# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 46

*Complete Course of Patrology*, or Universal Library … of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … **FIRST SERIES**

## Volume XLVI of Patrology

### Saint Aurelius Augustine

### Eleventh Volume

Printed at Paris; sold by the publisher on the street called d’Amboise, near the gate commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1845.

## Volume front matter

## Series title page

### Complete Course of Patrology

That is, a complete, uniform, comprehensive, economical universal library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices; corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indices following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: one of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily learn which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which places in their works they did so.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but collected for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Universal Library of the Clergy*, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

## Volume XLVI of Patrology

### Saint Aurelius Augustine

### Eleventh Volume

Printed at Paris; sold by the publisher on the street called d’Amboise, near the gate commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1845.

## The complete works of Saint Aurelius Augustine

Bishop of Hippo,

After the recension of the Louvain theologians, corrected anew against French, Vatican, Belgian, and other manuscript codices, as well as against earlier and more carefully corrected editions, through the work and scholarly efforts of the monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

The newest edition, corrected and enlarged, prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Universal Library of the Clergy*, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

### Eleventh volume

16 volumes: price 86 francs.

Paris; sold by the publisher on the street called Montrouge, beside the gate of Hell, in French: *près la barrière d’Enfer*. 1842.

[Col. 0022] They will be made together [Note: [Col. 0022] The passage is corrupt in the manuscript copies.], [lacuna] And thus the fact that the aforementioned holy Bishop Augustine, moved by the divine Spirit, produced books, treatises, and letters in the holy Catholic Church for the instruction of souls amounts to 1,030 works, except for those that cannot be counted because he did not specify their number.

[Col. 0021]

## Appendix: Works Whose Authors Were Already Known or Have Been Identified in This Edition, and the Names or Dates of Those Authors

### In Volume One

The *Principles of Dialectic* has as its author a certain Augustine, clearly different from the Augustine of Hippo, but perhaps not different from the author of the books *On the Miracles of Sacred Scripture*, who likewise calls himself Augustine.

The book *On the Eremitical Life*, addressed to a sister, is by Aelred of Rievaulx, abbot in England.

### In Volume Two

The *Letter to Demetrias* is by Pelagius.

The *Disputation of Augustine with Pascentius* is by Vigilius of Tapsus.

### In Volume Three

The three books *On the Miracles of Sacred Scripture* again belong to a certain Augustine, either British by nationality or from a neighboring people. He lived before Bede, but he wrote these books no earlier than the year 660.

The little work *On the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob* is a fragment of the *Questions on Genesis*, which Alcuin compiled for the most part from Jerome and Gregory.

The author of the *Questions of the Old and New Testament* indicates, in Question 44 from the Old Testament, that he wrote about three hundred years after the destruction of Jerusalem. His manner of expression also suggests an author not much more recent. Many attribute this work to Hilary the deacon, who flourished under Pope Damasus.

### In Volume Five

Sermon 9 is by Origen; several passages from it were also translated into Sermons 5, 6, 20, 24, 25, 26, 30, 31, and 33.

Sermon 235 is believed to be by Gregory of Boetica.

Sermon 36 was copied from Ambrose’s preface to his book *On the Holy Spirit*, just as Sermon 84 was copied from his widely circulated work *On the Sacraments*.

Sermon 155 is by John Chrysostom; according to two manuscripts, so are Sermons 43 and 268.

Sermon 236 contains a little book by Pelagius, and Sermon 71 reflects his teaching.

Sermon 72 is by Heraclius, who succeeded Augustine in the episcopate.

Sermons 133 and 148 belong to Pope Leo.

Sermons 80, 100, 122, 145, 152, 185, 203, and 248 belong to Maximus of Turin.

Sermons 61 and 199 are by Peter Chrysologus, though somewhat interpolated and abridged.

Sermons 119, 153, 154, 156, 161, 162, 176, 182, 196, 203, and 234 may be regarded as works of Faustus of Riez.

Sermons 2, 4, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 28, 29, 34, 35, 37, 38, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 63, 66, 67, 68, 69, 76, 77, 78, 89, 90, 91, 93, 104, 107, 110, 112, 115, [Col. 0022] 116, 129, 130, 139, 140, 141, 142, 173, 174, 224, 225, 228, 229, 230, 244, 249, 253, 256, 257, 258, 259, 260, 261, 262, 263, 264, 265, 266, 267, 269, 270, 271, 272, 273, 274, 275, 276, 277, 278, 279, 281, 282, 283, 284, 285, 286, 288, 289, 292, 293, 294, 295, 296, 297, 298, 299, 300, 303, 305, 307, 308, 309, 313, and 314 have been partly claimed for Caesarius of Arles and partly transferred here to support that attribution from works already published under his name.

In addition, the following Sermons appear to have been compiled by the same author from the writings of other Fathers: 5, 6, 14, 21, 24, 25, 33, 36, 53, 57, 58, 75, 101, 105, 111, 149, 168, 197, 198, 210, 220, 252, and 287.

The whole of Sermon 113, together with the final part of Sermon 234, was copied from Vigilius of Tapsus.

Sermon 208 should be attributed to Ambrose Autpertus; perhaps Sermon 195 and others that agree with these two in style should also be attributed to him.

Sermons 98, 108, 222, 280, 290, 291, 297, 302, and 304 already exist under the name of Rabanus Maurus among his works; Sermon 143 may perhaps be added to them.

Sermon 209 is by Bede or Alcuin, or certainly by a preacher familiar with Rabanus and older than he.

Sermon 171 should be restored to Odilo, abbot of Cluny.

Sermons 64, 74, and 247 belong to Ivo of Chartres; perhaps Sermon 223 does also.

### In Volume Six

This volume contains the following treatises:

*On Faith to Peter*, or *On the Rule of True Faith*, by Fulgentius of Ruspe, bishop.

*On Spirit and Soul*, by Alcher, a Cistercian monk. The book *On Loving God* and the *Manual* were written in a similar style.

*On Friendship* is a work by Aelred of Rievaulx, abbot in England and a Cistercian, abridged into an epitome.

*On the Substance of Love*, by Hugh of Saint-Victor.

The *Meditations*, either all or nearly all, are by John, abbot of Fécamp.

*On Contrition of Heart* is a work composed entirely from Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

The *Mirror* is the first part of the work which Father Chifflet published under the title *Confession of Faith of Alcuin*.

The *Ladder of Paradise* is by Guigo the Carthusian.

*On Knowledge of Life* is by Honorius of Autun.

*On the Christian Life* is by Fastidius the Briton.

*On Saving Instructions* is by Paulinus of Friuli, or Aquileia, patriarch.

*On the Seven Vices and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit* is by Hugh of Saint-Victor.

*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* is by Ambrose Autpertus, or Autpert.

*On the Antichrist* is a work written by Adso, abbot of Montier-en-Der, at the request of Queen Gerberga, wife of Louis IV, king of the Franks.

The *Psalter* is said to have been composed by the blessed Pope John at Vienne.

*On the Canticle Magnificat* is taken from Hugh of Saint-Victor.

*On the Consolation of the Dead* is by Saint John Chrysostom.

[Col. 0023] *On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct* is by Eligius of Noyon.

*On the Good of Discipline* is by Valerian, bishop of Cimiez.

We omit the minor works contained in Volume Seven concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Stephen, which are by known authors.

### In Volume Eight

The following appear in this volume:

The book *On Faith against the Manichaeans*, attributed to Evodius.

The *Dialogue against Felicianus, On the Unity of the Trinity*, restored to Vigilius.

[Col. 0024] *Questions on the Trinity and Genesis*, copied from Alcuin.

Two books *On the Incarnation of the Word*, addressed to Januarius, compiled from Origen’s work *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) according to Rufinus’s translation.

The book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, attributed to Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles.

Nor is it necessary here to list the various excerpts collected both in Volume Nine to illuminate the history of the Donatists and in Volume Ten to illuminate the history of the Pelagians.

**Whether Abraham was justified by faith or by works.** IV, 258. **Abraham pleased God by faith.** IV, 1948. **Abraham’s heart was chosen for faith.** V, 27. **Abraham’s work, whatever it might have been without faith, would have profited nothing.** IV, 259.

**In what year the promise was made to Abraham.** VII, 524. **A twofold promise was made to Abraham.** VII, 496, 509, 524. **A very extensive land was promised to Abraham.** III, 585. **The promise was made to give the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed.** VII, 499. **How the land of Canaan is promised to Abraham forever.** VII, 505. **The land promised to Abraham as an eternal possession must be understood either spiritually or according to a period whose end is not fixed.** III, 557.

**The offspring promised to Abraham from Sarah had not yet been given when he wished to receive one from Hagar.** VIII, 271. **Abraham did not sin when he approached Hagar the maidservant.** VII, 503. **Nor did he defile himself by any adultery.** VIII, 656.

**How Abraham’s body became dead.** X, 712. **Abraham’s body is called dead in relation to the aged Sarah.** III, 557. **It was not dead in relation to Keturah.** III, 557, 566. **Abraham received Isaac from Sarah by a miracle.** III, 557, 566. **Abraham’s fertility was restored, not his lust.** X, 449, 712. **When Abraham begot Isaac, concupiscence was not absent.** X, 449. **Abraham made good use of the evil of concupiscence.** X, 1439. **Abraham’s flesh simultaneously bore both the wound of transgression and the medicine for the wound.** III, 424.

**Abraham possessed the chastity of celibates in disposition, and the chastity of marriage in both use and disposition.** VI, 392. **In what respect Abraham is superior to those who practice continence.** VI, 392. **By merit of the continence he possessed in disposition, Abraham was not inferior to John.** VI, 391. **Abraham is praised because he used women manfully.** VII, 504. **What it signifies that after Sarah’s death he took another wife.** VIII, 557. **Abraham’s marriage with Keturah signifies something mystically.** III, 566. **Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were husbands for Christ’s sake and fathers for Christ’s sake.** VI, 396.

**Faustus accused Abraham of selling his wife to two kings for intercourse.** VI, 166. **Abraham is defended against Faustus’ accusations.** VI, 166; VIII, 420. **Abraham did not lie when he said that Sarah was his sister.** III, 555. **But through human prudence he kept silent about his wife.** VIII, 422, 423, 599. **What this prudence prefigured.** VIII, 424.

**What Abraham’s laughter signifies.** VII, 505. **Abraham’s laughter was one of wonder and joy, whereas Sarah’s was one of doubt.** III, 558. **Why a son was born to Abraham in his old age.** V, 504. **The banquet that Abraham celebrated on the day Isaac was weaned must be referred to a spiritual meaning.** III, 560.

**Abraham’s testing by God.** V, 28. **Abraham did not sin when, commanded by God, he wished to sacrifice his son.** III, 702, 811; VII, 35, 39. **Abraham’s act, when he wished to sacrifice his son, was obedience because God commanded it; if God had not commanded it, what would it have been but madness?** IX, 731. **Abraham’s faith and piety in offering his son.** V, 27, 31, 32. **And his obedience.** VII, 510. **Abraham’s obedience was great because a very difficult matter was commanded.** VII, 423. **Abraham’s faith in the offering of his son Isaac, and the sacraments of this event.** IV, 244. **Abraham is brought forward in the likeness of the eternal Father.** VII, 511. **Abraham is to be preferred to Isaac on account of obedience and faith.** VII, 514.

**Abraham was a prophet.** III, 1712; VII, 597. **Whatever Scripture says about Abraham both happened and is prophecy.** V, 31. **Abraham saw the Word in the bosom of the Father.** III, 1712. **The mystery of the Son of God was shown to Abraham.** VI, 334. **And Christ’s Incarnation was revealed.** X, 101. **Abraham knew the Lord’s Incarnation.** III, 1712. **Why Abraham made his servant swear beneath his thigh.** III, 1712; IV, 502.

**Abraham’s seed is said, by hyperbole, to be like the sand of the sea.** III, 556. **Abraham is the father of many nations in Christ.** VII, 507. **One nation called from all nations belongs to Abraham’s seed.** IV, 1392. **He lost Abraham’s lineage who departed from Abraham’s faith.** IV, 1948. **The Jews lost Abraham’s lineage by not believing.** IV, 1948. **The Jews boast of Abraham’s name without justification.** IV, 530. **Abraham’s two sons, the two Testaments.** III, 2133.

**Abraham’s seed, and who are his children.** IV, 1070, 1392, 1476, 1948. **Those who are from faith are Abraham’s children.** II, 894, 895. **We became Abraham’s children by believing.** IV, 244, 1948. **All the faithful are Abraham’s children.** VI, 334, 338. **Those who imitate Abraham’s faith are blessed in Abraham’s seed.** VIII, 332. **We are Abraham’s children by imitating his faith.** III, 1465. **By imitation of faith, those who believe in Christ became Abraham’s seed.** VIII, 421, 514. **How the kings of the nations are from Abraham’s son.** III, 557.

**Abraham as an olive tree.** X, 835. **The wild olive of the nations is grafted into Abraham.** X, 984. **Abraham belongs to the Church.** V, 39. **What God gave to Abraham through the promise pertains to our faith.** X, 592.

**Abraham was poor amid riches.** IV, 1083; V, 113. **And was not puffed up by good works.** V, 113. **What the gifts distributed by Abraham to the sons of his concubines signify mystically.** III, 566.

What is the abyss. IV, 1354, 1943. The abyss is the human heart. IV, 473, 980. By the name “abyss” the hidden hearts of mortals and their profound thoughts are signified. IV, 1748. There is an abyss in the good heart and in the evil heart; but both are naked before God. IV, 1749. The abyss of human conscience is naked to the eyes of God. I, 779. The abyss is the depth of sins, to which each person comes by despising God. IV, 348, 349.

The abyss is the preachers of the word. IV, 981.

By the name “abyss” the formless matter in Genesis is understood. VIII, 612. “The abyss and darkness were over the face of the abyss.” I, 827. What does “the abyss calls to the abyss” mean? I, 850.

## Academy

At the Academy, Polemo succeeded Arcesilaus, Xenocrates succeeded Polemo, and Plato succeeded Xenocrates. II, 439. Carneades was called the founder and leader of the Third Academy. I, 955. The Academy, Plato’s school. VII, 361. It was so called because it was separated from the people. I, 943.

Academic philosophy. VIII, 1073, 1074. It doubted even matters that were most evident. VIII, 1019, 1056. The disagreement between the two Academies, the Old and the New. I, 926. The New Academy was stirred up not so much against the Old as against the Stoics. I, 926. From what the doctrines attributed to the New Academy arose. I, 955.

The Academic philosophers were established by Plato. VII, 623. The Academic philosophers are the same as the Platonists. VII, 237. What the ancient Academics thought concerning the ends of good and evil. VII, 625, 626, 627. The ancient Academics strayed farther than the newer ones, placing blessedness in this life. VII, 630. In what the New Academics differ from the Old. VII, 623.

For the New Academics everything is uncertain. VII, 646. It was a tenet of the Academics that knowledge could not be attained by a human being. I, 923. And yet that a human being could be wise. I, 923. The Academics held that truth could not be comprehended. I, 923. That the whole task of the wise person consisted in seeking the truth. I, 923. The wise person ought to assent to nothing. For one who assents to uncertain things is in error. But everything is uncertain. I, 923. The suspension of assent is a great action of the wise person. I, 924. Nothing is more disgraceful than forming opinions. I, 923. The Academics could not call into question certain perceptions of true things that are in themselves most firmly established in the mind. VIII, 1075. Christians detest the doubt of the Academics as a kind of madness. VII, 646. The Academics, who thought error was sin and therefore that all assent should be suspended, are refuted. VI, 242.

The Academic philosophers held an opinion very different from what is commonly believed. II, 61. The Academic philosophers concealed Platonic doctrine, lest, when the masses and the uneducated rushed upon it indiscriminately, it should in no way be preserved clear and pure. II, 61. For the approval of falsehood had to be feared. II, 62. For some placed the discovery of truth itself in the senses of the flesh. II, 441. How Petilianus explains the Academics’ opinion concerning the deceptiveness of human sensation. IX, 359.

The arguments of the Academics caused trouble even for educated people occupied with affairs. I, 919. Or even for Augustine himself. I, 903, 904, 930. At the beginning Augustine inclined toward the opinion of the Academics. VIII, 78, 79. Nevertheless, he believes that they concealed their opinion by a definite plan and did not think as they are commonly supposed to have thought. I, 953 and following. Augustine himself wrote three books against the Academics while in retirement, before baptism. I, 903, 904, 930.

Academics called “Caducarians” by Monnica. I, 968. Cicero’s attractive passage on the Academics. I, 941.

Acatius, born with closed eyes, was cured by a poultice made from the Eucharist. X, 1315.

Acca, Romulus’s nurse. VII, 578.

To be sluggish. III, 953.

Ahab unjustly took away Naboth’s labors, whereas Israel justly took away the labors of the Canaanite. II, 811. Why Ahab was led astray by a spirit of deception. IV, 1001.

The Achaeans. VII, 86.

Achan. By what judgment of God Achan’s sons were slain by the enemies of Israel because of his sin. IX, 743.

Achilles. VIII, 585.

Ahithophel is interpreted as “Ruin of the brother.” IV, 97.

Achish, king of Gath. IV, 301. Achish is interpreted as “How is it?” IV, 302, 305, 308, 315. Achish is understood under the name Abimelech. IV, 301.

## To approach

One does not approach God or withdraw from God by distances of place: having become unlike Him, you have withdrawn far away; having become like Him, you approach very near. IV, 1273, 1217. We approach God or withdraw from Him not by place but by conscience; not by a vehicle but by the mind; not by the feet but by affections. IV, 1871. God is approached through repentance. IV, 314. The nations approach by following in faith, yearning with the heart, and running in charity. IV, 313. Let us approach Christ so that we may be enlightened, not so that we may be darkened. [Col. 0047] IV, 313.

Accents in Greek manuscripts are not to be disregarded. III, 592.

“Accessio” is what physicians call an attack or exacerbation. I, 719.

Approach to God. I, 673. See To approach.

## Respect of persons

II, 1636. What respect of persons is. X, 580. There is no respect of persons where there is no iniquity. X, 580. Respect of persons does not consist in grace being given to one person and not to another. X, 580, 581. Respect of persons in election to ecclesiastical honors is no slight sin. II, 740.

That God is not a respecter of persons is proved from the case of little children. II, 585.

An accident always indicates some change in a thing. VIII, 913. Separable and inseparable accidents. VIII, 913.

“To receive iniquity,” meaning to forgive or forget iniquity. III, 502.

Bread kills a hawk. I, 1349.

Acclamation of the people. V, 166.

The perverse accusation of fate, fortune, the devil, or God in connection with sins. VI, 358. How one should judge in the accusations of some people against others. IX, 610. The accusations of heretics against a Catholic presbyter can neither be admitted nor ought to be admitted. II, 1068.

Two kinds of accusers. I, 928. Many accuse another of what they themselves are thinking of doing in their own heart. IV, 800.

The vinegar offered to Christ on the cross, which He refused to taste: what it signifies. IV, 477, 851.

The ray of light by which light and darkness are distinguished is directed through the pupil of the eye. IV, 146.

From what the goodness or wickedness of an action is to be discerned. VIII, 446. The whole of a person’s good action is turning toward God. III, 382. What is to be sought in an action. VII, 647. In every movement of an action both its beginning and its end must be considered. VII, 200. What kind of action is directed toward the glory of God. II, 188. “What is done by you, God does in you. Nothing is ever done by you which God Himself does not do in you. But sometimes He does in you what is not done by you.” V, 380. Something should not therefore be thought to be done justly and well merely because God permits it to be done. VI, 583.

Why most people avoid the labor of action, although they may be suited to govern peoples. VIII, 436. The necessity of charity undertakes the just business of action. VII, 648. The action of the blessed will not be burdensome. VI, 342. Action and knowledge make a person blessed. VI, 299. The ordered harmony of action and knowledge is the peace of the rational soul. VII, 640, 642. See To act.

The active life is first and more abundantly made fruitful. VIII, 434. No one seeks the active life for its own sake, but for the sake of the contemplative life. VIII, 432, 433.

Some Manichaeans reject the Acts of the Apostles. II, 1033; VIII, 69, 368, 505. They do not wish to believe this book either. III, 1262. The reading of the Acts of the Apostles is customary in the Church. X, 962, note 2. The book of Acts was read every year in the Church. III, 1433. The book of Acts was customarily read from Easter Sunday onward. V, 1426.

The sting of death is sin: why. IV, 93. The vanity of exceedingly clever people is to be lamented. VII, 209.

Acindynus, prefect and consul. III, 1254.

A diamond is overcome by no other force except the blood of a goat. VII, 713.

Adam is interpreted as “Human being,” a designation common to both sexes. VII, 460. In the Hebrew language Adam signifies “human being.” X, 1583, 1585. Adam signifies the world in his name. IV, 1236. In the name Adam the four parts of the world are indicated. III, 1465, 1473. The number forty-six is also found. III, 1474.

Adam, the first human being. VIII, 211. The origin of Adam and Eve according to the Manichaeans, and their parents. I, 1375; VIII, 37. The Manichaeans say that Adam was created by the prince of darkness. VIII, 569.

At what age or stature Adam was created. III, 348. Adam and Eve were not formed on that day in which the spiritual creation was first made. III, 341. Adam was formed in no other way than as the primordial causes required. III, 349, 351. What God’s breathing into Adam signifies. III, 201. God’s breath in Adam is either the soul itself or was made by it. II, 348. Various difficulties if Adam’s soul was not created before it was breathed into the body. III, 370.

Adam’s ecstasy. III, 408. Through ecstasy Adam became a participant in the angelic court. III, 408. What Eve’s being formed from the rib of the sleeping Adam and joined to him in marriage signifies. III, 205. When God cast sleep upon him in order to make a wife for him from his side, he prefigured Christ sleeping on the cross. IV, 668, 1381; VII, 778. Adam is a figure of Christ, Eve a figure of the Church. IV, 461. Adam awoke as though full of prophecy. III, 408. For what purpose the woman was given to Adam. VI, 331. The Jewish old-woman’s tale that God created two women for Adam, from which endless genealogies arose. VIII, 637.

What Adam was like when created. VII, 790. How he was created in the image of God. VI, 331. Whether he was created wise. I, 607, 1305. Wisdom in Adam was most excellent. X, 1432. Adam was created just, and with a good will. V, 1426; VII, 418. The gifts of grace bestowed on Adam at creation. X, 935. If grace had been lacking to the human being, he would not have fallen through his own fault. X, 936. What the grace of the first human being was like. [Col. 0048] X, 274, 935. God left him most strong and permitted him to do whatever he wished. X, 940. Adam was not given as much grace as the saints. X, 937. The grace given in Christ is more powerful than Adam’s grace: through it a person is made willing to remain in the good. X, 935. See Grace. According to Catholic doctrine the first human being is proclaimed to have been created more good than in the Pelagian doctrine. X, 1536. The Manichaean, who denies that Adam was created good by God, is refuted not by the authority of Genesis or Paul’s epistle but by reason. X, 1537. “The human being first had to be made in such a way that he could will both good and evil; afterward he will be such that he cannot will evil.” VI, 336. Adam’s free servitude was advantageous. VII, 423.

Adam was in nature without guilt and defect. V, 172. Adam’s nature was created blameless and without defect. X, 247, 271, 932. Adam was not created in weak flesh, nor did he beget anyone before the sin. II, 588. He would have begotten descendants even if he had not sinned. I, 601, 605. Adam was not created in the likeness of sinful flesh. X, 149. Adam’s flesh is not a likeness of sin. X, 815. Adam and Eve were created blind. X, 416. What the opening of the eyes in Adam and Eve signifies. X, 417, 565. Adam would not have known evil unless he had done it. VIII, 613.

Adam’s happiness before the sin. VII, 434. How blessed and free in will the human being was before the sin. X, 1531. Before the fall the human being was blessed, but not completely so; he would have become perfectly blessed if he had stood firm. X, 932, 933. What kind of blessedness this was. X, 933. Adam in paradise before the sin was happier, with respect to the enjoyment of present good, than any just person. VII, 328. How exalted Adam’s nature stood before the sin. X, 1552, 1535.

Adam was made by God with a good will. X, 1496. The powers of Adam’s will before the sin. X, 935, 940. How Adam before the sin could do everything he wished. VII, 423. Adam was made in such a way that nothing at all would resist his will if he wished to keep God’s commands. VIII, 124.

Adam needed God’s light and love in order to persevere. VII, 422. Whether Adam received the gift of perseverance. X, 931. How Adam could have sinned by not persevering if he did not receive the gift of perseverance. X, 931. The first human being had received the grace necessary for persevering, but it was left to his own choice. X, 935, 938. See Perseverance.

Adam was created free for good action. X, 271, 1144. Adam could easily have kept the law if he had wished. X, 149. Adam could stand firm through his free choice. X, 933. Adam could have refrained from sin if he had wished. X, 1536. In the powers of the created human being lay the ability not to depart from God. X, 1001. It was in Adam’s power, with God’s help, to overcome the devil. VII, 435. It was not in Adam’s power to live well without God’s help, but it was in his power to live badly. VII, 435. His free choice was not sufficient for retaining righteousness unless divine help were provided. VI, 281. Adam did not need the help that is now necessary for resisting concupiscence. X, 933. The human being abandoned God through free choice. X, 933. Adam became evil by his own choice. V, 409. Adam lost by free choice the merits through which he had been able to possess them. X, 939. If Adam had persevered, the reward of his merit would have been the inability to sin. X, 936. See Freedom.

What Adam’s body was like. VII, 393, 395. According to the body Adam was earth. X, 110. Adam’s first body was animal. VII, 395, 397, 402. Before the sin Adam’s and Eve’s bodies were not corruptible. VI, 332. Some have thought that Adam’s body was first animal and afterward made spiritual. III, 352. This opinion is discussed. III, 352. Adam’s body would have been made spiritual as the reward of obedience. VII, 402.

Adam did not suffer discord between flesh and spirit, nor the necessity of fighting against vices. X, 172, 173, 1536; X, 802, 818. Adam’s body served his soul perfectly. X, 172. Adam’s soul before the sin, although his body was not yet spiritual but animal, nevertheless governed it according to its will. II, 589. Adam had complete dominion over his limbs. X, 565. If Adam had possessed concupiscence before the sin, he would have been miserable. X, 1531. The Pelagians make Adam miserable even in paradise. X, 1536. Adam’s foreknowledge would have made him miserable. X, 933. Before the sin Adam was naked of pretense but clothed with divine light. III, 208. Whether Adam had feelings of fear and grief before the sin. VII, 417. He could suffer no bodily illness. I, 601.

The doctrine of Caelestius that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin. X, 333; and the doctrine of the Pelagians. VIII, 48; X, 1170, 1178, 1362, 1559, 1560, 1561, 1570, 1571. Pelagius condemned this doctrine at the Palestinian council. X, 1178. He condemned his own heresy with a feigned heart. X, 1089. He condemned his own heresy so that he would not be condemned. X, 1536. Although Pelagius condemned his doctrine at the Palestinian council, the Pelagians nevertheless are not afraid to maintain it. X, 1275, 1279. As Augustine thinks, the Pelagians have ceased to say that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would have died bodily. II, 873. Adam did not fear death. X, 1536.

Adam was created immortal. X, 1598. Adam was created immortal in the sense that he could not die. III, 354. Adam could have avoided death if he had not wished to sin. [Col. 0049] X, 1536. Adam would not have died unless he had sinned. VII, 395, 397; X, 109, 1556. Adam was to be changed into a spiritual body. X, 110. If Adam had not sinned, he would have grown old without decay and, at the time God willed, would have passed from mortality to immortality without an intervening death. X, 110. Adam and his descendants could have been changed into an angelic form without death. III, 397. If Adam had lived justly, his body would have been changed into a spiritual condition and would not have gone into death. III, 353, 354, 355, 395. After begetting children, Adam would have been brought to better things without the intervention of death if he had not sinned. VI, 281. Adam, Eve, and their descendants, if they had not violated God’s command, would have lived—even in an animal body—as Elijah and Enoch now live. X, 1597. If Adam had not sinned, he would have had a life like that of the saints after the resurrection, without experiencing death. VII, 417.

Although Adam was spiritual in mind, he nevertheless had an animal body, even after being placed in paradise. III, 355. God formed Adam’s body not spiritual but animal. III, 351. Adam’s body was mortal precisely because it was animal. III, 353, 354. Because of the sin Adam’s body became not mortal but dead. III, 354. In what respect Adam was created mortal. X, 1090. Adam was mortal by the condition of his animal body, immortal by the benefit of the Creator. III, 354. Even if Adam had not sinned, he would have died unless he had eaten from the tree of life. VII, 396. In paradise Adam had refreshment from the fruits of the trees against decline, and from the tree of life stability against old age. X, 111. Before the fall Adam used the tree of life. X, 172.

Adam was handed over to death because he sinned. X, 1571. Adam died by the merit of guilt, not by the necessity of nature. X, 1560. From the time Adam and Eve sinned, through the changes of the ages, they went into death as though afflicted by a disease that had taken hold. X, 120. Adam can be said to have died on the very day on which he ate from the tree. VII, 396. In how many ways Adam died. VII, 387. Some incorrectly think that Adam earned by sin the death of the soul, not of the body. III, 353. Adam’s spirit was extinguished by a certain death of unbelief. X, 113. Through sin Adam became the old human being who is corrupted, and so forth. III, 354. Adam, made mortal, begot mortal human beings. VII, 379.

How God spoke to Adam. III, 392. In some bodily form. III, 387. Why the forbidden tree was given to Adam. VIII, 562, 615, 616. Why Adam was forbidden a good thing. IV, 896. Why Adam and Eve were forbidden the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. X, 172. The prohibition made to Adam against eating from the tree of knowledge is defended. VIII, 613, 615. In the prohibition, and so forth, God neither established something harmful, nor willed something impossible, nor fruitlessly willed to command what the human being would not keep. VIII, 615, 616. Therefore God gave him a very light command, to remind him that He was Lord. VII, 422. It was not food but forbidden food that destroyed Adam. II, 140. See Tree of knowledge.

Why Adam was created, when it was foreknown that he would sin. VI, 332. Why God commanded Adam and Eve what He knew they would not keep. X, 165. Why God permitted Adam’s temptation and fall. V, 172; VII, 435, 436. God would have preserved Adam in the salvation in which he had been created if He had foreknown that he would not sin. VI, 276. God was not ignorant that Adam would sin, but at the same time He foreknew what good and just thing He would make from the sinner. VIII, 614. Adam’s temptation and guilt were permitted for the benefit of his descendants. III, 435. Adam was first animal and afterward spiritual when, in paradise, he received the command of perfection. III, 201.

The cause of Adam’s fall. III, 1603. By what reasoning Adam was led to sin. III, 453, 454. Adam did not believe the serpent. III, 452, 453. The Apostle says that Adam was not deceived. VII, 419. Although Adam was not deceived, he was nevertheless no less guilty for that reason. VII, 419. Adam sinned not through error but through social necessity. VII, 419. And through a certain friendly benevolence, not overcome by the desire of the flesh. III, 453. Adam imitated Eve by sinning. X, 1225.

Adam’s sin began in the mind through elation. X, 685. Adam fell through pride. III, 2040. Adam’s sin first began from pride. VII, 420, 421. And from defection from the highest good. VII, 420, 421. Adam desired not to be under God’s dominion. III, 384. Amid the delights of paradise Adam did not wish to preserve righteousness. X, 183. Adam fell through avarice, since God could not be enough for him. III, 2039. He wanted to seize divinity and lost happiness. IV, 848. In Adam’s transgression the evil will preceded the evil act. VII, 420. Adam was conquered without a struggle. X, 1123. He fled into the shadow from the face of God. IV, 1854. He believed that God would easily grant forgiveness for the sin. III, 446. Adam’s and Eve’s excuses were full of pride. III, 449. In what sense God said, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us.” III, 451. Adam abandoned God before he was abandoned. VII, 387. Adam’s sin must be reckoned from the time when he was able to live either well or badly. III, 346.

Adam’s fall harmed God nothing. VI, 333. See Human being. Adam’s sin could not disturb God’s plan. [Col. 0050] VII, 418. Adam’s fall ought to serve us as a lesson for avoiding sin, not as an example for imitating it. He fell so that we might rise. IV, 539. It is absurd to believe that Adam’s sin was necessary. VII, 430. Even if Adam had not sinned, his descendants could nevertheless have sinned. VII, 418.

Adam sinned in paradise. X, 471, 794. Adam’s apostasy is ineffable. X, 1274, 1275. It was a great guilt. X, 1572. A great sin. X, 1179. The sin is graver in proportion as it was easier to avoid. X, 258, 937. Adam’s sin was graver in proportion as it was freer for him to abstain from it. X, 1148. See Freedom. Adam’s sin was greater than we can express. X, 471, 1555. Whether Adam’s sin was graver than Cain’s and that of the Sodomites. X, 1555. Why Adam’s sin was so grave. VII, 420, 423; X, 1440.

The greatness of Adam’s impiety is indicated both by divine Scripture and by the misery of the human race itself. X, 1277. Adam’s sin is to be assessed by the greatness of its punishment. X, 1555, 1556, 1572. Julianus contends that Adam’s sin should not appear great and that the punishment he deserved was light and almost nothing. X, 1569, 1572, 1573. The sins of Adam’s descendants, however horrifying, ought not to be equated with or preferred to Adam’s sin. X, 1553, 1554. Why Adam was questioned after the fall before Eve. III, 449.

Adam’s condemnation was just. VII, 423. Adam’s punishment. III, 450. The punishment for Adam’s sin was most just. X, 260. What Adam’s punishment was. VII, 422, 423. What Adam lost through sin. III, 355. How the statement that Adam lost the image of God through sin is to be understood. I, 640. Having lost blessedness, Adam was cast into misery. V, 209. On the punishments inflicted on Adam and Eve. III, 211. Into what miseries Adam fell through the evil use of free choice. VII, 386. After Adam’s free sin, his descendants were hurled into a condition of necessity. VIII, 124, 125. Adam’s descendants are freed from that necessity by grace. VIII, 125. Disobedience was repaid to Adam’s disobedience. VII, 423. This punishment was returned to the disobedient human being within himself: that he in turn should not be obeyed, even by himself. VIII, 613. Obedience would have been Adam’s reward; the punishment of disobedience is an example for his holy descendants. VIII, 614. Before Adam sinned he had neither sinful flesh nor the likeness of sinful flesh. X, 1384. Adam was not made such as infants born today are. X, 1496. Adam’s and Eve’s condition was one thing, that of their descendants another. X, 1532. Adam was not reduced by sin or punishment to infantile dullness and weakness. VII, 379. What was voluntary in Adam became natural in us. VIII, 166. On Adam’s punishments, which pass to his descendants. I, 1297; III, 211. Adam’s nakedness was proclaimed through sin. X, 1070. See Members; Nakedness. Why Adam was clothed in tunics of skins. IV, 1341.

Adam was expelled from paradise. III, 451. Why Adam was dismissed from paradise. X, 183. Adam had to be separated from the tree of life. III, 451. Adam was as one excommunicated. III, 451. Why Adam was placed opposite paradise. III, 451. After the sin Adam is said to have been dismissed from paradise by God, not excluded: why. III, 213. Adam, a citizen of Jerusalem, became through sin a pilgrim. IV, 1658. Adam was the human being who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho. III, 1340. In the punishment of Adam and of the other sinners, God was neither heedless of the future, nor powerless, nor malicious, nor jealous. VIII, 614, 616, 617.

The doctrine of Caelestius that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race. X, 338. And the doctrine of the Pelagians. X, 431. In what sense Pelagius understood the claim that Adam’s sin harmed not Adam alone and that infants are not in the condition in which Adam was before the sin. X, 393. Adam first received the serpent’s bite with its venom. V, 1342. Adam’s guilt is the death of all. II, 825, 826; X, 1157. And through his transgression he polluted everyone. X, 1227. Adam was one human being and the entire human race. III, 1473. In Adam the human race was established as though at its root. III, 345. In Adam we were all one human being. X, 115, 194, 444, 1219, 1401. We were all in Adam when he sinned. VII, 386. All sinned in Adam. X, 933. Adam’s descendants are bound by the bond of condemnation. II, 843, 858, 859. In Adam they were all present by reason of the seed when he was condemned. VII, 378; X, 1442. Everyone is born subject to the sin and death of the first human being, and is reborn joined to the righteousness and eternal life of the second human being. X, 121. Original sin is drawn from Adam. I, 649, 654. Adam’s sin is drawn by every person born, even from reborn parents. X, 471. Adam’s descendants are subject by the natural laws of descent both to sin and to condemnation. X, 1555. All Adam’s children are naturally evil. X, 1251. Through Adam’s sin the human race became a wild olive tree. X, 433. From and through Adam many sins are born. IV, 1735. How Adam’s sin is both alien to us and ours. X, 1210.

Adam. The Pelagians taught that the beginning of sin came from Adam insofar as the others imitated him. II, 679, 684. The Pelagians, who taught that the beginning of sin came from Adam insofar as the others imitated him, are refuted. II, 684. Whether Adam corrupted his descendants merely by the example of sinning. X, 1161. Adam is indeed an example for those who sin by choice, but he is the origin of those who are born with sin. [Col. 0051] X, 114, 115. If all sinned in Adam by imitation because he was the first to sin, then all are justified in Abel because he was the first to live justly. X, 119. All sinned in Adam, not merely by imitation but by contagion. X, 251, 868, 1217. Adam’s sin passed to everyone not merely by imitation but by descent. X, 462, 463, 1186. The likeness of the transmission of sin from Adam. X, 1218. Everyone born from that succession of descent belongs to Adam, just as everyone reborn in Christ through the abundance of grace belongs to Christ. X, 1211, 1224. See All.

Adam and Christ are set forth by the Apostle, the former as author of generation, the latter as author of regeneration. X, 1165. When the Apostle sets forth Adam and Christ, the Pelagians oppose imitation to imitation, not regeneration to generation. X, 1202. The Apostle teaches otherwise. X, 1265. In Adam, according to Julianus, there was not the first form of sin but the greatest; similarly, in Christ there was not the first form of righteousness but the greatest. X, 1557, 1573. Adam is the form of sin because of generation, not because of imitation. X, 1233. What it means to sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. X, 116.

Before the fall Adam did not need Christ’s blood. X, 933. For what purpose repentance benefited Adam. X, 1582. Adam is rightly believed to have been released from the bonds of hell through Christ. X, 1523, 1582. The Church believes that Adam was freed from the pains of hell through Christ’s grace when Christ descended to hell. X, 1553. Adam was freed from hell by God’s mercy. X, 258. The Church agrees that Adam was released from the pains of hell. II, 711. The first parents were saved. X, 183. The Tatiani contradict Adam’s salvation. VIII, 30.

The first Adam and the second Adam. X, 1553. In what respect Adam is a figure of the future second Adam. X, 462, 1171, 1223, 1225. How Adam is a figure of Christ. II, 684. All in Adam, all in Christ. V, 1333. Christ in Adam, and Adam in Christ. IV, 1296. No one enters death except through Adam; no one enters life except through Christ. II, 843. Adam’s flesh simultaneously possessed both the wound of transgression and the medicine for the wound. III, 424. Innocentius says that Adam could not have been rescued from his transgression unless the coming of Christ the Lord had restored his former condition of freedom. II, 785. Because Adam fell, Christ descended; Adam fell through pride, Christ descended through mercy. IV, 1596. Christ provides more to the reborn than Adam had harmed them. II, 684.

Adam conquered in Job. III, 2007. Adam, conquered in paradise, conquered in the dung heap. III, 2007. Adam in the dung heap was more cautious than Adam in paradise. IV, 220. In Scripture we are called human beings from Adam, and children of human beings from Christ. II, 548. Not everywhere, however. II, 548. Adam was a human being, not a son of a human being. IV, 350. Why only the names of certain sons of Adam are expressed in the genealogical sequence. VII, 456.

It cannot be affirmed whether Adam had begotten only Cain and Abel before Seth. VII, 456.

Whether Adam customarily saw God with bodily eyes is not clearly apparent. VIII, 856.

Six thousand years have not yet elapsed since Adam. VII, 599.

If Adam were to die today, he would have lived only a few days. V, 1518.

Adam is the origin of the two cities. VII, 466.

The Adamite heretics and their doctrines. VIII, 31.

Adelphius, from Thasbalta. IX, 222.

Adeodatus, Augustine’s natural son. I, 769. His intellect was a source of alarm to Augustine, I, 769, and promised something great. I, 962. Adeodatus speaks in the book *On the Happy Life*. I, 965, 968. Everything reported in the role of the other interlocutor in the book *On the Teacher*, published at Rome when he was about sixteen years old, is his own thought. I, 769. He was baptized with Augustine at about fifteen years of age. I, 769. Adeodatus was carried off by a premature death. I, 769.

Adeodatus, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Adeona, goddess. VII, 128, 196.

The fat of wheat. IV, 1046, 1930. The Jews do not eat fat as food. III, 684.

How great a good it is to cleave to God. VII, 350. To cleave to God is supremely blessed. I, 1322. It is good for a created spirit always to cleave to God, lest through turning away it lose the light it gained through conversion. I, 846. One who can see God invisibly can cleave to God incorporeally. II, 613. We cannot cleave to God except through devotion, love, and charity. I, 1322.

Adimantus, a disciple of Mani. V, 100; VIII, 129, 130. He was called by the first name Addas. VIII, 129, 130, 665. The work or book of Adimantus. VIII, 207, 665, 232. Adimantus’s error concerning the soul is refuted. VIII, 144. His slanderous objection drawn from the Apostle. V, 100. Faustus preferred Adimantus alone among the Manichaeans. VIII, 207, 232.

“I adjure you,” meaning “Swear to me.” III, 492.

God’s help is necessary for us. [Col. 0052] V, 108, 121, 375, 856, 894, 895, 1167, 1171. It is to be requested in prayer for doing good. X, 1292, 1293. See Grace. When God ceases to help, you can labor but cannot conquer. IV, 1424. Without God’s help a person cannot understand or obey with the eyes and ears of the heart. III, 770. Help was necessary for an angel and for the first human being; if it had then been lacking, they would not have fallen through their own fault; now, for those to whom it is lacking, it is the punishment of sin. X, 936. If God’s help is absent, that does not excuse human fault. III, 771. God helps us to do the commands of the one from whom we hope to receive the promises. V, 1669. What God commands is not harsh or burdensome, since He helps it to be done. V, 584. He helps not only by sanctifying and illuminating, and so forth, but also by giving charity. X, 1291. All the saints are helped by God, but inwardly, where no one sees. IV, 625. Two kinds of help. X, 321. Help without which something does not happen, and help by which something happens. X, 936. See Grace.

Admetus, king. VII, 571.

What causes admiration. VIII, 874. Admiration arises from something unusual and unexpected. I, 981; III, 179. It is not without a certain fear. IV, 1412. Certain things worthy of admiration in a faithful person. IV, 469. By admiring the faith of believers, Christ indicates that we ought to wonder at it. III, 180.

Admiration in place of praise. II, 707.

“To name a woman,” that is, to make her one’s wife. III, 624.

Very few adolescents avoid committing any blameworthy sins from the beginning of adolescence. VII, 730. What vices usually abound in adolescence. VII, 556. In adolescents who devote themselves to literary studies, impulses of rivalry and empty boasting must be restrained. I, 991. Rules of conduct are handed down to adolescents. I, 1006.

What **Ἀδολεχῆσαι** means. III, 565.

Adonai is interpreted as “Lord,” in the manner in which God alone is called Lord. VIII, 313.

Adonis was killed by the first tooth. VII, 185.

Adoption of sons. V, 348. The ancient custom of adoption among the people of God. III, 1072. The bond of adoption was not alien to the customs of the ancients. VIII, 215, 216; nor to the sacred writings. V, 349. Various examples of adoption. VIII, 215. One who adopts may be said to have begotten the person whom he adopted as his son, not by flesh but by love. III, 1073. The law of adoption adopted even the children of a deceased person. I, 633. There are two kinds of adoption. VIII, 206.

The name “adoption” has very great force in the sacrament of our faith. VIII, 215. What the adoption of the children of God is. III, 1268. How human beings are adopted by God. VIII, 215. The Pelagians acknowledged the adoption of infants in baptism. X, 578, 583. God’s mercy and benevolence in adopting human beings. III, 1394. Our adoption has already taken place in spirit, not in body. III, 2075. Our adoption will not be perfect except in heaven. VII, 729. The adoption and glorification of the human being arise not from his merits but from God’s grace. III, 1276.

To adore and to ask are not interchangeable. VIII, 751. Adoration of Christ’s humanity. IV, 1264. No one eats Christ’s flesh unless he has first adored it; and we not only do not sin by adoring, but would sin by not adoring. IV, 1264. A human being becomes like the one whom he adores. III, 1466. Creatures are not to be adored, from whom some likeness is taken in order to signify Christ or the saints. IV, 1193. Christians worship no dead person and adore as a divinity nothing made and created by God. II, 83. To adore in the temple and toward the temple are different. IV, 86.

What “to acquire” signifies. VII, 537.

Adrastus of Cyzicus, a distinguished mathematician. VII, 720.

Adrumetum. IX, 204.

Monks of Hadrumetum were disturbed by certain people who preached grace among them in such a way as to deny free will and God’s repaying each person according to his works; this arose from an incorrect understanding of Augustine’s letter to Sixtus, about which they consulted Evodius. II, 969. Evodius wrote a reply to them concerning Augustine’s letter. II, 969. See the Notes. The presbyter Sabinus interpreted Augustine’s letter to Sixtus for them, but the dispute was not settled. II, 976. Cresconius and Felix were monks of the monastery of Hadrumetum. II, 969. Cresconius and Felix went to Augustine before the feast of Easter, II, 970; and another Felix went with them, and they celebrated Easter with Augustine. II, 971. Augustine asked Valentinus to send to him the man by whom they said they had been disturbed, II, 970, namely Florus. II, 973. Florus came to Augustine. II, 977, with a letter from Valentinus by which he was cleared of suspicion of error. II, 976. The monks of Hadrumetum, divided among themselves concerning grace and free will, consulted Augustine, who wrote a book for them on this subject. I, 656. Augustine wrote for them the book *On Grace and Free Will*. II, 972. Augustine sent them writings that had been composed against the Pelagian error. II, 972. On the occasion of the monks of Hadrumetum, the book *On Rebuke and Grace* was published. II, 1002.

The feasts of the Ascension and of the coming of the Holy Spirit were received by tradition. II, 200.

Christ’s Ascension is the pledge of ours. V, 1210. No one ascends into heaven unless he clings to Christ. V, 570.

The inward ascent to God. IV, 413, 1629, 1639; it begins from humility. IV, 1605, 1672.

People who come from elsewhere are called immigrants or outsiders. IV, 1518.

Christ’s coming is twofold. IV, 1235, 117; V, 124, 128, [Col. 0053] either in the Church or in his own body. II, 920. How Christ’s first and second comings differ. III, 1624. See *Christ*. The two comings are compared with one another. IV, 1258. Daniel’s weeks signify that Christ’s coming has already taken place, not that it is future. II, 899, 911. The interpreters of that same prophecy hold this view. II, 912, 917, and this is also the opinion of Hesychius. II, 905, 911. Whether Daniel’s weeks refer to both comings. II, 911. What benefit Christ’s coming brought. IV, 1766.

Some believe that the Lord’s coming for judgment will occur, counting the years from Adam, after seven thousand years. IV, 90. This opinion is refuted. IV, 90. Both the person who says that the Lord’s coming will occur sooner and the person who says that it will occur later are in error. II, 924, 925. Christ’s coming is to be desired. IV, 811; how. IV, 811. He is to be loved and awaited. II, 909. If we love Christ, we ought certainly to desire his coming: for it is perverse—if indeed it is true—to fear that the one whom you love may come; to ask for his coming and fear that your request may be granted. IV, 1913. Christ’s coming is harsh for the harsh, gentle for the devout. IV, 1257. Christ brings tribulations to inflame souls with longing for his coming. IV, 125. It is in your power how you await Christ’s coming; therefore he delays coming, so that when he comes he may not condemn you. IV, 1257. The person who lives devoutly truly desires and awaits the Lord’s coming. II, 904, 905, 909. Everyone ought to prepare himself for it. II, 905, 906, 907, 908. Let us not resist the first coming, so that we may not fear the second. IV, 1235.

The hidden adversary is a great evil. VII, 632. Who the adversary is whom we must overcome in order to be crowned. VI, 289. The adversary is conquered with Christ’s help. VI, 291. Adversaries and harmful people are to be tolerated like the delirious, children, and the weak. III, 1258. Who your adversary is, to whom you must consent while you are on the way. IV, 342; V, 76, 245, 636, 1171, 1698. The word of God is the adversary of your will until it becomes the author of your salvation. V, 636.

Why adversities are common to the just and the unjust. VII, 20, 21. Lovers of this age more often lend their hearts’ ears to the truth amid adversity than amid prosperity. II, 938. In adversity, lovers of this age think more about escaping what distresses them than about grasping what might heal them. II, 938. Perseverance in enduring adversity. V, 623. In adversity one must not murmur against God. V, 1357. See *Scourging*, *Tribulation*. God does not fail his own in adversity. VII, 28. God permits those whom he loves to be afflicted. II, 424. Temporal adversities are necessary for exercising and perfecting virtue. III, 1220. Adversity is either the punishments by which sins are punished or the exercises by which they are cleansed away. VIII, 588. Temporal adversities may be commanded by God and must be endured for God’s sake. VIII, 451. Adversity is a gift from God who admonishes. II, 957. We cannot reach the seats of eternal happiness unless, exercised by temporal evils, we have not failed. II, 267. The devout are called blessed amid torments because, in hope of attaining blessedness, they endure the evils of this life courageously. II, 673. Any temporal adversity is easily endured so that eternal punishment may be avoided and eternal rest obtained. V, 444. In hope of attaining blessedness, the devout courageously endure the evils of this life. II, 668; those sound in heart endure the evils of the world. III, 1025. See *Afflictions*.

Adversities are useful to some and harmful to others. VIII, 451. No adversity breaks the person whom no prosperity corrupts. IV, 1058; or whom the prosperity of this age does not deceive. V, 687. Every bodily and spiritual adversity must be overcome by almsgiving, fasting, and prayers. V, 1042. Both adversity and prosperity must be guarded against: the former, lest it break us; the latter, lest it corrupt us. IV, 1824. Adversities are to be avoided when God is most clearly a helper. III, 613. Through wicked and unjust people God scourges whomever he wishes with temporal punishments. II, 995.

Flattery is seduction through deceptive praise. V, 1561; false praise. IV, 1824. People commonly lie through flattery. IV, 87. Flattery is the companion of every evil. IV, 142. Flattery is the sinner’s oil. IV, 1824; IX, 66. Let no one congratulate a person who prospers in his way, whose sins lack a punisher but have a praiser: this is a greater wrath of the Lord. IV, 126.

A flatterer. V, 579, 1229. Flatterers sell their praise like oil to fools. II, 571; IV, 1921; VI, 46. How great an evil it is to flatter sinners. IV, 581. The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins; for it is pleasing to do things in which one not only does not fear a critic but even hears a praiser. IV, 126. By flattery they draw to themselves those whom they entice into sins and, as it were, devour them. IV, 87. A flatterer is an accomplice of the deed. IV, 581.

Flattering friends corrupt; quarreling enemies often correct. I, 772. The reprover who heals loves more than the flatterer who anoints the head. II, 114. The flatterer’s tongue persecutes more than the hand of a murderer. IV, 869. You will not fear the one who threatens if you do not love him. IV, 675. Some speak our good with evil intent, others our evil with good intent: both must be guarded against. IV, 449.

Adulterers use the good of the body wrongly. X, 1451. The members of adulterers, and God’s works, are members of nature; nevertheless, through vice, and by that fact, they are subject to the devil. X, 1407. Adulterers are rebuked. V, 83. A Christian woman ought to grieve over a husband committing adultery not because of the flesh but because of charity. V, 83. The shameful excuse of adulterers. V, 84. Whether, with her husband’s permission, a woman may have intercourse with another man, and conversely. III, 1254. The story concerning this matter. III, 1254.

Although adulteresses were subject to some condemnation, they were nevertheless not punished with death. VII, 82. Why the adulterous woman was not stoned. IV, 1325. Concerning the adulterous woman. V, 109, 1389. The story of the adulterous woman was not found in most Greek copies. VI, 451. An adulterer who persists in adultery is not admitted to baptism. VI, 220, 482. Peace is rightly granted to adulterers who repent. II, 341. The law of Antoninus against adulterers. VI, 474. See *Marriage*.

Certain souls are adulterous, others fornicate. V, 117. See *Fornication*.

The adulterer is the ancient serpent. IV, 431.

Just as the adulterer rejoices in corrupted flesh, so the devil rejoices in a corrupted mind. IV, 432.

What adultery is. VI, 375; where the term comes from. V, 345. How extensive the evil of adultery is. V, 78, 83. From what it can be proved that adultery is evil. I, 1225. Adultery is not evil because it is forbidden by the Law; rather, it is forbidden by the Law because it is evil. I, 1225. Adultery is prohibited by a twofold commandment. V, 71. Adultery does not dissolve a marriage. VI, 452. Children born of adultery are not sinners for that reason. III, 418. God justly grants souls to adulterous conceptions. II, 778. Against adulteries some have entirely closed the way of penance. II, 340. A book on adulterous marriages. VI, 451. Adultery was common among the gods. VII, 81. Adultery of the flesh and adultery of the heart. V, 1439. The adultery of a soul that worships demons. V, 76. It is adultery to love a human being in place of Christ. III, 1497.

To distribute adulterated money. VI, 228.

An advocate who conducted a bad case is obliged to make restitution. II, 663.

Our advocates are the Martyrs, yet Christ alone is our Advocate. V, 1295.

The inner sanctuary of the temple. IV, 204.

There are two kinds of builders: those who build upon sand and those who build upon rock. III, 1444. What it means to build upon rock and to build upon sand. IV, 1335. Those who prepare for temptations build upon rock; those who promise earthly happiness build upon sand. V, 275. What it means to build with gold, silver, and precious stones. IV, 222. Those who love nothing except Christ build with gold, silver, and so forth. Those who love earthly things with Christ, yet do not prefer them to him, build with wood, straw, and so forth. IV, 222. Whoever builds the love of earthly things upon the foundation of the heavenly kingdom will be saved, yet as through fire. IV, 1044, [lacuna].

The building of the spiritual city. IV, 1620. The building and dedication of God’s house in us. V, 1471. Building takes place in labor, dedication in joy. V, 1476.

We are God’s building, because the one who cultivates us dwells in us. IV, 802. By God’s grace, not through preceding merits, we are built into God’s holy place. IV, 816.

Sick. See *Ill*.

Aegeria, regarded as the nymph-wife of Pompilius. VII, 223.

Aegialeus, the first king of the Assyrians. VII, 561.

The aegis, Jupiter’s shield. III, 1056. Why it is so called. III, 1056.

How another person’s illness is to be taken up in charity so that it may be relieved. VI, 80.

To be ill. To be born here in a mortal body is to begin to be ill. IV, 1320. A person does not have equal control over becoming ill and recovering. V, 850, 1269. The person who thinks himself healthy is ill more dangerously. V, 495.

Two kinds of sick people. V, 495. The difference between one who is ill and one who is weak. V, 277. A sick person should not dare to give advice to a physician. IV, 1914, 1915. The sick person’s harmony with the physician. V, 82. The sick person is not heard according to his will but according to his health. V, 1299. By observing the physician’s instructions, the sick person becomes healthy only gradually. V, 1270. Nothing is more arrogant than a sick person who mocks his medicine. IV, 1838. Illicit remedies of the sick. V, 1439. A sick person who refuses to be healed by superstitious remedies becomes a martyr in bed. V, 1301. One healthy person bears two sick people more easily than two sick people bear one another individually; so the good bear the wicked more easily. IV, 190. Christ the physician finds everyone sick. V, 495. By what remedy the sick are healed through Christ. V, 496. We are invited to take the cup by the example of Christ the physician. V, 543, 781. Many sick people conquering the devil in bed. V, 52.

The figurative healing of the sick at the pool. V, 686, 690, 693.

The Egyptians descended from the seed of Ham. IV, 1398. The kingdom of the Egyptians flourished in the time of Abraham. VII, 497. Isis handed down letters to the Egyptians. VII, 597, 599. The Egyptians’ fabricated wisdom is later than Abraham’s prophecy in antiquity. [Col. 0055] VII, 597; and later than that of our Patriarchs. VII, 599. The antiquity claimed for the Egyptians’ fabricated wisdom is refuted. VII, 599. The wisdom of the Egyptians, especially astronomy. VII, 599. The Egyptians loved geometry. III, 549.

The Egyptians’ custom concerning the bodies of the dead. V, 1605. The Egyptians excel in preserving the bodies of the dead. III, 502. Trismegistus foretold the downfall of the religion of the Egyptians. VII, 248, 251. He received this also from demons. VII, 248, 251.

Shepherds were abominable to the Egyptians. III, 605. The sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians. III, 605. The Egyptians are said to have been near to the Hebrews. III, 507.

The ten plagues of the Egyptians are expounded. IV, 1001; V, 67. Why the Egyptians were subdued by frogs and flies. III, 2039. In the Egyptians, a figure of the present age.

Faustus wrongly criticized the plundering of the Egyptians. VIII, 445. How God permitted the Egyptians to be deceived by the Israelites’ mutual taking of gold and silver. VI, 34. The wealth of the Egyptians, which the Israelites took away, was owed to the Israelites. IV, 1400. The Egyptians being plundered, a figure of Christians making progress through the knowledge of the pagans. III, 64. The drowning of the Egyptians in the Red Sea, a figure of the abolition of sins in baptism. III, 1722; V, 37.

Egyptian days. III, 2130.

Egypt. V, 291, 292, 768. Egypt, the land of Ham. IV, 1398. In the Hebrew language, Egypt signifies darkness or tribulations. IV, 1001. Egypt is interpreted as “affliction” and represents a figure of the age. IV, 1477, 1750. The location of Egypt. IX, 423. What was signified by God’s people being led out of Egypt. IV, 487. Israel’s departure from Egypt is expounded mystically. VIII, 269. In Egypt there is an abundance of grain from the flooding of the Nile, but pastureland, conversely, is scarce. III, 591.

Aeinan or Aeinaim is interpreted as “Fountains.” VIII, 457.

Aelianus, Proconsul. II, 399. Aelianus, Proconsul of Africa. IX, 540, 611, 649, 686. At what time he heard Felix’s case. IX, 687. Aelianus’s judgment by which Felix of Aptunga was cleared and acquitted. IX, 540.

Aelius, a deacon. IX, 513.

Aemilianus, bishop. II, 759.

Aemilius and Castus, martyrs. V, 1295.

When the good see the wicked flourishing, they are moved to want to imitate them. IV, 1201.

The difference between emulation and envy. III, 2142. Emulation is inclined to suspect evil. IV, 1435.

Aeneas’s father was Anchises, and his mother Venus. VII, 81. At what time Aeneas came to Italy. VII, 576. It is not true that Aeneas came to Carthage. I, 671. Aeneas is called pious. VII, 16. The house of Aeneas, that is, the Romans. VII, 462. Aeneas was made a god by the Latins. VII, 576, 577.

What a riddle is. VIII, 1068, 1069. A riddle is an obscure parable that is difficult to understand. IV, 546. Riddles are useful for sharpening the love of truth. VI, 320.

Poets are called riddle-makers. III, 739.

True equality, and true and first unity itself, is perceived not by the senses but by the mind. III, 146.

How equanimity is to be preserved. IV, 1212.

Equity is derived from equality. I, 1043.

God cannot lose equity. IV, 744.

How Valentinus admitted thirty aeons. VIII, 28.

See Ptolemy. Marcus.

Air was not omitted from the account of Genesis. III, 281, 282. When and why air was made. III, 238. Air is called heaven. I, 865; VI, 292; VII, 684. Air received the name of heaven and of the heavens. III, 265, 279, 281. Air is assigned to earth, water, heaven, and the firmament according to its purity or impurity. III, 238, 239, 274, 281, 282. Air is assigned to Juno. VII, 119. Anaximenes believed air to be a god. I, 782; II, 443. Anaximenes attributed the causes of things to infinite air. VII, 226, 230.

According to the poets, air is something different from the ether. VII, 119. Winds, thunder, clouds, rain, hail, and clear weather occur in the lower part of the air. III, 284; not in the higher part. III, 237. Air is felt to be dry in comparison with water. III, 238. It is proved that air is above water. III, 264. Air is believed to have been changed into a moist nature at the time of the Flood. III, 280. How air is suited to carrying the flights of birds. III, 238, 282, 286.

Air is nourishment. I, 1251. Without air, there is no sensation or movement of the body. III, 363.

Air is the prison of the sinful angels. III, 285, 730; IV, 1943. The creatures of the air are demons. I, 915, 1007. They surpass us in sharpness and subtlety of the senses, not in reason. I, 916.

Aerius, from whom the Aerian heretics are named. VIII, 39, 40.

What the Aerian heretics add to the Arians. VIII, 39, 40.

Bronze was discovered before iron. VII, 214. The ancients cultivated the earth with bronze. VII, 214.

Aeschines. IX, 468. Aeschines of Athens, a tragic actor, undertook public office. VII, 56.

Aesculanus, a god. VII, 128.

Aesculapius, the physician-god. VII, 128; summoned from Epidaurus to Rome. VII, 87, 97. When Aesculapius was sailing to Rome, an Epidaurian serpent clung to him as a companion. VII, 294. A temple consecrated to Aesculapius on the mountain of Libya. VII, 254. Aesculapius was both a human being and a god. VII, 254.

The fables of Aesop. VI, 538. Socrates rendered Aesop’s fables in verse. III, 1048.

What our summer is. IV, 1947. Summer signifies the prosperity of the age, winter its adversity. IV, 475, 804. Those fervent in spirit are signified by summer, and those newly established in faith by spring. IV, 941. Our summer is Christ’s coming; our winter is Christ’s concealment. V, 217.

To estimate God is to set things in order. IV, 1863. Who is an upright estimator of things. III, 29. He lives justly and holily. III, 29.

The six ages of the world. III, 1513, 1461; they are signified by the six jars. III, 1461. The six ages of the world are compared with the six days of creation. IV, 1182. Where each age begins and where it ends. III, 190. Those six ages are laborious; in the seventh rest is hoped for. III, 190. The seven ages of the world are signified by the seven days. III, 190. Four ages from Abraham to the end of the age. VIII, 138. Christ’s Nativity began the sixth age. VIII, 892. Why these ages are unequal. III, 193.

The stages of an age. II, 966. As many stages of an age as there are, so many deaths of ages. IV, 1686. Two ages: old age and extreme old age. IV, 894. The difference between the age of an older person and that of an old man. III, 191. There is no age where there is eternity. VIII, 773, 774. Although an age may seem long, when it has arrived at its end it is shown to have been short, because it comes to an end. IV, 1613.

Spiritual ages. V, 1081. The six ages of the human being, both of the old man and of the new. III, 143. The age of twenty signifies the faithful. III, 718. No age is excluded from the breasts of philosophy. I, 908.

Aetius, from whom the Aetians are named; they are also called Eunomians. VIII, 40.

What eternity is. VII, 751. All things stand in eternity. IV, 1623. In eternity there is neither anything past nor anything future, but only the present. IV, 71. Eternity has no “when.” IV, 1459. In eternity there is stability, but in time variation: in eternity all things stand; in time some things succeed others and some things occur. V, 666. Eternity is called the length of days. IV, 1613. Eternity is one day, many days, and many years. IV, 727. The days of eternity are all present together; therefore they satisfy. IV, 1147. The day of eternity neither comes nor passes, because it is not preceded by yesterday so that it may come, nor driven on by tomorrow so that it may pass. IV, 1463. Eternity consists in the word of four syllables, but in itself it is without end. IV, 1898. True eternity is where there is nothing of time. III, 1588. How eternity differs from time. VII, 321; how it is expressed in Scripture. IV, 1310.

True eternity belongs to God alone. VIII, 563. This world does not have the same eternity as God has. III, 175. God’s eternity is an eternity that always stands. I, 814. Eternity is God’s very substance, which has nothing mutable, nothing past, and nothing future; there is nothing there except “is.” IV, 1311. Even temporal happiness is better than a wretched eternity. VII, 241. Eternity does not exist without truth and love. VIII, 909. Eternity was made our refuge, so that we might flee to it from this mutability of time. IV, 1142. In heaven are eternity and truth; on earth, corresponding to these, are that which has come into being and faith. III, 1070. As much as eternity is valid with respect to what has arisen, so much truth is valid with respect to faith. VIII, 904. The name “age” sometimes signifies eternity. IV, 1715. There is a kind of imitation of eternity in the succession of times. IV, 120. All the fixed spans of the ages, when compared with boundless eternity, are nothing. VII, 359.

Eternity must be sought. III, 1658. Every human being seeks eternity, truth, and blessedness. VIII, 887. What we seek is not here. VIII, 887. Whoever wishes to contemplate the eternal years should rest from every external disturbance. IV, 976.

That whose time has no end is called eternal. III, 511, 556. The eternal precedes times and is not enclosed by time. IV, 913. In the eternal there is neither anything past nor anything future, but whatever is simply is. VI, 15. That must truly be regarded as eternal which is changed by no time. IV, 906. “Eternal” can be understood in two ways. III, 608, 680. What has a beginning yet is eternal is like a number. VII, 320. The Platonists falsely taught that nothing can thereafter be eternal unless it had always previously existed. VII, 311. Plato seems to have held the opposite view. VII, 311. Everything eternal is immortal, but not conversely. VI, 15. The Priscillianists held that “eternal” and “perpetual” differ from one another. VIII, 668.

Eternal goods must not be conceived carnally. IV, 488. The merit of eternal life is attained only by God’s gift. III, 419. How the mind may be made fit to attain eternal things. VIII, 903. By clinging to the eternal Creator, we too must necessarily be endowed with eternity. III, 131. The eternal, once attained, is loved more ardently than when desired. III, 35. God grants eternal things for enjoyment and temporal things for use. V, 413. The eternal hell. I, 768.

Aethan is interpreted as “Strong.” IV, 1120.

[Col. 0057] The ancient poets wish the ether to be one thing and the air another. VII, 120. The ether is more mobile than air. III, 225. The ether is the mind of the God of the world. VII, 212. The ether is assigned to Jupiter. VII, 119.

What the black Ethiopians signify in Scripture. IV, 938.

Aetiology. VIII, 68.

Mount Etna spews out rivers of flame. VII, 111. The sea is said to have burned so fiercely from the fires of Etna that rocks were scorched and the pitch of ships melted. VII, 111. The roofs of the city of Catina were destroyed by the force of the ash erupting from Etna. VII, 111.

Those who pursue evil, even though what they have done may benefit others for salvation, cannot find it good. IV, 212.

Our affections are movements of the soul. III, 1732. Affection is one thing, an affective quality another. X, 854. The affections called by the Greeks εὐπάθειαι (*eupatheiai*) and by Cicero “constancies” (*constantiae*) are three. VII, 411. The affections, or passions of the soul, called by the Greeks πάθη (*pathē*) and by Cicero “perturbations” (*perturbationes*), are four. VII, 258, 406. Why affections are attributed to God and the angels although they lack them. VII, 261. Whether the first parents had the affections of fear and grief before sin. VII, 449. The Platonists say that affections occur in the wise person; the Stoics deny it. VII, 258. The Stoics admit certain affections into the mind of the wise person. VII, 411. Christ was not without affections. VII, 415; yet not because of the weakness of his condition. VII, 415.

Christian discipline turns affections toward the uses of justice. VII, 260. Every right life has right affections, and every perverse life has perverse ones. VII, 416. If there are no affections, one is not living rightly. VII, 415. Even pious works have their affections or delights. IV, 978. The affections belong to this life, not to the future life that is hoped for. VII, 415. Nevertheless, there will be certain affections in the homeland. VII, 416. The three affections of the body are health, insensibility, and immortality. IV, 650.

Human affections are like feet. III, 1789. Our affections are our feet on the journey to God. IV, 1217. We run to God by our affections, not by our steps. VI, 681. There is no voice for God’s ears except the affection of the soul. VI, 322. An affection is punished even when the result does not follow. VII, 483.

Future relationships, even if Adam had not sinned. I, 605, 615; contrary to what Augustine had previously believed. III, 161. Spiritual affinity. III, 162.

The good suffer afflictions while the wicked flourish here. IV, 190. See *Why the good are afflicted by temporal evils*. VII, 20. It is beneficial for the just to be afflicted in this life. VI, 98. People are afflicted so that they may seek God, III, 863, and so that they may gather their affections away from the flow of earthly pleasures. III, 871. Through afflictions the Church is purified and exercised. III, 25. Some are spared in this world so that they may be tormented more abundantly in the next; others are not spared here so that they may be spared there. III, 1577. People are never afflicted without cause. III, 871. See *Adversity*, *Tribulation*, *Prosperity*.

Africa is the third part of the world. VII, 497. The dimensions of Africa. VII, 497. Whether Africa lies in the south. V, 291, 768. The location of Africa. IX, 423. Africa is not last in the order of believing. IX, 419. Whether Africa shares with the East and the East with Africa. IX, 538. Africa ravaged by barbarians. II, 529. In Africa you would more easily hear little horns than, and so forth. II, 436. The crime of the African traditores could not stain the whole world. IX, 100, 538, 539, 541. See *Donatists*, *Traditores*. Africa infected by the Pelagian heresy. X, 396.

Africanus wrote about Christ’s genealogy. I, 633.

Africanus, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Agamemnon, king of Mycenae. VII, 572.

Agapes. The Christians did not turn the sacrifices of the pagans into agapes. VIII, 383.

Hagar and her son signified the carnal people of the Old Testament. VII, 512. Hagar fleeing from Sarah’s face, a figure of heresies. V, 32.

The difference between ἄγαν (*agan*, “exceedingly”) and σφόδρα (*sphodra*, “very greatly”). IV, 1444, 1509.

The Hagarenes are interpreted as proselytes. IV, 1053.

Aulus Gellius, author of the *Attic Nights*. VII, 259; he recounts the disturbance of a certain philosopher during a storm at sea. III, 551.

Agenoria, a goddess. VII, 122, 125.

Nothing should be done that reason has not approved. III, 746.
