No one better orders what he should do than the person who is readier not to do what divine power forbids than eager to do what human thought has planned. VI, 326. Whatever you do, do it well, and you have praised God. IV, 341. The action of the soul ought to be such as tends toward tranquil security, not such as increases restless labor. IV, 1489. Good action leads to ever-watchful rest. IV, 1489. The activity of the peaceful and the leisure of the blessed. IV, 1463. Hope for doing good must not be placed in a human being. X, 886. See *Grace*, *Works*. What it means to act without bringing good or evil to completion. V, 818. See *Action*.

To be moved is more than to be ruled. X, 323. People are moved so that they may act. X, 373, 918. You act if you are moved, and you act well if you are moved by what is good. V, 718, 856.

Two agents in public affairs, once they had learned of Antony’s life, conveyed its report back to the world. I, 755.

[Col. 0058] Haggai: who he was and at what time he prophesied. IV, 1467; VII, 593. He was a prophet during the Babylonian captivity. IV, 1917. He prophesied the restoration of Jerusalem. IV, 1917. A passage from Haggai is defended against the Manichaeans. V, 330. Haggai does not support the schism of the Donatists. IX, 670.

Aggya. IX, 235.

Agilis and Romanus were sent by Paulinus to Augustine. II, 122; Augustine received them with great pleasure. II, 122.

Aginesis. II, 1063.

Agnes, virgin and martyr. V, 1250, 1565.

In Scripture, “to acknowledge” sometimes has the same meaning as “to regard with gratitude.” IV, 1374. In many passages of Scripture, to acknowledge God means to preserve; not to acknowledge him means to condemn. IV, 1836. For God to acknowledge sins means not to forgive them. IV, 947.

Agnosius, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 380.

Rams or ewes according to the time of the sheep’s giving birth. III, 572. The lamb is not to be killed in its mother’s milk: a prophecy concerning Christ. III, 652. The Paschal lamb, a figure of Christ. III, 608. Its mysteries. VI, 663. The lamb signifies the innocence of wisdom that chews the cud. IV, 1834. How Christ is the spotless lamb. IV, 763. To follow the Lamb wherever he goes is proper to virgins. VI, 407.

The Christian contest. VI, 289.

The Circumcellions were called “Agonists” by the Donatists. IV, 1732.

The devil is the organizer of the contest. IV, 1859.

The name “fields” is commonly used for villages, municipalities, and colonies. III, 1206. This world is the Lord’s field. III, 198; IV, 1950. The Church of God. IV, 1440. The cultivation of the Lord’s field. VI, 693. The two in the field are the clerics who govern the Church. IV, 1279, 1730.

Agrarian laws. VII, 107.

The farmer loses what he sows; so now the soul must be lost. V, 1456. The sins of farmers. IV, 886. God is our farmer. IV, 802. Human beings, however, are the laborers of this Farmer. IV, 802. Fruit is brought to God, as to a farmer, from what he has sown. IV, 1318.

Very many people take pleasure in agriculture. III, 1304. Its praise. III, 1304, 1305. Agriculture is the most innocent of all arts. VIII, 37. Among the Greeks it began to be practiced under King Argus. VII, 564. Before sin there was no affliction of labor. III, 378. The work of agriculture allegorically. III, 379. Why the Manichaeans permit agriculture to their hearers while condemning them in other matters. VIII, 37.

Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage. IX, 606; Cyprian’s predecessor. IX, 133. He first attempted to abandon the practice of not rebaptizing those baptized by heretics. IX, 133, 134, 140, 143, 159. An objection is raised. IX, 135. Although Agrippinus held a different opinion, he did not abandon unity. IX, 140.

Ajax. VIII, 585.

How Αἰών (*aiōn*) is usually rendered in Latin. IV, 1020, 1187, 1393.

Αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*). VII, 506.

The two wings of charity. IV, 1347, 1791, 1952. The two wings of prayer are fasting and almsgiving. IV, 482.

Alaric. V, 624; he overthrew Rome. I, 647. At the first siege of the city, at the end of the year 408, he inflicted this disaster on the Roman people. II, 365. Note a. After the city was captured, he ordered those who had fled to the holy places to be kept unharmed. VII, 13, note 2, 17, 45, 48. The humanity of Alaric’s soldiers. VII, 48.

Alba was built by Ascanius. VII, 89; at what time. VII, 577. Alba is a nearer mother of Rome than Troy. VII, 89. It was conquered by Tullus Hostilius. VII, 89. After Alba was founded, the kings of the Latins were called kings of the Albans. VII, 577. The Romans impiously brought war against the Albans. VII, 89; and unjustly. VII, 89.

Albicerus, a diviner by profession at Carthage. I, 925. He gave remarkable and certain answers to those who consulted him. I, 925. When someone asked him to say what the person’s soul was turning over, he replied that the man was thinking of a verse of Virgil; and he confidently recited that same verse, although uneducated. I, 915.

Albina, mother of Melania. X, 359. Note. Albina, Pinianus, Melania, and others. II, 471. Note. Through Jerome they sent greetings to Alypius and Augustine. II, 928.

Albinus, acolyte of the Roman church. II, 867, 868, 871, 874.

Whiteness on the skin is leprosy, not ordinary whiteness. IV, 937.

The river Albula, now the Tiber. III, 203.

The Manichaeans say that white belongs to God and black to Hyle. VIII, 396. Clothed in white garments after baptism. V, 678, 1092.

The sadness of Alcibiades. VII, 413.

Alcimus was made pontiff although he was unrelated to the priestly class. VII, 606.

Alecto, an infernal fury. VII, 88.

Alexander, king and high priest among the Jews. VII, 606.

Alexander of Macedon founded Alexandria. III, 795. His kingdom was great in extent but extremely brief in time. VII, 117; its power was most magnificent but by no means long-lasting. VII, 602. He sacrificed victims in the temple of God, but not with true piety. VII, 606. He wrote to his mother Olympias about the sacred rites of the gods. VII, 256, 358.

Alexander, an ancient heretic mentioned by Jerome. II, 252, 286. He left brief commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians. II, 252.

Alexandra, queen of the Jews. VII, 606.

Alexandria. VIII, 944, 966.

To be alienated from the life of God: how great a punishment this is. VI, 339.

Alienation may occur from the senses, from an evil spirit, and from a good spirit. III, 470; by what distinction. III, 470.

Who the foreigners are. IV, 648, 721. Foreigners: those who consider no happiness complete unless it is present happiness. V, 204, 205.

People possess what belongs to others when they possess what is superfluous. IV, 1922. What is alien from conscience is alien from action; what is alien from conscience seems alien from knowledge. IV, 334. Whoever gains nothing for you from what is yours is alien to you. IV, 553.

Nourishment. Besides food and drink, there is a third nourishment: the nourishment of the air. X, 513. Foods are daily medicines. VII, 690. Augustine was taught by God to approach food in the same way as he would approach medicine. I, 797, 798. Rules for taking food. III, 1337. Food is to be taken solely for the sake of health. I, 797. The use of food and of the tree of life in paradise. X, 772.

What allegory is. IV, 1347; VIII, 1068. Several kinds of allegory. VIII, 1068. Fourfold allegory: of history, deed, speech, and sacrament. III, 166. This rule must be retained in every allegory: what is said by way of likeness must be considered according to the meaning of the present passage. IV, 116. The usefulness of allegories. II, 214. Christ himself used allegory in the Gospel. VIII, 70.

Alleluia. See *Hallelujah*.

“To raise someone up,” meaning to kill. III, 824.

The bonds of contrition, the sacraments. IV, 1903.

The Allophyli mystically. III, 118; IV, 648, 721.

The river Almon, flowing into the Tiber not far from the city. VII, 50. Note (c).

Alogia is said to occur when a person indulges in banquets so as to stray from the path of reason. II, 141. *Alogiare* means to indulge in banquets in such a way as to deviate from reason. III, 1423.

The Alogi, heretics. VIII, 31.

The altar. I, 778; IX, 202. Christ’s altar. IX, 220. A wooden altar. IX, 190. The heavenly altar, which no unworthy person touches, and the visible altar, which many unworthy people touch. IV, 193. The lofty invisible altar, to which the unjust do not draw near: only the person who approaches that altar safely approaches this one. IV, 479. An altar erected over the relics of Stephen. V, 1438; and over the body of Cyprian. V, 1425. Altars are not erected to the Martyrs themselves but to God. V, 1251, 1438. At the altar of God, Martyrs and deceased holy women are commemorated in their proper place. VI, 423. The Martyrs are commemorated at the altar in a more honored place. V, 1251.

Altars: offering. II, 637. Sacrifice of the altar for the dead. VI, 609. Monnica, at the end of her life, desires that remembrance of her be made at the altar. I, 778. The altar, or what is received from the altar. V, 562. The holy victim is dispensed from the altar. I, 778. At Carthage, the custom of singing psalms at the altar is adopted. I, 634.

Spiritually, we must understand the altar as faith. III, 1242. Our heart is the altar of God. VII, 280.

The eagerness for quarrelling is condemned. III, 1308.

The alternations in mutable creation ought not to disturb us. VI, 131.

Height. There is no body that lacks length, breadth, and height. I, 1038, 1048. The height of a body, and its other dimensions, are explained. I, 1038. Spiritual height. IV, 1728.

God is high, and is reached by the humble. IV, 947, 1205.

Alypius was born at Thagaste. I, 724, of parents who were leading municipal citizens. I, 724. He was short in bodily stature. I, 967. Romanianus, a relative of Alypius. II, 110. Alypius was younger than Augustine. I, 724. He was Augustine’s closest friend from his earliest years, and was called by him “the brother of his heart.” I, 724, 766. Alypius attended Augustine’s lectures in rhetoric at Thagaste and Carthage. I, 724. From early youth Alypius displayed a great natural disposition toward virtue. I, 724. At Carthage he was seized like a thief, but was soon released. I, 726. At Carthage he was devoted to spectacles, but was recalled from the madness of the Circus by Augustine’s rebuke. I, 725. He came to Rome before Augustine in order to study law. I, 726. Alypius, an exceptionally courageous master of his body, trampled the icy Italian ground barefoot in an unprecedented undertaking. I, 769. He was seized with an incredible love of gladiatorial spectacles, incredibly carried away by it. I, 726. He became involved with Augustine in the superstition of the Manichaeans. I, 726.

Alypius went to Milan with Augustine. I, 727. He lived with the greatest continence. I, 730. He prevented Augustine from marrying, so that they might both devote themselves freely to wisdom. I, 730. He served three times in the office of assessor. I, 727, 754. While serving beside the Comes of the Italian largesses, his integrity was tested by a most powerful senator, both by promises and by threats. I, 727. Out of love of justice, Alypius abstained from using the praetorian treasury. I, 727.

Alypius thought that Catholics believed that Christ had neither a human soul nor a human mind, and therefore he was slow to move toward the faith. Later, however, he understood that this was the error of the Apollinarists. I, 746. Alypius joined himself to Augustine’s good purpose after Augustine’s conversion to God. I, 761. He withdrew with Augustine to the estate at Cassisiacum, a catechumen with a catechumen. I, 766. He discussed with Augustine the ends of good and evil. I, 732. He disdained to introduce the name of Christ into those literary nocturnal studies, but later came to his senses. I, 766. There he gave Augustine his assistance in publishing the books On Order and Against the Academics, taking the role of interlocutor in them in such a way that the very words committed to writing were his own. I, 908. Alypius returned to Milan in order to give his name for baptism together with Augustine. I, 769. Alypius was baptized. IV, 169.

Alypius, bishop of Thagaste. IX, 697, 700. Jerome greets Pope Alypius and his brother. II, 156. Paulinus sends Alypius the history of Eusebius, bishop of Constantinople. II, 212; he also sends one loaf of bread. II, 100. How highly Augustine valued Alypius. II, 90. Alypius praised for renouncing the world, rejecting flesh and blood, and embracing solitude. II, 95. Augustine promises that he will write the history of Alypius for Paulinus. II, 110. Alypius writes back to Sixtus. II, 867. Alypius and Augustine instructed Juliana and her household in good morals. II, 848. With Alypius and Augustine urging her on, Demetrias sent back word even though the wedding had already been arranged. II, 848. Alypius received with the greatest kindness and sincerity by Pope Boniface. X, 549. When the people of Hippo were demanding Pinianus for the presbyterate, they shouted many insulting and unworthy things against Alypius. II, 477, 481. Julian’s slander against Alypius. X, 1065, 1066. Alypius called by Julian “Augustine’s little household slave of sins.” X, 1053. By Augustine’s own testimony, Augustine became Alypius’s teacher in words, and Alypius Augustine’s teacher in deeds. I, 1007.

Amaccura. IX, 221.

Amalek, interpreted as “the people who lick.” IV, 1053.

Haman, interpreted as “his brother.” IV, 1110.

“Those who make bitter.” IV, 88, 796, 816, 1750.

Bitterness. Wherever the soul turns, it finds bitterness in earthly things; it has nothing from which it may become sweet unless it raises itself to God. IV, 1085, 1086. Why God mingles bitterness with the sweetness of temporal life. IV, 1213, 1793. God mingles bitterness even with innocent pleasures, so that we may have love only for eternal life. IV, 458.

It is not found what the prophet Habakkuk foretold, or when he prophesied. VII, 587.

The misery of the ambitious. I, 724.

Ambivius, bishop. II, 759, 778.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan. X, 866; he is praised. I, 717. His celibacy, occupations, and studies. I, 720, 721. Ambrose learned in secular and ecclesiastical literature. X, 1157. Every Sunday he expounds the word of God to the people. I, 721. Monnica loved Ambrose as though he were an angel of God. I, 719. Ambrose kindly received Augustine, who listened attentively to his preaching. I, 717. When Augustine asked Ambrose what he ought chiefly to read in Scripture in order to prepare himself for baptism, Ambrose prescribed Isaiah. I, 769. Augustine was converted and baptized through Ambrose. X, 645. It was chiefly through the mouth of Ambrose that God freed Augustine from error, and through Ambrose’s ministry granted him the grace of saving baptism. II, 152, 620.

The persecution of Ambrose. II, 177. Ambrose suffered persecution from the Arian empress Justina. I, 770. The people kept vigil in the church, prepared to die with their bishop. I, 770. At that time it was instituted, and has been retained ever since, that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, so that the people would not waste away from the tedium of grief. I, 770.

Ambrose forbids synaxes at the memorial shrines of the martyrs. I, 719. Ambrose miraculously discovers the bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius. I, 770; VII, 761; IX, 430. While Ambrose was still alive, demons begged him to spare them. VI, 608. In observing the Sabbath fast, Ambrose replied that the custom of the Church in which each person lived ought to be maintained. II, 151, 201.

Through Paulinus’s love for Ambrose, Paulinus was nurtured in the faith. II, 102. Paulinus calls Ambrose his father. II, 102. Paulinus is regarded as Ambrose’s presbyter. II, 102.

Ambrose’s death occurred in the year 397, on April 4. II, 151, 152. See the notes.

Ambrose, conqueror of heretics. X, 1368. Ambrose is set against Pelagius. X, 381. Ambrose’s doctrine opposed to the Pelagians. X, 681. Ambrose acknowledged original sin. X, 1052, 1157. He taught that no one is without sin. X, 284. Ambrose’s position in favor of original sin. X, 378, 409. Ambrose’s testimonies against the Pelagians. X, 632. Ambrose’s doctrine opposed to Julian’s three errors. X, 674, 675. Not even an enemy, as Pelagius testifies, dared to criticize Ambrose’s faith and his most pure understanding of Scripture. X, 1052. Julian said that, if Ambrose were alive, he would first correct himself and then everyone else concerning original sin. X, 1408, 1414. However holy Ambrose may have been, he must by no means be compared with the authority of canonical Scripture. X, 381.

Pelagius is said to have called Ambrose a certain beautiful flower that had shone forth among ecclesiastical writers. 1228, 1230. Ambrose greatly praised in Pelagius’s own words. X, 381, 383, 384, 409, 410, 436, 445, 466, 632, 661, 671, 695, 1070, 1080, 1157, 1274, 1345, 1378, 1402, 1411, 1412.

Ambrose defended Mary’s virginity. X, 445. For this reason he was called a Manichaean by Jovinian. X, 445. Ambrose wrote against those who claimed that the Lord had advanced by means of Plato’s books. II, 125. Ambrose’s understanding of Christ’s righteousness. X, 1084. Augustine embraces Ambrose’s view concerning the vision of God. II, 620. Commending it as a kind of rule for interpreting the Old Law, Ambrose often said while preaching: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” I, 722. In some matters Ambrose followed Origen’s interpretation. II, 261.

Ambrose’s exposition of Isaiah. X, 632, 633, 634, 647. On Psalm 48. X, 646. On the book of Tobit. VI, 579. On Luke. X, 645, 1024. Ambrose’s book On Isaac and the Soul. X, 671. On the Sacrament of Regeneration, or On Philosophy. X, 683, 687, 690. Apology of the Prophet David. X, 632, 645, 1024. Ambrose’s book On Flight from the World. X, 633, 634, 689, 1003. On Noah’s Ark. X, 632, 674. On the Good of Death. X, 635. Book I, On Repentance, against the Jovinians. X, 632. Book On Paradise. X, 682, 688.

Ambrosian verses. I, 777.

The Ambrosian Basilica. I, 770.

To walk according to the flesh and according to the spirit. V, 846. To walk not according to man but according to God. VI, 356. Our walking means burning with zeal in the paths of good works. IV, 290. It is better to walk sluggishly on the road than to run energetically off the road. IV, 259. Whoever walks on the road of faith is brought to the vision. IV, 1854.

Amen, a Hebrew word. III, 1694. Why it was not translated. III, 1694. What it signifies. Ibid. Amen means the same as “true.” V, 1633. Amen is interpreted as “true,” not in an ordinary way but according to mystical religion. VIII, 313. In response to the invocations of bishops, the people say “Amen.” VI, 320. The faithful respond “Amen” when receiving the Eucharist. V, 1247, 1469. “Amen” and “hallelujah” are sung throughout the world on the days of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection. IV, 177. “Amen” and “hallelujah” have been retained because of their more sacred authority. III, 42. “Amen” and “hallelujah” will constitute the whole activity of the blessed. V, 1530. “Amen, amen” is used to affirm something. III, 649.

What friendship is. VI, 22; X, 550. Friendship is agreement concerning human and divine things, accompanied by goodwill and charity. I, 941; II, 1071. Friendship consists in mutual love. VI, 173. Friendship is formed by similarity of character. III, 243. True friendship flows from love of eternity and truth. II, 667. It is not true friendship unless God joins together those who cling to one another in charity. I, 696. Friendship is faithful nowhere except in Christ. X, 550. This is the most just law of friendship: that each person should love a friend neither less nor more than himself. I, 873.

No one’s friendship should be rejected. VI, 82. Human friendship is of little benefit and sometimes does great harm; the friendship of Christ may be desired securely. IV, 1718. Friendship should be offered to those who do not dare to ask it of us. VI, 83. We may say that someone has been received into friendship when we dare to pour out all our counsels to him. VI, 83. One must beware of a rash judgment of goodwill toward someone whose good qualities alone are immediately apparent. VI, 83. Someone whose faults are initially all that become known should not be driven from the heart. VI, 83. Without faith, friendship cannot be established. VI, 173. The love of friendship loves what is not seen. V, 1692.

One friendship arises from habit, another from reason. V, 1691. Whether friendship should be sought for its own sake alone. VI, 21. The love of friendship should be gratuitous. V, 1692. Friendship should not be weighed by temporal advantages, but should be valued for gratuitous love. II, 667. When friendship perishes, the bonds of marriage, kinship, and affinity will not remain in the soul. VI, 173. Nothing is more bitter than pretended friendship. VII, 632. Friendship is full of fear and anxiety. VII, 634.

Friendship is hostile to evils. I, 682. Friendship with this world is fornication against God. I, 670. When you cultivate friendships with the citizens of Babylon, beware lest Babylon begin to delight you and you forget Jerusalem. IV, 1768. Every soul bound by friendship with mortal things is miserable. I, 697.

Nothing is friendly to a human being in any human affair without a human friend. II, 495. Someone aptly said of his friend, “Half of my soul.” I, 698. There is no friend among the unrighteous. IV, 1179. He truly loves a friend who loves God in his friend, either because God is in him or so that God may be in him. V, 1472. He loves a friend for God’s sake who loves the love of God in his friend. VIII, 451. A friend possesses his friend more securely in God. II, 72. He alone loses none of them who has all those dear to him in the One who is not lost. I, 699. Blessed is the one who loves God and a friend in God, and an enemy for God’s sake. I, 699. The sign of true friendship is agreement in religion. I, 941. Those who agree only in human matters are not friends. II, 1072. The constancy of one who is a friend through charity is not to be feared. II, 250.

The unfeigned faith and mutual love of true and good friends consoles us in this life. VII, 634. Friends who fear to rebuke are often less useful than enemies who quarrel. II, 247. Shame should not prevent a friend from admonishing a friend. II, 671. Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor everyone who beats an enemy. II, 323. Nothing proves a friend so much as carrying a friend’s burden. VI, 80. The faults of friends are not to be loved. V, 325. A friend giving evil advice. V, 501. Friends and good people are very powerful for good, and evil people for evil. V, 537. No one can truly be a friend of a human being unless he first belongs to truth itself. II, 667. He is not a friend of what is right who would prefer that what is right not be commanded. IV, 823.

Nowadays a friend and an enemy are scarcely distinguishable. V, 322. A friend’s good will is not seen but believed. VI, 171. Nor is his goodwill established for us without faith. VI, 171.

The death of a friend is bitter, and his change is more bitter. VII, 635. What truly consoles one in the death of friends. VII, 635. It is of some benefit to recognize what is bitter and sorrowful concerning those dearest to us. II, 365.

No one becomes a friend of God except through the purest conduct and sincere charity. III, 175. If anyone desires to know God’s will, let him become a friend of God. III, 175.

A friend awakened at midnight to give three loaves to refresh a friend. V, 619. Nature avoids the loss of the things it possesses. III, 386. In the loss of temporal things, nothing perishes for the saints. VII, 23.

Someone is said to have lost something when he has not received what he hoped for. III, 355.

The Ammonites descended from Lot. III, 762.

Amedera. IX, 221.

Ammon, interpreted as “son of my people,” or “son of sorrow.” III, 818; IV, 1053.

Ammonianus, bishop. X, 652, 663.

Ammonius, physician. VII, 761.

I love. What it is to love. VI, 23. We love nothing unless it is beautiful. I, 701, 1183. A person loves that by which he thinks he will become blessed. VI, 672. Whether unknown things can be loved. VIII, 952, 954, 971, 873, 974, 910. Whoever loves does not labor. III, 1741. Not everything that must be used is to be loved. III, 27. Whatever you love for a time is either taken away from you, or you are taken away from it. V, 1653. Things possessed with love do not perish without pain. VI, 156, 265. In this world there is nothing that a Christian can love. VI, 679.

The love songs of our homeland, not the old ones, should be sung. IV, 807.

Lovers of slippery things, provided that they are handsome and deceitful, do not care about truthful reprovers. IV, 282.

Love God; you will find nothing better. V, 1531. A great stimulus to the love of God is drawn from Christ’s incarnation. VI, 314, 339. See Love. God cannot be loved unless he is possessed. V, 211. When God is loved, he is continuously possessed. V, 211. God is to be loved more than parents. V, 1512. God is to be loved gratuitously. V, 905, 1646. To love God gratuitously is piety. V, 568. What it is to love God gratuitously. IV, 626, 658, 265, 1404, 1745. To love God gratuitously means to hope for God from God: he himself is sufficient for you; apart from him nothing is sufficient for you. V, 1469. If you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way. III, 2049. See Charity, Love. What is nothing other than possessing is knowing; it cannot be absent while it is loved. VI, 23. The command to love God with one’s whole heart leaves no part of our life that ought to remain vacant. III, 27. This love is compared with a river. III, 27.

God is to be loved for his own sake, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. V, 1472. To love a human being in place of Christ is adultery. III, 1497. We love God from God. V, 210, 923. God knows in each of us both how to hate what we have done and how to love what he has made. III, 1923. God loves what is his own even in the morally defective person, either by the benefit of healing or by the judgment of condemnation. III, 1923. Why it is necessary to know how much, and what kind of people, God has loved. VIII, 888.

He rightly loves his neighbor who acts so that the neighbor too may love God with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. III, 27. Whoever loves his brother loves God—why. VIII, 957, 958. Who love both their neighbor and themselves justly. VIII, 956. We ought not to love people as gluttons love thrushes. III, 2038. We love people in whom there is some spark of charity, and conversely. III, 1405. From what source someone is loved who is thought to be righteous but is not. VIII, 966. Imitate the good, tolerate the evil, love everyone. VI, 347. Those who are not yet righteous are to be loved so that they may become so; those who already are righteous are to be loved more ardently. VI, 344. What is to be loved in them. VI, 348. The soul is loved more than the body, even in another person. II, 1420. Someone who loves need not be stirred up to bring help to a friend. II, 1750. Augustine wished to be loved not in himself but in Christ. II, 1425. Those in higher positions also love and are loved by those beneath them. VI, 315. To love. See Love.

A person always loves himself and his own body. III, 27, 29. A rule should be prescribed for how a person is to love himself and his body. III, 28. To love oneself, and to deny oneself. V, 1456.

You love with charity whatever you love well. V, 160. See Friendship, Love, To love. The fuller we are of love, the healthier we are from the swelling of pride. VIII, 957, 958.

The proper manner of loving inferior things. V, 1654. Though the world has become bitter, it does not cease to be loved. V, 1419. If love of the world dwells within, there is no room for the love of God to enter. III, 1993. By loving God we become gods; by loving the world, we are called worldly. V, 678.

Love is a weight by which the soul is borne wherever it is borne. I, 848; II, 677; VII, 342. Love is to souls what weight is to bodies. II, 212, 213. Love is the hand of the soul. V, 694. The foot of the soul. IV, 124. Through love the soul is moved as toward the place toward which it tends. IV, 124. Love is a course. IV, 441. Love cannot remain idle. IV, 260, 1618. In what is loved, either one does not labor, or one loves the labor as well. VI, 448. Whether love can be free from pain. IV, 398. The wound of love. V, 1366.

Love makes all savage and monstrous things altogether easy and almost nothing. V, 444. Through love every hard thing is softened. V, 444. The soul is drawn by love. III, 1608. Nothing is so ironlike and hard that it cannot be conquered by the fire of love. I, 1328. There is no greater invitation to love than to anticipate another by loving. VI, 314. Is love itself to be loved? VI, 23. Love itself, by which what ought to be loved is loved well, is to be loved in an orderly way. VII, 467. Love itself is loved. VII, 341. Reciprocity of love is sought in the beloved. V, 211. We habitually direct our mind most intensely toward the things we love. I, 1184. Whenever someone seems to possess what he loves, he is called happy; but he is truly happy not if he possesses what he loves, but if he loves what ought to be loved. IV, 202. Love—but see what you love. IV, 260. Nothing else should be a matter of concern regarding how one lives except choosing what ought to be loved. V, 585. Love of the soul. See Soul. Love and fear lead to every right deed and every sin. IV, 1026. Each person lives from his own love, either well or badly. VIII, 228. In this life there is no virtue except loving what ought to be loved. II, 671, 673. When love is perverse, it is called desire or lust; when it is right, love or charity. IV, 124. Love and charity do not differ. VII, 410.

Love either rises or descends. IV, 1629. Love is commanded only toward God and one’s neighbor. III, 27. The love of God and neighbor is the end and fullness of Scripture. III, 34. How true love is to be ordered. V, 1654.

God commands that he be loved by man; and unless man does so, he threatens immense miseries. I, 663. We are commanded to strive toward God with the greatest love. I, 1316. Because God knows that it benefits us to love him, he makes himself lovable by praising himself. IV, 1869. God shoots the heart of the lover in order to help the lover; he shoots it in order to make a lover. IV, 1599. The virtue that leads to the blessed life is nothing other than the highest love of God. I, 1322. Everything tells us to love God, and everything continues telling everyone so that they may be without excuse. I, 782. The beauty of the world arouses love of God. IV, 1887, 1892.

Love of God with the whole heart is the worship of God, true religion, right piety, and due service. VII, 281. Piety is the worship of God, and he is not worshiped except by loving him. II, 556. The highest and true wisdom is contained in that first commandment, “You shall love,” and so forth. II, 556. Love is the sweetest incense offered to God. VII, 279. Love is the dove’s groaning. III, 1425. The new wine of lovers is the devout tears of the afflicted. IV, 1064. Our love toward God is not without hope, nor hope without love, nor are both without faith. VI, 232. Whoever loves rightly also believes and hopes rightly; whoever does not love believes and hopes in vain. VI, 286. The soul is better when it forgets itself for the sake of the love of God. I, 1308. God is to be loved chiefly and alone, because nothing is better than he. II, 672. The way to love God is to love without measure, from a letter of Severus. II, 419. We cannot measure how much love we lack in order to know how much would be enough for us. I, 848. He who made you demands your whole self. V, 212.

The gratuitous love of God does not abolish hope of reward. V, 1483. Just as the devout love Christ gratuitously, so the impious hate him gratuitously. IV, 1432. God is to be worshiped with chaste love. IV, 626, 658, 928, 1404. He loves God less who loves something together with God that he does not love for God’s sake. I, 796. What is not loved for its own sake is not loved. I, 881. Chaste fear comes from love. IV, 1682. Where fear is chaste, love does not perish through fear. IV, 1592. Love is the cause of why good is rightly done. X, 586, 788. Everything that can love loves God, whether knowingly or unknowingly. I, 869. We cannot love God fully because we do not see him. IV, 1892. If we wish to know him, let us first love him with complete charity. I, 1331.

Love makes God present. II, 672. The love of God causes death not merely to be despised but even to be desired. Whoever loves God alone and his neighbor for God’s sake is unconquered. III, 160. There is the place of undisturbed rest where love is not abandoned, if it itself does not abandon us. I, 701. Though standing on earth, you are in heaven if you love God. IV, 1085. By loving, the heart is lifted to God. IV, 1085. The more you love, the higher you ascend. IV, 1063. By loving God you ascend; by loving the world you fall. IV, 1667. Someone who would choose always to remain amid an abundance of worldly goods and not see the face of God has not yet begun to be a lover of God. IV, 1089. Someone must love God little if he considers himself made good not by God but by himself. II, 576. How shameful not to wish to labor out of love of God. VI, 448. Through love one asks, through love one seeks, through love one knocks, through love one receives revelation, and finally through love one remains in what has been revealed. I, 1325.

No one gives the love of God except God himself, and he gives it only through Christ. VII, 730. God would not be loved except through the Holy Spirit. I, 745, 848. Whoever is full of love is full of nothing except God. VIII, 968. Who praises truly except one who loves sincerely? II, 557. You freely praise what you love by praising it. IV, 1745. Love for God becomes apparent when God’s gains are loved. V, 1358. We must act so that others may love God together with us. IV, 929. The love of God is the beginning of the heavenly city; love of self is the beginning of the earthly city. VII, 436.

The love of God for human beings is commended. VI, 314. God always loves, whether he caresses or threatens. VIII, 964. The pledges of Christ’s love for the bride are the Holy Spirit and blood. IV, 1170. We are certain only of Christ’s love for us. IV, 1292. By what means it may be proved whether Christ is loved. IV, 1681.

One who loves God has no need to fear either temporal punishments, imperial laws, or hell. II, 803. Christian love is owed to God; human fear is owed to kings. IX, 45. If we refer all the movements of human action to love of God and neighbor, we shall be cleansed. I, 1186. Through the power of love for God, a person orders inferior things and is not defiled by them. I, 1187.

Love of neighbor. A good and honorable life is formed from nothing other than loving God and one’s neighbor. II, 525, 557. The soul maintains order by loving with its whole self what is above it—that is, God—and loving companion souls as itself. I, 1187. You do not love your neighbor as yourself if you do not lead him toward the good toward which you yourself are striving. I, 1332. If souls please you, let them be loved in God and drawn to him. I, 702. Learn to love the Creator in the creature and the Maker in what he has made, lest what was made by him hold you fast and you lose him by whom you yourself were made. IV, 439.

A human being is to be loved according to God, because you must love yourself in this way as well. IV, 1816. Whoever leads his neighbor, insofar as he can, to a similar love of God loves him as himself. II, 499. The rule of love of neighbor is this: whatever good each person wishes to happen to himself, he should wish for the other; and whatever evil he does not wish to happen to himself, he should not wish for the other. III, 161. Whoever loves his neighbor does everything possible so that the neighbor may be safe in body and safe in soul; and, as regards the soul, so that he may first fear and then love God. I, 1334. Since a person cannot benefit everyone whom he loves equally, he is unjust unless he prefers to benefit those closest to him. III, 163. A human being is not to be loved in the same way as relatives and fellow citizens are loved, on account of temporal ties, which ought to be hated. III, 161. To love a human being in order to obtain from him some temporal pleasure or advantage is a foul and detestable vice. III, 161. It is easy to hate the wicked because they are wicked; it is rare to love them because they are human beings. II, 654. The commandment concerning love of God and neighbor is not to be compared with the writings of philosophers or the laws of cities. II, 524. Whoever does not love the one who made man does not know how to love man rightly. II, 1072. One must fear above all that someone may believe he will come to the God whom he loves while despising his neighbor. I, 1332. There is no surer step toward the love of God than one human being’s charity toward another. I, 1187, 1331. In love of neighbor there are, as it were, the cradles of the love of God. I, 1187.

One kind of human love is right, another perverse. V, 1690. The degrees of licit love. V, 1690. Love of parents. V, 1512. Love of one’s wife. V, 501, 1513. Love of children. V, 566, 1513. It is inhuman not to love in a human being what is human, but to love what is one’s son. I, 161. Let us love the Lord; let us love his Church—him as a father, her as a mother. IV, 1140.

Love of enemies. Why the Lord commanded that enemies be loved, while parents and children were to be hated. I, 615. Whoever hates an enemy ravages himself by that hatred more severely than he ravages the enemy or is ravaged by the enemy. I, 674.

Two loves: the social and the private. III, 437. All loves are first directed by human beings toward themselves, and then toward something else. V, 1654. Whoever loves himself wishes to be nothing other than blessed. VII, 279. Only the person who loves God knows how to love himself. I, 1331. He loves himself spiritually who, with all that lives in him, loves God. I, 132. Unless he loves God, no one loves himself. II, 499, 768. To wish to be feared and loved by human beings not for God’s sake is a wretched life and shameful boasting. I, 803. Only two commandments of charity were given because a human being loves both God and himself with the same love. II, 672. Love of self does not long remain within itself but quickly vanishes into empty things. V, 585. Those who please themselves greatly displease God. I, 806. If the soul pleases itself, it becomes smaller in proportion as it desires to be greater. I, 1308. Perverse love of self is more truly contempt of self. V, 1457. Love of self is the cause of turning away from God toward the lowest things. VIII, 1006, 1007. Love of self is the first destruction of the human being. V, 585. Private love and pride are the sources of evils. III, 436. Love of self disturbs the soul. VII, 396.

The love of God and love of the world are opposed. V, 482, 633, 694, 1512. God alone is to be loved; this whole world, that is, all sensible things, is to be despised, though these things are to be used for the necessities of life. I, 1327. If a creature is loved by someone who neglects God, it becomes a punishment for its lover. I, 138. The love of God and love of neighbor are called charity; love of the world, love of this age, is called desire. IV, 260. Vices that exist in love. VII, 632. Love of vain and harmful things is the punishment of the first sin. VII, 784. Disordered love of things, not the things themselves, is the fault. VII, 356. Sin itself is not loved; rather, the disordered love of the creature is sin. V, 143. Love of the world does not coexist with love of God. V, 694. Love of God diminishes love of the creature, and conversely. III, 1647, 1691. Love of temporal things is conquered only by some sweetness of eternal things. I, 1190. Love of earthly things is birdlime on spiritual wings. V, 646, 1415. You love the world—it will swallow you; it knows how to devour its lovers, not to carry them. V, 482. Through love of things perceived externally, the inner parts decay. III, 845. Through love, human beings are subjected to creatures, and those who are subjected cannot judge. I, 783. God commands us to tolerate present things, not to love them. IV, 251. Through love of even permitted things, hay, straw, and so forth are built up. IV, 1045. In loving harmful things people are miserable; in possessing them, more miserable. IV, 202. God is merciful when, because we love wrongly, he denies us what we love; when angry, he gives the lover what he wrongly loves. IV, 202. When we love what God wills us to love, he will undoubtedly give it to us. IV, 202. Love of the world is laborious. I, 1186. True and divine philosophy warns us to restrain the most destructive love of bodily things. II, 63. What remedies God has set against love of vain and harmful things. VII, 785. Augustine strives to separate his love from what, against his will, can be absent from him. II, 63.

Useful love and harmful love. V, 1654. Illicit love. V, 1530. Tartarean love. IV, 1816. Shameful, vice-favoring lust imagined that God is love. VIII, 374. The force of impure love. V, 584, 883. What great troubles shameful love entails. IV, 1331. Unclean love casts one down to the depths; holy love lifts one to the heights. IV, 1618. Whoever loves carnally must love with destructive jealousy; but the love of wisdom is without jealousy. IV, 310. When the soul dies to bodily love, it lives sweetly. II, 72.

By loving the good, we become better. IV, 1869. People are such as their loves are. V, 584. No habits make people good or bad except good or bad loves. II, 672; V, 1417. Two contrary loves can exist in a human being. VII, 341.

A needy and unworthy love loves in such a way that it is subjected to the things it loves. III, 251. Love is more pleasing when it does not flow from need. VI, 315.

Chaste love of justice, and how it is proved. V, 965. See Fear. Love of justice, rather than fear of punishment, produces innocence. IV, 1190. The Law is fulfilled through love, not fear. V, 199, 1171. The new and old human beings, and the two Testaments, differ through love and fear. V, 81, 207. Love inflames; fear humbles. IV, 1027. From the varying affection of love comes virtue in four forms. I, 1322, 1330. See Love, Testament, Law, Charity, Human Being, Hatred.

The Amorites, interpreted as “those who make bitter.” IV, 1750.

What the prophet Amos foretold and at what time. VII, 583, 585. How sound was the eloquence of the prophet Amos. III, 96.

Ampelius, bishop. II, 759, 780.

The amphitheater. V, 334, 1026. The amphitheater of gladiatorial games. I, 726. The bloody contests of the amphitheater. VI, 639.

The fable of Amphion. VII, 570.

What magnitude is. VI, 22.

The valley of Amsanctus. X, 1069.

Amulius, brother of Numitor. VII, 577, 578. After expelling his brother, he ruled at Alba. VII, 91. Amulius was the fourteenth king in Latium after Aeneas. VII, 577.

Amurca, oil. V, 121, 137.

Amyntas, the eighteenth king of the Assyrians. VII, 569.

Ἀναβαδμοί (“Steps” or “Songs of Ascents”): what they are. IV, 415, 1596.

The institution of the anchorites is praised. I, 1338.

What analogy is. V, 364; VIII, 69.

Peter provided for the spiritual salvation of Ananias and his wife by means of bodily death. IX, 84. This correction was not excessively severe. V, 799. It must be believed that after this life God spared Ananias and Sapphira. V, 799.

Ἀνάστασις means “raising up,” ἐξανάστασις “resurrection.” III, 487.

Anastasius, Roman pontiff. IX, 300. Rufinus presented a little book to Pope Anastasius. II, 719.

Anastasius, Maximianist bishop. IV, 376.

Where the word “anathema” comes from and what it signifies. III, 510.

Augustine was prepared to anathematize the dead Caecilianus if the crimes charged against him were proved. II, 794.

The medical art contains anatomy. X, 528.

Anatomists, physicians. VII, 791.

The Gentiles killed the Anaunian clerics—Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander. II, 536.

Anaxagoras, a pupil of Anaximenes. X, 776. What he thought concerning the causes of things. VII, 226. He said that the sun was a burning stone, not a god. VII, 601. He says that Mind is God. II, 442, 443.

Anaximander, a pupil and successor of Thales. VII, 226. The period in which he flourished. VII, 582. What he thought concerning the principles of things. VII, 226. He admitted innumerable worlds. VII, 226.

Anaximenes, pupil and successor of Anaximander. VII, 226. The period in which he flourished. VII, 582. He believed that air was God. I, 782; II, 443. He attributed the causes of things to infinite air. VII, 226. Anaximenes believed that the gods arose from air. VII, 226. Cicero argues against the views of Anaximenes and Anaxagoras concerning God. II, 443, 444.

Anchises, father of Aeneas. VII, 81.

We are servants and slaves. IV, 1633.

A memorial to Stephen was erected at Ancona before the discovery of his body. V, 1445.

The Ancones and Auconisci. III, 764.

Ancus Marcius, king among the Romans. VII, 92, 582. The fifth king. VII, 591.

The custom of the Andabatae. X, 1057.

Andrew. Apocryphal writings under the names of Andrew and John. VIII, 626.

Andrew from the island of Capraria, a monk. II, 189.

Androgynes, or hermaphrodites. III, 294; VII, 486.

Andromache, wife of Hector, was carried off to Greece by Pyrrhus and married to him. VII, 88.

Andromeda, wife of Perseus, was received into heaven after her death. VII, 572. A star called by the name of Andromeda. VII, 572.

Anebon the Egyptian, to whom Porphyry wrote in order to be instructed about the diversity of demons. VII, 288.

Christ, the angle joining two walls. IV, 712, 1222.

One must walk along the narrow way so that the desires of the flesh may be stripped away. IV, 682. You have been confined in the earth; migrate to heaven. IV, 1736.

The name “angels” understood in a broader sense. I, 602. Angels, in Latin *nuntii* (“messengers”). III, 1596; V, 64, 230, 691; VII, 468. “Angel,” in Latin *nuntius* (“messenger”), is the name of an office, not of a nature. IV, 1348, 1757; V, 64. An angel is by nature a spirit; when sent, he becomes an angel. IV, 1348. Angels, rational spirits presiding over heavenly bodies. VI, 708.

The creation of the angels. III, 222; understood as having taken place through the light created on the first day. III, 228. The angels are not coeternal with God, yet they have not undergone the vicissitudes of time. I, 831. Whether the angels could always have existed. VII, 363. According to the Manichaeans, the angels were generated from the substance of God. VIII, 308, and were generated by the Father after Christ. VIII, 581. The Manichaean error concerning angels generated by the Father after Christ is refuted. VIII, 382.

When the angels were created. VII, 324, 347. Whether the creation of the angels preceded that of the world. VII, 345. Scripture did not express the creation of the angels explicitly. VII, 324, though Scripture did not thereby omit it. VII, 324, 347. The angelic creature was created first of all. III, 326, and why. III, 326. The angelic nature is the day first established. III, 334. How the angels were created, or how they are not coeternal with God, if they are understood to have always existed. VII, 364. Under what conditions it is permissible to discuss the creation of the angels. VII, 345.

The origin, formation, and blessedness of the angels are from the triune God. VII, 338. God established nothing better than the angels. VII, 751. The beauty of the angels. V, 136. In the angels, wisdom was created first of all. III, 313. The blessed angels are created wisdom. I, 831. God created the angels, at once forming their nature and bestowing grace upon them. VII, 357. The angels were not darkness first, for any interval of time. VII, 327. One must believe that the holy angels never existed without the love of God. VII, 357. The angels immediately adhered to the creating light. III, 317. From the moment they were created, the angels enjoy, in pious and holy contemplation, the very eternity of the Word. III, 270. Whether all the angels were created with equal blessedness from the beginning. VII, 329.

The angels’ morning and evening knowledge. VII, 343. What knowledge of the angels is called evening and morning. III, 354; day and evening. III, 313. In angelic knowledge there are day, evening, and morning. III, 315, 326; how this is so. III, 316, though this knowledge is not thereby less noble. III, 316. The angels saw the creating light and themselves in that light at the point of creation. III, 317; they also saw themselves in themselves. III, 317. In the very Word [Col. 0067] of God the angels first knew the eternal reasons of creatures, and afterward knew them in the creatures themselves. III, 313. Angelic knowledge does not remain in the creature, but refers the creature back to the praise of God. III, 313. At the sixth repetition of the angels’ morning and evening knowledge, the whole creation was completed. III, 313. Whether day, evening, and morning were simultaneously present in angelic knowledge at the beginning of creation and are so now. III, 316. The angels know in God not only what is hidden, but here also what becomes apparent when it is brought about. III, 335. How the angels know the Trinity. VII, 343. Through their most harmonious contemplation of the Word of God, the angels are one day, which the Lord made. III, 313. The angels know the creature better in the Word than in the creature itself. VII, 343. The order in which the angels came to know the works of God. III, 317, 320. In God the angels see unchangeable truth, and according to it direct their wills. III, 390. The angels have known the mystery of the kingdom of heaven from the ages. III, 354. The angels know our thoughts even if we do not wish them to; but we cannot know theirs unless they reveal them. III, 473. How they know sensible things. III, 269. From where the angels know temporal and changeable things more certainly. VII, 263. The angels are never deceived in their knowledge of future things. VII, 274, 275. What appears infinite to man is numbered by the angels. IV, 1906. The angels regard knowledge of temporal and changeable things as insignificant. VII, 263. In an ineffable manner they consult eternal truth concerning their actions as an unchangeable law. IV, 1009. How they consult the truth of God. VI, 146. God speaks to angels, whether good or evil, in many ways. V, 102; how he speaks to them. III, 391.

The whole nature of the angels is good. VII, 349. The angelic nature, by the very vice through which it is wretched, demonstrates that it was established as excellent. VII, 753. The angels are mutable by nature. I, 831; III, 133. The evil angels were not created evil by God, but became evil by sinning. VIII, 561; they departed from the highest good. X, 819. The angels were created with free will. VII, 751. The perseverance of the good angels and the fall of the evil, through free will. X, 932, 935. Why God did not take free will away from the evil angels, although he foresaw that they would use it badly. VII, 751.

Two kinds of angels according to Porphyry. VII, 303. Scripture does not establish that a twofold kind of angels must be admitted. III, 439. God divided the good angels from the transgressors either by foreknowledge or by action. VII, 346. The diversity of angels arises not from nature but from wills and desires. VII, 349, 353. When the separation of the good and evil angels took place. VII, 333. Two societies of angels, one good and the other perverse, signified by the names of light and darkness. VII, 346. Some think that the separation of the good and evil angels is signified by the name of the divided waters. VII, 347, 348.

To what extent the transgressing angels participated in wisdom before their sin cannot be determined. VII, 327. The transgressing angels did not attain the excellence of wise and blessed life. VII, 327. Whether the transgressing angels possessed some blessedness before their sin, though not foreknowledge. VII, 329. The transgressing angels either received less grace or were less assisted than those who stood firm. VII, 357. How the angels who stood firm were more greatly assisted than those who fell. VII, 357. How the angels are assisted from without. III, 391. God ordered the life of angels and human beings so that in it he might first show what their free will could do, and afterward what the benefit of his grace and the judgment of his justice could do. X, 932. The deserting angels are simultaneously immortal and dead. VII, 402. The angels could die because they could sin. VIII, 767.

The cause of the angelic fall was pride. III, 435, 437, 441; IV, 1608, 1623; VII, 751. The angels ought to have sinned all the less than we, inasmuch as they were better than we. III, 1925. The fall of the angels did God no harm. VI, 333. The guilt of the angels was judged all the more damnable inasmuch as their nature was more exalted. III, 1925. Why the angel fell irreparably. X, 1553. Why God contributed no grace toward restoring them. III, 1925, 2122. A portion of restored humanity will succeed to their place. VI, 246.

The angels fell from the spiritual paradise. VII, 1419. The sinning angels were thrust into the darkness of this air. III, 730. The air is like a prison to them. VII, 346. The deserting and corrupting angels are the possessors of, and sharers in, sinful humanity. VI, 245. The rejected angels are called exterminators and angels of wrath. III, 156; the last servants. III, 156; they are called flesh. VII, 470; they are to be cast into the second death after the final judgment. VII, 402; they will not be consumed in the common conflagration of the world. IV, 1313; they will not lack the sensation of pain. VII, 402.

Whether the angels have bodies. II, 355; VII, 467, 468. The bodies of the angels. I, 626; IV, 1094; V, 1262. In what sense the flesh of angels can be spoken of. V, 1622. The spiritual body of the angels. VIII, 870. What sort of bodies they were in when they appeared, and how they impress visions upon minds, is difficult to explain. VI, 260; VII, 870. The angels appear through a true body assumed by them. V, 104. They appeared in bodies that could be seen and [Col. 0068] touched. VII, 468. Since the angels are spirits, whether they can physically have intercourse with women. VII, 468. The angels truly ate with Abraham. V, 1617. The angels who appeared took food, not because they needed it, but because they wished and were able to do so. VII, 396. An angel eats not from necessity but from power, and so as to correspond with human beings. V, 1618. Whether, and how, Abraham and Sarah recognized God in the angels. III, 557, 558. The angel appearing in God’s place was called Lord. V, 65. The angel bearing the person of God appeared to Jacob. V, 57. What is signified by the angel wrestling with Jacob and unwilling to be held. V, 58. The angel who appeared to Manoah signified Christ. III, 824. Angels are living creatures. VII, 267. The voice of the Father on the mountain and the appearance of a dove could have been produced through the ministry of angels. II, 747. God sometimes speaks through an angel. IV, 1395.

The blessedness of the angels comes from God alone. VII, 220, 275, 349, 353. The angels owe God their existence, their life, their just life, and their blessed life. IV, 895. God gave the angels a command to praise him. IV, 1941. An angel is light, not in himself but in God. VII, 325. The angels are blessed from the same source as we are, even according to the Platonists. VII, 279. The blessed angels have never been exiles, but were so formed that, without any failure of contemplation and without any interval of change, they might enjoy the eternity and immutability of God. I, 831. The angels are more blessed because they have never been exiles. VII, 323. The angels in their lofty dwellings are not coeternal with God, but are secure in their everlasting blessedness. VII, 328, 329, 346, 357. The angels are established by God’s eternity, assured by his truth, and sanctified by his gift. VII, 284. The blessed angels are stable not by nature but by will, because they love God more than themselves. I, 133. The angels were made secure in a stability from which they would never fall. VI, 246. The inability to sin was made the reward of merit for the holy angels. X, 936. The angels would not be blessed if they were uncertain of their blessedness. III, 436, 437. We fear none of them, lest by sinning he become a devil. VI, 359; X, 1117.

It belongs to the nature of angels to adhere to God. VII, 350. The blessed angels serve God freely; and this benefits not God but themselves. I, 133. The angels freely, because joyfully, serve the eternal command of God. VIII, 418. The angels never recoil from the contemplation of God. III, 390. The angels become participants in the eternity, truth, and will of God. III, 390. The holy angels never abandon God. VIII, 614. When an angel turns away from God, he becomes unclean. VII, 325.

The bread of the angels. I, 1286. God himself is, as it were, the common life and sustenance of the angels. VII, 751. They are nourished by the Word of life as by their bread. III, 1978. The Word of God feeds the angels incorruptibly, making them incorruptible. IV, 995. The food and satiety of the angels. VI, 707. In the Word of God the angels rest in holy silence. VI, 331. The angels have their contemplation and their action. VIII, 418. As the angels see the face of the Father, so we too shall see God as he is. II, 606. Nothing unlawful pleases the angelic nature at all. III, 433.

The perfect justice of the angels. III, 1634; X, 601. An angel ought to live not according to an angel but according to God. VII, 407. In comparison with the justice of God, the angels are not just; how this is so. VIII, 677. The Priscillianists wrongly asserted that even the holy angels still had to be purged from their sins. VIII, 674. Christ did not die for the angels. VI, 261. The angels are works of Christ. III, 1823. Charity has been poured out in the angels through the Holy Spirit. VII, 357.

The number of angels is unknown to us. VII, 437.

The blessed angels are superior to rational souls in office, not in nature. I, 1287. The angels are indeed greater than a human being, but than a corrupt one. VIII, 803. The whole human race is compared with the multitude of angels as a single sheep. VIII, 727.

What the differences among the angels are, and whether the stars belong to their number, is uncertain. VI, 259. Augustine believes that the blessed spirits differ among themselves, but confesses that he does not know in what they differ. VIII, 678. To place human beings above the angels because Christ died for them: what is this other than wishing to glory in impiety? III, 1924.

Plato wished the angels to create bodies only, not souls. VII, 575. What follows from this. VII, 575. The angels cannot create. III, 404. Neither good nor evil angels are creators. VIII, 876, 878. They are not creators even of any nature, however small. VII, 373, 374. Whether they provided service to the Creator as he made the other things. VII, 374. Some angels can perform a certain service so that something may be created. III, 404. Angels, both good and evil, can use the corporeal matter of visible elements. IV, 1001.

Only God commands the blessed angels, whereas the whole world is subject to them. I, 1287. What creatures are subject to the blessed angels. III, 390. The angels appointed over heaven are set above the aerial powers. IV, 1385. By that law they bring about whatever occurs here. IV, 1385. God placed foreign nations under the angels, making the people of Israel his portion. IV, 1121. Why affections are attributed to the angels when they perform their offices. VII, 261. [Col. 0069] The office of the angels is to restore the soul before the presence of the Lord. VIII, 727. How an angel comes to God. VII, 484. Good angels cannot be intermediaries between wretched mortals and blessed immortals; evil angels can. VII, 268.

Neither good nor evil angels can be mediators for human beings in attaining blessedness. VII, 276. The favor of the good angels is necessary for us to attain blessedness. VII, 304. The angels have compassion on us and assist us at the Lord’s command. IV, 751. The angels offer our prayers to God. IV, 1009. How an angel is said to give understanding to a human being. IV, 1553. The angels rejoice over the salvation of human beings. IV, 1379. When the angels hear, God hears in them. VII, 291. Christians say that the holy angels are sent to human beings; the Platonists do not approve this. VII, 276. The angels are our helpers. VI, 69, 258. How great are the services of mercy they perform for us. III, 31. They perform them without pain or groaning. VI, 69. The angels could have been sent to serve Christ, not to assist him. IV, 666. When and how they carried Christ in their hands. IV, 1166. In the Church the angels ascend and descend upon the Son of Man; how this occurs. IV, 507.

How the redemption of humanity concerns the angels. VI, 261. Philosophers wish angels to be friends of the wise person. VII, 627. The friendship of the angels cannot be manifest to us. VII, 636. The friendship of angels is to be sought through likeness of good will. VII, 252. Angels cannot be friends with demons. VII, 252. We honor the blessed angels with charity, not with servitude. III, 170. Christians venerate and love the angels, but do not sacrifice to them. VII, 654. Even natural perception teaches that one must not sacrifice to those angels who command sacrifices to themselves. VII, 294, 295. The angels do not want us to sacrifice to them. VII, 284. The angels do not want divine honors and have sometimes rejected them most openly. VII, 298. The angels demand neither worship nor sacrifice. VII, 303, 304. For this reason the angel in the Apocalypse forbids a human being to worship him: he had appeared in such a form that he could have been worshiped as God. III, 564. The angels do not want to be worshiped in place of God. IV, 1090, 1246, 1757. The angels are soldiers; they do not know how to seek glory except that of the Emperor. But if they seek their own, they are condemned as tyrants. IV, 1357. The holy angels perhaps are nowhere called gods in Scripture for this reason: lest human beings offer them the worship of *latria*. IV, 1757, 1757. Porphyry advises that the angels be imitated rather than invoked. VII, 304. One should believe those angels who do not want service for themselves but only service to the one God concerning the blessed life. VII, 293. Angels and human beings are God’s living sacrifice and his living temple. VII, 303, 312, 357.

Good and evil angels have certain works in common. III, 445. God does many things through angels. VII, 220. How they operate in this world we do not know. III, 405.

How great the power of the angels is. IV, 1232. The good angels are more powerful than the evil. III, 444; VII, 717. Every human being desires the power of angels, but not their justice. IV, 1232. God makes good use of the evil angels. IV, 1002. Whether certain evil angels have been appointed over the evils that human beings suffer. IV, 1396. God uses evil angels not only to punish the wicked but also to test and reveal the good. IV, 1001. It is most fittingly believed that moral evils are inflicted by evil angels upon those who are subjected to them by divine equity. IV, 1001, 1003. Bodily pains are for the most part inflicted by angels of Satan. IV, 1709. Evil angels take pleasure in human punishment not because of justice but because of malice. IV, 105.

The rejected angels are called the lowest ministries. I, 156; IV, 105; and angels of wrath. IV, 105.

The angels are citizens of Jerusalem. IV, 1901. Holy angels and human beings are one city of God. VII, 284, 323, 357. We are fellow citizens of the angels. VII, 797. To what extent we can be joined to the angels even while living on earth under the condition of the flesh. VII, 252. The angels are to be regarded as our neighbors. III, 31. The human mind can be divinely snatched from this life into angelic life before it is released from the flesh through the common death. II, 610. Paul was snatched up into angelic life. II, 610.

The heavenly dwelling of the angels. IV, 1093. The blessed angels are the house of God. I, 830. The temple of God. IV, 1776; V, 1190. The heavenly court of the Emperor, the heavenly army. I, 748. The blessed angels are the most excellent and holy ministries of God. I, 170. The angelic ministries are called the chariot of God. VII, 692. The members of Christ have been brought, through the abundance of divine grace, to equality with the angels. III, 1924, 1925. To imitate the angels is a benefit of grace. X, 1164. We do not despair of becoming equal in the future to the angels whom the Lord of the angels served. III, 574; IV, 1776. The holy angels can be understood under the name “gods.” VII, 275. And they are so called in Scripture. VII, 275. The angels of God are also called human beings. VII, 468. In Scripture they are called men. VIII, 808, 810. They are customarily called by the name “men.” III, 802. But they are not customarily signified by the name “souls.” I, 601, 612.

Human beings who announce something are customarily called angels. VIII, 527. All who announce heavenly salvation to human beings are angels. V, 1544. Israel can be called angels. IV, 1901. They are called sheep and oxen. IV, 114. The angels are the organs of heaven. III, 879. The name “angels” is given to the entire heavenly city. III, 334. [Col. 0070] The blessed angels are called the heaven of heaven. I, 380.

Although we do not possess the power to see an angel, we do possess the grace of earning the power to see one. II, 604. Perhaps God is now seen by certain angels in the manner in which he is seen as he is. II, 603.

What the ascending and descending angels on Jacob’s ladder signify. IV, 1577. The angel who stirred the water of the pool. V, 600. Tichonius understands the seven angels of the Churches mentioned in the Apocalypse as the Churches themselves. III, 81.

The book of the angels. I, 852.

An angel assigned to each person. VII, 680.

An angel appointed over each visible thing. VI, 90. The angels preside over the judgment and administration of these corporeal things. III, 484.

The Angelic heretics. VIII, 32.

Anna, a widow of great merit. V, 1657.

Distress. Through distresses one passes to the place of spaciousness. V, 1366.

Anianus, pseudo-deacon of Celeda. II, 928. He supplies frivolous words for another’s—namely, Pelagius’—blasphemies. II, 928, note b. Jerome received his books from the presbyter Eusebius. II, 928. Anianus appears to designate Augustine or Jerome under the name of Traducianus. II, 928. He translated the homilies of John Chrysostom into Latin. II, 928.

The Anician family. II, 645; VIII, 574.

The soul. The question concerning the soul is exceedingly difficult. III, 355, 356; X, 520. Nor is it easily resolved from the Scriptures. III, 415. Whether, by the very fact that our nature differs from that of cattle, it knows how to investigate and discuss the origin of souls. X, 532. Whether it can and should be considered a fault that we are ignorant of many things concerning the nature of the spirit and of our soul. X, 530. Whether it is shameful for the soul to be ignorant of these things. X, 528. And a great detriment to the Church’s teaching. X, 498. It perhaps does not concern us to know in this life the origin of souls. X, 520. The mother of the Maccabees was uncertain about the origin of the soul. X, 814. Vincentius Victor’s opinion concerning the origin of souls is full of difficulties. X, 508. What must be avoided in the question of the soul’s origin. X, 493, 484. Four things to be avoided in the question of the origin of souls. X, 493, 494. Eleven things that must be avoided in the question of the soul. X, 546.

There are two opinions concerning the soul. III, 412. The origin of the soul can be understood in three ways. III, 410. Four opinions concerning its origin. I, 1296. Augustine was hesitant concerning the origin of the soul. X, 150, 489, 490, 501, 506, 523, 525, 547, 1400. Augustine defined nothing concerning its origin. II, 588, 717, 857. And, like Marcellinus, he consults Jerome. II, 864. Augustine found nothing certain in the canonical Scriptures concerning the origin of the soul. II, 862. Various testimonies of Scripture are weighed concerning the origin of souls. III, 412, 413, 414, 419. Four opinions concerning the origin of the soul. II, 776. Whichever of the opinions concerning the origin of the soul may be true, Augustine wished God undoubtedly to be praised in the book *On Free Will*. II, 587. Whoever wishes to defend one of Augustine’s four opinions concerning the origin of souls, rejecting the other three, should either produce from Scripture something that cannot be understood otherwise, or provide a reason so certain that no contradiction remains. II, 590. Verse 7 of chapter 12 of Ecclesiastes can be applied to support any one of Augustine’s four opinions concerning the origin of souls. II, 587, 589. In questions concerning the origin of souls, one must beware of denying original sin. II, 728, 729, 882, 732, 733. Whatever is argued in an inquiry or assertion concerning the origin of any soul, if it is contrary to original sin, cannot be true. X, 608. The soul, from wherever it comes, is from God. III, 366, 411, 412, 418.

The soul is not from itself. VI, 11. The soul has God as its author. VI, 11. Every soul can exist only from God. VIII, 93. The soul is to be attributed to God even more than sensible light is. VIII, 95, 99. All souls were created and established through Christ. VIII, 93.

The Manichaeans did not believe that the soul had been made from nothing; rather, they said that it was of the same nature as God. VIII, 34, 35. The Manichaean error concerning the soul. X, 1325. According to the Manichaeans, the soul is not God’s temple but his part or member. VIII, 380, 381. The Manichaeans say that the soul itself is the substance of God. III, 361. And that it is what God is. VI, 296. The Stoics, Manichaeus, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian held that the soul comes from God’s own substance. I, 1237, 1242. Priscillian’s error concerning the soul. VIII, 666, 667, 668, 671, 672. The Priscillianists did not believe that the soul had been made from nothing. VIII, 668, 669, 670. Rather, they said that it was of the same nature as God. VIII, 44. And that it was a part of God. VI, 523. So also did the Gnostics. VIII, 27. Victor’s error was to say that the soul was made by God, not from nothing but from himself. X, 477, 512. This is refuted. X, 477, 512.

The soul is from God, not of God. VIII, 117, 549, 669. The soul is not God. VIII, 116. It is not the substance of God. III, 366, 372; IV, 1822. The soul is not God’s nature, but by participating in it can be illuminated. II, 541. The soul is not from the very substance of God. III, 356, 358, 412. Since the soul is mutable, it cannot have been made from God, who is immutable. X, 477. Against the Manichaeans, the soul is not a part of God. II, 721; VIII, [Col. 0071] 549, 614. It is not a part of God but a great good. V, 853. To say that the soul is a portion of God is both blasphemy and heresy. X, 496, 498.

The soul is God’s breath, but not of his substance. VII, 373, 402. It is demonstrated that the soul is not a part of God’s breath. X, 512, 513. Elisha’s breathing into the boy’s face is adduced in vain to prove that the soul is a part of God’s breath. X, 514, 136. The soul and God are not of one and the same nature. X, 497. Philosophers distinguish the nature of the soul from the nature of God. III, 361. The Platonists believed the soul to be coeternal with God; on what basis. VII, 311. The Priscillianists asserted that the soul, angels, and demons were of one substance but were distinguished according to their merits. VIII, 668. They are refuted. VIII, 674, 676. The soul is not from the angels. III, 411. The soul’s causal principle was not inserted into the angelic nature. III, 368. Nor into corporeal creation. III, 368. Some philosophers thought that a rational soul arises from an irrational one. III, 360. Some supposed that a woman’s soul was made from a man’s soul. III, 407. They are refuted. III, 408. The soul is not from the earth. IV, 1518. Adam’s soul was not from any creature. III, 414.

The Western Church was accustomed to hold the propagation of souls. II, 864. Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the greater part of Westerners held that souls arise by transmission. II, 719. Concerning the transmission of souls: the opinion of Tertullian and Manichaeus. X, 1218. Catholics were accused by the Pelagians concerning this error. X, 1218. How souls can be transmitted cannot be explained. II, 862. The Traducianists maintain that the soul’s seed is transmitted through the seed of the one who has intercourse. III, 424. There is neither manifest material of seed nor a hidden principle of seed in the soul. III, 425. Augustine is uncertain whether souls arise by transmission or are newly created. III, 425. The opinion of the Traducianists appears to prevail over that of the new creation of souls. III, 426; their arguments. III, 415, 418, 422. From where some think they can establish the propagation of souls. X, 491. The testimonies of those defending the propagation of souls are resolved. II, 863. What the Traducianists must avoid. III, 426. Whether any testimony of Scripture proves that souls are made by God rather than by propagation. X, 484, 485, 486, 487, 488, 507. Whether the soul arises by transmission: Scripture contains nothing certain. X, 196. Nor can it be demonstrated from Scripture. X, 492.

If the soul does not arise by transmission, it is from nothing, not from God’s nature. X, 487. The soul was not born from God but created. II, 838. The soul was made by God, not from himself but from nothing. X, 477, 497, 499. Whether the soul is from nothing. III, 358, 414; it was made from nothing. VIII, 117. Pythagoras, the Platonists, and Origen thought that souls had fallen from heaven. II, 718. Plato taught that souls lived before they bore these bodies. VIII, 1011. The Platonic opinion concerning the soul’s life before the body is a fiction. X, 402. Concerning the soul’s incarnation: four opinions. II, 587, 723.

Origen held that souls earned different bodies according to the diversity of their sins. VII, 336; this is refuted. VII, 337. The soul is not thrust into a body because of its evil demerits. II, 717, 727, 731, 858. One must not say that souls were thrust into different bodies according to different merits. III, 345, 419. Souls have no merits before they are joined to a body. III, 413, 419, 421, 422. Souls are created in the flesh of sin so that they may acquire merit. III, 418. Whether the soul comes to the body by its own will or by God’s command. III, 368. If the soul was inserted into the body by its own will, it did not have foreknowledge of the future. III, 369.

Whether the soul descends from God or not appears to Augustine a great question. VIII, 116. The origin by which the soul comes to be in the body remained unknown even to Augustine in his old age. I, 587. Some churchmen thought that souls had once been created and were kept in God’s treasury. II, 719; they are pressed by objections. II, 732. Victor’s error was to say that God gives souls throughout infinite time, and thus always gives them just as he himself always exists. X, 515. Scripture does not permit one to believe that the souls of man and woman were created before their bodies. III, 343. Jerome indicated to Marcellinus that his own opinion was that new souls are made for each person born. II, 747; and he set out his opinion in his works against Rufinus. II, 719, 864. Augustine does not at all prohibit defending the infusion of new souls without propagation. X, 493. Difficulties concerning the new creation of souls. III, 410; X, 483. If souls are created individually for each individual, how do they contract original sin? II, 725. To what extent, according to Vincentius, souls are subject to original sin if they do not arise by transmission. X, 502. Victor’s error was to say that the soul deserved to become sinful before sin and to be defiled through the flesh. X, 477, 478, 516; this is refuted. X, 478, 481, 482, 502. Whether the soul had some state and some merit before the flesh. X, 501; Priscillianist error: that it possessed some good state and good merit. X, 515. It cannot be said that the soul sinned elsewhere before the flesh, so that it was condemned into the flesh. X, 482. Nor that, on account of offenses committed elsewhere, souls are thrust into bodies corresponding to their merits and afflicted in them to a greater or lesser degree. X, 126, 127. Victor’s error was to say that the soul lost some merit through the flesh, as though it had possessed good merit before the flesh. X, 515. The origin of the error concerning the soul’s sin before the body. V, 905.

[Col. 0072] The soul is subject to original sin only through the flesh. X, 479. Victor’s error was to say that the soul restores through the flesh its former condition and is reborn through the very means by which it had deserved to be defiled. X, 516. Augustine was uncertain how the soul contracts original sin. X, 507. What he thought should be held concerning the soul according to the faith. X, 525. Although souls do not come from Adam, they nevertheless find in him a just lot of condemnation unless they attain remission of sins by being reborn. II, 864. How are the countless souls of infants, whom God certainly knows will depart from their bodies without baptism, justly given over to condemnation? II, 778. God does not entangle innocent and pure souls in sin by mingling them with sinful flesh. X, 478. The soul was given to the body so that it might do good. VII, 310. The testimonies of those asserting that new souls are created are resolved. II, 863.

The Platonists thought that the passions of the soul arise from the mortal members of the earthly body. VII, 711; they are refuted. VII, 408. Because of original sin the soul is weighed down by wretched ignorance. X, 180. The soul’s vice is not its nature but something contrary to its nature; it is nothing other than sin and the punishment of sin. III, 141. The punishment of sin is no more in the soul’s power than sin itself is. I, 1171. Even a soul reborn cannot be free from every sin and ignorance in this life. VI, 60. The soul is disturbed by worldly movements according to its lower parts. IV, 1887. Beaten by the diversity of its desires, the soul bears wounded blows, divided among many loves. IV, 1887. When the health of the soul will be most secure. I, 1171.

Whether and how the soul was created in the first six days’ works. III, 358, 366, 368, 409. What the soul is can scarcely be expressed. III, 366. Whether the soul is corporeal. X, 534. The Seleucians maintain that the angels, not God, are the creators of souls, from fire and spirit. VIII, 41. Some thought that the soul is air. VII, 326. The soul is not aerial. X, 534; it is neither fire, air, nor any body. VIII, 981, 982; it is not from the elements. III, 358, 362, 363, 366.
