Aristotle said that the soul is a fifth body; Plato said that there is no such body. VII, 773. Lucretius writes that the soul is made of atoms. VIII, 72. Whether some matter preceded the creation of the soul. III, 358; what that matter would have been cannot be said. III, 359. If the soul was made from matter, it was at least made from spiritual matter. III, 370.

Tertullian maintained that the soul is indeed immortal but is a body. VIII, 46, 47; X, 499. Those who, following Tertullian’s opinion, think that souls arise by transmission wish them to be bodies. II, 861. Those who supposed that the soul is created from parents believed it to be a body. III, 425; others thought the same because of the rich man’s parched tongue. III, 376. Tertullian held this because he could not conceive of something incorporeal. III, 427. Tertullian attributes an aerial and luminous color, as well as sensation, to the soul. III, 427. Tertullian did not wish the soul to increase in substance. III, 428. What Tertullian thought concerning the soul’s growth. III, 428. What others thought who believed it to be a body. III, 425. It is absurd to say that the soul receives its form from the body and extends and grows with the body’s growth. X, 541, 543. Victor’s opinion was that the soul withdraws when limbs are cut off. X, 540. The soul has no quantity of mass, a subject treated extensively throughout the book published on this matter. I, 1037, 1038. But it has a quantity of power distinguished into seven degrees, in an order relating to the body, to itself, and to God. I, 1076.

The claim that the soul is a body is another error of Vincentius Victor. X, 477. The soul is not a body. III, 372, 425, 426, 365; nor does it arise from any body. III, 365. The soul is not corporeal. III, 480, 363, 364, 366; VI, 671; X, 538, 539, 544. It is not a corporeal quality. III, 426. It is not a mixture or temperament of the body. I, 1029. The soul is one thing, and the organs of the body another. III, 365. Nevertheless, it can have a likeness to the body and to bodily members. III, 480, 481, 363, 364. It is possible that there is in the soul a certain likeness of the body, while the soul itself is not a body. X, 540. Concerning the soul’s formation. VI, 27. When the messengers of sensation and ministers of movement cease, the soul departs. III, 364. When these fail, its attention is disturbed. III, 364. From this it comes about that the soul is withdrawn from the senses. III, 364. The soul takes pleasure when the bodily senses are gratified, or is saddened when they are offended. III, 1584. Sadness is no small evil of the soul. III, 482.

The soul is not subject to bodies, not even to celestial ones. III, 278. That either the soul may be affected by the body, or the body by the soul, is brought about by fitting principles that live immutably in the wisdom of God. VIII, 877. To what extent the soul experiences joy or sadness. X, 540. The soul truly experiences joy or sadness, even if it perceives not through bodies but only through likenesses of bodies. X, 540, 542. The voice of the soul in a sleeping person: what it is. IV, 1317. The soul grieves with the body, grieves alone within the body, and grieves even outside the body. VII, 711. In the soul there is one faculty by which we perceive true bodies, another by which we behold things resembling bodies but not bodies, and another by which we contemplate neither bodies nor likenesses of bodies. X, 542. It is false that, if the soul is incorporeal, it lacks form. X, 537. Whence arose the error of those who think that the soul is corporeal. VIII, 978, 979.

[Col. 0073] If the soul is a body, it follows that God too is a body. III, 426. If the soul is a body, it will also have sex. X, 542. Whether a human soul, summoned by magical incantations, could appear to the sight of the living, bearing the outline of a body. VI, 144. The soul’s body, or something like a body, which some call its vehicle. II, 78.

Whether the soul is spirit. X, 535, 545, 546. The soul is spirit, not body. II, 858; it is something simple and a substance of its own. I, 1035; it is spiritual, incorporeal, and near to the substance of God. IV, 1886.

The soul is called “flesh” when it still desires carnal goods. VI, 194. The soul, living according to itself, is carnal. V, 854. To what extent the soul’s desires are called “of the flesh.” X, 802. The soul is called “earth.” III, 223. An unrighteous soul is called “earth.” III, 1237.

The excellence of the human soul. III, 1451; V, 429. Nothing is more powerful, nothing more sublime, than the soul. III, 1585. The soul was made in the image of God. V, 562. There is nothing better in the nature of the soul than that it was made in the image of its Creator. VIII, 1039, 1040. In what respect the soul was made in the image of God. VIII, 1040. Rational souls are inferior to angels in function, but equal to them in nature. I, 1287. If anything created by God is ever better than the soul, this results from its sin, not from its nature. I, 1078. Some thought that the soul was made, but that the body was fashioned by God. IV, 1551. The superiority of the soul over corporeal things. III, 364. The philosophers’ opinions concerning the substance of the soul are refuted. VIII, 978, 981, 982.

The soul and spirit are two distinct things, but they are more often designated by one name. X, 495. “Soul” is sometimes understood together with the mind, and sometimes with the mind excepted. VI, 13. The soul’s head: mind and spirit. IV, 74, 77. The soul has a twofold part, intellectual and spiritual; the difference between the two. VII, 287. The higher part of the soul is the rational mind. IV, 1887. The lower parts of the soul. IV, 1887.

The Manichaeans posited two souls. VIII, 94, 93, 255. The Manichaean error concerning two souls, one evil and the other good, and concerning their mixture and struggle. X, 1318, 1510. That there are not two kinds of souls follows from the fact that one may deliberately choose the evil or the good side. VIII, 108, 109. Whether souls are of different natures because their wills are different. VI, 27. Varro’s three grades of soul. VII, 212. Rational souls are of three kinds. VII, 238. How much the Platonists attribute to the intellectual soul. VII, 308. See Mind. How the soul acquires knowledge either in dreams or when released from the body. X, 541.

Every soul derives from truth whatever makes it a soul at all. VI, 11. Once it begins to be capable of reason, it is either governed by a wise mind or by error. III, 1518. Our soul, entangled in error and folly, seeks the way—if there is one—of truth. VIII, 75, 76. The eye of the soul is the mind. III, 1658. God is the soul’s light. III, 479. Whatever the soul understands, insofar as it understands, is from God. III, 480. The soul, through its power of understanding, judges both the variety of things and thought itself. VIII, 186. When the soul sees God by intellectual vision, it sees him even above itself. VIII, 480. When the soul attempts to gaze upon that light, it trembles through weakness and is less capable. VIII, 479. The soul reads certain things in the eternal light of God. IV, 1888. In order to understand God and divine and spiritual things, the soul turns away from the light of the eyes. III, 362. Unless the soul pours itself beyond itself, it does not attain knowledge of the immutable substance. IV, 1712. Why the soul is commanded to know itself. VIII, 977. How it seeks itself. VIII, 979. God willed to sow in every soul the beginnings of understanding and the beginnings of wisdom. V, 667. The soul apprehends images of infinite things. IV, 1886. Some maintain that the human soul possesses within itself a certain power of divination. III, 464; they are refuted. III, 464. The soul would not learn evil if it did not do evil. VII, 310.

Plato promises the human soul false forms of blessedness. VII, 776. Whence the soul is blessed. VIII, 1051, 1052; whence it is troubled. VIII, 113, 115; whence it is wretched. VIII, 127, 1051, 1052. The soul does not remember lost blessedness, but it does remember God and the rules of justice. VIII, 1052. Porphyry says that, in order to be blessed, the soul must flee from every body. VII, 387, 390, 776, 799; this is refuted. VII, 390. An incorruptible body will not hinder the soul’s happiness. VII, 794. The soul will rejoice in the body in which it groaned. VIII, 794. The soul is blessed with God alone, in God alone, and from God alone. III, 1584, 1585; VII, 257. The soul’s rest is in God alone. II, 212, 213. The soul has nothing beyond God to desire. X, 240. The soul can make good use of bodily happiness by preserving order among creatures, if it makes that happiness serve the Creator. II, 539. The Platonists knew that the soul cannot be blessed except by participating in the light of its Creator. VII, 277. Plotinus knew this as well. VII, 279. Some maintained that the soul, even after receiving wisdom, could pass from blessedness into misery and back again. VII, 361; how impious and absurd it is to assert this. VII, 369, 370, 371; Porphyry himself rejected this opinion. VII, 310, 392, 795. If souls are to return to the body, they cannot be blessed. V, 1136. In that case the hope of souls would be more favorable here [Col. 0074] than in that blessedness. V, 1136. If the soul’s misery and blessedness are always alternating, it is not truly blessed. VII, 319. How truth is elicited from the soul’s passage from blessedness into misery and back again. VII, 795. In what the peace of the rational soul consists. VII, 640, 642.

The soul is immortal. III, 372, 1737. The soul’s life after death is established through numbers. III, 736. The immortality of the soul is proved. I, 896, 897. Likewise in the book written on this subject. I, 1021. Only a very few of the most gifted and learned have been able to arrive at an investigation of the immortality of the soul alone. VIII, 1023. What kind of blessedness those found who were able to arrive at an investigation of its immortality. VIII, 1023. The immortality of the soul has a certain limit or measure. VIII, 1040. The soul is immortal in its own manner. V, 428. The soul is immortal, but not as God is. II, 588, 721. The Arabians said that souls die with bodies and that both will rise again at the end of the age. VIII, 46. Some philosophers believed souls to be mortal, others immortal; the various positions of both schools. VII, 601. Many philosophers held that the soul is immortal and remains subject either to misery or to blessedness. II, 389.

Although immortal, the soul is mutable. III, 365, 1548, 1563; VI, 38. This is demonstrated against the Manichaeans from their own doctrine. VIII, 584, 585. The soul can be changed either for the worse or for the better. III, 356. What the mutability of the soul is. III, 359. Since the soul is immortal, how is it mutable? VIII, 669. Because the soul is mutable, it does not properly exist. III, 1685. The soul is in a certain sense mortal because it is mutable. III, 1588; VIII, 768. The soul can in some sense be understood as mortal. III, 372. In what way it is mortal. VI, 194; VIII, 885.

The soul has both its life and its death. VIII, 1040. God is the soul’s life. III, 1550, 1586, 1737; V, 415, 428, 881. The soul is the life of its body, and God is the life of the soul itself. V, 1248. Just as the soul is the whole life of the body, so God is the blessed life of the soul. I, 783, 791, 1263. Wisdom is the life of the soul. VIII, 614, 616. Truth. VI, 240. Faith is the soul of the soul. III, 1754.

How the soul can die. V, 428. The soul’s death is twofold. VII, 710. The soul’s death is to be abandoned by God. VII, 377. The soul’s death is folly. VIII, 614, 616. This is the death of the soul: not to know God. III, 835. What death of the soul is worse than the freedom of error? II, 963. The soul can be both immortal and dead at the same time, in a certain sense. VII, 402. The soul lives by avoiding what kills it through desire. I, 857. The soul has no other salvation, renewal, or reconciliation with its author than to despise all corporeal things and renounce this entire world, as is commanded in the mysteries. I, 1037.

The soul without charity is dead. III, 1462. What is signified by a dead soul. III, 711. The three movements of the dead soul are the arrogance of self-exaltation, the pleasure of lust, and the poison of curiosity. I, 857. The body is the tomb of the dead soul. IV, 1117.

The resurrection of the soul. III, 1550, 1552. The death and resurrection of the soul. VII, 665; VIII, 890, 898. The resurrection of souls occurs through the eternal substance of the Father and the Son; the resurrection of bodies through the dispensation of Christ’s humanity. III, 1591, 1592. How the soul rises again from sin. III, 432. Everyone diligently strives to postpone the death of the flesh; scarcely anyone cares to avoid the death of the soul. III, 1747. The soul cannot return without grace. VIII, 1007. It was able to wound itself, but not to heal itself. V, 1269. The raising of the soul differs from the raising of the body. IV, 893. Why living souls are so called. III, 239.

What the soul is like. VI, 639. The soul’s merit must not be assessed by the rank of the body it inhabits. VII, 240. Souls cannot be called more or less good except with respect either to morals or to differences in the constitution of bodies. III, 421. The soul is intermediate between God and the body. III, 1585. Between the Creator and creatures. II, 539. It has been placed in a kind of center of things. III, 201. Above the soul there is God alone. I, 1170. The soul has been placed beneath God and above all other things. VIII, 538, 547, 591, 592, 977, 1051. Beneath the soul is flesh; above it is God. VI, 710. The soul has God as its lord and the body as its servant. IV, 1887. In the order of things, the soul is nearest to God. I, 961, 1077.

The soul must be subjected to God; the flesh to the soul. V, 715. The soul must worship God alone, who alone is its author. I, 1078. The soul’s good is to adhere to God. VI, 38. The soul ought both to be governed by its superior, that is, God, and to govern its inferior, that is, the body. I, 1170. The soul, established in a kind of middle position, received the law of cleaving to what is above and governing what is below. IV, 1887. God subjects the body to the soul, the soul to himself, and thus all things to himself. I, 1079. The less the soul conceives God in its very thoughts, the less it is subject to God. I, 1201. If the rational soul serves its Creator, all other things will serve it. I, 1231. The more the soul is intent upon God, the more it is; the more it is intent upon the body, the less it is. I, 1170. So that the flesh may serve the soul, and the soul may serve God. VI, 711. The obedient flesh is the soul’s handmaid. IV, 1887. The soul is unhappy when it expects counsel from the body. IV, 1887. When the soul turns itself toward God, it is a sacrifice. VII, 283.

[Col. 0075] All the soul’s movements are nothing other than acts of will. VII, 409. The foot of the soul is love; it is moved by love as toward the place toward which it tends. IV, 124. The soul is not moved by feet but by affections. III, 1741. The soul must be lifted up to God, as a vessel is lifted to a spring. IV, 1854. Unless the soul thirsts, it will not be properly watered. IV, 1350.

The soul does not have light from itself, nor strength from itself, and so forth. IV, 704, 1858. The soul is beautiful and strong in virtue not through itself, but through participation in God’s light. VIII, 261. The rational soul ought to shine like the moon. III, 740. The soul cannot be just, saved, wise, or blessed except through participation in the immutable good. II, 571. The soul becomes good, chaste, devout, and so forth, through participation in the goodness, chastity, and devotion that are in God. III, 1684. The human soul is neither quickened, blessed, nor enlightened except by the very substance of God. III, 1584. Our soul stands in relation to God as air does to light. VII, 326. If the soul attends to its own light, it is darkened; if it attends to God’s light, it is enlightened. IV, 1261. From God’s light the soul gives itself counsel through the rational mind, and from this it conceives firm counsel in the eternity of its Author. IV, 1887. When the soul turns away from the light of justice, the more it seeks what it may find against justice, the more it is driven away from the light and plunged into darkness. IV, 765.

What the foulness of the soul is. VIII, 636. The soul’s beauty, virtue, and teaching of truth; its ugliness is vice. III, 359. The rational soul lives deformedly when it lives according to the trinity of the outward person. VIII, 988. If the soul follows itself in order to attain virtue, it follows something foolish. I, 1314. The nature of the soul is perfect when it is subject to its own spirit. VI, 194. The spirit of a human being is, as it were, the soul’s husband. VI, 58. The more the soul, purified by devotion, is less delighted by what belongs to it privately, the more it contemplates the law of the whole. VI, 90. By its own will the soul cannot make good for itself, but only evil. II, 571. The stronger soul sins, and after sin, under the divine law, is weaker and less capable of taking away what it has done. I, 1170. Just as the soul cannot illuminate itself from itself, so it cannot satisfy itself from itself. I, 853. In order to make the foul soul beautiful, Christ became foul. IV, 1338. If the human soul, though so greatly loved, is foul, how will it shine when beautiful? IV, 204. With what evils the soul of Christ was filled. IV, 1110.

The soul is sufficient to destroy itself; it belongs to God to make it safe. V, 138. The soul’s virtue is charity. IV, 1353. The soul’s bones—that is, its firmness and strength. IV, 92. Our soul, placed amid the temptations of the world, is weaker than anything. IV, 1634. Whence the soul is weak and dark. VIII, 1050. The soul consumes its strength all the more quickly the more it abandons him from whom its strength was given. III, 1344. The soul becomes worse through desire for inferior things. II, 539. The soul is nearer to God in proportion as it is more like him; it is more unlike him in proportion as it is more desirous of mutable things. VII, 271. The soul bound by love of earthly things has, as it were, birdlime on its wings and cannot fly. IV, 1618. What it means for the soul to be bent down. IV, 1849.

The soul captured by love of worldly things becomes an adulteress and an enemy of God. IV, 1178. How the soul turns away from God and commits fornication. VIII, 998, 999, 1005, 1006. What the soul’s fornication is. VIII, 138. The soul’s turning away from God. VIII, 102. From what the soul turns away from God. VIII, 977. Through pride the soul went out from God. III, 1603, 1605. That the soul is the cause of sin is shown by the repentance for sin itself and by forgiveness. VIII, 121, 123.

The soul is Christ’s bride. VIII, 424. The soul’s bread is the word of truth. IV, 752, 754. Its legitimate husband is the divine Word. VI, 58. The union of the human soul with the Word of God is difficult to understand. VIII, 425. The soul dies to sin and to the law of sin in order to marry Christ. VI, 62. Through faith and hope the soul is in Christ. IV, 1843. The holy souls are heaven and the dwelling place of God. IV, 530, 1186, 1260. The original region of the soul’s blessedness, the soul’s dwelling and homeland, is God. I, 587, 1036. A pure soul is the place of God. VI, 16. The soul of the righteous is God’s sword. IV, 324. The soul is our capital. IV, 388. The loss of souls is the shepherd’s loss. IX, 754. One must care for the soul not so that it may possess goods, but so that it itself may be good. V, 629. God alone can give the soul its goods. II, 591.

The Christian soul ought in this life to regard itself as desolate. II, 494, 496. And, as desolate, to pray. II, 506. The soul that understands itself to have been abandoned by every help except God alone is truly a widow. IV, 1725. While the soul is here in this flesh, it too has the consolations of the word, the consolations of prayer, and the consolations of discussion. IV, 753. The soul struggling with its diseases is kept from the physician for a long time, so that it may be persuaded into what evils it has plunged itself by sinning, may guard more carefully the health it has recovered, and may understand what great punishment is prepared for the ungodly who refuse to turn back to God. IV, 92. The soul’s riches. VIII, 165. The soul’s hunger. VIII, 636. Our soul, wrapped in a sluggish body, has become like snow. IV, 1932. The souls signified by the five virgins in the Gospel. IV, 1920. The souls that are to be handed over to beasts. IV, 942. The soul ought never to cease praising God. IV, 1316. Souls capable of and fertile in virtue often send vices ahead of them, by which they reveal to which virtue they would be especially suited if cultivated by instruction. VIII, 444. Evil befalls the soul without any substance being added or taken away. VIII, 193. The soul, while using creatures perversely, does not escape the Creator’s ordering. II, 539.

The soul, made by God, sinned through free choice, was polluted by sin, and through God’s mercy was freed in repentance. VIII, 547, 550. It was necessary that God give the soul free choice. VIII, 118. How it is shown that, according to the Manichaeans, only the souls that are good by nature sin. VIII, 107. That souls are evil by will, not by nature, follows from the usefulness of repentance. VIII, 109, 110, 119. And from their just condemnation. VIII, 106, 107. The soul, fallen through its own fault, is liberated by God’s mercy alone. II, 722. Lazarus in the tomb signifies the soul buried beneath earthly sins. VI, 59. The soul devoted to temporal pleasures is always inflamed by desire and cannot be satisfied. IV, 82. Hence the soul values bodily pleasure more highly than health itself. I, 1170.

The soul’s power over its body. VIII, 989. The manner in which the soul adheres to the body cannot be comprehended. VII, 725. The soul moves by itself. VI, 13. The soul is a certain kind of life. III, 1549; V, 880. It is the life of the body. III, 1586, 1737. The soul is the body’s highest good. I, 1313. What it provides for the body. I, 601, 1074. The human soul in some manner produces odors. III, 1451.

Scripture calls the administration of the body a “living soul.” III, 363. The soul animates and gives life to the entire body. VI, 301. It is wholly present in every part of the body. II, 723. It senses wholly in each individual particle. VIII, 185. The soul alone is simultaneously present not only to the entire mass of its body but also to each of its particles. I, 1034. When the body of a small worm is dissected, the soul is not cut apart. I, 1071. The soul’s function. VI, 711. How the soul moves the body. III, 388, 389. The soul is the mistress caring for a house of clay. VI, 667. The soul’s authority over the flesh. VI, 710. It administers the body through light and air. III, 363, 364. It has no laws over what is below unless they come from God, who is above. VI, 711. The soul cannot govern the body unless it itself is governed by God. IV, 887. Before sin, the soul of the first human being governed the body according to its will, even though the body was not yet spiritual but animal. II, 1108. After sin it governs, not in every respect according to its own will, but as the laws of the whole allow. I, 1287; II, 587. How great the soul’s power is for changing corporeal matter would take a long time to discuss. VIII, 877.

Whether the soul suffers anything from the body. I, 1167, 1168. Through the senses the soul receives whatever concerning corporeal things is not hidden from it. III, 363. How the soul is governed by the senses and how by the intellect. III, 1517. The body perhaps could do nothing in the soul if the latter had not been changed for the worse by the first sin. I, 1166. God alone can act upon rational souls, not through the body but through himself. I, 1185. Because of the condition of sinners, souls are permitted to act upon one another through their respective bodies. I, 1185. What burdens the soul suffers when it acts in a corruptible body. IV, 1320. Before sin, the body did not weigh down the soul. X, 1381. The soul is weighed down by the body because of original sin. X, 1268. Souls fitted to bodies are weighed down as though by forgetfulness. III, 418. The soul that has not yet suffered the vanity of sensible things and the senses is less exposed to falsehoods. II, 70. The soul is deceived not through any defect in the likenesses of things but through its own opinion. III, 475. The light of the eyes is an impediment to the soul’s understanding of spiritual things. III, 363.

Through memory the soul apprehends images of the greatest places. VIII, 185, 186. It thinks of things it has not seen by subtracting and adding. II, 69. How it sees and hears where it is not is difficult to explain. II, 517, 518. Through the body the soul receives some things that it changes and some that it does not change; through itself it likewise receives some things that it changes and some that it does not change. VI, 27. Whence the discord between soul and flesh has been turned into nature. X, 681. The Manichaean opinion concerning soul and body. X, 1319. The fellowship of soul and body. III, 1584. The soul is not defiled by the body except when it desires its mortal goods. VI, 187.

The soul naturally desires the body. III, 369. Through its desire to administer the body, it is held back from the vision of the highest heaven. III, 483. Hunger and thirst belong to the soul. IV, 217. Plato held that souls are not always in their own bodies and do not endure forever without bodies. VII, 392, 795.

The commendation of the soul. IV, 1885. How admirable is the soul of any animal. III, 1451. Our soul, although consumed by sins, is better than if it were changed into this visible light. I, 1276. The soul of a fly—indeed, every soul, even a vicious one—is superior to light. VIII, 96. A sinful soul is better than any supremely excellent body, not by merit but by nature. IV, 1885, 1886. Although vicious, the soul is better than even the soundest body. VII, 264. Even the lowest soul is preferred to the first body. I, 1279. The rational soul is to be preferred to those things that are regarded as gods. VII, 229. The faculties of the rational and irrational soul. VII, 154.

[Col. 0077] Nowhere in Scripture is the human soul said to be blood. VIII, 143. It is not signified by blood without reason. VIII, 650. In what sense the soul of an animal is called blood. VIII, 144, 146.

All animals possess a soul, or spirit. IV, 1272. The irrational soul in beasts. VII, 640, 642. The souls of living creatures are from God. VII, 374. To attribute rational souls to birds belongs to heresy. X, 330. Malignant spirits can corrupt the seeds of irrational souls, so that some are born with the vices proper to their kind. X, 1382.

“SouI” is used in Scripture in different ways. IV, 1411. “Soul” for life. III, 496, 535, 540, 704, 711, 1291. The soul is the life by which we live. IV, 1776. The vegetative principle is usually not called soul but life. III, 230. “Soul” for a human being. III, 517, 521, 588, 1740; VII, 408; VIII, 954. The soul is the inner human being. X, 156. “Soul” is sometimes used for the body. II, 863, 864. For animal pleasure. III, 744. Augustine sometimes uses the name “soul” for the whole incorporeal creation. I, 603. Why the soul was given to the world: Porphyry’s system. VII, 310. Why the soul is given to those who are dying. II, 726. How we should understand the claim that everyone brought all the arts with him and that learning is nothing other than remembering. I, 594, 787.

The souls of all Christians are one soul because of their one faith. IV, 1336.

“To lay down the soul” means to die. III, 1738.

“To seek someone’s soul” is said both in a good and in an evil sense. III, 504.

What it means to lose one’s soul. III, 75. To love and to lose one’s soul is understood in two ways. V, 1459. A certain perverse love of the soul, and a certain upright hatred. V, 1653. The soul’s perverse love is abundant, while upright love belongs to very few. V, 1653. The proper manner of loving the soul. V, 1653. The soul is not to be loved here. V, 1398. For whose sake we are commanded to lose the soul. V, 1394. What it means to hate the soul. III, 1767. How the one who loves loses the soul. III, 1767; V, 1653. To lose the soul so that it may be found. V, 1394. Does the one who destroys its carnal affection hate it? II, 1056. To hang up the soul together with money. V, 1457. The souls of the ungodly live in punishments. VII, 382. Those of the righteous are in rest. VII, 382, 392, 393.

Soul. What the philosophers thought concerning the state of souls after death. V, 1132, 1135. What happens to souls from the day of death until the resurrection. X, 978. The judgment of souls at the very departure from the body. X, 499. The receptacles of souls before the resurrection. VI, 158, 283. The various receptions of souls. III, 1751. The souls of the devout securely await the day of judgment in Abraham’s bosom. IV, 361. Souls cleansed of every contagion of corruption are established in peaceful dwellings until they receive their bodies. VIII, 1069. Immediately after death the soul enjoys rest, if it is worthy of it; but eternal life with the angels is given at the end. III, 1751. Before the resurrection of the body, the souls of the saints are indeed at rest, but not in that activity by which they are quickened after receiving their bodies. II, 327. Whether souls, when they have departed from the body, are contained in a bodily place. III, 376. According to their merits souls are carried to places either of punishment or of rest, places resembling bodies. III, 480, 481. The soul can be changed, not locally but temporally. III, 130. The soul in no way occupies spatial distances by its bulk. VIII, 184, 185. The soul’s place is not in any space, but in the delight with which it rejoices to have arrived through love. IV, 124. The body journeys through places; the soul journeys through affections. IV, 1604. The soul does not leave the body together with a body by which it could be carried to bodily places and contained in them. II, 699, 706. When the soul has left the body, it does not have any body. III, 480. The soul is carried to bodily places either only together with some body, or else it is not carried locally. III, 480. The soul’s punishment or joy after death is real, although it is not corporeal. III, 480, 481. Whether in the underworld it recognizes itself not through bodies but through likenesses of bodies. X, 540. There is one kind of rest or punishment for souls without bodies, and another with bodies. V, 1283, 1454. See Martyrs.

The purification of the soul. III, 832. The Manichaean doctrine that the soul, polluted when sent by God and unable to be cleansed when God was absent, is punished by an everlasting bond in a globe of darkness. VIII, 284, 285. The fantastical and ridiculous Euchite fable concerning the purification of souls. VIII, 40, 41. Porphyry’s opinion concerning the purification of the soul through sacrifices and consecrations. VII, 286, 287. Porphyry said that the spiritual soul could be purified by theurgic purification, but not the intellectual soul. VII, 306. He acknowledged that it could be purified by the virtue of continence without theurgic arts and initiations (*teletai*). VII, 306. Porphyry taught that through the *teletai* the soul is made fit to receive spirits and to see the gods. VII, 286. But not the intellectual soul, for seeing its God. VII, 287. Porphyry thought that the soul could not be purified from ignorance by any *teletai*. VII, 307. The Platonists profess that the purification of the soul lies in first principles. VII, 300. The soul is cleansed and healed by worship of the true God. [Col. 0078] VII, 288. Whether the souls of the dead know or care about what happens among the living. IV, 1437. The Platonic doctrine that the souls of the wise are carried to the stars, while those of fools return to bodies, whether human or animal. VII, 392. Porphyry taught that the souls of those who had lived dishonorably return to other human bodies in order to pay their penalties; Plato also taught that they return to the bodies of animals. VII, 375. The Platonists foolishly asserted that even purified souls return again to bodies. VII, 311. Concerning the return of souls into bodies after purification, Porphyry philosophized better than Plato. VII, 310. Virgil does not approve the doctrine of the return of souls into bodies. V, 1154. The transmigration of souls even into the bodies of animals was approved by Plato and Plotinus but displeased Porphyry. VII, 310. Porphyry taught that souls do not transmigrate into other human bodies. VII, 310. The Manichaean opinion concerning the transmigration of souls. VIII, 226, 231, 383, 384. The Manichaeans think that all souls except those of the Hearers and the Elect return into animals and into everything fixed by roots and nourished in the earth. VIII, 37, 143, 144. Not, however, into the smallest living creatures. VIII, 144. The opinion of the Manichaeans, who admit the transmigration of souls, is worse than that of the philosophers. III, 361. The futile opinion of some that human souls return into cattle, dogs, swine, and ravens. IV, 1911.

A certain heresy teaches that the souls of criminals are changed into demons and into whatever animals correspond to their merits. VIII, 45. Tertullian thought that the worst human souls become demons after death. VIII, 47. Plotinus said that human souls are demons after their bodies. VII, 265. The three kinds of demons into which souls can be changed. VII, 265. The nature of the soul is not converted into the nature of a body. III, 411. Nor into the nature of an irrational soul, nor into the nature of God. III, 411. Certain fictitious transmigrations of souls. III, 361. Plato, thinking that only souls were created by God and that they return into beasts, is refuted by Ambrose in his book *On Philosophy*. X, 686. The Catholic faith and truth do not admit that human souls can be transferred into animals or animal souls into human beings. III, 360, 361. Nor does similarity of morals prove this. III, 361. The doctrine that souls return to their proper bodies is taught by angels, prophets, Christ, and the apostles. VII, 310. The soul’s desire to return to its body. VII, 711, 794. Once the soul has taken up its body again, it will never lay it down through any death. VII, 794. Whether the number of liberated souls can always increase. VII, 371.

The mind is defined as a certain substance participating in reason and adapted to governing the body. I, 1048. The mind is the highest grade of the soul. VII, 212. This part of the soul is called the god of the world. VII, 212. The mind is too narrow to grasp itself. I, 785. We appropriately say that we know what the mind is because we too possess a mind. VIII, 953, 954. In a human being the mind is called the genius. VII, 212. The mind itself is most correctly called “sense.” VII, 318. The three parts of the mind. VII, 427.

The powers of the mind, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. I, 597, 1268. Every movement of the mind does something in the body. II, 72. The four disturbances of the mind. I, 788. From what it is known that the mind is mutable. VII, 231.

The mind is better than all bodies. III, 1561. The mind is better than the body. II, 65. No body is in any way more powerful than any mind. I, 1185. The mind is the body’s ornament; God is the mind’s ornament. III, 1643.

The mind becomes good only by turning toward God. VIII, 950. The mind’s beauty is justice. VIII, 954. When the mind inclines toward the body, it becomes corporeal in a certain sense. VIII, 588. And it is soiled by desire for earthly things. III, 1289; VIII, 89, 90. The mind becomes like God when it subjects itself to him; and the more diligently it does so, the more sublime and, with him alone ruling, the freer it becomes. I, 1319. The mind, too intently occupied with human actions, is in a certain sense emptied of God. III, 619. The mind becomes fuller of God in proportion as it extends itself more freely toward things above and eternal. III, 619.

The mind becomes weak by loving the body. III, 27. This is the mind’s sickness: it does not rise wholly, lifted up by truth, because it is weighed down by habit. I, 759. The health of the mind according to the Stoics. V, 1528; and according to truth. V, 1528. The mind is healed through wisdom. VII, 636. The mind’s health is to cling most firmly to the immutable God. III, 27. A mind that does not prefer eternal things to temporal ones must not be considered healthy. II, 499.

When the mind conquers itself in an ordered way, this is a matter of praise and virtue. VII, 431. The mind can in no way be subject to another mind’s power except by being subject to its own desires. I, 1032. To prostrate the mind means to seek the repose of the will in those things that are sublime among bodies. VIII, 898, 899, 1005, 1006, 1009.

A certain death and resurrection of the mind. III, 25. The person whose mind does not die to this age does not rise again to life but to punishments. III, 25. When the mind rejoices in itself as though in its own good, it is proud. II, 439. In this life the mind suffers hunger. III, 1281. Truth is the mind’s nourishment. II, 62. The more familiarly the mind moves about in truth, the more it is inserted into truth. II, 66. The mind must be refreshed with the food of instruction. III, 1287. The mind is nourished from the source of its joy. I, 863.

What kind of authority the mind exercises over the body. VII, 430. The mind does not properly rule the body if it itself does not serve God. VII, 656. The mind commands the body, and it obeys immediately; the mind commands itself, and resistance follows. I, 760. The mind rules the body more easily than it rules itself. VII, 430.

As ruler, governor, and inhabitant of the body, the mind sees things without a body. IV, 468. The mind can perceive something without images. III, 301. God is seen only by the mind, though not as a mind. IV, 469.

Human beings and demons would not be subject to passions in mind unless they were wretched. VII, 241. The mind’s place is its own affection. IV, 95. Augustine declares that he does not know whether the mind, after the resurrection, can know corporeal things without an organ of the body. II, 629. From habit the mind always seeks that from which it is accustomed to rejoice. VI, 46. Greatness of mind does not consist in killing oneself for whatever reason. VII, 35.

## Animals

Platonists held that mortal animals were made by lesser gods, or Angels. VII, 373, 375. The foolish Manichaean fable about the creation of animals in the nation of darkness is ridiculed. VIII, 395. Whether living creatures were multiplied in a single day. III, 240. The bringing forth of animals from the waters is narrated before that of those from the earth: why. III, 279, 280. Even harmful animals could have been created without doing harm, had there been no cause either for punishing vices or for testing virtue. III, 288. Harmful animals injure living human beings in punishment, exercise them beneficially, test them usefully, or teach them unwittingly. III, 289. Venomous animals appear to have been created before human sin. III, 289. Animals were truly brought to Adam so that he might give them names. III, 400. This has a prophetic significance. III, 400. How the animals were brought to Adam. III, 402. It is more credible that carnivorous animals did not live on flesh in the Ark. III, 550. The animals enclosed in the Ark signify the various nations destined to be brought into the Church. VII, 485. Whether animals were propagated on islands most remote from the mainland from those preserved in the Ark. VII, 485.

God gave living creatures fixed numbers of seeds. III, 240. Animals that arise without any preceding mating arise from the power inherent in the elements. VIII, 875.

Why certain animals were considered unclean in the Old Testament. VIII, 233. They were unclean to the Jews only for the sake of their signification. VIII, 498. What clean and unclean animals signify, and how Moses mentioned them through prophetic figures concerning Christ. VIII, 337.

Whether the movements of animals by which they seek or flee something should be called acts of will. VII, 151. The merits of animals must not be assessed according to the degrees of the elements. VII, 240. An irrational animal cannot be blessed. VI, 12. Some animals live amid flames. VII, 709. The sudden savagery of domestic animals at Rome: what it portended. VII, 104. A living animal is composed of soul and body. VII, 264.

## Animosity

It is a mark of greater intelligence to extinguish the flames of animosity by confession than to avoid the mists of falsehood by understanding. IX, 332.

## Anna

“Anna” is interpreted as “grace.” VII, 528. Anna, the mother of Samuel, is a figure of Christian religion and grace. VII, 528. From what does the prophetess Anna chiefly derive commendation? VI, 440. Why, although she had no children, did she refuse a second marriage? VI, 436.

## Annaeus Seneca

Annaeus Seneca flourished in the time of the Apostles. VII, 190.

## Annas and Caiaphas

The high priests Annas and Caiaphas customarily served in alternate years. III, 1937.

## Annianus

Annianus, consul. IX, 687.

## Hannibal

Hannibal won many victories over the Romans. VII, 180. Near Rome he was terrified by the thunderbolts of the gods. VII, 101. Hannibal was defeated by Scipio Africanus the Elder. VII, 102.

## Annibonius

Annibonius, bishop of Robautum. IV, 381.

## Rhaetian grain-supply

Rhaetian grain-supply. VII, 575.

## Year

The year was observed by the sun’s circuit. VIII, 893. What is the great year, or Plato’s year? III, 236. Which years are manifest and which more obscure? III, 236. Years were reckoned in different ways among different peoples. VII, 451. Egyptian years were once completed in four-month periods. VII, 358. Were the years of the first human beings equal to ours? VIII, 450. It is shown that the years of the first human beings were as long as ours. VII, 454. The number of years of the first human beings is recorded differently in the Hebrew manuscripts and in ours. VII, 449. From what did the difference arise in the reckoning of the years of the Hebrews and of the Seventy translators? VII, 453. In reckoning the years, the authority of the Hebrews is to be followed rather than that of the Seventy. VII, 452.

## Eternal years

Eternal years. IV, 752, 976. Years without years. IV, 418. God’s years are one day. I, 815. All God’s years stand together. I, 815. Those years do not fail which stand. V, 1623. Our years are said to fail either because in them we fail by loving things that pass away, or because they have been reduced to a small number. IV, 1145. Years stand in eternal life, whereas here they pass away—indeed, perish. VII, 531.

[Col. 0080] The number of years is to be reckoned for each person from the time when the first mortal birth took place. III, 875. That years are not added to those who are growing older but subtracted from them is proved by an example. IV, 795. A person’s years diminish rather than increase. V, 638.

Some falsely reckon many thousands of years in their history of time. VII, 358. This absurd vanity is refuted. VII, 358. From the creation of humanity to Augustine’s time, six thousand years had not yet been completed. VII, 358. Some defined the duration of this age as six thousand years. IV, 1143. ## Apostles

The Apostles are called *missi* (“sent”) in Latin. III, 1781. The number twelve among the Apostles is a great sacrament. IV, 1103, 1359. The Apostles are not of the world. III, 1677. What the Apostles left behind in order to follow the Lord. IV, 1371. Why Christ chose humble men as Apostles. VII, 611. Why he chose the weak. IV, 788. The Apostles thought that the Lord was merely human. IV, 1798; V, 1149. Ambrose says that not everyone saw Christ. II, 604, 610. The Apostles were afraid during the Lord’s Passion. IV, 1799; V, 493. In the Passion they abandoned him and lost faith. III, 1901. Doubting about Christ, they were defeated by the thief. IV, 1851; V, 749, 1116. The Apostles had lost hope. IV, 847, 1927. Stumbling during the Lord’s Passion, they were strengthened by his resurrection. IV, 1798, 1799. Before Christ’s death they were not yet mature for martyrdom. III, 1807. While under the Law, the Apostles were not yet free from desires. V, 794. It was appropriate for the Apostles, just as for us, to say, “Forgive us,” etc. IV, 1849. Julian’s slander that the Apostles were polluted by lust. X, 556. III, 124. And all nations. V, 159. The Apostles reached the ends of the earth. IV, 1674. How the words of the Apostles reached the ends of the world. IV, 1122. The oracles of the Prophets confirm the preaching of the Apostles. VI, 180. The Apostles’ utterances were marvelous deeds, not mere words. VII, 756. They appear to have performed greater miracles than Christ. IV, 1707. Through them God flashed miracles, thundered terrors, and rained consolations. IV, 1626. In performing miracles the Apostles did not arrogate to themselves the power of their Lord. IV, 1199. Christ prepared the Apostles like luminaries by his word and kindled them with the Holy Spirit. VII, 612. The Apostles, burning with divine fire like flaming logs, while they were driven from place to place, filled the whole forest of the world with their fire. IV, 253.

Having received Christ’s bride, the Apostles beget children for her. V, 1683. They founded churches not for themselves but for Christ. IV, 508.

At Jerusalem the Apostles decreed that no one should compel the Gentiles to Judaize, but not that anyone should prohibit Jews from Judaizing. II, 279. The Apostles did not take their Sabbath rest or fast on the Sabbath. II, 138. They were not accustomed to fast solemnly on the Lord’s Day. II, 149.

It is not incredible that some of the Apostles were granted a vision of the divine substance. II, 610. Why the Apostles did not request laws from the Emperors. II, 801. Petilianus says that sixty apostles, after abandoning the Twelve who remained with Christ the Lord, departed from the faith as apostates, yet were still considered apostles. IX, 271.

Augustine calls the Apostles rams. II, 1026. Rams of the flock. V, 749, 1414. Leaders of the sheep, principal members of the Shepherd. IV, 785, 916, 1849. The Apostles designated by the name “beards.” IV, 1733. The Apostles are oxen. III, 1470. Dogs who keep faith with the Lord and bark against his enemies. IV, 833. The Apostles are signified by the name “heavens.” III, 1664; IV, 288, 817, 1121, 1243, 1864. The Apostles became heaven because they were justified. IV, 1626. They are called hills. IV, 785. Columns. IV, 950, 1831. Columns of the living God. VI, 692. The columns that trembled during the Lord’s Passion were strengthened at the resurrection. IV, 950. The Apostles are sons of the bridegroom. IV, 1845. Sons of those who were cast out, because they are sons of the Prophets. IV, 1674, 1677. Foundations and columns of the Church. II, 553. Rivers raising their voice throughout the world. IV, 1187.

The Apostles are the foundations and gates of the Church. IV, 1103. Foundations of the heavenly city. IV, 1101. The twelve Apostles are the twelve hours of the day. III, 1750; IV, 650. IV, 814, 833, 1235. The Apostles are Christ’s eyes. IV, 1114. The eyes of the Church. III, 843. Bones, or the supports, of Christ’s body. IV, 168, 1297. The Apostles are fathers. IV, 513. The Lord’s feet. IV, 1167. Fishers of human beings. IV, 781. Princes. IV, 834. Thrones, or seats, of God. IV, 1625. For some people the Apostles are vessels of death and sharp arrows. III, 232. An unformed spiritual life can also be understood under the name “water.” III, 250. Water signifies worldly prosperity. IV, 797. Many waters signify various doctrines. IV, 269.

An arbitrator is said to be an intermediary appointed to settle a case. IV, 1383.

## Free choice

Free choice was acknowledged by Mani. VIII, 543, 538, 1087. The choice of the will was not given to all natures. III, 390. Free choice is asserted. VIII, 121. Free choice exists in Angels and human beings. VIII, 537, 538, 542, 543. Through his own free choice the first human being could stand upright by his own power. X, 933. Those who say that by our own choice we were made bad from good and can become good from bad are refuted. V, 409; X, 1541, 1542, 1544.

What kind of free choice is laudably free? X, 1102. Choice is truly free when it has been liberated. X, 234. Human choice must be liberated from slavery to sin, which now rules it together with death. VI, 282. The choice of the will is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. VII, 418. Choice is liberated only through grace. VI, 282. Free choice belongs to grace. X, 241.

Free choice must not be defended in such a way that God’s help is thought unnecessary. III, 1778. The Pelagians persuade people that the choice of the will can overcome temptations and fulfill God’s commandments without God’s grace. VI, 329. The Pelagians bring people to ruin by exalting free choice. X, 1246. One must not trust in the freedom of choice. VII, 467. The choice of the will is commended together with grace. X, 342. Free choice is not sufficient without grace. X, 202, 203. Free choice is assisted by grace, so that what we naturally desire—that is, to live happily—we may possess by living well. X, 1566. Nature’s free choice is insufficient for not sinning unless grace heals it by assisting it. X, 293. No human choice resists God when he wills to save. X, 942. God does not remove the choice of a good will but assists it. III, 757. See Liberty.

## Trees

How and when trees were created. III, 275. They were created on the third day according to causal principles. III, 259. Concerning herbs and trees it is said not only “according to kind” but also “according to likeness.” III, 287. Why the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was so called. IV, 897. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not harmful in itself, but through violated obedience. X, 172. The tree of paradise was good, and therefore it was not to be touched solely because God had forbidden it. IV, 896, 897. The tree of paradise was prohibited to commend the good of obedience. VII, 394.

The tree of life. III, 214. No one reaches it except through endurance and knowledge. III, 214.

What the good tree and the bad tree in the Gospel mean. X, 461, 1455, 1458. The good or bad tree is the will. X, 667, 668, 672, 754, 1454. In what sense a human being makes a tree good or bad. X, 370.

Grafting of trees. III, 405. How a tree comes from a seed and a seed from a tree. III, 358. Everything belonging to a tree was initially present in the seed through causal force and potential. III, 357. The Manichaeans think that trees live in such a way that they perceive and feel pain when injured. VIII, 37.

## The Ark of Noah

Noah’s Ark was made of incorruptible wood. IV, 1917. It was constructed of squared timbers: with what mystery? IV, 1103. How the Ark had two and three chambers. III, 349. Whether the cubits used in measuring the Ark were geometrical. VII, 474. Origen thinks that the cubits were geometrical. III, 349. Philo explained the Ark of the Flood according to the proportions of the human body. VII, 472; VIII, 274. Why the Ark was built over so many years. V, 1610. What Christ’s building another ark admonishes us about. V, 1611. Which animals were brought into the Ark. VII, 475. Why those who entered separately came out together. VIII, 265. The difficulties of those who attack the history of the Ark are answered. VII, 473.

The meanings of the Ark are expounded. VII, 472. An allegorical interpretation of Noah’s Ark. VIII, 262, 263. When the Ark and the Flood are under discussion, neither history alone without allegories nor allegories alone without historical truth is to be admitted. VII, 472. The allegory of the Ark coated with pitch, adapted to the error of the Donatists. IX, 397. Another allegory of the Ark, more consistent with the truth. IX, 397. Noah’s Ark is a figure of Christ. VII, 477. A figure of the Cross. III, 1464. And of the Church. III, 1434; IV, 1358; VII, 472, 476; IX, 397. In the Ark some things refer to Christ and some to the Church. VIII, 274, 275. How the Ark prefigured the Church. IX, 196. Just as it contained every kind of animal, so the Church contains all nations. IV, 1358. Noah’s Ark was a prophecy of our times. VII, 598. The Manichaeans attacked Noah’s Ark under the name *pancarpus*. VIII, 598.

The ark in which the Law was enclosed, whence it was called the Ark of the Testimony. VII, 295. The miracles performed through the Ark bear witness to the Godhead. VII, 295. The Ark of the Covenant may be understood as signifying a certain more sacred presence of the Lord. VI, 144. Mystical exposition of the Ark and the mercy seat. III, 633. The Ark of Christ’s sanctification: the Church, or the Body born of Mary. IV, 1722. How the Ark of the Lord remains forever. IV, 1005.

The Arcadians are said to have been transformed by Arcadian demons from men into wolves. VII, 575.

Arcadius the Emperor. VI, 722. Arcadius Augustus, twice consul. VIII, 111, 112. Arcadius, consul for the third time. IX, 529, 574. In the time of Arcadius, it was revealed that Constantinople would be destroyed by heavenly fire. VI, 722.

Archelaus, hearer and successor of Anaxagoras: what he thought concerning the principles of things. VII, 226.

Arcesilas, fellow student of Zeno under Polemo. I, 955. He succeeded that same Polemo. I, 955. He concealed the position of the Academy. I, 955. Arcesilas, founder of the New Academy. VII, 226.

Ἅρχιμάγειρος (*archimagirus*), a military commander or chief cook. III, 582, 584.

The geometrical writings of Archimedes, stubbornly attacked by Epicurus. VIII, 74.

The craft of workers in gold, silver, and metal is also called architecture. III, 654. Architectural work in textiles. III, 515, 516.

What the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue and the woman with the hemorrhage signify. V, 485, 486.

The Archontic heretics and their doctrines. VIII, 29.

What the rainbow in the clouds signifies. VIII, 265, 266, 630.

The bow of God stretched out: his threats. IV, 686. By the name “bow,” the Holy Scriptures are understood. IV, 106. What arrows the Lord’s bow has, and what weapons of death. IV, 106. The bow of the wicked: their ambushes. IV, 365.

Ardea, a city. VII, 93.

The Lord’s threshing floor: the Church. III, 127. The Lord’s threshing floor, in which there is now wheat, not without chaff. V, 119, 1174. The threshing floor must not be abandoned before the time of winnowing. IV, 190.

Arles. IX, 41.

The Council of Arles in the case of Caecilianus. II, 161, 169, 198; IX, 41, 640.

By the “sand of the sea,” the weak and carnal in the Church are understood. II, 336.

The Areopagus, the court of the Athenians. V, 808. Why it is so called. VII, 567.

Argentinus, a god, son of the god Aesculanus. VII, 103.

Argentius. II, 120.

Refined silver. III, 586. Who are those refined by silver? IV, 1429.

Argyrius rushed upon the Priscillianists either in ignorance or because he was entangled in the snares of that same heresy. II, 1034.

Inachus was the first to rule the Argives. VII, 597. Why Argos, or the Argives, are so called. VII, 564. The succession of Argive kings. VII, 562. The kingdom of the Argives arose at the same time as the descendants of Abraham’s nephews. VII, 562. The fall of the Argive kingdom. VII, 572.

Argus, son of Apis and king of the Argives. VII, 564. After his death Argus began to be regarded as a god. VII, 564.

The rebuking of the wicked. V, 78, 549. You must neither consent to the wicked by approving them, nor neglect them by failing to rebuke them, nor be arrogant by rebuking them insultingly. V, 550. He rebukes in mercy who rebukes without hatred. IV, 1824. Some will be rebuked in God’s anger and will not be corrected; others, through correction, will be saved. IV, 397. Whoever desires to be healed in this life does not wish to be rebuked in God’s anger. IV, 91.

The dry land. Not every dry place is earth. III, 234.

The ram caught by its horns, a figure of Christ crucified. IV, 244. The ram marked with red, a figure of Christ and the martyrs. III, 635.

The Council of Rimini. VIII, 710, 711, 730, 772; X, 1100. Augustine says that he is not bound by the authority of the Council of Rimini. VIII, 711.

Aristippus, a Socratic philosopher, said that pleasure is the highest good. VII, 227, 601.

Aristobulus, son of Alexandra, queen of the Jews. VII, 607. He was the first among the Jews to become both king and high priest. VII, 607. He was led in chains to Rome. VII, 607.

Aristodemus, a tragic actor, often sent by the Athenians as ambassador to Philip. VII, 56.

Aristonicus, defeated by the Romans. VII, 86.

Aristotle founded the Peripatetic school. VII, 237. Aristotle was a man of outstanding intelligence, though inferior to Plato in eloquence. VII, 237. He seemed to agree with Plato. I, 956. Aristotle trembles when Christ speaks in the underworld. IV, 1828.

Arithmetic is not derived from human institution. III, 61.

The story of Arion of Methymna, the most distinguished citharist. VII, 28.

Arius. V, 1641; VI, 714. The heresiarch from whom the Arians take their name. VIII, [Col. 0087] 39. Arius did not enter through the door into the sheepfold. III, 1721. The Arian heresy concerning the Son of God. III, 1609; IV, 288, 837, 1040, 1712; VIII, 923. Pascentius anathematizes Arius and Eunomius. II, 1039.

The Arians. V, 55; IX, 395, 469, 589. The Arian faith concerning the holy Trinity. II, 1049. They say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are different substances. II, 792. They used to say that the Father was invisible but the Son visible. III, 1779. They used to say that the Father was invisible, but the Son and Holy Spirit visible. II, 626; III, 1779. The Arians think that the substance of the Son of God, without assuming any body, is visible in itself. III, 392. And that the Father alone is invisible. III, 392.

The Arians deny that the Son of God is true God. VIII, 930. They say that the Father is one thing and the Son another. III, 1737. They say that the Father did not beget that which he is. II, 750. They deny that the Son is equal to the Father. III, 1672, 1711, 1796, 1820. And that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Son. III, 1796. They are refuted. III, 1537, 1559, 1560, 1802. The Arians either do not worship Christ or do not worship one God. VIII, 743, 763. Consequently, the Arians admitted two Gods and Lords. VIII, 769, 770. They believe that Christ assumed flesh without a soul. VIII, 39. See Christ, Son. The Arians are shown to assert different natures in the Father and the Son. VIII, 779, 780. Through their insult to the Son, the Arians falsely honor the Father. V, 772. How one should answer an Arian who asked whether God begot the Son willingly or unwillingly. VIII, 1087. The Arians sinned against the Holy Spirit. II, 814. The Arians are refuted when they assert that the Father is greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit much lesser still. VI, 640, 648, 658, 683, 692, 697. The Arians are refuted. V, 664, 665, 701, 746, 770, 774, 989, 1150, 1496, 1676, 1689. The Arians understand less than the Jews. III, 1744. Augustine observes that the Council of Sardica, which the Donatists cited, belonged to the Arians. II, 176.

The Arians accuse us of being Sabellians. X, 458, 1461. While fleeing from Sabellianism, the Arians fell into something worse. X, 1462. The Arians attempted to ally the Donatists with themselves. II, 176; IX, 516. The Donatists themselves at one time professed the Arian faith. II, 793. The difference between the error of the Arians and that of the Donatists. II, 793. An Arian and a Photinian, both heretics, divided against each other. V, 447. The Arians condemned. VI, 650.

When Arians returned to the Church, the degrees of honor were preserved for them. II, 813. Lucifer of Cagliari disliked this, and consequently fell into the darkness of schism. II, 813. Certain kings converted from the Arian heresy. VIII, 759. The Arians rebaptize. VI, 652, 692, 706; VIII, 39. Persecution carried out by the Arians. VI, 308. Imperial laws against the Arians. VIII, 709. The Arians rejected throughout the world. VI, 685. In Augustine’s time the Arian heresy was almost extinct, like a rotting corpse or a man at the point of death. III, 1689. An Arian once dead and coming to life again. VI, 696. The discourse, or summary of the Arians’ doctrines. VIII, 678, 679, 680.

Weapons on the right and left. IV, 426, 1215. God arms himself for us. IV, 323. It is a magnificent spectacle to see God armed for you. IV, 323. How God armed is to be understood. V, 1423. If we make good progress, we too shall be God’s weapons: how this is so. IV, 323. The strongest weapons against temptations are desires for eternal life. IV, 1774. The weapons by which the enemy is conquered, and the unconquerable shield. IV, 89. Weapons against the devil. VI, 637, 638. Our weapons must be burned with fire before God arms us with the evangelical weapons of truth, continence, and so forth. IV, 523. Weapons removed from the temples of the gods. VII, 100. The weapons of the devil. VI, 637, 638.

Armamiter, the eighth king of the Assyrians. VII, 562.

The estate of Armamiter. II, 235.

Those possessed by demons. VII, 50. Those possessed by idols, like frogs from the marshes. IV, 520.

The difference between a pledge and a security. V, 158, 858, 1673.

Arrogance must not be avoided in such a way that truth is abandoned. III, 1712. Although all arrogance is hateful, that of intelligence and eloquence is especially troublesome. III, 1794.

Why it is called an art. VII, 128. Art resides in the mind. I, 1024; III, 179. Art is a certain disposition of the mind. I, 1182. Art consists of imitation and reason. I, 1086. Three kinds of art. III, 57. The law of all the arts: equality and unchangeable unity. III, 147. Wisdom in the arts: in what sense. III, 515. See Study. Art has no defect and knows none. IV, 334. God’s art does not know defects, and judges defects. V, 579.

Two kinds of art. I, 1053. The usefulness of the liberal arts. I, 1015. What the vulgar art is. III, 146. Those who have chosen an evil art by which to make a living must be punished, because they wish to feed themselves from that by which they offend the one from whom all are fed. IV, 1692. Why teachers of the arts are so called. III, 1793. Knowledge of the arts contributes something to understanding Scripture. III, 57. Art is not found in brute animals. I, 1086.

There is scarcely any craftsman who does not have his art for sale at a monetary price. VII, 197.

How painful it is for children to learn crafts. VII, 728. The form of artifacts is conveyed through the craftsman’s hand from the wisdom of God. VI, 90.

Artemon, or Artemonius, the heresiarch. VIII, 34.

The arteries, veins of air. X, 527.

The five divisions of time. VI, 313, 338.

The Artotyrites: why they are so called. VIII, 31. Epiphanius joins the Artotyrites with the Pepuzians. VIII, 31.

The superstitious books of the haruspices. III, 50.

Asaph is interpreted as “synagogue.” III, 1347; IV, 916, 929, 1011; as “assembly.” IV, 970, 1035, 1051.

Asbestos, a stone of Arcadia which, once kindled, cannot be extinguished. VII, 715, 719.

Ascanius, son of Aeneas and the third king of the Latins. VII, 576. He founded Alba. VII, 89.

Ascatades, king of the Assyrians. VII, 568.

Ascension. See Adscension.

The Ascites, heretics. VIII, 42.

Asclepius, grandson of Aesculapius. VII, 253.

Asellus, a deacon. II, 718.

The Lord’s ass: the gentle people. IV, 272, 310.

Asia is said to be one third of the whole world when reckoned by its divisions, but half when reckoned by its size. VII, 561. The dimensions of Asia. VII, 578. Asia is the name of a province and also of a third part of the earth. III, 783; VII, 497. Asia conquered by Ninus. VII, 578. The Scythians once held almost all Asia. III, 794.

Asian luxury. VII, 103.

What Balaam’s speaking she-ass signifies. III, 742.

Asinius Pollio. II, 263.

The *Golden Ass*, a book written by Apuleius. VII, 574.

Aspasius Paternus, proconsul. V, 1410.

Asper the grammarian. V, 83.

So that the asp may not hear the voice of the charmer, it presses one ear against the earth and stops the other with its tail. IV, 680, 681; V, 1432. The deaf who refuse to hear the word of God are compared to asps. IV, 117. Asps are treacherous. IV, 684.

The Aspidisci. III, 636.

The house of Assaracus, that is, the Romans. III, 533; VII, 462.

Assur, figuratively used for the devil. IV, 1053.

The Assuri. IX, 235. The city of Assuritana. IX, 253, 507, 528, 550.

The Assuritani. IX, 108, 180.

“Assyrians” is interpreted as “those who direct.” IV, 1021. The Assyrian kingdom, extending far and wide from Ninus. VII, 116. The Assyrian kingdom ruled all Asia except India. VII, 497. The Assyrian kingdom at the height of its prosperity. VII, 560, 561. It flourished in the time of Abraham. VII, 497. The Assyrian kingdom lasted 1,240 years. VII, 117, 577. The Assyrian kingdom was transferred to the Medes. VII, 117, 577. When the Assyrian kingdom came to an end. VII, 577. The succession of the Assyrian kingdom. VII, 561.

Astaroth and Astarte, names of Juno. III, 797.

Asterisks in Greek manuscripts indicate passages that the Hebrews have but the Septuagint translators do not. III, 590; IV, 821.

Asterius, king of the Cretans. VII, 569, note b.

Asterius the subdeacon brought Jerome’s letters to Augustine. II, 237, 245. Asterius was made bishop. II, 276.

Asterius of Scythopolis interpreted the Psalms. II, 262.

Astrology and its invention. I, 1014. Astrology is a great argument for the religious but a torment for the curious. I, 1014. The vain predictions of astrologers. I, 694, 707, 737, 915. The Priscillianists maintain that astrology binds men to the fatal stars and that the body is composed according to the twelve signs of heaven. VIII, 44.

The trifles of the astrologers are refuted. VI, 112. Why astrologers sometimes give true answers. VII, 147. The perspicacity and blindness of astrologers. V, 438. See Mathematicians.

By “the crafty,” those of an evil disposition are understood. III, 431.

*Asystaton*. X, 1095.

Romulus and Remus established an asylum. VII, 45. The Romulean asylum, a kind of shadow of the remission of sins. VII, 161. The asylum of the Apostles is far safer than that of the gods. VII, 17.

The persecution of Athanaric, king of the Goths, in Gothia against the Catholics. VII, 616, and note b.

Athanasius of Alexandria, a Catholic bishop. IX, 516. A man of great steadfastness and sound faith. X, 1101. Constantine specifically sought him out. II, 1016. He preserved himself for the good of the Church. II, 1017. In the time of Athanasius almost the whole world had fallen away from the apostolic faith. X, 1100. Of the 660 bishops, scarcely seven remained with Athanasius in confessing the Trinity. X, 1100. Athanasius did not approve of melodies in the singing of the Psalms. I, 800. Augustine does not disapprove of that manner of singing. I, 800.

The Catholics were called Athanasians, or Homoousians, by the Arians. X, 1101.

The city of Athens was either restored or founded under King Cecrops. VII, 566. Why Athens was so called. VII, 566. It was given this name under King Cecrops. VII, 566. On what occasion. VII, 566, 567. Greece had nothing more illustrious than Athens. VII, 567. Athens derived no small glory from letters and philosophers. VII, 561.

The Athenians’ reputation among all peoples for every kind of learning. V, 808. The Athenians were distinguished in Greece more by reputation than by actual merit. VII, 561. At Athens the most loquacious philosophical heresies arose. IX, 454. The kingdom of the Athenians was changed into a republic. VII, 577. Athenian women took part in public deliberations. VII, 566. Why they were expelled from public deliberations. VII, 567.

How an atheist is to be convicted. I, 1246. Anyone who renders worship to something regards it in some measure as a god. III, 153.

Atlas, astrologer and king of Mauretania, brother of Prometheus and maternal grandfather of the elder Mercury. VII, 599. He flourished at the time when Moses was born. VII, 599. He was the first to observe the courses of the sun, moon, and stars. VII, 234, note 1. Why he is imagined to carry the heavens. VII, 565. Atlas the bearer. VIII, 307, 309, 374.

Mount Atlas. VII, 565.

The Atlantic philosophers. VII, 234.

Atoms, the principles of things according to Epicurus. VII, 230. Epicurus says that, through the chance collision of atoms, innumerable worlds, living creatures, souls, and the gods themselves come into being. II, 444. He is refuted by Cicero. II, 444, 445. The atom in body and in time. V, 1624.

Courtyards are understood as the more spacious areas of a house. IV, 1736. The courts of the Lord, in reference to future blessedness. IV, 1067, 1059, 1281. The holy court of the Lord: the Catholic Church. IV, 1233.

Attis, a handsome young man, castrated. VII, 185. The story of Attis. VII, 215.

What greed is. VII, 356. General greed, by which each person desires more than is enough. IV, 1530. Greed is the desire to be rich, not already to be rich. V, 523. Greed grows with abundance. IV, 1639. Insatiable greed. IV, 330, 422, 438; V, 1651. Let greed perish, and nature is rich. V, 395. The throat of greed is not closed by greater wealth but stretched; it is not watered but inflamed. V, 328. Greed often increased in those who restrained lust. VI, 448.

Greed is a grave sin. IX, 89. It is the work of an evil person, not of God. IV, 1691. The accusation and punishment of greed. V, 958. The burden of greed. V, 897. Greed is a chain on the feet. III, 2057. Greed is the enemy of Christ. IV, 1249. The losses of those who sin for the sake of profit. IV, 1645. Greed is excused under the appearance of devotion toward one’s children. V, 89.

A certain greed for life itself must also be avoided. V, 663. There is a kind of greed in lust and idolatry. V, 630. Greed is used for private love. III, 436. Those who reclaim what is theirs must beware of every form of desire. IV, 1570. Greed too loves unity. IV, 451. Greed attracts more people than expertise. VII, 197. The foolish counsel of greed. V, 527. God’s command ordering what greed commands. V, 529. Greed commands one thing against God, while God commands another against greed. IV, 675. All greed must be cut away. V, 627, 630.

The remedy for greed. IV, 1636. The teaching given to Christians for avoiding greed. V, 954. Greed obeys harsh commands eagerly. V, 257. A person serves greed, not God. V, 1205. Greed commands harsh things and is obeyed; God commands easy things and is not obeyed. IV, 1691. Christ frees us from the yoke of greed and luxury. V, 526. All greed is circumcised from us if God is worshiped freely. IV, 1531. The love of wisdom cleanses one from the filth of greed. VII, 204. “While your purse is being filled with coins, your soul is fevered with cares.” V, 403. When greed is rebuked, it begins to hate and accuse. IV, 1691. Greed is condemned in words by everyone, but not in deeds. V, 953. Greed and luxury are two mistresses issuing contrary commands. V, 526. See Desire.

Holy greed. V, 526.

Greed for eternal life, the best kind. IV, 1169.

The greedy. People would not be lovers of money unless they thought themselves more excellent in proportion as they were richer. III, 437. People are as greedy as they are proud. IV, 1909. The proverb of the greedy: “As much as you have, so much will you be; break the moon and make your fortune.” IV, 610; VI, 674. A greedy person is not only one who seizes another’s property but also one who covetously keeps his own. V, 628. The danger of the greedy, or of one who covetously keeps his own. V, 631. The greedy hoarder of his possessions is condemned. V, 961. The greedy person is dropsical. V, 410, 956. How great and how useless are the feverish passions of the greedy. V, 403. The greedy person is like a martyr of gold. V, 1461, 1470. He is tortured by gold, by which the merciful person is helped. V, 327. The greedy are poor. VII, 204. The greedy person does not possess so much as he believes he possesses. VI, 674. Faith is set before him as something more valuable. VI, 674. The madness of the greedy. IV, 422. The greedy person makes God the minister of his profit. IV, 250. The greedy person invokes profit, not God. IV, 250, 617. The cruelty of the greedy. IV, 1778. The burden of the greedy must be reduced by distributing it to the poor. VI, 673.

The foolish excuse of the greedy. V, 956. The false devotion of the greedy toward their children. V, 89, 528. The cruel excuse of the greedy, under the pretext of their children. VI, 673. The greedy person has the language of devotion but an excuse for iniquity. IV, 422. When a son has died, the greedy person must transfer his portion to him. V, 528. What was being kept for a living son is owed to the dead son. V, 528. Christ must be counted among the children when the inheritance is divided. V, 528; VI, 673.

[Col. 0090] The greedy compared with ants. III, 361. A sharp attack on certain blind greedy persons. VI, 674. Against those who desire what belongs to others. IV, 451. The greedy person labors so as to have enough to fill his chest, and loses his security. III, 2056. The greedy person loves what he loves with labor; God is loved without labor. III, 2056.

God is “greedy” for our salvation. V, 580. The greedy person and the love of God. VI, 674. “Greedy one, if God came to you without gold and silver, would you not want him? What of the things God made is enough for you, when God himself is not enough for you?” IV, 250. What is enough for the greedy if God himself is not enough for them? V, 141. The conversations of greedy people must be avoided. VI, 675.

Authority. We are impelled to learn by a twofold weight: authority and reason. I, 957, 1001, 1007. In time, authority comes first; in the matter itself, reason comes first. I, 1007, 1311. For learning, trusting authority is a great shortcut. I, 1042. Authority is twofold, divine and human. I, 1007. To seek the authority of human beings in order to strengthen reason is a sign of weakness. I, 1152.

The summit of authority and the light of reason have been established in the one name of Christ and in his one Church. I, 1009. By authority established by God, we are raised up to God as though by a kind of step. VIII, 89. How authority established by God moves us. VIII, 89, 90. To be deceived by authority is pitiable, but certainly it is more pitiable not to be moved by it. VIII, 89.

Authority is useful for persuading peoples to good morals. VIII, 90, 91. The life of the good is cleansed most easily, not by the winding paths of disputation, but by the authority of the mysteries into which we are initiated. I, 1007. It is helpful to follow the authority and precepts of the wise, and through these to believe that God speaks to oneself. I, 1075. Authority of a canonical kind must not be established in the writings of the Doctors. VI, 160. The opinions of any disputants whatsoever are not to be treated as canonical authority. X, 194.

Why there ought to have been few sacred authors. VII, 600.

The fowlers are treacherous. VIII, 67.

Hearers and catechumens. V, 754.

The duty of hearers toward teachers. V, 155. A negligent hearer must not blame the preacher’s faults. V, 971. Hearers are signified by the name “earth,” preachers by “heaven.” V, 1234. Which hearers are carnal and which spiritual. V, 156. Of those who hear the divine word, some build upon rock and others upon sand. V, 971. The acclamation of hearers. V, 135, 1373, 1388, 1415.

What it means to hear before God. IV, 193. Let the one who wishes to be heard by God hear God. V, 126. Not to hear, as though not to build, is evil. V, 971; IV, 1812. To hear and not to do is to build on sand; to hear and to do is to build on rock; neither to hear nor to do is to build nothing. IV, 1335. Whoever hears good things and does evil produces thorns in place of the gentle rain. IV, 1345. How can one be strong in doing who fails in hearing? IV, 1211. By hearing we believe, and by believing we shall see. IV, 510. First hear, then see. IV, 537. Whether hearing and perceiving with the ears differ. IV, 544. To hear the voice of praise means to understand inwardly, because whatever evil is in you is yours, while whatever good there is belongs to God. IV, 193. To hear the word of God is safer than to preach it. V, 966. Let the servant of God desire to hear rather than to speak. IV, 1812. To hear, to be drawn, and to learn from the Father. X, 972. Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to Christ. X, 971. To hear and learn is to eat. IV, 1874.

Hearers among the Manichaeans. VIII, 35; IX, 357. Rightly alienated from the evangelical commandments. VIII, 228. The Manichaeans believe that the souls of their hearers are dissolved into the Elect or into food for the Elect. VIII, 37. See Manichaeans.

Hearing occurs through the striking of the air. I, 252. Hearing is twofold, good and bad. IV, 344, 1236. The desire to hear, even in sacred songs. X, 89, 770.

Adurus, the name of an estate. VII, 767.

Aventinus, king of Latium, added to the number of the gods. VII, 577.

Mount Aventine. V, 63. Why it is so called. VII, 577.

The pit of Avernus. X, 1069.

To turn away. God must be asked not to turn his face away from us, but from our sins. V, 132.

The turning of the will away from the unchangeable good toward a changeable good—whether one’s own, external, or inferior—makes a person proud, curious, or wanton. I, 1269. By turning away from God, a person is darkened; by turning toward God, he is enlightened. IV, 193.

How the birds were created by God from the waters. III, 183. Birds do not fly in the firmament but according to the firmament. III, 283. Birds cannot fly in the higher air. III, 237. Four-footed birds. I, 636. The life of birds is highly skilled both in memory and chatter, and in building nests and raising their young. III, 283. Birds possess strong memory. I, 790. Some birds do not drink water. III, 237. Birds are called not living souls but flying creatures of living souls. III, 284. Why Abraham did not divide the birds in the sacrifice. IV, 1362.

The name “grandfather” is sometimes applied to a father. III, 494.

The difference between “to take away” and “to remove.” IV, 908.

[Col. 0091] Augendiarensis, or Augendus, bishop of Arles. IV, 381.

How unlawful auguries differ from lawful signs. III, 564.

Cicero ridicules auguries. VII, 136.

Augustine was born on the Ides of November. I, 962. At Thagaste, a municipality of Africa. I, 677. Born and raised among the inland peoples. II, 70. He calls the people of Madaura his brothers and parents. II, 1029. His parents were Patricius and Monnica. I, 870. His father, a citizen of Thagaste, was very poor. I, 677. Augustine professes that he was a poor man born of poor people. V, 1580. Augustine’s parents differed in faith and morals. I, 669, 677. His brother was Navigius. I, 962, 980.
