His sister was placed over a community of nuns. II, 959. His cousins were Lastidianus and Rusticus. I, 962. His kinsman was Licentius. II, 106. And Severinus the Donatist. II, 194. His mother and the whole household, except his father, believed in Christ. I, 669.

Augustine’s infancy. I, 664. From whom he learned to speak. I, 666, 671.

Augustine’s childhood. I, 666. From his mother’s womb Augustine was brought up in the Christian religion. I, 668, 921. His parents placed him among the catechumens. I, 729. He was marked with the sign of the Cross and initiated with the sacrament of salt. I, 668, 921. Monnica strove that God should be Augustine’s father. I, 669. His father did not overcome in him the right of his mother’s devotion, so as to prevent him from believing in Christ. I, 669. While still a boy and suffering from stomach trouble, Augustine earnestly and devoutly demanded baptism. I, 669. When his health was restored, baptism was postponed. I, 669.

Augustine was sent to school to learn letters. I, 667. He recoiled from the rudiments of letters, where one learns to read, write, and count. I, 670. He loved Latin letters and hated Greek. I, 670. He learned Latin letters amid the coaxing of his nurses. I, 671. At that time he understood, as best he could, that there was some great God who could hear and help even without appearing to the senses. I, 667. How greatly he feared being beaten at school. I, 667. He confesses that he sinned by writing, reading, or thinking about letters less than was required. I, 668. He loved to play, proud victories in contests, and having his ears scratched by false stories. I, 668. By innumerable lies he deceived his tutor, teachers, and parents. I, 674. His thefts at home. I, 674. He sought fraudulent victories in play. I, 674. He was devoted to gluttony and anger. I, 674. What was rightly set before him as the way to live. I, 667. His only concern was to become eloquent. I, 677. While exercising himself in school, he was applauded above many of his peers and fellow students. I, 673. Because of his progress in letters he was called a boy of good promise. I, 673. He was brought back from Madaura, to which city he had traveled in order to acquire literary and rhetorical learning. I, 677.

At the age of sixteen Augustine spent a year in his father’s house, his studies interrupted, indulging his temperament and his lusts. I, 675. During the intervening leisure, the brambles of lust grew. I, 675. He regarded his mother’s admonitions as fit for women. I, 678. Yet he was never insulting or harsh in speech toward his mother. I, 776. Augustine committed a nocturnal theft. I, 678. Among his peers he was ashamed of being guilty of a lesser disgrace. I, 678. He enjoyed doing evil, not only because of the pleasure of the deed but also because of the praise it brought. I, 678. For this reason he pretended that he had done what he had not done. I, 678.

At the age of seventeen Augustine was sent to Carthage for his studies. I, 683. He was captivated by theatrical spectacles. I, 683. He was captivated by love. I, 683. To be loved and to love was sweet to him, especially if he could also enjoy the body of the one who loved him. I, 683. During the celebration of sacred festivals he lusted within the walls of the church. I, 685. For this sin he was scourged by God. I, 685. Augustine became advanced in the school of rhetoric. I, 685. His studies tended toward the contentious courts. I, 685. Augustine recoiled from the brazen behavior of his fellow students, who were called “subverters,” yet he was ashamed with an impudent shame that he was not like them. I, 685, 712. About this time he lost his father. I, 685.

Augustine continued his studies, with his mother supplying the expense. I, 685. Romanianus, his Maecenas, also assisted him. I, 920. Cicero’s *Hortensius* kindled Augustine’s pursuit of wisdom. I, 685, 757, 961. He burned to fly back from earthly things to God. I, 686. How deeply he had absorbed the love and reverence of Christ’s name from childhood. I, 686. He neglected Scripture, considering it unworthy of comparison with the dignity of Tullian eloquence. I, 686.

As a young man, a layman and catechumen, Augustine fell into the heresy of the Manichaeans. I, 686; VIII, 174, 304; IX, 591. He was deceived by the Manichaeans. IX, 545. He was deceived in a twofold way. VIII, 102. Why he fell in with the Manichaeans. VIII, 66. Among the Manichaeans he was not an Elect but a Hearer. VIII, 113. His errors at that time concerning God. I, 687, 703, 704, 705, 715, 736. Concerning Christ. I, 716. Concerning the nature of evil. I, 715. Concerning the Old Law. I, 688. Concerning the cause of sin. I, 735. In investigating this he was tormented. I, 736. Concerning rational and irrational nature. I, 703. Concerning the fruits of the earth. I, 691. Augustine led others into the Manichaean heresy. I, 693. Among them was Romanianus. I, 920. And Alypius. I, 725. He remained in it for nine years, namely from the nineteenth to the twenty-eighth year of his life. I, 692, 710, 1326, 1374; VIII, 66, 180. His preconceived opinion concerning the holiness of Manichaeus. I, 710. In the difficulties Augustine raised, he was referred to Faustus. I, 710. Monnica, detesting his errors, withdrew from Augustine’s companionship. I, 691. Before God she mourned his ruin. I, 691. Monnica was warned in a dream of his future recovery. I, 691. And by the reply of a certain bishop. I, 691. Augustine was himself called “the son of tears.” I, 692.

Augustine taught the liberal disciplines. I, 693. And rhetoric. I, 693. First at Thagaste. I, 696, 925. Then at Carthage. I, 712, 724. He had moved there because of the impatience of his grief at the death of a certain friend. I, 698. And also for the sake of a more distinguished profession. I, 920. In both cities he had Alypius as a hearer. I, 724. He turned him away from the madness of the circus. I, 725. Driven by a desire for empty glory, he entered a poetic contest. I, 693. He detested the haruspex who promised him the prize in the literary competition. I, 694. Augustine was accustomed to consult the astrologers. I, 694. The old man Vindicianus tried in vain to call him away from them. I, 695. And so did Nebridius. I, 696, 737. He finally understood that this kind of divination was vain after hearing Firminus’s account, and rejected it entirely. I, 737. Augustine kept a concubine and remained faithful to her bed. I, 693, 732. By her he had a son named Adeodatus. I, 769. See Adeodatus.

At about the age of twenty Augustine understood Aristotle’s *Categories* and the books of the liberal arts by himself. I, 704. How great were Augustine’s intellectual skill and clarity. I, 705. He was erring in the teaching of piety with shameful deformity and sacrilegious disgrace. I, 706. At that time he held false ideas about God. I, 705. How he fell into love of things that are seized by time. I, 701. Augustine wrote two or three books on the Beautiful and the Fitting. I, 701. At about the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year of his life. I, 704. He dedicated them to Hierius, an orator of the city of Rome. I, 702.

Faustus, long desired and long awaited by Augustine, came to Carthage. I, 707. Augustine began to become alienated from the Manichaeans when he discovered Faustus’s incompetence, at about the age of twenty-nine. I, 711. Yet he did not withdraw completely. I, 711. From the beginning of adolescence Augustine burned with a desire to find and retain the truth. VIII, 65, 66, 78, 79. Augustine believed that, through his mother’s prayers, he had been granted a mind that placed nothing whatsoever before the discovery of truth. I, 1019.

Weary of the laxity of the Carthaginian students, Augustine sailed to Rome. I, 712. His mother was unwilling and deceived. I, 712. At Rome Augustine was seized by a fever and fell dangerously ill. I, 713. He recovered in the house of a certain Manichaean. I, 714. At Rome he associated with both Manichaean Hearers and Elect. I, 714. He was not yet free from their insane opinion concerning the nature of evil. I, 714. He despaired of finding the truth among the Manichaeans. I, 715. He supported the Academics, who judged everything uncertain. I, 715. Familiarity with the Manichaeans weakened his zeal for investigating the truth. I, 715. His errors concerning evil, the nature of God, and the Incarnation. I, 715. What held Augustine in error. I, 716.

Augustine taught rhetoric at Rome. I, 716. Augustine’s students at Rome were quieter than those at Carthage. I, 716. Many suddenly conspired together so as not to pay the teacher’s fee. I, 716. Why he then hated such people. I, 716.

Augustine was sent to Milan by Symmachus, prefect of the city, to teach rhetoric. I, 717. Augustine was kindly received by Ambrose. I, 717. He was captivated by his affection. I, 717. And delighted by his eloquence. I, 717. He despaired that truth could be found in the Catholic Church. I, 717. By listening to Ambrose, he gradually admitted the truth. I, 717. He decided that the Manichaeans must be abandoned. I, 717. What recalled Augustine from the Manichaean sect. VIII, 66. He was moved by Helpidius’s disputation against the Manichaeans at Carthage. I, 716. And also by Nebridius’s argument against them. I, 734. With what fear and desire he abandoned the Manichaeans. VIII, 577, 578. How he was recalled from admitting two natures. VIII, 130. After hearing an exposition of one or another passage of Scripture, Augustine recognized that the Catholic faith could be defended against the Manichaeans. I, 718. Yet, still doubting everything, he decided to remain a catechumen in the Catholic Church until something certain should become clear. I, 718. He would have recoiled easily from error if he had been able to conceive of a spiritual substance. I, 718. Why Augustine’s attempts to investigate the truth were fruitless. I, 720.

Augustine, in his thirtieth year, is neither a Manichaean nor a Catholic. I, 719. He reports this to his mother Monica, who was arriving at Milan. I, 719. He understands the Church’s teaching more and more clearly as Ambrose preaches. I, 721. He recognizes the necessity of faith and the authority of the Scriptures. I, 722. He still longs for honors, profits, and marriage. I, 723. He is taught the vanity of ambition and desires when he sees a beggar joking and rejoicing over wine. I, 723. Augustine delivers a panegyric in praise of the Emperor. I, 723. Perhaps of Valentinian the Younger. I, 723. He delivered a panegyric at Milan to the consul Bauton. IX, 362.

Augustine is anxious about the way of life he should undertake. I, 728. He postpones his conversion from one day to the next. I, 729. Alypius tries to dissuade Augustine from entering upon marriage. I, 730. A wife is sought for Augustine, so that he may be baptized as a married man. I, 730. His mother seeks a revelation concerning his future marriage, but in vain. I, 729. After permitting his concubine to return to Africa, Augustine himself obtains another. I, 730. Augustine was being recalled from the whirlpool of carnal pleasures by fear of death and of the future judgment. I, 732. This fear never departed from his heart. I, 732. He deliberates with his friends about living a common life. I, 731. About ten were soon to form one association; from their number, two at a time would provide for the necessities of the year, while the others remained at rest. I, 731. This plan is abandoned. I, 731.

Augustine, in his thirty-first year, still wanders enveloped in the darkness of ignorance concerning the nature of God. I, 733. Yet rising gradually through contemplation, he finally reaches what truly is, though he cannot fix his gaze upon it. I, 745. Augustine believes in Christ with a firm faith, but one not yet formed. I, 737. And an erroneous one. I, 746. He gradually becomes accustomed to the Church’s teaching, which he had condemned so vehemently. I, 721. And he prefers it to the teaching of the Manichaeans. I, 722. His parents had always commended the Catholic Church to him. I, 718.

By what path Augustine came to the Catholic religion. VIII, 78, 79. He never doubted the existence of God. I, 723. Nevertheless, he did not think rightly about God, because he was still compelled to conceive of something corporeal. I, 723. Reading the books of the Platonists helps him to discover the truth. I, 740, 961. From these books he emerges more learned, indeed, but also more inflated. I, 746. Augustine turns to Sacred Scripture, and especially to the Apostle. I, 747. Through reading him he makes remarkable progress. I, 747, 921.

In his thirty-second year Augustine is displeased with conducting himself in the world. I, 749. Yet he is held back by love of a woman. I, 749. The power of bad habit over Augustine. I, 754. He was bound, not by another’s iron, but by his own iron will. I, 753. How entangled he had once been in the life of this world. VIII, 67. Augustine approaches Simplicianus. I, 753. He is moved and distressed when he hears from Simplicianus about Victorinus’s conversion. I, 751. He is moved when Pontitianus recounts the life of Antony. I, 755. And when he hears of the conversion of two agents in the imperial service. I, 756. As a young man Augustine asked God for chastity, but did not wish to be heard quickly. I, 763.

Augustine withdraws into a garden, with Alypius following him. I, 758. The struggles of his spirit and flesh. I, 758. Augustine neither fully wished nor fully did not wish to convert; therefore he contended with himself. I, 759. In him the worse, long-established habit had greater power than the better, unfamiliar one. I, 760. Concerning the difficulties he overcame himself. I, 921, 961. Augustine withdraws a little from Alypius, throws himself down beneath a fig tree, pours forth a flood of tears, and implores God’s mercy. I, 761. At the prompting of a voice Augustine reads the Apostle and is wholly converted. I, 762. He informs his mother. I, 762. His mother rejoices, exults, and triumphs over her son’s conversion, and blesses God. I, 762.

Augustine is freed from error chiefly through the mouth of Ambrose, and is baptized by him. II, 621; X, 436, 645. He was baptized across the sea in a Church known throughout the whole world. IV, 394. Augustine’s conversion was granted through the faith and daily tears of his mother. X, 1026. Augustine embraces a celibate life, abandoning every hope of the world. I, 762. He postpones abandoning his profession of rhetoric until the autumn vacation. I, 762. He excuses this delay of only a very few days. I, 764. Although he does not deny that it was not free from blame. I, 765. Augustine finally abandons his teaching office. I, 767. Certainly compelled by anguish of heart. I, 764, 769, 907, 961, 980. But more strongly attracted by the desire to devote himself to God. I, 764; II, 67.

During the autumn vacation Augustine withdraws with his companions to Verecundus’s estate at Cassiciacum. I, 765. He spends the leisure of the countryside in the study of wisdom. I, 907. For the sake of discovering truth, he was accustomed to remain awake for nearly half the night. I, 981. With daily weeping he asks God that his wounds may be healed. I, 991.

By letter Augustine asks Ambrose what, above all, he should read in the Scriptures so as to prepare himself worthily for baptism. I, 769. He is instructed to read Isaiah. I, 769. Augustine composes several books there and writes letters to Nebridius. I, 766. Augustine takes care in educating his pupils Licentius and Trygetius. I, 908, 980. Every day before dinner he listens to half a volume of Virgil. I, 989, 924. He teaches them precepts of conduct. I, 620. He restrains childish impulses of rivalry and empty boasting. I, 991. He asks that they repay their teacher’s fee by being good. I, 991. Augustine begins the books Against the Academics a few days after his withdrawal, at the end of his thirty-second year, in the year of Christ 386. I, 905, 908. Augustine writes the book On the Happy Life on the Ides of November in the year of Christ 386, on which day he was entering his thirty-third year. I, 959, 962. He disputes with Alypius and Nebridius about the ends of good and evil. I, 732. He publishes the books On Order at the same time. I, 977; 980. Augustine later completes the books Against the Academics. I, 924. As a catechumen taking leisure in the country with the catechumen Alypius, Augustine is deeply moved by the recitation of the Psalms. I, 766. He meditates on the fourth Psalm, piously burning against the Manichaeans. [Col. 0094] I, 766. Augustine is tormented by extremely severe toothache. I, 768, 880. Augustine prays with his companions, and the pain departs. I, 768. Augustine writes the Soliloquies in his thirty-third year, in the year of Christ 387. I, 869, 878. What his character and feelings were at that time. I, 877.

Augustine returns to Milan to enroll among those to be baptized. I, 769. There, in the year of Christ 387, he writes the book On the Immortality of the Soul. I, 1021. And he begins the books on the Disciplines. I, 591. Augustine is baptized with Alypius and Adeodatus. I, 769. His spiritual joy after baptism, when all anxiety about his former life had departed. I, 769. Tears and movements of devotion at the hymns and songs of the Church. I, 769, 801.

Augustine undertakes the return to Africa with his companions. I, 771. At Ostia on the Tiber Augustine converses with his mother about eternal life, and both are carried away into contemplation of it. I, 774. This world and its pleasures become worthless to them. I, 775. Then, scarcely five days later, Monica falls ill; on the ninth day of her illness, in her fifty-sixth year and Augustine’s thirty-third year, she is released from the body. I, 776. Augustine mourns her death. I, 776. He follows the funeral, celebrated according to solemn custom, without tears. I, 777. Augustine prays for her salvation. I, 778. Augustine remains in Rome, and there, in the year of Christ 387, writes the books On the Morals of the Catholic Church and On the Morals of the Manichaeans. I, 1310. There also he begins the books On Free Will in the same year; he later completes them in Africa in the year 395. I, 1222. After returning to Africa Augustine writes two books On Genesis Against the Manichaeans. III, 171, 172. Around the year of Christ 389. III, 174. About that time he completes the books On Music, which he had begun at Milan in the year 387. I, 1082. Likewise the book On the Teacher with Adeodatus. I, 769, 1194. The book On True Religion, while he was not yet a presbyter. III, 121, 122. See below, where Augustine’s works are discussed. Augustine traveled across the sea; one went, another returned. IV, 394. When he returned to Africa. IX, 362.

Augustine’s delights: to be occupied with the remembrance of God. I, 794. His hope rests only on God’s very great mercy. I, 796. Augustine withdraws from necessary activities, as far as he can be released from them, into the contemplation of God. I, 807. His chaste delights are the divine Scriptures. I, 810. If he has any free time, he spends all of it on them. I, 810. Augustine, at one time considering a withdrawal into solitude, is forbidden by God, so that he may live not for himself alone but for others. I, 808. His love for God is intense. I, 782, 795. He loved God not with a doubtful but with a certain conscience. I, 782. Augustine is incited by the devil to ask God for some sign. I, 803. He regrets that he once attended spectacles. IV, 1919.

As a young man, having abandoned every hope of the world, Augustine comes to Hippo while seeking a place to establish a monastery, in order to visit a friend whom he wishes to have with him in the monastery serving God. V, 1569. Augustine establishes a monastery at Hippo in a garden given by Valerius. V, 1569. Augustine’s monastery. X, 1017.

Before his presbyterate Augustine enjoys a reputation among the servants of God. V, 1569. The people of Hippo seek Augustine for the clerical order. II, 480. Augustine is seized and becomes a presbyter. V, 1569; and he is ordained unwillingly. II, 88. Valerius lays upon Augustine the burden of preaching. II, 117. Augustine asks for a period of time until Easter, so that in retirement he may devote himself to prayers and study. II, 89. Augustine is permitted to remain silent only very rarely wherever, in Valerius’s presence, it is necessary to speak to the people. I, 584. Now created a presbyter of Hippo, Augustine disputes against the Manichaean Fortunatus. I, 612. And for two days against Felix. I, 633.

Augustine is made Valerius’s co-bishop. II, 123, 126; V, 1570. With Christ’s Nativity approaching. II, 123. How intensely he feared the episcopate. V, 1569. Augustine is ordained by Megalius, bishop of Calama. IX, 357, Note (a), and in Appendix 834. He sheds tears at the time of his ordination. II, 88. Augustine is ordained and takes his seat as bishop while Valerius is still alive, both of them unaware that this had been prohibited by the Council of Nicaea. II, 967. Augustine wishes to preside over the Church not so much as to benefit it. II, 511.

Augustine abandoned everything. II, 692. He says that, when he became a bishop, it seemed to him not that he had abandoned riches but that he had come to riches. II, 480. Augustine maintains with himself a monastery of clerics in the bishop’s house. V, 1570. Petilianus charged Augustine with having instituted the monastic way of life. IX, 372. Augustine wore shoes. V, 809.

Augustine’s household was administered with vigilant care. II, 271. Augustine decides to be content with only the food necessary for bodily health. VIII, 67. Augustine considers it improper for him, in food and clothing, to have anything that is not suitable for his fellow members, the deacons and subdeacons. V, 1580. Augustine does not allow the clerics to possess anything privately; but, thinking well of his brothers, he pretends not to investigate. V, 1569. Augustine does not permit his men to lunch or dine outside. V, 1580. He does not accept anyone’s inheritance when the children have been disinherited. V, 1571. He grieves bitterly over a will made by Januarius the cleric. V, 1570. Although Januarius’s will was made for the benefit of the Church, he regards it as invalid. V, 1570. Augustine is compelled to address the people concerning the life of his clerics. V, 1575. Augustine’s concern for his reputation. V, 1577. Augustine had decided to ordain no one who was unwilling to embrace the purpose of the holy community, so that if he later departed he would lose the clerical office; after changing his mind, he offers clerics permission to depart while retaining their clerical status. V, 1575. Finally, after learning the firm resolve of his companions, he decides that any cleric who violates the purpose of poverty is to be struck from the clerical register. V, 1580. Augustine wishes what the faithful offer to his clerics to be surrendered for common use. V, 1579.

Augustine was never absent from Hippo through self-indulgent freedom, but through necessary servitude. II, 470. Augustine went to Caesarean Mauritania because of an ecclesiastical necessity. I, 650; II, 869. See the Notes. Sent by Pope Zosimus. II, 857. Augustine finds it burdensome to write lengthy letters, lest he fail in his pastoral duty. II, 421. Augustine places every other duty, even those of charity, below the obligations of his rank. II, 421. He complains that for a whole day he is entangled in people’s affairs, as before. II, 968. He asks for leisure so that he may devote himself to the Scriptures. II, 968. The people of Hippo had agreed that, because of Augustine’s care for the Scriptures, no one should trouble him for five days of the week. II, 967. How diligently Augustine meditated on the law of the Lord. VIII, 823. At times, when he approaches the divine Scriptures without a devout mind, he is deceived. V, 356.

In speaking Augustine does not fear the grammarians’ criticism, provided that everyone is instructed. IV, 1796, 274; V, 228. Augustine, unprepared, delivers a sermon as the occasion arises. V, 1549. Augustine preferred to follow God’s will in the reader’s error rather than his own intention in the Psalm he had previously planned to expound. IV, 1784. Augustine carries Scripture in his hands while preaching. III, 1685; V, 221. Augustine reads from a codex. V, 1628. Augustine often uses non-Latin words so that the people may understand. IV, 1644. On solemn days Augustine postpones his sermon because there are many for whom the word of God is burdensome. V, 333. Augustine leaves something for his hearers to ponder and discuss. V, 364. In sermons to the people he admits that he had always avoided the question of sins against the Holy Spirit. V, 449. Impelled by God, he treats it. V, 449. When Augustine is appealed to by the poor, he asks, advises, and orders that things be given to them, as though he were their representative. V, 413. Augustine becomes a beggar of beggars. V, 433. Augustine’s exhaustion during the Easter vigil. V, 1442.

Augustine’s prudent charity in instructing the uneducated. VI, 328. Augustine’s modesty and restraint in publicly reproving women. V, 205. When Augustine preaches, the hearers acclaim him. V, 134, 530, 1374. During Augustine’s preaching tears arise in the hearers. II, 117. Augustine dissuaded the people of Caesarean Mauritania from the savage custom of civil combat. III, 115. Augustine calls himself the watchdog of the flock. IX, 353. Augustine’s modesty in preaching. IV, 741, 1668, 1945. Augustine does not commend himself to the people, but God, to whom he also commends them. IV, 1952. He spoke to the people from a place that was, as it were, higher, but through fear he was beneath the feet of his hearers. IV, 812. Augustine urges his people to sustain him by living well. V, 1481. Augustine delights only in the progress of his hearers. IV, 812. And in the good life of his sheep. V, 128. Augustine does not wish to be safe without his sheep. V, 125. Augustine does not want his reward to be secure through lost and disobedient sheep, but through sheep that have been found. V, 514, 1597. Augustine is a shepherd, not a hireling. V, 762. Augustine’s zeal to assist ministers of the word of God. VI, 311. Augustine rereads what had been read, taking the book from the deacon. V, 1574. Augustine takes Cyprian into his hands and reads him. V, 1347.

Augustine is again called the founder of the ancient faith. II, 891. Augustine labors against heretics by disputing, convincing, meeting with, and terrifying them, while nevertheless loving them all. IV, 433. Augustine defeats the Manichaean Fortunatus in debate. II, 273. See the Notes. He held a public debate with Fortunatus. II, 174. Augustine, having undertaken with great trepidation to introduce the mystery of the Trinity lest he weary the slower minds, thanks God that matters turned out otherwise. V, 363. A letter bearing Augustine’s signature is sent concerning Leporius. II, 992. Augustine writes to Provectus and Cillinnius asking them to receive Leporius, now penitent and reformed. II, 992.

With what state of mind Augustine disputed against the Donatists. IX, 449, 450, 451. With what attitude he approached refuting the Council held at Carthage by Cyprian. IX, 202. Augustine refrains from cataloguing the Donatists’ crimes and excuses them as far as he can. V, 306, 1595. He tries to avert the death penalty from certain Donatists accused of grave crimes. II, 535, 536. Augustine writes letters to lay Donatists. II, 537. He held that laws should not be sought from the Emperors against the Donatists. II, 804. He had believed that no one should be compelled to the unity of Christ. II, 329. Later he changed his mind. II, 329. Augustine held that Theodosius’s law against heretics should be observed. II, 804. When Augustine spoke and exhorted at Cirta, many Donatists were converted. II, 591. Augustine’s inward anguish when a Donatist returning to the Church was rejected by the brothers. V, 1358. Augustine is called a heretic by those whom he could have called by that name but does not. V, 1348. Augustine often suffers the Donatists’ ambushes. IV, 1605. Augustine’s fortunate error at the crossroads. VI, 239. Augustine responded to Orosius in one book concerning the Priscillianist heresy and certain opinions of Origen. II, 748.

Augustine and the other African bishops begin to be involved in opposition to the Pelagians. II, 537. In the year of Christ 411 or 412. II, 537. Augustine reports four opinions concerning the origin of souls in the books On Free Will. II, 723. He defines nothing concerning that origin. II, 857. Augustine is accused, together with the Catholics, concerning the transmission of souls. X, 1218. He is rashly accused of already being a Manichaean. IX, 545. If Augustine is a Manichaean because he asserts original sin, then Ambrose too is a Manichaean. X, 1402, 1404, 1414, 1417.

Augustine admits that he once held an incorrect view of the grace of God. X, 964. At one time he believed that faith was not a gift of God. III, 2061, Retr. He did not attend the episcopal judgment held at Carthage against Caelestius. I, 644. He detests and abhors the denial of grace in the Pelagians’ debates. X, 252, 272. Augustine had not initially grasped the Apostle’s meaning concerning the election of grace. III, 2061. And *Retr.*, book 1, chapter XXIII. Bishop Claudius sends Julian’s books to Augustine. II, 949. Augustine sends another work against Julian to Bishop Claudius. II, 950. Julian’s calumny against Augustine concerning grace and free will. X, 762, 1122. Julian tries to make Augustine an Apollinarian. X, 814. He calls Augustine the Epicurus of his own age. X, 726, 1464. He calls him a worshiper of the devil. X, 720. A letter written by Primas against Augustine is condemned in a council of bishops. IX, 591.

The Fathers of two councils, of Numidia and Carthage, entrusted Augustine with the care of the Scriptures. II, 968. Honorius and Theodosius write to Augustine concerning the Pelagian heresy. II, 927. See the Notes. The Massilians and Semi-Pelagians decree that the testimony Augustine had cited from Wisdom 4:11, as non-canonical, should be omitted. II, 1009. Augustine’s faith concerning the Holy Trinity. II, 1042, 1050. All heretics detest Augustine and Jerome. II, 891.

Augustine loved Jerome with the deepest affection. II, 289. Augustine dissuades Jerome from translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew. II, 242. How he wishes the books of the Old Testament to be translated by Jerome into Latin. II, 112. He urges Jerome to render the corrupted and varying version of the Septuagint according to Latin truth. II, 244. He requests this interpretation of the Septuagint which Jerome had published. II, 291. Augustine receives Jerome’s apology against Rufinus. II, 247. He grieves that the evil of discord had arisen between persons so close—namely Jerome and Rufinus. II, 248. He asks Jerome to expose the errors of Origen and of the heretics. II, 157. He requests letters and writings from Jerome. II, 241. He receives letters from Jerome. II, 154. Julian calls Augustine Jerome’s follower. X, 1417.

Augustine debates with Jerome concerning observance of the Law. II, 257, 260. In what Augustine’s and Jerome’s opinions differ concerning observance of the Law. II, 260. Augustine concerning Peter rebuked by Paul. II, 111, 156, 253, 255, 257. Augustine’s opinion agrees with the view of Cyprian and Ambrose. II, 286. Augustine denies that he wrote a book against Jerome and sent it to Rome. II, 237. Certain people at Jerusalem accused Augustine of seeking popular glory in writing his letter against Jerome. II, 244. In Augustine’s letter to Jerome, Jerome himself judges certain matters to be heretical. II, 244. Augustine replies to Jerome with humility. II, 246, 249, 289. He asks Jerome’s pardon. II, 246, 276, 290. And asks to be instructed. II, 276. Jerome came over to Augustine’s opinion. II, 290, note 779.

How devoted Augustine was to truth. VIII, 887. In what manner he prepared himself to investigate the truth. VIII, 68. And with what state of mind he debated questions. VIII, 822. How he prepared himself to resolve an ambiguous question. VIII, 98. Augustine once held the opinion that the future bodily resurrection would occur before the universal resurrection. VII, 667. Augustine does not approve what is instituted contrary to custom, so that it may appear to be an observance of the Sacrament. II, 221. He does not wish pagan idols to be broken unless permission has first been given. V, 422. The habit of swearing was overcome by him. V, 977, 1407.

Augustine’s modesty amid praise. II, 848, 1076. How he conducts himself toward human praise. I, 804; II, 93, 109, 420; V, 414, 1480. Augustine, knowing that false detraction increases his reward, does not want that reward to come at another’s expense. V, 1581. He preferred to be rebuked by one who censured falsehood, even though he was not conscious of it himself, rather than to be praised by his praiser. VIII, 823, 824, 844. What sort of praise, and from whom, Augustine forbids himself to receive. II, 1023. Augustine is less delighted by the voices of those who praise than by the voices of those who confess, and by the deeds of the upright. IV, 812.

How Augustine conducts himself toward temptations of carnal lust. I, 796. And toward temptations of gluttony. I, 797. Augustine was never a drunkard. I, 798. How he conducts himself toward the allurements of odors. I, 799. How he conducts himself toward the second kind of temptation, namely curiosity. I, 800. How he conducts himself toward the allurements of the eyes. I, 800. How he conducts himself toward the third kind of temptation, pride. I, 804. How he conducts himself toward pleasures of the ears. I, 799.

Augustine’s modesty. III, 1574; VI, 146, 159; VII, 337, 363, 365, 682, 686, 776; VIII, 678, 911; X, 523, 526, 547, 1027, 1034. Augustine’s devotion and modesty. VIII, 678, 911. Augustine’s modesty after expounding a difficult passage of Scripture. V, 466. Augustine’s modesty amid calumnies. II, 136; IX, 351, 353, 355. Augustine did not fear human detraction. IV, 1152. Augustine clears himself of detraction but does not name the detractors. V, 1579. What Augustine was like in accusations and calumnies brought against him. IX, 351, 353, 355. On account of his rhetoric, Petilianus designated Augustine by the appellation of Tertullus the orator. IX, 356. Having written maliciously about Augustine while he was still a presbyter, Petilianus asked pardon from the holy Council and obtained it. IX, 357. He said that Augustine was a Manichaean. IX, 354, 356, 545. And he said that Augustine was a presbyter of the Manichaeans. IX, 357. Petilianus said that Augustine possessed the condemnable genius of the Academic Carneades. IX, 359. And he rashly said that Augustine had been struck by the judgment of the proconsul Messianus. IX, 362. Whenever Augustine replies to anyone, whether in speech or writing, he does not return insults for insults. IX, 347. Cresconius’s foolish calumnies against Augustine. IX, 544. Augustine’s confidence in his own conscience. IX, 545. Augustine concedes to Cresconius that he does not yet know how to decline nouns. IX, 467.

While Augustine was established at Milan, he appeared in a dream—without knowing it himself—to Eulogius, the rhetor of Carthage, and expounded a passage of Cicero. VI, 601. He also often appears to two sick men, while remaining equally unaware of it himself. V, 1444, 1445.

Augustine strives to separate his love from what can be absent from him against his will. II, 63. In judging, or in suspecting anything evil of anyone, Augustine is especially cautious. II, 267, 269. Augustine’s gentleness and mercy toward the wicked shine forth on the occasion of someone being beaten in a riot. V, 1389. Augustine takes great pains to reconcile to himself a bishop whom he had offended with rather harsh letters. II, 623. He receives with a kindly and even temper the books of a young man who had written arrogantly against him. X, 473.

Augustine’s humility. II, 516; III, 121. His modesty. III, 411, 393, 431, 469, 470; X, 523. Augustine says that many things remain hidden from him in the Sacred Scriptures. II, 222. He says that he does not know the Hebrew language. II, 369. Augustine is not very familiar with the Greek language. VIII, 868, 869. Augustine’s modesty in defining matters. IX, 242, 243, 575. His attitude in accepting the answers of a wise man. VI, 597. Augustine does not wish to be regarded as a teacher. V, 155.

Augustine loves learning more than teaching. II, 643. He prefers listening to speaking. VI, 161, 170; IV, 1612. Augustine, already an old man, does not disdain learning something through the work and studies of young men. IV, 1354. Among preachers, he calls himself a cloudy cloud. IV, 1345. Augustine is almost always displeased with his own speech. VI, 311. Not so with that of others. VI, 312. Augustine does not cling stubbornly to his own opinion. III, 315. “Anyone can easily defeat Augustine,” he says of himself. II, 1048. Speaking about the generation of the Word, Augustine says: “If I am unable to explain it, do not suppose that the reason has failed, but that the man has failed.” V, 664.

What Augustine asks of his readers. VIII, 822, 823. How he wished his books to be read or corrected. VIII, 869. He does not wish canonical authority to be attributed to his writings. II, 628, 873. How much authority he wishes to be attributed to his writings. II, 585. He does not wish anyone to embrace all his writings so completely as to follow him, except in those matters where that person has seen that Augustine did not err. X, 1027. Augustine committed his meditations to writing so that they would not escape through forgetfulness. VIII, 823.

Augustine wants his short works to be read in the order in which they were written. I, 584. Augustine’s three books Against the Academics. I, 905. He wrote the books on the Academics to restore to hope of finding the truth those whom the Academics’ position had perhaps deterred from grasping realities. II, 62. Augustine writes at Rome the book On the Quantity of the Soul, around the beginning of the year 388. I, 1036. Augustine’s three books On Free Will. VIII, 588; X, 286. He sends these books to Paulinus. II, 125. Augustine wrote On Genesis Literally. VI, 166. Augustine undertook to demonstrate that an exposition of Genesis according to the literal sense is neither impossible nor contrary to the authority of Scripture. III, 401; and he explains the matter literally. III, 374. At the beginning of his conversion he wrote two books On Genesis Against the Manichaeans according to allegory. III, 373. Why. III, 373. In the books on Genesis Augustine speaks according to the proper meaning of the events that occurred, not according to the enigmas of figures. III, 259. Why Augustine, in interpreting Genesis, often asserts nothing. III, 261. Augustine fails when expounding the Scriptures according to the literal sense. III, 219.

Augustine ennobled poetry through the books On Music. II, 513, note. Augustine completes at Rome the books On Music, which he had begun at Milan in the year 387. I, 1082. For what purpose Augustine wrote the books On Music. II, 369. Augustine’s six extant books On Music deal only with rhythm. II, 369. Augustine’s sixth book On Music contains the whole benefit of those that survive. II, 359. Augustine intended to write another six books on melody. II, 359.

Augustine wrote something concerning the Catholic religion. II, 81. He wrote the book On True Religion while not yet a presbyter, around the year 390. III, 121, 122. At what time Augustine’s book On the Usefulness of Believing was written. VIII, 63, 64. And with what attitude. VIII, 65, 66. Augustine’s book Against Adimantus. VIII, 664, 665, 666. Augustine delivers a sermon On Faith and the Creed at the plenary council of Africa at Hippo. I, 612. Augustine sent books against the Manichaeans to Caelestinus. II, 85. Augustine’s two books to Simplicianus. X, 1027. The books On Christian Doctrine. VIII, 461. The books of the Confessions. VIII, 186. The third book of the Confessions. IX, 357. Augustine publishes the books of the Confessions around the year 400, already long a bishop. I, 658, 659. Darius requests Augustine’s books of the Confessions. II, 1022. The books of the Confessions were written before the Pelagian heresy arose. X, 1026. What Augustine’s character was during the period when he wrote the books of the Confessions. I, 779 and following, to the end of book X.

Augustine’s work against Faustus. III, 555, 597, 1045, 1573; VI, 166, 442; VII, 473; VIII, 664. Augustine promises a work On the City of God. III, 437. Book 1 of On the City of God. III, 816. Augustine began the books On the Trinity as a young man and published them as an old man. II, 758. Augustine sends the completed and corrected books to Aurelius. II, 758. Augustine does not wish to publish the books On Genesis and On the Trinity sooner, because they contain extremely dangerous questions that must be carefully examined. II, 587. Augustine’s books On the Trinity, On Genesis Literally, and Against Faustus. IX, 245, 246, *Retr.* Augustine’s *Brief Summary* of On the Trinity. VIII, 1058, 1059. For what purpose and at what time Augustine wrote the twelve books On Genesis. III, 244. Cassiodorus praises these books. III, 244. Augustine’s books On the Good of Marriage. X, 142. Augustine writes On the Good of Marriage and On Holy Virginity. VI, 442, 450; X, 142. At Juliana’s request Augustine writes On the Good of Widowhood. VI, 431.

Augustine’s work On the Baptism of Infants. VII, 379. Augustine’s book to Marcellinus. X, 254, 260, 335, 1401, 1402; a letter against Petilianus. IX, 480. Augustine’s book On the Spirit and the Letter. III, 83; VI, 211; On Faith and Works. VI, 149, 154. Augustine writes a memorandum to Fortunatianus of Sicca concerning Seeing God. II, 596. Augustine’s book On Nature and Grace. X, 338, 347. Augustine’s books On the City. VIII, 34, 613, 1023. Augustine completes the first five books On the City. II, 742. Augustine disputes against Emeritus at Caesarea in September of the year 418. I, 650. When Augustine’s book On Marriage and Concupiscence was written. X, 555, 1049. Augustine sends the first book On Marriage and Concupiscence to the Count Valerius. II, 950. Some excerpts from Julian’s books against Augustine had been sent to Count Valerius. II, 950; Augustine had answered them in book 2 of On Marriage and Concupiscence. II, 950. Julian publishes four books against Augustine’s writings On Marriage and Concupiscence. II, 950. Augustine’s books against Julian. X, 1051. Augustine’s *Enchiridion* on Faith, Hope, and Charity. VI, 154, 158; a sermon On the Ten Plagues and Commandments. IV, 1001; the book On Care for the Dead to Paulinus. VI, 157; the book On Grace and Free Will, written because of a disturbance in the monastery. X, 875, 876, 911, 912, note (a). Augustine’s book On Rebuke and Grace. X, 1027.

Augustine revises his short works and at the same time responds to Julian. II, 1001. As an old man Augustine writes the books of the *Retractions*. I, 583. Why he began the plan of reviewing his writings. I, 584. The purpose and date of composition of Augustine’s books of the *Retractions*. X, 1028. Augustine recognized that his books numbered 232. I, 659; II, 1000. Some books were written by him after the *Retractions*. I, 656, note. Augustine had not revised his homilies in the year 418, nor had he dictated anything concerning the revision of at least most of his letters. II, 1001.

On what occasion Augustine’s *Unfinished Work* was written. X, 1049, 1050. Augustine’s short work against Porphyry. X, 973. The letter to Proba. VI, 450. The letter to Pelagius. X, 349. He writes the letter to Pelagius to be sent through Innocent. II, 770. Augustine’s letter to Innocent, written jointly with four other bishops. X, 389. Augustine’s letter to Hilary. X, 334, note 8. To Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church. X, 879, 880, 1027. To Mercator. VI, 159. The tenth letter On the End of the World to Hesychius. VII, 664. Augustine’s letter to the holy Paulinus of Nola. X, 1028. In his letters Augustine inserts matters more necessary to others than to those to whom he writes. VI, 431, 441.

Augustine’s book On Heresies, written at the request of Quodvultdeus. VIII, 21. How he followed Epiphanius in the book On Heresies. VIII, 41. Augustine’s *Speculum* is a work that should be especially kept in memory. III, 902. Augustine’s purpose in the *Speculum*. III, 889. The other books written by Augustine. See the *Retractions*. I, 655. Index of Augustine’s short works. II, 576.

Augustine compared Sacred Scripture with the Septuagint translation. III, 547. Augustine expounded Psalm 72 on the night when the solemnity of the most blessed Cyprian was dawning. II, 543. At the funeral of a certain believer he expounded a psalm. IV, 1352. At the command of the brothers and fellow bishops he interpreted several psalms. IV, 322, 363, 1216, 1352, 1803. He did not interpret the Psalter, but corrected some errors in the Latin codices. II, 1077. Jerome says that Augustine’s interpretation of the Psalms differs from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks. II, 246. Augustine’s sermons on the Psalms are taken down in writing. IV, 599. Augustine’s forty-fourth sermon *On Various Subjects*, praised. III, 567. Certain short works were brought to Spain under Augustine’s name. X, 331. What Julian thought about Augustine’s books. X, 1053.

Augustine and Alypius instilled Juliana and her family with good morals. II, 848. At the urging of Augustine and Alypius, Demetrias sent word that she would not marry, although the wedding arrangements had already been made. II, 848. Augustine’s desire to see and speak with Paulinus. II, 108. Augustine receives bread from Paulinus. II, 103. He sends bread to Paulinus as a gift. II, 125. He promises Paulinus that he will write Alypius’s history. II, 110. Augustine gratefully received the hair shirts sent by Palatinus. II, 990.

Augustine is so tormented by fear and grief over the danger facing the people of Fussala and their bishop Antonius that he considers withdrawing from the exercise of the episcopal office. II, 956. Augustine desires to be free from the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, if this can be done without abandoning his office. II, 481. Amid his most pressing occupations. VI, 431. And bodily illnesses. VI, 576. He would prefer to work at fixed hours in the manner of monks. VI, 576. The Gospel terrifies Augustine, lest, after laying down the episcopal burden, he choose a more secure life. V, 1481. Augustine would not wish to have dealings with secular authorities. V, 1392.

Augustine of weak health. II, 470. He suffers, owing to a swelling, from the pain of fissures (*rhagades*) and protrusions (*exochades*). II, 152. Augustine was old through age, but through bodily infirmity he had already been old beforehand. V, 719, 1574. Augustine seeks familiarity with death. II, 74. Augustine desires the presbyter Heraclius as his successor. II, 967, 968. The people received his election with applause. II, 967, 968. Augustine transfers the burdens of his occupations to Heraclius. II, 968. Augustine could scarcely speak because of bodily weakness when Boniface came to him. II, 993.

For Augustine’s deeds, see his life written by Possidius. I, 38.

Augustine’s pupils: Alypius. II, 90. Boniface. II, 268, 271. Donatus. II, 227. Evodius. II, 697. Licentius. I, 908, 981. Privatus. II, 697. Possidius. II, 368. Profuturus. II, 111, 697. Servilius. II, 111, 697. Trigetius. I, 908, 981. Among Augustine’s intimate associates was Saint Paulinus. II, 107. Augustine and Alypius were two only in body, not in spirit. II, 111.

Eulogy of Augustine. II, 644. Augustine is called an example of integrity and justice. II, 514. Augustine praised by Ambrose. X, 1081. Paulinus calls Augustine a teacher in the faith. II, 470; both a teacher and a spiritual physician. II, 349. Paulinus says that Augustine is dead to the world. II, 349. Paulinus greatly esteems Augustine’s knowledge and learning. II, 347, 350. He calls Augustine the blessed Doctor of Israel. II, 462. The salt of the earth, and a lamp worthily placed upon the Church’s lampstand. II, 101. He calls Augustine’s mouth a pipe of living water and a vein of the eternal spring. II, 101. Paulinus marvels at Augustine’s books as words dictated by God. II, 99. He calls Augustine’s words heavenly. II, 126.

Audax calls Augustine the oracle of the Law, the consecrator of justice, the restorer of spiritual glory, and the dispenser of eternal salvation. II, 1076. By reading Augustine, Darius despised pagan rites. II, 1022. Nectarius compares Augustine with Cicero. II, 386. Augustine’s letters sounded of Christ, Plato, Plotinus, and Nebridius. II, 67. Orosius, a young presbyter from the farthest part of Spain, came to Augustine, inflamed by his ardor for learning. II, 748. Augustine is praised by Secundinus. VIII, 574. Theodosius writes to Augustine asking him to attend the Council of Ephesus. II, 927. Note: Vincentius says that Augustine, still far removed from the Christian faith and formerly devoted to literary studies, was a lover of tranquility and uprightness [*honestatis*; the reading is somewhat uncertain]. II, 348. “When one comes to Augustine, whatever may have happened that is unknown is lacking from the Law,” according to Volusianus. II, 514.

A certain Augustine, a bishop among the Donatists. IX, 48.

Augustus Caesar, the adopted son of Gaius Caesar. VII, 110. He waged civil wars with many opponents. VII, 109. The piety of Augustus. X, 1034.

The month of August, so called in honor of the emperor [Col. 0100] Augustus. III, 51; VIII, 346.

Avitus: two Spanish citizens of this name. VIII, 667, 668.

Diversion of the heart. IV, 202.

The favor of the court is a fragile thing. I, 756. Courtiers reach a greater danger through many dangers. I, 756.

Aurelian, persecutor of the Christians. VII, 614.

Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage. II, 389, 392; 490, 493, 577, 758, 779, VI, 547; VII, 762; VIII, 817, 818, IX, 700; X, 319, 386. Aurelius prompted Augustine to publish the book *On the Work of Monks*. I, 639. Sixtus writes to Aurelius. II, 867. And Paulinus [writes to him]. II, 101. Augustine copied out Sixtus’s letter to Aurelius. II, 867. The praiseworthy deed of Aurelius of Carthage. V, 1572. The anniversary of Aurelius of Carthage’s ordination. V, 643.

Aurelius of Utica. IX, 228.

Aurelius of Chullabi. IX, 238.

Charioteer. V, 136, 562, 1026, 1511; VI, 560, 638. The charioteer and the hunter among those who provided spectacles for the people. IV, 438, 439, 626, 1954. The people praise a charioteer in the theater according to their party loyalties. VII, 262.

The Romans did not worship the god Aurinus. VII, 135.

Pleasure of the ears. I, 779. Sins of the ear. V, 382. “You have heard the word; let it die within you, spoken by an angry man.” V, 323. The ear of God is to be understood as the power by which he hears. IV, 130. God requires the ears of the heart, not of the body. IV, 544. “Ears that hear” means the will to obey. X, 1016. See *to hear*. The right ear cut off by Peter from a servant, allegorically applied to the Donatists. VI, 306. It is not impossible for God to give the ears the capacity of seeing and the eyes the capacity of hearing. X, 339.

Gold is the pallor of the earth, silver its lividity. V, 136. Gold shining from the earth. V, 1655. Gold and silver are earth to the soul that is not earth. IV, 1481. God made gold, and placed you above gold, so that you might be its master, not its slave. IV, 1646. Gold ought to follow you, not you gold. V, 1417. It ought to be led, not to lead; to be possessed, not to possess. V, 1417. Gold is good in itself and by its nature, though it is not the highest good. V, 328. Why gold is given to the good and the wicked. V, 327. It was created for the praise of the Creator, for the testing of the good, and for the punishment of the wicked. V, 328. Gold and silver belong not to human beings but to God, because God not only created them but administers them according to his will—giving them to some for support and testing, and to others for punishment. V, 326, 327. The miser is tormented by the gold from which the merciful person is assisted. V, 327. Desire for gold is condemned, while its proper use is commended by the Lord. V, 329. What use of gold is good and what is bad. V, 148. The person who knows how to use gold possesses it; the person who does not know how to use it is possessed by it, rather than possessing it. IV, 1646. Gold properly belongs to the person who uses it well; and yet in truth it is God’s. V, 327. Gold and silver are evil for the wicked and good for the good. V, 468. Gold and silver are good—not because they make you good, but because they provide the means by which you may do good. V, 410. Through gold the good person does many good things, the wicked person many evil things. V, 1417. The person who uses gold well is the one who adorns gold itself. V, 148. Gold is preferred to God by the greedy. V, 144. And to faith. V, 146. Many lose their faith in order to acquire gold. IV, 1645. “You acquired gold and lost sleep.” III, 2056. Martyrs of gold: the greedy. V, 1461, 1470. See *Riches*. Gold cannot rightly be condemned. V, 328, 329. Contempt for gold commended in the prophetic writings. V, 332.

Gold and silver allegorically understood. V, 331. Gold signifies wisdom. III, 633. Wisdom is represented by gold, prudence by silver. IV, 823, 911. Gold is faith, hay is desire. IV, 1242. The good resemble gold, the wicked hay. IV, 1375.

Ausafa. IX, 236, 507, 528, 550.

Ause was the former name of him who was later called Joshua. V, 1553; VIII, 327.

The south wind, a hot wind. IV, 1664. In the holy books the south wind does not signify anything evil, just as the north wind signifies nothing good. III, 876. The south wind signifies the fervor of charity. II, 561.

Ausuaga. IX, 230.

The necessity of divine assistance for doing good. See *Help*; *Grace*. When Julian asks for God’s help in writing his books, he unwittingly confesses that God works in human wills. X, 1249. God’s help is called just because it is already granted to one who is just. IV, 104. The devil persuades us to distrust God’s help. IV, 325. Help is to be sought from the Lord. IV, 326. Faith, which is in Christ Jesus, obtains the help of grace. II, 760. The help of grace is present to some. VIII, 82.

Auxilius anathematizes Classicianus together with his entire household. II, 1066.

Axa, daughter of Caleb. III, 793.

Aymnius of Ausuaga. IX, 230.

Aynan is interpreted as “their sorrow.” VIII, 457.

Matthew calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fifth day of the week. II, 150. During the days of Unleavened Bread it was a defilement for Jews to enter the dwelling of a foreigner. III, 1936. How the eating of unleavened bread is to be understood and observed spiritually. VIII, 237, 503.

[Col. 0101]

## B

Baal, the name of Jupiter. III, 797. *Baalsamen*, meaning “Lord of heaven” in Punic. III, 797.

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” IV, 773, 774, 1659, 1761; VII, 482, 490, 497, 550, 601. Babylon was founded by Nimrod. VII, 482. The pride of those who built the Babylonian tower. VII, 482, 490. How this pride was punished. VII, 490, 491. Babylon was founded in the innermost regions of Persia. IV, 773. Babylon, the capital of the Assyrian kingdom. VII, 497. Babylonia, as it were the first Rome. VII, 561. Semiramis founded or restored Babylon. VII, 561.

Babylon signifies this world. IV, 336, 1659. Babylon, the city of the devil. VII, 550; IX, 56. A type of the society of the wicked. VI, 337. The city of Babylonia is the society of all the lost, and it itself possesses an earthly kingdom. IV, 208. Babylonia was first our mother. IV, 208. It first gave birth to us in captivity. IV, 1795. Babylon and Jerusalem are figures of the righteous and the reprobate. IV, 773. Babylon began with Cain, Jerusalem with Abel. IV, 733, 773. Babylon has the devil as king, Jerusalem has Christ as king. IV, 733. Babylon and Jerusalem are now intermingled. IV, 773. Who belong to that city and who to this one. IV, 733, 1106. Two loves make Babylon and Jerusalem: the love of God makes Jerusalem, the love of the world makes Babylon. IV, 773. Babylonia has its own lovers, and what kind they are. IV, 1762.

Babylonia: how to flee spiritually from the midst of Babylon. VII, 574. The person who begins to love begins to leave Babylonia. IV, 774. Although the body is still held in Babylonia, the heart should be sent ahead to Jerusalem. IV, 1940. Those who live faithfully in Babylonia do not perish, because they are predestined to be citizens of Jerusalem. IV, 1762. The citizens of Babylonia are foreign sons. IV, 1770. How Babylon itself is the daughter of Babylon. IV, 1773. The little ones of Babylonia. IV, 1773. The rivers of Babylon are all the things loved here and passing away. IV, 1762. The joy of Babylonia is temporal peace. IV, 1761. The captivity of the Jews in Babylonia is a figure of our captivity in the world. IV, 1659.

The Babylonian captivity and the events that took place in it: what they signify. VI, 336. When the Babylonian captivity of the Jews occurred. VII, 582. What the deportation to Babylon and the return from it signify. VIII, 272, 273. The Babylonian deportation as a figure of the Gospel’s passage to the Gentiles. V, 340.

The Bacchae, women distinguished less by virtue than by frenzy. VII, 571.

The Bacchanalia. II, 84. The Bacchanalia, rites instituted for Father Liber. VII, 571. The Bacchanalia were prohibited by the Senate in the city of Rome. VII, 187, 571.

Bacchus. See *Liber*.

The staff of mercy. V, 1650.

Elisha’s staff as a figure of the Law. V, 176.

A reed staff. IV, 1058.

The church of Badesilitana. II, 233.

Badi or Beda. IX, 211.

Bagai and Thamugadi, the chief towns of the Donatists. IV, 177.

The town of Bagai. IX, 209, 503.

The Council of Bagaia, or Bagaitanum. IV, 645, 685; IX, 47, 54, 113, 137, 251, 370, 503, 504, 506, 509, 519, 583, 585, 704. The Council of Bagai against the Maximianists, held in the year 394. II, 580; IX, 529. The Council of Bagai of three hundred and ten bishops. IX, 527, 547, 555, 585, 586. The names of some of them. IX, 555. At this Council the Donatists condemned Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri, and later received them back into the same episcopates in which they had been condemned, compelled by Optatus of Gildon. II, 192, 198, 265, 309. The Council of Bagai granted a postponement to the other persons constituted in the same Maximianist schism, including even those who had condemned Primianus, solely because they had not participated in Maximianus’s ordination. IX, 528, 550, 552, 555, 569. The deadline of the postponement. IX, 530, 550, 572. Praetextatus and Felicianus remained with Maximianus even after the appointed day. IX, 574. The sentence of the Council of Bagai against Maximianus and the twelve ordainers. IX, 506, 550, 552, 709, 745. The sentence of the Council of Bagai dictated by Emeritus of Caesarea. IX, 507, 704. The Council of Bagai said of the Maximianists: “The shores are full of the funerals of the dead.” II, 756. The basilica of Bagai was burned by the Donatists, and the sacred books were thrown into the fire. IX, 636.

The Bagradas River. VII, 769.

The town of Baiana. IX, 528, 550.

Bala is interpreted as “grown old.” VIII, 434, 435.

Balaam, reprobate and condemned. VI, 136.

Balbus in Cicero. X, 766. Balbus debates in Cicero’s book *On the Nature of the Gods*. VII, 149.

Baleus, the tenth king of the Assyrians. VII, 563.

The bath is so called because it drives anxiety from the mind. I, 777. The effect of bathing. I, 777. The use of baths is permitted to nuns once a [Col. 0102] month. II, 963.

“To be baptized.” This word comes from Greek; Latin usage treats it in such a way that it is not ordinarily understood elsewhere except with reference to the sacrament of regeneration. X, 837.

The end of John’s baptism. IX, 182. John’s baptism serves Christ, just as the ancient sacraments of the Law performed a precursor and prefigurative function. IX, 599. John’s baptism did not belong to Christ’s baptism as a part or stage of it. IX, 289. Regeneration did not take place through John’s baptism. VI, 255. Nor were sins forgiven, except in hope. IX, 183. John gave those being baptized instructions concerning morals. VI, 210. Christ received John’s baptism. VI, 256; IX, 174. He received it for the consecration of that sacrament itself. V, 1335. And on account of the pride of those to come. IV, 1164. Why John’s baptism did not continue. IX, 182. The baptism administered by John was called John’s; but the baptism administered by Paul was not called Paul’s—why. IX, 435.

Christ’s baptism. V, 947, 1303. It is to be distinguished from John’s baptism. V, 1048. Baptism, a sacrament. III, 70. The sacrament of birth, a great, divine, holy, ineffable sacrament. III, 2016. Its institutor. II, 180. Baptism belongs to Christ’s dispensation, which was accomplished through his humility. X, 131. Baptism, consecrated by Christ’s death. V, 1562, 1635; and by his blood. IV, 1420. The water of baptism is consecrated in Christ’s name and marked with his cross. V, 1551. The power of water through the consecration of the word. VI, 694. The spiritual person can judge concerning the solemnity of the sacraments, whether of baptism or of the mystery in which that fish—that is, Christ—is presented. I, 861. Baptism is administered in the name of the Holy Trinity. I, 851; V, 803. Therefore it is called the baptism of the Trinity. V, 1235.

The mystery of baptism is intimated at the beginning of the book of Genesis. VI, 133. Baptism was signified by the Flood. VIII, 263. And represented by the Israelites’ passage through the Red Sea. III, 1723; IV, 917, 1037, 1411, 1420, 1760; V, 37, 1551, 1555, 1562, 1635, 1637; VI, 335, 695. The water of sprinkling signified Christ’s baptism. III, 735, 736; VIII, 651. And Christ’s walking upon the waters. VI, 694. Circumcision was a figure of baptism. X, 833. And formerly served in place of baptism. II, 845. Christ gave the sacrament of baptism in the Church in place of circumcision. II, 1085. Baptism expresses spiritual circumcision. X, 403.

The Seleucians reject baptism. VIII, 41, 42. So do the Manichaeans. VIII, 38.

Why baptism was instituted. X, 1120. A second birth was instituted because the first had been condemned. X, 857. Because generation was condemned in Adam, regeneration is sought in Christ. V, 1345. The second birth is from God and the Church. V, 680. The womb of the mother; the water of baptism. V, 674. Before baptism a human being is under the devil, yet is not thereby removed from God’s power. X, 857. Hence those who are not regenerated remain under the devil. X, 821. Julian’s empty sophistry: that God and the devil entered into an agreement with one another, so that whatever is washed belongs to God, while whatever is born belongs to the devil. X, 837.

Baptism is necessary for everyone. VI, 253; X, 189, 190, 199. Even after John’s baptism. IX, 182. Paul baptized after John with Christ’s baptism. II, 343. Baptism is necessary even for those living perfectly. III, 1495. And at every stage of the inward person’s progress. IX, 173. No one comes to baptism innocent. IX, 338. Pope Innocent asserts the necessity of baptism. X, 576.

It is proved that Judas and the other Apostles had been baptized before the Lord’s passion. II, 178. When Peter denied the Lord, the Apostles had not yet been baptized—not with water, however, but with the Holy Spirit. II, 1086. It is more credible that the Apostles were baptized by Christ. II, 1088.

For what purpose the Pelagians believed baptism necessary at every age. X, 609, 613. Why the Pelagians exalt baptism so greatly. X, 621.

Christ’s baptism is necessary for infants. III, 418; V, 657. The baptism of infants is not superfluous, because they are bound by original sin. II, 678. Baptism is necessary for infants because of original sin, not because of personal sin. X, 121. Whoever is born carnally needs to be regenerated spiritually. X, 121. No one is freed from Adam’s condemnation except by being reborn in Christ. VI, 256. Baptism suffices for infants, so that after death they are not harmed by what carnal generation contracted along with death. VII, 730.

Infants ought to be baptized so that they may be freed from the devil’s power and from sin. X, 1438. Through baptism, dying infants are rescued from the power of darkness. II, 982; X, 426. Infants cannot be freed from original sin except through Christ’s baptism. II, 683. Infants are baptized not only so that they may be righteous, but so that the illness of original sin in them may be healed. X, 122. Infants are baptized for the forgiveness of sins. V, 751. The baptism administered for the forgiveness of sins is false in those who have no sin at all. X, 978. Parents ought to be diligent in having infants baptized. X, 199.

For what purpose the Pelagians admitted the baptism of infants. [Col. 0103] VIII, 48; X, 570, 1067, 1438. Concerning the baptism of infants: Pelagian doctrines and paradoxes. X, 705, 708. Pelagius says that baptism is to be celebrated for infants with the same sacramental words as for adults. X, 396. The Pelagians deny that infants should be baptized for salvation, on the grounds that they drew no contagion of condemnation from Adam. II, 761, 763, 773. Some Pelagians admit that forgiveness of sins takes place in infants through baptism— in what sense. X, 146. Although Pelagius and Coelestius admit that infants are baptized for the forgiveness of sins, they deny that infants have any original sin. X, 377, 385, 387, 388. The people of Marseilles seem to have doubted that infants are rescued from the power of darkness through baptism. X, 1009.

The Pelagians concede that infants should be baptized, not for eternal life but for the kingdom of heaven. V, 1336; X, 142, 394, 395. Coelestius’s doctrine that infants possess eternal life even if they are not baptized. X, 334. The Pelagians added that infants could be granted the rewards of eternal life without the grace of baptism. II, 788. Infants need baptism not only to obtain the kingdom of heaven but also for the forgiveness of sins. X, 121. Without baptism, infants cannot possess life in themselves. X, 615. No one can attain salvation and eternal life apart from fellowship with Christ. X, 122, 128, 196. Unbaptized infants remain in darkness. X, 129, 131. Vincentius’s error that infants who die without baptism can reach the kingdom of heaven. X, 480, 481. Vincentius promises forgiveness of sins to those who die unbaptized, and separates paradise from the kingdom of heaven. X, 503, 504, 518, 520, 522. Whether infants who die before or after receiving baptism will rise again. II, 730. Vincentius’s error that the sacrifice of Christ’s Body ought to be offered for infants who die before baptism. X, 480. The Pelagians did not dare promise the kingdom of heaven to unbaptized infants. X, 481, 520. They grant them salvation and eternal life, but exclude them from the kingdom of heaven. X, 123. A place of second happiness constructed by the Pelagians for unbaptized infants. X, 1130. They promise them an intermediate place between the kingdom of heaven and condemnation. X, 481. And for this reason they were condemned by the Councils and the Apostolic See. X, 505. That intermediate place is attacked. III, 1813; X, 481. The Lord’s statement excluding the unbaptized from the kingdom of God, as the Pelagians themselves admit. V, 1340. Unbaptized infants are condemned. X, 188, 189. They will be in condemnation with the devil. X, 140, 189. Yet in the mildest condemnation. X, 120.

The children even of the faithful are to be baptized. X, 175, 812, 847. Why the children of baptized people are baptized. X, 177, 178. Neither an unregenerated father harms his regenerated son in attaining eternal life, nor does a regenerated father benefit his unregenerated son in this respect; and likewise in the other cases. X, 1272, 1273. No one who was not born can be reborn in his parent. X, 177. The children of baptized people are not baptized without reason. X, 194, 195, 199.

Christ benefits infants who are baptized. V, 1346. The Church counts baptized infants among the number of the faithful. X, 124. And Christ incorporates them into his body through grace. X, 114, 196. Infants offered through the sacrament and the charity of the faithful, as though incorporated into Christ’s body, which is the Church, are reconciled to God. X, 131. In baptism they are adopted from being sons of human beings into being sons of God. X, 578, 583. Church tradition admits no one to the altar except one who has been baptized. IX, 138. It is unfathomable why some infants die deprived of baptism and others do not. X, 125. In the question why one infant is baptized and another is not, one must take refuge in divine authority. V, 1339. Vincentius’s error that it is written concerning infants dying before baptism: “He was taken away lest wickedness,” etc. X, 517. Whether it can be said that baptism is procured for infants whose future piety God foresaw had they lived longer. III, 419, 420. Augustine devised this for the purpose of refuting it. III, 420. Various answers, according to the various opinions concerning the origin of the soul. III, 419, 420. It is not by fate, fortune, or favoritism that one infant rather than another comes to the grace of baptism. X, 581. Not through the merit of the parents or of the infant itself, nor through foreknowledge of good or evil works. II, 885; X, 578. What should be said about an infant who dies without baptism through the negligence of its parents. III, 419.

It benefits infants to be baptized through the faith of those who offer them and of the Church. I, 1304. The faith of another benefits infants. III, 418; V, 1537. The response of those who offer them serves for the consecration of infants. IX, 175. The infant believes through another, because it sinned through another. V, 1342, 1346. It is healed through another’s words, because it is wounded through another’s deed. V, 1342. The willingness of those who offer infants for baptism benefits them through their fellowship in the one and same Spirit, from whom regeneration comes. II, 360. For infants are offered not so much by those carrying them as by the entire fellowship of the faithful. II, 361. Therefore the perverse intention of those who offer them cannot hinder the power of the sacrament. II, 361, 362. Infants may be offered for baptism by persons other than their parents. II, 362. Dying infants are rescued through baptism from the power of darkness, because, although the infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, the sacrament of faith nevertheless already makes the infant [Col. 0104] faithful. II, 364. When a person reaches the use of reason, he does not repeat the sacrament of baptism but understands it, and conforms himself to its truth with a corresponding will. II, 364.

The baptism of infants, an ancient rule. V, 939. And an apostolic tradition. III, 426; X, 131. It is not counted as guilt against infants that they receive baptism while resisting. II, 841.

Donatus asserted that Christ’s baptism existed only within his own communion. I, 618. Every smallest part of Donatus asserts that the true baptism has remained neither throughout the whole world nor in the greater part of Donatus, but only among themselves. IX, 114. The Donatists called their own baptism holy, but everyone else’s nothing. IV, 1890. The Donatists said that baptism was not true unless it was administered by a righteous person. II, 311. The Donatists wished baptism to be empty unless they themselves administered it. VI, 306. Yet they wished the person whom they had baptized to be justified. II, 809. They want baptism to be such as the person from whom it is possessed, administered, or received. IX, 286. Their statement, “As I am who baptize, so I make those whom I baptize,” is refuted. V, 1323. By this very utterance they are condemned. X, 287.

The minister of baptism is not to be considered, but God. IV, 1890. This is demonstrated from Christ’s example. IX, 77. It is also demonstrated from the Donatists themselves. IX, 76. The testimonies cited by the Donatists do not pertain to this matter. IX, 367. In the question of baptism, one must not consider who gives, possesses, or receives it, but what is given, possessed, or received. IX, 163. The power of baptism does not depend on the minister’s merits. II, 401. Nor on his goodness or wickedness. III, 1421. Rather, it cleanses through God’s grace. V, 602. And its own holiness is established. IX, 559, 560. Baptism is to be considered in itself, consecrated by the evangelical words, without the added perversity either of those who receive it or of those who administer it. IX, 163.

How Christ’s baptism is to be recognized and approved. IX, 142. Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit has Christ as its author, not any human being. IX, 279. Baptism administered according to the Gospel belongs to Christ, not to the ministers. IX, 110, 260, 262, 345, 438. Christ’s baptism, whether administered by an evil or a righteous person, is nothing other than Christ’s baptism. IX, 368, 369, 371, 372. Christ’s sacrament is holy even when administered through a less holy or unholy person. IX, 361. If no human being, whoever he may be, ought to usurp the right of baptism for himself, no one would dare to baptize. IX, 487. The holiness of baptism is not unequal because its ministers are unequal. II, 344; III, 1428; IX, 173, 435, 499. Baptizing by authority is one thing; baptizing by ministry is another. III, 1417. The power to baptize passes from the Lord to no one; ministry passes to everyone, whether good or evil. III, 1419, 1428, 1437. It is not the minister but Christ himself who baptizes. II, 311. Jesus baptized and did not baptize—how. III, 1511. The baptism administered by the Apostles before Christ’s passion and after Christ was not theirs but Christ’s. II, 344; IX, 435. None of the Apostles administered Christ’s baptism in such a way as to dare to call it his own. IX, 385, 386. Just as [no one calls] either the Gospel or the ministry [his own]. IX, 185. Baptism given by sacrilegious persons belongs to Christ, just as Christ’s name belongs to Christ when spoken by sacrilegious persons; but neither benefits them. IX, 602, 603. No one returns from baptism such as the person was from whom he was baptized. IX, 338, 374, 375, 376, 377. Otherwise the Donatists return as sinners. IX, 338, 340. All who were baptized by Optatus became Optatus’s; IX, 338, 340; it would follow that very many Donatists would have to be baptized again, yet they do not rebaptize them. IX, 287, 366, 367, 368.

Those who think that the righteous have one baptism and the wicked another speak of two baptisms. IX, 280. Baptism is common to the good and the wicked. V, 561. To the righteous and the unrighteous. IX, 195, 196. In the weeds and in the chaff there is true baptism. IX, 280. The sacrament of baptism is holy in itself even among sacrilegious persons. IX, 346. Baptism is good even in a sacrilegious person, just as the Law is good in an evil Jew. IX, 181, 596. The holiness of baptism cannot be polluted by anyone’s crimes. IX, 144, 167. Baptism exists even among the perverse and is not made perverse by anyone’s perversity. IX, 190, 191, 197, 198, 200, 214, 215, 223. This is shown by examples drawn from the Old Testament. IX, 223. Sacraments celebrated according to the evangelical rite, even if they were held by traditors, are not sacrilegious. IX, 602. The wicked indeed possess baptism as long as they are wicked, but they do not possess the salvation of which baptism is the sacrament. IX, 217. Baptism remains whole in the wicked, but does not benefit them for salvation. IX, 174, 219, 221. When a person abandons wickedness, what was previously present for destruction begins to benefit him for salvation. IX, 179, 509. Baptism can exist in the perverse and can even be openly administered by them. IX, 240, 286.

The false teaching of Petilianus—that the conscience of the person who gives baptism must be considered as what cleanses the recipient—is refuted. IX, 247, 260, 353, 356, 358, 363, 364, 373, 374, 377, 481, 556. The Donatists thought that baptism was rightly given by an impious person whose wickedness was hidden, but not by one whose wickedness was manifest. IX, 73, 230. If God or an angel then cleanses by himself when the baptizer’s polluted conscience is hidden, it is better to be baptized by a hidden evil person than by a [Col. 0105] manifestly good person. IX, 67, 248, 250, 373, 374, 375, 376, 377, 378, 480, 481, 502. This consequence is not Augustine’s, but he demonstrates that it is necessary. IX, 376. Whether the giver’s conscience should be considered only according to the reputation—true or false—that surrounds it. IX, 478, 480, 481, 498, 500, 557. The Donatists do not give true baptism if the guilty person, whether hidden or manifest, does not give it. IX, 279, 280, 281. The arguments by which the Donatists proved that baptism given by the faithless was nothing are turned back against them. IX, 250.

To be baptized by a dead person: what this means. IX, 218. Those are baptized by the dead who are baptized in temples of idols. IX, 484. And in the name of the gods. IX, 486. Whom the Donatists might understand by “dead baptizers.” IX, 250. If no sinner can baptize because he is dead, neither can one whose evil is hidden. IX, 485, 486. Baptism given by evil and wicked persons cannot be said not to have been given. IX, 75. Baptism given by evil persons, whether their evil is hidden or manifest, remains whole. IX, 509. Baptism given through a contemptible person is just as effective as baptism given through an Apostle. IX, 184. Like the Gospel, baptism can be dispensed by God through good and evil persons. IX, 498, 500. If the dispenser of the evangelical word and sacrament is good, he is a companion of the Gospel; if evil, he is not therefore not a dispenser of the Gospel. IX, 384. Judas is brought forward as an example. IX, 385.

The power of baptism, like that of the Gospel, does not depend on the minister. IX, 260, 261, 262. The justification of the baptized does not depend on the righteousness of the baptizer. IX, 145, 369, 370, 371, 374. The merit of the baptizer is not to be considered in the grace of baptism. IX, 64, 435, 499. Idolaters themselves do not think that they receive from their priests the sanctification they suppose they possess, but from their gods. IX, 484, 486. If the innocence of the baptized is expected from the innocence of the baptizer, many difficulties follow. IX, 261. The hope of the baptized is vain and empty if the baptizer’s conscience is considered. IX, 247, 260. The person who considers the baptizer’s conscience places his hope in a human being. IX, 500. Hence schisms arise. IX, 502. Hope must not be placed in the baptizer. IX, 378, 379, 380. Whether one receives the sacrament of baptism from a faithful or from a faithless person, all one’s hope must be in Christ. IX, 249, 260. The sole head and origin of the baptized, or of Christians, is Christ. IX, 500, 502, 518, 560. Finally overcome by the force of truth, Petilianus conceded this. IX, 490.
