The baptizer is not to be followed. IX, 350. One is not baptized in the name of the baptizer. IX, 353. Why Christ did not wish the ministers of baptism to be distinguished by some sign of superior holiness. IX, 184. The sacrament is one thing, its effect and use another. IX, 197. Yet it is not permissible for just anyone to baptize. IX, 489, 498. Whether only a faithful and most righteous worker should be employed in the sacrament of baptism. IX, 500. It is preferable that the minister of baptism be righteous rather than unrighteous. IX, 499. Why. IX, 361. How God works differently through good and evil ministers. IX, 67. Those baptized by people seeking their own interests and loving the world are like the children of a slave woman. III, 1486. An evil minister is a stone channel. III, 1422.

The Donatist doctrine that baptism is lost by departing from the Church. IX, 590. It is refuted by the manner in which the Maximianists are received. IX, 588, 590, 593. By the same arguments with which the Donatists blow away the baptism of the whole world, they blow away their own. IX, 293. Baptism is not lost by departing from the Church. IX, 109, 145, 193, 236, 237, 262, 298. This follows from the Donatists’ own agreement. IX, 109. Nor is the character of baptism erased in apostates. IX, 71, 72. In a soldier who wanders and deserts, the crime belongs to the deserter, but the character does not belong to the deserter; it belongs to the emperor. IX, 691. Heretics possess baptism as a deserter possesses his military character. VI, 636. They are condemned on account of it, not crowned. VI, 636. Their baptism is not changed when they return. VI, 636. Baptism is not lost by departing from unity; when one returns, it begins to benefit. IX, 204, 207, 208, 244. Baptism can be common to those who do not share a common Church. V, 1232; IX, 232, 238, 464. A person who makes baptism common to the Church and to heretics does not betray Christ’s bride to adulterers. IX, 230. Baptism is one, and it is in the holy Church, but not in the Catholic Church alone. IX, 210, 219. Nor is it found only among the saints. IX, 219. Baptism can exist both where the Holy Spirit has withdrawn and where the Church is not. IX, 193. Baptism and the Church can be divided and separated from one another. IX, 186, 191, 193, 206. The truth of baptism administered in the Church, attacked by Petilianus through various arguments and examples, is defended. IX, 280. The truth of baptism is not to be denied, rejected, or destroyed among heretics on Christ’s example; rather, their wickedness is to be rejected. IX, 601. The water of baptism flows outside paradise like the river Euphrates. IX, 210, 221, 227, 229, 476. That Christ’s baptism can exist outside the Church is proved by the water that came forth from the Lord’s body. IX, 440.

Baptism, which cannot be lost, cannot lose the right of administering baptism. IX, 70, 72. For the integrity of the Sacrament, it makes no difference what the faith of the recipient is. IX, 146. Nor that of the minister. IX, 147. Neither the goodness nor the wickedness of the one who receives, possesses, or gives it matters. IX, 199, 200, 212. Baptism consecrated by the evangelical words is not deceptive water. IX, 557. It exists among heretics too, just as the Gospel does. IX, 239. The testimonies of Scripture that appear contradictory are reconciled concerning the reality of baptism administered outside the Church. IX, 114. Baptism must also be acknowledged among heretics. IX, 630. Incense-bearers, traditors, and persecutors can baptize. IX, 558. Those who receive baptism, even deceitfully, possess it when they receive it in the Church, or where those who administer it think the Church to be. IX, 243. Some can possess true baptism even if they do not possess true faith. IX, 604.

There are not two baptisms because heretics can baptize. IX, 230. The wicked do not possess the power to baptize, if heretics do not. IX, 158, 160, 215, 216, 217, 221, 222, 230, 231, 236, 244. Baptism consecrated in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, when administered among heretics, belongs to Christ and the Church, not to them. IX, 121, 140, 145, 151, 165, 220, 231. The same is true of ordination: it belongs not to heretics but to Christ. IX, 691. The Catholic Church alone, through possessing what belongs to it within separated communions, generates spiritual children. IX, 117, 121, 123, 126. Baptism administered according to the evangelical rule remains complete even when administered by a heretic who dissents from the unity of the Trinity. IX, 597.

Baptism administered by heretics is good, just as baptism administered by the wicked is. IX, 190, 191. The baptism of Christ cannot be violated by the perversity of heretics when it is administered and received among them. IX, 177, 178, 179. The baptism of the wicked is invalid if the baptism of heretics is invalid. IX, 193, 203, 204, 205, 206, 207, 209, 211, 212. That baptism can be administered by heretics and schismatics was defined at the Council of Nicaea. IX, 72. Before the definition of the plenary council, great men disputed, without breach of peace, whether baptism could be conferred outside the Church. IX, 114, 124. Whatever Cyprian and his colleague said about the baptism of heretics at the Council of Carthage can be said about the baptism of the wicked. IX, 239; and in books 6 and 7 *On Baptism*. Arguments drawn from Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus that appear to prove that Christ’s baptism cannot be conferred by heretics are refuted in volume IX, books 3 and 4 *Against the Donatists on Baptism*. The Donatists are no longer permitted to remain ignorant of the value of baptism received outside the Church. IX, 113. Baptism administered in schism was approved by the Donatists. IX, 630. Petilian claimed that Catholics did not possess baptism; Augustine proves the same thing concerning the Donatists. IX, 286. There is now no controversy between Catholics and Donatists concerning the goodness of baptism conferred outside the Church. IX, 113. It was brought to an end by the Maximianists. IX, 630, 551. From the schism of Maximian the Donatists learned that Christ’s baptism can be administered outside the Church. VIII, 43, 44.

One baptism is also administered outside the Church by the ignorant, just as the one God himself was worshiped outside the Church by the ignorant. IX, 599, 604. Neither, however, is beneficial. II, 408, 415; IX, 599, 604. That baptism is also valid outside the Church is shown by Christ’s saying, “Whoever is not against you is for you.” IX, 313. The wicked do not receive baptism if heretics do not receive it. IX, 228, 229, 233, 244. Even if baptism exists among the Donatists, it does not follow that it ought to be received there. IX, 460, 462, 466, 467, 550. Water outside the fellowship of the Church not only does not avail for salvation but rather avails for destruction. VIII, 263, 264, 265. One who is born through baptism from the Catholic Church is born as from Sarah; one who is born from heresy is born as from a slave woman, but from Abraham’s seed. III, 1477. Wherever baptism is conferred, it is to be venerated. II, 301. Of two people equal in error and wickedness, the one baptized outside is worse than the one baptized inside. IX, 169. Whoever chooses to be baptized in schism, knowing that baptism is not rightly administered there, is perverse and wicked. IX, 110, 111, 112. When it is a question of where baptism should rightly be received, what is certain must be preferred to what is uncertain. IX, 113. For the sake of the Church’s peace, Cyprian does not think that those baptized outside it should be separated from the Church’s offices. II, 339.

Baptism conferred among heretics is valid and must not be repeated. II, 362; V, 462, 797. Donatists who pass over to the Catholic Church need not be rebaptized. II, 343. Followers and even founders of heresies who were baptized in the Catholic Church are not rebaptized when they return. IX, 223. After those who administered baptism—although they were heretics and perverse—one is not baptized, because it is not their baptism but Christ’s. II, 343, 344. Whoever imposes baptism upon baptism places stone upon stone, but one of them will be destroyed. IV, 433, 1229. Whoever rebaptizes does not make baptism cease to exist, but makes it count toward punishment. IV, 432. The fact that baptism is not to be repeated for those coming from heretics is shown by an apt comparison. IV, 181; V, 797. The Donatists are pressed with the charge that they rebaptize Catholics. IV, 134. By giving baptism a second time, the Donatists teach the baptized person to profess that he is not a Christian. IV, 432, 1895. Baptism cannot be repeated. III, 1477, 1485; IX, 70, 72. Baptism ought not to be repeated whenever one sins. X, 435. Rebaptism is a great crime. IX, 54. Just as, when Jews become Christians, God’s good things are not to be destroyed but their evil things are, so, when schismatics or heretics become Catholics, the Sacraments are not to be violated but schism or heresy is to be cut away. IX, 596. Baptism is impiously repeated because of the crime of traditio, whether unknown or unproved. IX, 515. One should not be baptized after heretics if one is not baptized after drunkards, sexually immoral persons, and so forth. IX, 218, 437. It is shown that baptism given by heretics or by the wicked must not be repeated. Volume IX, books 3 and 4 *On Baptism*. Baptism must not be repeated for one who believed wrongly. IX, 77. The Church receives those baptized outside. IX, 186. The Church’s custom of not repeating baptism. IX, 226, 227, 234, 237. And of not rebaptizing those baptized in heresy or schism. IX, 219, 220, 491. Even before Cyprian. IX, 143. And deriving from apostolic tradition. IX, 133, 134, 135, 159, 170, 194. Agrippinus, Cyprian’s predecessor, began, as it were, to correct—or rather corrupt—this practice. IX, 133. Cyprian changed it on Agrippinus’s authority. IX, 159. To rebaptize heretics, as Cyprian wished, was then a human error; to rebaptize Catholics, as the Donatists still do, is always a diabolical presumption. IX, 606. The Catholic Church judged that those baptized outside the Church were not to be baptized again before Donatus’s party existed. IX, 465. If those baptized among heretics did not possess baptism, then, since they were admitted to the Church without baptism, one of two things must be admitted: either the Church had then perished, or even another person’s known sins are not harmful. IX, 175. The Donatists cannot prove from the canonical Scriptures that someone coming from heretics was baptized again. IX, 465. In Scripture, neither do schismatics find heretics coming to the Catholic Church baptized again, nor do Catholics find heretics received in the baptism they had received in heresy. IX, 604. It does not follow that baptism must be repeated from the fact that the Apostles baptized after Moses or John. IX, 501, 563, 599, 606. Why Paul baptized after John’s baptism. IX, 181, 183. Gospel testimonies used to support the repetition of baptism are resolved or explained. IX, 601, 602. The Apostles prescribed nothing concerning whether baptism should be repeated after heretics. IX, 192. How we learn from the Apostles that baptism is not to be repeated. IX, 605. The custom of not repeating baptism has already been confirmed by a plenary council. IX, 158, 159, 162, 190, 192, 197, 199, 206, 219, 223, 232, 234. God revealed to the Church that heretics should not be rebaptized. IX, 221. Even the Donatists themselves agree that those coming from heresy are not to be rebaptized. IX, 745. The Donatists received those baptized by their own schismatics. IX, 251, 253. The baptism conferred in Caecilian’s party is shown to be excellent against the Donatists. IX, 69. The Donatists must either baptize after Primian or not baptize after Caecilian. IX, 520. If no one rebaptizes those baptized in schism for the unity of Donatus’s party, then, for Christ’s unity, the true and complete law of that inheritance ought to be acknowledged. IX, 509. People detest the repetition of baptism through some unknown inspiration of God. IX, 180. Even heretics themselves do so. IX, 180. That the repetition of baptism is perverse is shown from Cresconius the Donatist himself. IX, 469, 470, 471. Neither heretics nor Catholics ought to rebaptize, but for different reasons. IX, 145. Why Catholics do not repeat baptism. IX, 346. What Cyprian thought concerning those admitted from heresy into the Church without baptism. IX, 490, 492. How heretics who wished to come to the Church because they thought they did not possess baptism were to be instructed. IX, 179. Whether it is more harmful not to be baptized than to be rebaptized. IX, 138.

Baptism given by heretics or by the wicked remains complete. IX, 207, 244. But it does not avail for salvation. IX, 110, 144, 170, 235, 236, 239, 257, 437, 756. Nor is it rightly administered. IX, 110, 111. Heretics and the perverse possess legitimate baptism, but not legitimately. IX, 180, 186. They possess it legitimately when they turn to Catholic unity or to a life worthy of so great a Sacrament. IX, 180, 186. When those baptized outside the Church return to it, there is added what cannot be given except inside: the unity of the Spirit. V, 462. Whether those baptized outside the Church belong to forgiveness. IX, 138, 146. Baptism is all the more effective for destruction in one who is separated, the more effective it could be for salvation in one who is united. IX, 200. Heretics and the wicked can possess baptism, but they do not possess the remission of sins. IX, 227, 228, 232, 238, 244. Baptism given outside the Church does not avail for the remission of sins until one has been reconciled to unity. IX, 119, 121, 200. Even through baptism given in schism sins are remitted, but they are repeated because of perseverance in schism. IX, 120, 227. Nevertheless, one ought not to rebaptize. IX, 120, 121, 227. Outside the Church baptism does not avail for irrevocable remission of sins. IX, 146, 147, 149, 150. Hence baptism given inside the Church by wicked ministers remits sins. IX, 149. The Church’s baptism can exist outside the Church, but the gift of blessed life exists only inside the Church. IX, 155. Among heretics it is valid and sufficient for consecration, but not for participation in eternal life. II, 362. Heretics have received baptism up to the celebration of the Sacrament, but they do not attain eternal life except through the Sacrament of unity. IX, 155, 219. The water of baptism is like the water of the flood: it is salutary for those situated inside the ark, but deadly outside the ark. IX, 221. [Col. 0108] Baptism begins to be beneficial when one passes over to the Church. IX, 109, 113, 487, 711. What is granted to those baptized in schism when they return to unity. IX, 372, 551. Whether baptism received from the wicked effects the remission of sins. IX, 165, 166. Heretics and the perverse can give baptism, but they cannot give the remission of sins. IX, 192. The Sacrament sometimes harms the giver and benefits the recipient. IX, 488. Good and wicked people can possess and give baptism; the good beneficially, the wicked ruinously. IX, 199, 200. Who receive and administer baptism beneficially, and who do so without benefit. IX, 241. Those who give baptism without possessing the charity of unity give it to their own destruction. IX, 71, 72. There is a great difference between the faithful and the faithless—not with respect to the Sacrament, if each gives or possesses it, but with respect to merit. IX, 560, 562, 563.

The good and the wicked can give baptism, but only Christ can cleanse the conscience. IX, 482. The minister of baptism does not justify; Christ does. IX, 249, 260, 261. The Sacrament of baptism is applied bodily through the work of ministers, but through it God spiritually effects the consecration of the human being. IX, 192. The consecration of a person in baptism belongs uniquely to Christ. IX, 596. Those baptized by heretics or wicked people, if they turn with an undeceitful heart, are baptized by Christ. IX, 219. Christ baptizes not through visible ministry but through hidden grace. IX, 379, 385. Visible water is not sufficient for cleansing; in addition, that sealed fountain is required, with which no outsider shares. IX, 476. Water, outwardly exhibiting the Sacrament of grace, and the Spirit, inwardly effecting the benefit of grace, regenerate the human being. V, 312. Various questions concerning those who truly or deceptively receive or administer baptism. IX, 242. Many in the Church went astray in the question of baptism. III, 1422. Two councils were held in Africa concerning the question of baptism. IX, 144. Exhortation to baptism. V, 754, 1555.

The power of baptism. VIII, 572; IX, 165. Its effect. X, 570, 847. Without it no one enters the kingdom of heaven. I, 857. Punic Christians call baptism itself nothing other than salvation. X, 128. In dangers the catechumens ran to baptism. VII, 674. Many were baptized in the East and Africa because of an earthquake. V, 136. Christ’s baptism removes all sins. V, 53, 382, 383, 390, 401, 752, 1064, 1537, 1635; VI, 262, 288, 659; VII, 40; X, 430, 600, 688. Baptism grants forgiveness of all sins and removes crimes; it does not shave them away. X, 562, 563. Perfect cleansing is found not in John’s baptism but in the Lord’s baptism. II, 178. None of those who came to Christ through baptism is excluded from the grace of the remission of sins. X, 140. After baptism, the whole person is clean. III, 1789, 1790. Having been consecrated in Christ’s font and blood, the soul ascends wholly beautiful. VI, 689. Baptism drives out the destroyer from us if our heart receives the Savior. III, 1759.

The extent to which baptism benefits infants and adults. X, 123. The baptism of infants. IX, 174. Its value. IX, 175. Grace conferred on the baptized. V, 1093. Grace is secretly infused into infants in baptism. X, 114. Infants are renewed in baptism. X, 1077. Through baptism, even in infancy, the penalty of original sin is dissolved. III, 419. Through baptism, with the Church’s charity commending them, those who die before attaining the use of reason are freed from condemnation. II, 364. One imbued with the Sacrament of regeneration does not perish if he dies before attaining the use of reason. VI, 288. How sin is emptied out in infants and likewise in adults through baptism. X, 150. Through the Sacrament of baptism every guilt of sins committed against the Ten Commandments of the Law is washed away. VIII, 263. The baptized person has either come out of the inn healthy or is healthy within the inn. X, 276. Whoever is rightly cleansed by the Sacrament of baptism is spiritually cleansed in both flesh and soul. III, 736. The effect of baptism is that the guilt of past sins is dissolved in all, while in adults the will is also healed and prepared by the Lord through the spirit of faith and charity. I, 604. Not only sins but the very sinful desires are cleansed by the washing of baptism. X, 407. Even if full and complete remission occurs in baptism, there is nevertheless not yet complete renewal. X, 177.

Baptism removes all sins, but does not immediately heal every infirmity. V, 752; X, 590. In baptism the guilt of vices is dissolved, but infirmity remains. X, 682, 683. Guilt is remitted, but not the sickness which the guilt deserved. VI, 360. Baptism does not remove concupiscence. X, 678, 1116. But it leaves it without guilt. V, 391, 752, 820, 1537. That is, for the struggle. V, 391. Hence the necessity for the baptized saints to fight. X, 679, 856. Although the baptized have died to sin, they possess something in themselves that must be put to death. X, 846. Even for the baptized the flesh is opposed to them, and therefore grace is necessary. X, 276, 280. The extent to which baptism frees one from concupiscences. X, 846. A young man will not subdue carnal concupiscence unless aided by the Sacrament of baptism. III, 419. Augustine’s friend was baptized unknowingly and was wonderfully changed in spirit. VI, 696. Regeneration provides more than generation. X, 1183, 1188. Jovinian taught that after receiving baptism a person could not sin. [Col. 0109] VIII, 45, 46. A person can not only sin after baptism but also commit some sins, even if they are venial. X, 1117. There is one baptism, but in prayer we receive that by which we are washed daily. V, 401. Why the baptized pray, “Forgive us our debts.” X, 563. The baptized are released from the guilt of evils that remain after baptism. X, 853. Generation from Adam binds through one offense; regeneration from Christ dissolves both that offense and whatever is subsequently added through the wicked works of human conduct. II, 679. In baptism the whole guilt is dissolved, together with everything we have done, said, or thought in obedience to it; and thereafter the sickness from which unlawful desires are stirred would not harm us if we never obeyed them. IV, 1507. The baptized person is free from every sin, but not from every evil. X, 850. The force of habit is not put aside in baptism. X, 666. Baptism does not exempt us from the punishments of this life. VII, 728.

Through the holiness of baptism not only sins but absolutely all evils are to be removed. X, 435. Why the baptized are not immediately rescued from every evil. X, 1179. Nor are they immediately given the resurrection of the saints. X, 1180. From which evils complete health and newness are perfected in baptism. X, 855. The absurdities that follow from the opinion that no evils remain in the baptized. X, 853. Through the benefit of baptism one also reaches the perfection of the future age. X, 844. All remission of sins through baptism, and complete healing and liberation from every evil in the resurrection, must be attributed to the gift received. X, 434, 591. The infirmity that remains after baptism will be consumed in the resurrection. X, 590.

The body also is sanctified through baptism. X, 844. The body of the baptized is restored to the condition of the first human being before sin. VI, 694. Many sick people were healed in baptism. VII, 764.

The newly baptized are so called. V, 1092. They are called infants. V, 1092, 1099, 1101. Why they are so called. V, 1101.

What it means to be baptized into Christ’s death. X, 824. To be baptized into Christ’s death means nothing other than to die to sin. X, 660. Baptism is the likeness of Christ’s death and resurrection, both in infants and in adults. VI, 256. In baptism no one fails to die to sin. VI, 253. In baptism infants die to sin. X, 824, 827, 830, 1239. Mystical death in baptism. X, 683. Baptism is given so that we may both die and live again. VI, 253. Those baptized into Christ’s death die to sin so that they may live for God. VIII, 744, 745. Whoever desires baptism desires new life. VI, 677. The baptized person is marked with a royal character. II, 307. The baptized person ought to imitate God’s rest and activity. III, 305. How the baptized are both still children of the world and nevertheless children of God. X, 157, 844. The infants who are washed in baptism are chosen from the world. X, 823. After baptism is the time to guard against all future sins, since all past sins have been removed. VII, 40. After baptism the guilt of offenses is greater. I, 669. The newly baptized are admonished to display innocence of conduct. V, 1560. They should imitate good Christians, not bad ones. V, 796, 1092, 1094, 1102, 1670.

Baptism does not benefit everyone. IX, 462. Wherever baptism itself is, it is baptism; but the one who receives it is not therefore himself the same everywhere. II, 301. The laver of regeneration is common, but the grace itself is not common to all. IV, 984. A person can be baptized with Christ’s baptism and yet the remission of sins may not occur in him. IX, 118, 119. Whoever possesses Christ’s baptism must not therefore be secure concerning the remission of sins. IX, 218. In baptism both good and wicked people put on Christ up to the reception of the Sacrament, but only the good put him on up to the sanctification of life. IX, 193. Baptism is life for some and death for others. IV, 1760. Whom it gives life and whom it does not. IX, 189. Those who receive baptism and renounce the world in words but not in deeds possess true baptism, but are not brought to life. IX, 189. Baptism, like an implanted mark, adorns the soldier and convicts the deserter. IV, 433. How it is to be understood that those baptized anywhere and in any manner do not thereby obtain baptismal grace. IX, 167.

Augustine’s opinion: those possess baptism who, wherever and from whoever, receive it consecrated by the evangelical words, without their own pretense and with some faith, but without charity; yet it does not benefit them. IX, 243. The Sacraments, knowledge, prophecy, and faith are indeed great things, although the person who possesses them without charity is nothing. IX, 601. Baptism without charity benefits nothing. III, 1432. Whether one who approaches baptism deceitfully receives the remission of sins. IX, 119. Anyone who approaches Christ in good faith can receive Christ’s baptism without contamination from a wicked minister. IX, 386. Through the same baptism good Catholics are saved, while wicked Catholics or heretics perish. IX, 198.

Baptism given by heretics or by the wicked benefits neither them nor those who receive it unless they are changed. IX, 156, 157. Salvation is completed through baptism and conversion of heart, but either one can exist without the other. IX, 176. Baptism without righteousness does not lead to the kingdom, nor righteousness without baptism. IX, 437. Some wrongly say that the two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor refer one to those being baptized and the other to the baptized. VI, 207. [Col. 0110] Some wrongly thought that baptism without observance of the commandments was sufficient for life. VI, 210. Whether baptized sinners will come out of Gehenna. VI, 149, 154. Some promise liberation from eternal punishment to all the baptized, even heretics. VII, 733. Some promise it only to those baptized among Catholics, even if they live wickedly. VII, 741, 742. Temporary punishment must not be promised to those baptized who live criminally. VI, 226. Unless life corresponds to baptism, the kingdom of heaven will not be obtained. VI, 227.

The form or rite of baptism. II, 97; X, 145. Infants to be baptized are brought to the Church. V, 1333. The order of healing to be observed toward those being baptized. VI, 221. Faith is necessary for receiving baptism. VI, 649. Baptism does not benefit if faith is absent. III, 736. The person being baptized was asked whether he was turning to God and believing in him. IX, 352. Whether he was renouncing the world. IX, 190. Why another should not answer on behalf of one who can answer. IX, 175. The Creed was handed to those being baptized, and they were required to return it. VI, 206. Seven-year-old children recite the Creed when they are baptized. X, 481, 517. We are baptized while professing the rule of faith. V, 1614. At Rome, those being baptized customarily made a memorized profession of faith before the faithful from an elevated place. I, 751. Those presenting an infant for baptism answer, without lying, that the infant possesses faith because of the Sacrament of faith and turns to God because of the Sacrament of conversion. II, 364. Infants become believers through those by whom they are presented for baptism, and unbelievers through those who, because they believe baptism benefits nothing, do not believe that the infants should be presented. II, 870, 984. The Church lends infants the feet of others to come, the heart of others to believe, and the tongue of others to confess. V, 950. If you say that the one whom you present possesses something in him that may be saved, by confessing you erase it; if you say that he does not possess it, by denying you retain it. V, 950. If you do not have this faith in your heart for those on whose behalf you answer, by denying it you kill them. V, 944. In what sense Cyprian says that infants lost through their parents’ sacrileges what they had obtained. II, 361.

Repentance for one’s previous sins must precede baptism, although it is not useful unless the person is also baptized. II, 1088. The same applies after baptism if they sin after it. II, 1088. Peter enjoined on those being baptized not faith alone but repentance as well. VI, 204. Repentance not only for unbelief but for the former life, which must be changed into a new one. VI, 204. Obstinate adulterers and prostitutes were barred from baptism. VI, 150, 470. To bar obstinate wicked people from baptism is not a new practice. VI, 219. The error of some who admit everyone indiscriminately to baptism, including known and obstinate adulterers. VI, 197. The teaching of morals is to be given only after baptism. VI, 197. The error of saving all the baptized on account of Christian faith, even if they have not corrected morals that are as wicked as possible. VI, 197. Threefold error is refuted here. VI, 202. What those being baptized should avoid, what they should love, and for whom they should pray. VI, 692. Abstinence, fasting, exorcisms, and continence are necessary preparations for baptism. VI, 202. Psalm XXII is expounded to those being baptized. V, 1646.

Those being baptized renounce the devil. II, 889; X, 408, 427. Exorcism and exsufflation in baptism. II, 890; VI, 628; X, 649, 653. Why the Church breathes upon and exorcizes those being baptized. X, 1073, 1078, 1079, 1081. The water of baptism is consecrated by the sign of the cross. V, 1064; X, 861. The power of the water comes through the consecration of the word. VI, 694. It is not Christ’s baptism if the evangelical words constituting the Creed are not present. IX, 214. Baptism cannot be consecrated without those definite evangelical words. IX, 214. Heretics who do not baptize at all are more easily found than those who baptize without those words. IX, 214. Baptism is not invalidated by a perverse understanding of the evangelical words, whether on the part of the minister or the recipient. IX, 166, 167, 168, 170. An error arising through ignorance in those words does not destroy the Sacrament’s integrity. IX, 213, 214. The intention of the one praying overcomes the defect of the prayer. IX, 214.

One baptism. VI, 706. Those who wish to duplicate baptism must necessarily seek divided hearts. II, 97. To say that baptism is consecrated in three stages is a great error. IX, 284, 285. The baptized person is anointed with oil. VI, 693. Hands are imposed upon him. V, 1447. The Holy Spirit is invoked over him. V, 1163. The baptism of infants and communion. V, 943. In baptism a kiss was given to infants. X, 625. Whether baptism should be conferred before the eighth day. X, 625. The eighth day should not be awaited for baptizing infants. X, 190, 191. The Sacrament of baptism on Saturday. III, 305. Baptism can be given on any day. V, 1048. A superstitious baptism in the sea on the birthday of Saint John. V, 1021. Baptism during the Paschal solemnities. IX, 180. Why the number of those being baptized is greater on these days. V, 1048. Seven or eight days of the Paschal period are assigned to the Sacraments of infants. V, 1101. Why the Lenten fast precedes the celebration of Christ’s baptism. V, 1048. The newly baptized are clothed in white garments. V, 678, 1092. The sign of Christ appeared at Jerusalem on the garments of the baptized. V, 137. The eighth days of baptized infants. V, [Col. 0111] 1101, 1196, 1201, and note, 1560, 1669. Those who touched the earth with a bare foot during their octaves were customarily punished severely. II, 221. The octave in white garments. II, 133. The heads of the baptized are uncovered on the day of the octaves. V, 1669. What is celebrated on the eighth day of the baptized. IX, 290. An infant must be baptized alive. III, 420. Divergent opinions on whether baptism should be given at the end of life to catechumens who do not request it and cannot answer. VI, 469. Augustine holds that baptism should be given in the proposed case even to those retaining adulterous marriages. VI, 469. What it means, according to Julian, to be baptized for the dead. X, 1596. What baptism accomplished in Cornelius. IX, 174, 175. Whether those baptized by Christ’s disciples before his death received the Holy Spirit. VI, 53. Some bring infants to receive baptism because they think that by this remedy they retain or recover temporal health. II, 361.

The baptism of blood: what it is. IX, 276. Martyrdom and genuine conversion at the moment of necessity fulfill the place of baptism. IX, 173. For those unwilling to deny Christ, suffering is counted as baptism. II, 1087. Kindness supplies what necessity has excluded. IX, 175. Baptism was reckoned as given to the believing thief, and what could not be given to his crucified body was regarded as received in his free soul. VI, 53. Daily baptism. V, 1005.

Baptism cannot be administered without a minister. IX, 499. Whether baptism administered theatrically and jokingly should be regarded as valid. IX, 243. The right to give baptism is held in ordination. IX, 71. It is indicated that a presbyter customarily baptized. II, 343. A layperson baptizes in an emergency. IX, 71. Baptism given by a layperson without any necessity cannot be said not to have been given, but it was given illicitly. IX, 71. This is explained by examples. IX, 71. In extreme necessity baptism can also be received from a heretic or schismatic. IX, 109, 200, 242. Whether baptism can be given by those who have never been Christians. IX, 242.

The second coming of Christ will remove baptism just as the first removed circumcision. II, 96. A certain mother, intending to curse her sons, ran to the sacred font. V, 1443.

The idolaters had their own baptism. IX, 250. A certain prominent member of the Heavenly Ones instituted a new baptism. II, 180.

Barabbas is understood under the name of a gnat. III, 1329.

A beard is an ornament of manhood, not a defense. VII, 791. A beard is understood only in the perfect. IV, 1736. Christ’s divine virtue is represented by a beard. IV, 309. The beard signifies the strong. IV, 1733. Bearded Fortune. VII, 122.

Barbarisms. VIII, 417. What barbarism is. III, 44.

During the sack of the City, the barbarians spared Christians for Christ’s sake. VII, 14, 17. The barbarian period. VI, 699.

A barbarian, a servant of God. II, 698.

Bardesanes, from whom came the heretics called Bardesanists. VIII, 31, 32.

Barjesus, a magician. IX, 372.

Barnabas singing psalms with Paul in prison. III, 1935. Paul rightly reproved the pretense of Barnabas and Peter. VI, 536.

Barnabas the presbyter. II, 966; V, 1580.

Pinianus sends Barnabas, a servant of God, to Augustine when the people were forcing him into the presbyterate. II, 479.

Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe. VII, 591.

Bazan is interpreted as “dryness.” IV, 832. “Confusion.” IV, 832, 1751, 1760.

The asylum of basilicas is venerable even to the barbarians themselves. VII, 14, 17, 20, 45, 110, 113, 170. Those fleeing to holy places during the sack of the City were saved by the barbarians. VII, 170. See *Church*.

The Basilica of Celerina. V, 316, 939. The Basilica of Faustus. V, 643, 1202. The Basilica of Florentia. V, 1597. The Basilica of Gratian. V, 849. The Basilica of Honorius. V, 889. The Basilica of Leontius. V, 1201, 1207. The Greater Basilica. V, 1194. The basilica of the elders at Carthage. V, 209, 902, 1335; X, 334. The Basilica of the Scillitan Martyrs. V, 840. The Basilica of the Twenty Martyrs. V, 799. The Basilica of the Eight Martyrs. V, 1522. The Basilica Novarum at Carthage. V, III. The Basilica of Peter at Carthage, in the third region. V, 116. The Basilica of Restituta at Carthage. V, 132, 185, 559, 643, 1257. The Basilica of the Tricillae. V, 364.

The form of basilicas. III, 660.

Basilicas burned by the Donatists near Carthage. IX, 709.

Basilides, from whom came the heretics called Basilidians. VIII, 26. Basilides was the first to dare say that the God worshiped by the Jewish people was not the true God. VIII, 664.

The basilisk is said to excel among serpents by a kind of royal nod. IX, 54. The basilisk is king of serpents, just as the devil is king of demons. IV, 1168.

Basil, a Greek by nationality. VIII, 668. Bishop of Caesarea. X, 865. Whether Basil supports those who deny original sin. X, 650. Basil’s testimony concerning original sin. X, 652. Basil’s sermon on fasting. X, 652. His book against the Manichaeans. X, 649.

Bassus the Syrian. VII, 767.

A *basterna* [covered litter]. II, 73.

A *bastaga*, a carrying litter. II, 181.

Bathanarius, count of Africa. VII, 714.

The bitterness of Bator. V, 1503.

Augustine delivered a panegyric at Milan for the consul Bauton. [Col. 0112] IX, 362.

Everyone desires blessedness. I, 792, 793, 1220, 1312; IV, 293; V, 365, 366, 1401; VII, 277. Everyone seeks blessedness, eternity, and truth. VIII, 887, 1018, 1034. Everyone wishes to be blessed. X, 1521, 1524. Even the lost do. II, 497. The wicked are wicked for this reason: so that they may be blessed. IV, 1502. They wish to be wicked so that they will not be miserable. IV, 203. Even the philosophers of this age, and the Academics who doubted everything, were compelled to confess that everyone wishes to be blessed. X, 1567. The industry of all philosophers appears to have been devoted to blessedness. VII, 226.

How great is the variety of opinions concerning blessedness. VIII, 1018, 1019. The Academics placed it solely in the search for truth. I, 908. Blessedness is not in the mind, as the Stoics maintained. II, 439. The philosophers falsely asserted that the wise person is blessed amid pains and torments. II, 667, 668. The blessedness of proud philosophers is laughable and pitiable. VIII, 1021. One should not be called blessed who lives according to his own will. II, 497. Blessedness is not living as each person wishes. VIII, 1019, 1020. Cicero’s distinguished judgment on this matter. VIII, 1019. Where blessedness lies according to Cicero. VIII, 1046. Plotinus’s distinguished saying concerning blessedness. VII, 271.

What blessedness is. V, 1401. Blessedness, the sum and culmination of all good things. IV, 72. Knowledge of blessedness has been impressed upon our minds. I, 1254. Blessedness is attaining the highest good. I, 1254, 1260. The highest good is called that to which all things are referred. II, 438. The blessed life consists in what is to be loved for its own sake. III, 26. Blessedness consists in enjoyment of the true and highest good. VII, 233, 703. Everyone is blessed through enjoying that for whose sake he wishes to possess other things, since he loves it no longer for the sake of something else but for its own sake. II, 438; VII, 621. Blessedness is adherence to the highest good. VIII, 950.

Beatitude is God himself. I, 848, 965, 968; II, 503; VIII, 163, 554. The beatitude of man is God, or knowledge of God. II, 840. Attainment of God. I, 1315, 1319. Enjoyment of God. I, 587. Clinging to God. I, 795. Rejoicing in God, toward God, for God’s sake. I, 793. Running from many things toward the One, and remaining with the One. V, 587. Beatitude is joy in the truth. I, 793. Perfect knowledge of the truth, which is to be enjoyed. I, 976. Beatitude consists solely in the certain and perpetual vision of God. III, 1288. From what its perpetuity derives. V, 663. The beatitude of human beings and angels comes from God alone. VII, 217, 220, 269, 279, 280, 290, 349, 656. And the Platonists recognized this. VII, 279, 290.

For the Epicurean, the blessed life is bodily pleasure; for the Stoic, virtue of mind; for the Christian, the gift of God. V, 812. Nothing should more properly be called God’s gift. I, 962. Beatitude does not consist in riches, even if someone knows with certainty that he will not lose them. I, 965. They place beatitude in earthly goods only if they do not belong to the regeneration of the children of God. II, 669. One should not call him blessed who has attained temporal well-being in himself or in others whom he loves. II, 498.

No one who knows the blessed life is miserable. VI, 24. Two conditions of beatitude: enjoyment of the unchangeable good and security that it will not be lost. VII, 328. The blessed life is nothing unless it is eternal. V, 1403; VI, 24; VIII, 605. Promises of eternal beatitude in the Prophets. VII, 753. Eternity, truth, and happiness are beatitude. VII, 369. Eternity and security are required for beatitude. V, 1404; VII, 327, 360, 370, 433. An insecure possession of beatitude destroys love of God. VII, 371. Beatitude is deceptive and false when future misery is either unknown or feared. VII, 371. He is not blessed who fears that he may lose what he possesses. I, 965. He who foresees that he will fall into misery. X, 932, 933. We have learned that future beatitude will truly be everlasting, not through human arguments but through the aid of faith. VIII, 1023. Only the immortality of perfect beatitude can fill its measure. VIII, 607, 1022. The immortality of beatitude becomes credible through the incarnation of the Son of God. VIII, 1023.

The beatitude of the future life is perfect. VIII, 1018. In the heavenly city no calamity will have to be endured and no desire restrained; only love of God and neighbor will be retained. II, 525. There are life and good days where nothing desires anything against the spirit, where it is not said, “Fight,” but “Rejoice.” IV, 1862. In beatitude there will be nothing to fight against and nothing to sting; everything will yield to peace. IV, 1860. There nothing will remain, either in soul or in body, that rebels against the love of God. IV, 1862. In beatitude there is victory and truth; in beatitude, dignity and holiness; in beatitude, peace and happiness; in beatitude, life and eternity. VII, 78.

Beatitude is not found in this world. I, 701. True beatitude does not belong to this life. VII, 433, 628, 631. It is not to be sought here. 1106, 1363. What we seek is not here. VIII, 887. Where the blessed life is to be sought. V, 1106. There is no blessed life here except the life lived in philosophy. I, 928. What sort of beatitude can there be in this life? VII, 636. In this life beatitude is held only in hope. VII, 631, 648. What perfect beatitude may be here. V, 1179. Our beatitude in this life is inward. III, 1236. Beatitude is not found here in social life. VII, 631. [Col. 0113]

Not all who desire beatitude attain it. II, 393. There is no error in desiring it or in striving toward it. I, 1254. Why so few reach it. I, 1237. Many do not desire to attain it as much as is sufficient for them to have the strength. I, 793. Everyone indeed desires beatitude, but most do not know how it is reached. IV, 1502. Few desire that without which it cannot be reached. IV, 1502. To know how a human being can be blessed is true knowledge and must be preferred to everything. II, 436. Through sin humanity lost beatitude, but did not lose the ability to recover it. I, 1280. No sure way to beatitude is found without divine authority. VII, 600. One must proceed toward beatitude through faith. VIII, 1020, 1033. He proceeds toward it who lives well. I, 1321. It is reached through good works. I, 976, 1018. No one can be blessed unless he has knowledge of God and imitation of him. VII, 233. The one God must be worshiped in order to obtain beatitude. VII, 280. The way to beatitude is likeness to God. VII, 271. The Platonists deny that anyone will attain beatitude who has not clung to the unchangeable God in the purity of chaste love. VII, 277. The way to beatitude is Christ. V, 813. See Happiness. Beatitude and immortality cannot be possessed except through Christ. X, 747. Scripture presents both one way and many ways to the heavenly homeland. II, 393. The blessed life is not possessed if it is not loved. VII, 433. The labor of kings, princes, and others in securing peace for peoples is useless for the blessed life unless they ensure that this very peace is referred to the worship of God. II, 680. The name “beatitude” is extended even to people placed in different conditions. VII, 328. Carnal beatitude promised in the Old Testament taught that spiritual beatitude was to be expected in the New. VII, 539. The life of the blessed was signified by the bodily paradise in which Adam was. III, 478.

Who is blessed? I, 989. He is blessed who needs nothing, that is, who is wise. I, 976. The truth must be sought if we wish to be blessed. I, 919. “Why do you wish to be blessed by things of the lowest order? Truth alone makes people blessed, and from it all things are true.” IV, 79. He is blessed who reaches the highest degree through truth. I, 976.

Two things make a person blessed: willing what is good and being able to do what one wills. VIII, 1020. He is not blessed who does not have what he wants; yet not everyone who has what he wants is blessed. I, 964. He should be called blessed who has everything he wants and wants nothing wrongly. VIII, 1020, 1021. Or anything unsuitable. II, 498. To want what is unsuitable is most wretched. I, 964. Why, when they cannot have both, do people prefer to have everything they want rather than to want everything rightly, even if they do not have it? VIII, 1020. One cannot call blessed either the person who does not have what he loves, whatever it may be; or the person who has what he loves, if it is harmful; or the person who does not love what he has, even if it is the best thing. I, 1312. Truly blessed is not the one who has what he loves, but the one who loves what ought to be loved. IV, 202. And the one who enjoys what is best. I, 1312. One must not immediately call blessed anyone who enjoys what he loves. VII, 233. No one is blessed except the person who enjoys virtue and the other goods without which virtue cannot exist. VII, 626. No one is blessed unless he has reached the place where he cannot die, be deceived, or be offended at all. VII, 433. No one is blessed except the just. VII, 433. Which people are a blessed people? V, 206. Blessed in hope are those who search the testimonies of God—not because they are searching, but because they will find what they seek. IV, 1503.

A human being cannot make himself blessed. VI, 672. In this life the philosophers wished, with astonishing vanity, to be blessed and to make themselves blessed. VII, 627. Everyone wishes to be blessed by possessing something, but it is impossible for an inferior thing to make you blessed. IV, 293. “You will be blessed by this alone: by something better than you are. God is better than you, who made you. Love this; possess this. For what you want, you will have; and you will have this freely.” IV, 294. We are blessed from God himself, through him, and in him. VIII, 928. “Make us blessed, Lord, from you, not from gold, not from estates, and so forth.” V, 651. No one makes a human being blessed except the one who made the human being. II, 667, 669, 670. Therefore a human being must become blessed from the source from which he becomes good. II, 495. A blessed human being and a blessed city do not come from different sources. II, 669, 670. We shall be blessed by possessing God. IV, 295. “He who mercifully looked upon me when I was placed far away—how will he bless me when I am placed with him?” IV, 214. What makes the most blessed. VIII, 63, 64, 1061.

The reward of the blessed will be God himself. VII, 801. God himself is the spectacle of the blessed. IV, 1901. God is the food of the blessed mind. V, 709. Truth will be the rest and food of the blessed. V, 1633. To live blessedly is to enjoy God fully. III, 30. How a human being enjoys God. VII, 233. The blessed are not changed into God’s substance. X, 265.

The condition of the blessed. III, 476. All the blessed possess God’s house, and each possesses it whole. IV, 1061. When you hear, “They will recline with Abraham,” and so forth, understand not the belly but the mind. V, 489. When the blessed life is under discussion, mention of bodily touches should not be made. VII, 271. The joy of the blessed. IV, 1108. [Col. 0114] In order that nature may be blessed inwardly, instruction is supplied outwardly. III, 380. The blessed are already placed in the light of truth. IX, 188. Eternal peace, final beatitude. VII, 636, 637. This surpasses all understanding. VII, 796. The reward that God will give the blessed at the end cannot be explained in words. III, 25. They will possess the highest peace in themselves, among themselves, and with God. VII, 797. For the blessed, enjoyment of God will take the place of every good. V, 1189. God will be all in all. V, 376, 867. Whatever different things you seek here, there God himself, one and undivided, will be everything for you. V, 376. The joy of the blessed. VII, 691. In beatitude there will be true glory, true honor, and true peace. VII, 801. The blessed will pass from rest to rest. VII, 694.

Knowledge and action make a human being blessed. VI, 299. Someone is called blessed either by possessing or by doing. IV, 1061. What the blessed will possess and what they will do. IV, 1061. What the action of the blessed will be. V, 1147. The blessed will have leisure, see, love, and praise. V, 1185; VII, 804. In heaven there will be praise of God without cessation or weariness. V, 1147. The activity of the blessed will be nothing other than praising God. IV, 1061, 1062, 1403; V, 235; VII, 801. And singing “Alleluia.” V, 1147, 1176, 1186. Perpetual praise of God will be the occupation of those at rest: no one will then approach it, and no one will then depart from it. VIII, 314, 315. In the rest of the homeland there is not sluggish idleness, but a certain ineffable tranquility of restful activity. II, 212. Neither the praise of God nor the love of God will satisfy the blessed. IV, 1062. The blessed praise because they love; they love because they see. IV, 1916. The blessed will also devote the members of their bodies to the praises of God. VII, 801. The entire activity of the blessed will be to say “Amen” and “Alleluia.” V, 1632. Not with passing sounds, but with the affection of the mind. V, 1632. Nothing will be more joyful to the blessed than song in praise of the grace of God. VII, 803.

The blessed will see God in the very body. VII, 797. Whether they will see God through the body. VII, 797. With bodily eyes already made spiritual, they will see incorporeal things. VII, 799. They will not need bodily eyes to see everything. VII, 798. Bodily eyes will have their own function. VII, 798. When they are full of God, all the blessed will see one another divinely. V, 1146. They will see one another’s thoughts. V, 1145; VI, 387. They will see everything from which they are bodily absent. VII, 797. They will come to know what is outside. VII, 784. They will come to know the punishments of the condemned. VII, 784. Truth and knowledge of friends without fear of deception must belong to the blessed life. V, 1404. The knowledge and wisdom of the blessed will be full and perfect. VII, 724.

All the blessed will be immortal. VII, 751. The immortality of the blessed cannot be taken away by sin. VII, 403. The blessed will not perform works of iniquity, because there is no iniquity there; nor works of necessity, because there is no necessity there; nor works of mercy, because there is no misery there. IV, 1062, 1099, 1108, 1941. What the free will of the blessed will be like. VII, 802. In the blessed there will be an unlosable will for piety and equity, just as there is for happiness. VII, 802. In the blessed there will be no will to sin; in the condemned there will be no ability to sin. VI, 283. How the blessed will forget their evils. VII, 803. The blessed will have an insatiable satiety. V, 1633.

How beatitude is equal and diverse for all. V, 533. In beatitude there will be certain degrees of reward. VII, 802. Yet there will be no envy. VII, 802. The happiness of the blessed and the misery of the condemned will be greater in some than in others. VI, 283. Who are the lesser and greater among the blessed? X, 225. The saints will share one eternal life; although separated by different degrees of honor, they will shine together in harmony. VI, 285. In the blessed life there will be one virtue embracing all virtues, or rather, one that itself will be all the virtues. II, 671, 673. In place of the virtues with which the soul, established in labor, now operates, certain corresponding powers are to be hoped for in the life to come. I, 1191. Similar actions and virtues indicate the blessed life. III, 243. Faith, hope, and patience will not exist in the blessed life. III, 479. Most blessed are those for whom possessing God is the same as knowing him. II, 840.

The goods of beatitude are to be inferred from the goods of this world. VII, 792. From the death of Christ. VII, 792. The just labor very little for beatitude, and in it they reign truly and forever. VII, 77. Many are blessed, not because of what is present, but because of what will be present. IV, 1504. Blessed in hope are those who search the testimonies of God, not because they are searching, but because they will find what they seek. IV, 1503. If the rewards of future beatitude did not console the martyrs, who could endure such things? V, 1425. The beatitude and glory of the martyrs will be greater after the resurrection. V, 1283, 1454. In hope of attaining beatitude, the devout endure the evils of this life bravely. II, 668. Hence they are called blessed amid torments. II, 673.

Just as resurrection is promised to the flesh, so beatitude is promised to the soul. IV, 751. See Happiness. Beatitude is also the reward of good works for bodies. X, 239. The body of the blessed will be wholly subject to the spirit. VII, 802. What beauty the bodies of the blessed will possess. VII, 781. The beatitude of the body will be the fullness of health, that is, the strength of incorruption. II, 439. Although the bodies of the blessed will be spiritual after the resurrection, they will have tongues and voices with which to proclaim divine praises. II, 350.

[Col. 0115] Whether beatitude is obtained immediately after this life or only at the end of the age is a major question. III, 1351. See Eternal Life. It is rightly asked whether holy people who have died possess beatitude. VIII, 63, 64. Those who live well depart from here for rest and beatitude. VI, 677.

Between beatitude and misery there is no intermediate state in which a rational creature can exist. VII, 266.

God is truly blessed. VII, 328.

He alone lives as he wills who is blessed. VII, 433.

What it means to live blessedly. VI, 24.

The rational creature alone is capable of beatitude. VIII, 554.

The perfection of our beatitude is in the denarius, because it returns to the beginning. II, 218.

The eight Beatitudes are, as it were, steps toward perfection. III, 1233. The Beatitudes are compared with the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit. III, 1234; V, 1525.

Bebius was dragged by a hook and died with his entrails scattered. VII, 107.

Another Bebius, during Sulla’s victory, was torn apart by the hands of those tearing him apart. VII, 108. Note (c): “He died with his entrails scattered.” VII, 107.

Bejanus, of Bajanum. IX, 507, 528, 550.

How beasts know. I, 1066. Whether they possess reason and knowledge. I, 1063. Beasts possess the power of sensation, not of knowledge. I, 1066. This power is, as it were, an image of the knowledge that exists in human beings. I, 1067. Animals cannot judge the differences among the external senses. I, 1226. Human beings are superior to brute animals, not by making numbers but by understanding. I, 1018. They have no fellowship with beasts. I, 1368, 1370. We are surpassed by most animals in sensation, but surpass them in mind, reason, and knowledge. I, 1067. What it signifies allegorically to rule over beasts. III, 187. Those who tame beasts are called tamers. I, 1233.

The story of Bellerophon. VII, 570.

Bellona, the wife of Mars. VII, 191. A temple of Bellona established at Rome. VII, 105.

Christian teaching does not condemn all wars. II, 530. It makes a great difference for what reasons and under whose authority people undertake wars. VIII, 447, 448. A war undertaken with God as its author is undertaken rightly. VIII, 447, 448. It is not lawful for everyone to wage war. III, 781. Authority and deliberation for undertaking war should belong to the ruler, while the duty of carrying it out should belong to the soldiers. VIII, 447, 448. A just man may rightly wage war under a sacrilegious ruler. VIII, 447, 448. The causes of the wars of the earthly city. VII, 440. Cicero judged that war could be undertaken by the republic for the sake of safety. VII, 758. To wage war solely from desire to rule is great brigandage. VII, 117. Only necessity compels good people to wage war. VII, 124. What is rightly blamed in wars. VIII, 447. What is harmful and destructive in war. VII, 658.

The end of those who fight is peace. VII, 440, 637. War cannot exist without some peace, and conversely. VII, 641. Peace is not sought in order to stir up war; war is waged in order to acquire peace. II, 856. The soldier’s will ought to have peace, and necessity ought to have war. II, 856. To kill wars by a word rather than human beings by the sword, and to acquire peace through peace rather than war, is the greater glory. II, 1020. If the republic observes Christian precepts, wars will not be waged without benevolence. II, 531. Nor without mercy. II, 531. When a just war is waged, one fights because of sin and against the opposing side. VII, 643.

Which wars are just? III, 781. The Israelites waged just wars. III, 739. See Enemies. Even just wars cause pain to the wise person—why? VII, 634. The manifold disasters and dreadful necessities of wars. VII, 634. The miseries of wars are real. VII, 634. What should be considered amid the calamities of wars. VIII, 450, 451. Whoever thinks about or suffers the miseries of wars without pain is more miserable because he has lost the human feeling. VII, 634. Why prosperity and adversity alternate in wars. VII, 522.

The times and outcomes of wars depend on God’s judgment. VII, 168, 170. Through wars God corrects human morals, exercises virtue, and increases it. VII, 15. Even that war which is waged from desire does not merely fail to harm God or the saints; rather, it benefits them. VIII, 448. Why men great in virtue desire war. VII, 155. The bravest are indeed great and possess their own glory, but especially great are the most faithful warriors, through whose labors, with God’s help, the unconquered enemy is defeated and rest is secured for the republic. II, 1020. Wars broke out following the example of the gods. VII, 73, 74. Ninus was the first of all to bring war against neighboring peoples. VII, 116. How many wars afflicted the Romans after the altar of Concord had been founded. VII, 106. The fiercest wars under the emperor Gallienus. II, 918. The Social Wars. VII, 106.

The calamity of civil war. VII, 88. Civil wars are more bitter than all wars against enemies. VII, 109. And more pitiable. VII, 634. In the Roman civil war, a brother, recognizing that he had killed his brother, killed himself. VII, 73. The civil war of Marius and Sulla. VII, 106. The war of the fugitive gladiators. VII, 168. The Mithridatic War lasted forty years. VII, 169. The war against the pirates. VII, 168. The Samnite War, disastrous to the Romans, dragged on for nearly fifty years. [Col. 0116] VII, 169. The First Punic War lasted twenty-three years. VII, 169. The Second Punic War weakened Roman strength over eighteen years. VII, 169. What damage it inflicted on the Romans. VII, 169. The Third Punic War was completed in a short time. VII, 168. The Servile War. VII, 106. Note (b). The Romans wrongly attribute the length of the wars to Christian times. VII, 169. On the chain of wars that preceded Christ’s coming, numerous and very serious. VII, 109. Wars, great games of demons. VII, 99. The great war is called the war of the Lord. III, 738.

We have two kinds of war. IV, 959, 1858. The war of a human being against himself. IV, 959. A good person carries his own war with him wherever he goes. V, 169. War against vices. VI, 393; VII, 730. The origin of the war within us. VI, 360. The war of the flesh against the spirit arose from sin. VII, 729. “Through sin you have been divided against yourself: you have within you something against which to fight, something within you to conquer.” IV, 1859. Thus he is punished for rebelling against God, so that the one who refused to have peace with God becomes a war against himself. IV, 891, 960. How spiritual war begins with suggestion, is kindled by delight, and is completed by consent or resistance. IV, 1859. While spiritual war is being waged, it is not one contrary nature fighting another, but something like a husband and wife in one household. IV, 1860. A person’s struggle with vices does not prove that he is vicious. X, 153.

The inner war of soul and flesh in the just. V, 169. See Desire, Struggle, Fight. The intestine war with the enemy, desire. X, 853. The internal wars of the saints do not cease in this life. X, 856. How troublesome the inner war is. IV, 1858. No war is graver or more bitter than that of will and passion without any victory. VII, 658. It is a great war for us not to see our enemies and yet to conquer them. IV, 1854. War with hope of eternal peace is better than captivity without any thought of liberation. VII, 729. After the resurrection nothing from within us will resist us. VI, 274. See Fight.

The war of the spiritual against the carnal is that correction carried out in love; their sword is the word of God. IX, 507. Impiety wages war against God. IV, 523. As though by civil wars, the Church is shaken by heretics. IV, 1423.

The war of the five elements, or of the nation of light and the nation of darkness, according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 35.

Belocus, the ninth king of the Assyrians. VII, 562.

Belus, the first king of the Assyrians. VII, 561. Father of Ninus. VII, 577.

The Bema of the Manichaeans. VIII, 173, 174. Celebrated in March with great festivity. VIII, 346.

We cannot be well off as long as we are exiles from the Lord. IV, 1059. A human being wants nothing else except to be well off; but he does not seek it in the region where it ought to be sought. IV, 1063.

Blessing, and good speech. VI, 320. Why blessing was bestowed by God only upon human beings, birds, and fish. I, 860. What the blessing that God gave living creatures for multiplication is. III, 240, 241. What God’s blessing effected in the first parents. X, 405. Jacob’s and Esau’s blessings are interpreted of Christians and Jews. V, 37, 38, 56. The blessing of the just is to glory in God and to be inhabited by God. IV, 89. The blessing of Christians through the flesh of Christ. V, 57. A comparison between the blessing by which we bless God and the blessing with which he himself blesses us. IV, 802. When God blesses, he does what he says. IV, 1444. Human beings wish to be blessed by God in many ways. IV, 803. God’s blessing is eternal life. IV, 1441. What the blessing of the Lord from Zion is. IV, 1686, 1738. A rain of blessing. V, 312. The blessing of bishops over the people. II, 761, 775.

God is to be blessed at all times. IV, 278, 308, 309, 563. God is to be blessed every day. IV, 1870, 1871. God is to be blessed in days and nights, in prosperity and adversity. IV, 1737. To bless God in the churches means to live in such a way that God is blessed through each person’s conduct. IV, 196. Those who dwell in concord bless the Lord. IV, 1736. If you wish to bless the Lord, do his word, do his will. IV, 1335. When you begin to bless the Lord through a good life, his works bless him, not your merits. IV, 1335. Some bless with their mouths and curse in their hearts. IV, 737, 1736. A blessing extorted. V, 50. Supplications are made before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; prayers while it is being blessed; intercessions or petitions when the people are blessed; and after all these, thanksgivings. II, 636. The blessing of bishops over the people. II, 761, 775. It was especially the custom among the Jews for passersby to bless those engaged in work. IV, 1695. Blessing is given by utterance in the marketplace, by a vow in the Church. VI, 320.

“To bless” is used for “to curse.” III, 800; VI, 534.

Divine honors were once decreed to benefactors. VII, 51.

That which charity does for the benefit of one’s neighbor is called beneficence. III, 72. We are not beneficent when we do what is asked of us, but when we do what does not harm those who ask. II, 391. A human being sins in beneficence in two ways. X, 299. Benefits are to be expected from God alone. VII, 293. God’s benefits are of two kinds. IV, 345. God’s benefits to humanity are to exist, live, sense, and understand. V, 254. Temporal benefits are common to the just and unjust. IV, 658, 804, 1282. God’s benefits are extended to everyone, good and bad alike. V, 1186. God does not cease to call, neglect to instruct the one called, cease to perfect the instructed, or neglect to crown the perfected. IV, 1319. God does good by turning back the one who has strayed, helping the one who fights, and crowning the victor. IV, 1954. Because punishment was not to be inflicted without cause, the benefit was therefore freely bestowed. IV, 158. The benefits of God’s grace are to be recalled. IV, 1739. The memory of God’s benefits is to be recalled through solemn festivals. VII, 280. Whatever benefits angels or human beings can bestow upon human beings lies in the power of the one omnipotent God. VII, 292. Whoever bestows a benefit lends at interest. III, 1264. Two kinds of bestowing benefits. III, 1264. Good must be done to human beings for the sake of their eternal salvation. III, 1288.

Beneficiary. IX, 638, 640.

Benenatus. IV, 376. Bishop of Tugutium. II, 1069, 1070; IV, 381.

Benevolence is that by which we benefit anyone whom we can. VI, 514. Perverse benevolence. IV, 1919. Benevolence by which a human being wishes to care for his neighbor: a fountain and a river. III, 2039, 2040; IV, 657.

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” IV, 1022. What does Benjamin, the young man in ecstasy, signify? IV, 834.

The highest, holy, and just kindness belongs to God. III, 250.

Berecynthia, mother of the gods, from Pessinus. VII, 50, 87. Whether Berecynthia gave birth to Cynocephalus and fever. VII, 87. Berecynthia was washed every year in the river Almo. VII, 50. Note (c): An image of Berecynthia was brought into the city by Scipio Nasica. VII, 50. How shameful were the rites of Berecynthia. VII, 87. The rites of Berecynthia, the mother of the gods, were hideously cruel and more disgraceful than other rites. VII, 216.

Beersheba is interpreted as “well of satiety” or “seventh well.” VIII, 458.

Barzillai the Gileadite assigns the king David’s benefits to his son, a young man. II, 244.

The names “beasts” and “cattle,” and which animals they customarily designate. III, 241, 286. On the sixth day God fashioned the beasts of the field through an operation distinct from that by which he created everything simultaneously. III, 342. Why beasts that harm one another were created. III, 288. See Harmful Animals. The fact that beasts now harm human beings is a punishment for the first sin. X, 657, 663. In paradise beasts would neither have died nor become savage. X, 1307. The opinion concerning the transformation of beasts into human beings and human beings into beasts. III, 445. The spirit of beasts. VIII, 779. A soul is also present in cattle. VIII, 1057, 1061. The souls of beasts live, but do not understand. VIII, 975, 979. Beasts lack understanding. IV, 480, 1939. Beasts do not possess the reason by which they understand, but they do possess the spirit of an animated body and manifest life: desiring food, taking what is useful, and so forth. IV, 1939. Beasts sense, remember, and desire. VIII, 999. Many beasts surpass human beings in keenness of sensation, strength, movement, and length of life. VII, 240. Beasts use their senses and sensory movements to seek what is useful and avoid what is contrary. VIII, 675. Beasts possess certain signs among themselves. III, 37. Images in the part of the soul belonging to beasts. VIII, 979. Just as they are incapable of beatitude, so they are not subject to the punishment of condemnation. X, 408. Peoples are signified by the beasts of the forest. IV, 1358. What does it mean that the Apostle Peter killed and ate beasts? IV, 1359.

Beast-fighters. V, 203.

Beta means one thing among the Greeks and another among the Latins. III, 54.

Bethel, Ulammaus, and Luz are the same city. III, 577.

Bethlehem is still called a village. VI, 339.

Bethsan is today called Scythopolis. III, 795.

Bias of Priene, one of the seven wise men. VII, 582.

All sinners drink the same cup in this world, but some drink the dregs and others the wine. IV, 955.

Two-horse chariots. VII, 626.

Biger or Birger. See Abbir.

Bilta. IX, 202.

The leap year occurs after four years. III, 275; VIII, 893.

Bishop of Byzacena. II, 759, 781.

Blasphemers are enemies of God. IV, 1178.

To blaspheme is to speak evil words about God. I, 1354. To blaspheme is worse than to swear falsely. VI, 545. Bad Christians cause God to be blasphemed. IV, 196. They hinder unbelievers from salvation. IV, 196. Few are now found who blaspheme Christ with the tongue; many do so by their life. III, 1621. God is blasphemed through an evil work. IV, 1899. It is no wonder that human beings disparage the servants of God, since they do not cease to blaspheme God himself every day. II, 266.

When will the blasphemies of unbelievers against Christians cease? [Col. 0118] IV, 250. What is the unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit? V, 448. Any other blasphemy is forgiven, the sin against the Holy Spirit being excepted. V, 457. The blasphemy against the Son is not forgiven more readily than that against the Spirit because the Son is lesser insofar as he is human. V, 457.

Light-shunning cockroaches. VIII, 363.

Bobba or Obba. IX, 229.

The great spring of the royal Bullenses. III, 284.

The martyrs of Bollita or Volita. V, 849.

Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church. I, 655; II, 955; X, 549. His prudence in the case of Antonius. II, 955.

Boniface. VIII, 534, 535.

Boniface, bishop. II, 536, 631, 652. Bishop Boniface, bearer of Marcellinus’s letter to Augustine. II, 585.

Boniface, bishop of Cataquum. II, 358, 359. Note: successor of a certain Paul. II, 357. He was especially careful to avoid lying. II, 361.

Boniface, a presbyter, between whom and a certain member of the monastery of Saint Augustine named Spes a dispute arose. II, 266. What that dispute was. II, 268. Spes began to act more turbulently, so that Boniface the presbyter would not be permitted to remain in his rank; Boniface was prepared rather to suffer harm to his honor among human beings than to proceed uselessly to the disturbance of the Church. II, 269. Augustine found Boniface the presbyter guilty of no offense. II, 266, 268. Augustine neither wished nor dared to order Boniface’s name removed from the number of presbyters. II, 266, 267. Augustine sent Boniface and Spes to the tomb of Blessed Felix of Nola; Boniface humbly concealed his priestly dignity during the journey. II, 267.

Boniface, count of Africa. II, 995; V, 652. While still a tribune, Boniface pacified the barbarian peoples of Africa by defeating and terrifying them. II, 995. Once made Count of the Household Troops and Africa, he allowed them to rampage. II, 995. Amid military concerns he desired to know what belongs to God. II, 792. How greatly Boniface was entangled in affairs. II, 993. Boniface was occupied with matters necessary for Roman peace. II, 793. A rule of right living was prescribed for Boniface as he served in the army. II, 854. Nevertheless, Boniface married while sailing. II, 994. But only after she had first become Catholic. II, 994. Yet his daughter was baptized by those who deny that the Son of God is true God. II, 994. And there is a report that he was polluted by intercourse with concubines. II, 994. It is hoped that he may persuade his wife to continence, so that he may render to God what he owes. II, 997. And that he may undertake the monastic life. II, 997. Boniface is urged not to delay doing penance. II, 994. And to pay less attention to what people have deserved from him than to what he ought to do according to God. II, 995. A book on the correction of the Donatists is to be sent to him. II, 792. After the recent death of his former wife, Boniface desired service to God. II, 994. That is, the life of monks. II, 994. By the advice of Augustine and Alypius he was recalled from this course. II, 994. Afterward he ought not to have taken a wife. II, 997.

Boniface, whose inheritance Augustine refused to accept. V, 1572.

Bonosus praised by the Arian as a most learned man. II, 1053.

What the true good is. V, 468. A good entirely free from every evil is a complete good. VI, 237.

What the highest good is. II, 438; VII, 232. The highest good is that by participation in which other things are good. IV, 1740; VI, 17. And a human being can become blessed. VII, 227, 624, 625.

Where the highest good exists in a human being. VII, 232. The beatifying good. X, 756, 759. What the good of a human being is. VII, 281; X, 759. The disagreements of philosophers concerning the highest good. VII, 227, 232. Dinomachus’s opinion concerning the highest good. X, 852. Aristippus placed the highest good in bodily pleasure, Antisthenes in virtue of mind. VII, 601. The Platonists placed the highest good in God alone. VII, 232. Two conditions of the highest good: that nothing be better than it, and that it be such that one does not lose it unwillingly. I, 1312. The good by which you are truly good, and which you neither receive nor lose unwillingly. V, 469.

The highest good is incorruptible. VIII, 607. The good is simple and unchangeable. VII, 325. The highest and wholly unchangeable good is God himself. VII, 349; VIII, 101, 549, 551. God is the sum of all good for us; God is our highest good. I, 1316. “Highest good, this is your good, O soul; there are also lesser goods, which are good for different people.” IV, 1322. The good of every good, from which every good comes—the good to which nothing is added to specify what the good itself is—the simple good: this is what we ought to desire. IV, 203. The whole and true good of a human being is the light perceived not by the eyes but by the mind. IV, 81. By what eyes the highest good is seen. VIII, 206. The highest good cannot be loved as long as the evils of the body and of chance are feared. VIII, 89. No one can attain the highest good unless he has loved it perfectly. VIII, 89. No one can perfectly possess or know a good that is not loved. VI, 24.

Every good thing is either God or from God. I, 1265, 1270; [Col. 0119] III, 137. God, who is good, made all good things. I, 743, 811. He created all good things. VIII, 665. From the highest good all spatial and temporal natures receive their form and appearance. VIII, 206. Even the lowest good can exist only from the highest good. VIII, 606. You will find absolutely no good that is not good from God. IV, 1741. All good things, whether great or small, come only from God. VIII, 193, 551, 555, 586, 597. Even the smallest and earthly things. I, 597; VIII, 448, 560, 595. The things that have been created are good, though not supremely or equally good; taken together, however, they are very good. VI, 235. For something to be good, it is not required that it be equal to God. VIII, 606. All things are good. I, 743, 744. All creatures possess some good of their own. IV, 1322. Yet in comparison with God, created things are not good. I, 828.

God created all things good, but not equal to himself. VIII, 548. Some good things are better than others. VI, 379. Some things, lower than others, are created from nothing by the Omnipotent. VIII, 191, 586. Everything that exists is good, but things are unequal. VII, 335. Created goods ought not to have been equal to one another. VIII, 606, 607. Only the good is praised. IV, 1741.

Good things can exist without evils, but evils cannot exist without good things. VII, 418. What difference there is between the Manichaean and the Catholic concerning the nature of good. X, 1117. The Manichaean holds the nature of good to be changeable, but the nature of evil unchangeable. X, 1113. Jovinianus said that there is a necessity of good. X, 1418. How both good and evil can naturally be lost. X, 1343. Whatever is generated is good, though not without evil. X, 846. There would be no conflict between good and evil if no one had sinned. X, 756. Unless good had remained in nature, there would be no pain over lost good in punishment. III, 385. The Manichaean doctrine concerning the purification and liberation of good from evil. VIII, 35.

There are three kinds of good. VII, 232. The highest good is God; the great good is the soul; the small good is the body. V, 853. Good is threefold: great, intermediate, and least. I, 1268. Great goods are those by which one lives rightly—virtues; intermediate goods are those without which one cannot live rightly—the powers of the soul; least goods are those without which one can live rightly—the forms of bodies. I, 1268. Good is twofold: good that is good through another good, and good that is good through itself. IV, 1740. Good is twofold: one kind makes a person good, and another is that by which one does good. V, 320, 410. Some goods are to be sought for their own sake, others for the sake of something else. VI, 380. One good is superior in name, while others of different kinds are inferior. V, 144. God’s goods are of two kinds. IV, 345. There is a good that God does not give to the wicked, an evil that he does not give to the good, and certain intermediate things—both good and evil—that he gives to both good and wicked people. IV, 658. Let us seek goods that we do not share with the wicked. V, 1299.

The good of the soul is that which is better than the soul. IV, 293. God is the good of the soul. IV, 294. One must seek the good of the soul—not something that merely hovers over it in judgment, but something to which it clings in love. VIII, 949. The soul is the good of the body. IV, 293. Whatever goods the body itself may possess, such as beauty, strength, and health, come only from God, who created and perfects nature; how much more, then, can no one but he bestow the goods of the soul? II, 591. Goods of either body or soul, without virtue, are not truly goods for the person who possesses them. VII, 626.

According to the Stoics there is no good except virtue. VII, 258. The end of the good life is to live according to virtue. VII, 233. The blessed life is the reward of good things. V, 809. You seek good and do evil; you run in the opposite direction—when will you arrive? V, 809. There is great disagreement among philosophers concerning the end of the good. VII, 281. The philosophers’ opposing opinions concerning the end of the good. VII, 601.

Temporal and eternal goods. V, 498. The Lord’s goods are sweet, immortal, incomparable, everlasting, and unchangeable. IV, 210. The good for which we sigh will be peace—but what kind of peace? IV, 1688. What are the goods of the heavenly Jerusalem? IV, 779, 1679, 1686. The goods of the future age have no appeal to the ungodly. IV, 251.
