The good that should be desired is the kingdom of God and his righteousness. III, 1292. How eternal goods should be sought, and how temporal goods should be sought. V, 1567.

Only inward goods should be loved; other things should be used as necessity requires, not enjoyed for delight. IV, 81. Those who love inward goods are not easily found. IV, 81. A person begins to desire good when it begins to become sweet. X, 586. When good gives delight, that is a great gift of God. IV, 1547. See Good Work. God gives sweetness so that we may do good truly and well—that is, not from fear of bodily evil, but from delight in spiritual good. IV, 1565. Even the desire for imperfect good is a gift of grace; otherwise grace would be given according to merits. X, 583, 584, 586. No one possesses anything good unless he has received it from the one who alone is good. IV, 1670. The desire for good is charity, which comes wholly from God. X, 586. Whatever good you have is found in God’s justifications. IV, 193. Nothing is commanded of a human being that is not given by God. X, 588. God will not take away spiritual goods unless you abandon them; but he himself takes away carnal and temporal goods, and anyone else who takes them away does so by his permission. IV, 201.

[Col. 0120] Charity is the root of good things. X, 269, 270, 374. Without charity no work is rightly called good. X, 374. No good work is credited. X, 374. No one can will anything good unless he has received free grace through faith. X, 553. Nothing good exists without grace. X, 370. God makes human beings’ good within them. X, 1133. God does many good things in a person that the person does not do; yet a person does nothing that God does not enable him to do. X, 586. God brings about many good things from our evils and sins. II, 727. God himself works good in you. IV, 1335. No one can do good except through Christ. IV, 141. And unless he has come to know the one God. IV, 141. A person does both good and evil by his own will, but in different ways. X, 1484. In what sense good is voluntary. X, 314. Good will is given and aroused by God. V, 108. God’s good will precedes a good and upright will. IV, 89, 151. The source of an evil will is falling away from the unchangeable good. X, 370. Certain goods of the soul perish through an evil will in such a way that they cannot return through a good will unless God does what a human being cannot do. X, 1541, 1543, 1546. Either unwillingness to do what is good or inability to complete it comes from original sin. X, 1517.

We can neither begin nor complete good without God. X, 560, 586. It is not simply a matter of failing to do good, but of completing it. X, 306. Here one is given the ability to do good, not to complete it. VI, 362. What it means to complete good. X, 560, 734, 803. A person does good when he does not consent to an evil conscience; but he does not complete good if he still desires evil. V, 818. When is good not completed? X, 306, 431. All the good we possess comes from our maker; for what we have made in ourselves we are condemned, while for what he has made in us we are crowned. IV, 1280. Some good things can be done by people who do not do them well. X, 749. Good must be done to the praise of the one from whom you have received the ability to do good. You have the ability to do evil from yourself, but the ability to do good from God. III, 2030. When good is done from fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness, it is not done well; nor is what appears in the deed accomplished in the heart. X, 586. Among spiritual gifts, count as yours what you love in your brother; let him count as his what he loves in you. V, 1040. Our goods are God’s institutions and gifts; our evils, however, are our sins and God’s judgments. I, 781. The good do with God what is good; from the evil, God brings about what is just. VI, 294. A person is corrected if, in doing good, he measures himself by comparison with someone worse. V, 89. See Good Work. Force may be used to compel someone toward the good. II, 754, 757, 803.

Having abandoned a superior good, do not bend yourself toward an inferior good. V, 144. What good should someone seek when God is present to him? Or what could suffice for one to whom God is not sufficient? V, 366. Heir of Christ, why do you rejoice because you are a companion of cattle? Raise your hope toward the good of all goods. IV, 1322. Inferior goods contain delights, but not like God, who is the delight of upright hearts. I, 679. These things you seek are good, but they will become evil for you if you abandon the one from whom good things were made. IV, 1322. See Temporal Things. To be deceived by false goods is to judge things inferior to oneself worthy of admiration and desire. I, 1328. Philosophers understood that external goods should not be sought for their own sake. VII, 233. All created goods are changeable. VII, 349. From where changeable goods are good, and from where they are changeable. VIII, 607. There would be no changeable goods unless there were an unchangeable good. VIII, 950. Changeable goods are good and are not; they do not remain, but slip away and flow. IV, 1686. Goods are corruptible and subject to evil because they are not supremely good. VI, 236. Changeable goods are not good through themselves. IV, 203. Things should not be called goods if they do not make people good. V, 1511. If you seek good things, first become what you seek. But if, being evil, you have found many good things, what benefit is it to you, since you have perished? V, 187. You wish to possess good things but do not wish to be good; your life contradicts your desires. V, 521. Do you not see that you blush because of your goods if your house is full of good things while it has you as an evil person? V, 469. The silent voice of goods against the person who possesses them without God. V, 469. Everyone wants to possess all good things except life and himself. V, 141, 187, 469, 513, 630, 1362, 1482. What have you done against yourself? What evil have you deserved from yourself? Among your good things you do not want anything to be evil except yourself. V, 1112, 1363. Good things harm, and bad things benefit, according to the character of those to whom they are given. III, 1801. Whatever a good person suffers is good; it is not a punishment’s torture but an opportunity for a crown. V, 1364.

What are the goods of this life? VII, 641. Temporal goods are gifts of God. VIII, 163, 165. They are to be expected from God alone. III, 568; IV, 346, 803, 1686. From the one true God alone. VII, 139. Goods are for necessary use, not for the affection of charity—as a traveler’s lodging, not as a landowner’s estate. V, 954. Temporal goods are not goods in themselves, nor are they given to human beings except by the one who possesses authority over all heavenly and earthly things. II, 996. God looks after the benefit of those whose prayers for temporal goods he does not hear. II, 545. God does not give earthly goods to all who ask for them, so that they may worship him gratuitously. VII, 20. Goods should not be highly valued if even the wicked obtain them. V, 468; VII, 660. The wicked abound in goods that are sometimes lacking to the righteous. IV, 351, 1678. [Col. 0121] Why God gives temporal goods even to the wicked. V, 1418. Temporal goods are given to the wicked so that the good may despise them and seek better things. V, 1418. Temporal goods, when desired, kindle desire; when acquired, become worthless; when lost, vanish. V, 861. Nor do they cease to inflame desire for what is coming, corrupt what is arriving, and torment what is passing away. V, 861. Before Christ, the righteous governed temporal goods prophetically. II, 540. The goods of this age are also given to evil people so that the good may not value them highly. III, 1647.

Good and evil things are shared by the good and the wicked. V, 236. Why God gives and takes away temporal goods from the good, and likewise gives and takes them away from the wicked. IV, 803. Temporal goods are given to the good so that they will not be thought evil, and to the wicked so that they will not be thought great and supreme goods. II, 996. Temporal goods are taken away from the good so that they may be tested, and from the wicked so that they may be tormented. II, 996. The distinction between the righteous and the unrighteous in the goods and evils of this life. VI, 295. See Evils. Whoever perversely loves the good of any nature, even if he obtains it, becomes evil in relation to that good and miserable because he has been deprived of something better. VII, 356. A good person is not exalted by temporal goods. VII, 20. Some goods belong particularly to the good, while others are shared with the wicked. V, 409, 1417, 1460. Goods reserved as the particular possession of the righteous. V, 159, 1187. Why the goods and evils of this life, but not those of the next, are shared by the righteous and unrighteous. VII, 20, 21, 48, 173, 661. Some goods God gives even to his enemies; others he reserves only for his friends. IV, 755, 803, 918, 1068, 1088.

Such is the power of good that even the wicked seek it. V, 145. Wherever you sin, you are, as it were, seeking good. IV, 1322. Even when you happen to sin, you are deceived by your eagerness to choose the good, because you do not heed God’s good counsel about what should be despised and what chosen. IV, 1322. Earthly goods are desired, but because of Babylonian confusion. IV, 779. Those who seek God do not seek passing and dying goods. IV, 122. The attainment of inferior goods produces joy, but abandoning better things is wickedness. VIII, 557, 562. The beginning of the goods of this life is without providence, and their end is accompanied by repentance. II, 938. In them there is deceptive sweetness, fruitless labor, perpetual fear, and dangerous elevation. II, 938. An earthly good becomes worthless when acquired, although it had inflamed desire when sought. IV, 1323. God commands us to endure present things, not to love them. IV, 251. Why one should not rejoice in temporal goods. III, 847. Goods bring true happiness to no one because they do not extinguish insatiable desire. IV, 1411. Earthly goods belong on the left. VII, 302. Even if bodily goods diminish, they do not diminish a good and just life. VII, 31. The good have no reason to fear the loss of temporal goods. IV, 804. In the loss of temporal goods, the wicked are struck by a greater loss. IV, 804. By losing temporal goods we learn whether or not we love them. III, 163. It is foolish to trust in vanity and labor to acquire perishable goods without any fear of losing them. III, 882.

Present goods should be despised. V, 1397. Christ taught by his example that earthly goods should be despised and evils not feared. VI, 339. Christ did not wish to possess temporal goods, in order to show that they should be despised. IV, 250. Temporal goods should both be requested from God and despised for God’s sake. VIII, 451, 452. Only those who do not belong to the regeneration of God’s children place blessedness in earthly goods. II, 669. What kind of good are riches? V, 468, 1419.

How temporal goods should be used. I, 1238; VII, 645. What is possessed badly is another’s good; and the person who uses something badly possesses it badly. II, 665. Even certain goods should be used in such a way that we nevertheless do not love them. X, 317. Whoever does not use goods for the purpose for which they were established sins—sometimes venially, sometimes damnably. VI, 380. Temporal goods should be used well, to obtain eternal goods. VII, 641, 642. Temporal goods should be referred to eternal good. IV, 1404. Use inferior things well, enjoying the superior good. V, 144. It is evil to use good things badly, and good to use evil things well. I, 639. The four differences between the good and evil use of things. X, 147. Some goods can be used badly, while others cannot. X, 169. If goods are not necessary to someone, he acts better by not using them. VI, 380. Abstinence from earthly goods is easier than their temperate use. VI, 390. No one uses them well unless he can also refrain from using them. VI, 390. The goods we have received from God should be proclaimed so that they may benefit others. IV, 655. Every earthly possession is both an exercise of humanity and a punishment of desire. V, 327. Nectarius thinks it more grievous to be stripped of one’s resources than to be killed. II, 386. Civil laws do not make people good users of goods, but make bad users less troublesome. II, 666. How many distribute and abandon their own goods within the Catholic communion. VIII, 225. There are and will be faithful people who surpass others in temporal prosperity. II, 549.

What the temporal goods promised to the Jews signified. VIII, 165. The Jews expected temporal goods in Christ, and he heaped those goods upon them. II, 546. The goods of the Old Testament had to be denied to the Church so that it might learn to desire and hope for the goods of the New Testament. II, 544. From the goods of this world one should infer the goods that God will give in heaven. VII, 792. Which are falsely thought to be good days. [Col. 0122] V, 245. See Days.

Many things are good in themselves yet have the meaning of evil in Scripture. X, 834. Small goods, in comparison with greater ones, are called by contrary names. VIII, 555. Why the devil scatters evils among good things. V, 568. Through prudence good is known by means of evil, and through experience of evil, good. III, 385. Christ alone was pleased with good without experiencing evil. III, 385.

The Syllaean good. X, 852.

God alone is good, and all other good things come from him. V, 119, 185, 559. God alone is supremely good, together with whatever comes from him. VIII, 202. He alone is simply and without qualification good. IV, 1740. God is uniquely good, and a human being is good from God but evil from himself. II, 658. One God is good according to the right and true good. VI, 701. How uniquely proper to God it is to be good. IV, 1496. In what sense God alone is good. X, 308, 309. God alone is good through himself, not through a good received by participation from elsewhere. IV, 1740. The difference between those who are good through themselves and those who are good through participation. I, 1347. God alone is good, but, in a certain proximate measure, the human being too is good. V, 119.

We are good insofar as we exist. III, 32. No one is good who has not been evil. VII, 438. A human being is evil from himself but good through God’s gift. V, 1428. No one becomes good from evil except through God. V, 409. The one who is always good makes good from evil. V, 409. No one is good from his own resources, but from the one who is never evil. V, 120. God not only foreknows the good but himself makes them good. X, 938. We are God’s handiwork not merely so that we may be human beings but also so that we may be good. III, 383. Each person begins in mortality and wickedness in order later to become good. IV, 734. Human beings are good only in a certain respect. VI, 701. All creatures bear witness to God’s goodness and greatness. IV, 1630. The good are vessels of mercy. III, 606. God’s mercy embraces the good in order to nurture them. VII, 20. Socrates said that, for those who prefer nothing more than to be good men, the rest of education is easy. II, 1030.

A man is rightly called good not because he knows what is good, but because he loves it. VII, 341. A good person is one who, when he can do evil, does not do it. IV, 1190. Someone is called good when his good qualities prevail. II, 658. Do not praise yourself even when you are good; for by praising yourself as good, you become evil. Humility had made you good, but pride makes you evil. IV, 193. Let the good person not think that he alone is good, nor the wicked person that no one is good. IV, 191. When someone thinks that no one is good, he himself becomes no one. V, 569. If you have begun to be good, believe that others are good as well. V, 1162. The good lie hidden here because their goodness is inward and concealed in the heart. IV, 621. No one is good through fear of punishment, but through love of righteousness. II, 660. Earthly prosperity does not make a person good. V, 135. However good you may be, you will not be without some evil. V, 119. No one is good through another’s good, nor evil through another’s evil. V, 213.

The good are mixed with the wicked in this age. VII, 46. Concerning the mingling of good and evil. IV, 539, 540, 773, 1603, 1604. The good person should not fear amid the mingling with the wicked. IV, 191. The good are not defiled by contact with the wicked. IX, 78, 629. This follows even from the judgment of the Donatists themselves. IX, 629. Christ’s own example also teaches this. IX, 77, 78. Be good among the wicked, and you good people will be without evil. V, 1162. The example of King Jehoshaphat cited by the Donatists does not support them at all. IX, 78. A wicked person does not defile the good in two ways. V, 559. The good groan amid the temporal mingling with the wicked because of their iniquities. IX, 103. The good are separated from the wicked not by place but by disposition. IV, 95. The marks by which the good are distinguished from the wicked. IV, 773, 1604. The good and spiritual make progress by patiently enduring association with the carnal. V, 48. Sometimes a good person is ashamed to be good among the wicked. IV, 1209. The wicked do no harm to the good. VI, 295. The wicked truly harm no good person, but benefit him. V, 202. What the good should do when the wicked deter them from their godly purpose. V, 546, 548, 586. While the good are still weak, they need, in certain respects, the mingling with the wicked. III, 1371. The wicked are necessary for the good. V, 1564.

The good are mixed with the wicked not only in the world but also within the Church itself. IV, 192, 1275, 1693. Good and wicked people are in the Church. II, 952; V, 470, 549, 1164, 1167, 1417. The good are sometimes expelled from the Church by seditious people. V, 852. Their virtue at such a time is patience. V, 852. Every good person in the Church is the oil of holiness in the winepress, a vessel for honor in a great house, gold in the furnace, and grain in the granary. V, 120. The good must not be abandoned; the wicked should rather be tolerated than the good abandoned, so that the wicked may be separated. II, 417, 418. The good should be imitated, while the wicked must be tolerated until the separation is made at the Last Judgment. V, 52, 471. The separation of the good from the wicked is postponed until Christ’s coming. II, 258.

The good often suffer evils in this age as though they were wicked. VII, 661. The temporal misery of the good and prosperity of the wicked are a stumbling block to many. VII, 703. At times the good are justly scourged temporally along with the wicked. VII, 21. Why the good are tested here while the wicked prosper. IV, 470. Why the good are punished with the wicked, and how much they benefit from it. VI, 701. God’s scourging teaches the good patience. VII, 20. [Col. 0123] The good surpass others in the truest and most certain happiness. VII, 71. The wicked are not truly well off, nor are the good truly badly off. V, 319. The good suffer for a time, and the wicked flourish for a time. IV, 1191. When we see the good suffering here and the wicked flourishing, it is a dangerous temptation. IV, 190. Because of the wickedness of the evil person the good are scourged, and through the servant the son is corrected. IV, 1213. How much God provides for us through evil people. IV, 1214. How the good use the world. VII, 444. Even if the good person is a slave, he is free. VII, 114. Whether the good fight among themselves, and in what way. VII, 442. The more good a righteous person is, the more burdensome he is to the sinner. IV, 364. Whoever is good will easily find good people. VI, 344, 347. See Wicked. The fellowship of the good should be loved, but hope should not be placed in them. VI, 344, 348. No one is good without fruitfulness. X, 749. God himself will be the reward of the good. V, 1460. Jovinianus’s blasphemy that the good and wicked will have equal honor before God. X, 1418. A person is good to his neighbors if he is good to himself. V, 213.

The good are called handsome in body. VII, 469.

The good are compared to gold, the wicked to hay. IV, 1375. The good are designated by the name “mountains.” IV, 349.

The Borborites, or Gnostic heretics. VIII, 26.

The Egyptian god Apis, a bull. VII, 564.

The ox—that is, the Jews—recognized its owner, and the ass—that is, the Gentiles. IV, 1675. Who are the oxen that thresh? IV, 114. The oxen are understood as those who have dispensed the holy Scriptures to us. III, 1470. What it means in the New Testament to yoke together an ox and an ass for work. VIII, 238. Certain historians report that oxen spoke. VII, 110.

Botrus, bishop in Numidia and accuser of Caecilianus. IX, 26.

A cluster and a grape among thorns. V, 285, 473, 762. Christ is the cluster of grapes. IV, 109.

The arm of the Lord is Christ. IV, 484, 894, 1253.

Whatever has an end is short. IV, 727.

A summary of the proceedings of the Carthaginian conference. II, 537.

Brixia. IX, 539.

Brutus. II, 529. A kinsman of Tarquinius. VII, 94. A relative of Lucretia. VII, 32. Brutus was one of the first two consuls elected by the people after the kings had been expelled. VII, 61. Brutus’s injustice toward Collatinus. VII, 94. Brutus expelled Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, his colleague, from the city. VII, 94. Brutus killed his sons for the sake of his country. VII, 162.

The goddess Bubona, who watched over cattle. VII, 140.

A morsel. How many Judas, though healed, fills—those who unworthily receive the morsel. IV, 1854.

Buda, a garment made of rushes. II, 305. Note.

Bulbs. VII, 194.

Among the Romans, the bulla was an insignia of rank. VII, 101.

Bulla. IX, 233. The Bullensian Field. II, 234.

Busiris. VIII, 601. A tyrant, son of Neptune by the mother Libya. VII, 570. He sacrificed his guests to his gods. VII, 570.

The Buslaceni. IX, 234.

Byrrhus. V, 883, 1579.

Byzacium. IX, 430.

The Byzaceni. IX, 395, 586.

Byzantium, involved in the schism of the Maximianists. II, 333.

## C

The Cabarsussitan council of the Donatists. II, 580; IX, 503. Its letter against Primianus. IV, 376; IX, 807 apparatus. Primianus was condemned by this council. II, 579.

Cacus, half-human, so called because of his unsociable savagery. VII, 638. Cacus, half-human: a poetic fiction. VII, 639.

A corpse is ordinarily called nothing other than a lifeless body. VII, 693. “Corpse” derives from falling. VII, 675, 693. Because, when its inhabitant departs, the body falls. V, 1134. The corpses of the dead signify sins in the Law. III, 592.

Falling and descending are different. V, 1608. Many wish to fall with David but do not wish to rise with David. The example proposed is not that of falling, but of rising if one has fallen. IV, 586. The fall of the great should not be a delight to the lesser; rather, the fall of the great should be a terror to the lesser. IV, 586. A healthy person did not heed the physician’s command not to fall; let him at least heed it when sick, so that he may rise. IV, 458, 951. You fall by loving the world; you rise by loving God. IV, 546. A human being could be capable of his own fall, but is not capable of his own resurrection. IV, 1696.

“Cades” is interpreted as both “changed” and “holiness.” III, 775.

Those who suffer from epilepsy are called caducarii. I, 967.

Caecilianus, bishop. II, 756; IV, 135; V, 1587. Because Caecilianus had been appointed bishop of the church of Carthage against their will, the Donatists created a schism. VIII, 43. Augustine does not know whether Caecilianus was ordained by traditors. II, 794. The Donatists falsely accused Caecilianus. II, 794. The Donatists attacked his innocence with savage suspicions. IX, 86. Caecilianus was accused of handing over the Scriptures and of offering incense. IX, 323. He was attacked with slanderous charges. VI, 201. The sin against the Holy Spirit was unjustly charged against Caecilianus. IX, 554. Piety, truth, and charity do not allow the Donatists’ testimony against him to be accepted. II, 794.

Caecilianus refused to come to the lodging of his colleagues, who had been perverted by his enemies. II, 163; IV, 375. The Donatists could prove no evil against him. II, 757. Nevertheless, the Donatists thought that he and Felix, his ordainer, should be condemned together. II, 160, 162; IV, 375. The Donatists said that Caecilianus had been condemned, together with his colleagues and ordainers, by approximately seventy bishops. II, 160; IV, 383. Caecilianus was condemned in his absence and though innocent. V, 900. Many of those who condemned him are counted among the traditors. II, 160. As the proceedings of the Council of Cirta in the year 305 report. II, 580. Majorinus arranged for him to be condemned in his absence, and a bishop was ordained against him. II, 172. The Council of Secundus of Tigisis ought have no more force against the absent Caecilianus than the Council of the Maximianists against the absent Primianus, and so forth. II, 173; IX, 653, 654, 655. Caecilianus is excused by Catholics on the same grounds on which Primianus is excused by the Donatists. IX, 585. The Donatists refused to refer the case of Caecilianus and his ordainers to the church overseas. II, 163.

The Donatists accused Caecilianus before Constantine. II, 302, 310, 328, 331, 581. They did so through Anulinus, the proconsul. II, 302. A council was held at Rome to examine Caecilianus’s case. II, 399. It was presided over by Miltiades. II, 399. A written accusation against Caecilianus was submitted at Rome to Miltiades and the bishops sent by Constantine. II, 166. Donatus proved nothing when arguing the case with Caecilianus at Rome. VI, 307. Caecilianus, falsely accused before Constantine, was acquitted. I, 645. He was cleared through the Apostolic See. IV, 382. He was declared innocent and confirmed in his episcopate. II, 161, 166, 167, 399.

The Emperor Constantine arranged for Caecilianus’s case to be examined and settled more carefully at the Council of Arles. II, 161, 169, 198. The Donatists referred Caecilianus’s case, after the episcopal judgments, to the judgment of the Emperor Constantine. II, 794. The Donatists falsely claimed that Caecilianus had been condemned in Constantine’s court. II, 794, 580. In an overseas judgment Caecilianus defeated the Donatists three times, before judges whom they themselves had requested. IV, 383; V, 900, 1595. The Donatists unjustly believe that those who communicate with Caecilianus are defiled. II, 412. They were never able to demonstrate that Caecilianus or those who adhered to him harmoniously were weeds. IX, 91. Caecilianus’s case is shown to be victorious by the Donatists’ own words. IX, 682. Caecilianus’s case does not prejudice the case of the Church. IX, 667. Even if his crimes had been true. IX, 833. Especially since the case of the Maximianists does not prejudice the Donatists. IX, 667, 675. Caecilianus did not defile the overseas churches, if Maximianus did not defile the companions of his schism. IX, 740. Caecilianus is neither a head nor a root for those who came after him. IX, 577, 833. Caecilianus’s case is compared with Primianus’s case. IX, 703. The judgments by which Caecilianus and Primianus were condemned and acquitted are compared with one another. IX, 552, 553. Caecilianus’s case could not harm the Church spread throughout the whole world. IX, 654.

At the Carthaginian Conference the Catholics acted to show that Caecilianus’s case did not belong to the case of the Church. IX, 655. Although Caecilianus’s case did not pertain to the case of the Church, the Catholic bishops undertook to defend it at the Carthaginian Conference. II, 580. This was done so that the Donatists’ slanders might be exposed. II, 580. Valentinian, Gratian, Theodosius, and his sons most firmly upheld Constantine’s judgment in the case of Caecilianus. II, 400. From the Donatists’ own principles it is proved that Caecilianus belonged to the Church. II, 796. Augustine recited the proceedings relating to the case of Caecilianus and Felix to Glorius and Eleusius. II, 160. Augustine was prepared to anathematize Caecilianus after his death if the charges brought against him were proved. II, 794. Caecilianus was baptized in unity and administered baptism lawfully. IX, 52. Caecilianus’s name was recited at the altar after his death. IX, 832. Caecilianus’s ordination, deposition, accusation, acquittal, and so forth. See Donatists.

Caecilianus, magistrate of the Aptungitani. II, 304; IX, 540, 780. Former duumvir. IX, 540, 779, 780.

Caecilianus, bearer of Innocent’s letter to Augustine. II, 646. Why Caecilianus came under suspicion as though he were an accomplice in Marcellinus’s murder. II, 647. Augustine is distressed that Caecilianus remains a catechumen. II, 652.

Caecilius, son of Celer, proconsul of Africa. II, 223.

Caecilius of Bilta. IX, 202.

The speeches of Caecilius. VIII, 76.

Blindness and weakness are diseases of nature. X, 293, 296. “Blindness” is sometimes said to exist even when only some objects are not seen. III, 559. The blindness of all human beings from birth. V, 746. The blindness of the inward eyes is failure to understand. IV, 1552. Blindness of mind is the loss of understanding of truth, when someone is given over to a reprobate mind. IV, 94. Whoever is given over to it is excluded from God’s inner light, though not completely while he is in this life. IV, 94.

How great a misfortune is blindness of heart. IV, 860. Blindness is the sinner’s first punishment. V, 664. It is the punishment of the ungodly. III, 865. Blindness of heart, when one sins because one does not know what justice forbids, is not only sin but also the punishment of sin. X, 1539. Blindness of heart is a severe punishment and at the same time a sin. X, 258, 1068. Blindness of mind comes from God’s most just, though most hidden, judgment. VIII, 655. God spreads punitive blindnesses over unlawful desires. I, 674. Blindness of heart is the cause of sin. X, 787. The blindness of human beings who glory in blindness. I, 685. To be free from blindness of heart is not within human power. X, 1539. The blindness of the Jews is a great evil of unbelief and a great cause of sin. X, 787. The blindness of the Jews increased at Christ’s coming. V, 752. It is a hidden vengeance. IV, 860.

Paul’s bodily blindness was a true punishment. II, 803.

Every unrighteous and ungodly person is blind in heart. III, 1388. Those blind from their earliest age, when asked about light and colors, cannot find an answer. II, 70.

The illumination of the man born blind. V, 750. The error of the man born blind who thought that sinners are not heard. V, 751. The blind man healed at Milan at the bodies of the martyrs. I, 604; VII, 761. What the healing of the two blind men signifies. V, 544.

Caelestius, disciple of Pelagius. I, 644. From him the Caelestians derive their name. VIII, 32, 47. A man of exceptionally sharp intelligence. X, 574. Inflated by the wind of false doctrine. X, 388. Caelestius and Pelagius argue against God’s grace. II, 865. Caelestius admits no grace beyond the natural freedom of the will except in law and teaching. X, 375. He attempts, by means of other testimonies, to evade the scriptural testimonies which Catholics bring against possibility and freedom of choice. X, 304. Caelestius had begun to insinuate himself toward the honor of the presbyterate, but was brought before episcopal judgment. II, 685. Caelestius attained the presbyterate in Asia. II, 760, 764. Heros and Lazarus accused Caelestius and Pelagius of error. II, 759, 764. Caelestius’s principal propositions concerning grace were condemned by the Palestinian judges. X, 337, 338. To what extent the Palestinian bishops approved the propositions of Caelestius that were charged against Pelagius. X, 357. Orosius gave the Council of Carthage the letters of Heros and Lazarus against Caelestius. II, 759. The council judged that Caelestius and Pelagius ought to be anathematized unless they anathematized their errors. II, 760. Caelestius was condemned at Carthage. X, 389, 355. He was also excommunicated. I, 644. He refused to condemn the error concerning original sin in the Carthaginian judgment. X, 386. At last Caelestius confessed that the redemption of infants takes place through baptism. II, 685, 764. Part of the proceedings of the Carthaginian judgment against Caelestius. X, 386. Caelestius deceitfully professes that he agrees with the letters of Pope Innocent. X, 574, 575. He offers a statement of faith to Pope Zosimus. X, 386, 574. In what sense the statement was called Catholic. X, 386, 574.

Caelestius, now seemingly corrected by his own profession, was spared by the Apostolic See in its most benign leniency. X, 576. Whatever was dealt with more mildly in the case of Caelestius was the most merciful exhortation toward correction, not approval of his most destructive perversity. X, 574. Letter of the African council to Zosimus, exposing the tricks and frauds of Caelestius. X, 574. While attempting to clear himself, Caelestius was bound by Zosimus to consent to the letters of the Apostolic See. X, 574, 575. Caelestius withdrew from examination by the Apostolic See. X, 574, 575. The libellus of Caelestius was cited among the proceedings at Rome. X, 388. Caelestius condemned by Zosimus. X, 389. Pelagius likewise. X, 574. Proceedings in the case of Caelestius before Zosimus. X, 575. In the later condemnation of Caelestius and Pelagius under Zosimus, the Roman clergy held nothing different from what they had held earlier under Innocent. X, 573, 576.

Caelestius condemned at Constantinople. X, 703. Caelestius and Pelagius condemned by episcopal councils, by Innocent, and by Zosimus. II, 865. The Fathers of Milevis preferred that Caelestius and Pelagius be healed within the Church rather than, their salvation being despaired of, be cut off from the Church. II, 764, 773. Augustine sent Optatus examples of the sentence passed against Pelagius and Caelestius by the councils, by Innocent, and by Zosimus. II, 865. Caelestius deprived of Catholic communion. II, 894. Those who defend his doctrine. II, 785. Bishops who neglected to subscribe to the condemnation of Caelestius and Pelagius were punished by loss of their episcopal office, were forbidden [to exercise it], expelled forever from their cities, and deprived of communion. II, 927. The prescribed penalties against the Pelagians were imposed on those who delayed expelling or betraying Caelestius and Pelagius. II, 927. No imperial sanction against Caelestius and Pelagius. II, 927. It was decreed that Pelagius and Caelestius should be expelled from the city of Rome. II, 927. Augustine suspected that Caelestius was teaching doctrine at Hilary’s [place] in Sicily. II, 685.

Definitions of Caelestius. X, 292, 293. Augustine refutes them. X, 292, 293. The doctrines of Caelestius were charged against Pelagius as his teacher, but were understood by him otherwise. X, 357. And rejected by Pelagius himself. X, 334, 344. Caelestius was bolder than Pelagius. X, 388. Caelestius was the more open and obstinate heretic, Pelagius [Col. 0126] the more concealed and deceitful. X, 391.

The Caelestian heresy strangled by Augustine and Alypius. II, 928.

Caelestian heretics. V, 980. They were called Pelagians. II, 685. Note a. Why the Caelestians and Pelagians hated Jerome. II, 928.

Caelestinus the deacon. II, 868. Installed in the Roman See without any division among the people. II, 953.

Caelestinus, to whom the Books against the Manichaeans were sent. II, 85. Caelestinus, a friend of Augustine. II, 85. Caelestinus, Augustine’s presbyter. II, 429.

Caelestis, the goddess, held in the highest honor among the Africans and Carthaginians. IV, 752, 1270; V, 624; VII, 75. Note a. The shameful rites of the goddess Caelestis. VII, 75.

For a celibate person of holy life, every intercourse is illicit, since even conjugal intercourse is not permitted to such a person. X, 1390. Daniel, maintaining celibacy, a figure of the servants of God. IV, 1731.

Among the Punic people, the heavens are called *Samen*. III, 797.

They imagine Caelum to be the father of Saturn. VII, 209. They assert without number that Caelum is Jupiter. VII, 210.

Plato assigned the place of heaven to fire. VII, 236. Basilides said that there were 365 heavens. VIII, 26. Some maintain that there are seven heavens, others eight, others nine, or even ten. III, 478. The first, second, and third heavens signify the corporeal, spiritual, and intellectual realms. III, 483. On the occasion of the third heaven, some wish to understand the distinctions among the corporeal, animal, and spiritual human being. III, 484. How much broader the heavenly spaces are than the earthly is obscure. V, 1262. Among bodies, nothing is better than a heavenly body. III, 232. What place is called the gate of heaven. III, 570. We must not think that the heavens stand still because of the name “firmament.” III, 272. Various questions about the motion of heaven. III, 271. Concerning its shape. III, 270. In the ethereal heaven all things are peaceful and firmly established; beneath it all things are changeable and dissoluble. III, 232. The turbulent qualities of this lower heaven are not driven about by chance events. III, 336. The lower heaven is reckoned under the name of earth. III, 336. How the aerial heavens are to be understood as having perished in the Flood. III, 279. Whether the heavens will perish in the conflagration of the last judgment. VII, 697. Which heavens are to perish by fire is debated among the learned. IV, 1313. How heaven will be made new after the judgment. VII, 682, 684.

The “heaven of heaven” is the heaven that we do not see. I, 826, 830. The “heavens of heavens” are the higher heavens; the lower heavens are the spaces of the air. IV, 1313. We labor greatly to discover how the higher heavens are placed one above another, how many there are, in what ways they are distinguished, with what inhabitants they are filled, and by what arrangement they are governed; nevertheless, we strive to reach the place where our homeland is. IV, 288.

By “heaven and earth” is understood the formless matter created at the beginning. III, 178, 223, 257, 272, 326. The ethereal structure. III, 235. The whole of creation. I, 815; III, 197, 199, 223, 248, 321, 322, 334, 750. The world. I, 1317. The angels. I, 830, 833. By “heaven” is understood spiritual creation. III, 252, 258. Spiritual and carnal people in the Church. I, 850; III, 264; V, 380, 388.

Heaven, protecting the earth on every side, is a figure of divine mercy. IV, 1331. “Heaven” signifies Holy Scripture. IV, 1341, 1909. The heavens are the books of both Testaments. IV, 112. They are the Apostles. IV, 157, 1473. Hence “heavens”: weak human beings. IV, 1959. The Apostles, as heavens, poured out the Lord’s mercy everywhere. IV, 288. The Evangelists are heavens. IV, 154, 170. Holy souls are heavens. III, 1256. The saints are heavens. IV, 157, 159; V, 891. They are, as it were, suspended from the earth, bearing God, thundering with his commandments, and flashing with wisdom. IV, 159. The saints and the just are rightly called heaven. VII, 698. By heaven the just person is signified, and by earth the sinner. IV, 136, 275, 276. Heaven means the saints; earth, earthly people. V, 370. Any believer can be heaven. IV, 1243. Those on whom the kingdom of heaven is built up among the saints and faithful are called the foundations of heaven. IV, 1049. How the heaven stretched out like a skin is to be understood allegorically, Augustine explained in *Confessions* 13.15. III, 271. The ethereal heaven signifies spiritual beings. IV, 1748. Heaven is the Church; the earth itself is the enemy of the Church. V, 380, 388, 394. How heaven and earth are to be understood in the Lord’s Prayer. X, 997. In the Lord’s Prayer, heaven and earth are suitably understood as man and woman. III, 1279. Heaven is the mind, earth the flesh. V, 380, 388, 394, 401. The heavens pertain to signifying the serene understanding of truth. III, 264. By the upper heavens, charity is to be understood. IV, 1342.

The kingdom of heaven is expressed under various names. III, 1235. It was also promised in the Old Testament. II, 768. One must strive toward heaven with complete desire. V, 932. See “Kingdom of heaven.” Heaven is closed to no one except the one who has excluded himself. V, 1450. People are driven back from their heavenly homeland by the blasts of wicked conduct. III, 23. Whoever wishes to ascend to heaven must be united with Christ. IV, 1630. Do you wish to ascend? Hold fast to the one ascending; be his member, who alone ascends. V, 570. Christ, in the form of a servant, laid down the way; in the form of God, established the homeland. V, 571, 573. The Apostles ascended to heaven. V, 570. By faith, hope, and charity we [Col. 0127] are in heaven with our Head, because he himself, through divinity, goodness, and unity, is with us on earth. IV, 205. God has offered the kingdom of heaven for sale. IV, 1211. It is bought for as much as each person is able to possess. IV, 1470; V, 707. The unlearned seize heaven. I, 757. The thief was the first to enter heaven; Stephen invaded it by force. V, 1425. Those in heaven, where there is no misery, do not need mercy, yet they do need the Lord. IV, 287. In the homeland there will be no place for prayer, but only for praise. V, 868. In the future age, those who are well established will not be able to sin. X, 1235.

The work of the heavenly homeland. V, 615. In the homeland of heaven there are evening, morning, and midday, but no night. III, 316.

The chief founder of the new baptism among the Caelicolae. II, 180.

To perform ceremonies. V, 1412.

C. Caesar’s war against Pompey. VII, 109. Caesar, victorious over Pompey, exercised his civil victory with clemency. VII, 109. Caesar was slaughtered in his own house during the Marian victory. VII, 107. He was slaughtered in the very senate-house as one seeking kingship. VII, 109. Caesar Augustus wrested freedom, already languishing, from the Romans by every means. VII, 103. He restored and renewed the state as though from its foundations. VII, 103. Caesar was accustomed to forget nothing except injuries. II, 528. Caesar’s clemency. II, 528. The Romans raised Caesar to the immortal gods. III, 1057. The matter in which Sallust placed Caesar’s praise. VII, 155.

Those who succeeded Caesar Augustus were called Caesars. VII, 577.

Caesar’s village. IX, 216.

Caesarea of Cappadocia. V, 1443.

Caesarea, a city of Mauretania. II, 857. The province of Caesarea. IX, 395.

Cain is interpreted as “possession.” VII, 460, 461. How Cain could have built a city when there were only three or four people. III, 548; VII, 445. Scripture did not state how much time elapsed between the creation of the first parents and Cain. III, 396. How Cain and Romulus differ. VII, 441. Why Cain, the reprobate, was born before Abel, the elect. VII, 437, 438. Cain hateful to God because of his envy. VII, 444. He killed his brother out of diabolical envy. VII, 441. And out of hatred. III, 2013. Cain’s guilt seems great and his punishment slight, but this is how it appears to human judgments. X, 1556. Cain fears bodily death more than spiritual death. VIII, 260. He was punished with the life of a murderer. IX, 34, 319. Whether the curse by which Cain was punished with the sterility of the earth is contrary to the Gospel. VIII, 134.

Cain’s daughters are called the daughters of men. VII, 469. Why Cain’s descendants are not listed in sacred history. VII, 456. Cain’s succession is closed within eight generations from Adam. VII, 463. It ends with the number eleven. VII, 465. Why daughters are listed among Cain’s descendants and not among Seth’s descendants. VII, 460. Why some thought that Cain begot children from Eve his mother. X, 268. Cain’s sacrifice expresses the earthly riches of the Old Testament. VIII, 258. Cain, son of the devil. III, 2013. Cain is the first citizen of the earthly city. VII, 437, 441. The Babylonian city began with Cain. IV, 733, 773. Cain, having received from God a sign lest he be killed, is a type of the Jews. IV, 442, 705, 997. Cain is a figure of Judas and of the Jews. VI, 688; VII, 445; VIII, 258, 259, 260. And of those who persecute the righteous. VII, 456.

The origin of the name “Cainites” for the heretics. VIII, 28, 29. Their doctrines. VIII, 28, 29.

Caiaphas and Annas, both high priests, customarily served in alternate years. III, 1935.

Gaius Caesar. See “C. Caesar.”

Gaius Servilius, praetor. VII, 106.

Calama, a city. VII, 433, 766. The town of Calama. IX, 337, 385, 523, 524. The memory of Saint Stephen was brought to Calama by Bishop Possidius. VII, 766. The miracles performed at Calama in memory of Saint Stephen, brought there by Bishop Possidius. VII, 766, 768. The colony of Calama. II, 313. Its violence and injustice toward the Catholics and the Church. II, 316. What Augustine did while he was there. II, 317.

Sin is the cause of all calamities. V, 1131. Public calamities must be attributed to divine providence. VII, 15. In a time of calamity, the multitude should be rebuked. IX, 95. The impious, placed amid calamities, justify themselves and accuse God. IV, 1637.

The reed signifies the Scriptures. IV, 836.

How the devil watches the heel. IV, 548.

The profession of calculators and copyists, as it were a kind of infancy of grammar. I, 1012.

Caldonius, a bishop. IX, 192.

Calibius the younger, curator of the city of Aptunga. IX, 540.

The person who begins to wish to grasp the truth suffers a darkness that he had not previously perceived. IV, 1933.

Calligonus, a eunuch, struck with a sword because he had assaulted a prostitute. X, 845.

The philosopher Caliphon’s view of virtue and vice. X, 1083, 1084.

Whether the cup is to be understood for good or for evil in verse 9 of Psalm 79 is uncertain. III, 80. To receive the cup of salvation is to imitate the Lord’s sufferings. IV, 1318. If the physician had not first drunk from the cup, the sick man would fear [Col. 0128] to touch it. V, 1455. The Lord’s cup ought to contain water mixed with wine. III, 111. Augustine, speaking of the cup of cold water that God commands to be given, inflamed the cold hearts of human beings. III, 106. What is meant by the cup in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine with something mixed into it? IV, 954. Why the punishment of sinners is called a cup. IV, 137.

The seat of heat is in the liver. III, 362.

Calphurnius Lanarius is called Rufinus. II, 238.

What the place of Calvary signifies. V, 1085.

What Elisha’s baldness, mocked by the boys, signifies. IV, 1056, 1069.

The estate of Calvianus. IX, 521.

Calumny exists only when a neighbor is injured by the accusation of a false crime. III, 707. Calumnies should be refuted without quarrelling. V, 1579. How calumnies are to be endured. IX, 351, 352. The calumnies of unbelievers, heretics, schismatics, and demons are overcome when Christ crucified is contemplated. IV, 1578. Why God’s help is delayed for one who has suffered calumny. V, 1510. Neither the praise of the flatterer heals a bad conscience, nor the abuse of the reviler wounds a good one. IX, 352. Since calumny is a false accusation, it does not make a person guilty except before a human judge; but where God is the judge, no one is harmed by a false accusation, because it is charged not to the one against whom it is brought but rather to the one who brings it. IV, 1582. The greatest calumny of the Gentiles and Jews against Christians is their malicious assertion that Christians worship one whom they put to death. IV, 1578. Those who seek to construct tangled calumnies become entangled before those whom they strive to entangle. IV, 654. Greek calumny. I, 948.

Calumniators lie in wait for every word. IV, 654. The calumniator is the devil. IV, 905.

A miracle involving limestone. VII, 713. Why limestone is called living. VII, 713. Limestone soaked with oil does not become hot. VII, 713, 719.

Camaena, the goddess, teaches singing. VII, 122.

Diana mourned Camilla. VII, 86.

How ungrateful Rome proved to Marcus Camillus, although he had deserved extremely well of her. VII, 62. Although Rome had proved ungrateful, he nevertheless liberated her again from the Gauls. VII, 117.

The furnace signifies the day of judgment. IV, 1362. The furnace signifies the flatterer’s tongue. IV, 869.

What the *campestria* are and why they are so called. VII, 426; X, 467.

Who are called *campestrati*. VII, 426; X, 565.

*Cancellus* or *cancellum*. VIII, 534. To be placed within the railings, a mark of honor. II, 132.

Cancer is curable by no medicines. VII, 763. The miraculous cure of cancer. VII, 763.

Who the candlestick is. V, 1479.

Candidianus, a presbyter. VI, 610.

Candidus, a bishop. II, 759, 780.

Candidus of Villa Regia, a Donatist bishop who became a bishop among the Catholics. IX, 473.

Candorius, a bishop. II, 759, 780.

Dogs are not always to be understood in a bad sense. II, 634. The dogs of Christ keep watch and bark, both for the house and for the Lord, and for the flock and for the shepherd. II, 634. Dogs that bark not for truth but for custom. IV, 175. A dog as the lowest of either human beings or animals. III, 507. And as something contemptible. III, 805. Dogs: heretics. IV, 1925. The abusive are compared with dogs. II, 271. A dog recognizing its master, already forgotten by his own people. I, 1087.

To sing in jubilation is to understand that what is sung in the heart cannot be expressed in words. IV, 283. This is to sing well to God: to sing in jubilation. IV, 283. See “To sing.”

What is the difference between singing and psalmody? IV, 814, 1173, 1390. We must take care to understand what we sing. IV, 157. Singing knowingly was granted to human nature by the divine will. IV, 157. No one sings what is worthy of God unless he has received from him the ability to sing. IV, 323. Whoever desires, even if his tongue is silent, sings in his heart. IV, 1101. When singing to God, let us fear that we may not sing well. IV, 283. One must sing to God with both one’s mouth and one’s conduct. V, 211. One must sing with the heart, not with the flesh. IV, 774. One must sing with mouth and heart. V, 1024. We sing with the voice to stir ourselves; we sing with the heart to please God. IV, 1917. The singing of your lips is required from your heart. IV, 563. The new song is sung with charity. V, 207. One who does not have charity may carry the psalter, but cannot sing. IV, 1866. Singing is the activity of lovers. V, 207. The singer belongs to the lover; the voice of this singer is the fervor of holy desire. V, 1472. Do not pay too much attention to the voice of the one singing, but to the conduct of the one acting. IV, 1950. The one who lives for God sings to God; the one who works for his glory sings psalms to his name. IV, 814. You will not be able to prove how true the things you sing are unless you begin to do what you sing. IV, 1604. Who are those singing on the ten-stringed instrument? V, 81. Singing itself is confession: confession of your sins and of God’s power. IV, 808.

[Col. 0129] What is the difference between a song and a psalm? IV, 78, 813. The old and new song. V, 81. The new song. VI, 678. To sing the new song. V, 209, 890. The old song is sung by desire of the flesh; the new is sung by the charity of God. IV, 1227. The new song is nothing other than the praise of God. II, 557. It is love itself. IV, 1227. The new song belongs to grace, to the new human being, and to the New Testament. IV, 283, 1866, 1949. The song of Jerusalem is our language; the song of love for this world is a barbarian language, a foreign language that we learned in captivity. IV, 1771. The new song is the song of peace, the song of charity. IV, 1949. God’s song is holy joy. IV, 1917. The divine songs are the delights of our spirit. IV, 1884. The new song is the new commandment. V, 1471. Our song ought to harmonize with our conduct as in a dance. V, 1416. A song with the lyre signifies speech joined to good works. IV, 1174. The song that no one sings except virgins. VI, 410. The new song pertains to the new human being, the old to the old. IV, 435, 807. God teaches us no other song than that of faith, hope, and charity. IV, 1171. In the song of the Passion, Christ is, as it were, the leader of the singing, while the martyrs are, as it were, the responders. IV, 1109. What is the song of the rich and poor concerning the songs of Zion? IV, 1768.

The Song of Moses is expounded. V, 1634. There are fifteen Songs of Ascents because there were the same number of steps of the Temple. IV, 1960. What the Songs of Ascents mean mystically. IV, 1596, 1639, 1667. The Song of Songs: holy songs of love, and so forth. V, 289. Riddles. V, 289. The Song of Songs commends the holy loves of Christ and the Church. III, 925. It is extremely difficult to understand. III, 925. It shows how greatly divine charity ought to be desired and valued. III, 925. The narrative in the Song of Songs belongs to a form of speech concerning figurative things. III, 372. The Manichaeans’ love song. VIII, 507.

A song is a beautiful sound. I, 843. Its melody is greatly useful. I, 800. It is useful for moving the soul toward piety. II, 221. The singing of psalms in the Church. IV, 157. Ecclesiastical singing was instituted at Milan by Saint Ambrose. I, 768. Augustine was affected by it in a wondrous manner. I, 768. The pleasure of the flesh must also be avoided in divine singing. I, 799. One sins when the singing gives more pleasure than the subject itself. I, 799. The insolence of raging youths was quieted by the gravity of song. X, 797.

The dangerous pleasure of vain songs. V, 79. People are more inclined to vain songs than to hearing salutary admonitions. V, 79. Profane songs and dances were driven from the church where Cyprian was buried. V, 1415. Those singing shameful things are reproved. IV, 157. He himself sings in us, by whose grace we sing. II, 558. The time, usefulness, and holiness of singing in the church. II, 221. The Donatists sing psalms composed by human ingenuity and mix them with drunken revelries. II, 120, 220.

Capernaum, the chief city of Galilee. III, 1106.

We do not feel it when our hair is cut; why? I, 1171. It is not proper for women, even married women, to uncover their hair. II, 1060. Hair signifies the superfluities of temporal things. IV, 605. Hence the wiping of the Lord’s feet. IV, 605, 1820.

King Tarquin built the Capitol. VII, 87. The Capitol was dedicated to Jupiter. VII, 119. Mars, Terminus, and Juventas refused to yield the Capitol to Jupiter. VII, 130. The burning of the Capitol. VII, 72. The Gauls spared the Capitol, but not Sulla. VII, 109.

The Capitoline stone, a stone image of Jupiter in the Capitol. VII, 77, Note c. The Capitoline hill, preserved by the vigilance of the goose. VII, 70, 84.

The island of Capraria. II, 189.

By the name “goats,” the Church from the Gentiles is signified. IV, 1362.

Capses. IX, 235.

The captivity of the righteous must not be a disgrace to the Christian religion. VII, 30. Even pagans knew that captivity endured voluntarily for the sake of religion. VII, 28. In the Holy Scriptures there are great consolations for captivity endured for the sake of religion. VII, 28. Captivity is permitted by God for testing or correction. VII, 37. The captivity of Marcus Atilius Regulus. VII, 28. The captivity of chaste and holy women is greatly to be mourned; may God not abandon them. II, 426.

Our first captivity. IV, 891. The whole world is under captivity. V, 179. Our captivity is demonstrated. IV, 1765. In what our captivity consists. IV, 1765. Captivity is our pilgrimage. IV, 1917. The devil possessed the whole world as a mass of unbelievers. V, 890. Human captivity arises from sin. V, 188. The captivity of a person who abandoned God the Emperor and went over to the deserter, the devil, is not unjust. IV, 990. The captivity from which we are freed through Christ. V, 179. Our Redeemer erased the instruments of our captivity with his blood. V, 890. We became captives because we were sold under sin: we were able to sell ourselves, but cannot redeem ourselves; we sold ourselves by consenting to sin, and are redeemed through faith in righteousness, by the innocent blood given for us. IV, 1231, 1658. Confess that you are in captivity, so that you may be worthy to be freed. IV, 1071. Our captors are the devil [Col. 0130] and his angels. IV, 1765.

The captivity of the Jews is a figure of our captivity. IV, 772, 876, 1658, 1765. A fortunate captivity, by which people are captured for the good. IV, 830. What it means to capture captivity. IV, 830.

The pride of the wicked is the head of their circuit. IV, 1810. To raise one’s head is a sign of levity and pride. IV, 401. Who the heads of dragons are. IV, 937. The head of the calf that Moses threw into the fire was the body of the wicked. IV, 736. Why the head of those insulting Christ was nodding. IV, 1339. How Christ will shatter the heads of his enemies. IV, 831. Africans covered their heads in mourning; Jews uncovered them. III, 690.

Christ is the head of all the righteous and of the angels. IV, 385. Christ is the head of the good; the devil, the head of the evil. IV, 1807. How Christ is our head and the Church is the body. IV, 1803. One cannot speak of a head where there is no body of which it is the head. IV, 1803. The superiority of the head over the other members. IV, 217. The head adheres to its body through the bond of charity. IV, 231. “Where the head is, there the other members are” is a proverb. IV, 223. How the head and body are one. IV, 231. In the head, the voice of the members must be recognized. IV, 1295.

Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, who followed the Marian party, was defeated by Sulla and killed by Pompey. VII, 69, Note d. The cruelty of Gnaeus Papirius Carbo. VII, 107. There were many Carbones of the Papirian family. VII, 69, Note d.

Coals are incorruptible. VII, 713, 719. Therefore they are placed beneath boundary markers. VII, 719. What it means to heap fiery coals upon another’s head. III, 75. In the Apostle’s “coals of fire” (Rom. 12), they signify not God’s indignation but the fire of repentance. IV, 1018. Those who turn to the Lord are called coals because they come back to life from the dead. IV, 1601.

A carbuncle shines in the darkness. III, 47.

Carcedonius. II, 230, 231, 232.

Deserts make the prison. IV, 1842. Freedom makes one dwelling a home for one person, while servitude makes it a prison for another. IV, 1842. A prison is broad for a joyful person, and a meadow is narrow for a sorrowful one. IV, 1844. This world is a prison. IV, 1843. Some call the body a prison. IV, 1843. And the flesh, because of corruption. IV, 1843.

Carchabia. IX, 507, 528, 550.

Cardea, the goddess placed in charge of the hinge of the door. VII, 119.

Astrological pivots. VII, 145.

To lack. There is no difficulty in lacking unless there is desire in possessing. III, 76.

What charity is. V, 143; VI, 25. Charity is the virtue by which what ought to be loved is loved. II, 739. The Pelagians deny that charity is a gift of God. X, 1292. Why the Pelagians refuse to name charity among the helps of grace. X, 1296. The darkness of the Pelagians, when they wish knowledge of the Law to come from God but charity from ourselves. X, 905. To be able to have faith or charity belongs to human nature; actually having them belongs to the grace of the faithful. X, 968. Charity does not come from free choice but from the gift of God. X, 302, 303. Charity is not poured into our hearts through our own, that is, human, powers. II, 990.

Charity is a gift of God. II, 576, 595; V, 210, 577, 620, 715, 793, 1223, 1241, 1462; X, 237, 240, 290, 904, 905. Charity is the greater gift of grace. X, 905. No gift of God is more excellent than charity. VIII, 864, 865. Whatever God has given you is less than charity. V, 793. The charity by which the commandments are fulfilled does not come from us but from God. X, 903. Charity is wholly from God. X, 586. Charity and knowledge are from God. X, 905. If knowledge of the Law is from God, charity much more so. X, 1112. Charity and eternal life are the inheritance bestowed upon the children of promise. III, 566. We cannot possess charity from ourselves, but from God through the Holy Spirit. X, 1105. Charity is a gift of the Spirit. III, 2067. Charity is the heart’s enlargement by the Holy Spirit. V, 923. It is the effect of the Holy Spirit’s presence. V, 1673. Charity is more truly called a pledge than earnest money. V, 159. We must pray that charity be given by the one who commands it to be given. II, 595, 1016. Charity is obtained through faith. II, 818. Insofar as charity is present, it must be exercised by living well; insofar as it is lacking, it must be obtained by asking. V, 1046.

Charity cannot exist without faith. V, 564. Where love is, there necessarily are faith and hope. III, 1846. Charity grows weak when faith falters. III, 35. What it means to have charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. III, 36. Without faith, hope, and charity, no soul is healed so that it can see God. I, 876. After this life, charity alone remains. I, 876. Charity alone always remains. V, 867. See “Love”; “Affection.” Charity cannot in any way be right if the things loved are not true but false. III, 119. Nothing is higher than the way of charity, and only the humble walk on it. IV, 1837.

Charity commended by the Apostle. X, 902. Charity is commended. III, 1461, 2033; IV, 1949. How great a good charity is. V, 764; the greatest of all goods. II, 811. Praise of charity. II, 854; V, 1533, 1534. Charity is God himself. II, 818. Charity is so completely a gift of God that God [Col. 0131] is called charity. V, 852. In charity there are three things, as it were an imprint of the Trinity. VIII, 857, 858, 960. These three things are considered. VIII, 961, 962. Reconciled to God through the Mediator, let us cling to the One, enjoy the One, and remain one. VIII, 895, 896.

Charity is a great and true virtue. II, 737; V, 1397. It is a virtue of the soul. IV, 1353. It is the virtue of the city of God. IV, 541. What the true charity of Christians is. IV, 1816. Charity is greater than faith and hope, because when the object arrives these cease, whereas charity increases. IV, 1171. Charity must be possessed in all things and above all things. I, 1340. In whose hearts it is poured out. X, 297. Charity is new and eternal. IV, 1949. Charity is the grace of the New Testament. III, 755. Charity is the life of the heart. II, 564. Charity is a great way and possesses a great miracle. IV, 1837. It is the new commandment. V, 1236. The brief and clear precept. VI, 669. The completed and shortened word. II, 854; VI, 670. Charity is the end of every commandment. VI, 288. The end of the commandment—not that by which the commandments are consumed, but that by which they are perfected. IV, 261.

Charity holds the highest place in Scripture. IV, 1232. What Moses wrote pertains to charity. I, 840. The harmony of both Testaments concerning the commandments of charity. I, 1316, 1317. See “Love of God and neighbor.” Charity is the breadth of the commandment. III, 2058. In charity there is breadth; in hatred, narrowness. IV, 1736. The breadth, length, height, and depth of charity. II, 564, 565, 611. It is figured in the cross of Christ. II, 565, 612. Whoever has understood the breadth, length, height, and depth, and the charity of Christ surpassing knowledge, has seen Christ and has seen the Father, according to Ambrose. II, 604. Charity creates breadth, so that God may walk about within us. V, 889. The commandment of charity contains the well-being of physics, logic, ethics, and the state. II, 524.

The two commandments of charity must always be thought about and meditated upon, and so forth. III, 1531. The two commandments of charity signified by the two days Jesus remained in Samaria and Galilee. III, 1522, 1523. The two feet of charity. IV, 313. Augustine finds the two commandments of charity in all the discourses of Scripture. II, 223.

Charity is called the love of God and neighbor. IV, 260. Through charity we love both God and one another. III, 1852. Charity is the bond by which people are connected to one another and to God. III, 878. God and neighbor are loved with one charity, although those who are loved are not one. V, 1223. Through the binary number in Scripture, charity divided into two parts is commended. III, 1531. Charity is the movement of the soul toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. III, 72. Charity is love of God, of neighbor, and of oneself according to God. VII, 410. One charity is divine, another human. V, 1529.

God is worshiped through charity. II, 737. Charity is the glue by which the soul is joined to God. IV, 758. God is to be loved in such a way that, if possible, we forget ourselves. V, 779. To love God freely is not to place outside him some reward that one expects from him. V, 568. If you love, love freely; if you truly love, let the one you love himself be your reward. V, 905. This is to love God freely: to hope for God from God, to hasten to be filled from God, and to be satisfied with him himself. V, 1469. Let each person do everything with charity, not expecting temporal recompense but the face of God. V, 865. If, upon hearing that you must deny the face of God in exchange for any promised goods, you were terrified, then you loved freely. V, 966. Job is found to have loved God freely, loving him not because he had given something, but because he had not taken himself away. V, 569. God is loved for our good, not for his. IV, 1952. God will not possess less divinity if a human being does not have charity toward him. IV, 1952. God’s charity toward us is greater than ours toward God. IV, 1353. God is our abundance through charity. IV, 1628. God sits in the one who has charity as in heaven. IV, 1951. There is no true charity of God in the one who is ungrateful to the Holy Spirit. IV, 903. Through charity and humility we now draw near to God. V, 142.

We cling to Christ through charity, not through fear of punishment. II, 595. No one reaches Christ except through charity. IV, 149. The charity of Christ is in his unity. II, 229. Charity cries out to Christ from us; charity cries out from Christ for us. IV, 1817. If Christ is with us on earth through charity, through that same charity we are with him in heaven: Christ is below through the compassion of charity, and we are above through the hope of charity. IV, 1630. The Lord ascended above the heavens and from there sent charity. IV, 1344. How Christ walked on the way of charity. III, 1985.

Charity makes people capable of receiving divine things. V, 705. Charity admits us to the divine state. II, 533. Divine charity does not tolerate the illicit love of a prostitute. V, 1531.

Through charity the faithful are one in the one unchangeable One. X, 109. How Christ wills all to be one in him. VI, 712. Charity is the strongest bond of unity. VI, 137. Charity makes one heart out of many human hearts. III, 1538. The fervor of charity fuses many into one. III, 2056. Those who do not have charity do not dwell in unity. IV, 1736. The commendation of brotherly charity. III, 2014.

Charity is the mark of Christ’s disciples. III, 1809. Why the Apostle John [Col. 0132] commends almost this one thing. III, 2037. The charity of Paul and Stephen is commended. III, 2014.

Those do not have charity who have been cut off from communion with the Catholic Church, or who do not love unity. IX, 148, 149. Charity cannot be preserved except in the unity of the Church. IX, 312. It is not possessed outside the Church. V, 1223. Charity praises the Lord; discord blasphemes the Lord. IV, 1950. The source of charity is the Holy Spirit, the principle of unity in God. III, 1684. Charity makes the framework; the framework embraces unity; unity preserves charity; charity reaches glory. IV, 239. There is no charity in a Christian from whom the unity of Christ is not preserved. V, 1422. How Mother Charity grieves when unity is divided. III, 1434. Whoever has charity is secure: no one removes him from the Catholic Church; and if he begins to possess it outside, he is brought in, like an olive branch by a dove. IV, 176. Charity is life; dissension, death. VI, 713. To attack fraternal charity is a sin against the Holy Spirit. III, 1267. Dissensions sometimes arise from charity, or test charity. II, 957. The tribulation of others is common to those who share a common trial, hope, love, and spirit. II, 365. Charity looks more to the common good than to private advantage. II, 564. Each person also possesses something he himself lacks when he loves it in another. III, 1812. Whoever, through some necessity, cannot fulfill what God commands, should love the one who fulfills it, and fulfill it in him. IV, 1627. Nothing is more hostile to charity than envy. VI, 315. Who cannot have charity. IV, 1343, 1344. Charity is present in the one who does not seek his own in this life. IV, 1629. The two cherubim commend the fellowship of charity. III, 634. Those who have charity bear one another’s burdens; those who do not have it are burdensome to themselves. IV, 1698. The greater the charity, the greater the wounds caused by the sins of others. IV, 1269. The one who loves the wicked out of charity, does good to them, and intercedes for them, is not a partner in their iniquity. II, 654, 655, 658. Prayer for a brother is more pleasing to God where a sacrifice of charity is offered. II, 87. Charity alone extinguishes sins. III, 1982.

The unity of charity must be preferred to the earthly advantage of inheritance. V, 1577. The faithful rejoice in the rest of their brothers, even amid their own anxieties. II, 593. Everyone who sins acts against charity; hence whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all. II, 739. One who does not flee hostile disasters lest he abandon a ministry necessary to Christ’s people finds a greater fruit of charity than one who, fleeing for his own sake, is captured, does not deny Christ, and accepts martyrdom. II, 1015.

Charity is twofold: severity and gentleness. IX, 84. Forgiveness and punishment must both be exercised out of charity. II, 660. Just as severity is ready to punish the sins it finds, so charity does not wish to find what it must punish. II, 958. Charity that rages. IV, 1733. Charity strikes; iniquity flatters. III, 2033. Charity rages in the manner of a dove, not a raven. III, 2035. How far charity may be angry. IV, 1373. Sometimes it should not fear being troublesome to friends. V, 539. Charity within must not cease; its duties must be performed according to the occasion. III, 2037.

The duties of charity. VI, 328. Charity is not expended like money. II, 869. Charity is a sweet exactor. III, 2045. Charity is always owed, and alone, even when repaid, always holds the debtor. II, 869; V, 800. Charity always keeps us debtors, because it alone, although repaid daily, is always owed. IV, 307, 393. When charity is expended, it does not diminish. VIII, 272. It grows when distributed. IV, 1922. Whoever shows mercy distributes charity. IV, 1922. Love of God should be gratuitous; love of neighbor beneficent. V, 571. It is difficult to find anyone who has nothing with which to benefit another. V, 571. Charity always has something to give. IV, 371. Charity forgives; charity gives. IV, 1861. Charity does not permit you to fail to provide whatever you can, even to enemies. IV, 260. What each person ought to provide for his neighbor. V, 571. The matters with which charity ought to occupy itself. V, 1599. Love of neighbor is summed up in this: “Whatever you do not wish to be done to you,” etc. IV, 281. This saying extinguishes every outrage and crime. III, 74. The charity of God consists in three things; the charity of neighbor in seven. IV, 281.

The order of charity. VII, 643. To order charity. V, 603. Not in the order of loving, but in the order of giving assistance, he places the weaker before the stronger. II, 537. Charity must extend to enemies. V, 564. Charity is cautiously expended on enemies and confidently returned to friends. II, 869. Charity embraces not only those present but also brothers scattered throughout the whole world. III, 2025. We must show charity not only to brothers but also to those who are outside. IV, 299. The work of charity in the age to come. II, 565.

The charity by which people of evil conscience love one another. V, 562. Even robbers have among themselves what they call charity. VIII, 223. Human affection is partly lawful and partly unlawful. V, 1529, 1530. Lawful human affection. V, 1529, 1530. Charity must extend to enemies. V, 564. Charity is cautiously expended on enemies and confidently returned to friends. II, 868. Charity embraces not only those present [Col. 0133] but also brothers scattered throughout the whole world. III, 2048. We must show charity not only to brothers but also to those who are outside. IV, 299. The work of charity in the age to come. II, 565.

Charity is the root of all good things. X, 370, 374. Just as desire is the root of all evils. IV, 1154. From charity, as from a head, the other good things arise. III, 1852. A fruit is not good if it does not grow from the root of charity. X, 217. Take away charity, and you have no motive by which to move toward a good work; or, if you do move, you move as a slave. V, 369. Without charity a human being is nothing, whatever else he may possess. III, 1439. Charity alone works well. V, 904. It alone makes good use of God’s gifts. VI, 137. By charity you love whatever you rightly love. V, 160. Whatever is done without charity is in no way done well. X, 903. Where charity is absent, justice cannot exist. III, 1236. All good works are one work of charity. IV, 1148. When the work of the Law is truly done, it is done through charity, not fear. III, 755. The Law is not fulfilled without charity. V, 267, 696, 1241. The breadth of charity is necessary, lest whatever good you do perish. V, 904. No good would be done unless charity existed; and when charity is present, good cannot fail to be done. X, 374. What is more precious, more luminous, stronger, or more useful than charity? V, 764. Where charity is, what can be lacking? But where it is not, what can be beneficial? III, 1141, 1151, 1845. With charity everything is possessed; without it, nothing that can be possessed is beneficial. III, 1646; IV, 1627. Add charity, and everything is beneficial; remove charity, and the rest is beneficial for nothing. V, 44, 562, 575, 764, 783. Without charity all good things are of no benefit. II, 229, 755. Whatever holy things may be possessed are of no benefit. IX, 193. Neither truth, nor sacraments, nor knowledge, nor prophecy, nor faith. IX, 312, 314, 601. Whoever does not possess the one thing by which all things are to be used possesses everything uselessly. V, 550. If charity is absent, the rest are possessed in vain; if it is present, everything is possessed rightly. III, 1462. The other gifts will be taken away from one who does not have charity. IV, 1905. Take charity from the heart, and only falsehood remains. V, 1643. The good are distinguished from the wicked by charity alone; the rest they possess in common. V, 583. Unless the pleasure of charity conquers the pleasure of sin, the necessity of servitude remains unconquered. X, 1121.

Charity is called good will. VII, 410. Charity operates through you when you act willingly. V, 793. Charity causes as much to be credited to the one who gave little as to the one who gave much. IV, 1627. Charity kills what we were, so that we may be what we were not. IV, 1628. Charity conquers the desires of the flesh. III, 2061, 2062. *Retr.* We were slaves of desire; once liberated, we become slaves of charity. III, 1696. Charity does not rejoice in private excellence, and therefore it is not puffed up. III, 437. Charity must be pursued so that conceit may be avoided. V, 783, 1565. Excessive anxiety lest, where charity burns, humility be lacking. VI, 427. Charity must be earnestly sought, so that other pleasures may be despised and every passion endured. IV, 1548. Whoever has not been wounded by the wound of charity cannot reach true health. IV, 399.

The law of charity is the law of freedom. II, 740. Many things must be done on the counsel of charity, though they are not commanded by the precept of the Law. VI, 459. The law of charity is compared with the old Law. IV, 1698. Charity is a light burden. IV, 823; X, 289. The burden of passions is heavy for weakness, light for charity. X, 901. It was light for Peter when he suffered for Christ, not when he denied him. X, 901. Through charity the commandments become light. V, 584. The commandments are easy only for charity. III, 632. By the commandment of charity a person would be admonished without fruit to seek God’s gift unless he first received something of love. X, 903. Punishments produce a crown through charity. IV, 1844. The better the things that await charity, the more violent are present things for weakness. II, 593. As desire holds nothing without distress, so charity holds nothing with distress. III, 1348. The burdens of charity must be taken up in place of the burdens of desire. V, 897.

The power of charity. IV, 541. Persecutions are resisted by charity alone. IV, 124. Charity is stronger than all difficult questions. V, 1612. Charity is as violently powerful for saving as death is violently powerful for taking away. IV, 541. Why the strength of charity is compared with death. IV, 1628. Charity transfers us from death to life. III, 2017. Charity produces evangelical death in us, says Paulinus. II, 349. For the sake of charity we must patiently endure even the hatred of the world. III, 1853.

Charity casts out fear, but servile fear. II, 560. How. IV, 1680. Charity drives out one fear and introduces another. V, 883. Through chaste fear charity fears to sin, even if impunity should follow; for it does not judge that impunity will follow when, through love of justice, it counts sin itself as punishment. IV, 1576. Fear acts so that you do not do something; charity so that you do not wish to do it, even if you could commit it with impunity. V, 882, 883. Charity must be built upon fear. VI, 316. Piety begins with fear and is perfected through charity. III, 136. The sign of charity’s progress is the diminution of fear; the sign of its perfection is the absence of fear. VI, 25. Charity will then be perfect when punitive fear has entirely departed. X, 304. Perfect charity tolerates neither desire for the world [Col. 0134] nor fear. VI, 309. How one may recognize that a person is moved by charity and not by fear. V, 793. The Old Testament pertains to fear, the New to charity. III, 2074.

Knowledge serves charity. II, 223, 737. All knowledge and prophecy serve faith, hope, and charity. III, 35. Whatever is conceived soundly in the mind, spoken by the mouth, or drawn out from any divine page has no end except charity. IV, 1815, 1816. “In no Scriptures should you seek anything else; let no one prescribe anything else to you. Whatever is obscure in the Scriptures is hidden there; whatever is plain there is open there.” IV, 1816. Charity leads to understanding the truth. III, 1876, 1877.
