Charity makes it possible for us to understand divine things. I, 1324. The fullness of knowledge must necessarily be followed by charity. IV, 1022. Whoever holds charity in his conduct also holds what is evident and what is hidden in the divine utterances. V, 1534. By charity the whole doctrine of the Scriptures is possessed. V, 1534.

The sweetness of charity. IV, 1729. Charity cannot exist without joy. IV, 974. Charity is loved, yet is not felt. V, 160. Without charity there is no peace. IV, 1685. Charity is the broad commandment by which peace is restored. V, 1588. Charity takes delight only in what is lawful. X, 236. Whoever has charity should attend to his conscience, and there he sees God. IV, 1951.

Charity and desire in a human being. V, 562. People are submerged by the weight of earthly things and earthly affections, and emerge through the lifting power of charity and the spirit of holiness. I, 847. Those who excel in the fruit of charity may nevertheless have something requiring purification. IX, 125. A person is fuller of iniquity in proportion as he is emptier of charity. II, 740. Whoever refuses to serve charity must necessarily serve iniquity. IV, 163. If charity is lacking, there will be iniquity. IX, 601. The more God’s charity reigns in anyone, the less iniquity dominates him. IV, 1582. Carnal desire reigns where the charity of God is absent. VI, 287. Carnal charity belongs to those who hope for carnal happiness in the age to come. V, 34. The poison of charity is hope of acquiring or retaining temporal things. VI, 25. A soul that loves earthly things, or even itself, falls away in proportion as what it loves is less than God. V, 779. From the abundance of iniquity comes the torpor of charity. IV, 433. Once charity is born, it grows by advancing; by growing it will be perfected; once perfected, it will remain. V, 858. The greater charity is, the better is the one in whom it exists. VI, 286.

Charity can always be increased here. II, 739. What measure of charity Christ has enjoined upon us. IV, 661. How charity is nourished. V, 966; VI, 25. The nourishment of charity is the diminution of desire; in the perfect there is no desire. VI, 25. As charity grows, desire diminishes, until it reaches here such greatness that it cannot be greater. VI, 288. Begun charity is begun justice; advanced charity is advanced justice; perfect charity is perfect justice. X, 290, 295. Whatever is lacking in charity arises from fault. X, 269. Charity is greatest in this life when life itself is despised for its sake. X, 290.

The source of charity is the highest good. V, 159. Charity makes citizens of Jerusalem. IV, 773. None are holy except those who have had charity. V, 44. The sons of the heavenly Jerusalem are conceived and born through Charity the mother. IV, 1923. Whoever has been joined together in charity with living stones belongs to the house of God. IV, 1721. When souls attain to understanding God, nothing will be taken away from charity; rather, much will be added to it. I, 876. Then it will be most full. I, 593. Whether charity has anything by which it may grow when life has passed out of mortality. X, 290. See *Love*. The abundance of God’s charity makes it impossible for the blessed to fall. X, 933.

Why charity is compared with water. IV, 1353. Charity is signified by the upper heavens. IV, 1342. The scarlet symbol of charity. III, 734. The tabernacle of ten curtains. III, 634. See *Commandment, Scripture, Law*. Charity is the fruit that rises above Lebanon. IV, 912. Charity is the law of the city of God. IV, 1261. Charity is light. II, 561; III, 1598. The precious pearl of the Gospel. VI, 670. Charity is like a ship. IV, 1699. Charity is oil. III, 1435; V, 575. Bread. III, 1342. Our root. IV, 557, 607. Charity is the wisdom of God. II, 557. The tunic of Christ woven from above. IV, 176. Christ’s garments are his saints, his whole Church. IV, 507. The tunic woven from above is charity. IV, 176; V, 149. Charity is the wedding garment. V, 563; IX, 669. Faith, hope, and charity are signified in the fish, egg, and bread in the Gospel of Luke. II, 500. The charity of the Church figured in Rebekah. V, 44. The two wings of charity. IV, 823, 1791, 1952. At what price charity must be acquired. V, 211. Charity costs nothing. III, 2034.

That which is not cheapness should be called charity. V, 1527.

## Flesh

On the origin of flesh: the error of the Manichaeans. V, 189. The Priscillianists attribute the making of flesh not to the good and true God but to evil angels. VIII, 44. The Manichaeans believe that flesh has one author and spirit another. VI, 709. They consider flesh a fetter and a prison. [Col. 0135] VI, 710. The error that flesh does not belong to the human being. V, 1191. From where and how animated and sentient flesh comes into being. III, 404. God is the maker of flesh, against the Manichaeans. VIII, 392, 393, 394, 395. Flesh created by God is not evil. V, 852. But it is a small good. V, 853. Through flesh the Lord blesses us. V, 58. It is not the nature of flesh that is evil, but its vice. X, 1529. The incarnation of Christ shows that the substance or nature of flesh is not evil. VII, 301. The defilement of flesh and spirit. V, 268.

The flesh of sin is that which is born through desire. X, 1237. The flesh of sin belongs to all who are born from sexual union. X, 421, 1384, 1403, 1404, 1406. Why the assumption of mortal flesh is called sin. III, 2072. The flesh of Christ alone is not the flesh of sin. V, 823. The flesh of all other human beings, in relation to Christ, is nothing but the flesh of sin. X, 1220, 1589. Every flesh except Christ’s flesh is from God, from flesh, and from sin. X, 678. What is the difference between the flesh of sin and the likeness of the flesh of sin. V, 1114. In the flesh of sin there are death and sin; in the likeness of the flesh of sin, death without sin. V, 844.

What it means for the flesh to desire against the spirit. III, 416. The Manichaeans admitted another soul that desired against the spirit together with the flesh. III, 1350. Whether flesh feels pain and desires without the soul. VII, 424. How can flesh desire without the soul? III, 417. Flesh and spirit are like a kind of marriage. VI, 710. For the flesh to desire is for the soul to desire carnally. X, 845. The disobedience of flesh is sin dwelling in our members. X, 172. The less flesh is subject to the soul, the more it desires against the spirit. VII, 629. Flesh is now burdensome because it is needy, weak, mortal, and corruptible. V, 1259.

The discord of flesh and spirit does not come from the Creator. X, 1352. It followed not upon a bodily union with the devil entering in, but upon the withdrawal of God’s spiritual grace. X, 864. The struggle of flesh against spirit is vice, not nature. X, 278. It is deformity. X, 1355. It comes from the transgression of the first parent. X, 1324, 1336. The corruption of flesh contracted from sin is not sin but punishment. VII, 406. The desire of flesh against the spirit is the just punishment of the disobedience of the first parents. III, 400; X, 417. It comes from the condemnation of the human being. X, 287. Thus it is the sin of disobedience, so that it is the punishment of sin. X, 173. From Adam we have received the frailty of flesh, the torment of pains, the bond of death, and the snares of temptations. IV, 1072. The rebellion of flesh is the punishment of humanity, but the rebellion of humanity is not the punishment of God. VII, 424. Although human flesh and the flesh of cattle agree in material, they would nevertheless differ in their origin as well as in their end if humanity had not sinned. X, 1359.

The disobedience of flesh did not exist in the first human beings before sin. X, 172. Even after the remission of sin in baptism, flesh remains captive under the law of sin. X, 433. Flesh is contrary even in the baptized. X, 276, 280. How justly God exercises us through flesh. VI, 362. In this life we cannot be free from the troubles of flesh. VI, 60. The works of flesh are our enemies. VI, 354. The two carnal works by which the holy and prudent are distinguished from the imprudent. V, 346. Our inner Eve is our flesh. IV, 548. Just as the devil overthrew Adam through Eve, so he wishes to overthrow us through flesh. IV, 548. The works of flesh are human works; but human works are those that are not God’s. VI, 369. The works of flesh are enumerated. VI, 60.

How flesh is disciplined. VI, 681, 709. The mortification of flesh is our work in this life. V, 854. The flesh of sin must be trained through labors and troubles. X, 183. The pleasure of flesh must be restrained somewhat even from lawful things. VI, 711. “Serve the one who made you, and let what was made for you serve you: if you disdain to serve your God, you will never make flesh serve you.” IV, 1860. Whoever wants flesh to serve him is himself admonished to serve God. V, 715; VI, 362. Flesh fighting against spirit is like a wife against her husband. IV, 1860. Your flesh is your wife, your maidservant: call it whatever you will; it must be subjected. IV, 1860. Flesh is to be loved and chastised like a wife. IV, 1826. Flesh is to be loved for the sake of the soul. I, 625. Flesh is the soul’s maidservant. IV, 1884, 1885, 1887.

Everyone loves his own flesh, even when he has subjected it to himself. VI, 710. When the vices of flesh are resisted, flesh itself is loved because it is being healed. VI, 361. The saints love and desire their own flesh. VII, 393. A person who chastises his body does not hate his own flesh. VIII, 391, 392. No animal, however lowly, hates its own flesh. VIII, 391, 392.

The spirit provides for flesh in two ways. VI, 364. The works of the flesh kill those who do not mortify them through continence. VI, 355. Although the works of flesh have been prescribed to be mortified, the wounds of sins do not disappear. VI, 357. Even if the law of sin occasionally holds some part of flesh captive, it does not reign. X, 433.

When the desire of flesh and the good will be perfected. X, 733. The sense of flesh must be distinguished from desire. X, 1352. The affection of flesh. X, 432. “Flesh acts on its desires; act on yours as well.” V, 820. “Permit flesh nothing beyond its needs.” V, [Col. 0136] 820. Through the desires of flesh—hunger, thirst, and so forth—although they are blameless, some fall into guilt. X, 282.

The sins of flesh must not be despised. V, 511, 512. Those who say that God does not care about them are also refuted. V, 511, 512. The devil makes the sins of flesh seem light, although they are serious and deadly. V, 1094. The pleasure of flesh is one of the three vices into which all sins are gathered. IV, 115.

In the Lord’s Prayer, the baptized ask that harmony be made between flesh and spirit. X, 676. It is not human virtue but divine grace that creates harmony between spirit and flesh. X, 676. In the struggle of flesh against spirit we need God’s help. VI, 80. We mortify the works of flesh through our spirit because we are moved by God’s Spirit. VI, 357. Do not say, “I cannot hold, carry, and restrain my flesh”; you are helped so that you can. IV, 457. What flesh possesses, or by whom it is possessed. V, 1620. The bed of pain is the weakness of flesh. IV, 457. If flesh is subjected to spirit, there is right peace; but if it dominates spirit, the peace is perverse. IV, 1860. Whoever conquers flesh will immediately overcome the devil. IV, 1858. Flesh is cleansed through the heart. VII, 303. What good works are performed through flesh? IV, 1060.

To serve God in the flesh. V, 915. To be not in the flesh. V, 847. And what does it mean to be in the flesh? X, 178. Those who live according to flesh are said to be in the flesh. X, 255. Those who have been reborn through God’s grace are not in the flesh. X, 178. To trust in flesh. V, 917. To live according to flesh. VII, 404, 405. What it means to walk according to flesh. V, 846. To live according to flesh belongs to the Epicureans; according to the soul, to the Stoics. V, 853. Let the soul live according to God, and flesh according to the soul. V, 853. To live according to flesh is evil. V, 853. We are in flesh and are not in flesh—how? IV, 1490. Not to fall in the flesh is a great thing; yet no one can avoid slipping in it. IV, 1490. The pleasure of flesh is hostile to justice. X, 726. The prudence of flesh and spirit. V, 846. Carnal affections. IV, 200.

What carnal life is. III, 166. Every holy person in this life is both carnal and spiritual. V, 836. A human being is wholly flesh when he is flesh in body and carnal in mind. V, 299. The soul will be carnal if it wishes to live according to itself. V, 854. Who is wholly carnal, who partly carnal, and who wholly spiritual. V, 836. Who are the carnal in the Church? X, 195. “Carnal” is used in two senses. VI, 105. A carnal Christian is one who rejoices in having carnal happiness here, or hopes for such happiness in the future. V, 34. The carnal and the animal, who are still little ones in Christ. V, 462; VI, 122. The carnal are earth; the spiritual are heaven. IV, 1748. All the carnal are enemies of the spiritual. IV, 1603, 1772. The carnal in the Church belong to the lot of Esau. V, 39. The carnal of the Old and New Testaments are figured by Hagar and Keturah. VII, 512. The carnal divide among themselves. VII, 502. Demons are nourished by the division of the carnal. VII, 502. Carnal Christians serve the spiritual, not the reverse. V, 49. The carnal will be judged through fire at the end of the age. VII, 504. Some of the carnal will be saved through fire; some will be condemned in fire. VII, 504. The carnal are signified by night, the spiritual by day. IV, 940. Carnal things are not to be expected in the kingdom of heaven. V, 488.

Our flesh is a river. V, 674. Our flesh is grass. V, 269. The beauty of flesh must be referred to the one from whom all beautiful things come. I, 626. How our flesh thirsts for God. IV, 751. All flesh will come to God, because Christ assumed the firstfruits of flesh from a virginal womb. IV, 776. “All flesh,” that is, from every kind of flesh. IV, 776. The flesh of Christ is the vehicle by which he came to us, a garment, a beast of burden, and a temple. V, 676. Human flesh is the bride of Christ. III, 1452. The flesh of Christ was crucified and given for the life of the world. V, 57. Some asserted that the flesh of Christ would be changed into the substance of God. V, 57.

The flesh and blood of Christ are food and drink. III, 1612. It is not enough merely to eat the flesh and blood of Christ in the sacrament. III, 1621.

The Aerianists do not eat meat. VIII, 40. The Priscillianists. V, 801; VIII, 44. The Tatianists. VIII, 30. The Patricians considered flesh so detestable that some of them are said to have wished, by inflicting death upon themselves, to be rid of flesh; why. VIII, 42. The Manichaeans do not eat meat. VIII, 36, 37. Among the Manichaeans only the priests ate meat. VIII, 491. How the Manichaeans allow their “hearers” to eat meat. VIII, 37. Why the eating of meat is forbidden by the Manichaeans. I, 1361; VIII, 150, 151, 154, 493, 494. The Manichaean fabrication concerning the origin of all flesh. VIII, 234, 235, 396. The Manichaeans considered all flesh unclean. VIII, 227, 232. Why. VIII, 233, 234, 235, 236, 320. For the same reason that the Manichaeans refused to eat meat, they ought to have abstained from other foods. VIII, 232, 233, 235. That meats are more unclean than grains is not something the Manichaeans can properly teach. VIII, 235, 236. To abstain from eating meat because it is considered unclean is contrary to faith. II, 222. Eating meat does not defile if it is consumed without any offense, any weak scruple, or any lust [Col. 0137]. I, 1360. Why certain foods of meat were prohibited in the Old Testament. VIII, 151, 152, 233. What meats the Israelites desired in the desert. II, 617. That Christ removed all meats from his disciples’ diet but permitted secular people freedom regarding foods: a lie of Faustus. VIII, 337. In the fact that the New Testament regards no animal flesh as unclean, it does not oppose the Old Testament. VIII, 233. Abstaining from meat is good. I, 1358. Why the Apostle said that it is good not to eat meat. VIII, 149. The first fathers abstained from meat not in order to condemn it but in order to signify something. VIII, 493. Why Christians abstain from meat. VIII, 193, 194. Many of the first Christians did not eat meat; why. V, 801.

The Archontics deny the resurrection of the flesh. VIII, 29. The Cainites. VIII, 29; Carpocrates. VIII, 27. Cerdo. VIII, 29. The Hieracites. VIII, 38, 39. Marcus. VIII, 28. The Severians. VIII, 30. Simon Magus. VIII, 25. Valentinus. VIII, 28. Plato, Varro, and other pagans had some knowledge of the resurrection of the flesh. VII, 795. It is more excellent to know that flesh will rise and live without end than to teach whatever they were able to pronounce about its nature. X, 532. The resurrection of the flesh is asserted. IV, 752. The flesh of the saints rests in hope. VII, 393. What is to be hoped for concerning flesh. V, 848. The restoration and immortality of flesh are promised to the godly. V, 848. The flesh of a human being that has been taken by another as food will be restored to the human being in whom human flesh first began to exist. VII, 783. If the world believed the resurrection of flesh without miracles, that itself would be a great miracle. VII, 756.

After the resurrection flesh will be spiritual. VI, 361; VII, 393. After the resurrection it will become spiritual. X, 434. How great is the spirituality of flesh must be inferred from the gifts God bestows in this life. VII, 784. After the resurrection flesh will not be flesh according to corruption, but will be flesh according to substance. VIII, 129, 130, 143. In the resurrection flesh will no longer be corruptible. IV, 775. The household of God, gathered from all nations, will possess the kingdom of God in incorruptible flesh. X, 1602. After the resurrection flesh will be far more perfect than it was in the first parents. VII, 393. How. VII, 395. The supreme harmony of flesh and spirit after the resurrection. VI, 274. Whether the vision of God has been promised to flesh in the Gospel (Luke 3:6). V, 1266. At the judgment Christ will be seen by all flesh. V, 1266.

The future transformation of flesh. V, 269. Human flesh will be changed into the body of an angel. V, 269. The change of flesh for the better will belong to the saints. V, 1623.

In Scripture “flesh” is used for “human being.” II, 542, 543; IV, 217, 1761; V, 725; VI, 94, 356; VII, 404, 408; VIII, 690, 851, 852. Flesh is called “human being,” a figure in which the part stands for the whole. X, 491, 1168. “Flesh” for wife. III, 1395. It is used for brother. III, 496. For body or blood relatives. III, 44. For mortality. VIII, 250, 335. For corruption. VIII, 250. Under the name of flesh and blood the Apostle named the corruption of flesh and blood itself. I, 613, 631; II, 943, 945, 946; V, 1625. Or the works of flesh and blood are understood. II, 943. Under the name of flesh and blood either carnal prudence or corruption may be understood. X, 1602. The habit formed by the soul together with flesh is called “flesh” in Scripture. I, 1181. Carnal habit is signified by death. VI, 79. Why flesh is called the body of death. X, 676. How flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. II, 948; V, 1619.

*Caraenum*: boiled wine. I, 1365.

Carosus, a subdeacon. IX, 513.

The goddesses Carmentes, who sing the fates to those who do not know them. VII, 122.

Carneades, the Greek philosopher. I, 909. An Academic. IX, 359, 360, 459. The founder and leading figure of the Third Academy. I, 955. The champion of Arcesilas. I, 955. He proposes to tear down the Stoics and Chrysippus. I, 955. No Academic slept less deeply than Carneades. I, 945. Carneades was unable to discover the truth. II, 62.

The Carpi. IX, 217.

Carpocrates the heretic. VIII, 27. His heresy. VIII, 27. Carpocrates asserted that the world was not made by God but by demons. VIII, 664. From him came the Carpocratians. VIII, 27.

Carraria. V, 1578.

The city of Cartennae. II, 332; IX, 697. In Caesarean Mauritania. IX, 697; and II, 332.

Carthage. II, 163; V, 166, 195, 624, 809; VIII, 954, 966; IX, 209. A very famous city and the capital of Africa. IX, 137. Founded by Dido. IV, 537. Under the name of Tarshish it is understood. IV, 536. Carthage is the kingdom of the heavenly goddess. IV, 1270. The beginnings of the kingdom of Carthage surpassed those of other peoples in navigation. IV, 537. Three wars were waged between the Carthaginians and the Romans. VII, 62. *Note c.* Scipio Nasica did not wish Carthage, Rome’s rival, to be destroyed; why. VII, 43, 62. Carthage was destroyed by Scipio Africanus. VII, 102. Carthage, when overthrown, harmed the Romans more than when hostile. VII, 102. Carthage and Rome, two cities that shaped the shores of Latium. II, 436. The condition of Carthaginian affairs [Col. 0138] while Marinus Comes was raging there. II, 647. Augustine congratulates the citizens of Carthage because they do not wish the Roman gods, driven out of Rome, to remain in Carthage. V, 165. Carthage remains in the name of Christ. V, 624. The authority of the Church of Carthage over the other churches of Africa. II, 92. Its prerogative. II, 163. Basilicas at Carthage. V. *Basilica*. It was customary for the bishop of Carthage to be ordained not by bishops from Numidia but by bishops from the nearer regions. IX, 641. The clergy of Carthage. V, 293. The genius of Carthage. V, 419.

The Council of Carthage. See *Council*. The Donatist Council of Carthage against Caecilianus and his associates. IX, 512. It consisted of nearly seventy bishops. IX, 553. It condemned the absent Caecilianus. IX, 644. The Carthaginian Council of schismatics against Caecilianus. IX, 639. It has neither consul nor date. IX, 639, 642. The Council of Carthage held without date and consul. IX, 663. The Donatist Council of Carthage, consisting of forty-three bishops. IX, 552. It conducted itself with greater caution, moderation, and diligence against Primianus than the council of Bagai acted against the Maximianists. IX, 552. The Carthaginian judgment against Caelestius. X, 386. See *Caelestius*.

*Cartigare*. IV, 422. *Note 1.*

Carus. II, 224.

Those who build houses in villages, or wish to have them built, although they are Christians, are censured. IV, 1035.

The Artotyrites offer cheese and bread. VIII, 31.

Caspaliana, the name of an estate. VII, 767.

Praise of Castor. II, 239.

Cassianus, a Donatist bishop. IX, 334, 335.

Cassianus, a deacon. IX, 640. Accused of *traditio*. IX, 662, 663.

Cassiciacum, the estate of Verecundus, where Augustine was preparing to receive baptism. I, 765.

Cassius of Macomades. IX, 215.

Cassius plunders the temple of Jerusalem. VII, 607.

Chastity is a gift of God. I, 681; III, 639; V, 1505, 1507. Chastity comes only from God. II, 850.

True chastity is in God. III, 241. What chastity of soul is. VI, 515, 545. Chastity of mind, the beauty of the king’s daughter within. VIII, 315, 316. Chastity must exist in the mind. V, 1439. In what chastity consists and by what it is corrupted. VI, 514. See *Continence, Modesty*. Chastity is not violated without the consent of the will. VII, 30, 32, 41. The integrity of chastity has such force in the mind that, if it remains inviolate, even bodily modesty cannot be violated, although its members may have been overcome. II, 427. Violence inflicted upon the body while the mind resists is to be reckoned not as the shame of corruption but as the wound of suffering. II, 427. Chastity is not violated by violence if it is preserved in the mind. II, 1071. One must fear more that the chastity of faith perish through the corruption of the inner sense than that women be violently violated in the flesh. II, 1016.

Chastity is commended to men, women, the unmarried, and those already bound by a vow. V, 735. In preserving chastity, many men are surpassed by women. V, 735. Women are restrained by the guardianship of their parents, the modesty proper to their sex, and fear of the laws; hence the chastity of men is more glorious. V, 736. Whoever does not preserve chastity, do not approach the Eucharistic bread. V, 736. Chastity and concupiscence. X, 803. Chastity commended in both Testaments. VIII, 134. The profession of chastity and continence among Catholics. VIII, 225. The reward of chastity. VIII, 168. The reward of virgins and married women is unequal, but both possess an eternal reward. V, 1507. Zeal for chastity in Joseph and Susanna. V, 1439, 1463. Even the impure, or the impure themselves, love chastity in others. V, 1059. A chaste wife. V, 759. The chaste affection of one sleeping. I, 797. The desire and struggle of a chaste man. V, 718. By what judgment of God hostile lust was permitted to sin against the bodies of the continent. VII, 41. How the chaste mortify fornication. X, 846. Nothing that is chaste is shameful. III, 405.

What it means to seek God chastely. V, 760. He lives chastely who attends to God alone. I, 969. A chaste heart, by which God is loved freely and no other reward is sought from him. IV, 928. A heart is not chaste if it worships God for the sake of reward. IV, 658.

Castor and Pollux counted among the gods. VII, 134.

“Camp” used for battle lines drawn up for combat. III, 539.

The fortress of Galba. IX, 207.

Castus of Sicca. IX, 143, 219.

Castus and Aemilius: how they were first overcome in the torments, and how afterward they became conquerors. V, 1295.

A chasuble. V, 630.

Chance is what has a hidden reason and cause. I, 585. Absolutely nothing can happen without a cause. I, 983, 985. Nothing happens by chance in the world. VI, 17. To hold that everything is governed by chance is an impious doctrine. IV, 270, 924. See Fall.

Catacarposis: the remains of a holocaust which the fire consumed. III, 678, 679.

Catamitus in the Bucolics. VIII, 77.

The Cataphryges, heretics. II, 438. Their founders, doctrines, and name. [Col. 0139] VIII, 30. The Cataphryges assert that the Lord’s promise to send the Holy Spirit was fulfilled in Montanus and Priscilla. II, 1034, 305. They also assert that they themselves received the promised Paraclete. VIII, 506, 507. They condemned second marriages. VIII, 506, 507. This error, condemning second marriages, was publicized by Tertullian. VI, 43. The Cataphryges created a schism in Phrygia. V, 1174.

A poultice made from the Eucharist. X, 1315.

The Bishop of Cataquensis. II, 358.

The Catarists, a sect of the Manichaeans. VIII, 36, 37.

A platform or scaffold. V, 1255.

Catastolium. VIII, 375.

The Cathari, heretics: why they were so called; they were also called Novatians. VIII, 32. The Cathari denied that the Church could forgive all sins and forbade widows to marry. VI, 308.

Catechisms for those to be baptized. VI, 210, 219, 220, 228. The office of catechizing is taught through the precepts that have been handed down. VI, 311. Formulae of prayer for catechists. VI, 328, 345.

Catechumens. V, 136. A catechumen is one to whom baptism is at some time owed. IX, 357. The stages of catechumens. VI, 203. The initiation of catechumens. VI, 344. Anointed catechumens. III, 1714. The sacrament of catechumens. IX, 172. Note. Their sacrament, although it is not the body of Christ, is nevertheless holy, and holier than the foods by which we are nourished. X, 176. Note a. Catechumens are sanctified, in a certain manner, through the sign of Christ and the prayer of the laying on of hands. X, 176. The sanctification of catechumens is not sufficient for entering the kingdom of heaven or for the remission of sins unless they have been baptized. X, 176. Catechumens are invited to Baptism. V, 135.

Baptism is necessary for catechumens so that they may be enlightened. III, 1714. Their preparations for baptism. VI, 636, 660. After catechumens had given their names for baptism, they were cleansed by abstinence, fasts, and exorcisms, and abstained from marital intercourse. VI, 203. Whether baptism should be given at the end of life to catechumens who do not request it and are unable to answer on their own behalf. VI, 469. The opinion denying this is rejected, though it is not condemned. VI, 469. Caecilianus, believing that the faithful cannot administer public office, wishes always to remain a catechumen; Augustine does not approve this. II, 652.

A dismissal is made for catechumens after the sermon. V, 325. Why the sacraments of the faithful are not disclosed to catechumens. III, 1875. Catechumens do not know what it means to eat the Lord’s flesh. V, 754. They are urged, as Easter approaches, to give in their names; and if the festival does not move them, curiosity should lead them to learn what this means. V, 135. A Catholic catechumen burning with divine love is to be preferred not only to a heretic but even to a wicked baptized person. IX, 172. The voice of catechumens in the Psalm, hastening toward the grace of the holy washing. IV, 464.

Whether catechumens among the Manichaeans are the same as the Hearers. IX, 357.

The seat of our teacher, heaven. V, 1203, 1237, 1320. The wood of the one hanging became the chair of the teaching master. V, 1116, 1430. The seat of pestilence is called the earthly kingdom with pride. IV, 1.

The name “Catholic,” a mark of Christ’s Church. VIII, 175. The Church is called Catholic even by its own enemies. III, 128; IV, 643. The Donatists contended that the Catholic Church was more truly among themselves than among their opponents. IX, 623, 625.

Why it is called Catholic. IX, 292, 391, 741. Why the Donatists wish it to be so called. IX, app. 621, 830. Catholic communion. V, 53. The Catholic faith. V, 1123. The Catholic people. V, 762. See Church. Catholics innocent of the Donatists’ calumnious accusations. IX, 333. The gentleness and leniency of Catholics toward the Donatists. II, 306, 307. Catholics do not persecute the Donatists but defend themselves. II, 300. They do not act against the Donatists in order to seize their property. II, 345, 808. Why they seek the Donatists. II, 343, 811. The Catholics’ dispute with the Donatists is one of love, not litigation. V, 1586. Catholics look to the Donatists’ salvation when they compel them to unity. II, 401. The Donatists act against Catholics with fury and savagery, yet say that they suffer persecution. II, 307. The Donatists call Catholics “Macarians.” II, 301. The reason for the different manner in which the Donatists treat Catholics and Catholics treat Donatists. V, 288.

To rebaptize a Catholic is a most monstrous crime. II, 95. Even if Catholics were proved to be persecutors or traditors, they should nevertheless not be rebaptized. IX, 274. New heretics impose a new name on the Catholics from whom they depart. X, 1053. The Pelagians and Jovinian called Catholics “Manichaeans.” X, 552. Why. X, 571. The Catholic position lies between the position of the Manichaeans and that of the Pelagians. X, 607. Yet it condemns both. X, 611.

Good Catholics. III, 1369. Bad Catholics. III, 1368. Whether a Catholic of the worst morals is to be preferred to a heretic merely because the other is a heretic. IX, 171. Bad Catholics are converted more easily than heretics. IX, 163. Some promise salvation to Catholics who persevere in the Church, although they have lived very wickedly. [Col. 0140] VII, 734.

Catholic writers gave certain people an opportunity to contrive heresy. VI, 319.

Catiline. X, 751. A very wicked man. VII, 71. Not wicked without cause. I, 680. His endurance was extraordinary. I, 1356, 1357. It was not courage but hardness that made him endure hunger, cold, and sleeplessness beyond expectation. II, 736. Catiline’s conspiracy. VII, 80. Civil war. VII, 109. Catiline was overthrown in the civil war. VII, 71.

The roofs of the city of Catinia were destroyed by the force of ash erupting from Mount Etna. VII, 111.

The god Catius makes people *cati*, that is, sharp or discerning. VII, 128.

The praise of Cato. VII, 156. Cato’s virtue was closer to truth than Caesar’s. VII, 156. Cato the Younger killed himself at Utica so that Caesar could not boast that he had spared him. VII, 36. Cato destroyed himself through impatience. VII, 630. Cato’s friends attributed his voluntary self-killing to weakness. VII, 36. He himself indicated in the case of his son that it should be attributed to weakness. VII, 36. Cato’s witty answer to a superstitious man. III, 51. Cato was praised for handing his wife over to another man. VI, 203, 388. Cato of Utica ceded his wife Marcia to Hortensius. X, 810.

The innocence and wisdom of both Catos passed into a proverb. VII, 36. Note b. It is safer to imitate Cato than Jupiter. II, 315.

Catosus, a thoroughly good Christian cook. VII, 766.

Catulinus, a Donatist subdeacon. IX, 513.

The civil war of Catulus. VII, 109. Catulus withdrew himself from the hands of his enemies by drinking poison. VII, 107.

The cubs of lions roaring and seeking food: demons when they tempt. IV, 1292.

Caudium, a town of Samnium. VII, 97. Note 1.

A cause may be accidental, natural, or voluntary. VII, 151. The causes of everything that happens are nothing other than the volitions of that nature which is the spirit of life. VII, 151. Socrates also held this view. VII, 226. Good and evil are to be distinguished not by deeds and punishments but by their causes. II, 324.

The original cause of all things is God. VIII, 877. The cause of everything God made is his will. IV, 1745. The cause of good things is God’s goodness; the cause of evil things is the will that falls away from mutable good. VI, 244. The secondary causes of evils are both ignorance and concupiscence. VI, 244. Whether knowing the causes of things belongs to human happiness. VI, 238. Which causes we ought to know. VI, 235, 238.

He loses his case who asks for more than is owed to him. IV, 1542. Christians’ cases are to be brought before ecclesiastical judges, not before the civil forum. IV, 1570. If anyone neglected to pursue his case within a year, it was established at the Council held at Carthage on 13 September in the year 401 that thereafter no one should hear his complaint. II, 235. It was established at the Council of Carthage in the year 348 or 349 that a presbyter’s case should be settled by six bishops. II, 235. To plead a case at the second hour. II, 169. “Neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person,” a maxim of the Donatists. II, 580, 584; V, 901; IX, 667, 676. To what extent the Donatists wished that saying, so often retracted by them, to be understood. IX, 667. They are refuted. IX, 667. By this saying the Donatists strangled themselves. IX, 653, 684.

The devil held a bond against us; Christ erased this bond, this written obligation, with his own blood. IV, 1127. The debtor’s bond erased by the blood of the Redeemer. V, 745. The bond of God’s promises is the Gospel. V, 1469.

Caiaphas. In him the prophetic chrism acted so that he prophesied; but his wicked life acted so that he prophesied unknowingly. VIII, 331.

Cecrops, king of the Athenians. VII, 565, 568.

Cedar is interpreted as “darkness.” IV, 1603.

Cedias, or *cesas* or *chesas*. IX, 209.

The cedar and the palm are not bent even in storms. IV, 1180. The cedars of Lebanon are the heights of the world. IV, 1024. Cedars are people exalted by the splendor of earthly nobility. IV, 213. The crushing of the cedars signifies the humbling of nobles in imitation of Christ’s humility. IV, 213. Cedar wood, a symbol of hope. III, 734.

Celer, proconsul of Africa. II, 223. His procurator was Spondeus. II, 536. Celer, a man of rank, now exercises no authority anywhere. II, 954.

The basilica of Celerina. V, 316.

The resurrection compared with the speed of a ray emitted from the eye. V, 1263.

Caelestius, or Caelesius, bishop in Numidia and accuser of Caecilianus. IX, 26, 775.

Celsinus. I, 921.

C. Celsus. II, 273.

A certain Celsus completed, in six not-small volumes, a survey of the opinions of all philosophers down to his own time. VIII, 23.

Celsus. I, 881. His opinion concerning the highest good and the highest evil. VIII, 168.

The history of Celticchius, a catechumen and later a bishop. VI, 165.

[Col. 0141] Censure. Justice breaks unjust bonds. V, 510. Augustine does not think that innocent souls should be punished for another person’s crime. II, 1067.

What the census is. III, 610.

The fable of the Centaurs. VII, 570.

Centos. VII, 548.

“Centre” is used for the whole. VII, 696. Geometers call the middle of the earth the centre. VII, 390.

A century or cohort of one hundred. V, 263.

A centurion. IX, 639, 640. The humility of the centurion. III, 1526; IV, 428. Humility and faith. V, 415, 487, 1503. The centurion and Regulus are compared with each other. III, 1525. The Gentiles are represented in the centurion. V, 416.

Centurius, a lay Donatist. I, 138.

For some, Cephisos is the same as Mesappus. VII, 563.

The fable of Cerberus. VII, 570.

The Cercopitheci, or apes. VII, 487.

Cerdon admitted two gods. VIII, 664.

The Cerdonians, heretics, and their doctrines. VIII, 29.

The three ventricles of the brain. III, 364. The anterior part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is situated toward the forehead. III, 364.

Augustine's praise of the candle. VII, 468.

They report that Ceres is the Great Mother, or Earth, and Juno. VII, 207. Ceres is placed over the seeds together with Liber. VII, 207. The rites of Ceres. VII, 185, 210. See Eleusinian rites. Some think that Christians worship Ceres and Liber because of the bread and cup. VIII, 379.

Ceretius, a bishop. II, 1034.

“Ceremony” from *carendo*, as though *carimonia*. I, 646.

Cerinthus, a heretic, and his opinions. VIII, 27. Cerinthus and Hebion were anathematized because, according to Jerome, they diminished the ceremonies of the Law in relation to Christ’s Gospel. II, 257.

The Cerinthians, heretics. VIII, 27.

Grace now establishes the struggle and will later perfect health. X, 1198. Even under grace the spiritual person struggles. X, 966. In this age strength for the struggle is granted; in the future there will be everlasting peace. X, 1199. Struggle unto blood. V, 1438. Victory is given to the one who struggles through Christ. V, 1367. He who has imposed the struggle helps the one who struggles. V, 1511.

The same degree of certainty is not to be sought in everything. I, 722. In matters pertaining to the salvation of the soul, to prefer uncertainties to certainties is a grave sin. IX, 111, 113. Nothing is certain on this earth except death. IV, 428.

The properties of deer are expounded allegorically. IV, 465, 1698. Deer signify those who repel poisonous tongues. IV, 214. Wicked deer, spiritually transcending all the thorny brush and forests in their running. IV, 1372.

The nature of deer when they cross a strait. VI, 81. Those with stiff necks are called proud. IV, 1694.

That Abraham fathered children by Keturah is not to be attributed to incontinence but to allegorical significance. III, 566. Keturah and her sons signify the carnal people of the New Testament. VII, 512.

The size of whales. II, 382. Whale ribs fixed publicly at Carthage. II, 382.

Chaeremon, skilled in the sacred rites celebrated for the gods. VII, 290.

Chaldaea belonged to the kingdom of the Assyrians. VII, 492.

The Chaldaean philosophers. VII, 234.

Ham is interpreted as “hot.” VII, 477. Ham, Noah’s son, was the father of Canaan. IV, 1398. Canaan is cursed in his son because of the prophecy. III, 551. The Egyptians arose from the seed of Ham. IV, 1398. Ham was a figure of those who live utterly depraved lives. VII, 478. [He was also] a figure of heretics. VII, 477.

The chameleon. VIII, 988.

Chemosh, the name of a certain god. III, 809.

Canaan is interpreted as “humble.” IV, 1394. Prepared for humility. IV, 1751. Their movements. VII, 478. At what time God’s promise concerning the land of Canaan was fulfilled. VII, 524. How the land of Canaan belongs forever to Abraham’s seed. VII, 499.

Why the Canaanites are called accursed seed. X, 1426, 1428. Under the name of Canaanites, the seven nations hostile to the Israelites are sometimes understood. III, 783. The Canaanites’ labor Israel took away justly, whereas Ahab unjustly took away Naboth’s labor. II, 811.

The Canaanite woman, an example of humility. V, 483, 487. The Canaanite woman’s perseverance in asking. V, 487. What sort of faith in her was praised. VI, 154.

The Greeks call *chaos* matter confused and formless in the beginning. III, 178.

The character of a Christian—the cross on his forehead—teaches him what he professes. V, 1386. The Lord’s character. V, 1350. The baptized bear it. II, 754, 803. The Lord had placed the character on Stephen’s forehead. V, 1437. The character of the sacrament. See Apostate. The royal mark among soldiers. II, 803.

[Col. 0142] Charus, a citizen of Hippo, but an Oriental deacon. X, 352.

“Cherubim” is called in Latin “fullness of knowledge.” III, 214; IV, 1021, 1260. The cherubim are rational creation in the multitude of knowledge. III, 634. A mystical explanation of the cherubim placed upon the mercy seat. III, 633. They represent the two Testaments. III, 634. They commend the fellowship of charity. III, 634.

Chettaeus is interpreted as “cut off.” VIII, 450.

ΧΙΔΙΑΣΤΑΙ [Chiliasts], or Millenarians. VII, 667, 668.

Chilo of Lacedaemon, one of the Seven Sages. VII, 582.

Why surgery is so called. I, 1088.

The good faith of a certain Alexandrian surgeon. VII, 762.

A bad *choraula*, a good *symphoniacus*. II, 228.

Strings. Concerning the ten strings. V, 75.

A chorus is the agreement of singers. IV, 1953. A chorus signifies harmony, which consists in charity. IV, 1109. The chorus of Christ is now the whole world. IV, 1953.

Augustine consoles Chrisimus, who was deeply disturbed by adverse circumstances. II, 1059.

Chrism. V, 1100. The sacrament of chrism, among the visible seals, is most holy, just as baptism itself is. IX, 342. It can also be found among the worst people. IX, 342.

Christinus. II, 1070.

Christ, the name of the sacrament. III, 2000. “Messiah” in Hebrew, “Christ” in Greek, “anointed” in Latin; he anoints his whole body, the Church. IV, 1370. Christ is named from chrism. III, 1648; VII, 549. Or from anointing. IV, 200, 1370; VIII, 53, 54, 645, 689. When he was anointed by the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1093.

Christ did not cease to be preached from the beginning of the human race. II, 376; X, 973. Nor were there lacking those who believed in him. II, 376. The five periods of time through which he did not cease to be foretold. VI, 314. What was done so that the Jews would not think Christ’s promise had been fulfilled in any one of their kings. VI, 338. Christ is encountered and gives nourishment throughout the sacred Scriptures. VIII, 269. Christ foretold by many Prophets. V, 1674. The truth of the prophecy concerning Christ is proved from the Jewish books. III, 1052. Testimonies of the Prophets concerning Christ. III, 1658, 1660, 1661. Their predictions concerning him. VII, 584. The prophecy concerning Christ: Eliezer’s oath. VII, 512. Job prophesied Christ. X, 283. Christ is to be understood in the deeds and writings of the Old Testament. V, 31; VIII, 275, 276, 277. The figures of Christ were either those that appeared mystically to our fathers through angelic miracles or those performed by the fathers themselves. VIII, 895. The things read in the second chapter of Genesis speak beforehand of Christ. VIII, 280. Christ foretold in Psalm 44. VIII, 53, 54. And in Psalm 68. VIII, 54. Psalm 71 is to be understood of Christ, not of Solomon. IX, 406. Christ foretold in Isaiah’s prophecy. VIII, 57, 58, 59. Christ promised and foretold by the Prophets. VIII, 282, 283, 284, 643. Miracles would not have announced Christ sufficiently without prophetic testimonies. VIII, 279. Christ is compared with Jonah. VI, 666. Jonah foretold Christ not so much by his words as by a certain suffering of his own. VII, 587. The coming of Christ is foretold. VII, 584, 588, 592, 593. Christ himself also preached in the Prophets. IV, 1845. The Prophets, full of Christ, announced Christ. IV, 1845. They foretold him as God and man. II, 521. Christ prophesied in the ancient Law. II, 634. The Scriptures were made on account of Christ. IV, 1779. Whatever difficulty a person encounters in the Scriptures, let him not depart from Christ: when Christ has been revealed to him in them, let him understand that he has understood. IV, 1237. Many things said about Christ are not to be understood literally. IV, 1597.

Christ had to be foretold by certain sacraments when he was going to come, and announced by others when he had come. II, 528. Testimonies of foreigners concerning Christ. VII, 609. Responses of oracles concerning Christ. VII, 650, 651. The oracles do not proclaim Christ as God but only as a man. VII, 652. They confessed him to be holy and immortal. VII, 305. The oracles praise Christ in such a way as to blame Christians; why. VII, 652. Why Christ had to be foretold. IV, 1447. Many heralds preceded Christ as a great judge. IV, 1258.

How great was the desire for the Christ who was to be born among the ancient saints. V, 890, 1658. Christ’s incarnation benefited the ancient fathers even before it had occurred. X, 401. Through faith in Christ who was to come, the fathers were justified. IV, 385, 596. Christ is the same for the ancient fathers and for us. V, 1553.

Christ is celebrated in figures in the ancient Law. VI, 42. Christ was figured in the meats supplied to the people of Israel in the evening and the breads supplied in the morning. III, 616. Christ was foretold in the ancient sacrifices. VIII, 347. A figure of Christ. III, 791. The various figures of Christ from the Old Testament are catalogued. VIII, 268, 269, 270, 271. The figure of Christ: the tree of life. VII, 701. Noah and the ark. III, 2022; VII, 472. Isaac. III, 1464; IV, 245; V, 133; VII, 511; VIII, 852. The ram seen by Abraham. [Col. 0143] VII, 511. The marked or blood-colored ram. III, 635. Jacob’s stone, Moses’ staff. VIII, 853, 880. Christ figured by the angels, by Isaac, by the rock, and by the ram. VIII, 772. By three birds. IV, 1299. By the serpent lifted up by Moses. IV, 1578; X, 1138. Christ as rock, manna, pillar, cloud, and so forth. VIII, 269, 270. Christ in the angel wrestling with Jacob. IV, 506, 1936; V, 682. Christ in Moses. V, 758. Joshua as a figure of Christ. VIII, 328. Christ and the Church are figured in the times of the Judges and Kings themselves. VIII, 271. The present age exhibits the name of Christ and the Church just as past ages announced them. VIII, 285. Christ in Samson. V, 1640. Christ prefigured in Jeconiah. V, 341. Christ in the lamb, bull, and goat. V, 133. Christ crucified in the likeness of sinful flesh, figured in the bronze serpent lifted up. V, 1342. Christ lies hidden under the veil of the Law as the marrow lies beneath the chaff. V, 725. Christ signified by Lazarus. III, 1352.

Some think that Christ was visible before he assumed flesh. VII, 508. And that he appeared to Abraham. VII, 508. Christ appeared to Abraham in the person of an angel. III, 563. Some reasonably believe that Christ’s incarnation was also revealed among the nations. VII, 609. Christ speaks as the Lord God in the prophetic books, and yet Christ appears. VII, 705.

The pagans said that Christ was nothing other than a man, although one of the most excellent wisdom. I, 636; III, 1048, 1069, 1071. They invented the claim that he had published books on magic. III, 1049. They said that these were inscribed with the names of Peter and Paul. III, 1049. Some dared to say that Christ had learned his opinions from Plato’s books. III, 56. The heretic Marcus asserted that Christ suffered not truly but merely in appearance. VIII, 28. Cerdon held the same view. VIII, 28. Cerdon taught that Christ was neither born from a woman nor possessed flesh. VIII, 29. Cerdon taught that the God announced in the Old Testament, the God of the Law and the Prophets, was not the Father of Christ. VIII, 29. The Marcionites taught the same. III, 1711. The Cerinthians said that Christ was merely a man. VIII, 27. So did the Ebionites. VIII, 27. Photinus. II, 459. The Ophites consider Christ to be a serpent. VIII, 28, 29. Some say that the Sethians considered Christ to be the son of Shem. VIII, 29. The errors of the Manichaeans, Photinians, and Apollinarists concerning Christ’s incarnation. X, 1033, 1034. The Photinians wished Christ to be merely human, and the Manichaeans merely divine. V, 229. Some said that Christ was only God, others only man; the faith confesses both. III, 1663.

The Manichaeans call Christ the serpent of paradise. VIII, 37, 38. The Manichaeans said that Christ was not only fixed, bound, and compacted in heaven and the stars but also on earth and in everything that grows upon it. VIII, 211, 212, 379. How, according to the Manichaeans, Christ bound up in all things could be helped. VIII, 211, 212. They said that Christ was the son of the first man whom they imagined. VIII, 211. They said that he was this visible sun. III, 1652; V, 36. The error of the Manichaeans that Christ had no flesh. X, 1586. What the Manichaeans and Pelagians believe concerning Christ’s flesh, and what the Catholics believe against them. X, 1385. The Manichaeans worship Christ not as real but as phantasmal. V, 28. The Manichaeans deny that Christ possessed a vulnerable and mortal body. VIII, 304. They thought it unworthy to believe that Christ was born from a womb. VIII, 178, 213, 217. They attempt to assert that Christ had no mother. IV, 129. They taught that Christ pretended to the appearance of flesh, the death of the cross, the wounds of the Passion, and the scars of the resurrection. VIII, 37, 38, 179, 223, 238, 217, 256, 299, 300, 321, 322, 483, 487, 488, 489, 494, 495, 598, 599. Many said that Christ had no flesh and did not rise again in his body. IV, 871.

The Paulinians assert that Christ did not always exist, but that his beginning was when he was born from Mary, and that he was nothing more than a man. VIII, 34. The Origenists introduce Christ as a creature. VIII, 33. What the Arians thought concerning Christ. VIII, 680, 681, 686, 687. The Arians taught that Christ suffered contamination from human flesh not according to the form of God but according to the form of man. VIII, 725. They said that Christ was the God of every creature. VIII, 721. The Noetians wish Christ to be the very same person as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. VIII, 32. The Sabellians and Priscillianists held the same view. VIII, 44. Petilianus said that Christ was the middle person of the Trinity. IX, 372. The Proclianists deny that Christ came in the flesh. VIII, 41, 42. All heretics deny that Christ came in the flesh. V, 989. All wicked Catholics also deny it. V, 992. The error of certain people who deny that Christ’s body was formed from a woman and think that it came to be in the same way as the body in which the Holy Spirit appeared as a dove. VI, 302.

The Arians and Apollinarists teach that Christ assumed flesh without a soul. VIII, 39, 40, 686, 687, 689. Certain heretics believed that in Christ the Word was in place of the soul; others, in place of the human mind. II, 833. There was a heresy that said the Word of God was in him in place of mind, understanding, and reason. [Col. 0144] V, 1124. The Apollinarists dogmatized that Christ did not assume a rational soul. III, 1737; VII, 404. The Apollinarists held that in Christ the Word was in place of the soul. III, 716; VIII, 40. The Apollinarists said that Christ had only a soul, without a human mind. IV, 217. Some who arose from that heresy said that he lacked even the soul itself. IV, 218, 1084. It is rash to say that a rational soul came to Christ after he had already been born. II, 552. From where Christ received his soul. III, 422. Christ’s soul is not derived by transmission. III, 422. Even the Traducianists themselves admit this. III, 424. According to some, Christ says in Wisdom 8: “I obtained a good soul.” III, 413. This is examined. III, 421. The question concerning Christ’s soul is exceedingly difficult. VIII, 784.

The Apollinarists teach that Christ’s flesh was not assumed from Mary’s flesh and that something of the Word was converted into flesh. VIII, 40. Valentinus taught that Christ brought with him a spiritual body and assumed nothing from Mary, but passed through her as through a stream or conduit. VIII, 28. Apelles taught that Christ did not take flesh from heaven but received it from the elements of the world, and returned it to the world when, rising without flesh, he ascended into heaven. VIII, 30. What the Priscillianists thought concerning Christ’s flesh. VIII, 668. The Ebionites say that Christ did not rise but will rise. VIII, 27. Some judged that Christ’s human form was to be changed into the divine substance. VIII, 708. Porphyry despised Christ in the flesh. VII, 301. What the Pelagians think concerning Christ. X, 609. The error of the heretics concerning Christ is divided into three kinds. III, 1332, 1666. What is to be believed concerning Christ. X, 1034. What Christ was before the incarnation. V, 1095.

Christ’s twofold coming. IV, 117, 1235; V, 202. Christ’s coming into the world is to be understood with reference to the flesh. V, 939. The whole Trinity made Christ as man. VI, 251. Christ’s Incarnation is the work of the whole Trinity. V, 1096. Why Christ came to us. V, 945; VI, 668. The chief reason for Christ’s coming was the commendation of love. VI, 314. Christ had no reason for coming except to save sinners. Take away diseases, take away wounds, and there is no reason for medicine. V, 945. Christ came to procure human salvation. IV, 1089. Because Adam fell, Christ descended. IV, 1598. If you, O man, had not abandoned God, God would not have become man for you. IV, 372. God became man so that, since as a man you could come to man, though you could not come to God, you might come to God through man. IV, 1741. It was not our good merits but our sins that brought Christ from heaven to earth. V, 944, 1074. The human race would not be liberated unless the Word of God deigned to become human. V, 939. If he were not man, man would not be liberated. IV, 766. Christ would not seek the one he had made unless he himself became what he had made. III, 1622. Christ became man so that man might not perish. V, 174. Unless the Son of man had come, man would have perished. V, 895. Beautiful passages concerning Christ’s coming to us in the flesh. I, 701, 746.

Christ assumed human nature in order to teach that what ought to be worshiped by man is what every intellectual creature ought to worship. III, 170. In no way was the human race more beneficially provided for than when the very Wisdom of God assumed the whole man. III, 134. Christ became a participant in our mortality so that we might become participants in his divinity. IV, 1546, 1785. Christ came to human beings as teacher and helper. II, 521. Christ appeared to us through a mortal body because we had to be healed through the humility of the Son of God. II, 946. From the incarnation of the Son of God one can see how great a place man has among God’s works. VI, 297. Christ assumed flesh so that man would not cling to carnal things. II, 1057. He became man so that he might make us gods. V, 1012. He assumed our nature so that the devil might be defeated through the very nature he had deceived. VI, 291.

Christ’s generation and birth are twofold, and each is wondrous. V, 260, 773, 1007, 1015, 1017, 1019, 1073, 1655, 1659, 1661, 1675, 1676. How Christ was incarnate. V, 1061. How wondrous Christ’s incarnation is. V, 1011. It is ineffable. VI, 249. The form of a servant was added; the form of God did not depart. V, 990. The Word did not withdraw from the Father. V, 1097. Christ was here through divine majesty and came through human weakness. V, 940. Christ’s mission was his self-emptying. III, 1615. Christ emptied himself before human beings, concealing what he was and displaying what he had become. V, 1003. Christ goes while hidden, comes while appearing, and remains while ruling. III, 1815. The man in Christ was not assumed by the Wisdom of God in the same way that other human beings become wise through it. VI, 301. Man was assumed by the Word in such a way that he became God together with it. IV, 73. Christ became man without ceasing to be God. III, 1621; V, 999, 1203, 1205. Christ the man was never so man that he was not the only-begotten Son of God, because of the only-begotten Word. X, 1137. Christ, God from God, light from light. III, 1635. Why Christ is called the true Son of God. V, 774. The Son of God equal to God. V, 691. The only Son of God. V, 1061, 1068, [Col. 0145] How he is the only Son of God the Father. V, 769. According to the form of God, Christ is invisible in the same way as God the Father. IV, 1789.

Christ, the true and truthful Son of God and of man. VIII, 211, 216, 222. Christ is always the Son of God by nature, and the Son of Man by grace, having been assumed in time. VIII, 688, 702. Christ is the Son of God by nature, not by grace; true, not adopted. V, 990. Nowhere in Scripture is Christ called the Son of God by adoption. VIII, 581. Those who say, “He who is the son of man became the Son of God, but he who is the Son of God did not become the son of man,” are refuted. V, 999.

Christ is Word and man. III, 1737. God and man. IV, 528; V, 229, 196, 547, 573, 685, 1149, 1279, 1398, 1495. Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh. III, 1836; IV, 1084; VIII, 690. Just as one man consists of soul and flesh, so one Christ consists of God and man. V, 940, 997. Christ is not a semi-God, as though he were God in part and man in part, but wholly God and wholly man. V, 1332. True God and true man. VI, 300, 459; VIII, 211. Christ is God hidden in flesh. V, 1330. God and man are not two but one Christ. III, 1737, 1739, 1836; X, 144. In Christ there is a twofold substance, divine and human; both are not two but one Christ. III, 1836; V, 727.

Christ took visible human form into the unity of his person. VIII, 756, 757. God is not a part of Christ’s person. VIII, 765. In the unity of his person Christ joined the nature of God and man in such a way that he both elevated the customary through the uncustomary and tempered the uncustomary through the customary. II, 519. The same person is God and man, not by a confusion of natures but by the unity of person. V, 999. Christ is simultaneously God and man in the unity of person. VI, 249. The Lord makes one person with the servant. V, 436. There is one person in Christ. II, 543; III, 1553, 1617, 1817; V, 568; VIII, 688; X, 1034. There are not two Christs, nor two Sons of God. V, 1341. Christ the Son of man was in heaven even when he was speaking on earth. III, 1617; V, 436, 1340. Because of the unity of person, Christ both remained in heaven and walked on earth. X, 144. In Christ there are two substances, God and man, but one person, so that the Trinity may remain a Trinity and, with man added, not become a quaternity. V, 728, 999, 1205. In Christ the form of a servant is to be distinguished, not separated or alienated and constituted as another person. V, 309. In Christ, because of the unity of person, each nature communicates its designation to the other: the divine to the human and the human to the divine. VIII, 257. The Son of man is said to have descended from heaven, and the Son of God to have been crucified. VIII, 789, 790. Different things are predicated of the same Christ because of the different natures of the hypostasis. VIII, 840.

Christ, a giant of two substances, obedient in one respect and equal to God in another. VIII, 689. Christ lesser than the Father and equal to him. VI, 250. Christ both Only-begotten and Firstborn: how. VIII, 581, 583. The Manichaeans wanted “firstborn” to be understood of Christ not according to his assumption of humanity, but according to the excellence of his divinity. VIII, 473, 382. Because of the form of God, Christ is called the Beginning, the Firstborn, and the Lord of glory; because of the form of a servant, the Bridegroom proceeding from the bridal chamber, the Head of the body, the Church, and so forth. VIII, 835. For Christ as man, God is both Father and Lord. VIII, 691. For him, God the Father is Father of the form of God and Lord of the form of a servant. IV, 1785. The fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ: how. II, 846; III, 459. By what distinction divinity dwells in Christ and in his members. II, 846. In Christ neither divinity was changed into a creature nor the creature into divinity. VIII, 829. By the incarnation, Christ the Son of God is the same person as the son of man. V, 1000. How we ought to believe Christ to be the son of man. VIII, 223.

As man, Christ belongs to the same nature as we do. V, 941. Christ is himself, precisely as he was made the son of man, yet distinct from us. V, 680. Christ came to what he was not; he did not lose what he was. V, 680, 685. Christ’s participation in what is inferior to us, and our participation in what is superior in him, are dissimilar. X, 174. One thing in Christ is permanent, another transitory. IV, 1449. Christ’s earlier things are his divinity; his later things, his humanity. IV, 1609. Christ, the Only-begotten of God, was not made from nothing. X, 1481. How Christ is Creator, and how created. II, 835. Christ is unchangeable insofar as he is the Word. V, 689. The Son of God was not changed through the incarnation. V, 105, 308. Christ became man without change in himself. VI, 339, 345. Christ is therefore our firmness, because our weakness did not change him. V, 106.

Christ is perfect man. II, 833. Christ assumed a complete human being. V, 436. The whole human being. V, 1124; VI, 186, 302, 355; VII, 305. Through the spirit he assumed a soul, and through the soul a body. VI, 300. Christ had a soul. VI, 302; and a human mind. VI, 301. Christ neither lacked a soul nor lacked a rational soul. II, 542. If Christ had assumed only a soul, his members would be nothing but our souls. V, 878. Whether his soul was propagated from Adam or created. II, 717. See above. Christ’s soul was not subject to original sin. II, 866.

[Col. 0146] Christ’s flesh is the vehicle by which he came to us and raised us to the Father. V, 675. Likewise it is a garment, a beast of burden, and a temple. V, 675. Christ’s flesh is real and was assumed from Mary. V, 1619. Christ’s flesh is real because it is not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. V, 844. Those who deny that Christ had a true body, saying that what appeared to the eyes was something that did not exist, are refuted. V, 477. Christ’s having true flesh, against the Manichaeans and Priscillianists. V, 1122, 1125. Because of the Word, the flesh of the Word is dear to the Father. III, 1923. Christ had a true body. VI, 14, 300. Christ’s flesh, wounds, and scars were real. VIII, 250, 251, 340. He did not feign any of the affections of the human condition, but displayed them fully—not by the necessity of his condition, but by the will of a teacher. VIII, 484. The Son of God assumed our weakness. VI, 296. Christ assumed the affections of human weakness, just as he assumed the flesh itself and the death of the flesh—not by the necessity of his condition, but by the will of compassion. IV, 1111, 1208; VI, 94, 95; VII, 414. Christ’s weakness arose from power. VII, 415. Christ hungered and thirsted because he condescended to do so, not because he was compelled. V, 968. Sleep, food, and human affections in Christ prove that human nature was assumed, not consumed. II, 519. Christ shared our evils with us in order to give us his goods. V, 680. Against the Apollinarians it is shown that Christ possessed everything human except sin. IV, 218.

Christ’s conception has no parallel. II, 707. Christ was born of the Holy Spirit—not as from a father, but of Mary as his mother. VI, 251. Christ was conceived without concupiscence. II, 844; III, 422. His mother conceived Christ not by concupiscence but by grace. V, 823. Christ’s flesh came from our mass, not from the knot of concupiscence between man and woman. V, 928. Christ was made of a woman, with no intercourse intervening. III, 405. He was conceived through his mother’s faith. VI, 249. The Virgin conceived Christ not through carnal desire but through spiritual belief. IV, 826. How he was in his mother’s womb and in heaven. VI, 27. Christ came into this world for a wedding. III, 1452. The wedding of Christ to which Jews and Gentiles are invited. V, 559, 1662. Christ was born mortal in order to remove death. V, 1113. He assumed mortality in order to give immortality. V, 688. Christ came in the flesh to cleanse the defects of the flesh. V, 1019. Christ clothed himself with death in the virginity of his mother; he will clothe himself with life in the equality of the Father. IV, 1942. Christ came to assume our death and promise his life. IV, 1942. He came for this purpose: to undergo the death of the cross. IV, 857. He died from what was ours; from what was his own he could not die. V, 710. Our Priest received from us what he was to offer for us. IV, 1701. He received from you that by which he might die for you. IV, 1942. He received death from what was ours in order to give us life from what was his. V, 688, 1110. Because he came to suffer, he came hidden. IV, 567. Christ came not to do what sinners do, but to suffer what sinners suffer. IV, 1198. Christ came so that souls might rise from iniquity and bodies from corruption. III, 1586. Christ came for this purpose: that you might believe in God. IV, 1898. And that after the life of faith he might confer eternal life. III, 1727. In Christ’s flesh there was punishment without guilt, so that both guilt and punishment might be healed. V, 1374. By assuming punishment and not guilt, Christ destroyed both guilt and punishment. V, 934, 1343.

Christ assumed our iniquity in order to bear and heal it, not to possess it. V, 1331. He assumed flesh, not the iniquity of flesh; he assumed clean flesh, cleansing flesh. IV, 1850. He assumed flesh from the Virgin’s womb in order to offer the clean for the unclean. IV, 1953. From the Virgin’s body Christ did not assume what he was to heal, but that by which he was to heal. V, 1341.

Christ’s flesh is signified by the psaltery and the lyre. IV, 672. Christ’s flesh is called sackcloth because of its likeness to sinful flesh. IV, 335. Christ’s flesh is a sack. IV, 852, 1854. It is called the lamp of wisdom. IV, 1793. Christ’s flesh is the tabernacle and the Bride of the Word. IV, 1163.

The claim that Christ was not free from sins: Julian’s slander against Catholics. X, 561; 559. In Christ, human nature was without sin because of the union. VIII, 688. Christ suffered no contagion from human flesh. VIII, 720, 744. Christ descended to earthly contagion in such a way that he had no sin, even according to the confession of the Arians. VIII, 761. Christ was conceived without sin in order to dissolve sin. V, 817. He was born without sin because he was conceived without lust. V, 442, 785, 823, 832. Christ had no sin, either original or personal iniquity. V, 824, 928. Christ did not contract original sin. X, 1553. Christ alone was without original sin. X, 1416. How he was alien from original sin. IV, 591. Christ alone was born without sin. X, 142, 253, 1085. He alone could be born in such a way that he would not need to be born again. VI, 255. Christ alone in the flesh was without sin and ignorance. VI, 60. Christ alone was without sin in this life. III, 733, 867, 1696, 1697, 1847; X, 184. Why. X, 815. Christ would have made sin greater if he had possessed it as a child. X, 815. In Christ, human nature was incapable of sin. X, 934.

[Col. 0147] To equate Christ’s flesh with the flesh of others is blasphemy. X, 1375. The Pelagians equate them. X, 1418, 1429. Julian thinks that Christ’s flesh possesses the same purity as that of other human beings at birth. X, 813. Julian attempts to introduce lust into Christ. X, 1371, 1375. Christ’s birth from the flesh: in what respect it resembles and differs from ours. X, 174. Christ’s flesh is distinguished from ours not by the nature and substance of flesh, but by its freedom from participation in the common defect. X, 1587, 1588, 1608. Christ did not assume sinful flesh, although he came from his mother’s sinful flesh. X, 174. Because Christ was not born from the concupiscence of the flesh, he did not have sinful flesh. X, 1590. In Christ there was the reality of limbs, not the desire of sins. X, 1370. Christ did not transfer sin into his flesh, but death. X, 145. Christ drew mortality from his mother’s mortality, but not sin. X, 814. It seems that Christ’s flesh, by growing old, would in any case have proceeded toward death. X, 180.

Christ did not possess the desire of vices. X, 1366, 1369. Christ did not possess concupiscence and therefore, just as he did not commit sin, so he did not desire it. X, 1390. Since Christ was not born through concupiscence, he desired nothing illicit. X, 1373, 1374. Christ did not therefore need to possess concupiscence because he offered himself for imitation. X, 1338, 1390. The rationale of his example is not removed in Christ even if he did not possess the concupiscence common to us. X, 815. If Christ had possessed the concupiscence of the flesh, he would not have healed it in us. X, 816. Those who deny concupiscence in Christ do not thereby agree with the Apollinarians. X, 814. Christ alone did not possess concupiscence. X, 562. The devil found no concupiscence in Christ. X, 1341, 1366, 1384, 1387. Why concupiscence did not pass into Christ’s flesh. X, 814. In Christ there were sensations of the flesh, but not concupiscence. X, 1367.

Christ’s flesh was not sinful flesh, since it was not born from carnal pleasure. VI, 64. Christ’s body was not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. III, 422; V, 179, 744, 844. Christ alone possessed the likeness of sinful flesh that was not sinful flesh. X, 1384, 1385. How Christ’s flesh was in the likeness of sinful flesh. VIII, 297; X, 813. The likeness of sinful flesh in which Christ came to us was called sin. VIII, 744. Christ was without sin, yet was made sin. VI, 252. In what sense. V, 825, 845; X, 599. How he was called sin. X, 403. How he is said to have sins and transgressions who committed no sin. IV, 172, 400; V, 1607. Christ was the receiver of transgressions, not their perpetrator. IV, 849. He made our transgressions his transgressions so that he might make his righteousness our righteousness. IV, 172. Among human beings, Christ alone, being God-man, could truly say: “If you have found sin in me, say so.” IV, 590. In Christ there was integrity without sin, repayment without debt, and scourging without deserving it. IV, 463. He would not free others from bonds unless he himself were free from bonds. IV, 1850. How Christ was sent to condemn sin on account of sin. V, 745, 823. Through Christ alone original sin is dissolved. VI, 255. And other things added to original sin. VI, 256. In what respect Christ as man is something greater than other human beings. IV, 217.

Christ’s human nature did not begin to exist before it was assumed by the Son of God. VI, 252, 301. In Christ, the man who was assumed was not first created and afterward assumed; he was created in the very act of assumption. VIII, 688. Christ was not first the Son of Man and afterward the Son of God; by that very assumption he was made the Son of Man. V, 941. The Son of God assumed the whole human being, which had not previously merited him, but did so entirely by grace. V, 941. The Pelagian heresy leads to the belief that Christ earned by the power of his own will that he should be assumed by the Word of God. X, 1386. Christ is the most brilliant light of predestination. X, 982. The supreme example of grace. VII, 308.

Christ was predestined. III, 1907; X, 982. Whoever denies that the Son of God was predestined denies that he is the same Son of Man. III, 1907. That a man was assumed into the unity of the Only-begotten’s person is a matter of grace, not of nature. III, 1828. Human nature belongs by grace to the person of the Only-begotten Son of God. III, 1844. Christ did not earn that he should be assumed. VI, 250. From his beginning, Christ as man was Son of God not through merits but through grace. X, 1157, 1158. What impiety against the grace proper to Christ follows from the Pelagian doctrine. X, 1137. In a certain sense grace was natural to Christ. VI, 252. Through it he was made incapable of having any sin. VI, 250. This grace is indicated by the manner in which Christ was born of the Holy Spirit. VI, 251, 252.

Christ was from Adam’s seed, but was not begotten by a seminal process; in him he did not sin along with the others. X, 1401. Whether, and how, Christ was in Abraham’s loins. III, 424. From Abraham’s flesh Christ drew not the heat of the wound but the material of the medicine. III, 424. If Christ had been in Abraham according to the soul, he could not have failed to be tithed. III, 425. How Christ was not tithed in Abraham. X, 1552.

Christ is the Lord’s man. VI, 26, 42. Christ is the heavenly man. VI, 409. Also according to the flesh. X, 1602. Christ’s divinity [Col. 0148] is set against the divinity of Romulus. VII, 757, 759. That Christ is God is demonstrated by the miracles and prophecies fulfilled in him. VII, 757, 759. The constant confession of the martyrs persuades us that Christ is God. VII, 676, 758. Note. The woman understood that Christ was God when she believed that he could forgive her sins. V, 599. The divine deeds performed by Christ reveal his hidden divinity. V, 700. Christ proves that he is God. III, 1812. Christ acts in words and deeds so that he may be believed God and man. III, 1622. Christ was never separated from the Word. III, 1817. He was never abandoned. IV, 79. Nor was he cast away from the Word by the humiliation of the Passion. IV, 74. Christ’s soul was never separated from the Word. III, 1738. Christ is called even simply “flesh” and simply “soul.” III, 1739, 1740, 1836. In Christ, the Church too was assumed by the Word. IV, 77.

According to the fact that he is the Son of God, Christ has no earthly genealogy. VIII, 239. Christ’s carnal origin is from both righteous people and sinners. III, 769. Christ is from both royal and priestly stock. III, 809, 1072. How Christ is the son of Abraham and David. V, 337. Christ is Son of God and Son of David. VIII, 468, 469. Christ is the son of David. III, 1742. He is both Son and Lord of David. V, 343. Christ does not deny that he is the son of David. V, 572. He is said to have been begotten by David as from a womb. IV, 1459. The authority of all books and languages proclaims, against the Manichaeans, that Christ is from David’s seed according to the flesh. VIII, 248, 249. Christ would rightly be called the son of David even if Mary derived no origin from David. III, 1072. The question posed to the Jews concerning Christ. V, 572. What is to be believed about Christ. V, 1073, 1149. Christ does not deny that he is the son of Joseph. V, 342, 343. The genealogies from Abraham to Christ. V, 337.

Matthew recorded Christ’s genealogy differently from Luke: why. VI, 49; VIII, 214. Matthew and Luke do not lie when, in naming different progenitors of Christ, they mention different ancestors. V, 350; VIII, 216. Why Matthew counts Christ’s generations by descending and Luke by ascending. V, 351. Why they are counted through Joseph and not through Mary. V, 342, 350; VIII, 470; X, 810. Concerning the number forty in the Lord’s genealogies. V, 352. Why Luke counts seventy-seven generations of Christ. V, 353. Why sinners are included in Christ’s genealogy. VIII, 440. Why Christ did not wish to be born from the tribe of Levi. VI, 50.

Christ’s two births. III, 1488, 1648. Before he was born, and before all ages, Christ existed. IV, 1186, 1187. He was born of a woman not in the form of God but in the form of a servant. VIII, 217, 218. Why he wished to be born of a woman. V, 105, 334, 1007; VI, 141, 186. Christ was born by his will and died through mercy. IV, 1241. Christ made for himself the mother from whom he would be born. IV, 958. Christ’s birth from the Virgin. VI, 643. Why Christ chose to be born of a Virgin. VIII, 440. It was fitting that the God-man should be born of a Virgin. VI, 174. Christ is the Virgin’s Son and the Bridegroom of virgins. V, 1018; VI, 397. There was nobility in the virginity of the one giving birth, and nobility in the divinity of the one being born. V, 1029. Why Christ wished to assume flesh from Mary. III, 405. Christ was not therefore born of the Virgin Mary because he could not otherwise exist in true flesh. VIII, 483, 488.

Christ was born without injury to his mother’s virginity. V, 999, 1004, 1005, 1011, 1068, 1075. With her integrity remaining uncorrupted. VI, 186, 249. He was born through closed doors. V, 1074, 1157. In Christ’s emergence through the inviolate Virgin’s virginal organs, and his entrance through closed doors, the whole explanation of the event lies in the power of the one who accomplished it. II, 519. Christ was born without sin because he was not born through concupiscence. X, 1384, 1385. According to Ambrose, Christ’s carnal birth was therefore free from transgression because it did not arise from the union of the two sexes. X, 444, 1389. Christ alone was begotten from a single womb. IV, 1459. Christ was born in solitude because he alone was born of a Virgin. IV, 1845. Christ’s birth was full of wonders. VI, 663; VII, 314. Signs at Christ’s birth. VI, 643. When Christ was born. VII, 109, 608. On what day and under which consul he was born was known in Augustine’s time. III, 1592. How many years were counted from his birth or resurrection. II, 911. Christ has a birthday here as man, not as God. V, 1302. Christ was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. III, 629; VIII, 894; IX, 572. Christ was conceived and died around the eighth day before the Kalends of April. III, 629; VIII, 894. Christ was born when the days were beginning to grow longer, whereas John was born when they were beginning to grow shorter: the meaning of this mystery. IV, 1735. Christ was made before John—that is, was placed before John. V, 1678. The correspondence between Christ’s birthday and Christ’s work. V, 1000, 1007, 1013, 1015. Why Christ’s and John’s birthdays are celebrated, but not those of others. V, 1301, 1313. How Christ is born in us. V, 1659.

Why Christ came after so long a time. X, 973, 974. Why Christ did not come earlier. III, 1638. Why he did not come at the beginning of human sin. VI, 28. Yet he came in the youth and in the old age of the world. I, 626; V, 504. In the sixth age of the human race. VI, 55. Why he came after the Law had been given. [Col. 0149] V, 28. Christ wished to appear to human beings and preach his teaching among them at the time and place where he knew there would be people who would believe in him. II, 374.

Why Christ was born an infant and weak, although he was free from sin. X, 149. Christ, God, became an infant for our sake. V, 108, 1020. The wondrous harmony in the infant Christ of attributes that seem opposed. V, 997, 1001. In the infant Christ there was neither ignorance nor weakness of mind. X, 180.

Christ’s homeland is the Jewish people. III, 1524, 1526. And we ourselves as well. III, 1526. Christ was born in Judaea, but not for Judaea alone. IV, 1243. Christ founded Zion and was born in Zion.
