IV, 1846. Once born, Christ immediately joins Jews and Gentiles in himself. V, 1026. How Christ was not received by his own people. V, 1503. At Christ’s birth every rank of the faithful bears witness. V, 1019, 1657, 1659. Christ was revealed to the Magi at his birth. V, 1663. To Jews and Gentiles. V, 1668. Christ’s beauty. IV, 495.

Christ’s manger produces confidence in the forgiveness of sins and forgetfulness of the anxieties of a bad conscience. III, 881. Christ is both small and great. IV, 1230. His greatness is before days, beyond days, without day. IV, 1230. Christ performed all miracles, even before he was born as a human being. IV, 1150.

Christ’s poverty is extreme. IV, 844. Christ wished to be born poor. III, 696. Why Christ became needy. V, 243, 916, 1129, 1591. Christ came to fill the poor, having become poor himself. IV, 455. He deigned to need, so that he could repay the reward of the work. V, 968. Christ wished to be needy for your sake, so that you would have somewhere to sow the earthly things he gave and reap eternal life. V, 91. Christ’s poverty is our wealth; likewise, his weakness, foolishness, and mortality are our strength, wisdom, and immortality. IV, 454. How Christ is both poor and rich. V, 115, 215, 685. What are Christ’s riches? IV, 844.

Christ’s humility is commended in the incarnation. IV, 302. Christ’s humility. III, 1390, 1681, 1787. Christ’s humility cannot be explained, much less his divinity. III, 1402. Christ is called a worm because of the humility of his flesh, perhaps also because of the Virgin’s childbirth. II, 385. Christ’s humiliation could only have been profound. IV, 1735. Christ so humbled himself that he could not have appeared lower. III, 1903. He sets aside his divinity by concealing what was his; what he had received becomes visible. V, 488. The humble things narrated about Christ pertain to his flesh; the exalted things to his divinity. III, 1662. Christ’s humiliation is mercy, not weakness. IV, 1239. He emptied himself by assuming what he was not, not by losing what he was. V, 573. In the same flesh in which he came forth small, he entered, raised through closed doors, great. V, 1074, 1157. Why Christ came to us with such humility. VII, 221. Because of the great sin of pride, God came in humility: this cause, this great sin, this enormous disease, brought the omnipotent physician of souls down from heaven. IV, 163, 302. Christ was incarnate in order to teach the way of humility. V, 1321. Christ is the humble way; Christ is the exalted one and God, the truth and the life. V, 778. Christ appeared humble so that we might grasp him. IV, 1239. The Word of God, the bread of angels, becomes milk through the incarnation so that it may reach little ones. IV, 303, 1710. Christ is the same food of angels in heaven and of human beings in the manger. V, 1016. Christ, the creator of angels, became man so that he as man might eat the bread of angels. V, 1016. Christ in the manger is food for the faithful beasts. V, 1008. The food that we were too weak to grasp was sent to the flesh, and the Word became flesh so that the wisdom of God might become milk for our infancy. I, 745, 1286. Unless Christ were humble, he could neither be eaten nor drunk. IV, 303. Humility, the flesh, and the crucifixion of Christ are milk sufficient for little ones. IV, 1615. Christ wished to precede exaltation with humility. III, 1624. Whoever does not stumble over the humble Christ will not fear the exalted one. III, 2000. Christ remained hidden in order to offer an example through weakness. III, 1622. Christ gave us a great example of humility. III, 1631. Christ’s sign is his humility: he did not wish his sign among the faithful to be a star on the forehead, but his cross. III, 1396. Whoever rejects Christ’s humility is proud and far from health. V, 687.

Christ was a teacher not only by speaking but also by being born. VIII, 440. In himself he wished us to learn what should be despised in this life and what should be hoped for in the next. II, 543, 549, 550, 551. Through Christ’s birth, righteousness was brought to us. V, 1005, 1013.

Christ’s circumcision took place on the eighth day to signify his resurrection. II, 680. Prophecy that Christ would not be killed in infancy. III, 629, 652. Christ was carried into Egypt; by the deeds already accomplished by his limbs, he was speaking so that his persecuting enemies might flee. V, 1034. At twelve years of age the elders marveled at Christ’s wisdom. III, 422. Christ’s being subject to his parents concerned not divine majesty but human age. VIII, 786, 787. Christ’s obedience is set against Adam’s disobedience. VII, 423. Christ’s life described in brief. III, 135. Why Christ wished to be baptized. III, 1411, 1415, 1418; V, 1322; VI, 255; IX, 77, 182, 290. Why he wished to be baptized, although he had no stains. IV, 1164. He assumed medicines to be commended, not wounds. V, 1335. Why he assumed the sacraments of the old Law. V, 1048. He was baptized to accord with penitents. X, 1376. To teach the way of humility. V, 1321. By wishing to be baptized, he commended his humility still more profoundly. II, 843. Why he was not baptized by John alone. IX, 238. The Gospel authority maintains that Christ was baptized at about thirty years of age. III, 55. Why Christ baptized no one. III, 1305. Christ baptizes all those whom his ministers baptize. III, 1417.

Why Christ fasted for forty days. V, 1211. Why, when hungry, he did not make bread from a stone. IV, 1164. Just as at the wedding he made wine from water. V, 686. Christ’s hunger and thirst looked toward our good works and the faith of the peoples. IV, 336, 736, 851. Why Christ allowed himself to be tempted by the devil. V, 685. When Christ wished to be tempted by Satan, he transformed us into himself. IV, 724. Christ’s temptation is our instruction. IV, 1149. He was tempted in order to teach his own to resist the tempter. V, 685. Christ’s temptation is threefold, corresponding to the three kinds of vice: the pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity. IV, 116. Christ’s mystery was revealed in the Old Testament. V, 1377.

Christ here did not possess good things but endured evil things. V, 134. Christ wore sandals. V, 608. Christ testing Philip. V, 28. Some thought that Christ had lied in some respect and that what he threatened against the wicked would not come to pass. V, 478. Whence this opinion arose. V, 478. See “Son of God, Word.” Christ vindicated from a charge of falsehood in John VII. V, 737, 740, 741. How true his testimony about himself is. V, 713. When Christ was asked to order a brother to divide the inheritance, why he refused to do so. V, 1592. What Christ teaches by refusing to be a divider of an inheritance. V, 606. Christ Jesus was passing by when he was called upon, and he heals. V, 545. What it means that Jesus Christ was passing by. V, 544, 547, 1531.

Christ’s miracles. VII, 608. Some things were common to him and others; but it was proper to him to be born of a Virgin, to rise from the dead, and to ascend into heaven. II, 522. Unbelievers slanderously claim that Christ performed what he did by magical arts. V, 256, 447. Christ’s deeds also signified something, as though they were words. V, 486. Something other than what they displayed outwardly. V, 592. What words Christ’s deeds were. V, 582. Christ acted in the role of a reader. X, 140.

The purpose of each of Christ’s actions. V, 1615. In everything he did, Christ admonishes us how we ought to live here. V, 475. What Christ does comes to us; and what we do for his sake returns to us. V, 1475. What Christ did to heal a laboring human being. V, 543. Why he first chose the poor and uneducated, not the rich, not orators, and so forth. V, 537. Christ was wholly known both to the Apostles and to us; yet he was not wholly seen either by them or by us. V, 660. How our visions help one another. V, 660. By paying the tax, Christ foreshadowed that he would pay the death he did not owe. V, 845. By frightening the Jews, Christ recalled them to mercy toward the woman caught in adultery. II, 657, 658. When Christ hides himself, he takes account of our weakness; he does not diminish his power. III, 1774. Christ did not weep for the dead man, but for the death that man acquired for himself by sinning. V, 938.

Christ’s prayer on the mountain. V, 475. Christ prays for us as our Priest; he prays in us as our Head; he is prayed to by us as our God. IV, 1081. From the point at which Christ is man, he is also weak; from the point at which he is weak, he also prays. IV, 216. Christ as God the Word has no one to whom, or reason for which, he prays. IV, 216, 337. Christ prays and gives what he prays for. V, 1083. Christ prayed for all whom he redeemed, whether then living or destined to live afterward. III, 1917, 1919. He prayed in order to teach us to pray; he suffered in order to teach us to suffer; he rose in order to teach us to hope for resurrection. IV, 665. Christ’s prayer is an indication of our weakness. IV, 79. It is for the disciples’ edification. III, 1902.

Christ celebrated Passover before his Passion, on the evening when the first day of Unleavened Bread began. II, 993. How great was Christ’s humility when he washed the disciples’ feet. III, 1787. Christ washes our feet every day. III, 1789, 1790, 1794. Even before his death, Christ changed his flesh into whatever he wished. V, 1618. What Christ’s agitation signifies when Judas was about to depart. III, 1799. As the hour of the Passion approached, Christ was troubled by his own power. III, 1797, 1799. He was troubled because he wished to be. III, 1755. It was in his power to be affected in this way or that, or not to be affected. III, 1755. Christ was troubled for us. III, 1798, 1799. He was troubled so that we would not despair. V, 1399. How great a good we ought to hope for from participation in Christ’s divinity, whose agitation calms us and whose weakness strengthens us. III, 1798. In Christ our weakness is troubled. III, 1799. Christ transferred his members into himself and assumed their affection. III, 1769, 1799. When Christ was sad, he represented his weak members in himself. IV, 481, 1208, 1368; V, 193, 1398. Christ speaks as a sinner [Col. 0151], but in the person of his members. III, 422. Christ’s sadness was real, but was assumed voluntarily, like the flesh itself. IV, 1208. The cause of Christ’s sadness. IV, 858. As Christ was about to die, he was afraid, not in himself but in us, because of what he possessed that was ours. IV, 230. The human will in Christ recoiling from death. V, 1513. What Christ’s sweating blood from his whole body signifies. IV, 1817.

Christ’s betrayal, both by Judas and by God. V, 1383. What Judas sold, the Jew bought, and the Christian acquired. V, 1474. Christ patiently endured the betrayer. III, 1786. Christ’s patience toward Judas the betrayer. IV, 73, 135. Christ’s abandonment of Judas the betrayer is figured by David fleeing from the face of his son Absalom. IV, 72. Christ is said to have hoped in Judas because certain faithful people hoped in him. IV, 461. Christ handed himself over. III, 1802. He handed himself over to the Jews so that he might accomplish his will through those who did not know it. III, 1931. He who is the author of the cup of his Passion is himself the one who drinks it. III, 1932. Christ was handed over by the Father, by himself, and by Judas. II, 324; III, 2032; IV, 793. The wicked unjustly desired Christ’s death; God justly permitted it. IV, 745. Why Christ did not offer the other cheek to the one who struck him. III, 1934, 1935. Christ did not wish to punish the one who struck him, in order to teach us peace. III, 1934, 1935.

Christ’s Passion. VII, 585, 588, 591. Whatever the man Christ suffered, it cannot be said that God did not suffer it. IV, 1711. Christ is rightly called crucified God. II, 746. Since the whole Christ is Word, soul, and flesh, whatever concerns him as sad in the soul alone, crucified in the man alone, or buried in the flesh alone is referred to the whole Christ. V, 1068. When Christ was crucified, the darkening of the sun was truly prodigious. II, 917. Christ is rightly said to have died, although his divinity does not die. IV, 455. Because the sheep were hiding among thorns, Christ did not reach them to find them until he was crowned with the thorns of the Passion. V, 554. What Christ’s hands extended on the cross signify. IV, 755.

Christ was crucified so that no one would shrink from any kind of death that human beings regard as most disgraceful. VI, 187. He was crucified so that on the cross he might show the passing away of our old man. V, 1105. Why Christ was silent in the Passion. IV, 407. Christ teaching the rule of piety from the chair of the cross. V, 1430. He endured insults as an example for us. IV, 353, 1152. On the cross he taught us to be patient toward human tongues. IV, 551. The slanders of unbelievers, heretics, schismatics, and demons are defeated when the crucified Christ is considered. IV, 1578. Why Christ nodded his head at those who insulted him. IV, 1339. Christ’s steadfastness on the cross. IV, 1096. Christ did not wish to descend from the cross because he was teaching patience. III, 1397, 1675; IV, 462, 767, 882. On the cross he delayed displaying his power and made his mercy public. III, 1665. See “Cross.” Christ delayed descending from the cross so that he might rise from the tomb. III, 1487. Christ’s strength created you; Christ’s weakness recreated you. III, 1512.

How Christ was made sin and a curse. VIII, 297, 744. Christ did not deserve a curse, although he hung upon the wood. VIII, 166. It is no more an insult to Christ when Moses called him accursed than it is praise of Christ when the Manichaeans deny that he had mortal flesh. VIII, 298. Christ suffered not on account of the merit of iniquity but in the service of his mercy. VIII, 543. Christ’s Passion arose not from need but from mercy. VIII, 542, 547. Christ could be born without being sown, and suffer without being born. VIII, 485, 486, 487, 488. Christ’s love in the Passion. VI, 656. A medicine prepared from Christ’s blood for his killers. V, 946, 998.

Christ was beautiful, but became disfigured for the sake of his disfigured bride, in order to make her beautiful. V, 582. Christ prays for those who crucified him. V, 196, 524. From Christ’s disfigurement came the beauty of the Church. V, 259. He became dearer and sweeter to the bride the more disfigured he became. V, 259. In order to make the soul beautiful, he became disfigured. IV, 1338. Christ is both disfigured and beautiful. V, 181. How. V, 766. Christ’s disfigurement is our beauty. V, 181. Christ possessed beauty even on the cross. IV, 495. Christ appeared disfigured to those by whom he suffered. IV, 1681. The shameful appearance of the crucified one gave birth to the beauty of the resurrection. V, 1184. Christ was therefore dishonored and crucified here in order to teach us to despise the good things of this age more than to love them. II, 993. A certain heresy said that divinity suffered in Christ when his flesh was fastened to the cross. VIII, 44. Christ spoke in the person of his members: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” II, 544, 550; IV, 567, 623, 693, 882. And in the person of the martyrs. II, 550. Christ often speaks in the person of the Church. II, 545. In his Passion Christ, while praying, bore our weakness. II, 545; IV, 172. Christ cried out in the Passion but was not rescued. IV, 173. Christ was forsaken not so that we might be foolish, but so that we might become wise. II, 550. In Christ the Church suffered, and in the Church Christ suffered. II, 545.

Christ’s side was opened so that all might enter through it. VI, [Col. 0152] 704. Christ is the door; the entrance was opened when his side was pierced. V, 1415. From it water and blood flowed forth: in the one is your cleansing, in the other your redemption. V, 1415. Christ’s spouse, the Church, was formed from the side of him who slept on the cross. IV, 1324, 1381, 1672, 1684, 1785. When Christ’s side was opened, the purse containing the price of our redemption was poured out. V, 1454, 1473. Christ’s side was pierced by a lance, and our price flowed forth. V, 1064. If Christ’s blood had not been poured out, the world would not have been redeemed. V, 683. Christ blotted out every sin with his blood. V, 824. He made an eye-salve for us from his blood. V, 753. The blood and water issuing from Christ’s side are the two sacraments of the Church. IV, 461, 1785; VI, 689, 696. When that cluster of grapes was pressed, that flowed forth from which the inebriating and most glorious cup came. IV, 649. Christ’s blood on earth has a mighty voice. VIII, 259.

Christ’s death was voluntary. VII, 520. Spontaneous. VIII, 898. Christ suffered and died by power and will, not by necessity. IV, 1104; V, 1083; X, 256. And this is our price, by which he redeemed us through death. X, 256. Inasmuch as he was human, God died; and inasmuch as he was God, the human being was raised. IV, 1711. Christ accepted death by the will of obedience. X, 180, 182. If he had not died, Christ could not have been Christ. V, 1121. Christ became obedient for us. VIII, 781. In Christ there are eternity and, at the same time, the humility of death. III, 1775.

Christ, the Son of God, is life in himself: how, then, did he die? V, 710, 1061. Christ died when the flesh died. III, 1817. From where Christ’s mortality came. V, 1607. Mortality was his by condescension, not by nature. V, 1110. The mortality of the flesh, arising from human sin, was also effected in Christ. VIII, 297. Christ was mortal not from his own substance but from ours; so we are immortal not from our own substance but from his. IV, 1906. Christ’s death killed death. III, 1490. The dead Christ killed death. V, 1114. By accepting death Christ overcame it. X, 198.

Christ died when he wished. III, 1638, 1673, 1674, 1675, 1739. And because he wished it. III, 304, 1674, 1736; V, 54. Christ suffered what he wished to suffer, and when he wished to suffer it. III, 1475, 1744, 1770. Christ ought not to have died except when the proper time had come. III, 1457. In the sixth age of the world he restored the human being whom he had formed on the sixth day. IV, 1182. “The hour of Christ,” “the time of Christ”: how it should be understood. III, 1674. The time of Christ’s death. VII, 619. Some mistakenly thought that Christ suffered at the age of forty-six. III, 55. The Evangelists are reconciled concerning the hour at which Christ was crucified. IV, 763.

Whether it may rightly be inferred from Christ’s having died that he was a human being. VIII, 479, 482. Who placed the soul in Christ’s death, and what soul. III, 1737. The Word did not place a soul in Christ’s death. III, 1738. Nor did Christ’s soul place itself. III, 1738. How Christ’s flesh itself placed the soul. III, 1738. How Christ himself placed it. III, 1739.

Christ’s contest with the devil in his passion. VI, 664. Christ conquered the devil by the truth of justice, not by force of power. VI, 255. Christ, having been wounded, wounded the devil. IV, 1126. By Christ’s death, as by his own trophy, the devil was defeated. V, 1209. From his cross, to which he was nailed, Christ killed the devil; and from that cross he is our king. IV, 1952.

Christ killed death, bound the bond, and took captivity captive. IV, 1850. If he had not been killed, death would not have died. V, 1209. He alone can say that he suffered here without cause. IV, 1936. By enduring punishment without guilt, he dissolved both guilt and punishment. V, 754, 1131. Unless he paid what he did not owe, he would never have freed us from what we owed. V, 845. He was able to redeem who could not sell himself. IV, 1703. Christ was the most perfect victim for cleansing our faults. VIII, 901. Christ was a priest who, finding nothing pure in the world to offer, offered himself. IV, 1733.

Christ’s death was foretold in the sacred Scriptures. VII, 552, 553. Christ’s death was signified in the blessing of Judah. VII, 520. A prophecy concerning Christ’s being lifted up on the cross. III, 776. Christ’s death was prefigured by the serpent lifted up in the desert. X, 145. How Moses asserted that Christ’s death would be real. VIII, 297, 298, 299. Christ’s passion was prefigured by Noah’s nakedness. VII, 478. By the red heifer. III, 733. Christ’s passion was the evening sacrifice. IV, 1818. The sacrifice of a sheep was a figure of Christ’s passion. VI, 335. Christ offered himself as the sacrifice in place of all sacrifices. IV, 71. Christ’s passion was prophesied in the Book of Wisdom. VII, 554. Christ’s passion is treated throughout Psalm 63. IV, 760. Christ’s passion was foretold in the Psalm of dedication. V, 1473.

The mysteries and stages of Christ’s passion are explained. V, 1084. The sacrament of Christ’s passion and resurrection. V, 1104. Christ’s death had one purpose, and his resurrection another. V, 1120. Christ’s passion was his exaltation. III, 1773. Christ’s passion is our purification. III, 1787. Christ’s passion is a distinction between spiritual and carnal goods, temporal and eternal. III, 733. The fruit of Christ’s passion. VI, 644, 645, 656.

Why Christ accepted death. X, 1181. Christ, the Son of God, was crucified and died for us. V, 1069, 1074, 1089. Christ’s blood was poured out for our redemption. V, 1473, 1513. Neither death nor life was owed to us by Christ. V, 1110. Christ’s death, though not owed, freed those liable to death. VIII, 1027, 1028. From where Christ received the liability to die. III, 422. How he died to sin. X, 1241. How fittingly Christ’s death was chosen, so that we might be justified in his blood. VIII, 1030. In dying for the ungodly, Christ may have companions in endurance, though in the cause he can have none. X, 1215. Christ could therefore release sins by dying because he both died and did not die for his own sin. VII, 301.

The whole world was redeemed by Christ’s blood. IV, 177, 179, 1236. Christ bought brothers for himself with his blood; rejected, he proved them accepted; sold, he redeemed them; insulted, he honored them; killed, he gave them life. V, 935. Christ redeemed all captives. IV, 1697. The apostolic statement is both authoritative and true, because Christ is the Savior of all human beings. V, 1322. The one redeemed by Christ’s blood does not perish. V, 1253. He bought the whole, who paid so great a price. IV, 1254. According to Peter, he seems to have suffered only for those who follow in his footsteps. V, 1396. Christ suffered for all. V, 1396. Christ’s blood is the price for slaves, and a pledge for the bride. IV, 1634. Christ’s blood was poured out for the forgiveness of all sins in such a way that it could also blot out the very sin by which it was poured out. III, 1863. Christ’s death is like the forgiveness of sin. VI, 256. The claim that Christ died for nothing follows from the Pelagian heresy. II, 768. Christ conquered the world for us not with an armed soldier but with a mocked cross. IV, 760. Christ is sacrificed for us daily by the very remembrance of the Savior’s benefit. IV, 966. Christ dies for each person when that person becomes a participant in his death through baptism. X, 828. Christ’s blood is salvation for one who wills it, punishment for one who does not. V, 1515. Christ was killed so that fear might be changed into love. IV, 1167. Christ wished to die so that we would not fear this death, but rather that death from which he freed us through this one. IV, 831. Christ removed every fear from the martyrs not only by word but also by example. IV, 866. After Christ passed through tribulations, the way was made clear by his passage. IV, 720. Christ wished to suffer in order to console those who suffer. IV, 1176. Through Christ’s passion we are taught to seek eternal happiness. II, 542, 548. Christ’s death is the pledge of the life given to us by him. V, 1468. In Christ, through patience, the human being acquired heaven, and God benefited believers through the human being. IV, 121. What Christ did is greater than what he promised; it is more incredible that the eternal one died than that a mortal should live forever. IV, 1942. Christ gave his death to the ungodly; what does he reserve for the righteous except his life? IV, 1942. Christ came to be despised and honored, confessed and denied, and so forth. III, 1660. His name was sown through Christ’s death. IV, 453. The grain fell in one small place, but produced abundant fruit. IV, 866, 1377. Christ was preached to us in weakness so that we might choose his reproach all the more. IV, 623. Christ is to be imitated by us not in the power of miracles but in endurance of sufferings. IV, 1149. Participation in Christ’s sufferings through love. V, 923. Christ’s sufferings, not pleasures, are to be imitated by the Christian. V, 275. Why one should not be ashamed of Christ’s death. V, 1278, 1279. Christ’s appearance, against the serpent’s bite, is metaphorically applied to the Pelagian heresy. X, 1138. How the devil leads his own into contempt for Christ’s death. VIII, 900. Why there is mention of a new tomb in connection with Christ’s burial. VI, 187. God’s resting from his works on the seventh day was intended to foretell the day on which Christ would rest in the tomb. III, 305. Only Christ’s flesh lies there, and I say, “Our Lord,” because I behold the garment and adore the one clothed in it. V, 1062.

Christ descended to the underworld. II, 710, 711, 715. Why. VII, 541. Christ was in the underworld according to his soul. II, 833. Whether Christ descended to the place of punishments. II, 834. Christ descended as far as the places where sinners are tormented. III, 481. In the underworld Christ helped some. V, 436. He released some from torments. II, 834; III, 481. A certain heresy holds that, when Christ descended to the underworld, the unbelievers believed and thereafter all were freed. VIII, 45. Some think that those whom Christ freed from the underworld were people who had not heard the Gospel. II, 714. Others say poets and orators who exposed false gods to ridicule; others, pagans of praiseworthy life. II, 710. It is rash to define whom he freed from the underworld. III, 1697. Christ, penetrating the regions below and rising from there victorious over death, performed a great miracle for the dead. IV, 1115. How Christ was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights. III, 87.

Christ’s resurrection. VI, 187; VII, 584, 587, 592. The Manichaeans say that Christ’s resurrection was imaginary. VIII, 488, 489. Christ’s resurrection ought not to have been long delayed. II, 548. Nor should his flesh have been reserved for the final resurrection. [Col. 0154] II, 554. Christ raised himself, and the Father raised him. V, 1399. He was raised by the Father as a human being, and raised himself as God. IV, 452, 666, 1442. Christ died by power and rose by power. V, 1399. On the cross Christ displayed patience; in the resurrection, power. VI, 665. Christ’s body rose in the same condition in which it had been placed in the tomb. VI, 304. Christ’s resurrection was a unique sign, which existed in him alone. IV, 791. That one rose, never again to die. IV, 1672. No one before Christ rose to eternal life. IV, 1642, 1701. How Christ, after the resurrection, is understood to have been wholly God. I, 622. Faith believes that Christ entered through closed doors after the resurrection and, at his birth, came forth through his mother’s incorrupt womb. V, 1010. Unbelievers deny both. V, 1010. There is still a report among the Jews that Christ was taken from the tomb by the disciples. V, 261. The soldiers’ vanity selling vanity to vanity. V, 261. Why his linen cloths and the napkin were found in the tomb. VI, 60.

Why Christ’s resurrection was first announced to men by women. V, 266, 1108. Christ appears to Magdalene. V, 1148, 1154. A difficulty in Christ’s words to Magdalene. V, 1143, 1148, 1151, 1154. Christ enters to the disciples through closed doors. V, 1157. The disciples are rebuked for thinking that they saw a spirit. V, 1122, 1123. When Christ rose, the glory in his body should be believed to have been hidden from the disciples’ eyes rather than absent. VII, 781. Christ joins the disciples on the road. V, 1118. Christ is recognized in the breaking of bread. V, 1111, 1127. Why Christ preserved the scars in his body. V, 539, 645, 658, 1140; VI, 647. He preserved the scars in his body to heal the wound of doubt in the heart. IV, 1134. After the resurrection Christ showed scars, not wounds, to those who doubted. II, 372. Those scars which Christ showed after the resurrection to those who doubted were not fictitious. II, 372. Why Christ suffered in the sight of all but did not rise in the sight of all. II, 548. How Christ was recognized and not recognized after the resurrection. II, 643. Christ may rightly be said to have pretended. V, 556. It was a figurative fiction, not a deceptive one. V, 558. The claim that Christ could neither be deceived nor lie is vigorously defended. V, 737. After the resurrection Christ lived among his disciples so that they might be strengthened in faith. V, 1212. Why Christ spent forty days with his disciples after the resurrection. V, 1211, 1216. After the resurrection Christ took food and drink. VII, 395. After the resurrection Christ ate by power and love, not by necessity. V, 659, 1360. After the resurrection Christ was not subject to the need of hunger and thirst. III, 1806. Christ’s resurrection showed that nothing belonging to human nature perishes. III, 135. Some have said that, through Christ’s death, a resurrection was granted to the righteous of the kind promised to us at the end. II, 711. Christ’s birth and resurrection were his own unique and singular miracles. VII, 314.

Christ’s death and resurrection were prefigured in Abel and Seth. VII, 461. The burning of the red heifer was a sign of Christ’s resurrection. III, 734. Amos foretold Christ’s resurrection. VII, 584. Hosea did so as well. VII, 584. Christ’s resurrection was the glorification of the Father and the Son. III, 1903. The one death and resurrection of Christ’s body corresponds, for our salvation, to our twofold death and to the resurrection of body and soul. VIII, 889, 890, 891. Christ’s cross, burial, and resurrection are figures of the Christian life. VI, 257. Christ’s resurrection is the hope of our resurrection. IV, 1700. Christ’s resurrection circumcised us. III, 1634; V, 1105. Christ’s death is for us so that we may not fear; his resurrection is for hope. III, 422. By his death and resurrection Christ taught what we should not fear and what we should hope for. IV, 899. By his passion Christ showed what we ought to endure for the truth, and by his resurrection what we ought to hope for in eternity. VII, 612. By being born Christ won love; by dying and rising again he drove out fear. VIII, 89. We ought to place faith, hope, and love in Christ’s resurrection. III, 734. Christ lives in those who struggle against desires. X, 866. Faith in Christ’s resurrection distinguishes Christians. V, 1075, 1133. This is truly to wish to kill Christ: to extinguish the name of his resurrection. IV, 694.

Why Christ withdrew his presence from the world after his resurrection. X, 182. Christ withdrew bodily so that faith might be built up. V, 1119. So that, in the absence of the flesh, his divinity might be contemplated. V, 1214. Christ’s humanity, to which they clung with human affection, had to be taken away from the disciples’ eyes. V, 1238. Christ ascended so that the disciples would not remain attached to the flesh. V, 1212. Why the Holy Spirit could not come unless Christ departed. V, 1238. Christ’s resurrection and ascension. V, 1070. Christ’s two glorifications. V, 1222. Christ’s glorification is recognized in the resurrection and ascension into heaven. III, 595. The glorification resulting from Christ’s victory was completed by the resurrection and ascension. V, 1209.

Christ’s ascension into heaven. VI, 187. Christ ascended into heaven with his body. V, 1210. How the one Christ ascended into heaven. III, 1488; V, 570, 780, 1341; X, [Col. 0155] 144. For how many people Christ has not yet ascended. V, 1155. Christ’s resurrection and his ascension into heaven with his body are proved credible. VII, 755. And it is shown that they are now believed. VII, 756. Many miracles bore witness to Christ’s ascension. VII, 760. Christ’s ascension was a great and salutary miracle. VII, 760. Christ descended to us out of mercy and ascended to the Father through justice. V, 789. The ascension of Christ the Lord should be celebrated in such a way that we ascend with him. V, 1202. The Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven support our faith. III, 24. In Christ’s glorification sins are dissolved and abolished. III, 594. Christ ascended into heaven so that, as head, he might help from above the members laboring on earth. V, 932. Whoever wishes to ascend into heaven must be united to Christ. IV, 1630. As Christ ascends, he raises us, to whom he descended when we had fallen. IV, 203. Christ’s passage, in his passion and resurrection, from this mortal life to another, immortal life is commended. II, 205. In the evening the Lord was on the cross, in the morning in the resurrection, at midday in the ascension. IV, 640. Christ was the pelican in his birth, the night-raven in his death, and the sparrow in his resurrection. IV, 1300. How Christ goes to prepare dwelling-places that already existed in the Father’s house. III, 1814. The last words of Christ ascending into heaven should be highly valued. III, 2061. Christ’s last words were despised by schismatics. V, 1222. The head, about to ascend into heaven, commended the members on earth and departed. III, 2060. The prophecy of Christ’s ascension. V, 1208. The footprints of Christ on the Mount of Olives. III, 1735. Christ’s birth, resurrection, and ascension are perhaps a more powerful work than the world. II, 522.

The Seleucians assert that Christ did not take flesh to the right hand of the Father, but that it could be in the sun. VIII, 41, 42. The pagans did not understand how an earthly body could be in heaven. VI, 188. Christ’s very body was raised into heaven. VI, 304. It is pointless to ask how the Lord’s body is in heaven. VI, 188. How Christ is now believed to be in heaven. II, 833. Christ’s body is in heaven as it was on earth when he ascended into heaven. II, 942. Christ’s body is not subject to corruption. II, 943, 945.

Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father. V, 1075. As a human being Christ sits at the Father’s right hand; as God he is wholly everywhere. VI, 658. How Christ’s sitting at the Father’s right hand should be understood. VI, 188, 304. Insofar as he is God, Christ is everywhere; insofar as he is human, he is in a particular place. II, 834, 836. Christ is nowhere absent. III, 483. Christ is everywhere. V, 1341. Wholly everywhere. V, 1264. As God he is wholly everywhere at once. V, 1264. How Christ changed place and did not change place. V, 547. Christ’s threefold presence. V, 1602. Christ is both here and above. V, 683, 685. Scripture recognizes Christ as both like and unlike Moses. VIII, 325, 326.

Christ commanded something greater than what was commanded in the Old Testament. VIII, 129, 130. Christ neither wished to turn any Jew away from his God nor violated any of the commandments given through Moses. VI, 349, 350. Christ did nothing by force but everything by persuasion and admonition. III, 135. How this should be understood. I, 604. Christ brought truth as teacher, gentleness as liberator, and justice as judge. III, 1648, 1649. Christ’s teaching is not hostile to the state. II, 532, 533. Christ’s discipline drives from the mind the inflated and turbulent desire for things beyond our control. II, 485.

Christ is both our wisdom and our knowledge. VIII, 1034. In what sense Christ is said not to know the day and hour of judgment. VIII, 312.

Christ is both our example and our help. V, 608. Christ became an example for angels and human beings. III, 1069. Christ is the singular example of obedience. III, 385. Christ’s example would not suffice unless the Holy Spirit were sent. III, 1864. Christ is proposed for imitation to the human being who had imitated the devil. I, 1308. Imitation of Christ. V, 784, 1447; VI, 26. Whether we can imitate Christ. X, 1588. To what extent we imitate Christ. X, 1390. We should not excuse ourselves on account of Christ’s excellence, as though we should not strive to imitate him according to our measure. X, 1390. The example of perfection in Christ is to be imitated in such a way that we strive and desire not to have desires. X, 1373. We must all follow Christ. V, 1395. Where and by what way Christ is to be followed. V, 586. In what ways it is permissible to follow Christ apart from martyrdom. V, 1396. The various degrees of those who follow Christ, and what it means for them to look back. V, 588. Why one who professes that he will follow Christ is rejected. V, 602, 603. Another called by Christ. V, 603. Someone called by him, wishing to delay because of carnal affection, is urged onward. V, 603. A third called by him, who looks back toward his own people, is blamed. V, 604. Christ hates the one who remains behind, turns back, or wanders away. VI, 681. We ought to follow Christ, not precede him. IV, 449. Whoever wishes to live by his own counsel wishes, as it were, to precede Christ. IV, 868.

Christ’s yoke is gentle. II, 485. Christ’s yoke is light. II, 200.

Christ is king and priest. VI, 48. Christ was foretold as king and priest throughout the entire arrangement of the Old Testament. [Col. 0156] VIII, 290, 370. Christ’s priesthood and kingship were foretold in Samuel and David. VIII, 271. Christ is king of the blessed lights. VIII, 579, 580. Christ is king of angels and human beings. VI, 336. By what title Christ is King of Israel. III, 1765. Christ the truest Lord. IV, 1809. Melchizedek prefigured Christ’s priesthood. II, 769. Christ is sacrifice and priest. III, 1695; IV, 200, 1733. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews indicates that Christ’s priesthood was prefigured in Melchizedek and places it above the Levitical priesthood. X, 1552. Through Melchizedek, Christ’s priesthood is distinguished from the priesthood of Levi. III, 423. Christ is the priest by whom we appease God. VII, 280. Christ is priest and sacrifice both in the human being and according to the human nature he assumed. VII, 298, 313. Christ is victor and victim, priest and sacrifice. I, 808. Christ, priest and victim, fulfilled the sacrifice of praise. VIII, 57. Christ alone is the chief of priests, who did not need to offer sacrifice for his own sins. X, 162. Christ, in the form of a servant, preferred to offer sacrifice rather than receive it, so that no one would think that sacrifice ought to be offered to any creature. V, 1252; VII, 298. Christ at the right hand of the Father is our priest. IX, 59.

Christ is sacrificed daily in the sacrament. II, 364. The sacrifice of Christ’s body is the sacrament of the faithful. II, 563, 569. Christ’s sacrifice is offered in the Church throughout the whole world. VI, 49. Through the sacrament of his body and blood Christ gives himself to human beings as food. III, 879. From the altar the holy victim is distributed, by which the bond that stood against us has been erased. I, 778. Receiving the flesh and blood is necessary for possessing life. X, 1268. Christ’s blood intoxicates the mind so that it forgets the love of the world. VI, 696. The sacrament of Christ’s body is far from the hearts of the proud wise. II, 840. When Christ’s blood has been received, all nations respond, “Amen.” VIII, 259. Those who do not imitate Christ merely adore and are not nourished by his body and blood. II, 567. The rich of the earth are not nourished by Christ’s body and blood. II, 567. Infants who have not eaten Christ’s flesh will not attain eternal life, according to Innocentius. 785, 826. Christ’s blood was prefigured by the ancient sacrifices. X, 809. All the sacrifices of the Law and the prophets were shadows of Christ’s sacrifice. VI, 249. The New Testament was dedicated in Christ’s blood. X, 328. You possess Christ in the present through faith, in the present through the sacrament of baptism, and in the present through the food and drink of the altar. III, 1763. To eat the Lord’s body and drink his blood is to remain in him. III, 1614, 1616, 1618. To believe in Christ is to eat the living bread. III, 1601, 1607.

Christ’s body is twofold. III, 82. Christ is spoken of in three ways in Scripture. V, 1485, 1500. The first way is when he is proclaimed as God. V, 1485. The second is when he is presented as God and human being. V, 1486. The third is when he is understood as head and body. V, 1486. Christ is head and body. V, 754, X, 144, 145. Everything announced about Christ concerns the head and the body. IX, 392, 395. Christ and his members are one Christ. III, 1488; V, 570, 755, 789, 1341, 1500. Christ is above in himself and below in his own people. V, 683, 685. Christ is sometimes spoken of as the head and sometimes as the whole body of the Church. VI, 79. Christ is the head of the Church. V, 265. The head of the Church, of all the righteous and of the angels. IV, 385, 749, 786, 1159. Christ’s very flesh is the head of the Church. IV, 1613. When the Church is joined to his flesh, Christ becomes whole, head and body. III, 1979. Christ and the Church, head and body, are one human being, one Christ. IV, 161, 232, 250, 453, 629, 662, 693, 695, 723, 730, 761, 866, 948, 1082, 1156, 1679, 1784, 1817, 1819, 1846. Christ in his entirety, together with his members, exists for the sake of the Church. X, 1001. Christ’s substance is his people. VII, 544. Christ’s body is the Catholic Church alone. II, 815. It was gathered at the beginning through humility, not power. II, 757. Christ strengthened the Church with authority and armed it with reason. II, 448. Christ is whole in the body and in the head. III, 1622. Christ is in his members. III, 1622. “See how great is the grace by which we reach God, since he himself willed to be one with us who is one with the Father.” IV, 1846. Christ is one with the Father in one way and one with us in another. V, 789. He who did not disdain to assume us into himself did not disdain to transform us into himself and to speak in our words. IV, 230, 231. He is with us on earth through divinity, goodness, and unity; we are with him in heaven through faith, hope, and love. IV, 205, 1630. Here Christ gives birth and suffers in his members. IV, 613. Christ resides as head in heaven and labors as feet and body on earth. IV, 1105, 1163, 1167, 1178, 1846. Christ speaks from heaven when his members are trampled on earth. III, 2060. Christ usually transfers to himself the person of his members. VII, 552. It is in the person of his members that he says he has ceased hoping in God. IV, 847. He is said to receive in his members the gifts that his members receive. IV, 829, 830. Christ as a whole is to receive the Father’s inheritance; he has not yet received it. V, 154. We suffered in Christ, and he suffers in us; we rose in him, and he rises in us. [Col. 0157] IV, 749. A prophecy concerning Christ the head is applied to us, his members. V, 1474. In the prophets Christ speaks now in the person of his members, now in his own person. IV, 79, 436. Christ is always the origin, root, and head of the Christian. IX, 248, 249, 260, 374, 375, 382. Christ is the creator and head of Christians. IX, 576, 577. Christ makes a body for himself from all of us as members. VI, 712. We have become not merely Christians but Christ. III, 1568.

How we become Christ’s members. V, 1341. Not everyone passes over to Christ, but those from whom the veil is removed. VIII, 655. No one passes into Christ’s body unless he has been stripped of carnal garments. III, 1325. Christ cannot be understood by one who has despised the nourishment of milk from the apostolic and prophetic breasts. VIII, 279. No one becomes a member of Christ except either through baptism in Christ or through death for Christ. X, 480. Who belong to Christ’s mystical body and who do not. II, 839. What it means to come to Christ. X, 888. To come to Christ is to believe. X, 553. Christ is to be conceived through faith and eaten through works. V, 1012. Faith in the incarnation of the Son of God. VI, 300.

Christ is the distinctive foundation of the Catholic faith. VI, 233. Faith in Christ is necessary for salvation. X, 398, 400. See Faith. No one has ever belonged to the spiritual Jerusalem unless Christ was revealed to that person. V, 610. Christ is held through faith. III, 1759. Everyone, even heretics, teaches that Christ must be believed. VIII, 86. To believe in Christ is God’s gift. X, 972. No one comes to Christ unless it has been given to him, and this is given to the predestined. X, 1014. Knowledge of Christ is God’s gift, granted to those whom he wished and when he wished. VII, 313.

Knowledge and worship of Christ come from his grace. III, 648. Eminent knowledge of Christ will not exist except in the other life. X, 602. Not all the apostles saw Christ, according to Ambrose. II, 604, 610. Whoever knew the breadth, length, height, depth, and the surpassing knowledge of Christ’s love saw both Christ and the Father, according to Ambrose. II, 604.

Through faith in Christ the righteous of ancient times could also be cleansed. VII, 302. Some of Christ’s members preceded the advent of Christ’s incarnation. IV, 731. The ancient fathers were called Christ’s even before there was an anointing, perhaps because they were already Christians. IV, 1395.

Christ exists among heretics in name only. VI, 233. The prophecy concerning Christ and the Jews who would believe in Christ is the promise made to Moses concerning the vision of God. III, 648, 649, 650. A prophecy concerning the blessing that Christ would give to the new people. III, 774. Christ’s preaching among all nations is Jacob’s blessing. VII, 513. The world’s belief in Christ was the work of divine power, not of human persuasion. VII, 759. Christ’s righteousness cannot benefit those who do not believe. X, 152. No one can be righteous as long as he is separated from the unity of Christ’s body. II, 811, 815. Christ rejoices in unity. VI, 712.

The unity of Christ’s body is commended by our sacrifice. II, 839. The gathering of the saints to Christ is Christ’s perfect stature. IV, 227. Christ’s bones, heart, belly, and tongue are allegorical. IV, 175. Christ’s heart is sacred Scripture. II, 554; IV, 175. The tongue signifies the preachers of the Gospel. II, 554. His garments signify his sacraments. IV, 176. The apostles. V, 486. The Church. V, 490. What Christ’s garment, shining like snow on the mountain, signified. IV, 1932. The seamless garment signifies love, which cannot be divided. V, 149.

Christ is bridegroom and giant, beautiful and strong. V, 1662. Christ is the bridegroom. III, 820; IV, 333, 495. When you hear “Christ,” do not separate the bridegroom from the bride. IV, 333. Christ and the Church are one body. X, 1001. Christ and the Church are sometimes indicated as one person. III, 82. Christ and the Church are the true seed of Abraham. III, 789. Christ’s body and the Church, his bride. See Church. Christ is bridegroom and bride. IV, 1295. The bridegroom is in the head, the bride in the body. V, 571. Christ left father and mother to cling to his wife. VIII, 258. How this should be understood. IV, 501, 1295; V, 570. The statement that Christ left father and mother and clung to his wife, rightly understood. III, 215.

Christ loved his bride while she was still ugly. IV, 495. Christ loves sinners so that they may not always remain sinners. V, 947. Christ loved nothing in us except God. III, 1809. The bride’s affection for Christ. V, 766. How the words of Christ’s bride are to be understood. V, 766.

Christ is to be loved. V, 727. He is to be loved above all things. IV, 222. The devout love Christ freely; the ungodly hate him without cause. IV, 1432. Those who love Christ must hate what he hates. IV, 1248, 1249. What it means to have Christ as one’s foundation. VI, 155, 264. To have Christ as one’s foundation is to place nothing before him. VII, 743. When Christ crucified is loved, love itself is loved. IV, 1681. Elijah will teach the Jews love for Christ. VII, 704. Christ is the life of hearts. II, 566.

Christ’s first and second advents. III, 1327, 1406, 1624, 1675. Christ came first to save and later to judge. [Col. 0158] III, 1664, 1665. One advent of Christ is hidden, the other manifest. V, 124, 128. Christ’s advent for judgment. VI, 188. Christ’s advent for judgment was foretold. V, 1219. Christ is preached as crucified, humbled, and judged so that he may come exalted, come alive in power, and come to judge. IV, 1262. It is expressed not so much in the Old Testament as in the New that Christ the judge will come from heaven. VII, 705. Where it is read that God will come to execute judgment, Christ is to be understood. VII, 707. As a human being Christ received the power to execute judgment. III, 1580; VIII, 222. Insofar as he is the Son of Man, Christ received the power to execute judgment from the Father, from himself, and from the Holy Spirit. VIII, 691. He will judge the whole world because he paid the price for the whole world. IV, 1236. Everyone of every order will give an account to Christ. II, 1028. See Advent. What Christ’s final advent will be like. V, 1369.

What Christ will be like when he comes. VI, 647, 658. The judge will come in visible form. V, 1070. Christ will be the future judge in the form of a servant. V, 711. Christ will come in human form to judge. IV, 1096; VIII, 691. As a human being Christ will judge human beings. III, 1553. When Christ judges, the form of a servant will be seen, while the form of God will remain hidden. III, 1553; VIII, 222. The ungodly will see Christ in the form of a servant, the righteous in the form of God. X, 223. When Christ was being judged, he was teaching so that he might judge those whom he had taught. IV, 291. Christ will judge with great power because he was judged with great humility. IV, 408. At the judgment he will appear like fire, for the punishment of the ungodly and as light for the righteous. IV, 814. Christ is the defender of the penitent, the petitioner for pardon on behalf of the confessing, and the judge of the innocent. IV, 809. Who are the living and the dead whom he will judge. VI, 188. Christ is now silent with respect to judgment, but not silent with respect to commandment. III, 1406. Now he is silent about vengeance, but not silent about admonition. IV, 568.

Christ not to be feared as judge, because he is an advocate. IV, 568. We ought not merely to await Christ’s coming with confidence, but also to desire it. IV, 1913. On awaiting and desiring the coming of Christ the Lord. V, 632, 1369. His second coming is called: “He will come, the Desired One.” V, 330. It is shameful for a Christian not to desire Christ’s coming. V, 1610. For one who loves Christ, the only punishment is to be without him. V, 766. When Christ’s coming is to occur cannot be known. II, 907, 908. The disciples’ inquiry concerning the time of Christ’s future coming. V, 1219. Christ’s answer concerning his coming. V, 1219.

Christ was not recognized by the Jews. IV, 304. Why God was not recognized in the flesh. III, 2007. Christ’s flesh is the cloud by which the world’s light is tempered, not obscured. III, 1653. Christ was not recognized by the Jews because the Lord’s hand lay heavily upon them. IV, 1789. The Jews alone do not recognize Christ in the Scriptures, although the Scriptures were made on his account. IV, 1779.

The Jews believe that Christ will come, but not that he will die. VII, 553. The Jews expected temporal goods in Christ. II, 546. The Jews are convicted that Christ has already come, both by the faith of the nations and by what has taken place among the Jewish people themselves. VIII, 278. Christ is proved to be the Messiah against the Jews. V, 567. From that very city where they killed him, all were expelled. IV, 1723. Concerning Christ’s coming: as great as the distance between the angels’ proclamation and the demons’ confession, so great is the distance between the authority of the Prophets and the curiosity of the sacrilegious. VIII, 290. Heretics agree in this: they deny that Christ came in the flesh. V, 988. To doubt that Christ came in the flesh is common equally to bad Catholics and to heretics. V, 992. Christ’s coming became as salutary for believers as it became destructive for unbelievers. III, 1856.

Why Christ came, and what benefit he brought to the human race, is explained against the complaints of the pagans. IV, 1766. The benefits bestowed upon us through Christ’s coming. V, 894. The incarnation of Christ the Son of God: how great a grace it is. V, 1314. Christ’s incarnation is the beginning of our cleansing. VII, 301. Christ took upon himself our two evils, in order to give us his two goods. V, 1279. He shared our evils with us, in order to give us his goods. V, 680, 1598. Christ bound the devil by the sacrament of his incarnation. IV, 821. The incarnate Word is an eye-salve. III, 1656, 1660. In what sense Christ was sent only to the Israelites. V, 483. God sent Christ, his Son, on behalf of those foreknown and predestined, to be called, justified, and glorified. V, 845. Christ’s good works benefited only the predestined for eternal salvation. IV, 1115. Who are meant by those given to Christ. X, 928. In what sense it is said, “All shall be made alive in Christ.” VII, 398. How fitting was the manner of liberating humanity through the incarnation and passion of the Son of God. VI, 297.

Christ is the one mediator between God and human beings. I, 601; IV, 216, 1159, 1741; V, 310, 503, 680, 1332, 1607; VII, 268. Christ is the Word with God, flesh among us, and the Word made flesh between God and us. III, 385. See Word. He himself is the mediator in the middle; had he not come, the way of mercy would have perished. IV, 1383. Jesus Christ is the one mediator between God and human beings, in both the Old and the New Testament. X, 399, 400. [Col. 0159] No other mediators are to be sought apart from Christ. VII, 269. How Christ became mediator. VII, 302. What is required for this mediation. VII, 268, 271. Through what Christ is mediator. X, 402. Christ is mediator not because he is God, but because he is human. III, 1843; IV, 1383; VII, 269. Christ as human being: redeemer, mediator, head of the Church, and so forth. III, 1811. Insofar as Christ is human, he is mediator; insofar as he is the Word, he is not “in the middle,” because he is equal to God. I, 808. He is truly mediator: mortal with human beings, righteous with God. I, 808.

Christ is the way, the truth, and the life. III, 33, 1578, 1816. Christ is the truth, even when he is proclaimed without truthfulness. III, 118. Christ, remaining with the Father, was truth and life; by clothing himself with flesh, he became the way. III, 1656. Christ is our way. VI, 681. The only way to salvation. I, 760; II, 637. Christ’s incarnation is the universal way for the soul’s liberation. VII, 313. The only most secure way to God. VII, 318. Christ became our way. III, 25, 313. The way by which we go. III, 1852. Christ is the way, so that by walking in him we may proceed securely. IV, 806, 807, 1137. Christ made himself the way for us into heaven. VI, 339. Christ made himself the great road and pathway by which he leads us to our homeland. V, 91. Christ is the way to the homeland, to life, and to truth. V, 685, 777, 778, 780, 952, 1405. Christ is guide, way, and homeland: he leads us as guide, leads us in himself as the way, and brings us to himself as the homeland. IV, 1640. Christ is king of the city toward which we journey; he himself made himself the way by which we might reach the city. IV, 1101. In the form of a servant Christ paved the way; in the form of God he established the homeland. V, 571, 573. He himself is the homeland to which we go; he himself is the way by which we go. V, 573, 685. Through the flesh Christ became the way for himself and for us by which we might return. III, 1817. Through Christ we go to Christ and to the Father. III, 1816. Through the human Christ you proceed toward the divine Christ. V, 1206. Christ’s humanity is the way to his divinity. III, 1702; V, 1217. By becoming a participant in our humanity, Christ provided a concise means for our participation in his divinity. VII, 269. By forgiving sins Christ opened the way to the homeland. III, 25. There is no way of salvation without participation in Christ’s body and blood. II, 637. One must not cling to Christ insofar as he is the way. III, 34. Christ belongs both to us and to the Father. IV, 1728. Christ is our brother. IV, 549. Christ is our neighbor. III, 31; V, 933; VII, 704. Distant and near. V, 932. Christ is mediator not between the Father and human beings, but between God and human beings. IV, 216. Christ reconciles us with God, correcting our will toward justice and bending God’s judgment toward mercy. IV, 1384. Between the Trinity of God and the weakness and iniquity of humanity, the mediator became a human being who was not unrighteous but nevertheless weak, so that by what was not unrighteous he might join you to God, and by what was weak he might draw near to you. IV, 216.

The grace of Christ the mediator is commended. III, 1842. Christ’s mediation was necessary. III, 1070; IV, 1159, 1741. No one is born here in such a way that he does not need Christ the physician. III, 1445. All need the benefit of Christ the mediator. X, 131. Just as no one dies except in Adam, so no one is made alive except in Christ. X, 140. By the grace through which Christ was good from the beginning, others are made good from evil. X, 1137, 1139. The Pelagian assertion that Christ did not die in vain, but so that we might be justified more easily. X, 1226. Pelagius thought Christ necessary for us only so that we might learn how we ought to live. X, 270. The Pelagians acknowledged in Christ only the authority of a teacher of doctrine and example. X, 705. In what respect Christ’s cross is emptied of its force. X, 250, 251, 260, 270.

Christ is our physician. III, 1397, 2054; V, 1370. The great physician. V, 945. From his own blood he made medicine for the mad murderer. V, 943, 846. Christ is the Samaritan helping the wounded man. V, 933. How Christ the physician gradually heals us. V, 1270. Christ the physician, who first drank the cup for the sick. V, 542, 781. Christ, in the incarnate Son of God, is medicine bringing aid to all. VI, 298. Christ is our health. IV, 481. In Paul Christ displayed the greatness of his art. IV, 1708. The Pelagians admit that Christ the physician was necessary for infants because of bodily evils, but not so that they might be freed from the devil’s power. X, 1306. They say Christ the physician is necessary for them so that they may avoid envy. X, 1308. Christ also died for infants. X, 122. Christ died only for sinners. X, 825. Julian the Pelagian admits that Christ also died for infants. X, 469.

Christ is our Redeemer. V, 726. Christ is the salvation of God. III, 788; IV, 331, 445, 1595; V, 890, 1266; VIII, 611, 624. Christ is the truth and salvation of God. IV, 445. Christ is our hope. IV, 725. Christ is the one Savior. V, 1061. In Christ is the salvation of all nations. III, 872. No one is free from the wounds of the slaughterer except by the grace of the Savior. II, 843, 858, 884, 859, 374. Christ is the liberator. I, 1355. He overcame the devil by the law of justice: killed without guilt, born without lust. I, 1286. Christ’s blood is our price, which Augustine both drank and distributed. I, 810. No one will pour innocent blood back upon him, nor restore to him the price with which he bought us, so as to take us away from him. I, 778. The Pelagians do not want Christ to be Jesus for the infants themselves. X, 1308. In what respect Christ restores what was shattered through Adam. X, 1178. How all things are restored and reconciled in him. VI, 261. Christ did not die for the angels. VI, 261. Christ, both in the form of God and in the form of a servant, is Lord of the angels. III, 334.

Christ is Savior, judge, and advocate. V, 1062, 1370. Christ is advocate only for those who believe in him. VI, 223. Christ wished to present himself to the Father as an intercessor in such a way that he would remember that he was our teacher. III, 1902.

Christ is the prophet of prophets. VI, 537. Christ is prophet and Lord of the prophets. III, 1596.

Christ is the true teacher. VI, 678. Christ is truly the good teacher because he is God. I, 855. Christ is the good teacher, teaching what it is beneficial to know. V, 1221. Christ is the teacher who knew both how to teach what benefited and how not to teach what harmed. IV, 355. Christ is teacher of all. V, 742. Christ is the preacher of the world. V, 396. Christ is teacher in heaven, not only of human beings but also of angels. III, 1487. He has his teaching chair in heaven. VI, 678. He teaches inwardly. I, 875. His school on earth is his body. VI, 315. Christ’s deeds are also signs. III, 1747. They are also kinds of utterances. III, 1598. In everything the Lord did, he admonishes us how we should live here. V, 475. Christ also speaks through deeds. V, 1171. Through Christ’s temporal acts we are instructed for eternal life. V, 1614. The Word of God would have been insufficient if he had commanded by speaking without also going before us by doing. I, 782. Christ’s whole life was a discipline of morals, by which we are taught what should be desired and what avoided. III, 135. By his words, deeds, death, life, descent, and ascent Christ cries out that we should return to the heart and find him. I, 701. He taught us his power by his deeds, his mercy by his humility, and his nature by his command. I, 1007. In Christ crucified human beings learn many things. VI, 207. What things Christ teaches us. I, 1007. Christ teaching what he wishes to be learned from him. V, 897. Christ is the Father’s command. V, 775. How useful Christ’s commands are. VII, 65. Christ gave commands for the best conduct against corrupt morals. VII, 74.

Christ is the teacher of humility. V, 191. The teacher of humility. VI, 413, 414, 416. Christ’s weakness is the teacher of humility. I, 745. Christ’s humility is the medicine for our pride. V, 684, 688. By charity and humility Christ healed humanity’s twofold sickness. VI, 315. Christ’s humility is the highest medicine and a profound sacrament. VIII, 952. Great is the misery of a proud human being, but greater is the mercy of humble God. VI, 314. Revealing the New Testament of the eternal inheritance, Christ taught by his example that earthly things should be despised. VI, 339. Christ’s disciples are called by this name in two ways. X, 929. The chair of Moses prefigured Christ’s chair. IX, 305.

Everyone ought to live for Christ, not for himself. II, 568. Whoever has been born spiritually is bound to raise up offspring for Christ. VIII, 302. Christ’s poverty satisfies the person who not only despises temporal goods but also endures evils. II, 567. Christ is despised in himself and in his members by those who love what he despised. IV, 250. Christ’s charity was so great that he wished to have coheirs. IV, 565. Christ himself will be our possession in the future. V, 1469.

Christ has his own commonwealth. IV, 1911. Christ governs us only from above. IV, 1774. Christ’s kingdom is spoken of in different ways. VI, 76, 77, 78. How Christ’s kingdom was spread among all nations. IV, 389. The pagans repeatedly claimed that the name of Christ would last only 365 years. IV, 453, 454. The devil is conquered in Christ’s name. VII, 300. Whatever wonders are performed are performed in Christ’s name. V, 1431, 1440.

Christ’s authority. VII, 589, 593, 594, 595. Christ was praised even by those who did not believe in him. IV, 1370. The pagans honor Christ as supremely wise but deny that he is God. I, 636. The pagans did not dare to blaspheme Christ. IV, 1243. The pagans were forbidden by their gods to blaspheme Christ. III, 1061. They shamelessly attribute present misfortunes to Christ, although they are not permitted to worship him. VII, 109, 110. Certain things befit Christ insofar as he is God, and certain things insofar as he is human. II, 835. Many things are said about him in Scripture according to the form of God, and many according to the form of a servant. II, 1042. These must not be confused. II, 1042. Christ says that the Father is greater than he insofar as he assumed the form of a servant. II, 751. It is not easily found that Christ called the Father “Lord.” III, 563. The Son assigns everything to the Father because he himself is from the Father, not the Father from him; he gives everything to the fountain from which he was born. V, 1083. Why Christ continually calls himself the Son of Man. V, 1113. In the Gospel he calls himself the Son of Man in order to distinguish himself from Adam, who is a human being but not the Son of Man. II, 547. Christ’s divinity must not be separated from his humanity, whether he is called the Son of God or the Son of Man. II, 835. Christ is called πρωτότοκος (*prōtotokos*, “firstborn”), not πρωτογενής (*prōtogenēs*, “first-generated”); μονογενής (*monogenēs*, “only-begotten”), not μονότοκος (*monotokos*, “only-born”). III, 759. Christ’s outward movements are not signs of a disturbed mind, but of a teaching master. III, 180. How the testimony Christ gave about himself is true. VIII, 322. Christ was able to do many things that he did not wish to do; and what he wished was the better course. VIII, 485, 490. Christ deemed it worthy to perform greater works through his disciples than through himself. III, 1823. Christ did not see the Father with bodily eyes. II, 320, 707.

Christ’s comparison with Adam. III, 1401, 1463. With reference to the first human being and to Christ, “the first and the last Adam” is understood, or with reference to each human being considered in different ways. II, 946. Why Christ is called the second Adam and the second human being. X, 1512. In what way Adam was a figure of Christ. II, 684. Conversely, Christ is the figure of Adam. X, 1555. In Scripture we are called human beings from Adam and sons of human beings from Christ, though not everywhere. II, 548.

Christ is called vine, sheep, lion, lamb, rock, and cornerstone by way of likeness. III, 1839. The name that properly belongs to Christ is “the Word in the beginning.” III, 1729, 1736. Christ is called the Lamb. V, 45, 1209. How he is the spotless Lamb. IV, 763. The Angel of great counsel. IV, 315; V, 64, 691. The Angel and Lord of angels. III, 1596. Christ is the eagle. III, 884. Christ is represented by the ram caught by its horns. IV, 245. Christ is called bull, ram, and he-goat in the figures of the divine utterances. VIII, 346. Christ is the grape-cluster. VIII, 271. The cluster of grapes pressed in the winepress. IV, 109, 649. The arm of God. III, 1346; IV, 484, 894. Christ is understood under the name of camel. III, 1360. Christ is food for angels. IV, 995. Christ is food for great and small. IV, 1598. He is food for the mind, restoring without being consumed. V, 183, 1006, 1016. He is food that satisfies the hungry and remains whole. V, 183. Christ is a heavenly human being from heaven. V, 1621.

Why Christ is called David. VI, 168. Christ is called David because he is from David’s seed. IV, 1869, 1870. Christ is both son and Lord of David. IV, 1870. Christ was prefigured under the name of David. IV, 646, 663. Christ is God of gods. IV, 564. Our day. V, 932. Day from day. V, 1005, 1099. The day whose twelve hours are the shining Apostles. IV, 650. Christ is the Father’s teaching. III, 1629. Christ is the Lordly human being. IV, 67, 78, 105, 109, 114.

Christ is Emmanuel. III, 385. Christ is signified by the honeycomb. IV, 1497. Christ is our end, an end that perfects, not destroys. III, 1785. Christ is the end of the Law, not because he consumes it, but because he perfects it. IV, 78, 514, 628, 662, 723, 785. Christ is the firmament. IV, 911. Christ is the fountain from which all received—whether those sent beforehand before the incarnation or those sent by the incarnate Christ. V, 1311. Christ is our foundation and head. V, 1616. Christ is the foundation even of those who belong to the Law and the Prophets. IV, 1560. Christ is compared to a hen. III, 1330; IV, 526, 698. Christ is the giant of giants. IV, 1116. Christ is the grain that must die and multiply. III, 1766. The grain that fell into the earth in the Passion. IV, 720. The grain multiplied through death. V, 1397. For what reason Christ is called ἰχθύς (*ichthys*, “fish”). VII, 580. Christ is the door. V, 755, 780, 1647. Christ is the heavenly jurist. IV, 1849.

Christ is the great mountain from the small stone. IV, 522, 533, 554, 680. Christ is the stone cut from the mountain without hands. III, 1407, 1465; IV, 1294. Christ is the stone cut from the mountain, which by lying low shakes the one who stumbles against it, and by coming in exaltation crushes the proud. V, 567, 573, 681. Christ is the cornerstone. III, 1839, 2082; IV, 534; V, 42, 341, 544. Christ is the stone of stumbling for all the wicked. III, 2000. Christ is the stone anointed by Jacob. III, 1449; IV, 506. Christ is the anointed and rejected stone. III, 376. Christ is the lion. III, 1728, 1736; V, 45, 1209. Christ is figuratively lion, rock, and calf. IV, 1153. Through the sun, the lion, and so forth, Christ is signified by likeness, not by the propriety of substance. VIII, 266. Christ is the tree of life in the spiritual paradise. III, 376. Christ is called a lamp. IV, 1567. Christ is the illuminating light. III, 1782. The Lord’s light. IV, 155. “Light” is said properly, whereas “stone” is figurative. III, 315. The light of the world. III, 1652. The unquenchable light. III, 1575.

Christ is the hand of God. IV, 1595, 1865; V, 1317. Christ is the pearl for which everything must be sold. III, 1371. Christ is the physician. IV, 353. The physician who made medicine from himself for the sick. V, 725. Christ is the merchant. IV, 866. What kind of commerce Christ has with the human race. V, 689. Christ is the merchant who carried our price in a sack: he was pierced by a spear, the sack was opened, and the price of the whole world flowed out. IV, 178, 179. Christ came here for an exchange: he brought goods and received evils. IV, 1942. Christ is continually called a mountain in Scripture. IV, 74, 77, 517; V, 45; VI, 52. Christ is the mountain of mountains. IV, 1116. The fertile and cheese-producing mountain. IV, 827. Mountain and valley. IV, 1597. Christ is a wall against the enemy’s ambushes. III, 1440. Christ is the heavenly merchant, who came to receive insults and give honors; to drink in pain and give salvation; to undergo death and give life. IV, 231. Christ is the cloud from the Virgin. IV, 1124.

Christ is oil. III, 710. The doorkeeper. III, 1728. The door. III, 1728, 1734, 1735. The sheep. III, 375, 1728, 1735. The bread. V, 265, [Col. 0162] 725, 1463. The true bread. III, 1602, 1607. The heavenly bread prefigured by manna. V, 45, 1551. The heavenly bread eaten by the true Israelites. V, 1551. The bread of angels. I, 1286. The bread of angels and the ration of combatants brought from the Lord’s storehouses. IV, 1863. Christ is bread and drink. III, 1612. Whoever hungers for Christ the bread hungers for righteousness. III, 1607. Christ is the Paraclete. III, 1828. The shepherd. III, 1728, 1734; V, 308, 1647. Shepherd and door. IV, 1102, 1103. Christ is peace. V, 170. Our peace. III, 1834. Christ is our peace and the true peacemaker. IV, 1655, 1668. In what sense Christ can be called a persecutor. IX, 265. Christ is the rock. III, 375, 737, 791, 804, 1729, 1736; V, 45. The rock upon which Gideon placed the flesh of a kid and unleavened bread, a figure of Christ. III, 112. The rock upon which the Church was built. I, 618; V, 1238, 1348. The rock against which the greater enemy must be killed and the lesser dashed. IV, 1774. Christ is our price. V, 1591. Christ is the beginning. III, 1681; V, 24. Christ is ruler, bridegroom, and redeemer of the Church. IV, 1784. Christ is king of the Jews. IV, 526, 759. Christ is king and priest. III, 1045, 1594.

Christ is called priest because he sanctifies us, and king because he rules us. IV, 504. Christ was prefigured through Solomon. IV, 1668. Christ is our savior. IV, 1728. Christ is the Samaritan. IV, 1765. Christ is the Holy of Holies. IV, 1116. If you consider the sacraments, he is the Holy of Holies; if the flock subject to him, the shepherd of shepherds; if the building, the foundation of foundations. IV, 1102. Christ is the wisdom of God, present everywhere. III, 1659. Christ is called the sun; hence the Manichaeans’ opportunity for error. IV, 132, 1947. Christ is temple and altar. III, 1329. Christ is the tower of strength. IV, 725. The divine Word is the grape, Christ the cluster of grapes. IV, 109. Christ is truth and mercy. IV, 667. Why Christ is a worm. II, 384, 547; IV, 174. Christ is the power of God, the wisdom of God, and truth. I, 1321; III, 170. Christ is the fountain of life. V, 1113. The fountain and light of life. III, 1654. Christ is the life of the sacraments. V, 92. Christ is eternal life. III, 1610, 1818. Christ as human being is the vine; according to his divinity, the cultivator. III, 1839. Why Christ called himself the vine and his disciples the branches. III, 1841. Christ is called the calf because of the sacrifice. V, 45. Christ is the vulture. III, 885.

The Christian religion is the true religion. I, 602. It existed among the ancients. I, 602. The Christian religion took its beginning from Jerusalem. VII, 618. It is found in the Catholic Church alone. III, 127. The healing power of the Christian religion. VII, 76, 79. To one who asks why the world was without the Christian law for so long a period of time, the answer is given. II, 373. How all now sing of Christ. II, 1028. The method of Christian teaching is exceedingly excellent. III, 134. The Christian religion persuaded human beings of what Plato could not persuade them. III, 123. What was foretold in Scripture concerning the Christian religion comes to pass in such a way as it was foretold that it would pass away. II, 1028. When Christian kings were made, Christ’s Gospel penetrated everywhere in a short time, says Hesychius. II, 904. Its enemies boasted that the Christian religion would last only a short time. IX, 894. Whether Christianity makes progress through deaths. IV, 321. The truth of the Christian faith is evident from the blood of martyrs and the chastity of virgins. III, 125.

The Christians were first so called at Antioch. I, 622. Christians are so called because of the mystical chrism. VII, 676. We may rightly call Christians “Christs.” VII, 532. Christians were prefigured in Jacob. V, 43, 55. Good and bad Christians were foreshadowed in the same blessed Jacob and limping Esau. V, 58. Figures of Christians in the things that happened to the Israelites. V, 37, 38. The Christian people was preferred to the Jewish people. IV, 990. The Jews are servants of Christians. V, 56.

Some Christians existed before Christ. V, 1376, 1377. The ancient saints were saved through faith in Christ’s future Passion. I, 808. Christians are children of the Patriarchs, not by descending from their flesh but by imitating their faith. IV, 933. Christian kings are called from Christ. II, 1055.

A Christian is understood under the name “brother.” III, 1266. Christians are truly Christ’s brothers by adoption. VIII, 215. Christ’s brothers and children. III, 1829. Whoever first believes receives Christ’s sign on the forehead. V, 1075. Christians believe in Christ, not in Peter. VII, 620. Christ wished his sign to be impressed on our foreheads, so that a Christian would not blush at Christ’s reproaches. IV, 252. The name “Christian” was once cast at people as an insult and reproach. IV, 486. At one time it was a crime and disgrace to be a Christian; now it is an honor. IV, 719, 856, 1138. No error now dares to exalt itself without seeking the coverings of the Christian name. II, 447. Christians should not regard themselves as worthless, since God daily pours out for them the most precious blood of his only-begotten Son. V, 1378. Why what a person is as a Christian pertains more to him than what he is as a human being. II, 1420. Catholics, or orthodox Christians, are so called—that is, guardians of integrity and followers of what is right. III, 127. A Christian must be guided by the weight of authority. V, 1600. It is enough for a Christian to believe that all things were created by the supremely good Trinity, and that they are good. VI, 235. Not all Christians are the temple of God, but only those who live well. IX, 671.

[Col. 0163] Two kinds of Christians. III, 127. Christians of three kinds. V, 53. Four kinds of Christians according to the manner of their birth. III, 1479. Good and bad Christians. V, 559, 561. Who are true Christians. IV, 373; IX, 151. Christians ought to differ from the customs of the nations. V, 1025. Faustus’s slander—that Christians changed nothing in the customs of the nations—is refuted. VIII, 435. Catholic Christians are defended against Faustus’s slanders. VIII, 347.

A Christian ought not to have a crime. III, 1697. The conduct and morals of Christians. VII, 647. The true adornment of Christian men and women is not merely the absence of every deceptive cosmetic, nor even the splendor of gold and clothing, but good morals. II, 1060. Their attitude toward created things and toward God himself. VI, 331. The order of Christian life. I, 866, 867. One must not flatter oneself about the Christian profession unless works also follow. IV, 1043, 1044. Christians ought to imitate Christ. V, 53. In what respect Christians express Christ’s holiness. IX, 274. Christian life must be conformed to Christ’s cross, burial, and resurrection, and so forth. VI, 257.

A Christian, simply because he is a Christian, will suffer something more in this age. V, 276. He is a Christian in vain if he is not in that condition for which Christ suffered. IV, 176. If you think you have no tribulations, you have not yet begun to be a Christian. IV, 649. The courage of Christians against tyrants’ threats. IV, 1591. A Christian, after Christ’s example, becomes strong in tribulation. IV, 649, 653. For Christians, martyrdom for Christ is the best end. X, 995. When a Christian cannot be killed, an attempt is made to dishonor him. IV, 732. Christians should patiently endure injuries for the instruction of others. II, 529. Christian steadfastness. V, 277. A Christian ought to be like a square stone. IV, 1103. The security of Christians under Christ their patron. V, 728. Christians learn what they ought to do for their heavenly homeland from what the Romans did for their earthly one. VII, 160, 162.

Earthly kings persecuted Christians without cause. IV, 1591. The gentiles could not destroy the Christian name. V, 1637. After Christ’s death, the Christian name was spread through the sufferings of the martyrs. IV, 453, 454. Christians’ struggles are now not with tyrants but with the devil and with the flesh. IV, 1687. The Apostle described a Christian, not a Jew still placed under the Law. X, 995. The world is hostile to a Christian. IV, 649.
