The life of Christians in this world is like trees that appear dead through the winter. III, 1627.

The wealth of Christians. VII, 23. Those who are Christians are altogether poor. IV, 863. Christians ought not to be disturbed by losses. II, 1060. The Christian’s heart is distressed not because of loss, but because he does not yet live with Christ. IV, 1631. The person who wishes to become a Christian for temporal advantage is rebuked. VI, 330. A Christian was not made for this purpose: to flourish in this age. IV, 190. Whoever is a Christian so that he may abound in temporal goods fails when these things fail. IV, 1701. The Christian who wishes to become one for earthly happiness still remains in darkness. IV, 1673. He is not yet a Christian who does not attend to God’s promises concerning the future age. V, 78. Christians who serve God in hope of a bodily reward belong to the Old Testament. V, 32. It belongs to Christians to suffer temporal evils and hope for eternal goods. V, 1356. Christians were not made for the goods of the present time. V, 705. Christians exist in order to overcome present things and hope for future ones. IV, 1154. We are Christians not for the sake of temporal life but for eternal life. V, 632, 1196, 1356, 1386, 1650. We ought to be Christians for the sake of everlasting life. II, 550. He is truly a Christian who professes the religion for the sake of future rest. VI, 331. They are Christians for the sake of one eternal life. VII, 189.

A Christian is one who recognizes that he is a stranger here. V, 642. Christians use earthly goods as strangers, without being captured by them; through evils they are either tested or corrected. VII, 42. Three things are commended to the Christian: continence, justice, and hope of an eternal reward. V, 633. A Christian may not doubt the resurrection. V, 1614. Faith in the resurrection is proper to Christians. V, 1112. It is shown that the Christian heart ought always to seek heaven, like a burning torch. V, 1117. The whole life of good Christians is a holy desire. III, 2008. Whoever passes over to Christ passes from fear to love. V, 199. For the Christian who loves, the law is not a burden but an adornment, not a torment but an ornament. V, 207. You are a Christian: hear Christ; you are a servant: hear your Lord; you are a son: hear your father. IV, 160. The pastures of the Christian soul. V, 1647. How the good Christian is devoured in the food of bread. IV, 617.

The life of perfected Christians is praised. I, 1337. The life and morals of Christians living together in a city. I, 1338. When a Christian is required to leave father, mother, or wife. II, 689.

Christians are priests. VII, 676. The sacrifice of Christians. V, 284.

All Christians have one commonwealth. VI, 573. Christians are recalled to unity. VI, 712, 713, 716. By the very fact that you received the name of Christ, you were born by a certain sacrament in the womb of the Church. IV, 678. Christians do not have many souls, but one soul—the one and only soul of Christ. II, 1056. All Christians are one human being. IV, 1316, 1336, 1634, 1704. We are all in Christ, Christ’s, and Christ himself. IV, 200, 1679. How a Christian, when another Christian performs miracles, also performs them himself. IV, 1707. In Christians who are still carnal when they die, the spirit perfects whatever is lacking, because they have not withdrawn from the unity of Christ’s body. II, 843. Good Christians are forbidden by the lukewarm to be led along as though by the authority of crowds. V, 546, 548.

Some are Christians in name, empty in deed. V, 1562. The distinction between Christians who love this world and those who despise it. II, 486. Half-Christians. VIII, 207. Bad Christians. VI, 343, 347. False Christians. VII, 674. Fictitious and bad Christians are not to be counted among Christ’s members. VII, 742. Fictitious and bad Christians: “the mystery of iniquity.” VII, 686. Christians who do not have good morals are both called God’s and not God’s: God’s because of his sacraments, not God’s because of their own vice. IV, 539. Bad Christians carry the holy name to their own punishment. V, 548. Bad Christians do injury to Christ. III, 1760. They fill the churches on the feast days of the Christians just as they fill the theaters on the solemn days of the pagans. VI, 343. Temptations assail Christians through pagans, Jews, heretics, and especially bad Christians. VI, 343, 347. Just as formerly the insults of pagans lay in wait for the virtues of the righteous, so now do the insults of bad Christians. IV, 1151, 1152. Bad Christians are more harmful insofar as they are more inward enemies. VI, 180. Bad Christians live worse than Jews and pagans: the latter are compared to wild wood, the former to a cut branch. IV, 242. Those who bear only the name of Christian are called beasts of the reed. IV, 836. Many who wish to become Christians are offended by the bad morals of Christians. IV, 243. The Church must not be despised because of the morals of bad Christians. I, 1341. Whoever gathers into the Church ought not to be disturbed by the wicked morals of many Christians. VIII, 291. Good and bad Christians are mingled together here; why this is so. IV, 248, 249. Their opposed ways of life. III, 128. The wicked are tolerated as straw. III, 127. Nor are they cut off from the Church. I, 1341. Good Christians are encouraged to tolerate the bad. V, 471. Bad Christians are urged to change their life. V, 471. Curses directed against bad Christians fall upon all Christians. IV, 582. How Christians are more numerous than the number would suggest. IV, 440. Good Christians are few in comparison with the multitude of the bad, but considered in themselves they are many. VIII, 291. The pagans have nothing they can bring against Christians except Christian dissension. V, 314. It is the greatest slander if Christians are reproached for worshiping a dead man. IV, 1578. Christians worship no dead person. II, 85. Porphyry accused Christians of worshiping demons. VII, 653, 654. The evils inflicted upon the Roman Empire by certain Christian emperors are unjustly attributed to Christian teaching. II, 532. The Roman pagans attributed all the evils they suffered to the Christians. VII, 49, 111. These accusations are refuted. VII, 111. Christians strive—even with the testimony of pagans—so that those afflicted may not feel the duration of their calamity. II, 387, 389. Seneca neither blames nor praises Christians. VII, 192. In Julian’s time Christians were forbidden by law to teach literature and rhetoric. I, 753. A Christian ought neither to be led astray by the empty loquacity of false philosophy nor terrified by the superstition of false religion. III, 262. A Christian speaking about natural matters as though in accordance with Christian writings should affirm nothing rashly before unbelievers. III, 261, 264. The remarkable conversion of the enemies of the Christian name. VII, 612. The enemies of the Christian name partly believed, partly perished; only a few fearful ones remained. IV, 1782.

Christians are Israelites and sons of Abraham. II, 896. They are Jews and Israelites not carnally but spiritually. II, 895, 896. Although Christians are spiritually Jews and Israelites, they ought not to assume these names for themselves. II, 896, 897. Aptus taught Christians to Judaize. II, 897. Christians ought not to Judaize. II, 892. In celebrating Easter, Christians observe it so that the Sabbath may coincide with it. II, 211. Yet they do not observe days and years, months and seasons. II, 209, 210. They celebrate Easter according to the calculation of the sun and moon. II, 209, 210. Christians, if they can, ought not to allow anything to be taken from the threshing floor or winepress for sacrifices to demons; but if something has been taken without their knowledge, they use the remaining fruits, which are clean. II, 185. Christians are not permitted to use anything in honor of the gods, even if they despise them in their hearts. II, 185. It is not permitted to appropriate anything from temples, idols, or sacred groves that are being overthrown for private uses. II, 185. The Donatists said that no one, even an evil person, ought to be killed by Christians and the just. II, 177. Whether some will become Christians during the final three years and six months. VII, 671.

Chromatius, bishop. X, 652, 663.

Chrysippus. I, 955; IX, 459. Chrysippus, one of the leaders of the Stoics. VII, 259, 261. When Carneades was about to debate with him [Col. 0165], he thought that his heart should be purged with hellebore, etc. IX, 459. Chrysippean arguments. II, 82.

Chrysostom. X, 685. According to Julian, outstanding among the learned and the saints. X, 661. Why he did not speak so explicitly about original sin. X, 656. Chrysostom’s testimonies concerning original sin. X, 656, 657. Chrysostom embraced Origen’s and the ancients’ view concerning Peter’s being rebuked by Paul. II, 254.

Chullabi. IX, 238.

Chusi, interpreted as “silence.” IV, 97.

Cibaliana. IX, 232.

The delirium of the Manichaeans: that foods are purified and cleansed by being eaten and belched up. VIII, 226, 230. Adimantus slanderously claimed that Christ had said, only to the crowds, “It is not what enters that defiles a person, but what comes out.” VIII, 232. No foods are unclean. VIII, 151. Foods do not pollute. I, 799. It was not food that destroyed Adam, but forbidden food that destroyed him. II, 141. Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh that was suitable for food. I, 799. John was not polluted by locusts that served as food. I, 799. Religious observance concerning foods. I, 1340. Those who are overly superstitious in the choice of foods should be fraternally admonished. I, 1341. Foods are clean for the clean, but luxury is clean nowhere. V, 1040, 1043. One should fear not the uncleanness of the dish but that of desire. I, 799. One should be blamed not for the kind of food but for immoderate greed. VII, 515. Frugality in food and drink. X, 723. What temperance in food and drink would have been like in paradise. X, 772.

The eternal law permits food and drink only for the preservation of health. VIII, 426. Food should be taken as medicine. I, 797. Great is the person who, in eating, is not carried even slightly beyond the limits of necessity. I, 799. What is enough for health is too little for pleasure. I, 797. Food is not taken without pleasure, in order to live. VII, 622. The necessity of food is a calamity, yet it is called a delicacy. I, 797. In food there lies in wait the snare of desire, and dangerous pleasure attaches itself like a handmaid. I, 797. It would be happier to take food and drink without any seductive sweetness of taste. X, 771. Food that no longer has flavor in the stomach has, as it were, flavor in the memory. I, 786. Appetite for food is greater amid cares. I, 924. How bodily food should be taken to the praise of God. IV, 1899. One should not glory in abstinence from food. I, 798. Costly foods are indulged in for the weakness of the rich; cheap and choice foods provide nothing more. V, 413. Whether food pertains to the body or to the soul. I, 963.

Earthly food and heavenly food. VI, 707, 708. Why spiritual food is superior to bodily food. V, 1481. The soul has its own proper food and its own hunger. I, 963. Food of the mind. V, 709. The mind is nourished by that in which it rejoices. I, 863. Our food is God: he alone restores and does not fail. IV, 597. A human being does not live from one source and an angel from another. IV, 1742. The godly person is nourished by the food of righteousness, the ungodly by that of pride. IV, 1290. If you do not wish to be the serpent’s food, do not be earth. IV, 1386. The food of the eyes is light. V, 183. Egyptian food. I, 741. Note (a).

A scar in Scripture also signifies a mark of color alone. III, 519, 696. When is a scar said to run? X, 315.

Ciceion or ciceia, a kind of shrub. II, 263.

Cicero. II, 391, 395. An Academic philosopher. VII, 136; VIII, 1056; X, 1566. A most eloquent man and the most vigilant weigh­er and measurer of words. VIII, 636. Philosophy both began and was perfected in the Latin language through him. I, 910. Nothing is superior to Cicero in the Latin language. I, 1204. Cicero is praised. II, 498. Cicero says that he had found the Latin language deficient, so that he gave less suitable names to things that he perceived. I, 932. Everyone admires his tongue, but not his heart to the same degree. I, 685. Even in his works there are solecisms. I, 1015. His speech by which Rome was saved seemed barbarous. I, 1015, 1016. Cicero’s speeches called the Verrines are the most illustrious. I, 1204. In praising his own eloquence, Cicero does not fear arrogance. III, 1793. Cicero’s dialogue entitled *Hortensius*. I, 686; VIII, 1019, 1046, 1056; X, 774, 802. In the *Hortensius*, Cicero saw human misery but did not recognize its cause. X, 778. Cicero’s discussion against the views of Anaximenes and Anaxagoras concerning God. II, 443. Cicero’s view concerning the definition and division of the virtues of the soul. VI, 20. *On the Happy Life*. I, 909. A passage of Cicero from the *Tusculans* is attacked. II, 667. Another passage is more truthful. II, 668. A passage concerning friendship is praised. II, 1071. A passage of Cicero. II, 1074. The style of Cicero’s letters. II, 1075. Cicero’s books *On the Republic*. VII, 648; X, 767. They perished. VII, 53. Note (a). Whom Cicero called “almost consular philosophers.” II, 389. Cicero praises Caesar’s clemency. II, 529. Cicero’s saying about the actor Roscius. III, 1068. Cicero’s statement about someone—“He never uttered a word that he would wish to recall”—is rejected. II, 586. Cicero expresses indignation at the establishment of images and at fabulous opinions about the gods. VII, 136. He mocks augury. VII, 136. When Augustine was asked many questions about Cicero’s books, what he replied. II, 432. Cicero’s codex could not be found at Hippo. II, [Col. 0166] 436. Cicero’s murder and its cause. VII, 110.

Some have thought that Cilicia was called Tharsis [Tarshish]. IV, 536.

Haircloth. II, 189. The haircloth of a poor person. V, 1402. Haircloth pertains to the signification of sin. III, 1077. It pertains to the confession of sins. V, 518. In it there is remembrance of sins. VII, 465. Haircloth is the flesh of Christ because of mortality and likeness to sinful flesh. IV, 335, 852. Augustine received with the greatest gratitude the haircloths sent to him. II, 989, 991.

The poverty of Cincinnatus the dictator. VII, 164.

Ashes of repentance. IV, 1301. Penitents roll about in ashes, thereby testifying that they are like them. IV, 1933. The ashes of the red heifer signify the fame that followed Christ’s passion and resurrection. III, 734.

Cinna, consul. VII, 107. Cinna was called fortunate because of his license to sin. VII, 174. Cinna brought war against the City and devastated it. VII, 69 and Note (c), 107.

Circe, the most famous sorceress. VII, 573. She transformed the companions of Ulysses. VII, 575.

Circus charioteers are to be separated from communion for as long as they are driving. IX, 787.

Virtue is compared with a circle. I, 1051.

The spectacles of the Circus. VI, 638, 700. The madness of the Circus. V, 1026. Those who attend the Circus and amphitheater are reproved. IV, 585, 1035, 1919. For what reason the Circus spectacle was instituted by Romulus for Neptune the equestrian god. VII, 61, Note (c). At first the Romans used only Circus games. VII, 44. Whence the Circus games were called Consualia. VII, 61, Note (c).

Circumcellions. VIII, 43; IX, 28, 96, 725. Whence the Circumcellions, or Circillions, were named. IV, 1730. The wicked behavior of the Circumcellions. IV, 1730. Drunkenness and license. IX, 53, 54, 62, 257, 268, 320. Fury against themselves and others. VIII, 43. The fury of the Circumcellions who threw themselves down cliffs in the mountains. IX, 106. The voluntary deaths of the Circumcellions. IX, 631, 636. It is characteristic of the Circumcellions to wish to die without cause. V, 422. The leaders of the Circumcellions. V, 306, 307. The daily violence of Circumcellions roaming about under bishops and presbyters as leaders. IV, 134, 1234. Circumcellions, the satellites of Donatist clergy. IX, 580, 581. The leaders of the Circumcellions were clerics. II, 397. The Circumcellions have herds and women, including religious women. II, 135. The furies of the Circumcellions. V, 306. Their fury. IX, 45, 46, 283, 306, 317, 319, 320, 322, 423, 429. Innocentius after his eye had been dug out and his finger cut off, and the presbyter Restitutus, were killed by them. II, 509. The savagery of the Circumcellions. II, 97, 98, 307, 413. They ravage the churches in the region of Hippo so thoroughly that perhaps the deeds of the barbarians are milder. II, 422. The crimes of the Circumcellions and examples of their cruelty toward Catholics. IX, 520, 522, 560, 631, 636. The savagery of the Circumcellions toward bishops. II, 306. Against the bishop of Bagai. II, 307. Against Catholic clerics. II, 302, 306. Against the clerics of Hippo. II, 511. Against laypeople. II, 307. The fury of the Circumcellions against Paul and Macarius. IX, 47. Against Rogatus. IX, 704. The weapons of the Circumcellions. IV, 645. Wood, iron, and slings. IX, 46, 320, 333. The clubs of the Circumcellions, called “Israels.” IV, 134. The Circumcellions attacked human eyes with lime and vinegar. IX, 636. The license of the Circumcellions is rightly reproved, even when they use violence against certain very wicked people. IX, 432. The Circumcellions invaded the Catholic basilica at Hasna and smashed the altar. II, 120. See *Donatists*. The Circumcellions’ formula of greeting was “Praise be to God.” IV, 1732; IX, 306. The Circumcellions’ formula of greeting was more feared than the roar of a lion. IV, 1732. Concerning the savagery of the Circumcellions: the complaint of the clergy of Hippo to Januarius. II, 306. A law enacted against the Circumcellions. IX, 48. Many of the Circumcellions themselves were genuinely corrected by the force of the laws. II, 322. Circumcellion courage. IX, 328. The Circumcellions are called Agonistici by the Donatists. IV, 1732.

Why circumcision was commanded at the time of Isaac’s birth. VII, 506. It was also commanded for Abraham’s entire household. VII, 506. In circumcision the name was changed. VII, 505. Circumcision was rightly imposed on servants and rightly understood by free people. VIII, 157. Circumcision is the sign of the Old Testament; why it was given in hidden flesh. V, 876. The sign of circumcision was given in a fitting part of the body. VIII, 479. What circumcision foretold. IX, 290. Circumcision is a prophecy of Christ. V, 876; X, 403. The sign of the grace of Christ, who removes original sin. X, 1173. Circumcision represented regeneration in Christ. X, 1073. And Christ’s grace. X, 1206. The sacrament of circumcision prefigured the baptism of our time. X, 504. The necessity of circumcision. VII, 506. Its usefulness. II, 96, 415. Its effect. IX, 175. Circumcision purged original fault. X, 450, 834. It delivered from eternal death. X, 720. The command that infants be circumcised under the terror of so great a punishment proves that nature had been corrupted. X, 402, 403. The command of circumcision demonstrates original sin. X, 450, 686. Why circumcision was commanded on the eighth day. V, 916; VIII, 228, 335; X, 833, 1429. Circumcision of the flesh on the eighth day pertains to the prophecy of Christ [Col. 0167]. And of his resurrection. II, 679. Circumcision once took the place of baptism. II, 845; V, 1548; IX, 309. Comparison of circumcision and baptism. X, 686. Carnal circumcision signifies spiritual circumcision. III, 1634. Circumcision is a matter of great sacramental significance, and from it circumcision of the heart is understood. IV, 954; V, 801. Circumcision of the heart. X, 208. Circumcision signified renewal. VII, 505. Regeneration. VII, 505. And the stripping away of carnal life through Christ’s resurrection. V, 1105.

So that Paul would not seem to detest circumcision as though it were idolatry, he circumcised Timothy; he did not circumcise Titus, lest people should think that without it there was no salvation. II, 280. Timothy’s circumcision was not performed as a pretense. VI, 492. Circumcision was observed by the ancients as a figure of the baptism to come. IX, 464. The rite of circumcision after Christ is superfluous, not harmful, except to one who placed hope of salvation in it. III, 2113, 2134. Why circumcision is no longer observed. VIII, 353. Why the yoke of circumcision should not be imposed on the Gentiles who believe in Christ. VIII, 156. Circumcision benefits neither the Gentiles nor harms the Jews. VI, 492. The Jews should neither be prohibited from it nor the Gentiles compelled to it. VI, 492. When the Manichaeans mock circumcision, they contradict themselves. VIII, 478. How we are circumcision and righteousness. V, 916.

Whether cycles of times and temporal things are to be admitted. VII, 361, 369. “Circuit” signifies desire for temporal things, by which a person is rolled about like a wheel through the repeated cycle of seven days. IV, 139.

Cirta. IX, 208, 511. When it was called Constantina. IX, 512. Note 2. Augustine went to Cirta for the purpose of ordaining a bishop. II, 180. The people of Cirta and Augustine burned with a mutual desire to visit one another. II, 592. The people of Cirta attributed their conversion to Augustine, although he was absent. II, 591. He denied that it should be attributed to him, even if it had occurred while he was among them and speaking. II, 591. The schismatic Council of Cirta in the year 311, under the presidency of Secundus of Tigisis. II, 161, 162, 580; IX, 639, 755. It consisted of scarcely eleven or twelve bishops. IX, 663. The Donatists maintained that the Council of Cirta was false. IX, 642, 643, 755. It is shown, against the Donatists’ objections, that the Council of Cirta was genuine. IX, 643, 644, 663. The judge orders an investigation into whether it was false. IX, 643. The date of the Council of Cirta. IX, 643. The Council of Cirta has a day and consuls recorded. IX, 663. The acts of the Council of Cirta. IX, 510. Note (a).

Cison, interpreted as “their hardness.” IV, 1054.

The distinction and mystical significance of the harp and psaltery. IV, 280, 479, 671, 672, 900, 1964.

What a city is. VII, 447. Properly, a city is understood as the people who inhabit it. IV, 1621. Not its walls. VI, 721. A city is a multitude of people brought into a certain bond of harmony. II, 529. A harmonious multitude of people. II, 670. “The Roman City” means the Roman kingdom. III, 1106. A city is truly said to flourish when it excels in chaste, honorable, and upright morals. II, 314.

When “city” is used in Scripture without qualification, it is understood as the City of God or the Church. IV, 912. The two cities. VII, 437. From the beginning of the human race. VI, 333, 337. One of the righteous, the other of the wicked. III, 436. Both cities consist of angels and human beings. VI, 284. Among all nations, although distinguished from one another by such great variety, there are no more than two cities. VII, 403. One is predestined to reign with God, the other to be tormented with the devil. VII, 437. Both cities arose in the first human being by foreknowledge. VII, 376. Good and evil are common to both cities, but their use is different. VII, 620. Some prophecies pertain to the heavenly city, some to the earthly, and some to both. VII, 525. Neither city—the godly and the ungodly—has ever been absent from the earth. VII, 489.

The two cities are distinguished in the history of Genesis by their different lines of descent. VII, 446, 460. The course of the two cities. VII, 620. It is expressed through the succession of Cain and Abel. VII, 456, 460, 467. The mystery of both cities in Cain and Seth. VII, 456, 460, 466. The origin of the two cities is found in two loves. VII, 421, 436. Scripture establishes that the City of God exists. VII, 315. The City of God consists of angels and human beings. VII, 349, 284. The City of God was ordered by foreknowledge before Adam’s sin had been committed. VII, 418. The City of God, ever enduring the earth and hoping for heaven, is called Jerusalem and Zion; it begins with Abel, just as the evil city begins with Cain. IV, 1846. Knowledge of the City of God is clearer in Abraham. VII, 496.

Whence the origin, formation, and blessedness of the City of God come. VII, 338. Christ is the founder of the City of God. VII, 64. The building of the spiritual city. IV, 1620, 1621. The City of God is born from faith and lives from hope. VII, 461, 466. The holy Church is the City of God. IV, 1261. All the faithful—past, present, and future—together with the angels, make one city and one house of God. IV, 1668, 1669. Many who are full of charity make a city for God [Col. 0168]. IV, 1261.

The spiritual city, where no one is born because no one dies. V, 42. The rest and happiness of the heavenly city. IV, 1096, 1916. A city is not blessed from one source and a blessed person from another. II, 669, 670. In the City of God, God’s will is the law. VII, 63, 284. The law and virtue of the City of God are charity. IV, 541, 1261. In the heavenly city, truth is king, charity is law, and eternity is its measure. II, 533. The figure of the heavenly city. VII, 438, 446, 463. The heavenly city is a pilgrim here. VII, 438. The heavenly city has journeyed among the holy people of God, and in all others it has been foreshadowed sacramentally. VII, 481. While journeying on earth, the heavenly city does not possess peace in faith. VII, 645. From what source it has peace with the earthly city, and from what source discord. VII, 645. It refers earthly peace to heavenly peace. VII, 646. While journeying on earth, the heavenly city follows the laws and institutions of nations insofar as they do not impede religion. VII, 646. The guardians of the City of God are the bishops. IV, 1669. The citizens of God are blessed in this life through hope. VII, 648. The illnesses and healing of God’s citizens in this life. VII, 442. Citizens of the heavenly homeland existed even among other nations besides the Jews. VII, 609.

The beginning of the earthly city. VII, 524. Corrupted nature gives birth to citizens of the earthly city, whereas liberating grace gives birth to citizens of the heavenly city. VII, 439. The ungodly city began to appear with the division of languages. VII, 489. The earthly city will have earthly generations until the end. VII, 461. The victories of the earthly city are deadly, or at any rate mortal. VII, 440. Two forms are found in the earthly city. VII, 439. The war and peace of the earthly city. VII, 440. The ungodly city is signified by the name “beast.” VII, 674, 679. The city of the devil, and the senate, ministers, and people of this city. IV, 120. Sometimes the citizens of the evil city are shown administering good actions by the example of the good city, and conversely. IV, 735. Why God permits the city of the wicked to be more numerous. VI, 337. The captive city of Jerusalem is to be liberated from the Babylon of this age after the passage of time. VI, 323. How greatly the two cities differ from one another. VII, 161. And the distinction between the two. VII, 436.

The two cities are mingled in this age, sharing iniquity. VII, 46, 467. Jerusalem and Babylon are already separated in the heart. IV, 1761. See *Babylon*. In this world the two cities, Jerusalem and Babylon, are mixed together for the time being; at the end they will be separated. III, 436; IV, 735, 773. After the judgment the two cities will exist in eternal blessedness or misery. VI, 284. Augustine promises a work *On the City of God*. III, 436. The first five books of *The City of God* completed. II, 742.

What is the city of circumstances? IV, 255, 722.

What is the city of contradiction? IV, 637.

Cizan, in the diocese of Hippo. II, 232.

Disasters and devastations are useful to Christians. V, 621.

What it means to cry out to Christ. V, 545. One must cry out amid crowds that forbid crying out. V, 548. The crowd forbids crying out to Christ. V, 546.

The cry of the heart. V, 858. The cry of the heart is the ardor of charity; the silence of the heart is the coldness of charity. IV, 404. A cry to the Lord in the feeling of the heart. IV, 74, 83, 254, 971, 1834. See *Prayer*. A cry at midnight. V, 576. “Cry” used of shamelessness and the freedom of iniquity. III, 491. “Cry” for manifest sins. III, 858.

Clarentius. II, 240.

Clarus of Mascula. IX, 237.

Classicianus is condemned by anathema together with his entire household. II, 1066, 1067.

The poet Claudian was alien to the name of Christ. VII, 172.

Claudius, bishop. X, 639, 640. Claudius the bishop sent Augustine four books of Julian against one of Augustine’s works. II, 949. Augustine sent Claudius his replies to Julian’s books, so that Claudius might judge them. II, 949.

Claudianists or Claudianenses. IX, 555. The Claudianists were admitted to communion by Primianus. IV, 379.

The keys of the Church. V, 1545, 1549, 1711; VII, 673. The keys were entrusted to the Church. III, 25. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter, who represented the person of the Church. V, 802, 1349; VI, 308. The keys were given not to Peter alone but to the Church. V, 802. The keys of the kingdom of heaven are in the Church. VIII, 572. The power of the keys of the Church. II, 356. The keys were given to the Church so that it might not only remit sins but also punish them. VIII, 623. Spiritual punishments are far more serious than bodily ones. VIII, 619, 623. The person who is punished more severely is the one who, as it were, has been left unpunished. VIII, 623. How “Whatever you loose on earth” is wrongly understood by the Donatists. V, 600. The keys of the Church are administered through bishops. V, 1545. Christ first raises up; then the Church looses. V, 1349. It belongs to the disciples to loose those whom Christ has raised up. V, 594, 595. They loose the bonds of guilt itself. V, 595. The person who is not in the Catholic Church has no part in those keys. V, 802.

Clauthmon, a mountain. III, 796.

The mind ought to be more full of clemency the purer it is from wickedness. II, 659.

Clementius, bishop. X, 652, 663.

[Col. 0169] Cleo. VII, 54.

Cleobulus of Lindus, one of the Seven Sages. VII, 585.

Why Cleombrotus threw himself from a wall. VII, 36.

Cleophon. VII, 54.

People love the clerical office. V, 1575. The clerical office is more a burden than an honor. V, 1575. Penitents did not accept the clerical office, nor did they return to it, because of the strictness of discipline; nevertheless, a dispensation could be made in their case. II, 812. The honor of the clerical office is not taken away from Donatists returning to the Church. II, 811, 813.

Whence clerics were named. IV, 824. The praise of clerics. I, 1339. The continence of clerics elected even against their will. VI, 486. How clerics ought to conduct themselves toward one another. II, 1018. The life and conduct of Augustine’s clerics in the monastery. V, 1569. Augustine did not dare to degrade clerics departing from the commitment to common life. V, 1572. Eventually he declared that he would erase them from the clerical register. V, 1580. Those who had left or been expelled from a monastery should not become clerics. II, 233. A good monk scarcely makes a good cleric, etc. II, 228. Clerics are not to be received into the monastery. II, 233. Clerics are exempt from all public functions. IX, 777.

To degrade a cleric. VI, 271. No cleric who has not yet been convicted ought to be suspended, unless he fails to appear. II, 269. The humility of Boniface the presbyter is praised: he did not even accept the letters by which he could have received his honor while traveling abroad. II, 269. Augustine asked the clergy and people whether it pleased them that the name of accused but unconvicted presbyters should not be recited at the altar. II, 269. It was established by the strictness of discipline, not by despair of mercy, that no one should accept the clerical office after repentance for a crime, return to it, or remain in it. II, 812. It is permissible to act otherwise when the usefulness of the Church requires it. II, 812. Augustine gives an account to Primatus concerning presbyters removed from office by him. II, 234. He also gives an account to the Council. II, 234. If someone neglects to conduct his case within a year, no one thereafter should hear him. II, 234. Ecclesiastical discipline does not permit a cleric of one Church to transfer to another. II, 231, 232. It was established that no one should receive another Church’s cleric. II, 233. To whom clerical inheritances belong. II, 293. Augustine judged that presbyters made from monks should leave the property of the Church in which they had been ordained, although previously he had granted only half of it. II, 292. Ambrose wished to reclaim the presbyter Paulinus for his own clergy, even though Paulinus lived in different places. II, 100. By the Gentiles, all clerics were called instigators of the most empty superstition. IX, 645.

Clerics are represented by Noah. IV, 1731. By the name “clerics,” the testaments themselves are signified. IV, 824. And the inheritances themselves. IV, 824. Clerics are designated by the phrase “the two in the field.” IV, 1279, 1730.

What a client is. V, 728. How the client of a powerful person should defend himself against another’s threats. V, 728.

Cloacina, a goddess. II, 84. Whence she was so called. VII, 118, Note 1. Tatius dedicated Cloacina as a goddess. VII, 190.

The name Cloacina was given to Venus. VII, 118, Note 1.

*Cluere*, that is, “to cleanse.” VII, 118 and Note 1. *Cluere* means the same as “to be powerful.” X, 1147.

Gnaeus Manlius, proconsul, celebrates a triumph over the Gallo-Greeks. VII, 102.

How coeternal and coeval differ. V, 666.

They displayed the inscription of the books on the title page. II, 155.

Codrus, king of the Athenians, liberated his homeland by his death—how this happened. VII, 576. Codrus was regarded as a god by the Athenians. VII, 576. What the quarrels of Codrus were. VII, 576.

The people of Cos. II, 534.

Heaven; see *Caelum*.

The Lord’s Supper is called the reception of Christ’s body. II, 203. The Supper consecrated by the hands of the Lord. V, 645. The mystery of the Lord’s Supper is that we should lay down our life for the one whose blood we drink. V, 1395. The Lord gave his supper; he gave his passion: the one who imitates him is satisfied. IV, 178. See *Eucharist*. No one should hesitate to come to the supper. V, 647. The Jews were invited to the supper; we were led and compelled. V, 643. They must be compelled to enter the supper: let necessity be found outside, and willingness is born within. V, 647. The three excuses of those unwilling to come to the supper. V, 643. On the day of the Lord’s Supper, in some places only the evening offering is made. II, 202. In other places the body and blood of the Lord are offered in the morning for those who have eaten, and in the evening for those who have fasted. II, 204. Some approve of offering and receiving the body and blood of the Lord after food on this day. II, 204. The disciples did not receive the Lord’s body and blood while fasting. II, 203. Augustine does not dare to define whether communion should be received before or after a meal. II, 202. Concerning communion on the day of the Supper, let each person do what he finds practiced in the Church to which he has come. II, 202. The custom of washing the body on the day of the Supper and relaxing the fast. II, 203. This arose because, during the observance of Lent, the bodies of those who were to be baptized had become dirty and were washed on that day. II, 204. Many refused to adopt the washing of the feet on the day of the Supper as a custom. II, 220. Some did not hesitate to remove the washing of the feet on the day of the Supper from customary practice; others transferred it to the third day of the Octave or to the eighth day itself. II, 220.

The custom of the ancient Romans of dining and taking lunch in public. X, 1357.

The Coenobites are praised; their institution. I, 1338. The life of the Coenobites is described in the Acts of the Apostles. V, 1574.

Mud as a remedy for wounds caused by fire. I, 1350.

To compel. Force may be used to compel someone toward the good. II, 754, 757, 802. Someone must be compelled into the Church. V, 648. Let necessity be found outside, and willingness is born within. V, 648. Heretics and schismatics can be compelled through fear of punishments. II, 329, 803. How. II, 320, 322, 326. One must consider not the fact that someone is compelled, but the nature of that to which he is compelled. II, 329. The person who is compelled does not will. X, 1117. A person is not thereby compelled to will the good because he cannot will evil. X, 1117. Care that merely compels people, rather than teaching them, is more burdensome than useful. II, 367.

That is properly called “thought” which is gathered together in the mind, that is, compelled together. I, 787. Democritus maintained that our thoughts arise only from images of bodies entering the mind. II, 445, 446. Epicurus likewise. II, 445, 446. Four kinds are found in thought. VIII, 996. In thought there is formed a unity of three things: memory, internal vision, and will. VIII, 988. Thought brings knowledge of things stored in the hidden recesses of the mind before the mind’s gaze. VIII, 1042. Thought presupposes the word. VIII, 1070. Thoughts are both utterances and visions—how this is so. VIII, 1070. Whether we can sometimes see our own thoughts. VI, 31. Why we wish our thoughts, now hidden, to be made manifest in heaven. V, 1145. Human beings are able to think of nothing except bodies. II, 517. When the mind thinks of bodies, their incorporeal likenesses appear before it. II, 614, 618. The Stoics and Epicureans cannot think except of corporeal things. II, 444. Some were not unaware of the understanding of incorporeal things. II, 444. Almost innumerable things are thought incorporeally and intelligibly by those who know how to think such things. II, 445. From this Democritus’ opinion concerning the cause of our thoughts is refuted. II, 445. Whence thought is carried toward various things. VIII, 994. To draw thought away from habit is a mark of great intelligence. II, 517. Thoughts are not hidden in heavenly bodies. III, 213. It is one thing to think and another to desire. X, 584. To think of the good is less than to desire it. X, 584. Sins are committed most easily and quickly in thought. X, 584. Thought becomes sin when consent is added in some way. X, 243. Just as sin is committed before human beings, so before God there is the sin of thought. V, 928. In thought each person is innocent; in thought each person is guilty. IV, 1571. Everyone sails in his own heart; he does not suffer shipwreck if he thinks good thoughts. V, 424.

Pious thought comes from God. I, 976. Good thoughts come only from grace. II, 818. In what pertains to piety, we are not capable of thinking anything as though it came from ourselves. X, 1013. A person’s thought cannot be changed permanently without grace. X, 448. It cannot happen that someone who has good thoughts has evil deeds. IV, 1838. For one who thinks about justice, something is present that is wholly everywhere. V, 1486.

What a blameworthy thought of evil is. X, 327. “For evil not even to enter one’s thoughts,” a statement of Pelagius’ that was brought against him in the episcopal Synod, insofar as he explained it himself. X, 324. To take pleasure in illicit thoughts without consent is not yet complete death, but is death begun in some manner. V, 594. The pleasures of illicit thoughts are sins. VIII, 1009. Evil thoughts kill the soul, even though they are not carried out in deed. IV, 1190. The struggle of evil thoughts in the heart of each person. IV, 1277. Evil thoughts must be cleansed. V, 268. Brooding thoughts. X, 596. It is difficult to distinguish thoughts introduced by the evil spirit. III, 465. They are distinguished only by God’s gift. III, 465. One should not judge concerning the thoughts of another. III, 1859.

Spiritual kinship with Christ is to be preferred to his bodily relationship. VI, 397.

The various ways of knowing are explained. II, 456, 457. The order by which knowledge comes about. III, 316. God knows in us even what we ourselves do not know. III, 1644. People are said to be known by God when he makes himself known to them. III, 303. Angelic knowledge. See *Angels*. A human being cannot possess full knowledge in this life. VI, 60. The knowledge of a creature has an evening and a morning—how this is so. VII, 322. Knowledge of each thing in the Word of God belongs to the day; knowledge of the thing in its own nature belongs to the evening. III, 313. There is a great difference between the two. III, 313. We know bodily things outside ourselves; spiritual things within ourselves. VIII, 954.

Knowledge of God. I, 872, 873. What is necessary for knowing God. I, 875, 876. Let us first love with complete charity the one whom we wish to know. I, 1331. If anyone desires to know God’s will, let him become God’s friend. III, 175. Unhappy is the person who knows other things but does not know God. Blessed, however, is the person who knows God, even if he knows nothing else. I, 708. Most blessed are those for whom possessing God is the same as knowing him. II, 840. No one comprehends the fullness of God. II, 606. It is no small beginning of the knowledge of God to know what he is not. II, 459. He is known better through not knowing; perfect knowledge of God belongs to the future life. I, 588. Knowledge of God through negations. III, 1588. The knowledge of God in the human soul consists in knowing how it does not know him. I, 1017. He is not known by bodily sense. I, 784. What knowledge of God is true and leads to eternal life. VI, 223. No one knows God unless he understands that God is the highest and unchangeable good, by participation in which one becomes good. II, 575. Creatures lead to knowledge of God. I, 745, 1275. Those who, knowing God through the things that have been made, do not obey the truth are without excuse. II, 895. When we know God, this too must not be attributed to ourselves but to his mercy. II, 574. The person who understands that even the ability to understand and know the Lord is given by the Lord himself understands and knows the Lord to no small degree. VII, 531. The reward of knowledge is granted according to the merit of faith. VI, 71. God is not found by the proud, even when they are learned. I, 707. The more we progress in the knowledge of God, the more we tend to live. III, 1905. To know God and not glorify him as God is impiety and foolishness. X, 212. The eminent knowledge of Christ will exist only in the next life. X, 545.

Knowledge and consideration of oneself. III, 1649. What kind of self-knowledge is useful. V, 756. Knowledge of oneself surpasses other sciences. VIII, 885. A human being is unknown to himself. I, 782, 979. It is difficult for each person to judge himself perfectly. IV, 1921. Withdrawal from the senses and recollection of the mind into itself are necessary for a human being to attain self-knowledge. I, 979. Whoever knows only what bodily sense touches seems to be not only with God, but not even with himself. I, 996. What affections self-knowledge arouses in the soul. VIII, 886. Knowledge of oneself makes a person displeased with himself, and thus pleasing to God. IV, 266, 267. One must pass from knowledge of oneself to knowledge of God. III, 1542.

Cognition that is certain and easy: whence it comes. VIII, 608. Cognition of truth with the heart purified. VI, 310. Cognition and action make a person blessed. VI, 299. “Cognition” is sometimes used for faith, sometimes for vision. III, 1922. “To know” sometimes means the same as “to approve.” IV, 1288.

**Cognitor (judicial commissioner).** V, 599.

The names of wicked men are not to be adopted. X, 511.

We are properly said to know someone when his character and life are not hidden. III, 1859. No one is known except through friendship. VI, 82.

Scripture defines worshiping God as true wisdom. I, 655. That worship is owed to the true God which the false god demands for himself. IV, 1220. Many forms of vain worship are rejected. III, 169. The wicked angel is not to be worshiped. III, 169. That no creature is to be worshiped by the soul: these are the very words once impressed upon the faithful by the Church. I, 1077. Nothing at all that any mortal bodily sense perceives is to be worshiped. I, 585. Since God is found to be greater and better than all things, he must be loved above all things in order to be worshiped. IV, 996. We ought to worship God freely and with chaste love. IV, 488, 617, 626, 658, 928, 1404, 1531, 1745. God is to be worshiped with faith, hope, and charity. VI, 232. For that is worshiped which is loved. IV, 996. God is worshiped by a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving. X, 214. All who worship God in a carnal manner are represented by Ishmael; the Old Testament belongs to these. IV, 1603. When the devil could not overthrow the Christian name, he suggested that, just as God was worshiped for heavenly things, so he himself should be worshiped for earthly things. IV, 456, 457. The same worship was offered to demons as to the true God. IV, 1220. Not only God but also human beings, and even other creatures, are said to be worshiped. VII, 278. See *Worship*. Atheists, who think that nothing should be worshiped, nevertheless serve their vices. III, 155. We do not worship God as though he were earth. I, 845. We worship God as Lord, and he worships us as his earth. IV, 295. God worships you and you worship God—not so that he may be fruitful, but so that you may be fruitful. IV, 1891; V, 316.

The *coloni* are so called from inhabiting, not from agriculture. VII, 278.

Collatina, the goddess placed over the hills. VII, 118.

Collatinus, Lucretia’s husband. VII, 32. See *Tarquinius*.

The contribution of private wealth for public uses. VII, 100. The Church’s public contribution for the needs of a man overwhelmed by debt. II, 1092.

The Carthaginian conference with the Donatists. II, 488; X, 336, 346, 704. Many on the Donatist side desire a conference between their bishops and the Catholics. IX, 523, 689. The Catholic bishops assembled at Carthage in council decided to meet the Donatists and offer them a conference. IX, 523, 810. A conference was offered to the Donatists repeatedly. IX, 391, 593. The Donatists refuse it. IX, 391, 593. The Donatists repeatedly refused the conference. IX, 43, 259, 651. And a meeting with the Catholics. IX, 656. Why they refused the repeatedly offered conference. IX, 449, 453. Because they distrust their bad cause, they do not wish to confer with the Catholics. IX, 592. The Donatists criticize the conference offered by the Catholics under the faulty name of contentiousness. IX, 548. A conference is a more expedient way of pursuing the cause of truth and unity than a lawsuit. IX, 548, 549. Primianus litigated against Maximianus in court through advocates. IX, 548. The Donatists are not to be approved because they refuse to confer with the Catholics concerning baptism. IX, 466, 467.

The emperor Honorius orders a conference to be held between the bishops of both parties. IX, 613. The decree of Honorius concerning the holding of the conference. IX, 816. Honorius wishes Marcellinus to preside in the principal place at the conference. IX, 817, 818, 819. Marcellinus’s edict by which the bishops of both parties are summoned. IX, 614. By what benefits the cognitor invites the Donatists to confer. IX, 614. Marcellinus’s edict concerning the place and procedure of the conference. IX, 614. The Donatists refused to agree to Marcellinus’s edict, which proposed the conditions for holding the Carthaginian conference. II, 490. The Catholics’ letter in which they reply that they agree to everything arranged in that edict. IX, 615, 821. With what attitude the Catholic bishops came to the conference. V, 1588. The Donatists’ formal notice. IX, 615, 805. The place assigned for the conference: the Gargilian Baths. IX, 620, 679, 819. What day was appointed for the conference. IX, 622, 818.

How the Carthaginian conference was conducted. II, 578. On what day and in what year the conference with the Donatists was held. IX, 613, 614, 616. How many bishops from each side the cognitor had designated to attend the conference. IX, 615, 677. The Catholics granted that all the Donatists who had come should be present. IX, 615. The number of Catholic and Donatist bishops who came to Carthage for the conference. IX, 620, 677, 827. By coming to the conference, the Donatists acknowledged that the Catholics were not traditors. IX, 651. What the Catholic bishops proposed they would do for the sake of peace if the truth of the Church were demonstrated either on Donatus’s side or in their own communion. IX, 615, 700, 701. The Catholic bishops did not enter Carthage with the pomp with which the Donatists entered it. IX, 618, 679. The opening of the conference. IX, 815. The Donatists did everything they could to prevent the conference from taking place and to prevent the proceedings from being easily read. IX, 613, 618, 688. The Donatists feared that the Catholics might retain any of their words. IX, 255, 257. They never wished proceedings to take place where they feared being defeated. IX, 679, 680. Their fear itself was their judge. IX, 680. The Donatists objected to the Catholics that other bishops had been added to the ancient episcopal seats in order to increase the number. IX, 618. It appeared that they themselves had done this in the diocese of Musti. IX, 618, 619. The Donatists were convicted of falsity in the reading of their bishops’ names. IX, 619, 677. The Donatists proposed to the Catholics that they should determine how they wished to proceed in the conference: by testimony from the Law or by public records. IX, 626, 831. The Catholics’ response. IX, 627, 679, 831. The Donatists’ formal notices and mandates, together with the Catholics’ responses. IX, 820, 821, 822, 827. The Catholics’ mandate, in which the entire case was summarized and the defense of the Catholic position was entrusted to seven bishops chosen for the debate. IX, 821. Thus, on the second day, the Catholics conducted the case in the drafting of the mandate in such a way that the Donatists could find no response. IX, 678. The Donatists’ evasions on the third day of the conference. IX, 679, 680. The Donatists tried to bring discredit upon the Catholics because they had requested a human cognitor. IX, 636, 637. It is apparent that the Donatists themselves had requested a human judge. IX, 636, 637.

Whether the Catholics were the petitioners in the conference. IX, 622, 623, 625, 679. Why the Catholics at times refused to assume the role of petitioners. IX, 624, 679. There is no doubt that the conference was requested by both sides. IX, 679, 818, 829, 830. The Donatists refused the meeting offered by the cognitor. IX, 619, 827. Why. IX, 621, 634. Their reason is rejected. IX, 621, 634. The Donatists confessed that they had no case against the transmarine Churches. IX, 682. From this their unjust separation is proved. IX, 682. The Donatists acted, spoke, and read out many things against themselves. II, 578, 579, 582. Caecilianus, accused in the conference. IX, 639. He is excused. IX, 641. To what extent the Catholic bishops wished the case of Caecilianus and the other bishops to be pursued in the conference. IX, 655, 826. The Donatists were more unjust toward Caecilianus than toward Primianus. IX, 553, 554, 641. And toward Novellus of Tysica and Faustinus of Turubis. IX, 676. In the pamphlet they produced and in the emperor’s letters, the Donatists show that they themselves had been condemned by Constantine rather than Caecilianus. IX, 685. Why the Donatists raised the case of Felix of Aptunga in the conference. IX, 686.

The conference cleared Caecilianus’s case. IX, 752. The Donatists requested and received a delay of six days. IX, 678, 828. After receiving the delay, the Donatists were unable at the conference to answer the Catholics’ mandate. IX, 682, 683. The cognitor’s judgment concerning everything done during the three days of the conference. IX, 653. The Donatists long refused to subscribe to the records of the conference. IX, 660. Later, when the judge insisted, they agreed. IX, 660. They rejected the name “brother” offered by the Catholics. IX, 749. The Donatists’ slander concerning Marcellinus, the cognitor of the conference. IX, 699. The Donatists said that the judge of the conference had been corrupted by a bribe. IX, 651, 655, 660, 676, [Col. 0173] 687. The Donatists complain that the judgment was pronounced against them at night. IX, 661. Their complaint is unjust. IX, 661, 689. The Donatists complained that they had been shut up as though in a prison. IX, 689. A response to the Donatists’ complaints about the human freedom taken away from them—freedom that God had granted them. IX, 716, 719. Whether freedom of choice was granted to the Donatists by the emperor. IX, 648, 650. Julian granted the Donatists the freedom of perdition. IX, 722. The Catholics refuted the Donatists at the Carthaginian conference. IX, 651, 652. And defeated them. II, 795. After the Carthaginian conference, nearly all the Donatists were converted. IX, 699.

The proceedings of the conference with the Donatists. V, 599. The records of the conference are customarily read publicly throughout the Churches on the days of Lent. IX, 700. *Brief Summary of the Conference with the Donatists*. I, 646. A book written against the same people after the conference. I, 646. Augustine refers Boniface to the summary of the Carthaginian conference. II, 795.

The hills signify the people of the faithful. IV, 1479.

The Collina Gate of Rome. VII, 125.

Conversation is the bond of fellowship. I, 1011.

Eye-salves for healing the sight of the mind: what they are. III, 1543.

A *collyris*, a bread baked under ashes. III, 377.

Color exists only in bodily things. V, 1498. Color is not a body but a certain quality of a body. I, 1197. Color is one for everyone—or rather, there is no color at all if light is removed. V, 1498. Colors properly belong to the sense of sight. VIII, 98. Whence the variety of colors in Jacob’s sheep. VIII, 877.

Colorbasus and his heresy. VIII, 28.

The nature and character of doves. III, 1366, 1427. The simplicity and other qualities of the dove are to be imitated. V, 426. What is signified by the dove sent from the ark and returning with an olive branch. VIII, 265. The dove signified the Holy Spirit. IV, 1706. The Father’s voice was heard on the mountain and the form of a dove was seen, without the ministry of a life-giving soul. II, 746. These things could have occurred through the ministry of angels. II, 747. In the dove the Holy Spirit was shown not in his own nature but in a symbolic form. II, 747. The dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared was a real dove. VI, 302. What it means to buy and sell a dove. IV, 1706. The dove is used as a sign of love. IV, 634.

The pillar of cloud was withdrawn when Jesus served as guide. III, 777.

Coluthus, from whom the Coluthians derive their name. VIII, 42.

**Comes.** II, 100. *Comes largitionum Italicianarum* [Count of the Italian largesses]. I, 728. An official of the *comes*. II, 430.

“To be reminded by commandments,” that is, to be admonished. III, 706.

*Commentarienses*. IV, 1200. Who they are. IV, 1200, note.

The divine dealings accomplished with us through the incarnate Christ. IV, 231, 1942. Christ’s dealings with us. V, 688, 725. The transaction of our redemption through the Son of God. IV, 1321, 1925.

Conjugal intercourse is good. X, 1411. The intercourse of chaste marriages for the purpose of procreation is a good work. X, 1437. The good of marriage. X, 1409. Conjugal intercourse is to be attributed to God. X, 1412. Not all intercourse of bodies is evil. X, 709, 710. The devil did not institute conjugal intercourse. X, 837. Conjugal intercourse would have existed even if no one had sinned. X, 837. The union of the sexes would also have occurred in paradise. X, 709. Conjugal intercourse would have been such that either there would have been no lust or it would not have been troubling. X, 837.

All who depart from the mercy of God’s love suffer agitation. VIII, 261.

The Apostle calls what is common “unclean” and “defiled.” I, 1360.

**To share.** See *To Give*.

The Donatists say that the good are defiled by communion with the wicked. I, 637. The Donatist rule: “Whatever those with whom communion has been shared were like, all become like them, and so does the whole mass.” IV, 378, 379. What it means to share in the sins and wickedness of others. IX, 517, 565, 657, 658. To share with the wicked is to consent to them. II, 265; IX, 79, 80. One shares in evil when one joins to another’s deed a partnership of will or approval. V, 549. Even known wicked people do not harm the good within the Church if either the power to exclude them from communion is lacking or some consideration for preserving peace prevents it. II, 297. Communion with the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments but through consent to their deeds. II, 579. Augustine does not act so that anyone should be compelled unwillingly to Catholic communion. II, 132, 135. When someone writes to members of another communion concerning a property matter, he is not criticized; but when he writes concerning a matter of the soul, it is not without suspicion. II, 160. Augustine writes to them letters of the sort that may be used with pagans. II, 154. Only spiritual fellowship with the wicked, and consent to their deeds, is forbidden. IX, 672, 673. They share at the altar, not with the wicked, whom they dislike even while tolerating them. II, 170. Christians become mutually sharers in labor and rest. II, 187. Whatever one person is less able to do, the person who is able does on his behalf, if he loves in the other what the other does not do because he is unable. II, 507. Augustine declares that he cannot share communion with one who does not share communion with Aurelius. II, 232. The emperors of our communion—that is, of the Catholic Church—issued laws against all heretics. IV, 684. Those who are not of their communion they call heretics. IV, 684.

Sometimes those who refuse to restore what they have taken away are deprived of communion at the holy altar. II, 663. They are excluded from it only if they have confessed voluntarily or have been lawfully convicted. V, 1541. See *Excommunication*. Preparation for communion. III, 1611, 1846. Daily communion. II, 201; VI, 691, 696. In some places communion is received daily, in others at fixed intervals of days. III, 1280, 1614. In the eastern regions most people do not receive communion at the Lord’s supper every day. III, 1280. Communion of infants. V, 943.

Common life. VI, 549. The common life of nuns is praised. IV, 1058. Let everything be held in common in the monastery. I, 1377, 1378. Things possessed in common do not generate the lawsuits, enmities, and other evils that arise from possession of private property. IV, 1748. What benefit did it bring the first Christians to make common property out of private possessions? IV, 1748.

Even pagans acknowledged that comedies could in no way have been accepted in writing or performance unless the morals of those who accepted them corresponded to them. II, 315.

**Comparison.** People are not to be compared with one another on the basis of isolated goods; rather, everything in each person must be considered as a whole. VII, 514. The force of the comparative degree. IX, 542, 544. The comparative degree does not always increase the thing it compares. IX, 583.

*Compartus*. VIII, 598.

Through the compassion of charity Christ is below and we are above through the hope of charity. IV, 1630. The tongue cries out through compassion when the foot is trodden on, not through friction. IV, 1105. What one member suffers becomes less when the other members suffer with it. II, 365.

The fetters of God’s discipline and fear. IV, 1305. Our fetters are mortality. IV, 1895. The persecutors released fetters by killing people and turned them into crowns. IV, 1306. See *Bonds*. Some people bound in fetters flee into the Church and are released; but there the fetters of marriage are fastened more tightly. IV, 1959.

“To shorten someone,” that is, to kill. III, 824.

**Competentes.** V, 1556. Whence they are so called. VI, 202, 203, 603. *Competentes*, as though “those petitioning together.” V, 1076. The Lord begins an agreement with the *competentes*. V, 1077. The creed of faith was delivered to the *competentes* to be memorized. I, 612; VI, 180. The creed was delivered to the *competentes* first, and the Lord’s Prayer afterward. V, 377. At the Easter vigil the *competentes* recited the creed, not the Lord’s Prayer. V, 399.

Self-complacency, the cause of the first sin. VII, 433.

A fellow presbyter. VI, 610.

Who is called “pierced in heart.” IV, 1440. Compunction arising from awareness of sin, fear of death, and fear of judgment. IV, 215.

**Endeavor.** “You have indeed given me free will, but without you my endeavor is nothing.” IV, 208.

How human conception proceeds and is completed. VI, 39. Why the Manichaeans command that conception of offspring be avoided. VIII, 420.

The most salutary authority of councils. II, 200. Obscure questions are not to be settled immediately even in a universal council. IX, 129. The letters of bishops and the decrees of provincial councils yield to greater councils. IX, 128. The earlier plenary councils themselves are corrected by later ones. IX, 129. And later councils are preferred to earlier ones by posterity. IX, 135. A plenary council. II, 200. A plenary council remains after the Roman judgment. II, 169. A bishop does not have control over the acts of a council when the Primate objects. II, 164. Catholic councils always had consuls and dates. IX, 639. The Catholics proved this both from the council of Miltiades and from Scripture. IX, 642. Whether it is proved from Scripture that councils ought to have a date and consuls. IX, 663.

Two African councils concerning the question of baptism. IX, 144, 145, 159. The council of the bishops of Africa and Numidia under Agrippinus. IX, 606. The Council of Carthage under Cyprian. IX, 141, 143. Its opening. IX, 128. The Council of Carthage was not followed concerning the rebaptizing of heretics. IX, 234. And it is refuted. IX, 161, 162. The Council of Carthage concerning the baptism of heretics condemns the Donatists. IX, 219. And accuses them of schism. IX, 220, 225. How devoted the fathers of the Council of Carthage were to unity. IX, 214. The Council of Carthage of all Africa concerning summoning the Donatists. IX, 523, App. 810. The Council of Carthage, the universal council of Africa, concerning the reconciliation of the Donatists. IX, App. 809. Various councils held at Carthage against the Donatists. IX, App. 802, 806, 807, 814. The Councils of Iconium and Synnada. IX, 495, 496, note. The plenary council at which the question of not repeating baptism was discussed. IX, 114, 135. The Council of Zerta in Numidia against the Donatists. I, 647; II, 577. The plenary Council of Hippo Regius of all Africa. I, 612; II, 92 note, 115 note, 233. Augustine, a presbyter, delivered a sermon there. I, 612. The Roman Council in the case of Caecilianus, under Miltiades. II, 399, 794. The Council of Arles in the case of Caecilianus. II, 161, 794; IX, 40. The Council of Milevis against the heresy of Pelagius. II, 762, 784. The Councils of Carthage and Milevis. X, 648. The writings of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis sent to Pope Innocent. X, 576. Two councils against the Pelagians sent to the Apostolic See. V, 734. The Council of Diospolis, or Palestine, in the case of Pelagius. II, 776, 827. See *Pelagius*. The Council of Carthage in the year 256. II, 339. The schismatic Council of Carthage in the year 311. II, 163, 492, 579. The Council of Carthage in the year 348 or 349 under Gratus. II, 235. The Council of Carthage in the year 397. II, 269. The Council of Carthage in the year 401. II, 228, 233, 235. Called plenary. II, 233. The Council of Carthage in the year 404. II, 805. The Carthaginian conference. II, 488. The Council of Carthage against Caelestius. I, 644; II, 759. Augustine did not attend it. I, 644. Another Council of Carthage against the heresy of Pelagius. II, 759, 779. Another Council of Carthage, concerning which letters were sent to Zosimus. II, 972. Another Council of Carthage called the plenary council of Africa. II, 972 and note.

The Council of Sardica belonged to the Arians. II, 176; IX, 516. It was convened against Athanasius, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria. IX, 516. The beginning of this council’s letter bears the name of Donatus, bishop of Carthage. IX, 516. It listed, without the names of their cities, the bishops to whom it was addressed. IX, 516.

The Donatist councils: the Council of Cirta, in the year 305. II, 161, 580; IX, 510. See *Cirta*. The schismatic council against Caecilianus. V, 960. The schismatic Council of Carthage against Caecilianus. IX, 533. Of seventy bishops. IX, 426. Under Secundus of Tigisis. IX, 443, 639. The Donatist Council of Carthage’s letters, sent throughout Africa, were readily believed. IX, 443. False accusation had alienated many from Caecilianus. IX, 443. Once the sacrilegious dissension against the entire Christian world had been exposed, many bishops, clergy, and people abandoned the Donatists and returned to Catholic peace. IX, 443. Another Carthaginian council of 270 schismatic bishops. II, 342 note. The Council of Carthage of forty-three bishops against Primianus. IX, 552. See *Carthaginian*. The Council of Bagai. II, 813; IX, 98, 426. See *Bagaitan*. The Donatists call it plenary. II, 192. The Council of Cabarsus. II, 580; IX, 503, 552. See *Cabarsus*. The Carthaginian council of thirty bishops after the conference. IX, 736. The council of the Maximianists against Primianus. V, 960.

**Concio (sermon).** Prayer during preaching. II, 117.

Those preaching. VII, 105, 106.

Augustine calls “fellow clergy” the clerics to whom he writes. II, 470.

God is the author of harmony and agreement. I, 1174. What musicians call harmony in song is concord in a state. VII, 66. The commandments of concord are taught in the Churches of Christ. II, 529. The worshipers of false gods did not possess commandments of concord such as are taught in the Churches of Christ. II, 529. Concord is the people’s salvation. VII, 655. Concord cannot exist without justice. VII, 66. The kind of concord with God required of human beings. V, 82. Why concord among brothers is rare. V, 1590. Concord among brothers in the heavenly inheritance. V, 1593. The concord of those who place their hope only in secular things is not very firm. IV, 625. The concord of pagans who quarrel over the worship of disputing gods. VI, 712. Why the devil introduces quarrels among Christians but not among pagans. VI, 713. The usefulness of such quarrels. VI, 714. Every effort must be made to restore those who quarrel to concord. VI, 714. The concord of bodily members recalls Christians to unity. VI, 712. The perfect concord of flesh and spirit after the resurrection. VI, 274. In the homeland there will be supreme joy and supreme concord. III, 1656. Perfect concord and security among those who praise God exist only in heaven. V, 1190.

Concordia, the goddess. VII, 105, 132. Concordia was vainly regarded as a goddess by the Romans. VII, 106. A temple of Concordia was built in a place of seditions and slaughter. VII, 105, 106.

*Concordialis*. II, 592.

Concubines are sometimes called wives. VII, 513. Every concubine is a wife, but not every wife is a concubine. III, 571. It is not permissible to keep concubines. V, 1710. Any concubine other than a wife is a prostitute. V, 1094. When a dismissed concubine has professed that she will know no other man, it is rightly questioned whether she should be admitted to baptism. VI, 221. The sons of concubines signify heretics and carnal Jews. VII, 513.

Intercourse is established solely for the sake of procreation. VIII, 438. Conjugal intercourse undertaken with the intention of procreation is not sin. X, 421, 816. When intercourse is honorable, when venial, and when culpable. X, 819. Conjugal intercourse undertaken through incontinence is sin. VIII, 494. See *Marriage*, *Nuptials*. Intercourse for the sole pleasure of lust [Col. 0176] is not free from guilt, but because of marriage it is venial. X, 423, 807. The Law says that a person is made unclean by conjugal intercourse. I, 652. The intercourse of male and female is a sign of mortal bodies. III, 293. How intercourse of the ancients with slave women could occur without adultery. V, 349. Even conjugal intercourse seeks a bed removed from observers. VII, 426.

**Lust.** X, 719, 829, 868, 1236. Lust concerns things present as well as absent, whereas desire concerns only things absent. IV, 1521. That lust exists in human beings is demonstrated. X, 279. No one is born now without lust. II, 844; X, 1097, 1223. Anyone who admits lust does not agree with the Paterniani or Venustiani. X, 800. Some lust is praiseworthy, other lust condemnable; the latter is understood whenever the term is used without qualification. IV, 1520. If it is not stated what sort of thing is desired, “lust” is understood in an evil sense. VII, 411. The lusts in us are evil when we take pleasure in what is not permitted. VI, 362. Every evil lust is rightly called fornication. III, 1247.

Carnal lust and spiritual lust. VI, 352. The flesh lusts against the spirit in good people, for in evil people it has no one against whom to lust. V, 717. The discord that exists between spirit and flesh strives toward concord. V, 821, 849. Carnal lust is considered in relation to the four degrees of human beings. III, 2065. Carnal lust signifies lovers of the lowest pleasure. III, 153. The lust of the eyes signifies the curious, and worldly ambition the proud. III, 153. Even if lust sometimes makes use of the eye, ear, tongue, or fleeting thought, we must not therefore despair of salvation. V, 846. Esau condemned not the food itself but the food he desired, even to the point of despising the sacrament that he possessed in his primacy. II, 141.

The desire for another’s property that is forbidden by the tenth commandment. V, 71. It is not permitted to desire one’s neighbor’s property, even if a lawful succession is being sought there. V, 71. One is reproved for desiring another’s property. IV, 451.

Three contrary opinions concerning carnal lust. X, 1434. What the Manichaeans think about lust. V, 815, 821; VIII, 38; X, 1324. The Manichaeans attribute lust to the nation of darkness. X, 1334, 1336. The Manichaean says that lust is an evil substance. X, 1320. It is not a defect of a good substance. X, 1325. How opposed the Catholic faith is to the Manichaean error. X, 1325. Concerning the discord of flesh and spirit, the Manichaeans and Pelagians are altogether mistaken. X, 1514. The Manichaean and Pelagian opinions concerning lust. X, 1435. According to the Manichaeans, whence comes the lust of the flesh against the spirit and of the spirit against the flesh. X, 1510. According to the Pelagians, the discord of flesh and spirit arises from the force of habit; according to the Manichaeans, from the mingling of the natures of good and evil. X, 1322. How the Manichaean and Pelagian errors concerning lust differ from one another and from the Catholic faith. X, 1350. How greatly the Catholic faith concerning the discord of flesh and spirit abhors the Manichaean error. X, 1510. The Catholic doctrine concerning lust is contrary to both errors, that of the Manichaeans and that of the Pelagians. X, 1321. Although they say in common that lust is evil, the Manichaeans and Catholics differ very greatly from one another. X, 1469.

Julian said that lust was, in itself, a natural and innocent affection. X, 1094, 1095. Julian calls lust natural, not carnal lust. X, 297. Julian praised lust. X, 769. The Pelagians are ashamed to name lust but are not ashamed to praise it. X, 446. Lust praised by Julian as a good and placed in paradise. X, 1274, 1275, 1284. Julian places the discord of flesh and spirit in paradise. X, 1408.

The Pelagians place lust in paradise. X, 1093, 1236, 1327, 1336, 1340, 1341. Even lust of the kind that exists now. X, 1514, 1531, 1536. Lust would not have existed in paradise. V, 717; X, 1344, 1357, 1359. Carnal lust against the spirit would not have existed in paradise if human beings had not sinned. X, 1091, 1092, 1093, 1344, 1358, 1359. The law in the members resisting the law of the mind did not exist in paradise. X, 439, 1438. It did not exist before sin. X, 732. Lust did not exist in the body of that life which existed in paradise before sin. X, 1439. If lust existed in paradise before sin, then even at that time free will was not effective in the first parents. X, 1514. Either there was no lust in Adam before sin, or it was corrupted in him through sin. X, 1553. What carnal lust might have been like if no one had sinned. X, 1347, 1359, 1360, 1363. Carnal lust either did not exist in paradise before sin or, if it did, it was not such as to resist the will. VIII, 1032; X, 772, 802.

Lust is not a sense but a quality. X, 856. Sense is one thing, lust another. X, 1379. The power of sensing and the power of desiring are different. X, 1353. The horrifying absurdity that follows from the Pelagian error concerning lust. X, 1367, 1369, 1370. Julian says that carnal lust, mingled with the senses of the whole body, existed in Christ. X, 1370.

[Col. 0177] Julian called lust good. X, 1120. Julian considers carnal lust good even when what is desired is evil. X, 1335. Lust is not good. X, 798, 815. Lust is neither truly condemned by the Manichaean nor truly praised by Julian. X, 1346. Lust is evil. X, 738, 739, 740, 742, 775, 799, 801, 802, 817, 820, 842, 1098, 1350, 1351, 1374, 1376, 1379, 1390, 1461. Carnal lust is an evil accident of our nature, not to be removed by separating it off from God, but to be healed by God’s mercy. X, 607. Ambrose calls lust “sacrilegious hunger.” X, 1095, 1096. Lust is evil both in married people and in the continent. X, 740, 741. Lust would not be evil if it moved someone to permitted intercourse solely for the purpose of procreation. X, 762. Whoever fights against lust admits that it is evil. X, 724, 725, 727, 728. Carnal lust is evil. X, 764, 1379. Lust is evil even according to the opinion of the philosophers. X, 852. Lust exists here and must be restrained and diminished, but in the blessed it must be completely healed. X, 1317. Lust is evil because it impels one toward evil. X, 1120. Carnal lust, whether now running toward unlawful things or merely impelling one toward them, is evil. X, 1452. For Julian, not lust itself but only excess was evil. X, 716. Lust itself is evil, not merely its excess. X, 722. In Julian’s opinion, lust itself is not evil even when it is immoderate. X, 1348. Lust itself is evil, and did not begin to exist until after sin. X, 1436. Why lust is worse than ignorance. X, 741. Augustine convicts Julian in his own words when he discusses lust. X, 723, 724, 727.

Whence and by whom the defect of lust can be healed. X, 276. Lust is not from the Father. X, 768. The human being is God’s work, not lust, without which human beings are not generated. X, 446. Julian taught that carnal lust began to exist in humanity before guilt. X, 1352. The form of the limbs does not demonstrate that carnal lust existed in such a form before sin. X, 1438. An evil will preceded lust. X, 1095. Lust did not exist before sin. X, 1605. Lust would not exist if humanity had not first sinned. X, 413. Through the transgression of the first human being, lust was turned into our nature. X, 239, 1097, 1147, 1274, 1345, 1350, 1361, 1394, 1408, 1414, 1453, 1514, 1608.

Lust is our languor, not another nature. V, 816. Lust is a disease. X, 717. Whoever acknowledges the remedy for lust acknowledges the disease of lust. X, 723. Lust is a defect of nature. X, 800. Lust is either a defect or something that has been corrupted. X, 1237. Lust in human nature was either born from sin or corrupted by sin. X, 1360. Lust is an evil arising from the depravity of our nature, corrupted by sin. X, 1453, 1461, 1469. The holy Fathers before the Pelagians said that lust had corrupted human nature. X, 1095, 1097. Lust and the other evils of the human race arise only from the good nature established by God but corrupted through the transgression of the first human being. X, 1325, 1328, 1338. According to the Catholics, the discord of flesh and spirit arises from the sin of the first human being. X, 1322.

Lust comes from sin. X, 820, 1081. Everyone born from Adam carries with him the transmission of iniquity. IV, 734. Lust could exist only in this body of death. III, 400. Carnal lust against the spirit arises from the first sin. VII, 788. Lust is innate in us and arose from the first sin. V, 817.

The punishment of lust. X, 630. Lust is the punishment of sin. VI, 362; X, 261, 1378. This resulted from the punishment of sin: that the human being should be divided against himself, because he refused to be subject to one ruler. IV, 891. See *War*. The violence of lust, by which one who knows what he ought to abstain from is overcome, is not only sin but also the punishment of sin. X, 1539. Carnal lust is a punishment for human beings, not for animals. X, 1359. Why lust is not evil in animals. X, 776.

Lust is sometimes called sin. I, 608; VI, 353. Lust is sin. X, 1336, 1605. It is not sin for one who does not consent to it. II, 893. The Apostle calls lust by the name of sin. X, 560. Why carnal lust is called sin. V, 840; VIII, 93, 94. And in what sense. X, 428, 563, 696, 1243. It is called sin because it occurred as the deserved consequence of sin. V, 717. Carnal lust is the law of sin. X, 432. Why lust is called the law of sin and why it is called sin. X, 1096. Lust is both sin, the punishment of sin, and the cause of sin. X, 787. Carnal lust is the daughter and mother of sin. X, 429. Lust is the same thing as the law of sin resisting the law of the mind. X, 1097. Lust resists the law of the mind. X, 798. Human beings justly suffer lust. V, 821. One must not murmur against God on account of lust but seek his mercy. X, 260.

Lust is a foul law, a wretched law, a wound, corruption, and languor. [Col. 0178] V, 819. Lust itself is accused by its own movements. X, 742. The movement of lust is its act. X, 859. Why people are ashamed of carnal lust. X, 1445. The carnal disobedience that is both penal and shameful. X, 1378. Lust would not be shameful if humanity had not first sinned. X, 467, 1085. Humanity would have been procreated without lust if sin had not preceded it. X, 446. There would have been intercourse of bodies, but without lust, if sin had not preceded it. X, 730.

Carnal concupiscence is not to be charged against marriage. X, 606, 424, 607. The evil of concupiscence must be distinguished from the goodness of marriage. X, 414.
