What difference exists between Catholics and Pelagians concerning the use of concupiscence. X, 723, 727. Who is to be judged to use the evil of concupiscence without being overcome by it. X, 419. The Apostle does not condemn the use of carnal concupiscence. X, 1324. God gave Abraham and Sarah fertility; He did not arouse concupiscence. X, 449. Carnal concupiscence does not produce the semen, but arouses it. X, 451. The good use of concupiscence is praised in marital intercourse. X, 1462. In marriage one must not serve concupiscence; rather, concupiscence itself must be compelled to serve the propagation of offspring. X, 424. Concupiscence must also be restrained in marriage. X, 807. The disease of concupiscence in marriage should arise not from the will but from necessity. X, 418. Concupiscence serves in marriage, but reigns in adultery. X, 421. The marriages of the faithful convert carnal concupiscence to the service of righteousness. X, 416. The goodness of marriage does not extinguish the evil of concupiscence, but moderates it. II, 844. Chaste marriages make good use of the evil of concupiscence. X, 178, 730, 1437. A parent also makes good use of the evil of concupiscence when he begets a son chastely, and God does so when He creates a human being providentially. X, 723. Conjugal chastity resists concupiscence. X, 1236.

Carnal concupiscence is not found only in the pleasure of the genitals, but in every bodily sensation. X, 1352. What it means to desire the flesh. X, 845. To desire the flesh means to desire the soul itself in a carnal manner. X, 301. The cause of carnal concupiscence lies not in the flesh alone, but also in the soul. III, 416.

The devil found no concupiscence in Christ. X, 444. Christ did not possess carnal concupiscence resisting the spirit. X, 1374. There was no concupiscence in Christ. X, 816. Christ’s virtue was not to possess concupiscence; our virtue is not to consent to it. X, 1365. See Christ. All, with one exception, are formed from the pleasure of concupiscence. X, 684, 720. Whatever is born through concupiscence is rightly subjected to the devil on account of sin. X, 428. Original sin arises from this vice. X, 1193. Original sin is derived not from marriage but from concupiscence. X, 730. Concupiscence is inherited by those who are begotten carnally even from parents who have been regenerated. X, 563. Concupiscence, which is expiated only through baptism, transmits the bond of sin to descendants. X, 428. The guilt of concupiscence makes a person guilty originally. X, 829. The law of sin with guilt in unbaptized infants. X, 434. Concupiscence binds unbaptized infants under guilt. X, 152.

Concupiscence is an evil, and remains after baptism. X, 852. The guilt of concupiscence remains in the children of those who have been regenerated until it is washed away by baptism. X, 407. Concupiscence remains in the baptized. X, 848, 850, 1117. But without guilt. V, 590, 752, 820. Carnal concupiscence remains in the offspring even when its guilt has been absolved in the parent. X, 407. The most courageous conquerors of concupiscence are not defiled by its evil. X, 1322.

The guilt of concupiscence is released only by baptism. X, 855. Concupiscence is so forgiven in baptism that, although it has been transmitted into those who are born, it does no harm to those who are reborn. X, 563. Concupiscence is forgiven in baptism, not brought to an end. X, 678. Its guilt is released in baptism, yet weakness remains. I, 609. If nature were healed from every weakness just as it is healed from guilt through regeneration and the forgiveness of sins, the spirit would not desire against the flesh. X, 1452. How the evil of concupiscence remains after it has been put to death in the baptized. X, 178, 430. In what sense concupiscence is dead after baptism, when it already arouses so many evil desires. X, 696. Concupiscence is present in one who is born and in one who is reborn; it harms the former but does not harm the latter. X, 407. The guilt of concupiscence is released after baptism while concupiscence itself remains. X, 178, 179. Concupiscence is forgiven with respect to guilt, but remains in its activity. X, 676.

The extent to which concupiscence exists in us. X, 152. The hidden force of concupiscence after its guilt has been released, until the complete transformation takes place. X, 434. The force of concupiscence is dormant in an infant. X, 1246. And hidden. X, 679. In what sense concupiscence remaining after baptism is called iniquity. X, 683, 793. Whether, and when, concupiscence in the baptized is sin. X, 678. Concupiscence without consent is not sin. II, 893; X, 428, 1316. Concupiscence does not harm the baptized; only consent to it does. X, 152, 1605. It does not make people evil when what pleases the evil inclination is not done because a good pleasure prevails. VI, 362. Concupiscence [Col. 0179] would not harm us if we obeyed none of its unlawful desires. IV, 1507. The devil will harm you in no way if, when you withdraw your members from him, he does not hold them. V, 1077. Just as concupiscent disobedience is without guilt in the body of one who is asleep, so it is without guilt in the body of one who does not consent. VII, 39. Whoever consents to concupiscence cannot say, “It is not I who do it,” and so forth. X, 560. Many defeated by damnable concupiscences excuse themselves with the Apostle’s words, “So that you do not do the things you wish.” V, 716. Concupiscence does not entail the necessity of crime. X, 815. Evil concupiscence displeases God even in the baptized. X, 848. It is sin not merely to feel concupiscence, but to follow it. X, 789.

The saints do not lack the movements of concupiscence in this life. III, 2061, 2062, Retr.; V, 718. The holy married Fathers permitted themselves intercourse with their wives as far as was lawful; but they did not endure the force of concupiscence as far as it was lawful. III, 422. Chaste and good marriage laws do not allow concupiscence to prevail except to the extent that they can use it to provide for the succession of the human race. III, 424. The Apostles groaned because of carnal concupiscence. X, 562. How concupiscence held the Apostle captive. X, 432. The Apostle did not say without reason, “Let there be no concupiscences,” or “Do not produce them,” but “Do not bring them to completion.” V, 716, 717, 719, 815. Whether we wish it or not, we have them. V, 718. The Apostle himself was not without concupiscence. V, 834. Carnal concupiscence is nothing other than the desire for sin. X, 297. The desires of concupiscence are evil. X, 430. Why God does not remove all carnal concupiscence from us altogether. X, 752.

Why concupiscence remains in the baptized. X, 829. Concupiscence was made a punishment from sin, but from the punishment merit can arise. III, 400. The extent to which concupiscence promotes innocence. X, 742. The guilt of concupiscence has been released through regeneration, but its struggle has been left for the contest. X, 1096, 1097. Concupiscence is not completely extinguished by baptism; it remains for combat. X, 150. Concupiscence whose guilt has been released does no harm when one fights against it. X, 861. The struggle against concupiscence. X, 679, 682, 683. See Contest, Struggle, Combat. From the time we desire Jerusalem, concupiscence contends against us. IV, 775. If there is no quarrel in you, see whether perhaps there is no war because the peace is perverse. V, 189. Only warriors of the virtues and conquerors of vices experience the battle against concupiscence. VI, 353. The whole life of the saints is a war. V, 818, 821. It is better to fight with concupiscences than to have peace with them. VII, 729.

Concupiscence is greater in some and lesser in others. X, 1424, 1428. Whom concupiscence attacks more fiercely. X, 855. Youth has more aggressive enemies; old age has smaller ones, but it still has them. V, 719. Concupiscence is less powerful so long as one sins not knowingly but ignorantly. X, 1605. Concupiscence is believed to be stronger or weaker through weakness and ignorance, according as each person is better or worse. X, 152. Concupiscence has room to grow. X, 1605. Concupiscence strengthened by habit is more vehement. X, 855. Both sins committed voluntarily and the habit of sinning add strength to concupiscence. X, 1605. By following concupiscences, strength is added to them. III, 1699. Concupiscence has strength over one who is subjected to it. V, 816.

Through the vice of concupiscence a person commits many things, either through weakness or blindness. X, 261, 263. The fire of concupiscences does not allow one to see the truth. IV, 688, 689. Sins of concupiscence occur in the use of things that have been permitted and are lawful. X, 300. Certain venial falls of concupiscence. X, 696. Whoever yields to carnal concupiscences, whether thinking them good or knowingly following them as evil, is wholly carnal. V, 836. Carnal concupiscence is the punishment with which God strikes the carnal. III, 828. How God hands people over to concupiscences. X, 793. He hands them over not by compelling them, but by abandoning them. V, 391.

Concupiscence is not lust until it is brought to completion. X, 1383. What it means to bring concupiscences to completion. V, 719; X, 733. Even when the law in the members resists the law of the mind, there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ. X, 433. How concupiscence does evil without bringing it to completion. V, 818. How it does not allow good to be brought to completion. V, 938. Not to desire at all belongs to the perfect; not to follow one’s desires belongs to the person who is fighting. V, 816, 836. The threefold degree of those who obey concupiscences, represented by the three dead persons whom the Lord raised. V, 720.

Concupiscence must be resisted. V, 597; X, 775. Concupiscence can be resisted, although one cannot be entirely without it. X, 799. Carnal concupiscence, with which we are born through transmission, must be conquered quickly. IV, 688. Concupiscences do not want to follow you; do not follow them. They rebel—rebel against them; they fight—fight; they assault—assault; only see to it that they do not conquer. V, 816. A great reward is prepared for those who conquer concupiscence through grace. III, 400. It is not impossible to conquer concupiscence. III, 400. Concupiscence can be subdued by its assailants, not by those who praise it. X, 1343. [Col. 0180] How one must resist concupiscence and evil habit. V, 719, 816; VII, 38. Concupiscence is not extinguished by the commanding letter through fear of punishment, but by the assisting Spirit through love of righteousness. VIII, 654. Knowledge of the law is not sufficient to conquer concupiscence. V, 794.

The evil of concupiscence was unknown before the Law. V, 828. Concupiscence is not even counted as an enemy by those who do not know God’s Law. VI, 353. When concupiscence becomes known through the Law, it increases and becomes unconquerable. VI, 103, 353. Concupiscence is increased by the prohibition of the Law, not healed. II, 893, 894; III, 2065, 2068, 2070. Concupiscence was increased through the Law, not conquered. V, 829. When you hear, “You shall not covet,” if grace is absent, you have heard your punishment. V, 792. It is not enough for a person to impose laws upon the innate movements within himself. X, 820. One who trusts in himself must fear lest sin thereby gain much greater dominion over him. VI, 357. If you place your hope in the spirit by which you are human, your spirit will again relapse into the flesh. V, 830. Concupiscence is not removed by fear of punishment. V, 949. Concupiscence rages in the person who abstains from evil deeds not through delight in righteousness but through fear of punishment. V, 82. God’s commandments are weapons against concupiscence. V, 719.

Concupiscence is an evil, and it is resisted only with God’s help. X, 1096. Concupiscence is conquered only through grace. VI, 353. Charity conquers the concupiscences of the flesh. III, 2061. Retr. The evil concupiscence is not yielded to when the delight of righteousness prevails. VI, 225, 287. The delights of concupiscence and of God’s Law. V, 830, 838, 839. It is God’s Spirit who fights in you against you, against that which is in you and against you. V, 717. Christ lives in those who fight against concupiscences. X, 866. The languor of concupiscence is a tyrant; if you wish to be its victor, invoke Christ as commander. V, 190. The final three petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are to be used against concupiscence. X, 153. Although the struggle with concupiscence is not damnable, it is nevertheless pitiable. X, 440. The struggle with concupiscence diminishes spiritual delight and the perfection of righteousness. X, 742. Even vigorous warriors are not without wounds from sins. VI, 357. A part that is somewhat free resists the remnants of servitude. V, 189. Concupiscence, once conquered, neither reigns nor fights, yet it remains present. IV, 1860. When your members are not made weapons of iniquity, iniquity is indeed in the members, but it does not reign. V, 190.

In whom concupiscence reigns. X, 1243. Concupiscence reigns when its desires are obeyed. III, 417; V, 719; VI, 354. So that it may not reign, hold your members and do not arm your adversary with them against you. V, 719. Grace ensures that concupiscence does not dominate. VI, 357. The kingdom of concupiscence is overthrown only through grace. V, 190. Nothing except grace frees one from the domination of concupiscence. III, 2061. As far as the saints are concerned, concupiscence loses its kingdom in this life and perishes in the next. V, 840, 841. When concupiscence does not reign, the mind has more authority to hold the members of the flesh than concupiscence itself has to move them. V, 841. From the one who gave a person victory over concupiscence, so that he would not be dragged away by pleasure, he also receives strength for endurance, so that he will not be broken by pain. IV, 1577. When concupiscence is rightly overcome. X, 788.

Concupiscence is diminished. X, 855. How. X, 856. Concupiscence can be diminished in this life, but cannot be consumed. X, 851. The diminution of desire is progress in holiness. X, 845. Concupiscence, or our necessity, is diminished through grace and brought to an end through grace. X, 1279. Concupiscence is diminished in those who are making progress and increased in the incontinent. X, 430. Continence crucifies the concupiscences of the flesh in a certain manner. VI, 355.

Concupiscence exists both in married people and in those who practice continence; why. X, 742. Why it is not completely extinguished in those who practice continence. X, 742. Women are not immune from the movement of concupiscence. X, 798. Concupiscence lays ambush for the saints in such a way that it does to them while they sleep what it cannot do while they are awake. V, 819. It is not in human power to be free from the violence of concupiscence. X, 1539. It is not in the soul’s power not to desire, so long as sin remains in the members. III, 417.

Concupiscence can be diminished as long as we live, but cannot be brought to an end. V, 817. Concupiscence can be conquered until it is healed completely, just as a wound in the body is healed by a perfect cure. X, 722. In this mortal life it is difficult even for those under grace to fulfill in every respect what is written in the Law, “You shall not covet.” VIII, 552. The commandment “You shall not covet” is not perfectly fulfilled here. II, 893. Why does the Law say, “You shall not covet,” if it is not fulfilled here? X, 432. It shows not what we are capable of here, but toward what we are to strive by making progress. II, 893. We ought in every way to wish to root out unlawful concupiscences completely, although this is not granted in this life. V, 892. Which words belong to those fighting against concupiscences, and which to those triumphing over them. V, 892. The destruction of concupiscence must be among our desires. V, 189, 815, 820, 892. You are a person of evil desire if you do not wish to be free from such an adversary. V, 189. When all concupiscence is present. X, 1605. To have no concupiscence does not belong [Col. 0181] to the present life but to the future. X, 1383. Concupiscence first leads those who follow it, then drags those who resist; after grace has been received, it neither drags nor leads, but still contends; after the contest comes victory. IV, 775. Not to covet is the fullness of virtue, the perfection of righteousness, and the palm of victory. V, 816. Concupiscence is eventually to be put to death by the grace of Christ. V, 819. There will be no concupiscence at the end. X, 153. The rebellious movements of concupiscence will not rest in the righteous until they possess incorruptible flesh. I, 623. Concupiscence will not exist when we no longer possess a mortal body. X, 1243. Concupiscence will not exist in the perfection of righteousness. X, 300. Then a person will be free from every evil, when there is nothing for him to resist. X, 1452. Concupiscence will not exist in the bodies of the blessed after the resurrection. X, 433, 562. The carnal concupiscence that is now a pleasure to the ungodly will afterward be turned into torments. X, 852. The ungodly person is not freed from concupiscence by dying. X, 277, 561. See Body of sin, Law, Lust, Flesh.

Concupiscence represented by hay. IV, 1242. Carnal concupiscence is compared to a river. III, 1308. Concupiscence is represented by the woman, and the mind by the man. VI, 579. Concupiscence is dropsy. V, 410.

Condemnation on account of original sin. X, 440. Grace alone, the grace of Christ, frees from the condemnation into which everyone is born. X, 116.

Augustine calls a deacon whom he is discussing a “con-deacon.” II, 630, 644, 758, 868, 999, 1001.

We are all fellow disciples under Christ the teacher. V, 155.

Confession is the same as the creed of faith. VI, 276. Those who professed the Christian faith in order to be admitted into Christ’s household were called “confessors.” VII, 45. Note (a). Confession of faith without shame. V, 1279. What it means to confess to God. I, 779. Nothing is nearer the ears of God than a confessing heart and a life proceeding from faith. I, 677. It is little to have Christ in one’s heart and refuse to confess Him when reproach is feared. IV, 1436, 1437. The great fruits of such confessions. I, 781. Confession is twofold: of sin or of praise. IV, 108, 225, 513, 1020, 1218, 1405, 1463, 1495, 1774, 1844, 1878. Confession is sometimes used in praise of God. III, 1366. Confession is twofold: that of one who praises and that of one who repents. V, 186, 435, 952. Both are owed to God. V, 186. In either matter—that is, in your sin, because you committed it, and in a good deed—confess to the Lord because He accomplished it. IV, 1173. When things go badly for us, let us confess our sins; when things go well, let us confess praise to God; nevertheless, let us not be without confession. IV, 225. We always have something to confess. IV, 1281. Confess now what you have done against God, and eternally you will confess what God has done for you. IV, 226. Let the person who wishes to reach divinity confess his weakness. IV, 1907.

Confession of sins. III, 635; V, 90, 153; VI, 358. Confession of sins is necessary for salvation. V, 138, 186, 756. The medicine of confession. V, 139, 982. The medicine of confession and repentance is necessary for the sinner. VIII, 419. On the usefulness and necessity of confession. IV, 408, 253, 808, 959, 1079, 1080, 1219, 1232, 1318, 1761, 1827, 1853, 1861, 1883. Confession is a sacrifice to God. IV, 1233. The confession of a sinner is itself also praise of God. V, 433. First accuse yourself; having accused yourself, praise God. IV, 1908. When confession is lost, there will be no place for mercy. IV, 854. The confession of a human being is human humility; God’s compassion is God’s exaltation. III, 1504. Confession of sins belongs to the righteous; defense of merits belongs to the proud. V, 1382. The first grace of God’s benefaction is to bring a person to confess his weakness, so that whatever power we have may come from Him. IV, 428. God questioned Adam in order to compel him to confess his sin. III, 207. Let a person confess what he is, so that he may be healed by the One who always is what He is. III, 1982. Before the Lord comes, let us condemn by confession what we have done, so that He may find something to crown rather than something to condemn. IV, 1219. Human righteousness itself consists in not sparing oneself in confession. III, 839. Just as God hates one who defends his sins, so He raises up one who confesses them. IV, 1885. It is a pact of fellowship with iniquity to take pleasure in confessing it rather than avoiding it. VI, 425. Are you afraid to confess, although by failing to confess you cannot remain hidden? You will be condemned in silence, though you could be freed by confessing. IV, 808. Why do we confess to God, who knows everything? I, 809. Confession of evil works is the beginning of good works. III, 1491, 2006. Reformation begins with confession and is completed through good works. IV, 1281, 1338, 1908. The sinner who confesses proceeds from darkness into light. III, 1578. The smoke of confessing sinners draws tears from proud persons who have been humbled. IV, 1865. When the name of confession was heard, the people used to beat their breasts. IV, 1495, 1774, 1844; V, 186, 435.

Confession comes before everything, then love. III, 1982. A person corrected by his own confession is reproached with greater and truer glory than any erring person is praised by the mouth of another. X, 548. Do not be secure after you have confessed a sin, as though you were always ready both to confess and to commit sin; take care that you may be healed. IV, 409, 1335. The confession of sins must be joined with praise of God; otherwise it is not devout unless it does not despair and asks God’s mercy. IV, 1406. After confession God will not bring punishment if you also do not repeat the iniquity. V, 300. Through confession the scruple of conscience must be removed. V, 300. What benefit does the Church provide for one who confesses, if he first had to be raised from the dead by the Lord? V, 434. In confession of sins the Church opened her mouth to receive the blood of Christ. VIII, 259. The confession of the rich man in hell. IV, 93. Confession commended in the commandment concerning not eating what has been strangled. VIII, 265.

The books of the *Confessions*, written around the year 400. I, 652.

One must trust in God alone, not in an angel. IV, 1496. Not in oneself. V, 829. To trust in a human being rather than in the Lord is wretched and deadly. IV, 1889, 1890. One must trust in Christ not because He is the Son of Man but because He is the Son of God. IV, 1890.

*Confit.* II, 80.

The conflict of flesh and spirit also exists in the saints. X, 1527. The conflict of flesh and spirit is described by Gregory of Nazianzus. X, 1528.

Conformation, which is one of the original goods: what it is. VII, 788. How many fraternal congregations there are in the Catholic communion. VIII, 225. The various kinds of people who have undertaken a life in congregations. VIII, 225.

What confusion is. IV, 856. Lust is the cause of confusion. VII, 778. There is a certain salutary confusion. IV, 328. Confusion is the beginning of conversion. IV, 868. One confusion is temporal, another eternal. IV, 233. Temporal confusion is useful: it is the disturbance of the mind as it looks upon its sins, is horrified by seeing them, blushes with horror, and corrects itself through shame. IV, 232. A Christian should not fear temporal confusion; if he does not have it, he will have eternal confusion. IV, 232. Confusion that leads to sin, and confusion that leads to grace. II, 346. At the judgment those will be ruinously confounded who now refuse to be salutarily confounded. IV, 1098.

Why it happens that soothsayers sometimes foretell the truth. VII, 722.

The blasphemy of the Manichaeans that marriage comes from the devil. VIII, 367. What the Manichaeans find hateful in marriage. VIII, 310, 365. The Manichaeans condemn the use of marriage. I, 1344, 1372, 1373. Ambrose and the Catholics praise marriage. X, 1407. What is disputed between Augustine and Julian concerning marriage. X, 811. Whether marriage is a species of nature. X, 1461.

The sacrament of marriage is great in Christ and the Church, but least in husband and wife. X, 427. Marriage is made not by carnal intercourse but by conjugal love. V, 344. The union of souls is dearer than the mingling of bodies. VIII, 470, 471. There was a true marriage between Mary and Joseph. X, 420, 810. Spiritual marriage in a human being. III, 206. A mutual vow of chastity does not dissolve a marriage. X, 420.

At first, marriages between brothers and sisters were necessary. VII, 458. Why the ancient fathers sought marriages with relatives. VII, 459. Why such marriages were prohibited. VII, 459. Marriages between brothers and sisters were condemned among the pagans. VII, 458. Why they were prohibited by religion. VII, 458. Marriage between Abraham’s relatives was no longer lawful even in Abraham’s time. VIII, 422. Marriages with relatives were prohibited not by divine but by human law. VII, 459. Custom itself recoils from contracting marriages with relatives. VII, 458.

Cyprian asserts that marriage with unbelievers is not lawful. VI, 221, 469. A marriage between Catholics and Donatists is mentioned. V, 279.

Marriage is not dissolved because of sterility. VI, 385. The bond of marriage is released by death alone, not by fornication or the separation of the spouses. VI, 473, 479. Married people are permitted to divorce only on account of fornication. VI, 100, 451. Pollentius holds that spouses who separate from each other on account of fornication may marry others, but he is refuted. VI, 451. A man who dismisses an adulterous woman and marries another commits adultery. VI, 467. Even if he marries her in order to make her a Christian. VI, 468. Augustine thinks that no command concerning this is found in the New Testament. VI, 468. In the Old Testament it was altogether prohibited to receive a wife contaminated by another man. VI, 474. Reconciliation after adultery with a repentant spouse: how fitting it is for a Christian. VI, 474. Those unwilling to reconcile with adulterous spouses should maintain continence. VI, 479, 485. The complaints of the incontinent against Christ’s law forbidding marriage to another after dismissing an adulterous wife. VI, 476. Pollentius thinks that it is not lawful to dismiss unbelieving spouses; Augustine says that it is lawful but not expedient. VI, 459. Separation from an unbelieving spouse is not prohibited by a command of the Law, but is advised by the counsel of charity. VI, 100, 461, 463, 464.

What the good of marriage is. X, 141. The manifold good of marriage. VI, 375, 379, 432. The threefold good of marriage. X, 404, 688, 810. The book *On the Good of Marriage* against Jovinian. I, 639; III, 397. *On Adulterous Marriages*. I, 653. What married people seek when they seek the good of marriage. X, 738. For whom marriages were instituted. X, 1582. Marriages should be joined only for the sake of begetting children. [Col. 0183] VIII, 310. The end and intention of pious spouses. X, 738. A woman ought to marry for no other reason than to become a mother. VIII, 365.

The rendering of the marital debt. VI, 379. Conjugal honor consists in the chastity of procreation and fidelity in rendering the carnal debt. VI, 382. Marital intercourse is not to be condemned. X, 555. Intercourse necessary for generation is blameless, and it alone is marital. VI, 381. When the use of marriage is blameless. V, 1272, 1540; X, 1451. By using excessively that very thing which has been permitted, you corrupt the temple of God within you. V, 1272. You are a violator of the covenant. V, 1272. Marital intercourse would have existed even if no one had sinned, but without lust. X, 765. There are damnable and venial sins among married people. X, 429. In the use of a spouse, what is without guilt, what carries venial guilt, and what carries mortal guilt. X, 423. See Intercourse. Even with a lawful wife one has intercourse unlawfully and shamefully when conception of offspring is avoided. VI, 479. The sin of spouses who obstruct the generation of children. X, 423. The venial sins of married people. X, 724. The use of marriage that is not without venial sin. X, 1353. Marital intercourse undertaken to satisfy concupiscence carries venial guilt. VI, 269, 377, 381. Marriage does not encourage this offense, but pleads for pardon for it. VI, 381. To consent to lust solely for the sake of carnal pleasure is sin, although it is granted to married people by way of indulgence. X, 563. When married people use lust well and when they use it badly in a venial way. X, 810. In chaste spouses there is both willingness in the procreation of offspring and necessity in lust. X, 806.

The struggle of married people against concupiscence. X, 724. It is not the bodies of married people but their offenses that are attributed to the evil author. X, 445. Earthly pleasures and loves connected with marital union are not damnable. VII, 743. The pleasures and loves of married people, though not damnable, are consumed by the fire of tribulation and bereavement. VII, 743, 744. A certain intemperance is to be tolerated in married people. X, 423. Even chaste marriages are ashamed of the disobedient movements of the members. X, 565. Married people are ashamed of lust alone in the mingling of bodies. X, 1304. Marital intercourse should be sought with sorrow. V, 348. It is Adam’s punishment. V, 348.

What perfect conjugal chastity is. X, 724. The summit of conjugal chastity is reached when nothing is done because of concupiscence. X, 741. How the holy Fathers formerly used marriage. X, 419. They used marriage in a marital manner. VI, 394. They maintained obedience in conduct and continence in custom. VI, 395. Even the married life of the ancients was prophetic. VI, 397. See Marriage. Both marriage and the human being are good, and yet original sin must be admitted. X, 728. The Pelagian argument in praising the innocence of marital intercourse, in order to remove original sin. X, 555. Whether abstaining from marriage is good. VII, 463. Before the Flood no one is found to have abstained from marriage. VII, 463. In both cities many abstain from the work of generation. VII, 463. Married people abstain by mutual consent. V, 344. Marriage remains even when continence is maintained by equal consent. III, 1071. Married people may not observe continence except by mutual consent. VI, 453. Those marriages are happier in which the spouses are able by equal consent to maintain continence between them. III, 1249. A marriage in which continence is observed is by far the most excellent. III, 1250. A faithful married person is better than an unbelieving celibate. VII, 515. Faithful married people are preferred to the virgins of unbelievers. X, 763.

Jovinian equated the merit of conjugal chastity with that of sacred virgins. I, 639. How much inferior the good of marriage is to the good of holy virginity. VI, 401. And to the good of widowhood itself. VI, 433, 434. Humble married people are better than proud continent people. V, 1564, 1567. Humble marriage is better than proud virginity. IV, 1280. There are many difficulties concerning marriage, widowhood, and virginity. VI, 442. Many chaste marriages have been proved by the calamities of husbands, to which the wives rendered greater assistance. IV, 658.

The mutual duty of spouses. II, 1078. Husband and wife receive a command and an example concerning what they ought to be toward one another. VI, 364. Whether spouses ought to conceal their good works from each other. III, 1272. Whether one spouse may give alms without the other knowing it. III, 1272. A husband should tolerate even very troublesome faults in his wife, provided they do not amount to the crime of fornication. III, 1257. The disposition of an adulterous wife and of a chaste wife. II, 560. A good wife both calls her husband “lord” and regards him as such in her heart. V, 225. She counts the marriage contract as the instrument of her purchase. V, 225. Faithful married people, already eating the body of Christ, are admonished to preserve chastity. V, 755, 1710. In married people themselves, luxury is intemperance in misuse. III, 76. The violator of another man’s wife fears being punished by death. V, 871. Married life is represented by the thirtieth fruit. VI, 423. Married people yield a thirtyfold fruit. III, 1549. The games of holy married people with their wives and children are not idle but prudent. VI, 451. The age at which spouses can beget children. X, 714. An old man cannot beget children by every woman. X, 712. The deformed king of Cyprus used to place a beautiful picture before his wife during intercourse, lest she give birth to deformed children. [Col. 0184] I, 655. A kind of alliance resembling marriage exists among certain animals. X, 416.

Those who conspired with Catiline were perjurers. VII, 80.

There are no marriages except where death is present. III, 1361.

Conscience, like an altar on which sacrifice is offered to God. IV, 578. An erroneous conscience binds. I, 1360. If someone considers good what is evil and does it, he nevertheless sins by that very judgment. II, 186. Conscience is the belly of the inner person. III, 1643. Whoever is ashamed of his conscience places a limit upon iniquity. V, 1457. The conscience of the godly is the seat of God. IV, 520. Just as the conscience of the ungodly is a great punishment, so that same conscience is a great joy to the godly. IV, 625. Just as a bad conscience is wholly in despair, so a good conscience is wholly in hope. IV, 261. In tribulations a sound conscience is a refuge, where a person will find God. IV, 515. The dwelling and repose of conscience in the desert. V, 311. The joy of a good conscience is paradise. III, 482. Conscience is a desert where rest and consolation are found. IV, 635. Conscience is now a great solitude. V, 312. In heaven there will no longer be a desert. V, 312.

The better virtue is content with the testimony of conscience. VII, 156. A good conscience is sometimes not enough. II, 475, 480. When it is sufficient. V, 302. Concern for one’s reputation must be added to a good conscience. V, 1508, 1568. A good conscience is not sufficient if one’s conduct before people is negligent. V, 301. For human opinion, a great number of witnesses is needed; for God’s sight, conscience alone is required. IX, 545. A bad conscience is the pit into which the ungodly falls. IV, 670. There is no greater tribulation than the conscience of offenses. IV, 515. The conscience of a wicked person surpasses all prisons and even hell itself in horrible and punitive darkness. II, 651. A bad conscience does not flee from itself. III, 1694. A human being, you can flee whatever you wish except your own conscience. IV, 234. A bad conscience is compared with a bad wife and an inconvenient dwelling. IV, 312, 344, 515, 1286. Examination of conscience. V, 110. The abyss of conscience lies naked before the eyes of God. I, 779. Conscience must be cleansed quickly. V, 300. How it must be cleansed. IV, 312. The consciences of the wicked are healed by nothing except forgiveness. IV, 516.

No one, however outstanding in grace, should dare to refuse the sacraments of consecration. III, 745.

The consenting gods were summoned to Jupiter’s council. VII, 130.

To consent. Consent is a word of the heart. VI, 350, 351. Each person becomes guilty under the divine laws by a word spoken in the heart, even when no act has been admitted through the body. VI, 351. We sin not in the evil desire itself but in our consent. III, 2066. How the consent of the will can be distinguished from sin. X, 431. Consent to another’s sin becomes your own sin. IV, 1699. What it means to consent to those who commit evil. IX, 37. No one can be bound by another’s chain of iniquity if he has not consented to it by any act of his own will. II, 359. Innocentius judges that there is not much difference between the mind of the perpetrator and the favor of the person consenting. II, 786. The person whom no one supports usually unlearns his error. II, 786. Every evil person persecutes the good for this reason: the good person does not consent to him in evil. IV, 1690.

To consent to a calling or dissent from it belongs to one’s own will. X, 240.

Consentius. VI, 517. Consentius sends his books to Augustine to be examined and approved. II, 452. Consentius’s character, integrity, and humility. II, 452. Consentius proposes questions about the Trinity to Augustine. II, 448. Augustine responds to Consentius’s questions. II, 942. Consentius was personally unknown to Augustine. II, 942.

The preservation of every creature by God is necessary. VII, 375. If God withdraws from nature the intimate operation by which He sustains and makes it, immediately, as though extinguished, nothing will remain. III, 304, 404.

God’s plan concerning our predestination remains forever. IV, 292. It is utterly foolish to say that something new arose in God’s plan. I, 1016.

Evangelical counsels. I, 855. How the Lord’s counsel is distinguished from a commandment. VI, 402, 466. One must be encouraged toward the counsels in such a way that a life brought into conformity with the rule of the commandments is not condemned. II, 691, 692.

What the gift of counsel accomplishes. III, 40. Counsel, the fifth step toward wisdom. III, 40. See Moses. True counsel, from whatever soul it proceeds, must be attributed to God. III, 18. Nor should it be despised. III, 619. Counsel is unnecessary except in adversity. IV, 140. Counsel must be sought from Christ amid the tribulation of this world. V, 402, 404. The rich person needs counsel: you give counsel, and you have provided alms. IV, 1665. A just judgment or true testimony must not be sold, although a just defense and true counsel may be sold. II, 663. “He has good sides and bad sides” is a proverb about one who lives and is governed by good and bad counsels. IV, 1684. One who seeks counsel for salvation, yet does not willingly listen. V, 524.

God consoles the good heart and torments the evil heart. IV, 1748, 1749. Whatever prosperity God provides for us is the consolation of the miserable, not the joy of the blessed [Col. 0185]. How the soul of the just refuses to be consoled. IV, 974. Our consolations in the desert. IV, 753. Our consolation is in hope, our groaning in reality. IV, 165. Whence true consolation comes to us. II, 495. That will be true consolation which will give what cannot be lost. V, 365. Whoever wishes to console someone does not raise him up unless he grieves with him. IV, 1199. Consolations as though they were drink. III, 831. A consolatory letter to a widow on the death of her husband. II, 309. Consolation concerning a brother’s death. II, 1083, 1084.

Constancy cannot exist without corresponding actions and virtues. III, 244. Constancy does not allow a person to become depraved; obstinacy does not allow him to be corrected. II, 224. If obstinacy tries to possess unconquerable strength, how much strength constancy ought to possess. II, 309. The constancy of the saints is fire in relation to their persecutors. VII, 677.

What and how many are the *eupatheiai* (εὐπάθειαι), the good emotions. VII, 411.

Constantina, a city. II, 133; IX, 337, 371. The church of Constantina. IX, 246.

Constantinople. VIII, 1017. An ally of the Roman Empire and, as it were, the daughter of Rome herself. VII, 171. Constantinople both has grown and is growing. V, 624. Constantinople, corrected and divinely preserved through fear of the fire threatening it. VI, 722.

Constantine the Great, Augustus. II, 169, 304; IX, 512. Emperor. IX, 540. Consul for the second and third time. IX, 687. The Donatists brought Caecilian’s case before him. II, 399, 580, 794. They asked him for episcopal judges. II, 161, 166, 264, 302. Constantine did not dare to judge the bishop’s case. II, 399. Constantine ordered the parties to come to an episcopal trial in the city of Rome. II, 303. Constantine’s letters to Probianus the proconsul concerning Caecilian. II, 303. To Verinus the vicar. II, 581. To the proconsul, ordering Ingentius to be sent to him. II, 582. Everything is fully attested by Constantine’s letters. II, 162, 170. The Donatists did not accept the episcopal judgment. II, 162, 170. He granted that a second episcopal trial be held in the Gallic city of Arles. II, 162, 170. Some of the most obstinate and litigious Donatists appealed to the same Emperor. II, 162, 170. Constantine did not dare to judge the judgment of the bishops. II, 170. Later he himself was compelled to conclude the episcopal case. II, 170, 303. He declared Caecilian completely innocent. II, 170, 304. Judging most justly in favor of Christ’s unity, he deserved to be accepted by the Donatists, though they had not appealed to him. IX, 326. Parmenianus complains that he condemned the Donatists to capital punishment, “at the urging,” he says, “of Hosius the Spaniard.” IX, 43. See Donatists. In Caecilian’s case Constantine acted far more properly than his accusers. II, 328. He ordered the basilicas to be taken away from the Donatists. IX, 326. He was the first to establish, against the Donatists, that their places of assembly should be claimed for the treasury. II, 303. Matters belonging to them. II, 328. Constantine was by no means hostile to the Christian name, but plainly glorious in the Christian name. IX, 326. Unlike the other emperors, Constantine’s father did not carry out persecution. IX, App. 778. Why God bestowed so many successes upon the Emperor Constantine. VII, 171.

Constantine the Younger, Caesar. IX, 512.

A certain Constantine, a friend of Augustine. IX, 593, 594, *Retractationes* 595.

Constantius, a bishop. X, 378.

Constantius the Emperor, a heretic. VIII, 771. He specifically wished to seize Athanasius. II, 1016.

Constantius, consul. II, 786.

Constantius the Roman, a Catholic Christian formerly a Manichaean. VIII, 223.

What a constellation is. III, 51.

The imperial constitutions against the Donatists. IV, 135.

Habit arises from the will. X, 1398. The force of deeply rooted habit. I, 754, 1350; VII, 194, 730; X, 1523. The pestilential sweetness of habit. I, 1307. The force of habit conceded by Julian. X, 1108. The Pelagians understand the Apostle’s words to mean that the unwilling person is compelled to sin by the force of habit. X, 1393. The Pelagians attribute to the violence of habit what the Apostle says: “Not what I will,” etc. X, 1524. Habit is like a chain. I, 753. Habits of carnal pleasures are bonds. III, 865. Even a bad habit is observed as a law. V, 78. Habit is, as it were, a second nature. I, 1173; X, 1119, 1398, 1605. Habit introduces necessity. VIII, 124. The necessity of habit. IV, 238. Habit becomes necessity when it is not resisted. I, 753. The various stages by which one reaches that necessity. I, 753. Vice does not become less voluntary through habit. VII, 351. Habitual evil does not allow one to see that it is evil. V, 593.

A bad habit, a monstrous kind of death. III, 1748. Bad habit, the stone of the tomb in which the sinner lies. III, 1578. Habitual evil signified by Lazarus buried and already stinking. V, 519, 720. Whoever is crushed beneath the mass of a bad habit is like buried Lazarus. V, 435. One oppressed by the weight of habit is not to be despaired of. V, 595. Much loud reproach is needed for those who have grown hard through habit. V, 594 [Col. 0186]. What that reproach ordinarily produces. V, 594.

The struggle against bad habit. V, 816. To overcome habit is a hard struggle. IV, 238. How vicious habits are overcome. II, 92; III, 1257. How the impulse of carnal habit is broken. I, 1181. The stronger the habit, the greater the effort it demands. V, 978. A bad habit must be struck down before it grows strong, while desire is still small. IV, 1773. How, once restrained, it gradually weakens and dies. V, 977, 979.

The sins of habit must not be despised. V, 125. The sins of habit are difficult to undo. VIII, 1756. The retinue of continuing habit. I, 732. The burden of habit weighs one down. I, 807. It is regrettable that the things most salutarily commanded in the divine books are cared for less, while various customs and presumptions are observed exactly. II, 221. Human actions are not to be condemned or approved according to the rule of custom. VII, 71. Human custom does not excuse what is forbidden by God’s eternal law. I, 712.

Which customs in the Church should be changed. II, 221. In matters concerning which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of God’s people or the institutions of the ancestors are to be held as law. II, 136, 200. Whatever is not contrary to the faith or to good morals and contains something conducive to encouraging a better life, wherever we see it established or learn that it has been established, let us pursue it with praise and imitation, unless someone’s weakness is so obstructive that greater harm would result. II, 221. Disturbances very often arise from contentious obstinacy in retaining customs. II, 201. A change of custom, even one that brings benefit, causes disturbance through its novelty; therefore a change that is not useful is harmful. II, 203. One should not easily depart from custom unless it is opposed to reason. I, 1108. Custom must yield to reason. IX, 144, 157. It must yield to truth. IX, 143, 144, 220. But when truth supports a custom, nothing ought to be held more firmly. IX, 157. Augustine calms the defenders of an ancient but very bad custom by receiving them gently. II, 118. He also answers their objections. II, 118. How one should judge another person’s custom. III, 74.

Your consubstantial one. V, 384.

To consult means either to impart or to seek counsel. V, 1412. God acts by a hidden impulse upon those who consult and those who are consulted, though they do not know it, so that while each person seeks advice, he hears what he ought to hear, according to the hidden merits of souls. I, 739. The tongue of worldly friends contradicts the devout as though offering counsel, and, like food, ordinarily consumes him through affection. I, 764.

How it is appropriate to consult for oneself. V, 1411.

Consuls are so called from consulting. VII, 154. The consuls quickly extended and enlarged the Roman Empire. VII, 154. The Donatists maintained that, according to ecclesiastical custom, councils of bishops were not recorded with consuls and dates. IX, 642. Catholic councils always had consuls and dates. IX, 639. The Catholics proved this both from the Council of Melchiades and from the Scriptures. IX, 642. Imperial enactments are not called into doubt even when the consuls are not recorded. IX, 647.

The distinction between completion and consumption. III, 2057. A thing is completed when it is ended in such a way that it is perfected; it is consumed when it is ended in such a way that it no longer exists. IV, 709. Completion does not stand together with faith. III, 1924.

Consus, the god who provides counsels. VII, 122. Consus, the god Neptune of horses. VII, 61, note (c). The Consualia, Circus games, and why they are so called. VII, 61, note (c).

The touch of a dead person is human iniquity. III, 735.

Contemplation. V, 925. The goal toward which all who are converted strive. VIII, 432, 433. The promised contemplation, the end of all actions. VIII, 831, 834. Contemplation is reached only through the labor of actions and the suffering of trials. VIII, 433. The excellence of contemplation of heavenly things. II, 128. The sublimity of contemplation, granted even to certain very humble people who persevere most steadfastly on the way of faith, but denied to those more intelligent. II, 454. It ought to be contemplation of truth, whether by inquiry or discovery, not idle leisure, that gives delight. VII, 647. The contemplation of God, the unchangeable good. IV, 203. The contemplation of God may be sought and hoped for without presumption. IV, 204. Hence, those who rightly worship God pass into eternal contemplation of His form, even while the time of faith remains. II, 527. Everything that we contemplate or grasp in thought we grasp either by sense or by understanding. I, 1026. Contemplation is a holy intoxication of the mind withdrawn from temporal things sinking below and beholding the eternal light of wisdom. VIII, 276. In contemplation of eternal things the mind’s gaze does not remain long. VII, 1010. In contemplation, love of truth seeks holy leisure. VII, 647. Contemplation surpasses action. VIII, 1070. It is good that even the contemplative life should merit popular honor. VIII, 436. Why the contemplative life is barren. VIII, 434. No one is forbidden contemplation. VII, 647.

Contempt of the world. V, 242, 586, 1415.

To contend over words is most disgraceful. I, 946, 947. Whoever contends over words through ignorance should be taught; whoever does so through malice should be abandoned. I, 949. What it means to contend with words. III, 119. To contend in court over earthly things is a fault. IV, 1045. Contend with evil, but concerning goodness. IV, 364. The true contest is that one should be good against evil, not that there should be two evils. IV, 364. Contentious hostility is of two kinds. IX, 559. The desire for contention and human praise is the mother of pride. II, 92. Contentions and dissensions are produced only by the animal-minded. V, 73. Those more eager for contention than for truth, where they are accustomed to seek hiding places for their defense. II, 1039. These words are wrested away by writing them down. II, 1039. The contentious have no means by which to see God. V, 162. The contention of Catholics with the Donatists is one of love, not litigation. V, 1586.

Continence and endurance are two virtues of this life. V, 139, 235, 236. Continence from the allurements of the flesh is fivefold. VI, 45. Continence from the allurements of the world is commanded by the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. IV, 1463. Continence is necessary for restraining every sin. VI, 359. The struggle of continence against lusts as long as we are here. VI, 352, 362. The evil of concupiscence is not overcome except by the good of continence. VI, 353. Continence in a certain manner crucifies the very desires of the flesh. VI, 355. Continence must be observed according to each person’s station. V, 735, 736, 1200. Continence must be observed, whether marital or more excellent. VI, 484. Marital continence. VI, 368. Continence from the lust of the flesh, and continence of the mouth. VI, 349. Continence of the heart, commended by Christ under the name of the mouth. VI, 351. Continence of the flesh is to be counted among the goods of the mind. VI, 400. Continence is of very great value in spiritual warfare. VI, 355. Against the harmful sweetness by which concupiscence prevailed, the Lord grants a beneficial sweetness by which continence gives greater delight. VI, 353.

The chaste dignity of continence is serene, cheerfully composed but not dissolute. I, 761. Continence is luminous and beautiful. II, 852. Continence is not sterile but fruitful through the Lord God as husband. I, 761. Through continence we are gathered toward the one God from whom we have flowed into many things. I, 796. When continence does not yield to the impurity of carnal desires, the body itself is sanctified. VII, 31.

Continence is preferred to marriage. VI, 380; VII, 515; VIII, 597; X, 758. By divine right. VI, 397. Continence is now better than the procreation of children, provided that it is observed in order to think about the things of the Lord. VI, 394, 478. Before Christ was the time for marrying; after Christ is the time for continence. X, 422. Why perpetual continence was unusual among the ancients. VI, 435. Continence, like the other virtues, must be distinguished as habit and action. VI, 390. Among the ancients continence was to be maintained as a habit; now it is to be maintained in action. VI, 380, 391. Continence should be recommended to those who are capable of it. VI, 449. Now only those ought to marry who do not practice continence. VI, 380. If continence were worthily observed by everyone, the city of God would be filled more quickly. VI, 381. Continence and virginity commended in the Old Testament. VIII, 302.

The vow of continence. VI, 412; X, 740. Whoever does not fulfill the vow of continence is condemned. V, 1201. Those who have professed continence may not desire marriage. X, 741. A vow of continence must not be broken for any hope of compensation. VI, 468. For those practicing continence, spiritual delights should take the place of carnal ones. VI, 447. Continence can be observed by those who wish to observe it. X, 819. Those who have professed continence can observe it, although those who have not professed it are often compelled to observe it. VI, 447. Those practicing continence should beware lest money take the place of love for a husband and, once lust has been restrained, avarice grow. VI, 447.

A vow of perpetual continence undertaken by mutual agreement between married partners. II, 1012. Continence cannot be vowed without the consent of both spouses. II, 487, 997; III, 746; IV, 1959; VI, 468; X, 957, 958. A wife who undertakes continence while her husband does not yet wish it does not do so according to sound doctrine. II, 1078. A woman who, with her husband’s consent, does not engage in sexual intercourse must in other matters serve her husband with the obedience proper to a married woman. II, 1078. A woman who lives continently with her husband’s consent must do nothing concerning clothing, gold, or any other possessions without his decision. II, 1079.

Those bound by a vow of continence. V, 736. The continence of clerics who have been chosen unwillingly is contrasted with men unwilling to practice continence after divorce. VI, 486. Continence freely chosen becomes necessity, and what is guarded out of necessity can become voluntary—how this happens. VI, 485. Continence is sometimes violated without violating the body. VI, 351. If continence is preserved, bodily continence is not violated. VI, 352. The continence of certain people is impure, so that by magical arts they may gain access to other men’s wives. VI, 367.

Married people must observe continence on certain days of the year. V, 1052. It must be observed during Lent. V, 1047, 1052. The continence of those who practice it is attacked by the envious in order to test it. V, 1564.

Continence and endurance are gifts of God. V, 1286. Continence and chastity are gifts of God. III, 639; VI, 349, 372, 421, 442 [Col. 0188]; X, 807. How great a gift continence is. VI, 444. No one can be continent unless God grants it. X, 297. Continence is a gift of God and is given to one who asks. I, 729. Continence must be requested from God. X, 236. Prayers are more effective for loving and possessing the good of continence than exhortations. VI, 445. God commands and gives continence. I, 796; II, 677. Continence comes from the gift of God and free will. X, 886. So that one may not fall away from it, one must not presume upon one’s own strength. VI, 355, 357. Your spirit is not continent if it is not restrained by another who is higher. V, 830. The place of those practicing continence is more excellent in Christ’s body. V, 1564. Those practicing continence occupy a very high place with God. II, 855. Yet married people can be better than those practicing continence. VI, 392.

Continence without faith is not true continence. VI, 368. In addition to continence and good works, charity is required. V, 575. The good of obedience is greater than that of continence. VI, 392. A woman who abstains from marriage is excessively to be detested if she does not abstain from sins. VI, 383. Those practicing continence while living contrary to their resolution are censured. VI, 415. It would be better for them to marry than to burn. VI, 415. The various kinds of continence, and which is more excellent. VI, 484, 485.

Those practicing continence must especially beware of pride. V, 1567. A continent person should consider what he lacks, not what he has. V, 1565. A humble married person is better than a proud continent one. V, 1564, 1567. In what manner God either punishes or prevents the pride of those practicing continence. VII, 41. It is beneficial for the proud continent to fall. V, 1567. Against those who think that continence is beneficial only for the present life. VI, 401. Those practicing continence in this age should not think disparagingly of the holy fathers who were married. VI, 395.

Human contracts bear certain imprinted traces of heavenly justice. VI, 120.

The world’s contradiction. V, 1531. Whoever begins to follow Christ suffers contradiction. V, 586.

Contraries belong to the beauty of the universe. VII, 332. The reciprocal relation of contraries. X, 858. The meaning of certain words must be understood from their opposite. III, 800. Most unknown things are understood from signs opposed to them. III, 386. The dialecticians say that two contraries cannot be present in anything simultaneously. VI, 238.

What contrition of heart is. IV, 947, 1902. Those who do not crush their hearts are not healed. IV, 1902. Contrition of heart is a loud cry for God’s mercy. I, 739. The striking of the breast is a sign of contrition. IV, 1903. Temporal sacraments are the bonds of contritions. IV, 1903.

Soldiers are called *contubernales*, as though having tents together. IV, 143.

The insults of heretics are to be regarded as praises. X, 1254.

Fellow recruits (*contyrones*). V, 1077.

Congruity and incongruity are universal good and evil. I, 1350. All harmonies are beautiful. III, 146. Truth is the highest harmony. III, 154. Harmony is maintained in bodily pleasure. III, 154.

Care should be taken for good conduct before the brothers. V, 301, 303. For their benefit, not for our dignity. V, 302. Conduct without complaint, according to the law. V, 929.

Conversion to God. I, 988. In order for a human being to be something, he turns toward the one by whom he was created. IV, 896. We must always be made and always perfected by God, adhering to Him and remaining in that conversion which is toward Him. III, 404. The spiritual life is formed and perfected by conversion to the Creator. III, 247. By turning ourselves toward sin, we lose illumination; by turning ourselves toward God, we receive illumination. III, 1566. How the soul’s conversion to God takes place. III, 418. Conversion arises both from shame over sin and from hunger and thirst for righteousness. IV, 832. “By my own good it was bad for me without you; for if it had been well with me without you, perhaps I would not have wished to return to you.” IV, 1787. God pursues the back of the one who flees and illuminates the face of the one who returns. V, 780. “As you flee, you have a judge; as you return, have a father.” V, 780. Paul was converted through the infliction of blindness. II, 803.

To be converted is to raise oneself from the immoderation of vices into virtue and temperance. I, 988. Renunciation of this world must precede conversion to God. V, 1654. No one can be converted to God unless he turns away from this world. VIII, 102. The soul is not converted to God except when it turns away from this age, nor does it turn away from this age more suitably unless pains are mingled with its harmful pleasures. IV, 121. As long as one lives, there is always a place and always a time for changing an evil life into a good one. VI, 772. The time for conversion is now; in the other life there is only the recompense of merits. IV, 93. A human being is twice wretched before conversion. IV, 1658.

Most people wrongly postpone conversion by hoping. V, 140, 244, 536. Some postpone it by hoping, others by despairing. V, 139, 244. Conversion must not be postponed until tomorrow. V, 141, 150, 241, 245. Those who postpone their conversion hear in themselves the raven’s voice: “Tomorrow, tomorrow.” IV, 1330. God promised forgiveness for your conversion, but He did not promise tomorrow for your delay. IV, 1301, 1877; V, 513, 536. Those who did not wish to have conversion unto salvation will have conversion unto shame. IV, 96.

Impediments to conversion. I, 1170. Whence the labor and difficulty of conversion arise. IV, 93. Why the difficulties and illnesses of souls turning to God are not immediately removed. IV, 92. The distress of a person converted to God but not refreshed by spiritual joy. III, 1341. Conversion does not take away pleasure from a person, but changes it. IV, 946. Our perfect conversion finds God ready. IV, 92. After conversion all sins are completely forgiven, and once debts have been remitted, a new account is made with God. V, 535. If you are changed, God is changed. V, 152. For the converted person, a change of life is not enough unless satisfaction for the committed offenses is also present. V, 1548.

Conversion: the sinner cannot rise from sin by himself without grace. V, 137. We cannot turn ourselves to God unless He Himself arouses and assists us. X, 169. Conversion is to be attributed to God, not to human works. II, 591. Conversion comes from God’s grace. III, 1779; IV, 1119, 1073. It does not come from merits. V, 1648. Our conversion to God is God’s gift. X, 888. The soul turning to God prays that God may turn toward it. IV, 92. Whoever is always good makes good from evil. V, 410. The sinner has it within free will to be converted. V, 48, 51, 56. God is more to be praised for the conversion of sinners than for the resurrection of the dead. IV, 1123. Just as it is harsh to show indulgence to sinners, so it is impious to deny a hand to the converted. II, 784. God and the angels rejoice more in the conversion of sinners. I, 751. Why there is greater rejoicing over the conversion of noble people. I, 752. The joy we experience when some people are corrected and changed for the better cannot be compared with any joy in this life. II, 1085. An exhortation to change one’s life for the better. V, 1482. Those who are not converted now, while Christ is building the Church, deserve greater reproach than those who were not converted in former times while Noah was building the ark. V, 1611.

The conversion of the nations is symbolized. III, 1333. See Sinner; Ways of the Lord.

We eat with strangers, with pagans, more readily than with brothers and Christians if they live badly, and this for the sake of correction and healing. IV, 1289, 1290.

How insults contribute to the benefit of the just. IX, 355. How one ought to conduct oneself after hearing an insult. IV, 1185, 1434. How Augustine endured a grave insult from a presbyter. II, 136. An insult must not be repaid with an insult. V, 1584. If you strike someone who has insulted you, that is not courage, because you have been overcome by anger. IV, 1184.

The Lord’s banquet is twofold: one is here for the faithful, the other in heaven for the blessed. V, 559. The bread of the heavenly banquet is righteousness, and its drink is wisdom. V, 417. What sort of person the one who invited to the banquet is. V, 582. The one reclining without a wedding garment is rejected. V, 583. Who are to be understood as the wicked excluded from the banquet. V, 560. One person excluded from the banquet signifies many excluded. V, 560.

Augustine arranges for the banquets customarily held in churches to be abolished. II, 115, 116. Banquets formerly held in the basilica of Blessed Peter. II, 119. The Jews are not said to have held luxurious banquets in the temple. II, 115.

Every abundance that is not God is poverty. I, 848.

For what purpose marital intercourse was instituted. X, 730. Marital intercourse would take place without concupiscence if no one had sinned. X, 730.

God is the light of hearts. II, 560, 561. Christ is the life of hearts. II, 564, 565. God deigns to visit our heart with His word as His field and seeks fruit from our heart. IV, 706. The heart is the root from which either thorns or fruits proceed. V, 569. God seeks the heart, examines the heart; inwardly He is witness, judge, approver, helper, and one who crowns. IV, 1746. A person is in his heart, whoever he is. I, 781. An emperor sits in a person’s heart: if he is good and commands good things, good things are done; if he is evil and commands evil things, evil things are done. IV, 1938. God judges hearts, not words. III, 726. The heart has its own mouth. VIII, 1070. The mouth and tongue of the heart. IV, 1660, 1661, 1775. Whatever proceeds from the mouth of the heart, if it is evil, defiles us; if it is good, cleanses us. IV, 1660. With the heart you praise; with the heart you place sacred victims upon the altar of conscience. IV, 1746. Tears are the blood of a wounded heart. II, 1081, 1082. Through the heart the flesh is cleansed. VII, 303. God places His law in the heart so that it may be loved with chaste love. IV, 1565. It is utterly impossible for something done from fear of punishment, rather than from love of righteousness, to come from the heart. IV, 990, 991.

The human heart with its treasure. V, 1519. Where the heart should be placed. V, 136. Heaven is the place of our heart and treasure. IV, 1170. The slow heart is secure when it is in heaven; an acute heart is nothing when it is on earth. II, 296. The heart must be fixed in the eternal God so that it may stand firm. I, 814. Our heart is restless until it rests in God. I, 661. When our heart belongs wholly to God, it is not lost to us. V, 212. A heart flying about amid the past and future movements of things is still vain. I, 814. How many imaginings the human heart produces. VIII, 887. God’s grace converts the heart from multiplicity to unity. V, 1290. By sincere devotion, He Himself gradually cleanses the hearts of those who seek God from the pollution of earthly affections. I, 775. A pregnant heart. IV, 1775. “Your heart had rotted in the earth; you do not hear ‘hearts above’ without reason, lest it rot.” IV, 271, 1941.

“Heart on high.” V, 135, 168, 170, 369, 523, 623, 904, 956, 1456. When “lift up your heart” is an expression of devotion and when of pride. V, 1202. To have the heart lifted toward oneself is pride; toward God, obedience. VII, 421. To have the heart lifted toward God is God’s gift. X, 1013. When the heart is lifted toward God, it is His altar. VII, 280. How the heart is poured out before God. IV, 739. The coldness of charity is the silence of the heart; the ardor of charity is the heart’s cry. IV, 404. Christ is the foundation of our heart, provided that worldly things are not preferred to Him. V, 1616. Fear and disturbance of the heart arise from the loss of our fortitude. IV, 404, 405. The heart driven to grief by temporal loss is ashes. IV, 1631.

What a right heart is. VI, 162. What kind of heart is right. IV, 991, 1207, 1287, 1468, 1649. Who are right-hearted and who are perverse-hearted. IV, 273, 274, 277, 352, 1649. A person is perverse-hearted who wishes to bend God’s heart, which is always right, toward the perversity of his own heart. IV, 771. A person is right-hearted who praises the father’s scourge. V, 146. When the heart is not straight, its works are not straight, even if they appear straight. IV, 991. How the right-hearted and the pure-hearted differ. X, 311. The simple and pure heart. III, 1304. A pure heart is a simple heart. III, 1232. No one has a simple, that is, pure, heart except the person who rises above human praises and looks only upon the one who alone examines the conscience. III, 1270. Who is truly pure in heart. III, 40. The chaste heart. IV, 658, 928, 1246.

From what the heart is cleansed. V, 569. Through what the heart becomes spotless. IV, 1556. How one reaches purity of heart. X, 286, 310. The heart must be crushed so that it may become pure. V, 134. Purification of the heart, the sixth step toward wisdom. III, 40. The heart must be cleansed so that God may be seen. V, 1204. The pure in heart will see God. II, 604, 608, 618, 620, 621. Faith cleanses hearts so that the inner eyes may be opened and brightened. IV, 1552. The heart is like an eye by which God is seen. III, 1269. The eye of the heart is required for seeing God. III, 1510, 1527, 1539. The image of God is in the heart. III, 1542. God wishes to dwell in a pure heart. V, 1205. The heart of the faithful is not too narrow a temple for God. V, 158. The hearts of the saints are great tabernacles of God. IV, 508.

God is the life-giving delight of the pure heart. I, 857. The pleasure of the heart. III, 1608. Good pleasures are attributed to the heart; bad ones to the kidneys. IV, 104, 192. Tranquility of heart comes from the serenity of a good conscience. V, 1242. When our heart is said either to accuse or not to accuse us. X, 305. The heart of the wicked is the bottom of the sea. IV, 782, 1425. How the storm of the heart is calmed. III, 1755.

The chamber of the heart. IV, 1834. The heart is the holy bedchamber of virtue. VIII, 448. The heart of the just is his house. VI, 162. The heart of a just man is his house, where he dwells more abundantly with God’s approval, etc. IV, 1469. We gladly dwell in the heart if we cleanse it from iniquity. IV, 943. See Conscience. The feathers of the heart, by which it flies to its own home, are faith, hope, and love. IV, 1060. Whoever strives to be free for God should return into his heart. I, 834. And find Him there. I, 701. The heart must be carefully closed. IV, 1834. The door of the heart has, as it were, two leaves: desire and fear. IV, 1835. The seduction of the tongue violates the virginity of the heart. III, 1499. What disturbs the silence of the heart, so necessary for prayer. I, 803. The multitude of human beings has the heart not in the heart but in the eyes. IX, 43. The heart in the ears. IX, 338. The double heart of a liar. V, 739. The faithless person is crafty to his own harm. I, 972.

The human heart is an abyss. IV, 473, 1749. Matters of the heart can have no judge except God. V, 569. Christ is the accuser and examiner of the heart. V, 569. A closed heart does not exclude the eye of God. I, 705. The innermost parts of the heart are naked before God. I, 779.

The twisted and hard heart. IV, 1903. “To strengthen the heart,” used for “to harden it.” III, 783. See Hardening. What the stony heart and the fleshly heart are. X, 898. How the fleshly heart and the stony heart are to be understood. III, 85. Hardness of heart arises from each person’s vice. III, 601. Hardness of heart persisting to the end of life is sin against the Holy Spirit. II, 814. The hardness of human hearts does not repel God’s hand; rather, God releases that hand when He wishes, whether showing mercy or taking vengeance, and no one can hide from His heat. I, 705. God acts in human hearts and inclines them wherever He wishes. X, 907, 908, 909. God works good in the hearts of the elect. X, 909. He works conversion in the human heart. X, 1296. God acts in human hearts, including upon the movement of their will. X, 908. God acts in the hearts even of the wicked, whatever He wishes. X, 907. God uses the hearts of the wicked for the praise and assistance of the good. X, 907.

What it means for the heart to be enlarged. IV, 79. Enlargement of heart may be understood both in good and in evil. III, 532. Enlargement of heart comes from charity. V, 158. Enlargement of heart is delight in righteousness. IV, 1527. We shall see one another’s hearts after this life. V, 321, 322.

Corax, king of the Sicyonians. VII, 569.

*Core* is interpreted as “bald,” “baldness,” or “skull.” IV, 464, 482, 493, 514, 525, 533, 605, 1056, 1069. It is also a figure of Christ. IV, 1069.

Cornelius Rufinus was expelled from the Senate because he was discovered to possess ten pounds of silver in vessels. VII, 164.

Cornelius Celsus held that wisdom was the highest good and bodily pain the highest evil. I, 881.

Cornelius the Censor. II, 263.

Cornelius and those who were with him were the first upon whom the Holy Spirit descended while they were not yet baptized. IV, 1247. Before visible baptism Cornelius received the Holy Spirit. III, 735; V, 1235. Cornelius the centurion received the Holy Spirit without the laying on of hands. V, 601. Almsgiving cleansed Cornelius the centurion in a certain manner. V, 802. Cornelius the centurion prayed and gave alms not without some faith. X, 970. Cornelius was handed over to Peter for instruction. III, 18.

Before becoming a catechumen, Cornelius had corrected himself from the vice of sexual immorality with the most restrained will. II, 1074. By not flattering his depraved habits, Augustine showed himself his true friend. II, 1075.

“You will hear little crows more easily in Africa than …,” a proverb. II, 436.

It is implied that there are no cornel trees in Africa. II, 70.

The horn signifies height, not carnal but spiritual. IV, 1728.

Cornutus, a presbyter. II, 899, 901.

Cornutus, the grammarian. VIII, 77.

A crown is promised to those who conquer. VI, 289. No one can be crowned unless he has conquered, nor conquer unless he has struggled. IV, 724. The crown is owed to those who preserve the faith. V, 1369, 1371. The owed crown would not be given unless undeserved grace had first been given. V, 1366. In order that the crown may be given to the worthy, grace is given to the unworthy. X, 341. God crowns us with mercy. V, 753. Unless God first spared through mercy, He would not find anyone whom He could crown through judgment. IV, 1282. God will crown His gifts, not your merits. IV, 895, 1280, 1321, 1783, 1784.

Christ’s crown of thorns. IV, 1942. However much you may suffer, you will not reach those insults, those scourges, that shameful garment, that crown of thorns, and finally that cross. IV, 366.

A golden crown shown to Sulla in a calf’s liver during a sacrifice. VII, 72, 73.

Corpus fabricated by the devil according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 380, 386. And the workmanship of the nation of darkness. VIII, 498. The Manichaeans detest earthly bodies as though they belonged to the nature of evil. VII, 408. The Paterniani say that the lower parts of the human body were made not by God but by the devil. VIII, 46.

Every body is from God. VI, 14. Bodies can be formed and created by God alone. VIII, 95, 556. Some have said that the body was fashioned by God, but that the soul was made by him. IV, 1551.

In how many ways the term “body” may be understood. II, 722. What the body is. X, 534, 544. A body is any nature that occupies a spatial place by length, height, and breadth. III, 366. Take away spatial extension from bodies, and they will no longer exist. II, 838. Some think that what is not a body has no substance at all. II, 619. No body exists without parts. I, 1023. A body cannot be imagined or perceived without the peaceful continuity and likeness of its parts. VIII, 195, 199. A body has innumerable parts. I, 1252. A body is better in proportion to the number of its parts. I, 1167. Strictly speaking, a body cannot be called one. I, 1252. Even the smallest bodies are divisible without limit. VIII, 998. Any body can be cut infinitely. I, 1027; II, 64; III, 266, 301. No body whatever is not smaller in a part than in the whole. VIII, 185.

It is proper to a body to be in a place and to move from place to place. V, 360, 361. The order of bodies arises from the diversity of their weights. V, 1142. The swiftness of the heavenly bodies. V, 1266. The movement of certain heavier bodies is faster. V, 1142. Higher bodies are not more powerful than earthly bodies. III, 278. Very few know the proper movement and nature of the body. X, 528. Not even the soul itself knows the nature of the body. X, 527. Questions concerning the nature of the body. X, 527.

How bodies exist in the intellect. VII, 231. A body has no power to form anything spiritual. III, 470. It is not the body that makes the image of the body in the spirit, but the spirit that makes it in itself. III, 467, 470. The image of the body is more excellent in the spirit than the body itself in its own substance. III, 467. Of what nature are the likenesses of bodies that we have in dreams? X, 540. Bodies that are displayed either in dreams or in ecstasy are, as it were, spiritual rather than corporeal matter. X, 539. To judge corporeal things according to incorporeal and eternal principles belongs to a higher kind of reason. VIII, 999. The more someone prefers the light of the mind to the light of the body, the better he is. II, 616.

A body cannot exist without some form. VIII, 195. A body is contained by some form and appearance. I, 901. In it, beauty alone is praised. II, 64. In the body there is a certain beauty of rational order. VII, 791. For them, being is not the same as being beautiful. I, 846. How beautiful and admirable is the structure of the human body! VII, 790. Even if the members of the body are beautiful individually, they are more beautiful in the structure of the whole body. III, 296. The structure, composition, and workmanship of the body indicate its craftsman, the true God. VIII, 392. How the body was made in the likeness of God. VI, 32. The body cannot receive the image of God. X, 537. The condition of the body is not deformed by the difference of the sexes, even if the union of the two sexes were always evil. X, 710. In the constitution of the body, dignity was preferred to necessity. VII, 791. The four elements and qualities of the body. IV, 91. The body as earth. VII, 531. The physicians’ opinion concerning the human body. III, 362. The diverse functions of the members, with complete harmony in the body. IV, 1707. The health of the body is the harmony of its members. VI, 712. The structure of the body as a symbol of charity. VI, 125.

Why the beauty, size, and strength of the body are common goods of the good and the wicked. VII, 471. The Stoics do not wish to call bodily things good or bad, but advantages or disadvantages and externals. VII, 258, 260. This is merely a contest over words, not an examination of things. VII, 260. The goods of the body come only from God. II, 568. If the goods of the body are diminished, a good and just life is not thereby diminished at all. VII, 31. Bodies are not subject to angels, but angels govern them as things subject to themselves. VIII, 870. Augustine proves that it is more probable that angels have bodies. II, 355. The body is not a good of the soul. II, 438. The body, insofar as it is raised toward heaven, is suited to the rational soul. III, 348. The soul is the good of the body. I, 1313. Even while paying the penalty for its sin, it adorns the body. I, 1284. The body is the garment of the soul. IV, 1314.

The body is given life only through the soul. III, 1585. Whence the senses of the body arise. III, 466. Whence the powers of the body are greater. I, 1056, 1057. How the powers of the body are weakened. V, 1617. Three conditions of the body: health, insensibility, and immortality. IV, 650, 651. There are three kinds of its growth. I, 1054. Any incorporeal nature, even if vicious and miserable, is better than the body. II, 561. A very base soul is superior to the most excellent body. IV, 1885. The mind is better than the body. II, 64. Nothing is found between body and soul that is better than the body and worse than the soul. VI, 38. Nothing is worse than a body. VI, 38.
