The pagans said that they did not worship bodies, but the divinities presiding over the governance of those bodies. IV, 1484. Some consider bodies to be prisons of souls that sinned elsewhere. V, 1259. Every movement of the soul does something in the body. II, 72. It is difficult to know how the body is changed by an affection of the will. VIII, 871. Some people use their bodies as they wish to produce marvelous effects. VII, 433.

According to Tertullian, everything corporeal is subject to suffering. III, 427. Perhaps the body could do nothing at all to the soul if sin had not preceded it. I, 1166. The higher cause of every corporeal change is the will of God. VIII, 871. This is demonstrated by an example. VIII, 871. The condition of the body before Adam’s sin was one thing, and its condition now is another. X, 1449. Our first parents ruled over their bodies. III, 283. Before sin the body was governed at the soul’s discretion, although it was not yet spiritual. II, 588. After sin the body is governed by the ordered soul, as the laws of the universe permit. II, 587. The mind commands the body in one way and lust in another. X, 767. Our body is in a worse condition than Adam’s. III, 354. The bodies of the people of former times were larger than those of people today. VII, 447, 448. Before sin the human body was the best of its kind. III, 134. It did not suffer illness. I, 601. Whether the body can suffer and yet not die. VII, 710, 711.

Adam’s body before sin was not corruptible. VI, 332. Adam’s body was simultaneously mortal and immortal. III, 354; V. Adam. The immortality of Adam’s body came from the tree of life. VII, 394. The animal body of the first human beings, and of those who would have been born from them if no sin had occurred, could have passed into a spiritual condition without an intervening death. X, 1599. If our first parents had not sinned, their bodies would have received an angelic form. III, 283. After sin the body began to be subject to death. III, 200. The death of the body resulted from sin. X, 114. How the body died because of sin. X, 112. The Apostle calls it “dead” because of this necessity of dying. I, 628. The body is destined to die in us even when we live justly. III, 354. Why the Apostle calls it the body of death, or a dead body, rather than a mortal body. III, 354, 399. Even now the body is said to be dead so long as it does not perfectly serve the spirit. VI, 62, 65. The body is the tomb of the dead soul. IV, 1117. What “body of flesh” means. X, 545. Whether “body of death” should be understood as sins or as flesh. X, 1089. “Body of death” is said of vice, not of substance. X, 279. Congenital defects of bodies or minds prove original sin. X, 1432. Natural defects of bodies or souls are not to be attributed to God the Creator. X, 1420. [Col. 0193] Bodies would not be born defective if there were no sin. X, 1194, 1288. And if nature had not been corrupted by sin. X, 1290.

The loss of the body’s grace was the punishment for Adam’s sin. X, 120. Two things must be considered in the body: God’s creation and the punishment merited. IV, 1843. “God made your body good, because he is good; the just one brought corruption upon it, because he is judge.” IV, 1843, 1844. Although human and animal bodies have common material, corruption and lust need not therefore be common to them. X, 1363. The custom of covering the body arose from sin. X, 1376. The peace of flesh and spirit is not present in this body of death, but it was present in that body of life belonging to human beings before sin. X, 1531.

What an animal, dead, and spiritual body are. VII, 397. Which bodies are animal and which spiritual. VII, 395. And how they differ. VII, 402. Animal bodies, that is, animated bodies. VII, 401. A body is called animal because of the dissolution of death, but spiritual because it is already immortal with the spirit—not because it is changed into spirit. II, 945. Some have asserted that every body can be changed into every other body. III, 362. And it is credible that this can happen. III, 365. No body can be converted into a soul or into an incorporeal nature. III, 362. A corruptible body would not burden the soul if there were no sin. X, 1529. The burden of the body always remains in this life. V, 1260. All bodies are corruptible, but they burden some souls less and others more, according to the diversity of God’s hidden but nevertheless just judgments. X, 1424. Our body was our ornament; we sinned, and from it we received fetters. IV, 1896. The body is man’s heaviest bond. I, 1328. The body is a servant and is common to human beings and beasts. VII, 264. The body is the servant of the soul. III, 400.

The body must be disciplined so that the devil and the world may be conquered. VI, 294. The body must be subjected to service. VI, 294. This happens if we first subject ourselves to God. VI, 294. To subdue the body. V, 107. By not sparing the body, one takes care of it. V, 1258, 1261. Why we sin by loving bodies. VIII, 109. No one hates his own body. III, 28. And even if something is loved more than the body, the body is not thereby hated. III, 29. Porphyry taught that every body must be shunned. I, 590; V, 1108. For the purification of the soul. VII, 375. So that the soul may be blessed. VII, 308. The discipline of the body is a sacrifice. VII, 283. The bodies of the faithful are a sacrifice to God, members of Christ, and a temple of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 791.

The body of the faithful is the temple of God. X, 433. Our bodies, because of Christ’s body, are members of Christ, as are our souls. V, 878. Our bodies, because the Spirit of Christ dwells in them, are temples of the Holy Spirit. V, 878, 880. And because they were purchased with Christ’s blood. V, 886. How the Holy Spirit dwells in them. V, 881. To what extent the body is sanctified by baptism. X, 847. The perfect sanctification of bodies is hoped for, not possessed. X, 425. What it means to abolish the body of sin. III, 2069. The body becomes holy through the practice of a holy will. VII, 30. The violence of another’s lust does not take holiness away from the body. VII, 32. The body is called man’s vessel and house. IV, 561. The bodies of the righteous are like vessels and instruments used by the Holy Spirit for good works. VII, 27. The saints give little attention to the burial of the body. I, 775, 778.

Both the death and resurrection of the body. III, 25. The resurrection of bodies, denied by the pagans, is asserted against them. VII, 754. The Manichaeans deny the resurrection of bodies. VIII, 146. The world does not rashly believe in the resurrection of bodies. VII, 793. The life of the body is to be hoped for, since the life of the spirit has already preceded it. X, 113. The resurrection of bodies is necessary for the soul’s perfect blessedness. III, 483. The body will not obstruct the soul’s happiness. VII, 794. What is now a burden will then be an honor; what is now a load will then be a relief. V, 1259. No bodies, considered in themselves, can be either blessed or miserable. I, 1283. The resurrection of bodies, and what it will be like in the age to come. X, 112, 113. Human bodies, even though animal and earthly, are owed resurrection and eternal incorruption. X, 1359, 1362. Bodies are restored to such a condition when they are healed as mortal nature, after sin, has already received—a nature that compels them to die. X, 1449.

The bodies will be saved in the resurrection of the dead. III, 1527. To depart from this body of death is one thing; to be delivered from it is another. X, 299. Those who will rise for punishment are not delivered from this body of death. X, 433. The body of death returns to the wicked in the resurrection. V, 840. What will happen to our body after death need not greatly concern us. III, 289. It will be the same body as before. I, 613. How bodies will be restored in the resurrection. VII, 27. In the future life the body will be restored to its former stability. I, 603; III, 132, 133.

What the bodies of the saints will be like after the resurrection. VII, 393, 403. The body will be better after the resurrection than that of our first parents was in paradise. I, 601. What the human body will be like in heaven. VII, 793. It will be spiritual. I, 620, 647. [Col. 0194] How it will become spiritual in the resurrection. VIII, 145. Our bodies, now earthly and animal, will become spiritual after the resurrection, and how this will happen. II, 355, 618, 629; VI, 188, 274. Augustine has no doubt that the quality of bodies after the resurrection will be spiritual, although he is unable to explain it. II, 355. See Resurrection. Why spiritual bodies are called spiritual after the resurrection. V, 1143. The body will be subjected to the spirit without inconvenience. I, 588. It will not need nourishment. I, 603. The bodies of the saints will be spiritual in such a way that they will eat, if they wish, by possibility and not by necessity. VII, 395. The swiftness of the spiritual body. V, 1263. The heavenly body, like Christ’s, will be able to enter a house through closed doors. V, 1264.

The body will be incorruptible and immortal. I, 588. Perfect health of the body is the immortality of the whole person. II, 438. The body remains incorrupt if incorruption does not depart from the mind. VI, 495. The body’s immortality and incorruption arise from the health of the soul. III, 27. It is the reward of the merit that Adam lost. III, 355. The immortality of bodies after death. VII, 240. And their eternity. VII, 309. It seemed absurd to philosophers that the body should be immortal and eternal after death. VII, 389. It is shown that the immortality and eternity of bodies after death are not impossible. VII, 390. According to Plato, to live forever in a body is a great gift of God. VII, 392.

How an earthly body will be in heaven. V, 1140. That earthly bodies cannot be in heaven was a philosophical dogma. VII, 390, 773. It is refuted. VII, 772. How our body will be in heaven if there is no corruption there. V, 1622. See Resurrection. It is more marvelous for incorporeal minds to be joined to earthly bodies than for earthly bodies to be raised to heavenly ones. VII, 755. Thoughts are now hidden in the body, but not in the same way in the heavenly body. III, 213.

Whether corporeal things can be seen by the body alone. VII, 800. Whether God will be seen through a spiritual body. V, 1264. Whether through a spiritual body a substance that is not seen in a place can be seen remains unknown. V, 1265. Whether loving corporeal appearance is a form of alienation. VIII, 817, 818, *Retractationes*. Whether knowledge can arise apart from bodily form. X, 537. “Body” signified by the term “pavement.” IV, 1525.

“Body” is used for the whole person. III, 1739. The handing over of bodies. III, 265. “Bodies” used for things possessed corporeally. III, 265. And for slaves. III, 496.

“Corporeal” is used both properly and figuratively. III, 459. Those who voluntarily enslaved themselves to corporeal things are justly oppressed by corporeal servitude. I, 740.

The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. III, 612; V, 729. See Eucharist. The reception of Christ’s body and blood. III, 704. Daily reception of Christ’s body, and its reception as non-daily in some places. III, 1280, 1614. What it means to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood. III, 1614, 1618. Our bodies are members of Christ because of Christ’s body. V, 878. Christ’s body, which is the Church, is called Christ; and the devil’s body is called the devil. III, 442. We are joined to Christ’s body by faith and given life by understanding. III, 1618.

Correction of anyone is not to be despaired of, except the devil’s. IV, 630. Correction of life must not be postponed. V, 512, 1095. See Conversion. It is dangerous to defer correction of one’s morals. III, 1651.

Fraternal correction. III, 708; IX, 81, 82. Reproof and discipline must not be neglected. V, 111, 549; IX, 98; X, 918. Even though they are disliked. II, 247, 957. Correction must not be neglected when it can be carried out by advice, authority, or power. III, 1263. To neglect fraternal correction is a grave evil. IX, 83. “He who strikes is pious; he who spares is cruel.” V, 111. To neglect reproof out of desire or weakness is a sin. VII, 21. Correction must be administered. X, 931. The necessity and usefulness of reproof. X, 919, 921. Reproof is useful and necessary even though grace depends on God. X, 920. Although predestination is certain, or although none of the predestined can perish, correction must nevertheless not be neglected. X, 945. Since it is uncertain to us whom God has determined to save, we ought to seek the salvation of all and of each person by our desire, preaching, and correction. X, 944. Correction must be applied to everyone. X, 946. The good are reproved as sons; the wicked are dismissed as strangers. IV, 883, 1177. Whoever is forgiven in the future age is reproved for his sin in this age. IV, 595. Correction serves not only the one corrected but also the good of others. VII, 644. Correction is a remedy against certain sins. VI, 228. The Lord’s command concerning the correction of the wicked. VI, 200.

Everyone is obliged to administer correction. VII, 21. Especially bishops. VII, 21. And those who are set over others. VII, 21. The duty of reproving is imposed on those in authority. V, 124, 1697. He does not rule who does not correct. IV, 504. We must not neglect to reprove those entrusted to our care. V, 549. Shepherds must not spare the vices of the multitude in order to win its favor. V, 274. To reprove is the work of a true shepherd. V, 762. Not to reprove is the work of a hired servant. V, 761. Whoever neglects correction is justly scourged temporarily together with those who do evil. VII, 21. Augustine’s frankness in reproving a friend who had asked him for consolation over his wife’s death. [Col. 0195] II, 1074.

What correction is permitted, and to what extent. IX, 432. With what disposition the duty of reproving is to be undertaken and fulfilled. III, 1261, 1262, 1263, 1298, 2143. With what disposition correction must be administered. II, 531; V, 507, 549, 1698; VI, 199. How fraternal correction must be given and received. I, 1381. The correction of the restless is not returning evil for evil. IX, 350. In correction, good rather than evil is returned for evil. X, 946. It is not permissible to rage against the wicked. V, 1389. “Do you wish to overcome wickedness by wickedness? There will be two wickednesses.” V, 1389. If the one who reproves wishes to return evil for evil to the person who resents his reproof, he was not worthy to reprove but was plainly worthy to be reproved himself. II, 958. Correction must not be given in order to insult, but in order to heal through shame. V, 779. So that the soul that had gone forth in dissipation may return in shame. V, 780. Correction must be given with charity. X, 902. Correction proceeds from charity. X, 942, 944. Correction is a duty of love. V, 54. Whoever reproves out of charity does not lose charity by applying severity. II, 530. It is better to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness. II, 323. Much must be done even against the unwilling, who must be punished with a certain kindly harshness. II, 531. The final punishment is justly demanded when no opportunity for correction remains. II, 530.

When correction is beneficial. X, 920. Whence correction derives its power and effectiveness. X, 942. Whence it derives its usefulness. X, 944. It is God who makes correction beneficial. X, 946. Correction is beneficial only through God. X, 921. Human correction occurs only through divine assistance. X, 1246. Correction without grace working inwardly is of no benefit. VII, 442. Why those who do not obey are justly reproved, even though they have not yet received the grace to obey. X, 920. Whether they are regenerate or not. X, 921. Correction is a healing medicine for the predestined, but a punitive torment for the reprobate. X, 942. “To be reproved by God” and “to be instructed” are referred to the same gentleness. IV, 1145. The use of command, correction, and prayer. X, 919. Corrections are made by rebuke, admonition, and prayer. II, 231. Correction and grace do not cancel each other. X, 942.

How correction must be administered. IX, 83, 84; X, 946. Correction varies according to the diversity of faults. X, 944. Correction must sometimes be private and sometimes public. V, 510. When it should be private and when public. V, 510. Why it is done privately. V, 511. Publicly, only public sins are to be reproved. X, 946. “If you alone know that your brother has sinned and wish to accuse him before everyone, you are not a corrector but a betrayer.” V, 510. Public correction in the Church. V, 127. Great consideration is needed in administering correction, lest one sin. II, 353. Augustine confesses that he sins daily in administering correction. II, 353. A small person is better corrected than a stubborn one broken; and a teachable, unlearned person is better corrected than a headstrong one. II, 873; VI, 160. Correction is sometimes omitted out of a counsel of charity. VII, 21. Those who cannot be corrected must be tolerated. IV, 1692.

Correction must not be rejected or despised merely because it comes from an inferior. II, 290. Against those who refuse correction. X, 920. An answer is made to the excuses of those unwilling to be corrected. X, 921. Those who take correction badly call quarrelsome and contentious the people who deal earnestly with them. IX, 450. Whoever does not wish to be made healthy in himself becomes mad against the one who reproves him. V, 78. To be ashamed of correction is a fault of the proud. VII, 309. How the more honorable make good use of correction. I, 725. It is easier to see what to correct in another and to correct it than to see what must be corrected in oneself and willingly accept correction. III, 2114. It is much more marvelous and praiseworthy willingly to accept someone correcting us than boldly to correct someone who has gone astray. II, 286. By humbly accepting correction from Paul, Peter left posterity a rarer and holier example than Paul did by reproving Peter. II, 285. Sins seem more pardonable when the guilty person promises correction. II, 654. When the truth is spoken to us with some harshness, we are corrected not by the human being, who may perhaps be a sinner, but by Christ. II, 130. Paul does not spare the vices of those who show him honor. V, 273. How God corrects. VIII, 159. The scourging of God when he reproves must be patiently endured. V, 146. See Scourging. How correction of heretics should be attempted. VIII, 173. The correction of a man through a vision of being beaten. V, 1410.

The corruption of character and disposition reveals itself in children through many signs. I, 674.

In this life the body is subject to continual corruption and change. IV, 752. Whence corruption comes. VIII, 202, 203. Natures are corruptible because they were made from nothing. VIII, 554. Corruption tends toward non-being. VIII, 204. Through corruption all things tend toward non-being. I, 1348. But God does not allow them to reach that point. I, 1349. Corruption is not nature but contrary to nature. VIII, 201. Corruption is not a substance but exists in a substance. I, 1348. Nothing is corrupted except what is good. I, 1349. Corruption is nothing other than the destruction [Col. 0196] of the good. VI, 238. Wherever there is corruption, there was once good. VIII, 201.

Why corruption is permitted by God. VIII, 203. God’s goodness orders the things that are corrupted in a most fitting way. I, 1349. Not every corruption deserves blame. I, 1290. Only corruption that is vicious is blamed. I, 1291. The corruption of the soul through illicit desires. IV, 1920, 1921. Corruption begins with bad faith; from there one proceeds to shameful morals, and from there to the most grievous iniquities. IV, 614. It is corruption of the mind to be disgusted by what is sweet. IV, 1425.

Those who corrupt themselves are not innocent. V, 1272. Who can be corrupted by another and who cannot. I, 1290.

Flashes of lightning signify miracles. IV, 1865.

The raven sent out from the ark could have perched on a corpse. III, 551. What is signified by the raven sent out from the ark that did not return. VIII, 264. Ravens signify the pagans; the young of ravens, the children of the pagans. IV, 1911, 1912. The raven’s voice. V, 512, 1095. The raven’s voice, “tomorrow, tomorrow,” in those who postpone conversion. IV, 1330. God does not seek delay in the raven’s voice, but confession in the dove’s groaning. IV, 1330. See Penitent sinners.

Why a rib was taken from the sleeping Adam and not from the wakeful one. IV, 668.

Tarquinius cut a whetstone with a razor. VII, 294.

Cotta argues in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*. VII, 149.

Quails were not given to the Israelites in the wilderness, but *ortygometra* [a distinct bird]. III, 617.

Cranaus, successor of King Cecrops to the throne of Athens. VII, 568.

The two Crassi, father and son, were slaughtered in each other’s sight at the time of Marius’s victory. VII, 107.

“Tomorrow, tomorrow,” the raven’s voice, by which many remained outside after the door had been closed. V, 512.

Tomorrow. How one must not think about tomorrow. VIII, 167. How the command not to think about tomorrow is to be understood. III, 1803; VI, 507.

Crates of Thebes embraced the Cynic sect. X, 1362.

To create and to establish are the same. VI, 184. In Scripture, “to create,” “to establish,” “to constitute,” and “to make” are used interchangeably and with the same meaning. VIII, 632, 633. No creature can create. III, 602. Therefore human beings cannot fashion something from nothing, because they work through the body. VI, 90.

Creator. Who alone is the Creator. VIII, 877, 878. God alone can be the creator of any nature whatsoever. III, 403, 405. The Creator must not be blamed for any offense arising from vices, but must be praised in consideration of all natures. VII, 353. Nothing in creation is coeternal with the Creator. VII, 365. The omnipotence of the Creator. III, 406. How marvelous are the works of the Creator. III, 1450. The Creator is omnipotent through the power of wisdom, not through reckless power. III, 406. The Creator’s omnipotence is the cause of every creature’s subsistence. III, 304. The Creator is justly praised in all the things he made, because they are all very good. III, 369. To have created mutable and temporal things without mutable and temporal movements requires considerable, or at least some, wisdom. II, 948. Creatures are steps toward knowledge of the Creator. I, 744, 745. We must not love the creature while neglecting the Creator; rather, let us attend to the creature and praise the Creator. V, 1204.

The Arians thought that “created” meant the same as “begotten.” VIII, 633, 634. The offspring of the Creator is not a creature. VIII, 583, 584. The offspring of the Creator is entirely equal to him. VIII, 585.

The benefit of creation. V, 172. Three things must be known about a creature: who made it, through what he made it, and why he made it. VII, 334. How marvelous is the wisdom of the Creator in the creation of the universe. VIII, 391. The works of creation should not be regarded as unbelievable. VII, 376. God made the whole creation not through some creature but alone. IV, 1758. Nothing is born unless God works it. IV, 1552. There is no creature that was not created by the omnipotent one. VI, 183. Scripture did not omit any kind of creature in its account of creation. III, 341. That a thing can exist belongs to the nature of things; that it will come to be belongs only to God’s will. III, 350. The creature cries out everywhere, “God made me.” IV, 205. Creatures cry out, “He made us”; their cry is their appearance. I, 783. The whole creation proclaims that it has the most excellent Creator. VIII, 1061. Although creatures can be nothing without God, they are not what he is. VII, 220.

Creation. God made all things from nothing. I, 811, 828; III, 137. Why. VIII, 117. Against those who deny that something can be made from nothing. I, 1191. The creature was made not from God’s nature but from nothing. III, 247. Creatures were made from nothing, not from God. VIII, 559. How creatures are from God. X, 497. To have been made from nothing is the same as not being God’s nature. X, 1479. Whatever is made cannot be equal to the one by whom it is made. VI, 11. Creatures possess within themselves the limit of their nature, by which they are not what God is. III, 309. The creature is neither consubstantial nor coeternal with God. III, 247. From Paul it is shown that the creature is neither alien to God nor of the same substance as he. [Col. 0197] VIII, 583. How the creature was made by God, not begotten from God. VIII, 548. God established all creatures from his goodness alone, not from need. I, 845.

Creatures are in God. III, 332. Whatever creatures exist are life in God. III, 1387. How. III, 1387. Creatures are life not in themselves but in God. III, 332. What kind of life they are. III, 332. Things that have been made are better in God, because there they are truer, eternal, and unchangeable. III, 332. Before they were made, all things existed in the knowledge of their maker. III, 332. Before it was made, the creature was life in God’s wisdom. III, 1397. Creatures are in God’s own wisdom. III, 287. How creatures existed in God’s wisdom before creation. VIII, 674. The Priscillianists taught that all things, before appearing as made, always remained made in God’s wisdom. VIII, 668. How this can be rightly understood. VIII, 674. All creatures were established by God’s power and wisdom. VIII, 586. Just as the movement of wisdom is most effectively accomplished with ease, so God easily established all things. III, 318. All creatures are in God’s Word. III, 1674. Every creature, except light, was first in the Word of God, then came to be in the knowledge of rational creation, and afterward in its own kind. III, 269. Creatures exist in one way in the Word of God, in another way as they were first established by God, and in another way as they are now produced. III, 331.

All creatures were made by God through his Son. VIII, 579. The Father’s command that all things should be made is nothing other than the Father’s Word, through which all things were made. VIII, 685. Why, in the account of creation, the Son is mentioned sometimes as the Beginning and sometimes as the Word. III, 248. The opinion of some that God made all things by the Word but made man, as more excellent than the rest, with his own hands is refuted. IV, 158. God established the whole creation through the Son in the unity of the Holy Spirit. III, 221, 241. Whoever denies that the creature was made from nothing by God the Father through the Son in the goodness of the Holy Spirit, and that it is mutable, is compelled to speak sacrilegiously about God. VIII, 584.

The creation of the world is the work of the whole Trinity. VIII, 129. Every creature receives being, form, and order from the creative Trinity. III, 129. Traces of the Trinity in creation. VII, 342. The Holy Trinity is indicated in the beginning and perfection of creation. III, 251. The eternal Wisdom is the beginning of spiritual creation. III, 250.

The creature was made not before the ages, but with the ages. III, 335. Arguments by which the creation of natures in time is attacked. VII, 366. They are resolved. VII, 366. It is not impossible for God to make new things for the world without having a changeable will. VII, 371. It is violent to try to demonstrate that something can now be made from nothing. III, 411. The opening of Genesis concerning the creation of heaven and earth can be understood in various ways. III, 247. All things were created simultaneously. III, 231, 234, 317, 322, 327, 328, 330, 388. How, then, are six days narrated? III, 319, 326. And how are separate operations assigned to separate days? III, 231. All things were created simultaneously in the principles of spiritual creation. III, 234. The other creatures were not made without the knowledge of spiritual creation. III, 312. In what way creatures are known by God and by angels. III, 334. God’s creature is known to angels in one way and to us in another. III, 325. Our mind is not capable of seeing creatures with God in the principles according to which they were made. III, 333. Why we do not know creatures as easily as we know God. III, 219, 220. We know creatures in God’s Word and in the first creation not through the senses but by believing divine authority. III, 331. Many creatures are unknown to us. III, 334. In creatures, morning signifies their form and evening their privation or defect. III, 235. Knowledge of the creature in itself produced evening. III, 314. Nevertheless, it is not unfittingly called day in a certain respect. III, 312. The creature has evening in itself, not in God. III, 308.

How the works of creation were completed on the sixth day and yet remain begun. III, 318, 348, 393. Only one day was created, by the repetition of which the many days so called pass away. III, 310, 314, 321. The order of the creation of things through six days is not an interval of time but a connection of causes. III, 325, 326. Why particular works were produced on particular days. III, 273. The beginning of creation in the Creator’s rest is signified by the morning of the seventh day. III, 309. It does not appear when the seventh day was created. III, 310. See Day. On the seventh day of creation, fullness and rest are commended. VII, 344. The number of the days of creation is mystical. VII, 347. How things that move through temporal intervals to accomplish what belongs to each kind were established. III, 318. The first creation of things took place without bodily delay, but their administration did not. III, 330. The production and succession of things that now occurs is the unfolding of the ages that God implanted in the whole creation. III, 336. In the creation that is narrated as having been made without intervals of temporal delay, a wonderfully distinct order of things is found. VIII, 609, 610. There is a twofold kind of creature not subject to time. I, 831.

The species of the whole creation is formed solely by the work of God. VII, 374. All things made by divine skill both display a certain unity in themselves and possess form and order. VIII, 932. Creatures have their own measures, numbers, and orders. [Col. 0198] III, 288. All creatures were established in their respective degrees and distinguished by their orders. VIII, 538. The degrees, order, and number of creatures were known to God before creation. VIII, 674. Measure, form, and order are universal goods in things made by God. VIII, 553. In what sense “measure” is sometimes said to be evil, etc. VIII, 558. In creatures there is an order of reason, an order of usefulness, and an order of justice. VII, 331. All creatures are arranged in determinate degrees, either by intervals of place, by natural merits, or by the merits of rewards and punishments. VIII, 586, 595. How marvelous and diverse is the beauty of creatures. VII, 791. From where creatures receive their form. I, 845. They would hang formless if they had drawn existence from God alone. I, 845. The marvelous ordering of creatures. IV, 1878. All creatures are governed according to a certain order. VIII, 873.

The creation of heaven and earth. I, 811. How what Scripture says about the creation of things is variously understood. I, 841, 842. How one should answer someone asking what God was doing before the creation of heaven and earth. I, 815. God created man through his Word, and through the Word recreated him. IV, 1855. The wonders, or miracles, of creation are unusual for this reason: they were the first. III, 373.

That all creatures are good, against the Manichaeans. I, 743. Every creature is good in its own kind and order. VIII, 538, 607. But not equally so—why? VIII, 606. Since God made everything, why did he not make everything equal? VI, 27. How it can be proved that God made all good things from nothing, “very good.” VIII, 580. The creature was made from nothing, not from God, and therefore is not supremely good. VIII, 593. Creatures are good insofar as they have received existence. III, 32. The goodness of a creature’s nature is shown by its corruption and even by the blameworthiness of vice itself. I, 1289. All creatures are so good that reason demonstrates even those created with vices to be good, through the testimony also of the vices themselves. X, 1537. The Manichaeans must always be pressed concerning the goodness of creatures, so that they may acknowledge God, whom they deny, as the author of their good. X, 1537.

To what extent Catholics praise the creature. X, 611. Why the Pelagians praise it. X, 606, 609. In praising the creature the Pelagians seem to have recovered from the error of the Manichaeans, but they perish from another plague of their own; both are refuted by the Catholics. X, 611. The true praise of creatures. VIII, 300. To what extent the works of the Creator are to be praised. X, 770.

Creatures, when not compared with God, exist, because they are from him; but when compared with him, they do not exist. IV, 1741, 1863. A rational creature that avoids evil only by comparison with other evils is nevertheless no small good. III, 434. God did not create the defect of creatures, but ordered it. III, 240. Nothing happens to man in respect of bodily defects that God does not will. III, 598. Every creature sinned of its own accord and became hostile to the truth; but, so that it might justly be punished, it was subjected to vanity not of its own accord. IV, 1532. God’s love for his works proceeds from his beneficence. III, 250, 251. God applies the effectiveness of his power to establishing the things that arise daily. II, 948. God creates inwardly; outwardly, the works of the creature are employed. VIII, 876. If God’s goodness withdraws from created things, they relapse into nothing. X, 712, 858. A creature, whether bodily or spiritual, is always manifold. VIII, 928.

The subjection of creatures to God and to one another. III, 390. God placed spiritual creation above bodily creation. III, 388. Apart from man, the other things that the Lord created he subjected, with supremely wise ordering, either to good or to evil angels. X, 1421.

The creation of spiritual creation. I, 846. The rational creature: how great a good it is. VIII, 554. Intellectual creation has its place in the rest of God. III, 309. How it is evident how weak spiritual creation is. I, 848. A creature is good insofar as it exists; insofar as it falls short, it shows that it was not begotten from God but made by him from nothing. VIII, 191. Why creatures fall short and are changeable. III, 136. All creatures are changeable, not because they are from God, but because they were made from nothing. X, 666, 667, 1481. And yet they are good. X, 1495. Bodily creation can be changed through times and places, spiritual creation through times alone. III, 388. Intellectual creation, through contemplation of the truth, transcends all times. III, 252.

Which rational creature is better. VIII, 614. Through participation in the Creator, incorporeal rational creatures become better. II, 562. Spiritual creation can possess formless life—why? III, 249. The formlessness of creation is its turning away from unchangeable wisdom, while its beauty is its turning toward it. III, 249. Spiritual creation is an imperfect and dark abyss so long as it does not turn toward the Creator. III, 247, 252. When a creature abandons the unchangeable light, it is darkened in itself; when it turns toward that light, it becomes light—not in itself, but in the Lord. VIII, 602. How a creature can be illumined. III, 247. And be called light. I, 846. A creature then imitates the form of the divine Word when it turns toward the Creator of its substance. III, 249. Eternal Wisdom never ceases speaking to intellectual creation, so that it may turn toward the one from whom it comes. III, 249. A creature that has not turned toward its Creator tends toward nothingness. III, 247. Since a creature was made from nothing, when it sins it can incline toward nothingness—how? VIII, 583, 584, 587, 590, 594. When a rational creature clings to its Creator in the obedience of love, it preserves its nature in his eternity, truth, and love. VIII, 595.

A rational creature is either blessed or wretched. VII, 266. Origen taught that the alternating changes of blessedness and wretchedness among rational creatures have always existed and will always exist. VIII, 33. In what the happiness and perfection of spiritual creation consist. I, 846. Rational creation was made in such a way that it cannot itself be the good by which it becomes blessed. II, 561, 568. A rational creature’s turning away from the unchangeable good is vice and misery; its turning toward it is virtue and blessedness. II, 561, 568, 569. For those who turn away from God, creatures are converted into punishment. IV, 1887.

A rational creature is either mortal or immortal. VII, 266. All creatures began to exist, but some cease and others remain. VIII, 604. What is created in time can be immortal. II, 727. God would not create any creature whom he foreknew would become evil unless he also knew for what good uses he would employ it. VII, 332. Is it cruel for God to create those whom he knows will be damned? X, 1442. No creature ought to live according to itself. VII, 408. Nothing but God is sufficient to satisfy the needs of creation. VII, 349. The true food of rational creation is God alone. X, 255. Spiritual creation is the heaven of heaven. III, 252. Spiritual and bodily creation as a whole is often called heaven and earth. III, 273.

Creatures are the traces and signs of God. I, 1264. How God is contained in creatures. IV, 1480, 1481. All the works of God bear witness to God’s goodness and greatness. IV, 1580. How all creatures praise God. IV, 205, 845, 846, 1691, 1878, 1946. The forms of creatures are voices praising their Creator. IV, 206. All creatures bore witness to Christ. III, 1398. Creation was made a spectacle for man. IV, 1851. Creation is a very extensive and immense commonwealth. VIII, 873. The whole of creation is a great book of the nature of things. VIII, 509. God does not enjoy creation but uses it. III, 32. How God is described as using all creatures as he wills. VIII, 872. Creation never surpasses the will of its Creator. IV, 1464.

How created things are to be loved. III, 1995. A creature can be loved both well and badly. VII, 467. A creature is harmful to its lover for no other reason than that it is preferred to the Creator. IV, 1028. Those who prefer a creature to God are reproved. V, 144. Love of creatures is drunkenness. I, 677. It scatters and tears a person apart, as it were. I, 675. No creature may be worshiped with the worship owed to God alone. VII, 217. Whoever worships a creature with wicked and obscene rites sins twice against God. VII, 217. From creatures one must rise up to the Creator. V, 699.

No creature of God is evil, but to use it badly is evil. VIII, 562. See Evil. Sin. How a creature is to be used or enjoyed. VIII, 968. Without love of the Creator, no one uses creatures well. X, 755. The use of creatures is the solace of the wretched and condemned, not the rewards of the blessed. VII, 792. A soul that uses a creature perversely does not escape the ordering of the Creator. II, 539. In how many ways a creature is taken as a sign. VIII, 879. The creature of man in man. VIII, 583. Every creature is partly bodily and partly incorporeal. II, 378.

The Manichaeans violently insulted believers. VIII, 183. In religion it is not shameful to believe before knowing. VIII, 81. How necessary belief is in many matters for human society. VIII, 84, 85. Sometimes believing is without fault, sometimes with fault—when? VIII, 83. What difference is there between believing and supposing? VI, 488. How believers are removed from the rashness of those who merely suppose. VIII, 84.

To believe is to think with assent. X, 963. One believes what one does not grasp. III, 1667. There are things that we do not believe unless we understand them, and other things that we do not understand unless we believe them. IV, 1552. One believes in order to understand. III, 1667. Believing is not the same as beholding with the mind’s gaze. II, 597, 599. Absent things are believed; present things are seen. II, 600. To refuse to believe anything except what one sees is perverse. V, 698. In what sense we are said to see things believed with the mind. II, 600. When we believe certain bodily things that we have read or heard but have not seen, the mind must form for itself something in the outlines and shapes of bodies; and this is useful for some purpose. VIII, 951, 952. Believe what you do not yet see, so that you may not be ashamed when you see it. IV, 1208. One may believe or disbelieve human witnesses or testimonies according to the judgment of how much weight they possess, or do not possess, for producing belief. II, 598.

What it means to believe in God. III, 1631. To believe in God means, by believing, to cling to him so as to cooperate well with God, who works good. IV, 988. To believe is to approach God. III, 1741. We do not believe in an Apostle or in a human being—why? III, 1781. You live if you believe; if you believe, you become a temple of God. IV, 1620, 1704. Three degrees among believers. V, 1297. Faith in Christ, poor and crucified. V, 251, 730. Whoever does not believe in Christ is condemned. V, 1343. Believing Christ and believing in Christ are different. V, 788. What it means to believe in [Col. 0200] Christ. III, 1778. To believe in Christ means to love Christ. IV, 1704. To possess the faith that works through love. VI, 217. See Faith. Believing in the heart is not enough unless Christ is also not denied with the mouth. VI, 526. Those who are unwilling to speak what they believe do not believe perfectly. IV, 1492. It is difficult for one who believes rightly to live wrongly. V, 321. To come to Christ is to believe. X, 568. For infants, to believe is to be baptized. X, 132. Many say that they do not wish to believe in Christ because no one can fulfill what he commands. IV, 1370. See Faith. If you believe in Christ born in the flesh, you will reach Christ born from God. IV, 1641. What is to be believed concerning Christ. V, 1072, 1124. See Christ.

To believe the Gospel is a gift of God. X, 972. Belief is given to us by the Father. III, 1618. No one believes except one who has heard from the Father; and everyone who has heard and learned comes. X, 970. From where the will to believe comes. X, 237. The will is not sufficient for believing without grace. II, 830, 831. The will to believe is not attributed to God merely because it proceeds from the free choice that we received when we were created. X, 240. Those who attribute too much to their own powers cannot believe in Christ. III, 1778. To believe is the work of God, and that same work is righteousness. V, 320. How God works in a person the very will to believe. X, 240. Both believing and doing good are given through the Holy Spirit, and at the same time they are ours. X, 964. In what sense believing and willing are ours. III, 2061, 2062. Retr. Difficult things are neither believed nor grasped unless God grants it. III, 1815. No one can believe unless touched by some calling. VI, 126. We are called by God’s mercy so that we may believe; and believers are granted the ability to do good. III, 2061, 2062. Retr. The Jews and those who, together with them, do not believe, do not believe through the fault of their will. II, 830. It is a just punishment that people do not believe with a blinded heart; but it is free grace that they believe with a free will. X, 1518. Whether the ability or inability to believe is beneficial or harmful is of no advantage or detriment unless predestination is taken into account. X, 1014. Although some are naturally disposed to believe when certain words or deeds are presented, these are nevertheless not presented to them if they are not among the predestined. X, 1014. It did not benefit the Tyrians that they could believe, because they were not predestined; nor would it have harmed the Jews that they could not believe, if they had been predestined. X, 1014. Why it was given to some to believe and not given to others is God’s inscrutable judgment. X, 1016. Not all the people of every nation, but people from all nations, will believe in Christ. II, 923.

Three kinds of believable things. VI, 31. From what God has done it becomes believable that he has promised. V, 727. Faith in things more believable is strengthened by believing things that are less believable. X, 144. Things that are extremely joyful are scarcely believed, even when they are certain. IV, 1927.

There is a great difference between the gullible and the believing person. VIII, 80. The term “gullible” is ordinarily used as a reproach. VIII, 80. One must not believe every spirit. V, 984. See Faith.

The duty of a creditor and a debtor. III, 764. God calls his creditors to himself so that they may receive. V, 525.

Crescens of Cirta. IX, 208.

Crescentianus, Bishop of Mures. IV, 381.

To grow. “They grew young men” means “they became young men by growing.” III, 493.

Cresconius, tribune. II, 428, Note (b).

Creconius, a monk of Hadrumetum. II, 968, 971.

Cresconius, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 376.

Another Cresconius, a Maximianist. IV, 376.

Cresconius, a Donatist grammarian. I, 641.

Cresconius, bound to no clerical office. IX, 447.

Creso, Bishop of Conjustiacum. IV, 381.

Creso, or Cresoconius, of Titianum. IV, 381.

Physicians call a critical accession the phase through which one passes to health. IV, 923.

Creusa, the wife of Aeneas. VII, 576.

Criasus, king of the Argives. VII, 565.

Criatus, fifth king of the Argives. VII, 565.

A crime is a grave sin. III, 1697. Some have thought that there are only three deadly crimes. III, 995. They are refuted. III, 995. It is better to choose an uncertain crime concerning the future than a certain one in the present. VII, 570. To take pleasure in a false crime is a genuine crime. VII, 570. A false crime, which is slander, does not make a person guilty except before a human judge. IV, 1582. What is natural to a horse is a crime in a human being. IV, 1339.

Another person’s crime does not stain one. II, 86; IX, 31, 40, 233. Especially if it is unknown. II, 86; IX, 31, 40, 233. See Evils, Sins, Tradition. Even if the crimes are true, they do no harm to the love of the good, which tolerates everything in unity for the sake of unity. IX, 57. No one becomes a participant in another’s crime except one who does or approves what is unjust. IX, 79. Even if we are far from crime, we are nevertheless not without sin. IV, 1508. Many can be without a crime; no one is without sin. X, 563. See Sin.

Any crimes are forgiven in the Church. VI, 262. Crimes are not redeemed by almsgiving unless life is changed. VI, 265. See Sin. Sometimes crimes are punished by crimes, and the punishments of sinners are not torments but increases of vices. VIII, 635. To suffer accusations from the enemies of the Church together with the Church herself is glorious. IX, 611.

The long-haired monks are chastised. VI, 578. Why long hair was praiseworthy in Samuel and other ancients. VI, 578.

Crispina, martyr. IV, 1616, 1775, 1777, 1783; V, 1298, 1565; VI, 422, Note (a).

Crispinus, Donatist bishop of Calama. IX, 523, 528, 555. He is called a “yesterday’s recruit.” IX, 523.

Crispinus, presbyter of Crispinus of Calama, the Donatist. IX, 523. His savagery. IX, 523. Why the Catholics brought laws into action against Crispinus. IX, 524. Crispinus appeals to the sons of Theodosius. II, 306; IX, 524, 525. Through Catholic clemency, Crispinus was not permitted to be struck with the penalty of ten pounds of gold. II, 236, 306, 307. Through the intervention of Possidius. IX, 524. Crispinus acquired an estate near Hippo. IX, 316, 336. Crispinus did not hesitate to submerge nearly eighty souls by rebaptizing them. IX, 316, 336. Crispinus, a heretic, rebaptized the Mappalians, who had been subjugated by fear and money. II, 236.

Crispulus, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Crispus, consul. IX, 687.

“Critical” is what physicians call an accession in other cases. I, 719.

The crocodile alone moves its upper jaw when chewing. I, 891; X, 831. The shore of the crocodiles. VII, 253.

The distinction between χρόνοι (*chronoi*, “times”) and καιροί (*kairoi*, “appointed times” or “occasions”). II, 900.

God does not delight in torments, but in our justice; nor is the question what each person suffers, but why. V, 1293. All bodily torments that are inflicted either exercise those who have turned to God, admonish them to turn, or justly prepare the hardened for final condemnation. IV, 117, 118. Bodily torment afflicts the wicked and purifies the good. VI, 295. If the person being tormented gains no good from it, he grieves over the loss of salvation. VII, 641.

How light torment is when compared with Gehenna. VI, 719.

Why Christ chose the punishment of the cross. VI, 17, 630. Christ accepted the most shameful kind of death so that Christian freedom would fear not only no death but no kind of death. VIII, 166. Jesus carrying his cross: a great spectacle. III, 1945. What is signified by Christ’s carrying his cross. V, 1084. The inscription above the cross. V, 1084. Why Christ did not come down from the cross. V, 535, 543. By the cross Christ conquered the world. V, 334. The cross is the mousetrap by which the devil was caught. V, 726. By the power of the cross heresies are crushed, as the serpents of the magicians were crushed by Moses’ staff. VI, 696. The wickedness of the people who crucified the Son of God appears to have reached its completion; but greater is that of those who refuse to live rightly and hate the commandments of the truth, for which the Son of God was crucified. IV, 103.

The cross is the worst kind of death. III, 1665. Nothing seemed more accursed than the punishment of the cross. IV, 1829. The cross has now been removed from the punishment of the human race, since no one is crucified. IV, 366. The cross is no longer used among the Romans in the punishments of the guilty. III, 1664. It passed from places of punishment to the foreheads of emperors. IV, 366. That cross on which enemies insulted is now fixed on the foreheads of kings. IV, 637, 663, 1839. Christ conquered kings through his cross and, after subduing them, fixed the cross itself on their foreheads. IV, 1228. The sign of the cross is now more precious on the foreheads of kings than the jewel of the diadem. IV, 292, 934. Christ established the shame of the cross in the place of our shame. IV, 1839. Why he honored his cross here. V, 543. Since he gave such honor to his punishments, what does he reserve for his faithful? IV, 292, 366. Those who mock Christ’s cross are devoured by demons as by wild beasts. IV, 525.

The cross is the key of the Old Testament. V, 1377. It was the key by which closed things would be opened. IV, 514. Everything was revealed through the mystery of the cross. V, 1378. The cross is the sign of the New Testament, just as circumcision is of the old. V, 876. The cross is the rod of Christ’s kingdom. VI, 696. Christ’s cross was a tribunal. III, 1642. It was a tribunal, not a punishment. VI, 69, 695. The tribunal of the judge. V, 1293. The tribunal from which Christ condemned the one who insulted him and crowned the one who confessed him. V, 1460, 1471. Christ’s cross is a great candlestick. V, 1311, 1436. The cross is Christ’s school and chair. V, 1116, 1430. Christ accepted the cross not as a demonstration of power but as an example of patience. III, 1397. On Christ’s cross power was hidden, just as the number of seeds lies hidden in a grain. IV, 720. The cross itself was also made for the persecutors themselves. IV, 487.

The great exchange of the cross. V, 1454. To take up the cross. V, 586, 1456. Which cross must be taken up in order to follow Christ. VIII, 166. A Christian must bear the cross in the present life. II, 215. Christ’s cross must be embraced, lest we be swept away and swallowed in the whirlpool of this world. II, 335. Christ’s cross is the ship in which we cross the sea of this age. III, 1389, 1390. We must be carried by the Lord’s cross so that we may cross over to our homeland. V, 475. A Christian must hang continually on the cross. V, 1039. One must not depart from the cross, and it will itself lead us to our homeland. III, 1389. It is better not to see with the mind what truly is and not to depart from Christ’s cross than to see it with the mind and despise Christ’s cross. III, 1389. [Col. 0202] Christ’s cross strengthens us against the filth of the human race’s worst morals. II, 533.

The cross must not be regarded with shame. V, 1074. A Christian is not ashamed of the cross but bears it on the forehead. IV, 1839. Let glorying be in Christ’s cross, not in our righteousness. V, 877. The cross is a medicine. IV, 1838. The cross is a sign of humility, by which the swelling of pride is healed. IV, 1838. The humility of the cross is the way to exaltation. V, 875. The wood of the cross is called life. III, 1386.

The sign of the cross. I, 668; II, 694. The sign of the cross overcomes the enemies of the Church. V, 1638. Christ’s cross is Christ’s sign; unless this sign is applied, nothing is properly completed in the celebration of the sacraments. III, 1950. The cross, burial, and resurrection of Christ are to be observed in the celebration of Easter. II, 215. The sign of the cross on the forehead. V, 181, 201, 876, 941, 1293, 1386, 1501; VI, 335. The people are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s passion for the protection of salvation. VIII, 270. Christians immediately make the sign of the cross on their foreheads if they become frightened for any reason. IV, 585. A dying young man began to make the sign of the cross on his forehead. II, 694. The striking of Goliath on the forehead, where he did not have the sign of the cross, is not without mystery. IV, 1857. The cross is like a trophy on the foreheads of the faithful. III, 1396, 1665, 1709, 1780, 1946. If you bear on your forehead the sign of Christ’s humility, bear in your heart the imitation of Christ’s humility. V, 201. For the faithful the cross is triumph and a standard against the devil. VI, 664. The cross on the foreheads of catechumens. III, 1476. Through the sign of the cross the Church receives catechumens. VI, 659. A cancer cured by the sign of the cross. VII, 763. The sign of the cross appearing on the garments of the baptized. V, 136. The power of the nails of the cross. V, 1646.

The cross allegorically. III, 1949. Our cross is our mortality. II, 1058. In a certain sense, the person who governs his mortality through continence takes up his cross. V, 1085. The four dimensions of the cross. V, 371, 903. What the dimensions of the cross signify. II, 566, 611; IV, 1348. The breadth, length, and depth of the cross describe all Christian action. III, 64. The breadth of the cross signifies joy; its height, expectation of reward from the sublime justice of God; its length, endurance; its depth, the hiddenness of the sacrament. II, 216. The depth of the cross: that grace is given to one person and not given to another. V, 905. How one is to ascend the four steps of the cross that lead to heaven. VI, 698.

Noah’s ark was a figure of the cross. VI, 334. So too was Moses extending his hands. VIII, 901. The wood cast into the waters so that they might become sweet. III, 616. The Greek letter T. III, 804. The staff with which the rock was struck. III, 737. The two pieces of wood of the cross were signified by the double striking of the rock. III, 1612.

To know Christ crucified is great wisdom. V, 874. We have been crucified and have risen with Christ. III, 2063. The cross, burial, and resurrection are enacted in hope and faith. II, 215, 216. On the Lord’s cross the crucifixion of the old man is signified. III, 2069. The crucifixion of the inner man: the pains of repentance and a certain health-giving torment of continence. VIII, 891. The serpent lifted up by Moses was a figure and likeness of the likeness of sinful flesh to be crucified in Christ. IV, 1578. What it means to be crucified to the world. VI, 207. Who was crucified to the world, and to which world he was crucified. V, 1312. What “to injure the cross of light” means among the Manichaeans. IV, 1823.

Cruelty that spares, mercy that rages. II, 660.

What crystal is and how it is formed. IV, 1914.

Our inner bedchamber is our heart. IV, 343, 515.

The geometric cubit is equivalent to six of our cubits. III, 549; VII, 474. By the geometric cubit the capacity of the area for containing all animals is demonstrated. III, 549.

According to the Manichaeans, gourds are killed when they are plucked. VIII, 230.

The people of Cuicul. IX, 236.

Julian acknowledged that guilt is also the punishment of the sinner. X, 1354.

The worship of God cannot be expressed in a single word. VII, 278. Worship called *latria* is owed to God alone. VII, 279, 280. The Christian religion consists in worshiping one God, because only one God makes the soul blessed. III, 1585. What the worship of God consists in. X, 211. The worship of God is love of him. VIII, 1010. The worship owed to God consists in consecrating some of our possessions, or ourselves, through the rites of religion. VII, 277. A person becomes like the one whom he worships. III, 1466. The worship of God is piety; nor is he worshiped except by loving him. II, 557, 737. It benefits us to worship God, not God himself. II, 377. We worship God, and God tends us. V, 316, 531, 651. The worship of God is freely given. IV, 207, 488; V, 207, 865. The servitude of the old law occurs when God is worshiped for the sake of earthly things. V, 167. Whoever seeks earthly happiness in place of the worship of God assigns that worship a most contemptible price. V, 135. Only the free worship of God satisfies the soul. V, 865. God himself is the reward of those who worship him. V, 136. What kind of worship of God is servile and what kind is free. X, 597.

True worshipers of God are gods. VII, 279. The saints are our fellow servants, not to be worshiped in God’s place. V, 1442. Martyrs are to be honored; God is to be worshiped. V, 1249. The saints shudder at having the worship owed to God offered to themselves. V, 1251. Worship offered by pagans to dead human beings. V, 1249. The worship of many and false gods is fornication. III, 1702. See *Latria*.

The Cumaean Sibyl sang many things about Christ. VII, 580. The Cumaean prophetess perhaps heard something in the spirit concerning the one Savior. II, 1073. The Cumaean song. II, 393; III, 2089. Songs about Christ are attributed to the Cumaean Sibyl and circulated under the name of the Erythraean Sibyl. VII, 580.

Cumana was a Greek colony. VII, 86.

Cradles used for nursing. I, 841.

Cunina, the goddess who oversees infants’ cradles. VII, 118, 122.

What desire is. VI, 24, 25; VII, 409. Desire is a wicked will. I, 1295. Desire is improperly called affection (dilectio). VIII, 956. Love is called desire when it is perverse. IV, 124. Desire is love of things that one can lose against one’s will. I, 1227. When desire is mentioned without specifying its object, it can only be understood in an evil sense. VII, 411. The term desire is used of evil and disgraceful things. III, 1303. Things sought for the sake of something else are not to be called desires. I, 880.

No one except the Pelagians denies that desire is evil. X, 1366. Evil desire is not from God. IV, 291. Before sin there was no desire in Adam resisting the will. X, 1530. Desire makes us unlike God. VII, 271. Desire is culpable not because of its object but because of its disorder. III, 1824. Desire is the root of all evils. IV, 1154; X, 370. Desires are harlots. I, 705. Desire is threefold: of pleasure, domination, and knowledge. I, 807; III, 153. Christ, tempted by the devil, conquered these desires. I, 807; III, 153. Love of gold, praise, and women is more appropriately called desire or lust. I, 1329. Love of the world, love of this age, is called desire. IV, 260. Humility drives from the soul a windy and turbulent desire, greedy for things placed beyond our power. II, 483. There is toil wherever many things are sought and loved, for attaining and retaining which the will is not sufficient. II, 485. Desire does not know where necessity ends. X, 773. Desires are not brought to an end but increased if present things are despised for the sake of earthly promises. V, 263. Desire for eternal things must not be mixed with desire for temporal things. V, 204.

Temporal things do not extinguish desires. IV, 1411. They increase desire even more in those who possess temporal things. IV, 1639. While we scratch the heat of desire, we kindle it. I, 684. Desire is birdlime. IV, 1792. He is master of his possessions who is not entangled in desire; but whoever is held by desire is possessed, not a possessor. IV, 544. The dangers of one who jealously guards his possessions. V, 631. How desire for temporal things is unjust toward one’s neighbor. V, 203. Desires and lusts commonly arise from the sudden success of earthly happiness. III, 799. Desire is a bad master. IV, 163.

All the desires of this life are its satellites. V, 1282. Desire is a weight. I, 847. One’s own desire is each person’s storm. V, 482; VI, 456. Two things produce all sins in a person: desire and fear. IV, 1026. Desire is the soul’s advance; fear is the soul’s flight, etc. III, 1732. Desire and fear are two doors for the devil when he tempts. V, 200, 201. Through them the enemy enters and reigns. VI, 310. Through desire the devil reigns in a person. VI, 291. Invisible powers are conquered when desires are conquered. VI, 291. Evil desires are the gates of death. IV, 123. Desire is called sin. VI, 106. Each person sins through desire for lower things. IV, 950. The greater desire is, the stronger it makes a person to endure any evils. VI, 618, 622. So long as desire is in our members, it resists the law of the mind according to a law of its own. II, 771.

Some desires are born with us; others we acquire through habit. V, 817. Desire is strengthened by nature and habit. VI, 106. The desire of the world has its beginning in the choice of the will, its progress in the pleasure of delight, and its stability in the bond of habit. VI, 619. Human will should not be called free so long as it is subject to desires that conquer and bind it. II, 593. How great a good it is to be released from the bonds of desire. I, 763. When desires are strong and we serve them, they are called necessities. IV, 238. Frustrated desire turns into pain. VII, 711. The fullness of desires is not so much satisfaction as oppression. III, 846. Desire, like the root of thorns, turns sweet rain into punishments. IV, 1803. Every desire is followed by its own guilt. I, 674. In the soul itself, where the will’s appetite is the measure of all human actions, punishment immediately follows guilt, usually becoming greater through the heavier blindness of the person who does not perceive it. II, 381. In what sense the desires of the soul are called desires of the flesh, and how they are cured. X, 802.

Desires thought to belong to innocence, and to be lawful and permitted by the laws. VI, 613. Desire makes citizens of Babylon. IV, 773, 774.

Evil desires at birth: the little ones of Babylon. IV, 1773. [Col. 0204] Desire, while it is small, must be struck down. IV, 1773. Desire must be killed here so that it may be consumed, not postponed so that it may be satisfied there—in heaven. IV, 1466. There will be no desire among the blessed. VI, 289.

Each person bears the burden either of his desire or of his love. V, 898. The better the things awaiting love are, the more violent present things are for weakness. II, 593. How desire and love differ. VIII, 967. Carnal desire reigns where the love of God is absent. VI, 287. People are submerged by the weight of desire and earthly attachments, and emerge through the uplifting power of love and the spirit of holiness. I, 847. In place of the burdens of desire, the burden of love must be taken up. V, 897. Desire had wickedly subjected you; may love subject you beneficially. V, 897. Desires are more easily cut away in those who love God than in those who love the world and are sometimes satisfied. II, 994. Desire decreases as love increases. VI, 288. The beginning of the diminution of desire is fear of God. VI, 25. The more the kingdom of desire is destroyed, the more love increases. III, 72. The servitude of desires becomes a burden when they begin to cool. I, 749. The diminution of evil desires is progress in holiness. X, 845. One desire is driven out by another desire. X, 747. It is not healed. X, 594. There is a great difference between desire being overwhelmed by the soul’s despair and being driven out by health. I, 879. When the business of evil desire is not fulfilled outwardly because of fear of punishment, it remains inwardly as an enemy. II, 593. Desire is restrained by resting. VII, 445. The desire for life is the last and greatest of all. X, 691. The victor over all desires is the one who subjugates love of this life. V, 1282. We are freed from the dominion of concupiscence by the grace of God alone through Jesus Christ. I, 620, 621. See Concupiscence and Lust.

When desire is to be considered subdued. V, 963. Desire of the flesh, expelled through repentance, sometimes returns more greedily. III, 1325. It does you no good to lack resources while burning with desire. IV, 609. It is not money but avarice that is condemned. IV, 609. God does not regard one’s resources but one’s desire. IV, 1727. Those who, through desire, are excessively intent on outward things in this world are signified by the raven sent out from the ark. VIII, 264.

Why Cupid is represented as a flying and shooting boy. VIII, 374.

The Cupsonians. Donatists living among the Cupsonians. V, 293.

The end of cares is pleasure. IV, 103. Since security can scarcely be hoped for here, one must act so as to strip ourselves of useless cares and clothe ourselves with useful ones. II, 85. God cares for everything insofar as universal providence is concerned; he does not care for oxen—that is, he did not give man a command concerning them. IV, 1893. Unhappy man: God cared that you should exist, but you do not care that you should live well? IV, 1201.

Whoever wishes to be healed must not reject the hands of the omnipotent physician. IV, 712.

Curator. II, 162.

Curator of a city. II, 304.

The curia seems to be named from *cura*, “care.” VII, 285. Rome has thirty-five curiae of the people. IV, 1624.

The contest of the three Curiatii against the three Horatii. VII, 89.

Curiosity takes its name from *cura* (“care”), and is inimical to security. I, 1184. Curiosity is called the desire of the eyes. III, 1996. Why it is so named. I, 802. Curiosity is one of the three kinds of vice under which all sins are comprehended. IV, 115. On the vice of curiosity. I, 802. Every unlearned soul is curious. VI, 293. Whatever curiosity has grasped, it admires less. X, 832. We are admonished by curiosity to contemplate the truth. III, 164, 165. Curiosity seeks to know through the senses; pleasure seeks to enjoy. I, 802. The dangers of curiosity. I, 726. Curiosity is an impediment to faith through the five senses. V, 644, 645. Vain curiosity about difficult or useless matters usually separates one from God, unless charity prevails—the charity that invites us to spiritual things. III, 2077. The honor owed to God forbids attention to curious matters. I, 687. Those who ought to devote themselves to their own salvation and the usefulness of the Church should not have time for handling curious questions. III, 271, 277. Time should not be occupied with curious questions, but devoted to better things. II, 75. Scrutiny of the Scriptures as a remedy for curiosity. III, 166. Curiosity is prohibited by the Sacred Scriptures. I, 1327. The Apostle reproved the curiosity only of the carnal person, not of the spiritual person. VI, 70. The punishment of curiosity. VII, 722. At the instigation of curiosity, divine honors were offered to demons. VI, 584. Against curiosity, the judgments of God are incomprehensible. X, 832.

Curious: in what respect he differs from the studious person. VIII, 80. To restrain and curb curious people is among Augustine’s greatest concerns. II, 432. Human beings are curious in learning about another’s life, but sluggish in correcting their own. I, 780.

Curma, a member of the curial order. VI, 602.

Curma, a blacksmith. VI, 603.

[Col. 0205] To run is to make progress. X, 315. All who run perseveringly in our stadium receive a crown; and the one who arrives first waits to be crowned together with the one who comes later. IV, 441.

The public post. I, 717. Note (a).

Curtius threw himself headlong into a sudden chasm in the earth for his country. VII, 127, 163.

Curubis, a town. V, 1410; VII, 764.

One is called “bent down” who has made himself prone toward earthly desires. IV, 595. One who has an earthly mind. IV, 1849. One who, pressed down by the weight of sins, cannot raise himself up. IV, 401.

“Bent”: one who praises God in prosperity but blasphemes in adversity. IV, 278. To think about lower things—that is, to have a bent back. IV, 860.

Custody. The law by which a person is granted thirty days in which to conduct his affairs under moderate custody in the city where he is being detained. II, 429, 430.

The watches signify periods of the night. III, 718.

The Donatists in the city of Rome were called Cutzupitae. II, 196. See Note (a).

A man from Curubis, formerly an actor and suffering from paralysis, was restored to health when he was baptized. VII, 764.

Certain animals move their skin only where they feel something; a human being cannot do this. VII, 432.

Cylinnius, bishop. II, 991.

Cynegius, son of Flora. VI, 157, 591.

The Cynic philosophers. I, 956. Where they got their name, and in what respect they differ from others. VII, 624. The Cynics’ manner of dress makes no difference in religion. VII, 647. They take pleasure in a certain freedom and license of life. I, 956. The disgrace and shamelessness of the Cynics. VII, 428; X, 428. The Cynics’ Herculean aids. I, 943.

Cynocephalus, one of the Roman deities. VII, 59. Cynocephalus came to Rome from Egypt. VII, 87.

The Cynocephali. VII, 485.

Cynomyia, a dog-fly. V, 69. It signifies canine behavior. IV, 1000.

Cyprian, martyr. IV, 1099; VII, 255. His praenomen was Thascius. V, 1412. Bishop of Carthage. IX, 239. What Cyprian was like before his conversion to the faith. V, 1420. How wicked, how impious, how detestable his life was. V, 1416. Cyprian was truly made “of *cyprus*” when he became a Christian. V, 1421. The benefits of grace bestowed on Cyprian. V, 1422. Cyprian was transformed from a forensic orator into a preacher of Christ. V, 1023, 1421. Cyprian restrained his tongue from excess and curbed it into a weightier and more moderate eloquence. III, 102. Cyprian’s exile. V, 1410. Cyprian’s return from exile. V, 1410. After returning, he stayed in his gardens. V, 1410. Cyprian, a good shepherd. V, 763, 764. Cyprian’s pastoral solicitude. V, 1411.

Cyprian’s arrest by two officials. V, 1411. The proconsul’s words to Cyprian, and Cyprian’s reply. V, 1411. Cyprian’s words. V, 1412. The sentence against Cyprian. V, 1412. Cyprian the martyr proclaimed his confession, remained in the faith, shed his blood, and conquered the devil. V, 110. In place of the blood of Christ that he drank, he did not hesitate to shed his own blood. VI, 689. Cyprian received his sentence from below and his crown from above. IV, 391. Cyprian suffered martyrdom for faith in Christ who was born. VIII, 225. The place where he was killed. IV, 290. The location of Cyprian’s tomb. V, 1422. The table of the martyr Cyprian. IV, 1056, 1046; V, 107. At Carthage. V, 320, 652, 729, 833, 915, 1413. The memory of Cyprian. V, 1415. An altar erected over his body. V, 1424. The memory of the martyr Cyprian not far from the sea. I, 713. Cyprian’s solemnity. II, 648. The natale of Cyprian the martyr is celebrated throughout all Africa. V, 1412. Augustine desires to be aided by Cyprian’s prayers. IX, 188. And he asks for this. IX, 225. On the night when the solemnity of Blessed Cyprian was dawning, Augustine expounded Psalm 72. II, 543. The Church of Carthage was ennobled by Cyprian’s episcopate and martyrdom. V, 1413. Cyprian was renowned throughout the world both for his suffering and for his writings. V, 1413, 1422. Cyprian suffered martyrdom before the rise of the Manichaean heresy. X, 466. Cyprian had kindled many people, through the most ardent exhortations, to conquer the devil. V, 1412, 1421.

Cyprian condemned spectacles. VI, 639. Cyprian is mentioned by Pelagius with due honor. X, 623. Cyprian the Punic was a great punishment for the Pelagian heresy even before it was born. X, 1053. Cyprian defended original sin. X, 466. Cyprian’s testimony on behalf of original sin. V, 1347; X, 623. In his teaching on the origin of concupiscence, Cyprian opposed the future Pelagians. X, 1511. Cyprian’s testimony concerning the grace of God. X, 626.

Cyprian held a different view of baptism from that maintained by the Church’s form and custom. II, 310. Cyprian judged that the baptism of Christ was not present among heretics and schismatics. IX, 197, 199, 201. Cyprian says nothing about baptism administered among heretics or schismatics. IX, 208. He admits that in the past those who had been baptized elsewhere were admitted into the Church without being baptized again. II, 339. And although he considers them to be without baptism, he nevertheless does not believe that they should be separated from the Church’s benefits. II, 339. What he thought concerning the salvation of those baptized outside the Church. IX, 138. Cyprian taught that heretics were to be baptized again. IX, 124, 131, 607. How he fell into error. IX, 134. Cyprian is excused. IX, 124, 129, 130, 490, 491, 606. Cyprian’s reasons are more plausible than true. IX, 159. Cyprian erred concerning baptism just as Peter did concerning circumcision. IX, 225, 232. Cyprian corrected, on the basis of the Church’s faith, those who thought that an infant should not be baptized before the eighth day. II, 731. He himself, together with certain fellow bishops, judged that a newborn infant should be baptized promptly and properly. II, 731; X, 190, 191. Augustine seems somewhat uncertain whether Cyprian thought that heretics should be baptized again. IX, 465. Some maintain that a wrong opinion concerning baptism was falsely attributed to Cyprian. II, 340. Augustine considers it to have truly been Cyprian’s opinion. II, 340, 410. On the sole authority of Agrippinus, he changed the custom of not repeating baptism. IX, 159. Cyprian would have changed his opinion after the decision of the plenary Council. IX, 129. Augustine conjectures what Cyprian would have done if the question of baptism had been settled by a plenary Council. IX, 157, 159.

How learned and teachable Cyprian was. IX, 157, 194. Whether Cyprian changed his opinion is unknown. IX, 129. Although it is not found in the record, it is nevertheless reasonably believed that he corrected his opinion concerning baptism. II, 340. The correction of Cyprian’s opinion concerning baptism may perhaps have been suppressed. II, 340. Augustine judges that Cyprian later either corrected his erroneous opinion concerning baptism according to the rule of truth, or covered this blemish, as it were, with an abundance of charity and had it cleansed by the pruning knife of martyrdom. II, 340, 341, 409. Why the Lord did not reveal the true opinion concerning baptism to Cyprian. IX, 124, 129, 159. And why He permitted him to think incorrectly about baptism. IX, 198. And that many fellow bishops agreed with Cyprian’s opinion. IX, 200. Cyprian supports Augustine’s opinion concerning Peter’s rebuke. II, 286. Why the Donatists value Cyprian’s authority so highly. IX, 739.

Cyprian’s council either did not take place, or was overcome by the other members of the unity from whom he was not separated. IX, 465. Cyprian’s council has a date. IX, 663. The authority of Cyprian blunts the Donatist error. II, 340. Cyprian’s authority confounds the Donatists rather than helping them. IX, 141, 489. Cyprian condemns the Donatists for abusing his authority. IX, 225, 231. Cyprian’s letters and actions are of very great force in refuting the Donatists. IX, 107, 108, 109. How one should respond when the Donatists bring Cyprian’s authority against the Catholics in the question of baptism. IX, 126, 746. What difference there is between Cyprian’s error and that of the Donatists. IX, 126. Cyprian correctly refutes the argument that they were bringing from the Apostle against rebaptization. IX, 160. Cyprian’s authority should be presented as favoring the Catholics rather than the Donatists. IX, 139. Cyprian’s authority does not bind Catholics. IX, 490. How Cyprian’s statements and those of other teachers should be understood. IX, 490. Cyprian’s holiness is not prejudiced by his error concerning baptism. IX, 186. Although Cyprian thought differently about baptism from what the truth showed, he was nevertheless a branch in the root of Christ, which the Father would cleanse, and so forth. IX, 746. Although Cyprian held a different opinion concerning baptism, he did not abandon unity. IX, 124, 130, 151, 161.

How greatly Cyprian loved the unity of the Church. V, 1422. Cyprian was most devoted to unity. IX, 88, 89, 90. And most loving. II, 340, 341, 410; IX, 566. He did not abandon the root of unity. II, 340. How devoted to unity Cyprian showed himself at the Council of Carthage. IX, 201. How greatly Cyprian cultivated and guarded the charity of unity. IX, 187, 188, 198, 200. How highly Cyprian valued the unity of the Body of Christ. IX, 491, 496, 497. Cyprian’s testimony concerning the unity of the Church. II, 410. In Cyprian, God displayed an example of charity and unity. V, 1422. Cyprian thought that one should remain in unity with those who did not hold that persons coming from heretics should be baptized. IX, 194, 198. Cyprian did not want bishops who held different opinions to be removed from the right of communion. IX, 201, 203, 214, 219, 226, 227, 234, 244. Cyprian did not separate himself from his evil colleagues, but rebuked them severely. IX, 85. When this occurred. IX, 88, 89. Cyprian not only tolerated colleagues who held different opinions through the patience of charity, but also manifestly evil men. IX, 95. He tolerated the avarice of his colleagues. II, 318. And he reproved it. II, 410. Cyprian and his colleagues tolerated in unity both the perverse and those who thought differently from them. IX, 228, 229, 231, 233, 234, 244. Cyprian always taught that the Church should not be abandoned because the wicked are mingled with the good. IX, 492, 494, 495, 521. Cyprian was crowned not merely because he suffered for Christ’s name, but because he suffered for Christ’s name within the embrace of unity. II, 410. Cyprian is an example to the Donatists that they should not withdraw from unity. IX, 138, 139, 140.
