Cyprian’s letter to Antonianus. II, 340; IX, 157, 158, 165. To Donatus. V, 1421. To Fidus, bishop. X, 624, [Col. 0207] 644. To Jubaianus. IX, 239, 490, 496. This letter is examined. IX, 141, 143, 144, 145. It was read aloud at the Council of Carthage. II, 340. Cyprian’s letter to Magnus. IX, 202, 240. To Maximus. II, 410, 411; IX, 492, 742. To Pompeius. IX, 192, 193, 201. To Quintus. IX, 192, 201. To Quirinus. X, 627, 630. To Saturninus, Maximus, and others. IX, 192, 201. To Stephanus. IX, 208.

Cyprian’s letter on patience. X, 624. The booklet *On the Good of Patience*. IX, 161, 187. The letter *On the Lapsed*. II, 690; VI, 220, 230; IX, 161. A passage from it is explained concerning parents who murder their children. II, 360. Cyprian’s book *On Mortality*, laudably known to many—and almost all—who love ecclesiastical writings. X, 624, 629, 690, 979, 1528. For what purpose he wrote this book. II, 986. Cyprian’s letter *On Works and Almsgiving*. X, 629, 691. The treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*. X, 626, 629, 676, 877, 878, 922, 996, 997. In the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, Cyprian taught that everything by which we live rightly must be requested from our Father who is in heaven. II, 972, 979, 980. Cyprian’s book *Testimonies*. X, 623. Cyprian’s letter on unity, or the book *On the Simplicity of Prelates*. IX, 491. The letter *On Zeal and Envy*. IX, 161, 164. Cyprian’s style has a certain distinctive character. II, 340.

Cyprian’s encomium. IX, 141, 187, 198. Cyprian was free from envy. IX, 161. Cyprian’s soul, a great sword of God. V, 1424. Cyprian, a chosen grain. V, 1417. A precious stone. V, 223.

Cyprian, one of the Fathers of the Council of Carthage. II, 759, 780.

Cyprian the deacon, bearer of Augustine’s letter to Jerome. II, 241, 245, 251, 288, 291.

Cyprian, bishop of Thubursicubure and a Donatist, condemned by Primianus. IX, 368. He was discovered in a brothel. IX, 368.

The king of Cyprus was accustomed to display a beautiful picture to his wife during intercourse, lest she give birth to ugly children. I, 655.

Cyrus, king of the Persians. VII, 117. He also ruled the Chaldaeans and Assyrians. VII, 583. Cyrus caused fifty thousand Jews to return from Babylonia to restore the Temple. VII, 583.

## D

Dacianus. V, 1257, 1260.

Δάκτυλος (*dáktylos*), “finger.” VIII, 42.

The story of Daedalus. I, 894; VII, 570.

Definition of demons according to Apuleius. VII, 263. According to Plato. VII, 241. Demons were so called because of their knowledge. VII, 273. The knowledge of demons without charity. VII, 273. Some do not think that demons were heavenly or superheavenly angels. III, 285, 430. Porphyry distinguishes demons from angels. VII, 287. The Platonists thought that demons were made from human beings. VII, 265.

The sin of demons was pride. VII, 221, 353. Love of arrogance and honor. VIII, 585, 592. Why demons are proud. VII, 273. Demons were blessed before their fall, but not completely. X, 933.

The demons were cast down from heaven. IV, 1220. They fell from the spiritual paradise. VII, 419. Demons dwell in the lower heaven—that is, in the air—not in the highest heaven where the sun and stars are. VI, 291. Demons were thrust down as into a prison of this murky air. II, 378; III, 285, 443; V, 1091; VIII, 562, 875. The dwelling-place of demons is in the air. VII, 239. As if in a prison suited to them. VII, 246. Demons, turned away from the light and warmth of charity, grew numb as if with icy hardness; therefore, figuratively, they are placed in the north. II, 561. Demons are creatures of air or ether. II, 72; III, 284. The most contemptible creatures of the air. I, 916. Demons surpass us in the subtlety of their senses, not in reason. I, 916; II, 72. Why demons are not dissolved by death. III, 284. The airy body of demons. VI, 584, 585.

Demons share something with gods and human beings. VII, 239. According to Apuleius, demons resemble the gods only in the eternity of their bodies, not in mind. VII, 263. How absurd this is. VII, 263. Demons are corporeal. VII, 239, Note (a), 337, 710. Demons surpass human beings neither because of their airy bodies nor because of their higher dwelling-places. VII, 239, 240, 246. Why God willed demons to surpass human beings in bodily excellence, although they are inferior to them in goodness of life. VII, 210. Goodness of life in a human being is to be preferred to the bodily excellence of demons. VII, 240, 246. Demons are more miserable in an eternal body than human beings in a mortal one. VII, 265. Why. VII, 265. It does demons no good to be eternal if they are miserable. VII, 271. The eternal body of demons is the bond of the condemned. VII, 265.

Some have called demons by the name of gods. VII, 255. How a demon became a god from a human being. VII, 252. Demons are called not simply gods, but gods of the nations. IV, 1757. Some demons are greater, others more contemptible. IV, 1375. Some have distinguished demons from gods. VII, 257.

Some placed demons between gods and human beings. VII, 257. Demons are either unclean, if intercourse with a human being is contamination, or better than the gods. VII, 269, 270. To what extent demons can be intermediaries between gods and human beings. VII, 266. Demons persuaded some that they were gods, and others that they were at least messengers of the gods. VII, 247. Although Hermes asserts that demons were made gods by human beings, he did not say that they were messengers and intercessors. VII, 252. It is absurd to imagine demons as messengers and interpreters of the gods. VII, 245. Demons are falsely imagined as intermediaries between gods and human beings, so that human beings might be commended to the good gods. VII, 243, 244, 245, 246. And might be reconciled to them. VII, 257. Through demons, human beings vainly seek the friendship of the gods. VII, 264. Some unhappily worshiped demons as mediators for returning to God. I, 807. See *Devil*. Demons not only do not provide a way to God, but prevent the way from being followed. VII, 272. Demons are false and deceptive mediators. VII, 264, 272. The mediation of demons benefits human beings nothing. VII, 268, 269, 270, 272. It contributes nothing toward attaining blessedness. VII, 275. Even earthly happiness is not in the power of demons. II, 534. Porphyry inquires into various matters concerning demons from the Egyptian Anebo. VII, 288. Porphyry said that association with demons should be avoided. VII, 287. Porphyry thought that everyone should make use of the friendship of some demon. VII, 287.

Demons conduct their business so that they may be regarded and worshiped as gods. VII, 72. Demons wish to be worshiped through miracles. VII, 296. The Romans advise that the good demons, **ἀγαθούς** (*agathous*), be invited, and the evil ones, **κακούς** (*kakous*), appeased. III, 1053. Some judged that certain demons were evil and others good, and that the latter should be worshiped for the sake of eternal life. VII, 257. What should be thought about them. VII, 257. Apuleius denies that demons are gods, but does not separate their worship from the religion of the heavenly gods. VII, 247. Some did not dare to say that demons were entirely unworthy of divine honor. VII, 248. The souls of demons were summoned and placed in images and mysteries. VII, 253, 254. Demons were invited by the affection of the nations to possess images. IV, 1483. How demons are enticed. VII, 717. The worship of demons was introduced by the rulers of cities. VII, 139. It was difficult for the less educated populace to avoid the worship of demons. VII, 139. What sort of worship pagans offered to demons. IV, 1220. Dishes of food were offered to demons. VII, 49. Why demons rejoice in sacrifices. VIII, 901. Health for little children was sought through sacrifices to demons. II, 359. How many absurdities and contradictions there are in the worship and invocation of demons. VII, 288. When things that have been used for the worship of demons may be converted to one’s own uses. II, 185. When something from our own storehouse, intended for sacrifices to demons, may be taken away without our guilt. II, 185.

Demons are not to be worshiped. VII, 276. The worship of demons is attacked. IV, 209, 1246. Demons are not to be worshiped, neither on account of what they now are nor even if they possessed virtue and wisdom. VII, 241. It is more dangerous to serve demons than idols. IV, 1245. Sinners sacrifice to them in more than one way. I, 673. The sacrifice of Christ and the gift of the Holy Spirit free us from the worship of demons. VII, 138. Plato admonished people to detest the uncleanness of demons and their impure commands. VII, 239.

Because of the uncleanness and weakness of their desires and punishments, demons are unable to behold and consult the present truth within. VI, 146. Demons do not contemplate the eternal causes of times in God’s wisdom. VII, 274. How demons foresee the future. VI, 143, 164; VII, 274. From where they foretell future events. VI, 586. Because of the keenness of their senses, the swiftness of their movement, and their long experience, demons predict many future events. VI, 584. Nor should they therefore be preferred to human beings. VI, 584. How far their divination falls short of the height of divine prophecy. VI, 586. Demons foretold certain things that they had learned from prophetic or angelic oracles. VI, 587, 588. Why they kept these things silent for a long time and then brought them forth. VI, 587. It is not surprising that demons announce things that happened long ago somewhere far away. III, 467. Demons are often mistaken in their knowledge of future events. VI, 586; VII, 274. When they foretell something true, they mix in deceptions. VI, 143.

How demons deceive. VI, 587. Why demons are sometimes found to have spoken the truth through their prophets. VIII, 903. If a lying spirit says something true, it should not for that reason be denied merely because a detestable spirit said it. IX, 368. Whether it is unworthy for truth to become known through them. VI, 586. How demons are moved by outward signs to do or not to do something. VI, 146. How they discern the dispositions of human beings that have been conceived only in thought. II, 72, 73; VI, 582, 586. Demons can perceive what has entered our memory, as when we recall a verse. I, 916. Thus, with their help, Albicerius divined a verse that one of Augustine’s disciples was turning over in his mind. I, 915. At the memory of the saints, demons confess at Milan in a marvelous and terrifying manner. [Col. 0209] II, 269. Demons confessed Christ as the Son of God out of fear, not as Peter did, out of love. V, 993, 1117.

Demons take pleasure in certain creatures of God. VII, 717. Why demons delight in the obscenities of games and the fictions of poets. VII, 238, 239. What Apuleius said about the morals of demons, and what he found in them to praise. VII, 239, 240. Apuleius judged that only demons ordered from the moon downward are stirred by passions. VII, 304. Demons are stirred by passions. VII, 242. Why. VII, 242, 257, 261, 263. It is thereby shown that demons are not to be worshiped: they resemble us in being subject to passions. VII, 242.

Demons are especially corrupted by the arrogance of pride and the malice of envy. VI, 585. The envy of demons toward human beings. VII, 78; VIII, 585, 592. Human beings’ eternal happiness is a punishment to demons. VII, 78. Demons feed upon the misery of the condemned and, through their malevolence, are tormented by the liberation of the good. III, 156. They take pleasure in human error and are fed by it, in a manner of speaking. II, 378. Those who rejoice in the miseries of others are like demons. III, 156. By what art of harming do demons wish either false or true accusations against themselves to be reported? VII, 55. It is characteristic of their malevolence that, whether they are appeased or entreated, they do not cease to wish to harm. IV, 209, 1246.

The greatest vices of demons are pride and deceit. VIII, 409. Demons have the greatest desire to deceive. VII, 139. Demons are extremely watchful in deceiving. VII, 84. How demons persuade the wicked to do evil. VI, 586. While demons teach the precepts of morality to a few but display shameful spectacles to everyone, they carry out the work of deception. VII, 75, 76. Demons wished, by their example, to provide crimes with something like divine authority. VII, 73. Demons stir up wicked minds by a hidden impulse. VII, 75.

Demons boast above all in possessing the hearts of mortals. VII, 717. Demons possess the hearts of mortals especially when they transform themselves into angels of light. VII, 717. Demons transform themselves into angels of light in order to test those whom it is necessary either to instruct in this way or, justly, to deceive. VII, 636. Demons cannot possess anyone unless they have deceived that person. VII, 139. Demons would perhaps deceive less if they found idle people less often. VII, 84. Demons would not test human beings if they could discern the inner appearance of virtues in them. III, 467. Through every sensory entrance, the demon violates the soul’s holiness. VI, 14.

What is the food of demons? IV, 1292, 1374, 1375. Demons feed on the division of carnal people. VII, 502. The devil devours no one unless he has overthrown that person through tribulation. IV, 1292. Demons conquer no one except through partnership in sin. VII, 300.

Some believe that the demon is the author of this world; why. VIII, 651, 655, 659. The lowest part of the world has been subjected to the rebellious angels. III, 52. This visible matter does not serve demons at their command, but God, and so forth. VIII, 875, 876. Of what world are demons the rulers? IV, 630. Demons are rulers of the world that they made. IV, 1854. The whole earthly city is subject to demons. VII, 634. How demons are the rulers of darkness. VI, 292.

Demons perform many marvels. VI, 584, 585. Demons do certain things resembling the holy angels, not in truth but in appearance, not in wisdom but in sheer deceit. II, 383. Demons taught human beings the art of magic. VII, 717. Demons summoned by magical arts are not creators. VIII, 876, 878. Demons do not create natures but alter them. VII, 575. Demons perform the lowest services. III, 156. The lowest servants. III, 156. God uses even evil spirits as ministers, either to avenge the wicked or to test the good. VI, 131. Demons are called destroyers and angels of wrath. III, 156.

The power of demons over human beings comes from God’s high and just judgment. VII, 224. Demons cannot do in bodily goods and evils what is commonly thought. VII, 78. Demons do nothing to human beings except when, and to the extent that, they are permitted by God’s high and secret providence. VII, 70, 251. The power of demons to inflict diseases. VI, 586. Demons first suffer the punishment of their own sins in order to do harm. VIII, 586. Demons cannot harm anyone or accomplish anything unless power has been given them from above. VIII, 663, 875. Why and how the power to harm is sometimes given to demons from above. VIII, 875, 876. Demons do nothing except what God has permitted. VII, 574. Demons cannot do what they are not allowed to accomplish. VII, 224. Demons do greater harm by doing good. VII, 251. The noonday demon: a more intense persecution. IV, 1154. The power permitted to demons to stir up persecutions is useful to the Church. VII, 298. The greater power we see them to possess over these lower things, the more tenaciously we must cling to the Mediator. VII, 574. Demons must be fought with patience and prudence. VIII, 586. What God intends from the struggle against demons. VIII, 586.

Some people suffer demonic attacks. VII, 628. Even baptized infants suffer them. VII, 714. Why God permits this. VII, [Col. 0210] 786. Demonic attacks do not harm baptized infants. VII, 714. A young man was freed from a demon at the memorials of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius. VII, 765. And a woman of Hippo was freed when she had anointed herself with oil. VII, 765. The saints expel demons by exorcising, not by appeasing them. VII, 399. No one should boast about the expulsion of demons. IX, 303.

Demons are kept for punishment at the judgment. III, 443. What the misery of demons is. VII, 349, 353. The misery of demons would not be eternal unless their malice were great. VII, 267. It is not surprising that the heavenly bodies of transgressing demons—if indeed they possessed such bodies—were changed into an airy quality, so that they could suffer something from fire. III, 285. Even if demons are incorporeal, they can be afflicted by the bodily punishment of fire. VII, 724. How. VII, 724. The despair of demons. VII, 240. What the martyrs will do in judgment against demons whose temples they overthrew by dying. V, 1422. Demons, while Ambrose was alive and entirely unaware of them, begged him to spare them. VI, 608. The faith of demons. II, 878. Demons are signified by lions and lion cubs. IV, 1292, 1374. Demons are kites. IV, 1161. Demons are pirates. III, 842. Vulture’s young. III, 829, 841. Demons were seen fighting one another on a plain in Campania. VII, 73.

In the Scriptures, demons are understood in a negative sense. VII, 273. The pagans also understand demons in a negative sense. VII, 273. The name “demons” is so detestable that it ought to be removed from the holy angels. VII, 276. Everyone, or almost everyone, abhors the name of demons. VII, 239.

A demoniac, situated at home, saw a priest coming to him from twelve thousand [units; reading uncertain]. III, 468. When a demon speaks in demoniacs, they do not know what they are saying. III, 444. How demoniacs sometimes speak the truth. III, 464.

Damascus, a city flourishing in wealth. V, 1034.

Damasus. The dissension of the Roman people over the election of Pope Damasus. X, 842.

The condemnation of carnal generation on account of original sin. X, 160. The cause of condemnation in infants who die without baptism is original sin, not the acts they would have committed had they lived. X, 1006. It was a matter of justice that all should be condemned. X, 250. All human beings are entirely in the mass of perdition, from which no one is freed except by the grace of the Redeemer. X, 402. No one is released from the bond of condemnation except through Christ. II, 843, 858, 859. There is no condemnation in the saints here. V, 841. No one is freed from the condemnation deserved by original sin except through mercy and undeserved grace. VII, 727; X, 1606. How great are the thanks owed by those who are freed from condemnation through Christ. X, 250. Whoever is left in condemnation has no grounds for complaint. VII, 727. The condemned will have no excuse. V, 151, 152. That the souls of infants are condemned if they depart from this life without baptism is attested both by Holy Scripture and by the holy Church. II, 317.

Those who are not freed by grace are justly condemned. X, 250. Those who could not be justified are also condemned. X, 251. It is inscrutable why God creates from the condemned human race people who are destined to be condemned. X, 837, 1130. Some are indignant that God creates those whom He foreknew would be condemned. X, 1071. If every human being were freed from condemnation, what sin deserves through justice would remain hidden; if no one were freed, what grace bestows would remain hidden. II, 875. God does not wish to condemn us. V, 150, 152, 154. Since God is just, He cannot condemn anyone without evil merits. X, 721. God condemns no one except with the most equitable truth. II, 820, 882. All who are condemned are condemned by God’s justice and truth. IV, 1583. To approve falsehoods as truths and to be unable to restrain oneself from lustful acts is the punishment of condemned humanity. I, 598.

The misery of the condemned is deprivation of participation in God. VII, 269. For the condemned to perish from the kingdom and be alienated from the life of God is so great a punishment that no torments known to us can be compared with it. VI, 285. The punishment of the condemned is more incredible than the happiness of the blessed. VII, 709. Various opinions concerning the punishments of the condemned. VII, 731, 732. The final condemnation of the wicked is compared to wax flowing away from the face of fire. IV, 814. The condemnation of the wicked is called their destruction. VII, 684. Condemnation is the second death. VII, 658, 666, 675. For all the condemned, that perpetual death will be common, although their torments will vary. VI, 285. In condemnation, death is said also to exist according to the body; why. VII, 378. The condemned are concerned about their own people. IV, 1437, 1438. Whether the condemned have knowledge of what is happening within the joy of the Lord, which they will not know. VII, 694. What sort of battle the condemned will endure. III, 658. The condemned are most fittingly placed in punishment. I, 604, 1349. There is no intermediate place between condemnation and the kingdom of heaven. X, 140. See *Infants*. *Original Sin*.

Degrees of condemnation. X, 117. In that condemnation, some will be punished twice as much as others, the sons of Gehenna. X, 250. The misery of some of the condemned is greater than that of others. VI, 284. Some of the condemned will be condemned more tolerably than others. IV, 1106; VI, 275. Whose punishment among the condemned is the mildest. VI, 275. Each person will have a condemnation more tolerable in proportion as he had less iniquity. VI, 275. Whether the punishments of the condemned will at some time be alleviated. IV, 1406. That the prayers of the Church may benefit certain moderately wicked condemned persons by mitigating their punishment. VI, 283. Note (a). How it can be said that God does not withhold His mercies from the condemned. VII, 739.

How the bodies of the condemned will be able to remain animated and alive amid eternal torments. VII, 709. They may not improperly be called corpses. VII, 693. How the bodies of the condemned will be incorruptible if they suffer, or corruptible if they cannot die. VI, 274. How the unquenchable fire and ever-living worm of the condemned are to be understood. VII, 694. How the pain of the condemned will not end. VII, 658. The punishments of the condemned are more severe after the resurrection. V, 1453.

Some think that no one will be condemned at the last judgment because of the intercessions of the saints. VII, 732. They are refuted. VII, 736. Some think that the punishments of condemned human beings, but not those of demons, will cease. VII, 731, 733. Origen thought that the punishment of the devil and the condemned would not last forever. X, 325. Some promise liberation from eternal condemnation to all the baptized, even heretics. VII, 733. They are refuted. VII, 741. Others make this promise only to those baptized among the Catholics, even if they live wickedly. VII, 734. These too are refuted. VII, 741, 742, 743. Some grant this same thing to all Catholics who persevere in the Church, even if they have lived most wickedly. VII, 734. They are refuted. VII, 743. Some grant it to all who have given alms, even if they have not changed their conduct. VII, 734. They likewise are refuted. VII, 746. Against all these it is shown that faith without works is insufficient for salvation. VI, 211. It is proved against certain people, indeed against very many who think otherwise, that the punishment of the condemned will be eternal. VI, 284. More are condemned than are saved. VII, 727.

To suffer loss. V, 1474.

Fear no loss except that of God. V, 207. Other losses are beneficial when they cut away what is superfluous. V, 202. Why God permits temporal losses. II, 1060. The Christian’s heart should not be troubled because of loss, but because he does not yet live with Christ. IV, 1631. Losses inflicted by pagans are endured or repaired by Christians; by this example we wish the gains of souls not to be hindered. II, 317.

Danae. I, 672. What it signifies that Jupiter desired intercourse with Danae through a shower of gold. VII, 571.

Danaus, the tenth king of the Argives. VII, 569.

Daniel the prophet. III, 461, 462. What he prophesied and at what time. VII, 593. Why he confesses his own sins and those of his people. X, 159. Daniel was a quiet man, who was secure even among lions. IV, 1731. The lions recognized Daniel as superior to themselves. III, 2039. David, serving God in celibacy, represented the servants of God, that is, monks. IV, 1731. What Daniel, Job, and Noah signify. VI, 716.

Daniel was learning the mystery of the weeks from the Angel. II, 911. Hesychius does not think Daniel’s weeks were fulfilled at Christ’s birth and passion. II, 904, 911. Some interpreted them of Christ’s second coming. II, 901. Daniel’s weeks were completed at Christ’s former coming. II, 911, 917. They signify not Christ’s future coming but his past coming. II, 899.

Dardanus, illustrious in worldly rank. II, 832. Augustine’s dearest friend. II, 848. Augustine answers his questions in the book *On the Presence of God*. II, 833.

To give. God alone does not know how to do anything but give. V, 108. He who has no superior has no giver. V, 108. How the command to give to the Almighty is to be fulfilled. V, 1592. One must give what, as far as a human being can know or believe, harms neither oneself nor another. III, 1264. Who should be preferred when something cannot be given to two or more people. III, 30. From whoever is given more, more is required. II, 883. Every thing that is not diminished by being given, while it is possessed but not given, is not yet possessed as it ought to be. III, 19. Who are understood as having been given to Christ. X, 928.

Dares. VIII, 574.

Darius. II, 801. King of the Persians. VII, 583.

Darius, a count sent to arrange peace. II, 1014. He writes back to Augustine. II, 1014. If he did not extinguish and end the wars, at least he postponed them. II, 1015. Although Darius was born of Christian parents, whenever pagan rites occasionally stirred his feelings, he utterly rejected them through Augustine’s reading. II, 1016. How pleasing this was to Augustine. II, 446. Darius was Christian not outwardly, but in Christian charity. II, 1025. He asks Augustine for the *Confessions*. II, 1022. He also receives it from Augustine himself. II, 1025. Together with the other books that are listed. II, 1026. Darius greatly valued Augustine’s words. II, 1020. He also assisted his library. II, 1026. Darius gave medicines to be delivered by the presbyter Lazapus to Augustine. II, 1022.

Datianus, bishop of Camicetum. IV, 380.

[Col. 0212] Dativus of Badis. IX, 211.

Dative. In place of the Greek dative case, Latins use the ablative. III, 487.

David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” and bore the figure of Christ. IV, 148, 154, 302, 628, 646, 716, 1238, 1717, 1845; VIII, 458. He is also interpreted as “desirable.” IV, 323; VIII, 458. David was chosen by God on account of Christ, and the tribe of Judah on account of David. IV, 1007. Why David is called chosen according to God’s heart, although he committed such and so many offenses. VI, 168. David was small in stature but great in faith. IV, 1856. David was transferred from the pastoral care of sheep to rule over human beings, whereas Christ was transferred from oxen to sheep, from the Jews to the Gentiles. IV, 1007.

Saul permitted David to fight Goliath, understanding that there was something divine in him. V, 197. David’s confidence in God as he advanced against Goliath. V, 197. What mystery David’s five stones contain. V, 198. David burdened with Saul’s armor signified a human being under the Law. IV, 1859. David’s contest with Goliath is expounded mystically. IV, 1855, 1856. David earned envy in return for a good deed. IV, 301. David received, as a figure of the New Testament, his wife, whom her father Saul had given to another. VI, 474.

David’s humility and gentleness. IV, 1716. His gentleness toward Saul. VIII, 161. David fulfilled Christ’s command to love enemies. VIII, 161. Why David did not hold the kingdom until he had first been freed from his persecutors. IV, 600. David, guilty of perjury, chose the lesser of two sins. V, 1408. How David was struck by the deaths of so many people because of the census. VIII, 618, 619. The death inflicted on people who were at some point going to die did them no harm because of the census. VIII, 619, 623. David was abandoned for a little while by the Ruler’s medicinal providence, lest he himself abandon the Ruler through deadly pride. VI, 372. Why David offered sacrifice. VIII, 625.

David was moved not by his own injury but by his son’s sins. III, 77. David was not unjustly cast down by the persecution of his son, but humbly chastened in piety. IV, 1845. David’s gentleness toward his son Absalom. III, 77.

Although David fell into adultery, he was far removed from the excess of the lustful. III, 77. In David there was not persistence in immoderate lust, but a passing through it. III, 77. David’s humble confession. III, 449. David would not have risen from sin unless Christ’s grace had lifted him up, from the letter of Innocent. II, 782. Although forgiveness was granted to David by the Prophet, why did what God had threatened nevertheless follow? X, 1582. David’s repentance. VII, 554. Those who seek grounds for sinning in David’s fall are chastised. IV, 586. What David’s sin prefigured. VIII, 458. David’s virtues and vices. VIII, 441. Why faithful Scripture did not conceal David’s sins and merits. II, 534.

David’s very extensive kingdom. VII, 525. How many years David reigned. VII, 577. During David’s reign a certain turning point and the beginning of the youth of God’s people occurred. VII, 522.

With what disposition David loved musical harmony. VII, 547. He loved pious music. II, 369. David was the author of the Psalter. V, 197. The whole Psalter is attributed to David’s name, and its psalms are called Davidic. IV, 130. Davidic verses. II, 369. Which psalms David wrote. VII, 547. He says certain things differently from the way they are read in other books of Scripture, lest it be thought that he is recalling past events rather than prophesying future ones. IV, 1476. David was a man in the Old Testament, but not a man of the Old Testament. III, 2137.

Christ is signified by the name David. V, 308. David is a figure of Christ. VI, 336. A figure of Christ’s body, or of the Church. IV, 600, 619, 713. In David’s suffering Saul’s persecution, the kingdom of eternal salvation was prefigured. IV, 600. David fleeing into a cave is a figure of Christ hiding himself in the flesh. IV, 663. A figure of Christ placed in the tomb. IV, 664. David’s betrayal by Doeg is a figure of Christ’s betrayal. IV, 603. What David detained by the Philistines signifies. IV, 648. David pretending madness before Achish is a figure of Christ preaching the sacrament of eating his flesh. IV, 305, 315. David fleeing from Absalom is a figure of Christ abandoning Judas the betrayer. IV, 73. David represented the person of the priest when he ate the showbread. III, 1045; IV, 601. David speaks in the person of Christ. IV, 723. The promises made to David are found in his Son—not in Solomon, but in Christ. VII, 540.

Christ paid our debts. IV, 1783. Daily debts. V, 381, 392. Debts to brothers and enemies are to be forgiven. V, 53, 324, 514, 516, 652, 1274. To release a fellow servant from debt is an alms of great profit, so that the Lord may release you. V, 1055. The covenant of forgiving debts in the Lord’s Prayer. V, 383, 1056. The debt owed to one who wishes to litigate is to be forgiven. III, 1282. He loses his case who has demanded more than is owed to him. IV, 1531.

No one owes anything except to the one from whom he received the obligation. I, 1292. God owes nothing to anyone, because he provides everything freely. I, 1293. The Lord himself made himself a debtor, not by receiving but by promising. I, 714; IV, 1068, 1445; V, 640, 863, 1184. In order that a human being might demand a debt, he first received what was not owed. V, 1428. He has become a faithful debtor; be an avaricious exactor yourself. IV, 286. If the Lord wished to repay, he would have repaid nothing except the punishment that was owed. V, 177. Everything owes God, first whatever it is, then whatever better thing it could be if it wished, and whatever it ought to be. I, 1293. The soul renders to God what it owes, either by doing or by suffering. I, 1293. Whoever does not do what he owes immediately suffers what he owes. I, 1293. The debtor is held at the time of judgment because he was found to be a giver in the time of mercy. IV, 1283. Every human being is God’s debtor and has a brother as debtor. V, 381, 515. We have debtors and are debtors: how our debts may be forgiven. V, 983.

The obligation of debtor and creditor. III, 764. Debtors should not be pressed too hard. V, 1129.

The ten-stringed psalter. V, 79.

The Decalogue. V, 517. The Manichaeans reject and violate the Decalogue. VIII, 303, 307, 309, 310, 311. The division of the commandments of the Decalogue. III, 620; V, 1165. Three concern God, seven human beings. V, 79; VIII, 306, 310. The first three commandments of the Decalogue pertain to indicating the individual persons of the Holy Trinity. II, 213. All the commandments of the Decalogue are contained in the commandment, “Whatever you do not wish to be done to you,” and so forth. V, 86. In the commandment to love God is the chastity of the Church’s marriage; in the commandment to love one’s neighbor is the unity of its members. VIII, 306. The individual commandments of the Decalogue are expounded. V, 76. The Decalogue was given not only to the Jews but also to us, to establish a rightly ordered life. X, 215, 594. We are bound to observe the commandments of justice contained in the Decalogue. X, 222. The Decalogue also kills unless grace is present. X, 215. The commandment to observe the Sabbath alone among the others was placed in the form of a figure of the shadow. X, 217.

Deans of the monks. I, 1338. Their office. I, 682.

Tithes. V, 89. Whether it is sufficient for a Christian to give a tenth of his possessions. V, 522.

To deceive no one is a supreme and almost divine virtue. VI, 35. The degrees of this virtue. VI, 34. How God permits someone to be deceived. VI, 35.

Decius. IX, 323, 328. Decius the emperor, persecutor of Christians. VII, 614. Decius and his son devoted themselves for their country. VII, 127, 163.

To decline to the right means wishing to attribute to oneself what is right, rather than to God’s grace. III, 769.

One who wishes to behead the Church. V, 725.

The beauty of God’s house. V, 116.

A city decurion. II, 304. Ingentius is not tortured because he asserted that he was a decurion of the Ziquensians. II, 304.

The dedication of a previously profane temple. V, 889. See *Church*. The dedication of candlesticks. V, 1478. The dedication of God’s temple in us has not yet occurred, but only its building. V, 890. The foundation of the Church has already been dedicated; we too shall be dedicated when we rise. V, 661. The dedication of the house now being built amid tribulations will occur at Christ’s second coming. V, 178; IV, 221. It has already taken place in the Head, as the dedication of the foundation. IV, 221.

We tolerate deficiency in intelligible things more painfully than in sensible things. VIII, 99. Although deficiencies are numbered among intelligible things, they should not for that reason be preferred to sensible things. VIII, 98. Deficiency is not always to be assigned to guilt or punishment; there is also a deficiency that is praiseworthy or desirable. IV, 1558. Not every deficiency is blameworthy, but only voluntary deficiency. I, 1291; VIII, 590. Deficiencies that are not voluntary are either for the punishment of sin or for the beauty of the universe. VIII, 590. God is not the author of evil. I, 1346. Nor of defection. I, 1347. The deficiencies and advances of creation are not without contributing to the beauty of the universe. III, 259.

You can fall away from God, but you cannot restore yourself. IV, 1224. To fail is to tend toward nothingness. VIII, 587, 592. Things fail or can fail because they were made from nothing. II, 439.

“Is lacking.” II, 833, 1076.

The defense of sins is great iniquity. IV, 701, 854, 1793, 1808, 1821. See *Sin*.

The distinction between a defender and an intercessor, and the office of each. II, 657.

A definition should contain nothing foreign to the matter. I, 913. The parts of a definition. I, 1038. How a definition should be examined. I, 1038. The usefulness of definition. VII, 67.

The deformity of bodies shows how punitive is the condition of mortals. VII, 781. It will not remain after the resurrection. VII, 781, 783.

The hidden dwelling places of the pious dead. VII, 28. Whether the spirits of the dead suffer the fire of temporary tribulation. VII, 745. The spirits of some of the dead suffer punishments. VII, 738. The faithful dead are members of the Church. VII, 674. Their commemoration is customarily made at the altar. I, 778. At the altar one prays for the dead commemorated there, but not for martyrs. V, 867, 1291, 1295. Prayer for the dead. III, 1847. Offerings for the dead. II, 92. The sacrifice of the Mass for the dead. II, 694. A sacrifice for the dead, with the corpse placed beside the tomb. I, 777. What Monica requests for herself. I, 778. Augustine wishes prayer to be offered at the altar for his father Patricius and his mother Monica. I, 780. He himself also prays. I, 778. The sacrifice of the altar and almsgiving are performed for all baptized dead. VI, 283. The exercise of mercy toward the dead. III, 1350.

The souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living relatives. VI, 283. The spirits of the dead are aided by the Church’s prayers, the saving sacrifice, and almsgiving, and the extent to which they are aided. V, 936, 937. That they may be commemorated in their appointed place at the sacrifice itself, and that it may be commemorated that the sacrifice is offered also for them—this, handed down by the Fathers, is observed by the universal Church. V, 936. These rites do not create new merits for the dead. V, 937. For which dead persons prayers are heard. VII, 737. The sacrifice, prayers, and alms benefit those who, while alive, merited that these things should later benefit them. VI, 283. These acts of piety are expended on the dead in vain if, while they were here, they lacked the pledge of this benefit. V, 937. Those whom they benefit receive either complete remission through them or a mitigation of the condemnation itself. VI, 284, Note (a). For the very good, they are thanksgivings; for those who are not very bad, intercessions; for the very bad, whatever consolation the living can provide. VI, 283. A Mass for a dead person whose soul is uncertain. VI, 284, Note (a). Prayer is not offered for impious and unbelieving dead. VII, 736. No aid of mercy can be offered to certain dead persons. III, 1351.

The commemoration of the dead. IX, 655.

What the funeral rites of the dead admonish us to reflect upon. V, 937. Funeral processions and the like are, whatever they may be, consolations for the living, not aids for the dead. V, 936. Nevertheless, since these acts are counted among good works in Scripture, each person should perform them according to his ability. V, 937. Funeral praises and the like are performed for the sake of those who live. II, 1074.

The dead await the redemption of their bodies. I, 606. The dead should rather be called absent than dead. IV, 1897. See *Dead*.

The degradation of a cleric, a punishment inflicted by ecclesiastical discipline. V, 1575; VI, 199, 271. To whom and when it is permissible to degrade someone. IX, 669.

Deborah, judge and prophetess among the Hebrews. VII, 572.

Pleasure is the end of care. IV, 103. Pleasure is as it were the soul’s weight. I, 1179. Wherever its pleasure is, there is its treasure. I, 1179. Nothing is loved except what gives pleasure. V, 869. Sometimes what gives pleasure is believed beneficial even if it harms. II, 963. What is recognized as desirable is not desired unless it gives as much pleasure as it ought to be loved. X, 242. Often we see what ought to be done but do not do it, because it gives no pleasure to do it, and we wish it would give pleasure. IV, 1522. Unless what is recognized as to be done is also pleasing and loved, it is not done, undertaken, or lived well. X, 203. The more certainly we know that something is good, the more strongly we desire it and the more ardently we take pleasure in it. X, 167. A good work gives greater pleasure the more God is loved. X, 168.

May God give pleasure—he from whom comes everything that gives pleasure. V, 143. Who gives such pleasure as the one who made everything that gives pleasure? IV, 281. Good things give pleasure although they are not good in themselves; what will the pleasure of the unchangeable Good be? IV, 203. The pleasure of praising God is promised to the pious and not given to the impious. V, 1188. The pious take pleasure in God after earthly things have been lost. V, 147. The occupation of the blessed is to contemplate the pleasure of the Lord himself. IV, 203. We should take pleasure neither in our past life nor in our present life, but focus on what is promised to us. IV, 681. No creature pleases itself and takes pleasure in itself as much as a good mind does. X, 752. The mind’s pleasure in justice and faith. V, 869. No pleasure should be compared with the heart’s pleasure in the light of truth. V, 969.

Pleasure in the good is a gift not of the letter but of the spirit. X, 203, 217. When the good gives pleasure, it is a great gift of God. IV, 1547, 1565, 1566. Pleasure in the good must be attributed to grace. X, 561. Pleasure in justice is God’s gift. V, 919. Why justice sometimes gives more or less pleasure and sometimes none. X, 168. Unless pleasure in justice conquers the pleasures of other things, we are defeated in the struggle against sin. VI, 271. When pleasure in justice conquers, one does not yield to evil desire. VI, 287.

Pleasure in God’s law and pleasure in concupiscence. V, 830. Lawful and unlawful pleasures of the senses. V, 868. Harmful pleasure follows desire; fruitful pleasure follows charity. IV, 124. When pleasures become unlawful lusts. VIII, 419, 420. Not to restrain pleasure in what is unlawful is sin. VIII, 419. To consent to some unlawful pleasure is sin not only in dreadful crimes but also in lesser matters. X, 244, 996. Whoever restrains the pleasure of the flesh from none of the lawful things is close to unlawful pleasures as well. VI, 711. Pleasure in justice must surpass whatever pleasure or pain from other things obstructs. X, 242.

Pleasures and pains must be conquered. V, 1470, 1510. There is always some titillation in pleasure, even in one who has overcome temptation. IV, 1860. A person is wounded by the pleasure of wanton thoughts, even if he departs victorious by not consenting. V, 391. Bodily pleasure does not harm those whose greater pleasure is the pleasure of the word of wisdom and of God’s commandment. IV, 345. Why God mingles bitterness with earthly pleasures. IV, 458, 1213, 1793. Holy people have the power to restrain unlawful pleasure. III, 433. Whoever believes in Christ will pass beyond the pleasures of perishable things. IV, 794. Good pleasures are attributed to the heart, evil ones to the kidneys. IV, 103, 104.

The pleasures of sinners are fleeting. V, 861. In pleasures nothing should be sought except complete bodily health. II, 496, 497. A Christian should not seek pleasures but imitate Christ’s sufferings. V, 275. Pleasures are to be despised. II, 496, 497. Riches are the mothers of pleasures. II, 497. A life in temporal pleasures, compared with eternal life, should be called not life but death. II, 223.

There are pleasures of justice as well as of iniquity. V, 919. What spiritual pleasures are. VI, 447. Christ is our pleasure. IV, 1793. Holy pleasures in the divine Scriptures. IV, 413. Pleasures are scattered through the holy Scriptures by the Holy Spirit. IV, 1803. Spiritual pleasures are presented enigmatically in sacred Scripture. VIII, 308. The pleasures of our spirit are divine songs, in which tears are not without joy. IV, 1884. Pleasures are not taken away from the converted person but changed. IV, 946. The pleasure of the gentle is peace. IV, 362.

Why offenses are so called. IV, 950. Offenses are not understood, just as darkness is not seen. IV, 162. Two kinds of offenses: one’s own and those of others. IV, 162. Christ made our offenses his own, so that he might make his justice our justice. IV, 172. The offender is justly abandoned, so that he himself becomes his own punishment. X, 1355.

Delphinus, bishop. II, 537.

Delphinus of Bordeaux. II, 100.

Why Demaenetus was changed into a wolf. VII, 573.

Demetrias, a virgin. X, 378. Daughter of Juliana. VI, 433, 442. At the urging of Alypius and Augustine, Demetrias sent word that she had renounced marriage when the wedding had already been arranged. II, 849. Demetrias, willingly and by request, was offered to God as a virgin. VI, 441. Pelagius’s letter to her. II, 854. Alypius and Augustine point out the poison in the books written to Demetrias. II, 850. Demetrias’s virginal holiness is praised everywhere. II, 645. Her praise. II, 645.

Demetrius of Lepti-minus. IX, 222.

Demetrius, a presbyter forbidden communion by Primianus. IV, 379.

Democritus. I, 945. Democritus’s opinion of God. II, 445. And of the cause of our thoughts. II, 444, 445. Democritus is said to differ from Epicurus in natural questions in that he perceived some animal and breathing force to be present in the collision of atoms. II, 445.

Demosthenes, the most illustrious of orators. IX, 468. He included all the rules of eloquence in delivery. II, 442. When Aeschines objected to his insolent diction, Demosthenes replied that the fortunes of Greece did not depend on whether he used one word or another. IX, 468.

A hundred denarii may perhaps be a thousand asses. V, 516. The denarius as a reward. V, 696. The denarius paid equally to all for work in the vineyard does not abolish the difference between rewards. VI, 410.

The number ten signifies totality. VI, 38; VII, 696. The Law. III, 1442; V, 517, 1240, 1241, 1243. Perfection. V, 1240. The perfection of blessedness. III, 1336. Also the discipline that signifies God as Creator and the creature as created. VI, 39. The significance of the number ten. V, 352, 353. And its mystical explanation. III, 48. The perfection of our blessedness is in the number ten because it returns to the beginning. II, 218.

Teeth help us to speak as they help us to chew. V, 1145. If the teeth become numb, what remedy is there? IV, 562. How teeth differ from bones. X, 527. A tooth of a huge beast on the Utican shore. VII, 448. Who are the teeth of sinners and the teeth of the Church? IV, 75, 1007, 1224.

To weigh down. V, 1513.

A description of public depravity. VII, 65.

Supplications are used in avoiding evils, prayers in seeking good things. II, 635.

Abandonment. See *To abandon*.

When God does not answer in temporal goods, he does not thereby abandon us. II, 545, 563, 575.

To descend and to fall differ in the proper sense. IV, 1598, 1631. The one descending from Jerusalem to Jericho is the human being descending from immortality to mortality. IV, 1134. To descend to something in the exercise of duty is one thing; to fall into it through desire is another. V, 346.

A human being deserted the emperor and fell away to the deserter. IV, 892. God will not abandon his work if he is not abandoned by his work. IV, 1890; X, 261. God abandoned Adam because Adam himself abandoned God. IV, 693. The anger of the Judge handed some people over to their desires, not by compelling them but by abandoning them. V, 391. When God abandons someone, blindness immediately occurs. X, 256. The human being then goes into evil. X, 567. The tempter takes possession. V, 590. God helps those who have turned toward him and abandons those who have turned away. X, 153. He abandons only those who deserve it. X, 259. God abandons a person somewhat lest we become proud. X, 151, 200. Those are more miserable who do not at all perceive the evil of their abandonment. III, 432. A human being who asks God is not abandoned by him. V, 171. You help what you created; you do not abandon what you made. IV, 208. God fed you while you despised him, and will he abandon you while you fear him? IV, 315.

The world itself is a desert because of its dryness and barrenness. IV, 1760. How the desert places were filled with servants of God. IV, 634. Any faintheartedness and storm in the desert seems less troublesome to me than what we either suffer or fear amid the crowds. II, 354. For the pious, conscience itself is a desert. IV, 635.

Desire is longing for absent things. IV, 1522. Desire is the soul’s thirst. IV, 750. It is the bosom of the heart. III, 1691. Through desire, even what is hastened in time seems slow. II, 905. Things long desired are obtained more sweetly. V, 411. The mind is extended by desire for the desired thing, not by joy in the thing obtained. IV, 434. Unlawful desires corrupt the soul. IV, 1920, 1921. When are we not held captive by evil desires? III, 2071. We sin not in an evil desire but in consent. III, 2066. Unlawful desires arising from innate concupiscence do no harm if they are not obeyed, whether in action, speech, or silent assent. IV, 1507. The origin of the evil desires of concupiscence. X, 430. We ought to will that evil desires not exist. X, 431. It is one thing to have evil desires of the heart and another to be handed over to them. X, 789. What it is to be handed over to evil desires. X, 789. Only the reprobate, not the predestined, are abandoned to perish according to their desire. X, 324. God hands a person over to evil desires not only through patience but also through power. X, 790. The fruit of a forbidden desire is sweeter. III, 2070. The soul, scourged by the diversity of its desires, bears wounds, divided among many loves. IV, 1887. Whoever abandons both what he possesses and what he hopes to possess abandons the whole world. II, 692.

Holy desire is the whole life of the good Christian. III, 2008. Holy desires come from the spirit alone, not from the flesh. III, 416. Our desire should now be directed only toward heaven. V, 932. The desire for God’s kingdom is produced by tribulations battering us from every side. IV, 290. Whoever does not groan as an exile will not rejoice as a citizen, because desire is not in him. IV, 1641, 1940. Our desire must always be extended until it reaches the vision of God. IV, 1147. The desire for Christ in all the just, from the beginning to the end of the world. IV, 1557. Desires for eternal life are weapons against temptations. IV, 1774. The desire of the just is to contemplate the delight of the Lord himself. IV, 203. Your desire is your prayer; and if your desire is continual, your prayer is continual. IV, 404. The pattern of desires in the Lord’s Prayer. V, 378. What desire God promises to hear quickly. IV, 1296, 1888. The desire of the just is delayed so that it may grow, and grows so that it may receive. IV, 1057. God extends desire by delaying; by making the soul desire, he extends it; by extending it, he makes it capable of receiving. III, 2008. Nothing prevents God’s justifications from being possessed except that they are not desired. IV, 1522.

The desolate possess the consolation of the Father of orphans. IV, 815.

To despair. A person must rejoice more when what he had despaired of comes. IV, 1927. Despair in sins thinks that it will destroy itself if it has not done something to which lust urges it. X, 266. Nothing concerning God is to be despaired of. V, 36. Nor concerning the forgiveness of sins. III, 871. God is so full of the fatness of mercy that those who turn to him— not only any sinners but even the impious—must not despair. IV, 597. By despairing, the soul loses more than by sinning. V, 138. Sin accompanied by despair is certain death. IV, 588, 1703. The soul is suffocated by despair of forgiveness. V, 1558. Both hope and despair in sins are to be feared. IV, 1877. Despair and hope are causes of impenitence and destruction. V, 139. One must walk between despair and presumption. V, 778. Let no one presumptuously rely on himself, and let no humble person despair of the Lord. IV, 946. Lest people live worse through despair, God promised a harbor of forgiveness; and again, lest they live worse through hope of forgiveness, he made the day of death uncertain. IV, 1302, 1876. No one should be despaired of as long as he lives. IV, 370, 630; V, 456, 1548; IX, 698. When the enemy suggests despair of salvation, by what unconquerable shield is he repelled? IV, 89.

To shore up crumbling fables with answers from destinies. V, 106.

[Col. 0217] Some are destroyed by God so that they may be built up; others are destroyed in such a way that they are not built up. IV, 1120, 1462.

Detraction is more biting than truthful criticism. V, 1561. As you grow angry with another when he speaks ill of you, so grow angry with yourself when you speak ill of another. V, 635. Just as one should not readily believe a friend who praises, so one should not readily believe an enemy who disparages. IX, 354. When we are disparaged, we must first pray for ourselves, so that we may overcome the desire for vengeance, and then for our detractors themselves. IV, 1434. Fortitude is necessary when one is disparaged in one’s presence—not to repel the insult but to endure it. IV, 1184. Through false disparagements the reward of God’s servants increases, and the punishment of those who disparage them increases. V, 1581. Augustine does not desire this kind of reward. V, 1581. Detraction by those who seem to be persons of influence is a scandal to the weak. IV, 582.

At what time Deucalion’s flood occurred. VII, 568. It did not reach Egypt. VII, 568.

Deuerra, a pagan deity. VII, 188.

A self-devotion is made with a curse. III, 738.

Offerings of devoted people. V, 1572. “Now let it not be driven from the understanding of the devoted that the Father does everything through the Son,” and so forth. V, 356.

God’s existence is proved. *On Free Choice of the Will*, book I, chapters V–XV. God’s existence is known by faith and reason. I, 1262. Reasoning does not establish that God must exist. II, 705. Vanity seeks knowledge of God through disputation; piety seeks it through belief. V, 1203. The error of those disputing about God arises from three causes. VIII, 819. Which is worse. VIII, 820. God is recognized from the works of creation. IV, 944; X, 211. God is known to philosophers from created things. V, 776, 1133. How the Platonists arrived at knowledge of God. VII, 231. Just as the soul is understood from the movements and administration of the body, so God is understood from the administration of the world and the governance of souls. V, 1022. Such is the power of true divinity that it cannot be wholly and completely hidden from a rational creature already using reason. III, 1910. The name of God could not have been wholly unknown to the nations before they believed in Christ. III, 1910. An unbeliever can reach such darkness as to deny that God exists. IV, 1117. How one should deal with an atheist. I, 1242. Rare are those who say in their heart, “There is no God.” IV, 613. No one dares say that God does not exist, even if he has dared to think it. IV, 141. To deny God himself is open madness. VII, 152. The madness of those who deny God belongs to only a few. V, 441. The true God was recognized even through the responses of oracles. VII, 651. Varro designated the true God by the name Jupiter. VII, 650.

What God is. III, 1658. To think as truly as possible about God is the truest beginning of piety. I, 1224. To be mistaken about God is dangerous; to lie about him is ruinous. V, 157. God is not possessed together with falsehood. I, 807. Various opinions about God. I, 721; III, 123, 164, 169. The nations’ opinion concerning our God. III, 1055. Varro approved the view that God is a soul governing the world by motion and reason. VII, 138. All nature proclaims that it is not God. VI, 653. What the whole of nature teaches us about God. VIII, 1061. What the Church teaches. I, 1317.

What God is, or what God is not. I, 783; V, 143, 1689. We can more easily say what God is not than what he is. IV, 1090. In divine matters pious ignorance is better than presumptuous knowledge. V, 663. It is no small part of knowledge to know what God is not before one can know what he is. II, 459; III, 1588; VIII, 948.

Everyone understands God as that than which nothing is better. I, 807; III, 22. God is that than which nothing is superior. I, 1248. God’s excellence. III, 1383.

Being belongs properly to God. VII, 236. God supremely and primarily is. III, 32. He alone properly is. III, 1680. God possesses in himself a mode of being utterly different from that of creatures. III, 333. God is such that, in comparison with him, the things that have been made are not. IV, 1741. God supremely is because he neither advances nor declines through any changeability. II, 439. In God everything that is said is identical with him. V, 1498.

God’s simplicity. VII, 231. God is the simplest nature. VIII, 1062, 1076. God cannot be part of anything. VIII, 765. God is simple and manifold. VIII, 928, 929, 936. God, although triune, is simple and unchangeable good. VII, 325. How. VII, 326. In God power is not one thing, wisdom another, and the other virtues something else. V, 1498. For God, being is the same as being able. III, 1558. Being is the same as being great and being good. VIII, 947. Being strong, being just, and so forth. VIII, 927, 929, 931, 933, 943. Being wise. VIII, 947, 1076.

What God’s nature is. III, 1876. God’s nature is understood from his workmanship. VI, 662. God is a certain substance. IV, 844. The highest substance. X, 255. He is a certain most excellent and immortal nature. III, 21. Unchangeable. III, 357, 362. Invisible and wholly present everywhere. III, 647. Whatever can be understood in God is substance. VI, 192. In God, “substance” is said abusively; “essence” properly. VIII, 912. Whether God is called substance or essence, it is said with reference to himself, not relatively to something else. VIII, 942. Whatever appears to be said of God according to qualities must be understood according to substance or essence. VIII, 1062. In God nothing is said according to accident, but according to substance or relation. VIII, 913, 914. The Arian doctrine that everything said or understood of God is said according to substance is false. VIII, 912, 914. In what Catholics and Manichaeans agree concerning God’s nature, and in what they disagree. X, 1468.

In his essence God is identical with supreme being and supreme living. I, 665. For him, being and living are not different things. I, 665. Philosophers understood that God is a certain wise eternal life, making others wise. V, 776. This was understood from consideration of the world. V, 776. God’s life is God himself. III, 1548. God’s life is unchangeable. III, 1548. God is said tropically to have a soul, just as he is said to have bodily members. VII, 534. God is the supreme source of life. VIII, 93. In God there are both the cause of subsisting, the reason for understanding, and the order of living. VII, 228. God is not of the same nature as the soul. VII, 230. Some have said that the lives and souls of all living things are taken by lot from God’s soul. VII, 123. God’s soul is his will. III, 716. God has neither sex nor age nor defined bodily members. VII, 134.

### What is to be thought when God is mentioned

What is to be thought when God is mentioned. V, 35. What God is like cannot be grasped by thought. III, 790. God is incomprehensible. I, 661; IV, 1742, 1743, 1872; V, 360, 663. Certain things were therefore set forth beforehand in the Gospel, so that we might be admonished that we ought not boast of a rash comprehension. II, 1053. Plato says that God cannot be comprehended. VII, 270. God is more truly thought than spoken of; and he exists more truly than he is thought. VIII, 939. To touch God to some small degree with the mind is blessedness; to comprehend him is impossible. V, 663. The incomprehensible God is always to be sought. VIII, 1057. Nothing concerning God can be understood without piety and a certain peace of mind. VIII, 92. For God to be understood, even in however small a part, requires only great groanings and sighs. VIII, 174. The soul dares to speak of God more easily than to see him; and it speaks of him so much less the more sincerely it has been able to see him. VIII, 187. God must first be known through unfailing faith, so that he may be loved. VIII, 951. One must approach God by the intellect alone. VIII, 90. The fantasies that the heart imagines for itself concerning God. V, 1204. One who thinks of God carnally: how he is to be instructed. V, 157. Every carnal thought must be rejected, so that one may grasp how God is truth. VIII, 948. How God is to be thought of. III, 2035. Whoever thinks of God as he is not, necessarily carries in his thought an alien and false god. III, 790. Some wish God to be something like that which was figuratively shown to the spirit of the saints. III, 427. We perceive God more easily with the mind than creatures. III, 333. God is interior and exterior, older and newer than all things. III, 333.

### God ineffable

God is ineffable. I, 662, 663; III, 21, 333; IV, 1090. In what way. I, 662, 663; III, 21, 333; IV, 1090. God’s majesty can be thought by spiritual beings, but cannot be uttered by anyone. II, 1053. God is ineffable, and by keeping silent one may sense more about him than one can say. V, 665. Honourable silence rather than any human voice is fitting for God. VIII, 142. Woe to those who are silent about God, for the talkative are mute. I, 662, 663. Everything can be said of God, and nothing is said worthily of God. III, 564; V, 1498; VI, 138; VIII, 138, 142, 627, 628. No worthy comparison can be found for speaking about God. VIII, 728. We must not rashly say something about God that we do not read in his Scripture. III, 302. Power, prudence, and similar things are said of God not properly, but because nothing better can be said. V, 1497. Human words are attributed to divine realities, but there they are to be understood with their imperfections removed. VI, 140.

### The name of God

The twofold name of God declared to Moses. V, 61, 66. The name of God, the τετραγάμματον (the four-letter name), is ineffable. III, 638. The name of God is being itself. IV, 1741. God’s name is delightful to those who love him above all delights. IV, 612. Why God is called a consuming fire. VIII, 148. Light. VIII, 938, 939. Light-producing Light. VIII, 404. God is the light of truth that illuminates every human being. X, 130.

### God as spirit and as incorporeal

According to the Platonists God is spirit; according to the Stoics he is body. III, 1056. Tertullian maintains that God is corporeal, as is the soul. X, 499. And that he is body. II, 861; III, 427; VIII, 46. Some attribute a body to God, lest he fail to be a substance. II, 619. Some have imagined him to be an fiery body, others the brightness of light. III, 164. But he is incorporeal. I, 721. To suppose God corporeal is altogether impious. II, 622, 623. God is not something corporeal, nor anything of such a kind as can be formed by our thought. V, 35, 369. Whatever presents itself as corporeal, and whatever is changeable among spiritual things, is not God. VIII, 958. Even the ignorant common people proclaim that nothing touched by bodily sensation should be worshipped as God. VIII, 90. It is proved that God is not body. VII, 230.

How absurd it is to ascribe limbs to God. II, 459. God is defined by no bodily form. VI, 188, 304. He is not to be thought of as having a body extended in space. V, 359. How statements made bodily about God are to be understood. I, 1318; III, 166, 186. The limbs attributed to God are to be understood spiritually. [Col. 0219] II, 628. God’s limbs are the power of his operations. IV, 130. They are the effects of his operations and powers. III, 716. God is wholly eye, wholly hand, wholly foot. II, 628. God’s face is the power by which he makes himself known to those worthy of it. IV, 137. God’s ear is not a bodily limb, but the power by which he hears. IV, 130. What God’s face, hands, and feet mean. V, 366. God’s arm and hand are Christ. IV, 484, 894, 1146, 1444, 1253. The Son and the Holy Spirit. IV, 1551; VII, 373. God’s hand is God’s power. III, 347; IV, 484, 1551, 1613; VII, 373. His power. VIII, 692. God’s right hand is eternal happiness. IV, 1146, 1782. God’s finger is the Holy Spirit. II, 218; IV, 111. In what sense God’s jealousy, anger, mercy, patience, repentance, hands, feet, and so forth are spoken of. VI, 34, 139, 140, 249, 611. God’s anger and jealousy are without disturbance. III, 558, 599, 651. God is not subject to disturbances. III, 2065. In God, position, clothing, years, and place are spoken of metaphorically. VIII, 817.

### God’s beauty and fullness

God’s beauty. IV, 1075. His fullness. I, 845; III, 133. In God nothing is lacking and nothing is excessive. I, 894. How the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ. II, 847. What distinction there is between the way divinity dwells in Christ and in his members. II, 847.

### God’s speech

How a statement about God is to be understood. III, 227. God’s speech in his substance; the immutable Word of God, who is Christ. IV, 1788. The Word of God. III, 348. God speaks the coeternal Word. III, 250. How God speaks with the angels. III, 447; VII, 484. The angels hear God’s speech in ineffable ways and convey it to human beings. VII, 293. How, and in how many ways, God speaks to human beings. IV, 566; VII, 317, 484. God speaks either through his own substance or through a creature subject to him. III, 392. God speaks either in thought itself or through a bodily creature. III, 1284. He speaks inwardly to those who make room for him. III, 2005. God himself sounds everywhere through many organs, by touching, modulating, and inspiring. IV, 566. How God spoke with the first human beings. VII, 443. After the sin, God spoke to the first parents through a creature subject to him. III, 392, 447. He spoke inwardly with them in other ways. III, 392, 447. God spoke to Moses through an assumed creature, not through his own substance. IV, 1788. At times God speaks to his servants in the very persons of his servants. III, 394. Various questions are raised concerning God’s speech. III, 252. How it could have occurred naturally is difficult to discover. III, 252. In Scripture he speaks to human beings in human fashion. III, 558. He has messengers for our sake and for their own. III, 334.

### God invisible

God is invisible. V, 1266. Not only the Father, but the whole Trinity, is one God invisible by nature. II, 605. In what sense invisible, when the angels always see his face. VIII, 763. God is not invisible to angels and to those who will be like them. VIII, 768. God cannot be seen by bodily eyes. VI, 663. God is invisible to bodily eyes but visible to the mind. II, 318, 319; V, 663; VIII, 171. God is invisible to the bodily eyes of all, but known to the very pure hearts of a few. IV, 1481. God can be seen only by the mind, though not in such a way that the mind itself can be seen. IV, 468. Even when you see God, you will not be able to say, “This is God.” V, 369. God cannot be seen in a place in the manner of a body. V, 1264. God is called invisible lest he be believed to be a body. II, 618. God is light, but the light of the heart. II, 561.

“No one has ever seen God,” because no one has comprehended with mind or eyes that fullness of divinity which dwells in God, according to Ambrose. II, 604. Ambrose intimates that the Son of God was seen in the Old Testament. II, 604. How God made himself visible to the Fathers. VII, 291. Through a creature, God used to appear to the first parents in human form. III, 448. God’s appearance to Moses. V, 59, 160. How Moses saw God. VI, 662. Moses desired to see God in the substance in which God is. III, 477. The pious who desire to see God wish to behold the substance by which he is what he is, not the appearance in which he appears as he wills. II, 605. God’s appearance to Moses took place through an angel. V, 60. Why it was in the bush that was not consumed by the flame clinging to it. V, 60. God customarily appears in fire. VI, 659. God can at the same time appear here and remain hidden: appear in appearance, remain hidden in nature. V, 161. When God appears in bodily form, his substance does not appear. III, 394, 632. It cannot be refuted that either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—if indeed it was a vision of the Holy Spirit—can be seen in the form chosen by the will and not fashioned by nature, since we also received a vision of the Spirit in the form of a dove. II, 604, 605. According to Ambrose. II, 618. God deigns to appear through his substance, as he is, only to pure hearts. V, 59. There is an inner manifestation of God which the impious do not know. III, 1831. God’s form will be seen by the pious alone; Christ’s form as servant will be seen by everyone. V, 711.

### Whether God is to be seen

Whether God is to be seen by bodily eyes. VII, 798, 799, 800. Whether he will be seen through a spiritual body. V, 1264. Whether he could at least be seen through a glorified body. II, 619. Some have said that not only the saints but also the impious will see God after receiving bodies in the resurrection. II, 319. Others think that those who rise to eternal life will see [Col. 0220] God through the body. II, 619. Even in the resurrection God will not be seen by the sight of the eyes. II, 606. The holy Fathers—Ambrose, Jerome, Athanasius, Gregory of the East, and others—taught that the invisible God is seen invisibly. II, 624. Whoever can see God invisibly can himself cling to God incorporeally. II, 613. If bodily vision of God is ever granted, it will not impede spiritual vision. II, 629. How the angels see the face of the Father, and how we too shall see God as he is. II, 605. Perhaps God is now seen by certain angels in the manner in which he is seen as he is. II, 605. Even in the resurrection God will not be heard by the hearing of the ears. II, 609, 618. God cannot be seen by bodily eyes. II, 319, 618, 619, 622, 623, 625, 626, 627; not even by Christ. II, 707.

To see God is the highest happiness. I, 1018; V, 711. God will be seen by his children as he is. V, 161. The vision of God is the reward of faith. VI, 661. Why it is deferred. VI, 662. In how many ways God can be seen by the blessed. VII, 801. He will be seen with the eyes of the heart. VII, 799. What is required for God to be seen in perfect vision. VIII, 171. The mind must be changed in order to see him. VI, 14. The soul must be purified. III, 23. The eye of the heart must be cleansed. V, 542, 670. God is the light of purified minds, not of the bodily eyes. II, 318. Even in the resurrection it is not easy to see God, except for those who are pure in heart, according to Ambrose. II, 604, 608. Through God’s help, a pure heart must be prepared for seeing him. II, 622. In the future age the impious will not see God, but only those pure in heart. II, 607, 608. The pure in heart will see him. II, 618, 620, 621. We shall see God to the extent that we shall be like him. II, 319. We do not now see God to the extent that we are unlike him. II, 319. How God is already seen. VI, 661. How the Apostle says that we now see God through a mirror. VIII, 1067. God is seen by those who die to the world. III, 40. God can be seen only in that life in which, in order to live, one must die to this life. III, 649. God shows himself to those who love him and is sufficient for them, so that they do not turn away from him. I, 833. God is everywhere hidden and everywhere manifest; no one is permitted to know him as he is, and no one is permitted to be ignorant of him. IV, 952.

How “to see God’s face and not be able to live” is to be understood morally. VIII, 864. The vision of God’s face is his manifestation. VIII, 797. From where God’s “back parts” can be seen. VIII, 865. God’s back parts were seen by the Israelites. VIII, 865. Christ is God’s back parts. VI, 663. The flesh of Christ. VIII, 863, 864. God’s invisible things are intellectually perceived through the things made in the body. VIII, 392. Divine things are seen by understanding, not by gazing with the eyes of the flesh. VIII, 712. Concerning the vision of God. V, 155, 366. Quarrels and disputes arose over the question of the vision of God. V, 162. To know what God is. VIII, 951. Through knowledge of God a human being becomes blessed. V, 663. To the extent that we know God, we are like him, but not like him as equals. VIII, 969.

### God’s attributes and beauty

God’s attributes are inexplicable. I, 662. God’s attributes are described in summary. I, 662.

God’s beauty is ancient and new. I, 795. By imitation of it, other things are beautiful; in comparison with it, they are ugly. I, 1018. All beauty comes from it. I, 801. And every form. III, 131. God’s beauty is in intelligible and immutable truth. II, 444; and in justice. II, 462.

### God’s eternity

God’s eternity. VII, 362. God remains with and in himself as complete and perfect eternity. V, 1073. God was not made by anyone. X, 571. God is, and truly is, and precisely because he truly is, he exists without beginning or end. IV, 1743. God neither began to exist, nor grew weary of his inactivity, nor became sluggish through ceasing, nor laboured through working. VIII, 604. God alone is eternal. V, 208. He surpasses all time. X, 401. He does not know times. I, 814. God precedes all past things. I, 815. In God’s nature there is nothing that is as though it did not yet exist, or that was as though it no longer existed; there is only what is, and this itself is eternity. IV, 122. God’s very substance is that which contains nothing changeable: there is nothing past there, as though it no longer existed; nothing future, as though it did not yet exist; there is nothing there except what is. IV, 1311. In God alone the present is found. III, 1680. God’s eternity is one day. I, 815. It surpasses all future things. I, 815. There truth is eternal and love eternal; there love is true and eternity true; there eternity is dear and truth dear. VIII, 887. God creates all times without a temporal will. VIII, 335.

### God immutable

God is immutable. I, 664, 1248, 1318; IV, 1142; VII, 220, 362; VIII, 518, 551, 558, 887, 911. The Manichaeans posited mutability in God’s nature. VIII, 595. God alone is immutable. V, 986; VIII, 912. God is immutable goodness. III, 384. No mutability of time can be found in the substance of the highest good. VIII, 594. God is above everything that is changeable. I, 1248. He is not at one time one thing and at another time another, nor at one time one way and at another time another, but always the same and the same. I, 828. In him stand the immutable causes of all unstable things; the immutable origins of mutable things remain; and the eternal principles of irrational [Col. 0221] and temporal things live. I, 664. God knows and wills immutably. I, 853. Remaining immutable, he forms and renews all things. I, 1265. In God there is no new movement. I, 815. Always the same and unmoved, he acts upon all things. III, 389, 390, 391. How God, unmoved, moves creatures can be discerned from the example of the soul. III, 388. God does not act through temporal movements. III, 200. How temporal movements in temporal things come about when God commands non-temporally is extremely difficult to grasp. III, 252. God’s plan is not changeable. III, 300. God persists in immutable will, truth, and eternity. VIII, 372. God is not changeable because he commanded one thing to be offered in the Old Testament and another in the New. II, 528. God does not change his will, but the things he willed. VIII, 660. When God changes, he is said to repent because of the change in the work itself, not in the plan, which is immutable. IV, 1416, 1723. God changes when you change: his sentence changes, not his justice. VI, 141. God is immutable, the author of all good. VI, 360. God alone is immortal, because he alone is immutable. VIII, 768.

### God incorruptible

The Manichaeans said that God’s nature was corruptible. X, 1325, 1328. He is incorruptible. VIII, 518. He has no nature opposed to him. VI, 185. Except that which does not exist. VII, 350; VIII, 586. God cannot be harmed or injured, nor can any other nature be so harmed except with his permission. VIII, 555, 563. God cannot suffer any necessity. VI, 16. Nor can he be violated in any respect. VIII, 114.

### God’s immensity and omnipresence

God’s immensity. II, 837; VII, 220. God is everywhere. I, 707, 795. God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are simultaneously everywhere. II, 837. It is difficult to discover where God is, more difficult where he is not. I, 1077. Nothing is more hidden than he, nothing more present. I, 1077. Augustine’s false conception of God’s immensity, still Manichaean. I, 733, 736. He is so diffused throughout all things that he is not the quality of the world but the creating substance, ruling without labour and containing the world without burden. II, 837.

God is wholly everywhere. II, 443, 517, 622; III, 1640, 1654; V, 1264, 1268. How he is wholly everywhere in himself. II, 838. Divinity is wholly everywhere, divided nowhere. V, 560, 367. God is present everywhere. IV, 952, 1125. Present everywhere and seeing everything. V, 441. He is present to created things by spiritual presence. IV, 1047. God’s presence in things is the cause of their existence. I, 661. An indication that God’s presence is known to all is even the oath used by the wicked: “God is my witness.” V, 101. When God, who is everywhere present, is considered to be simultaneously present to each of us. VI, 14. Whatever understands God is with God. I, 995. What God’s hidden place is like, into which God’s servant enters. III, 1603, 1604. The wretched can be where God is, but only the blessed are with him. III, 1927. God is neither stretched out by bulk nor diminished by division. VII, 280. God’s nature is everywhere whole and everywhere present, not smaller in one part and greater in another; without any bulk, it is great, and is not extended across the intervals of places. VIII, 184. If the soul is not extended through places, much less is God. VIII, 188. He is wholly everywhere and is nowhere in places. I, 721, 795. He is present everywhere not through the spaces of places but through the power of his majesty. III, 1277.

### God and place

God is not in a place. V, 367, 548, 1265, 1268; VI, 15, 661. If he were in some place, he would not be God. IV, 953. God is moved neither through place nor through time. III, 387, 395. How he is said to descend. VII, 483. And to be in a bodily place. III, 752. To be in the heavens while being wholly everywhere. II, 459. He makes his presence known to human beings through the effect of a miracle. IV, 484. God is nearer to us than many creatures are. III, 333. God is more inward to a human being than the human being’s own heart. IV, 853. He is to be sought within our interior. I, 795. It is proclaimed in both Testaments that God does not dwell in places constructed by human beings. VIII, 141.
