God’s dwelling made by human hands is understood in both Testaments as signifying something. VIII, 141. God blesses his temple; he does not need it in order to be blessed. VIII, 604. The temple of God is angels and human beings. VIII, 604. God’s holy seat is heaven and the soul of the just person. IV, 529, 530. If you wish, you are God’s seat. V, 367. God is in the holy and the just. III, 1276. God is everywhere through the presence of divinity, but not through the grace of indwelling. II, 837. God is not present to certain people. III, 1392. He does not dwell equally in human beings through grace. II, 837. He is possessed by human beings according to their capacity. II, 838. He dwells in the elect even though they are still carnal. II, 842, 843. He is said to dwell in little children because he secretly works in them so that they may be his temple; and he brings this to completion in those who make progress and persevere in progress. II, 841. By indwelling, God contains; he is not contained. V, 1502. He bears and contains those in whom he dwells; if he withdraws, they fall. IV, 1632, 1633.

God is present to every conscience: to the good as a father, to the wicked as a judge. V, 101. Do not think of God as being in places; he is with you according to what you are: a helper if you are good, an avenger if you are evil. IV, 952. God’s presence is joy to Adam the just, punishment to the sinner. V, 542. To God, who is everywhere and contained by no place, we draw near not through places: to draw near to him is to become like him; to withdraw is to become unlike him. IV, 337, [Col. 0222] 1217. Love presents God as present. II, 670. The wicked do not escape God’s presence. I, 766. Who is said to hide himself from his sight. III, 208. Before he made heaven, earth, and the saints, God dwelt in himself and with himself. IV, 1632. How God the Word was in the world. III, 1393, 1398. God does not fill the world like water, air, or light. II, 517. No one comprehends God’s fullness. II, 606.

### God’s greatness

God is great not in bulk but in power. II, 519. God’s substance is not bounded by quantity. V, 157. How God grows. III, 1504. God is not great by participation in greatness. VIII, 918. God is so great in great works that he is not smaller in the smallest. V, 1060; VIII, 391, 665. God is immutable greatness; how he is magnified by us. IV, 1337. Porphyry acknowledges that God is great. VII, 650.

God is wise, eternal, and so forth, not by participation in wisdom and eternity, but by the wisdom and eternity of which he himself is the author. VI, 16. God’s wisdom is simply manifold and uniformly multiform. VII, 368. God’s wisdom and power in the first creation are not to be measured by customary and daily works. VII, 373. God is present to the minds of the wise without being contaminated. VII, 270.

### God’s knowledge

God possesses knowledge of all things. I, 590. God alone knows himself as he altogether is. I, 853. Nothing is hidden from him. I, 590. What God’s knowledge is like. VIII, 1075. God’s knowledge does not vary. I, 826; VII, 291. Nothing departs from him or succeeds to him. VIII, 931. God’s knowledge comprehends the infinite. VII, 367. There is an abyss both in a good heart and in an evil heart, but these are naked before God. IV, 1749. No one can evade God’s eyes. IV, 1200. God sees present, past, and future immutably. VII, 334. To God future things are present, as past things are. VII, 291. With God everything is present. VI, 15. The knowledge of God is the cause of all things. I, 736. God knows all creatures not because they exist, but they exist because he knows them. VIII, 931, 1076. God does not know in the way a human being or an angel knows, but in an incomprehensible way. IV, 576, 577. God’s knowledge is so great that, in an ineffable way, all things were present to him before they were created. IV, 577. Compared with God’s knowledge, our knowledge is ignorance. I, 811.

To deny that God knows the future beforehand is manifest insanity. VII, 149. What God’s knowledge and foreknowledge are like. VI, 136. God’s foreknowledge, like his judgment, is certain and fixed. VII, 472. In God’s disposition, all the times that are to come have already been made. VII, 291. God is not the author of everything he foreknows. I, 1276. Sins are not to be imputed to him. I, 1280. God’s foreknowledge is reconciled with freedom. I, 1273.

### How God is said to know, not to know, and to test

How God is said to know, not to know, and to test. VI, 48, 106. Scripture customarily attributes to God what he brings about in us, wherever it can appropriately be said of him. IV, 75, 615, 616. Just as certain praiseworthy things about human beings are not rightly said of God, so certain blameworthy things about human beings are rightly understood in God. VI, 141. God is said to know what he causes to be known. VII, 511. He is said to see what he causes to be seen. IV, 697, 699; VII, 483, 753. He is said to know when he is known or causes something to be known. III, 334, 563; IV, 490, 615, 697. God is said to see when he has mercy. III, 1756. When God saw that what he had made was good, he taught that it was good; he did not merely say so. VII, 334. God tests in order to know—that is, in order to cause someone to know through his gift. III, 757; IV, 490. How God is said to learn. V, 29. It is not incompatible to say that God was amazed. VIII, 406. Why Scripture says that God does not know, repents, and similar things. V, 1498. How God is said to repent. V, 152. How God is said not to know sinners. IV, 69. To command and speak to us. V, 98, 102. What God’s thought and reconsideration mean. VII, 472. God must not be tested. III, 574. How God is said to test. V, 29.

### God as truth

God is eternal truth, which is the food of the mature. I, 742. God is the truth presiding over all things. I, 807. God’s face is nothing other than the very truth for which we sigh. I, 988. God is truthful in a way different from a human being. III, 1685. When he promises, he can deceive no one. I, 826.

### God’s will

God’s will is not a creature. I, 814. God’s will and God’s power are God himself. I, 736. The cause of everything he has made is his will. IV, 1745. He wills all that he wills once, simultaneously, and always. I, 832. God did not create the world by a new act of will. I, 832. God can do many things that he does not will. X, 250. How God wills many things that he does not do. VII, 753. According to Plato, no force overcomes God’s will. VII, 389. God’s will is always unconquered and never evil, whether he has mercy or hardens. VI, 279. Nothing happens apart from God’s will, even when something happens against his will. VI, 279. Through the same will of the creature by which what the Creator did not will came about, God himself fulfilled what he willed. VI, 279. Every creature serves God, willingly or unwillingly. VI, 294. God’s good will is always fulfilled through the good wills of human beings just as through their evil wills. VI, 279. God’s will was fulfilled concerning the sinful human being. VI, 282. The good God would not allow something to be done badly unless he were omnipotent and able to bring good out of evil. VI, [Col. 0223] 279. Nothing can happen to a human being according to bodily vices that God does not will. III, 598. God wills all things justly. III, 598. What God’s will was concerning the salvation of Adam, whom he foreknew would sin. VI, 281. No one knows God’s plans except his friends and children. VI, 71. No one comprehends God’s judgments, and no one justly reproves them. VII, 71. God’s will is called what he brings about in the hearts of those who obey his commands. VII, 753. God causes human beings to do what he commands. X, 975. God’s best servant is the one who looks not so much for hearing from God what he himself wants, but rather for willing what he has heard from God. I, 795. God’s will was better known to the prophets than to the philosophers. VII, 389.

God’s power and God’s will are God himself. I, 736. They are the cause of creatures’ existence. I, 736. How God does everything whatever he wills. VII, 753. He does whatever he wills; whatever is done badly, he does not will. VI, 627. Let us grant that God can do something which we admit we cannot investigate. II, 519. God has no master. I, 803. He rules without pride. I, 804. The mind becomes like him when it subjects itself to him. I, 1320.

### God omnipotent

God is omnipotent. V, 1060, 1067. He alone is omnipotent. VI, 640. Not even a pagan denies that God is omnipotent. V, 1131. God is called omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills. VII, 719. God is omnipotent, being unable only to do what he does not will. V, 1067. By the will of omnipotent God, what otherwise cannot happen comes about. V, 1141. Whether the will of almighty God can be called fate. X, 577. Nothing is impossible for God. VII, 716. God is rich in omnipotence, not in money. VII, 204. If you do not know how something happens, believe that what God permits or does does not happen unjustly. V, 319. Nothing is taken away from God’s omnipotence by the fact that he cannot sin or die. V, 1061, 1068; VII, 349, 793; VI, 627; VIII, 482; X, 285. Whatever God is said not to be able to do, he can do not defectively but powerfully. VIII, 693. God omnipotent is not overcome even when the wicked do many things against his will. V, 1067. God was not defeated by the devil when Adam was deceived. VIII, 615.

### God the creator

God alone is Creator. VIII, 878. The only true Creator. III, 603. Whatever appears better in accordance with true reason, know that God made it. I, 1277. Whatever does not praise the Lord, the Lord did not make. III, 2002. Human nature naturally senses that it has been made by God. X, 247. With God, both the ability and the ease of creating things are incomparable. III, 302. If God could not make good things, he would possess no power; but if he could and did not, he would possess great envy. III, 307. Whether God can be called the cause of things. III, 21. How the Platonists knew that God is the first cause. VII, 231. All things are from him, not from his substance. VIII, 560. God is the Creator of all things that we see and of the better things that we do not see, although the manner in which he made them cannot be comprehended. VIII, 610, 611. God the omnipotent Maker is shown through three powers. VIII, 547, 549. Those who think that God did not make the world from nothing but from a nature coeternal with himself deny that God is omnipotent. VI, 181. God would not be omnipotent if he needed matter in order to make what he willed. VIII, 117. How God’s command, power, and goodness are understood in the creation of things. III, 228. One must not think that God’s works were fashioned by bodily limbs. VII, 373. He did not create the world by a new will. I, 832. God works by an immutable plan and will. VII, 366, 367. God made new things without being new; temporal things while eternal; changeable things while knowing no change. V, 1204.

God is the Creator of times. III, 310. The belief that whatever God generated is coeternal with God and of the same substance as he is, is a Manichaean error. VIII, 532. God created everything in time, yet according to an immutable and eternal plan. VII, 362. When God works, nothing comes to be in his nature that was not there before. VII, 367. Whatever God does in time, he does while his plan remains immutable. VII, 320. Whatever is said to begin or end in God is to be understood not in his nature but in his creature. III, 227. For God, what he has made is nature. III, 349. God arranged everything according to measure, number, and weight. III, 299, 300. How. III, 299, 300. From God comes every measure of measures, the equality of numbers, and the order of weights. III, 337. God is both measure, number, and weight. III, 299. How. III, 299. God possessed everything in wondrous ways before he made it. V, 958. He knew everything before it came to be. III, 332. Why. III, 333. Where he saw the basis from which he would arrange everything. III, 300. In his own life God saw everything when he made it. III, 332. God’s having seen his works means that he approved them. III, 228. God knows everything immutably. III, 334. God is the author of all those works for which the natural philosophers imagined many gods. VII, 219. A concise description of God’s works. I, 865.

God the Creator made heaven and earth without any extension of his activity. I, 826. God created both heavenly and earthly things, including the smallest among them. VIII, 606. God is the Creator of every [Col. 0224] nature, however small. VII, 373, 374, 376. God is great in his smallest works. III, 399. God is so great an artificer in great things that he is not smaller in small things. VII, 335. How much the omnipotence of God the Creator shines forth in the smallest things. II, 519. God the Creator is not small in small things, but indicates great things through the smallest. II, 519. In creating the human being, he displayed his goodness. I, 1272. God is the Creator of both soul and body. X, 686. He is the Creator of the body. III, 131. God made the human being; he did not make the human being’s vices. III, 2002. God is the Creator of visible and invisible things—not insofar as vices are concerned, but insofar as the natures themselves are concerned. III, 227. God is the Creator of those who are born, but in such a way that he is the author of their natures, not of their vices. X, 1300, 1301, 1303, 1312, 1313. No one is excluded from God’s kingdom. V, 1638. God is not the generator of evils. VIII, 632, 633. What God does in every kind and operation of nature. VII, 788. God’s power over all natures and wills. VII, 435. No one is excluded from God’s kingdom. V, 1638. What God is to rational beings, irrational animals, and bodies. VIII, 372. The charge that God sins through weakness in mysteries, excess in precepts, and brutality in judgments: Julian’s slander against Saint Augustine. X, 1418. God the Creator applies the efficacy of his wisdom to fashioning the things that arise each day in their appointed times. II, 948.

God even now creates the things that are born. III, 325. God continues to work until now. III, 304, 334. How, when he created everything simultaneously. III, 337. He always works and always rests. I, 868; III, 1534; IV, 1181. God’s cessation from work is without idleness, and his work is without labour. VII, 367. God did not labour in working. III, 302. Whether he literally rested. III, 302.

### God’s rest from his works

How God’s rest from his works is to be understood. III, 304, 320, 336, 338; V, 80. Because God is perfectly blessed in the good that he himself is, he rested in himself from the good things that he made. III, 298, 307. God can be said to have rested insofar as he granted rational creation rest in himself. III, 302, 303, 306. Since we rest, God says that he rests. IV, 1725. God is always at rest; his rest is himself. I, 868. God’s rest is without beginning and without end. III, 310. He has neither morning nor evening. III, 308, 309, 310. Why God rested on the seventh day and blessed it. III, 305, 306. Having ordered the causes of things, through the immutability of his most secret plan he arranged what he makes known and present at their appointed times, and has already made future things. IV, 1416. God does nothing that he did not foreknow from eternity that he would do. IV, 1416. He does what he promised he would do. X, 224, 1206, 1208. How God made the things that are still future. III, 1814. God does certain things through himself; certain things he commands or permits to be done through a creature serving him: what those things are. VI, 36, 37. God works through his ministers in such a way that they too are fellow workers with God. VII, 483. Why he wished to create the world: it is useless to ask. III, 175.

God made all things out of goodness, not necessity. IV, 1745. God loves the creature so that it may exist and remain. III, 251. God’s love for his works arises from beneficence. III, 250, 251. In God there is a love for his works arising from beneficence, not from need. VI, 166, 167. God gained nothing for himself from the works of the good. III, 435. He needs no good things, whether made or to be made. III, 306, 308. Nor did he need things to be made, since he has no need of things already made. VIII, 606, 608. For the increase of blessedness. VIII, 606, 608. God owes to no one what comes from him, because he is blessed. III, 306, 308. God needs no creature in order to be better, more powerful, or more blessed. IV, 896. He would not have been less had he not made the world, nor more blessed when he had made it. III, 306. God is the judge of wills, the creator of natures. VIII, 544. God creates natures in goodness and orders wills by power. III, 389. God is the best creator of natures, but the most just ordainer of sinners. III, 296. God alone restores creatures. III, 408.

God, being omnipotent, does nothing without reason, though the human mind cannot give an account of that reason. VII, 716. In marvelous things that transcend nature, the whole reason for the deed is the power of the one who performs it. II, 519. God has hidden within himself the causes of certain acts, which he did not implant in created things. III, 406. Very hidden and abstruse is the power by which God acts, so that even things lacking sense immediately obey his will. IV, 1410. The usefulness of God’s hidden works. X, 832. Some things in God’s works are more difficult to know than God himself, insofar as he can be known. X, 527. Just as human custom speaks through words, so divine power speaks through deeds as well. II, 383. God is the maker of created things, the light by which things are known, and the good by which things are done. VII, 233, 234. God is the beginning of nature, the truth of doctrine, and the happiness of life. VII, 233, 234. God is the author of natures, the giver of understanding, and the inspirer of the love by which one lives well and happily. VII, 338. The Platonists recognized these things. VII, 230. What answer should be given to one who asks what God was doing before heaven and earth? I, 815.

The Epicureans deny that God cares for human affairs. VIII, 376. The impious doctrine of the wicked is that God’s providence does not care for human affairs. IV, 924. That the governance of human affairs does not belong to God is a suspicion held by some. V, 318. God’s providence governs all things. I, 978, 979, 1223, 1349; III, 126, 145. God administers the universe. III, 285. How. III, 390; VII, 220. How God administers the human race. III, 391. And wills as well. III, 390. He cares for each one of us as though he cared for that one alone, and for all as though they were individuals. I, 692. Those who are perverse in heart hold three opinions about God: either that God does not exist, or that God is unjust, or that he does not govern human affairs. IV, 273. God, infused into flesh, did not abandon or lose the care of governing the universe. II, 517. God’s general and particular benefits toward human beings. VII, 220. If God withdraws his effective power from things, they can neither act nor continue to exist. VII, 788. If God were to cease governing things, they would immediately fall apart. III, 304. God administers even the lowest and most contemptible parts of the world. III, 336. By a twofold work of providence God administers the whole of creation. III, 390, 402, 404. God both does and orders certain things, while he merely orders others. III, 229. God’s providence in the governance of things and in the ordering of evils. V, 318, 692. God’s providence is called into doubt or criticized by some because of the happiness of the impious. V, 126, 128, 135, 318. God is upright and is not pleasing to the perverse. V, 322. God does not need the justice of an upright person, much less the wickedness of a perverse one. III, 433. Why God makes rich and poor. V, 523. Music was granted to human beings to indicate the harmony of divine governance. II, 726. God governs all things, and why he does not avenge evils. VI, 661. God makes good use of everything. I, 809. Even of human error. I, 670. The wickedness of sinners. I, 772. And the malice of the devil. III, 219. God knows how to make good use not only of good people but also of evil people. VII, 435. How, and for how long, he allows evil people to prosper and good people to suffer. V, 319. When God made the devil good, he foresaw how he would use him even when he became evil. VII, 332. Faustus said that the God of the Old Testament was improvident, ignorant of the future, envious and fearful, desirous of human blood, jealous, wrathful, a killer of human beings. VIII, 406.

God is one. V, 1073, 1076. There is no true God except one. VI, 387. The one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. V, 1333. What is God? Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. IV, 216. What is to be believed about God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. V, 1072. It is shown from Scripture that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and Lord. II, 1045, 1046. In God there is one essence, three hypostases for the Greeks, and three persons for the Latins. VIII, 917. When the Greeks wish to signify the one true God, they add the article. III, 575.

God is the highest good. VII, 233. The Good that needs no good. I, 845, 868. That God is good is identical with his very being. X, 369. To be good in himself, absolutely and without qualification, is proper to God. IV, 1496, 1740. God is the good of all good things, the good from which all good things come, the good without which nothing is good, and the good that is good without the others. IV, 1742. From the fullness of his goodness creation subsists. I, 845. God is for us the sum and supreme source of all good things. I, 1316. Our good always lives with God; and because we have turned away from it, we have become perverse. I, 706. What kind of good God is is commended by the fact that no one who departs from him is well. III, 432; VIII, 554. God alone is the good by which an intellectual nature becomes blessed. VII, 162, 349. How God is recognized as the highest good. VIII, 949, 950. All creatures bear witness to God’s goodness and greatness. IV, 1865. Cerdon taught that God was not good but just. VIII, 29.

God alone is supremely good, and so is what is from him. VIII, 202. God is good by his own goodness, not by a goodness participated from elsewhere. IV, 1740. God is good in a unique way, while a human being is good from God but evil from himself. II, 658. God alone is good from himself, and from him come all other good things. V, 119, 185, 559. No one possesses anything good unless he has received it from the one who alone is good. IV, 1280, 1670. God is so good by the property of his nature that he cannot be corrupted; creatures are otherwise. X, 1537. God is good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, presiding without position, containing all things without any condition, wholly everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. VIII, 912. God is found in all good things, whether correcting, consoling, testing, crowning, cleansing, or illuminating. IV, 1655. God’s goodness is not to be accused because of the creation of evil things. V, 851. This is that marvelous goodness of God by which he makes good use even of evil angels or human beings. IV, 1398. God is so good that he makes good use even of evil things. II, 539; III, 1619, 1620; X, 1495. From human beings’ very sins he brings about good. II, 727; V, 95. From evils he makes good things. VI, 359. God acts well even by allowing whatever is done badly to be done. VI, 276. God makes good use of the evil works of human beings, just as they misuse the good works of God. IV, 1396, 1397. He rightly uses even the evil wills of souls, when they perversely misuse good natures. III, 431. God makes good use of evil hearts for what he wishes to show or accomplish for the good. III, 601. God acts in hearts so as to bring about the outcome he has determined for events. III, 801. For the benefit of the good, he spares those whom he foresees will become evil. III, 606. God used even the sins of human beings to signify what he wished. III, 815. God is not the author of sins but their ordainer, through the distribution of merits. III, 259. God uses the wickedness of the wicked to exercise the good and admonish them by comparison. II, 860. God gives and foreknows all things; but he foretells sins, threatens punishments, and promises benefits. II, 558. God consoles our sadness over evils by showing that they contribute to the advancement of the saints. II, 1085. God permits evil people to exist only as far as he knows is useful and sufficient for admonishing and exercising his holy household. II, 1085. God knows where to place a sinner, just as a painter knows where to place black color. V, 1382. The whole world is a goldsmith’s furnace: the just are like gold, the impious like chaff, tribulation like fire, and God like the goldsmith. V, 1383.

God is merciful. I, 1333. His sweetness. I, 1315. There is no injustice with God, whether he chooses or rejects; how this is so. VI, 120, 121, 122. When God has mercy on whom he wishes and hardens whom he wishes, he is not unjust. II, 822, 823; VI, 72. Nor is he a respecter of persons. II, 875. God has mercy on whom he wishes, not through justice but through the grace of mercy; and he hardens whom he wishes, not through iniquity but through the truth of retribution. II, 876. How God can still complain when he has mercy on whomever he wishes. II, 880, 888. God complains of sinners justly and mercifully. VI, 121. Whatever a human being may have done, he finds God praiseworthy in his deeds. VI, 332. How great a mercy God has shown toward us, he demonstrates in those toward whom he has not shown it. IV, 704, 707. Why God is called our mercy. IV, 712, 713. How God wills all human beings to be saved. VI, 280. God does not cease inviting to repentance those whom he foreknows will abandon justice or persevere in sins. V, 807. God has mercy on no one in vain. VI, 119. God’s preceding and following mercy. V, 1650. God converts human beings through mercy and truth. III, 604. God’s grace does not wait for human wills to come before it. II, 987. God prepares the will. III, 2061, 2062, *Retractationes*. Not only the instruction of the mouth but also the opening itself belongs to God’s will and grace. III, 598. God does not deceitfully command what he knows the person commanded will not do, so that he may receive a just judgment. III, 600. God does not love to condemn but to save; and God is patient toward evil people so that he may make the evil good. V, 129.

God’s patience toward us. V, 467. God’s patience is useful to some, according to the hearts of human beings, for repentance, but useless to others, who resist God, and so forth. III, 603. God’s patience invites the wicked; his scourge teaches the good patience. VII, 20.

God is not the author of evil. VI, 16. He is not the author of sin. X, 235. Not even of the lightest sin. IV, 1398. He is not defiled by human sins. VIII, 560. God is not the author of guilt in the reprobate. II, 884. God hardens no one except on account of merit. II, 823. He abandons no one unless he is himself abandoned. I, 699, 700, 707. He does not abandon those who live by faith in him and worship him devoutly. II, 525. If God abandons us, what virtue remains to a human being? II, 553. “It is necessary that by the help of whom we conquer, by his not helping us we should again be conquered,” says Innocent. II, 782. When God abandons, he does not abandon when he does not grant temporal goods. II, 563. God sometimes joins very biting medicines to gentle remedies. II, 323.

God’s mercy and severity. III, 1290. He rages mercifully against sinners. I, 676. He also exacts temporal punishment from the elect. III, 775. For God to be with stiff-necked people means that he is present by avenging and punishing. III, 647. God never falls silent regarding a commandment, but for a time he is silent regarding punishment. IV, 952. How God’s mercy and patience will be followed by justice. V, 482. God’s turning away and turning toward. V, 780. The unjust person promises himself much from God’s mercy, so as to make God unjust as well. IV, 728. A sweet father when granting gifts, sweeter when forgiving sins. I, 673. His mercy is necessary even for the saints. I, 778. Who would presume so much upon his conscience as to be certain that it could suffice for him at God’s judgment, unless God judges mercifully those who are merciful? II, 571, 573. If God were judge alone and not merciful, no one could stand before him. IV, 1698, 1700. In God alone we should glory concerning our good works. II, 851, 852. When God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts. II, 880. The harmony of God’s justice and mercy. III, 134. God is just and merciful. V, 151. Neither can mercy take justice away from God, nor justice take mercy away. IV, 505.

God is just. I, 1296; X, 688. Although God cannot be unjust, he is nevertheless not unfree. X, 1116. It is madness to doubt God’s justice. I, 1296. God’s equity may be hidden from you, but injustice cannot be there. V, 179. God is just both when he condemns and when he has mercy. IV, 1922. God is always just, whether rewarding or condemning. VIII, 538. He rewards or condemns free choice. VIII, 540. How God both condemns the impious and justifies the impious is hidden. VIII, 390. How God hates none of the things he made, while hating the reprobate. VI, 122. God hates and loves the unrighteous. X, 1422. God does not demand what he has not given, and he has given everyone what he demands. IV, 575. How God spares no one, neither the just nor the sinner. VIII, 407, 411, 412. Whether through punishments or rewards, God orders all things under the governance of justice. VIII, 159. God is just even when he forgives sins. IV, 1263. God does not leave the sins unpunished even of those whom he forgives. IV, 592. God is truly just when he protects the just in such a way that he himself illuminates them, and orders sinners in such a way that they are punished not by his but by their own wickedness. IV, 108. God was always just, even before there was evil for him to punish. I, 1004. God is just even when he punishes. I, 1241. And innocent. I, 680. God’s severity is exemplified in the cutting off of the Jews, and his goodness in the grafting in of the nations. VIII, 51. God’s severity in inflicting punishments is no greater in the Old Testament than in the New. VIII, 616, 617, 618, 619, 620, 621. Just as goodness is especially commended in the time of love, so God’s severity is especially commended in the time of fear. VIII, 167. In the Law God terrified people with carnal punishments, in the Gospel with spiritual ones. VIII, 620, 622. He rages mercifully, sprinkling forbidden pleasures with bitterness. I, 676. By an inexhaustible law he scatters punitive blindnesses over forbidden desires. I, 674. The sinner, fleeing from the gentle and good God, runs into the just and severe God. I, 706. Amid punitive evils, God grants many good things even to the wicked. VIII, 1026. Both Testaments proclaim God’s mercy and justice. VIII, 138. Why Scripture commends God’s goodness and severity. VIII, 617. God is just even when he does what would be unjust if a human being did it. X, 1256, 1257. Not everything God permits is just. VI, 581, 582. The just God permits unjust things, even in matters pertaining to religious worship, but not with impunity. VI, 582. God orders all things. I, 999, 1001. Even sins. I, 668, 1180, 1285. The just God and the jealous God are not opposed to each other as contraries. VIII, 142.

God’s justice is so called not as that by which he is just, but as that with which he clothes a human being. X, 209, 220, 237, 603. God alone is just and justifies. II, 809. God is the fountain of justice, by which all who are just are just. IV, 744. The fountain of justice, from which no one worthy is barred. V, 1515. The fountain of justice, which cannot approve unjust things. V, 649. Whoever thinks that evil deeds please God does not think of him as God. IV, 614. God is not constrained by necessity so that he cannot sin. X, 1116, 1117. God heals what has been corrupted immediately from guilt, but gradually from weakness. X, 679.

What God’s anger is. VII, 472. God is disturbed by no passion, although he is said to become angry. VII, 261. God becomes angry with tranquility. IV, 690. Disturbance does not befall God. IV, 92, 1415. God’s anger is not a disturbance of the mind but a fixed and just vengeance. II, 860; VIII, 1030. It is also the force by which he avenges most justly. IV, 70. The vengeance for the first sin, and for the sins added to it, is called God’s anger because it comes from God’s judgment. IV, 690. What happens at his left hand is called his anger because it happens through his laws. IV, 92. The anger by which God punishes is not in him but in the souls of his ministers. IV, 105. God’s anger can be understood as the very obscuring of the mind that follows those who transgress God’s law. IV, 70. God’s anger is the movement that occurs in the soul that knows God’s law when it sees that same law being disregarded by a sinner. IV, 70. God avenges both in anger and in favor. X, 166. God is gentle in his anger. V, 166. God’s fatherly anger: through tribulations he becomes angry and leads onward; he rages and saves; he terrifies and calls. IV, 655. God sometimes grants temporal goods and sometimes usefully withdraws them. II, 575. God brings evils upon the wicked—not sins, but punishments. II, 558. God’s greatest anger is that by which the sinner does not suffer what he keenly hates but does what he shamefully desires. VIII, 635. God’s anger is greater against the sinner whose sins lack an avenger and have a praiser. IV, 126. God is very angry when he does not inquire, when he seems to forget and pay no attention to sins, and when people reach wealth and honors through frauds and crimes. IV, 126. See *Anger*. God then punishes most severely when he leaves sins unpunished; he opposes mercifully when he makes abundant lusts destitute. II, 531. In this age God lavishes good things upon the faithless and the despairing. II, 957.

What God’s hatred is. IV, 85. God loves in the sinner what belongs to nature and hates what belongs to guilt. IV, 504. God is sometimes said to abominate, not for destruction but for discipline. IV, 1415.

How God’s derision and mockery are to be understood. IV, 70.

In what sense God is said to repent. VII, 418, 472, 539. Plato said that God was lifted up with joy by the perfected universe. VII, 334. What God’s repentance, anger, mercy, jealousy, and forgetfulness are. VIII, 141, 147, 148, 410, 412, 627, 628, 629, 661.

The deity as the unity of the Trinity. VIII, 829. The unity of the Godhead and the distribution of the persons. V, 309. How the Trinity exists within God’s very simplicity. VIII, 1063. God is Trinity, but not triplex. VIII, 929. The unity of the Godhead and the plurality of the persons are intimated in the creation of the human being. III, 291. Many believe the nature of God in the Trinity, but few understand it. III, 356. There are not several gods, but one God of one substance. IV, 844. Whatever is said substantially of God is said individually of each person and simultaneously of the Trinity itself. VIII, 916, 917. What belongs absolutely to God as essence is said of the Trinity in the singular, not the plural. VIII, 918. What is said of God in relation to time is said relatively, not accidentally. VIII, 922. And without any change in him. VIII, 922. What God begot is equal to him, unlike what he made. VIII, 190, 546, 547, 548, 551, 579, 584, 585. It is impious to say that God is mutable and begot a mutable offspring. VIII, 585. God the Trinity is the reality to be enjoyed. III, 21. God is one in three persons. VI, 189. Some believe that the very communion, or deity, of the Father and Son, and the love of each for the other, and the charity of both, is the Holy Spirit. VI, 191. Christ may rightly be called the crucified God. II, 746.

God makes himself our debtor, not by receiving but by promising. I, 714; IV, 1068. God becomes a debtor because he has become a giver. IV, 1283. God is an able promiser and a faithful fulfiller. IV, 433, 434.

What God’s oath is. VII, 511. God’s oath is a confirmation of his promise. IV, 1122.

We have God himself as God, Lord, and Father. VIII, 216. He is properly called the God of those who love him. IV, 657, 1809. God belongs to all, and is not divided among all his own people, but is possessed wholly by each. V, 315. God does not belong to all in the same way: he is more ours, since we live from him. IV, 294. God is properly called the God of one whom he has more familiarly, as among his slaves and household property. IV, 575. We carry the title of God in our hearts. V, 163. How the things that belong to God become ours. V, 909. God protects us because he is God, so that we may not die; he rules us because he is king, so that we may not fall. IV, 542. God is my supporter, lest I fall; my deliverer, lest I remain trapped; my protector, lest I be struck. IV, 1862. God is our refuge. V, 377. Things contrary to us must be diligently avoided even when God is most manifestly our helper. III, 614.

God is called Lord in relation to time. VIII, 922. From what time he began to be called Lord. III, 382. Augustine does not dare say that God was always Lord. VII, 363, 365. All things, whether miserable or happy, need the Lord. IV, 287. God is our supreme usefulness and salvation. III, 382.

God is our Father. V, 409. How he is Father of Christ and of human beings. III, 1565. It is one thing when God is commended to you because he is God, another because he is Father. III, 1546. What God demands from us—that he be our Father—is a matter of mercy. III, 1276. God can become our Father at no cost, but solely through a good will. III, 1276. Some are called children of God according to predestination, not according to regeneration. II, 846. God’s children do not cease to be children of the world during the present life. X, 590. God was not called Father by the Jews, but Lord. III, 1275. Porphyry praised God in such a way that he called him both God the Father and king. VII, 793.

God is to be praised with the heart and with love. V, 1643. God is to be praised in prosperity and adversity. IV, 309, 1794.

To worship God is the proper duty of justice. X, 283. We are commanded to love and worship one God. III, 70; VII, 646. Varro taught that only one God should be worshiped. VII, 138. This is also proved by the fact that his gifts are counted among the gods. VII, 132. The pagans did the greatest wrong to the true God by worshiping him together with false gods. VII, 134. By wishing to have God together with many others, idolaters more easily brought it about that they did not have him than that they mixed him with many or false gods. II, 842. The pagan deities dread God. VII, 754, 793. The labor of upright rulers in securing peace for peoples is useless for the blessed life unless they take care that this very peace be referred to the worship of God. II, 671. The God of the Hebrews alone is to be worshiped; by enjoying him alone, his worshiper is blessed, and conversely. VIII, 371; VII, 141.

God is to be worshiped gratuitously and with chaste love. IV, 626, 658, 660, 661, 928, 1028, 1402, 1404; V, 29. See *Worship*. When we glorify God, it benefits us, not him. IV, 436. It is of great benefit to a human being to serve God. III, 384. God is to be worshiped not only for eternal but also for temporal benefits. VII, 202. Socrates said that each person ought to worship God in whatever way God himself commanded him to be worshiped. III, 1053. To worship the true God with disgraceful and criminal worship is sacrilegious. VII, 217.

Sacrifice must be offered to the true God alone. VII, 654. We must serve that God with sacrifices of whom we ourselves ought to be a sacrifice. VII, 295. The Jews worshiped God through a rite signifying future things. VIII, 290. It is sacrilegious for a Christian to place an image in a temple for God. VI, 188. The worship of *latria* is owed to God alone. II, 749. To God is owed λατρεία (*latreia*) as God, and δουλεία (*douleia*) as Lord. III, 631. God cannot be served with perfect servitude. III, 790. With what conduct God is to be worshiped. VII, 653. God is worshiped through charity. II, 737. Through faith, hope, and charity. II, 282. What benefit comes from believing in God with right faith, worshiping him, and knowing him. VI, 223. God walks in us through the presence of his majesty if he finds breadth of charity. V, 889. The worship of God consists above all in the soul’s not being ungrateful to him. X, 210. God is worshiped solely through the piety of obedience. X, 172, 210. How God’s name is sanctified. III, 1278. It is possible that the same one God is worshiped even outside the Church. IX, 463.

God is to be loved above all and alone, because nothing is better than he. II, 672. Since God is unchangeable wisdom, he is to be preferred to all things. III, 22. God is to be loved more than every human being, indeed more than oneself. III, 29. Nothing given by God is to be preferred to God himself. V, 29. How God is to be tasted. III, 1562. How he is to be loved as money is loved. VI, 675. God is not to be loved for the sake of a reward. III, 1405. One clings to God more closely the less one loves what is one’s own. VIII, 1006. God is not loved as much before he is seen as he will be loved when he is seen. X, 603. God works all things together for good for those who love him. X, 931. For which people who love God do all things work together for good? X, 929. Love God: whatever you love comes from him. V, 1204. How God is called charity. VIII, 1080. God himself is the life-giving delight of the pure heart. I, 857. God becomes for a human being the whole of those things that the human being loves. III, 1495. We should desire and strive that all people love God. III, 30. The commandment was given concerning the love of God and neighbor, indeed also of oneself. III, 29. Why the commandment to love God is distinguished from the love of neighbor. III, 33. God commands nothing that benefits him, but what benefits the one to whom he gives the command. II, 527. God can never be loved wrongly. VII, 467.

God is both loved profitably and feared. VIII, 617. How God is lovable and dreadful. IV, 1874. God alone cannot be feared without love. VI, 25. What must be done in order that he may be feared. VI, 25.

God is always to be sought in this life. III, 1804. Both the appearance of all things and some inner awareness—I do not know what—urge us to seek God and serve God. VIII, 89. God is to be sought so that he may be found; he is to be sought even when found. III, 1804. Once found through faith, in what way he is always to be sought. IV, 1391. Where and how God is to be sought. VIII, 957. He is to be sought chastely. V, 759. God is sought through Scripture and through creation. VIII, 845. After death we shall not become more capable of finding God. III, 1804. Inquiry concerning God purifies; imitation deifies the affection. VII, 653. The action of the right path is that which looks toward the glory of God. II, 189. What kind of action this is. II, 189. God considers our benefit more than our will. IV, 277.

God is witness and judge. III, 1669. God wished human beings to have witnesses, so that human beings might also have God as witness. III, 1979. God judges not words but hearts. III, 726. What it means for us to come to God and for God to come to us. VIII, 704. We move toward God, who is present everywhere, not in places but through good conduct. III, 23, 25. Not by bodily movement but by the will of the heart. III, 1608. Not with feet but with conduct. II, 672. God is inaccessible to our powers, but he is approached through his gifts. IV, 1515. With God, the one who brings more has more standing—not silver, but faith. V, 316. What it means for a human being to be with God and for God to be with a human being. VIII, 1018. We become more like God the more we advance in his knowledge and love. II, 319. How the blessed approach God, since he is inaccessible. VIII, 539. One departs from God not through distances of place but through an aversion of the will. III, 383. Not with feet but with the heart. IX, 62. If a human being does not make himself fall away from God, God never makes himself depart from the human being. III, 1654. No one will take God away from you; you take him away from yourself if you flee from him. IV, 1249. If one does not wish to have the Lord his God, where will he flee from the God of all? IV, 1809. A human being draws near to God by living piously and withdraws from him by sinning. II, 838. He draws near through likeness and withdraws through unlikeness. VII, 271; VIII, 946. The more desirous the soul is of temporal things, the more unlike God it becomes. VII, 271. God’s likeness in us. V, 361. God’s likeness is sought even in sins. VIII, 991. Turned away from the image of God. VIII, 1005. How this happens. VIII, 1006. Only sins separate God and human beings. X, 123.

Those who oppose God’s rule, not by nature but by vices, are called God’s enemies. VII, 350. What it means to be an enemy of God. VI, 65. Who are understood to have embittered God. IV, 88, 89. Many do evil because they think they are not seen by God. V, 441. How one can forget and remember God. VIII, 1049. Whoever despises divine things must necessarily judge human things otherwise than he ought. II, 1072. Without grace the soul does not return to God. VIII, 1007. Only humility and piety receive God as favorable and saving. III, 646. It is no wonder if people malign God’s servants, since they do not cease blaspheming God himself every day. II, 266. God’s benefits toward the sinner. IV, 371.

God is high, and is reached by the humble. IV, 947, 1205. God is so most high that our misery and our groaning are not far from him. IV, 665. Whoever understands God is joined to God. VI, 38. Whoever begins to think worthily about God will find silence to be praised with the ineffable voice of the heart. V, 1498. The knowledge of God sometimes shines through for wise men when they have withdrawn from the body. VII, 270. A human being does not touch God unless he has passed beyond the soul. III, 1562. The more freely the mind stretches toward heavenly and eternal things, the fuller it becomes of God. III, 619. A mind too intent on human actions is, in a certain sense, emptied of God. III, 619.

God himself, the promiser, is the end of our desire; he will give himself immortal to immortals because he gave himself mortal to mortals. IV, 477. God is the end of every desire. VII, 280. He himself is our reward. IV, 575. He is our inheritance and possession. IV, 294. How God is the inheritance of human beings. III, 1394. God is the land that the meek will inherit. III, 1232. God both possesses and is possessed, and all this for our sake, so that we may be blessed. IV, 295. Above all the things God gives to good and evil alike, he preserves himself for the good. IV, 918, 1028. What will he give to one who loves him, except himself? IV, 1840. God is sought from himself; he promises himself. III, 1655. God would not satisfy me completely unless he promised me himself as God. V, 865. God is sufficient for us; without God nothing is sufficient. V, 492, 865, 958. Whatever is present to us apart from God is not sweet. IV, 1090. For the blessed, God will be whatever we desire here as something great. V, 1189, 1190. No one readily dares say “my God” except one who believes in him and loves him. V, 315.

Nothing is better than clinging to God. IV, 928. Whoever clings to what is higher tramples on what is lower; but if he withdraws from what is higher, these lower things are turned into punishment for him. IV, 1887. God is not to be used but enjoyed. VI, 20. To enjoy God is to live blessedly. III, 30. The soul has no rest except in God. I, 661, 699; II, 213. When will God be all in all? VIII, 708. In God our being will have no death, our knowing no error, and our loving no offense. VII, 342. Envy no one God; you will all possess him wholly, each individually. IV, 929.

God is the light of the soul. III, 479; V, 36. Our morning light. III, 1532. The higher light by which the mind is illuminated. III, 1517. God is to the soul what light and air are to the body. IV, 893. God is light, fragrance, and food to the heart. V, 183. God is bread, water, and light to a human being. III, 1495. The light of minds for learning all things. VII, 232.

God is the fountain of life. III, 131. The life of souls and the life of lives. I, 687. To dwell in God is to live. I, 870. By indwelling, God contains; he is not contained. V, 1502.

The true God is the one whom Christians serve. VII, 650. It is demonstrated that the God of Israel is the true God. III, 1054, 1060. The God of Israel is neither Jupiter nor Saturn. III, 1061. Those who reject the God of Israel do not worship all gods; nor does the one who worships others worship him. III, 1059. Nothing was foretold against the God of the Hebrews by the pagan prophets. III, 1055. Why God wished to be called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. III, 1479, 1486; VIII, 454. The God of the Law and the Prophets is not to be accused of cruelty. VIII, 618. God is not impure because he foretold shameful punishments to the impious. VIII, 633.

How God is the God of gods. VII, 317. Created gods are gods by participation in the true God, not by their own truth. VII, 422.

Who is the God of the Manichaeans? III, 165. How unworthy are the Manichaeans’ thoughts about God. VIII, 381. The Manichaeans’ errors concerning the nature of God. VIII, 92. They admitted one good principle and another evil one. I, 1317. It is shown that the Manichaeans admit two gods. VIII, 389, 390. It is unnecessary to invent two gods, one good because of the benefits of gifts, the other evil because of the judgments of punishments. VIII, 389, 394. The battle of God with the race of darkness, a fiction of the Manichaeans. VIII, 398, 400, 533, 534, 536, 585, 595; X, 1071. The Manichaeans’ error in supposing that God feared for himself and his kingdoms from the race of darkness. VIII, 333, 566, 595. The Manichaeans’ invention concerning the mingling of part of God’s nature with a contrary and rebellious nature. VIII, 214, 414. The error of the Manichaeans in holding that part of God’s nature had been mingled with and polluted by the nature of demons and had to be bound, defiled, and so forth. VIII, 536, 537, 539, 544, 545, 565, 595. The Manichaeans say that God’s nature was first corrupted by necessity and afterward irredeemably by will. III, 436. The Manichaeans maintain that God’s very substance was partly corrupted by the substance of evil and brought into a necessity of sinning. II, 724. God’s substance, according to the Manichaeans, is corruptible. VIII, 113, 248; X, 1325, 1328. God is incorruptible; the race of darkness could not harm him. VIII, 534, 535, 536, 539, 547, 548, 596. How, according to the Manichaeans, the part of God’s nature mingled with and polluted by the nature of demons is purified. VIII, 540, 544, 551, 567, 569, 570, 571, 585. The Manichaeans preached that God’s part is bound, oppressed, and defiled in all conceptions, and that afterward it cannot be liberated in its entirety. VIII, [Col. 0231] 218, 222, 229. The Manichaeans thought that the members of their god were bound in foods and were restored and liberated by belching and eating. VIII, 230, 231, 232, 284, 294, 320, 597. Especially in the Elect. VIII, 35. The Manichaeans maintained that the substance of their god was not only defiled but could not be recovered and gathered back from every part. VIII, 233. The Manichaeans’ god mingles his own part wretchedly, purifies it disgracefully, and condemns it cruelly. VIII, 540, 546, 566, 595, 596, 597. The mourning of God, according to the Manichaeans, until his members are purified. VIII, 214. The Manichaeans teach that the God of the Law and the Prophets is not the true God. VIII, 37. The things that the Manichaeans confess about their god are more absurd than the things they criticize in the Old Testament as supposedly unworthy of God. VIII, 413, 1414. The Manichaeans’ god is worse than human beings. VIII, 416. In what respect Catholics and Manichaeans agree concerning the nature of God, and in what respect they disagree. X, 1468. Someone dared to blaspheme the God of Israel as not only a demon but worse than the other demons. VIII, 640. Some said that the soul of the world is God. VII, 123. Some said that only rational animals are parts of God. VII, 123. They are refuted. VII, 123. To what extent Apelles admits two gods. VIII, 29. Cerdon. VIII, 29. The nations had not fallen into false gods to such a degree that they abandoned belief in one true God. VIII, 383. Christians do not derive their belief in the monarchy of God from the nations. VIII, 383. How correctly certain pagans thought about God. IX, 224. Pagan writers could not remain silent about God. VIII, 290. The gods of the pagans never dared to predict or say anything against the God of Israel. VI, 589. Their most learned authors sought more to discover who God was than they were able to deny God. VI, 589. It is proved that he alone is the true God and alone is to be worshiped. VI, 589, 654. The Prophets had foretold that the worship of demons would yield to his worship. VI, 654. What was foretold is fulfilled daily. VI, 591, 592. God is terrifying to the gods of the nations, who are demons, but beloved by the gods whom he made his sons. IV, 566.

“Praise be to God” (*Deo laudes*), the Circumcellions’ formula of greeting. IV, 1732; IX, 306, 318. “Thanks be to God” (*Deo gratias*), the customary form of greeting among monks. IV, 1732. Unjustly criticized by heretics. IV, 1732. “Thanks be to God”: we hold nothing better in mind, express nothing better with our mouth, and set nothing better down with our pen. II, 158.

The pagans believed that many gods had to be reconciled to human affairs. VII, 645. Mad desire itself boils over into many divine powers. VII, 211. Philosophers held differing opinions about the nature of the gods. III, 123. Varro’s opinions about the gods are ambiguous. VII, 208. By what reasoning Varro discovered the multitude of the gods. VII, 189. Varro rejected the popular belief concerning the gods. VII, 137. The sharpest intellects suffer constriction when interpreting the stories of the gods. VII, 209. More intelligent and weightier Romans understood the things proclaimed about the gods to be vain. VII, 136. In matters concerning the nature of the gods, it belongs to humanity to form opinions and to God to know. VII, 208. Maximus writes that there is one supreme God, but that his powers, diffused through the work of the world, are invoked under many names. II, 81. Augustine ridicules him for this. II, 83.

Some gods are natural, others instituted by human beings. VII, 183. To call the gods of the nations certain members of the one great God is sacrilegious wit. II, 83. Whether the gods are, as it were, powers, members, or parts of Jupiter. VII, 123. They attempt in vain to refer all the gods to the world. VII, 218. Whatever the natural philosophers referred to the world and its parts must be referred to the true God. VII, 219. One must not invent as many gods as there are works in the world of the true God. VII, 219. Those who think human works are gods are more deeply sunk than those who think God’s works are gods. III, 70. The pagans sometimes make several things one god, and sometimes one thing several gods. VII, 207.

According to the pagans, all gods are of one substance, although they have different duties, works, and powers. VIII, 376. Heraclitus believed that the gods are from fire, Pythagoras from numbers, and Epicurus from atoms. VII, 181. Anaximenes held that they are from air. VII, 226. Plato thought they were made by one God. VII, 175. According to Plato, the gods are animals. VII, 241. By their nature they are not immortal, but they are immortal by the will of God. VII, 794. The gods made by the supreme God possess immortal bodies. VII, 388, 390. According to Plato, they are enclosed in heavenly bodies. VII, 794. According to Plato, it is a great benefit for the gods made by the supreme God to possess immortal bodies. VII, 390. This is refuted. VII, 388. According to Plato, God promised the gods eternal permanence in heavenly bodies. VII, 794. Trismegistus says that some gods were made by the supreme God and others by human beings. VII, 247. Error in making gods. VII, 250. It is said that gods are made by human beings when invisible spirits are joined to images by a certain art. VII, 247, 250, 251. Unbelief is the cause of this error. VII, 250. For the gods, a demon serves as soul and an image as body. VII, 254.

The gods are unclean spirits. VII, 221. Most deceitful demons. VII, 111. Those who fashioned gods for themselves were possessed by demons. VII, 251. The gods are more rarely called by the name “demons.” VII, 255. Apuleius carefully distinguishes the gods from demons. VII, 239. It is absurd to assert that the gods are more readily mixed with demons than with human beings. VII, 315. It is a false Platonic saying that no god is mixed with a human being or contaminated by such contact. VII, 269. It is absurd to say that the gods need demons as messengers and interpreters. VII, 245. From what point the gods of the nations began to be named in Scripture. III, 572.

The gods of the pagans were human beings. V, 1349. Euhemerus wrote that the gods had once been human beings. VII, 184. Maro and Tullius thought so. II, 84. Cicero admits it. III, 1056. Leon, an Egyptian priest, declares it and disclosed it to Alexander. III, 1056, 1057; VII, 229. And this is more credible. VII, 208, 217, 253, 254. Several dead people were transferred into the number of the gods through the vain superstition of the Greeks. VII, 565. In the time of the Caesars, no one was enrolled among the gods through error, but through flattery. VII, 581. It is easier for a human being to cease to be human than for those whom a human being made to be able to be gods. VII, 250. The gods differ from human beings in place, eternity, and blessedness. VII, 266. Varro said that it was useful for the gods to pretend that they had been begotten as human beings. VII, 81.

The distinction among the gods according to Labeo. VII, 105. Some gods are celibate, others joined in marriage, and so forth. VII, 191. Plato assigns male gods to heaven and female gods to earth, and afterward confuses them. VII, 218. Certain and uncertain gods. VII, 87. Three classes of gods. VII, 133. Three orders. VII, 58, note (c). The selected gods. VII, 130, 193, 194. There is no rational basis for the selection of the gods. VII, 195. Why the selected gods are so called. VII, 196. The selected gods are distinguished by the nobility of their crimes, not by the dignity of their virtues. VII, 221. The selected gods are more associated with injuries than with honors. VII, 197. The selected gods became more widely known because of their disgraceful acts than the others did. VII, 217. There is scarcely one of the selected gods who is not disgraced; among the lower gods, scarcely one who is disgraced. VII, 198. They wish the selected gods to be this world. VII, 207.

Some have thought that the gods are both good and evil. VII, 255. Apuleius wanted all the gods to be believed good and blessed. VII, 263. Some have thought that the gods are good only. VII, 247, 255. Plato held this opinion as well. VII, 126, 237. The Platonists perhaps called the good gods holy Angels. VII, 275, 276. We call the good gods holy Angels. VII, 252. Why Plato deprived only the evil gods, or demons, of the pleasure of theatrical spectacles. VII, 239.

Porphyry subjected the higher gods to disturbances. VII, 304, 305. He also asserts that, through theurgy, they are subjected to them. VII, 288. Apuleius distinguished them from the stain of disturbances. VII, 304. The Stoics distinguished them likewise. VII, 262, 263. Why. VII, 242. Porphyry said that the gods could be bound by incantations. VII, 304, 305. The Stoics hold that the struggles of conflicting desires belong to demons, not to gods. VII, 262. Discord among the gods. VII, 188. Varro wanted quarrels and lawsuits to be foreign to the gods. VII, 567.

The worship of the gods, an institution of demons. VII, 179, 187. The demons carry out their business so as to be regarded and worshiped as gods. VII, 72. Although later times did not establish dead human beings as gods, they nevertheless did not cease to worship those who had been established as gods. VII, 581. The pagans omitted many things by which they could have conferred divine honors. VII, 127. The Platonists judged that several gods should be worshiped. VII, 277. Porphyry admitted the worship of the gods contrary to what he understood. VII, 303, 304. Porphyry said that sacrifices should be offered to good and evil gods; Plato, only to the good. VII, 237. It is shown that the gods should not be worshiped merely because they were made. VII, 251. The Manichaeans worshiped a multitude of gods. VIII, 142, 307, 308, 321. The good gods whom the Platonists call gods do not wish to be worshiped in place of God. VII, 281, 284. Why it is impious to worship the gods. VII, 217. The worship of many gods is fornication. VII, 303. Scripture often and properly calls it so. III, 70. False gods do not forbid others to be worshiped along with them. III, 1058. A Christian must not use anything in honor of foreign gods, even if he despises them inwardly, lest he who cannot see the mind be led by him to honor such things. II, 185.

The worship of false gods itself took various forms. II, 373, 375. Varro vainly boasts that he imparted to the Romans knowledge of the gods who should be worshiped. VII, 122. Labeo believes that evil gods are appeased by bloody victims and gloomy supplications, and good gods by games and pleasant services. VII, 56, 237. The appeasement of the gods through the obscenities of the games is more harmful to their names than their anger would have been. VII, 76. Plato deprived only the evil gods, or demons, of the pleasure of theatrical games. VII, 238. With what evil disposition the gods ordered theatrical games to be exhibited for them. VII, 75. The gods are unworthily worshiped by honorable people when they are appeased by shameful acts. VII, 78. The gods are thereby proved obscene, because they ordered obscene games to be exhibited for them. VII, 53. For this reason they ought to have appeared unworthy of divine honor to the Romans. VII, 57, 58. Fictitious crimes were shamefully enacted in the games as service to the gods. VII, 582. The disgraceful acts of the gods, which are even presented for viewing in the theaters. II, 533. The false gods delight in the evil morals of their worshipers. V, 1025. The gods are thereby proved false, because they delight in their own crimes, whether real or fictitious. VII, 78, 111. The gods took no care to prevent evils of character from befalling their worshipers. VII, 60, 74, 79. They never gave their worshipers any commands concerning uprightness. VII, 49, 51. They never gave the Romans any commands against luxury and greed. VII, 64, 69. Laws for establishing good morals or correcting bad ones are not to be expected from gods who took care to sow and increase disgraceful behavior. VII, 59, 74. It is shown that the gods were present to fulfill desires, but did not preside over restraining them. VII, 70.

The gods are spectators and supporters of crimes. VII, 92. They testify that they are authors of a wicked and impure life. VII, 74. The gods are authors and teachers of sins, not avengers. VII, 81. The gods are not to be approved because they punished crimes in some people but did not avenge them in others. VII, 82. The gods, as though offering divine authority for committing crimes, demand theatrical games. VII, 111. Even pagan philosophers themselves prove that, through imitation of the false gods, the most wicked people become worse. II, 315. For nothing makes human beings so unsociable. II, 314. The examples of the gods move people more than the precepts of philosophers. VII, 52, 53.

The Romans vainly attribute the causes of their misfortunes to the destruction of the gods. VII, 101. The gods cannot be said to have established, increased, or preserved the Roman Empire; why. VII, 119, 135. Nor did they grant peace to the Roman Empire. VII, 84, 85. The pagans thought that, because the worship of the gods had been forbidden, disasters were inflicted on the human race. VII, 29. The gods are worshiped in vain for the advantages of this temporal life. VII, 173, 174, 316. The pagans are compelled to admit this. VII, 29. It is also shown by examples. VII, 29. The variations of temporal affairs do not depend on the favor or anger of the gods. VII, 70. It follows that the gods are either worshiped needlessly or are unjust. VII, 70. They did not avert carnal evils from their own worshipers. VII, 79. By deceiving and misleading their worshipers they harmed them, rather than helped them. VII, 113. The functions of the gods accord more with comic buffoonery than with divine dignity. VII, 187. The gods are worshiped in vain for the sake of eternal life. VII, 175, 183, 187, 193, 256. There is no help from the gods for the kingdoms in which they are worshiped. VII, 117. Nor for the cities entrusted to them. VII, 83. It is absurd to ask one god for what is under the protection of another. VII, 175, 176. When virtue and happiness are present, the innumerable crowd of gods and goddesses is unnecessary. VII, 128, 129, 130. The gods of the pagans are dead gods. IX, 65. They are compared to barley bread. III, 802. The temples of the gods are poorly protected as places of asylum for those who flee to them. VII, 15, 17, 18.

The Romans worshiped the gods without images for more than 170 years. VII, 138, note (b). At what time images of the gods were established. VII, 581. For what purpose they were devised. VII, 198. Varro taught that the Romans worshiped the gods more chastely without images. VII, 198. The temples of the gods were overturned and their images broken at Carthage. VII, 620. Alexandria lost its gods. V, 624. Golden gods and wooden gods differ in price but are equal in having eyes and not seeing. V, 624. The temples, idols, and sacred groves of false gods can be converted to common use or to the honor of the true God. II, 185. It is useless to recite in the temples salutary interpretations of what was written in ancient times about the life and morals of the gods. II, 315.

The various names of the gods. II, 84. What nonsense the pagans have uttered about Saturn and Jupiter. III, 1056. The gods who are Jupiter’s parasites. VII, 184. The *Dii Manes*. VII, 253. Only through the Christian religion could the gods’ deception be exposed. VII, 221. The gods of the pagans are not to be compared with the Martyrs. V, 1250.

The name “gods” is common to Angels and human beings. VII, 275. Whether Angels should be called gods. IV, 1757. Human beings called gods. IV, 1248, 1776. Human beings are gods not through their own merits but through God’s grace. IV, 1048. Human beings are gods by participation, not by nature. IV, 1221, 1545. Human beings are deified by grace, not born from the divine substance. IV, 565.

Deogratias the Deacon. VI, 309. He reported to Augustine the pious fervor of Restitutus. II, 1065.

Deuterius, a Donatist bishop. IX, 691.

Deuterius of Macriana, a Donatist bishop. II, 342.

Deuterius, metropolitan of Caesarea. IX, 697, 700.

Deuterius, a bishop. II, 1033.

The *Deuterosis* of the Jews, their traditions. VIII, 637, 642.

The right hand is used in praise. III, 769. The right hand is named in connection with all good things. III, 493. The right hand of God. V, 1062, 1070. The right hand of the Father, power. VI, 646, 658. Blessedness. VI, 304, 646. The right hand signifies what is more precious. III, 1259, 1261. What someone places first. IV, 1435. The right and left signify blessedness and misery. VIII, 597. Our right hand is eternal life; the left, temporal life. IV, 1770. Salvation in the right hand is eternal salvation; salvation in the left is temporal salvation. IV, 1782. The right hand is spiritual charity; the left, carnal desire. V, 806. The right hand signifies prosperity. III, 493. Those who place blessedness in temporal things make the right what is left. IV, 1770. One sits at the right hand in the more honorable place. [Col. 0234] VIII, 792. What it means to go to the right or left after foreign gods. III, 770. What the right hand of iniquity signifies. III, 770; V, 204.

The Devil is called *accusator*—“accuser”—in Latin. III, 741. The Manichaeans thought that the Devil has a father. III, 1704. They do not wish him to be counted among God’s creatures. III, 436. They are pressed by the argument. III, 436. Some have thought that the Devil was not among the number of the heavenly Angels but of the worldly ones. III, 438. The Devil is from the same source as the other Angels. III, 1703. The Devil is the prince of the angels who fell. X, 932. How he was in the midst of the Angels. V, 103. The Devil is king of demons, as the basilisk is king of serpents. IV, 1168. The Devil became a devil from being a good Angel. I, 1308. He was once a good Angel. IX, 162. He enjoyed the One who is supreme. III, 133. He rejoiced in sublime truth. III, 209. He was in the truth, but did not remain there. X, 922. In what sense it is said that the Devil did not stand in the truth. VII, 330.

The origin of the Devil’s fall. VIII, 615. Some say that the Devil fell because he envied the human being made in the image of God. III, 436. By loving himself more than God, he refused to be subject to him, swelled with pride, and defected from the supreme essence. III, 133. The Devil became a devil from an angel when he wished to be his own self and to rule himself. IV, 1623. And because he took more pleasure in himself than in the One by participation in whom he was blessed. III, 313. The Devil is proud. VII, 419. The Devil fell from what he was going to receive, not from what he had received. III, 441. Various opinions about the Devil’s creation and fall. III, 443. The Devil is superior by nature to all beasts. III, 431. Some thought that the Devil was created in wickedness. III, 439. They are refuted. III, 439, 441. The Devil was not always evil. VII, 330. The Devil was created good and upright. X, 670. The Devil is the author of vices: good by nature, evil through vice. X, 1537. The Devil was made good by God. X, 734. The source of the Devil’s evil. VIII, 592. The Manichaean heresy that the Devil has a certain proper nature of evil, as though from an opposing principle. VII, 329. The Devil’s nature, insofar as it is nature, is not evil. VII, 641. The Devil, insofar as he is an angel, is not evil, but insofar as he is perverse through his own will, he is evil. III, 133. The Devil was not blessed before sin. III, 436, 438, 441. The Devil was never blessed if the Angels know what they are and foresee what they will later become. II, 248. Some said that the impious would see God and that God had been seen by the Devil. II, 602. They are refuted. II, 607, 608. He fell from the sublime dwelling of heaven and from the company of the higher Angels, and with his angels was condemned to this air as to a prison. IV, 1220, 1382, 1385, 1913. He has his seat in the North. IV, 1127. The Devil’s body is aerial. III, 436. The Devil’s present condition is explained by comparison. IV, 1385. The statement, “How you have fallen from heaven,” etc. (Isaiah 14:12), is to be understood of the Devil’s mystical body. III, 441. Likewise the statement, “You are the seal,” etc. (Ezekiel 28:12). III, 442. Where the Devil and his angels dwell among the heavenly beings. V, 1090. The Devil’s body is called “the Devil.” III, 442. The Devil fell at the beginning of time. III, 437. The Devil is a devil through two evils, pride and envy. VI, 413. The Devil fell through pride alone and is therefore to be punished for that alone. IV, 709. From defect came need, and from need envy, by which the Devil is a devil. III, 133. The Devil envied the human being who stood, because he himself had fallen. VII, 419. The Devil is the human being’s adversary because of envy. IV, 709, 1245, 1623; VIII, 592.

The Devil was not permitted to tempt the woman except through the serpent. III, 431. Nor the man except through the woman. III, 443. Why the Devil chose the serpent to tempt Eve. VII, 419. The Devil spoke in the serpent, not in the woman. III, 443. The Devil was cursed in the serpent. X, 1576. How the Devil heard the voice of God. V, 102. And how he came into God’s presence. V, 101, 103. The Devil was a murderer from the beginning. III, 1703; IX, 266. How. III, 437. The Devil was truly the first sinner. V, 1344, 1345. In what sense it is said that the Devil sinned from the beginning. VII, 330. A perpetual will to sin holds him. I, 1278. The Devil has no free choice for doing good, but his will has been hardened toward the greatest malevolence by the punishment of his crime. II, 982.

The Devil is the father of unbelievers, not by creating them, but because they are his sons by imitating him. IV, 501; V, 1552. Who are the Devil’s sons. IX, 266. Imitators of the Devil are sons of the Devil. III, 2011, 2023. Through the Devil, sin entered the world, so that sinners might imitate it. X, 1162, 1163. The sons of the Devil are one thing, the sons of the world another. X, 589. Not every sin makes people sons of the Devil. X, 589. Unbelief makes sons of the Devil. X, 589, 590. The Devil works his evil works in the sons of distrust: distrust and unbelief. II, 982. The Devil is called the ancient sinner, the one appointed over death, and the prince of this world, that is, of all sinners. I, 748, 1286. The persuader to evil works, the exactor of punishment. IV, 1850. The Devil is the prince and king of vices. VI, 357. The Devil and his angels are the rulers of the world. V, 1090. Through sin the Devil is the prince of this world. III, 1872. Of what world he is prince. X, 1546. In what sense “prince.” [Col. 0235] III, 1173, 1838; VI, 291. The prince of the world, that is, of the wicked, who dwell in their hearts only in this world. IV, 209, 1841; V, 790. The prince of sin, and therefore the prince of this age. V, 100, 435. The Devil is the head of evils. IV, 1807. Our captor. V, 726. He held us only by the bonds of sins. V, 726. The origin of the Devil’s dominion over humanity. I, 1285. Those who belong to the Devil’s kingdom. V, 447. All sinners are subject to the Devil as their prince. X, 429. Whether a human being can be subjected to the Devil through sin. X, 862, 863. All are subject to the Devil because of Adam’s sin. X, 444. They were handed over to his power not by God’s command but by his permission. VIII, 1026. If they are not reborn in Christ. X, 455. God does not create for the Devil those whom he knows will be born under sin. X, 454. Through vice, the human being is under the Devil. X, 1269. The Devil’s punishment is to have sinners in his power. III, 209. The Devil was heard according to his own will, but for condemnation. IV, 173. The sinner was given as food to the Devil. VI, 291. See “Demons.” All were handed over to the Devil’s power because of Adam’s sin, yet they are not outside the law of God’s power. VIII, 1026. The Devil himself is not outside the power of the Almighty, just as he is not outside his goodness. VIII, 1026. Neither the sinful human being nor the Devil is removed from God’s power. X, 705, 719, 837. Those alone are not possessed by the Devil whom Christ’s grace liberates. X, 1107. The Devil received power over the lowest things and lost the highest and supreme things; and this power is not the power of one who is angry but the punishment of one who is condemned. IV, 201. The Devil is not the author of human nature. X, 857. The Devil sometimes claims for himself certain things that were instituted naturally. X, 1436. Whatever is subjected to the Devil by God’s judgment is in his power in such a way that it cannot be outside God’s power, under which the Devil himself has also been established. X, 1035.

The Devil was expelled through Christ’s power. V, 445, 447, 787, 1090. And through Christ’s death. I, 1286. Christ redeemed us from the Devil’s captivity. IV, 1657. How the Devil was defeated by our Redeemer. V, 726, 745. The Devil was defeated by Christ through the truth of justice, not through violent power. VI, 256; VIII, 1026. And he must now be defeated in this way. VIII, 1026. How the Devil was defeated by Christ’s power. VIII, 1028. How by justice. VIII, 1027, 1029. The Devil’s trap is mortality and the Lord’s cross. V, 745, 726, 1209. The Devil was defeated by his own trophy, since, in killing the last human being, he lost the first from his snares. V, 1209. Although the Devil seemed for a time to prevail after the human being was overcome, even so he was defeated eternally when the human being was restored. VIII, 615. To bind the Devil means to restrain his power from seducing and possessing human beings. VII, 668, 670. The Devil has been bound so that he may not seduce the nations of which the Church consists. VII, 670. Why the Devil’s release will be permitted. VII, 670. And when it will occur. VII, 670.

The Devil is said to have been “sent outside,” not because he is outside the world, as certain heretics think, but because he has been expelled from the minds of the pious who do not love the world. VI, 291. In the mysteries, the Devil is sent outside through exorcism and exsufflation. X, 1383. Once excluded by believers, the Devil began to possess the impious more fully. VII, 668. Whether the Devil was not expelled from the hearts of the righteous before Christ’s advent. III, 1772. The Devil, sent outside, who ruled inwardly, fights outwardly. V, 787. The Devil is permitted to attack externally for the sake of our exercise. V, 787. The Devil does nothing and can do nothing unless sent or permitted. III, 880, 1441; IV, 201, 1001, 1150, 1246; X, 757. If the Devil could do anything, none of us would remain. IV, 1246. Permission is given to the Devil against human beings either for testing, or for vengeance inflicted for condemnation or correction. III, 880. No one can be tempted by the Devil unless God permits it, either to condemn the impious or to test the pious. IV, 1375. He is allowed to tempt only as much as benefits those who are making progress. IV, 761. And the elect. VIII, 1029. The Devil has the will to tempt, but not the power either to act or to determine how he will act. III, 444. The will to harm does not cease in the Devil even when power is not granted. III, 886. God turns the Devil’s temptations to the benefit of the Saints. VII, 332.

God created the Devil so that he himself might benefit the good through him. III, 440. God uses the Devil for the salvation of the faithful. VIII, 900. God makes good use of the Devil’s persecutions.
