X, 757. The Devil’s unceasing war against us becomes beneficial to us. X, 692. The Devil is the hammer of the whole earth, by which, when placed in God’s hand, the pliable trumpets are struck. IV, 1255. The Devil is the agent and executor of divine providence. III, 2128. The Devil does not know how many good things are brought about through him, even when he rages. IV, 1709.

The Devil is the *Agonothete*—the arranger of the contest. IV, 1859. A practiced enemy. III, 2006. The Devil is called “the enemy-man.” IV, 1805. The Devil’s fury is insolent toward God, wicked toward us, and destructive to himself. V, 1080. The Devil’s struggle against Christ and Christ’s faithful. VI, 664. As a most malevolent consolation in his own condemnation, the Devil seeks those with whom he may be condemned. VI, 343. The fallen Devil envied the standing human being and acts so that the human being may not reach the place from which he himself was expelled. IV, 709, 1807. The Devil presses in every way, seeking how he may cast us down. IV, 758. What he persuades the sinner to do. V, 139. He does nothing except block the way to God. IV, 1751. He does everything so that people will not believe in God and will not come in faith to the Mediator by whom his works are undone. II, 982. The Devil is the worst hunter of the world. V, 334. The Devil does not cease to persecute, either openly or by ambush. III, 1467. How he lies in wait. III, 1441. The Devil’s angels are cowardly in the hiding places of their ambushes. III, 1441. The Devil does not dare lie in wait for us if we have not departed from the way, that is, from Christ. IV, 1660. It is sometimes hidden even from the Devil what kind of person someone is: unless he tempts him, he does not discover it. IV, 660. The Devil examines all our sins with the diligence of envy. V, 928. He attacks us with our own weapons. V, 1077. We give the Devil room through an evil will. V, 435. For the Devil who tempts, there are two doors: desire and fear. V, 200, 201. The Devil tempts only what is dominant in you in the flesh. IV, 1858. The Devil rules in a human being through desire. VI, 291. He holds in his power those whom he ensnares with desire for this life and terrifies with death. IV, 227. The Devil enters the heart by implanting wicked suggestions in the thoughts of the wicked. III, 1159. The Devil’s head is the beginning of an evil suggestion. IV, 548. The Devil’s phantoms are for ensnaring souls. VII, 289.

The Devil’s kingdom is a kingdom of deceptions. VIII, 897. The Devil is the father of lies. III, 1704. The Devil is more to be feared when he deceives than when he rages. IV, 432. In how many ways the Devil deceives human beings. VIII, 897. The Devil allows some people to possess certain things resembling good works. II, 982. The Devil and his angels are the external darkness of unbelieving people. II, 562. The Devil does not deceive the one whom God does not abandon. IV, 1577. Wherever the Devil finds an empty place, there he attempts to make a nest. V, 1567. The Devil’s vessels are those who give him room through unbelief. V, 806. The Devil, both by himself and through the sons of unbelief, attacks the sons of light. VI, 615. Through his vessels the Devil carries out persecution of the body, so that inwardly there may be ruin of the heart. IV, 1841. The Devil is the corrupter of the Church’s virginity. V, 575. The Devil and Judas persecuted Christ’s soul; now the Devil remains for the persecution of Christ’s body, while Judas has been succeeded by the Jew. IV, 1849.

The Devil will rage against the Church for three years and six months in the last times. VII, 670. The fiercer the Devil’s persecution will be in the last times, the stronger will be the Christians’ endurance. VII, 671. The Devil is enclosed in the hearts of those who hate Christians. VII, 671. By afflicting, the Devil exercises but does not harm; by raging, he benefits us for the crown. IV, 1129. We ought to prefer fleeing from the pursuing Devil to following him when he leads. IV, 119. The Devil attempts to overthrow us and break our spirit through human insults and the slander of evil tongues. II, 270. The Devil is a slanderous adversary. V, 568. A slanderer. IV, 905. He knows that his false accusations have no force before God; he spreads them among human beings—for what purpose. V, 568. The Devil persecutes those whom he already possesses as captives, not in order to gain them, but because he possesses them and makes use of them. IX, 720. Although expelled outside and no longer reigning, the Devil does not cease to tempt. III, 1772.

Why does the Devil, who fights with us, not conquer us? III, 1993. The Christians’ struggles are now no longer with tyrants, but with the Devil. IV, 1207, 1687. It is a great battle not to see the enemy and yet to conquer him. IV, 1854. Who rebels against the Devil. X, 863. How the Devil subjects us and how he is overthrown by us. V, 1542. Concerning the Devil: whoever conquers himself inwardly triumphs over him outwardly. V, 29. And whoever conquers the flesh. IV, 1858. Our adversary the Devil is defeated when desires are defeated. VI, 291. Nothing defeats him so much as our being merciful. IV, 1860, 1861. As with Goliath, the Devil’s head is cut off with his own sword. IV, 1857. The Devil is defeated by boys and girls through grace. V, 787. To resist the Devil, one must ask for God’s help. X, 281.

The Devil, when tempting, holds the person who consents but does not compel the unwilling. V, 200. When the Devil tempted Adam, he did not have the power to compel but the cunning to persuade. III, 1489. He was not the oppressor of one unwilling—Adam—but the tempter of one willing. VIII, 539. The Devil works in the sons of unbelief by no other force than the fellowship and bondage of sin. V, 455. The Devil’s contest with Job. IV, 1382. The Devil conquered in paradise but was overcome on the dung heap. IV, 1383. The Devil is mystically described in the case of Job. IV, 1384. To renounce the Devil, his pomp, and his angels. VI, 291. Those who do not give the Devil room give room to God. III, 2005. If the Devil is expelled, God is admitted. IV, 391.

The Devil is to be punished more severely than human beings. X, 429. How the Devil is ordered by God’s justice in punishment. VII, 641. The Devil is mocked by the Angels. IV, 1385. Origen’s error concerning the Devil’s return to the good. X, 1518. And concerning his salvation. VII, 731, 735. To whom it seemed that the Devil could obtain God’s mercy, with Origen reportedly as the authority. X, 1484. The doctrine of the Priscillianists that the Devil, together with the condemned, will at some point be saved. VIII, 668. It is refuted. VIII, 672. [Col. 0237] Origen taught that the Devil, his angels, and all the impious, after being purified and liberated after exceedingly long ages, would be restored to God’s kingdom and light, and that after exceedingly long ages they would again fall back into these evils. VIII, 33. The Devil is not liberated together with the human being, because he sinned more greatly. I, 1285, 1287. Only the correction of the Devil and his angels is to be despaired of. IV, 630. Why the Church does not now pray for the Devil. VIII, 737.

The Devil as a dragon, enemy of the Church. IV, 1381. The Devil signified by the name “strong” and “powerful.” IV, 695, 910. Prefigured by Goliath. IV, 302. The Devil as a lion. V, 1209. The Devil as lion and dragon. III, 1167. The lion and the dragon on account of ambushes and wrath. III, 879. The lion in attack, the dragon in ambush. IV, 867, 434, 1168. The Devil as a wolf. III, 1731. The Devil called death. IV, 556. He is signified by the name of death and hell. VII, 681. The Devil appointed over death. IV, 223. The Devil as a scoundrel and pirate. V, 1649. Why Petilianus attempted to portray the Devil as learned in the law. IX, 299. If the Devil had not known that the temple, priesthood, and sacrifice were owed to the one true God, he would never have demanded these things for himself from his worshipers. II, 377. The Devil’s temples are overthrown everywhere, idols are smashed, and priests and those possessed are killed. V, 1453. The worship of demons is adultery of the soul. V, 76. See **Demons**.

**Deacon**, in Latin *minister*. V, 1441. Deacons in the third rank of the priesthood. IX, Appendix 773. How dangerous the office of a deacon is. II, 88. The deacon’s office is to minister the blood of Christ. V, 1385. By the deacon’s voice the common prayer is announced. II, 221. The falling away of deacons who had come to the Church from the party of Donatus. II, 271.

Diagoras the atheist. IX, 360.

**Dialectic**, a Greek name. IX, 456, 457. It is expertise in disputation. IX, 455. It is the discipline of disciplines. I, 1012. It both wishes and is able to make people knowledgeable by itself. I, 1013. Many things are apprehended through it. I, 949. Dialectic teaches nothing other than to demonstrate consequences—whether true things from true premises or false things from false premises. IX, 459. The science of defining and dividing is not false, even when applied to falsehoods. III, 60. The invention of dialectic. I, 1012. The truth of connections was not established by human beings but observed by them. III, 58. From where the truth of propositions and connections is to be extracted. III, 58. The usefulness of dialectic. III, 60. Dialectic is of the greatest value for understanding Scripture. III, 57. Cresconius criticizes dialectic. IX, 455. Neither dialectic nor eloquence is to be feared by defenders of the truth. IX, 466. Christ made use of dialectic. IX, 458. And Paul as well. IX, 456. The wise man is skilled in it. I, 949. Dialectic was intensely loved by the Stoics. VII, 232. It flourished among them to the greatest degree. IX, 455. And among the Epicureans. IX, 455. Ecclesiastical judges do not judge according to dialectic. X, 819.

Who should be called a dialectician. IX, 455, 457, 459. Dialecticians do not make it possible that, if something is true, it should be false, or that, if it is false, it should be true. IX, 480. The dialecticians’ rule—that no thing can simultaneously contain two contraries—fails when applied to evils and goods. VI, 238.

Diana is regarded as the sister of Apollo, as the Moon, and as mistress of roads. VII, 207. Why she is called a virgin. VII, 207. Pagans interpret Diana as virtue. III, 1059.

What the *diapsalma* is. IV, 80.

A dictator was created only in the greatest dangers. VII, 97. The dictatorship was greater in honor than the consulship. VII, 164.

Dictinius, bishop of Astorga. VI, 522. Dictinius’s book entitled *The Balance*. VI, 522, 543, 548.

Augustine laments that he wept over Dido’s death. I, 670.

What the didrachma is. IV, 1783.

Didymus, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Didymus the Blind left commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians. II, 252, 262. He wrote a book on the Holy Spirit. III, 604. Jerome criticized Didymus the Blind. II, 286.

The word “day” is used in different ways. III, 231; IV, 1115. How the name of day and night is to be understood. III, 230, 295. “Day” is called that light which night precedes and, when departing, follows. III, 255. The distinction between days and nights. III, 183. The enumeration of days and nights serves to establish a distinction between God and creatures. III, 235. It is impossible to conceive the first days of the world’s creation, much more to describe them. VII, 322. How one day was completed, whether in the creation or after the creation of light. III, 253. How day and night could have existed before the creation of the sun. III, 231, 275. How three days and nights succeeded one another before the creation of the sun. III, 255. It is not proved that day and night existed before the creation of the sun through the emission and contraction of light. III, 258. How “day,” “evening,” and “morning” are to be understood in the account of creation. III, 314, 317. All things were made simultaneously and nevertheless were made over six days. III, 319. How the six days of creation are to be understood. III, 295, 309, 314, 323, 338; VII, 322. How day and night can apply to sensual and rational light. III, 231. How spiritual light displayed day and night, morning and evening. III, 311. The day that was made first is the angelic nature. III, 326. A certain wise light was called “day.” III, 310. Day, evening, and morning in angelic knowledge. III, 314. In what sense day can be called an intellectual creature. IV, 1567. The interpretation given of the spiritual day is not to be considered figurative. III, 314. We must understand the beginning of day and the beginning of night as the primacy of each. III, 237. The seventh day without evening. V, 80. Why the seventh day had a morning but no evening. III, 306, 314, 326. The seventh day is the seventh repetition of the day first created. III, 311. The cessation of the seventh day is to be understood as having occurred with the making of the creatures themselves, not with the administration of those creatures said to have been made. II, 948. The allegory of the seven days concerning the Christian person’s progress in good works. III, 191. The seven days mystically signify the seven ages of the world. III, 190.

Day is produced by the revolution of the fixed stars. III, 236. “Day” now means the sun’s duration above the earth, and now the duration of its entire circuit from east to east. I, 821. The whole circuit of the sun is more correctly called a day, not from east to west but from east to east. II, 911. The customary seven days of the week differ greatly from the seven days of Genesis. III, 314. What they signify. III, 320. In Genesis the day begins with light and ends with darkness; now the reverse—why. III, 1325; V, 1089. In earlier times the day had twenty-four hours, as it does now. VII, 455. The winter day has as many hours as the summer day, although they are shorter. III, 159. The seven days of the week were named by the Gentiles after their gods. VIII, 346. And after the planets. IV, 1192. This manner of speaking is disapproved in the mouths of Christians, who would use the ecclesiastical manner of speaking more appropriately. IV, 1192. Holidays. V, 1201. Intercalary days. VII, 451.

Some days belong to heaven, others to earth. IV, 1130. The day of eternal life is one day without setting. IV, 202. Eternal days have been called both “many days” and “one day.” V, 528. Properly speaking, they are not many but one. V, 520. The day of eternity is always today. VI, 255. The day that truly exists is not here. IV, 418. Days join themselves to one another, follow one another, and do not remain fixed. IV, 419. In Holy Scripture “day” is used for time. VII, 659. Especially when “day” is used in the feminine gender. IV, 1115. It is used for an indeterminate period. III, 197. Sometimes for a multitude of years. II, 911. According to the Scriptures, one day is a thousand years. II, 911. The three days of the age: one before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. IV, 224.

To observe days and months before beginning something, because they are considered favorable or unfavorable times, is a great sin. VI, 270. Choosing a day for marrying, planting, or sowing is foolish. VII, 146. Which observance of days is culpable. II, 210. Christians observe the days in the celebration of Easter according to the councils of the Fathers. II, 217. In celebrating Easter—a figure of the Lord’s Passion—the Jews do not take account of whether the Sabbath occurs or whether it coincides with the third week of the new moon. II, 215, 218. The custom of the Church has confirmed that the eight days of the neophytes should be distinguished from the others—that is, that the eighth should correspond to the first. II, 220. The mystery of the eighth and seventh day. V, 1197.

Day signifies prosperity, night adversity. IV, 1110, 1737, 1793, 1794. What human beings’ days are like. IV, 1487. Evil days from the beginning of sin. V, 168. The evil days are those in which sinners appear to flourish and the righteous to labor. IV, 1204. The present day is one of labor and sadness. V, 1051. Evil days signify the evils perpetrated during the days. II, 916. The days of the wicked and of the faithful are different. IV, 123. There is no good day for a person who is evil. V, 245. Two things make evil days: wickedness and misery. V, 909. Wicked people make evil days. V, 168, 1363. Which are the good days and where they are to be sought. V, 123, 169, 170, 633, 635, 1014. There are always evil days in the world, always good days in God. IV, 317. Days are evil because one passes away so that another may come; the good days will be one eternal day. V, 1084.

The last day is the end of the age for the entire human race, but for each individual person it is the day of death. V, 76, 589, 932. Every day is to be reckoned as the last. V, 1411. God beneficially established the day of death as uncertain. V, 241. It cannot be known when the day of the Lord will come. IV, 90. Hesychius says that the signs Christ gave to signify the last day have been fulfilled in part. II, 903. Whoever confesses that he does not know when the last day will come agrees more with the Gospel than one who says it will come sooner or later. II, 924. The last days were spoken of even in the earliest times of the Apostles. II, 913.

The Lord’s Day. V, 916. It is called the first day of the week, the second day of the week, the second weekday, and so forth. IV, 1192, 1960. The Lord’s Day, which is the eighth and the first, began to be proclaimed from Christ’s resurrection. II, 215. It signifies the resurrection. II, 215. This was not unknown to the ancient Fathers. II, 215. Nevertheless, only the Sabbath was handed down for celebration, because at that time there was rest but not the resurrection of the dead. II, 215. The Lord’s resurrection consecrated the Lord’s Day for us. V, 916. By faith in the resurrection, not by the custom of refreshment, the Lord’s Day is placed before the Sabbath. II, 141. The Priscillianists used a testimony from the Acts of the Apostles in support of fasting on the Lord’s Day. II, 148.

The Day-Father is from no day; the Son is day from day. V, 1084. Christ is day from day. IV, 1417.

The Day-Father: God who brings forth childbirth into the day. VII, 122. See **Dis Pater**.

To refer someone for accusation, that is, to accuse. I, 1203.

How and among whom difficult matters are to be treated. III, 99. In difficult and obscure matters, rashness must be avoided. II, 862. What is sought with greater difficulty is usually found with greater sweetness. IV, 1352.

Difficulty: what purpose it served in the first human being after sin, and what purpose it serves in others. I, 1298. If difficulty had belonged to the human being’s origin, the human being would not for that reason alone have been condemned. I, 1302. Ignorance and difficulty are two punitive things for every sinful soul. X, 287. If ignorance and difficulty are natural, the soul begins from there to rise toward the blessedness of wisdom and rest. I, 1302. If it neglects this, it is plunged into another difficulty, which is punitive. I, 1302. What is assigned to guilt in difficulty. I, 1297, 1302. Whether difficulty is natural or not, God is nevertheless to be praised for it. I, 1303. Difficulty justly spread to Adam’s descendants. I, 1297. Difficulties must necessarily exist so that it may be shown to a human being that he is human. V, 1559. Difficulty is for the godly an admonition to progress and the beginning of perfection. I, 1298. For the diligent it contributes to a crown, for the negligent to punishment. I, 1299. God’s help must be entreated for overcoming it. I, 1297, 1303. Through it, a work of piety becomes easy, even if it had been difficult or impossible. I, 620. Difficulty in doing good causes us finally to acknowledge God as the giver of this good. IV, 1421. When difficulty is overcome, the demon is conquered by the very means by which it had conquered the human being. I, 1299. Therefore the difficulty of a work does not always increase the measure of merit. X, 857.

Distrust of God’s help is suggested to us by the Devil. IV, 325.

The finger of God is the Holy Spirit. III, 604; IV, 111; V, 74. The fingers of God are his ministers, through whom the Scriptures were produced when they were filled with the Holy Spirit. IV, 111. Who the fingers are with which the body of Christ fights. IV, 1857, 1858. In the fingers, a division of operation and the root of unity are understood. IV, 1857. To flash or gesture with the fingers. VIII, 953.

To take on condescension. I, 720.

What dignity is. VI, 22.

What it means to be enlarged in heart. IV, 79. Enlargement of the heart proceeds from love. V, 758. It is the delight of righteousness. IV, 1527. It is God’s gift that in his commandments we are not constricted by fear of punishment but enlarged by love and delight in righteousness. IV, 1527.

*Dilectio* is not distinguished from *amor*. VII, 410. What is neither known nor believed cannot be loved. X, 243. In what sense love is God. III, 2031. The love with which God loves is incomprehensible, immutable, and eternal. III, 1923. God loves all things in their kinds with the greatest order. III, 1924. The Father has no other reason for loving the members of the Son than that he loves the Son. III, 1923. God’s twofold love of souls. X, 1422. In a wondrous and divine manner, when God hated us, he loved us. III, 1923. We were loved when we were displeasing, so that there might be in us something by which we could become pleasing. III, 1898.

There is one commandment of love, if it is understood. VI, 672. The commandment to love God and neighbor is explained. VI, 670, 671. There are four things to be loved, and what they are. III, 27. In the two commandments of love, a human being finds three things to love: God, one’s neighbor, and oneself. VII, 643. The order and measure of love. VIII, 959, 963. What ordered love is. III, 29. The love of God and the love of one’s neighbor, although sometimes set separately in Scripture, imply one another. VIII, 956, 958, 1050. Whatever is commanded or urged is rightly done when it is referred to love of God and neighbor. VI, 288. Love of God and neighbor. V, 563, 564, 1461, 1527, 1648. All perfection consists in love of God. VIII, 136. We are all the more righteous the more we love God. X, 604. We would not love God unless he had first loved us. V, 210; X, 904. He who gave himself to be loved, though not loved, loved us. III, 1898. What else should we love in ourselves except God—either because we possess him or so that we may possess him? V, 1189. A difficult question arising from the Lord’s words, in which he says that the one to whom more is forgiven loves more. V, 597. Whoever does not love God is said to hate himself. VIII, 1049. How we ought to love God with our whole heart. X, 528. The commandment of love will be perfectly fulfilled only in the future life. X, 301. Why the commandment to love God with one’s whole heart is imposed here, when it is not fulfilled here. X, 243. Our love of God benefits us, not God. V, 212. We love ourselves if we love God. II, 499.

The love of God is first in the order of commanding; the love of one’s neighbor is first in the order of doing. III, 1531. A good and honorable life is formed from nothing other than loving God and one’s neighbor. II, 524. The reason why God and the human being are to be loved. III, 30. Every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake, whereas God is to be loved for his own sake. III, 29. Whoever does not love the one who made the human being does not know how to love a human being rightly. II, 1072. The Church is loved for the sake of one’s neighbor, God for God’s sake. IV, 1615. We are commanded to love one another for the sake of the kingdom of God. V, 1461. Piety belongs to love of God; innocence and benevolence to love of one’s neighbor. VI, 514. Love of God should be gratuitous; love of one’s neighbor should be beneficial. V, 571. The love with which we love one another ought to imitate the love with which Christ loved us. III, 1808. We can return no better fruit of love to Christ than the example of imitation. V, 1395. The fullness of love is to lay down one’s life for one’s brothers. III, 1846.

This rule of love is fixed upon the human being: by imitating the Father, one should love one’s enemy. IV, 631. Love of one’s enemy is perfect love. III, 2042. The perfection of mercy. III, 1264. “Love your enemies,” lest, through carelessness, you hate your friends as well. V, 1404. Love of enemies. V, 383, 496, 1426, 1436. Loving an enemy is salutary, although bitter. IV, 447. Nothing in God’s commandments is more marvelous than love of enemies. IV, 1518. Nothing in Scripture contradicts the commandment to love enemies. III, 1265. Why we should love our enemies. III, 30. See **Enemies**.

How great love of one’s neighbor ought to be. IV, 1170; V, 1461. Do not love the vices of your friends, if you love your friends. V, 323. Do not love vice for the sake of the person, nor hate the person for the sake of vice. V, 323. Loving the good, or those believed to be good, benefits the one who loves. II, 87. This is the one error to be avoided. II, 87. Let each person love in others what he himself does not possess, and love Christ in them. V, 589. One’s neighbor himself is now loved through faith. VI, 288. The commandment to love one’s neighbor implies the commandment to love God, and conversely. III, 1809, 1846.

By loving one’s neighbor, one travels the way to God. III, 1532. Love of one’s neighbor is a sure step toward love of God. VIII, 136. Through love of one’s neighbor, the eye is cleansed for seeing God. III, 1531. God grants us love of our neighbor. III, 1809.

Love must be extended so as to draw everyone toward God. V, 566. All are to be loved equally. III, 30. Parents are to be loved, but Christ more. V, 1532. Another human being is to be loved more than our own body. III, 30.

Love of one’s neighbor receives its rule from love of oneself. VII, 34. No commandment is needed for each person to love himself. III, 34. What perverse self-love is. III, 27. Who loves himself and who loves his neighbor badly. VI, 674. Who knows how to love himself. V, 715. Whoever does not yet know how to love himself should learn from one who knows how to love his neighbor. V, 715. Whoever does not love God does not love himself. V, 212. Those who love themselves in order to possess God love themselves properly. III, 1846. The commandment to love one’s neighbor and oneself concerns body and soul. III, 29.

How the sinner is to be loved. V, 43. Whoever intercedes for the ungodly is not a companion in wickedness. II, 660. Nor is one who loves the ungodly out of charity and does good to them. II, 654, 655.

What true love is. VIII, 956. Love must be demonstrated by works, lest the name be an unfruitful designation. III, 1830. Love alone is always to be returned. V, 1201. To love this world is to live wickedly. VI, 299. See **To love**. Character is usually judged from what each person loves. II, 672. Each person is such as his love is. III, 1997. Labor cannot end unless each person loves that which cannot be taken away from him against his will. IV, 107. From this it is evident that you love what is good if you are found to hate what is evil. IV, 1249. Christ is not worthy to be loved together with avarice. IV, 1248, 1249. To love righteousness and hate iniquity—this is the whole scepter of Christ’s kingdom. IV, 504. Love is light; hatred is darkness. IV, 633. Love is preached in vain to one who loves the world. IV, 254. Learn not to love, so that you may learn to love; turn away, so that you may be converted; empty yourself, so that you may be filled. IV, 254.

Love produces a certain death in us. IV, 1628. Love is our death to the world and life with God. III, 1808. Love is the work of faith. III, 2054. Love alone distinguishes between the children of God and the children of the Devil. III, 2016. Love is the virtue of the city of Jerusalem. IV, 1628. Why the commandment of love is called the new commandment and the commandment of Christ. III, 1845, 1808. Love belongs to the New Testament. III, 623. The commandment of Christ is love, through which sins are forgiven. III, 2013. The commandment of love is not burdensome. X, 289. To whom it is burdensome. X, 290. Love can be formed by admonition and persuasion; it cannot be imposed by forcing someone unwilling. VIII, 565.

Ambrose teaches that love belongs to the benefit of grace. X, 582. Grace accomplishes this: that God’s commandments, which could not be fulfilled through fear, are fulfilled through love. IV, 1579. A commandment truly becomes a good work when it is performed with love as its end. IV, 1540. Hope usually kindles love. IV, 1487. Love, and do whatever you wish. III, 2033. Love is now present in desire, not yet in satisfaction. III, 1852. Love of God and neighbor remains forever. IV, 1563. By loving we become truly strongest—not through proud harshness but through secure righteousness. V, 1526. Peace and abundance come through love. IV, 1628. Love and faith are proved more fully through heresies. II, 793. Love is our fruit. III, 1852. The reward of love is the one who is loved. IV, 1563. See **Love**, **Charity**.

A person ought not to trust in his own diligence. X, 253.

The Ogygian flood. VII, 566. Deucalion’s flood. VII, 568. The universal flood in the time of Noah. VII, 566. In what year from Adam the universal flood occurred. VII, 463. Why it occurred at that time rather than another. VII, 471. The duration, increase, and decrease of the flood, and so forth. III, 550. At the time of the universal flood, none of Seth’s sons perished. VII, 471. Objections against the flood are resolved. VII, 566. See **Ark**. The flood is defended against slanders. VIII, 631. Whether any writers remembered the universal flood. VII, 566, and note. To recall the memory of the flood, kings of Greece instituted sacred rites for false gods. VII, 569. The sacrament of the flood. VI, 334; VIII, 631. What kind of flood the saints suffer in this age and how they escape it. IV, 214, 269, 270, 1354.

The four dimensions in the Apostle: breadth, length, height, and depth. V, 371. The dimensions of the cross. V, 903. See **Cross**.

Forgiving debts to debtors. VI, 266. We ought to regard as wholly forgiven to us whatever evil has not been committed by us under God’s governance. VI, 420, 427. See **Sins**. The forgiveness of another’s sin is a remedy given by God for obtaining mercy. IV, 1469, 1698. In this kind of good work there is no excuse, where the will alone is the whole capacity. V, 1053. Forgiven sins are imputed again to the one who does not forgive. V, 517. See **Debts**. One must not despair concerning the forgiveness of any sin whatsoever, since even the killing of Christ was forgiven to those who confessed. IV, 707.

A Christian is required to leave father, mother, wife, and so forth, whenever the necessity arises that, for example, either the father or Christ must be abandoned. II, 689, 690. The person who does not place hope in riches and uses them rightly, and so forth, abandons riches. II, 690. The person who abandons both what he has and what he desires to have abandons the whole world. II, 692. The person who despises not only as much as he could have but also as much as he wished to have despises everything. II, 124. Paulinus renounced everything. II, 102, 107.

Dinocrates, brother of Saint Perpetua the Martyr: whether, having died before baptism, he was freed from condemnation through his sister’s prayers. X, 481, 503, 505, 516, 517. Dinocrates deserved to be freed from misery through the prayers of his holy sister. X, 541.

Dinomachus’s opinion concerning the highest good. X, 852.

Diocletian. IX, 323, 328. Consul eight times. IX, 510, 513. Consul nine times. IX, 643. Diocletian, persecutor of Christians. VII, 614.

Dioga of Leptis Magna [reading uncertain]. IX, 239.

Diogenes of Apollonia, a student of Anaximenes, recognized certain principles of things. VII, 226; X, 777. Another Diogenes, the Cynic. X, 777.

The depravity and shamelessness of Diogenes the Cynic. VII, 428.

Diomedes made a god by the Greeks. VII, 573, 576. The birds of Diomedes flatter those of Greek origin and pursue foreigners. VII, 576. The transformation of the birds of Diomedes. VII, 576. The island of Diomedes. VII, 573.

Dion of Naples, a distinguished mathematician. VII, 720.

Dionysius the Areopagite, that is, the chief man of the Athenians. V, 808.

Dionysius, the same person who is called Father Liber. VII, 569.

What Dionysius the Tyrant did in order to have beautiful sons. X, 813.

Dionysian or Josinian. IX, 230.

Dioscorus, a Greek youth. II, 436. Sent to Carthage to learn literature. II, 436. He asks Augustine to explain questions from Cicero’s books to him. II, 431.

Dioscorus the chief physician, brought to the Christian faith by repeated miracles. II, 1012.

The bishops of the Diospolitan Synod. X, 652, 663. A summary of the points that Pelagius anathematized at the Council of Diospolis and that a Catholic ought to profess. II, 828. Pelagius was said to have been cleared by the acts of the Diospolitan Synod. II, 761, 765. At the Diospolitan trial Pelagius evaded the issue; he did not clear himself. II, 787. The Diospolitan Fathers who absolved Pelagius are not to be accused. II, 765. Augustine requests the acts of the Diospolitan Synod from John of Jerusalem. II, 776. Innocent doubts the acts of the Diospolitan Synod. II, 787. After the Council of Diospolis, Pelagius did not write sincerely about the help of grace. II, 829.

Diptychs. See **Tablet**.

To depart. Not to depart from God is a work of grace. X, 1001.

What it means to learn. I, 787. A question raised by an opponent becomes an opportunity for learning. VII, 477. We are led to learning by authority and reason. I, 957, 1007. Authority must precede reason. I, 1007, 1311. How punitive it is for children to learn letters or crafts. I, 1300. The torments of learners in this life belong to the miseries of this age. X, 1516, 1525. The force of habit in learning. III, 46. In learning languages, free curiosity has greater force than fearful necessity. I, 671. What children often learn in trivial matters can be learned more safely in matters that are not trivial. I, 671, 672. More useful things, rather than more marvelous ones, are to be learned. I, 1054. No age is too late for learning what is necessary. II, 720. Learning letters for the sake of temporal advantage—how customary and how vain it is. VI, 675. See **Teach**. Many learn God’s ordinances and yet do not learn them. IV, 1550. One ought to learn the divine ordinances as those who do them learn them, not as those who merely remember them in order to have something to say. IV, 1513, 1514. No one is taught unless he learns; no one learns unless he is taught. IV, 1548. No one rightly learns what pertains to living with God unless he is made teachable by God. III, 104. Whoever learns through grace does everything he has learned must be done. X, 367. And he comes to Christ. X, 368. There is some similarity between learners and those who eat. III, 101. Those who learn are happier than those who teach. IV, 594. Truth is the reason why we learn; necessity is the reason why we teach. II, 194. Augustine loves learning more than teaching. II, 194. Some who are unwilling to learn, lest they become proud, are criticized. IV, 1712. What negligence in cultivating a tree is, sluggishness in learning is for the soul. III, 380.

“Discipline” is derived from “learning.” I, 1223; VI, 669. Discipline is knowledge of all kinds of things. I, 1021. Reason is the inventor of all disciplines. I, 1011. The liberal disciplines are so called undeservedly unless the pursuit of Christian piety is present. II, 368. Discipline has two parts, one of life and the other of instruction. I, 1006. Discipline is good, not evil. I, 1223. The usefulness of the liberal disciplines. I, 988. They raise the intellect toward divine things. I, 1015. Augustine is displeased that he had assigned too much importance to them. I, 588.

Christian discipline or instruction: what it is. IV, 1204. Christ is the teacher. VI, 678. The school is his body. VI, 678. The house of discipline is the Church. VI, 669. There one learns to live well so as to reach eternal life. VI, 669. Ecclesiastical discipline is founded on Christ’s words. VI, 200. It is directed above all against pride, the mother of envy. VI, 413.

Discipline is signified by the endangered situation produced by gathering a multitude in the Church. V, 1168. The rigor of discipline is relaxed for the sake of peace. II, 812. Augustine laments that many disturbances arise in matters belonging to discipline. II, 201. When discipline differs, what the prudent Christian ought to observe. II, 151, 200. Ecclesiastical discipline concerning the recitation of martyrs at the altar. V, 866. Discipline and correction are not to be neglected. V, 111, 506, 518, 900. It is dangerously neglected. II, 231. What it ought to regard. IX, 81, 84. How ecclesiastical discipline is to be exercised. IX, 84, 86, 92. However vigilantly household discipline may keep watch, no one dares claim that the household is without evil people. II, 271, 272; IV, 1328, 1329. Discipline is to be exercised toward the wicked, but judgment is not to be rushed. V, 299. Discipline and correction are to be applied without hatred. V, 385. See **Correction**. Discipline is to be given when necessary, but charity must never be abandoned from the heart. V, 518. Christ willed discipline to be gentler in the New Testament. IV, 1413. Discipline produced through corrective tribulation is learned by undergoing it. IV, 1548. Ecclesiastical discipline administered by presbyters. V, 1221.

Christ’s disciples are called such in two ways. X, 929. They were more truly his brothers. III, 1468. Christ found the hearts of the disciples dead. V, 1118. They had lost hope and faith. V, 1119. In Christ’s death. V, 1120. How the disciples’ soul alternated in faith. V, 1109. Christ’s disciples were unable even to imitate the thief’s faith. V, 1110. The unbelief of Christ’s disciples. V, 493. Especially when they heard of Christ’s resurrection. V, 658, 1104, 1108, 1122, 1151, 1154. Before the resurrection Christ’s disciples thought he was merely human. V, 1149. They were held by human affection for him. V, 1238. The disciples, doubting at Christ’s death, were prefigured in Moses. V, 1554. The disciples’ error represents the errors of heretics. V, 477, 478. How the disciples did greater works than Christ. III, 1821. Christ’s words to the disciples apply equally to us. V, 721. Everything must be renounced in order for one to become a disciple of Christ. III, 1343. To be Christ’s disciple is to build a tower and fight against a stronger king. III, 1343.

How disagreements are to be settled. I, 772. Especially between husband and wife. I, 772. How a friend of both parties ought to conduct himself in the disagreement of two people. V, 323. Discord blasphemes the Lord. IV, 1950. See **Harmony**, **Division**. The causes of dissension. VII, 560. The discord that exists between spirit and flesh works toward harmony. V, 821.

Discord, the goddess. VII, 105. She provoked the Trojan War. VII, 105.

To distinguish. Who distinguishes the vessels of mercy from the vessels of wrath? X, 582. Discrimination from the mass of perdition. V, 446. Through grace. X, 923. No one is distinguished except by the grace of the Savior. X, 923, 1422, 1428. Faith working through love distinguishes the children of God. X, 590. Everything necessary for eternal salvation is provided for those who have been distinguished, that is, for the elect. X, 924. See **Election**, **Grace**.

Discretion. Great and spiritual men take the utmost care not to do publicly anything that they understand is not yet timely to do with the people. III, 144. They conceal certain things from the little ones but tell no lies. III, 144.

Dis Pater. VII, 122, 207, 213, 218. See **Orcus**, **Pluto**.

God can make exceptions concerning laws established by him. III, 803. What is done through inspiration against a commandment is to be counted as transgression. III, 803, 816. What “dispensationally” means. II, 228.

The dispensation of Christ’s flesh. V, 1217.

The dispensation of our salvation. V, 1122.

What displeases God ought to displease a human being, and conversely. V, 134. Let what you are always displease you, if you wish to attain what you are not yet. V, 926. Nothing in you pleases God except what you have from God; what you have from yourself displeases God. V, 108.

What it means to dispute. IX, 457. In disputations, contention must be avoided. IX, 548. It is dishonest to add something to another person’s words against which you are disputing. IX, 210. Matters that can be common to both parties must not be brought into a dispute. IX, 396. Nor should figurative or obscure matters be brought into it. IX, 398.

Certain conditions for disputing are proposed. II, 276. What is more contentious than disputing over a name when the matter itself is agreed upon? II, 1040. Nowhere do I find so little to say as where the matter being discussed is clearer than everything said about it. X, 147. Truth is sought by disputation, not disputation by truth. III, 547. The life of the good is not purified by the meanderings of disputation but by the easy authority of the sacred mysteries into which we are initiated. I, 1007. One disputes with the Almighty by seeking, not by attempting to defeat him. III, 885. It is no small progress in philosophy when, in comparison with the discovery of what is right and true, the disputant’s victory is despised. I, 910. The authority of no disputant is to be placed on a level with the canonical books. X, 623.

Dissension is the death of a Christian; charity is life. VI, 713, 714. Dissension among Christians is Satan’s triumph. V, 1053. Dissensions should never be loved, although they sometimes arise from charity or test charity. II, 957. Dissensions without the loss of charity. VI, 388. From where the dissension of flesh and spirit arises. X, 1096. See **Desire**.

We depart from God through unlikeness. IV, 337.

“To distinguish with one’s lips,” meaning to define. III, 675.

**Long.** What is long when there is an end? V, 688, 1385. Weakness makes what is brief seem long. IV, 361. Whatever has an end is not long. IV, 234, 1889.

A lodging-place of the saints, that is, a monastery. I, 1340.

Divine and incorporeal things are wholly everywhere. V, 1486. It is difficult to communicate divine things to carnal people. V, 665.

Divination is named from divine things. I, 917. Divinations of demons. I, 1007. God sometimes grants demons a share of divination. VI, 143, 164. See **Demons**. The divinations of astrologers are deceptive. I, 737. Divinations and predictions are full of destructive curiosity, tormenting anxiety, and deadly servitude. III, 53. Astrological divination is a kind of fornication of the soul. III, 52. The demons take care to entangle human minds in the nets of this harmful curiosity. VII, 722. Divination by blood. VII, 223. By water. VII, 223. How the statements or responses of diviners are to be understood. III, 757. The marvelous divination of certain young men at play. III, 472. And that of another person who predicted that a man would be killed by a lion. III, 473. The divinations of Albicerius are marvelous. I, 914. But they are to be despised. I, 914. Some wish the human soul to possess within itself a certain power of divination. III, 464. This is refuted. III, 464. See **Astrologers**. Divination was prohibited in the cities of the nations before Christ’s coming. VII, 223. Various questions about diviners raised by Porphyry. VII, 289.

Divinity, why it should be sought. VII, 193. Divinity can in no way be seen by human sight. VIII, 826. It is clear that divinity is not present in civic theology. VII, 193. Why pagans worshipped divine gifts among the gods. VII, 131. Their arguments are refuted. VII, 132.

Division of body into infinity. III, 266. Both local and temporal spaces admit infinite division. I, 1174.

Desire wishes to divide, just as charity wishes to gather together. V, 1224. Those who are divided among themselves may both belong to the kingdom of the devil; but the two cannot likewise both belong to the kingdom of Christ. V, 446, 447. Division has no place in the inheritance of Christians. VI, 716.

Riches: why they are called “the mammon of iniquity.” IV, 552; V, 650; VII, 749. Riches are one thing, money another. VII, 204. For the unjust, riches are nothing but money. III, 1349. Riches are of many kinds. IV, 1293. True and false riches. V, 328, 650. The desire for riches is insatiable. V, 956. How dangerous the desire for riches is. V, 242, 1457. It is an enervation of body [Col. 0244] and soul. VII, 155. In riches, desire is reproved, not possession. VII, 24, 25. Whose love of riches hinders salvation. VI, 216. Those who do not possess riches but desire to possess them are counted among the rich who must be reproved. IV, 1057. Riches are for the sake of life, not life for the sake of riches. V, 1518. Riches have harmed many. IV, 624. The enticements of riches. I, 880, 906, 907. Riches are sought through pride. IV, 545. And they generate pride. IV, 922, 1769. The greater people are in the world, the more they love riches. IV, 1909. Through riches a nest is gathered for pride, in which it may be nourished and grow. V, 957. The worm of riches is pride. V, 215, 242, 412, 521. Riches will not harm you if you remove pride. V, 242. If you are puffed up on account of riches, do not consider when you will become the prey of men: you are already the devil’s prey. IV, 1727.

Riches are a dream. V, 1517. Riches ought to be called another’s property. III, 1349. They do not make a person happy. I, 906; VII, 162. Earthly riches are evidence not of strength but of weakness. V, 488, 1189. They are supports of weakness, not ornaments of power. V, 232. Those are not true riches which, as they increase, increase poverty; and which, however great they become for their lovers, do not bring satisfaction but inflame desire. IV, 224, 1638; V, 328. They are called “abundant poverty.” I, 670. You possess riches: poverty has increased, not power. V, 956. You possess riches and desire more: it is sickness, not wealth. V, 410.

The emptiness and disadvantages of riches. IV, 1727. Riches bring nothing except anxiety. V, 1520. The burden of riches. V, 899. The weight of riches prevents a person from following Christ. III, 1655. When a person seeks what is superfluous, he wishes to load his own fetters. IV, 864. Riches are rivers that carry away those whom they lift up. IV, 1769. From riches come pressures and fears. IV, 1057. The richer you are, the more fearful you are. IV, 1762. Riches blind the wicked when they are offered, and torture them when they are taken away. V, 328. Earthly riches are perishable and full of dangers. V, 114, 217. They cannot be taken away from here by those who are dying. V, 114. To possess riches is not blameworthy; but to love them, place one’s hope in them, or prefer or compare them with truth, justice, and so forth, is blameworthy. VIII, 165. Hope must not be placed in riches. V, 958. Let your heart flee from gold, and it will be your servant. V, 955. In this matter, if you do not wish to be a slave, be a fugitive. V, 955. Those who prefer to be tortured rather than surrender their riches are not good Christians. VII, 25. How one should conduct oneself toward riches, both when they are lacking and when they are present. II, 856. How riches should be sought from God. IV, 624.

God grants riches to the good for testing, and to the wicked for punishment. V, 327, 328. An abundance of riches is also found among the just, but they do not set their hearts upon them. IV, 1867, 1868. To one whose mind is not earthly, gold and silver are earth. IV, 1481. Riches are possessed badly by the wicked, and possessed all the better by the good, the less they are loved. II, 665. It is more remarkable not to cling to riches when one possesses them than not to possess them at all. I, 1329. It is not contrary to the New Testament for God’s friends to possess riches. VIII, 162, 163. Nor does the New Testament command that they be sold, but it gives this as advice. II, 687. It is more useful to hold earthly wealth humbly than to abandon it proudly. II, 124. Temporal riches were also despised in the Old Testament. VIII, 163, 164. Abraham was poor in the midst of riches. IV, 1083. Riches, if possessed without desire, are not to be blamed. V, 956. The love of riches is such that they cannot be lost without pain: it is wood and hay built upon the foundation. VI, 216. Those who love riches with carnal affection, yet do not prefer them to Christ, will be saved through fire—how this is to be understood. VI, 153, 155.

Riches are not to be loved, but only used. III, 1691. No one should be considered to possess riches except one who uses them well. V, 327. How they should be used. I, 163. The use of riches in good works. V, 90, 217, 219, 242, 328, 415, 522, 959. Through them God supplies the good with opportunities for benefaction, while he torments the wicked with fear of losses. V, 327. Christ’s riches are to be distributed to the poor. VII, 162. As long as riches are on earth, they are not riches. V, 650. The great wealth of Christians is the needs of the needy, if we understand where we ought to store what we possess. V, 1389. If riches are loved, they should be stored where they cannot perish. II, 485. Where they are safely placed. VII, 24. They are placed in safety when they are distributed. V, 239. The safe place for riches is heaven, to which they are carried by the hands of the poor. IV, 423, 549, 550. Riches must migrate from earth to heaven. V, 239, 240, 405, 413, 1519. All who live badly leave their riches to others. IV, 553.

The riches of Christians—what they are. VII, 23. The riches to be sought are those that cannot be taken away. IV, 1645. Those are true riches which, once we possess them, we cannot lose. V, 650. What those riches are. V, 651. Spiritual and true riches. IV, 316, 863, 864, 1638, 1639. The riches of the soul. VIII, 165. Inward riches that cannot be lost in shipwreck. V, 147, 218, 955. The fountain of inward riches is not hidden if the heart is open: the key of faith opens the heart. V, 955. Gold shines for many, but faith does not shine. IV, 365. Your riches are your God. V, 955. Whoever wishes to be rich should cling to God. IV, 545. Even if you wish it, perhaps you will not have gold; when you wish for God, you will have him. IV, 294. Every abundance that is not God is poverty. I, 848. What will the riches of the one whose poverty makes us rich do for us? V, 916. True riches are in heaven. IV, 620. True riches are immortality, because true abundance is where there is no need. V, 216, 232. True riches are to be sought from God. V, 220, 651, 1520.

Who should be called rich. VII, 204. There are the rich of the world and the rich of God. V, 957. The rich of this age and the rich of the age to come. V, 521. The rich who are not of this world. V, 215. The rich of the age are in need. IV, 316, 317. You think someone rich who would be less in need if he had less. V, 328. He is rich and full, yet empty. V, 366. He is always a beggar. V, 1521. The rich acknowledge that they are poor. IV, 1628. They are devastated by desires, scattered by cravings, tortured by fears, and wither away in grief. IV, 224. The rich in fact and the rich in desire differ. V, 412, 956. The rich man is compared with the dropsical man and with the bent woman mentioned in the Gospel. III, 1343. If you are master of gold, you make of it what is good; if you are its slave, it makes of you what is evil. V, 955. To wish to grow rich through another’s poverty is utterly unjust. V, 1591. Let the rich man know that he is a traveler, and that he entered riches as though entering an inn; he does not take away with him what he found in the inn. V, 114.

How the rich and the poor can mutually share and lessen their burdens in turn. V, 899. By giving to the poor, the rich man lessens the burden. V, 414. Let the rich give alms readily. IV, 549. The Lord made both rich and poor: through the one who has, he helps the needy; through the one who has not, he tests the one who has. V, 243, 523; IV, 1649, 1650. It is falsely said that the rich have done good for themselves as long as they lived. IV, 561. If you keep it, it will not be yours; if you distribute it, it will be yours. V, 961. The foolish and luxurious rich man, who plans to store up or feast rather than distribute. V, 529, 629. Let the rich man fear that, while wishing to be a predator, he may become the prey of a greater, and that the smaller fish may be devoured by the larger. IV, 422. Let the rich use what is superfluous in such a way that they give the poor what is necessary. V, 413. The superfluous possessions of the rich are the necessities of the poor: when they possess what is superfluous, they possess another’s property. IV, 1922. God questions the rich and the poor in their hearts, not in their chest and house. IV, 545.

What the Apostle wishes to command the rich. V, 521. The rich must beware of pride. V, 112, 956. Praise the humble rich man; praise the rich man who is poor. V, 112, 113. The rich are proud in spirit and, because of their abundance, do not seek eternal things. IV, 1814. The rich do not consider themselves equal to others. IV, 920. Why the rich and noble ought not to be proud against the poor and lowly. III, 1276. Let the rich man not disdain being called the poor man’s brother. V, 217. The rich man who despises the poor is wretched when life has ended. V, 249, 250. Rich and poor are equal in birth and death. V, 412. Let the rich man be humble; let him rejoice more because he is a Christian than because he is rich. V, 217. Those who flatter the rich. V, 250. The rich—that is, the proud—must be emptied; and the hungry—that is, the humble—must be filled. V, 1315. The rich man who is not lifted up by his many financial resources is poor. IV, 545, 1057. If the rich man therefore considers himself great, he is proud and needy: he swells in the flesh but begs in the heart; he is inflated, not full. V, 215. The mind that conquers its riches is greater than its riches, not by desiring them but by despising them. V, 215.

The foolish labor of proud rich men. III, 882. The rich labor more bitterly in their thoughts than the poor in their work. X, 1578. A comparison between the greedy rich man and the peaceful poor man. VII, 114. The rich man who is secure in conscience sleeps more safely on the ground than the rich man in purple. V, 216. The rich, less secure amid the disturbances of the world, not only lost their possessions but perished themselves because of them. V, 217. Proud rich men are compared with ostriches. III, 881, 882. The foolishness of the rich in caring for burial. IV, 555. The humble and merciful rich are the true poor. V, 113. The ancient patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others—were rich. II, 686. The rich of the earth worship Christ, but are not filled with his wisdom and justice. IV, 1726. They are not filled with Christ’s body and blood. II, 566.

The rich of this world were not despised by Christ. V, 216. They are saved with difficulty. V, 521. How their conversion takes place. III, 882. It is easy for God to bring the rich into the kingdom of heaven. II, 494. The rich do not accept correction. IV, 920. It is difficult for them not to contract more sins than others. IV, 1731. Which rich are not heard by God. IV, 1083.

The Pelagians falsely taught that a rich man remaining in his riches could not enter the kingdom of God, and so forth. II, 686, 687, 688. The Pelagian doctrine was that baptized rich people, unless they renounced everything, were not credited with any good they appeared to do, and could not possess the kingdom of God. II, 686, 687, 688; X, 334. Augustine does not compel the rich to eat the food of the poor. V, 414. Rich people who build churches or monasteries are cedars of Lebanon, in which sparrows make their nests. IV, 1371, 1372. [Col. 0246] Rich and very distinguished persons of both sexes were exalted by the glory of martyrdom. II, 691.

The idea of the Christian rich man. II, 691. Every rich man is God’s beggar. V, 686. If the rich man does not have God, what does he have? V, 492, 521. Some rich people are numbered among the Lord’s poor. IV, 1197.

The rich man in the parable was a wicked Jew. V, 249. Why he was condemned. V, 962, 1651. He was digesting in hell what he had eaten in heaven. IV, 561. In hell he became merciful too late. V, 113. His punishments. VI, 719. The flame by which he was tormented was spiritual. VII, 725. How the flame of hell, the bosom of Abraham, and the other matters related in the story of the rich man are to be understood is scarcely, or never, discovered. III, 376. Various matters concerning the rich man who was buried in hell. IV, 561. Comparison of the rich man and Lazarus. V, 217, 249, 530, 611, 911, 1518, 1650.

Divorce. The law of the world concerning divorce differs from the law of the Gospel. X, 420.

Nothing is lasting in which there is an ending. VII, 359.

The office of teaching is highly excellent. III, 18. The office of teachers is dangerous; the condition of hearers is safer. V, 155. To learn, the sweetness of truth ought to invite us; to teach, the necessity of charity ought to compel us. VI, 161. Augustine loves learning more than teaching. VI, 161, 170. The precepts of teaching are not superfluous, although God makes people teachers. III, 103. God established that people should be taught by people, not by angels—why. III, 18. Some of the saints are taught by God alone. IV, 1486. Very few have been granted the ability to receive the doctrine of salvation without the ministry of any human being. X, 1023. After judgment, a person will not be taught by another person; rather, all will be taught by God. III, 1278.

The duty of a Christian teacher. III, 91. It is the teacher’s duty to ask God for understanding of the mysteries, so that he may be able to answer those who ask about the faith. V, 619. Whoever honors a teacher honors truth. X, 495. Those who teach what we do not know must be endured with the greatest patience. X, 526. A person who is wicked is not a teacher. I, 1223. One who teaches good things while doing evil is necessary, is a hireling, and is of some benefit. V, 1169. Let those who are to receive something from you become attentive to your conduct. II, 437. “I do not want you first to teach something that must later be unlearned, so that you may teach what is true.” II, 437. Whoever does not do what he teaches others, if he is sometimes useful, does not do it himself, but God does. III, 1305. Wicked teachers are thorns bearing a cluster of grapes. III, 1730. To terrify and not to teach is wicked domination. II, 322. One must teach without pride and envy. III, 18. A teacher must most carefully guard against the vice of pride. II, 1090. This is especially necessary for one whom exaltation easily invades. II, 1090. The teacher’s consolation. II, 1090. We ought not to wish for the ignorance of others merely so that we may teach what we know. II, 1090.

God teaches in one way, a human being or an angel in another. X, 130. The human teacher is an external cultivator of the tree. III, 1610. The sound of words strikes the ears; the teacher is within. III, 2004. The human teacher’s voice strikes the bodily ear; God strikes the ear of the soul. IX, 697. Christ teaches within; a human being admonishes. I, 1219, 1220. We have Christ as our teacher within. III, 1557. He who teaches hearts has his chair in heaven. III, 2004. How God teaches through grace. X, 368. The school of God the Father is very hidden. X, 970. When God wishes to teach, he first gives understanding, without which a person cannot speak of matters pertaining to divine teaching. IV, 1548. God teaches in such a way that we know what must be known by opening the truth; he teaches in such a way that we do what must be done by inspiring sweetness. IV, 1549. Although grace is freely given, exhortation to teaching is nevertheless necessary. X, 1023. Why the Father does not teach everyone to come to Christ. X, 971. We are taught by God even when we listen to human beings. II, 874. And also when we learn the things that pertain to true piety. VI, 161. Who should be called teachable. IX, 193. Holy teachers are children of the Church by learning, and fathers by teaching. X, 1406. There are some matters on which even the most learned and best defenders of the Catholic rule do not always agree among themselves, while preserving the structure of the faith; and one says something about a single matter better and more truly than another. X, 655. To what extent the authority of holy teachers ought to prevail. II, 277, 339, 628, 873. Jerome considers it dangerous to judge the opinions of the teachers of the churches and to prefer one to another. II, 904. Teachers are called mountains, and so forth. III, 1380.

Who is truly learned and wise. III, 62. See Teacher. The learned in the Church are precious stones. V, 223. They lie in darkness if they are not part of the Church’s adornment. V, 223. They lose their value when they do not have charity. V, 223. Some learned men think they are nothing unless they try to tear apart the labors of others. VI, 441. Why God sometimes permits learned men to be mistaken in certain matters. IX, 129. Some learned men prefer to be learned rather than just. IV, 1503.

Two kinds of doctrines among the pagans. III, 50. Every doctrine concerns either things or signs. III, 19. The multiplicity of doctrines is a flood of waters. IV, 269, 270. Many doctrines are either superfluous or harmful; one is useful and salutary. II, 1030. [Col. 0247] Socrates taught the remaining doctrine easily to those who had been persuaded to desire nothing more than to be good men. II, 1030. Secular doctrines are husks on which pigs feed. III, 1344. Saving doctrine consists partly in things to be believed and partly in things to be understood. VI, 496. Christ’s doctrine commands humility. V, 876; VI, 413. It condemns corruption of morals. VII, 64, 74. How doctrine can be called grace. X, 367. The doctrine and law of God, although holy, just, and good, nevertheless kills if the Spirit does not give life. II, 983. Aids to doctrine, when administered through a human being, benefit the soul when God works so that they may benefit it. III, 104. God has placed the doctrine of truth in the chair of unity. II, 403. Doctrine once received must not be communicated with a bitter heart. V, 300. Doctrine that is open is like honey; but what is expressed concerning the more hidden sacraments is like a honeycomb. IV, 1566.

“Doech” is interpreted as movements. IV, 601.

Dogmas are the settled opinions of sects. III, 1326.

The salvation of members of one’s household must be secured with every vigilance. V, 581.

What pain is. III, 364. Pain is twofold: that of the flesh and that of the soul. VII, 424. What produces pain in the soul and in the body. VIII, 557.

What bodily pain is. III, 132, 364. Pain of the flesh is an offense of the soul arising from the flesh, and a certain disagreement with its suffering. VII, 424, 711. The pain itself that is called bodily pain cannot exist without the soul. IV, 1110. No fear of the flesh, as it were, precedes pain of the flesh. VII, 424. Bodily pain is harmful because it attempts to tear apart what was one. I, 1017. The pain felt by animals indicates that they desire unity. I, 1305. Pain of the flesh is a judgment of life, not evidence of death. VII, 712. The death of the flesh does not always follow pain of the flesh. VII, 710. Why pain of the flesh kills. VII, 710.

Pain of the soul. III, 132. The soul’s pain is disagreement with those things that have happened against our will. VII, 424. It is called sadness. VII, 424. Pain of the soul is preceded by fear, which is not in the flesh. VII, 424. Pain and fear are two torturers of the soul; they do not torture simultaneously but alternate in causing torment. V, 687. Pain and pleasure are two incentives to sin. V, 1286.

Pain can exist wherever desire can exist. VII, 711. Whatever a person possessed only with enticing love, he does not lose without burning pain. VII, 744. Pain exists only in good natures. VIII, 557. Pain is testimony to a good that has been taken away and to a good that remains. VII, 641. Just as joy over an abandoned good, in sin, testifies to an evil will, so pain over a lost good, in punishment, testifies to a good nature. VII, 641. Souls have no pains except those outside God. I, 699.

One pain is fruitful, another fruitless. IV, 621. Saving pain is the pain caused by a physician when cutting. IV, 1489. The pain of incision must be endured so that we may be healed. V, 1270. Endure medicinal pain, thinking of the future healing. IV, 1319. The pain arising in the hearts of the devout, whom the conduct of the wicked persecutes, benefits those who suffer—why. VII, 614. The pain of the soul is always alleviated. I, 698. Pain over the loss of things in which a person rejoiced while enjoying them is the fire through which he will be saved. VI, 153, 155, 216; VII, 744, 746. The pain of this life passes; that of the other life will not end. VII, 658. From him we receive the strength of patience, so that we are not broken by pain; from him we receive victory over desire, so that we are not carried away by pleasure. IV, 1577. For the image of God, it is punishment to be compared with the condition of animals in suffering. X, 1563. It is more fitting that the unjust person should suffer in punishment than rejoice in sin. VII, 641. Everyone flees pain more than he seeks pleasure. VI, 25. Not to suffer pain at all is evidence of savagery in the soul and insensibility in the body. VII, 415, 417. It matters whether someone does not suffer because of health or because of insensibility. V, 1528. Many have endured pains through vice, not through virtue. V, 1254, 1287.

Deceit is present when one thing is done and another pretended. III, 1446; IV, 86, 143; V, 45, 739, 1561. To speak deceitfully is to bring one thing forth with the lips and close another within the breast. V, 123. The term “deceit” is used figuratively. V, 45. God never approves deceit, but permits it. IV, 1400. The deceit of a powerful evil person is compared with a razor. V, 421. Many less proficient in Latin used *dolus* for *dolor*—“pain.” III, 1466.

Deceitfulness is a kind of fraud: expressing one thing in words while thinking another. IV, 581.

The deceitful person does not follow Christ. V, 603.

Domiducus, a god. VII, 188.

A person desires to rule over others. III, 27. And this is intolerable pride. III, 27. See Servitude. The desire to rule is the first vice: taking pleasure in one’s own power. V, 644. From what time the lust for ruling began especially. VII, 90. It is harmful. VII, 90. It devastates mortal hearts. VII, 644. Fathers are more obliged on account of their ruling than servants are to endure on account of their serving. VII, 644. Just as humility benefits those who serve, so pride harms those who rule. VII, 644. Domination was included among the praises of the Romans. VII, 155.

*Dominicarius.* II, 146.

To celebrate the *dominicum* and to come to the *dominicum*. V, 205, and note (b). To conduct the *dominicum* and the assembly. IX, 643.

The Lord’s Day. V, 916. It began to have its own festival with the Lord’s Resurrection. II, 215. On the Lord’s Days we pray standing and sing “hallelujah”—with what meaning. II, 218. Augustine does not know whether people everywhere stand when praying on these days. II, 220. On these days someone would fast not without scandal. II, 136, 143, 148, 150.

The Lord’s son. V, 1357.

The Lord God alone. III, 382. God is truly Lord because he does not need a servant, while the servant needs him. II, 527. The Lord was worshipped by the Fathers in the angels who represented his person. V, 65. See God.

Any human being may be called “lord,” because of the service of charity. II, 94. Human beings are not very truly lords, since they need servants. IV, 872. What masters owe servants, and servants masters. I, 1329. Do not fear the human master outside you; fear the evil master within you—your desire. IV, 163. Unjust and difficult masters must be endured. IV, 736. In the customary form of letters, even non-Christians are called “lords” in greetings. X, 349. The person who is not entangled in desire is master of his own possessions. IV, 544.

“The Lord be with you.” VIII, 1049.

Domitian, most cruel. VII, 168, 614. The greater part of Nero’s reign. IX, 323, 328.

Domitius, a god. VII, 188.

A human being is the tamer of beasts; God is the tamer of human beings. V, 375.

“Domnaedius” is said to mean “lord of houses.” IV, 429, note 3; IX, 316, note 4.

Domnio. II, 100.

*Domnus.* V, 643, 967. “Lord, poor man.” V, 113.

A house is used to mean both a building and its inhabitants. V, 1503. It is used for a city. VII, 462. For a bedroom or tent. III, 494. How a house and a tabernacle differ. IV, 202. Hence a marble house is bad, and a smoky house good. V, 929.

The inhabitants themselves are God’s house. V, 1477. Be God’s house, and it will be your house. IV, 252. The Church is the house of our prayers; we ourselves are God’s house. V, 1471. How this house is built. V, 1471. God’s house is built by singing, founded by believing, raised up by hoping, completed by loving, and dedicated at the end of the age. V, 178, 1471, 1476. The Church is God’s house, outside which God does not hear anyone unto eternal life. IV, 478, 1721. You enter your own house in order to inhabit it; you enter God’s house in order to be inhabited by it. IV, 1721. All the faithful and the angels make one house of God and one city. IV, 1668, 1669. Whoever is joined together in charity, as living stones, belongs to God’s house. IV, 1721. God’s house is still being built: by growing, it has occupied many nations and will occupy them all. IV, 1228. What it means to love the beauty of God’s house. V, 116.

Donatianus, primate of the province of Byzacena. II, 759, 780, 891.

Donatianus, a Donatist bishop. IX, 326, 555.

Donatianus, a Maximianist. IV, 376.

Donatus, proconsul of Africa. II, 366.

Donatus, former proconsul. II, 427, 428.

Donatus, who voluntarily left the monastery with his brother, against Augustine’s wishes. II, 228.

Donatus, a rebaptized deacon. II, 536.

Donatus, one of the Fathers of the Council of Zerta. II, 577.

Donatus. VI, 714.

Donatus. V, 1587. The false miracle of Donatus. III, 1501.

Two Donatuses, one of Casae and the other of Carthage. IX, 646, 662. See below. Donatus of Casis Nigris, author of the schism. II, 813. And leader of the Donatist heresy. VIII, 43. Donatus is sometimes a precious stone by reason of doctrine or eloquence. V, 223. Lifted up by pride, he made a party for himself. V, 279.

Donatus, a Donatist bishop. IX, 528, 529, 555.

Donatus of Bagai, a schismatic. II, 175, note. A Donatist pseudo-martyr. III, 1483.

Donatus of Belma, bishop. IV, 381.

Donatus of Carthage, a schismatic. II, 175.

Donatus of Cebresuta, bishop. IV, 380.

Donatus of Cibaliana. IX, 232.

Donatus of Fiscianum, bishop. IV, 380.

Donatus of Macomades, formerly a Donatist bishop and later a bishop among the Catholics. IX, 473.

Donatus of Masculi, a traditor. IX, 511, 612; Appendix 773. A schismatic. II, 197.

Donatus, presbyter of the village of Mutugenna. II, 756. Augustine attempts to overcome his great obstinacy in the schism. II, 754.

Donatus of Sabrata, bishop. IV, 381; IX, 507, 528, 530.

Donatus of Samurda, bishop. IV, 381.

Donatus, a Donatist bishop in the place of Turris. IX, 618.

Donatus Urbanus. IX, 510.

[Col. 0249] Donatus, from whom the Donatist schism arose. IV, 134, 177, 347, 1925; VI, 201. Two Donatuses belonging to the same schism: the first, from whom it begins, was the bishop of Casis Nigris in Numidia; the other, after Majorinus, was the second bishop of the party of Donatus of Carthage. I, 617, 618, and note (a). Some wish the Donatists to have been called after him. VIII, 43. The Donatists were so called either after Donatus of Carthage or Donatus of Casis. IX, 468. The party of Donatus in Africa. V, 49, 55, 268, 280, 288, 291. It arose from Numidia. V, 293. At first, at Carthage, it was called the party of Majorinus. II, 302. The party of Donatus arose through the agency of Secundus of Tigisis, a heretic. V, 293. The apparent leaders of the Donatists were Donatus, Majorinus, and Parmenianus. IX, 96. The proud authors of the schism of the party of Donatus. V, 304.

Donatus of Casis Nigris was the first to set up altar against altar. IX, 468. He was the first to sacrifice outside the Church. IX, 469. At Rome he was convicted—Caecilianus still being a deacon—of having created a schism at Carthage. IX, 637, 642. He is said to have greatly strengthened the Carthaginian heresy. IX, 468, 469. The Donatists proclaim Donatus above all others. IX, 664. They call him the ornament of the Church of Carthage and a man of martyrial glory. IX, 664. They greatly praise his eloquence. IX, 448. Donatus is said to have performed wonders. IX, 428. The Donatists were accustomed to swear by the white hairs of Donatus. IV, 134. In the clearest voices they used to say to him, “Well done, well done, good leader, illustrious leader.” IV, 870. Whether Donatus is to be understood as the prince of Tyre. IX, 423, note 3. The principal places of the Donatists were Bagai and Thamugadi. IV, 177.

The Donatists. A council was held in the house of Urbanus Donatus. II, 197. Or in that of Urbanus Carisius near the city of Cirta. IX, Appendix 774. It consisted of eleven or twelve factious bishops, presided over by Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia. II, 161. He leaves the present and confessed traditors to be judged by God, and permits them to remain in their episcopal sees. II, 161, 162, 164; IX, Appendix 775. Especially Donatus of Masculi, Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae, and Donatus of Calama. II, 197. He condemned the absent through the judgments of those present. II, 161, 162, 164, 264. Secundus of Tigisis feared that suspicion of treason was sufficiently probable against him. II, 162, 164. By him Silvanus was ordained bishop of Cirta. II, 197. When Mensurius had stated his case before the Emperor concerning the deacon concealed in his house, he was ordered to return, but was unable to reach Carthage. IX, Appendix 775. After Maxentius restored liberty to the Christians, Botrus and Celesius, wishing to be ordained at Carthage, arranged for ordination to be carried out in the absence of the Numidian bishops, by neighboring bishops alone. IX, Appendix 775. Caecilianus was chosen by the suffrage of the entire people, and was ordained bishop when Felix of Autumnita laid hands upon him. IX, Appendix 775. The disappointed aspirants, Lucilla and the elders to whom Mensurius had entrusted money, fabricated charges against Caecilianus so that his ordination might be declared invalid. IX, Appendix 776. The Numidian bishops who had held the council at Cirta were summoned as traditors. IX, Appendix 776. Then another perverse and wicked council was assembled at Carthage. II, 160, 163, 164. Seventy schismatic bishops gathered. II, 160, 166, 579; IX, 426, 639, 640, 684. And traditors as well. II, 164; IX, 511. Against Caecilianus. II, 172. Secundus of Tigisis, the primate, presided. II, 166; IX, 519. Lucilla fomented this council. II, 172. She was a Spanish woman. IX, 395. Extremely wealthy. II, 167; IX, 37. And extremely factious. II, 167; IX, 37. Caecilianus, while still a deacon, had offended her against ecclesiastical discipline. II, 167, 172; IX, 37, 426; Appendix 775. Lucilla corrupted the minds of the bishops with money, as the deacon Nundinarius testified in the proceedings before Zenophilus, the consular governor. II, 167, 168; IX, 426; Appendix 798. She also purchased Caecilianus’s condemnation. IX, 426, 443. She gave four hundred *folles*. IX, 513; Appendix 798, 799. The bishops present at this council had been bought and incited, and were also displeased that they themselves had not ordained the bishop at Carthage. II, 168; IX, 26. Caecilianus refused to visit the lodging of his colleagues. II, 164. He perceived that they had been perverted by his enemies against the truth of his case. II, 163, 168. And he always regarded them as suspect. II, 163, 165, 168. He reserved his case intact for the churches overseas. II, 164, 167, 168. He sent word to the Numidian bishops that, if there were anything that could be proved against him, an accuser should come forward and prove it; he declared himself ready to be ordained again if Felix had contributed nothing to it. IX, Appendix 776. The Numidian bishops did not communicate with Caecilianus. IX, Appendix 776. At that time nothing had been fabricated by his enemies against Caecilianus himself; rather, he had been defamed on account of his ordainer, whom they falsely called a traditor. IX, Appendix 776. The council condemned Caecilianus, although innocent and absent, because he had refused to come to them—as though he had been ordained by traditors, and because it was said that, while he was a deacon, he had prohibited food from being brought to martyrs held in custody. II, 161, 162, 163, 166; IX, 639. The customary form of judicial proceedings was not observed. IX, 26, 37. The schismatics had given the people an intervener from their own communion. II, 177. Caecilianus was deposed, and another was ordained. IX, 37. This occurred at Lucilla’s insistence, inflamed with furious hatred. IX, 512. They raised up Majorinus against Caecilianus. [Col. 0250] II, 161. And they ordained him. IX, 469, 553. Majorinus had been a lector in Caecilianus’s diaconate and was a member of Lucilla’s household. IX, Appendix 776.

The party of Donatus arose against the Catholic Church from the schism at Carthage. IX, 637. It is reported that throughout Africa the traditors were condemned at Carthage. II, 164. The Donatists charge the Catholics with the crime of treason. II, 264, 396, 403, 578, 588. They circulated false imperial indulgences in favor of the schism. II, 398. Communion with the whole world remains with Caecilianus. II, 168. Constantine arranged for three thousand *folles* to be counted out to Caecilianus through Ursus, financial administrator of Africa. IX, Appendix 777. He also instructed him that, if he needed any money, he should request it from Heraclides, the manager of his estates. IX, Appendix 777. Constantine entrusted Anulinus, the proconsul, and Patricius, the deputy of the prefects, with the task of restraining those who, as he had learned, were corrupting the people of the Catholic Church. IX, Appendix 777. He made the clergy exempt from all public duties. IX, Appendix 777.

Certain Donatists, having gathered a multitude of the people with them, thought that Caecilian should be opposed. IX, App. 778. They refer Caecilian’s case to the Emperor. II, 302, 310, 327, 329, 331, 392, 580, 794. Through Anulinus the proconsul, they sent the crimes that they alleged against Caecilian by bringing accusations. II, 302; IX, 554, 555, 610, 626, 627, 631, 636, 640, 679, 695, 739. They present two petitions to be directed to Constantine. IX, App. 778.
