Petitions of the bishops of Majorinus’s party to the Emperor Constantine. IX, App. 778. The Emperor does not dare to judge the case of a bishop. II, 399. The Donatists choose to conduct the case against Caecilian before two overseas churches. II, 169. They ask the Emperor for judges. II, 161; IX, 27. From Gaul. II, 198. The Emperor consented. IX, 27, 40. And he writes to Miltiades that a council should be held at Rome. IX, App. 778. A council is compelled to meet at Rome. II, 166, 399; IX, 27. In the house of Fausta in the Lateran, in the year when Constantine was consul for the third time and Licinius for the third time, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, a Friday. IX, App. 779. The names of the bishops who took part in the council. IX, App. 778, 779. Melchiades, the Roman bishop, presided over it. II, 161, 399; IX, 40. Constantine orders ten bishops from each side to sail to Rome to conduct the case. IX, 637, App. 778. Anulinus replies that both parties have assembled and promised to send bishops. IX, 637. Donatus of Carthage was sent to the episcopal tribunal of Melchiades against Caecilian. IX, 662. When conducting the case against Caecilian, he proves nothing. The case of Caecilian was examined at Rome by order of the Emperor Constantine, in the episcopal tribunal of Melchiades, the Roman bishop, and of the other Gallic and Italian bishops. IX, 637. A petition is produced. II, 167. The Donatists can prove nothing against Caecilian. II, 161, 166, 167. Donatus of Casis Nigrae was convicted in the presence of the assembly of having created a schism at Carthage while Caecilian was still a deacon. IX, 647. Donatus was condemned in person. II, 399; IX, 637, 642. Therefore he was struck by the sentence. IX, App. 779. Caecilian is pronounced innocent and confirmed in the episcopate. II, 167, 399. Caecilian, condemned in his absence at Carthage by the judgment of Secundus of Tigisis, was later acquitted in person by the judgment of Melchiades at the Roman council. IX, 779, 519, 645, 661; App. 779. The sentence of Miltiades. IX, App. 779. The bishops Eunomius and Olympius, sent to Africa, declare where the Catholic Church is and strengthen the sentence pronounced in favor of Caecilian. IX, App. 779. The seditious party of Donatus did not allow this to happen, and daily disturbances arose from factional zeal. IX, App. 780. They denounce Felix of Aptunga, Caecilian’s ordainer, to Constantine as a traditor. II, 400. After Caecilian had been cleared at Rome, Felix is ordered to be cleared in Africa. IX, 594, Retr. 610; App. 780. Felix is acquitted of the charge of traditio by the judgment of Aelianus the proconsul. II, 162, 164, 400, 492, 582; IX, 532. Ingentius confesses that he had fabricated a false charge against Felix. II, 582. The proconsular proceedings by which Felix was acquitted. IX, App. 780.

Donatus asked that he be permitted to return, but not to approach Carthage. IX, App. 779. Through Filuminus, his supporter, it was represented to the Emperor that, for the sake of peace, Caecilian should be kept at Brixia. IX, App. 780. The Donatists maintained that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor’s judgment, at the accusation of his superiors, to live in exile at Brixia. IX, 539, 541, 664, 666, 684, 695. The Catholics proved that this was false. IX, 539, 541, 664, 666, 684, 695. Caecilian was not condemned but kept at Brixia for the sake of peace. IX, 685. Donatus returned voluntarily and first to Carthage. IX, App. 780. When Caecilian heard this, he hastened to his own people, and thus the factions were renewed. IX, App. 780.

Donatus believes that an appeal should be made from the bishops. IX, App. 779. The Donatists do not accept the episcopal judges given to them by Constantine. IX, 426. Why. IX, App. 785. Later they accuse them before Constantine as unjust judges. II, 169, 264, 303, 399; IX, 426. The Christian Emperor did not dare to regard their disorderly and deceitful complaints in such a way that he himself would judge the decision of the bishops who had sat at Rome. II, 169. He appointed other bishops. II, 169. [Col. 0251] The Council of Arles is summoned to take place before the day of the Kalends of August. IX, App. 785. Constantine writes to Ablavius, the vicar of Africa, ordering him to command the parties between whom the dispute existed to go to Arles for the council. IX, App. 785. Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse, is ordered to proceed to the Council of Arles. IX, App. 786. The names of the bishops who took part in the Council of Arles. IX, App. 786. Constantine arranges for the matter between the Donatists and Caecilian to be more carefully examined and settled at the Council of Arles. II, 161, 169, 198. Caecilian was acquitted at the Council of Arles. IX, 41, 640. What was done at the Council of Arles. IX, App. 786. Constantine, detesting the Donatists’ obstinacy, orders the bishops who had taken part in the Council of Arles to return to their provinces. IX, App. 788. But he orders the Donatists to be brought to his court, so that they might live there and make provision there for their own death. IX, App. 789.

The Donatists appeal from the ecclesiastical judgment to Constantine. II, 161, 198, 310, 327, 794; IX, 27, App. 426. At the Donatists’ request, Constantine had granted an episcopal judgment both at Rome and at Arles. They accuse the first before Constantine; from the second they appeal to him. IX, 326. They approach Constantine himself so that he might decide that Caecilian’s case should be examined even after the Council of Arles. IX, 41. Constantine orders the parties to meet at Rome to conduct the case. II, 169; IX, App. 789. I do not know for what reason Caecilian did not appear. II, 168. When the same people petitioned him, the Emperor ordered them to proceed to Milan. Some withdrew; the Emperor had the rest brought there under guard by his officials. II, 169. Constantine orders Ingentius, convicted of falsehood, to be sent to his court, so that it could be made clear to the Donatists who were petitioning that they were vainly trying to bring Caecilian into disrepute. IX, 540. The judgment of Constantine held at Milan. IX, App. 790. With both parties present, the Emperor judges Caecilian innocent and declares the Donatists slanderers. II, 169, 399; IX, 640, 647, 648, 649, 650, 664, 685. Constantine’s sentence. IX, 647. The codex in which Constantine’s judgment is read has neither date nor consular year. IX, 664. When the Emperor heard the parties, the Donatists were found and condemned as slanderers. IX, 371, 429. Caecilian was acquitted both by ecclesiastical and imperial judgments. IX, 615, 626, 643, 681, 687, 695. Caecilian was condemned once in his absence and acquitted three times in his presence. IX, 362, 668. Caecilian was acquitted by an overseas judgment. IX, 503, 533. Constantine’s letter to Eumalius concerning Caecilian’s vindication. IX, 687. And to Probianus. IX, 540, 649. The Donatists said that the overseas judges had been corrupted by Caecilian. IX, 533. And that Constantine himself had been corrupted by favor. IX, 41, 533. The Donatists’ murmuring against the judges by whom they had been condemned. IX, 41, 42. In Caecilian’s case the Donatists prefer human traditions to divine Scripture. IV, 1924. The Donatists were condemned three times by the judges whom they themselves had requested. IV, 383.

The Donatists do not cease even after being defeated so many times. II, 400. Although Caecilian was pronounced innocent by the Emperor at Milan, they nevertheless lie that Caecilian himself was condemned in that judgment. II, 794. They remained in the same obstinacy of fury. IX, 426, 429. Defeated everywhere, they rebaptize. IX, 27. The Donatists did not wish to be corrected even after being overcome. IX, 39. Constantine promises that he will come to Africa to judge between Caecilian and Donatus concerning the schism that had arisen in Africa. IX, App. 789. Constantine was the first to enact many measures against the Donatist error. IX, 329. Constantine ordered the basilicas to be taken away from the Donatists. IX, 326. Constantine ordered their meeting places to be claimed for the treasury. IX, App. 791. The Donatists present Constantine with a petition in which they say that they will in no way communicate with his bishop, that scoundrel, and that they are prepared to endure whatever he might wish to do to them. IX, 648. Constantine judges that the Donatists’ insolence should rather be tolerated than punished. IX, App. 791. Constantine wrote to Valerius, the vicar, concerning the remission of the Donatists’ exile and their fury being left to God as avenger. IX, 648, 685, 687. After the Donatists occupied a basilica that Constantine had ordered to be built in the city of Constantina, he grants them another place belonging to the treasury and orders a basilica to be erected at the treasury’s expense. IX, App. 792.

The Donatists’ petitions to Julian the Apostate. IV, 374. From him the Donatist bishops living in exile obtain permission to return. IX, App. 802. The Donatist bishops’ dreadful crimes after their freedom had been restored to them by Julian. IX, 803. The Catholics send envoys to Honorius. IX, App. 811. The memorandum given to the envoys. IX, App. 811. The law of Honorius confirming the constitutions previously issued against heretics and declaring that they also apply to the Donatists. IX, 522, App. 815. The same emperor’s law repealing the law by which freedom of choice had been granted to heretics. IX, App. 815.

Donatists. The universal Council of Carthage in Africa, seeking to deal gently and peacefully with the Donatists, sends envoys to explain to them that nothing just can be brought forward against the Church. IX, App. 810. A second Council of Carthage [Col. 0252], from all Africa, decides that the Donatists should be summoned. IX, App. 810. The form of the conference with the Donatists. IX, App. 810. The petition given by the Council of Carthage to Septimius, the proconsul, concerning the conference with the Donatists. IX, 626, App. 811. After the Council had been held, the Catholics invite the Donatists to peace and to confer together peacefully, as had been decreed at the Council of Carthage in the year 403, on 25 August. II, 306, 308. The command of Honorius concerning the conference to be held. IX, App. 816. Marcellinus’s first edict, by which the bishops of both parties are summoned after it has been sent through the provinces. IX, App. 817. Why the earthly authorities provided the Donatists with a place and time for the examination. X, 1054, 1055, 1056.

The Catholics propose the conditions of the conference to the Donatist bishops. II, 488, etc. They promise that they will not seek episcopal honors if it is shown that the Church has remained only in Donatus’s party. II, 488. The Donatists’ formal notices. II, 501. The Catholics respond to the Donatists’ formal notices. II, 490. The Donatists had nowhere wished to confer with the Catholics, as though they were fleeing from speaking with sinners. II, 401. The conference was held with the Donatists. I, 646, 650; V, 1582, 1586, 1590. At the conference, the Donatists refuse to sit with the Catholics, although the presiding judge had offered them seats, lest they be defiled by them. V, 599. By the very excuses with which they avoided sitting with the Catholics, they were convicted of not even having had the right to enter. V, 599. At the conference the Donatists insisted that the case should not be heard, on account of which the bishops from both parties had been compelled to assemble. II, 578. They said and recited many things against themselves. II, 579, 580, 582. They confessed that they had nothing to say against the Catholic Church. II, 579, 580.

The Donatists were defeated. VI, 696. Condemned by their own judgment. V, 901. The Donatists, already caught, say: “We do not wish to contend.” V, 286. They professed that Caecilian had been accused before the Emperor Constantine by his predecessors. II, 580. When they said that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor, they were convicted of lying. II, 580. They said that Marcellinus, the presiding judge at the Carthaginian conference, had been corrupted by a reward. II, 577. Especially by Augustine, so that he would judge in his own favor. V, 901. The Donatists’ lies. II, 577, 579, 580, 582. The Donatists convicted of lying. II, 577. The Donatists remained obstinate in the schism after the conference. II, 161, 170, 172, 265, 309, 400; V, 286, 899. How many crimes they are guilty of. V, 900. What should be answered to them when they say: “I do not communicate in the sins of others, nor ought I to bear one whom I know to be evil.” V, 900. I think that even the devil, if he were defeated so many times by the authority of the judge whom he had voluntarily chosen, would not be so shameless as to persist in that case. II, 309. The Donatists resist by raging or by becoming sluggish, like the frenzied or the lethargic. II, 312. Augustine calls them a heretical, incurable, and contentious soul. V, 901. And yet he immediately orders that they be treated gently and that insults be avoided. V, 902. The Council of thirty Donatist bishops after the Carthaginian conference. IX, 736. The foolish excuse of certain obstinate Donatists. V, 1596.

Two evils are charged against the Donatists: error concerning the question of baptism and separation. IX, 497. The Donatists are convicted of schism. IX, 226, 233, 517, 519. By what they are convicted. IX, 306. The clergy sent by Secundus of Tigisis did not wish to approach the clergy of Carthage; they appointed a Visitor and were received by Lucilla. V, 293. The Donatists are guilty of schism, whatever they say or invent about traditio and persecution. IX, 387, 388, 392, 394, 395, 493. By the definitions of Cresconius they are both heretics and schismatics. IX, 469, 470, 471, 472. It is evident that the Donatists do not communicate with the Churches founded outside Africa through apostolic labor. IX, 629. They repel Catholics from their communion. V, 288. They never wished to celebrate the day of Epiphany with the Catholics. V, 1033. They thought that the sacred places and instruments touched by Catholics had to be cleansed. II, 414. See the notes. They do not accept letters of communion from Catholic unity. II, 160, 170, 173. They vainly attempt to affirm that they are Catholics on the testimony of the blessed Cyprian. IX, 741. They maintained that the Orientals belonged to their communion. IX, 576. Fortunius maintained that the Council of Sardica had sent letters of Donatus’s communion to the African bishops. II, 176. The name Donatus was found among the bishops of the Council of Sardica. IX, 576. What should be thought about this. IX, 516, 576. It is not established that the Donatus mentioned in the council’s letter was that founder of the schism. II, 176. The Donatists cut themselves off from unity by execrable sacrilege. IX, 256, 258. The Donatist schism is sacrilegious. IX, 293. Unjust. IX, 26, 28, 41, 49, 121, 585. Separation is the greatest and most evident crime. IX, 264, 266, 267. The Donatists, unwilling to communicate with all nations, are pressed on this point. III, 1464. Augustine’s dilemma addressed to the Donatists. II, 592.

The Donatists were with the Catholics in baptism, in the Creed, and in the other sacraments of the Lord, but not in the spirit of unity. II, 343. The Donatists’ mind is alienated from unity. V, 1583. They lack charity. V, 1256. That charity is not in Donatus’s party is shown by the very schism they created. IX, 311, 312, 313. The Donatists are signified by the raven that did not return to the ark. III, 1434. They are urged to return to unity. [Col. 0253] III, 1434, 1435, 1436. The Donatists are refuted. V, 41, 73, 74, 267, 286, 313, 628, 722, 763, 768, 991, 1126, 1161, 1228, 1234, 1235, 1256, 1326, 1350. The Donatists cannot excuse their separation. V, 304. They have no cause for separation. IX, 62, 177, 179, 254, 256, 265, 266, 279. They severed themselves from the Catholic Church without cause. II, 173, 195, 224, 240, 297, 298, 314, 328; IX, 130. The Donatists had no cause for withdrawing from unity, or their cause was rash. IX, 50, 130, 131. How they left the Church. III, 2000. And why. IX, 364. The Donatists rashly withdrew from the Church on account of the charge of traditio. IX, 36, 538. They separated because the crime of traditio had been alleged, not because it had been proved. IX, 141. The Donatists’ schism cannot please anyone prudent who wishes to profess Christianity. V, 306.

The Donatists boast that they preserved the Scriptures from the fire. V, 310. The Donatists undeservedly abandon so many Christian nations among whom a traditor is unknown. IX, 515, 516, 519. The charge of traditio should rather be brought against the Donatists than against the Catholics. IX, 266. See Traditio. The Donatists are traditores. IX, 131. Their ancestors handed over the holy codices. II, 265; IX, 426. And the Church’s instruments. II, 265. How this is shown. IX, 736. They are shown in the ecclesiastical and municipal proceedings to have been detected and confessed as guilty of traditio. II, 403. It is read in ecclesiastical and municipal proceedings that the Donatists were betrayers of the sacred books. IX, 254. In the proceedings of the Council of Cirta. II, 580. The Donatists condemned the charge of traditio when it was alleged against others, but granted it even when confessed against themselves. IX, 37. What they themselves say about traditores rests on no adequate authority. V, 289.

The Donatists maintained that there were no Christians throughout the whole world. IX, 62. And that they alone were Christians. IV, 1234; IX, 36, 410. They taught that the Church had perished from the whole world. IX, 425. See Church. The Donatists do not dare to say that the Church perished in Cyprian’s time because people coming from heresy had been admitted to the Church without baptism. IX, 176. The question between the Donatists and the Catholics is where the Church is. IX, 391, 392. The question must be settled by divine words, not by those that are brought forward by either side. IX, 391, 394, 396. The Donatists ought to demonstrate their Church only by the canonical authority of the holy books. IX, 427, 430. They do not recognize the Church by the authority of the divine writings. II, 793. They wrongly call Donatus’s party the full Church. IX, 587. Donatus’s party is in Africa alone. II, 952. Hence it is not the Catholic Church. II, 190, 194. The Donatists occupy Mauretania and Numidia. IX, 586. They predominate in Numidia. IX, 51. Donatus’s party is unknown to a large part of the Roman world and to barbarian nations. II, 297. Outside Africa the Donatists have only a few members, and even these are not conspicuous. IX, 535. They customarily send one or two bishops, or at most three, to these people. IX, 535. From Africa they used to send a bishop to Rome for a few Montenses. IX, 346, 494, 516. And to Spain, to the household of one woman. IX, 346.

The Donatists wrongly glory in their small numbers. IX, 296, 403, 537. The Maximianists are fewer. IX, 537, 582. The arguments of those wishing to commend the Donatists’ small numbers are refuted. IX, 416, 418. Scripture says that the Church is spread throughout the whole world, but the Rogatists deny it. II, 331. The Donatists deny it. III, 1407. And they affirm that it flourishes only in Donatus’s party. VI, 306. And that Christ remained with two languages. III, 1991. They ought to show that the Church is either to be retained in Africa alone or restored from Africa among all nations. IX, 428, 430. They can produce no testimonies from Scripture showing that the Church remained in Africa alone. IX, 442, 443. They wish somehow to behead the Church. V, 725. That Donatus’s party is not the Church is also evident from Cresconius’s own words. IX, 536.

The Donatists undeservedly say that the world has been polluted by Caecilian’s sins. II, 799, 801. They created a schism because they supposedly did not wish good people to be among the wicked. IV, 191. And they said that the mixture of the wicked harmed the good in the Church. IV, 837. This was the principle of the Donatists: that whatever those were like with whom communion had been shared, everyone and the whole mass became like them. IV, 378, 379. The Donatists arose from the Church that tolerates the wicked. IX, 90. The Donatists’ judgment concerning the purity of the Church. IX, 247. Their presumption and arrogance concerning the truth and holiness of their own Church. IX, 95, 97. The Donatists said that their bishops were without sin and that one ought not to pray for them. IX, 343. The Donatists’ leaders are prejudiced by their vain presumption concerning the holiness of their Church. IX, 103. The Donatist association is full of wicked men. IV, 134. Among them are traditores, drunkenness, lending at interest, and interest upon interest. V, 306, 307. A multitude of sins. V, 306, 307. They do not consider themselves defiled by those whom they receive, although they have been condemned in sacrilegious schism. II, 198. The Donatists themselves did not withdraw from wicked men. II, 801. They communicate with the Maximianists, who are schismatics. II, 412, 413, 414. And they receive them with their honors intact. II, 579, 804, 812. They confirm the baptism given by the Maximianists. II, 308, 406, 490, 580, 800. Donatus communicated with Deuterius, who admitted traditores without baptism, and with all the bishops of the Moors. [Col. 0254] II, 342. The Donatists decreed in the Council of 270 bishops that traditores, if they did not wish to be baptized, should be admitted to communion as intact members. II, 342. They received Felicianus of Musti, whom the Council of Bagai had called an adulterer of the truth and a chain of sacrilege, with honor. II, 240, 403. The Donatists are separated from the whole world by a far greater crime against schismatics than the crime they condemned in the Maximianists. II, 194. They received the Maximianists as intact, although they had previously condemned them as ruined. V, 550.

The Donatists have no origin for their communion if the communion of the wicked destroyed the Church in Cyprian’s time. IX, 140. They have no defense for their separation if it did not destroy the Church. IX, 140. If the Church perished because wicked people were tolerated within it, the Donatists cannot show where they themselves came from. IX, 273. The Donatists rashly prefer Donatus’s party to Churches founded by the Apostles. IX, 535. They rashly accuse the overseas Churches. IX, 40, 41, 46, 510. With what arrogance they judge the world. IX, 298, 300. They dared to condemn the whole Christian world—an unprecedented act. IX, 51. The Donatists are unjust: they detest those unheard by themselves, yet receive those condemned by themselves with all their honors intact. IX, 79. The Donatists do not wish to believe the crimes circulated about their own people, but they believe the report spread about innocent people as though they were traditores or murderers. IX, 277, 280. They do not wish to erase with their tongue the words of Scripture that they boast they preserved from the flame. IV, 678. The Donatists do not know how they have acquitted the Church of the whole world. V, 900. This was said especially: “Neither does one case prejudice another, nor one person another.” V, 901. The Donatists pretend not to know the sins of their own people that are manifest throughout Africa; but crimes alleged by Africans against Africans, unproved and indeed acquitted, they do not allow to remain unknown to Easterners and Westerners. IX, 565, 567. When the Donatists do not dare to condemn their own manifestly wicked people, they rashly condemn the whole world. IX, 503, 504. And although they communicate with the Maximianists, they rashly refuse to communicate with the whole world. IX, 426. They think that a person’s iniquity has greater power to contaminate another than a person’s righteousness has to purify another. IX, 293. The Donatists have no charity, since they charge the world—unknown and unrecognized even by themselves—with crimes committed by Africans, without even proving them. IX, 337, 338. The world could not have been polluted by a crime alleged against Africans but not proved, if the manifest crimes tolerated among the Donatists themselves do not pollute them. IX, 277, 282, 319. It follows from the Donatists’ own principle that they are polluted by the sins of others. IX, 278. The Donatists boast vainly in the name of Donatus, although they are polluted by Optatus’s rapacity and the Circumcellions’ drunkenness. IX, 293. The Donatists are polluted if communion with heretics and wicked people pollutes. IX, 225, 227, 233, 234, 337. The communion of Catholics does not pollute the Donatists if that of the Maximianists does not pollute them. IX, 252, 571, 572, 575, 581. And it is shown from the Apostle that wicked people, if they are in the Church, do not pollute the good; or, if they are outside, that the sacraments are present among them as well. IX, 314.

The Donatists have no way to defend their schism. IX, 283. They unjustly bring forward testimonies of Scripture in their defense. IX, 734, 737, 738. The testimonies of Scripture by which separation from the wicked is commanded do not favor the Donatist schism. IX, 670, 673. The testimonies that they produce from Scripture turn back upon the Donatists. IX, 49, 105. And so does everything that they charge against the Catholics. IX, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55. The testimony of Ezekiel gives the Donatists little help in defending their schism. IX, 518. The Donatists are confounded by Israel’s very secession from the kingdom of Judah, which they set up as an example of their schism. IX, 417. Psalm 49:16–17 and following is applied to the Donatists: “Why do you recite my ordinances,” etc. IX, 61. By the same reasoning by which the Donatists refuse to communicate with the Orientals, they ought not to communicate with the Maximianists. IX, 576. The Donatists cut their own throats by their own judgment in the case of the Maximianists. IX, 252, 253, 255, 257, 258, 377, 378, 585, 592, 641, 703. They wounded their own case in the judgment of the prefecture by certain thoughtless and rash replies. IX, 625. The Donatists have no cause for separation if the wicked do not pollute the good in unity. IX, 244. The Donatists impiously separated themselves from the world while tolerating wicked people among themselves. IX, 273, 277. Nor do they rebaptize those baptized by themselves. IX, 275. Psalm 22, which they brought forward on their own behalf against the Catholic Church, is explained against the Donatists. IX, 297. The reproaches and insults that they directed from the Psalms and the Gospel against the Catholics are turned back upon the Donatists. IX, 267, 268, 269, 270, 271, 309, 310, 311. The Donatists are obstinate because they refuse to believe so many scriptural testimonies concerning the Church. IX, 414, 431, 434, 444. If refusing to yield to the Emperor has some appearance of courage, there is no praise in openly contradicting the truth. IX, 105, 106.

Cyprian’s authority does not favor the Donatists. IX, 126, 128, 129, 133, 135, 606. The Donatists’ case was utterly shipwrecked by Cyprian’s own authority. IX, 176, 177. The Donatists are convicted of schism by the very unity that Stephen and Cyprian maintained, although they held different opinions. IX, [Col. 0255] 607. Whatever the Donatists charged against the Maximianists can be charged against the Donatists. IX, 303, 304, 531, 533, 534, 546, 547, 549. The Donatist schism from Catholic communion is demonstrated by the schism of the Maximianists from Donatus’s party itself. IX, 553. From what they suffered at the hands of Maximian, the Donatists learned that they had impiously separated themselves from the world. IX, 105. If they wish, they can see their own depravity as in a mirror in the case of the Maximianists. IX, 567. By the reasoning with which they prove that their own schismatics could not withdraw from them, they are convicted that they themselves could not separate from the whole world. IX, 101. The charges that the Donatists bring concerning traditio, persecution, and false baptism are answered solely from the case of the Maximianists. IX, 258.

The Donatists tolerated the most manifest sacrilegious people for the sake of Donatus’s false peace. IX, 27, 51, 62, 63, 74, 86, 88, 105. Donatus’s party is full of chaff. IX, 96. Their communion contains the vices that they reproached the whole world for possessing. IX, 293. How many and how serious are the crimes in Donatus’s party. IX, 96. In Donatus’s party there are unjust, lying, dead, sinful, and fictitious people. IX, 63. There are many wicked bishops among the Donatists. IX, 58. Donatist bishops and presbyters have been convicted of sexual misconduct with pregnant women. IX, 280. The Donatists are guilty and wicked, not because of the crimes committed by some of their members, but because of the crime of schism. IX, 333. The crimes committed in their party do not pertain to all Donatists. IX, 312. For the sake of Donatus’s unity they endure the notorious and infamous evils of Optatus, but for the sake of Christ’s unity they refuse to endure things uncertain and unknown. IX, 308. By the reasoning with which they excuse Optatus, they ought also to excuse the whole world. IX, 531. By the reasoning with which they wish the wicked of their communion not to harm the good, the Catholics likewise act. IX, 277, 283. The Donatists are contaminated if the good are contaminated by communion in the sacraments with the wicked. IX, 56. The Donatists violate peace with the Catholic Church, but preserve it among themselves in such a way that they receive people condemned in sacrilegious schism. II, 172, 192, 195, 198. Nor do they consider themselves defiled by them. II, 198. To the Donatists’ error, who refuse to tolerate the wicked, another contrary error is added, arising from Scriptures wrongly understood. VI, 201. Whether the Donatists were the first to judge that the wicked should be expelled from the Church. IX, 96.

The Donatists are unjust: they admit the baptism of the Maximianists while ritually exsufflating the baptism of the whole world. II, 172, 193, 266, 404, 405. The Donatists make not only laypeople but also clergy, presbyters, and bishops into catechumens if they can transfer them to themselves. IX, 605. They persuade Catholics coming over to them to say that they are pagans. II, 135. The person whom they are preparing to rebaptize they teach to deny before the minister of baptism that he is a Christian. IV, 431, 432, 1895. Anyone of the faithful who crossed over to the Donatists was baptized. II, 179. The Donatists’ arguments and evasions. IV, 1895. The Donatists lead those whom they can seduce through certain secret caves and rebaptize them. IV, 1895. The Donatists rebaptize. V, 769. And they subject those returning to them to penance. V, 1359. The Donatists receive and rebaptize a young man guilty of killing his mother and still breathing out murder. II, 132. Likewise, a degraded subdeacon. II, 134. A certain Donatist returned to the Church. V, 1598. A Donatist who returned to the Church and confessed the sin of rebaptization was rejected by certain brothers. V, 1358. Augustine both excuses and disapproves this action. V, 1358. The Donatists even rebaptize Christians coming from Mesopotamia, Syria, and elsewhere. IV, 134, 383.

The Donatists are reproved because they rebaptize. III, 1420. The Rogatists said that they followed the authority of Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus in rebaptizing. II, 339. They try to defend themselves by Cyprian’s authority. I, 637. In the letter to Jubaianus. II, 339. Donatus of Carthage did not establish that Christians should be rebaptized. I, 618. The Donatists’ objections concerning why they rebaptize are answered. III, 1430, 1431.

The Donatists insist that baptism is void unless they themselves have given it. VI, 307. They say that the person whom they have baptized is justified by them and that they are in the Church that is without sin. II, 809. The Donatists said that baptism given by them was holy, but that baptism given by others was nothing. IV, 1890. “What we give is holy”: a statement of the Donatists. IV, 1890. They say that the sacraments are holy only when they are administered by holy people. IV, 134. And that baptism does not remove sin unless it is given by a holy minister. III, 1410, 1421, 1422. The Donatists’ words, “I sanctify; I justify; what I give is holy,” are refuted. V, 723. To the extent that the Donatists say, “I justify; I forgive sins,” they are worse than the Pharisees. V, 600. The Donatist error that the Holy Spirit is not given except through holy ministers. V, 1225. The Donatists said that they baptized by power, not by ministry. III, 1419. The Donatists are likewise pressed on this point. III, 1498, 1499, 1500. The Donatists’ foolish objection. V, 278. A passage from the Song of Songs brought forward by them in vain. V, 289, 768. Likewise a passage from Habakkuk. V, 292. And a Gospel passage concerning the tree and its fruit, wrongly transferred by them to the minister of baptism. V, 1323. The Donatists’ argument from the words of Matthew 18, in which they contend that sins are forgiven through human beings. V, 600. The Donatists admit that a baptized person is justified [Col. 0256] by a hidden sinner. V, 1325. And that this person is then born from God. V, 1325. Among the Donatists salvation depends on the lives of their leaders. V, 724. The Donatists falsely claimed for themselves the power to give salvation. IV, 1890, 1891. The Donatists’ proud declarations. V, 599, 1296, 1320. A Donatist who says that he is righteous is proved to be wicked. V, 305.

The Donatists, with monstrous sacrilege, execrate the baptism of the overseas Churches while accepting that of the Maximianists. IX, 31, 40, 108, 137, 223, 252, 427, 569, 570, 740. They neither rebaptized nor reordained their own schismatics. IX, 73. They did rebaptize some of their schismatics, but did not rebaptize others. IX, 99. They did not rebaptize the Maximianists. IX, 137. They received them with their honors intact and rebaptized none of them. IX, 549, 554. The Donatists are ridiculous: although they judged the sacraments by the morals and actions of human beings, after Optatus they rebaptized no one. IX, 291. The Catholics have already settled the case that they have with the Donatists concerning baptism, since they do not repeat baptism after the Maximianists. IX, 556, 557, 558, 559. In the case of the Maximianists, the Donatists declared both that unity should not be abandoned on account of the wicked and that Christ’s baptism given outside the Church should not be destroyed. IX, 683. What troubles the Donatists concerning the sacrament of baptism has already been resolved in the case of the Maximianists. IX, 371, 372, 551, 558. And throughout Book 4 against Cresconius, the scriptural testimonies by which the Donatists think the necessity of rebaptization is proved are turned against the Maximianists. IX, 558, 563. Likewise Cyprian’s authority. IX, 559. Since the Donatists do not rebaptize after their own sinners, they ought not to rebaptize after the whole world either. IX, 485. Most of the Donatists’ ministers do not baptize if wicked ministers do not baptize. IX, 64, 74, 75. The Donatists’ rebaptization is refuted by circumcision itself, which was not repeated after wicked ministers. IX, 309. What Paul said to certain schismatics—“Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” and so forth—applies to the Donatists. IX, 381. In rebaptizing, the Donatists spiritually shed blood. IX, 54. The imperial constitution against Donatists who rebaptize. IX, 805, 813.

### The Donatists

The fury of the Donatists. X, 704. Unbridled license. II, 132, 135. A monstrous and savage manner of acting. II, 413, 799, 800. They perpetrate daily acts of violence everywhere through the Circumcellions. IV, 134. See Circumcellions. The evils that followed the Donatian schism. II, 131, 415. The crimes of the Donatists summarized. IX, 720. The dreadful deeds of the Donatist bishops after Julian had restored their freedom to them. IX, 803, 812. Most of the Donatists, including bishops, presbyters, and clerics, inflicted killings and slaughter even upon their own people. II, 177. Through extremely violent mobs they even attack Catholic churches of their own accord, wherever they can. IX, 272. The Donatists ordered the Eucharist to be poured out for dogs. IX, Appendix 803. Then the dogs tore their masters to pieces. IX, Appendix 803. The Donatists prevented Catholics by violence from preaching the truth. II, 397. Catholic teachers often suffered the Donatists’ ambushes. IV, 1605. The cruelty of the Donatists toward those who wished to pass over to the Catholic Church. II, 397, 798, 800. They subjected Marcus, presbyter of Casphalianum, and Restitutus of Victorianum—who had embraced Catholic unity of their own accord—to punishments. II, 397; IX, 525. They beat the subdeacon of Marcianus of Urgensis, who had become Catholic under no compulsion, almost to death, and buried him beneath stones. II, 397.

The Donatists were lovers of homicide. II, 797. Murderers of the Prophets. IX, 268. Various crimes of cruelty and savagery that the Donatists committed are reported. IX, 316. They forbid bread to be baked for Catholics. IX, 316. How cruelly the Donatist clerics raged against Catholic clerics. IX, 521. The Donatists poured lime mixed with vinegar into people’s eyes. IX, 521. By blinding them with lime and vinegar, were they not more cruel toward Catholics than the devil was toward Job? IX, 636. They killed Restitutus and Innocentius, gouging out the latter’s eye as well and cutting off his finger. II, 509. The region of Hippo was harassed by the Donatists’ audacity. II, 296. An armed band of Donatists lay in wait for Augustine’s passage. VI, 239. The cruelty of the Donatists toward Maximianus, the Catholic bishop of Bagai. IX, 521. They lay in wait for Possidius, bishop of Calama, like brigands. II, 397; IX, 523. They threw out the presbyter of Siniti with grave insult. II, 397.

The fury, drunkenness, voluntary deaths, precipices, and sacrilegious cult of those who cast themselves from them among the Donatists. IX, 590. They inflame their drunkenness to the accompaniment of psalm-singing composed by human ingenuity. II, 221. The madness and fury of certain Donatists. V, 1596. The Donatists’ voluntary deaths. IX, 526. The Donatists slaughtered themselves. II, 797, 798, 799, 940. Three kinds of death frequently practiced by the Donatists. IX, 724, 725. For the Donatists it was a daily game to kill themselves by throwing themselves from precipices, into water, or into fire. II, 798. Why they did not also resort to the noose. IX, 736. They thrust themselves upon the pagans to be killed. IX, 725. And offered themselves to be slaughtered. II, 798. Donatus, a Donatist presbyter of Mutugenna, when apprehended, [Col. 0257] refused to make use of an animal brought to him, struck himself violently against the ground, and threw himself into a well. II, 754, 755. The Donatists’ voluntary deaths, precipices, and so forth, so that they might be honored by human beings. IX, 429. The Donatists’ voluntary deaths are censured. VI, 616; IX, 721, 723, 725. Since the Donatists do not spare their own lives, they are guilty. IX, 709, 711. In this they imitate the devil. IX, 299. From him they learned voluntary deaths. IX, 299. By killing themselves at the devil’s instigation, they imitate the betrayer. IX, 736. Augustine compared not any human being in the party of Donatus, but the error itself, to Satan. IX, 591. The Donatists bring forward in vain something from the Sacred Scriptures in support of their insane doctrine of voluntary death. IX, 726, 728. The Donatists kill themselves mystically. IX, 276.

### Donatists: imperial laws against them

The laws of the emperors against them. V, 900. Constantine was the first to issue an extremely severe law against the Donatists. II, 399. His sons Constantius and Constans imitated him. II, 399. Valentinian, Gratian, Theodosius, Honorius, and Arcadius also issued laws against them. II, 400. Theodosius’s law imposing a fine of ten pounds of gold upon heretics was extended also to the Donatists who raged against the Church. II, 804; IX, Appendix 806, 812. The law concerning ten pounds of gold against the Donatists was first cited. IX, 316. The laws of Honorius against the Donatists. I, 641, 654. The edict of Macedonius against them. II, 673. The punishments inflicted upon the Donatists by imperial laws are noted. II, 331. No royal law ordered the Donatists to be killed. IX, 319, 327. And this perhaps arose from God’s greater wrath. IX, 319. The emperor imposed upon the Donatists only the penalty of exile, not of death. II, 940; IX, 717. Monetary fines were decreed against all Donatists, and exile against their bishops or ministers. II, 805. The Donatists were not even permitted by the emperors’ laws to remain in the cities. IX, 316. Catholics hold the Donatists in their estates and cities as hostages. IX, 433. This was so that the Donatists themselves would not be expelled from the countryside on every side. IX, 317. The Donatists were deprived of the ability to make wills or donations. IX, 788, Appendix 812. And of receiving anything from them. IX, 788, Appendix 812. The emperors rightly refused to recognize the validity of Donatist wills. V, 310. They were ordered, according to the laws of earthly kings, to lose their earthly possessions. II, 345. The sites of their congregations were claimed for the treasury. II, 303, 328. Imperial laws do not allow them to retain the basilicas. IX, 326. Not even those which they had built while in schism. IX, 47. Yet they did not restore all those which Unity had held from the beginning. IX, 48. The Donatists do not possess earthly things rightly. II, 345. Whoever has lost all earthly things for Christ’s peace has God; but whoever has lost even a few coins for the party of Donatus has no heart. IX, 336. The Donatists boasted that they feared neither the loss of wealth nor death itself. IX, 335, 336, 337. Augustine at one time held that laws against the Donatists should not be requested from the emperors. II, 804. He invites Maximinus to a conference and promises that soldiers will be absent, lest any Donatist think that he wished to act in a more tumultuous manner. II, 98.

### The Donatists’ objections concerning imperial constitutions

The Donatists object to the Catholics on account of the emperors’ constitutions. IV, 135. They complain unjustly that Catholics bring their complaints before the emperor. II, 328, 580. Or that Christian emperors have enacted laws against them. IX, 46, 47, 631. Or that Catholics seek something from the kings of the earth against the enemies of Christ. II, 794. They themselves were the first to do all these things. II, 327, 492, 795. They obtained commands from the rulers against the Rogatists and Maximianists. II, 192, 266, 327. And they employed earthly powers against the Catholics. II, 301, 413. They appealed to Julian, the deserter of Christ and idolater, and declared that justice alone had a place with him. II, 327, 400. The Donatists attribute the voluntary deaths of their own people during persecutions to the Catholics. IX, 518, 327. Whether they threw themselves from precipices, or were thrown by order of some authority, is uncertain. IX, 273. They bring against the Catholics crimes committed by bad Christians during the time of persecution, which crimes are said to have been committed by their own leaders. IV, 133. The Donatists spread the report that Marculus and Donatus had been killed by Catholics. IX, 268, 273. The Donatists’ unjust complaint concerning the persecution of Paul and Macarius. IX, Appendix 800. They make Catholics odious on account of Macarius. IV, 134, 135. They called the Catholic Church “Macarian.” II, 190.

The Donatists unjustly charged the Catholics with persecution. IX, 531, 532. They complained unjustly that they were suffering persecution. II, 307, 310; III, 1482, 1483; IX, 317, 327, 432, 434. The response to their complaints about persecution. IX, 666, 684, 709, 710, 715. They themselves persecuted the Maximianists. II, 413, 414. Through Optatus Gildonianus. IX, 137. When the Donatists complain of persecution, the very persecution they inflicted upon the Maximianists closes their mouths. IX, 254, 295. If persecution is not permitted, the Donatists persecuted the Maximianists. IX, 531, 532, 534. The Donatists complain unjustly that the emperors ordered the possessions of their churches to pass to the Catholic Church. II, 809. It is shown that the places held by the Donatists belong to the Church. IX, 303. The places which the Donatists had begun to possess after separating, when they pass over to the Church, are rightly possessed by [Col. 0258] the Church from them. IX, 304. The Donatists took away the Maximianists’ basilicas. IX, 47, 737, 740. Julian the Apostate restored the basilicas to the Donatists. IX, 47, 329, 334. The Donatists are convicted of contradiction when they complain that they are persecuted by Catholics. IX, 664, 665. They never spared their own schismatics. IX, 55. By the reasoning with which they excuse the cruelty of the Primianists toward Salvius, the severity of the Catholics toward the Donatists is excused. IX, 108. If the one who suffers persecution is better, the Maximianists are better than the Donatists. IX, 636. What the Donatists complained about concerning Caecilianus, the Maximianists likewise complained about concerning Primianus. IV, 376. Augustine shows that the Donatists do not suffer persecution, or do not suffer it according to the Gospel. IX, 272. The Donatists endure persecution; the Catholics endure suffering. II, 414. The Donatists rightly suffer by the commands of the rulers. IV, 1894, 1895. Whatever they suffer, they suffer justly. IX, 43. If they suffer anything, they suffer justly on account of the schism. IX, 272. The Donatists suffer persecution from themselves. IX, 725. Whatever evil happens to them, they suffer from themselves when they resist the laws of the authorities. IX, 433. Why they arouse the severity of the authorities against themselves. IX, 106. It was within the power of the Donatists to suffer no losses, even while following their heresy, if the Catholic Church suffered no violence. IX, 434. The Donatists commit worse things than they suffer. IX, 43, 46. The Church suffers more grievously from the Donatists than they do from the emperors. IX, 434. The Donatists have shown themselves before the emperor to be persecutors of the innocent. IX, 649, 695. The Donatists are more cruel toward Christ and the Gospel than those who persecuted the name of Christ and wanted the Gospel, once burned, to be abolished. IX, 319. Indeed, more cruel than the Jews. IX, 320. Worse even than the Jews themselves. III, 1991. The Donatists imitate the crime of Antichrist. V, 723.

The Donatists’ persecution of the Church is more grievous than that of the emperors. III, 1420, 1482. How zealously the Donatists seek to deceive Christ’s weak sheep. IX, 132. By persuasion they do what the persecutor did not do by killing. IV, 1895. See Baptism. The Donatists are vipers. IX, 267. It is shown that the Donatists are not only not Christ’s sheep, but are wolves. IX, 309. The Donatists are wolves and thieves. V, 760. The Donatists’ schism is the fruit by which they are recognized as ravenous wolves. IX, 270. The Church advanced through the Donatists’ persecution. II, 807.

How the Catholics persecuted the Donatists. IX, 315. For what purpose laws of fullest coercion are employed against the Donatists. IX, 433. The earthly authorities decreed that the Donatists should suffer either on account of their error or so that their attacks might be driven away from their salvation. IX, 526. The emperor strives not only to take away from the Donatists the license to rage, but also to bring them back to Catholic unity by coercion. II, 806; V, 295. The Church seeks not their death but their conversion and peace. II, 807. The severity of the laws against the Donatists arises from God’s mercy and from the love of the Christian Catholic emperors. IX, 136, 307, 324. Kings terrify the Donatists not cruelly but mercifully; the Donatists, however, do not fear bravely but obstinately. IX, 336. Whatever is done with the Donatists is done out of charity. IX, 332. If any war is waged against the Donatists, it is out of love, not hatred. IX, 307. The Donatists resist the truth, some by raging and others by growing sluggish. II, 312. The Church heals both groups. II, 322, 323. The Donatists’ foolish objection against Catholics who call them back from error. IV, 160, 299, 300. More concerning the Donatists. IV, 131, 170, 171, 177, 246, 639, 641, 781, 961, 962, 1067, 1091, 1228, 1229, 1231, 1253, 1269, 1270, 1309, 1310, 1613, 1656. The Donatists are piously punished by the emperors’ laws so that they may recover from error. II, 798. The Donatists complain unjustly that the kings of the earth have established laws against them for the sake of Catholic peace. II, 492. That they are compelled to unity by the commands of the kings of the earth. II, 397. Catholics care for the Donatists’ salvation when they compel them to unity. II, 401. The Donatists ought to consider for what reason they suffer anything at the hands of Catholics. IX, 433. They complain unjustly that Catholics seek them—indeed, that God seeks them through Catholics. IX, 291. Why and for what purpose the Donatists are sought. III, 1435, 1448; IX, 333, 334, 432, 693, 740. The Catholics do not act against them in order to acquire their possessions. II, 345, 808; IX, 737. The punitive laws enacted against the Donatists do not compel them to do good, but prevent them from doing evil. IX, 315. The Donatists boast unjustly of their gentleness, because they compel no one to join their communion. IX, 315. The Donatists are sought through the Scriptures, through peaceful words, and through the scourges of temporal tribulations. IX, 292. If the party of Donatus suffered any affliction, it suffered like Hagar from Sarah. V, 52. The Donatists are like the servant of the high priest whose ear was cut off; but those Catholics who persecute the Donatists are like Peter. IX, 321. The Donatists interpret the deed of Simon of Cyrene in their own favor. V, 294. Either the Donatists rightly suffered persecution, or, if the proper measure was exceeded, the chaff was responsible. IX, 254, 256, 265, 482. If anything beyond measure and against the will of charity is committed against them, this belongs to the chaff of the Church, not to the wheat. IX, 48, 434. It does not belong to those by whom people who act in such ways are laudably tolerated [Col. 0259] for the peace of unity. IX, 520, 526. None of the good in the Catholic Church approves this, if anyone—even a heretic—is savagely treated to the point of death. IX, 526. Nor, even far short of death, if the desire for revenge repays evil with evil through harassment. IX, 526. Nor if anyone takes away another’s property as though on behalf of unity. IX, 526. A Christian who persecutes the Donatists, whether out of hatred or greed, by force of the imperial laws acts most wickedly. II, 345, 346. The Donatists slanderously disparage Augustine’s reputation. IV, 393, 394. Augustine tries to avert the punishment of death from certain Donatists guilty of great crimes. II, 535. Augustine did not say that persecution ought to be inflicted upon the Donatists. IX, 520. Genethlius, of blessed memory, bishop of Carthage before Aurelius, restrained a constitution against the Donatists, for which reason they praised him greatly. II, 178.

The Donatists complain unjustly that they suffer persecution for the faith and on account of the Son of Man. IX, 718. They boast vainly of the glory of endurance. IX, 106, 753. If they suffer anything for the schism, they say that they are baptized in their own blood. IX, 279. They wish to be regarded as martyrs. IX, 136, 317. The memorial observances of the dead Donatists. IX, 428. Crowds of drunkards and shameless people flock to the tombs of their dead whom they honor. IX, 430. The Donatists honored the corpses of those who had voluntarily cast themselves from precipices. IX, 257, 308. They celebrated their birthdays or feast days. IX, 106. They swore by the gray hairs and bodily remains of their false martyrs. IX, 106. The Donatists unjustly called themselves martyrs of the truth. IX, 43, 45, 62. The Donatists live like thieves and boast that they die like martyrs. IX, 315. They live like thieves, die like Circumcellions, and are honored like martyrs. II, 307. The Donatists’ false martyrs. III, 1436, 1483. The Donatists cannot be called martyrs. IX, 653. They seek the glory of martyrs for themselves unjustly. VI, 617. They rashly claim for themselves what is said about martyrs in the Apocalypse. IX, 723, 724. The Donatist martyrs are censured. V, 630, 1448.

It is not useless for the restless Donatists to be restrained and corrected through the authorities ordained by God. II, 321. Very many Donatists were corrected by the imperial laws. II, 359, 795, 806. And they rejoiced that they had been compelled to come to the Church. II, 321, 322, 330. The story of a certain Donatist who was converted out of necessity. IV, 369, 370. A certain Donatist subdeacon converted wholeheartedly to Catholic peace. IV, 370. Many Donatists were converted from the schism to the Church. V, 1595.

The error of the Donatists had spread far and wide throughout Africa; only a few now remain in it. IX, 449. The number of Donatists who pass over to the Church is far greater than that of those who remain in Donatus’s dissension. IX, 726. Many cities that had previously been Donatist, through fear of the laws, now ardently love Catholic unity. II, 329. The conversion of some Donatists consoles the Church for the destruction of others. II, 808. Concerning the exclusion of the Donatists: thanksgiving for the church of Carthage, together with the bishops’ letters, is to be sent to the Imperial Court. IX, 814. The Donatists’ error is not unforgivable. IX, 475, 478. Patience ought to be shown toward them. V, 902. Charity is commended toward the Donatists. IV, 299. They are brothers, although bad brothers. V, 288. They are called brothers by the Catholics. IX, 691. With them there is both dispute and concord. V, 1590.

The Donatists who hasten to the Church are not rebaptized. II, 803, 811. The Donatists’ sacraments are not hostile to Catholics. II, 312. Donatists returning to the Catholic Church are purified in the same way, without a repetition of baptism, in which they judged Praetextatus and Felicianus to have been purified. IX, 555, 556. The extent to which the Donatists are to be received by Catholics. IX, 691, 806. They are not received into the Church in the condition in which they were. IX, 472, 476. Those Donatists who come to unity receive the benefit of charity. IX, 312. Donatists who hasten to the Church must do penance. II, 811. If any who had been degraded among the Donatists wished to pass over to the Catholics, they were received only in the humiliation of repentance. II, 135. When Donatists pass over to the Church, the dignity of the clerical or episcopal office is not taken away from them, for the sake of peace or out of clemency alone. II, 229, 489, 812, 813. The bishops of the Donatists are received into Catholic unity in such a way as appears suitable to the peace and usefulness of the Church. IX, 474. Augustine cannot be the authority, according to Possidius, for ordaining someone who was baptized in the party of Donatus. II, 1061.

Why the Donatists seek a stricter discipline. IX, 81, 85. The Donatists criticize Catholics because they sing the sober divine songs of the Prophets in church. II, 221. Penance in the party of Donatus. V, 1359. Many Donatists distributed many things to the poor and were ready to accept death. III, 2020. The Donatists’ good works are false and vain. III, 1436. The Donatists cannot say, on the basis of their deeds, “Lord Jesus.” V, 1236. The Donatists despise God, rather than glorify him. IX, 80. They believe what they see among their own people. IX, 428. The Donatists’ calumny against Catholics: that the Catholics placed something else upon God’s altar. II, 330.

### Donatist and Catholic doctrine

What the doctrine of the Donatists and Catholics is. V, 724. Donatus’s writings prove that he did not think correctly about the Trinity. [Col. 0260] VIII, 43. The union of the Donatists with the Arians, and the distinction between the errors of the two groups. II, 176, 792. Some Donatists deny that the Son is equal to the Father. V, 991. The Donatists are insulting toward Christ. V, 724. They regard Donatus as Christ. V, 1023. They are convicted of boasting that they are in place of Christ. V, 1323. They believe neither Moses nor Christ, even when he is risen. V, 724. What keeps the Donatists in error. V, 901. What prevents the Donatists from recovering their senses. IX, 136.

Donatus, who attempted to divide Christ, was himself divided from his followers. VI, 306. The party of Donatus was split into many parties. II, 334; V, 50, 447; VIII, 43; IX, 40, 101, 114, 136, 113. Maximianus split the Donatian schism with a new schism. II, 172, 580, 800. And so did Rogatus. II, 326. The Donatists and Maximianists divided against one another. V, 447. The congregations of the Donatists, Maximianists, and Rogatists. V, 769. The Donatists are the same as the Parmenianists. VIII, 32. The council of the Donatists against the Maximianists. IX, 63. The councils of the Donatists. See Councils.

### Donatian or Donatist

Donatians, or Donatists. VIII, 43. Augustine agrees that they should be called Donatians rather than Donatists, after Donatus. IX, 468. Why the Donatists were called by this name, and not rather Christians. IX, 552. Just as Maximianists and Claudianists are so called, so Donatists is also a proper designation. IX, 555. At Carthage they were first called the party of Majorinus. II, 302. They were called Montenses or Cutzupitae in the city of Rome. II, 196; Note VIII, 43; IX, 346, 395. The origin of this. IX, Appendix 805. To the Donatians or Donatists, who are called Montenses at Rome, they customarily send a bishop from Africa. VIII, 43.

Donatulus of Capsa. IX, 235.

### Gifts

Certain gifts of God are common to the good and the wicked. IV, 1343; V, 1460. The gifts of God are ours, although they do not come from us. II, 851. What is given to us is also ours. V, 1464. God’s gifts become a human being’s when he loves what he receives and gives thanks to the one who gave it. V, 908. No one should envy God’s gifts: how they can be common to all. V, 1040. He who gave us being gives us also the ability to be good. IV, 1379. See Benefits. The wicked also possess many gifts of God. V, 764. The more someone knows God’s gifts to be God’s, the more blessed he is by them. VI, 442. No one is blessed by God’s gifts if he is ungrateful to the giver. VI, 443. It is better to give thanks to God even for a small gift from him than to wish others to give thanks to oneself for a great one. II, 110. Some gifts belong to sons who are heirs, others to sons who have been disinherited. VI, 624. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are diverse, but the Spirit is the same. II, 839. There is a division of gifts, and concord makes one body. III, 1509. God’s gifts are multiplied among human beings when they distribute them to others. III, 19. The gift of the Holy Spirit is signified by water or by fire. III, 804.

The soul cannot receive or possess God’s gifts except by consenting. X, 241. We should pray that God’s gifts may increase in us. IV, 1548. It is God’s task to preserve his gifts in us. V, 1362. The gift of God is itself the human being’s gratuitous merit. II, 820. The merits of a human being are God’s gifts. V, 1367. When God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts. II, 880. The particular gift that is given here or preserved for the future belongs to the good. V, 583, 1460. The distinction between a gift and something given. III, 526. What someone did not wish to receive when it was given is demanded of him. IV, 287. It is one thing to be unable to receive, another to be unwilling: in the former there is the excuse of necessity, in the latter the guilt of the will. IV, 287. The one who received less seems to walk more safely; but this is so only if he does not perversely seek what he did not rightly receive. IV, 1709. Who is to be preferred when something cannot be given to two or more people? III, 30. Let no one seek anything in Christ’s body except health. IV, 1709.

God seeks no gift more than you. V, 508. For there is nothing better in all earthly creation. V, 317. By giving yourself to him, you will be good. V, 707. Eternal life is worth as much as you are; give yourself, and you will have it. V, 707. What do we gain by giving ourselves to God? V, 212. You give to God from what belongs to God: from what he gave you, he receives from you. V, 913. Zacchaeus, Peter, and the widow gave different things; but they arrived at one destination because they did not love different things. V, 315. The spiritual gifts that God gives he will not take away unless you abandon them; but he himself takes away bodily gifts, and whoever else takes them away does so by his authority, since he grants the power. IV, 201.

“Until” is used in the sense of “no longer.” VI, 77.

Christ sleeps in a boat tossed by temptations when faith sleeps in the heart. IV, 1169, 1915. When Christ sleeps, the heart is tossed by waves. IV, 1915. Those who love present things sleep. IV, 963.

“Sleep” is used in Scripture for death. IV, 74.

“Sleep” is used for remaining and ceasing. III, 514, 534. For lying with someone. III, 497.

Turn your back toward what is falling and your face toward what remains. IV, 190.

What the drachma sought by the woman means allegorically. IV, 1379, 1792.

Dragons are the largest of all animals. IV, 1943.

Marcus Drusus. VII, 106.

The dual number is used by the Greeks and Hebrews. VII, 695, 696.

“You have two” is a customary expression. IV, 201. To plead a case before two. II, 169.

### Doubt

One doubts in the truth, not about the truth, who knows with certainty that he doubts. III, 155. On what matters it is permissible to doubt. VII, 646. It is better to doubt about hidden things than to quarrel about uncertain things. III, 376. Faith in history perishes if what has been established by authority and time is called into doubt. I, 1335. Doubt signifies a mind that is by no means rash; it is the greatest safeguard of tranquility. I, 1213. The verb of doubting is sometimes used as a rebuke. III, 1671.

### Sweetness

The sweetness of God’s name is far preferable to the sweetness of the world. IV, 612. Deceptive sweetness: what it is. VI, 104. Only those who have tasted the sweetness of God know it. IV, 612. An exhortation to taste God’s sweetness. VI, 296. God’s sweetness is hidden from those who fear and revealed to those who hope. V, 791, 794. God conceals the sweetness of love from those for whom fear is useful. IV, 229. The sweetness of this life is a trap in which the unwary are caught. IV, 1647, 1648.

Pleasure is sweet, but God is sweeter. V, 1286. As long as iniquity flatters and iniquity is sweet, truth is bitter. V, 830. If things in the world are sweet, they are digested with bitterness. IV, 612. The harmful sweetness of sin should be digested through the bitterness of tribulation. V, 1.

### Dulcitius

Dulcitius, tribune and notary. VI, 147, 148; IX, 705, Retractations 706, 707. In Africa, an executor of the imperial laws against the Donatists. I, 654; II, 939. Augustine instructed him and he wishes to know how he should conduct himself toward the Donatists. II, 939. First, by an edict, he admonishes them at Thamugadi. II, 939. He explains this edict in a second one. II, 939. He writes to Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi. I, 654. He treats him more honorably than was appropriate for a heretic. II, 939. He sends Augustine Gaudentius’s rescripts for refutation. I, 654.

The number twelve is used for totality. VII, 663. The number twelve is perfect. IV, 715. The number twelve is consecrated. III, 1621. The number twelve of the Apostles has a great sacramental meaning. IV, 1103.

The double heart of a liar. V, 739.

The Lord commanded difficult things, but he made great promises. V, 120. The things that are difficult for those who labor become gentle for those same people when they love. V, 444.

The hardness of sinners is dissolved into tears of repentance before God’s face, just as wax flows before the face of fire. IV, 814. Even if the predestined are extremely hard and have become, as it were, crystal, they are nevertheless not too hard for God’s mercy. IV, 1935.

Dusii are certain demons, so called by the Gauls. VII, 468.

The office or rank of a duumvir. VI, 602.

### E

Ebionite heretics. VIII, 27.

Holy drunkenness. V, 1098. Its effects. IV, 351, 955, 1369. Sober and praiseworthy drunkenness of the mind. VI, 296. Spiritual drunkenness. V, 160. Drunken martyrs were led to their passion. IV, 352, 955.

Drunkenness is a sin. X, 159. Through habit the sin of drunkenness has become cheapened and is despised. V, 125. The people have now become accustomed not only to mentioning drunkenness without honor, but also to praising it with hilarity. IX, 171. Nothing is more insane than a drunkard. IV, 1370. The struggle against drunkenness and bad habit. V, 816. Drunkenness must be avoided. V, 1098. The eternal law condemns it. VIII, 426. Drunkenness was frequent in Augustine’s time. II, 345. Even among ministers of Christ. II, 344. Augustine laments that drunken celebrations in honor of the holy martyrs were customarily held every day. II, 91. Those who become drunk at their solemnities persecute the martyrs with cups. IV, 723. Augustine censures drunkenness. II, 116. Augustine drove drunken celebrations from the solemnity of Saint Leontius, not without danger to himself. V, 1174. The drunken celebrations customary at martyrs’ solemnities ceased in all, or nearly all, the churches overseas. II, 91. The Donatists inflame their drunkenness to the singing of psalms, as though to trumpets. II, 221. “Drunkenness” is frequently used in Scripture for satiety. III, 586.

There is a very great difference between a drunken person and one who is drunk. VIII, 427.

Ecbola. IX, 639, 640.

Various names of the Church. IX, 241. The Church is called from its being a calling or vocation. III, 2089. It was instituted entirely for the worship of one God. VI, 259.

The antiquity of the Church. IX, 122, 123. The Church was first in heaven. III, 335. The Church was foretold in chapter 2 of Genesis. VIII, 258. And in the ark of the Flood. VI, 334, 346. It was promised in the blessing of Abraham. VI, 174. The Church is the true seed of Abraham. III, 789. The Prophets’ predictions concerning the Church. VII, 584; VIII, 289. The Church, already figured and prophesied in those very promises, then gave birth to the foreknowledge of the saints. VIII, 305. The prophecies concerning it have been fulfilled. VI, 175.

The Church is the reconciled world. V, 588. The body of Christ. III, 25; V, 266. He himself is its head. V, 753. It is one great body, belonging to one great head. II, 584. One household. II, 584. The Church and Christ—head and body—are one human being and one Christ. [Col. 0262] IV, 161, 232, 250, 453, 629, 662, 693, 695, 723, 730, 761, 866, 948, 1082, 1156, 1679, 1784, 1785, 1817, 1819, 1846; V, 571, 754; VII, 532; VIII, 896; X, 145.

The Church was also assumed by the Word in Christ. IV, 77. The Word himself is not a part of the Church, but, as its head, became flesh. IV, 1942. The Church is joined to Christ’s flesh and becomes the whole Christ, head and body. III, 1979. The Church is Christ’s body, temple, household, and city; Christ is its head, inhabitant, sanctifier, and king. IV, 1717. The Catholic Church alone is Christ’s body. II, 815. In Christ’s body: what are the head, the beard, and the edge of the garment? IX, 341.

Christ and the Church are sometimes indicated as one person. III, 82. Christ often speaks in the person of the Church. II, 545. The voice of the Church and of Christ is one. V, 722. The Church suffered in Christ, and Christ suffered in the Church. II, 545.

The Church is Christ’s wife. III, 25; IV, 1672, 1684, 1784. Christ’s bride. V, 563, 991, 1233. She is Christ’s bride in secret. VIII, 423. The Church, Christ’s bride, left her mother, the Synagogue, in order to cling to him. V, 570. The Church is the daughter-in-law of the Synagogue. IV, 501. The Church’s marriage is celebrated. III, 1990, 2013. The marriage of Christ and the Church is joined together by great love. IV, 1140. The Church’s marriage with God is most intimate; no one offends one while pleasing the other. IV, 1140. The Church’s marriage document. VI, 668. The Church was endowed by the God to whom she is married, adorned by him, redeemed by him, and healed by him. IV, 510. Endowed with Christ’s blood. V, 1331; VI, 645, 668. The Church loved the promise of eternal life in the gifts of her bridegroom. VIII, 305. In order to establish the Church, Christ put on beauty for those whom he pleased, and strength for those whom he displeased. IV, 1182, 1183. Christ loved the Church while she was still ugly; he overturned her ugliness and fashioned beauty. IV, 495. Christ’s ugliness made her beautiful. VI, 690. The Church is whitened and adorned. VI, 289, 290. The Church’s beauty proceeded from Christ’s passion as from a root. V, 258. If you marvel at Christ’s humility on account of the Church, do not now marvel at the Church’s exaltation on account of Christ. IV, 1340. Whatever the bride possesses that pleases Christ, she has from him. IV, 510. Christ is the Church’s ruler, bridegroom, and redeemer. IV, 1784.

The Church is born from the bridegroom. VI, 645. From Christ’s side. III, 216, 1513; V, 55. The Church marries when the bridegroom dies. VI, 645. The formation of the woman mystically signified the formation of the Church. III, 407, 1463; IV, 564, 1784. The Church’s womb is, as it were, the font of baptism. V, 379. The Church’s nest is made from the wood of Christ’s cross. IV, 1300. Why the fellowship of the Church’s unity is properly the work of the Holy Spirit. V, 463. To the Church the Holy Spirit is what the soul is to our body. V, 1231. Those who deny that the Holy Spirit is in the Church are like the Pharisees who denied that he was in Christ. V, 448. The entire Church is one widow. IV, 1726. The Church is a widow in the bridegroom’s absence. IV, 1897. The Church is Christ’s sister from the Father. VIII, 425. Christ’s Church is his sister by his blood, nearest by approach, a dove by the Spirit, and perfect by the word. III, 1791. The Church is our mother. IV, 1140, 1141. The Church is called a daughter because of succession, and a mother because of precedence. IV, 1773. The Church is Christ’s wife, mother, children, brothers, and sisters. IV, 1684, 1685. He will not have God as Father who refuses to have the Church as mother. VI, 668. The Church is both mother and children to herself. III, 1327. The Church is a mother, and her two breasts are the two Testaments. III, 1998. The Church must be loved as a mother. V, 1512. Let us love God as Father and the Church as mother. IV, 1140. An exhortation to love the Church. VI, 692.

The Church’s concern for her children. VI, 692. How great a care the Church ought to have for a girl entrusted to her. II, 1069. The Church’s gentleness toward those who were first deceived and later corrected. II, 337. The Church is Christ’s bride and a fruitful virgin. VI, 645. The Church has been called a virgin. III, 859, 1498. The whole Church is called a virgin. IV, 1920; VI, 438. One entire virgin. IV, 1920. All the Church’s ranks are one virgin. III, 1499. In what the Church’s virginity consists. V, 1005, 1012. In its entirety she must be a virgin in chastity and integrity of heart. IV, 570. A prostitute was found and made a virgin. V, 1063. She is a virgin in this age and will marry in the future. VI, 47, 48. She is both virgin and mother. V, 768, 1005, 1010, 1012, 1018, 1063. Just as Mary was. VI, 397. She becomes fruitful throughout the whole earth when Christ is exalted above the heavens. VI, 645. The Church is called barren, as one that did not give birth. III, 1064. The Church is fruitful without corruption, virgin and mother. VIII, 305. She gives birth every day and is a virgin. VI, 249. The churches give birth through the Gospel. III, 880. With labor. III, 880.

The apostles are the Church’s supports and pillars. II, 553. They are its bones and strength. IV, 175, 1297. Its foundations and gates, as are the Prophets. IV, 1103. The Church’s daughters are daughters of the Apostles and daughters of kings. IV, 508. The stability of the heavenly Church. VI, 259. The Church’s strength is its love. IV, 1628. Christ is the Church’s foundation and head. V, 1615. The Church’s foundation is above, in heaven, and why. IV, 223, 1103. The Church [Col. 0263] is built not upon human beings but upon Christ. V, 479. In the Church there is the true and salutary, and, in a certain sense, genuine and radical Christian society. VIII, 289.

The Church is foretold as to be gathered from all nations. VII, 585, 586, 592, 593. It is gathered from all ages. III, 821. It was gathered at the beginning through humility, not power. II, 757. Christ is the door of the Church. III, 1721, 1726. For what purpose one must enter the Church. III, 2013. To what extent pagans come into the Church and heretics return to it. IX, 478. One enters the Church through humility. III, 1721. Through present humility the Church acquires future exaltation. VII, 611. To what height it has been raised. V, 314. The Church of Christ is exalted by the cross. VI, 688.

The Church’s doctrine and faith. I, 1336; III, 128. The Church teaches what it has believed, not what it knows. V, 1613. The Catholic Church demands faith from those who come to it; heretics promise rational demonstration. VIII, 19. In the Catholic Church, the simplicity of believing, not quickness of understanding, makes the common people most secure. VIII, 175.

The Church hungers for those whom it wishes to win. IV, 242. No one enters the body of the Church unless he has first been slain. IV, 1642. In a certain sense the Church eats those whom, through its saints, it transfers into its own body. IV, 242.

The Church is one, true, and catholic. V, 49. The Church is above in the angels and below in all the faithful. IV, 1776; VI, 260, 261. The Church is partly on pilgrimage and, for the greater part, dwelling in heaven. IV, 1952. Nevertheless, there is one Church. V, 1500. It is one through the bonds of love. VI, 259. The Church, blessed in the holy angels, helps its pilgrim part. VI, 258.

The Church is one, from Jews and Gentiles. V, 757; VI, 341. It is gathered from the uncircumcised and the circumcised. IV, 534, 1011, 1012. The Church of Christ was planted where the thorns of the Synagogue were uprooted. IV, 462. The difference between the Church and the Synagogue from the meaning of their names. IV, 1047. The Church of the Gentiles is a proselyte, an adopted newcomer to the fathers—not born of their flesh, but their daughter by imitation. IV, 1896. The Church existed even before Christ’s coming, in the saints. V, 38. The members of the Church were the saints who preceded Christ. VI, 313, 335.

The Church is one. IX, 391. The Church is unique—certainly none other than the one Catholic Church. II, 556; V, 447. Christ calls the Church his one Church. II, 555; IV, 176. How the Church is one and manifold. IV, 1837, 1961. Many churches are indeed mentioned in the Scriptures, but they are understood to be members of that one Church. IX, 415, 635. From all the sons of kings one particular queen is made. IV, 509. Particular churches are called islands. IV, 1240. We speak in the languages of all nations within the unity of the Church. III, 1645. The Church is unity. IV, 1309.

The Church’s unity is commended. III, 1432, 1433, 1489; IV, 513, 538, 889; V, 693, 1076, 1224, 1233, 1586, 1587, 1595. Christ binds the Church with the knot of unity and love as with a bond of health. III, 25. The Church is preserved by the structure of unity. IX, 341. Unity is anointed just as priests are anointed. IX, 341. Those are in the unity of Christ’s body who are in Christ’s peace; and those are in Christ’s peace who are of good will. IX, 160. Heretics, Jews, and pagans formed unity against unity. V, 423. The peace of the Church remits sins. IX, 146, 147, 150. This peace is not among the wicked, whether they are inside or outside the Church. IX, 150. Through love the members adhere to one another and to the head. IX, 392. Cyprian taught, both by prophetic testimony and by the significance of the sacraments, that the Church consists of those who are unanimous and harmonious. IX, 240. How greatly the prayers of the saints who are in the Church avail. IX, 149.

The perfection of unity consoles the Church in its grief over lost children. II, 940. The unity of the Catholic Church was signified by the gift of tongues. V, 534, 1225. The one who was healed in the pool represented the unity of the Church. IV, 889, 1733; V, 693. So too did the sheep entrusted to Peter by Christ. V, 1350. All things cry out for unity. IV, 1925.

That one unique Church, the dove, is formed from the saints alone. IX, 219. Heretics and schismatics do not belong to it. VI, 193. No one can have Christ as head unless he has been in his body, that is, in the Church. IX, 429. Whoever, while thinking heretically, refuses to leave a church for the sake of some secular advantage must be regarded as separated from it all the more criminally, inasmuch as he adds the deceit of dissimulation to error and division. IX, 169. Those are outside the Church who dissent from Christ’s testimony either concerning Christ the head or concerning his body. IX, 395. Many who are outside the Church and are called heretics are, according to God’s foreknowledge, better than many good Catholics. IX, 156. All heresies went out from the Church, like useless branches cut off from the vine. VI, 635.

Through heretics the Church is shaken as though by civil wars. IV, 1425. If by your impatience you shake the sides of Mother Church, she indeed shakes you out with grief; but more to your harm than to hers. IV, 678. As Rebecca gave birth, the Church distinguishes those whom she carried as twins in her womb. IV, [Col. 0264] 1673. Why God allows the Church to be disturbed. V, 1496. The Church is disturbed by the separation of schismatics and heretics. III, 1799. Some members, or grains, of the Church have been overshadowed by the rebellions of heresies and schisms when these prevailed. IX, 443. The Church sometimes suffers temporal storms in its grains, so that in certain places it is not recognized; nevertheless, even there it remains hidden. IX, 443. A part of the Church trampled underfoot. IX, 444. Some part completely cut off. IX, 444. How the good, expelled from the Church by seditious people, ought to conduct themselves. III, 128.
