The Church makes use of all who err for its own advancement. III, 127. What ought to keep a Christian in the Church. VIII, 175. The little ones grow feathers in the Church’s nest and nourish the wings of love on the food of sound faith. I, 706.

There is an inner Church and an outer Church. IV, 512. Not only schismatics, but also the perverse, do not belong to the Church. IX, 117. Many who seem to be outside are within; many who seem to be within are outside. IV, 1428; IX, 196. There are many in the Church who do not belong to it. IX, 155, 156. One who is mingled with Christ’s sheep only by bodily association must not be said to be in the Church. V, 462. The Church’s separated chaff, and its inner chaff. IX, 538. Whether the external wicked are worse than the internal wicked is a major question. IX, 163. As long as someone remains attached to the Church, his healing is not to be despaired of; otherwise it is when he has been cut off. V, 754. False Christians within the Church, and sons of the Church among the impious. VII, 45. Not all who are in the Church reign with Christ. VII, 673. The wicked do not belong to the Church. III, 1431, 1433; IX, 160, 189, 195, 199. The greedy and the other wicked do not belong to it. IX, 149, 150, 155, 156. Although bodily in the Church, the wicked are spiritually outside it. IX, 207. Heretics have fallen from the Church by open and bodily separation, but the wicked by hidden and spiritual separation. III, 442. Although Donatists are not rebaptized when they pass over to the Church, they are nevertheless not received as they are. II, 940. Even one who is mingled with the congregation of the saints in carnal hardness has always been separated from the unity of that Church which is without spot or wrinkle. IX, 123, 124.

The Church is in those who build upon the rock, not in those who build upon the sand. IX, 436, 437, 440. Those who hear Christ’s words and do not do them are outside the rock. IX, 228. All the faithful who have existed, who exist, or who will exist belong to the Church. IV, 749. The predestined can in no way be separated from the Church. IX, 491. Nor are penitents excluded or separated from it. IV, 1295. Those separated from the Church cannot be good as long as they think against it. II, 952. Outside it, schismatics must necessarily perish eternally. V, 1596. Outside it, schismatics feed not Christ’s sheep but goats. V, 1296. Whoever exists outside it neither hears nor sees; and whoever is in it is neither deaf nor blind. IV, 538. Truth remains in the Church’s womb; whoever is separated from it must necessarily speak falsely. IV, 678. Those cut off from it boast of their form in vain. V, 1232. Some things are done outside in Christ’s name, not against the Church; and inside, some things are done on the devil’s side against the Church. IX, 164. It can also happen that the good teach something useless while preserving love, and that the wicked teach something salutary without love. IX, 164. Good works performed outside the Church are useless. IV, 1060. Outside the Church’s unity, whatever heretics do is of no benefit. IX, 54. It is of no benefit to preserve virginity. II, 952. Or to die for Christ’s name. II, 410. Martyrs are to be honored only within the Church’s unity. V, 1295. The Holy Spirit, as the soul of the Church’s body, is not possessed outside it. V, 461, 1221, 1231, 1232. Nor is the remission of sins. V, 465. Outside it no one is heard unto eternal salvation. IV, 478, 1270, 1721. It is proved by the example of Cornelius that whatever good may be present in prayers and almsgiving cannot benefit outside the Church. IX, 115. It can indeed be said of human beings that outside the unity of the Church God has none of his own, but this is not said of the sacraments. IX, 162. Outside the Catholic Church everything may be possessed except salvation. IX, 170, 695. Except love. IX, 476. How greatly the prayers of the saints who are in the Church avail. IX, 149. Whom they help and whom they do not. IX, 149.

The holy Catholic Church—which one? V, 1063, 1071; VIII, 78. Why it is called catholic. III, 221. The Church is called catholic because it is spread throughout the whole world. II, 194. There is no Catholic Church except the one spread throughout the inhabited world. IX, 112. That the Church has been spread throughout the whole world and extended among all nations is shown against the Donatists. II, 189, 194, 195, 198, 264, 583, 794, 952; IV, 244, 513, 566, 640, 642, 669, 807, 1159, 1630, 1924, 1925; V, 289, 659, 722, 723, 1126, 1221; IX, 79, 252, 264, 265, 268, 269, 283, 284, 306, 310, 318, 319, 330, 370, 380, 582, 587, 589, 628, 653, 718; VI, 174, 306, 307. By what praises the Church is proclaimed, by what mysteries commended, by what sacraments concealed, and by what preaching revealed. IV, 1677. Praise of the Catholic Church. VI, 652, 660. The great Church is the Catholic Church alone. IV, 443. The Church is a human being spread everywhere, whose head is above and whose members are below. IV, 476. Now the whole body speaks in the languages of all; and in those languages in which it does not yet speak, it will speak. IV, 1929. The universality of the Church was represented by the four days. III, 821.

The Church is everywhere. VII, 609. From the ends of the earth it cries out to God. IV, 1602. It is summoned from the four quarters of the world in the name of the Trinity. IV, 1104. The Church of the saints is the Catholic Church, not the church of heretics. IV, 1951. The Catholic Church is throughout the whole world, whereas each heresy is confined to its own part. V, 280. The same Catholic Church is everywhere; heretics are not everywhere, but are one group here and another there. IX, 538. The Catholic Church is the Lord’s tabernacle; the churches of heretics are the tabernacles of a man, the tabernacles of sinners. IV, 1912. The Catholic Church is not Donatus’s party. II, 189. It is not confined to Africa alone. II, 396. A church that does not communicate with all nations is not Christ’s Church. IX, 400. The Church overseas. V, 292, 293. The whole Church is one tree. IV, 1743. The Catholic Church bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world. IX, 616. The glory of the Church rising from a despised root among all nations. V, 259. The Church’s harvest sprang up more abundantly through the blood of the martyrs. IV, 454, 595, 1595; VII, 758. The Church’s expansion is the fruit of Christ’s abandonment, tribulation, and prayer. II, 556. The Scriptures promise that the Church will one day exist among all nations. II, 491. God’s promises concerning the Church’s extension throughout the entire world. IX, 35, 38. For the most part fulfilled. IX, 36. How the Church began at Jerusalem and from there proceeded through all languages. IX, 412.

By what indication the Church is to be recognized. VIII, 289. And from where it is to be demonstrated. IX, 427, 429, 430. Each of us does not seek the Church in his own righteousness, but in the divine Scriptures. II, 335. The Church’s location must be sought only in the Lord’s words. IX, 392, 395, 396. The Catholic Church is recognized in the Scriptures. II, 401, 491. It is commended in Holy Scripture. IX, 466. It is signified in Scripture. IX, 633, 428. It is proved from Scripture. IX, 632. By countless testimonies. V, 288, 294, 797. First, it is shown from the Law. IX, 398, 415. From Genesis. IX, 431, 441, 534. From the Psalms. IX, 405, 431, 441. From the Prophets. IX, 400. From Isaiah. IX, 431, 441. From the Gospel. IX, 407, 430, 431, 438, 441. It is recognized from Luke’s Gospel, chapter 24. V, 1125. From the Acts of the Apostles. IX, 409, 430, 431, 442. From the apostolic Epistles. IX, 430. From the Apocalypse. IX, 430. The gift of tongues bestowed upon the Apostles foretold that the Church would exist among all nations. IX, 476. The Catholic Church was shown to Peter in a vision. V, 802. Wherever Christ appears in the writings, his Church also appears. II, 491, 794; IX, 536. The Church spread throughout the whole world—how small it was when it was foretold to Abraham. V, 335. The Church must exist among all nations, but not in such a way that everyone who is there will believe. II, 923. The bridegroom of the Church is above all the heavens; the bride is over the whole earth. V, 308. The Prophets spoke more obscurely about Christ than about the Church, because they foresaw that greater disputes would be raised about the Church than about Christ. IV, 244, 245. The Church of Christ cannot be doubted more than the body of Christ, who rose from the dead. IV, 1928. The blindness of heretics concerning the Church is equal to the blindness of the Jews concerning Christ. V, 260. There are not as many heresies against the Church as there are testimonies of the Law for the Church. IV, 1925. How ineptly the Donatists respond to the testimonies of Scripture that foretell the Church’s spread throughout the whole world. IX, 406. The Catholic Church is established and defended against Vincentius’s objections. II, 331. He maintained that it is called catholic because of the observance of all the commandments. II, 333, 346. And, to prove that the Church is not spread everywhere, he adopted a passage from Hilary. II, 333. The passage explained. II, 335, 337. How the universality of the Church is shown against the Donatists from their own arguments. IX, 588. And from their own confession. IX, 583. The Catholic Church is named even by its enemies. III, 128.

The true Church is not covered over and invisible. IX, 422. It cannot be hidden. IX, 343. It is clear and conspicuous to all. IX, 493. It escapes no one. IX, 284. It cannot remain hidden. V, 222. It is constituted in manifestation. IV, 160, 161. It is not to be recognized under the name of a supposedly secret and apocryphal truth, or on the basis of a small number of people. VIII, 290. It is well known throughout the whole world and is not to be sought in a desert or in private rooms. IX, 443. After this age the Church will not be hidden in any part. IV, 514. The Church’s doctrine: for Julian, a popular dogma. X, 1143. The Donatists dared to say that the Catholic Church was a human fabrication. IX, 732.

The Donatists want the Church to have perished from the inhabited world. IX, 35, 36, 37, 49, 79, 294, 340. Through the contagion of the wicked Africans. IX, 494. Through Caecilian’s sin. IX, 713. Because of Caecilian’s crimes, whether true or false. VIII, 43. And to have remained in Africa alone. IX, 49, 52. The Donatists attempt to reduce the Church to a small part of the earth. IX, 300, 312, 330. Ignorantly or deceitfully the Donatists cite certain testimonies of Scripture to show that the Church has perished from the whole world. IX, 417, 418, 419, 421, 424. They say in vain that it will perish. V, 289. The Donatists rashly condemn the churches of the whole world. IX, 300, 312. They accuse them rashly and unjustly. IX, 494. They called the Catholic Church a prostitute. IX, 696. Scripture shows that the crimes of Caecilian were impiously and calumniously brought against the Church spread throughout the whole world. IX, 633. The Church’s holiness is not polluted by the contagion of the wicked. IX, 177, 178, 179, 275. The sins of others do not stain it. IX, 370, 371. The evils committed within it do not belong to it. IX, 310, 312, 315. Those who are wicked within it do it no harm. IX, 234, 616, 617. The sins committed within their communion do not injure the just. IX, 417. At the conference the Donatists confessed that the overseas Church was not contaminated by the crime of the Africans. IX, 681. The Church must be considered to have perished if another’s sin contaminates it. IX, 228, 244. Whether the wicked stain the good when they share the same communion, before Cyprian. IX, 493. If the Church perished from the inhabited world through the contagion of the wicked, it also perished among the Donatists. IX, 393. The Donatists do not dare to say that the Church perished in Cyprian’s time. IX, 746. If the Church had already perished in Cyprian’s time, whence then came the origin of Donatus and Majorinus? IX, 131, 133, 607, 608. The African traditores cannot pollute the Church if the Maximianists did not pollute the Donatists. IX, 583. The Catholic Church could not perish through the crimes of the Africans. IX, 414, 415, 611. Nor could it be stained. IX, 252. The Church’s personification addressed to the Donatists. IX, 31, 41. The Church’s condition, and how it did not perish in the time of the Arians. II, 86, 87.

The Church cannot be interrupted without perishing. IX, 140. Whether it was interrupted from the Flood until Abraham. VII, 475. At one time the Church existed in a single person, at another in a single family. IV, 1689. The whole Church is to be understood in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. IV, 1743. The Church, passing from some who depart to others who come, has been founded forever. IV, 894, 901, 906, 1007, 1309. Those who are not in it say that the Church has perished. IV, 1309. The Donatists want to behead the Church. V, 725. The Church was not destroyed by communion with the wicked. II, 339, 341, 342. It is shown that the Church has not perished from the whole world. IX, 424, 425. The Church is not conquered, uprooted, or overcome by any temptations until the end of the age comes. IV, 726. The Church can neither perish nor be brought low. IV, 1353. The Church’s faith endures to the end. V, 224. The Church will not fail. VI, 53.

The Church has the good mingled with the wicked throughout the whole world. II, 338, 345; III, 1431; IV, 190, 1693; V, 299, 307, 1092; VI, 341; VII, 611; VIII, 291. The chaff and the weeds are mingled with the wheat throughout the whole world until the day of judgment. V, 119, 1174; IX, 296, 297, 312, 444, 536, 537. Nevertheless, the weeds are not among the wheat in the Church, but in the world. IX, 629, 632, 634. The Church is not here without spot or wrinkle. I, 593, 617, 637; II, 842; X, 336, 435, 621. Pelagius was accused of saying that the Church here is without spot. X, 336. In what sense Caelestius said that the Church is without spot, and in what sense Pelagius did. X, 336, 356. The Pelagians taught that, in the present time, the Church exists only in the just. X, 998. The Church here is not without sin. V, 981. Nevertheless, it is called the kingdom of heaven. V, 1169. The Church that has no spot or wrinkle is not to be understood as though it already were so, but as the Church that is being prepared to become so. IX, Retr. 107, 108. Here it is being prepared to be without spot or wrinkle in heaven. V, 982. The bodily separation of the wicked from the Church will take place at the end of the age. II, 338. The Church will become pure from all mingling with wicked human beings only after this mortality. IX, 658. This earthly Church is to be gathered into heaven after the resurrection. III, 335. Only in the future age will the holy Church attain spotless purity. X, 285. Without spot or wrinkle only after the resurrection. II, 810; X, 310. What the Church will be like after the resurrection. V, 1197, 1243. How great the Church’s splendor will be after judgment. VII, 682. Then the Church will contain only the good. V, 1175. The Church of the saints, the Church of the grains. IV, 1950. The Church among the wicked as a lily among thorns. IV, 1802. The Church’s beauty is already wondrous. IV, 1340.

The periods of the Church must be distinguished. IX, 658, 659. The Church is now mortal; in the age to come it will be immortal. IX, 632, 635. The Church has two periods. IX, 632. Yet there are not two Churches. IX, 635. The ages of the Church. IV, 385, 894. The Church’s old age will be white through rightly performed deeds, but it will not be corrupted by death. IV, 1179. The Church’s old age is youthful and green. IV, 1179. Christ’s Church is no longer under the Law but under grace. VIII, 309, 311.

The conduct of the Church, Christ’s spouse, etc. VIII, 309. Three classes of people living in the Church. VII, 40. Three kinds of human beings. III, 1357. Each contains its own good and its own wicked. IV, 356, 1279, 1730. Two kinds of people exist in God’s house. IX, 241. Two kinds of workers, the good and the hypocrites. V, 94. The Church contains the strong and the weak. V, 1640, 1670. It can exist neither without the strong nor without the weak. V, 480. It contains the spiritual and the carnal. IX, 195. The life of both. IX, 195. The Church consists of the spiritual and the carnal, as of heaven and earth. IV, 1748. The carnal within the Church are in Esau’s portion. V, 39. Those in the Church who love their honors and advantages are chaff. V, 50, 1175. The Church either shelters the little ones like eggs beneath vigilant wings or nourishes them like infants with milk. VIII, 305. The Church teaches, and in it God grants the character traits that distinguished philosophers sought for practical life rather than formed in others. II, 315. Those who live badly in the Church make God’s house a den of robbers. IV, 1705. Those who seek their own interests in the Church, not those of Jesus Christ, sell sheep, oxen, and doves. III, 1469. How the Church takes care not to soil its feet while proceeding toward Christ. III, 1789. How the prophetic rebukes addressed at times to the whole multitude are to be understood. IX, 417. Christ addresses any one person from the Church as though addressing the Church. V, 292. The good and the wicked in the Church. IX, 162, 167, 192, 417, 420, 427. According to the Donatists’ own confession. IX, 629, 659, 660. The Church is presently lame, containing good and wicked. V, 59. The Church is dark and beautiful. III, 83. The Church is not therefore to be abandoned because the wicked are found in it. II, 411, 794, 951. Even pastors. II, 951, 952. The Church is not to be abandoned because of the weeds or the wicked who are in it. IX, 348, 349, 417, 514, 566, 585, 657, 658, 675. Nor because of manifest traditores. IX, 517. Examples. II, 329, 341; IX, 370, 371. This is Cyprian’s consistent teaching. IX, 165, 514, 564, 683, 741, 742, 744, 747.

The sins of wicked Christians do not stain the Church. IV, 1801. No bodily mingling with the wicked causes it disturbance. IX, 295. The Church has what it must bear outside and what it must mourn within. IV, 1847. The Church is here in labor and pain—why? IV, 613. As long as the Church is in labor, its children, good and wicked, are within. IV, 1673. Reconciliation of the Scriptures concerning the mingling of the good and the wicked in the Church. IX, 632. Within the Church are the good and the wicked; outside it there can be no good. IX, 610. The wicked eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord together with the good. IX, 669. The wicked also ascend into the apses; in the apses there are grains, and there are also weeds. V, 472. In comparison with the wicked, the just are few. IX, 417, 418. In the Church, the inheritance of God is shared with the few, but with the many his seals are shared. VIII, 291. The Church now separates itself from the wicked by difference of conduct, while tolerating them in sacramental communion. V, 1071.

Church. The wicked in the Church are now so mingled that not only are those who lie hidden unknown, but those who are known are often tolerated for the sake of the unity of peace. IX, 631. The wicked are to be tolerated in the Church. II, 329, 403; VIII, 292. For the Church’s unity, the sins of others must be tolerated. V, 42, 49. The weeds must be tolerated. IX, 517. The Church tolerates many things that it does not approve. II, 222. The Church does not consent to the deeds of the wicked but tolerates them. IV, 1802; V, 55, 56, 59. The Church’s prayers for its good children against the wicked. II, 1057. The Church is not to be blamed because of the conduct of wicked Christians. I, 1342. These are tolerated as chaff. I, 1342; III, 127. The sin or error of anyone has long been endured until he either finds an accuser or stubbornly defends a perverse opinion. III, 127. The fellowship of the wicked mingled with the good does not prejudice the Church. II, 329, 492. Whether they are to be barred from communion, if either the power to do so is lacking or concern for peace prevents it. II, 297. The fellowship of the wicked would prejudice neither the Church nor innocent Christians, even if some traditor had crept into the succession of bishops extending from Peter to Anastasius. II, 197. In the Catholic Church the good tolerate the wicked for the sake of the good of unity, but hate them for the sake of the good of equity. II, 170, 179, 198, 335, 338. How the perverse are to be tolerated in the Church: Tychonius treated this, and Augustine approves his work. II, 1065. In the Catholic Church the good do not share in the deeds of the wicked, but in Christ’s altar. II, 170, 265, 298. The crimes charged against them belong to the chaff, not to the wheat. II, 198. Ecclesiastical discipline is not therefore neglected. IX, 370. Ecclesiastical correction is called bloodless discipline. II, 657. Ecclesiastical discipline must be vigilant in correcting the wicked, not only by words but also through excommunications and degradations. IX, 631. See “The Wicked.” Separation from the Church and reconciliation. VII, 674.

The Church has been given the power to forgive sins. III, 25. The Church alone received the power to remit sins. VI, 263. Some fettered people flee into the Church and are released. IV, 1959. The keys of the Church. V, 1545, 1711. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to the Church when they were given to Peter. VI, 308. That is, to Peter as representing the person of the Church. V, 802, 1349. The keys were given to one because of the Church’s unity. V, 1349. Christ first raises sinners, and then the Church releases them. V, 1349. How the Church benefits sinners by releasing them. V, 434. The Church opened its mouth in confession of sins to receive Christ’s blood. VIII, 259.

The authority of the Catholic Church. VI, 319; VIII, 91, 246; IX, 466. All heretics attempt to surpass the deeply founded and most stable authority of the Church, as though in the name and promise of reason—why? II, 448. How the Lord fortified the Church’s authority. II, 448. How great the Church’s authority is, even in matters attested by its records. V, 1333, 1346. The authority of the apostolic churches above that of the others. II, 164, 175. The authority of the Western Church. X, 648. The faith of the Eastern and Western Churches is one. X, 649. Whatever the whole Church believes must be accepted, even if it can neither be investigated by reason nor explained in speech. X, 829. The Church’s ancient, canonical, and deeply established custom. V, 1343. The truth of the Scriptures is upheld when what the universal Church has approved is done. IX, 466. The rule concerning the differing observances of different churches. II, 151, 200, 202. The predestined Church, the pillar and foundation of truth. IV, 1350. Perfect truth exists in the Church alone. I, 1325. It alone possesses the truth, both in its milk and in its bread. VIII, 305. Unless the Lord inhabited the Church, however diligent a speculation might be, it would fall into error. IV, 122. There are various languages in the Church, but one doctrine. IV, 509. The Church must keep watch against profane novelties. X, 141. Christ referred to the Church the examination of matters pertaining to doctrine. III, 1355. The rulers granted the Church such authority that whatever was judged in it could not be undone. IV, 196. The condemnation of heretics makes clear what the Church thinks. I, 752. The Church, fighting against all heresies, cannot be defeated. VI, 635. The devil is not permitted to harm the Church in anything. VII, 613. The Church will never be seduced by the devil. VII, 670. The Church has different discipline according to the variety of circumstances. II, 812. What the whole Church commonly practices must be observed. II, 202.

The Church is never without persecution. VII, 613, 614. As long as the Church is here, there will be no lack of enemies who desire its ruin. IV, 1012. The Church is in great glory among all nations, but also in great temptation. IV, 724. It is at once in the breadth of joy and the narrowness of tribulation, because it embraces both good and wicked. IV, 239. Now it is threshed like a threshing floor with chaff. IX, 587. It always suffers persecution for righteousness, even if not always through bodily tortures. IX, 420. The Church’s persecution is threefold: first by tyrants, second by heretics and false brothers, and third by the Antichrist. IV, 128. The Church is the mother of martyrs. V, 221. It grows through persecutions. V, 1351.

Ten persecutions of the Church are counted. VII, 614. Whether, from these ten until the eleventh, which will be from the Antichrist, the Church will suffer no other persecution. VII, 614. The final persecution of the Church—what it is. VII, 676. At the time of the final persecution the Church will be spread everywhere. VII, 676. After the final persecution the Church must still be purified by certain tribulations. III, 1326. The Church’s persecutions were not signified by the plagues of Egypt. VII, 615. The time of persecution and peace of the Church was represented by King Nebuchadnezzar. II, 325.

The Church’s greatest tribulation comes from evil works. IV, 720, 721. From the beginning the Church was attacked by the impious. IV, 1689, 1690. In times of persecution it was as though the whole Church were being attacked at once, but now individuals are tested one by one. IV, 761. The Church suffers persecution from the pride and impiety of the carnal, whom it tries to correct through temporal troubles and terrors. II, 324. The Church is instructed through fears, pains, labors, and the dangers of temptations. VII, 611. God purifies and disciplines the Church through certain medicinal troubles. III, 25. In prosperous circumstances consolation is provided for the Church so that it is not broken by adversity; in adverse circumstances discipline is provided so that it is not corrupted by prosperity. VII, 613. The Church is now being built in labor and hardship; afterward it will be dedicated in glory. IV, 219; V, 1471, 1476. The building of the heavenly Church. V, 1475. The dedication of the Church. V, 1475. Since pagans have nothing in it to criticize, they bring forward the dissension of Christians. V, 314.

Tyrants exercise the Church’s patience, heretics its wisdom, and enemies its benevolence or even beneficence. VII, 613. For the sake of temporal safety the Church did not fight against impious persecutors. VII, 758. If it wished to use the sword, it would seem to be fighting for the present life. IV, 723. How greatly ecclesiastical people abhor the desire to kill. II, 367. It abhors willing what cannot be done without bodily tortures. II, 395. The Catholic Church has been strengthened against the attacks of enemies not by resisting but by enduring. VI, 298. How it now conquers its enemies. VI, 298. It conquers its enemies through gentleness, just as Christ conquered. IV, 1717. One must pray for the Church’s persecutors. II, 637. Pious works must be performed to obtain peace for the Church. V, 1585. A Christian must not avenge himself against the Church by attacking the Church. VII, 162. No sober person will think against reason, no Christian against the Scriptures, and no peaceable person against the Church. VIII, 895. Those who crossed over to the Church were cruelly harassed by the Donatists. II, 798, 800.

When the Church is attacked by abortive sons who are waging war against it, it rightly and properly seeks aid from its other sons. II, 1057. It is permissible to seek the protection of the Church from the emperors. IX, 327, 334. It belongs to Christian kings of this age to desire that the Church be peaceful. III, 1483. This includes even acting harshly against the Church’s enemies. III, 1483. It belongs to their care to ensure that no one rebels against the Church with impunity. IX, 733, 739. And that no one sins against divine matters. IX, 749. The Church rightly compels its lost children to return. II, 803. It compels them beneficially. II, 312. It possesses the power not only to invite but also to compel people to what is good. II, 757. It seeks not the death of the lost but their conversion and peace. II, 807. The Church must not be deterred by the loss of some from securing the salvation of others. II, 799. Even one person’s conversion consoles the Church in its grief over lost children. II, 808.

The Donatists call the Catholic Church “Macarian.” II, 190. The Church benefited from the Donatist persecution. II, 807. And from the emperors’ good and bad laws. II, 398, 795. When the Church suffers, Christ suffers. IV, 613, 749, 1119, 1132. The Church suffered in Christ when he suffered for the Church; just as Christ himself suffered in the Church when the Church suffered for him. II, 545. A Christian is Christian in vain if he is not in the lot for which Christ suffered. IV, 176. Whether that Church is to be called the true Church which suffers persecution, rather than the one that inflicts it. IX, 664, 665. Through Christ the Church learns to offer itself by the daily sacrifice. VII, 298. The Church’s universal sacrifice through the great priest. VII, 284.

Ecclesia inops et peregrina. IV, 1119. The Church is poor and a pilgrim. IV, 1119. The goods of the Old Testament had to be denied to the Church, so that she might already learn to desire and hope for the goods of the New Testament. II, 544. The Lord indicated that the Church would have purses, since he himself had a purse. III, 1762, 1803. Ecclesiastical goods are possessed under human law. III, 1437. The Donatists complained unjustly that the Emperors had ordered the possessions of their churches to pass to the Catholic Church. II, 809. Offerings made to churches: when they should be accepted or refused. V, 1571. The necessities of the Church’s ministers are to be supplied before they ask. IV, 1910. Bishops are thought to use and enjoy the Church’s estates, and in reality some use them with the attitude of a master. II, 480. Augustine tolerates their administration but does not love it, and wishes to be free of it, if he can do so without neglecting his duty. II, 481. If ecclesiastics possess privately what is sufficient for them, the Church’s goods are not theirs but the poor’s. II, 809. Ecclesiastical cases were chiefly entrusted to the tribune Marcellinus, yet they belong to the Proconsul. II, 510. We do not wish the sufferings of God’s servants to be avenged, as though by the law of retaliation, with equal punishments. II, 509, 510, 511. The sufferings of God’s servants, which ought to be the Church’s glory, must not be dishonored by the blood of enemies. II, 536. This was readily obtained from the Emperors in the case of clerics killed by pagans. II, 536. Although some, stirred up more turbulently by more recent events, disapprove of this, they will nevertheless praise it afterward. II, 536.

The Church is a field. V, 46. God’s field. IV, 1744. The Lord’s field. VI, 685. The Lord’s field is at first full of thorns. VI, 688. God’s most fruitful field. III, 926. The field watered with Christ’s blood. VI, 688. The Donatists did not want the Church to be Christ’s field, but held that the world outside the Church was. IX, 742.

The Church is God’s maidservant. IV, 1140. The Church called a corner. V, 557. It is Noah’s ark. III, 1434. In it the saints are kept safe. IV, 214. The Church is a threshing floor. V, 119, 1174. A threshing floor containing both chaff and grain. IV, 109, 115. In the Gospel the Donatists attempted to deny that the Church was like a threshing floor. IX, 660. The Church is the Lord’s holy court. IV, 1233. The City of God. IV, 533, 534, 680; VII, 387, 585. Why it is called the city of the great King, Zion, Jerusalem. VII, 550. The Church is a city set upon a mountain, which cannot be hidden. IV, 680. A city on a mountain, and a sheep on the shepherd’s shoulders. V, 222. The Church is heaven. III, 834. A silvered dove. IV, 823. The Church is confession and beauty. IV, 1340.

The Church is God’s house. IV, 194; V, 1647; VIII, 1085. In the Creed the Church is rightly joined to the Trinity, as to the inhabitant of the house. VI, 258. The building and dedication of the Church, God’s house. V, 1471, 1476. The Church is called a firmament. IV, 532, 533. Lightning. III, 1330. God’s inheritance. IV, 394, 1012. The Church as the new Jerusalem descending from heaven: how this is to be understood. VII, 682. This Church begins with the earthly Jerusalem and ends with the heavenly one. IV, 1929. Israel according to the spirit. VIII, 628. The Church is a mountain. IV, 70, 478, 533; V, 265. God’s holy mountain. III, 442. A ship. IV, 1188, 1380, 1381. A ship tossed by a storm. V, 415. Christ’s sheepfold. III, 1721. Paradise. III, 207, 442, 478, 482; IV, 539; VII, 395. A rock. III, 885, 886. The rock upon which the Church was promised that it would be built is Christ himself. V, 1238, 1348.

The Church is understood by the name of orphans and widows. III, 850. Why it is called queen. VII, 549. It is called a kingdom. III, 821. The kingdom of heaven. VI, 409. Christ’s kingdom. VI, 76. God’s kingdom. VII, 672. The Church is a net cast into the sea. IX, 25. Sun, moon, and stars. II, 919. A stall. V, 752. The universal Church is called the moon; particular churches are called stars. IV, 112. In the small number of the stronger and more illustrious, the Church is compared with the stars; in the multitude of the weak and carnal, with the sand of the sea. II, 336. The Church is Christ’s robe. VII, 520. God’s tabernacle. III, 1064. The tabernacle stands against heresies, schisms, and so forth. IV, 252, 253. The Church militant is God’s tabernacle; the Church triumphant is his house. IV, 252, 469, 1720. The Church is the temple of the supreme Trinity. VI, 259. The land of the blessed and the land of the living. III, 85. It is compared with a winepress. V, 121. The churches are winepresses. IV, 109, 1056. The Church is called a turtledove. IV, 1300. Christ’s garment. V, 490. Christ’s garment, which is cleansed so that it may have no spot and stretched so that it may have no wrinkle. IV, 1734. The Church’s varied and gilded clothing: how this is to be understood. IV, 509. The Church is compared with a vine. III, 1990. It puts forth shoots like a vine and is pruned. VI, 341.

The Church is represented by Noah’s ark. IV, 115, 1103; V, 1216; IX, 196, 397, 632. The Church, like Noah’s ark, is tossed about in this life. II, 847. It is represented by Gideon’s dry fleece. III, 813. A representation of the Church destined to serve under the kings of this age. VI, 337. The churches are represented by hinds. III, 880. The Church was represented by Eve. III, 215; IV, 1673. By the Flood. IV, 1354. By Jephthah’s daughter. III, 823. It is compared with the moon. II, 209; IV, 132. The type of the Church in the Canaanite woman. V, 486, 487, 544. In Mary Magdalene. V, 58. In Christ’s mother. VI, 660. In the mother of the Maccabees. V, 1380. In the woman to whom the risen Christ said, “Do not touch me.” V, 1144, 1153. In the prostitute whom Samson married. V, 1640. In Peter. V, 479, 802, 1348, 1350. The Church, with respect to the present and future age, is represented by Martha and Mary. III, 1341. It is represented by Mount Paran. III, 775. The Church and the Synagogue are the two women who disputed before Solomon over a son. V, 92. The woman suffering from a flow of blood is a type of the future Church from the Gentiles. III, 820, 1641. The Church was represented by the woman who anointed Christ. IV, 171. By the creation of the world. I, 850. In the blessing of Noah’s sons. VIII, 265. In the fishing before and after Christ’s passion. V, 1158, 1161, 1164, 1167; IX, 196, 397, 632. It was represented by Rebekah. IV, 1673; V, 38. By the second Sabbath. IV, 532. The Church, enduring persecution in its beginnings, was represented in Samson. IV, 1126. The image of the present Church is in Zion; the image of the future Church is in Jerusalem. IV, 122, 70, 1107. The Church is signified in the vessel shown to Peter. V, 802. In Jacob’s garment. V, 46. In the high priest’s garment. III, 687. In the garments of the transfigured Christ. V, 490.

The Church is properly called the people contained within the basilica. II, 863.

The Church is also called the place where the Church, or the faithful, assemble. III, 704, 711. The form of churches. III, 660. The apse of a church. II, 474, 477. The construction of a church is a good work insofar as it proceeds from faith and charity. V, 1475. It is sacrilegious to place an image of God in a Christian temple. VII, 188. Churches adorned with memorials of the martyrs. IV, 1590. What is done in churches. VII, 76, 77. In them some are rightly occupied and some wrongly. V, 196. Those who have their body in church but their heart elsewhere are rebuked. V, 423. Churches were established for hearing the word of God. VII, 52. In churches men sit separately from women. VII, 76, 77. Why the overseers of churches sit in a more elevated place. V, 569. Some come to church not out of devotion but because of the occasion of a solemn festival. V, 1600. Those who fill the theaters also fill the churches. V, 1165, 1174. On solemn days the Church is filled with people who would rather leave sooner than come. V, 1212. Women who come to church in proud attire are reproved. V, 205. The walls of churches sufficiently protect the bodily safety of those who feared being executed. II, 647, 651. Those who flee to a church usually wait there until their affairs are settled through the bishop’s intercession. II, 430. Augustine considers it part of his duty not to abandon a man who had fled in this way to his church. II, 429. He might have been carried off outside it, though he was less cautious. II, 430. He complains that the laws had not been observed, so that the man was carried off in this way. II, 430. Augustine wished to raise the question, or even consult the Apostolic See, whether those who flee there in order to break faith with their guarantors should not be expelled from the church. II, 1067. After the ecclesiastical records had been completed, the sentence of anathema was imposed on the man who appeared to have led perjurers away from the church, although he said that they had first left voluntarily. II, 1066. A man overwhelmed by debt flees to the Church for help, and the creditors press Augustine to hand him over to them. II, 1092.

Why most people avoid ecclesiastical duties and the governance of peoples. VIII, 436, 437. Most are compelled to undertake them by force. VIII, 437. The churches have different offices in their various members, but one common life. V, 1231. Showing partiality in conferring ecclesiastical honors is no slight sin. II, 1092. If the Church has desired a monk’s service, he should neither accept it with greedy self-exaltation nor reject it through flattering indolence. II, 188. Those in the Church who offer excuses to avoid undertaking the steward’s office are compared with the servant unwilling to distribute the talent. VI, 218. What rule should be observed in conferring ranks of honor upon those received into the Catholic Church. IX, 478. This is the order in the Church: some go before and others follow; and those who go before have someone whom they follow. IV, 436. These men ought to watch over the peace with vigilant attention. IV, 901. Priests and Levites in the Church. VII, 693. The care and dangers of the Church’s rulers. IV, 1425. At this very time nothing is easier or more pleasant for a bishop, presbyter, or deacon than the office, if it is performed perfunctorily; nothing is more difficult if the work is done as God commands. II, 88. When the danger of devastation threatens, when ecclesiastics may or may not flee. II, 1013. At such times some usually demand baptism, others reconciliation, and all consolation and the administration and distribution of the sacraments. II, 1016. See “Flight.” The Church’s bishops invoking God with barbarisms and solecisms, and not understanding the words they utter. VI, 320. Whether holding the Church and holding primacy are the same thing. IX, 187.

Ecclesiastes is held by the Jews to be a book in the canon of sacred Scripture. VII, 661.

Ecclesiasticus is not in the canon of the Hebrews. VI, 165. By others it is called Jesus Sirach. VI, 125. Because Jesus Sirach is the author of this book. III, 947; VI, 606. Ecclesiasticus is attributed to Solomon because of the similarity of its style. VI, 606; VII, 554. The books of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus are not Solomon’s. III, 947.

Ecdicia, a devout woman. II, 1078.

Sea urchins increase and decrease according to the moon’s waxing and waning. VII, 146.

Eclipse. See “Sun.”

What ecstasy is. III, 391, 464, 470; V, 102; VI, 129. Ecstasy is an excess or alienation of the mind. IV, 226, 338, 834, 1492. It arises either from fear or from some revelation. IV, 1492. In it incorporeal things take on the likeness of bodies. VII, 725. And the images that are seen signify something. III, 465. Description of ecstasy. V, 360. What ordinarily happens in a more violent ecstasy. II, 610. Saint Peter’s ecstasy. V, 1228. Rusticanus, in ecstasy, knew both that he was awake and that he was seeing something not with bodily eyes. III, 455.

The rack of the heart. V, 110.

Eden, that is, delights, or pleasure, or a feast. III, 202; VIII, 261.

Some people are the more gluttonous because they are filled with more cares. I, 924.

Desire for eating. V, 771.

Edesius, an official recorder. IX, 513.

Edom is the name of Esau. III, 579. Why Esau was called Edom. IV, 1772. Edom is interpreted as “earthly.” IV, 715. In Punic, Edom is said to mean “blood.” IV, 1772.

Educa, or Edulica, a goddess. VII, 122, 140.

God placed in things the seminal principles, as it were, of unusual and supernatural effects. III, 406. People love to investigate what they have not experienced and to seek the causes of unusual things. III, 469.

He is effeminate who has lost endurance. IV, 211.

The monstrous ferocity of all animals under Roman rule. VII, 104.

A burglar. V, 422, 1585. A burglar becomes a miner. V, 693.

Whether everyone who is wretched is in want. I, 970, 971, 972. He is needy and poor who is not perfect. IV, 872, 873. The poor need you, and you need God. IV, 410. One needy person seeks you; you ought to seek another. IV, 1911. Let the needy person rejoice in what you have given, so that you too may rejoice in what God has given. IV, 410. We are all in need, and God, who in himself needs nothing, is in need in the needy. V, 408. The Lord helps the needy through the one who has, and through the one who does not have he tests the one who has. V, 523.

Poverty and fullness of mind. I, 974. The greatest poverty is to lack wisdom; and whoever does not lack wisdom can lack nothing at all. I, 973. That poverty is to be feared which is diminished neither by abundance nor by want. II, 389. “A destitute life produces everlasting misery,” says Nectarius. II, 387. Augustine did not read this anywhere. II, 388.

“I am in the flesh; I am in the mind; but I am more in the mind than in the flesh.” V, 837.

God’s going forth is understood when he appears in works of grace. IV, 816. In what sense Christ is said to go forth. IV, 1114.

The vice of exaltation. VII, 421, 422. Pride attempts to creep into great things. II, 881.

The Elcesaites, heretics. VIII, 31. Epiphanius associates them with the Ebionites. VIII, 27.

Elchasai, a false prophet. VIII, 31.

Election to the kingdom. X, 924. Election according to grace. V, 604. The ineffable election of grace. III, 1851. Why one person is chosen from the same mass and another rejected: this is unsearchable. V, 177. And it must be referred to God’s inscrutable judgments. VI, 121, 122. God’s hidden judgments in the election of human beings. VI, 127, 275. See “Grace.” Election from the mass of perdition is gratuitous. X, 581. Election is from grace and purpose. VI, 114. Predestination and election proceed from God’s good pleasure. X, 987. From that mass of perdition which arose from Adam, God alone distinguishes a person in order to make him a vessel for honor rather than dishonor. II, 969. The cause of election is love. III, 1831. Election is through mercy and judgment. X, 925. The election of grace is not from works. II, 821, 823, 827; VI, 125. It is not from preceding merits. X, 924, 1133, 1140, 1142. Neither from the merits of parents nor of infants. II, 887. The election of the Gentiles must be attributed not to merits but to grace. IV, 1744. Election does not presuppose merit. III, 1851, 1853. It precedes all human merits. VI, 620. [Col. 0272] Not even faith itself precedes election and calling. X, 998. The election of grace would not be grace if any merits preceded it. I, 621. Election is spoken of where God does not find something made by another that he may choose, but himself makes what he finds. X, 582. Election is not based on foreknowledge of works. II, 888; X, 792, 1132. The Pelagians, ascribing election to future works, are foolish. X, 582. The calling of the elect proceeds from God’s purpose. X, 987. Only the elect have a calling according to God’s purpose. I, 621; III, 2061, 2062. *Retr.* Thus God predestines his elect adults by grace that he may also prepare their wills. I, 595. Divine election does not show partiality, even though it does not proceed from merits. X, 580. Election from the world, or calling, presupposes election before the foundation of the world. X, 986. God chose before the foundation of the world those whom he predestined. X, 987. The mystery of election is displayed in the calling of ignorant shepherds and impious magi. V, 1030. What the election of grace was like, Augustine had not understood at first. III, 2061, 2062. *Retr.* Election to glory. See “Calling.”

The elect, those who are called according to God’s purpose. II, 825; X, 924. Loved according to election, predestined. II, 639. God himself makes people elect; he does not find them so. II, 886. Those who do not yet exist are chosen, and the one who chooses does not err. V, 173. God chose those whom he willed according to his grace and according to their righteousness. V, 604. The elect owe everything to God’s grace. V, 604. We were chosen and predestined not because we were going to be holy, but in order that we might be holy. X, 987. God chose the righteous, not those whom he foresaw would become such by themselves, but those whom he predestined to make such. X, 987. The Pelagian position concerning Esau and Jacob is refuted. II, 887. Christ finds all people evil and makes them good by his grace. V, 587. The Apostles chose Christ because they were chosen, not because they chose him and were therefore chosen. X, 904. Why the lowly were chosen by Christ first. V, 537, 1163. How God chose the rich in faith. X, 986. God works so that we may be to the praise of God’s glory. X, 988. The elect are called God’s children and Christ’s disciples in two ways. X, 929. All good believers are rightly called elect. VII, 194. Only the good belong to election. III, 579. How those who will not persevere can be called elect. X, 925. None of the elect perishes. X, 792, 924, 930. God causes even the sins of the elect to work for good. X, 930. They are led to repentance. X, 792. Why there are more reprobate than elect. II, 860. Why they are sometimes said to be few and sometimes many. IX, 418. They are few in comparison with the reprobate, but many in themselves. II, 338; IV, 1208, 1475. The number of the elect will be fixed, but their multitude will be so great that no one can count it. V, 1161, 1165. The elect are stars, which are numbered by God; those who are not elect are counted beyond the number. IV, 1904. In the elect and the reprobate alike, God’s goodness and equity are rightly proclaimed. III, 434. Election is to be attributed to mercy; reprobation to God’s judgment. II, 823. Through the reprobate and the elect, God’s riches are made manifest. II, 824, 876. In the reprobate the elect recognize what divine mercy has bestowed upon them. II, 822, 824, 860, 876, 887, 986. The objection of those who say, “Why does he still complain?” and so forth, is resolved. II, 822, 882, 884, 888. The elect are spoken of in praise. III, 1619. The name “elect” is not found in an evil sense except when the wicked are chosen by the wicked. III, 579. The various symbols and figures of the elect. III, 632. The elect are compared with the apple of God’s eye. VII, 705. The elect are signified by the number of the fish. V, 1168.

The elect of the Manichaeans. IV, 1822; VIII, 35; IX, 357. The life of these elect and their foolish sacrileges. VIII, 226. These elect are not those whom God saves, but God’s saviors. IV, 1823. See “Manichaeans.”

Almsgiving in Greek is *eleēmosynē*, “mercy.” V, 1043. Almsgiving is a work of mercy. VI, 268. Almsgiving is commended. III, 2023, 2024; IV, 423, 963, 964, 1922; VII, 25. The good of almsgiving. V, 524. Its power for redeeming sins. V, 407. The Lord commands that alms be given. II, 1092. Almsgiving to the poor is the Christian’s sacrifice. V, 252. Almsgiving is the beginning of charity. III, 2019. Alms are gifts in which the King is worshiped. IV, 511. God’s command concerning almsgiving is now to be embraced. V, 530. Christ silently demands alms; and the voice of the silent one is greater, because in the Gospel he does not remain silent. IV, 1910. One needy person seeks you; you ought to seek another. IV, 1367, 1911. God wished to be in need of you, and you draw back your hands. IV, 1922. Let the poor person not first weep because of you, so that the poor may rejoice because of you. IV, 1863. Christ is in need in the poor person. V, 240, 243, 1129. He deigns to present himself to be fed in the poor person. V, 615. God receives and is fed in the poor person. V, 524, 1041. Christ gives from heaven and receives on earth. V, 253. Christ asks nothing from you except what he gave you; the giver himself wishes to become a debtor. V, 686. When God commands almsgiving, he commands that it be given not from the property of the one to whom he gives the command, but from his own property. V, 326. Let people consider how great is the merit of feeding Christ when he is hungry, and what a crime it is to despise Christ when he is hungry. V, 408. The one who gives alms out of charity feeds two people: the one who hungers for bread and the one who hungers for righteousness. III, 2041. We entrust to God what we give generously to the poor. II, 1092.

Almsgiving is a pious loan to God. V, 239, 1706. The almsgiver’s commerce. V, 410. Wealth should be sent ahead into heaven. V, 405. A person gives necessities in order to live here longer, even miserably; he does not give what is superfluous in order to reign eternally with Christ. V, 1387. “Consider what your alms are buying, when you buy, and at what price you buy.” IV, 1326. Those who do not cease giving alms pay the price of the redemption of their souls. IV, 549. You will not be poor by giving, because the heavenly treasure is possessed more securely. IV, 1469. Do you wish to find something in your hands afterward? Do not now despise the hand of the poor; and look upon empty hands if you wish to have full hands. IV, 963, 964. Those to whom we should give alms must be sought out. IV, 1366, 1367.

Alms are to be given not from plunder but from honest labor. V, 648, 962. God wishes to be given a portion of what he has given. IV, 1922. Whoever gives alms to the poor does not give from his own property but from the Lord’s. V, 326. You give from the property of the one who commands you to give; be a distributor, not an invader. IV, 1923. Almsgiving is a repayment, not a gift. IV, 1236. It is similar to fraud if someone does not give his superfluous possessions to the needy. V, 1041. The superfluous possessions of the rich are the necessities of the poor. IV, 1922. Other people’s property is possessed when superfluous possessions are possessed. IV, 1922.

Alms: set aside something as a debt, as though it were to be returned to the treasury. IV, 1911. A fixed amount should be designated for alms, either from annual produce or from daily earnings. IV, 1911. For you seem to be giving from something living, and your hand must tremble when you extend it toward what you had not vowed to give. IV, 1911. In what measure and for what purpose alms should be given. V, 243, 253. To give a tenth of your income is little. IV, 1911. The Pharisees, whose righteousness yours ought to surpass, gave tenths; but you do not even give a thousandth. IV, 1911. There is a proper measure in almsgiving, not in the amassing of wealth. V, 89. See “Wealth.” Whoever gave something to a poor person and then lost something else should see that he lost what he did not give. IV, 388. An evil thought, like a moth, turns a person back from giving alms. V, 959. Avarice excuses itself under the appearance of devotion toward one’s children. V, 89. Christ ought to receive a share of the inheritance along with the children. IV, 424, 552; V, 1572. “I am saving it for my children”: a voice of affection, an excuse for iniquity. IV, 422. People do not lose what they give away: they entrust it to a servant and it is safe; they entrust it to Christ and it perishes? IV, 423, 552, 1769. God himself preserves what is given to the poor. V, 524. The only thing that does not perish is what you give to the poor; other things that you do not give, though they abound for you, you either lose while alive or leave behind when you die. V, 253. Money is not lost through almsgiving, but is preserved. V, 405. The portion of the dead son is owed to Christ. V, 90.

How almsgiving should be practiced. III, 1272, 1273, 1274. Almsgiving is forbidden to be mixed with the desire for temporal advantages. V, 806. It should be done from the heart. IV, 482. It should be given with humility and cheerfulness. V, 1200. It should not be done proudly or sparingly. V, 89. The one who helps a poor person should not exalt himself over that person. V, 1128. The almsgiving of the Pharisees is insufficient. V, 626. Almsgiving is often done by sad and complaining people so that they may escape the annoyance of the petitioner, not so that they may refresh the needy person’s inward parts. IV, 482. If you give bread sadly, you have lost both the bread and the merit. IV, 482. Almsgiving proceeds from the heart. If you extend your hand but do not show mercy in your heart, you have done nothing; but if you show mercy in your heart, even if you have nothing to extend, God accepts your almsgiving. IV, 1660. How we are commanded to give alms to everyone who asks and forbidden to give them to a sinner. IV, 1327. Almsgiving even to poor people who pretend to be needy. V, 251. Give alms even to an evil person, so that you may reach the good as well. V, 251. Show mercy to the wicked, not as wicked; give to God’s work, not to the human being’s work. IV, 1326, 1327. God considers not to whom something is given but with what intention it is given. VII, 748. A wife should not give more generous alms without her husband’s consent. II, 1079, 1080.

How the poor can give alms. IV, 1664, 1665. The one whose breast is full of charity always has something to give. IV, 371. Where he does not find the means, God crowns the will within. IV, 1351. What is reckoned for the one who gives a cup of cold water. IV, 1665.

Almsgiving should be done in secret. IV, 512. How it should be done publicly. IV, 512. The almsgiving of one who gives with his own hand is double. V, 1200. See “Works of mercy.” Friendship with the poor should be acquired through almsgiving. V, 250. Works of almsgiving should be increased during Lent. V, 1042, 1045.

Alms greatly assist prayer. II, 503, 507; VII, 747. Almsgiving and fasting are the two wings of prayer. IV, 482; V, 398. Prayer must be supported by almsgiving and fasting. V, 811, 1041, 1046. These are the three forms of human righteousness in this life: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. IV, 482. These three are remedies for lesser sins. V, 88. How almsgiving itself makes prayer. V, 1044.

[Col. 0274] Those who live badly do not give worthy alms. VII, 747, 748. For whom alms will be beneficial at the judgment. VII, 750. They benefit those who have changed their lives. V, 243; VI, 265, 267, 268. They benefit nothing those who have not abstained from lusts and crimes. II, 675. “Your coins are turned into good, while you remain evil?” V, 650. If you give for the purpose of always being allowed to sin with impunity, you are not feeding Christ but attempting to bribe the judge. V, 243. Everyone is first bound to give alms to his own soul. VI, 268; VII, 748. Whether almsgiving can cleanse without faith. V, 626.

Many kinds of almsgiving. VI, 265. The two kinds of almsgiving are forgiving and giving. V, 252, 1041, 1199, 1557. One kind of almsgiving is from the heart, the other from possessions. V, 398. Another kind of almsgiving is sparing one’s enemies. V, 1042, 1045, 1053. Nothing is greater than that kind of almsgiving by which we forgive from the heart whatever each person has sinned against us. VI, 266. No one is poor in this kind of almsgiving. V, 1042, 1053. The true almsgiving that is commanded to be performed. V, 626. By almsgiving every form of goodwill and beneficence is signified, whether giving or forgiving. X, 300. No almsgiving is greater than that which was bestowed upon us through God’s incarnation. V, 1043.

Alms for the dead. VI, 158. See “Avaricious.” “Money.” Almsgiving must not be mercenary. IV, 1327. The reward for almsgiving. V, 253, 525, 1025. From where recompense for almsgiving is inferred. VII, 27. Why only almsgiving is mentioned at the judgment. V, 407, 1700. Exhortation to give alms. V, 90, 642, 686, 1651, 1671, 1700.

The elements of the world. VII, 120. The four elements of the body. IV, 91. The five elements of the Manichaeans. VIII, 35, 210. Whether there are four elements or more is investigated beyond the faith. X, 398. The order of the elements according to the philosophers. V, 1140. The order and position of the elements are not unchangeable. VII, 774. The elements are distinguished not only by places but also by their proper qualities. III, 263, 264. The elements possess their own determinate power and quality. III, 406. In the elements lie hidden certain occult seeds of things that come into being bodily and visibly. VIII, 875. Some philosophers assign particular animals to each element. III, 284; VII, 242. Various opinions concerning the transformation of the elements. III, 280. The weights of the elements. V, 1141. The elements were not omitted in the account of the works of creation. III, 227, 238, 280.

A person afflicted with elephantiasis. V, 489. Elephantiasis. IX, 507, 528, 550.

The Eleusinian rites. VII, 210.

Eleusinus. V, 1580, 1581. Eleusinus, a tribunician man. VII, 768. Among the people of Thamugadi, a tribune. II, 941.

Eleutherius, bishop. X, 652, 663.

Elijah and Enoch were not permitted to live here, because no one can live here without sin. II, 872. Perhaps they live in the paradise from which Adam was expelled. X, 1598. They do not fail through illness or old age. III, 397. Elijah’s state is intermediate between that of those who are already blessed and that of those who are still pilgrims. III, 396. His translation does not prove that death is not the punishment for sin. II, 871. According to some opinions, Elijah and Enoch will one day die. II, 871; V, 1375. And they will return to this life to pay the debt of death. III, 397.

Elijah’s coming before the judgment. VII, 704. At the second coming Elijah will be what John was at the first. III, 1408. Elijah will teach the Jews love for Christ. VII, 704. And he will teach them to understand the Law spiritually. VII, 704. Some heretics thought that Elijah’s soul had passed into John. III, 725. Elijah raised the dead. II, 521. He is believed not to have taken a wife or fathered children. III, 396. He lawfully offered sacrifice outside God’s temple. III, 702. Why he is sent to the widow. III, 1416. He is sent to the widow to be fed, so that a benefit might be bestowed upon the one who fed him. V, 98, 1128, 1258. Elijah represented the person of prophecy. V, 1216.

Eliezer’s oath, a prophecy concerning Christ. VII, 512.

Choosing the good is from God. X, 314. We do not choose God unless we are chosen first. V, 210. See “The Elect.”

Elizabeth was descended from the daughters of Aaron. III, 809.

In the raising of the child, Elisha bore a type of the Lord. V, 176. In Elisha’s deed, the insufficiency of the Law and the necessity of grace were prefigured. V, 176, 753.

The allegory of Elisha and his staff. X, 617. Elisha raised the dead. II, 521. What Elisha’s baldness, mocked by the boys, signifies. IV, 1056, 1069.

Hellebore is sometimes food, sometimes poison, and sometimes medicine. I, 1350.

Ellipsis is familiar to Greek and Hebrew expression. III, 524.

Elpidius the Arian sends Augustine to Bonosus and Jason, men whom he describes as highly learned, thinking that Augustine is in error and wishing to recall him from that error. II, 1053.

*Elogium*, that is, blame or reproach. V, 1571.

To speak little, even though one talks much. II, 1023.

What eloquence is. IX, 447. The power of eloquence. IV, 1762. Its emptiness. IV, 1762. Plato reports that some judged eloquence should be expelled from the state and from human society. IX, 448. Cresconius accuses eloquence. IX, 447, [Col. 0275] 448, 455. The accusation against eloquence is refuted. IX, 547. The defense of eloquence. IX, 447. The extent to which eloquence is useful. IX, 448. Things wrongly said with fluency are very harmful. X, 495. What is said ineptly is in no way eloquent. IX, 283. Eloquence is joined with wisdom in the sacred authors. III, 92. And in sacred Scripture. III, 93, 94, 95. Wisdom without eloquence benefits states little; eloquence without wisdom harms them greatly and is usually never useful. III, 91. Who speaks wisely. III, 92. What it means to speak eloquently and wisely. III, 119. One who speaks wisely and eloquently but lives wickedly does indeed instruct many, although he is useless to his own soul. III, 118. What is the bad use of eloquence. X, 476. Eloquence was not instituted by human beings. III, 60. The fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine* treats eloquence’s purpose, function, and parts throughout. One may rightly be called eloquent who teaches, delights, and moves. III, 104. The eloquence that pleases this age does not nourish faith. IV, 995. The eloquent are mute when, while praising the creature, they forget the Creator. IV, 1873.

The divine utterances are salutary to those who understand them well, but dangerous to those who wish to twist them according to the perversity of their own hearts. IV, 543.

The joys of the blessed appear to be signified by the Elysian fields. VII, 310.

Emmaus. The opening of the disciples’ eyes at Emmaus is not to be taken figuratively. III, 446.

The one who corrects out of hatred must himself be corrected. IV, 1824. You also love greatly those whom you correct. IV, 229. Whether God comforts or corrects, he instructs the one for whom he is preparing an inheritance. IV, 628. A right heart neither resists a father who corrects nor distrusts one who promises. IV, 1468. A father often corrects his children through the most wicked servants. IV, 1499.

Correction should not be postponed. III, 1651.

To buy. V, 662, 910. Everyone wants to buy cheaply and sell dearly. VIII, 1017. An example contrary to this saying. VIII, 1018. To buy at auction. II, 357. How one who wishes to buy another’s estate is unjust. V, 204. God does not wish those whom he bought to perish. V, 153. A powerful person cannot lose what he bought with his gold, while Christ loses what he bought with his blood. V, 1253.

Emeritus, a Donatist bishop. IX, 690, 698, 699. At Caesarea. IX, 697, 698. Endowed with a good intellect and educated in the liberal disciplines. II, 297, 298, 301. One of the seven selected to dispute with the Catholics at the conference in Carthage. I, 650. At the second conference, held at Caesarea, he fell silent while Augustine was arguing. I, 650. Augustine had previously sent him a letter. II, 299. Emeritus remained stubborn in the Donatist schism. IX, 708, 731, 732, 743. He dictated the sentence of the Council of Bagai against the Maximianists. IX, 53, note (b). The proceedings involving Emeritus. IX, 712, 739.

Medical science contains the empirical art. X, 528.

Ἐναντίον (*enantion*), “opposite” or “against.” VII, 483.

*Encaenia*, the festival of the dedication of the Temple. III, 1741.

What the *Enchiridion* is. VI, 233.

The Encratites. VIII, 30. According to Epiphanius, Tatian’s schismatics. VIII, 30.

Endor is interpreted as “fountain of generation.” IV, 1054.

Ennius, the poet. VIII, 1018. He translated Euhemerus’s history into Latin. VII, 217. Ennius’s saying concerning the desire for praise. II, 1024.

Ἔννοιαι (*ennoiai*), “concepts” or “notions.” VII, 232.

Enoch is interpreted as “dedication.” VII, 460, 461, 462. Whether Enoch was Cain’s first son. VII, 447.

Enoch was translated. III, 397. Enoch and Elijah are believed to have been translated to the place where the tree of life is. X, 1581. Where they are is investigated beyond the faith. X, 398. Grace was also granted to them so that they might not sin. X, 1581. They still live, but have not been changed after the resurrection into the spiritual condition promised to the body. X, 111. They live in the bodies in which they were born. X, 398. From what source they live. X, 111. They are believed to return here and die. X, 1581. What Enoch, the seventh from Adam, being taken away signifies. VII, 598; VIII, 262. It can be said that Enoch prophesied. VII, 598. Why Enoch’s writings were not regarded as authoritative. VII, 470, 598. Enoch fathered children. III, 397. See “Elijah.”

Enos is interpreted as “man,” a designation proper only to a male. VII, 460.

Entellus. VIII, 574. The boxing gloves of Entellus. II, 238, 247, 249.

An *entheka* is a repository for treasure. V, 1572.

Epaphus, the father of Libya, the mother of Busiris. VII, 570.

Those who inspect ephemerides are censured. IV, 456.

The ephod, or *ephud*, is one of the sacramental signs of the tabernacle. III, 806. The ephod is a sign of priestly honor. III, 806. Only the high priest wore the ephod. III, 807.

Ephrata is interpreted as “mirror.” IV, 1720.

Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” IV, 719, 1022.

Passengers (Ἐπιβάται), marines. II, 977, note (a); X, 915.

Epictetus, Stoic philosopher. VII, 259.

[Col. 0276] **Epicurus.** VIII, 72. Heir of Democritus. I, 946. He did not believe that the sun or any of the stars was a god. VII, 601. He maintained that neither Jupiter nor any of the gods dwells in the world, to whom human prayers might reach. VII, 601. He placed happiness in pleasure. I, 942; VIII, 1019. He called bodily pleasure the highest good. IV, 944. He was called a pig by the philosophers themselves. IV, 944. He refused to believe that after death there remains life for the soul and a continuation of merits. I, 732; IV, 944. He was hostile to the geometrical writings of Archimedes. VIII, 74. The atoms of Epicurus. II, 64, 445. They are refuted. II, 63. See Atoms; Principles.

**Epicurean philosophers.** VII, 230, 232. Skilled in dialectic. IX, 455. Their ignorance of the liberal disciplines not only did not embarrass them, but even delighted them. IX, 655. Epicureans and Stoics placed the rule for grasping truth in the senses, the Platonists in the understanding alone. II, 441. The Epicureans said that the bodily senses are never deceived; the Stoics, that they are sometimes deceived. II, 441. What the Epicureans thought about the soul. V, 811. They think that death is the end of all evils, as do those who consider the soul mortal. II, 389. They deny a future life. V, 1528. They thought that after death there is absolutely no sensation. II, 668. They also deny that God cares for human affairs. V, 1528. Epicureans live according to the flesh, Stoics according to the soul. V, 853. The Epicurean view of the blessed life. V, 809. When pain is present, they nourish themselves with the image of past pleasure. V, 1528. They placed the highest good in the body. II, 439. They are refuted. II, 439. Epicureans and Stoics compared with the Apostle. V, 809. They contradicted Paul, who was sowing the seed of faith beforehand. II, 442. Some Christians in their morals were Epicureans. V, 811. The sects of the Epicureans and Stoics have died out. II, 442. The ashes of the Epicureans no longer even retain heat. II, 437.

Epidaurus, a town of Achaea. VII, 87, note (b).

Epimenides of Crete. VIII, 646.

**Epiphany**, the manifestation of Christ. V, 1028. The festival was rightly instituted for this reason. V, 1035. The whole Church of the Gentiles celebrates the day of the Epiphany. V, 1033. It is thirteen days after Christ’s birth, on the day, namely, on which he is said to have been adored by the Magi. V, 1035. The Donatists never wished to celebrate the day of the Epiphany with Catholics. V, 1033. What will the tribunal of the Judge be like, when the cradles of an infant terrified proud kings? V, 1029.

Epiphanius of Cyprus, bishop of Constantia, or Salamis. VIII, 23, note (a). Famous with deserved praise in the teaching of the catholic faith, he collected eighty heresies from before and after the Lord’s coming. II, 999; VIII, 23, note (a), 41; X, 1366. How far he brought his book On Heresies. VIII, 41. This Epiphanius was much more learned than Philaster. II, 999.

**Bishop:** where the name comes from. V, 580; VII, 647. In Latin episcopus means “overseer” (*superintentor*), because he exercises oversight. IV, 1669. For this reason a higher place was assigned to him. IV, 1669; V, 1367. The bishop’s higher position is dangerous. IV, 1669. The episcopate is the watchtower of a vinedresser, not the summit of one who is proud. IX, 702. “Bishop” is the name of a task, not of an honor. VII, 647. Bishops are guardians and shepherds, but under Christ, the Guardian and Shepherd. IV, 1669. Those who have been Christians but have been led astray by pagans or heretics cannot become bishops when they return to the Church. IX, 478. Why a bishop may not be ordained unless he is the husband of one wife. VI, 387. Nor may one who has had another wife, even while he was a pagan or catechumen. VI, 387. This is not required as a merit of a good life, but as the mark of ecclesiastical ordination. VI, 388. What is this mark? VI, 388. A bishop’s private blessing. VII, 762.

The episcopate is greater than the presbyterate according to the terminology of honors that ecclesiastical custom has now established. II, 290. The episcopate itself, and all the authority of this name, arose from Peter; from Innocentius. II, 780, 784. With what disposition the episcopate should be undertaken, and how one should live in it. VII, 647. Compulsion is needed with very many people so that they will accept the episcopate. II, 754.

**The duties of episcopal office.** V, 1484. The bishop’s office according to the mind of Paganus. II, 313, 316. The episcopate is not a device for passing one’s deceptive life. II, 296. He is not a bishop who loves to preside rather than to benefit. VII, 647. Bishops are called fathers. IV, 513. A bishop is the son of a layman and the father of his father. IV, 1450. Bishops are servants of the Church. VI, 577. Bishops exist not for themselves but for those to whom they administer the word and sacrament of the Lord. IX, 474, 702. Augustine seems to act against his office if he spends the moments of his time on matters other than the necessities of his service. II, 421. Augustine is entangled in people’s affairs before and after midday. II, 968. He asked that for five days no one disturb him, because of his care for the Scriptures entrusted to him by two councils: the decision was made and the proceedings completed, yet this arrangement did not last long. II, 968. It is disgraceful for a bishop distracted by ecclesiastical cares to expound the little questions of Tullian dialogues. II, 432, 436, 437.

**The weight of the episcopal burden.** V, 960, 1480, 1482, 1687. What a bishop’s burden, well borne or badly managed, deserves. V, 1480. The urgency of preaching is entrusted to the bishop. IX, 453. A bishop must be not only learned but also teachable. IX, 157, 194. The burden of preaching is heavy, but it must not be abandoned by him. V, 1481. Even if he is not heard. V, 1481. A bishop speaks from a higher place. V, 608, 761. Nor does he give what is his own, but what belongs to the one from whom he himself receives. V, 608, 618. How a bishop is bound to refute those who teach what ought not to be taught. II, 133, 135. How great a concern for the salvation of others is imposed on a bishop. V, 1480. A bishop exists for the duty of correction. VII, 23. How adulterers betrayed by their wives should be corrected by a bishop. V, 511. Augustine is deeply distressed, in his capacity as bishop, that he is said to have to present himself humbly toward a man who had committed abominable deeds. II, 647. Whether bishops are mediators. IX, 59, 60. In the Church the bishop intercedes in a clear voice. II, 221. Even wicked bishops, when they pray for the people, are heard. IX, 60. See Priest. A bishop’s blessing upon the people. II, 761, 775. The claim that episcopal blessing is useless follows from the Pelagian heresy. II, 761, 775. Bishops were harassed by litigants. IV, 1570. A devout bishop is compelled to deal with secular authorities and to suffer many indignities. V, 1391. It is the duty of the priesthood to intervene on behalf of the accused. II, 652, 654. It is approved that this proceeds from religion. II, 654. With what disposition it should be done. II, 654. How those who fear being sent to prison should approach a bishop. V, 879. Augustine asks as a friend, advises as a bishop, indeed commands, that a judge do nothing other than what he advises. II, 510.

A bishop administers the affairs of the poor. II, 809. Bishops are guardians of orphans. V, 950. Bishops are thought to use and enjoy ecclesiastical goods as possessors and masters. II, 474, 480. The Vadiani created a schism by censuring wealthy bishops and celebrating Easter with the Jews. VIII, 39. A bishop should take care of his good name and especially ensure that he is not thought avaricious. II, 292. Paul did the same. II, 293. Bishops ought to be free even from the mere malicious appearance of avarice. II, 292, 293. The disgraceful avarice of bishops in Cyprian’s age. II, 410. Bishops are under an obligation to receive guests. V, 1570. Bishops’ houses. V, 1569, 1670. There are false bishops, just as there are false angels and false apostles. IX, 271. The vices of certain bishops reported by Cyprian. IX, 518. A bishop should not think that an unjust agitation cannot creep into him because he is a bishop. II, 1067. Wicked bishops do not harm good peoples. IX, 55–58.

Bishops are to judge ecclesiastical cases. II, 169. A bishop’s lawsuit is to be heard by bishops. IX, 579. A bishop cannot be judged by another any more than he himself can judge another. IX, 128, 141, 201. It is rebellion against the First See for a bishop to wish to condemn some whom the primate wishes to defer. II, 164. Three kinds of punishment inflicted on bishops. II, 955. When the people refuse to receive a degraded bishop, they can neither be compelled nor ought they to be. II, 234. Whoever tries by any acts of violence to recover the honor he has lost does not wish to serve Christ, who wills this, but to rule Christians who do not will it. II, 234. A bishop, unless he has lost his order, cannot have lost the power to baptize. II, 193. A visiting bishop sits beside his colleague. II, 489. Every bishop of the catholic Church, whatever his status, if he has not been condemned by an ecclesiastical judgment, is the colleague of the others. II, 295. Bishops who are not primates are to be named in the *Tractoria* in the order in which they were made bishops. II, 226. Augustine sincerely regrets that, in writing, he had not sufficiently considered the episcopal standing of another person. II, 623. Why Augustine, writing to a Donatist bishop, does not mention the title “bishop.” II, 94. When bishops write to bishops, they do not add the names of their cities. IX, 576. Augustine admits that he cannot refuse letters written to commend someone. II, 646. Bishops may not take it upon themselves to write to a people who have not been entrusted to their administration. II, 234. A bishop’s care extends only to his own church; in other churches he does what their bishops permit or desire. II, 133. After several previous examples, Augustine undertakes the burden of a co-episcopate. II, 123. Augustine arranges for a bishop to be ordained in a village forty miles from Hippo, although it was not sufficient for him to exercise the necessary diligence. II, 953. The primate is summoned because of this ordination. II, 954. Augustine offers, without being asked, a young man who had only been placed in the rank of lector, and he is accepted as bishop. II, 954. Later accused and judged before Augustine, he appealed to the Apostolic See. II, 954. The faults of bishops can be punished without violating the honor of the episcopate. II, 954. Augustine prepares to confer the episcopate on a presbyter, but the presbyter prevents him by resisting in every way. II, 953, 954. After the departure of bishops, churches are accustomed to be disturbed by ambitious or contentious men. II, 966. A bishop was ordained at Milevis, designated by the preceding bishop. II, 966. Not without some sadness among certain people, because he had designated him only before the clergy, having said nothing about him to the people. II, 966. Augustine says before the clergy and people: “I want the presbyter Heraclius to be my successor.” II, 966. The proceedings concerning this designation. [Col. 0278] II, 966. The Council of Nicaea provided that no other bishop should be ordained while a bishop was still living. II, 967. Alypius is said to have been placed in the Apostolic See. II, 99. Alypius is praised for combining the monastic life with the office of bishop. II, 99. Bishops are free, without prejudice to the right of communion, not only to seek the truth but also to hold a different opinion. IX, 141.

**Episcopal proceedings.** V, 1576. The transfer of bishops is unlawful. II, 954. Cyprian did not forget that he was a bishop even when martyrdom was pressing upon him. V, 1411. Augustine withdrew from Carthage, where he was being compelled to do what was unbecoming. II, 646. No one appointed himself “bishop of bishops.” IX, 142.

The office of the episcopate is sometimes commendably laid down. IX, 474. Episcopal dignity will be more fruitful for us if it gathers in the flock after laying down its burden than if, by retaining it, it scatters the flock. II, 489. To lay down the burden of the episcopate in order to avoid dangers for the Church is far more glorious than to undertake it in order to govern the helm. II, 239. Maximianus gloriously relinquished the episcopate of Vaga. II, 239 and note. All the Catholic bishops who were present at the Carthaginian conference were ready to lay down the episcopate for the unity of Christ. IX, 615, 700, 701. An offer of fellowship in the episcopate was made to the Donatists. V, 1588, 1595.
