The honor of the episcopate or clerical office is not taken away from Donatists who pass over to the Church, for the sake of the good of peace and solely out of clemency. II, 812, 813. Each bishop orders and directs his own conduct, knowing that he will render an account of his purpose to the Lord. II, 341. Whether bishops, or superiors of churches of a lower order, should be understood by the likeness of fishermen. VI, 219. The unbroken succession of bishops from the very sees of the Apostles. IX, 506. The office of the episcopate imposed on every head of a household. V, 580.

**Formal letters.** II, 175. The epistolary style derives from the practice of the ancients. II, 1054. The usual form of letters need not be observed, nor was it observed by the ancients, when they were dealing with something that could not be briefly explained. II, 839.

Some denied that the Letter to the Hebrews was by the Apostle Paul. VII, 500.

**Epithalamia**, or songs customarily recited by schoolmen at weddings. IV, 494, 495.

A swelling or tumor given to the Apostle. V, 835.

The banquets of this earth are daily medicines. V, 489. The devout heart has its banquets, and the proud heart has its banquets. IV, 1290. God’s banquets seek minds, not bellies. V, 581.

Mares of Cappadocia conceive by the wind, and their offspring live no longer than three years. VII, 715.

The name “horse” signifies temporal honor. IV, 297, 1912. The power of the horse signifies pride. IV, 1912. Horse and mule signify the proud. IV, 272.

**Heraclius, presbyter.** II, 966. He delivers a sermon in Augustine’s presence. V, 1717. The proceedings by which he was designated as Augustine’s successor. II, 966. Augustine transfers to him the affairs that the people brought to Augustine himself. II, 968.

Heraclius, presbyter. VIII, 709.

Heraclius, deacon. V, 1577.

Eratus, king of the Sicyonians. VII, 564.

The wilderness signifies the world. IV, 917. For the Christian, this world is the wilderness. V, 37. Christians should know where they are: they are in the wilderness, and they sigh for their homeland. IV, 917. The wilderness of conscience. V, 311.

Erichthonius, fourth king of the Athenians. VII, 569. Why he was believed to be the son of Vulcan and Minerva. VII, 570. From where he received this name. VII, 570.

Eridanus. To migrate from the Mincius into the Eridanus. II, 434.

No one raises anyone to the level at which he himself is unless he himself descends somewhat to the level at which the other is. II, 77.

To distribute is the servant’s task; to demand an account is the Lord’s. V, 1481. To distribute spiritual goods is everyone’s task. V, 580. Money must be distributed so that justice may be obtained. V, 410.

Eros, a Gallic bishop. See Heros.

Eros, very dear to Augustine, different from Herote the Gaul. II, 189.

**Error**, what it is. VI, 239. It is the approval of what is false as true. I, 912. Error is the adultery of the soul. II, 62, 529. To approve falsehoods as truths and so err unwillingly is not the nature of a human being as created, but the punishment of one condemned. I, 598; III, 840. No one errs in the truth. IV, 807. A person should not be thought to be in error when he knows that he does not know something, but when he thinks he knows what he does not know. II, 924. How much each person should shun error and falsehood. VI, 240. No one wishes to err with just anyone. II, 286. Error is not free from disgrace. VIII, 83. The Academics considered error a sin that could not be avoided unless all assent were suspended. VI, 242. The errors of the nations are especially prominent in two sects that have lasted into Christian times. II, 442. Error in every matter must be avoided with the utmost care. VI, 239. Errors are avoided with the greatest difficulty. VIII, 173. Error on a bodily path is sometimes useful, but not on the path of morals. VI, 239. It matters greatly how much and in what respect each person errs. VI, 239, 241. It also matters how readily he corrects himself, or with how much obstinacy he tries to defend his error. [Col. 0279] X, 1028. The most outstanding intellects fell into greater errors in proportion as they ran more confidently, as though relying on their own powers. II, 669. One never errs more safely than when one errs through excessive love of truth. VI, 487. See To Be Deceived. There is no worse death of the soul than the freedom to err. II, 400. When an erring disputant should be tolerated. V, 1348. Two vices that are most difficult to tolerate in human error. VIII, 845. Obstinacy in error must especially be avoided. X, 375. To err is human; to remain in error through spitefulness is diabolical. V, 901.

Error is more easily defined than ended. I, 911. How error grows strong. X, 194. In various sects, error is strengthened by the succession of a continuous series. IV, 837. “For the most part, the person to whom no one agrees unlearns how to err,” says Innocentius. II, 786. He loves himself excessively and perversely who wishes others to err so that his own error may remain hidden. II, 586. It is characteristic of error that whatever displeases a person, he thinks also displeases God. III, 208. Nothing is safer than that there should be many who refute errors. II, 870. Those in error are more inclined to seek what they can answer against the objections made to their error than to consider how salutary those objections are, so that they may be free from error. X, 260. It is not surprising that errors arise; rather, one must be watchful lest they do harm. II, 1084. It is useful for the saints to be instructed by the trials of errors. II, 1084. If someone errs in some matter, provided he is humble, God will bring him back. IV, 1715. The procedure and example to be followed in correcting one who has fallen into error. II, 991, 992. Those who err throughout the whole face of the earth. V, 280.

**Blushing of the first parents:** its origin. X, 444. Blushing because of disobedient members. X, 417. The shame of the members is the punishment of sin. X, 564, 565, 712. Modesty makes an honorable face blush, even at the accusation of a false crime. IV, 856. If it is a crime to blush, the guilt belongs to the one who makes the false accusation, not to the person accused. IV, 856. In insults, no face blushes except that of the proud. IV, 314. One must not be ashamed of Christ. IV, 850, 851; V, 1278. “Be bold; what do you fear for your forehead, which you have armed with the sign of Christ’s cross?” IV, 851. See Christ.

**To belch forth.** You eat when you learn, you belch forth when you teach; you eat when you hear, you belch forth when you preach. IV, 1874. If you wish to belch forth grace, drink grace. IV, 1875.

Who is worthy of the name “learned”? I, 1015. Christ did not place the learned and the experts in the Law among his disciples. III, 1446.

God instructed human beings in many ways. IV, 1202. For this he will demand an account. IV, 1202. No one can be instructed without labor and pain. IV, 1145. Instruction produced through hardships is called discipline in ecclesiastical writings. IV, 1547, 1548.

The speeches of Erutius. VIII, 76.

When the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied. VII, 579, 581. Her poems about Christ. VII, 579.

**Esau and Jacob:** blessings. V, 38, 56. Esau and Jacob had one and the same lot from their father, mother, conception, and birth; they differed only through God. II, 887, 888. In what sense did God hate Esau, who hates nothing that he has made? VI, 122. Why the gift of faith was withdrawn from him. VI, 117. Why he was not called in a corresponding manner. VI, 119. Whether he was rejected on the basis of foreknowledge of his future will. VI, 117. How his rejection was just. VI, 113, 115. Esau is not condemned as one who was undeserving. II, 823. How different he was from Jacob in character. VII, 144. Esau was not condemned because of food, but because of the food he desired to the point of despising the sacrament that he possessed in his primacy. II, 141. Esau did not lose his birthright because of a pork dish, but because of a dish of mashed lentils. V, 1045. He lost his birthright through Egyptian food. I, 739, 799. What Esau, losing his primacy because he was overcome by desire, signifies. IV, 527, 558, 1772. How Esau was supplanted by Jacob. V, 47.

What Esau’s being worshiped by Jacob signifies. IV, 1135. Esau served Jacob as far as the time of King Joram. III, 567. How. III, 567. Esau signifies the proud and sinners. IV, 527. Esau, hairy, and Jacob, smooth, are two kinds of Christians born in the womb of the Church. V, 41, 48. Esau signifies the carnal among the people of God. III, 567; IV, 1772. Jacob signifies the spiritual. V, 34. Why Esau, signifying the carnal, is called the elder. V, 37. Esau bore the figure of the ancient Synagogue. IV, 1015, 1477. Esau is the symbol of the Jews, Jacob of Christians. V, 55.

Food either delights or offends according to what suits each body. VIII, 397. The Manichaeans believed that souls are present in foods. VIII, 230, 232.

**Ezra:** when he wrote. VII, 596. In a certain manner he prophesied about Christ. VII, 596. He was regarded more as a recorder of events than as a prophet. VII, 596.

All things, both sensible and insensible, seek to exist and to preserve that existence. VII, 340. No one fails to desire existence. VII, 340. Nonexistence is chosen by no one. I, 1281. Not even by those who take their own lives. I, 1281. Nothing is permitted by divine providence to reach the point of not existing. I, 1349. No one truly says that he would rather not exist than be miserable. I, 1279. [Col. 0280] Existence itself is a great good, which both the blessed and the miserable desire. I, 1280. The more existence is loved, the more eternal life is desired. I, 1280. All things are true insofar as they exist. I, 744. Everything that exists is rightly to be praised, because it is good. I, 1280. Everything that exists, insofar as it is some substance, is good and can exist only from God. III, 436. Insofar as we are good, we exist; insofar as we are evil, we exist less. III, 32. A human being exists, knows that he exists, and loves both to exist and to know this; in these three matters the human being is not deceived. VII, 339. Existence belongs to light; nonexistence to darkness. IV, 109.

To exist is nothing other than to be one. I, 1349. To exist truly is always to exist in the same manner. III, 1679. If any thing is mutable, it does not truly exist. III, 1680, 1685. That truly exists which remains unchangeably. I, 742; III, 32; IV, 1741; V, 61. What truly exists is without beginning and without end. IV, 1743. True, sincere, genuine existence belongs only to what does not change. V, 66. “Existence” is the name of immutability. V, 66.

True existence is proper to God. VIII, 557. The proper name of God. V, 61, 66. God alone is true existence. IV, 1741. Creatures, in comparison with God, do not exist. IV, 430. In what sense sinners do not possess existence. IV, 430. Whoever turns away from the one who truly exists turns toward nonexistence. IV, 431. Every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is compelled to exist. IV, 109. Whatever is no substance is absolutely nothing. IV, 844. To exist, to live, and to understand. I, 1244. From understanding, existence and life are inferred. I, 1244. To be something in something is said in two ways. I, 895.

“To be,” meaning “to be considered.” III, 586.

**Essence:** what it is. VII, 350. Essence is ordinarily understood in no other way than substance. VIII, 939. Essence and substance—that is, what the ancients called nature. I, 1345. No essence is contrary to God. VII, 350. The degrees of essences ordered by God. VII, 350.

Esther, a book of Sacred Scripture. X, 569. When the book of Esther was written. VII, 596.

Those who hunger for righteousness. V, 365.

If the pagans were able to possess anything divine and upright in their teachings, our saints did not reject it but corrected it. IX, 224, 231.

Ethan means “strong.” IV, 940.

Etruria. The Romans’ serious war with Etruria. VII, 63.

The tortures of the Etruscan kings. IX, 379.

**Eve, the first mother.** V, 1439. What Eve signifies. III, 207, 215. Why she was called “life.” III, 212, 215. Eve sinned through curiosity. III, 446. She gave the fruit to the man, perhaps also with persuasive speech. III, 445. She considered it more probable that death would not follow than that it would follow as she had feared. III, 446. Even if Eve had forgotten the divine commandment, she would not have ceased to incur the greatest guilt. III, 445. Eve’s mind contained a love of her own power and a certain proud presumption about herself. III, 445. The extent to which Eve was corrupted by the serpent. X, 864. Eve’s transgression is inexcusable. III, 445. Why Eve was clothed in tunics of skin. IV, 1341. The pains of Eve in childbirth arose from the condemnation of guilt, not from the condition of nature. X, 1564, 1566. Eve’s name means “life”; it is a great sacrament of the Church. X, 442. Eve is a figure of the Church. IV, 461. Eve’s formation compared with the formation of the Church. V, 1475. Eve’s reliquary. I, 713. The inner Eve for us is our flesh. IV, 548.

What it means to “destroy the body of sin.” III, 2069.

Evagrius. II, 758, 780.

**Authority of the Evangelists.** VIII, 213. What the Evangelists wrote must be considered to have been written by Christ. III, 1070. Because one Spirit spoke in them, what one of them said is also true. V, 1118. In what order the Evangelists wrote. III, 1043. There are four Evangelists because there are four regions of the earth. III, 1043; IV, 1359. The four Evangelists are understood in the four living creatures of the Apocalypse. III, 1666. Some understood them more aptly than others. III, 1046. The Evangelists vary while preserving the truth of their account. V, 1117, 1130, 1153. Their writings are not contradictory to one another. VIII, 515. In composing Christ’s genealogy, they do not disagree with one another. VIII, 217. The agreement of the Evangelists concerning the division of Christ’s garments. III, 1947. Why Matthew, Mark, and Luke gave more precepts for living than John. III, 993. The Evangelists are called heavens. III, 870; IV, 154. Angels. III, 873. The feet of the Lord. IV, 1167. Arrows. IV, 150. They are signified by ascending and descending angels. VIII, 268. Philip the deacon is properly called an evangelist. V, 1226, 1227. “Evangelist” in the sense of preacher of the Gospel. V, 600.

**Gospel:** where the name comes from. IV, 1417. In Latin, *evangelium* means “good news” or “good proclamation.” V, 266, 740; VIII, 210, 214. The Gospel is both an Instrument and a Testament. V, 1436. How the Gospel is not hostile to the Law. VIII, 656. The Gospel is the law of the New Testament. V, 167. In the Gospel the grace of the New Testament is revealed, which was veiled in the Law. IV, 1856. According to the Manichaeans, from where the Gospel both began to exist and received its name. VIII, 209. According to the Catholics, from where it came. VIII, 213. How Faustus defines the Gospel. VIII, 219. The Manichaeans read and praise the Gospel. III, 180. From it the Manichaeans accepted some things and rejected others. VIII, 321, 323, 342. They said that certain things were false. VIII, 339. The Apostles divided the Gospel in its administration but joined it in charity. IV, 541, 542.

**Authority of the Gospels.** III, 1041. Falsehood cannot enter the Gospel. V, 740. Augustine would not have believed the Gospel except for the authority of the Church. VIII, 176. Paul would not have had confidence in preaching the Gospel unless the judgment of Peter and those who were with him had confirmed it. II, 255. It is confidently believed that there is no disharmony among the Gospels, until it is understood. V, 336. Greater faith should be placed in the Greek copies of the Gospels. III, 1259. The fifth Gospel translated by Jerome. X, 1389, note (a). John’s Gospel surpasses the others. III, 993. The opening of John’s Gospel contains matters belonging partly to wisdom and partly to knowledge. VIII, 1013. Some things can be known through bodily sensation, others through the reasoning of the mind. VIII, 1015. A certain Platonist said that the beginning of the Gospel according to John ought to be written in letters of gold. VII, 309. What was foretold in the Gospel is now fulfilled. V, 417. The evangelical light is represented by the lamps enclosed in the jars of Gideon’s faithful soldiers. III, 815.

The faith of the Gospel has been received throughout the whole world. V, 335. The Gospel has not yet been preached among certain peoples. IX, 205. Not yet among very many communities of Africa. II, 922. The Jews believed that the grace of the Gospel was owed to their merits and was not to be given even to the Gentiles unless they received the sacraments of the Law. VI, 111. Even if it were true that people were afflicted with worse evils after the preaching of the Gospel than before, these things would nevertheless befall them deservedly. II, 422. The Gospel must be heard as though the Lord were present. III, 1632. The Gospel is the mouth of Christ. V, 520. In it also the Lord is now with us. V, 784. The four Gospels are four drachmas, by which we are freed from the exaction of this age. IV, 1783. There our sins are released. IV, 1783. The Gospel must be placed against the heart, so that it may be healed of sins. III, 1443.

The Gospel is the rod of Christ’s power. VII, 551. The wine that was kept at the wedding. III, 1459. The evangelical sacraments, marked by Christ’s words and deeds, are not evident to everyone. VI, 54. The Gospel is a teacher for the mature, while the Law is for children and acts as a pedagogue. VI, 37. Through the Gospel we are taught what we ought to love, what to despise, what to do, what to avoid, and what to hope for. V, 1357.

The Gospel without baptism does not lead to the kingdom of heaven, nor does baptism without it. IX, 385. What it means to accept the Gospel. VIII, 220. Does a person not accept it if he does not abandon everything? VIII, 226. The various degrees of those who fulfill the evangelical commandments. VIII, 226, 228. How one who follows the evangelical life should live with those who are less perfect. II, 352. When Christ prepares people through the Gospel, he does not want the excuse of carnal or temporal affection to be interposed. V, 603.

Whether the administration of the Gospel is superior to baptism. IX, 385. The preaching of the Gospel became clearer and more powerful through the sufferings of its preachers. VII, 612. The preachers of the Gospel fought for the truth by enduring suffering and conquered by dying. VI, 179. The evangelical light increased through the death of the martyrs. III, 815. Ministers of the Gospel ought, by their manner of living, to be an example to the faithful. I, 857. To preach the Gospel opportunistically. V, 609. Those who preach the Gospel without purity. IV, 139. Many minister the Gospel, but minister to themselves. IV, 1291. Those who wish to evangelize should leave their water jar. III, 1521. The Gospel must not be sold. V, 273. What the Gospel was for which Paul labored even to imprisonment. IV, 1448. Preachers of the Gospel should receive from the people support for their necessities, but the reward of their administration from the Lord. V, 273. It was permitted, but not commanded, for the Apostles and others to live from the Gospel. VI, 553. One who evangelizes may receive material things in return for spiritual things. IV, 1366, 1367, 1910, 1911. One who evangelizes should be assisted before he asks. IV, 1366, 1367, 1910. The Gospel is placed on the head when it aches. III, 1443.

Eucaddires. II, 83.

**Eucharist.** III, 71, 1723; VIII, 382, 658, 879, 881; IX, 202, 290, 669. A sacrament. II, 200; IV, 1348; VII, 520, 741. The sacrament of our price. I, 778. “The Eucharist is our price, which I eat and drink and distribute,” says Augustine. I, 810. The Eucharist, the sacraments of the altar. V, 584. It is also called the sacrament of the altar. V, 401. It is also called the body of Christ. V, 401. Almost everyone, as a matter of sacramental terminology, calls it the body of Christ. V, 1563. Bread and cup are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another understood. V, 1247. The bread is Christ’s body; the cup is Christ’s blood. V, 1246. The Eucharist is called communion in the Lord’s body. I, 720. Christ’s table established in the midst of the Church. V, 735. The table of the Lord’s body and blood. III, 1733. The great table from which we receive Christ’s body and blood. V, 193. In the Church the body and blood [Col. 0282] of the immaculate Lamb are received. II, 147. Christ gave a saving nourishment from his body and blood, so that there would never be a lack of what could refresh you. V, 729. He gave those who thought it had to be divided into parts a brief answer concerning its integrity. V, 729. If we did not have Christ’s flesh, we would not eat the bread of the altar. V, 726.

The Eucharist is spiritual nourishment received from God’s altar. V, 389. The food and drink of the Eucharist. V, 233. The Eucharist is a life-giving banquet. V, 1649. From the Lord’s table we taste not cheap foods or lowly drinks, but the flesh and blood of Christ himself, who was slain. V, 1662. The distinction between the Eucharist and temporal food. III, 1613. It is not every bread, but the bread that receives Christ’s blessing, that becomes Christ’s body. V, 1116. It becomes mystical for us. VIII, 379. “That bread which you see on the altar, sanctified by the word of God, is Christ’s body; that cup—or rather what the cup contains—sanctified by the word of God, is Christ’s blood.” V, 1099, 1246. Christ gave the disciples the supper consecrated by his own hands. V, 645. It is this same supper that is now prepared. V, 645. By faith we eat this same supper daily. V, 645. Christ gave the first Eucharist, prepared by his own hands and commended by his own mouth, to Judas as to the other Apostles. IV, 135; V, 453. He included Judas in the banquet at which he commended and handed over to the disciples the figure of his body. IV, 73. The Eucharist is a sign of Christ’s body. VIII, 144. Some thought that the Lord would give pieces cut from his flesh. IV, 1265. Christ seemed to the disciples to be insane when he said, “Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood,” etc. IV, 305. Christ carried his body in his hands when he said, “This is my body.” IV, 306, 308. To impress the greatness of that mystery more forcefully, the Savior wished this final teaching to be fixed more deeply in the hearts and memory of the disciples. II, 203. The Lord’s Supper after the resurrection, confirmed by his own hands and mouth. V, 643. Christ is recognized and held at the breaking of bread. V, 558, 1111, 1118, 1127. The breaking of bread in the sacrament of Christ’s body. II, 148. Christ did not wish to be recognized by the disciples except in the breaking of bread, for our sake, since we were not going to see him in the flesh and yet were going to eat his flesh. V, 1118.

**The Eucharist prefigured.** IV, 305. It was represented in the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek to Abraham. VII, 500. We now see this figure fulfilled; how it is fulfilled is kept silent for the sake of the catechumens. V, 1407. How the spiritual food of the Israelites is the same as ours. V, 1551.

The Eucharist is a sacrifice. VII, 655. An offering. IX, 58. The holy victim distributed from the altar. I, 778. It nourishes not by what is seen but by what is believed. V, 645. The Christians of Africa call the sacrament of Christ’s body nothing other than life. X, 128.

Catechumens do not know the Eucharist. III, 1477. Catechumens and Hearers see the Eucharistic table but do not approach the banquet. V, 735. The faithful know what they receive, because they are blessed through the flesh. V, 58. The faithful person knows where we recognize Christ; the catechumen, however, does not know. V, 1111, 1116. Catechumens are stirred up so that, by enrolling for baptism, they may soon be able to approach such banquets. V, 754. They have not yet heard anything about the sacrament of the holy altar that the baptized saw today. V, 1102, 1246. The daily bread is what the faithful receive and what the baptized are going to receive. V, 381. What the faithful know, from the wheat and wine. V, 48.

### Eucharist

The Eucharist pertains to those who have been regenerated. X, 1265. It is the sacrament of the faithful. V, 649, 729. It is granted only to those who have received baptism. III, 1477. They cannot eat the body of Christ unless they have been baptized. II, 826. Nor can those who have not eaten it have life. II, 785, 826, 984. Apart from baptism and participation in the Eucharist, no human being can attain not only the kingdom of God but even salvation and eternal life. X, 128, 129. This statement, “Unless you eat my flesh,” etc., applies to everyone, including infants. X, 123, note (a), 124. They cannot eat the body of Christ unless they have been baptized. II, 826. Nor can those who have not eaten it have life. II, 785, 826, 984. Participation in the Eucharist is necessary for little children to attain eternal life. X, 576, 648. The Eucharist administered to little children. X, 1154. Infants become participants at the Lord’s table so that they may have life within themselves. V, 943. The blood which the murderers shed in their madness, they drank through grace. IV, 517, 791. Believers drank the blood which they had shed in their violence. V, 485, 497, 538, 554, 1550, 1685.

### Reception of the Eucharist

The reception of the Eucharist. VI, 202, 470. It is called the Lord’s supper. II, 203. With what disposition the sacrament of the Eucharist should be received. III, 1610. No one will eat Christ’s flesh unless he has first adored it. IV, 1264. Those who eat Christ’s flesh and drink Christ’s blood should consider what they are eating. V, 754. Although the sacrament of the Eucharist must necessarily be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly. IV, 1265. Then Christ’s body and blood will be life for each person, if what is taken visibly in the sacrament is eaten and drunk spiritually, in the very reality itself. [Col. 0283] V, 729. Even the impious receive the true body and blood of Christ in the sacrament. IX, 181. Many wicked people can approach the altar set up in the Church, but they cannot approach the other altar in heaven. V, 1543. Heretics eat Christ’s body only sacramentally; Catholics eat it in reality. VII, 734. What it means to eat Christ’s body truly, and not merely sacramentally. VII, 742. The Eucharist must be eaten with the heart. III, 1612. A particular manner of eating Christ’s flesh belongs to the devout. V, 453.

Chastity is commended to those who are about to receive the Eucharist. V, 735, 736. “You know to whom you approach, what you eat, and what you drink—indeed, whom you eat and whom you drink; keep yourself from fornications.” V, 85. Christ’s humility, displayed in the Incarnation and in the sacrifice of the altar. IV, 303, 306, 312. Unless Christ were humble, he would neither be eaten nor drunk. IV, 303. “The Lord gave his supper; he gave his passion: the one who imitates him is nourished.” IV, 170, 178, 545. Even the rich of the earth eat the body of their humble Lord, but they are not nourished until they imitate him; nevertheless, they adore him. IV, 170. Those proud people too come to Christ’s table and receive some of his body; but they merely adore and are not nourished. II, 567. “The poor have eaten and have been filled,” having suffered such things as they have eaten. IV, 178. We are nourished from the Lord’s cross because we eat his body. IV, 1290.

The Eucharist gives life to the good and brings death to the wicked. III, 1762. In the Eucharist the faithful have where they may live and from which they may live. III, 1612. “Eat life, drink life; you will have life, and life is complete.” V, 729. Christ willed our salvation to be in his body and blood. IV, 303. The cup of the Eucharist intoxicates the martyrs for the attainment of heavenly things. IX, 298. The Jews were darkened by Christ crucified; we, by eating and drinking the crucified one, are illumined. IV, 313. The Eucharist is the sacrament of devotion, the sign of unity. III, 1612. The mystery of our peace and unity, which is therefore consecrated in bread and wine. V, 1100, 1103. Concord and union are the effect of the sacrament of Christ’s body. III, 1613, 1614. Only those eat Christ’s body who are within the structure of his members. VII, 742. The power understood in the Eucharist is unity itself: so that, gathered into Christ’s body and made his members, we may be what we receive. V, 589. Not all who receive the sacrament of Christ’s body will have with him the place promised to his members. V, 1563.

### The Eucharist and confession of faith

After receiving Christ’s blood, all the nations respond, “Amen.” VIII, 259. Our price is received, and “Amen” is answered. IV, 1663. Every day, in receiving Christ’s pledge, you say, “Amen.” V, 1469. Those approaching the Lord’s table there utter the words of faith. V, 145. Those who approach the Lord’s table and there utter the words of faith are called the faithful. V, 145. The faithful are those to whom Christ’s body is distributed. V, 649. “You receive your mystery; you answer ‘Amen’ to what you are, and by answering you ratify it.” V, 1247. “You hear, ‘The body of Christ,’ and answer, ‘Amen’: be a member of Christ’s body, so that your ‘Amen’ may be true.” V, 1247.

### The Lord’s Prayer before receiving the Eucharist

Why the Lord’s Prayer precedes reception of the Eucharist. V, 127. With the words “Forgive us,” etc., we approach the altar with a cleansed face and share in the Lord’s body and blood. V, 127.

### The Eucharist as our daily bread

The Eucharist is our daily bread. V, 381, 389, 394, 645. Daily reception of the Eucharist. X, 627, 998. The faithful ought to receive the Eucharist every day. V, 1099. Some communicate every day, others on specified days. II, 200. The person who does not dare to receive the Eucharist every day, and the person who does not dare to omit it on any day, each honors the Lord’s body and blood. II, 201. This food desires only not to be despised, just as the manna was not to be treated with disgust. II, 201.

### Worthy and unworthy reception

The good and the wicked receive the Eucharist together. V, 584. In the very Eucharist many eat and drink judgment upon themselves. V, 645. Those who eat unworthily truly eat, even though they eat judgment upon themselves. V, 1229. How many Judases Satan fills while they unworthily receive the morsel. IV, 1854. What is good cannot benefit one who receives it badly. IV, 1854. What is given is not evil, but what is good is given to the wicked for judgment. IV, 1854. See Sacrifice.

“If you live well, you will have Christ as your food; if you withdraw from Christ, you will be food for the dragon.” IV, 1386. An account is required from the one who eats concerning what he eats; the minister should not forbid him to eat, but should warn him to fear the one who will demand an account. IV, 545. When someone sees another approaching the altar whom he knows to be unworthy, when there is nothing for him himself to fear from this. V, 899, 900. Separation from the Eucharist on account of some more serious offense. X, 627, 998. Crimes that separate one from communion with Christ. X, 628. Those who do not persevere in a good life are separated from the bread of the Eucharist. V, 395, 401. Separation from the sacrament of heavenly bread through ecclesiastical discipline must be humbly embraced by the penitent. V, 1543. A little girl, struck by the sacrileges of demons through her nurse, later rejected with extraordinary movements the Eucharist brought to her in church. II, 361.

[Col. 0284]

### The Eucharist celebrated at martyrs’ memorials

The Eucharist celebrated at the memorials of martyrs. I, 720. A table constructed at the burial place of Cyprian, on which sacrifice is offered to God. V, 1413. The multitude honoring Cyprian’s anniversary drank Christ’s blood. V, 1413. Receiving Christ’s body and blood at the altar. V, 384. The deacon Laurence administered Christ’s sacred blood. V, 1395. The Eucharist was formerly accustomed to be placed in the hands. IX, 277. It was received with hands joined. IX, 58.

### Fasting and the Eucharist

The disciples first received the Lord’s body and blood while not fasting. II, 203. Christ did not prescribe the order in which it should thereafter be received, in order to preserve this matter for the Apostles. II, 203. The Eucharist should be received by those who are fasting, and this is the custom of the whole Church. II, 203. Some have been pleased, on the day of the Lord’s Supper, to offer and receive it after food, as a more solemn commemoration. II, 203. What Augustine thinks about this. II, 203. From this it pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the Christian’s mouth before any other food. II, 203. A poultice made from the Eucharist. X, 1315. The sacraments that are brought by the bishop’s hand are adduced in support of the statement. II, 650. How the Ophites consecrate the Eucharist. VIII, 28. The Cataphrygians. VIII, 30. The Pepuzians. VIII, 31. The Manichaeans. VIII, 35.

Eucharius, a presbyter, healed of a kidney stone through the memorial of Saint Stephen. VII, 766. “And he was raised up.” VII, 766.

Eucratius of Thenae. IX, 220.

The Εὐχεταί (Euchites), heretics. VIII, 40.

Eudaemons. VII, 265. Eudaemons cannot be intermediaries between gods and human beings. VII, 266.

Eudoxus the astrologer. VII, 500.

Public conveyance. I, 717.

Overthrows. I, 716; III, 156.

Those who cause overthrows. I, 685; II, 799. Namely, those who want laughter and frivolous spectacles to be provided for them through the overthrow and error of others. III, 156. One who causes an overthrow. II, 799.

Euphrates the presbyter, converted to the unity of Christ. II, 583.

Eugenius of Ammedera. IX, 221.

The tyrant Eugenius, successor of Maximus, defeated by Theodosius. VII, 172.

Euhemerus. III, 1056. He wrote a sacred history. VII, 217. He reports that Saturn, Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto were human beings. III, 1056; VII, 184. Euhemerus was translated into Latin by Ennius. III, 1056.

Eulogia, blessed bread. IX, 357. The term *eulogia* is used when bread sent as a sign of unity is received. II, 100. That is, it is blessed by being received. II, 103.

Eulogius the bishop. X, 325, 652, 663.

Eulogius the deacon and martyr. V, 1247, 1249. His answers. V, 1249, 1251.

Eulogius, rhetorician of Carthage. VI, 602.

Eumalius, vicar of Africa. IX, 541, 640, 687.

Eunomius, from whom the heretics called Eunomians, or Aetians, derive their name. VIII, 40, 707, 1087. Eunomius, who said that the Son of God was a son not by nature but by will, is refuted. VIII, 1087.

The Eunomians. III, 1836; V, 448, 988, 990; IX, 395. They sinned against the Holy Spirit. II, 814. The Eunomians were in the East, not in Africa. V, 280.

The eunuch of Queen Candace received the Holy Spirit without human ministry. V, 601, 1227.

Evodius, a native of Tagaste. I, 770. While serving as a soldier in the *agentes in rebus*, he was converted to God and baptized before Augustine. I, 771. In the books *On the Quantity of the Soul* and *On Free Choice of the Will*, he takes the role of interlocutor. I, 1033. He joined Augustine as a companion in the holy purpose and returned with him to Africa. I, 771. He sang a psalm at Monica’s death. I, 776.

Evodius conversed with Proculeianus. II, 129.

Evodius, the bishop who went to Italy with Theasius. II, 273.

Evodius mentioned by Paulinus. II, 100.

Evodius, bishop of Uzalis. II, 693; V, 1446; VII, 768. He writes back to Valentinus concerning the letter to Sixtus. II, 975, note (a). He presents many matters to Augustine in various letters, and Augustine replies to him. II, 693.

Eupasia. VI, 475.

The Euphemites, heretics. VIII, 41.

Euphrates. III, 378. The name refers to the great river. III, 787.

Europa, carried off by Xanthus, king of the Cretans. VII, 569.

The measurement of Europe. VII, 497.

Europs, the second king of the Sicyonians. VII, 561.

Εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*), piety. VII, 279.

Eusebia the Manichaean, as though a nun. VIII, 36.

Eusebius. VI, 597; VIII, 27. He composed a history of the times pertaining to sacred Scripture. III, 62. Rufinus added two books to Eusebius’s histories, which he translated into Latin. VIII, 46. The Chronicles of Eusebius. VII, 497, 566, 587. Eusebius’s view concerning the time when the promises were made to Abraham. [Col. 0285] VII, 496. Concerning the years of the Israelites’ servitude in Egypt. III, 612. Eusebius of Caesarea interpreted the Psalms. II, 262. Paulinus calls him “of Constantinople”; Paulinus sends his history to Alypius. II, 99.

Eusebius of Vercelli. II, 263.

Eusebius of Emesa. II, 286. He left brief commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians. II, 252.

The presbyter Eusebius sends Jerome the books of Annianus the Pelagian. II, 928.

Eustasius from the island of Capraria, a monk. II, 189.

Eustochium and Paula send greetings to Augustine. II, 753. Jerome grieves over the death of Eustochium. II, 928.

Eutomus the bishop. X, 652, 663.

Eutropius the bishop. VIII, 665.

Eutychianus, consul. VII, 620.

The Eutychians, heretics. VIII, 50, final note.

The injustice of the tax collector who demanded again what had already been returned to its owners, as though it had been given without his authorization, is censured. II, 1062.

The most exalted angels of the devil. V, 883.

To exalt God means to confess that he is exalted. V, 1681. God exalts the humble in such a way that he does not make them proud. IV, 1472. See Pride.

The prayers even of sinful human beings are heard. V, 748, 751. When a person prays to God, the doubt of one who is uncertain whether he is heard is removed. V, 171. We have from this a certain claim upon God that he should hear us, because he made us. V, 295. God anticipates our desires. V, 494. When someone asks for trifling things, God in his mercy does not hear him in order to grant them, but hears him in order to heal him by not granting them. V, 203. If God has not given something, know that it is beneficial to you, because a good father does not give it. V, 204. God sometimes hears certain people in anger and does not hear others in mercy. V, 147. Sometimes God does not hear us so that we may understand what we ought to ask of him. IV, 623, 624. See Prayer. Whoever wishes to be heard by God should first hear God. V, 126.

To hear a murmuring means to recognize it. III, 509.

### Blindness

Blindness is the greatest punishment. IV, 688, 690, 691, 692. Each person is either disciplined for purification, warned for conversion, or—if he has despised God’s call and discipline—blinded for condemnation. IV, 116. Why one person is blinded and another illumined must be left to divine judgment. III, 1777. A sinister intention blinds a person. IV, 1839. Arrogance is the cause of blindness. IV, 790, 794. The blindness of unbelievers can be caused by the devil. VIII, 393. In one and the same evil deed, one element comes from the cunning of the tempter, another from the wickedness of the one who wills it, and another from the justice of the one who punishes. VIII, 394. In a certain respect the blindness of unbelievers may pertain to the true God. VIII, 389. And not unjustly. III, 1777, 1780. God blinds by abandoning. III, 1777. The blindness of the Jews arose from pride. III, 1778, 1779; VI, 20. Blindness is sometimes beneficial. III, 1372. It benefited very many Jews. III, 1779.

Three kinds of excellence. V, 1590.

An exceptor, or court secretary. V, 1390. Judicial secretaries. II, 578, 581.

Excess in matters granted for use is much more tolerable than excess in matters not granted. VI, 382.

How those excluded from the Church may benefit the Church. III, 127.

Silversmiths are called *exclusores* when they know how to produce the form of a vessel from a confused mass of metal. X, 210; IV, 643, 836, 837.

### Excommunication

Excommunication. III, 451, 764, 1763; VI, 199, 473; IX, 45, 444, 669. Excommunication from the table. IX, 94. Excommunication is merciful severity. VI, 199. It is a remedy against certain serious sins. VI, 228. “Let us rebuke, chastise, excommunicate, and separate—even while retaining love.” IV, 635. There is no greater punishment in the Church than excommunication. X, 944. Those cut off from the Church are exposed to every danger and to the teeth of wolves. Innocentius. II, 783. Excommunication must be carried out only by legitimate authority and with judgment. V, 900, 1546. A subdeacon excommunicated by his presbyter. II, 419. Likewise, a deacon excommunicated by his presbyter. II, 419. Where excommunication should be applied. IX, 92, 93, 95. The excommunication of a sinner. III, 1732. The incontinent are excommunicated. V, 1094. One should sometimes prudently refrain from excommunication, lest the person struck become worse through the scourge. V, 125. Especially when disturbance and disruption of the Church are feared. V, 51. The Fathers preferred the Pelagians to be healed within the structure of the Church rather than cut off from its body, if necessity allowed it. II, 685, 764, 773. Augustine proves that a person who deserved excommunication was not excommunicated when there was a danger of schism. II, 298.

What excommunication ought to take into consideration. IX, 62, 94. It can be beneficial. X, 944. How it is salutary. IX, 92. Separated from Christ’s body either by penance or by a bad conscience. VII, 674. Just as, before visible excommunication, anyone who harbors a hostile disposition toward the truth by which he is convicted and accused has already been cut off, so after reconciliation he may remain cut off. IX, 444. If the crimes alleged against Caecilianus [Col. 0286] could be demonstrated, we would anathematize him as already dead. II, 794. The separation of false brothers cannot take place before the time of harvest without disturbing the Church. III, 1799. It does not separate from fraternal charity those whom Paul commands to be separated from the fraternal congregation. IX, 84, 85, 86, 92. Excommunication does not harm innocent and spiritual people, but proves them. IX, 123. It does not harm a person that human ignorance does not wish him to be read from the Church’s register, provided unjust conscience does not erase him from the book of the living. II, 269. If a faithful person has been unjustly anathematized, the one who commits the injustice will be harmed by it more than the one who suffers it. II, 1068. How those unjustly excommunicated ought to conduct themselves. III, 128. Augustine finds no justification for having an entire household struck with anathema because of one person’s sin, nor did he dare to do so. II, 1066. To excommunicate a layperson and degrade a cleric. VI, 271.

A former curator. II, 304.

Human pride thinks itself excused when what it does wrong appears to arise from ignorance rather than from the will. II, 883. Pelagius says that the wicked will excuse themselves on the ground that they did not receive the grace to live well. II, 882. Every sinner is shown to be without excuse. II, 882. Scripture calls those who sin knowingly “without excuse,” even according to the judgment of their own pride, by which they place great confidence in the powers of their own will. II, 883. Those who excuse their sins seek, by a circuitous route, to come to accuse God, because they are unwilling to come by the direct route to appease God. IV, 268. The impious accuse God in order to excuse themselves. IV, 1172, 1691. Excusing sin is wicked and is suggested by the devil. V, 138, 186; VI, 357. Excusing oneself in manifest sins is a more condemnable form of pride. VII, 422. By refusing to admit guilt, a person rather increases his guilt. VI, 357. It removes not the punishment but the possibility of pardon. VI, 357. There are various excuses for sins: fate, fortune, the devil, and God himself. VI, 358. When you wish to be your own defender, the devil, your accuser, triumphs over you. V, 186.

Who the sons of the cast out are. IV, 1674.

A former duumvir. II, 304.

Exedra. IX, 697. A place from which the bishop spoke to the people. VII, 770.

Reason must be preferred to examples. VII, 36. Examples move more than commands. VII, 53. They strengthen the faith of the weak. IV, 1402. The examples of the saints kindle some people and discourage others. IV, 1812. Examples are like embers that leave desolation. IV, 1600. We are pressed by examples toward conversion. IV, 1600, 1601. Those who lead in the Church ought to offer themselves as an example to those who follow. IV, 436. Whoever presents an example for good imitation offers a greater mercy than one who provides food for restoring the body. V, 804. An example should not be taken from the many, but from the few who are just. IV, 437. An example of sin should not be taken from the fall of great men. IV, 539, 586. Evil examples do not excuse anyone, and good examples are not lacking. V, 1547. By excusing himself through the example of the wicked, a person seeks not a defender for a bad case but a companion for punishment. V, 758.

*Exenia*, for *xenia*, a gift or hospitality. IV, 195.

To exercise. Sometimes God, through the temporal power of those who are to be condemned, exercises discipline upon those who are to be delivered. IV, 935. See Tribulation.

Those who have been disinherited are commonly called abominated. IV, 86.

The purpose for which exhortation is employed. IV, 1501. The power of exhortation comes from grace. VI, 444. Exhortation accomplishes nothing unless the one who is within reveals it. III, 1609.

More is required from the one to whom more is given. II, 882.

### Exorcism

What exorcism is. I, 968. The exorcism of infants at baptism. IV, 797; X, 829, 1073, 1325. Also the blowing upon them at baptism. X, 1192, 1220, 1383. Exorcism among the rites of baptism. I, 968; X, 408. It is a very ancient rite. X, 465. The most ancient tradition of the Church. X, 467. Diabolical power is exorcized at baptism. X, 426. See Baptism. Exorcism by adjuring in the name of Christ. V, 1080, 1100, 1103.

The ecclesiastical exorcisterium. IX, 578.

To deviate (*exorbitare*) means to go outside the track. III, 1739.

*Expalmatus*. IV, 1230. “He might be struck.” III, 2031.

The difference between what is expedient and what is unlawful. VI, 461. When something is expedient and when it is not. VI, 463. What is lawful but not expedient should be avoided not under the constraint of the law but through free love. VI, 461.

Experience corrects those whom words do not correct. V, 405. Constant experience gradually removes the stimulus of wonder. VII, 714.

To be displayed in pomp (*expompari*; meaning uncertain). V, 268.

The solemn observance of funeral rites. IV, 1352. “For three days we praised the Lord together in hymns over the tomb of the deceased, and on the third day we offered the sacraments of redemption.” II, 694. What reaches the spirits of the dead at funerals. IV, 554. Funerals are more consolations for the living than aids for the dead. VII, 27. Funerals of the rich. IV, 322, 554.

[Col. 0287] To expire means to be outside the spirit. III, 1739.

### Blowing upon those being baptized

Blowing upon those being baptized. X, 408, 455, 829, 1073. The blowing upon infants is a very ancient rite. X, 465. It is also the most ancient tradition of the Church. X, 467. A rite of the universal and most ancient Church. X, 1305, 1307, 1439. The blowing upon infants at baptism is performed so that they may be rescued from the power of the devil. X, 1323. It would not be permissible to blow upon the image of God in baptism unless it were to be rescued from the power of darkness. X, 1333. A grave and conspicuous injury would be done to God himself if his images were blown upon and exorcized without sin being involved. X, 1414.

To go into exile means to be removed from one’s soil. III, 1739. An exile is nowhere without being a Christian. V, 1410. Exile, if one loves one’s homeland, is a great punishment; if one does not love it, it is a worse punishment of the heart. V, 1339. The servants of God choose exile voluntarily every day. VIII, 225.

Exultation is of two kinds, good and bad. IV, 1217. You ought to exult in the Lord piously if you wish to mock the world securely. IV, 1217. To exult in one’s beds means to exult in one’s hearts. IV, 1955. The exultation of the saints is not yet present in reality but in hope. IV, 629. Everyone ought to exult with trembling, because what causes his exultation is God’s gift, not his own merit. IV, 1955. The exultation of the unjust is in the world and therefore passing; that of the just is in the Lord and endures. IV, 277.

“Arise” in the sense of “awake.” III, 497.

External things should not be loved. IV, 1813. External things cannot be clean for those whose interior things are unclean. IV, 1661. Let us rejoice in inward things and have need of outward things. IV, 1813. A person dies to external things more as he draws nearer to God; just as, when he withdraws from God, he directs all his powers toward external things. II, 208.

Outermost things. To advance into outermost things means nothing other than to cast away innermost things—that is, to put God far from oneself. I, 1185.

To exalt. It is not enough for a person to acknowledge that the good within him comes from God unless he also does not exalt himself over the one who does not yet possess it. IV, 878. See Pride.

Hezekiah, an excellent and most devout king, reigned in the time of Romulus. VII, 578. By destroying the groves, temples of idols, and high places that had to be destroyed, he served the Lord. II, 801. Hezekiah was going to die according to certain causes relating to future events, and how fifteen years were added to his life. III, 351.

Ezekiel: what he was and when he prophesied. VII, 592. He prophesied during the Babylonian captivity. IV, 772. Ezekiel speaks of sons and fathers living their lives separately when he says that the father’s injustice does not harm the sons. X, 1273, and frequently above. Ezekiel’s prophecy in chapter 18 pertains to the foretelling of the revelation of the New Testament. X, 1281. Jerome published commentaries on Ezekiel. II, 719.

## F

A Persian fable. VIII, 92.

Fabiola. II, 719, 1091.

Fabius. X, 745. Destroyer of the city of Tarentum. VII, 19. He abstained from plundering statues. VII, 19.

The construction of buildings. IV, 1036.

Fabricius. II, 390; X, 745, 751. An eminent Roman. VII, 164. His voluntary poverty. VII, 164.

Fabricius. VIII, 639. A heretic. VIII, 664.

A fable is a lie composed for usefulness or pleasure. I, 894. The Pagans try to interpret their fables according to the nature of things or the morals of human beings. VIII, 374. And to refer them to certain obscure “physiologies” or “theologies.” VIII, 275.

### To make

Whatever anyone makes is either from himself, from something else, or from nothing. VIII, 547. Nothing generates or makes itself. I, 1028. “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another”: the truth was written by the hand of our Maker in our very hearts. IV, 673. No one was permitted to be ignorant of this, so that there might be a basis for judging those to whom the law was not given. IV, 673. “Do with me”—what does this mean? IV, 1442. Numbers that produce are to be preferred to numbers produced. I, 1165. Deeds are speeches by which the just person will be defended in judgment. IV, 1469. Care must be taken not to speak, like the philosophers, of certain human acts as intermediate between right action and sin. II, 280. Examples of certain acts that are neither good nor evil. II, 281.

A faction: the agreement of unjust members of the nobility. VII, 67. If the person brought to judgment sees that there is a faction, he ought to reserve his case for a better judgment. IV, 375.

The face of God is his presence through the Church. IV, 814. It is the power by which he makes himself known to those who are worthy. IV, 137. It is truth. I, 988. It is his revelation and his future presence in judgment. IV, 838. The face of the favorable and assisting Lord is upon those who do good, and the face of the angry Lord upon those who do evil. IV, 1593. The face by which God is to be seen. II, 620, 622, 625. The remarkable likeness and unlikeness of human faces. VII, 721.

A crime is what desire does in order to harm another. III, 72.

[Col. 0288] Resources are called riches. V, 1189. Resources are nothing other than indications of weakness. V, 488, 1190. God does not consider one’s means but one’s desire. IV, 1727. And one’s will. IV, 1057. God crowns the will inwardly when he does not find the means. IV, 1351.

Dog-like eloquence. II, 752.

To reap or mow. IV, 318.

Deception makes bad use of the tongue. III, 1620.

The deceptive differs from the lying. I, 892; III, 149. A deceptive person is one who has a desire to deceive. I, 892. A false person must be instructed; a deceptive person must be avoided. I, 925.

### The difference between being deceived and lying

The difference between being deceived and lying. V, 157, 738. To lie is worse than to be deceived. V, 738. Sometimes lying is more tolerable than being deceived. VI, 241. With respect to the human will, being deceived is a lesser evil than lying. VI, 241. Those who deceive by lying are more miserable than those who are deceived by believing liars. VI, 240. In some matters we are deceived with great harm, in others with little harm, in others with no harm, and in others with some benefit. VI, 241. But error itself, whether great in a great matter or small in a small matter, is nevertheless always evil. VI, 241, 243. Many want to deceive, but no one wants to be deceived. I, 794; V, 984, 1405; VI, 240; VIII, 340. The good do not wish to deceive; neither the good nor the wicked wish to be deceived. V, 984. How naturally the soul hates being deceived. V, 813. Here it is difficult not to be deceived. II, 275. The human heart is deceived about sin and the punishment of sin. IV, 87. “Do what you can to come to the life in which you will not be deceived; live now in such a way that you do not deceive.” V, 1405.

Falsehood is nothing in itself, but is spoken of when something is thought to be what it is not. I, 744. The mind itself deceives, not the eyes. III, 149. Falsehood does not arise from things themselves or from the senses, but from sins. III, 149, 150. Falsehood is not in things but in the mind’s perception. I, 887. A soul that has not yet suffered the vanity of sensible things and the senses is less subject to falsehoods. II, 70. Falsehood draws falsehood after it. IX, 462. This is a realm of falsehood. V, 973. Falsehood is a capital crime. V, 1471.

### The false

What the false is. III, 60. On the notion of the false. I, 898. The false is nothing other than what is not as it appears. I, 889. Certain things are true in the same respect in which they are false. I, 893. No one knows false things unless he knows that they are false. VIII, 1070. Something is not true merely because it is expressed eloquently, nor false merely because it is expressed inelegantly. I, 710. Why we usually think false things. VIII, 997. A person is more deeply embedded in false opinions the more familiarly and habitually he wallows in them. II, 66. Knowledge of the truth is capable of judging and overturning every falsehood, if only it is put forward, including things previously unheard. II, 437. It is never permissible to tell a falsehood. IV, 86. False testimony must not be given even under threat of death. V, 123. False testimony must be avoided even at the risk of property and life. V, 631. False witnesses are blinded and, without knowing it, say things by which they appear to be false witnesses. IV, 373, 374.

Care must be taken concerning a good reputation. V, 1508, 1569; VI, 448. A good reputation is cruelly despised. VI, 448. Popular reputation should not be the goal of one’s endeavors. II, 433, 434. A good reputation is a good fragrance. III, 1760. A good reputation is for some the fragrance of life leading to life, and for others the fragrance of death leading to death. III, 1760. A ruined soul strives to acquire a reputation for itself by evil arts. IV, 127. When we have done everything we rightly can for the sake of our reputation, if someone detracts from it, let there be the consolation of conscience—and indeed complete joy. VI, 449. Our life is necessary for us; our reputation is necessary for others. VI, 448. Sometimes there is a situation in which conscience is insufficient. II, 475, 480. To his own destruction, a person is considered good by the good when he is secretly evil. III, 465. How the just are proved by good and bad reputation. IX, 355. Nothing is cheaper than the authority of reputation. I, 928. Human rumor is compared to the winds. II, 1308.

Hunger and thirst are pains. I, 797. Hunger is a disease whose medicine is food. IV, 398, 1396. The person who fasts for seven days is consumed by hunger. IV, 1638. Abraham and Isaac suffered hunger. IV, 384. How, then, do the just not seek bread? IV, 384, 386. What it means when God called it hunger, etc. IV, 1396. Good hunger. VII, 25. The famine at Rome. VII, 26. The famine at Saguntum. VII, 101.

Hunger of the heart. V, 262. “Now is the time of hunger; afterward will be the time of fullness.” IV, 298. The hunger of the perfected is the conversion of sinners. IV, 241, 242. We ought to be hungry for God: before the sight of his door, let us beg in prayers. IV, 1895, 1896.

How a household should be administered. VII, 644.

Three measures of flour. V, 641.

To bewitch, in the sense of “to envy.” III, 536.

Fascius, overwhelmed by debt, fled to the Church. II, 1092.

When relief is given to weariness, another weariness begins. IV, 1320, 1321, 1638.

### Folly

Folly is a great evil. X, 707. Folly is natural—why? X, 1314. Folly was introduced not by the mingling of another nature but by the corruption of our own nature. X, 1429. Certain people are born foolish, compelling acknowledgment of original sin. X, 707, 1314. [Col. 0289] Delight in the absurdity of fools arises only from carnal affection. X, 148. The foolish virgins, for whom conscience is insufficient. IV, 1921. The foolish virgins are stirred to good works not by the strength of a good conscience but by the prompting of another’s tongue. IV, 1921. He does not say to his brother, “Fool,” when, in saying this, he is offended only by his brother’s sin. VII, 748.

### Fate

“Fate” (*fatum*) may be derived from *fari*, “to speak.” VII, 150; VIII, 213. What is commonly understood by the name of fate. VII, 141; X, 579. Fate fabricated from the arrangement of the stars. V, 1007, 1027. Why the three Fates are imagined at the distaff and spindle, twisting thread from wool with their fingers. VIII, 374. Nothing happens by fate. VII, 150. The mathematicians themselves overturn their doctrine of fate by their own actions. II, 1061. This doctrine is no small evil, since it turns people away from the medicine of confession in order to defend sin. II, 1061. That something happens by fate although it does not happen deservedly: this is the Pelagian position, which is refuted. X, 761. The cause of sin must not be converted into fate. II, 1061. Whoever attributes his evils to fate attributes them to God. IV, 1173. Catholics do not assert fate under the name of grace. X, 577, 579. Why this was alleged by the Pelagians against Catholics. X, 577. The accusation of fate is turned back against the opponents. X, 578, 579. By the name of fate some understand not the position of the stars but the totality of God’s will. VII, 148. Why one should refrain from calling it fate. VII, 150.

What fatal things are. VII, 141. The proponents of fatal stars are attacked. VII, 141, 144, 145.

Faventius, lessee of the Paratian forest. II, 429, 430.

Faunus, son of Picus and the second king of Laurentum. VII, 573. He was enrolled among the gods. VII, 573.

The incubi, or fauns. VII, 468.

Faustinianus the bishop. II, 759, 762, 780.

Faustinus of Tuburbi. IX, 676.

Faustinus the Donatist forbids bread to be baked for Catholics at Hippo. IX, 316.

Faustinus, a Donatist bishop. III, 1436.

Faustinus the deacon. V, 1576.

### Faustus

Faustus the Manichaean. VI, 166, 442. A bishop of the Manichaeans. I, 707, 710, 711. Faustus’s homeland, qualities, and so forth. VIII, 207, 223. His intelligence. VIII, 333. His softness. VIII, 223. The false virtues of which he boasted. VIII, 224. Faustus denied that anything concerning Christ had been prophesied in the books of the Hebrews. VII, 473. Julian calls Faustus Augustine’s teacher. X, 1203. Faustus was a snare of death for many and an occasion of salvation for Augustine. I, 711. Because he was a Manichaean, Faustus was banished, along with several others, to an island by proconsular judgment. VIII, 225.

Faustus of Timida. IX, 233.

Faustus, bearer of the letter to Boniface. II, 854.

The basilica of Faustus. V, 643, 1202.

Faustulus, the shepherd, husband of the nurse of Romulus and Remus. VII, 578.

The teaching of wisdom, expressed from obscure mysteries, is like a honeycomb. IV, 1566. The honeycomb signifies Christ. IV, 1497.

Fever, the goddess of the Romans. II, 84; IV, 1396; VII, 59, 88, 125. The Romans built shrines to Fever and Pallor. III, 1053; VII, 105.

Fever does not fear a silver bed, does not fear the pomp of the rich, and does not fear the weapons of the warrior. V, 1260. Fevers of the soul. V, 83.

From where the month of February received its name. VII, 200. February was named from the sacred rites of the Luperci. VIII, 346. The month of February was dedicated to the god Terminus. VII, 200.

Gall grows through the ease of becoming angry, and as gall increases, the ease of becoming angry increases. II, 73. Christ rejected gall on the cross because those who grow bitter do not enter into his body. IV, 852.

## Fertility

By his ineffable words God implanted the power of seed in the first human beings. X, 405. Fertility existed before sin and was not removed by sin. I, 1297. The fertility granted to human beings was not taken away after sin. I, 1297; VII, 788; X, 1438. It is not what it would have been had they not sinned. VII, 789. Fertility, not the arousal of the shameful members, is God’s gift. X, 450. Although the fertility of women has now become burdensome, it was iniquity, not fertility, that caused this. X, 1560. God makes women’s wombs fruitful, not by a constrained power, but freely and most powerfully. X, 837.

## To the virgin Felicia

A consolatory or exhortatory letter, so that she may not suffer scandal because of evil shepherds. II, 950.

## Felicianus of Musti

IV, 376, 381. A Maximianist. IX, 76, 108, 109, 137, 178, 371, 507, 528, 530, 550. Ordainer of Maximian. IX, 253. Felicianus and others conspiring with him condemned Primianus. II, 412. Felicianus is accused of the entire conspiracy. II, 413. Titianus brings a complaint against him. IX, 574. A complaint against Felicianus for excluding him from the places of Musti. IX, 529. Felicianus was one of the twelve accused before three or more proconsuls so that they might be expelled from their sees. II, 407. Proceedings were brought before the proconsul to exclude him from the basilica. II, 241. How long this conflict lasted. IX, 530. Felicianus is condemned by Primianus. II, [Col. 0290] 404, 405. By the Donatists. II, 580. By the Council of Bagai. II, 192, 198, 309, 405; IV, 382; IX, 63, 73, 107, 251. Felicianus is called an adulterer of the truth and a chain of sacrilege. II, 405, 414. Felicianus passes from the party of Donatus to the Maximianists. IX, 655. He communicates with Maximian and baptizes many outside the communion of the Donatists. II, 241. Felicianus is forcibly restored through Optatus. IX, 251, 252, 316, 565, 581, 704. Felicianus is reconciled with Primianus. IX, 107. Felicianus, condemned by the Donatists, was later received back by them without baptism and in the same rank, after he had returned to them out of a desire for concord. II, 192, 198, 309, 405, 407, 413; IX, 39, 584, 618, 655, 740. Under compulsion from Optatus Gildonianus. II, 198, 405. Although condemned, Felicianus of Musti was received again by the Donatists as though he were unblemished, supposedly for the sake of peace. IX, 54. Those whom he baptized in Maximian’s schism were also received with him. II, 241. The Donatists neither rebaptized Felicianus nor those whom he had baptized in the schism. IX, 97, 98, 113, 262, 504. Felicianus of Musti now lives as a bishop among the Donatists. IX, 426.

## Felicitas and Perpetua

Martyrs. VI, 703. Felicitas, a woman martyr. V, 1280. By giving birth, Felicitas experienced Eve’s punishment. V, 1284.

A letter. II, 942.

## Felix

Augustine sends two of his own men to Nola, to the memory of blessed Felix, so that it might become clear which of them was guilty. II, 269. Felix’s basilica. VI, 157, 591. Felix the confessor appears to human eyes themselves. VI, 606.

IX, 221.

## Felix of Aptunga, ordainer of Caecilianus

I, 642, 644; IX, 593, 594; Retr. 610. Acerbius is accused at the Carthaginian Council of the schismatics. IX, 639. The Donatists charged him with the crime of handing over the sacred books. II, 581. He was called the source of all evils at the Donatist Council. II, 303, 492. Constantine caused the case of Felix of Aptunga to be heard first by the proconsul Aelianus. IX, 593, 594; Retr. 610. The case of Felix of Aptunga was pursued by the Donatists with much greater hostility and criminal accusation than the others. II, 161. The Donatists falsely claimed that Felix of Aptunga had been convicted before the proconsul’s court of handing over the sacred books by a certain Vincentius. IX, 539. Ingentius confessed during the inquiry of the proconsul Aelianus that he had acted falsely against Felix. II, 581. Felix of Aptunga rightly allowed a certain man to be hung on the rack during the inquiry into his case. II, 166. By Constantine’s order he was cleared in the official proconsular proceedings. II, 161, 492. He was also acquitted of the charge of handing over the sacred books. IX, 532, 539, 553, 610, 649, 650, 686. And by Constantine’s rescript. II, 581; IX, 540, 553. The official proconsular proceedings by which Felix was acquitted. IX, App. 780. A copy of the letters by which he was declared innocent. II, 304. Felix of Aptunga was indeed cleared by a proconsular judgment, but he himself had not sought this judgment. II, 165.

## Felix the bishop

## Felix the bishop

He is commended to Valerius the Count. II, 949.

## Felix the Manichaean

I, 633; VIII, 519. He said that he was prepared to be burned in defense of his master’s teaching. VIII, 527. He anathematized Manichaeus. VIII, 551. There is a suspicion that Letter 79 was written to him. II, 273. Note (a).

II, 969, 971; X, 911, 914.

II, 971, 975.

## Felicitas, the goddess

VII, 126. Lucullus was the first to establish a temple to Felicitas. VII, 129. If Felicitas is a goddess, she alone ought to have been worshiped. VII, 129, 131. The Romans were mistaken, who worshiped felicity as a goddess only so late. VII, 129, 130. Felicitas is preferable to a kingdom. VII, 130. Felicitas is not a goddess but a gift of God. VII, 131, 140, 193. It is not Felicitas who must be worshiped, but God. VII, 131.

What distinction is there between felicity and good fortune? VII, 126. God grants true felicity only to the good. VII, 139. True felicity. VII, 370. How great true felicity will be. VII, 801. Felicity is the fullness of all desirable things. VII, 140. It is participation in God. VII, 153. Felicity can be conferred only by the one true God. VII, 71. God is our blessedness; for one who turns away from him there will be nothing but misery. IV, 898. See *Beatitude*, *Prosperity*. The felicity of the first human beings before sin. VII, 434.

Where human beings place felicity. II, 531. Felicity must not be placed in temporal things. V, 202. He is foolish and perverse who thinks that human felicity consists only in temporal possessions, pleasures, and so forth. IV, 1611. Temporal felicity belongs to the Old Testament. III, 630. Spiritual Jews understood that through Christ they were to expect not earthly and carnal felicity but heavenly and spiritual felicity. VII, 546. The New Testament was figuratively foretold by the earthly felicity of the Old Testament. II, 540. Whoever seeks earthly felicity from God within the Church belongs to Ishmael. IV, 1603. Earthly felicity was despised even in the Old Testament. VIII, 163. The temporal felicity of the pagans is to be attributed to God’s hidden providence, not to the favor of the gods. VII, 71. Temporal felicity is common to the just and the impious. III, 650; V, 129, 1386. It is often granted even to the wicked. VII, 595. It is a most beneficent providence that it not be sought by the good as something great. II, 543. Temporal felicity is called the left hand; eternal felicity, the right. IV, 1612, 1770, 1867, 1868. The good possess perpetual felicity at the right hand and temporal felicity at the left. V, 204. Whoever sets his heart on temporal felicity makes what is left into what is right. IV, 1867, 1868, 1869. The sin is not failing to possess this felicity, but making it the right hand when it is the left. IV, 1612, 1770, 1867. Felicity according to the perverse opinion of human beings. II, 531. Temporal things confer true felicity on no one, because they do not extinguish insatiable desire. IV, 1411.

Those who flourish for a time should not be considered happy. IV, 883. Even the impious do not retain their felicity in the present. IV, 1636. A wicked person is thought happy because felicity is not understood. III, 1625. The wicked person is the more unhappy the happier he seems to himself. V, 1165. Truly happy is not the person who has what he loves, but the person who loves what ought to be loved. IV, 202. See *Blessed*. Nothing is more unhappy than the felicity of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and an evil will is strengthened like an internal enemy. II, 531. The felicity of the impious is a source of scandal to some. V, 126, 134, 168, 203, 1164. The devout should not be disturbed by the worldly felicity of the impious. V, 1383. Those who are scandalized by the felicity of the wicked are not upright in heart. V, 318. The felicity of the wicked is not to be envied. III, 1605. For one turning away from God amid adversity, the false felicity of the wicked becomes a true snare. IV, 1655. Whoever patiently endures the felicity of the wicked and the hardships of the good is already blessed in this respect. IV, 1191.

The felicity of the impious is a great wrath of God. V, 1357. Whoever is pleased by this world should regard himself as being in distress. IV, 1059. The felicity of sinners is their own pitfall. IV, 1204. The wicked flourish through false goods and perish through true torments. IV, 626. Felicity is the dream of one who sleeps. IV, 925, 1719. Especially the felicity of the impious. VII, 302. Temporal felicity is the river of Babylon. IV, 1764. Felicity will wither and fall like the flower of hay. IV, 620. Deceptive felicity is a greater unhappiness. IV, 1697. The felicity of the world is not an honor but a burden to the devout. V, 1384. Worldly felicity is more a danger than an ornament to us. V, 1562.

Earthly felicity should be considered neither evil nor of great importance. VII, 71. Earthly felicity is a gift of God. II, 533, 539. It is given by God to the just so that they may be free for what enables them to obtain eternal good. IV, 1401, 1402. Felicity and the abundance of temporal things in this world are consolations during our pilgrimage. IV, 579. Both felicity and unhappiness are to be feared. IV, 946, 1058. Earthly felicity is more to be feared than misery. IV, 587, 840, 841. Earthly felicity is to be despised. V, 204, 205, 206, 1070. The kingdom of earthly felicity is pride. IV, 1050. The felicity of the good is to have God in their conscience. III, 1605. Christ did not promise the felicity of this age. IV, 360; V, 1356. Christ as man was not to be commended for earthly felicity, lest people serve God for its sake. II, 543. Whether the felicity of human affairs has been diminished in Christian times. III, 1068. Felicity is not to be sought here. V, 134. Whoever wishes to become a Christian for the sake of earthly felicity still remains in darkness. IV, 1673. Whoever seeks earthly felicity in return for worshiping God sells that worship for the cheapest price. V, 135. Psalm 72 introduces a repentant person who had served God for an earthly reward and intended to recognize why the impious flourish in earthly felicity. II, 543. Against those who seek carnal felicity and do not see themselves answered. V, 147. Against those who think felicity exists in this life and doubt the next. V, 1381. To seek earthly felicity and patiently await eternal felicity is to sleep among the middle ranks of the clergy. IV, 825.

God mixes bitterness into earthly felicities so that another felicity may be sought, whose sweetness is not deceptive. V, 621. If God did not mix bitterness into the felicities of this age, we would forget him. IV, 1212, 1213. It is a mark of great virtue to struggle against felicity, so that it may not entice, corrupt, or itself overthrow us. V, 483. No unhappiness breaks the person whom no felicity corrupts. IV, 1058. It is a great felicity not to be conquered by felicity. V, 483. Earthly felicity is to be used in the service of the Creator. II, 539. And for eternal gains. II, 356. Heavenly felicity is compared with earthly felicity. V, 136. The felicity of souls is one thing before the resurrection and another after it. V, 1282. What full felicity is. X, 1498. Most blessed are those for whom possessing God is the same as knowing him. II, 840. Felicity does not belong to the body; it belongs to the one who enjoys and understands. II, 439. It is situated in eternity, truth, and charity—that is, in stable, certain, and complete felicity—where everything is clear to those who remain, see, and love. II, 744. When we love God for his own sake, and ourselves and our neighbors for his sake, we must not yet consider ourselves established in the blessed life, as though there were nothing more for which we should pray. II, 499. Eternal felicity is the right hand of the Father. VIII, 692. The people of the world are happy unhappily, while the martyrs are unhappy happily. IV, 1679. The martyrs endured torments because they saw felicity. IV, 1678. The two eternal felicities introduced by the Pelagians are futile. X, 1188. What sort of felicity is to be hoped for in the future age. V, 34, 36, 135, 1384. Carnal thought concerning future felicity. V, 1189.

## Woman

Woman was made from man. IV, 1784. She was made in the image of God. III, 293. She was made outside the six days of creation. III, 343. Through a woman came death; through a woman, life. VI, 303. Through a woman came poison; through a woman, salvation. V, 334. See *Woman*. The reproach borne by women before Christ was erased by grace. VI, 704. Woman’s subjection to man. I, 866; III, 204. For a woman to serve men is the natural order. III, 589. And the law intended it so. III, 762. A woman placed under her father or husband cannot make a vow without their consent. III, 744, 745. See *Vow*. Women once practiced philosophy. I, 993. Women took part in public deliberations at Athens, but were later expelled; why. VII, 566. The Voconian Law forbade making a woman an heir. VII, 103. The female sex was fashioned for the production of offspring, though not with lust, unless human beings had sinned. III, 400. What use of women is natural and what is contrary to nature. X, 456, 457, 723, 1450, 1452, 1453. The Nicolaitans taught the detestable disgrace of using women indiscriminately. VIII, 26. Simon Magus. VIII, 25. Saturninus. VIII, 26. Among the Manichaeans, the conception of women is the prison and bond of God. VIII, 597. Why Plato judged that women should be used promiscuously. X, 1551. Why prostitution of women was prohibited. VIII, 438. A woman is desired and desires not only by touch but also by affection and sight. II, 961. Nothing casts a manly spirit down from its citadel more than feminine blandishments. I, 878. Why the devil spared Job’s wife. III, 2023. It is not fitting even for married women to uncover their hair. II, 1060. Women are to be permitted to adorn themselves only for their husbands, by concession, not by command. II, 1060. What harm women’s desire for external ornaments causes, and what benefit their rejection of them brings. V, 884. The honor of the female sex is found in Christ’s mother. V, 1008. Why Christ accepted service from religious women out of their resources. IV, 1367, 1368. Women were the first announcers of Christ’s resurrection. V, 335. Why Christ’s resurrection was announced to men through women. III, 1998. Women victorious over the enemy. V, 1285. The transformation of women into the male sex. VII, 110.

## Thigh

The thigh signifies flesh. IV, 1183. The fruit of the thigh is one thing, the fruit of the womb another. IV, 1724. The breadth of Jacob’s thigh signifies the multitude of his descendants. IV, 506. What girding the sword around the thigh signifies. IV, 1183.

Dishes offered to the gods. VII, 50.

V, 1201.

Iron signifies tribulation. IV, 1397.

Let us burn with zeal in the journeys of good works, for this is our walking. IV, 290.

The goddess. VII, 129.

## Festival

God’s festival is joy without deficiency. IV, 470. Certain festival days of the pagans. V, 1610. The festival days of Christians and the solemn days of the pagans. VI, 343. A profane festival. IV, 1038. Human festivals are passing joy, full of luxury. IV, 470. Why festivals are celebrated annually in the Church. VIII, 503. How festivals should be observed. II, 1404. Carnal celebration of festivals. V, 1178. Certain festivals celebrated with the joy of diners at public tables. V, 274. The festival days of the gentiles were marked by an abundance of food and drunkenness. II, 118. Why, at the beginning of the Church, the festival days of martyrs were permitted to be celebrated with similar luxury. II, 118. The festivals of the martyrs were instituted so that we might be admonished to imitate them. V, 52, 1293, 1352, 1364, 1414, 1447. To honor the festivals of the martyrs without imitating them is nothing other than flattering them deceitfully. V, 1447. In various places, on Sundays, during the fifty days after Easter, on the solemn days of martyrs, and on every festival, people dine. II, 146. The feast of the Lord’s Ascension and the deposition of Saint Leontius are celebrated on the same day. V, 1208. The festival of a certain woman’s blood. III, 1439.

Festus is called upon against the Donatists of the Hippo region. II, 309. Since the letters previously given had accomplished nothing. II, 312.

## Fetus

When a fetus in the womb begins to live. VI, 272.

## Fetal matters

V, 1014.

## “Let it be, let it be”

In the Psalms, “Let it be, let it be” is the subscription of God’s security. IV, 1114.

## Fiction

Fiction is not always falsehood. VI, 538. Christ figuratively pretended not to know what he knew, and also pretended that he was going farther. VI, 537.

## Fig tree
