A fig tree with leaves but without fruit signifies the Jews and Pharisees, who had words but not deeds. IV, 264. The leaves of the fig tree signify the itch of lust. V, 442. What is meant allegorically by the man seen by Christ beneath the fig tree. IV, 264. Egyptian figwood does not float in water. VII, 715. The barren fig tree for three years. V, 553, 555, 638.

## Confidence

What confidence is. VI, 21. How great is the security of one who trusts in God. IV, 201.

## Fidentianus

A bishop. II, 758, 780.

## Fidentius

A bishop. V, 1448.

## Faith, the goddess

Faith was believed to be a goddess, and had a temple and altar. VII, 127.

## Faith: its origin and nature

Why faith is so called. III, 1760; VI, 515. It is called *fides* because what is said (*dicitur*) is made (*fit*). II, 285; V, 320. Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. V, 699. Faith is conceived from the canonical Scriptures. VII, 646. Catholic faith is gathered from the testimony of reading and founded on apostolic truth. V, 355. Faith falters if the authority of the divine Scriptures falters. III, 35. The books of the Jews support our faith. VI, 178. Faith has its own light in the Scriptures. V, 698. It has its own eyes, by which in a certain way it sees that what it does not yet see is true, and by which it sees most certainly that it does not yet see what it believes. II, 456. What has not yet shone upon our understanding must not be abandoned from the firmness of faith. VIII, 947. Faith is believing what you do not see. III, 1690. This is faith’s praise: that what is believed is not seen. III, 1837. Faith properly concerns things that are not seen. VI, 235. When we see the Church, we ought to believe in Christ whom we do not see, just as the apostles, seeing Christ, believed in the Church which they did not see. V, 1126, 1143. What a Christian does not need to know. VI, 235.

Faith is removed if assent is removed, as the Academics would have it. VI, 243. God’s will seeks faith, not inquiry. V, 1438. Faith must be embraced before questions are finished, lest life end without faith. II, 386. Where reason has ceased, there the building of faith begins. V, 1157. And progress. V, 1008. To what extent faith sometimes precedes reason and is always preceded by reason. II, 453. It is permissible to seek and receive an account of faith. II, 453. The deceitful Manichaean commands faith in uncertain matters and promises knowledge of certain matters. VIII, 183, 184. As much as eternity is worth in relation to what has come into being, so much truth is worth in relation to faith, according to Plato. III, 1070. When faith is at issue, there is no need for a lengthy speech. V, 1075.

Various arguments for the Catholic faith. VIII, 175. The firmness of faith lies in the fact that everything that happened in Christ was foretold. III, 1989. What we now see fulfilled should move us to believe what we have not seen. VI, 176, 178, 341, 346. The first Christians were moved by miracles to believe what was foretold would happen. VI, 341. If the manner in which the world came to believe is considered, it is found more incredible than the things it believed. VII, 756. Divine signs and indications are not lacking, by which we may be led to faith. V, 700. Faith confirmed by signs. VI, 174. The faith of the whole world was wonderfully won for Christ. VI, 179. The whole world bears witness to our faith. V, 1603. Whoever still seeks prodigies in order to believe is himself a great prodigy. VII, 760. Faith is stronger the more it no longer seeks miracles. X, 183. It is permissible to believe or not to believe human witnesses or testimonies, insofar as one weighs how much force they possess for producing or failing to produce faith. II, 598. Our faith must not depend on the conduct of human beings, however holy their profession may be. IV, 1592.

Faith does not belong to the proud. V, 656, 874. Faith first, and then precepts for living, subject the soul to God. VI, 299. Faith possesses humility. III, 1670. Faith is milk for little children. VIII, 821. When we are little children, we must be nourished with the simplicity of faith. VI, 309. The simple Catholic faith is the one salvation of little children: by this single milk they reach, with assured strength, the firmness of more solid food. IV, 132, 133. A simple faith that may suffice for us does not suffice for others. V, 619. The most correct discipline is to receive the weak as fully as possible into the citadel of faith. II, 448.

Faith is the firstborn of our heart. V, 72. Faith is a matter of the heart, not of the body. VIII, 1016. Faith is not a matter of a body that greets, but of the believing mind. VI, 316. Faith’s companions are hope and charity. V, 369. Faith is the eye of the heart. IV, 1169. Our faith is our first fruits. IV, 1749. All knowledge and prophecy serve faith, hope, and charity. III, 35. Here we need firm faith, hope, and charity. IV, 1171. God is to be worshiped through faith, hope, and charity. VI, 232. These alone are to be followed in religion. VI, 233. Faith without hope and without charity is not devout. II, 456. How faith relates to each of these. II, 457. [Col. 0294] Faith can exist without hope, but hope cannot exist without faith. VI, 234. Hope is faith’s friend. V, 248. Faith can exist without charity, but charity cannot exist without faith. V, 564; VI, 235. When faith falters, charity grows weak. III, 35.

The work of faith is love. III, 2054. True faith is faith that works through love. III, 1631. Praiseworthy faith—the faith of the faithful—is itself the true faith of grace that works through love. V, 564, 852. Whoever does not love believes and hopes in vain. VI, 286. Faith works through love in the heart, even if it does not emerge outwardly in action. V, 32. Faith without charity is death. III, 1578. Dead faith belongs not to Christians but to demons. VI, 217. The faith of demons. II, 878. The faith of those who live badly is close to the faith of demons. V, 993. Corruption begins with bad faith; from there one proceeds to shameful conduct. IV, 614. The faith of Christians must be distinguished from the faith of demons. II, 878; V, 369, 865, 912, 1116. What Christian faith is. VI, 286. Faith with love is Christian faith; without love, it is the faith of a demon. III, 2055. Those who do not have faith are worse than demons. III, 2055.

What faith pertaining to religion is, and what matters it concerns. VI, 234, 299. The division of matters belonging to the object of faith. II, 456. What is sufficient to believe. VII, 235. The principal matters of Christian faith. V, 808, 1116, 1133. Historical and temporal faith; spiritual and eternal faith. III, 166. By the temporal faith of the history administered for our salvation by the incarnate Word, infants are nourished—that is, those not yet capable of understanding spiritual and eternal things. IV, 110.

The first and greatest duty of faith is to believe in the true God. VII, 127. Faith in God the Creator is not sufficient for salvation. X, 249. Without faith in Christ no one has ever been reconciled. IV, 1396. No human being has ever been able to be justified or saved. X, 399, 401. No one is delivered from the condemnation that came through the faith of Jesus Christ. X, 923. None of the just, even among the ancients, could have been saved from the condemnation of the entire mass of perdition except through faith in Christ. III, 1918; VI, 287. Whoever died in a region where he could not hear Christ’s name could not be justified. X, 249. Faith in Christ is not necessary for salvation if a person can live justly without it. X, 248. The faith of Christ is to be preferred to works of the Law. III, 613. Christ is the certain and proper foundation of the Catholic faith. VI, 233. Christian faith properly concerns the case of two human beings, Christ and Adam. V, 190; X, 399. Faith in Christ’s resurrection is the faith of Christians. IV, 1609. The fullness of faith concerning Christ. V, 1196. What the faith of Christ is. III, 1778. Faith in Christ is the way to God. VI, 243; VII, 318. Through faith in Christ born in the flesh one reaches Christ born of God. IV, 1641.

True faith was one and unchanged from the beginning of the human race. II, 374. The faith of the Old and New Testaments is not different but one. II, 681. From the beginning of the human race Christ never ceased to be prophesied, nor were there ever lacking those who believed in Christ. II, 375. The ancient righteous were saved by the same faith by which the faithful of our time are saved. II, 845, 858; III, 1722. The faith of the righteous of the Old and New Testaments is the same. VIII, 356; X, 272, 399, 400, 450, 569, 595. Before the Passion, the righteous lived by faith in Christ. X, 284. And they were saved. II, 681, 769, 858. The faith in Christ possessed by us is the same as that possessed by the fathers of the Old Testament. IV, 596; V, 133; VII, 610. Just as we were saved through faith in Christ’s past Passion, so the ancient saints were saved through faith in that same Passion as future. I, 808. They were saved by believing that Christ would come, just as we are saved by believing that he has come. VI, 332. The faith of the Old Testament belonged to the grace of the Spirit. IV, 283. There is one faith even amid different observances. II, 146. Why God spread one faith abroad in many and varied ways. IV, 524. How faith is common and one among all believers. VIII, 1016, 1017.

Faith is necessary here. V, 236. Necessary for salvation. V, 784, 1341. Without faith no one has ever been or will be righteous. VI, 621. How long faith is necessary. I, 877. Without faith it is impossible to please God. X, 755. Faith is the first commandment and the beginning of religion. V, 237. The beginning of salvation. V, 912. The beginning of correcting the heart. X, 314. The beginning of a good life. V, 254; VI, 204, 621. The beginning of a better life and of inward renewal. IV, 1749, 1750. Faith is the beginning of the Christian person; martyrdom for Christ is the best end. X, 995. Faith is necessary for living devoutly. VII, 610. Faith is a step in piety. III, 1574. Your faith is your righteousness. IV, 279. Righteousness comes from faith, not from works. II, 819. Righteousness comes neither through the Law nor through the possibility of nature, but from faith, and so forth. II, 768. All righteousness takes its beginning from faith. II, 877. The justified person begins from faith. IV, 1464. Faith is the resurrection of the sinner. III, 1568. Through faith the soul comes back to life. IV, 1116. Justification by faith without works. V, 31. What it means, according to the Apostle, to be justified by faith without works. VI, 88. The extent to which the Apostle distinguishes faith from works. X, 969. Why the Apostle said that we are justified by faith rather than by works. X, 969. What should be thought about faith without works. IV, 257. Paul asserts that a person is justified by faith without works, so that no one may presume that grace was received on the merit of works. IV, 261. Faith without works is of no benefit, just as works without faith are of no benefit. IV, 258, 259, 261. Faith without works is not sufficient for salvation. X, 892. Faith without works saves no one. X, 598. It is idle. VI, 87, 88. A root without fruit. IV, 259. Augustine refers to his book *On Faith and Works*. II, 948. The freedom of faith must not become a covering for malice among the faithful. VI, 225. Some promise themselves the kingdom of heaven on account of faith, even though they live badly. V, 368. The error of those who think that the baptized are to be saved because of Christian faith, even if they do not correct their utterly evil conduct. VI, 197. It is refuted. VI, 150, 210, 370. Faith in God must not prevent human beings from doing what must be done. III, 574. God performs the work of the Law in a person through his grace, and the person, receiving grace through faith, is a fellow worker with the assisting God. III, 756.

Faith does not come from works but belongs to grace. III, 613. Not from merits. III, 1400. Faith does not come from good works; rather, good works come from faith. V, 32; X, 892. Faith is the beginning from which good works begin. X, 341. The grace of faith precedes good works. VI, 111, 621. Before faith there is no good work. III, 1851. Good works depend on faith and are preceded by it. III, 613. Without faith no one performs good works. II, 875; V, 72. Without right faith, no abundance of praiseworthy works is beneficial. X, 598. Works performed before faith, although they appear praiseworthy to human beings, are empty. IV, 259. Whether someone who gives alms without faith should be called devout or impious. IV, 262. Whatever is not from faith is sin. X, 754. This was said not of the goods of soul and body, which are gifts of God even in sinners, but of their actions: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.” X, 752. Faith is in the soul like a good root that turns rain into fruit. IV, 1803. Faith obtains the grace of doing good, or charity. II, 819. It obtains help so that the Law may be fulfilled. V, 851. It obtains justification. II, 820. Justification and salvation are obtained through faith. X, 232, 233. Faith preserves the grace of justification. II, 878. Woe to the faithful person unless the Lord protects his faith. IV, 1614. What faith obtains does not cease to be a freely given gift. II, 878, 879. On the way of faith, those to whom sins are not imputed are regarded as not sinning. IV, 1508. Before faith, only evils are owed in return for evils. IV, 1516.

Faith is the beginning of merit. II, 878. How. III, 2061, *Retr.* How mercy is attributed to a preceding merit of faith. III, 2061, *Retr.* Faith begins merit, but the merit of faith itself is also a gift of God. X, 965. And from his mercy. X, 965. It is not repaid on account of any merits of ours. X, 377. Faith is from God. III, 83. It is God’s work. III, 1602. The gift of God. I, 622; IV, 1116; V, 254, 730, 911, 913, 915, 1362; VI, 111, 115, 116, 247; X, 552, 553, 897, 975, 976, 989, 1605. Faith does not arise from preceding merits but is God’s gratuitous gift. II, 878, 879, 880, 969. An altogether gratuitous gift. X, 399, 616, 673. A gift denied to the proud. V, 436. Faith is from grace. X, 972. God produces our faith in our hearts. X, 963. Faith arises in a person, and without it no one performs good works. II, 878. Although faith obtains the grace of acting, faith itself is a gift of grace. X, 341. It does not precede God’s mercy. II, 879. That we believe in God and live devoutly depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who has mercy. II, 982. God must be prayed for on behalf of those who do not wish to believe, so that they may wish to believe. II, 984, 987, 988, 989. Saint Cyprian admonished us to pray for our enemies who have not yet believed in Christ, so that they may believe. II, 972, 980. We would pray in vain for unbelievers to believe unless the Church believed that, through God’s grace, even the evil and unbelieving wills of human beings can be converted to good. II, 972. Thanks must be given to God for those who have believed after being unbelievers. II, 989. Faith is not reached through merits of works. X, 341. From what source each person becomes worthy of faith. X, 975. The passage by which the Massilians attempt to prove that faith is not God’s gift, and its explanation. II, 375, note (a). The righteousness of faith comes from the Holy Spirit after Christ’s departure. V, 786. Faith is strengthened through baptism. III, 264.

Certain beginnings of faith are like conceptions. VI, 111. Faith is aroused through obedience, with God’s mercy preceding and calling. IV, 991. No one is sufficient for himself either to begin or to perfect faith. X, 963. The beginning of faith is God’s gift. II, 979, 988; X, 961, 962, 989, 990, 1024, 1026, 1027. It is pride to attribute the beginning of faith to a human being. X, 963. Vitalis used to say that the beginning of faith was from ourselves, while the remaining goods of the religious life were from God’s grace. II, 989. He used to say that it was up to us to believe in God and consent to the Gospel. II, 978. Yet, insofar as it lies within him, God brings about our willingness to believe, namely by making his sayings known to us. II, 978. If consenting to the Gospel does not come from God’s gift but from the will, the Church prays in vain that those to whom the Gospel is preached should believe, and so forth. II, 978, 980. [Col. 0296] In the beginning of faith there is also the beginning of a good—that is, a devout—will. II, 989. Not only the beginning of faith but also its growth is God’s gift. X, 992, 995. Grace is not given freely if the beginning of faith is from a human being but its increase is from God. X, 963. A human being could claim the entire work of salvation for himself if he were sufficient to begin or perfect faith. X, 963. Whatever precedes faith, accompanies faith, or follows faith must be attributed to God. X, 970. Between the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance lie those things by which we live rightly; even the Pelagians agree that these too are given to us by God, with faith obtaining them. X, 1028, 1033.

Perfect faith and faith in its beginning are gifts of God. X, 966. Perseverance in faith is a gift of God. X, 940. That faith and perseverance are gifts of God is attested by the whole Church in its prayers. X, 1031, 1032, 1033. The Church’s prayers are for the faithful, that they may persevere, and for unbelievers, that they may believe. X, 1606. Both faith and the salvation promised to faith are gifts of God. X, 976. Faith is from God’s gift. III, 1631. Against this Augustine initially held a different view. III, 2061, *Retr.* When Augustine came to recognize that the beginning of faith is God’s gift. X, 1026.

How faith is within one’s power. X, 235. Those who believe in the Lord with their own heart do so by their own will and free choice. II, 984, 987. Those who wished to believe did believe. V, 787. And unbelievers themselves, if they wished to believe, would be prevented by no one. V, 787. Our faith is in free choice in such a way that it needs divine assistance. III, 1778. Both willing and believing are ours, and at the same time they are God’s gift. X, 965. Why the faith of Christ is called our faith. X, 209. It is safer to entrust one’s faith, hope, and charity to God’s will than to one’s own. X, 976.

**Faith is not possessed by all.** IV, 1118, 1803. Why the gift of faith is not given to all. X, 972. Why one believes and another does not, when both hear the same thing: this is the depth of God’s judgments. II, 878. To what extent those who were going to believe in Christ were foreknown by Christ. X, 974. The impossibility of faith and conversion: what it is and whence it comes. III, 1778, 1779. One must submit to having faith preached by a human being, although faith can be given to a human being without a human intermediary. X, 920. To very few it has been granted to receive faith without any human preaching, or even through angels. X, 1023. No one receives faith from a minister of the word or sacrament, whether he is faithless or faithful. IX, 501. Fathers of faith. V, 1104.

**Faith is a great possession.** V, 248. Faith is demanded from us, salvation is offered; what is promised is precious, while what is commanded is done freely. V, 1112. Faith is to be preferred to gold. V, 218. Gold shines for many, but not faith. IV, 366. Faith, even in despised matters, is a great good of the soul and must be preferred to bodily salvation. VI, 376. Faith is gold, carnal desire is hay. IV, 1242. Carnal faith. V, 34. Faith is a costly thing; you have sold it for something cheap. IV, 262. You hoped for earthly happiness on account of good works: you are impious. IV, 262. You hoped for eternal life on account of works, but not from the one from whom it ought to be hoped for: you are impious. IV, 262.

**Faith is the safer path to religion and must be held by all.** VIII, 82, 86, 91. Faith is the word that fulfills and abbreviates what the Lord accomplished upon the earth. VI, 124. Through faith the way to God is open. IV, 1751. Let faith be with you, and God is with you. IV, 1169. What faith contributes to the knowledge and love of God. VIII, 960. Moral uprightness pertains to loving God and neighbor; the truth of faith pertains to knowing God and neighbor. III, 71.

**Who is a son of faith?** X, 214. By faith we have received the power to become children of God. IV, 1614.

Faith draws us to Christ. II, 878. Through faith one truly approaches Jesus. III, 1101. Faith in Christ. V, 773. Faith concerning Christ: Christ is in the heart. III, 1755. Through faith and hope our soul is in Christ. IV, 1843. One must not doubt that a devout and faithful person is with Christ through faith. III, 1927. As long as Christ dwells in a person through faith, that person is the temple of God according to faith, not according to appearance. IV, 1632. The pagan renounces the world; then he is sacrificed: he believes in God; then he is eaten. IV, 1642.

Faith alone in Christ cleanses. IV, 1137. If faith in Christ is present, no sins will remain. V, 788. Christ benefits nothing those who do not believe. V, 1345. The veil that is in the Old Testament will be removed when each person passes from it to Christ. II, 549. Jesus in the boat, faith in the heart. IV, 324, 1169. When our faith is awake, Christ is awake in us. V, 424. When faith is asleep in the heart, as Jesus sleeps in the little boat, we are endangered, driven about by the waves of temptations. IV, 190, 1169, 1611. Faith in the heart, like Christ asleep in the boat, must be awakened. V, 240, 1602. You are tossed by a storm of doubt: awaken Christ, awaken your faith. IV, 1915. Forgetfulness of faith is Christ’s sleep in the heart. III, 1755. Faith present, watchful, forgotten. V, 504.

Faith is the purpose of the incarnation. VIII, 914. Faith is the saving medicine of the faithful in the holy Church. VIII, 822. The medicines of faith were prepared by the hands of God. I, 722. The Lord came with this medicine in order to command the peoples to have faith. II, 448. Before you know why something was said, believe that it had to be said in the way it was said. IV, 1915. Christ thirsted on the cross for the faith of those for whom he prayed. IV, 851.

Faith is life. III, 1577, 1727, 1753, 1815. Right faith is the right way. IV, 262. Right faith is the beginning of a good life. V, 254. A right life must be joined to right faith. V, 993, 994. As we are distinguished by faith, so let us be distinguished in conduct; so let us be distinguished in works. V, 1117.

Faith is the foundation of the spiritual building. X, 970. What it means to have faith in the foundation. VI, 215. What it means to build wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation of faith. VI, 151.

Faith precedes prayer. II, 878. Faith is the source of prayer. V, 655. No one prays except by faith. V, 913. If faith fails, prayer perishes. V, 655. Let faith pour out the prayer, and poured-out prayer obtains firmness for faith. V, 655. To the extent that faith advances, temptation diminishes, and conversely. V, 655. Faith obtains from God what the Law commands. IV, 1545; VI, 287. It obtains grace for fulfilling the commandments. IV, 1549. Through faith those things were fulfilled that could not be fulfilled through the Law. III, 2066. By faith the judgments of God’s justice are preserved. IV, 1567. Intention makes a good work; faith directs intention. IV, 259.

**Full faith.** V, 912, 1196; V, 1345. Most Catholic faith. X, 237. True faith, or Christian faith, by which the righteous person lives. X, 237. What it means to live by faith. X, 182. It is a command that the righteous person live by faith, and eternal inheritance is promised to this faith. IV, 1393. No one lives by faith unless he does not see what he has believed. IV, 1452. How one must both believe what is to be understood and understand what is to be believed. V, 257. Understand, so that you may believe, my word; believe, so that you may understand, the word of God. V, 258. God has given us sight, by which we can believe what we do not see. V, 700, 727. One who understands by true reasoning what he had previously only believed is to be preferred to one who desires to understand what he believes; but if he does not even desire this, he does not know what use faith serves. II, 456. There are things that we do not believe unless we understand them, and other things that we do not understand unless we believe them. IV, 1552. With God’s help and gift, understanding advances toward understanding what it believes, and faith toward believing what it understands. IV, 1552. Faith is believing what you do not yet see; the reward of faith is seeing what you believe. V, 254. Faith in some way begins knowledge. VIII, 961. Faith is a step toward understanding. I, 1224, 1243; III, 129. Faith is the most wholesome and necessary step toward acquiring knowledge. IV, 111. Faith must precede understanding. VI, 299. True reason leads to understanding; faith prepares the mind. II, 454. Faith leads to knowledge of the truth. II, 447. Through faith one arrives at certain knowledge. VIII, 183. And at understanding. III, 1741. Understanding follows faith. II, 447. The reward of knowledge is granted on account of faith. VI, 71. Faith ought to precede understanding, so that understanding may be faith’s reward. V, 257, 672, 698, 770. The fruit of faith is understanding. III, 1574. Faith has stronger eyes with which to behold the end of the impious who prosper here. IV, 1897.

The reward of faith is certain, and so is the punishment of unbelief. V, 1119. The reward of faith is the salvation of souls. III, 1850. Contemplation. VIII, 832, 833, 835. The Christian mind must first be nourished by simple faith, so that it may become capable of understanding heavenly and eternal things. VIII, 279. Faith makes people capable of receiving divine things. VIII, 822. By faith the mind is purified so that it may be attuned to eternal things. VIII, 904. By faith hearts are cleansed so that the inner eyes may be opened and brightened. IV, 447, 1552, 1640. Through faith in temporal things a person reaches eternal truth. III, 1070. No one becomes fit to find God unless he has first believed what he will afterward come to know. I, 1243. Faith exists when, in hope, one awaits what is not yet seen in reality. VII, 379. Future things are believed in such a way that they are also hoped for as things to be seen. II, 456. Faith, regeneration, hope, and love are, in this life, consolations for the wretched, not the joys of the blessed. IV, 1555. Faith desires to see what it believes. VI, 661. By believing we strive toward seeing. III, 1923. Faith must labor so that at last it may see. VI, 662. Faith is believing what you do not yet see; the reward of faith is seeing what you believe. V, 254. What would the reward of faith be unless what we believe were hidden? The reward of faith, then, is seeing what we believed before we saw it. IV, 1451. Faith leads to vision. V, 103, 571. Through faith one must arrive at vision. IV, 510. The reward of faith is the vision of God. III, 1691. The reward of faith is to be defined as the vision of the things that were believed and hoped for. III, 1927. The time of faith and the time of sight. V, 236. Through faith we walk toward sight. V, 1523. Faith belongs to the present life; sight to the future. III, 1830. A mind imbued with faith tends, by living well, to reach sight. VI, 233. We are nourished by faith, while sight is what will nourish us. V, 708. He will make happy in the homeland the one whom faith does not console on the journey. V, 541. When will our faith become reality? VIII, 904. In the temporal retention, contemplation, and love of faith there is a certain trinity, but not yet properly the image of God. VIII, 1038.

Faith admits us to the commonwealth of God. II, 533. The way of faith leads to possession of blessedness. VIII, 63, 64. Faith prepares the saints for the kingdom of God. III, 1815, 1816. Why faith is necessary for attaining blessedness. VII, 627. Faith and piety are preparations for entering the wedding feast with the bridegroom. II, 574. By faith the mind is purified so that it may be able to see God. V, 36, 368, 541; VIII, 951. God is the reward and prize of faith. V, 136. In some people the grace of faith is such as is not sufficient for obtaining the kingdom of heaven. VI, 112. The Catholic faith is secure under God’s governance. VI, 293.

Whatever is contrary to the Catholic faith must, without any doubt, be believed to be utterly false. III, 262. The Catholic faith is opposed to the errors of the Manichaeans and Pelagians. X, 1607. What the Catholic faith maintains. III, 221. Augustine declares his faith at greater length. II, 1042. More briefly. II, 1050. The rule of faith: the creed. V, 999, 1614. The profession of faith, formulated in definite words, customarily handed down to the Competentes to be memorized. I, 612. And recited in the presence of the Church. I, 751. The profession of Christian faith. VI, 190.

Faith must be confessed freely. V, 1278. Constancy in the Christian faith. VII, 646. Temporal death is left for the exercise of faith. II, 683. Eusebius says that the Elcesaites taught that faith was to be denied during persecution. VIII, 27. Whether faith is ever to be desired. VI, 376. Faith must be held in the heart and on the lips. IV, 444. Those who believe in their heart but deny or conceal it with their lips are reproved. IV, 444, 445. So that faith may not fail during persecution, the Lord gives life. IV, 446. To prevent faith from being lost, everything must be lost. IV, 618. Christian faith can be denied in two ways. IV, 761. Many have lost faith through love of visible things. IV, 1643. Those who lost faith buried their birthright in their heart. IV, 1750. There is one faith even outside the Church, but without love. IX, 463, 464. The faith of heretics ought not even to be called faith. VI, 368. Faith is the virginity and chastity of the heart. III, 1453, 1454. A Catholic woman married twice is preferred to a professed heretical virgin. X, 599.

Faith and love are proved more fully through heresies. II, 793. God’s mercy does not abandon those who live by faith in him and worship him devoutly. II, 525. One who knows how to defend the faith is more learned, not more faithful. V, 1131. This is necessary for those who waver, not for those who believe. V, 1131. How we know the faith that is in us. VIII, 1014. How the mysteries of faith are to be handed down to the people. III, 1333. Questions beyond the faith: what they are and examples of them. X, 397, 398. In questions beyond the faith, a person may be said to err without nevertheless being judged a heretic. X, 397, 398. The rule to be observed in more difficult questions of faith. VIII, 947. The Christian authorities of the earthly commonwealth ought not to give the opponents of the faith a place and time for examination. X, 1054. No one is to be compelled unwillingly to faith; but perfidy is customarily punished by severity, indeed even by God’s mercy. IX, 315.

A eulogy of the Catholic faith. V, 1690. Faith is preferred to the Law. X, 898. The faith of those under the Law differs from the faith of children. X, 236. Faith is indeed on the earth, but it is scarcely found complete. V, 655. The integrity of faith is a matter of no small importance. IX, 146. There is no defect in faith. VIII, 80. Christ’s saying in Luke 18 is to be understood of faith. V, 655. The faith of the nations is Christ’s glorification. III, 1766. The faith of the nations foretold in Scripture. VII, 357, 359.

Faith is an eye-salve. III, 1655. Faith is signified by a fish. III, 1342. Why devout faith is a good fish. V, 620. Faith is great, like a grain of mustard seed. V, 488. Hyssop is a symbol of faith. III, 734. Faith in what the Lord temporally did and endured for us is the tabernacle of protection against the contradiction of tongues. IV, 229. Faith is both a tunic and a breastplate. V, 399. Those who are steadfast in faith are the immovable world; those who waver in faith are the movable world. IV, 1185. One faith is ordinary, another is higher, from which believers are so called. V, 145.

It is not right to deny a matter merely because it happened only once. II, 590.

The baptized little ones are called faithful on account of the sacrament of faith. II, 984. The faith of those by whom a little child is brought to be consecrated benefits the child. I, 1304. Who the faithful are. X, 1180. People become faithful only by free choice, and yet they become faithful by the grace of the one who freed their will from the power of darkness. II, 981. How this is so. II, 982. In the faithful four things are to be considered: predestination, calling, justification, and glorification. III, 1614. The faithful are called children of light, children of peace, children of the Church, and members of Christ. IV, 1867. Those approaching the Lord’s table are called faithful. V, 145, 649. False believers. V, 1201. There are those who are called faithful but are not, and in them Christ’s sacraments suffer insult. V, 1092. Christ can never be absent from his faithful. IV, 1498. The love of unity and tolerance of faults are commended to the faithful. III, 879. The faithful rejoice in the rest of their brothers even amid their own anxieties. II, 593. The faithful are signified by Zion and Jerusalem. IV, 598. All the faithful, together with the angels, make one house of God and one city. IV, 1668, 1669. Compared with the life of unbelievers, the life of the faithful is day; compared with the life of the blessed, it can be called night. III, 312; V, 321. The multitude of the faithful, or their migration to various places because of persecutions, is represented by locusts. IV, 1443. The faithful are compared with shorn sheep. III, 38. The faithful are God’s tabernacle on earth. IV, 469. The faithful in the Church are like a kind of woven fabric. III, 879. Comparison with the faithful is a reproach to unbelievers. III, 1871. The faithful, holy and good, are few in comparison with the many wicked; yet in themselves they are numerous. II, 336, 338. The fewness of the faithful is called fewness like that of grains in comparison with chaff; in themselves, however, they are a multitude. VIII, 388.

A faithful human being is one who believes God when he promises; a faithful God is one who provides what he promised to a human being. IV, 283, 284. What is small is small; but to be faithful in a small matter is great. III, 105.

Faith is twofold: the faith by which we believe, and faith in promises. X, 235. One faith concerns human agreements, another is that by which the baptized are called faithful. II, 184. Faith is also necessary in human affairs. VI, 171. If faith were removed from human affairs, what terrible confusion would follow. VI, 173. Everyone loves faith. V, 144. Faith shines even more brightly in the eyes of the wicked than gold. V, 218. Faith is necessary for servants. III, 591. Faith is honored in a servant. V, 145. Faith owed to God must not be withheld, although it is demanded from a servant. V, 87, 145, 219. They praise faith and wish it to be shown to them even when they do not wish to show it to God. V, 87. What you rejoice to receive from an inferior, render to a superior. V, 219. Faith is both rendered and possessed; indeed, if it is not rendered, it is not possessed. V, 219. You love faith in order to demand it; love it in order to show it. IV, 365. Christ is the neighbor to whom faith must be kept. V, 251. Christ himself demanded faith above all. VIII, 88. Faith in returning a deposit. IV, 618, 674. Faith given in agreements and arrangements. VI, 376. Faith must be kept toward a friend in his poverty. V, 247. Faith must be kept not only toward a friend but also toward an enemy. II, 856. Armies hostile to one another observe the faith of an oath, even when it was extorted. II, 482. The faithfulness of the Romans is worthy of praise. X, 389. The faith of Regulus and of the Saguntines. VII, 101, 759.

A guarantor deceived by the person for whom he stood surety paid the lawful penalty on that person’s behalf. II, 661. Augustine wishes to discuss at a council whether those who flee to a place where they may break faith with their guarantors should not be expelled from the Church. II, 1066. For it seemed unworthy that they should find, in the very house of faith, assistance for violating faith. II, 1066, 1067. It is permissible to make use of the pledged fidelity of one who, in order to keep it, has sworn by demons. II, 184.

Confidence in oneself or in a human being is a deceptive horse for salvation. IV, 276. His mercy, not our merit, gives us confidence in God. IV, 1120.

Fidus the bishop. X, 652, 663.

To become or be made. II, 288.

Those who fix or fasten. II, 694.

Every proud person is fictitious; every fictitious person is a liar. IV, 1811. Every profession has hypocrites. IV, 357.

The Figulinian estate. II, 397.

God is a potter when he makes us fragile, weak, and earthly. IV, 1211.

A figure is said to exist when some space is enclosed by a line or lines. I, 1041. At length on mathematical figures. I, 1042. The figure ἑτέρωσις, by which one number is taken for another number. VI, 253.

The figure antiphrasis, when words are spoken by way of contraries. V, 634. The figures of Scripture adhere to events that truly occurred. V, 30, 557, 558. Our figures are the things that happened to the Israelites. V, 37, 38, 1551. The figures of the Old Testament seek an inquirer, not a critic. V, 62. Just as in good things there is much more good in what is signified through the figure than in the figure itself, so the reverse is true in evil things. IV, 985. The ancient figures were annulled through Christ. V, 474. The figure of the Body and Blood of Christ. IV, 73.

The daughter of Babylon is Babylon itself, and the daughter of Zion is Zion itself. IV, 1773. The unhappy daughter of Babylon, and why. IV, 1773. The daughters of Judah—not Jews, but daughters of confession. IV, 540. The daughters of Tyre are the daughters of the nations. IV, 511. The daughters of kings are souls raised up to Christ through the apostles. IV, 508. They are both daughters of the apostles and of Christ. IV, 508. The daughters of kings are also cities founded by kings that believed in Christ. IV, 509. Evil daughters, that is, evil people in the Church, among whom the good are like a lily among thorns, or grains among chaff. IV, 538. Those who do not live as Christians after baptism are also called daughters because of the form of piety; and not daughters, or outsiders, because they have lost virtue. IV, 539. The Voconia law forbade making an only daughter an heir. VII, 103.

Those who say that the Son of God is the very one who is the Father are excluded by the Catholic faith. VI, 184. So also those who say that he is a creature. VI, 184. Arius said that the Son of God began in time; the later Arians, however, did not hold this view. VIII, 923. At Ariminum the Arians pronounced anathema on those who said that the Son of God was made from nothing. VIII, 730. The Arians taught that the Son of God was begotten perfect, not progressing toward perfection; but that his perfection was less than the Father’s. VIII, 780, 787, 803. According to the Arians, the Son of God is degenerate. VIII, 748, 761. Some said that the Son of God was a plan or will. VIII, 1087. Against what they say: certainly the Father willed and the Son accomplished, as is shown by the fact that the Son wills and the Father does. V, 748. The Arians profess that the Son of God is a son not by nature but by grace. VIII, 802. Eunomius said that the Son of God is a son not of nature but of will. VIII, 1087. How the Arians deny that the Son is coeternal with the Father, and how this is proved by Catholics. V, 664. A certain heresy confesses that the Son is coeternal with the Father, but not that he has always been the Son. VIII, 45. The Arians wanted the Son of God to have been anointed by God before the incarnation. VIII, 734. They also said that, by his very nature and substance, he was visible and corruptible. II, 1047; III, 1403. How, according to the Arians, the Son of God sees the Father. VIII, 728. Their position is refuted. VIII, 745, 746. The Arians acknowledged the Son of God as God, Lord, King, and so forth. VIII, 732. For this reason they thought him less than the Father, because he fulfilled the Father’s commands. VIII, 804. They even maintained that he worshiped the Father according to the form of God. VIII, 728. By refusing to equal the Son with the Father, lest they do injury to the Father, they do injury to both. V, 772. Whoever makes the Son of God lesser insults God the Father. VI, 667. Those who denied the Son’s equality with the Father were expelled from the Church. III, 1666, 1668. Some say that the one who is the son of man became the Son of God, whereas the one who is the Son of God was not made the son of man. V, 999.

The eternal generation of the Son of God is to be understood in the words, “Today I have begotten you.” IV, 71. The Son is “from the womb” because he is from the substance of the Father. V, 747. The Son was begotten without passion. II, 751. Far from Solomon having said that God has no son, as Porphyry wishes, he said that God has a son. II, 382. The Father always begets, and the Son is always born; but one must beware lest the generation be thought incomplete if we say not “born” but “being born.” II, 1047. The likenesses of the Son’s birth in creatures are imperfect. V, 666, 668. The Son’s generation, coeternal with the Father, is illustrated by the likeness of radiance generated from flame. II, 749.

The Son of God is not so by grace or adoption. II, 541, 542. The Son of God is God. VI, 628, 640. This is proved. III, 1749. The Son of God is the one true God with the Father. VI, 629; VIII, 683. No one besides Christ would dare say that he is one with the Father. V, 774. Prophecy concerning Christ the Shepherd, teaching that he is one with God. V, 308. The Son of God is called God in relation to himself, and Son in relation to the Father. IV, 845.

The Son of God is not of a nature different from the Father’s nature, because he is born. VIII, 719. The names “Son” and “Father” do not in themselves indicate natures, but the persons of one in relation to the other. II, 750. It is wrong for the Arians to say that the Father and the Son have different natures because one is father and the other son. II, 750. Or because one is from no one and the other from another. II, 750. The Son of God is of the same substance as the Father. VIII, 825. The Son is in no way truly God’s son if he was not born from the Father’s substance. VIII, 771, 773, 778, 786. The Son of God is of the same nature as the Father. VIII, 685, 686, 748. Of the same substance as the Father, equal to him and coeternal with him. V, 708, 747, 770, 771, 774, 1019, 1150, 1213, 1497. The Son of God is another than the Father, not another thing. X, 500. The Son according to substance—that is, what the Father is—not according to his relation to another. IV, 845. **Note 1:** Or, according to what he is in relation to another. IV, 845.

The Son ascribes to the Father, not to himself, everything that he has and can do, because he is from the Father and not from himself. II, 751. The Son of God frequently says, “The Father gave me,” so that it may be understood that the Father begot him. VIII, 839, 847. Whatever God the Father gave to God the Son, he gave by begetting him. III, 1912; VIII, 1081. The Son of God lacks nothing that the Father has. VI, 630. The Son of God is called Son because the Father is what he is, and because he has his being from the one from whom he comes. V, 668. The Son of God received life from the Father, but not as though he had ever been without life. VIII, 716. Because the Son of God is from the Father, and not the Father from him, he receives life and commandment from the Father and is taught by him. VIII, 706.

The Son is coeternal with the Father. II, 751; V, 990; VI, 15, 631; VIII, 683, 773. The Son of God, insofar as he is the only-begotten, cannot be said to have been or to be going to be, but only to be. VI, 185. The Son of God is equal to the Father. II, 751; V, 990; VI, 32, 74, 191, 630, 641, 683; VIII, 702, 706, 716, 719, 723, 747, 773, 774, 775, 776, 778, 779. The Son’s coeternity and equality with the Father are proved against the Arians. V, 770. He is born as Son and equal to the one who begets him. II, 1054. The Son, born equal, is always equal just as he is always born. II, 751. In everything said of his substance, the Son of God is equal to the Father. VIII, 927. Either God did not wish to have an equal Son, or he could not; if he did not wish to, he is envious; if he could not, he is weak. II, 1048.

The Son is most like the Father. III, 1819. He cannot be unlike the Father in any respect. VI, 17. Because the Son of God is the perfect image of the Father, he is equal to him. VIII, 931. The only-begotten is solely the image of God, not made according to an image. I, 626. The Son is the Father’s full, perfect, supreme image. VIII, 701. He is the likeness and image of the Father, the form of all things, supremely filling the one from whom he is. III, 159. The Son of God is equal to the Father, even though the Father gave and the Son received. VIII, 774, 800. Even though he obeyed the Father. VIII, 688, 691, 776, 781, 786. The Son’s obedience does not indicate inequality. VIII, 688, 691. The Son of God is not for that reason unequal to the Father because he was glorified by the Father. VIII, 848. Nor because he was sent by the Father. VIII, 685, 905, 906. Responses to testimonies by which the Son of God appears to be asserted to be unequal. VIII, 773, 774, 798. If the Son of God is not equal to the Father, there are two gods, and the Father was envious. VIII, 777, 780. The Father is not for that reason more powerful than the Son because he begot the creator, whereas the Son did not beget. VIII, 768.

The Son of God is almighty. VI, 629, 640. According to his divine nature, the Son of God is God, almighty, invisible, immortal, and wise, just as the Father is. VIII, 720, 724, 725, 745, 746, 762. The Son possesses the power, immortality, and so forth that the Father possesses. IV, 502. The Son’s will is the same as the Father’s. VIII, 686. The will of the Father and the Son is one according to the equality of the form of God. V, 860. The works of the Father and the Son are the same. V, 703, 746, 748. Carnal understanding proposes the Son and the Father to itself as though they were two craftsmen. V, 702. The Son likewise does the same things that the Father does. III, 1535–1564, throughout the treatise. The Son of God was not made in the form of God, to such an extent that all things were made through him. VIII, 723. The Son of God did not fail to beget because he could not, but because it was not fitting. VIII, 768. Whatever the Son does, he does not do without the Father, and conversely. III, 1560. Whether, because the Father does nothing without the Son and the Son nothing without the Father, it follows that the Father should be said to have been born, suffered, and so forth. V, 356. The works of the Son and the Father are the same because the Father does what he does through the Son. V, 702, 704. Because the things belonging to the Father belong to the Son. V, 746. The Son does not act without the Father in doing what he promised to do. III, 1826. Whether the Father acted by commanding and the Son by obeying. V, 747. Even if this were granted, it would not follow that the Son is less than the Father. V, 747. The Son of God created all things at the Father’s command. III, 241. Let us not doubt that all things are ruled through the one through whom all things were made. V, 356. Where it is said, “The Son can do nothing of himself,” and so forth, it is as though one were saying, “He would not be the Son unless he were born from the Father.” V, 705. How the Son does what he sees the Father doing. V, 701.

The Son of God is immeasurable, just as the Father is. VIII, 813.

For the Son of God, being is the same as knowing. III, 1689. The Son knows the last day in the Father. V, 589. For the Son of God, being Son is the same as seeing the Father. III, 1566, 1567. The Son’s knowledge and the Son’s vision are the same as the Son himself. III, 1567. In the nature of the Son of God, being, hearing, and seeing are the same. VIII, 693, 696.

The Son is invisible just as God the Father is; when he wished, he appeared—not as he is, but as he wished. V, 64. Even when sent, the Son of God, being equal to the Father, was not seen. VIII, 905. Some hold that the Son of God spoke either to the prophets or in the prophets. VIII, 849. Whether the Son of God is invisible because he cannot be seen with human eyes. VIII, 729. The Arians’ uncertain position concerning the visibility of the Son of God before the incarnation. VIII, 803. The occasions on which they think the Son of God was seen by a human being are refuted. VIII, 804, 805, 806.

The Son of God is the incomparable splendor of incomprehensible light. VIII, 610. This is shown from Scripture. VIII, 611. The only-begotten Son of God is God’s peace; he himself is God’s splendor. II, 617. Day from day. V, 891. The Son of God is light. VIII, 611. True light. I, 740. How the true light illuminates every human being. X, 130, 131. The Son of God is rightly called God from God, light from light, life from life; but not Word from Word, and why. VIII, 696.

The Son of God is called Word, Beginning, Wisdom, Truth, and Power of God. I, 813. Why he is called the Word. VI, 183. How he is the Power and Wisdom of the Father. VIII, 936. Why Scripture indicates him especially under the name of Wisdom, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom. VIII, 936, 937. The Son of God is the Beginning. III, 222. He is the Beginning not for the Father but for all creation. III, 251. From the one from whom the Son of God has his being as God, he also has that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. VIII, 1095. What the Father’s love for the Son is like. III, 1509. See **Word**. The Son of God and the Father love one another equally. VIII, 802.

There can be only one Son of God, and why. VIII, 202. The Son of God is both only-begotten and firstborn. VIII, 202. How he is the firstborn of all creation. VIII, 706. When the Lord uses “Son” without qualification, he wishes the only-begotten Son to be understood. IV, 116. The Son of God is not from the Father in the manner of all creation. II, 749. The only Son is like the Father by being born; we are like him by seeing. IV, 565.

The mission of the Son of God is wholly ineffable. VIII, 686. How it is to be understood. VIII, 849, 850. The Son of God is not said to be sent simply because he was born from the Father. VIII, 907. Whether the Son of God is to be said to have been commanded or sent by the Father. VIII, 708. How he was sent and foretold. VIII, 905, 906. He was sent by the Father, by the Holy Spirit, and by himself. VIII, 790, 848, 850. The mission of the Son of God is his appearance in the flesh. VIII, 905. The Son was sent in such a way that he did not depart from the Father. III, 1689. The Son of God is sent in one way so that he may be with a human being, and in another so that he may be a human being. VIII, 907. He is sent to each person when he is recognized by anyone. VIII, 907. But the Father is not sent. VIII, 908. For the Son of God, just as being born means being from the Father, so being sent means being recognized as being from him. VIII, 908.

Although the Son was sent by the Father, he is nevertheless not less than the Father. III, 1573. The Son of God is not less than the Father. VIII, 721. In himself he is not less through the incarnation. V, 1214. In the form of a servant he is less not only than the Father but also than himself and the Holy Spirit. VIII, 828, 836. There is a twofold rule for understanding the scriptural statements about the Son of God. VIII, 845. Ambiguous statements concerning the Son of God can safely be understood according to either rule. VIII, 847. Many scriptural statements indicate not that the Son is less than the Father, but that he is from the Father. VIII, 847. Whatever is brought forward from Scripture that appears to show the Son of God as less than the Father must either be understood of the form of a servant, or taken as said so that one may be demonstrated from the other. VIII, 775. The Father is not called the God of the Son before the incarnation except in prophecy. VIII, 782. The Son of God truly said that the Father was his God, also on account of the form of a servant; he did not falsely assume this humility. VIII, 781. The Son of God is less than the Father, indeed less than the angels, because of weakness. VIII, 687. As a human being, the Son fulfills the Father’s command; as God, he himself is the Father’s Commandment. VIII, 706, 802.

The Son of God was not made and is not less than the Father. VI, 184. The Son of God was not made. II, 1053. The Son of God was made only in the form of a servant. VIII, 756. How the Son of God, equal to the Father, emptied himself. IV, 699. The Son of God is truly said to have been born and to have suffered without any change in his divinity. VI, 303. The Son of God was not changed in assuming humanity. VIII, 812. In taking flesh the Son was not changed, just as one who puts on a garment is not changed into a garment. V, 1214. The Son of God always remained unchanged. III, 1566, 1567. While remaining in his own nature, the Son of God became a participant in our nature, so that we, while remaining in our nature, might become participants in his nature. II, 542. Participation in our nature did not make the Son of God worse; participation in his nature makes us better. II, 542.

Why the Son of God became outwardly manifest and deigned to appear in humility. VIII, 202. The Son of God was incarnate so that human beings would fear being exalted through human pride more than being humbled by God’s example. II, 1029. The human birth of the Son of God is both humble and exalted. VI, 630. The Son of God became for us a temporal way through humility, which through divinity is our eternal dwelling. VIII, 938. The Son of God is an example for us without having an example himself. VIII, 938. In the form of God he is an example to the angels who did not fall, and in the form of a servant to human beings so that they may rise again. VIII, 938. The Son’s obedience is the first cause of human salvation. VIII, 687, 688. Birth from a virgin belongs to the Son alone, but it was effected by the Father and the Son, just as were his passion and resurrection. V, 357, 1063. The Son of God assumed the whole of human nature, but free from every bond of sin. VI, 249. The Son of man could not be contaminated in the Virgin’s womb. VIII, 598.

According to the form of divinity, the Son of God is everywhere; according to the flesh he assumed, he is in heaven. IV, 969. He sits at God’s right hand and intercedes. VIII, 723, 760. In what form the Son of God will judge, and from whom he received the power to exercise judgment. VIII, 840, 842. The righteous and the impious will see the Son of God according to the form of a human being. VIII, 841, 842, 844. According to the form of God, only the righteous will see him. VIII, 844. The vision of the Son of God according to the form of God will not be the supreme good of the righteous. VIII, 844. The Son of God is subject to the Father only according to his humanity. VIII, 750, 829. How will he be subject to the one who subjected all things to him? VI, 75. After the kingdom has been handed over to God and the Father, the Son of God will no longer intercede for us. VIII, 835.

The Son of God is called the arm of God. IV, 484. He is the hand and arm of the Father. III, 1744, 1775. He is food for angels insofar as he is the Word of God with God; but in order to be food for human beings, the Word became flesh. III, 879. The Son of God is teacher, defender, intercessor, and giver. III, 1564. The Son of God is the hand of God. V, 1377. The Son of God is regularly called king in Scripture. IV, 84. Peter said it, and the demons also said it: “You are the Son of God”—an equal confession, but not an equal love. IV, 566.

Many are sons of God by grace, one by nature. V, 770. God the Father did not wish the Son whom he uniquely begot to be one alone. IV, 811. The Son of God willed us to be his brothers. V, 387. The Son of God has no brothers insofar as he is the only-begotten, but does have them insofar as he is the firstborn. VI, 185. See Christ. Why the Son of God became human. VI, 184. The Son of God became the son of man so that the sons of men might become sons of God. V, 680. The Son alone with respect to divinity, not alone with respect to inheritance. V, 702. He alone was begotten from the substance of the Father; the others were adopted into his family through him. V, 702. It is not impossible for people to become sons of God, for whose sake the Son of God became the son of man. V, 675. Power was given so that we might become sons of God. V, 1504. This power is from God. X, 285. It does not come from free choice, but from the gift of love. X, 1001, 1292. For the sons of men to become sons of God [Col. 0303] is less than for the Son of God to become the son of man. V, 675, 1504. Some are sons of God according to grace received in time, others according to God’s eternal foreknowledge. X, 928. Those who have not yet been regenerated are called sons of God according to predestination. II, 846. We are already sons of God through grace, faith, the sacrament, and the blood of Christ. V, 503, 691, 709, 774. Spiritual sons are begotten through the Gospel in Christ Jesus. IX, 66. The sons of God are human beings renewed according to his image. VIII, 136. And those who practice conduct appropriate to their newness. X, 157. Each person becomes a son of God insofar as he begins to exist in newness of spirit. X, 156. The teaching of Caelestius: people cannot be called sons of God unless they have been made wholly pure from every sin. X, 345. We are sons of God in hope, not in reality. IV, 565. Those for whom God is lovable are sons; those for whom he is terrifying are not sons. IV, 566. “Sons of promise” is equivalent to “sons of grace” and “sons of mercy.” II, 559. If we have become sons of God, then we have become gods. IV, 565. The sons of Christ and the wife of Christ: the Church herself. IV, 1684. The sons of the bridegroom: the Apostles. IV, 1684, 1845. Those sons must be peacemakers. IV, 1685. Who are the sons of God and the sons of the devil. See God; Devil.

The sons of Abraham, the sons of David, and the sons of the Patriarchs are those who imitate their faith and piety. IV, 933, 1725. The sons of Esau and the sons of Edom are all carnal; Jacob’s sons, however, are spiritual—less in age, greater in power. IV, 1772. We are sons of Abraham or of the devil, not by being born, but by imitating. V, 1552. The one who made the promise makes people sons of Abraham’s faith. V, 911. Who are the sons of men? IV, 125, 349, 350, 544, 616. See Human Being. Who are the sons of those who have been put to death? IV, 1019. Sons of those who have been cast out. IV, 1673. The son of a wicked man sometimes flourishes in this world, and sometimes, having become righteous, flourishes in Christ. IV, 399. A father often corrects his sons through the most wicked servants. IV, 1499. If sons are scourged, what should the most wicked servants expect? IV, 1210. The name “sons” is understood in various ways in Scripture. I, 619; VIII, 129, n. 3, 130. Sons of night and of darkness. IV, 757. God alone divides the sons of day from the sons of night. I, 851. The sons of the kingdom are those prepared for the kingdom of God. VI, 252. The sons of Gehenna are those prepared for it. VI, 252. Sons of wrath. IV, 398. Our sons are good works. IV, 1688, 1724. The fruit of these works is sons’ sons. IV, 1688. Alien sons are the citizens of Babylon. IV, 1783. The younger son in the Gospel. V, 1458.

The begetting of children is a benefit from God. VII, 440. It belongs to the glory of marriage, not to the punishment of sin. VII, 428. The begetting of children in paradise would not have occurred without the joining of the sexes. X, 555. The multiplication of children comes from the Lord’s blessing. IV, 1778. Having children is no longer happiness; having good children is. IV, 1686. For children to be born to their parents belongs to fertility; for them to live, to happiness; for them to be properly instructed, to will and ability. VI, 441. Against those who rejoice that children have been born to them, or grieve that they have not been born. IV, 1686. Not everything born from someone is called that person’s son. VI, 252. One is called the son of a grandfather, great-grandfather, or some still more remote ancestor if he is descended from him. III, 494. Legitimate sons and natural sons. X, 721. Adopted sons, natural sons, and marital sons. V, 348. Sons born of legitimate marriages are more under the authority of the father than of the mother. II, 1082. Children born not only from marriage but also from adultery are in some respect a good. X, 456. Even if children are generated through a wound inflicted by the devil, the devil nevertheless has no power over them. X, 757.

Little children sometimes undergo a common punishment through divine judgment on account of their parents’ sins. X, 1252. Certain sins of parents of whatever kind are visited upon their children. X, 1254. Scripture shows that children are punished on account of their parents’ sins. X, 1253, 1254, 1256, 1258, 1275. Why God judges parents and children differently, and why he entrusted human beings with judging differently. X, 1261, 1262, 1263, 1264. God’s judgment is not bound by the law that commands a human judge not to put a son to death for his father. X, 1252, 1253, 1254, 1255, 1256, 1257, 1258. It belongs to the grace of the New Testament that a son is not liable for his father’s debts. X, 873. Children are raised up before God by the virtues of their parents. X, 1272. How the blessedness of children is promised on account of the merit of their fathers. IV, 1724. Wicked children, living ruinously, persecute the piety of their parents. II, 310.

Who truly loves his children. VI, 702. A father does not give a sword to his weeping son. V, 498. Nor does he lift him onto a horse. V, 147, 498. One who destroys his sons’ pleasures offers to God a sacrifice like Abraham’s. VI, 702. If someone’s son dies, he mourns him; if he sins, he does not mourn him—and yet we are Christians. IV, 409. Everyone labors for his children; no one for himself. IV, 1659. Against the avaricious, who say that they are preserving their possessions for their children and refuse to give to the poor. IV, 422. You have children? Count one more, and give something to Christ. IV, 424. Christ must be counted among one’s children in the division of the patrimony. V, 529. What you wrongly preserve for your children will harm both you and your children. V, 529. One who divides the share of a deceased child among the surviving brothers teaches parricide. V, 529. Children’s piety toward their parents should not be for sale. V, 264. Children [Col. 0304] in a particular sense among the Jews. V, 350. The sons first mentioned in the genealogy of the first human beings are not firstborn. VII, 456, 457, 464.

**Fimbria.** A most depraved man, who followed the party of Marius against Sulla. VII, 83. He cruelly destroyed Ilium. VII, 83. He was slaughtered in his own house. VII, 107.

Touching the fringe. V, 1278.

**Fingere.** Sometimes means “to pretend,” sometimes “to form.” IV, 427. *Fingere* with a pretended lie means to compose or fabricate something. VII, 399. “To pretend” is not always the same as “to lie.” IV, 1210. In a certain manner, what is said figuratively is “fabricated.” V, 558. Christ’s figurative representation was symbolic, not deceitful. V, 558. See Fiction. One who fabricates what he says labors. IV, 1811.

**End.** What the end is. VIII, 653; X, 749. “End” is used in two ways: either that by which something ceases to be what it was, or that by which what had been begun is brought to perfection. IV, 230, 628. There are two kinds of end: completion and destruction. VI, 77. The end of destruction and the end of perfection. V, 366. An end is spoken of where nothing further to which something might extend or be referred can be found. II, 438. Everything that ends is small. II, 1310. What is “long” when it has an end? V, 688, 1385. There is no end to misery so long as the end of our duties is placed in an unstable thing. II, 435. As to when the end of the world will come, the view that conforms more closely to the Gospel is the one that confesses ignorance. II, 924. On the end of the world: *A Book to Hesychius*. II, 899.

Christ is our end—not one who destroys, but one who brings to completion. IV, 628, 662. The end of all completion is to have life without end and without sorrow, attained through the sorrows of this life. IV, 1561. When the psalm says “To the end,” hearts should be turned toward Christ. IV, 1804.

What difference there is between the end and the duty. VIII, 653. What the end of a good work ought to be. IV, 1533. What it is. VII, 227. The end to which every work is referred makes it either praiseworthy or blameworthy. I, 1356. What are the ends of our good and evil? VII, 621. The ends of our good and evil are placed either in the mind, or in the body, or simultaneously in both. VII, 621. Concerning the ends of good and evil, Varro counted two hundred and eighty schools. VII, 621. God is the end for whose sake everything that is rightly done is done. X, 788. When God’s gifts are not referred to their author, those who use them become unjust by that very fact. X, 746. When a person does something in which he does not appear to sin, yet does not do it for the reason for which he ought to do it, he is shown to be sinning. X, 749. Whatever good is done by a person, if it is not done for the reason for which true wisdom commands it to be done, is sinful through an improper end, even if it appears good as a duty. X, 749. Virtues are distinguished from vices by their ends, not by their duties. X, 749. Unbelievers sinned in this respect: they did not refer their works to the end to which they ought to have referred them. X, 751. Evil can never become good through a good end. VI, 528.

**Firmament.** It is named from distinction and appearance. III, 232. The firmament is the same as heaven. III, 232. Not every firmament is heaven. III, 233. The firmament is the same as the air. III, 266. What is the firmament of heaven? III, 238. The firmament is heaven; allegorically, a firm heart. IV, 159. The firmament signifies the Law. IV, 1194.

The Firmian war. IX, 316.

**Firminus.** A liberally educated man. I, 737. He relates a certain divination of the astrologers. I, 738.

The firmness of the soul is called a mouth. IV, 1796. Grace makes a person firm; yet however firm someone may have been, one must fear for him because he is a vessel of clay. IV, 878. Christian firmness consists not only in doing what is good, but also in enduring what is evil. V, 277.

No one will be firm before God except one who recognizes himself as weak in himself. V, 481.

**Firmus.** Bishop of Thagaste, when questioned, can be compelled by torture neither to lie nor to betray a human being who is being sought. VI, 504.

**Firmus the presbyter.** X, 411, n. 1. His faith and virtue. X, 411, n. 2. Firmus the presbyter brought two letters from Count Valerius to Augustine. II, 926. He was sent to Ravenna, and from there to Africa and Sicily, on business concerning Eustochium and Paula. II, 754. He sent a letter of Sixtus to Hippo. II, 867. Through him Augustine sent a longer letter to Sixtus. II, 874.

**Firmus**, to whom Augustine sends a letter. II, 1065.

**Firmus**, from whom the Rogatists are said to have called other Donatists “Firmians.” II, 301.

**Firmus**, barbarian king. IX, 46. A most savage enemy of the Romans. IX, 46.

Christ’s treasury. IV, 1911. A treasury is a public sack. IV, 1911.

**Flaccianus.** Proconsul. VII, 579.

**Flaccianus.** A very learned and distinguished man. I, 915. He consulted Albicerius the diviner. I, 915. He mocked that art of divination. I, 916.

The Lord’s scourge is upon all flesh. IV, 1748. The world is now deservedly scourged with severity. V, 469. Everyone is worthy of the scourge, because no one is without sin. VI, 700, 717, 720. As no one is without sin, so no one is without a scourge. IV, 1132. Your scourge is within you, from yourself. IV, 960. God made a scourge out of the sinner. IV, 362, 366. God justly scourges us, however much righteousness we may seem to preserve. II, 423, 425. Why the good are scourged along with the wicked. VI, 701. Why God sometimes strikes the more innocent and spares the more wicked. IV, 1180, 1945. God already punishes some wicked people, so that his providence may become known; he does not punish others, so that divine patience may be preserved. IV, 255. The scourge is punishment for the wicked, discipline for sons. IV, 274. He scourges every son whom he receives. No one is excepted: even the only-begotten, though without sin, was not without the scourge. IV, 274. If you are exempted from suffering the scourges, you will be exempted from the number of sons. V, 276.

God’s scourge is our admonition. V, 150. God’s scourge is both punishment and grace: what does he preserve after punishment, he who by grace administers punishment? IV, 427. When God scourges some people on earth, it is admonition, not yet condemnation. IV, 568. The scourge is medicine against sins. IV, 409. When God chastises the world, he does not wish to condemn the world. V, 935. His anger is great when he spares sinners. V, 935. God is angry when he does not punish. V, 1636. It is a great mercy not to leave wickedness unpunished. V, 935.

God scourges and loves. V, 54. Even when the Father strikes, he loves. V, 111. God greatly loves even those whom he corrects. IV, 229. He is both a Father who promises life and one who imposes discipline. VI, 719. It is better for God to scourge you and receive you than to spare you and abandon you. V, 377. Let the Father’s scourges be sweet to us, lest the Judge’s sentence become bitter. IV, 1793. Scourges are prepared by which eternal inheritance is prepared. IV, 409. Do not fear being scourged, but fear being disinherited. IV, 1131. One who flees from God who scourges him is not cast away by God; rather, he alienates himself from the inheritance. IV, 1132. Let us who are scourged not fear that we shall be rejected, but rather trust that we shall be received as justified. V, 860. Do not abandon the one who reproves and exhorts, terrifies and consoles, strikes and heals. V, 277.

People grieve over their own scourges, but do not grieve over why they are scourged. IV, 409. They grieve over loss of money, not loss of righteousness. IV, 409. Let no one consider what he suffers, but what he does. VI, 719. Whatever he may have suffered here, if he is not corrected even then, there is a double condemnation. VI, 720. How one should use God’s scourges and gifts. IV, 770. Therefore, whether in gifts or in scourges, praise him. IV, 1871; V, 134. The one who praises the Father’s scourge is upright in heart. V, 147. Praise of the one who scourges is medicine for the wound. IV, 1871. Let the Father’s judgments be praised in the scourge, if his promises are loved in the reward. IV, 1592. By God’s scourge we are disciplined here for what hope. V, 376. The scourge of God the disciplinarian must be endured. V, 376. Compare any human punishments with Gehenna, and everything you imagine is light. VI, 720. We should consider what Christ endured. VI, 724. Let the sinful son not disdain the scourges endured by the only-begotten without sin. IV, 1131.

A certain person scourged in a vision. V, 1410.

**Flagitium.** That is called *flagitium* which desire does in order to corrupt its own soul and body. III, 72. Shameful acts and crimes. III, 2064. Shameful acts precede crimes. III, 72. Acts contrary to nature are to be detested everywhere and always; those contrary to human customs are to be avoided according to the diversity of customs. I, 689. All shameful acts belonging to bad morals pertain to love of this world. VI, 207. Three deadly shameful acts, punishable by excommunication. VI, 220. Compensation for shameful acts is admitted with the greatest danger. III, 559.

**Flamen.** A priest of distinguished rank among the Romans. VII, 60. There were only three flamines among the Romans: Dialis, Martialis, and Quirinalis. VII, 60.

**Flame.** The pot of iniquity burns, but the flame of love is greater; do not let yourself be overcome. IV, 721.

Breath is nothing other than moving air. X, 534.

The breath of God is called the soul. IV, 1776.

“Breath” sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit. X, 484.

**Flavianus.** Formerly Vicar and a member of Donatus’s party. II, 300.

Those who are not broken by adversity weep as though they were not weeping. IV, 1917. The divine discourse, teaching one to weep in joy and rejoice in sorrow, appears to teach something perverse. IV, 1764. You ought to weep, but while remembering Zion. IV, 1763.

Weeping and laughter. V, 943. See Tears. Why weeping is sweet to the miserable. I, 697. Babylonian weeping. IV, 1763. Many weep with Babylonian weeping because they rejoice with Babylonian joy. IV, 1763.

**Flora.** A widow. VI, 157, 591.

**Flora.** A mother. III, 1068. The goddess who presides over flowering grain. VII, 118. How obscene the stage games of Flora were. II, 315; III, 1068; VII, 76.

**Florentia.** A basilica. V, 1597, 1598.

**Florentina.** II, 1089.

**Florentinus.** II, 429. An official of the Count. II, 430.

[Col. 0306] Florentinus, well known at Hippo. II, 1029. He delivered the letter of the people of Madaura to Augustine. II, 1029.

**Florentius.** A bishop. II, 587.

**Florentius.** A bishop. II, 991.

**Florentius.** Bishop of Hadrumetum. IV, 380.

**Florentius.** A Donatist bishop. IX, 528, 555.

**Florentius.** A sower who obtained by a miracle the means to buy clothing. VII, 765.

**Florinus.** From whom the heretics called Florinians took their name. VIII, 42.

**Florus.** A pagan. IX, 511.

**Florus.** An Hadrumetian monk, from the district of UZalis. II, 975. His journey to his homeland at UZalis, and from there to Carthage. II, 975. He brought Augustine’s longer letter to Sixtus to the monastery at Hadrumetum, II, 975. The book in question was *On Grace and Free Choice*. X, 913, n. 2, 915. Valentinus was moved by this book, and disagreement arose among the brothers. II, 975. They wrote to Augustine. II, 974. Augustine asked that Florus come to him. II, 970, 974. Florus went to Augustine. II, 976. Florus’s faith concerning grace, free choice, and retribution on the day of judgment was sound. II, 976. And Catholic. X, 917. It was not erroneous, as his brothers had said. II, 969, 970.

**Florus.** Julian’s associate. X, 1327, 1341.

A work of Julian’s undertaken on the authority of Florus, the bishop, against Augustine. X, 1051. And dedicated to him. X, 1316.

A flower signifies glory. IV, 1728. Those who flourish through the prosperity of this world perish in the power of God. IV, 626. They flourish for a time and perish forever. IV, 626. The righteous sometimes waver when they see the wicked flourishing and abounding. IV, 1648, 1649. Those who flourish here are compared with hay. IV, 607. If you cling to the flower of hay, since it will wither, you too will fall with it. IV, 607.

The rivers of paradise are real rivers. III, 378. From where they arise. III, 328. Whether their sources are known or unknown. III, 378.

The rivers of Babylon are all the things loved here that pass away. IV, 1762. They are the various desires of human beings. IV, 1763. They are riches that carry away those whom they exalt. IV, 1769. The river is the mortality of this age. IV, 795.

A river is signified in Scripture for both good and evil. V, 198. The river of God is the people of God. IV, 783. Many rivers and one river. IV, 783. The name “river” designates the world. IV, 1857. There is a certain river consisting in this entire order of passing things. IV, 794. The rivers of Ethan dry up when they accomplish nothing. IV, 940. The rivers of Ethan are those who presume upon their own strength and virtue. IV, 940.

What hay and the flower of hay are. IV, 1333. The name “hay” is also applied to grain crops. IV, 1400. The hay of the rooftops is grass that grows on roofs; it appears high up but has no root: what it signifies. IV, 1694. The wicked are like hay, the good like gold. IV, 1375. “Hay” signifies carnal things. IV, 1909. Hay is desire. IV, 1242. The mountains produce hay when the powerful distribute the fruits of the earth to the poor. IV, 1909, 1910.

Scripture calls what is lent at interest *foeneratio*. III, 534.

Interest-bearing lending is both a profession and an art. IV, 638. Interest-bearing lending is a detestable sin. IV, 386. Pious interest before God is almsgiving. V, 239, 524, 525, 1128, 1200, 1586. What it means to engage in maritime lending. V, 253. Interest-bearing lending is called a body, as though necessary to the state. IV, 638.

In Latin, *foenerari* is said both of the one who lends and of the one who receives a loan. IV, 386. It is clearer to the people if one says *foenerare*, “to lend at interest.” IV, 386. The one who forbids you to be a lender at interest commands you to be one: lend at interest to God. IV, 386. One lends at interest to the Lord who has mercy on the poor. IV, 387. The lender at interest wants to give less and receive more: give little, receive great things; give earth, receive heaven. IV, 387. The sinner lends at interest and does not repay when he fails to give thanks to God, from whom he received so many good things. IV, 371. The Church rebukes the lender at interest, and everyone curses him. V, 525. Lenders at interest who excuse themselves by saying that they have no other means of livelihood are refuted. IV, 1692. One who does not forgive sins or demands revenge is a lender at interest in injuries. IV, 638.

One hundred bags; one thousand bags. V, 263, 1704.

**Spring.** What a spring is and what it signifies. IV, 939. The spring of paradise irrigating the whole earth may perhaps have been dried up so that the labor of its inhabitants might be increased. III, 328. Various questions concerning that spring. III, 328, 329. On the origin of springs and rivers. III, 239. Summer tests a spring or torrent; temptation tests the person in whom the Word of God has become a spring of water. IV, 939. The spring and the light are with God. IV, 465. One who is still laboring in the poison of wickedness does not desire the spring of wisdom. IV, 465, 466. Run to the spring like a deer. IV, 465. One who has killed the serpents runs more eagerly to the springs. IV, 465. Destroy the serpents of iniquity, and then you will desire the spring of truth more greatly. IV, 465. A vessel is brought to the spring when the soul is raised to God. IV, 1854. A spring among the Garamantes is cold by day and hot by night. VII, 715, 718.
