A spring in Epirus in which lighted torches are extinguished and extinguished ones are kindled. VII, 718, 719.

**Fonteius.** A Carthaginian who, while still a pagan, wrote about cleansing the mind in order to see God. I, 624; VI, 14.

[Col. 0307] **Forculus.** The god appointed over doors. VII, 119, 184.

**Form.** The supremely One is the principle of every form. III, 233. A certain unformed and unmade form—the Word of God—is a form without time or place. V, 662. There is an eternal and unchangeable form through which all things are formed. I, 1264. No thing can form itself. I, 1264. All things that exist, once form is removed, will be nothing. I, 1265. Form has limits determining from where and how far it extends. V, 665.

To be formed is to be reduced to unity. III, 233. Adam was called a form of the future, but in reverse. III, 2067.

Written letters. II, 175.

**Formianum.** A town. II, 348.

The ant gathers during summer what will benefit it during winter. IV, 475. God’s ant gathers during the summer of prosperity what will sustain it in the winter of adversity. IV, 805. How the ant should be imitated spiritually. VIII, 168. It is beneficial to have the heart of an ant. V, 238.

Fear is always joined in some way with wonder. IV, 1412.

An iron furnace: harsh tribulation. III, 531.

Fornication is twofold: of the flesh and of the spirit. VI, 469. Of the heart and of the flesh. V, 1063. Fornication is condemned in Scripture by divine law. VIII, 439. When fornication was prohibited in the Law. III, 763. Fornication is a great evil. III, 743. It carries deadly guilt. VI, 378. It excludes one from the kingdom of God. V, 879, 1462. It is an offense injurious to God. V, 85, 86, 878. Through the vice of fornication, God’s image and temple in a human being are corrupted. V, 86, 1271. And injury is done to God’s grace. V, 86, 1271. Participation in the body and blood of Christ ought to deter one from fornication. V, 85. Spare Christ in yourself; recognize Christ in yourself. V, 878. The fornication on account of which a wife is permitted to be repudiated, and how far it is to be understood. III, 1251. In the Lord’s words, fornication, on account of which it is permissible to dismiss a wife, is not to be understood as only that committed in sexual misconduct. I, 616. To what kind of fornication this permission is to be limited is an extremely obscure question. I, 616. How absurd it is to classify death as the fornication that dissolves the marital bond. VI, 472, 473. The heart of a fornicator properly and familiarly becomes the servant of the body. V, 887, 888. Then it cannot be said that he possesses his own mind, but that the whole human being is flesh. V, 887. Why fornication alone is called a sin against one’s own body. V, 886. Fornication exists not only in bodily luxury but also in the soul’s dissipation. V, 1079. Fornication may be committed licitly, but not according to God’s laws. V, 828. What perversity there is in the human race in committing fornication and adultery. V, 84.

Fornication of the heart existed in everyone; in a few it existed in the flesh, in everyone in the heart. V, 1063. The fornication and adultery of the soul that worships demons. V, 76. What it means to fornicate away from the Lord. V, 778. The general fornication of the soul is that by which, instead of clinging to God, it clings to the world. V, 887, 889. Every soul that, having abandoned the eternity of truth, delights in earthly filth, fornicates away from the Lord. V, 92. How fornication of the soul and adultery of the soul differ. V, 117.

A brothel: the place of a prostitute. VI, 351.

“Perhaps” and “possibly” for the Greek ἄρα, although not entirely equivalent. IV, 1644, 1645.

**Fortitude.** What fortitude is and its parts. VI, 21. Fortitude is that by which we endure all troublesome things. IV, 1066. Fortitude is an affection of the mind by which we disdain all disadvantages and losses of things not placed in our power. I, 1235. It is also love that easily endures everything for the sake of what is loved. I, 1322. Fortitude and temperance belong to the lower part of the mind. III, 205. Duties of fortitude. VII, 629, 631. Examples of fortitude. I, 1329. The highest examples of pagan fortitude. VII, 127. Fortitude is not killing oneself. VII, 631.

From where our fortitude comes. IV, 1797. Christian fortitude arises from hunger and thirst for righteousness. III, 1257. The fortitude of Christians comes from love; that of the pagans from desire. X, 1104. Through the gift of fortitude one hungers and thirsts for righteousness. III, 39. Fortitude is the fourth step toward wisdom. III, 39. Fortitude is a vice when it is employed for pride. IV, 427. All fortitude lies in humility. IV, 1184. If fortitude is human and not God’s, it is hardness. IV, 1388. No one falls except one who wants his fortitude to belong to himself. IV, 1498. Fortitude must be implored from the one who commanded us to be strong; unless he himself makes us strong, we will not be what he commanded. IV, 477. The fortitude of Christ’s soldiers against the devil. VII, 671, 672. The more violent the assault of war, the greater the glory of not yielding. VII, 678. Fortitude is necessary for restraining anger when insult is hurled in our face. IV, 1184. This is not fortitude if, after being insulted, you strike, since you have been conquered by anger. IV, 1184. Knowledge and fortitude are therefore extremely rare, because nature has been corrupted by sin. X, 1431, 1434.

False fortitude and true fortitude. V, 1525, 1528. Strong in a bad sense. V, 305. One person is called stronger than another on four grounds. VIII, 586. Those strong with damnable strength: (1) the devil; (2) those who presume on riches; (3) those who presume on their own righteousness. [Col. 0308] IV, 695. These are compared with madmen, whose death is nearer the stronger they are. IV, 696. Some are called strong because they presume on their own righteousness. IV, 940. The strong in the Church, although they are not disturbed by the persecutions of outsiders, are nevertheless disturbed by the wickedness of their brothers. IV, 242. The strong often yield to scandals. IV, 476. One who is strong through true virtue neither dares rashly nor fears thoughtlessly. II, 736. He is strong who is strong not in himself but in God. IV, 265. No one is strong in this age except in the hope of God’s promise. IV, 1120. God is strong in his own power, whereas we are strong through participation in that power. IV, 795.

What accidental events are. VII, 141. Accidental events are divinely given through hidden causes. III, 571.

What fortune is. III, 571. By the name “fortune,” Augustine understands the accidental outcome of things, not a goddess. I, 585. Nevertheless, he disapproves the use of this word. I, 585.

**Fortune.** The goddess takes her name from accidental events, over which she is thought to preside. VII, 122, 126. Fortune is not any divine power. III, 571. She is worshiped as a goddess without justification. VII, 126. On what basis is Fortune thought to be a goddess, when she can be evil? VII, 126. Fortune was depicted as blind. I, 1273. Why she is called blind. VIII, 374. Fortune recklessly bestows her gifts on each person. VII, 197. The good things of Fortune: the truly wise, whom alone it is right to call blessed, wished neither to fear nor to desire them, and so forth. II, 65. The image of Womanly Fortune spoke through the cunning of demons. VII, 126. Bearded Fortune, who gives adults a beard. VII, 122.

**Fortunatianus.** II, 759, 780. Bishop of Sicca. I, 647; II, 622. See note (c).

**Fortunatianus.** Presbyter of the church of Thagaste. II, 273.

**Fortunatus.** A bishop. II, 430, 431. A Catholic bishop at Constantina. IX, 245, 337, 371.

**Fortunatus.** Bishop of Dionysiana. IV, 380.

**Fortunatus.** From Thuccabor. IX, 212.

**Fortunatus.** Successor of Profuturus. IX, 611.

**Fortunatus.** A Manichaean presbyter. I, 612; VIII, 111, 112. Fortunatus the Manichaean was defeated in debate with Augustine. II, 272, and note.

**Fortunius.** Bishop of Tubursicum belonging to the Donatist party. II, 173; IX, 528, 555. Augustine held a public disputation with him. II, 174. Summary of Augustine’s disputation with him. II, 175, 176. Fortunius maintained that his communion existed throughout the whole world. II, 175. He also maintained that the Council of Sardica had sent a letter to the African bishops who belonged to Donatus’s communion because the name Donatus was read among the other bishops. II, 176. Augustine replied that it was not established that the Donatus mentioned in the council’s letter was that African Donatus who founded the schism. II, 176. Augustine soon realized that the Council of Sardica whose letter Fortunius displayed had been Arian. II, 176. He proved this from the fact that Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and Julius, bishop of the Roman Church, were condemned in it. II, 176. Fortunius said that the overseas churches had remained innocent until the time of Macarius. II, 176. He praised the life of the Catholic bishops but denied that they were in the Church. II, 175. He wished to show that his people were Christians because they endured persecution. II, 175. Augustine proved that those belonging to the Donatist party suffered persecution not on account of righteousness. II, 175. Fortunius’s character and intention pleased Augustine so much that he believed it would be extremely difficult to find anyone so useful among the Donatists. II, 178.

The pit of sinners is itself the happiness of sinners. IV, 1204. A pit descends downward; the proud seem to go up into heaven but sink into the earth. IV, 1204.

**Digger.** II, 230. **Diggers.** IX, 513.

To dig a pit for a sinner means that God, by hidden justice, spares the sinner. IV, 1204. Everyone who prepares a pit for his brother—that is, a deception—must fall into it. IV, 670. The pit is a bad conscience and blindness. IV, 670.

The breaking of bread. V, 1111, 1116, 1127. See Eucharist.

It is suggested that strawberries do not exist in Africa. II, 70.

What a spear is. IV, 1955. Properly, a spear is a sword; figuratively, the tongue of persecutors. II, 555. The spear of God is the sword of God. V, 1424. The spear of God is the soul of the righteous. IV, 324; V, 1424. The enemy’s spears are various opinions of error. IV, 120.

“Break the moon and make fortune.” VI, 674.

Brothers or sisters, as a general term, are customarily called male or female blood-relations among the ancients. VIII, 422. And in Scripture. V, 737. They may refer to any degree of kinship. III, 489, 1374, 1467, 1623. “Brother” is understood in terms of the flesh. III, 496. Every human being is a brother. II, 95; III, 507. We are all brothers in hope of the heavenly inheritance, and neighbors by the earthly condition of our birth. IV, 189. All the baptized are our brothers. IV, 299. Whoever says to God, “Our Father,” says to Christ, “Our Brother.” IV, 549. He himself is the brother: if a brother does not redeem, a man will redeem. IV, 549. Let no master disdain to have as his servant a brother whom the Lord Christ wished to have as a brother. V, 393. Under the heavenly Father, servant and master are brothers. V, 400. How someone is a brother, sister, and mother of Christ. IV, 1685.

False brothers are to be tolerated within unity. IX, 311. If someone cannot endure a brother, what can he endure? II, 188. False brothers seize upon every word to find snares in it. IV, 459. The persecution of false brothers is more serious than that of enemies. IV, 638, 639, 653. What the danger from false brothers is. V, 119. They did not know how to cease from dangers caused by false brothers until the end of the world. V, 910.

How we prove that we love brotherhood. III, 1992. A sermon on fraternal harmony. V, 1054. Let the weaker not hinder the stronger, and let the stronger not press the weaker. II, 507.

The deceitful suffer deceit while they seek to practice it. IV, 925. A fraud is not for that reason no fraud because it is committed against the treasury. II, 356. The servants of God endure the hardship of poverty better than they obtain the means necessary for life with a guilty conscience arising from fraud. II, 356.

Frigidity occurs only in men. X, 989.

Whatever is dull is cold. IV, 1935.

Coldness occurs when God abandons the sinner. IV, 1934. The coldness of love is silence of the heart. IV, 404. Spiritual cold and ice arise both from iniquity and from the good works of others. III, 869.

There is a forehead on the face, and there is also a forehead in the conscience. V, 630. The forehead is the praise of our modesty. IV, 1839. One who has no forehead is shameless. IV, 1839.

**Fronto.** A servant of God. VI, 521.

**Fructesea.** A goddess. VII, 128.

**Fructuosus.** A bishop. II, 759, 780.

**Fructuosus.** A bishop and martyr. V, 1247.

**Fructuosus.** A digger. IX, 513.

The Manichaeans said that a fruit experiences pain when it is plucked from the tree, cut down, crushed, cooked, and eaten. VIII, 230. The plucking of fruits was homicide according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 230, 235. During Lent almost all Christians abstain from certain fruits of the earth; some abstain always. VIII, 493. The fruits by which a tree is recognized. III, 1306. Grace is necessary for a person to produce good fruits. X, 370. Our fruit does not make God richer, but makes us happier. V, 531. The hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit, understood in various ways. VI, 423.

Frugality was called by some the mother of all virtues. I, 974. Frugality was, in Cicero’s view, the greatest of the virtues. I, 975.

What it means to enjoy. VI, 19; VII, 339; VIII, 981, 982. Broadly, to enjoy means to use with delight. III, 33. To enjoy is to have at hand what you love. I, 1312. Properly, to enjoy is to cling to something through love for its own sake. III, 20. It is to place the end of one’s joy in it. III, 33. One must not enjoy oneself. III, 26. One must not enjoy a human being. III, 26. Whoever enjoys a human being in God enjoys God rather than the human being. III, 33. God alone is to be enjoyed. III, 33. And only eternal things. III, 26. In what sense is God said to have given everything for enjoyment, when only he is to be enjoyed? V, 958. Enjoyment and use. V, 958. The one who enjoys God stands firm; the one who wishes to enjoy himself—that is, the proud person—falls. IV, 1620. It matters whether a person wishes to enjoy body and time, or divinity and eternity. II, 539. God does not enjoy us, but uses us. III, 32. In what sense enjoyment is spoken of with reference to uses. VII, 339. It is not entirely unreasonable to think that beasts enjoy food and every bodily pleasure. VI, 19.

The fatness of grain. IV, 1930. Christ’s grain groans among the weeds. IV, 476.

Falsifying with pigments is an adulterating deception. II, 1060.

It is permissible to flee during persecution. III, 1731. How and when it is permissible to flee from city to city when persecution presses. II, 1014, 1015. To whom it was commanded or permitted. IX, 272. One who is specifically sought by persecutors may flee, while others who are not similarly sought remain for the Church’s necessary ministry. II, 1014. The Apostle Paul fled because he was being specifically sought. II, 1014, 1015. Augustine’s advice is that bishops or clergy whose ministry is necessary to the people should not withdraw when there is imminent danger of siege or destruction. II, 1013. If persecution rages only against the ministers of the Church, the Church is not for that reason to be abandoned. II, 1017. Some may flee for the benefit of the Church if there are not lacking others through whom ecclesiastical ministry can be supplied. II, 1016. If it is necessary for some of the clergy to flee for the benefit of the Church, and there is a dispute of charity among them, lots should be drawn to determine who will remain and who will flee. II, 1017. One who flees in such a way that, when he has fled, the Church is not deprived of necessary ministry does what the Lord commanded or permitted. II, 1018. Those suffer on behalf of others who, although they could rescue themselves from evils by fleeing, preferred to remain rather than abandon the needs of others. II, 1014. One who flees while the people remain amid persecution is a hireling. II, 1015, 1018. One who flees because he has been overcome by fear does not burn with charity, and ought to fight against fear. II, 1015. Ministers ought not to remain where there are no longer people whom it is necessary to serve. II, 1015, 1018. Even if bishops and clergy do not flee, the people should not for that reason be forbidden to flee. II, 1018. To flee bodily because of persecution is permitted; to flee in spirit is not. IV, 1810. Christ provided an example of fleeing. V, 741.

The ungodly flee from the face of God, not by hiding but by fearing. IV, 814. How a sinner can flee from the face of God. IV, 1790, 1791. If you wish to flee from God, flee to him: flee to him by confessing, not by hiding from him; for you cannot remain hidden, but you can confess. III, 2021. There is nowhere for a person to flee from an angry God except to a reconciled God. IV, 953, 1217. We can flee neither our conscience nor God. IV, 234, 235.

The flight of the flesh and the flight of the spirit. IV, 814. What is meant by flight in winter and on the Sabbath. III, 1151.

The Fugalia festivals. VII, 51.

Fulgora, a widowed goddess. VII, 191.

Coots are sea birds or birds of the marshes. IV, 1350. The homes of coots. IV, 1372.

Nocturnal thunderbolts were attributed to the god Summanus, daytime thunderbolts to Jupiter. VII, 131. Why thunderbolts sometimes strike a mountain—that is, a good person—and not a robber. IV, 1945.

Fulvius, a consul, killed with his children in the uprising of the Gracchi. VII, 105.

Smoke is, by a certain unity, what it is. VIII, 196. Creatures are compared with smoke. IV, 1863. The larger a globe of smoke is, the more insubstantial it becomes. IV, 370. Mountains smoke when, touched by God, the proud offer prayer to him in return. IV, 1388, 1389. Because a person feared, his days became days of smoke. IV, 1302.

The foundations of heaven, upon which the kingdom of heaven is built: Christ, the Apostles, and so forth. IV, 1049. Christ is our foundation if he holds the first place in our heart. V, 1616. Our foundation is above, not below. V, 1477. Just as the foundation of a bodily structure is at the bottom, so the foundation of a spiritual structure is at the top. IV, 1103. Because our foundation is in heaven, let us be built toward heaven. IV, 1621. “The foundations of the earth”: those made prosperous by an abundance of earthly goods. IV, 1049. How the foundations of the earth are shaken. IV, 1049.

Fundanus the rhetorician, although one-eyed, fathered a one-eyed son. X, 832.

God is rightly called our foundation. V, 651.

The cords of sinners are the impediments of enemies. IV, 1546. The righteous sometimes entangle the body, but not the spirit. IV, 1546.

A tightrope walker. Peter was not a tightrope walker but a sea-walker. IV, 440.

Care for the dead is praiseworthy. VII, 27. The pomp of a funeral. V, 611, 612, 936. The pomp of a funeral consists for the living in whatever consolations they may have, not in aids for the dead. V, 936; VII, 26. See Funeral rites.

Furius Camillus. See Camillus.

Furius defended injustice against justice. IX, 559, 560. Note (a).

A tenant baker. IX, 316.

Furnae. IX, 233.

There is no theft except when, by secretly taking what belongs to another, one harms one’s neighbor. III, 708. Theft forbidden. V, 70. How the commandment against stealing differs from the commandment against coveting another’s property. III, 621. Theft is against the law of nature. I, 678. No thief tolerates another thief with equanimity. I, 678. No one has an unjust gain without a just loss. V, 70. Whether the children of Israel committed theft by despoiling the Egyptians, and whether anyone may imitate them. IV, 1400. The Israelites did not commit theft by despoiling the Egyptians. III, 608.

The killing of a thief. See The Twelve Tables. If a nighttime thief is killed, it is not treated as homicide; if a daytime thief is killed, it is. III, 627. It is not injustice, by bodily afflictions, to compel thieves to return the money they took. II, 662. One should intervene on behalf of thieves, not so that they may fail to return what they took; otherwise one would enter into partnership in the crime. II, 663.

Fussala, a fortified settlement adjoining the territory of Hippo. II, 953. Fussala was forty miles distant from Hippo. II, 953. Fussala had formerly belonged to the parish of the Church of Hippo. II, 953. There was not a single Catholic at all in Fussala. II, 953. The error of the Donatists held the people. II, 953. Through great labors they adhere to the unity of the Church. II, 953. The Donatists rage against the priests appointed to gather the people of Fussala. II, 953. Augustine commends the priest of Fussala to Quodvultdeus. II, 1001.

The territory of Fussala. VII, 764.

The distinction between the spindle and the distaff is explained allegorically. V, 227.

Those things are truly future which God wills. III, 350. Future things have efficient causes in God’s wisdom. III, 1902. Those things are necessarily future which God has foreknown. III, 350. With God, what is future by his arrangement is already accomplished. IV, 1396. What is the basis for believing in future things. VII, 720. In how many ways future things are foreknown. VIII, 902. In predicting future things, the Prophets use verbs in the past tense. IV, 1354, 1476. Cicero denied knowledge of future things. VII, 148. Why. VII, 149.

[Col. 0311] G.

Gabbarae. V, 1605.

Gabinus. IX, 710, 732, 733. Gabinus, formerly a Donatist, now returned to the Church. IX, 711.

Gabinianus became not only a Christian but a very good and faithful man. II, 1012.

Gades, an island of Spain. VII, 158.

Gaeson: they interpret it as shield, spear, or lance. III, 539.

Gaianus. IV, 376. Bishop of Tigualis. IV, 381.

Gaius. V, 253.

Gaius, whose character is praised. II, 86.

Gajuseius. III, 1436; IV, 883, 1826.

Galaad is interpreted as “one who casts away” or “revelation.” III, 818, 820. Also, “heap of testimony.” IV, 719.

Galatia is not one church, but a region containing innumerable churches. IX, 414.

Galerius Maximus recites from a petition a decree against Cyprian. V, 1412.

Galilee is interpreted as “revelation.” III, 1216.

The unbelieving Galileans, a figure of the Jewish people. III, 1525.

Galla, a widow carrying the relics of Saint Stephen, is commended to Quintilian. II, 965.

The Gauls afflicted by disasters. II, 422.

The Gallic invasion of the City. VII, 108. They set Rome on fire, with only the Capitoline Hill remaining. V, 1356. Camillus rescues his country from the Gauls. VII, 62.

The Galli, as the priests of Berecynthia were called, from the river Gallus. VII, 52. Note (a). They had been castrated. VII, 185, 213, 214. The castration of the Gallic priests is attacked. VII, 214, 215. These men begged alms from the peoples. VII, 215. Note (b).

The fighting of cocks. I, 989.

Cockcrow. The customary time for praying after cockcrow. IV, 1587.

Under the emperor Gallienus, the end of the world could have been thought to be near. II, 918.

Whether a hen has an embryo is recognized from its voice, feathers, and so forth. IV, 1152, 1153. The hen alone among other birds becomes weak with its young through maternal affection. IV, 698, 1153. Wisdom is rightly compared with a hen. IV, 1152. The Gospel hen. V, 625, 1213, 1224. Hens are said to bring forth their own young from ashes. II, 703. The transformation of hens into the male sex. VII, 110.

Gallionus, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 381.

Gamalius, a Donatist bishop. IX, 528, 555.

The Ganges was formerly called the Phison. III, 203; 378.

The story of Ganymede. VII, 132, 571.

Garbe. IX, 511.

Mount Garganus. VII, 573.

The Gargilian baths. IX, 620.

Who are called babblers. IV, 975, 976, 977, 1515.

Garum. V, 1587. Garum sauces. VIII, 302.

Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi. I, 654. One of the seven chosen to defend the Donatist cause at the conference. IX, Retr. 705, 706, 707, 708. Two letters of his. IX, Retr. 705, 706, 707, 708. Augustine replied to him. II, 942. Two books were written against him. I, 654. In his letter, Dulcitius addresses Gaudentius of Thamugadi more honorifically than was fitting for a heretic. II, 940.

Gaudentius brought Augustine a letter from Severus of Milevis. II, 419.

Gaudentius, a count of the emperor Honorius. VII, 620.

What it means to rejoice in the Lord. V, 935. To rejoice toward God, in God, and on account of God: this is the blessed life itself, and there is no other. I, 793. To live blessedly is nothing other than to rejoice in true and certain goods. I, 1237. Those who are not corrupted by prosperity rejoice as though they did not rejoice. IV, 1917. A person rejoices more truly and pleasantly in a good conscience amid hardships than in a bad conscience amid delights. VI, 330. The wicked man rejoices in the tavern; the martyr rejoices in chains. IV, 1809. If you rejoice for a time, do not trust in it there; if you are sad for a time, do not despair. IV, 1212. A person must rejoice more when what he had despaired of has arrived. IV, 1927. The saints rejoice only in hope, when they rejoice soundly. VII, 611.

Greater joy is preceded by greater hardship. I, 752. Babylonian joy. IV, 1763. What the joy of the ungodly is like. IV, 1251. Joy from the world is impure. IV, 1661. The world’s happiness is unpunished wickedness. V, 935. Joy in earthly goods is troublesome and dangerous. IV, 1777. The joy of the rich of this age is the joy of the insane. III, 1438. Carnal joy comes from sickness of mind. V, 1189. Insane joys are not joys. VI, 330. There is no joy except in good things. III, 1306, 1307. The consolation of captives is one thing, the joy of free people another. IV, 1764. Whatever prosperity God now displays is not the joy of the blessed, but the consolation of the miserable. IV, 1864. There is a joy that is not given to the ungodly but to those who worship God freely, whose joy is God himself. I, 793. We do not place our joys in external things, having God within. I, 1188. Let joy be in the Lord, not in the world. V, 933. Do not rejoice in the world; rejoice in Christ, rejoice in his word, rejoice in his law. IV, 1212. The joy of the righteous comes from faith, hope, charity, and the truth of the Scriptures. IV, 691. The blessed life is joy in the truth. I, 793. There is security in no human being, and certain joy from no human being. IV, 1085, 1086.

The joy we receive from correcting the wicked cannot be compared with any joy in this life. II, 1085. When we rejoice over the faithful and the righteous, their goodness benefits both them and us; but when we grieve over the unfaithful and the wicked, both their wickedness and our sadness harm them alone. II, 1085. God mingles tribulations with earthly joys so that we may learn to desire eternal sweetness. IV, 1777. The joy of Christians in tribulation. IV, 1796, 1797. The martyrs were patient in tribulation because they rejoiced in hope. IV, 1679, 1680. The hope of one who rejoices contains great joy. IV, 1679. Hope cannot exist without joy. IV, 1885. Nor are we now without joy. V, 861. The joy of Christians is already in hope of what is future; afterward it will be in reality. IV, 271, 559, 1640, 1679.

The ungodly do not know the joy of the righteous. IV, 1775. The joy of the godly is a song to God. IV, 1917. Our joy, our peace, our rest, and the end of all our troubles is none other than God. IV, 1073, 1077. Firm joy is found in God alone. IV, 1870. What is eternal joy. V, 479. It is found only in God. III, 1502. When is joy complete. V, 142. Complete joy is not carnal but spiritual joy. III, 1896. Complete joy is found in fellowship itself, in charity itself, and in unity itself. III, 1980.

Gazuufala. IX, 237.

The treasury is God’s chest, where the things sent for the needs of God’s servants were collected. IV, 765.

Gebal is interpreted as “a vain valley,” that is, “deceptively humble.” IV, 1053.

How Gideon and Phua were brothers, although they belonged to different tribes. III, 809. Gideon sinned by making the ephod. III, 813, 815. How, then, is he praised in Scripture. III, 813. Gideon fell somewhat short of faith. III, 814. He tested the Lord. III, 813, 814. Gideon’s soldiers’ torches enclosed in earthen jars, a figure of evangelical light. III, 815. The number of soldiers chosen by Gideon contains a great mystery. IV, 833. What Gideon’s fleece prefigures. IV, 521, 907. It is interpreted mystically. IX, 398. Gideon’s fleece is a figure of the people of Israel; the dry threshing floor is a figure of the Church. III, 814.

How greatly the fire of Gehenna should be feared. V, 1616. We do not read the threat of Gehenna among the threats of the old law. IV, 1413. The martyrs were strengthened by fear of Gehenna. IV, 526. Who would not drink the cup of temporal tribulation, fearing the fire of Gehenna? IV, 843.

The church of Gelizitana. II, 162.

Gelosus, a priest. VII, 762.

Gemelius, bishop from the Tanabaeans. IV, 380.

The Twins. IX, 239.

Gemini is interpreted as “right-handed.” IV, 97.

Geminius, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 376.

Geminius from Furni. IX, 233.

The similar and dissimilar health of certain twins: to what should it be attributed? VII, 142. Hippocrates recognized two sick twins. VII, 144. The actions of certain twins are sometimes different, as are their characters. VII, 143.

The constellation of Gemini discussed. I, 739.

The groaning of the heart and the groaning of the flesh. IV, 403, 404. Why the faithful groan. IV, 1657. Those who groan or rejoice wrongly make themselves objects of groaning. IV, 1298. One groans well who sighs for his homeland, not one who is crushed by troubles. III, 1425. No matter how far a person has advanced, he will not lack here something over which to groan. IV, 471. In paradise you did not groan but enjoyed yourself; placed outside, groan. IV, 225. Groan over present things, sing over future things; pray over reality, sing over hope. IV, 224. There is groaning only among the miserable, and prayer only among the needy. IV, 206. Let us groan now and pray now; praise will follow prayer, and joy will follow groaning. IV, 206. God seeks our hidden groaning. IV, 344. The groaning of devout desire—even if a servant of God sometimes appears to laugh—never departs from God’s ears. IV, 404. Our groaning is in reality, our consolation in hope. IV, 1659. One who does not groan as a pilgrim will not rejoice as a citizen, because desire is not in him. IV, 1940. Groaning is something that possesses joy as well. IV, 1295. The groaning of the godly comes from the gift of the Holy Spirit. IV, 199. The Spirit is said to groan because he makes us groan. III, 2076.

Gems belong not to chests but to consciences. V, 147.

Genealogy. In a genealogy, placing women in place of men is not the custom of Scripture. III, 768.

Generation before sin would have been without lust. X, 756, [Col. 0313] 737. It would have proceeded from the obedience of the members, not from their power. X, 447. If they had not sinned, the first parents would have used their genital members, like their other members, according to the decision of their will. VII, 432, 434. See Lust. The disobedience of the genitals as punishment. X, 468, 469. The genitals were not shameful before sin. X, 1255. How they became shameful. X, 404, 406, 564, 565. The shameful movement of the genitals would not have existed in marriage had sin not preceded it. X, 467, 468. The involuntary movement of the genitals is shameful. X, 768. Everyone, modest and immodest alike, is ashamed of shameful movements. X, 566. The chaste experience the punishment of the disobedience of the genitals; the impure exult in the heavier punishment of the mind over this punishment of the flesh. X, 468. Not to blush at shameful movements is most shameless. X, 565. Generation is attributed first and chiefly to the father. X, 1285. The beginning of generation comes from the man. X, 1166, 1175. If the human mind fails in explaining human generation, who could recount divine generation? II, 1054. At what age a person can beget children. IV, 1393. The age at which spouses can beget children. X, 714. At how many years it ends. IV, 1393. An older man cannot father children with an older woman. III, 557. How generation from Adam differs from and does not differ from generation from other fathers. X, 1277. Human generations compared with the leaves of trees. IV, 1311. In Scripture, generations are counted not by years but by successions of people. III, 614. In Matthew, the generations of the Lord are found as three groups of fourteen, with Jechoniah counted twice. V, 339. Why he is counted twice. V, 340. See Christ.

The Apostle contrasts generation with regeneration. X, 1187. See Baptism. Carnal generation makes children of the flesh, children of death, children of the age, and children of wrath; spiritual generation does the opposite. X, 187. The first generation was mortal, from God’s wrath; the second generation will be immortal, from God’s mercy. IV, 1073. Carnal generation holds a person in a condemned stock. X, 406. See Original sin. Generation is from a human being; regeneration is from God alone. X, 1272. There is one generation by which we become faithful, and another by which we shall rise from the dead. IV, 1752.

Christ taught by his example that kinship of earthly lineage must be disregarded for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. VIII, 248.

The integrity of Generosus of Consular Numidia. II, 430.

Genesidius. VIII, 209, 214.

Some begin the history of Genesis, according to the literal character of the events narrated, from the point at which Adam and Eve, having been expelled from paradise, begot children. III, 372. Their arguments are satisfied. III, 373. The narrative in the books of Genesis is not a form of speech about figurative things but about things that happened. III, 372. They maintain that the works of Genesis, understood also bodily, more firmly support the narrative of divine speech. III, 373. What is the aim of the writer of the history of Genesis. VII, 456, 457, 462, 464. The unfinished book On Genesis Literally. I, 613; III, 219. Twelve books On Genesis Literally. I, 640; III, 245. Two books On Genesis against the Manichaeans. I, 599; III, 173. Augustine’s judgment concerning the books he himself published on Genesis. I, 613. The beginning of Genesis is explained in the last three books of the Confessions. I, 845.

Gennadius hears hymns of the blessed in a dream. II, 699.

Genethlius, of blessed memory, bishop of Carthage before Aurelius, suppressed a constitution against the Donatists; hence he was greatly praised by them. II, 179.

Astrologers. VII, 796. Those commonly called “mathematicians” are superstitious. III, 51. They are deceivers. III, 1457. They give empty responses. VI, 112. See Mathematicians. Their science is to be referred to certain agreements with demons. III, 52. Astrologers are refuted. III, 1456.

Genius, a god, so called from generating. VII, 205.

The genius of Carthage. V, 419.

Gennadius is warned not to doubt whether there will be any life after death. II, 699.

The Manichaean dream of a race of darkness rebelling against the kingdom of God. VIII, 113. It is refuted. VIII, 115, 116.

Seventy-two nations arose from the sons of Noah. VII, 481, 484. The nations were divided by languages. VII, 483. The number of nations increased far more than the number of languages. VII, 485. The difficulty concerning the number of nations is resolved. VII, 491. They worshiped a false human being in place of the true God. IV, 1481. What they worshiped in bodies. IV, 1483, 1484. The nations that did not know God were a wilderness; all nations are called the boundaries of the wilderness. IV, 785. Which are the nations that naturally do the things of the law and are said to have the law written in their hearts. X, 227, 228, 229, 749, 750. The calling of the nations. IV, 1238, 1239. How the nations were converted to Christ. III, 1641. The Gospel transmitted to the nations. V, 607. God caused the nations to will what they could also have been unwilling to will. X, 1207. The Jews were rejected because of pride, and the nations were grafted in, or the Gentiles added, because of humility. II, 559; V, 488, 490. The nations as the wild olive. IV, 1743, 1744. The greater praise of the nations than of the Jews. V, 485. Through the preaching of the Gospel, the nations became the spoils of the Israelites. VII, 706. The conversion of the Gentiles in Augustine’s time. IV, 1864, 1865. The Church’s joy over the calling of the Gentiles. [Col. 0314] IV, 1247, 1248. The calling and conversion of the nations foretold. VII, 555, 584, 585, 589, 592. Prefigured in Isaac. VII, 505. Foreshadowed through the mystical disk. IV, 1248. The salvation of all nations and their reception into the Church prefigured. V, 802, 1036. The Jews called the nations “dogs.” V, 487, 679; IV, 702. The nations as dogs licking Lazarus’s sores. III, 1352. The nations are called stones of the field. III, 830. Why the nations are stones. V, 679. The nations were called stones because they worshiped stones. IV, 530. The nations are signified by the sea and by Ethiopians. IV, 524, 937, 938. Against the Nations. V, 1130, 1133, 1138. There are two nations and two kingdoms: one of Christ, the other of the devil. II, 918. The name “nations” can refer to the wicked. IV, 544. To be mixed with the nations and separated from them. V, 1024.

The invention of geometry. I, 1014. The Egyptians devoted themselves to geometry. III, 549. Geometers are rare in the human race. VIII, 1011.

The river Geon, now the Tigris. III, 203.

Girba. IX, 209.

Germanianus, a bishop. II, 759, 780.

Germaniciana. IX, 228.

The Germaniciani. II, 1068.

Germanus, a bishop. II, 759, 780, 788.

Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs. V, 1297. Their bodies are discovered. I, 770. At Milan by Ambrose. VII, 761. The discovery was illuminated by miracles. V, 1299, 1437. A blind man was given sight. VII, 761. The memory of Gervasius and Protasius is celebrated on the day on which they were found, not on the day on which they died. V, 1299.

The myths say that Geryon had three bodies. VIII, 948.

Public records. II, 133; V, 1594. Episcopal records. II, 580; V, 1576. Ecclesiastical records. II, 161, 162, 1066; V, 1575. They are to be removed where they have been made rashly. II, 1067. Proconsular records. II, 161, 162. Municipal records. II, 265. Before Zenophilus. II, 413; IX, 542, App. 793. At Cirta before Munacius Felix, flamen, etc. II, 197; IX, 583, 793. Before Aelianus. IX, App. 780. Records of the Council of Cirta. IX, 510. Note (a), 542. Judicial records. II, 413. Why Augustine wishes the sacrilegious crime to remain attached to the public records. II, 133, 135.

Gestures, as it were the natural words of all nations. I, 783. Gestures are certain signs. I, 1206.

Geta. IX, 323, 328.

Geth is interpreted as “winepress.” IV, 648.

Getulia, a part of Africa. VII, 93. Note (d). It suffers from continual drought. I, 1001; IV, 1944.

Getulicus, bishop of Victorianum. IV, 381.

Mount Giddaba. III, 1988; V, 267.

In the Hebrew language giants are called Raphain. III, 749. Giants are people of towering stature. VII, 82, 448. Why they were created by God. VII, 471. Whether they were begotten by human beings or by demons. III, 549. The age of the giants. VII, 469. There were more giants before than after the Flood. VII, 471. Giants existed in both sexes. III, 549. A gigantic woman was born at Rome in Augustine’s time. VII, 469. The proud are signified by giants, IV, 1116, as also are those who excel in spiritual strength in the Church. IV, 1116.

Whether Scripture distinguishes between begetting and giving birth. III, 759.

Gildo. II, 299. The time of Gildo. IX, 316. See Optatus.

The church of Gippitana. II, 234.

Glabis. III, 856.

Gladiators, professors of public disgrace, are not admitted to Christ’s sacraments. VI, 220. A gladiatorial spirit. IV, 875. To devote oneself with a gladiatorial spirit to satisfying one’s lusts. V, 140.

A sword can be understood in a good sense. VII, 691. In a bad sense, it stands for a discordant tongue. VI, 306. The benevolent sword and the malicious sword. IV, 1866, 1867. The two-edged sword is God’s word in the Old and New Testaments, promising eternal and temporal things. IV, 1956. Relating the past and promising the future. IV, 1866. Christ’s sword is his word. IV, 500. God’s sword cuts away corruption and heals Christ’s members. IV, 1866. The ungodly are the devil’s swords. IV, 1857. The devil uses them to slaughter souls. IV, 1837. The sword stands for tribulation. II, 644. A sword was given to Esau, but not to Jacob himself. V, 50.

The offspring of Glaucia. II, 79.

What glory is. VI, 22. What human glory is. VII, 156. Frequent report about someone with praise. III, 1905. Clear renown with praise. VIII, 770. Glory is not in the mouth of the crowd but in the things themselves. II, 428. Disgraceful glory: secular honors. I, 670. The Romans’ immense desire for glory. VII, 154. Human glory, the reward rendered for the Romans’ good morals. VII, 154, 160, 161. It is regarded as the glory of vanity to believe in no powers of truth. VII, 173. How the desire for glory differs from the desire for domination. VII, 165. The desire for glory is hostile to faith. III, 1623; VII, 159. The more free a person is from the desire for glory, the more like God he is. VII, 159. The desire for glory must be overcome by love of justice. VII, 159. To despise glory is a great virtue for one who possesses virtues. VII, 165. Virtue is the road to glory. VII, 156. See Praise. The vice of vain glory must be avoided especially, or even solely, by the perfect: for the vice by which the soul first fell is the last it conquers. IV, 100. Often a person boasts more vainly of his very contempt for vain glory. I, 806. The Apostles did not seek human glory; nor do those defend themselves against it who, while scorning others’ judgments, seem wise to themselves and please themselves. VII, 167. To expect glory from one another and not seek that which is from God alone is the leaven of the Pharisees. V, 721. Those delighted by vain glory have nothing in their conscience. IV, 1984.

One must seek not one’s own glory but God’s glory. III, 1632. God’s glory is that one who becomes good should glory not in himself but in the Lord. IV, 194. God’s glory in the gratuitous justification of human beings. V, 998. God’s glory by which we, though unworthy, have been saved. IV, 158, 159. A person recognizes this more readily while constrained by want. IV, 159. Not only human beings, but even the righteous, if indeed we are righteous, he made us, and not we ourselves. IV, 159. We must glory in God alone for our good things. II, 851, 852. When we act well, let us understand that God acts through us; and let us claim nothing as our own, deceived by the desire for vain glory, the one evil by which we are plunged from the highest things to the lowest. I, 1078. No one can glory before God. X, 939. One must glory in God, not in merits. X, 980. Not in one’s own righteousness. V, 872. One must glory in nothing, since nothing is ours. X, 628. Boasting is excluded through faith. X, 210, 237. The Lord’s Prayer itself shows that one must glory in God alone. X, 1001. To glory in God is God’s blessing. IV, 89. One who glories in himself glories in a fool. V, 873. The righteous person’s glory is in himself, but he is not himself his own glory. II, 852. Of one who does not glory in the Lord, I do not hesitate to say that whatever else he has, he has in vain. X, 1033.

To glorify God and to give thanks are the same thing. V, 439. We glorify God not by making him glorious, but by calling him glorious. IV, 436. Where knowledge is perfect, there is the highest glorification. III, 1905. Boasting is signified by oil. IV, 1921.

In what people God’s glory dwells. IV, 195. In what sense all lack God’s glory. IV, 233. God’s glory is our glory and benefits us. V, 1680. When we glorify God, it benefits us, not him. IV, 436. Our glory is secure in the Lord’s glory. V, 303. When it is sometimes permissible to glory without arrogance. III, 1794. A true manner of glorying exists in conscience. IV, 1955. Solid glory is possessed in conscience before God, where there is no boasting. IV, 100. God’s glory is set in Christ Jesus through grace for the remission of sins. IV, 157, 158. How great a merit it is to glory in Christ’s cross. V, 875, 876. The calling to glory is not according to human merits but according to God’s mercy. III, 648. Our future glory will be to be equal to the angels and to see God. IV, 368. God took away our glory in order to give us his: he took away the vain to give the full, the wavering to give the solid. IV, 789. By glory we shall be wholly light, having in ourselves nothing that resists charity, opposes truth, or is subject to weakness. V, 987. A certain excellent and singular glory in heaven is to be granted for a praiseworthy vow. VI, 402.

The Gnostic heretics: whence they arose and why they are so called. VIII, 26.

Goetia, a kind of magic. VII, 286.

Gog is interpreted as “roof.” VII, 676. The wars of Gog and Magog, and the building of the Temple in Ezekiel, are difficult to understand. II, 719.

Who Goliath was. V, 197. Goliath’s single combat with David. V, 197. It is explained allegorically. IV, 1856. Goliath is a figure of the devil. IV, 302.

The story of the Gorgon. VII, 570.

Gor. IX, 227.

The power of the Goths. VII, 115. The Goths, having gathered an army, ravage Italy. VII, 115. The Gothic invasion of the City. VII, 109. The pagan Goths, attacking Rome, are defeated. V, 624. The Gothic heretics conquer. V, 624. Gothic gladiators. VII, 90. How the Donatists try to win the Goths over to themselves. II, 793.

Tiberius Gracchus was killed by Scipio; for what reason. VII, 66. The head of Gracchus was sold for as much gold as it weighed. VII, 105. The uprisings of the Gracchi. VII, 66, 69, 104. The death of the Gracchi. VII, 105.

Gradation, or κλίμαξ, a figure of speech. III, 93.

The four stages of the human being: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and in peace. III, 2065. The Songs of Ascents, in Greek ἀναβαθμῶν—that is, “of those ascending,” not descending. IV, 413. There are as many as there were steps of the Temple. IV, 1960.

Greece became a Roman province. VII, 52.

The Greeks, after Troy was destroyed and they were returning to their own lands, were crushed by various disasters. VII, 573. The Greeks’ empty superstition and custom of placing the dead among the number of the gods. VII, 565. The kingdom of the Greeks. See Argos. The Greeks were called frivolous. VII, 18. The Greek language predominates among the nations. VII, 235. The contests of the Greek gymnasia differ from those of the Roman forums. II, 436. The Greek language, as the earlier language from which Scripture was translated into Latin, deserves greater credence. IV, 1539. The Greeks count by letters. III, 1473.

Grammar is called in Greek grammatikē and in Latin litteratura. I, 1012, 1099. Grammar is the guardian and disciplined regulator of articulated speech. I, 894. It professes to preserve history. I, 1012, 1099. Is it the task of grammar to teach sounds and accents? I, 1010. The laws of grammar are carefully observed, while God’s commands are neglected. I, 673. Curtains hung at the entrances of grammar schools. I, 670; VI, 713. A book on grammar written in dialogue form by Augustine when he was at Milan preparing to receive baptism. I, 591. How that book was lost. I, 591.

Grammarians, wearing the paenula. I, 672. Grammarians contemptuously called “letter-men.” II, 445. Note 1. Grammar judges the poets. I, 1014. Let a preacher not fear the grammarians’ criticism while instructing everyone. V, 228, 1371. The laws of grammar are to be observed less carefully in sermons if, by chance, the people understand better through a barbarism. IV, 386, 1796.

Hail is wickedness that takes away another’s property. IV, 1000.

The grain multiplied through death. V, 1397.

The cruel enemies of grace, the Pelagians. X, 688, 693. And the Caelestians. VIII, 47. What grace is according to Pelagius and Caelestius. II, 760. Pelagian grace. X, 272, 361, 1291. Pelagian grace is multifaceted. X, 1111. Concerning the help of grace, Pelagius says that it is to be referred either to nature, doctrine, free will, the remission of sins, or the example of Christ. II, 760, 768, 774, 849, 853, 877. According to the Pelagian teacher, grace is to be understood as that which is common to pagans and Christians, the ungodly and the godly, the faithful and the unfaithful. II, 816. Nature is common to all, not grace. V, 172, 173, 174. The Apostle speaks not of natural gifts of God but of gifts of grace: “For who makes you different?” X, 967, 968. Just as the Law is not grace, so nature itself is not the grace by which we are Christians. X, 896. When grace is discussed, we are not speaking of that which pertains to the establishment of nature but to its restoration. X, 252, 277. The false defender of nature is under the yoke of iniquity. V, 190. He is refuted by the experience of his own weakness. V, 188. [This is demonstrated] from the prayers of the Church. V, 191. By asking for continence, the wise person asks not for nature, free will, knowledge, or remission of sins, but for the strength by which he may be able to remain continent. II, 853. Although the nature with which we were created can in a certain sense be called grace. II, 767, 768. Nature is not to be considered grace except because it too was granted freely. V, 172, 176. Pelagius says that there is no grace of God except our nature, created with free will. X, 345, 347. At times, and that only faintly and not openly, he joined to it either the help of the Law or the remission of sins. X, 347. Grace given without any preceding merits is not the remission of sins. II, 877. The false defender of nature is ungrateful to the physician. V, 189.

The Pelagians call the grace of God by which we are helped not to sin “the Law.” X, 617, 893. And Pelagius professes nothing concerning grace that cannot be understood as referring to the Law and teaching. X, 375, 376. Grace does not consist in the Law. X, 212. The Law is one thing, grace another. X, 364. What difference there is between grace and the Law. V, 791. Through the Law it was brought about that sin should be recognized, increased through transgression, and that thus one should flee to divine grace. II, 769. By teaching and commanding what cannot be fulfilled without grace, the Law demonstrates to man his weakness, so that, once his weakness has been demonstrated, he may seek the Savior. II, 593. Neither the priesthood nor the Law introduces anyone into the eternal inheritance, but grace through faith. III, 743. God accomplishes the work of the Law in man through his grace; and man, receiving grace through his faith, etc., is a fellow worker with the God who helps him. III, 756. True Israelites glory in grace, not in the Law. II, 893.

### The assistance of grace, according to Pelagius, placed solely in the revelation of teaching. X, 379, 380.

The grace of Christians does not consist merely in knowledge. II, 852. If grace is absent, teaching itself is also harmful. II, 983.

### Pelagian grace as an interior and manifold illumination of the mind. X, 364.

This grace does not differ from the grace of the Law and of teaching. X, 364. The revelation of wisdom is not perfect grace. X, 366. Grace operates not only so that we may know what must be done, but also so that we may do what we have learned, etc. X, 367, 373. Grace not only shows what must be done, but also helps so that it can be done. X, 153, 241, 363. God operates not by the Law and teaching sounding outwardly, but by an inner, hidden, wondrous, and ineffable power in human hearts, producing not only true revelations but also good wills. X, 373. The revelation of wisdom belongs to teaching; it also belongs to teaching when every good thing is commended. X, 366. How grace can be called teaching. X, 367. Man established under the Law; man established under grace. I, 620. The condition of man established under grace. V, 64, 66. Fear under the Law, hope under grace. V, 791.

Grace in the proper sense is not nature, nor knowledge of the Law, etc. X, 352. The Pelagians contend that grace—which is neither the Law nor nature—has [Col. 0317] force only so that past sins may be forgiven, not so that future sins may be avoided. X, 896. Grace is neither nature together with free will, nor knowledge of the Law, nor forgiveness of sins, etc. X, 352. The Pelagians placed grace in the forgiveness of sins and in Christ’s example. X, 361, 379, 774, 1243. Grace in the proper sense, the grace of Christ, is, for Pelagius, Christ’s example. X, 381, 1202. Pelagius understood grace as that in which we were created by God with free will. X, 333. The grace of the Pelagians is nothing other than free will given by God and the teaching of the Law. X, 262. The view that God does not give grace for individual acts, but that it exists in free will or in the Law and teaching, is Pelagian. II, 979. Pelagius condemned this at the judgment of the Eastern bishops, although with a deceitful heart. II, 979. Pelagius says that there are three things by which divine commands are fulfilled: possibility, will, and action. X, 361. He attributes possibility to God, but the other two to man. X, 362, 363. The Pelagians defended free choice of the will in such a way that they left no place for the grace of God. I, 595. Grace is not free will. X, 333. The grace of Christians does not consist in the nature of free will, nor in the Law and teaching. II, 849, 852, 983, 985; X, 338. Augustine did not assert the Pelagian position in his earlier works on free will. I, 596. Not possibility alone, but also will and action are helped when God teaches through grace. X, 368, 373.

### The Pelagians eventually acknowledged grace

The Pelagians eventually confessed grace. V, 856. What sort of grace they confessed. X, 1484. And the extent to which Pelagius professed that it is given for individual acts. X, 361. Pelagius required grace only for acting more easily. X, 374, 375, 380, 871. Through the sacrament of Christ’s death and resurrection, he maintained that there is merely a more convenient way, not that another way is impossible. X, 872.

Grace is not given merely in order to act more easily. X, 584. Pelagius is refuted, since he taught that grace is given out of abundance or for easier action. II, 829, 830. Pelagius attacks the grace of God through Christ. II, 775. The grace by which the ungodly are justified and by which we are Christians. I, 647. Yet he does not dare to attack it openly. II, 760. Porphyry acknowledged grace, but not grace through Christ. VII, 307.

### Grace in the general and the particular sense

I, 624; III, 2087. *Retr.* Grace is of two kinds: one common to all, namely, the grace of creation; the other proper to Christians, namely, the grace of election and deliverance through Christ. V, 172, 173. The opponent of grace is injurious to Christ. V, 921. The grace of Christ is set against the Jews like a cloud. III, 656. Augustine asks Pelagius to confess the grace of Christ. II, 776.

The Pelagians asserted that grace is given according to our merits. I, 595; X, 376, 377, 570, 887, 888. Apart from the sole grace of the forgiveness of sins. X, 890. They taught that men merit grace through the good use of free will. X, 372. Scriptural testimonies by which the Pelagians prove that grace is given according to merits. X, 888. They misuse the testimony of Zechariah. X, 888. Other passages of Scripture that they misuse. X, 888. The Pelagian dogma that grace is owed to faith. X, 377. Faith is the merit of grace. X, 377. Prayer is the merit of grace. X, 633, 758, 897. Grace is owed to the first desire for the good. X, 567, 583. And to conversion of heart, or a good intention. X, 585, 686, 888. The Pelagian dogma that grace is given according to merits was condemned by the Synod of Palestine. X, 338. Pelagius himself condemned it at the Synod of Palestine. II, 877; X, 587, 961, 962, 1011. So that he would not be condemned by Catholic judges. II, 985; X, 584, 1027, 1128. Yet after that Council he did not write sincerely about grace; rather, he taught that grace is given out of abundance or for easier action. II, 829. And that it is given according to merits. X, 371, 554. Some people, unless they assign to themselves something that they may give first and receive back as a reward, think that they are restrained from every pursuit of piety. X, 977. The teaching that grace is given according to our merits is a doctrine of Caelestius. X, 344. Caelestius’s errors concerning grace. X, 357. They were condemned by the Palestinian judges. X, 358. And by Pelagius and Caelestius themselves. X, 358. By the grace of creation one who deserved nothing good was created; by the grace of election one who deserved much evil was saved. V, 176.

Pelagius confesses grace in deceptive words. X, 332. He anathematizes those who say that grace is not given for individual acts, but exists in free will or in the Law and teaching. X, 338. The Synod of Palestine believed that Pelagius confessed the grace that is widely known in the Church. X, 333. Pelagius and Caelestius nowhere confessed true grace. X, 375, 378.

### The rejection and defense of grace

Pelagian grace is rejected. X, 872. The grace of God must be defended against the Pelagians. X, 885. What one should think about grace together with the Church. II, 817. Twelve statements concerning grace. II, 984. Augustine says that he knows these to belong to right and catholic faith. II, 985, 987. Grace is the justice of God. X, 896.

Grace was promised in the New Testament through a prophet. X, 231. The grace of the New Testament was hidden under the old. X, 400. Like Gideon’s rain upon the fleece. II, 770; IV, 1779. Grace was represented and explained through Samuel’s mother. VII, 528. The ancient sacrifices signified grace but did not effect it. II, 633. The [Col. 0318] earlier tablets given through Moses signified it. III, 653. The commandment concerning observance of the Sabbath. III, 655. And the manna. III, 634. Grace was hidden in the Old Testament and revealed in the New. IV, 1856; V, 167, 753; X, 217. Why this is so: “O the depth!” etc. II, 770. Grace and truth are realities of the New Testament. III, 1396.

### The necessity of grace

Grace is necessary. III, 871, 1397, 1402, 1778, 1841, 1843; X, 170, 280, 281. It is beyond nature and the Law. V, 174. It is not man alone who belongs to the grace of God: the angels themselves owe God that they exist, that they live, that they live justly, and that they live blessedly. IV, 895. The help of grace is necessary in both conditions of man, but greater in the present condition. VI, 282. Human nature itself, even if it had remained in the integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. II, 830. Even when intact, nature could not preserve salvation without grace. II, 830.

Because grace heals, it is called medicine. X, 1308. Nature would not need grace if it were healthy. X, 285. Whoever denies that human nature, at any age, needs Christ the physician is an enemy of the grace of God. X, 402. Medicinal grace. V, 850. What this means according to Pelagius. X, 266. Grace is medicine: whoever wishes always to remain sick is ungrateful toward medicine. V, 852. Those who think themselves healthy rave against the physician. V, 943. Grace assists both little ones and adults. V, 907. The Pelagians in fact deny the medicine of Christian grace to little ones. X, 1308.

Grace is liberating. V, 940. All who are delivered are delivered through grace. II, 776, 822. And apart from the grace of the Savior, which has never been absent from the human race, no one can be delivered. VII, 315; X, 315, 316. Grace delivers from the devil. V, 446. It alone delivers from the miseries of this life. VII, 786. And from sins. II, 885. From the law of sin. V, 842. From the dominion of concupiscence. I, 620; III, 2061. From this body of death. II, 769. Grace alone removes sin. III, 2065, 2068. Through grace transgressors of any law are saved. II, 681. Even David himself would not have risen from sin unless grace had raised him up, according to Innocentius. II, 782. There is no soul, except Christ’s own, for whose deliverance from sin Christian grace is not necessary. III, 416. Pelagius taught that man can be without sin without grace. X, 281. To assert that man can be sinless through grace is tolerable. II, 771, 772. The dominion of iniquity over man before grace. V, 187. The justice of God alone sets me free; what is mine alone is nothing but sins. IV, 895. The necessity of liberating and assisting grace. IV, 233, 234, 890, 895.

Grace is necessary even for the baptized. X, 277. If the grace of God does not govern you, you fall; if it does not raise you up, you lie prostrate. V, 855. If you could not make yourself, how can you remake yourself? IV, 524. You can fall away from yourself, but you cannot restore yourself; the one who restores you is the one who made you. IV, 1224. You could do nothing in yourself except destroy yourself; nor do you know how to find yourself, unless the one who made you seeks you. V, 108. Nature is not restored by itself, but by the grace of God. III, 406, 418; IV, 891, 998.

Grace is necessary so that the soul may return to God. VIII, 1007. We are sufficient for ourselves for sinning; but for returning to righteousness, we are not. X, 259. Grace wiped away all sins and supplied assistance to our will as it struggled not to sin. V, 843. Grace is necessary both for the beginning of conversion and for progress and perseverance. IV, 892, 893. And for embracing repentance. VI, 271. What is the first grace that a sinner receives? III, 1400.

Grace must be requested from God so that the devil may be resisted. X, 281. Grace must be sought in temptations. III, 761. Grace is necessary for overcoming temptations. V, 190. Do not say, “I cannot hold, carry, and restrain my flesh”; you are helped so that you can. IV, 457. The weakness of a person deprived of the help of grace. IV, 1746. God carries and sustains those in whom he dwells; if he withdraws, they fall. IV, 1632, 1633. A person deprived of divine grace must necessarily perish, ensnared in the devil’s traps. Innoc. II, 785. Unless God’s grace, implored by great prayers, descends upon us, we do not at all attempt to overcome the errors of our earthly body. Innoc. II, 782. All the saints testify that they can do nothing without God’s help. Innoc. II, 782. We must necessarily be overcome again if the one by whose help we conquer does not continue to help us. Innoc. II, 782. While fighting against sin, we are overcome unless we are helped by God, so that not only may we see what must be done, but also so that the delight of righteousness may conquer in us the delights of other things. VI, 271. Man needs God’s help not to sin and to act justly. X, 153. Even one who is perfectly justified needs the help of grace in order to live rightly. X, 261. So that he may walk in the right way. V, 751. The will both to believe from the beginning and to persevere to the end belongs to the grace of God. II, 985. Those who have been sanctified need God’s help in order to become more holy. III, 1915. Pelagius himself confessed that without grace man cannot be perfected. X, 343. It is given by God so that it may be known from whom every good thing is given. III, 1850. When we know God, not even this must be attributed to us, but to his mercy. II, 575.

Grace is necessary for explaining the mysteries of faith. V, 355. Good thoughts come only from grace. II, 818. For believing, the will is not sufficient without grace. II, 830. Man cannot illuminate himself. IV, 193. Healthy and open eyes, if [Col. 0319] external light is absent, remain in darkness. IV, 1858. Apart from God, we are darkness and weakness. IV, 200. Not sinning, both in an intact nature and in a corrupted one, comes from God’s help, as does the ability not to sin. X, 274. No one can will righteousness except through grace. X, 1520. Grace must be proclaimed not only on account of possibility, but also on account of will and action. X, 373. Adults ought not to trust in the power of their own will. X, 1292. We must not rely on our own powers, but prayer must be joined to our efforts, so that he who deters us from evils may fill us with goods. VI, 480. The whole appearance and countenance of the Holy Scriptures admonishes us that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord. VI, 278. Let no one presume, by his own strength, to render what he has vowed; the one who urges you to vow also helps you to fulfill it. IV, 1717. Man ought to rely on God’s mercy, not on his own virtue. X, 693. Mercy and judgment are exercised in human wills. X, 968. Man cannot will the good unless he is helped by the one who cannot will evil. X, 1114. Man fell into the evil he committed not compelled by any necessity, but by his own will; yet he can be recalled to the good he abandoned only by God’s grace, not by the will of the freedom that he deservedly lost through iniquity. X, 1518. God cannot be reached by free choice alone and without the help of grace. X, 372. “You did indeed give me free will, but without you my effort is nothing.” IV, 208. God grants the movement of the will, diligence in striving, and works fervent with love; God bestows them. VI, 127. Adam’s descendants cannot change themselves, but are changed by God. X, 1251.

Grace is necessary not merely so that one may act more easily, but so that one may be able to act at all. V, 856. It is necessary so that man may do something good. X, 370. Nothing good is done without God’s help. V, 856. Nothing upright. X, 264. The more or less a person is helped by grace, the more or less he can do what contributes to eternal life. II, 354. Whatever is good is given by God. III, 1850. It comes from God that we love him. II, 576. Man would not have lived well except through the grace of God. III, 431. Unless God’s grace frees the will from slavery to sin, mortals cannot live rightly and piously. I, 596. Man cannot do anything well as though from himself. III, 382. The first benefit of God’s grace is to bring us to confess our weakness, so that whatever good we can do, we may do in God. IV, 428. Without grace we can in no way either think or act according to God. II, 969. Without grace, people do absolutely no good, whether in thinking, willing and loving, or acting—not only so that, with grace itself showing what must be done, they may know it, but also so that, with grace itself providing the power, they may do with love what they do. X, 917. Unless grace helps us, we can possess no piety or righteousness, either in action or even in the will itself. II, 818. Without it the will cannot be good. II, 851.

### Good living must be attributed to grace

That one lives well must be attributed to grace. IV, 584, 789, 1575, 1784, 1814. Grace alone produces in us every good merit of ours. II, 880. We possess true righteousness only through grace. V, 921. Man receives from God both that he is a human being and that he is righteous. V, 107, 872. God worked so that you might exist; if you are good, he himself works so that you may be good. IV, 1851. From the one from whom I received existence, I received goodness as well. IV, 713, 1379. Whatever we are, we are by his mercy; whatever we are from ourselves, we are evil. IV, 876. If a man wishes to be something good, he must not derive it from himself. V, 639. Whatever good a man possesses, he possesses only from the one who is all our good. IV, 1073. Whatever evil is in you from sins is yours; whatever good is in justification is God’s. IV, 193, 1280.

The opponents of the grace of the New Testament do not attribute their goodness to God, but rather wish to claim it for themselves. II, 575. Let us claim nothing for ourselves, lest we also lose what we have received. V, 178, 191. We owe God that we are human beings, that we have lived well, and that we have understood rightly. V, 953. Christian discipline is this: whatever someone does badly, he should attribute to himself; whatever he does well, to God; nor should he exalt himself over the one who does not do well. IV, 1204. Those who think that they should attribute to themselves, rather than to God’s grace, the fact that they live well, no longer live well, however many good works they may appear to perform. IV, 902. If someone walking in the right way attributes this to himself, he perishes from the right way. V, 750, 751. Those who are entrusted to themselves and are moved by themselves are not good, because they are not children of God. X, 805. Hope for acting well must not be placed in man. X, 885. Whatever evil we have not done must be credited to grace. I, 681.

The person who thinks that nature is sufficient for observing the commandments opposes grace. II, 741. Grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled. X, 221. Grace is necessary for fulfilling the Law. V, 75, 894, 1160, 1162, 1165, 1170. The grace that helps is necessary so that the command of the one who commands may be fulfilled. IV, 757, 889; VI, 421. The commandments of the Law cannot be fulfilled except through grace. II, 674–677, 769, 894, 898. Human weakness does not conform to God’s upright and difficult commandments unless the love that goes before comes to its aid. IV, 1512. Through helping grace the commandments are [Col. 0320] fulfilled, even in the Old Law. VIII, 359. If the divine Spirit does not yet help him, the person who wishes to live according to the Law is defeated and knowingly sins. VI, 287. The Law would not command unless there were a will; nor would grace help if the will were sufficient. II, 766. Grace, making us love what the Law commands, can command those who are free. VI, 354. Through the Law human presumption is removed; through grace, captivity. V, 793. The Law commands; the Spirit helps: the Law acts with you so that you may know what to do, the Spirit so that you may do it. V, 1163. It was grace, not the Law; the Spirit, not the letter, that made provision against sin. X, 1173. God gives man the means by which he may do what he commands. IV, 1549. God himself gives the strength so that what he helps may be fulfilled. V, 200. The Law without grace is a letter that kills. V, 1239. It does not remove sin, but increases it. IV, 1572. It remains to convict iniquity, not to give salvation. IV, 888, 989, 1581. The Law is useful for this purpose: that it may send us to grace. IV, 1575. Grace both frees from sin and grants that the letter may be fulfilled. V, 1239. With the Spirit’s help, what God commands is done with joy and delight. V, 1171. Those who hear divine testimonies are not moved to faith when the hidden grace does not operate in them so that they may believe. IV, 1117. Those who are deterred from faith by the difficulty of the commandments should come, relying not on their own powers but on God’s grace; they should come to be helped, not judged. IV, 457.

The grace by which God’s commandments are fulfilled is obtained through humble prayer. IV, 1581. It is obtained through faith. IV, 1549, 1560. Grace is not thereby unnecessary to the will because the Apostle said, “Let him do what he wills.” X, 314. Those who deny the necessity of grace must be resisted with the greatest sharpness and force. X, 202. The necessity of grace for doing any good work is shown by an analogy. X, 261. The clearest testimony to grace is prayer. II, 766, 979, 990; X, 887. The help of grace for not sinning would not be requested unless it were necessary. X, 313, 314, 1534. Innocentius teaches the necessity of grace. II, 781, 785. He says that it is unjust and ungrateful to deny grace. II, 781, 782, 784. Ambrose teaches this. X, 382, 383. There was a dispute between Augustine and Pelagius concerning the necessity of grace. X, 276.

### True grace opposed to Pelagian grace

What true grace is, as opposed to Pelagian grace. X, 374. What should be called true grace. X, 332, 378. What true grace is according to Paul. II, 853. What grace is proclaimed in the Church. X, 338. What grace the catholic faith proclaims. X, 1213. The catholic position concerning grace. X, 980, 1033. The grace of Christians. II, 767, 768. What the grace of God through Jesus Christ is. X, 917. In what grace is defined. X, 231. In what the Christian faith recognizes grace as consisting. X, 220.

### Definition of the grace of Christ

The grace of Christ is defined. X, 378. Grace is the inspiration of love. X, 617. Grace in the proper sense, the grace of Christians. II, 1321. The grace of the New Testament is love. II, 853; III, 84; X, 374. Love is poured into hearts so that the healed soul may do good not from fear of punishment, but from love of righteousness. X, 233. Grace is certain knowledge and victorious delight. X, 170. The effects of grace are illumination and delight. X, 167. How God teaches through grace. X, 368. God teaches sweetness by inspiring love; he teaches discipline by giving patience; he teaches knowledge by illuminating the understanding. IV, 1549. Whether God teaches everyone through grace or not. X, 971. Whoever learns through grace does absolutely whatever he has learned must be done. X, 367, 368. Whoever has learned through grace comes; whoever does not come has not learned. X, 368. The grace professed by Christians is that by which the good is not merely suggested but made persuasive. X, 366. “Then I learn to act, if you teach me in your sweetness.” V, 830.

True grace is the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which delight in and love of the good arise in the soul. X, 203. Grace gives the delight in righteousness by which the excess of concupiscence is overcome. VI, 225. How grace frees from the law of sin and death. VIII, 125. It frees the delight of the will from consenting to pleasure. X, 560. Through the Holy Spirit it comes about in us that we delight in not sinning, where there is freedom; apart from this Spirit, we delight in sinning, where there is slavery. X, 218. The sweetness of grace makes what is commanded more delightful than what hinders it. X, 233, 561. Grace is the blessing of sweetness. X, 586. When the things by which we advance toward God delight us, this is inspired and supplied by the grace of God. VI, 127. Grace is signified by the terms “milk” and “honey”: it is sweet and nourishing. V, 167. Nothing signifies grace more than an abundance of milk. V, 199. Grace is signified by milk, because delectable mercy is poured freely into little ones. IV, 827, 1857. Spiritual grace is understood as love of God and neighbor. III, 2063.

The grace of God brings about the fulfillment through love of God’s commandments, which could not be fulfilled through fear. IV, 1579. God gives sweetness so that we may do good truly and rightly—that is, not from fear of carnal evil, but from delight in spiritual good. IV, 1565, 1566. Whoever does not yet act—whether by not doing at all or by not acting from love—should pray to receive what he does not yet have. X, 948. See “Prayer.” The power and sweetness of divine grace is understood only by the one who loves, etc. III, 1609. Grace is hidden from those who fear punishment. X, 233. Grace works inwardly. X, 316. It [Col. 0321] operates within. X, 114. God does not help outwardly but inwardly. X, 226. How hidden grace is and how far removed from the senses. X, 971. People can because they so will; they so will because God works through his grace in such a way that they will. X, 900, 939. Who is capable of willing and being able, unless the one who, by calling, granted that we should will, helps us by inspiring us so that we can? V, 1014. Grace brings it about not only that we wish to do what is right, but also that we can. III, 2066. “I wish you to will, but it is not enough that you will; you must be helped so that you may will fully and fulfill what you will.” V, 894. Sometimes God does in you what is not done by you; but nothing is ever done by you that he does not do in you. V, 380. God works in us in such a way that we also work; he shows himself to be the worker who calls upon the helper. V, 108. “I can thirst for you, but I cannot water myself.” IV, 1852.

The grace of God makes us do good works. X, 1142. It makes us act. X, 367, 901. It does so by supplying the will with the most effective strength. X, 367, 901. It is boastfulness to say, “We do what God promises.” X, 1208. What God promises that human beings will do, God himself brings about. X, 976. The one who promises promises what he does, not what you do. V, 894. What is done by you, God himself does in you. V, 380. The grace of God not only effects the forgiveness of sins, but also makes the human spirit cooperate with it in the performance of good works. IV, 988. God prepares the will, not merely by applying the Law and teaching to man’s free choice, but by so acting upon the mind that he inclines it to assent to the Law and teaching. II, 980, 987. Nothing meritorious on the human side precedes the grace of God; rather, grace itself merits increase, so that, once increased, it may merit perfection, with the will accompanying but not leading, following but not preceding. II, 819.

### The power of grace

The power of grace. III, 25, 84. Its potency and energy. X, 936, 971. The source of grace’s power and efficacy. X, 936, 971, 972. The power of God’s grace to convert human wills. X, 568. Grace, or God’s will to save, is certain and most effective. VI, 276. The gentle force of grace. V, 730. Grace inclines our heart wherever it wills. X, 372. God can convert the evil wills of human beings, whenever he chooses, to good. VI, 277. The grace of the Savior so acts upon the will that it is said to be moved by grace. X, 323. We will, but God works in us the will; we act, but God works in us the action. X, 1013. The weakness of the human will has been assisted so that it is moved by divine grace unfailingly and irresistibly. X, 940. Through the help of grace, it comes about that they most invincibly will what is good and most invincibly refuse to abandon it. X, 940. Grace is that which no hard heart rejects. X, 971. The will of God, who wishes to save, is not hindered by human will. VI, 276. Grace is given so that hardness of heart may be removed. X, 971. The grace of God anticipates those who resist, so that they become willing. X, 618. God’s grace makes the unwilling willing. X, 1299. Grace removes the heart of stone—that is, the most obstinate will, utterly inflexible toward God. X, 898, 971. The efficacy of grace, in the extent to which it moves, is shown in Peter. X, 382. The basis on which Paul proves that grace was not empty in him. X, 342. The nature and power of grace are recognized from prayer. X, 980. Scriptural testimonies on behalf of grace. X, 618. Testimonies from Cyprian. X, 626, 628. From Ambrose. X, 633.

Catholics do not assert fate under the name of grace. X, 577. Why the Pelagians make this objection against Catholics. X, 577. The difficulty of reconciling free will and grace. X, 383.
