The question concerning God’s grace and free will is extremely difficult and intelligible to few. II, 970, 972. The question is obscure. X, 981.

Grace must not be defended in such a way that free will is removed; nor must free will be exalted in such a way that we are judged ungrateful toward grace. III, 1778; X, 168. Neither should God’s grace be denied, nor should free will be defended in such a way that it is separated from God’s grace. II, 969–972, 974, 981. This is proved from the Scriptures. II, 973. Those who proclaim grace in such a way as to deny human free will are in error. II, 969. Those who believe that free will is helped by God’s grace so that we may think and do what is right hold the correct view. II, 969. If there is no grace of God, how does Christ save the world? If there is no free will, how does he judge the world? II, 969. Both grace and free will are asserted. X, 877, 888. Both are required for salvation. X, 893.

Grace does not remove free will. X, 233. It does not drive free will away, but rather recalls it after it has been driven away by vices. X, 1296. Through God’s grace free choice is truly made free to choose and do good. II, 987. The freer the will, the healthier it is; and the healthier it is, the more subject it is to divine grace. II, 676, 677. All the pages of Scripture teach us that free will can do nothing when deprived of heavenly support. Innoc. II, 785. Through the hidden inspiration of God’s grace, the will is prepared by the Lord. II, 987. What freedom is like without grace. V, 856. Freedom without grace is not freedom but defiance. II, 682. Without grace, man falls headlong through free will. X, 889. God’s grace frees free will so that it may be free for doing what is right. I, 625. What can we do by free will unless the one who commands us helps us? IV, 1792.

### The cooperation of grace and free will

The concurrence of grace and free will. V, 902. Grace and free [Col. 0322] will are required for living well. X, 886. The effort of our will must be joined to God’s grace. X, 154. To incline the heart toward God’s testimonies is at once a divine gift and an act of one’s own will. IV, 1569. When Christ crucified is preached, one hearer despises him and another ascends; let the one who despises attribute it to himself, and let the one who ascends not claim it for himself. V, 730. The children of God are moved by the Spirit of God—not because they themselves do nothing, but so that they may not fail to do anything good; they are moved by the good so that they may act. IV, 1581. You act and are acted upon, and you act well when you are acted upon by the good. V, 855, 717. No one is helped by grace unless he himself also acts. X, 315. The one who made you without you does not justify you without you. V, 923. Exhortations, commands, and instructions demonstrate free will; prayers, however, demonstrate grace. X, 349, 350. One must not presume upon either grace or free will. X, 579. Pelagius said that all graces and virtues can be possessed by each person in one way, Caelestius in another. X, 556.

The distinction between grace given before and after the fall. X, 933. What sort of help of grace was granted to the first man in the state of innocence. X, 935. The help of grace would have been present in the state of intact nature. X, 274. Like light to healthy eyes. X, 274. Our weakness now needs to be helped by greater gifts of grace. X, 939. A more powerful grace is needed after the fall than before it. X, 934. The grace given in Christ is far more powerful than the grace given to the first man. X, 936. There are two kinds of help from grace: one without which something does not happen, and another by which it happens. X, 936. This is explained by the examples of nourishment and blessedness. X, 936. What help of grace man now needs. X, 937. The help of grace does not assist without our will. X, 204, 209, 212. Did the Pelagians remove the diversity of graces? X, 339. The distinction between the gift of perseverance granted to Adam and that granted to other human beings. II, 1010. One grace belongs to the person struggling, another to the victor. X, 1186.

### Prevenient and subsequent grace

Prevenient and subsequent grace. V, 942, 952, 1650. Grace goes before us. III, 1843, 1851. It goes before us so that we may love God. X, 1131. God’s mercy everywhere goes before us. V, 1014. Who is capable of willing and being able, unless the one who, by calling, granted that we should will, helps us by inspiring us so that we can? V, 1014. Grace does not cooperate with a will that already exists first, but goes before it so that it may work upon it. X, 1112. Far be it from us to put ourselves first in God’s gifts and God second. X, 586. Before man acts, God acts first. X, 1135. How grace goes before us in all things. V, 952.

### Operative and cooperative grace

Operative and cooperative grace. X, 901. Grace works without us so that we may will; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, it cooperates with us. X, 901. Without it—whether operating so that we may will or cooperating with us when we will—we are entirely powerless for works of piety. X, 901. Grace helps each person’s purpose, in what sense this is said catholically. X, 618. The will must strive. X, 156. We too work, certainly, but we cooperate with grace as it works. X, 264.

True grace helps in two ways. X, 1244. The help of grace is twofold. X, 1534.

To attribute to grace, and not to oneself, what is done through grace is a duty of piety and humility. X, 342. When grace is under discussion, everything must be attributed to God. X, 1000, 1001. We live more safely if we attribute everything to grace, rather than entrusting part to it and part to ourselves. X, 1001. God’s grace should be understood in such a way that, from the beginning of one’s transformation to the end of one’s perfection, whoever boasts should boast in the Lord. X, 588.

The grace of Christ abounds much more greatly than Adam’s sin, in what sense. X, 116, 118, 462, 826, 1229, 1230. It benefits more than sin harmed. X, 1181, 1182. Does sin benefit because of the abundance of grace? X, 205. How grace abounded. III, 2068; X, 1200. To what extent it surpasses sin. X, 1236. The benefits of Christ’s grace are more abundant than the harms of Adam’s fault. X, 1179, 1180. Grace abounded for many, not for a greater number. X, 1229, 1230, 1231.

Benefits of divine grace. I, 1296; IV, 279, 488, 499, 1319, 1321, 1322, 1429, 1430, 1629; V, 894, 952. What grace contributes. III, 2065. It works in us. II, 817. Grace distinguishes from the mass of perdition. II, 817, 820, 851, 860, 969. It distinguishes the redeemed from the lost. VI, 278. The grace of God is properly that which distinguishes the good from the evil. X, 968. And by which we have been made sheep and believers. V, 173. How grace can be common in one person and another, even without the person’s knowledge, whereas guilt cannot be so. II, 360. Grace makes human beings children of God. V, 691. The grace of the New Testament is to be born from God. II, 541. Grace makes the very persons who were evil good. X, 1133. The Savior’s benefit is twofold: first, the remission of sins; afterward, the healing of illnesses. X, 1514. Grace both erases sin and grants that it not be committed. X, 261. God grants grace in two ways: by forgiving past iniquity and by helping us not to enter into temptation. X, 1120. Grace causes the Law to be fulfilled, nature to be liberated, and sin not to rule. X, 897. God justifies by grace not only by forgiving evil deeds, but also by granting charity for doing good. X, 1212. By grace the sick are healed, the sluggish are roused, and those who are willing are helped. II, 831. The grace of God contributes nothing more useful to us here than that we may die to sin. [Col. 0323] II, 974. In each human being, the reign of death is destroyed solely by the grace of the Savior. X, 116.

Four benefits of grace are enumerated: first, the remission of sins. V, 752. Second, the healing of the illness remaining after baptism. V, 752. Third, redemption from every corruption and concupiscence. V, 752. Fourth, the crown of righteousness. V, 753. Liberation from four temptations through the grace of God. IV, 1421. Every weak person is made powerful by grace, and through it becomes conscious of his weakness. I, 781. The grace of God makes people strong in tribulation. IV, 1560, 1561. Now it belongs solely to the grace of God that we approach God and do not depart from him. X, 1001. For some, grace is the water of contradiction; for others, the water of sanctification. III, 737. Whoever remains chaste from the beginning is governed by God; whoever becomes chaste from being unchaste is corrected by him; and whoever remains unchaste to the end is abandoned by him. VI, 422. Through grace a human being is created anew. III, 412. Whether grace makes a completely new person. X, 844.

Various effects of grace. X, 1192. Even those who have become hardened through long practice of sin can be restored through repentance, according to Pelagius. X, 379. We have been restored through Christ’s grace and reborn as a better person, according to Pelagius. X, 379. Every work of grace belongs to the renewal of the age to come. VII, 729. The soul is illumined by grace as a cloud is by the sun. III, 870. With God granting and assisting, understanding advances toward understanding what it believes, and faith toward believing what it understands. IV, 1552. Grace is the water by which inner thirst is irrigated. III, 737. Grace makes the slow equal to the gifted. III, 882. To end this life with a will consenting to saving doctrine belongs to the elect. II, 982. Grace brings those predestined and called according to the purpose to the highest perfection and glorification. X, 367. The grace of God makes steps for a person by which he may ascend to blessedness. IV, 1063. Grace is the way by which one reaches the heavenly homeland. II, 393. God does not give such salvation as anyone could extort. IV, 200. A person will receive immortality through grace, which he would have received through merit had he not sinned. VI, 282. In eternal life the saints will know more fully what good grace has bestowed upon them. VI, 275. The true grace of God can be defended even if there were no original sin, as Pelagius wished. X, 1010. Through God’s grace we become both debtors and renderers of payment. V, 1368.

Grace is from God. X, 917. It is God’s gift. V, 788. Obedience and repentance, self-restraint and wisdom, are gifts of God. VI, 421. The cause of grace, through which sinners are saved, is hidden in God. III, 406, 407. Whoever denies that the good which is from God is from God does injury to the whole Trinity. II, 852.

Grace is from Christ as God and human being. III, 1842. Our salvation is from God, so that we would not be liberated through Christ either if he were not God. VI, 282. Grace has been placed in Christ, great and full. IV, 157. How great is the grace of Christ’s humility and passion. III, 1402. Everything good that you have belongs to Christ. IV, 450. Without Christ, nothing; in him we are capable of everything. IV, 232. The common source of grace. V, 1437. The source of grace opened in Christ. VI, 283. The grace Christ bestowed upon us is his joy in us, and our joy. III, 1845.

Grace is and is called grace because it is given freely. I, 597; V, 177. Grace is given freely. X, 909, 1003. Unless it is free, it is not grace. VI, 282. Grace is what a mother gives freely, and she is distressed if there is no one to receive it. IV, 1857. Gratuitous grace. II, 875, 877; X, 249. It is not grace if it is not gratuitous. IV, 158, 488, 891, 892, 895, 998, 1364. Grace is not owed but freely given. X, 1131, 1133. The gratuitous grace of God is the oil of the lamps. III, 1583.

The ineffable grace by which God chose us. III, 1851. Grace does not find people to choose; it makes them. II, 821. It finds everyone unrighteous. VI, 622. The election of grace is not made on the basis of any preceding merits, whether of parents or of infants, nor on the foreknowledge of works. II, 887. Grace is called by the name of “lot” because in a lot there is no election, but the will of God. IV, 246. Jacob was loved and Esau hated before either had any personal merits. VI, 277. In Esau’s hatred, a punitive judgment is imposed on one who deserves it; in Jacob’s love, mercy is bestowed on one who does not deserve it. VI, 277. God liberates no one except by gratuitous mercy. II, 820, 882. An example of gratuitous grace is found in infants. II, 814; X, 909. That grace is not given according to merits, and that no one is punished except for his own merits, is most clearly inferred from infants. X, 1008.

We have been called and predestined freely. V, 863. Calling belongs to the grace of God, not to merits. IV, 89. Grace is not given according to merits. III, 871. After the fall, the liberation of human beings is gratuitous through grace. X, 933. The grace by which the will is liberated precedes the will. I, 597. Julianus vainly exalts the merits of the will against grace. X, 1140. Grace is the effect of God’s mercy, not a payment for human willing. X, 1007. God’s good will precedes our good will; and this is the invincible shield by which the enemy suggesting despair of salvation is repelled. IV, 89, 151.

[Col. 0324] Grace is not given according to merits, whether to adults or to infants. II, 984, 985, 986. It is utterly false that grace is given according to our merits. II, 970, 971; X, 572, 554, 567, 758, 873, 875, 877, 889, 981, 1012, 1028, 1031, 1032. Grace is not from our merits but from the mercy of God. II, 984, 985; X, 219, 577. Truly gratuitous grace, owed to no merits. X, 1133, 1135. Grace is not bestowed on us for the merits of a preceding life. X, 127.

Grace precedes merits. VI, 115, 620; X, 628. Merits do not precede grace. X, 374, 479, 898, 964. Nothing of yours preceded, so that you might receive it. IV, 891. Your merits did not precede; the benefits of God came before you. IV, 234, 585. Grace does not find righteous people whom it might crown, but offenses which it might forgive. IV, 754. Good gifts—namely, grace—are rendered for evil merits. X, 620. Grace is given freely, and it is given to the undeserving. X, 340. Grace was given to the undeserving so that the crown might be rendered to one who deserved it. X, 341, 342. Punishment is not rendered to many as something owed; grace is not given as something owed. X, 1132, 1133. Since punishment would not be imposed freely, the benefit was therefore bestowed freely. IV, 158. Grace is no longer grace if we insist that merits preceded it. III, 1851. If any merits precede it. III, 2061. *Retractationes*: It is no longer given freely but is rendered as a debt. V, 177. Grace both for beginning and for persevering to the end is not given according to merits. X, 1012. The grace by which the heart of stone is taken away is preceded not by good merits but by evil ones. X, 898. The gratuitous grace of God, with no preceding merits, is not unjust. X, 125. To what extent grace can be said to be given according to our merits. X, 890.

Grace precedes good works. X, 1131. Works arise from grace, not grace from works. II, 817. Grace precedes faith. VI, 620. The grace of faith is not given on the merit of works. IV, 262, 263, 1116. Whether one who is justified by the election of grace can be called or said to be worthy by designation. X, 345. Whether the Apostle was at least worthy through faith, so that such great grace might be given to him. X, 340. Those who say that they ask God in faith to grant them perseverance in the good things they have and to add those they lack—and thus that everything is given by God—are refuted. V, 913. When you begin to bless the Lord in a good life, his works bless him, not your merits. IV, 1335. God finds nothing to demand unless he has granted what he finds. III, 1031. Grace is defended without merits, even if there were no original sin. X, 1010. To say that grace is given according to merits is to deny grace. X, 1026. It is to destroy grace. X, 553. Those who glory in their works do not attain grace. IV, 887. If you wish to be a stranger to grace, boast of your merits. IV, 263. To what extent it can be said that human nature deserves grace. X, 744. Grace is not given according to merits; rather, when it is given, it gives merits themselves. II, 980; VI, 620. When grace helps the righteous person, it seems to be repaid for merits; but it does not cease to be grace, because it helps what it itself bestowed. VI, 621. You were loved first, so that you might become worthy to be loved. V, 781. We were loved so that we might love. V, 942. Both faith and prayer are from the grace of God. V, 915. Grace is added to those who live piously. X, 371. Grace for grace, eternal life: it is a reward, and yet it is grace. II, 880; III, 1399; IV, 262; VI, 282. Gratuitous and effective grace is proved from the words of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. X, 620.

The evident proof of divine grace is the singular assumption of a human being by the Word. II, 847; VI, 250; VII, 308. Grace shone forth especially in Christ. V, 435, 940; X, 168. Grace without merits, in the righteousness of Christ’s humanity, is an example of the grace by which we are justified. X, 1138. Outstanding examples of grace and predestination are found in infants and in Christ. X, 977. By the same grace by which Christ was made, the Christian person is made. X, 982. Christ did not demand what was owed; he paid what he did not owe. IV, 498. He came with the kiss of grace. IV, 498. Grace shines forth especially in the robber. V, 435. In Peter. V, 480. In Paul. V, 1268. From this it is proved that grace is not given according to merits. X, 888.

How hidden is the distribution of grace. X, 569. The inscrutable judgments of God in the distribution of grace. X, 980, 1009, 1011. The gifts of grace are given from the depth of God’s judgment. V, 181, 1294. Grace is an inscrutable depth. V, 907. Grace is given according to the good pleasure of God’s will. X, 1009. It is hidden in his will. V, 371, 372. The dispensation of grace is very hidden, but nevertheless just. VII, 443; VIII, 451. The grace of God is not unjust. VII, 376. The distribution of grace occurs for hidden yet just reasons. VIII, 451. Not everyone belongs to grace. IV, 1394. Of two infants, one reaches grace and the other does not. V, 177, 178. Why the grace of God comes to one through Jesus Christ and does not come to another may be a hidden cause; it cannot be an unjust one. X, 125. It is not by fate that some infants receive help and others do not. X, 1011. Grace in the election of certain infants for baptism. X, 824. The inscrutable height of grace in the distinction between infants who reach baptism and those who do not. X, 1523. It is inscrutable why God liberates or punishes one rather than another. X, 1003. Why one is liberated and another condemned belongs to the inscrutable judgments of God; nevertheless, there is no iniquity with God. [Col. 0325] X, 761. Nor is he therefore a respecter of persons or unjust. II, 875, 885. Thus neither does mercy hinder the truth by which one who deserves punishment is punished, nor does truth hinder the mercy by which one who does not deserve it is liberated. II, 877. No one is liberated except through undeserved mercy; no one is condemned except through deserved judgment. VI, 275. Even if no one were liberated, no one could rightly reproach the justice of God. VI, 278. Those who are liberated had to be liberated in such a way that, from the many who were not liberated, what the entire mass deserved might be shown. VI, 278. All deserve condemnation; if all were liberated, what is owed to sin by justice would remain hidden, and if no one were liberated, what grace bestows would remain hidden. II, 875. Why one person receives help and another does not must be referred to the hidden judgments of God. X, 910. Why grace is given to one and not to another. V, 905. Why it is not given to everyone. X, 971, 1009. Since grace is given freely. X, 1002. Why it is not given to all, or not always to the saints. X, 170. God is not unjust when he does not give grace to everyone, and gives it to one rather than another. X, 1002. Some receive help from grace before baptism, some not even after baptism. X, 1115. Grace is given to some from mercy, while to others it is not given according to truth. X, 169, 170. Why he makes some religious and not others belongs to the depth of God’s judgments. X, 1135. Why one person is persuaded in such a way as to be convinced, but another is not so persuaded. X, 241. Why some receive grace for a time and are allowed to live here until they fall. II, 983. Those to whom grace is not given do not receive it by the just judgment of God. II, 984, 986. Grace both justifies the ungodly and helps the righteous. VI, 620. But when he does so, he does it through mercy; when he does not, he does not do so through judgment. VI, 277. The grace of God by which human minds are revived so that they can hear the commands of health is exceedingly hidden. IV, 1116. Grace releases some sinners who confess their sins, and raises others who even defend them. IV, 816. Grace was given to Paul, who was unbelieving and a cruel persecutor. V, 913. Grace does not move one so much when it is bestowed on the undeserving as when it is denied to others equally undeserving. X, 125. Augustine does not know why one is helped in this way and another in that way, or even why one is not helped; nevertheless, he knows that God does this with the highest equity, known to God himself. II, 354.

Grace is voluntary rain. IV, 819, 1735; VIII, 887. The dew of Hermon. IV, 1735. In God, who has mercy on whomever he wills, there is no iniquity. V, 179. Why God has mercy on whomever he wills is beyond human understanding. V, 179. Let the equity of God, who has mercy on whomever he wills, be believed now, until it is seen afterward. V, 180. God has mercy through great goodness and hardens through no iniquity. VI, 278. See “God’s will.” Grace is help in the vessels of mercy and a warning in the vessels of wrath. X, 581. Grace is not given to everyone, and to those to whom it is given it is given neither according to the merits of their works nor according to their will. II, 984, 985. How is it to be understood that God wills all human beings to be saved? II, 985. Whether, in the election of grace, greater intelligence, fewer sins, honorable and useful learning, or the will itself is taken into consideration. VI, 127, 128. Grace is not given according to the qualities of intellects. X, 126. By the grace of God, human wills are preceded, and through it they are prepared rather than grace being given on account of their merit. II, 987. God is neither prevented by fatal necessity from conferring that benefit on those who are to be condemned, nor does he confer it on others through respect of persons. X, 1505. Why the good Lord God sometimes grants not even to his saints either certain knowledge or victorious delight with respect to some righteous work. X, 170. Why God heals his saints and faithful servants more slowly from certain vices. X, 170. By delaying the help of grace, God is present. V, 892, 893. In human beings there is a cause why they are not helped by God. X, 167. For those to whom grace is absent, this is already the punishment of sin; for those to whom it is given, it is not given as something owed. X, 936. At no time has the remedy of grace against sin been denied to the predestined. X, 179. The grace of Christ was not lacking, even before his coming, to those to whom it was fitting that it be imparted. VI, 288. Through the gift of grace and faith, the ancients too were justified beforehand. VI, 621. The power of the grace of the Sacraments. IV, 984. Grace does not depend on visible Sacraments. III, 712.

Who are helped by grace. II, 678. A person begins to receive grace from the moment he begins to believe in God. VI, 111. Before the remission of sins, grace inspires faith and the fear of God by imparting salutary feeling and effect in prayer. II, 885. Faith merits the grace of doing good. II, 818. And obtains it. II, 760. The grace of God is given to those who ask, seek, and knock in faith. II, 989. Knowledge of one’s own weakness is necessary for obtaining grace. V, 481. To desire grace is the beginning of grace. X, 917. How do you wish to receive the grace of divine goodness, when you do not open the bosom of your will? V, 903. For God to wish to give, you too must adapt your will to receive. V, 903. You must bring a receptive faith, so that through the inundation of grace you may humble yourself, entreat God, and presume nothing about yourself. V, 200. God both commands and brings it about that the will to receive God’s grace precedes it. III, 598. Grace is rain: the low places are filled, the high places are dried. V, 730. The proud person loses the grace given to the humble. V, 200. A person is not yet wholly cut off from the inner light of God while he is in this life. [Col. 0326] IV, 94.

Grace is given to adults for each individual act. II, 828, 983, 984. Love and delight in righteousness are signs of grace. X, 918. The excuse of the perverse is dissolved when they say that they did not receive grace. II, 882. Grace must not be defended in such a way that people, as though secure because of it, love evil works. II, 974. God will not abandon his work if he is not abandoned by his work. IV, 1890. Grace must also be urged upon the pious and those who fear God. X, 275. Who are not subject to the grace of God. X, 896. In the Epistle to the Romans, the Apostle spoke in his own person and in the person of others who are still under grace, not under the Law. X, 557, 561, 562. From the Catholic teaching concerning the defect of origin and grace, the disadvantages alleged by the Pelagians do not follow. X, 1409. Scriptural passages from which the Pelagians took an opportunity for error are explained. X, 585. Before Pelagius, interpreters of Scripture touched only briefly on the difficult questions concerning grace. X, 980. The depth of gratuitous grace. II, 564, 569. In this depth the understanding of many is crushed. II, 565. Those who wished to debate the depth of God were submerged in the depth, and from this arose the error concerning the sin of souls before the body. V, 905. In the mystery of grace and election, faithful ignorance is better than presumptuous knowledge. V, 179. Some foolish people think that the Apostle, in answering the question concerning election and rejection, failed and, lacking an answer to give, exclaimed, “O man, who are you?” and so forth. VI, 278. Augustine did not at first find the grace by which God chose us. III, 2061. *Retractationes*: The question concerning the distribution of grace is inscrutable. X, 621. To what extent it is resolved by the Apostle. X, 621. Whoever dislikes this answer, “O the depth,” and so forth, should seek more learned authorities, but beware lest he find presumptuous people. X, 241. Why Augustine did not discuss grace, predestination, and so forth in the books *On Free Will*. X, 1008. The books *On Free Will* are wrongly brought against Augustine in the question of grace. X, 1010. Augustine himself answered the objection drawn from the books *On Free Will*. X, 1010.

The commendation of grace. III, 1607; IV, 1851. The grace of God that liberates us commends itself to us throughout all the holy Scriptures. IV, 874. And especially in Psalm 70. IV, 875. How the Apostle commends grace. II, 887. The praise and proclamation of grace are the condemnation and reproach of sins. X, 205. The grace of God is to be proclaimed at the feasts of the martyrs. V, 1286. Grace and glory are sometimes said to have been given already through the firmness of the promise, although they are to be given only at their proper time. III, 85. Why Augustine took such great pleasure in discussing grace. X, 242. The book *On the Grace of the New Testament*, written by Augustine on account of the new heresy hostile to the grace of God. I, 645. Two books, *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin*. I, 650. The book *On Nature and Grace*. I, 647. The book *On Grace and Free Will*, written for the monks of Hadrumetum. I, 656. The book *On Correction and Grace*, sent to the same men. I, 656.

What grace or gratitude (*gratia*) is. VI, 20, 21. An innate force implanted this. VI, 20, 21. How necessary knowledge of God’s grace and gratitude are. V, 1286. Thanksgiving and prayer are necessary. II, 851, 856. Thanksgiving is a testimony to grace. X, 154, 996. Thanksgiving and prayer show that the will is prepared by preceding grace, not that grace is given on account of a preceding merit of the will. II, 988. Thanksgiving is illusory if thanks are given to God for something he himself neither granted nor accomplished. X, 996. If one human being were to thank another for something he thought the other had not provided, or knew the other had not provided, it would more truly be called flattery or mockery than thanksgiving. X, 989, 1245. Thanks are to be given to God not only when he does good but also when he corrects. IV, 562, 563; 1171, 1172. Thanksgiving is owed to the physician by everyone. V, 950. One who gives thanks for a little is incomparably better than one who exalts himself over much. II, 110; V, 1287. From this comes the greater thanksgiving owed to God. VIII, 624. The whole purpose of thanksgiving is to prevent us from being ungrateful. II, 576. In thanksgiving nothing else is done except that whoever glories may glory in the Lord. II, 576. We may give thanks to him, but we may not repay him. IV, 498. God demands thanksgiving for his benefits. IV, 371. Human beings are not sufficient to give thanks to God for both general and particular benefits. VII, 221. We give thanks to God in words, but retain them in deed. IV, 1140. The gifts of grace become one’s own when one loves what one receives and gives thanks to the one who gave it. V, 908. Thanksgiving is a more sacred sacrifice of praise. VIII, 624. The faithful know where it is said, “Let us give thanks.” V, 439. Thanksgiving to the Lord our God is a great sacrament in the sacrifice of the New Testament. II, 558. What is the difference between supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings? II, 636. Prayers are made before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; prayers when it is blessed; intercessions or petitions when the people are blessed; and after all these, thanksgivings. II, 637.

Emperor Gratian. II, 400. Gratian made Theodosius his partner in the empire in preference to his own brother. VII, 171. Gratian was killed by the tyrant’s sword. VII, 171. He was avenged by Theodosius. VII, 171.

Basilica of Gratian. V, 849.

Gratianopolis, a city in Gaul. VII, 719. Not far from the city of Gratianopolis is a spring in which lighted torches are extinguished and extinguished ones are kindled. VII, 719.

The difference between congratulation and prayer. IV, 1337.

Gregorianus. VI, 475.

Gregory, an Eastern bishop. II, 626; X, 649, 677, 866, 1024. His first apology concerning his flight. X, 677.

Unless God directed human steps, they would always go astray. IV, 372.

The security of God’s flock. V, 296.

God governs without labor what he has made. V, 692. God, having entered into flesh, did not abandon or lose care for governing the universe. II, 517. Government is best when all things are ordered and administered in their proper times. VI, 566. Music was granted to human beings to indicate the harmony of divine governance. II, 726.

The birthday of the martyr Guddens. V, 1335.

The temptation of gluttony. I, 797, 798. Gluttons described. III, 97.

Guntasius. IV, 376. Bishop of Benevento. IV, 381.

Whirlpools. IX, 236.

Gymnosophists, a sect of philosophers among the Indians. VII, 426, 462.

H.

Recognize that you possess what you possess, and that of yourself you possess nothing, so that you may be neither proud nor ungrateful. IV, 1084. “As much as you possess, so great you will be”: a proverb of the avaricious. IV, 609. A person is called blessed by possessing or by acting. IV, 1061. A person is truly happy not when he has what he loves, but when he loves what ought to be loved. IV, 202. You are unworthy to possess what you do not wish to be. V, 630. Each person should be said to possess something when he uses it well. V, 327. He who does not know how to use gold does not possess it, but is possessed by it. IV, 1646. Something can be possessed without its being known that it is possessed. V, 462. No one gives himself what he does not have. IV, 744.

How God is said to dwell on high and yet to regard the lowly. IV, 1472. God is high; he does not dwell in you if you wish to be high. IV, 1186. Dwelling together in unity belongs to the perfect. IV, 1729, 1734, 1736. Those in whom charity is not perfect, when they are together in unity, disturb the others, just as a restless beast breaks with its kicks what is yoked to it. IV, 1736.

Our dwelling should not depart from heaven. IV, 557. Our dwelling is in heaven or in the world according as we love God or the world. V, 928. God’s dwelling in Christ is far otherwise than in the saints. IV, 828.

The Apostles, angels, and preachers of truth are God’s dwelling-place. IV, 296. By good works we become a dwelling-place for God. V, 1478.

*Habitus* is said in many ways. VI, 84. What *habitus* is. VI, 396.

A matron’s dress is distinct from a widow’s and a nun’s garment; it can suit married women without compromising religious observance. II, 1081. The dress or manner of life by which each person follows the faith does not concern the City of God. VII, 647.

Hadrian surrendered Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Assyria to the Persians. VII, 135.

What the woman with the issue of blood signifies. V, 485, 486.

To cling to God is life; to depart from him is death. IV, 1889.

What heresy is is altogether difficult to define. II, 999. What Cresconius thinks is the difference between heresy and schism. IX, 469. Heresy is properly an inveterate schism. IX, 471. Not every error is heresy, although every heresy reckoned as a fault cannot be heresy without some error. VIII, 23. There is no heresy that does not call itself truth. VIII, 507. No heresy is Catholic. IX, 589. Heresy is later than the Church. IX, 122. All heresies went out from the Church like useless branches cut off from the vine. V, 53, 55, 280; VI, 635. In what sense heresies are daughters of the Church, and what they have in common with it. V, 233.

How heresies and schisms arise. IX, 153. Heresies arise from Scriptures not rightly understood. III, 1536. The author of a heresy is a mountain where sheep sometimes find pasture, but from God’s rain, not from the mountain’s hardness. V, 279. Leaders of heresies are designated by the name of mountains. IV, 347, 1651, 1652. Only great men have produced heresies. IV, 1652. Heresies and schisms are the Church’s dung. V, 53. They occur through carnal people. V, 49. They were foretold by the Prophets. VIII, 288. Why the devil introduced them after idolatry. VI, 713. Why they are permitted. IV, 106.

Heresies are useful. VII, 477, 612. They benefit the Church, and how. I, 746; III, 130, 173. What good they bring to the Church by occasion. VI, 341, 713; X, 1026. Through them it becomes conspicuous what the Church of God thinks and what sound doctrine contains. I, 746. Faith and love are proved more soundly through heresies. II, 793. Where sound faith is absent, justice cannot exist. III, 1236. Heresies would not be allowed to spring up over the earth unless contradiction itself exercised sound discipline. VI, 180. God permits heresies so that we may apply ourselves to the study of the Scriptures. III, 173. Heresies are like torrents that roar for a time. IV, 685. The first heresy arose among Christ’s disciples. IV, 643. Ignorance of heresies is safer. V, 988. The gathering of a synod to condemn heresies is not always necessary. X, 638.

Philaster counted 128 heresies. VIII, 33. Epiphanius, however, eighty. VIII, 23. Philastrius and Epiphanius differ about the number of sects for no other reason than that one of them thought one thing to be heresy and the other another thing. II, 999. Various heresies against faith in the Trinity and the Incarnation. VI, 299, 300. Quodvultdeus asks Augustine to explain all heresies from Christ onward, with their errors and rites. II, 999. Especially the heresies after which the Church baptizes, yet does not rebaptize. II, 999. The Pelagian heresy was raised by monks. X, 355. Its principal tenets. X, 557. It was condemned in the Synod of Palestine. X, 333, 334, 335. And by the universal Council held at Carthage, in what year. X, 558, 559. Note: Heresies crushed by the power of the cross. VI, 696.

Heresiots. II, 157.

Who should be considered a heretic. II, 160; VII, 612; VIII, 65; X, 331. What makes a person a heretic cannot be encompassed by a fixed definition at all, or only with the greatest difficulty. VIII, 23. A heretic is not the same as one who believes heretics. VIII, 65. A person does not depart from the Catholic rule if he believes that a heretic falsely professing Catholic doctrines is Catholic. VI, 521. One who says foolish or false things is not immediately to be judged a heretic. X, 330. No one is a heretic unless he resists the doctrine of the Catholic faith once made known. IX, 169. Obstinacy makes a heretic. X, 523, 524. The forehead of heretics is no forehead. X, 751. Heretics and schismatics have made private property for themselves of the Lord’s stolen goods. V, 796. All heretics are heretics not because they despise the Scriptures, but because they do not understand them. II, 459. And because they obstinately assert their false opinions against the Scriptures’ truth. III, 360. Heretics, reading with an evil intention through sin, are compelled to understand wrongly, so that this itself is the punishment of sin. IV, 106. From the obscurity of the sacrament and the enigma of the reading they arm their shamelessness. IX, 400. When they cannot accuse and obscure the truth of divine Scripture, they bring into hatred the people through whom it is preached. II, 272. By their perverse will they procure for themselves both the present desert of blindness and, if they remain untaught through obstinacy, that of future eternal punishment, etc. II, 1084.

Heretics are not in the Church. IX, 440. They do not belong to the Church. VI, 193. They are outside the Church. V, 292, 980, 1167. Hence they are excluded from Catholic communion. III, 127. Heretics are born of the same seed as Catholics, but excluded from the inheritance because of pride. V, 33. When they became puffed up in defending their erroneous opinions, they were excluded from the Catholic Church. IV, 1710. Sometimes good people are expelled from the Church under the name of heresy or schism. III, 128. How many, born in heresy, remain in it, believing that it makes no difference where they hold Christ’s faith. II, 330. Among heretics Christ exists in name only, not in reality. VI, 233. How heretics belong to the people of God. IV, 1427.

Whether a heretic is worse than a heathen or pagan. IX, 223. He is worse than unbelievers. VII, 742. Whether, by the very fact that he is a heretic, he has other vices. IX, 171. Heretics and schismatics differ. III, 127. Heretics could divide the sacraments, as though Christ’s garments; they did not divide charity, or the seamless tunic woven from above. IV, 176. So far as lies in them, heretics destroy the praise which God perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children, since they do not allow little ones to be nourished with the milk of faith. IV, 135. They attempt to overcome the authority of the Church under the name and promise of reason. II, 448. And by this deceptive promise they deceive. I, 1194. Heretics do not prescribe faith to those coming to them, but promise reason. VIII, 79.

Heretics are with us in many things. II, 343. Though they celebrate the same sacraments, they differ in judgment. III, 127. Among them there can be sacraments displaying the form of godliness, but the invisible and spiritual power of godliness cannot be among them. V, 463. They can have many gifts; they cannot have charity. IV, 1343; VI, 137. Whatever they may possess, although holy in itself, they themselves are nevertheless nothing. VI, 137. Neither the faith nor the continence of heretics is true. VI, 368. Fasting does not benefit them. VI, 711. If heretics have performed any miracles, one should be the more on guard. IX, 428. Heretics claim for themselves the glory of martyrs if they suffer anything. [Col. 0329] IX, 105, 106. In vain do they call themselves martyrs and servants of God. IV, 1494.

Heretics would not exist if there were no pride. III, 142. Pride, their one mother, gave birth to all heretics. V, 280. Every heretic is consequently foolish. X, 330. Heretics are always restless because the Holy Spirit opposes them. II, 219. By the restlessness of heretics, our diligence is roused as though from the sleep of idleness. II, 891. The Church is shaken by heretics as by civil wars. IV, 1423. Heretics are useful to the Church. V, 339; VIII, 267. The Church uses them to test its doctrine. III, 127. They exercise the Church’s wisdom and benevolence. VII, 612, 613. By their death, the children of the Catholic Church are awakened from sleep and advance to an understanding of the divine Scriptures. IV, 106. Heretics benefit the Church not by teaching truth, which they do not know, but by stirring it to uncover truth. III, 129. They gave occasion for matters hidden in the Scriptures to be disclosed. IV, 643, 644, 837. By going out from the Church, they benefit the Church in that we are given both zeal for inquiry and an example of fear. IV, 1428. The discovery of truth is more pleasant by comparison with heretics. IV, 126. When heretics are answered from necessity, Catholics are built up to advantage. IV, 1429. From those who think wrongly, those who think rightly are proved. IV, 643. The heretic: enemy and defender of the Christian faith. IV, 111.

**Hatred of heretics** is a sign of greater glory. II, 891. The errors of heretics are true persecutions for those who wish to live piously. VII, 613. Their snares are destructive to the carnal-minded. IX, 148. All heretics are soldiers and auxiliaries of the devil. X, 1545, 1546. Sons of the devil. V, 286. Heretics commonly commend themselves by their small number. III, 1305. They glory in their small number. VIII, 664. This is the voice of all heretics. X, 781, 782. All heretics are confined to a few and to a part. IV, 265, 1428. All heretics give different names to the antiquity of Catholic truth; each of them claims his own particular name. VIII, 707. There is no sect of error that so opposes Christian truth that it does not strive to glory in the name of Christ. VI, 180. Heretics call all who are not of their communion heretics according to their own laws. IV, 684, 685. When heretics are convicted by the truth, they customarily say: “We are sheep; the bishops will have to give an account concerning us.” V, 282. The Apostle declares that heretics attempt what the magicians of Pharaoh attempted. II, 219.

Heretics are compared with a serpent. III, 216. And with chaff. III, 217. They were prefigured by Ham. VII, 477. By foxes dragging fire in their tails. V, 1641. By the sons of concubines. VII, 513. By Ishmael, the other son of Abraham. V, 33. By Samson’s companion who took a wife. V, 1641.

Heretics are antichrists. VII, 686; VIII, 664. Thieves and robbers. III, 1721. They are called dogs. IV, 1925. Wolves of the roads. VI, 682. Beasts of the reed. IV, 836. False prophets. IV, 101. Serpents hardened by indignation. IV, 684. They are called bulls. IV, 836. How certain heretics are in the Church. IX, 444. Some are in the great house of the Church like vessels destined for dishonor. IX, 157. The learned Christian either grieves at or laughs at the vanity of heretics. III, 176.

Heretics are to be healed rather than destroyed. VIII, 173. They are to be recalled from destruction by every means. II, 795. With what disposition one should rise against heresies, and what benefit results from this. X, 397. Why one should answer the writings of heretics. X, 551. Heretics strive not for correction but for contention. IV, 837. Gentleness is to be shown toward heretics who quarrel and revile. V, 1584. Against them one must act not with disputes but rather with prayers before God. V, 1584. Not so much by disputations as by prayers. X, 260. Instruction and prayer are owed to heretics and Pelagians. II, 830. One must pray for heretics and schismatics. IX, 260.

Heretics are to be slain by the spiritual sword, the double-edged blade of both Testaments. VIII, 333. Heretics are convicted all the more forcefully the more avenues are open for avoiding their snares. VIII, 844. Augustine does not wish private crimes to be brought against heretics, but only the fact that they are not Catholics. II, 271. By what method Augustine wished to refute them in his books *On Music*. I, 1194. Augustine’s gentleness and clemency toward them. I, 1311. Those who attack heretics are helped by God. III, 173. Once the author of a heresy has been corrected, the others are more easily recalled. II, 788. Heretics do not defile those who come to communion. IX, 226, 227. It is lawful to deal with a heretic or schismatic concerning the business of the soul, just as it is lawful to deal with them concerning a piece of land or the settlement of a lawsuit. II, 155. During Augustine’s time the Donatists, Maximianists, Manichaeans, Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, and Cataphrygians were flourishing. II, 438. The impious doctrines of heretics are to be refuted by any Catholics whatever; but their impious acts are to be punished by bishops who are present or nearby. X, 558. Innocent says that heretics are to be cut off like rotten members. II, 781, 782, 784.

Heretics are to be recalled to the Church by every means. VI, [Col. 0330] 714. Augustine wishes heretics to be corrected in such a way that they are taught. II, 367. “If they were frightened but not taught, it would seem like a kind of wicked domination; if they were taught but not frightened, they would be moved more sluggishly.” II, 322. Augustine does not refuse to teach a heretic, however proud and obstinate. II, 155. God mercifully admonishes heretics through human authorities. IX, 106, 108. Heretics, schismatics, and pagans can be restrained by severe laws for the sake of religion. II, 802; IX, 44. The usefulness of temporal troubles in bringing heretics back. II, 321, 322, 330. It is piety to trouble them. VI, 715. The action against heretics and schismatics should not be called persecution. III, 1482. Great mercy is shown to heretics (the Donatists) when, through the emperors’ laws, they are unwillingly snatched from their sect, and so forth. II, 798. The emperors’ laws against heretics. IV, 684, 716, 1309. The general law of Theodosius against all heretics. II, 804. The penalty of ten pounds of gold imposed on heretics by Theodosius. II, 804. And by the emperors. II, 306. Laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics were sent to Africa, while Stilicho was alive, through the care of Theodosius’ son. II, 358. The emperors’ laws order heretics to be excluded from the basilicas. IV, 684, 685. The emperor regards as one and the same fault those who, whether by dissembling and conniving or by failing to condemn, have afforded heretics harmful support. II, 927. Augustine pleads with the prefect of the praetorium that the pride of heretics should be healed by frightening them rather than cut away by punishing them. II, 297. Augustine wishes heretics to be corrected, not killed. II, 367. Heretics falsely call those things their property which they have been ordered by the laws of the emperors to surrender. II, 345. Many truly hold and defend Catholic unity, although they approached it through fear. II, 321. Heretics who were falsely thought to have transferred to us were found, in trials, preferable to long-standing Catholics. II, 312. “Because of the imperial law, whoever persecutes you not from love of correcting you but from hatred and hostility is displeasing to us.” II, 345. “Whoever greedily desires your property is displeasing to us.” II, 345. “So too is anyone who holds, not through justice but through avarice, the property of the poor or the basilicas which you held under the name of the Church.” II, 345.

Heretics returning from heresy, even after relapse, are to be received kindly. V, 1358. Heretics and schismatics are to be received into the Church in one way, pagans in another. IX, 478. How heretics are to be received into the Church. IX, 437, 440. It is established that the Easterners at some time judged that heretics should be baptized again. IX, 495, 497. Note (a). Scripture nowhere commanded that those baptized among heretics should be baptized again. IX, 221. When heretics return to the Church, baptism is not to be violated. VI, 137.

A person is made a heretic by perverse dissent, not by the Christian sacraments. II, 343. Heretics coming to the Church were admitted without baptism. IX, 175, 177, 178. Cyprian determined that they should be received not through baptism but through repentance. IX, 145. And Crescens of Cirta judged at the Council of Carthage that they should be reconciled by the laying on of hands alone. IX, 208. Why hands are laid upon them. IX, 193. Heretics passing over to the Church are cleansed by charity, not by repetition of baptism. IX, 711. What heretics ought to seek in the Catholic Church. IX, 185. What is conferred upon them when they come to the Catholic Church. IX, 197, 238, 330, 466, 474, 476, 477. When they return to the Church, the baptism they received outside begins to be useful to them. IX, 237, 242. It is established that heretics confer true baptism of Christ because even the wicked who are within the Church confer it. IX, 139, 140, 176. See *On Baptism*, Books 3 and 4. To what extent it is fitting that repentant heretics be received in the same grades of honor. IX, 474.

Some promise heretics release from eternal punishment. VII, 733, 741, 742.

**Hallelujah.** III, 2035; IX, 312. It is interpreted as “Praise God.” IV, 1938; V, 996, 1147, 1184, 1190, 1192, 1632. It was retained because of its more sacred authority. III, 42. Why it is doubled in certain Psalms. IV, 1419. Psalms of Hallelujah. IV, 1404. Hallelujah is sung solemnly at a fixed time according to the Church’s ancient tradition. IV, 1419. Hallelujah and Amen are sung throughout the whole world on the days of the Lord’s Resurrection and Passion. IV, 177. Hallelujah is sung solemnly after Easter. IV, 1937, 1938. That is, for fifty days, and this according to ancient tradition. V, 1052, 1176. During the Easter season Christians relax their fasts and sing Hallelujah, which is a sign of the Resurrection. II, 217. On other days it is sung differently in different places. II, 220. Hallelujah is now for us the song of the traveler. V, 1186. Hallelujah is the song of the future life. IV, 1938. “Hallelujah will be our food in heaven, Hallelujah our drink, Hallelujah the activity of rest; everything will be Hallelujah.” V, 1176, 1186. In heaven Hallelujah will exist in reality, but now in hope: now hungry love sings it; then love enjoying its object will sing it. V, 1188.

**Hannibal.** VIII, 574. Quintus Maximus broke Hannibal, exulting in youthful fashion, by his patience. II, 244.

**Soothsayer (*hariolus*).** A soothsayer should not be called wise. I, 916.

**Haruspices.** The haruspices offered sacrifices to the demon. I, 694. Augustine despises the haruspex who promised him victory through his rites in the contest of theatrical poetry. I, 694. The books of haruspices and augurs are superstitious. III, 50.

**Hasna.** II, 126.

**Daniel’s weeks.** Whether they refer to Christ’s first coming, his second coming, or both. II, 912. There were some who thought that they referred to both. II, 912. Augustine holds that Daniel’s weeks were completed at Christ’s first coming. II, 899. Many interpreters of this prophecy agree. II, 912. They were not completed before the Lord’s Passion. II, 915. Hesychius does not think that they were completed at Christ’s first coming. II, 904, 911. If they refer to the second coming, they would already have had to be fulfilled. II, 912. Jerome marks as rashness the view of one who interprets Daniel’s weeks as referring to Christ’s future coming. II, 901. Hesychius favors this opinion. II, 904, 911.

**Ebionites.** According to Jerome, they pretend to be Christians. II, 257.

**Heber.** The name “Hebrews” derives from him. VII, 598.

**Hebrews.** Why they were so called. I, 636; III, 552. Whether they were surnamed from Heber or from Abraham. VII, 481. Before the Law, the Hebrews were not without preachers of God, or angels. VII, 302. The Hebrews offered victims to the one God, the creator of all. VIII, 386. Of all the nations, they alone did not worship gods. VII, 154. Whether, apart from idols, they retained all the rites of the nations. VIII, 386. What was the condition of the Hebrews in Egypt after Joseph’s death. VII, 564. The Hebrews had to be disciplined in Egyptian servitude so that they would desire the help of their Creator. VII, 565. Hence among the Hebrews the humiliations of toil and the prosperity of consolations alternated. VII, 570. A considerable trace of justice in the Hebrew people. VII, 491. The Hebrews won victories not so much because of their own merits as because of the sins of the nations they conquered. VII, 522. The division of the Hebrew kingdom. VII, 557. Its reunification after the division. VII, 558. The various ages of the Hebrew people, and where they are to be taken from. VII, 522. Hebrew names were translated first into Greek and then into Latin. IV, 302. Among the Hebrews no one was permitted to write Hebrew letters except the scribes. VIII, 365. See *Jews*.

**Hebrew language.** It received its name from Heber. VII, 400. It was the first of all languages. VII, 400. When it was invented. VII, 522. It remained in the house of Heber. VII, 400. It was transmitted only to the people of God. VII, 490. Hebrew letters before Moses. VII, 598. The Hebrew language, together with its letters, was preserved through the succession of the fathers. VII, 598. Hebrew was very closely related to Punic. III, 488. And joined to it by a certain similarity of meaning. V, 648.

**Hecate.** Her oracle praised Christ. VII, 652.

**Hecates.** The soul of the world. V, 1137.

**Hector.** VIII, 585.

**Helen of Greece.** II, 157, 237. Menelaus’ wife, corrupted by adultery with Paris. VII, 81.

**Helen.** A certain prostitute whom Simon Magus wanted to be believed to be Minerva. VIII, 25.

**Eli the priest.** Judge of the Hebrews. VII, 577. Why Eli’s sons were punished by death. VIII, 618.

**Heliopolis.** The city of the sun. III, 584. It is more than twenty miles distant from Memphis. III, 584.

**Helle.** A myth. VII, 570.

**Helpidius.** He debated against the Manichaeans near Carthage. I, 716.

**Helvidius.** From whom the Helvidians derive their name. VIII, 46.

**Her.** It is interpreted as “skin-clad.” VIII, 456.

**Heraclitus.** VII, 181.

**Plants.** How and when they were created. III, 273, 326. For what purpose thorny and poisonous plants were produced. III, 182. The life of plants, according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 37. The ever-living plant. III, 1742.

**Heracleonites.** Heretics named after Heracleon, and their doctrines. VIII, 28.

**Hercules.** V, 164, 1249, 1250; VII, 639. When he lived, and why divine honors were accorded to him. VII, 565. Larentia, the prostitute of Hercules. VII, 185. Labeo numbers Hercules among the demigods. VII, 58, 59. Hercules was called the god of strength. V, 166. The custodian of Hercules, playing with himself as though with Hercules. VII, 185. It is said in more secret histories that there were several Herculeses. VII, 569. The twelve great deeds of the Syrian or Tyrian Hercules. VII, 569. They report that he was burned by himself on Mount Oeta. VII, 569. The idol of Hercules with its inscription. V, 164. With a gilded beard at Carthage, which was shaved there. V, 166. The Suffetani killed sixty Christians because of the idol of Hercules. II, 191. Hercules removed at Rome. V, 166. The spirits of Hercules and Juno divided against each other. V, 447; VI, 712. The Herculean aids of the Cynics. I, 943.

**Inheritance.** Whoever desires to possess another’s property as though by right of inheritance sins. V, 72. In a division of an inheritance, the division belongs to the elder brother, while the choice belongs to the younger. V, 1576. The inheritance of the Old Testament is earthly happiness; that of the New Testament, eternal immortality. IV, 824, 825. The inheritance in which we are joint heirs with Christ is not diminished by the abundance of its possessors, nor made narrower by the number of fellow heirs. IV, 565. We are God’s inheritance, and God is ours. V, 796, 1593; VI, 87. God is called our inheritance because he feeds and sustains us; and we are called God’s inheritance because he administers and rules us. IV, 83. The inheritance promised to us and already manifested in Christ our head. V, 154, 858.

**Heir.** Who is the heir of the Old Testament. X, 328. We have been made heirs of God, not so that we may succeed him, but so that we may live with him forever. IV, 1807. Why we are called heirs and co-heirs of Christ. VI, 86, 87. Christ is to be written as heir together with his children. V, 1571. Augustine does not accept anyone’s inheritance when the children have been disinherited. V, 1571. When the Church ought to accept or refuse an inheritance. V, 1570.

**Hedgehog.** A figure of those who are covered by lighter sins. IV, 1372, 1373.

**Hermaphrodites.** VII, 486; VIII, 1002.

**Hermes the Egyptian.** What he thought about idolatry. VII, 247.

**Hermias.** From whom the Hermians derive their name. VIII, 41.

**Hermogenes.** The origin of the name Hermogenians. See *Sabellians*. VIII, 32.

**Hermon.** It is interpreted as “exalted light.” IV, 1735. Also, his anathema. IV, 1127. Anathema. IV, 472.

**Hermogenianus.** II, 61.

**Herod.** A foreigner, king among the Jews. VII, 607. Murderer of infants. VI, 655, 664. Herod’s fear and savagery. V, 1029, 1664. Fearing that he would lose his kingdom, Herod did not deserve to acknowledge the King. IV, 536. Christ crowned the innocents whom Herod killed. IV, 536. Herod was in danger of committing either perjury or a bloody crime. V, 1408. It is uncertain whether Herod married the wife of his brother while the brother was dead or alive. VI, 221. The two Herods provide an opportunity for charging the Gospel with falsity. IX, 662. The persecution by King Herod after the Lord’s ascension was most severe. VII, 615.

**Hero.** Why he is so called. VII, 299. The souls of the dead who have acquired some merit are called heroes. VII, 299. The name “heroes” is not readily found in Scripture. III, 500.

**Heros.** A Gallic bishop. X, 320, 343, 355. Heros and Lazarus accuse Pelagius and Caelestius as authors of a wicked error. II, 759, 764. The presbyter Orosius brought their letter to the Council of Carthage. II, 759. Pelagius replied to the charges of Heros and Lazarus. II, 776.

**Hesiod.** The poet gave the Muses their name. III, 49.

**Hesperius.** A former tribune. VII, 764.

**Hesperus.** The star of Venus. VII, 720.

**Hesternus.** Used in place of “young man.” IX, 523.

**Hesychius.** Bishop of the city of Salona. II, 899, note (b); VII, 664. A holy man of God. II, 924. Augustine writes to Hesychius. II, 899. Hesychius replies to him. II, 901. Augustine in turn writes back. II, 904.

**The cruelty of the Etruscan robbers.** X, 778.

**Hieraca.** From whom the Hieracites derive their name. VIII, 38.

**Hierius.** VIII, 707, 708. An orator of the city of Rome. I, 702. Augustine dedicated to him the books *On the Beautiful and the Appropriate*. I, 702.

**Jeroboam.** He established idolatry in his kingdom. VII, 557.

**Jerome.** I, 649. A venerable presbyter. X, 286. A man of God. II, 625. A most learned man. II, 864, 904. Especially learned in Scripture. II, 628. From adolescence into old age he labored and lived in a monastery. II, 245. In the monastery, he complains that he was shaken by various waves and endured the hardships of exile. II, 154. Jerome was unknown to Augustine in person but joined to him in unity of spirit. II, 155. Jerome does not deliberately defend either that Peter sinned or that Paul arrogantly rebuked his superior. II, 253. In a recent work he followed Cyprian’s and Augustine’s opinion on this matter. II, 779. Augustine seems to say that Jerome admitted “useful lies” in sacred Scripture. II, 156. Jerome reproached Augustine concerning the latter’s letter circulated throughout Italy. II, 244. And concerning the violation of the right of personal relationship. II, 245. Augustine urges Jerome to a *παλινωδία* (*palinōidia*, recantation). II, 157.

What Jerome thought concerning the origin of the soul, he explained in his little works against Rufinus. II, 719. He wrote to Marcellinus that it was his opinion that individual souls are newly made for those being born. II, 748. He left the question of the origin of souls for Augustine to solve. II, 747. Jerome’s testimony in favor of original sin. X, 665. Jerome established the doctrine of original sin in his book against Jovinian and in his commentaries on Jonah. II, 723, 730. Jerome’s opinion concerning the vision of God. II, 621, 625. He holds that the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be seen by the eyes of the flesh. II, 621, 626. And that an incorporeal reality cannot be seen by bodily eyes. II, 621. Jerome’s opinion concerning the members of God, against the Anthropomorphites. II, 628. Augustine sends Jerome’s explanations of Daniel’s weeks to Hesychius. II, 899, 903. Hesychius says that these leave the reader in suspense. II, 904. Augustine agrees with Jerome, who marked as rashness a certain opinion concerning Daniel’s weeks. II, 901. Jerome calls the question of the gourd in his book of explanations on Jonah ridiculous. II, 275. A certain bishop, because the people were rioting, was compelled to correct Jerome’s interpretation of a passage in the prophet Jonah as though it were erroneous. II, 242. Jerome reproves Origen. II, 286. Augustine asks him to disclose the errors of Origen and the heretics. II, 157. Jerome teaches that it is dangerous to judge the opinions of the teachers of the Churches. II, 904. In the East Jerome struggled against Pelagius on behalf of Christ’s grace. II, 764; X, 699. His work against Pelagius under the name of Critobulus. II, 779. Pelagius complained about Jerome because, as a rival, he had envied him. X, 700.

Jerome translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech. VII, 603. Augustine does not possess the Psalter translated from Hebrew by Saint Jerome. II, 1077. Jerome interprets Job from the Hebrew. II, 242. Jerome’s translation of the prophet Jonah from Greek into Latin is more accurate. II, 242. Jerome replies concerning his translation of the prophet Jonah. II, 263. Jerome’s commentaries on Ezekiel. II, 719. His books on Daniel. VII, 695. On Malachi. VII, 699. He translated the Gospel from Greek with the greatest fidelity. II, 243. In his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, he says that he followed Origen’s commentaries. II, 252. And also those of other Greeks. II, 252, 253, 254. Why, after others, he undertook a new translation of the canonical books. II, 262. He cannot devote himself to the Septuagint edition, as Augustine wished, because of the shortage of copyists. II, 753. In translating the canonical books, he preserved the truth of the meanings rather than the order of the words. II, 261. What the Jews think of Jerome’s translation. VII, 603. Jerome wrote a book on the best method of interpreting Scripture. II, 261. Augustine requests it. II, 291. Two of Augustine’s books were dedicated to Jerome. II, 752. They are extant. II, 720, 733. Jerome was resolved to love, esteem, and honor Augustine, and to defend his statements as though they were his own. II, 753. Jerome’s book against Rufinus is praised. II, 727. His work against Jovinian. II, 735, 737. Jerome’s work in which he discusses the resurrection of the flesh splendidly. II, 779. Jerome’s letter to Marcellinus. II, 718. It is praised by Augustine. II, 723, 724, 747, 864. Augustine requests Jerome’s little work on heresies. VIII, 49. Jerome’s *Chronicle*. VII, 566, 587. Jerome’s book, which some called an *Epitaph*, should be called *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. II, 252. This book came into Augustine’s hands. II, 155. Augustine indicates certain additions that should be made to it. II, 157. Jerome composed the epitaph of the presbyter Nepotianus. II, 252. Jerome writes that a two-membered human being was born at Lydda. VI, 273. Note (a).

**Eulogy of Jerome.** X, 192, 665, 699. His intellect was golden through divine gift. II, 156. Jerome’s mind is known to no small degree through his writings. II, 155. Through Jerome’s teaching, ecclesiastical literature in the Latin language was advanced as far as it had ever been able to advance. II, 741. No discourse of Jerome is too long, however much time it may occupy. II, 155. Unfortunate is the person who does not honor Jerome’s labors worthily or give thanks to God for them. II, 741. How highly Augustine valued Jerome’s knowledge. II, 247. Augustine admits that Jerome surpassed him in knowledge of sacred literature. II, 247. According to Augustine’s own testimony, Augustine was inferior to Jerome in many matters. II, 290. Augustine sends two books to Jerome. I, 649. How intensely Augustine burns with longing for Jerome. II, 237, 241, 247, 248. Augustine would have wished, if it were possible, to have Jerome present every day. II, 720. Jerome does not allow even a single hour to pass without mentioning Augustine. II, 891. Jerome writes to Augustine through Firmus. II, 275, 276, 291. He sends greetings to Alypius. II, 291. Alypius visits Jerome. II, 111. Augustine commends Paul, one of his brothers, to Jerome. II, 158.

**Hilary.** X, 283, 866. An eminent doctor of the Churches. X, 693. A man of no ordinary authority in the interpretation of Scripture and the defense of the faith. VIII, 931. Hilary, a Gallic bishop, a most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church against heretics. X, 645. His teaching concerning Christ’s flesh. X, 1587. He demonstrated that it was not a lie when Christ said that he did not know the day of judgment. II, 778. He taught that no one is without sin. X, 283. Hilary’s books. VIII, 931. A treatise on Psalm 118. X, 691. A homily on Saint Job. X, 692. His exposition of the first Psalm. X, 692. And of Psalm 51. X, 693. Hilary translated Origen’s work on the Psalms. II, 262. Hilary’s statement concerning the Trinity. VIII, 1059. Hilary’s interpretation of a passage of the Apostle. X, 614. Vincent opposed Hilary of Poitiers’ book—namely, *On the Synods*—against the Church growing everywhere. II, 332, 337. Note (a). Augustine interprets the passage of Hilary that had been brought forward. II, 337.

**Hilary of Arles.** He is moved by certain statements of Augustine, but in all other matters he is a follower and admirer of Augustine’s teaching. II, 1007.

[Col. 0334] **Hilary of Syracuse.** He consults Augustine. Augustine gives him a satisfactory answer. II, 674.

**Hilary.** A Gallic layman. II, 1007. He appears to have been from Narbonne. II, 771. Note. He indicates that he had been Augustine’s disciple. II, 771, note; 1012; X, 957. He sent Letter 226 to Augustine. II, 1007. He mentions that he had previously sent another letter to him. II, 1011. Augustine’s letter to Hilary. X, 334. It is Letter 178. II, 771. Note. Augustine commends himself to his prayers. II, 771. He explains the Pelagian inventions to him. II, 771. Hilary requests Augustine’s books *Retractions* and *On Grace and Free Will*. II, 1011.

**Hilary the Tribunician.** A Catholic. I, 634. He disapproved of hymns from the Psalms being sung at the altar; Augustine published a book against him. I, 634.

**Hilarense.** A town. II, 1019.

**Hippocentaur.** What is the Manichaean hippocentaur? VIII, 313.

**Hippocrates.** He frees a woman who was to be punished on suspicion of adultery. III, 572. Certain books were falsely attributed to Hippocrates and were not accepted by physicians. VIII, 514.

**Hippo Diarrhytus.** VII, 486; IX, 236.

**Hippo.** IX, 337. Hippo-Regius is called a Roman city. II, 135. Note (a). The Church of Peace at Hippo-Regius. II, 966. The estates of the Church of Hippo, which the bishop is considered to possess as owner. II, 480. Augustine reproaches the people of Hippo because they had forgotten the custom of clothing the poor. II, 471. The people of Hippo wanted Saint Pinianus to live in their city. II, 476. And they desired him as their presbyter without any shameful ambition. II, 480. With what tumult they asked that he be ordained their presbyter. II, 478. In that tumult they said many insulting things against Alypius. II, 481. They requested that, if Pinianus should ever consent to undertake the clerical office, he consent only in the Church of Hippo itself; Pinianus agreed to this. II, 479, 482. The weakness of the people of Hippo, and how much Augustine suffers from them. II, 473. The landowner and master of the region of Hippo praises Augustine with ironic flattery. II, 515.

**Deacon of Hippo.** V, 1576.

**Council of Hippo.** Held in the year 393. VI, 181, note (a). At the Council of Hippo in 398, canon 38, and at the Third Council of Carthage in 397, canon 47, it was determined which Scriptures are canonical and ought to be read among the people of God. II, 233.

**Hyrcanus.** Son of Alexandra, queen of the Jews. VII, 607. He was confirmed in the pontificate. VII, 607.

**Goats.** Some goats will not be on the left. IV, 799.

**Hispania.** So many provinces of Spain began to experience evils from which they had previously been untouched. II, 422. False doctrines slaughter the souls of the Spaniards far more unhappily than the barbarian sword. II, 721.

**History.** History should not be numbered among human institutions. III, 56. History resembles demonstration. III, 56. The extent to which history belongs among the liberal disciplines. II, 368. Its credibility perishes if what has been established by the agreement of people and ages is called into doubt. I, 1335. Even profane history helps in understanding the sacred books. III, 55. Ecclesiastical history, written in Greek by Eusebius and translated into Latin by Rufinus. VI, 597. The occasion of history. I, 1012.

Historians of the nations, since they disagree with one another on many matters, do not deserve belief. VII, 716. Greater credence should be given to historians who do not contradict divine history. VII, 600. Historians commonly, when they come to their own person, weave their account in such a way as though they were narrating about someone else what they are narrating about themselves. VIII, 342.

**Actor.** V, 562, 1026, 1461. The gestures of actors have force by convention, not by nature. III, 54. Actors can in no way be skilled in music. I, 1089. Actors, charioteers, hunters, and others who love watching spectacles are criticized. IV, 438, 439, 440, 626, 1327. Actors are not permitted to approach the Christian sacraments unless they have abandoned their profession. VI, 219. Among the Greeks, actors were admitted into the administration of the state. VII, 55.

**Hoc.** It signifies one thing when it is shortened and another when it is lengthened. III, 1940.

**Kids.** Two peoples. V, 42. The kids are not to be separated before the judgment. V, 298, 304.

**Holocarpoma.** III, 678, 679.

**Holocaust.** A sacrifice is called a holocaust when it is wholly burned. IV, 576, 599, 776, 798, 1775. Whoever wishes to offer a holocaust to God should burn completely with the fire of divine love. IV, 1775. Not every sacrifice was a holocaust. III, 823. See *Sacrifices*. No one ate from a holocaust. III, 823. God disapproves of human holocausts. III, 810, 815, 816. Holocausts with marrow, mystically understood. IV, 799. *Holocaustosis*: the remains of a holocaust consumed by fire. III, 678.

**Homer.** When he lived. VII, 80. Note (a). Homer, the sweetest but most vain poet: his reading was bitter to Augustine as a boy. I, 671. He invented many things, attributing them to the gods for shameful men, so that shameful acts would not be thought shameful, and whoever committed them would seem to be imitating not depraved human beings but heavenly gods. I, 671.

[Col. 0335] **Human being.** What is a human being? VII, 626. A human being is a rational animal. V, 255. Made from earth. V, 1588. A mortal rational animal. I, 1009, 1062; VIII, 939. Why a twofold distinction is included in this definition. I, 1009, 1062. The human being is composed of soul and body. I, 963; II, 65; V, 717, 810. The whole human being is soul and flesh. IV, 402. The whole nature of the human being is ordered by the rule of the soul and the service of the body. VI, 126. Apart from soul and body, nothing belongs to his substance and nature. V, 810. The human person is a mixture of soul and body. II, 520. This mixture seems more incredible than the mixture of God and man in Christ. II, 520. The human being is a great miracle. V, 700. Whether the soul alone can be called a human being. I, 1313.

A description of the human being according to Apuleius. VII, 263. The Manichaean fable concerning the first human being. VIII, 210, 221, 246, 375. Concerning the war of the first human being with the race of darkness. VIII, 210, 211, 223, 234. The Manichaean says that human beings are children of smoke. VIII, 197. Why the Manichaeans try to introduce an evil maker of the human being. X, 1532. Some have thought that human beings always existed. VII, 357. Their answers to the objections raised against them. VII, 357.

**Creation of the human being.** III, 186, 241. The structure of the human flesh itself testifies that God is the maker of the human being, from whom all good things—whether heavenly or earthly—come. X, 1532. The creation of the human being is joined to, and also distinguished from, the creation of the other animals. III, 241. Why the human being is called God’s preeminent work. III, 347, 348. Some suspect that the inner human being was made first and then the human body. III, 293. God made the human being, like the other creatures, through his Word. III, 371. How the human being was made into a living soul. III, 363. Whether the human being was then animated when God breathed into his face. VIII, 614. God breathed into the human face because it contains, as it were, the organs of sensation. III, 23. The human being was made invisibly, causally, and potentially on the first day of creation; on the sixth day he was made visibly. III, 343, 344, 346, 347, 349, 410. The human being was created on the sixth day and re-formed in the sixth age. VIII, 257. The human being was made in the image of God. I, 626, 858; III, 186. The human being is God’s coin. V, 82. The human being made in the image and likeness of God is a great reality. III, 26. The human being’s likeness to God. V, 164. The human being was made in the image of the Trinity itself. III, 244; VIII, 1001, 1055. Whether only the man, and not the woman, was made in the image of God. VIII, 1003, 1005. It is said of the human being before he sinned that he was made in the image of God. VIII, 135. How, and in what respect, the human being was made in the image of God. III, 243, 292, 347, 366, 409, 2039; VII, 373, 400; VIII, 475, 695, 1003. The human being was made in the image of God in his soul. V, 353; VI, 628. The human being was made in God’s image because he understands, possesses wisdom, and distinguishes good from evil. IV, 218. The human being bears within himself a symbol of the Trinity, namely, being, knowing, and willing. I, 849. The human being was made in the image, and is the image, of God. V, 361. This image is far removed from God. V, 362. The true honor of the human being is the image. VIII, 1006. How the Apostle calls the human being the image of God. III, 243. When it had been said that the human being was created in the image, why “and likeness” is added. III, 241, 242, 244, 749. The human being was made in the image and likeness, but he is not himself that very image and likeness equal to the Father. III, 243. The likeness in which the human being was made is the very Word of God. III, 243. Whether he was made in the image in one respect and in the likeness in another. VI, 33.

The human being is twofold, inner and outer, and the rationale of each. VI, 32. Which of the two was made in the image and likeness of God. VI, 32, 33. A certain heresy said that the human body, not the soul, is the image of God. VIII, 45. He is the image not because of the body but because of the mind. III, 186. The human being was made in the image of God not according to the body but according to the rational mind. VIII, 1004. The human body, insofar as it has an upright form, can be said to have been made in the likeness of God. III, 243. The human being indicates in his very body that he was made in the image of God, because he was made with an upright stature. III, 347. By the upright stature of his body, the human being is admonished not to pursue earthly things like the animals. III, 347. Rather, he should direct his mind toward eternal things. I, 1313; III, 186. Through sin the human being did not lose everything of the image of God that he possessed. I, 628. He lost only the perfection of God’s image. III, 186. Although through his origin the human being is in the kingdom of the Devil, he is nevertheless the image of God. X, 1082. The creation of the human being is explained allegorically. I, 858.

What kind of being the human being was made by God. VII, 386, 399, 400. How he was made upright. VI, 282. The human being is upright when the spirit commands and the flesh serves. III, 1395.

For what purpose the human being was made. VI, 628. The end of the human being is eternal life. III, 144. The human being was made in time, but according to God’s immutable and eternal plan. VII, 362. What answer should be given to those asking why the human being was created so late. VII, 359. The human being’s condition before sin. VI, 244; X, 172. In paradise. VII, 417. The first human being was created in a nature without guilt and without defect. V, 172. Without concupiscence or conflict between flesh and spirit. V, 717. Before sin, the human being was blessed in hope of a future transformation. III, 438. He was good within his kind. III, 296. Perhaps God did not say that the human being was good because he foresaw that he would sin. III, 295. The human being was created in the knowledge of God, and is renewed in it. III, 292.

- Whether, if he had not sinned, man would have been destined to be miserable through fear of death. X, 1530, 1536. If man had not sinned, he could have avoided death. III, 354. And this is indicated by death itself in man. III, 353. His descendants would not have been subject to death. VII, 403. They were destined to be joined to the angels without the intervention of death. VII, 377. If man had not sinned, he would not have been liable to death. VII, 720.
