It is the faith of the whole Church that human nature was divinely instituted in such a way that, if man had not sinned, he would not have died. X, 1561. Man would have been immortal if he had not sinned. VIII, 615. Man would have been immortal through the fruit of the tree of life. VIII, 615. Whether he had eaten from the tree of life before the curse. VIII, 615. The ability not to die was granted to him from the tree of life, not from the constitution of his nature. III, 354. If man was made immortal, how he could have needed food is difficult to say. III, 293.

- What man’s body was like before sin. VI, 373. It was not corruptible. VI, 332. Mortal human beings are generated from Adam, who was made mortal through sin. VII, 378. According to Julian, man was created mortal, not as a punishment but by nature. X, 1312. From the moment human beings are conceived, they begin a certain sickness by which they are necessarily destined to die. III, 399. Plotinus judged that the fact that human beings are mortal in body belongs to God’s mercy. VII, 265.

- That it is not contrary to God’s wisdom for the human race to have a beginning. VII, 370. Certain philosophers are compelled to admit that the human race first existed without human beings who generated it. VII, 359. Various opinions about the propagation of children if man had not sinned. VI, 373. How the multiplication of human beings would have occurred if they had remained immortal. III, 292. And if Adam had not sinned. III, 396. If human beings had not sinned, they would have multiplied the human race without lust. VII, 428, 429, 430. Augustine’s opinion that man could have been sown in paradise at will, with the genital members obeying. X, 1444, 1447. Whether the first human beings abstained from intercourse until the age at which they are said to have begotten children. VII, 456, 465.

- Why God willed to create all human beings from one ancestor. V, 563, 1233; VI, 373. Human beings were begotten from one ancestor to commend the closer bond of kinship and the bond of unity. III, 398. To commend fellowship. VII, 372, 376, 403. Nothing is so discordant through vice, yet so social by nature, as the human race. VII, 376. Every human being was made in the first human being, in respect of origin and seed. IV, 1551. How the whole of creation is in each human being. VI, 68; VIII, 675. Whether monstrous races of human beings arose from Adam or from the descendants of Noah’s sons. VII, 485.

- Man sinned by his own will through guilt; he was ordered by God’s justice through punishment. III, 431. The dogma of Jovinianus that human beings imbued with the mysteries of God cannot sin. X, 1417, 1418, 1419.

- Why the temptation of man was permitted. III, 431, 432. Man would not have been destined for great praise if he could live well for the reason that no one urged him to live badly. III, 431.

- The fall of man. VII, 727. Why it was permitted by God. V, 172. Man was cast down by the tempter because he was proud. III, 431. And because he followed the deceiver’s pride. III, 1787. Because, with his heart exalted, he withdrew from God. VIII, 615. Man was upright; by his own choice he became evil. V, 409. The figure of fallen man in the one who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho. V, 752, 1646. He did not wish to stand with the Lord; he fell and was broken, like a vessel falling from a man’s hand. V, 717. Man was handed over to himself because he abandoned God by pleasing himself. VII, 433. Because he wished to use his own will, he delighted in breaking the commandment, so that, with no one ruling him, he might become like God. IV, 897. The price of man’s sale was a small pleasure from the forbidden tree. V, 188. Man sinned by his will, not by necessity. III, 432. He had been made in such a way that no necessity compelled him to abandon God. VIII, 614. So that he could not sin if he did not wish to. VIII, 614. Man was not incapable of sinning. VIII, 419. Man was made in such a way that the possibility of sinning came from necessity, but sin itself from possibility. X, 1494. Why he was not made in such a way that he would not wish to sin. VIII, 614. He was made with the power to sin and not to sin, destined to receive as his reward the inability to sin. VI, 359. God made him in such a way that he would crown him when standing, order him when fallen, and help him when rising. VI, 332.

- Man was created with free will. VII, 752. Why he was created free. VI, 11. If he did not have free will, he would excel less in the order of nature. III, 369. Free choice of the will was given to man in such a way that he nevertheless necessarily lives under the power of one who is better. VIII, 613. Man would not have lived well except through God’s grace. III, 431. Why God did not take free will away from man, although he foresaw that he would sin. VII, 752. Why God creates man, whom the devil is to possess. X, 408. God foresaw that man would sin, and at the same time foresaw that a people of the godly would be joined to the holy angels and called to adoption. VII, 372.

- From where and to what man fell. III, 138. The higher rational nature itself is, the worse its ruin; and the more incredible its sin, the more damnable it is. X, 1553. Because he was made to live a blessed life if he lived well, therefore the one who lived badly will live a miserable life. IV, 1302. The transgressor man, having lost blessedness, was cast into misery. V, 209. Man’s misery after sin. VI, 244, 363, 628. Human beings have two evils: iniquity and mortality; one is guilt, the other punishment. V, 934. Human beings are mortal, fragile, weak, carrying earthen vessels that cause one another distress. V, 440. In this age man has no other destiny than to be born, labor, and die. V, 726. Man deserved to be his own punishment. IV, 405. Man suffers inwardly from himself, but outwardly from those among whom he lives. IV, 405. Every human being seeks the blessed life. V, 810. Whether human beings can be happy in true blessedness while they are mortal. VII, 268. As long as human beings are mortal, they must be miserable. VII, 268. Man is not blessed because he does not live as he wishes. VII, 133. And even if man lived as he wished, he would not be blessed if he lived shamefully. VII, 133. Man owes himself to God, and must be returned to him in order to be blessed, since he received from him the fact that he exists. II, 486. Man is satanic from what is his own, but blessed from God. III, 1750.

- Human beings are born in the body of death and in the flesh of sin. X, 134. They are born for the world before they are born for God. X, 823. From where human beings, both greater and lesser, are guilty. X, 708. Why a just person is not born from just parents. X, 177. The human race is under the devil’s power because of sin. X, 1122. Insofar as human beings are human beings, they are God’s work; insofar as they are sinners, they are under the devil. X, 567. Human beings are subjected to the power of darkness, that is, to the devil’s power. II, 982. By what right they were handed over to the devil’s power, and by what right they were freed from it through Christ. I, 1286. The captivity from which Christ redeemed human beings is voluntary. VIII, 543. Man is subject to vanity because he did not wish to be subject to truth. IV, 1549. We were made by the hands of truth, but because of sin were cast into the days of vanity. V, 403. The things over which man ruled were justly made penal for him. VIII, 203.

- Human nature was created good. X, 1516. But it is vicious through an evil will. III, 1703, 1705. Human nature is from God, not iniquity. III, 369; X, 1124. Every human creature was corrupted in Adam. IV, 1549. All human beings were one. V, 906. What is the cause that man is worse. VI, 12. Whether he is worse with God as author. VI, 11.

- Human nature is capable of virtue and perfection. X, 688. According to Julian, man was made not of a good but of an evil nature, because in him the evil action by which he could not act well prevailed more strongly than the good action by which he could not act badly. X, 1522. What Julian criticizes in human nature created by God, he ought to criticize in angelic nature as well. X, 1517, 1518. Although human beings are damnable because of their corrupted origin, goodness is nevertheless shown to them. X, 857, 858. Human beings whom God creates from an origin deservedly and justly condemned are nevertheless something good. X, 1443. Man is a great good. III, 384. But mutable. III, 384. Although man has lost natural goodness and voluntary evil has become inseparably attached to him, he was nevertheless well constituted. X, 1541, 1543. Nothing harms man except his own iniquity. VII, 114. Let man erase what he has done, and he will please the one who made him. V, 587.

- After sin, man has consolations mingled with punishment. VIII, 203. Man was not abandoned without mercy. VIII, 203. Human nature is both good and capable of being free from evil. X, 298. When it is freed from evil. X, 298. All human beings are one mass of sin. VI, 71, 121, 124. All those born as children of wrath needed a reconciler. VI, 248. If you, O man, had not abandoned God, God would not have become man for you. IV, 372. Man must be reformed by the clemency of the one by whose goodness he was formed. I, 1067. The one who created, formed, and made man himself recreates, reforms, and restores him. IV, 524. The Son of God was sent to them so that all might be freed. VI, 345. Man was formed on the sixth day and reformed in the sixth age of the world. IV, 1182. Man cannot rise again from himself. I, 597. Man grew old through sin and is renewed through grace. IV, 1949. He was capable of wounding himself, not of healing himself. IV, 1263, 1696. He cannot be restored by merits or free will. VI, 246. But by grace. VI, 247. His reformation comes from God’s mercy alone. VI, 245. How justly he was condemned, and how mercifully he was freed. VI, 685. Man was made freely, and freed freely. IV, 488. Man’s liberation corresponds to the manner of his captivity. X, 407, 408. Man is restored by the same steps by which he had perished. VI, 655.

- To what end man was renewed. III, 1636. The restored portion of humanity will take the place of the angels who deserted their station. VI, 246. The elect are chosen to restore the part of the angels that fell, perhaps in greater number. VII, 752. Why neither all human beings are condemned nor all are freed. VII, 727. We carry something of the old man with us until the last moment of death. V, 202.

- The generation and double life of man: one according to the body before Christ, the other according to the soul after Christ’s coming. IV, 90. The great difference between a sound man and a fallen man. X, 271. Man both a human being and a sinner. V, 132, 323, 565. Who is a good man and who is an evil man. X, 370. One man can at the same time be good by nature and evil by vice. X, 1260. From what evil each person should pray to be freed. V, 253. Julian does not make clear from where man is good or evil. X, 1491. Man is evil from himself, but good from God and through God. III, 1706. God alone is good in a distinctive sense, and man is good from God but evil from what is his own. II, 658. By withdrawing from God man grows cold; by approaching him he grows fervent; by withdrawing he grows dark; by approaching he grows bright. IV, 896, 1175, 1379. Man is not godly, chaste, truthful, and so forth except through the godliness, chastity, and truth that are in God. III, 1685. Human beings are servants of God through the oil of his mercy, not through their own strength. III, 1583. It belongs to God not only that man exists, but also that his well-being comes from none but him, from whom he has his existence. III, 484. Man is a sinner from himself, but not righteous from himself. III, 834. How man is his own and not his own. III, 700. Man is not justified by himself. X, 873, 875. Nothing is more contemptible than man without God. V, 1527. Without God man is nothing to himself except a guide into destruction. I, 693. Nothing is man’s own except, perhaps, falsehood. III, 18; V, 200, 953.

- All man’s evil is error and weakness. V, 987. Human beings are blind from birth. III, 1713. Man cannot rescue reason from errors unless God, the light of minds, is present. II, 669. Man is, at best, an eye without light. V, 437. When God is present to him he is illuminated; when God is absent he is immediately darkened. III, 383. Man was hiding from himself; the Law was given so that he might find himself. V, 833. What it means for man to recognize himself. V, 488. By teaching and commanding what cannot be fulfilled without grace, the Law demonstrates man’s weakness, so that, once his weakness has been shown, he may seek the Savior. II, 593. A man’s being is one thing, and his ability another. III, 1558. It lies within his will what he wants, but not what he can do. I, 630. He had received great powers of free will, but lost them by sinning. V, 752. By willing evil he lost the ability to do good. V, 188. Whether man can change his will for the better. I, 620. How man can avoid sin. VIII, 419. Man falls by loving the body and abandoning God. III, 132. To live according to man and to live according to the flesh are the same. VI, 355. How we ought not to be “human.” III, 1381. Why human beings are rebuked for being human. V, 503, 908. Man ought not to love himself for his own sake. III, 27. Man is not to be loved for his own sake. III, 26. Hope must not be placed in man. IV, 246, 1651, 1652. In what does man exist more—in the flesh or in the mind? V, 837, 838. How much good or evil human beings contribute to our happiness or misery. II, 495. Amid the evils by which they are oppressed, human beings indulge in pleasures. II, 919.

- Man was called by God not to be man but God—not by nature but by God’s gift. V, 909. It belongs to man’s nature to be able to adhere to the nature that is the highest good. III, 384. Man is something only so long as he clings to the one by whom man was made. IV, 896, 962. Man becomes better by adhering to God. III, 384. The less man clings to God, who supremely is, the less stable he feels himself to be. II, 439. God himself is sufficient for you; besides him nothing is sufficient for you. V, 1469.

- By the just order of nature, man ought to be subject to God. VII, 629. By his mind man is closer to God than by any other part of himself. VII, 318. Man is not man unless he keeps God’s commandments. VII, 601. The true man is the penitent who asks God for help. III, 831. He is at his best when his whole life advances toward unchangeable life. III, 26. Man is directed from human things toward divine things when the divine will is preferred to the human will. III, 1770. If man thinks well, he is in God; and if he lives well, God is in him. III, 1745. Man’s excellence. III, 241. Man was not made like cattle, a tree, or a stone. V, 173. What man shares with other created things, and what is peculiar to him. V, 254. We have being with trees and stones, life with trees, sensation with beasts, and understanding with angels. V, 255. Even an evil man is better than any animal. V, 1187. The fact that a man is not like a corpse, a tree, or an animal may be called grace. II, 767. Some have thought that man, as the more excellent creature, was formed by God’s hands, while the rest were made by his word. IV, 158, 1551. Man is midway between angels and beasts. VII, 268, 372. Their life is midway between that of angels and cattle. III, 1546. Human beings resemble cattle in their manner of life. III, 360. Man’s punishment is that he has been compared with irrational animals. X, 1359. Man’s dignity above the other animals. IV, 1272, 1302. By what reasoning man is proved to surpass the beasts. VI, 14. Man rules the beasts. III, 186. He lost this dominion after sin. III, 186, 187. Man is of such excellence in comparison with cattle that a vice in man is the nature of cattle. X, 408. What is a crime in man is natural in a horse. IV, 1379. Man differs from cattle only by the mind. VI, 186.

- Man could not behold unchangeable truth with his mind if he had not been made for it. III, 159. Those are censured who are capable of thinking about nothing but bodies. II, 517. Man alone among living creatures perceives eternal principles in bodily things. VIII, 999. Man is unclean until the end of this life. III, 735. Man has that by which he is above the sun and that by which he is beneath the sun; that by which he belongs to truth and that by which he belongs to vanity. IV, 421. He must be judged wholly by what holds the chief place in him. III, 243. Only God is better than the human mind. IV, 294. That which is best in man is what is best for the soul. I, 1314. How highly God values man. IV, 1863. What pledges of salvation God has given to man. IV, 1942. In man memory, understanding, and will are shown to be separable but operate inseparably. V, 562. Before experiencing evil, man could have understood what evil was. III, 386.

- Man is a great miracle. V, 700; VII, 291. It is worthy of wonder in human beings that each has an individual face. VII, 721. Man is a great depth, whose hairs are more countable than his emotions. I, 702. The human heart is impenetrable to itself. IV, 473. There is something in man that even the spirit of man, which is in him, does not know. I, 782. Ignorant of the future, man lives by faith. III, 369. Perhaps every person knows what he is when he speaks; who knows what he will be tomorrow? V, 798. Man is said to judge matters over which he has the power to correct. I, 860. Just as man surpasses all beasts by understanding, so by living well he is better than demons. VII, 240. Man is an earthly animal, but worthy of heaven. VII, 752. Man is a worm, and yet is placed in heaven. III, 1385. Man is called earth and heaven. I, 587. Man is a dead skin, foul pus. V, 1396.

- Human beings are called gods in Scripture. VII, 275. Why they are called gods more clearly than the angels themselves. VII, 275, 276. By loving God we become gods; by loving the world we are called “the world.” V, 678. There are three things in human nature by which it differs from the gods. VII, 265. Man is called to divinity, not by nature but by gift and adoption. V, 909. Faithful human beings are midway between carnal human beings and angels. VI, 708. Man is midway between beasts and angels: he subjects to himself what he shares with beasts, and subjects to God what he shares with angels. VIII, 419. By piously obeying God’s commandments, man passes into angelic fellowship; by disobeying, into the bestial condition. VII, 372. Human beings are destined to become angels, and this can happen. V, 270, 728, 1442. Human nature, perfected, will equal the angels. IV, 294, 1945.

- Man’s dignity comes from God’s condescension toward him. V, 1661. It is known through the Incarnation. VIII, 1031. Of all that is not God, only God himself is greater than the human nature Christ assumed. VIII, 803. Through the incarnate Word man was made such that he could receive God. III, 1510. The man whom God assumed, when compared with other human beings, is separated from them by a greater distance than the sun is separated from the other stars by comparison. II, 80. Everything that was made was made for man’s use. VI, 20. The difference between “human beings” and “sons of men.” IV, 113, 136, 349, 350; V, 160, 1113, 1187. In Scripture we are called human beings from Adam, and sons of men from Christ, though not everywhere. II, 547; III, 1634. Every man is Adam, and every man is Christ. IV, 891. Sometimes man is Adam both according to the flesh and according to the spirit; sometimes according to the flesh alone. III, 418. See Adam.

- Man, a son of God. V, 503. A son of God not by nature but by adoption. VIII, 581. Every human being is one’s neighbor. II, 673. The threefold life of man: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. III, 2138. The four conditions and actions of man: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and in peace. III, 2065; VI, 52, 64, 287. In man a twofold operation of providence is found. III, 380. How God works upon man. III, 382. For man, “to be made” means to recognize the Word of God through whom he is made. III, 292. Man’s salvation is attended to through authority, reason, history, and prophecy. III, 141. God comes to his aid through himself, through angels, and through human beings. III, 131. Man must be reformed by living according to God’s will. I, 858. He is restored by God’s grace, conquering desires and loving God. III, 132. Man must first return to himself in order to return to God. VII, 342. From where human beings are loved. I, 707. Why they should be thought well of. I, 1008. Man’s whole duty. II, 85.

- What the carnal, animal, and spiritual man is. VI, 68. Two kinds of human beings: one thinking about earthly things, the other about heavenly things. IV, 603. The two kinds of human beings, the just and the wicked. IV, 363. The outward or old man, and the inward or new man. IV, 90, 91, 190, 191. Who he is. III, 143; V, 81, 908, 1660; VIII, 476. What he is like. VIII, 997. In what he consists. VIII, 475. Comparison of the inward and outward man. III, 143. The end of the outward man is death. III, 144. The outward man has six ages. III, 143. The outward man is corrupted either by the progress of the inward man or by his own decline. III, 156. What it means to put off the old man and put on the new. IV, 188, 189; X, 157. The course of both men throughout the entire human race. III, 144. The inward man has six ages. III, 143. The old man can exist without the new, but not the new without the old. III, 144. The man called inward enjoys and is illumined by the inward light of truth. I, 1217. The beauty, justice, and virtue of the inward man. II, 462. Where the inward man is recognized. VIII, 1005, 1008. In the inward man there is a certain secret marriage. VIII, 1007. The spiritual man does not judge sacred Scripture, even if something there does not shine clearly. I, 859. What kind of man someone is, such are his actions. V, 1325. The man kindled by the fire of divine love and striving toward God’s embrace is God’s sacrifice. VII, 296. In this life the spiritual man is a sacrifice; in the next he will be a whole burnt offering. VI, 69.

- Human beings are harder to tame than wild beasts. VI, 25. By their gluttony human beings surpass any four-footed animal. VIII, 198. Man desires to rule others. III, 27. And this is intolerable pride. III, 27. The three parts of a human craftsman: nature, instruction, and practice. VII, 339. Man, as some assert, is formed in the womb over forty days. V, 1039. By the name “man,” carnal people are understood. VI, 121.

- “Man” is frequently used for any part of himself. VII, 399. In Scripture he is signified by the name of the soul alone or of the flesh alone. VI, 355, 356. “Flesh” is used in Scripture for “man.” II, 542. “Man” is also used for his body alone. X, 1219.

- Whether Christ can be called “the Lordly Man.” I, 616.

- The bestial man. VI, 672.

- Plato’s man. II, 64.

- The human race as the fig tree. III, 1331. The human race is a great ornament to the earth, even when only a few live rightly and laudably. III, 369, 398. Whoever would not have man exist among created things contradicts God’s goodness. III, 398. Two kinds of human beings useless to the human race. VIII, 456. In a certain sense the whole human race consists of two human beings. X, 1211. The human race is a great sick person. V, 537. The entire human race is the Gospel man on the road, left half-dead. V, 933. What Christ provided for the suffering human race in order to heal it. V, 542. God visited the human race at three times. V, 467. The human race rests on two supports. V, 346. Human emotion must be conquered by Christ’s example. V, 1513. The human race is like a river or torrent. VII, 788; VIII, 902.

- The prohibition of homicide. V, 70. Whether homicide committed with a conscience filled with fear, or perpetrated with exultant boldness, is now culpable. X, 763. In voluntary homicide both God and man act; in involuntary homicide God alone acts. III, 448. In voluntary homicide, although the person killed is one whom God wishes killed, the killer is nevertheless worthy of punishment. III, 625. Homicide is to be punished by excommunication. VI, 220. Whether and when homicide is lawful, either under divine or human laws. I, 1225. The Donatists love homicides so much that, when they cannot carry them out against others, they carry them out against themselves. II, 797. Every wrongful movement to harm one’s brother is counted as a kind of homicide. VIII, 361. It is homicide to strike even a condemned person without due order. V, 1390.

- A homicide is one who hates his brother. III, 2017. Also one who persuades his brother to do evil. III, 1704.

- Homogynes was the first to yoke oxen to the plow. VII, 564. Hence divine honors were conferred on him. VII, 564.

- Pascentius demands that ὁμοούσιον [*homoousion*, “of the same substance”] be anathematized because it is not found in Scripture. II, 1039. Although ὁμοούσιον is not found in the sacred Scriptures, it is possible that what this word is rightly judged to apply to may be found there. II, 1039. And that the term, stated in the confession of faith, should be defended. II, 1040. That ὁμοούσιον is rightly said of the Father and the Son. II, 1048. That things are said in Scripture of the Father and the Son which are said only of those who are of one substance. II, 1049. The *homoousion* was confirmed at the Council of Nicaea and attacked by the heretics at Ariminum. VIII, 772, 785. Some unlearned Catholics rejected the *homoousion*. X, 1101. Catholics were called “Homousians” by the Arians. VIII, 707; X, 1101.

- Moral nobility is intelligible beauty. VI, 19. Moral nobility itself does not condemn what is condemned by the pride of those who love to be called honorable but do not love to be honorable. VI, 560.

- What is honorable. VI, 19.

- God is honor. VII, 128.

- The proud and the humble love honor in different ways. VIII, 593. To desire honors: when it is fitting and when unfitting. II, 498. Honor ought to seek you, not you honor. V, 242. Whoever loves honor imitates God. VIII, 593. Many things have been taken from divine worship in order to be rendered as honors to human beings. VII, 281. Honors and powers should not be desired either for their own sake or for some other good that comes from them. II, 498. Human honor, even when bestowed according to merit, should not be regarded as something great. VII, 161. Honor is the smoke of time. V, 136. Honor is a flattering name, but an evil servitude and a sickly outcome. II, 128. What honors here burden in the other life; what lifts here weighs down there. II, 96. If honor is loved, let it be possessed where no unworthy person is honored. II, 486. True honor is in heaven. VII, 801. Virtue is the road to honor. VII, 156. Humility. IV, 1597. Just honor is owed to virtue, not to vice. VI, 486. Honor is owed even to unjust authorities. IV, 1653. Honor is not owed to error, but to the good qualities of the person who errs. II, 129. Honor benefits the sick nothing. IV, 1320. “Honor nourishes the arts”: Cicero’s maxim. VII, 158.

- Ecclesiastical honors. V, 569. Showing partiality in granting ecclesiastical honors is no slight sin. II, 747. The temples of honor and virtue were joined at Rome. VII, 156. Lucifer of Cagliari was displeased that the ranks of honor were preserved for Arians returning to the Church. II, 813. One’s personal honor should be despised so that the unity of the Church may be preserved. V, 96. The Donatists received the Maximianists with their honors; the Church did the same. II, 814.

- An honorarium is what is given for the sake of honor. I, 999.

- Honoratus of Tucca. IX, 144, 237.

- Honoratus the Manichaean, a close associate of Augustine. X, 1464. Deceived by the Manichaeans. VIII, 63, 64, 66. Augustine wrote the book *On the Benefit of Believing* to him. VIII, 63, 64.

- Honoratus, to whose questions Augustine’s Book or Letter 140 responds. II, 538.

- Honoratus the presbyter. II, 293.

- Honoratus, bishop of Thiava. II, 1013, note (b). In his letter to Augustine he approves the view that, when the danger of devastation is pressing, bishops should migrate to safe places. II, 1014. Augustine does not agree. II, 1013.

- The emperor Honorius. VII, 620. Consul. II, 786. Consul again. IX, 529, 574. Sixth consul. VIII, 519. Ninth consul. II, 583. Twelfth consul. IX, 697. The laws of Honorius against the Donatists and Pelagians. I, 641. Honorius and Theodosius wished those who delayed either expelling or exposing Pelagius and Caelestius while they were hiding in any part of the provinces to be subject to the penalty prescribed for these heretics. II, 927. The laws of Honorius against the Donatists. IX, 445, 446; *Retractationes*, 489; appendix, 813, 815, 816. Against the pagans. II, 316. Against heretics and idolaters. II, 357, 358. Honorius and Theodosius venerated God with sincere confession in accordance with the Nicene synod. II, 927.

- The Basilica of Honorius. V, 889.

- Honorius of Milevis, degraded in the Catholic Church. IX, 372.

- An hour is not wholly present. I, 817. It is driven along by fleeing moments. I, 817. At the fifth hour one goes to the table. V, 1521. The final hour, that is, the final time. III, 1998.

- Marcus Horatius, consul. VII, 95. The three Horatii fought against the three Curiatii; the Horatii prevailed. VII, 89. Horatius killed his sister because she mourned the death of one of the Curiatii to whom she had been betrothed. VII, 89.

- Horace the poet. VI, 538. His saying, “Dare to know.” I, 1059. A Horatian maxim. II, 586.

- Barley. A drink made from it quickly intoxicates. I, 1365.

- What a horoscope is. VII, 143. The vanity of horoscopes. VII, 146.

- The granaries of Celica. IX, 235.

- Dominicus Horrearius. V, 923.

- Hortensianus, from the household gods. IX, 215.

- Hortensius was made dictator. VII, 97.

- *Hortensius*, Cicero’s dialogue. VII, 92. It stirred Augustine to a passion for philosophy. I, 685.

- The Lord’s garden. V, 1396.

- It is said that “Hosanna” could not be translated into another language. III, 42. “Hosanna” is the interjection of one rejoicing. III, 43. Or the utterance of one entreating. III, 1764.

- The Donatists used to say that Hosius of Córdoba had been condemned by the Spaniards but acquitted by the Gauls. IX, 38. Later the Spaniards yielded to the judgment of the Gauls. IX, 39.

- Here we are all guests. V, 643. In receiving unknown guests, it is much better to endure a bad person than to exclude a good one, while taking care not to receive a bad one. II, 153. Sometimes, without knowing it, people received angels by welcoming those whom they did not know. V, 615.

- Hospitality is commended. V, 506, 642, 967, 1118, 1121, 1127, 1585. When Christ wished to be fed, he provided for the one who fed him. V, 613. In sending Elijah to the widow, he himself had not become needy but was preparing to bless the widow. V, 613. Among most people it is customary to wash the feet of guests. III, 1794.

- Hostanes the magician. IX, 224.

- The purpose and origin of sacrificing human victims. VII, 209. The victims of the Old Law are figures of the sacrifice of Christ and of the righteous in heaven after the judgment. VII, 701. We sacrifice to God a victim of humility and praise on the altar of the heart, with the fire of fervent love. VII, 280. The sacrifices pleasing to God are mercy, humility, confession, peace, and love. IV, 1236. Confession is a sacrifice to God. IV, 1253. Enter the house of God with a humble heart, and you have entered with a sacrifice. IV, 1233.

- Hostilina, the goddess appointed over crops, when the new ears are made level. VII, 118.

- Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, consul. VII, 103.

- *Hostire*, that is, “to make equal.” VII, 118.

- Enemy. Why God often does not free his servants from the fury of enemies. VII, 42. You conquer a visible enemy by striking, an invisible one by believing. V, 435.

- What is owed to humanity is rendered when one person rashly suspects no evil of another and does not readily believe anyone who makes an accusation. IX, 610. See *Man*.

- Who is called human. V, 940.

- The way of humility is not found in the books of the philosophers; it comes from Christ. IV, 270. Christ is the teacher of humility. V, 191. And its instructor. VI, 413, 414. To be little is so great a thing that it could be learned only from Christ, who is so great. VI, 415. A humble heart brings God down from heaven so that he may draw near. IV, 1205. The proud man is in great misery, but the humble God is in greater mercy. VI, 316. See *Pride*. We were humbled by truth unto death; by mercy we are restored to life. IV, 1555. Human pride pressed you down so heavily that only divine humility could lift you up. V, 1004. At last earthly pride recognized that among earthly things nothing is more powerful than divine humility. II, 1029.

- Christ’s humiliation could only have been exalted. IV, 1735. Christ’s humility from the beginning of the Incarnation to the cross. V, 115. Humility was commended by the Lord, who was soon to die, in the washing of the feet. VI, 414. The reason for Christ’s humility was our weakness. V, 778. Christ especially commended righteousness through humility. V, 1322. Humility is to be learned from the incarnate Word. V, 671. It is almost the one discipline of Christianity. V, 1538. Christ wishes us to learn from him not to perform miracles but to be humble. V, 441, 782. Christian doctrine is the commandment of humility. V, 876.

- Christ’s humility is to be imitated. III, 1604, 1606. It is not to be rejected through pride. V, 684, 687. Christ’s humility displeases the proud; but if it pleases you as a Christian, imitate it. IV, 1203, 1204. Christ’s example of humility is a medicine for pride. V, 1396. Certain members of Christ are exalted even in this age so that greater humility may be present in them. IV, 1119. Christ’s humility is our salvation in Christ. V, 1295. Humble Christ is the way to the homeland. V, 685. Humility is to be pursued. V, 354, 1560. It was necessary so that we, who fell through pride, might return to God. VI, 185. The rationale of humility among the saints. X, 161. Pride does its own will; humility does God’s will. III, 1604. Those who have not yet joined their devout necks to the Lord’s gentle yoke cannot easily be called humble. IV, 1473. Humility of heart is a sacrifice. IV, 1705. Whatever makes you righteous, attribute to God’s mercy; whatever makes you a sinner, to your own iniquity. V, 605. The whole appearance and countenance of the holy Scriptures admonishes us that whoever glories should glory in the Lord. VI, 278. It is incomparably better to give thanks to God for a small thing than to exalt oneself over a great one. V, 1287. The trembling of humility is better than the confidence of pride. IV, 1388. A humble sinner is better than a proud righteous person. IV, 1203; V, 930. A humble married woman is better than a proud virgin. IV, 968, 1280. See *Pride*. *Virginity*.

- Humility is holy infancy. V, 1561. The whole of human humility consists in recognizing oneself. III, 1604. A person is humble insofar as he acknowledges how many gifts of God have been bestowed on him. IV, 1429, 1430. Because of humility, it is useful for everyone, or nearly everyone, not to be able to know what they will become. II, 983. To be humble means not to wish praise for oneself. IV, 310. By what means one person can regard another as superior to oneself. VI, 82, 424.

The usefulness and necessity of humility are commended. IV, 314, 320, 428, 993, 1165, 1233, 1234, 1366, 1387, 1462, 1472, 1597, 1669, 1670, 1671, 1715, 1725, 1726, 1727. So great is the usefulness of human humility that even divine sublimity commended it by its own example. III, 1787, 1794. Humility is the foundation of the spiritual building. V, 441. And of perfection. III, 1690. It itself is our perfection. IV, 1714. The ways of humility are the ways of life. IV, 145. Humility is necessary for us to ascend to God. I, 701. The exalted God is approached through humility. V, 142, 1535. God is high, and is reached by the humble. IV, 947. Humility is the way to obtain truth. II, 442. No rash person should wish to reach the height of wisdom before possessing the humility of obedience. IV, 1566. God wills us to be both humble, to avoid pride, and lofty, to grasp wisdom. IV, 1712, 1713. It is excessive anxiety to fear that, where charity is burning, humility might be lacking. VI, 427. Nothing is loftier than the way of charity, and only the humble walk in it. IV, 1837. In the weakness of humility the virtue of charity is perfected. VIII, 887. Certainly God is great: he is burdensome to the strong, but light to the weak. Weakness in humility is greater strength. IV, 1186. All strength is in humility. IV, 1184. Victory is obtained through humility. V, 893. What dispositions and affections of humility Christian discipline prescribes. IV, 1203, 1204. The devout discipline of humility drives from the soul its windy and turbulent desire, greedy for things placed beyond our control, and in a certain way breathes it out. II, 485. Whoever is humble is truly poor even amid riches. V, 112. If a person removes his own righteousness from the midst and humbles himself, God’s righteousness will come and be exalted. IV, 1128 [Col. 0343]. The Lord draws near to the humbled, but withdraws far from the exalted. IV, 1082. How God gives grace to the humble. IV, 1427.

Humility distinguishes the city of God from the city of the devil. VII, 421. The humble becomes a member of Christ. III, 1604, 1606. A humbled heart is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. VI, 419. The house of the Most High God. I, 826. God makes the humble his heaven. IV, 1472. Small sins that creep upon the watchful grow through pride and are destroyed by humility. VI, 425. Humility is a remedy against swelling. V, 780. Something can perish from the swollen; nothing perishes from the little. III, 1606. Unless humility both precedes, accompanies, and follows everything we do well, pride snatches the whole thing from our hand. II, 442. What the humble obtains, the proud loses. V, 108. The unhappy prodigal son obtains happiness through humility and shows himself worthy precisely by confessing himself unworthy. IV, 159. Those who have learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be gentle and humble in heart make greater progress by thinking and praying than by reading and listening. II, 596. Through humility charity is both acquired and preserved. VI, 413. The measure of humility given to each person corresponds to the measure of that person’s greatness. VI, 413. God exalts the humble. V, 1278. He exalts them in such a way that he does not make them proud. IV, 1472. The proud person is entangled in evils so that he may be humbled; the humble is rescued from evils so that he may be exalted. IV, 1589. The excellence of Christ’s glory has its beginning in humility. IV, 1454. Humility exalts. VII, 421. Humility is the merit of glory, and glory is the reward of humility. III, 1905. Loftiness delights everyone, but humility is the staircase. V, 586, 671. The firmest humility is more powerful and safer than the most windy loftiness. VIII, 957. Humility is the way by which one reaches eternity. V, 685. Humility prepares a safe and true way to heaven. VII, 482. The humble is received by entering through the door; the proud is cast down by climbing up another way. IV, 1229. Humility is especially to be pursued in the monastery. I, 1379. The humble person [acts] disorderly. V, 107.

A certain perverse humility by which a person turns toward earthly things. IV, 1142. To be humbled by God is sometimes both punishment and grace. IV, 427. An evil and penal humiliation. IV, 1751, 1752. Humility is twofold: of confession and of tribulation. IV, 1541. Likewise, voluntary and penal. IV, 1550. Whoever is not humbled by confessing iniquity is humbled by the weight of God’s hand. IV, 267. Humility that is false and feigned. IX, 63. God does not accept false humility. V, 981. The pretense of humility is a greater pride. VI, 421. What does it profit that what you say appears humble to people, if God sees that what you think is lofty? IV, 1505. In wondrous ways it happens that a person becomes more inflated by false humility than if he had displayed pride more openly. II, 642. Humility will be genuine only if it is not displayed merely on the tongue. IV, 1505. A lie under the appearance of humility is a sin. V, 981. The praise of humility must not be partly assigned to falsehood. X, 265, 267.

Humility is difficult to instill. VII, 13. The first and great gift of the Spirit is humility and gentleness. III, 2138. Christ placed the sign of humility in the stature of childhood. I, 674. Humility is signified by a valley. V, 1524. Scripture commends humility more in those who were from the Gentiles than in the Jews. V, 1036. The humility of the Centurion. IV, 428; V, 1503. Of the tax collectors. IV, 446, 447. Of the Canaanite woman. V, 483, 487. Humility in the Canaanite woman had produced great faith. V, 1036.

The four humors by which the nature of the flesh is regulated. II, 943.

Hydromancy, a kind of divination brought from the Persians. VII, 223.

Dropsy of the heart: the avaricious person. V, 410, 956. Dropsy cannot be cured. V, 489.

Winter raging at Rome with incredible severity. VII, 98. Our winter and summer: what they are. V, 216. Winter, a figure of adversity. IV, 370. In winter dead and living trees look alike, but the coming summer distinguishes them. IV, 1947. Winter, this present life. IV, 389, 1947.

What *hyle* is. VIII, 379, 380, 556. What the Greeks understand by this term. VIII, 379. *Hyle* as the principle and nature of evil according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 370, 379, 369. It is shown that *hyle* cannot be the principle of things. VIII, 390. The absurd Manichaean teaching concerning *hyle* is refuted. VIII, 380, 395, 401. They commonly call the demon *hyle*. VIII, 387.

Hymenaeus. VIII, 575.

Honey of Hymettus. I, 966.

A hymn is a song containing praise of God. IV, 914, 1947. A hymn ought to have three things: praise, of God, and song. IV, 914, 1947, 1948. The singing of hymns in churches. IV, 487. The singing of hymns was instituted at the altar in Carthage. I, 634. Hilary attacked it, and Augustine defended it. I, 634. The eternal hymn is the reward of the saints. IV, 1948. The hymn said to be of our Lord Jesus Christ is usually found in the apocryphal Scriptures. II, 1034. Its words are set down in an exceedingly obscure manner. II, 1034. More passages are reported. II, 1035 [Col. 0344]. The hymn of the three boys belongs to Scripture. VII, 324.

To sing hymns. IV, 320.

What hyperbole is. VII, 499; X, 788.

Hyperbolus. VII, 54.

Hippocrates. I, 695.

The origin of hypocrisy: what it is. III, 208. The desire for human praise often generates hypocrisy. II, 92. Hypocrisy shines outwardly; inwardly it is mud. IV, 1229.

Who is a hypocrite. III, 1271.

Underground chambers. V, 267.

Hyssop, a lowly but medicinal herb. IV, 593. Hyssop is suitable for cleansing the lungs. IV, 593. Hyssop is a symbol of cleansing the heart. IV, 593.

## I. J.

Jabin is interpreted as “wise.” IV, 1053.

Jacob—that is, “supplanter”—because at birth he held his brother’s heel. IV, 987, 1937. He is the same person later called Israel. V, 47, 681. That is, “seeing God.” V, 41; IV, 1937. Concerning his two names. V, 681. Given for different reasons. IV, 987. Why Jacob was called Israel. VII, 518. Why, after receiving the new name, he retained the former one. V, 682. Jacob and Esau as constellations. I, 739. Jacob and Esau had one and the same lot from their father, their mother, their conception, and their birth; they differed only by God. II, 887. Whether Jacob was approved through foreknowledge of his future will. VI, 117. Whether he was chosen through foreknowledge of future faith. VI, 114. In him God loved not the fault that he was removing, but the grace that he was giving. VI, 123. See Election. The blessings given to Jacob and Esau. V, 39, 56.

Jacob and Esau are two peoples. IV, 527, 1135. Jacob is a figure of Christians, as Esau is of the Jews. V, 55. Jacob signifies the spiritual among God’s people. III, 567; IV, 1771, 1772; good Christians. V, 34, 37. Esau signifies the carnal. IV, 527; V, 34, 37. Jacob’s blessing: whether it was fraudulently stolen without deceit, and what it signifies. VII, 515. Jacob received the blessing without deceit, through deceit. III, 567; V, 41, 557. Jacob is defended against the charge of lying. V, 45. When that prophecy was fulfilled: “The elder shall serve the younger.” IV, 527, 1135.

Jacob’s dream was a figure. V, 681. Who are signified by the angels seen by Jacob ascending and descending on the ladder. IV, 1597, 1598. The stone anointed by Jacob, a figure of Christ. VII, 517. Jacob’s wrestling with the Angel. V, 57, 681. What it signifies. IV, 1936. Jacob’s wrestling with the Angel, a prophecy concerning Christ. III, 574. And concerning Christ’s Passion. VII, 518. The Lord wrestled with Jacob in the person of the Angel. IV, 1936. Jacob prevailing over the Angel, a figure of the persecutor prevailing against Christ. IV, 1022. Jacob bore the figure of the Church. IV, 1015. The striking at the breadth of the thigh signifies the multitude of unbelievers. IV, 506. What Jacob blessed and limping signifies. V, 57, 681; VII, 518. Blessing among those who believed; limping among those who did not believe. IV, 506. The various colors among Jacob’s animals: whence they came. VIII, 988. Jacob’s four wives are wrongly brought forward as a crime against him. VIII, 428, 430. With what intention Jacob took several wives. VII, 517. And what the four wives prefigured. VIII, 432. Jacob’s chastity. VII, 517; VIII, 430, 431. In what year of his life Jacob went down into Egypt. VII, 563. In what year of his life he died. VII, 564. Jacob blessing Joseph’s sons. I, 801; V, 1275. Jacob is often named in his sons. III, 596.

How James is the brother of the Lord. III, 2110.

The feast day of James and Marianus, martyrs. V, 1288.

James. II, 1070.

James and Timasius. X, 247. Young men of highly honorable birth. II, 774. Good servants of God and honorable men. X, 347. At one time disciples and admirers of Pelagius. X, 333, 347, 348. At Pelagius’s urging they renounced the world and lived continently. II, 767, 774. Augustine’s works recalled them from Pelagius’s error. II, 767. They ask Augustine to refute a book which they assert to be Pelagius’s. II, 767, 774, 816. They thank Augustine for the book on nature and grace that he wrote for them. II, 741. Their letter is praised. II, 767.

What boasting is. VII, 356, 424. Boasting is the final plague and more harmful than the others. I, 992. Boasting amid the very filth of mourning. III, 1287. Boasting makes many people generous and martyrs. III, 2020. Remove boasting, and what are all human beings except human beings? VII, 161.

The loss of your possessions does not mean that the one who gave them has been taken from you, although what he gave has been taken away. IV, 281.

Ejaculatory prayer. The brothers in Egypt indeed have frequent prayers, but very brief ones, launched forth, as it were, in haste. II, 1020.

Jader of Midila. IX, 229.

Iamblichus, a Platonic philosopher. VII, 237.

Jambus of Germaniciana. IX, 228.

The feet called iambi. I, 1098.

Janiculum, a mountain now called Montorium. VII, 97. Note 2.

Janiculum, a city. VII, 198.

The two doors through which the enemy enters and reigns: desire and fear. VI, 310.

January. IX, 384.

Januarius, a bishop. II, 759, 780.

Januarius, a Donatist bishop. II, 302; IX, 528, 555.

Januarius of the village of Caesar. IX, 216.

Januarius of Lamboese. IX, 206.

Januarius of Muzula. IX, 222.

Januarius, a gravedigger. IX, 513.

Januarius, bearer of Augustine’s letter to Paulinus. II, 816.

Januarius, at whose inquiries two books were written. I, 638; II, 199.

Januarius the presbyter retained his private property contrary to the law of the monastery. V, 1570. He made a will. V, 1570.

January was named from Janus. VIII, 346. And was dedicated to Janus. VII, 200. The solemnity of the January Kalends. V, 1020, 1021, 1024. Superstitions. V, 1020, 1024, 1025. Augustine warns that the customary superstitions should not be practiced on the January Kalends. V, 1020. On the January Kalends one should either fast or at least eat lunch soberly. V, 1025.

Why Janus is imagined with two faces. VII, 200. And with four faces. VII, 201. Janus is more innocent than the other select gods. VII, 198. He is not properly distinguished from the god Terminus. VII, 200. Nor from Jupiter. VII, 203. Why he is placed before Jupiter. VII, 201. Beginnings of things belong to Janus. VII, 200. Janus is the world. VII, 200, 203. The gates of Janus were open in war and closed in peace. VII, 84.

Japheth is interpreted as “breadth.” VII, 477.

Jason, praised by the Arian as a most learned man. II, 1053.

Jasus, son of Triopas, king of the Argives, enrolled among the gods. VII, 565.

The story of Icarus. VII, 571.

The Council of Iconium. IX, 195, 196. Note (a).

The twinkling of an eye. V, 1624.

What ideas are. VI, 30. How great a force is established in ideas. VI, 29. Plato is said to have been the first to call them ideas. VI, 29. Plato’s ideas. VII, 218. The ideas of all things exist eternally in the divine mind. VI, 31.

Idioms, the distinctive features of a language. III, 485, 557.

The “same thing” is the supreme and unchangeable good that God is. VIII, 872. “The same thing” is “I am who I am.” IV, 1622. Or, that which always exists in the same way. IV, 1622, 1906. No one possesses this “same thing” from himself. IV, 1623.

Jeduthun is interpreted as “Leaping over them.” IV, 412, 729, 970.

Why those who worship idols become like idols. IV, 1754. It is deservedly that a human being falls away from the one who made him, when he himself places above himself what he made. VII, 249. Who are called idolaters. VIII, 827. The false natural philosophy of idolaters is rejected. VII, 217. The beginning of idolatry. VI, 685. Its origin. VII, 221, 224. Idolatry arises from pride. V, 1022. And from vanity. X, 212. Idolatry, instituted in Egypt, became more widespread and much more shameful. IX, 597. Nothing is greater, nothing more superstitious. V, 1022. The world was flooded with the fabrications of the Egyptians. V, 1022. The Jews who desired earthly and temporal happiness were easily converted to idols. IV, 351.

Idolatry is a great evil. III, 743; VIII, 540. The sins of idolatry are also punishments. V, 1022. How insane the worshipers of idols are. IV, 1754, 1957; V, 777. Those who want to have God along with many others more easily brought it about that they did not have him than that they combined him with many false gods. II, 842. Idolaters are pressed hard. III, 1061. The Apostles’ teaching against idolatry is vindicated from the prophecies. III, 1066. Idolatry cannot be defended. VII, 221, 222. They say in vain that they do not worship images but what is signified by images. V, 1023. The excuses of idolaters are refuted. IV, 1244, 1245, 1246. Idolaters possess something worthy of approval. IX, 587. Idolatry was punished or restrained among the Jews. VIII, 290. It was punished by Moses. VIII, 462. By destroying the sacred groves, temples, and high places of idols, Hezekiah and Josiah served the Lord. II, 801. By granting Daniel power to break the idol and by throwing his enemies to the lions, Darius served the Lord. II, 801. The worship of idols was forbidden and their temples closed by the laws of the emperors. IV, 1788, 1789. Idols overturned. V, 151, 162, 165. Idols should not be broken unless legitimate authority is granted. V, 422. The unjust complaints of idolaters. V, 423. The Roman disaster did not happen as a result of the idols being overturned. V, 623, 624. The Donatists acknowledged that the crime of idolatry was justly punished by the emperors. IX, 45. Under the pretext of breaking idols, the Donatists went to pagan festivals so that they might be killed by the pagans. II, 797. Those people vowed to their idols as many victims as they killed from among them. II, 797.

Idolatry is to be punished by excommunication. VI, 220. The rejection of idols was foretold. III, 1062; VII, 248, 588, 592. Idolatry was destroyed by the opposite causes from those by which it had been established. VII, 250 [Col. 0346]. Idolatry was overthrown through the name of Christ and the faith of Christians, in accordance with the prophecies. III, 1061. The grace of the truest Savior overturned idolatry. VII, 248. Idolaters became angry with Christ their Lord on behalf of their idol; if they had become angry with their servant on behalf of their idol, they would have deserved condemnation. IV, 1258. One should not be angry with idolaters, but pray for them. V, 423. The various forms of idolatry. III, 152. The idols of the heart. VI, 643. If a craftsman gave his idol not only its shape but also a heart, the idol itself would be worshiped. V, 777. How the weakness of human thought tries, through the habit of visible things, to establish idolatry in our heart. II, 798. How idolatry is avarice. V, 630.

Idol-meat. Those who dine in an idol shrine with pagans are reproved. V, 417. Some recline in an idol shrine out of fear of some important person. V, 418. The foolish excuse of those reclining in an idol shrine. V, 419. It is better to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols. VI, 385. If someone is uncertain whether a piece of meat has been sacrificed, and it has not been sacrificed, then, provided that he has retained the knowledge that it was not sacrificed and eats it, he certainly does not sin. II, 186. A person does not sin who later eats unknowingly food which he previously rejected as though it were idol-meat. II, 185. If it is certainly known to be idol-meat, it is better not to eat it, even if there is danger of death and no occasion of scandal exists. But if it is known not to be idol-meat, or if this is unknown, it may be taken for necessary use without any scruple of conscience. II, 187. A Christian ought not to use anything in honor of foreign gods, even if he despises them in his mind, lest he edify those who cannot see his mind toward honoring them. II, 185. Idols, temples, and sacred groves may be converted to common uses or to the honor of the true God. II, 185. A Christian may use the vegetable produce that grows in the garden of an idol’s temple, or the spring or well that is in the temple, even if some sacrificial offering is thrown into the well or spring with the intention of sacrificing to the waters. II, 186.

Idumaea is interpreted as “earthly.” IV, 721.

The Idumaeans, the people of Edom, descended from Esau. III, 579; VII, 520. They are interpreted either as “blood-colored” or as “earthly.” IV, 601, 602, 1052. The Idumaeans were made tributary to the Israelites by David. III, 567.

Jebus, a city which, after being destroyed, Jerusalem was built upon. IV, 734, 773.

Jeconiah is interpreted as “preparation of God.” III, 1076. Jeconiah is a figure of Christ. V, 341.

For the partial obedience that Jehu displayed, motivated by his desire for his own rule, he received the temporal kingdom as a temporary reward. VI, 520.

Christ’s spiritual fast. IV, 336, 851.

Fasting, a great work, a Christian work. IV, 1108. Christian fasting: what it is. III, 1339. Our fast differs in its purpose from the fast of pagans, Jews, and heretics. VI, 711. With what intention fasting should be observed. III, 1287. Those who fast so that they may eat a more sumptuous lunch are conducting business for the belly, not for religion. IV, 1108. Fasting fights against the belly and the throat; sometimes it serves them. IV, 1108. Fasting serving luxury and the belly. IV, 488. Fasting is necessary for subduing the flesh. VI, 709. Fasting is defrauding the flesh and profiting the mind. VI, 706. One should fast when we are engaged in a sharper struggle with the enemy. V, 1049. Fasting is either in tribulation or in joy. III, 1339. Fasting belongs to the will; hunger to necessity. IV, 476.

Which fasts are acceptable to God. V, 1042. Fasting together with prayer and almsgiving. V, 811. Fasting without prayer and almsgiving is insufficient. IV, 482. The prayer of one who fasts should be free from desire and hatred. V, 1044. Fasting without mercy is nothing to the one who fasts. V, 1043. The meal omitted through fasting should be distributed to the poor. IV, 482. Let hungry Christ receive what the fasting Christian takes less for himself. V, 1053. Let the voluntary deprivation of the well-to-do become the necessary abundance of the poor. V, 1053. Add to almsgiving what you subtract from yourselves by fasting. V, 1040, 1047. Fasts, prayers, and almsgiving belong to the clothing of the sheep. III, 1306. Fasting is commanded in the New Testament. II, 147.

Fasting before the solemnity of Christ’s Passion is especially fitting. V, 1050. Why it was instituted with the number forty. V, 1051. The fast of Lent has authority both in the ancient books and from the Gospel. II, 217. Lenten fasting is prescribed for us by the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. IV, 1463. Why Christ’s fast, like those of Moses and Elijah, lasted forty days. V, 695, 1039, 1216. What it signifies. III, 48. What kind of fasting and abstinence is required in Lent. V, 1043. The Manichaeans did not celebrate the fast before Easter. VIII, 178. The fasts of Christians during the days of Easter and during other solemnities in Christ, and their fasts for pagans during the pagans’ profane festivals. IV, 1261, 1262. The fast of the Nativity of the Lord. II, 234. Fasting on Wednesday, because on that day the Jews are found to have taken counsel to kill the Lord. II, 150. The Roman people customarily fasted on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. II, 140. The Romans do not seem to fast on Thursday. II, 140. Even those who eat lunch on other Saturdays fast on the Saturday preceding Easter. II, 150. Throughout the Church the Sabbath is a day for eating, except among the Romans and a few Westerners. II, 139. Many nearby, and sometimes more distant, churches observe the Saturday fast together with Rome. II, 281. The much greater part of the world does not observe it. II, 281. Some fast on Saturday because of the humility of the Lord’s death; others relax the fast because of God’s rest. II, 150. The sermon of a certain Urbicus, by which he proves that one should fast on Saturday, is most injurious to the universal Church. II, 137, 138. The arguments of that Urbicus by which he proves that one should fast on Saturday are refuted. II, 139, 140, 141, 142. Some Romans believe that the Saturday fast originated from the fact that Peter, about to contend with Simon on the Lord’s Day, had fasted the preceding day; others think this false. II, 146. In observing the Saturday fast, the custom of the bishops should be followed. II, 151. One must also ensure that the fellowship of those among whom we live and with whom we live for God is not offended. II, 148. A traveler does best when following the fasting customs of the place where he is staying. II, 202. The Church forbids fasting for several days for certain reasons. V, 1052.

Fasting is not observed, especially on feast days. II, 145, 146. Christians relax their fasts during Eastertide, pray standing, and sing “Alleluia,” which is a sign of the resurrection. II, 218; V, 1048, 1052. Fasting on the Lord’s Day is not unlawful, but no one should assign this day to fasting without just cause for scandal. II, 138, 144, 149, 150. The Apostles were not accustomed to fast solemnly on the Lord’s Day. II, 149. The Manichaeans assigned the Lord’s Day for fasting to their hearers. II, 149, 150. The days on which one should or should not fast are not fixed. II, 148, 151. From where the Priscillianists derive their approval of fasting on the Lord’s Day. II, 149. The Aerians refuse to celebrate officially established fasts; each person is to fast whenever he wishes. VIII, 40. Daily fasting is recommended, except on those days when the Church forbids fasting. V, 1052. Except for Saturday and Sunday, many people fast throughout their entire lives, especially those established in monasteries. II, 140. Daily fasts, as well as three-day fasts, without food or drink. I, 1340. Frequent, daily, or even incredibly prolonged fasts in the Catholic communion. VIII, 225. Augustine heard from the brothers that someone had fasted for forty days. II, 149. Fasts were also customary among women. I, 1340. If you cannot fast, feed the poor person instead, so that through his being filled you may receive forgiveness. V, 811. Every chastisement of the body is signified by fasting. X, 300. The great and universal fast is to abstain from iniquities and the unlawful pleasures of the world. III, 1529. To fast from this world. V, 695, 1212. Why one must mourn and fast in this life. V, 1050. Jovinian said that fasts were of no benefit. VIII, 45. For fasting to benefit heretics, they must return to the Church. VI, 711. The children at Nineveh were rightly compelled to fast because of original sin. II, 723.

Jemini is interpreted as “right-hand.” IV, 97.

Jephthah, that is, “opening.” III, 817, 818. Jephthah was a judge of the Israelites, not a king. III, 819. Jephthah’s vow is examined. III, 810. Whether Jephthah’s vow displeased God. III, 812. Whether Jephthah made the vow by inspiration of the Holy Spirit. III, 814. Whether Jephthah killed his daughter at God’s command is rightly questioned. VII, 35. Whether Jephthah acted rightly in carrying out the vow. III, 812. Jephthah’s vow, a prophecy concerning the Church. III, 815, 820. Jephthah, a figure of Christ. III, 817. Jephthah’s faith. III, 816.

How Jeremiah was known to God before he was formed. III, 344. Some believe that he was sanctified in the womb according to predestination. II, 846. The innate holiness of Jeremiah and John the Baptist. X, 1428. Jeremiah and John, though sanctified in the womb, nevertheless bore original sin. X, 1429. What kind of holiness was then present in them. X, 1429. Some understand Jeremiah’s sanctification as a type of the Savior. II, 846. Jeremiah foretells the seventy-year captivity and other disasters for the Jews. VII, 582, 583. And the future restoration of the city of Jerusalem. IV, 1917. What Jeremiah prophesied and at what time. VII, 591. Jeremiah was born approximately one hundred years before Plato. VII, 236.

Jericho is interpreted as “moon.” IV, 728. The fall of Jericho’s walls in the presence of the Ark expresses the destruction of the hope of this world through the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit. II, 209.

Jerusalem was called Jebus. III, 783, 795; IV, 773. And Salem. IV, 303. Jerusalem itself is Zion. IV, 774. Jerusalem, a city shared by the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. III, 795. Its overthrow is treated throughout Psalm 73. IV, 929. Of the signs that Christ foretold as future, some pertain to the destruction of Jerusalem, some to the Lord’s coming through the Church, and some to the final coming at which he will judge the living and the dead. II, 214. Jerusalem was overthrown during the celebration of Passover. IV, 932. Under King Zedekiah. VII, 582. Josephus writes that such evils then befell the Jewish people at the destruction of Jerusalem that they scarcely seem bearable. II, 216. The Jews were forbidden by the Roman emperor to approach the city of Jerusalem. V, 57. How the promises made concerning earthly Jerusalem are to be understood. VII, 543. In Augustine’s time Jerusalem was full of Christian worshipers and had no Jew. IV, 759, 773. Many were baptized at Jerusalem because of an earthquake. V, 136. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” IV, 122, 598, 734, 1656, 1755, 1761; VII, 637. It has eternal peace as its end. IV, 1761. The prerogatives of Jerusalem. IV, 253. Why Jerusalem is called the holy city. VII, 438. The true Jerusalem, the Church of the saints. IV, 1952. The world was set ablaze by the fervor of the Church of Jerusalem. V, 660. From Jerusalem the Church began; it is to be understood not as invisible but as visible. IX, 409. Spiritual Jerusalem belongs no more to the Jews than to the Gentiles. IV, 1467. Jerusalem is partly on pilgrimage and partly abiding in heaven. IV, 1952. Its citizens are also angels. IV, 1761. The Babylonian city and the city of Jerusalem, so that they may be opposed to one another. See Babylon. A captive portion of Jerusalem is held in Babylon on account of sin. IV, 1761. Jerusalem begins to be freed in its heart from captivity through confession of iniquity and love of righteousness. IV, 1761. Each person becomes a suitable citizen of heavenly Jerusalem as soon as he has renounced this world. IV, 1477. The children of heavenly Jerusalem are brought to birth and born of their mother, charity; they are enclosed as charity gathers them together. IV, 1923. Jerusalem is a type of the heavenly city. VI, 336. And a shadow. IV, 1620, 1650, 1656. In Jerusalem there is an image of the future Church, just as in Zion there is an image of the present Church. IV, 122. Jerusalem signifies our eternal mother in heaven, whether in the angels themselves or in those who are saved in hope. III, 478. Heavenly Jerusalem will receive from human beings as many citizens as it lost from the angels, or even more. VI, 246. To love Jerusalem is to walk toward it. IV, 1918.

Jesus in Hebrew, **Σωτήρ** (*Sōtēr*) in Greek, *Salvator* in Latin. VIII, 1025. Jesus is interpreted as “Savior,” or “Saving One.” V, 944, 1334, 1370; VII, 553, 785.

Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the people into the promised land. VII, 522, 568. When Joshua son of Nun died. VII, 568. He was called Auses. V, 1553.

Jesus. The foolish prattle of the Manichaeans about him is beaten down. VIII, 376. That a suffering Jesus is born from the earth, with the Holy Spirit conceiving, and that he himself hangs from every kind of wood: a Manichaean heresy. VIII, 376.

The Pelagians begrudge human beings Jesus as Savior. X, 1123. The Pelagians themselves deny that Jesus is Jesus for little children. X, 1302, 1303. Jesus is Jesus also for little children. X, 190, 473, 1143, 1189, 1190, 1192, 1214, 1281, 1379, 1380, 1467, 1606. Jesus is scarcely sought for Jesus’ sake. III, 1600. Jesus is strong and weak. III, 1512. How much more affectionate and sweeter it is to name Jesus than “Savior.” VII, 591. To say Jesus in words and deeds. V, 1237.

Indolence. Leisure should be enjoyed for devotion, not for indolence. II, 188.

Fire as the principle of things according to the Stoics. VII, 230. They also regarded it as a god. VII, 230. The perpetual fire dedicated to Vesta. VII, 77. It is proved that fire is superior to air. III, 265. Above the air, pure fire is said to be heaven. III, 265. Why fire is found in the lower part of corruptible air. III, 283. Even this fire itself is praiseworthy. VII, 352. Lower fire penetrates everything in order to produce movement in them. III, 281. It cannot grow cold. III, 281. It can be changed into another element. III, 283. It cannot rise into the higher heavenly tranquility. III, 283. The ancients attributed a certain purity to fire. VII, 121. There are many wondrous things in fire that cannot be explained. VII, 712, 719. That animals live in fire was unknown to Augustine. VIII, 198.

Fire, the Holy Spirit. V, 254. Whether the fire over the Apostles on the day of Pentecost was seen with the eyes or with the spirit may be debated. VIII, 852. Why fire is first used in the sacraments, in catechizing, and in exorcizing. IV, 797.

Fire is a symbol of adversity, just as water is a symbol of prosperity. IV, 797. The fire of the temptation of tribulation. V, 254; VI, 155, 264. The fire by which each person’s work is tested. IV, 222. Who is burned by it and who is not. VI, 264. The fire of the furnace acts in different ways: it turns straw into ashes and removes impurities from gold; so does tribulation. IV, 173. Fire may be understood in a good sense. VII, 692. The term “fire” signifies punishment. III, 779. The fire preceding Christ’s coming, both for the punishment of the wicked and for the salvation of the redeemed. IV, 1240, 1241; VII, 503. How the fire of the final judgment should not be feared. IV, 569. Purgatorial fire after this life. III, 212; VI, 156, 217, 264. One thing is not harmed by fire; another is saved through fire. IV, 222. See Purgatorial.

The Priscillianists taught that the fire by which sinners are punished is neither real nor eternal. VIII, 668, 672. According to some, the fire of Gehenna is used for the pain of a soul that repents fruitlessly. VII, 723. The punishment of eternal fire is joined to exclusion from the kingdom of God. V, 879, 1337. The fire of Gehenna is the future punishment of sinners; the fire of desires is their present and hidden punishment. IV, 686, 687, 688. The fire of Gehenna pertains to body and soul. VII, 723. The punishment of fire will be assigned to human beings and demons. VII, 724. Whether that fire is bodily. VII, 724. How spirits can be tortured by bodily fire. VII, 725. The eternal fire of hell and eternal burning. VI, 214. Eternal fire. VII, 682. It is not eternal in the same way as God. VIII, 563. Eternal fire is not evil. VIII, 563. According to the diversity of merits, eternal fire will be lighter for some and heavier for others. VII, 731. In what part of the world the fire of hell will be, no one knows. VII, 682.

Ignorance and weakness, the two causes of sin. VI, 271. Ignorance and weakness are vices that hinder the will from being moved to do a good work or to abstain from an evil work. X, 167. Certain acts done through ignorance are nevertheless disapproved and judged in need of correction. I, 1297. They are sins. I, 1295. To cause someone harm through ignorance is a sin. VII, 728. Sins of ignorance. X, 148, 243, 255, 287, 851, 1118, 1239. What these are. II, 186. Sins of ignorance are called human sins. III, 721. Sins arising from ignorance are voluntary. VII, 665. A certain necessity of sinning arising from ignorance. X, 1118, 1120. One sins more seriously when knowingly than when unknowingly. X, 884. Nevertheless, one must not therefore flee into the darkness of ignorance in order to seek an excuse there. X, 884, 885. Ignorance is twofold: that of those unwilling to know, and that of those simply lacking knowledge; neither excuses. X, 885. See Knowledge. Ignorance is not a just excuse. II, 883. Nor does ignorance excuse in such a way as to free one from punishment. X, 884. To what extent ignorance excuses. IX, 485. For this reason those who sin knowingly are called inexcusable, because they also see by their own judgment that they are inexcusable. II, 883. When ignorance and difficulty are reckoned as guilt. X, 288. Julian calls perfect ignorance by the name of justice. X, 721. The doctrine of Caelestius: ignorance and forgetfulness are not subject to sin, since they occur not according to the will but according to necessity. X, 345. Ignorance and difficulty belong to the misery of just condemnation. X, 1009. Ignorance, the punishment of the first sin. VII, 784. Ignorance and difficulty are a just punishment arising from the condemnation of humanity. X, 287. How great is the ignorance of little children. X, 149, 150. Ignorance is an evil even in one who has been baptized. X, 851. Ignorance and weakness—so that a person either does not know what he ought to will or cannot do everything he wills—arise from the hidden order of punishments and the inscrutable judgments of God. VIII, 451. They are called sins because they derive their origin from the sin of free will. I, 1298. They are the most just punishment of sin. I, 1297. Ignorance itself, in those who were unwilling to understand, is without doubt sin; but in those who were unable, it is the punishment of sin. II, 883. Although, on the hypothesis, it be conceded to the Manichaeans that ignorance and difficulty are not punishments of nature, the faith concerning original sin must nevertheless be defended against the Pelagians. X, 1009. Even if ignorance and difficulty were humanity’s natural beginnings, God would still not be blameworthy but praiseworthy. X, 1009.

How ignorance and difficulty can be overcome. X, 288. The evil of ignorance can not only be diminished but also consumed in this life. X, 851. From what source it is diminished. X, 851. A person cannot be freed from ignorance without labor, pain, and fear. VII, 784, 785. Faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge. V, 179. A person ought not to be ashamed to confess that he does not know what he does not know, lest, while pretending to know, he never become worthy to know. II, 862. Confession of ignorance is a step toward knowledge. V, 1382. It is better not to know than to err. III, 1553. In matters concerning God, ignorance is more devout than presumptuous knowledge. V, 663. Let there be rather a devout confession of ignorance than a rash profession of knowledge. V, 663. Augustine chooses to confess cautious ignorance rather than false knowledge. II, 901. Augustine confesses to those who ask that he is ignorant of the origin of the soul, as of many other things. II, 724, 732. How ignorance of certain matters should be patiently endured. II, 732. For what reason this is permitted by God even in the learned. II, 724. A certain learned ignorance through the Spirit of God. II, 505. It is one thing to be ignorant of what it is evil not to know; another, of what either cannot be known, or need not be known, or is irrelevant to the life we seek. II, 733. Of which ignorance it is said, “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored.” II, 743. Was Christ ignorant of anything? IV, 333. Christ was ignorant of sin—not by judging it, but by not committing it. IV, 333. God is said not to know in the way that an art does not know vices. IV, 334. The symbol of ignorance is darkness. IV, 326; V, 576. Ignorance is the mother of wonder. I, 857. *I do not know* (*ignoro*) sometimes means the same as “I do not approve.” III, 2071; V, 838; VI, 106. “It is unknown” is used of what is foreign to the work. IV, 334.

God’s forgiving is not knowing; and not knowing means not taking notice of or not exacting punishment. IV, 947. God forgives better than he recognizes. IV, 947. God forgives the person who confesses, but who punishes himself. IV, 592. Sometimes God chastises in this age the person whom he forgives in the age to come. IV, 595. See To Spare.

One must forgive a brother. V, 653, 1055, 1556. One should quickly forgive the person who asks pardon. II, 856. And even the person unwilling to ask pardon. V, 1056. Only the person whose guilt is utterly certain receives forgiveness. II, 165. One must forgive a brother as often as necessary. V, 515, 652. In this kind of good work there is no excuse, where the will alone is the entire capacity. V, 1053. The person who forgives loses nothing; enriched by love, he returns home. V, 252. The merciful gentleness of forgiveness does not serve to leave wickedness unpunished. VIII, 624. Nor should discipline be neglected. V, 518. One must forgive or punish out of love. II, 661, 662.

Each person is unknown to himself before the questioning of temptation. IV, 698.

Ilia, or Rhea, the mother of Romulus. VII, 578. They maintain that Ilia conceived twins by Mars. VII, 578.

Ilium was destroyed by Fimbria. VII, 83. By the Greeks. VII, 91. The ancestral gods did not prevent the destruction of Ilium. VII, 83.

“Ille” (“that one”), used in place of a proper name. V, 964.

Worldly allurements are to be despised. VI, 447. To allure. VI, 314.

What is illicit. VIII, 419.

Illumination is twofold, spiritual and bodily. X, 130. There is illumination through faith and illumination through direct vision. III, 2010. The opinion of the Arians was that illumination returns by stages all the way to the Father. VIII, 711, 712, 713. A person is illumined by turning toward God, not by turning toward himself. IV, 193, 200.

Illusion is a great persecution. III, 1481. Just as illusion is the punishment of the soul, so truth is the soul’s reward. IV, 402. How great the soul’s illusions are. IV, 402. Their complete cessation is a gift of God. I, 797. Nocturnal illusions, though involuntary, nevertheless require repentance. II, 797.

What imagination is. III, 464. Imagination is nothing other than an impression inflicted through the senses. II, 69. Imagination is not something bodily. III, 366. The power of imagining is explained by the soul’s capacity to remove or add to what it has apprehended through the senses. II, 70. The imagination of a body in the soul is better than the appearance of the body, but the likeness of God is not so. VIII, 969. The power of mothers’ imagination over fetuses. III, 572. How difficult it is to drive imaginary forms away from the inner sight. II, 615. What must be done to drive them away. II, 616. How imagination is useful to faith. VIII, 951. Two evils to be avoided by the mind while it imagines. VIII, 990. Cattle and birds delight in imagination. III, 366.

What an image is. III, 242. Three kinds of images: of things perceived, things imagined, and things held to be true. II, 69. We have impressed in our heart an image of the things we think about. IV, 1813. The imagination receives images of things not from itself but from the senses. II, 69, 70. How images are formed in the soul can scarcely be explained. II, 706. Images of bodies are not bodily. II, 706. Bodies’ images are perceived by the spirit through a certain likeness of the body, although that likeness is incorporeal. II, 618. The source of the images of sleepers, madmen, and others. VIII, 989. Image, equality, and likeness are not the same. VI, 85. Images are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are. VI, 143, 163. Vast mirrors do not make images larger; in small mirrors, even if a large face is presented, a very small image is formed according to the size of the mirror. II, 65. What difference there is between image and likeness. III, 749. The image of a beast in a human being. VIII, 1006.

The image of God is twofold. V, 82. “Image of God” is one thing, and “according to the image of God” another; both are said of human beings, but of Christ only the first. I, 626. Which creature should be called the image of God. VIII, 991. How a human being is according to the image of God. VI, 332. The image of God is within the human being, not in the body. IV, 564, 629. The image of God is in the mind. IV, 480; VI, 628. The image of God must be sought in the immortality of the rational soul. VIII, 1038, 1040. Whether a woman’s mind did not bear the image of God. III, 452. The image of God remained in Adam after the sin, but disfigured. I, 640. It has not been entirely erased in unbelievers. X, 230. We have been able to disfigure the image of God in us, but cannot restore it. V, 255. Sin erased the image of God in humanity; grace restores it. III, 355; X, 229, 230. The grace of righteousness. III, 355. How the image of God is restored in a human being. VIII, 1053, 1054. It cannot be restored without God’s grace. I, 1067. The image of God is disturbed by a perverse life. IV, 959. Those who reduced the image of God to nothing in their earthly city are worthy of having God reduce their image to nothing in his city. IV, 926.
