When and in what respect a human being is made according to the image of God. VIII, 473, 475. When God’s image in a person is perfect. II, 562; VIII, 1050.

His image must be returned to God. IV, 1379. It is the most precious deposit in a human being. I, 1067. The person who always clings to God truly preserves his image. IV, 896. “Image and likeness of God” is one thing, and “according to the image and likeness of God” another. VI, 33. To will to be like God is praiseworthy in one sense and perverse in another. IV, 895, 896. You begin to become like him when it displeases you to be unlike him. IV, 959. The image of God seeks truth, not vanity. V, 566. In a human being, likeness to God will then be perfect when the vision of God is perfect. VIII, 1054, 1055. One image belongs to the earthly human being, another to the heavenly human being. X, 1601. How we bear the image of the heavenly and earthly human being. III, 352. The image of God would not be subjected to the devil except by God’s judgment. X, 1547. See Original Sin. It was just that stability of life should be granted to the image of God, unclouded by any sin. X, 1598.

Our weakness arises from sin. VI, 296.

Imitation of God. V, 653. Perverse imitation of God in sins. I, 681. The devil wished to imitate God, but perversely: he did not wish to be subject to God’s power but to have power against him. IV, 896. God’s patience toward sinners is to be imitated by human beings. II, 654, 655, 656. Imitation of Christ is the better fruit of love that we can offer him. V, 1395. Christ’s passion benefits only those who follow in his footsteps. V, 1396. In what we ought and ought not to imitate Christ. IV, 1149, 1150. To imitate Christ’s ways is to enter through the door. IV, 1149. Imitation of good people and of Christ himself. IV, 436. Imitation of the martyrs. V, 1405, 1447, 1547. To honor without imitating is nothing other than flattering deceitfully. V, 1447. A considerable part of imitation is rejoicing with the virtues of those who are better. V, 1283. To wish to imitate a human being and depend upon him belongs to the imperfect. IV, 246. If you wish to imitate the crowd, you will not be among the few who walk the narrow way. V, 1094. Whom we ought to choose as models. V, 1102. What someone should do if he finds no one worthy of imitation. V, 1547. If you do not find someone to imitate, become someone whom another may imitate. V, 1102. Those who imitate the wicked seek companions for themselves to go to Gehenna, not patrons for the kingdom of heaven. V, 759, 796. Sin is committed through imitation. X, 1163. Misplaced imitation. IX, 606. Imitation is generally to be disapproved, although what is proposed for imitation is not disapproved. VIII, 109. Sin did not enter the world through imitation alone. X, 1156. See Sin. When speaking of Adam and Christ, the Apostle opposes regeneration to generation, not imitation to imitation. X, 1224.

Who are called immaculate. X, 312.

The immensity of God. See God.

Excesses are restrained in some way under God. VIII, 557.

To be sacrificed is to die to God. V, 1368. Why the Apostle forbade Christians to eat sacrificial food. VIII, 503.

True immortality. V, 428, 1059. God’s immortality is immortality in the true sense. V, 428; VIII, 1062. Immortality belongs to no creature. VIII, 821. The immortality of the soul is proved because the soul itself is the subject of a discipline that is eternal. I, 896, 1021. It is also proved by the nature of numbers, which is immutable and adheres to the soul without its being lifeless. I, 1023. And because reason, which is immutable, cannot be separated from the soul. I, 1025. Because the soul cannot be without life. I, 1028. Because it has no contrary. I, 1029. Because it knows the truth. II, 65. Because nothing is contrary to the truth, from which the soul is what it is, insofar as the truth itself exists. I, 1030. Finally, because it cannot be changed into something else. I, 1031. The better philosophers defended human immortality in their writings. V, 1132. Pherecydes the Assyrian was the first among the Greeks to discuss the immortality of the soul. II, 521. Pythagoras of Samos, having heard a discussion of the soul’s immortality, became a philosopher from being an athlete. II, 521. A devout man who doubted the immortality of the soul is instructed by seeing divine things. II, 699. Human immortality is twofold: the first, by which one was able not to die; the second, by which one will be unable to die. VI, 281. Immortality is of two kinds, greater and lesser: lesser immortality is that by which someone can avoid dying. X, 1580. Greater immortality is that by which someone is unable to die. X, 1581. Which immortality Adam lost. X, 1581. By not sinning, Adam could have been changed from the lesser immortality to the greater. X, 1581, 1582. If Adam had not sinned, he would have received, without the intervention of death, the inability to die and the inability to sin. X, 1522. From the lesser life, in which Adam could either die or not die, he would have reached through persevering obedience the greater life, in which he could not die. X, 1598. Immortality was supplied to Adam from the tree of life. X, 1580. Adam can be said to have lost bodily immortality, since through sin he could not attain it. III, 355. Through the sin of the first human being, our nature was changed from the possibility of immortality into the necessity of death. X, 1512. The immortality of the first human being differs from the immortality that will exist after the resurrection. X, 1096. Adam’s immortality consisted in being able not to die; the immortality of the blessed will consist in being unable to die. VII, 803. That final immortality of the whole human being will be the body’s perfect health. II, 439. The body’s immortality and incorruption arise from the health of the soul. III, 28. It is a certain incorporeal excellence. II, 836. Immortality does not suffer pain, for all corruption has been removed. IV, 651.

The desire for immortality and incorruption is in us. X, 110. So too is the natural appetite for blessedness. X, 747. If the reward of immortality were given to the faithful in this age, it would no longer be faith. X, 181. The pledge of immortality for us is our mortality, assumed by Christ. IV, 1906. Just as Christ was mortal not from his own substance but from ours, so we are immortal not from our substance but from his. IV, 1906. Some philosophers wrongly deny that human beings would have been immortal had they not sinned. VII, 392.

A person is called immortal in two ways. X, 1560. What difference there is between immortal and eternal. VI, 15. Something created in time can be immortal. II, 727. The first human being was created immortal insofar as he could avoid dying. III, 354.

Whether uncleanness is to be removed by another through inflicting an injury on someone. VI, 506. No uncleanness is counted as existing in foods; nevertheless, people abstain from them in order to restrain desire. V, 1044, 1047. How nothing is clean to the unclean. IV, 1661. How the command not to touch what is unclean is to be understood. V, 551. The animals prohibited in the Old Testament were considered unclean not by nature but by their symbolic meaning. VIII, 233, 236.

Immutability belongs to God alone. V, 986. God is not therefore changeable because he commanded one thing to be offered to him in the Old Testament and another in the New. II, 527.

Those who are impatient because they do not wish to suffer evils suffer worse ones. VI, 611.

Impeccability in God arises from his nature; in a human being, from God’s gift. VII, 802. Whether there is any rational creature that cannot be delighted by anything illicit is a great question. VIII, 419.

The soul cannot rule well over one inferior to it unless it has not disdained to serve one superior to it. IV, 530. In the house of the righteous person who lives by faith, even those who command serve those over whom they appear to command. VII, 643.

An emperor exists within each human being and sits in the heart: if he is good and commands good things, good things are done; if he is evil and commands evil things, evil things are done. IV, 1938.

It is lawful to speak to an emperor concerning religion. IX, 44. The care of emperors concerns not only earthly matters but also ensuring that no one may sin against divine things with impunity. IX, 749. Possidius of Calama sailed to the emperor to plead the case of his Church. II, 352. Note (a). What legal authority Christian emperors possess to restrain and punish heretics and schismatics. IX, 45. Valentinian, Gratian, Theodosius, and his sons most firmly upheld Constantine’s judgment in the case of Caecilian. II, 400. The Donatists wrongly reproached the Catholics for pleading the Church’s case before the emperors, although they themselves professed to have done the same. II, 580. The Donatists say that Christians ought not to ask anything from Christian emperors against the enemies of Christ, although they themselves acted first. II, 305, 794. They persecuted the Maximianists through the earthly authorities. II, 192, 265. Yet they complained against the Catholics of persecution through judicial authority, which they themselves had invoked. II, 305. The emperor Julian, a deserter from Christ, granted the party of Donatus freedom to perish when Rogatianus and Pontius petitioned him. II, 399, 414, and Note. See. The Donatists complain unjustly that the emperors ordered the possessions of their churches to pass to the Catholic Church. II, 809. The emperor strove not only to remove from the Donatists the license to act savagely but also to bring them back to Catholic unity by coercion. II, 806. Catholic emperors compel the Donatists to unity. V, 295. The imperial constitutions against the Donatists. IV, 135, 684. They invalidate the wills of schismatics. V, 310. The usefulness of imperial laws, whether they are enacted for truth against falsehood or for falsehood against truth. II, 795. Thagaste, Augustine’s city, was converted to Catholic unity through fear of the imperial laws. II, 330. If something is requested from the emperors for the benefit of the Church, this does not mean that hope is placed in them. IX, 334. Petilianus rashly dares to say that Catholic emperors are not permitted to know the Holy Scriptures. IX, 330. Nor to accuse them of persecution. IX, 331. Petilianus badly proves that Catholic emperors and judges perished by persecuting the Donatists. IX, 323, 328. We are wrongly reproached with the claim that many evils befell the Roman Empire through Christian emperors. II, 532. Some letters of emperors bear the date and the consuls; some do not. IX, 664. The happiness of Christian emperors. VII, 170. Someone despised an emperor because of a fortified position. IV, 878. The Eastern emperor. V, 294.

The expansion of the empire. VII, 124. The Western Empire was later in time but more illustrious in greatness. VII, 158. Imperial power comes from the one true God. VII, 168. Virtue is the way to empire. VII, 156. It makes no difference under whose empire a mortal human being lives, provided those who rule do not compel him to impious and unjust acts. VII, 160. The most exalted summit of the noblest empire supplicates at the tomb of the fisherman Peter, its diadem laid down. II, 1028. Human dominion over human beings does not derive from the order first established by God. VII, 643.

Imperfect. When Christians who are still carnal and not yet perfect die, the Holy Spirit perfects whatever is lacking in them, because they have not withdrawn from the unity of the body. II, 843.

Lack of knowledge is no small punishment of this life. VII, 728.

What impiety properly is. IV, 596, 597. God hates impiety, and in some he punishes it through condemnation, while in others he removes it through justification. VI, 123. To justify the impious is a greater act of mercy than to create the righteous. III, 1823. Just as there is great piety in the few, so there is also great impiety. V, 441. In impiety itself, the more condemnable the vice, the more certainly praiseworthy the nature. VIII, 1068. The name “impiety” is applied even to a slight sin. III, 767. The impious, joined to one another in imitation, are one kind, one lump, one mass. VIII, 649. The devil is one with all the impious of whom he is the head, as with a certain body of his own. V, 790. Some of the impious sin more and others less; the reason for this. X, 1185. The impious are fools. III, 829. The impious do not know how even to think about the good things of the age to come. IV, 251. The impious often obtain good things in this life as though they were good. VII, 661. By the hidden administration of divine providence, the impious are given time to flourish and reign. III, 727. In his most beneficent providence, almighty God has granted earthly happiness even to the impious, lest the good should seek it as something of great value. II, 543. In Psalm 72 a repentant person is introduced as having served God for an earthly reward and as intending to recognize why the impious flourish in earthly happiness. II, 543. The impious flourish in false goods and perish in true torments. IV, 626. The impious unjustly ridicule the devout because they hope for their happiness rather than possess it. IV, 1635. When the impious are miserable and when they are called happy. IV, 919, 920, 1636. The impious do not live but seem to themselves to live. IV, 690. The life of the impious is compared with grass, which remains green through winter and withers in summer. IV, 556, 557. The impious are compared with smoke. IV, 392. The impious feed on the food of pride. IV, 1290. The hearts of the impious are an abyss. VII, 668. The conscience of a criminal overcomes prisons and hells with dreadful and penal darkness. II, 651. The punishment of the impious may be similar, but the cause of the martyrs is different. II, 796.

The impious tempt. III, 432. An impious person who persuades others to impiety is a murderer. III, 847. A perverse person harms himself more than others. II, 651. The impious persecute the devout by their conduct. VII, 613. Why the impious were created by God. VIII, 608. In what sense they can be called good. VIII, 608. The impious have their own place, which they fill in created things for the benefit of the saints. III, 433. The impious person lives for the devout person, and the sinner for the righteous. III, 144. It benefits the devout to grieve over the evil conduct of the impious. VII, 614. The correction of the impious brings the greatest joy to the devout. VII, 614. The impious have a place here among the righteous, not in the other life. V, 1384. The expulsion of the impious by God. IV, 88. The punishments of the impious are without end. VII, 637. The impious are called by the name of the world. III, 1862.

Impenitence is the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit. V, 455, 464. Both despair and hope are causes of impenitence. V, 139. See Repentance.

By the laying on of hands, bishops offer their peoples to God at the altar’s offering. II, 637.

The impossibility of conversion and faith—what it is and from where it comes. III, 1778. God does not command the impossible. X, 271, 288. See Commandment. “Cannot” is sometimes said of what can be done by power but cannot be done by justice. IX, 726. “Cannot” is sometimes used in place of “does not wish.” III, 1776.

When the Psalmist appears to invoke evils, he does not wish them but foresees them. V, 378.

All wickedness arises from weakness of spirit. III, 1259.

A person is imprudent who does not provide for himself in the future. IV, 551.

What immodesty is. X, 763. How broadly it extends. V, 84. Immodest love is not love. V, 1509. The immodest are unworthy not only of ecclesiastical ministry but also of communion in the sacraments themselves. II, 91. Immodesty is to be punished by excommunication. VI, 220.

Sin cannot go unpunished. V, 133, 139, 187. Those who promise themselves impunity for wickedness from divine mercy are refuted. IV, 257, 701, 997. The wicked person wants God to be wicked, so that he will not punish sin. V, 82. It is a great mercy not to leave wickedness unpunished. V, 935. By sparing, God acts harshly, but he acts harshly justly. V, 935. When God leaves sins unpunished by forgiving them, he then punishes more severely; he mercifully opposes the person when he renders abundant lusts powerless. II, 531. Impunity is the greatest punishment. II, 392. The greatest vengeance. V, 935. Punitive impunity is nourished by prosperity. II, 531. To permit impunity is not part of Christian gentleness. II, 316, 317. It belongs to God’s more vehement anger if he wishes evil to remain unpunished for a time in those who have not been corrected. II, 316. The person who truly repents does nothing other than refuse to allow what he has done wrongly to remain unpunished. II, 316. Pernicious impunity is not permitted by Christian gentleness. II, 390. Just as there is mercy that punishes, so there is cruelty that spares. II, 660.

Inachus, the first king of the Argives. VII, 562, 597.

Those who are said to have embittered God [*inamaricasse*: reading uncertain]. IV, 88.

What emptiness is. I, 733, 900. How it differs from nothing. I, 733; III, 177.

Earrings, suspended high on the ears of men on one side, are reckoned among binding ornaments. II, 1060; III, 50. Those who wear them wear the sign of the devil. II, 1061. Earrings are called phylacteries of idols. III, 576.

Ino, the wife of Athamas, was enrolled among the gods. VII, 572.

Enchanters mix the name of Christ into their incantations. III, 1440. Virgil recounts how much the enchantress promised. VII, 718. The remedies of incantations are illicit. V, 1439, 1671.

The mystery of the Incarnation did not cease to be foretold from the beginning of the ages. VI, 332. The ancients believed that Christ’s Incarnation would take place. II, 846. It was foreknown by Abraham. X, 401. And by Melchizedek when he blessed Abraham. X, 401. Among the Hebrew people, what has been happening from Christ’s coming until now and thereafter was foretold. VII, 221. The Platonists denied the Incarnation. VII, 307. It is asserted against them. VII, 308. The Manichaean doctrine concerning the Incarnation of the Word. VIII, 585. The error of the Apollinarists: that Christ did not have a human soul or mind. I, 746. Leporius had denied that God became human, lest any unworthy change or corruption of the divine substance result. II, 932.

The Incarnation of the Word. X, 934. Christ’s Incarnation is Christ’s mission. III, 1667, 1702. Christ’s Incarnation is incredible to unbelievers. III, 393. Christ’s Incarnation is the greatest of all miracles. III, 1527. The Incarnation of the Word is ineffable. X, 982, 983. What is to be believed concerning the Incarnation. VIII, 910. The Word of God assumed a human being in a manner far different from that in which he is present to other creatures, and made himself and that human being one. II, 520. The human being approached the Word; the Word did not undergo a convertible transformation into a human being. II, 745. Flesh approaches the Word; the Word does not perish in the flesh. V, 1315. The Word of God was not changed by assuming flesh. II, 518. In assuming a human being, God was not consumed. VII, 318. “The Word became flesh” by taking what he was not, not by losing what he was. V, 1317. It should not seem incredible that the Word took a body from the Virgin in such a way that he lost nothing belonging to the divine nature. II, 518. Sleep, food, and human emotions prove that Christ assumed human nature, not that he was consumed by it. II, 519. God himself remains God; humanity approaches God and becomes one person. V, 1332. Christ joined both natures in the unity of one person. II, 519. The human being was fitted into the unity of the person of the Word of God, while the Word remained unchangeably in his own nature. II, 745. The person of Christ is a mixture of God and human being, just as the human person is a mixture of soul and body. II, 518, 519, 746.

Christ is the Incarnate Word. V, 1310. God and human being are not two but one Christ. X, 143. See Christ. By assuming a human being, the number of persons in the Trinity was not increased. II, 543, 745. The statement found in ancient codices that the Word became flesh through the assumption of an inferior person: how it is to be understood. III, 215. Note 1. How the Word assumed human nature in the Incarnation. VII, 729. He assumed the whole human being. I, 746; III, 134. He graciously undertook to free in us everything he had made. VI, 367. In the human being whom he assumed, the Word assumed our entire nature—that is, both a rational soul and mortal flesh without sin. II, 1085. He assumed our nature without sin, but not without the condition of the sinner. I, 1166. Through a rational soul the Word became a participant in flesh. II, 542. The mixture of the Word of God and a soul ought to have seemed more credible than the mixture of soul and body. II, 520. The Word wished to unite himself with the human being in a certain manner, so that the whole human being might be fitted to him as a body is fitted to a soul, except for mutable composition. II, 521. The Incarnation of the Word is a marriage. III, 1329; IV, 495. The Word of God remains as he is and is wholly everywhere. II, 518. God, infused into flesh, neither abandoned nor lost the care of governing the universe. II, 517.

The cause of the Incarnation is sin. V, 944, 945, 951. Why the Son of God assumed a human being from Adam’s race and from a virgin. VIII, 1032. For the salvation of the faithful, the eternal Word willed to become human from a woman. II, 540. So that no sex might think itself despised by its Creator, he assumed a male human being, born from a woman. III, 134. Both sexes were honored through Christ’s Incarnation. VI, 186. See Christ. Because the Word of God is unchangeable, we do not fear believing that he was born from a Virgin. VIII, 585. The Son of God was not contaminated either by the human being with whom he clothed himself in the Incarnation or by the human beings among whom he lived. VII, 272. He demonstrated that true divinity cannot be contaminated by flesh, and that demons are not therefore better than we are because they do not have flesh. VII, 272. In the flesh Christ showed us two lives, one laborious and the other blessed. VIII, 543, 547. Why Christ wished to undergo the cross. VIII, 543. Christ descended even to the places where sinners are tormented. III, 481. Through the Incarnation, how God became close to humanity, and from what state he had previously been distant. V, 934.

The Incarnation of the Word demonstrates the dignity of human nature. III, 134. Especially because he graciously undertook its wound. I, 1166. Why the assumption of humanity is properly attributed to the Son. II, 70, 71. “The Word became flesh”: not the Father or the Holy Spirit, but the whole Trinity made the Son’s flesh. V, 1063.

Whether the Incarnation occurred because of Christ’s merits. X, 1137, 1138. See Christ. That union by which the Word and flesh together were called the only-begotten Son of God was not merited by that human nature through works. IV, 1442. The grace of the Incarnation is the greatest of all. III, 1844. The assumption of the human being by the Word is wholly unique. II, 836, 847. No soul can bring it about through the merit of free will that it should be another Christ. II, 847. The personal union with God in Christ arises from a singular grace, not from the merit of free will. II, 847. Christ surpasses other human beings not merely through a more perfect participation in wisdom but through being himself the person of truth. I, 746. What belongs to knowledge and what to wisdom in the incarnate Word. VIII, 1033. If a reason is sought for the Incarnation of the Word, it will not be marvelous; if an example is demanded, it will not be unique. II, 519.

The necessity of the Incarnation. V, 573, 710, 998, 1006, 1099. There is no greater grace than that of the Incarnate Word, and it has no cause other than grace. V, 999. The human race would not be liberated unless the Word of God were shown to be human. V, 940.

The wisdom of the Incarnation. VII, 308. No other way of liberating humanity from the misery of mortality was more fitting than the Incarnation of the Word. VIII, 1024. The benefit of the Incarnation. VII, 220, 222. How great the benefit is. IV, 898. The benefits provided for us through the Incarnation. V, 1016, 1018; X, 174. In no way was humanity provided for more beneficially than through the Incarnation of the Son. III, 134.

The purpose of the Incarnation. VIII, 533, 541, 546, 547, 585; X, 131. The purpose of the Incarnation is the adoption of human beings as sons of God. VII, 729. God became human so that we might become gods. V, 909. The Word became what we are so that we might attain what we are not. V, 670. Through the Incarnation it came about that human beings would not seek divinity in vain. II, 521. Since the Word became flesh, one must not despair that human beings can become sons of God. II, 542. The Word graciously assumed from a human being the name of humanity, generously bestowing on him the name of divinity. II, 521. The Word assumed a human being whom human beings could see, so that, healed through faith, they might afterward see what they could not then see. II, 540, 545.

The usefulness of the Incarnation. IV, 1766, 1767. Its various advantages. VIII, 1031. The incarnate Wisdom of God is the most convenient way to religion. VIII, 88. Through the Incarnation, a certain discipline of life and an example of the commandment are impressed upon us. II, 70. The Incarnation of the Word is the Wisdom of God made like milk for our infancy. I, 745. The Word came in Christ as instruction and assistance for human beings to attain eternal salvation. II, 520. The Incarnation of the Word is an eye-salve for the eyes of our hearts. III, 1395, 1399. It is the clay by which the blindness of the human race was healed. III, 1714. A great medicine against pride. I, 1167; V, 487. Pride does not perceive the mystery and power of the Incarnation. VII, 273, 301. How much thanksgiving must be offered for the benefit of the Incarnation. VII, 220, 221. The Incarnation founded faith. VII, 318. All the righteous, whether before or after the Incarnation, lived and live only by faith in Christ’s Incarnation. II, 859. The ancient righteous were justified by faith in the Incarnation, just as we are. X, 400, 401, 403. And they were saved. II, 680. Faith in the Incarnation is necessary as long as we dwell here. V, 1216. See Christ.

In the flesh. V, 670.

The incarnation of the soul. II, 723, 729, 733.

A mother turns food assimilated into her flesh into milk. V, 670.

All temporal things are uncertain. II, 495, 496, 506. Everything here is uncertain except death. V, 590.

What those beginning a good life usually suffer from their opponents. V, 548, 586.

A resident (*incola*) is one who dwells in a foreign land. IV, 1602. *Incola* means the same as “immigrant” or “stranger” (*advena*). IV, 1398. How *incola* and *inquilinus* differ. IV, 1518. The unbelievers cannot properly be called residents and pilgrims here. IV, 1519.

Safety consists in life itself and in health, as well as in the soundness of mind and body. II, 499. The care a person naturally has for his own safety is a trace of the most hidden unity from which he comes. I, 675.

Incontinence among married couples is venial because of the marriage. III, 397; VI, 458. See Marriage. Continence.

Every incorporeal nature is called “spirit” in Scripture. II, 1043. Any incorporeal nature, even if vicious and wretched, is superior to every body. II, 561. Evodius thinks that God alone is always without any body. II, 698.

Incorruption. God preserved the three men in the furnace either by adding incorruption to their flesh or by removing from the fire the power to corrupt; the latter method is more marvelous. II, 942. The type of incorruption in the timbrel and strings. IV, 1964.

Unbelief and faithlessness are death. III, 1753. Just as the fact that the Lord cannot deny himself is praise of the divine will, so the fact that the Jews could not believe is blame of the human will. III, 1778.

Incubi. VII, 468.

[Col. 0356] Lack of earthly goods troubles the soul. III, 2073. The mutual dependence of masters and servants. III, 2044.

To be unlearned is a lesser evil than to be unwilling to learn. I, 942.

Truce. VI, 35.

Indulgence is to be hoped for not by the obstinate, but by those who turn away from sin. VI, 223. The forgiveness of sins belongs among the uncertain and hidden matters of God’s wisdom. IV, 592. Forgiveness is promised to the sinner who turns back, not to tomorrow. IV, 1301, 1877; V, 141, 245.

“To be hardened” means “to be made strong.” III, 543.

How Pharaoh was hardened. III, 601. The cause of Pharaoh’s hardening was also God’s very patience. III, 603, 607. The heart is hardened when God abandons it and the enemy takes possession of it. III, 784.

Those who display themselves in women’s clothing are legally regarded as infamous and incapable of making a will. I, 899.

Why infancy is so called. VII, 522, 730. Infancy lies subject to the flesh without any resistance. VII, 522, 730. No one would not choose to endure death rather than infancy. VII, 728.

An infant in its mother’s womb is not part of its mother’s body. X, 847. It is related that infants not yet born cried out certain words from their mothers’ wombs. VII, 110. The weeping of infants at the beginning of this life is a prophecy of the miseries into which they are entering. VII, 728. Infants are weaker than the fetuses of other animals. VII, 379. Why an infant who is destined to die immediately or soon is born is hidden. III, 420. How great is the weakness of infants. X, 150. How great their ignorance is, and where it comes from. X, 148. The ignorance of infants is penal. X, 149. Whether the mind of infants knows itself. VIII, 1040.

The doctrine of Caelestius: infants newly born are in the state in which Adam was before the transgression. X, 334.

Infancy is subject to sins. I, 665, 666. A one-day-old infant is not free from sin, not because of what it has committed, but because of what it has contracted. V, 928. Infants themselves also need a liberator and baptism. V, 1333. Christ is also the Savior and Redeemer of infants. X, 128, 129. Before baptism, infants are exorcized and exsufflated. II, 890. Unbaptized infants are under the power of the devil. X, 426. Because of original sin. X, 708. See Baptism, Little Ones. Personal sin must not be attributed to infants. X, 121. Infants are called both believers and penitents. X, 123. Consecrations of infants. I, 1080. The error of Victor: infants who die before baptism can attain forgiveness of original sins. X, 516. The condemnation of infants who die without baptism is the lightest. X, 809. In what bodily size infants will rise again. VII, 776.

How Babylon found us as infants and strangled us. IV, 776, 777, 1773. Who the infants and nursing children are in the Church. IV, 110. The infancy of regeneration is new life. III, 1982. The newly baptized are called infants. III, 1982; V, 1092, 1099, 1101, 1203, 1246. Seven or eight days are assigned to the sacraments of infants. V, 1101. The octave of infants. V, 1201. A sermon delivered on the octave of infants. V, 1560. To wean someone prematurely during spiritual infancy is harmful. IV, 1713, 1714.

Infants killed for Christ are martyrs. VI, 655. Their suffering is vividly described. VI, 644, 655. See Innocents.

We cannot at all will unhappiness. X, 274. Awareness of one’s own unhappiness is no small approach to blessedness. III, 1247. Unhappiness is represented by fire, prosperity by water. IV, 797. See Happiness, Tribulation.

He tramples on lower things who clings to what is higher; but if he withdraws from what is higher, those lower things will be turned into punishment for him. IV, 1887. See Temporal Things and Happiness. In spiritual terms, all lower things are more sorrowful. III, 483. A person who loves lower things is assigned a place among the lower regions. III, 132.

Hell is understood in various ways. III, 582, 586. Hell means either the place of the ungodly after death or the blindness of soul that receives and envelops the sinner. IV, 93. By the word “lower regions” the lower parts of the earth are designated. III, 730. Why. III, 482; IV, 1943. The lower regions are beneath the earth. I, 640. Some assert that hell is explained as existing in this life and not after death. III, 481. The pagan sages did not doubt the substance of the lower regions. III, 481. There is indeed a substance of the lower regions, but it is spiritual, not bodily. III, 481. Scripture nowhere uses the name “hell” for something good. II, 711, 834; III, 482. In Greek, the lower regions are called ᾅδης, Hades, because they contain nothing pleasant. III, 483.

Hell is twofold, upper and lower. IV, 1093, 1094. The lower depths, that is, the heavier punishments suffered by the condemned after this life. III, 167. There is no remembrance of truth there, no reasoning. III, 167. Once excluded from the kingdom of heaven, nothing remains except the punishments of Gehenna. V, 962. Degrees of punishment in hell according to the diversity of crimes. IX, 171. The torments of hell are harsher for some and milder for others. V, 879. The milder punishments there are worse than those feared here. V, 879. The infernal angels are compared with torturers who conduct interrogations. [Col. 0357] V, 680. They are called the exceedingly dreadful angels of the devil. V, 883. It is absurd to think that pain, whether of body or of soul, will be absent in hell. VII, 723. No one in hell will be freed from the eternal fire once he has been cast into it. VII, 750. No one is withdrawn from the torments even by dying, lest the punishment itself also die at the same time in the dying person. VIII, 621. Why the eternity of these punishments in hell seems harsh and unjust to human feelings. VII, 726. See Fire.

There is no intermediate place between hell and the eternal kingdom. VII, 741. It is not absurdly believed that places most remote from the torments of the ungodly were assigned to the ancient saints, although they were among the lower regions. VII, 681. The lower regions are not called the place where the souls of the righteous rest. III, 481. Christ descended to the lower regions. II, 710, 712, 714, 834, 835. And in the lower regions he freed certain persons. II, 714. The Church agrees that Adam was released from the pains of hell; some add that this was also granted to the ancient saints, but Augustine disapproves. II, 711. Some have thought that the poets and orators who exposed false gods to ridicule, as well as pagans of praiseworthy life, were freed by Christ when he descended to the lower regions. II, 710. Some think that those who did not hear the Gospel were released. II, 713, 833. It is rash to define who those are whom Christ freed when he descended to the lower regions. II, 710. From what part of hell the rich man could have seen Lazarus established in rest. IV, 93. The gates of hell are the dominion of death. V, 1642. The dangers of hell deceive people more amid the prosperity of the world. IV, 1488. The dangers of hell find people, and are not found by them. IV, 1488. Christ alone rescued his soul from the hand of the lower regions. IV, 1438. Those who know that the evil they do is evil descend alive into hell. IV, 639.

Faithlessness is death. III, 1577. Faithlessness begins the claim to punishment. III, 2061. *Retr.* It makes people children of the devil. X, 589. Faithlessness is transmitted to an infant. X, 847. Faithlessness is signified by the name of iniquity and sin. IV, 1508. Faithlessness is properly called sin, as though it were the only sin, when the particular kind of sin is not specified. X, 589. Why the sin of faithlessness against Christ alone is charged. V, 785, 787. The faithlessness of the world is without excuse. V, 787.

Whether unbelievers can perform good works. IV, 259, 260. See Faith. An unbeliever cannot be a good tree. X, 754. The works of unbelievers. X, 341, 755. By what standard the works of unbelievers are to be examined. X, 230. The works of unbelievers are not good. X, 755. Even those that seem good are sins. X, 753, 754. How. X, 753, 754. Among unbelievers there can be bodily virginity, but not virginal chastity. X, 763. We read of certain works of unbelievers that we cannot condemn but rightly praise. X, 311, 754. It is very difficult to find the life of any extremely wicked person without some good works. X, 754. You will find people living well who are not Christians: they run well, but the farther they run, the more they go astray. V, 777. The good works performed by unbelievers are not theirs, but belong to the one who makes good use of evil things. X, 754, 755. An unbeliever is condemned despite praiseworthy conduct, while a believer is saved despite less commendable conduct. X, 598. Unbelievers cannot keep the words of God. IV, 1516. When unbelievers do not believe the Gospel, they act against God’s will, yet they do not overcome it. X, 238. We do not pray for unbelievers that their nature may be changed or that doctrine may be preached to them, but that their will may be corrected, that they may consent to the doctrine, and that their nature may be healed. II, 983. The hearts of unbelievers and ungodly people are lions’ dens. IV, 1376. Unbelievers and ungodly people are represented by the sea. IV, 1748. How they move about in the waters of the sea. IV, 1380. Unbelievers and ungodly people are darkness. IV, 248. Converted to God through faith, they become light. II, 562. Unbelievers are water; Christians are wine. III, 1452. Unbelievers who become believers are prefigured by the calf’s head crushed by Moses and scattered into the water as a drink for the children of Israel. IV, 1129. See Pagans. Unbelievers and ungodly people are not strangers in the land. IV, 1519. The devil uses them like swords against the faithful. IV, 1857, 1858.

Nothing can be joined to the infinite. II, 443. No finite thing, however great, can be compared with the infinite. IV, 373. There are infinite parts in a body. I, 1252. A line can be cut transversely without limit. I, 874.

Human weakness in general is explained against the Pelagians. X, 689, 690, 692. Weakness and blindness are diseases of nature. X, 293, 295. What the dullness and weakness of the minds and bodies of infants indicate. VII, 378. The weakness of the flesh in infants is penal. X, 150. Human weakness cannot be without sin in this age. I, 593. The weaknesses of the soul have multiplied, not for destruction, but so that a physician might be desired. IV, 144. Weakness had besieged us irremediably, so that we were not even allowed to go to the physician. V, 778. Weakness is a warning not to be proud. X, 742. “Because there is no strength in me, nor is there hope for me from myself.” IV, 472. “You who wished to be powerful in yourself, God made you weak so that he might make you strong from himself, because you were becoming weak through yourself.” IV, 525.

Weakness and ignorance are two causes of sin. VI, 271. The weakness and corruptibility of the body are shackles. IV, 1019. In ourselves weakness alone is the cause of fighting. [Col. 0358] X, 742. The better future things are in relation to love, the more violent present things are in relation to weakness. II, 593. Weakness of both body and soul must be acknowledged so that a person may be perfected. X, 367. So that grace may be obtained. V, 481. In weaknesses nothing should be sought except God’s help. III, 1444. The weakness that remains after baptism will be consumed in the resurrection. X, 591, 602. The weaknesses of others must be endured, and they must be helped. III, 1237, 1258, 1261, 1262. See Burdens. The weakness of thirty-eight years. V, 694. In Scripture, weaknesses are used to signify sins. II, 633.

The difference between a weak person and a sick person. V, 277. How the weak are to be strengthened. V, 276. How the weak are to be treated in monasteries. I, 1380. Why they are stronger in mind but weaker in body. VIII, 586. The weaker are oppressed by the more powerful. IV, 1646.

Inflation and swelling imitate greatness but do not possess health. IV, 420.

Every praiseworthy talent, without true piety and religion, withers into pride. VII, 51. The most outstanding intellects have fallen into greater errors to the extent that they proceeded with greater self-confidence. II, 669. The natural slowness and stupidity of certain people arise from original sin. X, 1381, 1382. Those born dull-witted are so by merit of original sin. X, 1441. However highly gifted people may be, how far they fall short of Adam’s intelligence. X, 1432, 1433. To be born talented is a matter of good fortune. VII, 128. Augustine asks Jerome where the diversity of talents arises from. II, 728.

The Father is rightly called “unbegotten,” even though Scripture does not use this word. II, 1039, 1040.

Ingentius, decurion of the city of Ziqua. II, 304; IX, 540, App. 784. Ingentius, public notary. IX, App. 780. Ingentius, secretary of Augentius. IX, App. 782. Maximus, a former duumvir, maintained that Ingentius had forged Caecilianus’s letter. II, 304; IX, 540. He himself confessed during the inquiry of Aelianus the proconsul that he had committed a forgery against Felix, Caecilianus’s ordainer. II, 582; IX, 686. The emperor orders Ingentius to be sent to his court. II, 582; IX, 540, 649, 686. Why. II, 582. The codex of Optatus proves that Caecilianus was cleared by the emperor. II, 581. A petition given to the emperor Constantine by the Donatists. II, 582. The emperor’s letter to Verinus, the vicar. II, 582. The emperor’s letter to the proconsul ordering that Ingentius be sent to his court. II, 582. Nor did the emperor later condemn the man whom he had cleared. II, 582, 583.

Through the vice of ingratitude even great men have fallen into the disgrace of idolatry. X, 211. The ungrateful are described. III, 97. The ungrateful person toward God is the sinner who lends at interest and does not repay. IV, 370, 371. The soul is ungrateful when it attributes to itself what it has from God, especially righteousness. X, 211. He has without having who does not know whence he has: God takes away his possession, and his iniquity remains to him. V, 1287, 1290. Ungrateful free will cast humanity down. V, 1289.

Hostilities live by three vices: negligence, stubbornness, and proud shame. V, 1046. Three remedies correspond to these three vices. V, 1046. Hostilities either should never have arisen or should quickly have died, before sunset. V, 1046. Hostilities must be avoided with the greatest care, endured with the greatest fairness, and ended with the greatest speed. I, 1006. It is not enough for a human being merely not to provoke or increase the hostilities of others; he must also strive to extinguish them. I, 773.

“Enemy” and “enemy.” V, 323. Who are God’s enemies. IV, 630, 1178, 1801; VII, 350. Whoever was an enemy of Christ will be under his feet, either adopted or conquered. IV, 1452. Who the enemies of the Church are. IV, 242. Two kinds of human enemies. IV, 324, 325. As long as you are your own enemy, you have the word of God as an enemy. V, 637. The enemy whom the ancients were permitted to hate and whom we are commanded never to love is the devil. V, 806. Enemies are not permitted to attack the faithful except insofar as this benefits their testing and proving. V, 421. Hatred of enemies must be turned against the devil, who persecutes us through them. IV, 1841. Invisible enemies must be conquered invisibly. V, 435. All the carnal are enemies of spiritual people. IV, 1772. It is a dreadful evil to disclose the words of angry enemies to their angry enemies. I, 773. If two of three friends become enemies, what should the third do? V, 323. Enemies can do no harm. V, 1430. An enemy can rage; he cannot strike if God does not will it. IV, 366. There are two enemies in persecution, one hidden and the other open. IV, 632, 649. The enemy is inwardly his own enemy who hates another. V, 507. He first and more greatly harms himself than the person against whom he rages. V, 507. A raging enemy cannot harm you in any way as much as you harm yourself if you do not love your enemy. V, 383. Nothing harms the righteous person who can even make good use of an enemy. III, 163. God turns enemies to the use of his own people, not only when enemies are conquered but also when they are feared. III, 795. Human enemies, whatever they may be, are not to be hated, lest, when a wicked person hates the wicked person he has to endure, there be two wicked people. IV, 248.

[Col. 0359] Love of enemies is commended. IV, 1273, 1274; V, 53, 383, 384, 564, 1404. Nothing in God’s commandments is more marvelous than love of enemies. IV, 1518, 1524. The ancient law also commanded this. V, 807. Learn to love your enemy if you wish to guard against an enemy. IV, 1273. Loving an enemy is salutary, although bitter. IV, 447. The command to love enemies is difficult, but it has a great reward. V, 120, 1435, 1684. He tramples the waves of this age who loves his enemies. IV, 631. He becomes like God. IV, 1274. With what disposition an enemy is to be loved. III, 2038, 2041. Why he is to be loved. III, 30. Whoever loves an enemy loves a brother. III, 2041. Even wicked enemies are to be loved. IX, 120. An enemy must be loved in such a way that he is nevertheless corrected. V, 53. How hatred and love of enemies are not contrary to one another. VIII, 362. Punishment of an enemy can proceed with charity. VIII, 158, 159. The killing of enemies was fitting for the Jews as a people still carnal. VIII, 158, 159. With what disposition those who were holy and spiritual within the Jewish people killed enemies. VIII, 158, 159. Gentleness toward enemies. V, 1430.

We are bound to spare our enemies. V, 299. At least to those who ask, forgiveness must be given. V, 384. An enemy who repents and asks forgiveness must be forgiven. V, 381; X, 300. Whoever refuses forgiveness to an enemy harms not the enemy but himself. V, 385. An enemy is defeated by nothing so much as by our being merciful. IV, 1860, 1861. Sparing enemies is the greatest kind of almsgiving. VI, 266. See Almsgiving. Forgiving debts. Forgiving.

For whom and against whom one should pray concerning enemies. IV, 248. We have no enemy except the devil; we must pray for the rest. IV, 238. How difficult it is to pray for enemies, and how great the fruit of this work is. V, 120. We must wish our enemies as much good as we wish ourselves. IV, 435. What prayer against enemies is unlawful and what is lawful. V, 564. How wicked it is to pray for evils to befall enemies. V, 1686. One must pray against the malice of the enemy, not against his nature. V, 384. What kind of death should be desired for an enemy. V, 565. People should not pray that their enemies die; they should pray that they be corrected, and then their enemies will be dead. IV, 404. Why the Church now prays for enemies. VII, 737. The Church did not pray for enemies without reason. V, 151. To confer a benefit on enemies is to take away what is harmful to them. II, 390. What is meant by heaping coals on an enemy’s head. V, 807.

Love of enemies is perfect love. III, 2042. Love of enemies is our victory over the devil. IV, 1214. Love of enemies is a gift of God. V, 1436. The example of loving enemies was given by the heavenly Father. V, 325, 1433. Another example is found in Christ. V, 1435, 1685. Another in Stephen. V, 525, 1436, 1685.

Iniquity is not a substance. IV, 845. Rather, it is the perversity of a will twisted away from the highest substance toward the lowest. I, 744. Whoever refuses to serve charity must necessarily serve iniquity. IV, 163. Iniquity is an evil master in the heart. IV, 163. You are rightly subjected to iniquity, the master whom you made for yourself, because you refused to be subject to the one who made you. IV, 163. The heads of iniquity sprout from the lust to rule, to watch, and to feel. I, 690. Nothing is more laborious than iniquity and impiety. IV, 127. Iniquity is the flesh resisting the spirit. X, 861.

Great iniquity is sterility. IV, 1571. What useless moisture is to a tree, a persuasion toward iniquity is to the soul. III, 380. Iniquity is a fever by which the palate of the heart is destroyed. IV, 251. From the abundance of iniquity comes the torpor of charity. IV, 433. Iniquity alone makes you far from God; throw down the wall of sin, and you are with him. IV, 1775. You cannot withdraw from the wicked, but withdraw from iniquity. IV, 1185, 1402. Some try, as it were, to search out their own iniquity, and fear finding it. IV, 343. How many defend their own iniquity. IV, 343. The adversary of iniquity is the word of God: cling to it, and iniquity is destroyed and conquered. IV, 342. You either kill iniquity or are killed by iniquity. IV, 764. Iniquities are not natural to us, but they can be changed. IV, 1195. No one commits injustice except in vain. IV, 1646.

The iniquity of those who live badly is, for the time being, to be tolerated. III, 1624. How to make progress through the iniquity of one’s neighbor. IV, 800. Iniquity first harms the unjust heart from which it proceeds, before it harms the righteous person against whom it proceeds. IV, 107. Iniquity committed through blood is called “blood.” IV, 597. Human iniquity is signified through contact with a dead body. III, 736. Every iniquity, whether small or great, must necessarily be punished, either by the person himself through repentance or by God through vengeance. IV, 701. No iniquity goes unpunished except that which the blood of the Savior has expiated. X, 861.

A person becomes unjust when he loves for their own sake things that are to be taken up for the sake of something else, and desires for the sake of something else things that are to be loved for their own sake. VIII, 451. The unjust misuse God’s good works. III, 1620. What the unjust person did unjustly, God permitted justly. IV, 745. Let the unjust will be condemned, and let the just permission be glorified. IV, 746. For the unjust themselves, if they are not corrected, he reserves eternal punishments who justly uses their wickedness to inflict temporal evils on others. II, 993. An unjust person is not truly a friend. IV, 1179. The unjust have two voices. IV, 1201. An unjust person is no small punishment to himself. IV, 605. The humiliation of the unjust is truly wretched. IV, 255. The unjust are suited to the lower parts of creation insofar as they are unlike God; they become suited to the higher parts insofar as they become like God. I, 744.

The unjust are called foreigners, sons of strangers, waters of contradiction, and a wicked sword. IV, 1867. The unjust are like dogs licking Lazarus’s wounds. III, 832. The unjust are compared with hail. III, 875. They are designated by the name of dust. IV, 328. The unjust are darkness. III, 1398; IV, 325, 1607. All the unjust are in darkness. IV, 557, 564. From the darkness of dreams, the unjust will pass into the darkness of torments. IV, 564. The unjust constitute one body with the devil and receive one judgment. V, 790.

An injury is not what you suffer lawfully. IV, 1894. There are three kinds of injury. III, 1261, 1263. An injury that can be restored concerns either money or service. III, 1263. Whoever injures another in our presence injures us. V, 511. What the person who has committed an injury ought to do. V, 508.

With what disposition a Christian should endure injuries and losses of temporal goods. II, 529. Injuries must be endured with the greatest patience. III, 1257, 1258. The Apostle exhorts you not merely to endure distress, but to endure injury. IV, 1894. God avenges those who suffer injury by punishing those who inflict it. IV, 1894. What the person who has suffered an injury ought to do. V, 508. You have suffered evil: forgive, lest there be two evil people. IV, 638. The person who has suffered an injury and wishes to be avenged seeks a remedy in another’s punishment and finds a great torment. V, 684. If you show mercy, you will await judgment securely—not so much secure in your own justice as in God’s mercy. IV, 1922. Who is the usurer of injuries. IV, 638. The forgiveness of injuries is mercy that costs nothing. IV, 1922. The complete remission of injuries is commanded in the New Testament and foretold in the Old. VIII, 139. The forgiveness of injuries and the commandments concerning patience must especially be retained in the preparation of the heart. II, 530. A ruler of the state ought to forget injuries. II, 528. The forgiveness of injuries is useful to the commonwealth, far from being harmful. II, 529. When Romans received an injury, they preferred to forgive rather than prosecute. II, 528. Cicero said that Caesar was accustomed to forget nothing except injuries. II, 528.

To injure. V, 288.

It is better to suffer injustice than to commit it. IV, 1655. Another person’s injustice torments you only insofar as you have departed from your own. IV, 1268. Injustice first and properly harms the unjust person alone. IV, 365. Every unjust person is wicked. IV, 1805, 1806. What is done unjustly, God justly permits to happen. VII, 728. An unjust person, whether gentle or fierce, is harmful both to himself and to others. IV, 1805. It would not be enough for you to be unjust unless you also wished the person from whom you did not want vengeance against yourself to be unjust. IV, 478. The unjust person must be punished, whether he is converted or not. IV, 364. The unjust person is compared with a burning torch, which is always being consumed but does not always burn others. IV, 1241. What the unjust say when admonished by the righteous. IV, 1200. Two unjust people scarcely tolerate one another. IV, 364. What sort of harmony exists between them. IV, 364. See The Unjust.

Who is innocent. V, 1272. No one is more innocent than the person who is perfect in virtue. III, 1259. The innocent person is one whose heart is harmless. IV, 1663, 1662. One who harms neither another nor himself. IV, 1286. A person is not innocent, although he does no harm, if he wishes to do harm. IV, 1190. Each person is innocent not through fear of punishment but through love of justice. IV, 1190. Christ alone is innocent. V, 928. It is the duty of the innocent not only to inflict evil on no one, but also to restrain people from sin or punish them. VII, 644. Why the innocent suffer here. I, 1304. The consolation of oppressed innocents is God as judge and conscience as witness. IV, 408.

The Innocents, martyrs of Christ. I, 1304; III, 426. The blessed ignorance of the Innocents, who were able to suffer for Christ, whom they were not yet able to confess. V, 1027. Christ crowned the Innocents whom Herod killed for him. IV, 536. The Innocents were granted the name and crown of martyrs. V, 1664, 1668. See Infants.

Innocence is the virtue by which we harm no one. VI, 514. This is true innocence: it does not harm even an enemy. IV, 102. Innocence of conduct. V, 1560. Especially toward God. V, 1561. Innocence of heart is required; innocence of hands is not enough. IV, 1008. All justice is reduced to the one word “innocence.” IV, 1286. Your innocence, even in sleep, is the voice of your soul. IV, 1317. Innocence is to be preferred to all riches. IV, 1068. Hold on to innocence as, when you were greedy, you held on to your little money-bag so that it would not be taken from you by a thief. IV, 392. Let that be your inheritance. IV, 392. Simulated innocence is not innocence but a double iniquity. IV, 765. Whether innocence lost through sin can be restored through repentance. X, 1543.

Innocentia, a deeply religious woman, healed from cancer through the sign of the cross. VII, 763.

[Col. 0361] Pope Innocent. X, 376, 378, 389, 574. The Council of Carthage writes to Innocent against Pelagius and Caelestius. II, 758. Likewise the Council of Milevis. II, 762. Likewise five bishops. II, 764. Likewise Aurelius with others, somewhat more carefully. II, 972. Innocent replies to these letters with four other letters. II, 779. Pope Innocent’s letter to the Council of Carthage. X, 575. To the Councils of Carthage and Milevis. X, 648. His letter to the bishops of Numidia. X, 576. Innocent’s rescripts to the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, as well as to the bishops’ private letters, are praised. II, 817. Augustine received Innocent’s letter through Caecilianus. II, 646. Innocent’s judgment concerning the Palestinian proceedings. X, 389. He did not think that Pelagius had been cleared. II, 787. He condemned Caelestius and Pelagius together with their doctrines. I, 649; II, 865; X, 574, 699. Innocent’s censure of Pelagius’s book. II, 788.

Innocent, bishop. II, 577, 758, 780.

Innocent, bishop of Thebaltis. IV, 380.

Innocent, the presbyter who carried Jerome’s letters to Augustine. II, 928.

Innocent, the presbyter killed by the Circumcellions after his eye had been gouged out and his finger cut off. II, 509, 511.

Innocent, former advocate of the vicariate prefecture, miraculously healed near Carthage. VII, 761.

Infants cannot be renewed unless they have drawn along with them the oldness of sin. X, 1308.

What “to nod” means. VIII, 1071.

An unmarried woman ought to please God with the full intention of her soul. VI, 445.

What disobedience is. III, 377. Disobedience is a great evil. III, 383. Adam’s disobedience. IV, 897. The disobedience of the flesh, the first punishment for human disobedience. VII, 386, 426; X, 564. See Adam, Obedience.

Poverty. The servants of God endure the hardship of poverty better than they obtain the means for necessities with a guilty conscience. II, 357.

The disordered soul. I, 670. God commanded, and so it is: every disordered soul is its own punishment. I, 670.

Who is called a tenant. IV, 429, 1945. How a tenant differs from an inhabitant. IV, 1518. You are a tenant on earth; you will be a possessor in heaven. IV, 1946.

“To pollute” used for “to pronounce polluted.” III, 519.

Insects were created by God. III, 287. When. III, 287. In insects there is greater scope for the reflection of a thoughtful observer and more abundant praise of the omnipotent craftsman. III, 288.

Insensibility is by no means praiseworthy. IV, 650, 651.

Ambushes are called bows. IV, 763. The enemy does not dare to lie in wait for us if we have not departed from the way, that is, from Christ. IV, 1660. No ambushes are more hidden than those concealed under the appearance of duty. VII, 632. Ambushes are not placed unjustly in a just war. III, 781.

A foolish person is one who does not understand what evil he is in. IV, 551.

Foolishness is no small punishment of this life. VII, 728. In what sense Christ possessed foolishness. IV, 849.

Which human institutions are to be avoided and which embraced. III, 55.

God’s breathing into the face is the creation of the soul. VII, 373. Augustine does not approve what is instituted contrary to custom, so that it may function as a kind of observance of a sacrament. II, 221. Among non-superstitious human institutions, some are superfluous and luxurious, others useful and necessary. III, 54. Which those are. III, 54.

The instruments handed over to the Church. II, 265.

The ungodly now mock, though later they will themselves mock themselves. IV, 1637.

The intellect is something belonging to the soul. III, 1516. It is called the “man” of the soul. III, 1516. The intellect is called hidden sight. IV, 296. The difference between intellect and reason. V, 254. Nebridius: the intellect is warned by sense to see intelligible things rather than receiving something from sense. II, 67. What we perceive through the intellect. II, 597, 599, 613, 615, 616. Sound is, as it were, the vehicle for expressing the intellect. V, 185. What we know is contained in the intellect, and only by it can it be grasped. I, 996. The universals are in the intellect—or rather, the intellect itself is the universals. I, 1007. The intellect is finite. VI, 14. The distinction between intellect and speech. VI, 311.

The intellect, lest it go astray, needs divine instruction and assistance. VII, 642. The intellect comes about in us by consulting God, whether the mind itself understands through its own power or through the senses. II, 78. God alone is the light of the intellect. IV, 1553. A good intellect comes from the Holy Spirit. V, 1645. It is no small matter of understanding to know from whom understanding must be requested. IV, 1552. Intellect and wisdom are to be sought from God. X, 911, 912. How an angel is said to give understanding to a human being. IV, 1553. One reaches understanding through faith. II, 522; III, 1618, 1619, 1630; X, 125. Why David asks for understanding. IV, 1552. An impious mind even hates understanding itself, lest it be forced to do what it has understood. V, 850.

Intelligence is the most excellent thing in a human being. I, 1223. Our intelligence is a nature that is not one thing here and another there, but possesses everything it has all together in one. II, 616. No one sufficiently knows the powers of his own intelligence. X, 530. What the first intelligence and the intelligence that follows from it are. IV, 263, 264. A perfect understanding of each thing is given, beyond which nothing more excellent can exist. VI, 22. Faith must precede intelligence. V, 556, 570, 571. Unclean hearts cannot bear the light of spiritual intelligence. VI, 470. Conduct leads to intelligence. III, 1540. A good life is to be preferred to easy intelligence; it deserves to understand more. V, 1179.

Understanding is more excellent than being or living. I, 1244. Understanding, believing, and supposing are neighboring states in human minds. VIII, 83. How they differ from one another. VIII, 83. Understanding occurs in us in two ways: either through the mind itself or through a warning received from the senses. II, 78. Understanding is always without fault. VIII, 83. Understanding belongs only to one who perceives the truth. V, 157. What understanding the truth means according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 372. One person cannot always understand each thing more than another. VI, 22. The speed of understanding and sharpness of discernment are gifts of God. I, 705; III, 1689. A person understands more sincerely to the extent that he withdraws the mind’s attention from bodily senses. I, 1029. For the carnal person, the whole rule of understanding is the habit of seeing. V, 1139. Understanding superfluous things does no harm; but perhaps learning them was harmful—why. VIII, 83. We fail to understand some things because we cannot, others because we do not wish to. IV, 342, 343. Some things we do not believe unless we understand them, and other things we do not understand unless we believe them. IV, 1552. See Faith. What must be done so that we may be able to understand what we believe. V, 570. The stages of understanding are faith, the merit of faith, and intellect. V, 698.

What intelligible things are. VII, 231. Intelligible things surpass sensible things. VIII, 96, 99. But the deficiencies of the two kinds cannot be ranked one above the other. VIII, 99. Philosophers place riches in intelligible things and poverty in sensible things. II, 64. We understand intelligible things through intelligible forms. VII, 341.

Intent is light. III, 1289, 1339. It is not what each person does, but with what disposition he does it, that must be considered. III, 1289. Each person must be assessed according to his disposition for the recompense of reward or punishment. IV, 460. When the good and the wicked do the same things and suffer the same things, they must be distinguished not by their deeds and punishments but by their causes. II, 324. Right intention. V, 804, 805. Culpable intention. V, 805. Which intention is wrong and which is right. V, 303, 375. Intention makes a work good; faith directs intention. IV, 259. A person scarcely knows the intention of his own heart. IV, 1837. It is known to God alone. IV, 1837. The intention of a good conscience is the oil by which the lamps—that is, the good works of the wise virgins—are nourished. II, 571. An evil intention blinds a person. IV, 1839. Whatever a person does in order to obtain earthly advantage, he does as a slave. V, 208. How one should act so that the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. IV, 1834.

How great a sin intemperance is. V, 1272.

The distinction between an intercessor and a defender, and the duty of each. II, 657, 662. To intercede for another seems to every person a duty of humanity. II, 657. It is commended by the Lord. II, 658. One must intervene on behalf of thieves, not so that they may in no way restore what they have taken—for otherwise one would enter into partnership in their crime. II, 662, 663. Rather, it is so that an opportunity may be given them to correct their conduct. II, 655, 656. The evils that sometimes follow from the liberation of the guilty are not to be charged to intercessors, but the good things they have in view are. II, 661. How much the intercession of the saints avails for others before God. IV, 1412.

Intercidona, a goddess. VII, 188.

The one who offers a person to be killed kills him. III, 1937.

Interjections, when they are transferred into the use of another language, cannot be conveyed by translation. III, 43. Interjections indicate emotion more than they signify any particular thing. III, 1764.

The inner things, not the outer, are to be loved: let us have the former by our will, the latter by necessity. IV, 1813.

How intercessions, supplications, prayers, and thanksgivings differ. II, 635. Prayers (*precationes*) are made before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; prayers (*orationes*) when it is being blessed; intercessions or petitions when the people are blessed; and after all these, thanksgivings. II, 636.

The diversity of interpretations of Scripture is useful. III, 43. From where a fault in translation can be corrected. III, 44. Why Jerome undertook a new translation of the canonical books after others. II, 262. See Jerome. Augustine thinks that the interpreters of Scripture are to be granted very great authority. II, 112. Augustine calls the edition of the interpreters of the Septuagint the Vulgate. VII, 489. See Septuagint.

A question does not demonstrate ignorance. VIII, 408, 630.

*Interventores*. IX, 610. Note (a). An *interventor* was one who governed the Church while the see was vacant. II, 177. Note (a).

To find: what it is. VIII, 979. The capacity for finding cannot be lacking in minds that piously seek God. I, 1049. Part of discovery is knowing what you are looking for. III, 547. A thing that has been found must be restored to its owner. V, 963, 965. What you found and did not return, you stole. V, 965. Ignorance is no excuse if avarice is not mastered. V, 964. An excellent example concerning this matter. V, 964.

Inventius, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Another Inventius, bishop. II, 780.

Anger that grows old becomes hatred, and so forth. II, 153.

How envy and emulation differ. III, 2142. Envy, hatred of another’s happiness. III, 436; IV, 1399; V, 1561. Envy, the daughter of pride. V, 783, 1561, 1565; VI, 315, 413, 450. Pride, the mother of envy. II, 561; IV, 1290. And its companion. IV, 709. Envy follows pride; it does not precede it. III, 436, 437.

How great an evil envy is. IX, 160. Envy is a monstrous vice. III, 160. Envy is hateful to God. VII, 444. Nothing is more wretched than envy. VII, 268. Nothing is more opposed to charity. VI, 315. Envy ought to be absent from the faithful. III, 879. Envy is a diabolical vice. VI, 315, 413, 673. A diabolical evil. IX, 314. The devil’s sin. III, 2017. Through this the devil is the devil. III, 133. The devil’s body is composed of the envious. IV, 1807. Envy is both a diabolical sin and the punishment of sin. X, 821, 822. Envy is the cause of all seductions and overthrowings. IV, 1807. Diabolical envy, which... VII, 441. Envy prevents a person from possessing what another possesses. III, 1646. Each person also possesses what he does not have when he loves it in another. III, 1812. In spiritual goods, regard as yours what you love in your brother; let him regard as his what he loves in you. V, 1040. The false righteous must envy the true righteous. IV, 1807. There is no envy in heaven because of the difference in rewards. VI, 412; VII, 802.

A person is envious who desires to be better than another. III, 2040. No one envies another for something he neither wishes to be nor to appear to be. IV, 1807. No envious person, when he wishes to harm another, is not first a torment to himself. VIII, 586. An envious person is called a sinner by a distinctive mark. IV, 414.

Invisible things appear in a manner appropriate to themselves, and therefore they are more certain than those reached by the bodily senses. II, 456. Invisible things are better than visible things. V, 869. Certain eternal things are called invisible because they cannot possibly be seen by these mortal eyes. II, 456. God is the greatest of all invisible things. VII, 319. To whom faith must be given concerning invisible things. VII, 318. The Arians established a hierarchy of invisibility, not only in the Trinity but also among the heavenly virtues. VIII, 727, 745, 766. They are refuted. VIII, 763.

How a person is said to act unwillingly. X, 234. No one does a kindness unwillingly, even if what he does is good. I, 669. By God’s power no one is compelled unwillingly either toward good or toward evil. X, 567.

What it means to invoke God in truth. IV, 1087, 1882, 1883. Who properly invokes the Lord. III, 1307. Only the rational soul knows how to invoke God. IV, 1911. It is not fitting to invoke God without purity of heart. IV, 249. No one has invoked God whom God himself did not first call. IV, 1488. The wicked both invoke and do not invoke God. IV, 249. To invoke God is to call him into oneself. IV, 249. You invoke whatever you love. IV, 1087. Whoever invokes God for the sake of earthly goods does not invoke God. IV, 250, 617, 618. A person does not truly invoke God if he desires what displeases him. IV, 142. Something not belonging to God but to human beings is sometimes called an invocation. III, 501. We ought to commend ourselves to the martyrs’ prayers. V, 868. The invocation of Saint Stephen. V, 1447.

Io, also called Isis, daughter of Inachus, was regarded as a goddess in Egypt. VII, 563.

Joab is interpreted as “enemy.” IV, 715.

Augustine was uncertain whether Joachim was Mary’s father and whether he belonged to the tribe of Levi or of Judah. VIII, 471.

Job before the Law. V, 500. Job was neither a native nor a proselyte, but of the Idumaean people. VII, 609. He was three generations later than Israel. VII, 609, 610. He used what he had received like a good traveler; he possessed things, but was not possessed by them. VI, 704. Job demonstrates that God also gives and takes away temporal things. IV, 327. He remained alone of his possessions, alone of his household, alone of his children, full of God. IV, 660. His wife alone was left to him, like Eve, an ally of the devil, not a comforter of her husband. IV, 220, 660, 1150, 1151, 1382, 1732, 1738, 1881; VI, 632, 704, 719. After all his possessions had been taken from him, the devil kept Job’s wife for himself as a servant to deceive her husband. IX, 727. He did not say, “The Lord gave; the devil took away,” because the devil would not have taken anything away unless the Lord had permitted it. IV, 1150. Job was a drawn trumpet which, struck by tribulation, produced a strong and sweet sound. IV, 1255, etc. He worshiped God without seeking payment. IV, 660, 1752, 1794; V, 264, 569, 1692. Having lost everything, he delighted in God. V, 147. Why Job was tempted and tested. III, 1697. God permitted him to be tempted so that the human being might be tested and the devil conquered. IV, 1150, 1612. Job was handed over to the devil to be tempted, so that, when Job had been tested, the devil might be tormented. III, 2023. Job did not see the devil but understood God’s power. [Col. 0364] IV, 1150. Whether the devil spared Job’s eyes with greater cruelty in the flesh so that they might remain to witness the wound he had inflicted upon his entire body. IX, 636.

Job was trained against the devil. III, 2007. He was more cautious than Adam. VI, 616, 719. Through Job, Adam conquered on the dungheap, though conquered in paradise. IV, 220, 327, 539, 1207. Job, rotten in the dungheap, was better than Adam, whole in paradise. IV, 1255. Job on the dungheap—how rich! V, 1511. Poor outwardly, rich inwardly. IV, 255. Job suffered no scandal in his distress. V, 500. When the fire of temptation approached, it found gold, not straw; it removed the impurities but did not reduce him to ashes. V, 569.

Why Job suffered so much. X, 305. Job was not afflicted on account of sins. X, 162. He surpassed all who at that time could be righteous on earth. X, 162. Nevertheless, he was not without sin. X, 159, 162. In justice and piety, no human being of Job’s time was his equal. VII, 609. God permitted Job himself to be tempted so that he might be offered to us as an example for imitation. IV, 660. Job is described as patient. VI, 615, 632, 704.

Job, fortitude. I, 1329. Job was great in enduring tribulations. X, 162. Job was strengthened to endure by foreseeing Christ’s passion. X, 161. Job prophesied Christ. X, 283.

Job is a figure of those who worship God in marriage. IV, 1732. He seems to have said something harsh against God, but only to those who do not understand. IV, 1383. He is defended against blasphemy. IV, 1384. Job’s glory is perhaps no less than that of the martyrs. VI, 719. Job and the other saints who preferred to endure evils rather than inflict death upon themselves are to be preferred to Cato. VII, 37. Since Job received back not twice as many sons but the same number he had possessed, faith in the resurrection was commended. II, 549. What Job, Daniel, and Noah signify. VI, 716. Through the inner light Job is indifferent whether he has the darkness or the light of this life. IV, 1794. The book of Job is received by the Jews as authoritative Scripture. VII, 609. Jerome first translated Job from Greek speech and then from Hebrew. II, 242. In the later version such diligence is not observed. II, 242.

Jobinus. II, 702. He who serves God’s maidservants. II, 708.

The delight of the godly in the Lord, even in this life. V, 142, 146, 147. Now delight is mingled with fear; it will be complete in the future. IV, 1092. Fear belongs to the present life, delight to the future. IV, 1554.

John the Baptist. His excellence. IV, 1833. Sanctified in the womb. See Jeremiah. Whence John’s exultation comes and what it signifies. II, 840. John was born with sin and needed a Savior. V, 1335. Whether the use of reason and will was hastened in John. II, 840. He was sent before Christ as a lamp before the light. V, 1502. Not the light, but a lamp. V, 437, 1502. A lamp. III, 1657. The lamp that God prepared for his Christ. III, 1582; IV, 1728. Light and not light. III, 1503. He was light, but not the true light. III, 1391. He was illuminated light. III, 1658. He was not the light that is not illuminated by participation. II, 541. How the true light is distinguished from illuminated light—that is, Christ from John. II, 541.

John the forerunner was not born so wondrously and made so great without cause. V, 1308, 1316, 1328. John was, as it were, a boundary of the former dispensation. V, 1328; X, 595. John, bearing the person of all the prophets. V, 1306, 1307. And of the whole of prophecy. VI, 42, 44. John was more than a prophet. V, 1302. Why he was called more than a prophet and said to have had no greater among those born of women. IX, 289. He was so great a man, greater than whom no one existed, so that by humbling himself before Christ he might show that Christ was more than a human being. V, 1310, 1313, 1316, 1329, 1331, 1674.

Whence John’s greatness is commended. V, 1303. Whoever is greater than John is God. V, 1301, 1321. Among human beings, Christ alone is greater than John. V, 431, 1308. He is greater than John who among the angels is lesser. V, 431. John the Baptist did not want to grow through the words of human beings, because he had grasped the Word of God. V, 431. John the Baptist, the voice of one crying in the wilderness. V, 1304. As Christ, the Word himself, grows, the voice diminishes. V, 1307. John is properly the voice, as though the seal of all the voices that foretold Christ. V, 1306. John, the herald of the Lord. V, 1302. The bridegroom’s friend. V, 1303. At the bridegroom’s wedding, the best man. V, 1332. John’s remarkable abstinence. I, 799. John is thought to be Christ. V, 1303, 1308, 1329. Certain heretics supposed that Elijah’s soul had passed into John. III, 725. John is Elijah, and is not Elijah. III, 1408. John’s humility. III, 1496, 1498, 1503, 1658. He rejected false honor in order to find true glory. IV, 594. By abasing himself, he commends Christ. V, 1302, 1310. Whether John doubted about Christ. V, 432. Since he was not among the Lord’s disciples, but had disciples together with the Lord, he becomes his more credible witness. V, 1320, 1331. The testimony of John the Baptist concerning Christ, and Christ’s concerning John. III, 1657; V, 430, 431, 1308, 1312. Why John’s testimony concerning Christ was sought. III, 1660, 1661; V, 714. How John bore witness to the light. [Col. 0365] III, 1392. John’s testimony proves Christ’s divinity. II, 540. John the Baptist’s statement, “I ought to be baptized by you,” was fulfilled. V, 1335.

John’s baptism is different from Christ’s baptism. V, 1018; IX, 290. John’s baptism belongs to the foretelling of Christ. IX, 289. The baptism of John after which Paul baptized cannot be brought forward by the Donatists as an example to prove that rebaptism is necessary. IX, 290.

The killing of John the Baptist: on what occasion it occurred. V, 1406. A comparison of John the forerunner and Christ at their births. V, 1301, 1327. The difference between John and Christ in their births and passions. V, 1013, 1015, 1302, 1308, 1311, 1681. The custom of celebrating John’s nativity was received through the tradition of the ancestors. V, 1319. The superstitious and pagan solemnity that had been observed on John’s birthday was corrected. V, 1021. Why only the nativities of Christ and John are celebrated, and not those of others. V, 1302, 1319.

John the Baptist is a martyr, because he was killed for the law of truth, although not for the name of Christ. IV, 1832, 1833. John the Baptist, a mountain. III, 1391.

John the Evangelist was loved by the Lord above the others. V, 1148. John customarily called himself the disciple whom Jesus loved. III, 1932. Who that disciple was who followed Christ with Peter when he was led to Annas cannot safely be affirmed, because it is not stated. III, 1932. Perhaps that disciple was John. III, 1932. John’s purpose in writing the Gospel. III, 1375, 1377. John took care to express the Lord’s divinity. III, 1045. He spoke more sublimely than the others about the Lord’s divinity. III, 1662. Hence he is placed far above the other three. III, 1045. Among the four Evangelists he is the most eminent. III, 1085. John transcended all creatures in order to reach the Word. III, 1381, 1743.
