John the Evangelist is an eagle. III, 1510. He is rightly compared with an eagle. III, 1662, 1666, 1686. Why John reclined upon the Lord’s breast. III, 1556. He drank the secret of the divinity from the Lord’s breast more abundantly and, in a certain way, more familiarly. III, 1045. And he drew his teaching from it. III, 1382, 1663. John the apostle was a most eager banqueter. IV, 1874. A great belcher, he drank the heavenly secrets from the Lord’s breast. V, 210. What John the Evangelist said about the Son of God can arouse the minds of little ones, but exercise and nourish those somewhat more advanced. III, 1536. John the Evangelist, a mountain. III, 1390. His humility. III, 1382. John is concerned with the contemplative virtue, while the other Evangelists are concerned with the active. III, 993, 1046. John the apostle, a virgin. VIII, 493. He experienced no marriage. VI, 391. Although he did not suffer martyrdom, in the merit of patience he is not inferior to Peter. VI, 391. How the Lord wishes John the Evangelist to remain until he comes. V, 1181. John the apostle is found to have died long before five thousand five hundred years had been completed from the beginning of the human race. II, 910. The Alogi reject John’s Gospel. VIII, 31. John’s First Epistle was written to the Parthians. III, 1333.

John, bishop of Jerusalem. IX, 300; X, 342, 343, 351. He is said to have loved Pelagius greatly. II, 774. Augustine writes to him and asks that he himself be answered by him. II, 774. He sends him Pelagius’s book together with the response he made to that same book. II, 775. John of Jerusalem refutes Pelagius. II, 829.

John, bishop. X, 652, 663.

John of Constantinople. II, 286; X, 865. What he thought about sin. X, 285. He acknowledged original sin. X, 1513, 1516. The passage of John Chrysostom improperly cited by the Pelagians to deny original sin is answered. X, 654. John Chrysostom’s homily on Lazarus raised from the dead. X, 656, 657. Letter to Olympias. X, 656.

John the hermit, endowed with the spirit of prophecy. VII, 172. The elder Theodosius consulted him about the outcome of the war. VI, 607. He was questioned with the greatest patience and answered with the greatest wisdom. VI, 608. He never allowed women to see him. VI, 607, 608. To a woman who anxiously pleaded through her husband, he appeared in her dream, as he had promised. VI, 607, 608.

What Joel prophesied and at what time. VII, 583, 587.

Jonadab is interpreted as “the Lord’s spontaneity.” IV, 876, 890. Jonadab was an example of obedience for his sons. IV, 875, 876.

What Jonah prophesied and at what time. VII, 585, 587. He announced wrath, not mercy. V, 1610. That Jonah was in the whale’s belly for three days is no more incredible than that Lazarus was raised on the fourth day, Christ rose on the third day, or three men walked about in the furnace. II, 382, 383. Jonah is a figure of Christ. II, 383, 384. Jonah prophesied Christ not so much by speech as by a certain suffering of his own. VII, 587. A comparison of Jonah and Christ. VI, 666. Jonah’s passage, which differs in the Hebrew from the version of the Septuagint, stirs up turmoil in the Church. II, 242. What Augustine thinks about that passage. II, 291.

The Ionic philosophers. VII, 225, 233.

The Jordan. Near the Jordan, at the beginning of spring, there is a wheat harvest. [Col. 0366] III, 777. At that time the Jordan is fuller than during the winter. III, 777. Christ’s teaching began at the Jordan. V, 1303, 1587. The Jordan is a figure of baptism. IV, 1479. What the Jordan turning backward signifies. IV, 1479.

Joseph signifies increase. IV, 1021, 1037. Joseph’s dream of the sheaves bowing down to his sheaf is best understood of Christ. III, 582. Joseph was called *Psontomphanech* by Pharaoh. III, 582. Why he was more a prophet than Pharaoh. III, 461. In what year of his life Joseph was elevated by Pharaoh, and in what year he summoned his father to Egypt. VII, 563. Joseph’s family was freed from the danger of famine through his care: a prophecy concerning those freed through Christ. III, 588. Joseph’s chastity. VII, 563. And his struggle against sin. V, 1439, 1592. Joseph, an example of purity for men. V, 1509. In what year Joseph died. VII, 564. Joseph is a figure of Christ. II, 919; III, 588, 594; IV, 1037, 1404. The blessing of Joseph’s sons is a prophecy concerning Christ. III, 593. Joseph is used for any brother. III, 98.

How Joseph, the virgin’s husband, could have had two fathers. I, 633, 635. The question of the two fathers is resolved. III, 767, 768, 1072, 1073, 1334; V, 348; VIII, 215, 216, 486. Joseph has one father and another grandfather according to Matthew, and another according to Luke. VIII, 213. Because of the dignity of the male line, Christ’s generations are traced from Joseph or to Joseph. VIII, 214. Joseph and Mary were truly married, not merely in human opinion. X, 810, 811. Joseph was Mary’s true husband. V, 342. He was chosen as a witness to the perpetual virginity of his wife. VI, 560. Joseph was the guardian, indeed the witness, of virginal modesty. V, 1096. Joseph’s justice was sincere, not harsh. V, 338. Joseph was a witness of the Virgin’s childbirth. III, 1637. He is rightly called Christ’s father. III, 1071. How he was Christ’s father. V, 342, 348; X, 421. Joseph was Christ’s father not by flesh but by love. V, 351. Because of a certain holy and virginal marriage with Christ’s mother, he deserved to be called Christ’s parent. VIII, 214.

Josephus, writer of Jewish history. II, 916.

Josiah was revealed to a certain prophet long before he was born. VII, 548. By destroying the sacred groves, temples of idols, and high places, he served the Lord. II, 801.

Joshua was previously called Auses. V, 1553; VIII, 327. What the change of his former name signifies in Joshua. VIII, 327. At Joshua’s command the sun stood still, but time continued to pass. I, 821. Joshua is a figure of Christ. V, 1553; VIII, 271.

Whether Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, worshiped the true God. III, 619.

Jovian, Julian’s successor. II, 400. He ruled for a short time. VII, 171.

Jovinian, a monk from whom the Jovinianists took their name. VIII, 45; X, 445. His doctrines. VIII, 45. Heresy. VI, 372; X, 1114, 1115, 1116. His errors. X, 1418. His error concerning marriage. X, 193. He equated the marriages of the faithful with sacred virginity. X, 458, 643. He considered the preference given to virginity an accusation against marriage. X, 1415. He did not want to have a wife not because of greater merit, but so as not to suffer the troubles of married life. VIII, 46. He destroyed the holy Mary’s virginity. X, 552, 643. Jovinian’s heresy gained strength at Rome. I, 639. Augustine opposed it by publishing a book, *On the Good of Marriage*. I, 639. Jovinian’s heresy was suppressed by the Roman Church. I, 639. Jerome rejected Jovinian’s empty talk. II, 723. The Jovinianists’ questioning is exploded. VI, 392. In defending the equality of sins Jovinian was a Stoic; in pursuing and defending pleasures, an Epicurean. II, 735. Why he branded Catholics with the charge of Manichaeism. X, 458, 643. Jovinian called Ambrose a Manichaean. X, 1419. What distinction there is between Jovinian, the Manichaean, and the Catholic. X, 1115. The Pelagians are worse than Jovinian. X, 1418. Julian compares Augustine with Jovinian and abusively declares him worse. X, 1482, 1483.

Jovinus, bishop. X, 652, 663.

Jove. See Jupiter.

Jovius, Count of the Emperor Honorius. VII, 620.

How Iphigenia, daughter of King Agamemnon, was transformed. VII, 575.

What anger is. VI, 140. Anger is a turbulent desire to remove those things that hinder freedom of action. II, 73. It is a movement of the soul provoking one to inflict punishment. IV, 92. It is a desire for vengeance. V, 396; VII, 424. Anger is used for vengeance. VIII, 410. Before sin, anger was not vicious. VII, 427. The Platonists confessed that anger was a vicious part of the soul. VII, 427.

How much harm anger does. V, 1431. There is a true light—justice and wisdom—which the mind ceases to see when overcome by the disturbance of anger as by a cloud. V, 476. Anger is a scorpion. V, 1430. The movement of anger arising from the punishment of sin is not within one’s power. IV, 80. If anger creeps upon a Christian, it must not be held for long and become yesterday’s anger. IV, 189. One must beware lest anger turn into hatred. IV, 241. It is nourished and grows through evil suspicions. V, 397. And it is brought to hatred. V, 506. Anger that grows old becomes hatred. II, 153; IV, 189, 1373; V, 324, 397. What difference there is between anger and hatred. IV, 632; V, 1054. Anger disturbs the eye; hatred extinguishes it. [Col. 0367] IV, 241; V, 507. Anger is a shoot which, unless quickly uprooted, grows into a beam. IV, 241; V, 397. By retaining anger, one avoids an enemy outwardly but keeps something much worse within one’s heart. V, 1045. This causes one to provide the devil access through it as through a door. V, 1045. “Let not the sun go down upon your anger,” lest the sun of justice abandon the mind itself. V, 1045. As vinegar corrupts a vessel if it remains there too long, so anger corrupts the heart if it lasts into another day. II, 958.

Through the ease of becoming angry, bile increases, and through the increase of bile we are compelled to anger more frequently. II, 73. Anger is an enemy beyond whom the other enemies scarcely do any harm. V, 1430. A description of an angry person and of another who patiently endures. IV, 1241. What anger without sin is. V, 649. Not everyone who becomes angry hates—indeed, sometimes a person is proved to hate more if he does not become angry. V, 506. There is a great difference between one who is angry and one who hates. V, 307. If a father becomes angry with his son in order to correct him, he loves through becoming angry. V, 1054. What it means to become angry with one’s brother. III, 1229, 1230. What it means to become angry with one’s brother without cause. I, 615. One does not become angry with a brother when one becomes angry at the brother’s sin. I, 615.

Whence the anger of the godly arises. IV, 240. Sometimes it is permissible to be angry with those who live badly, but not to shout, when they cannot be corrected, and hence there is inward disturbance. IV, 241. It is much better that we become angry with no one, even justly, than that, by becoming angry as though justly, we slip through a hidden facility of anger into hatred of someone. II, 153. The enormity of anger is signified by fire. IV, 1000. The anger of the nations was fire, consuming more those who persecuted than those whom they persecuted. IV, 1241.

It is human to become angry. V, 1054. Anger is a speck; hatred, a beam. V, 1054. To become angry with oneself. V, 649. Every person who repents becomes angry with himself. V, 1358. Anger cannot be killed, but it can be restrained. V, 1431. It is more praiseworthy to triumph over conquered anger. IV, 1469.

What the anger of God is. VIII, 142. God’s anger is his vengeance. VI, 139, 249. According to the Apostle. III, 2065. A just and fixed vengeance. II, 860. Vengeance for iniquity. IV, 1014. The just rationale of vengeance. IV, 1054. The turning away of his face. IV, 207. God does not return anger except when it is deserved. X, 621. God’s anger arises from the sins of the people. V, 1393. God’s anger against the wicked is not without goodness. VI, 246. God is gentle even when angry. V, 166. What human mercy contributes to those with whom God is angry. IV, 996. He is angry with his servants as a father correcting them, not as a judge condemning them. IV, 1022, 1023. Very few know the power of God’s anger, because toward most people he is angry precisely when he spares them. IV, 1145. The greater anger of God is the vain and deceptive happiness of the wicked. IV, 1145. Whatever the wicked willingly do and whatever they unwillingly suffer belongs to God’s just anger. VI, 246. God’s anger passes over the righteous; it does not remain. IV, 1119. Human anger has power here alone and over the body; divine anger has power both here and after death. IV, 1145. There is an anger of consummation, and an anger of consumption. IV, 710, 711. From where God’s anger usually creeps upon his ministers. V, 1540. Sons of wrath, that is, those bearing vengeance. IV, 398. We are said by nature to have been sons of wrath because in hope we are no longer so, although in reality we still are. IV, 398. How Julian understood our being by nature children of wrath. X, 841. See Original Sin. Nothing frees from the anger of God except the grace of God through Jesus Christ. X, 125.

Iras is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” VIII, 457.

Irenaeus of Lyons, bishop, asserts original sin. X, 644.

Irenaeus of Olulis. IX, 232.

Irenaeus the collector. VII, 767.

How irony and antiphrasis differ. III, 81.

Irreverence, almost shamelessness: when it is necessary for a Christian. IV, 850.

Christ is still mocked by countless people. IV, 171. How the mockery and derision of God are to be understood. IV, 70.

Isaac is interpreted as “laughter.” VII, 510. Isaac signifies grace. VII, 505. Isaac was conceived by a miracle. X, 714. Isaac, the son of promise, signifies the calling of the Gentiles. VII, 505. Isaac is a figure of the sons of promise. III, 566. God’s command that Isaac be killed by his father displeases only the impious. V, 27. Isaac carrying wood is a figure of Christ carrying the cross. IV, 244, 245; VII, 511. Christ’s sacrifice was prefigured in Isaac. V, 133. Isaac is a figure of Christ. VIII, 810. He prefigured the Lord’s passion and resurrection. IV, 603. What Isaac’s sport with Rebekah signifies. VIII, 427. Why he called Rebekah his sister and concealed that she was his wife. VIII, 427. What Isaac and Rebekah prefigured in the blessing of Jacob. V, 38. Isaac understood a figure in Jacob’s deception. V, 44. Isaac was carried away into ecstasy after giving Jacob his blessing. III, 569. This blessing is not without prophetic significance. III, 569. Isaac is a figure of the citizens of heaven. VII, 439, 440. The history of Isaac is both true and figurative. V, 31.

Isaiah prophesied much more than the other prophets about Christ and the Church. VII, 585. Isaiah’s prophecy resembles the Gospel. V, 259; IX, 503. Isaiah is called by some more an Evangelist than a prophet. VII, 585. Isaiah saw God, but not as he is. III, 1779. Isaiah was killed by Manasseh. VII, 582. Augustine was ordered to read Isaiah in order to prepare himself for baptism. [Col. 0368] I, 769. The Pelagian interpretation of Isaiah. X, 1137, 1138, 1139.

Isis, or Io, daughter of Inachus. VII, 597. Wife of Osiris. VII, 254, 256. She gave the Egyptians writing. VII, 597, 598, 599. They thought that the dead Isis was to be worshiped as a great goddess. VII, 599, 563. It was forbidden, under penalty of death, to say that Isis had been a human being. VII, 564. When Isis is angry she harms many; when favorable she helps many. VII, 254.

Ishmael’s sport with Isaac was persecution. V, 33. Ishmael is a figure of the citizens of the earthly city. VII, 439. Of those who worship God carnally and seek earthly happiness. IV, 1603.

The Ishmaelites are interpreted as “obedient to themselves.” IV, 1052.

Israel is interpreted as “seeing God.” IV, 959, 1254, 1609, 1624, 1656, 1937, 1951; VII, 518; VIII, 741. Israel is the name of election. IV, 575.

Why the Israelites are called sons of God. X, 1428. The people of Israel were tithed in Abraham. X, 1552. The Israelites did not conquer their enemies quickly, lest they perish, puffed up by prosperity. III, 788, 798. The Israelites did not commit theft by despoiling the Egyptians. III, 608. Israel justly took away the labor of the Canaanite, whereas Ahab unjustly took away the labor of Naboth. II, 811. The Israelites’ clothing and shoes lasted for many years in the wilderness. II, 942. The deliverance of the Israelite people from Egypt is described. VI, 694. How many years the Israelites served in Egypt. III, 610; VII, 502.

The beginning of the Israelite kingdom. VII, 577. And the succession of its kings. VII, 577. All the kings of Israel were rejected. VII, 558. The ten tribes of Israel were defeated by the Chaldaeans and led into captivity. VII, 581. Why the Israelites fell into idolatry. III, 1404.

The carnal and spiritual Israelites. VI, 334, 336. They were spiritual members of the Church. VI, 335. They understood what was signified by the sacraments of the Law. VI, 336. The Israelite people were a prophetic nation. II, 376. It was a prophet of Christ. VI, 435. The sayings and deeds of this people were prophecy. VI, 335. Israelite is interpreted mystically. VI, 49, 694. No Christian should consider himself a stranger to the name of Israel. IV, 1476, 1743. Many born from Israel are not Israelites, and conversely. II, 895, 896. The seed of Israel consists of those born into new life and restored to the vision of God. IV, 169. Israel comprises all the faithful. IV, 1743. All the saints. IV, 1948. The children of the Church. IV, 1952. Whatever happened to Israel in Egypt and the wilderness is applied to the conduct of Christians. V, 1551; VIII, 269. The captivity and liberation of the Israelites are figures of the captivity and liberation of Christians. IV, 917. Israel led out of Egypt is the human being freed from sin through baptism. III, 1626.

The vision of God promised to Israel. V, 683. The name of Israel conveys the promise of seeing God in the homeland. III, 577. The people of God will truly be Israel in the heavenly Jerusalem. VII, 547.

The Israelites called the clubs of the Circumcellions *Israeles*. IV, 134.

A large part of Italy was once called by the name of Greece. VII, 225. Italy’s disasters. II, 422. Italy ravaged by gladiators. VII, 115. The illustrious poet mentioned the flowers of Italy. II, 314. The Italians mock Augustine over the sounds of words, and are in turn criticized by him. I, 1015. The Italians pray for clear winters. I, 1001.

Italica, a very powerful woman. II, 318, Note (b), 364. Augustine’s letter to her is mentioned. II, 703.

One path is the path of mortality, another the path of piety. V, 955.

Ithacus. VIII, 1047.

Jubaianus, bishop. IX, 128, 141, 142.

God commands difficult things, but promises great things. V, 120. God gives what he commands. X, 899. God causes human beings to do what he commands to be done. X, 976. God assists what we have willed if we do what he commands. V, 165. See Commands; Precepts. The one who commands acts when it is not permissible to refuse the service. III, 622.

Jubilation, a sound of joy without words. IV, 1254, 1255, 1272. Jubilation is an amazement of joy that cannot be expressed in words. IV, 528, 1218, 1323. A person understands jubilation when he knows how to rejoice in the Lord, not in himself, and in God’s grace, not in his merits. IV, 1128. Jubilation befits the ineffable God. IV, 283.

A *jubilum* is a certain sound signifying that the heart is in labor with what it cannot say. IV, 283.

Judah is interpreted as “confession.” IV, 540, 835, 865; VIII, 457. The tribe of Judah is signified by the name Judah. III, 793. Jacob’s prophecy concerning Judah pertains to Christ. VIII, 440. What Judah’s intercourse with Tamar signifies. VIII, 456. Scripture neither approved nor condemned Judah’s deed, but left it to be weighed. III, 812. Judah fornicated insofar as it lay within him. III, 812. Judah’s intercourse with Tamar is a sin. VIII, 439.

Judas Maccabaeus cleansed the temple of every contamination of idolatry. VII, 606.

The Epistle of Jude is among the canonical Scriptures. III, 1831.

Judas: Christ chose Judas as an Apostle. VII, 611. Christ chose him in order to give us an example of endurance of evils. IV, 329. Judas was not chosen for blessedness. III, 1796. He was chosen for the work of temptation; the other eleven Apostles for the work of testing. IV, 653. Among the chosen Apostles he is not listed last without reason. V, 95. Judas had not abandoned everything in such a way as sincerely to break the bond of cupidity. IV, 1438. Judas used to take away what was put into the money-box. IV, 195, 1438. Why Christ entrusted the money-boxes to the thief Judas. VI, 552. Although Judas was an unfaithful keeper of the Lord’s money-boxes, he was sent with the other disciples to preach the kingdom of heaven. IV, 135. Christ entrusted to him, as to the other Apostles, the first Eucharist, prepared by Christ’s own hands and commended to them by his own mouth. II, 178, 329; IV, 135; V, 153. Christ admitted him to the meal at which he commended and handed over to the disciples the figure of his body and blood. IV, 73. Judas ate the Lord’s bread; against the Lord he ate punishment. III, 1796. The wicked man received Christ’s body wickedly. III, 1612, 1801. After the bread of Christ had been wrongly received, the devil entered Judas in order to possess more fully what had already been handed over to him. III, 1802. The devil would not have entered Judas’s heart unless Judas had given him room. IV, 1766. The morsel by which the Lord wished to designate Judas was not the Lord’s body. III, 1802.

Judas did not have a right understanding of Christ’s divinity. IV, 1438. He did not become perverse at the moment when, corrupted by the Jews, he betrayed the Lord. III, 1761. On Judas’s betrayal. III, 1802, 2032. Judas the betrayer, the spy upon the Shepherd, the ambusher of the Savior, the seller of the Redeemer. III, 1786. Judas is not praiseworthy because of the usefulness of Christ’s betrayal, but damnable because of the willfulness of his crime. III, 1932. In betraying Christ, he did evil in such a way that good came from the one betrayed, a good of which he was unaware. III, 1620, 1786. From Judas’s crime God worked our salvation. V, 95, 339, 1067. In betraying Christ Judas did the same thing as God the Father and Christ himself, but not with the same intention. IV, 793, 1214. Judas’s treachery is beautifully expounded. VI, 688.

Judas freely betrayed Christ, although Scripture had foretold that he would betray him. IX, 407. Judas’s voluntary death was a great sin. VII, 31. It was not so much the crime he committed as his despair of pardon that made Judas perish utterly. V, 1558. Judas feared God, but it did him no good because he did not hope. IV, 1912. Psalm 108 is explained entirely as concerning Judas. IV, 1431. See Christ. Judas was evil by his own will, yet by God’s ordering providence he obtained his appointed place. V, 693. Judas, the son of the bridegroom pursuing the bridegroom, prefigured by Absalom. IV, 73, 97, 1847. Judas was called the son of perdition, predestined to perdition. III, 1914. Judas was a wolf covered with sheep’s clothing, tolerated among the sheep by the profound counsel of the master of the household. III, 1930. The Caians regard Judas the betrayer as something divine, and his crime as a benefit. VIII, 29. Judas represents the enemies of Christ. IV, 1432. He signifies the body of the wicked. III, 1762. Now there is not one Judas, but many. IV, 1441. Judas and the devil persecuted Christ’s soul; and now that same devil remains for the persecution of Christ’s body, while Judas is succeeded by a Judas. IV, 1849.

Judaea is interpreted as “confession.” IV, 959. Why it is called the desirable land. IV, 1412, 1413. Judaea and the Jews were named after Judah, Jacob’s son. IV, 956, 957; VII, 447.

Why the Jews are called Amorites and Hittites. III, 1703. The reason for the greater glory of the Jewish nation above others. IV, 1077, 1078, 1221. When the Jews were led captive into Babylon. VII, 582. After the Babylonian captivity the Jews had no kings. VII, 596, 607. The captivity of the Jews was dissolved by Cyrus. VII, 582. After the restoration of the Temple the Jews had no prophets. VII, 606. Hence they became worse. VII, 606, 610. The kingdom and priesthood of the Jews were a prophecy of the coming king and priest. VIII, 409, 417. The whole Jewish nation and kingdom was a prophet of Christ and of the Christian kingdom. VII, 221; VIII, 283, 290. The kingdom of the Jews was established without the aid of gods and preserved by the one true God alone. VII, 140.

The Jews received the Law so that they might become liable, not so that they might be freed from guilt. IV, 233. Their hardness was signified by the stone tablets. IV, 1369. The Jews did not understand for what dispensation the Law had been given. III, 2068. To the carnal Jew the Law was a burden and torment. V, 207. Why the Law worked wrath for the Jews. X, 208. They did not have the word of God within themselves, but in the letters that they read. VIII, 649. Why the Jews were under the servitude of fear. III, 615, 623. See Grace. They are heirs not from the Law, but from the promise. X, 1209. Temporal rewards were appropriately promised to the Jewish people. VIII, 162, 164. Because they desired earthly happiness, they easily turned aside to idols in adversity. IV, 351.

The Jews were afflicted with pride. V, 945. What their boasting was like. X, 208. Their empty boast concerning the Law and their free will. V, 851. They thought that they fulfilled God’s Law by their own righteousness. X, 208. The Jews were in error: first, because they were not subject to God’s righteousness, wishing to establish their own righteousness; second, because after Christ’s Passion they judged that the ancient sacraments had to be celebrated as necessary for salvation; third, because they persecuted preachers of grace [Col. 0370] as though they were enemies of the Law. II, 145, 156. They thought that they were justified by the Law; the Pelagians are like them. II, 770, 893. The Pelagians Judaize, not indeed in name but in error. II, 893. What sort of righteousness the Jews had. V, 921. The Jews are truly to be compared with sponges. V, 1086. The Jews are by nature from God, but by vice not from God. III, 1705. They are sons of Abraham by origin of flesh, not by likeness of life. III, 1701, 1705. The Jews are not sons of Israel. IV, 1948. They degenerated and lost Abraham’s offspring. IV, 1948. The Jews are sons of the devil by imitation, not by birth. III, 1703. Sons of the Old Testament. X, 593. Why they were called sons of the kingdom. V, 417. Called Christ’s own. V, 678.

The blindness of the Jews. III, 1936. Especially when Christ appeared. V, 260; VI, 643, 664. The Jews were blinded by their opinion of their own righteousness. V, 873. And deservedly so because of their pride. IV, 1789. The blindness and unbelief of the Jews. V, 260, 721, 751, 1029. In what way they are both seeing and blind. V, 752. The blindness of the Jews as a hidden vengeance. IV, 860. It came from other hidden sins known to God. VIII, 288. The Jews did not recognize Christ in his humility. IV, 522, 790, 862. Because the hand of the Lord lay heavily upon them, and God did this by repaying them justly rather than raging against them—not by wounding them, but by not healing them. IV, 862, 1789. In the resurrection of the dead they hoped for carnal goods. IV, 786. Why they hoped that they alone would rise to blessed life. IV, 786. The Jews were disturbed by the truth, Christ. III, 1633. The Jews are reproved for despising the Son of God in the form of a servant. III, 1573. They expected temporal goods in Christ. II, 546. They falsely boasted that Christian grace was owed to them. V, 93.

The Jews believed neither Moses nor Christ. V, 250. The unbelief of the Jews was prophesied. VIII, 288. The Jews were inexcusable because they did not believe in Christ. III, 1858. What sin the Jews would not have had if Christ had not come. III, 1857, 1860; V, 450. Why the Jews could not believe. X, 1014. They could not believe because they did not want to. III, 1776, 1778. The Jews, and those who do not believe with them, do not believe through the fault of their own will. II, 830. God foretold the unbelief of the Jews; he did not cause it. III, 1776. The unbelief of the Jews was a sin. III, 1775. In the sin by which they killed Christ, the Jews were blinded because of the merits of other hidden sins. III, 1051. The Lord showed the Jews only his bodily presence. III, 1735. Christ found the Jews full of sins. V, 450. The Jews were more dangerously ill. V, 945. They raged against the physician. V, 496, 945.

The cruelty of the Jews. III, 1937. They sinned more by calling the Lord demon-possessed than by killing him. III, 1633. They killed the Lord because they envied his authority. IV, 765. And because they feared losing earthly things. IV, 932. They killed Christ with the sword of the tongue. IV, 763. They killed the Lord to test whether he was truly a human being capable of dying, or something above human beings. IV, 762. In killing the Lord they themselves were killed, because in them iniquity lived. IV, 765. How much they suffered after the Lord was killed. IV, 666, 759, 1439, 1723. Why they immediately suffered persecution and were scattered. VI, 341. Why God allowed them to be subjugated by the Romans. III, 1051. The Jews were most rightly handed over to the glory of the Romans. VII, 165. They were excluded from their ancestral land by order of the Roman Emperor. V, 57. They were made tributaries of the Romans by Pompey. VII, 607. They became tributaries because of sin. IV, 682. They deservedly lost the land for which they killed the Lord. IV, 1137. The Jews are servants even of the rulers of the earth. III, 1693. This dispersion was foretold. VII, 584. The Jews remained without any anointing of king or priest. III, 1052; VII, 533. In Augustine’s time there was no Jew in Jerusalem. IV, 759, 1650. That nation did not so pass under Roman jurisdiction that it lost the form of the Jews. IV, 706, 707. Why the Jewish sect was not utterly destroyed. VI, 179. The Jews serve the Christian people. VII, 513. How the Jewish people, though greater, serves the Christian people, though smaller. IV, 1771, 1772. Why the Jews were preserved and scattered throughout the whole world. X, 594. They are necessary for believing Gentiles. IV, 705. The Jews were not scattered everywhere without divine providence; they retain the kind and name of their nation. V, 1032. They were not conquered by the Romans without reason, nor destroyed; they remained in their Law and ancestral customs so that by their rites and Scriptures they might show Christ. V, 1667. Israel appears in vain among all the nations. IV, 1136. The Jews remain marked, figured by Cain, who received a sign from God so that he would not be killed. IV, 442, 463, 705, 997; V, 1032; VIII, 261. The Jews were scattered throughout the whole world for the sake of the testimony of the Scriptures. VII, 140, 221, 608, 610. So that they might be witnesses of Christ through the Law itself. II, 634. And of the faith whose enemies they are. V, 268, 1032, 1038. And of Christian truth. III, 1061. Their books support our faith. VI, 178. The Jews remain to carry our books to their own confusion. IV, 666. So that everywhere they might carry the sacred books in which Christ and the Church were foretold. II, 523. They carry the divine writings, not for the assistance of their own salvation, but as testimony to our salvation. V, 1030, 1032, 1034. They carry the lamp of the Law to others, not to themselves. [Col. 0371] VI, 664. The Jew carries the book from which the Christian believes. IV, 666. The Jews are servants of Christians and custodians of our books. V, 56, 57, 1667. Christian archivists. VIII, 266, 267. Book-carriers. IV, 463. They are our scribes. IV, 666. The Jews are stones at the milestones. V, 1027, 1665.

The Jews, unwilling to be sheltered under the wings of that hen, Wisdom, gave an example by which we ought to learn fear. IV, 1140. The unbelief of the Jews contributes something great to our use. VIII, 329. The Jews’ abandonment by God was foretold through Isaiah. VIII, 59. More clearly through Malachi. VIII, 61. The Jews expelled Christ from the earthly Jerusalem; Christ expelled them from the heavenly Jerusalem. IV, 1650. Why the Jewish people is cursed. VIII, 259. Even though untamed, the Jewish people has not been abandoned by God. IV, 1225. The Jews were rejected, but not all of them. IV, 1221, 1222. Some Jews were chosen. III, 1765. Some of those who were persecuting Christ. III, 1687. From the Jews, as from the Gentiles, there are vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy. VI, 124. The multitude of the Jews, rejected deservedly because of faithlessness, belongs rather to Esau than to Jacob. IV, 1476, 1477. Many Jews were converted through consideration of the prophecies concerning Christ. VII, 608. Many after hearing Peter. V, 484, 947. In the converts, Christ’s prayer from the cross was effective. IV, 1199. The Jews are the broken olive tree. V, 1503. Before Christ the Jews were in the root of the olive tree; now they are broken branches. VIII, 241. The Jews were rejected because of pride, and the Gentiles grafted in because of humility. II, 559; V, 487, 1503. In the Jews there was the earlier grace; in the Gentiles greater humility. V, 1036. The Jews who crucified Christ obtained forgiveness through humility and confession. IV, 1198, 1199. The blood which the Jews, raging, poured out, they drank as believers. IV, 791; V, 485, 497, 538, 554, 1550, 1685.

The converted Jews were ardent in devotion to the evangelical life. VI, 340. In fervor they surpassed the Gentiles in conversion. IV, 1304. The Jews, though conquered, gave laws to their conquerors. VII, 192. With the Jews defeated, their God showed that he himself had not been defeated, by the overthrow of idols and the conversion of all the nations. III, 1051. How greatly God’s works in the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles are to be feared. IV, 789, 790, 794. The Jews are transgressors, dust. IV, 1303. From that dust came a wall of so many thousands of believers. IV, 1303. Not only did the Jews refuse Christ as king; even now many refuse to have him reigning everywhere. IV, 647. The Jews who crucified Christ walking on earth sinned less than those who despise him seated in heaven. IV, 859. For the sake of the elect, God does not cease spiritually to perform the signs that he once performed bodily for the Jews. IV, 1751, 1840, 1841. The fact that Christ has come is hidden from the Jews—but it is hidden from them because they want it so. V, 567. The Jews who have not been converted still await Christ. IV, 936; V, 567, 572. They believe that Christ will come, but not that he will die. VII, 553. They pretend not to understand and see the Scriptures through which Jesus Christ was announced. II, 448. The blindness of the Jews is to be refuted from the Scriptures of the Old Testament. VIII, 51. The adversary is refuted from the documents of the enemy. IV, 463. Thus the Jews appear in relation to Scripture as the face of a blind person appears in relation to a mirror: it is seen by others, but not by the blind person himself. IV, 666. With what disposition of mind the Jews are to be invited to the faith. IV, 110. The Jews will rush into the snares of Antichrist. IV, 1418. At the final time before the judgment they will be converted to Christ. VII, 704. Those who will be converted in the last days will mourn Christ’s death, not with the feeling of guilt for a crime, but with an affect of piety. VII, 706. Hosea foretold the conversion of the Jews to Christ before the judgment. VII, 581. The Jewish error concerning the resurrection. V, 1622. Christ rose to judge the Jews. IV, 1723. They have already been judged, and in what way. IV, 1752.

How much superior the religion of the Jews is to that of the pagans. VIII, 290. The Jews show Christ through their rites and Scriptures. V, 1034. The sacraments of the Jews and what they signify. V, 1242. The kingdom, Temple, priesthood, and mystical anointing of the Jews were assigned to the foretelling of Christ. III, 1051. The Jews could not sacrifice among the Gentiles. I, 600. Nor could they slaughter the Passover anywhere they wished. I, 600. Note (a). For the Jews it was a pollution to enter the dwelling of a foreigner during the days of Unleavened Bread. III, 1936. The Jews observed the Sabbath carnally. III, 189. Their abstinence from unclean animals was figurative. V, 800, 801. Seneca criticized the Sabbaths and sacraments of the Jews. VII, 192. How the religion of the Jews was weakened. VII, 529. Once the New Testament had been revealed, the ancient observances were not necessary. II, 894, 897. Augustine judges, following Jerome, that Gentiles who had believed in Christ were free from the burden of the Law, whereas those who believed from among the Jews were subject to the Law. II, 253, 257. After Christ’s coming, Jewish observances were neither harmful to Jews nor necessary for Gentiles. VI, 492. Christian doctrine did not compel Jews to Judaize, but the decree of the Apostles did not prohibit it either. II, 279. Jerome declares the ceremonies of the Jews to be both harmful and deadly to Christians; Augustine holds the same, provided that revealed grace is posited. II, 258, 283. With what intention Jews were permitted to observe the Law after Christ. II, 278. Why the precepts of Jewish observances are read to Christians. V, 801. Christians are Jews spiritually, not carnally. II, 895, 896. Although a Christian is spiritually a Jew and an Israelite, he ought not to apply these names to himself. II, 895, 897. Who should be considered alien to carnal Judaism. II, 391, 394. A certain person is said to Judaize carnally and to call himself a Jew and an Israelite. II, 899.

Moses represents the Jews. IV, 1789. The Jews are foreshadowed in Cain. VI, 688; VIII, 258, 260. They are compared with the workers on Noah’s ark. V, 1665. They are figured in the bush that was not consumed. V, 63. In the water of the pool. V, 687, 690. In Gideon’s fleece. IX, 398. The Jews are signified by the ox, and the Gentiles by the donkey. IV, 1675. The carnal Jews are foreshadowed by the sons of the concubines. VII, 513. The Jews and Christians are signified by the rich man and Lazarus. III, 1350. The Jews and Christians are figured by Jacob and Esau. IV, 1771. Esau represented the Jews. V, 55. He who did not obtain his father’s blessing. VII, 516. The blessings seemed to regard the Jews as the elder son; but they come to the Christians as the younger. V, 43, 44. The Jews are signified by the earth and the dry land, and the Gentiles by the sea. IV, 524, 937; IX, 398. The Jews alone, from among the ancients, do not seek the covering of the Christian name. II, 448. The Jews, Arians, and others sinned against the Holy Spirit. II, 814. The Jews do not accept the Book of Wisdom as canonical authority. I, 638; II, 199. The traditions of the Jews are unwritten. VIII, 637, 638, 642. The Jews are marked at the Kalends of January. V, 1020.

When the Book of Judges begins. III, 791.

A judgment of the mind concerning so many things does not take place without some inner light. II, 615. One must not judge concerning visible and invisible creation according to human perception. VIII, 609. Concerning what we may or may not judge. III, 2085. How miserable and lamentable human judgments are. VII, 632. One must judge no one. IV, 1804. To what extent judging the deeds of others is prohibited. III, 1296. One must pronounce judgment on no one in either a good or an evil direction. IV, 370. Judgment must not be passed on a person one does not know. VI, 82. Judge what you see; leave to God what you do not see. V, 323. One must not judge hidden matters concerning human beings. III, 1859. Judgment concerning hidden matters must be reserved for God. II, 267.

Everything is full of rash judgments. V, 285. Rash judgment. III, 1297. Do not judge rashly, since you do not see with what heart someone acts. V, 1145. Who rashly judge uncertain matters. III, 1298. It is difficult for all people not to seem to you as you are. IV, 339. Augustine was especially cautious in judging or suspecting something evil concerning anyone. II, 267, 268. The time for judging has not yet come: when it will come. V, 322.

How difficult it is to judge ourselves. IV, 1921. How uncertain our judgment is, even concerning ourselves. V, 285. What each person is today, scarcely anyone knows—not even the person himself. V, 285. It is unjust for anyone to wish to judge another and not wish to be judged himself. II, 1039.

The judges are called gods. III, 628. The office of judging is foreign to human beings. V, 299, 304. Human society draws a person into exercising the office of judge. VII, 633. What must be considered in a judge. X, 700, 701, 702. This security of faith in a judge is that he does not fear being judged himself. IX, Appendix 820. Judges are puffed up because they judge capital cases. V, 1504. Let the judge pronounce judgment first upon himself, then upon others. V, 110. Let judges judge human beings with trembling. V, 108, 109. How unjust precipitate judgment is. V, 298. Debtors arrogantly judge from whom punishment should be demanded and to whom it should be granted. VI, 121. Mercy is necessary for judges. II, 656, 658, 659. Because they themselves also need mercy. II, 656. Judge yourself without flattery, and your neighbor with love. V, 322. When you judge, love the person and hate the vice. V, 323. How a judge ought to fulfill the office of a compassionate father. II, 509. The gentlest men carefully examine a hidden crime for this purpose: to find those whom they may spare. II, 509. I usually hear that it lies within the power of a judge to avenge more mildly than the laws command. II, 536. Judges may bend a sentence toward leniency, even in cases that are not ecclesiastical. II, 512. Let a judge love to frighten, but let him love. V, 111.

The severity of judges is not useless. II, 660, 661. How a judge ought to recognize the true misery of this life and the necessity of investigating the truth by means of torture. VII, 633. Let a judge pursue sins, not the sinner. V, 110. Let him not pursue him to death, lest he destroy the human being; a person should not be killed, so that there may be someone to correct himself. V, 110. Why judges are said to “take action.” V, 138. The custom of appealing from a milder sentence. II, 512. When a judge asks where the defendant is hiding, and someone who knows says that he does not know, he gives false testimony and kills his own soul. VI, 503. To judge in the absence of and without hearing the other party is a sacrilege. II, 165.

To judge personally. III, 1636. In judging, no one assumes another’s person if he does not assume his own. V, 960. In judgment one must favor neither the poor nor the rich. III, 628. It is not permissible to favor the poor against the truth. IV, 285, 286. What can be done for the benefit of a person after judgment has been pronounced. IV, 286. Whoever either spares the guilty or attempts to destroy the innocent will not escape serious danger. IV, 377.

Whether a judge accepts any gift, God alone knows. IV, 195. A person accepts a gift not only when he judges badly for the sake of gold and silver, but also when he judges badly for the sake of praise. IV, 195. The danger faced by a judge who does not seek what belongs to others but nevertheless greedily guards his own. V, 631. A just judgment or true testimony must not be sold, although just advocacy and sound advice may be sold. II, 663. If the office of a judge is purchased with money with the intention of serving justice, it is not to be condemned. V, 110.

A judge ought to regard a provincial case differently from an ecclesiastical case. II, 508. Judgment is twofold: ecclesiastical and forensic. X, 598. Secular judgments were referred to bishops. IV, 1570; VI, 576. The rule of ecclesiastical judgments. V, 1546, 1547. We neither can nor ought to admit the accusations of heretics against a Catholic presbyter. II, 1068. The judgment in which a bishop accused gives an account of his case. II, 954. He is punished while his episcopate is preserved. II, 954. Augustine judges a presbyter. II, 234. Although it had been decreed that the presbyter’s case should be concluded in a council of six bishops. II, 235. What the presbyter denied, Augustine left to God. II, 234. How he tempered judgment with mercy. II, 234. Two of his own men accused one another and denied the charges in turn; by mutual agreement he sent them to the tomb of Blessed Felix, where one or the other would be compelled to confess the crime. II, 269. The use of blows is often accustomed to be employed by bishops in judgments. II, 509. Episcopal judgment is indissoluble. IV, 196. Constantine’s law required that the sentences of bishops should always be preserved inviolate and incorrupt. IV, 196.

One must not contend in court. III, 1260. Christ prohibited having a lawsuit against another concerning secular matters. VI, 269. And it is a fault, as the Apostle teaches. IV, 1045; VI, 269. But a venial one. VI, 269.

A perverse judgment is not judgment. V, 317. To do judgment and justice. V, 317. Not only the person who has lost a good case, but also the person who has been defeated most justly murmurs against the judge. IX, 41. Judges used to be appointed by lot and superstition at the Kalends of January. V, 1020. Solomon’s judgment between two prostitute women is expounded allegorically. V, 92.

How inscrutable God’s judgments are. III, 1771, 1777; V, 177; X, 980. To whom and in what way they are called inscrutable. IV, 1514. The height of God’s judgments. X, 1126. Deep. V, 905, 907. Abyss. IV, 473, 474. To wish to scrutinize inscrutable things is like wishing to see invisible things and speak ineffable things. V, 182. For us there are consideration, wonder, trembling, and exclamation, because there is no penetration; for God himself there is glory. V, 118, 1294. God judges now and has judged from the beginning of the human race. VII, 659, 687. Nothing here happens without God’s judgment. VII, 660. Certain examples of God’s astonishing judgments. X, 926. And of his inscrutable judgments. X, 1004.

Judgment is twofold: hidden and manifest. IV, 117. Hidden judgment is the punishment by which each person is now either exercised for purification, admonished toward conversion, or blinded toward condemnation. IV, 117. God’s judgment in the varied affections and dispositions of human beings. X, 744, 745. Without God’s judgment no one is slow in mind or lame in body. IV, 1515. God’s judgments in the mystery of grace are not to be investigated by reason. V, 181, 1294. God’s hidden judgments in the predestination of human beings. VI, 275. God’s hidden judgments: why a reprobate is born from one who is predestined, and one who is predestined from a reprobate. X, 846, 847.

How the world is now judged. III, 1771. Judgment is twofold: one of condemnation, the other of discrimination. III, 1113, 1576, 1709, 1719, 1771. The judgment of discrimination takes place in this life. III, 1771. The devout, when they ask God to judge them, ask to be distinguished from the wicked. IV, 191. The Lord judged his people by separating the good from the evil. IV, 1752, 1753. “Judgment” is sometimes understood as discrimination. IV, 191. God now judges some things, not everything. V, 129. Where you speak iniquity against God, there he judges you; he does not postpone judgment, but punishment. IV, 953. For this reason many things are reserved for judgment, while some are judged in the present, so that those whose judgment is delayed may fear and be converted. V, 129. God judges no one because of what he would have done had he lived longer, but only because of what he actually did. X, 482, 483, 977, 981, 1007. The Pelagians themselves saw that it is false that a person is judged according to foreknown merits. X, 979. Those who think that each person is judged according to foreknown merits oppose the Catholic teaching concerning original sin. X, 978. They favor the Pelagians. X, 979. It is absurd to say that anyone is judged according to the merits he would have had if he had lived a long time. X, 978, 1004. They were compelled to say this about infants, even those who wished to remain separate from the error of the Pelagians. X, 1011. God’s judgment upon sinners. V, 126. God exercises judgment in mercy itself and in the forgiveness of sins. IV, 285. When the defendant changes, God the judge changes. V, 152.

God’s judgments are hidden in this life. VII, 660. And nevertheless just. [Col. 0374] V, 1381. God’s judgments are secretly just and justly secret. VII, 687. The faith of the devout is not unaware that what is hidden is just. VII, 661. The equity of God’s judgments is to be believed for the present, until it is seen clearly in the homeland. V, 180. Unless divine judgments are believed, they are not understood. IV, 1393. God’s judgments will be revealed in the homeland. III, 1777. God’s judgments benefit the good and harm the wicked. III, 603. Which judgments of God the Church knows. IV, 1514. Who seem to wish to enter into judgment with God. IV, 1848. Whoever sees a faction formed against himself ought to reserve his case for a better judgment. IV, 375. “Judgment of God” is sometimes applied to evil and sometimes to good. VI, 258. Where it is stated without qualification, a just judgment is understood. IV, 903, 1576, 1577. Usage nevertheless permits both a good and an evil judgment to be spoken of. IV, 903, 1576, 1577. God’s judgments are of three kinds: first, intermediate, and last. VII, 660.

The final judgment. V, 124. Why the last judgment is so called. VII, 659. Why it is called the day of judgment. VII, 659. The day of judgment is asserted to be certainly forthcoming. IV, 944, 945; VI, 305. From where faith in the judgment is confirmed. VI, 342, 346. It is confirmed by the authority of the Old and New Testaments. VII, 661. Certain testimonies of Scripture that seem to concern the judgment pertain to other matters. VII, 663. The future judgment is proved beyond doubt by so many other things foretold and already fulfilled. II, 1028; V, 151, 640, 1453. The Flood as an example of the divine judgment. VI, 334. Faith in the divine judgment ought not to waver because of the prosperity of the wicked. IV, 357. Even if no one had sinned, creation would not have been endowed with blessedness by God without judgment. VII, 659.

The day of the coming judgment is hidden. V, 271. No one knows the final time of the world, the day, or the hour. II, 899, 900, 901, 902, 903. Christ is said not to know it because it was not part of his teaching office that we should know it through him. IV, 355. And because he makes us not know what would not have benefited us to know. IV, 355. God wisely wished that day to remain hidden, so that the heart might always be prepared. IV, 351. Christ did not reveal the day of judgment to the Apostles. II, 906. Some think that it will occur after a fixed number of thousands of years. V, 576. The time of the final judgment cannot be discovered by a definite computation of years from Adam. IV, 90, 1143. Six thousand years have passed. V, 576. Augustine does not dare to count the times concerning the Savior’s coming, which is awaited at the end. II, 899. What the Apostle Peter proclaims concerning the last judgment. VII, 683. Paul did not say after how much time the final judgment would come, but how it would come. II, 906, 907. We can conjecture the final time of the world from the signs. II, 903, 909. Of the signs that Christ foretold would occur, some refer to the destruction of Jerusalem, some to the Lord’s coming through the Church, and some to the final coming at which he will judge the living and the dead. II, 914. The evils that will precede the Lord’s final coming will not be common to the good and the wicked. II, 918, 919. The signs of the judgment’s imminent coming have existed since the time of the Apostles; nevertheless they continue to correspond to the final days and to be signs. II, 913, 914. Nearly all the signs of judgment spoken by the prophets have been fulfilled. V, 576. The end of the age will not come before the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world. II, 900. Yet not in such a way that everyone will believe. II, 923. The final days of our judgment are not far off. V, 128. Even if the day of judgment is far off from the world, the final day of each person’s life is near. V, 271. The final judgment will come quickly. V, 76. The day of judgment is delayed until the number of the Church’s members is complete. V, 228. The more judgment is delayed, the more forcefully it will come. IV, 717. The day of the final judgment cannot therefore be known merely because the days are to be shortened. II, 912. In what sense the day of judgment is rightly understood as the eighth day. IV, 90, 91. For how many days the final judgment will extend is uncertain. VII, 659.

What the last judgment will be like. IV, 1236. How it will be carried out. III, 1554. This is difficult to comprehend in the holy Scriptures. X, 326. Judgment will take place immediately at the Lord’s coming. VI, 159. The Father will not appear at the last judgment. III, 1553, 1571. The Father judges and does not judge, according to different judgments. III, 1708. The Father will not judge by manifesting his presence, but Christ will. VII, 707. Christ will judge as the Son of Man. IV, 950. The Son will come in human form to judge. III, 1571, 1580. All who are to be judged will see the judge in the form of a servant; the form of God will be reserved for the good alone. IV, 546, 547, 1096; V, 711, 1071, 1267. The wicked will see the Son of God in the flesh for punishment, not for reward. III, 1831. Christ will come to judge in the same manner in which he came to be judged. III, 1832. The order of events to be carried out in the final judgment. VII, 709. The living and the dead are to be judged. II, 873; VI, 258, 634, 666. From the Apostle, some appear to be destined to be caught up alive to Christ’s judgment; difficulties are raised against this. II, 873; VII, 688, 690. At the judgment the Lord will come like fire to those for whom his coming will be punitive. VII, 692. Where the saints will be during the conflagration. VII, 684. The separation of the good and the wicked at the judgment. VII, 702. From this the Son of Man will be glorified. III, 1804, 1806. There will be a separation not only of the wicked, but also of the good from the good, so that some will stand at the right hand to judge, while others will sit with the Lord to judge. [Col. 0375] IV, 570. Not only the twelve Apostles will judge, nor will only the twelve tribes be judged. VII, 662. All the perfect will judge. IV, 570, 572, 1156. Those who will sit to judge are called heaven; those who will stand to be judged are called earth. IV, 573, 1626. Justice becomes judgment when the righteous receive the power to judge. IV, 1407. At the judgment the books of the Old and New Testaments will be opened together with the book of life. VII, 680. Human beings will be judged in various ways. III, 1783. God judges not only universally, concerning the race of demons and human beings, but also concerning the deeds of individuals. VII, 659.

Judgment will be according to his works. X, 877, 878. A person will receive neither good nor evil except according to what he did through the body, not according to what he would have done had he lived longer. II, 984, 986. How this is also true of infants. II, 985. See Adrumetini, Florus. In judgment, the judge is justice itself, and the witness is an evil conscience. VI, 658. Hence the good conscience trembles in judgment. V, 578. Between the just Judge and your conscience, fear nothing except your own case. IV, 408, 809, 1913. A person will be defended by his own deeds. IV, 1469, 1470. In judgment the Lord will be the witness. VII, 702. God is the Judge; consider what sort of case you are carrying in your heart. IV, 1835. Let us rejoice that our judge is such that he cannot be deceived by the devil. V, 568. At the last judgment God is an incorruptible judge. V, 75, 299, 649. The Lord questions you not in order to learn from you, but to confound you. V, 299. How severe the Judge will be. IV, 1197, 1198. However righteous a person may seem to himself, he is found perverse by the rule and judgment of God. IV, 1849. The time of mercy is not without judgment, nor the time of judgment without mercy. IV, 1587. No one dares boast before God the Judge that he has a chaste heart. X, 309. A purified life is difficult to find when he judges who knows how to judge with complete precision. IV, 481. How much each person will need to be judged mercifully, and who may hope for this. II, 571, 573. If God were judge alone and not merciful, no one would stand before him. IV, 1698, 1700. Woe even to the praiseworthy human life if God examines it after removing mercy. I, 778. There is no hope unless the mercy of the Judge triumphs. II, 741. Whoever awaits judgment without mercy as though secure provokes the most just wrath. II, 741. To whom God will administer judgment without mercy. IV, 1236, 1469. In God’s judgment there are pity and mercy. X, 239. In God there are both mercy when he judges and judgment when he shows mercy. II, 741; IV, 284, 285. Judgment and mercy are not contrary to one another. IV, 284. As generously as God dispenses mercy in the present age, so severely does he threaten judgment in the future. V, 75. When the time of judgment comes, there will be repentance, but fruitless because it will be too late. IV, 608. Some will be reproved in God’s wrath and will not be corrected, while others will be saved through correction. IV, 397. After the resurrection, there will be some in judgment to whom mercy may be shown, so that they are not sent into the eternal fire. VII, 738. In judgment, certain purifying punishments will await certain people. VII, 700. How secretly the Judge’s final sentence is written. V, 297. God’s judgments will appear entirely just on the last day. VII, 660.

Whoever has begun to believe in the day of judgment has begun to fear it. III, 2046. The final judgment strikes fear into the negligent. III, 25. The day of judgment is terrifying to those who do not wish to live well in security but wish to live badly for a long time. IV, 354. The final judgment is something not to be feared but desired. V, 1063. God’s judgment is to be feared by the wicked because of punishment and loved by the good because of the crown. IV, 1283. Whoever fears the Judge who is to come should change and correct his conscience now. IV, 548, 569, 809, 1913. The good await the final day of judgment securely; the wicked await it trembling. V, 299. Whoever despises this life awaits the day of judgment securely. IV, 1916. Whoever lives piously truly desires and awaits Christ’s coming. II, 904, 909. It is fitting for the pious to desire Christ’s coming for judgment. V, 1369. Augustine loves and desires the Lord’s coming. II, 925. Among such lovers, who is more in accord with the Gospel: the one who says that the Lord will come sooner, the one who says that he will come later, or the one who confesses that he does not know which? II, 925.

God threatens that he will come as Judge so that, when he comes, he may not find anyone to punish. V, 150. Do to yourself now what God threatens you with; be your own judge. IV, 583. Each person has himself as judge, so that he may have God as defender. IV, 947. He who will then be Judge is already an advocate. IV, 809, 1913. Whatever is required for judgment to be carried out is found within the person himself. IV, 675. Preparation for the final day. V, 589. Live as though God were coming to judgment today, and you will not fear when he comes. V, 1221. May the father’s chastisements be sweet to us, lest the Judge’s sentence be bitter. IV, 1793. We are warned by Noah’s example to await the final day of judgment. V, 1610. The day of judgment is represented by a furnace. IV, 1362. Why the final judgment is called a drawn bow. IV, 717. “Judgment” used of punishment. III, 1576, 1577; V, 1630. Used of eternal punishment. II, 947; V, 1258. Used of condemnation. V, 1343; VI, 224, 305. There is some distinction between judgment and justice. IV, 1407.

Judith: The Jews are said not to have accepted the book into the canon of Scripture. VII, 583. At what time the events written in the book of Judith took place. VII, 583.

Juga­tinus, the god appointed over mountain ridges. VII, 118. Juga­tinus, the god who joins spouses together. VII, 122, 188.

The yoke laid upon infants is just because they are born with sin. X, 1250. It is unjust if there is no original sin. X, 1278, 1281. See Misery, Original Sin.

To bear Christ’s yoke is nothing other than to live piously in Christ. V, 443. Desire had subjected you badly; let charity subject you beneficially. V, 897. Whoever is subject to Christ’s yoke has all other things subject to him. III, 151. Christ’s yoke is to the Christian what feathers are to a bird. IV, 719. Christ’s yoke appears hard. V, 442. Christ’s yoke is easy. II, 200. How it becomes easy. V, 443. It is gentle for one who loves, but hard for one who does not love. V, 192, 1507.

The household of Juliana, no small church of Christ. II, 849. Juliana says that her household is separated from those who seem to have even minor errors. II, 849. Augustine and Alypius instruct Juliana and her family in good morals. II, 848. They also instruct them against the Pelagian poison in the book addressed to Demetrias and given to her. II, 848. Juliana receives pious admonitions with gratitude. II, 849. At her request the work On the Good of Widowhood was written. VI, 429. Augustine’s congratulatory letter to Juliana. II, 645.

Julian succeeded Constantius and Constans. II, 399. The outstanding natural gifts of Julian the Apostate were deceived by a love of ruling and sacrilegious curiosity. VII, 168. Julian’s army was routed because it trusted the oracles too much. VII, 136, 168. Christian soldiers obeyed the temporal lord, although he was an unbeliever, for the sake of the eternal Lord. IV, 1654. By an issued law Julian forbade Christians to teach letters. I, 753. Teaching and learning. VII, 615. Julian’s times. II, 316. Persecution against the Church. VII, 615. The cheerfulness of a young Christian singing psalms amid tortures deterred Julian from torturing the others. VII, 615. How the Donatists praised Julian. IX, 324, 326, 327, 334. How greatly they flattered him in a pamphlet they issued. II, 327. How shamelessly Rogatianus and Pontius flattered him. II, 400. The praises by which the Donatists exalted him were full of impiety. IX, 47. He received flattering prayers from the Donatists. IV, 374. In view of them he granted the Donatists a rescript. IX, Appendix 808. At the supplication of Rogatianus and Pontius he granted the party of Donatus freedom of perdition. II, 399, 415, and Note. He returned the basilicas of the catholic unity to the Donatists. IX, 47, 316, 334. Julian’s words on behalf of the Donatists. IX, 334. They are explained against the Donatists. IX, 335. Jovinian succeeded Julian. II, 400.

Julian of Marcelliana. IX, 235.

Julian of Telepte. IX, 233.

Julian delivered Alypius’s letters to Paulinus and Therasia. II, 99.

Julian, the Pelagian heretic. X, 1049, 1050. An outstanding young man. II, 365. Memorius, Julian’s father, had made him very dear to Augustine. X, 647. Augustine loved and desired him intensely. II, 369. Julian was an exceedingly self-confident young man. X, 694. Inflated by secular learning. X, 1157. He boasted of the skill of dialectic. X, 705. Julian was married. X, 725. Later he professed continence. X, 727. He was possessed by Pelagian impiety. X, 455. Julian was baptized in the Catholic Church. X, 1143. He abandoned Catholic truth. X, 1052. He withdrew from communion with the Catholics. X, 455, 1260. Once Julian had been defeated, he would have had no leisure to write unless he had obtained these things from human beings. X, 1249.

What was disputed between Julian and Augustine. X, 643. Julian’s reasoning, by which he denies original sin, favors the Manichaeans. X, 668, 669. Julian mocks the opinion that God could have granted a blessed man the ability to sow offspring from his own seed without shameful lust, just as wheat is sown. X, 1445, 1447. Julian does not cite the Scriptures faithfully. X, 452, 1106. His calumnies against Augustine and the Catholics. X, 552, 554, 1055, 1057. Everything that Julian objects against Augustine and the Catholics is turned back against him. X, 1558. Julian must be slain by the Manichaean with his own sword. X, 1313. Julian’s objections against Augustine’s first book On Marriage and Concupiscence. X, 437 and following. Julian boasted that he alone was defending the abandoned truth. X, 699, 835. He wrote four books against the first book On Marriage and Concupiscence. I, 651; II, 949; X, 637, 638, 641. After Augustine had responded to excerpts from these books, he subsequently answered the whole work. II, 949. In four books. I, 654. Julian does not cease to scatter the poisons of faith everywhere. II, 949. Augustine’s second book On Marriage was written against him. I, 651. Julian published eight books after those four to which Augustine had already responded. II, 1001; X, 1063. Alypius sent them from Rome to Augustine, pressing him strongly not to delay responding to them. II, 1001; X, 1063. Julian’s work addressed to Saint Turbantius. X, 1353.

Julian’s complaint against the judges who condemned Pelagius’s heresy. X, 701, 702. He appeals to the bishops of the East. X, 648, 649. He demands learned judges. X, 1141. He asks for an examination already conducted before the Apostolic See and at the Palestinian judgment. X, 1183. He complains that an episcopal examination and judgment are being denied him. X, 700. He awards himself the palm against God’s bishops. X, 1146. Julian’s little document. X, 437, 440. Julian’s letter sent to Thessalonica. X, 571. Sent to Rome. X, 437, 1056. Julian’s two letters to Zosimus. X, 1057.

Julius, the bishop rejected by the council said to have been held at Sardica. II, 176.

Julius the bishop brought the letters of the Council of Carthage to Innocent. II, 780. Those of the Council of Milevis. II, 784. And likewise those of Aurelius and others. II, 786.

Julius Obsequens, author of a book On Prodigies. VII, 73.

Julius Proculus. VII, 91.

The month of July, so called in honor of the Emperor Julius. III, 51; VIII, 346.

The word *jumenta* (“beasts of burden”) is derived from *juvare* (“to help”). III, 764. In the Church, those who walk simply but are useful and full of faith are called beasts of burden. IV, 1427. Christ’s beast of burden is a gentle man who does not wish to be praised but is content with carrying the one whom he bears. IV, 310. We should not be ashamed to be God’s beast of burden. V, 1007.

“Junior”: the new man, the child of grace, the singer of the new song—not Cain but Abel, and so forth. IV, 1512. “Junior” and “senior” sometimes have the same meaning as “younger” and “older,” although neither is an old man. IV, 1564.

Junius Brutus killed his sons and his brother’s wife. VII, 94. The death of Junius Brutus. VII, 94. See Brutus.

The consulship of Junius Quartus. II, 784, 787.

Junius, a bishop from Naples. IX, 192, 239.

Junius, a notary. IX, 513.

The month of June, named after Juno. VIII, 346.

Juno. I, 673; V, 1250. She is said to be the air. V, 1024. Juno is said to occupy the air alone. III, 1063. They claim that Juno is the earth. VII, 207. Why Juno is called both the sister and the wife of Jupiter. VII, 119. And also his mother. VII, 120. Soranus said that Juno was nothing other than Jupiter himself. VII, 203. The spirits of Juno and Hercules divided against one another. V, 447; VI, 712. The contest of Juno, Minerva, and Venus over beauty for the sake of the golden apple—a story regarded as false even by the pagans themselves. VII, 567. Juno, the goddess of childbirth. IV, 200. Juno is *iterduca* (“she who leads the way”) for children. VII, 195. Juno’s asylum at Troy liberated no one from the Greeks. VII, 17. The spirit of Juno. V, 447. Juno is called Astarte. III, 797.

Jupiter. V, 1249. He is understood to be the ether. VII, 119. The later Platonists wish Jupiter to be the soul of this world. III, 1058. Some also approve this view. VII, 122. Others consider him to be the world. VII, 202. If Jupiter is a god, he must be called not the soul of the world but the world itself. VII, 202. How, according to Varro, all things are understood to arise from Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. VII, 218. All things are full of Jupiter. VII, 120. Jupiter’s power in the efficient causes of things. VII, 201. Jupiter’s weakness in coming to the aid of the people. VII, 97. Jupiter is said to be male and female. VII, 202. He is called the begetter and begetress of the gods. VII, 202. King of all gods and goddesses. VII, 119. If this king is the star of Jupiter, it ought either to be brighter than the others or higher than Saturn. VII, 206. Jupiter himself is Saturn. VII, 205. He himself is Mercury. VII, 205. He himself is Genius. VII, 205. He himself is all the gods. VII, 205. He is worshiped under the names of all the gods collectively. VII, 121. Jupiter is worshiped under another name by those who worship one God alone without an image. VII, 119. The various surnames assigned to Jupiter refer to one and the same being. VII, 203. Among his other surnames, Jupiter is called Money. VII, 203, 204. What a wise person should think about the surname “Money” attributed to Jupiter. VII, 205. Jupiter would more readily be called Wisdom than Money if the theology of the nations contributed anything to eternal life. VII, 205. As a young man Jupiter indulged in many sexual outrages. VII, 97. Jupiter, adulterer of wives and ravisher of Ganymede. VII, 132. He was changed into a bull and a swan so that he might sleep with some woman. VII, 134. Why poets invented Jupiter as both thunderer and adulterer. I, 672. To call Jupiter both the ruler of the world and one who flows away in sexual outrages is contradictory. VII, 202. A painted panel of Jupiter inflamed a young man’s lust. II, 315. In Arcadia Jupiter was called Lycaeus. VII, 574. Jupiter is called Stator. VII, 89. Jupiter pitched camp on Mount Olympus when he was waging war against his father. II, 83. Virgil imposed upon Jupiter the role of speaking falsely. V, 623. Virgil introduces Jupiter speaking falsehoods while he himself speaks more truthfully. V, 623. Homer called Jupiter a demon. VII, 256. Apollonius was much better than Jupiter. II, 533. At first Jupiter had no temple at Rome. VII, 87. Varro thought Jupiter was the God of the Jews. III, 1055. The Romans customarily worship nothing higher than Jupiter. III, 1055. The oath by the stone of Jupiter was the most sacred oath among the Romans. V, 77. Note (c).

What God’s oath is. V, 511. God’s oath by which he bears witness to himself. IV, 1459, 1460. God’s oath is confirmation of a promise. IV, 1122, 1459. The Prophet calls an oath what he establishes by a solemn pledge. IV, 1567. An oath means one thing in the mouth of the person swearing and another in the prophet’s signification. IV, 99. Why God forbade swearing. VII, 1660. Why it is said that one must above all abstain from swearing. V, 977. Although God and the Apostle made use of an oath, we must nevertheless avoid it. V, 972, 974, 1406. Swearing must be avoided, and it is safer not to swear. II, 693. Because the Apostle swore in his letters, swearing ought not therefore to become a game for us. II, 693. What kinds of oath are lawful. III, 1255, 2110. Under what condition an oath should be used. V, 977. The person who does not know how to lie swears securely. V, 1407. One who swears does not swear for himself but for his neighbor. V, 979.

Faithfulness to an oath must be maintained. II, 481. Even when the oath was extorted. II, 482. The mind ought to be so firmly fixed on keeping God’s commands that what it resolves concerning their observance should count as an oath. IV, 1567. It is rightly said that the oath must be fulfilled not according to the words of the person swearing but according to the expectation of the person to whom the oath is sworn—an expectation known to the one who swears. II, 476, 482. The Hebrews kept their oath to the Gibeonites even though the latter had lied. III, 781. The scrupulous observance of the oath by a certain Regulus. II, 476. Augustine admits that the question concerning an oath seemed difficult to him and that he always avoided it. V, 974. Why Augustine avoided it. V, 979.

What it means to swear. V, 975. To swear is to promise firmly. IV, 1717. It is to call God to witness. IV, 1459, 1460. God alone swears securely because he cannot be deceived. IV, 1122. Let God swear, whom nothing deceives and from whom nothing is hidden. V, 973. What God has promised by swearing will undoubtedly come to pass. IV, 1725. How greatly we ought to fear God when he threatens and swears. IV, 1226.

How swearing is forbidden altogether. VI, 507, 512. A person is rightly forbidden to swear lest he slip into perjury. IV, 1122, 1459. The farther one is from swearing, the farther one will be from perjury. IV, 1459. Because perjury is a grave sin, Scripture has given you a shortcut: do not swear. V, 973. Whoever swears is close to the precipice of perjury. V, 974. How much the danger of perjury must be feared. V, 973. To swear truthfully is lawful; not to swear is safer. V, 974. Even though one does not sin by swearing to the truth, the hearts of human beings, because of their frailty, are more safely preserved from perjury by not swearing. VIII, 362, 364. Even one who swears to the truth approaches a false oath. V, 1407. It is not a sin to swear truthfully, but to swear falsely is a very grave sin. II, 693. A great sin. V, 1406, 1407, 1408. A false oath is deadly, a true oath dangerous, and no oath secure. V, 974. To swear falsely by idols is perjury. V, 978. One must not only refrain from swearing, but no one should be compelled to swear. II, 184. To demand an oath from another in order to place faith in him—I would not dare say that this is not a sin; nevertheless, it is a human temptation. V, 978. Scripture says that we should not swear, but it does not say that we should not accept an oath from another. II, 184. Whether the person who makes a pagan swear by false gods for him commits a sin. II, 184. One who swears by false gods and does not keep faith sins twice. II, 184. One who swears after being challenged by another does not sin in the same way as that other person. V, 1409. Whoever compels someone whom he believes will swear falsely is worse than a murderer. V, 978, 1409. It is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by a false god than to swear deceitfully by the true God. II, 184. Whether someone who knows that another is swearing falsely is obliged, and under what circumstances, to expose him. III, 673. A servant of God must not, even when death threatens, swear that he will do something illicit or wicked. II, 475. A rash oath must not be fulfilled if doing so would involve murder. V, 1408. David swore that he would kill Nabal, but by not killing him he sinned less. V, 1408. Someone who swears that he will not withdraw from a bishop is not guilty of perjury if he withdraws with the bishop’s permission. II, 230, 232. We may make use of the peace that has been established between other people who have sworn oaths. II, 184, 185. It is permissible to rely upon the faithfulness of someone who, in order to keep it, swore by demons. II, 184.

The habit of swearing is very bad. V, 1409. How the habit of swearing is uprooted. V, 979. Augustine was sometimes subject to the habit of swearing. V, 977, 1407. Augustine swears when necessity compels him. II, 480. And he does so following the Apostle’s example. II, 481. How Augustine swears when compelled by great necessity. V, 977. Tutuslymenus was scourged by divine correction because of the sin of swearing [reading uncertain]. V, 1409.

Various forms of swearing. V, 975. One swears who says, “God is my witness.” V, 102, 975. The practice of swearing by the Gospel. II, 1066. A common oath: “By my eyes.” V, 55. Swearing by one’s eyes was formerly customary. III, 1659. Socrates used to swear by the dog, by the stone, and by whatever objects came before him; why. III, 123. The Donatists swore by Donatus’s gray hairs. IV, 134. “Swear, forswear yourself, but do not reveal the secret”: a saying of the Priscillianists. VIII, 44. To swear by an imprecation is the gravest kind of oath. IV, 99. An oath is sometimes called an imprecation. III, 568. A curse. III, 565.

[Col. 0379] Right is what is just. IV, 1894. Right and wrong are opposites. IV, 1894. There is no right where true justice is absent. VII, 648. Unjust human enactments ought neither to be called nor considered laws. VII, 648. It is falsely said that right is whatever is useful to the one who has greater power. VII, 648. Divine right. VI, 395. Heavenly right. V, 357. The jurist of heaven. V, 654. The right of the forum and the right of the pole. V, 1572, 1710. Divine right and human right in the possession of earthly things. II, 345. Making wills according to Roman law. II, 331.

Civil laws do not make people use good things well; they make those who use them badly less troublesome. II, 665. A person does not possess a right over what he does not handle justly. V, 327. What natural right and customary right are. VI, 20, 21. How many kinds of customary right there are. VI, 21.

Ecclesiastical law. IV, 196. Formerly there were no legal formulas, but the discretion of the will was regarded as the norm of law. V, 549.

Justina, mother of the younger Valentinian, was seduced by the Arians and persecuted Ambrose. I, 770.

The history of Justin. VII, 116.

The origin of the term “justifications.” III, 631. Justifications are not words but acts of justice. IV, 1514, 1520. They are called God’s justifications, although they are performed by us, because they cannot be performed unless he grants them. IV, 1514. How God’s justifications are taught. IV, 1516. How they are to be learned. IV, 1514. By what stages one reaches them. IV, 1522. Among the Lord’s justifications, none is more difficult and wonderful than that each person should love his enemies. IV, 1524. What it means to covet or desire God’s justifications. IV, 1521, 1522.

What it means to be justified. X, 228. The ungodly person is justified when he becomes pious from being ungodly and moves from the possession of the devil into the temple of God. IV, 100. The justification of the sinner. III, 1491. To justify, that is, to make just, is beyond human power. V, 1324. There is no one who is just and justifies except God. II, 809. No one restores except the one who creates; no one repairs except the one who made. V, 952. He made not only human beings but also the just—if indeed we are just—and we did not make ourselves. IV, 159, 193. Nothing is more magnificent than the justification of the ungodly. IV, 1464. Whether creating the just is greater than justifying the ungodly. III, 1823. In what sense the Pelagians acknowledge God as the author of justification. X, 208. Christ is just and justifying; we, however, are justified by his grace. II, 810. We are justified in Christ alone. X, 115. No one justifies except Christ. X, 119. How all are justified through Christ. X, 463. Faith in Christ is necessary for justification. V, 784. How our justification in the blood of the Son of God is explained. VIII, 1025. Through Christ’s flesh, justification by grace also takes place in our flesh. X, 679.
