We are justified from sins by the same grace by which Christ received the ability not to sin. VI, 250. Christ made our offenses his offenses so that he might make his righteousness our righteousness. IV, 172. In justification, a comparison from opposites is rightly made. X, 1236. To redeem humanity, a contrary path was undertaken to the one by which it had been led into captivity. X, 407. One who has not heard the name of Christ could not be justified. X, 251.

Human justification is gratuitous. IV, 158, 704, 707; X, 210. What it means to be justified freely. X, 228. God saved us not according to the works of righteousness that we performed, but according to his mercy, and so forth. II, 569, 570. Calling precedes our justification; it is not a matter of merits but of God’s grace. IV, 89. Our justification takes place through the call of mercy and the fear of judgment. IV, 1963. God most justly judges that the mercy of justification is not to be granted to certain people. VI, 121. The very fact that God justifies human beings he does by a judgment too hidden for us to grasp. II, 569. Our justification is from grace, but not without our will. V, 922. God does not build his temple from you as though from stones that have no movement of their own. V, 857. The one who made you without you does not justify you without you. V, 923.

How justification occurs through grace. X, 209. Justification is carried out in this life in three ways. X, 689. Faith obtains justification. II, 818, 819; V, 864. Justification is obtained from faith. X, 232. A person is justified not by the law of works but by the law of faith. X, 215. Justification by faith without works. V, 31. How this is to be understood. VI, 88. A person begins to be justified by faith, so that good works may show not what he has merited as antecedents, but what he has received as consequents. IV, 1464. God justifies the ungodly only if he believes and confesses. IV, 332. Faith preserves justification. II, 878. Repentance precedes justification. IV, 1786.

Our justification and perfection. V, 454. Whether we are already justified. V, 864. No one is justified as long as he lives this life. V, 930. Our justification here is incomplete. V, 867. It will be completed when our hope is completed. V, 790. Justification is perfect in the martyrs. V, 867. What the sinner destined to be justified has received is a pledge of what he will receive when glorified. IV, 1465. Justification is entirely grace; eternal life is both reward and grace. X, 936. The Lord’s righteousness justifies the ungodly; human righteousness does not make a person pious but proud. [Col. 0380] IV, 1544. No one is justified in the sight of God—how? X, 312. How, just as all are brought to condemnation, so all are brought to justification. X, 827.

What justice is and where it comes from. VI, 20. Justice is the virtue by which each person receives what belongs to him. I, 1235; IV, 1065; VII, 649; X, 1063, 1064. Whatever God wills is justice itself. V, 700. Another definition of justice. I, 1189, 1322. In what justice consists. III, 1337. Justice is a great virtue of the soul and especially worthy of praise. IV, 1577. Justice pertains to every part of the soul. III, 204. The function of justice. VII, 629. The unchangeable rules of justice, known even to the ungodly. VIII, 1052. Does one not sin who fails to see the unchangeable rules of justice? VIII, 1047. The reasoning of justice considers not only what was done but also why it was done. VIII, 426.

Justice appears to be returning evil for evil, but this is not God’s justice. IV, 87. When God punishes sinners, he does not inflict his own evil upon them but abandons them to their evils. IV, 87. The order of God’s punishing justice. VII, 641. God’s justice is not cruel. VII, 376. God is not so merciful that he is unjust. IV, 1330. Nor is he so just that he is not merciful. IV, 446. If justice is pronounced without mercy, it will find something to condemn in everyone. IV, 1922. All deserve condemnation; if all were liberated from it, what is due to sin by justice would remain hidden, while if no one were liberated, what grace bestows would remain hidden. II, 875. The very justice by which good things are repaid to us is not without mercy. IV, 1517. God is a just Judge even when forgiving sins. III, 2093. Justice and mercy are repeatedly commended in Scripture. III, 565, 591. The first justice of a human being is to punish yourself as evil and to let God make you good. IV, 1080. God’s supreme justice makes good use even of the wicked. IV, 1001. Whatever evils unjust masters inflict upon the just is not punishment for a crime but a testing of virtue. VII, 114. Certain traces of heavenly justice must be preserved in human contracts. VI, 121. Justice in earthly affairs becomes a step toward heavenly justice. VI, 37. Justice is firm and inflexible, an iron rod. IX, 405. What true justice is. VII, 649, 656, 730. The origin, age, genus, and species of justice. X, 1063, 1064.

God’s justice and human justice. II, 1607. The virtue and justice of God are all the more necessary because he wills them in such a way that he cannot will otherwise. X, 1498. The constancy of divine justice. III, 2094. The higher divine justice is, the farther it is from human justice. X, 1256, 1257. There is a certain enduring justice that even the unjust perceive: if you approach it, you are just; if you withdraw from it, you are unjust; it neither increases nor diminishes. IV, 744. In the love of the just we are inflamed by the love of the unchangeable form itself. VIII, 959. In many just people there is one justice of God, shared by all, as though one face were looking into many mirrors. IV, 137. The justice by which the soul lives is to be understood as living in itself. II, 461. And without doubt this is God. II, 461. God is the light of justice. V, 36. Some have mistakenly thought that there is no justice existing in itself. III, 74. The discipline of human justice is to love in oneself nothing except what belongs to God and to hate what is one’s own. III, 2093. All justice is reduced to the one word “innocence.” IV, 1286. Human justice differs from the justice by which God is just. X, 895. God’s justice is called that which God does. X, 211. By it he makes us just from being ungodly. V, 753. We are God’s justice when we live justly. II, 569. It is not the justice by which God is just, but the justice by which human beings are just—those whom his grace justifies. II, 570. God’s justice also becomes our justice when, by cleaving to him, we live justly. II, 461. God’s justice is so called because it comes to a human being from God. III, 618; X, 895. Why it is called ours. X, 209. The justice of God, which… X, 247. Justice from God comes not through the Law but through grace. X, 896. The justice of the Law, justice in the Law, and human justice—what each is. X, 603. God’s justice, or justice from God, and justice from the Law—what they are and what each means. X, 367, 368, 895, 1209.

Human justice, in or from the Law, and God’s justice—that which comes to a human being from God—in the spirit of grace. X, 603. The justice that comes from the Law is called ours because the Law commands through the letter but does not help through the spirit. II, 818. Justice comes from the Law when one obeys the Law through fear. V, 919. God’s justice is “without the Law,” although it is manifested not without the Law. X, 209. God’s justice was manifested through the Law and the Prophets. X, 209. The justice that is in or from the Law does not fulfill the Law’s justice; rather, the justice in the spirit of grace does. X, 603. Justice is not from the Law. X, 616. The promise is destroyed if justice comes from the Law. X, 1210. Justice comes neither through the Law nor through nature. X, 249. If justice comes through nature and the will, Christ died for nothing. X, 746, 896. Those who assert justice from the Law are enemies of the cross of Christ. X, 605. Justice from the Law removes a person from Christ—why? V, 918. To the Apostle it appears a loss. V, 926. Paul abhors his own righteousness so that he may have righteousness from God. V, 921. Why Paul despised the justice that comes from the Law. X, 602, 603. God’s justice, unknown to the Jews and Pelagians. V, 753. The justice of the Pharisees is to say and not to do: “Let yours abound,” so that you both speak good things and live well. V, 1170. There is a kind of justice without complaint in the eyes of human beings, but not in the eyes of God. V, 929, 930. If justice comes from imitating the just, Christ died for nothing. X, 1202. Justice was brought to us through Christ’s incarnation. V, 998. The Pelagians’ calumny concerning the justice of the Prophets and Apostles. X, 597. How Christ’s justice is ours. V, 790. Those who are said to wish to establish their own justice. X, 895. Our justice comes neither through the Law nor through the possibility of nature, but from faith in God through Jesus Christ. II, 769; X, 232.

Justice from faith. X, 1209. Justice from faith is that by which we believe that justice is given to us, not produced by us within ourselves through our own powers. II, 818. Justice from faith is the “pistic ointment” (*unguentum pisticum*). III, 1760. The justice of the just is human in such a way that it is God’s—that is, given by him. IV, 233, 877. Our justice comes from nowhere except God. V, 872, 915, 923, 930, 1515. God possesses the storehouse and fountain of justice. X, 154. A person does not possess justice from himself. X, 1102. It is not born with him. V, 922. True human justice is not that which comes from free choice but that which comes from God. X, 1542. God’s justice is not without grace. X, 1249. There is no justice in human beings except by the benefit of grace. III, 755. It comes from God’s gift. X, 231, 1064. Living well is a divine gift. X, 204. To say that justice can be perfected without the help of inward grace is a crime of impiety. X, 245.

Charity, not fear, produces God’s justice. X, 236. Only divine grace enables true justice to be loved and to give delight. VII, 380. No part of justice can be fulfilled unless God grants it. V, 877. Whoever denies that one can attain any progress in true and pious grace except with the help of the Savior’s grace is not a Christian. X, 282. There is no true justice without faith in Christ’s grace. X, 605, 606. There is no justice apart from Christ, although there may be some sin apart from Adam. X, 120. Justice is the life of the soul. II, 461. What is required in order to perform justice. X, 242. Human nature alone is insufficient to work and perfect justice and fulfill God’s commands. II, 760, 768. A just life is present when we will it, because to will it fully is itself justice. II, 485, 595. But this very full willing will not exist in a human being unless the grace of the Spirit heals and helps him so that he can will it. II, 595. No one possesses justice badly, and whoever does not love it does not possess it. II, 665. A person is not good through fear of punishment but through love of justice. II, 660. Bodily punishment, although it does not proceed from the will, nevertheless recalls a person from sinful action; justice, however, must be loved in such a way that even bodily punishments should not restrain us from its works. II, 594. Force may be applied to compel someone toward justice, since Paul is read to have been driven to the Church by force, and Sarah beneficially subdued Hagar’s pride. II, 323. Children thirst for justice, not slaves. X, 236. Justice must be served generously. VI, 61. Service to justice is true freedom. VI, 247. Justice deserves more service than people customarily offer to sin. II, 594. The enemy of justice is the person who does not sin through fear of punishment; he will be its friend if he does not sin through love of it. II, 594. Those who are restrained from sinning by fear of punishment do not yet love justice. IV, 1958. A person is not a friend of what is right if, were it possible, he would prefer that what is right not be commanded. IV, 823. Love makes justice easy. IV, 239, 823. The love of justice is chaste. V, 965. A person loves justice if he would prefer that theft did not exist even if there were no hell. IV, 282. How unworthy it is that pleasure should lead to sin while fear compels one toward justice. V, 870. The justice of the martyrs is perfect. V, 867. There are certain stages of progress in the love of justice. V, 868.

Justice is to be pursued with delight and love. V, 870. Whoever knows justice perfectly and loves it perfectly is already just. VIII, 968. Justice from the Law through fear does not produce sweetness of heart, but justice from faith does. VII, 739. The fruits of justice are sweeter than those of iniquity. VI, 330. Justice affords greater delight than riches. V, 1470. It is to be preferred to all other delights. V, 869. Among all things that delight, let justice delight us most. V, 868. It is to be preferred to all good things. V, 1470. How it happens that justice now delights more or less, and now does not delight at all. X, 168. A good work delights all the more, the more God, the supreme Good, is loved. X, 168. Justice should delight in such a way that it conquers even lawful pleasures. V, 869. Love and delight in justice are signs of grace. X, 918. Justice must not be loved so much in peaceful times that it is abandoned in times of turmoil. IV, 1522. Justice is laborious except for those who love it. X, 1200. The burden of justice is not a weight for the burdened, but wings for those who will fly. V, 898. Why obedience to justice has now become burdensome: the cause is pride. X, 170.

Justice is the beauty of the soul. VIII, 954. Justice has its own beauty. IV, 780; V, 87. It is seen by the eye of the heart. IV, 780. It pleases the eyes of the heart. IV, 282. It is loved even amid bodily ugliness. IV, 780. A bent and misshapen old man is handsome and lovable when accompanied by justice. IV, 282. For the lover of justice it is enough to please the eyes of Wisdom; he cares nothing for the others. IV, 282, 283.

The justice of the first state in paradise, and where the justice after the fall resides. X, 173. One kind of justice now belongs to human beings for receiving everlasting salvation; another belonged to the human being in paradise, so that he would not lose that same salvation. VI, 99. The beginning of our justice is confession of sins. III, 2006. Christ especially commended justice through humility. V, 1323. To recover justice lost through sin, one must strive through labors and hardships. X, 183. The justice of this life is comprehended in three things: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. IV, 482; X, 299. God takes pleasure in our justice, not in torments. V, 1293. Works of justice are of no benefit without baptism. X, 1265. What limit there is to human justice. IV, 322. Justice must consist not in words of the lips alone but also in deeds. IV, 674. He truly speaks justice who does not make one thing resound upon his lips while concealing another in his heart. IV, 675. Why justice is involved in Christ’s going to the Father. V, 789. The justice concerning which the world is convicted. V, 788.

How “to do justice” and “to perfect justice” differ. X, 283. Four questions concerning the perfection of justice. X, 155. The perfection of justice is possible in this life. X, 204. Even though it is not found here. X, 242, 245. The justice of this life is imperfect. VII, 657; X, 603, 604. Why. X, 243. Perfect human justice is imperfect. X, 162. When you have contemplated the standard of justice in the Scriptures, no matter how far you have advanced, you will find yourself a sinner. IV, 1827. In this life human beings are partly still children of the world and partly children of God. X, 157, 158. What sort of justice can be posited as existing in this life without sin. X, 244. Justice is compatible with conflict against vices. X, 690. No one in this life is so clean that he does not need to be cleansed more and more. III, 1840. However much justice there may be in us, it is dew beside the fountain of God’s justice. IV, 1638. Here we have something of justice, and something we do not have. V, 864. Let us be grateful for what we have, so that what we do not have may be added and what we have may not be lost. V, 864. Testimonies of Cyprian concerning the perfection and imperfection of our justice in this life. X, 629. Of Ambrose. X, 634. All those who in this life are proclaimed in the testimonies of Scripture with praise of justice were not without some sin. X, 164. The perfection of justice and full security were not even found in Paul. V, 834; X, 601, 604. Justice without any sin will exist only in the age to come. X, 1234.

The justice of this life. X, 1514. What kind it is. V, 91. And where it resides. VII, 657, 658. What the paths of justice are. V, 1648. In what sense a person’s justice is said to be perfect here. X, 602. From where the perfection of justice comes. X, 206. Justice is perfect when we love the greater things more and the lesser things less. III, 164. The perfection of justice requires nothing more than a perfect will. II, 485. What part of justice can be fulfilled without some continence? V, 877. Your faith is your justice. IV, 279. Degrees of charity produce degrees of justice. X, 290. A person is called perfect in justice who has advanced greatly in it. X, 165. In the justice that is to be perfected, the person who has advanced greatly in this life is the one who, by advancing, has recognized how far he is from the perfection of justice. X, 243. For the sake of justice, not only pleasure must be despised, but pain also endured. V, 871. True martyrs are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice. II, 796. The justice of the martyrs is perfect. V, 871, 1295. Perfect justice, or a life without sin, although it pertains to the human being, is also a divine gift. X, 201, 202. Just as death is paid back as the wages deserved for sin, so eternal life is paid as the wages deserved for justice. II, 881. How little the justice of this life is to be valued in comparison with the justice of the future. V, 930. It is far inferior to that by which we shall be made equal to the angels. VIII, 889. Our justice is through faith, not through sight. III, 2010. When justice will be perfected. III, 2006. Justice cannot be as great in this life as in the future life. X, 601. The perfection of justice belongs only to the other life. X, 299, 300.

The justice of the other life is most perfect. X, 606. Where the justice of the other life resides. VII, 658. Justice is perfect where peace is perfect. IV, 1930. True justice is peace. IV, 904. Justice and peace kiss one another. IV, 1078. Justice will then be true and perfect, when we are able not only to do nothing evil but not even to think anything evil. IV, 1639. Justice is food for souls. III, 1494. Here we hunger and thirst for the justice of God, so that afterward we may be filled with it. VII, 740. God is justice; the justice for which we certainly hunger and thirst is our justice in this pilgrimage, while the justice with which we shall afterward be filled is our full justice in eternity. II, 461. Hunger for justice prepares us for complete satisfaction. VI, 707. Justice is hungered and thirsted for through the gift of fortitude. III, 39. Satisfaction with justice in eternal life. III, 1609. We shall not be satisfied with justice until this life has ended. IV, 751. Justice is perfect when God is seen. V, 931. Here the fullness of justice is hoped for in the commandment; there it will be received as the reward. X, 622. Now it must be done as a commandment; after death it will be received as a reward. X, 631, 632. The perfect justice of the future life will not be a commandment but the reward of the commandments observed here. X, 600. The perfect justice of this life produces merit; the most perfect justice of the future life becomes the reward. X, 606. Justice belongs to this life; power to the other. VIII, 1026, 1028.

Perfect justice exists only in the angels—and scarcely even in the angels, if they are compared with God. III, 2006. The perfection of justice and full security are found in the angels. X, 601. Whether justice will cease in the future life. VIII, 1046.

The law of justice is inscribed in everyone’s heart. IV, 673. Justice is bread. IV, 562. It is signified by bread and wine. IV, 1370. The life of the just is signified by the bodily paradise in which Adam was placed. III, 478. See Human Being; Saint. The perfection of justice is signified by the number forty. V, 694. Noah, Daniel, and Job as examples of eminent justice. IX, 343. The sacrifice of justice in the temple of the mind. I, 1195. The justice of God. See God.

What the justice of the unjust is. IV, 1433. We are called “justice,” and in what sense we are so called. V, 916. How we are justice and circumcision. V, 915.

Justice and judgment differ somewhat. IV, 1407. To do judgment and justice means to live rightly. VII, 531. How justice is changed into judgment. IV, 1406.

Who is a just person. VIII, 451. What a just mind is. VIII, 955. No one is just except the one who serves God. V, 649. The just person is under the yoke of justice. VIII, 126. What it means to live justly in this life. VIII, 419. What else is living justly than hearing the precepts of the law and doing them? V, 1270. This is the whole life of the just: to set the testament of God above sacrifices. VII, 699. The life of the just must not withdraw from heaven. IV, 557. To live justly is itself our way. III, 1658. Whoever is just is immediately good. IV, 1577. A person may be called just who has drawn very near to the perfection of justice. X, 304. Those are not just who do what they do out of fear. V, 32. They are deceptively called just who think they do what they do not do with the spiritual charity that comes from God. X, 603. In what sense a just person is said to be like God. III, 2010.

Before the election of grace there were no just people. VI, 621. What distinguishes the just from the unjust. X, 597. A person is made just by the one who can never be unjust. IV, 1446. A person becomes just in the same way that air becomes luminous. III, 383. A person must not turn to the Lord in such a way that, once made just by him, he then departs from him. III, 382. The just person believes that he cannot preserve justice without God. V, 605. To live justly is God’s work, although it is carried out through us. X, 242. God knows the ways of the just and himself brings about their works. X, 877. Why God is said to work the works of the just. VI, 331. God works upon a human being so that he may be just, provided that the human being does not depart from him through pride. III, 380. Although the just are justified freely, they nevertheless have their own merits. I, 1346. There is in the human being a certain just order of nature. VII, 629. No one can be just as long as he is separated from the unity of the body of Christ. II, 811, 815.

The works of the just are Christ’s works. III, 1823. People who are reborn in Christ become just by the same grace by which Christ, the just human being, was born. X, 1139. There never was and never will be a just person without faith in Christ. VI, 621. The ancient just were saved only through faith in Christ. II, 858, 859; VI, 621; X, 450. They were liberated only by the grace of Christ. X, 315, 403. The same grace and faith in the Mediator liberated the ancient just. X, 1127. The faith of the ancient just and our faith are the same. X, 399, 500. Pelagius and Caelestius deny that the ancient just lived by faith in the Incarnation. X, 1223. And that they were saved through Christ. X, 400. The ancient just were Christians in reality, even if not in name. X, 595. All the just, including those who lived before Christ’s coming, belonged to the members of Christ. IV, 385, 731. The ancient just did not belong to the letter of the Law but to the grace of Christ who was to come. X, 116. The Pelagian view concerning the salvation of the ancients. X, 569. The ancient just belong to the New Testament. X, 596. The ancient just were not of perfect virtue, but were just because of their faith. X, 599. See Saints; Testament. Where the ancient just were dwelling before Christ’s coming, and whether his Passion transferred them to something better—this must be investigated. VIII, 513.

No one is just except the humble and devout. IV, 585. Unbelievers do not enter the just way; the proud perish from it. V, 107. The just person focuses more on his faults than on his virtues. VII, 167. The just have reason to humble themselves because of the danger of falling. VI, 419. A humble sinner is better than a proud just person. V, 930. Let no one please himself or compare himself with those who live badly. V, 932. Or insult others. V, 933. Many just people are inferior in merit to converted sinners. VIII, 443, 444.

The just person who stands usually falls. V, 669. Those who are about to fall are mingled with the just, so that fear may increase through their fall. VI, 419. A just person can be led astray, but not to eternal damnation. VII, 669. No one is just in all things. X, 161. Some sins are found here even among the just. VII, 21. The just, who live by faith, are not without sin. X, 244. Nevertheless, there are those who live without blame. VI, 262. All the just in this life are good in one respect and bad in another. V, 559. The life of some just people is neither good nor bad. VII, 750. The ancient just were not without sin. X, 622. Even in the fruitful branches the farmer who is in heaven finds something to cleanse. IX, 746. The just according to the divine standard, and the just according to the human standard. VI, 718, 720, 721. Those who presume upon their own justice are sometimes called just in Scripture. IV, 696. Here there is no just person who does not fail through certain human impulses directed toward himself and thus sin. VI, 262. However much justice the just may possess, there is always reason not for boasting but for repentance. V, 1538. The just rightly pray for the forgiveness of their sins. II, 842; VII, 657. The forgiveness of sins is necessary for everyone without exception. VI, 262.

Why the just suffer many things in this world. IV, 1637. God is not therefore unjust or powerless, nor does he therefore fail to care for human affairs, because he allows the just to be afflicted. VI, 98. It is beneficial for the just to be afflicted in this life. VI, 99. The labor of the just is the Father’s scourge. IV, 1204. God always delivers the just from tribulations—not bodily, indeed, but spiritually. IV, 319, 320. The humbled just are not wretched except in the eyes of the wicked. IV, 255. The humbled just have not fallen, because God, to whom they cling, is their height. IV, 255. In public temporal misfortunes among the pagans, the just suffer doubly: from the wicked and with the wicked. II, 423. Nothing harms the just. IV, 366. Whoever harms the just truly harms himself, not the just person. I, 600. Nothing just displeases the just. III, 140. What the king’s furnace was for the three boys, the burning world will be for the just marked with the Trinity. IV, 1314. A person is not therefore more just because he suffers persecution; this is demonstrated by examples. II, 177. The just are never without persecution here. V, 910. How they always suffer persecution for the sake of justice. IX, 420. The just person and the unjust person are burdens to one another. IV, 364. What the labors of the just are. VII, 787. The labors of the just are a stumbling block to certain wicked people. VI, 38. The just person advances when he sees the punishment of a sinner. IV, 690, 691. From where the just person’s cause for disturbance arises here. IV, 241, 471. The just sometimes waver when they see the wicked flourishing and abounding. IV, 1648, 1649. The life of the just in this age is like a tree that appears dry during winter. IV, 358, 556, 557. The life of the just here is warfare, not yet triumph. V, 814. The struggles of the just. VIII, 586, 587. The just are affected not only by their own affairs but also by the affairs of others. VII, 414. The just have rightly ordered passions. VII, 413, 416. The just person escapes shipwreck rich and naked. V, 1511.

Why the just person is loved even when unknown. VIII, 971. How one who is not yet just can recognize the just person whom he loves. VIII, 953, 954, 955, 959, 966. If a just person has departed from the justice in which he lived for a long time and dies in the impiety in which he lived—not merely for one year but for one day—he will go to the punishments due to the wicked, and his past justice will profit him nothing. X, 979. Who will be found just at the last judgment. X, 304. For the liberation of the just, life will not suffice at the judgment without the support of the saints. VII, 749. The just will in a certain way be purified at the judgment, when the wicked are separated from them. VII, 700. The just themselves will be sacrifices in the kingdom of heaven. VII, 700. What fruit there is here for the just. IV, 691. The just rejoice here and in heaven: here in hope, there in reality. IV, 1679. After their good works the just will keep an eternal Sabbath. IV, 1181, 1182. According to hope, the just person is more blessed than Adam placed in paradise. VII, 328. How the just are few. IX, 296.

The just properly rule the earth. IV, 544. They properly inhabit the world. IV, 544. Everything belongs by right to the just. II, 665. How the seed of the just is powerful on earth. VI, 161. How the just person does not seek bread. IV, 387, 388. One who acts justly will receive praise from authority, whether that authority acquits or condemns. V, 110. What it means to receive a just person in the name of a just person. IV, 1327.

Just persons have been called either angels or sons of God. III, 319. Fields and hills are called just. IV, 784, 785. The heavens are called just. III, 1277; IV, 1314, 1625, 1626, 1632; V, 1590. The just person is light. III, 826. He is day. III, 826. Unless a person turns toward and remains established in the unchanging Good, which is God, he cannot be formed as just and blessed. III, 381. The just are Christ’s kingdom. VIII, 830, 834. The just are compared with palms and cedars. IV, 1179, 1480. They are called the seats of God. IV, 1625, 1626. They are the seats of God, who judges from them as from a throne and directs them. IV, 1240, 1626. An angel carries the just who depart from here into paradise. V, 638. The three kinds of the just are signified in Noah, Daniel, and Job. II, 423; VI, 717; X, 158. How God loves the unjust. VI, 621.

That which is contrary to truth cannot be just. VI, 540.

“Jusum susum.” III, 2036, 2060.

Juventas, a goddess. VII, 122.

Youth is defined as extending to about thirty years. VII, 777. The proposed method of educating youth is rejected. I, 672. The youth of a Christian is spent in labors and hardships, but his old age is made white by righteous deeds. IV, 1178, 1179. Life should be corrected especially in youthful age. IV, 1512.

A passage of Juvenal. II, 532.

K.

The solemnity of the Kalends of January is superstitious. V, 1020, 1021, 1024.

[Col. 0385] L.

Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” VIII, 432.

Labdon, a judge among the Hebrews. VII, 576.

Labeo. Three men of this name existed, distinguished for their knowledge of civil law. VII, 56, note (a). Labeo the philosopher. VII, 795. Labeo, highly skilled in antiquity. VII, 56. How Labeo distinguishes the gods. VII, 105. By what means he distinguishes good divinities from evil divinities. VII, 56. Labeo, a demon-worshiper. VII, 272.

The lips of the inner and outer human being. IV, 900. Deceitful lips increase the punishments of those whose tongues thirst in the underworld. IV, 250. Let your lips agree with your heart; while seeking peace from God, be at peace with yourself. IV, 444. Labor of the lips is pride. IV, 1810, 1811.

How labor has been commanded for us. IV, 1211. It is nobler to provide oneself with food and clothing by the labor of one’s hands than to receive them from others. II, 692. The labor to be chosen by servants of God is labor undertaken with a free mind, without anxiety and greed. VI, 560. See Work.

Some people think themselves learned unless they undertake to examine the labors of others—not by judging them but by tearing and rending them apart. VI, 441.

Whence labor comes here. V, 440. No human being is exempt from the punishment of labor. X, 1578. The labors belonging to several conditions of life are listed. V, 443. The Greeks call labor and pain by one name. VIII, 410. Labor exists wherever many things are sought and loved, for acquiring and retaining which the will is insufficient. II, 485. Labor cannot end unless each person loves what cannot be taken away from him against his will. IV, 107. Let a person labor to hold what he easily lost; what he has held after labor he will hold securely. IV, 1936. Everyone labors for his children; no one for himself. IV, 1159. Labor is the seed of iniquity; sin is the conception of labor. IV, 107. People labor for their desires but do not wish to labor for God’s promises. V, 237. The labor of the wicked is in a circle. IV, 1810, 1811. A good work does not labor much; an evil work involves labor. IV, 1181, 1811. Nothing is more laborious than iniquity and impiety: pain follows that labor, because the labor is undertaken not only without fruit but also to one’s destruction. IV, 127, 142. The labor of the just is the Father’s scourge, while the prosperity of sinners is their pit. IV, 1204. If you wish to endure labor, look to the reward. IV, 372. The labor is brief and not without consolation. IV, 1212. The labors of this life, because they pass away, are nothing; but they are followed by goods that do not pass away. V, 728. Labor is the price of the kingdom of heaven. IV, 1211. Now is the time of labor, the time of sowing, the time of cold: sow even amid winds and rains; summer will come to make you joyful. IV, 391. Lovers do not feel what they labor at, and they labor all the more when someone tries to prevent them from laboring. V, 585. The labors of lovers are in no way burdensome; for in what is loved, either there is no labor, or the labor itself is loved. VI, 447, 448. No one undertakes the labor of cleansing flesh and spirit unless invited by a reward. V, 263.

Rest is purchased by labor. IV, 1211. What the end of all labors and actions ought to be. V, 85. The soul’s action ought to be such as tends toward peaceful security, not such as increases restless labor. IV, 1489. Whatever you labor at, you labor for this purpose: that you may see. IV, 1170.

Milk. You are a little child; you still need to be nourished with milk; do not become angry with the breasts. IV, 644, 784. Be nursed so that you may be nourished; nourish others so that you may grow; grow so that you may eat bread. IV, 1713. The bread of angels became milk for us. IV, 235, 1710, 1711. Humility, the flesh, and the crucifixion of Christ are milk sufficient for little ones. IV, 1613. Christ in humility is our milk; the same Christ, equal to the Father, is our food. III, 1998. The same thing can be both milk for little ones and food for the mature. X, 1017. Milk signifies grace in a wonderful way. IV, 827, 1857; V, 167. The milk of the flock. V, 271. See Shepherd. The Manichaeans do not partake of milk as nourishment. VIII, 37.

Those being nursed in the Church are people who are not yet capable of understanding spiritual and eternal realities; they are nourished by faith in the temporal history administered for our salvation by the Incarnate Word. IV, 110.

The mothers of Lacedaemon, so that their sons might pour out their blood for their earthly fatherland, aroused them to military contests more ardently than the sound of the standards. II, 1057.

Lacerna, a cloak. V, 883.

Tears are witnesses of grief. V, 1536. The tears of newborns are witnesses both to their misery and to the prophecy of that misery. V, 909. The tears of the saints in this life. VII, 683. Why every just person weeps more abundantly here. V, 194. Why the devout have cause for tears. IV, 429. Perhaps your conscience burns because of guilt; extinguish the flame of sin with tears. IV, 1224. The smoke of confessing sinners wrings tears from proud persons who have been humbled. IV, 1865.

Tears are the blood of the penitent. V, 1542. To sow in tears is the lot of all Christians. V, 192, 194. The tears of the devout are compared with the weeping of the wicked. V, 195. Tears and laughter over perishable things are empty. V, 194, 195. The tears of those who pray are sweeter than the joys of the theaters. IV, 1683. The devout tears of those who share in affliction are the new wine of lovers. IV, 1064. The bread of tears is eaten day and night. IV, 467. Why tears are called bread and not drink. IV, 457, 1683, 1684.

Lactantius inserts certain prophecies of the Sibyl into his work. VII, 581.

Lacturnus, the god presiding over ripening grain. VII, 118.

A lake is the depth of misery or of hell. IV, 1111, 1853; VII, 594. The lowest lake is the deepest misery. IV, 1112. A lake is the depth of the world and the abundance of luxury. IV, 223. The lake of misery is the depth of iniquity arising from carnal desires. IV, 434, 1853. Those who immerse themselves in lust descend into the lake. IV, 223. So do those who lose the confession. IV, 1853. How opening and digging out a lake differ. IV, 107.

Iniquity first harms the unjust heart from which it proceeds, before it harms the just person against whom it proceeds. IV, 107.

Laelius is introduced as an interlocutor in Cicero’s discussion of the Republic. VII, 67.

What joy is. VII, 409. Joy exists in both good and evil. VII, 411, 412. The joy of the wicked in temporal goods is blindness and the greatest misery. VI, 295. The joy of the world is vanity. III, 1438. Joy in evil is a pit. IV, 671. Joy itself is death in the enjoyment of what someone has desperately desired, when he obtains it. IV, 123. The sadness of one who suffers wrongdoing is better than the joy of one who commits wrongdoing. IV, 671. The joy of the world is unpunished wickedness. V, 935. Joy is not to be sought outside but within. IV, 82. Let the heart rejoice in God. V, 182. A right heart always finds delight in God. IV, 1251. The joy of the saints arises from the fact that the Lord is in them. IV, 829. The joy of the mind is acquired by ceasing from the joy of the flesh. VI, 711. The cause of your sadness is sin; let the cause of your joy be justice. IV, 478. Let us rejoice in the Lord, not in ourselves, because our good is not ourselves for ourselves, but he who made us. IV, 118, 273, 770, 794. Nothing is more excellent than the joy found in the word of God. III, 483. The clouds of the Scriptures produce the nourishment of joy. IV, 1909. Let joy not be without fear. IV, 1092, 1093. When joy will be full and perfect. IV, 1092, 1275. When heavenly and ineffable joy has been received, the human mind in a certain way perishes and becomes divine. IV, 351. The day will grant joy; the night demands patience. IV, 1853. Things that are very joyful, even when certain, are scarcely believed. IV, 1927.

A solemnity is called joy. II, 115.

A letter to Laetus, who was being troubled by the desire to return to the world that he had despised. II, 1055.

Layperson. V, 653, 758, 1540. Laypeople of a lower calling—that is, those other than monks. I, 639.

Lamasba. IX, 236.

Lambaese. IX, 206.

The plate on the forehead of the high priest signifies sanctification and the removal of sins. III, 641. It also signifies confidence in a good life. III, 638.

A rescript to Lampadius concerning the question of fate and fortune. II, 1061.

Lampares, the twenty-third king of the Assyrians. VII, 572.

Lampius of Barcino. II, 100. Through him Paulinus was suddenly consecrated at Barcino in Spain by force of an inflamed mob. II, 100.

What wool and linen signify. V, 224. Wool is the material of clothing and designates the predestined. IV, 1932.

The weakness of our nature. IV, 1319, 1507. Weakness contracted through fault. VI, 360. The weaknesses endured as punishment for sin even by the citizens of the heavenly city. VII, 442. Weakness after baptism. V, 752. By whom our weaknesses are healed. IV, 1319.

A Laodicean left commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians. II, 252. Jerome says that a Laodicean had recently departed from the Church. II, 252, 286.

Laomedon built Troy. VII, 79. He deceived Apollo and Neptune by perjury. VII, 80.

The Manichaeans say that stones are the bones of the rulers. VIII, 306. Stones and earth exist in the world like the nails and bones of God. VII, 212. The nations that worship stones are called stones. IV, 530; V, 679. The pagans worshiped dead stones; we have found the living stone. IV, 1244. Christ is the cornerstone. V, 42. All the faithful are one stone. IV, 1228. The anointing of the stone placed beneath Jacob’s head is a figure of the anointing of Christ. III, 570. To be shattered by Christ the stone is one thing, and to be ground to powder is another. IV, 522. The stone of demonstration and truth. III, 634. David’s five stones. V, 198. Living stones and dead stones. V, 163. Christ the stone shatters the small one but will crush the great one. IV, 936. Precious and living stones in the Church. V, 223. Those who believe by loving Christ are living stones from which the temple of God is built. IV, 512, 1704. All the prophets are stones of Zion. IV, 1303. A boundary stone of a field. V, 1511. Stone milestones filled with inscriptions teach the way. V, 1547.

The fall and restoration of the human being. III, 132.

The hunters’ snare is the sweetness of this life. IV, 1647. How people fall into the snare and are rescued from it. IV, 1151, 1647. The devil sets snares not on the road but around the road; the road, however, is Christ. IV, 1151. There are two things in the devil’s snare: error, by which he entices, and terror, by which he breaks. IV, 236.

Larentina, Hercules’ prostitute: by what merits she obtained divine honors. VII, 185.

The Lares, good demons made from human beings. VII, 265.

A letter of Largo concerning contempt for the things of this age. II, 938. Whether this is the same man who held the proconsulship of Africa. II, 938, note (c).

The Larvae, harmful demons made from human beings. VII, 265.

One who repels a lascivious impulse, if he has thought of something more pleasurable, does not depart without a wound. V, 391.

The sides of a person are called those who cling to him. IV, 535, 1684. Those who grow proud of their perfection fall away from the side of the Lord. IV, 1156. Those who have left everything stand at the side of Christ. IV, 1156. “The man is good, but he has bad sides”: a proverb. IV, 535, 1684.

Here Christ wished to remain hidden, and the good likewise remain hidden. IV, 621.

Lastidianus, Augustine’s cousin. I, 962.

The Latin language was vernacular in Africa in Augustine’s time. I, 671. The lack of Latin in the regions around Hippo greatly hampers the administration of the Gospel. II, 294. The Italians criticized Augustine over many verbal expressions. I, 1015.

Latinus, son of Faunus, from whom the kingdom of the Latins began to be called. VII, 572, 576. The kings of the Latins were called Silvii. VII, 577.

Latinus, bishop of Mugiensis. IV, 381.

Latria. VIII, 698, 703, 799, 827, 828. What latria is. VII, 278. Latria is the service owed to God. III, 536, 564, 628, 631; VIII, 313, 384, 385. It is to be offered to God alone. VII, 160, 173, 221, 646. To the one Creator. II, 749. And to each person of the Trinity. II, 749. How we offer latria to God within ourselves. VII, 280.

The breadth of charity. V, 904.

Banditries are small kingdoms. VII, 115.

Bandits have among themselves what they call charity. VIII, 223. So that bandits may be more safely hostile to the peace of others, they wish to maintain peace among their associates. VII, 638. The obstinacy of bandits amid tortures, so that they do not betray their accomplices or their own names, is not without great love. V, 923.

The bandits at Christ’s right and left. V, 1085, 1451. The conversion of the bandit crucified with Christ. III, 1678; V, 150. His faith and confession. IV, 332, 443. By confession he poured out the corruption from himself and became fit for the Lord’s food. IV, 848. How great was the merit of the bandit’s faith on the cross. V, 150. How great it was when the disciples wavered. V, 1110, 1293. The bandit believed on the cross when faith had failed in the very teachers. III, 1918. The apostles were defeated by the bandit, who believed when they failed. IV, 847, 1851. The faith of the bandit is compared with the disciples’ defection. X, 480. The bandit’s justification on the cross through faith, with no preceding merits. VI, 125. The bandit was justified and saved freely on the cross: from the jaws—that is, from banditry—to judgment, from judgment to the wood, and from the wood into paradise. IV, 332, 655. Mercy offered the bandit what misery had delayed. V, 436. To the believing bandit, by the ineffable power of the reigning God, baptism was reckoned as having been received in the soul, since it could not be received in the crucified body. VI, 53. Whether the bandit to whom Christ promised paradise on the cross had been baptized is uncertain. I, 627, 638; IX, Retr. 107, 108; X, 503, 505, 516. It is more credible that he had been. I, 653. The bandit on the cross was a martyr baptized in his own blood. X, 480. Or he was drenched by the water that flowed from Christ’s side. X, 480, 481. The sanctification of the sacrament was absent from the bandit bodily through necessity, but present through piety. IX, 173, 174, 175. The example of the bandit must not be used to override the Savior’s command concerning baptism. X, 481. “Today you will be with me in paradise”: Christ said this to the bandit insofar as he is God. II, 834. How the bandit was in paradise with Christ on the day of Christ’s death. II, 833. Where his soul was placed in paradise. III, 483. The bandit understood under the parable of the prodigal son. VI, 705.

To make a proposal (laturam facere). V, 1519.

The bearers of the loads of the rich are the poor. V, 130, 240, 406.

Superstitious baths on the feast of Saint John. V, 1021. The bath of water receives the effect of complete cleansing through the word after this life. I, 593.

How washing and watering differ. IV, 94. As an example of humility Christ washed the disciples’ feet, not as a sacrament of cleansing. IV, 1184. What it means to wash one’s hands among the innocent. IV, 193. The custom of washing on the day of the Lord’s Supper. II, 204.

Praiseworthy things are precious through their own radiance, not through the speech of the common people. II, 428, 433. Whatever we praise, we praise because it is good. IV, 1741. Many praise many things; the wicked praise wicked things. IV, 418. Do you praise what is being done? Then you are approving the deed. IV, 581, 1741. Incautious praisers of the Church or of certain professions. IV, 1278. No one praises except what pleases him. IV, 1939. Praise is free from the law governing the weaving of history. IV, 1400.

To praise God is to accuse ourselves. V, 434. What praise is pleasing to God. IV, 1900. The angels and heavenly beings have the command to praise God. IV, 1941. In what manner God is praised by the angels and in what manner by us. V, 1016. Every creature praises God. I, 705. How even inanimate creatures praise God. IV, 1691, 1878, 1939, 1946, 1947. The very forms of creatures are voices praising the Creator. IV, 205, 206. It is not safe to turn even a fingernail’s breadth from the praise of the Lord to praising oneself. V, 435. Whoever praises himself does not praise God but turns himself away from God. V, 932. For a human being to praise himself is arrogance; for God to praise himself is mercy. IV, 1869. It belongs to God to please you by his beauty; it belongs to you to praise him in thanksgiving. IV, 500. The supreme work of the human being is nothing other than to praise God. IV, 500. Why God wishes to be praised by the human being. IV, 1318. God mercifully commands us to praise him, not arrogantly. IV, 1739. God neither becomes greater if you praise him nor smaller if you criticize him. IV, 1738, 1739. Through praise, as though through eating, strength is acquired, and the one who is praised becomes sweet. IV, 1281.

We have many reasons for praising God. IV, 598. God moderated his praise of himself so that he could make us capable of receiving it. IV, 1742. God himself praised himself so that he might be rightly praised by human beings. IV, 1869. All his praise is contained in God’s goodness. IV, 1740. Sacrifices of praise are acceptable offerings. IV, 836. The praises of God are a sacrifice of justice. IV, 599. The sacrifice of justice is more pleasing to God than the sacrifice of a calf. IV, 864.

God is always to be praised. V, 1185. The teaching is brief: praise God always. IV, 1871. Let the sound of voices alternate according to the occasion; let the interior voice be perpetual. IV, 1317. You praise God all day, if you wish: whatever you do, do it well, and you have praised God. IV, 341, 1938. The tongue praises for an hour; let life praise always. IV, 1899. You cease to praise God when you turn aside from justice. IV, 1938. God is to be praised in prosperity and adversity. IV, 280, 628, 885. You are crooked if you praise God when things go well for you and blaspheme when they go badly. IV, 278. The praise of the one who scourges is medicine for the wound. IV, 1871. To praise God wholly concerning oneself is to praise him with tongue, voice, conscience, life, and deeds. IV, 1938, 1939. God is to be praised in speech, understanding, and good works. IV, 1390, 1949. Life and tongue. V, 1190. God is to be praised in all our works. IV, 1316, 1317. In vain does the tongue bless God if life curses God. IV, 580, 583. Whoever lives badly and praises God is discordant with himself. IV, 1900. Only the secure person praises God, who has no reason to displease him. V, 1186. The praise of the ungodly offends God. IV, 1900. Their works praise God; greed and lust do not praise him, because he did not make them. IV, 1691. He does not yet praise God who lives badly, or who attributes to his own merits the fact that he lives well, or who exalts himself above another. IV, 540, 584. To hear the voice of praise is to understand inwardly that whatever evil is in you is yours, while whatever is good is God’s. IV, 193, 796. The voice of praise belongs to God, because whatever good we are, we are by his grace. IV, 796. God is to be praised in truth—that is, from what is his, not from what is yours. IV, 193, 194. Whoever thinks he possesses some good from himself departs from the praise of the Lord. V, 435. Since the Spirit of God praises him in his servants, what is this but his praising himself? IV, 1869. The praises of the saints are the praises of God. V, 1423. The works of the commandments are the praises of the one who works in his own people. IV, 1407. The rich praise themselves; the poor praise the Lord. IV, 178, 943.

Confession ought to precede praise. IV, 1908. No one praises God suitably, yet no one fails to praise him in some manner. III, 106. Those who submit themselves to the Lord praise him. IV, 275. To wish to praise is itself to praise. IV, 1746. The eloquent are mute when, while praising the creature, they forget the Creator. IV, 1873. If servants do not praise the Lord, they will be proud, ungrateful, and irreligious. IV, 1738. And God must be praised by them all the more, so that they may deserve to be both servants and sons. IV, 1739.

God is to be praised with heart and love. V, 1193, 1643. When you praise with the heart, you place victims upon the altar of conscience. IV, 1746, 1220. God’s ears are open not to the mouth but to the heart, not to the tongue but to the life of the one who praises. IV, 1900. To praise God is to love and praise; to praise in love and love in praises is a labor that is never idle. IV, 1916. Praise without love is neither true nor acceptable to God. V, 1643. Let the tongue praise God, let life praise him, but let it possess limitless charity. V, 1186. Who praises truly except one who loves sincerely? II, 557. Do not fear that you will be unable always to praise the one whom you can always love. IV, 1062, 1063. Let God be praised by the will and loved with charity; let what is loved and what is praised be offered freely. IV, 626. Sacrifices of praise offered not from fear but from charity are called voluntary offerings of the lips. IV, 1568. In praising what you love, you praise freely. [Col. 0389] IV, 1745. No one praises God unless his deeds agree with his mouth, by loving God and neighbor. V, 209, 211. Charity praises the Lord; discord blasphemes. IV, 1950. The new song is nothing other than the praise of God. II, 557. Prayer ought to begin with the praise of God. IV, 1390, 1882. Our praise possesses joy; prayer possesses a groan. IV, 1937.

The safe path to the praise of God must be sought in Scripture. IV, 1869. Praise is to a well-fed heart what belching is to a stomach that is belching. V, 1188. At present hungry love sings; in heaven love that enjoys will sing. V, 1188. The praise of God alone will be the occupation of the blessed. IV, 1062, 1100, 1107, 1108, 1463, 1889; V, 1147, 1176, 1186. There our food will be, and there our drink; action will be rest, and everything will be joy. V, 1177.

Praise without end exists in heaven because love is without end. IV, 1281, 1844. Begin to praise now if you are going to praise forever. IV, 1870.

One should not seek one’s own praise but God’s. III, 2058. How a person may praise himself without arrogance. IV, 1873. Do not praise yourself, even when you are good: by praising yourself as good, you become bad; humility had made you good, but pride makes you bad. IV, 193. Not wishing to be praised in oneself is humility. IV, 310. Those who court human praise. V, 577, 579. All mortals desire to be praised. VIII, 1018. True is the praise that God does not keep silent about. IV, 1432. One who acts rightly ought not to look to human praise. III, 1269, 1271, 1272. How a mind accustomed to human praise will fail when judgment approaches. II, 573, 574. Human praise is not to be sought in one’s studies. II, 433. Whoever seeks human praise through his works is represented by the foolish virgins. V, 577. Whoever seeks human praise in a pious profession fails when reproved by people. V, 1564. The foolish virgins do good works for that empty praise itself, not for the sake of their conscience. II, 571. Whoever judges badly for the sake of praise receives a reward. IV, 195.

The love of praise is a vice. VII, 158. It holds a chief place among vanity’s manifestations. IV, 1532, 1533. They thought this vice useful to the commonwealth. VII, 158. Through love of praise many have restrained other vices. VII, 158. Such people are not saints, but they are less shameful. VII, 158. It is better to resist the desire for human praise than to yield to it. VII, 158. The danger of human praise. V, 478. The desire for praise is the mother of the pride of contention. II, 92. Greed for praise often produces hypocrisy. II, 92. Whoever wishes to be praised by people while God reproves him will not be defended by people when God judges, nor rescued from God when he condemns. I, 804. Desire for praise makes people miserable. I, 1231. By his grace God grants people the means by which they may be praised. X, 208. It is dangerous even to be praised for God’s gift. II, 804. One ought not to live badly in order to avoid being praised. I, 805. Augustine regrets having raised certain people up by excessive praise. I, 587. Praise is removed from vanity where even reproach is free from offense. II, 428.

Human praise is not always to be condemned. IV, 1533. When human praise does not harm. V, 804, 805. Praise is the companion of a good life. I, 805. Human praise is useful to those who praise when, in a person’s good life, they honor God rather than the person. III, 1269. When someone is praised, let him redirect the praise to Christ. IV, 450. When the good are praised, the benefit goes not to those praised but to those who praise. II, 1024. Those who praise the good indicate that they are pleased by the good whom they sincerely praise. II, 1024. How the righteous conduct themselves when they are praised. II, 93, 1024; III, 171; VII, 166. How Augustine conducted himself. II, 109. How prelates ought to receive praise and honor. II, 93. In praise, truth is to be sought and vanity avoided. II, 1023. For what purpose Themistocles said that he enjoyed hearing his own praises. II, 1023. To desire to be praised is partly to be approved and partly to be avoided. II, 1023. The Lord taught us through his Apostle not to place the end of our righteousness in human praise, yet nevertheless to seek human praise for the sake of those very people. II, 1024. We ought to be moved by human praise not for our own sake but for the sake of our neighbor. I, 805. How the praise of the good may benefit even those whom they praise, although the praised persons do not possess what is being praised in them. II, 1024. Augustine does not wish to be praised by those who live badly. V, 1480. By those who live well, he neither wholly wishes it nor wholly does not wish it. V, 1480. Sometimes it is permissible to praise oneself without arrogance. III, 1793. To live rightly and not wish to be praised—what else is that but to be hostile to human affairs? III, 1269. It is easy to lack praise while it is withheld; it is difficult not to enjoy it when it is offered. II, 92.

False praise is flattery. IV, 1824. You would do better to reproach than to praise deceitfully. IV, 1600. Flatterers sell praise. V, 578. The praise of a flatterer is to be rejected. IV, 870.

Lavinia, wife of Aeneas. VII, 576.

Lavinium, the city in which Aeneas established his kingdom. VII, 91, 210.

Laurentius the Martyr. V, 1385; VI, 689. Archdeacon. V, 1388, 1393. His cruel martyrdom. III, 1621. The courage of Laurentius. III, 1621. Its source. III, 1621. Compared with the fervor with which he burned inwardly, the external flame was cold for Laurentius. V, 1397. The body of Laurentius at Rome. V, 1355. The memorial of Laurentius near Ravenna. V, 1445.

[Col. 0390] Laurentius, bishop of Caesarea in the province. II, 955.

Laurentius, brother of Dulcitius. VI, 154, 229, 231.

Laurentum, the beginning of the kingdom. VII, 572. Picus, the first king of Laurentum. VII, 572. Roman origin is said to have come from the Laurentes. VII, 572.

Lazapus, presbyter. II, 1022.

Lazarus means “helped.” III, 1350; IV, 872. Although Lazarus was a figure of the sinner, he was greatly loved by the Lord. III, 1749. The raising of Lazarus signifies something allegorically. VI, 59. Lazarus raised from the dead, a figure of the sinner rising again. V, 433. And of penitents. IV, 1306. Lazarus represents a type of the Church of God. IV, 872.

Lazarus, the poor man covered with ulcers, carried into the bosom of the rich Abraham. V, 113. Lazarus and Epulo exchanged places after death. IV, 550. Lazarus possessed not the merit of poverty but of piety. IV, 610. Why Lazarus’s name is stated, but not the rich man’s. V, 248. See Rich Man. Comparison of Lazarus with the rich man. V, 248, 1650.

Lazarus, a Gallic bishop. X, 320, 343, 355. The presbyter Orosius brought the letters of Lazarus and Heros to the Council of Carthage. II, 759. Heros and Lazarus accuse Pelagius and Caelestius as authors of a wicked error. II, 759. Pelagius replied to the objections of Heros and Lazarus. II, 776.

Lazarus, presbyter. II, 966.

Lazarus, deacon. V, 1574.

Reading is necessary for us here, not in our homeland. IV, 1193. Divine readings raise us up against despair and frighten us against pride. V, 778. When you read, God speaks to you; when you pray, you speak to God. IV, 1086. A person makes progress all the more quickly when he reads good things, the more quickly he does what he reads. VI, 565. Perverse zeal for reading is censured. VI, 565. Readings and singing in the Church. V, 950.

The lector read aloud the psalm that was to be explained to the people. IV, 1784. The lector ascends; the expositor speaks. V, 124, 131. Readers sound forth the word of God even when expositors are silent. V, 204. The lector recites the Gospel. V, 433, 1117. The lector singing in church the psalm he himself chose. V, 1550. He is not an ecclesiastical reader who has read a non-ecclesiastical Scripture, even though he read it in church. II, 234. Those who had once performed the office of lector in a particular church could not be claimed by another church. II, 233 and Note. Boys among the order of lectors. III, 1049; V, 1550.

The error of readers is threefold. VIII, 72. The errors of slower readers are not to be attributed to the author. VIII, 823. Whoever cannot read should continually hear the word of God. IV, 1159. Those who have learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be gentle and humble in heart make more progress by thinking and praying than by reading and hearing. II, 597. In Christian assemblies there was alternating reading and psalm-singing. II, 119.

Lectisternia, couches spread in honor of the gods. VII, 96.

A bed is sometimes a symbol of carnal pleasure and worldly delight. IV, 93. Rest is represented by a bed. IV, 1730. Those who serve God in leisure are said to be in bed. IV, 1730. The bed of pain is the weakness of the flesh. IV, 457. Bronze beds. VII, 102. A silver bed. V, 1402. A silver-plated bed. V, 114.

Leges, a city. II, 1094.

Lemures, harmful demons made from human beings. VII, 265.

The lentil stew cooked by Jacob and eaten by Esau: what it prefigured. V, 39. Lentil stew, food of the Egyptians. IV, 527. Alexandrian lentil stew is magnified. IV, 527.

Leo, a priest of the pagans. VII, 256. High priest of the Egyptian rites. VII, 229. He reveals the origin of the gods. III, 1057.

They think that Leo the acolyte is the same Leo the Great who later succeeded Sixtus in the Roman see. II, 867, Note (b). Sixtus writes to the elder Aurelius through Leo the acolyte. II, 867.

It is more credible that lions did not live on meat in the ark. III, 550. The lion is used in praise and also in reproach. IV, 583. Christ is signified by the lion. IV, 1375. The lion signifies both Christ and the devil. II, 79; V, 471. The lion was conquered by raging; the Lamb conquered by suffering. IV, 1958. The lion in its lair is called the Antichrist, in whom both force and deceit will operate. IV, 127, 128. The lairs of lions are the hearts of unbelievers. IV, 1376. The cubs of lions are the Jewish people; the lions are the chief priests. IV, 667. Lions and lion cubs signify demons and their rulers. IV, 1374, 1375.

Leonas, servant of God. VI, 518.

The Leon­tiana basilica. V, 1201, 1207. Its founder was Leontius himself. V, 1208. The solemnity and burial of Leontius. V, 1208.

Leontius, deacon. II, 1002, 1012.

The civil war of Lepidus. VII, 109.

Leporius denied that God had become man and introduced a fourth person into the Trinity. II, 991. A doctrine contrary to the error of Leporius. VI, 249. Leporius was rightly corrected by Proculus and Cylinnius. II, 991. And condemned. II, 991. Leporius went to Augustine, who received him in order to heal him. II, 991. And he was in fact healed. II, 991. Those who came with him were healed as well. [Col. 0391] II, 992. He asked that he be received through a letter signed by himself. II, 991.

Leprosy of the mind: varied and inconsistent teaching. V, 953.

Leptimagne. IX, 239.

Leptiminus. IX, 222.

What the hare signifies. IV, 1372, 1373.

Those suffering from lethargy. V, 538. They are endangered by sleep. IV, 340, 341. Why lethargics are so utterly enervated. I, 1057. The lethargic person wishing to sleep, a symbol of the sinner wishing to perish. V, 246, 538, 1596.

Lethe, the river—or river of oblivion—in the underworld. VII, 310.

Levana, a goddess. VII, 122.

The soul must be lifted up to God as a vessel is lifted to a fountain. IV, 1854. The heart must be lifted upward lest it decay. IV, 1085, 1629, 1630. To lift oneself up to God, and to lift oneself up against God. V, 1536.

Leucippus, eighth king of the Sicyonians. VII, 562.

Leucius, a bishop. II, 759, 780.

Leucothea, a goddess. VII, 572.

Why Levi was not tithed. X, 175. Levi was hidden in Abraham’s loins. III, 407.

Levites. Whatever pertained to the Levites was considered to pertain to God. III, 719. God appointed the Levites to himself in place of the firstborn sons of Israel. III, 719.

Leutius wrote acts in the manner of the Acts of the Apostles. VIII, 539.

The word *lex* (“law”) is derived from *legere* (“to read”) or *eligere* (“to choose”). III, 681. Law is understood both generally and specifically. III, 2087, 2088. *Retr.* The law of the universe is divine wisdom. VI, 90. One law is eternal and another temporal; concerning both, there is an extended and excellent discussion. I, 1229. The eternal law is divine reason, or the will of God commanding that the natural order be preserved and forbidding it to be disturbed. VIII, 418, 420, 438, 446. The everlasting law of God. III, 618. The law of God is the will of God. IV, 386. The concept of the eternal law. I, 1229. The eternal law remained in the hearts of the devout before the written law. V, 500. It is right to know the eternal law, but wrong to judge it. III, 148. Those who cling to the eternal law have no need of the temporal law. I, 1238. The threefold law: given in paradise, implanted naturally, and promulgated in writing. IV, 1574. The law was given to the upright person so that the virtue of obedience might be commanded. X, 1534.

Natural law. II, 681. It is called the law of reason. II, 683. No one is permitted to be ignorant of the law of nature. IV, 1574. It is proved to exist in all human beings. IV, 673, 1574. Why was the written law given when it had already been written in the hearts? IV, 673. Natural law was restored, increased, and strengthened through the written law. IV, 1574. The law is contained in the five books of Moses. V, 198, 199. Under the name “Law,” all the utterances of the Old Testament are signified. VIII, 1081. The heart of the Law is recognized in the Ten Commandments. VIII, 262.

Three kinds of laws. VIII, 347. Law and testimony are two names for one thing. IV, 987. How the law bears witness to the justice of God. X, 596. The divine laws are expressed more clearly and securely within the mind. VIII, 105. The temporal law was also given by God. I, 689. The temporal law can be changed over time. I, 1229. The written law was written by the finger of God. VI, 335. The law was given through angels, in whom the person of God appeared. VII, 293. The law was given on the fiftieth day after the killing of the lamb: what this signifies. IV, 1167. Why the law was written on stone. IV, 1326. Moses was the minister of the law; Christ its promulgator. IV, 590. The breaking of the tablets signifies that the law serves for condemnation. III, 756. The repetition of the law signifies the New Testament. III, 653. Why the law was given before the people with terrifying display and wondrous signs. VII, 292.

For what purpose was the law given? V, 689, 833, 842, 850, 927, 1535; VIII, 351, 543; X, 205, 297, 1238. The law is the cause of transgression. VI, 211. It makes sin known. VI, 103. The law, by prohibiting sin, became the power of sin. VI, 353. Why and how it is the power of sin. VII, 380; X, 198, 1605, 1606, 1607. The law increased concupiscence. VI, 103, 108, 353. Through the giving of the law, one who previously did not know himself to be a sinner became a transgressor. V, 818, 829, 831, 928. Let the letter of the law display sin; let the law of grace remove sin. V, 825. Transgression comes from the law. II, 769, 892. Through the law, sin that was hidden appeared. V, 175. Why the law is called a ministry of death. VIII, 652, 653. What is the law of sin and death? V, 842; VI, 61. The abundance of wrongdoing through the law. X, 205.

Carpocrates rejected the law. VIII, 27. The Cainites blaspheme and deny that God is the author of the Law. VIII, 29. So did Marcion and Mani. X, 603. The Manichaeans oppose the Old Law. III, 2065. In their furious ignorance they habitually criticize it. VIII, 255. Faustus blasphemed that it differed in no way from paganism. VIII, 320. The Manichaean error concerning the Old Law. VI, 109. And their slanders against it. V, 23, 175; VIII, 403. They are refuted. V, 823, 828; VIII, 404, 643. A summary of the scriptural passages that Augustine defended against slanders. VIII, 659. The Pelagian slander concerning the use of the Old Law. X, 587.

The law is not to be censured as evil. X, 557. The Apostle does not disapprove of the Law. [Col. 0392] III, 2065. The praise of the Law according to the Pelagians. X, 610, 616. What the Pelagians intended in praising the Law. X, 616. To send the Law to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel is a doctrine of Caelestius. X, 333, 334. To what extent Catholics should praise the Law. X, 611. Even the Old Law is from God. X, 594. The Law is not evil, but good. VI, 108, 109. Its goodness is demonstrated. V, 822, 828, 831, 842. It is good and holy. VII, 380. In what way it is good. III, 2065. The law is good for one who wishes to do what the law wills. X, 432.

The law was beneficially enacted. VIII, 71. The usefulness of the Law. II, 676; V, 750; VI, 61, 103, 116, 279, 312, 348, 486. For whom it is useful. X, 1111.

For whose good was the law given? II, 859. The law leads to grace like a pedagogue. VI, 353. It is useful for this purpose: to send one to grace. IV, 1575. The law was given to show how tightly bound were those who presumed upon their own powers. III, 2068. A law had to be given that would show a person himself more clearly, lest the proud human mind think that it could be righteous from itself. II, 860. The Law was therefore given so that, as sin increased, the proud might be humbled; once humbled, they might confess; once confessing, they might be healed. IV, 1329. The law was given so that a person might discover himself, though he had been hiding from himself. V, 833, 927. The Law itself was also given as an aid, but not in the same way as grace. V, 850. It was given as an aid so that you would not think yourself healed. V, 850. The law was given so that weakness might be discovered, indeed increased, and so that the physician might thereby be sought. V, 842, 850. By teaching and commanding what cannot be fulfilled without grace, the law demonstrates to a person his weakness, so that the weakness thus revealed may seek the Savior. II, 593, 893. How the law reveals sickness, cures pride, and leads to the physician. V, 753. The Law was given to the Jews so that they might flee to grace. VIII, 652. The Law made fences for you, so that, unable to find a way out, you might rush to grace. V, 894. The law shows that not only a teacher but also God as helper is necessary. X, 205. The law was given to the wicked so that, sensing their wickedness, they might desire grace. X, 1534. The Law was a pedagogue for the Jews, by whom they were to be led to the grace that is in faith in Jesus Christ. III, 615.

The weakness of the Law. III, 1402. Its weakness for justifying. IV, 888, 889. Why the Law is called weakened and weak. IV, 818. The inability of the law of Moses to heal. V, 689, 753. Neither natural nor written law could take away sin. X, 116. Nor could it free from sin. X, 556, 557. The law condemns the deed but does not remove the evil. X, 634. Without grace, the law does not remove sin but increases it. IV, 1572. Sins were not taken away through the Law. III, 2067. Neither the Law nor the priesthood introduces anyone into the eternal inheritance, but grace through faith does. III, 743. The law could not reconcile. X, 826. The Jews thought they were justified by the Law, as the Pelagians also think. II, 769. The letter of the Law justifies no one. X, 219, 556, 1227. Without grace, the Law not only accomplishes nothing but does very great harm. X, 364, 365. It makes transgressors, either unto the completion of an evil deed or at least in the will alone. X, 221, 904. The Law did not produce justification but transgression. X, 230. The Law of Moses is like Gehazi’s staff placed upon the face of the child. IV, 889; V, 176; VIII, 272. The Law is like a stone placed upon a dead man. III, 1756. The Old Law is a stone of stumbling for those who do not have grace. IV, 1167. The weakness of the Law arises from the flesh. V, 844.

Why does the Law command? X, 214. The Law commands what is good but does not give it. VI, 353. It knows how to command, not to help. V, 822, 1171. The Law was given to show a person his weakness, so that the weakness thus revealed might seek the Savior. X, 209. The Law without grace. X, 887. The Law without grace is insufficient. X, 896. It makes the enemy known but does not conquer him. V, 794. The Law without grace is powerless. V, 1165. The Law is not evil, although without grace it is harmful. VIII, 312. The Law is always good, whether it harms those who are empty of grace or benefits those who are full of grace. VIII, 312. How the Law harms. III, 2065. Without grace, the Law is not the correction of the sinner but the power of sin. X, 1605, 1606. The Law gave sin its power—not because it commands evil or forbids good, but because desire was increased by prohibition, not extinguished. II, 892; V, 841, 894; X, 203, 204. Somehow the very thing that is desired becomes more pleasurable while it is forbidden. X, 204. The more the law forbids something, the more one desires it, because it is less permitted. VI, 106. How the Law is the power of sin although it is good. V, 109.

Without grace, the Law produces sin. VII, 730. It makes people more guilty. V, 753. It produces wrath. X, 894. How it does so. X, 208. To sin after knowing the Law is more serious. I, 1338. Those instructed in the divine law who do not obey the law are more inexcusable. II, 884. We are transgressors of the Law when we fail to do what we already know ought to be done, or do what we know ought not to be done. VI, 271. Without the gift of charity, the Law can command but cannot help; indeed, it can make one a transgressor as well. VI, 287. Those who sin against the Law incur the charge of transgression. III, 2065, 2068. Those to whom grace is not given become transgressors when the Law is added, not righteous. X, 1427.

Through knowledge of the Law, the excuse that people usually offer for their sins is removed. X, 882, 883. Those who know the Law and have not fulfilled it by the powers in which they trusted are inexcusable before themselves. [Col. 0393] II, 884. The Law convicted sinners but did not absolve them. III, 1528. Those who sinned during the middle period between the two Laws—although, according to Julian, not free from sin—were nevertheless not transgressors. X, 1223. All sinners on earth are to be regarded as transgressors of the Law, whether it was given in paradise, written in the heart, or given through Moses. II, 681. The Law could shut the mouth of everyone, but could not convert the mind. X, 634. How those guilty of violating the Law are healed. III, 1397.

The ancient Law was truly a heavy yoke, though it became light. V, 444. The Law helps so that grace may be sought. X, 365. The Law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled. X, 221. The Law is not grace, and nothing is done rightly through it without grace. X, 607. Just as the Law is not grace, neither is nature itself the grace by which we are Christians. X, 896. The Law without grace is the letter alone. IV, 888. The letter kills. X, 203, 205, 213, 217, 903. Hence it kills. X, 589. In what respect the letter helps the predestined. X, 1111. What health is to the eyes for seeing the sun, grace is to minds for fulfilling the Law. VIII, 312. Where grace was absent from the Law, the flesh resisted with invincible force. V, 844. The Catholic faith concerning Law and grace. X, 587, 588.

What it means to fulfill the Law. VIII, 344, 352. Why the Law could not be fulfilled. III, 1401. It is not my weakness that fulfills the Law, but my will praises the Law. V, 837. It is impossible to fulfill the Law through the flesh. X, 588. The Law is insufficient for free choice. II, 683. Human powers are insufficient for fulfilling the Law. II, 393, 595. From the opinion of those who say that the Law can be fulfilled by one’s own powers, it follows that we ought not to pray. II, 595. The Law is not a testimony to free will. X, 1534. The Law would not command unless there were a will; nor would grace help if the will were sufficient. II, 766. The righteousness of the Law is not fulfilled when the Law commands and a person acts as though by his own powers, but when the Spirit helps and the person’s free will—freed by God’s grace—acts. X, 603. To fulfill the Law naturally means the same as according to nature restored by grace. X, 229. Those who naturally do the things of the Law, if they are strangers to grace, will be punished more mildly. X, 230. Even if a person can naturally, or by the powers of nature, do some things belonging to the Law, this is nevertheless not enough to obtain eternal life. X, 230, 231. The Catholic faith concerning Law, grace, and free will. X, 917.

The Law is fulfilled not by fear of punishment but by love of justice. V, 199, 1170, 1241; VI, 222; X, 221, 368. The Law terrified concupiscence but did not extinguish it; it produced fear of punishment, not love of justice. V, 833. The Law instills fear but does not grant charity. X, 280. The Law knows how to threaten, not to help; to command, not to assist. V, 822. It shows sin but does not remove it. V, 823. The Law threatens in vain when iniquity rules. V, 188. To abstain from what the Law forbids out of fear of punishment, not love of justice, is sin. VII, 417. Whoever performs the work of the Law out of fear of punishment rather than love of justice certainly does it unwillingly. IV, 1528. And he is an enemy of the Law. IV, 1528. The Law terrifies the one who presumes upon himself; grace helps the one who hopes in God. V, 792.

Why the Law’s harsher vengeance raged in the Old Testament. II, 660. In the Old Law fear prevailed; in the new, love. IV, 986. Why the Law was given in such a form. IV, 1064, 1580, 1581, 1698. The Old Law knew only how to punish sins. V, 28. The Law commanded the Jews not to spare evildoers. III, 1937. The Law is more commonly called “law” when it threatens, terrifies, and takes vengeance. VI, 110. The Law is unnecessary except for those for whom servitude and fear are useful. VIII, 71. Why God terrifies through the Law. X, 617. The purpose of the Law’s threats. X, 219, 253. The Law is a most troublesome pedagogue. V, 851, 856, 857. It leads to grace. X, 247, 248.

The Law cannot be fulfilled without grace. IV, 457, 1857. No one fulfills the Law unless grace helps him. III, 1607. The Law was not unfulfilled through any fault in the Law, but through the fault of the wisdom of the flesh. X, 221. The letter of the Law can only command, not help. X, 116. The precepts of the Law cannot be fulfilled except through grace. II, 769, 893, 894, 898; V, 73, 188, 894, 1170, 1240. The Law, which is not fulfilled by fear, is fulfilled only by charity.
