III, 653, 755; IV, 281, 282, 829, 990, 991. Nothing fulfills the Law except charity. III, 2136; VI, 109, 336. Many things must be done not at the command of the Law but through free charity. VI, 459. The Law is fulfilled when everything it commands is done not from desire for temporal things but from love of the one who commanded it. VI, 338. Whatever the Law commands is completed only with the help, inspiration, and gift of the one who commands. X, 1606. The Law knows how to command, but weakness succumbs to it; grace knows how to help, through which charity is poured in. X, 557. What could not be fulfilled through the Law was fulfilled through faith. III, 2065. The Law can be fulfilled only by spiritual people. III, 2061, 2062. *Retr.* The law of God’s mercy is the law of charity. IV, 1698. The law of charity grants pardon for sins, erases the past, and gives warning concerning the future. IV, 1698. The same commandment is law to those who fear and grace to those who love. VI, 110. The Law is merely the letter for those who do not fulfill it through the Spirit of charity. VI, 110. Through transgression, the Law binds the offender, commanding what people cannot fulfill because of weakness unless they turn in devotion to God’s grace. VI, 108. Whoever cannot fulfill the Law ought to pour out prayers and flee to mercy. III, 1442. Through the Law comes knowledge of sin; through faith, the obtaining of grace against sin; through grace, the healing of the soul from the defect of sin; through the soul’s healing, freedom of will; through free will, love of righteousness; through love of righteousness, the performance of the Law. X, 233. The Law leads to faith; faith obtains a more abundant Spirit; the Spirit spreads charity; charity fulfills the Law. II, 593. How concupiscence ruled before the Law and under the Law. III, 2065.

The Law makes people subject to it guilty. III, 1397. What it means to be under the Law. VIII, 306. Who is said to be under the Law. X, 280, 603. Who are damnably under the Law. II, 284. One is under the Law who does not fulfill the Law. III, 1397. A person remains under the Law as long as he lives in sin. VI, 61. Those are under the Law whom the Law rules. VI, 108. Those under the Law are slaves of the desire that rules them. VI, 106. To be under the Law is to presume, with proud exaltation, upon one’s own powers for carrying out God’s commands. II, 284. The one under the Law is guilty; the righteous person is with the Law. III, 1756. Under the Law, people desiring carnal goods did not love the righteousness of the Law. III, 2072. Under the Law, activity is vain when lust ravages the mind and is restrained by fear of punishment rather than overwhelmed by love of virtue. I, 1337. What distinguishes a person placed under the Law from one placed under grace. I, 620. To be under the Law, to be in the Law, and to be without the Law are different things. IV, 67; VI, 558. Righteous people existed during the time of the Law, yet they were not under the Law but under grace. X, 399. The condition of a person placed under the Law. VI, 63, 108. The person under the Law is represented by David burdened with Saul’s armor. IV, 1859. What it means to sin in the Law. III, 1857.

Knowledge of the Law is not absolutely necessary in order not to sin. X, 321. Pelagius is confronted with the statement—allegedly his own—that no one can be without sin unless he possesses knowledge of the Law. X, 321. Pelagius’s reply to the objection. X, 321. The matter is examined. X, 321. It is one thing to be helped by knowledge of the Law so as not to sin, and another to be unable to be without sin unless one has knowledge of the Law. X, 321. What is understood by “knowledge of the Law.” X, 322. Knowledge of the Law without charity puffs up. X, 617. Those who fulfill the Law in life cannot fail to keep it in memory. IV, 706. God places his Law in the heart so that it may be loved with chaste love. IV, 1565. One law is written and imposed upon the servant; another is perceived by the mind of one who has no need of letters. IV, 67. The Christian heart in the book of the Law is like a luminary in the firmament of heaven. IV, 1195. A person attends devoutly to the law of God and the words of his mouth when humility inclines his ear, not when pride raises his neck. IV, 984. How one may retain the Law of God in memory and meditate upon it fruitfully. IV, 706, 707, 1195, 1510, 1555. Whoever remembers the Law but does not love it has its memory written as a stone within him—not to adorn him but to weigh him down. IV, 1529.

The Apostle’s threefold law: the law of faith, the law of works, and the law of sin. V, 821, 823. What the law of sin is. III, 2071, 2139. And what it means for the Apostle. X, 432, 433. Which law is the power of sin. X, 1605, 1607. The law of sin with guilt in unbaptized infants. X, 434. How the law of sin is remitted through baptism and remains. X, 675. See Concupiscence. The law of sin is the force of habit. I, 754. The law in the members and the law of the mind fight against each other. X, 433. The law of God, the law of works, and the law of faith. X, 218. How the law of works and the law of faith differ. X, 210, 211, 213, 214, 216, 218. Through the law of works the Lord says, “You shall not covet”; through the law of faith he says, “Without me you can do nothing.” X, 226. Through the law of works God says, “Do what I command”; through the law of faith one says to God, “Give what you command.” X, 214. In the law of works there is the justice of God who commands; in the law of faith, the mercy of the one who helps. IV, 1527. Those who do the works of the Law are justified not through works but through grace. X, 228. Which works of the Law are those through which a person is not justified. X, 232. The Apostle could have been inwardly a transgressor of the Law in his corrupt affections and yet fulfilled the outwardly visible works of the Law. X, 557. What the law of faith is. IV, 1527. The Law is not nullified through faith but established. X, 233. The law of faith is a great abundance of sweetness, that is, charity. X, 233. To delight together in the Law of God according to the inner person is a gift not of the letter but of the Spirit. X, 217. Delight in the Law of God comes from the great grace of God. X, 432.

The Law written on tablets and the Law written in the heart. X, 219. What it means for the Law to be written in hearts. X, 222, 227, 229. The Law inscribed in each person’s heart for discerning the just. IV, 673. If the Law of the New Testament is said to be written in hearts, how do the faithful differ from the Gentiles, who have the work of the Law written in their hearts? X, 227, 228. To have the Law written in the heart is to belong to the New Testament. X, 225, 228.

The law of the Spirit of life: what it is. VI, 61. How it frees from the law of sin and death. X, 434. The New Law is a testimony to the liberation of the will. X, 1534. The law of liberty is charity. X, 280. What it means to serve the Law of God with the mind but the law of sin with the flesh. X, 433. [Col. 0395] By grace alone a person serves the Law of God with the mind. X, 561. The law of the mind and the law of the members are signified by the *tragelaphs*. III, 880.

The Law of the City of God is charity. IV, 1261. In heaven the fullness of the Law will be preserved without any fear of sinning. IV, 1538. The Law will not be fulfilled so that absolutely nothing is lacking except in the other life. X, 604. The Law is not read in heaven, and why. IV, 1194, 1360.

Whether a Christian is bound to observe the precepts of the old Law. X, 594. One must pass from slavery to the Law into the freedom of sons. X, 236. Why Christians now reject the observances of the Law. X, 215. Jerome says that observing the Law is not indifferent between good and evil, but rather evil. II, 260, 280. Augustine teaches that it is neither good nor evil. II, 280. A Jew who had believed in Christ could remain in the observances of the Law, although they were superfluous. VIII, 156. With what intention Paul undertook to celebrate certain lawful rites. II, 278, 279, 282. He observed them without deceit. VI, 536. At that time they were permitted to Jews who believed in Christ. VI, 536. Augustine holds that Peter and Paul practiced the commandments of the Law out of fear of the Jewish believers, whereas Jerome holds that they merely pretended to do so. II, 156, 260. After the Lord’s resurrection, the Law lost, as it were, the life of its function. II, 281. It was not immediately to be abandoned, but reverently escorted to burial. II, 281, 284. The Apostles imposed nothing from the old Law upon those from the Gentiles who believed, except three things. III, 994. Gentiles were not compelled to observe the Law. VI, 536. Some thought that they had to be compelled, as though they could not be saved without those observances. VI, 536. Peter’s fear pretended this; Paul’s freedom rebuked it. VI, 537. Augustine judges, on the basis of Jerome, that Gentiles who had believed in Christ were free from the burden of the Law, whereas those who believed from the Jews were subject to the Law. II, 251, 258. The Cerinthians wanted the precepts of the Law to be observed. VIII, 27. The Ebionites. VIII, 27. The Nazaraeans. VIII, 27. The observance of the Law was not to be rejected all at once, but gradually. II, 281, 282, 285. At the beginning of the revelation of grace, observance of the Law was not harmful; but as time progressed, it had to be abandoned by Christians. II, 282. Now anyone who wished to observe it would have to be regarded as an impious violator of a burial. II, 282. This is no longer permitted in any way. II, 283. Why we do not observe the sacraments of the ancient Law. IV, 1856. We no longer observe them because Christ fulfilled them. VIII, 353, 354. How Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets. VIII, 352, 359, 365, 368, 370. Which Law and which Prophets Christ did not come to abolish but to fulfill. VIII, 348, 351. Faustus thought that Christ fulfilled some things in the Law and abolished others. VIII, 359. This is refuted. VIII, 359. The old Law could have been changed without altering the order of divine providence. II, 526. The Law is not abolished in Christ, but the veil of the Law is. VIII, 71. The servile observances of the Law have been removed, but their interpretations are retained by free persons. VIII, 154. What belongs to the Law is no longer to be observed, but what those things signify is to be read and understood. VIII, 156, 157. Hope must not be placed in the shadows themselves, but in the realities signified by those shadows. VIII, 156. In the old Law mysteries were veiled. VIII, 71. Whatever was prophetically prefigured in the Law and the Prophets, whether through historical events, the celebration of sacraments, or forms of speech, is fulfilled in Christ and in the Church. VIII, 348. Christ was prophesied in the ancient Law. II, 634. The Jews were scattered throughout the whole world so that, through the Law itself, they might be witnesses to Christ. II, 634. The Jews did not understand Christ in the Law. VIII, 652. Except for some of them. VIII, 653. Many precepts of the Law were more suitable to the Jews because of their stony heart than they were true. VIII, 545.

All the precepts of the Law had been figures of us. VIII, 346, 351. The precepts of the Law were medicines; at the Lord’s coming, the medicines themselves were medicated. IV, 680. The Law is observed in part in the Christian faith. III, 743. What Christians now observe from the Law and the Prophets. VIII, 345, 359. What is signified by the Law is no longer commanded to be done, but is read in order to be understood. VIII, 345.

How the Law is to be understood. III, 2065; VIII, 403. It is to be understood spiritually, lest the carnal sense fall into murmuring. VIII, 703. Nothing is more harmful than taking anything in the Law literally; nothing is more beneficial than having it revealed by the Spirit. VIII, 71. The Law promised temporal things. III, 1602. Why it promised visible rewards. VII, 292. Eternal things were signified through earthly promises. VII, 293. The promises of the Law were understood by few. VII, 293. The promises of the old Law are to be understood spiritually. V, 167. Whoever receives the law of God for the sake of earthly things is himself an heir of the Old Testament. X, 328. What sort of life is promised to those who observe the Law. X, 616. To what extent the old Law is spiritual. X, 594. It is fulfilled only by spiritual persons. VI, 105. Not all who know the words of the Law are just. IX, 299. A person must be a doer of the Law, not its judge. I, 859. Whoever loves the law of God honors even what he does not understand in it; and when something seems to sound absurd to him, he judges rather that he himself does not understand it. IV, 1592. Four ways of expounding the Law. III, 222. The Law of Moses, which seems to promise only earthly rewards, also contains spiritual things beneath its veil. IV, 1149. The Law given to the Jews is the “voluntary rain” that God set apart for his inheritance. IV, 818. The old Law understood spiritually is the Gospel. V, 168. In the Law the grace of the New Testament was veiled; in the Gospel it is revealed. IV, 1856. Every legal observance possesses a hidden efficacy for understanding the grace of Christ. VIII, 259. Why the power of understanding the grace of Christ is not given to the Jews. VIII, 260. How the Law becomes grace and truth through Jesus Christ. VIII, 312. The Christian Law is praised even by unbelievers themselves as powerful, divine, and ineffable. IV, 457.

Comparison of the Mosaic and new Laws. X, 218. The distinction between Law and grace. IV, 1528; V, 792; VIII, 652, 653, 654. Their harmony. V, 843. The old Law ministers death; the new, righteousness. X, 219. The old Law is barley in relation to the Gospel’s wheat. V, 725. The precepts or admonitions that Christ seems to set against the precepts of the Law are found in the ancient books themselves. VIII, 366. The Law in Christ; the Law together with mercy. IV, 209.

To use the Law lawfully. V, 851; X, 616, 917. It is possible for someone to be in the Law and yet not use it lawfully. IX, 461. To what extent the just and the unjust use the Law lawfully. X, 209. These two propositions are not contradictory: that the just use the Law lawfully, and that the Law is not laid down for the just. X, 210. How the Law is not laid down for the just. X, 209. He uses the Law lawfully who, understanding why it was given, flees to grace. II, 593. The Law is not an aid to acquittal; rather, it becomes a bond of guilt for the person who trusts in his own powers to fulfill it. II, 593. To walk blamelessly in the Law. V, 918. The saints are not granted to perfect the Law in this life. V, 838. To agree with the Law. V, 837. How someone misuses the Law. VI, 105. Good works arise in one who uses the Law well, and evil works in one who uses it badly. IV, 720. It is one thing to perish without the Law, another to be judged by the Law. III, 1857. “Those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” is to be understood of the law of Moses. IV, 1572. The opinion that those who sinned under the Law will not perish but will be cleansed through temporary punishments is rejected. IV, 1573. Whoever refused to do the Law is justly dealt with by the Law. I, 1180.

The old and the new Law. V, 857. From what source both are called “Law.” X, 221, 222. “Old Law” is used sometimes specifically for one part of the Old Testament, sometimes generally for the whole Old Testament. I, 624. The Law despised by the Jews. V, 1642. Those who hear the Law, although they are not just before God, may nevertheless be heard when they speak the truth. IX, 714. The Christian Law is praised even by unbelievers, but they excuse themselves from embracing it on account of its difficulty. IV, 457.

The Law in the ark is sanctification in the Lord’s body. II, 219. The Law of Moses prefigured by the five porticoes. V, 689. And by the denarius. V, 1240. The Law of God is the firmament. IV, 1194, 1195. The immaculate Law of the Lord is the Holy Spirit. IV, 161. The Law of the ten commandments is the ten-stringed psaltery. IV, 161. The Law of the Lord is Christ himself. IV, 155. The author whom Augustine calls an adversary of the Law and the Prophets was not a Manichaean. VIII, 664.

All laws seek blessedness. II, 393. A law that is not just is not a law. I, 1231. Through human law, certain things are permitted that are forbidden and punished by divine law. I, 1232. Certain things are approved by the law of the world, not by the law of the Creator of the world. V, 828. How far the power of human law extends in exacting punishment. II, 1224. A judge may not judge the laws that have been established, but must judge according to them. III, 148. Whoever does not love the laws is subjected to them. I, 1188. Human laws must be learned. III, 62. The heavenly city does not hesitate to obey the civil laws of the earthly city. VII, 645. The Emperor does not violate his own laws when he grants pardon to those who confess. IV, 590. The Church benefits from the good and bad laws of emperors. II, 399, 796. Good people are tested by bad laws, and bad people are corrected by good laws. IX, 527. When the king’s heart is unfaithful, good people are either tested or approved; when it is faithful, evil people are either corrected or punished. IX, 739. Augustine, together with others, held that laws should not be sought from the emperors against the Donatists; others held the contrary. II, 804, 805. The Apostles did not ask laws from the emperors; why. II, 801. Christians may appeal to the emperors’ laws, following the example of the Apostle Paul. II, 806. What was decreed at the Council of Carthage concerning requesting laws from the emperors. II, 805. The emperors’ laws against heretics. IV, 1309. Against pagans. V, 313. The emperors’ laws punish heretics with fines and exile, but punish pagan sacrifices capitally. II, 326. Laws for destroying idols and correcting heretics were sent to Africa while Stilicho was alive. II, 358. On their account many were converted either to the Christian religion or to Catholic unity. II, 359. Vain men claim that these laws were issued without the Emperor’s knowledge or against his will. II, 358. The law of Theodosius imposing a fine of ten pounds of gold upon heretics was extended to Donatists who raged against the Church. II, 804. The Donatists were ordered to lose their possessions according to the laws of earthly kings. II, 345. The complaint of heretics against the laws of Catholic emperors. X, 703, 704. The emperors’ penal laws are defended on behalf of the Catholic Church against heretics. IX, 616. The coercion of laws does not remove free will. IX, 317. The usefulness of the imperial laws against the Donatists and others. II, 796, 798, 802, 806; IX, 315, 425, 733. Very many Donatists were corrected through the emperors’ laws. II, 796, 806. Catholics do not use the severity of the laws against heretics. II, 305, 306. Augustine pleads that the severity of the laws be spared the Donatists. II, 366. The law of Antoninus against adulterers. VI, 475. The Julian Law. VI, 475. The unjust Voconian Law. VII, 103. Secular laws. II, 166.

Leah is interpreted as “laboring.” III, 1046. Leah is a figure of the active life. III, 1046.

Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening” or “whiteness.” IV, 912, 1370. Lebanon is understood as representing the dignity of this age. IV, 912, 1370. What the fruits of Lebanon are. IV, 911, 912, 1370.

The Libellatics. IX, 157.

Booklets. V, 1442. Booklets were distributed so that miracles might be recited among the people. V, 493, 1300, 1443; VII, 768, 769, 770.

The goddess Libentina, so called from *libido* (“lust”). VII, 118.

From what source the god Liber and the goddess Libera are so called. VII, 187. Liber Pater, also called Dionysus, was regarded as a god after his death. VII, 569, 571. Liber was the discoverer of wine. VII, 569. Liber is placed before Ceres among the seeds. VII, 207. How shameful the rites of Liber are. VII, 210, 214. The pagans think that the rites of Liber should be entrusted to the eyes of a few initiated persons. II, 83.

The god Liber who presides over conception is distinct from Bacchus. VII, 195. Note (a).

Liberalis, a bishop. IX, 192.

The liberal arts have nothing appropriate to freedom except what they have appropriate to truth. II, 367. Hence the arts of poets, philosophers, and orators are for the most part improperly called “liberal.” VII, 367.

What is understood by the name “books of life.” VII, 680. The book of life is the predestination or foreknowledge of God. VII, 681. How the erasure of someone from the book of life is to be understood. IV, 862. The book of life will be opened at the judgment. VII, 680. Which book is understood in the words, “In the heading of the book it is written,” etc. IV, 1962. The divine books are sprinkled with certain holy and good delights. IV, 413. “Let the divine page be a book for you; let the world itself be a book for you. In these books only those who know letters can read; in the whole world even the uneducated person can read.” IV, 518. A book is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach. IV, 492. It is useful for many books to be produced by many authors in different styles but with one faith, even concerning the same questions. VIII, 823; IX, 595. The authority of books that we write not as exercises for making progress but with the authority of instruction. VIII, 248, 254. Although the same truth found in sacred writings may also be found in books written by human beings, their authority is nevertheless vastly unequal. VIII, 249. Books written by human beings are to be read not with the necessity of believing but with the freedom of judging. VIII, 248, 249. Those who criticize the books and sermons of others often sin, and seriously. II, 353. At the end of a book the reader’s attention is refreshed, just as the traveler’s labor is refreshed by lodging. VIII, 636. The books of profane authors are waters not common to everyone. IV, 1360, 1361. In the books of foreigners there are excellent precepts of morals and discipline, but not humility. IV, 270. Reading disapproved books, for those whom it might not harm. X, 510. How Augustine reads the canonical books and others. II, 277, 286. The pontifical books of profane rites. VI, 583.

What the right of children is. X, 714. Note 1.

“Freedom” is understood in various ways. X, 1105, 1106. Natural freedom: serving no one. VII, 643. Our freedom should consist in not serving sin. VII, 114. What death of the soul is worse than the freedom of error? II, 400.

Free will is an intermediate power. X, 238. Free will, which can freely incline here and there. X, 169. What free will is according to Julian. X, 1515. How he defines it. X, 1102, 1103, 1104, 1293. How the Pelagians define it. X, 1466, 1518, 1519. The Pelagian definition of free choice is such that they must take freedom away from God. X, 1299. The equilibrium of freedom is not found even in the Pelagians’ opinion. X, 1297. According to the Pelagians, free will is not established without the possibility of sinning. X, 1483. Pelagius wants the possibility of free will to extend equally toward good and evil, as though weighed in an even balance, but he is inconsistent with himself. II, 829, 830. In God and in the blessed there is free will without the possibility of sinning. X, 1518. The ability both to sin and not to sin does not belong to the nature of free will. X, 1474. The possibility of evil is not required for freedom. X, 1521. Free will is supreme in God. X, 1474. Although he cannot do evil. X, 1117, 1118. For someone to be free, it is not required that he be able to will both good and evil. X, 1116. The ability to vary between good and evil does not belong to free will. X, 1543. Julian thinks that free will is incompatible with necessity. X, 1299. A certain blessed necessity that does not take away freedom. X, 1116. How Augustine explained free will while he was still a presbyter. III, 2078. Catholic faith does not deny free will either toward an evil life or toward a good one. II, 973.

To say that free will was taken away through Adam’s sin is Julian’s slander. X, 552, 564. Free will has not been taken away from the ungodly. X, 553. No one is compelled unwillingly toward either good or evil. X, 567. God does not heal anyone against his will. IV, 1320. Free will is affirmed. VIII, 451, 540. Free will was given to the soul. I, 595, 1079, 1241; III, 133. Our will is free because it lies within our power. I, 1275. Through free will we use free will itself. I, 1268. What is considered to lie within our power. I, 596, 1275. What we do by free will and what by necessity. IV, 1745, 1746. If freedom is taken away, all human life is overturned. VII, 149. Those who confess that every person who believes in his heart believes only by his own free will do not deny free choice of the will. II, 987. Free choice of the will in human beings is proved by the divine precepts. X, 882, 884, 885. By the very fact that something is commanded and enjoined, our obedience is required; and this cannot exist without free will. II, 971. From the fact that the Lord came to save the world and will come to judge it, grace and free will are both affirmed. II, 969; X, 874, 875 and following. Whoever thinks that a person who, by reason of age, was able to use free choice of the will is not judged according to his works is in error. II, 971. If human beings had not received free will and reason, just condemnation would not follow them when they sinned. IV, 1302. Free will was given to human beings, yet punishments for sinners were most rightly established by both divine and human laws. II, 940. One must not believe astrologers, lest we suffer shipwreck concerning free will. II, 210. Free will is not removed by God’s foreknowledge. I, 1274. Free will was not given in such a way that whatever a person attempts through it can disturb any part of the divine order and law. I, 595. The creature was established in free choice, but not in such a way as to overcome the Creator’s will, even when it acts against his will. IV, 1464. To raise the horns of false freedom against God. I, 166. It belongs to God’s omnipotence to permit the evils that arise from free will. VI, 581.

Why free will was given to human beings. VI, 11. Why it was given capable of turning toward evil. I, 1242. Free will was given to human beings so that they might serve God not by necessity but by choice. VI, 296. It was given for living rightly, not for sinning. I, 1242. Free will in human beings is directed toward virtues and vices. X, 286. Sin and right action lie within free choice of the will. VI, 16. God wished it to lie within your choice whom you would obey: God or the devil. IV, 1938. God gave free will to human beings; and if a person wishes it, what was yesterday straw becomes wheat today. V, 1175. Sinners who try to excuse themselves before God are accused for this reason: they possess free will. X, 883. Human beings were created with free will, by which they themselves consent to sin. IV, 268. Through free will people sin, especially those who sin with delight and love of sin, finding pleasing what they desire. X, 1110. A certain harmful freedom. IV, 1306. Free will is the cause of sin. I, 595, 733; III, 133. And in the books written on that subject. I, 1221. From human free will came the seed of death. V, 1269.

Free will is a good work of God. X, 1489. It belongs among God’s gifts. X, 155. It belongs among God’s gifts not merely that free will exists, but also that it is good. X, 155. Free will is reckoned among intermediate goods. I, 598. Why God left angels and human beings to free will. X, 932. What the freedom of the will was worth in the excellence of that first condition appears in the angels who stood firm. X, 1001.

What the free will of the first human being was like. V, 1269; VII, 802. One must speak differently about the freedom in which the first human being was created and the freedom in which he now exists. X, 287. Free will was perfect in the first human being. III, 2066. Adam possessed the fullest strength of free will. X, 1513. The first human being received free will upright. VI, 685. In the first state free will was sufficient by itself for sinning, but not for retaining righteousness unless divinely aided. VI, 281. We possess free will for doing evil without God’s help; although, in doing evil, it is not free but a condemnable slave. V, 856. The good use of free will comes from God. I, 598. Freedom deceived the first human being when he used its reins too indulgently. II, 785. What free will can accomplish without assistance was demonstrated in Adam himself. VI, 685. The weakness of free will is seen in Adam. V, 852, 940.

The Pelagian dogma that free will remains as intact as the harmless nature possessed by each person before the exercise of his own will. X, 1149. Whether free will is as complete after sins as it was before sins. X, 1108. What kind of freedom exists in human beings after sin. X, 1101, 1103, 1104. Free will is not now what Adam received, but has already been corrupted and must be healed. X, 1294. Free will corrupted by its own evil use. X, 1524, 1529. The free will by which human beings could act rightly failed through the evil of sin. X, 1523, 1524. Human beings received great powers of free will when they were created, but lost them by sinning. V, 752. By using free will badly, human beings lost both themselves and free will itself. VI, 246. What human free will is innate and wholly incapable of being lost. X, 1521. A certain innate and unchangeable freedom of the will. X, 1524. The free will by which we wish to be blessed and do not wish to be miserable cannot be taken away from us. X, 1565, 1566. The will is free even in that by which we wish to be blessed in such a way that we cannot at all wish to be miserable. VI, 281. Through the enormity of the first sin we lost our free will for loving God. II, 983. Through an evil will human beings lost the power to do good. V, 188. Human beings received such free will for standing and falling that they could avoid sin; after righteousness was lost through sin, there followed an inability to act rightly. X, 1522. What remains of free will in this mortal life. VI, 108. Julian’s opinion that the freedom to do good or evil cannot perish through its own evil use. X, 1520. Adam lost this. X, 1520. What freedom perished through sin. X, 552, 1110. Freedom from sinning perished as the punishment of sin. X, 1118. For once the will was conquered by the vice into which it had fallen, nature was deprived of freedom. X, 296. Whatever the cause of the will may be, if it cannot be resisted, yielding to it is without sin. X, 286. How, then, can it be resisted? X, 286. Freedom would not have perished if the good will had remained. X, 296. The freedom to act rightly in which human beings were created, and which now has less power, is the punishment of sin. I, 1296.

Free will must neither be denied nor credited with too much. X, 879, 880. Some attribute too much to free will. X, 151. How much the Pelagians attribute to it. X, 570. Pelagius is an arrogant defender of free will. X, 373, 374. The Pelagians attribute to their own free will the fact that they approached Christ by believing. V, 192. Some attribute their righteousness to free will. V, 172. They also judge that it is sufficient for righteousness. V, 852. The Pelagians asserted free will in such a way that they left no place for grace. I, 595. By exalting free will into pride, they throw it down rather than raise it up. V, 1467. The Pelagians oppress free will by defending it. X, 1290. In what sense the Pelagians admitted free will. X, 441. The praise of free will according to the Pelagians. X, 610. What their intention was in praising free will. X, 617. Against those who presume upon free will. V, 1466. How vain it is to boast of bare free will. II, 975. The first human being possessed the fullest disposition toward free choice; now free will in human beings is wounded. *De libero arbitrio* II, 974. Note (a). From what source free will is free in relation to good, and from what source in relation to evil. X, 553. What free will amounts to when it has been sold under sin. VI, 126. Caelestius’s opinion that free will would not be free if it needed God’s help. X, 345. Free will must not be defended in such a way that God’s help is judged unnecessary. III, 1778. Free will must be defended in such a way that room is left for grace. X, 885. Whoever denies that free will needs grace nullifies the reward of Christ’s death. X, 260. Even freedom restored to its former state needs the help of grace. X, 1520.

To what extent the freedom of the will is defended according to grace. X, 926. Human nature was capable, through free will, of wounding itself; once wounded, it is no longer capable of healing itself. V, 850, 877, 1268. It could fall, but it could not rise. I, 598; X, 1009, 1520. Let free will be credited only so far that God’s grace may be honored more greatly. II, 739. “You could do nothing to yourself except lose yourself; nor do you know how to find yourself, unless he who made you seeks you.” V, 108. Free will abandoned by divine help will in no way possess the solidity of righteousness, but only a destructive swelling. II, 676. It is worth nothing without God’s grace. V, 172, 174. It is not sufficient for good. X, 324. It is sufficient for evil, but insufficient for good unless it is helped by the omnipotent Good. VI, 685; X, 577, 935. “What can we do by free will unless he who commands us helps us?” IV, 1792. Although there is no doubt that the power of the will exists for not sinning, its power is nevertheless insufficient unless weakness is helped. II, 675, 676, 766. Freedom without grace is not freedom but defiance. II, 682. Free will is insufficient for doing good, according to Innocent. II, 782. It does contribute something to the conversion of the heart. X, 899. Free will without God’s grace can neither be converted to God nor make progress in God. II, 970, 973. Free will must not be separated from God’s grace, as though without it we could in any way think or act. II, 969. By the free will through which human beings changed from good to evil, they cannot be changed from evil to good. V, 172. Free will, having been taken captive, is effective only for sin; for righteousness it is ineffective unless divinely freed and helped. X, 607, 620. No one is free to do good without God’s help. X, 1293, 1294, 1295, 1296, 1297, 1299. Free will is insufficient for knowing how one ought to live and for living well. X, 270. Nor is it surprising that, either through ignorance, a person does not possess free choice of the will for choosing what he ought rightly to do, or, while carnal habit resists, sees what ought rightly to be done and wills it but cannot fulfill it. X, 287. If those whose spirit already desires against the flesh need God’s grace for each individual act, lest they be conquered, what freedom of the will can those possess who have not yet been rescued from the power of darkness, while iniquity rules, and have not even begun to fight? etc. X, 1535. Free will is insufficient for overcoming temptations unless the Lord grants victory to one who prays not to enter into temptation. X, 887. If the will were sufficient for our not entering temptation, we would not pray; yet if the will were absent, we could not pray either. II, 990. Those who say that, once they have received free choice of the will, there is no need for prayer that God help them not to sin are accused by the Pharisee himself. X, 154.

Those who think that the Law is sufficient through their own free will are refuted. V, 851. The Law is not sufficient through free will. II, 683. Free will is insufficient without grace for fulfilling negative precepts. X, 628. A person does not possess the keeping of God’s command in his power of choice in such a way that he can accomplish it without needing any help. IV, 1510. Free will is insufficient without grace. X, 895. It is insufficient for not sinning. X, 285, 293, 294. Before grace, free will in us does not enable us not to sin, but only not to wish to sin. III, 2066. What freedom those who do not wish to commit sin need. X, 1107, 1110. Pelagius said that all are ruled by their own will, insofar as the episcopal Synod approved that statement. X, 322. That statement of Pelagius rightly troubled some of the brothers. X, 323, 324. No one can use free will well except through grace. X, 571, 572. A person ought not entrust himself to his own direction. X, 323. “You love your free will—why entrust yourself to yourself? He can preserve you better who was able to create you before you existed.” V, 941.

Freedom toward good comes only from grace. X, 1144, 1145. Free will is effective for good works if it is divinely helped. II, 675. The will remains free even if it needs divine help. II, 828. Free will and God’s grace are commended together. X, 887. Scripture admits both. X, 879. How it commends both. II, 973. To incline the heart toward God’s testimonies is at once a divine gift and an act of one’s own will. IV, 1569. The grace of love, without which no one lives piously and with which no one lives except piously, must be asserted so that free will may truly be defended. X, 1299. Free will may exist by itself in a person if he does not come to Christ; but if he comes, it can exist only with help. X, 368.

Free will is weak here, even in the baptized and the saints. X, 1514. Its weakness is repaired only through grace. X, 1295. Free will must be restored and helped by grace. X, 1278, 1279. The freedom to act well, once lost, does not return except through grace. X, 1544. The good that human beings abandoned can be restored only by God’s grace, not by the freedom of the will, which they deservedly lost through iniquity. X, 1518. Lost freedom cannot be restored except by God. VII, 418.

True freedom comes from grace. X, 552. Through grace. X, 938. Free will truly becomes free through grace. II, 760. We are made free through the help of grace. X, 1534. No one is free from the law of sin except through grace. V, 842. Christ’s coming restored the state of former freedom. Innocent, II, 785. Freedom is promised by the Liberator to believers. X, 296. We then become truly free when God creates us—not as human beings, which he has already done, but so that we may be good. VI, 247. In the first Adam it became clear what human choice could accomplish toward death; in the second, what God’s help could accomplish toward life. II, 843. The will does not obtain grace through freedom; rather, through grace it obtains freedom. X, 926. In doing what is right there is no bond of necessity, because freedom is charity. X, 286. Health itself is true freedom. X, 296.

Free will is not abolished through grace but established. X, 233. It is not taken away when grace is preached. VI, 443; X, 265. It is not taken away by the Apostle. III, 2071. The choice of the will is not therefore taken away because it is helped; rather, it is helped because it is not taken away. II, 677. Free will has been given to us by God, although our effort is nothing without him. IV, 208. What is required from a human being because of free choice of the will is requested from God because of the help of his majesty. V, 903. We should understand that we possess free will for this purpose: that we may invoke the Lord with a pious will. II, 676. Whoever attacks the grace by which our free will is freed for turning away from evil and doing good wants his own will still to remain captive. II, 981. Those who attack God’s grace attack free will more truly, since through that grace it becomes free for choosing and doing good things. II, 987. Do not defend free will in such a way as to attribute good works to it without God’s grace; nor defend grace in such a way that, as though secure because of it, you love evil works. II, 974.

The difficulty of reconciling free will and God’s grace. X, 383. Who is free for evil. X, 1298. A person is free for sinning when he is enslaved and devoted to sin. VI, 246. Freedom from righteousness is servitude under sin. III, 156. A person possesses free will in evil when either a hidden or manifest deceiver has implanted in him delight in wickedness, or when he has persuaded himself of it. X, 1110. Those who are free from righteousness possess free will in evil; those who are slaves of sin do not possess free will in good. X, 1115. People become free from righteousness only by the choice of freedom; they become free from sin only through the grace of the Savior. X, 1110. We are truly free there where we do not take delight unwillingly. X, 432. Who are free to perform works of piety. X, 1105. Who is free for good. X, 1298. A person will not be free for doing what is just unless, freed from sin, he begins to be a servant of righteousness. V, 246.

What free will is. III, 1696. The first freedom is to be free from sins. III, 1697. Freedom from sin. X, 982. In vain those who are slaves of sin boast of free will. X, 233, 234. The will is not to be called free so long as it is subject to desires that conquer and bind it. II, 593. Freedom exists when not sinning is a delight. X, 218. The freedom of the New Testament is that those freed by grace do not serve sin unto death. X, 938. Choice will then be most free, when it cannot serve sin. X, 936. Choice will be freer when it will be altogether unable to serve sin. VI, 281. The denial of permission and impunity to sin does not conflict with freedom of choice. IX, 716. The elders of the Donatists also judged in this way. IX, 717. A person freed from evil by himself cannot be harmed by anyone. V, 253, 1363, 1364. Only the just person is free. V, 883.

True freedom is to serve Christ. II, 128. A creature is free when it offers service to the Creator. IV, 1493. God alone is served with supreme freedom. I, 1170, 1320. Freedom from temporal law and from the domination of inferior things belongs to those who cling to the eternal Law. III, 218. Freedom from the worship or domination of creatures, in which through the Christian religion we rejoice in God’s service. I, 1078. Freedom from the condition of sin belongs to those who submit themselves to truth. I, 1261. The free will is freer the healthier it is, and healthier the more subject it is to divine mercy and grace. II, 676. There is a free servitude with the Lord, where service is rendered not by necessity but by charity. IV, 1275. This is true freedom because of the joy of right action, and at the same time pious servitude because of willingness to obey the command. VI, 246. Freedom, true and sound freedom, exists when a good work is done not from fear but from love. IV, 820. The freedom of the New Testament is love; the servitude of the old is fear. I, 1334. Freedom excludes fear. III, 1698. The law of freedom is the law of charity. II, 740. The spirit of servitude and the spirit of freedom. V, 857.

## Liberty

There are two kinds of liberty: one belonging to merit, the other to reward. VII, 802. There is now greater liberty in the saints than formerly in Adam. X, 937. The liberty of the righteous is not as great in this life as it will be in the next. X, 1116. What difference there is between being able not to sin, die, or abandon the good, and being unable to sin, die, or abandon the good. X, 936. Full liberty in eternity. III, 1697, 1699. And most perfect liberty. II, 982. What the free choice of the blessed is like. VII, 802. Twofold liberty: immortality and perseverance. X, 936.

## Liberator

What, according to the Manichaeans, is the need for a liberator? X, 1105.

It is said that one is liberated in two ways. V, 743. Christ liberates both by taking away iniquity and by inspiring charity. X, 1104, 1106. No one is free in the good unless he has been liberated by the grace of Christ. X, 917. Those whom the Son has liberated are truly free. X, 440. What the Liberator has not liberated will not be free in the good. X, 1110. In what sense Christ is said to liberate everyone. X, 1198. In those whom God liberates, mercy is to be recognized; in those whom he does not liberate, judgment is to be acknowledged. X, 1071. God liberated man, not the devil, because man sinned less. I, 1284. What it means to be liberated from the body of death. X, 677. The purpose of the books *On Free Choice*, and against whom they were written. X, 1008.

## Libido

What libido is. VI, 496. Libido, the pleasure of the senses. X, 770, 771. Libido, a general term for every desire. VII, 424. Some desires have their own proper names, others do not. VII, 424. When nothing is added, *libido* usually means obscene bodily movements. VII, 424. Desires must be distinguished from sensations. X, 1367, 1368. The vivacity, usefulness, and necessity of sensation are one thing; libido is another. X, 770. In the senses of smell, taste, and touch: to what extent libido can and ought to be distinguished and subdued. X, 770. Love is called libido when it is depraved. IV, 124. The Platonists confessed that vicious libido is a part of the soul. VII, 427. In what sense. X, 854.

Libido arose after sin. VII, 428, 429. And arose from sin. VII, 430; X, 405, 406, 427. The origin of libido. III, 398, 446. When Julian is embarrassed to name *libido*, he calls it the strength and power of the members. X, 471, 472. Natural appetite. X, 446. Genital heat. X, 739. Manliness. X, 816. The Pelagians take pleasure in libido. X, 1248. How great, though false, is Julian’s praise of libido. X, 1144, 1160, 1279. Yet he is ashamed even to name libido. X, 446. Julian champions libido. X, 687. And places it in paradise. X, 1159, 1167. Whether libido could have existed in paradise before sin. X, 565. Libido would not have existed in paradise. X, 818. Nor did it exist in man before sin. X, 450, 1001. Great was the grace of God there, where the earthly and animal body did not possess beastlike libido. [Col. 0402] X, 781. Libido would not exist if man had not sinned. X, 1449, 1451. Libido as it exists now was not in paradise. X, 1158, 1193, 1449, 1451. Before sin there would either have been no libido in paradise, or it would not have been shameful. X, 1450, 1451. Or it would not have resisted the will. X, 1449. And would not have displayed its movements against the will’s command. X, 1321. Rather, it would have been subject to the will’s command. X, 566.

Libido is not subject to the will. VII, 425, 427, 430. It would have been subject to it if man had not sinned. VII, 430, 431, 432. Marriage would not have had the quarrel between libido and the will. VII, 431, 434. Nothing makes the mind a slave of libido except its own will. I, 1232. Before sin, mothers would have conceived without libido and given birth without pain. X, 453, 454. The act of married couples in begetting children could have taken place without libido. X, 451. Two people can be one flesh without libido. X, 1167. What libido might perhaps have been like in paradise. X, 1094, 1160. Libido before sin was not vicious. VII, 427.

Libido is evil. X, 768, 801, 1155. Cicero himself recognized that libido is evil. X, 768. The devil is the author of libido. X, 801. In venereal libido lies the evil of original sin. X, 142. Libido as it now exists is either a vice or has been corrupted. X, 1451. Not only its excess is blameworthy, but its impulse also is vicious. X, 1360. Libido as it now exists is evil. X, 1094. Libido that resists the spirit is evil. X, 1161. Libido is a disease. X, 469, 765. A wound of nature. X, 732. The punishment of sin. X, 120, 287, 288, 787, 1354. The penalty imposed on the will for disobedience. X, 429. Libido derives its origin not from the first establishment of nature but from the evil will of the first man. X, 764. The inability to abstain from libidinous acts because of the pain that resists and torments the carnal bond is not the nature of man as he was created, but the punishment of the condemned. I, 598. In what sense libido is natural to us. X, 801. By eternal law, dominion over libido has been granted to the human mind. I, 1232. In a perverse man reason is enslaved and libido rules. IV, 108.

Even when licit, libido seeks a hiding place. VII, 426, 427. It is more shameful than other desires. X, 756. One is rightly ashamed of libido. VII, 425, 428, 431. Why. VII, 431. Why libido is now shameful. X, 1161. When it began to be shameful. X, 451, 452, 457. The members are shameful because of libido. X, 451. Libido is shameful only because of sin. X, 1160, 1167. And because it is the punishment of sin. X, 1449. Before sin there would not have been generation without sexual intercourse, but there would have been sexual intercourse without shame. X, 458. The Pelagians say that sexual libido was created by God, but that in human beings it must be covered by shame. X, 1362. Why the movement of libido is more shameful to some than to others. VII, 427, 430, 431. Whether libido can be called God’s work because Abraham and Sarah, who conceived with libido through God’s gift, possessed it. X, 712, 713. Original sin is derived from libido. X, 1160. Libido is not the good of marriage. X, 422. Nor is the evil of marriage present in marriage itself. X, 460. Rather, it is the evil of carnal concupiscence. X, 406. The evil of libido must not be imputed to marriage. X, 406. Nor does it remove the good of marriage. X, 418. Libido does not come to marriage from its institution, but from Adam’s sin. X, 460. Condemnation of libido is not condemnation of marriage. X, 416, 418. Libido is culpable not only outside marriage. X, 687.

The disease of libido must be distinguished from the business of marriage. X, 1090. It is a venial fault to lie with one’s spouse solely for the sake of pleasure. X, 1090. See *Intercourse*. *Spouse*. The fact that marriages now cannot exist without the evil of libido, although libido can exist without them, belongs to the condition of this mortal body. X, 460. To make use of libido is not always a sin. X, 817. To make good use of the evil of libido is a good work. X, 1443. Although libido is evil, one can use it well or badly. X, 457. Who uses it well or badly. X, 1304, 1317. Marriage makes good use of libido. X, 404, 1193. Conjugal chastity makes good use of it. X, 172, 1155, 1167. Against it, the incontinent employ the remedies of marriage, while the continent undertake glorious struggles. X, 820. Conjugal chastity makes good use of libido; religious widowly continence and sacred virginal integrity make better use of it by not using it. X, 1451. Those who use libido not for libido’s sake but for the propagation of offspring do not perform the devil’s work. X, 1442, 1443. Marriage orders the movement of libido; continence restrains and curbs it. III, 400. Holy married people would not wish to suffer libido in the begetting of children. VII, 425. When libido harms regenerated spouses. X, 413. Those who make good use of libido are not defiled by its stain. X, 763.

Libido is not comparable to hunger and other annoyances. X, 773. The impulse of libido is not moderated of its own accord. X, 737. In dreams libido generally reaches an end resembling the act itself and the movement proper to it. X, 460. Libido is imperious toward the unchaste, to be subdued by the chaste, and shameful to both the chaste and the unchaste. X, 460. It is not without reason that libido is hateful to Christ’s soldiers, by whom it is defeated. X, 1237.

Venereal libido absorbs the mind. X, 773, 774. It does not allow one to think holy thoughts. X, 808. It stirs up the whole person and claims him for itself. VII, 424. It prevents the mind from rising to eternal things. [Col. 0403] VII, 227. The fellowship that ought to exist between God and us is violated when the same nature whose author he is is polluted by the perversity of libido. I, 689. See *Desire*. Libido rules in every evil deed. I, 1225. Some are led by libido, others by reason, to the necessities of life. V, 340. Threefold libido. I, 690.

No one is so wise that he has no conflict at all against libido. VII, 629. In this life the saints struggle and contend against the libido of the senses. X, 773. Libido must also be curbed in married people. X, 716, 717. The extent to which chastity conquers libido both in married people and in the continent. X, 1160. When libido is conquered, the devil is conquered. X, 801. Should one therefore not resist libido because it is the punishment of sin? X, 788. One consents to libido rather than commands it. X, 798. An eighty-four-year-old man bought a female lyre-player for his libido. X, 713. The impulse of libido, broken by the gravity of a song. X, 798. “Does libido rise? Hold your members; what will she do now that she has risen?” V, 719. “She knows how to rise, but does not know how to conquer; by rising constantly without cause, she learns not to rise.” V, 719. “Let her burn without cause, and she consumes herself.” V, 719. At the perfection of our salvation, libido will perish like an infirmity. X, 1443. In those in whom it will not be healed, it will be condemned. X, 1155. Why libido is not evil in animals. X, 756, 757, 1193, 1194, 1372, 1373, 1374, 1453. Libido belongs to the nature of the animal, but to the punishment of man. X, 1360, 1363, 1372, 1373. See *Concupiscence*.

The libidinous do not believe that the ancient righteous could have used many women temperately. III, 76. The libidinous are described. III, 97. Why those who go after their desires are called loose and dissipated. IV, 687.

## Libosus of Vaga

Libosus of Vaga. IX, 143, 220.

## Libra

*Libra*, the book of Dictinius. VI, 522, 543, 548.

## Libyan Philosophers

Libyan philosophers. VII, 233.

## Licentius

Licentius, son of Romanianus. I, 928, 1080; II, 110. Augustine’s concern for him. II, 126. Augustine rightly claims for himself the affection of a father and mother toward Licentius. II, 126. Augustine recalls Licentius from disorderly and libidinous behavior to the pursuit of wisdom. II, 106, 107. Augustine commends Licentius to Paulinus. II, 110. And asks him to be willing to exhort and instruct Licentius. II, 110. Paulinus sends five blessed loaves to Romanianus and Licentius. II, 126. While living with Augustine at Cassiciacum, Licentius takes the part of interlocutor in the books written there. I, 905. And in the books *On Music*. I, 1081. Licentius was devoted to poetry. I, 922, 923, 933. And a student of philosophy. I, 907, 987, 988. Licentius’s poem to Augustine, his teacher. II, 104. Licentius’s golden talent. II, 107.

## Liciatum

Liciatum. VII, 777.

## Licinius

The Emperor Licinius. II, 304.

Licinius, consul. IX, 687.

## Licit Things

Some things are licit but not expedient. VI, 460, 463.

## Binding

No one is to be bound because of an offense except justly, for justice breaks unjust bonds. V, 509. How the faithful exercise the office of binding and loosing. V, 509.

Superstitious bindings. II, 1060; III, 50. Sacrilegious binding used to recover health. V, 1301, 1439. To use bindings. IV, 318.

## Limata

Limata. IX, 511.

## Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil. VIII, 613, 614, 660. A true and harmless tree. III, 377, 383. Why it is so called. III, 377, 384; VII, 425; X, 171, 172. It would rightly have been called this even if the first parents had not sinned. III, 385. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not forbidden because it was evil. III, 384. Yet it is evil for no other reason than that it was forbidden. VII, 420.

## Tree of Life

The tree of life was endowed with invisible power. III, 451. What it was to provide. X, 172. It kept old age away. VII, 394. And death. VII, 394, 396; X, 1598. Through its power the first parents could have been subject neither to disease nor to change with age. III, 447. The tree of life provided food by which the human body would be strengthened in stable health. III, 377. Through eating the tree of life, what takes place in the flesh of the first parents would have occurred, as it occurs in angels through participation in eternity. III, 447. Adam ate from the tree of life. X, 1581. Adam used to take the sacrament from it, and food from the other trees. VII, 394; X, 1580. The tree of life is both spiritual and bodily. X, 1598. The food of the tree of life signified something great. III, 377. The tree of life was both truly created and a figure of wisdom. III, 375, 376, 377. The tree of life is a type of wisdom. X, 172. And a sacrament. III, 447, 451; VIII, 615, 616. What is signified by the tree of life planted in the middle of paradise. III, 203. It signified Christ. VII, 701. After the first parents had been expelled from paradise, the tree of life remained as a memorial signifying the spiritual tree of life. VIII, 616. Whether anyone now eats the food of the tree of life—unless perhaps Enoch and Elijah—must not be asserted rashly. VIII, 616. Enoch and Elijah are believed to have been translated to where the tree of life is. X, 1581.

The wood carries us upon the waters of the sea. IV, 1380. Imperishable wood, from which the ark was built. [Col. 0404] IV, 1917. The wood by which the waters were made sweet, a figure of the cross. III, 616. The wood on which the limbs of the dying Christ were fixed was also the teacher’s chair from which he taught. III, 1950. He subdued the wood that did not subdue iron. IV, 1228. Fruit-bearing trees in the field, allegorically. V, 313. The trees of the field are the peoples’ communities. IV, 1370. The trees of the forests are the pagans. IV, 1234.

## Limatensis

The bishop of Limatensis. II, 162.

## Limentinus

Limentinus, the god appointed over the threshold. VII, 119, 184.

## Charcoal

Charcoal is placed beneath the boundary markers. VII, 713.

## Clay

The clay of the earth from which man was formed. III, 201. Those who fall from justice become clay of the deep. IV, 843. Clay and mud signify carnal concupiscence. IV, 434.

## Line

What a line is. I, 1041. A line can be divided transversely without limit. I, 874.

## Tongue

“Tongue” is understood in two ways. VIII, 296. The tongue testifies to what the heart wills. IV, 1191. Tongues are good or evil where the mind is good or evil. V, 1418. The tongue is not made guilty except by a guilty mind. V, 973. The temptation of the tongue. V, 1300. It is difficult sometimes not to be struck by the temptations of the tongue. V, 1526. A tongue placed in moisture easily slips on what is slippery. V, 978. The tongue is not in moisture without reason, since it slips easily. IV, 414. Silence is the remedy against this. IV, 414. A deceitful tongue is one that bears the appearance of giving advice while intending harm. IV, 1599, 1600. The flatterer’s tongue persecutes more than the murderer’s hand. IV, 869. “You do not give your belly foods of bitterness, yet you give foods of iniquity to your wicked tongue; as you choose what you will eat, so choose what you will say.” IV, 606. The tongue of the Jews, the sword by which Christ was killed. IV, 668, 669. How difficult it is, even in pious duties of preaching, exhortation, and so forth, not to sin with the tongue. IV, 414, 580. The tongue alienates one human being from another more than one animal from another. VII, 633. The tongues of the wicked are in the devil’s hand. IV, 1867. It is more tolerable to slip with the tongue than with one’s life. X, 728.

The tongue must be restrained. V, 635, 978. How difficult it is to tame the tongue. IV, 1827. No one can tame the tongue without the help of grace. X, 254. God is the ruler of the tongue. V, 375.

Why God’s tongue is called a pen. IV, 497. Christ’s tongue, his preachers. IV, 175. Popular speech is for the most part sound teaching. IV, 279. Our tongue is the song of Jerusalem. IV, 1771. A barbarous tongue is one that does not praise the Lord. IV, 1478. What every person has on his tongue must be held in the heart: “What God wills.” IV, 279. A priest whose tongue was cut out. V, 1596.

The tongue, for the sound uttered by the tongue. III, 1952. For speech made through the tongue. IV, 597. In the beginning there was one language, before the tower of Babel. III, 401. Whence the diversity of languages arose. VII, 483. Proud impiety introduced the diversity of languages, while humble piety brought them into the unity of the Church. IV, 636; V, 1245. Three languages chiefly excel throughout the world: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. IV, 692. Hebrew was the first of all languages. VII, 522. Whence the Hebrew language received its name. VII, 522. Hebrew, Punic, and Syriac are related languages. III, 1520. By what figure the Greek and Latin languages are spoken of. IV, 335. Knowledge of languages is necessary for understanding the Scriptures. III, 42. The original language is to be trusted more than its translation. VII, 454, 455.

The gift of languages was formerly a very great sign of the Holy Spirit descending upon believers. VII, 612. What the gift of languages signified. IV, 161, 1706; V, 461; VII, 612. What the languages of all nations in one person at Pentecost signify. V, 497, 946, 1230, 1232, 1234, 1550. All languages were shown to be destined to believe, when all languages were already sounding. III, 1991. Christ and the Church now speak in the languages of all peoples. IV, 161. Whoever is in the body of Christ speaks in the languages of all. IV, 1929. Now, in the Church itself, unity speaks as one in the languages of all nations. V, 534, 1246. Why the gift of languages is not now granted. V, 1230. Nor do those who believe speak in languages. IV, 1706.

When we speak, we endeavor to bring our very mind into the mind of the hearer, so that he may perceive it. VI, 183, 184. From where a child learns to speak. I, 666. ## Games

Games were first instituted for King Telxion of the Sicyonians. VII, 562. Games sacred to the gods below. VII, 99. Circus games. I, 725. At first used only among the Romans. VII, 44. Funeral games. VII, 253. The secular games renewed at Rome. VII, 98. The secular games are to be despised. IV, 1046. Why games were instituted for the gods. VII, 569. Processional games. V, 148. The trifling acts of iniquity: games and empty spectacles. V, 81, 83, 88.

“Games,” that is, places for presenting games. V, 203.

How the mockery of demons takes place. VII, 574.

The sevenfold number there confirms mourning. III, 596. See *Novemdial*.

How those who mourn are blessed. IV, 1099. The children ought to mourn when the bridegroom has been taken away. V, 1049.

## Moon

According to the Manichaeans, the moon was made from good water. VIII, 35. And is the ship of light. VIII, 35. What the moon was like when created. III, 275. It is absurd to say that it was originally made full. III, 236. It was perfected every day. III, 236. It is always full. III, 276. There are two opinions concerning where the moon receives its light. IV, 131, 132. The Manichaeans’ delirium concerning the moon’s increase and decrease. II, 207. Whence its increase and decrease arise. IV, 131, 132. The moon’s waning and waxing arise because it is more or less illuminated by the sun; or, if it has its own light, because it displays or conceals the part of the hemisphere in which the light is located. II, 207. The moon was presented as being lowered through an imaginary deception of the senses. VII, 295. It is not the moon itself that changes, but what is illuminated. III, 276. How ineptly some people speak falsely about the moon. IV, 1194. The Manichaeans worshiped the moon. VIII, 242, 300, 320. Moses does not revile the sun and moon. VIII, 300. Christians do not observe days, years, months, and seasons, although they celebrate Easter according to the calculation of the sun and moon. II, 209. In Scripture the moon allegorically signifies the Synagogue. II, 208; IV, 137. The Church. IV, 131, 908, 1373. Just as the moon appears larger to our eyes when it recedes from the sun and smaller when it approaches the sun, so the soul, receding from the sun of justice, advances toward outward things, but by approaching it turns toward inward things. II, 207, 208. By the name of the moon, the mutability of mortality is signified. IV, 728, 908, 1134, 1846. Likewise, knowledge. IV, 1760. The moon is an image of the resurrection. IV, 1324. The moon signifies Christ’s flesh. IV, 941. It denotes the carnal and foolish. IV, 944. “Break the moon, make fortune,” a saying of the avaricious. VI, 674.

## L

Twofold is the light: God, and the light that he made. VIII, 609. The Manichaeans do not distinguish between the light that is God himself and the light that God made. VIII, 404. Eternal and unchangeable light. I, 742, 801. What sort of light God is to be conceived as. V, 36. How excellent is the light that God is. VIII, 372. The light that God gives is not such that it can be darkened by anyone. IV, 200. We are light in the Lord, darkness without the Lord. V, 321, 1472. God is the light of the heart. IV, 206, 207. They see that light only who are pure in heart. IV, 206, 806. Whoever is given over to blindness of mind is shut out from the inner light of God. IV, 94. The pagan, though apparently living well, is in darkness with his eyes open; the Christian, though living badly, is in the light, but with his eyes closed. IV, 196, 197. From the light of God the soul itself receives counsel. IV, 1887, 1888. In the eternal light of God the rational soul reads certain things. IV, 1887, 1888. The light of human beings, the light of minds. III, 1398. The inner light, by whose aid we see and judge so many things. II, 615, 616. It is called the judging light. II, 616. The light is truth shining with its own splendor, from which souls are kindled like lamps. IV, 102, 103. The light of the most pure and unchangeable truth, by which things are made manifest. V, 524. The true light: righteousness and wisdom. V, 476. The soul is suffused with intelligible light so that it may perform righteous works. IV, 1191. The light of righteousness is seen by the eyes of the heart. III, 1659. The light of righteousness is a punishment to the disturbed mind before it is healed. V, 542. The disturbed mind neither dares nor is able to contemplate the light of righteousness. V, 542. The light of the heart is charity. II, 560. Love of the inner light. V, 1531. How the visible light of the sun and the invisible light of the Word of God differ. V, 676. The inner light compared with the visible light. V, 547. The visible light forms the colors of bodies; the invisible light forms the affections of souls. V, 1498. When we repent of sin, we are in the light. IV, 162. God made the light when Christ rose from the dead. IV, 532.

One light illuminates, another is illuminated. III, 1502, 1658; IX, 74. The true light must be distinguished from illuminated light. II, 541. A human being cannot be light for himself. V, 987. “You are not light for yourself, just as you are a great eye, powerless without light.” V, 437. The light by which every human being is illuminated. V, 437. Christ alone is the true light. V, 35. The light of God and the truth of God—and both of these are one Christ. IV, 478. How the true light illuminates every person coming into this world. X, 130. See Every. The thing that has been illuminated must beware of the wind of pride. V, 437. How holy men are the light of the world. V, 36. The light of the living. IV, 660.

Created light is twofold: spiritual and corporeal. VIII, 405, 611. One corporeal light is common to the wicked and to beasts, and another is the light of the righteous. IV, 1250. Light is threefold: ethereal, sensory, and rational; and so is the contrary of each. III, 228. It is not easily perceived by a human being that there is some light beyond the heavens. III, 228. How great is the difference between the light by which we see and the light by which we understand. VIII, 372. The Manichaeans nowhere distinguished the light by which we see from the light by which we understand. VIII, 372. The Manichaeans say that corporeal light is God’s nature. VIII, 35. The Manichaean fable about the battle of light with darkness. VIII, 293, 294. On the purification of light. VIII, 35, 36. Various difficulties concerning the created light on the first day. III, 254. God himself was the light of Adam’s eyes. IV, 405. Whether light is the first creature. III, 248. What sort of light was made in the beginning. III, 227, 228. And what its nature was. VII, 322. Whether it was something corporeal or spiritual. III, 232, 248. Whether God said “Let there be light” in temporal time or in the eternity of the Word. III, 248, 251. Why, in the creation of light, “And God made” is not added. III, 252, 269. Nor is it said, “And so it was made.” III, 292, 317. How the division made between light and darkness is to be understood. III, 228. How it is to be understood in spiritual creation. III, 254. The light made first is the formation of the spiritual creature. III, 311. It is intellectual life. III, 253. Light may be said to have been made when uncreated wisdom transfers itself into holy souls so that, once illuminated, they may shine. III, 258. The interpretation given of spiritual light and day should not be considered improper or figurative. III, 314.

Light is a divisible body. VIII, 185. Light is wholly present everywhere. VI, 658. The light of the sun causes forms and colors to be distinguished. V, 676. Light is the queen of colors. I, 800. Light is the most excellent of bodies. I, 1279. No sense, and no spontaneous bodily movement of the soul, exists without light and air. III, 363. The light by which we distinguish everything is as certain for us as it makes certain the things we see. II, 457. The eyes are nourished by light. III, 1495; V, 709. Light is the food of the eyes. IV, 1114; V, 183. Whence the light that shines through the eyes comes. VIII, 675. What it means to rise before the light. IV, 1670.

### Maccabees

The fire did not acknowledge the Maccabees, although it acknowledged the three youths. III, 2040. Why. V, 1380. The Maccabees and the three youths had different outcomes in persecution, yet the same protection of God was present. V, 202, 1380. More was granted to the Maccabees than to the three youths. V, 1300. God crowned the Maccabees secretly, but openly delivered the three youths. IV, 1945. In the fire the Maccabees failed in the flesh, not in faith. IV, 389. The Maccabees became martyrs for the ancient sacraments. II, 156. And for Christ. V, 1379. The Maccabees were Christians not merely in name but in reality. V, 1377. A solemn feast was rightly instituted for the Maccabees. V, 1377, 1379. A basilica was erected in their memory at Antioch. V, 1379. The mother of the Maccabees was seven times a martyr. V, 1379. Her courage is praised. IV, 855, 856, 868. From her, mothers should learn to love their children. V, 1379. The mother of the Maccabees represented the Church. V, 1380. She was like Mother Church. IV, 855.

The Jews do not possess the books of the Maccabees as they possess the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. IX, 729. The Church regards them as canonical. VII, 596. Why. VII, 596. They were not received by the Church without benefit, provided that they are read or heard soberly. IX, 729.

### Machaera

What Machaera is. IV, 1955. The sword of the tongue is greater than one of iron. III, 2062.

### Macomades, Macomadia

IX, 215, 473.

### Macrobius

A Donatist bishop. II, 536; IX, 755. Macrobius was a young man of good character. II, 406. He was ordained bishop of the Donatists at Hippo. II, 406; Note (d). Macrobius was asked in a letter from Augustine not to rebaptize Augustine’s subdeacon. II, 407. How unjust his reply was. II, 407, 408. Augustine convicted Macrobius of manifest injustice. II, 408, 409. Macrobius reproved the deeds of the Circumcellions through a Punic interpreter. II, 416.

### Mactaris or Mattaris

IX, 225.

### Madaurenses

The idolaters of Madaura, writing to Augustine, call him “father” and wish him salvation in the Lord. II, 1025. Augustine exhorts them to the true religion. II, 1027. The forum of Madaura, occupied by a multitude of deities. II, 81. What images are there. II, 82.

### Madiam

“Madiam” means “declining judgment.” IV, 1053. He was Abraham’s son by Keturah. III, 739.

### Midianites

The Midianites were descended from Abraham through Keturah. III, 582. The Midianites are sometimes called Ishmaelites. III, 582. And Ethiopians. III, 727. They are now called Saracens. III, 727.

### Maelith

“Maelith” means “giving birth” or “suffering.” IV, 613.

### Magdalene

Whether the sinful woman Magdalene was the sister of Lazarus is uncertain. III, 1748. Her conversion. IV, 810. Magdalene became more forward in seeking salvation than she perhaps had been in fornication. IV, 1660, 1661. She received healing because she regarded herself as sick. III, 1447. Christ appears to her, but she is forbidden to touch him. V, 1148, 1154. The meaning of Christ’s words to Magdalene. V, 1143, 1148, 1151, 1154. Magdalene represents the Church. V, 58.

### Magic

Porphyry at one time praises magic and at another condemns it. VII, 286. The impiety of magic is demonstrated. VII, 243.

The inventor of magical arts was Zoroaster. VII, 728. Magical arts arise from the vice of curiosity. I, 802. They are practiced through the teachings and works of demons. VII, 244. How the demon taught human beings magical arts. VII, 717. Magical consecration. V, 1439.

### Pharaoh’s magicians

V, 74, 562. Why they performed certain miracles like Moses. VI, 90, 696. Through demons the magicians can do whatever they can do. VIII, 875. God alone also creates those things that are transformed by magical arts. VIII, 875, 876. The water that Pharaoh’s magicians changed into blood was either seawater or water from the region in which the children of Israel were. II, 585. Whether the magicians raised the dead. II, 521. Apuleius the African, despite all his magical arts, could not attain even a single judicial office in the commonwealth. II, 534. David, without magical arts, rose from shepherding sheep to royal dignity. II, 534. The magicians are not to be compared with the prophets, much less with Christ, as regards miracles. II, 535. The Egyptian magicians were defeated by Moses. II, 521. When it is uncertain whether a medicine is magical or not, what matters is the intention with which each person uses it. III, 57. The magicians were burdened with many sins. V, 1036. Their impiety lay in sacrilege. V, 1030. The magicians were severely punished even among unbelievers. VII, 243.

A star appeared to the Magi on the day Christ was born. V, 1033. This star was a magnificent tongue of heaven. V, 1031, 1035. It had never appeared among the stars before, nor did it appear afterward. V, 1031. The authority of a splendid solemn feast proclaims everywhere on what day Christ was worshiped by the Magi. V, 1030, 1035. The gifts of the Magi. VI, 664. In the Magi, the first fruits of the nations were offered. V, 1033.

### Teacher

No one who teaches a human being knowledge is teacher except God. I, 602, 813. This is treated explicitly in the book *On the Teacher*. I, 1193. A human being admonishes outwardly; God, the truth, teaches inwardly. I, 1216. We testify that we have an inner teacher when, with an unerring judgment, we approve someone who gives good admonition. II, 576. He who admonishes outwardly through his ministers by signs teaches inwardly, by the realities themselves, through himself. II, 591. The one Teacher, Christ himself, taught Moses through Jethro, Cornelius through Peter, and Peter through Paul. II, 724. We are all fellow disciples under Christ the teacher. V, 155, 1367. The teacher is the temple from which God gives answers. III, 18. See *Teach*, *Doctor*.

### Master of memory

The official responsible for dictating and recording what the emperor answered orally. II, 431; Note (b).

### Gowned teachers

I, 672.

### Teaching authority

Teaching authority is dangerous; the disciplined person is secure. V, 155.

### Magistrates

Magistrates of an evil state administer certain acts of a good state, and conversely. IV, 735.

### Great matters

A great matter requires great men. I, 909. When the greatest matters are sought from small men, they usually make those men great. I, 909. God is great not in bulk but in power. II, 517. Among things that are not great in bulk, what is greater is what is better. VIII, 929. We can be great in God if we are little under him. IV, 758.

### Magnanimity

What it is. VII, 35. See *Greatness of spirit*.

### Magnates

Magnates are compelled to satisfy the desires of those who attach themselves to them. II, 994. To satisfy them, it is necessary that many things displeasing to God be done—and even then they do not satisfy them. II, 994.

### Magnet

A magnet is brought from India. VII, 714. The magnet’s power is astonishing. VII, 714, 719. It does not act upon silver. VII, 714. When a diamond is placed beside a magnet, it does not draw iron. VII, 714. An iron image suspended in a certain temple by magnetic stones. VII, 717.

### Magnificence

What magnificence is. VI, 21. The Lord’s magnificence is this: the justification of the sinner. IV, 1464. How great are magnificence and power in angels. IV, 1232. “You were seeking magnificence; love holiness. When you have been sanctified, you will be magnificent.” IV, 1232.

Let God always be magnified, never man. IV, 871. We magnify God not by making him great, but by praising him and acknowledging him as great. IV, 913. Wisdom, immortality, and health possess greatness, but not in the wicked. II, 836. There is a difference between greatness and swelling pride. V, 537.

### Magog

“Magog” means “from the roof.” VII, 676. The wars of Gog and Magog and the building of the temple in Ezekiel are difficult to understand. II, 719.

### Major Caelicolarum

II, 180.

### Major Basilica

V, 1194. Or the Basilica of the Majores, at Carthage. V, 209, 902, 1335.

### Superiors

Superiors are not to be offended, and who they are. V, 418.

### Majorinus

A bishop. II, 759, 780; IX, 90, 96. Bishop of Carthage. I, 617; II, 759, 780. Ordained bishop of Carthage by Donatus against Caecilian. IV, 375; VIII, 43; IX, 469, 533. The party of Majorinus was initially called that which was later called the party of Donatus. II, 302.

### May

The month of May takes its name from Maia, the mother of Mercury. VIII, 346.

### Malachi

Malachias, or Malachi, the prophet, is called an angel, and is believed by some to have been the priest Ezra. VII, 699. What he prophesied and at what time. VII, 593.

### Malacia

V, 623.

### Malchus

“Malchus” means “about to reign.” III, 1931. John alone explicitly gives this name. III, 1931. And Luke alone reports that the Lord healed his ear. III, 1931. The ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signifies hearing renewed after the old age was cut away. III, 1931.

### Slanderers

The freedom to slander does not make anyone blessed. VII, 174.

There is a class of slanderers who, whenever a bishop, cleric, monk, or nun has fallen, believe, proclaim, and insist that all such people are the same, although not all can be exposed. II, 270. They should not spread slanderous writings among those who are at odds, writings that those who are reconciled cannot erase. II, 250.
