The teeth of slanderers consume not the human being but his carnal desires. IV, 197. Those who live badly, even if their tongue is silent, curse the Lord by their life. IV, 1335, 1737. A curse is like oil in the bones of those who think themselves strong because they are permitted to do evil with impunity. IV, 1441. The person who glories in iniquity before human beings is covered with a curse as with a garment. IV, 1441. The person who deliberately attacks evil girds himself with a curse. IV, 1441.

### Curse

Why a curse is expressed in terrifying words. VIII, 636. God’s curse upon Adam belongs to the sentence of the one who punishes, not to the anger of one who curses. VIII, 616. When curses are spoken prophetically, they do not arise from the evil wish of one who invokes harm, but from the foreknowing Spirit who announces what will happen. VIII, 330. “Curse” is sometimes said because of the malicious error of those who speak, not because of any evil in the words themselves. IV, 460. Why Christ refrained from cursing the Jews. IV, 353. What barrenness Christ cursed on the tree. IV, 334. A rare example of a mother’s curse. V, 1443; VII, 769.

### Hammer

The devil is the hammer of the whole earth. IV, 1255.

### Malliana

II, 1034. A subdeacon of Mallianum. II, 1033.

### Malice

What malice and malignity are. IX, 87. Malice is the love of doing harm. V, 1560. The vice of malice is not nature but against nature. VII, 331. The malice of infants is natural. X, 1426. Malice may be called natural without any reproach against God’s institution and constitution. X, 1420. Malice was originally derived from Adam. X, 909. Human malice can possess a desire to do harm, but not the power to do so. IV, 291. What the depth of malice is. IV, 349. Malice is compared with fire. IV, 329, 330. Through the malice of the wicked, the good person is scourged, and through the servant the son is corrected. IV, 1213. Unchangeable malice belongs not to God but to the human being. X, 1423. “Malice” in the sense of punishment. V, 1400. Misery is the inseparable companion of malice. IV, 293. Malice is the lack of good. X, 1481.

### Evil

What evil is. VIII, 586, 587, 607. The Manichaean view of evil. X, 1529. It is refuted. VIII, 588, 589. The Manichaean error concerning evil. X, 1104, 1105. From what source they judged evil and good. VIII, 509. They think evil is not an accident but a substance. X, 1330. Evil is not a substance. I, 743, 1350; VIII, 193, 538. There is neither an evil nature nor a love of an evil nature. VIII, 393. Evil is not nature but against nature. VIII, 200, 201. For every kind of thing, that is evil which is against nature. I, 1347. It is an incompatibility hostile, as it were, to substance. I, 743, 1350. Evil is nothing but the privation of good. I, 688; VI, 13; VII, 325, 335; X, 743, 1495. The cause of evil is a falling away from good. VII, 357; X, 666, 672. A will falling away from the unchangeable good toward changeable good. VI, 244. There is no nature of evil; rather, the loss of good has received this name. III, 384. Evil is nothing other than corruption. VIII, 200. Corruption of natural measure, form, or order. VIII, 553. The entire term “evil” has been derived from the privation of form. VI, 13. For nature, evil is to fall away from being and to tend toward nonbeing. I, 1348. Evils have arisen from goods. X, 669, 1478, 1480, 1481, 1495, 1496. Evil proceeds only from good. X, 671. It can arise only from a good nature. X, 464, 669, 731. Evils arise not from nature but from the defect of nature. V, 987.

There is no supreme evil. VI, 13. It cannot be known without the supreme good. VIII, 101. Evil cannot exist without good. X, 1335. Evil is nothing except that which is also good. VI, 237. Evil can exist only in a good nature. VII, 353. Only in some good. X, 1124. Evils that are vices exist from goods and in goods. VI, 238; X, 1085. How evil is removed from nature. VII, 418. Good can be made from evil. X, 404. Evils can arise from good because good was made from nothing. X, 1481. Evil could arise in the human being because he was made from nothing. X, 1470–1475.

Where evil comes from is a major question for the Manichaeans. VIII, 101. It is also argued against the Manichaeans. VIII, 202, 203, 415, 596. The Seleucians assert that evil comes sometimes from God and sometimes from matter. VIII, 41. Whether God is the father of evils. VIII, 631. The Coluthians denied that God makes evils; the Florinians said that he created evils; both were heretics. VIII, 42.

How many kinds of evil there are. VIII, 607. “Evil” is used in two ways. VIII, 169. Everything called evil is either sin or the punishment of sin. I, 735, 1222; III, 132, 221. The evil of guilt proceeds from free choice. I, 595, 612. This is treated explicitly in the books *On Free Choice*. I, 1221; X, 1509. Evil comes to us from ourselves. V, 375, 1363. Each wicked person is the author of his own evil deed. I, 1221. Is anything evil except the act of the will that justice forbids the perpetrator to commit? X, 1456. The false principle of Julian: that the evil of the will cannot be attributed to nature. X, 1486. Evil wills have within themselves their own inner punishment, namely their own iniquity. III, 390. It belongs to God’s omnipotence to permit evils arising from free choice. VI, 359.

God is not the author of evils. I, 1235, 1346; III, 1703; VI, 16. Of the two kinds of evils in the world, which belongs to God? VIII, 117. The evil that is punishment is inflicted by the Lord. VIII, 169, 170. The evil of punishment is justly inflicted by God. I, 742, 1221. God brings evils upon the wicked—not sins, but punishments. II, 558.

The origin and source of evils. X, 465, 666. Sin. VIII, 123. The philosophers judged that evils occur because of sins committed by souls in another life. V, 1132. The Manichaeans and Catholics alike acknowledge the evils of this life, but they completely disagree about their origin. X, 1528. The Manichaeans want the evils of the human race attributed to some evil principle coeternal with God’s eternity; the Pelagians do not want them attributed to sin. X, 1339. Evils are not natural. III, 221. Is the evil with which we are born natural? X, 1127. It is false that evil cannot be refuted because it is natural. X, 1457. Sin is the cause of all our evils. V, 1131. There would be no evils if there were no sin. VII, 752. There would be no evil if we had not committed it. III, 384. Congenital evils come to us from a nature corrupted by sin. X, 1528. If no one had sinned, congenital evils would not have existed in paradise. X, 1529, 1549, 1550. The evils suffered by infants demonstrate original sin. X, 1269. They arise only from a corrupted nature. X, 821, 822. The distance between the Manichaean heresy concerning natural evil and the Catholic doctrine of original sin. X, 1263. The Pelagians do not refer evils to original sin. X, 1608. When the question is where evil comes from, the Pelagians assist the Manichaeans. X, 1538. On the question of evil, Catholics can easily answer the Manichaeans, but Pelagians cannot. X, 1509. The Catholic doctrine that nature was corrupted by sin must be confessed in order to defeat the Manichaean. X, 1532. What evil is according to Julian. X, 1494. Julian foolishly attempts to prove that evil must be traced back to God himself. X, 1487, 1488. Sin is the cause of the evils we suffer from creatures. III, 1386. The evils of this life arise only from sin. X, 1546, 1550. The evils of body and soul sprang from the root of sin. X, 1315, 1316. The evils seen in Adam’s descendants arise from original sin. X, 1488. The evils of those being born are to be attributed to the sins of their parents. X, 1382. We would not perceive evil except through experience. III, 384. Before experiencing evil, a human being could have understood what evil was. III, 386. See *Affliction*. The whole world is afflicted by temporal evils. II, 422. These evils, since they were foretold in the Prophets and in the Gospel, are not to be wondered at. II, 422. In what spirit the Prophets speak of evils as though they desired them. IV, 328, 329. Evils and goods here are common to wicked and good alike. IV, 1017; V, 236. It is otherwise after the judgment. VII, 661. Each person measures evils according to desire and habit. VI, 513. If piety and charity are absent, what is tranquility and rest from the world’s evils except material for lust and destruction, whether as invitation or assistance? II, 1026. Prosperity is the gift of God who consoles; adversity is the gift of God who admonishes. II, 957. Whence evil times and evil days come. V, 498, 909, 1363, 1416. See *Days*. It is the mark of fools and wicked people to accuse the order of things when they think the times are worse than they were. IV, 81. The evils that occurred in the Roman Empire through certain Christian emperors are unjustly charged against Christian teaching. II, 532.

There are certain evils of which God is the author. X, 711. How one and the same evil can be from God and from the devil. X, 806. The evil attributed to an angel or human being is not attributed to the one by whom they were created. X, 1499. Augustine attends rather to the higher causes of temporal evils. II, 995. How evils are from God. VIII, 204. For what purpose God permits them. VI, 236; VIII, 203. Why God permits life in this age to be spent amid various evils. IV, 329; X, 709. The evil that comes to you from God is not evil, because it is just. IV, 278.

God knows how to make good use of evils. VII, 435. He knows how to work well from evil. X, 1442. He knows how to make good from evil. VIII, 427, 429. God makes many good things from our evils and our sins. II, 727. Almighty God would not allow evils to exist if, in his supreme goodness, he could not use them well. X, 1495. God judged it more powerful and better to do good even from evils than not to allow evils to exist. VI, 245; VII, 751. Evil is not from God when good is made from evil. X, 1442. Evils benefit and goods harm according to the persons to whom they are given. III, 1801. Nothing evil happens to the saints that is not turned to their good. VII, 23. Evils are permitted for testing and correction. VII, 42. They serve our instruction. III, 1441. They test the virtue of the righteous. VII, 114. The good, whether they live or die, cannot perish through transitory evils. VII, 74. Amid these pressures, the sour lees of those who murmur and the oil of those who confess never cease to flow. II, 422. Present evils either pass from us while we live or are forgiven us when we die. V, 402. God makes good from evils, either by healing them through mercy or by ordering them through judgment. III, 1924.

How one may use evil well. X, 142. The evils of this life, which it is impossible to avoid, matter greatly in respect of the reason for which, the hope with which, and the end toward which each person suffers them. II, 938. God’s servants suffer temporal evils in two ways. II, 422. Temporal evils are not to be feared. VI, 724. What good people also suffer is to be endured with an even temper. VII, 660. For the sake of faith and piety, all bodily evils are to be endured. VII, 313. If you truly love what is good with all your heart, you will bear every evil patiently and with equanimity. V, 1397. It is characteristic of Christians to suffer temporal evils and hope for eternal goods. V, 1356. Whatever evils belong to this life are not to be compared with eternal ones. V, 937. In comparison with eternal fire, they are not small but nothing. V, 150. So that we would not fear evils, Christ endured them all in himself. VI, 339. See *Goods*. Augustine shows that the evils afflicting the world are not signs of the imminent coming of the judgment. II, 918, 919.

The two evils of the human being are mortality and iniquity. V, 934. The root of evils is desire. X, 370. The two evils of the human being are error and weakness. V, 987. Ignorance and concupiscence are the sources of all human misery. VI, 244. Moral evils are to be counted either as the only evils or as the greatest. VII, 112. The wicked shrink from bodily evils, but not from moral evils. VII, 113. The wicked care to enjoy only bodily goods and not to suffer only bodily evils. VII, 78. The wicked count as evils only bodily and external disadvantages. VII, 79. The wicked regard possessing every good except themselves as the greatest good. VII, 79. It is one thing to be evil and another to suffer evil. V, 319. There is no other evil except sin. VIII, 117. An evil deed is done only by the wicked. VII, 421. An evil deed is one in which lust rules. I, 1224. Whatever evil in you comes from sins is yours; whatever good is found in justifications is God’s. IV, 193. Human beings sometimes do evil voluntarily and sometimes under compulsion. X, 1494. Those who refrain from evil through fear, while they find opportunities, do not become evil; they are revealed as having already been evil. IV, 1190. A Christian is not held accountable if some evil happens to another through things that he does or possesses for a good and lawful purpose. II, 187. Every evil deed involves toil. IV, 1811. Those seeking permission to do evil seek examples from people who live badly. V, 1579. Evil must not be done so that good may come. X, 808. Whoever seeks evil, although what he has done may benefit others, cannot discover good. IV, 212. Whatever is learned not through wisdom but through experience is happily not known. X, 1532. Things done badly are to be mourned, even if later they are corrected as far as possible. II, 231. Evils without grief are worse. VIII, 557. Through the equity of his governance, God both makes good use of the wicked and rightly orders perverse things. VIII, 329. God makes good use of the evils of sinners. VIII, 563. God permits the wicked to do evil because he is eternal and sees what he has reserved for them. IV, 1178.

What it means to complete evil. X, 431. The evil against which the baptized struggle comes from original sin. X, 680. Who is said to abstain from every evil thing. X, 306. How the Apostle said that he does the evil he does not want. X, 560. Congenital evils are overcome through grace. X, 1427. To turn away from evil and do good is not possible for the human will except through grace. X, 1297. It is not in the power of the children of human beings to be freed from evil unless grace gives them the power to become children of God. X, 1144. What it means to be freed from evil. V, 1364. When a human being asks to be freed from evil, he asks to be freed from himself. V, 986, 987. Christ frees from congenital evil. X, 1123. What the end of our evils is. VII, 621.

To repay evil for evil appears to be justice, but this is not God’s justice. IV, 87. It is the justice of the unjust, if it may be called justice. IV, 1433. When a human being repays evil for evil, doing so with an evil intention, he himself is first evil, since he wishes to punish evil. IV, 87. Whoever does not repay those who repay him with evils is perfect. IV, 99. See *Avenge*. Whoever reproves the person by whom he has been troubled does not always repay evil for evil. II, 322, 323.

How evils are from God and not from God. VIII, 100. Can the wicked be counted among the works that God made very good? III, 440. God made the wicked with respect to nature, not with respect to guilt. V, 587. The wicked receive their evil will from themselves, but from God they receive a good nature and a just punishment. III, 434. God creates the wicked in the same way as he feeds and nourishes the wicked. X, 1504. This is not contrary to God. X, 1506. Why God creates those whom he knows will become wicked. X, 1200. God protects the wicked as his own sheep. IV, 350. The wicked are vessels perfected for destruction. III, 606. If God willed it, even the wicked would be good. III, 434. God could have turned the will of the wicked toward good, but he did not; why he did not is in his own keeping. III, 434. The wicked were created for the benefit of the saints. III, 433, 434, 440.

### The wicked

What a wicked person is. X, 370. Each person is wicked by his own will. VII, 50. We are all wicked. V, 467, 559; VI, 662. No one can claim that the wicked are not within his discipline. II, 272. The wicked and heretics are described from various testimonies of Scripture. IX, 204, 217. The wicked are wicked for this reason: so that they may be blessed. IV, 293, 1502. To the extent that we are wicked, we are less. III, 32. No wicked person does good. V, 409. No wicked person fails first to harm himself. IV, 329. We are not wicked with impunity, because God is just. III, 32. God does not need the punishments of the wicked. III, 434. Through the punishments of the wicked, God provides for the salvation of the good. III, 434. The wicked person is his own punishment. V, 1364. To the good person, the wicked person is grievous, even to look upon. V, 117. The wicked insult the good. IV, 1209. They scourge the good. IV, 1213, 1214. Only the wicked rage against the wicked. V, 1392.

The happiness of the wicked is a source of scandal to some. V, 126, 134, 168, 203, 1154. It is also an occasion of falling. VII, 703. It gives the weak an occasion to murmur. IV, 190, 357, 620. Their complaints are restrained. IV, 190, 620–622, 1196. Even good things harm the wicked. III, 603. The wicked are not truly well off, nor are the good truly ill off. V, 319. Even if the wicked reign, he is a slave. VII, 114. How miserable the wicked are in tribulations. IV, 369. The wicked have two kinds of knowledge and two kinds of forgetfulness. VII, 803. The wicked want every good except themselves. V, 187, 468, 512, 630, 1362. Whoever has been freed from his own evil is secure from other evils. V, 253, 1364.

The wicked surround God’s servants on every side. V, 55. We must live among the wicked. IV, 329, 1464. How great a punishment is the necessity of living among the wicked. IV, 1268. The wicked are mixed among the good. IV, 735, 1604, 1605, 1693. Let the good person who is mixed among the wicked be secure. IV, 194. The wicked are manifest, while the good are hidden. IV, 1767. The wicked are mixed among the good in every gathering of a multitude. IV, 634, 635. In every way of life. IV, 356, 1278, 1279, 1730. In households, even the more holy ones. II, 272. This is proved by examples. II, 272. There will be no wicked when there are no people tested through them. IV, 362. If the wicked did not exist, there would be no reason to pray for enemies. V, 120. God, knowing that we are to be exercised, mixes in with us those who will not persevere. IV, 635. The wicked are far more numerous than the good, who lie hidden among the wicked like grain among chaff. IV, 539.

- The wicked mixed with the good in the Church. IX, 96. From the Donatists’ own confession: [the wicked are] in the Church, even though hidden; by whom they were sown. IX, 634. How the Donatists attempted to evade the Gospel parables concerning the mingling of the good and the wicked in the Church. IX, 742. The wicked are not in Christ’s body. IX, 345, 346. They may appear to be inside, but are outside. IX, 481, 482. They are outside the Church, because they are upon the sand, not upon the rock. IX, 212, 216. At times the Church permits the wicked, even unwillingly, to use the sacraments, lest disturbance and schism occur. V, 51. The wicked must be tolerated by the good. V, 1093, 1165. They must be tolerated both outside and inside. V, 119, 319, 471, 1093, 1546. They must be tolerated in the Church. II, 411; IV, 190, 460, 635, 636, 637, 653, 654, 736, 1604, 1605; VI, 228; IX, 30, 32, 48, 51, 56, 83, 104, 493, 742, 744. Why they must be tolerated. IX, 69. They must be tolerated for the sake of unity. IX, 88, 90, 91, 92, 94, 370, 629. See Weeds. The wicked whom we cannot correct or condemn must be tolerated. IX, 746. Let a person mercifully rebuke what he can; what he cannot, let him bear patiently, and let him groan and grieve with love. IX, 94. The wicked should rather be tolerated than rashly removed by judgment. V, 1546. The wicked must be tolerated for the sake of the good; the good must not be abandoned for the sake of the wicked. II, 329. To tolerate the wicked for the sake of unity is worthy of no small praise, much less of any reproach. II, 171. We ought to desire to tolerate the wicked here rather than to be tolerated by the good. VI, 604. The wicked are more easily tolerated by the good than by the wicked, just as one healthy person more easily bears two sick persons than two sick persons bear one another individually. IV, 190. No Scripture fails to admonish us that the wicked are to be tolerated in the Church. II, 1065. The Lord himself taught this by tolerating Judas. III, 1762. The Church must not be abandoned because of the mingling of the wicked. II, 410. Sound doctrine teaches that one must neither withdraw from the Church on account of the wicked nor neglect discipline toward the wicked themselves. VI, 199, 200, 201. Although the wicked are not separated from the people of God, ecclesiastical discipline nevertheless does not sleep with respect to them. IX, 669. Tolerance of the wicked does not exclude the corrections of ecclesiastical discipline. IX, 656. Emeritus denied that the wicked should be tolerated by the good in unity and for the sake of peace. IX, 743. Tichonius and the other Donatists said that they should be tolerated, even if true crimes were charged against the wicked. IX, 96, 254, 257. When the contagion of sin has invaded the multitude, not excommunication but the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. IX, 93. Gaudentius taught that the good perish even through the contagion of wickedness that has gone unrecognized. IX, 743.

- If the wicked are in the Church, they can harm no one. IX, 29, 50, 51, 53, 55, 56, 57, 69, 275, 276, 655, 656, 657, 658. How innocence may be preserved among the wicked. IX, 393. Be good among the wicked, and you will be good without the wicked. V, 1162. The wicked do not harm those who have not consented to their deeds. VI, 201. Those who tolerate the wicked do not share in their sins, just as Paul did not share in the sins of the false brothers, nor the apostles in Judas’s theft and crime. IX, 344. The wicked are spiritually separated from the good; but if they are also separated bodily, they become worse. IX, 200. Separation of the heart from the wicked, not bodily separation, is commanded. V, 549, 551, 553; IX, 349, 633. The mingling of the wicked with the good is not eternal but temporal, and not spiritual but bodily. IX, 349. Throughout this life the wicked are separated from the good not by bodily segregation but by difference in conduct. IX, 566. This bodily separation from the wicked is reserved for the end of the age. IV, 735; VII, 611; IX, 249. See Sin.

- The wicked are not in this world without purpose. IV, 630. Why the wicked are in this world. V, 118. The wicked here are placed in their proper position for good uses. V, 1382. The abundance of the wicked exists for the purification of the good. V, 118, 120. Although the wicked are wicked through their own fault, God brings good out of their wickedness. IV, 1398. The wicked use God’s good works for evil. IV, 1396. It belongs to the wicked to use good things badly; God, by contrast, uses wicked things well. V, 117, 1382. God makes good use of the wicked. II, 539; X, 1303. How. II, 1084. Just as the wicked use God’s good things badly when they are not corrected, so God, conversely, makes good use even of their wickedness—not only for his own justice, etc., but also for the training and advancement of his saints. II, 1085. God uses the wicked not according to their perverse will but according to his own upright will. V, 1067. God makes good use of the wicked and adapts their wickedness to train and admonish the good. II, 860. In what way the wicked benefit the good. VII, 478. The wicked person does the righteous no harm but benefits him. V, 202, 253. How many good things God grants us through wicked people. IV, 1214, 1215. Power over the good is given to the wicked for the benefit of the good. VI, 93. The righteous are tested through the wicked. IV, 362. The wicked exist for the admonition or training of the good. III, 601, 606, 788, 794. Every wicked person either lives so that he may be corrected, or lives so that the good may be trained through him. IV, 630. The wicked serve others as an aid to training and an example of fear. III, 434. A wicked person is a sharp razor. V, 202. A powerful wicked person is an excessive razor that cuts away what is superfluous. V, 421. God will repay the wicked according to their wickedness, not according to the benefit that the righteous have derived from it. IV, 1214, 1215. Because the wicked willingly and unjustly use good things, they will justly be tormented by evil things against their will. II, 554. Why God spares the wicked. IV, 1204, 631. The wicked are preserved here so that good people may be born from them. V, 1383. Wicked Christians are more to be feared than Jews and pagans. VI, 343. It is not lawful to rage against the wicked. V, 1389. Why and how the wicked are to be loved. VII, 22. The wicked are to be loved so that they may cease to be wicked. II, 659. Whoever deals with the wicked in such a way that they repent of their wickedness knows how even to benefit them through indignation. II, 649, 651. The wicked perish either through conversion to righteousness or through the loss of their power against the good. III, 1359. If a wicked person becomes displeased with himself, once corrected he will become pleasing to himself. V, 513. A wicked person who has died is to be mourned twice over. V, 1392. One must not be led by the authority of those who live badly and prevent others from living rightly. V, 546, 548. From the bad life of those who were thought good, nearly all good people come under evil suspicion. IV, 243. The wicked will have no place in the future life. V, 1383. The wicked are like hay. IV, 1375.

Mamitus, the twelfth king of the Assyrians. VII, 564.

Nurslings (mammantes). IV, 1235.

Mammon is interpreted as “riches.” III, 1349; IV, 620. Among the Hebrews, mammon means “riches”; among the Punic peoples, “profit.” III, 1290; V, 648. Whoever serves mammon endures a harsh and destructive master. III, 1290. Why riches are called “mammon of iniquity.” IV, 552; V, 250, 328, 648, 650.

Nurslings reared by a nurse (mammothrepti). IV, 246.

Manasse is interpreted as “necessity.” III, 820. “Forgetting.” IV, 719, 1022.

Slaves are so called because they were captured by hand. III, 590.

What the holy commandment is. VI, 226. How the commandment leads to life and to death. VI, 104. Know that the commandment is a weapon—not one by which it kills you, but one by which the enemy is killed by you; yet do not presume upon your own strength. V, 831. We ought to look into God’s commandments as into a mirror. IV, 1510. They are rightly hidden from those who understand earthly things. IV, 1520. They are understood more perfectly when they are practiced. IV, 1550. The divine commandments, which especially correspond to the will itself, display free choice. X, 883. It would have profited the faithful of ancient times nothing to have loved God’s commandments unless Christ had set them free. IV, 1593. Human weakness is not brought into conformity with God’s upright and arduous commandments unless his prevenient love assists it. IV, 1512.

[Col. 0416] God’s commandments are fulfilled only through grace. I, 796; V, 1162. “If you wish, you will keep the commandments”: in what sense this was said. X, 900. To keep God’s commandments is to persist in his love. IX, 151. Grace brings it about that God’s commandments, which could not be fulfilled through fear, are fulfilled through love. IV, 1579. The ways of the Lord are hard for fear but easy for love. X, 290. If a commandment is performed from fear of punishment, not from love of righteousness, it is performed slavishly, not freely; and therefore it is not truly performed. X, 217. “The commandment is broad”: this means charity. IV, 1561, 1562. The new commandment makes a new person. V, 1533. How God’s commandments are to be sought. IV, 1539. Whoever attempts to fulfill God’s commandments for the sake of an earthly reward does not fulfill them, because he loves not the commandments themselves but something else. IV, 1563, 1579. The Gospel commandments are more sublime than what many people in Catholic communion practice. VIII, 225. Why not all the commandments are fulfilled by every saint. X, 1297.

A mandate made by the Donatists concerning the Conference. II, 577. Not without the charge of falsehood. II, 577.

Mandrake apples are rare. VIII, 435. Their qualities. VIII, 435. Some believe that mandrake apples produce fertility in barren women. VIII, 435. Mandrake apples symbolize popular glory. VIII, 435.

Eating is not a sin; rather, sin consists in using immoderately the gifts of God, which he has provided for their proper uses. V, 800. What is a just reason for eating and drinking. V, 346. Christians have been granted permission to eat everything with moderation, blessing, and thanksgiving. V, 802. A human being eats from necessity; an angel, from power. V, 1618. After the resurrection there will be the power, not the necessity, to eat. V, 1618. To eat food that does not perish is to believe. III, 1602. Why David refused to eat with the proud, although we read that the Lord ate with them. IV, 1289. In a certain manner the Church eats those whom it transfers into its own body. IV, 241, 242. To eat Christ’s body. See Eucharist.

How “morning” should be understood in the creation narrative. III, 235, 240, 296, 312, 314. When morning will come. V, 58. It will be morning when we see what we believe. IV, 1853. “Morning” signifies the prosperity of the age. IV, 782. The time of consolation. IV, 1173.

We remain in Christ through need; he remains in us through mercy. V, 742.

Manganae. II, 71.

To wear sleeves (manicare). III, 808.

The pagans considered all the dead to be Manes gods. VII, 253. They also considered them to be the souls of human beings whose merits were uncertain. VII, 265.

Manes the Persian. VIII, 485, 487. Or Manichaeus. VI, 305. Why he was later called Manichaeus or Mannichaeus. VIII, 34, 361. Manichaeus usurped the name “apostle.” I, 1341; VIII, 38, 519, 530; IX, 271. He prefixed this opening to all his letters: “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ.” I, 1341, note 1. Why he called himself an apostle of Jesus Christ. VIII, 177. He falsely calls himself Christ’s apostle. VIII, 283. His disciples called him this foolishly. VIII, 69, 520, 526. It cannot be proved that he was Christ’s apostle. VIII, 176. His disciples said that the Holy Spirit had come to us through Manichaeus. VIII, 69. They also said that the Lord’s promise concerning the Holy Spirit had been fulfilled in their Manichaeus. II, 1035. Manichaeus himself said that the Holy Spirit was personally present in him with full authority. I, 709. Manichaeus was believed by his followers to be the Holy Spirit. VIII, 177, 178, 292, 525. What is written in the New Testament concerning the Paraclete cannot apply to Manichaeus. VIII, 507.

His disciples boasted that Manichaeus had come to disclose the figures of the ancients. VIII, 189, 308. His disciples praised Manichaeus for speaking naked and proper truth after removing the coverings of the figures. VIII, 307, 308. Manichaeus’s books are full of fables. I, 707, 710. Manichaeus had twelve disciples, corresponding to the apostolic number. VIII, 38. Manichaeus was killed. VIII, 178. The feast of Manichaeus’s birthday was celebrated with great solemnity during Easter. VIII, 178, 179. Manichaeus was called “father” by his disciples. VIII, 207. The ravings of Manichaeus. VIII, 181. His precepts. VIII, 223. His errors committed to writing. I, 710, 1355, 1356. Manichaeus’s writings. VIII, 517, in the Admonition 518, 529, 530. His epistle. X, 1318. Found at Constantinople. X, 1316. Julian assisted by the speeches of Florus. X, 1316, 1327. Manichaeus’s letter to Patricius. X, 1325, 1404. To the daughter of Menoch. X, 1404. In a written letter Manichaeus provided a rule of life extremely difficult to observe. I, 1376. Manichaeus’s Epistle of the Foundation. VIII, 400. Manichaeus’s foundation, which Augustine calls ruinous. VIII, 580. His writings contained many things about the stars, written with extreme ignorance. I, 709. Manichaeus was deceived in the question of the cause of sin. X, 1464. Manichaeus and Melitidis. X, 1462.

Manichaeans. III, 1875; V, 551, 573, 657, 659, 984, 1122, 1641; IX, 469. They caused a schism in Persia. V, 1174. Manichaeans in Paphlagonia and in Gaul. VIII, 570. Manichaeans, disciples and successors of the heretics Hymenaeus and Philetus. VIII, 219. Why the Manichaeans were called Catharists. VIII, 36. Their doctrines. VIII, 34. Their fables are full of blasphemies. IV, 1907. Various heads of the Manichaean heresy. VIII, 510. The Manichaean error concerning the nature of God. VII, 336; X, 1126. What they thought about God. IV, 1040, 1907, 1908. Their mad opinion concerning their god. VIII, 466. The Manichaeans’ blasphemies concerning the nature of God. VIII, 565, 566, 567, 571, 595, 598. They believed in two gods, one good and the other evil. I, 1317. Or rather, in two natures or substances and two mutually opposed principles. I, 1346; III, 130. Their error concerning the two natures. III, 1305, 1703, 1705; IV, 108, 1922; V, 821, 847, 985; X, 666. The Manichaeans imagined the whiteness of immense light extending everywhere through infinite spaces, but split on one side, as it were, by a certain black wedge; thus they taught that there were two opposing kingdoms. III, 165. They asserted that the kingdom—or race—of darkness was eternal and the supreme evil. I, 1346. They further said that evil was earth, a gloomy and deformed mass immensely deep and long, and also mind, or a thin and subtle mass wandering through the earth. I, 716, 1351. They wish the nature of the race of darkness to have always been evil, without any beginning. VI, 363. They professed that the kingdom of light was truly God and granted it a simple, immutable, impenetrable, and incorruptible nature. I, 1346. The Manichaeans do not even understand what a body is. V, 106. They can do nothing but confess an immutable God. V, 105. The madness of the Manichaeans concerning two natures in conflict with one another. VI, 360, 364. Their fiction concerning the struggle between the God of light and the prince of darkness. X, 1071. Concerning the race of darkness rebelling against God. VI, 292, 358. When the race of darkness once rebelled against God and attempted to invade the kingdom of light, they dreamed that the good God, unable to find any other way to resist the enemy, was compelled by necessity to send here a good soul, a certain portion of his substance; that the enemy was tempered by its mixture, and that the world was fashioned. I, 1352, 1355, 1356; III, 130. They maintain that God’s substance was corrupted in part by the substance of evil and brought into the necessity of sinning. II, 724. They said that a portion of the good God, mixed with the princes of darkness, polluted and bound throughout the whole world, was purified through the food of their Elect and through the sun and moon; but whatever could not be purified from it was, at the end of the age, to be bound in an eternal and punitive bond. II, 1034. The Manichaeans’ god is captive, polluted, and so forth. VIII, 35, 36. The Manichaeans say that divine help is given to the merits of the good nature. X, 573. The Anthropomorphites have an even more intolerable and dishonorable conception of God. VIII, 189.

The Manichaean error concerning the cause of the world’s creation. VII, 335; VIII, 35. They confess that the good God fashioned the world, though from an alien nature and matter. VIII, 603. They rave that this world was fashioned from the members of God, with the entrails of the race of darkness mixed in. IV, 1822. They said that God fashioned the heavens, but not from his own substance. I, 864. They said that there were eight earths and ten heavens, that Atlas carried the world, that Splenditenens suspended it, and so forth. VIII, 508. In that kingdom of evil were five caves of the elements: one full of darkness, another of waters, another of winds, another of fire, and another of smoke; and animals were born in each of those elements—creeping things in the darkness, swimming things in the waters, flying things in the winds, quadrupeds in the fire, and bipeds in the smoke. I, 1351. They said that the world was fashioned from these things. I, 1351. By the good God. I, 1317. The Manichaean error concerning the twofold earth, the kingdom of light, and the kingdom of darkness. VIII, 533. The origin of their fantasies concerning the earth of darkness. VIII, 197. They say that the good God is not the author of all natures. X, 572. The Manichaean opinion concerning the origin of flesh. V, 189. They invent the claim that all corporeal nature comes from the race of darkness. V, 105, 106. They deny that God is the creator of bodies. III, 217; X, 1125. They say that bodies have an origin coeternal with themselves. X, 651. They said that flesh, the tiniest animals, and everything that clings to the roots of the earth are generated and formed by the evil mind. I, 864; VIII, 475. They thought that rational souls existed in beasts. I, 1370. And in trees. I, 1368. They attributed the power of understanding to plants. III, 229. They believed that trees hear our voices, understand words, observe bodily movements, and even perceive thoughts. I, 1369. They held that plants and stones possess the sensation of pain and groaning. III, 2074. They said that a fig tree weeps when it is plucked, and that the vine feels pain, senses, sees, and hears. I, 1074. For this reason they thought one should abstain from slaughtering animals and tearing up plants. I, 1368. They held that to kill a tree or an animal is homicide. II, 1368. The Manichaean error concerning the commandment against killing. VII, 34. They believed that a human being was reincarnated into a tree. I, 1369.

The Manichaeans thought that some portion of God was present in vegetables, lettuces, fruits, and so forth. I, 1362. The Manichaean god, bound and polluted in food, is purified by being eaten. VIII, 498. They said that the soul, according to the merits of its pollution, enters a human being through food and drink. X, 613. They did not offer bread to one who was eating. IV, 1823. They said that wine was the gall of the princes of darkness, although they did not spare the grapes themselves from being eaten. I, 1364. Their refined abstinence. I, 1357. Gluttony. I, 1367, 1374. Impurity. I, 1374. The Manichaeans said that it was more advantageous for a person to be a moneylender than a farmer; why. IV, 1823. Gold was unjustly accused by the Manichaeans. V, 329. They considered it unlawful for the faithful to possess fields, houses, or money. I, 1343, 1345.

The Manichaean error concerning the sun. VIII, 391. The Manichaeans worshiped the sun. I, 1351; III, 199, 216; IV, 189. As a particle of light in which God dwells. III, 199. As God himself. V, 105. As the Creator himself or a part of him. V, 329. They believe that the sun is not a body. V, 106. The Manichaean delirium concerning the moon’s waxing and waning. II, 207. Their fiction concerning intercourse between the prince of darkness and a woman. X, 864. The Manichaeans say that human beings were created by the eternal prince of darkness from the mingling of two natures that had always existed, one good and one evil. X, 441. They say that human beings were not instituted by God. X, 570, 607, 611, 612. They wove a long fable concerning the creation of Adam and Eve. I, 1375. They thought themselves to be the nature and substance of God. VIII, 261. They said that souls belonged to Christ, bodies to the devil, and that both sexes came from the devil. VI, 365. The Manichaean error concerning the soul. VII, 336; X, 1325. They teach that our soul is what God is. VI, 297. That it is a part or particle of God. V, 986; X, 572. They assert that the souls not only of human beings but also of animals are of God’s substance and are parts of God. II, 718, 841, 1033. In wishing the soul to be part of God, the Manichaeans futilely refer its stain and weakness back to the body. II, 720. The Manichaean heresy concerning two souls is completely overturned by the definition of sin and will. VIII, 105, 107. The Manichaean opinion concerning the transmission of souls. X, 1218.

The Manichaean error concerning Christ’s incarnation. X, 1034. The Manichaeans say that the God announced in the Old Testament is not Christ’s Father. III, 1711. They do not deny that Christ is God. V, 104. But they say that he is God alone. V, 229. They believed that Christ extended toward our salvation as if from the mass of God’s most radiant substance. I, 715. They never dared to say “Father and Son” except as being of one substance. V, 105. The Manichaeans blaspheme the virgin birth. X, 573. They say that Christ had no mother. IV, 1685. They attempt to assert this from Matthew, chapter 12. IV, 129. They deny that Christ was born of a virgin and that his flesh was real. I, 715; II, 1032. They are refuted. III, 1452. The Manichaeans deny that Christ was human. V, 573; VI, 682. They teach that Christ had no body. V, 104, 477. Nor was truly human, but a phantom. V, 658, 659. They say that Christ had no flesh, or only simulated flesh. IV, 411, 1208; V, 659, 985, 1125; VI, 365; X, 613. They say that he did not undergo a true death on the cross. IV, 411, 1208. Rather, that he was crucified in a phantasm. I, 713. They said that Christ was crucified throughout the whole world. IV, 1823. How, and by whom, they dreamed that the cross of light was harmed. IV, 1823. The Manichaeans vainly boast that they think more highly of Christ because they call him spirit alone. V, 1123. By denying Christ’s flesh, they empty the whole mystery of our redemption. V, 1122.

The Manichaeans attack Christ’s grace, nullify his baptism, and dishonor his flesh. X, 573. They do not wish the creature to be liberated by Christ’s flesh and blood. X, 612. They consider baptism superfluous at every age. X, 613. The Manichaeans worshiped the sun and said that it was Christ. IV, 132, 133, 1194. They are censured. V, 35. The Manichaeans thought that Christ was the serpent who led Eve to eat from the tree of life. III, 216. Hence the sect of the Ophites. III, 216.

The Manichaean error concerning evil. X, 1463. They think that the nature of evil is coeternal with God. X, 1008. They mix the immutable substance of evil with the nature of their god. X, 1104, 1105. Thus they make God’s nature corruptible and captive under an alien nature. X, 1104, 1105. The Manichaeans introduce a nature of evil endowed with its own principle and opposed to God. II, 722. They affirm that the cause of sin is an evil nature. X, 612. They say that vices are natures and substances. X, 1085. They say that an evil nature has been mixed into the human being. X, 441. They thought that there were two souls in one body: one from God and a part of God, the other from the race of darkness, proceeding from its own evil principle and coeternal with God. I, 608; III, 130. They said that these souls struggle with each other in a human being when the flesh desires against the spirit. I, 758, 759. The Manichaeans referred all good things to the good soul and all evil things to the evil soul. I, 608. One Manichaean did not fear death because he said that it was the separation of good from evil. II, 272. The Manichaean error concerning the struggle of flesh and spirit. VI, 709, 710. The Manichaeans’ extreme madness in saying that the nature of good is compelled to do evil. X, 1113. The Manichaean error concerning desire. V, 815, 842. They thought that desire was of the evil substance, coeternal with God. X, 1318. They criticized desire not as an accidental vice but as a nature evil from eternity. X, 572. They denied that sin took its beginning from free choice. X, 572, 607. They also denied that original sin had passed to all from the first human being, who was initially pure and later corrupted through free choice. X, 613. They denied that free choice arose from what previously was not evil. X, 608, 611. They said that the Creator God was blamed when the origin of evil was traced to free choice. I, 594. They attributed their sins to the race of darkness. IV, 270, 1821, 1822. They said that they sinned when the nature of evil prevailed over the nature of God. VI, 358. Paulinus extols Augustine’s five books against the Manichaeans with praise. II, 101. He believes their dictated words to have been divinely inspired. II, 100. He calls them the Pentateuch. II, 101. The books concerning Free Choice were written against the Manichaean heresy because of the question, “From where does evil come?” I, 1211; the treatises that follow are contained in this volume.

Julian’s slander that Catholics agree with the Manichaeans concerning the origin of evil. X, 1113. Julian called those who acknowledged original sin Manichaeans. X, 1149, 1155, 1191, 1193. Pelagius charged the Catholic Church itself, as well as its teachers, with contagion from the Manichaean plague. X, 1276. Julian brands Catholics with the stigma of Manichaeism. X, 643. Jovinianus does so as well. X, 643. Julian accuses Catholics under the name of Manichaeans. X, 863. He also reviles Augustine. X, 1338. And he maintains that the name is rightly imposed upon them. X, 1462. The Pelagians branded Catholic teachers with the charge of Manichaeism. X, 703, 1051, 1054, 1060, 1074, 1143, 1462. Julian calls Catholics by the names of Manichaeans and Traducianists. X, 1380, 1381. Novelty in an insulting name must not be feared so much that the truth of a most ancient Catholic doctrine is abandoned. X, 1286. Catholics are far removed from the Manichaeans in the question of evil. X, 1592. The Catholic truth is contrary to the Manichaean error concerning the nature and origin of evil. X, 1508. How different the Manichaean error is from Catholic doctrine, and how insane it is. X, 1311. Those who affirm original sin are not Manichaeans. X, 1188. Catholics, although saying certain truths together with the Manichaeans, nevertheless recoil far from their errors. X, 1468. Pelagian doctrine concerning original sin favors the Manichaeans. X, 816. Those who deny original sin assist the Manichaeans. X, 666, 667, 668, 669, 1187, 1290. Julian supports Manichaeism when he argues against the Catholic doctrine of original fault. X, 1515. The heresies of the Manichaeans and Pelagians are mutually opposed and equally rejected by the Catholic Church. X, 572, 573. To what extent the Manichaeans and Pelagians are joined in error, and to what extent they are separate. X, 573. Although the Pelagians are opposed to the Manichaeans, they nevertheless favor them. X, 819. And support them. X, 1335. They open an entrance for their error. X, 1434. And they assist them. X, 1314, 1328, 1336, 1338, 1339, 1435, 1592, 1608. The Pelagians, fleeing perversely from the Manichaeans, assist those very people. X, 1463. Julian assists the Manichaeans. X, 1313, 1320, 1369, 1379, 1382, 1453, 1478, 1502, 1527, 1529, 1539. Manichaeism is so assisted by Pelagian error that it becomes unconquerable. X, 1318. Pelagians cannot answer the Manichaean who says that human flesh was evil even before it sinned and that nature was created miserable. X, 1529. The Pelagians cannot defeat the Manichaean who introduces an evil creator of flesh. X, 1530. Julian attacks the Manichaeans in such a way that he raises them up against the Savior. X, 1478. How the Catholic faith extinguishes both errors, of the Pelagians and the Manichaeans. X, 1339. Catholic doctrine is opposed to both errors, that of the Manichaeans and that of the Pelagians. X, 1310. The Catholic Church’s judgment concerning evil avoids both Manichaeans and Pelagians. X, 1463. The difference among Manichaeans, Pelagians, and Catholics concerning the nature of evil. X, 1125. Not only Catholics but also all heretics who are not Manichaeans detest the Manichaeans’ foolish and harmful impiety. X, 571. Manichaeism is utterly overthrown by Catholics. X, 1314. How the Manichaean plague is refuted by Catholics. X, 1490. The Catholic faith defeats the Pelagians together with the Manichaeans. X, 1338, 1339. And truth rebukes them. X, 1301, 1310. The Manichaean opinion concerning evil is most decisively overthrown. II, 763, 882; VI, 236. The Manichaeans are defeated. VI, 696.

The Manichaean doctrine concerning humanity, the law, and marriage. X, 570. They affirm that marriage was not instituted by the good God. X, 570, 607, 611. They attribute marriage to the prince of darkness. X, 615. They condemn marriage and the procreation of children. I, 1343, 1344, 1372. Why they abstained from intercourse. VIII, 229. How they take care that prostitutes do not become pregnant. VIII, 453. The shamefulness of the Manichaeans laid bare. VI, 683. Their impurity is marked. III, 1876.

The Manichaeans mock the sacred Scriptures. IV, 1907. Their error concerning the Old Law. VI, 109. They oppose the Old Law. III, 2065. Their slanders against the Old Law. V, 23, 24, 822, 826. They say that the Law given through Moses was not from the true God but from the prince of darkness. II, 1032; X, 570, 607, 611. They condemn the Law and the Prophets. VIII, 603. They accuse as false and inserted by corrupters whatever the apostle incorporated into his discourse from the Law and the Prophets. VI, 70. They dare to blaspheme the saints of earlier times. X, 611. They criticize the patriarchs praised in the Old Testament. I, 688. They slander the fathers of the Old Testament concerning their having several wives. VI, 395. They do not accept the Old Testament. X, 1008. They attack it. I, 598; III, 173, 189, 216. They also disparage it before the unlearned. VIII, 67. They did not accept everything from the books of the New Testament. VIII, 505. They say that the Old Testament is from an evil god. V, 927. From the prince of darkness. I, 654; V, 175. They err concerning the Old Testament not by accepting it otherwise than they ought, but by not accepting it at all and by detesting it, they blaspheme. III, 373. The Manichaeans’ slanders against the Book of Job. V, 100. Against the Prophets. V, 330. Against the prophecy of Haggai. V, 326. They accept neither the Old Law and the canonical Prophets nor everything contained in the canonical Scriptures of the New Testament. II, 1033, 1034. Some of them reject the Acts of the Apostles. II, 1034. They read the Scriptures of the New Testament. III, 180. Nevertheless, they say that they have been falsified. I, 716, 1317, 1368. They say that the passages recounting original sin were inserted. I, 598. The Manichaeans’ fraud in their use of Scripture. V, 332. They say that the sacred Scriptures which convict their errors have been corrupted. II, 278. They say that the two Testaments do not agree with one another. IV, 1893. Scriptures not received by the canon are accustomed to pervert minds. II, 233. Neither the antiquity of the authority of Scripture, nor the power of miracles, nor soundness of morals, nor the truth of reason supports the Manichaeans. VIII, 285.

The Manichaean Church consists of two professions: the Elect and the Hearers. VIII, 35. The Elect were said to be superior; they professed to observe the three seals. I, 1357. The Manichaean Elect, who ... IV, 1822. The Manichaean Elect are to be laughed at: they abstained from plucking fruits or vegetables and ate what the Hearers had plucked. VIII, 230, 235. The Manichaean Elect frequently received the Eucharist. VIII, 114. The second rank of the Manichaeans was that of the Hearers. I, 1080. The Manichaean Hearers knew nothing concerning morals but only concerning faith. VIII, 114. The Hearers kneel before the Elect so that hands may be imposed upon them as suppliants—not only by their presbyters, bishops, or deacons, but by any of the Elect. II, 1033. Together with the Elect they worship and pray to the sun and moon, and they fast on the Lord’s Day. II, 1032. The Manichaeans established Sunday for their Hearers as a lawful day of fasting. II, 148, 149. The Hearers eat meat, cultivate fields, and, if they wish, have wives; none of these things are done by those called the Elect. I, 1079, 1368; II, 1032. The Manichaeans have thirteen teachers, seventy-two bishops, presbyters, and deacons. VIII, 38. By whom bishops, presbyters, and deacons are ordained. VIII, 38.

The Manichaeans deceitfully fulfill the commandments. VIII, 223, 224, 225. They pray to the sun and moon. VIII, 38. They cannot offer God simple and pure prayers. VIII, 382. There is nothing shameful in the Manichaeans’ prayers, but only something contrary to the faith. VIII, 93. The Manichaeans almost charged the pagans with a crime because they thought God should be worshiped with altars, shrines, images, victims, and incense. VIII, 380. In the worship of many gods the Manichaeans are worse than the pagans. VIII, 369, 374, 375. The many gods of the Manichaeans. VIII, 376. The Manichaeans both enumerate and commend a very numerous family of gods. VIII, 142. In what they differ from the Gentiles, the Manichaeans are vain; in what they resemble them, they are worse. VIII, 383. Faustus is refuted by admitting temples, images, and sacrifices for the worship of God. VIII, 381, 382. Which temples, which images, and which sacrifices Faustus admitted. VIII, 369, 380. It is shown that the Manichaeans cannot be a rational temple of God. VIII, 380.

The Manichaeans deal with the unlearned not through truth but through fraud. V, 332. Their cunning for deceiving the unlearned. VI, 293. They deceive only when they promise knowledge that they do not provide. VI, 70. Manichaeus not only fails to provide knowledge and truth but speaks falsehood. VIII, 184. The Manichaeans replied that certain points of their doctrine could not be explained because of their sublimity. VIII, 576. The Manichaeans sacrilegiously and rashly attack those who, following the authority of the Catholic faith, believe what they are not yet able to see. VIII, 65. The Manichaeans are more eloquent and copious in refuting others than firm and certain in proving their own doctrines. VIII, 66. A saying of the Manichaeans concerning deserters from their sect. VIII, 67.

The utterly depraved sect of the Manichaeans. IV, 1907. Their error is most pestilential and destructive. IX, 258. Their doctrine compels the perpetration of horrifying indecencies. VIII, 570. The Manichaeans are few and extremely wicked. X, 1143. They cannot do otherwise than love their own flesh. VIII, 392. The misery of the Manichaeans’ god. VIII, 513. Among the Manichaeans and those falsely called Manichaeans, those who are falsely called such are wicked, while those who are not falsely called such are vain. VIII, 224, 228. The Manichaeans are censured. VIII, 91, 92. Why one should deal more gently with the Manichaeans. VIII, 180. It is shown that Manichaean authority is far inferior to the authority of the Gospel. VIII, 508, 510.

Manichaeans designated by Paul. VIII, 314, 578. The doctrine of the Manichaeans foreseen by the Apostle in the First Epistle to Timothy. VIII, 523. The Manichaean heresy arose after Tertullian and Cyprian. VIII, 283; X, 626. The Manichaeans signified in Ham. VIII, 267. The books of the Manichaeans are elegant, costly, and beautiful. VIII, 285, 294. The Manichaean *Treasury*, a book. VIII, 538, 568, 570. The subdeacon Victorinus was teaching the blasphemies of the Manichaeans, and was exposed while teaching them. II, 1033. When questioned by Augustine, he could not deny his error, but confessed that he was a Hearer, not an Elect. II, 1032, 1033. Augustine, horrified by his imposture, arranged that he be restrained under the guise of a cleric, removed from the clerical order, and expelled from the city. II, 1033. Even though he was asking to be recalled to the way of truth. II, 1033. Nevertheless, Augustine wishes that an opportunity for repentance be granted to him when he asks for it, provided that he exposes the Manichaeans who are hiding in Malliana and throughout the province. II, 1033.

## Manifest

That is especially to be endured which, once it is manifestly wrongly done, cannot be undone. II, 231.

## Manlius Theodorus, consul

VII, 620. A learned Christian man. I, 588. The book *On the Blessed Life* was dedicated to him. I, 959.

## Manna

V, 58. The voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance. IV, 817. That manna tasted to each person according to his own will can be proved only from the Book of Wisdom. II, 199. Manna could taste according to the desire of the faithful, but not of those who murmured against God. I, 638. To some, manna tasted like Christ. V, 1552. It signified Christ. III, 1603. Manna, a figure of Christ’s heavenly bread. V, 1551. The shadow of the sacrament of the Eucharist. III, 1612. Manna and the altar of God signified the heavenly bread. III, 1612. How those who ate manna died. III, 1611. Manna ceased after the crossing of the Jordan. III, 617. The manna enclosed in the ark, a symbol of grace. III, 633.

## Many dwelling places

Many dwelling places in the kingdom of God. III, 1812. Many dwelling places, that is, diverse rewards and lights of merits in heaven. VI, 410. How Christ goes to prepare the dwelling places that already exist. III, 1814. The desire of love is the preparation of a dwelling place. III, 1816. Whether dwelling places outside the heavenly kingdom should be assigned to the unbaptized. X, 518. See *Intermediate Place*. To lodge. V, 1262.

## Mansuetarii

Who they are. I, 1232.

## Meekness

Meekness is commended. I, 858; IV, 310, 1717. Meekness is necessary for maintaining patience. V, 860. Meekness and humility are the first and great gift of the Spirit. III, 2138. Christian meekness can be preserved while punishing offenses. II, 317, 531, 660. Commendation of ecclesiastical meekness. II, 509, 511, 535, 649. Meekness is to be shown toward heretics who quarrel and revile. V, 1584.

## Mantua

Virgil the Mantuan rhetorician. II, 82.

## Manturna

The goddess Manturna. VII, 188.

## Manubia

Spoils acquired in war. VII, 93.

## Manumission

The tablets concerning it were broken. V, 145. A document of manumission read aloud in the church. V, 145.

## The hand of God

What the hand of God is. See *God*. The hand of God is heavy upon the proud and light upon the humble, yet strong against both. IV, 267.

The hand signifies power. III, 497, 498, 1745. “In the hands,” the same as “in the power.” IV, 1956. “Hand” for the person whom another employs to do what he wishes. III, 1745. For human work and writing. III, 1745. For a bodily member and for writing. VIII, 296. The hand signifies good works. IV, 1853. The extension of the hands is the practice of good works. IV, 1115. The right hand signifies a beloved helper in good works. III, 1248. God is to be sought with the hands. IV, 1853. The hand signifies vengeance. IV, 837, 838. By the word “hand,” force is signified in Scripture. I, 1190. “Let not our hands be upon him,” that is, let us not inflict violence upon him. III, 496. He “washes his hand in the sinner’s blood” who, while considering the death of the wicked, cleanses himself from sins. IV, 691. “The hand of pride,” for the work of pride. III, 525. “The hand of the sinner,” the activity of one giving evil advice. IV, 353. Hence the command that we lift our hands in prayer. IV, 755. The laying on of hands, according to Nemesianus, is the sacrament of regeneration. IX, 205. The laying on of hands cannot be repeated in the same way as baptism cannot be repeated. IX, 149. Why the laying on of hands is administered to one coming from heresy. IX, 193.

## Mappalia

V, 422.

The Mappalienses understand Punic alone. II, 236. Nearly eighty of them were rebaptized while resisting. II, 235; IX, 316.

## Maratus

Maratus, king of the Sicyonians. VII, 568.

## Marazana

IX, 229.

## Marcelliana

IX, 235.

## Marcellina

A certain member of the Carpocratian sect, who worshiped images of Jesus, Paul, and Homer. VIII, 27.

## Marcellinus

A bishop. II, 759, 780.

Marcellinus, bishop of the Romans, was accused of having offered incense after the books had been burned, so that he might not perish. IX, 323.

Marcellinus. I, 646; VII, 13. Tribune and notary. X, 109, 201; II, 487, 490; IX, 613. Most devoted to the divine Scriptures and exceedingly dear to Augustine as a friend. II, 864. He urges Augustine to publish books on Genesis and the Trinity. II, 587. Augustine’s book addressed to Marcellinus. X, 335. The books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* and *On the Spirit and the Letter* were written to him. I, 645. Marcellinus the tribune frequently visited Volusianus at his mother’s request. II, 514. He writes to Augustine asking him to answer Volusianus’s letter. II, 514. Marcellinus writes to Augustine through Bishop Boniface. II, 585. Likewise through the presbyter Urbanus. II, 585. Augustine writes back to Marcellinus, satisfying the questions he had proposed. II, 525. This work is mentioned. II, 537. When Marcellinus was uncertain about the origin of souls, he asked Augustine, who confessed his own perplexity and ignorance. II, 864. Jerome wrote to Marcellinus that it was his opinion that individual souls are newly made for those being born. II, 747. Jerome’s letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychia on the origin of the soul. II, 718. He is praised by Augustine. II, 723, 864.

Ecclesiastical cases were entrusted especially to Marcellinus the tribune. II, 510. He was the judge at the Carthaginian Conference. IX, 700. Augustine explains to Marcellinus how he wishes those convicted of crimes among the Donatists to be treated. II, 535. He gives him an account of his occupations and nocturnal labors. II, 536. The Donatists claimed that Marcellinus, the judge at the Conference of Carthage, had been corrupted by a reward. II, 577, 582. Marcellinus is cleared of the charge of handing over the sacred books. IX, 610. Marcellinus’s integrity. IX, Appendix 820. The murder of Marcellinus is recounted, and the cruelty of Marinus is set forth. II, 646, 647, 648, 651. Marcellinus was taken away one or two days before the solemnity of Saint Cyprian. II, 649. Praise of Marcellinus. II, 650.

Marcellinus, a deacon among the Catholics, was excommunicated by his presbyter. After passing over to the Donatists, he was rebaptized by Proculeianus and made a deacon; he was killed during a nocturnal attack. II, 417.

## Marcellus

A bishop. II, 759, 780.

Marcellus, presbyter of Marcellinus, bishop of Rome, is cleared of the charge of handing over the sacred books. IX, 610.

Marcellus of Zama. IX, 232.

## Marcellus

Marcellus captured Syracuse. VII, 19. He wept over the Syracusan city that he was attacking. VII, 90. The edict of Marcellus in defense of inviolate chastity. VII, 19.

## Marcianensis estate

II, 702.

## Marcianus

Marcianus of Urgensis chose Catholic unity of his own free will. II, 397.

## Marcion

Marcion the heretic. IX, 231. A disciple of Cerdo. VIII, 664. Deceived in the question concerning the cause of sin. X, 1464. From him came the Marcionite heretics and their doctrines. VIII, 29; IX, 469, 589.

The Marcionists condemn the Law and the Prophets. VIII, 603. They deny that these belong to the good God. II, 1033. They tell empty stories about the world and the Law of Moses. I, 654. The questions of the Marcionists and Sabellians had already fallen silent in Augustine’s time. II, 438.

## Marcuclius

A subdeacon. IX, 513.

Marcuclius, a gravedigger. IX, 513.

The Donatists complained that Marculus had been thrown down by Catholics. IX, 320. Whether Marculus’s fall was voluntary or decreed by order of the law. IX, 526. Marculus, the Donatist pseudo-martyr. III, 1483. The passion of Marculus and the transfer of his name into the martyrologies. IX, 526, note (a).

## Mark

Mark, the equal of the Apostles. V, 1127. The attendant and abridger of Matthew. III, 1044, 1045. The face of a man is attributed to him. III, 1666.

Mark of Mactaris. IX, 225.

Mark of Casphalus became a Catholic of his own free will. II, 397.

Mark the heretic and his doctrines. VIII, 28.

## Sea

What the sea is. I, 853. Among the Hebrews, “sea” means every gathering of waters, including fresh waters. III, 182. Why God rains upon the sea. IV, 1944. The Aegean Sea. I, 935; IV, 1037. The crossing of the Red Sea, a figure of baptism. V, 1551, 1555, 1635. Whether the sea will be dried up in the conflagration of the world is uncertain. VII, 682.

Allegorical interpretation of the sea. I, 853. The human race is compared with the sea: deeply curious, stormily swollen, and fluidly unstable because of the fault of the first man. I, 911. The sea is used for the world. VII, 680. The sea, in a figure, is this present age, bitter through falsehood, turbulent through its waves, and so forth. IV, 780, 1478, 1479. Three kinds of sailors on the sea of this age. I, 397. What the crossing of the sea in a ship signifies. V, 475. The sea is a figure of the present life. VII, 682. The sea: all unbelievers. IV, 1748. Persecutors of the Church. IV, 1126. The bottom of the sea, the heart of the ungodly. IV, 782. In its bitterness, the sea represented the Gentiles. IV, 937, 1126.

## Mariambulus Petrus

IV, 440.

## Margarita

A girl not yet twelve years old, violated by the Manichaeans for the sake of their criminal mystery. VIII, 36.

## Miriam

The tambourine of Miriam, the sister of Moses. V, 1638.

## Mary

Mary the virgin was conceived through the concupiscence of her parents. X, 813. And born from the carnal concupiscence of her parents. X, 1553. Mary, descended from Adam, was dead because of sin. IV, 335. Mary was not handed over to the devil by the condition of her birth because that condition is dissolved by the grace of rebirth. X, 1418. Mary was of a royal and priestly tribe. VI, 50. Mary belonged to the seed of David. VIII, 471, 472. Why Christ wished to take flesh from Mary. III, 405. Why Gabriel came to Mary and not to Joseph, as he had come to Zechariah. V, 1317. The question of Zechariah and Mary was similar, but their dispositions were different. V, 1314, 1318. The virgin could have been afraid, or certainly ignorant of God’s plan, namely, how he wished her to have a son. V, 1319. Mary did not doubt God’s power, but asked how she was to conceive. III, 726. Mary’s resolve of virginity. V, 1096, 1318. Mary had vowed herself to God as a virgin before she heard that Christ would be born from her. VI, 398. In the marriage of Mary and Joseph, all the goods of marriage were present. X, 421. See *Marriage*, *Nuptials*. Mary was freed from Joseph’s false suspicion. V, 1507. Mary’s husband was not one who removed her virginity, but its guardian—or rather not its guardian, since God was the guardian—but a witness to her virginal chastity. V, 1096.

Mary’s modesty and humility are to be imitated by women. V, 343. Mary is blessed among women. V, 1318. Mary is blessed because she keeps the word of God. III, 1468. Mary was more blessed by receiving Christ’s faith than by conceiving Christ’s flesh. VI, 398. According to the Arians, the Holy Spirit came upon Mary to sanctify and cleanse her. VIII, 736. Mary became the mother of the Son of God by grace. V, 1319. Mary conceived Christ’s flesh through faith. VIII, 490. She conceived him in her mind before conceiving him in her womb. V, 1074. Through pious faith, the virgin Mary merited that the holy offspring be formed in her. X, 175. There was carnal material in Mary’s body from which Christ took flesh, but carnal concupiscence did not sow Christ in her. X, 1553. Although the virgin’s flesh came from the propagation of sin, she did not conceive from the propagation of sin. III, 422. Mary conceived not through lust but through faith. V, 442. She conceived without the heat of concupiscence. V, 1114. She conceived with the love of faith burning within her. V, 1069. Mary alone is both mother and virgin in spirit and body. VI, 399.

Mary’s womb, the bridal chamber of the union of the Word with flesh. III, 1452; IV, 1942; V, 1319. Mary’s womb conceived nothing mortal either before or after. III, 1623. The Antidicomarianites maintain that Mary was joined to her husband after Christ’s birth. VIII, 40. The Helvidians destroyed Mary’s virginity. VIII, 46. Jovinianus destroyed it. VIII, 45; X, 552, 1417. Catholics rejected Jovinianus’s argument against the inviolate virginity of holy Mary. X, 643. Mary is called both virgin and woman. V, 343. Mary’s virginity. X, 445. Mary is perpetually virgin. V, 990. Mary conceived through faith and gave birth as a virgin. VI, 249. Mary was a virgin conceiving, a virgin giving birth, and a virgin dying. VI, 339. The virgin believed, the virgin conceived, the virgin gave birth, and the virgin remained so. V, 343, 1019. Christ brought fertility to the virgin but did not take away her virginity. V, 442, 997, 1004, 1010, 1019, 1073, 1105. He found Mary a virgin when he was conceived and left her a virgin when he was born. V, 640. By being born, Christ did not take away the glory of Mary’s virginity, to which he had brought the gift of fertility. VIII, 490. Mary did not lose her integrity. III, 1467. Faith believes that Christ emerged through her incorrupt limbs. V, 1010. Nothing is more undefiled than the virgin’s womb. III, 422. Mary’s purification was according to the custom of the Law rather than necessity. III, 696. From Mary the dignity of virginity began. V, 348. Mary lived without any sin. X, 267. Regarding Mary, Augustine wishes, out of honor for the Lord, that absolutely no question be raised when sins are being discussed. I, 746.

An encomium of the Virgin Mary. III, 113. Salvation was offered through her for the restoration of humanity. V, 335. Through a woman came death, and through a woman life. V, 1108. Mary the virgin, the dignity of the earth. III, 216. Mary’s merits, apart from the integrity of her flesh, are distinctive. VI, 396. Mary is spiritually the daughter of Christ the Head, spiritually born from him, but the mother of his members, because she cooperated through love so that the faithful might be born in the Church. VI, 399.

Mary as a figure of the Church. VI, 659, 660. The Church, like Mary, both gives birth and is a virgin. V, 1063. What Augustine wrote confirms Mary’s virginity. II, 590. Mary is found to have prophesied as a virgin. VII, 559.

## Mary and Martha

The differing duties of Mary and Martha. V, 925, 967, 1186. Both were good. V, 614, 615, 967. Why Mary’s portion is better. V, 615, 617, 968. To be nourished by truth: Mary’s portion, which does not pass away. V, 969. Mary was eating the very one whom she was hearing. V, 969. Her work is taken away, not her reward. V, 968. Martha’s ministry was not reproved by Christ. V, 616. It tends toward Mary’s repose. V, 615. The two lives represented in Martha and Mary. V, 617, 1188.

## Maria

The mother of the martyr Marianus. V, 1288.

The feast-day of the martyrs Marianus and James. V, 1288.

## Marius

The most bloodthirsty author of the civil wars. VII, 70, 71.

## Marianus

A bishop. II, 759, 780.

## Marica

The goddess Marica. VII, 71.

## Marinus

A traditor from the waters of Tibilis. IX, 511, 612.

Marinus’s cruelty in the killing of Marcellinus. II, 646, 647, 648, 649, 651.

## Husband

A woman deserved to have a husband as her lord not by nature but by fault. III, 450. A husband may not practice continence without his wife’s consent. IV, 1959. An intemperate husband is an adulterer against his wife. X, 687. What a wife should do when her husband falsely suspects her. V, 1508. The soul has God as its legitimate husband. V, 759.

## Marius

Marius the young man. VII, 107. Marius, a municipal citizen of Arpinum, was made consul at Rome seven times. VII, 69, note (b). The cruel victory of Marius. VII, 107. Marius, defeated by Sulla, fled to Minturnae and was commended to the goddess Marica. VII, 71. Sulla’s victory avenged the cruelty of Marius. VII, 107.

## Marratius

A Maximianist bishop. IV, 381.

## Mars

The god of war. VII, 206. The maker of deaths. VII, 196. Guilty of homicide, yet acquitted. VII, 567. Mars and Vulcan are enemies. VI, 712. The star of Mars. VII, 206.

Mars was one of those who attended the Donatist council at Cirta. IX, 513.

Mars the deacon. IX, 513.

## Marsi

The Marsi attempted to shake off the Roman yoke. VII, 168.

## Marsus

An enchanter. II, 210; IV, 679.

## Martialis

Martialis of Pertusa. IX, 507, 529, 550.

## Martianus

Martianus of Sullectum. IX, 507, 529, 550.

## Martinianus

A bishop. II, 966.

Martianus, Augustine’s oldest friend. II, 1071. Augustine urges him to receive the sacraments of the faithful without delay. II, 1073. And to enroll his name among the candidates for baptism. II, 1073.

## March

The first of the months. VIII, 346.

## Martyrs

Why they are called martyrs. IV, 1523. *Martyr* in Greek, *testis* (“witness”) in Latin. III, 1979; V, 1297, 1452; VIII, 448. *Martyrium* in Latin means “testimony.” IV, 1539. Martyrs are witnesses of Christ. III, 1866, 1868. In the martyrs there is a great heap of testimony to Christ. IV, 719, 722. We would more elegantly call martyrs “heroes,” if the Church’s customary speech allowed it. VII, 299. Description of a martyr. III, 882. In martyrdom, confession comes first; then courage, and afterward breadth of spirit. IV, 835. Martyrs are patient in torments, faithful in confession, and truthful in speech. IV, 444. The bitterness of death endured by the martyrs. V, 1360. The martyrs lost everything, even their very souls, so that they would not lose the faith. IV, 618. What did the martyrs find that they could repay to God? IV, 1318.

For the martyrs, fighting for salvation meant despising salvation for the Savior’s sake. VII, 758. The courage of the martyrs for despising the threats of the world. V, 220. They conquered errors and terrors. V, 1414. They conquered the world’s allurements and harshnesses. V, 1290. Pleasures and pains. V, 1282, 1470. The martyrs were tempted by the allurements of carnal parents. V, 1288. The martyrs were so “drunk” that they did not recognize their own people. IV, 352, 955. The martyrs were happily unhappy. IV, 1679. Drunken men persecute them with cups. IV, 723. The sacrifices of the martyrs. III, 811.

Why the persecutor does not terrify God’s martyrs. V, 427. Why they did not feel bodily sufferings. V, 1282. The martyrs’ courage came not from themselves but from God. V, 34, 1289, 1368, 1455; VI, 607. The martyrs are armed by God and helped by the same God who armed them. V, 1423. The martyrs could never endure such great tribulations in the flesh unless they conceived great repose in the mind. IV, 760. The martyrs’ security under God’s protection. V, 1463, 1467. Christ suffered first and gave the martyrs the power to suffer. V, 1451. The martyrs’ strength came from Christ’s example. IV, 760, 762. Christ is the head and model of the martyrs. IV, 762. While the martyrs lay down their lives, Christ lays down his. IV, 1840. When they suffered, it was Christ himself, the one Christ, who suffered. III, 1733. The martyrs imitate the Lord’s Passion in a very different way. III, 1332. In the martyrs, Christ bears witness to himself. V, 713. The martyrs were bound by judges with chains, but by God with fetters. IV, 1305. The martyrs were fettered in heart by the wisdom to which they bore witness through their sufferings. IV, 1146, 1147. By the martyrs’ blood, as by oil, the fire of love was kindled in Christ. IV, 77. Christ is glorified in the sufferings of his servants. III, 1770. Through the martyrs’ passion, in a certain way, Christ rose among the Gentiles. IV, 491. The martyrs’ strength came from hope and the vision of promised happiness. IV, 1678, 1679, 1680, 1702, 1703. Because when one thinks with great love about where one is going, one treads the way with great courage. V, 1366. What joys will there be in the strength of those who reign, when such great joys belong to those who die for the truth? V, 1255. The martyrs’ strength came from fear of hell. IV, 1647. The freedom and joy of a most steadfast young martyr singing psalms amid torments. VII, 615. Answers of certain martyrs to the persecutor’s questions. V, 1450. The saying of a certain woman martyr during her confession: “Honor Caesar as Caesar; but fear God.” V, 232.

There are true and false martyrs. V, 1297. The devilish spirit fills its martyrs so that they despise torments. V, 1254. Martyrs of gold. V, 1461, 1470. Heretics wish to be called martyrs. V, 1451. The Donatist martyrs are criticized. V, 630, 1448. The punishment of the ungodly may be similar, but the cause of the martyrs is different. II, 796. The cause distinguishes a martyr from the endurance—or rather the hardness—of criminals. V, 1253. It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr. II, 310, 413, 940; IV, 333, 340, 482, 483, 848; V, 1254, 1293, 1448, 1450, 1451, 1470; IX, 44, 524. The disposition toward martyrdom makes a martyr. V, 1354. The honor lies in the goodness of the cause, not in the harshness of the punishment. IV, 848. To suffer for the truth belongs to martyrs; to suffer for falsehood may belong even to the ungodly. V, 1453. It is a greater victory to be killed for the faith of the truth. VIII, 449.

There were martyrs even in the Old Testament. VIII, 449. John the Baptist is a martyr because he was killed for the law of truth, although not in the name of Christ. IV, 1832, 1833. Many prophets are martyrs, although they did not die for Christ. IV, 1832. No one died before Christ for confessing the name of Christ. IV, 1832. The acts of the martyrs who suffered because they refused to hand over the sacred books. IX, 643.

True martyrs are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness. II, 796. One who is killed for righteousness is called a martyr. V, 632. Perfect martyrs are lovers of righteousness. V, 871. Our righteousness: God does not delight in torments. V, 1293. The martyrs’ righteousness is perfect. V, 1295.

The martyrs’ strength comes from love. IV, 541. While the martyrs were being beaten, they were conquering, because love was not conquered. IV, 1733. Martyrdom without love profits nothing. V, 764. Nor do other good works. III, 1436. In martyrdom, faith, hope, and love are commended. IV, 835. By loving Christ, the martyrs attained the virtues and strength of the Church. III, 926. He conquered in them who lived in them, so that those who lived not for themselves but for him would not die even when dead. V, 1282. Those who do not have the life of Christians cannot have the death of martyrs. II, 940.

Martyrdom outside the Church, even if undergone for the name of Christ, profits nothing. II, 756; IX, 169, 695. Nor does it profit those who live in the Church without love. IX, 170. Cyprian judged thus. II, 410. When a martyr was asked by someone to pray for him, he replied that he ought to pray for the Catholic Church. V, 1249.

The martyrs conquered not by resisting but by dying. VII, 771. The persecutors could harm the martyrs in nothing. IV, 1813. The martyrs were killed and yet rescued from their enemies. IV, 761, 762. The martyrs were abandoned, yet not abandoned, into the hands of the ungodly. IV, 390, 722. The martyrs triumphed over their persecutors. IV, 670. The martyrs were victorious over their persecutors.
