V, 206. The persecutors of the martyrs were converted to Christ. IV, 1782. The persecutors’ plan was to destroy the martyrs; the martyrs’ plan was to find their enemies lost. IV, 1524. The blood shed by the Donatists won many of them over. II, 808.

The martyrs are conquerors of demons. VII, 299. Not through supplicatory gifts, but through divine virtues. VII, 299. The martyrs’ victory over demons, now so evident. V, 1422. The smoking altars of demons were extinguished by the martyrs’ blood. V, 1422.

The martyrs’ patience conquers both Jews and Gentiles. II, 802. The martyrs abolished false religions. VII, 136. The martyrs’ victory is an argument for the Christian religion. VII, 758. The martyrs bear witness to our faith. VII, 771. By dying they assert Christ more than by living. V, 1298. What the martyrs’ sufferings achieved. VII, 612. The martyrs won this homeland for us by their blood. VII, 77.

The martyrs’ blood is seed. V, 151. From the martyrs’ blood, as from sowing, the Church’s harvest arose. IV, 431; V, 1298, 1380. And it sprang up more fruitfully. IV, 695, 1754, 1829. The death of the martyrs was the multiplication of Christians. VII, 751. Thousands of martyrs were killed. V, 338, 1548. Thousands of crowned men are found if even a single day of the martyrs’ passion is counted. V, 1176. The earth was filled with thousands of martyrs. V, 151. The earth was made purple. V, 1377. Sixty Christians of Suffectum were slaughtered. II, 190. The bodies of the martyrs were burned and their ashes scattered into the Rhône. VI, 597. Why God permitted this. VI, 599. The death of the martyrs, the richness of the earth. IV, 1829. The earth, heaven, and Church, and the times themselves, are adorned by the merits of the martyrs. IV, 1590. The number of martyrs will be completed in the time of Antichrist. IX, 724. How the martyrs are avenged. III, 1268. If the martyrs still seek human praise, they have not yet conquered. V, 1352. They seek nothing from us for themselves, but for our own sake. V, 1352. Where the enemy turns the name of Christ into a crime, there Christ turns punishment into praise. V, 1422. The martyrs’ fetters were turned into a crown. IV, 1306. The more courageously the martyrs contend, the denser the crown of martyrdom. VII, 678.

The merits of the martyrs. VII, 255. Martyrs have greater merit than those who die after receiving baptism. VII, 381. Martyrdom is [baptism] for the unbaptized. VII, 381; IX, 173; X, 480, 505. The death of the martyrs is precious. V, 333, 1298, 1454. The martyrs occupy the highest place in the churches. IV, 835, 1523. The happiness of the martyrs is one thing before the resurrection and another afterward. V, 1283, 1454. Before the resurrection, it is a small portion of the promise, or rather the consolation of delay. V, 1283. The martyrs did not despise the body but took good care of it. V, 1259. By dying for Christ, they benefited themselves, not Christ. V, 1459.

The martyrs’ complete victory. V, 1291. And the greatest rewards. V, 1281. The martyrs’ reward is prepared for those who follow Christ and keep the faith. V, 1369, 1394. The martyrs’ glory is hidden from the foolish. V, 1400. The martyrs, killed publicly and falsely triumphed over, were truly crowned in secret. IV, 220, 476, 1259. They hastened, freed for happiness. V, 1449. The spirits of the martyrs, like many exceedingly sweet fruits from the Lord’s garden, passed over to the heavenly table. IV, 1013. The more courageously the martyrs contend, the more glorious are the citizens of the city of God. VII, 299. By dying, the martyrs passed to goods that are utterly certain. V, 1425. The blessed possess the land of the living. V, 1420. At rest with Christ, they await the redemption of their bodies. V, 1420, 1454. They are joined to Christ. V, 1425. Wherever they are, they are with God, where all is well. V, 1366. They violently invaded heaven. V, 1425. They reign with Christ. V, 1434; VII, 673. There they see one another, hear our speech, and are able to pray for us. V, 1434. They are where Christ is. V, 1441. They have passed from this world to the Father. V, 1459. Perhaps scars will appear on the bodies of the martyrs. VII, 782. Why the martyrs are friends of Christ. V, 1461. An innumerable company of holy martyrs entered the kingdom of heaven courageously and forcefully for confessing Christ—something that the one who received the keys of his kingdom formerly could not do. III, 1933. The martyrs bear a hundredfold fruit. III, 1325.

The Church is honored by the relics of the martyrs. V, 1475. The martyrs’ blood is held in veneration by Christians. VII, 612. Memorials of the martyrs. IV, 1782. A basilica of the eight martyrs. V, 1578. The feast-day of twenty martyrs. V, 1447. A basilica. V, 799. A most renowned memorial near Hippo. VII, 765. Christians honor the memorials of the martyrs. VII, 255. Why Christians celebrate the memorials of the martyrs. VIII, 384. How Hermes attempts to bring Christianity into disrepute on account of the memorials of the martyrs. VII, 253. Only memorials, not temples, are built for the martyrs. VII, 772. Why altars are placed over the bodies of the martyrs. VII, 255. Temples, altars, priesthoods, and sacrifices are not established for the martyrs. V, 1251, 1437; VII, 255, 772. But for God himself. VIII, 348, 385. The martyrs are honored neither with divine honors nor with human crimes. VII, 256. The martyrs are not worshiped with the worship of *latria*. VIII, 384. Martyrs are to be praised and loved; the God of the martyrs is to be worshiped. V, 1252. A martyr in the Lord is praised when the Lord is praised through him. V, 1420. Praise of the martyrs redounds to God. V, 1423. The martyrs are not invoked by the priest who offers the sacrifice, but merely named. VII, 772. The martyrs are recited at the altar’s sacraments in their proper place. V, 1251, 1291, 1360; VI, 423. The acts of the martyrs, to be recited at their solemnities, are scarcely to be found. V, 1426. When the martyrs are recited, prayer is not made for them. V, 868, 1291, 1295, 1360. No prayer is made for the martyrs. III, 1847. It is an insult to pray for a martyr. V, 867. The Church commends itself to the martyrs’ prayers. V, 1291, 1360. God is propitiated by the martyrs’ prayers. III, 635. The martyrs are our advocates, yet Christ alone is our advocate. V, 1295. The martyrs are still sad because they intercede and groan for us. IV, 1099. The martyrs pity us and pray for us. V, 1283. Why God grants temporal benefits through the martyrs’ prayers. V, 1385. An apt comparison concerning this matter. V, 1385. How the martyrs are present to help the living. VI, 607. What is seen by both the living and the dead may be attributed to angelic activity. VI, 600, 604. Through the martyrs, health is not granted to everyone, but immortality is granted to their imitators. V, 1299. If we are less worthy to receive, let us ask through the friends of Christ. V, 1462.

Why God especially commends the merits of the martyrs through their memorials. VI, 607. At many memorials of the martyrs, demons are tormented and expelled from possessed bodies. VII, 254. Faustus accused Christians of turning idols into martyrs. VIII, 384. The martyrs are honored far more worthily than the gods of the pagans. VII, 772. The memorials of the martyrs succeeded the shrines of the gods. VII, 253. Booklets concerning God’s benefits through the martyrs, read aloud in the church. V, 493, 1300, 1443. The birthdays of the martyrs are celebrated. VI, 676. Those who held banquets on the birthdays of the martyrs called them “joy.” II, 115. Why food was brought to the memorials of the martyrs. VII, 255. It was not brought to them by the better Christians. VII, 255. Whatever religious services are performed at the places of the martyrs are adornments of the memorials, not sacrifices for the dead. VII, 255. At the solemnities of the martyrs, certain Christians insult them by their extravagance. IV, 867. Whoever wishes to celebrate the birthdays of the martyrs properly should desire to imitate the martyrs. IV, 869. To honor and not imitate is nothing other than to flatter deceitfully. V, 1447. Why the solemnities of the martyrs were established, and how they should be celebrated. V, 1248, 1252, 1283, 1447. See *Festivals*.

The martyrs are to be imitated. V, 51, 52, 1389, 1405, 1548. They followed the hard way after Christ and smoothed it for us. V, 1405. The martyrs are spices. V, 1250. The martyrs teach contempt for the world by their example. V, 1415. They provide us an example of patience. V, 1292. Martyrdom in daily temptations. V, 1439. You will emerge as a martyr if you overcome all the devil’s temptations. V, 52. Martyrdom in bed. V, 1300. Martyrdom is the fire by which each person’s work is tested. VII, 745. The martyrs’ passion and reward foretold in Psalm 125. V, 195. The martyrs prefigured in the reddened ram. III, 635. The martyrs’ passion signified by Christ’s bloody sweat. IV, 1206, 1817.

## Martyriani

Heretics. VIII, 41.

## Masinissa

The kingdom of Masinissa in Africa. VII, 112.

## Mass

One mass of perdition in which all are bound together. VI, 278. The entire mass was corrupted. X, 1136. The mass of sin, the mass of wrath. V, 153. The mass of perdition from which we were chosen. V, 177. If no one were freed from the condemned mass, no one could justly criticize God’s judgment as unjust. X, 933, 972. Separation from the mass does not occur through merits, fortune, or fate, but solely through God’s good pleasure. X, 581. Why all are not freed from the mass, but some are left in it. X, 581, 582. See *Grace*.

## White mass

IV, 571, 1880; V, 1400. So called from Utica. V, 1417.

## Massaliani

Heretics. VIII, 41.

## Massephat

Interpreted as “intention.” VII, 539.

## Massilians

The Massilians’ position concerning original sin and the grace of regeneration. II, 1003, 1008. Concerning predestination. II, 1008, 1009. The position of the Massilians and certain others in Gaul concerning predestination and calling. X, 953, note 2. Concerning God’s will to save all. II, 1004, 1011. Concerning the number of the predestined. II, 1005, 1009, 1010, 1011. Concerning election based on foreseen good or evil acts that infants would have committed had they lived longer. II, 1004, 1005. Concerning the purpose of the grace that calls. II, 1004, 1008. Concerning Christ’s death for the whole human race. II, 1005. Concerning preaching being made to some and not to others, and at some times and not at others. II, 1009. Concerning the two things that bring about human salvation: grace and human obedience. II, 1005. Concerning human freedom to do good and evil. II, 1004. Concerning human sufficiency to begin and complete a good work. II, 1008. Concerning the beginning of good will. II, 1008, 1009. Concerning perseverance. II, 1010; X, 955, note 4. The Massilians reject testimony from the Book of Wisdom as coming from a noncanonical book. II, 1010. The Massilians’ position concerning the interpretation of the blessed Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. II, 1004. Certain Massilians were offended because they did not understand Augustine’s books. X, 947, note 2.

The Massilians’ position is partly Catholic and partly Pelagian. X, 949, note 3. The extent to which the Massilians departed from the Pelagians. X, 961. How harmful these remnants of the Pelagian heresy are. X, 951, note 7. A virulent remnant of Pelagian perversity is nourished among the Massilians, and it is not of moderate poisonousness. II, 1007. The Massilians think that whatever Augustine argued in his books against the Pelagians concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose is contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding. II, 1003. With certain exceptions, the Massilians admire Augustine in all his deeds and sayings. II, 1012. In particular, Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles. II, 1007. After reviewing the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, some Massilians became more intelligent. X, 949, note 2. Concerning the remaining doctrines of the Massilians, see *Faith*, *Grace*, *Predestination*, *Perseverance*. Also the letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine. X, 917 ff.

Few dare to oppose the Massilians. X, 951, n. 7. Prosper declares himself unequal to dealing with the Massilians. II, 1007. He asks Augustine to reply to the Massilians and proposes questions to which he wishes an answer. II, 1007. When the Massilians were troubled by Augustine’s statements, they preferred to blame their own slowness and request a clearer exposition of his position rather than criticize what they had not understood. II, 1003. The Massilians were moved by the same considerations as the Hadrumetines; their questions were fully answered in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*. II, 1003. The Massilians and those who agree with them are men outstanding in their devotion to every virtue, and the less discerning follow their authority without judgment. II, 1003; X, 947, n. 2. Some of them are bishops. II, 1007; X, 951, n. 7. The Massilians’ view of the distinction between the grace of an innocent human being and that of a fallen human being. II, 1010. How the Massilians rely upon authority. II, 1004, 1011. How they wish Augustine’s opinion—even if true—to be kept silent without danger, and expressed only with harmful consequences. II, 1004, 1011. Hilary thinks that the Massilians cannot be overcome by reasoning alone unless authority is added as well. II, 1012. Many Massilians are such that, by ecclesiastical custom, laypeople must show them the highest reverence. X, 957.

**Martyrs of Massilia.** V, 1286.

**Mascula.** IX, 237, 511.

**Male and female could come into being only according to the body.** III, 293.

**Earth, the mother of the gods.** VII, 186. See *Berecynthia*.

**Mothers.** The lusts of mothers generally reveal the offspring. VIII, 988. The soul of a mother, being disposed in one way or another, can impress certain qualities upon the fetus, as it were. VII, 374. Comparison between the mother’s food, which she transforms into flesh and from which she produces milk, and the incarnate Word. V, 670. The Church forbids striking one’s mother. II, 132. A certain mother’s curse upon her ten children. VII, 769. A mother treated insultingly by her son. V, 1443. She strangled herself with a noose. V, 1443. Her evil imprecations against him and her other children are heard. V, 1443. See *Parents*.

**The mother of Christ.** Commended by Christ himself as he was dying. V, 1086. Maternal kinship would have profited Mary nothing had she not borne Christ more blessedly in her heart than in her flesh. VI, 398. How someone can be Christ’s mother, sister, and brother. IV, 1685.

**Matter.** Some pagans join matter to God as coeternal with him. VIII, 380. The matter from which the world was made is neither absolutely nothing, nor coeternal with God, nor made by anyone other than God. VIII, 609. It was created together with the world. VIII, 609. The matter of heaven and earth was created simultaneously with them, and did not exist before them. V, 1067. Matter called formless, capable of forms and subject to the Creator, is convertible into whatever the Creator chooses to make. V, 1067. Formless matter is not absolutely nothing. I, 827. Rather, it is something intermediate between formed things and nothing. I, 828. Matter was made from nothing, and everything was made from it. I, 829; III, 178. Formless matter is not earlier in time than formed things. III, 257, 388. God created it together with things. III, 276. It could not have been the matter of any natures unless it came from God. III, 274.

By what names matter is designated. III, 178. In the book of Genesis, matter is more appropriately called by the name “water” than “air.” III, 225. Let the human mind attempt either to know matter by not knowing it, or to fail to know it by knowing it. I, 827. The end, formlessness, and subjection of matter under the craftsman are indicated. III, 226.

**Mathan.** I, 633.

**Astrologers and astrology.** The divinations of astrologers. I, 737. The science of astrologers is uncertain. VI, 29. It is vain. VII, 144. The error and ignorance of astrologers regarding twins. VII, 142. The astrologers’ foolish doctrine of fate is demonstrated by their own actions. II, 1061. How the expertise of astrologers is tested. VII, 147. Why astrologers sometimes speak the truth. III, 278; VI, 29. Association between demons and astrologers. III, 53. They are deceived by transgressing angels who are believed to be astrologers. III, 52. Astrologers, and those who consult them, are censured. IV, 456, 747, 1821. To consult astrologers, haruspices, or sorcerers is to commit fornication with demons. V, 76. Astrologers are to be avoided even if they speak the truth. III, 52; 279. In evil deeds astrologers introduce the accusation that God, the author of the stars, rather than human beings, the authors of crimes, is to blame. III, 278. Astrologers try to take away from us the reasons for prayer. III, 278. If we believe the ravings of astrologers, we suffer shipwreck concerning free will. II, 210. They object in vain that we too celebrate Easter according to the calculation of the sun and moon. II, 210. An astrologer converted to better things. IV, 746. The books of astrologers were burned. III, 1455. The ancient writers did not call “astrologers” those who are now called by that name. VI, 28. See *Genethliaci*.

Priscillian wanted astrology to prevail. VIII, 667.

**Methuselah.** Whether he lived fourteen years after the Flood. VII, 449. Whether he survived the Flood or not is investigated apart from the danger to faith. X, 398. According to the Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint, Methuselah died six years before the Flood. III, 548; VII, 454.

**Marriage.** From what it derives its name. VIII, 365. The Manichaeans condemn marriage. VIII, 597. The threefold good of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. III, 397. What must be considered in that threefold good. III, 397. Marriage confirmed by an oath. II, 97. Marriage contracts. I, 772; V, 1272. The bishop signs them. V, 1463. Conjugal honor consists in the duty of governing the marriage and receiving children. I, 730. What the disposition of the faithful ought to be in the use of marriage. X, 416, 419. The procreation of children is the one legitimate reason for sexual intercourse. VI, 368. There is no sin in the duty of begetting children. III, 288. Marriage contracts existed for the purpose of procreating children. V, 88, 225, 345. When sexual intercourse within marriage is a venial sin. V, 345, 1272; VI, 269. See *Wife*. There is no marriage where efforts are made to prevent the wife from becoming a mother. I, 1373. In that case she becomes a prostitute. I, 1373. The good of marriage does not extinguish but moderates carnal concupiscence. II, 844. See *Conjugal union, Weddings*. Unjust husbands rage against adulterous wives even though they themselves are adulterers. VI, 474. Husbands should be moved to spare adulterous wives not by license for lust but by concern for piety. VI, 481. Whether it is lawful to marry unbelievers. VI, 221.

Marriage is indissoluble. X, 420. Scripture attributes to both God and Adam the words expressing the indissolubility of marriage. III, 408. The marriage of women who have fallen away from their resolve should not be dissolved. VI, 438. After the husband’s death, a true marriage can be formed with one with whom there had previously been adultery. X, 420. Continence by mutual consent does not dissolve marriage. X, 422. Nor does a mutual vow of chastity. X, 420. Nor does the infertility of a spouse. X, 420.

**Mattarians,** a sect of the Manichaeans. VIII, 36, 223.

**Matthew.** Matthew is said to have written in Hebrew speech. III, 1044, 1139. The others wrote in Greek. III, 1044. Matthew undertook to narrate the Lord’s Incarnation according to the royal lineage. III, 1044. And his generation according to the flesh. III, 1071. Matthew and Luke chiefly commended Christ’s humanity. III, 1044. The lion was assigned to Matthew. III, 1666. Matthew’s authority is asserted against Faustus. VIII, 341.

**Matthias** received the episcopate of the apostle who had perished. IX, 263.

**Matuta,** the goddess, mother of Melicertes. VII, 572. She presides over ripening grain. VII, 118.

**Mauritania.** IV, 179. Mauritania Sitifensis. VI, 165. Mauritania Caesariensis. IX, 316, 588. Mauritania Caesariensis is closer to the western than to the southern region and does not wish to be called Africa. II, 333. The Mauritanian provinces have their own primates. II, 226. Augustine went to Mauritania Caesariensis because of an ecclesiastical necessity. II, 857, 869. Note.

**Maurentius, bishop.** II, 762.

**Mauri.** IX, 586.

**Maurusius.** II, 224.

**Maxentius, emperor.** IX, 645, 662.

**How we are commanded to offer the other cheek to one who strikes the jaw.** VI, 506, 507.

**Maxima, a servant of God.** II, 1084.

**Maximian, emperor.** VII, 614; IX, 323, 328, 540. Consul seven times. IX, 510, 513. Consul eight times. IX, 643.

**Maximian, bishop of Bagaia, a Catholic.** How much he suffered from the Donatists and Circumcellions. IX, 521. His dreadful scars moved the emperor against the Donatists. II, 306. The slaughter of Maximian, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Bagaia. II, 805.

**Maximian, a Donatist.** III, 1470; IX, 180. Founder of the Maximianists. IX, 530.

**Maximianists.** V, 769. Schismatics from the party of Donatus. I, 645; V, 447; IX, 105. History of the Maximianist schism. IX, 703. Founders of the schism. IX, 251. The council of the Maximianists against Primian. V, 901. Maximian, deacon of Primian, bishop of Carthage, and the circumstances in which he created a schism within the party of Donatus. IV, 375; IX, 703. Maximian raised altar against altar. IX, 553. The Maximianists condemned Primian. IV, 375. They complained about Primian in terms like those in which the Donatists complained about Caecilian. IV, 376. The council of Secundus of Tigisis against Caecilian ought to have no more force than that of the Maximianists against Primian. II, 173. A *tractoria* issued by the Maximianists at the council of Cabarsussa. IV, 376. Maximian, a relative of Donatus, cut himself off from communion with Primian, whom he condemned in his absence, and against whom he was ordained bishop. II, 173; IV, 375; VIII, 43; IX, 563. Maximian was made bishop from the diaconate after creating a schism. II, 800. When Maximian was set up against Primian, twelve Donatist bishops joined him; they were accused before more than three proconsuls so that they might be expelled from their sees by judicial authority. II, 406. Maximian affirmed that he had remained in the party of Donatus, while Primian and his associates had created the schism. IX, 552. Maximian the Donatist became, as it were, a mountain. IV, 347. Primian was cleared by the other African bishops of his communion of the charge brought against him by Maximian’s faction. II, 173. Maximian was condemned, together with twelve others, by the Donatists. II, 800. Three hundred and ten bishops condemned Maximian at the council of Bagai. II, 406; IV, 382, 645, 684, 685; VI, 696; IX, 73, 426. Together with the twelve who ordained him. IX, 251, 262, 507, 527, 549. On the appointed day they granted the others belonging to that part of the schism the opportunity to return. Later, for the sake of peace, they received back into their offices some of the twelve themselves and some of those to whom a postponement had been granted when they returned after the appointed day; the Catholic Church did the same. II, 800, 814; IX, 704, 705. The sentence of the 310 Donatist bishops at Bagai against the Maximianists, pronounced in the year 394. II, 406, 407, 580; IX, 47, 98, 99, 269, 506, 550. Those to whom the council of Bagai granted a postponement of time were outside the Church. IX, 567, 570, 571, 573. Maximian yielded the Vaginensian episcopate for the sake of peace. II, 239.

Primian the Donatist separated the Maximianists from his communion. IX, 96. Why the case of the Maximianists was raised against the Donatists at the beginning of the Conference. IX, 616, 617. The case of the Maximianists cuts the Donatists to pieces. IX, 634, 636, 740. The Maximianists were produced for the purpose of convicting the Donatists of schism. IX, 257. The Donatists are separated from the whole world by a far greater crime of schism than the one they condemned in the Maximianists. II, 193. Why the Maximianists refused to yield to the judgment of Primian and the 310 bishops. IX, 39.

The Donatists approved the baptism of the Maximianists. IX, 113. But not all of them. IX, 114. A person is rebaptized after Maximian, but not after Felician or Praetextatus. IX, 253. The Donatists confirmed the baptism given in Maximian’s sacrilegious schism. II, 406, 580, 800. And they accepted it. IX, 99, 141, 180, 262. The Donatists were unjust in accepting the baptism of the Maximianists while repudiating the baptism of the whole world. II, 192, 265, 404. There is no better reason for not rebaptizing the Maximianists than for not rebaptizing other schismatics. IX, 99. The baptism of the Maximianists is null if baptism given by the wicked is null. IX, 509. Primian condemned Maximian and those who condemned him along with the others, yet received the condemned and rejected men back into their former offices and accepted the baptism conferred by them. II, 756; V, 553. The Maximianists were received by the Donatists just as they had been, honored, neither purified nor degraded by any more severe humiliation of penance, and not rebaptized. IX, 532, 630. Cresconius foolishly defends the reception of the Maximianists, together with those whom they had baptized, even into their offices. IX, 505, 507, 508.

The Maximianists, condemned at the council of Bagai and expelled from their basilicas but nevertheless received by the Donatists without any question concerning baptism, prove that people do not perish because of the crimes of others. IX, 371. The Donatists held that those who had communicated with the schismatic Maximian were not defiled, but that those who had communicated with Caecilian were defiled. II, 412. The Donatists complained against the Catholics—and indeed against Caecilian and Felix—of persecution through judicial power. II, 305. Yet they themselves persecuted the Maximianists through secular authorities. II, 192, 265. How fiercely they persecuted them. IX, 46, 47, 55, 254, 258, 316, 432, 704. Maximian suffered persecution both from Optatus and from Primian. IX, 578. Primian seized Maximian’s own house for use as an ecclesiastical exorcisterium. IX, 578. Maximian’s church was destroyed to its foundations. II, 177. Maximian asked assistance from a Christian emperor, not so much to avenge himself as to protect the Church entrusted to him. II, 806. Although the Maximianists had killed no one bodily, why were they accused by the Donatists as though they had shed blood? IX, 269. The Maximianists were expelled from their basilicas by the Donatists through public courts. IX, 48, 55, 137, 273, 630. To expel the Maximianists from the places they held, the Donatists used the laws enacted against heretics. IX, 303, 549. The Maximianists were expelled from the places belonging to the party of Donatus by orders of the judges. IX, 303, 531. To what extent the Donatists defended this action. IX, 48, 55, 137, 273, 630. The Maximianists sought a conference with the Catholics, but were rejected. X, 704. How the Donatists taunt the Maximianists. IX, 251, 262.

The Maximianist schism was less serious than that of the Donatists. IX, 432. In the two testimonies commonly used by the Donatists, the Maximianists defeated them. IX, 441. The Maximianists were fewer than the Donatists. IX, 586, 587. They were later than the Rogatists. IX, 46. The Maximianist schism broke out in Byzantium and Tripoli. II, 333. The Maximianist party occupied a few Tripolitan, Byzacene, and Provincial communities. IX, 395, 430, 586. The Maximianist schism lasted nearly three years. IX, 704. Maximian’s vigils. V, 1598. The Donatists compared Maximian and the Maximianists with those earlier schismatics whom the earth swallowed alive. IX, 132, 588.

**Maximian, bishop of Erumminum.** IV, 381.

**Maximilla,** the second prophetess of Montanus. VIII, 30.

**Maximinus, emperor.** VII, 614.

**Maximinus the Arian.** VIII, 707, 708. Bishop of the Arians. V, 773; VIII, 732. His faith concerning the Trinity. VIII, 711, 716, 717. His conference with Augustine. VIII, 742.

**Maximinus, bishop of Sinita.** VII, 764. Perhaps the same man who had previously been a Donatist. II, 94. And the same who, when accused of having rebaptized a Catholic deacon, was challenged by Augustine’s letter. II, 94. After converting to the Catholic Church, what he suffered from the Donatists. II, 397.

**Maximinus, the Catholic bishop who took part in the council of Zerta.** II, 577.

**Maximus.** IX, 755.

**Maximus the tyrant.** IX, 362. He killed Gratian. VII, 171. He expelled Valentinian, Gratian’s brother. VII, 172. He was killed by Theodosius. VII, 172.

**Maximus, bishop.** II, 759, 780.

**Maximus, bishop of Pittana.** IV, 381.

**Maximus of Madaura.** II, 81, 83.

**Maximus, presbyter, returned from schism to the Church.** IX, 492.

**Maximus, the presbyter to whom Cyprian writes.** IX, 192.

**Maximus, sent by Augustine to Macrobius.** II, 404.

**Maximus, converted from the Arian heresy in old age.** II, 752. He is urged to strive to bring his entire household, and those whom he had perverted, back to the Church. II, 748, 752. Alypius and Augustine are concerned whether he gratefully received the letter sent to him. II, 752.

**Mazuroth.** III, 877.

**Medea.** III, 1191; VIII, 601. Flying Medea. I, 687, 898.

**Mediator.** Who the Mediator is. IX, 60. Christ is the Mediator of life; the devil, the mediator of death. VIII, 896, 897, 898. How the Mediator of life overcame the mediator of death. VIII, 899. What the office of a mediator entails. VII, 269, 272. What is meant by “the Mediator between God and human beings.” V, 174, 1133. The Mediator had to possess something like God and something like human beings. I, 807. Christ is Mediator insofar as he is human. V, 1332. The necessity of the Mediator. V, 852, 1333. How the Mediator destroyed the pride of the captor through the humility of the redeemer. X, 409. The mystery of the Mediator was preached to the ancients through prophecy, and to us through the Gospel. III, 1070. Why the angels are not raised up through the Mediator. III, 1924, 2122. What the Mediator’s grace provides for us. VII, 300. We must cling to the Mediator all the more tenaciously the greater the power of demons we see in these lower regions. VII, 574. Through the one Mediator we are gathered from many into one. VIII, 895.

**Medicines.** Certain medicines are the daily restorations of our needs. IV, 1320. A medicine prepared by a wise man. IV, 681. Every illness of the soul has its medicine in the Scriptures. IV, 357; V, 207. The medicines themselves are torments. VII, 786.

**Medicine.** Medicine has two functions: one by which illness is cured, and another by which health is preserved. IV, 104. Medicine should not be neglected because the plague of some people is incurable. II, 522. The more medicine is praised, the more the disease from which it heals is blamed. X, 205. Medicine compared with agriculture. III, 380. The experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many medicines. II, 813. Medicine should not be rejected after sin. V, 127. Daily medicine in the Lord’s Prayer. V, 127.

**Physician.** Who is properly a physician. V, 1269. A physician must be endured even when he cuts. IV, 1319. It is a matter of skill, not cruelty, to deny certain things to someone not yet healthy so that he may be able to have everything when healthy. V, 1300. A physician is cruel who listens to a person and spares the wound and the putrefaction. IV, 319. The more hopeless the patient was thought to be, the more highly the physician is praised. IV, 1219. One who receives a physician is ill with hope; one who strikes him in madness is ill without hope. V, 943. The patient’s concord with the physician. V, 83, 1595. Why a physician of the body does not always heal. IV, 1319. God both heals surely and heals freely. IV, 1320. God deals with us in the manner of physicians. IV, 319.

**Christ the Physician.** V, 537, 539. He came to heal the human being. IV, 353, 1308. The earlier physician drank the bitter cup so that the patient would not fear drinking it. IV, 1259. What killed the physician benefited the patient as a medicine. IV, 1447. The physician’s blood as medicine for his own killer. V, 943, 946. The art of Christ the physician commended in Paul’s healing. IV, 1708; V, 949. For the omnipotent physician no illness is incurable. IV, 1319. The physician himself is salvation. V, 1499. See *Christ*. Comparison with a physician. V, 324, 495. Physicians as preachers of the word. IV, 1116. The proud are signified by the name “physicians.” IV, 1116.

**Milan.** V, 964. Relics were discovered at Milan. V, 1438. At Milan, at the Memorial of the Saints, demons confess wonderfully and terribly. II, 269. Meditation on the law of God. IV, 1555, 1570.

**Meditation on God** has its own inner affections and certain delights. IV, 778.

God is said to be in the middle, caring equally for everyone, just as something situated in the middle has equal distances from all its boundaries. IV, 520. Someone is said to be in the middle when the chief honor is shown to him. IV, 1445.

**The empire of the Medes** was transferred to the Persians. VII, 117.

**Megalius, bishop of Calama, primate of Numidia,** and Augustine’s ordaining bishop. IX, 357, Note (a), 628. While Augustine was still a presbyter, he wrote against him in a hostile sense. IX, 357. Before the holy council he asked and obtained pardon for having sinned in this way against Augustine. II, 152 and Note; IX, 357. The death of Megalius. II, 152.

**Megasius, bishop.** II, 759, 780.

**Honey.** Hymettian honey is sharply sweet. I, 966. Scholastic honey. I, 966. Honey from the rock signifies the wisdom of Christ. IV, 1046. Clear teaching of wisdom is like honey; teaching expressed from more obscure mysteries is like the honeycomb. IV, 1566.

**Melania.** II, 478, 928. Daughter of Albina and wife of Pinianus. X, 385. Melania lived in a monastery. II, 348. Melania lived at Thagaste with Albina and Pinianus. II, 473. Melania’s restraint in mourning the death of her only son, Publicola. II, 347. Melania was praised by Augustine. II, 918.

**Melanthus,** the sixteenth king of Athens. VII, 577.

**Melantonice,** wife of King Criasius, enrolled among the gods. VII, 565.

**Melchi.** I, 633.

**Melchiades,** presbyter of Marcellinus, bishop of Rome, and later himself bishop of Rome. IX, 40, 610, 637. He presided over the council at which Caecilian was acquitted. II, 399; IX, 40, 610, 637. The council of Melchiades has a date and consuls. IX, 663. The Donatists accuse Melchiades of the crime of handing over the Scriptures. IX, 40, 645, 646, 661. He is cleared of the crime of handing them over. IX, 610, 661. The judgment of Melchiades in favor of Caecilian. IX, 613. When it was held. IX, 687. He did not usurp this judgment. II, 166. The Donatists wished to destroy Melchiades’ judgment in favor of Caecilian. IX, 646, 661. Melchiades confirmed Caecilian in the episcopate and rejected Donatus. II, 161. Melchiades, son of Christian peace and father of the Christian people, presented letters of communion even to those who were known to have been ordained by Majorinus, so that in whatever places there were two bishops produced by dissension, he wished the one to be confirmed who had been ordained first. II, 167.

**Melchizedek.** Some question whether Melchizedek was a human being or an angel. III, 567. Melchizedek represented Christ. III, 111. His priesthood prefigured Christ’s priesthood. II, 769. So too did he prefigure the Eucharist when he offered bread and wine. VII, 500.

**Melchizedekians,** heretics. VIII, 31.

**Melech.** In Hebrew, the word signifies “choir.” IV, 1109.

**Meletius,** a heretic from whom came the Meletians, who are now said to be joined to the Arians. VIII, 39.

**Melicertes,** son of King Athamas, enrolled among the gods. VII, 572.

**Mellona,** the goddess concerned with honey. VII, 140.

**Melody.** The usefulness of melody in ecclesiastical song. I, 800. To be attracted by melody rather than by the subject matter is a sin. I, 801.

**Melos.** When Augustine was considering writing six books on melody, other affairs turned him elsewhere. II, 369.

**Melonitanus.** II, 694.

**Melza, Melzita.** IX, 507, 528, 550.

**Members.** Some members are for use, others for beauty. V, 1146. The members of the body are either the dwelling place or the instrument of something inward. V, 371. The members of the body, except those that serve lust, are moved by the will. VII, 427, 431, 432. Those that serve lust would also have been moved at the will’s command if the human being had not sinned. VII, 432. Julian thinks that shame concerning the members was implanted from the beginning of creation. X, 779. Even the philosophers recognized that the genital members are shameful. X, 766. Concerning the modesty of the members. X, 1363. The disobedience of the members is the punishment of sin. X, 472. Why the genital members are called “shameful.” X, 173. From where the term “shameful members” comes. X, 405, 406, 417. The origin of dishonorable members. X, 780. Why they are called dishonorable. X, 806. The first parents covered their members out of shame. X, 780, 781. See *Shame, Blushing*. Sin caused certain members to be dishonorable and shameful. X, 1356. Monstrous members would not have been born if no one had sinned. X, 1438.

The different functions of the members and their common life. V, 1231. One spirit. V, 1232. Harmony and concord among the members. V, 165, 502, 1145. Their marvelous mutual agreement. IV, 1707. All the members serve one another because of the unity of the body. III, 1541. The concord of the members is a symbol of charity. III, 1645; VI, 125, 126. In that concord each possesses what the other possesses. III, 1646. The members of the body share one another’s suffering. IV, 231, 1296. A severed member retains its form but not its life. V, 1232.

**Members of Christ.** V, 1530. Their union with Christ the head, and an apt comparison concerning this. V, 1606. The world’s hatred of the members of Christ. V, 1563. Charity makes us members of Christ. III, 1618. The voice of the members must be recognized in the head. IV, 1295. Christ still labors and thirsts in his members. IV, 1284, 1285, 1630. Just as in our members there are different operations but one health, so in Christ’s members there are different ministries but one charity. IV, 296.

In what sense bodily members are attributed to God in Scripture. III, 210. The members attributed to God are to be understood spiritually. II, 628.

**Membresa.** IX, 107, 234, 507, 528, 549, 550.

**Memor,** father of Julian. X, 833. Augustine’s friend. X, 648.

**Memory.** How the mind remembers. VIII, 993, 994, 995. Whether memory concerns present things. VIII, 1047. The unfathomable treasury of memory. X, 530. The remarkable and excellent memory of Simplicius. X, 529. Confidence in memory. X, 529, 530. Even animals are perceived to possess memory of bodily things. VIII, 185. Cattle and birds possess memory. I, 790. A certain kind of memory exists in human beings which animals do not possess. VIII, 1090. How much memory contributes to certain thoughts that we foresee as though they were future. VIII, 1066. A kind of trinity in memory. VIII, 993. Memory, understanding, and will are essentially one, but three relatively. VIII, 983. How memory remembering itself, understanding itself, and loving itself forms a Trinity. VIII, 1046. Memory, understanding, and will are three equal things, not only each equal to each but each equal to all. VIII, 983. In memory, understanding, and will, aptitude and use are observed. VIII, 982.

The memory of God over us—how sweet it is. IV, 1874. God is said to forget when he does not act, and to remember when he acts. IV, 1112.

Whether memory should be attributed to the mind or to the body. I, 1040, 1087. Although not every image belongs together with memory, Nebridius nevertheless thinks that no memory can exist without an image. II, 67. Memory can exist without an image. II, 68. How memory is aroused. III, 1589. The power of memory. I, 784. Memory preserves incorporeal likenesses of sensible things. II, 614.

**Memorials of the martyrs.** I, 719. The communion of the Lord’s body was customarily celebrated at them. I, 719. It seems remarkable that a memorial of Saint Stephen was built before his body was discovered. V, 1445. At Milan, at the Memorial of the Saints, demons confess wonderfully and terribly; a thief was compelled to confess his theft. II, 269. Augustine sends two of his men to the Memorial of Blessed Felix of Nola so that it might become clear which of them was guilty. II, 269. It is remarkable why miracles occur in some places and not in others. II, 269.

Memorials of the martyrs. See *Martyrs*. Those very people who persecuted the martyrs seek out their memorials, either to worship there or to become drunk there. IV, 1782. Ambrose forbids banquets to be brought there. I, 719, 720. The memorial of the martyr Cyprian, not far from the sea. I, 713. “Memorial” is used for relics or for the reliquary containing relics. VII, 768. Marble memorials of wealthy dead people. IV, 322, 554.

**Memorius** desires Augustine’s books *On Music*. II, 367, 368.

**Memorius, presbyter.** IX, 513.

**Memphis,** the city where the pharaohs lived. III, 584.

**Mena,** daughter of Jupiter and stepdaughter of Juno Lucina. VII, 195. The function of the goddess Mena. VII, 195. Mena presides over women’s menstruation. VII, 122.

**Menander,** a heretic from whom came the heretical Menandrians. VIII, 26.

**Lying.** What lying is. VI, 488, 489. A lie occurs when someone knowingly says what is false, whether anyone is harmed by it or no one is harmed. III, 708. A lie is a false signification with the intention of deceiving. VI, 537. Anything contrary to the Law and the truth is called a lie. IV, 1175. What difference there is between lying and deceiving. I, 892; III, 149. A person who lies or does not lie must be judged not from the truth or falsity of the matter but from the judgment of his own mind. VI, 489. The fault of one who lies is the desire to deceive in making a statement. VI, 489. In one who lies there is a will to learn what is false. III, 34. One who unknowingly says what is false does not lie; rather, one lies who says what is true while thinking it false. V, 739; VI, 240. Concealing the truth is one thing; uttering a lie is another. IV, 85; VI, 533. Whether the intention to deceive in the speaker is required for a lie, or whether it suffices. VI, 489.

A lie is not something that lacks a double heart. IV, 86. The heart of one who lies is double. VI, 488. Fictions in words and actions are not always lies but sometimes figures. III, 1362. Tropes are not lies. II, 778; VI, 533. Nor are jokes. III, 587; VI, 487. Lies told to please through flattering speech are to be avoided. VI, 501. People generally lie through flattery. IV, 87. There are two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, though they are still not without fault: when we joke, or when we lie in order to benefit someone. IV, 86. Such lies are not found in those who are perfect. IV, 85. Those who lie only in this way will at some time deserve to be freed from every lie. IV, 85, 86.

The itch to lie. III, 208. The desire to lie arose in Adam after the sin. III, 212. A lie is not a substance or nature but belongs to what is not, not to what is. IV, 85. Whether it is ever proper for a good man, indeed a Christian, to lie, is a major question. II, 285. An extremely obscure question. V, 738. Whether lying can ever be useful or lawful. VI, 491, 513. Some have held that a lie may be uttered never by the mouth of the heart, but sometimes by the mouth of the body. VI, 508, 510.

There is not only one kind of lie. III, 2000. Here human beings have a treasury of lies. V, 1185. A well-intentioned lie. VI, 496. Whether some lies are honorable, when they benefit certain people and harm no one. VI, 502. Whether it is lawful to use them. VI, 501, 502. Some admit them. III, 622. Well-intentioned lies are praised not for their content but for their disposition. IV, 85. A perfect and spiritual person ought not to lie for the sake of this temporal life. IV, 85. Whether one should lie so as not to betray either a murderer or an innocent person being sought for execution. VI, 503. What an interrogated person who knows where the person sought for execution is should answer. VI, 504. Firmus, bishop of Thagaste, neither wishes to lie nor can be forced by torture to betray the person being sought. VI, 504. Whether a good person may ever lie for another’s safety. VI, 541. One must not lie for anyone’s temporal safety. VI, 494, 495. Nor must one lie with the intention of preserving others for eternal life. VI, 496. No one is to be led to eternal salvation with the help of a lie. VI, 516. In danger to eternal salvation, just as no one ought to be helped by sexual violation, so no one ought to be helped by a lie. VI, 546. Whoever lies only for a person’s safety has made very great progress; what should be praised, or even rewarded, is not his deceit but his benevolence. VI, 244, 492, 541. Whether one should lie for the sake of chastity. VI, 495, 515. Human judgment says that one should lie to conceal from a sick person something that would bring him death; the light of the mind does not say this. VI, 543. Truth would then wrongly be called murderous. VI, 543. If lying is permitted in the proposed case, access is opened to perjuries and blasphemies. VI, 544. Lies must not be used to expose heretics in hiding. VI, 518, 519, 520, 521.

The Priscillianists wish lies to be used to conceal matters from outsiders. VI, 519. Among heretics they alone hold this opinion. VI, 519. Lying and perjury are familiar to the Priscillianists. I, 654. A book against lying was written on the occasion of the Priscillianists. I, 654. An earlier book on lying. I, 630. Some think that a lie should be used to avert a more serious evil inflicted upon them by another. VI, 497. They are refuted. VI, 497. Lies are either to be avoided by acting rightly or confessed through repentance. VI, 547. How insulting to God is the lie of someone confessing sins that he did not have. VI, 720, 721. A lie in the guise of humility is a sin. V, 981. It is not permissible to lie even for the sake of modesty. X, 265. A lie is not to be admitted under any apparently good intention. VI, 527. A lie must never be used in religious teaching. VI, 500, 535, 536.

It is not permissible to lie to anyone. IV, 189. Eight kinds of lies. VI, 505. One must never lie by any of the eight kinds of lies listed. VI, 516. It must be firmly believed that lying is entirely absent from the authors of the sacred Scriptures. II, 285. Lying does not enter the Gospel. V, 740. How dangerous it is to attribute any lie, even a well-intentioned one, to Scripture. II, 112; VI, 404. If well-intentioned lies were admitted in Holy Scripture, its authority would collapse. II, 113, 155, 156, 157, 278.

Examples of lying sought in the Scriptures are examined. III, 708; VI, 492, 533. The rule by which passages brought forward from Scripture as examples of lying are to be evaluated. VI, 543. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are defended against the charge of lying. V, 45; VI, 533, 534. The Egyptian midwives who lied are approved because of their disposition toward moral improvement. VI, 492. Whether the lie of the Egyptian midwives deserved a reward. III, 597. In the case of the Hebrew midwives and Rahab, it was not deceit but benevolence that was rewarded. VI, 540. They would have done better to abstain from lying. VI, 541, 542. The lie of the Egyptian midwives is not to be imitated. III, 597. Nor are the true lies narrated in the Old Testament to be imitated. VI, 539. Who the spirit of lying sent to deceive Ahab was. VI, 146. Gospel passages that seem to support lying are discussed. VI, 537. No example of lying is available from the New Testament. VI, 492, 536, 537. Christ is defended against the charge of lying. V, 740. It is vigorously defended that Christ did not lie when he said, “I am not going up to the feast,” and nevertheless went up. V, 737. One who promises something and does not do it does not always lie. V, 738. Whether certain acts of the apostles favor lying. VI, 536. Augustine grieves that Jerome undertook the defense of lying. II, 112.

Mendacium an possit excusari. III, 708. Whether a lie can be excused. III, 708.  
Nullum mendacium potest esse justum. VI, 539. No lie can be just. VI, 539.  
Mendacium divina lege vetitum. V, 502, 907. Lying is forbidden by divine law. V, 502, 907.  
Mendacium quia injustum erat, ideo prohibitum. III, 708. Lying was forbidden because it was unjust. III, 708.  
Mendacium omne esse peccatum. VI, 240, 243, 516, 547. Every lie is a sin. VI, 240, 243, 516, 547.  
Diabolus homines possidet, quando mendacium eos possidet. III, 1453. The devil possesses people when a lie possesses them. III, 1453.  
Mendacium animam occidit. V, 429, 502, 880. A lie kills the soul. V, 429, 502, 880.  
Mendacio vita aeterna amittitur. VI, 495. Through lying, eternal life is lost. VI, 495.  
Ab aeternitate tanto quisque discedit, quanto a veritate discedit. VI, 496. Each person departs from eternity to the extent that he departs from the truth. VI, 496.  
Mendacium magis obest mentienti, quam ei qui per illud decipitur. VI, 239, 240. A lie harms the liar more than the person deceived by it. VI, 239, 240.  
Mendacium in Anania et Sapphira punitum. V, 799. The lie of Ananias and Sapphira was punished. V, 799.  
Mendacii doctores acute impugnantur. VI, 544, 545. The teachers of lying are sharply refuted. VI, 544, 545.  
Defensores mendacii quam caeci. VI, 517. How blind are the defenders of lying! VI, 517.  
Omne opus malum cogitatum, mendacium ducem habet. IV, 1811. Every evil deed conceived in thought has a lie as its guide. IV, 1811.  
Mendacium, peccatum omne potest appellari. VII, 407. Every sin can be called a lie. VII, 407.  
Inter multa mendaciorum genera, quaenam pejora. VI, 516, 520, 521. Among the many kinds of lies, which are the worse. VI, 516, 520, 521.  
Mendacii signa et prodigia. VII, 687. Signs and wonders of lying. VII, 687.  
In vetere homine mendacium, in novo veritas. V, 908, 909. In the old person there is lying; in the new, truth. V, 908, 909.  
Homo de suo non habet nisi mendacium. V, 1185, 1193. A human being has nothing of his own except a lie. V, 1185, 1193.  
Nihil est hominis proprium, nisi forte mendacium. III, 18. Nothing is proper to a human being, except perhaps a lie. III, 18.  
In ore hominum veritas non est, quia cor eorum fallitur de peccato, et de poena peccati. IV, 87. There is no truth in the mouth of human beings, because their heart is deceived concerning sin and the punishment of sin. IV, 87.  
Mendacium loqui laborant homines; nam veritatem tota facilitate loquerentur. IV, 1811. People struggle to speak lies; for they would speak the truth with complete ease. IV, 1811.  
Merces caventium mendacium amore veritatis. III, 213. The reward of those who avoid lying is love of the truth. III, 213.

Mentiri et falli in quo differant. V, 157, 738. In what lying and being deceived differ. V, 157, 738.  
Mentiens et mendax differunt. VI, 501. A person who lies and a liar are different. VI, 501.  
Mendax qui aliud loquitur, aliud agit. III, 2002. A liar is one who says one thing and does another. III, 2002.  
Omnis homo mendax ex se ipso, verax ex Dei gratia. V, 1452; X, 307. Every human being is a liar by himself, truthful by the grace of God. V, 1452; X, 307.  
Si mentiris, verum dicis, sophisma Chrysippi. IX, 483. “If you are lying, you are telling the truth”: a sophism of Chrysippus. IX, 483.

## Beggar

Mendicus. The beggar.  
Qui, a quibus, quidve petunt hîc mendici nostri. V, 411. Who these beggars of ours are, from whom they ask, and what they ask. V, 411.  
Mendico debetur eleemosyna. IV, 1367. Alms are owed to a beggar. IV, 1367.  
Vide Eleemosyna. See Almsgiving.  
Mendicus plerumque ostiatim cantat Dei praeceptum. V, 205. A beggar usually sings the commandment of God from door to door. V, 205.  
Mendicus est qui Deum non habet, licet bonis omnibus aliis rebus affluat. IV, 1883. A person who does not possess God is a beggar, even if he abounds in every other good. IV, 1883.  
Mendicus es quamdiu pannosam mortalitatis carnem portas. IV, 1885. You are a beggar as long as you bear the ragged flesh of mortality. IV, 1885.  
Omnes sumus mendici Dei. V, 366, 380, 410, 515, 686. We are all beggars before God. V, 366, 380, 410, 515, 686.  
Mendicemus ante januam conspectus Dei in orationibus. IV, 1896. Let us beg in prayers before the door of God’s presence. IV, 1896.  
Mendicus inferni. V, 612. The beggar of hell. V, 612.  
Mendicat ante te anima tua: quo pane egeat. V, 627. Your soul begs before you: what bread it needs. V, 627.

Menelaus maritus Helenae. VII, 81, 82. Menelaus, the husband of Helen. VII, 81, 82.

[Col. 0435] Menestheus rex Atheniensium. VII, 576. Menestheus, king of the Athenians. VII, 576.

Meniana. V, 77. Meniana. V, 77.

Mens dea. VII, 128, 196. Mens, the goddess. VII, 128, 196.

Mens quid sit. IV, 480; X, 545. What the mind is. IV, 480; X, 545.  
Mentis nomine quid intelligendum, ut ferri possit Anaxagorae sententia de Deo. II, 443, 444. What is to be understood by the term “mind,” so that Anaxagoras’ opinion about God may be acceptable. II, 443, 444.  
Mentem incorpoream esse probatur. VII, 230. It is proved that the mind is incorporeal. VII, 230.  
Mentis humanae excellentia demonstratur. VII, 789. The excellence of the human mind is demonstrated. VII, 789.  
Optimum in homine est mens et ratio. I, 586, 908. The best thing in a human being is the mind and reason. I, 586, 908.  
Mens, ratio et spiritus vocatur. I, 1232. It is called mind, reason, and spirit. I, 1232.  
Mens omnis spiritus est, non omnis spiritus mens est. VIII, 1053. Every mind is spirit, but not every spirit is mind. VIII, 1053.  
Mens pars est superior et caput animae. IV, 73, 74, 1887. The mind is the higher part and the head of the soul. IV, 73, 74, 1887.  
Ratio et intelligentia menti naturaliter inest. VII, 318. Reason and understanding are naturally present in the mind. VII, 318.  
Sapiente et rationali mente, nihil praeter Deum praestantius. I, 1233. To a wise and rational mind, nothing is superior except God. I, 1233.  
Supra mentem Deus. VIII, 1057. God is above the mind. VIII, 1057.  
Mens coelum. V, 380. The mind is heaven. V, 380.  
Mens atque intelligentia oculis et hoc vulgari aspectu est melior, quia magis sunt illa quae intelligimus, quam ista quae cernimus. II, 66. The mind and understanding are superior to the eyes and ordinary sight, because the things we understand are more substantial than those we see. II, 66.  
Mens etsi amissa Dei participatione obsoleta sit et deformis, Dei tamen imago permanet. VIII, 1044. Although the mind has become worn and deformed through losing participation in God, the image of God nevertheless remains. VIII, 1044.  
In qua parte mentis Trinitas et imago Dei. VIII, 1000. In what part of the mind the Trinity and the image of God are found. VIII, 1000.  
Mens imago Trinitatis in sui ipsius memoria, intelligentia, et voluntate. VIII, 984. The mind is an image of the Trinity in its own memory, understanding, and will. VIII, 984.  
Mens, amor, et notitia, vestigium Trinitatis. VIII, 963. The mind, love, and knowledge are a trace of the Trinity. VIII, 963.

Mens humana sui numquam non meminit, se non intelligit, se non diligit. VIII, 1049. The human mind never fails to remember itself; it does not understand itself or love itself. VIII, 1049.  
Etiam in infirmitatis et erroris malis. VIII, 1050. Even amid the evils of weakness and error. VIII, 1050.  
Mens, amor, et notitia ejus, substantialiter eadem sunt, et relative dicuntur. VIII, 964, 965. The mind, its love, and its knowledge are substantially the same, and are spoken of relationally. VIII, 964, 965.  
Tria haec unum et aequalia. VIII, 963. These three are one and equal. VIII, 963.  
Singula sunt in se ipsis et tota in totis. VIII, 965. Each exists in itself, and the whole exists in the whole. VIII, 965.  
Sunt inseparabilia. VIII, 964. They are inseparable. VIII, 964.  
Sed non partium instar juncta. VIII, 964. But they are not joined like parts. VIII, 964.

Mens praeferenda memoriae. VII, 196. The mind is to be preferred to memory. VII, 196.  
In mente hominis quasi masculus et femina reperitur. III, 291. In the human mind, as it were, a male and a female are found. III, 291.  
In mente una, ratio superior, quae ad contemplationem; et inferior, quae pertinet ad actionem. VIII, 999, 1009. In one mind there is a higher reason, which pertains to contemplation, and a lower reason, which pertains to action. VIII, 999, 1009.  
Quomodo in mente ratio superior et inferior regendae. VIII, 1004, 1007. How the higher and lower reason in the mind are to be governed. VIII, 1004, 1007.  
Mens nostra quomodo formanda. VIII, 1009. How our mind is to be formed. VIII, 1009.  
Mens omnis tria de se ipsa certo scit, intelligere, esse, et vivere. VIII, 980. Every mind knows three things about itself with certainty: that it understands, exists, and lives. VIII, 980.  
De se ipsa certo scit se velle et meminisse. VIII, 980. It knows with certainty about itself that it wills and remembers. VIII, 980.  
Mens quomodo et se cogitat, et se novit. VIII, 1041. How the mind both thinks of itself and knows itself. VIII, 1041.  
Se ipsam per se ipsam novit. VIII, 962. It knows itself through itself. VIII, 962.  
Non ex parte, sed totam se cognoscit. VIII, 976. It knows itself not partially, but as a whole. VIII, 976.  
Mens eo ipso se cognoscit, quo intelligit praeceptum se cognoscendi. VIII, 980. The mind knows itself precisely by understanding the command to know itself. VIII, 980.  
Unde errores mentis de sua ipsius substantia. VIII, 977, 978, 979, 980. The source of the mind’s errors concerning its own substance. VIII, 977, 978, 979, 980.  
Unde mentis falsa de se ipsa existimatio. VIII, 978. The source of the mind’s false opinion about itself. VIII, 978.  
Mens infantium an se noverit. VIII, 1040. Whether the minds of infants know themselves. VIII, 1040.  
Cur sicut notitia mentis est proles, non etiam amor partus ejusdem sit. VIII, 970. Why, although the mind’s knowledge is its offspring, love is not also its offspring. VIII, 970.  
Mens amat se ipsam non incognitam sibi. VIII, 975. The mind loves itself, and it is not unknown to itself. VIII, 975.  
Mens se diligendo, diligit Deum; quem si non diligat, se ipsam odisse dicenda est. VIII, 1049. In loving itself, the mind loves God; if it does not love him, it must be said to hate itself. VIII, 1049.  
Ad memoriam mensura, ad visionem numerus, ad voluntatem pondus pertinet. VIII, 998. Measure pertains to memory, number to vision, and weight to the will. VIII, 998.  
Quanta intentione, in ista quae foris sunt sensibilia, mens feratur. VIII, 1041. With what intensity the mind is directed toward those sensible things that are outside. VIII, 1041.  
Quisquis mente cernere aliquid potest, intus est discipulus veritatis, foris judex loquentis. I, 1218. Whoever can perceive something with the mind is inwardly a disciple of truth and outwardly a judge of the speaker. I, 1218.  
Mentis lumen Deus. VII, 232. God is the light of the mind. VII, 232.  
Mentes rationales non habent veram lucem suam, nisi ipsum Verbum Dei. III, 331, 332. Rational minds have no true light of their own except the very Word of God. III, 331, 332.  
Ab omni iniquitate et errore mundatae, poterunt participes esse Verbi Dei. III, 331, 332. Once cleansed from every iniquity and error, they will be able to share in the Word of God. III, 331, 332.  
Mens primo purganda fuerat fide ad incommutabile lumen perferendum. VII, 318. The mind first had to be purified by faith in order to bear the unchangeable light. VII, 318.

Mens et ratio velut in arce collocata, ad regendas libidines et iram. VII, 427. The mind and reason are placed, as it were, in a citadel to govern lust and anger. VII, 427.  
Mens a nullo cogitur servire libidini. I, 1232. The mind is compelled by no one to serve lust. I, 1232.  
Huic obtemperare convenit caetera quaeque in homine sunt. I, 585, 909. Everything else in a human being ought to obey it. I, 585, 909.  
Mentem sevocare a sensibus, magni est ingenii. II, 517. To withdraw the mind from the senses is a mark of great ability. II, 517.  
Mens regit carnem, caro regitur. V, 837. The mind governs the flesh, and the flesh is governed. V, 837.  
Recte regit, cum a Deo regitur. V, 842. It governs rightly when it is governed by God. V, 842.  
Serviat meliori, ut serviat sibi inferior. V, 821. Let it serve what is better, so that what is inferior may serve it. V, 821.  
In clausis cubiculis orare, est in mentis penetralibus orare. I, 1195. To pray in closed rooms is to pray in the inner chambers of the mind. I, 1195.  
Unde mens turbetur in articulo mortis. IV, 481. The source of the mind’s disturbance at the moment of death. IV, 481.

## Table

Mensa Domini. V, 145, 193, 1649. The table of the Lord. V, 145, 193, 1649.  
Mensa potentis. III, 1733, 1846; V, 1395, 1462. The table of the powerful. III, 1733, 1846; V, 1395, 1462.  
Mensa magna, ubi epulae sunt ipse Dominus mensae. V, 1455. The great table, where the Lord himself is the feast of the table. V, 1455.  
Mensa magna ad quam Dominus nos invitat. V, 1107. The great table to which the Lord invites us. V, 1107.  
Vide Eucharistia. See Eucharist.  
Mensa S. Cypriani. V, 107, 320, 652, 729, 833, 915, 1397. The table of Saint Cyprian. V, 107, 320, 652, 729, 833, 915, 1397.  
Mensa Deo constructa, cur dicatur Cypriani. V, 1413. Why a table constructed for God is called Cyprian’s. V, 1413.  
Hora ad mensam accedendi, quinta. V, 1521. The hour for approaching the table was the fifth hour. V, 1521.  
Not. (a). Note (a).

Menses in prioribus saeculis tales fuerunt, quales nunc. VII, 454. The months in earlier centuries were such as they are now. VII, 454.  
Mensibus quibusdam deorum gentium nomina imposita, caeteri a numeris nominantur. VIII, 346. The names of the gods of the nations were assigned to certain months; the others are named from numbers. VIII, 346.  
Mensem veteres observaverunt talem, quem circuitus lunaris ostendit. VIII, 893. The ancients observed a month such as the lunar cycle reveals. VIII, 893.

Mensurae nomine, aut res quae metitur, aut mensura qua metitur, intelligitur. II, 380. By the term “measure” is understood either the thing that measures or the measure by which it measures. II, 380.  
Non omnis mensura circumscribitur tempore. II, 379. Not every measure is bounded by time. II, 379.  
Mensura temporis. I, 822. The measure of time. I, 822.  
Mensura, numerus, et pondus etiam in spiritalibus. III, 299, 300. Measure, number, and weight also in spiritual matters. III, 299, 300.

Mensurius Carthaginensis episcopus a Donatistis traditionis accusatus. IX, 638. Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, accused by the Donatists of delivering up the sacred books. IX, 638.  
Et a Petiliano. IX, 323. And by Petilianus. IX, 323.  
Mensurius vindicatur. IX, 611. Mensurius is defended. IX, 611.  
Mensurii epistola ad Secundum Tigisitanum. IX, 638. Mensurius’ letter to Secundus of Tigisis. IX, 638.  
Ejus veritas unde assorebatur. IX, 644. From where the truth of his account was confirmed. IX, 644.  
[Col. 0436] Mensurius in communionis unitate defunctus est, antequam se scinderet pars Donati. IX, 362. Mensurius died in the unity of communion before the party of Donatus separated itself. IX, 362.

Mercator quem filii nomine appellat Augustinus. VI, 159. Mercator, whom Augustine addresses by the name “son.” VI, 159.  
Mercator rescriptum Augustini non accipiens, alias ei asperiores litteras scribit. II, 869. Mercator, not accepting Augustine’s reply, writes him another and harsher letter. II, 869.  
Simulque mittit librum adversus novos haereticos, sanctarum Scripturarum testimoniis refertum. II, 869. At the same time he sends a book against the new heretics, filled with testimonies from the holy Scriptures. II, 869.

Mercatorum pericula et peccata. IV, 886. The dangers and sins of merchants. IV, 886.  
An mercatura sit licita. IV, 886. Whether commerce is lawful. IV, 886.

## Reward

Merces. Reward.  
Attende mercedem, si vis tolerare laborem. IV, 372. Keep your reward in view if you wish to endure labor. IV, 372.  
Merces transitoria, data obedientiae exhibitae ex dominationis cupiditate. VI, 520. A passing reward, given for obedience rendered out of desire for domination. VI, 520.  
Qui negligens est in exhibendo opere, impudens est in exigenda mercede. V, 1112. Whoever is negligent in performing the work is shameless in demanding the reward. V, 1112.  
Quidam putant perire opera sua, quia non eis redditur merces peritura. IV, 1168. Some think that their works perish because the perishable reward is not paid to them. IV, 1168.  
Merces nisi finito die non est petenda. IV, 360, 372, 1201. The reward is not to be sought until the day is finished. IV, 360, 372, 1201.  
Mercedem si vellet Deus reddere, poenam redderet. III, 2066. If God wished to repay us according to our deserts, he would repay us with punishment. III, 2066.  
Merces nostra, gratia vocatur. IV, 262. Our reward is called grace. IV, 262.  
Coronat Deus in misericordia et miseratione. X, 239. God crowns us with mercy and compassion. X, 239.  
Merces cultus Dei, quaenam exspectanda. V, 135. What reward for the worship of God is to be expected. V, 135.  
Bonorum operum merces non isto tempore speranda. V, 99. The reward of good works is not to be hoped for in this present age. V, 99.  
Merces aeterna promissa, quid. X, 222. What the promised eternal reward is. X, 222.  
Merces aeterna pertinet ad novum Testamentum. X, 225, 226. The eternal reward belongs to the New Testament. X, 225, 226.  
Per Jeremiam praedicta est. X, 224. It was foretold through Jeremiah. X, 224.  
Merces summa haec est, frui Deo et aliis in ipso. III, 32. The highest reward is this: to enjoy God and others in him. III, 32.  
Quomodo omnium erit merces aeterna. X, 224. How the eternal reward will belong to all. X, 224.  
Merces te erigat, si opus turbat. V, 1517. Let the reward lift you up if the work disturbs you. V, 1517.  
Merces consoletur, si opus fatigat. V, 70. Let the reward console you if the work tires you. V, 70.  
Mercedis a Deo promissae certitudo. V, 237. Certainty of the reward promised by God. V, 237.  
Merces sine fine, opus cum fine. V, 1278. A reward without end, a work with an end. V, 1278.  
Mercedis promissae memoria perseverantem facit in opere. III, 2003. Remembrance of the promised reward makes one persevere in the work. III, 2003.  
Mercedis spem non tollit amor Dei gratuitus. V, 1482. The freely given love of God does not remove hope of reward. V, 1482.  
Vide Beatitudo. See Blessedness.

Mercenarii merces, dicitur sanguis. III, 704. The reward of the hired worker is said to be blood. III, 704.

Mercenarius pastor, quis. III, 1729, 1732. Who the hired shepherd is. III, 1729, 1732.  
Mercenarius est, qui peccantem non libere audet arguere. III, 1732. A hired worker is one who does not dare freely to rebuke the sinner. III, 1732.  
Mercenarii fuga quatenus intelligenda. IX, 713. How the flight of the hired worker is to be understood. IX, 713.  
Mercenarii fugientes, dum iniquis favent. V, 762. The hired workers flee while they favor the wicked. V, 762.  
Vide Ovis, Pastor. See Sheep; Shepherd.  
Mercenariorum opera Ecclesiae necessaria. III, 1730. The work of hired workers is necessary for the Church. III, 1730.

Mercimonium. Antiqua commercia mutatis rebus fiebant. V, 497. Trade. Ancient commerce was conducted by exchanging goods. V, 497.  
Mercimonium coeleste. V, 496. Heavenly trade. V, 496.  
Mercimonium Christi. V, 1114. The commerce of Christ. V, 1114.  
Mercaturam quodam modo Dominus vult nos cum ipso exercere. V, 959. In a certain manner the Lord wishes us to conduct commerce with him. V, 959.

Mercurius nepos Atlantis ex Maia filia, quo tempore fuit. VII, 565, 599. Mercury, the grandson of Atlas through his daughter Maia, and the time in which he lived. VII, 565, 599.  
Quare in deorum numerum relatus. VII, 565. Why he was reckoned among the gods. VII, 565.  
Mercurius appellatur nuntius. VII, 205. Mercury is called a messenger. VII, 205.  
Mercurius, quasi medius currens. VII, 205. Mercury, as if “running between.” VII, 205.  
Mercurius mortalis fuit. VII, 254. Mercury was mortal. VII, 254.  
Cur alatus pingitur. VII, 205. Why he is depicted with wings. VII, 205.  
Mercurii officia. VII, 205. The functions of Mercury. VII, 205.  
Mercurius litterarum repertor dicitur. III, 49. Mercury is said to have discovered letters. III, 49.  
Eloquentiae praeerat. VII, 128. He presided over eloquence. VII, 128.  
Not. (a). Note (a).  
Et mercibus. VII, 205. And over merchandise. VII, 205.  
Sepultura Mercurii in civitate Hermopoli. VII, 254. The burial of Mercury in the city of Hermopolis. VII, 254.  
Mercurius avus Trismegisti. VII, 254, 599. Mercury, the grandfather of Trismegistus. VII, 254, 599.

Mercurius Trismegistus, nepos Mercurii majoris. VII, 254, 599. Mercury Trismegistus, grandson of the elder Mercury. VII, 254, 599.  
Non praecedit tempore Patriarchas, neque ipsum Moysen. VII, 599. He did not precede the Patriarchs in time, nor Moses himself. VII, 599.

Meretrices cur toleratae. I, 1000. Why prostitutes are tolerated. I, 1000.  
Meretrices ad sacramenta Christi non permittuntur accedere. VI, 213, 219. Prostitutes are not permitted to approach the sacraments of Christ. VI, 213, 219.  
Meretricis domus, inferni imaginem tenet. V, 1642. The house of a prostitute bears the image of hell. V, 1642.  
De meretrice dictum. Luc. VII, Cui plurimum dimittitur. V, 97. What is said about the prostitute in Luke 7, “To whom much is forgiven.” V, 97.  
Meretrices lupae vocatae. VII, 578. Prostitutes are called she-wolves. VII, 578.

Meridies, quid sit. V, 767. What midday is. V, 767.  
Meridies multifarie intelligitur. V, 292. “Midday” is understood in many ways. V, 292.  
Meridies mundi, Aegyptus. V, 291, 292. The midday of the world is Egypt. V, 291, 292.  
Meridies in Scripturis quid significet. IX, 422. What midday signifies in the Scriptures. IX, 422.

Merinthiani haeretici a Merintho. VIII, 27. The Merinthians, heretics named after Merinthus. VIII, 27.

Merita in nobis seu bona, seu mala. X, 873, 874. Merits in us, whether good or evil. X, 873, 874.  
Merita nostra faciunt nobis terrorem. V, 1199. Our merits cause us terror. V, 1199.  
Meritum incipere per liberum arbitrium, dogma Pelagianum. X, 633. That merit begins through free will is a Pelagian dogma. X, 633.  
Non nos discernunt merita, sed gratia. V, 1333. It is not merits but grace that distinguishes us. V, 1333.  
Meritis gratia non datur. IV, 1364. Grace is not given according to merits. IV, 1364.  
Vide Gratia. See Grace.  
Meritum gratia praecedit. V, 917. Grace precedes merit. V, 917.  
Merita bona esse non possunt, nisi per gratiam. X, 889. Merits cannot be good except through grace. X, 889.  
Omne bonum meritum nostrum non in nobis facit, nisi gratia Dei. II, 860; X, 968. The grace of God alone makes every good merit of ours exist in us. II, 860; X, 968.  
Meritum sine gratia, nec in primo statu hominis ullum esse potuisset. VI, 282. Without grace, there could have been no merit even in humanity’s original state. VI, 282.  
Merita ex gratia, non gratia ex meritis. V, 917. Merits arise from grace, not grace from merits. V, 917.  
Gratia est omne meritum in electis. X, 924. Grace is every merit found in the elect. X, 924.  
Merita nulla nostra fuerunt, cum ad nos venit Dominus. V, 1647, 1648, 1650. We had no merits of our own when the Lord came to us. V, 1647, 1648, 1650.  
Merita nostra non praecesserunt, pro quibus Filius Dei moreretur. IV, 1082. Our merits did not precede, for which the Son of God would die. IV, 1082.  
Salvator non invenit merita bonorum, sed invenit merita suppliciorum. IV, 233, 585, 890, 1848. The Savior did not find merits deserving rewards, but found merits deserving punishments. IV, 233, 585, 890, 1848.  
Non invenit Salvator quod coronet, sed quod damnet. IV, 233. The Savior did not find something to crown, but something to condemn. IV, 233.  
Meritis operum nullis praecedentibus in tantam celsitudinem subvecta est humana natura, ut totum simul Verbum et caro unigenitus Filius Dei diceretur. IV, 1442. With no preceding merits of works, human nature was raised to such a height that the only-begotten Son of God was called at once both Word and flesh. IV, 1442.  
Meritorum nostrorum non est vocatio et electio, sed benevolentiae et misericordiae Dei. IV, 89, 788. Our calling and election are not due to our merits, but to the goodwill and mercy of God. IV, 89, 788.

Meritum incipit ex fide. X, 377. Merit begins from faith. X, 377.  
Quomodo. III, 2061. How this is so. III, 2061.  
Retr. Illud initium meriti accipitur sine merito. X, 377. *Retractions.* That beginning of merit is received without merit. X, 377.  
Merita omnia bona a fide incipiunt. II, 877. All good merits begin from faith. II, 877.  
Meritum orationis debetur fidei, quae data est non oranti. II, 877, 879. The merit of prayer is owed to faith, which was given to one who was not praying. II, 877, 879.  
Meritis vel operum, vel orationum, vel fidei suae nemo dicat sibi traditam Dei gratiam. II, 970. Let no one say that God’s grace was granted to him on account of his works, prayers, or faith. II, 970.  
Meritum tamen est sive bonum [Col. 0437] piorum, sive malum impiorum. II, 970. Yet there is merit, whether the good merit of the devout or the evil merit of the impious. II, 970.  
Qui dicunt gratiam secundum merita nostra dari, meritum in eo esse dicunt quod sumus cum Deo; ejus autem gratiam secundum hoc meritum dari, ut sit et ipse nobiscum. X, 888. Those who say that grace is given according to our merits say that merit consists in our being with God, and that his grace is given according to this merit so that he himself may also be with us. X, 888.  
Meritum nostrum in eo esse, quod quaerimus eum; et secundum hoc meritum dari ejus gratiam, ut inveniamus cum. X, 888. They say that our merit consists in seeking him, and that his grace is given according to this merit so that we may find him. X, 888.  
Merita sunt justorum; sed ut justi fierent, merita non fuerunt. II, 876. There are merits belonging to the righteous; but there were no merits by which they became righteous. II, 876.  
In meritis non necessitatem natura facit, sed voluntas culpam. VIII, 539. In matters of merit, nature does not create necessity, but the will creates guilt. VIII, 539.  
Non in meritis nostris gloriandum. III, 648, 870. We must not glory in our merits. III, 648, 870.

Meritis suis nihil tribuunt pauperes, sed totum misericordiae Dei. IV, 1814. The poor attribute nothing to their own merits, but everything to the mercy of God. IV, 1814.  
Merita tua nusquam jactes, quia et ipsa tua merita Dei, dona sunt. IV, 1876. Never boast of your merits, because even your merits are God’s gifts. IV, 1876.  
Merita vera hominum non sunt nisi Dei munera. I, 778; V, 753, 1361; VI, 282; VIII, 1024, 1051; X, 341. The true merits of human beings are nothing other than God’s gifts. I, 778; V, 753, 1361; VI, 282; VIII, 1024, 1051; X, 341.  
Dona Dei gratuita. II, 820. The freely given gifts of God. II, 820.  
Avulsit Deus merita nostra, et inseruit dona sua. IV, 1855. God tore away our merits and grafted in his gifts. IV, 1855.

Merita non comparantur nisi per corporis tempus. X, 977. Merits are acquired only during the time of the body. X, 977.  
Merita hîc comparantur, in coelis praemia redduntur. X, 1182. Merits are acquired here; rewards are bestowed in heaven. X, 1182.  
Frustra homo post hoc corpus inquirit, quod in hoc corpore sibi comparare neglexit. VII, 740. In vain does a person seek after this body what he neglected to acquire for himself in this body. VII, 740.  
Cum hinc exieris, recipieris pro meritis, et resurges ad recipienda quae gessisti. Tunc Deus coronabit non tam merita tua, quam dona sua. V, 932. When you depart from here, you will be received according to your merits, and you will rise again to receive what you have done. Then God will crown not so much your merits as his own gifts. V, 932.  
Non judicari quemquam a Deo secundum merita quae habiturus erat, si diutius vixisset. III, 420. No one is judged by God according to the merits he would have had if he had lived longer. III, 420.  
De meritorum futurorum praescientia. X, 979. Concerning foreknowledge of future merits. X, 979.  
Mortui non judicantur secundum opera quae facturi fuerant: gratia non datur secundum merita. X, 1011. The dead are not judged according to the works they would have done; grace is not given according to merits. X, 1011.  
Meritis praecedentibus redditur vita aeterna, quae tamen et ipsa vocatur gratia. II, 881. Eternal life is bestowed on the merits that precede it, yet it too is called grace. II, 881.  
Cum Deus coronat merita nostra, nihil aliud coronat quam dona sua. II, 880; IV, 1264; V, 1466; X, 890. When God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts. II, 880; IV, 1264; V, 1466; X, 890.  
Meritum non auget operis difficultas. X, 856. The difficulty of the work does not increase merit. X, 856.  
Merita esse diversa, quamvis eadem facientium aut patientium. II, 324. Merits are different, although the actions or sufferings may be the same. II, 324.

Merra, amaritudo interpretatur. III, 615. Merra is interpreted as “bitterness.” III, 615.

Merula flamen dialis, praecisis venis, Jovi suo sanguine litavit. VII, 107. Merula, the *flamen Dialis*, having cut his veins, offered a sacrifice to his Jupiter with his own blood. VII, 107.

Mesappus nonus rex Sicyoniorum. VII, 563. Mesappus, the ninth king of the Sicyonians. VII, 563.

Messianus proconsul. IX, 362. Messianus, proconsul. IX, 362.

Messis duplex, una ventilata de cruce, altera in fine ventilanda. IX, 29. There is a double harvest: one winnowed from the cross, the other to be winnowed at the end. IX, 29.  
Messis et messores Christi. III, 1522. The harvest and reapers of Christ. III, 1522.

Messe pro ungue Punice dicitur. III, 1520. In Punic, *messe* is said for “claw.” III, 1520.

Metallicus ex effractore. V, 693. Metallicus, from *effractor* (“burglar” or “breaker-in”). V, 693.

Metangismonitae haeretici. VIII, 41. The Metangismonites, heretics. VIII, 41.

Metaphora. VI, 533. Metaphor. VI, 533.

Metaplasmi. VIII, 417. Metaplasms. VIII, 417.

Metellus Romanorum laudatissimus, quinque filios consulares habuit. VII, 71. Metellus, the most highly praised of the Romans, had five sons who became consuls. VII, 71.  
Metellus rerum temporalium felix fuit. VII, 71. Metellus was fortunate in temporal affairs. VII, 71.
