Metellus Pontifex in flammas irruit ut vestalia sacra abriperet. VII, 99. The pontiff Metellus rushed into the flames to rescue the sacred objects of Vesta. VII, 99.

Metreta nomen mensurae. III, 1461. *Metreta* is the name of a measure. III, 1461.

Metrum graece, latine mensio seu mensura, quid. I, 1115. What *metrum* means in Greek, and *mensio* or *mensura* in Latin. I, 1115.  
Metra quodammodo innumerabilia. I, 1146. Meters are in a certain sense innumerable. I, 1146.  
Metra quae duas in partes divisibilia sunt, caeteris praestant. I, 1146. Meters that are divisible into two parts are superior to the others. I, 1146.  
De metro copiose tractatur. I, 1124. Meter is treated at length. I, 1124.  
Summa omnium metrorum. I, 1136. A summary of all meters. I, 1136.

Metrodorus. I, 956. Metrodorus. I, 956.  
Hic primo confessus est, non decreto placuisse Academicis nihil posse comprehendi. I, 956. He was the first to acknowledge that the Academics’ position that nothing can be comprehended was not accepted by decree. I, 956.

Metus quid. VII, 409. What fear is. VII, 409.  
Metus alios animi motus comitatur. VI, 23. Fear accompanies other movements of the soul. VI, 23.  
Metuendi causa quae sit. VI, 22. What the cause of fear is. VI, 22.  
Metu triplici commovemur, amissionis eorum quos diligimus, doloris, et mortis. I, 877. We are moved by three kinds of fear: fear of losing those whom we love, of pain, and of death. I, 877.  
Neque non amandum est non metuere; neque id solum amandum. VI, 23. Not being afraid is also something to be loved, but it is not the only thing to be loved. VI, 23.

Metymna Lesbi insula. VII, 28. Methymna, on the island of Lesbos. VII, 28.

Micare digitis. VIII, 953. To signal by finger movements. VIII, 953.

Micipsa filius Masinissae. VII, 112. Micipsa, the son of Masinissa. VII, 112.

Midila. IX, 229. Midila. IX, 229.

Miggenes fossor. IX, 513. Miggenes, a gravedigger. IX, 513.

Miggenes Elefantariensis. IX, 507, 528, 550. Miggenes of Elephantaria. IX, 507, 528, 550.

Migginus. IV, 376. Migginus. IV, 376.

Migginus alter Maximianista episc. IV, 377, 381. Another Migginus, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 377, 381.

Migginus ab Elephantaria episc. IV, 380. Migginus, bishop from Elephantaria. IV, 380.

Migirpa. IX, 203. Migirpa. IX, 203.

Miles pro carnifice et quaestionario aliquando sumitur. VII, 39. “Soldier” is sometimes used for “executioner” and “torturer.” VII, 39.  
Not. (c). Note (c).

Militare non prohibuit disciplina Christiana. II, 531. Christian discipline did not prohibit military service. II, 531.  
Militantium est tabernaculum, et ipsorum est nomen contubernales. IV, 143, 202. The tent belongs to those serving as soldiers, and their name is “tent-companions.” IV, 143, 202.  
Militibus data Imperatoris signa. II, 301. The Emperor’s standards were given to the soldiers. II, 301.  
Et regalis character. II, 307. And the royal mark. II, 307.  
Militis voluntas pacem habere debet, bellum necessitas. II, 856. A soldier’s will ought to seek peace; war is a necessity. II, 856.  
Militum violentia extorquentium aliquid a possessoribus, quod publice non jubetur. VI, 92. The violence of soldiers extorting something from landowners, when it is not publicly ordered. VI, 92.  
Milites qui Deo auctore bella gerunt, non sunt homicidae. VII, 35, 39; VIII, 447. Soldiers who wage wars with God as their authorization are not murderers. VII, 35, 39; VIII, 447.  
Miles in hoste interficiendo minister legis est. I, 1227. In killing an enemy, a soldier is a minister of the law. I, 1227.  
Hostem perimat necessitas, non voluntas. II, 856. Let necessity, not the will, kill the enemy. II, 856.  
Vic­to vel capto misericordia debetur, maxime ubi pacis perturbatio non timetur. II, 856. Mercy is owed to the defeated or captured, especially where no disturbance of peace is feared. II, 856.  
Milites non bene facere prohibet militia, sed malitia. [Col. 0438] V, 1391. It is not military service but wickedness that prevents soldiers from doing good. V, 1391.  
Militares viri Deo placere possunt: Exempla. II, 855. Military men can please God: examples. II, 855.

Militis Christiani hostes. VI, 693. The enemies of the Christian soldier. VI, 693.  
Valde turpe est, ut quem non vincit homo, vincat libido; et obruatur vino, qui non vincitur ferro. II, 856. It is extremely shameful that lust should conquer one whom a human being cannot conquer, and that wine should overwhelm one whom iron cannot defeat. II, 856.  
Milites Christi impugnat mundus duplici acie. V, 1256. The world attacks Christ’s soldiers with a double battle line. V, 1256.  
Militiam Dei militantibus, arma dextera et sinistra. IX, 502. For those serving in God’s army, weapons are on the right and left. IX, 502.

Militariter loqui. II, 445. To speak in military fashion. II, 445.

Milevis. II, 133. Milevis. II, 133.  
Milevitana Ecclesia post obitum Severi cum pace accepit Episcopum, quem vivus designarat. II, 966. After the death of Severus, the Church of Milevis peacefully received the bishop whom he had designated while alive. II, 966.  
Milevitani Concilii epistola. II, 762. The letter of the Council of Milevis. II, 762.  
Memoratur. II, 773, 784, 972. It is mentioned. II, 773, 784, 972.

Mileum. IX, 511. Mileum. IX, 511.

Mimi cujusdam facetissima urbanitas. VIII, 431. The exceedingly witty urbanity of a certain mime. VIII, 431.  
Mimus est generis humani tota vita tentationis. IV, 1686. The entire life of the human race is a mime of temptation. IV, 1686.

Millenarius numerus pro universitate ponitur. VII, 668. The number one thousand is used for totality. VII, 668.

Millenarii. VII, 691. The Millenarians. VII, 691.  
Et Not. 4. And Note 4.  
Seu Chiliastae a Cerintho. VIII, 27. Or the Chiliasts, deriving from Cerinthus. VIII, 27.

Milliaria lapidea litteris plena viam docentia. V, 609. Stone milestones covered with inscriptions showing the way. V, 609, 1027, 1547, 1665.

Milliarii. VII, 667. Milestones. VII, 667.

Minae Dei, arcus Dei. IV, 686. The threats of God are God’s bow. IV, 686.  
Arcus et suspensiones. IV, 474. The bow and hangings. IV, 474.  
Minis Dei prohiberis a malo, invitaris ad bonum. IV, 569. By God’s threats you are restrained from evil and invited to good. IV, 569.  
His qui non movetur, non credit. IV, 569. Whoever is not moved by these does not believe. IV, 569.  
Minae saeculi contemnendae. V, 220. The threats of the world are to be despised. V, 220.  
Minae cujusdam nec ad malum compellere, nec a bono deterrere debent. IV, 569. The threats of anyone ought neither to compel us to evil nor deter us from good. IV, 569.

Mincius. De mincio in Eridanum emigrare. II, 258. The Mincio. Its flowing into the Eridanus. II, 258.

Minente die, pro exstante. V, 402. “With the day impending,” meaning “with the day standing forth.” V, 402.

Mineorum haeresis, qui et Nazaraei nuncupantur a Pharisaeis. II, 258. The heresy of the Mineans, who are also called Nazarenes by the Pharisees. II, 258.

Minerva, Graece Ἀθηνά. VII, 566. Minerva, in Greek Ἀθηνά (*Athēnā*). VII, 566.  
Minervae Athenarum civitas consecrata. II, 186. The city of Athens was consecrated to Minerva. II, 186.  
Minervam vel summum aethera, vel lunam esse dixerunt. VII, 207. They said that Minerva was either the highest heaven or the moon. VII, 207.  
Minerva quare de capite Jovis nata canitur. VII, 120, 566; VIII, 373. Why Minerva is sung of as having been born from Jupiter’s head. VII, 120, 566; VIII, 373.  
Minervam ideas intelligi vult Varro. VII, 218. Varro wishes Minerva to be understood as the Ideas. VII, 218.  
Minerva artibus et ingeniis praeposita. VII, 128, 207. Minerva placed over the arts and talents. VII, 128, 207.  
Not. (a). Note (a).  
Minerva quo tempore vixit, quare Tritonia dicta, et in deorum numerum relata. VII, 566. When Minerva lived, why she was called Tritonia, and why she was reckoned among the gods. VII, 566.  
Minervae ludos instituit rex Erichthonius. VII, 569. King Erichthonius established games for Minerva. VII, 569.  
Minervae ludorum praemium, oleum. VII, 569. The prize of Minerva’s games was oil. VII, 569.

Minimi Christi, quinam. V, 648. Who are the least of Christ’s people. V, 648.

Minister Dei optimus, quis. I, 795. Who is the best minister of God. I, 795.  
Minister fictus, quis. IX, 64, 68. Who is a false minister. IX, 64, 68.  
Homines non sunt attendendi, cum sanctum aliquid homo accipere desiderat. IX, 75. Human beings are not to be considered when someone wishes to receive something holy. IX, 75.  
Dona Dei perveniunt ad eos qui cum fide accipiunt, etiamsi talis sit per quem accipiunt, qualis Judas fuit. IV, 135. God’s gifts reach those who receive them with faith, even if the person through whom they receive them is like Judas. IV, 135.  
Vide Baptismus. See Baptism.  
Ministri Ecclesiae non deserant munus ecclesiasticum, populorum peccatis commoti. III, 1334. Ministers of the Church must not abandon their ecclesiastical office because they are disturbed by the sins of the people. III, 1334.  
Ministros Christi qui blasphemant, Christo resistunt. III, 2002. Those who blaspheme Christ’s ministers resist Christ. III, 2002.  
Ministris Ecclesiae subsidia corporis debentur. I, 862. Material support is owed to the ministers of the Church. I, 862.  
Eisque victum suppeditare debent fideles, prius quam petant. IV, 1910. The faithful ought to provide them with food before they ask for it. IV, 1910.  
Ministri Ecclesiae ad temporalia attendere non debent. III, 1294. Ministers of the Church ought not to attend to temporal matters. III, 1294.  
Non faciunt contra praeceptum, qui procurant necessaria. III, 1294. Those who provide necessities do not act against the commandment. III, 1294.  
Ministri Christi necessarii sunt in persecutione, quia multi tunc ad Ecclesiae sacramenta concurrunt. II, 1016. The ministers of Christ are necessary during persecution, because many then hasten to the sacraments of the Church. II, 1016.  
Utitur Deus ministris etiam spiritibus malis, ad vindictam malorum, et ad probationem bonorum. VI, 131. God uses as ministers even evil spirits, for the punishment of the wicked and the testing of the good. VI, 131.  
Ministris non solum bonis et sanctis utitur Deus ad opera congrua, sed etiam malis ad opera digna. VI, 146. God uses not only good and holy ministers for appropriate works, but also evil ones for works suited to them. VI, 146.  
Ministeriorum distributio varia esse debet. VI, 36. The distribution of ministries ought to be varied. VI, 36.

Minos Xanthi filius ex Europa. VII, 569. Minos, son of Xanthus by Europa. VII, 569.

Minotauri fabula. VII, 570. The story of the Minotaur. VII, 570.

Minturnae Campaniae oppidum. VII, 71. Minturnae, a town of Campania. VII, 71.

Minuscularii, vectigalium conductores. VII, 197. *Minuscularii*, collectors of taxes. VII, 197.

Mira non solent homines mirari, nisi rara. VII, 721. People usually do not marvel at wonderful things unless they are rare. VII, 721.

Mirabiliarii. III, 1501. Wonder-workers. III, 1501.

Mirabilia. Voluntas omnipotentis, sufficiens ratio credendi in mirabilibus. VII, 719. Wonders. The will of the omnipotent one is a sufficient reason for believing in wonders. VII, 719.

Miraculum, quid et quotuplex. VIII, 90. What a miracle is and how many kinds there are. VIII, 90.  
Miracula plerumque, quae contra naturam fiunt, appellantur. VIII, 481, 489, 490. Miracles are generally called things that occur contrary to nature. VIII, 481, 489, 490.  
Miracula multa videntur, quae fiunt ab hominibus usu creaturarum. VII, 718. Many things appear miraculous that are done by human beings through the use of creatures. VII, 718.  
Miracula proprie quaenam. VIII, 879. What things are properly miracles. VIII, 879.  
Miracula quomodo fiant, ab homine non potest comprehendi. VIII, 881. How miracles occur cannot be comprehended by a human being. VIII, 881.  
Miracula multa, aut magicarum artium ope, aut per ipsos daemones fiunt. VII, 717. Many miracles occur either through the aid of magical arts or through the demons themselves. VII, 717.  
Miracula magica, pleraque specie tenus, mortalium sensus imaginaria ludificatione decipiunt. VII, 295. Most magical miracles, in outward appearance only, deceive the senses of mortals through an imaginary illusion. VII, 295.  
Miracula Pagani magicis artibus tribuunt. VII, 721. Pagans attribute miracles to magical arts. VII, 721.  
Miracula quaedam Gentilium referuntur. VII, 294. Certain miracles of the Gentiles are reported. VII, 294.  
Miracula Martyrum et falsorum deorum comparantur. VII, 772. The miracles of the martyrs and of false gods are compared. VII, 772.  
Miracula deorum cum nostris non sunt conferenda. VII, 294, 295. The miracles of the gods are not to be compared with ours. VII, 294, 295.  
Miracula nostra excellere, finis quo discernuntur ostendit. VII, 294. The purpose by which our miracles are distinguished shows that they are superior. VII, 294.  
Miracula quae a daemonibus fiunt, spernenda. VIII, 897. Miracles performed by demons are to be despised. VIII, 897.  
An miracula credenda sint. VII, 716. Whether miracles are to be believed. VII, 716.  
Respondetur his, qui miracula in Scripturis sacris relata, falsa esse dicunt. VII, 296, 297. A response is given to those who say that the miracles reported in the holy Scriptures are false. VII, 296, 297.  
Si coeperis humano sensu miraculorum discutere rationem, timeo ne perdas fidem. V, 1157. If you begin to investigate the rationale of miracles by human judgment, I fear that you will lose faith. V, 1157.  
Miracula varia recensentur. VII, 770. Various miracles are recounted. VII, 770.  
Miracula quam multa in veteri Testamento facta ad commendandum Dei cultum. VII, 286. How many miracles were performed in the Old Testament to commend the worship of God. VII, 286.  
Attestabantur [Col. 0439] promissis Dei. VII, 285. They bore witness to God’s promises. VII, 285.  
Miracula quae per arcam testimonii facta sunt, Divinitati attestantur. VII, 295. The miracles performed through the ark of the testimony bear witness to the divinity. VII, 295.  
Miracula Dei universa, ideo ab infidelibus non creduntur, quia ratio eorum non videtur. II, 454. God’s miracles as a whole are not believed by unbelievers because their rationale is not apparent. II, 454.  
De quibusdam miraculis ratio reddi non potest, non tamen non est. II, 454. An explanation cannot be given for certain miracles, but that does not mean that there is none. II, 454.  
Nec propterea incredibilia esse debent. VII, 714. Nor should they therefore be considered incredible. VII, 714.  
Non ideo aliquid non fuit, vel futurum non est, quia ratio non potest reddi. VII, 714, 715. Something did not therefore fail to exist, or will not therefore occur, merely because its rationale cannot be given. VII, 714, 715.  
Tota ratio facti, est voluntas facientis. II, 519. The entire rationale of an act is the will of the one who performs it. II, 519.  
Miracula fiebant simplici fide pietatis, non incantationibus. VII, 286, 291. Miracles were performed by simple faith and devotion, not by incantations. VII, 286, 291.  
Inusitata prodigia opportune reservavit Deus, quae infirmitas hominis novitati intenta meminerit. IV, 1465. God fittingly reserved unusual prodigies, so that human weakness, attentive to novelty, might remember them. IV, 1465.  
Tres viros ab ignibus, et Danielem a leonibus Deus liberavit, ut consuleret saluti regum illorum, a quibus in illa supplicia tradebantur. II, 425. God delivered the three men from the fires and Daniel from the lions in order to contribute to the salvation of those kings by whom they were handed over to those punishments. II, 425.  
Miraculum magnum ipse homo mirator. V, 700. The human being himself, who marvels, is a great miracle. V, 700.  
Insolita fecit Christus, ut et in ipsis solitis agnosceres artificem tuum. V, 700. Christ performed extraordinary things so that, even in ordinary things, you might recognize your Maker. V, 700.  
Miracula Christi et opera verba sunt. III, 1860. Christ’s miracles and works are words. III, 1860.  
Miracula quaedam fecit Christus, quae nemo alius fecit: quaedam alii fecerunt, quae Christus non fecit. III, 1861. Christ performed certain miracles that no one else performed; others performed certain miracles that Christ did not perform. III, 1861.

Miracula majora fecisse videntur Apostoli, quam Christus. IV, 1707. The Apostles appear to have performed greater miracles than Christ. IV, 1707.  
De miraculorum potentia quare nemini gloriandum. IX, 302. Why no one should glory in the power to perform miracles. IX, 302.  
Miracula aliter a Christo, aliter a Sanctis patrata. V, 1432, 1440. Miracles performed in one way by Christ and in another by the saints. V, 1432, 1440.  
In miraculis faciendis Apostoli non sibi potentiam Domini sui arrogabant. IV, 1199. In performing miracles, the Apostles did not claim for themselves the power of their Lord. IV, 1199.  
Miracula non sunt signa sapientiae. III, 1307. Miracles are not signs of wisdom. III, 1307.  
Miracula faciunt boni et mali. V, 562. Good and evil people perform miracles. V, 562.  
Miracula quaedam etiam scelerati homines aliquando faciunt, qualia sancti facere non possunt. VI, 92. Sometimes even wicked people perform certain miracles such as saints cannot perform. VI, 92.  
Cur a malis fieri miracula aliquando sinitur, aliquando non. VI, 92. Why miracles are sometimes permitted to be performed by evil people and sometimes not. VI, 92.  
Miracula alio fine, aliaque potestate et jure fiunt, per magos et per Sanctos. VI, 91, 92. Miracles are performed for one purpose, and with another power and authority, by magicians and by saints. VI, 91, 92.  
Aliter per bonos, et aliter per malos Christianos. VI, 92. In one way by good Christians, and in another by evil Christians. VI, 92.  
Cur facere miracula non omnibus conceditur. VI, 92. Why performing miracles is not granted to everyone. VI, 92.  
Miracula sanitatum cur non omnes obtineant. V, 1299. Why not everyone obtains miracles of healing. V, 1299.

Miracula necessaria fuerunt antequam crederet mundus, ad hoc ut crederet mundus. VII, 760. Miracles were necessary before the world believed, so that the world might believe. VII, 760.  
Multi sunt quos ad invisibilium fidem, visibilibus miraculis excitari opus est. II, 454. There are many who need to be stirred to faith in invisible things by visible miracles. II, 454.  
Miraculis visibilibus, velut quibusdam primordiis lactescentibus, fides germinavit. X, 182. By visible miracles, as by certain nursing beginnings, faith sprouted. X, 182.  
Miracula fidem firmant. III, 1752. Miracles strengthen faith. III, 1752.  
Fidei nostrae attestantur. VII, 771. They bear witness to our faith. VII, 771.  
Miracula ut fidem facerent innotuerunt; et per fidem quam fecerunt, clarius innotescunt. VII, 760. Miracles became known in order to produce faith; and through the faith they produced, they become more clearly known. VII, 760.  
Miracula Domini in corporibus et in animis. V, 591. The Lord’s miracles in bodies and in souls. V, 591.  
In miraculis Christus saluti animarum magis consuluit, quam saluti corporum. III, 1527. In his miracles Christ took greater care for the salvation of souls than for the salvation of bodies. III, 1527.  
Miraculum de quinque panibus. V, 725. The miracle of the five loaves. V, 725.  
Miracula Christi propter significationem facta. V, 592. Christ’s miracles were performed for their symbolic meaning. V, 592.  
Apta huic rei similitudo. V, 592. A fitting comparison for this matter. V, 592.  
Miraculis corporalibus aedificabat fidem Christus. V, 539. Christ built up faith through bodily miracles. V, 539.  
Ecclesiae postea fides sine miraculis laudabilior. V, 539. Afterwards, the faith of the Church without miracles is more praiseworthy. V, 539.  
Omnia quae fecit Dominus Jesus, non solum valent ad excitanda corda nostra miraculis, sed etiam ad aedificanda in doctrina fidei. III, 1458. Everything that the Lord Jesus did is effective not only for stirring our hearts by miracles, but also for building them up in the teaching of faith. III, 1458.  
In miraculis est quaedam Dei eloquentia. VII, 770. In miracles there is a certain eloquence of God. VII, 770.  
Miracula ad intelligendum Deum de visibilibus mentem humanam admonent. III, 1592, 1593. Through visible things, miracles admonish the human mind to understand God. III, 1592, 1593.  
Miracula habent linguam suam. III, 1593. Miracles have their own language. III, 1593.  
Miracula Apostolorum, persuadebant quae dicebant. VII, 756. The miracles of the Apostles persuaded people of what they were saying. VII, 756.

Miracula an nulla modo non fiant. VIII, 63, 64. Whether miracles are ever not performed. VIII, 63, 64.  
Cur modo non fiant. VIII, 90. Why they are not performed now. VIII, 90.  
Aut raro fiant. I, 604; III, 142. Or are performed rarely. I, 604; III, 142.  
Miracula sunt etiam consueta. VIII, 871, 874. Ordinary things are also miracles. VIII, 871, 874.  
Miracula quotidie in rerum natura eduntur, quae prae consuetudine vilescunt. II, 519; III, 1458, 1592; IV, 1164; V, 699, 725, 1139, 1157; VII, 291, 713. Miracles occur daily in the nature of things, but become cheap through familiarity. II, 519; III, 1458, 1592; IV, 1164; V, 699, 725, 1139, 1157; VII, 291, 713.  
Et videndi consuetudine mira non sunt. II, 372. And through the habit of seeing them, they are not regarded as wonderful. II, 372.  
Miracula Deus quotidie facit, quae homines non mirantur. III, 1450. God performs miracles every day at which people do not marvel. III, 1450.  
Inusitata quaedam servavit, quae faceret ut dormientes homines excitaret. III, 1450. He reserved certain unusual things so that he might awaken people who were asleep. III, 1450.  
Quae fiunt praeter usitatum ordinem naturae, ideo movent quia rara sunt. III, 1592. Things that occur beyond the customary order of nature move us because they are rare. III, 1592.  
Novit Deus quomodo miracula sua debeat commendare, novit agere ne vilescant. V, 1299. God knows how he ought to commend his miracles; he knows how to act so that they do not become cheap. V, 1299.

Miracula etiam nunc fiunt in nomine Christi. VII, 760, 769. Miracles are still performed now in the name of Christ. VII, 760, 769.  
Miracula nunc majora Christus operatur. V, 540. Christ now performs greater miracles. V, 540.  
Miracula facta in translatione corporum SS. Gervasii et Protasii. I, 770. Miracles performed during the translation of the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. I, 770.  
Severi in regione Sitifensi episcopi neptis sanitatem tribus barbaris a Deo impetravit, propter quod captivitate liberata est. II, 426. The niece of Severus, bishop in the region of Sitifis, obtained healing from God for three barbarians, on account of which she was freed from captivity. II, 426.  
Qui per miraculum beneficia percipiebant, libellos dabant qui legerentur in populo. VII, 768, 769, 770. Those who received benefits through a miracle gave written accounts to be read before the people. VII, 768, 769, 770.  
Miracula quare in aliis locis fiant, in aliis non fiant, consilium Dei. II, 269. Why miracles occur in some places and not in others is God’s counsel. II, 269.  
Miracula quae nunc fiunt, non tanta, quanta prima gloria illustrantur. VII, 760. The miracles that occur now are not as great as those by which the first glory was illumined. VII, 760.  
Miracula an fiant operationibus Martyrum, an precibus tantum eorum. VII, 771. Whether miracles are performed through the actions of the martyrs or only through their prayers. VII, 771.  
Miracula quae operantur non regenerati, fiunt a Deo vel ab Angelis sanctis. II, 846. The miracles performed by those who have not been regenerated are performed by God or by holy angels. II, 846.  
Quomodo Christianus in alio faciente miracula, ipse faciat. IV, 1707. How a Christian himself performs a miracle when another is performing it. IV, 1707.  
Deus tentatur, cum miracula flagitantur, non ad salutem, sed ad experientiam. I, 802. God is put to the test when miracles are demanded not for salvation but for experimentation. I, 802.  
In eos qui miracula facere volunt. IV, 1706, 1707. Against those who wish to perform miracles. IV, 1706, 1707.  
Potentius est conjungi Omnipotenti pia voluntate, quam propria potestate et voluntate posse, quod contremiscant qui talia non possunt. VIII, 957. It is more powerful to be joined to the Omnipotent One by a devout will than to be able, by one’s own power and will, to do what those who cannot do such things tremble at. VIII, 957.  
Miracula sola veritas facit. VIII, 874. Truth alone performs miracles. VIII, 874.  
Miracula qui facit praeter unitatem, nihil est. III, 1501. Whoever performs miracles outside unity is nothing. III, 1501.

[Col. 0440] Mirari, quid. VIII, 608. What it means to marvel. VIII, 608.

Miseratio Dei in homines, gratuita. X, 621. God’s compassion toward human beings is freely given. X, 621.  
Miserationes Domini multae: attendit contemptores ut corrigat, nescientes ut doceat, confitentes ut ignoscat. IV, 588. The Lord’s compassions are many: he attends to the contemptuous in order to correct them, to the ignorant in order to teach them, and to those who confess in order to forgive them. IV, 588.  
Miseratio ex gratia, obduratio ex judicio. X, 1139, 1142. Compassion proceeds from grace, hardening from judgment. X, 1139, 1142.

Miseri sunt homines, quamdiu sunt mortales. VII, 268. Human beings are wretched as long as they are mortal. VII, 268.  
Miser est qui Deum amisit, aut illi non adhaeret. VII, 349, 650. Wretched is the person who has lost God or does not cling to him. VII, 349, 650.  
Aut illum non colit. VII, 281. Or does not worship him. VII, 281.  
Miser quisque dicitur, quando illi subtrahitur quod amat. IV, 202. Each person is called wretched when what he loves is taken away from him. IV, 202.  
Miseri multi magis habendo quod amant, quam carendo: amando res noxias, miseri; habendo, sunt miseriores. IV, 202. Many are more wretched through possessing what they love than through lacking it: by loving harmful things they are wretched; by possessing them they are more wretched. IV, 202.  
Velle quod non decet; idem ipsum miserrimum est. ex Cicer. II, 498. To desire what is improper is itself the most wretched thing. From Cicero. II, 498.  
Occulte sunt miseri, qui gaudent in malis. II, 632. Those who rejoice in evils are secretly wretched. II, 632.  
Miser est qui fruitur re creata, quam perverse amat. VII, 356. Wretched is the person who enjoys a created thing that he loves perversely. VII, 356.  
Miserum genus humanum effectum propter peccatum Adami, tandem fatetur Julianus. X, 1573. At last Julian admits that the human race was made wretched because of Adam’s sin. X, 1573.  
Sub Deo justo nemo miser, nisi mereatur. X, 1065. Under a just God no one is wretched unless he deserves it. X, 1065.  
Miseri cum praeter ordinem non sint, nonnulla pace gaudent. VII, 641. Although the wretched are not outside the order of things, they enjoy some peace. VII, 641.

Miseria creaturae rationalis, aversio ejus ab incommutabili bono. II, 561. The misery of a rational creature is its turning away from the unchangeable good. II, 561.  
Miseriae generis humani. X, 782. The miseries of the human race. X, 782.  
Miseriae hujus vitae, quantae. VII, 628. How great the miseries of this life are. VII, 628.  
Falsa felicitas, vera miseria est. IV, 1099. False happiness is true misery. IV, 1099.  
Miseria hominum a primis fletibus nascentium, usque ad extremos halitus morientium. X, 1073. The misery of human beings extends from the first cries of those being born to the final breaths of those dying. X, 1073.  
Ah ortu ad interitum. X, 1184. From birth to destruction. X, 1184.  
Miserias hujus vitae Tullius vidit et lamentatus est. VII, 628. Tullius saw and lamented the miseries of this life. VII, 628.  
Causam nescivit. X, 767. He did not know the cause. X, 767.  
Miseria generis humani a Philosophis cognita, non nisi ex peccato originali nascitur. X, 782. The misery of the human race, recognized by the philosophers, arises only from original sin. X, 782.  
Miserias Deo naturarum institutori tribuunt Pelagiani. X, 1566. The Pelagians attribute these miseries to God, the creator of natures. X, 1566.  
Et in paradiso futuras fuisse asserunt, etiamsi nemo peccasset. X, 1249, 1448, 1449, 1559, 1573, 1575. And they assert that they would have existed even in paradise, even if no one had sinned. X, 1249, 1448, 1449, 1559, 1573, 1575.  
Miseria mortalium quo sensu potest dici naturalis. X, 1509. In what sense the misery of mortals can be called natural. X, 1509.  
Miseriae corporis post peccatum. IV, 397, 398. The miseries of the body after sin. IV, 397, 398.  
Miseriae quibus humanum genus merito primae praevaricationis obnoxium est. VII, 784. The miseries to which the human race is liable by reason of its first transgression. VII, 784.  
Miseria hominis, inobedientia ejus ipsius adversus eum ipsum. VII, 423. Human misery is a person’s own disobedience against himself. VII, 423.  
Miseriae hujus vitae ex originali peccato veniunt. VII, 790; X, 1077, 1248, 1276, 1311, 1501, 1509, 1513, 1515, 1527, 1528. The miseries of this life arise from original sin. VII, 790; X, 1077, 1248, 1276, 1311, 1501, 1509, 1513, 1515, 1527, 1528.  
Miseria mortalium nulla esset, si non esset peccatum. X, 1408. There would be no misery among mortals if there were no sin. X, 1408.  
Adami grande peccatum, causa miseriarum generis humani. X, 1511, 1512. Adam’s great sin is the cause of the miseries of the human race. X, 1511, 1512.  
Aerumnae generis humani et majoribus et parvulis communes, fateri cogunt peccatum originale. X, 1559. The afflictions common to the human race, both adults and little children, compel one to acknowledge original sin. X, 1559.

Miseria omnis naturae rationalis ex ignorantia rerum agendarum, et concupiscentia noxiarum. VI, 244. All misery of rational nature arises from ignorance of what ought to be done and desire for harmful things. VI, 244.  
Miseria ex amore temporalium bonorum nascitur et augetur. VII, 441. Misery is born from and increased by love of temporal goods. VII, 441.  
Miseria nulla alia quam stultitia. II, 64. Misery is nothing other than foolishness. II, 64.  
Miseriae non est finis, quamdiu finis officiorum nostrorum in re instabili collocatur. II, 435. There is no end to miseries as long as the goal of our duties is placed in an unstable thing. II, 435.  
Miseriarum testimonia fidelia sunt ipsae virtutes. VII, 631. The virtues themselves are faithful testimonies to miseries. VII, 631.  
Miseria hominis, ut et misericordia Domini, plena est terra. IV, 287. The earth is full of human misery, just as it is full of the Lord’s mercy. IV, 287.  
A miseriis non liberat-nisi gratia Salvatoris. VII, 786. Nothing except the grace of the Savior frees us from miseries. VII, 786.  
Non semper liberat, ne propter hoc religio quaeratur. VII, 786. It does not always free us, lest religion be sought for this reason. VII, 786.  
Ad hoc adjuvat gratia meliores, ut fortiore corde tolerentur miseriae. VII, 786. For this purpose grace helps the better people, so that miseries may be endured with greater courage. VII, 786.  
Miseriarum remedia plena labore ac dolore. VII, 785. The remedies for miseries are full of labor and pain. VII, 785.  
Liberatio ab his miseriis, proprie in altera vita. VII, 786. Deliverance from these miseries properly belongs to the other life. VII, 786.  
Qui se agnoscit in vera esse miseria, erit in vera felicitate. IV, 1099. Whoever recognizes that he is in true misery will be in true happiness. IV, 1099.  
Tota ista miseria generis humani, dolor medicinalis est, non sententia poenalis. IV, 1793. All this misery of the human race is medicinal pain, not a penal sentence. IV, 1793.  
Quid miseriae hujus vitae nos edoceant. VII, 729. What the miseries of this life teach us. VII, 729.  
Miseriae similitudo, cordis duritiam solvit. V, 1199. The likeness of misery dissolves hardness of heart. V, 1199.  
Ad eos qui non sunt in potestate, ubi mala vident aut audiunt, non pertinet nisi misereri. V, 1392. Toward those who are not under their authority, when they see or hear evils, people have no duty except to show mercy. V, 1392.

## Mercy

Misericordia quid. VII, 260. What mercy is. VII, 260.  
Est virtus. VII, 260. It is a virtue. VII, 260.  
Quaenam virtus, et unde dicta. VIII, 142. What kind of virtue it is, and from where it gets its name. VIII, 142.  
Misericordia generali nomine dicitur, quia misero subvenitur. IV, 1469. It is generally called “mercy” because help is given to a wretched person. IV, 1469.  
Misericordia a miseria nomen habet. VI, 139; X, 1065. Mercy gets its name from misery. VI, 139; X, 1065.  
Misericordia ex eo appellata est, quod miserum cor faciat condolentis alieno malo. I, 1333. It is called mercy because it makes the heart of one who feels compassion for another’s evil sorrowful. I, 1333.  
Misericordiam Stoici in vitio ponunt. II, 394; VII, 260. The Stoics count mercy as a fault. II, 394; VII, 260.

Misericordia qualis Deo conveniat. VI, 140. What kind of mercy is appropriate to God. VI, 140.  
Misericordia est in Deo sine cordis miseria. VIII, 143. In God there is mercy without misery of heart. VIII, 143.  
Misericordia Dei magna, magnae humanae miseriae est necessaria. VII, 636. The great mercy of God is necessary for great human misery. VII, 636.  
Qui magnam misericordiam deprecatur, magnam miseriam confitetur. IV, 588. Whoever begs for great mercy confesses great misery. IV, 588.  
Misericordia non indigent coeli, ubi nulla miseria. IV, 287. Heaven has no need of mercy, since there is no misery there. IV, 287.  
Misericordia Dei quanta erga hominem. V, 153. How great God’s mercy toward humanity is. V, 153.  
Misericordia Dei in sanctos, aeterna est. IV, 1420. God’s mercy toward the saints is eternal. IV, 1420.  
Erga omnes tam sanctos quam reprobos, universae viae Domini misericordia et veritas. IV, 1588. Toward all, both saints and reprobates, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. IV, 1588.  
Misericordia Dei in sanctos non terrena, sed coelestis. IV, 346. God’s mercy toward the saints is not earthly but heavenly. IV, 346.  
Misericordia Dei ubique nos praevenit. V, 1015. God’s mercy everywhere precedes us. V, 1015.  
Praevenit voluntatem. I, 628. It precedes the will. I, 628.  
Deus non miseretur, nisi voluntas praecesserit; sed ipsum velle Deus operatur in nobis. VI, 73. God does not show mercy unless the will has preceded; but God himself produces the willing in us. VI, 73.  
Misericordiam fides non praecedit. II, 879. Faith does not precede mercy. II, 879.  
Ad misericordiam Dei pertinet vocatio, quae etiam fidem praevenit. I, 628. Calling belongs to the mercy of God, and it also precedes faith. I, 628.  
Misericordia fideli quidem datur, sed data est etiam ut esset fidelis. III, 2061. Mercy is indeed given to one who is faithful, but it was also given so that he might be faithful. III, 2061. *Retractions.*  
Misericordia quomodo praecedenti merito fidei tribuitur. III, 2061. *Retractions.* How mercy is attributed to the preceding merit of faith. III, 2061.  
Misericordia Dei et vocamur ut credamus, et credentibus praestatur ut bene operemur. I, 623; III, 2061. By God’s mercy we are both called so that we may believe, and it is granted to those who believe so that we may do good works. I, 623; III, 2061.  
Misericordia et gratia [Col. 0441] Dei convertit hominem, ut justificetur impius, et incipiat habere meritum bonum, etc. II, 970. The mercy and grace of God converts a person, so that the ungodly may be justified and begin to have good merit, etc. II, 970.  
Misericordia Dei non deserit eos, qui ex ejus fide vivunt, eumque pie colunt. II, 525. God’s mercy does not abandon those who live by faith in him and devoutly worship him. II, 525.  
Quidquid sumus, Dei misericordia sumus; quidquid autem ex nobis sumus, mali sumus. IV, 876. Whatever we are, we are by God’s mercy; whatever we are from ourselves, we are evil. IV, 876.  
Veritate humiliati sumus in mortem, misericordia instauramur ad vitam. IV, 1555. By truth we have been humbled to death; by mercy we are restored to life. IV, 1555.  
Magna est misericordia Dei, peccata donare. IV, 446. Great is the mercy of God in forgiving sins. IV, 446.  
Misericordia, medicina quotidiana quotidianorum vulnerum leviorum. II, 740, 858; V, 1198. Mercy is the daily medicine for daily lesser wounds. II, 740, 858; V, 1198.  
Misericordiae unda ignis peccati extinguitur. IV, 1861. By the wave of mercy the fire of sin is extinguished. IV, 1861.  
Ex misericordiae promissione non debemus polliceri, quoniam quidquid fecerimus, non perimus. IV, 1132. From the promise of mercy we must not assure ourselves that, whatever we do, we will not perish. IV, 1132.  
De misericordia Dei nemo sibi multum blandiatur. IV, 505, 1282. Let no one flatter himself too greatly concerning God’s mercy. IV, 505, 1282.  
Non sibi blandiatur qui non conatur adversus peccata. V, 154. Let no one who does not struggle against sins flatter himself. V, 154.  
Tempore misericordiae utendum ad poenitentiam. V, 636. The time of mercy must be used for repentance. V, 636.

Misericordia gemina. V, 1199. Mercy is twofold. V, 1199.  
Duplicis generis. IV, 345. Of two kinds. IV, 345.  
Misericordia non semper bona. X, 754. Mercy is not always good. X, 754.  
Est misericordia puniens, est crudelitas parcens. II, 660. There is a mercy that punishes, and a cruelty that spares. II, 660.  
Misericordia crudelis. X, 1082. Cruel mercy. X, 1082.  
Misericordiae magnae est nequitiam impunitam non relinquere. V, 935. It is great mercy not to leave wickedness unpunished. V, 935.  
Misericordia non tantum vocantis est, sed et verberantis. IV, 1131. Mercy belongs not only to the one who calls but also to the one who chastises. IV, 1131.  
Ad misericordiam Dei pertinet, etiam flagellis exercere. IV, 854, 855, 1145. It belongs to God’s mercy even to discipline by scourges. IV, 854, 855, 1145.  
Misericorditer dat Deus, cum dat; misericorditer aufert, cum tollit. IV, 1871. God gives mercifully when he gives, and takes away mercifully when he removes. IV, 1871.  
Deus non dando quod male petitur, magis misericors. IV, 1087. God is more merciful when he does not give what is wrongly requested. IV, 1087.  
Quia magis crebra sunt mala, dulcior erit misericordia. IV, 474. Because evils are more frequent, mercy will be sweeter. IV, 474.  
Multum sibi in hac carne tribueret homo, nisi usque ad mortem sub venia viveret. VII, 300. A human being would attribute much to himself in this flesh if he did not live under forgiveness until death. VII, 300.  
Misericordia nulla major, quam quae nobis a Christo praestita. V, 1043. There is no greater mercy than that which Christ has shown us. V, 1043.

Mercy’s time is now. IV, 284, 1282, 1284. The time of judgment will come. IV, 1291. The mercy and justice of God. V, 75. Mercy has gone before; judgment will follow. III, 1664. The time of mercy is not without judgment, nor the time of judgment without mercy. IV, 1587. When you have received mercy, use it well, so that at the time of judgment you may render a good account. IV, 287. Mercy triumphs over judgment. III, 634, 641. Otherwise there is no hope. II, 741; III, 641. We must flee to the mercy of God in order to obtain forgiveness of sins. III, 641. In God there is both mercy when he judges and judgment when he shows mercy. II, 740. God neither loses judgment in mercy nor mercy in judgment. IV, 284, 285, 446, 1861. The mercy of God does not prescribe against his justice, nor does his justice take away his mercy. V, 152. Mercy shown without judgment is false or cruel. IV, 285, 286. If God were only judge and not merciful, no one would stand before him. IV, 1698, 1700. Unless God first spared through mercy, he would find no one whom he could crown through judgment. IV, 1282. Mercy is granted beforehand; afterward severity will be rendered. V, 201. We need the mercy of God more than the most exact judgment. V, 930. Mercy is gratuitous, whereas judgment is owed. X, 981. Even at the judgment we shall need the mercy of God. X, 941. However justly a person may live, that person needs the mercy of God. IV, 481. Woe even to a praiseworthy life if God examines it after removing mercy. I, 778. No merit precedes mercy; judgment presupposes merits. X, 969. At the final judgment, mercy will be granted to the pious in recompense for the merits of good works, according to a just judgment; but it is not so now. X, 941, 942. God is merciful, repaying not only good for evil but also good for good. IV, 1517.

The commendation of divine mercy. IV, 234, 997, 1330. How mercy has been magnified even to the heavens. IV, 673. Scripture loves to join mercy and truth together. III, 565, 592; IV, 1117, 1480. We too ought to render mercy and truth to God: how this is to be done. IV, 1129, 1776. God wishes mercy to be sought from him. IV, 287, 299. God wishes us to show mercy more than to be freed from misery. V, 619. God will more readily restrain anger than mercy. IV, 977. Do not, because you have crossed over, wish to destroy the bridge of God’s mercy. IV, 1196. Silent contritions of the heart are great voices calling upon the mercy of God. I, 739, 740. No one is less worthy of mercy than a proud wretch. I, 1286. Those who stubbornly resist their father’s discipline do not deserve mercy. IV, 1133. Why are they called vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath? X, 1129.

What mercy is to be shown, and to whom. IV, 1326. Mercy is to be bestowed especially upon the soul. V, 627. Whoever is cruel to himself cannot be merciful to another. IV, 1283, 1284. The duty of mercy is owed to everyone. III, 31. Even to the unjust? IV, 1326. Judges ought to be moved by mercy toward the accused, because they too need mercy. II, 656, 657. The mercy by which priests customarily intervene for the accused is commended and explained. II, 654. Mercy is owed to the defeated. II, 856.

Works of mercy are commended. IV, 1236, 1328, 1469, 1860, 1861. Where works of mercy are absent, “Turn away from evil” may be present; but because “and do good” is absent, it is insufficient. V, 407. Works of mercy ought to increase when public calamities become more frequent. II, 471. Mercy is twofold in a good work. V, 1478. Mercy is true almsgiving. V, 626. Mercy that costs nothing is the forgiveness of injuries. IV, 1922. By showing mercy to another, we attend to our own advantage. III, 32. Whoever shows mercy expends charity. IV, 1922. Mercy must not be opposed to judgment. III, 628. False mercy is to spare in a way that nourishes vices. II, 391, 395. Perverse mercy is to conceal heretics. V, 754. What helps us greatly with God is that we grieve mercifully for the wicked, and for that very grief groan and pray. II, 1085. The wicked cannot fulfill the duties of mercy. III, 1326. Disobedient mercy, or merciful disobedience, is rightly rejected. X, 505. Works of mercy come from the merciful God. VI, 116.

Mercy is the true sacrifice. VII, 283, 284, 699. If mercy is not shown for God’s sake, it is not sacrifice. VII, 283. God is appeased by sacrifices of mercy. II, 665. Sins are expiated. II, 659; III, 1443. Works of mercy are remedies for abolishing sins. X, 152. Mercy reconciles us to God. V, 1198. Christ taught by himself that mercy must be granted beforehand so that justice may be fulfilled in us. V, 789. Because God is just, he executes judgment without mercy upon the one who has not shown mercy. IV, 1469. The counsel for escaping miseries is to be merciful. III, 1287. Works of mercy are our seeds. IV, 1664. The seed of the future harvest. VI, 161. Mercy is nowhere placed among objects of reproach in ecclesiastical writings. VIII, 410.

The merciful. V, 366. Even if human beings did not need mercy, they ought to be merciful after the example of Christ. II, 659, 660. The enemy is conquered by nothing so much as by our being merciful. IV, 1861. Whoever, moved not by grief but by the duty of goodness, supports a neighbor is considered merciful. I, 1333. No one can be merciful without love. III, 2079. Let no one think that God’s mercy will be shown toward him if he himself is unmerciful. IV, 1326. By frightening the Jews, Christ recalled them to mercy toward the woman caught in adultery. II, 656, 657.

The Mass of the catechumens takes place after the sermon. V, 324. Mass for the dead. II, 694. For a deceased person whose soul is in doubt. VI, 284. Note 4. See Sacrifice.

Mithridates, king of Asia. VII, 103. He ordered all the Romans found in Asia to be killed on a single day. VII, 103. The Mithridatic War. VII, 72.

How the meek and the merciful differ. III, 1257. Who the meek are. V, 365, 499, 500. God is meek when he grows angry. V, 166. Christ meek and humble: how he neither remains silent nor relents. V, 1276. Those who have learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be meek and humble in heart make more progress by thinking and praying than by reading and hearing. II, 597.

Mnesarchus the Stoic. I, 956.

Mnestheus, king of the Athenians. VII, 576.

Moab was the son of Lot. III, 739. It is interpreted “from the father.” IV, 1052.

The Moabites were descended from Lot. III, 762. The Moabites signify evil works. IV, 720.

Mociacensis. IX, 513.

Christian moderation. IX, 526, 527.

Where modesty gets its name. I, 711, 975. It is more beautiful for the temperance of the mind to confess its ignorance than for knowledge of things. I, 711.

Where “modica” gets its name. VIII, 557.

What it means to modulate musically. I, 563, 564.

Whether “mode” is in any way applicable to God. VIII, 558. The highest mode is God the Father. I, 976. Mode, the father of order. I, 1018. Mode, species, and order are general goods in things made by God. VIII, 553. Wisdom is a certain mode of the mind. I, 975. Why “mode,” and also “evil species,” is sometimes spoken of as evil. VIII, 558. A mode approved by everyone, recognized by few. I, 990. How difficult it is to maintain moderation in the use of things granted to us. V, 1272.

“Moechia” is the general term signifying every illicit sexual union. III, 622. Properly, however, it is usually understood to mean only adultery. III, 622, 763. Moechia is also the lust itself of the woman. VIII, 361. The prohibition of adultery. V, 69. Adultery is prohibited by the sixth and ninth commandments. V, 71. Adultery is forbidden to men no less than to women. V, 83. How the commandment against adultery differs from the commandment against coveting a wife. III, 622. Augustine discusses the commandment against adultery at length: why. V, 78.

Adulterer. Some in Africa thought that peace should be granted to adulterers. II, 341.

The mill, a figure of this world. IV, 356. Those who live in the world are in the mill. IV, 1730, 1731.

God commands us to endure the hardships of life, not to love them. I, 793. The hardships that a person now suffers by obeying God’s commandments are suffered either from the illness itself, which has not yet been healed, or from the assistance of the remedy. VI, 99. The usefulness of bodily hardships. X, 259. [Col. 0443] Threefold usefulness. II, 504. Temporal hardship is to be used for salvation. II, 470. Temporal hardships ought to admonish us so that we may avoid eternal ones. II, 470. Increasing hardships compel us to desire eternal rest. II, 593.

Effeminate men consecrated to the Mother of the Gods. VII, 215. They were also employed in the rites of the gods. VII, 185.

Where monks get their name. IV, 1732. Heretics insult Catholics because of the name “monks.” IV, 1730. Monks are simply called “servants of God.” II, 993; V, 1070. Monks living in holy fellowship in the desert. IX, 423. Monks are praised. IV, 1730. The institution of monks, anchorites, and coenobites is praised. I, 1338. The monastic way of life, famous throughout the world. IX, 372. Its brief commendation. IV, 1277. The monastic life is compared with a harbor. IV, 1277. The psalm “Behold, how good…” gathered monks together like a trumpet. IV, 1729. The profession of monks is signified by Matthew XXIV: “Two in bed,” etc. IV, 357, 358, 1279. Monks are prefigured by Daniel. IV, 1731. Monks are Christian soldiers. VIII, 226. Soldiers of Christ fighting in silence, etc. II, 997.

The good pursuits of monks. IV, 1278. What monks customarily do and with what disposition they ought to do it. II, 190. Many fast throughout their entire lives every day except Saturday and Sunday, especially those established in monasteries. II, 139. Some Carthaginian monks supported themselves by their own hands, while others lived on offerings from the faithful; hence great disputes arose. I, 638. On what occasion the book On the Work of Monks was published. I, 638. The Massalians said that monks were not permitted to work for the sake of sustaining life. VIII, 40. Monks gathered into holy fellowship who are unwilling to work are punished. VI, 549, 560. Idle and wandering monks. VI, 575. Monks carrying hypocrisy around for sale. VI, 578. If servants, freedmen, peasants, craftsmen, and commoners are not admitted to the profession of serving God, it is a grave offense. VI, 568. Those abuse this profession who seek, through it, to be fed, clothed, and honored by people by whom they had been accustomed to be despised and crushed. VI, 568. See Work. Alms given by a woman to two monks as though they were poor men, without her husband’s knowledge, cause scandal. II, 1079. If a monk of Thagaste died without having sold his property or transferred it to anyone by an open donation, only his heirs succeeded to it: an example. II, 293. Long-haired monks. I, 638. They disturbed the Church. VI, 580. They are rebuked. VI, 578. Even in a monastery, the wicked must be tolerated for the sake of the good. IV, 1278, 1279. What kind of mercy it is to safeguard the good reputation of God’s servants. V, 569.

What deserters from the monastic life are like. IV, 1279. The monastic purpose must not be abandoned. IV, 1058. If the Church desires some service from a monk, he should neither accept it with ambitious self-exaltation nor reject it through flattering indolence. II, 188. We customarily admit only the more proven monks into the clergy. II, 228. Deserters from monasteries are not to be chosen for the clergy. II, 228. “Thanks be to God,” a greeting customary among monks. IV, 1732. Monks who shut themselves in for many days and allow no one access to them. VI, 570. The holy and numerous flock of the Egyptian monks is indicated. V, 769. Egyptian monks killed by barbarians. II, 422. Augustine hopes that the monastic purpose will flourish throughout all Africa, as it does in other lands. VI, 576. Augustine commends himself to the prayers of monks as more watchful and more sober. II, 188. Alypius joins the monastic life with the office of bishop. II, 99. It was decreed concerning clergy alone, not laity, that those coming from elsewhere should not be received into a monastery. II, 233. Eustasius and Andreas from the island of Capraria (monks). II, 189. The Apostolici admit only monks and nuns, and those who have no marriages. VIII, 52. The Hieracites. VIII, 38. The Aeriani. VIII, 39.

The profession and dwelling of nuns. I, 1339. Food and clothing are to be distributed to the nuns by the superior, not equally to all. II, 960. They are to dress from a common wardrobe and not care whether they receive the garment they had put away. II, 963. Nuns should take care that, in the monastery where they can become rich through labor, they do not become pampered paupers. II, 962. If a nun marries, she will be considered an adulteress. IV, 1058. Nuns must not call anything their own. II, 961. How they ought to regard one another, whether they had been poor or rich in the world. II, 961. They should consider those richer who have been stronger in enduring frugality. II, 962. Their dress should not be conspicuous; no hairnets should appear beneath their head coverings; they should have no hair bare on any side; they should walk and stand together. II, 961. In walking, standing, dress, and all movements, nothing should be done that might entice anyone’s lust. II, 961. They should fix their eyes on no one and avoid lustful glances. II, 962. No one should take any food outside the hour of the midday meal, except when ill. II, 961. The nuns should admonish one another; they should report to the superior those who, after being admonished, have neglected to correct themselves; and they are not innocent if they fail to report them. Those who are convicted should undergo corrective punishment; those who refuse to bear the punishment should be expelled. II, 963. They must not accept gifts or letters from a man. II, 963. They must avoid murmuring. II, 963. The nuns should work in common; whatever is sent to the religious women should be under the superior’s authority; anyone who conceals something given to her is to be condemned as a thief. II, 963. Clothing is to be washed according to the superior’s decision. II, 963. The use of baths is to be allowed once a month. II, 963. How sick nuns are to be treated. II, 962, 963. Care of the sick is to be assigned to someone; when it is necessary to go to the baths or anywhere else, fewer than three must not go; they must not choose their companions but receive them from the superior. II, 963. Nuns should not be troubled if something is indulged to the sick or to others. II, 961. They should request books at a fixed hour each day. II, 963. They should have no quarrels, or settle them as quickly as possible. II, 963. Whoever has injured another should repair what she has done by making satisfaction as quickly as possible. Those who have injured one another should make satisfaction to one another. II, 964. Those who have exceeded moderation in restraining their juniors are not required to ask forgiveness from them. II, 964. They should obey the superior as a mother, and much more the priest who cares for all of them. II, 964. The office of the superior. II, 964. They should observe the Rule not as slave women under the Law but as free women established under grace. II, 965. The Rule is to be read once a week. II, 965. The priest who cares for the nuns is called the superior. II, 959, 960. Nuns wishing to change their superior ask for something contrary to sound discipline. II, 959. The habit of a nun differs from that of a married woman, but is one that a married woman may wear with her husband’s permission. II, 958. When the nuns disagree, Augustine denies them his presence and deals with their affair before God through tears. II, 959.

A monastery of clergy. V, 1570. Flocks of monasteries. I, 755. See Fraternal Congregations. The Church has produced monasteries on the hem of Christ’s garment. IV, 1734. Petilianus the Donatist censures monasteries and monks. IX, 372. See Augustine. The monastery at Milan, full of good brothers, outside the city walls, under Ambrose its nurturer. I, 755. Augustine saw several monasteries, or refuges of the saints, at Rome. I, 1340. Monasteries begin to be established at Carthage. I, 638. A monastery first instituted by Augustine in a garden and afterward in the bishop’s house. V, 1569. The occupations of well-governed monasteries. VI, 576. It was decreed at the Council of Carthage held on 13 September 401 that those who had left a monastery or had been expelled from one should not become clergy elsewhere or superiors of monasteries. II, 234. Augustine found it difficult to encounter better people than those who had made progress in a monastery, and he did not encounter worse than those who had fallen in monasteries. II, 272. Rich people who build monasteries: what they are compared to. IV, 1371. A book brought into the monastery at Hadrumetum without the abbot’s knowledge, and what disturbances it caused there. II, 975.

Monaxius, consul. II, 927.

We are God’s coin. III, 1691; V, 566.

Most wholesome admonitions belong to grace. III, 1833.

Monnica, wife of Patricius and mother of Augustine. I, 780. She was brought up soberly and chastely. I, 771. In a Christian household that displayed uprightness of conduct among the members of the Church. I, 770. She was trained in propriety not so much by her own mother as by a certain aged servant woman. I, 770. Monnica was trained by discipline and under the governance of Christ, who already instructed her in the fear of God. I, 770. Through Christ Monnica was subject to her parents, rather than through her parents subject to Christ. I, 771. Monnica, gradually seized by a love of wine, was cured of this vice through the taunt of a maidservant who was quarreling with her. I, 771. Monnica was torn apart by Julian’s insult. X, 1090. She was freed by God’s grace from a childish vice. X, 1090. Monnica, given in marriage to Patricius, served him as though he were her lord. I, 771. She labored to win him for God. I, 771. From the time she was reborn in Christ, although not yet released from her husband, she led a distinguished life in faith and conduct. I, 779. How she conducted herself toward her husband, who was far removed from her faith and conduct. I, 771. How she conducted herself toward her mother-in-law, who had been stirred against her by the whisperings of wicked maidservants. I, 772. How she conducted herself toward her parents and her household. I, 772.

Monnica nourished her children, giving birth to them again and again whenever she saw them straying from God. I, 773. Monnica gave birth to Augustine both in the flesh, so that he might be born into this temporal light, and in her heart, so that he might be born into eternal light. I, 770. She gave birth to Augustine in spirit with greater anxiety than she had borne him in the flesh. I, 714. She placed Augustine among the catechumens from his earliest years. I, 669, 729. When Augustine was still a boy and was in sudden danger of death, she hurried anxiously to have him initiated into the saving sacraments. Yet when Augustine recovered, she judged that baptism should be postponed. I, 670. When Augustine was sixteen years old, God had already begun in Monnica his temple and the beginning of his holy dwelling. I, 677. Monnica was accustomed to come to church twice a day, morning and evening, to pray or hear the word of God. I, 714. Obedient and serving the saints, Monnica never omitted an offering at God’s altar. I, 714. Monnica was exceedingly devoted to the sacred Scriptures. I, 993. How she conducted herself toward the servants of God. I, 773. How she conducted herself toward married women who brought complaints about their husbands. I, 772. How she conducted herself toward minds divided and at odds with one another. I, 773. Monnica frequently gave alms. I, 714. Near the end of his life she led her husband to faith in Christ. I, 773.

Widowed from her husband, Monnica nevertheless provided expenses for Augustine, who was then studying rhetoric at Carthage. I, 685. Monnica admonished Augustine with immense anxiety to shun fornication, and especially adultery. I, 678. Monnica mourned Augustine’s falling into the heresy of the Manichaeans and rejected his company. I, 691. Monnica was warned of Augustine’s future repentance through a dream and through the reply of a certain bishop, who declared that it could not happen that the son of such tears should perish. I, 692. There was one reason why she wished to remain here for a while: namely, that she might see Augustine a Catholic Christian before her death. I, 775. Monnica followed Augustine, who was sailing to Rome against her will. I, 713. Shortly afterward, having boarded the ship, she comforted the sailors amid the dangers of the sea, having been divinely assured of a safe arrival. I, 719. When Monnica came to Milan, she found Augustine, after hearing Ambrose, already estranged from the Manichaeans. I, 719. Monnica loved Ambrose as an angel of God. I, 719. When she brought food to the memorial shrines of the martyrs in Africa, she did not set down more than one small cup measured out for herself, from which she might take a small draught. I, 720. At Milan, when Ambrose forbade these offerings, Monnica most willingly complied with him. I, 720. While the people of Milan kept vigil in the church, Monnica held the first place among those keeping vigil. I, 769. She lived by prayers. I, 769. Monnica was concerned whether she ought to fast on Saturday at Milan and accepted Ambrose’s reply. II, 151, 201. In praise of Monnica, Ambrose would often burst forth upon seeing Augustine, congratulating him on having such a mother. I, 196.

When Monnica heard of Augustine’s conversion, she rejoiced, exulted, triumphed, and blessed God. I, 762. She withdrew with Augustine to the estate at Cassiciacum. I, 765. She took part in the discussion on the Blessed Life. I, 962. On Order. I, 991, 993. Augustine had experienced her intelligence and her mind inflamed toward divine things. I, 991, 993. In the discussion on the Blessed Life she offered outstanding opinions. I, 962, 976. Augustine reports one notable opinion of hers. I, 775. Monnica thought that the Academics should be called “Caducarians.” I, 967.

Monnica accompanied Augustine back to Africa after he had received baptism. I, 777. At Ostia on the Tiber, shortly before her death, she conversed with Augustine about eternal life. I, 774. Both were carried away into contemplation of eternal wisdom. I, 774. Monnica declared that she now took pleasure in nothing in this life. I, 775. After about five days she took to her bed with fevers. I, 775. Monnica was carried into ecstasy. I, 775. When she returned to her senses, she said that no concern should be shown for burying her body outside her homeland. I, 775. She asked them only to remember her at the Lord’s altar. I, 775. Finally, on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her life and the thirty-third year of Augustine’s life, she departed from this life. I, 775.

Monnica’s funeral. I, 776. The sacrifice of our price was offered for her, her body already placed beside the tomb, before it was laid within, as was customary there. I, 776. How Augustine mourned his mother’s death. I, 775. Monnica’s eulogy. I, 772. Augustine believes that he owes his whole life to his mother’s merit. I, 960. Through her prayers, he believes he was given the mind that placed nothing before the discovery of truth. I, 1019.

Monnulus of Girba. IX, 209.

The unicorn signifies pride. III, 881.

The single combat of Goliath and David. V, 197.

Monster. V, 771. Derived from “to show” (*monstrare*). VII, 722. Whether monsters may rightly be called errors and sins of nature. X, 814. Monsters in human bodies would not have been born if no one had sinned. X, 1125. Why monsters were created by God. VII, 486. Various monstrous human races are reported. VII, 485. A two-membered human being born in the East. VI, 273. Monstrous offspring will rise again with nature corrected. VI, 272.

Montanus. VI, 305. Founder of the heretical Cataphrygians. VIII, 30. Through him, they say, the Holy Spirit came. II, 1035.

Montanus the presbyter. IX, 513.

Good mountains and evil mountains. IV, 519, 1257. When Scripture mentions mountains in a good sense, it immediately names the Lord there. IV, 1651. Mount Zion, the mountain of Esau, the dense mountain: what they signify. VII, 588, 589. The mountains of Israel, where there is good pasture. V, 284. Christ is signified by the name “mountain.” IV, 74; V, 265, 266. The righteousness of Christ. IV, 74. The exaltedness of the angels. IV, 1141, 1142. The synagogue. V, 267. The Church. IV, 70; V, 267. Ministers of the word. IV, 1479. And the devout through whom Scripture is handed down. IV, 1651. The mountain from which the stone was cut signifies the kingdom of the Jews. IV, 1270. The mountain that rose from the cut stone signifies the Church. IV, 70, 478, 1270; V, 267. The mountains surrounding Jerusalem [Col. 0446] are preachers, angels, apostles, and prophets. IV, 1650. Great mountains—that is, preachers—give light, but are themselves illuminated first. IV, 1651. The name “mountain” signifies illustrious and spiritual men of the Church. IV, 437. Men eminent in holiness within the Church. IV, 904. Help comes to you from the mountains, but not from the mountains themselves. IV, 347. The mountain signifies the excellence of Christ’s charity in eternal life. IV, 143. The name “mountain” signifies the powers of the world. IV, 519. The proud. IV, 1865. The leaders of heresies. IV, 347. How Christ’s saying, “You will say to this mountain, ‘Move into the sea,’ and it will happen,” was fulfilled. IV, 517, 518. The mountain cast into the sea by the apostles. V, 554.

The Montenses, or Donatists. VIII, 43. Thus they were called at Rome. II, 196.

A monument is so called because it reminds the mind. VI, 596. The new tomb in which Christ was buried corresponds to the Virgin’s womb. VIII, 894.

Moral philosophy. VII, 232.

The Pelagians place diseases in paradise. X, 1248. There would have been no diseases in paradise. X, 802. The origin of diseases in infants. X, 707, 801, 802. They are arguments for original sin. X, 707. How many diseases afflict the body. VII, 786. Once the hardship of illness has been experienced, the pleasantness of health becomes more evident. VII, 425. In almost all diseases, medicines are torments. VII, 785. A disease that resists every effort of the physician is incurable and unconquerable not through the physician’s fault but through the patient’s. VII, 173. Every disease of the soul has its medicine in Scripture. IV, 357. How Julian understood the “disease of desire” in the Apostle. X, 807.

Precepts of conduct are handed down to the young. I, 1006. In matters pertaining to life and conduct, not instruction alone but exhortation is necessary. VI, 431. Depraved acts that violate human customs are to be avoided according to the diversity of customs. I, 689. Conduct is usually judged from what each person loves. II, 672. Only good or evil loves make good or evil conduct. II, 672; V, 1417. Good conduct is itself the dignity of human beings. VII, 161. God himself makes a person’s conduct good. X, 1208. Upright conduct, even among pagans, comes only from God. II, 591. How usefully good conduct is commended to peoples. VIII, 90. Recognition of truth comes through good conduct. I, 1334. Paganism does not condemn corruption of conduct as Christianity does. VII, 64, 69, 70, 74. How greatly people neglect the evils of conduct. VII, 79. Evil conduct brings more harm than raging enemies. VII, 43. Evil conduct torments the hearts of those who live piously. VII, 613, 614. The corruption of conduct before Christ’s coming. VII, 64, 74. Where likenesses of conduct come from. X, 500. To praise God by conduct and by words. V, 1190. How greatly Eunomius is an enemy through his conduct. VIII, 40.

Fools. II, 728; X, 707. They utter no word that they would wish to recall. II, 586. Fools as the delight of the thoughtful. X, 148. Fools providing the thoughtful with the delights of foolishness. X, 127. A certain fool who was most patient under his own sufferings but a fierce avenger of insults against Christ. X, 127.

Custom, or usage, is extremely powerful either for attracting or presenting something to human understanding. VII, 458. The custom of the Church to which we have come must be observed if we do not wish either to suffer or cause scandal. II, 151, 201. Which practices introduced from various customs ought to be cut away. II, 221.

The death of the body is the separation of the soul from the body. IV, 556, 893. Certain philosophers do not wish death to be a punishment. VII, 387. Julian maintains that bodily death would have occurred in paradise even if no one had sinned. X, 1585. Julian introduced into paradise not the rest of the good dead but the sufferings of the dying. X, 1575. According to Julian, punitive death owed to sin is only eternal death. X, 1222. Bodily death itself is also punitive. X, 1222. Punitive death dissolves the soul from the flesh. X, 1593. The ordinary death of the body occurs deservedly because of sin. X, 1596, 1603, 1604. The Pelagians say that death passed to us through Adam, and in this they cut their own throats. X, 613, 615.

Death was threatened to the first parents. V, 1439. The human being was created in such a way as not to have the necessity of dying; but through sin the condition of nature was so changed that it became necessary for the human being to die. X, 1112. If no one had sinned, human beings would not have undergone even a gentle death in paradise. X, 1572. Unless Adam had sinned. X, 1181. This human being would not have died unless God had struck him. IV, 861. The very death of the human being indicates that he would have been without death if he had not sinned. III, 352, 353. The cause of death is the frail structure of the limbs. VII, 710. By sinning, the human being was forced into the necessity of dying. II, 547. Not death alone but sin also passed into us through Adam. X, 613, 614, 1169.

Death has been decreed for everyone. V, 1280, 1506, 1513. It is a debt that no one escapes. V, 1192. Every human being except Christ is born bound by the condition of death and the laws of hell. V, 1105.

Death comes from sin. II, 873; III, 353; VII, 377, 378, 380, 387, 391, 396, 403; X, 111, 197, 406, 826. The necessity of dying exists from birth itself. V, 489. The necessity of death is the merit of sin. X, 113. Death is the punishment of sin. V, 906, 936, 938, 1104, 1773, 1775; X, 613, 1571. It is not the cause. X, 260. Death is owed to sinful flesh. III, 2072. Death follows sin. X, 1248. It accords with God’s judgment that the sinner should die, yet death does not accord with his work. X, 1354, 1355. From death comes that weariness which we find in all our refreshment. IV, 1076. The guilt of dying appears in the involuntary movement of the flesh. III, 422.

The Lord assumed the death of the flesh not from the necessity of his condition but by the will of compassion. IV, 1111. Death in the Lord was a sign of the sins of others, not a punishment for his own. V, 1607. Christ was not destroyed but transferred from temporal life to eternal life, from the Jews to the Gentiles, and so forth. IV, 1139. What the Lord’s death accomplished. III, 2072. The devil brought about death, and by Christ’s death he himself was taken captive. V, 715. Christ died as the slayer of death. IV, 600. To be healed by looking at the serpent is to be saved from death by believing in the one who died. IV, 933. How our death was dissolved by Christ’s death. VIII, 889. Christ’s death is the pledge of the inheritance. V, 726. Christ alone endured death without sin. X, 613. In Christ, death was not the punishment of sin but a gift of mercy. III, 1401. It was a matter of gracious condescension, not of debt. III, 2072. The translation of Enoch and Elijah does not prove that death is not the punishment of sin. II, 871.

Death does not come from God. I, 919. Death was sown by the serpent. IV, 933. How death comes from the devil and how from God. X, 806. To what extent it comes from the devil upon human beings. X, 114. Why the devil is said to have the power and dominion of death. X, 181. The devil is death, not because he himself is death but because death comes through him. IV, 556. The sting of bodily death is sin. X, 1604, 1607. How this is so. X, 197, 614. How death is called sin. IV, 335. Death is called sin because it comes from the punishment of sin. VIII, 296, 297. Whether, because the sin of the first human being caused us to die, the Savior’s coming ought to have caused us not to die. X, 180. Why those who are freed from sin through baptism remain subject to death. VII, 379; X, 181. Why death, which is the punishment of sin, remains although sin does not remain. II, 872; V, 1375. Why temporal death is left for a time to the faithful, while everlasting death is taken away from the guilty. X, 1181. Temporal death is left for the exercise of faith. II, 683; V, 1375; X, 182, 183, 184, 186, 260. The punishment of death has been turned to the uses of justice. VII, 379.

The reign of death. VII, 403. When death reigns over infants, it is a sign that they are liable to original sin. X, 1228. What the reign of death means in the Apostle. X, 116, 462. What kind of reign of death it is. X, 1171. Death reigned in the world because of original sin. X, 1221, 1224. The Savior’s grace alone destroys the reign of death in each person. X, 116. Death, accompanying sin as its punishment until everlasting destruction, unless divine grace heals generation through regeneration. X, 1261. The reign of death is not in those who, reborn by Christ’s grace, belong to his kingdom. II, 683. How grace frees from the law of death. VIII, 125.

Death is twofold. VIII, 890, 900; X, 1171. There are two deaths: one of the body, common to the good and the wicked, and the other of the soul through sin. X, 1584. Death is twofold: one temporal, the other eternal. III, 1710. The death of the soul and the death of the body. VII, 377. Twofold death passed to everyone. X, 1170. Twofold death, the first and the second. V, 1105, 1513; VI, 275; VII, 378. The first death: what it is. VII, 378. One is the first death, brought by the first human being through sin; another is the second death, which the second human being will bring through judgment. X, 1584, 1593, 1604. Whatever death there is, up to the one called the second, God threatened to the first parents. VII, 385, 387. Death both of soul and of body would not have followed if sin had not preceded it. VI, 160. The first death is common to all, but not the second. VII, 398. The first must necessarily be undergone by all; the second is prepared only for the wicked. V, 1513. Those who are freed from sin suffer only the first death. VII, 379. The first death endured for the sake of truth frees from the second. VII, 382. The death of the flesh belongs to that fire by which each person’s work is tested. VII, 745. The second death: what it is. VII, 377; X, 116. It is eternal death. VII, 193. What eternal death of soul and body is. V, 430. Eternal death is called the second death. X, 140. The second death is called condemnation. VII, 658, 674. The second death is the worst. VII, 385. The second death belongs only to the wicked. VII, 378. What the first death is in the mortal city, the second death is in the immortal city. VII, 384. How great the danger of eternal death threatens everyone. V, 1541. Everyone would rush into the second death unless God’s grace freed some. VII, 403. The second death is called both death, and yet no one there dies. V, 1402. Death will die in us but will live in the condemned. V, 1114. One resurrection of the blessed removes both deaths. X, 1181. How Christ’s single death was expended for our double death. VIII, 891, 892. Christ’s temporal death killed human beings’ eternal death. III, 1402. Death died in Christ. V, 496, 1114, 1354.

[Col. 0448] It is not opinion but nature that dreads death. V, 936, 1360, 1373, 1374. It is necessary to die, and no one wishes to. IV, 238. There is a certain sweet bond of the body, and a person is bound by it and does not wish to be released. V, 1366. Nature’s first and greatest voice is that a human being should flee death. VII, 630. Why everyone shuns death. VII, 340. Fear of death. VI, 676. Whether he would have been destined for paradise without sin. X, 1530, 1536. Fear of death congenitally implanted in Adam’s descendants. X, 1530. God made fear of death for the sake of discipline. IV, 1162. Fear of death is torment. X, 1570, 1571. Death is feared more than hardships. X, 1571. How much a person labors to avoid death. V, 706. How vain the fear of death is. V, 881. Fear of death pricks most sharply when things are going well for us. V, 238. What must be done so that we may not die. V, 881. Death is something which, if you wish it, will not exist. V, 1513. The death of the soul must be feared more than that of the body. V, 430, 880, 1247. It is not temporal death but eternal death that must be feared. V, 1280. His death is bitter to us whose life is sweet. VII, 635. To whom Cicero promises a pleasant death. VIII, 1056. With how vain a fear human beings are held by death. V, 881. Those who fear dying and do nothing except die later—why do they not act so as not to die? V, 881. Why everyone, or almost everyone, tries to postpone the day of death. II, 544. An accelerated death is useful to some. III, 780. No one labors to avoid death altogether, but only to postpone it. III, 816. One should not be concerned how quickly, or by what kind of death, this life is ended. VII, 25. The manner of death does nothing to the good that could harm them after death. VII, 471. Do not concern yourself with where a person dies, but with where he is going after death. IV, 1945. You who do so much to die a little later, do something so that you may never die. V, 1387. Those who are disturbed when death threatens should look upon Christ himself, who was disturbed for the same reason. III, 1798. Everyone shuns the death of the flesh, but few care about the death of the soul. III, 1747. Fear of bodily death makes people guilty. X, 1603. Death is not to be feared. II, 649. Temporal death is not to be feared. III, 1710. The whole of human life can be made fearless in the face of death. II, 74. The wise person fears neither bodily death nor pains. I, 971. It is better to undergo one death by dying than to fear them all while living. VII, 25. To overcome the fear of death is no small virtue. X, 183. It is a greater virtue to despise death than hardship. X, 1571. The fact that the faithful overcome fear of death belongs to the struggle of faith. X, 182. Christ showed by his death and cross that neither death nor the manner of death is to be feared. VI, 664. Fear of death in Peter and Christ. IV, 1143, 1144. Why Christ feared death and Paul did not. IV, 1287. Christ’s death teaches that death is not to be feared to such an extent. V, 1354. Christ removed the fear of death by rising again. V, 799. We fear death, although it ends weakness. IV, 1143, 1144. Death is not a punishment for an old man. IV, 1268. No one invokes death with words, but with a bad life. IV, 473. Death is called for by the wretched; when it is present, they flee it with all their might. V, 519. Death cannot be loved, but it can be endured. V, 1373. Although we wish to cling to Christ, we nevertheless do not wish to die. IV, 842. By reason of the mind the devout person desires to be released, but by the feeling of the flesh he shuns it. II, 544. The Apostles fleeing after Christ’s death are prefigured by Moses fleeing from the serpent. IV, 933.

Death must be endured with an even temper. III, 1402. It must be endured patiently, following Christ’s example. IV, 831. When God commands, it must not be refused, at whatever time. III, 361. This house has been leased to you, not given to you. IV, 1945. The master of the house, when he wishes, says, “Move out”; he did not make a contract with you and bind himself by an agreement to a fixed term. IV, 429. Death is not to be avoided through sin, but endured for justice, if the opportunity is given. VII, 301. The wise person ought to bear death patiently, when it comes from some source other than himself. VII, 630. It is not permitted to inflict death on oneself. II, 755; VI, 616. Whatever the reason. VII, 30, 34, 35, 38, 39. Inflicting death on oneself does not belong to greatness of spirit. VII, 35. Plato judged voluntary death ought to be prohibited. VII, 36.
