Death must not be inflicted on oneself. III, 1767, 1770. Nevertheless, it is preferable to choose it rather than sin. III, 1767.

Fourfold kind of death. III, 1752. Threefold kind of death. III, 1747. Three kinds of death frequently practiced by the Donatists. IX, 724, 725. The two most disgraceful and customary deaths of those who kill themselves are hanging and jumping from a height. IX, 299. One who inflicts death on himself, even while being compelled to evil, perishes eternally. II, 755. He who inflicts death on himself is worse than a parricide. VI, 617. Some die with patience; the perfect live with patience. III, 2046. Love of God makes death despised, indeed even desired. I, 1328. Death is to be desired. IV, 1843. Yet not excessively. IV, 1843. How a just person may desire death in a most bitter life. IX, 727. One ought to desire to hasten more quickly toward Christ when a swift death comes to one’s aid. X, 630. Why Paul desired death, and why the other Apostles did. X, 631, 632. For the faithful, unwillingness to die is not advice for them to make progress, but an indication that they have made too little progress. III, 1376. The more we enjoy God either through a mirror or in an enigma, the more ardently we desire to end our pilgrimage. III, 30. Death is a vehicle to the kingdom. VI, 668. The death of the flesh is called sleep. [Col. 0449] IV, 825. It is like sleep. IV, 1701. Death is called sleep because of the future resurrection, which is like awakening. II, 572. The Manichaeans said that death was the separation of good from evil. II, 272.

Death is not an evil, according to the Pelagians. X, 610. According to Julian, death was promised—or rather indicated—to the transgressor as a benefit, so that he would not think his labor eternal. X, 1570, 1571. Death is not a good. VII, 380, 381. When death occurs to mortals, it should not be considered anything dreadful. III, 778. Death is the just vengeance of sin, yet it shows more of God’s mercy than of his severity—why. III, 134. The fact that human beings must necessarily die in the body is no small benefit of Christ’s grace. X, 113. Some have discussed the good of death appropriately. X, 613. According to Cyprian, death is not only not useless to the faithful, but even useful. X, 979, 980, 981. Through the temporal deaths of mortals, God imposes the usefulness of fear of him upon peoples. VIII, 412. Through bodily deaths God has sometimes punished even those who had not committed sins. VIII, 660, 661, 662. The remains of death turn to the good of the elect. VIII, 1029. Through God’s mercy death is turned to good uses. X, 613, 614. Bodily death is punitive, but through God’s grace it becomes precious. X, 1585, 1593. Death becomes the just person’s merit. VII, 380, 381. Who make good use of death, which is the punishment of the first sin. X, 178. The Martyrs, making good use of the evil of death, strive onward. X, 1575. He who contends for the truth to the point of death, or is killed by enemies whom he has offended for the sake of justice, offers God a pleasing sacrifice. III, 811. Death turns either to what is worse or to what is better. III, 1588.

Death is evil in all who are dying, but among the dead it is evil for some and good for others. X, 1575. Whether death is good for the good and evil for the wicked. VII, 378, 381. Death is evil for the wicked. VII, 378. What kind of death is truly good or evil. V, 611. Nothing makes or proves death evil except what follows death. V, 612; VII, 25, 26. Whatever harms those who are dying comes from life, not from death. II, 649. For the dying person, either life or punishment will be his companion. V, 811. Death should not be considered evil when a good life has preceded it. VII, 25. It is not within human power by what outcome one ends this life, but it is within human power how one lives, so as to end life securely. V, 1400. To die in sin is the greatest evil. III, 1678. He who has lived well cannot die badly. V, 1162; VI, 676. Live in such a way that, when dying, you may find the Father as judge, the Angel who lifts you into Abraham’s bosom as a harsh minister, and paradise as a prison. V, 638. When someone dies immediately after a true conversion, God does not take account of his ability but crowns his intention. V, 131. Death is the end of evils, but only in those whose life is chaste, devout, faithful, and innocent. II, 389.

How the death of the just and that of sinners differ. IV, 321. The impious do not understand what death is, even when they see wise people dying. IV, 551. Death must be understood in relation to the soul as either most evil or most good. IV, 322. What kind of death is best. IV, 825. The death of the saints is precious. VII, 381. The price of holy deaths is the death of one. V, 1454. Death is good for the devout person from whatever source it comes. IV, 1945. Through the death of the soul, if it has not lost its God, it will be in him whom it did not exclude from itself. V, 881. A splendid example of dying. II, 694, 697. Just as death is paid as a wage in return for the merit of sin, so eternal life is paid as a wage in return for the merit of righteousness. II, 881. Adam is the author of death; Christ, of resurrection. X, 1593. It is the doctrine of Caelestius that neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does it rise again. X, 334. Some maintained that through Christ’s death resurrection was granted to the just in the same form as that promised to us at the end. II, 712. There will be no death in the age to come. VII, 683. Through the more wondrous power of grace, the just revive from death to eternal blessedness, rather than never enter into the experience of death. II, 873. Bodily death will be destroyed in the resurrection. X, 1603. The victory of death will be overcome by the resurrection of bodies. X, 198. In the resurrection only the just will be freed from the body of death. V, 839. No one at all wishes to die. V, 939. Those who remain at the end will not feel death, being changed suddenly. X, 181. The rapture of living believers at Christ’s coming does not prove that death is not the punishment of sin. II, 872.

The thought of death is often buried with the dead person after burial. V, 1601. One ought truly to think only about a person’s final departure, which is called death. II, 74. Amid restless noises, gatherings, and running about, there is no familiarity with death. II, 74. Death alone is certain here. V, 590. Everything else is uncertain. IV, 428. God in great mercy has hidden the day of death from us. IV, 332; V, 241. Why God wished the day of death to be uncertain. IV, 1301, 1876. The last day is hidden so that all days may be watched. V, 241. The day of death is uncertain, but near. V, 241, 839. The day of each person’s death is his last day. V, 932.

What the body of death is, and who are freed from it. X, 561. What the shadow of death is. X, 1522. The shadow of death is the way of sin. V, 1649. Death was prefigured in Saul. IV, 601. Who is called dying. VII, 382. Whether the time of death should be said to exist among the dying or among the dead. VII, 382.

What spiritual death is. III, 1547; V, 1617. The death of the soul. V, 1059. The soul can and cannot die. V, 428, 1247. The death of the soul is the loss of God. III, 1737; V, 415, 428. Separation of the soul from God. IV, 556, 893. The death of the soul is wickedness. III, 131. By what signs the death both of body and of soul is recognized. V, 429. He who lives badly is death to himself. I, 830. Life amid temporal pleasures, compared with eternal life, should be called not life but death. II, 223. It is sharply proved that we love death more than life. VI, 676. The death of the soul is more dreadful and more to be feared than that of bodies. VIII, 618. Sinners are killed when, with their understanding darkened, they are alienated from the life of God. IV, 1800. The death of dead souls lies beneath the weight of the body. IV, 1117. How the soul is said to be dead through sin. III, 2069. The true death is to descend into the depth of sin. IV, 703. The death of the soul is understood when it has been put to death by sin or punished by condemnation. II, 717. Through bodily deaths many have died because of the sins of others; no one through the death of the soul. VIII, 619. A certain death is the transformation of a bad life. V, 1106. Certain deaths belonging to the stages of life. IV, 1686. The death of the Egyptian livestock. V, 69.

How the mortal, the one destined to die, and the dead differ. X, 111. Our mortal condition, by which we were created mortal, is a divine gift. VII, 376. Mortal things, although punitive, have their proper place of beauty in the beauty of the ages. VIII, 607.

Mortality became like a second nature. VI, 107. The origin of mortality and lust. III, 446. Mortality derives from sin. V, 62, 63, 67, 1607. It is the punishment of sin. VI, 107, 332. Mortality is real in Christ. V, 1609. Why it was assumed by Christ. V, 62, 63. Mortality ought to benefit a human being by fostering humility. V, 589. There will be no mortality after the resurrection. X, 112. The mortality of the age is a river. IV, 794, 795. The mortality of the age is compared with a torrent. IV, 1462.

“Morticinum” (“something dead”) is a term used only of the dead, whereas “mortale” (“mortal”) is also used of living bodies. IV, 1013. Why the Apostle prohibited Christians from eating carrion. VIII, 503, 504.

What it means for Christ’s faithful to be put to death and made alive. VII, 529. The members must be put to death. VI, 370. See Flesh. The spirit does this in subduing the flesh, so as to make it subject. III, 28. This is our work in this life: to put to death by the spirit the actions of the flesh, daily afflicting, diminishing, restraining, and killing them. V, 855. While you do not consent, you put pleasure to death; when it begins not to please at all, you have put it to death. V, 855. In this contest, when we struggle, we have God as our spectator; when we labor, we ask God to be our helper. V, 855. In putting the flesh to death, one must not rely on one’s own spirit. V, 855. Otherwise, what does it benefit you not to be an Epicurean if you are a Stoic? V, 855. Those who chastise the flesh strive to imitate the state that will exist after the resurrection. III, 28. Nor do they hate their own body. III, 28. We must die an evangelical death, so that by a voluntary departure we may anticipate the dissolution of the flesh. II, 349. So that we may live the evangelical life. II, 352. Mortification, fasts, and almsgiving greatly aid prayer. II, 504, 507. We must die so that we may live. V, 924. What it means to die to the age. III, 1808. He whose spirit does not die to this age does not rise to life but to punishments. III, 25. Unless by the mortification of our members we imitate Christ’s death on the cross, we do not attain his resurrection from the dead in glory. From Paulinus. II, 350. Love causes a certain death in us. IV, 1628. Various kinds of mortification. X, 849.

The souls of the dead are held in hidden receptacles, each according as it is worthy either of rest or of affliction. VI, 158, 283. The dead are not judged according to the deeds they would have done if they had lived. X, 1005, 1006. The souls of the devout dead are not separated from the Church. VIII, 558. We do not lose those who depart from this life, but send them ahead to life, and so forth. II, 318. The dead, whether good or bad, sleep. III, 1751. Scripture’s most truthful usage calls the dead “those who sleep.” V, 576, 936. So that they may be understood to awaken and rise again. IV, 1112. To the one who can awaken them, the dead are sleepers. V, 592, 593. The Platonic doctrine is that just as the dead always arise from the living, so the living arise from the dead. VII, 510. Why death is not burdensome to the deceased saints. VII, 393. For the just living in rest, it would be better to live with their own bodies in good health. VII, 392. From what perspective one may mourn the dead, and what ought to console this mourning. V, 936, 937, 939. Let those who mourn be consoled by the services of their brothers and sisters. V, 937. Mortal grief over beloved dead persons is not to be reproved, but enduring grief ought not belong to the faithful. II, 1083. Augustine consoles a sister afflicted by the death of her brother. II, 1082.

The memory of the dead. IX, 576. The memory of the devout dead in communion in Christ’s body. VII, 674. The Aerianists say that offerings ought not to be made for the dead. VIII, 39. The Heracleonites are said to redeem their dead, as it were, through oil, balm, water, invocations, and so forth. VIII, 28. The place of burial does not by itself benefit the dead; and the extent to which it benefits them. [Col. 0451] VI, 596, 610. When Christian people lack burial, this takes nothing away from them. VI, 594, 596, 600. The dead receive no help from the pomp of the funeral or the ornamentation of the tomb. IV, 552, 560. The solemn services for the dead: sacrifices of the altar, prayers, and almsgiving on their behalf. VI, 609. The whole Church is accustomed to pray for the departed. VI, 592. Even in the general commemoration for all the departed in Christian and catholic fellowship. VI, 596. In the priest’s prayers, which are poured out before God at his altar. VI, 593. Whether the offering made on behalf of the dead benefits them. VI, 157. Paulinus’s difficulty: how these prayers can benefit them. VI, 593. According to the kind of life they led, the dead are benefited or not benefited by whatever is devoutly done for them. VI, 157, 158. The place of burial, the pomp of the funeral, and so forth, are more consolations for the living than aids for the dead. VI, 594, 596. Why care for the funeral and burial is praiseworthy. VI, 595. A mother wishes the corpse of her dead son to be placed in the basilica of the blessed confessor Felix, and obtains her wish. VI, 591, 592. Paulinus judges that the feelings of the faithful who take such care for their relatives’ bodies are not empty impulses. VI, 592. The custom of the Egyptians concerning the dead. V, 1605. See Deceased. Whether, to what extent, or how the spirits of the dead know what is happening around us is a difficult question. IV, 1437. The dead do not take part in the affairs of the living. VI, 604. The dead can learn what is happening here either from those who go from here to them, from Angels, or through God’s revelation. VI, 605. They themselves can also be sent to the living. VI, 606. Visits of the dead that foretold events subsequently confirmed by what happened. II, 697, 698. Evodius asks whether a soul departing from the body takes the warm element with it. II, 697. Several dead persons were seen entering houses just as they had been accustomed to do. II, 697. Many testify that during the night there are disturbances and prayers in the places where bodies have been buried, especially in basilicas. II, 697. A holy presbyter was a witness of such a vision. II, 696. From the Gospel it is understood that the dead have some concern for us. IV, 1437. A deceased wife is represented as concerned for her husband. II, 1075.

Two kinds of dead. V, 591. All the wicked are customarily called “dead” in a mystical sense. IX, 262. All unbelievers and all wicked people are dead. IV, 893. One who lives luxuriously is more dead than one who ends his luxury by dying. IV, 409. The raising of the dead and the justification of sinners are God’s greatest praise. IV, 885. The three dead whom the Lord raised signify three kinds of sinners. III, 1747; V, 592, 720. The dead of the age—who they are. IV, 1850. “Let the dead bury their dead.” V, 603. What dead works are. VI, 208.

“Sin was dead” means that it did not appear. III, 2070.

Numerous motions—rational and irrational, counted and numbered, compounded and proportioned. I, 1092. Motion occurs in six parts. VI, 19. Motion through places implies motion through times, but not conversely. III, 388. Things that move more quickly move more ardently. III, 267. The interior parts of a round mass move more slowly, the exterior parts more quickly. III, 266. In the motions of bodies it is wholly impossible for anything identical to be produced by two agents. II, 79. Every motion of the soul does something in the body. II, 72. The soul’s perverse motions must be restrained by continence, by denying consent and rejecting even the pleasure of thought. VI, 369. The disobedient motions of the members are the evil of original sin. X, 142. See Concupiscence; Members.

When Moses was born. VII, 565. Moses was older than all Greek poets and philosophers. VII, 596, 599. Whether Moses’s deed in the killing of the Egyptian is to be justified. III, 597. Moses was summoned on Mount Sinai by an Angel with divine words. VIII, 444. The Angel wished to kill Moses’ infant son because he was not circumcised. II, 96. God himself appeared to Moses, but while hidden. V, 161. How he appeared. V, 59, 63. Moses spoke with God mouth to mouth. VI, 662, 663. God spoke to him through an assumed creature, not through his own substance. IV, 1788. Some held that it was Christ who spoke to Moses. V, 63. Others held that an Angel appeared to Moses. V, 64. The Angel who bore the Lord’s type spoke with Moses. III, 1403. Moses saw the Lord’s brightness. II, 610, 611. How Moses saw God. VI, 662. He desired to see God in the substance in which God exists. III, 477. Moses did not see God through his own substance. VIII, 811, 812. And as he truly is. III, 1779. The promise made to Moses concerning the vision of God was a prophecy about Christ. III, 648. Moses saw God’s “hind parts” by prophesying Christ. VI, 663. Moses’ face was radiant. V, 474. Moses prophesied Christ. VII, 568.

The signs given to Moses when he was sent to free the Israelites are explained allegorically. V, 61. The Egyptian magicians were overcome by Moses. II, 521. When Moses led the people out of Egypt. VII, 568. The song of Moses. V, 1638. God gave Moses the tablets of the Law. V, 81. Although God spoke with him, Moses nevertheless received advice about governing the people from his father-in-law. III, 18. Moses’ humility is praised in this. III, 619. God wished Moses to be admonished by a foreigner, where pride could tempt him. III, 619. Moses stood between God and Aaron. III, 599. In Moses there was leadership; in Aaron, ministry. III, 619. Not only the offices but also the deaths of Moses and Aaron were signs of things to come. III, 743. Moses should not be criticized for having waged wars. VIII, 450. Moses’ hands against Amalek, now raised and now lowered. V, 1556. Whether Moses distrusted God’s ability to provide meat in the desert. III, 726. What Moses’ various deeds signified. VIII, 461. Moses striking the rock with his staff as a figure of the Jewish people placed under the Law. VIII, 326. Moses’ doubt was figurative. V, 1553. With what punishment it was avenged. IV, 1267, 1414. Moses raged against the idolatrous Jews with no cruelty but with great love. VIII, 452. Moses’ perfect hatred. IV, 1802. Moses hated the iniquity he punished in such a way that he loved the humanity for which he prayed. IV, 1802. In the silence of his voice, Moses cried out in his heart. III, 614. How confidently Moses said, “Blot me out of the book of life.” V, 553. It is not to be believed that Moses was alienated from the eternal fellowship of the Saints because of his sin. VIII, 325. At what age Moses died. VIII, 568. What Moses’ death on the mountain signifies. V, 1554; VIII, 326.

Moses was a priest. III, 684; IV, 1265. Whether he was the high priest. III, 684. When Scripture clearly says that Moses first offered sacrifice. III, 633. Why Moses could not enter the tabernacle when the cloud descended, but did enter the cloud where God was. III, 656.

Moses was the most faithful steward of the prophetic mystery. VIII, 331. Minister of the Law. V, 689. Minister of the Old Covenant and prophet of the new. IV, 1141. In understanding, Moses belonged to the New Covenant. IV, 1802. The five books of Moses. V, 198, 199, 687. They were signified by the five porticoes of the pool of Bethesda. IV, 889, 1329. By the five stones David took against Goliath. IV, 1857. By the five barley loaves. III, 666. Moses represented the Jewish people. IV, 1789. Moses is a figure of Christ. III, 1723. He represented Christ. V, 758, 1635. From Moses the anointing began from which the name “Christ” became known. VIII, 331. Everything Moses wrote concerns Christ. VIII, 320, 321, 323, 330, 332. And this must be believed as a matter of faith. VIII, 334. His particular testimonies concerning Christ. VIII, 329. For one who believes Moses, it does not follow that he also believes Christ. VIII, 334. The teaching of Moses and Christ was not different, but the time was different. VIII, 334. Moses sometimes signifies those who become participants in God’s innermost truth, and sometimes those who do not understand God’s grace. III, 656. The praise of Moses. VIII, 443, 444. Faustus’s insults against Moses are refuted. VIII, 427.

Moses’ seat prefigured Christ’s seat. IX, 305. Moses’ radiant face bore the figure of truth. V, 474. Through the punishment of his doubt, Moses represented those who wished to be under the Law and did not wish to be under grace. IV, 1267. Moses himself, terrified and fleeing from the serpent, prefigured the Apostles fleeing after Christ’s death. IV, 933. All the saints are to be understood in Moses. IV, 1329.

By a peculiarity of the Hebrew language, “woman” (*mulier*) denotes every female, whether untouched by a man or already joined to one. II, 540; III, 492, 493, 744, 1111; V, 1000, 1318. The Apostle’s passage saying that Christ was born of a woman. V, 358. The formation of woman was accomplished by no one other than God. III, 403, 404. Why woman was formed from man. VII, 372, 376. Woman was made as a helper for the sake of offspring. III, 395, 396, 397. Even if the necessity of dying had not arisen from sin. III, 398. Woman was made so that the man would rule over her. III, 450. Through the woman’s turning toward the man, the servitude of condition rather than of love is signified. III, 450. Whether the woman’s mind did not bear the image of God. III, 452. Woman was tempted before man because she was weaker. VII, 419. If the woman alone had sinned, she alone would have been punished with death. VIII, 12. Before sin, woman could have conceived while preserving the integrity of the virginal womb. VII, 434. The punishment inflicted on woman must be understood figuratively and prophetically. III, 450. The formation of woman is mystically called a building. III, 402, 403. The formation of woman, in the manner in which it is narrated, occurred so that something might be foretold. III, 402. The formation of woman mystically signified the formation of the Church. III, 407, 408. Whether a woman’s chastity is violated when, at her husband’s command, she gives herself to another’s lust in exchange for her husband’s life may be debated with particular scrupulousness. VIII, 424. Hippocrates frees a woman from punishment on suspicion of adultery. III, 572. The command not to approach a woman during her menstrual blood is not to be taken figuratively. X, 199. To approach her at that time is a sin. III, 706. Women deceive men through simulated whiteness and redness and applied cosmetics. VI, 446. The sight of women is to be avoided. IV, 586. Although the woman is far away, lust is near. IV, 587. Greater vigilance is applied to a woman because her weakness is greater. V, 84. Women who come to church in proud attire are reproved. V, 205. But modestly and with consideration for their modesty. V, 205. The two women litigating before Solomon over a son. V, 92. The woman bent over in illness for eighteen years. V, 639, 1709. The woman touching Christ’s fringe while the crowd pressed around him. V, 416. The adulterous woman. V, 108, 1380. The absolution of the woman caught in adultery. IV, 589. The sinful woman reclining at the Lord’s feet. V, 595. The woman anointing Christ, a type of the Church. [Col. 0453] IV, 171. The woman who had lost a drachma. I, 791. Faithful women accompanied the Apostles so that they could provide them with necessities. VI, 552. As Christ also did. VI, 552. Solomon’s riddle about a woman sitting on a seat at the doors. I, 688. The Athenian woman accustomed to poisons. I, 1350. Woman signifies concupiscence; man signifies the mind. VI, 580. The Pepuzians grant women such honor that they are honored among them with the priesthood. VIII, 30. After a woman has given birth, three gods were appointed as guardians. VII, 187. Those who display themselves in women’s clothing are rightly considered infamous and legally incapable of making a will. I, 899.

Womanizing. VI, 391.

Augustine judged that the pagan Calamens ought to be punished with many pecuniary penalties. II, 390.

What loquacity is. I, 583. How it differs from eloquence. IX, 447.

Various kinds of multiplication. IV, 1778. Blessing is usually and properly understood especially in multiplication. IV, 811. What it means to be multiplied in the soul. IV, 1778. The multiplication of children comes from the Lord’s blessing. IV, 1778. A certain blameworthy multiplication by which people multiply through desire for temporal things. IV, 82, 139. A certain multiplication not of abundance but of poverty. IV, 1778.

When and how the multitude should be rebuked. IX, 95. How the sins of the multitude are punished. IX, 91. One person must be treated differently from a multitude. IX, 674. Whatever crime and iniquity intoxicates the multitude causes it to lose the truth of judgment. IX, 89.

Many who are said to belong either to Adam or to Christ are themselves “all.” X, 871. Whom the Apostle calls “many” when he says, “Many were made sinners.” X, 871.

Munatius Felix, perpetual *flamen*, curator of the colony of Cirta. IX, 513, 583. Proceedings conducted before Munatius Felix. II, 265.

Everything God created is clean; and certain animals are called unclean only because of their symbolism. IV, 1833, 1834. How all things are clean to the clean, but nothing is clean to the unclean. IV, 1661.

To cleanse and to heal have the same force in spiritual matters. IX, 74. Faith in God cleanses the heart; the clean heart sees God. V, 368. Cleansing can be attained in this life, but it will not be perfect until after the resurrection. X, 691.

External purity without interior purity is nothing. IV, 1660. Interior purity necessarily brings external purity. IV, 1660. Purity of heart alone is the reason we shall see God. II, 609.

A certain heresy admits innumerable worlds. VIII, 45. Anaximander admitted them. VII, 226. Epicurus dreamed that they are generated and dissolved by the accidental motions of atoms. VII, 320. The philosophers held various and conflicting opinions concerning the unity, beginning, end, and governance of the world. VII, 601. Plato admitted two worlds: one intelligible, the other sensible. I, 588, 954. What he understood by the name of each. I, 588, 954. Plato and other philosophers perceived that this world is an animal. I, 602. Philosophers call the world a great animal without bodily senses, whose soul is Jupiter or Hecate. V, 1137. The Platonists teach that the world is the greatest animal. VII, 388, 390. A most blessed and everlasting animal. VII, 308. The structure of the world’s body. VII, 212. Some thought that the world was God’s body. VII, 123. According to the pagans, the body of the world is not God, but its soul is. VII, 202. The soul of the world and its parts were considered true gods. VII, 211. Varro held this view as well. VII, 198, 199, 202. It is refuted. VII, 202. Varro believed that the individual parts of the world have different souls, yet divine ones. VII, 199. The soul of the world enclosed in all corporeal elements. VII, 390. Whether the world has a soul is a great and hidden question. III, 1058. Some pagans regard the whole world as the greatest of the gods. VIII, 370. Varro judged that the world is God. VII, 199. Plato did so as well. VII, 390.

The world is imagined to be eternal. V, 1137. The created world is not from eternity. VII, 319. The Platonists thought that the world was both made and yet eternal. VII, 311, 319, 320, 359. Some believe that Plato thought contrary to what he says. VII, 359. The Platonists’ arguments are refuted. VII, 320, 321. Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Simon Magus, Menander, and Saturninus asserted that the world was not made by God. VIII, 26. The Nicolaitans did likewise. VIII, 26. Priscillian’s error concerning the prince of this world. VIII, 666, 667, 668, 671. The Priscillianists wish the world to have been made by an evil prince. VIII, 44. How and from what the world was fashioned according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 113, 375. A battle was fought before the constitution of the world. VIII, 182. The Manichaean attributes the structure of the world to the good God the craftsman, but the animals, everything that grows from the earth, and humanity itself to the race of darkness. X, 1325. The Seleucians wish the matter of the elements from which the world was made to have been made not by God but to be coeternal with God. VIII, 41.

The world was created by God. VII, 318. Why the world is not as old as God. VIII, 605, 609. From what beginning the world was made or could have been made. VIII, 605. The Priscillianists thought that the world was made last so that souls that had sinned previously might be purified. VIII, 668. They are refuted. VII, 674, 675. Three things must be investigated in the creation of the world. VIII, 334, 337. How the world was made from nothing if it was made from unformed matter. VI, 181, 182. The world was made from unformed matter, but that matter was created simultaneously with the world. VIII, 610. The world is pregnant with the causes of things that are born. VIII, 877. When the world was created, it possessed, as it were, the seed of everything that now comes into being. III, 338. The world is like a great tree of things. III, 1305. Whether the creation of the world is to be understood as having been accomplished through the Son of God in both Testaments. VIII, 129. How the world was created in six days. III, 326. See Day; Creation.

Why God wished to make the world. VI, 18. There is no other reason for creating the world except that good things might be made by the good God. VII, 334. Plato recognized this. VII, 334, 336. Origen recognized this. VII, 336. The Manichaeans did not think so. VII, 337. The pagans concede that the world is administered by God’s providence from the highest to the lowest. VIII, 410. The lowest part of the world is subject to the transgressing Angels. III, 52. The Gentiles believed that the world was made by God but administered by gods whom God had made. VII, 318. Why the world is so large, when it could have been larger or smaller; why it is in this place rather than that one, Augustine does not know. II, 65. In the course of debate we say that there are three worlds, one above another. II, 69.

Mundus

The magnitude of the world commends the magnitude of God. IV, 1887, 1892. Varro considers nothing to be more excellent than the world. VII, 182. The world itself silently proclaims both that it was made and that it could have been made only by God. VII, 319. The world is a greater and more excellent miracle than all the miracles it contains. VII, 291, 718, 724. The beauty of the world consists in the kinds of immortal and mortal animals. VII, 376. The beauty of the world is blameless in these three respects: through the condemnation of sinners, the testing of the righteous, and the perfection of the blessed. III, 141. The beauty of the age is like a great song of some composer, leading toward the eternal contemplation of the beauty of God. II, 527. The world is beautiful and ugly. V, 498. Should the things that displease us in the world therefore be condemned because they do not suit us? VII, 335. Why certain things in the world displease us. VII, 335. Even things that are ugly in themselves contribute to the beauty of the world. III, 156. The beauty of the world confesses the beauty of its Creator. V, 1134. The beauty of the world should be contemplated so that its Maker may be loved. IV, 1887, 1892; V, 438. Why we are warned to turn away from this world and turn toward God. VI, 13. The creatures of the world were made as a spectacle, through which the goodness and gracious gift of the Creator are perceived. IV, 1851. Contemplation of the world leads to immortal things. II, 145.

Some think that this world is not eternal, but comes into being and perishes innumerable times; others admit innumerable worlds. VII, 359, 360. Some have maintained that after the revolutions of the ages everything will return to the same order and the same appearance. VII, 361. Plato maintained this. VII, 361. Origen likewise. VII, 361. Certain heretics said that after the resurrection the world would remain in the condition in which it now is and would not be changed in any way. VIII, 42. The opinion of those who wish everything in the world to return to the same order and appearance after the revolutions of the ages must be rejected. VII, 362. Cicero agrees with the Platonists that the world will not perish. VII, 759. Porphyry charged the Christians with folly because they said that the world would perish. VII, 696. The end of the world. VI, 667. In what sense Scripture says that the world will perish. VII, 697. How the world will perish. VII, 683. The world will pass away not by complete destruction, but by a change in things. VII, 679. The world’s alteration concerns qualities alone. VII, 682.

The division of the world into four parts. VII, 199. Into seven ages. VII, 804. Six ages of the world are counted. IV, 1182; V, 691, 1197. Each consists of a thousand years. VIII, 892. The age of the world beginning from the creation of man. V, 1518. The apostle John is found to have died long before 5,500 years had been completed from the beginning of the human race. II, 911.

The Donatists wished “world” always to be understood in an evil sense. IX, 658. Scripture sometimes uses the name “world” in a good sense. IX, 632. “World” is used both in a good and in an evil sense. IX, 658. “World” is said of human beings both in an evil and in a good sense. III, 1773; X, 1383. In Scripture “world” is used in two ways. X, 1347. The world is twofold: good and evil, redeemed and condemned, hostile and reconciled. III, 1853, 1920, 1921, 1929; V, 500, 588, 678, 1088, 1502. Christ prayed for this world, not for the other. III, 1920, 1921. What John indicates by the name “world.” X, 1349. Which world is said to lie in the power of the evil one? X, 822. Which is that world of which Christ was not a part, and from which he chose the Apostles? X, 823. “World” is said of human beings not according to God. X, 1348. By the name “world” the inhabitants of the world are understood. X, 370. Lovers of the world. IV, 249, 1766, 1841. Lovers of the world, or the ungodly, or the carnal. IV, 630; VIII, [Col. 0455] 508. Sinners. IV, 975; V, 928. The unrighteous. IV, 1854. Why the unrighteous are called “world.” V, 790. The devil is one with all the ungodly, as with a kind of body of his own. V, 790. The righteous are not called “world,” because although they dwell in it in the flesh, they are with God in heart. IV, 1842. Those who love the world are called “world,” because they inhabit it by loving it. IV, 1842. The devil, as prince and head, rules the world—that is, the children of unbelief. V, 790, 1088, 1090. One is the world God made, another the world the devil rules. IV, 1841. The faithful world: all believers. III, 1921. The condemned world rightly did not know Christ; the reconciled world, however, knew him not by merit but by grace. III, 1929. The world conquered for us through Christ. V, 590. He conquered the world not by fighting but by suffering. III, 1941. The good world made from the evil. V, 587. The conversion of the world is a great miracle. VII, 756. That the world believes in Christ was the work of divine power, not of human persuasion. VII, 759. Christ freed the world from the world. III, 1925. By generation we are of the world; by regeneration we are freed from the world. III, 1910, 1915.

The world rules through unlawful pleasures, pageantry, and curiosity. VI, 294. This world is a slave. VI, 294; V, 1357. A Christian ought to use the world, not serve the world. IV, 1235. The good use the world in order to enjoy God; the wicked do the opposite. VII, 444. The will of the unrighteous belongs to the world. VI, 620. What it means to be of the world. III, 1677. Christ was never of the world, because he was born of the Holy Spirit. III, 1915. That someone is not of the world is due to grace, not to nature. VI, 620. To die to the world so that one may live for God is a sacrifice. VII, 283. It is one thing to send fire into the world, another to send the world into fire. IV, 715. The world is full of pressures. IV, 1189. A winepress overflowing with pressures. V, 137. The pressures of the aging and failing world. V, 504. The world is now so crushed that it has even lost the appearance of seduction. II, 483. The ruin of the world does not warn us to migrate elsewhere. V, 241, 405. As much as those who did not deign to flourish with the flourishing world deserve praise, so much do those deserve reproof who delight in perishing with the perishing world. II, 483. How would you gather the flowers of the world if you do not withdraw your hand from the thorns? V, 241.

The world persecutes the world. V, 587. The world is a great sea in which smaller fish are devoured by larger ones. IV, 422. The world wants to swallow you; you swallow the world. IV, 341. By its wickedness the world can rage, but not beyond the limit set by the Creator. IV, 1127. Let the world rage: it does not break us, because we belong to Christ; let the world flatter: it does not seduce us, because we belong to Christ. V, 728. The world’s opposition. V, 1531. The world flatters in order to deceive, or terrifies in order to break. V, 1256. As the end of the world approaches, errors increase. III, 1598. To what extent the world’s loves, terrors, and errors are conquered. X, 937. The evils of the world should be regarded as bearable in hope of the future. II, 508. What answer should be made to the promises of the world? V, 1291. Not to believe in the world’s happiness is self-restraint; not to yield to the world’s unhappiness is endurance. V, 235. One should labor to prevent the world from capturing one, rather than fear that it may fall. V, 590. Whoever cannot overcome the flattering world cannot overcome the raging world. V, 1470. This world is more dangerous when flattering than when troublesome, where piety and charity are lacking. II, 593, 1026. Whatever in temporal matters the world smiles upon in us is more a danger than an adornment. V, 1564. The happiness of worldly people is a dream, in which everything is, as it were, [incomplete]. IV, 559. One trusts the deceptive world, not God. V, 859. There is nothing in the world for which God should not be preferred to it. V, 586. The sweetness of God is set against the sweetness of the world. V, 866. To those who do not use, or use rightly, the evils of this age—whether pleasant or fierce and harsh—God has promised a future age in which they will suffer no evils. X, 1178. How the world loves itself. III, 1853. How we ought to love it. III, 1853. How the world loves and hates what belongs to it. III, 1855.

The lovers of the world follow what is fleeing. VI, 661. They love what is bitter. VI, 661. You wish to hold the perishing world impurely; what would you do if it remained? V, 622. Whether the world is happy or overturned, God must always be blessed. V, 622. The bonds of the world have real harshness and false pleasure; certain pain and uncertain enjoyment, etc. II, 104. Nothing is more burdensome to the friends of this world than not to labor. III, 151. The world is loved although ugly and bitter; what if it were beautiful and sweet? V, 241. For healing the minds of lovers of this age, whether in prosperity or adversity, wisdom can scarcely be found suitable. II, 938. Some lend the ears of their hearts to it: more rarely amid prosperity, more frequently amid adversity. II, 938. God mingles such great consolations with sufferings and acts wonderfully so that we may not love the world and may not fail in the world. II, 352. By love of the world the soul fails in proportion as what it loves is less than God. V, 779. Love of the world adulterates the soul. V, 779. For those who love the world, the Sacraments remain in them for condemnation, not as supports for salvation. III, 1994. This world is dear to human beings, and they have become cheap in their own eyes. II, 160.

[Col. 0456] Contempt for the world. V, 622, 1517. This entire world—that is, all sensible things—is to be despised; they are nevertheless to be used for the necessities of life. I, 1327. How the world becomes contemptible, whether by promising or by threatening. III, 2004. For those called by Christ, the pleasure of visible things diminishes. VI, 55. Whoever abandons the whole world abandons both what he has and what he hopes to have. II, 692. He despises everything who despises not only as much as he could have, but also as much as he wished to have. II, 124, etc. All the baptized, not yet enjoying the promised homeland, are in the world as in a desert. VIII, 270. Abstaining from love of this age benefits no one except the faithful. I, 857.

The various meanings of “world.” III, 1393, 1398, 1828, 1838, 1875, 1912, 1995, 2007, 2017. In Scripture the world is called a field. III, 198. This world is the Lord’s field. IV, 1950. By Christ the world is called a dog and a lion. II, 556. The world is a dog barking from habit, not reason, against unfamiliar truth. II, 556. In certain passages Scripture calls this world the city of circumstance. IV, 703, 711. The world is compared with the desert in which the Israelites wandered. III, 1627, 2029. For a Christian this world is a desert. V, 37. This world is like a furnace for potters. V, 420, 1383. The upper hell. IV, 1093. An overflowing and abundant but bitter sea. IV, 1223, 1852. It is compared with a millstone. IV, 1730, 1731. And with a mill. IV, 356. The world is a scorpion. V, 621. “World” used for the Church. IX, 658.

Munera

The gifts of God are of two kinds. IV, 345, 346. God seeks you more than your gift. V, 252, 508. “But I am evil,” you will say, “and perhaps he will not accept me.” By giving yourself to him, you will become good. V, 707. Only the humble offer gifts to God. IV, 969. The gifts God now desires are alms. IV, 511. If God forbids people to accept gifts from their own, why does he himself accept them? VIII, 662. What it means to accept gifts when this is counted as a fault. IV, 195. He accepts a gift who judges wrongly for the sake of praise. IV, 195.

Munus

A gift as a spectacle. V, 333. The day of the games. V, 132, 333. Organizers of games or spectacles. IV, 1918, 1919.

Municipal records. II, 413, 415. To be questioned in municipal records or proceedings. II, 429, 430, 431.

Murcida

The goddess Murcida makes a person excessively inactive. VII, 125.

Murcidus

“Murcidus,” that is, sluggish and inactive. VII, 125.

Muressis

A friend of Optatus. II, 857.

Murmur

Murmuring is a great sin. III, 1612.

Those who murmur are described. IV, 1736. Those who murmur against God’s scourge are rebuked by the example of Daniel, who confessed his sins. VI, 716, 717. Those who murmur against the times are restrained. V, 621, 1416. In tribulations one must not murmur against God. II, 330, 426. Those who murmur against God because of the prosperity of the wicked. V, 126. See Felicitas. People murmur against God because the wicked fare well in this life while the good suffer. IV, 543. The godly should not murmur if they see the ungodly tolerated by God. IV, 1196. Or if they see them abound in earthly possessions. IV, 918, 919, 922, 923, 930, 951. Your murmuring does not aim to prevent you from serving, but to make you serve as a bad servant. IV, 1275. You would not now be the one who murmured if the person who first murmured about you were heard against you. IV, 1196. Let us diminish sins and murmuring. V, 1358. By murmuring against God you are a blasphemer. IV, 1196.

Muses

The origin of the fable of the Muses. III, 49. Varro shows that the Muses are daughters of Jupiter and Memory. III, 49. The poet Hesiod gave the Muses their name. III, 49.

Musaeus

The theological poet Musaeus. VII, 572, 597.

Flies

The generation of flies. VII, 475. Someone said that flies were not from God; consequently, he was compelled also to say that human beings were not from God. III, 1386. Fireflies. VIII, 363.

Muscarium

A fly-whisk. V, 293.

Muscipula

The devil’s snare contains terror and error. IV, 235, 236. Everyone who does not hope in God falls into it. IV, 235.

Music

Music is the science of modulating well. I, 1083; II, 726. The invention of music. I, 1014. Consonance implanted in us by nature. VIII, 889. The power of reason in perceiving what pertains to music, where nothing except equality gives pleasure. I, 1177. What “raising” and “placing” mean in music. I, 1110. Lovers of pleasurable music. III, 98. Music can be practiced wisely by the wise. III, 98. David loved pious music. II, 369. Augustine wrote a short work on this subject, and what is thought of it. II, 368, 369. Music was granted to human beings to indicate the harmony of divine governance. II, 726. Music suggests the unity of a well-ordered city. VII, 547. Augustine ennobled poetry through his books on music. I, 1081; II, 513, note. Augustine’s purpose in publishing these books. I, 1163, 1165.

Mosaic painting. VII, 485.

Musta or Mustita. IX, 507, 528, 550.

The diocese of Musti. IX, 618. The city of Musti. IX, 253. The people of Musti. IX, 108, 180.

Mustum

Certain remarkable things about must. I, 1364.

[Col. 0457] Mutability is not improperly called mortality. VIII, 855. Everything is subject to mutability: the body, heavenly bodies, animals, and so forth. IV, 1623. Everything touched by bodily sense cannot remain in the same condition even for a moment of time. II, 63. Heaven and earth proclaim that they were made because they change. I, 811. The soul is mutable temporally, not locally; the body in both ways. III, 137. Everything that has been made is mutable; God alone, and that which he has begotten, cannot be changed. VIII, 551. Natural and human things can be changed according to the suitability of the times, while the principle according to which they are changed remains unchanged. II, 526. Change is blameless, indeed good. IV, 714.

Mutigena. IX, 755.

Mucius Scaevola extended his right hand into the flames. VII, 127, 163. Mucius Scaevola, a pontiff, was killed at the altar of Vesta. VII, 108, 109, 110.

Everyone who receives borrows, even if he himself will not be the one to repay. III, 1264. See Mutuum.

Mutugenna

Donatus, presbyter of the estate of Mutugenna. II, 753, 756. A deacon of Mutugenna who was rebaptized. II, 95.

Mutunus

The god Mutunus, the same as Priapus among the Greeks. VII, 122.

A mute and deaf man at Milan, understanding others only through bodily movement and himself indicating what he wished in no other way. I, 1052.

A loan must be given without interest, and debtors must not be pressed excessively. V, 1128.

Muzula. IX, 221.

Myrmecoleon. III, 828.

Myro

An artisan in casting images. I, 893.

The obscurity of the mysteries is useful; without it they would not be sought diligently, nor would truth be found with delight. III, 136.

The mysteries are sweeter the more obscure they are. IV, 1803. How the mysteries should be investigated. III, 426.

Sacred mysteries. VI, 443. In them we are commanded to have our hearts raised upward, to give thanks, and so forth. VI, 443. See Sacramenta.

“Mythicon” is called “fabulous” in Latin. VII, 181.

N

Nebuchadnezzar found mercy. V, 1381. It was granted to him to believe in God and escape the eternal punishments of Gehenna. V, 1507. The laws of King Nebuchadnezzar. II, 796, 806. Before and after his conversion. II, 398. Nebuchadnezzar symbolized two periods: one in which kings compelled people to worship the idol, another in which laws were enacted on account of God. II, 325. The edict of King Nebuchadnezzar was read in the Gothic office of Holy Saturday. II, 398.

Why Nahor is not mentioned in Terah’s departure from the region of the Chaldeans to Mesopotamia. VII, 493.

Naenia, a goddess. VII, 189.

Naevius, a poet approximately contemporary with Plautus. VII, 54. Note (e), 57.

Naevius, a man of remarkable height. II, 80.

“Naid” is interpreted as “agitation.” VIII, 261.

Namphanius. II, 82. It signifies “a man of good foot.” II, 83. This name suits Hercules in Virgil. II, 84, 85.

To what extent narration varies without lying. III, 1090.

Birth

How visible things are born. VIII, 876. A human being is said to be born in two ways: in the womb and from the womb. IV, 678. A child still in the womb cannot be called born. II, 844. To be born here in a mortal body is to begin to fall ill. IV, 1320. A newborn child cries because it is entering this life. IV, 1664. Children are born in this age so that they may displace their parents. IV, 756, 794. Everyone born from Adam is born condemned from one who was condemned. IV, 1735. No one is born without drawing punishment, drawing the merit of punishment. IV, 591, 734. No one is born from the Spirit unless he has been humble. III, 1487. No one is born of water and the Spirit unless he is willing. III, 1998.

Natalicus, bishop of Thelensis. IV, 380.

The Matins of the Lord’s Nativity. V, 333. The day of the Lord’s Nativity returns on the same date because it is not celebrated as a sacrament, but only as a recalling of the fact that he was born. II, 205. The Church celebrates only the nativity days of Christ and John. V, 1301, 1319. Augustine celebrates his own birthday. I, 588, 962. The Church calls precious deaths “nativity days.” V, 1412. The nativity of a city. IV, 437.

Natalis of Oea. IX, 239.

The birth anniversaries of the saints should be celebrated with sobriety. IV, 1141.

Potential births created. III, 326.

There are two Nathans. I, 627, 637. Nathan, son of David. VIII, 215. He is confused with the prophet through whom David was rebuked. V, 352.

Nathanael was not among the number of the Apostles. III, 1445. Nathanael was not chosen among the disciples because he was learned in the Law. IV, 788. Nathanael recognized divinity in Christ. [Col. 0458] V, 681. How he recognized it. V, 557. Nathanael under the fig tree: the human race under sin. V, 680.

Our birth is twofold. III, 1478, 2011; V, 679, 1669.

Nature is nothing other than that which is understood to be something in its own genus. I, 1346. The ancients used “nature” for essence and substance. I, 1346. Philosophers divided the whole of what pertains to nature into bodies, the void, and the properties that belong to these. II, 447. The natures themselves are called substances. V, 844. Everything that is nature, insofar as it is nature, is compelled to exist. IV, 109. No nature or substance is contrary to truth. IV, 85. Nature is threefold: nature mutable in place and time; nature mutable in time alone; and nature mutable neither in place nor in time. II, 85. The nature of God cannot fail. VII, 355.

There is no nature that is not either God himself or made by him. X, 966. God is the author of all natures. III, 276, 389; V, 1066, 1344; VII, 331, 374, 719; VIII, 199, 556. Not the devil. X, 1383. No nature can have a creator except one who creates good things. X, 1536. The small works of nature are more astonishing than the immense ones. VII, 791. Nature produces nothing randomly. I, 983. The course of nature has its natural laws. III, 406. Beyond the natural course of things, the Creator can make from all these things something other than what their so-called seminal principles contain. III, 406. Things that occur beyond the course of nature do not occur against nature. III, 349. What is considered to be against nature. VIII, 480. It is not against nature when God works in any nature whatsoever. VII, 720, 721. It is not impossible for God to change natures. VII, 722. Things belonging to nature usually displease us because they are harmful. VII, 352. What the first or primordial natures are. VII, 622, 628. The first natures are to be desired for their own sake. VII, 626. Some things are congenital and begin to appear at the age when the use of reason begins. X, 1427. The Romans thought that the natures of things, established under the rule of the true God, should receive religious worship. VII, 136. Our usefulness, not an equitable principle, is what we use to judge a nature. VII, 352. Obscure matters concerning natural things should be treated by inquiry, not by assertion. III, 220. The seeds of all natures are God’s works. X, 1441. In every form and mode of nature the Creator is worthy of praise. VII, 353.

All natures were created good, although unequal to the Creator, because they were created from nothing. X, 966. Nature, insofar as it is created by God, is always good. X, 1312. Every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. I, 1289; VIII, 199, 200, 551, 556; X, 1124. Even that which can be corrupted. VIII, 553. Nature is God’s good work. X, 1489. No natures could in any way be good if they had not been made by God. VII, 353. All natures, made good by God from nothing, are good, but some are better than others. VIII, 191. All natures are good. VII, 352. A nature in which there is no good cannot exist. VII, 641. A nature that cannot be miserable should not for that reason be judged better. VII, 349. Every nature is a great good if it cannot be corrupted, a small good if it can. VI, 237. A nature that cannot be corrupted is the highest good. VIII, 553. A nature of a higher order, even when corrupted, is sometimes better than an inferior nature, even when uncorrupted. VIII, 553. Nor would nature be corruptible unless some good existed. VI, 237, 238. The corruption of nature is its evil. VI, 237. Nature, insofar as it is nature, is good; insofar as it is vicious, it is evil. VI, 238. Every nature was good before it was evil. VII, 331. No nature is evil in itself, but through defect. VII, 351. However greatly any nature may be disfigured by vices, its institution is always good. X, 1409. An evil nature is good insofar as it is nature. X, 1332, 1334.

How created spiritual nature is administered. III, 391.

God alone is superior to rational nature. VIII, 202, 203. Human nature, although mutable, is good insofar as concerns what was created. X, 1117. The nature that was made so that it could avoid sin if it wished is not evil. III, 443. Better is the nature that does not wish to sin at all. III, 443. Manichaeus detestably censures human nature; the Pelagian praises it cruelly. X, 1302, 1305. The five pestilential natures of the earth: a delirium of the Manichaeans. VIII, 184, 194. Manichaeus removed the natures of animals from the workmanship of the true God. X, 1453. The Manichaeans admitted two natures in the human being. VIII, 113. They are refuted. VIII, 115, 116, 120, 122. The twofold nature, namely of good and evil, admitted by some. VIII, 552. Manichaeus posited two natures or substances, namely of good and evil. VIII, 34. Manichaeus posited them wrongly. VIII, 537, 539, 579, 602. The fiction of these two natures is rejected. VIII, 509, 593. The number of natures in the Manichaean phantasm. VIII, 190. How many goods the Manichaeans place in the nature of evil, and how many evils in the nature of good. VIII, 563. The absurd Manichaean opinion concerning different natures. VIII, 396, 400. The Manichaean error concerning human nature—how different it is from Catholic doctrine, and how insane. X, 1311. Nature and vice. V, 132.

[Col. 0459] Nature is not evil. X, 1159. Human nature is not evil, yet something evil is present in it. X, 457. Human nature is indeed a good, but evil is present in it. X, 1304, 1309. Whoever says that nature is not good denies the Creator of the good that was created; but whoever denies that evil is present in it begrudges the corrupted nature its merciful Savior. X, 1334, 1335. The Pelagians deny that human nature was corrupted by the sin of the first man. X, 1424. Rational nature was initially made capable of both good and evil, but afterward, according to merit, it would be capable either of good alone or of evil alone. X, 1492. The nature in which Adam was made blameless must be considered differently from this nature in which we are now born. X, 288. Human nature is not now sound. X, 1107. The misery of the human race itself indicates that human nature has entirely collapsed through Adam’s ruin. X, 1275. Nature was created sound and afterward corrupted by sin. X, 249. Nature, at least in the unbaptized, is corrupted. X, 276. Human nature is now corrupted. X, 450. Corrupted and ruined by sin. X, 256, 257. How nature could have been corrupted by sin, since sin is not a substance. X, 257. The defect of nature comes from original sin. X, 249. Human nature is a great good, but dead through a great evil. X, 1459. Sin cannot exist except in a nature. X, 1410. It is shown that nature could be changed through sin. X, 1572. And that it was in fact changed. X, 1575. The nature of earlier times was no less corrupted by evil customs. X, 402. The state of nature was changed by human sin. X, 1112. The devil is not the author of nature but of guilt. X, 1385. Although God is the author of nature, original evil can nevertheless exist in it. X, 731. The substance of nature is good even in great sinners. X, 729. Human nature is evil, but it is not an evil. X, 1329, 1330, 1337. Whoever says that human nature is an evil is compelled to deny grace—not whoever says that it is evil. X, 1329. If human nature were an evil, it ought not to be saved; if it were not evil, it ought not to be saved. X, 1328, 1329, 1330, 1331. Human nature was made not only without defect, but even when it is made evil through defect, it is capable of the good by which it may become good. X, 1117. Human nature was created not evil; even though an evil will has done evil in it, it cannot return to the good by its own powers. X, 1522.

Nature is neither sound nor sufficient for righteousness by itself. X, 250. Nature is not sound insofar as, through blindness, it does not see what ought to be done, or through weakness does not accomplish it. X, 293. Pelagius defends nature as though it were sound. X, 285. Augustine and the Catholics defend and proclaim created nature; they criticize and condemn sinful nature. X, 1502. Julian tries to excuse nature. X, 1497, 1498, 1500. How Julian understands that nature, when it first did evil, had an evil will not from necessity but from possibility. X, 1499. It is shown against Julian that natures sin whether from possibility or from necessity. X, 1502. Nature corrupted by its own will cannot be healed without God’s grace. X, 297. Whoever defends nature against grace is not acting for God’s cause. X, 266. He acts for God’s cause better who acknowledges grace than he who defends nature. X, 271. The defender of nature, while seeming to protect it as sound, excludes the Savior from the sick. V, 189. Human nature, even if it had remained in the integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. II, 830. Nature does not remain in good condition once it has withdrawn from its maker. III, 432.

Pelagius defended the possibility of nature. II, 768, 770, 785. Whoever asserts that nature can suffice for avoiding sins and fulfilling commandments opposes God’s grace. II, 762. God creates nature; he heals defect. X, 1159, 1167. Corruption of nature through sin, renewal through Christ. X, 173. Coelestius confessed at Carthage that nature needs a Redeemer. X, 706. How human nature is capable of justification. X, 690. The human race falsely complains about its nature. X, 247. Nature should not be thought to be grace—or thought to be so merely because it was granted freely. V, 172, 173, 176. Nature is common to all, not grace. V, 172. There is no one in the human race to whom love is not owed: if not the love of mutual charity, still love for the fellowship of common nature itself. II, 499. In a certain sense nature is the grace of God. II, 767, 768.

Punitive nature: punishment for sin. X, 249. What was punishment for the first man is nature for us. IV, 398. By condemning nature, God neither took away everything he had given nor removed it from his power. VII, 788. The world would be full only of good natures if no one had sinned. VII, 336. Rational nature, even when miserable, is superior to irrational or insensible nature. VII, 349. Whether each person is bound to recognize his own nature, so as to differ from animals. X, 525. We scarcely recognize our own nature. X, 527, 528, and following. “Nature” is said in two ways of the human being. I, 600, 610, 1297. “Nature” for the member through which the nature of animals of the same kind is propagated. X, 1450.

Shipwreck. V, 1517. All lovers of the age have suffered shipwreck, and all came out naked. IV, 1645.

Navigius, Augustine’s brother. I, 962, 980. He took part in the writing of the books at the villa at Cassiciacum. I, 965. Navigius was present at Monnica’s death and funeral. I, 775. The spiritual instruction of Navigius. VI, 680. Navigius was splenetic. I, 968.

The benefits and disadvantages of navigation. IV, 1762.

Ships are endangered both at sea and in harbor. IV, 1277. We are all in one ship: some work, others are carried; nevertheless all are endangered together in the storm and saved together in the harbor. IV, 190, 1425. A ship tossed by a storm. V, 475. Jesus in the ship, faith in the heart. IV, 190, 324. Two ships, two peoples. V, 1173. A ship made immovable by the great efforts of men and oxen was dragged by a single little woman with her belt. VII, 294. Ships called churches. IV, 1380, 1381, 1425.

A sailor who has lost his destination: the more skillfully he steers the ship, the more dangerously he steers it. IV, 259.

When Naum prophesied is not found. VII, 587. What he prophesied. VII, 588.

In the Law, those who temporarily held a vow were called Nazaraeans. III, 822.

Nazaraeans, heretics. VIII, 27. Some called them Symmachians. VIII, 349; IX, 465. The heresy of the Nazaraeans. II, 282. They observed circumcision, the Sabbath, and most of the other precepts of the Law. VIII, 349. They added circumcision to baptism. IX, 465. The heretical Nazarenes still persist. IX, 225.

Nebridius. II, 63, 65, 67, 68, 71, 72, 73. His homeland was near Carthage. I, 728. Very dear to Augustine, a very good and very cautious young man. I, 696. Nebridius had a remarkable soul. I, 737. Through him his entire household became Christian. I, 765. Nebridius came to Milan for no other reason than to live with Augustine in the pursuit of wisdom. I, 728. Nebridius taught under Verecundus, the grammarian at Milan. I, 755. Nebridius tried to dissuade Augustine from consulting astrologers. I, 696. Nebridius was an ardent seeker of the blessed life. I, 728. Nebridius’s argument against the Manichaeans. I, 734. Nebridius, who had at one time gone astray concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, later became Catholic; he served God in perfect chastity among his own people in Africa. I, 765. Nebridius hated a brief answer to a great question. II, 263. Nebridius died not long after Augustine’s baptism; he is believed to live in Abraham’s bosom. I, 765. Letters to Nebridius. I, 765. Augustine’s letters to Nebridius sounded of Christ, Plato, and Plotinus. II, 67. Victor, Nebridius’s brother. II, 73.

The one necessary thing. V, 614, 1188; X, 605. Many things are necessary to a human being here because he is weak. V, 232. God sometimes permits necessities to be lacking to his servants. III, 1296. What the lack of necessities for life produces in the righteous. VII, 28. Whoever wishes sufficiency of necessary things for himself and his own wishes appropriately, and wishes no more. II, 499. Earthly goods should be for the use of necessity, not for the affection of charity. V, 954.

What is understood by the terms “necessary” and “possible.” X, 1499. The distinction between necessary and possible. X, 1481, 1482, and following.

Necessity is twofold. VII, 152. Heavenly necessity according to the astrologers. VII, 142. How we are compelled by necessity neither toward virtue nor toward vice. X, 286. Necessity and will can exist together. X, 1398. Necessity does not consume the will. X, 1398. A certain necessity of the will. X, 1393. The necessity of the good is found together with voluntary virtue. X, 1498. Pressing necessity against one’s will has no place in an act of justice, but sometimes exists in an act of sin. X, 1299. A certain necessity of doing evil. X, 1492, 1500. The punitive necessity of sinning in the devil, who nevertheless is not excused from guilt. X, 1484. Whence the devil’s necessity of sinning arises. X, 1484. The necessity of doing evil in us, which was not present in the human being when he first sinned. X, 1485. The human being was created in such a way that he had no necessity of sinning, and would not sin if he did not wish to sin, since he could always also refuse to wish it. X, 1490. The necessity of vice in the present life. X, 1500. A certain necessity of sinning. X, 286, 296, 1118, 1120. This necessity is the punishment of sin committed without necessity. X, 1118, 1119. Just as in reward there will be the inability to sin, so in punishment there is the inability to act rightly. X, 1518. Some things done by necessity are also to be condemned; they would be no sins if this were not the punishment of the human being but his nature. I, 597, 1296. Necessities: powerful desires. IV, 238. Evil habits. IV, 238. Necessity introduced by habit. I, 753. The Pelagians understand the necessity of habit in the Apostle’s words. X, 1398. The pious and true sense, according to the Catholic teachers, of Paul’s saying about himself, “For I do not do the good that I wish,” etc. X, 1493. The Pelagians say in vain that those words belong not to the Apostle but to a person weighed down by bad habit. X, 1493. The necessity of sin in Adam’s descendants is not healed except by grace. X, 1496. Not every necessity harms freedom. VII, 152. Nor does every necessity conflict with freedom of choice. X, 273. A certain blessed necessity that does not take away freedom. X, 1116. A certain necessity of the will, and a blessed one. X, 1487. If the inability to sin is to be called necessity, that necessity is altogether most blessed. X, 1118. The happy necessity of virtue in the future life. X, 1500. God is not pressed by necessity so that he cannot sin; nor are the blessed pressed by such a necessity, but they enjoy it. X, 1118.

Every necessity must be endured rather than any iniquity perpetrated. IV, 920. The humble are freed from necessities. IV, 238. When God instructs us through necessities, he wants us to love him more. IV, 754. The harsh necessity of dying, and the unwillingness to do what is necessary. IV, 237. Necessity, the mother of all human actions. IV, 1061. The harsh necessity of the present life: not knowing another’s heart, indeed not even one’s own. IV, 237.

Temporal necessities: why they are to be hated. III, 1249. These do not exist in the kingdom of heaven. III, 1249.

Necromancy, a type of divination. VII, 223.

Nectarius the elder. II, 153. Perhaps the same as that Pagan who wrote to Augustine on behalf of his native Calama, and to whom Augustine replied. II, 313, 386.

To deny Christ by one’s actions. V, 991. Denial is not merely with the tongue, but also by one’s actions. III, 2001. It is not only Pagans and Jews who deny Christ, but all who live wickedly. IV, 614. As great as the life of confessing Christ is, so great is the death of denying Christ. III, 1810. To deny that one is a Christian is to deny Christ. III, 1933. To deny oneself. V, 585, 1456, 1459.

Wisdom is denied to the negligent. IV, 1378.

“Business” (*negotiatio*) is called so in Greek from action, and in Latin from “denied leisure” (*negatum otium*). IV, 887. Whether business is a sin. IV, 886. The benefits and disadvantages of business. IV, 1762.

A merchant is exposed to fraud and perjury. V, 1391. The perverse desires of sellers and buyers for profit and cheapness. V, 1541. Whether a merchant may sell for more than he paid. IV, 886. The merchant, insane and ruinous. V, 144. A merchant, shipwrecked because of gold, loses his soul. V, 1517. Those are merchants who take pleasure in their own works. IV, 887.

The business of the blessed, free from idleness, is to praise God. IV, 1463, 1916, 1941. Certain likeness of divine justice has been impressed upon human affairs. VI, 120, 121.

Neat. V, 228.

Nemesianus, a boy martyr. V, 1298.

Nemesianus of Tubunae. IX, 204, 205.

Nimrod, a giant. III, 551; VII, 491.

Naples. IX, 239.

What the new moons signify. VIII, 354.

The beginnings of the newly baptized. VI, 208. In order that the days of the newly baptized might be distinguished from the others—that is, so that the eighth day might correspond to the first—the custom of the Church established this practice. II, 220.

Naphtali is interpreted as “my enlargement.” IV, 835.

From where Neptune is called a god. VII, 212. They claim that Neptune is the waters of the world. VII, 207. The sea is attributed to Neptune. IV, 209; VII, 119. In the statue of Neptune the Gentiles worshiped the sea. IV, 1483. Neptune ignorant of the future. VII, 80. Neptune’s servile services in the building of Troy. VII, 79, 80. Neptune, a lie made by man. V, 1023.

From where wickedness (*nequitia*) derives its name. I, 964, 974. The wickedness of those who hate the precepts of truth, for which the Son of God was crucified, is greater than that of those who crucified the Son of God. IV, 103. It is wickedness to love this world. VI, 299.

Q. Nero’s luxury and cruelty. VII, 166. He was the first to persecute Christians. IX, 323, 328. Nero set Rome on fire, wishing to see how Troy had burned. V, 1356. Some suspect that Nero will be the future Antichrist. VII, 686.

What it means to say that God does not know something. IV, 69, 334, 354, 355. God’s “not knowing” means disapproval. V, 579. It is right for a human being, when he does not know, to say, “I do not know”; but when he knows and says, “I do not know,” he bears witness against himself. V, 714. Not knowing another’s heart is a harsh necessity. IV, 237. Many do not even know themselves. IV, 1519.

Catholic doctrine is contrary to the error of Nestorius. VI, 249, 250, 251, 252.

The Nestorian heretics. VIII, 50. Note 2. Their heresy. X, 934.

The nerves are instruments of bodily movement. I, 1057. Dryness and moderate heat invigorate the nerves and make them more mobile. I, 1057. Strength resides in the nerves of bodies. I, 1057, 1058.

The Council of Nicaea. VIII, 772, 779, 785. Augustine and Valerius were unaware that the Council of Nicaea had prohibited two bishops from being in the same see. II, 967. The emperors profess the faith of the Nicene Synod. II, 927.

Nicodemus was buried with Stephen and was responsible for the discovery of Stephen’s body. V, 1433.

Nicholas, one of the seven deacons, from whom the Nicolaitans derive their name. VIII, 26. His heresy. VIII, 26.

Nicomedes of Segermes. IX, 209.

The nest of fear. IV, 1923.

Nigidius the mathematician: why he was called “the potter.” VII, 143.

[Col. 0462] The Manichaeans say that black belongs to Hyle. VIII, 396.

That which is absolutely nothing is that which is no substance at all. IV, 843. God made things from nothing because he did not make them from himself. X, 1470. A human being is something only so long as he clings to the one by whom he was made; when he withdraws from him, he is nothing. IV, 962. Whoever abandons the one by whom he was made and inclines toward nothingness is held fast in this sin. IV, 109. That which is very small in comparison with another thing is regarded as nothing. V, 795. Nothing and darkness are not the same. X, 1480.

The Nile, the river called Gihon in Scripture. III, 203, 378. At the cataracts of the Nile, the inhabitants are deprived of the use of their ears by the noise of the rushing waters. X, 1419. At a fixed season the Nile spreads into stagnant waters over the plains of Egypt; at another season it returns to its banks. III, 329.

Ninyas, son of Ninus, the fourth king of the Assyrians. VII, 561, 562.

What “too much” (*nimis*) usually signifies. IV, 1444, 1509. “Too much” in the sense of “very.” IV, 1509. “Nothing in excess,” a proverb praised by Greeks and Latins. IV, 1509. “This is the first useful rule in life: nothing in excess,” from Terence. I, 975. Too much is often more disadvantageous than too little. I, 975.

By whom Nineveh was built. VII, 480. How the statement is reconciled that the Hebrew manuscripts say Nineveh would be overthrown after three days, whereas the Septuagint says after forty days. VII, 605. Nineveh was overthrown in an evil sense after Jonah’s preaching, but built up in a good sense. IV, 592. Overthrown through repentance. V, 1610. Nineveh as a figure of the Church. VII, 605.

Ninus, the second king of the Assyrians. VII, 561. He was the first to wage war against neighboring peoples. VII, 116. He is said to have conquered all Asia. VII, 561. At what time he subjected Asia. VII, 578. The desire of Ninus. VII, 116.

Anaxagoras used to say that snow was black. X, 1397. What Christ’s garment shining like snow on the mountain signified. IV, 1932. “Snow like wool”: the predestined are still cold. IV, 1932.

Nobles are restrained from sinning only by the fear of God. IV, 1958. The grace of Christ also reaches the nobles. IV, 1370. Many among the nobility chose poverty in this world and nobility in Christ. IV, 1958. The conversion of nobles is a cause of greater joy for the Church. I, 752. Pride at noble birth is suppressed. V, 1312.

Nobility according to God and according to this world. III, 1259. The devil holds the proud more tightly under the name of nobility. I, 752.

Nobilius, bishop. II, 1093.

The will to harm may arise from each person’s own mind, but the power to harm comes only from God. III, 431. The will to harm is from the evil one; the power comes only from God. IV, 220, 291, 1292, 1385. By God’s hidden dispensation, the power to harm is permitted against one person for punishment, against another for testing, and against another for a crown. IV, 220. One will be harmed from the very point at which one attempts to harm another. IV, 329. One is harmed in two ways: either by being made wretched or by being abandoned while wretched. IV, 1285. The powerful of this world cannot harm the godly. V, 220. The wicked person does no real harm to the good person, but benefits him. V, 202, 1364. When God does not will it, no one harms you; when he permits it, you are corrected, not destroyed. IV, 1246. Whoever harms the righteous does not truly harm him, but himself. I, 600. No wicked person fails to harm himself first. IV, 329, 1286. It is possible for your wickedness not to harm another; but it is impossible for it not to harm you. IV, 330. The lover of iniquity harms only his own soul. IV, 136. God harms no one; rather, each person is bound by the cords of his own sins. IV, 151. The guilty person cannot be humble, and the proud person cannot be innocent. V, 1561.

The “Nocturnal,” as it is called, a type of sacrifice and superstition. VI, 703.

Nodotus, the god appointed over the joints and knots of grain stalks. VII, 118.

Noah may rightly be called a prophet. VII, 598. Everything Noah did was prophetic. VII, 477. One reprobate was found in Noah’s ark. II, 272. Noah’s ark signifies the Church. IV, 1358. Noah and his household were saved through water and wood; Christ’s family is marked through baptism by the passion of the cross. VIII, 262. Noah signifies the rulers of the Church. IV, 1731. Noah drunk and naked, a figure of Christ. VIII, 266, 267. Noah as a figure of the Lord’s passion. III, 111. Of Noah’s sons, Scripture mentions only those who produced nations. VII, 481. Those who now do not convert while Christ is building the Church deserve greater reproach than those who formerly failed to convert while Noah was building the ark. V, 1611. What Noah, Daniel, and Job signify. VI, 717.

Noema is interpreted as “pleasure.” VII, 465.

Νοερόν (*noeron*, “intellectual” or “intelligible”). VIII, 910.

Noetus, from whom the heretics called Noetians derive their name. VIII, 32.

Nola attacked by barbarians. VI, 606. And ravaged. VII, 24. With what obstinacy certain people in the city of Nola adhered to the error of Pelagius. II, 826.

“Name” (*nomen*) is so called as though from “designation” (*notamen*). III, 230. A name is not a name on its own account, but because of what it signifies. IV, 122. Names were imposed on things as each person pleased. I, 1116. [Col. 0463] To impose names on things is a sign of the highest wisdom. X, 1432. Once the matter is established, one should not labor over the name. IX, 469. A name is of no benefit where the reality is absent. III, 2007.

What the name of God is like. IV, 1311. How it has been adapted to human understanding. IV, 1392. In what way God’s name is sanctified. IV, 1337. How it is sanctified in the elect. X, 899. Knowledge of God’s name. IV, 122. If you seek God’s name, he also seeks yours; if you neglect God’s name, he too erases yours. IV, 1173. If the one who invokes the Lord’s name wishes that name to benefit him, let him depart from iniquity. V, 447. To take the Lord’s name in vain. V, 68. The name of Christ is his reputation: his name was small, but it became great. IV, 1262.

“Not,” the negative particle added to a term, does not change its category. VIII, 915. Non-beings and similar things, which are known not in their form but in its privation, are in a certain manner known by not knowing. VII, 355.

“To know” used in the sense of “to do.” IV, 1526. There are two ways of knowing human beings, and accordingly we are affected toward them in different ways. II, 942.

Nothing is ours except sin. V, 953.

Notaries. III, 55. A notary who receives dictated material in notes or writes it down. II, 694. Notaries of the Church. II, 967. The notary and the tribune. II, 488, 490. The poverty of Latin speech among the notaries in Palestine. II, 753.

The *Notaria* or *Notoria* of the Donatists. II, 490, 493, 509, 511; IX, 621, 622, 677, Appendix 821, 828.

Knowledge is produced by the knower and the known. VIII, 970. Knowledge of a thing exists in one way in the thing itself, and in another way in the eternal truth itself. VIII, 965. Knowledge of God is one thing, and human knowledge another. IV, 576. God is not known except in Judaea. IV, 956. The fullest, truest, and happiest knowledge of God belongs to those for whom possessing God consists in knowing him. II, 840. Those who are known by Christ. IV, 1114.

What night is. III, 255. Night serves the day, not day the night. IV, 885. Whatever you do by God’s command should not be done for the rewards of the flesh, lest the day serve the night. IV, 885.
