Midnight is called “deep night” (*intempesta*) because it is unsuitable for the activities of those who keep watch. IV, 1586. See *Day*. The night in which no one can work: what it is. III, 1715. Night is the iniquity of this age. IV, 85; V, 58. Night signifies adversity. IV, 67, 1173, 1737, 1793, 1853. Tribulation. V, 225. The time of this life. IV, 557, 973, 1292, 1792. The flesh and those who are carnal. IV, 159. The humility of mortality. IV, 1544. Ignorance. IV, 1161. Judas and the Jews. IV, 160. “As long as you do not see my heart, and I do not see yours, it is night.” IV, 1291.

A razor, a wicked person. V, 202, 421.

Nova. IX, 233.

The Novatians. IX, 469, 589, 747. They rebaptized. IX, 145. A certain Novatian said that Peter had not been baptized. II, 1086. And that the apostles had performed penance in place of baptism. II, 1088. The heresy of the Novatians, which condemns second marriages. VI, 433.

Novatus, a heresiarch. VI, 714.

Novatus, a bishop. II, 1019, 1020, 1021.

Novatus, a bishop, perhaps of Sitifis. II, 294. Note (b).

Novatus of Thamugadi. IX, 204.

To renew. VI, 687.

Novellus of Thysica. IX, 676.

The *Novemdial*: nine days of mourning at the funeral of Pagans. III, 596. This custom of observing a nine-day period should be prohibited among Christians. III, 596.

The number nine is imperfect. III, 1356.

The dangerous desire for novelty. I, 1353. How antiquity yielded to novelty. VI, 677, 678.

In what sense it is said that nothing is new under the sun. VII, 361. The renewal of the new human being is signified on the Lord’s cross. III, 2069. The old human being is in labor, but the new human being is born. IV, 536. We must always be new. IV, 1716. New life begins now in faith and is lived in hope, but will not be perfect until the resurrection. II, 217. The new human being, the new song, and the New Testament belong to one kingdom. V, 210.

The last things and the ancient things: what they are. IV, 1787.

The church of the *Novorum* or *Novarum* at Carthage. V, 111; IX, 638.

Many things are harmful that are not evil. VIII, 312.

To marry. A person who has vowed continence may not take a wife, even in order to make her a Christian. VI, 468. See *Marriage*. To marry after a vow of continence is condemnable. IV, 1058. Yet such marriages are not to be condemned. VI, 437. Nor are they to be dissolved. VI, 438. Virgins who regret their profession would do better to marry than to burn. VI, 415. Falling away from a holy purpose is evil, but the marriages of those who have fallen are good. VI, 439. Against those who say that the marriages of women who have fallen from a holy purpose are adulteries. VI, 438. If a nun marries, she will be regarded as an adulteress against Christ. IV, 1058. In giving a daughter in marriage, nature places the mother’s will before all others, unless the girl is of an age at which, with greater legal freedom, she may choose for herself what she wishes. II, 1070. See *Marriage*.

[Col. 0464] A cloud is water. III, 237. How a cloud signifies the ascent to heaven. IV, 1344, 1345. The cloud is Christ in the flesh. IV, 1124. The Apostles are clouds. IV, 346. Elijah, Jeremiah, John, and the other prophets and announcers of God’s word are clouds. IV, 1125. Clouds are preachers of truth, from whom God flashes, thunders, and waters. I, 852; IV, 136, 346, 672, 1345. Clouds are the sacraments and figures. IV, 1909. The cloud is sacred Scripture. III, 198; IV, 137. Christ was prefigured in the pillar of cloud. IV, 1266.

The first parents did not notice their nakedness until after sin. III, 448. After sin there is shame at nakedness, but not before. V, 817. Nakedness would not have caused shame if iniquity had not preceded it. V, 638, 680. Why the first parents were not ashamed of their nakedness before sin. III, 430; VII, 425. Why the first parents covered their nakedness after sin. X, 685. Shame at nakedness is born with every human being. X, 565.

The trifles of adults are called business. I, 668.

Numa Pompilius, successor of Romulus. II, 529; VII, 60, 84, 582. To protect Rome, he added other gods to the Trojan gods. VII, 87. He taught the Romans to worship the gods in a manner different from before. II, 375. He was the founder of the Roman religious rites. VII, 222. His books were burned by decree of the Senate, lest the reasons for the rites become known. VII, 222, 223. Numa Pompilius reached the secrets of demons through illicit curiosity. VII, 222, 223. He established certain laws for governing the city. VII, 60. He did not deserve to be counted among the gods, although he worshiped them. VII, 582.

Numantia, a city of Hispania Tarraconensis. VII, 103. Note (d). The Roman treaty with the Numantines, an unfortunate one. VII, 103.

The goddess Numeria teaches people to count. VII, 122.

Number. Whatever reason can do, it can do through numbers. I, 1015. The most effective numbers are present in the seeds of things. III, 326. And in all things, even the least important. I, 1258. Wisdom manifests itself through the numbers impressed upon each thing. I, 1263. In wisdom and from wisdom there is number; in number and from number there is wisdom. I, 1258. Spiritual and eternal numbers. I, 1181. The unchangeable nature of numbers. I, 1252, 1257, 1355. Infinite numbers. VII, 367. Whatever is counted is counted by number; but who counts number itself? IV, 1906. The infinity of numbers is not incomprehensible to God. VII, 368. Number without number. IV, 418. The beginning of number is from one, and its end is in nothing. VIII, 605. Why, in counting, progression toward God proceeds from one and then returns from him to one. I, 1095. Although intelligible number increases infinitely, it does not therefore diminish infinitely; the case is the opposite with sensible number. II, 64. Number, and beyond number. V, 116, 1168. Those who are “extra-numbered.” IV, 1904. The occasion for numbers. I, 1013. Traces of numbers in carnal pleasure. III, 157. On numbers, at length and excellently. I, 1094, 1163, 1257. The singular number used for the plural. IV, 1443. The plural number used in place of the singular. IV, 1442. In numbers Scripture makes use of a solid total. III, 613. And by the name of the whole it generally signifies the greater part. VII, 471. It is the custom of Scripture not to count what exceeds certain numerical units. V, 352. Which numbers are called imperfect, perfect, and more-than-perfect. III, 298. The most sacred numbers in Scripture, full of mysteries. III, 589.

Various numbers are explained mystically. IV, 570. The mystical interpretation of three and four. V, 1177. The number three pertains to the soul, and four to the body. IV, 91. The number three is especially prominent in many sacraments. II, 220. The numbers four and twenty. III, 718. In the number four there is a mark of temporal things. V, 1178. The number five is commended in the Old Testament. III, 717. In the number five the Jewish people placed under the Law is understood. IV, 571. Continence of the five senses is understood. IV, 570. The five virgins signify all the souls that will enter the kingdom of heaven. IV, 1920. The Law is prefigured by the numbers five and ten. V, 198. The mystical interpretation of seven. V, 353, 652, 1161, 1166. What seven signifies. IV, 1019, 1960. The number seven often signifies universality. II, 209. Perfection is represented. V, 518, 581. The Holy Spirit is commended. V, 1160, 1170. Creation is represented by the number seven. II, 218; V, 1177. What eight signifies. IV, 90. The eighth number signifies the resurrection. II, 215. The mystical interpretation of ten. V, 352, 353, 1177, 1240. The mystery of the number ten. V, 518. The number ten signifies the whole of wisdom. V, 1216. It signifies eternity. IV, 1961. It expresses the Law. IV, 1961. The perfection of our blessedness is in ten, because it returns to the first number. II, 218. The numbers seven, ten, twelve, and all other numbers are often used for the whole course of time. III, 86. The mystical interpretation of eleven. V, 353, 518. Of twelve. IV, 572. The number twelve is most sacred. IV, 1359, 1436. The number fifteen signifies the harmony of the two Testaments. IV, 1144, 1960. What the number seventeen signifies. IV, 571. In the number seventeen a wonderful sacrament is found. II, 220. What the number eighteen signifies. III, 805. What the number twenty-five signifies. [Col. 0465] III, 1599. The mystical interpretation of forty. V, 352, 1039, 1051, 1177, 1216. The present life is represented by forty, and the future life by fifty. II, 218. The number forty indicates the completeness of the ages. IV, 1226. It commends temporal dwelling together in this world. IV, 1961. The mystical interpretation of fifty. V, 1177, 1178. The fiftieth day is commended not only in the Gospel but also in the ancient books. II, 218. The number fifty has great significance. IV, 1960. It demonstrates blessed eternity. IV, 1463. The figure of the number fifty. V, 1051. The significance of the number seventy-seven. V, 353, 518. The number one hundred fifty and the number fifteen are sacred. IV, 1144. The mystical interpretation of numbers and of the 153 fish. V, 1170. What the number of fish caught after the resurrection signified. IV, 1961. A thousand, because of its perfection, includes all the other numbers. IV, 1394.

The Numidians. IX, 586.

Numida, a heretic and originator of the Donatist schism. V, 293.

Numidia. IV, 178; IX, 588. The location of Numidia. IX, 430. It has fertile, grain-producing fields, but no olive groves or forests. V, 293. The frenzy of the Donatists arose in consular Numidia. II, 225; V, 293. Except in consular Numidia, the Donatists are outnumbered by Catholic bishops in the other African provinces. II, 493.

Numidius, a bishop. II, 759, 780.

The Gentiles worshiped the powers that presided over bodies, not the bodies themselves. IV, 1483. See *Gods*. The Abadires among the divine powers. II, 83.

Numitor, grandfather of Romulus and king in Latium. VII, 578. Driven from Alba by his brother Amulius. VII, 91. Rome was founded in the first year of Numitor’s reign. VII, 578.

Numitorius was dragged by a hook and died with his entrails scattered. VII, 107.

Nummasius, an advocate, spoke on behalf of Restitutus, the Donatist bishop, against Maximian. II, 413. He acted so that the church of Membresitana might be handed over to the communion of Primian. IX, 549, 550.

The human being is God’s coin. V, 82. God seeks from us his own coin—that is, his own image. IV, 1318.

Nundinarius, a Donatist deacon. IX, 512, 513. Degraded by Silvanus of Cirta. II, 168. And excommunicated. II, 197. Before Zenophilus he opened Lucilla’s market. IX, 426, Appendix 798.

Nundinus, an exceptor. IX, 513.

Marriage. X, 710, 806. To what extent marriage is to be defined. X, 818. The Adamites condemn marriage. VIII, 31. So do the Tatianists. VIII, 30. The Manichaeans. X, 1462, 1463. Why the Manichaeans condemn it. VIII, 37, 494. And condemn it more than intercourse. VIII, 597, 598. No marriages are to be condemned. VI, 449. Against those who slander marriages condemned by the Apostle. VI, 404, 405. Marriage is not condemned by Catholics. X, 442, 820. It is a calumny of the Pelagians to say that those who assert original sin are condemn­ers of marriage. X, 1058. It is Julian’s calumny to say that marriage was not instituted by God. X, 554. Marriage was instituted by God. III, 1458; X, 564. And when. X, 554. Even marriages that take place now were instituted by God. X, 468. Marriage was blessed by God and is good. X, 1161. Why the blessing of marriage was given before sin. VII, 428, 429. How the blessing bestowed by God on human beings so that they might multiply was removed by sin. X, 448.

There would have been marriage even if no one had sinned. X, 405, 414, 1085. The natural use of intercourse, and one without blame, could have existed in paradise even if no one had sinned. X, 1451. Marriage before sin would have been very different from what it is now. X, 405. Julian admits lust accompanied by shame into paradise. X, 1178. Concupiscence would not have existed in marriage in paradise. X, 1081. Apart from lust, marriage before sin would have been like marriage now. X, 731. There would have been marriage without lust, or at least without lust accompanied by shame, if there had been no sin. X, 607, 1161, 1167. How marriage is now different after sin. X, 468. Marriage now does not exist without lust. X, 1341.

Although marriage can no longer exist without the evil of concupiscence, it is not thereby evil. X, 730. Marriage is not an evil. X, 404. It is not a sin. VI, 381. Marriage is good, but concupiscence is evil. X, 725, 726. Marriage is not evil, nor do spouses make good use of a good thing; rather, they make use of an evil thing. X, 728. Those who use their spouses’ bodies to beget children, for the purpose of generating those who are to be regenerated, do not serve the devil through lust. X, 1403. Although marriage does not exist without lust, marriage itself is not therefore condemned, nor does lust cease to be a disease. X, 765. Marital intercourse in itself is good and is not a sin. X, 406. The work of marriage is good even among the impious. X, 758. Marriage is good and honorable. III, 397; X, 686, 687. Marriage is good. X, 763. In what respect it is good. X, 717. The good of marriage. X, 1084. The marital goods: which they are and how they are to be loved. X, 424. How the good of marriage differs from the evil of concupiscence. X, 418. The three goods of marriage. X, 732, 810. Offspring, chastity, and the sacrament. X, 406. Offspring, fidelity, and the sacrament. VI, 394. The good of marriage is the procreation of children. VI, 269.

Marriages are celebrated in order to have children. III, 1452. To use marriage in a marital manner. VI, 394. The only marital intercourse is that which takes place for the sake of procreation. VI, 381. The propagation of children is the first, natural, and legitimate reason for marriage. VI, 394, 479. Intercourse for the sake of propagation is not a vice but a duty. VIII, 598. Marriages are honorable and free from every fault of lust if spouses make good use of them with the intention of propagating children. X, 1557. The law of marriage is honorable and useful, so that children may be born through ordered propagation. X, 1459. The fruit of marriage is a human being. X, 442. The ordered acceptance of children. X, 729. Only the lustful do not intend conception or childbirth in the use of marriage. X, 447. Who misuse the natural good of marriage. X, 415. And turn that good into sin. X, 415. Unbelievers turn the good of marriage into evil; believers turn it to the use of righteousness. X, 757. The work of marriage is good; nevertheless, fornication and adultery must not be committed in order to beget children. X, 758. How marriage differs from adultery. X, 1084. The good of marriage cannot be accused because of original evil, nor can the evil of adultery be excused by the natural good. X, 413.

The good of marriage is conjugal chastity. X, 404. Even in marriage there is culpable lust. X, 687. What the “tribulation of the flesh” in marriage is, of which the Apostle speaks. VI, 403. The good of marriage moderates concupiscence but does not extinguish it. II, 844. The marriages of believers turn the concupiscence of the flesh to the use of righteousness. X, 416. Formerly marriage was obedience to the Law; now it is a remedy for weakness and a consolation of human nature. VI, 437. Marriage, which could have been a duty for the healthy, is a remedy for the sick. III, 397. Marriage provides for the weakness of incontinence. X, 424.

The sacrament of marriage. X, 420. The sacrament of marriage is not lost by separation or adulteration. X, 420, 424. The Lord came to the wedding so that conjugal chastity might be strengthened and the sacrament of marriage might be revealed. III, 1459.

Praise of marriage according to the Pelagians. X, 610. What the Pelagians’ intention is in praising marriage. X, 615. To what extent marriage is to be praised. X, 611. Marriage should be praised in such a way that it is not considered a criticism of marriage that all human beings are born subject to original sin. X, 643. The dispute between Augustine and Julian on this matter concerns the foundations of faith. X, 643. Marriage by its nature and institution is not a cause of sin. X, 460. Sin did not arise from the goods of marriage. X, 427. What in marriage belongs to God and what belongs to the human being. X, 805. Everything in marriage is from God except concupiscence and sin. X, 445. Whether praise of marriage is shared with lust. X, 803.

Jovinian praised marriage excessively, but did not deny original sin. X, 445. Jovinian equated marriage with sacred virginity. X, 193, 552, 1418. Marriage is good, but virginity is better. VIII, 494. By divine law virginity is placed before marriage. VI, 397. Virginity should be preferred to marriage in such a way that marriage is not condemned. VI, 404. Christian Catholic marriages, even those of women who have not been married only once, are to be preferred to Vestal virgins and to the virgins of heretical groups. X, 416. Married women are also holy in body, although less so than unmarried women. VI, 434, 435. In former times it was dutiful, not lustful, for holy men to have intercourse with women according to the right of marriage. VI, 385. They descended to marriage by a step of piety, whereas now people ascend to it by a step of honorability. VI, 386. In the time of the Law, holy women married not because concupiscence compelled them, but because obedience did. VI, 435. The fact that the ancients had several wives was not caused by lust of the flesh, but by concern for procreation. VI, 436. Their having several wives signified several churches subject to one husband, Christ. VI, 388. The sacrament of marriage has now been restricted to one husband and one wife. VI, 387. The carnal generation of the ancients belonged to prophetic dispensation. VI, 387. The ancients sought children from their marriages for Christ’s sake. VI, 389. Married people of the present age are not to be compared with the holy married people of the first age. VI, 386. In former times marriage was also to be embraced by the continent; in the present age it is to be chosen for the sake of children only by those who cannot remain continent. VI, 380, 383, 386, 478. The present age no longer has the necessity of marriage. X, 424.

The marital bond, even if the marriage is not followed by the procreation of children, is not dissolved except by the death of one of the spouses. VI, 394. It is unlawful for a woman who has left her husband by divorce to marry another while her husband is alive. VI, 394. Nor is it lawful to take another wife for the sake of begetting children after dismissing an adulterous wife. VI, 478. The marital covenant is not annulled by the separation of the spouses. VI, 378. The objections raised against the disadvantages of not being permitted to take another wife after dismissing an adulterous wife. VI, 482. Pollentius held that it was forbidden to marry another only if one had left a spouse who had not committed fornication, but not if one had left a fornicator. VI, 471. This is refuted. VI, 472. Pollentius’s view that a woman who leaves an adulterer is not forbidden by a command to marry another, but should avoid it only because of disgrace. VI, 454. Whether a husband who dismisses an adulterous wife and takes another should be considered an adulterer is so obscure in the divine judgments that anyone may be mistaken about it without grave guilt. VI, 221. Whether a virgin who unknowingly married another woman’s husband should be considered an adulteress. VI, 203. A man who refuses reconciliation with his adulterous wife cannot marry another. VI, 476. The Apostle commands that she remain unmarried, even if she has left an adulterer. VI, 455.

Some heretics condemned second marriages. VII, 513; VIII, 657. The Cathari do not admit them. VIII, 32. The Cataphrygians condemned second marriages as fornications. VIII, 30. So did Tertullian. VIII, 47. Second marriages were condemned by the Cataphrygians, Novatians, and Tertullian, but permitted by the Apostle. VI, 433. Marriage is not condemned by a profession of widowhood. VI, 433. God demonstrated that second marriages are lawful. VIII, 661. At the present time, both second and first marriages are to be held in contempt unless incontinence stands in the way. VI, 436.

The marriage of the holy soul in heaven. VI, 47. The wedding of the king’s son. V, 559. There will be no marriage in the future age: why. X, 1178. See *To marry*, *Concupiscence*, *Lust*, *Marriage*. Weddings are celebrated for seven days. III, 571.

The gods of marriage. VII, 188.

The wedding garment. V, 561.

The daughter-in-law of the Synagogue, the Church. IV, 501.

The righteous sometimes waver when they see the impious flourishing and abounding. IV, 1648, 1649.

The night raven as a figure of Christ. IV, 1299. And of preachers. IV, 1298.

Nymphidius, a bishop. X, 652, 663.

## O

Obedience. III, 400. A great virtue of rational creation subject to the Creator. VII, 394. The sole virtue of every rational creature acting under God’s power. III, 377. Obedience is a virtue that is radical, foundational, and wholly universal. VI, 395. Obedience is the mother of all virtues. VI, 393. The mother and guardian of virtues. VII, 420. The origin and mother of all virtues. VIII, 613. Nothing is more beneficial to the soul than to obey. IV, 891. In every rational creature, obedience is the origin and perfection of all righteousness. IV, 904. The piety of obedience, by which God alone is worshiped. X, 172. The excellence of obedience. VII, 372.

Obedience was strongly commended to humanity by God. X, 172. God demonstrated the value of obedience when he imposed a prohibition concerning a good tree. IV, 897. A prohibiting command was necessary for humanity, so that the virtue by which one might win the favor of one’s Lord would itself be obedience. III, 377, 379, 384. God required obedience not for the sake of dominion, but for the benefit of the one serving. X, 172. Obedience alone bears the palm; disobedience alone finds punishment. IV, 897. Whoever wishes that what is beneath him be subject to him should obey the one above him. IV, 1860. It arose from the punishment of sin that humanity should be divided against itself, because it refused to be subject to one authority. IV, 891. Through obedience to the commandments one reaches the hidden things of wisdom. IV, 1566. Obedience must be preserved in order to receive wisdom, and once wisdom has been received, obedience must not be abandoned. IV, 1566. Let no one seek to reach the height of wisdom before possessing the humility of obedience. IV, 1566. Obedience can belong only to the humble. VII, 421. To retain the first place for obedience. V, 1355. Avarice commands harsh things, and it is obeyed; God commands easy things, and he is not obeyed. IV, 1691. In this one matter alone a son should not obey his father: if his father commands something against God. IV, 875. Obedience is to be shown to all masters and authorities, even wicked ones. II, 994; IV, 1653. To obey kings is a general covenant of human society. I, 690.

Obedience is a gift of God. VI, 421. Obedience is a pious gift of God, and obedience from the heart. X, 1245. The good of obedience is greater than that of continence. VI, 393. The obedience of Abraham. V, 27. A promise of obedience is tested not by hearing but by trial. IV, 990. The obedience of the sons of Jonadab is commended. IV, 875. The obedience of the boy Jesus. V, 343.

How hardening comes from God, and yet not unjustly. III, 1777; VI, 121. God has mercy through a free gift, but hardens according to the most just merit. II, 888. God hardens no one except according to merit. II, 823. Hardening arises only from merit, whereas grace does not. X, 910, 911. Just as God has mercy through great goodness, so he hardens through no iniquity. VI, 278. God’s hardening is his refusal to show mercy. VI, 120. God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by withholding mercy. II, 879. God produces hardness of heart not by instigating or inspiring it, but by abandoning the person. III, 1777; IV, 1003. He brought this about among the Egyptians through evil angels. IV, 1003. Why one person is hardened and another is not must be left to divine judgment. III, 1777. Hardening arises from judgment. X, 1140, 1142. The hardening of sinners demonstrates God’s wrath toward the reprobate and his mercy toward the elect. VI, 124. Pharaoh’s hardening did not occur without free choice. X, 911. How this happened. III, 601. See *Pharaoh*.

Obelisks and asterisks in Greek manuscripts. III, 590.

Those who have become hardened through bad habit are to be rebuked; the effect of this rebuke. V, 594. The rebuke of a sinner, so that he may be healthfully put to shame. V, 779. A lover’s rebuke is sometimes bitter. V, 1437. A rebuker loves even when he strikes. V, 1229. A comparison of the rebuker and the flatterer. V, 1229. If a bishop neglects the duty of rebuking, he is called good; if he fulfills it, he is called wicked. IV, 1690.

The offering of the altar. I, 634, 714; II, 637. When it is not possible either to carry an offering to the altar or to offer it to God through a priest, what should be done. II, 426. You were asking what you could offer to God for yourself: offer yourself; nothing is better in all earthly creation. V, 317. God seeks you more than your gift. V, 508. An offering at the memorial shrines of the martyrs. V, 1251. It is made to God, not to the martyrs. V, 1251.

How “to forget” is said of God. IV, 1540. Forgetfulness does not befall God. IV, 123, 1540, 1541. The doctrine of Caelestius that forgetfulness is not subject to sin. X, 345. Forgetfulness of God is a distant region. III, 1344. A person must not forget from which sins he has been delivered. IV, 965, 966. Ungrateful forgetfulness of God’s benefits is to be avoided. IV, 1317; VII, 280. Forgetfulness of evils is of two kinds. VII, 803. The soul has forgotten itself by loving the world; let it forget itself by loving the maker of the world. V, 779.

Cicero teaches that obscenity of language is to be avoided in translation. VIII, 636.

Why the sacred authors spoke obscurely. III, 99. The obscurity of the sacred authors is not useless. II, 93. It is not to be imitated by Christian teachers. III, 98. In obscure and difficult matters, rashness must be avoided. II, 862.

How supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings differ. II, 866. Prayers of petition are made before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; prayers are made while it is being blessed; intercessions, or petitions, when the people are being blessed; and after all these, thanksgivings. II, 867.

What observance is. VI, 21. Innate nature implanted this. VI, 20. Observance toward authorities and toward anyone superior is to be properly ordered. V, 418, 420.

Which observance of days is blameworthy. II, 210.

Observance. What is the yoke of observances that Christ removed? X, 594. Once the New Testament had been revealed, the legal observances were neither harmful to the Jews, nor necessary for the Gentiles, nor salutary for anyone. VI, 494. The Apostle commands that the legal observances be despised as superfluous, not removed as harmful things. VIII, 156.

When the fear of a barbarian siege is imminent, whether clergy may flee to safe places. II, 1014.

Let him obey the Physician’s command to rise, who was unwilling to believe the Physician so as not to become ill. IV, 891.

The Hebrew midwives were rewarded for benevolence, not for deception. VI, 540. The lie of the Egyptian midwives is examined. III, 597. See Lie.

The slanders of detractors are to be refuted without quarrelling. V, 1579.

Christ’s setting, Christ’s passion. IV, 1374.

*Occentare*: to publish an infamous song naming a person. VII, 54, note 3.

Scripture frequently signifies the western region when it says “above the sea” or “from the sea.” III, 539; IX, 588. All Orientals and many Westerners do not fast on Saturday. II, 138, 140. The devastation of the western provinces, especially the city of Rome. II, 719.

To kill. Not everyone who is the cause of another’s death is guilty. II, 661. Sometimes the person who was the cause of death is more at fault than the one who killed. II, 661. When one person is killed by another, it makes a great difference whether this is done from a desire to inflict harm or unjustly to seize something, or in the course of vengeance or obedience, or from the necessity of escape or assistance. II, 660. The commandment not to kill admits exceptions. VII, 35. Who are exempted from the crime of homicide, although they kill people. VII, 35. The commandment not to kill is not violated when the law kills, or when God commands someone to be killed. III, 622. Elijah was righteous, although he killed many false prophets with his own hand. II, 178. It is not lawful for just anyone to kill the wicked. V, 1390. Whoever kills a person without any legitimate authority is a murderer. II, 940. Killing another who wishes and asks to die and is no longer able to live is shown by Scripture to be unlawful. II, 940. It is not lawful to kill an enemy either because he has sinned against us or so that he may not sin. VII, 38. It is not lawful to kill someone in order to protect one’s own life or that of others, unless one is a soldier or holds some public office. II, 186. He is not free from sin who kills a person so that he himself will not be killed by that person. I, 1228. It cannot be shown from the New Testament that any righteous person killed anyone. II, 179. The killing of an innocent person is unjustly perpetrated by a human being, although it is justly permitted by God. IV, 745.

A person ought not to kill the guilty, much less himself, who is innocent. II, 666. No innocent person is killed by himself. IX, 712. Those who worship the one true God may not kill themselves. VII, 36. It is not lawful to kill oneself for any reason. VII, 34, 35, 38. Not even to avoid sin. VII, 40. Nor so that the mind, while the body is oppressed, may not consent to lust. VII, 38. Nor even from fear of punishment or disgrace. VII, 30, 35, 39, 40. Christians ought rather to endure captivity and every other evil than to kill themselves. VII, 38. The Donatists, lovers of homicide, slaughtered themselves or offered themselves to be slaughtered. II, 797. Those who kill themselves defend themselves in vain by the example of Razis. II, 940. The example of Job demonstrates that no one may lawfully kill himself. IX, 727. Killing oneself is not courage. VII, 630. Some extend the commandment not to kill to animals. VII, 34. The Manichaeans extend it even to plants. VII, 34, 35. Why we may kill animals. VII, 35.

Sinners are killed when, darkened in understanding, they are alienated from the life of God. IV, 1800. God wishes to kill in a person what the person has made, and to save what he himself has made. IV, 1692. Let another’s iniquity destroy your flesh while truth preserves your soul. IV, 1026. Let no one kill his own soul for another’s body. IV, 86. Either you kill iniquity, or you will be killed by iniquity. IV, 764. Parents are called spiritual murderers when they attempt to bind baptized infants through the sacrileges of demons. II, 360. “To kill blood,” meaning to shed it by killing. III, 514.

The hidden things of the Son: what they are. IV, 117.

Hidden things. The rashness of human judgments concerning hidden things. IV, 1435.

God conceals what it is not beneficial for us to have revealed. IV, 356.

Occupation. A person excessively absorbed in human activities is, in a certain sense, left free for God. III, 619.

“To meet someone,” or “to meet up with someone,” meaning to kill. III, 824.

Oceanus. II, 719. Augustine asks him for Jerome’s book, in which Jerome discusses the resurrection of the flesh brilliantly. II, 779. Augustine writes one reply to his three letters. II, 777.

The tides of the ocean increase and diminish with the lunar waxing and waning. VII, 146.

Ochus. VIII, 601.

The octave of the regenerated. III, 1235. The octaves of infants. V, 1201, 1669. The holy day of the octave. VI, 581. Those who touched the earth with bare feet during their octave were customarily punished severely. II, 221. The eight days of the Neophytes, distinguished. II, 220. The third day of the octave, or even the eighth itself, was chosen by some for the washing of the feet. II, 220.

Octavian, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Octavius, bishop. II, 759, 780.

The head of the consul Octavius placed on the Rostra. VII, 107.

The eighth. IX, 237.

The Basilica of the Eight Martyrs. V, 1578.

The eye is named from swiftness. V, 382. Whether the eyes undergo anything in seeing: at length. I, 1059. The eyes do not see; rather, someone sees through the eyes. V, 699, 1134. The eyes are the windows of the mind. IV, 468. Other senses are signified by the name “eyes.” V, 646. The eyes are the chief of the senses. I, 802. The power of the eye’s pupil. I, 1048. Through the pupil the beam of light is directed, by which light and darkness are distinguished. IV, 146. The opening of Adam’s and Eve’s eyes, and of the disciples’ eyes at Emmaus, is not to be understood figuratively. III, 446. What the opening of the eyes in the first parents means. X, 173. An immodest eye is a messenger of an immodest heart. I, 1391; II, 961. The wantonness of the eyes must be restrained. IV, 587. A man must not fix his gaze upon a woman. I, 1391. The enticements of the eyes. VII, 232, 813. To entice the eyes. V, 1413. The loss of the bodily eyes is considered greater than that of the mind’s eyes—but by the blind. IV, 860. Light is food for the eyes. IV, 1114; V, 183.

The eyes are called lights. V, 35. We have other eyes besides the eyes of the flesh. II, 700. The eye is twofold, interior and exterior. III, 1493. The eyes of the flesh and the eyes of the heart. V, 869, 1300. The eyes of the heart. VI, 543. The eyes of the heart are superior to the eyes of the body. II, 615. No ray of the bodily eyes can approach the light of the mind; in the latter, spaces and intervals of place are not seen. II, 615. Whether God can be seen with the bodily eyes. V, 367, 1257. With bodily eyes God appeared not through himself but through visible creation. V, 59. Perhaps Job saw God with bodily eyes for an hour. VII, 799. Perhaps Simeon saw God with bodily eyes for an hour. VII, 799. God is not seen with the bodily eyes but with the mind’s eyes. II, 617, 622, 623, 625, 626, 628. God cannot be seen with bodily eyes even by Christ. II, 707. The bodily eye will not see God even in the age to come. II, 625, 626. The bodily eye can see nothing except what is corporeal and located within spatial extent and distance. II, 622, 623. God is invisible to the bodily eyes. II, 617, 619, 620. The bodily eye will never be able to see God. II, 319. Some go so far as to grant even the wicked the possibility of seeing God with the bodily eye. II, 319. Not even Christ could have been granted the ability to see the Father with bodily eyes. II, 320. If some think that God is to be seen with bodily eyes in the resurrection, let them show how they establish this. II, 618. The eyes of the blessed will see incorporeal things. VII, 799. The bodily eyes are not to be compared with the eyes of the heart. II, 615. The bodily eyes will see something in heaven. II, 622. The eyes of the heart prefer a deformed but faithful servant to a handsome but faithless one. V, 869. The eyes of the heart are now illumined by faith; afterward they will be illumined by vision. V, 366. The eyes of the flesh are greatly loved, while the eyes of the heart are greatly neglected. V, 542. Just as visible light is painful to the eyes of the flesh, so the light of righteousness is painful to the eyes of the heart. V, 542. How greatly the crowd of phantasms arising from the habit of carnal life disturbs the eyes of the mind. II, 615. What must be done by one who cannot drive imaginary forms of bodily qualities away from the mind’s vision. II, 615. By what illnesses the mind’s eye is troubled. IV, 1252; V, 542. The mind’s eye is troubled by anger and extinguished by hatred. IV, 241. Blindness of the inner eyes is failure to understand. IV, 1552. The eye of the inner person is healed with difficulty. VIII, 174. Our entire work now is to heal the eye of the heart. V, 542. The mind’s eye must be healed with the mordant eye-salve of the commandment. IV, 447. The eye of the heart, by which God is seen, must be cleansed through faith. V, 541, 670. Hearts are cleansed through faith so that the inner eyes may be opened and made serene. IV, 1552. What the simple and purified eye of the heart is. III, 1304. The eye of the heart is faith. IV, 1169. How strong and powerful the eyes of faith are. IV, 1897. Those who envy the prosperity of the wicked do not have the eyes of faith. IV, 392. No one can evade the eyes of God. IV, 1200. Against those who fear human eyes but do not fear God’s. IV, 342, 343.

God’s eyes are upon the one whose eyes are turned toward God. IV, 271. The eyes of Christ’s mystical body are its brighter and more eminent members. IV, 1114.

“To cast one’s eyes upon someone,” that is, to love. III, 496. “To have before one’s eyes” means to love. IV, 1286. To pluck out one’s eyes, to indicate great love. III, 729. “Eye” signifies a friend. III, 1248. It also signifies that which is loved intensely. III, 1247. “Eye” is used for intention. IV, 1532, 1533; X, 755.

Hatred is anger grown old. II, 153; IV, 189, 632; V, 324, 397. How hatred arises from anger. V, 324. Hatred creeps in when no angry person regards his anger as unjust. II, 153. From what source we love people or hold them in hatred. III, 1405, 1859. We must be watchful lest hatred for anyone occupy the innermost part of the heart. II, 153. Hatred extinguishes the eye. IV, 241. Love is light; hatred is darkness. IV, 633. The one who hates is in darkness and in prison. V, 1054. Our life is love; hatred is death. IV, 633. In charity there is spaciousness; in hatred, confinement. IV, 1737. Hatred blocks the fountain of charity flowing from the heart. V, 1557. Hatred of one’s neighbor lays waste the heart more grievously. I, 674. Hatred harms the one who hates more grievously than the other person. V, 507. The one who hates his brother is a murderer. IV, 189; V, 324, 397. Those who hate their brothers are men of blood. IV, 1801. The devil possesses more fully the one who is not only alienated from God but also hates without cause those who serve God. VII, 668. One hates without cause who seeks no advantage from hatred or escape from any disadvantage. III, 1862. What vice it is to hate unjustly. IV, 410. Do not conceive hatreds, or end them quickly. V, 137. Hatred must be laid aside quickly, lest it corrupt the heart. V, 1274. Anger is a splinter; hatred is a beam. IV, 632; V, 324, 506, 1054. There is a great difference between the sin of one who hates and that of one who is angry. V, 506. What hatred is lawful. VII, 409. Perfect hatred is such that one neither hates people on account of their vices nor loves vices on account of people. IV, 1801, 1802. The wicked are not to be hated, and why. IV, 630. Hatred is to be conceived not against the person but against what the person has done wrongly. V, 163, 324, 780. With security we hate wickedness in the wicked and love the creature. IV, 1569, 1804. Hatred is the greatest crime of the persecutor, even though it is the voluntary punishment of the sufferer. IV, 1434. Hatred must be directed not against the persecutor but against the devil who works through him. IV, 1766, 1841. What kind of hatred toward parents is commanded. I, 616.

What hatred of God is. IV, 85. If you hate what God hates, you will be God’s friend. IV, 504. Hatred itself of sinners begins to make us like God. IV, 1080. Christians ought to learn from Christ’s example to be hated without cause. IV, 847, 848. Hatred of the soul is love of wickedness, and conversely. V, 1472.

“Odollamites” is interpreted as “testimony in water.” VIII, 457.

The desire to smell. X, 771.

The good odor of Christ: all the faithful. IV, 171. The good odor: the saints. V, 1250. Through Christ’s good odor some are healed and others perish. IV, 507, 508. How this happens. V, 1250.

The tale of Oedipus. VII, 571.

Mount Oea. IX, 239.

Oenophorus. VII, 198.

Oeta. VII, 569.

Forgiving offenses according to Christ’s example. V, 1057. With what care Augustine tries to appease a bishop offended by somewhat harsher letters. II, 623, 629. See Forgive, Enemies.

The official of the Count. II, 430. What court officials may receive and what they are bound to return. II, 664.

The term “office” is less customary in ecclesiastical books; Ambrose was not afraid to use it. II, 285. Our office must be evaluated not by the office itself but by its end. IV, 1532. All offices must be directed toward attaining the good. VII, 297. The duty of giving is often the merit of receiving. II, 1089.

Public office. IX, 432, 513, 616, 621, 643, 649. The office of the consul. II, 430. The whole office proceeds before the judge. V, 431.

“Og” is interpreted as “heaping up.” IV, 1760. Conclusion. IV, 1751.

Ogyx, or Ogygus, or King Ogygius. VII, 720. Historians do not agree when he lived. VII, 566. The flood of Ogygus. VII, 566.

An olive branch is a sign of peace. III, 47.

Although the wild olive is good, in Scripture it nevertheless has the meaning of evil. X, 834. The wild olive and the olive tree. V, 563, 1032, 1036, 1086, 1503. The wild olive also grows from the seed of the olive tree. II, 890. The natural branches are cut off and the wild olive is grafted in: why? V, 489.

The Manichaeans ought to regard vegetables as more unclean than meat. VIII, 235.

Minerva, inventor of olive oil. VII, 569. Oil blessed for the administration of the sacrament. IX, 190. Visible oil is in the sign; invisible oil is in the sacrament; spiritual oil is within. IV, 505. Christ’s oil, even when administered by a sinner, is not the sinner’s oil. V, 1225, 1229. To carry oil with oneself. V, 577. Whoever has oil with him does not seek the sinner’s oil. IV, 1824. Foreign oil. V, 577. Those who buy and sell oil. V, 578. Flatterers sell oil. IV, 1921. The sinner’s oil is the false praise of a flatterer. IV, 1824; V, 578. Oil is glory. IV, 1824. It is glorying itself. IV, 1921. Oil within. IV, 1921. Oil signifies the testimony of a good conscience. IV, 1824. Grace and the Holy Spirit. IV, 1443; V, 1000. Spiritual joy. IV, 182.

Oil and lees. V, 120, 137. Oil and the olive tree. V, 500.

The fruit of the olive signifies charity. III, 1435. The example of the olive tree and the wild olive, however he explains it, shows how original sin can be inherited from parents who have themselves been regenerated. X, 471.

A pot signifies tribulation. IV, 720. The pot of hope in tribulations. IV, 721. The pot of iniquity burns, but the flame of charity is greater. IV, 721.

Olibrius. VI, 446, 447.

Olympias, mother of Alexander. VII, 256.

Olympius, a Spanish bishop. X, 644. His ecclesiastical sermon. X, 644.

Mount Olympus in Macedonia, the highest mountain. III, 184, 1988. The height of Mount Olympus. VII, 474. It is said that at the summit of Mount Olympus neither clouds are seen nor winds felt. III, 280, 550. Neither birds can fly there nor human beings live there for long. III, 280. Whether the floodwaters rose above Mount Olympus. III, 550. Olympus, dwelling place of the gods. II, 83. Jupiter encamped on this mountain while waging war against his father. II, 83.

“Omen,” a word formerly unused in sacred writings. I, 586.

“All”: how it is to be understood. X, 270. “All” in Scripture means all kinds. X, 1421. In this sense, all flesh will come to Christ. IV, 776. “All” for “many.” X, 1217. How “all” is not said of everyone. II, 872. It is not contradictory that the same people are many and all. X, 1203, 1204. How “all” and “many” are understood by the Apostle, etc. X, 1234. How the Apostle understands “all.” X, 1201, 1203. How all are said to be from one person unto condemnation. X, 1129. How all are sinners through Adam and all righteous through Christ. II, 843; X, 119, 463. All are brought through Adam to condemnation and all through Christ to justification. X, 141, 1198. All are brought through Adam to death and all through Christ to life. X, 871. How all are made alive in Christ. X, 1226, 1231. How God wills all to be saved. X, 759, 943. Not all are reborn unto justification, but all who are reborn are reborn only through Christ. II, 680, 729. “All are taught so that they may come”: in what sense this is correctly said. X, 971. In what sense it is said that every person is illumined by God. X, 130.

Nothing is taken away from God’s omnipotence by the fact that he can neither sin, nor die, nor kill himself. X, 274. God is truthfully called omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills, and the effect of his will is not hindered by the will of any creature. VI, 276. God is omnipotent by doing what he wills, not by suffering what he does not will. VII, 152. See God.

Ὁμοούσιον [*homoousion*, “of the same substance”]. VIII, 707.

By the name “wild asses” are understood those few who, free from every occupation, serve God. III, 881. “Wild asses” signify the nations. IV, 1360.

Oneus, the twenty-ninth king of the Assyrians. VII, 577.

Christ’s burden is light through charity. IV, 823. We are to bear one another’s burdens. VI, 80. Those who have charity bear one another’s burdens. IV, 1698. Nothing proves a friend so well as bearing a friend’s burden. VI, 81. We are urged, by Christ’s example, to bear the burdens of others. VI, 81, 82. By loving Christ, we easily endure another’s weakness. VI, 83. We bear the misfortunes of friends more firmly. VI, 82. How burdens are to be borne. VI, 81, 82.

Two kinds of burdens. V, 896. Some burdens involve sharing weakness; others involve rendering an account to God for our actions. III, 1113. The burden of poverty and of riches. V, 899. The burden of laziness. V, 897. Each person’s sins are his own burdens. V, 896.

Work. If the Church should require some work from a monk, he must neither undertake it with greedy self-exaltation nor reject it through flattering laziness. II, 188.

God performs all his works in tranquillity. IV, 1181. God is said to work when the righteous do good through his gift; he is also said to rest when they rest in him. VI, 331. God’s works existed in the Word before they were made. IV, 497. The works of the Father and the Son are the same. IV, 1442. In miraculous things beyond nature, the entire explanation of what happens is the power of the one who performs it. II, 519. Why God places his works before our eyes. IV, 1336. God’s works are narrated in summary. I, 865. All God’s works praise God. IV, 1691. Grace is intimated in all God’s works. IV, 1851. God works in a person both the willing and the doing. X, 918. Against those who say, “If we are acted upon, we do not act,” the answer is: “If you were not an agent, the Spirit of God would not be a co-worker.” V, 856. We are acted upon by the Spirit of God as he exhorts, illumines, and assists. V, 856. Know how to do good in such a way that the Spirit who directs is the helper. V, 856. You do indeed act, by free will, without his assistance—but badly. V, 856.

What kind of work human beings performed in paradise. III, 204. To work with the flesh and not with the spirit is useless; to work with the spirit and not with the flesh is characteristic of the lazy. V, 224. We must possess spiritual things and not perform carnal things in a carnal manner. V, 224. God’s servants are commanded to perform bodily work, so that they may support themselves by their own hands. VI, 551. Monks living by the work of their hands. I, 638, 1339. Against lazy monks unwilling to work. VI, 566, 569. They falsely claim that they are free for prayer, psalms, reading, and the word of God. VI, 564, 565. They preach their own laziness as though it preserved the gospel. VI, 569. How foolishly. VI, 569. They insult the better and more industrious monks. VI, 569, 577. They arrogate to themselves the name of holiness. VI, 578. If they work with their hands, they act more mercifully than when they have distributed all their possessions. VI, 573. Others lack an excuse. VI, 568, 573. It is wholly unfitting that in the life where hard-working senators are found, idle artisans should be found. VI, 573. Those who were wealthy in the world, if they plead weakness, are to be believed and endured. VI, 567, 572, 573. What works are to be imposed on monks. VI, 573. The command to work bodily was relaxed for the Apostles. VI, 554. And for ministers of the gospel. VI, 453, 567. Paul did not make use of this permission: why? VI, 558, 559. What honest work may be done to obtain a livelihood. VI, 560. The book *On the Work of Monks*. I, 638; VI, 547.

What servile works are. III, 1635. Do not think that you are doing anything unless you are doing it insofar as you are evil. IV, 1851.

Laborers hired to cultivate the vineyard. V, 531.

Some works are made good or evil by their end; others are sins in themselves and must not be done for any supposedly good end. VI, 528. What works are truly good. X, 763. From what source good works flow. X, 206. Intention makes a good work; faith directs the intention. IV, 259. Let us learn, amid similarity of actions, to distinguish the minds of those who act. II, 437. The end of good works. V, 85. Whatever a person may have done as though rightly, unless it is referred to piety toward God, ought not to be called right. VI, 204, 288. Works cannot be right when the heart is not rightly directed. IV, 991. Works are then right and pure when they are directed toward charity. III, 1289; IV, 1148. An action is then right, just, and pious when a good work is done to the praise of the one by whose grace it is granted that it be done. II, 568. A work is truly good when the agent’s intention is launched forth from charity and, returning as to its proper place, rests again in charity. VI, 323. A work is good when it is done for eternal life, provided that eternal life itself is hoped for from the Lord through Christ; otherwise it is impious. IV, 262. No good works exist before faith or without faith. II, 853. Faith does not come from good works; good works come from faith. V, 32. Where faith was absent, there was no good work. IV, 259, 838. Human beings perform good works, but faith is formed in the human being; without faith no human being performs those works. II, 877. Whether works that appear good, performed without faith in Christ, are good and useful. III, 1602, 1720. Works performed before faith are empty. IV, 259, 261, 262. No abundance of praiseworthy works is beneficial without right faith. X, 598. Let no one boast of his works before faith; once faith has been received, let no one be lazy in good works. IV, 263.

Good works are from grace. X, 239. Works do not precede grace but follow it. VI, 111, 112; X, 1142. Works are from grace, not grace from works. II, 817. A reward is owed to good works if they are performed, but grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed. X, 1133. Only those works are to be called good that are performed through love of God. IV, 838, 1540, 1569. There is one work in which all things are contained: faith working through love. IV, 1149. Good works are performed with rest when faith works through love. III, 655. All our good works are one work of charity. IV, 1148. No one should glory in good works before the grace of faith. III, 2137. Works not performed from grace are either merely human, or sins, or servile works. III, 655. A wicked person cannot possess good works. V, 467. Our root is charity; our fruits are our works. IV, 607. A fruit is not good if it does not arise from the root of charity. X, 217. A good work must be done from the heart, and therefore from love of righteousness, not from fear of punishment. IV, 990. A good work is not one done from fear but one done from love. V, 33. When a person acts from fear and when from charity. V, 792. The works you do with sadness are done from yourself; you do not do them. IV, 1174.

Good works are God’s gifts. IV, 1784; V, 1466; VI, 247. Good works come not from us but from God. III, 1843. For salvation it matters that good works and righteousness come to us from God and not from ourselves. X, 1141.

Works and faith are from God. III, 83. Our works are good because God gives them to us. I, 868. A good work is both God’s and ours. I, 622. Good works come from God and from the human being. III, 654. Good works arise simultaneously from free will and from God’s assistance. III, 1778. Willing and working are what God gives a person when he justifies the ungodly. II, 560. God works in us in such a way that we also work. V, 108, 856. You can perform no good thing unless illumined by God’s light and set aflame by his Spirit. IV, 1175. Our good works belong to God rather than to us. IV, 1783, 1784; VII, 804. The work is ours, but not ours alone; the reward of the work comes from God alone. V, 1464. Unless God assists our good works, we cannot complete them. IV, 232, 757. How we ourselves perform good works when God works in us. IV, 1876. “See your work in me, not mine; for if you see mine, you condemn me; if you see yours, you crown me.” IV, 1783, 1784.

Our good works are to be attributed to God. I, 1078; III, 190. They are not to be assigned to us. X, 879. They are to be attributed to God’s grace, not to our own powers. II, 688. Whoever assigns good works to himself turns aside to the right hand. II, 973, 974. One must not glory in oneself on account of good works. III, 1849. Those who glory in their own works are signified by the latter tablets given to Moses. III, 653. What it means to rejoice in God’s works. IV, 978. The servants of God are, in two senses, God’s works. IV, 1148. The works of the Father and the Son are the same. IV, 1442.

The necessity of good works. IV, 482, 1315. Works are necessary together with faith. IV, 259. The beginning of good works is confession of evil works. III, 1491. A person’s highest work is to praise God. IV, 500. Good works are practiced through abstinence from unlawful desires. III, 1530. Works of mercy are to be practiced in the present time. V, 97, 515, 612, 1053, 1198, 1206. Works of mercy will exist only in this life, not in the future life. V, 91, 97, 235, 617, 1631. Works of mercy must surpass our offenses. V, 1199. The more the tribulations of this world press upon us, the more extensively works of mercy must be practiced. II, 471. What another is less able to do is done by the one who is able, if he loves in the other what he himself does not do because he cannot. II, 507. Only works of mercy are mentioned at the judgment. V, 406. Works of mercy are works of righteousness. IV, 574. They are sacrifices. IV, 574. They are our seeds. IV, 1664; V, 193. Good works are effective for obtaining blessedness. VII, 804. “The work frightens you; look at the reward.” V, 422. The reward of good works is not to be expected in this present time. V, 99. Against those who think their works perish because a perishable reward is not given to them. IV, 1468. “Not from works”: in what sense the Apostle denies that we are saved by works. X, 893. Not from works but from God’s mercy: we are called so that we may believe, and those who believe are enabled to perform good works. III, 2061; *Retractationes*. Works of the Law do not justify a person except through faith in Jesus Christ and God’s grace. II, 892. Justification by faith without works. V, 31. Some works of the Law are superfluous after faith; others are nothing before faith. III, 2137. The works of the Law are divided into two parts. III, 2117. All good works love to be brought into the light. II, 510. Good works done openly have a twofold usefulness. V, 804, 1478. How good works are to be done before people and not before people. V, 303, 372, 803, 804, 1479. For what purpose good works ought to be done before people. IV, 787, 788. We are forbidden to seek our own praise in a good work. V, 1479. What disposition a living person has toward a future work and toward a past work in good works. V, 227. Good works are not always to be interrupted because some people are scandalized by them. II, 1080. Nevertheless, they must sometimes be abandoned with regard to particular persons. II, 1080. The works of the churches by which God is honored are a kind of weaving. III, 879. Human works are called their children. II, 632. Good works are like the children of our life. VIII, 1004. Good works do not benefit those outside the Church. III, 1500. “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done had he lived longer.” II, 985, 986. God will repay each person according to his works. X, 911, 912.

What evil works are. VII, 418. Those who praise evil works are like dogs licking Lazarus’s sores. III, 1350. Dead works must be put to death so that we may live. VI, 208. Works of the flesh. See Flesh. A good work does not involve much labor; an evil work brings labor. IV, 1181. In our evil works, God’s works are good. I, 1180. The occupation by which the works of unbelievers are defended as though they were good. X, 754. Some good works, without which the life of even the worst person is scarcely found, do not benefit the ungodly unto eternal salvation. X, 230. The good works performed by unbelievers are God’s gifts. X, 754. The fact that Polemo was freed from drunkenness through Xenocrates’ philosophical discussion is to be attributed to divine, not human, work. II, 591. How much more is this true when others are converted to God. II, 592.

The great riches of Christians are the needs of the poor. V, 1389.

The Ophites, heretics or Serpentines. III, 217; IX, 589. From where they arose and why they were so called. VIII, 28.

How opinion and understanding differ. I, 1282. What can neither be understood nor perceived gives rise to an excessively rash and foolish opinion. II, 78. The crowd is more inclined to rush into false opinions. I, 955, 1042. The rashness of asserting an uncertain and doubtful opinion scarcely avoids the name of sacrilege. III, 221. The difficulty of refuting an erroneous opinion. VII, 47. It is no small evil, through perverse opinions, not only to be led by the lure of pleasure into committing sin, but also, in order to defend sin, to be turned away from the medicine of confession. II, 1061. If a person is more deeply embedded in false opinions the more familiarly and constantly he wallows in them, this happens much more easily in matters that are true. II, 66. One must not adhere to the opinion and example of the many against the law of God. VI, 344. When contradicting another’s opinion, it must be done without prejudice to charity and truth. II, 289.

To opine is never without fault. VIII, 83.

Ops, the god who brings aid to those being born. VII, 122, 128.

No one desires what lies within his own power of choice. IV, 1509. The figure of a person expressing desire in the Prophets is understood as the foreknowledge of the one announcing it. V, 148. And approval of the divine decree. V, 149.

Optatus of Milevis, bishop of the Catholic communion. IX, 37, 430. The book of Optatus produced by the Donatists. II, 581. They ask that it be read at the Conference of Carthage. IX, 647. Optatus embraces Caecilianus’s vindication rather than his condemnation. IX, 685.

Optatus, bishop. II, 577, 795.

Augustine’s response to Optatus’s question concerning the origin of the soul. II, 857.

Optatus of Thamugadi, Donatist bishop. II, 171; IX, 55, 58, 337, 528, 555, 738, 740. Called Gildonian. II, 198, note (a); IX, 50, 82, 565. Why he was so called. IX, 51, note (a), 55. Optatus, Gildo’s satellite. IX, 76, 338, 340, 504. For Optatus, God is the Count. IX, 277, 281, 286, 340. And faith. IX, 250. Optatus’s statement about his ordainers. IX, 641. Optatus’s cruel deeds. IX, 276. Optatus was loudly proclaimed a robber everywhere. IX, 62. Thief, robber, traitor, oppressor, separator. IX, 288, 340. Optatus the King (*basileus*). IX, 54. Optatus attacked the Catholic Church atrociously and as an enemy, on land and sea, with armed crowds. IX, 316. All Africa groaned under his wickedness. II, 193, 297; IX, 301. For ten years. IX, 257. The Donatists disapproved of Optatus. IX, 50, 51. Yet they retained him in their communion. IX, 51. The Donatists feared to condemn Optatus, a criminal whom they had known for a long time. IX, 250. They tolerated him as long as they feared him. IX, 88. The Donatists anointed the power of Optatus the Gildonian with the oil of flattery. IX, 86. The flatteries, services, and so forth of the Donatists toward Optatus. IX, 277. The Donatists said that what Optatus had done did not belong to them. IX, 531. Through fear of Optatus, the Mustitani and Assuritani compelled their bishops to return to Primianus’s communion. II, 193, 198, 265, 309; IX, 532, 565. Whoever was baptized by him could not be cleansed, even according to the Donatists’ own judgment. IX, 503. Optatus the Gildonian died in prison. IX, 329. The Donatists called Optatus a martyr. II, 265. The Donatists attended his anniversary with great celebration. II, 407; IX, 277.

Optatus, presbyter. II, 223.

The abundance of minds: God. VII, 162, 164.

What reproach is. IV, 856. In the face of reproaches, when the person by whom they are uttered cannot be corrected, nothing remains except to pray. IV, 852. Reproach endured for Christ’s name. IV, 252, 850, 851, 1537.

Orata, a very fortunate man. I, 972, 973. How he was wretched amid his riches. I, 973.

## Orator

The Christian orator is always engaged with a weighty subject. III, 105–106. Let him place prayer and God first. III, 103–105, 120. Let him pursue truth rather than words. III, 119. He ought to refute every objection that can arise. III, 107. Let him act so that he is heard intelligently, willingly, and obediently. [Col. 0475] III, 103–105. Let him pursue clarity, and how he should do so. III, 99–100. In clarity there is a certain diligent negligence. III, 99. It is the orator’s task to teach, delight, and move. III, 101. How these three can be accomplished. III, 101. Teaching and delighting are useless unless the mind is also moved. III, 102. It matters more that the Christian orator speak wisely than eloquently. III, 91. From where one can attain the ability to speak wisely. III, 92. Those who speak eloquently are heard agreeably; those who speak wisely, beneficially. III, 92. Why even those who do not act beneficially are heard beneficially. III, 118. The ecclesiastical orator chooses a good life, but does not neglect a good reputation. III, 119. The Christian orator whose life corresponds to his speech is heard with greater obedience. III, 118. Christ won an orator from a fisherman, not a fisherman from an orator. IV, 372. One is not to be blamed who takes a discourse composed by a more skilled person to deliver before the people. III, 120. See *Preacher, Eloquence, Preacher*.

## Oratio

Prayer is a human being’s speech addressed to God. IV, 1086. Prayer is a sacrifice. IV, 475. Under the name of prayer are understood all the rules of holy desire. X, 300. What need there is to pray to God. III, 1275. If God knows what is necessary. V, 379, 494. Although God knows what is necessary for us, that is no reason not to pray. X, 1017. Because he wishes our desire to be exercised in prayers, so that we may be able to receive what he prepares to give. II, 500. God wishes to give, but he gives only to one who asks; he does not give to one who cannot receive. IV, 1324. What reason we have for praying, and why the angels announce our prayers to God when nothing is hidden from him. II, 568. Our prayers are announced to God, not so that God may be instructed, but so that we may be built up. II, 568. Why God wished that things which he could also give to those who do not pray should be requested from him. X, 1001–1002. God wishes to be asked so that he may be loved when he comes to our aid. IV, 1423. Regarding what we do not yet possess, God commands us to have it, so that he may remind us what we should ask. VI, 443.

Prayer is an argument for the necessity of grace. X, 314. The clearest testimony to grace. II, 766. From God is requested precisely what is demanded of a human being. V, 903. God must be asked to give what he has commanded. IV, 1510, 1581. When we pray, we say nothing other than, “Give what you command.” X, 154. To what extent the Massalians observe the command to pray. VIII, 40.

What the Pelagians thought prayers were necessary for. X, 376, 380–381. The necessity of prayer. X, 151, 317–318. It is asserted against the Pelagians. VI, 443. Prayer is necessary for those who are not led by grace. X, 918. It is necessary for those who gird themselves to do good. X, 918–919. Prayer is necessary for a human being not only so that he may be forgiven, but also so that he may not sin. X, 256. If the will were sufficient for us not to enter into temptation, we would not pray; yet if the will were lacking, we could not pray either. II, 990. In prayer a person recognizes from where he may receive what he wishes to have. X, 317. Prayer reminds us that we need the Lord’s help, lest we place our hope of living well in ourselves. II, 990. From the opinion of those who say that the law can be fulfilled by one’s own powers, it follows that we ought not to pray. II, 595, 761, 763, 775. It is foolish to pray that you may do what lies within your power. X, 256. God’s help must be invoked. V, 895. Prayer is necessary not because of what we have been, but because of what we shall be. X, 531. Prayer and thanksgiving are necessary. II, 851, 856. How prayer differs from congratulation. IV, 80, 1337.

## Orare

What should be prayed for. IV, 1087. We must pray that God give what he commands us to have. VI, 443–444. We must pray that he preserve what has been given and supply what has not yet been given. VI, 444. We must pray that God’s gifts in us may increase. IV, 1048. Let us trust that we shall receive what we have not yet received, since we are not ungrateful for what we have received. VI, 444. How we should ask in prayer for what we have received. X, 997. “Ask nothing from God except God.” V, 1461. “What will anything be to me that you give me apart from yourself?” V, 1469. We have received the remedy of prayer against sins after the integrity of remission. V, 752. We must ask the Lord not to sin. II, 775. The blessed life is to be requested; everything else is to be requested for its sake. II, 497, 499, 503, 505. How temporal and eternal benefits should be requested. V, 497. Those who ask temporal things from God ask for nothing. V, 794. Learn to ask this from God: that you may not fear being heard. V, 1445. Many cry out to the Lord for temporal things; scarcely anyone does so for the Lord himself. IV, 971. Bodily necessities must be requested from God alone, not from demons. IV, 752–753. We must pray that health, friendship, and sufficiency may be possessed, or, if they are already present, preserved. II, 499. Let us pray that, when by God’s gift we have come to sound judgment, we may be able to do what we have wished. II, 990. Knowing from whom you received it, ask him for its completion, from whom it was given that it might begin. II, 990. Those are deceived who think that God should be invoked only in adversity and not in prosperity. V, 482. Evil things are not to be requested from God. III, 1824. It is no small temptation if your petition is against your own cause. III, 1826.

We must pray for the persecutors of the Church. II, 637. We must pray for enemies and persecutors. V, 120, 806. If you have learned to pray for your enemy, you are walking on the Lord’s way. III, 1985. He does an injury to God who asks him to crush his enemy. IV, 436. Our prayer makes alms when it is poured out for enemies as for friends. V, 1044. Why the Church now prays for enemies but will not pray for them at the last judgment. VII, 737. Intercession for a brother is more pleasing to God when a sacrifice of charity is offered. II, 87. Let all the members pray for one another; let the head intercede for all. III, 1985. We are not commanded to pray for certain brothers. III, 1266–1267. Prayer is offered for unbelievers so that they may believe. V, 914–915. How the priest standing at the altar exhorts the people to pray for unbelievers, catechumens, and the faithful. II, 978, 988. The priest prays to God aloud at the altar that unbelieving peoples may be compelled to come to the faith. II, 988. For this reason God makes those who do not yet believe believe through the prayers of believers, to show that he himself accomplishes it. II, 988. The prayers offered by the Church—whether for unbelievers, that they may be converted, or for believers, that faith may be increased in them and they may persevere—are destroyed by the Pelagians. VIII, 48. For whom and against whom prayer should be offered. IV, 248, 438. It is not permitted to pray against anyone. III, 1267. The Church would not pray for the reprobate if they were known to be reprobate. VII, 737.

How useful the assistance of prayers is. IX, 478, 509. How much the prayers of the saints avail with God for others. IV, 1412. Even great men ought to commend themselves to God through the prayers of others. II, 1025. The Lord’s Prayer is effective only for those whose faith works through love. VII, 657. Let the martyrs rejoice over us, since they pray for us. IV, 1141. One who prays for the catholic Church omits no individual. V, 1249. The Church prays for all human beings, yet is not heard for all. VII, 737. For whom the praying Church is heard. VII, 508.

What must be observed in praying. IV, 1351–1352. How one should pray. III, 1274, 1467. We do not know what to pray for as we ought. X, 531. Two things must be avoided by one who prays: that he ask either for what he ought not, or from one from whom he ought not to ask. V, 378. One must pray in the manner Christ taught. IV, 1352. Prayer ought to begin with the praise of God. IV, 1882.

Prayer is twofold, interior and exterior. IV, 404. “Pray without ceasing” is to be understood of interior prayer. IV, 404. Prayer without ceasing is more certainly heard. II, 500. To pray without ceasing is to desire the blessed life from God alone without ceasing. II, 501. The frequent, very brief, and rapidly uttered prayers of the brothers who are in Egypt. II, 501. To pray for a long time when one is free—that is, when the duties of other good and necessary actions do not interfere—is neither wrong nor useless. II, 501. To pray frequently is not to pray with many words. II, 501–502. What it means to speak much and what it means to pray much. II, 501. Many words are to be avoided in prayer. V, 378. More diligent care regarding prayers is found to have been enjoined in Scripture especially upon widows. II, 506. We pray in words at fixed intervals so that we may recognize how far we have advanced in the desire for eternal life and may stir ourselves more ardently to increase it. II, 501. It is fitting to pray only spiritually, for those reborn in the Spirit. II, 502.

Prayer must be offered in the temple of the mind. I, 1195. What it means to pray in closed rooms. I, 1195. Prayer is not rightly offered unless it comes from the innermost heart. VI, 144. When you pray, close the door, lest the tempter enter. IV, 1834. Vocal prayer without attention directed toward God is empty. IV, 1585. What the voice of prayer is. IV, 1809. The prayer of many has sound but no voice. IV, 1809. Prayer is a cry to God, not with the voice of the body but of the heart. IV, 74, 83, 254, 1834. Our prayer scarcely occurs without wandering of mind. IV, 1086, 1585. God’s wonderful kindness in tolerating prayers made with wandering minds. IV, 1086. One who prays with the whole heart cries out when he thinks of nothing else. IV, 1585. Great concentration in prayer expresses the great feeling of the one praying. IV, 1585. Whoever grieves that his prayer is lukewarm, cold, and almost nothing is already praying. VI, 127.

The time for praying is the time of God’s grace. VI, 234. The time for prayer is after the cockcrow. IV, 1587. Concerning the place and manner of prayer. III, 1519. The petitioner’s feeling matters more than the place of petition. IX, 429. If someone praying at the memorial shrines of heretics is heard, he receives either good or evil not because of the merit of the place but because of the merit of his desire. IX, 428. No bodily posture is prescribed for praying. VI, 144. A posture suited to those who supplicate is to bend the knees, extend the hands, and prostrate oneself on the ground. VI, 597. To strike the forehead against the ground. V, 1419. Through these acts the feeling of the heart that preceded their performance increases because they have been performed. VI, 597. When someone cannot perform these acts, he lies prostrate in the most secluded room, where he is pierced with compunction. VI, 597. We pray standing for the fifty days after Easter and on all Sundays. II, 218, 220. Why those standing for prayer turn toward the East. III, 1277. Whether Christians everywhere pray standing during the Easter season and on Sundays, Augustine does not know. II, 220.

We must pray perseveringly. IV, 801. Persistence in prayer is commended. IV, 801, 1539. We must hunger for God; let us beg in prayer before the door of his presence. [Col. 0477] IV, 1895–1896. The prayers of the righteous are accompanied by tears and groaning. V, 195. The groaning of one who prays. IV, 224. The tears of those who pray are sweet. IV, 1683. What kind of prayer is pure. X, 302, 304. The two wings of prayer are fasting and almsgiving. IV, 482. The two kinds of almsgiving. V, 398, 1040–1042. From where prayer receives much assistance. II, 504, 507. Prayer must be assisted by fasts and almsgiving. V, 1046, 1585. This is human righteousness in the present life: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. IV, 482. Through their prayer the humble touch God. V, 267. Prayer should be chaste, so that we desire not what lust but what charity seeks. V, 1044. Prayer is more acceptable the more fully it accomplishes the effect proper to its spiritual nature. V, 1052. It accomplishes this effect more fully the more the mind is suspended from carnal pleasure. V, 1052. Those who have learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be meek and humble in heart make greater progress by thinking and praying than by reading and listening. II, 597. The heart that rightly asks, knocks, and seeks must be devout. V, 568. Life knocks, and the door is opened to life. V, 568.

The best prayer is a righteous life. VII, 653. How quickly the prayers of those who act well are received. IV, 482. Faith precedes prayer. II, 878. Faith is the fountain of prayer. V, 655. The merit of prayer is owed to the faith that was given to one not praying. II, 878, 880. Nothing prays except faith. V, 913. If faith fails, prayer perishes. V, 655. Faith, hope, and charity lead the one who prays to God. II, 504. In faith, hope, and charity, through continuous desire, we always pray. II, 502. Hope and charity pray, and therefore faith also prays. VI, 234. Let prayer always fast from hatred and always feed on love. V, 1044. Faith in Christ is the means of obtaining. III, 1328. No one asks in Christ’s name who thinks of Christ what ought not to be thought, or who asks for something unrelated to salvation. III, 1896–1897. What pertains to the order of salvation is requested in the Savior’s name. III, 1852. We do not ask in the Savior’s name whatever we ask against the usefulness of salvation. III, 1825. Prayer is not righteous except through Christ. IV, 1436. Prayer that is not made through Christ is itself sin. IV, 1436. We pray to him, through him, and in him. IV, 1082. He prays for us, prays in us, and is prayed to by us. IV, 1081; V, 1685. Christ prays and gives what he prays for. V, 1083. Christ prayed in order to teach us to pray. IV, 665. Christ teaches us to pray as a teacher and hears us as a Son. V, 1153. Christ exhorts us to pray through comparisons. V, 410, 618. God has granted the ability to implore, and in order that we might implore, he has stirred our heart. V, 952.

Desire prays even if the tongue is silent. V, 498, 820. A more worthy result follows prayer when a more fervent feeling precedes it. II, 502. Your very desire is your prayer; and if the desire is continuous, the prayer is continuous. IV, 404. Prayer rises from a faithful heart like incense from a holy altar. IV, 1818.

The grace of praying comes from the Holy Spirit. IV, 1539. Prayer is a gift of God. II, 878, 880. Those who wish faith in prayer to come from themselves and everything else to be obtained from God are refuted. V, 913. To pray to God is a gift of spiritual grace. X, 633, 1032. Prayer is the one hope amid the evils of the present age. V, 494, 497. When it falls asleep. V, 498. With what disposition the angels offer our prayers to God. II, 502. God does not allow those who cry out to him to perish in dangers. IV, 440.

## The Lord’s Prayer

The Lord’s Prayer is the rule for asking, given to the apostles by the heavenly lawgiver. IV, 1849. Why the prayer was handed down in words. III, 1275. Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer. II, 503; III, 1277; V, 377; VI, 285. The preface to the Lord’s Prayer. III, 1276. Its petitions number seven in Matthew and only five in Luke. VI, 285. In the Lord’s Prayer, three petitions concern eternal life and four temporal life. III, 1285. The final three petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are to be used against concupiscence. X, 153. The petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are compared with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the Gospel beatitudes. III, 1286. The third petition of the Lord’s Prayer—“Your will be done”—what it signifies. X, 676. The good say sincerely, “Your kingdom come”; the wicked do not say it in the same way. V, 299. The Lord’s Prayer and the Creed embrace faith, hope, and charity. VI, 234. The Creed is handed down first to catechumens, and afterward the Lord’s Prayer. V, 377, 386. The Prayer is recited by the *Competentes* after eight days. V, 400. The Lord’s Prayer pertains especially to the faithful. IV, 1849. The Lord’s Prayer in the celebration of the sacred mysteries. V, 324, 1101. The Lord’s Prayer is said daily at the altar. V, 399. Why it must precede the reception of the Eucharist. V, 127. Who asks for what is not found in the Lord’s Prayer? II, 504. The Lord’s Prayer contains whatever can rightly and suitably be prayed for, and all other prayers are referred back to it. II, 503. All the saints are heard for themselves, not for others. III, 1896. The pattern of desires in the Lord’s Prayer. V, 378. Whoever prays for what cannot pertain to this evangelical prayer prays carnally. II, 503–504. Unless you say the Lord’s Prayer, you are not praying. IV, 1352. If you say another prayer, you will not be heard. IV, 1352. The one who does what he says recites the Lord’s Prayer confidently. IV, 1352. In it is the covenant concerning the forgiveness of debts, by which we too are bound to forgive our brothers. V, 383, 1055, 1556.
