With what disposition “Forgive us our debts” should be said. IX, 63. The Lord’s Prayer concerning the forgiveness of debts is necessary for the righteous. VII, 657. He who dictated the prayers to you is your advocate; if you lie, he is your witness; if you do not correct yourself, he will be your judge. V, 654. The Lord’s Prayer is daily medicine. V, 127. The Lord’s Prayer is daily healing against lesser sins. VI, 228. Our daily cleansing. X, 435. The daily brush by which sins are wiped away. V, 983. As it were, a daily baptism. V, 1064. The Lord’s Prayer removes not every kind of sin, but small sins. VII, 748–749. It removes minor and daily sins. VI, 265; X, 200. If it is said truthfully, it forgives daily sins. X, 1232. It also removes grave deeds if one departs from them through repentance. VI, 265. Through the Lord’s Prayer whatever is done wrong in fasting and almsgiving is forgiven. X, 300. Venial sins are cleansed by works of mercy and prayer. II, 675.

## Those Whom God Hears in Prayer

Whom God hears when they pray. IV, 1390. Who can have confidence that he will receive what he asks. X, 311. God provides many things to those who pray, even anticipating them in prayer. I, 798. Those who remain in Christ receive what they ask. III, 1842. The blind man who had not yet seen with his heart said that the prayers of sinners are not heard. V, 749, 751. God hears only the poor. IV, 864. Being heard follows humble confession. IV, 253–254. Whoever wishes to be heard by God must first hear him. V, 126. The one prayer of an obedient person is heard more quickly than ten thousand prayers of one who shows contempt. VI, 565. People do not receive what they ask because they ask wrongly. III, 1824. We must pray that God not do what we ask wrongly. III, 1826.

Sometimes God, when angry, gives what you ask, and when favorable, refuses what you ask. V, 1567; IX, 429. To some impatient people the Lord God granted in anger what they were asking, just as, when favorable, he refused it to the apostle. II, 505. We must fear lest God, in anger, give us harmful things which, in his favor, he could have withheld. III, 1824. The prayers of demons were heard. III, 2024. God hears the devil more quickly for the purpose of tempting than Job for the purpose of healing him. IV, 1882. The apostle asks and does not receive; the devil asks and receives—why? IV, 173, 1882. Paul was not heard according to his will but according to his healing. V, 1566. How eternal things and temporal things should be requested, and with what disposition. V, 1566. Many are heard and in many ways—not only catholic Christians but also pagans, Jews, and heretics. IX, 429. Outside the Church many are heard for many things, but not for eternal life. IV, 478, 1270, 1704, 1721. How the prayers of the wicked are heard. III, 2024. Many are heard by God with closed mouths, while many are not heard amid great cries. IV, 1604. Some are heard to their condemnation, while some are not heard for their salvation. IV, 173. God hears some and does not hear others according as he knows what is expedient for each. IV, 1088, 1881. What desire God promised that he would hear. IV, 1296, 1888. One who asks for superfluous things is not heard by a favorable God. V, 203, 498. The one who does not ask for earthly things is heard quickly. IV, 1777. God does not abandon a person even when he does not hear him concerning temporal goods. II, 545, 563, 575. God does not hear us concerning temporal things so that we may understand that eternal things are to be desired from him. IV, 483. When God does not remove the tribulations for which we have prayed, let us not think that we are neglected by him, but hope for greater goods. II, 505. When a person would use badly what he wishes to receive, God, in his mercy, does not let him receive it. III, 1824–1825, 1834. God hears for healing, not according to the will. IV, 173, 1883. Do not regard being heard according to your will as a great thing; regard being heard for your benefit as a great thing. V, 1566. God is a father, and he does not give his children what is harmful. IV, 1899. Trust the Father, because if it were expedient for you, he would give it to you. V, 498. Nothing should be requested as though fixed, but only what God knows to be expedient for us. IV, 624. God knows what it is expedient for us to be given; we, however, should consider what it benefits us to receive. IV, 1899. When we love something wrongly, God in his favor refuses what we love; but in anger he gives the lover what he wrongly loves. IV, 202. When we love what God wishes us to love, he will undoubtedly give it to us. IV, 202.

God is present even when he delays; what he delays is present; and by delaying he is present, lest, by fulfilling the will too hastily, he fail to bring complete healing. V, 892. Prayer for a righteous person is easier; for the wicked it labors more. V, 326, 1429, 1433, 1441. When God sometimes gives more slowly, he commends the gifts rather than refusing them. V, 411. God delays giving what he wishes to give so that you may desire the delayed gift more greatly and the quickly given gift may not become cheap. V, 619. Perhaps God delays giving something, but he leaves no one who is hungry. III, 1557. Some things are not refused but delayed so that they may be given at a suitable time. III, 1896. He who cares knows the hour of giving. IV, 1881. If God does not give at the appointed hour, he exercises the one who seeks and does not despise the one who asks. III, 1557. Through prayers God wishes our desire to be exercised, so that we may be able to receive what he prepares to give. II, 502. The prayers of the saints are seemingly repelled by the delay of benefits and the adversity of tribulations, so that, struck as by the blast of a fire, they may blaze more intensely. IV, [Col. 0479] 1118. What we ask in the Savior’s name is delayed only, not refused. III, 1826. The faithful person asks for many things according to the present age and is not heard; but with regard to eternal life he is always heard. IV, 718. How prayers, supplications, and the like differ. II, 635. Supplications are made before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; prayers, when it is being blessed; intercessions or petitions, when the people are being blessed; and after all these, thanksgivings. II, 636.

Common prayer is announced by the deacon’s voice. II, 221. Through common and alternating prayers we accomplish more than through individual and private prayers. Innocentius. II, 788. Prayer before food. X, 176. Prayer for the dead at the altar. I, 780. Prayer for the departed. VII, 737–738. Augustine’s excellent prayers to God. I, 869, 888.

## Oratory

I, 1379. In an oratory no one should do anything except what it was made for, from which it also received its name. II, 960.

## World

The world is signified by the name of Adam. IV, 1236. The regions of the world. VII, 497. The world became Abraham’s possession not through observances of the Old Law but through faith in the Gospel. VII, 522.

The Roman world. VII, 171.

Orcus was the brother of Jupiter and Neptune. VII, 213. Orcus was the receiver of the dead. VII, 196. They hold Orcus to be the earthly and lowest part of the world. VII, 207.

## Ordination

The sacrament of ordination. IX, 109. The blessing of ordination. II, 229. The ordination of the clergy is carried out for the gathering of the people. VI, 394. Those to be ordained ought to be without crime. X, 563. Augustine refuses to impose the hand of ordination on a suspect person, or to introduce him to another bishop on his own commendation. II, 268. When asked whether one baptized in the party of Donatus ought to be ordained, Augustine does not advise it; but he adds: “It is one thing to do something if you are compelled, another to advise that you do it.” II, 1061. At the time of his ordination Augustine poured forth tears. II, 88. Afterward he experienced a burden much heavier than he had thought. II, 88. Once ordained, he beseeches Valerius to allow him to devote himself in retreat to prayer and study, so that he may become better instructed. II, 89. Augustine denies that Pinianus could be ordained in the Church entrusted to him by another bishop unless Augustine had been consulted and had given permission. II, 477. Ministers ordained in whatever places ought to remain in those places. IX, App. 787. The people of Hippo believed that it could not happen that someone ordained among them, even unwillingly, could depart from their city. II, 477. Augustine thought otherwise. II, 477. The sacrament of ordination may not be repeated. IX, 70–72. It is not lost. IX, 109. The sacrament of ordination remains in those who have been ordained. VI, 394. It remains even in one who is removed from office because of some fault. VI, 394. Those ordained even outside the Church are received with their honors. II, 813. The anniversary of Aurelius’s ordination. V, 643. Likewise, Augustine’s ordination. V, 1480, 1482. Peter was the ordainer of Stephen. V, 1365.

## Order

Order is an arrangement assigning to things equal and unequal their proper places. VII, 640. Order is that through which all things established by God are carried out. I, 991, 994. Order is the general good in things made by God. VIII, 553. What order among things is worth. VIII, 397. Everything is administered by God according to order. I, 984, 994. Evils too are contained within it. I, 985. Ordering compels being; disordering, nonbeing. I, 1341. Let order belong to him who knows how to order what he created. V, 1355. We have been fitted into the order of passing things according to our merits. I, 1179.

What is the order of nature in a human being? VII, 629. Order and peace require that a human being first be subject to God, and then the flesh to the human being. IV, 1860. To maintain order and to be maintained by order are not the same. I, 1187. The unjust are ordered justly and the ugly beautifully. III, 150. God ordered sinful humanity to be ugly, but not in an ugly manner. I, 1180. God knows how to order souls that desert him. VI, 333. Whoever orders himself unjustly in sins is justly ordered in punishments. II, 539.

Order is a guide to God. I, 990. The order of things must be preserved so that the soul may act well. II, 539. The order of life and education. I, 1006. That order is to be approved in which better things come first. VI, 326. There is no order when better things are subjected to worse. I, 1231. What is changed for the better tends toward being and order. I, 1348. No one should be disturbed if the prescribed order is disturbed, since it is uncertain what course of action may be more useful. VI, 326. We ought to arrange the things to be done according to our capacity. VI, 326. Let us not rejoice that we have carried out ordered things because they were pleasing to us, but because it pleased God that they be done in this way. VI, 326. Let everyone be ready to put God’s will first. VI, 326. Why order is sometimes called bad. VIII, 558. The books *On Order* were written toward the end of the year 386. I, 977. They were dedicated to Zenobius. I, 979. Why. I, 985.

A letter of the people of Madaura is written under the heading “Order.” II, 1026. To repeat laws in due order. II, 316.

## Childlessness

Childlessness belongs to the fire that consumes what is defective in the love between spouses. VII, 743–744.

## Oreb

Oreb is interpreted as “dryness.” IV, 1053.

## Organ

“Organ” signifies all musical instruments, although it is sometimes used only for those inflated by bellows. IV, 671, [Col. 0480] 1964. Musical organs signify the saints. IV, 1964. The citizens of Jerusalem have their organs: the Scriptures of God, God’s commandments, God’s promises, and so forth. IV, 1764. What the organist is like, such is the organ. V, 1383.

## Orestes and Pylades

I, 697.

## Easterners

Eastern heretics attempted in some manner to associate themselves with the Donatists. IX, 576. Whether they rescinded the judgment they had made concerning baptism is not established. IX, 559. The Easterners relax the fast on Saturday to signify the Lord’s rest, while, because of the humility of the Lord’s death, some Westerners fast; everyone fasts on Holy Saturday to renew the memory of the apostles’ grief over the Lord’s death. II, 150.

## Origen

I, 593; VIII, 667–668. His error was that everything returns to the point from which it deviated. I, 593. Origen’s error concerning the punishment of the devil and the condemned, which he thought would not last forever. X, 325. Concerning the salvation even of the devil. VII, 731. Some assert, and some deny, that Origen thought the devil could obtain God’s mercy. X, 1485. Origen’s opinion concerning the salvation of the devil is refuted. VII, 735. Origen was mistaken because he was too lenient. VII, 735. Pythagoras, the Platonists, and Origen thought that souls had fallen from heaven. II, 718. Origen’s books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). VII, 336. Origen added material from Theodotion to the Septuagint translation. II, 261. He interpreted the Psalms. II, 261. He wrote five volumes on the Epistle to the Galatians, and treats the same subject in Book 10 of the *Stromata* and elsewhere, according to Jerome. II, 252, 254. He asserts that neither Peter sinned nor Paul reproved him insolently, in order to answer Porphyry’s blasphemy. II, 254, 257. John Chrysostom embraced Origen’s and the ancients’ opinion concerning Peter’s being reproved by Paul. II, 254. Augustine asks Jerome to expose the errors of Origen and the heretics. II, 157. Jerome praises Origen remarkably and afterward criticizes him substantially, and on questions that were not insignificant. II, 286. Augustine wrote a book concerning certain opinions of Origen that the Church did not accept. II, 748. Why Origen was rejected by the Church. VII, 731.

## Origenians

The heretics called Origenians, or followers of the “Adamantine Teacher.” VIII, 33. The doctrines of the Origenians. VIII, 33.

Other heretics called Origenians, named after some Origen unknown to me. VIII, 33.

## Original Sin

Original sin. V, 928, 944, 1343. Everyone is subject to original sin. III, 1634; X, 270. Infants. VII, 506. An infant draws original sin from Adam because he was one with him and in him. II, 360. Generation from Adam, because of one offense, places a person under obligation; regeneration from Christ dissolves both that offense and whatever is subsequently added through the human way of life’s wicked works. II, 678–679. To be born from Adam is a necessity arising from condemnation; to be born through Christ is a matter of will and grace. III, 1401. No position concerning the incarnation of the soul should be maintained that denies original sin. II, 733. If souls are created individually for individuals, how do they contract original sin? II, 725. Original sin is both alien and ours. X, 1079. The original bond of condemnation. VI, 277. The punishment of original sin. VI, 107. Jerome established the doctrine of original sin in his book against Jovinian and in his commentaries on Job. II, 723, 730.

Pelagius denied original sin, and the Pelagians with him. II, 723, 865. Zosimus’s letter in which he asserts original sin. II, 865. The baptism of infants argues for original sin. III, 416. Original sin is washed away by baptism. IV, 591. The baptism of infants is not superfluous, because they are bound by original sin. II, 678. In original evil there are two things: sin and punishment. VII, 788, See *Sin*.

Propagation and conformity belong to the original good. VII, 788. Ὁρμή (*impulse, inclination*). VII, 628.

## Adornment

The more the adornments of the outward person are desired, the more they are detriments to the inward person, and conversely. V, 884. Augustine does not wish adornments of gold or clothing to be prohibited by a hasty judgment, except for those who are neither married nor wishing to marry and who ought to consider how to please God. II, 1060. The chief adornment of Christian men and women is good conduct. II, 1060. The wearing of gold, the curling of the hair, and other things of this kind, which are ordinarily employed either for empty display or to entice through beauty, have rightly been criticized. II, 1080. Women may adorn themselves only for their husbands, and this by concession, not by command. II, 1060. If a woman is compelled by her husband through some harsh condition to wear indecent adornment, let her have a humble heart beneath her proud dress. II, 1081.

## Orontius

II, 1071.

## Orosius

Orosius, a Spanish presbyter. I, 648; VIII, 665–666, 669; X, 343. He came to Augustine from the farthest part of Spain, inflamed by zeal for the Scriptures. II, 748. Augustine sent Orosius to Jerome. II, 721. Orosius’s memorandum. VIII, 669. Augustine answered Orosius in one book concerning the Priscillianist heresy and certain opinions of Origen. II, 748. Orosius brought the letters of Heros and Lazarus to the Council of Carthage. [Col. 0481] II, 759. He brought to Oceanus a book in which Jerome discusses the resurrection of the flesh splendidly. II, 779. Jerome calls Orosius his brother and Augustine’s son. II, 752. The eulogy of Orosius. II, 720.

## Orpheus

Orpheus, the theological poet. VII, 572, 597. He was the most renowned of all. VII, 581. He was placed in charge of the rites of the underworld. VII, 572. Whether Orpheus’s prophecies concerning Christ are more suitable for the Gentiles than those of the Hebrew prophets. VIII, 282, 290, 292.

## Orphans

“Orphani,” in Latin *pupilli*, “orphans.” III, 1829. The sword of God’s word makes orphans and widows. IV, 815.

## Orthodox

“Orthodox,” that is, those who follow what is right. III, 127.

## Orthopolis

Orthopolis, the twelfth king of the Sicyonians. VII, 565.

## Ortygometra

*Ortygometra*, a genus of birds not entirely unlike quails. III, 617.

## Mouth

The mouth is twofold: that of the body and that of the heart. VI, 351, 508–509. The mouth of the heart. IV, 1661, 1775. The mouth of the heart cries out many things that are not said by the mouth of the body. VI, 350. The mouth of the heart expresses consent as an inward word. VI, 350. The inner mouth is discerned by the inner ear. VI, 351. The mouth of the body produces nothing except what proceeds from the mouth of the heart. VI, 350. The hidden mouth in the heart, chewing the savory joys of God’s bread. I, 722. Of which mouth the saying “the mouth that lies,” and so forth, is spoken. VI, 509. The mouth of God is his utterance. IV, 1515. A barrier should not be placed on the mouth, but the door of continence. IV, 1819.

A bone, or hidden bone, signifies inner firmness. IV, 1796. In Scripture, bones signify the soul’s firmness or strength. IV, 92, 228, 1297, 1796. In the Lord’s body, all the righteous—firm in heart, strong, and so forth—are called bones. IV, 242, 332, 476, 1297. In Scripture, bones signify patience in faith. IV, 320. The Church’s bone signifies spiritual persons. IV, 492.

A kiss imprinted on another man’s wife is punished by flogging. VII, 726.

The custom of kissing relatives was accepted among the ancients. III, 570. The kiss of peace among the sacraments. V, 1101; IX, 277. A kiss was given to infants at baptism. X, 625.

## Hosea

Hosea, king of Israel, reigned in the time of Romulus. VII, 579.

What the prophet Hosea foretold. VII, 584. The apostles explained what Hosea’s marriage to a prostitute signified. VIII, 459.

## Osiris

Osiris, the husband of Isis. VII, 254, 256.

## To Display

“To display evil” means “to do evil.” III, 502.

## Omens

“Omens” (*ostenta*) is derived from “to display” (*ostendere*). VII, 722.

## Door

The door of the gate is the beginning of faith. IV, 306. The door of our heart has, as it were, two leaves: desire and fear. IV, 1835. The door of the heart must be carefully closed. IV, 1834.

How a Donatist doorkeeper should behave toward strangers. V, 288.

Otium gives opportunity to temptation. VII, 84. Leisure should be used for piety, not idleness. II, 188. In leisure, one should not delight in inactive repose, but either in inquiry or in the discovery of truth. VII, 647. Holy leisure is that devoted to acquiring wisdom. III, 1791. When holy leisure must be abandoned so that Christ may be preached. III, 1791. The love of truth seeks holy leisure; the necessity of love undertakes just business. VII, 647. A great withdrawal from the tumult of passing things is necessary for a person to come to fear nothing. II, 74. It is possible to be deified in leisure. II, 74. The business of the idle. IV, 1463, 1916.

The Manichaeans do not eat eggs. VIII, 37.

God himself takes care of the sheep. V, 283. Who are God’s sheep? V, 315. The sheep to whom Christ was sent. V, 484. Who are Christ’s sheep and who are not. III, 1742. Christ’s sheep are the predestined. III, 1725. None of Christ’s sheep perishes. III, 1743. Christ said to the Jews that they were not among his sheep because he saw them predestined to eternal destruction, not to eternal life purchased by the price of his blood. III, 1725. There are many of Christ’s sheep from the Jews, but they are not his only sheep. V, 42. Not only the shepherd, but the sheep also enter through the door. III, 1726. What it means to enter and go out through Christ. III, 1726. Before Christ’s coming, Christ’s sheep heard his own voice, not the voice of strangers. III, 1723. Whether those who were wandering and listening to the voice of strangers were Christ’s sheep. III, 1724. Not all who heard Christ’s voice were sheep. III, 1723. The security of the sheep brought back through Christ to the fold. V, 1647. The sheep are saved when they hear the shepherd’s voice. V, 307. The lost sheep, once found by the shepherd, is still sought by him. IV, 1595. The sheep of the people. IV, 1224. Shorn sheep signify the perfect. IV, 1224. “Sheep and oxen” in the Psalms are rightly understood as all holy spiritual creatures. IV, 114. The sheep’s hope, health, and rest are in God alone. V, 285. Wandering sheep are not neglected without danger to the healthy. V, 278. Christ demands that love be shown to his sheep. V, 1180. The shepherd is to be loved, the hired man tolerated, and the thief avoided. V, 756. See Shepherd. We are the sheep of his pasture and of God’s hands. V, 295. In hell there are sheep whose shepherd is death; in heaven there are sheep whose shepherd is life. IV, 556. Which sheep Christ’s fold contains. IV, 1418. Three persons come to the fold: the shepherd, the thief, and the hired man. V, 756.

An oxymoronic statement. X, 1480.

Uzziah, king of Judah. VII, 583.

[Col. 0482] P.

The agreement to forgive, so that we may be forgiven. V, 1054.

That one must repent of sin: this is the voice of nature. VIII, 109, 110. A place for repentance for every kind of crime is not denied in the Church. V, 448. The Cathari deny repentance. VIII, 32. Certain heretics became such by denying that repentance should be granted for sins. V, 1559. And they were excluded from the Church. V, 1559. The permission of a place for repentance in the Church stirred up the reproach of the pagans against Christians. IV, 1300, 1301. A reply is made to pagans who mock repentance. V, 1559. No one can pass from error to truth, or from any sin, whether great or small, to correction without repentance. II, 347. Three reasons for undertaking repentance. II, 1088. Three kinds of repentance. V, 1537, 1550. The first is that which precedes baptism. V, 1537, 1550. The second is that which here belongs to all and is perpetual. V, 1537, 1556. The third is more severe, for deadly sins. V, 1542, 1558. What kind of repentance is forgiven by God. III, 1266. It is not enough to change one’s conduct unless one also makes satisfaction to God. V, 1548.

Repentance is a certain anger directed against oneself. V, 133, 1358. Do you wish to flee from God? Flee to him; do you wish to flee from one who is angry? Flee to the one who has been appeased. IV, 1913. The soul, punishing itself, should be pierced with remorse, lest, condemned in God’s judgment, it be tortured. IV, 80. That everlasting salvation which was shamefully lost through pleasure is rightly recovered through pain. III, 289. It is divine justice that the one who willingly lost what he ought to have loved should, with sorrow, lose what he loved, while the Creator of all natures is praised everywhere. III, 385. The affliction of the penitent is the punishment of sin, although it is medicinal and salutary. III, 728. The pains of the penitent are like the pains of a woman in labor. IV, 536. The person who, hoping in God’s mercy, thereafter guards against sinning so that he begs forgiveness for past sins, appeases God. IV, 1913. The sacrifice of righteousness through repentance. IV, 81.

The more humble form of repentance. VI, 220. The salutary remedy of repentance is to attribute sin to no one but oneself. VII, 444. How necessary the humility of repentance is. V, 1535. Even for those who have been justified. V, 1538. The humility of repentance before justification. IV, 1786. Through the humiliation of repentance one approaches God. IV, 314. When the humility of repentance precedes, God is joined to human beings. III, 879. One must not return to one’s former life after repentance. V, 1035. Perverse repentance. V, 126. Repentance that must not itself be repented of. V, 1182. Those who relapse after baptism must embrace repentance. V, 1545. Not only in secret, but in the form in which it is practiced in the Church. V, 1711. When repentance must be undertaken in the knowledge of many or even of the whole congregation. V, 1545. To undertake repentance according to the custom of the Church when the cause is worthy of it. VI, 271.

Public repentance is undertaken for monstrous sins, not for slight ones. VI, 636. Mournful and lamentable repentance. VI, 18. Who are to be compelled to it. VI, 18. Priests subject those whom they have freed from punishment to the most humble repentance. II, 655. The ashes of repentance. IV, 1301, 1933. The public repentance of Theodosius. V, 1710. It belongs to Christian discipline that one should neither despair of anyone’s correction nor bar anyone’s access to repentance. VI, 503. Some completely closed the way of repentance to adulterers, while others allowed it, with the bond of unity remaining intact. II, 341. The Church rightly and deservedly maintains that peace should be granted to adulterers who repent. II, 342. Augustine was deeply distressed that a place of repentance had been denied by certain brothers to a Donatist returning to the Church. V, 1358. Why a place of repentance was granted to those who would not practice repentance and were devoted to death. X, 1427, 1428. The practice of repentance when, because of a crime committed, someone is separated from the body of Christ. VI, 262. Some asked for a place of repentance; others, having been excommunicated, were reduced to that place; and some do not wish to rise from it, as though the place had been chosen. V, 1111. No one is compelled to seek a place of reconciliation. V, 1359.

The time for repentance. V, 126. The periods of repentance are rightly established by those who preside over the Churches. VI, 263. In the practice of repentance, not so much the measure of time as of sorrow must be considered. VI, 262. The manner of undertaking repentance and the measure of satisfaction must be received from those who preside over the sacraments. V, 1545. The Lord leads the penitent, like Lazarus, to confession; thereafter the ministry of the Church completes the rest. V, 1558. The penitent must observe the physician’s instructions and endure the pain of the incision. V, 1270. Yet he is not thereby already healthy. V, 1270. Sins committed after baptism can be healed through repentance. VI, 254. Augustine acts alone with Marcellinus, lest there be anything that required greater and more distinguished repentance. II, 650. Repentance must be embraced when God scourges. VI, 699. When God does not punish, he has not lost his power, but demands repentance from you. V, 471. We ought to repent of this life, because it is subject to corruption and temptations. V, 1537. Let us now say fruitfully, “All things pass away like a shadow,” lest we say unfruitfully, “They have passed away.” IV, 284.

The postponement of repentance is extremely dangerous. IV, 1301. Those who practice repentance are said to have sinned against God; those who refuse to practice it are said not to have sinned against God. III, 773. Against those who take from others an example of neglecting repentance. V, 1545, 1547. Barren repentance is of no benefit. V, 408. What the fruits of repentance are. V, 408. Repentance is fruitful only in this life. VII, 739. Fruitless repentance. VI, 205. After judgment it is fruitless; now it is fruitful, when correction is free. V, 150. There will be repentance on the day of judgment, but it will be fruitless. IV, 284, 357. The repentance of the present time is medicinal pain; the repentance of the future time is penal pain. IV, 689. Repentance after judgment is torturous, not healing. V, 131. Late repentance. III, 865. Let the voice of Scripture make you repent; for at the voice of the present Judge, you will repent without cause. V, 150.

Repentance is a gift of God. II, 828; VI, 271, 421; X, 503. Repentance is given by God. X, 1422. It belongs to the gift of the Holy Spirit, because it makes the sinner displeased with what he has done. IV, 596. The call to repentance must be referred to the hidden judgments of God. X, 920. By what means God urges people toward amendment. V, 150. God brings some people to repentance through goodness, while according to his judgment he does not bring others to it. X, 793. Through the preaching of repentance people are called to Christ and the Church is gathered. IV, 1963. That forgiveness is not given to penitents according to grace, but according to their merits and labor: the teaching of Caelestius. X, 345. Ambrose teaches that repentance is accomplished through the Lord’s mercy and assistance. X, 382. What repentance from dead works is. VI, 208. Manure applied to a barren tree is a figure of repentance. V, 1183. Why David’s repentance was accepted by God, but Saul’s was not. VIII, 442.

Who in former times were properly called penitents. VI, 228. Those properly called penitents in the Church. II, 1086. These are people who have sinned after baptism in such a way that they deserve to be excommunicated and afterward reconciled. II, 1088. The penitent should do what benefits himself for salvation and others as an example. V, 1545. It belongs to the penitent both to acknowledge and to punish his own sins. V, 132. The penitent is a person angry with himself. V, 187, 649. He is himself his own punisher. V, 1273. Tears are the penitent’s blood. V, 1542. The penitent is a true human being. III, 831. The penitent is partly righteous and partly a sinner—and in what sense. IV, 1825. How the penitent is joined to God, and why it is advantageous that God intercede for him. V, 187. Penitents are among the members of Christ. IV, 1295, 1537. The penitent must strive to destroy all sins. V, 153. If the last day does not find you victorious, let it find you at least fighting. V, 153. The rest is easily forgiven when one is found striving. V, 153.

The reconciliation of penitents. VII, 674. True repentance receives forgiveness of sins even through a bad cleric. V, 466. The penitent’s resurrection and release are represented in Lazarus. IV, 1306; V, 595. The laying on of hands upon penitents, the imposition of prayer, and their examination. V, 1111. Penitents abound. V, 1111. When they are examined, they are found to be living badly. V, 1111. What ought to be a place of humility becomes a place of wickedness. V, 1111. When hands are laid upon them, an extremely long line is formed. V, 1111. An admonition to penitents. V, 1111.

In what sense God is said to repent. IV, 1416, 1460, 1723; VI, 141; VII, 539. Repentance in God is called a change of decision. V, 152. Why repentance seems less fitting to God than foreknowledge, anger, and similar attributes. VI, 141.

Faustus alleges paganism against both Jews and Catholics. VIII, 369.

Who are called pagans. I, 648. In what respect they differ from the Manichaeans. VIII, 376. From where the error of paganism arose. VII, 208. What pagans think about the beginning of things and what they think about the gods. VIII, 376. They worship the sun. IV, 189. One God is celebrated by pagans under various names. II, 82. The religion of the pagans was wholly occupied with dead human beings. VII, 253. They regard dead human beings as gods. V, 1249. Augustine calls pagans “demon-worshipers.” II, 159. Pagan priests are called dead, not only because of their impiety but because of their dead gods. IX, 65. The custom of playing and dancing was accepted in pagan festivals. III, 473. The games and rites of pagan worship are most shameful. II, 415; VII, 50. They are most cruel. VII, 52. Pagans become worse through imitation of their gods. II, 414. Pagans do not excuse their sacrilegious rites and images on the grounds that they interpret elegantly what each thing signifies. II, 378. The concord of pagans who quarrel about the worship of their gods. VI, 712. Pagans did not possess precepts of concord. II, 529.

The supposed virtues of the pagans are not true virtues. X, 747. See Unbelievers, Virtue. The virtues of pagans are barren. II, 710. For pagans it is of no benefit—not that they are already good, but that they are moderately bad. IV, 196. Even the respectable conduct of pagans comes only from God. II, 591. The prosperity of the pagan state is luxurious, licentious, and sacrilegious. II, 533. Pagans are heard with respect to certain temporal matters. IV, 1270. Pagans are thieves and robbers. III, 1720. Their teaching about virtues and vices is harmful. III, 1720. Pagans are in darkness. IV, 196. Pagans want Christ to have felt nothing against their gods, but to have worshiped them by magical rites. III, 1069. Pagans were compelled by their oracles to praise Christ. III, 1052. The pagan excuse for not becoming Christians. IV, 116. Pagans attribute the cause of evils to Christians. IV, 1033, 1034. Their complaints against the Christian religion arising from the devastation of Rome. V, 505, 1356. The pagan scandal caused by the world’s sufferings. V, 503. Pagans should not be drawn away from the Christian religion by the discord of Christians. VI, 713. Pagans believe inwardly but are ashamed to confess it. V, 1278. The pagans’ remarkable conversion to Christ. III, 123. Pagan superstition is destroyed. V, 166. Images were ordered to be broken by recent laws. IX, 44. Sacrifices are punished capitally. II, 326. Many pagans were converted to the true God through fear of the imperial laws. II, 334. From temples, idols, and sacred groves that are overthrown, a Christian may not appropriate anything for private use. II, 185. It is not lawful to seize the property of pagans. V, 963. Christians are distinguished from pagans by good works. V, 1025. Good Christians ate with pagans rather than with bad Christians. IV, 1289, 1290. The weakness of pagans is compared with the steadfastness of martyrs. IV, 1829. Pagans who come to Christ can become bishops. IX, 478. Pagans are called “the trees of the forests.” IV, 1234. Dead stones. V, 163. Paulinus wrote against the pagans. II, 159. Augustine requests this work of Paulinus. II, 181.

What παιδεία (“discipline”) means in the sacred Scriptures. IV, 1547, 1548.

The Palestinian judgment in the case of Pelagius. II, 816, 826, 827, 831, 876, 979. Which propositions Pelagius anathematized at the Palestinian council. II, 827, 979. See Pelagius.

The palate is called οὐρανός (“heaven”). VII, 200.

Palatinus, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Augustine advises Palatinus how he may progress and persevere in the Christian wisdom he has chosen. II, 989.

Straw has a cooling power, so that it preserves snow, and a warming power, so that it ripens unripe fruit. VII, 712, 719. Heretics are signified by the names “straw” and “weeds.” III, 127, 144. The unjust are also signified. IX, 29. Straw signifies those who seek carnal things, whether they are inside or outside. V, 1175. Straw signifies the envious and unjust person whom the wind of temptation carries away; opposed to him is the weighty people. IV, 339. Straw can become grain. V, 1175.

To sing a παλινῳδίαν, that is, a recantation. II, 157, 237, 244, 290.

Palladia was healed at Hippo at the memorial of Saint Stephen. VII, 770.

Palladius. II, 774.

Palladius, bishop of Tibagita. IX, 697.

Hercules wept for the dying Pallas. VII, 86.

Philosophers wearing cloaks are called Cynics. I, 942. The Cynics used a cloak and a club. VII, 428.

Pallor, a Roman god. II, 84; IV, 1396; VII, 125. Introduced by Hostilius. VII, 130, 190. The Romans built shrines to Pallor and Fever. III, 1053.

Pammachius. VIII, 574.

Pammachius brought his Donatist colonists to the Catholic Church. II, 225.

Why Pan was called Lycaeus in Arcadia. VII, 574.

Pancarius. II, 1068.

Pancarpus. VIII, 574. It is customarily eaten at public entertainments. VIII, 598.

Pancratius, bishop of Balianum. IV, 381.

To perform the pancratium means to box. IV, 679.

Pannonius, bishop. II, 759, 780.

Bread signifies everything necessary for nourishment. III, 496, 499, 509, 514, 652; V, 389, 394. Bread nourishes a human being and kills a hawk. I, 1350. Bread and unmixed wine were carried to the graves of the dead. IV, 554. Banquets were also celebrated there. IV, 554. In Scripture, bread appears both in a good and in a bad sense. III, 79.

God is bread. IV, 1726. God, the bread, descended to earth so that he might become milk for us. IV, 1726. The unfailing bread that ends our need is the Trinity. V, 620. The bread of heaven is Christ. V, 726. So that human beings might eat the bread of angels, the Lord of angels became human. V, 701, 726. Human beings and angels partake of the same bread, but they eat it in different ways. IV, 1742. The living bread that refreshes us on the way will satisfy us in our homeland. IV, 1814. Christ the bread must be eaten with labor and sweat. IV, 1784. The heavenly bread seeks the hunger of the inner person. III, 1607. Pieces of bread signify the members of Christ. IV, 1934. The bread that refreshes and does not fail is righteousness, truth—Christ himself. V, 969. The bread of angels and human beings is truth, wisdom, and the power of God. IV, 1742. The bread of the soul is the word of God. IV, 386, 1165, 1297. The bread of the heart is righteousness. IV, 562. The bread of truth is bitter to sinners. IV, 88. The bread of sorrow is for penitents. IV, 1786. The bread of the land of the living. V, 265.

The daily bread is twofold: bodily and spiritual. V, 389, 401. Daily bread is the word of God. V, 381, 389, 395. The readings and sacred hymns. V, 389. The Eucharist. V, 381, 389, 395, [Col. 0485] 401. Whatever is necessary for our soul or body in this life. V, 395, 401. The three loaves given to a friend. V, 620. Whoever asks God for three loaves asks to be filled by the vision of the Trinity. IV, 1324. Elijah’s hearth-baked bread was something different from ordinary bread. III, 377. Why Christ, when hungry, did not make bread from stones. IV, 1164, 1165. The multiplication of the loaves in the wilderness. IV, 1164. In the multiplication of the loaves, the Lord’s omnipotence was, as it were, a fountain of bread. III, 528. What the miracle of the five loaves signifies allegorically. III, 1600; VI, 48. And the miracle of the seven loaves. V, 581; VI, 51. The mysteries in those who were satisfied with the seven loaves. V, 581. Why the Manichaeans offered bread to a beggar. VIII, 160.

Paulinus sends five blessed loaves to Romanianus and Licentius. II, 126. Paulinus sends bread to Alypius. II, 100. And to Augustine. II, 103. And Augustine in turn sends it to Paulinus. II, 125.

The pantomime. III, 64; V, 1020. Pantomime pleases the unjust more easily than God. IV, 277. Pantomimes are theatrical and dishonorable. IV, 1347.

The pope. The preeminence of the Roman episcopate. X, 551. The Roman pontiff is first in rank among the other bishops. X, 648. When two councils were sent to the Apostolic See and replies came from there, the case of Pelagius was ended. V, 754. See Roman bishop.

The Papirian family among the Romans. VII, 69. Note (d).

Parable: what it is. IV, 852. The distinction between parables and propositions, or προβλήματα (“problems”). IV, 983. Some have thought that the parable of the ten virgins does not refer to Christ’s final coming. II, 922. The Lord’s parables are to be understood according to likeness and unlikeness. III, 1358. See Likeness.

Paraclete is interpreted as “comforter” or “advocate.” III, 1828, 1868.

Paradise properly means a wooded place. III, 482. A garden. V, 1505. “Paradise” is a general name for every place where life is enjoyed in happiness. II, 834. Every spiritual region, as it were, where the soul is well, may rightly be called paradise. III, 482. Some understand the paradise planted in Eden bodily, others spiritually, and others in both ways. III, 371. Augustine embraces the third opinion. III, 371. The location of paradise is most remote from human knowledge. III, 378. Where the paradise in which the human being was formed is located is sought apart from the danger to faith. X, 398. The supreme delight of paradise. IV, 1771. Some wish paradise and its features to be understood only spiritually. VII, 394. Certain Catholic interpreters have understood what Scripture relates about paradise as referring to spiritual paradise. X, 1599. Scripture shows the bodily paradise more clearly. X, 1599. Paradise can and should be understood according to the literal sense. III, 373, 555. What paradise would have been according to the Pelagian heresy, and how false it would have been. X, 1089, 1310, 1328, 1332, 1408, 1457, 1458, 1537. What the Pelagians’ paradise of delights would have been, even if no one had sinned. X, 1537. The Pelagians wish to introduce concupiscence into paradise. X, 803. Julian is forced to fill God’s paradise not only with human lusts but also with torments. X, 1560, 1561, 1564, 1571, 1572. And with deaths. X, 1581, 1583, 1585. He also places in paradise not only the punishments of death but deadly illnesses. X, 1594, 1598. The Pelagians, while denying original sin, are forced to admit every natural defect in paradise. X, 1457. In fact, the Pelagians place there all the defects of bodies and souls. X, 1537. The Pelagians’ opinion about paradise is comprehensible to no one. X, 1434. The blessedness of paradise would have admitted neither death nor so many bodily evils. X, 1307. The condition of the human being in paradise with respect to the senses. X, 797. Why the human being was placed in paradise, to work and guard it. III, 379, 380, 381. Whether the first parents needed food in paradise. X, 772. In paradise, children would have been begotten without lust. X, 818. In paradise, if anything useful were learned, it would be learned without labor. X, 1516. In paradise you did not cry out, but praised; you did not groan, but enjoyed. Cast outside, groan and cry out. IV, 225. The human being was expelled from the earthly paradise. III, 213. Paradise was both bodily and spiritual. VII, 419; X, 172. The spiritual and moral exposition of paradise. VII, 394, 395. What the delights of the earthly paradise signify allegorically. III, 202. By the bodily paradise in which Adam was, both the life of the saints now conducted in the Church and the life that will exist eternally after this one were signified. III, 478. The Apostle called the third kind of vision “paradise” and “the third heaven.” III, 478. Paradise is the blessed life. III, 202, 214. Whether the paradise to which the Apostle was caught up was in the third heaven. III, 482. Paradise promised to the thief. II, 712. How the thief was with Christ in paradise on the day of Christ’s death. II, 833. The thief could have been introduced into the paradise where the body of the first human being had been. III, 376. The Seleucians deny visible paradise. VIII, 41. Paradise is a type of the Church. X, 798. The Church was called paradise. III, 442, 478. In a human being, a certain joy of a good conscience is paradise. III, 482.

How the paralysis of the inner person is healed. IV, 385. What the paralytic lowered through the opened roof to the Lord signifies. V, 277. The paralytic allegorically. III, 1334. How the soul, loosened from good works, seeks Christ. III, 1334. The paralytic healed in baptism. VII, 764. A paralytic was restored to health at an oratory in which earth brought from Jerusalem had been buried. VII, 765.

The Jews also call Parasceve “the pure supper.” V, 1090.

The Paratian forest. II, 430; V, 1090.

Frugality should be joined to fasting. V, 1043.

God spares the wicked by hidden justice. IV, 1204. God spares in different ways. III, 645. Christ spared no one in speech, so that there would be people whom he might spare in judgment. IV, 1197. Unless God first spared through mercy, he would not find anyone whom he could crown through judgment. IV, 1282. Do you wish God to spare you? Do not spare yourself. V, 1358. It makes a great difference with what intention each person spares. II, 660. Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor everyone who beats is an enemy. II, 323. One who spares can be cruel; one who strikes can be devout. V, 111.

Paregorizare, that is, “to soothe” or “mitigate.” IV, 1638. Note 2. We are daily soothed by God’s medicines. IV, 1638.

Parentalia (ancestral rites). IV, 554; V, 1601.

When the first parents were created. III, 409. In what the sin of the first parents consisted. III, 432. The first parents believed that God would easily forgive their sin. III, 446. As soon as Adam and Eve transgressed the commandment, they were stripped inwardly when grace departed. III, 446. The very intimacy with God that had given the first parents confidence before sin weighed upon them after sin. III, 448. Why the eyes of the first parents were opened. III, 445. The opening of Adam’s and Eve’s eyes is not to be understood figuratively. III, 446. The first parents could have enjoyed the knowledge of good and evil if they had approached the tree at the proper time. III, 452. If they had not sinned, neither they nor their descendants would have died. III, 395. How this would have been so. III, 396. They began to die on the day on which they ate, and so forth. X, 1583. See Tree of life.

The first parents, even if they had not sinned, would nevertheless have begotten children. VII, 430. For the first parents there could have been honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage bed in paradise. III, 395. In immortal bodies there could have been such a condition that children would be born solely through the affection of holy love, with no concupiscence of corruption. III, 293, 395, 399. The first parents did not possess the appetite for carnal pleasure that these bodies now possess. III, 398. Why they did not have intercourse in paradise. III, 395. They did not beget children before sin. VII, 434, 435. They are rightly visited in the evening. III, 447. The fact that children are born under condemnation is not to be attributed to their parents. X, 809.

How parents should conduct themselves toward their children. IV, 1205. It is the natural order that children serve their parents. III, 590. The son ought not to obey his father in this one matter: if he commands something contrary to the Lord. IV, 875. The father is to be honored because he is a father, and God is to be honored because he is God. IV, 1685. Parents sometimes disown wicked children so that they will not be ashamed of them. III, 2132. Whether children are to be punished for the sins of their parents. III, 765. Christ taught by his own example that the iniquities of parents cannot harm their children. VIII, 440. How the sins of parents pertain to their children. IX, 633. And that God repays them to the children. VIII, 137, 138. To which children the sins of parents are repaid, and to which they do not bring harm. IV, 1437. Formerly it belonged to parents to give names to their children. V, 351.

Not to acknowledge or honor one’s parents is doglike. V, 69. How parents are to be honored. V, 603. A son who insulted his mother was punished by divine vengeance together with his other brothers. V, 1443, 1444; VII, 769. How greatly the curses of parents against their children are to be feared. V, 1445. The Gospel does not contradict the commandment about honoring parents. VIII, 136. Why parents and relatives are to be hated. III, 1249. How they are to be despised for Christ’s sake. I, 615. Parents are not despised with any impiety because of the proclamation of the kingdom of God. VIII, 136. The love and rejection of parents are commended in both Testaments. VIII, 137. To what extent the affection of parents and relatives is harmful. II, 1055. To what extent it should be ended. II, 1056, 1057. The groans of the carnal mother are opposed to the groans of Mother Church. II, 1057. Whoever wishes to give his possessions to the poor must first distribute them to his parents if they are poor. II, 1059. To what extent parents and friends are to be loved. I, 1238. To what extent love of parents is pure or impure. VII, 746. Christ ordered the love of parents; he did not abolish it. V, 1512. Two parents lead to death, and two to life. V, 154. The father and mother of mortal humanity allegorically. IV, 198. If we do not harm but love our parents—God and the Church—inheritance will follow. V, 154.

Pariatores. V, 1191. Note (b).

A full compensation for all Christ’s sufferings. IV, 731.

The pain of a woman giving birth is the punishment of sin. X, 1560, 1563, 1564. Whether animals suffer pain at the time of giving birth is not established. X, 1563.

The wall. Christ made one wall out of two; heretics make two out of one. IV, 1223. A whitewashed wall signifies hypocrisy. IV, 1229.

Parietinae means the same as ruins. IV, 1298.

Paris, son of Priam, king of the Trojans. VII, 82. Note (f). Paris’s adultery with Helen, the wife of Menelaus. VII, 81. Offended by Paris’s adultery, the gods abandoned Troy. VII, 82. The judgment of Paris is fabulous even to the pagans themselves. VII, 568.

Parmenianus. V, 1587; IX, 33. Bishop of Carthage among the Donatists, successor of Donatus. I, 637. Parmenianus confirmed Donatus’s error. V, 279. The Donatists greatly praised Parmenianus’s eloquence. IX, 446. The arrogance of Parmenianus and the other Donatists. IX, 546. Parmenianus’s letter to Tychonius. IX, 107, 108. In replying to Tychonius, Parmenianus restrains him but does not refute what he wrote. II, 342.

The Parmenianists are the same as the Donatists. VIII, 32.

The parish of the Church of Calama. VII, 433.

“Parish” used for “diocese.” II, 953, 955.

The patricide of one’s country contains every crime. I, 953.

A part is ugly when it does not accord with its whole. I, 689.

From where *parta*, *reperta*, and *comperta* are derived. VIII, 968, 972.

Parthenius. II, 94.

By participating in divinity we become immortal. IV, 1906.

To divide. It is now a peaceful custom among human beings that, when they divide earthly possessions, the elder makes the division and the younger chooses. VII, 498.

The labor of childbirth results from sin. X, 405, 1448. Childbirth with groaning is the punishment of the sinful woman. X, 1178. On the pain of women in labor. X, 1577. Women in labor, whether the pain is greater or less, nevertheless suffer; and this pain is either the punishment of sin, or pain existed in paradise. X, 1578.

Small things are not to be measured by their size but by the wisdom of their maker. VII, 335.

What kind of children would have been begotten in paradise if no one had sinned. X, 1332. The Pelagians cruelly defend infants. X, 472, 473. Julian defends infants in such a way as to separate them from the Savior. X, 1478. The Pelagians refuse to acknowledge that unbaptized infants are subject to the condemnation of the first human being. I, 598; X, 394. The holy Fathers taught, without suspicion of the Manichaean heresy, that infants are subject to original sin. X, 1212. Infants are subject to original sin. II, 871. Infants are shackled by the sin of origin. III, 1695; X, 188, 189, 470, 471, 1154, 1215, 1216, 1217, 1240, 1241, 1242, 1250. Infants are subject to sin because they derive their origin from the one in whom all sinned. X, 1123, 1124. The sin of infants comes from Adam. X, 463. Infants belong to the sin through which death entered the world. X, 1228. Infants are bound by the contagion of the first parent. X, 871. Infants themselves are poisoned by the serpent’s bite. X, 145. Because of original sin, infants are transgressors. IV, 1574. Infants are born from concupiscence, and concupiscence is evil. X, 736. Infants are born evil not through God’s creation but through the defect of a nature corrupted by sin. X, 1506. Just as infants are accounted righteous through regeneration, so they are accounted unrighteous through generation. X, 1307. Because infants are defiled through generation, they must be cleansed through regeneration. V, 906. Even if an individual’s own sins do not harm the parent after conversion, they nevertheless harm the parent’s child if the child is not reborn. X, 177.

The Pelagians say that infants possess sins of their own through free will. II, 820, 821. In infants there is no sin belonging to their own life. X, 147. In what sense infants are guilty by the will. I, 608.

Whether infants, at birth, belong to God or to the devil. X, 705. Original sin holds infants under the devil’s power. X, 427. Infants are not improperly subjected to the devil through sin. X, 465. Before they are baptized, infants are under the devil’s power. X, 838. Why. X, 1402, 1404, 1557. The Pelagians denied that infants are rescued from the power of darkness. X, 441. And in this they are heretics. X, 1343, 1378. Infants are rescued from the power of darkness. X, 829, 841. Through the sacraments. X, 1300, 1303, 1305, 1307, 1385. The very form of baptism declares that infants are subject to sin. X, 145. The sacraments of the Church themselves show that infants are rescued from the power of darkness. X, 407, 408. Exsufflations. X, 1504, 1506. And exorcisms. X, 1506. Infants are exsufflated and exorcized: why. VI, 628. See Baptism, Exsufflation, Exorcism. The soul of an uncircumcised infant cannot be cut off from the people without guilt of sin. X, 1206, 1210. Sacraments are provided for infants even before circumcision. X, 809.

Regeneration is necessary for infants. V, 657, 944; X, 132, 133. It is ruinous and deadly not only to the infant’s body but also to the soul to depart this life without baptism. X, 191. The infant would have perished without baptism. X, 145. This has always been held firmly and certainly by the Church. X, 191. Infants cannot be freed from original sin except by baptism. II, 678, 683. Infants are baptized for the remission of sins. X, 177. The universal Church has held from ancient times that infants obtain remission of original sin through baptism. X, 190. Infants too die to sin and are made alive in baptism. [Col. 0488] X, 1215, 1216, 1217. Infants die to sin in baptism; therefore they are guilty. X, 827, 828, 829, 830. Infants both are dead in sin and die to sin. X, 830. Through baptism, which is the wondrous grace of God, infants are compelled to be holy and just. X, 1506. They are conformed to Christ’s death. X, 177. Infants themselves also renounce the world in baptism. X, 1267. Infants believe through the faith and answer of those who carry them. V, 1346; X, 505, 570. And they are called believers. V, 1343; X, 123, 1078. To those wounded by another’s deed, help is given through another’s faith. V, 950, 1342. Infants are counted among believers and the faithful. X, 187. They can also be said to be called to repentance. X, 123. For infants, to be baptized is to believe; not to be baptized is not to believe. X, 132. How infants become believing or unbelieving: through those who believe or disbelieve. II, 871, 984. The faith of those answering for them in baptism must be orthodox. V, 951. Whoever presents an infant for baptism must share the Catholic faith. X, 146. Some Pelagians held that infants believed through those by whom they were presented. II, 870, 890. Certain people wrongly inferred from the Gospel that infants are enlightened as soon as they are born. X, 129, 130. Why the Pelagians say that infants should be baptized. X, 705. Infants cannot have eternal life without participation in the body and blood of Christ. X, 394. To what extent eternal life is owed to those reborn. X, 1133. Certain sacramental things are administered even to infants, who are still weak. IV, 784. The baptism and communion of infants. V, 943. Christ’s blood is administered to an infant so that it may have life. X, 1154. Infants eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood. II, 985. Infants who have not eaten Christ’s flesh will not obtain eternal life, according to Innocent. II, 785, 826. Whether parents harm baptized infants when they try to heal them through sacrifices to demons. II, 359. It is not counted as guilt against infants that they receive baptism while resisting it. II, 841. They are so ignorant of what they do that they are not even judged to have done it. II, 841.

Infants are born wretched. X, 147. See Evils, Wretchedness. Reason, as though still quiet and almost asleep, yet implanted and in a certain way sown within them, lies hidden in infants. X, 130. Ignorance and weakness of mind and body in infants. X, 147, 180. How great is the ignorance of infants. X, 148. In these shadows of ignorance the child’s soul lies not only unlearned but also unteachable. X, 149. From the deepest ignorance they advance toward babbling foolishness—which will not remain—as though progressing toward knowledge and speech. X, 148. Infants are neither wise nor foolish. I, 607. Infants pass from infancy to wisdom through the intermediate stage of folly. X, 795. Infants are weaker than animals. X, 150. This weakness of the body corresponds to weakness of mind. X, 150. The weakness of the flesh in infants is punitive. X, 150. Augustine asks Jerome why infants suffer the punishments of this life. II, 727. Why infants are born wretched according to Julian. X, 1353, 1354. His opinion is absurd and makes God unjust. X, 1574. The wretchedness of infants arises from original sin. X, 1179, 1187, 1191, 1332. They would not be in paradise. X, 1336. The punishments of infants would be unjust if they were innocent. X, 1175. It would be a great injustice if infants were oppressed by a heavy yoke without the merit of sin. X, 1201. The punishment of infants is unjust if original sin is denied. X, 1506. Whoever denies original sin cannot say with what justice infants suffer such great evils. X, 1505. If infants did not possess guilt merited through their origin, whatever evil they suffer would be unjust. X, 1334. God would appear unjust if he inflicted such great evils on infants who carried no sin at all. X, 697. Those who say that infants suffer such great evils without the merit of sin blaspheme God’s justice. X, 1300. God’s equity in punishing infants because of the defect of their origin. X, 1301. The death of infants results from the sin of the first man. V, 906. On the death and torments of infants. I, 1303. Whether these torments benefit the infants themselves or their parents. I, 1304. Infants would not be born with vices if they were not liable to original sin. X, 709. A heavy yoke lies upon infants, not without merit. X, 1194. That heavy yoke is unjust if original sin does not exist. X, 1199, 1200. And if Adam’s sin is not imputed to them. X, 1192. The fact that even baptized infants sometimes suffer attacks from demons arises from the merit of original sin. X, 840. The killing of infants, justly commanded by God, demonstrates original guilt. X, 1424. The infants consumed in the burning of Sodom are an argument that original sin exists. X, 1556. The gifts of grace necessary for salvation would not be denied to infants if they had no sin. X, 1076. Whether infants should not be counted among those whom God wills all to be saved. X, 760.

The Pelagians separate infants from the grace of Christ. X, 1187, 1190, 1193, 1210, 1211. And from the kingdom of God without any merit of sin. X, 1188, 1191. The grace of Christ also pertains to infants. X, 1190, 1191, 1192. The Pelagians confessed that infants needed redemption, but refused to state that the remission of sins was necessary for them. X, 185. In what sense Coelestius confessed the redemption of infants. X [Col. 0489] 395. Infants need reconciliation, which takes place through Christ. X, 870. Infants belong to the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s death as sinners. X, 1215. The Pelagians deny that infants need a Savior. X, 1305. They even dare to deny that infants are to be saved by the Savior. X, 571, 572. Infants need a Savior. V, 944. The Pelagians deny that Christ is Jesus for infants, except in the same way as he is for every mortal creature. X, 1345. Christ is also Jesus for infants. V, 943, 1334; X, 1077. Christ is the Savior of infants. X, 179. Julian inconsistently says that Christ died for infants while they are nevertheless not liable to original sin. X, 1213, 1214. Infants are bound by original sin because Christ did not die for those who had no sin whatsoever. X, 825.

From where infants are to obtain righteousness. X, 1182. Just as infants die in Adam, so they are made alive in Christ. X, 1171. Without any exercise of their own will, infants belong to the first and the second Adam. X, 1235. From Adam infants derive the guilt of sin and the punishment of death, while from Christ they receive participation in righteousness and the reward of eternal life, although in neither case have they done anything good or evil by their own will. X, 1554. Infants die in Adam and are made alive in Christ without any works of their own will. X, 1292. In the regeneration of infants, the will of those receiving it neither precedes, accompanies, nor follows. II, 820. The Holy Spirit dwells in baptized infants, even though they do not know it, because he secretly acts in them so that they may be his temple; and he brings this to completion in those who progress and persevere. II, 840, 841.

The Hieracites do not wish infants to belong to the kingdom of heaven. VIII, 38. It is an error—one anathematized by Pelagius—to say that infants have eternal life even if they are not baptized. II, 826. The Pelagians promise salvation and eternal life to unbaptized infants outside the kingdom of God. X, 570. Life outside the kingdom of heaven is promised them in vain, but condemnation remains for them. II, 871. Unbaptized infants cannot have life; why this is so. X, 978. Infants are condemned because of original sin unless they are regenerated. I, 649; V, 1339; X, 679. Those who are not joined through Christ’s baptism to his body and members belong to condemnation. X, 189. They remain in perdition and darkness. X, 132. God’s wrath remains upon them; they have been judged and will be condemned. X, 187. Unbaptized infants will be in condemnation with the devil. X, 140. Unbaptized infants undergo the punishment of the second death. X, 570. They are tortured by punishments. II, 723, 727. Nevertheless, in the condemnation of all, they will suffer the mildest punishment. X, 120. And the lightest. X, 809. Augustine seeks the reason for the condemnation of infants and reports a certain opinion on the matter. II, 730, 731. Why an unbaptized infant proceeds to condemnation: the reason may not seem sufficiently weighty because it is not found, not because it does not exist. V, 1339. If infants did not bear original sin, they would not justly be excluded from the kingdom of God. X, 715, 1191. Separation from the kingdom of God is a great evil, and this is not imposed on infants without merit. X, 840. God would be unjust if he condemned infants who were not liable to sin. X, 721. The whole Church of Christ agrees concerning the condemnation of those infants who have not been regenerated. X, 1191. Pelagius’s opinion concerning infants who die without baptism. X, 395. There is no third place besides the kingdom and punishment. X, 1073. Infants are sent either to the kingdom or into eternal fire. V, 1337. Whether infants who die before or after receiving baptism will rise again. II, 730. What the resurrection of infants will be like. V, 1140. Infants too will render account of their own bodily deeds before Christ’s tribunal. X, 839. Since baptized infants are counted among the faithful and believers, they are not judged. X, 146. Only infants who do not yet have works of their own, whether good or evil, will be condemned solely on account of original sin, if the Savior’s grace does not assist them through the bath of regeneration. II, 971. Infants receive good or evil according to what they have done through the body. II, 984. That grace is given freely is proved by the case of infants, who do not possess the use of the will and are not distinguished through free choice. II, 820, 826, 984, 985. Some infants are vessels for honor through grace, others vessels for dishonor through judgment. X, 1249. Why, out of two infants, one is brought to grace while the other is suffocated beforehand is a profound and inscrutable matter. V, 177, 905, 907. An infant who died before baptism was restored to life through Stephen’s prayers so that it might receive the sacraments. V, 1446. Infants cannot merit punishment or grace through free choice. II, 820. We ought to speak all the more earnestly on behalf of infants because they can do so little for themselves. X, 199.

Infants, that is, the humble. V, 436, 440. Who are the infants and sucklings in the Church? IV, 110. Infants in faith should not be sent into a premature passion. III, 629. Note. Infants, that is, the carnal. V, 156. The Scriptures are adapted to such people not so that they may remain carnal, but so that they may progress. V, 156. Infants are designated by the name “earth,” but as they grow they will become heaven. IV, 1486. The infants of Babylon are newly arising evil desires. IV, 1773. An excellent comparison involving a mother cherishing her infant. V, 156. Various fears are employed to restrain the vanities of infants. VII, 785. The blows and insults directed at infants are pleasing and delightful. X, 148. Yet no prudent person would approve of their being incited to these things out of a desire to provoke laughter and through the vanity of their elders. X, 148.

Let us feed Christ by living well, and he will feed us by granting us to live forever. IV, 568. It is one thing to be born of the Spirit and another to be nourished. V, 454. Christ’s twofold feeding of the people: the first from five loaves, the second from seven; the mystery of each. VI, 48, 49, 50, 51.

Pascentius publicly declares that Augustine did not dare to state his faith to him. II, 1038, 1041, 1049. In the words with which Pascentius stated his faith, he altered them as often as he repeated them. II, 1038. In the morning he had wished his own words and Augustine’s to be taken down by notaries, but after lunch he no longer approved. II, 1038, 1041, 1042, 1049, 1050. Pascentius praises Auxentius and anathematizes Arius and Eunomius. II, 1039. When Pascentius said that he had found Augustine far inferior to what rumor had proclaimed, Augustine’s reply. II, 1041. Pascentius wanted distinguished men to be present at his conference with Augustine. II, 1042, 1049. Other insults by Pascentius against Augustine. II, 1050. What Augustine replies to them. II, 1051. Augustine does not write Pascentius’s name in his letters to him. II, 1038, 1049, 1050. With what intention. II, 1049.

“Pascha” is a Hebrew name, not a Greek one. IV, 842, 1609, 1789. It signifies “passage” or “transition.” III, 1785. “Pascha” comes not from the Greek πάσχειν, “to suffer,” but from a Hebrew word signifying “passage” or “transition.” II, 205; III, 1785; IV, 841, 842, 1609, 1789; VII, 522. The Jews try to understand that a kid also must be taken for celebrating Passover. III, 609. Those who were unclean because of a dead person postponed the celebration of Passover to another month. III, 722. What Passover prefigured. IX, 290. Passover was a figure of Christ’s passion. VII, 322. The Passover of the Jews was a shadow of the true Passover. III, 1758, 1785. The truest Passover was celebrated in Christ. V, 844. The true Passover is Christ’s sacrifice. III, 1785.

The annual solemnity of Passover. IV, 171. Passover is enacted both in the sacrament and in remembrance of what took place. II, 205. The passing over signified by this word, “Pascha,” is now enacted in us through faith, hope, and charity. II, 205, 206. The agreement of the Old and New Testaments concerning the celebration of Passover and Pentecost. II, 217, 218. Passover was generally not celebrated among the Manichaeans, and occasionally only by a few with very tepid observance. VIII, 178. How and when the Tesseradecetitae celebrate Passover. VIII, 31. Why our Passover does not coincide with the day of the Jews’ Passover. VIII, 503. Christians do not observe days, years, months, and seasons, although they celebrate Passover according to the reckoning of the sun and moon. II, 209. They observe the arrangement by which the Sabbath coincides, something the Jews do not observe. II, 211. The Council of Arles judged that Passover should be observed throughout the whole world on one day. IX, App. 787. The Church’s custom established observance of the forty days before Passover. II, 220. Let us celebrate the vigil of Passover outwardly and inwardly, so that God may speak to us in his readings and we may speak to God in our prayers. V, 1088. The vigil of Passover is like the mother of all holy vigils. V, 1088. On this night the hostile world and the reconciled world keep vigil. V, 1088. Christian strength does not allow the one, nor demonic strength the other, to sleep during this celebration. V, 1088. How great Augustine’s fatigue was during the vigil of Passover. V, 1442. At the solemnity of Passover the story of the three youths is sung in the Church. IX, 330. And that of Daniel. IX, 332. Note (a). After the reading of Daniel’s story at the holy solemnity, they respond “Amen” and make the sign of the cross. IX, 322. Note (a). During the fifteen days of the Passover festivals, lawsuits cease. V, 1201. The period after Passover is spent in praise, with the fasts relaxed. IV, 1937, 1938. During the paschal season Christians relax their fasts, pray standing, and sing “Hallelujah,” which is a sign of the resurrection. II, 218. Augustine does not know whether Christians everywhere pray standing on the paschal days and Sundays. II, 221. The time before Passover signifies the tribulation in which we now are. IV, 1937. The octave of Passover. V, 1196. They complete the sacraments of infants. V, 1198, 1201. In celebrating Passover, the three days of the crucified, buried, and risen Christ must be observed: what the cross signifies we enact in the present life; what burial and resurrection signify we enact through faith and hope. II, 215. Passover signifies the life to come. IV, 1938. When Christ passed to the Father, hope was given to the members in the head of what was to follow for them. III, 1785. The paschal festival makes even those more fervent who are more sluggish during the rest of the year. IX, 330.

Paschasius. IV, 376. Bishop of Vicus Augusti. IV, 381.

Our pastures. V, 1647. True pastures in the other life. III, 1727, 1742.

Πάσσαλος, “stake.” VIII, 42.

Passalorynchites. VIII, 42.

The sparrows nesting in the cedars of Lebanon: whom they signify. [Col. 0491] IV, 1371. In comparison with a sparrow, any stallion is found to be extremely cold. VIII, 198. The Sparrow signifies Christ in his resurrection. IV, 1300.

The Lord’s passion is described in Psalm 68. IV, 846. The mysteries of the Lord’s passion are explained. V, 1084. Christ’s passion is noted under Pontius Pilate, both as an indication from which the chronology may be established and as a means of further commending Christ’s humility. V, 1070. Christ’s passion was prefigured by Jacob’s wrestling with the Angel. VII, 518. By Noah. III, 111. By the troubled water of the pool. III, 1528. The rosy evening sky resembles Christ’s passion. III, 1327. The Lord’s passion became a stumbling-block to many. IV, 1397. The Lord’s passion signifies the present life, and his resurrection the future life. IV, 1938. By his sufferings Christ demonstrated that it is not the gifts that seem to be promised in the Old Testament, but eternal things, that should be desired. IV, 1146.

How many blessings the Lord’s passion produced. IV, 745, 746. The Lord’s passion is the price of the whole world. II, 264. It is the root from which the glory of the Church proceeded. V, 258. The annual celebration of Christ’s passion. IV, 170, 171. The time of Christ’s passion is now the most festive time of the whole world. VIII, 179. On the anniversary of the Lord’s passion, Psalm 21 is sung. IV, 172, 178, 179. The Lord’s passion is read solemnly. V, 1084. But only according to Matthew. V, 1107. Augustine once wanted it to be read each year according to all the Evangelists; consequently the people were disturbed. V, 1107.

Christ’s sufferings are to be imitated; a Christian must not seek pleasures. V, 275. By imitating the Lord’s passion, the poor will be satisfied. IV, 545. The example of Christ’s sufferings is set before the afflicted. IV, 366, 373. Christ’s passion is an example of patience. VIII, 542. The cup of the passion is bitter and health-giving. V, 1455. The bitterness of the passion must be drunk until the bitterness of this age passes away. IV, 551. Why the bitterness of the passion was endured with joy by the saints. V, 1366. The Lord’s passion is like a potsherd with which sins are scraped away. III, 826. In what sense Christ’s sufferings are not in Christ alone and yet are only in Christ. IV, 730. Christ’s sufferings are our sufferings. IV, 406. Christ the Lord suffered willingly, we by necessity; he through compassion, we by our condition. IV, 333, 1104. No one shares in Christ’s sufferings without charity. V, 923. The burden of sufferings is heavy for weakness but light for charity. X, 901. See Christ.

A passion is a movement of the soul against reason. VII, 242. The Platonists supposed that passions arise in souls from earthly bodies and mortal limbs. VII, 711. To admit passions in the gods is a fiction of the poets. VII, 261, 262. Human weakness is not free from passions. VII, 258, 261. The Platonists or Aristotelians think that passions can befall the wise person; the Stoics deny it. VII, 258. The Stoics do not regard passions as vices if they have no power against the virtue of the mind. VII, 261. The Stoics said that the wise person necessarily suffers passions but does not yield to them, whereas the fool yields. VII, 258, 259, 261. When the Platonists and other philosophers speak about passions, they dispute more about words than about things. VII, 259, 260, 261. All the viciousness of human conduct is contained in four passions. VII, 408. The four passions of the soul are nothing other than love. VII, 410. Folly or misery causes passions to exist in human beings. VII, 242. The disturbance of the passions rules over fools and evil people. VII, 263. The disturbance of the passions indicates misery. VII, 267. The source of good and evil passions. VII, 410. In Latin, especially in ecclesiastical usage, *passio* has ordinarily been understood only in a condemnatory sense. X, 469. Christian religion does not so much analyze the passions as their causes. VII, 260.

True religion commands that passions be put away. VII, 242. Holy Scripture subjects the passions to the mind so that they may be moderated and turned to the uses of righteousness. VII, 260. By what method the mind does not permit passions to prevail within it against reason. VII, 260. The wicked and pagans restrain their passions only through pride. VII, 416. Whoever already serves the law of God in his mind dies to his passions. VI, 62. How the passions are to be moderated by temperance. I, 1328. Mortified passions are called holy, chaste, and good loves; the unmortified are called disturbances, lusts, and desires. III, 188. What evils proceed from the unmortification of the passions and what goods from their mortification. III, 188. By resisting the passions, the mind exercises the kingdom of virtue. VII, 260. The wise and good govern their passions in such a way that they would rather not have them than conquer them. VII, 263. See Disturbance.

Who are called passive. VIII, 167.

There are two aspects of pastors: one by which they are Christians, the other by which they are prelates. V, 270, 296. Good pastors are made from good sheep. V, 287. There are many good pastors, although none approaches the power and goodness of the Pastor of pastors. V, 765. There is one good shepherd because all the good are in one. V, 287, 763, 765. A bad pastor is bad through his own wickedness; a good pastor is good only through God’s grace. V, 1484. Who is a hireling pastor and who is a chaste one. V, 759. The hireling pastor fleeing. V, 760. Few are pastors; many are hirelings. V, 760, 762. How hireling pastors are useful. V, 760. A pastor is not one who is prepared for certain things but not for others, but one who is prepared for every good work. V, 760. The suitable pastor is one who is able to lay down his life for the sheep. V, 1354. He loves the sheep in such a way that he can die for them either in deed or in affection. V, 1354. Pastors feeding not the sheep but themselves. V, 270. The pastor is commanded to lay down his life for his sheep. III, 1733. When pastors have laid down their lives for their sheep, the one Christ himself has laid down his life. III, 1733. There is one pastor in the Church. III, 1730. There are two kinds of pastors in the Church: some care for Christ’s flocks, while others delight in their own temporal honors and secular advantages. II, 951. Pastors who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ are dead. V, 281.

The duties of the pastor and of the sheep. V, 796. What benefit there is in explaining the pastor’s duties to the people. V, 607. Instruction belongs to the pastor’s office. II, 635. The other pastors of the Church have been entrusted with what was entrusted to Peter. V, 1354. This is to feed in Christ: to feed in Christ and with Christ, and not to feed for oneself apart from Christ. V, 287. It belongs to pastors not to be silent; it belongs to the sheep, even if the pastors are silent, to hear the pastor’s words from the Holy Scriptures. V, 282. When evil people cannot speak good things, how can a bad pastor be heard? V, 473. A bad pastor is to be heard not in what he brings from himself but in what he brings from God. V, 283. It belongs to the pastor to explain difficult passages of Scripture. V, 716. The deeds of bad pastors are thorns, but their words are grapes—though from the vine, that is, from the cathedra. V, 762. It speaks about them, not they themselves. V, 761. The pastor’s voice must be heard with trembling. V, 295, 296. Those who listen to the pastor are rescued from the teeth of wolves. V, 313.
