The pastor’s voice is one in which the sheep hear Christ alone, not a stranger. III, 1725. The pastor must hear with trembling both what is said concerning pastors and what is said concerning sheep. V, 296. Augustine avoided the question of swearing, lest by admonishing and commanding he make more guilty those who would not listen. V, 979. It belongs to a pastor who seeks his own interests not to rebuke the erring. V, 273. The pastor’s negligence kills the person whom he does not admonish. V, 281. The one dies justly, and the other is justly condemned. V, 281. If, fearing to cause harm, he addresses people while promising them earthly happiness, he destroys them. V, 275. What makes a pastor more sluggish in rebuking. V, 961. Very few contradict the pastor by speaking, but many by living badly. V, 961, 963. It belongs to the pastor to recall wandering sheep to the fold. V, 278. The pastor must even be importunate toward those who neglect their salvation. V, 245, 246. What Augustine’s attitude was toward the wickedness of his people. II, 1063, 1064. Why a pastor must not conceal someone’s conduct because of that person’s merits toward him. II, 1074. Why he must strengthen weak sheep. V, 275, 276. Pastoral charity places the weaker before the stronger not according to the order of loving but according to the order of giving help. II, 537. The pastor’s sorrow over the evils of the sheep benefits him; yet he wishes nothing to be advantageous to himself unless it is advantageous to them. V, 514. It belongs to the pastor to say to his hearers with Augustine: “If I do not remain silent, I shall free my soul; but I do not wish to be saved without you.” V, 125. Likewise: “My delight in this life is nothing except your good life.” V, 128. Insofar as it depends on him, the pastor kills good sheep by living badly. V, 274. Although they live, he is nevertheless a murderer. V, 275. How the death of the sheep is charged to the pastor. V, 281. A sheep is not safe when it follows a wandering pastor. V, 282. How sheep are safe under bad pastors. V, 281. Bad pastors in the Church are like the Pharisees. V, 750. How God recalls sheep from bad pastors. V, 282. Hope must not be placed in good pastors. II, 951, 952. The good works of the sheep are consolations amid pastoral dangers. V, 611. Augustine counts no joy, comfort, or relief from his dangers except the good life of his people. V, 1112. What comforts the pastor in dangers is that he is helped by the prayers of his people. V, 915. The devout pastor’s vow. V, 124.

How dangerous an account pastors must render. V, 796. What account the pastor must render concerning the sheep. V, 762. When the pastor’s account concerning the sheep is complete. V, 763. The pastor’s burden must not be cast off. V, 513. Augustine discloses the scruples of pastoral care by which he himself was distressed. II, 352. The reverence due to the pastor. V, 611. Pastors have been given the power to receive milk. V, 272. Let them take milk in such a way that it benefits the sheep. V, 272. Pastors should receive from the people support for their necessities and from the Lord the reward of their stewardship. V, 273.

Patelana, the goddess appointed over the husks that open so that the ear may emerge. VII, 119.

“Father” and “Abba” signify the same thing. IV, 1012, 1419. Why the Apostle places them together. IV, 1012, 1419. The Arians, who call only the Father God, are refuted. VIII, 738. Why the Arians called only the Father God. VIII, 716, 718, 728, 738. The Arians believed that the Father was not God by nature. VIII, 778. The Father is the true God by begetting truth, not by participating in it. II, 1047. The Father is the source of the whole deity. VIII, 908. In the divine persons the Father is not alone but has a likeness. III, 244. The Father begot what he is. VIII, 723. The Father was able to beget what he is. V, 771. The substance of the Father and the Son is not different. VIII, 749. The Father is what the Son is according to substance, not according to what is said in relation to another. IV, 845. In the Trinity the Father is spoken of not in relation to himself but in relation to the Son; in relation to himself he is called God. IV, 845. Scripture shows that the Father begot the Son equal to himself. VIII, 764, 766. The fact that the Father begot a Son equal to himself is also shown from the births of animals. VIII, 761. The Father would not have begotten a Son equal to himself either from inability or from envy. VIII, 762. Whether the Father is not himself Wisdom but only the father of Wisdom. VIII, 924, 933. This is a very difficult question. VIII, 934. The Father is not merely the father of virtue and wisdom but is himself virtue and wisdom. VIII, 935, 936, 937. The Father and the Son together are one wisdom, just as they are one essence, although they are not together one Word. VIII, 936. Why the Father is not similarly the begetter of his own greatness, goodness, and so forth. VIII, 925, 933. With what praises the Arians extol the Father. VIII, 728. Why, according to the Arians, the Father alone should properly be called blessed and powerful. VIII, 729. Why he alone is wise. VIII, 730. Why he alone is immortal according to the Arians. VIII, 731, 733. The Arians called the Father alone incapable of suffering. VIII, 813. Even the Manichaeans do not say that the Father is invisible to the Son. VIII, 764. According to the Arians, the Father alone is invisible, while the Son is visible to the Father, though not to the heavenly powers. VIII, 728, 739. This dream is refuted. VIII, 745. Why some defend the view that the Father alone is invisible, while the Son and Holy Spirit are visible. VIII, 867. The Arians did not wish the Father to have appeared in any way, even through a created creature subject to him. VIII, 812, 813. It is excessively rash to say that the Father never appeared to the patriarchs or prophets through any visible forms. VIII, 866, 867.

Some words in Scripture belong to the Father alone; which they are. VIII, 857. How the Father speaks to the Son. III, 1386, 1689. No one knows this. VIII, 692. The Father’s command is his Word. VIII, 838, 839. From the Father’s temporal words addressed to the Son, the Son learned nothing. VIII, 803. The Father is not called “unbegotten” in Scripture. II, 1010. How the eternal Father eternally begets the Son. III, 1560. Although the Father begot the Son willingly, it does not follow that the Father’s will existed before the Son. VIII, 685. The works of the Father and the Son are the same. VIII, 694. The Father does not do one thing and the Son another; the Trinity performed the same works. V, 703, 746. The Father never does anything without the Son. VIII, 617. Whatever the Father God did, he did only through the Son. V, 702. The Father and the Son are one principle. VIII, 785. There is great love between the Father and the Son. III, 1508.

Why the Father alone is not said to have been sent. VIII, 686. The Father was not incarnate. III, 1667. The Arians called the Father the God and Lord of Jesus Christ even before the incarnation. VIII, 733, 734. The Father is not God’s God, but God is Christ’s God. VIII, 721. God the Father can be called the King of our Lord Jesus Christ. IV, 821. In what respect the Father is greater than the Son. VIII, 746. The Father is not greater than the Son because, being begotten by no one, he begot a Son equal to himself. VIII, 786. Christ called the Father greater than himself according to the form of a servant. III, 1835, 1837. Why the Father is said not to judge but to have given judgment to the Son. III, 1670; VIII, 842. The Father will be invisibly present with the Son in judgment. VIII, 787. What “the bosom of the Father” means. VIII, 764. The Father’s right hand, at which the Son sits, is eternal happiness. VIII, 692. The Father is not dishonored by an insult to the Son. V, 772.

God is our Father. V, 409. God is both our Father and our mother, and in what sense. IV, 208. For faith and eternal salvation, the Father is none other than God. IX, 627, App. 833. According to the age of this world, the devil is our father and Babylon our mother. IV, 208.

The head of a household’s concern and discipline regarding his family. IV, 599. The sin that does not displease you in your son pleases you. IV, 599. See Parents. A father is pious even when he strikes and cruel when he spares. V, 111. The head of a household ought to fulfill the episcopal office in his own house. III, 1768. The head of a household urges everyone in his family, as though they were sons, to worship and win God’s favor. VII, 644. He ought to take precepts from the law of the state by which to govern his household. VII, 645. An example of rejecting a father who gives bad advice, while preserving the honor due to him. V, 1284. Anyone is called someone’s father not only if he has begotten him but also if he has adopted him. VIII, 215, 216. Adoptive fathers beget more chastely in the heart those whom they cannot beget in the flesh. V, 348.

With what attitude Faustus censured the deeds of the patriarchs. VIII, 440. The Manichaeans’ calumnies against the patriarchs. VIII, 403. The patriarchs and prophets are defended against the accusations of the Manichaeans. VI, 395; VIII, 417. The chastity of the ancient fathers, even when they had several wives. V, 345, 347, 349. Even if the patriarchs had been lustful and cruel, they would still have been better than the god of the Manichaeans. VIII, 465. Why it is commended in the patriarchs that they were keepers of livestock. III, 589. Why the patriarchs and prophets reigned here. VIII, 449. Not only their speech but also their life was prophetic. VIII, 417. In them, both what they said and what they did [Col. 0494] were heralds of the Christ who was to come. V, 31. By believing in Christ, whom they proclaimed beforehand, they belonged to the Church. VI, 313, 314. We are sons through imitation of the patriarchs. IV, 1402. Some think that Christ released the patriarchs and prophets from the pains of hell; Augustine disapproves of this. II, 711.

Who are called “fathers” by Catholics. IX, 627, App. 833. The writings of the Fathers must be distinguished from the authority of the canon. II, 339.

The Paterniani, or Venustiani, heretics. VIII, 46; X, 800.

Paternus. II, 224.

Paternus, proconsul. V, 1411.

The Patricians. IX, 589.

The Patripassians. V, 448; IX, 589. The heresy of the Patripassians. V, 356. Faith is set against the doctrine of the Patripassians. V, 357. The Church removed the Patripassians from communion with the saints. V, 357.

To suffer. It is one thing to suffer punishment and another to suffer injury. IV, 1894. We suffer nothing in this life except as a consequence of that death which we merited through the first sin. IV, 398. Whatever God permits you to suffer is the scourge of one correcting, not the punishment of one condemning. III, 1441. Whatever we suffer in this life is to be attributed not to folly but to God’s plan for our healing. IV, 770. Whatever we suffer and whatever God bestows on us, we receive for consolation and suffer for testing. IV, 917. What we suffer here is God’s wrath. IV, 977. Why do you love to have what Christ had if you fear to suffer what Christ suffered? IV, 1250. Whoever strives to progress begins to suffer; whoever does not suffer does not strive to progress. IV, 1599. All perfection consists in contending for the truth until death and enduring every evil for the supreme good. IV, 1561. A person suffers both inwardly from himself and outwardly from those among whom he lives. IV, 405. When a Christian suffers, he must not readily turn against the person from whom he suffers as though out of hatred; rather, he must turn to prayer so that he does not lose love. IV, 632. It can happen that someone who confesses Christ suffers for the sake of human glory. IV, 490, 491.

What patience is. VI, 21, 613. God’s patience toward us. V, 467. Why God’s patience bears with the wicked. VI, 334, 343. We must not abuse God’s patience. V, 297.

## True and false patience

V, 1287. Not everyone possesses patience who endures every kind of pain with the greatest fortitude. VI, 368. False patience is earthly, animal, and devilish. VI, 619. The human will may suffice for it. VI, 619. The strength of false patience. VI, 618. It borrows its strength from worldly desire. VI, 622. It is like the stupor of an illness, not the strength of holiness. VI, 622. To glory in this is madness. VI, 622. Patience is worthy of punishment so much greater, the more it subjects the instruments of the virtues to vices. VI, 613. Patience is the companion of wisdom, not the servant of lust; the friend of a good conscience, not the enemy of innocence. VI, 611. Let patience praise God, not avarice; charity, not greed. VI, 633. How much the wicked suffer. VI, 611. The patience of the wicked is not patience but hardness. VI, 613. The patience of schismatics who endure evil so as not to deny Christ is to be praised. VI, 623. It benefits them in undergoing punishment more tolerably, not in attaining the kingdom of heaven. VI, 624. It is a gift of God. VI, 624. But it is the gift of the disinherited, not of sons. VI, 624. The cause for which one suffers distinguishes true patience from false. VI, 611.

The Lord now requires patience from us. V, 298. The necessity of suffering has rightly been imposed upon us. VI, 617. Endure, for you were born for this; endure, because perhaps you yourself have been endured. V, 298. Let the cause of patience be chosen well. V, 1453. Patience and long-suffering exist only in adversity. IV, 271, 1171. Patience in tribulations. IV, 480, 738, 1853. Patience is more easily preserved as long as we suffer outside the flesh. II, 552. Patience is especially praised in death undertaken for the sake of justice or scorned: why. X, 183. How evils are to be borne patiently. VI, 662. Those whom we cannot correct are to be endured patiently. IV, 633, 1276, 1328, 1329. Patience would not have been praiseworthy, but negligence blameworthy, if a bishop beaten by schismatics had not sought help from the Emperor for the Church entrusted to him. II, 806. Each person ought patiently to endure, while preserving the teaching of the truth, what he cannot correct. VI, 228. What right patience is, and how useful. VI, 611. Wisdom finds no place where there is no patience. V, 825. Without patience there is no hope of future life; without gentleness, patience cannot be preserved. V, 860. Patience benefits both soul and body. VI, 614. The exercise of patience in soul and body. VI, 614. The greater struggle of patience when the devil rages. VI, 615. One must beware lest patience be lost through the desire for revenge; it is more precious than everything that an enemy, even against his will, can take away. II, 530. The person is said to be filled with the poverty of Christ who not only temperately despises all temporal goods but also patiently endures evils. II, 567. A Christian ought to be prepared to endure everything. III, 1259, 1260.

The precepts of patience are to be fulfilled not by bodily display but by preparation of the heart. III, 1935. The precepts of patience and the forgiveness of injuries are to be retained especially in the preparation of the heart. [Col. 0495] II, 530. The command concerning offering the other cheek to one who strikes was violated neither by Christ nor by the Apostle. II, 530.

Patience is divine. VI, 619. God’s patience toward sinners is to be imitated by human beings. II, 654, 655, 656. What God’s patience is like. VI, 611. Christ’s patience is to be imitated. V, 54, 477. Patience is to be learned from Christ’s power. III, 1706. In his passion Christ displayed the example of patience, and in his resurrection its reward. V, 946. Whoever wishes to endure everything patiently should not descend from heaven, but should meditate on the law of God day and night. IV, 1195. The patience of Christ’s poor is rewarded eternally. VI, 625. Let patience look to an eternal, not a temporal, reward. VI, 632. Temporal evils are not therefore to be endured patiently so that, as happened to Job, they may be recovered twofold. II, 549. Through hope of attaining blessedness, the devout bravely endure the evils of this life, and for this reason they are called blessed amid torments. II, 668, 673. The power of desires produces endurance of labors and pains, and no one willingly undertakes to bear what causes suffering except for the sake of something that delights him. VI, 613. Patience is greater in proportion as charity is greater. VI, 619. Examples of patience are to be displayed for the progress of others. III, 289. True patience does not arise from the powers of free choice. VI, 617. Although patience may seem to conquer when someone trusts in his own strength, it is conquered by pride. V, 1253. Why true patience cannot suffer for justice and eternal life what false patience suffers for iniquity and temporal life. VI, 618.

Patience is a gift of God. V, 1252, 1286, 1288; VI, 624. Patience is given by God. IV, 298, 737, 738. Patience comes from the one from whom true wisdom comes. VI, 618. From the one from whom charity comes. VI, 619, 623. The Holy Spirit is his fire; unless the will, kindled by it, loves the impassible good, it cannot endure the evil it suffers. VI, 619. How patience given by God is nevertheless ours. V, 1463. From the one who gives us victory over desire, so that we are not carried away by pleasure, comes also the strength of patience, so that we are not broken by pain. IV, 1577. Although very rare, examples of patience unto death nevertheless existed among the ancient Fathers. II, 549. Job’s patience is described. VI, 615, 632, 704, 718, 719. The firmness of patience is signified by the bones. IV, 320, 1796.

## Fatherland

How great our love for our fatherland ought to be. II, 313. The fatherland is ordinarily regarded in the place of parents. I, 1238. All crimes are contained in parricide against it. I, 953. It belongs to the duty of virtue to live for one’s fatherland. VII, 622. Nectarius reports, on the authority of very learned men, that a singular reward is prepared in heaven for those who have deserved well of their fatherland. II, 387. Some retain the customs of their fatherland more stubbornly, others relinquish them more easily. II, 201, 202. Fatherlands, that is, cities or large families. III, 508.

## Heavenly fatherland

The heavenly fatherland. V, 241. Our fatherland is the heavenly Jerusalem. IV, 288, 1602. Praise of the heavenly fatherland. III, 1636. Description. VI, 686. Its blessedness. IV, 582, 756, 1099, 1107, 1108. There will be no temptation there. IV, 798. There the struggle that a person experiences within will end. IV, 775. Works of mercy will cease there, because there will be no misery. IV, 1099, 1108. What heat and refreshment will be like there. IV, 797, 798. There will be no place for prayer, but only for praise. V, 868. There will be vision without defect and love without weariness. IV, 1089. There will be joy without end, eternity without stain, serenity without cloud. III, 1626. The treasure of the heavenly fatherland is truth. VII, 160. The citizens of the heavenly fatherland are gathered through the remission of sins. VII, 161.

The heavenly fatherland is to be desired. III, 1662, 1691; IV, 774; V, 38. Whoever finds pilgrimage sweet does not love the fatherland. IV, 1089, 1195. Apart from the heavenly fatherland, everything that belongs to us is pilgrimage. IV, 734. The faithful pass out of the world; the unfaithful pass away with the world. III, 1785. We sigh for the fatherland by faith. V, 1613. We must hasten to the fatherland. VI, 679. It is not a path of feet but a path of conduct. VI, 699. We must run toward it by love, not by the feet of the body. IV, 1952. You are walking if you love; for we run toward God not with steps but with affections. VI, 681. See *Way*. The Platonists in some fashion saw the fatherland, but did not keep to the way. VII, 307. The fatherland is the life of Christ; the way is the death of Christ. III, 1624. To return to the fatherland, we need to be carried by the Lord’s cross. V, 475. What is the soul’s beast of burden, and how is it to be tamed? VI, 681, 709. The outfitting of the vessel for this purpose. VI, 680. What must be done for the eternal fatherland is shown by what the Romans did for the earthly one. VII, 160, 161, 162.

## Patricius

Patricius, Augustine’s father, a poor municipal citizen of Thagaste. I, 677. Beyond the resources of his household, he supplied his son with whatever was needed for his studies, even when the son was living far away for that purpose. I, 677. The character of Patricius. I, 772. Although Patricius was hot-tempered, he never struck his wife Monica. I, 772. Patricius became a catechumen. I, 677. He died a believer when Augustine was in his seventeenth year. I, 685.

Patricius, Augustine’s nephew. V, 1575. A subdeacon. V, 1575.

Patricius, from whom the heretics called Patricians derive their name. VIII, 42, 663.

The patrimony of a poor person is bodily health. V, 249, 1402. A person entrusts children more wisely to God the Creator than to his own patrimony. V, 89.

## Advocacy

A just judgment or true testimony must not be sold, although a just advocacy and true counsel may be sold. II, 663.

## Patron

Christ our patron. V, 728.

## Paventia

Paventia, a goddess. VII, 122.

## Pavibundus

“Pavibundus,” trembling with fear. V, 148.

## Pavimentare

“To pave.” V, 513, 1463.

## Paula

The devout life of Paula and Eustochium. II, 753. Paula called the niece of Alypius and Augustine. II, 929. Paula greets Augustine. II, 753. Jerome sits beside the sick Paula. II, 238.

## Paulina

Paulina. II, 483. Ready to dedicate continence to God. II, 487. Paulina, advanced in years. II, 597. She asked Augustine to explain fully to her whether God can be seen with bodily eyes. II, 596. This arose from the occasion of that brief letter of hers. II, 603. Augustine wrote her a book on seeing God. II, 596.

Augustine greets Paulinianus, who was staying with Jerome. II, 237.

## Paulinus of Nola

Paulinus, bishop of Nola. VI, 157; VII, 24; X, 1027. A noble servant of God. VIII, 588. He was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and, at Barcelona in Spain, was forcibly ordained by Lampius amid a suddenly inflamed crowd. II, 100. Paulinus was nurtured in the faith through his love of Ambrose, whose presbyter he is considered. II, 100. Paulinus was honored with episcopal dignity. II, 99, 103. Paulinus renounced everything. II, 102. An example is offered of Paulinus renouncing worldly pomp. II, 107. Paulinus’ humility. II, 102, 103. Paulinus and Therasia call themselves sinners in their superscription. II, 120, 347. Paulinus was exceedingly obedient to the divine will. II, 274. Paulinus’ astonishing occupations, although he was thought to be enjoying leisure. II, 356. Paulinus went to Rome every year. II, 355. Paulinus free from episcopal cares. II, 123, note (c).

Augustine praises Paulinus. II, 108. Paulinus’ breast is an oracle of the Lord. II, 125. Paulinus’ letters are highly praised. II, 108. Paulinus has his wife beside him, not as a leader toward softness but as one who restores strength to her husband’s bones. II, 108. Paulinus’ consolatory letter to Macarius is mentioned. II, 1073. The letter of Paulinus and Therasia to Alypius. II, 99. Another to Augustine. II, 101. Paulinus’ letters breathe the most genuine fragrance of Christ. II, 831. Paulinus appears as a most sincere lover and confessor of grace. II, 831. Paulinus’ words from his letter to Severus. II, 831. Augustine commends the pitiable boy Vestutinus to Paulinus, even though he is among the impious. II, 125. He also commends Romanianus and Licentius. II, 125. Augustine asks him to exhort and instruct Licentius. II, 110. Paulinus sends five blessed loaves to Romanianus and Licentius. II, 126. Paulinus wrote against the pagans. II, 159. Augustine requested this work. II, 125, 159, 181. Paulinus asks Augustine’s opinion concerning the burial of the dead and the Church’s prayers for them. VI, 591. He proposes certain questions from Scripture to Augustine. II, 465. Augustine replies to Paulinus. II, 630. Augustine sends him the books on free choice. II, 124. Paulinus receives from Aurelius Augustine’s five books against the Manichaeans. II, 121. Alypius arranged this. II, 101. Paulinus sends to Alypius the history of Eusebius, bishop of Constantinople. II, 100. Alypius and Augustine instruct Paulinus against the heresy of Pelagius. II, 815. Paulinus received letters from the bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus, and Severus. II, 125. Paulinus wrote to Aurelius of Carthage. II, 100. Augustine sends bread to Paulinus. II, 125. He promises him that he will write Alypius’ history. II, 110. Paulinus read Augustine’s book *On True Religion*. II, 109. He marvels at Augustine’s books as words dictated by God. II, 100. Augustine’s desire to see and speak with Paulinus. II, 107.

Paulinus, a presbyter. II, 645. A disciple of Paulinus of Nola. II, 644. Augustine calls him his son and fellow presbyter. II, 645.

Paulinus, a deacon. X, 387, 389, 575.

## Paul the Apostle

Why the Apostle is called Paul. I, 753; X, 207. Previously called Saul, after Saul. V, 1429. Paul means the same as “little” (*modicus*). III, 2037. And “humble.” V, 605, 914, 1278, 1429. Saul was a fierce persecutor at Stephen’s killing. V, 1429. He guarded the garments of those stoning Stephen, so that he might stone him with everyone’s hands. IV, 1934. Saul’s ferocity against the Church indicates great fruitfulness. VIII, 445.

Paul’s conversion. IV, 503; V, 167, 948, 1276. Paul’s conversion did not arise from prior merits. IV, 701. Paul’s own merits were nothing but evil. V, 1466. For Paul to be called from heaven and converted by so great and effective a calling was solely the grace of God, because his merits were great—but evil. X, 889. Paul obtained grace without any good merits, indeed with many evil merits. X, 890. In Paul grace appeared more evidently and clearly. X, 207. Good was repaid to Paul for evil, when he possessed evil merit. X, 888. Saul, raging, was forestalled by grace. V, 913, 914, 920, [Col. 0497] 1571, 1465. How the frenzied Saul was healed. VI, 656. Christ commended the power of his art in him as physician. V, 1370. Paul changed from a wolf into a sheep, and from a sheep into a shepherd. V, 949. From persecutor into apostle. V, 949. Paul was freed from evil by Christ himself. V, 1364. Christ struck Paul down with a rebuking voice and raised him with a merciful hand. IV, 1164. Paul was an extinguished coal, but was kindled by Christ’s voice. IV, 1812. Paul was hard and cold against the fire of God. IV, 1935. Christ slew Saul with his voice and, taking him into his own body, in a certain way ate him. II, 220. In Paul’s conversion Jacob’s prophecy concerning Benjamin is fulfilled. V, 1275, 1465. Paul is signified by the younger Benjamin in ecstasy. IV, 835. Paul’s transformation occurred because of Stephen’s prayer. V, 914, 1436. Paul obtained mercy so that, by looking to him, no sinner might ever despair. IV, 875. In Saul’s healing, hope of salvation was brought to the despairing. V, 951, 1268. Although the Apostle Paul was struck down and instructed by a heavenly voice, he was nevertheless sent to a human being to receive the sacraments. III, 17, 18. In what sense Paul was the first of sinners. V, 948, 951, 1370. Paul was first among sinners not in time but in wickedness. IV, 875. Paul became a preacher of Christ from a persecutor. V, 1268, 1351. How wisely and eloquently Paul spoke. III, 93, 94, 95, 96. Paul was especially skilled in dialectic. IX, 456. Paul was learned in divine law. V, 358. In how many ways Paul preached Christ by means of signification. VIII, 873. Paul was a flexible trumpet. IV, 1255. Paul is rightly called a sower of words. V, 606. He was a sower of words but a reaper of conduct. V, 808. Paul debates with the Epicureans and Stoics. V, 854. Paul preaching among the Athenians. V, 808.

The Jews accused Paul as an enemy of the Law. II, 279. Paul sometimes observed the ancient sacraments and sometimes did not, according to the dispensation of the time and the requirements of those with whom he was present. II, 280, 288. Paul observed the sacraments of the Jews but did not sacrifice with the Gentiles: how. II, 157. How Paul became a Jew to the Jews, weak to the weak, and so forth. II, 157, 257, 288, 289. Paul became all things to all people, not through the deceit of a liar but through the affection of one who shared their condition. II, 288; VI, 537, 557. With what intention Paul observed his ancestral practices. VI, 493. Paul did not observe them deceitfully. VI, 536. He aided the carnal Jew or pagan in the same way that he himself would have wished to be aided, if he had been in that condition. VI, 558. In order to shape the Church, Paul put on beauty for those whom it pleased and strength for those whom it displeased. IV, 1182, 1183. Augustine thinks that Peter and Paul practiced the commands of the Law out of fear of believing Jews; Jerome, however, thinks that they merely pretended. II, 157, 260. From James it is demonstrated that Paul did not observe the Jewish sacraments by pretence. II, 280. Paul rebuked deceptive pretence in Peter. II, 156, 257, 260. Jerome says that Paul too pretended to observe the Law. II, 256, 257. Jerome maintains that Paul rebuked Peter for what he had done, not because of a well-intentioned lie, but because of an honorable dispensation, having defended himself and others before him. II, 257. Paul rightly rebuked the pretence of Peter and Barnabas. VI, 536. Paul corrected Peter truthfully. II, 156, 277, 278, 285. In rebuking Peter, Paul did not speak tropically or metaphorically. II, 779. Paul did not lie. II, 779. Once Paul’s lie is admitted in the dispute he had with Peter, his authority collapses. II, 113. From Jerome: Paul could not have had confidence to preach the Gospel unless the judgment of Peter and those who were with him had confirmed him. II, 255.

Paul’s charity is preached. III, 2022. Paul tolerates false brothers. II, 297. He joins Jews and Gentiles in Christ through the bond of grace. III, 2089. While Paul was giving birth to the faithful, charity was giving birth. IV, 1923.

Paul claims for himself a father’s duty toward the Corinthians because of the preaching of the Gospel. VIII, 385. Paul bore toward his children not only a father’s heart but also a mother’s. IV, 1299, 1923. When shipwrecked at sea, Paul carried in his heart the patrimony of his faith. IV, 1645. How much the zeal for his neighbor tormented him. IV, 1269. Paul did not seek his own glory. III, 1471. What cause Paul had for boasting in the flesh. V, 917. His humility is seen both in heaven, because of the freedom of the spirit, and on earth, because of the servitude of the body. IV, 1473. How Paul endured tribulations. IV, 367. Paul and Barnabas singing psalms in prison. III, 1935. How Paul avenged the martyr Stephen in his own person. III, 1268.

Paul was caught up into paradise: whether in the body or outside the body. III, 453, 455. Paul did not know whether the soul had been separated from the bodily senses or whether he had altogether left the body. III, 458. That third heaven to which the Apostle was caught up was truly the third heaven. III, 456, 457. The Apostle was certain that he had seen the third heaven, uncertain how he had seen it. III, 456. How this could happen. III, 457. What Paul saw in his rapture he saw properly, not imaginally. III, 458. The Apostle was caught up as far as intellectual vision, in which God is seen in the form in which he is. III, 478. Paul was caught up to angelic life. II, 610.

Whether all graces were given to Paul. X, 339. Whether Paul was without sin because he said that the crown of righteousness remained for him. X, 165, 166. Paul was not yet perfected in the fullness of righteousness. X, 602. The perfection of righteousness is complete security, and this was not present even in Paul. X, 601, 604. In what sense Paul was understood by the Palestinian bishops to have possessed all graces. X, 339. Paul says of himself both that he is imperfect and that he is perfect. X, 602, 606. Paul professes himself imperfect. V, 834, 835, 924. By acknowledging his weakness he is perfected. V, 481. How Paul was without reproach according to the righteousness that is in the Law. X, 558, 602, 603. Paul, however perfect, still needed liberation. X, 162. Whether he spoke in his own person when he said, “Who will deliver me,” and so forth. X, 154. He speaks not in the person of the Jews but in his own when he says, “Wretched man that I am,” and so forth. X, 1088. Likewise, “Not the good that I want,” and so forth. X, 1116. Likewise, “But I am carnal,” and so forth. I, 620, 638. Paul speaks in his own person and in the person of others who are still under grace, not under the Law, when he says, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.” X, 557. How Paul called himself carnal and sold under sin. X, 559. How he does not know what he is doing. X, 561. How he said that he does the evil he does not want. X, 560. That Paul spoke there in the person of a person still existing under the Law may be seen from three considerations. X, 560. Why the passage immediately following Paul should be understood of a person established under grace. X, 561. Not only Paul’s flesh but also his mind was weak. X, 367.

That Paul and the other Apostles were polluted by lust is a slander of Julian. X, 556. Paul abstained from all intercourse. X, 886. Paul’s struggle against desire. V, 817. Why the thorn of the flesh was given to Paul and not quickly removed. V, 893. It was a remedy against exaltation in Paul. V, 835, 892. O poison, which is cured only by poison! V, 893. Paul was not without the thorn of the flesh until death. X, 166. God did not graciously hear Paul. V, 147. Paul was not heard according to his will because he was heard for his healing. IV, 1899; V, 836. Paul’s thorn of the flesh and buffeting: a certain bodily pain. IV, 1269, 1708.

Once an apostle, Paul learned a craft by which he could live. III, 1961. Paul lived by the labor of his hands so that he would not seem to sell the Gospel. VI, 557, 558. Nor would the weak hate it as though the Gospel were for sale. VI, 559. What this work by which he lived was. VI, 559, 560. When he was accustomed to undertake it. VI, 560.

Paul’s joy and words as his passion approached. V, 1366, 1368. Paul was strengthened by revelation concerning his future passion and victory. V, 1368. It is shown that Paul did not wish to die. V, 1374. Paul and Peter suffered for Christ on the same day. V, 1352, 1361, 1365. See *Peter*. How Paul will judge the twelve tribes of Israel when there are only twelve seats. IV, 1103, 1104. The crown is returned to Paul as his due because undeserved grace went before it. V, 1361, 1464. Pelagius did not consequently say that Paul was worthy to receive all graces. X, 344. Was Paul worthy to receive all the graces of apostleship? X, 341, 342. Paul, who found the giver during the time of mercy, retains him as debtor at the time of judgment. IV, 1283.

Paul’s merits are gifts of God. X, 341. Paul fights vigorously for grace. X, 207. Paul is a great preacher of grace. X, 341. A devoted preacher of God’s grace. X, 133. A most steadfast preacher of grace. X, 214. A vehement defender of grace. X, 224. The keenest soldier and most unconquered defender of grace. X, 990. Paul is a great teacher, confessor, and preacher of grace. X, 342. Paul’s grateful disposition toward God. III, 2037. Paul terribly rebukes the ungrateful. IV, 1118.

How reverently Paul receives the Scriptures of the Old Testament is apparent from his letters. VIII, 650, 651, 658. Paul’s letters are weighty and strong, as even his detractors have confessed. III, 96. When writing to the Corinthians, Paul did not correct what he had written to the Romans. VIII, 248. Certain matters in Paul’s letters are difficult to understand; hence some promised themselves salvation from faith alone. VI, 212. Distinguished defenders of the faith used the Epistle to the Hebrews as a witness. VI, 235. What Paul’s Gospel is. IV, 1448.

Praises of the Apostle Paul. VII, 414. Paul was a great and holy man. X, 601. An excellent member of Christ. X, 339. A soldier of the heavenly camps. I, 798. Paul’s modesty and zeal for Christ. IV, 348. Paul’s modesty in the knowledge of God. V, 1203. Paul, the Lord’s granary worker. V, 923. Paul as crystal. IV, 1934, 1935. Paul is dissolved into water so that those who thirst may drink. IV, 1935. Paul became bread to nourish others. IV, 1934. Paul stretched himself out like a psaltery; Christ touched it, and the sweetness of truth sounded forth. IV, 1954. Paul, Mount Sinai. IV, 819. Paul’s spiritual vessel. VI, 680. Paul, a man of the highest counsels. I, 1320. Paul earned primacy in the apostolate in the Gospel itself. X, 163. Paul’s letters have greater force in the Church than those of his fellow apostles. IV, 1708. Nothing in the Scriptures was better known to Paul, nothing sweeter, nothing more familiar. IV, 1934. Paul’s tongue, winged as it speaks mysteries. I, 862. Augustine read Paul above all others. I, 747, 762, 922. The Manichaeans falsely proclaimed that they especially accepted Paul the Apostle. VIII, 246. See *Apostle*. Why Paul the Apostle is loved even when unknown. VIII, 953, 954, 959. A painting displaying the stoning of Stephen and the conversion of Saul. V, 1437.

Paul the proconsul becomes, through baptism, a provincial of the great King. I, 753.

## Other persons named Paul

Paul, bishop of Cirta. IX, 584. He and the subdeacon Sylvanus handed over the Lord’s instruments. II, 197.

Paul, a bishop burdened with enormous fiscal debts. II, 356. Apparently the same man whom Augustine rebukes. II, 180.

Paul, a bishop. IX, 513, 514.

Paul, a bishop. VIII, 665.

Paul of Samosata and his errors. VIII, 34. From Paul of Samosata came the heretics called Paulianists, more commonly known as Photinians. VIII, 34.

Paul of Bobba. IX, 229.

Paul the deacon carries Augustine’s letter to Boniface. II, 993.

Paul, a brother. II, 1012, 1013.

Paul sent by the Emperor to Africa to eradicate the Donatist schism. IX, 48.

A certain Paul healed at Hippo at the memorial shrine of Saint Stephen. VII, 770.

It was established by the Council of Nicaea that the Paulianists were to be baptized in the Catholic Church. VIII, 34.

## Peacock

The flesh of a dead peacock does not decay. VII, 712, 719.

## Pavor

Pavor, a Roman god. VII, 125. Introduced by Hostilius. VII, 130, 190.

Fear is sometimes expressed by the word “ecstasy.” IV, 230. Fear is also present in the passion of the righteous. IV, 231. Was Christ afraid of death? IV, 230. See *Fear*, *Terror*.

## Poor

God generally makes his servants, whom he can feed, needy in order to find them working. V, 1128. The patrimony of the poor is health. IV, 610, 971; V, 249, 1402. Who are to be called poor. VII, 204. The true poor person. V, 115. The poor person of God is poor in spirit, not in purse. IV, 1727, 1814. The poor are not those who possess nothing, but those who have no hope except in God. IV, 1196. In the case of the poor righteous person, the empty chest is noticed, but the conscience full of God is not noticed. IV, 371. If a poor person has God, what does he not have? V, 492, 521. In what things the truly poor are rich. IV, 170, 1649. What vices the poor must avoid. V, 521. They must beware of the desire for riches. V, 522, 956. Nothing is lacking to the one who desires nothing. IV, 1639.

A tranquil poor person is to be preferred to a covetous rich person. VII, 114. Sleep comes more easily to hard ground than to a silver-plated bed. V, 114. It is more for a poor person to see the starry sky than for a rich person to see a gilded roof. IV, 1687. Many are poor but rich in desire. IV, 1371. A poor person possessed by desire is worse than a rich person. V, 114. It benefits a poor person nothing to lack means while burning with desire. IV, 609. Much has been abandoned by one who has abandoned not only whatever he possessed but also whatever he desired to possess. IV, 1371. A poor person who desires riches and is puffed up is counted among the reprobate rich. IV, 545, 1727. Whoever is not elated amid an abundance of possessions is counted by God among the poor. IV, 545, 1057, 1197, 1727. The true poor person is scarcely found in the crowd of the poor. V, 114.

Why God made the poor and the rich. IV, 1649, 1650. How the poor and the rich can mutually share and lessen their burdens. V, 899. The poor person is a citizen of the kingdom of heaven: through him we send there what we give him. V, 240. The poor have been appointed as lenders to the rich. V, 130, 240, 406. The poor are hidden channels through which our possessions go before us into heaven. IV, 424. The bellies of the poor are safer storehouses. V, 219. Distribution to the poor is seed in the earth. V, 265. God is the surety of the poor. IV, 387. When a poor person prays for you, he asks God to pay on his behalf. IV, 387. Who is the poor person abandoned by God. V, 111. Christ’s poor are to be counted among his children. VII, 162. The poor in the place of Christ. V, 1519. Christ is poor in us, with us, and for us. IV, 1295. The poor are the Lord’s feet. III, 1760. Christ is to be clothed and welcomed in the poor. V, 170. The custom of clothing the poor at Hippo. II, 471.

Care of the poor. V, 433. The goods of the Church belong to the poor when the clergy have sufficient provision from elsewhere. II, 809. The Church fed the poor. IX, 94. The bishop administers care of the poor. II, 809. Friendship with the poor is to be acquired through almsgiving. V, 250. The poor Lazarus was lifted into the bosom of the rich Abraham. V, 114. The poor person should not become proud because of Lazarus’ lot. V, 112. The poor and the rich share the same lot of blessedness if both are humble. V, 113. See *Rich*. The rich person who despised the poor person here should not hope for his companionship in eternal blessedness. V, 248. The poor person’s tents. V, 251. See *Almsgiving*.

[Col. 0500] Who are the poor in spirit. IV, 943; V, 364. The poor in spirit are understood as those humble and fearing God. III, 1232. Humble in heart. IV, 1726. Not presuming upon themselves. IV, 177, 1727. Blessed are the poor in their own spirit, rich in the Spirit of God. IV, 1836. A proud poor person is intolerable. V, 112, 218. The poor, that is, the humble in heart, hunger for righteousness all the more because they are empty of the world. IV, 1726. The poor person whose refuge is the Lord is the one who loves nothing that either abandons him while he lives or loves it, or is abandoned by him when he dies. IV, 121. The poor of God. IV, 902, 909, 910, 1649, 1650. Every human being is poor. V, 686. To take the part of a poor person in judgment is false mercy and true injustice. IV, 285. The treasure of the poor is a good will. IV, 371.

## Poverty

Poverty in itself is neither blessedness nor misery. V, 327. The pursuit of complete poverty belongs to evangelical perfection. IX, 423. Voluntary poverty belongs to Christian perfection. IX, 341. It is falsely said that a needy life produces eternal calamity. II, 389. The voluntary poverty of many distinguished Romans was stricter than that of Christians. VII, 164. The commitment to poverty among Augustine’s clergy. V, 1570, 1572. The confessor of holy poverty cannot be tormented without a heavenly reward. VII, 25. Even the pagans grieved more that Roman poverty had perished than that Roman wealth had perished. II, 532. Who is said to be filled with Christ’s poverty. II, 567. Christ’s poverty and riches. V, 215. If Christ had avoided poverty, we would not be without poverty. V, 916. Faith must be kept with a friend in his poverty. V, 247. The poverty of a failing spirit. V, 219. What poverty God should give his enemies. VIII, 164.

“Paupertacula,” a little poverty. V, 1570.

## Peace

What peace is. IV, 1075. The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order. VII, 640. Definitions of the peace of various things. VII, 640. All things desire peace. VII, 639. Peace is the end of all our devout intention and action. III, 1901, 1902. Eternal peace is the end of our goods. VII, 637. Peace is the end of all good desires. V, 912. Every human being seeks peace and rest, but not in his own region. IV, 560. The use of all temporal things is directed toward the fruit of peace, either earthly peace in the earthly city or eternal peace in the heavenly city. VII, 642. The value of the good of peace. VII, 637. What kind of peace is to be pursued. V, 170. Those who live by faith pursue peace from one source, and those who do not live by faith from another. VII, 645.

True peace. V, 912. What the true peace of a human being is. III, 1233. The true peace of a rational creature. VII, 646. In this life, the peace of a human being is obedience ordered in faith under the eternal law. VII, 642. Peace promised to the devout. V, 121, 123. There is no peace with God except through confession of sins. IV, 937. Peace is not complete as long as vices rule. VII, 657. Right peace consists in the flesh being subjected to the spirit, and the wife to the husband; if the reverse occurs, it is perverse. IV, 1860. Peace is attained through continence and justice. VI, 359. What kind of peace delights God. VIII, 166. What is repaid is pleasing when it is repaid from peace and in peace. IV, 1494. Peace heals rivalry. III, 2142. Peace consoles us in pressures and frees us from every pressure. III, 1902. Christ is truly our peace, the true peacemaker. IV, 1668. God is peace; Christ is peace. IV, 1656.

Christ’s peace is twofold: one in this world, the other in the future. III, 1834. The peace of the world differs from the peace of Christ. III, 1835. The peace of this world is not complete. III, 1834. The peace of the world is material for luxury and destruction, whether as an invitation or as an aid, if piety and charity are absent. II, 1026. True and perfect peace is not in this life. III, 1656; IV, 319, 560, 1075, 1076. It is not to be hoped for in this age. VII, 546, 547. It is not to be expected by a human being until after the resurrection. V, 331, 1211; VI, 66. Not until after the transformation of the body. III, 2066. The peace of a human being in this life, compared with the peace of blessedness, is found to be misery. VII, 636. It is consolation for misery rather than joy in blessedness. VII, 657. Perfect peace will then be ours when our nature, clinging inseparably to its Creator, is resisted by nothing within us. VI, 360. Where there is perfect peace, there is perfect justice. IV, 1930.

Eternal peace is the reward of victory over temptations. VII, 636, 637. No one passes into peace unless he has first waged war against vices. IV, 121. Eternal peace is the supreme good. VII, 648, 658. The peace of God surpasses every understanding, even that of angels. VI, 261, 262. The peace of the blessed surpasses every human understanding. VI, 261. Peace is the delight of the blessed. IV, 362. Peace is our inheritance. IX, 694. Peace is the possession, inheritance, and fatherland of the righteous. IV, 1655. The good for which we sigh will be peace. IV, 1688.

The peace proper to Christians is, here, with God through faith, and eternally it will be with him through sight. VII, 657. Everything we do as Christians is done for the sake of peace. III, 1901. For the sake of peace we believe, hope, love, and are instructed in the sacraments. III, 1902. Here we possess peace in hope. IV, 1930. To have peace is to have what one loves. V, 1582. Perfect peace follows a good will. III, 2066. The river of peace, the abundance of peace, is to be received. VII, 690. Peace and abundance are produced through love. IV, 1628. Peace is a benefit of the true God. VII, 84, 440, 441.

Temporal peace too is to be desired by God’s servants. VII, 656, 657. With what disposition the earthly city seeks peace. VII, 444. The peace of the earthly city: what it is. VII, 645. Peace is the end of those who wage war. VII, 440, 637. Beyond doubt, those who fight seek peace, if they are good. II, 1020. Peace is not sought in order to provoke war; rather, war is waged in order to obtain peace. II, 856. Peace ought to belong to the will, war to necessity. II, 856. Domestic peace: an ordered harmony of commanding and obeying. VII, 643. Everyone desires to have peace with his own people. VII, 637, 642. Peace with others: an uncertain good; why. VII, 632. Peace among us is commanded to us. III, 1656. Peace must always be spoken of. V, 1586. The most perfectly ordered peace: what it is. VII, 730. The order of peace with human beings here is first that one harm no one, and then that one benefit whoever one can. VII, 643. Without charity there is no peace. IV, 1685. The peace of the Church is commended. IV, 1604, 1605, 1629, 1656, 1949.

Peace is not in schism, but in the Church. IX, 308. The whole of salvation consists in the bond of peace. IX, 85. When the bond of peace is preserved, the demons’ power to inflict harm becomes ineffective, the snares of their ambushes are shattered, and their plans of destruction vanish. IX, 85. When Donatists pass over to the Church, the honor of the clerical or episcopal office is not taken from them for the sake of peace, and this happens solely out of clemency. II, 812, 813. “Peace be with you” was said in response to readers in the Donatist gatherings (perhaps also among Catholics). II, 170. In giving peace, the Donatists speak falsely. IV, 1629.

The sign of peace: a kiss. V, 1101. Peace is generally bestowed upon the unworthy. VII, 440, 441. How peace is to be used. VII, 441. We may use the peace that has been made between others under oath. II, 185. Praise of peace. IV, 1923. The Church of Peace at Hippo Regius. II, 966. In Scripture, peace and concord. III, 1546. In Sulla’s victory, peace and war contend in cruelty. VII, 108.

The peacemakers, sons of God. V, 162. God will be seen only by peacemakers. V, 162. Augustine’s peaceful disposition, even toward sacrilegious persons. II, 132.

The term “sin” is understood in various ways. X, 599. Some sins belong to conduct, others to the arts. X, 1516.

What sin is. I, 609; III, 221; VIII, 38, 105, 586, 587, 588, 590, 591, 592, 593, 595; X, 1148, 1157, 1464, 1466. Sin is the evil quality of a thing. X, 294. Sin occurs when a human being seeks pleasures, exalted things, and truths not in God but in himself and other creatures, and thus rushes into pains, confusions, and errors. I, 676. Sin is transgression of the law. III, 1077. Sin is something done, said, or desired against the eternal law. VIII, 418. Sin consists in two ways: either in doing what is forbidden or in failing to do what is commanded. X, 298. There will be no sin if something exists without its being divinely commanded not to exist. X, 165. Sin is the disorder and perversity of the human being. VI, 122. There is no other vicious and blameworthy life of human beings than one that uses and enjoys things wrongly. VIII, 981. No one would sin if nothing unlawful were pleasing. VIII, 419. Sin exists when either the charity that ought to exist is absent or is less than it ought to be. X, 298. Sin is a defective and voluntary movement. I, 1270. The definition of sin. X, 1077, 1118. But considered in Adam. X, 1067. What sin is according to Julian’s view. X, 1312, 1414, 1538. The definition of sin brought forward by Julian is a definition of that which is merely sin, not of that which is also the punishment of sin. X, 1066, 1148, 1157, 1174, 1486, 1539, 1550. Whether the definition of sin can favor the Pelagian heresy. VIII, 105, note (a). The genus, difference, and mode of sin. X, 1067. Sin is an act, not a thing. X, 294. Whether sin can arise from an evil cause or not is investigated. X, 1464, 1465.

The Manichaeans assign sin to a prevailing evil nature opposed to God’s nature. VI, 358. Sin cannot be imputed to us if we have been sent by God himself into a nature opposed to God. VIII, 126. According to the Manichaeans there are no sins. VIII, 541. Sin is not desire for an evil nature but abandonment of a better one. VIII, 557, 562. Sin is not natural. VII, 330, 331; X, 293. Sin is rightly called natural. X, 1476. Natural sins: what they are. III, 221. Sin cannot exist except in a nature. X, 1335. Julian maintains that sin can come only from what is possible. X, 1500. Pelagius argues falsely concerning the possibility of not sinning. X, 274. The possibility of sinning belongs to the human being, not to God. X, 1509. God cannot sin by nature; one who participates in God receives from him the inability to sin. VII, 802. Why God cannot sin, and why the human being can. X, 1471. The human being did not sin because he was made from nothing, but for that reason he was able to sin. X, 1494. Rational creation was able to sin because it was made from nothing. X, 1473, 1474, 1475, 1488, 1495. Not everything made from nothing was able to sin; rather, the nature that was able to sin was made from nothing. X, 1494, 1495.

How it is that it belongs to a human being using the freedom of the will both to be able to sin and not to sin. X, 1115. The difference between being able not to sin and being unable to sin. X, 936. God cannot sin; this has also been granted to the angels, and will later be granted to the righteous, that they cannot sin. X, 1117. The blessed angels received the inability to sin as the reward for their perseverance. X, 936, 1491, 1492. The human being too would have received it, if he had stood firm. X, 1491, 1492. At first, it was a great good for the human being to be able not to sin; afterward, as a reward, it will be greater not to be able to sin. X, 1490, 1491, 1494, 1495, 1509. For every rational creature to which it is granted not to be able to sin, this is not proper to its nature but is God’s grace. VIII, 768. Nothing compelled an angel or a human being to sin. X, 1472. Whether the possibility of avoiding sin applies to every sin, both original and personal. X, 1467. Rational creation was originally made in such a way that it would neither sin unwillingly nor be driven by any necessity to will sin. X, 1474. The first sin was committed by the human being under no compulsion. X, 1477. Sins arising from necessity proceed from those sins that were committed under no necessity. X, 1119. Which sins are said to be committed under a certain necessity. X, 161. They are imputed. X, 161. What the sin of the angel and of the human being teaches. VII, 436.

The first sin in paradise began with the mind. X, 794. The first sin is to take delight in one’s own power. II, 439. The first human being’s sin was ineffably great. X, 1119. Several kinds of sin are present in the first human sin. VI, 254, 255. Whence came the gravity of the first sin. VII, 419, 420. The first human being’s voluntary sin is the cause of original sin. X, 461. The origins of sins. I, 1285. Sin is twofold: original and repeated. VI, 106. Original and actual. VI, 262. The distinction between original and actual sin. X, 115.

Original sin. VI, 277, 278; VIII, 1026; X, 115, 198, 413, 463, 464, 533, 570, 649, 696, 720, 732, 784, 810, 811, 819, 824, 836, 874, 1052, 1053, 1058, 1059, 1061, 1082, 1128, 1145, 1174, 1197, 1198, 1199, 1239, 1240, 1244, 1249, 1258, 1263, 1276, 1277, 1396, 1426. Original sin derived from the first human being. V, 179, 383, 442, 587, 657, 751, 832, 927, 928, 950, 992, 1156, 1343, 1647. Adam’s sin did not remain at its source but passed through to everyone. V, 832. It is contracted from the whole stock of Adam. VI, 245. Hence guilt is both engendered and added. VI, 262. Original sin is transmitted from Adam alone. X, 118. The first human being made the whole mass a damnable one. V, 907. The poisoner struck the entire mass of the human race in the first human being. V, 944. By the sin of the first human being, the entire mass of the human race was condemned. VII, 727.

The Manichaeans deny original sin. X, 1008. The Pelagians deny it. II, 723, 762; VIII, 48; X, 114, 441, 481, 520. Julian’s view of original sin. X, 720. Julian said that it was a Manichaean position to confess that those born derive original sin from Adam. X, 648, 653, 654, 656. According to Julian, certain innocent persons exist to whom Adam’s guilt did not extend. X, 1202, 1203. Why the Pelagians deny original sin. X, 533. The principal objections of the Pelagians against original sin. X, 186, 187, 188, 672. Five Pelagian arguments for denying sin are demolished. X, 694. Julian’s arguments for destroying original sin. X, 721. And his reasonings. X, 1412. Objections against the transmission of original sin. V, 944, 1345; X, 465, 470, 714, 738, 812, 872. If Julian denies original sin, he is forced to admit certain things that must be detested and condemned. X, 1594, 1595. The Catholic position opposed to the Pelagians. X, 673.

The sin of origin is asserted against the Pelagians as deriving from Adam. IV, 591; V, 906, 943, 950, 1338; X, 129, 464, 465, 575, 576, 614, 653. From where original sin is proved. X, 796. The Pelagians maintain that the question of original sin lies outside the danger to faith. X, 397. Original sin is unquestioned in the Catholic faith. X, 1430. To deny original sin is contrary to the ancient opinion implanted in the Church. X, 188. The faith concerning original sin was handed down and established in antiquity. X, 1074. The entire Catholic Church teaches original sin. X, 1280. Before Augustine, the entire Catholic Church believed it. X, 1183. Discussion of original sin is new. X, 193. It is not established when people began to doubt original sin. X, 192. It must be believed as a matter of faith that infants are subject to original sin. X, 655. Various testimonies of Scripture prove this. X, 131, 132. Original sin is manifest both according to the holy Scriptures and in the fact that its remission through the washing of regeneration has been established by the authority and antiquity of the Catholic faith and is universally known through the Church’s clear celebration. X, 608. The sin of origin is revealed by holy Scripture, and it reveals itself. X, 1192. Original sin is proved from Scripture. X, 465, 1073, 1082, 1083, 1084. Original sin is asserted from Job. X, 161, 162. And from the testimony of the Apostle. X, 196, 438, 439, 462. Through one human being came sin, and through one came reconciliation. X, 869, 1227. Why it is said that sin entered through one, not through two. X, 1216, 1219, 1225. What sort of sin entered the world through one human being. X, 1163, 1164, 1400. The Pelagians’ escape when they are pressed by the Apostle’s words about original sin. V, 1344. The Pelagians taught that the beginning of sin came from Adam insofar as the others imitated him. II, 679. They are refuted. II, 684. One sin common to all, not by imitation but by transmission. X, 114, 115, 117, 118. When the Apostle says that sin entered the world through one human being, he means generation, not example. X, 1283, 1284, 1286, 1287. The sin of imitation entered the world through the devil; the sin of generation through the human being. X, 1163, 1164. Julian finally confessed that sin passed through the disobedience of one. X, 1235. The Apostle is wrongly cited against original sin. V, 1346. Original sin is narrated in the Old Testament. I, 598. It is shown that original sin was imputed under the Law. X, 1173, 1227, 1237. An argument for original sin is the circumcision of infants. X, 402. The commandment of circumcision. X, 720, 1194. Original sin signified by the foreskin. X, 835.

When Catholics assert original sin, the Pelagians charge them with the crime of Manichaean heresy. X, 632. How far the Catholic dogma concerning original sin differs from the error of the Manichaeans. X, 1287. Those who assert original sin are not Manichaeans. X, 1083, 1227, 1230. Catholics who assert original sin are far removed from the Manichaeans. X, 441, 1125. Nor do they accuse God. X, 1126. Of all human beings, although all are born under sin, God alone is the author. X, 469. Although the fetus, sex, body, and fertility are from God, the one born from them is nevertheless not without stain. X, 1313, 1344. That the devil’s work passes through God’s work, or through the work of God’s work, is not implied. X, 1501, 1502, 1505. It is not contrary to God’s goodness to create something that the devil’s malignity possesses. X, 408. Whoever denies that, by reason of original sin, infants are allowed to be afflicted by the devil accuses God’s judgment. X, 1437. Why God continues to create human beings whom he knows will be born under sin. X, 454. Before they are reborn, human beings are assigned to the devil not because of their substance but because of the sin of their first parent. X, 1415. Although original sin is congenital, it must be distinguished from the Creator’s act of instituting nature. X, 1442. It must be distinguished from nature. X, 1278, 1288. Why sin is called original rather than natural. X, 1438, 1439. Catholics and Manichaeans both hold that sin is natural, but for radically different reasons. X, 1469. The basis on which Julian proves that sin cannot be natural. X, 1500. Whoever denies original sin assists the Manichaeans. X, 667, 668, 669.

The cause of original sin. X, 756. And its origin. X, 1069. If original sin is referred to its origin, it is of the same kind as actual sins. X, 1187. Original sin and voluntary sin are of the same kind. X, 1187. The manner in which original sin is transmitted, although it cannot easily be investigated or explained in easy language, is nevertheless believed by the Church. X, 828. That is the ancient sin, than which nothing is better known for preaching and nothing more secret for understanding. I, 1328. The source from which original sin is derived is either learned at leisure, or may be unknown without harm to salvation. X, 794. Julian discusses by what means original sin is found in an infant. X, 1150, 1152, 1153. By what means sin is found in an infant. X, 1183. How original sin entered the world. X, 462. Two modes of contracting original sin. X, 794. The Apostle demonstrates how original sin entered the world. X, 1151, 1152, 1153, 1156. The Pelagian heresy is the claim that there is nothing in the nature of one’s ancestors by which a person at birth could justly be possessed by the devil. X, 443, 444. Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him we all perished. X, 1400. All who were to arise from Adam through the lust of the flesh were in Adam’s loins. X, 1070. A human being incurred guilt because he was one with and in the one from whom he derived it when what he derived was committed; but he does not derive it from another when he lives his own life. II, 360. Whoever comes from Adam was one in him when he sinned. II, 824. Condemned in the root before being born. X, 406.

All are subject to original sin. X, 128, 131. Original sin bound everyone equally. X, 1225. By the desert of original sin, the human race became the sport of demons. X, 864. Whence original sin comes. X, 697. The evil of original sin is hereditary. X, 684. The first human being’s sin was great and, in corrupting nature, worse than all the violence of habit. X, 1525. The sin of origin comes from the bond of carnal desire. IV, 591. All who are carnally born from Adam are subject to it. II, 825, 859, 871, 883, 983. Original sin comes from carnal desire. X, 406, 728, 1160, 1237, 1451, 1605. Original sin is transmitted through lust. X, 429. Through desire. V, 817; X, 443. Original sin is the guilt of desire carried from those being born. X, 1155. Whatever human beings are born through desire cannot be without sin. V, 929; X, 438, 1368, 1372, 1373. Either body and soul are derived from a corrupted human being, or one is corrupted in the other as in a corrupted vessel. X, 794. The difficulty of explaining how original sin is contracted raises the question whether souls are newly created. II, 860. If souls are created individually, how do they contract original sin? II, 725. Whatever position is held concerning the origin of souls, no position may be held that denies original sin. II, 587, 732, 733, 865.

The infants of the faithful are also subject to original sin. II, 889. Original sin must not be attributed to marriage. X, 1459. Whether evil can arise from good. X, 863. The cause of original evil is not marriage but Adam’s sin. X, 1455. Since marriage is good, from where is original sin derived? X, 729. Original sin can be transmitted by parents who are free from it. X, 833. The Pelagian position is that sins cannot be born from something free from sin. X, 816. Although original sin has been remitted in the parent, it passes to the offspring. X, 835. Why children of wrath are born from a holy marriage. X, 425. Although a sinner has begotten a sinner, it does not follow that a righteous person must beget a righteous person. X, 158, 175. A parent dead to sin and alive to God begets one dead to sin. X, 831. Why a righteous parent does not beget a righteous child. X, 177. A regenerated believer begets with the sin of the first human being because he begets according to the flesh, not according to the spirit. V, 944. Original sin does not make marriage evil. X, 404. Wherever a person is born, whether from marriage or fornication, he is guilty through original sin. X, 729. To what extent original sin is transmitted from regenerated parents to their offspring. X, 434. Just as it could happen that a non-Christian should be born from Christians, and a non-member of Christ from members of Christ, so it also happens that an unclean person is born from the cleansed. X, 195. How it happens that original sin is contracted from a parent in whom it is not present. X, 843, 844. Original sin is contracted only through generation. X, 120. Original sin is derived from the defect of the seed. X, 447. Original sin is ours by right of procreation. X, 1071. Sin comes by transmission, just as righteousness comes by regeneration. X, 119. It is shown by examples that parents can transmit to their offspring what they do not possess. X, 831. How what has been remitted in the parent is transmitted in the offspring is explained, in any event, by the example of a wild olive growing from an olive tree. X, 425, 426. Children are born guilty from faithful spouses, as a wild olive from an olive tree. X, 555. Original sin, already remitted in baptized parents, remains in infants, as is demonstrated by the example of the foreskin. X, 834. And by that of chaff among wheat. X, 195. Just as the spirit of righteousness belonging to those through whom infants are reborn conveys faith to them, so the flesh of sin belonging to those through whom they are born conveys guilt to them. X, 187. It is a Pelagian dogma that an alien sin cannot be imputed to infants by God, who is supremely just. X, 1148, 1149. In what sense original sin is alien. X, 194. In what sense it is also ours. X, 921, 1257. Julian’s false principle that a matter of the will cannot be applied to the seeds of generation. X, 1540, 1541.

Original sin is not absurdly called voluntary. I, 604, 608, 610. Original sin is not without the will. X, 1149. Original sin is not in the will of the one being born, yet it is not without the will of the first human being, at least. X, 1393, 1394. Although those being born derive original sin without their own will, the origin itself was corrupted through the will of the first human being. X, 1477. Original sin arose from Adam’s evil will. X, 464, 707. Original sin was propagated from a voluntary defect. X, 1417. Original sin, produced by the will of the first parent, passes by contagion to descendants without their will. X, 1396. Sin, including original sin, does not exist without free will. X, 1392. In what sense original sin is free. X, 838. Everyone except Christ is subject to original sin. X, 185. Infants are transgressors on account of original sin. IV, 1574. Christ’s soul was not subject to the sin of origin. II, 866. Because Christ was conceived without desire. V, 785, 823, 824, 832, 1341, 1342. In Christ alone the devil found nothing of sin. V, 928. Christ alone can say that he suffered here without cause. IV, 1936. Christ endured punishment without guilt. X, 1594. That is Christ’s unique glory. X, 1594. It does not follow that, because Christ did not have original sin, no innate perversity dominates the image of God. X, 1589.

The punishment of the first sin. VII, 372, 373, 433. Its effects. VII, 433. The miseries of this life. VII, 729. The disobedience of concupiscence and the necessity of dying. VII, 379. The necessity of sin and death. VII, 403. Sin is the cause of death. II, 873. By sinning, the human being was compelled into the necessity of dying. II, 547. After sin, the soul governs its body in an ordered way, not entirely according to its own choice, but as the laws of the universe permit. II, 587. The punishments of sin are ignorance and difficulty. I, 1296. Restlessness of mind. I, 732. Error and disordered love. VII, 784. The sins that flow from the first sin do not cease to be sins. I, 1296. And why. I, 1297. Through original sin, nature as a whole was changed for the worse. X, 732. Because of original sin, people are born slow-witted. X, 1380, 1381. By reason of original sin, mortal nature is more inclined to sin. X, 1484. Human beings add actual sins to original sin by their own will, not through Adam. X, 120. From Adam, and in addition to Adam, many sins arise. IV, 1735. Original sin belongs to the temporal condition of the body. X, 978.

Original sin is recognized from its punishment. X, 1577. The miseries of the human race show original sin. X, 1177, 1280. And the evils and sufferings by which infants themselves are afflicted. X, 196, 1540. The miseries of this life testify that the whole mass of the human race was condemned through the sin of the first human being. VII, 784, 787, 788. God allows no one to suffer any evil that he does not deserve. X, 1177. The punishment of the image of God would be unjust unless guilt had merited it. X, 1594. The heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam would be unjust if original sin did not exist. X, 1061, 1062, 1072, 1250, 1267, 1335, 1339, 1437, 1557. Such great misery would not be inflicted upon human nature unless there were sin. X, 1061, 1062, 1063. It is not just that the sons of Adam should be oppressed from their birth by a heavy yoke, without any merit of sins. X, 1147, 1149, 1150. It is contrary to the ordinances of God’s justice that punishment should be inflicted upon human beings by him or under him without merit. X, 1191. It would not have been just for Adam’s penalty to pass to his descendants without guilt. X, 1164, 1165. The soul is unjustly burdened by the body if original sin does not exist. X, 1268. God would be unjust in imposing a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam if original sin were denied. X, 1126. God, who is supremely just, would not permit a heavy yoke to be imposed upon infants unless he found sin in them. X, 1073, 1079, 1175. In the face of so many and such great evils suffered by infants, God would lose either his justice, his omnipotence, or his very care for human affairs if original sin did not exist. X, 1072, 1148. Those who deny original sin are forced to call God either powerless or unjust. X, 864. The Pelagians try to remove original sin by praising God’s works. X, 460. Even the soul born with original sin has reason to give thanks to God. I, 1297. Original sin is not to be imputed to parents. X, 730, 731. Original sin is demonstrated by the fact that God is faithful in his words, just in his judgments, and holy in his works. X, 1433. Infants are shown to be guilty of original sin. X, 1067.

Sin and death passed through one human being to all, and Christ removes both. X, 1180. Judgment from one offense unto condemnation; grace from many offenses unto justification. X, 871. All human beings are bound to condemnation by God’s just judgment because of original sin. X, 933. Original sin is sufficient for condemnation. X, 117. It draws those to whom it is not remitted into condemnation. X, 1180, 1181, 1182. Even if no other sins are added. X, 1185, 1188. Unless it is removed through regeneration. X, 1278. If original sin is not removed by God’s judgment or removed by God’s grace, when infants die they either pass from evils to goods by the merit of regeneration, or from evils to evils by the merit of their origin. X, 978. Some are indignant that unreborn infants who die before exercising their own will are condemned because of another’s sins. X, 1071. Whether, like the devil, the human being should not be condemned except for sins of his own will. X, 840. If original sin did not exist, the images of God would be unjustly excluded from the kingdom of God. X, 1251, 1268, 1280. No one is made alien to the kingdom of God without some evil. X, 815. The image of God, if without sin, should not be excluded from the kingdom of God. X, 142, 1082, 1154. It is an insult to the image of God to separate it from the kingdom of God. X, 1136. God does not reject his image unless he himself has been rejected. X, 1065. The injustice of the first human being is imputed to infants born from him so that they undergo punishment, just as the righteousness of the second human being is imputed to regenerated infants so that they obtain the kingdom of heaven. X, 1078, 1079. Just as death is paid as the wage of sin, so eternal life is paid as the wage of righteousness. II, 881.

Original sin was expiated by circumcision. X, 450. The abolition of original sin was signified by the circumcision of an infant. X, 1239. No one removes original sin except Christ. X, 760, 1428. It is dissolved only through Christ. VI, 255. It is removed only through regeneration. X, 505, 1271. Nothing but God’s grace liberates from original sin. VII, 428; X, 128. The sin of origin is removed by Christ’s baptism. IV, 591. Together with all the sins born from it. IV, 1507; X, 120. Those who have sinned after receiving baptism cannot be cleansed again by the same sacrament. III, 2102. The baptism of infants is not superfluous, since they are bound by original sin and remission of sins truly takes place in them. II, 678, 889, 890. It is a great insult to God if his image is exorcized and exsufflated unless the prince of this world, who is cast out, is being exorcized and exsufflated there. X, 1220. It is a crime against majesty to exorcize and exsufflate images of God in infants if this is not done to rescue them from the devil’s power. X, 155.

All sins are remitted in baptism, but weakness remains. X, 630, 638. Death remains. II, 872. Why the punishment remains. X, 1595. The punishments of sin, even after guilt has been removed, remain for the testing of faith. X, 182, 1563. So that faith may be tested. X, 1579. Sins pass away in two ways: in act and in guilt. X, 858. Sins pass away in act but remain in guilt; desire passes away in guilt but remains in act. X, 858.

The Catholic faith has believed in original sin from antiquity. X, 451, 829. The faith of the holy Fathers concerning original sin. X, 1074, 1075, 1080. The agreement of the Fathers in asserting original sin. X, 192, 194, 466, 697, 719, 1406, 1407, 1411, 1413. The most celebrated teachers of the Church confessed original sin. X, 1380. Testimonies of the ancients proving that infants are born subject to original sin. X, 190, 614, 662. Cyprian’s. X, 191, 623, 624, 625, 626, 644, 718, 1073. Ambrose’s. X, 409, 632, 1068, 1069, 1070. Zosimus nowhere denied original sin. X, 574. Ambrose acknowledged it. X, 1142, 1145, 1147, 1155, 1409, 1411, 1414, 1415. Other Fathers as well. X, 1143, 1147, 1155, 1157. The Catholic dogma concerning original sin was repeatedly and clearly declared by Ambrose. X, 1416. Ambrose is correct concerning the five points advanced by Julian in order to deny original sin. X, 686. Jerome’s testimony in favor of original sin. X, 192. Jerome established the dogma of original sin in the book Against Jovinian and in his commentaries on Job. II, 723, 730. From which teachers Augustine received and learned the dogma of original sin. X, 1548. Augustine follows the holy teachers in the question of original sin. X, 1404, 1405. Augustine never failed to admit original sin from the time of his conversion. X, 843. Paulinus taught original sin. II, 831. In asserting original sin, the Eastern bishops agree with the Western. X, 649. In what sense John Chrysostom said that infants do not have sins. X, 655. The sin of origin is proved from the infants brought to Christ. V, 659. At the Palestinian judgment Pelagius denied that he said infants newly born are in the state in which Adam was before sin. X, 1112. Pelagius acknowledged original sin. X, 653. Some heretics also acknowledged it. X, 978. Those who taught original sin were neither Manichaeans nor dreamers nor madmen. X, 1280. No one dares call the ancients who asserted original sin Manichaeans. X, 643, 644. When God says, “I will repay the sins of the children upon the fathers,” he condemns not imitation but generation. X, 1254, 1255, 1258.

The sins of fathers are repaid upon their children by divine justice, not human justice. X, 1278. In a certain sense, the sins of parents are both ours and alien. X, 839. It is probable that children are bound by the sins of their parents, and not only by those of their first parents. VI, 254. Children were bound by their parents’ sins in the Old Testament. X, 872. When God says both that the sins of fathers do not belong to their children and that he repays the sins of fathers upon their children, he is not speaking contradictorily. X, 1271, 1273. How the sins of parents are repaid upon their children. IV, 1437. How far the sins of parents are transmitted to their children must not be determined rashly. VI, 255. The sins of a father do not affect a son who lives righteously. VIII, 138. Alien sins must not be imputed to one who could have prevented them by a lesser sin of his own. VI, 498. Just as some parents aggravate original sin, so some lessen it. X, 1428. To what extent original sin increased. X, 1239. Original sin is sin in such a way that it is also the punishment of sin. X, 1068. Original sin is the reason why God’s wrath remains upon infants who have not been incorporated among the faithful. X, 125. Of two infants, one is received by grace and the other left to justice. X, 1065. Everyone born from Adam belongs in a certain way to the old city. IV, 734. Some refuse to attribute personal sin to children before the point of their fourteenth year. III, 417. They are refuted. III, 417. Sin is dead without the Law because it lies hidden, does not appear, and is unknown as though buried. V, 830, 832, 894.

Sin is turning away from eternal things and turning toward mutable things. I, 1240, 1269; VII, 354. It is a turning either toward one’s own good, toward something external, or toward something inferior. I, 1240, 1269. Sin is transgression, when a human being, desiring something more, exceeds the rule of justice. V, 353. Sin is admitted when, through an immoderate inclination toward these lowest things, the highest goods are abandoned. I, 679. It occurs when things Christ despised are desired or things Christ endured are fled. III, 135. Sin itself is not loved; rather, the disordered love of a creature is itself sin. V, 143.
