Through sin one falls away not toward evil things, but in an evil manner. VII, 355. Just as before human beings were made, so before God the sin of thought exists. V, 928.

God is not the cause of sins. I, 830, 1269; X, 731. Although sinners are accustomed to cast their sins back upon him. III, 209. Sin is not from God. V, 143. God makes what belongs to nature in sin; what belongs to guilt, he does not himself make. V, 587. Sin is explained by the likeness of limping. X, 294. The human being has sin from himself alone, not from God. IV, 1318, 1848. Sins arise not from God but from the will of those who sin. I, 1271; VIII, 560. Sins would not occur unless God permitted them; why he permits them. VI, 358, 359. It lies within the power of evil beings to sin; but that they should do this or that through their evil lies in God’s sole power. X, 984. Unless the will is the cause of sinning, nothing remains of justice in laws, institutions, or praises. II, 1061. The cause of sin is from the soul, not from the flesh. VII, 405. Whoever sins, sins willingly. I, 1294. Not by nature. I, 1270. Sin is wholly voluntary. III, 133. Sin would not be sin if it were not voluntary. I, 603. The first cause of sin is the will alone. II, 773. A failing will. VI, 244. Sin comes only from the will. VIII, 103, 121, 122; X, 1312. It lies in each person’s will whether he is darkness or light. III, 884. If we do not wish to, we do not sin. X, 152. The origin of sin lies in the will. X, 1477. Sins committed by the ignorant or by those under compulsion are not wholly without the will. I, 604. For whoever sins unknowingly nevertheless commits sin willingly. I, 609. Although sin can exist without the will to sin, it cannot exist without the will to perform the act. I, 609. It is indeed harsh that the habit of sinning makes love of wrongdoing, but nothing is harsher than that it extinguishes shame. X, 1056.

Sins committed under the force of habit, the Pelagians say, are not voluntary. X, 1505. Sin can remain without the will, although it cannot exist without the will. X, 1395–1398, 1410. How it is true both that sin cannot exist without the will and that it can remain without the will. X, 1396, 1397. Some sin is involuntary. X, 1393. It is shown that sin can be changed from voluntary into involuntary. X, 1505. Sin is not only voluntary and possible, but also necessary. X, 1493, 1495, 1500. The Manichaeans attribute the origin of sins not to free choice but to the necessity of an adverse nature. VIII, 566. And to the substance of the opposing race. VIII, 38. The necessity of sinning was not imposed upon human beings by the Creator. X, 1488. Whether all are compelled to sin, as though unwillingly, by the necessity of their flesh. X, 1110. A person is not compelled to sin, as though unwillingly, by the necessity of his flesh; but if he has already reached the age at which he exercises the judgment of his own mind, he is held in sin by his own will and by his own will is driven from one sin into another. X, 1110. There is a certain necessity of sinning. I, 753, 759; X, 286, 295. How someone falls into it. I, 753. Three things must be distinguished: sin, the punishment of sin, and that which is both sin and the punishment of sin. X, 1068. The same thing can be both sin, the punishment of sin, and the cause of sin. X, 787, 788. Sin that is the punishment of sin, by which a person sins unwillingly. X, 1396. A harsh necessity of possessing sin followed those who sinned. X, 296. Sin arising from necessity is claimed by Julian to be attributable to God. X, 1500. The unconquerable necessity of slavery under sin, unless the delight of charity conquers the delight of sin. X, 1121.

Sin arises only from free choice. VIII, 537, 538. Both sin and a right act lie within the free choice of the will. VI, 17. Whether, for something to be sin, it must necessarily be avoidable. X, 298. Sin does not exist through that by which it can exist—that is, through free choice. X, 1397. What cannot in any way be avoided is not sin. I, 1295; X, 286. Freedom is enslaved to sin. X, 1110. There are many things by which people do evil, from which they are free to abstain. X, 1068. All who sin with delight and love of sin sin especially through free choice; and they take pleasure in what they desire. X, 1110. Human beings were made with the power to sin, and as their reward they will receive the inability to sin. VI, 359. In heaven there is such freedom that there is also a voluntary and happy necessity of living well and never sinning. X, 296. What sins are those arising from necessity. X, 1119. Sins said to be committed by necessity are to be understood as sins of weakness. X, 287. Sin was not necessary in order to be the cause of God’s mercy. X, 261.

## Sin

Whether anyone in this life can be without sin may be a question. X, 199, 281, 286, 299. The heresy of Jovinian, that a person cannot sin after baptism. X, 1114, 1116, 1117. Some assert that a person can live in this life without any sin. VI, 426. Pelagius taught that a person can be without sin, and that some actually had been so; yet he contradicts himself. II, 776. John of Jerusalem refutes him. II, 829. The Pelagians said that the whole Church was without sin. V, 980. They are refuted. V, 980. The Pelagians believe that the life of the righteous contains no sin. VIII, 48. That a person can, if he wishes, be without sin: the teaching of Pelagius. X, 350. And the doctrine of Caelestius. X, 334. That doctrine was brought against Pelagius in an episcopal synod, and how it was explained by him. X, 329. Caelestius said that before Christ’s coming there had been people without sin; Pelagius, however, said that they had lived holy and just lives. X, 334, 335, 356. No one in this life is without sin. II, 674, 675; III, 1697, [Col. 0508] 1789, 1790, 1871; V, 132, 749, 893, 979; VI, 228, 720. No matter how righteous. VII, 657, 748, 749, 787, 788; VIII, 632; X, 1115, 1235. He spoke truly who said that a human being is not without sin. X, 265, 266. Christ alone is without sin. V, 1341. Except for the one Mediator, no one in this life is without any sin. X, 155, 156, 166, 179, 245, 630, 631, 638, 726, 753. Not even Paul himself. X, 166. No one except Christ was or can be without any sin. X, 171, 174, 306. This also belongs to the unalterable confession of faith. X, 184. Although it could happen that a person might be without sin. X, 201. The Lord was mortal, but not because of sin. IV, 592. The only infant who could have been innocent was one not born of Adam’s act. IV, 592. He alone came without sin who found us sinners. IV, 233. In Christ alone the devil found nothing. V, 929. In what manner Christ was ignorant of sin. IV, 333, 334. Sin is possessed either by drawing it from another or by adding to it; Christ had none. V, 824. Sin was neither in the soul nor in the body that the Word assumed. IV, 335. He alone, free from sins and the liberator from sins, found all people sinners. II, 669. Augustine does not think that one should resist too strongly the possibility that some besides Christ were without sin. X, 317. Those who say that someone here, besides Christ, either is or was entirely without sin are to be tolerated to some extent. II, 675. Concerning the holy Virgin Mary, for the honor of the Lord, I do not want any question at all raised when the subject is sins. X, 267. No saint besides the Virgin is without sin. X, 267. When Christ came, he found in human beings nothing but what he would condemn. V, 201. No one here can live without sin. V, 401. In what sense some people can be said to be without sin in this life. X, 384. It is one thing to live justly, another to be without sin. X, 335. A person can be just and yet not be without sin. X, 269. It is one thing not to have sin, another not to obey its desires. X, 283. The struggle against sin. X, 305. Hence, while struggling against vices, we are not without sin. X, 696. It is one thing not to sin, another not to have sin. III, 2140. What it means not to have sin. X, 453. No one lives so justly in this flesh as to have absolutely no sin. X, 316. It is one thing to be without sin, another to be without reproach. X, 304. It is one thing not to do good, another not to be without sin, even if a person does many good things. X, 307. Many are without crime; no one is without sin. X, 563. Someone can live without crime, but not without sin. VII, 415. Those who walk in the ways of the Lord do not commit sin, and yet they are not without sin. IV, 1506. Very few are those who, from the beginning of adolescence, commit no condemnable sins. VII, 730. As long as a person bears the flesh, he cannot avoid having lesser sins. III, 1982. When a person becomes without sin was not determined in the Palestinian judgment. X, 352, 356. Some sins are daily for ministers of the sacraments and the word of God; others are daily for the laity. V, 1538, 1540. The sins that are accustomed to creep in. V, 1541. That the perfect faithful are not without sin here is understood from the Lord’s Prayer. X, 300. And it becomes evident. X, 316. The righteous rightly pray for the remission of their sins. II, 842. In what sense the one born of God does not sin. X, 312, 370. And cannot sin. X, 254. And no one is without sin. X, 157, 158. Why no one is without sin in this life. X, 167. Why it is a person’s fault that he is not without sin, when without grace he cannot be without sin. X, 297. God wills a person to be without sin. X, 295. Why a person is commanded to be without sin. X, 295. A person is most wisely commanded to be without sin—why. X, 295. Why God commands people not to commit any sin, although he knows that no one will fulfill this. X, 165. Not to sin is given by God—in what manner. X, 1212, 1213. It was necessary for the removal of the occasion of pride that a human being should not be able to exist without sin. X, 262. Enoch and Elijah were not permitted to live here because no one here can live without sin. II, 872. The sins of those whose righteousness Scripture commemorates, although Scripture does not report them, nevertheless do not make these people sinless. X, 268. Testimonies of Scripture and examples by which it is proved that a human being is not without sin. X, 159. The Pelagian evasion is answered. X, 159. A person is not therefore entirely without sin because Scripture calls him perfect in some respect. X, 165. Although people are sometimes found in Scripture described as without reproach, no one is found described as without sin except Christ. X, 253. When the standard of righteousness in Scripture is considered, a person, however much he has advanced, is found to be a sinner. IV, 1269, 1827. Not even those whom Scripture praises for having kept God’s commandments were free from sins. IV, 1266. Why the sins of great men have been written down. III, 78; X, 266. No one among Christ’s members dares say that he has no sin. IV, 1818. Asking forgiveness for sins committed after baptism pertains to everyone, including the Apostles. IV, 1849. Whoever thinks that he lives without sin acts so as not to receive forgiveness. VII, 415. The saints do not say that they have no sin, not to avoid arrogance but to confess the truth. IV, 1505. If perhaps [Col. 0509] someone here is without sin, the greater he is, the more he humbles himself. VI, 426. Whoever denies that he has sinned makes God a liar, while he wants to make himself truthful. III, 1983. It would be a sin if someone who did not have sin said that he did. VI, 720. According to Ambrose, no one in this world is without sin. X, 384. That a person can be without sin in this life is not immediately to be denied—why. X, 155. A person can be without sin in this life, even if he is not such. I, 644, 645; X, 241. How. X, 155, 156. That a person can be without sin if he wishes—in what sense. X, 356. Since a person can live without sin, why is no one without sin? X, 356. Although we cannot be without sins, let us nevertheless hate them. V, 984. Who is most truly to be called without sin. X, 283. To be entirely without any sin does not yet make a person equal to God. X, 265. No one can live without sin, but one can die without sin. X, 267. Whether the saints died without sin. X, 266. Whoever does not neglect to cleanse the sins without which no one lives here will deserve to depart from here without sin. II, 675. To be wholly without sin is to be hoped for only in the resurrection. III, 2140. To have no vice at all is the righteousness of the future life, which will be the reward of the present life. X, 1514, 1515. After the resurrection there will be not only no sins but no sinful desires either. X, 407. No sins are forgiven in heaven—why. X, 848. There will be no sin in the kingdom of God. X, 1582. The inability to sin is the reward of the saints. X, 1523. The sins without which no one lives here are signified by the washing of the feet. III, 1789, 1794. No one exists for whom the remission of sins has not been necessary. X, 316. Although a person ought to be without sin, this is possible, but not without grace. X, 294. A person can be without sin, with the assistance of grace. X, 271. A person can be without sin only through the grace of Christ. X, 299. No one in this life is without sin, even through the grace of God; nevertheless, it is tolerable to assert that through grace a person can be without sin. II, 771. Although there is no doubt that the freedom of the will is free for not sinning, its power is nevertheless insufficient unless weakness is aided. II, 766, 775. For sinning, the soul is sufficient for itself; not for healing the sin that has clung to it. V, 138. So that we may not sin, free choice is not in us before grace, except insofar as we may wish not to sin. III, 2066. It is the most criminal impiety to deny that without the grace of God a person cannot be without sin. X, 252. The error of those who say that a person lives here without sin is less harmful. X, 201.

Sin can be avoided if corrupted nature is healed by grace. X, 293. To die to sin requires the work of grace. III, 2068. Human nature can be perfected and be without sin, but only through the grace of God. X, 281. Sin cannot be conquered without grace. VI, 103. There is no sin that one person commits which another person could not commit if the guide by whom the human being was made were absent. V, 598. Every crime, wrongdoing, or sin is our negligence; every virtue and holiness is God’s indulgence. V, 605.

Sin now rules human beings together with death. VI, 282. Who is a slave of sin. X, 1107. Not everyone who is a slave of sin commits sin; but whoever commits sin is a slave of sin. X, 1107. We have been taken captive because we were sold under sin. III, 1694; IV, 1658. The misery of slavery to sin. I, 1233. At length, concerning slavery to sin and the reign of desire. I, 1233. Let sin not reign in our mortal body. III, 1698. How and when it does not reign. III, 2069. The righteous struggle not so that there may be no desire in their body, but so that it may not reign. III, 417. Sin will not reign in us if we do not obey certain desires. III, 2066. The reign of sin is overthrown in two ways. III, 1268. The view of Julian that the reign of sin fell through the promulgation of the Law. X, 1235. It is discussed. X, 1226. How sin was dead without the Law. VI, 104. And how it came to life again. VI, 104; X, 559. What sin abounded through the Law. X, 1235, 1236, 1239. For sin not to be counted is for it itself to be unknown and not to be considered sin. X, 116. Whether sin is not imputed when there is no Law. X, 1227. Sin was not counted—that is, it did not appear. III, 2067. From what does a person know that sin dwells in his flesh? VI, 106. Sin is recognized through not understanding, just as darkness is recognized through not seeing. III, 2071. And it is felt. VI, 64. What it means to be ignorant of sin. V, 837. To be ignorant of sin is to refuse it and not approve it. X, 561, 562.

Who dominates sin. VIII, 258, 259, 261. What it means to empty the body of sin. III, 2069. How it is emptied. VIII, 891. To pave over sins. V, 1463. The sins of later times are not rightly compared with Adam’s sin. X, 1549. The condition of subsequent offenses was not like that of the first offense committed in paradise. X, 1550.

Sin is the death of the soul. III, 1748. The soul’s only death. VIII, 95. One ought to choose death rather than sin. III, 1767, 1770. Only sins are to be mourned; other evils are to be endured. IV, 409. Through sin a human being becomes like vanity, although he was like truth when he was [Col. 0510] created. IV, 1532, 1863. Only iniquity puts a person far from God. IV, 1775. By sinning a person withdraws from God; by living piously he draws near—how. II, 838. Sins alone separate from God. VII, 300. And from salvation and eternal life. X, 129. How they prevent entry into eternal life. VI, 513. Some sins so hinder arrival at the kingdom of God that nevertheless, through the merits of the saints, forgiveness is obtained. VII, 750. What sins these are. VII, 750. No one can obtain eternal salvation unless, confessing his sins, he has leveled all the empty heights of his pride, and so forth. II, 1029. In sin there are darkness and cold. III, 1579. Sins are the darkness of souls. IX, 118.

Confession of sins before God awakens hope. I, 675, 781. Daniel confessed his sins daily to God. II, 675. Sins are better accused so that they may perish than excused so that they may remain. IV, 1410. A perverse and excusatory confession of sins. IV, 268. A good covering and a bad covering of sins. IV, 266. Sins are added to sins when sins already committed are covered over with other sins. III, 1469. Do not cover your sins, and God will cover them. IV, 267. Excusing sin and perverse defense of it. V, 138, 143, 153, 186. See Repentance. Excusing sin is pride, worse and more condemnable. VII, 422. Those who do not confess their sins but defend them are compared with smoke that is fading away. V, 153. When we excuse our sins, the devil triumphs; when we accuse them, he groans and grieves. V, 186. When we acknowledge our sins, we commend God’s glory. IV, 1219. God erases sins by turning his face away; by turning it toward them, he writes them down. IV, 594. May God turn his face away from your sins, but not turn his face away from you. IV, 207. Do not turn your face away from your sins if you want God to turn his face away from them. IV, 505, 1632. When a person pays attention to sins, he accuses and punishes; when God does not pay attention, he defends and frees. IV, 266. Whoever does not want to see his own sins puts them behind his back and sharply observes the sins of others. IV, 1284. Those who defend their sins or attribute them to God are reproved. IV, 268, 434, 605, 701, 854, 1172, 1793, 1808, 1821. Confessions of sins are wounds bursting outward. III, 1350. How sins stink is perceived by anyone with a sound sense of smell. IV, 401. The burden of sins must be laid down quickly. III, 1474. The gravity of sin ought to trouble us. III, 1755. Sin ought to displease us. V, 134. A person’s sins displease him when God shines upon him. III, 1491. You do not truly mourn your sins if tears run while your hands remain inactive. IV, 410. So that we may not increase our sins through despair, the harbor of repentance has been set before us; and again, so that we may not increase them through presumption, the day of death has been made uncertain. V, 1560. Turning away from sin in order to obtain its forgiveness. VIII, 258. The turning from sin ought to be toward the human being—in what sense. VII, 444, 445. Sins, like diseases, are avoided in two ways. X, 287. Sins of three kinds are to be healed by a threefold remedy. VI, 228. Sin must not be avoided by means of sin. VII, 58.

There are two kinds of sin. IV, 816. There are three kinds of sin. III, 1747; VI, 17, 228. All sins comprise these three: the pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity. IV, 115. Three distinctions of sin. III, 1247. Like three deaths. III, 1247. There are two kinds of sins: against God and against human beings. V, 1271. What it means to sin against God and to sin to God. III, 773, 774. There is no reason for sinning against God. V, 1469. The sin of a human being or an angel harms God in no way. VI, 333. Sin does not harm God. I, 830. Nor can it harm him. I, 690. How, then, is it against God? I, 690. A person sins in two ways before becoming wise. I, 1306. All sins belong either to the corruption of shameful acts or to crimes of causing harm. V, 87. Sin against another human being is not to be disregarded. V, 507. Sin against another human being is committed in two ways: first, if he is harmed; second, if he is not helped when one can help him. I, 1332. Every sin harms the one who commits it more than the one who suffers it. VI, 240. Whether sin against the Holy Spirit can be called schism, and the handing over of the Scriptures. IX, 554. Whether that sin ought not to be charged against schismatics. IX, 554.

Some sins are against nature, others against morals, and others against commandments. VIII, 428.

The pleasure of sin is called sin. III, 417. The sin in the members of which the Apostle speaks is a certain violent allure­ment of the flesh in this body of death. III, 417. The law of sin is called sin. X, 178. Sin is called concupiscence because all sins arise from it. V, 840. What the law of sin in the members is. VI, 107, 108. The law of sin is the violence of habit. I, 754. The Apostle calls the illicit desires of the original sickness sin. IV, 1507. Sin unto death—what it is. III, 1266; X, 938. Sins of imitation in the world. X, 1162. The sin that the Jews would not have had if Christ had not come. V, 450. Why the world is convicted concerning the single sin of unbelief. V, 785, 787. One sin is merely sin; another is also the punishment of sin. I, 604, 608, 612; III, 156; X, 1467, 1474. There are certain sins that are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sins. [Col. 0511] IV, 687; X, 258, 790, 793, 906, 975. Some sins also arise from the wrath of God. III, 797. Sins are punished by sins. X, 1354. It comes from the punishment of sin that a human being is divided against himself, because he refused to be subject to one ruler. IV, 891, 1859. The ease with which certain sins are committed is the punishment of other preceding sins. VI, 91. Some manifest sins arise as punishment for certain hidden ones. VIII, 288. Manifest sin is useful for healing the hidden vice of pride. VII, 422. The judgment and punishment of sins, which is now carried out secretly. IV, 117. In the mind itself punishment immediately follows guilt, usually greater because of the blindness of one who does not perceive it. II, 381. God acts not by an evil work but by a just work when he makes certain sins also punishments of sin. X, 1355, 1356. An objection to the position concerning sin and the punishment of sin is answered. X, 790. Actual sin has a twofold origin. I, 1285. A twofold cause. X, 554. The cause of sin is twofold: ignorance and concupiscence. X, 563. Ignorance and weakness. VI, 271; X, 152, 167. Sin is one thing, the concupiscence of sin another. X, 1172. The cause of sins is either ignorance, weakness, or contempt. III, 729. The most just punishment of Adam’s sin is ignorance and difficulty. X, 287. All sins arise from that root of error and perverted love with which every son of Adam is born. X, 846.

Human sins are called sins of ignorance. III, 720. The sins of the ignorant. VI, 456. Sins arising from ignorance. X, 287. How is it that everyone who sins has not seen or known God? X, 313. The sin of one who knows is graver than that of one who does not know. IX, 157, 158; X, 884. Sins of ignorance are lighter than those committed by people who know. X, 148. Sin is without doubt ignorance itself in those who were unwilling to understand; but in those who were unable to understand, it is the punishment of sin. II, 883. The sins of those who are unwilling are the sins of those who are ignorant. III, 728. Sins of ignorance can also exist among the baptized. III, 2100. Sins of ignorance are all those cases in which someone thinks that what is done badly is done well. II, 186.

Sins arising from weakness come from the transmission of Adam’s first sin and from bad habit. VIII, 541. We all contract daily sins through the weakness of the flesh. V, 1541. If a sin of weakness has crept in, what should be done? III, 1983. How it is healed. VIII, 541. The two incentives to sin are pleasure and pain. V, 1286. Remedies against these two. V, 1286. Two things produce all sins in a human being: desire and fear. IV, 413, 1026. By sinning, each person sells his soul to the devil for the price of pleasure. III, 2071. If sin did not delight, it would not be committed; nor would it delight if there were health. V, 877. If righteousness delights less than sin, or does not delight, or delights less than it ought, this results from illnesses of the soul. V, 877.

Sins committed secretly are sweeter. III, 2070. The sweetness of sin is deceptive. VI, 104. Sin is like a buckthorn: at first it pleases, afterward it pricks. IV, 689. Sin is sweet, but the death to which it leads is bitter. V, 398. The things for which people sin they leave behind when they die here, but they carry the sins themselves with them. V, 398.

Sin is not committed without a cause. I, 679. It is committed only for the sake of usefulness or pleasure. VI, 513. Perhaps no one would wish to sin itself, but it is done for the sake of something else that the sinner does desire. III, 728. Whether sins can be admitted, if not for temporal advantage, at least for the sake of preserving holiness. VI, 513. Let a person do even what he can for the temporal salvation of human beings; where he can do nothing except by sinning, let him consider that he has nothing to do. VI, 542. Sins are never to be committed as though for some good. VI, 528. Compensatory sins are not themselves to be admitted. IV, 530, 533, 539. Sin is not only what appears to human beings in a shameful or unjust act; it is also sin if an act has the appearance of a good work and yet is done for the sake of temporal reward, not for everlasting rest. V, 208. A person vainly thinks himself victorious over sin if he does not sin only from fear of punishment. II, 593. Whoever does not sin solely from fear sins by the will. X, 558. You ought not to avoid sin from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness. V, 870. Whoever does not sin from fear of punishment is an enemy of righteousness; but he will be its friend if he does not sin out of love for it. II, 594. Each person hates sin only to the extent that he loves righteousness. II, 594.

In how many ways sins are committed. X, 563. There are many sins in inward words that are not found in outward deeds. VI, 351. Yet there are no sins in outward deeds that are not preceded by inward words. VI, 351. Who can avoid sins of the tongue and sins of the heart? IV, 1700. Even in things that are permitted, sins occur if the proper measure is exceeded. V, 88, 1273. Three or four stages in sins. V, 594, 720. Sin is completed through three things: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. III, 207, 1246. These three correspond to what happened in the temptation of our first parent. III, 207, 1246. We sin not in an evil desire but in consent. III, 2066. Sin is present when you take pleasure; it reigns if you consent. IV, 587. How sins are connected with sins. IV, 677, 1705, 1808. Everyone who sins acts against charity; therefore whoever offends in one matter has become guilty of all, since [Col. 0512] no sin exists except against charity, and so forth. II, 739. A person is fuller of iniquity in proportion as he is emptier of charity. II, 740.

The Stoics maintain that all sins are equal. VI, 539. Jovinianus said so. VIII, 45. Nectarius also thinks so; Augustine refutes him. II, 387, 393, 394. How sin and crime differ. IV, 1507, 1508. And the definition of each. III, 681, 682. Even in little children there are obligations and offenses. IV, 1381. Venial sins and crimes. X, 563. Condemnable and venial sins. X, 302, 1180. Great sins and small sins. III, 1491, 1492. Degrees in sins and in guilt. III, 1241. There are certain sins concerning which it is impossible to determine whether we shall perish because of them. IV, 1132. Which sins are light and which grave must be weighed not by human but by divine judgment. VI, 269. In every sin—more in a greater one, less in a smaller one—something is nevertheless desired against justice. VI, 367. A sin can be lighter than another by intention; yet the lighter one is not therefore to be committed, since it is often graver than a sin of another kind. VI, 529. The sins called crimes. V, 1206. Grave sins, for which a definite condemnation and separation from daily bread are owed. V, 88, 382, 1540. Sins that require more strenuous labor of repentance. V, 1273. Among Christians there are some sins more serious than the persecution of enemies. III, 1266. What venial sins are: the sins of the righteous. VI, 1718; X, 230, 244, 269. This life is not lived without venial sins. X, 230. Sins appear more pardonable when the guilty person promises correction. II, 654. Venial sins do not prevent the righteous from eternal life. X, 230. To what extent they are forgiven. X, 1180. Certain small sins are listed. V, 80, 392, 1206. Examples of venial sins. X, 268, 269. The multitude of venial sins in one person. X, 269. Small sins are not to be despised. V, 88, 382, 398. They are not to be neglected. VI, 680. If neglected, they kill. III, 1492. Sins are to be avoided, even those that appear small. IV, 447, 448. If sins are neglected because they are small, let them be feared because they are many. IV, 1700. If you despise light sins when you weigh them, be terrified when you count them. III, 1982. Light sins gathered together, like mange, either kill us or destroy our beauty. V, 1541. Light sins enter through small cracks like water into a drain. IV, 810. Daily small sins form a mass and a heap. IV, 1201. Even if they do not crush us individually by their weight, all of them together overwhelm us in a pile. IV, 1508. Small sins overwhelm by their multitude unless they are forgiven by God. V, 88, 382, 1207, 1273. Many light sins make one great sin. III, 1982. Small sins, if frequent, burden and oppress us like one great sin. II, 1089. Small sins that creep up on watchful people grow through pride and are destroyed by humility. VI, 425, 426. Each person ought to avoid the lighter sin that is his own rather than the graver one that belongs to another. VI, 499. Sins that appear light are sometimes extremely grave. VI, 270. Each person judges sins grave insofar as they injure the life he loves. VI, 513. Horrible sins appear light through habit. VI, 270. We shudder only at unusual sins. VI, 271. Woe to the sins of human beings, at which we shudder only when they are unusual; but by often seeing what is customary we are compelled to tolerate everything, and by often tolerating it, even to do some of it. III, 2130. What people think should be lightly regarded as sins of the flesh harms God himself. III, 560. Sins of the flesh are deadly. V, 507. Why the fornicator alone is said to sin against his own body, when other sins are attributed to the works of the flesh. V, 886. Hence the ungodly, whom grace does not assist, sin more or less. X, 1185. Grave sins are to be avoided; lesser ones are to be healed by a threefold remedy. V, 88. The cleansing and daily medicine of daily sins. V, 127, 299, 382, 983, 1207, 1272. Lighter sins are erased by the Lord’s Prayer. VI, 265. And by almsgiving. X, 302, 304, 563, 564. Repentance, fasts, almsgiving, and prayers for venial sins. II, 1089. Why light sins are not mentioned in Scripture. X, 268. Many sin while thinking that they are not seen by God. V, 441. If you want to sin, look for a place where God does not see you, and do what you want. V, 736.

Whether anyone can be liable for the sins of others. X, 839. No one else commits another person’s sin. X, 1147. How someone shares in the sins of others. V, 549; IX, 344. Or does not share in them. V, 551; IX, 79, 80, 82, 83. To share in the sins of others is to consent to them. IX, 228, 609. Whoever spares and favors the nourishment of vices so as not to grieve the will of sinners is no more merciful than one who refuses to take a knife away from a child lest he hear the child cry, and so forth. II, 395. In how many ways someone can be said to have sinned with another. IV, 1409. Whoever consents to a sinner is burdened by his own sins, not by those of another. IV, 1699. Sin is advised to another either through foolish benevolence or through malicious envy. VIII, 592. One who does not wish to restrain sinners by sinning does not consent to sinners. VI, 498. As it is harsh to show indulgence to sinners, so it is impious to refuse a hand to the converted. II, 784. The sins of others do not prejudice anyone. IX, 427. See Church, Evil. No one is to be calumniated on account of another’s sins, and no one need fear calumny on account of them. IX, [Col. 0513] 612. If the sins of others defile anyone, the Donatists prejudice themselves. IX, 612. The Donatists did not want the sins of others to pertain to them. IX, 306. If anyone thinks that the sins of others pertain to him, they do pertain to him. IX, 278, 287. The sins of others do not harm the salvation of others when the name of Christ is invoked. IX, 301. That the sins of others do not harm others is shown by the Donatists’ own acceptance of the Maximianists. IX, 371. No one’s crime defiles one who is unaware of it. II, 328. The Donatist bishops who had come to the Conference admitted that no one is defiled by sins of others of which he is ignorant. IX, 631. The sins of others do not defile. II, 339, 341; IX, 278, 279, 519, 520, 565. They do not defile anyone within unity. IX, 607, 608, 609. No one is contaminated by the sins of others; nevertheless, correction of others is not to be neglected. V, 896. The sins of others are to be borne patiently. V, 41. They are to be borne in such a way that the offenders may be corrected. V, 43. When someone sins, one should act so that another does not learn of it. V, 511. The sins of others are not to be watched with excessive curiosity. V, 152. Whether anyone ought to avoid the sins of others because of his own sins. VI, 499. Why the custom of accusing the sins of others before ecclesiastical judges is neglected. V, 1546. On the way of faith, those are regarded as not sinning to whom sins are not imputed. IV, 1508.

Sins of bad habit are difficult to undo. III, 1756. Intimacy with sin is to be avoided as one avoids intimacy with a serpent. V, 138. When sins become cheapened through habit, they are no longer even felt. V, 125. By not admitting one particular sin, the others are undone; by admitting it, the others are strengthened. III, 2013. It is difficult for perverse people, while avoiding vices, not to rush headlong into their opposites. III, 398. How the soul rises again from sin. III, 432. It is one thing to withdraw from every sin, another to have withdrawn. X, 308. It is little to withdraw from sins if one neglects to deal with past sins. V, 409. Through sin the soul can be dead, although sin itself seems still to live. III, 2069. When sin will die. III, 2070. Sin is diminished in the life of those making progress and consumed in the life of the perfect. III, 1697. The more someone advances, the farther he becomes from sin and the nearer to the fullness of righteousness. X, 308. Sins are easy to fall into, and righteousness is laborious except for those who love it. X, 1200. All sins are to be overcome by love and delight in righteousness. X, 161. Nothing tests a spiritual person so much as his treatment of another’s sin. III, 2143.

Sin cannot remain unpunished. IV, 505, 701; VI, 358. Those sin tolerably who are corrected and healed by the scourge. IV, 1133. It belongs to the natural order of justice that either sins should not be committed or that they should not be able to remain unpunished. VIII, 480. Sin is contrary to nature, but by punishment it is brought back into conformity with nature. VIII, 480. Sin must be punished either by God or by man. IV, 505. Sin must be punished either by the repentant person or by God the judge. V, 133, 139, 187. One who truly repents does nothing else than ensure that what he has done wrongly is not left unpunished. II, 655. You wanted to sin, but did not want to suffer; as though it were not enough for you to be unjust, unless you also wished him to be unjust from whom you did not want vengeance to be exacted upon you. IV, 478. The bitter draught of correction must not be rejected. V, 84. The usefulness and sweetness of repentance. I, 700. A place for the most humble repentance is granted in the Church only once. II, 656. So that the medicine might not be cheap and therefore less useful to the sick. II, 656. The works of those to whom a place of repentance is not granted in the Church are nevertheless not useless. II, 656. See Repentance.

If sin ought not to be punished, it would not be sin. IV, 505. How sins are punished or washed away. VIII, 480, 588. To punish and to forgive sins belongs equally to God. VIII, 561. For God to see sins is to punish them. IV, 264. Why God does not punish the sinner immediately. VI, 662. Many things here seem unpunished, but their punishments are reserved. VI, 263. Man sinned voluntarily, but was not condemned voluntarily. III, 2075. The punishment of sin is justly decreed. III, 384. By not punishing sins, the Lord does not favor sins. III, 1650. The punishments of sin are common to angels and human beings. VI, 244. Whether temporal sin is justly punished with eternal punishment. VII, 725. Eternal vengeance is deserved by sin. II, 381. The punishment and end of sinners is that they are first ravaged by the fire of desires, then cast out from the company of the blessed through the stench of evil works, and finally, carried away and submerged, suffer indescribable punishments. IV, 137. Sins deserving eternal punishments are punished by temporal corrections. VIII, 442. The punishments of sinners show what God grants to the elect. VI, 123, 124, 126. God neither permitted the sinful human being to remain unpunished nor abandoned him without mercy. VII, 153. The punishments of sin are just. I, 1241. And varied. I, 674. What the punishment of sin is. III, 221. The punishment proper to human sin. VI, 244. Each person’s punishment is made from his own sin. IV, 107. God does not punish in human beings the sins which he foreknew they would someday commit, as the Pelagians taught. II, 889. Why the punishment of sinners is called a cup. IV, 137. God does not produce from himself the means by which sins are punished, but so orders sins themselves that what had been pleasures to the sinning human being may be instruments to the punishing Lord. IV, 107, 108. The destructive sweetness of sin is digested through the bitterness of tribulation. V, 1271. By paying the penalties of its sin, the soul gains discernment of good and evil. III, 138. Through punishment we are instructed toward repentance. III, 134. Punishment makes sinners ashamed, which impunity would not have done. X, 1355. The punishment of the body, even if it does not proceed from the will, nevertheless recalls one from the work of sin. Justice, however, must be loved so that even bodily punishments should not restrain us from its works. II, 594. The transgression of the Prophet was punished by temporal death, but not by eternal death. VI, 598, 599. How holy men punished certain sins by death. III, 1262. For one person’s sin another is not to be punished in human judgment; but in God’s judgment someone is sometimes punished by a visible penalty. III, 778, 779. The sins of some are avenged by the bodily deaths of others. VIII, 660. Why this occurs. IX, 743. Whatever is sinned by many is not unpunished before God. II, 525. How the sins of a multitude are to be corrected. IX, 93. How those of private persons are corrected. IX, 92. Whoever orders himself unjustly in sins is justly ordered in punishments. II, 539. God is not the author of sins, but their disposer. VIII, 451. How the ordering of sins in punishments is punishment and how it is justice. VIII, 554. Sin does not disturb the order of God’s rule. I, 830. No one acts unjustly unless permitted to do so by the divine and most just judgment. VII, 659. Sin contributes to the beauty of the universe. VII, 336. Sinful souls contribute to the perfection of the universe. I, 1283. Although their sins are not necessary to that perfection. I, 1284. God makes many good things from our evils and our sins. II, 727. The world is not wholly filled with sins simply because sin exists. VII, 336.

No sin is unforgivable except perseverance in wickedness together with despair of God’s forgiveness. III, 2104. Sin against the Holy Spirit that can be forgiven in this life. II, 814; V, 447, 449. Sin against the Holy Spirit that is unforgivable. V, 465; VI, 272. What it is to sin against the Holy Spirit. III, 1267, 2097, 2098. He sins against the Holy Spirit who, despairing or despising the preaching of grace and peace, refuses to repent and persists to the very end. III, 2097, 2105. The sin against the Holy Spirit that is not forgiven is impenitence. V, 455. The unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit is hardness of heart until the end of life, and so forth. II, 814. The question of the sin against the Holy Spirit is perhaps the most difficult in all Scripture. V, 449. Augustine always avoided this subject in sermons to the people, and at last treated it when moved by God. V, 449. A short treatise on the unforgivable sin. VI, 272. The sin unto death. III, 1229, 1230. One must not pray for a person sinning the sin unto death. III, 1266. The sin unto death is such a great stain that it does not permit one to submit to the humility of petition. III, 1266. The sin of pride is contempt for the word of the Lord. III, 728. It was expiated by no kind of sacrifice. III, 728. It cannot be abolished without punishment of the person who commits it. III, 728. There is no sin concerning which forgiveness ought not to be hoped for. III, 1640, 1678, 1687, 1696, 1748. The forgiveness of sins is necessary for every person living here. VI, 262. The forgiveness of sins takes place in view of the future judgment. VI, 263. The forgiveness of sins applies to little children. X, 1191, 1196.

Sins are dissolved and abolished in Christ’s glorification. III, 595. Christ alone can take away sins. III, 638. Only he who came without sin can free from sin. III, 1694, 1695. That the poison of sin can be removed only by Christ’s death was taught by the serpent raised up in the wilderness. X, 145. Sins are taken away when Christ’s death is contemplated. III, 489, 490. No one is freed from sins except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ. II, 885; X, 1119. The sin of one’s own will is also dissolved and healed through Christ. X, 120. To what extent Christ takes away sin. X, 1172. Christ takes away sin in three ways. X, 1176. Sin is taken away by sin. X, 262. A person is not freed from sin by the Law but by grace. X, 896. No sin is taken away by the Law. X, 1173, 1176. Sins were not removed through the Law. III, 2067. Sin is taken away by grace alone. III, 2065. Sins are taken away only by the grace of faith, which works through love. III, 2106. The Law caused sin to be exposed; grace caused what had been done to be erased and guarded against being done. X, 1173. The forgiveness of sins does not occur only once through grace. X, 1232. In how many ways it occurs. X, 1232. To what extent a human being is healed from sins. X, 295. There are two kinds of liberation from sin. X, 1122. Julian’s slander against Augustine: that a human being cannot be cleansed from sins. X, 1115. How the cleansing of sins occurs in this life. VII, 300. In what ways sins are cleansed. IX, 475. Sins are forgiven in three ways. VI, 636. Remedies for sins: almsgiving, fasting, and prayer. IX, 63. Sins are expiated by prayer, and God is appeased. II, 665, 675. Sins are expiated by sacrifices of mercy. II, 659. Daily almsgiving is not sufficient to cleanse greater crimes. V, 88. Sins must be drained away daily through good works, lest they weigh down the ship. IV, 810. Through almsgiving God is to be propitiated for past sins, not bought, as it were, so that one may always commit them with impunity. VI, 265. Sinners are mistaken when they think that by almsgiving they can purchase impunity for remaining in their crimes. VI, 268. Almsgiving does not redeem sins unless one’s life is changed. VI, 265, 267. More serious sins are erased through the Lord’s Prayer if life is changed for the better through repentance. VI, 265. Sins, however monstrous, are forgiven in baptism. VI, 635, 636. All die to sin in baptism. VI, 253. Sins are not cleansed by baptism alone. IX, 475. The forgiveness of sins does not follow baptism unless baptism is not only lawful but also lawfully received. IX, 181. The error of not believing that sins are forgiven in the Church. VI, 272. Sins, however great, are forgiven in the Church through repentance. VI, 262. There is no sin that is not forgiven through the Church to one who repents and begs forgiveness. III, 1336. Sins are not forgiven outside the Church. VI, 263; IX, 146, 147, 150. Nothing is released outside the Church. V, 1349. Only repentance practiced in the true religion obtains forgiveness and cleanses what has been committed. II, 391. The Lord raises up by himself; through his disciples he releases. V, 1350. The release from sins can be granted through the Church, but the dead person can be raised only when the Lord himself cries out inwardly. IV, 1306, 1307. The forgiveness of sins is granted even through wicked ministers. IX, 67. Sins are not forgiven except to the baptized. VI, 636. For which sins there is easy hope of forgiveness. V, 153. One should not think that forgiveness is granted for sins committed for the sake of liberating people. III, 708. Ignorance of sin contributes to the ease of forgiveness. IX, 158. The condition under which our daily sins are released. V, 983.

To one who does not forgive sins, sins are not forgiven by God either. VI, 193, 267; VII, 749. For one who does not forgive others their sins there is no hope of salvation. V, 1273. Forgiving the sins of others is an antidote against all sins. V, 1271. A remedy for sins. IV, 1698; IX, 213. When and with what disposition forgiveness of sin is to be granted or denied. II, 391. To forgive an offense committed against oneself, so that God may forgive, is a great work of mercy. IX, 64. Forgiven sins return where fraternal love is absent. IX, 120. All sins are erased when we say, from a true heart and with full confidence, “Forgive us,” and so forth. IV, 1861. The necessity of forgiving the sins of others. V, 384. We ought to forgive one another our offenses and pray for one another concerning them. III, 1794, 1795. We must all beg forgiveness from God, not absolution. V, 152. The whole Church here asks that its sins be forgiven. V, 981, 982. Which sins we ask to be forgiven in the Lord’s Prayer. IV, 1507; IX, 120. Venial sins are erased in the Lord’s Prayer. VI, 636. God forgives the sins not of everyone, but of those whom he has foreknown and predestined. VIII, 660. When each person has departed from the body, all those debts are forgiven which he had in such a condition that they could be forgiven, since they are also forgiven in daily prayers. V, 982. Which sins God does not impute. X, 298. Certain sins are forgiven even in the future age. X, 848. The forgiveness of sins is the refuge of the citizens above. VII, 77. The Lord’s mercy is nowhere more abundant than in the forgiveness of sins. IV, 289. See Mercy. A deadly security in sinning, based on the hope of forgiveness promised to those who confess. VI, 425. All sins are to be regarded as forgiven when God guards people so that they do not commit them. VI, 421, 427. Burial signifies the forgiveness of sins. III, 592. See Forgiveness.

The depth of sins is signified by the abyss. IV, 348. Sins are signified in the Law by the corpses of the dead. III, 592. And by the eleven curtains covering the tabernacle. III, 635. Sins are the only bonds by which the devil held us. V, 726. Sins are not only bonds but also little hairs. IV, 677. In Scripture, infirmities are used for sins. II, 633. Sin is called by the name of lying. VI, 547. Every sin is a lie. IV, 1174; VII, 407. As regards sin, what it means to turn to the right or to the left. X, 184. Sin is nothing. I, 682. And human beings become nothing when they sin. III, 1385; V, 153. Sins have no substance. IV, 1645. Sin is a servile work. X, 218. Hairs are a symbol of sins. V, 41, 56. Sin is a sacrifice to the demon. I, 673. Sin is like a scorpion. V, 818. Sins are called interest and debts. IV, 910. They are called wounds. IV, 861. Sin is signified by the number eleven. VII, 465. How sin and vice differ. X, 294. In what sense Christ is called sin. VI, 252, 253. Christ is sin because he is the victim for sin. V, 825. How sins are in him. V, 1607. Why the assumption of mortal flesh is called sin. III, 2072. Why Christ’s flesh, and Christ himself, are so called. V, 745. The punishment of sin is called sin. III, 520; VI, 253, 540. Sins are called sacrifices for sins. III, 721, 731, 1695; V, 744, 825; VI, 253, 540.

The sinner is under the yoke of the devil. VIII, 126. Sinners are said to be from the father, the devil. VIII, 135. The Pelagians wish all sinners, because of the freedom of the will, to belong to the imitation of the first human being. X, 1204. In the general sense, a sinner is either a transgressor of the Law, if he received the Law, or an unrighteous person, if he did not receive it. IV, 879. Every transgressor is a sinner, but not conversely. IV, 1572. Those who did not want to confess themselves sinners became transgressors when the Law was added. IV, 1329. A sinner becomes a transgressor through the Law. V, 690. All sinners of the earth are to be regarded as transgressors of the law, whether the law given in paradise, written in the heart, or given through Moses. II, 681. He carries with him the inherited punishment of iniquity and the penalty of sin, assigned to death. IV, 734. Absolutely all human beings are dead in sins. VII, 665. Some sin from necessity, others from abundance; of the latter it is said that their iniquity proceeds from fatness. IV, 920. Some sin through ignorance or weakness, others through pride. IV, 1522, 1523. We are called sinners when we sin through ignorance, and transgressors of the Law when we sin knowingly. VI, 271. It makes no difference whether you yourself commit the crime or wish it to be committed by another for your sake. I, 1369. It is worse to lead another into sin than to be led by him. I, 1285. The human being sinned less by consenting to the demon than the demon did by giving evil advice to the human being. I, 1286. The sinner’s ears lie between God who warns and the serpent who suggests. IV, 1172.

The bread of truth is bitter to sinners. IV, 88. The sinner’s adversary is the word of God. V, 637. The sinner cannot flee from God, but everywhere finds the law of God in his own punishment. I, 699. The sinner who turns away from God becomes blind; he does not yet feel the punishment, but already possesses it. V, 664. Sinners are blind in heart. III, 1388. What they must do in order to be healed. III, 1388. In his sins the sinner weaves a rope for himself. III, 1460.

Each sinner abandons Christ the more, the more he loves what Christ disapproves. VII, 748. The sinner is worse if he rejoices in the harm done to equity. VII, 641. Nothing is more wretched than the prosperity of sinners. II, 531. In prosperity the sinner is compared with hay, which quickly passes away. IV, 1177. The peace of sinners is not to be envied. IV, 770, 771. Let no one congratulate a person who prospers in his way, whose sins lack an avenger and have a praiser: this is a greater anger of the Lord. IV, 126, 1266. The happiness of sinners is their own pit. IV, 1204. In prosperity the sinner is like a fish that already has the hook in its jaws. IV, 1176. Sinners do not displease themselves because they do not attend to themselves. IV, 1261. The sinner is said to despise God when he attributes no providence to God or does not believe that he belongs under it. IV, 1853. A description of the sinner in the discussion of his conversion. III, 1338. The sinner’s conversion and repentance. IV, 583, 655, 1460, 1799, 1933. The sinner’s conversion is to be attributed to God’s grace. III, 406, 407. The sinner is known and sought by God before he knows and seeks God. III, 1448. God sees and hates those who sin, even though he is now silent. V, 126. Christ loves sinners so that they may not love being sinners. V, 947, 949. Preceding merits in sinners leading to justification and hardening. VI, 72. The sinner’s first labor is to become displeasing to himself, to conquer his sins, to be changed for the better; the second labor is, because he has been changed, to endure the tribulations and temptations of this age and to persevere among them to the end. IV, 717. To obtain mercy, the sinner must acknowledge his sin. IV, 589. The sinner ought to rage when he recognizes himself as guilty. III, 1755. Even if the sinner confesses, he remains guilty unless the ministers release him. III, 1757. How the sinner is healed. III, 1340. God does not turn away from the sinner and then turn back. He turned away because you turned away: you made the fall from him, not he the setting from you. V, 780. Let the sinner perish, so that the human being may not perish. V, 152. Sinners are overthrown in two ways. VII, 739. For the sinner to rise again, he must imitate Christ raising Lazarus. III, 1755. The raising of Lazarus is explained allegorically as the raising of the sinner. III, 1578. In the sinner’s return to God, greatness of soul imitates virtue and instruction imitates wisdom. VIII, 587. Three kinds of sinners and three degrees of sin are represented by the three dead whom Christ raised. V, 593, 720. The sinner who wishes to perish must be compassionately helped, like a lethargic person. V, 246. Those sinners who denied that people should be admitted to repentance were excommunicated by the Church. III, 2099, 2100. Out of the rigor of discipline, repentant sinners did not receive clerical status, nor return to it; nevertheless, dispensation could be made in their case. II, 812. The sinner receives what was lost only gradually. V, 1270. If the human being returned quickly to his former blessedness, it would be a game for him to fall into death by sinning. V, 1270. One must rise quickly from sin. V, 595. The devil either turns the sinner away from the medicine of confession, drives him into despair of forgiveness, or leads him into presumption upon divine indulgence. V, 139. No sinner ought to despair of the mercy of almighty God. V, 1060. No sinner should despair, but should flee to God through repentance. V, 442, 1548. Paul confesses himself a sinner so that no sinner may despair of himself. V, 927, 949, 951. The sinner should presume upon God’s mercy in such a way that he does not cease to fear his justice. V, 262. Sinners should love gentleness in the Lord in such a way that they fear the truth. III, 1650. The sinner should not spare himself. III, 1491.

The sinner’s silence is a cry of impiety against God. IV, 256. A cry of presumption. IV, 266. The voices of sinners sunk into the depth of evils. IV, 1697. Sinners are roused to pray so that sins may be erased, diminished, and brought to an end. V, 749. God hears sinners. IX, 60, 61. God answers them. III, 1718. The dangers of those who strive to heal others held fast by vices. II, 352.

The excuses of sinners are various. VI, 358. No excuse of human beings is just; for if the excuse of sinners were just, it would no longer be grace but justice that liberated them. II, 883, 884. Every sinner is without excuse, either because of the guilt of origin or because of the addition of his own will, whether he knows or is ignorant. II, 883. It can never be well with the sinner. III, 384. But sometimes he does not feel it. III, 432. Sinners are already tortured in this life. IV, 689, 690. Sinners generally suffer punishment openly and always secretly from God for their deeds. VII, 659. The sinner rages against himself. VIII, 137. The conscience of a criminal surpasses prisons and hells in its fearful and punitive darkness. II, 651. God makes a scourge out of the sinner. IV, 362. The sinner wrongly thinks that his deeds please God because God delays vengeance. IV, 582. Why sinners are sometimes scourged less in this life. IV, 409, 770, 771. God scourges sinners here so that they may be corrected. IV, 1292. When God punishes sinners, he does not inflict his own evil upon them, but abandons them to their own evils. IV, 87, 151. Through comparison with sinners and their punishment, others are incited to live rightly. IV, 126. Jesus looks everywhere upon the sinner, not to help but to punish. V, 879. Why some grow old in crimes. V, 879. Many sinners are corrected, many tolerated, and many unknown. V, 1546. Punishment is reserved for the sinner from his own works. IV, 124. Divine providence does not make sinners but orders them. IV, 106. God’s sentence against sinners is changed if they themselves change. V, 152. Correction and future judgment await sinners who are not corrected at the present time. V, 125. The sinful nature is better ordered so that it may rightly suffer in punishment than that it may rejoice with impunity in sin. VIII, 554, 563. That sinners are not to be spared on the day of judgment, but exercised by eternal fires: this was approved by bishops as Catholic doctrine and brought against Pelagius as erroneous. X, 326. Pelagius did not distinguish sinners to be saved through fire from sinners to be punished by eternal punishment. X, 325, 326. The expulsion of sinners by God. IV, 88. What kind of sinner is worthy of condemnation. VIII, 419.

The sinful human being has two names: one God made, the other the human being. V, 110, 152. In the sinner both the guilt is to be rejected and the nature approved. II, 654. In sinners only sins are to be hated; the human beings themselves are to be loved. VIII, 161. The sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved. III, 29. The sinner is to be loved, not insofar as he is a sinner, but by pursuing the sin—just as a sick person is loved while the fever is attacked. V, 43, 110, 163, 780. In what sense sinners do not have being. IV, 430. Sinners are less than they were. III, 133. They do and do not do evil: how this is to be understood. IV, 1507. How sinners imitate the individual persons of the most holy Trinity. VIII, 586. Sinners imitate God the Father in impious pride, while the just imitate him in pious generosity. VIII, 586. The conversion of a proud sinner because of the dignity of this age is described. III, 881. The sinner’s place and use. IV, 362. Sinners, whether angels or human beings, do not disturb God’s providence. VII, 435. Sinners are useful as an example. III, 432. Why God created those whom he foreknew would sin. VII, 435. God did not compel either human being or angel to sin, although he foreknew what good would arise from it. VII, 435, 436. Sinners are like vessels of the devil, which he fills with his bitterness. V, 726. Sinners and ungodly people are one mass, in which are both Jews and Gentiles. VI, 124.

“Sinner” is sometimes used for “sin.” III, 75. Who are called sinners in Scripture. IV, 1412. The sinner is black in color. V, 693. Repentant sinners are compared with young ravens. III, 880. Sinners are called goats. IV, 779. Sinners are signified by kids. V, 43. Sinners are dead servants. V, 744. They are called darkness. IV, 1766. They are darkness. III, 258, 259, 826, 870. They are called earth. III, 1277. Sinners cannot save themselves; how they are understood when joined to oxen. IV, 799. The sinner is the footstool of God’s feet. III, 1257.

Beating of the breast. V, 133, 186, 433. An indication of contrition. IV, 265. The people used to beat their breasts when they heard the word “confession.” IV, 1495, 1774, 1844; V, 186. Whoever beats his breast and is not corrected hardens his sins rather than removes them. VI, 675. He paves over his sins. V, 1463. Beat your breast, but by striking your breast and inflicting wounds upon yourself, be corrected. V, 512. Bishops standing at the altar also beat their breasts. V, 1541, 1542. The priest too beats his breast. V, 749. The beating of the breast is a testimony to our sin. V, 751, 762.

Embezzlement: theft from the commonwealth. III, 1762.

An animal consists of soul and body. VIII, 418. The Manichaeans believed that animals possessed not only human souls but divine ones. VIII, 231, 232. Animals also have souls. V, 1181. What animals are understood by the term “cattle.” III, 241. What the life of animals is. III, 1540. What the good of an animal is. IV, 1322. Animals are God’s flocks. IV, 1911. Why the Manichaeans prohibited the slaughter of animals. VIII, 383. By the term “animals,” the uneducated are understood. IV, 1750.

Cattle bear young twice a year in Italy. III, 573.

Money as a goddess. VII, 128.

Money is so called from cattle; it is whatever human beings possess. VI, 672. Everything of which we are legally masters is included under the name of money. I, 1238. Copper money began to be used before silver money. VII, 128. Money and riches differ. VII, 204. Only iniquity regards money as riches. IV, 620. See Gold; Riches. Money is not improperly represented as round, because it does not stand still. IV, 1057. How great is the difference between money and God. VI, 674. See Covetous. In order to increase money, some lose faith. IV, 1645. Love of money is poison to right hope. I, 1006. Love of money extends even to contempt of the soul. V, 1457. Some call money their blood. V, 146. Money can help and harm. V, 498. Put your hand to money in such a way that you release your heart from it. V, 955. Money does not make one blessed. VI, 674. How just it is to divide money with one’s neighbor. VI, 673. Money is possessed badly by the wicked and possessed all the better by the good the less it is loved. II, 665. Whether it is permissible to save some money when the Lord has commanded us not to think about tomorrow. III, 1803.

Those who possess money are not rich if they are greedy. VII, 204.

Metrical feet: what they are and how many kinds there are. I, 1102. They are treated at great length. I, 1107.

The custom of washing guests’ feet exists among most people. III, 1794. This custom is praiseworthy. III, 1794. The one who washes guests’ feet is humble in heart. III, 1794. The things Christ did in washing the disciples’ feet are explained allegorically. III, 1787. Who anoints Christ’s feet with precious fragrance. III, 73. Feet are defiled even when one comes to Christ by way of the earth. III, 1789, 1790.

The soul’s foot is love. IV, 124. Our feet are our affections. IV, 1217. The foot of pride is so called because by it we withdraw from God. IV, 354. Which are the Lord’s feet. IV, 833, 1167. The two feet are the commandments of love. IV, 315.

The heresy of those who walk barefoot. VIII, 42.

Pegasius, a Donatist bishop. IX, 528, 555.

Pegasus. VII, 570.

A Pelagian bishop. II, 759, 780.

Pelagianus of Luperciana. IX, 229.

The Pelagian heresy. III, 2061, 2062. Its origin. III, 83. Pelagius and Coelestius, leaders of the unspeakable heresy. X, 1561. Pelagius, Coelestius’ teacher. X, 355. Pelagius was a more hidden and more mendacious heretic; Coelestius was more open and more obstinate. X, 391.

Pelagius, surnamed Britto, was once beloved by Paulinus as a servant of God. II, 816. Pelagius the monk. VIII, 47; X, 342, 345, 346. Pelagius and his followers are indicated to possess intellectual ability. II, 821, 830. A circumspect man. X, 196. A man, as those who knew him say, good and worthy of praise. X, 188. Pelagius was an eminently Christian man. X, 189. A Christian of no small progress. X, 189. Praised by some. X, 188. The praiseworthy character of Pelagius. X, 167. Pelagius was regarded as a holy man. X, 185, 186. Julian calls Pelagius holy. X, 1406. The bishops’ letters written to Pelagius were full of praise. X, 348. Augustine at times mentions the name of Pelagius with some praise. I, 644. In the greeting of a letter Augustine calls Pelagius “lord.” X, 349. Also “most beloved” and “most desired.” X, 349. Augustine replies to Pelagius with courteous letters. II, 596. Pelagius’ exhortations to a good life were vehement and in a certain sense ardent. X, 348.

Pelagius lived for a long time at Rome. X, 389, 396. Augustine first learned the name of Pelagius, then absent and established at Rome, with great praise of him. X, 346. How Pelagius became known to Augustine. X, 346. Pelagius came to Africa. X, 346. He was received on the shore of Hippo while Augustine was absent. X, 346. He went to Carthage at the time of the Conference with the Donatists. X, 346. There Augustine saw his face once and again. X, 346. Afterwards he hastened overseas. X, 346.

The main points of the Pelagian heresy. II, 674. Certain points. X, 355, 356. The principal points. X, 357. The three principal points of the Pelagian heresy. X, 606, 996. The five principal points of the Pelagians’ fog and slanders. X, 606. Augustine reports the dogmas of the Pelagian heresy. II, 772, 773, 774. The Pelagians’ dogmas concerning grace, free will, and the salvation of little children. X, 570, 571. The Pelagians’ paradoxes concerning the baptism of little children. X, 705.

The Pelagians denied original sin. I, 598, 608; II, 723, 762, 773; V, 1345. They attempt to make the flesh of every infant equal to Christ’s flesh. V, 992. Pelagius, a deceptive praiser of little children. X, 551. Pelagius’ argument against original sin. II, 865. The Pelagians maintain that no original sin exists in those being born. X, 114. They say that the miseries of the human race occur without the desert of that sin. X, 1098. They are compelled to place in paradise all the evils which we believe to be punishments of sins, and even lust itself. X, 1507, 1509, 1513. Pelagius’ error: that one who was such is free from guilt because he could not have been otherwise. X, 251. The Pelagians praise nature as though it were sound. X, 1060. They praise the concupiscence of the flesh as though it were a natural good: why. X, 436. They are refuted by the authority of Ambrose. X, 436. They asserted that ignorance and difficulty belong to the constitution of nature. I, 598, 608. Some of them say that every human being is created by God, even now immortal, and that all die according to their merits because all have sinned—not in Adam, but in themselves, since they were created. V, 906. They are refuted. V, 906. The Pelagians teach that death comes not from sin but from nature, and that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned. V, 1375. The Pelagians taught that the beginning of sin arose from Adam insofar as the others imitated him. II, 679. They are refuted. II, 684. The Pelagians did not want little children to be baptized for salvation. II, 761, 763, 773. They say that Christ is the Savior of adults, not of minors. V, 992. They thought that little children could be granted the rewards of eternal life without the grace of baptism. II, 785. They concede that little children should be baptized, not for eternal life, but for the kingdom of heaven. V, 1336. The Pelagian distinction between eternal life and the kingdom of God is plainly arbitrary. V, 1338. The Pelagians’ opinion concerning the place where the blessed innocents remain who departed this life without baptism. III, 1812, 1813. It is an error—which Pelagius anathematized—that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life. II, 826. The Pelagians unjustly shut the kingdom of heaven against unbaptized little children, since they do not acknowledge original sin. X, 175. They contradict themselves when they assert that unbaptized children are not to be condemned, yet think that they are not baptized because they would live badly. II, 889. The Pelagians, thoroughly convicted, even strive to persuade people that God is the avenger of sins not committed. II, 889. The Pelagians came not a little near the truth in the question of infant baptism, where they admitted that infants believe through those by whom they are presented. II, 870, 871, 890. The Pelagian heresy is shipwrecked upon the misery of little children. X, 1294. Neither reason, learning, piety, justice, nor sacred testimonies support the Pelagian error concerning original sin. X, 1147. The Pelagians agree with the Manichaeans in denying original sin. X, 613. By denying original sin, the Pelagians assist the Manichaeans. X, 863, 865, 1074, 1105, 1114, 1288. They rage against little children more cruelly than the Manichaeans. X, 1062. While the Pelagians try to avoid the Manichaean plague in the opposite direction, they are proved to hold views concerning the fruit of marriage more pernicious than those of the Manichaeans themselves. X, 1463. Just as the Arians hold something worse than the Sabellians concerning the Trinity, so the Pelagians hold something worse than the Manichaeans concerning marriage. X, 458. The Pelagians, avoiding the errors of the Manichaeans, stumble into others. X, 613. And while they avoid the Manichaean heresy, they introduce another. X, 571. In what respect the Pelagians and Manichaeans are joined in error, and in what respect they are separate. X, 573. When the Pelagians cast the name of Manichaean at Catholics, they think they are escaping the force of the truth. X, 607. The heresies of the Pelagians and Manichaeans are mutually opposed and are equally rejected by the Catholic Church. X, 572, 573. The Pelagians, attributing election to future works, are convicted by the case of twin children, one of whom died after baptism and the other without the grace of baptism. X, 583. In what respect the Pelagians overturn God’s judgments. X, 1097. The Pelagians are not heretics merely because they deny that souls are propagated by transmission. II, 865.

Pelagius, a haughty champion of free will. X, 373. Pelagius falls headlong by exalting the powers of nature. X, 375. The Pelagians, precipitators of free will. III, 1841; X, 554. Proud defenders of their own will. X, 585. Inflaters of free will. X, 1207. In what respect the Pelagians and Catholics disagree when they say that free will exists in human beings and that God is the creator of those who are born. X, 1289, 1290, 1291. The Pelagians attribute patience to the powers of free will. VI, 607. Pelagius denies that human nature has been corrupted or depraved by sin. X, 256. He teaches that nature is not corrupted and that free will is sufficient for salvation. II, 765, 768. The Pelagians thought that we possess from the Creator an implanted capacity for willing and acting. II, 816. The Pelagians are like those who glory in the Law. II, 676, 893. They say that, once the Law has been given, the human will can suffice for fulfilling it. II, 595. A Pelagian statement: “It was necessary for me to know through the teaching of the Law what I should do; I have free will—who will separate me from that way?” Refuted. V, 730. The Pelagians also said that a person in this life, once God’s commands were known, could attain such perfection of righteousness without the help of the Savior’s grace, solely through the free choice of the will, that it would no longer be necessary to say, “Forgive us our sins,” and so forth. II, 763, 772. The Pelagians’ position was that free will would be taken away if they did not grant that a person possesses even a good will with God’s help. II, 875. The Pelagians, impiously chattering and presuming on their own powers, say: “God made me a human being; I make myself righteous.” V, 656. “If I wish, I am righteous; if I do not wish, I am not righteous.” V, 1316. “You save yourself, if you are willing.” V, 409. “We act by free will so that we may be righteous.” V, 172. Against the heretics, the Pelagians boast that they possess by nature the good understanding by which God is praised. V, 1644. They boast that they came to Christ by their own free choice and their own will. V, 192. By praising nature excessively, they deceive. V, 754. They say that charity comes not from God but from us. I, 621. That a human being is sufficient for himself and does not need divine grace, from Innocentius. II, 785. That we need no divine help to keep God’s commandments. II, 772, 774. That without God’s grace a person can be without sin, and that some actually have been so; but they contradict themselves. II, 775, 776, 829.

The Pelagians are ungrateful toward grace, attributing much to needy and wounded nature. V, 752. The Pelagians are refuted because, while defending free will, they deny God’s grace. VI, 443. Pelagius contradicts Christ’s grace by defending nature. X, 260. Pelagius taught that a person could refrain from sinning without grace. X, 281, 285. The testimonies of the Fathers by which Pelagius proves that a person can refrain from sinning without grace are explained. X, 282. Pelagius corrupts a passage from the apostle James in order to deny the necessity of grace. X, 254. Pelagius could not tolerate the words, “Give what you command, and command what you will.” X, 1026. He believes that there is nothing he receives from God and that nothing remains for him to ask in order to be healed, from Innocentius. II, 787. From the Pelagian heresy it necessarily follows that we ought not to pray. II, 595, 761, 763, 774. The Pelagians say that they prayed so that God might give to them, and first believed so that they might pray. V, 913. They do not ask for God’s gift in order that they may not sin. X, 1098. Pelagius’s teachings concerning grace. VIII, 47, 48. The Pelagian error concerning grace is no small matter. II, 849. The emerging Pelagian heresy is to be abhorred, although it pretends to admit God’s grace. V, 174.

The Pelagians’ conception of grace. II, 652, 768, 849, 852; X, 1296. The Pelagians referred grace to nature, the Law, teaching, free will, Christ’s example, and the remission of sins. II, 760, 768, 852. According to the teaching of Pelagius, God’s grace is that which is common to pagans and Christians, the impious and the pious, believers and unbelievers. II, 816. Pelagius locates grace in the Law and in teaching. X, 364, 365. Where Pelagius places the Savior’s healing assistance. X, 266. Pelagius thought that Christ was necessary for us so that we might learn how we ought to live. X, 270. Pelagius taught that grace is given as something superfluous, or for acting more easily. II, 829.

The Pelagians teach that grace is given according to merits. I, 595; X, 577. At the trial in Palestine, Pelagius did not hesitate to anathematize this with his lips alone. X, 578. The Pelagians are deserters from the faith. X, 576, 585. Opponents of grace. X, 576. Not only deserters from God’s grace but also persecutors of it. X, 625. The Pelagians deserve much pity because they contend against manifest grace. V, 754. Pelagius and Coelestius oppose grace, though not openly. II, 760, 762, 774, 865. According to the Pelagian heresy, Christ died for nothing. II, 768. What is the person who impiously attacks grace, if the Pharisee is rebuked for giving thanks arrogantly? V, 657. The Pelagians’ deceitful humility. V, 981. The Pelagians are more arrogant than the Pharisee. V, 1315. The Pelagians’ position concerning perfection. X, 689. The Pelagian error that the righteous are free from every sin. X, 998, 999. In what sense, according to the Pelagians, a person can be without sin. X, 802. The Pelagians teach that a person can be without sin in this life. V, 833. That the whole Church is without any sin. V, 980. The Pelagians falsely taught that a rich person who remains in his riches cannot enter the kingdom of God, and so forth. II, 686, 687, 688. Doctrines opposed to the Pelagians, which the Catholic Church has always maintained, were confirmed by the Council of Diospolis. II, 828. An episcopal judgment had been rendered concerning the errors of Pelagius and Coelestius at the Council held at Carthage in the year 411. II, 759, 760.

Heros and Lazarus accuse Pelagius and Coelestius of being the authors of a wicked error. II, 759, 763. Pelagius replied to the charges of Heros and Lazarus. II, 775. Fourteen bishops presided as judges over Pelagius at the Palestinian synod. X, 652, 663. Their names. X, 663. Certain charges were brought against Pelagius at the Palestinian synod. X, 320. The chapters of Coelestius were brought against Pelagius, and he rejected them. X, 333, 334. These matters were condemned at the synod, and Pelagius himself would have had to be condemned unless he too condemned them. X, 338, 354. Other chapters sent from Sicily to Augustine were also brought against Pelagius, with mention of Augustine’s own name introduced. X, 334. Pelagius’s response to the chapters brought against him, and his profession of faith. X, 345, 346. Pelagius denied that certain statements of Coelestius were his own, but refused to anathematize others. X, 352. Summary of the chapters that Pelagius anathematized at the Council of Diospolis, and that a Catholic ought to profess. II, 828, 979. Pelagius condemned the proposition that Adam was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die. X, 1089. So that the Catholic synod might be deceived and a new heretic not be condemned, Pelagius anathematized those who say that infants newly born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression. X, 392. He condemned those who say that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race; that newborn infants are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression; and that they possess eternal life even if they are not baptized. X, 653, 703, 715, 1112, 1113. He did not condemn these things with a truthful heart. X, 1112, 1113. Unless Pelagius condemned the claim that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race, he would have been condemned by the Palestinian judges. X, 392, 1186. By saying that Adam’s sin harmed the human race through imitation, not propagation, Pelagius thinks that he had eluded the Palestinian judgment. X, 653. Unless Pelagius had condemned, in the presence and hearing of the Eastern bishops, the errors brought against him concerning infants, he could not possibly have emerged from there except condemned. X, 653, 703. In the question of infant baptism, Pelagius deceived the Palestinian judges. X, 390. He deceived the judges all the more secretly because he set out his position more craftily. X, 393. Pelagius’s fraud and craftiness. X, 393. Pelagius’s hiding places beneath ambiguity. X, 396. Pelagius inverted the question at issue concerning infant baptism. X, 394. Pelagius must certainly be condemned together with those whom he condemned as holding wrong opinions about infants, because he retained in his heart what he denied with his mouth. X, 653. Pelagius taught that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not his descendants, even after he had condemned that doctrine at the Palestinian synod. X, 391, 392, 393. Pelagius’s cleverness in suppressing God’s grace in certain passages of his book. X, 347.
