At an episcopal synod Pelagius condemned those who deny that grace is given for each individual act and place it in the Law and in free will. II, 979, 984; X, 338, 361. Pelagius’s suspicious profession concerning the necessity of grace for each individual act. X, 361, 365. Pelagius confesses grace in deceitful words. X, 331. Concealing his meaning beneath ambiguous generality, Pelagius used the word “grace” to dispel ill will and avoid offense. X, 379. At last Pelagius admitted true grace at the episcopal synod. X, 338. He did not confess God’s grace truthfully. X, 352, 361. The Palestinian synod believed that Pelagius was confessing the grace well known in the Church. X, 333. What was required of Pelagius in the question of grace. X, 383. Pelagius produced at the Palestinian synod Augustine’s letter addressed to him. X, 549. At the Palestinian trial Pelagius confessed that grace is not given according to merits. X, 887. Through fear of his condemnation, he condemned the proposition that grace is given according to merits. X, 619, 1011, 1028. He did not condemn it with a truthful heart. X, 371. Rather, he did so falsely. X, 567. And through deceitful fear. X, 577. He concealed his meaning with ambiguous words. X, 554. Fearing episcopal judgment, he denied that he taught that God’s grace is given according to our merits, and by anathematizing those who taught this, he condemned them. II, 877; X, 554. Unless Pelagius had condemned the proposition that grace is given according to merits, he would have been condemned by the Catholic bishops. X, 727, 887, 1133, 1212. Yet he is found defending nothing else in the books he wrote afterward. X, 554. His later books show that he anathematized it deceitfully. II, 877; VIII, 48; X, 887. Whatever Pelagius denies that he said at the wretched Council of Diospolis, he professes in his reply to Jerome’s letter. II, 928. What prayer Pelagius admitted to be necessary. X, 256. Pelagius was pronounced Catholic by fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine. I, 649; X, 319. Judged Catholic. X, 357, 358. Absolved at the Palestinian synod and, as some think, cleared. II, 761, 764; X, 333, 335. He eluded the proceedings; he did not clear himself. II, 788. He deceived the Palestinian judgment, and for that reason appears to have been cleared there. X, 389, 392. By deceiving the synod, Pelagius stole his acquittal from it. X, 392, 394. How he was acquitted. X, 394, 663, 697. At the Palestinian trial, the position that Pelagius ought to have held was acquitted. X, 394. Pelagius’s acquittal. X, 346. Pelagius’s clearance is regarded with suspicion. X, 346. What judgment Innocentius rendered concerning his clearance. X, 389. Augustine interprets benevolently what had been handled too incautiously by the judges in Pelagius’s case. X, 344. The Diospolitan Fathers, who acquitted Pelagius, are not to be accused. II, 764, 765. What Pelagius ought to do in order to appear corrected. X, 350. Pelagius’s written defense addressed to Augustine. X, 352. In it he did something that differs from what is contained in the episcopal records. X, 352, 353, 354. Pelagius boasts of the judgment of the fourteen Palestinian bishops as though it were a victory. X, 350. Part of the records of the Palestinian judgment in Pelagius’s case. X, 390. Innocentius’s judgment concerning the Palestinian proceedings. X, 389. Innocentius does not consider Pelagius cleared. II, 787. After Pelagius was acquitted, his heresy was condemned. X, 354, 355, 358, 699. Pelagius deceived the Palestinian synod. X, 390, 392, 393. How he eluded it. X, 653. Pelagius attempts to deceive the apostolic see. X, 394, 396. Pelagius’s letters, with a booklet of faith, sent to Innocentius. X, 376, 396, 397. Pelagius’s hostile complaints against his enemies. X, 376. Pelagius prepares refuges for falsehood in hiding places of ambiguity. X, 394, 396. Concerning Pelagius’s letter in which he boasts that his errors had been approved by the fourteen bishops. [Col. 0522] 350, 351. Pelagius deceived the Palestinian judgment, but could not deceive the Roman Church. X, 389. A booklet against Pelagius presented to the holy bishop Eulogius. X, 325. Pelagius’s condemnation. X, 394. Pelagius condemned at the Palestinian synod. X, 703. Pelagius and Coelestius condemned. X, 396. Rightly condemned. X, 410. The Pelagian heresy has been condemned by the bishops and is no longer to be examined but restrained. X, 1183. After the excommunication of Pelagius and Coelestius, many who adhered to them were converted. X, 394. Some of Pelagius’s disciples withdraw from their teacher’s doctrine. X, 583. After the Palestinian synod Pelagius did not hold a Catholic view concerning infants. X, 392. Nor did he write sincerely concerning the help of grace. II, 829. Pelagius published his books after the Palestinian synod. II, 829; X, 394. These books are noted. II, 826, 829. Although Pelagius acknowledges revelation through the Holy Spirit, he nevertheless does not depart from his doctrine. X, 381. Pelagius’s letter to Demetrias. X, 371, 378. He says that in it he most openly confesses grace. II, 854. What Augustine thinks about the book written to Demetrias. II, 850. Pelagius’s letter to Paulinus. X, 378. To Constantius. X, 378. Two letters of the Pelagians: one sent to Rome, the other to Thessalonica. X, 551. Julian sent the first, so that through it he might find or make as many of his own adherents as possible; the second was sent by eighteen men, apparently bishops, to the bishop of that place, so that, if possible, he might be brought over to their side. X, 551. A letter of the Pelagians sent to the East. X, 1218. The Pelagians falsely claimed that the Eastern Churches favored them. X, 335. And that throughout the entire West their dogma had been accepted, no less foolishly than impiously. X, 623. Pelagius used Augustine’s testimony. I, 596. The letter of Pelagius that he sent to Rome. X, 361. Pelagius’s book on behalf of free will. X, 379, 380. In the books he published on behalf of free will, Pelagius holds nothing other than what he condemned at the Palestinian synod. X, 361. Pelagius, imitating Cyprian, wrote a book of testimonies. X, 623. Or of chapters. X, 350, 351, 1420. Pelagius’s expositions of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. X, 185, 186, 343. In these he did not dare to attribute his errors to himself openly. X, 396. Pelagius’s book presented to Augustine by James and Timasius. X, 338, 347. His name was not stated, so that, while friendship continued, the error of friends might die. X, 348. Augustine refutes the book *On Nature and Grace*, without naming its author. X, 347. With his name suppressed. II, 816. Why Augustine ultimately refuted Pelagius by name. X, 348.

The Pelagian heresy must be condemned, even if Pelagius had been justly acquitted at the Council of Diospolis. II, 761. The Pelagians were condemned by the authority of the Catholic councils and the apostolic see. X, 505. A letter was written against the Pelagians from the African Council to Zosimus, and he sent a rescript from it to all the bishops of the world. II, 972. Augustine sent the decree established by the later plenary Council of all Africa against the error of Pelagius himself. II, 972. Two councils concerning this case—the Councils of Carthage and Milevis—were sent to the apostolic see, and rescripts came back from there. V, 754. Note (a). “The case is finished; if only the error were finished as well.” V, 754. A letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocentius against the Pelagians. II, 759. Likewise another from the Council of Milevis. II, 762. And another from five bishops. II, 764. This one is said to have been written somewhat more carefully. II, 972. Innocentius’s three rescripts in response to those three letters. II, 781. The Council of Carthage decrees that Pelagius and Coelestius ought to be anathematized unless they anathematize their errors. II, 760. Augustine sends Optatus copies of the letters written against Pelagius and Coelestius by the councils, as well as by Innocentius and Zosimus. II, 865. And to the monks of Hadrumetum. II, 972. Innocentius says that the Pelagians should be cut off like rotten limbs. II, 782, 784, 786. Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned by episcopal councils and by Innocentius and Zosimus. II, 865. Sixtus pronounced an anathema against the Pelagians before a very large crowd. II, 874. The Pelagians are convicted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church, with the letters of the African councils cooperating. I, 650. Pelagius’s error is condemned. II, 817. Unless Pelagius and Coelestius corrected themselves and performed penance, they were condemned throughout the whole world. II, 865. The Pelagians were condemned by the Church. X, 1211. Cast out from the face of the Church. X, 1258. The Pelagians were rightly expelled from the Church. X, 798, 1503. And rightly separated from the Church. X, 1187. They went out from the Church. X, 1292. Against the authors of the Pelagian heresy the episcopal councils, the apostolic see, the entire Roman Church, and the Roman Empire—which, by God’s favor, is Christian—were rightly stirred up. X, 394. The Pelagians were treated more leniently than the stricter discipline of the Church required. X, 574, 575. Some Pelagians were condemned, others corrected. X, 637. The Pelagians seek a universal synod of East and West. X, 638. It is not an equal matter to hold a conference with the Pelagians and to hold one with the Donatists. X, 704. The Pelagians kept boasting that a reply had been issued on their behalf by the Emperor. X, 703. They accused the Catholics of having recourse to the powers of the world, and so forth. X, 1183. They call Augustine a heretic, although he could rightly call them by that name, but does not. V, 1348. Pelagius and Coelestius, recently deprived of Catholic communion by a judicial sentence, persist in their condemnation. II, 894. The usefulness of Pelagius’s condemnation. II, 787. The Fathers of Milevis prefer that Pelagius and Coelestius be healed within the Church rather than cut off from it with their salvation despaired of; Augustine desires the same. II, 764, 773. Around the year 416 the Pelagians had not yet been clearly separated from the Church. II, 686, 773. Since Pelagius’s errors were condemned, some now defend them more freely, others sow them more secretly, and others, out of fear, keep silent about what they retain in their hearts. II, 867, 875. The first must be restrained more severely, the second investigated more vigilantly, and the last treated more gently but taught no less diligently. II, 875. The Pelagians’ calumnies against the Catholics. X, 1262. They charge Catholics with slowness of understanding. X, 115. Augustine laments the Pelagians and urges the people to have compassion on them. V, 754. He orders them not to conceal the Pelagians but to bring them to him. V, 754. Some have become entangled in Pelagian error without malicious intent. VI, 444. The Pelagians, who are spreading perniciously, must be avoided. II, 867, 875; V, 1376. Some Pelagians, known before this heresy was condemned by the clearest judgment of the apostolic see, suddenly became silent afterward. II, 867. The Pelagians begin to decline. VI, 696.

The Pelagians at last confessed grace, and Augustine therefore blesses God, hoping for better things. V, 856. But they want grace only to assist in acting more easily. V, 856. This is refuted. II, 856. Pressed by the voices of the pious, the Pelagians maintain that their own merit precedes the aid of grace. II, 876. The penalty imposed on those who refuse to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. II, 927. Pelagius and Coelestius were expelled from Rome by an imperial constitution. II, 927. By a new sanction, those who knew them to be hiding in any province were ordered to drive them out or betray them. II, 927. Jerome congratulates Alypius and Augustine that the Coelestian heresy had been strangled through their agency. II, 928. At the exhortation of Pelagius, Timasius and James renounced the world; after following one who held wrong views about grace, they were later converted through Augustine’s efforts. II, 767, 816. The Pelagians are to be received into the Church if they repent. II, 784, 786.

The Pelagians are still seeking a place to hide by introducing the unnecessary question of the origin of the soul. X, 608. The Pelagians’ five hiding places. X, 609. What they conceal in these hiding places. X, 611. The five principal heads of the Pelagian heresy proscribed by Cyprian and Ambrose. X, 637, 638. Many years earlier, Cyprian prepared an antidote against the Pelagian poisons that were to come. X, 996. The Pelagians’ five stratagems. X, 622. The Pelagians’ exceedingly strong and swift intellects. X, 250. Intellects not to be despised. X, 574. The Pelagians, sons of pride. X, 578. The Pelagians’ vanity, most arrogant, cruel, and impious. X, 623. The Pelagians’ most arrogant and ungrateful disputations. X, 1145. The Pelagians, inflated wineskins distended by the wind of exaltation. V, 980. Proud and contentious. V, 843. The Pelagians’ serpentine cunning. X, 615. The Pelagians falsely thought that their dogma could be commended to the Catholic minds of certain Roman clerics. X, 573, 574. Many in Rome favored Pelagius’s errors. II, 764. The Pelagians habitually exalt themselves because of Sixtus’s friendship. II, 867. It is reported that Sixtus favors them. II, 867, 875. During the time of Pope Innocentius, the Pelagians did not dare either to defend Pelagius at Rome or to boast of his doctrines. II, 787. Pelagius is said to have deceived many at Jerusalem. II, 764. Many in the city of Nola adhered to Pelagius’s errors. II, 827. Pelagius writes to Paulinus. II, 816. By whom he had been loved as a servant of God. II, 815. In letters sent to Paulinus, Pelagius says that he ought not to be thought to defend free will without God’s grace. II, 816.

The Pelagians’ refuge. X, 897. The Pelagians boast of their small number. X, 1143. The Pelagians are few in comparison with the Catholics. X, 1507. Among them are some priests. X, 1097. The Pelagians’ ruin of morals and destruction of modesty. X, 798. The Pelagians’ cruelty toward the servants and maidservants of God under Jerome’s care. X, 358. How unjust the Pelagian heresy is, and how ignorant of the whole of religion. Innocentius. II, 782, 783, 785, 787. The horrible monsters produced by the Pelagian heresy. X, 1370. The Pelagians ought not to reject the holy Fathers as judges. X, 697, 700, 701, 702. Testimonies of the ancients against the Pelagians. X, 623. Innocentius’s censure of Pelagius’s book. II, 788. Of John of Jerusalem. II, 829. Of Jerome. II, 764, 781. Pelagius complains about Jerome, saying that Jerome envied him as a rival. X, 700. Augustine’s first writings against the Pelagians. I, 644. Earlier private treatises written against them. I, 644. Augustine writes a letter to be sent to Pelagius through Innocentius. II, 771. For a time Augustine kept silent about their names, hoping thereby that they could be corrected more easily. I, 644. Augustine says that Pelagius must anathematize his own writings, or those published under his name. II, 771. Pelagius and Coelestius are intimated to deny that the writings published under their names are theirs. II, 763. Five bishops ask Innocentius himself to send to Pelagius a letter written by one of their colleagues. II, 771. A letter written to Sixtus against the new Pelagians, who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits. II, 969, 972. Pelagius is refuted. IV, 704.

The Pelagian heresy is not ancient. X, 886. The ancient Catholic faith demonstrates that the Pelagians are new heretics. X, 1054. The Pelagians’ novel doctrine is opposed to the most ancient foundation of faith. X, 1276. The Pelagian heresy arose after Ambrose. X, 636. It was aroused by monks. X, 355. The Pelagians are new heretics. X, 413, 426. Enemies of God’s grace. X, 551, 578. Pelagius was the most recent of the heresiarchs in Augustine’s time. I, 595. Honoratus is warned against them as having recently arisen. II, 575. They are described as people whom one should not lightly despise, since they are continent and praiseworthy in good works, and so forth. II, 575. By others the Pelagians are called Coelestians. II, 685, Note (a); VIII, 32. The Pelagian heresy greatly exercised Augustine. III, 83.

Pelagius of Tarentum. II, 815.

Pelasgus, or Pelagus, or Palaphus, king of the Sicyonians. VII, 576.

Where the pelican is born. IV, 1298. Its nature. IV, 1299. The pelican signifies Christ. IV, 1299.

The Peligni attempt to throw off the Roman yoke. VII, 168.

Skins signify mortality. IV, 1341, 1353. They indicate death. V, 1618. Goatskins. V, 41.

Pellonia, a goddess. VII, 129.

Why the Peloponnesians did not overcome the Athenians. VII, 576.

The images of the household gods that Aeneas brought from Troy are said to have migrated from place to place. VII, 294.

Bound wings create a burden. IV, 633. The wings of souls. IV, 1776, 1791.

Pentadius, a bishop. II, 759, 781.

Pentapolis is Libya; it is Cyrene. V, 294. It obeys the Emperor of the East. V, 294.

The feast of Pentecost, established from the weeks. V, 73. The agreement of the Old and New Testaments concerning the celebration of Easter and Pentecost. II, 218. The Pentecost of the Jews, a figure of Christian Pentecost. VIII, 503.

Masters wearing the *paenula*. I, 672.

Pepuza, a city. VIII, 31.

The heretics called Pepuzians: why they were so named. VIII, 30. They are said to have arisen from the Cataphrygians. VIII, 31.

Inquiry and interrogation differ. III, 67.

What is meant by the Lord’s “striking,” mentioned in Psalm 56. IV, 861.

To lose one’s soul so that it may be found. V, 1516.

The Lord seems not to know the lost. III, 1755. From the perdition in which we are born, no one delivers us except the Savior’s grace. X, 448.

The partridge is a contentious bird. V, 286. The partridge is an exceedingly contentious animal; driven by its eagerness for contention, it runs into a snare. VIII, 289. The partridge in Jeremiah 17, gathering without judgment, signifies the devil. V, 285.

To be absent from the Lord is death. IV, 1889. Hope of our sure return consoles and encourages us while we are absent. IV, 1884. This life is an absence from home. IV, 1781; V, 38, 1523. Our very absence is tribulation. IV, 579. It is captivity. IV, 1917. The cause of our absence is sin; the gift of our return is justification by grace. IV, 1658, 1659, 1761. See *Homeland*. Our absence is to be endured, not loved. VI, 679. This life is represented by the Israelites’ journey through the wilderness. V, 1637.

Who understands himself to be a stranger in the world? III, 1627. In what way human beings are strangers here. IV, 430, 1518, 1519, 1602, 1604, 1888. For the faithful stranger, remembrance of the heavenly Jerusalem is at once joyful and bitter. IV, 1884. The stranger does very well when he follows the custom of the fasts of the place in which he is staying. II, 202.

Peregrinus, a bishop. II, 748, 752.

Peregrinus, presbyter of the Church of Mustitana. IX, 529.

Peregrinus, a deacon. II, 536, 537, 644.

Peregrinus Comes, a praiseworthy and thoroughly Christian man. II, 1013.

Perfection of the good is its completion, and the end of evil. III, 1699.

There is a certain perfection in this life. V, 868. What sort of perfection exists in this life. I, 614; VIII, 960. What human perfection of righteousness is, and when it will be. X, 295. From where, when, and where it is to be hoped for. II, 739. Whoever strives toward perfection ought to endeavor, as charity advances, to diminish desire. III, 1699. The perfection of the good is that desire itself for sin should not be present in a person. I, 608. There are two kinds of perfection: the supreme perfection and that of those who are making progress. X, 253. By what way a person must be led toward perfection. X, 288. How far one must run toward perfection. X, 302. This is precisely what is being accomplished in us: by striving, laboring, praying, and obtaining, we are brought to that perfection in which we can behold God with a pure heart. X, 286. God is both the author and the helper of perfection. I, 1303. Not only perfection but also the beginning of virtue comes from God’s grace. X, 743. The perfection of virtue comes not from one’s own powers but from God’s grace. X, 691.

Christ is our perfection. IV, 628, 662. The person who imitates Christ is perfect. V, 783. The perfect person resists sin until death. V, 1439. The person who does not repay evil to those who repay evil is perfect. IV, 99. Those who know how to dwell together in unity are perfect. IV, 1734. Great must be the joy of spiritual maturity when a person has become a new spiritual person. III, 560. The perfection of love consists in loving enemies and loving them so that they may become brothers. III, 1984. We are perfect in love when nothing remains from weakness. II, 740. No one possesses complete perfection as long as he lives here. II, 739; X, 165, 306, 307. No one is truly perfect in this life. IV, 425, 1058, 1714. The reformation now taking place, compared with the perfection of the future life. X, 223. The perfection of this life does not consist in being without any sin. X, 599. What already appears perfect to human beings is still imperfect in comparison with God’s perfection. IV, 1267. The life of no righteous or holy person is perfect in comparison with the future life. III, 36. The very perfection of a person is to have discovered that he is not perfect. V, 931. Perfect travelers, not perfect possessors. V, 926. We are now being built into God’s temple, which will be dedicated at the end. X, 846. When perfection will come. X, 157. Where and when the fullest perfection of righteousness is attained, Augustine does not concern himself excessively, provided it is believed that it cannot be attained without grace. X, 288, 290. See *Righteousness*. Whoever denies that anyone can attain complete perfection without the aid of the Savior’s grace is not a Christian. X, 282, 284. Why the perfection of righteousness is rushed, although no one possesses it in this life. X, 301. A person is perfected in two ways. X, 296. Someone who has made great progress in righteousness is rightly called perfect in righteousness. X, 165. Nothing hinders perfection so much as pride. IV, 709. Our perfection is humility itself. IV, 1714. For the perfect, the vice of empty glory must be avoided either exclusively or above all. IV, 100. It is also counted toward perfection if each person knows that he is not yet perfect. X, 599. It belongs to the perfection of this life that we understand that we are not yet perfect. IV, 425; X, 599, 605. Let us confess our imperfection so that we may deserve perfection. V, 784. The perfect live here only for the sake of others. IV, 241. Let the perfect be an example to the faithful. IV, 436. The perfect will judge with Christ. IV, 1156. The perfect are signified by sheep that have been shorn. IV, 1224.

Periander of Corinth, one of the Seven Sages. VII, 582.

Pericles governed Athens for many years. VII, 54.

Dangers make the one who delivers sweeter. IV, 1210. Three dangers must be passed through by the members of Christ who are making progress. III, 820. Dangers from false brothers until the end of the age. V, 910. The dangers of hell deceive more amid the prosperity of the world. IV, 1488. Whoever does not guard against danger tempts God. VII, 498.

*Periodus*. III, 94.

The Peripatetics. I, 956. Aristotle, the founder of the Peripatetics. VII, 237. Their error concerning blessedness. VII, 630.

Whoever is separated from the blessedness that God gives his saints by punishment is said to perish for God. III, 1858.

There is a certain pitiable expertise: to distinguish soups, wine, and so forth with extraordinary discrimination by smell and taste. I, 1054.

The Periurgi. VII, 294.

Perjury: how it differs from blasphemy. VI, 544. Some establish limits and rules for swearing falsely. VI, 544. No reason can be offered why one ought to swear falsely. VI, 545. In how many ways perjury occurs. V, 972. Perjurers are those who, while keeping the words they swore, have deceived the expectation for which the oath was sworn. II, 476. Who would think that perjury ought to be committed because of uncertain—not, I say, losses, but death itself, which must be avoided? II, 475, 482. The danger of perjury in taking an oath. V, 973. Every oath is forbidden because of the danger of false swearing. V, 1406. No perjurer goes unpunished. V, 976. Perjury is all the more punishable insofar as the thing by which one swears is more sacred. II, 184. To swear falsely is a monstrous sin. II, 184. A great and grave sin. V, 972, 973. Deadly to the soul. V, 975. Perjury is graver than adultery. VI, 547, 548. David’s perjury was a great sin, although less than murder. V, 1408. Perjury was familiar to the Priscillianists. I, 654. “Swear, foreswear yourself, but do not reveal the secret”: their saying. VIII, 44.

What the *perizomata* are with which Adam and Eve girded themselves. X, 564, 685, 784, 785.

Perpetua, a martyr. X, 481. Perpetua dreamed that she was wrestling with an Egyptian after being transformed into a man. X, 539. The passion of the martyr Perpetua. IV, 541; V, 1281. Perpetua did not realize that she was fighting against an exceedingly savage cow. V, 1282. Perpetua was enlightened by divine revelations. V, 1281, 1284. Perpetua neither yielded to her father when he gave wicked counsel nor failed in the reverence owed to him. V, 1284.

How long the empire of the Persians lasted. VII, 117. The Persians worshiped only two gods. VII, 168. The Persians prohibit marriage to some people. III, 705.

[Col. 0526] Persian philosophers. VII, 233, 234. A Persian tale. VIII, 574, 578, 599.

Sometimes “to persecute” means the same as “to follow perfectly.” IV, 410, 411.

The persecution of the Church is twofold: one consists in the violence of persecutors, the other in the malice of those who plot. IV, 868. The persecution of the Church is threefold: first, violent persecution by tyrants; second, fraudulent persecution by heretics and false brothers; third, the more dangerous persecution by Antichrist, both violent and fraudulent. IV, 128. The various persecutions suffered by the Church. VII, 615. Persecutors could do nothing to harm the martyrs. IV, 1813. During the persecution at Jerusalem, burning pieces of wood were scattered, and the world was set alight. V, 660. Persecution raised in Persia against the Christians. VII, 616. Gaul free from persecution. IX, Appendix 778. The persecution of heretics succeeded the persecution of tyrants. VII, 612, 613. The final persecution of the Church: what it is. VII, 676. The sharper the assault of the war, the greater the glory of not yielding, and the denser the crown of martyrdom. VII, 678. Persecutions are useful to the Church. VII, 298, 299. The persecution of enemies turned to the Church’s honor. IV, 206. Persecutions are not absent even in this time, when tranquility seems to prevail. IV, 221, 136, 432, 634, 866, 1150, 1207. Persecution is twofold: of the heart and of the body. VII, 614. From the beginning the Church was attacked by the impious. IV, 1689.

The occasion for persecution and crowns is never lacking for Christians. V, 52, 910. How all the godly endure persecution. IX, 720, 721. What here persecutes the life of the good more than the life of the wicked? II, 1064. This persecution is continual. II, 1064. The life of the wicked persecutes the life of the good—not when it compels one to imitate what one dislikes, but when it compels one to grieve over what one sees. II, 1064. One who lives wickedly in the presence of a godly person, even if he does not bind the person who consents, torments the person who perceives it. II, 1064. Spiritual people suffer persecution from the carnal. IV, 1603. The devil persecuted Christ’s soul, and Judas the soul of the Master; and now that same devil remains for the persecution of Christ’s body, while Judas has been succeeded by a Judas. IV, 1849. The wicked have always persecuted the good, and the good the wicked—how this occurs. II, 395. Every wicked person persecutes the good for this reason: the good does not consent to him in evil. IV, 1690. The wicked suffer persecution from their own deeds. IX, 725.

The Donatists complain that they suffer persecution, although they themselves inflict it. II, 307, 310. Petilianus accuses the Catholics of persecution, and is refuted. IX, 269, 270, 272, 273. The persecution of the Catholics against the Donatists should not be called persecution of persons, since it is rather persecution of vices for the liberation of persons. IX, 709. The Donatists’ complaints about persecution are turned back upon themselves. II, 192, 266, 305; IX, 273. By the same argument with which they excuse themselves for the persecution carried out by their own side, the Catholic Church defends itself. IX, 273, 274, 276. The example of the Maximianists. IX, 577, 580. It is not a proof of righteousness that someone suffers insults and persecution. VIII, 224. No one is therefore more righteous because he suffers persecution. VIII, 224. This is demonstrated by examples. II, 177. Persecution is inflicted and endured both on account of righteousness and on account of wickedness. III, 1855. Just and unjust persecution. II, 797. Inflicting persecution is not proof of wickedness. IX, 665. Either persecution is not always unjust, or, when it is just, it ought not to be called persecution. IX, 666. Not every persecution is blameworthy. IX, 432. Some persecution can be just. IX, 483. It can happen that the just laudably persecute the unjust. IX, 578, 580, 696. In fact, the saints sometimes do inflict persecution. II, 797.

Persecution must be distinguished not by actions and punishments but by their causes. II, 394, 395; IX, 577, 580. Merit is acquired not from persecution itself but from a good cause. IV, 341, 483. The true martyrs are those who suffer persecution for righteousness. II, 796. There are two kinds of persecutors: those who censure and those who flatter. IV, 869. A good persecutor is one not of a person but of sin. IV, 1289. What difference there is between persecutors and correctors. IX, 432. Apostolic men should not fear persecutions. III, 1237. For whom suffering persecution is blessedness. IX, 719. Persecutors sometimes swallow up the living, but only those in whom the Lord is not present. IV, 1642. The persecution of the unjust purifies you and makes him guilty. IV, 365.

The usefulness of persecutions and tribulations. IV, 648, 653, 654, 655, 1126, 1215, 1259. The persecutions of the wicked are effective like fire applied to gold, not like fire applied to hay. IV, 1693. They exercise the good; they do not crush them. IV, 229. They shave the saints, as it were, like hair. IV, 605. By divine dispensation persecution is permitted against one person for punishment, against another for testing, and against another for a crown. IV, 220. Why God permits the saints to suffer persecution, although he once delivered the Israelites from Egypt with such powerful might. IV, 483. He who rules the sea tempers persecution as he wills. IV, 1126. God rescues some from persecution bodily, so that unbelievers may be confounded; others only spiritually, so that examples may be provided for the faithful. IV, 1169. Why persecution does not overthrow the predestined. IV, 1161, 1162. As an angry father beats his son with a rod soon to be thrown into the fire, [Col. 0527] so God uses the temporal power of the damned to exercise discipline upon those who are to be delivered. IV, 935. Persecution and tribulation are a winepress. IV, 648, 652. The evils inflicted by persecutors are to be avoided when possible, but they must be endured when they cannot be avoided without impiety. II, 1016. So that faith may not fail during persecution, the Lord gives life. IV, 1568.

Persecutors are to be loved. III, 1260. Persecutions are resisted by charity alone. IV, 124. During persecution, the one thing to fear is that the love with which the enemy is loved may be disturbed. IV, 632. In persecution one is crowned for service; in peace, for steadfastness. V, 1395. Prayer is to be offered for the persecutors of the Church. II, 637. When the Church prays for persecutors, the persecutors are nearly finished. IV, 1261. The conversion of the Church’s persecutors. VII, 612. A more severe persecution is signified by the noonday demon. IV, 1155, 1161. Persecution is a raging sea. IV, 1126, 1188, 1189, 1257. The people are not to be abandoned in persecution and dangers. II, 1019. During the Church’s persecutions some consent, some flee, and some suffer. III, 849. During persecution it is permitted to flee to another place. III, 1511. During persecution a private house was provided for the assembling of Christians. IX, 643. During the persecution, when the sacred books were being sought in order to burn them, Christian congregations were accustomed to assemble, martyrs were baptized in prison, and Christ’s sacraments were celebrated. IX, 663. Mensurius forbade Christians to honor those who, without being apprehended, offered themselves to the persecutions and voluntarily declared that they possessed Scriptures which they would not surrender. VIII, 638. The Jews persecuting the Apostles sent them into the forest like burning torches. V, 1434.

What perseverance is. VI, 21. To persevere in Christ is to persevere in his faith. VII, 742. The one who remains in Christ’s body and has learned from the Head the endurance of perseverance will persevere to the end. IV, 665. The Church’s perseverance to the end. V, 224. Not only the will to believe from the beginning, but also the will to persevere, is a gift of God’s grace. II, 986. Perseverance is a gift of God. IV, 1809; X, 921, 993, 995, 996, 997, 1018, 1021, 1024, 1026. Cyprian recognized this before Augustine. X, 1027. That God gives perseverance belongs to faith. X, 1002. Although perseverance is from God, correction of the one who has not persevered is not to be neglected. X, 921. The perseverance debated among theologians. X, 995. The perseverance that is God’s gift is perseverance to the end. X, 999. Perseverance is requested in the Lord’s Prayer. X, 922, 996. The saints ask for perseverance. X, 997, 998. The gift of perseverance can be obtained through prayers; but once it has been given, it cannot be lost. X, 999. Whether perseverance can be lost. X, 999, 1000. Whether perseverance can therefore be lost because someone voluntarily abandons God, so that he may deservedly be abandoned. X, 1000. God causes the predestined to persevere. X, 938. Perseverance is given to the children of God. X, 928. To the predestined. X, 927. And it is given only to the predestined. X, 1003, 1004, 1005. What kind of aid for perseverance was given to the first human being, and what kind is now given to the predestined. X, 937, 939. Now the aid is necessary not merely without which they could not persevere, but also by which they do persevere. X, 939. Whether, when Christ prayed that Peter’s faith should not fail, it would have failed had Peter wished it to fail. X, 926. When Christ prayed that Peter’s faith should not fail, he prayed for nothing other than that Peter might have the freest, strongest, unconquered, and most persevering will in faith. X, 926. No one to whom perseverance has been granted fails to persevere. X, 999. Once God’s gift has been granted to a person, so that he is not led into temptation, there is no saint who does not hold fast the perseverance of holiness to the end. X, 999. No one ceases to persevere unless he has first been led into temptation. X, 999. Those who did not receive the gift of perseverance were left to free will. X, 942. All who do not persevere have not been separated by predestination from the mass of perdition. X, 923, 925. Some of the reprobate possess true righteousness for a time, although they do not persevere in it. X, 928. To the question why one person perseveres and another does not, some answer by reference to human free will in such a way as to defend it against grace. X, 926. Why perseverance is given to one and not to another is inscrutable. X, 926. And it must be referred to God’s unsearchable ways. X, 927. There is no excuse for those who did not receive perseverance. X, 923. Those who, without receiving the gift of perseverance, have fallen back and died in sin are justly to be condemned. X, 923. Why God mixes those who will not persevere with those who will. X, 1012. Because of the danger of pride, God mixes those who will not persevere with those who will. X, 941. And so that, terrified when the former fall, they may walk the right path with fear and trembling. II, 984. Those who do not persevere were not called according to the purpose. II, 639. If you perish in the straw, you were not gold, but only pretended to be gold. V, 119. To persevere to the end is the condition of sheep hearing the shepherd’s voice. III, 1725. Whether someone has received perseverance remains uncertain as long as he lives. X, 993, 994. No one is certain of perseverance except by some revelation from God. VII, 328. [Col. 0528] For the sake of the most salutary humility, it is useful for all, or nearly all, that they cannot know what they will be. II, 984. The perseverance of martyrs is difficult. X, 995. Perseverance is necessary for us to deserve blessing. V, 58. Contradictors are overcome by perseverance. V, 548. To persevere is a great and difficult thing. IV, 1809. Perseverance is encouraged by the shortness of time. IV, 361, 362, 366.

Perseverantius, a Tibertine bishop. IV, 381.

Perseus, the husband of Andromeda, received into heaven. VII, 572. A star was named after Perseus. VII, 572.

Persius. II, 433, 1023. A satirical poet: he handed down moral precepts. VII, 52. Persius places above all punishments the punishment suffered by people who are compelled to acknowledge the vices they cannot avoid. I, 1211.

The persons of the Holy Trinity must neither be confused nor separated; the works of nature and grace are common to them. II, 744. The persons are neither, when confused, one, nor, when separated, three. II, 750. The names “Father” and “Son” do not indicate natures in themselves, but signify persons in relation to one another. II, 751. The voice that was heard was not joined to the unity of the Father’s person, nor was the appearance of the dove joined to the unity of the person of the Holy Spirit. II, 745. The Father’s voice heard on the mountain and the appearance of the dove were produced without the ministry of a life-giving soul. II, 746. They could have been produced through the ministry of angels. II, 747. See Trinity. A human person is a mixture of soul and body; Christ’s person is a mixture of God and man. II, 520, 745. Partiality. III, 1636. It is not permissible to favor the person of a poor man in judgment. IV, 285, etc. Christ did not favor the persons of the Jewish leaders. IV, 1196. The “person” of the body, as though in the body’s name and place. II, 545. “Neither the cause of a cause nor the person of a person prejudices another”: a saying of the Donatists. II, 580, 581, 584, 756; IX, 667, 676. See Cause.

Obstinacy is not therefore to be embraced because steadfastness is desirable. I, 1065. Obstinacy strives to be called steadfastness. II, 736. Obstinacy prevents a person from being corrected; steadfastness prevents him from being corrupted. II, 225.

Pertunda, a goddess. VII, 188.

The Stoics defined disturbance as a movement to which reason yielded. III, 559. There are four disturbances of the soul: desire, joy, fear, and sadness. I, 788; III, 1798. The Stoics wrongly deny that these can befall the wise person. III, 1798. Christians can arouse them within themselves. III, 1798. The Stoics did not exclude every disturbance from the soul of the wise person. III, 556. The Stoics admitted three disturbances in the soul of the wise person, and an equal number of steadfast dispositions. VII, 411. What difference there is between disturbances and steadfast dispositions. VII, 411. The citizens of the city of God possess rightly ordered disturbances of the soul. VII, 413. Disturbance does not befall God as judge and avenger. III, 2065; IV, 92, 1415. Disturbances very often arise from contentious obstinacy in retaining customary practices. II, 201, 202. See Passion.

Pertusa. IX, 507, 528, 550.

Who are called “perventors.” III, 1101; VIII, 516.

To break the bond of customary and almost familiar perversity requires greater strength. II, 224. If something right is found even among the perverse, once their perversity has been corrected, what is right must not be violated in the least. IX, 598.

Perversely obstinate. Nothing should be debated with such a person. I, 1242. Obstinacy is the desire to win. VII, 424.

A severe pestilence in Africa. VII, 112. At Rome. VII, 96, 97, 98. What cause the oracle declared the Roman pestilence to have. VII, 98. “The pestilence is asking for money; give it two coins, and let it go on its way”: a Punic proverb. V, 910. The seat of pestilence is the love of domination, or pernicious doctrine. IV, 67.

What one ought to ask from God. IV, 755, 756. One should ask not for the things he made, but for him who made them. IV, 330, 438. If you ask him for something else, you will wrong him and harm yourself. IV, 331. God gives only to the one who asks, so that he may not give to one incapable of receiving. IV, 1324. How petitions of the heart and of the flesh differ. IV, 358. What asking, seeking, and knocking are. III, 1302. Asking, seeking, and knocking are gifts of divine inspiration. VIII, 21.

Petilianus the Donatist. I, 640. Ingenious and eloquent. IX, 336. Before becoming bishop, Petilianus was a courtroom advocate. IX, 356, 357. Petilianus, formerly a catechumen in the Catholic Church, was ordained bishop by force by the Donatists. IX, 342, 696. He was established as bishop of Constantina. I, 644; IX, 391, 593, 594. Or, according to the *Retractationes*, of Cirta. IX, 445. Petilianus was the successor of Silvanus in the Donatist church at Cirta, but not his immediate successor. IX, 386. Petilianus’s letter in which the order of Donatus’s party is said to be set forth. II, 196. His letters against the Catholic Church. IX, 245, 246; *Retractationes*. And Augustine’s response to them. I, 640. Petilianus complained about Augustine’s response to his letters—for what reason. IX, 707. Petilianus’s frequent curses against the Catholics are turned back upon the Donatists themselves throughout Book 2 of *Against Petilianus’s Letter*. Petilianus often does not report the testimonies of Scripture as they stand. IX, 304, 305, 313. The scriptural testimonies cited by Petilianus are directed more against the Donatists than against [Col. 0529] the Catholics. IX, 379, 386.

Wantonness makes wrongful use of the eyes. III, 1620.

What the rock signifies. IV, 1363. The rock is Christ. I, 618. The rock is a symbol of Christ. III, 737. The rock struck by the rod is a figure of Christ. V, 1551, 1553. The rock upon which the Church was built is Christ himself. V, 479, 1238, 1348. The rock, Christ, melted itself in order to water the faithful. IV, 1480. The rock is everywhere our refuge. IV, 1373. Building upon rock and upon sand. V, 275.

Petronia, a most distinguished woman, was healed of an illness at the Memorial of Saint Stephen established at Uzalis. VII, 768.

Peter received his name from Christ, the rock. I, 618; V, 479, 1148, 1238, 1348. Why Peter’s name was changed. III, 1444. Peter was first and foremost in the order of the Apostles. V, 479, 481, 797, 1353, 1365, 1368; X, 648. The primacy of the Apostles stands out in Peter. V, 480; IX, 127. The episcopate itself and all the authority of this name emerged from Peter. Innoc. II, 781, 785. Peter’s apostolic principate is to be preferred to any episcopate. IX, 127. Whether revelation was made to Saint Peter when he confessed Christ as the Son of the living God through faith in so great a truth, or through a vision of what he saw, does not seem clear. II, 610. Peter’s confession of Christ, and immediately afterward his human thought and trembling concerning the same Christ. V, 1108, 1109, 1353, 1458; VI, 690. The cause of Peter’s confession and the cause of his trembling. V, 1239. Peter clung to Christ with a human and carnal affection. V, 1238. Peter was first called blessed and soon afterward Satan. V, 480. Why Christ called Peter Satan. IV, 1670. Peter, answering from the Father’s revelation, was called rock and blessed; speaking from the weakness of the flesh, he was called Satan. IV, 1799. What in Peter came from himself and what from God. V, 1292. From himself, he was a liar; by God’s gift, truthful. V, 1185, 1194. He was blessed not from himself but from the Lord. III, 1750. Blessedness came from God; Satan came from man. V, 1109. The apostle Peter was not lying when he said that he wished to lay down his life for the Lord. X, 530. But he presumed too much upon himself. X, 931. Peter’s presumption. III, 1810, 1811. Peter had presumed upon his own strength, not upon God’s gift, but upon free will. V, 1292. He promised more than he could do. V, 1352. When he promised that he would lay down his life for Christ, he saw what he wished but did not know what he could do. III, 1810. He had not yet received the strength by which he could fulfill his promise. V, 1180. He wished to go before the Lord. IV, 328. He did not have the strength for this. IV, 1832. Before Christ’s death, Peter was not yet fit for martyrdom. III, 1874. He could not yet die for Christ. V, 34. Peter’s presumption and denial. V, 797, 1359. Likewise concerning Peter’s denial. III, 788. Peter, a pillar most firm, trembled all over at the force of a single breeze. III, 1932, 1933. Peter was carnal-minded and weak. V, 34. What an abyss of weakness there was in Peter. IV, 473. In Peter were signified the Church’s strength and weakness. V, 480, 1350. Peter was weak and unknown even to himself. V, 755. He did not know himself when he said, “I am with you unto death.” IV, 490. Before the temptation he presumed upon himself; in the temptation he learned about himself. IV, 355, 647, 1797, 1798. Peter, feverish, declared himself healthy, but Christ touched the vein of his heart. IV, 1797, 1831. Peter was revealed to himself when, as the Lord’s passion approached, he presumed, and when it came, he faltered. V, 1104. Christ abandoned Peter, and Peter the man was found. V, 798. The presumptuous man is abandoned for a little while so that he may be shown to himself. V, 1294. For an hour his weakness trembled so that presumption might be overcome, not so that devotion might be destroyed. V, 1292. That was not Peter’s abandonment but his instruction. V, 1294.

Peter lacked charity when he denied Christ. III, 1863. He lacked perfect charity when he denied the Lord out of fear. X, 901. If Peter had gone away after denying Christ, what else would he have done but perish? III, 1933. The apostle Peter freely denied Christ, although Scripture had foretold his denial. IX, 407. Peter’s denial and conversion. VI, 690, 705, 706. Some try to excuse Peter. III, 1810, 1811. They are refuted. III, 1810, 1811. It is proved that Peter truly sinned by denying Christ. IV, 1831. Peter was within the lion’s teeth when he denied the Lord three times. IV, 1376. With what eyes Christ looked upon Peter. X, 382. The Lord looked upon Peter not with the eyes of the flesh but with the deepest mercy. V, 1293. Peter would not have denied unless he had been abandoned; he would not have wept unless he had been looked upon. V, 1294. Although Peter denied Christ for a time, shaken by fear, he was restored by weeping and later crowned by confessing. IV, 1537. Peter dies by denying life. V, 1180, 1297. He came back to life by weeping. III, 1811. Peter’s tears in response to the Lord’s regard. IV, 1798. Peter did not perform penance in the manner of those in the Church who are properly called penitents. II, 1086. Peter’s faith in the Lord was swallowed up when he was crucified. V, 1147. Peter, who had confessed that Christ was the Son of God, afterward thought carnally about his passion. VI, 131. He did not believe that Christ had risen. V, 1148.

Peter was presumptuous, a denier, a confessor, and a lover. VI, 694. A fervent lover of Christ. V, 1348. A greater lover of our Lord than a denier. V, 1353. Peter was exceedingly ready in the love of Christ. V, 479. How great Peter’s love of Christ was. [Col. 0530] IV, 1167, 1168. In the denial the Lord showed Peter to Peter; in love the Lord showed Christ to Peter. V, 1372. Peter’s fear before the Lord’s passion, and his love after the resurrection. III, 1863. Peter’s love was expanded on the day of Pentecost through the Holy Spirit. III, 1864. His zeal in bearing witness to Christ. III, 1864, 1865.

What Peter saw when he was carried away in ecstasy. IV, 1359. Concerning Peter’s vision in which he heard, “Kill and eat” (*Macta et manduca*). V, 800. Peter, representing the figure of the Church, heard, “Kill and eat.” V, 43. Peter kills all the animals. IV, 1359. Why Peter was asked three times whether he loved Christ. III, 1733. By a threefold utterance of love he canceled the threefold utterance of denial. IV, 407, 1168; V, 756, 765, 799, 1179, 1350. Three times he confessed love; three times fear was condemned. V, 799, 1372. Once Peter had come to love him, Christ entrusted the sheep to him. V, 1353.

The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter, who represented the person of the Church, and forgiveness was granted. VI, 308. Representing unity, Peter confessed Christ on behalf of all and received the keys from him. III, 1949. Peter represents the person of the Church. V, 478, 480. Especially in the passage where it is said, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” V, 802, 1239, 1350. Because of the primacy he held among the disciples, Peter represented the Church when it was said to him, “I will give you the keys,” and so forth. IV, 1432. The keys were given to Peter alone because they were given to the unity of the Church. V, 1349. Christ entrusted the sheep to Peter as the figure of the Church’s unity. V, 287, 1350. In him the unity of all good shepherds was represented. V, 798. Peter represents the figure of the whole Church. I, 618; VI, 691. He is the type of the one Church. V, 479, 1109. He left the whole world, and Peter received the whole world. IV, 1371. Peter signifies the body of the Church and the good within the Church. III, 1762. In Peter alone Christ forms the Church. V, 755. The Church is built not upon Peter but upon the rock he confessed. V, 1238. See Rock. Because Christ is the rock, Peter is the Christian people. V, 479. Peter walking upon the sea represents the Church. V, 478. Peter was not a tightrope-walker but a sea-walker. IV, 440.

Peter was foretold to suffer what he did not wish. V, 1359. Peter, previously weak in himself, was now, by Christ’s grace, mature for suffering. V, 1180. Thorns trampled by feet of stone. V, 1360. Before the Lord’s death Peter was weaker than the martyrs and even certain girls. V, 1297. How many—not only old men and old women, and young men and women of both sexes, but even boys and girls—despised death for confessing Christ: something that he once could not do, although he had received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. III, 1933. Peter was powerful not in himself but in the Lord. V, 482. How Peter would suffer unwillingly. V, 1373.

Why Peter was rebuked by Paul. III, 2113, 2114. Augustine holds that Peter and Paul observed the commands of the Law out of fear of believing Jews, whereas Jerome holds that they merely pretended. II, 156, 260. Paul truly corrected Peter. II, 155, 277, 278, 285. He did not correct him because he observed ancestral traditions, but because he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. II, 155, 259. Peter really was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, and he was not acting rightly. II, 278. Augustine’s view of Peter rebuked by Paul agrees with the thought of Cyprian and Ambrose. II, 286, 781. Jerome ultimately followed this view. II, 781. Peter was corrected by Paul because of his pretense concerning the works of the Law. VIII, 358. Peter fell into superstitious pretense. VI, 308, 493. Paul rebuked the deceptive pretense in Peter. II, 155, 260, 279. Paul recalled Peter from pretense. III, 2107. Peter willingly accepted correction from Paul. VI, 493, 494, 537. Peter, when rebuked, was more admirable than his rebuker. III, 2114. There is praise here for Paul’s just freedom in rebuking and for Peter’s holy humility in accepting rebuke. II, 285. In this matter Peter provided posterity with a rarer and holier example than Paul. II, 285.

Peter and Paul, despised in death, are honored after their passion to what extent. IV, 1830. Both shedding their blood as companions, they consecrated the same feast day. V, 1361, 1365. They suffered on different days. V, 1352. Peter and Paul were one. V, 1352. Peter’s memory is held in great honor at Rome. IV, 509. The basilica of Saint Peter at Carthage. V, 116. The feasts of Peter and Paul are to be celebrated with greater attendance. V, 1365. Augustine is saddened by the people’s sluggishness amid so great a celebration. V, 1365. The bodies of Peter and Paul at Rome. V, 1355. At the tomb of Peter the fisherman, the most eminent summit of the most noble Empire, with its diadem lowered, makes supplication. II, 1028; V, 1684. Peter and Paul are painted together with Christ in several places. III, 1049.

Peter and Paul are compared with one another. V, 1368, 1683. In Peter let us learn not to be proud; in Paul, not to despair. V, 1684. Peter strengthened us through his apostleship, martyrdom, and letters. V, 1050. Some Romans think that the Saturday fast originated because Peter, intending to contend with Simon on the Lord’s Day, fasted on the preceding day; others think this false. II, 145. Peter is vindicated from the accusation of magic. VII, 617. Peter ordained Saint Stephen. V, 1365. Peter had his cathedra at Rome. IX, 300. The apocryphal story of [Col. 0531] Saint Peter’s daughter and the gardener’s daughter. VIII, 161.

Peter the Spanish presbyter, to whom the second book *On the Soul* was written. X, 473, 474.

Peter of Hippo Diarrhytus. IX, 236.

There were two deacons named Peter in the city of Rome itself at the same time. IX, 646.

Phaedra. III, 1191; VIII, 601.

The bull of Phalaris. II, 667.

Phaliscus, the poet. I, 1144.

Fanatics. V, 553.

The power of phantasies. VIII, 989. Phantasy of memory. VIII, 969. Although not every phantasy is accompanied by memory, it nevertheless seems to Nebridius that there can be no memory without phantasy. II, 67. Memory can exist without phantasy. II, 68. Nebridius thinks that all images derive their phantasy from themselves rather than from sense perception. II, 67.

Phantasies, or visions of the soul. VII, 259. The difference between phantasies and phantasms. I, 1180. A phantasm is so called when our sense is deceived by the falsity of what is seen. III, 730. Phantasies occur when the soul moves the likenesses of bodies through the spirit; when it gazes upon things presented to it, they are appearances. III, 470.

Phantasms are fabrications derived from the form of a body and drawn in through bodily sense. III, 130. The deceptive play of phantasms is the source of all errors. I, 1180. A splendid description of the soul’s struggles with phantasms. I, 734, 740; III, 164. It is rare and difficult to overcome carnal phantasms through the serenity of a devout mind. I, 756. How fabricated phantasms are to be judged. III, 150. From where the mind judges phantasms. III, 154. To regard true phantasms as things known is the greatest error. I, 1180. A person’s phantastic condition can be conveyed to the perception of others. VII, 575.

Pharan is interpreted as “fruitful mountain.” III, 775. It signifies the Church. III, 775.

Pharaoh was the name of all the kings of Egypt. VII, 521. Pharaoh is not a person’s name but a royal dignity. III, 498, 501. Pharaoh is interpreted as “dissipation.” IV, 1750. Pharaoh, killing the males and sparing the females, signifies the devil choking virtues and nourishing desires. IV, 1771. The flies under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed signified the restlessness of the proud, that is, of heretics. II, 219. How Pharaoh’s hardening took place. III, 601. It was owed to his previous merits. V, 72, 73. God hardened Pharaoh’s heart by a just judgment, and Pharaoh himself by free will. X, 911. The fact that Pharaoh did not obey God’s commands already proceeded from punishment. III, 2080, 2081. Pharaoh was not held responsible for failing to obey at that time, since, with his heart hardened, he could not obey; rather, he was held responsible because by his earlier unbelief he had made himself worthy of having his heart hardened. III, 2080.

The Pharisees were certain leading men, as though separated from the common people for Jewish nobility, and, so to speak, the distinguished men of the Jews. V, 626, 917. This word is said to sound as though it meant “separation.” V, 917. The Pharisees are thieves and robbers. III, 1720. They were not healed by Christ because they seemed righteous to themselves. III, 1447. Christ’s saying about hearing the Pharisees but not imitating them applies also to wicked shepherds within the Church. V, 757. The Pharisees’ washings. IX, 339. Outward cleanliness. V, 625. Cleanliness in the body, not in the heart. IV, 1289, 1820. The Pharisees’ leaven. V, 721. The Pharisee who had invited the Lord: proud thinking. V, 596. The Pharisee and the Publican. V, 220, 656, 1315. The Pharisee’s boastfulness. IV, 265. In what the Pharisee sinned when he gave thanks to God. X, 154. The Manichaeans called the Catholics Pharisees. X, 1101.

A druggist promising an animal that would eat itself. X, 726.

Phegous, brother of Phoroneus, king of the Argives. VII, 562. Phegous taught the observance of periods by months and years. VII, 562. A temple was established at Phegous’s tomb, in which he was worshiped as a god. VII, 562. Why. VII, 562.

Pherecydes the Syrian philosopher. I, 954. Pherecydes the Assyrian was the first among the Greeks to discuss the immortality of the soul. II, 521.

**Φιλαργυρία (*philargyria*)**, love of money. IV, 1531. In Paul, this term signifies a genus through a species, that is, greed in its general and universal form. IV, 1531.

Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, was seen by Augustine at Milan with Saint Ambrose and wrote a book on heresies. II, 999. A very lengthy book. VIII, 33. He counted 128 heresies. VIII, 33. Among the Jewish people there were twenty-eight heresies before the Lord’s coming and 128 after the Lord’s coming. II, 999. Augustine implies that Philastrius included among the heresies some that are not heresies. II, 1000. He declares Epiphanius to be far more learned than Philastrius. II, 1000.

Philip the deacon, who properly deserved to be called an evangelist. V, 600, 601, 1226, 1227. He was different from the Apostle. V, 1227.

Philistines is interpreted as “those falling through drink.” IV, 1053.

Philo, the Academic philosopher. I, 926. The Greeks do not hesitate to compare Philo’s eloquence [Col. 0532] with Plato’s. VIII, 274.

Philocalia is love of beauty. I, 922. In incorporeal and supreme matters, *philocalia* is the same as philosophy. I, 586, 922.

Philocalus, a leading man among the people of Hippo. II, 999, 1000.

To philosophize is to love God, according to Plato. VII, 233, 236. The only reason for philosophizing available to a human being is to be happy. VII, 623.

The name “philosophy” arose from Pythagoras. VII, 225. The origin of philosophy occurred after the patriarchs, and even after Moses, around the time of Hermes Trismegistus. VII, 599. Philosophy is the love and pursuit of wisdom. I, 1327. Certain exceptionally acute philosophers thought that not even what is grasped by the mind deserved to aspire to the name of wisdom unless the grasp were so firm that the mind could not be moved away from it by any reasoning. I, 1068. The excellence of philosophy above the other disciplines. I, 987. What the glory of philosophy is. I, 922. Every age is mature for philosophy. I, 908. From its harbor one proceeds to the region of the blessed life. I, 959. The philosophy of this world is forbidden in the sacred writings. I, 956, 993. Questions about this world, although they bring some pleasure when investigated, must be feared lest they consume time that ought to be devoted to better things. II, 75. What the proper task of true philosophy is. I, 1002. Nothing more is found in philosophy than what the One is. I, 1016. Philosophy promises reason. I, 1002. Philosophy has two questions: one concerning the soul, the other concerning God. I, 1017. An exhortation to philosophy. I, 905, 919. The mountain of vainglory erected before the harbor of philosophy must be avoided. I, 960. On the praise and defense of philosophy: Cicero’s *Hortensius*. I, 685. How Augustine was inflamed with enthusiasm for philosophy. I, 685.

The three parts of philosophy. VII, 52, 228. The tripartite division of philosophy was not instituted by human beings but discovered. VII, 338. Namely, by Plato. VII, 338. Philosophy investigates either morals, nature, or the method of reasoning. II, 441; VII, 338. Ethics, physics, and logic are contained in the two commandments of charity. II, 524. Another division of philosophy is into active and contemplative. VII, 228. This is not contrary to the tripartite division. VII, 228. Christian philosophy is true philosophy. I, 961; X, 774. In every part of philosophy God holds the highest place. VII, 233. The discoveries of philosophy are useless without divine authority. VII, 52. Philosophy aims at attaining blessedness. VII, 339. Philosophy is the sole remedy against the miseries of this life. VII, 787.

The origin of the name “philosopher.” VIII, 1037. Philosophers are those who profess the pursuit of wisdom or wisdom itself. VII, 225, 234. The name “philosopher” comes from Pythagoras. X, 1432. They began to be called philosophers from his time. VII, 582. The true philosopher is a lover of God. VII, 225. The gentile philosophers came after the prophets. VII, 596, 597. Philosophers held, taught, and defended various opinions about the nature of the gods. III, 122. Philosophers who said that the gods were their friends fell among wicked demons. VII, 636. Honors ought to be assigned to philosophers rather than to the gods of the gentiles. VII, 52. After knowing God, how foolishly the philosophers served idols. V, 777, 1134. What the philosophers found through curiosity they lost through pride. V, 777. Because of pride they did not find the Creator through the creatures. I, 707. They understood many things about God and truth. V, 439, 776, 1133, 1644. From where they understood them. V, 776. The wisdom of the philosophers comes from God. VII, 52. The pagans themselves admit that philosophy can be given by God alone. VII, 787. The greatest philosophers among the gentiles philosophized without the Holy Spirit, although they did not remain silent about the Father and the Son. III, 604. The books of the philosophers speak about the only-begotten Son of God. III, 1390. The gentile philosophers wrote extensively that the soul is immortal, but they most openly deny that the resurrection of the flesh can occur. IV, 1134. The ancient philosophers are not to be consulted about the resurrection and future matters. VIII, 902, 903. The philosophers were deceived by human conjecture. VII, 390. The philosophers place riches in intelligible things and poverty in sensible things. II, 64. The philosophers labored in their studies for no other reason than to discover how blessedness might be attained. VII, 600. And this was their common pursuit. V, 809. The philosophers erred by placing blessedness in this life. VII, 627, 628. They taught that one could make a blessed life for oneself by the power of one’s own will. II, 830. Therefore true piety is absent among them, because they wished to manufacture a blessed life for themselves. II, 667.

## Philosophers

Whence the disagreements among philosophers. VII, 600, 601. Why they were tolerated so readily. VII, 601. No philosopher was so approved that the others, who held different and opposed opinions, were disapproved. VII, 601. The state in which philosophers are tolerated truly deserves the mystical name of Babylon. VII, 601. Philosophers did not know to what end the truths they knew ought to be directed. VII, 602. Out of fear, men did not dare to teach what was right. III, 126. Why they suppressed the truth in [Col. 0533] iniquity. VIII, 1034. The Gentile philosophers, enemies and defenders of the truth. IV, 111. Philosophers corrupt in heart. IV, 273. Proud wise men. III, 1390. The disease of philosophers: vanity. X, 212. Why philosophers are vain. II, 281. The thoughts of philosophers: great ravings of great learned men. V, 1137. The pride, envy, and curiosity of philosophers. III, 126. Blindness. I, 707. Vanity. I, 1327. The various schools of philosophers. I, 956. The two kinds of philosophers, the Italian and the Ionic. VII, 225, 234. The founder of the Ionic school, Thales of Miletus. VII, 225. Of the Italian school, Pythagoras. VII, 233. The names of various philosophers. X, 776. Consular philosophers. II, 389; X, 777. Philosophers wearing the pallium. VII, 389. When philosophers become Christians, they are compelled to change not their dress but their false doctrines. VII, 647. The divine Scriptures command that not philosophers altogether, but the philosophers of this world, are to be avoided and mocked. I, 993. Philosophers who philosophize according to the elements of this world must be shunned by a Christian. VII, 234. Philosophers approached the Christian faith in certain matters. X, 778. Which philosophers came closer to the Christians. VII, 233, 235. The Gentile philosophers seem to say something only until they are compared with Christ. IV, 1828. If one of them is found to have said what Christ also said, we congratulate him, but we do not follow him. IV, 1828. The pagan philosophers, unjust possessors of the sciences, arts, and so forth. III, 63. If anything was rightly said by them, it must be converted to our use. III, 63. As Cyprian, Lactantius, Victorinus, and Hilary did, and Moses before them. III, 63. All philosophers lacked the example of divine humility, which was made manifest at the most fitting time through our Lord Jesus Christ. II, 440. Whether philosophers favor the Pelagians in the question of original sin. X, 776, 777, 778. The opinions of philosophers have become altogether obsolete. II, 437, 442, 448. It is useless for a Christian teacher to inquire into the opinions of the ancient philosophers, since no one now proposes anything from them against the Christian faith. II, 437. In Augustine’s time all philosophers were either Cynics, Peripatetics, or Platonists. I, 956. They were very few indeed. I, 959. In Augustine’s age there were no philosophers except in their bodily garb. II, 61. The response of a certain philosopher disturbed in a great storm. III, 556.

## Phison

Phison, the river now called the Ganges. III, 203.

## Phlebotomize

To perform bloodletting. V, 146.

## Phlegm

The seat of phlegm is in the head. VII, 348.

## Seals

Seals, marine calves. III, 284.

## Phoenice

Which region of the Holy Land Phoenice is. III, 617.

## Phoenix

The phoenix, reborn from its own death. X, 543. It signifies the resurrection of bodies. X, 543.

## Phorbas

Phorbas, son of Criasius and Melantomice, the sixth king of the Argives, reckoned among the gods. VII, 565.

## Phoroneus

Phoroneus, the second king of the Argives. VII, 562, 566.

## Photinus

Photinus the heretic. VI, 714; VIII, 34; IX, 169. His heresy. I, 746. Photinus denied that Christ was God. V, 573; VII, 652. He considered Him merely a human being. V, 229, 573, 991, 1150, 1156. Yet he held that He surpassed all pious and holy men in excellence of wisdom and righteousness. V, 1155. The Photinian and Arian parties divided against each other. V, 447. Photinus did not enter through the door into the sheepfold. III, 1721. His error. III, 1609.

## Photinians

Photinians. III, 1737, 1738, 1875; V, 988. The Photinian error concerning Christ’s incarnation. X, 1034. Concerning the Trinity. V, 448. The Photinians attributed the Son’s beginning to the Virgin’s womb and refused to believe that He had existed previously. II, 605. The Photinians, Jews, and others sinned against the Holy Spirit. II, 813; V, 448. The superstition of the Photinians. III, 127. The heresy of Photinus arose in Pannonia. V, 1174.

## The Frenzied

The frenzied. V, 538, 945, 1596. Why they are stronger than usual. I, 1058. For the frenzied, death is nearer, and all the nearer in proportion as they are stronger. IV, 696. A frenzied man predicted the future death of a certain woman. III, 468.

The illness of the frenzied. V, 945.

## Phrygia

Phrygia divided by the Cataphrygians. V, 1174.

## Phrixus

The story of Phrixus. VII, 570.

## Consumption

A consumptive person cannot be cured. V, 489.

## Physics

The science of physics. VI, 235.

## Picentes

The Picentes attempt to throw off the Roman yoke. VII, 168.

## Painter

A painter knows where to place each color. V, 692.

## Paintings

Lascivious paintings. I, 671. Worshipers of paintings and tombs. I, 1342. A painting displaying the stoning of Stephen and the conversion of Saul. V, 1434.

## Picus

Picus, son of Saturn or Sterces, the first king of Laurentum. VII, 572, 573. Picus, a renowned warrior and augur. VII, 573. Romulus consecrated Picus as a god. VII, 190.

## Piety

What true piety is. VII, 159, 160. The beginning of piety is to think as highly as possible of God. I, 1224. The perfection of piety is love. III, 132. Piety is to love God gratuitously, without seeking reward. V, 568. Piety, according to the Greek term, means good worship. VI, 231. Piety is the true worship of the true God. II, 673; V, 523. God is not worshiped except by loving Him. II, 557. The same things are approved by the pious as please God. I, 865. The path of piety rises from humility to heavenly things. VII, 52. Leisure is to be enjoyed for piety, not for idleness. II, 188. Piety is the wisdom of man. VI, 231; X, 211. It is the second step toward wisdom. III, 39. If piety and charity are absent, what are tranquility and repose from those and the other evils of the world except material for luxury and destruction, whether as an invitation or as an aid? II, 1026. Piety is not to be sought for the sake of the goods or evils of this life, but for the sake of the future judgment. VII, 661. Piety suffices for true happiness. VII, 114. Faith and piety are preparations for entering the wedding feast with the bridegroom. II, 574. Piety is a great gift of God. VII, 114. Great piety, like great impiety, belongs to few. V, 441. A form of piety, but not virtue itself, can exist in those cut off from the Church. V, 463. Piety is shown not only toward God but also toward parents. VII, 279. Toward those related by blood and toward one’s country. VI, 21. Innate force implanted this. VI, 21. Piety is the most sacred bond of the human race. VIII, 84. The term “piety” is also commonly used of works of mercy. VII, 279. Piety is more than what came before, and so forth. III, 1685. The pious love Christ without seeking reward. IV, 1432. See Good.

The pious person is nourished by the food of righteousness. IV, 1290. How the pious suffer persecution. IX, 719. The impious live by the pious. III, 143.

## Pygmies

The Pygmies are so called as though they were a cubit tall. VII, 485.

## Cosmetics

Cyprian and Ambrose attacked cosmetics. III, 114. Women who color their appearance with cosmetics are worse than adulteresses. III, 114. They teach their husbands to commit adultery. III, 114.

## Pledge and Earnest

How a pledge and an earnest differ. V, 158, 159, 858, 1673.

## Sloth

The burden of sloth and its struggle with avarice. V, 897. See Acedia, Negligence.

## Pilate

Pilate is mentioned in the Passion of Christ to establish the chronology. VI, 187. Pilate was to some extent a participant in the iniquity of the Jews. IV, 762. Pilate and the Magi signified the nations that were to be gathered from East and West. V, 1031.

## Pilleatus

Pilleatus. III, 1440.

## Pilumnus

Pilumnus, a god. VII, 188.

## Pilus

Pinianus. II, 471. Melania’s husband. X, 359. Note. Pinianus wishes to swear to the people that, if he were ordained against his will, he would leave Africa altogether. II, 478. A pirate’s free reply to Alexander. VII, 115. The war against pirates. VII, 107.

The occupations of fishermen and hunters. VI, 714. Christ did not gain a fisherman from the orator, but an orator from the fisherman. IV, 372. Why fishermen and the weak were first chosen by Christ. V, 256, 537, 1683. The disciples’ two fishing expeditions, one before and the other after the resurrection, and the difference between them. VI, 97. The two miraculous catches of fish made at the Lord’s command, and how they foreshadow the condition of the present and future Church. V, 1161, 1244. What the catch of 153 fish signifies. IV, 1961; VI, 39. It demonstrates new life. II, 219.

## Fish

A mute fish. I, 1351. It is entirely certain that fish possess memory. III, 283, 284. The two fish with which the Lord fed the crowds on the mountain: what they signify. VI, 48, 49. They signify two persons, namely the royal and the priestly. I, 627; III, 1595. What is signified by fish and whales. I, 863. A fish lifted from the depths is eaten at a table prepared in the sight of believers. I, 858. A good fish: pious faith. V, 620.

## Pool

The sheep pool, Siloam. V, 687. What it signifies that a sick man went down into the pool after the water had been stirred, and that not many but only one was healed. V, 690, 693. The disturbed pool healed one person; hence it signified Christ’s Passion. IV, 1329. The five porticoes of the pool represented the five books of Moses. IV, 889, 1329.

## Mill

Being crushed in a mill, a punishment of slaves. V, 883.

## Pittacium

Pittacium. V, 964.

## Pittacus

Pittacus of Mytilene, one of the Seven Sages; at what time he lived. VII, 582.

## Pleasing God

Here we can scarcely please God, and the source from which we can do so. V, 295. God is to be pleased by true and sincere affections. VI, 446. The person pleases God whom God pleases. IV, 277, 1631. God will please you if you are upright. V, 317. The upright God does not please the perverse person. V, 322. Nothing in you pleases God except what you have from God; whatever you have from yourself displeases God. V, 108. Let a person erase what he has done, and he will please the one who made him. V, 587. To please oneself is dangerous; one must beware of becoming proud. III, 1793. Let no one please himself, as though he had lived justly here. V, 932, 933. Where you have pleased yourself, there you have remained. V, 926. You will displease God if you please yourself. IV, 472. Whoever pleases himself pleases a foolish man. IV, 1631; V, 303. To please oneself is the sin of pride. VII, 420, 421, 422. The proud soul wishes to please in the sight of men; the humble soul wishes to please in secret, where God sees. IV, 163. How the desire to please people may be uprooted. VI, 26. How one ought to please everyone, and yet not please people. IV, 1629. How we ought to please and not please people. II, 1024; V, 301, 372. Whoever pleases God and people at the same time does not really please people. III, 2109. The Apostle pleased people for the sake of their salvation; he did not please people for his own advantage. V, 374.

Placor. III, 951, 968.

The plagues of Egypt. IV, 999, 1000, 1399. The ten plagues compared with the Ten Commandments. V, 67.

The *plani*—diviners and mathematical impostors—devoid of piety. I, 694, Note 2; V, 261. And devoid of truth. I, 739.

Plantarium of peace. V, 314.
