## Plato

Plato. II, 67; IV, 1828; IX, 224. An Athenian, born of an honorable family. VII, 227. Plato’s remarkable intellect. VII, 227. His gifts. I, 926, 954. His eloquence. III, 124. Plato, a noble philosopher. VIII, 1011. The most distinguished of Socrates’ disciples. III, 1048; VII, 227. He far surpassed Socrates’ other disciples. VII, 597. Plato learned the theology of Pythagoras from his successors. III, 56. From Socrates he learned moral matters, and from the Pythagoreans natural and divine matters. VII, 228. For the sake of acquiring knowledge and perfecting wisdom, Plato undertook various journeys. VI, 30; VII, 228.

Plato is said to have composed a complete philosophical system. I, 955. He divided philosophy into three parts. VII, 228. The extent of the power of Plato’s Ideas. VII, 218. Plato admitted certain civic virtues resembling other true virtues. I, 955. According to Cicero, Plato placed in divine wisdom the end of the good, the causes of things, and confidence in reasoning; but the Epicureans and Stoics placed these in the nature of the body or of the soul. II, 441. Plato’s teaching is not wholly alien to the Church’s teaching. III, 124. With a few changes, the Platonists ought to bow their pious necks to Christ. II, 442. Plato’s opinion concerning the twofold world. I, 955. The one he believed to be an animal. I, 602. Plato’s “year.” III, 236. Plato, despising marriage, feared the perverse opinion of his time so greatly that he sacrificed to nature, so that the supposed sin might thereby be erased. III, 126. Plato’s opinion concerning the nature of the stars or gods. V, 1138. Plato’s conception of man. II, 64. Plato and his disciples thought sacrifices ought to be offered to many gods. VII, 237. Plato, who expelled the poets, was more worthy of divine honors than the gods who ordered theatrical games to be presented to themselves. VII, 58, 59. Plato’s philosophy surpasses the fabulous, civic, and natural theology of the pagans. VII, 229. Let the other philosophers yield to him. VII, 230, 231. Plato’s book on the ordering of the world. V, 1138. It agrees with the Book of Genesis. VII, 236. Plato wrote more pleasantly for reading than powerfully for persuasion. III, 124. He taught remarkable things but persuaded no one. III, 124. Some believe that he thought contrary to what he says. VII, 359. He deliberately sought to conceal his own opinion. VII, 228. Porphyry corrected many of Plato’s doctrines. VII, 309, 310. Plato left his school, the Academy, to his disciple Xenocrates. II, 440.

Plato’s distinguished eulogy. I, 954. Plato, almost the god of philosophers. X, 777. Labeo places Plato among the demigods. VII, 58, 59, 238. At what time and for how many years Plato flourished. VII, 235, 597. Note (b). Augustine once mistakenly believed him to have been Jeremiah’s contemporary. I, 632. Some have dared to say that Christ learned all His opinions from Plato’s books. III, 56. Ambrose wrote against them. II, 125. He shows that Plato was rather instructed by our people. III, 56. By Jeremiah? Augustine asserts this here, but later retracted it. III, 56. Plato neither heard Jeremiah nor read the prophetic Scriptures. VII, 235. Plato is not to be compared with any holy angel, prophet, apostle, martyr, or any Christian whatsoever. VII, 59.

## Platonists

The Platonists are the same as the Academics. II, 440. Most famous among Greeks and Latins. VII, 235. Deservedly the noblest of all philosophers. VII, 277. They are to be placed far above all other philosophers in every branch of philosophy. VII, 231, 232. Augustine preferred the arguments of the Platonists to the arguments of the other philosophers. I, 957. The Platonists placed the highest good in God. II, 440. The Platonists distinguished what is perceived by the mind from what is touched by the senses. VII, 232. The Platonists said that only what is immutable and eternal truly exists and can be perceived. II, 441. Plato wants the things we learn to remain always and not be able to perish; hence, they are not past things. II, 68. The Platonists were more enlightened than the other philosophers in proportion as they thought more correctly about the one God. VII, 237. The Platonists conceived God as incorporeal and as the creator of all natures that are not what He Himself is. VII, 231. Augustine read in their books certain things agreeing with Christian teaching concerning the divinity of the eternal Word, but nothing concerning the humility of the incarnate Word. I, 740. In them also he did not find what he found in the sacred writings, namely, the way of salvation and the teaching of humility. I, 747. Because of their lack of divine humility, the Platonists could not fulfill the role of true reason. II, 440. The superstition of the Platonists. III, 126. The Platonists require the worship of many gods in order to attain the blessed life. VII, 225. The Platonists believed that human souls, having fallen from heaven because of the merits of their sins, were thrust into bodies. I, 587; II, 718. The Platonist opinion concerning the soul’s life before the body is rejected. X, 403. The Platonist doctrine concerning the illumination and blessedness of the soul agrees with the Gospel. VII, 279, 280. The Platonists wrongly argue that an earthly body cannot exist in heaven. VII, 773. The Platonists believe that all punishments, whether of this life or of the future life, are imposed for correction. VII, 727. The Platonists guarded Plato’s sayings as mysteries. I, 954. Plato’s sayings are not easily understood by everyone. I, 954. The Platonists concealed their opinion. II, 440. Why they concealed it. II, 441, 448. The praise of the Platonists. I, 953. It is disapproved. I, 588. The Platonists are preferred to the Peripatetics. VII, 237. The Platonists, although at a considerable distance, are nevertheless closer to the truth than the other philosophers. VII, 320, 321. And closer to Christian doctrine. VII, 229, 230. They easily become Christians. III, 126. The beginnings of Platonic wisdom probably came from the sacred books. VII, 235, 236. Note (a). The Platonists disclosed their doctrine when the name of Christ began to be preached. II, 448.

## Applause

Pleonasm has a place in the Scriptures. IV, 1399.

Plotinus. II, 67. A Greek Platonic philosopher. VII, 237. Considered another Plato. I, 956. Plotinus is praised for having understood Plato more excellently than the others. VII, 265. Plotinus’ opinion concerning heavenly illumination and blessedness. VII, 279. Some disciples of Plotinus were corrupted by magical arts, while others passed over into the army of Christ. II, 448. The school of the Platonist Plotinus flourishes at Rome. II, 448.

Lead receives from a craftsman a form by which it can float upon water. VII, 773.

## Rain

Whence rain comes according to Priscillian. VIII, 667. How rain is formed. III, 266. What is meant by “it had not yet rained upon the earth.” III, 198. God rains upon a fish, and sometimes does not rain upon us: why. IV, 1944. Rain fails because of a Christian, a common proverb. VII, 49. Certain portentous rains. VII, 111. Voluntary rain is called grace because it is not given according to merits. IV, 1735.

Pneumatomachus, an opponent of the Spirit. VIII, 59.

## Podagric

A physician afflicted with gout who was healed of gout in baptism. VII, 764.

## Punishment

Punishment for sin is one thing; sin itself is another. I, 604, 608, 612. Every punishment, if it is just, is punishment for sin. I, 1296. Because of the punishment of sin, certain movements of the soul are not under our control. IV, 80. See Sin. Hidden punishments inflicted by God. X, 235. Ignorance in those who did not want to understand is without doubt sin; in those who could not understand, it is the punishment of sin. II, 883. Unbelief and impiety begin to deserve punishment, so that through the punishment itself people may do evil. III, *Retractationes* 2061, 2062. It is a great punishment to perish from the way of righteousness. IV, 72. The punishment of guilt is death. V, 1105. The bodily blindness of Paul at his conversion was a true punishment. II, 803. God willed this entire age to be punitive for human beings. X, 1192. God neither inflicts undeserved punishments nor permits them to be inflicted. X, 1270. God would be returning punishment if He wished to return a reward. III, 2066. When punishment is returned as owed, why is there no injustice with God? VIII, 554. Why God permits regenerated infants to be afflicted by various evils. VI, 263. Temporal punishments are for the exercise of the faithful. VII, 525. [Col. 0537] All punishments are inflicted either for sins or for exercising and manifesting virtues. VII, 728. Through punishments God either restrains the wicked or instructs those who are subject to Him. VIII, 446. God does not need the punishments of the wicked, but through them He provides for the salvation of the good. III, 434. It is read that punishments are inflicted on the wicked both by good angels and by evil angels; but it does not occur that the righteous are tested by bodily punishments through good angels. IV, 1002, 1003. The punishment of the wicked is among God’s good works. I, 625. See Sin. God turns our punishments to our advantage with wonderful kindness. X, 1578, 1585. Why punishment is still exacted after sin has been forgiven. X, 183, 184. What kind and how great a punishment is owed for each fault belongs not to human judgment but to divine judgment. VIII, 554, 561. No punishment: how great a punishment it is for the sinner. V, 935. Punishment on account of another’s sin. X, 722.

The Platonists believe that there are no punishments, whether in this life or in the future, except purgatorial ones. VII, 727. Some punishments are purgatorial in this mortal life. VII, 727. Some occur after death. VII, 728. Whoever arranges himself unjustly in sins is justly arranged in punishments. II, 539. Those who willingly use goods unjustly will justly be tortured unwillingly in punishments. II, 562. Some have thought that the punishments of the damned either will not exist at all or will end shortly. VII, 732, 733. They are refuted. VII, 732, 733.

## Eternal Punishments

Eternal punishments. V, 196, 218. Eternal punishments are to be feared more than temporal ones. VI, 703. No temporal torment can be compared with eternal punishments. VI, 342. In damnation, the punishments are unequal. X, 230. The punishments of Gehenna are different for different people. V, 879. Future punishment has two forms. IV, 686. The punishment of the damned is a kind of good. VII, 351. The punishment of the sinful soul does not disfigure the kingdom of God by any deformity of its own. VI, 18. Death among the damned is perpetual. VI, 342, 343. By a sufficiently hidden but nevertheless just disposition, God predestined certain people—the Donatist schismatics—to the ultimate punishments. II, 939. Eight kinds of punishment. VII, 725. By enduring punishment without guilt, Christ removed both guilt and punishment. V, 934, 1131. Some think that the punishments which the Lord threatened will not occur. V, 478. They are refuted. V, 478. Whence arose the opinion that people think Christ did not truly threaten the wicked. V, 478.

## Fear of Punishment

Fear of punishment is useful for restraining the wicked and enabling the good to live more peacefully among the wicked. II, 660, 802. It is better to lead people to worship God by teaching than to compel them through fear or pain of punishment. II, 802. Punishments should be applied to the guilty with the disposition of one who loves and corrects. V, 111. Whether by punishing or forgiving, one acts well only when one corrects human life. II, 661. No one becomes good through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness. II, 660. He is an enemy of righteousness who does not sin out of fear of punishment; but he will be its friend if he does not sin out of love of it. II, 594. He vainly thinks that he has conquered sin who does not sin out of fear of punishment. II, 593. Bodily punishment, although not arising from the will, nevertheless recalls one from the act of sin; but righteousness must be loved in such a way that even bodily punishments should not restrain us from its works. II, 594. We cling to Christ through charity, not through fear of punishment. II, 595. Punishments borne out of charity produce a crown. IV, 1844. Punishment does no harm if the cause is good. V, 1400. Fear of punishment is useful for compelling heretics into Catholic unity. II, 330.

## Poeni

The Poeni sacrificed their children to Saturn. VII, 216. The Poeni and the Canaanites are the same people. III, 2096.

## Poetry

The invention of poetry. I, 1013. What the ornaments of poetry are. I, 1000. Its trivialities are to be rejected. III, 166. Excessive devotion to it is disapproved. I, 982. Philosophy is to be preferred to it. I, 934. Augustine ennobled poetry through his books on music. II, 513. Note 2.

## Poets

Poets are called “enigmatists.” III, 739. Who the theological poets are. VII, 572. The theological poets were called wise men. VII, 581. The Greeks wrongly granted poets license to mistreat anyone they pleased. VII, 135. The license of poets toward human beings, but not toward the gods, displeased the ancient Romans. VII, 53, 54, 55, 56. It was considered more acceptable among the Greeks than among the ancient Romans. VII, 55, 56, 57, 58. Plato judged that poets, as adversaries of the truth, should be expelled from the city. VII, 58, 237. Among the Romans, poets were removed from the tribe and excluded from every honor. VII, 57. The law of the Twelve Tables forbids poets to damage the reputation of citizens. VII, 54, 58. The lies of poets. I, 1014. The comedies and tragedies of poets among the liberal studies. VII, 53. Poets are not altogether to be despised by philosophy. I, 940. The judges of poets are grammarians. I, 1014. The stories of poets are less obscene than the sacred rites of the gods. VII, 53. Poets are no less worthy of infamy than stage performers. VII, 58. Stage poets inflame lust. VII, 59, 60.

Polemo, Plato’s successor and Zeno’s teacher. I, 954. Polemo, Xenocrates’ immediate successor. II, 440. Polemo was the fourth after Plato to hold the school of the Academics. VII, 623. Through a discussion of the fruit of temperance, Xenocrates suddenly converted Polemo—who was not merely a drunkard but drunk at that very moment—to different morals. II, 591, 592; X, 647, 666.

Weight is the impulse of each thing, as though it were striving toward its proper place. IV, 222, 223. Weight is twofold. IV, 222, 223. The forces of weights in the elements. V, 1140. The weight of desire and the weight of charity. I, 847, 849; II, 677; VII, 342.

Ponticanus, an actor in the story of Romulus. II, 1063.

Pontius. IX, 324. A Donatist bishop. IX, 334, 528, 555. He is said to have performed miracles. IX, 428. Pontius’ false miracle. III, 1501. How Pontius pleaded with Julian. II, 399; IX, 326.

Popular tumults are to be restrained by each person according to his ability. V, 1392.

## People

A people is not every gathering of a multitude, but a gathering united by agreement in law and by a community of interests. VII, 67, 648. Where a true people is found. VII, 655. In what way the designation “people” can apply to the Romans and to other kingdoms. VII, 655. A people and a crowd differ. V, 614. Two peoples: the faithful and the unfaithful, the predestined and the rejected. III, 1507. The difference between the old and new peoples can be observed in each one of us. VI, 31. The people signified by the two goats, the two sheepfolds, the two walls, the two blind men, and the two ships. V, 43. No people except Israel was called the people of God. VII, 609. The people of God are now considered to include all who bear His sacraments, but not all belong to His mercy. IV, 538.

## Pig

The pig signifies the uncleanness of forgetful folly. IV, 1834.

## Porphyry

There were two Porphyries: one Sicilian, the other not. I, 643. Certain questions proposed by Porphyry—not the Sicilian one whose fame is most celebrated. I, 643; II, 370. Porphyry the Sicilian. III, 1052. Porphyry the Greek, a Platonic philosopher. VII, 237. The noblest of the pagan philosophers. VII, 754. Most learned. VII, 650. When he lived. VII, 313. He taught that every body must be fled from. I, 590; V, 1137. Porphyry’s books *From the Oracles of Philosophy* (*Ek logiōn philosophias*). VII, 650. His books on the return of the soul. VII, 308. Although Porphyry held erroneous views about the soul, he nevertheless corrected the opinion of the Platonists. VII, 310. He corrected many of Plato’s doctrines. VII, 309, 310. Porphyry confesses the true God, the great God. VII, 696. Porphyry’s inconsistency as he wavers between confessing the true God and worshiping demons. VII, 303, 304. Porphyry’s impiety. VII, 304, 305. Porphyry is to be blamed, also because he sacrificed to the gods. VII, 651. He says good things about Christ. VII, 651. Porphyry was first a Christian, later a deserter from and adversary of the faith. VII, 306. Note (a). A bitter enemy of Christians. VII, 650. And of the Christian faith. V, 1137. Porphyry’s calumny against Christ and Christians is refuted. VII, 653. Porphyry despised Christ because of the body He received from a woman. VII, 307, 309. He accused Christians of folly because they said that the world would perish. VII, 696. Porphyry consults the Egyptian Anebō about various matters pertaining to demons. VII, 288, 289. With what disposition he consults demons. VII, 288, 289, 290. Origen asserts that Peter did not sin and that Paul did not insolently rebuke his superior, in order to answer Porphyry’s blasphemy, according to Jerome. II, 253, 257. How Porphyry’s calumny concerning Paul’s rebuke of Peter is to be defended in the stronger manner. II, 286.

Porphyry, a bishop. X, 652, 663.

Another Porphyry, a bishop. X, 652, 663.

Porsenna, king of the Etruscans. VII, 63.

[Col. 0539] What the gates of death and the gates of the daughter of Zion are. IV, 123. The gate of God: confession. IV, 1281.

## Portents

Portents, from *portendere*, “to foretell” or “to indicate beforehand.” VII, 722. Portents seem to be contrary to nature, but are not. VII, 721.

## Portico

The five porticoes of the pool represented the five books of Moses. IV, 889, 1329; V, 689.

## Portion

In what sense God is called the portion of the pious. IV, 1545.

## Possessions

Christians are permitted to have possessions. I, 1343. Which possession of an earthly thing is legitimate by divine law and which by human law. II, 345. All possessions are held by human law. III, 1437. From what the innocence of possessing temporal things is recognized. V, 694. A litigant over an earthly possession. V, 1586. Lawsuits and many evils arise from possession of private property; these are removed when property is held in common. IV, 1748. God is our possession and we are God’s possession: how this is so. IV, 1891; V, 316. Blessed is the nation whose possession He is; blessed is the inheritance whose possessor He is. IV, 295.

## Possessor

Who should be called the possessor of something. V, 327. Who is a possessor in good faith. VI, 203. What is possessed badly is another’s; and the person who uses something badly possesses it badly. II, 665. Civil law does not make those who use goods well, but makes those who use them badly less troublesome. II, 665. You wish to possess the earth: see to it that you are not possessed by the earth. V, 365. You will truly possess the earth when you have clung to the one who made heaven and earth. V, 365. How it is permissible to possess all things. V, 781. You wished to possess everything; do not seek this through avarice, but through piety and humility. V, 781. The person possessed, not possessing, who is held captive by desire for things. IV, 544. It is one thing to possess God and another to possess a human being. IV, 576.

## Possible

Something possible can happen even though it has never happened. X, 201, 204. There are certain things that can happen, although there is no example showing that they have happened. X, 241. There are also natural possibilities. X, 1489. Being able to do evil is not evidence of freedom. X, 1103.

## Possibility

Pelagius called the possibility which nature received when it was created, together with free will, grace. X, 333. The possibility of not sinning in the state of unimpaired nature could in some manner be admitted, but was not inseparable from nature. X, 275, 276. Pelagius wrongly defends this possibility. X, 275. Pelagius confesses that possibility was given by the Creator, but wants the will and action to come from man. X, 362, 373. He argues that only possibility, not will or action, needs assistance. X, 381. Pelagius attributes grace to possibility, but not to action. X, 272, 273. In what sense Pelagius attributed the possibility of not sinning to God’s grace. X, 275. What grace of God is being discussed when the possibility of not sinning is at issue. X, 277. Possibility does not relieve the misery that oppresses man. X, 1497. Natural possibility was corrupted by the sin of the first man, according to Ambrose. X, 385. If natural possibility through free will is sufficient, Christ died for nothing. X, 270. And the faithful pray in vain, “Do not lead us into temptation.” X, 277. Pelagius said that the ability to do good belongs to God; but why did he not want to say that what we do belongs both to us and to Him? X, 369. From where man is able and from where he is unable. X, 271. “What I can do, I see; from where I can do it, I do not see—except that I also know that this too is from God.” V, 905. In the saints, possibility comes together with its effect. X, 271. The possibility of human perfection lies in God’s grace. X, 1279.

## Possidius

Possidius, bishop of Calama. II, 397; VII, 766. A Catholic bishop. IX, 523, 697. For what sad reason he is traveling to Paulinus. II, 352. Note (a). Possidius’ journey seems to inspire Nectarius with an idle fear. II, 388. The ferocity of Crispin, the Donatist bishop, toward Possidius, and Possidius’ gentleness toward Crispin. II, 397; IX, 523. Possidius was nourished by Augustine with the Lord’s bread. II, 368.

## Posidonius

Posidonius the Stoic, greatly devoted to astrology. VII, 142, 145.

Later things: do not look back upon them out of desire, like Lot’s wife; rather, look back upon them out of contempt. IV, 392.

Posthumianus, bishop. II, 759, 781.

Posthumius, a haruspex. VII, 72.

The powerful who in this age wish to thunder against the servants of God will be struck by lightning in the next. IV, 1158. The friendship of the powerful, when it harms salvation, must be despised. V, 537.

Free power was given to human beings by God. I, 1241. That is in our power which we do when we wish. I, 620, 1274. That which follows our will. I, 620. Because the will is in our power, it is free for us. I, 1274. Nothing is so much in our power as the will itself: how this is so. VIII, 129, 130. Power is spoken of when the ability to act accompanies the will. X, 234. For something to be done by power, the will must be present. X, 234. Each person is said to have in his power whatever he does if he wishes and does not do if he does not wish. X, 235. Any good action is in our power. I, 619, 620. And in what sense. I, 599, 619, 620, 629. What we perform is in our power. IV, 1831. Power was given to us against lust. V, 719. The power to live well is attributed not to free choice but to the grace of God [Col. 0540]. X, 1110. No saint rejoices in his own power, but in the power of the one from whom he has whatever capacity he possesses in due measure. VIII, 957. Power becomes complete through love. I, 599. How the one who does good merits praise by his power. V, 1389. God did not deny free will to his rational creature; nevertheless, he retained for himself the power by which he justly orders even the unjust. III, 2129. It belongs to God’s power to condemn the wicked. IV, 743.

Power exists only from God. VI, 131, 137; X, 235. Even the power to do harm comes only from God. VIII, 561. Why the power to harm is given to the devil and to the wicked. IV, 743, 744. The devil’s power in the lower realms is not the power of one who is angry, but the punishment of one who has been condemned. IV, 201. When God is pleased with you, demons can do nothing to you; when he is angry, they do whatever they wish. IV, 209. All the power of rulers and laws is from God. VI, 76. The power of kings ought to become the servant of God’s majesty, in order to extend his worship. VII, 170, 171. It is more powerful to be joined to the Almighty by a devout will than, by one’s own power and will, to be able to do what those who cannot do such things tremble at. VIII, 957. When power is given, necessity is not imposed. X, 235. The power to accomplish what an evil will intends comes from God’s judgment and is a punishment. X, 235. It is one thing to wish to use unjust power justly, and another to use just power unjustly. VI, 385. Rulers are permitted to persecute the wicked. II, 299. Why power is often given to worse people over better ones. VIII, 561, 586. Why the weaker are oppressed by the more powerful. IV, 1646. God grants the wicked power over the good, in order to judge the wicked and discipline the good. IV, 291. As an angry father strikes his son with a rod that will soon be thrown into the fire, so God exercises the discipline of those who are to be liberated through the temporal power of those who are to be condemned. IV, 935. When the terror of temporal powers attacks the truth, it is a glorious test for the strong among the just, but a dangerous temptation for the weak; when it proclaims the truth, it is a useful admonition for the discerning who have gone astray, but a useless affliction for the senseless. II, 331. Whether a power favoring the truth corrects someone, or a power hostile to the truth rages against someone, the person who is corrected by the former has reason to praise it, and the person who is crowned victorious over the latter has reason to praise it. II, 331. Honor and obedience are owed even to unjust authorities. IV, 1653, 1654. To what extent it is necessary to submit to earthly authorities. III, 2083, 2084. Observance toward authorities should be properly ordered. V, 418, 420. The powers of this age are signified by mountains. IV, 519. Power signified by the hand. IV, 1956.

Potina, a goddess. VII, 122.

Precentor and succentor. IV, 1109.

Commandment. The Manichaeans were accustomed to blame God because he gave the human being a commandment in paradise. VIII, 208. God did not command anything impossible to the human being. X, 155. A prohibiting commandment was necessary for the human being, so that the very virtue by which he might win the favor of his Lord would be obedience. III, 377, 379, 384. From contempt of the divine commandment came the experience of evil. III, 384. Some commandments are given to the healthy, others to the sick. V, 1269. The commandments of God, which were given to the healthy as very sweet, the human being made very burdensome for himself. V, 543. When the divine commandment thunders, one must obey, not argue. VII, 510.

The commandments of the Decalogue are hostile to the Manichaeans. VIII, 307, 309, 310, 311. Of the commandments of the Decalogue, three concern God and seven the human being. III, 620, 621. The three commandments of the Decalogue concerning God are fitted to the Trinity. V, 208. The other seven commandments concern human beings. V, 80, 209. The commandments of the Decalogue, except for the Sabbath alone, are to be observed literally and not figuratively. II, 214. The two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor are mutually connected. VI, 207, 210. The commandments for living well are contained in one brief and clear commandment of love, so that no one may have an excuse on the day of judgment. VI, 669, 670. All the divine commandments are to be referred to two. X, 296. The commandment concerning love of God and neighbor is not to be compared with the philosophers’ writings or the laws of cities. II, 524. Both commandments of love are fulfilled with respect to Christ. V, 1206. The gods never gave their worshipers commandments for ordering their lives. VII, 49, 51. “You shall not covet” is a general prohibition; “You shall love” is a general injunction. X, 296, 297. The commandment concerning honoring parents is called the first when reckoned with reference to the second tablet. V, 209. The ten commandments are compared with the ten plagues. V, 67. Some things are commanded generally to all, others to each particular class of persons. III, 75. One must observe at what time something is commanded or permitted. III, 75.

For what purpose commandments are given. X, 918. The usefulness of commandments. II, 739. God commands nothing for his own benefit, but for the benefit of the one to whom he commands it. II, 527. By commanding, God makes useful whatever he wishes to command. III, 384. The commandments of God are very good. X, 288. The great usefulness of commandments, provided free choice is granted only so far that the grace of God may be honored more greatly. II, 739. The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, etc. III, 36. Why God commands what he knows will not be observed. X, 165. And what we cannot fulfill without him. II, 677; VI, 443, 444. God commands nothing impossible. X, 152. God would not command us to do what he judged impossible for a human being to do [Col. 0541]. IV, 661. See Law. God commands some things that we cannot do, so that we may learn what we ought to ask of him. X, 900. God does not command impossibilities; rather, by commanding he admonishes us both to do what we can and to ask for what we cannot do. X, 271. By the commandment we are admonished to do what we attempt but cannot accomplish by our own strength, and therefore to pray for divine assistance. X, 254. A human being can fulfill God’s commandments if he wishes. III, 176. No one fulfills the commandments unless aided by grace. V, 1160, 1162. What is commanded through the letter is fulfilled not by the letter but by the Spirit. VIII, 644. The commandment “You shall not covet” was given so that you would know your enemy, not so that you would conquer him. V, 794. Free choice, without the help of God’s grace, is not sufficient to fulfill the Lord’s commandments. II, 675, 676, 677. Anathema on anyone who thinks otherwise. II, 762. The commandments were given so that there might be no excuse based on ignorance. X, 883. The commandment is an argument for free choice; prayer is an argument for grace. X, 303, 882, 883. The things that must be done would not be commanded unless our will were thereby to be revealed; nor would they be requested unless the weakness of our will were to be assisted by the one who had commanded. II, 775. Nothing is found in Scripture to have been commanded to a human being by the Lord merely to prove free choice that is not also found either to be given from his goodness or to be given in order to demonstrate the help of grace. X, 588. By the commandment free choice is admonished to seek God’s gift. X, 903, 904. This commandment is given to us: either to do what is already in our power, or to pray that power be granted to us. VIII, 776. God commands these things because they can be done; but he himself gave the ability to do them to those who can and do them, while by commanding he warns those who cannot to ask him for the ability. X, 1297. To fulfill what is commanded us, assistance must be requested from the one who commands. II, 682; X, 1280. The commandments are not fulfilled except by the one who gives them. VI, 421. The force of the commandments does not bring about their fulfillment; grace does. V, 199. God himself gives strength so that what he commands may be fulfilled. V, 200. God must give a human being what he commands him. X, 154. God himself causes human beings to do what he commands. X, 975. The commandments cannot be kept without grace. X, 886, 887. When one hears the commandment of the Law, “You shall not covet,” one has heard one’s punishment if grace is absent. V, 792. By saying “You shall not covet,” the Law established not what we are able to achieve here, but what we are to strive toward by making progress. II, 893. Whoever thinks that he fulfills the commandments of the Law by the choice of his own will, without the Spirit of grace, wishes to establish his own righteousness rather than receive the righteousness of God. X, 1209.

For whom the divine commandments are burdensome. X, 302. What one for whom the divine commandments are burdensome ought to do. X, 289. What he commands is neither harsh nor burdensome when he helps so that what he commands may be done. V, 584. Whatever is harsh in the commandments is made light by love. V, 584. Why Scripture declares that God’s commandments are not burdensome. X, 303. The commandments are made easy only by love. III, 633, 634. God commands nothing impossible, because all things are easy for love. X, 289. No one truly obeys God’s commandments except through love. X, 1296. Whoever keeps God’s commandments out of fear, not love, does not keep them. X, 593. See Fear.

The Jews were given lesser commandments, Christians greater ones: why this is so. III, 1231. Why the commandments are lesser in the Law and greater in the Gospel. III, 136. Most of the commandments of the Old and New Testaments are the same. IV, 930, 931. The Lord commanded difficult things but promised great things. V, 120. Eternal reward was promised to those who observe the commandments of the New Testament. X, 222, 223. God arouses people to observe them. I, 956. Christ commanded that the commandments be observed in order to attain eternal life. VI, 210. In what sense Pelagius and Coelestius said that we do more than was commanded in the Law and the Gospel. X, 337, 357. How this was approved by the bishops. X, 337.

Observance of the commandments is a sign of remaining in Christ’s love. III, 1843, 1844. Christ’s commandments are to be carried out not by bodily display but by the mind’s readiness. III, 1935. There are certain commandments that spiritual people grasp but carnal people do not. IV, 492. The commandments are not fulfilled merely by external action. III, 772, 773. To fulfill the commandments, the will is sufficient where external action cannot be performed. III, 773. The divine commandments are to be understood from the deeds of the saints. VI, 506. The commandments of God are guarded in vain by memory if they are not also guarded in life. IV, 1511. To meditate on and practice the divine commandments is our daily bread. III, 1280. God’s commandments are our paths. IV, 1808. By the commandment “You shall not covet,” we are ordered to subtract from the weight of desire whatever is added to the weight of love. II, 677. It does not profit one to fulfill God’s commandments where true faith is absent. VIII, 223. The commandments of conduct cannot be kept and observed without faith. VI, 210. The divine commandment must always conquer the human affection within us. VIII, 629. Few attain the commandments of life: through reason each person becomes capable of the commandment; through wisdom, an observer of it. I, 1306. The Pelagians’ calumny concerning the fulfillment of the commandments in the future life. X, 600. The commandment not to covet cannot be fulfilled here. V, 816. When the commandments are fulfilled as they ought to be fulfilled. X, 918. God’s commandment sung from door to door by beggars. V, 205. It is one thing to command virtue and another to permit weakness. V, 346. Whatever is permitted by the Lord is also lawful to do; whatever is commanded is sin if it is not done. VIII, 165. The difference between the Lord’s commandment and his counsel. VI, 402. God’s commandments and counsels change according to circumstances, not because of inconsistency in the one who commands, but because of the reason governing his dispensation. VIII, 450. People should be urged toward the counsels in such a way that a life brought into conformity with the rule of the commandments is not condemned. II, 691, 692. A commandment is sometimes disregarded when a more important duty carries one away. VI, 512.

You were prey to a lesser one; you will be prey to a greater one. IV, 1646.

What it means to predestine. X, 1018, 1019.

Predestination. VII, 435, 466; X, 945, 1002. What predestination is. X, 1014. Predestination is sometimes signified by the term foreknowledge. X, 1022, 1023. Predestination and foreknowledge are the same. X, 1023. We were predestined before we existed. V, 862, 864. The human being was not predestined on the sixth day, but before the ages, in the Creator’s foreknowledge. III, 347. How predestination and grace differ. X, 975. We were predestined gratuitously. V, 863. The grace of predestination. II, 768. Predestination comes not from human merit but from God’s grace. VIII, 614. Not from works. II, 639. The Antichrist is new, and he most openly contradicts the one in whom Christ spoke, who says that election comes from works, not from grace. X, 1132. The promise made to Abraham concerning the faith of the nations in his seed was made concerning God’s predestination, not concerning the power of our will. X, 975. Predestination does not arise from foreseen good works. II, 887; X, 792. Our predestination was not made in us, but secretly with God, in his foreknowledge. IV, 1962. Jacob was not elected for his own merits; he was first foreknown and first predestined. IV, 1744. Christ cannot be denied to have been predestined. III, 1907. See Christ. Christ Jesus is the most illustrious example of predestination. X, 981, 982, 1033. The predestination of Christ and his members does not arise from foreseen merits. X, 983. All the predestined are saved through one Mediator and through one and the same faith. X, 179.

Predestination is certain. X, 1015. The immovable truth of predestination. X, 985. Predestination is eternal and immovable. III, 1814, 1845, 1921. Hence Christ’s joy concerning us from eternity. III, 1844, 1845. The one who predestined all future things by certain and unchangeable causes has already done whatever he will do. III, 1905, 1906, 1908. None of the predestined perishes. VII, 614; X, 792, 929, 930, 941. Not one of those for whom Christ died perishes. II, 744. God erases none of those whom he wrote in the book of life. IV, 862. No one can harm the predestined. V, 862. The devil leads none of the predestined into eternal damnation. VII, 669. The wolf, thief, and robber do not destroy anyone except those predestined to destruction. III, 1743. The predestined sometimes err and are outside. III, 1725. But if they are predestined, they err for a time and do not perish forever. III, 1725. The kingdom of death is not in those who, reborn by Christ’s grace, belong to his kingdom. II, 683. The Lord, the founder of Jerusalem, knows which people he has predestined as its citizens and which he sees still to be redeemed from the devil’s dominion by Christ’s blood. IV, 774. None of the predestined will perish with the devil; none will remain under the devil’s power until death. VIII, 1030. If some of the predestined go astray and deviate, God causes even this to advance toward the good. X, 930. The predestined are not abandoned to perish through their own desire, but only the reprobate are. X, 324. Those who fall and perish were not among the predestined. X, 938.

The number of the predestined is fixed. I, 605; II, 825; X, 940. The number of the predestined is great. VIII, 614. How the predestined are both few and many. IX, 537, 582. In comparison with those who perish, those who are saved are few; without comparison with those who perish, they too are many. X, 1200, 1229, 1230, 1231. But why some are more numerous than others: many wish to know God’s purpose, but either very few human beings or none at all can know it. X, 1200. The number of the predestined is completed in two ways. I, 1288. That the predestination of infants to baptism can be impeded: Victor’s error. X, 517. God’s mercy accompanies the predestined in whatever condition they may be. X, 941. Those whom God predestined he calls to repentance. IV, 1932. He crowns as worthy the one whom, in mercy, he saw fit to call while unworthy. V, 442.

Predestination lies in the depth of divinity. X, 1064. The causes of predestination are inscrutable. II, 886. God’s hidden judgments in the predestination of human beings. VI, 275. And inscrutable. X, 126, 1007. From the same mass some are liberated by God’s grace, while others are not liberated by God’s judgment. X, 1136, 1140. Why miracles were not performed for the Tyrians and Sidonians who would have believed, though they were performed for others who would not believe, except by the inscrutable judgment of predestination? X, 1005, 1006. It did not benefit the Tyrians to be able to believe, because they were not predestined; it would not have harmed the Jews not to be able to believe, if they had been predestined. X, 1014. Why some belong to predestination and others do not: there may be a hidden cause, but it cannot be an unjust one [Col. 0543]. II, 639, 883. Why one believes and another does not, although both hear the same thing: this is the depth of God’s judgments. II, 879. Why God liberates this person rather than that one: let whoever can search it out, but beware of the precipice. II, 883. Why God makes some sheep and does not make others: an inscrutable question. X, 620, 621. If it were resolved according to the merits of wills, it would be evident. X, 1128. In order to show for what merit nature was condemned, not even the Almighty himself readily wills to liberate from so great an evil. X, 1200. In those who are liberated, and not only in them but also in those who are not liberated, God shows what he bestows. VII, 435. If the definition of predestination does not obstruct exhortations to wisdom and to the other gifts of God that opponents acknowledge, it ought not to obstruct exhortation to faith and perseverance. X, 1019. The Massilians themselves exhort people to those things that they acknowledge with us to be gifts of God, such as chastity. X, 1021. The testimonies of Cyprian and Ambrose show both that grace is gratuitous and that exhortations are nevertheless not thereby obstructed. X, 1023. What position the Pelagians and what position the Semi-Pelagians hold concerning predestination. X, 988.

Who the predestined are is hidden. VII, 668, 669. No one is certain and secure concerning his own salvation and predestination. X, 940. No one can assert anything certain to another concerning that person’s predestination. X, 1012. Through predestination and foreknowledge, only the one who was able to predestine and foreknow knows the sheep and the goats. V, 304. Predestination must be hidden in this life. X, 940. When security concerning predestination exists. X, 941.

The predestination defended by Augustine, and how certain it is. X, 1023. No one can argue against it except by falling into error. X, 1023. The faith concerning this predestination, which is now defended against the new heretics, is a faith that the Church of Christ has never lacked. X, 1031, 1033. Why Augustine defended predestination so vigorously. X, 1026, 1027. The objections raised against predestination can also be raised against foreknowledge. X, 1019, 1126. To contradict predestination or to doubt concerning predestination is excessive contentiousness. X, 1028. Predestination, preached through the Apostles and defended by Augustine against the new heretics, does not abolish obedience. X, 1025. It does not prohibit the preaching of faith and obedience. X, 1015. The doctrine of predestination is not opposed to the usefulness of preaching. X, 1013, 1014, 1015, 1025.

Predestination is to be preached. X, 1025. How it is to be preached. X, 1018. And when. X, 1017. The method of preaching predestination can be objectionable and inept. X, 1016. How predestination is to be preached without causing offense. X, 1028, 1029, 1030, 1033. A formula for preaching predestination that is offensive and to be avoided. X, 1030. When predestination is preached as it ought to be, it is not a cause of despair. X, 1031. It brings no more despair than exhortation. X, 1022. The preaching of predestination does not obstruct exhortation to grace. X, 1021. The predestined person is not merely prevented by the preaching of predestination from engaging in the work of salvation; rather, he is helped toward it. X, 1019. What opponents bring forward against preaching predestination can equally be said against the grace of God, from which they admit that the other gifts, except faith and perseverance, come. X, 1018. Opponents cannot deny that predestination belongs to those gifts of grace that they themselves acknowledge, while nevertheless their exhortations are not obstructed by this predestination. X, 1019. Just as the person whom God foreknew would be chaste, although he is uncertain of this, acts in order to be chaste, so the person whom God predestined to be chaste, although he is uncertain of this, does not for that reason fail to act in order to be chaste, since he hears that by God’s gift he will become what he hears. X, 1019. The definition of predestination does not prevent the correction of the unchaste and contentious; likewise, it does not prevent the correction of unbelievers and of those who do not persevere in faith. X, 1020.

Predestination to eternal life and to eternal death. X, 533. The human race that has been predestined to destruction. X, 308. By a sufficiently hidden but nevertheless just disposition, God predestined some to the ultimate punishments. II, 939. Those predestined to damnation and eternal destruction. III, 1742, 1743, 1914, 1920, 1921, 1929. To eternal fire. VII, 692, 792. Predestination to punishment arises from justice; predestination to grace from God’s goodness. VI, 279. Those foreknown to be damned could be taken from this life after baptism, before they sinned. X, 1505. Those beloved according to election are predestined. II, 638. The predestined are Christ’s sheep. III, 1725. Those who were not given to Christ are those to whom he will not give eternal life, although power over them too was given to him. III, 1925. Christ’s good works benefited only those predestined to eternal salvation. IV, 1115. The predestined from the Jews. X, 984. How Christ draws to himself those predestined to salvation. III, 1773.

The preaching of the divine word is to be received with fear. III, 1790, 1791. Nevertheless, when necessary, it is not to be omitted for the sake of holy leisure. III, 1791. Nor through fear of sinning. III, 1792. For the sake of preaching Christ, holy leisure must sometimes be abandoned [Col. 0544]. III, 1791, 1792. Nor are slight sins to be feared. III, 1792. If your preaching is supported by truth, let your teaching be public. VI, 683. To preach from the housetop. V, 1427. How true preaching can be distinguished from false preaching. VI, 682, 685, 686. Preaching belongs to spiritual people; compliance belongs to carnal people. IV, 1748. Who listen obediently to the preaching of truth. X, 1016. Preaching without grace working inwardly is of no benefit. VII, 442. The preacher’s labor is fruitless if there is no one within who works. V, 820, 825. Whoever neither fears nor is moved when he hears preaching is not worthy to be healed. IV, 716. Preaching and predestination do not obstruct one another. X, 1015. Preaching of God outside the Church is fruitless. IV, 929. There are still nations at the ends of the earth, although, as is reported, very few, to whom the Gospel has not yet been preached. X, 248, 249. The external preacher of God’s word is fruitless if he is not an inward hearer. V, 966. If you wish to be heard, hear yourself first. IV, 580. Preachers utter words; God gives understanding of the words. III, 1688. Preachers whose mouth gapes open while their heart does not are represented by Zilpah. VIII, 435. The preacher builds in human hearts an unconquered camp against the devil. V, 1539. Preachers raise up offspring for their dead brother, that is, for Christ. VIII, 502. The preacher’s profit is the good life of his hearers. V, 580. The preacher should seek the hearers’ ears for himself, and their hearts for God. V, 1149. Unless the minister who preaches is burning, he does not set on fire the one to whom he preaches. IV, 1353. It is difficult for a preacher not to give a slanderer an opportunity, either by sinning in his words or by teaching higher things. IV, 414. Nevertheless, the office of preaching is not for that reason to be abandoned. IV, 416.

The preachers of God’s word: where they find consolation when they are called deceivers. III, 1628. Preachers are commanded to bring peace. V, 610. If they choose not to tell others, they will not deserve to hear from God. IV, 416. Care must be taken lest something correctly said but incorrectly understood disturb a reader or hearer. IV, 1504. When reproving women, preachers should take account of their modesty. V, 205. Certain preachers do not announce the truth chastely or from the truth. IV, 139, 1491. A good reputation is necessary for a preacher. VIII, 436. Preachers whose faith and teaching are correct, even if their life is bad, are to be heard. IV, 395, 580. How preachers who seek their own interests are to be heard. V, 473, 610, 761. The sound teaching of a preacher who lives badly is like a grape hanging among thorns, yet growing from a vine. V, 283. “A good man preaches to you: pluck the grape from the vine. A bad man preaches to you: pluck the grape hanging on the hedge.” V, 610. One must not cease from persistent preaching. IX, 449, 450, 451, 452. Even if people will not assent but will contradict. IX, 449, 450, 451, 452. Whether the preacher of righteousness is received, rejected, or even suffers any temporal adversity, he will not be deprived before God of the reward of his office. IX, 449. If preachers accomplish anything, it must be attributed not to their strength but to God’s grace. IV, 817, 819, 1118, 1650, etc., 1668. The preacher asks those being baptized for prayers on his behalf, as though this were his payment. VI, 685, 692, 693, 699. For the preacher, the hearers’ expectation is a prayer. V, 333, 989. Prayer after the sermon. V, 213, 1633. Preachers pass from this life into another, but Holy Scripture remains. I, 852.

Preaching the word of God from a higher place. V, 580, 761. Preachers stand in a higher place for convenience, but from that very higher place the hearers judge them. V, 155. In preaching itself, preachers converse, explaining what they understand to those who do not yet understand. V, 158. During a sermon Augustine takes up a codex of Scripture and reads from it. II, 116. Carrying Scripture in his hands, Augustine speaks to the people. V, 221. At Siniti, where a Donatist bishop presided, a presbyter was sent to preach in a house under his jurisdiction. II, 397.

The ministry of preaching is dangerous. V, 155, 966. The danger facing preachers is that they may become proud. III, 1790. Truth is heard more safely than it is preached. III, 1790; V, 966, 970. When preachers are criticized, they are disturbed; when praised, they are puffed up. III, 1792. How preachers ought to respond to human praise, following Augustine’s example. V, 414, 1480. How they can rejoice in the benefits given to them. I, 860, 861. Augustine does not love the praiser, but rather despises in his heart the things he says. V, 513. The one who seeks his own interests does not perform the preacher’s work; rather, that work is performed through him. V, 610. The commandments established for preachers concerning not carrying a purse, etc., are not to be understood carnally. V, 608. What is necessary is owed to them, and how. I, 862. The needs of preachers must be relieved. IV, 1366, 1367, etc., 1368, etc. Preachers give gold and receive hay. IV, 1365. Preachers must not appear to proclaim the Gospel out of the necessity of their poverty. V, 272. Let them receive support for their necessities from the people and the reward for their administration from the Lord. V, 273. Let them expect a reward only from the source from which these people receive salvation. V, 273.

Preachers of God’s word are called the abyss. IV, 473. Angels ascending and descending. III, 1449. Dogs. IV [Col. 0545], 833. The teeth of the Church. IV, 1224. Beasts of burden and servants. IV, 1366. The tongue of Christ. II, 158, 553. Physicians. IV, 1118. They are physicians who care for the man wounded by robbers, but the Lord brought him to the inn. IV, 1118. They are called mountains. IV, 347, 781, 782, 1650. Eternal mountains, great mountains. IV, 961. Clouds. I, 852; IV, 347, 520, 672, 715, 980, 981, 1749. Clouds and heavens. IV, 1123, 1234, 1242. Clouds and winds together. IV, 1749. The nurses of the Church. IV, 241, 242. The feet of the Lord. V, 602. Preachers are represented by the pelican, the night-raven, and the sparrow. IV, 1298, 1299. Preachers are called ambassadors of reconciliation. IV, 837.

How predictions come about. VII, 315. Predictions that are not referred to the worship of the one God are the devil’s mockeries. VII, 291. Predictions whose fulfillment is seen in the Church. VI, 346. The certainty of God’s predictions and promises is demonstrated by those things that are already seen to have been fulfilled. V, 151, 241, 640, 862. How “to predict” and “to promise” differ in God. II, 556. Christ’s prediction does not excuse Peter for his denial, nor Judas for his betrayal. IV, 1831.

Voluntary precipitate self-destruction, characteristic of the Donatists. IX, 526. This was unheard-of in Roman laws. IX, 526.

To prefer. Who should be preferred when something cannot be given to two or more people. III, 30.

What the soul of a pregnant woman can do to the fetus. VII, 374. Pregnant women in the Gospel are souls who possess hope in this world. IV, 1235.

Praejectus, a bishop. VII, 766.

The prejudice of human presumption. IX, 567.

Let those placed over others strive to preside not in order to rule but in order to benefit. VIII, 436. The temptations and dangers of those placed over others. IV, 1422. A good superior is your nourisher; a bad one is your tempter. V, 420. Whether good or bad, a superior cannot harm the devout. V, 420.

The food of those who fight is the bread of angels. IV, 1863.

God sets a reward before us so that we may do what he commands by loving the good more than by fearing the evil. V, 123. God bestows good rewards from his own gifts. IV, 1517. There will be different degrees of rewards in heaven. VII, 802. Rewards corresponding to individual works in the sentences of blessedness. V, 367. God himself is the reward promised to us. IV, 928; V, 136, 491, 905, 1461.

God prepares the will. III, 2061, 2062, *Retr.* How preparing the heart belongs to the human being. X, 585.

The first place should be accorded to the superior, but he should not desire it. V, 569. Superiors should preside over the brothers in such a way that they remember they are their servants. IX, 94. In exercising authority, superiors should care not for themselves but for those subject to them. V, 271. Superiors are Christians for their own sake; superiors exist for the sake of others. V, 270. The duty of admonition is imposed on superiors. V, 124. Bad superiors are not to be imitated; an elegant comparison concerning this. V, 1547. The bad examples of superiors. V, 274. How bad superiors speak good things and are to be heard by their subjects. V, 473.

The foreskin of the flesh signifies sin. X, 686, 834.

Foreknowledge is knowledge of future things. VI, 138. As memory relates to past things, so foreknowledge relates to future things. I, 1276. Whether foreknowledge properly exists in God. VI, 138. Cicero denies God’s foreknowledge. VII, 148, 149. Those who establish astral fates are more tolerable than those who deny God’s foreknowledge. VII, 149. Whoever denies God’s foreknowledge denies God himself. VII, 152. God’s foreknowledge cannot be denied by anyone. X, 1126. God’s foreknowledge is certain and fixed. VII, 472. There is no foreknowledge unless it foreknows with certainty. I, 1276.

God’s foreknowledge cannot be deceived. III, 350, 351. Those things that God foreknew are truly future. III, 350. God foreknew sinners even in their mothers’ wombs. IV, 655. God is good in creating the creature, both the one whom he foreknew would sin and the one whom he foreknew would not sin. I, 1278. Believers and unbelievers belong differently to God’s foreknowledge. II, 878. The one whom God foreknew would sin must sin, although he is not compelled to sin. I, 1276, 1279. A human being does not sin because God foreknew that this would happen. VII, 153. God’s foreknowledge is not the cause of sins. X, 478. It does not compel anyone to sin. III, 1776. Just as God rightly punishes those whom he foresaw would sin, so he justly rewards those whom he foresaw would act rightly. I, 1277. God’s foreknowledge does not cause us to sin without free will. I, 1274. Nor does it cause us to do something else. I, 1275. It does not harm the creature’s freedom. I, 1275; VII, 149, 152, 153. Even though this harmony between foreknowledge and freedom torments many people. I, 1273. Laws, reproaches, prayers, exhortations, etc., are not pointless because there is foreknowledge. VII, 153.

Foreknowledge without predestination; predestination not without foreknowledge. X, 975. God’s foreknowledge is to be preached, even if some abuse this doctrine. X, 1016. The same objections can be brought against preaching foreknowledge as against preaching predestination. X, 1016. The number of the saints is certain and fixed for God. II, 825. We do not have foreknowledge of what sort our friends will be, or of what sort we ourselves will be. II, 248. Whether this exists in the holy angels. II, 248.

What the present is. IV, 418, etc. Things are called present because they are before the senses. VII, 318. Things that never stand still ought not to be called present. V, 621. Why present-minded people are so called. II, 1091. God is present everywhere and is wholly everywhere. IV, 1274. God is contained in no place; he is wholly everywhere in himself. II, 837. Why he is said to be wholly everywhere in himself. II, 838. “Everywhere I find you: if you are angry, as an avenger; if you are appeased, as a helper.” IV, 235. God’s presence is not to be judged by the senses. II, 848. God is wholly everywhere, yet he does not dwell in everyone. II, 837, 846. How God is absent from some people. IV, 1273, 1274. Who are said to be near or far from God. II, 838. Even in those in whom he dwells, God dwells unequally. II, 838, 847. To the one in whom he dwells he is wholly present, although that person does not contain him wholly. II, 839. It generally happens that several contain him less, while one contains him more. II, 839. God is the inhabitant of some who do not yet know him, but is not the inhabitant of some who do know him. II, 840. He also dwells in many who, as carnal people, still need milk. II, 844. The presence of majesty walks within us if it finds the breadth of love. V, 889. We shall have God more present to us the purer the love by which we move toward him. II, 672. Since you cannot flee from God’s presence, flee not from him but toward him. V, 442. God is said especially to dwell in the heavens because there he is perfectly obeyed. II, 848. A book concerning the presence of God. II, 832. The threefold presence of Christ. V, 1602.

Present life. V, 654.

Governorship, that is, the office of a governor. I, 729. What the Council of Arles decreed concerning governors. IX, App. 787.

God’s protection. V, 1468.

What Praestantius relates about the fantastic transformation of his father. VII, 575.

Why the prestidigitator is praised, and why he is blamed. III, 164.

Two kinds of presumption that one must avoid. IV, 257, 258. Do not presume to sin on the basis of God’s mercy. IV, 258. A person ought to presume upon God, not upon himself. IV, 457, 532. One must not presume upon oneself. X, 931. Presumption upon oneself is a person’s war against God. IV, 523. How that war is removed. IV, 523. One must not presume upon one’s own strength. II, 676, 677, 678; V, 200, 829, 855, 1294. If you presume upon your own strength, you will fall through that very thing on which you presumed. IV, 333. Many failed under torture; and I believe that those failed who presumed upon themselves. IV, 1155. Whoever presumes upon his own strength is struck down before he fights. V, 831. One who presumes upon his own strength while possessing knowledge of the law is hard pressed. V, 794. Peter’s presumption. IV, 448. Do not presume upon your justice in seeking the kingdom; do not presume to sin on the basis of God’s mercy. IV, 258. It is presumption if you think that you are a human being from God, but righteous from yourself. V, 107. The presumption of the human race in friends, in its own virtue, and in riches. IV, 548. One must presume upon no human being. IV, 1607, 1610. One must not presume upon glory and honor. IV, 925.

The past used for the future among the Prophets. IV, 1354, 1477, 1478. Why Scripture uses verbs of the past tense for the future tense. X, 930.

The praetexta, the toga worn by magistrates and boys. VII, 122.

Bishop Pretextatus. II, 759, 781.

Pretextatus, bishop of Assuras. IV, 376, 380; IX, 108, 180, 507, 528, 530. A Maximianist. IX, 137, 371. He passed from the party of Donatus to the Maximianists. IX, 549. Titianus brings a charge against Pretextatus. IX, 574. The charge against Pretextatus that he should be excluded from the places of Assuras. IX, 529. How long this conflict lasted. IX, 531. The Council of Vaga accuses Pretextatus of Assuras and Felicianus of Musti of cruelty. II, 414. Pretextatus was condemned at the Council of Bagai together with Maximianus. IX, 251. And together with Felicianus of Musti. II, 192, 198, 265, 309. Condemned by three hundred and ten bishops, he returned to his own condemners out of zeal for concord and was received by them without any loss of honor. IX, 39. And with his full honor intact, under compulsion from Optatus Gildonianus. II, 192, 198, 265, 309; IX, 426, 704, 740. Together with those whom he had baptized in the schism. IX, 504. Pretextatus was forcibly brought back to the party of Donatus by Optatus. IX, 251, 252, 565, 581. He died in the communion of Donatus. IX, 426. Although condemned, Pretextatus was again received by the Donatists as though unimpaired, as if for the sake of peace. IX, 54. Pretextatus was one of the twelve who were accused before three or more proconsuls so that they might be expelled from their sees. II, 407. Pretextatus of Assuras is said to have recently died. II, 408. Another had already been ordained in his place. II, 408. After the accusation had been publicized even by forensic tumult before so many consuls, he was received with his honors intact. II, 408.

The praetorian price. I, 728.

Who is to be regarded as a prevaricator. III, 2115; IV, 1287, 1572. You ought to hate prevaricators, not human beings. IV, 1287 [Col. 0547]. See Sinner. Little children too are prevaricators. IV, 1574.

God anticipates you in everything; anticipate his anger in at least something. V, 952.

Who is perverse in heart. IV, 1903.

Praxeas, from whom the Praxeans derive their name. See Sabellians.

What *precari*, *imprecari*, and *deprecari* properly mean. II, 635. *Preces* [prayers] are used in seeking good things; *deprecationes* [entreaties] in avoiding evils. II, 635. Prayer after a sermon. V, 213, 1633.

What prayers are useful for. VII, 153. What should be requested from God in our prayers. IV, 344; V, 247. After the judgment there is no place for prayers or merits. VI, 47. The prayers of the saints are always heard for salvation, but not always according to their will. III, 2023, 2024. It is a rule of forensic law that, if someone has lied in his petitions, what he obtained should not benefit him. III, 1443. Let him be deprived of the benefit, lose his case, and find punishment. V, 654. Prayers dictated by a heavenly jurist. V, 654. How, by not granting prayers, we often benefit people. II, 391, 395. Secular writings praise the ruler of his homeland who attends more to the people’s welfare than to their will. II, 391.

The goddess Prema. VII, 188.

The winepress. V, 983.

Oppression and scandal. V, 499, 503. We must not be deterred from good works by the world’s oppressions. IV, 1606. See Tribulation.

A presbyter: a designation for an age below old age but near to it. III, 566. The Aerianists said that a presbyter should be distinguished from a bishop by no difference. VIII, 39. Presbyters in the second priesthood. IX, App. 773. The ministry of preaching the word of God entrusted to presbyters. V, 141. A presbyter and a bishop speak from a higher place. V, 761. Presbyters began to give sermons in the presence of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. II, 158. Augustine requests that some of the sermons which these presbyters began to give in the presence of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, be sent to him. II, 159. A presbyter sent to Siniti, over which a Donatist bishop presided, to visit the Catholics and preach to those willing to hear. II, 397. In Augustine’s absence, presbyters imposed ecclesiastical discipline upon certain people. V, 1021. The Council decreed that the case of presbyters should be settled by six bishops. II, 235. Provided that he appeals within a year. II, 235. Augustine removes a presbyter from office. II, 235. Presbyters from Augustine’s monastery. V, 1578. Praise of Catholic presbyters. I, 1339.

The purse containing our price was opened on the cross. V, 1353, 1454, 1473. A thing for sale is bought, subjected, or surpassed by its price. V, 662.

Priam killed at the altar. VII, 15.

The god Priapus. VII, 59, 122, 123, 140, 184. Priapus, excessively masculine. VII, 188. The newly married woman used to sit upon Priapus’s *fascinum* and shaft. VII, 188, 215. The pagans interpret Priapus as the god of fertility. III, 1059.

The chief among the people of Hippo. II, 999. Orontius. II, 999.

The provinces of Mauretania have their own primates. II, 226. The primate sends letters summoning the Council. II, 227. Those disputing about the primacy must conduct their case before all the bishops of the province. II, 227. Meanwhile they must act concordantly, without prejudice to anyone. II, 227. By judicial sentence, two bishops of the province of Caesarea are excluded from the place of primate. II, 955. The primate is of the first see of the province of Numidia. II, 493. The term has the same meaning as “elder.” II, 490, 577.

Esau was condemned not by food, but by food desired even to the point of contempt for the sacrament that he possessed in his birthright. II, 141.

Primianus, a Donatist. III, 1470; V, 901; IX, 81, 90, 113, 180. Bishop at Carthage. IX, 113, 555. Primianus belonged to the larger party of Donatus. IX, 113. The ordination and deposition of Primianus, etc. IX, 252. Primianus was deposed at the Council of Cabarsussa, and Maximianus was appointed in his place. IX, 503, 508. Felicianus condemned Primianus, and was in turn condemned by him. II, 404, 405. Primianus separated the Maximianists from his communion. IX, 96. Primianus persecuted the Donatists. IX, 275. Felicianus condemned Primianus, and afterward was condemned on Primianus’s account by the party of Donatus. II, 580. Titianus accused Felicianus and Pretextatus of the entire conspiracy against Primianus. II, 413. Felicianus and the others who conspired with him condemned Primianus. II, 412. Primianus condemned Maximianus together with his associates. II, 580; IX, 527. Nearly one hundred Donatist bishops conspiring with Maximianus dared to condemn him. II, 406; IV, 375; IX, 549. The same crimes were charged against Primianus. IV, 378, 379. Primianus was condemned twice by the Maximianists. IX, 585. Condemned by two Donatist councils, he was acquitted by a third. IX, 552. In one Council Primianus was condemned by the judges, while in another he condemned others among the judges. IV, 382. Primianus was first condemned in his absence by one hundred colleagues. V, 900. Later acquitted in person by three hundred and ten. IX, 39, 519, 584, 684, 703. For the sake of the peace of unity. IX, 39. [Col. 0548] This condemnation did not prejudice him. V, 901. Primianus was cleared by the other African bishops of his communion of the charge brought by the faction of Maximianus. II, 173. The Council of Secundus of Tigisis against the absent Caecilianus ought to have no more force than the Council of the Maximianists against the absent Primianus. II, 173. Primianus both condemned his own condemners together with the others, and again received the condemned and detested men into his own honors and accepted the baptism conferred by them. II, 757. Victorianus of Carcavianum was one of the twelve bishops who supported Maximianus against Primianus. II, 414. He was condemned by the Council of Vaga. II, 414. Primianus refused a conference with the Catholics. IX, 652.

The Primianist schismatic party of the Donatists. IX, 46. The Primianists condemned the Maximianists. IV, 382. They tied the corpses of dead dogs around Salvius’s neck, and danced with him to shameful cries and songs. IX, 106, 107.

The original nature. VII, 625.

Wine’s first fruits were offered to images. III, 2085. Our first fruits are our faith. IV, 1749. The first fruits of the Spirit. See Spirit.

What the death of the firstborn signifies figuratively. IV, 1001.

Firstborn, primitive things, first fruits. III, 732. Why the firstborn were consecrated to God. VIII, 661. The firstborn of our heart is faith. V, 72. Christ, the firstborn from the dead. III, 2077.

Primulianus, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 381.

Primus Felix of Migirpa. IX, 203.

Primus, subdeacon of the Spanish church, defected from the Church. II, 134.

Primus, a lustful and frenzied Circumcellion. II, 135.

First in some art or skill. V, 1571.

“Beginning” is taken in various senses. III, 222. The Son of God is signified by the name “Beginning.” V, 24. Whether being the Beginning belongs only to the Son of God. III, 1682. How the statement in Genesis, “In the beginning God created,” and so forth, is to be understood. I, 836. The Heracleonites assert two principles, one from the other, and from these two many others. VIII, 28. Marcus supposed that the two principles were opposed to each other. VIII, 28. The Cerdonians held this view. VIII, 29. Marcion held this view. VIII, 29. Mani. VIII, 34. Some report that, in place of the two principles admitted by Marcus, Marcion, and the Cerdonians, Mani admitted two gods, one good and the other evil. VIII, 29. The Manichaean doctrine of two principles is refuted. VIII, 395, 398, 399. The various opinions of philosophers concerning the principles of things. VII, 225, 226, 230. Anaximander believed that the principles of things were infinite. VII, 226. The Platonists knew that the principle of things is in God. VII, 231, 232. To make oneself one’s own beginning and being is perverse exaltation. VII, 420. It is falsely said that no beginning exists without an end. VIII, 605.

The gods were called “princes.” III, 627, 628. The princes of this age. V, 100. An elegant conception of a Christian prince. VII, 170. Nothing is more fortunate than to be ruled by pious princes. VII, 166. Tullius said that the prince of a state ought to be nourished by glory. VII, 158. The prince of a state ought to forget injuries. II, 529. The power of princes ought to serve God in such a way that, through it, those who do not wish to serve his will are punished. IX, 734. The harsh necessity of princes, because they are compelled to satisfy the desires of others. II, 994. The prince of a state ought to attend to the people’s welfare rather than to their will. II, 531. Two kinds of princes do not act rightly: one consists of those who harm, the other of those who do no good. VIII, 456. The severity of princes toward heretics derives from God’s mercy. IX, 106, 108. What the terror of temporal authorities accomplishes when it attacks the truth, and what it accomplishes when it preaches the truth. II, 331, 398. Christ alone could say, “The prince of this world will find nothing in me.” V, 186.

Principalis of Cirta. II, 537. Note 1.

Prisca, Montanus’s prophetess, from whom the Cataphrygians derive their name. VIII, 30.

Priscilla. VI, 305. Priscilla and Montanus, prophets of the Cataphrygians. II, 1035.

In what respect Priscillianus was more wretched than the Manichaeans. VIII, 666. Priscillianus restored the Sabellian doctrine. VIII, 671. He established the Priscillianists in Spain. VIII, 44.

The various and shameful doctrines of the Priscillianists. VIII, 44. The Priscillianists think that Christ did not possess true flesh. V, 1225. They held that the Lord himself, speaking through his own mouth, was a deceiver rather than a teacher of truth. II, 1037. The Priscillianist error concerning the soul. VI, 523; X, 516. The Stoics, Mani, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian say that souls are from God’s own substance. II, 718, 722. The Priscillianists accept everything, both canonical and apocryphal, but pervert in their interpretations whatever is against them. II, 1035. The hymn called “of the Lord,” whenever they want it to have been spoken. II, 1035. Their claim that it was therefore not placed in the canon, lest the sacrament of the king should become known to carnal people, is ridiculed at length. II, 1035. That argument of theirs is not reasoning but evasion, by which they conceal what they believe. II, 1037. Another hymn to which they attribute divine authority. II, 1037, 1038. The Priscillianists used a testimony from the Acts of the Apostles to support fasting on Sunday. II, 148. Perhaps some heretics can be found more unclean than the Priscillianists, but none can compare with them in deceit. II, 1035. The Priscillianists are devoted to lying and perjury. I, 654. Their error concerning the use of lying. VI, 240, 519. The Priscillianist precept: “Swear, perjure yourself, do not disclose the secret.” II, 1035. The Priscillianists tell stories not very different from those of the Manichaeans. II, 722. Augustine had not yet heard of them when he wrote the books On Free Choice of the Will. II, 722.

Priscus, bishop of the province of Caesarea, is excluded from the primacy. II, 955.

Whoever aspires to heavenly things becomes accustomed to prefer what is common to what is private. IV, 1415. See Possession. No one will seek private possessions in heaven. IV, 1415.

Privatianus of Sufetula. IX, 215.

Augustine sent Aurelius the case concerning deprivation before receiving the man into the monastery. II, 234.

Privations in things are fittingly ordered by God. VIII, 556.

Privatus. II, 697.

Privatus of Sufes. IX, 215.

Something is said to be prior by eternity, by time, by election, or by origin. I, 842.

Proba Faltonia. II, 494. Note (a). Grandmother of Demetrias and mother-in-law of Juliana. VI, 446. A widow devoted to prayer day and night. II, 495. Augustine advises her how she should pray. II, 495. Augustine’s congratulatory letter to Proba. II, 645. Augustine returns Proba’s greeting. II, 507. Proba has sons, grandsons, and a large household. II, 506. She also has a daughter-in-law. II, 506. Holy widows and virgins have been placed under her care. II, 506.

What “probable” and “verisimilar” mean for the Academics. I, 931. How the Academics introduced the probable. I, 955. For the Academics, following the probable without assent is harmless; for Christians, sacrilegious. I, 952, 953. A person commits adultery or another crime even if he plausibly thinks that it is not a sin. I, 953. The disadvantages arising from probable opinion. I, 953. One may not live on another person’s probability. I, 952.

Probianus, proconsul of Africa. II, 304; IX, 540.

Everyone is moved by the praise of uprightness. VII, 75.

Problems—called *propositiones* in Latin—what they are. IV, 983.

To cast an insult at a prince is the more disgraceful the farther it is from the truth. VII, 55.

Proca, the thirteenth king after Aeneas in Latium. VII, 577.

The procession of the Word. III, 1702. No one can explain, when speaking of the Trinity, what difference there is between being born and proceeding. VIII, 770. It is sinful to want to mix processions of different kinds. VIII, 237.

The heretics called Proclianites. VIII, 42.

Proculeianus, Donatist bishop of Hippo. IX, 525. The mandate of the Proculeianists. II, 136. Their discipline was insulted on account of the fall of two deacons. II, 271. How he evades the conference convened to restrain the cruelty of the Circumcellions. II, 306, 398. How Proculeianus addresses Augustine as both honorable and most beloved. II, 129. Evodius held discussions with Proculeianus concerning Christ’s inheritance. II, 129.

Proculeianus. IV, 1951.

The proconsular province of Africa. II, 193.

Bishop Proculus. II, 759, 781. Proculus, a Gallican bishop. II, 991.

Proculus, bishop of Girba. IV, 381.

Who the procurators of the Jews were. VII, 607.

To be useful. The same things are not useful to everyone. IX, 460.

From where prodigies derive their name. III, 1524; VII, 722. Things are called prodigies because they portend something. IV, 522. Words are called prodigies and signs because they signify something. IV, 1399. Things produced by an unusual course of nature are called prodigies. VII, 376. Various prodigies. VII, 110, 111. A prodigy arising from the wildness of animals. VII, 104.

The story of the Prodigal is a parable. III, 375, 376.

Whatever pagans have said well must not be rejected. III, 49.

One must always make progress on the way to God. IV, 1798; V, 926. If you wish to reach what you are not yet, let what you are always displease you. V, 926. In the progress of the virtues, whoever says “It is enough” has remained on the road and does not know how to arrive. IV, 873. If you say, “It is enough,” you have perished. V, 926. Strive only to advance and not to fall away; God will readily forgive the rest. V, 153. In what the progress of this life consists. X, 244. See Perfection of righteousness. Everyone who advances withdraws from every sin. X, 308. We make progress in this life as desire diminishes and charity grows; we are perfected in the next life when desire has been extinguished and charity completed. II, 771. Whoever tries to advance begins to suffer the tongues of his opponents; whoever does not suffer them does not try to advance. IV, 1599. A person makes no progress if he does not feel tribulations together with the Church. IV, 221. Let us all wish to advance in such a way that we do not envy those who advance and do not insult those who fall back. V, 933. Progress is sometimes spoken of in an evil sense, and decline sometimes in a good sense. IV, 1556.

Three kinds of professions in the Church. IV, 1279, 1730. Every profession in the Church has good people and bad people. IV, 357, 1279, 1280, 1730. The profession of continence and contempt for marital pleasure in monasteries.

Profuturus, called by Augustine “another self.” II, 153. While preparing to travel to Jerome, Profuturus was meanwhile made a bishop and died shortly afterward. II, 241. Profuturus, perhaps the Catholic bishop of Cirta. II, 111. Note (c). IX, 611. Profuturus appears to Evodius after death. II, 697.
