Progress in the spiritual life. III, 820. See To advance.

Desire was made more ardent by prohibition. III, 2065, 2068, 2070; VI, 63. The prohibition of sins increases the desire to sin where the grace of the liberator is absent. VI, 61. Prohibition increases desire for an illicit act when the desire to sin is not overcome by the delight of righteousness. VII, 380. Projectus, the cleric who conveyed Caelestinus’s letters to Augustine. II, 868.

Who were called proletarians. VII, 97.

Prometheus, brother of Atlas. VII, 599. At what time he was born. VII, 565. Why he is said to have formed human beings from mud. VII, 565.

What difference there is in God between promising and foretelling. II, 558.

The promises of the Old and New Testaments are not the same. IV, 499, 930, 931. Carnal promises were made in the Old Testament; spiritual ones are made in the New. III, 1404. The temporal promises made to the Israelites were figures of things to come. IV, 915, 918. The figures of the Old Testament were promises of Christ. IV, 934. The promises made to the Jews in the Old Testament were partly fulfilled and partly remain to be fulfilled after death. VIII, 314. God’s promise is the foundation of our faith. III, 1656. Through his promises God has made himself our debtor. V, 863. God delays what he has promised; he does not take it away. IV, 475. He promised certain things which he did not give, but he must be believed on the basis of what he did give. IV, 1880. Something more incredible was done for us than what was promised. V, 1504. From what God has done, we ought to believe what he promises. V, 727. The one who promised is himself the one who fulfills. V, 175. What God promises, only God fulfills. II, 887; V, 894; X, 224, 375. Your promise is empty unless God does what you promise; but God’s promise does not depend on you, but on him. V, 911. The Lord commanded difficult things, but promised great ones. V, 120. The Eternal One promised eternal things. V, 622. The heavenly kingdom was promised to you so that you would not perish together with earthly things. V, 622. Life was promised to human beings, which they love greatly, and death was excluded, which they fear greatly. V, 706. God promised you nothing except himself. V, 760. God’s final promise. IV, 1446. Love of God’s promises and contempt for the promises of this world. V, 201. The promises of the world always deceive; God’s promises never deceive. Why the latter are to be preferred to the former. V, 859. Desires do not end but increase if present things are despised for the sake of earthly promises. V, 263. The certainty of God’s promises. V, 241, 861. Their firmness. X, 976. How all God’s promises were confirmed in Christ. IV, 911. A person entrusts himself more safely to the firmness of God’s promise than to his own weakness. X, 976. The bond or promissory note of God’s promises. IV, 1445, 1880. What pledges of God’s promise we have received. IV, 1942. For what purpose God’s conditional promises were made. X, 315. All the righteous before and after Abraham are children of the promise. X, 593.

How far the natural rights of descent extend through the succession of generations. X, 1551, 1552. These matters are ineffable in created beings and cannot be comprehended. X, 1551.

A prophet of God is nothing other than a declarer of God’s words to human beings who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God. III, 601. Prophets were called “seers” because they saw future things not with the body but with the spirit. II, 620. The distinction between prophets and seers. III, 470. From what point the time of the prophets takes its beginning. VII, 523. The prophets flourished especially when Roman rule began and Assyrian rule declined: why. VII, 584. The people of Israel had prophets until the time of Darius. VII, 583, 584. It had none after the restoration of the Temple. VII, 606. The prophets are earlier than the pagan philosophers. VII, 596, 597. Later than the theological poets. VII, 597. Not everyone who prophesies is to be counted among the prophets. VI, 130. Three kinds of prophets. VIII, 348. The spirit of prophecy foretells future things even through evil people. III, 1757. The gift of prophecy was granted even to the wicked. IV, 1343. It can be given to one rejected, envious, and ungrateful. VI, 138. In Scripture prophecy is spoken not only of good things but also of evil things. VI, 135. No contact with souls can stain the spirit of prophecy. VI, 129. Which prophecy is more certain. VI, 129, 130. Whether prophecy can exist without charity. VI, 136. How true prophets were distinguished from false ones. VII, 601, 602. The words of the prophets are understood from their deeds. IX, 100. The deeds of the prophets were themselves prophetic and mystical. VIII, 404.

How the prophets and seers foretold future things. III, 1059. The oracles of the prophets are from God, not from human beings. VII, 602. The prophets were filled with the Holy Spirit. VIII, 644. The prophets are taught either by the Wisdom of God or by angels. VII, 319. The various ways in which the spirit of prophecy affects prophets. VI, 129, 130. Prophecy belongs more to the mind than to the spirit. III, 461. He is not a prophet of the true and supreme God who, when visions divinely offered are presented, sees them either only with the body or even with that part of the spirit by which images of bodies are apprehended, but does not see them with the mind. VIII, 172. When the prophet speaks in his own person, the Lord himself speaks through him. IV, 662. The predictions of the prophets are far to be preferred to the predictions of demons. VII, 315, 316. The prophets sometimes foretell evils as though wishing for them. IV, 328. By using the figure of wishing, the prophet signifies the certainty of his vision and his approval of the divine decree. V, 148, 149. Prophets commonly foretell future things by the figure of imprecation, just as they express things that were to come by the figure of the past tense; they often sang in this manner. III, 1265. Why they generally announce future things as though they were past. IV, 75, 485. The prophets are defended against the adversary of the Law. I, 654. Against Faustus it is maintained that the prophets both foretold Christ, that their testimonies benefit us, and that they lived in accordance with their prophecy. VIII, 254, 255. How the faith of the prophets can be demonstrated. VIII, 285, 290. From what it is to be judged whether the prophets lived well or badly. VIII, 280. It is wrongly denied that prophets existed before Christ. VIII, 643, 648. Why so many prophets were sent before Christ. V, 1674. The prophets were not thieves and robbers. III, 1720. Which prophets are to be considered thieves and robbers. VIII, 322. The prophets who were sent did not come before Christ but came with him. VIII, 322. They announced Christ, being full of Christ. IV, 1845. The prophets foretold Christ as God and human being. II, 522. In them Christ sometimes speaks in the person of the head and sometimes in the person of the body. IV, 1784. Prophecy in which Christ is not understood is water. III, 1459, 1460. The prophetic books are tasteless and foolish when Christ is not understood. III, 1459. Prophecy concerning Christ was not lacking in any of the earlier ages. III, 1459. Every prophecy concerning Christ pertained to all nations. III, 1462, 1463. Hebrew prophecy was suited to the Gentiles so that they might believe in Christ. VIII, 282. Prophecy concerning Christ fulfilled. III, 1064. How Christ fulfilled the prophecies. VIII, 352. The prophecy lying hidden before Christ, signified by Zechariah’s silence. V, 1328.

There were many prophets, but the writings of only a few are preserved. VII, 583. Why prophets are called major and minor. VII, 585. Some prophets are called minor because of the brevity of their books. III, 927. All the prophets are beneath John. V, 1302. The utterances of the prophets are threefold. VII, 525. Their oracles pertain sometimes to the heavenly Jerusalem, sometimes to the earthly, and sometimes to both. VII, 525. Prophecy is a lamp lit to point out the way. IV, 1854. Every prophecy serves faith, hope, and charity. III, 35. How the prophets bear witness to God’s righteousness. X, 596, 597. Why the people of God were taught whatever pertains to knowledge of God or upright conduct not through contests of argument but through prophetic utterances. VII, 602. Prophetic speech is more effective for confirming faith. V, 256. Although the prophets spoke many evils against the wicked, none of them established for himself another temple, sacrifices, or priests. IX, 633. Many prophetic books are not received as canonical: why. VII, 598. The prophetic books were commended with their times previously noted and fixed. IX, 664. The Donatists criticized the Catholics because they sang the divine songs of the Prophets soberly in church. II, 221.

The prophets as oxen. III, 1470. Foundations of the heavenly city. IV, 1101. Foundations of the earth. IV, 150. Foundations and gates of the Church. IV, 1103. Stones of Zion. IV, 1303. Lamps. III, 1583. Mountains. IV, 1024, 1650. Clouds. IV, 136.

To draw near to God is to become like him. IV, 337.

Kinship. If human beings had not sinned, there would have been no kinships. III, 161. Augustine retracted this. I, 605. Kinship exists where there is agreement. IV, 1218, 1693. Whoever cannot benefit everyone whom he loves should benefit those nearer to him. III, 163. Spiritual kinship. III, 162. Spiritual kinship with Christ must be preferred to his bodily kinship. VI, 397, 398.

Atonement is made through a sacrifice. IV, 777.

The mercy seat was placed above the ark because the Law is not fulfilled in every respect by anyone who is making progress. III, 634, 640. Mystical interpretation of the mercy seat. III, 633.

God is not called propitious except in relation to sins. IV, 777, 1266. God is propitious both by forgiving sins and by avenging them. IV, 1266.

Retailers (*propolarii* or *propolae*). III, 1470.

[Col. 0552] Proportion is a kind of commensurability. I, 1192. A person possesses the power to judge the proportions of bodies, places, and so forth. III, 159.

A particular, universal, and indefinite proposition. V, 450.

Purpose. According to whose purpose the elect are called. X, 586. Calling and election of the predestined belong to God’s purpose. X, 587. Human purpose is assisted by subsequent grace, but it would not exist at all unless grace preceded it. X, 587.

The human being’s own possession is nothing except sin and falsehood. V, 200.

Whatever exists for the sake of something else is inferior to that for whose sake it exists. I, 1209.

Proscholus. V, 964.

At Rome it was permitted to kill the proscribed. VII, 108.

Who is called a proselyte. IV, 1201, 1896.

Proserpina, so called from *proserpere*, “to creep forth.” VII, 210. Proserpina, the wife of Pluto. VII, 119, 120, 213. Proserpina is said to be the lower part of the earth. VII, 213. Proserpina is set over germinating grain. VII, 118. Proserpina signifies fertility. VII, 210. The story of the rape of Proserpina is interpreted. VII, 210.

Prosper’s letter to Augustine concerning certain remnants of the Pelagians. II, 1002. Prosper appears to be the man distinguished in character, eloquence, and zeal with whom Hilary says he dealt. II, 1012. Although Prosper was personally unknown to Augustine, he had already written to him in other matters and had received letters from him. II, 1002. But only as an exchange of greetings. I, 1002.

Earthly prosperity, although shared by the wicked, is nevertheless given by God. IV, 280. Whatever God now gives to the prosperous is not the joy of the blessed but the consolation of the wretched. IV, 1930. Neither worldly happiness makes us blessed nor adversity wretched. IV, 1796. The prosperity of this age is not the lot of Christians. IV, 620, 621. A person ought not to be exalted by the prosperity and elevation of this age. IV, 621, 622. Prosperity is not blessedness for those whom an evil conscience torments. IV, 1180. Let no one congratulate a person who prospers in his way, whose sins lack an avenger and have a praiser; this is a greater wrath of the Lord. IV, 126, 1145. The most miserable condition is when the human mind seems to prosper in its iniquities and thinks that it is being spared, while it is being blinded and reserved for the final and appropriate vengeance. IV, 128. If, by remembering Zion, you weep, then when things go well for you according to Babylon, you ought to weep. IV, 1763.

Prosperous, or favorable, circumstances weary the minds of the wise. VII, 554. Prosperity is more to be feared than adversity. VII, 43, 44. There is greater danger in prosperity. IV, 1093. A prosperous condition is more dangerous to the mind than an adverse one is to the body. IV, 587. From prosperous circumstances arise ambition, greed, luxury, and so forth. VII, 43, 44, 62. Prosperity is useful to some and harmful to others: why. VIII, 451. In prosperity and adversity, use distinguishes the good from the wicked. VII, 20. Whoever advances in prosperous circumstances learns in harsh ones how much he has advanced. III, 164. Prosperity and adversity must both be guarded against: the former lest it corrupt, the latter lest it break. IV, 946. This world must be used indifferently, so that prosperity does not exalt and adversity does not break us. IV, 1794. God must be blessed in prosperity and adversity. IV, 309, 1794. The example of Job is proposed. IV, 309. See Job. Whoever despises present things and fears the prosperity of the age has become like a prodigy to many. IV, 881. God curbs the excess of excessive prosperity in the hearts of his own people. III, 795. The prosperity of the impious is for certain righteous people an occasion of scandal. IV, 560, 1175, 1176, 1178, 1180, 1189, 1190. The prosperity of this age is fragile. I, 907. Prosperity is compared with a reed staff. IV, 1058. It is represented by water. IV, 797. By day and summer. IV, 475. The prosperity of the age is day; night is adversity. IV, 467, 1793, 1794.

The feast day of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius. V, 1297. Their bodies were divinely revealed. I, 770; V, 1437. Through a revelation made to Ambrose. VII, 761; IX, 430. The commemoration of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius was celebrated on the very day of their discovery. V, 1299. Miracles performed at their translation. I, 770. A blind man of many years received his sight through them. VII, 761; IX, 430. At the memorial of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, a young man was freed from a demon. VII, 765. And many others were healed. VII, 765.

If God’s protection is absent, we are nothing. IV, 758.

Proteus. VII, 288. Proteus is said to be accustomed to be caught in the very way in which he would least be caught. I, 940. Proteus in poetry as an image of truth. I, 941.

Πρωτότοκα (*prōtotoka*), or firstborn: what is to be understood by these terms. III, 758, 759.

For the animal human being, all sayings of wisdom concerning an incorporeal and unchangeable substance are proverbs. III, 1897. A Punic proverb agreeing with Christ’s command. V, 910.

Some deny providence. I, 1272. Some confess it in a thoroughly mistaken way. I, 1273. What both groups must do in order to think about it piously. I, 1273. Whoever reckons that there is no providence, or does not believe that he belongs to it, enters into the depth of evils. IV, 1853. How far divine providence extends. VI, 37. The Epicureans denied that human affairs belong to the care of the gods; the Stoics asserted it. VII, 601. Plotinus proves that providence extends from the supreme God down to these earthly and lowest things. VII, 292. God’s providence extends to human beings and to all the lower and least things. I, 978; IV, 1446, 1892, 1943, 1944. Nothing occurs without God’s providence. V, 70. Everything is subjected to him. VIII, 450. All things are governed by it. I, 906, 978, 979. Everything is administered by it. VI, 17, 295. Whatever happens takes place according to the order and laws of providence. IV, 1946. All things are contained within its order and laws. I, 588; VII, 153. There would be no justice among human beings if God did not care for human affairs. VI, 98.

Arguments for divine providence. III, 337. There is no creature that, willingly or unwillingly, does not serve divine providence. III, 2128. Human conduct is subject to divine providence. III, 337. What happens opportunely, without any human planning, is to be attributed to divine mercy. V, 262. One who uses his own industry where he is able does not oppose providence. VI, 574. God cares for all things, especially the just. IV, 450, 451, 456. Why the wicked deny providence. V, 126, 129. Some deny providence because the wicked too abound in earthly goods. V, 1418. God’s providence, which brings good out of evil. V, 1067. In the world there is a twofold operation of providence. III, 379, 380. And in the human being. III, 379. The world is a furnace: straw is evil, gold is good, fire is tribulation, and God is the craftsman. V, 118. Under the hand of so great a craftsman, a speck of gold cannot perish in a great mass of straw. V, 118. He crowns some and condemns others; he nowhere errs: he tests some, proves his case concerning others, and orders all. V, 118. Demons are agents and executors of divine providence. III, 2128. Providence can use an evil person both to punish and to assist, and a good person both to condemn and to help. VI, 18. God’s providence in the labor of the good and in the prosperity of the wicked is a most profound sea. IV, 1176, 1191.

God’s providence is hidden. VII, 224. It belongs to God’s providence to determine what is suited to each time; this surpasses human planning. II, 375. God’s providence is neither constrained by fate, obstructed by chance occurrences, nor corrupted by any injustice. II, 886. When provision for the flesh is not blameworthy. III, 2085.

Distribution of provinces among the emperors. V, 294.

Province; provincial. IX, 395, 431, 586. Provincial. II, 532; V, 1391, 1540. A province is a multitude subject to tribute. V, 1540. “Provincial” is said of the common people who provide the soldier’s grain allowance. V, 1391, note (a). Tributary provincials. II, 532; VI, 341, 553, 561, 564. Most devoted provincials of the eternal King. VI, 569. Who is a provincial of Christ? IV, 1157, 1365. The Church has its own provincials. II, 691. Curses of the provincials. II, 1041.

Who is one’s neighbor? II, 1041. The neighbor is every human being. II, 672; IV, 143, 189, 1519; V, 563, 1596; VI, 671. Every human being is our neighbor. III, 31, 709. The angels also. III, 31. Christ himself also. III, 31. That person is one’s neighbor to whom the duty of mercy is, or would be, owed if he were in need. III, 31. The one to whom we show mercy is our neighbor. IV, 553. Even the person who is not yet a member of Christ with us is to be regarded as our neighbor. VI, 527. Since we do not know the future, we should regard everyone as our neighbor, not only by the condition of human mortality but also by hope of the heavenly inheritance. IV, 189. More truly called one’s neighbor is the person who attends to you closely—that is, looks upon you mercifully. V, 214.

How much the neighbor is to be loved, and for what reason. V, 212, 1461. One cannot love one’s neighbor who does not love God. III, 2138. People can lie about their love of God, because rarer temptations test it; this is not so with love of one’s neighbor. III, 2137. The benefit of one’s neighbor is to be considered even during leisure. VII, 647. Under the name “neighbor,” the command also includes loving an enemy. V, 807. See Love, Charity, Affection.

What prudence is. I, 1189. Definition of prudence. III, 2073. Definition and parts of prudence. VI, 20. Prudence is knowledge of the things to be sought and avoided. I, 1235, 1330. Prudence is the faculty by which we distinguish good from evil. IV, 1065. It is defined as love of God, skillfully choosing those things by which it is helped over those by which it is hindered. I, 1322. It should be attributed to prudence that the soul recognizes the eternal and higher things as more desirable than the lower. I, 1183. Prudence is established in the mind. I, 1228. They divided prudence into memory, understanding, and foresight. VIII, 1047. The function of prudence. VII, 629. Prudence of the flesh and of the spirit. V, 847. In what the prudence of the spirit consists. III, 2073. The prudence of the flesh: what it is. III, 2072; VI, 65; VIII, 125. The life and death of the prudence of the flesh. VIII, 326.

“Prudent” (prudens) is so called from “seeing ahead” (porro videns). IV, 945. Not only the good but also the wicked are commonly called prudent. IX, 709.

[Col. 0554] Hoarfrost, very fine hail. III, 876. What hoarfrost signifies. IV, 1000.

What it means to sing psalms. IV, 787. Not everyone who makes a sound with his lips sings a new song, but the person who sings in the manner enjoined by the Apostle, who says: “Singing and psalm-singing in your hearts to God.” II, 557. One should sing psalms intelligently. IV, 529. When a psalm-singer sings, not only should his voice sound forth God’s praises, but his works should agree with his voice. IV, 1173, 1899. In heaven, our entire life will be singing psalms to God. IV, 1389. Exultation in psalm-singing. IV, 1389.

How psalm, diapsalm, and sympsalm differ. IV, 80.

The singing of psalms in the Church. I, 800; III, 45; IV, 524, 525; IX, 330. The singing of psalms is celebrated throughout the Christian world. I, 766. The singing of psalms at the altar. I, 634. When the singing of psalms was introduced at Milan. I, 769. What Athanasius and Augustine thought about the singing of psalms. I, 800. The psalms were sung by the people standing. IV, 384. A psalm sung by one person. III, 1470, 1489. And by several. III, 1489. A psalm that was to be expounded was customarily sung by a lector. IV, 1100, 1784. A psalm partly heard and partly sung by the people. IV, 199. Psalm 21 was customarily sung in the Church during the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion. IV, 172, 178, 179. Psalms are sung at the funerals of the dead. I, 776. Augustine expounds a psalm at the funeral of a certain believer. IV, 1352.

The power and usefulness of the psalms. I, 767. The psalms are letters sweetened with the honey of heaven. I, 768. The psalms are voices full of grief; how they are more the voices of the Holy Spirit than our own. IV, 199. The psalms are our mirror. IV, 248. In the psalms one finds that Christ and his members are one person. IV, 866. Christ makes the words of certain psalms his own, to indicate that he himself spoke in them. IV, 237. It is scarcely possible to find voices in the psalms except those of Christ and the Church. IV, 713. Very often the voice of those persons is heard in the psalms as the voice of one person. IV, 866.

Augustine devotes himself to commenting on the psalms. II, 742. At the request of brothers and fellow bishops, Augustine expounds several psalms. IV, 322, 323, 363, 1216, 1352, 1803. Expositions of the psalms. II, 135, 140, 146, 742. Some psalms are deeper in proportion as they appear clearer. IV, 1501. The title of a psalm is like the psalm’s herald. IV, 1804. And like a door, it introduces one into its meaning. V, 178. Although the psalm was not written by Moses, why Moses’ name is used in its title. IV, 1141. Explanation of Psalm 4, “When I called.” II, 767. Augustine once dictated an exposition of Psalm 16. II, 632. Psalm 21 is read every year during the last week. III, 1500. Psalm 22 is expounded to those being baptized. V, 1646. Psalm 22 contains the mystery of the restoration of the human being. V, 1646. When Augustine dictated and treated Psalms 67, 71, and 77. II, 743. Augustine expounded Psalm 72 on the night when the solemnity of blessed Cyprian was dawning. II, 543. Augustine recommends reading this exposition. II, 543. What this psalm represents. II, 542. The subject and purpose of Psalms 50, 100, and 150. IV, 1962. The Psalter translated from Hebrew by Saint Jerome. II, 1077. Augustine did not translate the Psalter, but corrected the corruptions of the Latin manuscripts from Greek exemplars, and continues to correct them by comparing manuscripts day by day. II, 1077.

What the Psalter is, and how it differs from the lyre. IV, 280, 479, 671, 672, 900, 1036, 1064. The Psalter explained mystically. IV, 1953. What the ten-stringed psalter signifies. III, 48, 49. The ten-stringed psalter allegorically. V, 79, 207. The ten-stringed psalter signifies the Decalogue. IV, 275, 281, 1174, 1866. Carrying the psalter and throwing down the psalter. V, 81. The entire Psalter is attributed to David’s name, and the psalms are called Davidic. IV, 130.

Whether all the psalms contained in the Book of Psalms are by David. VII, 547. With what state of mind David composed the psalms. VII, 547, 548. Some have said that the Psalter consists of five books, but the authority of canonical Scripture proves that it is only one. IV, 1961. Origen, Eusebius, and many others who interpreted the psalms are listed. II, 262. The Catholics attempted to carry away a bishop whom the schismatics had left as though dead, with the psalms. II, 805. An acrostic psalm against the party of Donatus. I, 617. Acrostic psalms. IV, 1596. The Donatists sing psalms composed by human ingenuity. II, 221.

When female harpists were first introduced into banquets at Rome. VII, 102.

In the Gospel, false prophets are understood as heretics. IV, 101. The Lord orders false prophets in such a way that he rains snares from them upon sinners. IV, 136. Only a sinner falls into the error of following them. IV, 136.

Psonthomphanech: the name given to Joseph by Pharaoh. III, 584.

Ptolemy Epiphanes. VII, 606.

Ptolemy, son of Lagus, transferred many Jewish captives to Egypt. VII, 602, 606.

Ptolemy Philadelphus obtained the Scriptures from Eleazar the High Priest, and afterward the Seventy translators. VII, 602, 606. Ptolemy Philadelphus permitted the Jews held captive in Egypt to return freely. VII, 602, 606. Ptolemy Philadelphus sent royal gifts to the Temple. VII, 602. The library of Ptolemy Philadelphus. VII, 452. The Ptolemies reigned in Egypt after Alexander’s death. VII, 602.

Ptolemy, a disciple of Valentinus. VIII, 28. His heresy. VIII, 28.

Publianus, bishop. II, 759, 781.

A publican. V, 143. See Pharisee.

Publicola [uncertain reading]. II, 348.

Publius, brother of Gnaeus Scipio. VII, 54, note (2), 57.

Pudentianus of Cuicul. IX, 236.

The shameful parts. What causes us shame. X, 449. Why certain members are called shameful parts. VII, 425; X, 173, 451, 756. In beasts, the members belonging to the genitals and sexual nature are not shameful. X, 766. The cause of shame. X, 1364. The shameful parts would not be shameful if the law of sin did not enviously oppose the law of the mind. X, 786. What God made honorable in creating, we have made dishonorable by sinning. V, 638, 680; X, 779. The person who, while clothed with grace, had nothing on his naked body of which he was ashamed, once stripped of grace perceived what he ought to cover. X, 781. The members already existed before sin, but they were not shameful. X, 427, 444. Decency is observed with respect to the shameful parts when they are veiled. X, 780. Whether the shameful parts are to be covered. X, 767. Even barbarians cover their shameful members. VII, 426. The shameful parts of the human body are of two kinds. X, 1357.

The origin of shame in the human body. X, 416. The origin of the shame of the first parents. X, 784, 785, 1352. The cause of shame. X, 1363, 1375. Shame arising from sin. V, 638, 680; X, 427, 428. Shame concerning the genitals arises from sin. X, 1279. Shame arises not from the members themselves but from the disobedience of the members. X, 449. It is also a punishment for sin. X, 449.

What virginal chastity is. X, 763. The distinction between chastity and virginity. X, 762. To have subdued and ordered desire is the virtue of chastity. IV, 1001. The seat of chastity. I, 1228; VII, 31. Bodily chastity also dwells in the mind. VI, 545. To what extent chastity is to be preserved. X, 799. There is no bodily chastity unless it depends upon integrity of mind. VI, 495. Chastity is not violated by violence if it is preserved in the mind. I, 1228; II, 1016; VII, 31, 32. Chastity cannot be violated by another person’s lust. VI, 495, 496. No one violates bodily chastity when the soul neither consents nor permits it. VI, 514, 515. There may be some reason for permitting it, but none for consenting. VI, 514.

There are three kinds of chastity in the members of Christ. V, 1020. Conjugal, widowed, and virginal chastity are the three evangelical fruitfulnesses figured in Noah’s ark. VII, 473. What true conjugal chastity is. X, 416, 724. Conjugal chastity is the good of marriage. X, 404. To what extent it can be a beatifying good. X, 756. Conjugal chastity is the boundary of evil. X, 763. Conjugal chastity is a gift of God. X, 737, 742, 886. Nevertheless, it is lower than continence. X, 415. Conjugal chastity is a gift of God and yet is commanded: why? X, 415. In temptation, one must resist out of love for chastity, following the examples of Susanna and Joseph. V, 1510. A person who kills someone in order to preserve chastity is not excused from sin. I, 1228. Chastity, whether conjugal, widowed, or virginal, is not truly to be called chastity unless it is devoted to true faith. X, 416. The chastity of the impious is not true chastity. X, 762. Nor is that of unbelievers. X, 415, 743, 763. The loss of chastity was figured by the death of livestock. IV, 1000.

No one is truly chaste except a believer. X, 415. A man is not chaste if he does not preserve the fidelity of marriage toward his wife for the sake of the true God. X, 743.

The proper method of educating girls. I, 779. Cyprian, close to his martyrdom, commanded that girls be guarded. V, 1411.

The evils of children. X, 1525. The misery of children arising from original sin. X, 1311. See Misery, Infants. A child cries at birth because he is entering this life. IV, 1664. By crying at birth, he is a prophet of his own calamity. V, 909. The three boys remained in the fiery furnace for scarcely an hour. II, 143. Children attain the kingdom of heaven by humility, not by age. I, 674. “Child,” that is, “servant.” VII, 478.

Childhood is not yet capable of receiving a command. VII, 730. Childhood lies almost entirely in the grip of vicious pleasures. VII, 730. The vices of childhood pass into the succeeding ages. I, 674. How childhood is to be joined with old age. IV, 1472. Childhood is proposed both for imitation of humility and for avoidance of folly. IV, 525, 526. Childhood signifies humility; therefore only children praise the Lord. IV, 1472.

An unformed fetus does not fall under homicide. III, 626. Living fetuses in their mothers’ wombs. VI, 272.

To box is to engage in the pancratium. IV, 679.

Combat, spiritual battle. VI, 355. The conflict between love of God and love of the world. V, 1512. The battles of Christians are now not with tyrants but with the devil. IV, 1687. Combat against the devil. V, 51; VI, 280, 290, 291. Against the world. V, 1256. Let no enemy from outside be feared: conquer yourself, and the world is conquered together with the devil. V, 391. Combat [Col. 0556] against sin. IV, 345. We are defeated when fighting against sin unless we are divinely assisted. VI, 271. Even those who fight bravely are not without the wounds of sin. VI, 357. The conflict between body and soul. See Flesh, Concupiscence.

Interior combat. V, 85, 391, 716, 719, 815, 817, 820, 892. Where does the conflict that a person feels within come from? IV, 764. The conflict of flesh and spirit arises from weakness and vice contracted through fault. VI, 360. Once that has been healed, there will be no conflict. VI, 361. Who experience the internal conflict. VI, 353. It is far more tolerable never to have begun such a contest than to abandon it after beginning. VI, 372. In this battle there is a carnal army. VI, 354. To fight against the desires of the flesh is the work of the Holy Spirit in us. V, 717. When about to fight, first submit yourself to God; then, with him teaching and helping you, do battle. IV, 1860. God watches our battle not only in order to crown the victor but also to help the combatant. IV, 233. God does not watch us fighting as the people watch the hunters. V, 718. If God does not help us, we shall be unable—not merely to win, but even to fight. V, 855. A person who does not live justly does not fight but is dragged along. V, 821. Rather, he is not dragged along but follows willingly. V, 818. You labor by fighting, but you will rejoice in triumphing. V, 821. How grace conquers. VI, 353, 354. If the last day does not find you victorious, let it find you at least fighting, not captured and enslaved. V, 153. Treatise on the soul’s battle. V, 718. Several sermons discuss the same subject. V, from p. 817 to 847. The battles of the wicked against the wicked, of the wicked against the good, and of the good among themselves. VII, 441, 442.

What beauty is, and in what it consists. I, 701, 1184; III, 243. Beauty arises from likeness and a certain unity of the parts. I, 1223. The form of every beauty is unity. II, 85. Beauty composed of parts is much more praiseworthy in the whole than in a part. III, 188. Things that delight do so because they are beautiful. III, 148. Beauty is perceived everywhere and in everything. I, 989. Hence whatever is ordered, however ugly it may be, is beautiful. III, 156.

The origin of the beauty of the universe. VIII, 607. The beauty of temporal natures is accomplished through the passing of things and distinguished by the death of those being born. VI, 28; VIII, 205. The beauty of the world is like a great song by a certain composer, leading toward eternal contemplation of the beauty of God. II, 527. External beauties come from God’s beauty. I, 801. Justice has its own beauty. V, 87.

The beauty of the body. III, 155. Beauty is the harmony of the parts together with a certain pleasantness of color. II, 65. Beauty consists not in bulk but in the equality and proportion of the members. VII, 335. The defects by which beauty is distinguished should not be called corruptions. VIII, 205. Beauty is a good of God. VII, 467. God grants beauty even to the wicked, so that beauty may not appear to be a great good belonging only to the good. VII, 467. Beauty seduces those who pursue it. III, 139. Why beauty often deceives us. III, 150. One should not cling to inferior beauty. VIII, 206. When beauty is wrongly loved. VII, 467. Beauty is subject to many miseries. III, 155. The beauty of Christ. IV, 495, 496.

True beauty is in the soul. II, 65. In what the beauty of the mind consists. II, 462. The beauty of the soul is true virtue and justice. IV, 496, 704. Beauty is born from confession. IV, 1232. The beauty of creatures is their voice confessing God. IV, 1946. Sensation opposes the beauty of the soul. II, 65.

The distinction between the beautiful and the fitting. II, 527. Scripture calls the beautiful in body “good.” VII, 469. The Stoics said that only the wise are beautiful. VII, 232. A person whose body is beautiful but whose soul is deformed is more to be pitied than one whose body too is deformed. III, 119.

The augury of chicks. VII, 102.

What is the function of the lungs? IV, 1316. The lungs are like bellows. X, 513.

How great a magnanimity Pulvillus displayed in bearing the false report of his son’s death. VII, 162.

Dust designates the transgressing Jews. IV, 1303. And the unrighteous. IV, 328.

To use pumice on the face. IX, 706.

An indivisible point. I, 1045. Its distinction from a sign. I, 1046. The power of a point. I, 1046.

The Punic and Hebrew languages are joined by a certain closeness of meaning. V, 648; IX, 341.

Punic Christians call baptism nothing other than “Salvation,” and the sacrament of Christ’s body nothing other than “Life.” X, 128. Much wisdom was committed to memory in Punic books. II, 83. The disasters of the Punic wars. VII, 98, 99, 100, 101. A Punic proverb. V, 910.

To punish. One must forgive or chastise out of charity. II, 661, 662. Sin is punished either by the repentant person or by God the judge. V, 133, 138, 187. God orders sinners so that they are punished not by his malice but by their own. IV, 108. See Scourge, Sin, Punishment, Vengeance. When people are punished, they are punished by God alone. IV, 803. God punishes what you do in order to free what he made. IV, 1173. When God punishes, he does not take away all good, but removes some and leaves some. VII, 641. Through grace God imposes punishment. IV, 427. God punishes more severely when he leaves sins unpunished; he opposes mercifully when he renders abundant lusts powerless. II, 531. The Pelagians wrongly teach that evil works are punished by God—not those that a person has committed, but those that he would have committed. II, 889. Wicked people have places where, through Christians, they may be chastised not only gently but also beneficially. II, 317.

The power of the pupil of the eye. I, 1048. See Eyes.

Who is an orphan. V, 116. Who is the orphan for whom God becomes helper and father. IV, 129, 130. God’s orphan is the person who does not presume upon temporal things. IV, 1897. We are all orphans when the father is absent, not dead. IV, 1897. God is the protector of orphans and widows. IV, 1896. Bishops are guardians of orphans. V, 950. The Church or its bishops ought to care for the protection of all people, but especially orphans. II, 1069.

“To cleanse,” used for “to pronounce clean.” III, 519.

The purification of the soul is like a journey on foot and a voyage toward the homeland. III, 23. The example of the soul’s purification is incarnate Wisdom. III, 23. The beginning of human purification is Christ’s incarnation. VII, 301. Christians have purification of mind, spirit, and body in Christ. VII, 305.

The purgatorial punishments of certain people at the judgment. VII, 699, 700. See Punishment. Certain punishments are purgatorial in this mortal life. VII, 727, 728. Some occur after death, but none after the judgment. VII, 728, 730, 731. Purgatorial fire after this life. VI, 156, 217, 265. Purgatorial fire on the day of judgment. IV, 92, 1363. Some will be reproved in indignation and corrected, yet as though through fire; some who are reproved will not be corrected. IV, 397. Because it is said, “He will be saved,” that fire is despised; nevertheless, it will be more severe than anything a person can suffer in this life. IV, 397. “In this life purify me, so that I may no longer need corrective fire.” IV, 397.

Purpurius of Limata. IX, 511, 612. Purpurius charged Secundus of Tigisis with the crime of being a traditor. II, 162; IX, 755. Secundus Tigisitanus charged Purpurius with having killed in prison the sons of his sister Miseia. IX, 640. Purpurius confessed to homicide. IX, 714, Appendix 773.

Pusillus of Lamasba. IX, 236.

The difference between a well and a spring. III, 1512.

Pyramus and Thisbe. I, 982, 984, 989.

Pyrrhus, king of Greece, was summoned by the people of Tarentum and became an enemy of the Romans. VII, 97. The ambiguous oracle of Apollo concerning Pyrrhus. VII, 97.

Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes. VII, 164.

Pythagoras. IV, 1828; V, 1136. The Samian. VIII, 1011. The period in which he flourished. VII, 585, 596, note. Pythagoras acknowledged the immortality of the soul. I, 954. Pythagoras of Samos, after hearing a discussion about the immortality of the soul, became a philosopher from an athlete. II, 521. Pythagoras said that he was not a wise man but a philosopher. VIII, 1037. From him the name “philosopher” began. VII, 225, 596. And the name “philosophy.” X, 1432. Pythagorean philosophy was previously unknown. II, 375. Pythagoras devoted himself to the contemplative part of wisdom. VII, 228. At that time Greece had nothing clearer than Pythagoras in contemplative virtue. III, 1048. He wrote nothing either about himself or about any subject. III, 1048. Pythagoras’ judgment concerning the administration of the republic. I, 1020. Several errors of Pythagoras. I, 589. Pythagoras, the Platonists, and Origen thought that souls had fallen from heaven. II, 718. Pythagoras practiced hydromancy. VII, 223. Praise of Pythagoras. I, 953. It is rejected. I, 589.

## Q

What mystery the number forty contains. III, 48; V, 352, 695, 1039, 1051, 1177, 1178, 1216, 1239. It suggests the mystery of perfection. VIII, 895. The number forty is perfect and sacred. III, 1529. It is the sacrament of this laborious life. III, 1075. How. III, 1075. The number forty suits sometimes penitence and sometimes joy. III, 594, 595. Forty days before Easter and fifty afterward. V, 695, 1048, 1049, 1052, 1147, 1178.

The days of Lent are most sacred throughout the world. V, 1046, 1051. The season of the year and the number of days are to be observed. V, 1047. Lent is the principal observance of fasting. III, 594; IX, 700. Forty days of continuous fasting. V, 1178. What they signify. V, 1178. “Since you fast on the other days, increase during these days what you are doing.” V, 1040. What Lenten abstinence should be like. V, 1044. During Lent, people abstain from meat and wine. V, 1040, 1043. This observance is maintained not superstitiously but according to divine law. VIII, 492. If an infirm stomach cannot tolerate water, it would be more respectable to sustain it with customary and moderate wine than with elaborate beverages. V, [Col. 0558] 1053. The superstitious practice of those who avoid vessels in which meat has been cooked, as though they were unclean, is censured. V, 1047, 1052. During Lent, almost everyone abstains not only from meat but also from certain fruits of the earth. VIII, 491, 493. During Lent, everyone should imitate the food of the poor. V, 1053. Luxuries should be restricted, not replaced. V, 1043, 1044. Those who observe Lent while remaining luxurious. V, 1040, 1043, 1045, 1047, 1053. During Lent the body should be refreshed—or rather supported—not with laborious or costly foods but with those readily available and less expensive. V, 1044, 1045. Those who act otherwise are greatly mistaken. V, 1047. During Lent one must take up the cross of disciplining the body. V, 1039. Married people must preserve continence. V, 1040, 1043, 1045, 1047, 1052. More generous alms are to be distributed. V, 1040, 1042, 1045, 1046, 1047, 1052, 1053. Hostilities are to be ended. V, 1042, 1045, 1046, 1054. Above all, one must fast from lawsuits. V, 1040. Pious works are to be practiced more fervently. V, 1040, 1041, 1052. On the last Thursday, in some places the offering is made only in the evening, while elsewhere it is made both morning and evening. II, 202. Why it is offered twice. II, 204. Some neither bathe nor relax their fast on Thursday, while others do the opposite. II, 201, 204. Why the Lenten fast occurs before Easter and before baptism, when Christ fasted after receiving baptism. V, 1048.

The mystery of Lent is expounded. VI, 40, 96. The days of Lent signify the labor and humility of the present life. V, 1041. The sorrow of this life. IV, 1463. Lent figures the present Church. VI, 40, 97.

A Christian ought to be like a square. IV, 1103.

What animals are called quadrupeds. III, 241, 286.

To seek. What we seek at God’s prompting, we shall find through his own showing of it. I, 1243. By a certain divine providence it cannot happen that the ability to find is denied to religious minds that seek themselves and God—that is, truth—piously, chastely, and diligently. I, 1049. Some do not seek the truth piously, and therefore do not find it. I, 708. No person is deprived of the knowledge that what is ignorantly unknown can be sought profitably, and that weakness must be confessed humbly, so that God may help the one who seeks and confesses. I, 1297. Not all those from whom questions are asked can teach, nor are all who ask worthy. I, 1311. If wisdom and truth are sought as they ought to be, they cannot withdraw and hide themselves from their lovers. I, 1324. It is sought through love. I, 1324. When great things are sought from the small, they usually make them great. I, 909.

To seek God pertains both to praise and to condemnation. III, 1759. He who first sought the one seeking him will not despise the seeker. IV, 870, 871. God is not sought by those who turn away; rather, he himself calls those who turn away in order to fill those who turn back. IV, 288. There are two kinds of those who seek the Lord. III, 1676. To seek Christ wrongly is to die in one’s sin. III, 1676. Those who seek God no longer seek things that pass away and die. IV, 122. Those who seek God for the sake of earthly benefits do not seek him. IV, 996. Seek the Father for the sake of inheritance; seek the Lord for the sake of redemption; seek the patron for the sake of liberation. IV, 1855. Whoever seeks something from God other than God does not seek God chastely. V, 759. Seek nothing from God except God. V, 1461. What does the Lord seek from you except yourself? V, 317. God is to be sought without end because he is to be loved without end. IV, 1392. God is to be sought with the hands—that is, through works. IV, 1853. In tribulation, God is to be sought earnestly. IV, 326, 972. Anyone’s soul is sought in two ways: either for imitation or for destruction. IV, 407, 1840. In what sense God is said to seek a human being. VII, 537. To seek is the same as to possess one’s own. VII, 537.

“Interrogation” is suggested by the use of the rack, the raking of claws, and burning flames; or, more mildly, by blows with rods. II, 509, 511. A person suspended on the rack is tormented by claws. II, 166. An interrogator. V, 680, 1390.

Difficult questions are investigated not without benefit. VI, 260. There are three kinds of questions: whether something is, what it is, and what sort it is. I, 786. There cannot be more than three kinds of questions. VI, 15. An inscrutable question. X, 1128. Whoever does not see the question does not understand the solution. III, 1629. No question will delight in exposition unless, when proposed, it has engaged the mind. III, 1545. Often, in disputation, the proposer of a great question displays the persona of a great teacher. VIII, 107. Charity is stronger than all difficult questions. V, 1612. Seven books of questions. I, 651. Six questions against the pagans expounded. I, 643. A book on eighty-three different questions. I, 624; VI, 11.

Remove the bodies themselves from the qualities of bodies, and necessarily the qualities will not exist. II, 838. The four qualities of the body. IV, 91. A quality does not migrate from one substance into another. X, 855. Qualities pass to other bodies by affecting them, not by emigrating. X, 812. The qualities of bodily things pass from body to spirit in the same way as from spirit to body. X, 812. An evil quality can be present even when no temptation has been aroused. X, 859. An affective quality is something different from an affection. X, 854.

“Whenever” does not exist in eternity. IV, 1459.

Quantity is twofold: that of bulk and that of power. I, 1037. There is no body that does not have length, breadth, and height. I, 1038. The soul has no quantity of bulk, as is discussed at length in the book On the Quantity of the Soul. I, 1037. But it possesses quantity of power, whose seven degrees are assigned. I, 1074. Every body, however small it may be, has a half; and if it has a half, it has innumerable parts. III, 158. See Body. Grammarians and musicians attend to the quantity of syllables in different ways. I, 1099, 1100.

The just have a kind of sadness, but their joy has no “kind of.” IV, 559, 560.

The difference between quatuor (“four”) and quater (“four times”). VI, 40.

Complaint. To be without complaint is one thing; to be without sin is another. X, 163. See Perfection, Sin.

The Romans rightly wished the temple of the god Quies to be outside the gates. VII, 125.

Rest. What is at rest is not nothing; rather, it is more than what is restless. I, 1282. There is profound rest with God, and an undisturbed life. I, 682. How God’s resting from his works is to be understood. III, 189. God’s rest from his works is a symbol of our rest. V, 1242. How God will rest in us on the sabbath of eternal life. I, 868. The Holy Spirit is said to rest in those whom he causes to rest in himself. I, 846. Sloth seeks something like rest; but what rest is secure apart from the Lord? I, 680. Rest is found in God alone. I, 732. It is sought in vain in fleeting creatures. I, 700. The place of undisturbed rest is there where love is not abandoned, if it itself does not abandon us. I, 701. God made us for himself, and our heart is restless until it rests in God. I, 661. God shows how great a rational creature he made: nothing less than himself is sufficient for its blessed rest. I, 848. Rest is found only in the will of God. III, 886. Where there is rest, there is sanctification. II, 219. Everything is to be done for the hope of eternal rest. V, 80, 85. Good action leads to ever-watchful rest. IV, 1489. See Repose. Why Mary’s rest is preferred to Martha’s activity. III, 306. What kind of rest there is in heaven. II, 212. Rest is figured by a bed. IV, 1730.

Quietus of Buruch. IX, 218.

The number five is imperfect, whereas six is perfect. III, 1599. The number five is especially commended in the Old Testament. III, 717. The number fifteen signifies the concord of the two Testaments. IV, 1960. One eats after Easter for fifty days. III, 143. Fasts are relaxed, and we pray standing. II, 218. The Alleluia is sung everywhere. II, 220. The fifty days and the Alleluia after Easter are an ancient tradition. V, 1176. The number fifty is sacred in our religion. III, 48. It contains a great sacrament. IV, 1960. The mystery of the number fifty. II, 218; VI, 96. The reason. V, 75, 1052, 1177, 1178. The fifty days after Easter signify the days of the future age. V, 1084, 1178. The fifty-day period figures the future Church. VI, 97.

Quintasius, bishop of Capsa. IV, 381.

Quintianus. II, 232.

Galla, a widow, and Simpliciola, a virgin, are commended to Quintilian. II, 965.

Quintus at the plow. II, 390.

Quintus of Aggia. IX, 235.

Quintus, presbyter. II, 630.

Quintus, deacon. II, 351. He carried Augustine’s letter-book to Paulinus. II, 347.

The Quirinal flamen. VII, 60.

Romulus was surnamed Quirinus. VII, 60.

Quodvultdeus, deacon of Carthage. VIII, 21, 36. He asks Augustine to explain all the heresies from Christ onward, together with their errors. II, 998. Augustine excuses to him the difficulty of the work and notes that others have already attempted it. II, 999. Nevertheless, Quodvultdeus does not cease pressing his request. II, 999. He says that Greek eloquence is being assigned to him in vain, since he has not learned Latin. II, 1000. Augustine promises Quodvultdeus the work he requests, as far as his occupations permit. II, 1001.

Petilianus said that Quodvultdeus, convicted among the Catholics of two adulteries, had been received by the Donatists. IX, 366.

Quodvultdeus, bishop. II, 759, 781. Augustine wrote to him about what members of the clergy should do when fear of a siege was imminent. II, 1013.

## R

Rahab was rewarded not for her falsehood but for her benevolence. VI, 540. She would have done better to abstain from lying. VI, 541, 542. To what extent Rahab is to be imitated. VI, 542, 543.

[Col. 0560] What “Racha” means. III, 1240, 1241. The word of an indignant person. III, 1764. An interjection of an indignant person. III, 42, 43. “Racha” is said to be untranslatable into another language. III, 42.

Rachel is interpreted as “the beginning of sight.” III, 1046; VIII, 432. What Rachel prefigures. VIII, 432. She is a figure of the contemplative life. III, 1046.

The two roots of good and evil are charity and desire. X, 370. Charity is our root. IV, 124, 358, 557, 607, 1947. The apostate root. VI, 278.

The frog signifies exceedingly loquacious vanity. IV, 1000.

Birds of prey compared with kites. III, 361.

To seize. How God seizes a human being. I, 795.

Raphain, that is, Giants. III, 749.

Plunder is profit that causes harm. IV, 740. Plunder, together with theft, is forbidden by the seventh commandment. V, 71.

What punishment awaits those who seize other people’s property. V, 206. If the person who stores up his own property is foolish, find a name for the one who takes what belongs to others. V, 961. Those who seize property are reproved. V, 963. The alms of one who seizes property are not accepted by God. V, 649, 962. What you found and did not return, you seized. V, 965. The greater robber seeks you because he has found a lesser robber. IV, 1646.

The soul’s rapture is of two kinds: through spiritual vision and through intellectual vision. III, 476. In spiritual rapture revelation sometimes occurs. III, 476. The nature and excellence of intellectual rapture. III, 476. By divine power the human mind can be carried away from this life into angelic life before it is released from the flesh through the common death. II, 610. Paul was carried away into angelic life. II, 610.

Rare things are themselves marvelous. VII, 722.

Reason is the movement of the mind, capable of distinguishing and connecting the things that are learned. I, 1009. Reason is the mind’s gaze, by which it sees the truth through itself and not through the body; or it is the contemplation of truth itself, not through the body; or it is the very truth that it contemplates. I, 1026. Reason is the food of the mind. X, 680. It is common to human beings and angels, but not to animals. X, 330. Reason is, as it were, the head or eye of the soul. I, 1177, 1248. Evodius explains at length that reason is eternal. II, 701. Yet Augustine does not approve what Evodius says: that God is compelled to exist by reason, or that by reasoning God is made to have to exist. II, 705. The distinction between reason and understanding. V, 257.

Both the inner and outer senses are ministers of reason. I, 1245. Reason judges the inner sense. I, 1247. Reason is superior to the body and the senses. III, 146. There are two things through which its power can be brought even to bear upon the senses themselves—namely, works and words. I, 1010. In sight and hearing, and even in pleasure itself, there are certain traces of reason. I, 1011. Nothing in the human being is superior to reason. I, 1248. Through it human beings are superior to beasts. I, 1230. Hence in Scripture the human spirit is called reason, by which it differs from them. III, 202. Reason is known by reason itself. I, 1268. And it comprehends itself. I, 1246. Reason is the inventor of all the disciplines. I, 1012. Virtue is superior to reason. III, 147. Reason is placed, as it were, in a citadel to govern lust and anger. VII, 427. Reason ought, in the place of a husband, to govern every animal movement. III, 746. The dominion of reason was given to human beings to restrain the lower movements. V, 70. Reason does not rightly command the vices if it does not itself serve God. VII, 656. Reason is not absent in infants, but dormant. II, 361. Reason, dormant in the infant, must be awakened so that it may become capable of wisdom and truth. VII, 789.

How reason and authority contribute to learning. I, 1008. See Authority. Reason is to be preferred to examples. VII, 36. Error is not persuaded by reason, but by false reasoning. II, 455. Reason fails in the investigation of divine matters. I, 1315. Reason precedes faith, and faith reason. II, 454. If authority, such as that of the Holy Scriptures, is set against the clearest and most certain reason, the person who does this does not understand, and so forth. II, 588. If an argument is produced against the authority of the divine Scriptures, however acute it may be, it deceives through the likeness of truth; for it cannot be true. II, 588. Where human reason fails, faith suffices. V, 1008. Very few are capable of grasping reason. VIII, 81.

What is capable of reason. I, 1010. It appears in three things. I, 1012. The distinction between *rationabilis* and *rationalis*. I, 1010. In a rational creature, vice and misery consist in its turning away from the unchangeable good; virtue and blessedness, in its turning toward that same good. II, 561.

The breastpiece of the high priest. III, 637. They say that it contained a stone whose color changed, whether toward favorable or unfavorable signs, when the priest entered the sanctuary. III, 637. The breastpiece signified the Law and judgments. III, 640, 641.

Rationalis of Africa. IX, Appendix, 792.

Reasoning is thought that proceeds from certainties toward the investigation of uncertainties. I, 1021. Reasoning is an inquiry conducted by reason. I, 1065. The distinction between reasoning and reason. I, 1064. The use of both. I, 1065.

Ravenna. X, 437. The memory of Laurence at Ravenna. V, 1444. A constitution was issued at Ravenna. II, 927.

The example of Razius, who killed himself, does not help the Donatists. II, 931; IX, 728, 730. What it warns us about. IX, 730. Razius’s deed was great, but not good. II, 932. Scripture relates it but does not praise it. II, 931. In what sense Razius is praised in Scripture. IX, 729. Razius was not a wise man choosing death, but one impatient of enduring humility. II, 932.

What guilt is and where it resides. X, 860. The distinction between the guilt of sin and the punishment of sin—that is, between sin and the punishment of sin. I, 609. The guilt of sin. X, 430. Guilt is not removed except after baptism. X, 854. God allows the things whose guilt he removes to remain as a trial of faith. X, 182.

The error of those who rebaptize is refuted. III, 778. Why one must not be rebaptized. IX, 30. Rebaptism is something worse than death. IX, 319. To rebaptize is a grave crime. IX, 55. To rebaptize a heretical person who has received the signs of holiness transmitted by Christian discipline is altogether a sin. II, 95. The Donatists rebaptize Catholics, although among the heretics themselves the Church universal has agreed not to invalidate baptism. VIII, 43. The Donatists’ rebaptism is mocked in the party of Donatus. IX, 98. The Donatists did not dare to rebaptize those who had been baptized in Maximian’s schism. II, 800. Those who come over from the Donatists to the Church are not rebaptized, but must do penance. II, 803, 811. See Baptism, Donatists, Rebaptizers. V, 291, 293.

What Rebecca prefigured in Jacob’s blessing. V, 38. Rebecca is a figure of the Church. IV, 1673.

Reburrus. VIII, 227.

Recapitulation must be carefully observed in the Scriptures. III, 553.

One departs from God through dissimilarity. IV, 1217.

We have been reconciled to God—not as an enemy is reconciled to an enemy, as though God began to love those whom he had hated. III, 1923. No one is reconciled to God except through Christ. X, 141, 145, 826. Except through love. VI, 191. By keeping Christ’s commandments, we are reconciled to God. VIII, 119. The reconciliation of penitents. VII, 673, 674. Augustine wishes reconciliation to be granted at the danger of death to penitents, even those who retain adulterous unions. VI, 470. Reconciliation is a pledge of peace. VI, 470. A sermon on reconciliation. V, 1054. With what care Augustine worked to reconcile to himself a bishop whom he had offended by harsher letters. II, 623, 624.

Remembrance. The things we learn are not inserted into us as though they were new, but are recalled to memory through remembrance—an idea attributed to Socrates. II, 68.

Right actions are not right when the heart is not rightly directed. IV, 991. Actions are right when their end is love. IV, 1148. “Being upright, you will meet the Upright One, and without doubt God will please you.” V, 317. Who are upright in heart. III, 1605, 1625; IV, 104, 273, 275, 277, 278, 595, 770, 771, 991, 996, 1206, 1883. See Heart. A person is upright when, in the good that he does, God pleases him; but in the evil that he suffers, God does not displease him. IV, 883. However upright you may seem to yourself, God brings forth a rule from his treasury, fits you to it, and you are found crooked. IV, 1849. Those upright and not upright in heart. V, 317. By loving what is right we are corrected, so that, being upright, we may cleave to what is right. II, 672.

Ruler. V, 420. The dangers of the Church’s rulers. IV, 1425, 1426.

To reprove. In reproving God’s more sluggish steward, nothing is more effective than fear of a harsh word. V, 961.

Six distinctions among those who render, or do not render, good or evil. IV, 1432.

To redeem time. V, 122, 910.

The benefit of redemption. V, 1185. The mystery of Christ’s redemption was not absent in any former age. VII, 221. See Salvation. The mystery of redemption proclaimed in its various meanings. VII, 221. Our redemption is elegantly narrated. V, 726, 745. The transaction of our redemption accomplished by Christ. IV, 1321, 1925. See Christ. We have been redeemed by the blood of the Son of God. V, 153. He who redeemed us at so great a price does not wish those whom he bought to perish. V, 153.

A return to the former life of sin is forbidden. VII, 509. A person returns to something worse when he returns to himself. IV, 978.

The necessity of refreshment must be distinguished from the lust of gluttony. X, 771. Refreshments are daily medicines for necessities. IV, 1320. Seek refreshment from him by whom you were made. IV, 1855.

To reform. He who formed us is himself the one who reforms us. IV, 524.

Reformation begins with confession and is completed through good works. IV, 1908.

God is our refuge. IV, 234, 515, 878. Human regeneration is twofold. VII, 663, 667; X, 689. The benefit of regeneration. V, 1006, 1081. And grace. VII, 379, 506. The benefit of regeneration derives from Christ’s Incarnation. X, 174. The sacrament of our regeneration was intended to be manifest through the manifested Mediator; for the righteous of former times it was something hidden. II, 845. Scripture is silent on whether there was, and what there was, as a sign of regeneration before the Flood. VII, 459. Regeneration appears necessary for everyone except Christ alone. II, 844. A comparison of our regeneration and generation. V, 1081. Regeneration is opposed to generation. X, 188. [Col. 0562] In what manner spiritual regeneration takes place. X, 144, 145. The sacrament of regeneration is baptism. X, 177. Regeneration through Christ leads to justification of life. X, 177. What regeneration accomplishes. X, 187. Generation from the one Adam makes a person liable through one offense; regeneration from Christ removes both that offense and whatever is subsequently added through the wicked works of human conduct. II, 678, 679. Regeneration abolishes all sins at every age. VI, 287, 288. See Baptism. Regeneration, faith, hope, and love are consolations for the wretched in this life, not the joys of the blessed. IV, 1555.

The difference between being ruled and being moved. X, 323. A person who does not correct does not rule. IV, 504. Whom God rules and whom he abandons. X, 324. We are ruled by God in each act when we act rightly. X, 339. The spirit rules, the flesh is ruled; nor does the spirit rule well if it is not itself ruled. V, 915. Rule the earth, and you will be king of the earth. IV, 970.

The region of the living and the dead. V, 295.

To reign is said in two ways. VI, 77, 78. Whether wishing to reign more broadly is compatible with goodness. VII, 124. The desire to reign among the Romans. VII, 43. And in Ninus. VII, 116. When the Lord reigns, each person is so subject that he himself also reigns over his desires. IV, 647.

Earthly kingdoms are established by divine providence. VII, 141. They are granted. VII, 560. They are governed. VII, 154. The division of kingdoms results from desire or usefulness. VII, 560. In the earliest ages it did not follow that firstborn sons succeeded to the kingdom. VII, 464. Kingdoms cannot be given by the gods. VII, 176. Are kingdoms helped or abandoned by the aid of the gods? VII, 117. The one true God alone gives kingdoms. VII, 125. To good and evil, to the devout and the impious. VII, 139, 168. Why. VII, 139, 140. God distributes earthly kingdoms to whomever he wishes, and for as long as he wishes, either by permitting or by granting them. III, 1051. The Romans could not possess a kingdom against the true God’s will, but, after knowing him, they would have possessed it more rightly. VII, 135. God gives Christian emperors prosperous and unfortunate kingdoms; why. VII, 171, 172, 173. The kingdom of the good is useful not so much to themselves as to those over whom they reign. VII, 114. The kingdom of the wicked harms the rulers more. VII, 114. Kingdoms without justice are great robberies. VII, 115. A kingdom grows through another’s iniquity. VII, 124. In what sense the expansion of a kingdom can be called happiness. VII, 124. This is incongruously attributed to Jupiter if Victory is a goddess. VII, 124. To enlarge a kingdom through war is a great robbery. VII, 116, 117. To the wicked this seems happiness, to the good necessity. VII, 124. The form of a just and moderate kingdom. VII, 116.

The three more excellent kingdoms of the nations. VII, 497. Among earthly kingdoms, those of the Assyrians and Romans were more renowned than the rest. VII, 560. The four kingdoms of the world signified by the four beasts in Daniel. VII, 695. Changes of earthly kingdoms were foretold. V, 622. The alteration of the Israelite kingdom was prefigured in the Old Testament through Christ—where. VII, 526, 527. The kingdom of light and darkness, a fabrication of the Manichaeans, is overthrown. I, book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, chapters 3, 4, 5, etc. The rule of a wife. I, 732.

Three kinds of rule over rational creatures. V, 1638. Two kingdoms: one of Christ, the other of the devil. II, 918. The devil’s kingdom consists of those who are divided among themselves. V, 446. The kingdom of Christ is twofold. VII, 673. Christ’s kingdom is in this world, but not of this world. III, 1939. We are the kingdom of God if, believing in him, we make progress in him. V, 388. The kingdom of Christ and of the saints on earth after the separation of the wicked. V, 1197. Note (a). Christ’s kingdom remains undivided even when heresies and schisms arise. V, 446. The kingdom of the saints. VII, 673. And of the Church. VII, 548.

Why the Church is called the kingdom of heaven. VI, 409. The kingdom of heaven—that is, of the saints, who are called heaven. V, 490. The heavenly kingdom and the earthly kingdom are now mingled in this age. IV, 602, 603. The kingdom of heaven was not promised in the Old Testament. VIII, 129, 130. The name “kingdom of heaven” is not found in the ancient books, but in the new ones. VIII, 368. Why it was objected to Pelagius as erroneous that the kingdom of heaven had been promised in the Old Testament. X, 327, 328, 329. Whether it is in fact promised. X, 327. Through the earthly kingdom the righteous of former times imagined and foretold the heavenly kingdom. III, 73. The earthly kingdom of the Jews was a shadow of the heavenly kingdom. IV, 1603.

The kingdom of God, the kingdom of heaven, is still being built. III, 1815. The kingdom of God was promised. V, 641. To whom it was promised. I, 619, 674. Not only heretics, but also those who live wickedly, do not belong to the kingdom of God. IX, 170. Even one crime excludes a person from the kingdom of God. IX, 171. How flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. V, 1619. That a person can never enter the kingdom of God is a great punishment. X, 785. Only through the remission of sins do the baptized reach the kingdom of God. X, 142. Only fellowship with Christ brings one into the kingdom of God. X, 118. Where the kingdom of God is to be understood. X, 518. Outside the kingdom of God there is no eternal life reserved for unbaptized infants. X, 189. Between eternal fire and the kingdom [Col. 0563] of heaven there is no intermediate place of eternal life. V, 872, 1337. The price of the kingdom of heaven. V, 1521. At what different price the kingdom of heaven is bought. IV, 1468. It is worth as much as you possess. IV, 574. It is received in exchange for a cup of cold water. IV, 574. Who possess the kingdom of God. I, 612.

A description of the kingdom of God. I, 612. The kingdom of God is possessed wholly by all together and wholly by each individual. V, 549. Each person has in full what many possess harmoniously. V, 549. Everyone is invited to the kingdom of God. V, 549. We know what will not be there; what will be there we can love and desire, but cannot worthily conceive. V, 1121. There all our activity will be the praise of God. V, 1121. Who is great and who is least in the kingdom of heaven. V, 1168. The kingdom of God does not diminish as the number of its possessors increases, because it is not divided. V, 549. The kingdom of heaven has diverse rewards. VI, 410. What food there will be in the kingdom of heaven. V, 969. We already hold the pledge of Christ’s kingdom: the blood of Christ. V, 840, 848. Who rightly and who wrongly desires the kingdom of heaven. V, 489.

The unchangeable rule is the will of God. IV, 1206. Rules for understanding the Scriptures. V, 26, 30, 556. For understanding passages of Scripture concerning the Son of God. VI, 74. The rule of faith. VI, 259, 290. *Retr.* That is, the Creed. V, 999. Defenders of the Catholic rule. VI, 235.

Regulus. X, 745. Regulus would have brought the First Punic War to an end unless, through excessive desire for glory, he had imposed harsher terms on the Carthaginians. VII, 99. Regulus was captured in the First Punic War. VII, 99. The story of Regulus’s captivity. VII, 28. Regulus’s captivity, oath, and death compel the gods to blush. VII, 99. With what faith Regulus kept his oath to the Africans. VII, 164. Regulus freely endured the most certain tortures and a death of dreadful example rather than perjure himself. II, 475. Regulus judged it a great crime to kill himself. VII, 37. Regulus’s greatness of spirit. VII, 37. Regulus is to be preferred to Cato. VII, 37.

Relatives are sometimes the same, sometimes different. II, 750. In many relative expressions there is no word by which the terms referring to one another correspond mutually. VIII, 919.

For the sake of relaxing the mind, to take some pleasure after great cares is very proper; but to be seized by pleasure is sometimes disgraceful. I, 1086.

Religianus, bishop. II, 966.

The origin of the word “religion.” VII, 280, 281. Religion is so called because it binds us back to God. I, 605; III, 170. Or because it binds us to him. I, 605. What religion is. VI, 20, 21. True religion is that by which the soul, from which it had torn itself away through sin, binds itself back to the one God through reconciliation. I, 1080. An innate impulse implanted religion. VI, 20. The essence of the Christian religion. VII, 219, 220. The service of religion, called in Greek *latreia* (λατρεία), is owed to the Creator alone. II, 378. Whether religion can be offered to anything other than God. VII, 278, 279. The beginning of our religion. V, 237. True religion is inspired and taught by the true God. VII, 179. True religion has been one and the same from the beginning of the human race. II, 375, 379. The Christian religion among the ancients. I, 603. And its salvation was never absent from anyone who was worthy of it. I, 643. How this is to be understood. I, 643. An effective proof of the Christian religion: the prophets’ oracles concerning things dependent solely on God’s will. VII, 316. The faith of the whole world. VII, 760. And the fact that, because of Christ, the victors spared the vanquished. VII, 15. The Christian religion is the one saving religion. VII, 111. It was foretold in the Old Testament and revealed in the New. VII, 314. It was confirmed by various miracles. VII, 314. How religion was founded by Christ. VIII, 88. Where true religion or harmful superstition consists. II, 377. Religion properly has a place only in truth. IX, 748. The truth and marvelous spread of our religion are explained. II, 522. The truth of our religion is proved by the death desired by the Apostles for its sake. V, 1414.

False religions were abolished through the suffering of the martyrs. VII, 136. Error in religion arises from worshiping a creature in place of God. III, 130. There are various kinds of false religion. III, 169. Varro thinks it expedient to be deceived in religion. VII, 134, 137, 138. Deceiving the people in matters of religion was regarded as the business of the wise and prudent. VII, 139. The religion with which we were once imbued as children carries us away to itself even when we are unaware. I, 921.

True religion cannot rightly be entered without faith and without a certain weighty command of authority. VIII, 79. In religion alone these three things are to be followed: faith, hope, and love. VI, 232, 233. Some ridicule the Christian religion because it commands belief in things that are not seen. VI, 171. They are refuted. VI, 171. The holiness of the Christian religion is set against the impure worship of demons. VII, 76. The essence of religion is to imitate the one whom you worship. VII, 242. All religion exists for the sake of the soul. VIII, 75. Human beings cannot be joined into any name of religion, whether true or false, unless they are bound together by some sharing in visible signs or sacraments. VIII, 355. Religion is not sought unless it is believed to exist. VIII, 86. By what path religion can be found. VIII, 91. The incarnate Wisdom of God is the most convenient way to religion. VIII, 88. Religion should be sought among those who excel in widespread renown and in the allegiance of all peoples. VIII, 76. When the true religion is being sought, one must begin from the Catholic Church. VIII, 78. Nothing prevents religion from being sought among Catholics. VIII, 77. True religion is not to be sought among the pagans, nor among heretics, schismatics, or Jews. III, 163. But it is found among Christians. I, 603; III, 103. Whether one should refrain from investigating religion because it is found among only a few. VIII, 76. It is safer to follow the opinion of the majority in religion than the private opinion of one or a few. IX, 142. A person who approaches with a feigned heart is unworthy of religion. VIII, 81. The Christian religion is the royal road to the kingdom. VII, 312. The universal way of liberating the soul. VII, 313. Our religious liberty must not be burdened with servile obligations. II, 221. Our religion is not hostile to the commonwealth, but beneficial to it. II, 529. Even outstanding natural ability is insufficient for accepting religion unless God is present. VIII, 82. In religion there are two praiseworthy persons and three kinds of people to be disapproved. VIII, 83. The pagans’ false oracle concerning the time for which the Christian religion would endure. VII, 617, 618. The pagans complain unjustly about the Christian religion. VII, 65. The Christian religion is prefigured by Hannah, Samuel’s mother. VII, 528.

What distinguishes a religious person from a superstitious one. VII, 187. Augustine mentions a work on the Catholic religion written by him. II, 80, 109.

The relics of the martyrs. VI, 575. Honor divinely bestowed upon the relics of the saints. V, 1255. The relics of the saints are for the consolation of the faithful. V, 1257. They are for memorials of prayers, not for the glory of the martyrs. V, 1257. The relics of the martyr Stephen were transferred to Africa and, because of God’s benefits, became renowned everywhere. V, 1435. The relics of the martyr Stephen were placed in a sacred site. V, 1437.

A reliquary. III, 587, 588. Eve’s reliquary. I, 713.

The same remedy, applied to the same pain of the same person, was beneficial at first but harmful after several years. II, 527. Criminal remedies for recovering health. V, 52. God provides daily remedies through Innocentius. II, 782. Remedies for sins. V, 88, 982, 1207. See Sin.

Reminiscence: what it is. I, 787, 791, 1055, 1175. The Platonic doctrine of the soul’s reminiscence is rejected. I, 601. Plato’s and Pythagoras’s doctrine of reminiscence is refuted. VIII, 1011, 1012.

The remission of sins. VI, 193. The remission of all sins takes place in baptism. V, 41, 53, 390, 454, 752, 1635. Any sins can be forgiven. V, 1551, 1558. Sins are forgiven not by human beings but by God, both through human beings and apart from human beings. V, 599, 600. The remission of sins comes from the Holy Spirit. I, 995. Christ raises dead sinners; the disciples release those who are bound. V, 595. The remission of sins is where the Church is. III, 2062. It is not possessed outside the Church. V, 460, 463, 465. The Holy Spirit forgives sins through the Church. V, 454, 600. The sins we have avoided are to be counted among the debts that have been forgiven. V, 598. After the completeness of the remission of sins, we received the remedy of prayer. V, 752. There is one remission, given once in holy baptism, and another, given daily in the Lord’s Prayer. V, 396. For our sins to be forgiven, they must be forgiven to our brothers. V, 653. Whoever wishes to say effectively, “Forgive us our debts,” must say it truthfully, “as we also forgive our debtors.” V, 396. The daily incense of remission. X, 267. See Debt, Sin.

Remus was killed by his brother Romulus. VII, 82.

No one can be reborn who has not been born. II, 844; X, 177, 178. We are reborn from God and the Church. V, 680. Every human being is destined to perish eternally unless he is reborn. X, 1223.

Renatus, servant of God. X, 532. A monk. I, 653; X, 472, 474, 475. A layman. X, 495. From Caesarea he sent Saint Augustine two books written against his works. I, 653. He carried Optatus’s letter to Augustine in Caesarean Mauretania. II, 857.

The enjoyment of earthly things is attributed to the kidneys; why. IV, 103. When God possesses our kidneys. IV, 1795.

To be renewed in the spirit of the mind means to become spiritual. III, 355, 356. How a person is renewed through Jesus Christ. III, 221. In renewal, how we receive what Adam lost. III, 353, 355, 356. A person is not renewed unless he is renewed through Christ for what previously existed in Adam. III, 352. The complete and full renewal of a person does not take place immediately in baptism. X, 156, 157. The beginning and progress of renewal. X, 156. The order by which the illnesses of old age are healed as newness increases. X, 239. Where we are renewed in the knowledge of God. X, 542. The transition from old things to new takes place when outward things are corrupted and inward things are renewed. IV, 420. We are renewed through imitation of Christ’s passion. IV, 411. Renewal already takes place in the spirit and will later take place also in the flesh. III, 353, 354. Perfect renewal will take place in the resurrection. IV, 420.

The renunciation of Satan in the ceremonies of baptism. X, 408, 427. To renounce the world and the devil. VI, 291. Renunciation of the world and of the ruinous inheritance that comes from Adam. X, 1267.

[Col. 0565] To repair. Unless a person is repaired by God, he remains always in the deep. IV, 1696. The repair of the human being. See Reformation.

To be rejected by God means nothing other than not to be helped. IV, 1512.

Why repetitions occur in the sacred Scriptures. IV, 902, 948, 1219, 1317. Repetitions in books are not useless. IX, 125.
