Many reproach another for what they themselves are thinking of doing. IV, 800. A person who reproves in another what ought not to be reproved harms himself more than the other. II, 247. That reprover is just who has nothing in himself that can be reproved. IV, 590. Reproofs of the wicked benefit the good. V, 1564. One must pray for those who reprove. V, 1564. Quarrelsome enemies are generally more useful than friends who fear to rebuke. II, 248. When it is said that our heart does not reprove us. X, 305. See Correction, Rebuke.

Reprobation. Election is to be attributed to mercy; reprobation to God’s judgment. II, 823. How reprobation is not unjust. VI, 120, 121. The person who is rejected cannot rightly complain of God’s injustice. VI, 122. What God hates in the reprobate. VI, 123. Why one person is delivered and another is not is an inscrutable judgment of God. II, 876, 882. It would be unjust if vessels of wrath were made from a mass that had not been condemned. II, 822, 860. Augustine has not yet discovered where, or from what point, or when souls began to have the merit of condemnation, if they are new and did not yet exist. II, 861. God is not the author of sin in the reprobate. II, 884. The reprobate are abandoned to their own desire so that they may perish. X, 324, 942. When a person is given over to a depraved mind, he inwardly receives the merit of future punishments. IV, 1020. Some of the reprobate receive God’s grace, but they are temporary, do not persevere, abandon and are abandoned. X, 942. Some of the reprobate possess true righteousness for a time, but do not remain in it. X, 928. They are not among the number of the children, even when they are in the faith of the children. X, 928. God’s patience toward the children of perdition is neither empty nor fruitless. X, 1428. The reprobate are, in one respect, among the faithful, and in another respect, are not. III, 1799, 1800. See Predestined. Why the reprobate are created. II, 638, 778, 822, 825, 860, 884. Why God creates those whom he foreknew to be sinners and destined for condemnation. II, 824, 860. God does not withhold either the good of creation or the good of nourishment from those whom he foreknows will be punished with eternal torment. X, 1504, 1505. The reprobate are born and live for the benefit of the elect. VII, 544; X, 792, 1427. God makes good use of the reprobate. X, 1504. The reprobate are mingled with the elect in the Church. X, 611. The reprobate, of different kinds, are punished according to their merits. X, 942. The reprobate instruct the elect through their punishment. VI, 72. They serve the corrective purpose of the elect. VI, 123. God’s wrath, power, and mercy shine forth in the creation of the reprobate. II, 822, 860, 861, 876. Through the reprobate and the elect, God’s riches are made manifest. II, 824, 877. God uses the reprobate to display his grace in the predestined. IV, 1117. In the destruction of the reprobate, God makes known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy. X, 324. God acts very differently toward the reprobate and toward the elect. IV, 1205. God brings none of the reprobate to saving repentance. X, 793. The reprobate are more numerous than the elect; why. II, 861. Why there are so many reprobate. II, 861. See Elect.

The use of divorce among the nations and among the Jews. VI, 379. Why the Lord commanded that a certificate of divorce be given. VIII, 365, 367.

The rest of God. III, 303, 305, 306, 310; VI, 331. It is perceived only by the perfect. III, 306. God’s rest in Zion. IV, 1725. God’s rest from his works. III, 1556, 1557. Why it is mentioned by Scripture. III, 1557. God rested and always works. V, 691. See Rest. God’s rest on the seventh day. V, 80, 691. How it is to be understood that God rested on the seventh day. III, 189, 191. God’s rest signifies cessation from establishing the natures of things, but not from administering them. VIII, 131. God’s rest on the seventh day signifies that labor preceded it. VII, 323. It has no evening. VII, 344. The Lord’s rest on the seventh day signified the future rest that he would give human beings after good works. II, 213. God’s rest is so called because one rests in God. VII, 323, 345. God is said to rest when, by his gift, we rest. II, 213. God loves us so greatly that, because we rest, he says that he rests. IV, 1725.

Rest was not promised to the saints in this world. VIII, 264. The rest promised to us cannot be present in this age. X, 1579. Rest is not found in riches and honors. VI, 329. Nor in bodily entertainments and spectacles. VI, 329. Faith in rest and resurrection was commended in Noah’s ark. VIII, 264. We ought to hope for rest only after good works. III, 1556. Rest is bought through labor. IV, 1212. For eternal rest one would have to undertake eternal labor. IV, 372. Where there is rest, there is sanctification. II, 218. Those who seek no rest until after this life already taste a gentle rest here. VI, 330. God alone is the soul’s rest. I, 661, 732. Rest is loved everywhere, but certain and holy rest is found in God alone. [Col. 0566] II, 214. The creature’s rest in God. III, 302, 306, 307, 643. It has a morning but no evening. III, 308, 309. Before the Fall, human rest was in Christ’s divinity, and afterward in his humanity. VI, 331. The soul cannot rest except in what it loves; nor is eternal rest given to it except in the love of God. V, 208. Rest immediately after death. III, 1751. The rest of the saints in eternal life will not be idle. VI, 342, 343. The rest of the blessed is in contemplation of the truth. V, 1633. The angels’ rest is in the Word of God. VI, 331.

The causes of things are seen in the Word of God. VII, 274. Things are not learned through the words themselves. I, 1214. Which things are properly ours. V, 72. The instability of temporal things. I, 1281. It is not things but the people who misuse them who are to be blamed, since from good use one person becomes good and from bad use another becomes bad. I, 1240. Great things, when sought by small people, usually make them great. I, 909. Great things require great men. I, 909.

A rescript. III, 1443.

What the commonwealth is. II, 529. The commonwealth is defined as the people’s affairs. VII, 67, 648. In what sense the name “commonwealth” can apply to the Romans and to other kingdoms. VII, 655. What is the true commonwealth. VII, 655. A commonwealth cannot retain its name without justice. VII, 67, 68. What the commonwealth ought to aim at. II, 670. In what the safety of the commonwealth consists. II, 523; VII, 758. Christian teaching is not hostile to the commonwealth. II, 529. Rather, it brings it great safety. II, 532. The order of the commonwealth, a bond of a certain earthly peace that restrains even sinners, is highly effective. III, 398. In a commonwealth no one should care only for himself, but should diligently care for one another. III, 778. A commonwealth that worships idols is not a commonwealth. VII, 653. No commonwealth has true justice except one whose founder and ruler is Christ. VII, 69. Christ has his own commonwealth. IV, 1911. A commonwealth is not happy when its walls stand while its morals collapse. VII, 45. Nor is it happier because it is larger. VII, 114. The best commonwealth undertakes no war except for faith or safety. VII, 758. A description of the worst and most disgraceful commonwealth. VII, 65. These conditions are to be patiently endured by Christians. VII, 64. The commonwealth has no natural destruction. VII, 758. It was generally said that the commonwealth could not be ruled without injustice. VII, 66. The government of the commonwealth is threefold. VII, 67. Antisthenes said that the commonwealth should be administered by a wise person, while Aristippus said that it should be avoided. VII, 601. The administration of the commonwealth is completed through the agreement of very different people, like harmony. VII, 66. The books *On the Commonwealth* are praised. II, 314. A false opinion about the commonwealth. VII, 67.

To resist. Nothing resists us when we do not resist God. III, 2066.

God is said to regard someone when he has mercy. IV, 295. To look back. V, 476, 621, 622, 1202. It is common usage to use “regard” in the sense of love. IV, 800.

The cord of sins. IV, 1808.

Property belonging to others must be restored. II, 662. The commandment of restitution. III, 720. Sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored. II, 662. Interest must be repaid. II, 664. What court officials may accept and what they are likewise bound to restore. II, 663. An advocate who conducted a bad case is more obligated to make restitution than anyone serving in any other office. II, 664. One should intervene on behalf of thieves, not so that they may avoid restoring what they took—for otherwise one would become an accomplice in the crime. II, 662, 663. Restoring what belongs to others and giving one’s own goods to the poor are distinguished. II, 663. If someone is tortured because he is thought to possess something that he should return, even if he does not possess it, there is no injustice. II, 662. Nevertheless, in the very uncertainty, merciful people do not wish certain punishments to be inflicted for uncertain money. II, 662. Bishops rebuke some persons unwilling to make restitution secretly, others publicly; they even deprive some of communion at the holy altar. II, 662. No one can restore the price with which Christ bought us, so as to take us away from him. I, 778.

The restored Carthaginian basilica. V, 132, 185, 559, 643, 1257.

Restitutus was created by Primianus as Donatist bishop in place of Salvius of Membresa. IX, 579. Before the day of the delay granted to the twelve bishops who had adhered to Maximian had elapsed, he was ordained. II, 413. Restitutus clashed with Salvius Membresitanus over the small buildings and little fields, in order to drive him from the properties. IX, 592. Nor was he regarded as contentious. IX, 592. The advocate Nummasius spoke against Maximian on behalf of Restitutus. II, 412.

Restitutus, a presbyter of Victorianensis, voluntarily became a Catholic. II, 397; IX, 525. What he suffered at the hands of the Donatists. II, 316, 398.

Restitutus the presbyter was killed by the Circumcellions. II, 509, 511.

Restitutus the presbyter, whenever it pleased him, would lie there looking very much like a dead man. VII, 432, 433.

Restitutus and Florentius, bishops of Africa, sailed to the Emperor, against heretics and pagans, by decree of the council held at Carthage. II, 358.

Restitutus the bishop. II, 759, 781.

[Col. 0567] Restitutus, another bishop. II, 759, 781.

Restitutus the deacon and his pious fervor. II, 1065.

How Christ’s resurrection occurred on the third day. VI, 657. The three days of his crucifixion, burial, and raising. II, 215. How the three days of the resurrection are reckoned. VIII, 894. The Lord’s body rose again such as it had been buried. VI, 304. Christ’s body could be reduced in a moment of time to such subtlety that it entered through closed doors. VI, 304. Why Christ, when rising, retained his scars. II, 372. Christ alone rose never again to die. IV, 1673. No one rose before Christ to eternal life. IV, 1642, 1701, 1702. Circumcision was performed on the eighth day to signify Christ’s resurrection. II, 680. Christ’s resurrection was prefigured through circumcision. VIII, 336. It is a great thing to know the power of Christ’s resurrection. V, 922. Our resurrection is more wonderful. V, 922. Neither Magdalene nor the Apostles believed Christ’s resurrection. V, 1147. How Christ was recognized and not recognized after the resurrection. II, 643. The Lord’s resurrection took fear away from the disciples and gave them love. V, 1452. The resurrection was confirmed by Christ’s remaining with the disciples for forty days. V, 1218. In the celebration of Easter, Christ’s cross, burial, and resurrection are to be observed: the Christian ought to bear the cross in the present life; burial and resurrection are borne in hope and faith. II, 215. Christ’s resurrection is celebrated in the first month of the year, called the Month of New Things, because it signifies the renewal of life; it lasts three days because of the time before the Law, under the Law, and under grace; it is celebrated in the third week of the moon to signify perfection. II, 206, 208. The Lord’s resurrection, according to the four Evangelists, is customarily recited on the Paschal days. V, 1107, 1126, 1156. In what order. V, 1108, 1156. What John wrote about it is not read in a single day. V, 1156.

Faith in Christ’s resurrection. VIII, 864. Belief in Christ’s resurrection justifies us. VIII, 336. Why Christ was the first of all to rise. IV, 1162. Christ is the prince of the others who rise. III, 2091, 2092. Christ’s resurrection, his glorification. III, 1805. Christ indicates that his own resurrection and ours will occur at different times. III, 1829, 1830. We know that the resurrection has already occurred in the Head and will occur in the members. IV, 786. Our resurrection has already occurred in Christ. VIII, 251. In whom we had been crucified. III, 2063. We have already risen with Christ through faith. V, 1621. How our resurrection occurs on the third day. IV, 224. In the Lord’s resurrection the restoration of the new human being is signified. III, 2069. In the Lord’s passion and resurrection the passage from this mortal life into another, immortal life is commended. II, 205. Christ’s resurrection signifies new life. IV, 340. It shows us the life to come, just as his passion signifies the present life. IV, 1938. Christ’s resurrection is the strength of the martyrs. IV, 1616, 1617. Christ’s resurrection is the hope of our resurrection. IV, 1700, 1703. The Prophets did not remain silent about the resurrection. VIII, 368.

Isaiah signifies the resurrection of bodies. VII, 691. The Platonists unjustly deny the resurrection. VII, 392, 393. The Sadducees did not believe in the resurrection. VIII, 368. Hymenaeus and Philetus, mentioned by Paul, thought that the resurrection had already occurred. II, 206. The Seleucians do not think that there will be a resurrection, but that it occurs daily in the generation of children. VIII, 41. The Manichaeans denied that bodies would rise again. VIII, 220, 247. In a manner different from that of the Sadducees. VIII, 331. The Manichaeans promised their Hearers not a resurrection but a return to this mortality. VIII, 226. The Origenists reject the resurrection. VIII, 33. Philosophers, even those who excelled among the ancients, are not to be consulted about the resurrection. VIII, 903. Even among Christians one is sometimes found who contradicts the resurrection of the flesh. IV, 944. Resurrection belongs only to rational creation. VI, 650. Before the resurrection of the body, the souls of the saints are at rest. II, 214. All human beings will rise together. III, 1751. Both sexes will rise again. VII, 778. The Lord will bring back the bodies of the saints from every place. IV, 1945. The speed of the resurrection. V, 1624. There is a resurrection of all, but some rise to punishment and others to glory. IV, 1672. The difference between the resurrection of the righteous and that of the ungodly. III, 144. How the Apostle persuades us of the resurrection and of the difference among those who rise. II, 944.

What the resurrection will be like. VI, 650, 651. What the resurrection of the righteous will be like. V, 1614. Each person’s resurrection together with its cause. V, 1453. Some maintained that, by Christ’s death, a resurrection of the righteous had been provided, of the same kind as that promised to us at the end. II, 712. But Augustine does not find this sufficiently convincing. II, 712. What we shall be after the resurrection we shall know when we have become so; before we are so, let us not be presumptuous, lest we not be so. V, 1264. Many have thought that only souls would rise again. V, 1614, 1628. A resurrection of the kind that preceded in Christ is to be hoped for. V, 1616, 1622, 1630.

The resurrection is twofold. V, 591. In spirit and in body. V, 1627. The resurrection of souls and bodies, the goal of Christ’s preaching and dispensation. III, 1585, 1586. In no matter is the Christian faith contradicted so greatly as in the resurrection of the flesh. IV, 1134. The resurrection of the flesh has been denied by some. III, 1551. It is asserted against them. I, 601, 1077, 1170; III, 1554, 1580; V, 712, 713, 1131, 1600, 1603, 1609, 1626, 1629; VII, 754, 771, 795, 796. It is asserted against the Manichaeans. VIII, 247. We have already risen in mind, faith, hope, and charity; what remains is for us to rise in body. IV, 899. The resurrection of bodies is promised. III, 1332. The promised resurrection is opposed to the body’s death. X, 112. The resurrection of the flesh is preceded by the resurrection of the spirit. X, 232. The flesh will rise through the merit of the soul. V, 427. The future resurrection of the flesh belongs to all human beings. VI, 272. The Apostle deals with the death of the body and its resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, etc. X, 1584, 1585, 1586, 1593, 1596, 1601, 1602. This very flesh that is buried will rise again. V, 1192, 1217. The rising flesh will be changed and itself become a heavenly and angelic body. V, 1217. A spiritual body. V, 1142. There are some who think that then the flesh will be converted into God’s substance and will become what God is. II, 320. What our body will be like after the resurrection as a spiritual body. II, 628; III, 2061, 2062; VI, 274. Augustine does not refuse to learn what sort of spiritual body is promised to those who will rise. II, 618, 620, 623. Some think that the body must be changed into spirit. II, 618. Those who think that the spiritual body comes into being when it is changed into spirit are refuted. II, 945. The disadvantages that follow from this opinion. II, 619. Augustine thinks—though not with complete confidence—that the body should then be called spiritual because of a certain ineffable facility. II, 629. This resurrected mortal body is transferred into an angelic condition and a heavenly quality. IV, 1862. To Augustine, the qualities of spiritual bodies are as it were certain: mortality, corruption, and heaviness have been removed from them. II, 623. Other matters about which he is exceedingly uncertain. II, 623. The bodies of the saints will be immortal after the resurrection. V, 840. Because of the merit of righteousness, the body is to be made alive in the age to come—not merely so that it becomes living from dead, but also immortal from mortal. X, 113. See Body.

All will rise incorruptible, but among them the righteous will also be changed into that incorruptibility which no corruption whatsoever can harm. II, 947. After the resurrection the bodies of the saints will be wholly incorruptible, wholly immortal, and wholly agile and ready for movement. V, 1137. The stability of bodies after the resurrection. I, 603, 613, 620. In the bodies of the blessed there will be brightness, and different kinds of brightness, because the merits of charity are different. V, 1138. In the bodies of the blessed there will be beauty complete in every respect. V, 1146. The flesh will rise without defect. V, 1131. If the defects of the flesh will not rise, why are there scars in Christ? V, 1140. The bodies of the pious will rise without any defect, though the same in respect of the substance of the flesh. VI, 274. In bodily stature and appearance there will be nothing unbecoming. VI, 273. We ought to believe that we shall have bodies such that, wherever we wish and whenever we wish, we shall be there. V, 1140, 1143. How an earthly body will be in heaven. V, 1140. The body will easily be lifted into heaven if the burden of sins does not weigh down the spirit. V, 1211. The flesh that now causes you torment will then be your ornament. V, 1132, 1133. Whether the spirit will then need the body’s assistance to see bodily things, Augustine has not yet read anything sufficient for him. II, 629. Even in the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart, according to Ambrose. II, 604, 608. After the resurrection the body will be able to take food, but will not need it. II, 372. After the resurrection there will be the power, as in Christ, but not the necessity, of eating. V, 1139, 1618. The resurrected body would be imperfectly happy if it either needed food or could not take food. II, 372. After the resurrection body and soul will flourish through the Son of God and through the Holy Spirit. III, 133. Why there will be no marriages in the resurrection. IV, 786. The works of the flesh will not be the same after the resurrection. V, 1622. Life will be like that of the angels, without the operations of corruption and need. V, 1623, 1631. Nothing will resist our spirit. IV, 1688. Then true holocausts will be offered. IV, 798. In the resurrection the flesh will be spiritual and yet flesh. VII, 783. Through the glory of the resurrection the body will not lose mortality and corruptibility in such a way that it loses the very thing it is as a body and becomes spirit. II, 619. Then the body will itself be, and will not itself be. V, 840, 849. In the resurrection the bodies will then be spiritual, while all the limbs remain. II, 350. Some bodily members will be for use, others for appearance. V, 1145, 1146. Neither the inner members nor the hearts themselves will be hidden after the resurrection. V, 1145. The transformation of the whole human being for the better is to be completed in the resurrection. VI, 193, 194. Flesh and blood will be changed and become a heavenly and angelic body. VI, 309. It will no longer be flesh and blood, but only body. VI, 195. How superfluous parts will return to the body. VI, 273. The flesh of a human being that has passed into another’s food and flesh will be returned to the one whose it originally was. VI, 273. Various difficulties concerning the size of the bodies that will rise. [Col. 0569] VII, 776, 777. In what size each person will rise. VII, 783. Whether the bodies of all the dead will rise according to the measure of the Lord’s body. VII, 777. Whether aborted fetuses will rise. VI, 272. What was not yet complete will be completed, and what had been corrupted will be restored. VI, 272. Monstrous fetuses will rise with their nature corrected and amended. VI, 272, 273. A two-headed human being will not rise as one person, but as two human beings. VI, 273. Bodies dispersed in whatever ways will be restored whole in the resurrection. VII, 782. Hair and fingernails in the resurrection. VII, 780. From the bodies of those who rise, defects will be removed, but nature will be preserved. VII, 778, 781. The difference between the body before sin and after the resurrection. I, 603. Whether little children who died before or after receiving baptism will rise. II, 730. What the resurrection of little children will be like. V, 1140.

The resurrection of the body is for some a good and for others an evil. V, 709. What the bodies of the condemned will be like when they rise. VI, 274. How will they be incorruptible if they suffer, or how corruptible if they cannot die? VI, 275. What the bodies of the ungodly will be like when they rise. V, 1627. We shall not rise to the sufferings of pains, as the ungodly do, nor to the pleasures of carnal desires. V, 1059. The wicked will rise incorruptible in the integrity of their members, but subject to corruption through the pain of punishments. II, 947. In the resurrection of the dead, the glory of merits will differ. II, 944. After the resurrection the joy of the good will be greater, and the torments of the wicked more severe. III, 1751. The resurrection of bodies is necessary for the soul’s perfect blessedness. III, 483.

The resurrection is called regeneration (regeneratio). IV, 1873; X, 156, 591. Likewise adoption and redemption. X, 591. Complete renewal through the resurrection is the effect of baptism. X, 407. After the resurrection the whole human being, deified, will cling to unchangeable truth. V, 909. Some have thought that a first bodily resurrection and a future sabbath-rest of a thousand years would occur. VII, 667. Augustine once held this opinion. VII, 667. The resurrection is twofold. VII, 665, 666, 675, 690. Only those who will be blessed eternally belong to the first resurrection. VII, 665. The saints await the resurrection eagerly and patiently. VII, 393.

That through Christ’s resurrection the hope of resurrection was brought to us. V, 1607. The resurrection is the hope of our entire faith. VI, 659. The substance of our faith. VI, 650. Faith in the resurrection is characteristic of Christians. IV, 1308, 1609; IX, 673. It distinguishes them from pagans and Jews. V, 808, 1075, 1112, 1115, 1133. Once faith in the resurrection is removed, all Christian teaching collapses. V, 1599.

The possibility of the resurrection of the flesh is argued. IV, 751; VI, 194, 195, 342, 346, 347, 659. How it was argued by Christ. V, 658. Creation ought to give credence to the resurrection. V, 713. And so ought what Christ accomplished. V, 727. Christ raised certain people so that we might be prepared for the general resurrection. III, 1746, 1747. The growth of a tree from a small seed is no less, or perhaps more, marvelous than the earth’s womb returning whole the bodies destined for the future resurrection. II, 372. It is just as easy for God’s omnipotence to raise recent corpses as corpses that have fallen apart over a long period. II, 372. The promise of the resurrection is confirmed by so many other promises of God already fulfilled. V, 1143. Christ’s resurrection, not Lazarus’s, corresponds to the promised resurrection. II, 371. Faith in the resurrection was commended when Job’s children were restored to him—not twice as many, but as many as he had possessed. II, 549. Elijah and Elisha raised the dead. II, 521. Whether the Magi raised the dead. II, 521. The impossibility of the resurrection alleged by unbelievers is refuted by their own philosophers. VII, 794, 796. How the truth of the resurrection of the flesh is elicited from the contrary opinions of Plato and Porphyry. VII, 795. Christ was not compelled by Peter’s magic arts to foretell the resurrection. VII, 793. Christ foretold that the resurrection would be believed by the world. VII, 793. The whole world believed in the resurrection; whoever did not believe remained unclean. V, 658. Faith in the resurrection, plainly proved, is foolishly rejected by human beings. V, 1138. The resurrection was signified in Moses’ rod. VIII, 269. Concern for burial supports faith in the resurrection. VII, 27. The resurrection of the dead does not depend on their burial. III, 592. The resurrection is a benefit of grace. VI, 660. It is a more marvelous power of grace for the righteous to come back from death to eternal blessedness than not to enter into the experience of death. VI, 160. The likeness of the resurrection in the eagle and the moon. IV, 1323. The resurrection is the fruit of Christ’s mediation. VII, 268. Augustine wrote a letter about the resurrection of bodies. II, 631.

What the spiritual resurrection is. III, 1547, 1548. Resurrection according to the spirit, which now occurs through faith. V, 709, 1628. A human being cannot rise by himself when he has fallen by himself. IV, 1696.

Nets cast on the right side after Christ’s resurrection. VI, 304, 305.

[Col. 0570] The Rhaetian grain supply. VII, 575.

Reticius, bishop of Augustodunum, of great authority in the Church. X, 644. He took part in the Roman council at which Donatus, founder of the Donatist schism, was condemned while Miltiades was presiding. X, 644, 1078. His short work on baptism. X, 644.

Augustine notes that he was contemplating a work of Retractations. II, 586. Augustine calls this work exceedingly necessary. II, 1001. Augustine had completed two volumes of the Retractations in the year 418. II, 1001. For what purpose Augustine undertook a revision of his works. I, 585.

Retrarius. V, 621.

The fourfold kind of recompense. IV, 1516. Some recompenses were owed to us, others have been rendered. IV, 1317. God’s recompenses are not evil, since none are anything but just. IV, 1319. What recompenses of God there are toward human beings. IV, 1321, 1322. God repays good for evil, while human beings repay him evil for good. IV, 1493. Unless God repaid good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good. IV, 1517. What difference there is between God’s recompenses and those of human beings. IV, 1317. We are unable to repay anything to God. V, 1184. God does not wish to be repaid from what is yours; he wishes it from what is his. IV, 1318. What a human being ought to repay to God. IV, 1318. Christ repays on our behalf. IV, 1783.

What it means to look back. V, 621. After conversion one may not look back. IV, 874, 968, 1005, 1057, 1058. Whoever abandons the step by which he reached the one toward whom he was advancing looks back. IV, 1058. Who does not look back? V, 622.

What perfect revelation is. VIII, 172. Pelagius acknowledges the revelation of doctrine through the Holy Spirit. X, 381. Paul was strengthened by a revelation concerning his passion. V, 1368. The revelations of Blessed Perpetua. V, 1281, 1284. A revelation made to a military man. VI, 722.

“Revived” means “began to appear.” III, 2070.

The return of all things to the same order and the same appearance is not to be admitted. VII, 362. By what arguments philosophers prove that it ought to be admitted. VII, 366, 367. The answer made to them. VII, 366, 367.

A guilty person does not make another guilty. IV, 382. Whoever wishes to commit a crime is guilty before God even if he does not commit it. IV, 1662. Every human being considers it his responsibility to intercede for another. II, 657. It is the duty of the priesthood to intercede for the guilty. II, 653. This derives from religion. II, 655. With what disposition priests intervene for the guilty. II, 655. Those guilty persons who are freed from punishment through a priest’s intercession are nevertheless excluded from fellowship at the altar. II, 656. Augustine intercedes for the guilty so that an opportunity may be given them to correct their conduct. II, 655, 656. Judges ought to be moved by compassion toward the guilty, because they themselves also need compassion. II, 657. Christ found all people guilty. V, 201.

King. To rule. God rules the obedient and crushes those who resist. IV, 693.

“King” was originally the name of sovereign power. VII, 86. Kings are better named from ruling than from reigning. VII, 154. The first just men were appointed shepherds of animals rather than kings of human beings. VII, 643. It is easy to find someone who fears becoming king; no one wishes not to be happy. VII, 130. In former times kings and priests were anointed. IV, 1952. The anointing of kings is a type of Christ. VII, 543. The pursuits of the first kings of Rome. VII, 86. The duties of Christian kings. IX, 527. Kings serve the Lord both as human beings and as kings. II, 801. In one way as human beings, in another as kings. II, 801. How kings ought especially to serve God. IX, 330. You owe obedience to the king so that you may be able to rule. V, 715. Kings serve the Lord in fear by forbidding and punishing with religious severity whatever is done against the Lord’s commands. II, 801. It belongs to religious kings of the earth to restrain with appropriate severity not only adulteries, murders, and other such disgraceful acts or crimes, but also sacrileges. II, 940. A king can impose new commands on his subjects. I, 690. And it is a sin not to obey him. I, 690. When a king commanding something according to truth is resisted, truth is contradicted. IX, 105. Kings can issue edicts in favor of religion, as the faithful of old acknowledged. II, 399. It makes no difference under which king a person lives, provided he is not compelled to impious acts. VII, 160, 161. Catholics who make good use of friendship with Christian kings commit no sin. IX, 324. “The kings of the world have never experienced Christianity except as envious”: Petilianus’s statement, which is refuted. IX, 325, 326. Christians owe honor and obedience even to unjust and unbelieving kings. IV, 1653, 1654. Christ and his disciples also commanded by their own example that obedience be shown to kings. IV, 1591. Amid honors, kings should not forget that they are human beings. VII, 171. The greater their earthly exaltation, the more they ought to humble themselves before God. IV, 1779. A human being is king over human beings in human matters, but another is king in divine matters. IV, 647. The earthly king is under the heavenly King; the heavenly King is above all. IV, 647. The Jews sinned not because they said they had Caesar as king, but because they refused to have Christ as king. IV, 647. In Scripture the Son of God is usually called by the name “King,” rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit. IV, 84. Christ is our King. IV, 200. In the Church those who rule the desires of the flesh are called kings. III, 865; IV, 826. Description of the reigning king of the Manichaeans. VIII, 307, 309.

Rhadagaisus. V, 224. How the king of the Goths was defeated by the Romans in a single day, with great slaughter of his own men. VII, 169. The pagans boasted that Rhadagaisus could not be defeated because he worshiped the gods. VII, 170.

Rhadamanthus, son of Xanthus, from Europe. VII, 569. Judge among the dead. VII, 72.

Rhamnus, a kind of thorn, a figure of sin. IV, 689.

Rhea, or Ilia, the mother of Romulus. VII, 578. She is said to have conceived twins by Mars. VII, 578. See Sylvia.

How a rhetorician and a dialectician differ. IX, 457.

Rhetoric, victorious loquacity. I, 693. The invention of rhetoric. I, 1013. Its usefulness. III, 60, 61, 89. The precepts of rhetoric ought to be learned quickly by adolescents. III, 90. See Eloquence. Augustine teaches rhetoric. I, 693. At Thagaste. I, 695. At Carthage. I, 711. At Rome. I, 716. At Milan. I, 717. He abandons the profession. I, 763.

The heresy of Rhetorius, of extraordinary vanity. VIII, 44.

Rhinocorura, a city. III, 787; VII, 503.

What rhythm is. I, 1014. Rhythm is called numerus in Latin. I, 1014. The name “rhythm” has a broad application in music. I, 1116. At length, on rhythm. I, 1115.

The times for laughing and fearing must be distinguished. IV, 608. Laughter and weeping. V, 945. Laughter is the lowest characteristic of the human being. I, 1231. Reason must precede laughter. I, 913. Nothing is uglier than laughter deserving of mockery. I, 913. Laughter and joking delight only through a carnal feeling. X, 148.

Watering signifies weeping down to the inmost depths of the heart. IV, 94.

Ritanus, a Maximianist bishop. IV, 381.

A peaceful quarrel of doves. V, 426. The lust for quarrelling must be avoided. III, 58. There are quarrels even among the saints, but they do not destroy charity. IV, 318, 319.

Rogatianus, a Donatist. II, 399; IV, 376, 381.

Rogatianus of Nova. IX, 233.

Rogatus the Moor, III, 1470. Bishop of Cartenna. II, 301, note 1. Founder of the Rogatensians. II, 326. Or, the founder of a single schism within the party of Donatus. IX, 45, 46. Ordained in the place of Praetextatus of Assur. IX, 530, 704. Because of his defection from the Donatists, he suffered much at their hands. II, 361, note 1; IX, 316. The cruelty of the Circumcellions toward him. IX, 530, 704. Rogatus engaged in the legal dispute with the greatest ferocity. II, 326. Rogatus is now a Catholic. IX, 704. Rogatus lived in Augustine’s time. II, 320. Rogatus’s successor was Vincentius. II, 320.

The Rogatists. V, 769. Or the Rogatensians. II, 301. So called from Rogatus. II, 325. A fragment of a fragment, cut off from a larger fragment. II, 333. The Rogatensian schism did not arise before the year 361. II, 326, note 1. The Rogatists rashly cut themselves off from the Church. II, 333, 334. The Rogatists boast that they are neither earthly nor in the earth, but heavenly; Christ will find faith only among them. II, 345. The Donatists persecuted the Rogatists. IX, 46. The Rogatists called the Donatists Firmians. II, 302. The Rogatensians seem milder than the other Donatists, but are so only because they lack power. II, 326.

The Rogatensians, few in number in Caesarean Mauretania. IX, 422, 588.

Rome was founded by the Trojans. V, 505. By the descendants of Aeneas. VII, 80. By Romulus and Remus. V, 505; VII, 82. The authors do not agree about the date on which the city of Rome was founded. VII, 80, note (a). In what year of the reigns of Judah and Israel Rome was founded. VII, 578. And in what year of Numitor’s reign. VII, 578. Rome’s beginnings: an asylum for criminals and Romulus’s fratricide. III, 1050. After expelling the kings, Rome grew enormously in an incredibly short period. VII, 62. Rome, the capital of the nations. V, 166, 1684. Rome had thirty-five popular curiae. IV, 1624. Roman forums and Greek gymnasia are distinguished. II, 436. The expertise of the Romans. V, 1085. Rome was captured, plundered, and burned by the Goths. VII, 70, 96.

The first fire at Rome was caused by the Gauls, and the second by Nero. V, 1356. The public fire at Rome. VII, 99. Camillus freed Rome from the Gauls. VII, 117. Rome’s destruction by the Goths. VII, 469. Rome was overthrown by the Goths’ invasion under King Alaric. I, 647. It was devastated by a barbarian incursion. II, 485. The disaster inflicted on the Roman people during the first siege of the city by Alaric at the end of the year 408. II, 365 and note (a). Rome was captured and plundered by Alaric. VII, 14, 15, and note, and 19, 20. The third fire at Rome was caused by the Goths. V, 1356. God’s mercy tempered Rome’s destruction. VII, 45. The humanity of the barbarians toward most of the Romans. VII, 45. Those who had fled to holy places were spared. VII, 14, 15, and note, and 45, 48. Rome’s slaughter and destruction. VI, 718. Whether God truly spared the city. VI, 718, 721, 723. Whether there were then no righteous people at Rome for whose sake the city might be spared. VI, 718. The merciful acts performed during the city’s overthrow under Alaric are to be attributed to Christ. [Col. 0572] VII, 19, 20, 48. Rome’s devastation was falsely attributed to the Christian religion, or to the destruction of idolatry. V, 505, 623, 624, 1355. Rome was called a city for sale. II, 532. Rome was like a second Babylon. VII, 561, 578. The bodies of Peter, Paul, Laurence, and other martyrs were at Rome. V, 1355. Paulinus travels to Rome every year. II, 355.

The Romans descended from the Trojans. VII, 79, 81. And from the Laurentines. VII, 572. The houses of Aeneas and Assaracus were called Roman. III, 533; VII, 462. The life of the Romans under the kings. VII, 92. The beginnings of the Roman Empire under Numa Pompilius were peaceful for forty years. III, 800, 801. Under Numa’s reign the Romans enjoyed complete peace for thirty-nine years. VII, 84, 85. This was not due to the favor of the gods. VII, 85. What dreadful ends the Roman kings met. VII, 92. After expelling Tarquin, the Romans were freed from royal domination. VII, 583. Unable to endure kings, the Romans created consuls. VII, 154, 155. How greatly the Roman Empire grew in a short time under the consuls. VII, 154, 155. What the victories of the Romans were like from the time of the consuls onward. VII, 95. The Romans’ shameful treaty with the Samnites. VII, 97. The Romans borrowed Solon’s laws from the Athenians. VII, 60, 96. They also tried to improve them. VII, 60. By what right the Romans could claim for themselves the name both of “people” and of “state.” VII, 655. They had two illustrious orders, the equestrian and the senatorial. VII, 108. With what care the Romans examined those to be admitted to the Senate. II, 475. The most noble Roman men: Reguli, Scaevolas, Scipios, and Fabricii. VII, 77. The Romans were exempted from punishment by rods. VII, 63, note 1. The Roman republic never truly existed. VII, 648. From what time the Roman republic began to decline. II, 532. By what evils the Roman republic was harassed after the beginnings of consular rule. VII, 95. By what internal evils it was agitated. VII, 104. And how it in a certain way broke itself through its own greatness. VII, 607. Cicero’s opinion of the Roman republic. VII, 66. He mournfully laments its loss. VII, 67, 68. Sallust says more about the vices of the Roman republic. VII, 64. Sallust said that justice and goodness prevailed among them by nature no less than by laws. VII, 61, 62. At first from love of liberty, and later also from desire for domination and ambition for praise, the Romans accomplished many great things. VII, 155. Two things drove the Romans to remarkable deeds: liberty and the desire for praise. VII, 162. The first year of Roman liberty was funereal and Tartarean. VII, 95. Caesar Augustus wrested from the Romans, by every means, even their already feeble liberty. VII, 103. The Romans foolishly thought that the strength and stability of their empire were indicated by auspices. VII, 135. The fates of the Romans were sung by the Sibyl. III, 1054. Prefects are appointed by the Roman Empire over certain parts of Africa. II, 922. The Romans did no harm to the peoples whom they subdued and upon whom they imposed their laws. VII, 160, 161. They imposed not only their yoke but also their language on the peoples they conquered. VII, 634. All who belonged to the empire were counted as Roman citizens. VII, 161. The greatness of the Roman Empire was caused neither by chance nor by fate. VII, 141. Could the Roman Empire not have been great unless it was troubled by wars? VII, 85. The Romans impiously waged war against the Albans. VII, 89. And unjustly. VII, 90. The Romans’ war with the Etruscans. VII, 94. Various conspiracies of enemies against the Romans. VII, 97. The Romans were forced to form an army from slaves and criminals and to remove weapons from the temples. VII, 100. The Roman treasury failed to provide the soldiers’ pay. VII, 100. By how many disasters the Romans were worn down during the Punic Wars. VII, 98. And by Hannibal. VII, 100. By how many wars they were afflicted after the temple of Concord was founded. VII, 106. Roman armies were routed by the enemy. VII, 97, 168. A catalogue of Roman calamities. VII, 96. In their calamities they received no help from their gods. VII, 96. The overthrow of their homeland did not correct the Romans. VII, 45. The power of gladiators was terrifying to the Roman Empire. VII, 115. The boundaries of the Roman Empire were changed under the Emperors Hadrian and Julian. VII, 135. And under Jovinianus. VII, 136.

The Roman nobility was devoted to idolatry. I, 750. Rome was imprudently entrusted to the Iliac gods. VII, 84. How foolishly the Romans entrusted the city of Troy to the Penates for safekeeping. VII, 16. The gods of the Romans were innumerable. VII, 118. Apart from Numa’s constitution, the Romans added many gods. VII, 87. They established certain gods for themselves not by reason but by flattery. VII, 60. Juno together with Jupiter, and Venus as well, favored the Romans. VII, 88. The Romans built shrines to pallor and fever. III, 1053. They advise that good demons (ἀγαθοὺς daemonas) be invited and evil demons (κακοὺς daemonas) be appeased. III, 1053. They were accustomed to make the gods of the nations they conquered favorable to them by worshiping them. III, 1050. Why they refused to accept the God of the Jews. III, 1050. They are pressed by these arguments. III, 1053. They did not accept the God of the Hebrews because he wished to be worshiped alone. III, 1053. Even gods worshiped elsewhere among the nations were called Roman gods. V, 166, 505. The multitude of gods helped the Romans not at all. VII, 87. It is shown that the gods were not the guardians of the Romans’ prosperity and glory. VII, 101. The Roman Empire was flourishing. VII, 560. It cannot be said to have been established, increased, and preserved by the gods. VII, 119, 154, [Col. 0573] Why the Romans think that their empire was increased and established by Jupiter. VII, 124. Why God permitted the Roman Empire to reach such great glory. VII, 166. The Roman Empire was ordered by the true God. VII, 167. It is proved that Rome was not unhappy because it ceased to worship the gods. VII, 29. The Romans did not receive rules for living from their gods. VII, 60. The gods never showed any concern lest the Roman republic perish because of its evil morals. VII, 69, 71, 72. The Romans were wiser than their gods. VII, 59. The gods were cast down at Rome. V, 166.

Romans, while Carthage stood, lived according to excellent morals and in the greatest harmony. VII, 62. The Roman state rested on ancient morals and men. VII, 68. The virtues and vices of the ancient Romans. VII, 157. The Romans most eager for praise. VII, 58. And for domination. VII, 43. By what stages they reached this lust for ruling. VII, 43. They became famous in war and domination all the more because they gave themselves less to pleasures and greed. VII, 155–156. Venus did not preside over the first marriages of the Romans, but Bellona or Allecto. VII, 88. By what right and under what treaty they obtained their first marriages. VII, 88. Roman women afflicted by a severe pestilence. VII, 98. The morals of Roman matrons more grievous than the pestilence. VII, 97. The Romans long knew nothing of theatrical arts. VII, 58. By taking away from poets the freedom regarding human beings that they had granted regarding the gods, the Romans formed a better judgment of themselves than of the gods. VII, 56, 58. The Romans preferred to forgive an injury received rather than pursue vengeance. II, 529. The common people, who had no fields of their own, lived among the Romans from public resources. VII, 161. The Romans praised because of certain deeds resembling good works. II, 982. How much civil virtues accomplished in the Roman empire even without the true religion. II, 533. By what morals the Romans deserved that the true God should enlarge their empire, although they did not worship him. VII, 154. God repaid the Romans’ good morals with human glory as their reward. VII, 160–161. The Romans carried away nothing from their victories except empty glory. VII, 161. The virtues praised in the earliest Romans belonged to a few, not to all. VII, 157. How corrupt in morals the Romans were before Christ’s coming. VII, 64, 67, 69, 74. Various examples of Roman injustice. VII, 61. The Romans unjustly attribute evils to the Christian religion. VII, 43, 45, 46, 64, 68, 69. The evils that befall the Roman empire through certain Christian emperors are wrongly cast back upon Christian doctrine. II, 532. The Romans did something more difficult for their earthly fatherland than what is required of Christians for their heavenly one. VII, 162. The Romans’ ingratitude toward Christ. VII, 15, 48.

The succession of Roman pontiffs from Peter to Anastasius. II, 196. The authority of the Roman see. II, 781. In condemning heretics. II, 865, 869. In the Roman Church the primacy of the Apostolic See has always flourished. II, 163. The Fathers of the Council of Carthage judged that their decree against the Pelagians ought to be communicated to Innocent, the Roman pontiff. II, 760. Through Julius, the Fathers of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, together with five bishops, write to Innocent, the Roman pontiff. II, 782, 785, 788, 816. The Roman bishop is ordained by the bishop of Ostia. IX, 642. No Eastern Catholic ever wrote to the bishop of Carthage while bypassing the Roman bishop. IX, 516. At Rome, in the time of Innocent, the Pelagians did not dare either to defend Pelagius or to proclaim his doctrines. II, 788. There some favored Pelagius because they defended his doctrine; others because they did not believe that he had taught it. II, 765. In judgments the Apostolic See inclines toward mercy. II, 955. The practice of appealing from the judgments of African bishops to the Apostolic See. II, 955. The care of all the churches remains with the Roman see. Innocent. II, 786. The custom of consulting the Roman see about difficult matters has always been observed throughout the whole world. Innocent. II, 786. The concerns and occupations of the Roman Church, by which it responds to the consultations of different people. Innocent. II, 785. It handles consultations with faithful and moderate discussion. Innocent. II, 785. What can benefit all the churches throughout the world in common is referred to the Apostolic See. Innocent. II, 782, 786. When a difficulty arose, Augustine wished to discuss it in a council or even to write to the Apostolic See. II, 1068. Roman censure against certain people who had evaded an oath. II, 475. After a Roman judgment, a plenary council remains. II, 170. The Roman council concerning the case of Caecilianus. IX, 643. The Roman populace was accustomed to fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. II, 139. The Romans do not think that one should fast on Thursday. II, 139. New pilgrims continually come to Rome. II, 119. Daily drunkenness in the basilica of Blessed Peter there. II, 119. This basilica is removed from the bishop’s way of life. II, 119.

**Romanianus, bishop.** II, 781.

**Romanianus.** II, 80. Of Thagaste. I, 731. A relative of Alypius. II, 110. Father of Licentius. II, 111. Romanianus’ outstanding character. I, 906. His studies. I, 908. Romanianus’ abundant wealth. I, 731, 902, 906. Romanianus consoles Augustine, who had been deprived of his father; assists him; and, when Augustine was traveling to Carthage for the sake of his studies, received him into his house and supplied his expenses. [Col. 0574] I, 920. Romanianus became a Manichaean through Augustine’s influence. I, 908. Compelled by business to come to Milan, to the emperor’s court, while Augustine was teaching there. I, 730. Augustine urges Romanianus toward philosophy. I, 908, 919, 920. He proposes the example of his son Licentius, already a philosopher. I, 921. Romanianus is finally inflamed by Licentius’ enthusiasm for study. I, 921. Although he was held back by two obstacles from finding the truth. I, 922. Augustine envies him because he alone enjoyed his Lucilianus. I, 922. Romanianus, entangled in vexatious lawsuits, is inflamed by ardor for the blessed life. I, 920. Having been immersed in the world, he is rescued by adverse fortune. I, 908. Augustine promises to write for him a short work on true religion. I, 922; III, 128. He arranged for it to be published with Romanianus’ name inserted. I, 922; III, 128. Augustine praises Romanianus. I, 919. He recalls the benefits Romanianus had conferred upon him. I, 919–920. Romanianus is likewise praised in the book *On True Religion*. II, 109. Paulinus sends five blessed loaves to Romanianus and Licentius. II, 126.

**Romanus**, sent to Africa against the Donatists, acted according to the laws enacted against them. IX, 362.

**Romanus, bishop.** II, 759.

**Romanus and Agilis.** Paulinus commends them to Augustine. II, 121. Augustine receives them with great pleasure. II, 122. Augustine greets Romanus and Agilis. II, 159.

**Rhomphaea** (ῥομφαία), what it is. IV, 1955.

**Romulus.** II, 529. Son of Mars by Ilia Silvia, the Vestal. VII, 60, 61, 81. Whether Romulus and Remus were nourished by a she-wolf. VII, 578. Romulus, founder of Rome. V, 505, 623. Romulus called Quirinus. VII, 60. Romulus an imitator of Cain. VII, 441. He killed his brother so that one man alone might possess the whole domination. VII, 441. After killing his brother, Romulus ruled at Rome. VII, 91. Romulus was the fifteenth king in Latium after Aeneas. VII, 577. Some say that the Senate tore Romulus to pieces because of his savagery. VII, 91. Romulus made a god. VII, 577, 581. How. VII, 91–92. The Romans raised Romulus to the immortal gods through goodwill and fame. III, 1056. The writings maintain that Romulus was believed to be a god, not that he was made one. VII, 758. Roman flattery toward Romulus. VII, 91. The Romans preferred Romulus to many gods. VII, 60. They established a flamen for him. VII, 60. Romulus had not even one martyr when he was believed to be a god. VII, 758–759. Romulus is counted among the demigods. VII, 58–59. More private Roman doctrine commends him as a demigod rather than a god. VII, 60. Romulus’ divinity was remarkably believed because he became a god in an educated age. VII, 757. Rome believed in Romulus’ divinity not through the love of error, but through the error of love. VII, 757. Romulus’ divinity is set against the divinity of Christ. VII, 757. And it is rejected. VII, 758. The peoples subject to Rome called Romulus a god so as not to offend Rome. VII, 757–758.

**Dew**, whence it comes. III, 285. The dew of Hermon signifies God’s grace. IV, 1735.

**Rosae virgines** (“virgins of the roses”). II, 694.

**Roscius**, an actor. III, 1068.

**The wheel** is the world. IV, 981.

**Rotavia.** IX, 511.

**Rubigo**, goddess. VII, 129.

What *rubigo* signifies. IV, 1000.

The bush not burned although a flame clung to it: what it signifies. V, 63.

**Rucatensis, bishop.** II, 313.

The Manichaean delirium that the foods they ate were cleansed by their own belchings. VIII, 226.

**Rucuma.** IX, 228.

**Ruferius**, related to Armentarius. II, 483.

**Rufinianus, bishop.** II, 759, 781.

**Ruffinus**, consul. IX, 687.

**Ruffinus**, chief man of Cirta. II, 537.

**Ruffinus, presbyter.** X, 387. He published the sayings of the philosopher Sextus under the name of Saint Xystus, pope and martyr. I, 647, note (c). He offered a little book to Pope Anastasius. II, 719. Jerome wrote against him. II, 719. Ruffinus is called by the fictitious name Calpurnius Lanarius. II, 238. The friendship of Ruffinus and Jerome was known to almost all the churches. II, 248, 276. Augustine laments the discord that arose between them. II, 277. He wasted away with grief when he read Jerome’s *Apology against him*, although he admits that Jerome had moderated himself. II, 250. Ruffinus translated into Latin the ecclesiastical history that Eusebius wrote in Greek. VI, 597. He added two books to this history of Eusebius. VIII, 46.

**Ruffinus, deacon.** II, 630.

**Ruffinus, a Donatist bishop.** IX, 528, 555.

**Ρύγκος**, nose. VIII, 42.

**Ruma**, that is, a breast. VII, 203.

**Rumina**, goddess. VII, 122, 191, 203.

What it means to ruminate spiritually. VIII, 234. What is heard must be ruminated upon. IV, 525, 713.

**Ruminus**, Jupiter so called because he nourished animals at the breast. VII, 203.

[Col. 0575] **To weed grain**, that is, to remove it from the earth. VII, 118.

**Runcina**, goddess placed in charge of grain when it is hoed. VII, 118–119.

**Rusina**, goddess placed in charge of the countryside. VII, 118.

**Rusor**, god. VII, 243.

**Russica, Russicadia.** IX, 235, 386, 511.

**Rusticianus**, deacon of Mutigensis. IX, 754. A subdeacon in the Catholic Church. IX, 755. Excommunicated by his own presbyter, he flew over to the Donatists. II, 417. By them he was both rebaptized and made a deacon. IX, 755.

**Rusticianus, bishop.** II, 759, 781.

**Rusticus**, Saint Augustine’s cousin. I, 962.

**Rusticus**, whose son was a pagan. II, 1070.

**Rusticus, presbyter.** II, 966.

Letter to Rusticus and Felicitas. II, 958.

**Rusticus, bishop.** II, 759, 781.

**Another Rusticus, bishop.** II, 759, 781.

**Rusticus**, bishop of Cartenna. IX, 697.

Ruth, married twice: whether the widow Anna was more blessed. VI, 435.

## S

**Sabbatarius.** II, 146.

The rest of the Sabbath. V, 691. It is not without significance that, among all the works God made, sanctification first resounded there where he rested from all his works. X, 217. In the Law sanctification is mentioned only on the seventh day. V, 1170. Seneca criticizes the Sabbaths of the Jews. VII, 192. Faustus wrongly called the leisure of the Sabbaths a Saturnian chain. VIII, 346. Where the observance of the Sabbath began and where it ended. V, 1090. The spiritual and bodily observance of the Sabbath. V, 69, 77, 80, 85, 208, 752, 1160. Whoever still observes the Sabbath in the present age according to the sound of the letter understands it carnally. X, 216. Why the man who gathered sticks on the Sabbath was stoned at God’s command, although Christ healed the sick on the Sabbath. VIII, 167. Abuse of the Sabbath among the Jews. IV, 281. It would have been better for them to spend the Sabbath digging all day than dancing. IV, 281, 1172. What the observance of the Sabbath signified. X, 217–218. In this figurative command only what pertains to the Sabbath was hidden. X, 217. What the Sabbath’s cessation prefigured. VII, 323. The sacrament and mystery of the Sabbath. II, 212–213; III, 189, 1556. The bodily cessation of the Sabbath is a shadow of things to come. VIII, 334. The Sabbath was commended as bodily observance in leisure, so that it might be a figure of sanctification in the rest of the Holy Spirit. II, 212–213. The Sabbath observed by the Jews signified the height of grace. III, 655. Spiritual rest. III, 304–305; VIII, 132. It was a sign of the eternal Sabbath. IV, 396. The Sabbath signifies rest; the Lord’s Day, the resurrection. IV, 1960. The great Sabbath truly exists in blessedness. VII, 803. That Sabbath will have no evening. VII, 803–804. We ourselves shall be that true Sabbath. VII, 803–804. The seventh-day Sabbath without evening, a sign of everlasting rest. V, 37. The Sabbath of Sabbaths. V, 80, 208. The perpetual Sabbath. V, 1631. The Sabbath-rest of the saints on earth. V, 1197. The Sabbath signifies spiritual rest. II, 214.

**The spiritual Sabbath.** III, 1717. The spiritual Sabbath of Christians. III, 305; VIII, 131, 359. How Christians celebrate the Sabbath. VIII, 157. The command to observe the Sabbath spiritually. III, 1404. The Jews observed it slavishly. III, 1404, 1556. To rest on the Sabbath may perhaps already be superstitious. II, 143. Why the Christian no longer observes the Sabbath’s leisure. VIII, 353. The cessation of Sabbaths is now superfluous for observance, though not for reading and understanding. VIII, 230. The Sabbath’s cessation has its meaning among the prophecies written about Christ. VIII, 335. On the Sabbath the apostles did not rest, and they ate on the Sabbath. II, 142. The Lord prescribed nothing to the Hebrews concerning foods to be eaten or not eaten on the Sabbath. II, 142. The Lord’s Day is preferred to the Sabbath through faith in the resurrection, not through a custom of refreshment, and so forth. II, 146. The Christians’ Sabbath consists in the leisure and tranquility of a good conscience. IV, 1172. He truly observes the Sabbath who does not sin. V, 1242. A wicked person cannot possess the Sabbath. IV, 1172. Christ intimated the Sabbath through mercy, judgment, and faith. III, 1330. The Sabbath day, a day of joy. II, 142. Those who hunger for the word of God are especially accustomed to meet on Saturday. V, 716. What it means to remember the Sabbath. IV, 396. The special rite of Holy Saturday is confirmed in the Gothic liturgy. II, 399. The Lord’s Day is called the first day of the week; Monday, the second day of the week, and so on. IV, 532, 1192, 1960. The fast of the Sabbath. See **Fasting**.

**Sabellius**, a disciple of Noetus. VIII, 32. The heresy of Sabellius. III, 1631; IV, 84, 837. His doctrines. VIII, 32, 941. Sabellius did not enter through the door into the sheepfold. III, 1721.

**Sabellians**, heretics. VIII, 32; III, 1687, 1689, 1737, 1819, 1820, 1875. They are called Praxeans and Hermogenians. VIII, 32. More frequently, Patripassians. V, 448, 990; VIII, 32. The error of the Sabellians. III, 1667, 1668, 1672. Their heresy. VII, 301, 325; [Col. 0576] X, 1462–1463. Their doctrines. VIII, 671, 706, 754, 759, 918. Their position concerning the Trinity. V, 448. The Sabellians do not distinguish the Son from the Father. III, 1820. The Sabellians, confusing the Son with the Father, are forcibly pressed. III, 1775. The Arians accuse us of being Sabellians. X, 458. The disputes of the Sabellians are now silent. II, 438. See **Patripassians**.

The rape of the Sabine women. VII, 61.

**Sabinus**, consul. IX, 687.

**Sabinus**, a presbyter, read Augustine’s book with clear interpretations. II, 976.

**Sabrata.** IX, 1239, 507, 528, 550.

**Sack**, mortality. IV, 225. The sack of our price. V, 1353, 1454, 1473. The sackcloth of repentance. V, 1449.

There was one high priest. III, 685. By whom he was anointed. III, 685. At times there were several high priests to settle a dispute. III, 685. There were several high priests because of ambitions and conflicts among the Jews. III, 1757. Under the Law, the sons of priests succeeded deceased priests. I, 648, 652. The priest entered the Holy of Holies daily with incense, but once a year with blood. III, 640–641, 690. Whether, and at what time, the high priest engaged in begetting children. III, 711, 713. Why bodily defects were avoided in priests of the Old Testament. IX, 58. Why no one is found to have prayed for a priest of the Old Testament, but the situation is otherwise for one of the New Testament. IX, 60. Moral exposition of the high priest’s garments. III, 640–641. The priest’s manner of life symbolized by the bells of the priestly garment. III, 637. The Jewish priests bore the figure of the eternal priest. IV, 378. Egyptian priests performed no other duty besides service in the temple of their gods. III, 584. Christ priest and sacrifice, victor and victim. I, 794. As a human being, Christ preferred to be called priest and to be a sacrifice rather than demand a priest or sacrifice for himself. V, 1252. Who is that priest for whom no one prays? IV, 378. Christ alone was such a priest that he himself was also the sacrifice. IV, 200, 1733. See **Christ**.

Priests must be assessed not by their title but by their holiness. VII, 693. Study of Scripture, prayer, and reading are necessary for a priest. II, 88–89. The continence of priests. VIII, 46. The priest beats his breast with the people and asks pardon. V, 749. The priest’s blessing upon the faithful. X, 1032. All Christians are priests. VII, 676. Properly, however, bishops and presbyters. VII, 676.

**Priesthood.** IX, 202. The priesthood according to the order of Aaron has now ceased. IV, 1460; VII, 534. How Aaron’s priesthood is everlasting. III, 639. The future change of priesthood in the New Testament, prefigured in the Old. VII, 527, 532–533. Neither Aaron’s priesthood nor the Law introduces anyone into the eternal inheritance, but grace through faith does. III, 743. In Paul’s time the Jewish priesthood shone outwardly in name, but inwardly was filthy with muddy desires. VI, 507. Augustine asks whether force was done to him when he was advanced to the priesthood. II, 88. Augustine shed tears at the time of his ordination. II, 88. The second and third priesthoods. IX, Appendix 773.

**Saclas**, the Father of Adam and Eve according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 37.

**Pagan sacred rites.** V, 1022. How the sacred rites of the gods were established. VII, 256–257. Pompilius did not wish the reasons for the sacred rites to be known either to the people, the Senate, or the priests themselves. VII, 222. It happened through God’s hidden providence that he might receive them from demons, yet not be advised to burn them. VII, 224. How cruel were the sacred rites of the gods. VII, 52. Shameful. VII, 50, 52, 216. And dishonorable. VII, 185. Whether the sacred rites of the gods can be excused on the ground that they have their own interpretations. VII, 186. Varro tried in vain to make their shamefulness honorable. VII, 221–222. Some pagans understood that the sacred rites were theatrical performances. VII, 184. The fifteen men of the sacred rites among the Romans. VII, 178.

Sacraments are so called because in them one thing is seen and another understood. V, 1247. When signs pertain to divine things, they are called sacraments. II, 527. If sacraments did not possess some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. II, 364. Why we need sacraments. I, 856. Sacraments are bodily, as it were visible words; they are indeed sacred and holy, yet changeable. VIII, 356. The ancient righteous possessed some hidden sacrament of regeneration. II, 845. Scripture does not state whether, before Abraham, the righteous or their infants were marked by some bodily and visible sacrament. X, 402.

Seneca criticized the sacraments of the Jews. VII, 192. The Maccabees became martyrs for the sake of the ancient sacraments. II, 156. The Jews erred first because they were not subject to God’s righteousness, wishing to establish their own righteousness; second, because after Christ’s passion they judged that the ancient sacraments had to be celebrated as necessary for salvation; third, because they persecuted preachers of grace as enemies of the Law. II, 146, 156–157. Paul taught that a human being is justified not through those things but through the grace of Jesus Christ. [Col. 0577] II, 279. Certain Jewish believers insisted that those who believed in Christ could not be saved without the ancient sacraments. II, 278–279. The sacraments of the old Law were commanded solely for the sake of signification. X, 594. They were given by God to signify future things; for Christians they remain only to be read for understanding of the prophecy already set forth. II, 281. A sacrament not understood terrifies the soul piously; when understood, it produces pious joy. III, 2117. What the sacraments of the Old Testament signify. IV, 954–955. The ancient sacraments were shadows of things to come. X, 222. The sacraments of the Law foretold Christ who was to come. VIII, 355, 357, 359. The sacrament of the kingdom of heaven was veiled in the Old Testament, to be revealed in the New when the fullness of time arrived. IV, 983.

The ancient sacraments were necessary before Christ. II, 156. After Christ they were superfluous. II, 156. At that time Jews were permitted to celebrate them from customary solemnity, not from necessity for salvation. II, 156. Once the New Testament had been revealed, the sacraments of the old Law were not necessary. VI, 536. The ancient sacraments were neither harmful nor necessary for the first Christians. VIII, 357. The ancient sacraments are neither good nor evil. II, 281. Those seals of the Old Testament were not condemned, but, when more suitable ones succeeded them, they passed away. II, 96. The ancient sacraments were not to be imposed upon the Gentiles. VIII, 357. The Apostle undertook to celebrate the ancient sacraments of the Jews, lest he appear to condemn them as sacrilegious or as Gentile idolatry, and lest he be thought to teach secession from Moses. II, 278–279, 282. This was so that he might teach that they were not harmful. II, 156, 258. Paul showed that the ancient sacraments should neither be sought as necessary nor condemned as sacrilegious. II, 281. Augustine approves Paul’s procedure in undertaking to celebrate the Jewish sacraments. II, 282. The Apostle observed the ancient sacraments not through deceptive pretense but through prudent counsel. VIII, 357. Why the sacraments were permitted to Jews in the time of the apostles. VI, 536. See **Law**. How long the first Christians who believed from the Jews were permitted to observe the ancient sacraments. VIII, 357–358. It does not follow, from the fact that Christ did not abolish the Law and the Prophets, that the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets remain. VIII, 357, 359. Christ did not empty the ancient sacraments but changed them. VIII, 53. Why God instituted some things in the old Law and others in the new. III, 136.

It was fitting for Christ to be foretold by some sacraments when he was to come, and announced by others when he had come. II, 528. It is not surprising that some sacraments announce future things and others things already accomplished. VIII, 356. The secrets of the ancient sacraments were revealed to the faithful through Christ’s passion. VIII, 260. The sacraments were changed, not the faith. V, 133. One and the same faith has had different sacraments in different periods, according to the appropriateness of the signification. X, 179. The change made by Christ in the ancient sacraments was foretold in the Psalms. VIII, 53–55. We do not celebrate the ancient sacraments because what they promised has been fulfilled. IV, 1856. There are few sacraments in the New Testament; there were many in the Old. III, 136. The superiority of the sacraments of the new Law. II, 200. The difference between the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments. IV, 931; IX, 289. By very few sacraments, easy in observance and outstanding in signification, Christ bound together the society of the new people. II, 200. After the Lord’s resurrection, certain few signs were handed down in place of many: very easy to perform, most sublime to understand, and most chaste to observe. III, 71. The new sacraments are greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in performance, and fewer in number than the ancient ones. VIII, 355. The ancient sacraments were figured by the weapons David set down when he was about to fight Goliath. IV, 1856. The sacraments flowed from Christ’s side. III, 1513; IV, 461, 668, 1672, 1785; V, 1087; VII, 472. Sacraments generally receive the names of the things of which they are sacraments. II, 364.

Various sacraments are listed. IX, 190. The sacraments of initiation. I, 863. The sacrament of catechumens. X, 176. The sacrament of salt. I, 668, note (a). The sacrament of baptism. See **Baptism**. The sacrament of the Holy Spirit. V, 1100. The sacrament of chrism. See **Chrism**. The sacraments of the altar. V, 584; VII, 284. The sacrament of Christ’s blood. VII, 611–612. The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. VIII, 873. See **Eucharist**. The sacraments are hidden from pagans. IV, 1348. They are explained to infants. V, 1099, 1103, 1246. Why they are not disclosed to catechumens. III, 1875. In the sacrament received by a catechumen, the visible seals of divine things are present, but the invisible realities themselves are honored in them. VI, 344. In the sacrament by which we are anointed, something that we shall become is prefigured. IV, 200. A fish lifted from the deep is eaten at a table prepared in the sight of believers. I, 857, 860. See **Eucharist**. For whom the sacrament of baptism and of Christ’s body is beneficial. VII, 741. In the sacrament of the altar the whole Church is offered. VII, 284. In the mysteries we are commanded to despise all bodily things and renounce this entire world, [Col. 0578] because there is no other salvation of the soul, renewal, or reconciliation with its author. I, 1037.

Sacraments pertain more to the hope of future goods than to the retention or attainment of present ones. VI, 263. What Christ taught is handed down more secretly and more firmly in the sacred rites by which we are initiated; in them the life of the good is most easily purified, not through the winding paths of disputation but through the authority of the mysteries. I, 1008. The spiritual person judges concerning the solemnity of the sacraments by which we are initiated and of the Eucharist. I, 860. Christ’s sacraments have spread throughout the whole world through the works of God’s servants. I, 856.

The sacrament and the power of the sacrament are sometimes separated. III, 2026. The sacrament is one thing, the power of the sacrament another. III, 1611. The power of the sacraments is grace; it is not common to all, although the sacraments themselves are common. IV, 983–984. The sacrament is a visible word. III, 1840. The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. III, 1840. We are born spiritually through word and sacrament. III, 1486. God works through the ministers of the sacraments. I, 857. Through visible sacraments the minister sanctifies; through invisible grace, God does so. III, 712–713. Visible sacraments accomplish nothing without the sanctification of invisible grace. III, 712. Divine power attends the sacraments, whether for the salvation of those who use them well or for the destruction of those who use them badly. IX, 144. The effect of visible sacraments is piety. VIII, 355. Whoever receives the sacraments of faith in bed and has had no time to perform works is justified by faith without works. V, 31. Temporal sacraments are medicinal bonds of our contrition. IV, 1903–1904. God gives the sacrament of grace even through the wicked, but grace itself only through himself or through his saints. IX, 191. Although the Holy Spirit was given through human beings, what was given did not therefore belong to human beings. V, 1226. Since three things must be considered—the one by whom it is given, the one to whom it is given, and the one through whom it is given—the intervening minister does not intercept the benefit of the giver. V, 1225. Sacraments administered by sinners. V, 1225. The giver of the grace conferred through the sacraments is not the human being himself. V, 1226. The sacraments and spiritual works concerning present salvation are gifts of God, not of those through whom they are performed. IX, 152–153. The error of the Donatists: that the sacraments lose their own holiness because of the wickedness of their ministers. IX, 293, 296. The Donatists said that even those who disapprove evil deeds, or tolerate them for the sake of peace and unity, are defiled by communion in the sacraments. IX, 56. The wicked do not pollute the sacraments. IX, 73. The Donatists say that the sacraments are holy only if they are given by holy people. IV, 134. God’s gifts reach those who receive them with faith, even if the person through whom they receive them is like Judas. IV, 135. The sacraments remain holy even in criminal people. II, 172. Human conduct does nothing to God’s sacraments by which they might cease altogether to exist or become less holy. IX, 298. The sacraments harm all who handle them unworthily, yet benefit those who receive them worthily through them. IX, 65. Whether the effect of the sacraments depends on the goodness or wickedness of their ministers. IX, 67, 73. The holiness of the sacrament can exist where holiness of life does not. IX, 298. Through the power of the sacrament sins are forgiven, not through the merits of the ministers. IX, 156. The Cataphrygians are said to regard the sacraments as deadly. VIII, 30. The sacraments, like Scripture, can be common to heretics and the Church. IX, 146, 159, 162, 165, 170. Among heretics the sacraments are divine, not human. II, 312. They carry them to their own punishment. II, 312. Wherever the sacraments are, they are themselves. IX, 70. The sacraments do not lose the power of holiness when they pass to heretics while remaining as they are among us. IX, 747. The sacraments found among heretics and schismatics do not belong to them but to Christ. IX, 154. All the Lord’s sacraments come from the Catholic Church. II, 343. Why they are not changed when heretics return to it. II, 343. The sacraments and invocation of God’s name outside the Church belong only to the Church. IX, 473. Why the sacraments were not repeated before Cyprian and Agrippinus. IX, 154. The sacraments that schismatics have not changed are approved by us. II, 301. The sacraments of Christians must also be approved among heretics. II, 301. Among schismatics the sacraments can possess the visible form of piety, but not its spiritual power. V, 463. Those cut off from the Church bear and celebrate the bodily sacraments, but without spiritual power. V, 463, 465. A sacrament held outside the Church is held for destruction. II, 229. It is held for judgment. II, 583. All Christ’s sacraments, without the charity of Christ’s unity, are held not for salvation but for judgment. IX, 372. Among heretics the sacraments serve their condemnation rather than their salvation. IX, 179. Military standards are more dangerously held by usurpers than if they were not held at all. IX, 688. The wicked, whether inside or outside, can possess and administer the sacraments—not for salvation but for their own destruction. IX, 163–164, 167, 482. The sacraments are common to good and wicked alike. V, 561.

The use of the sacraments is sometimes not forbidden to the unworthy because of the necessity of the Church’s peace. V, 51. The sacraments of the Church [Col. 0579] are received in many different ways. IV, 1839. Sacraments are not always beneficial to those who possess them. IX, 461. Even if a righteous and an unrighteous person partake equally of the sacraments, it cannot therefore be said that participation in righteousness exists together with wickedness. IX, 294. The same sacraments are for salvation to the righteous, for condemnation to the unrighteous. IX, 293, 297–298, 435. In those who love the world, the sacraments remain for condemnation, not as instruments of salvation. III, 1994. Christ’s sacraments suffer injury in those who live badly. V, 1092. The holy visible sacrament must be distinguished from the invisible anointing of charity: the latter belongs properly to the good, while the former can exist in the good for reward and in the wicked for judgment. IX, 342, 345. Grace does not depend on visible sacraments. III, 712. Sacraments without charity benefit nothing. IX, 692. The life of the sacraments is charity. V, 92. Contempt for the power of the sacraments makes people sacrilegious. VIII, 355. For Christ’s sacraments a Christian ought to be more ready to endure everything than the ancients were for the sacraments of the Law. VIII, 355. The sacraments received among wicked people or through their ministry are not the sacraments of the wicked. IV, 1801. The sacraments are Christ’s garments; charity is the tunic woven from above. Heretics were able to divide the sacraments among themselves, but they did not divide charity. IV, 176.

To sacrifice voluntarily means to love freely what one praises. IV, 626–627.

What the true and perfect sacrifice is. VII, 283. Four things must be considered in every sacrifice. VIII, 901. Sacrifice is an ancient practice. II, 377. The antiquity of worshipping God through sacrifice. VII, 281. In paradise the first parents offered themselves to God as the purest victims. VII, 701. Only the first parents in paradise and the saints in heaven offer the sacrifice of righteousness. VII, 700–701. Sacrifices celebrated before the Flood. VII, 459. Although sacrifice is made or offered by a human being, it is nevertheless a divine matter. VII, 283. Sacrifice is owed to God alone. II, 377–378; V, 1249, 1667; VII, 255–256, 281, 654; VIII, 382. This is attested by the miracles performed through the ark of the testimony. VII, 296–297. A visible sacrifice must not be offered to anyone other than the one to whom the invisible sacrifice is owed. VII, 297. Why the demons demanded sacrifice. VII, 460. Demons demand that it be made for them because they know that it is owed to the true God. VII, 298. They delight not in the smoke of any bodily thing but in the mind of the suppliant. VII, 298. Sacrifice shows sufficiently to whom it is owed, whether the true God justly commands it or a false god arrogantly demands it. VIII, 409. The demons would not have sought sacrifice, priesthood, and temple for themselves unless they had known that these were owed to the one God. II, 377. Pagans are not to be blamed for sacrifices, but because they offer them to idols. II, 377.
