Sacrifice must not be offered to any bodily creature, nor to any spiritual creature, however righteous, and still less to an unrighteous one. II, 378. Not to good gods or evil ones. VII, 650. Not to angels or to the powers of God. VII, 654. Not to martyrs. VII, 255–256, 772. Angels and holy human beings rejected sacrifice, or divine honors. VII, 298. Other services offered to divinity human beings dared to claim for themselves; only very few are mentioned who wished sacrifices to be offered to them or wished through them to be regarded as gods. VIII, 624. Pagan sacrifices should not therefore be considered good because God did not prevent them from being performed. VI, 583. The nations made sacrifices in winepresses. III, 2085. Why the demon demands sacrifice for himself. VIII, 624.

Why God wished sacrifices to be offered to him. VII, 296. God does not need sacrifices; in accepting, rejecting, or receiving them, he consults only the interests of human beings. II, 377; VII, 281, 295–296, 654. Everything by which God is rightly worshipped benefits the human being, not God. VII, 282. To offer sacrifice and praise is useful to us, not to God. II, 527; VIII, 624. Why God commanded sacrifices to be offered to him when he did not need them. VIII, 231, 321.

Sacrifice of Abraham: what the account in Genesis 15 signifies. IV, 1361, 1362. The flame made from heaven in Abraham’s sacrifice was not a miracle: why. I, 648. Abraham’s sacrifice on the mountain. V, 31. The sacrifice of the Jews in animal victims. IV, 302, 303. Why only unblemished animals were formerly offered. VIII, 624. The sacrifice of victims, an odor of sweetness to the Lord. III, 639. God was not pleased by sacrifices of animals. III, 810. Why the children of Israel visibly sacrificed animal victims. VI, 31. The ancient sacrifices were imposed more suitably upon a perverse people than offered to a God who desired them. VIII, 346. Carnal sacrifices were given to the Jews so that they might not fall away into idolatry. III, 1468. Whether it was permitted to sacrifice outside the temple that was in Jerusalem. III, 702, 803, 804. What sacrifices were offered for the people, for the ruler, for the priest, and so forth. III, 686, 687. Sacrifices for sins called “sins.” VI, 253; VIII, 744; X, 403. Different sacrifices for sins. V, 1541. The command to offer a sacrifice for sin after a child’s birth is vain if original sin does not exist. X, 1192, 1227, 1237. Sacrifices for sins committed through forgetfulness, ignorance, and so forth. III, 676, 677. What animals were to be used for the sacrifice for sins, the burnt offering, the sacrifice of well-being, and so forth. III, 686, 693. The sacrifice for sin was not offered except together with a burnt offering. [Col. 0580] III, 675, 676. The saints do not offer sacrifices for sins. VII, 700.

The ancient sacrifices are symbolic. II, 377. The sacrifices varied according to the circumstances of the times. II, 379. The ancient sacrifices signified grace; they did not produce it. II, 633. By the sacrifices of the Old Testament sinners were convicted rather than cleansed. X, 139. Sacrifices in themselves can remedy no sin. III, 728. The sacrifice that God had commanded was suitable for the earliest times, but is no longer so. II, 527. The ancient sacrifices, like promissory words, were abolished when the sacrifice of Christ’s body was given. IV, 441, 442. Why the sacrifices of the ancients were changed. VII, 282. Although the sacrifices no longer exist in practice, they remain in the authority of their symbolism. VIII, 231. Everything pertaining to the ancient sacrifices was a figure of our own realities. VIII, 320. The sacrifices of animals were certain shadows of things to come. III, 810. The Manichaeans cursed the sacrifices of the Old Testament. VIII, 231. The sacrifices of the Fathers are not for that reason to be condemned, because the nations had sacrifices. VIII, 386. The difference between the sacrifices of the Hebrews and those of the pagans. VIII, 386. The critics of the Old Testament foolishly attempt to prove that all ancient sacrifices were offered to demons. VIII, 625, 626. What the sacrifices of the nations, the Hebrews, and the Christians are in relation to the true sacrifice. VIII, 382, 409. The sacrifice of our God abounded, and the sacrifices of the gods were prohibited. V, 1356. All sacrifices yielded to our sacrifice. VII, 655. Christ’s sacrifice was signified by the sacrifices offered for sins. III, 704. The ancient sacrifices of the saints were figures of the true sacrifice of Christ. VII, 298. All those sacrifices, in many and various ways, signified the one sacrifice whose memory is now celebrated. VIII, 231, 386, 409, 624, 625, 626, 661. Christ’s sacrifice foretold through many figures. V, 1667; IX, 154.

What is the true sacrifice owed to the one true God? VIII, 382, 386, 409. The sacrifice of Christ’s flesh, the true and only sacrifice for sins. X, 600. The sacrifice of the cross. V, 1501. Christ offered himself as a sacrifice in place of all sacrifices. IV, 71. Christ found nothing clean in human beings that he could offer for human beings; he offered himself as a clean victim. IV, 1953. The sacrifice of the New Testament. VIII, 626. The sacrifice of Christians. VIII, 382. The offering of the Lord’s body and blood. II, 115; IX, 461; X, 480. The truest and unique sacrifice. X, 211. The sacrament of the faithful. II, 563, 569. The Church’s daily sacrifice. VII, 298. Sacrifice to God in the Church. V, 1101, 1356, 1413. Christ is sacrificed for us daily through the very remembrance of the Savior’s benefit. IV, 966. The figure, reality, and memorial of the sacrifice owed to God. VIII, 386. The evening sacrifice. V, 1504. Where, when, and how the sacrifice of the New Testament is offered, only the baptized know. II, 558. The sacrifice Christ offered is known by the faithful. IV, 178. The sacrifice of Christians is offered everywhere on earth and in heaven. VIII, 61. The sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek is now spread throughout the whole world. IV, 303, 1427. A table was set up so that the sacrifice might be offered to God. V, 1413. Private sacrifices are prohibited. III, 702.

The sacrifice is sanctified through the word of God. V, 1099. To perform and offer sacrifice to God is not permitted to everyone. V, 759. It is not permitted to laypeople. V, 759. The bishop or presbyter offers the sacrifice. V, 1100. The order of the sacrifice. V, 1100. In this sacrifice there is a great sacrament, by which we give thanks to the Lord our God. II, 558. In our sacrifice the unity of Christ’s mystical body is proclaimed. II, 839. The sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood cannot be offered for the unbaptized. X, 480, 481, 504, 508, 520. The names of those for whom it is offered are not omitted. X, 509. Altar sacrifices and almsgiving for the dead. VI, 158, 283. Sacrifice for the dead. V, 936. It was customary to offer the sacrifice of our [reading uncertain: *protii*] price for the dead, with the corpse placed beside the grave. I, 777. The sacraments of redemption offered on the third day of the funeral rites. II, 694. The sacrifices benefit those for whom they are offered either by bringing about complete remission, or at least by making condemnation more bearable. VI, 158. In the celebration of the sacraments, four parts were designated by distinct names. II, 636. Then the bishops, as advocates, commend those entrusted to them through the laying on of hands to the most merciful power. II, 637. Then one should pray both for the persecutors of the Church and for the whole human race. II, 637. In some places no day is omitted on which it is not offered; elsewhere only on Saturday and Sunday; elsewhere only on Sunday. II, 200. On Thursday of the final week of Lent, in some places it is offered twice—that is, in the morning and in the evening—and elsewhere only in the evening. II, 200. Among the Donatists it was being spread about that the Catholics placed something else on God’s altar. II, 330. A kind of sacrifice in a superstitious spectacle. VI, 703.

By the sacrifice of Christ’s body, evil spirits were driven away. VII, 764. Augustine asks Longinianus many questions about purifying sacrifices: whether one who is clean needs them, and so forth. II, [Col. 0581] 1032, etc. There can be no way of salvation without participation in Christ’s body and blood. II, 638. The sacrifice, because of the name of the Lord that is invoked, is always holy; and it becomes for each person what the heart with which he approaches to receive it makes it. IX, 57, 300. The sacrifices of the ungodly harm the very people who offer them impiously. IX, 57. The sacrifice of those who sacrifice with a wicked purpose is not acceptable to God. VII, 444. What sacrifices we ought now to offer. IV, 659. What kinds of sacrifices God loves and crowns. III, 811. What kind of sacrifice is acceptable to God. IV, 1318. What is read as divinely commanded concerning sacrifices is to be referred to the signification of love of God and neighbor. VII, 283. God does not require the sacrifices themselves, by which the sacrifices he does require are signified. VII, 283. The sacrifices of the ancients signified those things that are enacted in us so that we may cling to God. VII, 282. God seeks us, not our possessions. V, 252.

We ourselves are a sacrifice to God. V, 317. No sacrifice is more acceptable to God than the just who offer themselves to God. VII, 700. We ourselves are the most excellent and best sacrifice. VII, 655. The sacrifice is Christ’s body, which we are. VII, 772. The visible sacrifice is the sacrament of the invisible sacrifice. VII, 282, 297. The human being himself is God’s invisible sacrifice in his heart. VII, 297. We always have a sacrifice that we can offer to God. IV, 659. Within us we have a sacrifice by which we may move God. IV, 475, 598. The sacrifice of righteousness through repentance. IV, 81. The sacrifice of a contrite heart. V, 133. God desires the sacrifice of a contrite heart, not the sacrifice of slaughtered cattle. VII, 282. Whoever punishes himself offers sacrifice to God. IV, 1824. Humility of heart is a sacrifice. IV, 1705. The sacrifice of praise in the New Testament succeeds the bloody victims of the Old Testament. II, 558. The sacrifice of praise, a freely given sacrifice. IV, 578, 1220, 1568. The sacrifice of praise, a more sacred sacrifice, is thanksgiving. VIII, 624. The sacrifice of righteousness. I, 1195. Of thought and tongue. I, 809. The sacrifices we offer must be kindled by love. IV, 659.

The Sadducees denied the Holy Spirit. V, 447. The Sadducees’ error concerning the resurrection. V, 1622.

Many things are called secular because they are done in this age in such a way that they pass away after a short time. VII, 506. The Tatianists have a taste for certain fabulous emanations of the ages. VIII, 30. See Aeons. The new ages constructed by the god of the Manichaeans upon the earth of darkness. VIII, 244. The ages were not created over the same span of time in which they pass away. III, 318. What “age of ages” means. VII, 368. How the ages are unfolded. III, 336. The beauty of the ages is woven together through the departure and succession of things. III, 251. The order of the ages is like a most beautiful song composed of antitheses. VII, 332. Why certain philosophers admitted the revolution of the ages. VII, 360, 361. We became parts of the ages through condemnation. I, 1179; III, 140. This age is delayed for no other reason than that the predestined number of the saints may be completed. VI, 449. Some said that the end of the world would come after six thousand years. V, 576. Six thousand years have already passed. V, 576. The end of the age is signified by evening. IV, 1362.

The term “age” sometimes signifies eternity. IV, 1715. Because of an ambiguous Greek word, it frequently happens that in the Psalms “age” is used for “eternal,” and “eternal” for “age.” IV, 1142. What is said to be “from the age” and “in the age.” III, 333.

The age: this desert. IV, 752, 753, 1760. A torrent. IV, 1644. A river. IV, 1857. The sea. V, 1173; VII, 680. A bitter sea, savage with waves. IV, 440, 780, 794, 1234. No one can cross this world’s sea except by being carried by Christ’s cross. III, 1389. God willed this entire age to be punitive for human beings. X, 1192. By “the age,” human beings are signified. X, 124. The age: sinners. V, 100. The age knows how to devour its lovers, not carry them. V, 482. Love of God and love of the age. V, 694. The investigators of this age are rightly censured in Scripture. III, 333. One ought not to be conformed to the age, but to imitate the imitators of Christ. I, 858. Those who cling to Christ conquer the age together with Christ. IV, 1189. This age must be fled not in body but in heart. X, 1004. No one turns his heart away from this age unless aided by the gift of divine mercy. IV, 1477. When Augustine had undertaken to renounce the age, his mother tried to call him back through her carnal affection; he is urged not to desist from what he had begun. II, 1055. A person who renounces the age will not be charged with less because he was not rich. II, 692.

The savage are compared with lions. III, 361.

Arrows: the words of God and his commandments. IV, 398, 503, 1600, 1865. By these arrows those who are wrongly healthy are wounded, and those who are rightly wounded are healed. IV, 1865. Arrows: the pains of soul and body that must necessarily be endured here. IV, 398.

Saguntum, once a most distinguished city of Hispania Tarraconensis. VII, 101. Note (a). It was besieged by Hannibal and destroyed in a great slaughter. VII, 101. The pitiable decision of the Saguntines when placed in extremity. VII, 101. The Saguntines preferred their entire city to perish rather than break the faith pledged to the Romans. VII, 759.

Agrigentine salt melts when brought near fire and crackles when brought near water. VII, 715, 718. What the transformation of Lot’s wife into salt teaches us. VII, 285.

Salacia, Neptune’s wife. VII, 120, 211.

The salamander lives in fires. VII, 712. It is not harmed by fire. X, 831.

Salem, the city later called Jerusalem. IV, 303.

What the willows signify. IV, 1764.

What the saliva running down David’s beard signifies. IV, 307, 309.

Sallust, a historian distinguished by the nobility of his truthfulness. VII, 18, 561. An excellent assessor of words. I, 974. Sallust is praised. II, 522, 735.

Salmana is interpreted as “shadow of disturbance.” IV, 1054.

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” IV, 901, 1668; V, 94, 96; VII, 541; VIII, 285, 450. The name Solomon is especially fitting for Christ. IV, 901. Solomon was a lover of women, an idolater, and rejected by God. IV, 1667. In Solomon, lust possessed the kingdom. III, 77, 78. Solomon was an idolater because he was unable to resist love of women. III, 453. Why the multitude of wives is reproved in Solomon but not in others. VIII, 453. What Solomon’s downfall prefigured. VIII, 459. Prosperity harmed Solomon more than wisdom itself benefited him. VII, 554. While asleep, Solomon preferred wisdom to everything. III, 466. Solomon became so wise that, had he not fallen, God’s promise concerning David’s seed might have been thought fulfilled in him, and hope concerning Christ would have been removed. IV, 1135. The promises made to David were fulfilled not in Solomon but in Christ. VII, 540, 541. The peace promised to Solomon’s kingdom was a shadow of the peace of the future kingdom. VII, 546. Solomon, whose figure he bore. IV, 1668. He was a figure of Christ. VII, 542. Solomon’s genuine books are Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, however, are attributed to him because of the similarity of their style. VII, 554.

The city of Salona. VII, 664.

To salt water floors. II, 414.

Those who like to joke. III, 208.

Dancers harmonizing with a spiritual song. V, 1416. The custom of dancing at the place where Cyprian was buried was abolished through the diligence of the bishop. V, 1415. Dancing with canine corpses, a punishment. IX, 579. The shameful dances of the Primianists. IX, 106, 107.

Strictly speaking, a *saltus* is a place still uncultivated and wooded. IV, 1720.

“Save” and “Savior” were not Latin words before the Savior came. V, 1371. God wills all human beings to be saved: how. II, 985; X, 760. Another interpretation of the Apostle’s passage, “who wills all human beings to be saved.” X, 945. God wills all human beings to be saved in such a way that he does not take away their free will. X, 238. Few are saved. V, 641. Why so many are not saved. II, 985. Since no one can will to be saved except by God’s willing it, why does he not turn the wills of all who are unwilling? X, 761. Are all not saved because they themselves are unwilling to ask? X, 759. A person is saved gratuitously when the Savior finds in him nothing to crown, but something to condemn. IV, 233; V, 917. When the Savior came, he found no one who was healthy. V, 847.

Why the Manichaeans consider a Savior necessary. X, 1463, 1469. Why Catholics do. X, 1463. The Savior is the help of the sick person; the Savior himself is the reward of the healed person. V, 851. Christ, the Savior of all human beings. V, 1322. There have been many saviors, but Jesus alone saves from sins. V, 1334. See Salvation.

Salvianus of Gazaufala. IX, 237.

Salvius of Ausafa. IV, 380; IX, 507, 528, 550.

Salvius of Membresa. IV, 380; IX, 507, 528, 550. One of the twelve who attended Maximian’s ordination and adhered to him. II, 413. Salvius had earned a bishopric in the party of Donatus. IX, 549. What he suffered from the Donatists. IX, 579. And from the people of Abitina. IX, 579. He endured immoderate persecution from the Donatists. II, 414. How badly Salvius was treated by the Primianists. IX, 106, 107. Why the Donatists demanded that Salvius be expelled from his church. IX, 549. Salvius was declared a heretic. IX, 532. The condemnation of Salvius at the council of Bagai. IX, 106. Salvius was driven from the church by the people of Abitina. IX, 106, 108. Salvius suffered worse things, while people danced with him, than if he had been burned alive. IX, 108. The attacks and harassment of that persecution could not force him to return to the party of Donatus. IX, 579, 581.

A temple of Salus established at Rome. VII, 105.

“Salus” in the Punic language means “three.” III, 2096. Human salvation is twofold. III, 1653. Bodily health is the poor person’s patrimony. IV, 610, 971. How bodily health is to be requested from God. IV, 455, 456. Bodily health comes from the Lord, regardless of through whom it is given. III, 1633. When the flesh is restored to health, death is not removed but postponed. III, 1633. The salvation of angels, human beings, and animals is from God. III, 1652, 1653. What salvation each person should be concerned about, and in what manner. IV, 1321. Some ask God as a great favor for temporal health, which he also gives to beasts of burden. IV, 349. A person should do what he can even for the temporal safety of other human beings; where he can do nothing except by sinning, he should consider that he has nothing left to do. VI, 542. Let him commit everything to God’s will and power. VI, 542. What salvation is proper to human beings. III, 1633, 1634. Salvation promised to the believer and the baptized. V, 453. This salvation must be distinguished from temporal safety. V, 1113. Salvation of the right hand and salvation of the left. IV, 165, 1782. Nothing whatever, not even this temporal life, is to be preferred to eternal salvation. IX, 335, 336. If this bodily safety is to be guarded so that even unwilling people are preserved by those who love them, how much more must that spiritual salvation be guarded, whose abandonment threatens eternal death. II, 756. If salvation is loved, it should be desired where, once attained, nothing is feared. II, 486. Our salvation is from God, not from ourselves. V, 952. Everything pertaining to salvation must be attributed to God. X, 983. Whether God helps through an angel or through a human being, he himself is our salvation. IV, 326. How God carries out the whole work of our salvation. IV, 738. God wills to kill in a human being what the human being made, and to save what he himself made. IV, 1692.

Salvation is Christ our physician himself. IV, 1499. “Salvation from the Jews” means nothing other than Christ from the Jews. IV, 540. Christ is the one way of salvation. II, 637. From the beginning of the human race there was one salvation through Christ. II, 374. There is no salvation for one to whom Christ has not been proclaimed. X, 126. The salvation of religion, and so forth, was never lacking to anyone who was worthy; and the one to whom it was lacking was not worthy. I, 643; II, 376; X, 973, 974. How this is to be understood. I, 643. How Augustine understood it. II, 370. God’s will was never altogether lacking for the salvation of mortals in righteousness and piety. II, 373. Before Christ, those who were not of Abraham’s seed also shared in this. II, 376. No one is made worthy of salvation by human will, but by divine grace. VII, 79. The saying of one who places his hope in a human being: “Except for Garseus’s safety, you can do nothing to me.” IV, 315. The ordering of divine providence concerning human salvation. I, 1315. The way of salvation is in Christ and the holy Scriptures. I, 737.

Why we must work out our salvation with fear and trembling. IV, 1851; X, 262, 264, 930, 931. The salvation of the city of God is acquired through faith, and it cannot stand without faith. VII, 759. There is no way of salvation without participation in the Lord’s body and blood. II, 637. In a lowly place there is salvation; in a high place, danger. V, 1569. Salvation can be obtained nowhere except in the Catholic Church. IX, 695.

The salvation of others is to be cared for out of charity. V, 492. The salvation of all must be pursued, since it is uncertain which people God has decreed to save. X, 945. Those who refuse to undertake concern for the salvation of others are rebuked. III, 1359. The Church must not be deterred from pursuing the salvation of others because of the loss of some. II, 798. To be a dispenser of eternal salvation through word and sacrament does not also mean to be a participant in it. II, 1077. Against those who promise themselves salvation apart from the kingdom of heaven. V, 1543. Salvation and eternal life cannot exist apart from the kingdom of heaven. X, 123, 140. Prophets, Apostles, martyrs, we, and those who will come after us will all receive everlasting salvation together at the very end. IV, 411. The salvation that will exist in the future age will itself be final blessedness. VII, 631. Why our salvation is delayed. IV, 338. Whoever arrives first at the finish of the race waits to be crowned together with the one who arrives later. IV, 441. Salvation is to be awaited from God with patience. IV, 1088. Some promise salvation through fire to those who, although believers, live most wickedly. VI, 225. See Faith.

The Salvation of God: Christ. IV, 1595, 1728. Desired by the ancients. V, 890.

“Greeting” is derived from “salvation.” V, 657. An ancient formula of greeting. V, 609. Why the Epistle to the Hebrews lacks a greeting. III, 2095.

The Samardaci: flat-nosed people. I, 952. Note 1.

Samaria commonly represents an image of idolatry. VI, 56. It is also used for idolatry itself. V, 1034.

The Samaritan woman. V, 606. Her conversion. VI, 54, 55. Jesus thirsted for the Samaritan woman’s faith. III, 1521. The Samaritan woman, a figure of the Church. III, 1513.

“Samaritan” or “Samarite” is interpreted as “guardian.” III, 1707. Christ is the true Samaritan. III, 1707. Because he is a guardian. IV, 235, 862, 1667, 1765. The Samaritans worshiped golden cows. VI, 56. The Samaritans who believed in Christ without seeing signs, a figure of the nations. III, 1525.

Among the Punic peoples, *samen* means “heavens.” III, 797.

When the Samian Sibyl lived. VII, 582.

The Samnites crush the Roman army at the Caudine Forks. VII, 97.

Samos, an island dear to Juno. VII, 185.

The gods of Samothrace. VII, 218.

The Sampsaeans, heretics. VIII, 31. Epiphanius associates the Sampsaeans with the Ebionites. VIII, 27.

Samson is interpreted as “their sun.” IV, 1041. Samson and his history allegorically understood. V, 1639. Samson strangling the lion, a type of truth, which endured persecution and conquered. [Col. 0584] IV, 1126. Samson’s death explained. VI, 702. How Samson is excused from the charge of homicide. VII, 35, 39. By the prompting of the divine Spirit, Samson killed himself together with his enemies. IX, 731. Samson, judge of the Hebrews, thought to be Hercules. VII, 576. Samson was a figure of Christ. IV, 1041.

Samsucius, bishop of Turris. II, 134, 293.

Samsuricus, a gravedigger. IX, 513.

Samuel. IV, 1343. Samuel is named among the sons of Korah, Aaron’s rivals. I, 648. Note (a). Samuel was not one of Aaron’s sons. VII, 533. Samuel was not only a Levite but also a priest. I, 652. Note (a). How Samuel could have been summoned by the female medium. VI, 142, 162. Whether Samuel appeared to Saul. VI, 606. It may have been a phantom of Samuel, not his spirit. VI, 142, 143, 163. Samuel is also said to have prophesied after death. VI, 165. The change of the ancient priesthood was prefigured in Samuel. VII, 532, 533.

Sanaem. II, 82.

To heal. A human being is fit to wound himself, not to heal himself. V, 138. We are to be healed of our vices by Christ the physician. V, 495.

To be sanctified, meaning to be regarded as holy. III, 521, 527. That which is offered from a vow and devotion is called sanctified. III, 713. The sanctification and cessation of work on the seventh day. V, 1242. The sanctifications of the Old Testament were shadows of true holiness. III, 1915. In what sense the vessels are said to be sanctified as a punishment of those who sinned. III, 731. God was sanctified in the ministers of the temple, even through punishment. III, 689. Jeremiah’s sanctification may reasonably be understood according to predestination. II, 848. The sanctification of God’s name is that by which we are made holy. V, 394. The saints are sanctified in one way, and God’s name in another. X, 228. When in the Lord’s Prayer we say to God the Father, “Hallowed be thy name,” what are we asking? X, 922. To be sanctified in truth is to be sanctified in Christ. III, 1915. The power of sanctification in Christ. IV, 1728. Whether some form of sanctification can be granted to those not yet born, and in what sense; the sanctification by which we are made temples of God is not granted to them. II, 846. The sanctification of catechumens through the sign of Christ and the prayer of the laying on of hands. X, 176. Whether the sanctification conferred by baptism is perfect in this life. X, 845. What sanctification consists in. VI, 80.

There are many modes of sanctification. V, 1346. Sanctification is manifold. X, 176. Sanctification of flesh and spirit. V, 268. Sanctification is from grace, not from works. II, 847. There is no true sanctification except from the Holy Spirit. V, 72. Sanctification is brought to completion in the fear of God. V, 269. The Lord sanctifies through invisible grace; the minister through visible sacraments. III, 712. Invisible sanctification does not depend upon visible sacraments. III, 712. Without the invisible sanctification of grace, visible sacraments benefit nothing. III, 712. At times God sanctifies even without a minister and sacrament, through himself. IX, 76. He also sanctifies through the wicked. IX, 189. The pagans do not think that they receive sanctification from their priests, but from the gods. IX, 250. To what extent a human being can sanctify himself. X, 313. To what extent spouses are sanctified by one another, or their children through them. X, 198. Our sanctification is complete. V, 1170. Sanctification and perfect holiness in the next life. VI, 80.

Consecrated women. V, 574, 1064. They are called so from holiness. VI, 428. Their institution. I, 1339. Their multitude in the Church. I, 1339. The common life of consecrated women is praised. IV, 1058. The common life of consecrated women is more excellent. VI, 423. Augustine commands that everything be held in common among consecrated women: food and clothing should not be distributed equally; they should not seek in the monastery what they did not have in the world; nevertheless, they should give those who were poor in the world whatever they need; they should beware of pride and devote themselves to prayer; when they pray to God with psalms and hymns, what is expressed by the voice should be present in the heart; they should discipline the flesh by fasting and abstaining from food and drink; outside the meal hour, one who cannot fast should take no food unless she is ill; they should listen to reading at table. II, 960. See Nuns. For a consecrated woman, it is a sin to wear the clothing of married women. VIII, 237. The virginity of consecrated women is not for that reason to be detested, because there were virgins of Vesta. VIII, 386. A consecrated woman who marries is to be condemned to eternal fire. V, 800. Some consecrated women in the city of Rome, infected with Jovinian’s heresy, married. I, 639. A consecrated woman captured by barbarians and returned honorably to her parents. II, 426. A subdeacon was forbidden to make undisciplined visits to consecrated women; when he did not obey, he was removed from the clergy. II, 134. Consecrated women of the Donatists. IX, 62. Deceased consecrated women are named in their proper place during the altar sacraments. VI, 423. Consecrated life. IV, 1280; V, 1004.

Holiness is said to derive from *sancire*, “to make sacred.” VI, 192. Human frailty cannot be brought into conformity with perfect service to divine holiness. III, 790. Augustine greets both the monk Renatus and the presbyter Peter with the title “Your Holiness.” X, 495. For the sake of holiness three things must be preserved: bodily modesty, purity of mind, and truth of doctrine. VI, 514. To feign a commitment to holiness. V, 1572. In what bodily holiness consists. VII, 31, 32. Whether “holy of holies,” “holy of the holy,” and “holy things” signify the same thing. III, 656. The holy place, a part of the Temple, was a figure of the Old Testament; the holy of holies was a figure of the New Testament. III, 635. The priest entered the holy of holies daily with incense, and once a year with blood. III, 642.

Holy. So that the Lord’s saying, “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” may be understood. VI, 470. “What we give is holy” was a saying of the Donatists. IV, 1696. “What we wish is holy,” an old proverb. IX, 572. Whatever is holy and true must always be acknowledged. IX, 747. Holy things can cause harm. III, 1432.

The ancient saints, children of the New Testament. X, 595. How the saints of the Old Testament were freed from sins. X, 555, 556. They were freed through Christ. X, 556. All the saints, including those of the Old Testament, were freed by the grace of Christ. X, 1107. The ancient saints believed in Christ who was to suffer. I, 808. The ancient saints were in the underworld until Christ’s redemption. VII, 681. A person lives justly and holily when he is an impartial judge of things. III, 29. Those are God’s saints who do not love the world. IV, 254. Some of the saints are taught by God alone. IV, 1486. In this life the saints and faithful are like trees stripped bare in winter. IV, 389. All the saints are to be praised in the Lord, not in themselves; nor were they without sin. X, 607, 611. The life of the saints can be without crime, but not without sin. VI, 262. They say that they have sin not to avoid arrogance but to uphold the truth. IV, 1505. The holier a person is, the more abundant are his tears in prayer. VII, 683. How there is no condemnation here among the saints. V, 841. In this life the saints are not free from movements of desire. III, 2061, 2062. *Retractations.* Quarrels also occur among the saints, but they do not destroy charity. IV, 318. The saints here do not do what they wish. V, 718. Wherever the saints are, they are with God. V, 1366. The saints rejoice in unity and are one in Christ. VIII, 217. All the saints are brothers among themselves through the same grace. VIII, 425. The saints advance, are tested, and are revealed through the perversity of the wicked. II, 1084. Nothing is lost to the saints through the loss of temporal things. VII, 23. The face of the earth is renewed through the grace of the New Testament by the multitude of the saints. III, 414. The death of the saints is precious. VII, 381. The saints would undoubtedly be wretched, even with every virtue, if they were always in pain. II, 673. All the saints belong to the Church. V, 38. The steadfastness of the saints on behalf of the Church. III, 128.

The saints are rightly called heaven. VII, 698. “Saints” and “spiritual” signify the mouth, while “carnal” signifies the belly. IV, 492. The saints are the teeth of the Church. III, 38. Imperishable wood. III, 1434. They are the temple of God, the house of God, and the kingdom of God. III, 1814; VIII, 673. Their hearts are God’s censers. I, 781. The saints and faithful are called musical instruments. IV, 1964. They are called rivers. IV, 1257. They are compared with the heavenly lights. IV, 1193, 1194. The saints, illuminated lights. III, 1670, 1671. The saints and spiritual people signify the sun, while carnal people signify the moon. IV, 941. The saints and faithful are God’s chariot. IV, 828.

The examples of the saints are set before every kind of human being. VI, 699. Examples of saints who spurned natural affections. VI, 702. People are not blessed because they are joined to the just and holy by kinship of the flesh, but because by obeying and imitating their teaching and conduct they cling to them. VI, 398. What was done by the saints through a special inspiration contrary to the law may not be imitated. VII, 39. What should be thought about those things known to have been done by the saints even though they were not permitted to be done. VII, 39. The fragrance of the saints: like jars of perfume, the more they were broken, the more abundantly it spread. V, 1250.

The saints’ reward is not in this world. VII, 160. Whether the saints are now in possession of blessedness is a major question. I, 606. The saints now reign with Christ and are his kingdom. VII, 673. We most truly say that Peter rejoices in repose with Christ. V, 1069. To possess God and belong to him is the highest and complete good for the saints. VII, 526. The saints shine in heaven with differing glory. III, 1812. The saints have unequal splendor, but heaven in common. V, 736. In heaven the saints will have their differences consonant, not discordant. IV, 1964. The saints live in Abraham’s bosom, mindful of us. I, 763. The intercessions of the saints do not pass away until our groaning has passed away. IV, 1099. We are aided by the prayers of the saints. VIII, 602. The saints now obtain benefits in the name of the one through whom they obtained them before they laid aside the flesh. V, 1442. The saints and angels do not permit hope to be placed in them. III, 32, 33. If you place your hope in them, they are saddened. V, 280. See Martyrs. The saints do not love their electors if they find them deserters of their companions. VIII, 217. The intercessions of the saints at the last judgment. VII, 732.

The saints are to be honored, not adored. III, 169. The cult of the saints. VIII, 602. Much of the worship belonging to God has been appropriated for the veneration of the saints. VII, 281. Holy people, like the angels, do not wish to be worshiped and adored by human beings as God. IV, 1245. Memorials of the saints. I, 719. Tombs of the saints. See Memorial. The small number of the saints is set in comparison with the multitude of sinners. VIII, 601. The total number of the saints is signified by the 153 fish. IV, 571.

Sancus, or Sanctus, king of the Sabines, enrolled among the gods. VII, 576.

“Blood” was called “soul.” III, 703, 711. And “the wage of a laborer.” III, 704. “Men of blood” are those who hate their brothers. IV, 1801. “Blood” denotes the iniquity committed through bloodshed. IV, 597.

Christ’s blood is the propitiation and sacrifice offered for us. IV, 1697. For servants, it is the price; for the bride, the pledge. IV, 1170, 1634. Why Christ sweated blood through his entire body. IV, 1206. We are watered with Christ’s blood. VI, 688. We are whitened and adorned. VI, 689. God pours out for us daily the most precious blood of his only-begotten Son. V, 1078. How Christ’s blood is to be received. VI, 689. Those who receive Christ’s blood respond, “Amen.” VI, 689. Christ made the blood of Christians precious. III, 1733.

Health is the absence of all unpleasant and burdensome sensation. V, 1260, 1262. The good of health. V, 1260. Its value. V, 1402. Bodily well-being is not to be despised because of life’s necessary uses. II, 497. Bodily health is the poor person’s patrimony. IV, 610, 971; V, 249, 1402. When health is present, what does the poor person lack? When it is absent, what benefit is anything the rich person possesses? V, 1187. Health is recovered only gradually. V, 1270. The health of this life is not true health. IV, 398. The illness is long. V, 488. Health is vaporous. V, 495. One day of health is better than many days of weakness. I, 1166. No one is more incurable than the person who seems healthy to himself. IV, 711. A human being does not have the power to regain health as he has the power to lose it. V, 1269. Health is from God. V, 1187. Health harms many people. III, 1443. Many are healed for themselves, not for the one by whom they are healed. IV, 1253. The health of the members lies in unity and charity. V, 754. Bodily health is the harmony of the things of which the body consists. V, 1259.

True health is immortality. IV, 402; V, 489, 1189; VII, 690. The perfect health of the whole human being comes after mortality has been completed. IV, 1902. God will grant this to the brokenhearted. IV, 1902. The mind that does not place eternal things above temporal ones is in no way healthy. II, 499. The heavenly physician does not receive the order of healing from the sick person, but from himself. X, 262.

## To be wise

To understand otherwise than the matter really is is a human temptation; but to love one’s own opinion excessively, even to the point of schism, is diabolical presumption. IX, 130.

## Saphrus

Saphrus, the fourteenth king of the Assyrians. VII, 565.

Sapida sent Augustine a tunic that she had woven for her brother. II, 1082. Augustine consoles her over the death of her brother. II, 1082.

## Wisdom

Wisdom properly exists in God. III, 242. All things, insofar as they exist, exist through God’s wisdom. III, 243. All things are in God’s wisdom. III, 1275. And they existed before they were made. III, 331. Divine wisdom is the law of the universe. VI, 90. Wisdom is infinite, not through spatial extension but through power. II, 443. From it comes the ordering and measure of all things. II, 443. The swiftness of divine wisdom is such that it is always everywhere and is enclosed nowhere. IV, 1931. God’s wisdom cannot be comprehended. VIII, 1066. The secrets of wisdom disturb those who are perverse in heart, but exercise those who are upright in heart. III, 1556. The Son of God is nothing other than God’s wisdom. I, 975. This was handed down as something to be believed in the profession of faith. I, 1262. God’s wisdom is the bread both of human beings and of angels. IV, 1742. Only a rational creature is capable of wisdom. III, 243.

What wisdom is. IV, 1759, 1760; VIII, 1037. Wisdom is defined as knowledge of divine and human things. I, 914. The definition is examined. I, 914. According to the Manichaeans, wisdom is the very light that is drawn in through the eyes. VIII, 316. Different conceptions of wisdom. I, 1253. Wisdom is a condition of the mind. I, 975. It is fullness. I, 975. Wisdom and number are the same. I, 1257. Why, then, is wisdom so precious and number so cheap? I, 1257. Wisdom is a certain ineffable and incomprehensible light of minds. I, 881. Spiritual and unchangeable light. VIII, 939. Wisdom is the greater luminary of the firmament. I, 854. How intellectual knowledge of eternal things comes about through wisdom. VIII, 1010. Wisdom pertains to the understanding of eternal things. VI, 140. Wisdom is truth itself. I, 916. In it the highest good is seen and held fast. I, 1254. Wisdom is the highest excellence in the soul. I, 880. It is the life of the soul. VIII, 615, 617. It is the right way of life. I, 913. Perfect wisdom is piously subjecting the creature to the Creator and distinguishing the Maker from what has been made. V, 1177. Wisdom is the love of God. II, 557. Wisdom is love without jealousy. IV, 310. Love of wisdom cleanses one from the filth of avarice. VII, 204. Insofar as we understand God’s wisdom spiritually, we die to carnal affections. VIII, 864. Wisdom is the true worship of the true God in the present age. II, 668. The true and principal worship of God. VIII, 886, 887, 1048. Human wisdom is piety. VI, 231. [Col. 0587] Piety by which the true God is rightly worshiped. VII, 436. What kind of wisdom is called piety, by which God is worshiped. X, 214. Wisdom, the fruit of piety. III, 441. Nature intended that nothing in our minds should be more clearly known to us than wisdom. I, 913. Whoever is blessed possesses it. I, 975. True wisdom directs its purpose toward eternal blessedness. VII, 648. Perfect wisdom in blessedness. VIII, 1056.

Wisdom, the richness of the soul. IV, 756. Wisdom, the mother of immortal delights. IV, 1466. What kind of appearance wisdom has. IV, 1908. How human wisdom is also God’s wisdom. VIII, 1048. God’s wisdom transfers itself into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets. VII, 319. The wisdom of the patriarchs and prophets is by far the most ancient of all. VII, 599. There is no true wisdom without true religion. VII, 51. The vision of immortal wisdom is dispensed in one way timelessly and in another way temporally. V, 1177. Human wisdom cannot be comprehended. VIII, 1066. How the spirit of wisdom is manifold. VII, 327. The Stoics are mistaken when they say that a person does not possess wisdom unless he is perfect in it. II, 738. Everyone sees that unchangeable wisdom must be preferred to what is changeable. III, 22. In unchangeable wisdom itself all good commandments are heard or seen. III, 392.

Whether wisdom is distinguished from knowledge. IV, 1759, 1760. How it differs from knowledge. VI, 140. What difference there is between the two. VIII, 1069. The functions of wisdom and knowledge are to be distinguished from Scripture. VIII, 1013. What the whole discipline of wisdom consists in. VI, 96. Whatever is sought for the attainment of wisdom concerns either morals, nature, or reason. II, 441. Eternal wisdom never ceases speaking to the intellectual creature, so that it may turn back to the source from which it comes. III, 249, 250. The sun of wisdom shines everywhere, but is not seen by fools. X, 130. Wisdom itself reveals itself to those who diligently pursue it. I, 1263. Few spiritual people attain to the most sincere knowledge of wisdom in this life. VIII, 175. Who are alienated from wisdom. I, 913. Everyone possesses wisdom as an artisan, but not everyone possesses light. IV, 1378. Although wisdom is everywhere, it is nevertheless far from the wicked. IV, 1908. A certain disposition is found midway between folly and wisdom. I, 607, 1305, 1307. The little child passes from infancy through childish vanity and intermediate ignorance to wisdom. X, 795, 821. Those seek wisdom perversely who seek it for empty glory. IV, 1585, 1586. Some do not find wisdom because they hate it. IV, 1585. The wicked seek wisdom in words but hate it in their conduct. IV, 1374. There is no other way to union with wisdom than through Christ. I, 590.

Since divine wisdom itself is our homeland, it also made itself the way to our homeland. III, 23. How God’s wisdom came to us. III, 23. Wisdom incarnate is the model for the purification of the soul. III, 23. God’s wisdom came to us so that we might cease to be childish in mind. III, 260. Wisdom healed the human being from certain opposites and from certain likenesses. III, 24. Through the incarnation God’s wisdom became weak, so that it might protect us beneath its wings like a hen protecting her chicks. IV, 1161. God put on flesh so that he might make his wisdom into milk for us. IV, 235, 1742. By what steps one reaches wisdom. I, 881. Seven steps to wisdom. III, 39.

Wisdom is not found unless it is desired with all the powers of the soul. I, 1324. Neither the presence of friends nor life itself is to be sought for its own sake, but for the sake of wisdom. I, 880. The harbor of wisdom does not receive a soul clinging to mortal things. I, 905. Solomon lost the wisdom he had acquired through spiritual love through carnal love. III, 77, 78. No one should wish to reach the height of wisdom before possessing the humility of obedience. IV, 1566. To find the way of wisdom, one needs a pure and simple eye. III, 1308. Wisdom finds no place where there is no patience. V, 825. Lovers of wisdom seek many people who will pursue it with them. I, 881. Christ does not conceal the treasures of wisdom in order to refuse them, but to awaken desire for what is hidden. V, 336. Wisdom is not denied to natural capacity, but it is denied to negligence. IV, 1368. To whom wisdom is given when they ask for it. X, 255. Augustine asks daily alms from the treasure of wisdom in a beggar’s prayer. II, 1076.

Where wisdom comes from in human beings. X, 485. Wisdom that is from above pertains to grace, not to free will. X, 255. Wisdom is God’s gift. VI, 421. Its great gift. VI, 444. The end of all gifts. III, 40. Why Scripture almost never says anything about wisdom except to show that it was made or created by God. VIII, 937, 938. How the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. V, 1524. The pursuit of wisdom is occupied with action and contemplation. VII, 228. The discovery of wisdom is to be preferred to treasures. I, 751. Who are understood as shackled in heart in regard to wisdom. IV, 1146. The bonds of wisdom. II, 103.

Wisdom signified by the name of gold. V, 331. The sacrament of wisdom, the tree of life. III, 376, 447, 451. Wisdom is the bread of the righteous person. IV, 390. Wisdom is called the sun. IV, [Col. 0588] 1760. In Scripture wisdom sometimes means cunning. V, 286. Often it means the wisdom of this world. II, 642. The wisdom of the world is folly to God. V, 1132. Christ destroys the wisdom that the wise arrogate to themselves, not the wisdom he has given them. VII, 307. Heavenly wisdom surpasses civic wisdom in authority and virtue. VII, 600. Wisdom is spoken of in the arts—in what sense. III, 515. Wisdom commended by Cicero. VIII, 1056.

The author of the Book of Wisdom. I, 631. Who he was is not apparent. III, 946, 947. On uncertain grounds it is believed to have been written by Sirach or Philo. X, 1420. The Jews do not receive the Book of Wisdom as canonical authority. I, 637; II, 199. The Massilians reject it. X, 955, n. 4, 979. The Book of Wisdom possesses the authority of canonical Scripture. X, 980, 981. Great and learned men who treated the divine utterances long before Augustine used the authority of the Book of Wisdom. X, 1019, 1020.

## The wise person

Who should be called wise. I, 1231; III, 61, 62; VIII, 84. Plato calls the wise person an imitator, knower, and lover of God. VII, 229. The functions of the wise person. I, 917. Constancy. I, 1002, 1020. The distinction between the wise person and the student. I, 936. And between the wise person and the fool. I, 1231. Against the Academics, the wise person must be perfect; but one who is still seeking the truth is not perfect. I, 917. The wise person should be an investigator of things, not a craftsman of words. I, 932. The wise person knows something—at least, he knows wisdom. I, 935. For the wise person wisdom is certain, and he assents to that which, if he had not grasped it, he would not be wise. I, 951. True knowledge exists in him alone. I, 915. The wise are more certain about those things that they understand beyond the appearance and likeness of the body. III, 484. In knowledge the wise person loves truth alone; in action, peace; in the body, health. III, 167. The wise person understands himself. I, 996.

The wise person is one who lives justly and prudently. I, 1256. He is at peace under the rule of the mind, with every desire subjected. I, 1231. The Stoics did not exclude every disturbance from the mind of the wise person. III, 556. The truly wise—those alone who may rightly be called blessed—did not wish the goods of fortune either to be feared or desired. II, 66. The wise person needs nothing. I, 992. The wise person alone does not sin. VIII, 85. The wise person is one who believes that he does not exist. X, 510. The wise person has not confined the pursuits of prudence within any limits or boundary. II, 512. The wise person is always fixed upon God, whether silent or speaking. I, 997. The wise person is joined to God in mind. VIII, 88. How people become wise. VIII, 937. Human beings are wise not from themselves but from God. II, 669. Whatever soul truly becomes wise does so through participation in God’s wisdom. III, 1058, 1069; VII, 326. When the inner human being truly becomes wise, he is illuminated only by the one who is the true light. X, 130. Hence, just as everyone wishes to be blessed, so everyone wishes to be wise. I, 1254. The authority of the wise person alone is to be valued. I, 908. It is safest to obey the wise. VIII, 84. No one seeks a wise person unless he is believed to exist. VIII, 85. In the Latin language, “wise” properly and laudably refers only to a good sense. III, 431. In Scripture, however, “wise” is sometimes taken in a bad sense. III, 431. The wise and prudent, from whom the mysteries have been hidden. V, 436.

## Sarah

Why Sarah’s name was changed, and the interpretation of both names. VII, 507. Sarah was barren. III, 2133. What Sarah’s barrenness signifies. VII, 440. The multiple cause of Sarah’s barrenness. ## Saturn

Saturn. IX, 262. Saturn is called **φαίνων** (*phainōn*, “shining”) in Greek. III, 236. Saturn is so called from sowing. VII, 205. Saturn is called so in Latin as though he were “sated with years.” III, 1057. According to the later Platonists, Saturn is named as if from the satiety of understanding. III, 1057. In Greek he is called **Χρόνος** (*Chronos*, “Time”). III, 1057. Why he holds a sickle. III, 1057. And why his image is represented with his head covered. III, 1057. Saturn is the length of time. VII, 120. Saturn is believed to have ruled in Italy before his son Picus. VII, 572. Saturn himself is Jupiter. VII, 205. Why Saturn is said to have castrated his father. VII, 209. And to have devoured his children. VII, 186. A stone was substituted for his son, and Saturn devoured it. VII, 202. Interpretation of the myths about Saturn. VII, 208. It is taken from ancient history that Saturn fled from Jupiter’s weapons. II, 84. Human sacrifices were offered to Saturn. VII, 209. By what arguments they proved that Saturn ought to be worshiped. VII, 209. Saturn’s star. VII, 206. The astrologers established Saturn among the stars as a maleficent god. III, 1058. Saturn completes the zodiacal circuit in thirty years. III, 232, 266. Saturn’s year consists of thirty years. III, 236. Why Saturn is extremely cold. III, 266. Saturn is slow because he is nearer the cold waters that are above the heavens. III, 232. Why Saturn was thought to be the God of the Hebrews. III, 1055. Some think that our ancestors were dedicated to Saturn because of the Sabbath. VIII, 379.

## Saul

Saul means “request” or “desire.” IV, 148, 600. How many years Saul, the first king of the Israelites, reigned. VII, 577. How the Spirit of God in Saul was both good and evil. VI, 134. How greatly David honored Saul because of the sacred anointing. IX, 298. Why David revered the anointing in Saul for so long. VII, 536. IV, 663; VII, 538. Saul was prefigured in Paul. V, 948. Saul was a very wicked king. V, [Col. 0590] 1278. Saul’s criminal character. II, 171.

The name Saul derives from Saül. IV, 916; V, 917, 948, 1429. What difference there is between Saul and Paul. III, 2037. He stoned Stephen by the hands of all. V, 1429. The free grace of God was demonstrated in the conversion of Saul as he raged. V, 913. Saul’s conversion may perhaps be owed to Stephen’s prayer. V, 806. When Saul’s heart was pierced, he began to suffer the same things as those whose hearts he had pierced. IV, 1441. ## Scandal

Scandal and affliction. V, 499. Scandal arising from the eye, the hand, and the foot. V, 501. Two scandals to be feared from heretics. IV, 1615. Scandal arising from the happiness of the wicked. Augustine tries to prevent scandals from being brought to the knowledge of the common people. II, 285, 286. Scandals are to be tolerated for the love of unity. VIII, 262. ## Schism

What schism is according to Faustus. VIII, 369. Schisms are divisions. V, 1165, 1244. Schism is a recent dissension within a congregation arising from some difference of opinion. IX, 471. Schism is discerned in departure, heresy in sacrilegious doctrine. IX, 747. No cause of schism is lawful. IX, 517. There is no just necessity for cutting off unity. IX, 69. There is no cause for a bodily separation of the good from the wicked. IX, 59. Separation of heart, not of body, is commanded. IX, 79, 80. One must not withdraw from Catholic bishops wherever they may happen to err by holding an opinion contrary to the canonical Scriptures of God. IX, 410. Israel’s secession from the kingdom of Judah was not schismatic. IX, 417. Hypocrisy must be opposed in such a way that the danger of schism is avoided. V, 94. Schisms are the dung of the Church. V, 53. Schisms are branches cut off. V, 53, 55. What follows from a vain and rash separation. IX, 105. Where charity is absent, justice cannot exist. III, 1236. Charity grieves when unity is divided. III, 1992. The Lord’s threshing floor could have sustained those who caused schisms as straw until the time of the final winnowing, unless they had voluntarily separated themselves from us. III, 127. How we know that no one rightly separates himself from communion with all nations. II, 334.

Under the Old Testament, schism was a crime more serious than the burning of a prophetic book and the making of an idol. II, 192. It is a wound more serious than idolatry or unbelief. IX, 115. The crime of schism is far more wicked than betrayal. IX, 349. More wicked than homicide. IX, 581. Schism is the most monstrous sacrilege. IX, 333. Nothing is more serious than the sacrilege of schism. IX, 69, 132. Schism is wound and death. IX, 137, 138. Schism or heresy is a more dreadful death than bodily death. IX, 43. Schism surpasses every crime. IX, 38. Whether schism is a sin against the Holy Spirit. IX, 554. God hates schisms. II, 172. The punishment of Dathan and Abiram indicates how highly schism is valued in the divine judgment. II, 298. Schisms are most justly punished by true unity alone. IX, 55.

From where schisms arise. III, 1984. The origin of schisms is hatred of one’s brother. IX, 118. Schisms arise from the very animal sense. IX, 122. All schisms are made by carnal people. V, 49. They could not have made a schism except by being maddened by swelling pride, deranged by the lividness of envy, corrupted by secular advantage, or perverted by carnal fear. IX, 104. The Donatists made a schism and heresy by persisting wrongly. II, 298. Augustine charged the Donatists with the crime of schism alone. II, 298. Communion with the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through agreement in their deeds. [Col. 0591] II, 579. The Donatists admitted this at the Conference of Carthage. II, 403, 409. Heresies and schisms are signified by the sons of Keturah. III, 2133. An exhortation to avoid schism. IX, 350.

## Schismatics

How schismatics differ from heretics. III, 1367. Heretics and schismatics were born of a young mother and an old father without a promise. III, 2134. They were born of a free woman, but according to the flesh. III, 2133. Schismatics boast that they alone are Christians and condemn the others. IX, 588. All authors of schism adopt this one argument: that the righteous are stained by the sins of others when they share the sacraments with them. II, 339. How false this is. II, 339. Some became schismatics because they feared being stained through association with sinners. V, 41. It is necessary to tolerate weeds and false brothers among the wheat until the harvest. III, 1799. Schismatics wish to show Christ as existing in one part, although he purchased the whole. III, 1984. Whoever loves a part is divided; if he is divided, he is not in the body; if he is not in the body, he is not under the head. III, 2060. Schismatics are worse than those who crucified Christ. IV, 311. Schismatics are to be counted among the dead and lost. I, 642. Those who have separated from unity and, by leading souls astray, destroy them shed blood spiritually, not bodily. IV, 645. Schismatics are murderers. IX, 274. Spiritual life is lost through schism. V, 1231. Schismatics do not belong to the Church. VI, 193. Schismatics tear the nets. IV, 781. Schismatics are connected with the Church in some respect and possess something sound. IX, 115. But through the deadly wound of schism, that sound element is dragged to destruction. IX, 115. In whatever they agree with us, schismatics are also with us. IX, 110. Schismatics belong to the people of God, if not through virtue, at least through the appearance of piety. IV, 1427. Although schismatics possess baptism, they do not possess the Holy Spirit. V, 462, 1235, 1236. Schismatics lack charity. IX, 121. Schismatics cannot be good. II, 952. The one who does not know how to err ought to separate. II, 952. Whatever good schismatics may be able to do does not benefit them. IX, 116. Whether the endurance of schismatics who endure tortures so as not to deny Christ is to be praised. VI, 623. Whether that endurance is a gift of God. VI, 624. Whether it benefits them. VI, 624. Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however laudably he may think he lives, will not have life because of this one crime: that he is separated from the unity of Christ. II, 579. Schismatics have no share in the inheritance of God. V, 797. Established outside the Church, you would be punished with eternal punishment even if you were burned alive for Christ’s name. II, 756. Christ does not take up schismatics because he takes up unity. IV, 779. Schismatics are opposed. IV, 1254. Schismatics are to be recalled peacefully to peace. V, 1583. Schismatics are rightly compelled to unity by emperors. V, 295. Augustine formerly did not approve of forcibly returning them to Catholic communion, but later, having learned by experience how much the diligence of discipline could contribute to changing them for the better, he changed his opinion. I, 641. Penalties decreed against schismatics by the law of Theodosius. IX, 48. Schismatics returning to the Catholic Church should be shown the piety of unity; the sacrament of truth must not be denied to them. IX, 603. It is permissible to deal with a heretic or schismatic concerning the affairs of the soul. II, 160.

## Knowledge

What knowledge is and how it exists in God. VI, 139. God’s knowledge is the cause of things, whereas human knowledge is caused by things. VII, 327. How God’s knowledge shines forth even in the smallest things. II, 519. God’s knowledge is unchangeable. VII, 334. The knowledge of approval in God. III, 647.

Whether knowledge is the same as wisdom. IV, 1759. Knowledge is distinguished from wisdom. VI, 140. What difference exists between them. VIII, 1009, 1013, 1012. Knowledge is the lesser luminary, wisdom the greater luminary. I, 854. The Stoics attribute knowledge to no one except the wise person. I, 874. Knowledge is the third step toward wisdom. III, 39. Knowledge exists when something has been perceived and known by a firm reasoning. I, 607, 1063. The idea that what we learn is not inserted into us as something new but recalled to memory through recollection was Socrates’ discovery. II, 68. Plato wishes the things we learn to remain always and not be able to perish, and therefore not to be past. II, 68. Knowledge pertains to those things we experience through the senses of the body. VI, 140. We know something both through sensory experience and through the testimony of witnesses. I, 607. How knowledge and sensation differ. I, 1066, 1067. The distinction between knowledge and experience. I, 1231. Certain knowledge of many things is given. VI, 243. Certain things in physics are known with certainty. I, 946. That is not to be called knowledge in which the person who professes it is sometimes mistaken. I, 915. Some kinds of knowledge are not human inventions. III, 55. Two kinds of these sciences. III, 55. The same or an equal knowledge belongs to dissimilar things. I, 874. Knowledge of human things is that which knows the light of prudence, the beauty of temperance, the strength of courage, and the holiness of justice. I, 915. Our knowledge consists of things seen and things believed. II, 600. We see some things through the senses and others through the mind’s intuition. II, 597, 599. Knowledge is attributed to the mind, whether it retains something perceived through the bodily senses or through the mind itself. II, 600. There can be no knowledge of false things. I, 936, 939.

Love of knowledge. VII, 341. No living creature except the human being possesses knowledge. VII, 341. The senses of irrational creatures contain a certain likeness of knowledge. VII, 341. We must beware of eagerness for empty knowledge. I, 1327. Knowledge can never be evil. I, 1230. Knowledge is food for the soul. I, 963. Two kinds of knowledge of evil. VII, 803. Those eager to learn the ancient and senile falsehoods of many people are restrained. II, 996. Listeners are won over through a collection of borrowed and conflicting opinions belonging to others. II, 999. This is called the most unskilled knowledge and is especially opposed to humility. II, 1005. Knowing the opinions of philosophers is not true learning and is opposed to the humility of Christ. II, 1005, 1007. How painful it is for children to learn the sciences. VII, 728. Why few and rarely attain knowledge. I, 918. To reach knowledge, the inner and outer senses must be surpassed. I, 1245. To impede the knowledge of things, the soul is weighed down by the body because of original sin. X, 1268. Knowledge does not puff up when charity builds up. X, 374. Compared with God’s knowledge, our knowledge is ignorance. I, 811. What knowledge is unnecessary for a Christian, and what knowledge is sufficient. VI, 235, 236. What kinds of knowledge, and to what extent, we ought to possess. VI, 239. Knowledge necessary for possessing the virtues. VIII, 1009. What knowledge is useful, and when. IV, 1548. What knowledge produces in the student of Scripture. III, 39. The knowledge of salvation is superior to all others. VIII, 885. This is the whole of great knowledge: to know that a person is nothing by himself, and that whatever he is comes from God and exists for God. IV, 874. Humility is necessary for the knowledge of God. V, 671. What each person is today, to some extent the person himself knows; what he will be tomorrow, not even he knows. V, 285, 971. Useful knowledge is that which accompanies charity and is the teacher of humility. IV, 1848. Knowledge is useful when joined with charity. III, 1617. All knowledge serves faith, hope, and charity. III, 35. Knowledge serves charity. II, 737. Knowledge employed toward the end of charity is very useful; in itself, without such an end, it has been shown to be not merely superfluous but even harmful. II, 223. Knowledge is given with complete certainty. VII, 646. It is of no benefit without charity. VII, 273. Whether knowledge should be avoided lest it puff one up. V, 1565. What kind of knowledge puffs one up. VIII, 1007, 1009. Knowledge without charity puffs up. V, 1241. Even if knowledge pertains to the law of God, if it exists in some respect without charity, it puffs up and harms. IX, 461. In addition to knowledge and delight in the law, grace is still required. II, 884. Charity is the fullness of knowledge. IV, 1260. Knowledge of God is his own gift. II, 574. Knowledge is less a gift than charity. X, 374. It is not in human power what a person knows. X, 242. By what means we shall learn the knowledge necessary for us from God without a teacher. II, 576. Great knowledge is confidence in God. V, 907. In knowledge of divine things, the gentle and humble make more progress by thinking and praying than by reading and hearing. II, 597. Knowledge itself punishes the conscience if what is learned is not put into practice. V, 1162. Knowledge is signified by the name of the moon. IV, 1760.

## To know

What we properly mean when we say “to know.” VIII, 63, 64. Everything we are said to know is grasped either through bodily sensation or through understanding. VIII, 93. We should not consider ourselves to know anything unless it is especially manifest to us. I, 923. We should not doubt that the things we have learned through the bodily senses are true. VIII, 1075. There are two kinds of things that are known. VIII, 1074. We know nothing as surely as we know that we are alive. VIII, 1073. And that we wish to be blessed. VIII, 1074. Whether knowing the causes of things pertains to happiness. VI, 239. Why what is known in this life does not make people completely blessed. VIII, 63, 64. Whoever says that he knows what he does not know is rash; whoever denies knowing what he does know is ungrateful. V, 1223. A person should not be ashamed to confess that he does not know what he does not know, lest, while pretending to know, he never become worthy to know. II, 862. Let no one ask me to know what I know that I do not know, unless perhaps he wishes to learn not to know what must be known to be unknowable. VI, 652. It is no small benefit if someone who wishes to learn something, thinking it would help him to know it, learns that it does no harm not to know it. VI, 609. God is said to “know” something as though for the first time when he causes us to know it. IV, 355, 615, 616.

The basilica of the Scillitan Martyrs. V, 840.

The Sciopods, so called as though they were “shadow-feet.” VII, 485.

## Students

Students. IV, 494. The license of students at Carthage. I, 712. The Romans were more restrained. I, 712. Yet they often cheated their teacher. I, 716.

[Col. 0593] A *scholasticus*, a legal expert. III, 1442.

A scorpion strikes with its tail. V, 621. A scorpion is struck down and eaten by a hen. V, 623, 625.

The scribes were not, among the Jews, those who served in the offices of judges or in the civic administration. V, 472. Their office. V, 472. The scribes were not learned in the kingdom of God. V, 472.

To be unwilling to withdraw one’s own writings, or to have them criticized by others when something has not been properly stated, is foolish. II, 585. Whoever could not attain the first rank of wisdom, namely, not to err, should attain the second rank of modesty, namely, to withdraw his errors. II, 586. Augustine does not approve of having one’s writings praised with a deceitful heart, or criticized before others while one remains silent. II, 301. Augustine wishes himself to be seen in what displeases in his writings, and God to be praised in what rightly pleases. II, 110. Marcellinus presses Augustine to publish certain of his writings, so that he may defend them while still alive. II, 586. He himself, however, delays, and is a strict judge of them, so that there may be fewer things open to criticism. II, 586, 587.

The sacred writers spoke with one Spirit. III, 1175, 1176. When they speak about themselves, they speak as though about another. III, 1800. The authority of ecclesiastical writers must be distinguished from canonical authority. II, 339. It is permissible to think differently from ecclesiastical writers when they have thought differently from what truth requires. II, 339.

The Manichaeans remove the authority of the Scriptures from consideration, accepting some passages and rejecting others. VIII, 508, 597, 606. They said that the testimonies of the Scriptures to which they could not respond were false. VIII, 245. They did not accept the books of the Old Testament, and accepted only such books of the New Testament as they wished. X, 1008. They asserted that these had been corrupted. X, 1009. They maintained that certain false statements had been mixed into the canonical Scriptures which they accepted. X, 1337. They recklessly taught that the Scriptures were corrupt. VIII, 69. The Manichaeans thought that they had been corrupted by those who transmitted them. VIII, 70. He does injury to the Scripture of the Old Testament with heretical impiety who, with the face of sacrilegious impiety, denies that it comes from the good, supreme, and true God. X, 328, 329. The critics of the Scriptures were humbled by God. IV, 1907, 1908. Faustus’s slanders against persons, or against their deeds as related in the Scriptures, are refuted. VIII. Throughout Book 22 Against Faustus. The Donatists boast that they preserved the Scriptures from fire. V, 310. The Lord’s codices were cast into the fire by the Donatists. II, 807.

The necessity of sacred Scripture arose from sin. III, 198. The praise and dignity of sacred Scripture. I, 854; II, 508, 524. The dignity and excellence of the Scriptures of the Old Testament. VIII, 74. In both Testaments the same commandments and the same promises are found. VIII, 134, 135. The divine authority of sacred Scripture. I, 723, 842, 852; VIII, 249. The authority of Scripture is marvelous. VII, 357, 359. And supremely eminent. VII, 318. Holy Scripture is placed at the highest and heavenly summit of authority. II, 277, 278. Whatever resists the history of our religion is utterly false. VII, 600. One must believe that only the authors of the canonical books did not err in writing anything. II, 276, 284, 285. The authority of the canonical Scriptures yields to no one. VIII, 517, 678. Sacred Scripture surpasses all others. IX, 128.

By whom the canonical Scripture was composed. VII, 318. In it God himself speaks. I, 864. And the Apostle demonstrates this. VIII, 646. The Scriptures of the Old Testament belong to the true and good God. VIII, 646. Sacred Scripture is God’s bond of indebtedness (*chirographum Dei*). IV, 1880. They are letters that have come to us from our homeland. IV, 1159, 1952. Sacred Scripture is the venerable stylus of the Spirit of God. I, 747. Scripture is used in place of God. VIII, 646. Sacred Scripture is discussed at length. I, 1335. From where the authority of the Scriptures is to be established. VIII, 245, 248, 283, 284, 452, 485, 486, 517, 626. Scripture proves its own credibility by the realities themselves. VIII, 284. How great is the authority of Scripture in its narration of historical events. VII, 599, 600. Scripture is truthful even if it is not demonstrated to be so. III, 329. The authority of the Scriptures of the Old Testament is commended by Christ and his Apostles. VIII, 637, 638, 647. The Jews themselves denied that the Scriptures of the Old Testament had been composed by Christians. VIII, 288. There is no room in Scripture for correction or doubt. VIII, 248, 249. The authority of Scripture must not be blamed on account of the sins it reports; rather, it must be praised and loved. VIII, 438, 439, 440. Concerning the authority of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Ecclesiasticus, and Wisdom. VII, 554. Likewise, of Malachi, Haggai, Zechariah, and Ezra. VII, 560. The Scriptures called canonical in the Church must be believed without any doubt. II, 598. God did not wish people merely to believe him when he spoke, but wished them to hold fast to his Scripture. IV, 1880. Christ wished nothing to be believed against the established authority of the Scriptures. VIII, 284. Whatever the authority of the divine Scriptures prescribes, or whatever the universal Church practices, must be observed. II, 202. Which writings among the canonical Scriptures have the greater authority. III, 40. Faith falters if the authority of the divine Scriptures falters. III, 35. Faith has been formed from the Scriptures. VII, 646. The city of God believes the canonical Scriptures. VII, 646. Scripture has now demonstrated its truth to the whole world. VII, 708. They try to undermine the authority of holy Scripture who attribute any lie to it. VI, 404. No matter how holy and learned a man may be, he must not be compared with the authority of the canonical Scriptures. X, 381. If an argument is brought against the authority of the divine Scriptures, no matter how clever it may be, it deceives by plausibility, for it cannot be true. II, 588. Those think that Christian teaching is incompatible with the welfare of the state who do not want the state to stand firm through the strength of virtues, but through the impunity of vices. II, 525.

The supreme truth of Scripture. I, 839, 860. And its great superiority to profane writings. I, 748. When Scripture takes a testimony from an author, it does not thereby confirm the rest of that author’s writings. III, 738. Comparison of sacred Scripture with profane writings. III, 65. Orosius, a young presbyter inflamed by zeal for Scripture, came to Augustine from the farthest part of Spain. II, 748. Sacred Scripture is Augustine’s chaste delight. I, 809. Sacred Scripture is sweeter than all the delights of the world. I, 810. In Scripture there is satiety without disgust. V, 30. In what manner one should devote oneself to the study of sacred Scripture. III, 42. The study of sacred Scripture is given by God. III, 90.

Holy Scripture is customarily read in the Church. IX, 330. How the Scriptures should be read. V, 354. How they are truly read. III, 92. With what disposition they should be read so as to be beneficial. VIII, 74. What those who read sacred Scripture seek. III, 38, 42. Those who recoil from sacred Scripture because of the roughness of its style are mistaken. III, 262. Sacred Scripture is accessible to all, but penetrable by few. II, 524. Its approach is open both to the small and to those capable of understanding. IV, 1360, 1361. Sacred Scripture has been brought down even to the dullness of infants. IV, 112. Holy Scripture has been adapted to the weakness of little ones. V, 156. Sacred Scripture is the heart of Christ, revealed when he was crucified so that it might be understood even by all the weak. IV, 175. What disposition should be adopted toward the difficulties of Scripture by one who is not yet a believer and by one who is already a believer. II, 386. The study of sacred Scripture requires a humble and gentle spirit. III, 64, 66. An explanation of Scripture that is not understood must be sought from God. III, 1539, 1540. Understanding of Scripture must be sought from God in prayer. III, 89. Human beings minister the Scriptures to us; God alone gives understanding of them. III, 1382. Understanding Scripture should not be expected in an unusual manner. III, 17. Whoever cannot understand Scripture should give God’s Scripture honor and himself fear. III, 261. When sacred Scripture is not understood, how it should be read. III, 1536. Whoever’s heart is full of charity understands the Scriptures without any error and preserves them without any labor. V, 1533. Sacred Scripture is free for the soul that serves, pure for the contaminated, and whole for the corrupted. I, 734. Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth frightens the attentive, by its truth nourishes the great, and by its friendliness feeds the little ones. III, 323. The same Scripture is called the Old Testament when it oppresses slaves, and the New Testament when it raises up the free. III, 2145. Scripture does not raise us unless it descends to us, just as the Word became flesh and descended in order to raise us. III, 1914. Those who read the Scriptures with an evil intention, through sin, are forced to understand them wrongly, so that this itself becomes the punishment of sin. IV, 106. Augustine advises beginning the reading of Scripture with the Apostles. II, 508.

The simplicity of sacred Scripture. I, 686, 723, 841. In the Scriptures there is a most salutary humility of wondrous height. VI, 319. The marvelous depth of sacred Scripture. I, 723, 810, 832, 1315; II, 516. The harmony of the Scriptures. VII, 600. Although the writers of the Scriptures are different, everything nevertheless agrees with everything else so completely that it is found to have been spoken as if with one mouth. VIII, 249. From whom the exposition of sacred Scripture should be sought. I, 1311. Sacred Scripture must be examined with respect for God’s servants who administered it. I, 843. One must not believe interpreters of the Scriptures who are hostile to them. VIII, 74. No one should judge sacred Scripture. I, 859.

The division of sacred Scripture. III, 1745. All Scripture is divided into two parts, the Old and the New Testaments. III, 246, 247. The canon of the books of the Old and New Testaments. III, 41. Which books of Scripture the Jews do not accept. III, 946. Legitimate Scriptures, that is, those containing the Law. III, 887, 888. Which is canonical Scripture and which apocryphal. VII, 470. Which writings are canonical Scripture was established by a council. II, 233. Whoever reads noncanonical Scriptures before the people causes them scandal. II, 233. Not everything that God spoke to the sacred authors has been written down. III, 690. Many writings are produced under the names of Prophets and Apostles. VII, 470, 471. The integrity and knowledge of the canonical Scriptures were guarded with such care that some people attempted in vain to fabricate writings in the names of the Apostles. II, 340. The Epistles to the Romans and Galatians are compared with one another. X, 733. In the Epistle to the Romans almost the entire discussion concerns grace alone, and does so so contentiously and in so many ways that it indeed tires the reader’s attention, though with a useful and salutary weariness. X, 207. The Epistle to the Hebrews was uncertain to some, but was counted among the canonical books by the Eastern churches. X, 137. The writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews is a faithful preacher of the faith. X, 1284. Distinguished defenders of the Catholic rule used the Epistle to the Hebrews as a testimony. VI, 235. The books of Scripture preserved by Catholic discipline have not been falsified. VI, 70.

Scripture was explained in the church. VII, 77. Treating the Scriptures is a great and difficult work. III, 19. It must be undertaken with God’s help. III, 19. When it is not rash to discuss the Scriptures. III, 19. Two vices are hostile to the treatment of the Scriptures. VIII, 845. The rule for understanding Scripture. IX, 673. Rules for understanding the Scriptures. V, 26, 30, 46, 149, 180, 198, 450, 456, 470, 556, 609. Fourfold method of treating the Scriptures of the Old Testament. VIII, 68.
