How Scripture should be understood and explained. VII, 473. Certain precepts for treating the Scriptures can be handed down. III, 15, 18. These are criticized by three classes of people. III, 15, 16. Their objections are answered. III, 16, 17. The treatment of the Scriptures rests on two things. III, 19. Rules for attaining the true meaning of the Scriptures. VI, 344, 345. Different interpretations of sacred Scripture can simultaneously be true. I, 838, 844. It is not harmful to think differently from others, provided that what we think is true. I, 836. Which meaning should be regarded as superior. I, 844. In all the Scriptures the greatest vigilance must be maintained, so that the exposition of the divine mystery may accord with the faith. VI, 55. In the Scriptures it is permissible to understand something the writer did not understand, but not something contrary to the rule of faith and truth. V, 63. The reliability of sacred Scripture must be established from the original language. VII, 455.

The various versions of sacred Scripture. VII, 603. From where Scripture was translated into different languages. III, 38. Ambiguity in Scripture in one language is removed by another. IV, 1536. Many translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek, and countless others also into Latin. III, 43. Scripture was translated from Greek codices into the Latin language. IX, 709. There are very few interpreters of the divine Scriptures in Latin, but countless ones in Greek. VIII, 214. Translation of the Old Scripture from Greek into Latin according to the Seventy translators. I, 592. Why certain things are found in the Septuagint version that are not in the Hebrew codices, and conversely. VII, 604. Both the Hebrew codices and the Septuagint version should be used. VII, 605. What obeli and asterisks signified in the Greek codices. III, 590; VII, 604. Asterisks in Scripture indicated that the words to which they were attached were not in the translation of the Septuagint, but were in the Hebrew. IV, 821. See *Lexicon*. Augustine compared the sacred Scriptures with the interpretation of the Septuagint. III, 547. The customary interpretation of Scripture. III, 1139. The Latin version of the Scriptures varies so greatly in different codices that it can scarcely be tolerated. II, 243. Augustine wishes to be rid of the great incompetence of the Latin interpreters. II, 291.

The Scriptures were so arranged by the Holy Spirit that some things in them were obscure and others clear. IX, 396. Why clear passages are intermingled with obscure ones, and obscure passages with clear ones, in the Scriptures. IV, 136. Although innumerable things lie hidden in the Scriptures, one does not reach what is necessary for salvation with such great difficulty in them. II, 516. The Scriptures are clear in matters necessary for salvation. X, 186. The obscurity of Scripture is useful. VII, 332. Indeed, it is not useless. III, 38. Why some things in the Scriptures are closed and others open. V, 849. In the Scriptures some things are hidden more secretly, so as to exercise those who seek them, while others are placed openly, so as to heal those who desire them. V, 196. Certain words of the Scriptures have benefited us by their obscurity, because they have produced many interpretations. IV, 159, 160. Certain mysteries of the Scriptures are closed, not so that they may be denied, but so that they may be opened to those who knock. IV, 1189, 1907; V, 1237. Something is obscure in the Scriptures so that the one who will receive it may be exercised and become more capable of receiving what is given. IV, 1907. And so that, after the labor of inquiry, the sweetness of discovery may be more delightful. IV, 413. And so that knowledge of something already known may itself become as though new. IV, 1803. The hidden places of the Scriptures are especially effective in sharpening love of truth and shaking off the torpor of disgust. VI, 320. Through the Scriptures God wishes to nourish us not only with what is clear, but also to exercise us with what is obscure. VI, 36, 539. In the holy Scriptures, what is placed obscurely to exercise the minds of the faithful should be welcomed if it is explained in many ways, provided that this is not done foolishly. VIII, 795. In the entire abundance of the holy Scriptures we are nourished by what is open and exercised by what is obscure: there hunger is driven away, here disgust. V, 450. The mysteries of God have been set high, lest we grow tired of what is offered, lest what is readily available become cheap, and so that what is sought with difficulty may be found with greater joy. IV, 1350. The Scriptures have been closed for the sake of delight. V, 1555. In Scripture we contemplate more sweetly those things that are extracted from its more hidden places. VIII, 262. God wished the prophecies to be obscure so that preachers, by interpreting them, might pour down spiritual nourishment from them as though from clouds. IV, 1909. The Scriptures are forests because of the density and shade of their mysteries. IV, 214. Pious faith and humble inquiry are necessary for understanding them. V, 336. We must not be content with the surface of the Scriptures. II, 920. In the obscurities of the Scriptures, their interpreters must not be followed rashly. II, 921. Searching the sacred Scriptures is a remedy for curiosity. III, 166. It is not only matters pertaining to the nature of God himself that we are forbidden to scrutinize. X, 527. In obscure matters where the Scriptures do not assist, rashness in judging must be avoided. X, 186. Sacred Scripture is criticized only rashly when it is not understood. VIII, 77, 91. The divine utterances are salutary to those who understand them well, but dangerous to those who wish to twist them according to the perversity of their hearts. IV, 543. The mysteries of the Scriptures build up those who have fallen and satisfy those who hunger. V, 30. Many things lay hidden in the Scriptures that were opened by responding to the questions of heretics. IV, 643, 837. What should be done when sacred Scripture is not understood. III, 1722, 1726, 1727, 1741. What the devout reader should do in obscure passages of Scripture. III, 262. Obscure passages of Scripture should be explained from clearer ones. III, 79. Or by recapitulation. III, 86. The obscure things of the Scriptures are revealed to the gentle and humble. IV, 1907. Obscure Scripture is received differently by the devout and the impious. III, 1721, 1722. Scripture that can yield a twofold meaning should not be interpreted with a hasty assertion. III, 260. Nothing prevents the same passage of Scripture from being understood in different ways. III, 80. What benefit may come from an interpretation of Scripture that proceeds by inquiry rather than assertion. III, 202. An uncertain passage is more safely explained through other passages of Scripture than through reasoning. III, 80. Obscure passages of Scripture should be explained by other clear and unquestionable passages. V, 264, 1634; VII, 332, 333. In the difficulties of Scripture, honor the word of God and defer understanding in piety. IV, 1907. Whoever loves God’s Scripture honors even what he does not understand in it. IV, 1592. Honor in it what you do not understand, and honor it all the more the more veils you see. V, 336. In approaching the divine Scriptures, piety and humility are desired more than intellectual sharpness. V, 336. Before you know why something was said, believe that it ought to have been said in the way it was said. IV, 1915. The difficulty of Scripture does not lie in obscure meanings when the Spirit assists. V, 820. Hold fast to and devoutly receive what is clear in Scripture, so that what is obscure may rightly be opened to you. V, 290. The very desire to understand is prayer before God. V, 820. Augustine admits that in the holy Scriptures themselves he knows far more that he does not know than that he does know. II, 222. The errors of those who do not observe moderation in understanding the Scriptures. VI, 200.

It can happen that Scripture is not understood because of unknown or ambiguous signs. III, 42. The ambiguity of Scripture lies either in proper words or in transferred words. III, 65. What should be done in the ambiguity of the words of sacred Scripture. III, 43, 44, 65, 66. The same word does not always have the same meaning in the Scriptures. III, 78. The Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, and other names found in sacred Scripture had been interpreted in Augustine’s time. III, 62. In the Scriptures everything that is said or done must be understood either literally, figuratively, or in both ways. V, 556. Three kinds of expression occur in the Scriptures. VIII, 846. Three distinctions in the Scriptures of every kind. VIII, 73. From where knowledge of an unknown word or unknown expression is to be extracted. III, 45. It is characteristic of the Scriptures that the conjunction *and* (*et*) is placed where no preceding statement exists to which the following one could be attached: what this signifies. IV, 79, 80. How indefinite propositions in the Scriptures should be understood. V, 450. Scripture sometimes puts the container for the contained. IV, 1414, 1415. It speaks of a part as though it were the whole. II, 638; IV, 1115. It uses the plural for the singular. VII, 519. It sometimes uses “many” for “all.” VII, 696. In Scripture and in the Fathers, speech is generally addressed to all, although it is to be understood as applying only to some. II, 337. Many things are spoken of as though they had happened when they are still matters of hope. II, 842. Scripture narrates future things as past. IV, 1476. It uses the future for the past and the past for the future. VI, 305; VII, 705. The past is often used for the future, but the future only rarely for the past. III, 723.

The predictions of Scripture are either already fulfilled or destined to be fulfilled completely. IV, 451, 452, 1881. Things predicted in the Scriptures can already be seen to have been fulfilled. II, 1028. The manner of counting used by Scripture. V, 352. Passages of Scripture in which one number is taken for another. VI, 253, 254. Scripture uses a complete number for calculating periods of time. III, 613. How ambiguity is removed from pronunciation. III, 67. And from diction. III, 68. The passage from John, “What was made in him was life,” etc.: how it should be punctuated. III, 331, 332. From what is read in the Scriptures, some things that are not read are also understood. VIII, 760. To what extent it is useful to bring forward by conjecture what Scripture leaves unspoken. III, 329. It is customary in the language of the Scriptures for what always exists to be said to occur in something when it begins to be recognized in it. VI, 75, 76. Knowledge of the stars contributes little, or almost nothing, to the treatment of the Scriptures. III, 57. Knowledge of animals, herbs, trees, and so forth contributes to understanding the Scriptures. III, 56, 62. Knowledge of the arts. III, 57. And dialectic. III, 57, 58. Whenever members of God are named in Scripture, the powers of his operations must be understood. IV, 130. It is customary in the divine Scriptures to attribute to the person of God what he does in us, wherever this can suitably be said. IV, 75. Scripture speaks about God in human fashion in order to commend him to us as infants at the breast. IV, 1713. Words by which something about God seems to be suitably expressed are more adapted to human capacity than to divine sublimity. VI, 138. Why Scripture, when speaking about God, also uses words that are ordinarily regarded as faults among human beings. VIII, 142. When Scripture uses our words in speaking about God, it shows that nothing can be said worthily about God. VIII, 138, 142. Why some things in the Scriptures are narrated with God’s judgment stated, and others with his judgment unspoken. VIII, 427. In the Scriptures there are things which, because they do not fit when heard carnally, admonish us to understand them spiritually. II, 459. What should be answered if something in Scripture seems absurd. VIII, 249. Things are not said pointlessly in the Scriptures that cannot fit events performed or to be performed by human or divine agency. VII, 526. The sacred Scriptures seem to quarrel. V, 164, 332.

There is no book of Scripture that, if certain statements are excerpted and torn from their context, does not appear to contradict itself. V, 332. Passages that appear contradictory in Scripture are reconciled. V, 164, 180, 213, 283, 372, 791, 804. Let each person have concord with God’s word in the heart, and there is no discord in the Scriptures. V, 510, 804. Through the Scriptures the Holy Spirit mingles certain things that appear absurd in visible realities, so as to compel us to seek them spiritually. IV, 1351. When speaking about natural things as though according to Christian writings, one must affirm nothing rashly before unbelievers. III, 261, 264. Whatever can be demonstrated about the nature of things by truthful evidence is not contrary to Scripture. III, 262. Where a natural matter is obscure and exceeds our measure, and the clear divine Scripture does not provide assistance, human conjecture must not rashly presume to define anything on that basis. II, 862. It is better to be ignorant with piety than to judge with madness. V, 740.

Sacred Scripture, once falsehoods have been removed, gradually raises us to divine things. VIII, 820. Many things are usefully repeated in the Scriptures. IV, 1817. The same things are stated in many ways so that variety of expression might remove weariness with the truth. IV, 525, 526, 1815. Passages of Scripture that appear to contain a curse were spoken not from ill will but as prophecy. IV, 88. When an oath occurs in the expression of a prophet, it should not be understood as it would be in the mouth of one who is swearing. IV, 99. Not everything narrated in the Scriptures signifies something. VII, 479. But whatever does signify something must be referred to Christ and the Church. VII, 479. In the history of Genesis, not all the people who then existed are named. VII, 446. What is the purpose of the history of Genesis. VII, 446. The kinds of events are distributed through the books of Scripture; the sequence of time is not woven together. III, 731.

The Scriptures do not always speak literally. III, 1303. Why Scripture speaks in figures. VI, 663. Figurative expressions in Scripture are mixed with prophetic ones. VII, 548. And with literal ones. VII, 691. In the things Scripture narrates, some may be understood according to the meaning of the figures, and others according to faith in the historical events. III, 247. Whether everything it reports as historically predicted and fulfilled signifies something to be fulfilled allegorically. VII, 526. To take figurative expressions of Scripture literally is a wretched slavery. III, 68, 69. The death of the soul occurs when understanding is subjected to the flesh by following the letter. III, 69. Augustine succumbs to the literal sense when expounding the Scriptures. I, 688. In the Scriptures many more things are conveyed through allegories and riddles, partly by words alone and partly also by the narration of events. VIII, 257. What cannot be explained according to the letter in Scripture is figurative and mystical. III, 401, 430. Nor can it be referred to the truth of faith or to moral uprightness. III, 71. How the metaphorical modes of speaking in sacred Scripture should be understood. III, 166. What rule should be followed in explaining allegories. IV, 116. No one should try with the utmost impudence to interpret something placed in an allegory as referring to himself unless he also has clear testimonies by whose light the obscure passages may be illuminated. II, 334. Everything signifying something in the Scriptures appears in a certain way to assume the persons of the things it signifies. VII, 610, 611. In the historical events Scripture narrates, it foretells the future. VII, 523, 524. Everything that has been written, even about the creation of the world, can be interpreted as signifying future things. IV, 532. Not everything narrated by the sacred Scriptures is proposed for imitation. IX, 729, 730. How passages of Scripture that suggest cruelty or disgrace, yet are reported in the person of God or of the saints, should be interpreted. III, 72, 73; VIII, 445, 446. And those passages in which certain deeds are praised that are contrary to the customs of good people today. III, 78. Or in which the sins of great men are reported. III, 78. What is generally a disgraceful act in other persons is, in a divine or prophetic person, a sign of some great reality. III, 73. Why certain changes and falls of the good, and again certain changes and advances of the wicked, are reported in the sacred Scriptures. VIII, 464. Why the Scriptures commemorate the falls of great men. IV, 586. In reporting the good and evil of human beings, the Scriptures judge some things and leave others for us to judge. VI, 539. Everything in the Old Testament admonishes the mind first to recognize that it signifies something and then to seek what it signifies. VIII, 274. Everything in the Scriptures either signifies future things or is placed there so that things signifying one another may be connected. VIII, 463. The fact that certain evil human deeds in the holy Scriptures signify good things does not make them good. VIII, 454. There is nothing in Scripture that is not there for the sake of signification. VIII, 273. The figurative meaning of the Scriptures should not be forced upon contentious or unbelieving people. VIII, 612. In the Scriptures, figures may be drawn from any things and words whatsoever, even from a shameful matter; they should be heard not disdainfully but wisely. VIII, 658. The same single reality is often suggested in the Scriptures through many different comparisons. IV, 109. Figures and tropes in sacred Scripture are delightful. III, 39. As the soul is to the body, so meanings must be preferred to words. VI, 320. The person who makes a pious mistake in interpreting the Scriptures must be corrected. III, 34.

In the Scriptures some things pertain only to faith and doctrine, while others concern the ordering of conduct. III, 887, 888, 889. Scripture asserts only the Catholic faith concerning past, present, and future things. III, 71. What is openly set forth in Scripture contains faith and the manner of life. III, 42. In Scripture, things divinely commanded must be believed either to form conduct and piety or to signify something figuratively. VIII, 464. Almost every page of Scripture sounds like nothing other than Christ and the Church spread throughout the whole world. V, 289; VIII, 463. The Scriptures were made for the sake of Christ. IV, 1779. The Old Scripture exists only to commend the coming of Christ and prefigure the Church. VI, 313, 315. The New Scripture narrates Christ and urges love. VI, 315. Throughout all the holy Scriptures, the grace of God that frees us commends itself to us. IV, 874. By Scripture’s manifold expression the soul is worn down, so that the grace of Christ, once glorified, may become sweet. VIII, 845. The whole appearance and countenance of the holy Scriptures admonishes us that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord. VI, 278. How Scripture forms human conduct. III, 71. The books of the Scriptures are full of what is permissible and impermissible. IV, 1921. Through divine Scripture, remedies are provided for the diseases of human wills. III, 38. Every disease of the soul has its own medicine in the Scriptures. IV, 357. Medicines in the holy Scriptures. V, 196. Scripture provides salutary commandments for the greedy, the lustful, and others. III, 125. It is the teacher of humility. I, 841, 852. The Scripture of God fortifies us against scandals. II, 266, 267, 270. Against the slanders and rash suspicions of human beings. II, 267, 271. It is lamentable that what is most salutarily commanded in the divine books is cared for less, while various customs and presumptions are observed exactly. II, 221. Whoever turns the meaning of Scripture toward the twofold love does not fall into a harmful error and does not lie. III, 34. Whoever holds charity in his conduct possesses both what is clear and what is hidden in the divine utterances. V, 1534.

All Scripture tends toward this one goal: that faith, hope, and charity may be built up in the soul. VIII, 951. Faith, hope, and charity are built up through the sacred Scriptures. III, 36. We read the prophetic and apostolic books for the remembrance of our faith, the consolation of our hope, and the encouragement of our charity. VIII, 294. A person supported by faith, hope, and charity needs the Scriptures only in order to instruct others. III, 36. The fullness and end of the Scriptures is love of God and of one’s neighbor. III, 34, 39. In the Scriptures there is a drink prepared for us by God for the love of himself in marvelous ways. IV, 1803. Whatever is conceived salutarily in the mind, spoken by the mouth, or drawn from any divine page has no end other than charity. IV, 1815, 1816. All the Scriptures teach you nothing else but continence from this world, so that your love may run toward God. V, 264, 695. Scripture commands nothing but charity and blames nothing but desire. III, 36, 71, 72. How both Testaments are ordered toward love of God and neighbor. VI, 315. Augustine testifies that he examines himself daily and finds nothing in the Scriptures in which he does not discover the two commandments of charity. II, 222. Whoever’s heart is full of charity understands the Scriptures without error and preserves them without labor. V, 1533. Whatever difficulty a person encounters in the Scriptures, let him not depart from Christ; when Christ has been revealed to him in them, let him understand that he has understood. IV, 1237. Why certain things are said in the Scriptures that do not pertain to the city of God. VII, 479. One must not depart from the teachings of sacred Scripture. I, 990.

The usefulness of the Scriptures. IV, 564. A spectacle provided by God in the meanings of the Scriptures. IV, 298; V, 322. Nearly all the Scriptures are contained in the power and mercy of God. IV, 743. Scripture is an adversary with whom we must quickly agree. V, 245. The Scripture of God is like a field where a building is constructed. III, 1582. Scripture, covered with figures and mysteries, is like a sky covered with clouds. IV, 1908, 1909. The books of the sacred Scriptures are called heavens. IV, 111, 113, 1341. The Scriptures are like the heart of Christ. II, 554. Feasts in the holy Scriptures. V, 581. Why Scripture is called a two-edged sword. VII, 692. The Scriptures are like lamps lit in the night of this age. III, 1662; IV, 1567. The authors of the Scriptures are called mountains and the summits of mountains. IV, 347, 911. Sacred Scripture is a cloud. IV, 137. The cloud in which the glory of Christ appears. VIII, 266. From the same cloud of the Scriptures, according to each person’s merit, there is poured upon the sinner a rain of snares and upon the righteous a rain of abundance. IV, 137. In this life we are nourished by the meanings of the Scriptures. III, 1530. Holy Scripture is pasture. V, 284. A mirror. IV, 1388. A faithful mirror. VIII, 438, 440. A most sincere mirror. IX, 89. A mirror that flatters no one. VI, 702. The holy Scriptures are holy mirrors. VIII, 269. Why Scripture is called a stylus and a pen. IV, 836. Holy Scripture is a divine treasure. V, 1481. The treasure of the Scriptures is great. VI, 670.

All the Scriptures must be heard attentively, but especially those that are effective against heretics. III, 1988. Heretics do not despise the Scriptures; rather, they seem to follow them while following their own errors. II, 459. Things should not be brought from the Scriptures into a dispute that could be common to both parties. IX, 396. Nor things that are figurative and obscure. IX, 397, 398. What should be done when someone perverts the Scriptures. V, 758. Wicked clerics attempt to pervert a passage of Scripture from the Gospel. V, 758. Study of the Scriptures, prayer, and reading are necessary for a priest. II, 88, 89. It belongs to pastors not to remain silent; it belongs to the sheep, even if the pastors are silent, to hear the Shepherd’s words from the holy Scriptures. V, 282. We must fear that the divine utterances may be stroked and flattered rather than treated. II, 353. The Scriptures and the Sacraments are shared by the good and the wicked. V, 48.

The monk Antony both retained the divine Scriptures by listening to them and understood them through prudent reflection. III, 17. The same is related of a Christian barbarian slave. III, 17.

The Scythians once held almost all of Asia. III, 796. Scythian philosophers. VII, 233, 234.

Scythopolis, formerly called Bethsan. III, 795.

The shield signifies different things in sacred Scripture. III, 79.

The *scyniphes* are extremely small gnats. VIII, 875.

Sebastianus. II, 1064. He is called Abbot. II, 1064. Note 1.

The usefulness and necessity of withdrawing from the turmoil of collapsing affairs. II, 74.

The usefulness of secrecy. V, 335.

What a sect is according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 369. There are different sects according to the various distinctions that can be established. VIII, 376.

The Secundian heretics. VIII, 28.

Secundianus of Thambeis. IX, 237.

Secundianus, a Donatist bishop. IX, 528, 555.

Secundianus, bishop of Prisciana. IV, 381.

Secundinus. IV, 376.

Secundinus the Manichaean, one of those whom they called “hearers.” I, 634; VIII, 571, 572. *Retr.*

Secundinus of Carpis. IX, 217.

Secundinus of Cedias. IX, 209.

Secundinus, or Secundus, bishop of Jacondiana. IV, 381.

Secundinus the Roman. VIII, 573, 594.

Secundinus, a presbyter. II, 1068.

Secundinus, a bishop. II, 991.

Secundus of Tigisisi. IX, 443. Primate of Numidia. IX, 37, 638. Author of the Donatist schism. V, 293. The ecclesiastical proceedings of Secundus of Tigisisi, held in the house of Urbanus Donatus. II, 197. The course that Secundus of Tigisisi ought to have followed. II, 163. Secundus of Tigisisi assembled a council against Caecilianus and his colleagues. IX, 493. At Carthage. IX, 639. The council of Secundus of Tigisisi at Cirta. IX, 510, 639, 774 *App.* See *Cirtan Council*. Secundus of Tigisisi left those who were present and had confessed themselves betrayers to be judged by God, and allowed them to remain in their episcopal sees. II, 161, 162, 164, 197. And, so that schism might not arise, he granted them peace. IX, 612. Secundus of Tigisisi feared that the suspicion of betrayal was sufficiently probable against him. II, 162, 164. And in fact he is accused of betrayal. IX, 511, 640. By Purpurius of Limata. IX, 612. Secundus of Tigisisi feared Purpurius of Limata, who had confessed to homicide, lest he should lose his primacy or his bishopric. IX, 714. And he writes back to Mensurius that he had refused to hand over the divine books to be burned. IX, 638, 659, 640, 735. The proceedings at Cirta and the letters of Secundus and Mensurius are examined. IX, 644. Secundus of Tigisisi was unable to clear himself of the charge of betrayal. IX, 735.

Secundus the Younger, a relative of Secundus of Tigisisi. II, 162. His nephew. IX, 511.

The laws concerning *securales*. II, 166.

The rights of the axe. II, 511.

The security given to a sinner by God’s ministers is of no benefit unless God approves it. V, 246. Perverse security. IV, 1916. God removes harmful security and implants a salutary fear. III, 1983. There is no security except in hearing God’s commands and awaiting his promises. V, 246. The security of a person who trusts in God’s protection. IV, 201. Security, when God is within. IV, [Col. 0600] 391. The security of the godly under God’s protection. V, 421. No one ought to be secure in this life, which is wholly a time of testing. I, 799. Security from evils is not found here, in the place of pilgrimage, but in the homeland. IV, 840, 841, 1093. True security is in heaven. V, 728.

Sedatus of Tuburbo. IX, 213.

To sit, equivalent to “to dwell.” V, 1062, 1070; VI, 634. To sit in the council of vanity is evil, not in body but in heart. IV, 192.

The conscience of the godly is God’s seat. IV, 520. All places in which God reigns are God’s seats. IV, 1133. The kingdom of Christ is signified by the word “seat.” IV, 1122, 1123.

The seditions of carnal Christians often drive good men out of the Church, by the permission of divine providence. III, 128.

“To seduce” is said both in a good and in a bad sense. III, 1628. Those are understood to be seduced who do not think that what they are doing is a sin. VII, 419.

Segerma. IX, 209.

Segetia, the goddess placed in charge of grain once it was already above the ground. VII, 119.

Segisvultus, a count. V, 773; VIII, 707, 708, 709.

Seia, the goddess to whom the sown grain was entrusted while it was beneath the ground. VII, 119.

Seir is interpreted as “hairy.” III, 774.

Selenite, a Persian stone whose inner whiteness increases and diminishes with the moon. VII, 715.

Seleuciana, a female servant of God. II, 1086.

Seleucus, from whom the Seleucian heretics took their name. VIII, 41.

Artisans who work in small shops. X, 836.

Selmon is interpreted as “shadow.” IV, 826.

Selom is interpreted as “his release.” VIII, 456.

Shem is interpreted as “named.” VII, 477. Shem as a figure of Christ. VII, 477. The generations of the sons of Shem are traced down to Abraham. VII, 488.

How the Lord could have ordered Shimei to curse David. X, 906. By his just and hidden judgment he inclined Shimei’s will—which was evil through Shimei’s own fault—toward this sin. X, 906. If he had obeyed God’s command, he would have deserved praise rather than punishment. X, 906.

Certain hidden seeds of seeds. VIII, 875. From certain hidden seeds, as from original principles, all things that are born receive the beginnings of development, the proper increases of size, and the distinctions of forms. VIII, 876, 877. The seeds of things, apart from the human being, which God created and subjected to angels, whether good or evil, can be corrupted by those to whom they are subjected. X, 1421. How much a grain of seed contains. V, 1158. All the members are latent in the seed. VII, 777. The seed of the woman. VII, 187. Although God is the author of seeds, it does not follow that corrupted seeds do not exist. X, 1441. The seed of man accursed. X, 447. God creates the seed, not the defect by which it is infected. X, 742. God works without defect even from corrupted seed. X, 1442, 1443. That the seed of man derives corruption from those who generate it is shown by natural examples. X, 833. The seed of generation and the seed of regeneration. X, 1430. Immortal and spiritual seed. X, 1429, 1430. The one seed of Abraham: Christ and the Church. III, 2125. The seed of the ungodly: the works of the ungodly. IV, 389. To sow in the flesh and to sow in the spirit. III, 2146. To sow in tears. V, 192. See *Tears*.

The Semi-Arians. VIII, 39.

The Semi-Pelagians. See *Pelagians*, *Massilians*, and *Vitalis*. VII, 561.

Semiramis, the wife of Ninus. VII, 561. Semiramis was incestuous. VII, 561. She is said to have been killed by her son. VII, 561. Semiramis either founded or rebuilt Babylon. VII, 561, 562.

A path is a narrow way. IV, 1836. Paths are counsels and thoughts. IV, 1802. Paths are God’s commandments. IV, 1808, 1837. Two paths to the kingdom of heaven. V, 1649.

Wolves of the paths. VI, 682.

“Always” is sometimes understood to mean “as long as one lives here.” IV, 1538.

The perfection of the number six. III, 296, 298, 301, 339; V, 343. Its origin. III, 301. The perfection of six commended in Scripture. VIII, 892. In the building of Christ’s body and of the Jerusalem temple. VIII, 893. The perfection of God’s works signified by the number six. VII, 343.

The senatorial age. I, 1006.

“Senate” is derived from *senium*, old age. III, 686.

Seneca was a senator of the Roman people. VII, 192. He worshiped the gods. VII, 190. What he thought about images of the gods. VII, 190. What he thought about their worship. VII, 192. Seneca’s book against superstitions. VII, 190. Seneca criticized the sacraments and Sabbaths of the Jews. VII, 192. Seneca flourished in the time of the Apostles. VII, 190. He neither praises nor condemns the Christians. VII, 192. Letters of Seneca to Paul are read. VII, 659.

The Greeks distinguish *senecta* and *senium*. IV, 894. Old age begins at sixty. VI, 43. It is not defined by any fixed number of years. III, 193. It usually lasts as long as the other ages. VI, 43. Old age, wholly white through upright deeds, is youthful. IV, 1179. The complaints and hardships of old age. V, 504. Everyone wishes for old age before it comes, and everyone complains about it once it has come. III, 1647; IV, 389. The desires of old age and of beauty cannot agree with one another. III, 1647. A worn-out old age, an old life. III, 1982. How old age is to be joined with childhood. IV, 1472. The old age of the Church is in joy, while its youth is in tribulations. IV, 1179.

The difference between *senex* and *senior*. III, 191; III, 541, 542. The age of *seniores* is less advanced than that of old men. III, 557, 566. Every old man is also a presbyter, but not every presbyter is also an old man. III, 566. Although it is more fitting for old men to teach than to learn, it is nevertheless better for them to learn than to be ignorant of what they should teach. II, 720. Spiritual enemies are weaker against the aged, but they are not absent. V, 719. The impious words of an old man in whom lust does not grow old. V, 879. An eighty-four-year-old man, after spending twenty-five continuous years with his wife, bought a female lute-player for his lust. X, 713. One who is subscribed as “the Elder of the Church of Summa.” II, 490. He is also simply called “the Elder.” II, 577. The same person subscribes as belonging to the chief see of the province of Numidia. II, 494. “Elder” used for “Primate.” II, 953, 954. Elder Aurelius. II, 867. Elder Donatianus. II, 891. Elder Alypius is named. II, 1012. Elder Saturninus. II, 94.

How sensations occur. III, 362, 363.

What sensible things are. VII, 231. Sensible things are so called not because they sense, but because they are sensed. VII, 341. We grasp sensible things through the bodily senses, but we do not judge them by the bodily sense. VII, 341. The Platonists held that sensible things should be placed below intelligible things. VII, 271. Philosophers place riches in intelligible things and poverty in sensible things. II, 65. Everything touched by bodily sense cannot remain in the same condition even for a moment of time. II, 63; VI, 13. The Manichaeans believed that plants and stones possess the sensation of pain and groaning. III, 2074. The Manichaeans say that earth, wood, and stones possess sensation and live with a more intelligent life, whereas flesh lives with a duller one. VIII, 306.

The nature of sense is discussed at length. I, 1058. Some senses are called bodily, others of the soul. I, 875; X, 496. Some are exterior and another is interior; the exterior senses are perceived by the interior. I, 1246. Not by themselves, however. I, 1246. The origin of bodily sense. III, 466. All the senses are diffused from a point, as it were from the center of the brain. II, 519. The five senses. V, 255, 574, 624; VIII, 94. Some relate the five senses to the four elements. III, 281. The five yokes of the senses. VI, 687. The five senses as five men of the soul. III, 1517; VI, 57, 58. The functions of the senses. I, 786. The five senses, a five-part gate. V, 574. The external senses are called the gates of the flesh. I, 786. They are messengers through whom the inner person learns. I, 783. Messengers of the flesh. IV, 1907, 1908. They are, as it were, the eyes of the mind. I, 875. The senses are windows of the house whose inhabitant is the mind. V, 428. They stand open in vain if the soul is absent. V, 428, 699. The senses do not sense by themselves; rather, there is another within who senses through them. V, 361. How the soul senses things outside its flesh. II, 518. Nothing is perceived by the senses unless the mind is present. II, 614. The mind leaves outside itself what is announced to it by the senses, committing their incorporeal likenesses incorporeally to memory. II, 614. Movement begins in all the senses from the subtlety of fire. III, 282. When one sense is dulled, the others become sharper. VI, 448. Some philosophers acknowledged that all the things the soul perceives through bodily sense can generate opinion, but not knowledge. I, 947. “The senses never deceive,” said the Epicureans; “do not assent to anything beyond being persuaded that it appears so to you, and there will be no deception.” I, 947. Geometry cannot be perceived by the senses. I, 874. Whatever is touched by sense is proved to be not one thing but many. I, 1252. One must not judge the order of things from the senses. III, 337. People devoted to the senses paint spiritual things in their hearts with shapes and colors. III, 426. Bodily sense must not be examined by bodily senses. II, 517, 518. Some philosophers thought that bodily senses should always be trusted, others that they should not always be trusted, and others that they should never be trusted. VII, 601. The person who never thinks the senses should be trusted is deceived more miserably. VII, 646. The senses should be trusted in the evident perception of each thing. VII, 646. In the senses certain traces of reason appear. I, 1010. The interior sense in a human being. VII, 341. The interior sense is the governor and judge of the exterior senses. I, 1247. It differs from reason. I, 1247. It exists in beasts. I, 1247. Curiosity about the senses is an impediment to faith. V, 645. Truth is perceived by no sense, yet it is loved. V, 870. All the interior senses take delight in justice. V, 869. Beasts also possess senses. V, 255. In some beasts they are sharper than in human beings. V, 1260. The senses of irrational animals contain a certain likeness of knowledge. VII, 341. The sense of demons is exceedingly acute; by comparison with it, ours should scarcely be called sense. II, 72.

There was no lust of the senses in paradise. X, 1095. What pleasure of the senses could have existed in paradise. X, 1096. Lawful and unlawful pleasures of the senses. V, 868. A beautiful movement soothes the sense, and through the sense the mind. I, 1010. Through the senses we are often struck by wounds in the soul. III, 126. Mortification of the senses. X, 769, 770, 771, etc. It is a mark of great intelligence to draw the mind away from the senses. II, 517. The senses must not themselves sense, nor should one use them like an animal, adding to the belly rather than to the mind. V, 699. Whoever uses the senses well enters into the joy of his Lord. III, 168. The pleasure of the senses, compared with the delight of eternal life, is not worthy even of remembrance. I, 774. Through the habit of abstaining from them and seeking better things, sensible things cease to delight us. II, 65. The five senses are gates; whoever does not admit corruption through them will be counted among the five virgins. IV, 1920.

What it means to sense. I, 1171. Sensing belongs not to the body but to the soul through the body. III, 282. The soul senses through the senses. V, 361. Sensing is an indication of animated and living flesh. III, 363. It is one thing to sense nothing through utter dullness, and another to sense nothing through perfect bodily health. I, 1171. The whole soul senses what it senses in the body, even when the body is not whole. II, 722. The whole soul senses when it senses something through the body, because this is not hidden from the whole soul. II, 444. The liveliness, necessity, usefulness, and lust of sensing must be distinguished. X, 770. It is not impossible for God to grant the ears the sense of seeing and the eyes the sense of hearing. X, 340.

The origin of the word *sententia*, “judgment” or “opinion.” VII, 318. How full of scruples it is either to pass judgment on others or not to do so, and to weigh the judgments of others about us in an even balance. II, 354. Three causes for changing one’s judgment are explained. II, 274. It is disgraceful to change a true and correct judgment; but to change a foolish and harmful judgment is both praiseworthy and salutary. II, 224. The first praise is not to be moved from a true judgment; the second is to change a false one. IX, 497. When the number of votes was equal, acquittal was usually preferred to condemnation. VII, 567. There are many in the Church who are held to a judgment by the authority of names, or transferred away from a judgment. II, 1011. Difference of opinion can exist among the dearest friends without harming affection. II, 289. How many flatter the judgments of the powerful. II, 1048. God’s judgment against sinners is changed if they themselves change. V, 152. The final judgment sends one either into the kingdom or into the fire. V, 1543.

Sentia, the goddess who inspires judgments. VII, 122.

To bail out a bilge. V, 1274.

Sentinus, a god. VII, 195.

Seon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes.” IV, 1750. Also, “useless shoot,” or “burning temptation.” IV, 1760.

How great a punishment it is to be separated from the face of God. IV, 569.

Plans of separation are futile, harmful, and sacrilegious, because they become both impious and proud. IX, 93. Separation of the heart from evils, not separation of the body, is commanded in Scripture. IX, 88, 90, 98, 668, 669, 674, 747. Jeremiah, Isaiah, David, the Apostle Paul, and Cyprian withdrew from evils in heart, not in body. IX, 100, 101, 102, 109. An objection against separation from evils only in the heart is answered. IX, 91. See *Donatists*, *Schism*.

One should take care, as far as one can, to bury the dead and construct tombs. V, 937. The Patriarchs did not care for the burial of bodies without reason. III, 592. See *Burial*.

The higher allegory of the seven days. III, 193. The seven ages of the world. III, 190.

The number seven. V, 518, 581, 652, 1161, 1166, 1170, 1242. The meaning of the number seven. III, 1336. Its perfection. VII, 345. Seven is a perfect number. III, 634. The number seven signifies universality. VII, 345. Also, the whole revolving span of time. IV, 1592, 1917, 1918. It pertains to the Holy Spirit. III, 326, 634; V, 75. It signifies grace. IV, 1961. And the perfection of the Church. VII, 529. The creature is represented by the number seven. II, 218.

Why the seventh day was sanctified by God. V, 80. The seventh day has no evening. V, 80.

“Seven times” in place of “always.” V, 652. Explanation of the number seventy-seven. III, 1335, 1336. By the number seventy-seven, the abolition of all sins is signified. III, 1077.

Why the Seventy translators differ from the Hebrew. II, 243; III, 1139; VII, 604. They do not differ from the Hebrew truth. VII, 606. The edition of the Seventy distinguished by asterisks and obeli. II, 753. Through the fraud of someone, Jerome lost much of his earlier work in preparing it. II, 753. Why strokes, or obeli, and asterisks were sometimes placed in the edition of the translators of the Septuagint. II, 261. Augustine urges Jerome to render this into Latin in accordance with the truth. II, 243. Why Augustine preferred a translation from the Greek rather than from the Hebrew. II, 242. The history of the Septuagint translation. VII, 603. This translation was commissioned by Ptolemy, king of Egypt. VII, 235. It is not established whether the Seventy translators translated separately in separate cells or compared their work with one another. III, 46. They did not compare their work with one another. VII, 603. The Seventy translators agreed with one voice in their translations. III, 595. Through prophetic authority, they translated the Scriptures with remarkable agreement. III, 784; IV, 1115, 1116; VII, 602, 603. The Seventy translators were distinguished not only by the gift of translation but also by that of prophecy. III, 595; VII, 604. The extent of the authority of the Seventy translators. III, 595; VII, 450, 470. The Seventy translators should be believed to have translated by the divine Spirit, by whom also those things were spoken that are contained in the Hebrew writings. IV, 1757. The translation of the Seventy carries considerable weight. II, 243, 290. It has greater authority among the Greeks. III, 46. The Jews prefer it to the others. VII, 603. Augustine asks that Jerome’s interpretation of the Septuagint be sent to him. II, 290. Why he asks for this. II, 290. Augustine does not want Jerome’s interpretation of the Septuagint from the Hebrew to be read in the Church, lest the people of Christ be disturbed by its novelty. II, 290. Some thought that the Greek codices of the Septuagint translation should be corrected from the Hebrew copies. VII, 604. The Septuagint translation is in use among the Latin churches. VII, 604.

“Sevenfold” in place of “the whole.” V, 518.

Tombs constructed with great labor. V, 611. A tomb is called a house. IV, 554. And a memorial. IV, 554. A marble tomb. VI, 677. Those who worship tombs and paintings. I, 1342. Immoderate extravagance concerning the corpses of the dead. I, 1342. An open tomb allegorically. IV, 87. The tomb of a dead soul is the body. IV, 1117.

We see how carefully burial is attended to. V, 848. Concern for burial exists in human beings from a natural affection for the body. VI, 598. Hence they grieve when those they love remain unburied. VI, 599, 600. The martyrs despised this affection. VI, 599. Why God allowed them to remain unburied. VI, 599. Although burial does not help the dead, it is nevertheless blameworthy to neglect it through irreligiousness. VI, 601. Scripture commends those who perform the duty of burial. VI, 600. Hence Scripture threatens the prophet who violates the word of God. VI, 598. The fact that the dead have appeared to the living and asked for burial does not prove that burial is a concern of the dead themselves. VI, 600. Whatever is spent on burying a body is not a protection of salvation but an act of humaneness. VI, 609. Whether burial in the memorials of martyrs benefits the spirits of the dead in any way. VI, 157. See *The Dead*. Forty days of burial signify a certain repentance. III, 594. The three days of the crucified, buried, and risen Christ. II, 215. In the celebration of Easter, the cross, burial, and resurrection of Christ are to be observed. A Christian ought to bear the cross in the present life; burial and resurrection are borne in hope and faith. II, 215. Burial signifies the remission of sins. III, 592. The burial both of Christ and of us takes place in the evening. IV, 224. Care for burial is praiseworthy. VII, 27. It pleases God. VII, 27. It supports faith in the resurrection. VII, 27. Christians can lack burial without harm to them. VII, 26, 27. Philosophers despised burial. VII, 26, 27. Often entire armies did so as well. VII, 26, 27. The circumstances of burial, funeral treatment, and so forth, are more consolations for the living than aids for the dead. VII, 26.

God is to be followed, not preceded. IV, 758. To follow Christ is to imitate him. VI, 411. To follow the Lamb wherever he goes is proper to virgins. VI, 410, 411.

Seranus, a deputy. IX, 316.

Seranus, a proconsul. IX, 579.

Serapis, the greatest god of the Egyptians; why he was so called. VII, 563. Whoever said that he had been a human being was liable to the death penalty. VII, 563. The delirious notions surrounding his worship. VII, 563. The overthrow of his temple foretold. VI, 581, 587.

Sergius Orata, exceptionally fortunate. I, 972, 973.

Speech often pleases the hearer but displeases the speaker. VI, 311. There is no greater reason for this than that people enjoy seeing something unusual and are wearied by speaking in the customary way. VI, 312. Speech proceeding from sadness is less agreeable. VI, 321. Among people who know one another affectionately, no subject of conversation is more fruitful than the source of our goodness and blessedness. II, 1030.

The word of God makes human beings gods. III, 1745. It does not always convert a person. VII, 443. Do we not handle the divine utterances rather than treat them properly? II, 353. The word of God is to believers as a hook is to a fish. III, 1700. It catches if it is itself caught. III, 1700. The word of God fears no one. IV, 1351. Whose adversary it is. IV, 342. The word of God is our adversary, and we must quickly agree with it. V, 76, 246, 637, 1171. The word of God is our daily bread. V, 381. What fruit those who agree with God’s word here have in death. V, 381. The word of God is a two-edged sword. IV, 1955. When the word of the Lord is scourged, the scourges against Christ are multiplied. III, 1469. Sermons heard while standing. V, 1253. “Speech” is called Mercury. VII, 206.

The serpent. Why the devil was permitted to tempt through a serpent. III, 435. The serpent did not dare speak to the man, but used the agency of the woman to bring him down; through the weaker it overcame the stronger. V, 1008. The serpent seducing by a promise of knowledge. V, 1495. Adam did not believe the serpent. III, 452, 454. How the serpent spoke to the human being. III, 444. The devil in the serpent. III, 206. The serpent’s curse is figurative. III, 449. The serpent’s curse refers to the devil who worked through the serpent. III, 449. The serpent’s enmity with Eve and its punishments. III, 210. The Manichaeans praised the serpent because, through its counsel, it opened the human being’s eyes. [Col. 0604] VIII, 208. The Manichaeans regarded the serpent as Christ. VIII, 313. The serpent from Moses’ staff. V, 61, 67. The bronze serpent hung in the wilderness. V, 61, 1342. Why it was lifted up in the wilderness, and why it was bronze. III, 2120, 2121. What it prefigures. V, 1562. What it signifies. VII, 286. It was a figure of Christ’s death. X, 145. Or of Christ lifted up on the cross. IV, 933, 1578. When the people began to worship the bronze serpent as an idol, King Hezekiah crushed it. VII, 286. Power is given to demons to move serpents at the incantations of human beings, so that the memory of the first event may be preserved. III, 444. Serpents are moved more by human songs than any other kind of living creature. III, 444. Serpents do not hear or understand the words of the Marsians except through the operation of demonic power. III, 444. The serpent occurs in Scripture both in a good and in a bad sense. III, 79. The nature and source of the serpent’s wisdom. III, 430, 444. The serpent’s cunning. III, 1366; IV, 681, 682, 1806. How it is to be imitated. IV, 681; V, 425. Good serpents allegorically—that is, not harmful for inflicting injury, but cunning for avoiding it. I, 858. Serpents live a long time. VII, 240. Serpents have exceptionally sharp sight. I, 1352; VII, 799; VIII, 197. And they delight in light. I, 1352. Some serpents are reported to have flown. VII, 110. Serpents that bask in the sun. I, 1352. To be eaten by a serpent. VI, 291. The serpent’s food is earth—that is, people who think earthly thoughts. IV, 1386. Visible serpents signify sins. V, 1343; VIII, 661. The serpent’s head is the first suggestion. IV, 1381. The serpent, a figure of heretics. III, 216.

The Serpentine heretics. III, 217.

Serotinus, a bishop. II, 759, 781.

Quintus Sertorius, a partisan of the Marian faction, proscribed by Sulla. VII, 109. He provoked civil war. VII, 109.

Gaius Servilius, a praetor. VII, 106.

Quintus Servilius, master of the cavalry. VII, 90.

Servilius, a monk. II, 697, 698.

Servilius, a bishop. II, 759, 781.

The servitude by which human beings are slaves to human beings arose as a punishment for sin. III, 450. It arose from sin. VII, 643. The law by which penal servitude is regulated. VII, 644. How many years Egyptian servitude lasted. VII, 502. Two kinds of servitude. III, 1849, 1854. Every servitude other than service to the Lord is full of bitterness. IV, 1275. Servitude is useful to some people. VII, 649. For this reason it can be called just. VII, 649. It is more fortunate to serve a human being than lust. VII, 644.

What is meant by servitude under sin. I, 1233; V, 943; VI, 282. Servitude exists when it is pleasurable to sin. X, 218. Servitude under vices is the most grievous of all. VII, 115. Nothing but Christ frees from it. V, 744. How much more advantageous service of God is than slavery to vices. V, 526. Service of righteousness is true freedom. VI, 247. Justice consists in the weaker reason serving the stronger. III, 590. Just servitude and just dominion, when animals serve the human being. III, 589. Servitude of the Law and freedom of the Gospel. I, 1334. Servitude under the Law is unfamiliar to some. VI, 288. What kind of spirit belongs to servitude. III, 2071. Whoever serves through love serves freely and obeys God without misery. III, 2137. Free servitude, where love serves rather than necessity. IV, 1275. The miserable servitude of idolaters. III, 151.

The origin of the word “slave.” VII, 643. A person captured from war was called a slave because he had been preserved from death. III, 590. The name “slave” was earned through fault, not nature. VII, 643. No human being is naturally the slave of another human being or of sin, for God originally created the human being in freedom. VII, 644. Iniquity or adversity made one human being the slave of another. III, 590. The name “slave” is nowhere found in Scripture before Noah’s curse on Canaan. VII, 643. The Apostle forbids Christian slaves to demand freedom from their masters. III, 624. A Christian who has become a slave should not disdain serving an unbelieving and bad master. IV, 1653. Unless, perhaps, he is ordered to do something against Christ. IV, 1654. When, at Christ’s command, you serve a human being, you serve not that person but the one who commanded you. IV, 1653. A slave of a human being is a slave of desire. V, 1503. What slaves owe their masters, and masters their slaves. I, 1337. How slaves were treated by the first fathers. VII, 643. Provision should be made for slaves as for sons, so that they may worship God. VII, 644. A Christian ought not to possess a slave in the same way as a horse or silver. III, 1260. The punishments of slaves. V, 883. How slaves can make their servitude somewhat free. VII, 644. A public slave of the city. II, 303. A faithful slave is emancipated. V, 145. The emancipation of slaves in episcopal proceedings. V, 1576, 1577. We are God’s slaves both because he created us and because he redeemed us. V, 146. Every creature, willingly or unwillingly, is subject to God. VI, 294. Everything serves God, either for the punishment of sins or for the liberation of the human being. III, 135. If the soul serves God, all else will serve it. III, 159. Faith demanded from a slave must not be denied to God. V, 87, 219. God’s runaway slave. IV, 1790, 1791. If we do not wish to be God’s slaves, we shall be under the devil and shall not escape the power of the true Lord. V, 231. God does not need slaves; slaves need God. III, 2044. God uses his slaves not for his own benefit but for theirs. V, 86. God sometimes visibly frees his slaves, and sometimes does not visibly free them; but he always frees them invisibly. III, 2040.

[Col. 0605] The Lord is to be served in fear, and rejoicing is to be combined with trembling. X, 930. To serve God is perfect freedom. I, 1078; II, 128. God wishes to be served voluntarily, not by necessity. III, 134. The righteous serve God generously, but the unrighteous serve him in chains. VI, 294. To serve God willingly and chastely is a great good. II, 87. Who serves God with the flesh and who with the spirit. V, 915. Whatever a person does with the intention of gaining earthly profit, he does slavishly. V, 208. Those who serve God for earthly things cannot serve with a true heart. V, 168. Those who serve God in hope of a carnal benefit belong to the Old Testament. V, 32, 167. This is righteousness: not to place slaves before the Lord, nor to equate them with him. IV, 904. God must be served with the whole, complete, and willing will. IV, 876. Whoever refuses to serve love must necessarily serve iniquity. IV, 163. You are rightly subjected to the iniquity that you have made your master, because you refused to be subject to the one who made you. IV, 163. Bishops have become servants of the faithful through Christ. IV, 1365, 1366. You serve Christ well if you serve those whom Christ served. IV, 1365. Augustine says that, in free service, he owes ministry to the devotion of the godly. II, 1089. Those who desire to be masters of mortal things become slaves of them. I, 1330. The servant of God, the people of God, the Church of God. III, 1470.

“Servants of God” used for monks. V, 1070. Those who supply the necessities of God’s servants are praised. VI, 578. Paul wants the necessities of God’s servants to be supplied by the faithful. VI, 561. They cannot procure these necessities for themselves because of their occupations or infirmities. VI, 562, 564. It is indicated that some of them are supported by pious believers and others by the work of their hands. II, 692. Augustine, servant of Christ and through him servant of his servants. II, 978. Rule for the servants of God. I, 1377.

Servius Tullius, king of the Romans. VII, 92.

What Servus, bishop of Thubursicum, suffered from the Donatists. IX, 521, 522.

The origin of *sesque*. I, 1093.

Sitting sometimes signifies honor and sometimes humility. IV, 1671, 1763. Sitting signifies humility. V, 967. Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father. V, 1070.

Seth is interpreted as “resurrection.” VII, 460, 461. In what sense Seth is said to have been born to Adam in place of Abel. VII, 457. The sons of Seth are called the sons of God and angels. VII, 469. Before they mingled with the daughters of men, they begot for God, not for themselves. VII, 469. Seth’s succession closes with ten generations and ends with the number twelve. VII, 463.

The origin of the Sethian heretics’ name and their doctrines. VIII, 29.

Severinus, a relative of Augustine, a Donatist. II, 194.

Severity, as though “savage truth.” V, 935. The temper of severity and charity. II, 958. It is better to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness. II, 323. Severity should be exercised against the sins of a few, while gentleness should be shown toward others. II, 92.

The Emperor Severus. VII, 602.

Severus, bishop of Milevis. II, 125, 229, 358, 759, 781, 1094; IV, 1227, 1715. Note (a). V, 1576; VII, 714. A fellow citizen and friend of Augustine. II, 294. Augustine extols him with great praises. II, 418. The niece of Bishop Severus, from Sitifis, carried away by the barbarians. II, 426.

Severus, a blind deacon. V, 1576.

The Severians, named from Severus, and their errors. VIII, 30.

Sextus the Pythagorean. I, 647.

The distinction of sex in creation. VII, 429, 430. Sex is not a defect in females but a part of nature. VII, 778. Some things born from water or earth have no sex. III, 287. The transformation of the female sex into the male. VII, 110, 111. Both sexes were honored by Christ’s birth. V, 1008. Both were led to hope of restoration. V, 106. Both sexes will rise again. VII, 778.

“If” is used in Scripture to mean “by no means.” VII, 543.

Varro relates that there were several Sibyls. VII, 579. The Erythraean Sibyl. VII, 579. The Cumaean Sibyl. VII, 580. The Samian Sibyl. VII, 582. The books of the Sibyl, a kind of oracle. VII, 98. Faustus taught that the predictions about Christ by the Sibyl, Hermes Trismegistus, or Orpheus were better suited to the Gentiles than the testimonies of the Hebrew prophets. VIII, 281, 282, 290, 292. The prophetess Sibyl, though not a prophetess of Christ, nevertheless foretold certain things about Christ. III, 2089. The Cumaean Sibyl may perhaps have heard in the spirit something about the one Savior. II, 1073. The Sibylline poem transferred by Virgil does not fit anyone other than Christ. II, 1073.

Sicca. IX, 219.

The town of Sicca. II, 1019.

Sichima is interpreted as “shoulders.” IV, 718.

The mountains of Sicily burn with flames yet remain intact. VII, 712.

Sicilibba. IX, 227.

“Just as” sometimes refers to likeness and sometimes to proper identity. IV, 1659. It does not always refer to equality. III, 1923, 2013, 2047.

[Col. 0606] The kingdom of the Sicyonians was very small. VII, 561. It flourished in the time of Abraham. VII, 497. How many years it lasted. VII, 577. When it was destroyed. VII, 577.

How the stars were made. III, 265. They said that the stars were parts of Jupiter, that they lived, and that they were gods. VII, 123. Whether Plato should be granted that the stars live by their own particular souls. VII, 388. To some, the stars appear to be luminous bodies without sensation. VI, 260. Whether the stars shine equally. III, 277. Each wandering star has its own sphere or orbit. III, 235. Whether the stars are angels is uncertain. VI, 260. Whether the stars are governed and animated by certain spirits. III, 279, 280. Flattery bestowed the names of human beings on the stars. IV, 1192. Observation of the stars is partly useful and partly vain. II, 211. Observation of the stars for learning the course of life is vain. III, 51. The mind’s wills are not subjected to the stars. VII, 146. Those who claim that the stars determine what we do and suffer overthrow the worship of God. VII, 141. If heavenly necessity is admitted, what judgment concerning human actions is left to God? VII, 141, 142. It is neither expedient nor appropriate to spend time investigating the intervals and magnitudes of the stars. III, 277. Knowledge of the stars contributes little, almost nothing, to the interpretation of Scripture. III, 57. It is properly and honorably disregarded. III, 57. We can derive nothing from it for our own actions. III, 57. By the name “stars” are understood those whose way of life is in heaven. III, 878. The Manichaeans worship no stars except the sun and moon. VIII, 346.

What it means to mark or signify. III, 1601.

## Sign

What is a sign. I, 1046. Definition of signs. III, 19, 20, 35. And their division. III, 19, 20. Various kinds of signs. I, 1198, 1199. Signs that signify themselves. I, 1205. The things signified are to be valued more highly than the signs. I, 1210. What is a mathematical sign. I, 1046. Its distinction from a point. I, 1046. Whether anything can be shown without some sign. I, 1196. Whether signs are shown by signs. I, 1084. A sign is learned more through the thing known than the thing itself through a sign that has been given. I, 1214. Signs and prodigies of falsehood. VII, 687. The distinction between lawful signs and unlawful auguries. III, 564. Whether it is lawful to ask a sign from God. III, 564. Among signs, words hold first place. III, 37. Signs are either proper or transferred. III, 42. Definition of both kinds. III, 42. How ignorance of proper signs is removed. III, 42. And of transferred signs. III, 46. In a sign—not only in words, but also in all the other signs of minds—nothing is to be sought except the mind itself. III, 1111. Signs are named after the things they signify. III, 497, 703. When signs concern divine things, they are called sacraments. II, 527. Of the signs by which Christ foretold future events, some concern the destruction of Jerusalem, others the Lord’s coming through the Church, and others his final coming, at which he will judge the living and the dead. II, 914. What it means to serve signs. III, 70, 71. The ancient Patriarchs and Prophets were not oppressed by servitude to signs. III, 70, 71. Jews and Gentiles were freed from servitude to signs in different ways. III, 70.

The sign of the cross on the forehead. IV, 252, 585. Believers receive the sign of Christ on the forehead. V, 1075. Bearing the sign of Christ inwardly on the forehead. V, 942. See Cross. The water of baptism is consecrated with the sign of the cross. X, 861. The sign of Christ drives away the destroyer if our heart has Christ dwelling in it. III, 1759. See Christ; Cross. We received the sign of the cross on the forehead, as on the seat of modesty, so that we may not be ashamed of it. V, 876, 941. The cross on the unshamed forehead is the sign of the New Testament, just as circumcision in hidden flesh was the sign of the Old Testament. V, 876. Christ was foretold by the sign of circumcision. V, 876, 916.

Roman military standards. IV, 935.

## Silence

Silence is to the ears what darkness is to the eyes. VIII, 197. How much the Passalorynchites value silence. VIII, 42. “Silence” is also called a suppressed voice. III, 1754. What silence signifies metaphorically. III, 886. Silence of the heart is the cooling of charity; you will be silent if you cease to love. IV, 404. Silence in music. I, 1125.

God is silent and is not silent. IV, 568, 1284, 1293. Because God himself is silent and cries out: he is silent in judgment, but not silent in command; so you too should be silent regarding arrogance, but not regarding invocation. V, 794. Christ is silent before the judgment, yet he is not silent. V, 124, 126, 129.

The whole earth had become a forest through the superstition of the Gentiles. IV, 1230.

Silvanus, a god hostile to pregnant women. VII, 187.

Incubi of Silvanus. VII, 468.

Silvanus, a Catholic bishop. IX, 700.

Silvanus, a subdeacon under Paul the bishop. IX, 584. The municipal records make the matter perfectly clear: he was exposed as an explicit traditor. II, 168, 197; IX, 386, 511, 513, 514, 583; II, 168. Nevertheless, he was ordained by the Donatists as bishop of Constantina, or Cirta. II, 168; IX, 256. By Secundus of Tigisis. II, 168. At the very beginning of the schism. IX, 387. Silvanus is wrongly excused from the crime of betrayal. [Col. 0607] IX, 384. Silvanus was driven into exile. IX, 514.

Silvanus, an old man of the church of Summis. II, 490, 577. An elder of the first see of the province of Numidia. III, 493.

Silvanus, superintendent of fields and forests. II, 1063.

Silvester, the presbyter of Marcellinus, bishop of Rome, is acquitted of the crime of betrayal. IX, 610.

Silvius, the posthumous son of Aeneas and the fourth king of the Latins. VII, 576.

Simeon the elder. V, 891, 1267, 1303, 1658.

Although the monkey’s body possesses the good of beauty, it possesses it to a lesser degree. VIII, 557.

When something is called similar, it is not understood to be similar in every respect. VIII, 324. From where do all similar things derive their similarity. VI, 16, 17. Everything exists, and is more beautiful to the extent that it has similar parts. III, 243. Like adheres to like; unlike flees from unlike. V, 117, 1102. Things may be called similar to God in many ways. VI, 32. A person begins to become like God when, because of his very unlikeness to him, he is displeased with himself. IV, 959. Whoever wishes to be like God should not depart from him. IV, 896. By grace a person becomes like God. X, 285.

## Similarity

Similarity, however, is opposed to truth. I, 891. Similarity is perceived not by the senses but by the mind. III, 146. In the mind there are only likenesses of the things we think about. II, 615. The likenesses of things are called by the names of the things to which they are similar. V, 745; X, 600. In likenesses, one thing can be called by many names, and things very far removed from one another by one name. V, 470. Scripture does not praise the thing itself in every case from which a likeness is drawn; it merely draws a likeness from it. IV, 679. Likenesses cannot be brought to perfection from every source. IV, 1332. Likenesses applied in Scripture to contrary things are explained from their surrounding context. IV, 1376. Whether, and in what respect, the likenesses brought forward by Scripture are true. IV, 812. Temporal likenesses cannot be found that can be compared with eternity. V, 666. Likenesses between created things and divine things have many differences. V, 670, 675. The usefulness of likenesses. II, 211.

What is the difference between likeness and image. III, 749. Some think that likeness is something more than image. III, 749. All things were created through the likeness of God; only the soul was made according to the likeness of God. III, 243. The likeness of God is properly called likeness. III, 242. The likeness of God was lost through sin. V, 82. When will our likeness to God be perfected, whether with respect to the soul or the body. VIII, 1055. The things from which some likeness is drawn in order to signify Christ or the Saints are not therefore to be worshiped. IV, 1193. Through likeness one approaches God. IV, 337, 1217, 1273, 1274.

The Donatists interpret the deed of Simon of Cyrene in their own interest. V, 294.

## Simon

Simon Magus. V, 601, 1023. His heresies. VIII, 25. Simon Magus asserted that he himself was Christ. VIII, 25. He sinned against the Holy Spirit. III, 2098. Yet Blessed Peter invited him to repentance. III, 2098. Simon Magus received the gift of the sacraments. IV, 1343. The crime of Simon Magus. IV, 247, 1464, 1706. Some Romans think that the Saturday fast originated because Peter, intending to contend with Simon on the Lord’s Day, fasted on the preceding day; others consider this false. II, 145.

Simonians, heretics. VIII, 25.

From what is the word “simple” applied to nature. VII, 326.

The ratio of one to two derives from the perfection of the number six. VIII, 892.

Those things that are divine are called simple principally and truly. VII, 326, 327.

Simplicianus, a presbyter of Milan. I, 749. The spiritual father of Ambrose. I, 749. Later his successor in governing the Church of Milan. I, 629; X, 966. Simplicianus, bishop of Milan. VI, 101, 102, 162; VII, 309; X, 1026. Simplicianus is consulted by Augustine. I, 749. Two books, *On Various Questions*, were written to the same man. I, 629.

Simpliciola, a consecrated virgin. II, 965.

Simplicity and fervor come from the Holy Spirit. III, 1426. The good of simplicity. III, 208.

The notable memory of a certain Simplicius. X, 529.

What is earlier and what is later can stand together. III, 319.

Some images are made by human hands, others by phantasms. III, 2090. Trismegistus asserts that images are, as it were, the bodies of gods. VII, 247. What the Pagans said they worshiped in images. IV, 1244, 1483. The Romans consecrated images of bodily vices. VIII, 374. The origin of the use of images. VIII, 409. When images were established for the gods. VII, 581. Images criticized by Seneca. VII, 190. Those who established images did not remove fear from the peoples but added error. VII, 119, 198. Cicero does not approve the institution of images. VII, 136. The ancients did not have images. VII, 581. Varro judged that religion could be observed more chastely without images. [Col. 0608] VII, 138. He confirms this by the example of the Jewish people. VII, 138. In images, demons gave deceptive oracles. VII, 581. It is impious for a Christian to place an image of God in a temple. VI, 188. How far worshipers of images have departed from the truth. VI, 90. Why Adimantus wished to appear favorable to images. VIII, 147. The destruction of the images of the nations was foretold by the Prophets. VIII, 286, 287. An iron image suspended by magnetic stones in a certain temple. VII, 717. In comparison with the images of the nations, not only a human being but even an animal is better. IV, 1482.

To pretend to have a resolve toward holiness is worse than to fall away from that resolve. V, 1572. Pretended equity is not equity but double iniquity. IV, 765.

Pretenders among the workers in the Church. V, 95.

A person who has fallen away from justice engages in pretense. III, 1325. Paul rightly reproved deceptive pretense in Peter. II, 260, 280. Paul rightly reproved Peter’s and Barnabas’s pretense. VI, 536.

Sina is interpreted as “commandment.” IV, 829. “Measure.” IV, 830. “Temptation.” III, 774.

The mustard seed signifies the fervor of faith. III, 1326. It is said to drive out poisons. III, 1326.

To purify. III, 1633.

What sincerity and truth are. IX, 87.

Those who rule love singularity by a hidden law of nature; those who are subject, however, are also subordinated decorously, in greater numbers, to one. VI, 387; X, 419.

What it means, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” IV, 1613, 1770.

The left signifies adversity. III, 492. Temporal things. III, 493. God scourges with the left in order to place the corrected person on the right. IV, 1146. Our left hand signifies temporal things and temporal prosperity. IV, 1611, 1770, 1867.

The different manner of acting among the Siniti and among Catholics and Donatists. II, 397.

The fortress of Sinitum. VII, 766.

The region of Sinitum. II, 428.

The Sintae. VI, 330.

The bosom signifies a secret place. IV, 1458. Abraham’s bosom. III, 481; V, 113.

## Sion

Sion is God’s rest. IV, 1725. Sion is interpreted as “contemplation.” IV, 70, 122, 598, 1006, 1261, 1307; VII, 549, 550. The true Sion is the heavenly Sion. IV, 1952. Sion is where everything stands and nothing flows away. IV, 1763. Sion is an image of the Church that now exists, whereas Jerusalem is an image of the Church that will exist in the future. IV, 122, 1261, 1307. Now stones are being fitted into the structure of Sion; when the building is complete, they will not be fitted in. IV, 1304.

Sisera is interpreted as “exclusion of joy.” IV, 1053.

Sitifis. II, 1019. The city of Sitifis shaken by an earthquake. V, 137. The Church of Sitifis. II, 795. A consecrated woman was carried away from Sitifis by the barbarians. II, 426.

Thirst of the soul is desire. IV, 750. The fountain of life is more delightful to those who have thirsted greatly. IV, 125. What Christ’s thirst on the cross signified. IV, 851. Why Christ did not wish to drink gall. IV, 852.

Sixtus the martyr. I, 647.

Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church. X, 1027. He was formerly proclaimed a patron of the Pelagians. II, 867, 874. They used to boast of his friendship. II, 867. Augustine grieved over this. II, 874. Sixtus wrote to Aurelius against the Pelagian error, defended grace against them, and was the first to pronounce an anathema against them before a very large congregation. II, 867, 874. Through the acolyte Leo he wrote a very brief letter to the elder Aurelius. II, 867, 874. Augustine copied this letter. II, 867. He also wrote another, longer letter, which he sent through Firmus. II, 866, 867. Augustine replied to Sixtus. II, 866. On the occasion of Augustine’s letter to Sixtus being carried to the monastery of Hadrumetum. II, 975. And on the disagreement that arose among the brothers therefrom. II, 975. Augustine himself explains the meaning and purpose of his letter to Sixtus. II, 969, 972. When some people had thereby been disturbed. II, 970.

Sixtus the Bishop. II, 759, 781.

Sixtus the philosopher. I, 647.

Human society is bound together by giving and receiving. VI, 120. How great is the bond of society. III, 778, 779. Every society naturally shuns a fraudulent associate. X, 416. The unity of society and the bond of concord are commended in the propagation of the human race through one man. VII, 372, 373, 376. Without the society of unity, established through the bond of charity, even the gifts of the Holy Spirit are of no benefit. VI, 137. Whatever cannot be shown to be contrary either to the faith or to good morals must be observed for the sake of the society of those among whom one lives. II, 200. A just society is one that serves God. I, 691. God is present to those who care for human society. VIII, 82. To what extent the society of the wicked is to be avoided. V, 549, 551, 553. The society of the lost is greatly harmful. VII, 107, 111. The good or the wicked will join themselves to us according as we live rightly or ruinously. V, 1102.

[Col. 0609] Socrates. I, 926. A pupil of Archelaus. VII, 226. The teacher of Plato. I, 954; VII, 226. Socrates was declared, on Apollo’s testimony, to be the wisest of all. III, 1048, 1053. He occupied himself with active virtue. III, 1048. He treated Aesop’s fables in a few verses. III, 1048. He did not wish to write anything. III, 1048. Socrates excelled in the active part of wisdom. VII, 228, 597. Why he wrote about morals while leaving physics aside is uncertain. VII, 226. What he thought about the gods. III, 123. Socrates’ demon. VII, 239. A saying of Socrates. I, 1035. The Socratic view concerning the ease of learning. II, 1030. Socrates rightly asserts that what we learn is not implanted in us as something new, but recalled to memory through recollection. II, 68. Why he customarily swore by any dog, by a stone, and by whatever happened to be at hand. III, 123. One of Socrates’ accusers was crushed and died through the power of the crowd; the other escaped death through voluntary exile. VII, 227. Why Socrates was condemned to death. VII, 227. The city of Athens publicly mourned Socrates, whom it had publicly condemned. VII, 227. Socrates is found in the chronicles after Ezra. VII, 597.

Companions, as though “those who eat together.” V, 766.

The land of the Sodomites compared with the paradise of God. III, 555; VII, 722. The appearance of the Sodomites changed. VII, 722. How great was the iniquity of the Sodomites. III, 558, 559. The apples of Sodom enclose inner ashes beneath a deceptive surface of ripeness. VII, 722. The punishment of the Sodomites is a preview of the future judgment. VII, 509.

The sun is called φαίνων (*phainōn*, “shining”) by the Greeks. III, 236. In the sun there are three things: being, shining, and illuminating. I, 877. Anaxagoras said that the sun was a burning stone. VII, 601. Anaxagoras denied that the sun was God, as did Epicurus. VII, 601. The sun, moon, and stars are to the world as God’s senses. VII, 212. The Platonists taught that the sun and stars were the most blessed and eternal living beings. VII, 309. The Priscillianists taught that the sun, moon, and stars were rational powers. VIII, 669. Whether this teaching of the Priscillianists is sound. VIII, 675, 676, 677. Whether the sun, moon, and stars are angels is uncertain. VI, 260. The Manichaeans do not think that the sun is a body. V, 106. The Egyptians regarded the sun as no small divinity. III, 584. The priesthood of the sun was a great dignity among the Egyptians. III, 584. How foolishly the Manichaeans think about the sun. VIII, 371. They called the sun the ship of light. VIII, 35, 539, 568. The Manichaeans taught that the sun was made from good fire. VIII, 35. They say that the sun is both God and a part of God. VIII, 597. The sun was worshiped by Pagans and Manichaeans. IV, 189. The Manichaeans worshiped the sun. III, 176; V, 329; VIII, 242, 300, 321. They worshiped the sun as a portion of the Creator. VIII, 591. They said that the sun was Christ. IV, 1194; V, 36, 105. The Manichaeans worshiped the sun as the divine substance and as the light of wisdom. VIII, 228. Why the Manichaeans worship the sun and moon. VIII, 369. Whoever worships the sun is cursed in a different way from one who hangs upon a tree. VIII, 301.

Philosophers say that the sun is eternal. II, 379. Why was the sun created if the first light was sufficient to make the day. III, 254. The poetic fiction that the sun plunges into the sea and then rises in the morning, complete, from the other side. III, 254. How swiftly the sun moves. V, 1262.
