It is not surprising that it is larger than the other stars. II, 80. The sun is set over the day alone, or even over the heat of the entire heavens. III, 1063. Astrologers and advocates of fate assign the chief part to the sun. III, 277. When the moon is full, the sun cannot be eclipsed. II, 917. A natural eclipse of the sun occurred at the death of Romulus. VII, 91. The eclipse of the sun at Christ’s passion occurred outside the regular course of the stars. VII, 92. And it was truly prodigious. II, 917. A notable eclipse of the sun occurred on 19 July 418. II, 903, note (a). It is recorded in the history of the nations that two suns were seen on one occasion. II, 917. Some people who sinned or failed to repay debts were ordered by judges to be placed in the sun. VII, 352. Christians do not observe days, years, months, and seasons, although they celebrate Easter according to the reckoning of the sun and moon. II, 210; VIII, 156.

The sun of righteousness is Christ, the truth. IV, 189. He does not rise for the ungodly. IV, 1374. The sun of righteousness does not rise for the wicked, the ungodly, or unbelievers. V, 1322. Just as the moon appears larger to our eyes when it moves away from the sun and smaller when it approaches the sun, so the soul, when moving away from the sun of righteousness, advances toward outward things, but when approaching it, turns toward inward things. II, 208. The power of the sun, and its distinction from the Word of God. V, 676.

The consolations of flesh and soul in this life. IV, 753. Earthly consolation is found more as desolation among human beings than as comfort. II, 495. True consolations are not found in riches, dignities, and so forth. II, 495. True consolation is in eternal life. II, 496. Good people also seem to provide substantial consolations in this life. II, 495, 496.

Solid coins. V, 964, 965.

Solitude is necessary for our mind to see God. III, 1533. Solitude is highly suitable for repentance. I, 761. It helps a person collect his thoughts. I, 979. The height of Christian perfection is to delight in solitude. I, 1337. Concentration of mind generates solitude for itself. VI, 145. The desire for solitude [Col. 0610] generally arises because of the crowd of tribulations and scandals. IV, 633.

A solemnity is so called from what regularly occurs each year. V, 1229. A solemnity offered to friends. V, 634. A solemnity does not conflict with truth when it does not permit the past to pass away. V, 1089. The solemnities of the Martyrs are to be celebrated by imitating their virtues. V, 1414. See Martyrs. A vernacular solemnity. V, 1208.

What a solecism is. III, 44. Solecisms and barbarisms sometimes contribute to the beauty of speech. I, 1001.

Solon of Athens, one of the Seven Sages. VII, 582. Solon gave certain laws to the Athenians. VII, 582.

Solon, a public slave of the city of Aptugni. II, 304; IX, 540.

The duty of binding and loosing was given to the Church, so that the bonds of those who have returned to life from sin may be loosed. V, 434, 594, 1549, 1711. Christ himself, who is not bound, loosed those who were bound. V, 176. No one is to be bound unjustly, because justice breaks unjust bonds. V, 509. See Keys.

The happy dreams of sleepers in paradise. X, 808. The visions of dreams are not bodily but resemble bodies, although many people of no ordinary acuteness think otherwise. II, 706. Whether they occur in the mind as letters made with ink on parchment, or like a seal in wax, and so forth, is not easily explained. II, 706. Nebridius asks Augustine how dreams arise, while explaining his own conjectures. II, 71. To what extent the visions of dreamers arise. X, 539, 540, 541. Dreams that occur through the agency of demons. II, 73. They can also be produced by the mind’s capacity to diminish or enlarge anything through thought. II, 73. Apparitions outside sleep and in sleep. II, 696. Gennadius hears the hymns of the Blessed in dreams. II, 699. Gennadius is admonished in a dream so that he will not doubt whether there will be a future life after death. II, 699. Erotic dreams can occur without sin. III, 466. The dreams of sleepers are the felicities of this age. IV, 1718.

The effect of sleep. I, 1032. Sleep makes the limbs grow weak. I, 1051. Sleep is often disturbed by dream visions. VII, 786. Sleep comes more easily to hard ground than to a silver-plated bed. V, 114. The praise of God is not interrupted by sleep; the innocence of sleep praises God. IV, 1900. Because of the soul’s good disposition, certain merits of the soul shine forth in dreams. III, 466. Sleep is twofold: good for the body, bad for the soul. IV, 750. Adam’s ecstatic sleep, a mystical interpretation. III, 205. Sleep is frequently used for death in Scripture. IV, 74, 1701, 1921.

Sound is threefold: either in the voice of an animal, or in what breath produces in instruments, or in what is produced by striking. I, 1013; IV, 1965. Sound is the vehicle of a word conceived in the mind. V, 185. The distinction of sound from number. I, 1163. From song. I, 842.

Scripture detests sophistries. III, 58. Sophistical profession condemned in Scripture. IX, 448. A speech is called sophistical when it pursues verbal ornament more abundantly than is proper. III, 58. The sophists, very eloquent authors of Latin literature. III, 505.

When Zephaniah prophesied. VII, 591.

Sor is interpreted as “anguish” or “tribulation.” IV, 1053.

Soranus, a most distinguished authority in medicine. I, 655; X, 639, *Retr.* 813.

A lot is not something evil, but, amid human uncertainty, indicates the divine will. IV, 246. The practice of reading lots from the pages of the Gospels is not pleasing. II, 222. Why grace is called by the name of “lot.” IV, 246, 247. When Augustine approves of casting lots. II, 1018.

Soothsayers. One must not turn to soothsayers and enchanters in illnesses. III, 1441.

The baths of Sossius. VIII, 111.

The chastity of eunuchs is less arduous. X, 845.

The Church of Spaniensis. II, 134.

What a *spatha* (sword) is. IV, 1955.

The first species, according to which, so to speak, all things have been given their species. VI, 17. Species will not make anyone glad in the homeland whom faith does not console on the journey. V, 541. “Species” is more commonly used of bodies or likenesses of bodies, although it is also spiritual. II, 606.

One species is generated in turn from another species. VIII, 996. Bodily and intelligible species. VII, 355.

How Christ is beautiful, although he is read to have had no outward form. IV, 1338.

Days of spectacles. V, 332. The empty spectacles of games. V, 85. The spectacles of theaters are unlawful. V, 868. They are dangerous. VII, 44, 45. They are harmful both to those who produce them and to those who watch them. IV, 1918. Spectacles were prohibited through the persuasion of Scipio Nasica. VII, 44, 45, 51. Christians are deterred from spectacles. V, 548. Through devotion to spectacles people become like demons. VI, 329. Mad. VI, 330. To permit spectacles is not the conduct of a true shepherd. V, 274. Harmful spectacles and the wholesome spectacles of the Church. VI, 638. Christians have their own spectacles. III, 1440; IV, 439, 1851, 1919, 1923; V, 333. God never ceases to stage for us a spectacle that we may behold with great joy. IV, 1033. It is a great spectacle to see God armed on your behalf. IV, 323. God himself is the spectacle of the Blessed. IV, 1901, 1916.

Spectators of trifles. 553.

Watchmen, that is, those set over the peoples. VII, 23.

Huge mirrors do not produce larger images; but in small mirrors, even if a large face is presented to them, a very small image is formed according to the size of the mirror. II, 65. The vanity of mirrors. I, 668, 683. Scripture is the mirror of the soul. IV, 248, 1338. The commandments of God are to be examined as in a mirror. IV, 1510.

Hope is only of good things, and only of future things, and concerns the person who hopes. VI, 235. The poet improperly said “to hope for pain.” VI, 234. “What I hold is better than what I hope for,” a common proverb. IV, 1646.

There is one hope among the nations and another among Christians. V, 1024. Carnal hope. V, 34. How empty and uncertain is hope in temporal goods. V, 861. Vain hope in money, honor, or a powerful friend. IV, 237, 610. Perverse hope deceives, just as good and upright hope sets free. V, 535. One hope concerns eternal rewards, another divine assistance. IV, 1541. Hope must be placed in God alone. VI, 344, 348. One must hope not in temporal things but in God alone. IV, 122. The person who does not hope in the Lord stumbles among the wicked. IV, 191. A Christian ought not to hope in himself. IV, 472, 1140. Miserable is the person who hopes in himself; still more miserable is the person who hopes in another human being. IV, 315. Cursed is the person who places hope in himself. VI, 285. Hope must not be placed in a human being. IV, 437, 961, 962, 1651, 1652, 1889, 1890. If you place your hope in another human being, you will be humbly disordered; if in yourself, you will be dangerously proud. V, 108.

All hope must be placed in God. V, 165. Not in the powers of free will. V, 902. Certain and fixed hope in God does not admit fear of anything. IV, 200.

The hope of Christians concerns eternal things. V, 859. Whatever is done should be done for the sake of future hope. V, 78. Our hope is the resurrection of the dead. V, 1599. The inheritance to be hoped for is not one such as is sought through evil desire, which must be wholly consumed here rather than satisfied there. IV, 1466. The hope of those who hope for something from God apart from God himself is insane. IV, 437, 438. We hope for equality with the angels. V, 834. The things that pertain to the hope of believers are contained in the Lord’s Prayer. VI, 285. Through the sacrament of the hope of eternal rest, the Church is joined together in the present age. VIII, 265. The hope of immortal life is the life of mortal life. IV, 1389. The hope of the saints of the Old Testament and of the New is entirely the same. VIII, 356. As with faith, so with hope: not seeing belongs to it. VI, 235.

The certainty of our hope. V, 861. How solid is the hope of Christians. IV, 1074. Our hope is founded on God’s promise. III, 1656. By what pledges of salvation from God our hope is raised. IV, 1941, 1942. If the Son of God was given even to those who were not yet believers, what is reserved for believers. V, 54. Because the salvation given to us in hope is certain, the Apostle speaks as though that same salvation had already been given. VIII, 251, 252. In our Head we see what we hope for. V, 860. Our hope is in Christ because what we hope has been promised to us has already been fulfilled in him. VIII, 251. The certainty of hope is the reason that what is to be done is spoken of as done. V, 180. Conversations with those who attempt to weaken our hope must be avoided. V, 859, 862. Their vanity is demonstrated. V, 860, 861. Hope exists only in some goodness of conscience. V, 865. Each person’s hope lies in his own conscience. III, 71. Let life follow wherever hope goes before. IV, 1774. Unless the joy of our hope were accompanied by the trembling of condemnation, security itself would be negligent in us and would become arrogant presumption. III, 883. Everything is to be hoped for from the mercy of God. IV, 210.

Hope and despair in sins are to be feared. IV, 1876, 1877. How people are endangered by hoping and despairing. III, 1651. How God provides for those who hope and those who despair. III, 1651. Perverse hope, by which conversion is postponed. V, 139, 536. So that people would not live worse in hope of forgiveness, God made the day of death uncertain. IV, 1301. For whom hope of easy forgiveness will exist. V, 153. Our hope in daily sins is humble confession. IV, 1828, 1884, 1885.

Hope is necessary here. V, 369. It is the companion of faith. V, 369. Hope cannot exist without faith, but faith can exist without hope. VI, 234. Faith that works through love cannot exist without hope. V, 866. Hope and charity pray; faith believes and prays. VI, 234. Hope cannot exist without love, nor love without hope. VI, 235. Hope is empty or nonexistent without charity. VI, 286. Hope usually kindles love. IV, 1487. Faith, hope, and charity enroll us in the divine commonwealth. II, 533. Hope obtains salvation and blessedness for us in this life. VII, 631. Hope is a consolation in this pilgrimage. V, 866. Hope nurses us, nourishes us, strengthens us, and consoles us here. V, 1188. Certain hope of our return consoles and encourages us when we are saddened in our pilgrimage. IV, 1884, 1889. The sweetness of God is revealed to those who hope. V, 791. Hope cannot exist without joy. IV, 1885. The Saints are always rejoicing, both here and in heaven: here in hope, there in reality. IV, 1498, 1659, 1679, 1703, 1889. The disciples had lost hope after Christ’s passion. [Col. 0612] V, 1110, 1115, 1118, 1120.

Hope and reality. V, 312, 313, 1188, 1219, 1456. There will be no hope when reality has arrived. V, 866. In the homeland there will be not hope but reality. IV, 1171, 1702. The hope of Christians is compared with an anchor. IV, 774.

The symbol of hope is cedar wood. III, 734. Hope is like a lamp burning in the night. V, 227. Hope is signified by an egg. III, 1342. Compared with an egg. V, 622. The hope of future life cannot be preserved without patience, nor patience without gentleness. V, 860. A person of good hope. X, 1028.

Spes. A dispute arose between Boniface and a certain member of the monastery of Saint Augustine named Spes. II, 267. What was that dispute. II, 268. Spes tried to advance into the clerical order; Augustine refused to lay hands on him in ordination. Spes began to act more turbulently, so that Boniface the presbyter would not even be permitted to remain in his position. Boniface was ready to endure the loss of his honor among human beings rather than proceed vainly to the disturbance of the Church. II, 268. Augustine sent both of them—namely Spes and Boniface—to the tomb of Blessed Felix of Nola. II, 269. Boniface humbly concealed his priestly honor during the pilgrimage. II, 269.

Speusippus, the son of Plato’s sister and his successor in the Academy. VII, 237.

The Sphinx, a monster. VII, 571.

Sphinxes. VII, 487.

According to the Manichaeans, plucking ears of grain is murder; according to Christ, it is innocence. VIII, 335, 381.

Why and when thorns, thistles, and barren trees were created. III, 290. Thorns came into being for human beings after sin, for the sake of labor. III, 291. Julian asserts that thorns, thistles, the sweat of labor, and the pain of childbirth were instituted before human beings sinned and were not imposed as punishment. X, 1569, 1576, 1577. Thorns in all the pleasures of life. IV, 1331. Whom the thorns that do not prick at the roots signify. IV, 1805.

The god Spiniensis. VII, 129.

The Spirit is spoken of in many ways. V, 717; VIII, 1053. The name “spirit,” insofar as it signifies some nature, is common to every incorporeal nature. II, 1043.

## Holy Spirit

The Holy Spirit. X, 484, 485, 486. The third Person in the Trinity. VII, 337, 338. The Holy Spirit is sometimes signified by the name “Spirit” alone. V, 451. Why the Holy Spirit is so called. VI, 336. From what he is properly called holy. V, 72. The Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Photinians, and Jews sinned against the Holy Spirit. II, 814. Some heretics altogether deny the Holy Spirit, while others wish him to be a creature; who they are. V, 448; VIII, 44. The Sabellians denied the Holy Spirit; the Arians denied that he was God; the Manichaeans fancied that he was corruptible and was sent only after three hundred years; the Cataphrygians denied his coming upon the Apostles but imagined that he had chosen prophets in Phrygia; finally, the Donatists blew upon his sacraments in repudiation. III, 2099; VIII, 30. The Sadducees denied the Holy Spirit. V, 447. The Macedonians were unwilling to acknowledge the Holy Spirit as equal to the Father and the Son and of the same substance with them. VIII, 797. What the Arians thought about the Holy Spirit. VIII, 680, 681, 736. The Arians said that the Holy Spirit was subject to Christ. VIII, 714, 716. The errors of the Arians, Eunomians, and others concerning the Holy Spirit. V, 448. Certain heretics thought that the Holy Spirit was the deity of the Father and the Son. VI, 191.

The Holy Spirit, God proceeding from the Father. I, 1321; V, 1071; VI, 258, 634, 684; VIII, 697, 703, 722, 742, 752, 790; IX, 378. The divinity of the Holy Spirit is asserted. II, 1046. Peter demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is God. III, 616. The Holy Spirit is the true God, equal to the Father and the Son. VIII, 788, 827, 828, 927. The Holy Spirit is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son. III, 1826; VIII, 928. Together with the Father and the Son, he is one wisdom. VIII, 938. The Holy Spirit is understood when the Father and the Son are named. III, 1461. Ambrose demonstrates that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son. III, 111. The Holy Spirit is intimated in several places in the Old Scripture. III, 584, 614. Yet he is not called the Holy Spirit, but the Spirit of God. III, 584. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. V, 454, 461. The Holy Spirit is common to the Father and the Son. VII, 337, 338. Whatever it is that is common to the Father and the Son is something common to them. VIII, 927, 928. This communion is a substance. VIII, 927, 928. It is more appropriately called love than friendship. VIII, 927, 928. The Holy Spirit is held in common by the Father and the Son because he belongs to both. V, 464. Yet he is distinct from both, as love is distinct from those who love. VIII, 928. Everything that the Father has belongs not only to the Son but also to the Holy Spirit. VIII, 848. Whatever seems to be said only of the Father or the Son is fittingly said of the Holy Spirit as God. VIII, 779, 783. The Holy Spirit is creator together with the Father and the Son. VIII, 783. He is sufficient for our blessedness in the same way as the Father. VIII, 832. The Father and the Son cooperate with the Holy Spirit, yet in these works there are not many but one Spirit. V, 459. The Holy Spirit alone is said to move over the waters; why. I, 848. How the Spirit of God was over the waters. III, 226; VI, 133, 167. What this signifies. VI, 133. According to the understanding of the Syriac language, the Holy Spirit was not borne over the waters but warmed them. III, 260. The Spirit of God was borne over the world while it was being made, and, once it had been made, is borne over it through the excellence of his power. III, 349.

The Holy Spirit is said in a particular way insofar as he is related to the Father and the Son. II, 1044. The Holy Spirit is spoken of in relation to the Father and the Son, but the term for the one to whom he is related does not correspond reciprocally to him. VIII, 919. Augustine more readily dares to call the Holy Spirit the holiness—or goodness—of the Father and the Son. VII, 337, 338. The Father and the Son are the one principle of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 920, 921. The Holy Spirit proceeds principally from him from whom the Son was born. V, 459. The Spirit of the Father and the Son, sent by both, begotten by none, the unity of both, equal to both. V, 1059. The Holy Spirit was not made by the Father and the Son, but proceeds. II, 749. Whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. III, 1888, 1889. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. VIII, 902. Why the Holy Spirit is said to proceed, but not to be born. VIII, 770. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is timeless, and he cannot be called the son of both. VIII, 1094. Why the Holy Spirit is not and is not called a son, although he proceeds from the Father. VIII, 920. The Holy Spirit is neither the Father’s son, nor the Son’s father, nor the Son’s son. V, 1071. He is God. V, 1071. The Holy Spirit cannot be called Christ’s father. VI, 251. The Holy Spirit was neither begotten as the Son from the Father, nor from the Son as the grandson of the supreme Father. VI, 191. Nevertheless, he owes to the Father what he is. VI, 191. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, equal to both. VI, 648. Why the Holy Spirit is not begotten and how he proceeds from the Father and the Son is understood only in blessedness. VIII, 1092. Although the Holy Spirit is not called begotten, he should not nevertheless be called unbegotten. VIII, 1095.

The Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son. VIII, 686, 697. What it means for the Holy Spirit to be sent. VIII, 908. How the sending of the Holy Spirit is to be understood. VIII, 850. The Holy Spirit is nowhere said to be less than the Father, or to have worshiped the Father. VIII, 723, 755, 757. He is nowhere said to be less than the Father, because he did not assume flesh. V, 1218. No one has ever said that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son. V, 458. The Scripture in which the Holy Spirit appears to be called less than the Father and the Son indicates his procession from both. VIII, 847. The Holy Spirit is not for that reason less than the Father and the Son, because they give and he is given. VIII, 1086. The Holy Spirit does not worship the Father. VIII, 750. In what sense the Holy Spirit is said to intercede with God for us. X, 531. In what sense he intercedes for us and cries, “Abba, Father.” X, 1032. The Arians do not wish the Holy Spirit to be worshiped. VIII, 807. The Arians maintained that no testimonies of Scripture could be produced concerning the worship of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 724. The Holy Spirit is owed λατρεία (*latreia*, worship). II, 749. The worship of the Holy Spirit is demonstrated. VIII, 760. The Holy Spirit will be invisibly with the Son in judgment. VIII, 787. Faith in the Holy Spirit. VI, 189. He sins against the Holy Spirit who, despairing or despising the proclamation of peace and grace, refuses to repent and persists to the very end. III, 2097. Concerning sin against the Holy Spirit. III, 2097.

The finger of God signifies the Holy Spirit. II, 218. The Holy Spirit is the finger of God. III, 604, 620, 1118; IV, 111, 1167; V, 74, 842, 857; VI, 335, 336; VII, 522; VIII, 791; X, 218.

The Holy Spirit is God’s gift, equal to the giver. VI, 231. Whether the Holy Spirit had not been given to the ancient righteous before Christ’s ascension. III, 1772. The Holy Spirit was upon the earth before the Savior’s coming. VIII, 644, 645, 646. How it is to be understood that the Holy Spirit was not an aid to virtue in the Old Testament. X, 591. Even in the time of the Old Testament, the Holy Spirit was for all the godly and holy not only an aid to virtue but also its giver. X, 597. The Holy Spirit not only assisted the good wills of the ancient righteous but brought them into being. X, 622. Concerning the sensible manifestation of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 909. The Holy Spirit came in the form of a dove. III, 2035. Why the Holy Spirit appeared in a dove, and the Son of God in a human being. VI, 25. The Holy Spirit was manifested in a dove not in his own nature but in a symbolic form. II, 747. Why the Holy Spirit was not born from a dove in order to appear in the form of a dove, just as Christ was born from a woman. VI, 302. The Holy Spirit has never assumed any creature into the unity of person. VIII, 909. A creature was not assumed by the Holy Spirit in the manner in which flesh was assumed by the Word. VIII, 851. Whether the Holy Spirit was not given before the day of Pentecost. VIII, 908. How he was not given before Christ’s resurrection. III, 1644, 1645, 1646, 1805. How the disciples were to receive the Holy Spirit whom they already possessed. III, 1826, 1827. Christ manifestly gave the Holy Spirit to the disciples twice. III, 1827; V, 1222; VIII, 180, 1093. Why he was given twice. V, 1222. The breath which the Lord breathed upon the Apostles was not the substance of the Holy Spirit but a figure. III, 412. The Holy Spirit is Christ’s gift, equal to him. V, 713. A gift purchased for us by Christ’s Passion. V, 1645. A great gift after Christ’s ascension. V, 786. The Holy Spirit poured out through Christ upon believers. VIII, 713. Christ was glorified for this purpose: that he might send the Holy Spirit, who would strengthen those who were failing. IV, 1443. He would free the faithful from fear. IV, 1167. The Holy Spirit delivers from fear of death. III, 2074.

When the Holy Spirit was sent. VIII, 179. The day of the Holy Spirit, as it were his birthday. V, 73. Just as the Law was given on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb, so the Holy Spirit came on the fiftieth day after Christ’s Passion. IV, 1167. A figure of the giving of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Christ’s sacrifice. III, 620. Why the Holy Spirit came on the tenth day after the Ascension. V, 1239. Why on the fiftieth day after the Resurrection. V, 73, 74, 1237. Joel prophesied the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh. VII, 586. And Nahum also. VII, 588. The old Law was given in one way, the Holy Spirit was sent in another. X, 218. The Holy Spirit was sent so that the Law might be fulfilled. V, 1239, 1243. The Holy Spirit came like fire, to consume the hay of the flesh and to cook and purify the gold. IV, 161. Why he appeared in the form of a dove over Christ, and in fire over the disciples. III, 1426. The coming of the Holy Spirit was a manifestation of him even to bodily eyes. VI, 54. It also signified that his fullness was poured more abundantly into human hearts. VI, 54. Why the Holy Spirit was given through sensible miracles at the very beginnings of the Church. IX, 148. Why he appeared in divided tongues. III, 1429. What the Holy Spirit signified by the gift of tongues. V, 461. He commended the unity of the Catholic Church. V, 1231, 1234. For this reason he caused those upon whom he first came to speak in the tongues of all peoples: he announced that he would gather the tongues of all nations into unity. IV, 161. Why he was formerly given in such a way that those whom he filled spoke in all tongues, whereas he is now not given in this manner. IX, 284. The errors of those who say that the promised Holy Spirit came in the Apostle Paul, or in Montanus and Priscilla, or in Manes. VI, 305, 306. The Manichaeans say that the promise of the Holy Spirit was fulfilled in Mani. VIII, 38.

What the benefits of the Holy Spirit are. VIII, 704, 717. With respect to the Spirit, being born and being nourished are different things. V, 454. The forgiveness of sins properly belongs to the Holy Spirit. V, 461. The Holy Spirit helps in one way when he does not yet dwell within, and in another when he dwells within: when he does not yet dwell within, he helps people to become faithful; when he dwells within, he helps those who are already faithful. II, 880. He fills in one way through sanctifying grace, and in another through a presence that bears witness and gives direction. VI, 133. Unless the Spirit of God rules you, you fall; unless he raises you up, you lie prostrate. V, 855. If the Spirit of God withdraws, the human spirit, weighed down by its own weight, turns back into the flesh and returns to carnal actions. V, 848. The Holy Spirit is called the grace of God. V, 787. The Holy Spirit is designated by the name of grace and peace. III, 2095. By the name of fellowship. III, 2095. Fellowship properly belongs to the Holy Spirit, through which we become one body of the one Son of God. V, 461. Through what they have in common, the Father and the Son willed that we should have fellowship both with one another and with them. V, 454. The Holy Spirit is the perfection of holiness. VIII, 716. Without Christ or without the Father, he neither sanctifies nor illuminates, and so forth. VIII, 705. He is said to do in us what we do through him. I, 865; II, 880. He is said to groan because he causes us to groan. III, 2076. Whom he causes to groan. III, 1425. The groaning of the godly comes from the gift of the Holy Spirit. IV, 199. See Trinity. The Holy Spirit is the pledge of future salvation. X, 1198, 1199. The same Spirit who is now the pledge of eternal life will later be its fullness. V, 932. The Holy Spirit is rather a down payment than a pledge. V, 858, 1673. The Holy Spirit is the pledge of Christ’s bride. III, 1452, 1644. The Holy Spirit and blood are pledges given by Christ to the bride. IV, 1170. In Christians who are still carnal, the Holy Spirit perfects whatever is lacking when they die, because they have not withdrawn from the unity of Christ’s body. II, 843.

The Holy Spirit is called the gift of God, a bestowal, fire, love, charity, peace, grace, our rest, and our place. I, 848, 1077; III, 171. The Holy Spirit is the gift of God. III, 1514; VI, 251. A gift not of the human minister but of God. V, 1225. In Scripture the Holy Spirit is properly named by the term “gift of God.” VIII, 1083. Why he is called a gift. VI, 191. Whether he was a gift before he was given. VIII, 921. The gift of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1086. The Holy Spirit is God and God’s gift. V, 80, 455. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are called the seven Spirits of God because of the sevenfold operation of one and the same Spirit. IV, 1960. Why the gifts of the Holy Spirit are diverse. II, 839. They are compared with the evangelical beatitudes. V, 1525. Some gifts of the Holy Spirit can be possessed without charity. VI, 135, 137. Nevertheless, they are of no benefit. VI, 137. The Holy Spirit, as though descending to us, begins with wisdom and ends with fear; we, however, ascending, begin with fear and are perfected in wisdom. V, 1161, 1166. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are compared with the stars. I, 842. They are called stars. IV, 1160. Although the Holy Spirit is one and the same, he is named differently because of his various operations. III, 615.

The Holy Spirit is a great river. IV, 1187. The inundation of the Holy Spirit, the river’s current that gladdens the city of God. IV, 519. The Holy Spirit is a fountain. IX, 476. The sword with which the Lord conquered the world. IV, 1183. The Holy Spirit is the Lord’s spotless Law. IV, 161. The oil of gladness. VIII, 782. The Holy Spirit is signified by oil and by water. IV, 1443. The Holy Spirit is the doorkeeper. III, 1729. The King. VIII, 792. How the Holy Spirit is called charity, and whether he alone is so called. VIII, 1081, 1086. In Scripture he is properly named by the term “charity.” VIII, 1082. In the Holy Spirit, God’s goodwill and love are understood. III, 251. The Holy Spirit is mentioned not only in connection with benefits but also with vengeance. III, 615.

Why the Holy Spirit could not come unless Christ departed. X, 182. Why the world cannot receive the Holy Spirit. III, 1828. The Holy Spirit is opposed to people who seek their own interests; he also harasses the harsh and proud with restlessness. II, 219. The place of the Holy Spirit is a humbled heart. VI, 419. The Spirit is given to human beings according to measure, but not to the Son of God. III, 1508, 1828. The Holy Spirit dwells in baptized infants even if they do not know it. II, 841. The Holy Spirit is still received through the laying on of hands. III, 2025. Some received the Holy Spirit before they were baptized. VI, 53. The Holy Spirit was given to Cornelius and one hundred and twenty people without anyone’s laying on of hands and before baptism. IX, 287. The Holy Spirit has at times been given through human ministry and without human ministry. V, 600, 601, 1227, 1235. The Holy Spirit is given only in the Catholic Church. IX, 148. He is not possessed outside the Church. V, 1232, 1235. He gives life to no one outside the Church. II, 815. The unity of the Church is, as it were, the Holy Spirit’s proper work. V, 463. Whoever does not adhere to the unity of Christ does not have the Holy Spirit. V, 73. Each person possesses the Holy Spirit to the extent that he loves the Church. III, 1646. The Holy Spirit is to the Church what the soul is to the body. V, 1232. Heretics and the perverse also possess the Holy Spirit, if baptism cannot exist without the Holy Spirit; but they possess him to their destruction, not to their salvation. IX, 193. The Holy Spirit is commended under the number seven. V, 1170, 1242. He is also often designated in this way. VII, 345. The Holy Spirit is the defender and leader of freedom. III, 2143. The Spirit of slavery and the Spirit of freedom are the same Spirit. V, 857. By God’s grace the human spirit becomes a participant in the Spirit of God. III, 725.

What the former signs were, and what the present signs are, of having received the Holy Spirit. V, 461, 1230, 1235, 1237. We cannot know the Holy Spirit unless he is in us. III, 1829. We recognize that the Spirit of God is in us by love of righteousness and by an unimpaired Catholic faith. V, 848. The sign of having received the Spirit is to say to God from the inmost depths of the heart, “Father.” V, 858. The effect of the Holy Spirit’s presence is charity. V, 1673. Without the Holy Spirit we can neither love Christ nor keep his commandments. III, 1826, 1827, 1828. When and how the upright spirit is restored in the soul. I, 1076. How the Holy Spirit is grieved. III, 302. “Do not extinguish the Spirit”: how this is to be understood. IX, 73. If the Spirit of God withdraws, the human spirit, weighed down by its own weight, turns back into the flesh. V, 848. The Spirit of God is the spirit of charity; the spirit of this world is the spirit of arrogance. V, 1287. What the voice of the Spirit is. III, 1486. What the first fruits of the Spirit are. VI, 69. The Spirit of God who is in us is also called our spirit. III, 725; VIII, 921. When the human spirit cooperates with the Spirit of God, then what God has commanded is fulfilled. IV, 988.

To serve God in the Spirit. V, 915. To be not in the flesh but in the spirit. V, 847. How one should walk according to the spirit. X, 588. To be led by the Spirit means to consent to the Spirit when he commands, not to the flesh when it desires. V, 815. Those who are not led by the Spirit must consequently be led by the flesh. III, 2139. The spirit rules and the flesh is ruled; yet the spirit does not rule well if it is not itself ruled. V, 915. Whoever follows his own spirit is proud. IV, 1836, 1852. The poor in their own spirit and the rich in the Spirit of God are blessed. IV, 1836. The kingdoms of the spirit and of desires are described. I, 1232. The struggle between spirit and flesh. I, 597, 614, 1296; V, 849. When the spirit fights against the flesh, it is not one contrary nature fighting another contrary nature, but rather it is like a husband and wife in a household. IV, 1860. The spirit’s struggle against the flesh is necessary. X, 1596.

What is understood by the name “Spirit of God.” III, 226. Whether the Holy Spirit is to be understood. VI, 132. Without qualification, “Spirit of God” is understood as the good Spirit. VI, 132, 134. The blessed spirits are the house of God. I, 818. They are called the heaven of heaven. I, 818. See Angels. Why an evil spirit is called the Spirit of the Lord. VI, 137. The Spirit of God is called good according to substance, but evil according to ministry. VI, 132, 134. The Spirit of the Lord acts through the good and the evil, the knowing and the unknowing, accomplishing what he knows and has ordained should be done. III, 814, 815. It is not absurd that an evil spirit should be sent by God. III, 808. An evil spirit has no power to harm except from God. VI, 131, 137. Evil spirits are permitted to harm only as much as God judges. VI, 146. God uses evil spirits either for condemnation, correction, or testing. VI, 137. [Col. 0616] For vengeance upon the wicked or for testing the good. VI, 13. Evil spirits were driven from a certain house by a sacrifice of Christ’s body. VII, 764. Unclean spirits are evil demons. VII, 56. “Unclean spirit” is said in two ways. I, 968. The affliction of unclean spirits is a punishment for original sin. X, 1177. The corruption of rational spirits is of two kinds: voluntary and punitive. VIII, 554.

“Spirit” is a general name for the soul. X, 546. Whether spirit and soul are the same. X, 545. What spirit properly is in a human being. X, 544, 545. In Scripture “spirit” is also used according to a certain distinction within the one soul of one human being. II, 1044. What the human spirit is. X, 546. What the spirit of the mind is. X, 546. The distinction between spirit and mind. III, 460, 475. It is extremely difficult for spirits without bodies to think with bodily thought. VIII, 949. The manner in which spirits adhere to bodies cannot be grasped. VII, 725. What the human spirit will be like in heaven. VII, 792. The spirit of life exists not only in human beings but also in animals. III, 550. The spirit of the world, also called the rulers of the world. V, 1091. The spirit of this world makes people proud. V, 1466. The spirit of this world is the spirit of pride. X, 214. “Spirit” used for husband. III, 1395.

“Spiritual” is said in several ways. III, 459. “Spiritual” is not always used as praise. III, 1786. The carnal person does not grasp spiritual things. V, 1230.

Spiritual people—who they are. IV, 1349. A spiritual person is one who is neither captured by temporal goods nor terrified by temporal evils. III, 2071. People become spiritual only through grace. III, 2061, 2062, *Retractationes*; VI, 105. The Holy Spirit makes spiritual people out of the animal-like. V, 1238. Spiritual people are not under the Law but with the Law. III, 2071. What the Spirit does against the flesh, spiritual people do against carnal people. IX, 507. The same person is both carnal and spiritual. V, 836, 837. The spiritual person too was sold under sin. I, 627. See Human Being. Spiritual people, that is, those who live spiritually within, can fall into temptation. III, 356. When spiritual people are unexpectedly overtaken by some offense, the affection of charity is somewhat restrained in them but not extinguished; then, growing warm again, it is restored to its former course. IX, 195. If spiritual people think something differently, God will also reveal that to them, provided they remain in the ardor and unity of charity. IX, 195. What the warfare and weapons of spiritual people are like. IX, 507. Spiritual people suffer persecution from carnal people. IV, 1603, 1772. Spiritual people are in no way divided among themselves, unlike carnal people. VII, 502. All nations are subjected to spiritual people. V, 49. “Spiritual” is said of the seat of God. III, 1256. The spiritual person is called greater, while the carnal person is called lesser—why. IV, 1771. Spiritual people are designated by the names of heavens, days, and deer. IV, 940, 1372, 1748. Spiritual people are signified by Jacob, carnal people by Esau. III, 567. Spiritual death and resurrection. V, 1627. To think spiritually is given by the Holy Spirit. V, 33.

A *spithamis*—a span. III, 636.

The “splendor-bearing weigher” (*splenditenens ponderator*). VIII, 307, 309, 374. What the Manichaeans think about the *splenditenens ponderator*. VIII, 375.

Petilianus made Splendonium, a deacon condemned in the Catholic Church, a presbyter after rebaptizing him. IX, 370. He later rejected him after experiencing his dreadful intrigues. IX, 370. Fortunatus proposed that the condemnation of Splendonium, sent from Gaul by the brethren, be read publicly. IX, 370.

What the spoils are that Christ takes from the defeated devil. IV, 821, 822.

Spondeus, procurator of Celer. II, 536.

The bride of Christ—who she is. III, 1452. When you hear “Christ,” do not separate the bridegroom from the bride. IV, 333. All the elect, or the Church, are Christ’s bride. IV, 494, 509, 512.

Our Bridegroom loved one who was foul in order to make her beautiful. IV, 1232. What it means to go out to meet the bridegroom. V, 575. Christ the Bridegroom is to be loved with the whole heart. VI, 427, 428.

Spurius Maelius, because he distributed grain to the people during a famine, incurred the charge of aspiring to kingship and was killed for that reason. VII, 96.

Squatting and an unkempt appearance in the profession of Christianity can be a cause of ostentation. III, 1287.

Inn women in Italy whom people claimed had turned men into beasts of burden. VII, 574.

What a *stater* is. IV, 1783.

Statilinus, a god. VII, 128.

“Station” signifies remaining in place. V, 967.

Who is a *stationarius*. IV, 1199, 1200.

Statius, the poet. VII, 54, 57. Note (f).

The three conditions of human beings. IV, 1279, 1730.

According to Plato, the stars are not immortal by nature but by God’s decision. V, 1138, 1141. They have intellectual souls of their own and are gods. V, 1138. Certain stars were called by the names of gods. VII, 206. The fictitious divinity of certain stars above the others is rejected. VII, 206. The stars are insulted when they are called by the names of gods. IV, 1194.

It is impious to say that wills are subject to the stars. IV, 924. The fictitious fate of the stars. V, 1007, 1027, 1031. No human birth is placed under the fate of the stars. VIII, 212. [Col. 0617] All the stars cannot be counted. VII, 500. How the stars will fall from heaven at the final judgment. VII, 697. The stars are the consolations of the night. I, 866. The Manichaeans thought that an insult was done to Christ because a star was said to have indicated that he was born. VIII, 211, 212. The star that the Magi saw did not rule Christ by decree but served him as a testimony. VIII, 212. It was not one of those that were created in the beginning. VIII, 212.

By the name of stars, the various gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified. IV, 1760. The stars that are said to be numbered by God are the elect; others are supernumerary. IV, 1904. The stars are certain lights in the Church that comfort our night. IV, 1904.

Sthenelas, the ninth king of the Argives, was enrolled among the gods. VII, 565.

Stephen. VI, 689. He is called a crown. IV, 695; V, 1426. Stephen was first among the deacons. V, 1431. Whether he adhered to the living Christ or turned to him after his death is uncertain. V, 1433. Stephen was simple and fervent. III, 1426. Stephen loved those by whom he was killed, because he was also dying for them. III, 2014. Stephen is stoned. V, 565, 1275. Stephen’s charity toward his stoners. V, 325. Stephen was gentle while being stoned, yet raged when he was heard. IV, 1734. Stephen rages and loves. V, 325. He seems to hate, he seems to rage: his tongue cries out, but his heart loves. IV, 1734; V, 1437. Stephen prays for his enemies on bended knee. V, 325. Why Stephen, standing when praying for himself, prays on bended knee for his enemies. V, 325, 1428, 1429, 1436, 1441. Stephen is our fellow servant, not to be worshiped as God. V, 1442. Stephen’s prayers obtain many things, but not everything. V, 1441. Paul’s conversion is attributed to Stephen’s prayer. See Paul. V, 1684.

The discovery of Stephen’s body. V, 1437, 1441; VII, 768. Note (a). An altar was erected to God over his relics. V, 1437. The memorial of Stephen at Hippo Regius. VII, 768, 770. It was outside the basilica. VII, 771. How many and how great miracles occurred at the memorials of Stephen located at Hippo, Calama, and Uzalis. VII, 768; V, 1444, 1446. Stephen’s relics were brought to the memorial at the waters of Tibilis. VII, 766. Bishop Possidius brought the memorial of Saint Stephen to Calama. VII, 766. At Calama, through the assistance of Saint Stephen the martyr, the presbyter Eucharius was healed of a kidney stone and later restored to life. VII, 766. Martialis was converted to the faith. VII, 766. Two people suffering from gout were healed through Saint Stephen’s relics. VII, 767. On what occasion Stephen’s memorial was built near Ancona before the discovery of his body. V, 1445. There the Lord performed many miracles through him. V, 1444, 1445. Galla and Simpliciola carried Stephen’s relics with them. II, 965. A blind woman was healed through Stephen’s relics. VII, 766. The wonders performed by Stephen, but through the name of Christ. V, 1431, 1440. Life was restored to a dead infant through Stephen’s prayers, so that the child might receive the sacraments. V, 1446. A girl was restored to life at the memorial of that same Saint Stephen at Hippo. VII, 767. A boy was restored to life at the memorial of Saint Stephen in the church at Audurus. VII, 767. The son of Irenaeus also revived after being anointed with Saint Stephen’s oil. VII, 767. Bishop Lucillus was healed of a fistula through Saint Stephen’s relics. VII, 766. Likewise, the infant Eleusinus revived after being anointed with Saint Stephen’s oil. VII, 768. A nun too was restored to life at the memorial of Saint Stephen. VII, 767. A little book concerning a man healed through Stephen’s prayers. V, 1443.

What Stephen, bishop of the Roman Church, thought about the baptism of heretics. IX, 192. He held that Christ’s baptism should in no case be repeated. IX, 607, 746. He thought that those who tried to overturn the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics should be excluded. IX, 194. The Donatists acknowledged his episcopate as unblemished. IX, 607.

Sterces, or Stercutius, a highly skilled farmer, discovered how fields could be fertilized with animal dung. VII, 573.

Dung was so called from Sterces, the highly skilled farmer. VII, 573.

Stercutius, a god. II, 84.

Two causes of sterility in women. X, 711. Christ cursed not the sterility of children but the sterility of fruit on a tree. IV, 334.

Stesichorus. II, 237, 290.

What are called stigmata. III, 2148.

The laws of Theodosius’s son against heretics and idolaters are attributed to Stilicho. II, 358.

Stimula, a goddess. VII, 122, 125.

The “thorn of the flesh” given to the Apostle. V, 1566.

Provincial stipendary officials. VI, 341.

A stipend, which is the payment owed for military service. VI, 282.

Why God did not bless the plants. III, 240.

The Stoics, Mani, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian say that souls are from the very substance of God. II, 718, 723. The Stoics attribute knowledge to the wise person alone. I, 874. The Stoics are mistaken when they say that a human being does not possess wisdom unless he is perfect in it. II, 738. The Stoics deny only verbally that passions affect the wise person. VII, 259. The Stoics do not exclude every disturbance from the soul of the wise person. III, 556. They place mercy among the vices. II, 395, 396. The Stoic error concerning the evils of this life. VII, 629. By placing the highest good in the soul, the Stoics turned the soul away from the flesh more than from the body. II, 440. The Stoic opinion concerning the blessed life. V, 809, 853. It is rejected. V, 812, 854. The Stoics maintain that all sins are equal. VI, 539. The Catholics denied this. II, 735. The Stoic doctrine of the equality of sins is refuted. II, 394, 395. The Stoic claim not to fear or grieve is ridiculed. V, 1528. The Stoics are to be judged as living according to the flesh. VII, 413. The Stoics are especially dialectical. IX, 455, 456, 459. They argue not so much about things as about words. VII, 404. They struggle more over opposition in words than over opposition in things. IX, 455. The Stoics’ ashes no longer even glow. II, 438. A Stoic philosopher turns pale in danger during a storm. VII, 259.

How some infants became cross-eyed. VIII, 1041.

The Strabonian estate. II, 234.

Christ himself makes himself the great road to the homeland. V, 91.

Strato the Peripatetic. VII, 190.

Straton, a deacon. IX, 645, 662. Whether he was a traditor. IX, 646, 662.

The celebration of New Year’s gifts. V, 1025. Alms should be given in place of New Year’s gifts. V, 1025.

Strenia, a goddess who makes people vigorous. VII, 122, 125.

The ostrich. Little loops made from ostrich bones worn on the fingers: a kind of superstition. III, 50.

What it means to desire earnestly. VIII, 972. The love of one who desires to learn is not love of something he does not know. VIII, 971, 974, 975.

Who is to be called a student. VIII, 80. How a student differs from a curious person. VIII, 80.

Study. What disciplines, sciences, and arts should be pursued, and how. III, 62. Those who ought to devote themselves to their salvation and the usefulness of the Church should not spend time on curious questions. III, 271, 277. In the study of all the sciences one must observe the rule, “Nothing in excess.” III, 62. How negligently the study of secular literature is pursued at Rome and in Africa. II, 436. How unbecoming it is for bishops. II, 436. Augustine does not wholly condemn it in a young man. II, 435. Augustine approves the fact that the rhetors of Carthage do not pursue certain curious questions. II, 437. Augustine devotes his studies to the people of God and cannot attend to other matters. II, 247. For what purpose men devoted to literature may seek human praise. II, 436. Prayer should precede study. I, 919. The studies of all learners belong to the labor imposed on humanity as a punishment. X, 1578. How learners’ studies are kindled. VIII, 972, 973. Tranquility of mind is necessary for the student. I, 1075. Human endeavor does not begin without grace. X, 588.

Folly, darkness of the mind. I, 999, 1307; V, 436. Folly is compared with darkness. II, 738. Folly is the poverty of the soul. I, 973, 974. True folly is false wisdom. V, 813. Folly is a vicious ignorance of things to be sought and things to be avoided. I, 1306. Folly embraces all the vices of the soul. I, 974. Folly is the greatest of the vices. I, 1306. Folly and childish vanity are effects of original sin. X, 821. Folly is also most wretched in the judgment of fools. I, 918. There is no other misery than folly. II, 64. Whether some other disposition can exist between folly and wisdom. I, 607. Something intermediate between folly and wisdom is found. I, 1306, 1307. This is explained by the example of little children. I, 608. A fool is one in whom the mind does not possess supreme authority. I, 1231. The distinction between a fool and a wise person. I, 1231. Every fool sins except in those actions in which he obeys a wise person. VIII, 85. Say that you are a fool—but say it inwardly—and you will be wise. V, 436.

A certain stupor far removed from health, by which a person is so much more insensitive as he is worse. IV, 650, 651.

Rape that cannot be avoided without personal sin is not the fault of the one who suffers it. VII, 36.

The sweetness of God’s grace should be sought so that the sweetness of iniquity may be despised. V, 831. Love of temporal things is overcome only by some sweetness of eternal things. I, 1190. God gives sweetness so that we may truly do good well—that is, not through fear of carnal evil but through delight in spiritual good. IV, 1565, 1366. Unless the Lord first gives sweetness, our land will possess nothing but barrenness. V, 920. See Sweetness; Grace.

Subdeacons from Augustine’s monastery. V, 1577.

Cities put up for auction in Sulla’s victory. VII, 108.

Subigus, a god. VII, 188.

Let the person who wishes what is beneath him to be subjected to him be subjected to what is above him. IV, 1860.

The higher the eminence, the more dangerous it is. IV, 1778.

Subsana, in the diocese of Hippo. II, 229, 230.

[Col. 0619] Subscudines. VII, 474.

The things to which “to subsist” is properly understood to refer. VIII, 942.

What substance is. III, 610. Substance is what the ancients called nature. I, 1346. Any substance: first, it is; second, it is this or that; third, in what it is, it remains as far as it can. II, 76. Substance means being something. IV, 844. Whatever is no substance is absolutely nothing. IV, 844. Whether any substance can be reduced altogether to nothing is a very subtle question. VIII, 607. Two substances, one good and the other evil, according to the error of Mani. X, 1320. Two substances contrary to one another, a fiction of the Manichaeans. VIII, 182. Substances are contrary to one another not in themselves but through their qualities. X, 278. No substance is evil. I, 703. See Nature. “Substance” is improperly said of God. VIII, 942. For the Greeks, it is the same as “person” for us. VIII, 942. It is used for riches. IV, 844.

God delays coming to the aid of someone so that what comes to the aid may be sweet. IV, 855.

The solemnity of the martyr women of the suburbs. V, 1521.

Even one who possesses another’s property by a lawful succession is condemned if he coveted it. V, 72.

Successus from Abbir Germaniciana. IX, 211.

What *succinctoria* are. X, 467, 685, 784, 785. The first parents made themselves girdles from fig leaves, not garments. X, 467.

What Christ’s bloody sweat signified. IV, 1817, 1818.

Sufes. IX, 215.

Sufetula. IX, 215.

The sixty martyrs of Suffectani were killed so that Hercules might be restored to them. II, 191.

To desire sufficiency in a proper manner. II, 498.

For God, a good will is sufficient—nothing is easier. V, 444. God alone is sufficient for us. V, 1189, 1461. What can be sufficient for one to whom God is not sufficient? V, 366, 620. “One is enough: be enough for the One.” IV, 207.

Strangled animals. What the command not to eat strangled animals teaches. VIII, 265.

The pagans know that the intercessions of the righteous benefit other people. VII, 750. They will benefit certain people at the judgment. VII, 749.

The first suggestion is signified by the head of the serpent. IV, 1381. Suggestion is followed by delight, and delight by consent or resistance. IV, 1859, 1860. How suggestions mingle with human thoughts is unknown to human beings. III, 1786. Some suggestions are good and others evil. III, 1786. The demon’s suggestion occurs spiritually. III, 1786.

Sullecte. IX, 507, 528, 550.

Summanus, the god to whom the ancient Romans attributed nocturnal lightning. VII, 131.

The highest good is eternal life; the highest evil is eternal death. VII, 627. See Good; Blessedness.

Sumticuli. V, 1578.

Something is said to be “above our head” when we take the greatest care over it. III, 495.

What pride is. VII, 356, 420. Pride is love of one’s own excellence. III, 436; V, 1565. Pride is the desire to appear to be what one is not. III, 199. Pride delights in everything that belongs to it and is, as it were, private to it. II, 564, 568. Pride is swelling. V, 1676. No one would be proud unless he were empty; if he were full, he would not be inflated. IV, 1233. The first and greatest fault of swelling is to wish to use one’s power for one’s own ruin. III, 377. Pride does not wish to have a superior, not even God. IV, 1471. It imitates God perversely. VII, 639. Whoever loves to be sufficient for himself becomes less when he falls away from the one who truly suffices for him. VII, 422. Pride approaches nothingness. VII, 421.

The origin of pride. III, 203. Where pride arises from. X, 206. How we are tempted by it. I, 804. How secretly pride lies in wait. X, 264. Pride arising from earthly prosperity. V, 206. Riches especially bring pride with them. IV, 1769. A nest of pride is gathered in riches. V, 957. Pride is the worm of riches. V, 112, 215, 412. Arrogance tries to creep into great things. II, 881. Pride lies in wait for things that are still greater. VI, 413. A striking description of pride. I, 1184.

## Pride

Pride is the chief of all sins. I, 1286. The head of all evils. III, 1603, 1604. The source of evils. III, 436. The first sin. IV, 156, 687. A great offense, and the head and cause of all offenses. IV, 163. One of the three kinds of vices by which all sins are comprehended. IV, 115. Pride is the cause of all vices. X, 168. The beginning of every sin. I, 1184. How this is so. X, 263. Not every sin is pride. X, 263. Pride comes first among the vices. V, 1575. How great an evil pride is. IV, 709. Nothing is more monstrous than this vice. I, 929.

### Effects of pride

I, 1190; V, 1561. Through this vice apostasy from God occurred. IV, 163. The pride of the devil. IV, 709, 1623. [Col. 0620] Pride cast down the devil, and envy following afterward overturned the human being who was standing where the devil himself had fallen. X, 263. Pride was the beginning of Adam’s sin. VII, 420. Adam’s pride. IV, 895. Humanity would not have perished had pride not swollen up. V, 684. Pride causes a person who has been injured to want revenge. V, 684. Through pride we fell, so that we came to this mortality. IV, 353. Through pride a person perishes from the right way. X, 265. Pride was the cause of the Jews’ blindness. III, 1778, 1779, 1780. The Jews were blinded on account of their pride. IV, 1789. Pride is the source of idolatry. V, 1022. And of other sins. V, 1022. The mother of all heretics. III, 202; V, 280. It gives birth to schism. V, 280. It is the mother of the desire for contention and human praise. II, 92. Pride and envy are diabolical vices. III, 1229. Pride is the mother of envy. II, 561; IV, 1290; V, 783, 1561, 1365; VI, 413, 673. Envy is its companion. IV, 709.

Pride is the greatest obstacle to cleaving to God. VIII, 1031. Through pride one departs from God. X, 206. The foot of pride is said to be that by which we depart from God. IV, 354. In proportion to the pride of the human heart is its distance from God. IV, 1205. Through pride we departed from God; we cannot return to him except through humility. IV, 302. Pride alone moves the foot toward ruin. IV, 1608. Pride prevents faith in Christ. V, 656, 874. Pride drives a person into his own darkness. X, 206. Pride closes the ears of the heart. X, 618. Pride and charity have the same outward effects. III, 2040. Pride extinguishes charity. III, 1982. Pride prevents or does not allow a person to be Christ’s disciple. VII, 309. Whoever loves pride does not wish to belong to the body of the humble head. V, 1568. Pride, presuming upon empty greatness, does not allow a person to walk by the narrow way and enter through the narrow gate. IV, 1471. Through pride the medicine of mercy is rejected. I, 1286. Why pride is to be feared by virgins. VI, 426. Nothing hinders perfection so much as pride. IV, 709. Pride is the reason why obedience to justice has now become burdensome. X, 170. From the point where pride seeks to rise above others, it is forced into confinement. III, 436, 437. Pride is leaven corrupting the dough. IX, 86. Pride is called the chair of pestilence. IV, 67. Pride is called stupor. IV, 1935.

How dangerous the disease of pride is. V, 945. By the cup of pride death was offered and poured into us. VI, 416. The greatness of the weak is deceptive: when it has taken possession of the mind, by raising it up it casts it down, by inflating it empties it, and by stretching it out it scatters it. V, 1561. Victorious human pride deceives itself. X, 351. Pride is the head of the serpent. IV, 354. The head of the circuit of the ungodly. IV, 1810, 1811. The Apostle attacks human pride in the passage, “What do you have that you did not receive?” X, 967. Above all, one must keep watch against pride. X, 171. Every other iniquity is exercised in evil deeds so that they may be committed; pride, however, even lies in wait for good deeds so that they may perish. II, 960. The other vices are to be feared in sins, but pride is to be feared even in rightly performed deeds. II, 442; IV, 709; X, 262, 263, 265. Pride must be guarded against once the desire to please human beings has been overcome. VI, 26. Pride increases all the more as the other desires yield to it. X, 788. The more holy a person professes something to be, the more carefully that person should beware of being deceived by pride. VI, 428. Pride is the first sin and the last for those returning to God. IV, 156. The danger of pride. X, 753. Where that danger comes from. X, 752.

### By what medicine the swelling of pride is healed

IV, 1523. Not even the humility of mortality subdued the exaltation of the proud. IV, 1542. Human pride is reproved by the humility of God. VI, 283. Divine medicine against pride. X, 168. Christ heals our pride by his humility. III, 1604. By his humility he casts it down. VII, 301. By his humility he heals it. VIII, 1031. Because of the great sin of pride, God came in humility. IV, 163, 302. Do you wish to be exalted? Submit yourself to him who cannot be humbled. IV, 1946. Pride pressed humanity down so greatly that only divine humility could raise it up. V, 1004. God become human is a great medicine against pride. V, 487. What pride can be healed if it is not healed by the humility of the Son of God? VI, 297. Let humanity at last blush to be proud, for whose sake God became humble. IV, 163. Through pride we fell, and while lying there we swelled up still more. IV, 1523. God subdues our pride through the most contemptible creature. III, 1386. Pride is the reason why God heals some of his saints more slowly from certain vices. X, 170. In some cases he does not even assist his righteous ones to perfect righteousness, because they can still become elated. X, 200. God abandons a person for a while, lest that person become proud. X, 262. Why God does not quickly heal pride itself. X, 262. Although the first exaltation cast Satan himself down, nevertheless the supreme physician employed, from the angel of Satan, a healing though burdensome medicine against the vice of exaltation. X, 601. Pride is a poison that is cured only by poison. V, 893. From the place where the devil fell, he casts others down. V, 893. The unicorn signifies pride. III, 881. The pride of the Pharisee. IV, 265, 446, 447. Pride is the spirit of this world. X, 214. Let no one glory in a human being, and therefore not in himself either. VI, 282. How the pride by which one person places himself above another is to be subdued. VI, 82.

### The proud

A person is proud when his own spirit lives in him. IV, 1852. And when he follows his own spirit. IV, 1836. The mind is proud when it rejoices in itself as though it were its own good. II, 439. Why this is sinful. II, 442. In astonishing ways a person becomes more inflated by false humility than if he were openly proud. II, 642. In Scripture, the proud are called those who please themselves. VII, 421. The proud soul wishes to please in the sight of human beings. IV, 163. The proud person flatters; love rages. III, 2041. Every proud person, since he wishes to appear to be what he is not, is counterfeit. IV, 1624, 1625, 1811. A person is proud who wishes to be praised in himself. IV, 310. By praising yourself as good, you become evil: humility would have made you good, whereas pride makes you evil. IV, 193. To call oneself holy is not the pride of an arrogant person, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful. IV, 1084. The proud praise themselves, not God. IV, 1471. A person is proud who either does not confess his sins, or claims for himself the good things he appears to possess, or, even if he attributes the good things he does to God, nevertheless exalts himself above others who do not do them. IV, 1203. The proud person loves to defend his own opinion, not because it is true, but because it is his. I, 839. The proud have their hearts lifted up, but against the Lord. V, 168. The proud wish to be worshiped in place of Christ. V, 1023. The perverse disposition of the proud. I, 1285. The proud person is marked by a particular characteristic of sin. IV, 414. The fall of the proud: whence it comes. I, 701. The proud person falls by the very fact that he considers himself lofty. IV, 1204. Where you become proud of God’s gift, there you lose what you had received. V, 751. The proud devil held only the proud through pride. IV, 1126. Whoever the devil has made proud, he conquers. III, 2030. God will be higher above you in proportion as you are more exalted. IV, 1780. The proud person rises up; God plunges him down. IV, 1205. God is high; he does not dwell in you if you wish to be high. IV, 1186. From whoever stands at the summit, the water of grace runs off. IV, 1836. God draws near to the afflicted and the confessing person, having abandoned the proud. IV, 225, 265. Those who are not proud in their understanding are poor in God. IV, 1083. See Humility, Poor.

### How God resists the proud

IV, 1426. It is a rule of divine law that whoever exalts himself shall be humbled. IV, 266. Even human beings count resistance to the proud among praiseworthy actions. VII, 13. Christ tramples the heads of the proud. IV, 1210. What he gives to the humble, he takes away from the proud. IV, 194, 1796. Mysteries are hidden from the proud. V, 440. The proud person is rejected from Christ’s discipleship. V, 415. The proud person loses what the humble obtain. V, 108. Proud mortals ought to blush before the devil: for although he is proud, he is nevertheless immortal. V, 590. It is useful for the proud to be confined more tightly and more openly. X, 365. And to fall into manifest sin. VII, 422. The proud are weakened so that they may be perfected. III, 414. Nothing is so unworthy of mercy as a proud wretch. I, 1285. To the proud, Christ is a stone of stumbling. V, 920, 921, 922. The sacrament of Christ’s body is far from the hearts of the proud wise. II, 840. The proud are not healed by Christ. III, 1446, 1447. It had to be shown to a soul that exalts itself how badly created nature fares when it has departed from its maker. III, 432. A celibate person, lest he at some time become proud, ought to consider what he lacks, not what he possesses. V, 1565. Against proud celibates. V, 1567. A humble married person is better than a proud celibate. V, 1564. How one should not dine with the proud, with whom Christ nevertheless deigned to eat. IV, 1289.

The proud are compared with smoke. V, 440. Why they are compared with smoke. VIII, 198. The proud, defending their sins, compared with smoke. V, 153. The proud are called the body of the devil. IV, 1807. Although the proud are lofty, they vanish like smoke. IV, 1184. The proud are compared with lions. III, 361. The proud freeze and fall like snow. III, 875. The proud person killed by his own sword. V, 831. The proud are called giants. IV, 1116. False righteous people. IV, 1807. They are represented by mountains. IV, 1243, 1865. The proud are darkness. III, 874. They are signified by the ninety-nine sheep left in the desert and by the nine drachmas. III, 1344. The flies beneath which Pharaoh’s magicians failed signified the restlessness of the proud—that is, of the heretics. II, 219.

## Superfluous things

Something is superfluous if it neither benefits nor harms. III, 2118. “Superfluous things do no harm,” an axiom of jurists. VII, 133. Those who keep only what is necessary possess many superfluous things. IV, 1921, 1922. If we seek empty things, nothing is sufficient. IV, 1922. Superfluous things burden rather than support; they load rather than honor. V, 523. Superfluous things should be distributed to the poor. III, 1760. The superfluous possessions of the rich are the necessities of the poor. IV, 1922; V, 243, 413. When superfluous things are possessed, they are possessed as another’s property. IV, 1922. Not giving one’s superfluous possessions to the needy is akin to fraud. V, 1041. See to whom your superfluous possessions will remain, lest, while you preserve what will keep you alive, you gather what will cause you to die. V, 629. Superfluous things are signified by hair. III, 1760.

Where the word “creed” comes from. V, 1058, 1072. Why it was instituted. V, 1066. The creed of faith. VII, 532. The creed of faith is called a confession. VI, 276. Even those cut off from the Church possess the creed. V, 1232.

## Time

What time is. VII, 363, 364. What time is is a difficult question. I, 839. A most intricate riddle. I, 820. Time is extension—but of what? Of the mind, perhaps? I, 822. There was no time when God had not yet made anything. III, 174, 175. There was no time before the world. VII, 321. Before creation, times are sought in vain. III, 325. Time always existed in time, and yet it was created. VII, 364. The creation of time and of the world has one beginning. VII, 321, 322. Time is a creature. III, 223. When time began. III, 223. Time began together with heaven and earth. V, 25. There is no time without creation. I, 826; VII, 364. Whether there can be time in the movement of incorporeal creation. III, 223. Time cannot exist without some movements of creation. VIII, 684. What are now called times began from the movement of the stars. VII, 364. The movements of the sun, moon, and stars are not time. I, 820. Time is not the movement of a body. I, 821. Rather, it is what we use to measure the movement of bodies. I, 821. The measurement of time. I, 816. How time can be measured. I, 819, 822.

Past, present, and future time. I, 816. In every movement of creation there is past and future, but not present. III, 1680. Words of time are used indifferently, although eternity is understood to remain without time. VIII, 699. In the heavenly dwelling time does not revolve, because its inhabitant does not fall away. IV, 1918. Of the whole time in which we exist, we hold only a moment as present. IV, 976. Things enclosed by the end of time are to be regarded as completed. IV, 1143. Time both is and is not. IV, 419. The three times do not properly exist. I, 818. How the differences of time should be named. I, 818. Past times are praised; Christian times are blamed. VI, 702. How past and future time can be long or short. I, 816, 817. The swiftness of time. IV, 361.

How time and eternity are distinguished. VII, 321. Time cannot be coeternal with eternity. VII, 364. In what sense time is called eternal. III, 175. How eternal times are to be understood. VI, 84; VII, 365, 366. Times are not indeed eternal, yet they did not begin to exist in time. VIII, 922. Times imitate eternity. I, 1179. Time is, as it were, a footprint of eternity. III, 236. What finite and infinite time differ in. VII, 360. Infinite stretches of time before the world are not to be imagined. VII, 320.

God governs times. VII, 139. The order of times [Col. 0626] is without time in the wisdom of God. VIII, 850. Phegous taught that times should be observed by months and years. VII, 562, 563. Superstitious observation of times was very common in Augustine’s day. III, 2130. How dangerous it is to the soul. III, 2130. What observation of times is blameworthy or harmless. II, 210. Those who observe times and days are reproved. IV, 456. One time is appointed for promising and another for fulfilling what has been promised. IV, 1445. Time, in relation to the order of human conduct, is fourfold: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and in peace. VI, 52. Time divided into three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. VIII, 892; IV, 1362. The five divisions of time. VI, 314. The six ages of the world. IV, 1182. The Pelagian division of time. X, 569. This is the fullness of time, when the Son of God came to teach contempt for temporal things. IV, 922. The two times of Christ: humility and glory. IV, 1461. Christian times. V, 505, 622. The two times of the Church: testing and crowning. V, 96. Here is the time of sorrow because of our sins, and afterward the time of joy because of the grace of the Savior. V, 1182. The time of sorrow and the time of joy are both represented by the forty days before Easter and the fifty days after Easter. V, 1184. Time is twofold: the time of mercy and the time of judgment. IV, 1282; V, 127. The time of faith and hope. V, 236. The opportune time is the time of grace. IV, 269. The time of good pleasure is the time of mercy. IV, 852. Some unjustly blame the times as though they were evil. VII, 78. Where evil times come from and how they are to be endured. V, 498. Evil times are made only by evil people. V, 1416. If people are not burdensome to themselves, to whom are evil times burdensome? V, 909. People always think the times are evil because of what they themselves do. V, 168. We ourselves are the times: let us live well, and the times are good. V, 498. What it means to redeem the time. V, 122, 910. Saint John used “hour” for “time.” II, 910. Time must not be occupied with curious questions about the world, but devoted to better things. II, 75.

## Temporal persons

X, 942. Temporal persons are those who do not remain in obedience to the end. X, 1029, 1030.

Temporal things are loved more before they are possessed, but become cheap when they arrive. III, 35. Temporal things do not satisfy the soul, whose true and certain dwelling is eternity. III, 35. Temporal goods both are and are not. IV, 1686. Temporal things have nothing except “it will be” and “it was”; what in them is future, when it arrives, immediately becomes past; it is awaited with desire and lost with grief. IV, 122. To take pleasure in temporal things, when they cannot be held, is wretched. IV, 1488. Whoever clings in heart to the Lord holds earthly things as though they were hairs. IV, 605. Temporal things must be relinquished in spirit. V, 997. The vanity of temporal things. V, 861. Temporal things, when desired, blaze up; when obtained, become cheap; when lost, vanish. V, 861. God often gives temporal things even to the wicked, so that they may learn from him to seek some other good. IV, 611. How temporal things are to be requested from God. IV, 624. Temporal things are given—and given by God himself, not by demons. IV, 327, 346, 931, 932, 1612, 1686. Those who seem to wish to worship God for eternal things and the devil for temporal things are rebuked. IV, 456. Whether God gives temporal things, takes them away, or does not give them, he is equally to be worshiped. V, 207. God mercifully takes temporal things away from those who abuse them. V, 203. He mercifully does not give them to those who would abuse them. V, 204. Those who place temporal things before eternal things clothe God’s benefits in reverse order. IV, 1868, 1869. Temporal things must be despised for the sake of eternal things. II, 529. The just and dutiful, and in its own sphere more peaceful and tranquil, administration of temporal affairs produces merit for receiving eternal things. II, 81. Those devoted to temporal things go around as though fastened to a wheel; they do not enter into truth because they do not love eternity. IV, 245. Some good must also be done through temporal things themselves. IV, 605. Those who know the name of God should cease to hope in and love temporal things. IV, 122. Temporal things therefore confer true happiness on no one, because they do not extinguish insatiable desire. IV, 1411. See Goods. It is not those who use temporal things who will perish, but those who prefer them to God. IV, 1606. When what has been made begins to perish, where will the lover of time be, who has lost eternity? V, 236. To envy temporal goods in others is characteristic of hired servants. III, 1405. See Earthly things, Transitory things.

Tenax, of Horreis Cesiae. IX, 235.

What darkness is. I, 826. Darkness is nothing other than the absence of light. VIII, 195, 197. Or air lacking light. VII, 326. There is no particular nature of darkness. IV, 109. Darkness is perceived only by comparison with light. III, 2071. Darkness is not corporeal. VIII, 195. God did not make darkness. III, 229. Yet he ordered it. IV, 108. Darkness has its order from God. III, 229. From when darkness began to exist. VIII, 609. Darkness was over the abyss. I, 818. The separation of darkness and light. VII, 332. What darkness God approved in the creation of the world. VII, 332. Darkness can produce nothing. VIII, 195, 197. The race and land of darkness: a delirium of the Manichaeans. VIII, 184. The five caves of the race of darkness. VIII, 186. The Manichaean delirium concerning the war against [Col. 0627] the race of darkness. VIII, 210. The fable of God’s war with the race of darkness is shown to be absurd. VIII, 244. The name “darkness” can signify nothingness. III, 240.

What the outer darkness is. IV, 94. The outer darkness and the binding of hands and feet. III, 168. For unbelieving human beings, the outer darkness is the devil and his angels. II, 562. The outer darkness is the punitive fellowship of the devil and his angels. II, 562. The outer darkness is bodily punishment. II, 562. At the end of the age God punishes the wicked with eternal darkness. IV, 998. Darkness belongs to the old human being, light to the new. III, 1985. What darknesses are to be feared. III, 1657. Wretched darkness in the human mind. X, 270. The darknesses of sins are twofold. IV, 1793. The name “darkness” signifies sins. IV, 108, 1195; X, 129. All the unrighteous and unbelieving. IV, 325, 1766, 1858. The darkness of sin exists by will, not by nature. IV, 1858. Those who are darkness today will be light tomorrow, if they wish. IV, 1195. Unbelieving people are darkness; converted through faith to God, they become light. II, 562. Darkness, a symbol of ignorance. IV, 328.

What it means to tempt God. VII, 498. So that we may not seem to tempt God, we must use our own diligence. VI, 574. Why God permitted Adam to be tempted and fall. VII, 435, 436. The temptation of the first parents explained allegorically. III, 208 and following. It is not permitted to tempt God. III, 574. A person ought not to tempt God when he has something he can do. VIII, 423.

Why human temptation is permitted. III, 431, 432.

Temptation is human life upon earth. V, 1050, 1051. Temptation is twofold: one of seduction or deception, the other of testing. III, 112, 113, 1708; V, 390, 452. One temptation leads to sin; another tests faith. V, 453. God’s temptation is a test, not a seduction to sin. III, 562, 616. In the sense of seductive temptation, the tempter is understood to be none other than the devil; in the sense of testing, God tempts. II, 948. How God leads into temptation. III, 1282. God tempts in order to teach; the devil tempts in order to deceive. V, 29. God does not tempt in order to know, but in order to make known. III, 616, 1282, 1708. Not so that he himself may learn, but so that he may disclose what lies hidden in a human being. V, 28, 29. The questioning of temptation reveals to each person the gifts of God that he possesses within himself. VI, 422, 424. A person is spared in that his weakness is not tested by temptation. VI, 424. Why and how temptations occur through Satan. III, 1284. No one is tempted unless God permits it. IV, 1292, 1382, 1383. A comparison is given. IV, 1384. Why God permitted temptations. VII, 670; VIII, 586. God seems to rage against those whom he permits to be tempted. IV, 796, 797. Those who are tempted are sometimes handed over, because of a hidden merit of their own, into the hands of the tempter. IV, 1292. God permits temptation so that the person may be tested and the devil conquered. IV, 1150. The devil is permitted to tempt according to measure. IV, 743, 1223. The devil is permitted to tempt only as much as benefits you, so that you may be exercised and tested. IV, 744. The devil tempts only what is ruled within you by the flesh. IV, 1858. In the devil’s trap there is error or desire by which he entices, and terror by which he breaks and carries away. IV, 236. The enemy afflicts us with daily temptations, introducing either something we may love wrongly or something we may fear wrongly. IV, 477. The tempter has two doors: desire and fear. V, 200, 201; VI, 348. Temptations arise from fear or desire. X, 152. The temptation of fear is threefold. III, 1332. Temptation through ignorance and weakness. X, 151.
