In every temptation two loves struggle with one another. V, 1512. The devil tempts not only by the assault of adversity but also by the seduction of prosperity. IV, 782, 797; IX, 720. There are two temptations: in prosperity and in adversity. III, 1492. Temptations arising from calamities have no power over us if temptations arising from pleasant circumstances have no power over us. III, 1286. Temptation is twofold: either the hope of obtaining a temporal advantage or the fear of losing one. III, 1306. A dangerous temptation occurs when we see the wicked flourishing and the good suffering. IV, 190. The devil’s temptations are three: to seduce by bad example; to break the spirit through human reproaches and the slander of evil tongues; and to persuade us to form judgments and malicious suspicions about our brothers. II, 270. Four kinds of temptations. IV, 1421. The first temptation is that of error and hunger. IV, 1421. The second is difficulty. IV, 1421. The third is weariness and disgust. IV, 1422. The fourth is anxiety concerning the dangers facing the Church. IV, 1422. Three kinds of temptations from the world: through pleasures, through displays, and through curiosity. VI, 294. In Christ it was shown that a threefold temptation must be avoided: that of pleasure, pride, and curiosity. III, 153. Augustine’s struggle against those temptations. I, 796. Temptation through Pagans, Jews, and heretics, but especially through bad Christians. VI, 343, 347. The storm of temptation is greatest when, defeated by desire, a person has the absent Lord. V, 476. Behold, the whole of human life is temptation, since a person is tempted even where he is adapting himself, as far as he can, to the likeness of heavenly life. II, 353. Three temptations of the spiritual life. III, 876. Temptation is twofold: to be esteemed by people and to be despised. III, 76, 77. The Apostles lacked neither. III, 76, 77. The temptations of demons arise from envy. VIII, 592, 599. The devil’s temptation vanishes unless the person being tempted [Col. 0628] gives him an opportunity. V, 29. Demons would not tempt human beings if they could perceive in them the inward appearance of the virtues. III, 467.

Temptations must be proclaimed to one approaching the service of God. V, 275. The baptized are not without temptation. V, 1555. No place here is free from the devil’s snares. II, 188. To be free from temptation is impossible in this life. III, 1284, 1285. After the remission of sins, we still remain amid the dangers of temptations. IV, 1319. He allowed himself to be tempted, as Emperor, in order to teach the soldier to fight. V, 334. In order to teach resistance to the tempter. V, 1049, 1291. The Lord’s temptation was manifold. V, 1291. Christ’s temptation was threefold, because of the three kinds of vice: the pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity. IV, 116. Christ was tempted so that the Christian might not be conquered by the tempter. IV, 1159. In the devil’s trap there is error or desire by which he entices, and terror by which he breaks and carries away; by both means he tempted the Lord—by desire in the desert, by terror in the Passion. IV, 236. In Christ the faithful person was tempted, and in Christ he conquered the devil. IV, 724. Whoever belongs to Christ is assailed by various temptations. IV, 758.

Not every temptation is to be blamed. VII, 510. Temptation is not useless. VII, 636. Temptation is twofold: harmful and beneficial. X, 1000. Temptation is beneficial. VII, 510. The usefulness of temptations. IV, 1223. In temptation what sort of person one is becomes apparent. III, 1730. In it a person comes to know himself. III, 289, 870, 871; IV, 355, 647. Temptation generally does not make a sinner but exposes him. V, 697. A person does not know himself unless he learns himself in temptation. V, 29. Temptation is necessary for the just. II, 856. It is necessary either to perfect, confirm, or test virtue. VIII, 411. Temptation is like an arena for combat. III, 832. Through temptation virtue is tested and exercised. III, 432. Our progress takes place through our temptation. IV, 724. Whoever is not tempted is not tested; whoever is not tested does not advance. IV, 870. How we are purified through temptation. V, 120. Temptations are like fire to straw for the wicked, but like fire to gold for the good. IV, 1375. Temptation is the fire that tests the work of each person in this life. VI, 155. The wind of temptation increases the fire rather than extinguishing it. V, 580. When the fire of temptation finds gold rather than straw, it removes the dirt but does not turn it into ashes. V, 569. A kind of martyrdom’s struggle occurs in daily temptations. V, 1439. It is better to be tempted and tested than to be rejected without having been tempted. IV, 1871. In this age we must always be instructed through temptations and tribulations. IV, 648. It is a more glorious crown not to have consented when tempted than not to have been able to be tempted. III, 432. Those who rejoice that they have progressed so far should not think, as human beings, that they can no longer be tempted. II, 992. The enemy does not cease and does not die except in the resurrection of the dead. IV, 1940. In the homeland there will be no temptation. II, 893.

The danger and burden of temptations. IV, 1940. Temptations are light when they do not press so hard as to compel; they are grave when they insist and weigh heavily. IV, 1154. In temptation suggestion comes first, pleasure follows, and finally consent or resistance. IV, 1859. It is one thing to take pleasure in suggestions and another to consent to them. IV, 1319. Do not converse with temptations. IV, 1774. Whoever conquers temptation does not extinguish desire. IV, 1860. Once temptation has been overcome, some tickling of pleasure nevertheless remains. IV, 1860. In temptations, the man, the woman, and the serpent are found in a certain sense. VIII, 1007. It is one thing to be tempted and another to be led into temptation. III, 1282, 1284. What it means to enter into temptation. X, 887. To enter into temptation is to depart from faith. V, 655. Why a person sometimes yields to temptation. X, 151. How one yields. III, 207, 208, 210. How one does not yield. III, 1284, 1285.

How Christ resisted temptations. III, 1996, 1997. How we should resist. III, 1996, 1997. What should regularly be done in temptation. III, 1467, 1770; V, 424. What is to be done when everything fails. V, 476. When the storm of temptations rages, faith must be awakened, like Christ sleeping in the boat. V, 240, 1602. The remedy for temptations is faith in the crucified one. V, 730. Temptation diminishes to the extent that faith increases. V, 655. The words and prayers of a person strengthening himself in faith against temptations. IV, 197. We do not know which temptations we can resist and which we cannot. I, 782. The saints conquer temptations by praying to God. VII, 299. In spiritual conflict we must hope for and request God’s help—not so that we do nothing, but so that, helped by him, we cooperate. III, 761. Without grace, the will is insufficient to conquer temptations. X, 887. We cannot overcome temptations through the choice of the will without God’s help. IV, 1142. Both grace and free will are necessary for conquering temptations. X, 887. Whoever conquers temptations does not conquer by himself, but God, who is in him, conquers. IV, 1643. In temptation God takes hold of a person so that he may not fall; rescues him so that he may not remain trapped; protects him so that he may not be struck. IV, 1862. When we are tempted, without doubt we are also consoled. IV, 1226. In temptations we must ask God for the virtue of self-control, so that enticing things may not seize us, and for endurance, so that hard things may not break us. V, 139. Whoever has already been cast down by fear of temptations must be raised up by God’s promised help. V, 276. Whoever denies that [Col. 0629] we ought to pray not to enter into temptation is plainly to be anathematized. X, 317, 318. Who would deny this? X, 317, 318. To be rescued from the temptations of this life is a great benefit of God. X, 981. To be tempted and not to be led into temptation is not evil, but rather good. X, 1000. Not being led into temptation is a gift of God. X, 1000. Not entering into temptation is not within the power of one’s own will without God’s help. X, 1293. The greatest temptation is to attribute the victory of conscience to one’s own will without God’s help. X, 1294. “Do not lead us into temptation” was twisted by Pelagius into a perverse meaning. II, 773. The strongest weapons against temptations are desires for eternal life. IV, 1774. Whoever conquers the flesh will immediately conquer the devil. IV, 1858. When temptation is brought upon someone, he should fast. V, 1048.

What human temptation is. III, 1284. Temptation signified by the wind. IV, 328. Temptation comes like a river; one must stand upon the rock. IV, 654.

The tempter is not conquered unless he is despised. V, 685. Christ taught us by his own example what we should answer the tempter. V, 685. The tempter does not cease knocking in order to break in; if he finds the door closed, he passes on. IV, 1834.

The terebinth exudes a medicinal tear. III, 792.

Terentianus. VII, 178. The poet Terentianus Maurus. VIII, 77.

A certain Terentius found Pompilius’s books by praying. VII, 222.

The poet Terentius, of African origin. VII, 57, note (b). Terentius was assisted by Scipio and Laelius in writing his plays. VII, 57, note (b). A passage of Terentius. II, 315, 802. Terentius’s advice given to a wretched man, so that he would not be more wretched. VIII, 1021.

The battle of the three pairs of brothers. VII, 89.

Terminus, the god of the Romans. VII, 135, 168. The boundaries of Roman affairs belong to Terminus, the Roman god. VII, 200. The sacred Terminalia, customarily celebrated in February. VII, 200.

The number three signifies the perfection of justice. III, 1261.

Earth is called a goddess because the part of the world-soul that is god permeates it. VII, 211, 212. Earth is represented under various symbols. VII, 213, 214. Earth has four names because of its fourfold power. VII, 213. To divide the earth among two or more gods is ridiculous. VII, 212, 213. Earth is called the mother of the gods. VII, 120. They wish Earth, Ceres, and Vesta to be one and the same. VII, 120. They think Earth, Tellus, and Tellumo to be different. VII, 120. The Manichaeans describe the land of light as cut off from the land of the race of darkness. VIII, 220. What shape they imagined the land of light and the land of darkness to have. VIII, 188. The shape of the land of light is more disgraceful. VIII, 188. Against the Manichaeans it is shown that the land of light is corporeal, if it is joined to the land of darkness. VIII, 188. Whatever kind of union the Manichaeans imagine between the land of light and the land of darkness, it can only be deformed and absurd. VIII, 191. The Manichaeans are shown that the land of darkness is not the supreme evil. VIII, 193, 195, 197. The Manichaeans wrongly said that the earth was coeternal with God. VIII, 532. The Manichaean delirium concerning an earth coeternal with God is refuted. VIII, 187. The Manichaean delirium concerning the five natures of the pestilential earth is refuted. VIII, 194, 195.

The globe of the earth is signified in the name of Adam. IV, 1236. When the earth was created. III, 256. Whether the earth was founded upon water. III, 264. How it was founded upon water. IV, 1759, 1760. Earth is higher than water. III, 583, 750. Earth is suspended upon nothing. VII, 391. That the earth possesses a certain unity, numbers, and order. I, 1192. The accursed earth producing thorns reminds human beings to turn away from sins and turn toward God’s commands. III, 181. The globe of the earth is, in a certain sense, the greatest island. II, 923. In the course of discussion we say that the earth is contained in a square figure. II, 69. How the earth was divided in the days of Peleg. III, 552. The earth is divided into three parts. VII, 497. The earth was divided by the diversity of languages. VII, 488. “Earth” is understood under the name of the lower heaven. III, 336. “Earth” is used for water. III, 614, 750. It is used for the weak part of the world. III, 614. It is used for the whole weak region of the world. IV, 1945.

Why it is called the promised land. X, 328. How extensive was the promise of the land made to Abraham. III, 555. The boundaries of the promised land. III, 787. The land flowing with milk and honey. V, 167. What the promised land signifies, and why it is called the land of Canaan. IV, 1394. Holy earth brought from Jerusalem is held in veneration. VII, 764. The land of the living and the land of the dying. V, 265. One is the land of the living, another the land of the dying: the latter will receive the dead whom it nourished alive. IV, 390, 1888. The land of the living can be understood as the body of those who rise again. V, 1420. This land is not the region of blessed life. V, 1107. The land of God, the heavenly homeland. IV, 144. Earth itself, by analogy, is the sea. IV, 981. “Earth” is used for life. IV, 390, 1811.

By the name “earth,” human beings are signified. III, 489, 497, 501, 506, 707. Likewise, the carnal in the Church. III, 264; V, 380. And sinful souls. III, 1256; IV, 136. The lower part of the human being. IV, 71. Earth, our flesh. IV, 391; V, 380, 388, 391, [Col. 0630] 401. Earth, the enemies of the Church. V, 388, 394. The lower parts of the earth, earthly desires. IV, 759. What the forgotten earth is. IV, 1117. Earth signifies the faith of little ones. III, 264. And stability in God. IV, 68. To judge the earth. V, 107. In what manner it is permissible to adore the earth. IV, 1264. In comparison with invisible creation, everything visible is called earth. III, 223. The earth is the temple of the whole world. VII, 248. The land of Tob, that is, the excellent land. III, 818.

Great earthquakes in the East and in Africa. V, 136.

Apuleius said that all earthly things undergo changes, transformations, and destruction. VII, 113. The need for earthly things troubles the soul. III, 2073. No one here is so perfect that he does not experience the inclination of mortal flesh toward earthly things. IV, 1525. Those who receive the Holy Spirit despise earthly things. X, 486. The condition of earthly things cannot in any way be equated with heavenly things. II, 1059. God sometimes grants temporal things beneficially and sometimes withdraws them beneficially. II, 575. If God gave earthly things as something great, he would not give them to the wicked. IV, 932. It is useful to seek even earthly goods from the one true God alone. VII, 302. The enemy would at least like to persuade us to worship God for heavenly things and the devil himself for earthly things. IV, 932. We must not cling to earthly things, even though God grants them. IV, 932. We must not cling to earthly things if we wish to see God, who is seen by the pure in heart. IV, 84. Everyone who desires earthly things against his own salvation is beneath the earth. IV, 759. Love of earthly things is birdlime for spiritual wings. V, 646. How the children of wisdom should use earthly things. III, 1337. Earthly goods ought to be subject, not pre-eminent; to follow, not to lead. II, 670. Earthly things are smoke. IV, 392. Love of earthly possession is the cause of discord. V, 1591. See Temporal things.

Those born of the earth are called sinners. IV, 544.

God terrifies from every side because he does not wish to find people whom he must condemn. V, 137.

Fear of the last day gives birth to security. IV, 1915. The terrors and blandishments of the world against Christ’s soldiers. V, 1256.

Tertullian. VII, 193, 194. An acute man. III, 427. He brought to light the heresies of the Novatians and Cataphrygians. VI, 433. He was the most eloquent supporter of those heretics. VI, 434. He maintained that God, like the soul, is corporeal. II, 861; X, 499. Tertullian’s error concerning the soul. III, 427. Tertullian held that souls are bodies. II, 861. He condemned second marriages. VIII, 657. How Tertullian became a heretic. VIII, 47. His writings were composed with great eloquence. VIII, 46.

The Tertullianists, heretics. VIII, 46. Their doctrines. VIII, 46. The very few Tertullianists who remained in the city of Carthage passed over to the Catholic Church and handed over their basilica to it. VIII, 46.

Tertullus, bishop of Abitina. IV, 381.

The Tessarescaedecatites, heretics. VIII, 31.

Clay is soft before the fire and hard after the fire: a figure of Christ, despised before his Passion and honored after his Passion. IV, 175.

Scripture calls a pact a “testament.” III, 491, 493, 539. “Testament” is used for every pact and agreement. IV, 1052. The difference between a divine and a human testament. IV, 395. Two Testaments. V, 36. Why one is called Old and the other New Testament. X, 221, 222, 597. Both Testaments were hidden before Moses; the Old was made manifest by Moses, in which the New was concealed. IX, 122. The Old Testament was revealed through Moses. X, 596. The New Testament is older than the Old, but was revealed later. X, 592. The various names of the Old Testament. X, 595. What the Apostle calls by the name of the Old Testament. I, 632. The name “Old Testament” is used in two ways. X, 327. One thing is properly the Old Testament, another is the Instrument. X, 595. All the canonical Scriptures administered before the Lord’s incarnation are reckoned under the name of the Old Testament. X, 327, 328. To what extent the books of the Old Testament are already useful. VIII, 237, 238; X, 138. The Old Testament is useful for convicting even the Gentiles. VIII, 328. The books of the Old Testament belong to Christians, and its precepts are better fulfilled through them. VIII, 52. Why, in the reading of the Old Testament, a veil is said to have been placed. X, 219. The Old Testament, the oldness of the letter, and the letter that kills signify the same thing. X, 595. In reading the Old Testament, the Catholic Church can in no way be convicted of error. VIII, 73. What Augustine thought concerning the Scriptures of the Old Testament and their authors. VIII, 73. The authority of the Old Testament is now retained not for imitation of Jewish servitude but as testimony to Christian freedom. VIII, 240, 243. Cerdon rejects the Old Testament. VIII, 29. The Severians reject it. VIII, 30. Marcion, Manichaeus, and others deny that the Old Testament is from the good, supreme, and true God. X, 328, 329. The Old Testament is from God. X, 594. In the Old Testament there are many things that offend the minds of the ignorant and those negligent of themselves. VIII, 67. Few are able to defend those things in popular [Col. 0631] fashion, and who those people are. VIII, 67. What seems perverse to the impious who do not understand either Testament is believed to be upright, though concealed, by the pious who do not understand. VIII, 408. What the Manichaeans object to in the books of the Old Testament. VIII, 73. Faustus thought that the Old Testament should be rejected for two reasons. VIII, 217. This is refuted. VIII, 217. What Faustus objects against God from the Old Testament, a Pagan could object against Christ from the New. VIII, 406. A Pagan who criticized certain things in Scripture as unworthy of God could be refuted by those same authors. VIII, 408. Certain things that Faustus criticizes in the old books as unworthy of God are explained. VIII, 406, 411, 412. The Manichaeans foolishly teach, and are refuted, that the testimonies of the Old Testament are useless before faith and superfluous after faith. VIII, 293. The Pelagian slander concerning the Old Testament and the ancient righteous. X, 591. The whole apparatus of the Old Testament foretold that Christ would come. VIII, 370. The people of the Old Testament were prophetic not only in speech but also in life. VIII, 219, 230. The same Scripture, which at that time exacted works signifying things, is now a witness to the things signified. VIII, 238.

Why the precepts of the Old and New Testaments differ. VIII, 449. In the Old Testament one must distinguish between precepts concerning the life to be lived and precepts concerning the life to be signified. VIII, 228. The precepts concerning the life to be signified were appropriate to that time in the Old Testament. VIII, 228, 236, 243, 244, 501, 504. The precepts concerning the life to be signified that were appropriate to the time of the Old Testament no longer need to be observed except spiritually. VIII, 237, 504. Christians observe the precepts concerning the life to be lived. VIII, 243. The Old Testament contains such precepts of justice as we are also now commanded to observe. X, 222, 594. The Old Testament is useful and has the greater authority for preaching Christ because it came to us through the Jews. VIII, 329. Why the vengeance of the Law was fiercer in the Old Testament. II, 660. The observances of the Old Testament could not be omitted without sin; now they are of no benefit. VIII, 243. The Manichaeans do not accept the Old Instrument and assert that the New has been corrupted. X, 1009. And falsified. VIII, 38, 501, 506, 514. In thinking that the New Testament has been corrupted and falsified, the Manichaeans contradict themselves. VIII, 506, 514. How it is proved that the New Testament has not been falsified. VIII, 506, 514. The Manichaeans accept from the New Testament only those things by which they think their heresy is assisted; they say that whatever opposes it has been falsified. VIII, 408. The Manichaeans cannot answer objections concerning the New Testament better than Catholics can answer objections concerning the Old. VIII, 244. How it is proved that the New Testament belongs to the Apostles. VIII, 509. The God of both Testaments is one and the same. VIII, 622, 623, 660, 661, 662, 663. The author of both Testaments is God. IV, 931. Through the Law he terrified; through the Gospel he healed those who had been converted. V, 28. The Manichaeans slanderously claimed that the two Testaments do not agree with one another. IV, 1893. But that they oppose one another. V, 23, 26. The Old and New Testaments are not contrary to one another. VIII, 622. The harmony of both Testaments. II, 218. The order of both is marvelous. I, 1334; III, 136. The New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New. III, 623, 633. The New was concealed in the Old like fruit in the root. IV, 914. As in the sediment of bodily sacraments. IV, 954. In the Old Testament there is the concealment of the New; in the New Testament there is the manifestation of the Old. V, 876, 1377; VI, 315; VII, 139, 140, 505. What was concealed in the Old Testament is now revealed in the New. X, 116. The New Testament was revealed in the Old. VIII, 623. What the Old Testament prefigured. VIII, 448. To those who understand it rightly, the Old Testament is a prophecy of the New. VIII, 302, 328. The New is the explanation of the Old. VIII, 451. The New Testament was foretold in the Old. I, 619. It was prefigured in the Old. IV, 1070, 1305; VIII, 448, 449, 623; X, 591. The testimonies of the Old Testament are proclamations of the New. VII, 662. The Old Testament is of no benefit except insofar as it bears witness to the New. VII, 539. In the New Testament the obscure things of the Old are revealed and the things foretold are fulfilled. VIII, 518. The grace of the New Testament was veiled in the Law and revealed in the Gospel. IV, 1416, 1856. The faith of the New Testament existed among the elect even when it was veiled; now, when it has been revealed, it does not exist among many who are called. IV, 996. In the Old Testament grace lay veiled and hidden; it was revealed in Christ’s Gospel through a most orderly arrangement of the times. X, 116, 217. This concealment was signified both by the veil of the temple and by Gideon’s fleece. X, 400. When the revelation of the New Testament took place. X, 597. A few of the ancients understood that the New Testament was prefigured for them. II, 540. These belonged to the New Testament. II, 540.

The distinction between the Old and New Testaments. II, 540; IV, 930; X, 220, 226, 227, 328. And their agreement. V, 37. The briefest and clearest difference between the two Testaments is fear and love. V, 207; VIII, 158. The law of the Old Testament is a ministry of death and condemnation, whereas the law of the New is a ministry [Col. 0632] of spirit and righteousness. X, 219. Fear prevails in the Old, love in the New. I, 1334. The New Testament belongs to charity. III, 2074. The Old belongs to fear. III, 2074. And to the old human being. III, 1636. It promised carnal things. III, 1636. The harmony of both Testaments lies in the commandment of charity. I, 1316, 1322, 1325. The promises and sacraments of the Old and New Testaments are different. III, 732. There are different promises of the Old Testament and of the New. IV, 327, 931, 1145, 1466, 1949. Only earthly happiness is openly promised in the Testament properly called Old. X, 328. Why that happiness was promised in it. X, 597. The Old Testament is so called because of its carnal promises. VII, 302. The Old Testament has temporal promises but spiritual meanings. V, 37. How the saints and spiritual men understood the promises of the Old Testament. VIII, 218. How the carnal men of that time understood them. VIII, 218. The promises of the Old Testament are predictions of the New. VIII, 218. Eternal and heavenly things are prefigured by the earthly and temporal promises of the Old Testament. X, 222. And were signified. VII, 139, 140. What is indicated by the temporal happiness of the Old Testament and the unhappiness of the New. VIII, 449. What is concealed in the Old Testament under the veil of earthly promises is revealed in the preaching of the New. X, 138. The New Testament is promised in the Old. X, 328. The promise of the New Testament made through Ezekiel. X, 1264, 1265, 1266, 1267, 1271. Why the Old Testament promised earthly goods, whereas the New promises heavenly goods. VIII, 162, 163. The New Testament does not remove the multiplication of earthly goods. VIII, 163. In the Old Testament the prefiguration of our possession is recognized; in the New Testament possession itself is held. VIII, 157. Everything that is done with us through the New Testament concerns nothing except the new inheritance of the new age. VII, 729. The distinction between the children of the Old and New Testaments. X, 594. The Old Testament gives birth to servants, the New to free people. VIII, 622. The two Testaments signify two lives and two hopes. VIII, 304. The holy men of the Old Testament had, in the New, hope of eternal salvation. VIII, 304. In the Old Testament some possessed future hope. IV, 351. The heir of the Old Testament. X, 328. In the Old Testament there were some heirs of the New. IV, 1466; X, 328. Who are the stewards and bearers of the Old Testament, and who are the heirs of the New. X, 591. What it means to belong to the New Testament. X, 228. Who belong to the New Testament and who to the Old. IX, 122; X, 593. Which of the ancients belong to the Old Testament. V, 37, 38. The saints of the Old Testament belong to the New. VIII, 456, 656; X, 591. Christians who serve God in hope of a carnal reward belong to the Old Testament. V, 32, 40. Under the Old Testament there were spiritual righteous people; under the New there are many carnal people. VIII, 623. Who is to be considered a person of the New Testament. V, 168. The “animal” people who belong to the Old Testament, if they die before becoming spiritual, are counted among the land of the living, preserved through the holiness of the sacrament. IX, 122. How both Testaments belong to the Israelites. VIII, 255.

The grace of the New Testament. II, 542. A book concerning the grace of the New Testament. II, 539. Through the grace of the New Testament, people learn—or ought to learn—to desire eternal life. II, 547. To what extent the promise of the kingdom of heaven does not belong to the Old Testament. X, 329. There is no mention of the New Testament in the ancient books except in Jeremiah. X, 221, 222. Christ is the mediator, seal, guarantor, witness, inheritance, and co-heir of the Testament. IV, 1130. The New Testament suffers injury if it is equated with the Old. X, 329. The New Testament must be preferred to the Old in dignity. VII, 662. The faith of the New Testament is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament. VIII, 258. The Old Testament compared with barley. III, 1594. Through the two Testaments, Old and New, the rule of discipline is handed down to us. I, 1334. Christ removed the extremely heavy yoke of the many observances of the Old Testament. V, 594. In the New Testament the sacrifice of praise succeeds the bloody victims of the Old Testament. II, 557. In the New Testament Christ wished discipline to be gentler. IV, 1413.

Testaments Two commend the mercy of God. III, 634. The Old Testament was signified in the earlier tablets. III, 653, 755, 756. The Law was given in stone tablets in the Old Testament, but in the New it is given in hearts. III, 753. The sign of the Old Testament: circumcision in concealed flesh; of the New: the cross on the unhidden forehead. V, 876. The two Testaments prefigured in Sarah and Hagar, Isaac and Ishmael. III, 566; IV, 302, 1603. In the two spies of Jericho. IX, 638. In the Holy Place and in the Holy of Holies. III, 635. And in the two cherubim of the ark. III, 634. The sign of the New Testament: the red heifer. III, 732. Repetition of the Law. III, 653. The Old Testament itself is also the law of Christ. III, 2145. Many things are called the Testaments of God, apart from those two great ones, the Old and the New. VII, 506. Which covenant of God did the newly born infant violate? [Col. 0633] X, 450. To acquiesce in the testimonies of both Testaments is to sleep between the two lots. IV, 823, 824.

The testaments of schismatics are invalidated by the laws of the emperors. V, 310. The Testament of peace. V, 310.

God wished to have human beings as witnesses, so that human beings might also have God as witness. III, 1979. The witnesses of God: the Martyrs. III, 1979. May that one be our witness by whose judgment we are crowned. III, 2021. The torture of witnesses for the purpose of seeking the truth. VII, 632, 633. The fact that false witnesses do not prevail is not evidence of great merit. V, 1506. One may believe or not believe human witnesses or testimonies, insofar as one considers how much weight they have, or do not have, for producing conviction. II, 598.

Testimony and law are two names for one and the same thing. IV, 987. The testimonies of God are those by which he deigns to prove to us how greatly he loves us. IV, 1515. With what disposition certain people search out the testimonies of the Lord. IV, 1503. A just judgment or true testimony must not be sold, although just advocacy and sound advice may be sold. II, 663. In many matters one must rely on human testimony. II, 598. Giving false testimony is forbidden. V, 71, 501, 631, 1506. No one may give false testimony against himself. VII, 34. How the prohibition against giving false testimony is to be understood. VI, 511. Neither promises nor threats ought to extort false testimony. V, 202, 220. False testimony against Christ, not only before his death but also after his resurrection. IV, 373.

Thabor is interpreted as “coming light.” IV, 1127.

Trabraca. IX, 217.

Thambei. IX, 237.

Thamugas. IX, 204. Thamugadi and Bagaï, the principal towns of the Donatists. IV, 177.

Tharassa. IX, 232.

Thasbalte, or Thasvalte. IX, 222.

Thagaste, the carnal homeland of Augustine. I, 677, 698; II, 473, 479. Where Augustine began to teach. I, 724.

The bridegroom’s chamber: the virgin’s womb. III, 1979.

Thales of Miletus, founder of the line of Ionic philosophers. VII, 225. He is said to have lived during the reign of Romulus. VII, 581. He was a natural philosopher. VII, 582. He thought water was the principle of all things. VII, 226, 582. He proved especially remarkable because he predicted eclipses of the sun and moon. VII, 226, 582. He committed his discussions to writing. VII, 226, 582.

Thamar is interpreted as “bitterness.” VIII, 456. Thamar means the same as “changing.” VIII, 457.

Thamna is interpreted as “failing” or “being deficient.” VIII, 457.

Terah, Abraham’s father, served foreign gods in Mesopotamia. VII, 492. Terah’s household suffered persecution from the Chaldeans on account of true piety. VII, 494. In Terah’s household the planting of the City of God was preserved. VII, 492. The generations of Terah. VII, 492. How many years Terah lived. VII, 494, 495.

Tharsis is interpreted as “humble command.” IV, 993, 1001. What Tharsis is. IV, 536, 537. Tarsus, Paul’s homeland. IV, 536. Whether Tarsus is Carthage. IV, 537.

Theasius, bishop. II, 273, 697, 759, 781.

Theasius, an old man. II, 697.

The theater. V, 1025. Why the theater was instituted. VII, 182. The curved form of the theater. VIII, 192. Theaters: caves of disgrace and public professions of wrongdoing. III, 1068. The disgracefulness of the theater. V, 1026. The evils of the theater. VI, 639. The theatrical crimes were instituted in honor of the gods whose crimes they were. VII, 121. The theatrical crowds. V, 1600. The Romans did not know theatrical arts for a long time. VII, 58. Scipio Nasica restrained the senate when it was attempting to construct the cavea of a theater. VII, 44, 45, 51. Those who frequent theaters are false Christians. VII, 46. The theatrical performers are to be separated from communion for as long as they perform. IX, App. 787.

Thebeste. IX, 220.

Thecla, a virgin. VI, 422, and Note (a). Thecla, already betrothed to a husband, was kindled by Paul’s preaching to love perpetual virginity. VIII, 492.

Theman is interpreted as “southerner” or “African.” VII, 589.

Themistocles replied that he did not know how to sing to the lyre, but that he did know how to make a great republic out of a small one. II, 438.

Theodorus. IX, 755. Theodorus, proconsul. IX, 530. Theodorus, outstanding in talent, eloquence, and wealth. I, 992. The book *On the Blessed Life* was written in reply to him. I, 959.

Theodorus of Heraclea. II, 286. He interpreted the Psalms. II, 262. He left commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians. II, 253.

Theodorus of Uzalis, bishop. IV, 380; IX, 507, 528, 550.

Theodorus, bearer of Augustine’s letters to Maximus. II, 404.

A certain Theodosius betrayed some Manichaeans. II, 1000.

Theodosius the Emperor. II, 400. Made partner in the empire by Gratian. VII, 171. Theodosius, consul for the third time. IX, 529. Consul for the eighth time. IX, 697. Theodosius fought against Eugenius more by prayer than by striking. VII, 172. A wind, fighting against the enemy from Theodosius’s side, by God’s power. VII, 172. Theodosius’s gentleness and moderation toward the children of his enemies. VII, 172. Theodosius’s faith and piety. VII, 172. Theodosius rejoiced more in being a member of the Church than in ruling on earth. VII, 173. Theodosius destroyed images of Jupiter. VII, 172. Theodosius’s repentance. V, 1710; VII, 173. Religious humility. VII, 173. Theodosius aided the suffering Church by laws against the impious. VII, 173. Theodosius’s law against heretics and schismatics. IX, 48. The elder Theodosius established a fine of ten pounds of gold for all heretics. IX, 524. Theodosius’s general law against heretics, by which they were fined ten pounds of gold. II, 804. Augustine considers this sufficient against the Donatists who were raging against the Church. II, 804.

The constitution of Theodosius and Honorius against the Pelagians. II, 927.

Theodotion, a Jew and blasphemer. II, 262. He translated Scripture from Hebrew into Greek. VII, 603. Note (b).

Theogenes of Hippo Regius. IX, 210. The memory of Theogenes. V, 1251.

Three theologies according to Varro: fabulous, natural, and civil. VII, 180, 192. Fabulous theology is adapted to the theater, physical theology to the world, and civil theology to the city. VII, 182. Fabulous theology is disgraceful. VII, 182, 183. The theatrical theology proclaims the crimes of the gods. VII, 223. Fabulous theology is unworthy of the gods. VII, 182, 186. It ought not to have been permitted to the populace. VII, 182, 186. Civil theology is more disgraceful than fabulous theology. VII, 185. It is more degraded than natural theology. VII, 199. Civil theology invited demons to possess human hearts. VII, 218. Civil theology is vicious, just like poetic theology. VII, 182. It indicates more criminal desires in the gods. VII, 223. Fabulous theology agrees with civil theology. VII, 187. Civil theology agrees with fabulous theology. VII, 183. Seneca criticized civil theology more forcefully than Varro criticized fabulous theology. VII, 190. Varro attempted to introduce natural theology. VII, 190. Civil theology was explained by Varro in sixteen volumes. VII, 193. This threefold theology—fabulous, physical, and civil—must yield to the philosophy of Plato. VII, 229.

Theologian-poets. VII, 572.

Theoprepia, a church belonging to the Donatists. II, 535.

**Θεοσέβεια** (*Theosebeia*, “godliness”). VIII, 1035; X, 211.

Therapius of Bulla. IX, 233.

The theriac remedy. V, 893.

**Θηριακή** (*Thēriakē*, “theriac”). X, 602.

The baths. VI, 330.

The treasure. To treasure up: what this means in Scripture. VIII, 621. How great are the heats of those who hoard treasures, and how empty their pretexts. V, 403. Treasure must be stored in heaven, not on earth. V, 403, 523, 1357, 1419, 1519. The treasures of God: God’s secret, from which he brings forth what corrects us. IV, 290. God’s treasure: one is found in mercy, another in wrath. IV, 1201. A false lover of his own treasures. V, 239. A faithful keeper. V, 239, 243. Carriers of treasure. V, 240. The good things of those treasures are to be desired, which all may possess with us without hardship. IV, 204. The place of our treasures and of our heart is heaven. IV, 1170. The treasure of the inner person. V, 147. Your treasure is your merit. IV, 387. The treasure of works, whether good or evil. V, 129, 130. The treasure of the poor is a good will. IV, 371.

Theurgy, the art of invoking the gods. VII, 286. Porphyry calls theurgy the conciliator of angels and gods. VII, 287. It is also a discipline for accomplishing both good and evil among gods and human beings. VII, 287. Theurgy is an invention of demons promising a false purification to souls. VII, 288. Porphyry wished theurgic purifications to be necessary for the spiritual soul and for other human beings apart from philosophers. VII, 305. What good was expected from theurgic purifications. VII, 305. Porphyry acknowledged that through theurgic art the soul could become immortal and eternal. VII, 305. Theurgy is a deceitful discipline full of error. VII, 305. Theurgy is to be feared either because of the dangers of the laws or because of the action itself. VII, 307.

Theurgists. VII, 294. Theurgists cannot purify the human spirit. VII, 305.

The church of Thiava. II, 291.

Thibaris. IX, 223.

Thimelic obscenity. VII, 186. Thimelic performers. VI, 330.

The Thimothean heretics. VIII, 50. Note 2.

Thomas became day. V, 1195. Thomas touched the man and confessed that he was God. III, 1980. The books of the Manichaeans are said to have claimed that the apostle Thomas took revenge on a certain man by whom he had been struck on the cheek. III, 1263. This is an apocryphal history concerning the apostle Thomas. VIII, 158, 161, 452.

Thomas, bishop. II, 759, 781.

Thorus, chaste with his wife [text uncertain]. IV, 1900.

**Θρησκεία** (*thrēskeia*, “religion” or “worship”). VII, 278.

[Col. 0635] Thubursicubure. IX, 368.

Thuccabori. IX, 212.

Thuriacus, or Thurimacus, the seventh king of the Sicyonians. VII, 562. The Sicyonians sacrifice at the tomb of Thuriacus. VII, 562.

Tibaga. IX, 697.

Romulus dedicated the Tiber as a god. VII, 190.

The Tiber was formerly called the Albula. III, 203, 378. The Tiber frozen solid. VII, 98. The overflowing of the Tiber. VII, 99.

Tibilis. II, 427.

The waters of Tibilis. VII, 766; IX, 511.

Tichonius, a Donatist. I, 613; IX, 33. Although he was a Donatist, he wrote against the Donatists. III, 81. On behalf of the Catholic Church. II, 342. He mentions living witnesses of what he wrote. II, 343. He separated himself from communion with the Africans, who were regarded as traitors. II, 342, 343. He taught that the sins of others do not defile one, and that Donatus’s own party had been corrupted by much leaven. IX, 80, 82. And that the wicked are to be tolerated among the good in unity for the sake of peace. IX, 96. Parmenianus wrote in reply against Tichonius. II, 342, 343. He also urges him to endure persecutions within Donatus’s party. IX, 105, 106. Tichonius acknowledged that the Church is spread throughout the whole world. IX, 34, 35. He was condemned by the council of the Donatists because he asserted the unity of the Church. IX, 35. Tichonius’s statement concerning the Donatists. IX, 73. In what Tichonius was mistaken. IX, 35. Why Tichonius is called a man of utterly absurd mind. III, 81. Tichonius composed a book of seven Rules. III, 81. These rules are examined. III, 81, 82, 83, 84, 611. Tichonius attributed too much to those rules, or keys. III, 81, 82. That book of Tichonius’s Rules must be read cautiously. III, 82. Tichonius’s view concerning the years of Israel’s servitude in Egypt. III, 611. Tichonius said that works are given to us by God on account of the merit of faith, but that faith itself is from us in such a way that it is not from God. III, 83.

Tigillus, an epithet of Jupiter. VII, 203.

Tigisa. IX, 510.

Tigisis, a city of Numidia. V, 293.

Tigisitana, bishop. See above, Secundus.

The Tigris. III, 203, 378.

Tilos, an island of India on which the trees are never stripped of their leaves. VII, 715.

Timasius. X, 247. At one time a disciple and admirer of Pelagius. X, 333, 347. Timasius, a servant of God. II, 479. A good servant of God and an honorable man. X, 347. Timasius and James, at Pelagius’s exhortation, renounced the world and lived continently. II, 767, 774. Timasius and James were recalled from the Pelagian error through Augustine’s work. II, 767, 774. Timasius and James sent Pelagius’s book to Augustine and received a reply from him. II, 767, 774, 816. The book *On Nature and Grace* was addressed to Timasius and James. II, 748. The letter of Timasius and James to Augustine after receiving the book *On Nature and Grace*. X, 347.

Timida. IX, 233.

To fear. Everything that can happen is prudently feared, even if it does not happen. IV, 1119. A person should not fear what he does not have the power to avoid. IV, 547. How much the body is feared. V, 879. A person has nothing to fear from another person. V, 427. Fear of God’s threats, contempt for human threats. V, 202. A Christian ought to fear nothing from enemies. IV, 1249, 1250. One must fear neither the north wind nor the seas, but God, their creator. IV, 1127. A mountain that does not fear is struck by lightning, so that a person who fears may be changed. IV, 1945. When you give discipline, you strike the earth so that the child may be frightened. IV, 1945. Do you wish to be feared by one lesser than you? Fear the greater. IV, 1762. God alone is to be feared. IV, 200, 291. Does a beast rage? Fear God. Does a person hate? Fear God. Does the devil attack you? Fear God. IV, 291. How God is to be feared. IV, 1262. No one fears God except one who is among the members of Christ. IV, 1679. Why we must work out our salvation with fear and trembling. IV, 1851. What the righteous have to fear. X, 262, 264. This is a time for fearing, not laughing, in this world. IV, 608, 1554. From the things one fears here, let each person infer what he ought to fear in the future. V, 880. When you recall God’s vengeance, fear. IV, 1748. There are two reasons for not fearing: hope in God or hardness of heart. IV, 650. Whoever has a sure, firm, and true hope in God fears no one. IV, 200. Fear ought to precede hope. IV, 1466. Fear is the flight of the soul. III, 1732; IV, 814. Fear and pain are two torturers of the soul, alternating in torment. V, 687. Fear and pain are the punishment of original sin. X, 1539. If no one had sinned, there would be no fear or pain in paradise. X, 1539. Epicureans and Stoics love to be without fear, but perversely. V, 1528. Fear arising from weakness of soul is not imputed. III, 792. Human fear prevailing over fear of God. VI, 699. Fear and desire are two doors through which the enemy enters and reigns. VI, 310. Fear and longing are two gates of the heart, to be closed to the devil and opened to Christ. IV, 1835. Empty fear and useful fear. V, 881. Fear exists in good and in evil. VII, 412, 413.

Two kinds of fear. III, 1849. Servile or penal fear, and chaste fear. III, 1708; IV, 155, 161, 992, 1534, 1680; V, 883, 1241; VI, 418. The distinction between chaste and unchaste fear. III, 2048, 2049. Servile fear. X, 236. Servile fear is the fear of burning with the devil; chaste fear is the fear of displeasing God. V, 883. Servile fear is afraid not to sin, but to burn. II, 594. The Law is not fulfilled through servile fear. IV, 281, 1167. Whoever does not kill because he fears being killed himself does not fulfill the commandment of justice. III, 2136. I dare to say: if you do not do evil because of fear of hell, I rejoice in your faith, but I still fear your wickedness. V, 965. Fear is compared with a wolf that does not dare seize its prey amid the barking of dogs. IV, 1190. Whoever performs a work of the Law from fear of punishment, not from love of justice, plainly does it unwillingly. IV, 1528. Those who obey the law through fear of punishment would prefer that there were nothing to fear. V, 1171. They would prefer that what is commanded did not exist. IV, 282. In fear, the will to do evil is held in check. IV, 281. Fear of punishment without charity does not prevent lust from ravaging the soul. I, 1337. Whoever does not desire something because of fear of punishment, I think, does desire it. V, 919. Just as a lion, robber, or wolf, when frightened, seizes nothing, yet is not changed at all. V, 965. Whoever abstains from the work of sin through fear of punishment, not through love of justice, is guilty in his will. X, 208. Whoever does not sin by willingness but by fear sins inwardly in the will itself. X, 558. If fear of punishment overcomes the pleasure of lust, the person is at least a transgressor in his will. X, 221. Fear compels a person to do in action what is permitted, while in his will he has something else—namely, he would prefer, if it were possible, that what is not permitted were permitted. X, 208, 236. One who fears punishment and does not love justice wishes to do what pleases him and not to have anything to fear. V, 792. In servile fear, although one believes in the Lord, one does not love justice but fears condemnation. X, 236. The person who does not keep the commandments out of love, but out of fear, does not keep them. X, 593. Through fear of punishment, a good action is not yet done well, nor is what appears in the deed accomplished in the heart. X, 586. Those who are restrained from sinning by fear of punishment do not yet love justice. IV, 1680, 1959. Innocence is produced not by fear of punishment but by love of justice. IV, 1190. Fear in which justice is not loved but punishment is feared is carnal, and with it the will to sin remains alive. IV, 1576. One who does not sin from fear of punishment vainly thinks himself victorious over sin. II, 593. He is an enemy of justice. II, 594. One who does not do evil from fear of punishment is not yet worthy of praise. V, 882. To act from fear rather than love belongs to one who has not yet been reconciled with his adversary. V, 81. To fear punishment is not the same as fearing God. III, 607. The demons confessed Christ to be the Son of God through fear, Peter through love: love is praised, fear condemned. V, 993. God is not worshiped through servile fear. IV, 996. Whoever still does good because he fears punishment does not love God; he is not yet among the children. V, 857.

Fear in the Old Testament is servile. IV, 1077. Fear belongs to the Old Testament. III, 623, 653. To act from fear, not love, belongs to the old person. V, 81. When something is done from fear of punishment without being referred to charity, it is not yet done as it ought to be done. VI, 288. See Law, Command, Precept.

Fear of punishment is not evil. V, 882. Whether it is sin. VI, 89. Fear of hell is good and useful, although it is not chaste. IV, 1682. God inserts useful fear. III, 1983. Fear is usefully employed to prevent wrongdoing. II, 186. The effect of fear. III, 39. Fear of punishment leads to love of justice. III, 1698. Fear drives away the habit of evil works and preserves a place for charity. II, 557. When people restrain themselves from sin through fear, a habit of justice arises, and what was hard begins to be loved. IV, 1680. Unless a person begins to worship God through fear, he will not arrive at love. IV, 1958. Do it—do it even from fear of punishment, if you cannot yet do it from love of justice; the mistress will come, and the slave will depart. V, 857. Whoever makes progress should rise from fear of God to wisdom. IV, 1599. Fear of God is the first step toward wisdom. III, 39; V, 1524. Just as those guided by love are better, so there are more people corrected by fear. II, 802. Fear must be driven out by charity, not by vanity. V, 1526. What a soul laboring under fear ought to do. X, 233. What must be done so that God may be feared. VI, 25. How charity is built from fear. VI, 316. Let fear be a tutor: let it not remain in you, but lead you to charity as to a teacher. V, 1533. Fear of punishment is a certain guardian and, as it were, a tutor of the Law. V, 882. Let it guard you and lead you to love. V, 882. Fear, as it were, prepares a place for charity. III, 2047. Fear of punishment is the servant of charity. V, 857. So that the devil may not possess your heart, let the servant go before in your heart and preserve a place for the mistress who is to come. V, 857. Christ was killed so that fear might be transformed into love. IV, 1167. Fear is medicine; charity is health. III, 2048. Charity casts out fear—but fear of temporal evils, not fear of the divine judgment at the end. VI, 418. Fear is excluded by charity. IV, 1534, 1681. Charity casts out servile fear. II, 559. Piety is begun through fear and perfected through charity. III, 136. Fear of God perfects sanctification. V, 269. Fear of God not only begins wisdom but perfects it. VI, 26. Through fear of God, empty fear must be driven away. V, 426. Fear of punishment departs to the extent that charity enters. V, 883. When charity has entered completely, there will be no fear. V, 883. Fear is not in charity. III, 655. Fear of God does not hinder love. V, 162. Servile fear of God and chaste fear: one is gradually to be expelled, the other is to remain. V, 1529. Charity does not expel chaste fear but takes it up. II, 559.

What chaste fear is. V, 1529; VII, 416. Chaste fear does not torment but makes the soul cling more tenaciously to that good which, if it abandons it, will cause it to fall. II, 561. How chaste fear remains forever and ever. VII, 416. Where fear is chaste, love does not perish through fear of God. IV, 1592. Chaste fear judges it a great punishment to be deprived of the light of justice. IV, 992, 993, 1682. Chaste fear comes from love. IV, 1682. Through chaste fear, charity fears to sin even if impunity follows. IV, 1576. Chaste fear hates sin itself as it hates hell. II, 594. Through servile fear one fears falling into the torment of punishment; through chaste fear, one fears losing the grace of a benefit. II, 558, 559, 562. Chaste fear is commanded even to those who, living by faith, are heirs of the New Testament. II, 559. How frequently fear of God is commended in Scripture. V, 1524. True strength is acquired through fear of God. V, 1526. What chaste fear is, explained by an analogy. IV, 1534, 1681. How one may determine what kind of fear a person has, servile or chaste. IV, 1681. Holy fear is the cross of which the Lord says, “Take up your cross.” III, 2142. The Prophet desires to be crucified with holy fear. III, 2142. Wounds are the friends of the fear of God. III, 2048. Let hope accompany fear of the Lord. IV, 1912, 1913. Fear has narrowness; love has breadth. V, 158. Fear of punishment has torment and is not in charity. II, 594. Fear of God, who is present everywhere, is commended. V, 736. Fear of God is a great protection for those advancing toward salvation. IV, 87. The spirit of fear is a great gift of God. X, 904. What spirit of fear is the gift of God. X, 905. How being driven by fear differs from being driven by love. V, 792, 793.

Timothy, a Carthaginian deacon. II, 1082. He carried Augustine’s letter to Severus. II, 419.

Timothy was ordained subdeacon at Subsanna’s place against Augustine’s advice. II, 230. What was done in his case is recounted and excused. II, 229, 230. Timothy had served in the office of lector at Subsanna, Turres, Cizan, and Verbalis. II, 232.

Tinisa. IX, 230.

The war of the Titans. VII, 137.

The bells on the priestly garment signify the conduct of the priest. III, 637.

The Titiana estate. II, 180.

Titianus, an advocate. IX, 549, 550. He requests that Felicianus and Praetextatus be expelled from the places they occupy. IX, 529, 551, 574. The words of the petition. IX, 574. Titianus accused Felicianus and Praetextatus of the entire conspiracy against Primianus. II, 413.

The title of a psalm introduces one into its meaning. V, 176.

The Israelites established titles, not in order to worship them as gods, but so that they might signify something through them. III, 573.

Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, joined to Romulus as partner in the Roman kingdom. VII, 89.

Titus Latinius, deprived of his son and afflicted with illness because he had not obeyed the command of the gods concerning the renewal of the scenic games. VII, 238. The dream of Titus Latinius. VII, 244.

Blind Tobias preceded his son with the foot of charity. I, 801. How Tobias was not blind in his blindness. V, 547. Tobias’s son held his father’s hand so that he could walk, but his father taught him the way so that he might live. IV, 1251.

Many examples of tolerating the wicked. II, 171, 178. The wicked must now be tolerated. V, 298. We ought to strive for this: to tolerate the wicked here rather than to be tolerated by the good. IV, 604. See Wicked. Toleration of the wicked in unity is the greatest victory. IX, 349. Toleration of the wicked does not exclude ecclesiastical discipline, correction, or the severity of charity. V, 299, 900; IX, 350. Those who practice tolerance among the wicked are compared with the stars of heaven. IV, 1193, 1194. Whoever loses tolerance has fallen from heaven. IV, 1194.

The difference between *tollere* and *auferre* (“to take away” and “to remove”). IV, 907, 908.

The origin of thunder according to Priscillian. VIII, 667. Thunder is called the voice of God. III, 507.

Topazion, a very precious stone. IV, 1578.

The winepress: the world. V, 137. The Church compared with a winepress. V, 121. In the Psalms, winepresses may be understood as Churches or as martyrdoms. IV, 109, 110. The winepress has three mystical elements: pressure, and from the pressure two products, one to be stored and the other to be cast away. IV, 1033. The nations performed sacrifices in winepresses. III, 2085.

“Torrents” properly denotes rivers that fail in summer but are flooded by winter waters. IV, 939. A torrent is water that comes with force. IV, 352. Human mortality is compared with a torrent. IV, 1462. Heretics are compared with torrents. IV, 685. All the impious and proud are so compared. IV, 685.

Torment. It is not injustice, through bodily troubles, to compel thieves to return the money they have stolen. II, 662. Through servile fear one fears falling into the torment of punishment, but through filial fear one fears losing the grace of a benefit. II, 558. Only those overcome torments who place their confidence in Christ, not in themselves. IV, 1157, 1158. Whoever makes progress feels the torments of the soul in the Church. IV, 221.

Torquatus killed his own son even though he was victorious, because he had fought the enemy against orders. VII, 37, 162.

The two torturers of the soul: fear and pain. V, 687.

Torture and judicial interrogations indicate that human judgments are uncertain and often mistaken. VII, 633. In torture, the judge’s ignorance is usually the calamity of the innocent. VII, 633.

*Tractoria*. II, 163. In the *tractoria* that Victorinus had sent to convene the council, Augustine criticized something, especially the fact that he was named before the others. II, 226.

In Paul, “he handed over” means the same as “he dismissed.” III, 2064.

Ancient and apostolic tradition. IX, 159, 174; X, 128. The handing down of ecclesiastical doctrine from hand to hand. X, 698. Unwritten apostolic traditions. X, 280. Through apostolic tradition the Church receives many things without writing. IX, 133. What we preserve not as written but as handed down—if it is observed throughout the whole world—is understood to have been commended and established either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils. II, 200. Whatever the universal Church holds, and which was not instituted by councils but always retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down solely by apostolic authority. IX, 174. Apostolic tradition is the most certain rule for investigating the truth. IX, 194. The perversity of the Pelagians is refuted by the rite handed down to the Church concerning the baptism of infants. II, 889. The tradition of the ancestors concerning the baptism of infants. V, 950. Concerning aid for the spirits of the departed. V, 936. Concerning saying “Alleluia” for fifty days. V, 1176.

The tradition of Christ. IV, 1214. See Christ.

Why they were called “traitors.” IX, 226. The ancestors of the Donatists handed over the sacred books and instruments of the Church to the persecutors. II, 265. What the crime of handing over consists in. IX, 53. Note 1. Petilianus compared them with Judas the traitor. IX, 263. God avenged upon the king who burned Jeremiah’s book the handing over of the books, by a death in war. II, 266. The Donatists call “traitors” those whom they either imagine or believe to have succeeded the traitors through the line of communion. IX, 386. Even if a traitor had slipped into the succession of bishops extending from Peter to Anastasius, this would prejudice neither the Church nor innocent Christians. II, 197. The Donatists themselves declare that those who communicated with Catholics could not have become traitors. IX, 636. If Catholics are defiled by the crime of handing over committed by their ancestors, the Donatists too are defiled by the crime of apostasy. IX, 226. The Church must not be abandoned on account of the crime of handing over. IX, 576. Why the crime of handing over could not have been a reason for the Donatists’ separation. IX, 538. The false crimes of the traitors. V, 1599. The crime of handing over and other charges brought by the Donatists are either untrue or do not belong to the Church. IX, 270, 272, 273, 274, 276, 283. Even if the traitors were manifest, the Church should not therefore be abandoned, since they did not establish it. IX, 517, 519. When the Donatists charge the whole world with the crime of handing over, they curse it. IX, 267. The whole world cannot be guilty of a crime of handing over that may perhaps have been true of the Africans. IX, 388, 392, 393, 394. Even if the crime of handing over were known, it could not have stained the whole world; how much less if it were unknown. IX, 37, 38. And if it had not been proved. IX, 254. The Donatists’ arguments to the contrary are refuted. IX, 38. The crime of handing over would not have defiled in unity those who disapproved of it. IX, 288. The crime of handing over charged by the Donatists does not stain the Church. IX, 265, 266. Even if the crimes of the traitors are true, they do not prejudice the Church; they belong to the chaff, not the wheat. IX, 428. The infidelity of the traitors does not nullify God’s faithfulness. V, 550. Catholics were charged with the crime of handing over. IV, 1234. The Donatists slanderously claimed that this had been committed by Caecilianus and other Catholics. IX, 53. Note 1. The crime of handing over was rashly alleged against Caecilianus and others by the Africans and was never proved. IX, 225, 228, 267, 288, 584. The Donatists unjustly accuse the Catholics of the crime of handing over. IX, 253. And the whole world as well. IX, 533. It is uncertain whether the charge against Catholics was handing over or offering incense. IX, 482. The handing over of the books occurred forty and more years after the passion of blessed Cyprian. IX, 176, 226. The crime of handing over should be attributed to the Donatists rather than to the Catholics. IX, 25, 288. It is judged without rashness that the Donatists succeeded the traitors. IX, 256. It is established that the Donatists were traitors; this crime could never be proved against the Catholics. IX, 510, 576. The acts of the council of Cirta in the year 305 show that some of those bishops who pronounced sentences against Caecilianus in his absence were manifest traitors. II, 580. In what sense Paul may be called a traitor. IX, 265. According to the Donatists, it follows from their admission that handing over the sacred books was not a crime, since the emperor ordered it. IX, 652. The Donatists tolerated the crime of handing over within their own party. [Col. 0639] IX, 256. The extent to which Cresconius defends the Donatist traitors. IX, 511. However vehemently the Donatists attack the traitors, they are accused in equally explicit terms. IX, 254. The same reasoning by which the Donatists repel the crime of handing over also removes it from the Catholics. IX, 514. Whether the Catholics are probably traitors, since the Donatists are more probably so. IX, 542. Secundus of Tigisis commended those who, after being arrested and refusing to hand over the sacred Scriptures, were killed, as worthy of honor for the merit of their martyrdom. IX, 638. Many, when they refused to hand over the sacred books, were tortured and killed. IX, 640. Mensurius forbade Christians to honor those who offered themselves to persecution without being arrested and who voluntarily declared that they possessed Scriptures they would not hand over. IX, 638. Let the person who quarrels against the testator’s will be regarded as having handed the Testament over to the flames. II, 172.

The Traducians. X, 1182. “Traducians” was a name given by the Pelagians alone to Catholics. X, 1101. “Traducians” was Julian’s term for those who confess original sin. X, 1053. The name “Traducians,” used insultingly of Catholics, can with equal right be used of the Pelagians and of Paul. X, 1286.

The tragelaphus, a goat-deer. III, 880.

To draw is the work of grace. III, 1607. Whom he draws and whom he does not draw, why he draws one and not another—do not judge, if you do not wish to err; let the one who is not drawn pray to be drawn. III, 1607. Who should be considered to be drawn to Christ. III, 1608, 1609. We are drawn to Christ by delight. III, 1608. The one to whom it is granted to believe in Christ is said to be drawn by the Father. X, 553. The Father draws by making willing persons out of unwilling ones. X, 568. The Father draws while teaching through delight. III, 1610. To be drawn by grace. V, 730. Whether the one who is drawn comes unwillingly. III, 1607, 1608. The drawing of grace is sweet. V, 730.

Trajan, the emperor. VII, 614; IX, 323, 328.

Goods transported by sea. V, 959. To engage in maritime transport. V, 240, 253, 528.

When we are tranquil, wisdom must be learned and the word of God gathered as food. IV, 474.

The Transfiguration of the Lord. IV, 1932. The allegory of the Lord’s Transfiguration. V, 490.

Transformations. What is to be believed about them. VII, 574.

Transgression is signified by the number eleven. III, 635.

Let us consider that we are passing over, and we shall sin less. V, 688. We have been attached, according to our merits, to the order of things that pass away. I, 992. Lovers of temporal things do not want what they love to pass away. III, 140. Only the impious are displeased by the administration of passing things. III, 141. We must not cling to passing things. III, 1469. Passage from transitory things to things that abide. IV, 419. From the pleasures of the world to spiritual joys. IV, 413. From the depths to things above, from what is later to what is earlier. IV, 420. From oldness to newness. IV, 420. From vanity to truth, and from visible things, through contempt of them, to invisible things, through desire. IV, 421. The passage of riches from earth to heaven through the hands of the poor, as through certain channels. IV, 422, 423, 424. Christ’s passage, and ours. IV, 842. God’s anger passes over the righteous; it does not remain. IV, 1119.

The migration of the Jews to Babylon. IV, 772.

Thrasymachus defined justice wrongly. VII, 648, Note (b).

The number three hundred suggests the sign of the cross. III, 804.

Treveri. I, 750.

*Tria* in Punic, *salus* in Latin. III, 2096.

Three things commended in the Gospel and by the Apostle: abstinence from evil, the performance of good, and hope of eternal reward. V, 633.

Tribulation—whence the word is derived. VI, 18. “Tribulation shall be whatever you will.” V, 503. No tribulation is greater than consciousness of sins. IV, 515. The tribulations of the unjust are none or few, after which they come to everlasting tribulation. IV, 320. How grievous are the tribulations of the wicked. IV, 369. Tribulation is near to the good of the soul, danger to the life of the body. II, 552. This entire life is to be regarded as tribulation. IV, 972; V, 687. Whoever thinks that he has no tribulations has not yet begun to be a Christian. IV, 649. For one who loves the other life, this life is tribulation, whatever prosperity may make it shine. IV, 1781. The Christian is afflicted throughout the whole time of life, even when things go well for him. IV, 1089. The Scriptures promise nothing in this age except tribulations. IV, 451. Pastors should not promise Christian peoples prosperity here, but adversity. V, 275. Tribulations foretold by Christ. V, 1356. The greatest tribulations do not arise against the Church except from those who misuse the law. IV, 721. Whether tribulations are greater in Christian times, and why. V, 1357. Tribulations befall human beings, even the faithful, on account of sins, although the glory of the martyrs flourishes from this. IV, 458, 1014.

Temporal tribulations are greatly beneficial. II, 491. The usefulness of tribulation. IV, 173, 378, 579, 587; VI, 723. Tribulations are the scourges of one who corrects, so that they may not be the sentence of one who punishes. IV, 797. God grows angry as a father when he sends tribulations. IV, 655. Tribulation is a warning, not yet condemnation. IV, 568. Tribulations are warnings and incentives to correction. V, 150. Tribulations for the testing of patience [Col. 0640]. X, 305. Tribulation is medicine for salvation, not punishment for condemnation. IV, 173. God burns and cuts like a physician, in order to heal. IV, 458. It is no small benefit that our sins are punished here. II, 650. God, like a good physician, mixes tribulations with the sweetness of this age. II, 957. The one who had no putrefaction was cut, and Christ himself, our medicine, did not refuse the medicinal fire. IV, 458. Through temporal tribulations one must flee from the wrath of the everlasting fire. IV, 717. The trial of tribulation makes one stronger. IV, 869. God sends tribulations so that faith may grow fervent and prayer may be exercised. IV, 1118. So that it may appear whether the soul worships God freely. IV, 487. So that we may begin to seek that rest which does not belong to this life. IV, 1057. Christ brings tribulations in order to inflame souls with desire for his coming. IV, 125. God mingles tribulations with earthly joys so that we may learn to desire eternal sweetness. IV, 483, 484, 1777, 1778. The kingdom of heaven is not reached except by the way of tribulation. IV, 600. This was prefigured in David. IV, 600. Through tribulations Christ gives eternal life to all his members. IV, 323.

Temporal tribulations are to be endured for the sake of future glory. V, 1277, 1355. Tribulation is both punishment and grace: what does the one who inflicts punishment through grace preserve after punishment? IV, 427. What is not mercifully granted to human beings by the Lord God, from whom even tribulation is a benefit? II, 958. Tribulation must be endured with an upright heart. IV, 770. Since we cannot be without tribulations, we owe patience to God. IV, 480. Endure tribulations—not once, not for two days, but from the beginning to the end. IV, 221. If you fail in tribulations, you have broken the lyre. IV, 480. One tribulation is that which finds us; another is that which we ought to seek and find. IV, 579, 1059. The difference between finding tribulation and being found by tribulation. IV, 1763, 1780, 1781. What should chiefly be done in tribulation. IV, 334. In tribulations the soul must not be surrendered, either against God or against those who inflict evil. IV, 883, 884. Those are upright in heart who, whatever they suffer against their will, attribute it only to God’s just will. IV, 273, 274, 277, 352, 353. In tribulations, attributing truth to God is the customary confession of the saints. IV, 1588. In tribulations one must beware of descending from spiritual elevation to carnal life. II, 917. When the good are harassed by tribulations and temptations, they return inwardly to themselves. IV, 804, 805. They imitate the ant. IV, 804, 805. Then what we have heard securely ought to be useful. IV, 474. In every tribulation one must flee for refuge to God. IV, 515. In tribulations one must invoke him who is powerful either to teach what should be endured or to heal what has been endured. IV, 579. Christ redeems people from tribulation, not on account of their merit, but on account of his name. IV, 493. God rescues his own from tribulations, not always bodily, but spiritually. IV, 320. In tribulation God does not hear his own according to their will, but according to their salvation. IV, 173. We do not know what we are praying for when we desire to be freed from every tribulation. II, 504. Grace makes people strong in temporal tribulation. IV, 1560, 1361. We should glory in tribulations. IV, 1796, 1797. What consolation there is in tribulation and temptation. III, 1466, 1467. The narrowness of tribulation comes to an end; but the breadth into which we pass has no limit. IV, 1496. It is not a great thing in tribulation if it is brief in duration. V, 402. In whatever tribulation you may be, there always remains for you a place in which you may delight. IV, 1870.

Every tribulation is punishment for the wicked and exercise for the righteous. VI, 18. For many it is for testing; for many, for condemnation. IV, 687. In one and the same tribulation, as in one fire, the godly is purified and the ungodly is devastated; God is praised in both. V, 1383. How differently the good and the evil conduct themselves in tribulation. VII, 20, 21. How tribulation contributes to the progress of the faithful, righteous Christian. VII, 21. The difference lies not in what sorts of things each suffers, but in what sort of person suffers them. VII, 20, 21. The good are governed through discipline, whereas the evil are shattered. III, 1075. The devil devours no one unless he has overthrown him through tribulation. IV, 1292.

The wind of tribulation is harsh, but beneficial. IV, 1658. Tribulation symbolized by night and by winter. IV, 370, 475, 1174. Through the name of iron. IV, 1397. Tribulation and temptation are fire. IV, 222, 797. The fire that tests each person’s work. VII, 743, 744, 745. Tribulation is called an iron furnace. III, 531. Tribulation is the goldsmith’s furnace: it purifies gold from its impurities and turns straw into ashes. IV, 255. Here God casts one into the furnace of tribulation, so that the vessel may be fired, not broken. IV, 1214. A vessel strengthened by fire does not fear water; if it has not been solidified by fire, water will dissolve it like clay. IV, 797. The world is the furnace; wicked people are straw; good people are gold; fire is tribulation; and God is the craftsman who purifies the gold. V, 118. Under the hand of so great a craftsman, a speck of gold cannot perish in a great mass of straw. V, 118.

A tribunal adorned with precious linens and furnished with five steps. VIII, 179.

[Col. 0641] When the tribunes were first created. VII, 62, 63. And Note (b). Ecclesiastical cases chiefly entrusted to the tribune. II, 510. A tribune appointed to guard the shore. II, 430.

Tribes are so called as distinct curiae and gatherings of peoples. IV, 956. Tribes may be called curiae, not properly, but by a neighboring term. IV, 1624. The tribe of the Lord and the tribe of the devil. IV, 1624. How many tribes there were in Israel. VII, 557. How the tribes of Israel numbered twelve, with the tribe of Levi excepted. III, 1073. There were thirteen tribes among the Jewish people, but the promised land was distributed among only twelve tribes. IV, 956. Women customarily married from one tribe into another. III, 809. What it means to be moved from one tribe. VII, 57, 58.

The Jews as tributaries. IV, 682.

What the number thirty signifies. III, 1599.

The basilica of Tricilla. V, 364. Note (b).

How the three days of the Lord’s burial are to be understood. III, 1199, 1325.

What a triangle is. IV, 1961.

The Platonists had some knowledge of the Trinity. VII, 307. Porphyry’s opinion concerning the Trinity. VII, 300. The error of Sabellius. IV, 84. The followers of Metangismon say that the Son is in the Father as a vessel is in a vessel. VIII, 41. The Manichaeans assign inaccessible light to the Father, the sun and moon to the Son, and air to the Holy Spirit as their dwelling places. VIII, 369, 372, 373. They are refuted. VIII, 373. In what the Manichaeans and Catholics agree, and in what they disagree, concerning the Trinity. X, 1468. The doctrines of the Arians concerning the Trinity. VIII, 679. And their faith. VIII, 729. The Arians teach that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of the same substance. VIII, 39. They say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have different substances. II, 792. The Arians argued from the terms “begotten” and “unbegotten” that the substance was different. VIII, 913, 914. They are refuted. VIII, 914, 915. The Arians introduced three gods into the Church. IV, 837, 1712. The Arians had said that the Father once existed without the Son, and later corrected this. II, 1047. The Arians impiously said that the Father did not beget what he is. II, 750. If some of the Donatists said that the Son was less than the Father, nevertheless they did not deny that he was of the same substance. II, 792. The Arians made the Father like an emperor, the Son a judge, and the Holy Spirit an advocate. VIII, 696. In making a difference of nature, the Arians did not demonstrate it. VIII, 696, 698. The Aetians, or Eunomians, asserted that the Son was entirely unlike the Father and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son. VIII, 40. Priscillian’s error concerning the Trinity. VIII, 666, 667, 668, 671. A certain heresy asserts that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are, as it were, three parts of the Trinity. VIII, 45.

The faith of the Trinity. VII, 337. The faith of the Trinity is expounded. V, 453. What faith teaches concerning the Trinity. VIII, 694, 716, 823, 945. What is to be held concerning it. II, 744. What is to be believed. VI, 193; X, 497. An explanation of the Trinity. III, 21. A description. II, 1028. The nature of God in the Trinity is believed by many and understood by few. III, 357. A name suitable to the Trinity cannot easily be found. III, 21. The mystery of the Trinity cannot be explained even in angelic words. VI, 659. The Trinity is one God. III, 1682, 1683; IV, 83; V, 64, 453, 614, 620, 703, 715, 853, 1059, 1063, 1071, 1076, 1198, 1218. The Trinity is one and the only God. II, 749. One, only, and true God. VIII, 714, 715, 721, 751, 762, 764, 769, 795, 798, 860. The Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, but together they are one Lord God. VIII, 741. The whole Trinity is one supremely good God. V, 853. God is one Trinity. I, 828. And a triune unity. I, 612, 828, 1321. The Lord whom we are commanded to adore: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. II, 750. In that peace of God which surpasses all understanding, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God. II, 1044. The whole Trinity is one God, not three gods or three omnipotent beings. V, 355, 1059, 1063, 1071.

The wondrous simplicity of the Trinity. II, 745. The Trinity is simple. VIII, 766. Unity in the Trinity. VII, 325. The unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is explained. II, 1042, 1043, 1044. The whole Trinity has one substance. III, 1862. The Trinity is of one and the same nature and substance. II, 750; VIII, 770, 772, 773, 775, 776, 777, 785, 786. There is one power, possessed by the threefold power; there is one substance, in which there are three subsisting realities. II, 450. The Trinity is one Lord, not three Lords; one God, one substance, three persons. V, 64, 65. The unity of the essence of the Father and the Son is established from the words, “We are one.” VIII, 706. The Father and the Son are not one and the same, but are one. VIII, 706, 722. In the Trinity there is no diversity of natures. VIII, 703, 704, 705, 706. The Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father, yet they are not two gods. VIII, 849, 851. It is not permissible to call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three gods. VIII, 308. The Son is worshiped both in the Father and in himself and in the Holy Spirit. VIII, 704. Of the Father and the Son alone it cannot be said that one is what the other is not, since both are so simultaneously. VIII, 925, 929. In the Trinity, the Greeks say “one essence, three substances”; the Latins, “one essence or substance, three persons.” VIII, 939. The opinion that the divinity of the Trinity is something other than the Trinity itself is refuted. [Col. 0642] II, 460. Some Latins, and especially the Greeks, said that the Trinity, which is God, is more properly an essence than one substance. II, 460. Why in the Trinity one person and three essences are not said. VIII, 943, 945, 947. For what reason the Greeks say in the Trinity “one essence, three substances,” and the Latins “one essence or substance, three persons.” VIII, 939, 940, 941. “Three persons” is said more suitably than “three substances.” VIII, 943. The terms “persons,” “substances,” and “essences” have not long been in use. VIII, 944. Scripture nowhere says “three persons” in God. VIII, 941. Why three persons are spoken of in the Trinity. VIII, 945, 947.

The persons of the Trinity. II, 1028. The persons of the Trinity are neither confusedly one nor separately three. II, 750.
