When three persons are spoken of in the Trinity, why are three gods not spoken of? VIII, 940. For God, to be and to be a person are not different things, but altogether the same. VIII, 943. We may not lawfully say “three gods,” although each individual person of the Trinity is called God. VII, 300, 301. In the Trinity the three persons are supremely one. VIII, 765. The Trinity is nothing other than that very being itself. I, 1321. One Trinity and a triune divinity. VI, 697. In the Trinity, whether one person or three together are called the one true God. VIII, 930. Those who denied the persons of the Trinity were expelled from the Church. III, 1666, 1668. The persons of the Trinity must neither be confused nor separated; the works of nature and grace are common to them. II, 744. The persons of the Trinity are inseparable. III, 1870, 1871. Although the Trinity appears separable, it is believed by right faith to be inseparable. V, 355. The inseparable distinction of the Trinity is not without purpose. VIII, 1081. The Trinity is not to be imagined as three living masses, as it were, nor is the divinity to be conceived as some fourth person. II, 455, 458. To believe that the divinity is everywhere but the persons exist only in heaven is an empty invention of carnal thought. II, 455, 459, 460. Sometimes no term is found by which the persons of the Trinity correspond to one another. VIII, 919, 920. The persons of the Trinity are marked by various properties and names. I, 976, 1077, 1336; III, 128. By the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is signified the way in which the persons refer to one another, not the substance by which they are one. II, 1043. The names “Father” and “Son” do not indicate natures in themselves, but signify the persons of one in relation to the other. II, 751. The distinction of the persons of the Trinity arises from relation to another. VII, 325. What is said relatively in the Trinity. VIII, 919. The Trinity is not spoken of relatively. VIII, 919. How “principle” is said relatively in the Trinity. VIII, 920, 921. “Person” is said of itself, not relatively. VIII, 943. What is said relatively of one another in the Trinity properly belongs to the individual persons; what is said of each in relation to itself is not said plurally of the three. VIII, 947. Whatever the Father and Son are said to be in relation to each other, neither is said without the other. VIII, 925, 927. What is said jointly of the Father and the Son, and what is not. VIII, 924, 925. On account of their inseparability, sometimes only the Father or only the Son is sufficiently named. VIII, 832, 834, 835. So that the Trinity, although inseparable, may nevertheless be understood as Trinity, many things are said separately of the individual persons. II, 744. In the Trinity, all are sometimes understood in one person. VIII, 833, 835. When the Son or the Holy Spirit adheres to the Father, the Father does not become greater than either of them individually. VIII, 930, 932. In the Trinity the three persons are not something greater than one. VIII, 947. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; neither is one the third part of this Trinity, nor are two a greater part than one, nor are all something greater than the individual persons. VIII, 983. The Trinity is no less in the individual persons than in all of them, nor greater in all than in the individual persons. II, 750. The Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. III, 1745. The Father and the Son possess the Spirit commonly, not divided within themselves. V, 460. Why the Holy Spirit is possessed in common by the Father and the Son, but the Son is not likewise possessed by the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth. V, 464. The Son adheres inseparably to the Father, if it is permissible to say “adheres” of that which never was and never can be entirely separated from any substance. II, 1052. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit adhere inseparably to one another. III, 1563. The difficulty concerning the inseparable Trinity. V, 355. The Father always begets, and the Son is always born. II, 1047. The Father was never previously aware that he would become the Father of the only-begotten God. VIII, 766. The Father is not from another God; the Son is from God the Father, yet for that reason the Son is not of another or different substance. II, 750. The Father, the fountain, begot the fountain; but both the begetting fountain and the begotten fountain, just as the begetting God and the begotten God, are one God. V, 1083. Who can explain how light was born from light, and yet the two are one light; how God was born from God, without the number of gods increasing? V, 1018. Since the Father has an only-begotten Son, either he did not wish to have an equal, or he could not: if he did not wish to, he is envious; if he could not, he is weak. II, 1047. Augustine demonstrates that the Son of God was not made and that he is equal to God. II, 1033, 1054. The Son of God is entirely what he has. III, 1743. Sound doctrine teaches that the Son was born, one from one God, and that the Holy Spirit belongs to both. VIII, 308. In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, quality is not one thing and substance another. II, 460. In divine things there is such fellowship of substance that it admits equality but not plurality. IV, 845. Whatever the Father is insofar as he is God, the Son and the Holy Spirit are also. IV, 844, 845. Everything that exists in the Trinity, whatever it is, is the supreme, true, immutable God. VIII, 702, 703.

The coeternity of the Trinity. VIII, 909. The Son is coeternal and equal with the Father. III, 1537, 1743. How the Father sanctified the Son. III, 1745. Whoever does not honor the Son as equal to the Father does not honor the Father. III, 1546. Because the Father loves and the Son is loved, and the Father bears witness while the Son receives it, there is not therefore diversity between them. VIII, 722, 754. What the Son speaks, the Father speaks. III, 250. How the Father shows the Son what he himself does. III, 1565. How the Son received a command from the Father. III, 1740; V, 775. In the sacred mysteries it was taught that God is omnipotent and “tripotent.” I, 1002. In the Trinity, three omnipotent beings are not to be spoken of, just as three gods are not spoken of. VIII, 715. The whole Trinity is omnipotent. VIII, 767. The Father, Son, or Holy Spirit must not be separated from one another, even in those things that Scripture attributes to one alone. VIII, 769, 826, 832. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one power, one substance, one divinity, one majesty, and one glory. VIII, 814. The Trinity has one will, one power, and one majesty. III, 1582. The Trinity is immortal, not the Father alone. VIII, 826. The nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must not be called changeable on the grounds that the things by which those persons were signified have passed away. II, 746, 747. The nature of the Trinity is immutable. III, 389. The whole Trinity is immutable. VIII, 757, 881. The entire nature of the Trinity is immutable and cannot be diverse. VIII, 685, 687. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are everywhere together. II, 837. Likewise invisible, equally and alike. V, 1266. The Arians said that the Father was invisible and the Son visible. III, 1779. The whole Trinity is invisible. VIII, 758, 854, 866, 881. Not the Father alone. VIII, 754. The Trinity belongs among those visible things that are neither bodies nor have any likeness to bodies. II, 457. Those who believed that the Father alone was immortal and invisible are refuted. VIII, 854. The Trinity in the knowledge of temporal things. VIII, 1012. How the Father and the Son know one another and all things. VIII, 1077. The Trinity is wise, not the Father alone. VIII, 1082. The Son is not unequal to the Father because he is the power and wisdom of God the Father; rather, for this reason he is coeternal with the Father. VIII, 923. Each person in the Trinity has his own wisdom, his own memory, and his own love. VIII, 848, 1066, 1080. Why the Son or the Holy Spirit is called “sent,” but not the Father. VIII, 869. The Son and the Holy Spirit are not therefore less than the Father because they are sent. VIII, 848, 869. Certain things are said in such a way that, to people of limited understanding, the Son himself may appear greater than the Father and the Holy Spirit be believed greater than the Son. II, 1046, etc. Why the gift of God is attributed to the Father. X, 970. The Father is supreme in all spiritual things. IV, 699. The attributes assigned by Hilary to the individual persons of the Trinity. VIII, 931. In the Trinity there is the perpetual stability of truth. III, 1669.

The works of the Trinity are the same. V, 704. The works are inseparable. II, 75, 745, 878; III, 1557, 1559, 1560, 1561, 1871, 1902, 1922; V, 356, 459, 1063; VI, 251, 463, 684; VIII, 308, 686, 691, 694, 705, 714, 827, 857, 858. The dwelling is inseparable when the operation is inseparable. V, 463. The operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable; nevertheless, for the Son to operate is from him from whom he himself is. VIII, 846. The origin of the works is from him from whom is the existence of the persons who cooperate. V, 459. Sacred Scripture measures the act of the Trinity not by a difference of powers but by the ineffability of its works. VIII, 697. Just as the Son does the will of the Father, so the Father does the will of the Son. VIII, 790. The power and operation of the Trinity are undivided. V, 356, 459, 703. The Trinity has equal power, one substance, and the same divinity. VIII, 714. To say that the Father can do something without the Son, and conversely, is contrary to the Catholic faith. III, 267. The Father and the Son are one principle. IV, 1457.

Nothing can be coeternal with the Trinity. III, 389. The Trinity created the world. III, 232. Whether the person of the Father and the person of the Son are distinguished in the creation of the firmament. III, 267. It is incompatible with the unity of the Trinity to understand the Son as having made the world as though commanded to do so. III, 268. Every creature receives being, form, and order from the Trinity. III, 128. Every creature in its entirety is from the whole Trinity. III, 128. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone are creator: a triune unity, one Trinity. V, 986. All things are not from the Father alone, but also from the Son. VIII, 827. The creation of the human being displays the plurality of persons and the singularity of the divinity. V, 703. As the Son does the works of the Father, so the Father does the works of the Son. V, 748. The forgiveness of sins belongs to the whole Trinity. V, 458. Nevertheless, it is understood to belong properly to the Holy Spirit. V, 460. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit perform certain things without one another. VIII, 824, 857. In the Trinity, certain works belong to one person, yet not without the cooperation of the others. V, 357, 459, 463. The individual works of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said to belong to each person insofar as they are manifested as pertaining to each of them [Col. 0644]. VIII, 694. The Arians and Catholics call the Father author, the Son creator, and the Holy Spirit teacher, guide, illuminator, and sanctifier—how this is to be understood. VIII, 761.

Since the Trinity works inseparably, it might seem to follow that the whole Trinity assumed the human being. II, 75. The Trinity wrought Christ’s flesh. V, 1096. But this belongs only to Christ. V, 363. When the human being was assumed, the number of persons in the Trinity did not increase. II, 746. The Trinity remains, and a quaternity of persons is not introduced when the human being is joined to the Word so that there is one Christ. II, 543. One must make or acknowledge a Trinity, not a quaternity. V, 727, 999, 1206. The Son of God proves that he is God. III, 1745. In the Trinity, human form must not be conceived except insofar as it pertains to the incarnation of the Word. III, 1687. The nature of God cannot be seen bodily; any person may appear through a created thing placed beneath him. VIII, 308, 868. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be demonstrated inseparably through a corporeal creature. VIII, 909, 910. Although they operate inseparably. VIII, 910. See Appearance. Neither the Father, the Son, nor the Holy Spirit has ever been seen through his own substance. VIII, 811, 812. The Trinity visibly manifested itself according to human capacity and for the salvation of human beings. VI, 649. The persons of the Trinity were intimated in Christ’s baptism. V, 354. The Trinity appeared perceptibly in Christ’s baptism. V, 353, 355. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not a threefold God, but one God. II, 1052. It is not a threefold person of God, because there is one form and one divinity. II, 1052. Augustine does not believe in a threefold person of God, as Pascentius wrongly charged. II, 1052. Neither was the voice heard joined into the unity of the Father’s person, nor the form of the dove into the unity of the Holy Spirit’s person. II, 745. The Father’s voice heard on the mountain and the form of the dove seen were produced without the ministry of a life-giving soul. II, 746. They could have been produced through the ministry of angels. II, 747. How one should rise toward knowledge of the Trinity. VIII, 1087.

The Trinity is represented in created things. VIII, 932. Traces of the Trinity in creatures. VII, 300. The Trinity is intimated in all the works of God. VII, 338. Especially in the holy angels. VII, 338. The mystery of the Trinity is intimated in Genesis. I, 847. In Genesis I. V, 26; VI, 167; VII, 345. Arguments for the Trinity from Scripture. VII, 484. What testimonies of Scripture compel us to confess the unity of the Trinity. II, 1044. Some understand “Trinity” as spoken of in the right spirit, in the Holy Spirit, and in the principal Spirit. IV, 596. The unity of the divinity and the distribution of the persons are shown by the words of Ezekiel XXXIV. V, 309.

The likeness of the Trinity in the human being. V, 362. The image of the Trinity in the human being. VII, 339, 342. Symbols of the Trinity in the human being. I, 849. How the Trinity is shown in the mind. VIII, 1040. The Trinity, which is the image of God, is to be sought in the principal part of the mind. VIII, 1044. The Trinity is the image of God in the mind insofar as the mind remembers, understands, and loves God, which is wisdom. VIII, 1048. The image of the Trinity in each person’s memory, understanding, and will. VIII, 1088, 1090. Memory, understanding, and will foreshadow the Trinity but do not express it perfectly. II, 745. Another trinity in the memory of one recalling a vision. VIII, 993. The image of the Trinity in the mind of one who knows and loves himself. VIII, 963, 972. A trace of the Trinity is also found in the outward human being. VIII, 983. The trinity of the outward human being is not the image of God. VIII, 990. One lives badly and deformedly according to the trinity of the outward human being. VIII, 990. The opinion that invents the image of the Trinity in the marriage of male and female and their offspring is not probable. VIII, 459, 1000. A trace of the Trinity in vision. VIII, 985, 991. The image of the Trinity is to be perfected in the Trinity. VII, 342. The traces of the Trinity are not sought in creatures without reason. VIII, 1058. Whether and how the Trinity who is God is shown through the trinities manifested in the human being. VIII, 1064, 1065. How one gradually reaches the Trinity who is God. VIII, 1087. How great is the dissimilarity between the image of the Trinity found in us and the Trinity itself. VIII, 1089, 1090. There is something in the human being by which, in some manner, what is said about the Trinity can be understood. VIII, 695.

The Trinity is elucidated by comparisons. VI, 189, 658, 692. The faithful, whose heart and soul were one, express in some manner the unity of the Trinity. III, 1684. A trace of the Trinity in love. VIII, 960. The Savior signified the Trinity by the name of bread. III, 2096. The Trinity may perhaps be figured in the three loaves which a friend asks a friend to lend him. II, 500. The threefold discipline of philosophy commends the Trinity. VII, 338. The first three commandments of the Decalogue pertain to the individual persons of the Trinity. II, 213.

Who now see the Trinity through a mirror. VIII, 1091. The eye of the mind, weak in such an excellent light, is not fixed upon it unless it is nourished and strengthened by the righteousness of faith. VIII, 822. A purified mind is fit to perceive the Trinity. III, 128. No one knows the Father except through the Son. III, 1734. Now the Trinity is seen through a mirror with the help of faith, so that it may be seen more clearly in the promised vision, face to face. VIII, 1091. Whether after the resurrection we shall see the Trinity with a spiritual body, Augustine seems to doubt. [Col. 0645] II, 460. Understanding the Trinity consoles the labors of the present life. III, 1341. It is food both from which you may live and from which you may feed others. V, 620. How the unknown Trinity may be loved. VIII, 952. Both the Father through the Son and the Son through the Father are glorified. VIII, 704. How the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit come to us, and we to them. III, 1832. The Trinity dwells in the saints as in a temple. III, 1833. How righteous people and sinners imitate the individual persons of the most holy Trinity. VIII, 586. We are commanded to imitate the Trinity through grace. VIII, 928. Believing in the divine Trinity and the triune unity, let us beware lest anyone seduce us from faith in the unity of God. V, 1076.

The faith of the Trinity is commended against various heresies. VI, 299, 643, 658, 667, 683, 698, 701. The confession of the Trinity issued by Consentius. II, 450. It is shown that the Trinity must exist. VI, 15. How one should inquire concerning the Trinity. VIII, 959, 961. Writing about the Trinity is necessary to no small extent, and certainly not superfluous. VIII, 869. How one should discuss the Trinity according to Augustine. VIII, 822. The mystery of the Trinity must be discussed according to a definite rule. VII, 300. Nowhere is error more dangerous than in discussion of the Trinity; nowhere is anything sought with greater labor, nor is anything found more fruitful. VIII, 822. Many things are said about the Trinity, not so that it itself may be stated, but so that it may be understood from those statements that it cannot be stated in them. II, 1054. The Arian is convicted of blindness, because he boasted that he could draw forth the naked truth concerning this mystery. II, 1054. Why Augustine writes concerning the Trinity. VIII, 869. Augustine keeps the books On the Trinity in his hands for a long time and thinks that they can be understood by only a few. II, 743. Augustine began these books as a young man and completed them as an old man. II, 758. They were stolen from him before he had completed and polished them. II, 758. He corrected them so that they differed little from those that had been stolen. II, 758. Otherwise he himself would have published them much more disentangled and clear. II, 758. The letter which he wishes to be placed before those books. II, 758.

Triopas, the seventh king of the Argives, enrolled among the gods. VII, 565.

Tripoli. IX, 430. The schism of the Maximianists broke out at Tripoli. II, 333. The people of Tripoli. IX, 395.

The story of Triptolemus. VII, 570.

Trismegistus. IX, 224. Whether the predictions of Trismegistus concerning Christ are more suitable for persuading Gentiles to believe in Christ than those of the Hebrew prophets. VIII, 282, 290, 292. The precepts of Trismegistus. II, 1031. See Hermes; Mercury.

What sadness is. VII, 409. Sadness, a contraction of the soul. III, 1732. Sadness is pain belonging to the soul alone. IV, 480, 1110, 1111. According to the Stoics, nothing in the mind of the wise person is sadness. VII, 411. What use the Stoics thought sadness served. VII, 413. Sadness is found both in good and in evil. VII, 411, 412, 413. Sadness concerning the things of the age is harmful. V, 1183. Sadness at another’s goodness is hateful to God. VII, 443. From what source sadness ought to arise. V, 1182, 1184. Godly sorrow. VII, 413. That sadness is praiseworthy which comes from the love infused by the Holy Spirit. III, 302, 303. The sadness we feel on account of evils relieves us, but burdens those who persist in their perversity. II, 1084. This sadness is pious and, if one may say so, a blessed misery: to be troubled by the vices of others without becoming entangled in them; to grieve without clinging to them. II, 1064. Sadness and pain among human temptations are not sins, but signs of human weakness. IV, 1111. Christian sadness has an “as if”; their joy has no “as if”; worldly people have the opposite. IV, 559, 560. The sadness of one who patiently suffers injustice is better than the unjust joy of one who commits it. IV, 671. The time of sadness comes before the time of joy. V, 1182. Sadness seems to dissolve the heart. II, 554. The better the mind, the more quickly and easily sadness is healed in it. VII, 635. Christ’s sadness before his death. IV, 274.

The fat or kidneys of wheat, that is, flour. III, 537. You are wheat; tolerate the chaff until it is winnowed. IV, 1950.

Tritonian Minerva. VII, 566.

The lake of Triton. VII, 566.

The time of threshing. V, 119.

The voice of those who triumph. V, 815, 893.

The history of Trogus Pompeius. VII, 116.

Neptune and Apollo, hired by Laomedon, built Troy. VII, 80. Troy, the mother of the Roman people. VII, 17, 79. The overthrow of Troy by Fimbria. VII, 83. By the Greeks. VII, 79, 80, 573. The gods who were worshiped at Troy did not prevent its overthrow. VII, 79, 80. The origin of the Trojan war and destruction. VII, 105. The Trojan gods. V, 505.

The Trojans, exiles under the leadership of Aeneas, founded Rome. V, 505.

Certain names of tropes, such as allegory, enigma, and parable, are found in Scripture. III, 80. Tropes are more commonly called “modes.” VIII, 1068. Why tropes occur in Scripture. VI, 534. The trope synecdoche is highly useful for understanding Scripture. III, 86. Knowledge of tropes is necessary. [Col. 0646] III, 80. The sacred authors used tropes. III, 80.

The scales of truth, not of desire. V, 1457.

Trygetius, a fellow citizen and pupil of Augustine. I, 963. At Cassiciacum he takes part in discussions in the books On the Academics, On the Happy Life, and On Order. I, 908. He loved history. I, 980. Trygetius had at one time entered military service. I, 908.

Which ductile and horn trumpets are meant. IV, 1255, 1256. May a horn trumpet raise you up against the devil, not a fleshly trumpet against your brother. IV, 1256.

Tubunae. II, 993, 997; IX, 204.

Tuburbum. IX, 213. The martyrs of Tuburbitana. V, 1521. Note (b).

The bishop of Tubursicum. II, 173, 180.

Tucca. IX, 231, 237.

The municipality of Tullium. VI, 602.

Cicero’s book On the Orator. IX, 455. See Cicero.

Tullius, a philosophaster who was to become an aedile. VII, 76.

Tullus Hostilius, the third king of the Romans after Romulus. VII, 92. He captures Alba. VII, 89.

He who teaches scarcely overcomes swelling pride. IV, 594. The effect and remedy of swelling pride. V, 780. Swelling pride must be healed by the medicine of humility. V, 780. The “poultice” of swelling pride given to the Apostle. V, 835.

Tumult: A great withdrawal from the tumult of collapsing circumstances is necessary for a person to become afraid of nothing. II, 74. Everyone ought, to the extent of his ability, to prevent civil tumults. V, 1392.

Leather tunics. III, 451; X, 1357. At one time Romans were not permitted to wear ankle-length and long-sleeved tunics. III, 74. Christ’s tunic, woven from above, signifies charity and unity. III, 1499, 1949; IV, 176; V, 149, 1086, 1222.

Beating of the breast. V, 133, 153, 186, 433, 1463. Beating of the breast is contrition of the heart. IV, 265.

The crowd and the people. V, 614. A crowd: a disturbed multitude. V, 614. An unordered multitude. III, 501.

Turbantius. X, 718. Bishop. X, 1051. Freed from the error of the Pelagians. X, 1051, 1146. And converted to the Catholic faith. X, 1353, 1435.

To indicate that shameful conduct must be avoided by naming certain shameful things is not itself shameful. VIII, 635, 636.

Turpilucrus. VI, 560.

The church of Turris. II, 134.

Towers in the diocese of Hippo. II, 232.

The turtledove, a symbol of the Church. IV, 1300. The turtledove signifies those who withdraw themselves from the busy occupations of human society. VII, 502.

Tusculum, a town near Rome. VII, 93.

A Tusculan quarrel. I, 938.

Tutilina, the goddess placed in charge of the grain that had been gathered and stored. VII, 118.

Tutunus. See Mutunus.

Tutuslymaeni, scourged by divine correction. V, 1409.

The river Tiber. See Tiberis.

Tychonius. See Tichonius.

The tympanist women signify those who praise God with the flesh subdued. IV, 834.

The tympanum, a figure of incorruption. IV, 1964. Mystical explanation of the tympanum and psaltery. IV, 1953.

What it means to play the tympanum. IV, 306, 308.

“Typhus” used for arrogance. II, 332.

A tyrant, an unjust king. VII, 67. Tyrants are thought to have been called “strong” by an ancient name. VII, 106. Tyrants are raised up only by the providence of God. VII, 106. Tyrants, without knowing what they were doing, brought gifts by sacrificing the holy martyrs. IV, 909. Under tyrants, Christians were tortured when they confessed, but released when they denied. IV, 1161. Tyrants and persecutors were made martyrs. IV, 1591.

Tyre is called Sor in the Hebrew language. IV, 1053. “Tyre” is taken for Carthage. IX, 421.

To the Tyrians, since it had not been granted them to believe, even the means by which they might believe was denied. X, 1014. It did not benefit the Tyrians that they were able to believe, because they had not been predestined by him whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways are inscrutable. X, 1014. The Tyrians, although they would have repented if the miracles performed at Chorazin and Bethsaida had been performed among them, will nevertheless be punished on the day of judgment—yet more lightly than those cities. X, 1006.

Augustine instructs and consoles Christ’s recruit, whose military service was being shaken by many temptations. II, 1055.

V

The red heifer, a sign of the New Testament. III, 732. A figure of Christ’s passion. III, 733. The cows signify souls that are easily led astray. IV, 643, 836. The Jewish people. IV, 1362.

The Vadiani, schismatics, not heretics. VIII, 39.

Vaga. IX, 220.

Vagaia. The Council of Vaga accuses Felicianus and Praetextatus of cruelty. II, 414. The judgment of the Council of Vaga, consisting of three hundred and ten bishops, against Maximianus. II, [Col. 0647] 406, 407. “Vagaitana privileges” for “Bagaitana.” IX, 427. See Bagai.

Who the vagi of the Romans are. VIII, 167.

The church of Vaginensis. II, 240.

Valens the Emperor, favoring the Arians, afflicts the Church. VII, 173. He persecuted the Catholics in the East. IX, 327. The persecution of the Emperor Valens. VII, 615, 616.

Valens the deacon. V, 1575.

Valentianus, a curator. IX, 511.

Valentinian the elder, a confessor of the Christian faith, was deprived of military service under Julian the Apostate. VII, 615. The successor of Jovian. II, 400.

Valentinian the younger, brother of Gratian. VII, 172. Consul again. II, 966. Taken into partnership in the Empire by Theodosius. VII, 172.

Valentinus, a Catholic bishop. II, 308, 577.

Valentinus the abbot. X, 881, 911 n. 1, 915. He greatly values the book on grace and free choice and Augustine’s letter to Sixtus. II, 975. Augustine writes one and another letter to Valentinus and the brothers who are with him. II, 968, 971. Valentinus writes back to Augustine. II, 974. He declares his faith concerning free choice and God’s judgment. II, 975.

Valentinus, bishop of Baia. II, 953. Note (c).

The Valentinians. IX, 589. From Valentinus. VIII, 27. The doctrines of the Valentinians. VIII, 27.

Valeriana, a martyr. V, 1448.

Valerian the Emperor. VII, 614; IX, 323, 328.

Valerius Licinianus Licinius, the emperor. IX, 540. Note 1.

Valerius, bishop of Hippo. II, 117, 131; IX, 755. He imposes upon Augustine the burden of preaching. II, 117. And the burden of the co-bishopric. II, 123. He often bears witness that his prayers were answered at Augustine’s arrival. II, 123. Augustine asks Valerius to allow him to spend some time in retreat. II, 89. While Bishop Valerius was still alive, Augustine was ordained bishop, although neither of them knew that the Council of Nicaea had forbidden this. II, 967. Valerius gives Augustine a garden. V, 1570.

Valerius Melzitanus. IX, 507, 528, 550.

Lucius Valerius, Roman consul. VII, 95. His poverty. VII, 164.

Publius Valerius was killed while defending the Capitol. VII, 96.

Valerius the count. I, 651; X, 411, 413, 437, 637, 639, 1049. Assistance from Count Valerius was requested against the Pelagians in the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. X, 1147. Eulogy of Count Valerius. II, 926. Augustine dedicates to him the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. I, 651; II, 915. Later he writes the second book to the same man, and on what occasion. II, 950. Valerius, a lover of peace and alien to empty arrogance. II, 131. Extremely observant of conjugal chastity. X, 414. Devoted to reading. X, 436. Augustine commends Bishop Felix to Count Valerius. II, 949.

Valerius the vicar, the same as Verinus. IX, 687. Note 2.

Valerius Soranus, the poet. VII, 203.

Valerius, an actor. II, 1063.

The Valesian heretics. VIII, 32.

The source of good health. X, 278.

Vallonia, the goddess placed in charge of valleys. VII, 118.

Who the “boasters” are. I, 1076; III, 139.

Vanity and truth differ by opposition. IV, 1531. Whatever passes away is called vanity. IV, 1863. Every creature is subject to vanity, that is, the human being. III, 2075. The angels are not subject to vanity. III, 2074. Man is subject to vanity because he refused to be subject to truth. IV, 1532, 1549. Every creature is vanity, not in itself, but because of human vice. III, 139. In what the vanity of this life consists. VII, 661. The vanity by which they call this life, established in miseries, blessed. VII, 629. The vanity of this age is explained briefly but vividly. II, 938. Vanity is more talkative than truth. VII, 174. Those who speak vanity do not listen to those who speak truth. IV, 1866. Vanity in human praise must be avoided; where it lies. II, 1023. What it means to observe vanity. IV, 237.

All human beings are being scourged; only the sons of God recognize that they are being scourged. IV, 1635.

Varro, a very learned man. VII, 111, 112, 561. The most learned of the Romans. VII, 650. More learned than the other pagans. III, 1055. No minor authority in history. VII, 559. An author worthy of belief. I, 1020. Varro is commended for the distinction of his intellect and his secular learning. VII, 177, 182. Although Varro did not attain knowledge of the true God, he perceived that the one God ought to be worshiped. VII, 138. He called the true God Jupiter. VII, 650. What he thought about the gods of the Gentiles. VII, 178. His doctrine concerning theology is insufficiently coherent. VII, 218. What he reports concerning the ends of good and evil. VII, 625. How, and into how many books, he divided his works on divine and human antiquities. VII, 178. Why he wrote more about human than divine matters. VII, 179, 182. Varro wrote about sacred buildings. VII, 98. He wrote about the people of the Roman nation. VII, 561, 720.

[Col. 0648] A vessel, a general name for all utensils. III, 699. The breaking of a vessel because of the compression of air. III, 265. A vessel is brought to the fountain when the soul is raised to God. IV, 1854. Vessels for honor and vessels for dishonor. V, 116. A vessel becomes one for honor through mercy, and one for dishonor through judgment. VI, 282. Vessels for dishonor would not exist unless they were evil. X, 1124. God prepares vessels for glory, and they themselves prepare themselves. X, 1135. How God makes vessels for dishonor. X, 1129. Which are the vessels of wrath and the vessels of mercy. X, 1129, 1141. Vessels of wrath made complete for destruction. IV, 1752. According to Julian, vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy are made from the wages of their own will. X, 1133, 1134. Vessels of wrath arise from judgment; vessels of mercy from undeserved grace. X, 1141. What benefit the vessels of wrath provide. VIII, 635. For what they are useful. X, 841. Vessels of destruction become useful for correcting others. VI, 123. Vessels of wrath, when God makes good use of them, benefit the vessels of mercy. X, 984. There is no third kind of vessel, neither for honor nor for dishonor. X, 1136, 1142, 1191, 1299. What the vessels of death are. IV, 106. The wicked, vessels of the devil, become vessels of Christ by believing. IV, 695.

Vaticanus or Vagitanus, the god who presides over the cries of infants. VII, 118, 122, 128.

The two breasts of Mother Church, the two Testaments. III, 1998.

The Veientes, or Veii, the most formidable enemies of the Roman people. VII, 62, 96.

The eleven curtains of the Tabernacle, symbols of sins. III, 634, 635. What the veil of the Temple, torn at Christ’s death, signifies. X, 400. Curtains hung at the entrances of grammar schools. I, 670; V, 964; VII, 713. The more curtains hang in a house, the more honorable each person is. V, 336.

The veil between the face of Moses as he spoke and the people listening. IV, 778.

To be veiled is equivalent to receiving the veil of sanctity. II, 959.

A farewell gift for veiling. II, 645.

To will is supremely free. VII, 152. Willing and being able are distinct. X, 234. To will what is unfitting is itself the greatest misery: it is not so miserable to fail to obtain what one wishes as to wish to obtain what one ought not. II, 498. What it means to will what is fitting. II, 498. See Will.

What Gideon’s fleece signifies. X, 400. Gideon’s fleece allegorically. IV, 520, 521, 907.

God has offered the kingdom of heaven for sale. IV, 1211.

Venantius, a bishop. II, 759, 781.

Venantius of Thinis. IX, 230.

The hunter. V, 85, 136, 333, 718; VI, 560. The labor of hunters. V, 444. Hunters fighting with bears. VI, 639. In the theater, the hunter is praised by the people according to the interests of his faction. VII, 263. The hunter and the charioteer among those who provided spectacles for the people. IV, 438, 439, 626, 1327. Hunters and actors who give away their own property are censured. V, 90. The duties of hunters and fishermen. VI, 714. The Lord hunted the lovers of hunters and the hunters themselves. V, 333. The devil, the worst hunter in the whole world. V, 334.

The perverse desires involved in selling and buying things, in charity and cheapness. V, 1541. Human beings were able to sell themselves, but were unable to redeem themselves. IV, 1231.

Sorcerers. The Donatists acknowledge that the force of the laws is rightly exercised against sorcerers. IX, 45.

Poisons themselves were created not only for the adornment of the universe but also for human benefit. VII, 335. The poisons of Roman matrons. VII, 97. A woman accustomed to poisons. I, 1352. Why the earth produces poisonous things. III, 182.

The Venetians. VIII, 236.

Sins are increased less by hope of forgiveness than by despair. IV, 1301. So that human beings would not live worse through despair, God promised a harbor of pardon; and again, so that they would not live worse through hope of forgiveness, he made the day of death uncertain. IV, 1301. Forgiveness should quickly be granted to those who ask for it. II, 857. Forgiveness must be given to a brother so that it may be received from God. V, 652, 653. He does not receive forgiveness unless his guilt is perfectly certain. II, 165. Forgiveness should be granted not for the impunity of wickedness but for the hope of correction. VII, 171. Forgiveness must be sought from the person who has been injured. V, 127, 1055. From certain people forgiveness must be sought only tacitly and by gentle persuasion. V, 1055.

Why the measure of venial sin is now unknown. VII, 750. Venial sins. X, 1117. See Sin.

Venilia, the goddess. VII, 122, 211.

“Belly” is used in Scripture for the inner parts. IV, 241. The belly of the Church in carnal matters. IV, 492. The belly of Christ, the weak within the Church. IV, 175.

A ventriloquist woman. III, 53.

What wind is. I, 1039. Wind is air moved and fluctuating. III, 225. Wind is nothing other than moving air. X, 534, 535. It receives different names from the different regions of the sky. I, 1039. What is praiseworthy and what blameworthy in wind. VIII, 196, 199. Souls are understood by the name “winds.” IV, 1346, 1347, 1776. Wind signifies temptation. IV, 328. To feed the winds is to feed demons, that is, by going astray to be a source of pleasure and mockery to them. [Col. 0649] I, 694.

Whence Venus received her name. VII, 188. Why Venus is called Vulcan’s wife and Mars’ adulteress. VIII, 374. Bald Venus. II, 84.

The function of Venus, or Liber, or Ceres. VII, 194, 195. Some wish Venus also to be a star and the moon. VII, 206. The star of Venus is called Hesperus, Vesperugo, or Lucifer. VII, 720, 721. The portent that occurred in the star of Venus. VII, 720. Venus was the adulterous mother of Aeneas. VII, 80. The rites of Venus. VII, 185. Before joining their daughters to husbands, the Phoenicians gave Venus a gift from the prostitution of their daughters. VII, 121. Whether there are three Venuses. VII, 121.

The Venustian or Paternian heretics. VIII, 46; X, 800.

Spring, for those new in the faith. IV, 941.

God is truthful in threats just as in promises. IV, 1226. A human being is not truthful unless God speaks in him. IV, 1432. Truth will be paid as a reward to the truthful person, and eternity will be paid as a reward to one who lives well in time. V, 1405.

Verbalis, in the diocese of Hippo. II, 232.

In Paul’s time it was not permitted for a Roman citizen to be punished with blows. II, 806.

Verbidium. VIII, 214.

“Word” is said in many ways. VIII, 968. What the word of the mind is. VIII, 1071, 1072, 1075, 1078. From things seen in eternal truth, we conceive and beget inwardly the word. VIII, 967. The word is conceived through love, whether of the creature or of the Creator. VIII, 967. In love of spiritual things, the word that has been born is the same as the word that has been conceived; it is otherwise in love of carnal things. VIII, 968. Whether only beloved knowledge is the word of the mind. VIII, 968, 969. The word precedes every work of a human being. VIII, 1073. The word necessarily precedes speech and action. VIII, 967. The word of the mind knowing itself is equal to itself. VIII, 969, 970. The word of the heart. V, 1097. The word of the heart, consent. VI, 350, 352. The human word passes to another while remaining in the heart. III, 1671. On the truth and falsity of our word. VIII, 1077. When our word is true. VIII, 1072, 1078. Our word cannot be, or be called, everlasting. VIII, 1078. Our word, even when we become like God, can never be equated with the divine Word. VIII, 1079. What our word will be when we become like God. VIII, 1079. Sound is the vehicle of the word conceived by the mind. V, 185, 677, 1097. The word that we speak is, as it were, one mind proceeding from another mind through which it discloses itself. VI, 183, 184. How word and voice differ. V, 1304, 1307, 1309. The external word, the voice of the internal word. VIII, 1071.

What words were instituted for. VI, 243. Words are necessary only for expressing the will. III, 499. The entire use of words lies in signifying. III, 20. The abuse of words extends widely through all languages. VIII, 410. Words admonish us to seek the things themselves; they do not present them to us so that we may know them. I, 1215. To linger over words when the matter is clear is shameful. I, 932. The meanings of words, not the words themselves, must be considered. III, 2097. “Word” used for “deed.” III, 503, 800. To love truth in words, not words themselves, is a mark of distinguished character. III, 100. Words are works. III, 1820. Scripture calls a long series of words a “word.” V, 456. An angry word should not be passed on; it should die within you. V, 323. Tullius says of a certain man that he never uttered a word he wished to recall—a statement more credible of someone excessively foolish than of a perfect wise man. II, 586. Whoever can understand the internal word can see the likeness of the divine Word. VIII, 1071, 1072.

The divine Word is compared with the human word. III, 1506. The nature of the human word cannot be comprehended; how much less that of the divine Word. III, 1671, 1672. The greatest possible dissimilarity exists between our word and knowledge and the divine Word and knowledge. VIII, 1073, 1075, 1077, 1078. Some wrongly thought that the Word of God was not only mutable but also visible. VIII, 854, 858, 861, 862. The impious assertion of Fortunatus that the divine Word is bound in the race of darkness. VIII, 121. What should be thought about the Word, the Son of God. VIII, 585. The Alogi refuse to receive the Word as God. VIII, 31.

The Son of God is called the Word of the Father, and why. VI, 183. Why the Son of God is called not the knowledge of God but the Word of God. VIII, 1079. What the Word of God is like. III, 1383. The excellence of the divine Word. IV, 496. The excellence of God’s Word must be understood from the property of the human word. V, 1124. The Word of God cannot be explained by a human being. V, 1003, 1124. Why God preferred to compare the utterance of his Word with writing rather than with sounds. IV, 498. The Word with God has neither syllables nor temporal durations. IV, 1378. God’s speaking is eternal. IV, 497. God’s own Word was not made. III, 1384. The Word of God, born without beginning, is coeternal with the Father. III, 227. From the one from whom he has being, he simultaneously has learned being. IV, 1564. In the Word, hearing and seeing, and so forth, are the same as being. III, 1541, 1542. The Word of God, God with God. III, 248. The Word of God is wholly equal to the Father from whom it is. VIII, 1076. The Word is the very same as the Father. VI, 183. The Word is predicated relatively, not absolutely. [Col. 0650] VIII, 936, 937. The Word, coeternal with God the Father, begotten, not made. V, 664, 672, 671. The generation of the Son of God is ineffable. IV, 496. No one understands how the Word of God was begotten except one to whom God himself has inspired it. II, 443. The Word, God with God, is eternally spoken, and through it all things are eternally spoken. I, 812. That Word remains unchangeably. VI, 183. The nature of the Word is to be and to be unchangeable. III, 1389. In the Word of God there is no “when” or “at some time.” III, 248. The Word of God remains in itself without aging and renews all things. I, 774. All things are simultaneously in the divine Word, principally and unchangeably; all are life and all are one. VIII, 888. In the divine Word, to be is not only the same as to live; to live is also the same as to live wisely and happily. III, 249. In the Word there is life, so that it is itself life. III, 268. Whatever is in the Word is life. III, 268. The Word of God does not possess unformed life. III, 249. The Word of God is the unchangeable light of wisdom. III, 250. The divine Word is truly truth, and in it that saying is supremely recognized: “Yes, yes; no, no.” VIII, 967, 968. The Word’s seeing is not other than the Word itself. V, 705. God knows in the Word all the things he made through it. VIII, 931. Through his Word the Father reveals himself. VIII, 937. The Word of God is wholly everywhere, and is not absent even from the minds of the impious. II, 540. The Word of God, wholly everywhere, is displayed through the likeness of our voice. II, 518. The Word of God is wholly everywhere. V, 676, 1486. Wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly in the angels, wholly with the Father, wholly with the Virgin, and so forth. V, 184. The vision of the Word and of the Father is not different but one. III, 332. The eternal Word is seen only by a most purified and simple heart. VIII, 140, 141.

The Word of God, the counsel of God. III, 1384. The command of the Father. V, 775. The Word of God before all creatures. III, 1399. Through his Word God made whatever he made. III, 249. Through it all things were made. III, 1384, 1385. All things were created. VI, 183. All things would not have been made through the Word unless it had existed before all things and had itself not been made. VIII, 888. The Word of God, through which God created all things, is eternal. III, 248. The Word of God is a certain art of the omnipotent and wise God, full of all living principles, and so forth. VIII, 931. The reason for creating each creature lived as coeternal life in the Word of God, coeternal with the Father. III, 268. The Word of God is a form not formed but the form of all things formed. V, 662, 1216. A form without place or time. V, 662. Existing in all things as their foundation, in which they exist, and as their summit, beneath which they exist. V, 662. The Word before times, through which times were made, and so forth. IV, 1311. In the one Word that he begot, God said all things before they were individually made. III, 268. In the Word the Father ineffably said all things. III, 1912. In the Word of God are all the things that are created, even before they are created. III, 268. The things made through the Word are in the Word in one way; the things that the Word itself is are in it in another way. III, 268. In the Word of God are the things that are to be and the things that have passed away. IV, 497. And all things existed before they came to be. IV, 742. What God does by the Word, he does by his hand. IV, 1313. The Word of God is called his hand. III, 348. Through the Word God created man, and through the Word he recreated him. IV, 1855. How a temporal creature comes to be when the Word is eternal. III, 248.

The Word, fountain and light. III, 1495. The true light of the human mind. III, 331. The Word itself is the teacher and principle by which we teach all truth inwardly. I, 813. The Father tells of himself through the Word. II, 1028. Through the Word God the Father makes himself known to the angels. II, 1028. The price of acquiring the Word is the one who acquires it himself. V, 662. Let him not seek outside himself what he might give; let him give himself. V, 662. Nor does he then lose himself, as he loses the price of the thing he buys. V, 662.

The Word, the bread of angels. V, 701, 1097, 1124. The Word of God is heavenly bread and treasure. IV, 1833. The angels are fed with the Word of life as with their bread. III, 1978. The Word is the food and bread of angels, by which they are nourished, live, are illuminated, understand, and are blessed. V, 401, 1020. Through the Word of God all rational minds are nourished without deficiency. V, 782. The Word is food, but not everyone is strong enough to take it. III, 1385. The Word is the bread of angels; the Word made flesh is the bread of human beings. III, 1494. Because man could not eat the Word, it became flesh so that man could suck it. III, 1385, 1386. The Word of God became flesh so that man might eat it, and dwelt among us. IV, 995. Through the incarnation the Word became, as it were, milk, so that we could take it. V, 670. The one whose Word does not depart from you is with you. IV, 390. The Word of God does not appear visibly except through some visible creature. VIII, 140.

The Word became flesh—not the Father, not the Holy Spirit—yet the whole Trinity made the flesh of the Son. V, 1063, 1096, 460. The incarnate Word is God and man. V, 1002. Heretics said that the Word of God was the mind, understanding, or reason in Christ. V, 1124. In the incarnation the Word assumed the whole human being. V, 1124. He assumed both flesh and soul. IV, 664, 665. In the incarnation the Word was not changed, nor did it depart from God the Father. V, 105, 671, 674, 680, 687, [Col. 0651] 995, 1001, 1002, 1097. When the Word put on flesh, it did not abandon the bosom of the Father. III, 1659, 1660. That the Word could proceed to us without departing from the Father is shown by the likeness of sound. V, 184. How the Word is handled with the hands. III, 1978. The Word that became flesh, so that it could be handled with the hands, began to be flesh from the Virgin Mary; but the Word did not then begin to exist. III, 1978. The Word became flesh but was not changed: an analogy. III, 24. The Word took flesh, but was not changed into flesh. III, 1045; VIII, 541. The Word was not defiled by a human body. VI, 187. Nor polluted by a female body. VI, 187. Nor contaminated in the Virgin’s womb. VIII, 177, 178. The mystery of the incarnation of the Word is commended. V, 675. And it is illuminated by comparison with the human word. V, 675, 677, 1097. Through that inseparable union of the Word itself, Christ is not such a man as other men are. IV, 211. The Word in the flesh as in a shell. IV, 1854. The divinity of the Word is not recognized by those who despise its weakness on the cross. IV, 1536.

The cause and necessity of the incarnation of the Word. V, 710, 845, 997, 1006, 1660, 1676. The Word of God was born in time for our sake. V, 1003. The human race would not be liberated unless the Word of God deigned to become human. V, 940. For us, on our behalf, from us, the Son of God became mortal. VIII, 541. The Word of God became incarnate so that it might bear what was worthy on behalf of the unworthy. V, 1009. The Word did not disdain to assume hay, lest the hay despair of itself. IV, 1333. The Word became flesh for us as the way. III, 1656. The first way to God. III, 33. The way by which we might return to our homeland. III, 1389, 1391. Through the incarnate Word one must reach the uncreated Word. III, 1388, 1494. One must cling to Christ according to what he became for us, so that one may reach him according to what he is. III, 1390. The Word became flesh, which we could see, so that what would enable us to see the Word might be healed in us. III, 1979. He wished to be born from a human being so that human beings might be born from God. III, 1395.

The infant Word, a teacher of humility. V, 1004. Since the Word was not ashamed to be born from a human being, human beings should not be ashamed to be born from God. III, 1399. Through the divine Word alone we can be good in whatever way we are good. IV, 496. The incarnate Word drives away our darkness. VIII, 888, 889. What was done by the Word is the word for us. III, 1593. The Word itself is not part of the Church, but the Word made flesh is the head of the Church. IV, 1942. The common storehouse of God’s Word in heaven. V, 581. The incomprehensible Word of God, revealed in the Gospel. V, 676. See Christ, Son of God, Incarnation.

The Word of God must be heard attentively. IV, 1884. Those unwilling to hear the Word of God are compared to an asp. IV, 679, 680. The Word of God must not be neglected because few do what they hear. IV, 692. The devout and the impious should hear the Word of God. IV, 1689. The heralds of God’s Word should speak to both the wicked and the good. VI, 677, 678, 687. Neglecting to do the Word of God is not excused by the preacher’s life. V, 971. One must not consider through whom the Word of God is administered. V, 695. We are all inward hearers of the Word of God; inwardly and outwardly we must all be doers. V, 970. Human beings hear from human beings, yet what they understand is given inwardly. III, 1609. What should be done when the Word of God is not understood. III, 1557. It is not enough to hear the Word of God in order to live; one must obey it. III, 1548. To receive the Word is to understand and hold on to it. III, 1911. The words of God must first be put into practice so that they may be understood. III, 631. Not to hear the Word of God is evil; to hear it and not do it is evil; what remains is to hear and do. V, 971. Those who hear and understand the Word of God are happy; those who follow in the happiness that comes next are those who believe even if they do not understand. V, 676. Everything lies open to the Word of God; nothing is hidden from the Word of God. V, 676. It is useless to praise the word of truth if it is not put into practice. V, 831. To hear the Word of God is to eat Christ himself. V, 969. The Word of God is our food and drink. V, 1648. It is bread that never departs from the mouth of the righteous. IV, 386. Our bread is the Word of God; we sweat in hearing it lest we die of fasting. IV, 286. He eats well but digests badly who hears the Word of God and does not do it. V, 183. When circumstances are peaceful, the Word of God must be gathered and stored in the innermost parts of the heart. IV, 369.

How effective Christ’s Word is. IV, 500. How swift and mobile it is. IV, 1931. It is compared with winds because nothing is swifter. IV, 1346. In some people the Word of God becomes a spring of water welling up to eternal life; others, hearing the Word, become torrents. IV, 939. The human heart repels from itself the severity of the Word of God and admits to itself the blandishments of the serpent that gives evil advice. IV, 543. How those who hear the Word of God well fail and progress. VI, 678. The Word of God, the seed that is scattered in hearts. III, 1396. The seed by which we are regenerated. IX, 249, 260. The Word of God is like an axe cutting rocks. III, 102. The words of God are arrows. III, 830. The Word of God is both an arrow and rain. IV, 981, 1600, 1601, 1803. The rain of God’s Word is turned by the wicked toward producing thorns, but by the good toward good fruit. V, 48. Desire, like the root of thorns, turns the sweet rain of the Word into pricks. IV, 1803. The Word of God in the heart frees one from the snare, from the crooked way, and from a slippery downfall. [Col. 0652] IV, 390. The clear words of Christ nourish; the obscure ones exercise. III, 1721. Christ’s words remain in us when we do what he commanded, and so forth. III, 1842. Those who think wrongly about the Word are not refreshed by the Word. III, 1385. The Word of God disturbs all perverse hearts, just as it exercises devout hearts. III, 1559. The Word of God is superfluous to many through their own fault. IV, 1689. It is not useful to everyone, because faith does not belong to everyone. IV, 1803. For whom it is harmful and for whom it is beneficial. IX, 65, 68. The fruit of God’s Word must be required even from one who does not hear. V, 204. What it means to remain in the Word of God. V, 742. How necessary this is for us. V, 743. How great the reward. V, 743, 746. The Word of God then rests in us when we consent to the Word of God. V, 1353.

The Word of God must not be hidden through fear of carnal disadvantages. III, 1338. Hunger, deprivation of the Word of truth. III, 1344. Weariness and disgust with the Word of God, a serious temptation. IV, 1422. Every human being who announces the Word is the voice of the Word. V, 1306. The Word of God comes when it is made manifest and departs when it is hidden. II, 518. The Word of God was heard by those standing. IV, 1062, 1930. The practice of sitting while the Word of God is heard, accepted in certain churches, is approved. VI, 325. One who hears the Word of God with weariness should be urged to sit down. VI, 325. There is labor in announcing and hearing the word of truth. IV, 286.

What modesty is. IV, 856. The source of modesty in the members of the body. X, 404. Modesty should not prevent a friend from admonishing a friend. II, 671.

Verecundus, a citizen and grammarian of Milan, and extremely close to Augustine and his associates. I, 755; II, 69. He asks Nebridius to assist him in teaching. I, 755. To Augustine, fleeing the world with his companions, he grants his country estate at Cassiciacum. I, 765, 980. Verecundus becomes a Christian during his final illness. I, 765. Verecundus dies while Augustine is acting at Rome. I, 765.

Verimodus, son of Darius. II, 1020, 1022, 1026.

Verinus. II, 231. Vicar. IX, 648, 650, 686. Constantine’s letters were addressed to him. II, 581.

Whose daughter truth is according to the Manichaeans. VIII, 211. According to the Manichaeans, truth is the very light that is drawn through the eyes. VIII, 316. Truth, the eternal law. VII, 484. Truth, which is eternal and surpasses all things, is God himself. I, 742, 807, 840, 1262; III, 147. The essence of truth, the Trinity. VIII, 948. Truth is called the likeness and image of the Father, and wisdom. III, 243. Truth, Christ. III, 2000. Christ, the principal truth. V, 184. Christ is the truth, to which we go through faith and through Christ. IV, 1640. Truth truly is. III, 1680. In it there is neither past nor future. III, 1680. In the substance of truth there is no greater except what is more truly so. VIII, 947. When truth possesses itself in the fullest measure. VIII, 73. Truth belongs to natural right. VI, 20, 21. Everything just comes from truth. VI, 540.

Truth and vanity differ by opposition. IV, 1531. Man was made like truth when he was created; through sin he becomes like vanity. IV, 1863. Truth cannot be humbled. IV, 1492. It surpasses everything. IV, 311. The bodily creature, which extends from the summit of heaven to the clouds, has the form of truth. III, 238.

Truth, the life of the blessed soul. VI, 240. Contemplation of truth, the life of the blessed. V, 1633. The blessed life is nothing other than joy in truth. I, 793. Truth alone makes people blessed, since all things are true through it. IV, 79. Truth, the treasure of the heavenly homeland. VII, 160.

Truth, the light of our mind. III, 1658. Truth exists above our minds. I, 1259; III, 147. For our minds judge other things not from truth itself but according to it. I, 745; III, 147. The human mind adheres to nothing except truth itself. III, 243. Whether the supreme truth generally contains the reason of each person. II, 80. Truth is both one and many, because there are many souls whom it illuminates. IV, 138. Philosophers saw from afar the fixed, stable, unturning truth in which all the principles of created things exist. V, 776. The law of unchangeable truth is the law of all the arts, and the art of the omnipotent Craftsman. III, 147. Some traces of truth are found even in the writings of profane authors. X, 767. Judgment about even bodily things is made according to the rules of eternal truth. VIII, 966. The Epicureans and Stoics placed the judgment of truth in the bodily senses. VII, 232. Truth is common to all. I, 840. It is common to everyone. IV, 969. Whoever wishes to possess a private truth should fear being deprived of it. I, 840.

Truth is found in God. VI, 14. All truth is from God. III, 1414, 1660. Wherever truth is found, it belongs to the Lord. III, 49. Everything true comes from him who says, “I am the truth.” III, 18. Whatever truth is found in a human being is not from the human being but from God. III, 2109. However truth may be spoken through a creature, it is spoken only by him who alone is truthful. VIII, 140. Whoever speaks truth speaks it because it is granted by him [Col. 0653] who is truth itself. II, 724. If the illumination of truth is taken away from a human being, he will be able to speak nothing but lies. V, 908. Whoever speaks truth speaks with his own mouth, but not his own truth. IV, 1120. Whatever is true in reasoning must be attributed to the light of truth. III, 1283. Things that do not come from truth usually overthrow themselves. VII, 210. Knowledge of truth is able both to judge and to overthrow all falsehoods, if only they are put forward—even those that had previously been unheard. II, 437. God placed the doctrine of truth in the chair of unity. II, 403. Truth that resists the sacred Scriptures must not, for any reason, be spoken or believed. VI, 156. Truth exists only in good works. IV, 1811. Truth alone is praiseworthy, even if it is not praised. II, 1023.

Everyone seeks truth, life, eternity, and blessedness. V, 776; VIII, 887. How great is our natural love of truth. V, 813. Truth would be sought less diligently if it did not have lying adversaries. V, 339. Our supreme task is to seek truth with the utmost earnestness. I, 933. The opinion of the Academics that blessedness consists in the search for truth, an opinion that is examined. I, 909, 966. Truth must be sought whatever the danger. VIII, 77. The disposition to seek what is true is safer than presuming unknown things to be known. VIII, 961. With what disposition of soul truth should be sought. VIII, 855. How it should be sought in disputations. VIII, 175. Truth is required by disputation, not disputation by truth. III, 547. I think that one can never err more safely than when one errs through an excessive love of truth and an excessive rejection of falsehood. VI, 487. Unless truth is desired with all the powers of the soul, it cannot be found in any way. I, 1324. The soul ought to desire truth more than itself. VI, 496. To find truth is exceedingly difficult. VIII, 65. Truth is found only through great labor. VIII, 174. If it is sought as it ought to be, it cannot withhold itself from those who love it. I, 1324. It is impossible that those who seek it piously, chastely, and diligently should lack the ability to find it. I, 1049. It admits all who seek it. I, 1261. Truth itself denies that one can reach it by such great detours, when it is so near, or by such great expense, when it is so freely given. II, 435. Truth speaks everywhere through whatever creature it chooses, to whatever creature it chooses. VI, 142, 162. How it speaks to a rational creature. VII, 484. Do not go outside yourself; return into yourself. In the inner person truth dwells. III, 154. Concerning all that we understand, we consult not the speaker who sounds outwardly, but truth itself, which presides within over the mind. I, 1216. No one sees that what he has read is true in the book or in the person who wrote it, but in himself. II, 86. Truth speaks within minds without sound. III, 1784. The voice of truth is not silent but cries out from the heart. IV, 675. How truth can be heard. III, 1784. Truth is a thing far removed from the minds of vain people. VIII, 65. Truth is present everywhere if the eye of the heart is open to it. IV, 234. Truth cannot be perceived by bodily senses. VI, 13. People see the rule of truth as unchangeable. III, 22, 23. Whoever begins to desire to grasp truth suffers a darkness that he had not noticed. IV, 1933. Whoever wishes to attain a clear understanding of truth should begin with confession. IV, 1908. A person cannot know all truth in this life. III, 1876. In what sense, nevertheless, he is said to know it. III, 1876. The truth we seek is not here. VIII, 887. Whoever boasts that he brings forth truth naked is thereby shown to be blind. II, 1054.

Truth is perceived only through divine assistance. I, 940. How, through the incarnate Word, we are made capable of perceiving truth. VIII, 889. Two vices hostile to the discovery of truth. VIII, 845. Knowledge of truth through a purified heart. VI, 310. The mind is capable of truth only when freed from vices. VI, 299. A sordid mind cannot cling to truth. VIII, 89. Through good morals we acquire recognition of truth. I, 1334. One enters into truth only through love. VIII, 507. Truth alone is possessed with security. I, 1261. No one loses it unwillingly. I, 1261, 1262. Nothing is firmer or calmer than truth. III, 238.

With what care the truth of doctrine and religion must be preserved. VI, 514. Truth is purity of mind. VI, 545. Truth is no more easily injured than bodily chastity. VI, 545, 546. Why people fear violating truth less than bodily chastity. VI, 546. Once the truth of doctrine has been corrupted, there is no way either forward or back to purity of soul. VI, 514, 515.

The sweetness of eternal truth. V, 615. Delight derived from the light of truth. V, 969. Nothing is more beautiful than intelligible and unchangeable truth. II, 443. The truth of God is the bread of angels and human beings. IV, 1742. Truth is bread. III, 1692. It is unchangeable. III, 1692. It is bread in this life and will be drink in the next. III, 1285. A common bread, by which both the preacher and the hearer live. V, 618. The bread of truth is bitter to sinners. IV, 88. Sound souls rejoice in the food of truth. IV, 89. The lover of truth cries out that what is true [Col. 0654] is sweet. IV, 1535. Love of truth is commended. IV, 310, 311. The recollection of truth is sweet. IV, 1227. Truth is sweeter than wickedness—but to the healthy. V, 831. Truth delights in truths. VI, 446. When hope of the future life had been set aside, some found it pleasant and joyful to be tormented by their love of truth. VI, 98. Eternal truth is food for the great; it is not changed into the one who receives it, but, conversely, changes him. I, 742. Truth changes all who behold it for the better; it is changed by no one for the worse. I, 1262. Truth is both sweet and bitter: when sweet, it spares; when bitter, it heals. II, 1062.

Divine truth must not be disclosed indiscriminately to its attackers and despisers. III, 1300. Truth should not be set before one who listens with an evil disposition. IV, 1767, 1769, 1770. Truth must not be concealed when some who are capable of receiving it are present. III, 1301. Truth must be preached insistently even to those who will not assent. IX, 449, 450, 451. It must also be pressed upon them through disputation. IX, 449, 450, 451, 352. Even to foreigners. IX, 454. Truth must not be concealed, even before the unworthy, for the sake of the worthy. IX, 523. Even unwilling people must be compelled to receive truth. IX, 722. Confidence in preaching truth is attributed to love, distrust to fear. VI, 192. No critic should be feared by the lover of truth. VIII, 843. All bodily evils must be endured for the commendation of truth. VII, 313. Whoever preaches truth must necessarily endure mockers. IV, 1768. Some meet death for truth courageously, others calmly, others willingly. III, 1369. The complete fulfillment is to fight for truth until death. IV, 1561. They are dogs who bark not for truth but for custom. IV, 176. Truth is heard more safely than it is preached. III, 1790. Truth is the reason why we learn; necessity is the reason why we teach. II, 874. How Psalm 14:3 is to be understood, where the one who speaks truth in his heart is praised. VI, 526. Likewise, the Apostle’s command that we speak truth with our neighbor. VI, 527. We ought to speak truth with our neighbor—that is, with everyone. IV, 189. To speak truth, and to speak vanity. V, 68. Those who speak vanity do not listen to those speaking truth. IV, 1865, 1866. It is nothing to preach truth if the heart disagrees with the tongue; and it is nothing to hear truth if no fruit follows from the hearing. IV, 812. Both those who do not believe the truth they speak and those who do not speak the truth they believe are rightly rejected. IV, 1491.

Two kinds of people oppose truth. VIII, 84. The doctrine of truth is hostile to demons. VII, 183. The wicked hate truth. III, 1860. People love truth when it gives light, but hate it when it reproves. I, 794. As long as wickedness is flattering and sweet, truth is bitter. V, 830. Why truth produces hatred. I, 794. When truth is spoken to us with some harshness, we are corrected not by the person—who may perhaps be a sinner—but by Christ. II, 130. No one can truly be a friend of a person unless he has first become a friend of truth itself. II, 667. People hate truth and prophesy without knowing it. V, 1427. People, though few, less often lend their ears to truth amid prosperity and more often amid adversity. II, 938. No one contradicts the clearest truth with his tongue, but he does so with his life. V, 963. Whoever resists the clearest truth opposes no one more than himself. IX, 177. When someone begins to resist the clearest truth, he is then cut off from the Church. IX, 444. Truth must be embraced whoever proclaims it. I, 984. Advice concerning truth, given through any person, must not be despised. III, 619. Truth must be loved for its own sake, not on account of the person by whom it is announced. III, 2108. Those who preach truth not in truth are tolerated, but not those who announce falsehood. VI, 527.

Truth can be hidden for a time, but it cannot be conquered. IV, 740. Truth must prevail, whether over one who denies or one who confesses. II, 1049. It is not good for one person to conquer another; rather, it is good for a person that truth conquer him willingly, because it is bad for him that truth conquer him unwillingly. II, 1049. Nothing conquers except truth; the victory of truth is love. V, 1586. Those who do not wish to be conquered by truth are conquered by error. V, 1586. We enjoy true freedom when we submit to truth. I, 1261. It is good to be caught in the nets of truth for food for the great King. V, 1326. The only person who lives well and honorably is the one whose life agrees with truth in every respect. I, 1051. The force of truth. IX, 678. Through the promise of truth we have a sure hope. II, 217. For a person to be able to take pleasure in truth, mercy must first have been shown to him. III, 604. Truth and mercy are repeatedly commended in Scripture. III, 565. Truth is frequently joined with mercy in Scripture. IV, 1117, 1480. Through truth and humility we are led to death; through mercy we are restored to life. IV, 1554, 1555. Truth is in heaven, mercy on earth. IV, 672. Like a shield, truth separates and distinguishes the humble sinner from the proud sinner. IV, 1153. A highly excellent exhortation to embrace truth, which alone makes people blessed. I, 1260.

What truth is. I, 888. The Academics said that truth could not be grasped. I, 924. The refutation of this. I, 945. Whence [Col. 0655] truth or falsehood comes. I, 891. Truth in the body is better than falsehood in the soul. I, 1167. God alone is the teacher of truth. I, 710. Everything true that we say belongs to God. I, 976. When truth is spoken, it is spoken under God’s inspiration. I, 861. True straw is better than light formed by an empty thought according to the will of one who merely suspects. III, 169. Truth is nourishment for the soul. II, 63. True things can be said unfaithfully, and untrue things faithfully. II, 420. Sometimes truth may be concealed without lying. III, 1301. Sometimes it is useful to remain silent about truth. X, 1017. The reasons for keeping silent about truth or not keeping silent. X, 1017, 1018. When truth should be spoken and when it should be kept silent. X, 1017. To keep silent about truth is one thing, to speak falsely another. IV, 85, 86. Sometimes keeping silent about truth is not blameworthy; speaking falsely is never permitted to the perfect. IV, 86. See “Falsehood.” Nothing permits speaking falsely; sometimes, however, it is useful to keep silent about some truth. III, 2111. One should not regret speaking truth, but it should be spoken cautiously. III, 1619. People labor to speak lies when they could speak truth with complete ease. IV, 1811.

The Academics’ probable opinion. I, 587, 927.

Various worms. V, 412. Some worms are found in springs of water and cannot exist outside them. VII, 709. Certain regions of Venetia eat some worms. VIII, 236. The worm: why Christ is called this. IV, 174. Christ was called a worm either to commend his humility or because a worm is born from flesh without intercourse, just as he was born from a virgin. II, 548. The worm of Gehenna signifies the pain of the soul. VII, 723. The worm of Gehenna also pertains to the body. VII, 723. When little worms are cut apart, their parts move. I, 1069. The cause of the movement of dissected little worms is investigated. I, 1070. Praise of the little worm. III, 156.

Versions differing from the Septuagint version. VII, 604. The Itala version is to be preferred to the other Latin interpretations of Scripture. III, 46. See “Scripture,” “Septuagint.”

Where the verse gets its name. I, 1014, 1149. Learned people call a verse something consisting of two members measured and joined together according to a fixed arrangement. I, 1126. The ending of a verse varies. I, 1149. A verse ought not to end with a complete foot. I, 1151. The ending of a heroic verse. I, 1151. How a heroic verse should be measured. I, 1151. On the excellence of six-foot verses. I, 1157. How six-foot verses should more conveniently be measured. I, 1158. Certain verses are named after their authors. I, 1107. The grammarian judges a verse by authority; the musician, by reason and perception. I, 1100. The minimum and maximum number of metrical units of which a verse can consist. I, 1127. How a verse is distinguished from rhythm and meter. I, 1116, 1147, 1151. A verse in the mind and a verse in the voice. IV, 120.

Veruclata. III, 801.

Verulus of Russicade. IX, 235.

Verus, a most perfect man and vicar of the prefects throughout Africa. II, 304; IX, 540.

The two Vespasians, father and son, most gracious emperors. VII, 168.

How “evening” is to be understood in the creation narrative. III, 314. How “evening” and “morning” are to be understood before the creation of the sun. III, 275. It is difficult to conceive of evening and morning during the first three days. VII, 322. What evening and morning signify. VII, 322. Evening signifies unformed matter. III, 240. It signifies the privation of creatures. III, 235. It signifies the sin of a rational creature. III, 259. See “Day,” “Morning.” Evening occurs in a person when the sun of righteousness sets for him. IV, 224. Evening began where the light of wisdom withdrew from sinful humanity. IV, 215. Evening signifies the tribulation of the world. IV, 782. It designates the end of the world. IV, 1362. The seventh day has no evening. V, 80.

Evening services. II, 120. They are customarily held every day. II, 120.

Vesperugo, the evening star, Venus. VII, 720.

The garment of the soul is the body. IV, 1314. Tearing one’s garments was an ancient practice of mourners. III, 711. Christ’s garments signify his sacraments. IV, 176. Christ’s garment is the Church itself. IV, 1932. Linen garments signify the inner parts. V, 224. How mixing purple with linen garments and wearing a linostima garment has now become sinful. VIII, 237. The high priest’s garment signifies the sacraments of the Church. III, 641. It also signifies the Church itself. IV, 1734. A person who seeks his own glory rather than Christ’s does not possess the wedding garment. III, 1464. The wedding garment is love. V, 562, 583; IX, 669. Christ’s garments were divided into four parts. V, 1086. The Lord’s four-part garment signified the four-part Church. III, 1949. Those who display themselves in women’s clothing are rightly regarded as infamous and incapable of making a will. I, 898. The *lacerna*, a type of garment. V, 883.

Vesta is said to be both the greatest of the goddesses, the earth, and, more often, fire. VII, 120, 121. She is said to be Venus. VII, 121. Among the Romans nothing was holier than Vesta’s temple. VII, 108. An everlasting fire burned in Vesta’s temple. VII, 77, 99, 108. Virgins were assigned to the Vestal fire because, just as nothing is born from a virgin, so nothing is born from fire. VII, 120, 121. How useless Vesta’s rites were for protecting the city. VII, 99. The burning of Vesta’s temple. VII, 99. A Vestal accused of fornication, as proof of her chastity, carried a sieve [Col. 0656] full of water to her judges. VII, 294, 774. Vestal priestesses discovered in fornication were buried alive. VII, 82.

What veteran soldiers endure in order to have a few days’ rest. IV, 373.

We carry something of the old person until the very end of death. V, 202. To put off the old person and put on the new. V, 81. The crucifixion of the old person is signified by the Lord’s cross. III, 2069.

How newness succeeded antiquity. VI, 677. Antiquity is carnality. V, 1230. Our antiquity must be crushed against Christ the rock. IV, 812.

Augustine commends to Paulinus the pitiable boy Vetustinus, pitiable even to the impious. II, 124.

Roman standards: eagles, dragons, and so forth. IV, 935.

The ways of the Lord are unsearchable: mercy and truth. II, 876; IV, 728, 1776. What the holy way is. VII, 569. In the holy place is the way of God. IV, 978. The right way exists only in the sight of the Lord. IV, 1593. The way of God is right faith. II, 979. The way is extended for pilgrims. III, 2054. It is one thing to be led to the way and another to be led along the way. IV, 1092. Who is said to keep the ways of the Lord. X, 305. What it means to turn aside and depart from the ways of the Lord. X, 305. You are on the way: remember that you have traveled some distance and that some remains; you have turned aside for refreshment, not for desertion. IV, 326. Do not remain on the way, do not turn back, and do not deviate. V, 926. It is better for a lame person to go along the way than for a runner to be outside the way. V, 926. Those who do not run along the way, the more they run, the more they go astray. V, 777. It is better to limp on the way than to walk vigorously outside the way. V, 778. Walk in Christ, so that you do not stumble, fall, remain on the way, look back, or depart from the way. V, 932. There are no ambushes on our way, but beside the way. V, 778. The enemy has been permitted to place these there so that you will not abandon the way. V, 778. Christ’s way lies amid snares: snares on the right are prosperity, snares on the left adversity. IV, 1839. What the broad and spacious way is. V, 1648. What the way of sinners is. V, 1897. The way of sinners is pleasing because its breadth is visible but its end is not. IV, 1897. The happiness of the wicked is transient; once their way has been completed, that happiness is finished. IV, 360. The sin of the way is not attributed to the one who commits it by deviating. IV, 1508. The narrow way leading to life cannot be traveled unless the heart has been enlarged. IV, 1530. The narrow way is difficult for one who labors, but becomes broad for one who loves. IV, 1530. The narrow way belongs to the few. III, 2122. When easier and fruitful things are fled from through lazy fear on God’s journey, harder and barren things are endured with troubled labor on the worldly journey. II, 1071. The thorny way, trampled down by the Apostles’ feet, became smoother for those who followed. V, 1298. Truth was discovered by the philosophers of this age, but not the way. V, 776. The way is Christ. V, 777, 780. It would have been too little for God to make his Son a guide to the way; he made him the way itself. IV, 1447. The prophetic lamp points out the way, and the Lord is in the flesh as in an earthen vessel. IV, 1854. Walk along the way toward prophecy, walk toward the words of God, walk toward the form of a servant, and you will be led to the form of the Lord. IV, 1854. Our way is love. IV, 1837. Nothing is higher than the way of love, and only the humble walk in it. IV, 1837. The way of God’s testimonies is Christ. IV, 1515. The ways of humility are the ways of life. IV, 145. One must not depart from the way of the virtues because of the insults of those who live badly. IV, 1151, 1152. “Ways” and “way” are read in Scripture because all are one. II, 393.
