What the ways and hedges signify in the Gospel parable. IX, 723. Stone milestones filled with inscriptions teach the way. V, 1547.

We are travelers here: what is appropriate for us in that condition. V, 926. Who is the perfect traveler. X, 164, 253, 602. The song of travelers. V, 1193.

The Manichaean traveler. VIII, 36.

To draw near. IV, 320.

Why the victims of the Old Testament were sought without blemish. X, 403. What the bloody sacrifices of Christians are. VII, 280. You place sacred victims upon the altar of conscience when you praise God in your heart. IV, 1746.

To sacrifice. III, 967.

Pope Victor. II, 196.

Victor, bishop of the province of Caesarea, is excluded from the primacy, and no bishop communicates with him anywhere except in his own diocese. II, 955.

Victor, bishop. II, 759, 781.

Victor, bishop. II, 759, 781.

Another Victor, bishop. II, 759, 781. Victor, whom Augustine calls “brother” and to whom he gives thanks. II, 153.

Victor of Altiburus, bishop. IV, 382.

Victor of Assuras. X, 235.

Victor of Aufidius. IX, 513, 583.

Victor of Castello. IX, 513.

Victor the gravedigger. IX, 513.

Victor the fuller gave twenty folles in order to become a presbyter. IX, 514.

Victor of Garbe. IX, 511.

Victor of Gor. IX, 227.

[Col. 0657] Victor the grammarian. IX, 513.

Victor, Nebridius’s brother. II, 74.

Victor of Octavum. IX, 237.

Victor, presbyter of Proculeianus. II, 133, 134.

Victor of Russicade. IX, 511. A traditor. IX, 612. Appendix, 773.

Victory is the subjugation of those who resist. VII, 637. It is natural for those who are defeated to prefer being subjected to victors, when they must be defeated, rather than being destroyed by warfare in every form. VII, 560. Victory is a gift belonging solely to the true God. VII, 125, 440, 441. Victories over enemies depend on the will and decision of the one true God. VIII, 448, 449. How victory should be used. VII, 440, 441. With what disposition the earthly city seeks victories. VII, 444. Victory must sometimes be attributed not to the merits of those who conquer but to the sins of those who are conquered. VII, 522. When victory comes to the wicked, divine judgment humbles the defeated, either correcting their sins or punishing them. VII, 643. Earthly victories are either deadly or, at any rate, mortal. VII, 440. Perfect victory over all the enemy’s devices. V, 1252. The teaching of Caelestius that our victory comes not from God’s help but from free will. X, 345. The holy Synod rejected this, as did Pelagius himself. X, 345, 346. The victory by which sin is conquered is nothing other than a gift of God. X, 887. Whoever presumes that he can conquer by his own strength, even if he seems to conquer through patience, is conquered by pride. V, 1253. Christ had from you temptation for himself, but from himself victory for you. IV, 724. The victory of the divine word. IV, 1956. See “To Conquer.”

The glassy joy of the victors, brilliantly fragile. VII, 114. It is an evil desire to wish to possess someone whom you hate or fear, so that you may be able to conquer him. VII, 124. To appear victorious in a disputation is not a great thing. II, 1048.

The Victoriana estate. VII, 765.

The Victorian estate. V, 1581.

Victorianus of Carchaba, or Carcavia. IV, 380; IX, 507, 528, 550. One of the twelve bishops who adhered to Maximian against Primian; he was condemned by the Council of Bagai. II, 414.

Victorianus, Catholic bishop of Mustitana. IX, 637.

Victoricius of Thabraca. IX, 217.

Victorinus. VIII, 667.

Victorinus, bishop of Leptimagnus. IV, 381.

Victorinus, bishop of Munatianum. IV, 380.

Victorinus, a subdeacon who, after being exposed as a Manichaean, was restrained, expelled from the clerical order, and driven from the city, and so forth. II, 1033.

Victorinus the rhetor of the city of Rome translated the books of the Platonists into Latin. I, 750. Victorinus earned a statue in the Roman Forum. I, 750. Victorinus read sacred Scripture and Christian books and publicly professed the faith. I, 750. He abandoned his school because of Julian’s law, by which Christians were forbidden to teach literature and rhetoric. I, 753.

To see. We use the verb “to see” to signify the operation of all the senses. II, 599. There are three kinds of things that are seen: one bodily, another resembling bodily things, and a third distinct from both. II, 457. Whether seeing well or badly refers to the outward eyes or the inward eyes. X, 369. The difference between seeing and believing is that present things are seen, while absent things are believed. II, 599, 600. God sees created things differently from human beings. I, 868. For God to see is the same as to show mercy. IV, 264, 295, 296. For God to see sins is the same as to punish sins. IV, 264. The desire to see. X, 770. See “Vision.”

The good of widowhood is superior to the good of marriage. VI, 432. The holy profession of widowhood. VI, 431. Second marriages are not condemned by the profession of widowhood. VI, 433. Exhortation to the good of widowhood. VI, 445. Comparison among three kinds of widows. VI, 440. A twice-married widow is sometimes to be preferred to one who has had one husband. VI, 440. The life of widowhood is signified by the sixtyfold fruit. VI, 423. The good of widowhood is not diminished by praise of the good of marriage but increased. VI, 435. What activities widows ought to pursue. VI, 447. Widows appear to have been charged with more diligent care of prayers. II, 506. Widows should beware of avarice. VI, 447, 448. Spiritual delights should take the place of bodily ones for them. VI, 447. A true widow is said to be one who has no one from whom she can receive support. III, 766. The attire of a widow is distinct from that of a married woman. II, 1081. It is indicated that she wears blackish garments. II, 1081. In the time of the patriarchs widows had distinctive garments. III, 583. Widows appear abandoned, but their help is strong. IV, 1726. God protects widows and orphans. IV, 1896, 1897. Every soul that understands itself to be abandoned by every help except God alone is a widow. IV, 1725. The soul that trusts in God alone is God’s widow. IV, 1897. The whole Church is one widow. IV, 1726. The Church is a widow in the absence of the bridegroom. IV, 1897.

Vigesilis. The people of Vigesilis steadfastly refused to receive their bishop, who had been degraded in the plenary council of Africa. II, 234.

Watchfulness is commended. V, 580. Watchfulness and prayer come from grace. X, 170, 171. One must always keep watch. IV, 1606. The enemy keeps watch while [Col. 0658] you sleep. IV, 801.

A watch does not last more than three hours. IV, 1144. Three-hour watches in military camps. III, 718. What the fourth watch of the night signifies. V, 476.

Sacred vigils. V, 1087. Vigils held for a sacred solemnity. IV, 1099.

The vigils of Maximian. V, 1598.

The Basilica of the Twenty Martyrs. V, 799. The feast of the Twenty Martyrs. V, 1447.

Let everything apart from God be held of little worth. IV, 252.

Villaregium. IX, 473.

To conquer a person is not a person’s good; rather, it is good for a person that truth conquer him willingly, and bad that it conquer him unwillingly. II, 1049. Nothing is more glorious than being conquered by truth. IV, 689. Whoever, by yielding, reaches what he does not lose unwillingly, conquers even when he seems to be conquered. III, 163. The person whose license to do wrong is taken away is usefully conquered. II, 531. One who has conquered vices cannot be conquered by another person. III, 160. The unconquered person is the one who loves only what cannot be taken away from one who loves it. III, 160. And the one who clings to God. III, 162. It makes a great difference what conquers within us. X, 591. How the pleasure of the flesh can be conquered. X, 804. Wickedness is conquered not by our strength but by God’s help. IV, 342. We are defeated while fighting against sin unless we are divinely assisted. VI, 271. You will conquer the one who usually conquers if the one who cannot be conquered dwells in you. III, 2006. We conquer through him who loved us. V, 1361. The one who conquered first will also make you victorious a second time. IV, 1321. We who have been defeated within ourselves conquer in God. IV, 1321. The Lion was defeated by raging; the Lamb conquered by suffering. IV, 1958.

Vincentius the Martyr, victorious everywhere. V, 1252. His praises. V, 1252. His feast days. V, 51, 1552. No region fails to rejoice in celebrating Vincentius’s feast. V, 1257.

Vincentius. IX, 539.

Vincentius, bishop. II, 759, 781.

Vincentius of Thibaris. IX, 223.

Vincentius Victor, formerly a Donatist, or rather a Rogatist. X, 510. Why Vincentius Victor wished Victor to be his cognomen. X, 773, *Admonition*, 475.

Where Vincentius took the name Victor for himself. X, 511. Vincentius Victor wrote against Augustine on the origin of the soul. I, 653. Vincentius Victor’s two books addressed to Peter. X, 495. Vincentius’s errors. X, 521. Vincentius was corrected moderately by Augustine and came to his senses. I, 653. Freed from the division of the Donatists or Rogatists. X, 503. Converted from the Rogatist faction to the Catholic Church. X, 473, *Admonition*, 475.

Vincentius of Carten., formerly a presbyter of Rogatus. II, 343. Later his successor. II, 321. He sits at Cartennis with ten Rogatists. II, 331. In Caesarean Mauritania. II, 332.

The bonds of wisdom are at first somewhat harsh; at the end they are neither harsh, because they are exceedingly sweet, nor soft, because they are exceedingly firm. II, 104. The bonds of the world have real harshness but false pleasure, and so forth. II, 104. Iron bonds are fear; golden bonds are love. IV, 1958.

Vindemialis, bishop. X, 411, note 1. He returned a letter to Augustine from the comes Valerius. II, 926.

Vindicianus, an old physician. I, 695. He had placed the agonistic crown upon Augustine when he was proconsul. I, 695. Vindicianus strove to recall Augustine from the astrologers’ nonsense. I, 695, 737. The physician Vindicianus’s remedy helped at one time and harmed at another. II, 526.

God’s vengeance is called his anger. IV, 710. Vengeance for sins is most certain. I, 1281, 1293. Vengeance follows sin most swiftly. I, 1292. The disgrace of sin does not exist in the nature of things even for a moment without the dignity of vengeance. I, 1292. Why God takes vengeance by killing whomever he wishes, whereas human beings do otherwise. VIII, 159. The right to avenge human sins, which belongs to God, proves that we were created by God. I, 1241. It is necessary that God avenge himself upon the unjust person. IV, 254. God avenges sins if he is just. IV, 589. Why at this time God repays vengeance neither to no one nor to everyone. IV, 255. God takes vengeance in anger upon the children of condemnation, but in favor upon the children of grace. X, 166, 167. Sometimes God takes vengeance in order to perfect; sometimes in order to condemn. IV, 710. Whatever is divinely avenged before the final judgment should be believed to serve not the destruction of human beings but their healing. VIII, 173. Do not murmur because God does not avenge himself upon the wicked, lest you be among those upon whom he does take vengeance. IV, 1196. Do not, because you have crossed over, wish to overturn God’s bridge of mercy. IV, 1196. Final vengeance is rightly demanded when no opportunity for correction remains. II, 530. How God’s vengeance extending to the third and fourth generation is to be understood. VIII, 137. The Manichaeans raged against the temporal acts of vengeance found in the Old Testament. III, 1263. Whether the two Testaments contradict each other concerning vengeance. VIII, 139. How the saints desire vengeance. IV, [Col. 0659] 1017. See “To Repay Evil.” How God’s elect pray that they may be vindicated. III, 1359.

There is a kind of just vengeance. VIII, 363. Good people can perform acts of vengeance with a good disposition. III, 1326. Vengeance against an enemy can proceed with love. VIII, 158, 159, 160. Vengeance is owed to nothing except sin. X, 166, 167. The twofold vengeance of sin: accompanying and consequent. VIII, 394. Whether and how vengeance should be carried out. IX, 83. With what disposition holy men carried out bodily vengeance. III, 1262. Vengeance that serves correction is not forbidden. III, 1261. Vengeance can be exercised both upon the body and upon the soul. VIII, 173. How vengeance should be carried out. VIII, 161. Vengeance must be carried out only by divine authority. VIII, 161. What the proper measure of vengeance is. I, 1006. To what extent vengeance should be exercised by rulers. VII, 171. Excess in vengeance. VII, 107. Vengeance easily exceeds the proper measure. III, 1258. You are permitted to avenge yourself because it is just; see whether you do not have something in yourself that ought to be avenged, and avenge that. IV, 1325. God does not restrain the justice of vengeance but extinguishes the pride of the avenger. IV, 1325. A person boasts vainly when, although he himself is human, he desires to avenge himself upon another human being and, while openly seeking to overcome a person, is secretly overcome by the devil. IV, 99.

What retaliation is. VI, 21. Innate force implanted this in us. VI, 20. How unjust the desire for vengeance is. V, 396. Pride produces the desire for vengeance. V, 634. The solace of vengeance is usually sought in what cannot be restored. III, 1261. Vengeance feeds the soul on another’s misfortune. II, 186. To avenge oneself is to feed on another’s misfortune. V, 1057. The person eager for vengeance seeks a remedy in another’s punishment and finds great torment. V, 684. It is a dreadful temptation to wish to take revenge. V, 391. Vengeance must not be sought. III, 708. We do not strive to feed our anger by avenging the past, but labor mercifully to provide for the future. II, 317. The desire for vengeance must be restrained by Christ’s example. V, 54, 396, 424, 684, 1396. A Christian must not inflict punishment out of a lust for revenge. II, 391. A Christian has not learned to avenge himself but to endure. IV, 255. One must beware lest patience be lost through the desire for vengeance; patience must be valued more highly than anything an enemy can take away even against one’s will. II, 530. Far be it from a Christian heart to be carried away to punish anyone by a lust for revenge. II, 391. Those who bitterly ask God for vengeance against an enemy are corrected. V, 1058. What the command to forgo vengeance altogether implies. VIII, 364, 367.

The vineyard planted by God. V, 531. Laborers hired for the vineyard. V, 320.

First fruits of wine offered in libation to idols. III, 2085. Why the Severians do not drink wine. VIII, 30. For the Manichaeans, drinking wine is not religion but sacrilege. VIII, 337, 379. The Manichaeans do not drink wine, although they eat grapes. VIII, 37. Why the Apostle said that not drinking wine is good. VIII, 149. The ability to drink wine without measure is considered either a gift of God or at least a pleasant, agreeable, and lawful good. V, 828. Whoever can do this receives the name of a strong man: all the worse, the more unconquerable he is under the cup. V, 828. Abstinence from wine during Lent. V, 1043, 1052.

The viper. The Jews are called “a generation of vipers” because of their conduct. V, 679.

The first partnership of man and wife. VI, 373. Whether several women may lawfully be joined to one man. X, 419. It was sometimes permitted for one man to have several wives, but never for one woman to have several husbands. VI, 387. Why. X, 419. Adulterous husbands are to be punished more severely than adulterous wives. VI, 474, 475. The immodesty of men is worse. VI, 475. Men ought to surpass women in chastity. VI, 486. It belongs to men both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example. VI, 475. The man is the head of the woman and ought to precede her in every good deed. V, 77. A man is not the head of a woman in what he does wrongly. V, 83. Is the domination of man a punishment for woman or the order of nature? X, 1566. A man is placed over his wife not to mock the weaker sex but according to the law of sincere love. I, 1336. In governing his wife, a man ought to resemble in spirit one who governs the flesh. VII, 443. It belongs to the man to command and to the woman to obey. III, 1395. Those who hate their brothers are men of blood. IV, 1801. By “man” a human being is understood from the more honorable sex, according to a mode of expression in which the whole is signified by a part. IV, 1511.

A virile woman. III, 963.

Strength. Nothing should be attributed to one’s own strength. III, 604. See “Power.”

## Rod

What many remarkable things Christ did with a rod. VI, 698. The rod: Mary, the rod; Christ, the rod; the cross, the rod. VI, 698. What the rod of Moses, changed into a serpent, prefigured. V, 61, 67. It was a figure of the Lord’s Passion. IV, 933. The rod enclosed in the ark, a symbol of power. III, 633. The rod of discipline. V, 1649. Even the good are ruled with an iron rod. III, 1075. The rod of Christ’s kingdom rules spiritual people and crushes carnal people. IV, 505. It is better to be instructed with a father’s rod than to perish through a robber’s flattery. IV, 1131. The colors of the rods that Jacob varied, by applying them, pass over into the souls of the animals’ mothers. [Col. 0660] X, 812. The blows of rods, a method of correction often accustomed to be employed in judgments by teachers, parents, and bishops. II, 509. It is also employed in the investigation of crimes. II, 509.

## Virgil the Poet

I, 671; VIII, 1047, 1050, 1079. The rhetorician from Mantua. II, 82. He sold words to the Romans. V, 623. Virgil had read much history supported by ancient authority. II, 84. Virgil praised by Augustine. III, 2089. Why Virgil is read by boys. VII, 16. Two verses of Virgil especially suitable to Christ. II, 521, 1073; VII, 305. Virgil’s opinion concerning punishments after death. VII, 727. A passage of Virgil. V, 622. Another passage contrary to it. V, 623. Passages of Virgil. II, 81, 84; VI, 239, 242, 253, 588, 593, 601.

## Virginity

Virginity received its name from abstinence from illicit things. V, 574, 575. Virginity is an imitation of heavenly life. VI, 398. It is an angelic portion and, in corruptible flesh, a continual meditation on incorruption. VI, 401. Even bodily virginity is itself spiritual. VI, 400. Virginity is honored because it is dedicated to God. VI, 400. The vow of virginity. VI, 412. The marking out of virginity. II, 229. Some vow virginity from an early age. IV, 967. A higher rank in the Church belongs to those who have vowed virginity. III, 1459. Those who vow virginity are not without marriage. III, 1459. Ambrose shows what virgins who have already taken the vow ought to be like. III, 113. Those who have vowed virginity lead the life of angels on earth. V, 736. They begin before death to be what the others will be after the resurrection. V, 736. Nor should they loosen the restraints of desire even with regard to things that are permitted. V, 736. Praise of the virginal profession. II, 645. Virginity is a work of supererogation, not a commandment. VI, 412. By divine law virginity is piously preferred to marriage. VI, 397. Jovinian equated the virginity of nuns and the celibate continence of holy men choosing a chaste life with the merits of chaste marriages. I, 639; VIII, 45. Virginity, which is not commanded, is more than conjugal chastity, which is commanded. X, 337. Virginity is to be preferred to marriage. X, 142. It is preferred to marriage. X, 416. No conjugal fertility can be compared with it. VI, 399, 400. Two contrary errors concerning virginity and marriage: one equating marriage with virginity, the other condemning marriage. VI, 405, 407. Virginity should be preferred in such a way that marriages are not condemned. VI, 404. Virginity is preferred to marriage not as good to evil, but as something better to something good. X, 1418. Virginity and chastity are not genuine unless devoted to the true faith. X, 416. To preserve virginity is more than conjugal chastity. X, 337. Because Catholics preferred holy virginity to marriage, Jovinian once called them Manichaeans. X, 458. Marriage should not for that reason be set alongside virginity, because it produces virgins. VI, 401. The birth of one virgin is the glory of all virgins. VI, 398, 399. Christ, the Son of a virgin and the bridegroom of virgins. VI, 397. How the dignity of virginity began with the Lord’s mother. V, 348. Christ’s birth according to the flesh from a virgin signified that his members according to the Spirit would be born from a virgin. VI, 399. Virginity could fittingly give birth only to the one who at his birth could have no equal. VI, 399. Mary’s virginity was dedicated to God by a vow before she heard about conceiving Christ. VI, 398.

Virginity is disgraceful without virtues. IV, 968. Virginity must be guarded by humility. VI, 396. Humility is especially commended to virgins. VI, 412, 413, 414. The greater virgins are, the more they should humble themselves in everything. V, 1020. The holier they are, the more humble they should be. VI, 427. A humble marriage is better than proud virginity. IV, 968, 1280. In what manner humility should be practiced by virgins. VI, 426, 427. What a virgin should think, so that she may not dare truthfully to prefer herself to a woman or to a married woman. VI, 422. So that a virgin may not become inflated, let her consider that perhaps she cannot suffer for Christ what a married woman might be able to suffer. VI, 424. The first thought of humility is that virginity is possessed as a gift from God. VI, 420, 422. God, the guardian of virginity, who gave it, dwells with the humble. VI, 426. Virgins should not despise married holy fathers. VI, 397. They should not consider themselves better than them. VI, 394. Nor should they think themselves free from sin here. VI, 425. The guardian of virginity is charity; the dwelling of this guardian is humility. VI, 426. The guardianship of chastity rests solely on charity. III, 2141. Many perplexities concerning marriage, widowhood, and virginity. VI, 442. If the heart is corrupted, the body’s virginity is useless. IV, 1168. Virginity in the flesh belongs to few; virginity in the heart ought to belong to all. IV, 1920; V, 575. If sacred virginity is lost through an unchaste will, one may return to chastity, but not to virginity. X, 1543, 1544. Lost virginity is compensated by no fertility of the flesh. VI, 400. A virgin who would not sin if she married; but if a nun marries, she will be regarded as an adulteress against Christ. IV, 1058.

Virginity of the flesh: an untouched body; virginity of the heart: an incorrupt faith. IV, 1920.

Virginity of the mind. V, 1495. Virginity of the mind: faith, hope, and charity. III, 1499. All ought to be virgins in faith. V, 1064. The virginity of faith exists among married people. V, 574. Virginity outside the Church is of no benefit. IV, 513. The virginity of the Church. [Col. 0661] V, 1005, 1010, 1063. The whole Church is called a virgin. IV, 1920; V, 575.

Virginity is commended. V, 996. Christ willed virginity to be free. VI, 398. Virginity is commended not by commandment but by counsel, in order to win a singular glory in the future life. VI, 402. Virginity should be loved not for this life but for the future one. VI, 407. Faithful and devout virginity has great merit, and merit of great honor, before God; hence—. III, 397. Those who preserve virginity should not immediately be judged to observe all the commandments of the Law and the Gospel. X, 337. Encomium of virginity. III, 112. Ambrose inflames virgins, with great eloquence, to undertake the purpose of virginity. III, 113. Augustine’s book On Holy Virginity. I, 640. “Virgin” is a name of integrity, not of age. III, 492. “Virgin” is a name of age, according to the Hebrew language. III, 575. Virgins were sometimes called women. III, 529. The integrity of a certain virgin was destroyed when a midwife examined it, as it were, by hand. VII, 32. Virgins are a more honorable member of Christ. III, 1499. Anyone who has not admitted corruption through the senses is counted among virgins. IV, 1920. Anyone who abstains from illicit movements of the senses. V, 574. The glorious struggles of holy virgins. X, 724. Virgins named for their distinctive and excellent holiness, also called nuns. V, 574. Their multitude. V, 574. Love makes sacred virgins. V, 883. Many also overcame the contrary efforts of their parents through the fire of heavenly love. V, 884. Fear is necessary for virgins themselves—not worldly or servile fear, but the chaste fear of God. VI, 418. Virgins still need to be given precepts concerning the very integrity of chastity. VI, 415. Virgins who regret their profession and purpose would do better to marry than to burn. VI, 415. After baptism, a woman who had been violated while a catechumen cannot be consecrated among God’s virgins. VI, 387. An obedient married woman is to be preferred to a disobedient virgin. VI, 422. A more obedient married woman is to be preferred to a less obedient virgin. VI, 392, 393. Mary is proposed to virgins for imitation. V, 1011.

The virgin’s womb, the bridegroom’s bridal chamber. IV, 161. The bridal chamber of the nuptial union of the Word and the flesh. IV, 495.

Virgins who strive to please people with more elegant clothing are reproved. VI, 415. Virgins do not maintain their profession merely through their manner of dress. X, 799. The number of virgins is greater among Catholics than that of women. VIII, 492.

Virgins themselves are mothers of Christ in the spirit. VI, 399. Why the birth of Christ is a cause of joy for virgins. VI, 664. Virgins should love their bridegroom with their whole heart. VI, 427, 428. The future glory of virgins is greater, with certain joys peculiar to them in heaven. VI, 410. To follow the Lamb wherever he goes is proper to virgins. VI, 411. The song of virgins, which no one else can sing. VI, 410. Virgins bear the sixtyfold fruit. III, 1325. Whether the virginal life is indicated by the hundredfold fruit. VI, 423. Exhortation to Virgins. III, 112. The martyr Cyprian wrote about the dress of virgins, not about undertaking the purpose of virginity. III, 113.

The parable of the wise and foolish virgins is explained. II, 571, 572; V, 573; VI, 44, 45. The five virgins in the Gospel signify all the souls that will enter the kingdom of heaven. IV, 1920. Virgins who do not bring oil. V, 804. The foolish virgins are those for whom conscience is insufficient. IV, 1921. And those who are stirred to good works not by the strength of a good conscience but by the prompting of another’s tongue. IV, 1921.

Games were exhibited for the Heavenly Virgin. VII, 50.

The goddess Virginiensis. VII, 122, 188.

The green of the field allegorically. III, 198.

Virtue seems to have been named from *vir* (“man”). II, 894, 1257. The pagans made Virtue a goddess. VII, 127. Virtue is not a goddess but a gift of God. VII, 127, 128.

What virtue of the soul is. V, 812. Definition of virtue from Cicero. X, 747. Virtue is called a habit and, as it were, a quality of a wise soul. I, 1314. Virtue is a habit of the soul consistent with nature and reason. VI, 20. Virtue is called a certain equality of life, everywhere agreeing with reason. I, 1050. Virtue is called either right or perfect reason. I, 876. Virtue is enjoying the things to be enjoyed and using the things to be used. VI, 19. The virtue of a rational creature is its conversion to the unchangeable good. II, 561. Virtue is the art of living well and rightly. VII, 128, 258, 789. Virtue is the art of attaining immortal happiness. VII, 128, 258, 789. Virtue is the order of love. VII, 467, 468. The true and unconquered virtue is charity. V, 1397. Virtue is charity, by which what ought to be loved is loved. II, 671, 673, 739. Virtue leading to the happy life is nothing other than the highest love of God. I, 1322.

What true virtue is. VII, 156, 636. Where the Pythagorean and Platonic philosophers placed true virtue. X, 745. Whether those who naturally do the things of the law possess true virtues. X, 750. This is true and the only virtue: not to serve arrogance, but God. V, 1293. No true virtue exists without true piety. VII, 166, 631. If anything praiseworthy naturally stands out in a person, it is purified and perfected only by true piety. VII, 77. Virtues are distinguished from vices not by their acts but by their ends. [Col. 0662] X, 749, 751. True virtues must serve God. X, 749. Unless virtues are referred to God, they are rather vices than virtues. VII, 656. Whatever a person may have done as though rightly, unless it is referred to the piety that is directed toward God, it ought not to be called right. VI, 204. Virtue of the soul is from God. V, 812. The virtue of the soul does not make one blessed; rather, the one who gave virtue does. V, 812. True virtues are not those that do not aim at eternal happiness. II, 670. Nor those that do not help a person attain true blessedness. X, 747. Christian virtues had to be commended not only for the harmonious fellowship of earthly society but also for attaining eternal salvation. II, 533. Virtues without faith are not true. X, 750. The virtues of unbelievers are not true. X, 751. Whether they are gifts of God. X, 744. Julian’s objection, defending the virtues of unbelievers, is answered. X, 751. The virtues of the pagans are sterile through empty glory. II, 710. Virtue is not true when it serves human glory. VII, 166, 167. Virtues serve human glory as shamefully as they serve bodily pleasure. VII, 166, 167. Virtues referred to themselves are inflated and proud. VII, 656.

Virtue is to be sought for its own sake. VII, 626. It is to be sought solely for its own sake. VI, 21. Virtue seeks everything for its own sake, even itself. VII, 626. Virtue makes good use both of itself and of the other goods that make a person blessed. VII, 626. Virtue places none of all the goods, whether of soul or body, before itself. VII, 626. Virtue loves, uses, and enjoys the primary goods, or goods of nature, for their own sake. VII, 625. No one makes bad use of virtues. I, 597, 1267. Goods of the body, even if diminished, do not diminish virtue. VII, 31. The soul that follows itself in order to attain virtue follows something foolish. I, 1314. Here virtue does nothing except wage perpetual wars against vices. VII, 629. Virtue wages perpetual wars against vices, not so that this life may be free of miseries, but so that it may be blessed—and saved—by hope of the future age. VII, 631. If the corruptible body did not weigh down the soul, a person would not strive toward virtue but would obey his God easily and happily, without effort. X, 1513. From its seat in the soul, virtue commands the bodily members. VII, 30. Whoever has virtues from the Spirit of God also loves enemies. VII, 127.

Virtue is the most excellent good among the goods of the soul. VII, 626. Nothing better or more useful than virtue is found here in a human being. VII, 631. The Stoics hold that no good of a human being exists apart from virtue. VII, 258. True virtue cannot exist except in a just person. X, 745. Virtues are goods among goods. X, 211. Virtue makes the soul most excellent. I, 1313. Virtues, by which one lives rightly, are great goods. I, 597, 1267. Virtue or vice is the reason for which we love or hate. III, 1859. How virtue is perfected in weakness. X, 742. The perfection of virtue is not to be despaired of. X, 673.

The virtues that exist in the human soul are not separated from one another. VIII, 927. All philosophers have approved that virtues are inseparable. II, 735. That opinion is proved. II, 735, 736, 737, 738. Zeno maintained the connection of the virtues. X, 1063. Although virtues are connected, one is nevertheless greater than another in one and the same person. II, 740. Virtue does not exist here without some vice. II, 737, 738, 740. In great souls certain virtues resemble the vices of lesser people. VIII, 417. A vice neighboring each virtue is found. VI, 21, 22. Two virtues are necessary here: self-control and endurance. V, 235.

Four kinds of virtue. VII, 127. The four parts of virtue: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. VI, 20, 51. The four virtues for the conduct of life: prudence, etc. IV, 1065, 1066. The order and connection of the theological virtues. IV, 261. From the various movements of the love of God arise those four virtues: prudence, justice, etc. I, 1322. How they are defined. I, 1235, 1332. The duties of the four virtues tend toward the love of God. I, 1330. The river of the earthly paradise divided into four parts signifies the four virtues. III, 203. The grades of virtues must be distinguished by one who applies his mind to the sacred Scriptures. VI, 34, 35. Virtues can exist both as habit and in action. VI, 390. Virtue, or wisdom, is compared with light; vice, or folly, with darkness. II, 738.

Virtues: justice, self-control, etc., do not arise from our own powers. II, 849, 850. Our virtues are not things that chance can give or take away. I, 916. The virtues with which the soul is adorned are from God. III, 1685. Virtue will not be ours unless God, by whom we are helped, is present. II, 669. No one acts rightly unless aided by divine assistance. VII, 659. Virtue is not from the human being but above the human being; it is what makes a person live happily. VII, 656. The virtue called ours is granted to us by God’s goodness. VII, 300. The virtue granted to us by God’s goodness must be attributed only to God’s grace. VII, 167. Virtue is given solely by God’s grace. VII, 128, 258, 789. True virtue is a gift of grace. X, 762. Why the Pelagians deny that virtues are gifts of God. X, 743. In what sense Pelagius understood that everyone could possess all virtues and graces, and the bishops approved it. X, 339, 340. How invisible power forms our virtues. V, 1498. The virtue of Christ will be in us when our virtue has failed. [Col. 0663] IV, 881, 882. Virtues are not seen by the eyes, and yet are loved. IV, 316. For all the virtues necessary in the valley of tears, Christ will give in heaven one virtue: himself. IV, 1065.

Whether virtues will cease in the future life. VIII, 1045. How virtues will exist and not exist in eternal life. II, 671. Here the same virtues exist in activity, after this life in effect; here in work, there in reward; here in duty, there in the end. II, 672. How virtues will exist in the blessed. I, 1189. The greater virtue that exists in the blessed together with the necessity of doing good. X, 1498. In the blessed life there will be one virtue that embraces all virtues—or rather, that itself will be all virtues. II, 671, 672. Two virtues: one active, the other contemplative. III, 1045. In heaven there will be one virtue, namely, contemplation of God. IV, 1066. Virtue is the way to glory, honor, and dominion. VII, 156. Among the Romans the dwellings of virtue and honor were joined. VII, 156. The virtues of the Romans are necessary examples of admonition for Christians. VII, 165. How much civic virtues achieved in the Roman Empire even without true religion. II, 533. The Romans preserved a certain integrity characteristic of their people. II, 533. True and only virtue. V, 1293.

## Force

Where the greater powers of the body come from. I, 1056. To repel force with force by killing someone who attempts to inflict sexual violation or death is illicit. I, 1227. Force may be used to compel someone toward good. II, 754, 757, 802, 803.

Nothing visible exists that is not changeable. VIII, 881. Three kinds of visible things. II, 457.

## Vision

“To see” is used in a general sense not only of the body but also of the mind. III, 623, 1958; V, 646. What difference there is between seeing and believing. II, 599, 600. When the desire to see God is evidence of gratuitous love. V, 965.

What vision is. VIII, 985, 986. How it occurs. I, 1058. From a visible thing arises the vision, or image, of the thing that is seen. VIII, 986, 987. How. VIII, 987. Vision through the emission of rays from the eyes. III, 258. The light that exists in the sense of the one seeing is not sufficient for seeing. III, 258. The view of Epicurus and Democritus that vision occurs through images coming to the eyes; they are refuted by Cicero. II, 446, 447. Those who do not attribute vision except to bodies should not be heeded. II, 620. Vision is not of either a more distant or a nearer thing. V, 1265.

Threefold vision: intellectual, spiritual, and bodily. VII, 286, 287. Note (a). One vision occurs through the eyes of the body, another through the mind’s gaze. II, 597, 599. What we see through the mind’s gaze. II, 597, 599, 613, 616. Nor is that vision to be despised: seeing what you do not know. II, 597. When the intellectual soul sees God through intellectual vision, it also sees him above itself. III, 480. Whether there are several levels in spiritual and intellectual vision. III, 478. There is a certain trinity in vision. VIII, 985. The three things that exist in vision differ by their nature. VIII, 986. How these three come together into one. VIII, 987.

The vision of God is twofold: one belongs to this time, the other to the future; the latter is by sight, the former by faith. IV, 1609, 1951. It is rightly said that we know God can be seen. II, 601. The Arians considered the Father invisible, but the Son and the Holy Spirit visible. II, 605, 626. Jerome’s view that not only the divinity of the Father, but also that of the Son and the Holy Spirit, cannot be seen by the eyes of the flesh. II, 622. There is no doubt that God’s nature is not seen in a place. II, 619. Ambrose proves by his authority that God is invisible to the eyes of the flesh. II, 603, 627. Jerome does likewise. II, 622, 623. So do Athanasius and Gregory. II, 626. Moses desired to see God in the substance in which God is. III, 477. It is probable that he saw him in this way. III, 477. God was not seen by Moses and other holy people in his own nature, but in the form in which he had wished to appear. II, 605, 607, 618, 626, 628. It is strange if Moses was not granted what he asked: to see God here as he is. II, 610. It is not unbelievable that this grace was granted to some who had not yet died, especially Paul. II, 610. But the mind must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision. II, 610. No one sees God in the form in which God is unless he first in some way dies to this life. III, 477, 478; V, 931. The divine substance cannot be known to a human being as it is known to itself. III, 301. The human mind cannot see the divine substance as the holy angels see it. III, 483. Even concerning the heavenly powers themselves we read, “No one has ever seen God,” from Ambrose. II, 602. In what sense. II, 602, 606, 609, 612. Seeing is one thing; comprehending the whole through seeing is another. II, 605. Some think that those who will rise to life will see God through the body. II, 619. Some have said that God is to be seen by the wicked and that he was seen by the devil. II, 602. They are refuted. II, 607, 608. The Manichaeans maliciously allege, according to our Scriptures, that the vision of the divine substance was granted to the devil. V, 104. Through the desire to see God, a devout life must be led by faith in this sorrowful pilgrimage. VII, 547. Vision face to face, the supreme reward promised to the just. VIII, 841, 844. Christ will be visible at the future judgment. V, 1267. Many questions about the vision of God are touched upon and resolved. [Col. 0664] II, 613. Scriptural testimonies that seem to speak contradictorily about seeing God are reconciled. II, 602. Concerning the vision of God, for the present it is enough to know that Christ as man sees the Father as he is seen by the Father. II, 620, 707. Whether the saints will see God through the body. VII, 797. The saints will see God in the very body. VII, 797. Some say that God will be seen through the body, but through a body that will already be spirit. II, 619, 623. Evodius confirms that God’s substance cannot be seen even by any glorified body, including the Lord’s own body. II, 703, 704. Augustine also confirms it. II, 707. By death the soul does not take away any body from the body. II, 253. Yet it removes certain eyes very similar to bodily eyes, with which it sees things very similar to those seen in dreams—but these too are not bodily. II, 253. When we have a spiritual body, we shall see the Trinity, whether with the mind or, in a wondrous manner, also with the body. II, 460. Whether God can be seen by the outer person or cannot be seen, it is certain that he will be seen by the inner person. II, 628. We can see God with the mind or with the inner sight of the heart. V, 670. God can be seen by the soul alone, yet not as the soul itself is seen. IV, 469. The vision of God face to face is reserved for the resurrection. IV, 485. The vision of God as he is, in the other life. III, 1779. In the heavenly homeland. III, 1662. What things draw one away from the vision of the Word. III, 1540. Angels enjoy the vision of the Word; animals turn away from it. Whoever desires it stands between the two. III, 1540. In heaven you will read the laws in the Word without a book. V, 181. What the vision of God will be like. VII, 797. We should not imagine a bodily face when the Apostle says that we will see God face to face. II, 620. No creature sees the face of God according to the property of his nature. II, 625. The vision of the God who sees. V, 441. When the one God is seen, the Trinity is seen. IV, 1075. There is no difference between the vision of the Father and the vision of the Son. IV, 1075. Nothing is more sublime than the vision of God. X, 601. What kind of rest and fulfillment of the will should be understood in the vision. VIII, 992. Without the vision of God, even if endowed with every other good, one is most unhappy, according to Plotinus as well. VII, 294. The vision and love of God both satisfies and does not satisfy. IV, 1100. The vision of the Savior will distress those who delight in illicit things. IV, 1916. The vision of God is our end. V, 366. To see God and praise God—this himself will be the harbor of our labors. V, 235. As this light is joy to healthy eyes and torment to unhealthy ones, so God is joy to pure hearts and torment to impure ones. V, 366. How great is the happiness of seeing God’s face. V, 931. Supreme happiness. V, 711. The reward of all the saints. VII, 518. The reward of faith. III, 1830. The vision of God after this life. III, 1654. The vision of Christ is our entire reward. IV, 1170. Hearts are cleansed by faith so that they may be fit to see God. IV, 1640.

The vision of God is specifically promised to the pure in heart. V, 368. God will be seen only by peacemakers. V, 162. See “Appearance of God.” The vision of God is reached through faith and good works. V, 103, 367, 571. Live well and presume that you will see the one by whom you are seen, but whom you cannot see if you live badly. V, 442. The proud think that they can be purified for seeing God by their own virtue; why they think this. VIII, 901. The faithful person ought to believe what he does not yet see in such a way that he both hopes for and loves the vision. II, 457.

Various kinds of visions. VIII, 171. Three kinds of visions. III, 458. Bodily, spiritual, and intellectual. III, 459. These will exist in the blessed. III, 484. How. III, 484. Bodily, spiritual, and intellectual visions occur in the same soul. III, 474. Bodily vision cannot exist without spiritual vision. III, 474. Spiritual vision can exist without bodily vision. III, 475. Bodily and spiritual vision can deceive; intellectual vision alone does not deceive. III, 475. In the other kinds, being deceived is not always harmful. III, 465. Bodily vision is referred to spiritual vision, and spiritual vision to intellectual vision. III, 462, 463. Intellectual vision is superior to spiritual, and spiritual to bodily. III, 474. Why the spiritual kind of visions is so called. III, 460. This kind is superior to the others. III, 458. The intellectual kind of vision. III, 461. In intellectual vision, the things seen in the soul are one thing, and the light by which it is itself illuminated is another. III, 479.

Causes of visions. III, 469. Visions sometimes arise from the body, sometimes from the spirit. III, 470. Things seen that have their cause in the body are not exhibited by the body. III, 470. They occur in two ways. III, 471. In the spiritual kind of vision, some things seen are, as it were, divine; others human. III, 479. Prophetic visions. X, 544. How angels introduce visions into minds is difficult to explain. VI, 260. The human spirit is not taken up by a good spirit to see visions unless the visions signify something. III, 472. Visions whose cause is in the body do not always signify something. III, 472. There are visions that appear to the spirit as though to bodily senses, through incorporeal forms resembling bodies. II, 747. In things seen, incorporeal things have the likeness of bodies. VII, 725. The things seen by dreamers are very similar to those seen by people who are awake. VIII, 1074. Blind people have more visions while asleep than while awake. III, 471. Things seen resembling bodies, into which the soul is snatched while awake, are not of a different nature. III, 472. How those things seen occur, from which divinations are made by hidden instinct or by chance, is exceedingly difficult to explain. [Col. 0665] III, 473. Through hidden and truthful visions God sometimes speaks in human hearts. IV, 1395. Every living soul, whether rational or irrational, is moved by things seen. III, 402. It is not in any soul’s power what things seen come to it. III, 403. The rational soul consents to what is seen or does not consent; but the irrational soul, touched by something seen, is driven onward. III, 402, 403. The devil entangles souls with fantastic visions. VII, 288. Through the obedience of angels, things seen reach animals, even the smallest. III, 403.

The apparitions of the dead cannot be denied. VI, 600, 601. Augustine holds that only likenesses of both the living and the dead appear, and indeed through angelic operations. VI, 601, 603, 604. Apparitions of the deranged. VI, 602. The portentous apparitions of Curma the Curial. VI, 602. When people see a dead person in dreams, they think they are seeing his soul; when they see a living person, only his likeness. VI, 601. Examples of apparitions are given. VI, 601, 602. Certain remarkable visions. III, 467. Remarkable visions of a sick boy. III, 468. Visions of the dead. II, 697. The vision in which a devout physician saw a city and heard there the hymns of the blessed. II, 700. The vision of a man who saw himself brought before a judge and beaten so that the marks of the blows appeared. V, 1410. Living people often appear to living people who are asleep, while the people themselves do not know that they are appearing. VI, 600. Augustine, still alive and unaware of it, appears to two sick men. V, 1444, 1445. Augustine, unknowingly, explains a passage of Cicero to Eulogius in a dream. VI, 602.

The sight of the mind must be treated in the same way as the sight of the body. III, 1542.

A visitor appointed by the schismatics. V, 293. The bishop of Siniti, a Donatist, under whose authority a presbyter was sent to visit the Catholics and preach in the house under his jurisdiction. II, 397. Augustine visits the churches belonging to his pastoral care. II, 223.

Some have thought that life is the body’s regulation. I, 1029. Even a dead soul is capable of furnishing life to the body. V, 429. Threefold life: seminal, sensory, and intellectual. VII, 153, 154. The life of trees and shrubs. V, 257. Every kind of life pertains to the highest principle of life. VIII, 94. Nothing can live without God. VIII, 101. To live, understand, remember, and excel with a lively intelligence are divine gifts. III, 1344. We do not have life in ourselves but in God; God, however, has it in himself. V, 710. Life comes from God the giver; death from God the avenger. I, 618. The Platonic view that the living are always made from the dead and the dead from the living. VII, 392. Whether anyone can be simultaneously living and dying. VII, 384. Colorbasus taught that the life and generation of all human beings depend on seven stars. VIII, 28. Each person’s life is best known to himself. VIII, 103. No one can be unaware that he is alive. VI, 242. Why human beings—and even beasts—not only sense that they themselves are alive but also that others and we ourselves are alive. VIII, 953. The misery of this life. I, 795; VII, 631, 632. To this life belong weeping and groaning. III, 1655. In this life false happiness is true misery. IV, 1099. In this life there are labor, oppression, tribulation, and temptation. IV, 559. This life is laborious. V, 402. To those who understand, this whole life is tribulation. V, 687. This life is true unhappiness and lying happiness. V, 1386. A life amid pains is not properly life. V, 813, 1402. Human beings do not enter the miseries of this life according to the merits of some previous life. II, 984. The whole life of a human being upon earth consists of his afflictions. IV, 1635. Life was made penal for us by the first sin. VII, 729. Mortal life itself is entirely punishment. VII, 728. It is the wrath of God. VII, 738. The wrath of God is not now greater over the children of Adam, because they live much less long than the ancients lived. IV, 1144. In this life many things seem prosperous to us that are adverse, and adverse things that are prosperous. III, 2076. In this world it is impossible not to fear, suffer, labor, or be in danger; but the cause makes a difference. II, 938. The good things with which the Creator filled this life, although it is subject to sin. VII, 788. The goods or evils of this life are intermediate things and, in comparison with eternal things, nothing. V, 938. The life of mortals is most miserable in comparison with the blessed life. VII, 648. To begin from a life entangled in carnal senses is a necessity; to persist in it is a matter of the will. II, 539. This life says to its lovers, “I am foul, I am hard, I am fleeting.” V, 1388. Love of this sorrowful life. V, 1281, 1385, 1388. Even a bad life is preferred by a person to all earthly goods. V, 122. How many labors, dangers, and deaths lovers of this transitory life undertake for its sake. II, 483. Eternal life commands its lovers nothing great when it commands itself to be loved in the way this life is loved by its own lovers. II, 484. To preserve life, human beings undergo every kind of labor. II, 483, 484. Many, in preserving it, even place eternal salvation in danger. II, 484.

### The brevity of life

The brevity of life. V, 128, 688. The whole life of a human being consists of a few days. IV, 373. As long as the age of the world revolves, understand that it is a point. IV, 234. That which has an end is not long. IV, 234. The longest human life is a morning breeze. IV, 361. The whole life of mortals hastens onward, and what appears more extended is a vapor only somewhat longer-lasting. IV, 996. Human life is vapor. V, 136, 687, 1387. Rather the shadow of life than life. V, 1538. The shadow of life: the life in which Adam was created. X, 1523. If Adam were still living and were to die today, it would profit nothing that he had lived so long. IV, 234. The present life is not even life. V, 121. It is conducted as though in dreams. V, 243. The human race is a mime; its whole life is one of temptation. IV, 1686. This life is death. IV, 1889. It is more truly death than life. V, 1522. It is called the dwelling-place of pilgrimage. III, 591. Human life decreases as it grows. V, 122, 237, 638. The course of life runs toward death. VII, 383. What is living long except running toward the end? V, 633. From the moment a person begins to live, he begins to die. VII, 383. The length of the lives of the first human beings, which— VII, 447, 448. How it is said that human life after the Flood would last one hundred and twenty years. VII, 471. Pliny also relates that in his own time a certain people lived for two hundred years. VII, 448. The first stage of human life, namely infancy and childhood, is devoted to the five senses. VI, 43. It ought not to be called life, but an everlasting and immortal torment. V, 813. This intermediate life is lived between the highest goods and the highest evils. V, 938. This life should be for you like an inn for a traveler, not like a house for an inhabitant. IV, 326. No one leaves this life except through death. VII, 553. Nothing makes the length of this life perceptible except the hope of living. IV, 96. Words by which the length of the human day and of this life is desired are words of sins, and so forth. II, 545. A long life is a long illness. V, 495; VI, 329. Make it good, and do not fear that it may be short. V, 122. Let life be loved, but let it be good. V, 1360, 1362. If life is to be long, let it itself be long in goodness. V, 245, 513. If life is to be long, it will be better if it is good. V, 513. If you wish to live badly, a long life will not be a true good, but a long evil. V, 122. The present life is night. III, 1654, 1655. What is living long except being tormented for a long time? V, 520. It is night for as long as this life is being lived. IV, 973, 1147, 1792. The present life is called the sea. III, 772. The worldly life is the abyss. IV, 874. The end of life is uncertain. V, 76, 1111. Why this mortal life was called an uncertain life by Coelestius. X, 395. Let us give thanks to God because he willed the final day of this life to be both short and uncertain. V, 688. We should not be concerned with how quickly, or by what kind of death, this life comes to an end. VII, 25. It is not a great thing to live long, or to live forever; but it is a great thing to live happily. V, 706.

### Life

Life. What it means to live well. V, 1106. The Latins use one name, *vita*, for both the life by which a person lives and the life by which someone is said to be of good character; the Greeks use two names. VIII, 410. Life cannot be good or bad before birth. III, 345. The human being has a twofold life. II, 539, 540. Spiritual life and spiritual death. III, 1576, 1577. What spiritual life is. III, 1547. Human life before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. III, 2138, 2139. The life of the human race is twofold: one according to the body before Christ, the other according to the soul after Christ’s coming. IV, 90, 91. The old life and the new life; mortal life and life that truly lives. IV, 1149. The new life was signified by Christ’s resurrection. IV, 340. What is meant by spiritual and bodily life in an unformed state. III, 247. The life of the faithful lived in this flesh may be called light and day in comparison with the life of unbelievers and the ungodly. III, 312. In comparison with the blessed life, however, it is night. III, 312, 313. That is the life of human beings in which the true light is present. III, 837. Intellectual life, unless it turned toward the Creator to be illuminated, would drift about without form. III, 253.

How the good life is to be ordered. IV, 811, 812. A good and honorable life is formed in no other way than by loving those things that ought to be loved, in the way they ought to be loved. II, 524. Nothing else should be a matter of concern regarding how one lives except choosing what ought to be loved. V, 585. Faith that works through love is itself the good life. VI, 224. To live well is to love God with the whole heart, the whole mind, and the whole soul. I, 1330. The rule of life, strengthened by the authority of both Testaments, is— I, 1329. The life of the soul is to run toward the fountain of life, so that it may see light in God’s light. V, 1059. Life under God, life with God, life from God, life that is God himself: such a life is promised to us eternally. V, 1363. The life of souls, and, as it were, the life of lives, is righteousness. II, 461. The person who practices judgment and righteousness lives rightly. VII, 531. A good life is like a stylus: it writes the good that is heard upon the heart. IV, 1216. A person is called human when he lives according to man; God when he lives according to God. V, 589. What it means to live according to God. VII, 407. What it means to live according to humanity. VII, 407. To live according to humanity is the same as to live according to the flesh. VI, 355. Carnal life is to be understood as arising not only from bodily vices but also from vices of the mind. VII, 403. From what source come the life and death both of the body and of the soul? X, 113. The life of the ungodly is false; they do not live, but only seem to themselves to live. IV, 690. What a wasteful life is. II, 1344. Life in sins is called death in comparison with a righteous life. VIII, 100. An evil life blasphemes God. IV, 1899, 1900. The case of those who knowingly lead a most wicked life is not milder than that of those who do so unknowingly; indeed, it is more serious precisely for this reason. VI, 227. Our life is love; our death is hatred. IV, 633, 635. Where the life of the heart resides. II, 564, 565. The life of the body is the soul; the life of the soul is God. IV, 893; V, 415, 428, 853, 880, 975, 1059. If the soul lives according to the flesh, or even according to itself, it fails. V, 853. Who lives according to the flesh, who according to the soul, and who according to God. V, 853. Life is misshapen where virtue serves pleasure as its mistress. VII, 622. The person who obeys God when he commands lives rightly. VII, 531. Let each person live not for himself but for Christ, doing not his own will but Christ’s. II, 569. We are stirred to live well by the daily dangers we face. V, 136. The person who wishes to live well pays more attention to God’s promises and threats than to those of this world. V, 201. Life must be corrected quickly. V, 75, 511. People wish to have every good thing except life. V, 122, 140, 512, 1482. If we live well, we have both died and risen again. V, 1105. The person who lives badly does not live: let him die, so that he may not die; that is, let him be changed, so that he may not be condemned. V, 1105. We ought to repent of this life because it is subject to corruption and temptations. V, 1537.

### The temptations and conditions of this life

The temptations of the spiritual life. II, 352, 353. The dangers and anxiety of this life. V, 1191. The poor consider only the rich to be truly alive. IV, 550. Lovers of the world regard nothing as life except daily pleasures. IV, 561. The life of the poor is for eternity, but labor only until the end; the life of the rich is only until the end, but labor for eternity. IV, 550, 561. The days of this life are days of tribulation; whether in distress or prosperity, everything is to be feared and lamented. IV, 1863, 1864. This life, however brightly it may shine with prosperity, is tribulation for the person who loves the other life. IV, 1781. When it is summer—that is, when life is prosperous—a person ought to gather for himself what will refresh him when winter comes. IV, 804, 805. The sweetness of this life was a snare during persecution. IV, 1647, 1830. Concern for the necessities of life soils the eye and makes the heart divided. III, 1288, 1291. With what disposition the necessities of life should be received. III, 1292. Apart from the obvious foods by which we are sustained externally, God works by a certain hidden act of his beneficence so that a human being may live. X, 731.

### Kinds of life

There are three kinds of life: leisure, activity, and a life tempered from both. VII, 623, 624, 647. In any kind of life, provided faith is preserved, each person can live and attain eternal rewards. VII, 647. The only difference concerns what love of truth holds fast to, and what it devotes to the duty of charity. VII, 647. Human life, when it administers something, is sustained by knowledge and action. VI, 43. The two lives are foreshadowed in Martha and Mary. V, 1188. The characteristics of the active and contemplative lives. III, 1045, 1046. What social life is. VII, 627. Social life belongs to the wise. VII, 631. The common life. VI, 423. The example of the common life among the earliest Christians. V, 1569. If you wish to become known to people, live in such a way even apart from the eyes of people. V, 716. How one who follows the evangelical life should live among the less perfect. II, 352. The fragrance of a good life is for some a fragrance of life, and for others a fragrance of death. III, 1760, 1761.

A good life in us comes from God, not from us. III, 1579. Living well is a divine gift. X, 205, 242. The power to live well is not given by free will, but by God’s grace. X, 552. Even a person who has been justified most perfectly cannot live rightly unless he is divinely assisted by the light of eternal righteousness. X, 260. In a human being himself, unless faith precedes, a good life cannot follow. VI, 204. No one can live rightly and do good works unless he has been justified by faith. VI, 126. A good and honorable life, if it does not arise from faith, is useless. III, 1720. We walk; and living itself is an approach. V, 638. The gods did not give commandments for ordering life. VII, 64, 69, 70, 74. Whoever has received from God the ability to live well should give thanks to him in such a way that he does not insult those who do not yet live well. V, 91.

### Temporal and eternal life

No earthly reward for a good life should be sought. V, 136. A good life cannot be followed by an evil death. VI, 676. Our life is twofold: eternal and temporal. IV, 725; VI, 513. Against those who doubt the other life. V, 1381. And against those who decide that one should live here as though nothing remained after death. V, 1601. Eternal life must be believed by faith. V, 1196. Faith in eternal life is established by the death of the Son of God. IV, 1942. It is more incredible that the eternal one died than that a mortal should live forever. IV, 1942. Testimonies to eternal life from the ancient books. VIII, 368. The pious physician is taught by a twofold vision that life remains after death. II, 699, 700.

If life is loved, why is the true life not sought? VI, 668. If life is loved, let it be acquired where it ends in no death. II, 486. Where the good life and the good day are found. V, 122, 634, 635, 1014. There is no life here. VI, 676. Life without any qualification, life alone, is eternal and blessed life. IV, 1555. Only the blessed life ought to be called life. VII, 666. There is no true life except that which is eternal and blessed. III, 1575; V, 519, 1402, 1403. In comparison with eternal life, the present life is to be reckoned not life but death. II, 223; IV, 1555. God mingles bitterness with even innocent pleasures so that we may love nothing except eternal life. IV, 458, 1793. We should continually sigh for eternal life. III, 1474. With what longing the Prophet sighed for it. III, 1404, 1405. How greatly people neglect eternal life in comparison with temporal life. III, 1747. Eternal life must always be set before the mind. III, 1640. How greatly it should be loved. V, 519, 706, 1385, 1387, 1513, 1515. Christians’ attention ought to be directed toward the life to come. V, 1196, 1650. The entire life of a good Christian is holy desire. III, 2008. Let us not cease asking for eternal life until we reach it. IV, 206. Everyone wishes for the blessed life. V, 1401. One does not live usefully in time except to acquire the merit by which one may live in eternity. II, 499. Everything else that is usefully and decently desired must without doubt be referred to that one life in which one lives with God and from God. II, 499. Because of the life that each person loves, he thinks that everything must be done. VI, 513. Both sufficiency and safety, whether one’s own or that of friends, must be rejected, so long as they are temporal, for the attainment of eternal life. II, 499. Against those who lose eternal life through love of temporal life. V, 1515. For the sake of eternal life, one must not tolerate what the Israelites tolerated for the sake of an idol. III, 644. See *Blessedness*.

The present life is the time for working out salvation. III, 1716. The present life is the time of mercy; after death comes the time of judgment. III, 1782. As you depart from this life, so you will be restored to that life. IV, 361. No one can be fit for the future life who has not trained himself for it. IV, 1937. Eternal life should be promised only to that faith which works through love. VI, 230. To what extent one should run toward the prize of eternal life. X, 301, 302. The reward of eternal life will be given to no one except the person who has acquired for himself its merit in this life. X, 299. After this life, nothing will be granted to anyone that he has not acquired in this life to be granted to him. VIII, 513. How this temporal life should be lived so that one may reach eternal life. II, 354. It is unworthy to despise even all necessities for the sake of transitory life, while refusing to despise superfluities for the sake of eternal life. II, 484, 485. Perishable life is redeemed at the cost of all good things. V, 1514, 1518. The present life must be despised in hope of the future life. V, 1517. A Christian ought not to hesitate to lose temporal life for the eternal life of his neighbor. VI, 495. The time of the present life, or the interval between baptism and the kingdom of heaven, is a time of prayer. X, 336. The present life is in reality a time of labor, but in hope a time of rest; in the flesh it is a life of oldness, but in faith a life of newness. II, 217. The night of this life calls for patience; the day will grant joy. IV, 1853. There is no life without the three dispositions of believing, hoping, and loving. V, 1024. The more we enjoy God—whether through a mirror or in an enigma—the more bearably we endure our pilgrimage and the more ardently desire to bring it to an end. III, 31. For now our life is hope; afterward it will be eternity. IV, 1372. Let life follow where hope goes before. IV, 1774. The life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life. IV, 1389. Temporal life is in faith; eternal life will be in direct vision. III, 1727. There we shall see what we believe. VI, 343. The vision of God. V, 34, 712. The vision of God in the form of God. III, 1572, 1573.

### Eternal life

Eternal life: what it is. VII, 193. Eternal life can be nothing other than the kingdom of God. X, 117, 118, 715. It is sufficiently clear that the blessed life is not found in the pleasure of the senses. II, 65. Eternal life is God himself. V, 1388. In eternal life we shall live with God, from God, and in God. V, 652. Eternal life is Christ. X, 175. The blessed life will come from the Word without a word. V, 925. Eternal life is the whole reward in whose promise we rejoice; it is also the very knowledge of truth. I, 1331. Eternal life is contemplation of truth. V, 1633. The life of the blessed soul is truth. VII, 240. The happiness of eternal life. V, 135, 813, 1090; 651, 660, 686. Its price. V, 707, 1518. Its goods. V, 707, 711. The eternal life of the saints. VI, 342, 343, 347. The exaltation of the saints is eternal life. IV, 1589. The praise of eternal life. III, 1647. In eternal life, nothing in one’s neighbor will be hidden from one’s neighbor. II, 318. In the rest of our homeland there is not lazy inactivity, but an ineffable tranquility of leisurely action. II, 212. In eternal life there will be neither laborious activity nor idle rest. VI, 343. Then the quiet work of charity without end will be to praise what it loves and love what it praises. II, 566. In eternal life there will be neither weariness nor hunger. III, 1405. But there will be the perfection of the justice of peace and of joy. X, 632. See *Perfection*. In the life to come, the desire of the righteous will be satisfied with good things. III, 1808. In the future life there will be no sin, nor any struggle with a desire for sin. X, 600. There will be no concupiscence with which to contend and which we would be commanded not to consent to. X, 153.

The blessed life is not blessed unless it is eternal. V, 1402. If a person is not granted everlasting life, what does living well profit him? III, 1720. In the other life, death is neither anxiously avoided by nature, nor shamefully feared by cowardice, nor bravely endured by wisdom. II, 484. In the righteous, what they love more in this life will be perfected after this life. III, 168. The same is true in the unrighteous. III, 168. The day of eternal life is one day without sunset. IV, 202. The length of days is eternal life. IV, 1169. The longest human life is nothing in comparison with God’s eternity. IV, 1176. Eternal life in rest before the resurrection. III, 1614. Human beings will all receive eternal life at the same time. III, 1751, 1752. The salvation of eternal life will be given to all together at the end. IV, 412. The person who reaches the finish of the stadium first waits to be crowned together with the one who comes later. IV, 441.

Eternal life is called grace. II, 881. Eternal life is grace for grace. X, 893. Yet it is given as though it were owed. III, 1400, 1401. Eternal life is the reward of labor. V, 422. The denarius that each person will receive. III, 1812. Just as death is given as the wages of sin according to the merit of sin, so eternal life is given as the wages of righteousness according to the merit of righteousness. II, 881. Eternal life is a reward and yet is grace. VI, 282. How it is both reward and grace. X, 892, 942. Eternal life is called grace, not because it is not given according to merits, but because the merits themselves have also been given. II, 881. Eternal life is indeed the wages of righteousness, but for you it is grace, since righteousness itself is also grace for you. II, 881. The blessed life is a possession held in common by all. V, 1401. Eternal life is equal for all, but honor is not equal. V, 1507. In eternal life all the blessed will be equal, although not in equal brightness. V, 533. In eternal life there will be different glory according to the diversity of merits. III, 1812. What each person will have will be common to all. III, 1812. There will be no envy. III, 1812. During the time of this life the good and the evil appear alike; the life of the good is hidden in the root, but summer will distinguish it. IV, 1947. The present life is signified by the number forty, the future life by fifty. IV, 1463.

The way to the blessed life was hidden from the philosophers, and it would be hidden from us too, unless it had itself come to us. V, 814. No one will reach eternal life unless he is reborn in Christ. X, 121, 122. Apart from baptism and participation in the Lord’s table, no one reaches eternal life. X, 128. Eternal life is the fruit of the Eucharist. III, 1613. Little children who have not eaten the flesh of Christ will not obtain eternal life; from Innocentius. II, 785, 826. Eternal life and charity are the gift of inheritance belonging to the children of promise. III, 566. It is signified by hyacinth-colored skins. III, 635. No one in this life is secure regarding eternal life. X, 1031. Nothing separates a human being from eternal life except sins. X, 129, 141. People are driven back from their homeland by the winds of their wicked habits. III, 23. By God’s hidden judgment it happens that more people reach eternal life from among the less educated and simpler than from among the learned. II, 744. The pledge of eternal life is the Holy Spirit. V, 1673. Our future life has already been completed in Christ our head. VIII, 249. The Apostle contemplates our future life, already completed in Christ, with such certain hope as though it were already present. VIII, 249, 250. Eternal life can be given by God alone. VII, 193, 194. It is sought from the gods in vain. VII, 175, 183, 187, 189.

### Vitalis

Vitalis, a learned man in the church at Carthage. II, 979. He teaches that the beginning of faith is not a gift of God. II, 978. How Augustine tries to lead him to the right faith. II, 978. Vitalis is criticized only for wishing the beginning of faith not to be a gift of God, but for claiming that we possess it from ourselves. II, 989. He agrees that God gives the other goods of religious life by his grace to those who already ask, seek, and knock through faith. II, 989. In this he shares with Augustine the struggle against the Pelagians. II, 988. Augustine does not believe Vitalis to be a Pelagian heretic. II, 987.

The vicious insult those who live well. IV, 1151, 1152.

### Vice

Vice is called that which is contrary to nature. I, 610, 1290. Vice exists in nature, but vice is not nature. X, 370. The Manichaeans say that the vices of substances and natures are themselves substances and natures. X, 1085. And the Manichaean thought so. X, 1453. Vice is not nature. X, 1159. It is neither nature nor substance. X, 1323, 1537. But it is contrary to nature. X, 1124. It is hostile to nature. V, 986. Vice is not so contrary to nature that it also destroys the furthest traces of nature. VII, 639. Vice bears witness that nature is good. VII, 349, 350, 351, 352. Vice can exist only in a created nature. VII, 418, 421. In vice, nothing else is displeasing except that it removes or diminishes what is pleasing in nature. X, 743. Vice is contrary to God. VII, 350. Vice cannot exist without causing harm. VII, 351, 353. How vice harms nature. VII, 351. Vice is the quality according to which the mind is evil. X, 294. Certain vices innate in bodies are removed by care. X, 1315.

The Platonists appear to think that the cause of vices arises from the flesh. VII, 405. Whether the devil, who has no flesh, is free from vices. VII, 405, 406. The vice of a human being is the nature of a beast. X, 408. Vices of the soul are privations of natural goods. VI, 236. Vices of the mind too—not all of them, however—are to be attributed to the flesh. VII, 405, 406. They are ascribed to the flesh. VII, 405, 406. Vice of the mind is a defect that is not to be counted among intelligible things. VIII, 98. God is not the author of our vices, although he is their good arranger. III, 229. Innate vices are to be attributed not to God’s workmanship but to judgment. X, 1427. Vice of the soul is nothing other than sin and the punishment of sin. III, 141. The cause of natural vices is original sin. X, 1429. The vice that darkens and weakens all natural goods was contracted from original sin. X, 249. The vice of origin is like ill health. X, 855. Original vice is in the seed. X, 833, 834. Vice propagates vice. X, 1167. The devil, the author of vices, would not be permitted to corrupt rational nature unless original sin existed. X, 1421. Our vices are to be attributed not to the divine work but to the human will and to the just vengeance inflicted upon it. X, 266. The origin of vices is from the human will. III, 605. The first vice of the rational soul is the will to do what supreme truth forbids. III, 138. Vice is using things that should be enjoyed and enjoying things that should be used. VI, 19. The vice of a rational creature is its turning away from the unchangeable good. II, 561, 571. Vice is a kind of tinder and, as it were, the root of sin. II, 737.

The Apostle set forth three kinds of vice to be detested and avoided. II, 91. The three kinds of vice—pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity—contain all sins. IV, 115. On the three vices individually. III, 154. These three kinds of vice are signified in the Psalms by the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea. IV, 115. Hence Christ’s temptation is also threefold. IV, 116. The vices that dwell in the members are called members. VI, 370. The commands of vices are contrary. V, 526. How grievous is the yoke of vices that command contrary things. V, 897. It is more difficult to serve contrary vices than Christ. V, 526. Names that properly signify vices are generally used to signify virtues. VIII, 410. The vices of some people are often indications of the virtues for which they are suited, if they are cultivated by instruction. VIII, 444. Some vices are openly contrary to virtues; others resemble them through a deceptive appearance. II, 735. Vices akin to virtues. X, 748. From the vices themselves we are admonished to strive toward God. III, 154. There are more vices than virtues. II, 736. Vices are not connected with one another. II, 735; IX, 172. They are not equal. II, 738, 739. The Stoics said that vices are equal; the Catholics denied it. II, 734. No one, however holy, is without vice in this life. IX, 58, 63.

The vices of the flesh must be steadfastly fought. VI, 370. The necessity of fighting against vices. X, 690, 691, 692, 695. How harsh and difficult this struggle is. X, 696. Vices are indeed dead in baptism through the remission of all sins, but we must in some way care for their burial. X, 696. A person must fight against dead vices. X, 696. It follows from the doctrine of the Pelagians that corrupted natural qualities would have arisen in paradise. X, 1419. The struggle with interior vices, and the body of this death, would not have existed in paradise. X, 1092, 1093. What a struggle with interior vices the saints endure because of the body that weighs down the soul. X, 1092. After the former and grievous ruin, God first willed us to struggle with vices so that afterward we might reign with him in eternal peace. X, 1535. The struggle with vices is a means of obtaining justification. X, 689, 690, 692. What measure should be observed in pursuing vices and offenses. IX, 527. Sometimes one vice is removed by another vice. II, 736. It was in our power not to fall into vices, but not to heal them. X, 266. Certainly, unless God is present, no one is fit to fight against vices. X, 1535. In this contest God preferred us to fight with prayers rather than with strength; why this is so. X, 1535. The vices of the soul are cured by the grace of Christ as physician. X, 802. It is more disgraceful to be conquered by vices than by a human being. III, 160. No one who has conquered his vices can be conquered by a human being. III, 160. Do not love vice for the sake of a person, nor hate a person for the sake of vice. V, 323. Vices in children, friends, servants, and all acquaintances should not be loved. VI, 703. The vices of others do not harm the whole world if they do not harm the Donatists who are in their communion. IX, 300, 301. The first person is corrupted by his own vice, by whose vice another may be corrupted. I, 1290. Vice or folly is compared with darkness. II, 737. War must be waged against vices. VII, 730. Vices are not mastered without conflict. VII, 657. Vices that have not been strengthened by habit are more easily conquered. VII, 730. How vices are conquered. VII, 731. Vices are not truly conquered except through delight in true righteousness. VII, 730. Unless through desire for the highest good. VII, 789. When vices are conquered without love of God, they are conquered by other hidden vices. VII, 730. The vices by which beasts, trees, and other irrational and insensible things are corrupted contribute to the beauty of the universe. VII, 351.

### Vine
