The wood of the vine is useful for none of the farmers’ purposes. III, 1842. They say that Liber Pater showed the vine to his host in the land of Attica. VII, 569.

We are more fragile than glass. V, 636.

Why the golden calf was cut into tiny pieces, scattered into water, and given to the people to drink. VIII, 462.

Vitumnus, a god. VII, 195.

The reproach of sinners contributes to the praise of God. I, 1289.

The soul gives life to the animal body in one way and to the spiritual body in another. II, 946.

Ulammaus, Bethel, and Luz are the same city. III, 577.

The desire for vengeance is vicious. IV, 1433. See *Vengeance*.

Owls. IX, 232.

The companions of Ulysses changed into beasts. VII, 573, 574. How this happened. VII, 575, 576.

### Shadow

What a shadow is. III, 255. A shadow consists of light and body. IV, 826. A shadow signifies this present life. IV, 1863, 1864. The shadow of the Holy Spirit is understood as a shelter from the heat of concupiscence. IV, 826.

Those of one mind become the holy dwelling-place of the Lord. IV, 815.

Ounces written with horizontal strokes. VII, 604.

### Anointing

When “Anointed” (*Unctus*) is heard, Christ is to be understood. IV, 505. How the ancient fathers were called Christs before there was an anointing. IV, 1395. Sacred anointing pertained especially to the royal and priestly person. I, 627. Prophets were also sometimes anointed. I, 627. Kings and priests were not anointed except in that kingdom in which Christ was prophesied. IV, 505. Anointing now pertains to all Christians; in earlier times it pertained only to the two persons of king and priest. IV, 200. Jacob’s anointing of the stone, a figure of Christ. IV, 510. Christ is our anointed head, and we ourselves are his body. IV, 200. Spiritual anointing and visible anointing. III, 2000. How anointing teaches us about all things. III, 2004. The sacrament of anointing, invisible anointing, is the Holy Spirit. III, 2004. We are anointed now in the sacrament, and the sacrament itself prefigures something that we shall be. IV, 200. Anointing the head belongs to joy. III, 1288.

What the ointment with which the Lord was drenched by a woman signified. IV, 171. “Pistic” ointment: righteousness from faith. III, 1760. Ointments made from the flesh of living creatures. I, 1362.

### Eleven

Eleven. V, 353, 517. The number eleven signifies transgression. III, 635, 1336. And sin. III, 1077; VII, 465.

The unicorn sometimes signifies pride, sometimes the exaltation of unity. IV, 1178. Unicorns: the proud. IV, 176. Also those whose firm hope is in the one God. IV, 1006.

The difference between “only-begotten” and “firstborn.” III, 2077. The only-begotten of God before the ages. III, 335. How the only-begotten of God is the Word of the Father. III, 227.

Priscillian asserts a unity in God without any existence or property. VIII, 667.

The union of Christ with the Church, and of the Church with Christ. IV, 618, 748, 749. Union among the faithful is commended through the union among Christ’s members. III, 1645.

### Unity

Unity is the form of all beauty. II, 85. Unity is perceived only by the mind. III, 149. Every nature desires unity. I, 1191. The unity of Christ and his members. V, 755. One Christ is both head and members. IV, 629. See *Christ*. The unity of the Church. V, 693, 765, 1225, 1231, 1232, 1236. The Church is unity. IV, 1309. See *Church*. The security of unity exists only through God’s promises, by which the Church is declared. IX, 104. God placed the doctrine of truth in the chair of unity. II, 403. Heretics divide unity for their own honor. III, 2028. The good of unity. IX, 138, 139. The unity of the Spirit and charity are the greatest of all goods. II, 811. Peace and unity are a great virtue of piety. VI, 308. Charity is the strongest bond of unity. VI, 137. Unity must be loved. III, 1618. The unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace must be diligently preserved. IX, 84, 87. One’s personal honor must be despised so that the unity of the Church may be preserved. V, 96.

For the good of unity and peace, everything must be endured. IX, 211. Each person must separate himself from the wicked in heart, not in body. VI, 180. Those who separate themselves from unity are emptied of the Holy Spirit. IX, 491. Whoever abandons unity violates charity. V, 550. Christ commanded us to gather together; he reserved separation for himself. II, 951. Christian unity is not divided by the division of kingdoms. IX, 417. To resist the unity of the Church with an unrepentant heart is an unforgivable blasphemy. V, 465. The charity of unity both covers error and covers a multitude of sins. IX, 177, 178. Cyprian presumed that those admitted into the Church without baptism, coming from heresy, belonged to forgiveness because of unity. IX, 178. Just as rightly received baptism avails for cleansing the sacrileges of the pagans, so the charity of unity avails for cleansing the sacrileges of schismatics and heretics. IX, 478. Cyprian asserts with complete confidence that those who are outside unity, even if they die for Christ’s name, can be killed but cannot be crowned. II, 410. So powerful is the charity of unity, whether for erasing sins or for confirming them, when it is preserved or violated. II, 410. How the mother charity grieves when unity is torn apart. III, 1992. How much Cyprian and others attributed to the bond of unity. IX, 178. How greatly unity must be loved is declared by the Carthaginian council itself. IX, 211. Human beings will be fully and perfectly one when they have reached that end at which God is all in all. II, 1043. The perfection of unity among the blessed. VI, 387. See *Concord*. The commendation of unity. IV, 1949. Unity is commended in the creation of things and in Christ’s birth. V, 1233. In Christ’s seamless garment. V, 1222. The unity of the Law, Prophecy, and Gospel. V, 491, 493. Avarice loves unity, but in matters where unity ought not to be loved. IV, 451.

The word “one,” without any addition, is not found in Scripture except concerning things that are of one substance. II, 1048, 1049. Where it is said of two or more that “they are one,” and nothing is added to say what they are one in, they are understood to be of one substance. VIII, 788, 789, 926. In Scripture something “one” is found concerning different natures, but what they are one in is added or understood. II, 1019. To be is nothing other than to be one. I, 1348. Simple things exist in themselves because they are one. I, 1348. Whatever is one is one from the Word of God. III, 151. The supremely One is the principle of every form. III, 234. “One” sometimes refers to what consists of many parts. IV, 1961. The one necessary thing. V, 617, 1188. One thing toward which we should strive when we labor amid the multitude of this age. V, 613, 614. In the multitude itself, only the one gives delight. V, 614.

### The universe

The universe consists of things similar to one another. III, 243. The indication of universality is the number seven. IV, 1592.

From what does the beauty of the universe arise? VIII, 554, 590, 591. The beauty of the universe comes from unity, from which it receives its name. I, 979; III, 189. The beauty of the universe is composed from the opposition of contraries. VII, 332. From the variety of harmful things. VII, 335. And from the vices by which irrational and insensible things are corrupted. VII, 351. Even ugly things, once restored to their proper place, contribute to the beauty of the universe. I, 999. The perfection of the universe results from the blessedness of those who do not sin and the misery of those who sin. I, 1284. Why the order of succession in the universe does not delight us. VII, 352. The beauty of the universe strongly commends the wisdom of God. VIII, 591.

### The origin of words

The occasion for words. I, 1011. It is fitting for a wise person to be an investigator of things, not a maker of words. I, 932. Ancient words are not to be despised, nor should one readily depart from customary usage, except where it is contrary to reason. I, 1106.

- The calling of human beings proceeds from God’s profound ordinance. VI, 73, 74.
- The predestination of the calling is hidden. VI, 59.
- All are called by the Lord. V, 549.
- Many who are called do not come; no one comes unless called. III, 2076, 2077.
- God’s calling is twofold. X, 792, 924, 983, 984.
- Some who are called are not according to the purpose, others according to the purpose. II, 825.
- The calling according to the purpose does not belong to all who are called, but only to the elect. I, 622; III, 2061. Retr., X, 965.
- Only the predestined are called according to the purpose. X, 586, 929.
- Those who do not persevere are not called according to the purpose. II, 639.
- Not all are called, but people are called from among both Jews and Gentiles. VI, 124.
- According to whose purpose the elect are called. X, 586.
- The calling and the whole work of the religious person are from God. X, 383.
- God’s calling precedes good merit. VI, 73.
- Calling is not a matter of merits but of God’s grace. IV, 89.
- Calling to glory is not according to human merits but according to God’s mercy. III, 648.
- Those who say that they were called because they worshiped God are refuted. V, 863.
- The calling of the elect is proper to them, not because they believed, but so that they might believe. X, 985, 986.
- One who is called according to the purpose cannot say, “I believed in order that I might be called in this way”; for God’s mercy goes before him, because he was called in such a way that he might believe. X, 985.
- We are called by God’s mercy so that we may believe, and those who believe are granted the ability to do good works. III, 2061, 2062. Retr.
- Whether calling is the producer of a good will. VI, 118.
- From calling according to the purpose all graces arise. X, 965.
- Congruous calling. VI, 118.
- A special calling. VII, 39.
- Our calling takes place through the preaching of repentance. IV, 1963.
- To consent to or dissent from God’s calling belongs to the proper will. X, 240, 241.
- How one should respond to God’s calling. IV, 1308.
- Those who are called ought not to procrastinate. V, 533.
- No class of human beings should despair of its calling. V, 1396.
- The fishermen and the uneducated were called first, while the orator, senator, and emperor were postponed; why. V, 256.

- The Voconian law, unjust. VII, 103.

- It is not without reason that birds are said to have been created from the waters. III, 282.
- In the first establishment of the causal reasons, birds were produced from the waters. III, 393.
- The fact that Adam gave names to birds and not to fish was done for some symbolic reason. III, 400, 401.
- What a winged bird is. III, 239.
- Which birds are four-footed. VIII, 817, 818. Retr.
- Birds signify spiritual hearts. IV, 1361.

- Volumna, a goddess. VII, 128.
- Volumnus, a god. VII, 128.

- One who wills is free from compulsion. VIII, 104.

- What the will is. I, 609; VIII, 93, 94, Note 3, 104; X, 1476, 1478, 1479.
- From what it is called. X, 234.
- Whether will belongs to irrational beings. VII, 151.
- Everyone’s own will is best known to that person. VIII, 103.
- Some wills of all people are known to each individual. VIII, 1017.
- The movement of the will is spontaneous. VI, 13.
- Properly speaking, will exists only in the good. III, 1303.
- We cannot will not to be happy. II, 669.
- The origin of the will according to Julian. X, 1489, 1494, 1495.
- Its origin according to Augustine. X, 1489, 1495.
- From what the will does not move, or from what it does not will. X, 167.
- The Stoics did not want wills to be subject to necessity. VII, 152.
- The will is changeable because it is from nothing. VII, 467.
- The will changes into these or those affections according to the variety of things that are desired or avoided. VII, 409.

- Willing is within human power. VI, 107.
- The will is free because it lies within our power. I, 1275.
- Nothing is so much within our power as the will itself. I, 620, 1275.
- There would be no will unless it lay within our power. I, 1275.
- It is by the will itself that one sins and lives rightly. 596.
- The mind becomes the slave of lust through nothing except its own will. I, 1272.
- The will is free insofar as it has been freed [Col. 0673]; and it is called will insofar as it is free. I, 609.
- The freer the will, the healthier it is; and the healthier it is, the more subject it is to divine grace. II, 676, 677.
- Human will should not be called free so long as it is subject to desires that conquer and bind it. II, 593.
- Laws, praises, exhortations, punishments, and so forth are undermined, and there is no justice in them at all, unless the will is the cause of sinning. II, 1061.

- Every will is either good, loving justice, or evil, not loving it; there is no middle position. X, 169.
- The will is always free, but it is not always good. X, 899.
- The origin of the good and evil will according to Mani. X, 1113.
- Whether the good and evil will, and likewise the possibility of willing, should be attributed to nature. X, 1499.
- The origin of the evil will. X, 370, 464.
- All power is from God, but not every will. X, 235.
- While Julian investigates where the evil will arose, he is shown to assert an unjust condemnation of nature. X, 1497.

- The evil will is not from God. VII, 151.
- Whether hardness of will is a divine punishment. VI, 119.
- The will can be evil without the instigation of an evil spirit. VI, 622.
- The evil will has not an efficient but a deficient cause. VII, 353, 355, 356.
- The evil will is rather a defect from God’s work toward its own works than any work. VII, 418.
- The evil will precedes the evil deed. VII, 420, 421, 422.
- The evil will arose from a human being who had been created good. X, 1478, 1480.
- Why a human being can possess an evil will. X, 1479.
- The will becomes evil when, abandoning what is higher, it turns toward lower things. VII, 354, 355.
- The evil will is contrary to nature. VII, 151.
- It is evidence of the goodness of nature. VII, 332.
- The saints will not have an evil will, in such a way that they cannot have one. X, 1498.
- By free choice alone the will can decline from the good; but from evil it cannot turn without God’s help. VII, 467.
- The will is evil from itself, but good only from God. X, 169.
- God is the author of the good will, whereas the sinner himself is the author of the evil will. X, 1479.

- An evil will must not be entrusted to its own freedom. II, 754.
- The power to persevere or not to persevere has been entrusted to a sound will. X, 938, 939.
- The will without grace is insufficient. X, 889, 892, 899.
- It is insufficient for fulfilling the commandments. X, 897.
- It is insufficient for possessing justice. X, 155.
- The will without grace is not moved toward the good. X, 744.
- The will is insufficient for not sinning. II, 766, 775.
- Prayer itself shows that the will without grace is insufficient for avoiding sins. X, 256.
- While Julian tries to excuse the will on the ground of possibility, he is shown to accuse nature even more inexcusably. X, 1497.
- The human will lost the power to perform good works, as the Pelagians themselves acknowledge. X, 1145.
- When the will does not will the good, it is a defect of the human will; when it wills the good, it is aided by divine grace. X, 323.
- The effort of the will without God is nothing. IV, 208.
- If the will did nothing, God would not be called its helper. IV, 1859.
- The will cannot be free for completing a good work unless it has been freed by God’s gift. VI, 444.
- For obtaining justice, willing is sufficient. II, 485.
- No one can will unless admonished and called, whether inwardly or outwardly. VI, 73.
- Without one’s own will there can be no sin in one’s own life. X, 147.
- Without our will, God’s justice will not be in us. V, 922.
- Without willing, we cannot do good. X, 213.
- Although we may have our own will, victory over temptations comes not from it but from God’s help. II, 828.
- By its own will the soul cannot make itself good, but it can make itself evil. II, 571.
- By his own will a human being could not heal himself. V, 409.
- The human will was blessed in paradise, but is now miserable. X, 1108.
- There is growth in the will where birth is in the will: no one is born of water and the Spirit unless willing; therefore, if one wills, one grows; if one wills, one diminishes. III, 1997, 1998.
- Two contrary wills sometimes exist in a human being. I, 759.
- The old carnal will and the new spiritual will in Augustine. I, 753.
- The strong and whole will, the half-wounded will, and the will rising in one part while falling and struggling with the other. I, 758.
- No one has sufficiently recognized the powers of his own will. X, 530.

- Every concubine is a wife, but not every wife is a concubine. III, 571.

- The wife of Christ is his Church, and we ourselves. IV, 1684.

## Z

- Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling of strength.” IV, 835.

[Col. 0679] What Zacchaeus’ climbing into the sycamore signifies. V, 941. Zacchaeus receives the Lord as a guest. V, 170. Zacchaeus gives half and reserves half for repaying frauds. V, 112, 243, 649.

What Zachariah prophesied and at what time. IV, 1467, 1917, 1940; VII, 593.

The nearly identical words of Zachariah and Mary, but not the same unbelief. V, 1314. Zachariah asks in despair; Mary in inquiry. V, 1314. What Zachariah’s mouth being closed first and then opened signifies. V, 1328. Zachariah and Elizabeth were not without sin. X, 162. How Zachariah and Elizabeth were blameless in all the Lord’s commandments. X, 312.

Zama. IX, 232.

Zeb, interpreted as “wolf.” IV, 1053.

Zebee, interpreted as “the wolf’s victim.” IV, 1053.

Before they were humbled, the sons of Zebedee wished to be exalted. IV, 1670. The sons of Zebedee, desiring eminence, are called to the way. V, 875.

Zilpah is interpreted as “gaping mouth.” VIII, 435. Zilpah represents preachers whose mouth gapes but whose heart does not. VIII, 435.

Where jealousy properly occurs. VIII, 142.

What zeal is. VI, 140; VIII, 142. What the zeal of God is. VIII, 138, 142, 147. Zeal is understood in two senses, and in which sense it can be attributed to God. VIII, 352. Zeal is taken in a good and a bad sense. VII, 677. By the name “the zeal of God” is understood the exacting of chastity, lest the soul, fornicating, perish from its God. IV, 1914. The zeal of God is the zeal of love. IV, 1583. The zeal of God is the whole hope of our salvation. VIII, 142. How we must all burn with zeal for the house of God. III, 1471, 1472. Impatient zeal. IV, 1196, 1279. Zeal not according to knowledge. V, 721. What zeal according to knowledge is. IV, 81, 1128. Whoever has zeal should be zealous for God, not for himself. IV, 1583. Why zeal seems less applicable to God than foreknowledge, anger, and similar attributes. VI, 141.

Zeno, one of the leading Stoics. VII, 259, 261. The chief of the Stoics. I, 954. Under Polemo’s instruction, a fellow student of Arcesilaus. I, 955. He said that God himself was fire, and that the soul was mortal. I, 955. He also said that there was nothing besides this sensible world, and that nothing in it occurred without a body. I, 955. Zeno placed blessedness in virtue. VIII, 1019. Zeno’s definition of the apprehension of truth. I, 925. It is examined. I, 943. Zeno’s opinion survived into Chrysippus. I, 955.

Zenobius. I, 977; II, 63. Zenobius is called “Master of Memory” by Dioscorus. II, 431. Zenobius encouraged Augustine to write the work *On Order*. I, 987. That work is named after him. I, 980. Augustine sought an encounter and meeting with Zenobius. II, 63.

Zenophilus, a consular. IX, 386, 426, 512, 513. Proceedings before Zenophilus the Consular. II, 168, 197; IX, 513. The acts of Zenophilus the Consular are cited. IX, 584.

Pope Zephyrinus. II, 196.

The council of Zertense. II, 577.

Ziph, a village from which the Ziphaeans are named. IV, 619.

The Ziphaeans are interpreted as “flourishing.” IV, 619.

The city of the Ziquensians. IX, 540.

What the tares are. VIII, 347. Tares properly denote those things that grow in the likeness of wheat. IV, 784. Inner and outer tares. IX, 163. Who are the tares sown by the enemy. III, 1367. Why the devil is permitted to sow tares over the seed. IX, 162. The Donatists contend that tares alone, and not wheat, have grown throughout the world except Africa. IX, 322. The parable of the tares against the Donatists. V, 298, 550. The tares must be allowed to grow in the Church until the harvest. IX, 52. The tares were commanded to grow with the harvest throughout the whole world. IX, 183. They were commanded not to be gathered up but tolerated. IX, 280. For the good of unity. IX, 582. Amid the tares, Christ’s wheat groans. IV, 476. Through tolerating the tares, the fruit of the wheat increases. IV, 781. Some tares are wheat in God’s foreknowledge. IX, 432. Known tares do not stain the wheat. IX, 493. Tares in the Church do not hinder faith or charity. IX, 205. Tares also signify heresies. I, 642; IX, 29. Tares and chaff in the Church. II, 264.

Zoboennus, bishop. X, 662, 663.

Zoninus, bishop. X, 662, 663.

Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians and inventor of magical arts, is said to have laughed when he was born. VII, 728. Zoroaster was defeated in war by Ninus, king of the Assyrians. VII, 728.

What difference there is between Ζωήν (*zōēn*, “life”) and Βίον (*bion*, “life”). VIII, 1004.

Zosimus, successor of Innocent. X, 648. A letter was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council against the error of Pelagius. II, 972. Zosimus replied, and his reply was sent to all the bishops of the entire world. II, 972. Augustine sends a copy of this reply to Optatus. II, 865. And to Valentinus and his brothers. II, 972. Pope Zosimus was deceived for a time by the Pelagians. II, 865. Note (a). Pope Zosimus is kindly excused. X, 388, 389. Zosimus’ exculpation. X, 574. A fragment of Zosimus’ letter in which he asserts original sin. II, 865. Zosimus, Roman pontiff, condemns the Pelagians. I, 650. He condemns Caelestius and Pelagius. X, 575. Julian accuses Zosimus, the Roman pontiff, of treachery. X, 842. Pope Zosimus sends Augustine to Caesarea on official business. II, 857.

Zozimus of Tharassa. IX, 143, 232.

The estate of Zubedi, belonging to Hesperius in the territory of Fussala. VII, 764.

GENERAL INDEX TO ALL THE WORKS CONTAINED IN THE APPENDICES TO AUGUSTINE

A.

Aaron represents the type of Christ the mediator. V, 1804.

Abba, a Greek name. II, 1161.

Abel held primacy in righteousness. III, 2154. He bore the type of Christ and Christians. VI, 748. He consecrated martyrdom. VI, 1740.

Abibas. VII, 811.

Ablavius, vicar of Africa. IX, 785.

Abraham was first called Illam [the reading is uncertain], then Abram, and finally Abraham. VI, 1311. With his father he worshiped idols. III, 2348. From a pagan he became a worshiper of God. III, 2274. He was skilled in astrology. III, 2360. The praise of Abraham. III, 2325. He represents the type of God the Father. V, 1753. Abraham was called a prophet, king, and father of many nations. III, 2323. He was set forth as an image to whose likeness the human race would return to God. III, 2324. The Hebrews were named from him. III, 2323, 2324. The Jews are Abraham’s children according to the flesh, and we according to faith. III, 2243. Abraham’s faith is praised and expounded at length. III, 2359; V, 1953. Abraham possessed the root of faith and of the Christian name. V, 1743. He observed whatever the law required by nature. V, 1743. His faith is the punishment of unbelievers; the unbelievers’ faithlessness is his glory. III, 2360. Abraham is compared with Jephthah. III, 2239. Abraham’s obedience in the sacrifice of his son is praised. V, 1751. Abraham slaughtered his son with the sword of obedience. VI, 1165. He knew that from his offspring Christ, the Lord of heaven and earth, would be born. V, [Col. 0680] 1753. In hope of the future Incarnation, he saw the Savior. III, 1359. He understood the mystery of the Trinity. V, 1748. The incorporeal majesty descended to him in the form of three men. V, 1744.

Abraham’s bosom, where the saints wait in blessedness. I, 1472.

Apse. VII, 835, 842.

Eulogies of absolution for the dead. VI, 1158.

Two kinds of abstinence. V, 2112. Abstinence from wine, meat, oil, and bathing. II, 1111; VI, 768, 777. To believe that those abstaining from wine or meat acquire no increase of merit is Jovinian’s view. VIII, 1219. The usefulness and proper measure of abstinence. II, 1114; V, 2029.

The twelve degrees of misuse. VI, 1079.

The upper abyss. VII, 850. The sinner’s threefold abyss. VI, 948.

Accidents are gathered together by the mind and thought. I, 1423. What they are. I, 1423. No accident can exist without a subject. I, 1424. Some accidents are within, some outside, and some both within and outside substance. I, 1425.

What acedia is. VI, 1089.

Achan’s sin, insofar as it harmed others. III, 2234.

Acratius. IX, 786.

What the intention of human actions ought to be. VI, 819. Whoever devotes himself to impiety does nothing. X, 1737. Charity is the form of every good action. VI, 1256. When we do good, God works in us and with us so that we may act. X, 1787, 1861. No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good. X, 1873. See *Work*.

Actors. IX, 818, 841.

What Adam was like when created. VI, 728, 774; X, 1771, 1773. Some say that Adam received the Holy Spirit at the beginning and lost it by sinning. III, 2369. They are prompted by the fact that he was made perfect. III, 2369. To possess the Holy Spirit is beyond the nature and perfection of man. III, 2369. It is clear that Adam does not now possess what he then possessed. III, 2370. In Adam the nature of all human beings was created together with him. X, 1812. It was without every fault. X, 1812. It was created with free will, and, had it not abandoned the Lord who was helping it, it could have attained blessedness. X, 812. What Adam could have done with respect to the beasts is shown in Noah. V, 1953. Adam’s body was made so that it could be dissolved; but the taste of the tree of life prevented corruption. III, 2227. Julian admits that those who think Adam was made mortal rely on no argument whatsoever. X, 1738, 1759. Those who say that Adam died by the necessity of nature, not by the desert of sin, are condemned. X, 1728, 1730. Adam possessed perfect human knowledge. VI, 815. It is falsely said that after the transgression he received knowledge of evil but did not lose knowledge of good. X, 1813. Since Adam was placed in the world as its lord, why did he receive a law from God? III, 2388. He was in paradise and remained a virgin as long as he fasted. V, 2026, 2031. From what he first fell. VI, 729. By what stages Adam and Eve fell into sin. VI, 1051. Adam sinned through hope of divinity, not through bodily desire. III, 2382. He admitted idolatry. III, 2277, 2278. Adam the thief. V, 2034. Adam was not therefore evil because he was the father of a murderer. V, 1740. Why God did not recall Adam, although he knew that he would sin. V, 1738, 1740. Some excuse Adam’s guilt. V, 1737. By doing so they wrong God. V, 1737, 1740. Adam alone, not God or the tree, must bear responsibility for his sin and its punishment. V, 1738, 1740. If Adam had accused himself, he would not have been exiled from paradise. V, 2202.

What Adam became after the fall. VI, 774; X, 1772, 1773. Adam’s sin stained the body. III, 2382. Human beings also became subject to corruption and death. III, 2382. Yet from this they gain profit if they obey God’s law. III, 2382. Adam’s sin changed the whole human being for the worse. X, 1785. It harmed not only him but also his offspring. X, 1785. Adam sold his own freedom and ours. V, 1944. He sold his race into sin. III, 2278. In Adam we all perished. X, 1812. Not by losing substance or will, but the light and beauty of the virtues. X, 1812. Adam and Eve are believed to have died on the day on which the necessity of dying was imposed upon them as punishment. VI, 1051. Adam was buried at the very place where Christ’s cross was fixed. V, 1750.

Adam’s change for the worse, and the contrasting change of the faithful for the better. X, 1878. A comparison of the first and second Adam. V, 2031; X, 1888. What it means to imitate Adam or Christ. VI, 1051, 1052.

Adelfius. IX, 787.

Adeodatus, a Donatist bishop. IX, 828, 831.

Adjutor, a *cornicularius*. IX, 816.

Adjutores, staff members of the proconsul’s office. IX, 816.

Adjutor, staff member of the vicar’s numerical office. IX, 816.

A young man without obedience, an abuse. VI, 1080.

Adore in God Christ as man, and in man God. I, 1468. On earth a king is worshiped as God’s representative. III, 2284. Imperial writings are addressed with “Adorata.” IX, 778. A cloak worshiped Saraca. II, 1097. The emperors worship Peter by falling on their knees. V, 2125, 2127.

What ascending to God means. VI, 791. Three kinds of ascent. VI, 817.

Christ’s Ascension is the pledge and earnest of ours. V, 2081, 2082. It is our glorification. V, 2083. We must ascend after Christ. V, 2082. Namely, in the heart. V, 2082. The vices themselves will become a ladder for us and raise us if they are beneath us. V, 2082. No vice ascends with our physician. V, 2082.

We subsequently discovered that the prefatory letter to Queen Gerberga should be ascribed to Adso, abbot of the monastery of Derbe, and that the book *On the Antichrist* should be restored to him. VI, 1129, 1130.

Adventius. III, 844.

Advent. VI, 1277. What Christ’s Advent accomplished for us. III, 2372. Christ’s second Advent will not take place secretly as the first did. V, 2051.

From what the adverb derives its name. I, 1402. What it is. I, 1403. The various endings of adverbs. I, 1402, 1404. Their meanings. I, 1402.

Adversity must be endured with equanimity. V, 1812. It is more to be feared if we suffer none or only slight adversity. V, 1813. Resources against adversity must be sought in time of peace. X, 1875. The adversity of the righteous is the price of eternal joys. III, 2439.

The destruction caused by flattery. VI, 1287. The vice of flattery has grown so much that it can no longer increase. II, 1113. Who the flatterer is. III, 2405. Flatterers are hidden cliffs. V, 1885. Everyone sells oil. V, 2350. The flatterer’s caress is the sinner’s oil. V, 2214; IX, 767. The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. X, 1870.

[Col. 0682] Adulterers are blinded by frenzy. V, 1783. There are many of them. V, 2289. Each must rebuke them, and after one or two rebukes separate them from his fellowship. V, 2289. They must be reported to the priests’ attention. V, 2289. Adulterers have no spark of faith. V, 2293. Adultery is punished by divine and human law. V, 2290. A practice has been introduced whereby the adultery of a woman, but not of a man, is punished. V, 2290. And men say that these things are permitted to them but not to women. V, 2290. Unless prolonged repentance and abundant almsgiving come to the adulterer’s aid, and he ceases from sin, he will perish eternally. V, 2290. Long absence from one’s wife does not excuse adultery. V, 2293. The first weapons of adultery are the eyes, the second the words. V, 1768.

The aedileship. IX, 782, 783, 784.

What distress of mind is. X, 1874. The sick person, as though between physician and disease, causes the one to whom he joins himself to prevail. V, 1876.

The Egyptians devoted themselves to vain philosophy more than other peoples. III, 2316. Their story concerning the origin of the world. III, 2218. The plagues of Egypt. III, 2164, 2165. What they signify. V, 1781. Egypt was justly struck in its firstborn. V, 1790. Who can extinguish the spiritual Egyptian? V, 1792.

Aelianus, proconsul. IX, 780, 781, 782, 784, 827.

The sons of Aelion. IX, 799.

Aelius Paulinus. IX, 780, 781, 782.

A work of Aetred on friendship, abridged into an epitome. VI, 831. And a book on the eremitical life addressed to his sister. I, 1451.

Various kinds of equivocal expressions. I, 1416.

What air is. VI, 1009.

The six ages of the world. VI, 742, 749. The six ages of the world and of human life. V, 1920. See *World*.

What “eternal” properly means. VIII, 1182. Eternity is neither corrupted nor changed. III, 2232. It rejects diversity. III, 2231. Nothing is eternal except what is simple. III, 2231. A period of one hundred years is no portion of eternity. VI, 991. All things imitate eternity. VI, 1020. There may be some distance among certain eternal things, but not in eternity itself. X, 1892. True eternity and immutability exist only in divinity. X, 1859, 1874. Meditation on eternal things restrains the mind’s instability. VI, 824. The happiness of eternal life. VI, 820, 822, 823, 828, 861, 862, 966. The severity of eternal punishments. VI, 821, 993.

The location of Ethiopia. III, 2171. The monstrous inhabitants of Ethiopia. VI, 1303, 1304.

Etymology is a matter of excessive curiosity and not of great necessity. I, 1411.

Aetius says that equality in the Trinity is by grace. VIII, 40.

What affection is. I, 1433.

The soul’s four affections. VI, 782. For what purpose they were given. VI, 813. What pious affection is. VI, 816.

The prayer of an afflicted soul. VI, 936.

Africa. IX, 784. The African provinces. IX, 816. What all Africa suffered in a severe persecution. IX, 773. In this persecution, apart from a few Catholics, everyone sinned. IX, 776.

The African Church suffers from a shortage of clergy. IX, 806, 808. It does not wish what it has decreed to be confirmed until the overseas Church has first been consulted. IX, 806, 807, 809. The Council of Carthage sends men to consult it. IX, 808. The Africans have their own law concerning rebaptizing. IX, 787. An African synod against Caelestius. X, 1699. Two African councils against the Pelagians, in volume 10. X, 1685, 1686. Aurelius was their leader, Augustine their intellect. X, 1685. The African council of the year 417 was brought before Zosimus. X, 1808. A letter was first sent to him. X, 1808. The African bishops complained before Zosimus as though he had lent Caelestius credence in everything. X, 1726. The reply of the African bishops to Zosimus is noted. X, 1731, 1775. It is praised by Caelestine. X, 1758. By others as well. X, 1775. The constitution of the African council of 417 was embraced by the whole world. X, 1724, 1837. How Cassianus marks it as an error. X, 1723, 1808. The universal council of Africa was held in 418. X, 1728. Two hundred and twenty-four bishops attended it. X, 1730. Caelestine embraces its decrees as though they were proper to his own see. X, 1757. The plenary African council of 418 is sent by order of the emperors from Aurelius to the bishops for their signatures. X, 1731. African bishops exiled to Sardinia. X, 1772, 1176.

A person who laughed only once in his life was called *agelastus*. III, 2357.

One field belongs to God, another to man. V, 2325.

Agesilaus. IX, 781, 783.

Agnes is proposed for consideration where chastity is being tempted. I, 1460.

The legal lamb is a figure whose reality is Christ, offered on the altar of the cross. V, 2066.

Agricola, prefect of the praetorium. X, 1727.

Agricola the Pelagian. X, 1753.

The two wings by which we are lifted to heaven are the two commandments of charity. V, 1745. The two wings by which souls are raised to heaven are charity and humility. V, 2312.

Albanus, a bishop exiled in Sardinia. X, 1772.

[Col. 0683] Albigistinum. VII, 830.

Albinus the dog. X, 1996.

Albinus Faustus, consul. X, 1765, 1771.

A white cloth, used for a book. II, 1108.

A book *On the Spirit and the Soul* attributed to Alcher. VI, 779.

Alcuin’s questions on the Trinity. VIII, 1172. His little work on Jacob’s blessings. III, 2199. His prologue to Charlemagne on the *Categories*. I, 1419.

Alethius, bishop. X, 1790.

A saying of Alexander. VI, 1339.

The custom of Alexandria. See *Priest*.

Alfius Caecilianus. IX, 780, 781, 782.

Alia and Sparsus, consuls. III, 2176.

The “Alleluia” is silent after Easter has been concluded. V, 2096. *Alleluia*, a customary word of praise, is omitted during Lent. I, 1457.

The inner and outer altar in Solomon’s temple, and how it is found in us. V, 2169. The altar at which Cyprian, Carpophorus, and others offered. IX, 776. Deacons defend the altar. IX, 803. The Donatists broke the altars. IX, 804. The invisible altar of God. X, 1875. The altar is each person’s heart. V, 2170. A feast for the consecration of the altar. V, 2166, 2168.

A little book written on parchment. IX, 778.

Alypius. IX, 816, 827.

Amacius, pope of Gaul. X, 1751.

Amahus, a disciple of Christ. V, 2127.

Bitterness. Through the bitterness of lower things, a person is taught to love better things. X, 1875.

The history of the Amazons. III, 2357.

Every word is ambiguous. I, 1416. But it can be explained by an unambiguous explanation. I, 1416. The distinction between ambiguity and obscurity. I, 1415.

Ambitausus. IX, 787.

The ambition of the clergy is cut away. V, 1804.

Ambrose. V, 1854; VI, 840, 841. A confessor. X, 1725. A bishop of holy memory. X, 1686. Ambrose’s words on Luke are praised. X, 1812.

The book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* is restored to Ambrose Autpert. VI, 1091.

What the amethyst displays. VI, 1230.

Friendship is a great and very rare thing. VI, 833. A friend is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve. VI, 1232. The most sacred bonds of friendship are consecrated at Bethany by the Lord’s authority. I, 1468. The source and foundation of friendship. VI, 837. Its origin, development, and abuse. VI, 834. What friendship is. VI, 831, 836. It does not embrace as many as charity does. VI, 833, 837. One kind is carnal, another worldly, another spiritual; the last alone is true. VI, 833. Childhood friendship. VI, 836. What spiritual friendship is like. VI, 836. Those among whom there is an agreement in vices falsely assume the name of friendship. VI, 833, 836. Friendship is the enemy of drinkers. V, 2243, 2303. True friendship begins here and is perfected in heaven. VI, 841. True friendship is eternal and cannot cease. VI, 833, 837, 839, 1049. Whoever wishes another reward from it does not yet know it. VI, 837, 840. Friendship is a certain degree near perfection. VI, 835. The perfection of friendship is reached by four steps. VI, 837. The fruits and advantages of friendship. VII, 835.

What a friend owes a friend. VI, 837. A friend ought to be the guardian of mutual love and of the soul. VI, 832. The joining of souls makes friends. V, 1954. Friendship makes one out of many. VI, 832, 836, 837. What friends ought to expend on one another. VI, 842. Love, affection, security, and joy are required for friendship. VI, 839. The law of friendship in asking and giving. VI, 841. Which friends should be chosen. VI, 837, 841. In friends, faithfulness, intention, discernment, and patience must be approved. VI, 840. When choosing them, one must beware of love’s impulse preceding judgment. VI, 840. How friendship should be cultivated. VI, 841. It is not rightly cultivated by those who do not preserve equality. VI, 841. How friends should be corrected. VI, 842. Friendship is not without blemishes, but for that reason it should not be avoided. VI, 836. Friendships should be loosened, not altogether broken. VI, 839. Reasons for dissolving friendships. VI, 838, 839.

To lose. To lose something temporarily for the sake of faith is to gain profit. III, 2224.

What love is. VI, 812, 845, 846. Impure love is not love. V, 1768. Love of the world is not love. VI, 1226. Charity that can be abandoned was never true. VI, 1049. Those who cannot return love are not to be loved. VI, 1081. Only that is rightly loved which can never be rightly lost. X, 1881. One may not love what does not always remain. VI, 1084. The sufficiency of love and its various degrees. VI, 959.

The effects of love in us. VI, 959. Through love the soul does not perceive itself. VI, 960. Love is also a sensation. VI, 807. Love is the life of the heart and therefore cannot be idle. VI, 846. Love joins those who are absent. V, 1877. Impatient love commonly despises dangers themselves. VI, 1165.

The multiple origin of love. VI, 837. Love of the world, love of sin, and love of God. VI, 963. The two streams of love are charity and desire. VI, 813. Two loves make two cities. X, 1877. See 1879. Love conquers by love. V, 2345. Good love and bad love can exist in one person. 1870. The fullness of the love of God excludes love of the world. V, 1848. Love and fear of God lead to every good work, while love and fear of the world lead to every sin. X, 1879. The manner of love produces different participation in the Word of God. VIII, 1190.

When love is ordered or disordered. VI, 846. Only the person who loves God loves happily. VI, 847. The different effects of love of God. X, 1893. We are made blessed through the love of God. VI, 807. To love God is righteousness and blessedness. VI, 1047. In what manner God loves us. X, 1787, 1789, 1864. It is impious not to love the one whom we cannot repay, even when we do love him. VI, 1188. What God has granted us through love cannot be repaid better than through love. VI, 939. Love alone among the soul’s affections can repay its Creator. VI, 807. Let the soul devote itself to this alone. VI, 807. Knowledge of God necessarily produces love of God. VI, 865. God wishes to be loved not only with words but with a pure heart and righteous works. VI, 1056. Two things belong to the love of God: the mind’s affection and the work’s effect. I, 1466. How the mind’s affection is nourished by salutary meditation on the mysteries. I, 1466. True love always confesses. VI, 860. Frequent remembrance of God’s benefits arouses, nourishes, and increases love of God. VII, 849. From this it is aroused. VI, 792, 961. It is specifically aroused by contemplating creation and redemption. VI, 849, 852. It is aroused by God’s supreme love for us. VI, 851. Love of God is necessary for obtaining forgiveness. VI, 1121. What preparation one who wishes to love God ought to make for him. VI, 961. What the mind of one who loves God is like. VI, 963. Who loves God. VI, 1038. When something is lacking from the purity of love. VI, 1120. The person loves God less who loves something together with God that he does not love for God’s sake. VI, 880.

Julian falsely says that our love is drawn from the body when it is troubled, and from the soul when it is exalted and continuous. X, 1741. Julian falsely says that holy love is implanted in us by nature and can persist through the powers of the soul alone without harming itself. X, 1741. The love of God comes only from God. X, 1741. We are bound always to love God, but we cannot unless he grants it. VI, 879. Through the gift of love we are made fit to enjoy blessedness. VI, 845. An ardent petition for the love of God. VI, 956. The lover of God is a lover of himself. X, 1891. The treatise *On Loving God* is composed chiefly from consideration of his benefits. VI, 847.

Through love God comes to human beings, comes into human beings, and became human. VI, 792, 807, 960. In what Christ’s friendship consists and how it should be cultivated. VI, 1049. Christ’s love is sweet and tranquil; love of the world is anxious and troubled. VI, 930. These two loves cannot be contained in one heart. VI, 930. An ardent supplication for Christ’s love. VI, 928. How great Christ’s love ought to be. VI, 1037. Whoever loves something more than Christ does not love Christ. V, 1881.

Love of God and neighbor is the double bond by which we come to contain God more fully. VI, 846. Love of God and neighbor is the way to life. VI, 847. The proper measure of love for God and neighbor. VI, 849. Love of neighbor is divided into innocence and beneficence: namely, that one harm no one and not wish to harm anyone, and that one do good to those whom one can help. I, 1465. Love of neighbor both avoids doing harm and takes care to do good. VI, 1039. Human beings, not their errors, are to be loved. X, 1859. Whoever loves God loves both himself and his neighbor, and conversely. VI, 1223.

Whoever loves himself, not God, does not love himself; and whoever loves God, not himself, loves himself. X, 1895. Why. X, 1895. No one can love another who does not love himself. VI, 813. Self-love is not sufficient for itself. V, 1828. The love of charity is rich and abundant for all, and grows by being distributed. V, 1828. How love of neighbors is taught through the mutual love of the members. V, 1949, 1951. Through the love of charity, another’s virtues become one’s own. V, 1950. Whoever loves everyone rightly rules everyone. VI, 782. What love or hatred of neighbor produces in us. VI, 1055. The wicked are to be loved so that they may become good, and the good so that they may become better. V, 1829. Friends are to be loved in God, enemies for God’s sake. VI, 1171. A sinner is not to be loved as a sinner, but as a human being. X, 1881. The manner of loving friends and enemies. V, 2157. Through love of enemies charity becomes complete. V, 1878.

Love of the world and love of God cannot dwell together in one heart. VI, 1084. To love God is equivalent to “Do not love the world.” VI, 1224. We must not wish to possess both Christ and the world. VI, 1188. Love of vanity is dust; love of iniquity is filth. VI, 848. How love of the present world must be opposed by love of the future. VI, 1103.

A sermon on virginity by Amphilochius of Iconium is mentioned. VII, 818.

Ananias, guilty of fraud and sacrilege, lost salvation. V, 1938.

Anastasius, supreme pontiff. X, 1681. Bishop of the Apostolic See, consulted by the Africans. IX, 808. He replied to them. IX, 809.

Anastasius the Librarian. VII, 817. Legate of the Apostolic See near Mantua. VII, 817. He translated into Latin the Greek history of the translation of Saint Stephen and Amphilochius’ sermon on virginity. VII, 817, 818. The former work, with a letter to Landuleus. VII, 817.

The unusual death of Anaxagoras. III, 2356.

Anaximenes’ opinion concerning God. VI, 888.

Andrew proceeded toward the cross secure and joyful. VI, 882. Out of charity he desired death. VI, 1120. A fabricated apparition of the Apostle Andrew. VIII, 1150.

To provide an *angarialis* [postal-service obligation]. IX, 790.

The two angels seen by Lot are understood as the Father and Son, one God. VIII, 1104. Under the name of an angel, the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush and to Joshua with a drawn sword. VIII, 1105. Our knowledge of angels is not especially clear. VI, 921. The Synod of Arles testifies to the presence of angels, as also of the Holy Spirit. IX, 787. Christ and his angels are called as witnesses. IX, 795. The case is said to be conducted with angels as witnesses and God also looking on. IX, 816. What angels are. VI, 1010. It is certain that angels are good and our helpers; what they are like, or when they were created, is less certain. VIII, 1177. The angelic nature was made on the first day. VI, 740. It is the beginning of God’s creatures. III, 2153. The angels were created while darkness still concealed water, and water concealed earth. VIII, 1215. They were created on the Lord’s day. V, 2274. All were created equal. VI, 738. Angels are living creatures. VI, 729. An angel is a spiritual nature. III, 2152. He was first placed in heaven. III, 2152. The distinction between angelic and human knowledge. VI, 1010. How angels are superior and equal to human beings. VI, 850, 870.

Why angelic sin is passed over in Genesis. VIII, 1176. Why it was left without a remedy. VIII, 1176. The fall of the angels is passed over because it was irremediable. III, 2153. It was irremediable because, having been established in the highest honor, the angel did not have a change toward a more excellent state, but only that he might be confirmed in the state he possessed. III, 2153. It is compared with the fall of man. III, 2153. The angels who fell are never to be restored. VI, 763. Why. VI, 763. For them to begin to be punished was nothing other than to be deprived of the love of blessed good. VI, 763. The eternal fire was also prepared for them. VI, 763.

How Christ’s cross benefited the angels. VI, 1192. The good angels are holy because they preserved the holiness of free choice. VIII, 1218. They continually read, choose, and love God’s will. VI, 927. Christ is the homeland of the angels. V, 1874. The bread of angels. V, 1997, 2035. Manna is called the bread of angels, not because they were nourished by it, but because through their ministry it was provided to the people, like the Law and the other things. III, 2168, 2228. The orders of angels. VI, 782. Their brilliance corresponds to their different ranks. VI, 1011. Although they are not to be judged, the angels tremble in the presence of our Judge. V, 2051.

Creation does not belong to angels. X, 1871. At God’s commands the angels can move every kind of living creature. VI, 746. They preside over the judgment and administration of bodily things. VI, 797. In wondrous ways they make their visions appear to be ours. VI, 1997. The power of angelic spirits over human beings. VI, 798. Through them the things occurring among insensible objects and sensible creatures are administered. VI, 1010. Angelic ministries are spread everywhere. VI, 800. Wind is raised and calmed by them. VI, 1009. All the wonders that God displayed among the people of Israel were accomplished through angelic offices. III, 2174. The exterminating angel of the Israelites feared the future work of Christ the mediator. V, 1804. The star that led the Magi to Bethlehem may have been an angel; angels transformed themselves into various forms for the sake of human beings. III, 2194. Angelic terror troubled Pilate’s wife on account of Christ. V, 2038. The one seen in the guise of a merchant is believed to have been an angel and a human being. VII, 851. Angels rejoice over the salvation of the world. V, 1986.

The angels’ services toward us. VI, 1324. How they present our prayers to God. VI, 850. For what reason they come to us. VI, 851. Two angels—one good and the other evil—are said to cling to each person. X, 1818. We have a guardian angel, and an evil angel is also present. VI, 1354. Everyone has an angel of God; an evil person repels the good one and takes on the malignant one. VI, 1182. An angel is assigned to each soul for its protection. VI, 856. The benefit of a guardian angel. VI, 1119. Guardian angels watch over our life. V, 1979. Their care and services toward us. VI, 885. Angels of peace receive the righteous when they die and rescue them from the devil’s power. VI, 1057. They attend the deaths of the saints, provide them help, and accompany their souls to Abraham’s bosom. I, 1472. Angels are present here for us and carry our souls to the other dead. VI, 799. They receive souls departing from here and place them either in Abraham’s bosom or in hell. VI, 1163, 1183. They raise the righteous to heaven. VI, 1350. The choir of angels meets the dying saints and leads them to Christ. VI, 1061. [Col. 0686] They lead them to paradise and delight them with spiritual song. VI, 1055.

A bishop, presbyter, or even layman is an angel of God. III, 2420. Those who do the will of God or of the devil are angels of God or of the devil. VI, 1071.

The origin of souls is hidden and known to God alone. VIII, 1208. Doubt concerning the origin of souls. X, 1784. The origin of souls is explained. VI, 809, 814. The Manichaeans and Priscillianists wish the soul to be from God’s substance. VIII, 1207. It is neither a part of God nor from God’s nature and substance, but from nothing. V, 2175; VI, 784, 809, 887; VIII, 1207; X, 1718. Souls did not exist before they were sent into bodies. V, 2183; X, 1718. Whether they are produced by transmission or not is uncertain. VIII, 1177. They are not produced by transmission. III, 2229. This is demonstrated from Scripture. III, 2229. They are not sown, but are created and infused when the body has been formed. VIII, 1216. Before the soul has been received, the body in the womb receives human form. VI, 784. The soul is infused into the body after forty-seven days. VI, 1276. It comes to the body at God’s command, not because it deserved to be enclosed in the flesh for deeds performed previously. VI, 784. Who contracts sin. VI, 810. Why God gives the soul to those who will die without baptism. VI, 810. Souls are of one nature. VI, 1023. Why one is more capable of learning than another. VI, 1024.

### Soul: what it is

What the soul is. VI, 781, 784, 788, 887, 921, 1009. A certain proper nature belonging to the soul, which can be understood but cannot be perceived by the senses. VI, 792. The soul is a certain power by which the body is made alive. VI, 727. In it there is one element called rational and another irrational. VI, 727. There are not two souls in one human being, one animal and the other spiritual. VIII, 1216. The sensory and rational soul are one. VI, 784, 814. Soul and spirit have the same essence but different properties. VI, 784. Whence it has these two names. VI, 784. As existing outside the body it is called spirit; as existing in the body it is called soul. VI, 1138. The soul’s threefold power: sensory, rational, intellectual. VI, 807. Why an intellectual spirit was given to the human soul. VI, 766. The soul’s substance is simple. VI, 789. Its powers and faculties are diverse. VI, 788. Whence its various names arise. VI, 788. When it is properly called soul, or mind, intellect, memory, reason, spirit, and sense. VI, 803. Life can persist without intellect, and the soul without mind. VI, 803.

Although incorporeal and simple, the soul is as though formed throughout the body, giving life to each of its members. III, 2229. Through the body’s pleasures the soul acquires a certain corporeality. VI, 813. This fault follows it even when it departs from the body. VI, 813. In essence the soul is simple, but in its functions manifold. VI, 803, 804, 825. It is rational, concupiscible, and irascible. VI, 781, 788, 812. From this it is shown that its senses, affections, and virtues arise. VI, 812. The soul’s powers are its own, but its virtues are not its own. VI, 789. The soul’s powers directed toward virtues and against vices. VI, 792. The soul’s powers by which it cleaves to God or becomes mingled with the body. VI, 794. It is falsely said that the seeds of virtues are naturally implanted in our souls. X, 1818. The soul’s capacity for knowing and loving is from nature, but knowledge of truth and the order of love are from grace. VI, 784. Souls are capable of good and evil by nature. VIII, 1191. Free choice is present in every rational soul. VIII, 1176.

The dignity of the soul, and the pledge and token of love given to it by God. VI, 851. God is proved to surpass bodies through the rational soul. X, 1896. The traces of the Trinity are present in the soul. VI, 783. The soul bears the image of God and of the Holy Trinity. VI, 805. Its likeness to God. VI, 805. Comparison of the soul with God. VI, 806. For what purpose the soul was made in the image and likeness of God. VI, 809. How, after departing from God’s likeness, it does not cease to bear his image. VI, 809. The modern legislators proclaim it to be in the image of God only because it is incorporeal, just as God is incorporeal. VIII, 1221. The image is found in eternity, the likeness in conduct. VIII, 1221. To penetrate the soul belongs to God alone. VIII, 1221.

No good is sufficient for the soul except the highest good. VI, 962. Nothing satisfies the mind except the true and certain eternity of incorruptible joy. X, 1881. Nothing fills it except God. VI, 887. When it desires something external, it is clear that it does not yet possess God within. VI, 887. The Trinity alone can fill the human soul according to its substance. VI, 799. How Satan is said to fill it. VI, 799. What angelic spirits can do within it. VI, 799. The soul’s blessedness depends upon continual remembrance and love of God. VI, 812. The soul’s prayer, by which it invites God into itself. VI, 953. The soul’s threefold power will be fulfilled in the blessed. VI, 829.

The soul is eternal. VI, 1023. Immortal. VI, 793, 811; VIII, 1173. The soul’s immortality was not called into doubt even by pagan philosophers. VI, 1161. This is also proved by the fact that it strives to live perpetually in the memory of posterity. VI, 1010. In what respect it is called mortal and immortal. VI, 784, 793, 821. The soul is the life of the flesh; how, then, does it receive death from the flesh? VI, 793. It is also said to be killed in Gehenna. VIII, 1173. Human souls alone are substantial, alone immortal. VI, 815; VIII, 1216.

It is proved that the soul is not a body. VI, 795. It is invisible and incorporeal. VI, 792. Yet in relation to God it is corporeal. VI, 792. It neither increases nor decreases. VI, 800, 805. It is utterly absurd to confine souls in bodily places. VI, 1029. There is no place in the soul. VIII, 1120. What is wondrous in it. VIII, 1120. The soul is, in a certain manner, everywhere within itself. VI, 800. Where it will be after leaving the body. VI, 800. It is without a place. VI, 1009. It can be called local and in a place, and yet not be in a place. VI, 793. It is wholly present throughout the body and in each of its parts. VI, 762, 794, 805, 810. It acts as a whole in whatever it does. VI, 794, 805. It is not itself diverse, but performs diverse actions. VI, 805. How it is wholly present in each member, yet there are not as many wholes as there are members. VI, 1024. God is the homeland of the mind. VI, 781. The soul has no local movement. VI, 762. Souls released from the flesh do not move, nor are they led to any bodily place. VI, 1029. Why some have seemed to be led upward. VI, 1029. How the soul moves through time and not through place. VI, 792. Through its own movement it is always in motion. VI, 796. It thinks while the body sleeps. VI, 796. The soul has a certain length, breadth, and height, so to speak. VI, 786. Every soul is greater than the whole world. VI, 1011.

It is not contrary to the soul’s nature either to receive God or to be joined to the body. VIII, 1191. What is lowest in the soul and highest in the body could be joined through personal union without confusion of natures. VI, 789. The soul’s friendship with the flesh. VI, 789. Twofold life. VI, 784. Twofold actions. VI, 789. Seven grades of action by which it displays its powers. VI, 825, 826. The mind’s sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence; how they are one and many. VI, 781. What these are. VI, 786. What is necessarily required and from what their activity derives assistance. VI, 787. What pertains to each of the senses. VI, 788.

What is the eye of the soul? VI, 785. Three things necessary for it to see. VI, 785. How many powers of perception there are in the soul. VI, 794. The soul is the likeness of all things. VI, 783. Capable of all things. VI, 783, 784. It sees itself and invisible things through itself, and visible things through the body. VI, 781. Within itself it sees what it remembers. VI, 747. It itself forms within itself images of the bodies it has seen. VI, 798. By what kind of visions it can be deceived or not deceived. VI, 797. The soul was created perfect within its own kind. VI, 815. It would know everything that can be known if the burden of the flesh did not exist. VI, 815. The soul’s dullness concerning itself and its discernment concerning others. VI, 921. Few are able to perceive soul with soul. VI, 781. Why. VI, 781. How the soul is understood to be released from the body, as it were, and to return to it, reporting what it has seen. VI, 1026. Whence it sees so many things in dreams. VI, 1024. Why it does not see itself. VI, 1024. Nothing is more known to the mind than itself. VI, 801. What prevents it from knowing itself. VI, 800, 801. How it can attain knowledge of itself and of God. VI, 812. What it must do to obtain this. VI, 804.

Whence the soul’s instability arises, and what teaches it. VI, 823. How it can be healed. VI, 824. In how many ways the soul descends to the body or ascends to God. VI, 801, 804. How greatly it matters that, having cast aside thought and desire for mutable things, it raise itself upward. VI, 801, 804, 814. The soul is urged to return to itself. VI, 801, 804, 814, 822, 827, 887.

The soul is not merely living, but life itself. VI, 806. How it gives life to the body, and in what manner they are mutually united. VI, 812. The threefold power by which the soul is mingled with the body: natural, vital, and animal. VI, 794, 795. How the soul rules its body. VI, 791. The mind is, as it were, the charioteer and commander of the body. III, 2323. It must govern the body with the restraints of divine law. III, 2351. The flesh was given to the soul as a kind of war. VI, 1074. The devil has power over the flesh, not over the soul. VI, 1074. The soul does not sin except through the flesh. VI, 1076. The soul will not rule the flesh well unless it has served God. X, 1875. It does not lack royal power when it rules well. X, 1879. The soul must be subjected to God so that the flesh may be subjected to the soul. V, 1917. How the soul is either ruled by its lawful king or laid waste by a tyrant. V, 1773.

The soul is loved less by many people than clothing. V, 2346. Greater care should be given to the soul than to the flesh. VI, 1334. What we owe to the soul and what to the flesh. V, 1916. Care for our soul is especially like the cultivation of earthly land. V, 2326, 2327. How blameworthy neglect of it is. V, 2326. God punishes this neglect with earthly losses. V, 2326. How unworthy it is that the flesh receive food twice a day while the soul scarcely receives the word of God after several days. V, 2022. The soul’s nourishment. VI, 1057. Food, drink, clothing, and rest. VI, 1351. The soul’s food is the word of God. V, 2318. For the soul, faith alone is sense, and charity alone is health. V, 1951.

What our soul is like, and what it ought to be like. VI, 826. The qualities of the Christian soul. VI, 961. The soul’s virtues compared with the orders of angels. VI, 782. Within itself the soul possesses that which enables it to dare aspire to the marriage of the Word. VI, 959. The wondrous division of the one simple soul through contemplation. VI, 803. When the mind thinks about eternal things it is masculine; when it thinks about temporal things, feminine. VI, 787, 805. The more it extends itself toward what is eternal, the more it is formed in the image of God. VI, 804. The mind is renewed by consideration of eternal life. VI, 820. By what virtues it reaches union with God. VI, 807. It approaches God through simplicity of essence and perpetuity of life. VI, 807. The soul as Jerusalem. VI, 1231. The city of God; its citizens, counselors, and soldiers. VI, 807. The soul is paradise, Jerusalem, the house of God, and the bride of Christ. VI, 807. The disordered soul. X, 1865. The misery of the soul that does not love Christ. VI, 953. The wicked are shown not to love their own souls. V, 2168.

For souls stripped of the body, daylight contributes nothing and the darkness of night does no harm. VI, 1024. Outside the body the soul sees or hears nothing corporeal in a bodily manner; or at that time it assumes an aerial body. VI, 1026. When the souls of the dead appear, they assume an aerial body. VI, 1026. The condition of souls released from the body until the day of judgment. VI, 1062, 1065. Human souls cannot pass into animals, nor the souls of animals into human beings. VI, 774. In the soul released from the body, the impressions and affections formed here remain. VI, 795, 800, 801, 812. Hence it is of the greatest importance that here it cleanse itself from attachment to bodily things. VI, 801. Among the Greeks a sect arose and came to the Latins that entirely denied Purgatory and maintained that souls receive neither rewards nor punishments until they have again been joined to bodies. II, 1127. This opinion is rejected. II, 1127. After this life souls have only two places in which they dwell eternally. X, 1654. The souls of the saints are in paradise. III, 2426. As soon as the soul is torn away from the body, it is either placed in paradise or in hell. VI, 1184. Beforehand the angels lead it before the tribunal of the supreme Judge. VI, 1183. After death the soul is received by angels and placed either in Abraham’s bosom or in hell. VI, 1163. The soul of the righteous person departing from here is raised by the hands of angels into Abraham’s bosom. V, 1948. The torments of the sinful soul at its departure. VI, 1356. Do condemned souls assume some body, or is hell incorporeal? VI, 1026. The soul departing from here is destined either to possess eternal blessedness or to be assigned to eternal punishment. III, 2232. Before the Lord’s Passion the souls of the saints were detained in hell. VIII, 1220. Now, when they leave the body, they go to Christ, just as the souls of sinners go into hell. VIII, 1220. Before Christ they were held in the prison of hell, though in a tranquil bosom. V, 2059. From the Passion of Christ onward, they enter paradise daily from the whole world. V, 2059. When Christ ascended, souls were seen going from the underworld into heaven. III, 2281. The holy souls are to be believed already to be with Christ. V, 2101. After the present life the souls of the righteous migrate to heaven. VI, 1350. They proceed into the heavens to God. III, 2371. The deceased person ascends into heaven from this life, from where the city of Jerusalem will descend for judgment. III, 2333. How the souls of the saints hear our prayers. VI, 1026. For their joy or punishment to be full and eternal, it is necessary that their bodies rise again. VI, 1027.

The Arians do not wish the Son of God to have assumed a soul, but say that the Word took the soul’s place. VIII, 1167.

According to some, there is a universal soul which is not joined to created beings but gives life to those being generated. VIII, 1166.

The soul of animals begins and ends living with their flesh. VI, 767. The souls of animals are not substantial. VI, 815; VIII, 1216. Nor are they governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think. VIII, 1216.

Four kinds of animals. VI, 729. Irrational animals lack intelligence. VI, 746, 747. Some think that animals on islands were produced from the earth. III, 2158. How different animals know their diseases and what remedies they seek. VI, 1338. What is signified by clean and unclean animals. V, 1939.

The distinction of Anician blood. II, 1114. The Anician house at Hippo Regius. II, 1156.

The consul Annianus. IX, 781.

Annianus. IX, 790.

The books of Annianus, the pseudo-deacon of Celeda. X, 1748. His statements in the letter to Orontius. X, 1749. Also in the letter to Evangelus. X, 1750.

The words of Anselm from the *Proslogion*. VI, 826, 964. Others from the *Prayers*. VI, 939.

Anulinus, proconsul of Africa. IX, 777, 778, 827.

The consul Anthemius. IX, 814.

The error of the Anthropomorphites. VI, 973. The anthropomorphite conceives God as physically represented in bodily form. VIII, 1215.

Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan. III, 2205. There are already many antichrists. VI, 1131. A book on Antichrist, concerning his parents, homeland, character, deeds, and so forth. V, 1131. This book is to be restored to Adso, abbot of the monastery of Der, in accordance with several manuscripts in which it is read under his name, with a prefatory letter addressed to Queen Gerberga.

Antioch, also called Reblatha. III, 2188.

Antiphons. V, 2323.

The antipodes. I, 1429.

A bishop is God’s vicar: he must daily act in Christ’s place, either offer sacrifice or anoint. III, 2386. Bishops can neither harm nor benefit those who receive the sacraments more than advocates can harm or benefit those whose cases they undertake. III, 2312.

Antonius. VI, 1104. He used to throw letters received from loved ones into the fire. VI, 1313. Antonius was told to flee from human beings. VI, 1994.

Apuan. VII, 815.

*Apátheia* (ἀπάθεια), freedom from passion. X, 1730. The heresy of *apatheia* and *anamartēsia* (ἀπαθείας καὶ ἀναμαρτησίας), “freedom from passion and sinlessness.” X, 1996.

Apis. III, 2218.

Bees were granted the ability to produce offspring without intercourse. X, 1646.

An exposition of the Apocalypse according to the allegorical sense. III, 2417. See John.

The error of Apollinaris concerning Christ. V, 2182, 2185. It is indicated and refuted. VIII, 1189. Apollinaris maintains that the Son of God assumed something lesser from human nature. X, 1717, 1735. He thinks that Christ assumed a soul without sense or reason. VIII, 1214.

The Apollinarists maintain that humanity passed into God through a change of nature. VIII, 1214.

Apollodorus. I, 1442.

Apoplexy. V, 2219.

Four kinds of apostles. VI, 752. The marks of true apostleship. VI, 752. The twelve apostles are the rays of the sun and an equal number of lamps of truth. V, 2088. What the Holy Spirit added to their perfection. V, 2088. What sentence each apostle spoke in the Creed. V, 2188, 2190. A panegyric of the apostles. V, 2156. Why fasting is not practiced on the vigils of certain apostles. VI, 1277.

Apostolic succession. Those who disturb the order begun by the apostle Peter and preserved down to the present through the succession of bishops. III, 2331.

The apparitors called *stationarii*. IX, 807. Apparitors of magistrates. IX, 816. An apparitor of the imperial retinue. IX, 816.

Constantine considers an appeal from the judgments of bishops disgraceful. IX, 779. With what striking words he condemns an appeal from the judgment of the Council. IX, 788. An appeal by the African bishops to Rome. X, 1687. By John of Jerusalem to Innocent. X, 1700.

Appetite. VI, 807.

Apronianus. IX, 782, 783.

Plato’s apsides. X, 1693.

Water is the matter of every liquid. III, 2163. From water the body of the dove was made in the beginning. III, 2196. There must be no doubt that waters exist above the heavens. VI, 743. How water rises upward and is changed into hail, snow, and rain. III, 2182. Frequent flooding of waters. V, 2077. Water changed into stones. III, 2169. Salt waters poured through the soil of excellent land become fresh, while fresh waters drawn through the ashes of marine plants acquire a saltier taste than the waters of the ocean. III, 2167, 2168. Why water was not cursed in Adam’s curse. III, 2155. Christ gave a blessing to all waters when he descended into the Jordan. V, 2012, 2013, 2015. After Christ’s baptism something more was conferred upon the waters than upon Mary. V, 2011. See Baptism. The Savior’s threefold water. VI, 1314.

The city of Aquae. X, 1721.

The metropolitan of Aquileia. X, 1763. He is reproved for having received Pelagians within the province. X, 1761. The province of Aquileia, Venetia. X, 1763.

Whitewashed altars. IX, 801.

Aratus, or the Arab, asserts that the soul dies with the body. VI, 815; VIII, 1216.

The canons of the Second Council of Orange. X, 1785. Transmitted by the Apostolic See. X, 1785. Approved and confirmed by that same See. X, 1790. The decrees of the Council of Orange are indicated as especially opposed to a certain letter sent to Caesarius. X, 1792. They are mentioned as the work of Saint Caesarius. X, 1792.

Arius. III, 2266, 2267. When he was born, how he lived, and how he died are known. VIII, 1110. He divides the nature of divinity. VIII, 1213; X, 1735. He places the Son below the Father because the Father says to him, “I have given you as a light to the nations.” VIII, 1112. Or because he himself says, “The Father sent me.” VIII, 1112. Or, “Father, glorify your Son.” VIII, 1113. The error of Arius arose from confusion between Christ’s two substances. V, 2081. The impiety of Arius is extensively refuted from Scripture. III, 2290, 2291. The faith opposed to Arius. V, 2181, 2185. The struggle between Arius and Sabellius serves the Catholic cause. VIII, 1112. Pascentius anathematizes Arius and Eunomius. II, 1157. The efforts of the Arians against the faith. V, 2181. Arian doctrine: the Father is greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit more than lesser. VI, 735. They say that God did not beget. III, 2229. Nor could he beget, since he is of simple nature. III, 2293. They likewise say that it belongs to God’s power to make false things true. III, 2291. Therefore Christ is called the true Son of God because he made him such that he is true. III, 2292. They also say of the Son, “There was when he was not.” III, 2292. They call the Son a perfect creature capable of ruling all creatures. VIII, 1162. They acknowledge the Son as God. VIII, 1108, 1110. But not as coeternal. VIII, 1110. They deny that the Son can be equal to the Father. VIII, 1101. They confess Christ to be equal to the Father. VIII, 1108. But in power and operation, not in eternity. VIII, 1108. They dishonor the Father by proclaiming the Son lesser. VIII, 1121. They deny that time existed before the Son. VIII, 1159. Yet their statement “There was when he was not” places time and space before him. VIII, 1160. They affirm that he was begotten from the Father’s will but not from his substance. VIII, 1161. They deny *homoousion*, “of the same substance,” lest he be understood as one divided into two. VIII, 1161. The Arians’ objections against Christ’s divinity and eternity are dissolved. V, 2198. The Arians believed that the Son of God assumed flesh alone, without a soul. VIII, 1167. They lead some astray by power and others by money. VIII, 1121. They rebaptize. VIII, 1129. The cave of the Arians, into which they invite a Catholic with money and, calling him a pagan, compel him to receive baptism from them. VIII, 1115. They uselessly give this cave the name of a church. VIII, 1130. The Arian heresy and the Catholic Church are represented by two prostitutes quarreling. V, 1822.

Augustine. IX, 816, 827. His eulogy. X, 1685, 1794, 1800. Augustine, a pillar of the Church. X, 1697. The strongest tower of the pastoral watchtower. X, 1830. He was ordained by Megalius, primate of Numidia. IX, 834. Innocent was beaten by heretics. X, 1708. Augustine speaks for the Catholic cause at the Conference of Carthage. IX, 828. He replies to the letters of the Donatists. IX, 838. The Jerusalemite assembly curses Pelagius as a blasphemer because he despises Augustine, through whose mouth the Lord granted the whole of Africa the health of unity. X, 1699. Augustine and Aurelius detect and convict Pelagius’s heresy. X, 1684. Augustine is the most vigorous defender of grace. X, 1740. Marius Mercator held Augustine in high esteem. X, 1737. So did Jerome. X, 1748. Jerome yields to Augustine the opportunity to contend against Pelagius. X, 1708.

Augustine and Jerome, lights among ecclesiastical teachers, are attacked by a certain Seneca. X, 1771. Augustine’s books on the predestination of the saints contain much that is troubling. X, 1849. Augustine’s teaching is defamed by a diabolical index, as though he approved what it contained. X, 1843. Certain priests in Gaul speak against Augustine as though he had exceeded the proper limit. X, 1757. When Augustine was already old, some spoke against him in secret whispers, as though he had removed free choice and introduced fatal necessity. X, 1794. Likewise, as though he wished two masses and two natures of the human race to be believed. X, 1794. That slander is rejected. X, 1801. Two epigrams of Prosper against a new detractor of the aged Augustine. X, 1857. Augustine’s books, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper, contain the Church’s faith concerning grace and free choice. X, 1778, 1784. Augustine died amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals while replying to Julian’s books. X, 1755.

Augustine’s writings, criticized by some in Gaul, are defended by Caelestine. X, 1753. By this pope’s testimony, he was everywhere beloved and honored by all. X, 1756, 1831. He was never touched even by a rumor of sinister suspicion. X, 1756. He always lived in communion with the Roman pontiffs and was always regarded by them as one of the best teachers. X, 1756. Caelestine’s distinguished testimony concerning Augustine, and the manner in which some try to obscure it. X, 1831. How futile this is. X, 1831. Pope Boniface commends Augustine’s teaching on grace. X, 1790. How highly he valued it. X, 1831. Those who slander Augustine’s teaching thereby wrong everyone, especially the Roman pontiffs, in this one matter. X, 1801. Their purpose is to persuade people that the Pelagians were unjustly condemned. X, 1801. Augustine’s teaching is defamed by publishing certain chapters from it under the title of condemnation. X, 1833. What those chapters are, and Prosper’s response to them. X, 1833. A summary of them together with the opposing opinions. X, 1840. They said that Augustine initially thought correctly when he said faith was from human beings, but later erred when he asserted that it was God’s gift. X, 1851. How rashly they said this. X, 1851. Augustine’s example teaches us to correct opinions formed imprudently. X, 1851. Augustine, torn apart by a rabid mouth, is defended. X, 1830. Throughout all parts of the world, all the children of promise agree with Augustine’s teaching. X, 1794. It is plainly evident that Faustus’s books are heretical because they oppose Augustine. An excerpt from Augustine’s letter to Sixtus. X, 1832. His homily on charity is mentioned. V, 2245. It is transcribed. V, 2247. His homily on the paralytic of thirty-eight years is likewise praised and briefly summarized. V, 2261. The second book of Augustine’s *Retractations* is praised. X, 1851. Likewise his work addressed to Simplicianus. X, 1851. Many of Augustine’s writings in support of grace are listed. X, 1831. Three books addressed to Marcellinus and a fourth addressed to Hilary are praised. X, 1708. His book *On Grace and Free Choice* is also praised. X, 1815. Likewise his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*. X, 1856. The occasion of Augustine’s books against Julian. X, 1737.

The charioteer. II, 1109; V, 1813.

Babbutius. IX, 791.

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” III, 2443. It represents the wicked, just as Jerusalem represents the saints. III, 2443. In one Church, Babylonians and Jerusalemites exist together. III, 2444. The conquest of Babylon under Cyrus. III, 2172.

The Flood was a likeness of our baptism. V, 2028. The figure of baptism in the waters that burst forth in the Flood, both those above and those below the heavens. III, 2157. Baptism is called the sacrament of Christ’s death and resurrection. X, 1845. The sacrament of faith and repentance. VI, 775. It is the sign of death conquered. III, 2275. An image of the future resurrection. V, 2070. Christ’s baptism is our burial. V, 1902.

The necessity of baptism. V, 1814; VI, 810; VII, 812; X, 1784. Baptized persons alone have the way of salvation. VIII, 1220. Catechumens, even when they die in good works, are denied eternal life except in the case of martyrdom. VIII, 1220. Comparison of the baptized and martyrs. VIII, 1220.
