The Pelagians denied that baptism was necessary for infants’ salvation; Caelestius confessed that through it they are redeemed. X, 1712. It is utterly foolish to deny this. X, 1714. To what extent Caelestius thinks that baptism for the remission of sins should be conferred upon infants. X, 1719. He is condemned for denying that infants should be baptized. X, 1728. Why they are baptized. X, 1728. Infants are baptized not only for the sake of the kingdom of heaven or so that they may merit adoption as children. X, 1772. But so that they may not be held by the second death. III, 2275. No one escapes the infernal Tartarus unless he has received this sign. X, 2275. Baptism is conferred for the remission of sins. X, 1708, 1728, 1769, 1772. Upon newborn infants. X, 1769, 1772. The necessity of baptism, and when it began. VI, 767, 775.

## Form of Baptism

X, 1728. In the solemn administration of baptism, all heretics agree in the use of the same words. IX, 765. A pagan, a Jew, a Sadducee, and others baptize; but there is one true baptism, that of Christ—and Christ’s baptism is that of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. IX, 765. Whoever is immersed in the name of Christ is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. X, 1655. There is no saint who rebaptizes after the Trinity. IX, 766. Those baptized among the Donatists ought not to be baptized again. IX, 764. Rather, they should be received according to the ancient order by the laying on of hands. IX, 809. Whether it is permissible to ordain those who had been baptized as infants among them. IX, 809. The baptism of the Church and that of heretics who baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is one and the same. VI, 750; VIII, 1217. For this reason the Church does not rebaptize them, because they were baptized in the name of the Trinity. VI, 750. This itself is the form of the sacrament. VI, 750. On their return they receive the power of the Holy Spirit, whom they did not receive outside. VI, 750. One who received baptism outside must come to the Church, not so that what was lacking may be supplied, but so that what was present may become beneficial. IX, 826, 837. Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is complete everywhere, but it benefits no one except within the Church. VI, 767, 776. Outside the Church it heaps up destruction. VI, 776. The baptism of an unwilling or hypocritical person is valid when he has repented. VI, 1119. A heretic is to be baptized if, when questioned about the Creed, he does not confess the Trinity. IX, 787. But if he does confess it, only the laying on of hands is to be performed. IX, 787. Heretics whose baptism is null. VIII, 1217.

## The Power of Baptismal Water

VI, 1209. The effects of baptism prefigured in the marriages of the Patriarchs. V, 1754, 1762. In the baptism of Christ. III, 2195, 2249. In the crossing of the Red Sea. V, 1791, 1955. All sins, and sins alone, suffer shipwreck in this washing. V, 1791. The power of baptism prefigured in the cleansing of Naaman. V, 1833. All the baptized are born infants, whether they are young or old. V, 1833. The nature of the baptized is changed. VI, 1203. Through baptism every guilt of sin is washed away. VI, 749. Through faith in the Church, the sins contracted in origin are forgiven for the person being baptized. VI, 1119. Through baptism all sins are removed from every believing person, both personal sins and original sin. X, 1834, 1841. The bond of original sin is broken, and the adoption of children, which had been lost, is restored. X, 1784. In baptism the Spirit, who brings faith into being, washes the soul from sins. III, 2254. The nature of baptism is spiritual, not earthly. III, 2254. The wondrous grace of baptism in infants and in those who receive it at the very end of their life, while their spirit is being breathed out. X, 1800. Baptism possesses the same fullness in all. X, 1730. Through baptism it is said that one drinks the cup of immortality, fashioned from our weakness and divine power. X, 1844. For one emerging from baptism, the gate of heaven is opened. V, 2015. The postponement of baptism until the end of life. III, 2376. Those who defer baptism do not know the gift of God. V, 1925. Through baptism our flesh becomes the land of the living, whereas previously it was the land of the dying. V, 1741. By it iniquity is erased, but weakness is not completely healed. I, 1463. Even one renewed by the grace of baptism needs God’s daily help to overcome the desires of the flesh. X, 1757.

## Baptismal Administration

Baptism is conferred by a presbyter. VII, 842. It was conferred upon Nicodemus by the Apostles. VII, 809, 811. The mysteries of baptism are not explained to catechumens until after baptism. VI, 1207. Exercises for those about to be baptized. VI, 1205. Infants to be baptized are presented according to the proper order immediately at the beginning of Lent. V, 1751. Mothers present them later, so that they will not be obliged to come to the vigils with them. V, 1751. Those about to be baptized are prepared by the Lenten fast. V, 2033. Baptism without repentance benefited no one who sinned voluntarily. VI, 1119. Those about to be baptized are catechized and exsufflated. X, 1656, 1759. So that the unclean spirit may be driven from them by exsufflations and exorcisms. X, 1759. No one approaches the baptismal font unless the unclean spirit has first been driven from him by the exorcisms of the clergy. X, 1759.

Those about to be baptized receive chrism and the oil of blessing. V, 1828. Why the ears and nostrils are anointed with blessed oil. VI, 1207. After the anointing of the ears, they are counted among the spiritual hearers. VI, 1208. Those about to be baptized are questioned concerning faith in the Trinity. VI, 1209. When asked whether we renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works, we reply that we will renounce them. V, 2334, 2335. In the case of infants, their parents are guarantors of this profession of faith. V, 2335. In this sacrament both those who receive and those who are received enter into a covenant with Christ. V, 2243, 2335. What sort of covenant this is. VI, 1169, 1209. In baptism, a promise is made to wash the feet of guests. V, 2220. 3. [Col. 0694] Sponsors are called fathers, and those sponsored are called sons. V, 2071, 2243. The duty of sponsors. V, 2071, 2238, 2243. The person being baptized is either sprinkled with water or immersed. VIII, 1220. He is submerged in the water under the sign of the cross. VI, 1115. That is, by a threefold immersion. V, 1791, 1825. What the threefold immersion of the head in the sacred font signifies. VI, 1211. The baptized person at the same time receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and communicates in the Eucharist. VIII, 1220. Honey and heavenly bread are provided for him. V, 1955. When baptism has been completed, chrism is poured upon the head: the meaning of this rite. VI, 1211. The newly baptized put on a white garment. V, 2070. Their feet are washed. VI, 1211.

## Baptism Is One

VI, 750; VIII, 1217. It is not to be repeated. VI, 767, 776, 779. Why it is not to be repeated. VI, 1115. It cannot be repeated, just as a mother’s womb cannot be entered again. X, 1888. To repeat baptism is called exorcizing the faithful and exorcizing the Holy Spirit. IX, 804. Those who repeat baptism are signified by that tail which cast the stars of heaven down upon the earth. III, 2434. How Catholics resist the Arians who compel the repetition of baptism. VIII, 1115, 1129. The Arians exsufflate him. VIII, 1129. The constitution of the elder Valentinian against those who rebaptize. IX, 805. Another constitution of Gratian. IX, 806. Two baptisms among the Pelagians. X, 1656.

Just as baptism is not repeated, so sins must not be repeated. VI, 1211, 1212. What the baptized must fear if they are sluggish. V, 1742. Those are not approved who wish to be found on the day of death as they emerged from baptism. V, 2232. Whoever does not put off the old person makes unworthy use of baptism and will therefore be condemned. X, 1781. Whoever has not kept the covenant vainly believes that baptism has not perished for him. V, 2336. The person who consults magicians forfeits the sacrament of baptism. VI, 1172. Or who practices superstitious rites. V, 2240, 2269.

## Blessedness

Blessedness can be prepared here, but cannot be possessed here. V, 2159. How blessedness differs in an impassible nature and in a passible nature. III, 2326. Angels and human beings received the gift of blessedness and eternity from God in the very creation of their rational nature. VI, 763. By sheer goodness God made us capable of blessedness and fit to taste it through the gift of love. VI, 845. Blessed is the person who lives as he wishes. VI, 725. A right will, even when it has not obtained what it desires, is nearer to blessedness than a wicked will, even if it has obtained what it desires. X, 1864. Nothing can make the soul blessed except righteousness. VI, 829.

## The Blessed Life

The blessed life is knowledge of divinity. V, 2324. It is joy concerning the truth. X, 1874. If the blessed life is not loved, it is not possessed. X, 1872. Reading seeks the sweetness of the blessed life, meditation finds it, prayer requests it, and contemplation tastes it. VI, 997. The blessedness of the saints after this life. V, 1964; VI, 807, 894, 1103, 1184, 1186. This comes both from the gift of grace and from the recompense of righteousness. X, 1861. To whom it should be granted. X, 1892. It was granted to the saints after the course of this life had run its course. V, 1876–1878. Jerome already rejoices in it. II, 1130. Vincentius also rejoices in it. V, 2097. See Soul; Heaven.

## The Joy of the Blessed

How great the joy of the blessed will be and from what it will arise. V, 1898. They will rejoice not in sensible things but in the highest good. VI, 1030. The joy of the blessed arises from love, and love from knowledge of God. VI, 967. The food, drink, and knowledge of the blessed. VI, 993, 996. The glory of the blessed is the vision of God. II, 1125, 1130. From the vision of God, delightfully impressed upon them, there will be both thirst and satiety. VI, 980. The blessed are eager and always full; they desire what they possess. VI, 920, 921. They are certain of the eternity of their happiness. VI, 828, 861. And, to the extent that God has given to each, they are perfectly and steadfastly good. VI, 775. They will enjoy God in three ways. VI, 829. The garments of the blessed are their merits. V, 2230. ## Charity

Charity is a short word, but great in reality. V, 1967. An encomium of charity. VI, 792. Charity is God’s way to human beings and the way of human beings to God. VI, 792. The fruit of the blessed earth. VI, 1223. The foundation of every good. V, 2245, 2312. The root of all good works. V, 1958, 1968, 2246. When this root is not alive, its branches [Col. 0698] with flowers and fruits are possessed in vain. V, 2261. Charity is the form of every good action. VI, 1256. The mother and teacher of heavenly virtues. V, 1958. The soul of all the Scriptures. V, 2247. The citadel of all virtues. V, 1960. Whoever has charity will be filled with every virtue. VI, 1188. Charity is the sum of every good. VI, 1149. It contains every good. V, 2247. Its highest reward is that of the saints in heaven. V, 1960. Charity is the sweet and salutary bond of minds. V, 1957, 1968. However far apart in body, it unites and joins them. V, 1957. Thus it loses none of them. X, 1874. It is harmony of minds, the fellowship of the elect, and the life of blessed souls and angels. VI, 809. Charity is our health. VI, 1065. Charity itself is good will. V, 2248, 2337. The whole perfection of charity consists in the goodness or will of the mind. V, 2256. Charity is properly called the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1174.

Charity is a gift of God—indeed, God’s gift. X, 1789, 1797, 1894. God, not ourselves, gives us charity. X, 1820. No gift is greater than this. VIII, 1174. Charity is a singular gift to the saints. VIII, 1174. No one was found worthy of this gift. X, 1797. Without it, many praiseworthy things may exist in a person that resemble piety but lack its truth. X, 1797. How great charity is: if it is absent, all other things are possessed in vain; if it is present, everything is possessed. X, 1888. Without it, the rich person is poor, and with it, the poor person is rich. V, 2247. Charity is rightly compared with oil. V, 1957. Charity is from God and flows back into God. VI, 1149. The wound of charity is demanded. VI, 935. The virtue of charity belongs properly to the saints; the other virtues may be shared by good and wicked people alike. X, 1859.

Nothing can be sweeter than charity, nor can anything be fulfilled more easily and happily with God’s help. V, 2245. Through the Holy Spirit it is poured into the hearts of all Christians in such a way that, if they wish, they can continually preserve it. V, 2245.

Four special virtues of charity are explained. V, 1952. Charity and covetousness cannot exist together in any way. V, 2245, 2247. Charity cannot be absent where covetousness is absent. V, 2245. The effects of charity and desire. V, 2170. Charity gathered the Church together. V, 2091. It renews human beings. X, 1882. It teaches the proper use of wealth. V, 1957. It causes all God’s commandments to be fulfilled with joy. V, 2245, 2247. Whoever rejoices in charity can be ignorant of nothing in the Scriptures, fail to fulfill none of the good works, and fear no one. V, 1968. Humility subjects the mind to God, purity joins it to him, and charity unites it. VI, 794, 807. Charity’s intimacy with God. VI, 819. A holy soul can never be without love. VI, 1150. The proof of love for God. VI, 1150.

Charity is an easy and gentle yoke. X, 1651. It customarily lifts rather than presses down. V, 2246. Charity holds first place among God’s commandments. V, 1960. It is sufficient in itself without certain works, while no works are beneficial without it. V, 2246, 2247, 2249, 2252. The commandment of charity admits no excuse. V, 1860, 2246, 2252, 2255. It embraces three things. X, 1872. The two wings of charity are love of God and love of neighbor. VI, 1149. Charity is twofold, like two feet for running along Christ’s road. V, 1875, 2161. Mutual charity is graphically commended. VI, 1065. Examples of compassionate charity in our members. V, 1949, 1951. In Christ, who now reigns. V, 1950. Charity is always sweet, even when it becomes angry or reproves. V, 1958. How great are the riches of charity. V, 1957, 1968. What charity possesses is available to all. V, 2249. The capacity for charity always increases. X, 1867. It grows through being distributed. V, 1828. Charity itself is such that its possession increases the more it is distributed. V, 2252. Human beings are vessels of charity; they are filled when they are loved. V, 1829. Charity makes its own what it loves in another among the saints. VI, 920. True charity embraces enemies themselves. They condemn second marriages. V, 2183; X, 1718, 1735.

Infants are catechized. X, 1768. Catechumens are to be mourned if they depart from this life without baptism. VI, 1166. The forehead of catechumens is signed. V, 1821. The mysteries of baptism are not explained to catechumens until after baptism. VI, 1207.

The ten Categories excerpted from Aristotle. I, 1419. In the *Categories*, Aristotle treats, first, things that exist; second, things that are perceived; third, things that are spoken. I, 1422. Or, as Themistius prefers, first things that are perceived, then things that exist, and afterward things that are spoken. I, 1422.

The Chair of Peter. IX, 805. The nativity-feast of Saint Peter’s Chair. V, 2100, 2101. It sometimes falls during Lent. V, 2101. The superstition customary on that day. V, 2101, 2102.

The seat of pestilence. III, 2330. The seat of life. III, 2330.

Cathinus’s colors [uncertain reading]. VI, 1110.

Who ought to be called catholic, and who ought not. IX, 830. What the Donatists understand by “catholic.” IX, 830. That is declared catholic which is spread throughout the whole world. IX, 780. Criminal Catholics will not possess the kingdom of heaven. VI, 776.

Catullinus, subdeacon. IX, 794.

The first cause of all bodily and spiritual movements is the will of God. X, 1864. What we know about unknown causes. X, 1873.

Celiel. VII, 815, 816.

The vain adornment of cells. I, 1462. In their oratory, the image of the Crucified should suffice, with Mary and John standing on either side of it. I, 1462.

Celsus, Vicar of Africa. IX, 780, 780.

Some make vows of wax or oil for the night lamps. V, 1978.

Cerdo posits two principles unknown to himself. VIII, 1217.

The brain as the heaven of our body. VI, 802. The seat of wisdom. VI, 1216. The brain’s three ventricles. VI, 795.

Candles lit before sacred relics. VII, 837. To provide little candles for churches. V, 2238.

Cerinthus. VIII, 1217. He hopes for sexual intercourse after this life. VIII, 1218.

Those who contend, considering how God regards and helps them. V, 1813. The time of our contest is short, but the reward is without end. V, 2135.

Beer. VI, 1286.

Deer are enemies of serpents and suffer nothing from their venom except thirst. VI, 1203.

To make a little deer, or little deer figures. V, 2001, 2003, 2004. To practice obscenity involving a little doe. V, 2239.

By what right the land of Canaan passed to the Israelites. V, 1811.

The Jews ask for Christ’s mark. VII, 827. Diabolical marks. V, 2071, 2239, 2272.

Engraved tablets. VIII, 1133.

Public documents. IX, 832.

A letter was given to Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse, instructing him to proceed to the Synod of Arles. IX, 786.

Chrism, the oil with which the faithful are anointed. II, 1161. What they are taught by that anointing. X, 1890. The mystery of the chrism poured upon the baptized. VI, 1211. Through the sacrament of chrism, a kind of diadem of royal anointing is placed upon the Christian as a mystery of the heavenly kingdom. II, 1116. And so that he may understand that he is not only a sharer in priestly and royal dignity, but is also made a combatant against the devil. X, 1890. The anointing with chrism of little children who had been baptized among heretics. VIII, 1217. See “Baptism.” A flask of chrism thrown through a window came down unharmed among the rocks. IX, 804.

Christ, from *chrisma*, “chrism.” V, 1761, 2192. Namely, from the infusion of the Holy Spirit. VI, 1191. He is called “anointed” in Hebrew. V, 2189. Christ is the arm of God. VI, 1141. The Only-begotten and Firstborn. V, 1996. The divine man. V, 2054. One of the Holy Trinity. X, 1778. The Law and the Prophets did not cease to foretell Christ’s mysteries. VI, 760, 772, 774. He was foretold in Isaac. V, 1758. In Isaac and the ram. V, 1750. In Jacob. V, 1760, 1761, 1763, 1764. In Joseph. V, 1765, 1773, 1924. In Moses. V, 1776. In Aaron. V, 1804. In the struck rock that brought forth springs. V, 1796. In the bronze serpent. V, 1807. In the grape-cluster brought from the Promised Land. V, 1800. In Gideon. V, 1817. In David. V, 1819. In Elijah. V, 1823, 1825. In Elisha. V, 1827. Christ is the fish of Tobit. V, 2125. In a certain way, the body of the shadows of the old Law. X, 1884. The name of Christ is truth. V, 1783. Christ, the Word of God, speaks not only through sounds but also through deeds. V, 1902. Before assuming flesh, he benefited the human race. X, 1735. The purpose of Christ’s mysteries in the dispensation of his work. V, 2043, 2044. Christ prepared roads for the Israelites through the sea. V, 1798. Christ was seen in Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace. III, 2391. Why Christ’s coming was delayed for so long. III, 2276. How great the devil’s power was before Christ’s coming, and how much it was thereafter diminished. V, 1819. The grace of Christ’s coming. V, 1925.

With Christ’s coming, the promise made to Abraham was fulfilled. III, 2210. And the seventy weeks were completed. III, 2213. [Col. 0701] With Christ’s coming, the fullness of truth was brought about. III, 2388. Christ was made from the woman whom he had made, and was made under the Law which he had given. VI, 772. He came in the sixth millennium of the world. III, 2320. How the eternal Son of God can be understood to have been born in time. VIII, 1166. How Christ came to Mary. VIII, 1170. In Christ’s conception, the husband signifies the Word, and the wife the ear. V, 1991. In Christ’s conception, the creation of the first man from raw earth is renewed. V, 1982. When the divinity came into Mary’s womb, it fashioned flesh for itself from her substance. V, 2199. The Holy Spirit made flesh from the Virgin for the Savior: the Power of the Most High—that is, Christ—overshadowed her, coming into flesh made by the Spirit, so that the Power of the Son might lie hidden in body and soul. III, 2250, 2251. Some most wickedly suppose that the Holy Spirit was present as seed in Christ’s conception. V, 2182. Christ was conceived not from the substance but through the power, command, and blessing of the Holy Spirit. V, 2178. Christ’s flesh was spiritually given its anointing in the Virgin’s womb. III, 2250. Christ alone was born without seed and therefore free from sin. X, 1619, 1620. He was born in true flesh from the Virgin’s womb through a mystical inspiration. X, 1615. In the manner of his conception, he compares himself to a worm. VI, 1191. He alone was born without sin. V, 1997. Nature, ever begotten, assumed our nature without sin. VI, 757.

Christ’s flesh was not conceived before it was assumed by the Word. VI, 772. The whole majesty of the Godhead was not enclosed in Christ’s body. VIII, 1189. The Father and the Holy Spirit filled Christ’s flesh, but by majesty, not by assumption. V, 2196. The whole Trinity made Christ’s body. III, 2251. He himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was the creator of his body; he alone personally possesses in himself that which is created. VI, 760. The whole Trinity fashioned the man whom the person of the Son alone assumed. VI, 736. Various heretical opinions about Christ are noted and rejected. VIII, 1213. The Arians held that the Word took the place of the soul in Christ. VIII, 1167. This is refuted. VIII, 1168. Through the mediation of a soul, without which it was impossible for God to be joined to a body, God became man. VIII, 1190. Although the Son of God came in the flesh, he nevertheless dwelt in his soul. III, 2390. Christ’s soul received all wisdom, truth, and life into itself. VIII, 1190. It was filled substantially with God. VIII, 1191, 1192. Because it adhered inseparably to the Word and received the whole of him in its entirety, it became with him, in a principal sense, one spirit. VIII, 1190, 1191. By merit of love. VIII, 1191. It chose the good before it knew evil. VIII, 1189. Christ’s soul possessed freedom, and there was no possibility of its sinning. VIII, 1189. Just as the motion of the body follows its shadow, so it unfailingly received the Word’s prompting. VIII, 1190. At one point Leporius thought that Christ had undergone everything belonging to suffering solely by the possibility of nature, without the aid of the Godhead. X, 1752. A similar, or even more destructive, heresy. X, 1752. Christ was made Grace in human nature. VI, 760.

Christ’s truth is established against the Jews by many testimonies from the Law and the Prophets. VIII, 1123. From Simeon and Zechariah. VIII, 1123. From Virgil, Nebuchadnezzar, and the Sibyl. VIII, 1126. From the elements. VIII, 1127. Artemon, Berillus, and Marcellus taught that Christ’s divinity began when he was born as a man. VIII, 1214. Christ’s divinity was attacked by Arian arguments and defended by catholic replies. V, 2198. Christ’s divinity was born from the Father’s nature. VI, 758. Christ was called the Word, Power, and Wisdom of God, so that he might be believed to be God and therefore one with him. III, 2285. Christ’s divinity is shown by the fact that everything predicated of God is likewise predicated of him. III, 2291. Christ’s humility is illumined by signs of his power. V, 1990. Christ is eternal in what is his own, mortal in what is ours. VIII, 1166. He is humbled in what he assumed and glorified in what is his own. VIII, 1167. Christ is proved to be God by the manner of his conception. V, 1983. And by the order of his birth. V, 1988, 1989. Christ’s birth shows him to be the son of man; his death revealed him to be God. V, 2057. Death revealed the man, resurrection revealed God. V, 2043. Where Christ is said to be the Son of God, his power confirms the testimony. III, 2345. Christ declared his divinity through many signs. V, 1927. He performed mighty works in two kinds. V, 1927. Christ is not a man apart from God or together with God, but man in God and God in man. VIII, 1215.

Christ’s flesh was not heavenly, passing through the Virgin’s womb as through another body. V, 2082. Christ’s body was not imaginary but solid. V, 2175. It was taken from sinful flesh. I, 2268. Christ’s flesh is Adam’s flesh. VI, 758. His body differed from ours in this one respect: it was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. VIII, 1176. He was born, suffered, and died in truth, not in appearance. VIII, 1176. Photinus wants Christ to be a mere man; Apollinaris denies that he was a complete man. V, 2182. Christ is one, God and man. III, 2390; V, 1925; VI, 913; VIII, 1122; X, 1890, 1892. He himself is one and of one nature with the Father, and of one nature with the Virgin. VI, 771. Fully and perfectly God, fully and perfectly man. VI, 756, 771. Perfect man and true God. V, 2180, 2185. [Col. 0702] In him there is the true form of a servant and the true form of God. V, 2084. He himself is our way and our homeland. V, 2083. He is mediator because he is both the same true God and true man. VI, 757.

Christ’s two substances and natures. V, 2003, 2081, 2176, 2182, 2185, 2198; VI, 736, 771; VIII, 1195. Perfect and complete. X, 1716, 1732. The error of the Easterners, who say that the Son of God and the son of man are of one nature, is refuted. V, 2081. Yet damnable is the blasphemy of those who wish, from the time of the assumed humanity, everything that belonged to the divinity to have migrated into the man, and everything that belonged to the humanity to have been transferred into God. V, 2182. Do not either confuse or divide the truth of the human and divine natures in one person. VI, 759. The Word assumed flesh; he was not changed into flesh. VI, 736. The Son of God assumed our nature in such a way that he did not alter his own. V, 1981. Humanity was joined to divinity; divinity was not changed into humanity. V, 2186. When Christ came to us, he did not depart from the Father. VIII, 1120. Assuming what he was not, without losing what he was. VIII, 1122. Although he was God, he was incarnate; and having become man, he remained what he was. VIII, 1176. He put on a garment that he had not possessed. VIII, 1107. Man approached God; God did not withdraw from himself. X, 1869. Christ came to us through what he assumed from us, and freed us through what remained his own. V, 2000. Entirely in heaven and entirely in the Virgin’s womb. VI, 1022. He showed his divinity and humanity in many ways. V, 1902. Some things he says and does as man, others as God. V, 2177, 2198.

Christ has two natures, not confused but united and inseparable in one person. V, 2198. There are not two persons but one. V, 2082; VI, 736, 771; VIII, 1195, 1206; X, 1716, 1732. In Christ, from divinity and humanity, there is one person. V, 1981. The one person of the Son. V, 2182, 2185. In him, the Son of God and the son of man are not two sons. VIII, 1195. As soul and flesh are one man, so the Word and man are one Christ. VIII, 1195. The Son of God in the Father’s heart, the son of man in the mother’s womb. VIII, 1122. Word, soul, and flesh are one Christ. VIII, 1122. Christ is one, not two, because his person is one, although his substance is not one. VIII, 1162, 1166. He preserved for each nature what was proper to it, but joined to each what belonged to the other. VIII, 1165. Something similar can be seen in man. VIII, 1166. Christ is true God and true man, one Son. VIII, 1213. Not by adoption or by designation, but by being born he bears the name “son” in both births. VIII, 1213. Christ is the unique Son of God by nature. VI, 1191. In the Lord, the servant was made at the same time as the one who is Lord. V, 1995. Christ’s flesh is adored, and why it is to be adored. V, 2200. The person of Christ’s flesh is divine from the very moment of its conception. VI, 758. The human nature was assumed by him into the unity of his person. VI, 759.

In what sense Christ is said to have been sent. X, 1890. In what sense he left father and mother to cling to his wife. VI, 748. Why he descended to us. VI, 1318. An unnamed heresy said that Christ lived in solitude, entirely free from any contact with sin, and came into this world not for our redemption but as an example. X, 1752. Christ assumed flesh to recall the whole world from sins and by his example, and to redeem it by suffering. X, 1732. There would have been no reason for him to assume flesh if the condition of human nature had remained intact. X, 1622. Christ bestows more upon us than Adam had obtained. III, 2370. Christ came to destroy the works of the devil. X, 1624. He deceived the devil by the same device with which the devil had deceived man. V, 2103. He set a trap in which he would free the whole creation. V, 1984. He assumed mortal man in order to make him immortal. VIII, 1122. Like Elisha, by humbling himself he restored life to the world. V, 1830. He became man to teach us the obedience in which alone our salvation lies. VIII, 1186. Having purchased from us his birth and death, he gave back resurrection and eternal life. V, 1999. Christ’s humility is the exaltation of our body. V, 1995. Christ willed to be born in every respect in Adam’s likeness, so that he might dissolve all human sins. V, 2031. To cleanse the flesh and soul of man, he assumed both. VI, 758. And this had to happen because man had died in both flesh and soul. VI, 736. There is in Christ a certain power of seed by which the soul restores souls and, through the flesh, raises the flesh of us all. VIII, 1172.

Christ’s two births. V, 2176; VI, 756; VIII, 1165. Both are equally incomparable. V, 1994. Equally wondrous. V, 1996. In those who deny either one, although their intervening arguments differ, the beginning and end of the error are the same. VIII, 1165. For this reason Christ is “yesterday and today.” V, 1998. Christ, who already had a father in heaven, had to choose only a mother on earth. VIII, 1146. Why Christ’s genealogy is divided into three parts. III, 2392. Why, although it contains only forty-one generations, the Evangelist appears to have counted forty-two. III, 2392. Why four were omitted. III, 2280. Apart from the order of his birth, Christ was truly begotten as a man. V, 1981. Christ alone was born of a virgin. VIII, 1122. How this was possible. V, 1989. Indeed, necessary. V, 1990. This manner of birth was prefigured in Adam. V, 1993. By being born of the Virgin, Christ did not incur the lots. VIII, 1107. He was born while his mother’s womb remained closed. V, 2003, 2066; VIII, 1122. What things contrary to one another are fitting to Christ at his birth. V, 1998. The fruit of Christ’s birth. V, 1989, 2145. Christ’s birthday foretells our growth. III, 2252.

The Magi recognized that Christ was God because the stars served him. V, 2015. Christ is invisible in himself but appeared visibly in man. VIII, 1145, 1147. Through his incarnation he made visible to us the God who is invisible in his immensity. VIII, 1180. He appeared, presenting man to those who saw, while preserving God for those who believed. V, 1996. While Christ was fleeing into Egypt, he is said to have been intercepted on the road by robbers and rescued through the favor of a young man, who was later crucified at his right hand and merited paradise. I, 1466. Christ served the Father in every condition. VIII, 1175. Angels served Christ while he was on earth. VI, 1146.

Christ first became known to the world at his baptism. V, 2015. Christ was born as the Son of God both according to the Spirit and according to the flesh. III, 2252. But he hears that declaration at baptism not for himself but for us. III, 2252. He was baptized not for himself but for us. V, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2015. Baptized in the flesh, he washes the baptizer in the Spirit. V, 2016, 2017. Nevertheless, he is said to have been consecrated in the Jordan, reborn through the sacraments, and begotten through the mystery. V, 2011. Christ’s baptism is called a second birth. V, 2012, 2013. And Christ’s regeneration. V, 2013. Christ’s humility in baptism. V, 2010, 2016. How fittingly he fasted in the wilderness. V, 2031. Christ’s temptations overcome through fasting are not written down. III, 2394. The devil was tormented when tempting him for two reasons. III, 2394. Christ’s temptation is the Christian’s instruction. X, 1868. What benefit it has brought us. III, 2196.

Christ preached for three years and six months. V, 1825. He taught us by word and example. V, 1866. In man he taught man from what he should withdraw, what he should endure, and toward what he should strive. VIII, 1146. Christ’s food is our salvation. V, 2172. Christ’s transfiguration manifested what was, as it were, hidden in his body. III, 2322. Then the divinity lying hidden in the body offered itself to be seen outwardly by the spectators according to their capacity. III, 2197. Some say that the Son of God was compelled by the necessity of the flesh to lie and was unable to do everything he wished. X, 1718, 1733. It is wholly impossible for Christ’s will not to be fulfilled. III, 2271.

Why Christ wept for Lazarus. VI, 1160. Why he both wept and rejoiced over Lazarus’s death. V, 1927. Why he asks what he does not fail to know. V, 1928. The power of Christ’s voice. V, 1928. How much Christ endured for us. V, 1955. An exhortation to imitate Christ’s endurance. V, 1956. Christ, the good physician, first tasted the cup that he was going to give us. V, 2031. The analogy between Christ and an experienced physician. V, 2201, 2203. Christ’s Passion is considered. VI, 905, 907. From where could man repay him with anything similar? VI, 906. Christ is still wearied by our weakness. V, 1924. He rests in the faithful. V, 1924. What Christ’s weaknesses have achieved for us. VI, 1194. He endured the true sensations and pains of his flesh in the Passion and before the Passion. VIII, 1214. Whatever weakness we read of in Christ must be attributed to the man he assumed. V, 1981. Christ suffered according to the substance that was assumed, not according to the substance that assumed. V, 2182. He hungered, thirsted, and grieved. V, 2175, 2186. As Son of God, he did not suffer; as man, he was not incapable of suffering. V, 2175, 2186. In the Passion he was humbled voluntarily and with the power of God undiminished in him. III, 2314. With his divinity whole and inviolate, he suffered in order to teach human beings endurance and humility. VIII, 1145. And to demonstrate the future resurrection. VIII, 1145.

How Christ does what he suffers, and conversely, being himself both the work and the author of the work. VIII, 1169. When he suffers, he is weak; when he acts, he is omnipotent. VIII, 1170. It is shown how things he suffered as man are attributed to the Lord, from the example of the human soul to which things belonging solely to the flesh are attributed. VIII, 1147. It is shown that he suffered by will, not by necessity. VIII, 1146. This is illustrated by a man forcibly thrown into prison and by a holy man who follows him in order to console him. VIII, 1147. Isaac as a figure of Christ suffering willingly. V, 1954. Christ’s killers were foretold in Jacob’s final words concerning Simeon and Levi. III, 2203. Christ’s soul was troubled and saddened on account of the disciples. V, 2037. He was sad not because of his own Passion but because of our dispersion. V, 2038. Sad unto death, not after death. III, 2391. What the Lord’s bloody sweat foreshadowed. X, 1865. Christ’s silence during the Passion proved his supreme innocence. V, 2040. It is a crime to imagine that Christ’s divinity became subject to suffering. V, 1981. Whoever asserts that it suffered is accursed. V, 2180. If anyone says that in the Passion of the cross the Son of God, who is God, felt pain, and not the flesh together with the soul, let him be anathema. V, 2176. Truly the Father’s divinity, clothed in our nature, mounted the cross. VI, 905.

The hour of Christ’s Passion must not be attributed to fate. X, 1894. Christ was crucified by the Jews, not by Pilate. III, 2260. Mark rightly declares that this happened at the third hour. III, 2260. [Col. 0704] How could it be both the third and the sixth hour? VI, 738. He suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which he is believed to have been conceived. VI, 742. The significance of this mystery. III, 2252. He suffered on the fourteenth day of the moon. III, 2317. He was crucified where Isaac was offered. V, 1751. Where Adam was buried. V, 1751. Why he was sacrificed in the open air and outside the city. V, 2048.

On the cross Christ was a worm and a beetle. V, 2039. Christ was both without sin and made sin. III, 2268. Man was betrothed to divinity, and by ascending to the marriage-bed of the cross he there established the marriage. V, 1987. In an exchange of mercy, Christ gave himself up to punishment for his spouse. V, 1987. On the altar of the cross he was both priest and victim. V, 2047, 2066. Priest and sacrifice, God and temple. V, 2203; VI, 760. For us, victor and victim, priest and sacrifice. VI, 910. Witness and judge. VI, 912. On the cross he thirsted for the faith of the unbelieving nations. V, 2042. On the cross he stretched out his hands, ready to embrace sinners. VI, 961. He bowed his head in order to give kisses to his beloved. VI, 961. Crucified, he abolished the sins of deeds and the desires of souls. V, 1816.

How many things on the cross testify that Christ is God. V, 2045. The thief’s sudden conversion and entrance into heaven greatly commends him. V, 2049. By converting the thief, Christ repaid the devil in kind. V, 2054. While Christ suffered, the sun failed at midday so completely that the stars were seen during those three hours. III, 2199. The resurrection proves that he did not die unwillingly or to no purpose. III, 2345. A cluster of flesh was brought to the press of the cross, from which the must of divinity began to flow. VI, 963. Christ’s blood is the physician’s blood, medicine for the delirious. VIII, 1114. Christ’s divinity experienced death through participation in the human feeling he had assumed, not through loss of its own power. VIII, 1169. Through participation in another’s sickness, not through possession of a wound of its own. VIII, 1172. Christ tasted death because he was man; he swallowed death because he was God. VI, 757.

Christ freed us from the devil’s just dominion by his unjust death. V, 1808. Christ’s death is my merit. VI, 961. Christ’s single death paid the debt of our double death. VI, 1193. Christ is not merely the receiver of some and the savior of others, but the receiver and savior of all. X, 1826. He is rightly said to have been crucified for the redemption of the whole world, and for those only whom his death benefited. X, 1838, 1842, 1844. Christ died for all—certainly for those who have believed or will believe; he also died for those who do not wish to believe, and in what sense did he not die for them? III, 2406. He shed his blood for the whole human race, for those who are predestined. VI, 1060. He suffered not only for the saints but also for sinners. VI, 1063. Christ’s blood, in the greatness and power of its price and with respect to the one cause of the human race, is the redemption of the whole world. X, 1844. But it does not heal if it is not drunk. X, 1844. Christ redeemed the whole world, giving more than it was worth. V, 2042. How Christ’s cross benefited the angels. VI, 1192.

At the same time Christ’s body was in the tomb, his soul in hell, and his divinity in paradise and everywhere. V, 2178. How Christ’s being three days and three nights in the heart of the earth is to be understood. VI, 738. Christ’s tomb is a womb. V, 2204. Why he was placed in another’s tomb. V, 2205. In dying, he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb. VIII, 1169. God lay in the tomb according to the flesh, and descended into hell according to the soul alone. VI, 757. Christ was in the tomb, in hell, and in heaven. V, 2083. It is impious to say that Christ’s soul was handed over to the custody of the underworld during the three days of his death. VIII, 1171. Nevertheless, it is not denied that he was among the dead. VIII, 1172. Christ descended to hell. V, 2204. According to his soul. VIII, 1203. His soul accompanying him. V, 2059. With the divinity accompanying him in the soul. V, 2189. His soul united to his divinity. V, 2059. Christ’s divinity descended to hell through the property of the flesh, and the flesh ascended into heaven through the merit of the divinity. VIII, 1166. The fruit of Christ’s descent into hell. V, 2062. Descending to hell, Christ deceived the devil. III, 2277. He bound the devil and there freed those who were held captive. V, 2195. From there he rescued the fathers who sat in darkness. VI, 391. From there he freed those who were detained there for original sin alone. VI, 1193, 1194. The voices of the ministers of hell at his descent. V, 2060. Likewise, the supplication of the righteous to him. V, 2060. Christ was in hell for thirty-six hours. VI, 742.

Christ is the firstborn from the dead, the offspring of the resurrection, and the death of hell. V, 2064. Ugly in death, beautiful in resurrection. V, 2085. Beautiful everywhere. V, 1999. Meditation on Christ’s Passion and resurrection. VI, 940. Christ raised himself. V, 2206. In the evening. III, 2322. On the very day on which he had also been conceived. V, 1994. Why he did not shine like the sun when he rose. VI, 738. Whether the saints who were then seen rose when he rose. III, 2199. Christ’s resurrection did not destroy the nature of his humanity. V, 2182. The Son assumed man so that he might remain so forever. VI, 737. He always possesses the flesh in which he was born of the Virgin. VI, 773. Christ entered among the disciples through closed doors. III, 2322. Nor should an explanation of this be demanded. V, 2072. Through closed doors he conveyed the substance of our body, having earlier emerged from the Virgin’s closed womb and from the sealed tomb. V, 2063, 2066. At Christ’s resurrection, all things smile and are renewed. V, 2067. In his body nearly the whole world rose again. III, 2279. In him we rose and reign. VI, 912, 957. Why Christ retained his scars. V, 2066. In Christ’s wounds there is medicine, or the treasure, of the human race. V, 2066. Christ’s wounds are a safe and secure rest for sinners and the weak. VI, 956. They are remedies against temptations. VI, 956. Through the openings in his body, the secrets of his heart lie open to us. VI, 956. A prayer to Christ in which the soul desires to become a participant in his resurrection and ascension. VI, 933.

Christ sits at God’s right hand, while the same nature of flesh remains in which he was born and suffered. X, 1717, 1732. He is at the same time in heaven and on earth. V, 1761. The proof that Christ reigns in heaven is the gift of the Spirit that he gives on earth. V, 2093. How Christ is judge of the dead and the living. V, 1805. At the judgment he will appear in such a form as can be seen both by those whom he is going to crown and by those whom he is going to judge. X, 1889. Then he will also display the cross and the wounds. V, 2052. How he will reproach the reprobate with his benefits. VI, 1186. Christ’s subjection and handing over of the kingdom. III, 2398; VIII, 1186.

Those who contend that Christ arranged, by magical arts, to be worshiped as one who had died are refuted from the prophecies. VIII, 1128. Invocation of Christ against the devil. VI, 1070, 1072. Christ now watches over and helps us who contend for him. V, 1878. Christ’s name impressed upon the mind of the reluctant Jew. VII, 827. Christ is to be praised both simply and in twofold fashion. V, 1855. In his divinity Christ became bread for us; in his humanity, milk. VI, 1267. To speak of Christ’s humanity and to be nourished by it is delightful and salutary for the dying. VI, 1152. Christ’s mysteries are reviewed in order to arouse a devout affection toward God. I, 1465. An ardent desire to love Christ joined with prayer. VI, 928. The misery of one who does not love Christ. VI, 953. Christ is one in himself but different to different people. V, 1807. To the believer he is salvation; to the unbeliever, a burden. V, 1800. To be without Christ is wretched; to have Christ with oneself is safe; to be with Christ is blessed. VI, 1337. If Christ walks in us in this age, he will dwell in us in the age to come. V, 2117. To have Christ remaining within oneself benefits the disciples, not Christ. X, 1788.

How Christ is a young goat, a sheep, and a calf. V, 1816. How he is a bull. V, 1818. A turtledove and a sparrow. V, 1849. Why he is like mustard. V, 1915. Christ’s eyes. III, 2204. His teeth. III, 2204. His mouth, hands, shoulders, and feet. V, 1907. Christ is our Savior, king, and only Lord. VI, 1191. Our true friend: the explanation of his various names. VI, 1049. Christ is the fountain of innocence and the fullness of righteousness. V, 2014. The fountain from which all the saints, whether before or after the incarnation, received. V, 2114. Our true joy. V, 1917. The end of the faithful. X, 1816. He is bought more dearly by some, more cheaply by others. V, 1765. Christ is accustomed to lighten, not burden, his load. V, 1800.

Those are to be called Christians who throughout the past have held the faith in the one God preached by the Savior. III, 2219. God their Father distinguishes Christians from Jews and makes them equal among themselves. V, 1867. Christians are called angels by comparison with the Jews. III, 2228. The hope of resurrection especially separates Christians from pagans. V, 1961. The times of Christians were foretold. V, 2348. The multiplication of the Christian peoples after Christ’s death was prefigured. V, 1773. A Christian is not born but made. III, 2274. Why we are called Christians, not Peterians or Paulians. V, 1780. The dignity and duty of the Christian. VI, 1033, 1036, 1037. Royal and priestly dignity is conferred upon him in baptism. VI, 1211. Through faith in Christ, forgiveness of sins is bestowed upon him. III, 2376. But faith benefits him nothing if it does not change his life. III, 2376. Knowledge of the Judge who is to judge urges a change of life. III, 2376. Those who defer accepting faith in Christ until the end of life are rebuked as mockers of God. III, 2376. The case of the pagan who believes at the end of life is better. III, 2377. Yet he does not possess the dignity or reward of one who has lived a Christian life. III, 2377. When he sees the latter’s glory, he will regret that he did not live, but died a Christian. III, 2378. How Christians who return to the devil’s spectacles after baptism will be accused by the devil on the day of judgment. VIII, 1119. Those who think that Christians cannot be condemned are refuted. VI, 1118.

The dignity of the Christian name alone does not make someone a Christian. V, 1896. Who is unworthy and who worthy of that name. VI, 1036. It is disgraceful to bear the Christian name without the corresponding reality. VI, 1036. Profession and life make a Christian. III, 2311. To be called a Christian while lacking Christian works is of no benefit. III, 2419. What works the Christian name requires. V, 2237, 2240. It is not enough for a Christian to have emptied his heart of evils unless he also fills it with good things. V, 1774. He is not a Christian who is not in Christ’s Church. VI, 1196. A contentious person is a Christian only in name. VI, 1083. One who is not chaste cannot be called a Christian. V, 1993. He is not a Christian who fears to die for the truth. II, 1134. What a true Christian is. VI, 1170. No one is rightly called a Christian who is not conformed to Christ in conduct. VI, 1084. The good Christian is always a citizen of heaven and a pilgrim in the world. V, 1877. As a pilgrim, how he ought to be disposed. V, 1955. He does not seek a reward in this life. V, 1965. Not possessing the world, he possesses the Savior entirely here. V, 1902. Good Christians are not separated from Christ even by tortures; but the lukewarm and negligent are sometimes separated by idle tales. V, 2270.

Instructions for the Christian life. VI, 1347. And throughout the treatise *On the Rectitude of Catholic Conduct*. VI, 1169. The Christian’s mouth, into which the sacraments of God are placed, ought always to praise God. VI, 1173. Worldly happiness does not belong to Christians. VI, 1068, 1070. In this life Scripture promises Christians nothing except tribulations. V, 1890. A Christian grieves if he appears happy in the world. III, 2354. One who follows Christ must prepare himself for battle. V, 1796. The whole life of a Christian, if he lives according to the Gospel, is a cross and martyrdom. V, 2129. Christ’s soldier must always keep watch. V, 1852. He must keep watch more carefully in peacetime. V, 1852. Here the Christian should be anxious, not secure. V, 1883. From what he ought to be secure, and why he nevertheless should not cease to be anxious. V, 1885. The Christian’s weapons against the devil. V, 1797. The Christian’s homeland, city, fellow citizens, parents, and king. V, 1877. Valentinian forbids Christians to serve pagans or Jews. X, 1751.

“Chore” means baldness. VI, 1203. The sons of Chore in the Psalms sing only joyful songs. VI, 1203.

Whom the chrysolite signifies. VI, 1230.

Whom the chrysoprase represents. VI, 1230.

Crystal is formed from snow freezing for a long time. III, 2169.

To use food well is properly characteristic of Christians. VIII, 1219. Who makes Christian use of food. V, 1939. A nun should avoid bright white bread and delicate foods as though they were the poison of immodesty. I, 1457. What foods ought to belong to her. I, 1453, 1457. To use sacrilegious food is a mortal sin. V, 2271.

Cicero teaches that memory is necessary for an orator. I, 1440. His speeches are praised. I, 1448. Also his book *On Friendship*. VI, 831, 835, 836, 839. Cicero did not know the virtue of true friendship. VI, 835.

Cicindilia [uncertain term]. V, 2238.

Sackcloth is woven from goat hair, and how suitable it is for the penitent. V, 2227.

The rite of ashes. I, 1457.

The charioteers called *Circissarii* are excluded from communion for as long as they are driving. IX, 787.

The circuit of the mind is best. VI, 732.

Circumcellions, the Agonistici recruited by Donatus of Bagai. IX, 801. They are called leaders of the saints. IX, 801. They allow no one to remain secure on his property. IX, 801. They wander about during market festivals. IX, 801. Most of them are killed at Octavensis. IX, 801. The bodies of those killed are placed beside whitewashed altars. IX, 801. Some of them, eager for a false martyrdom, threw themselves over precipices. IX, 801. The fury of the Circumcellions. IX, 811, 812. It was condemned by frequent imperial sanctions. IX, 812. The mobs of the Circumcellions must be suppressed. IX, 841. They are fined separately. IX, 842.

Circumcision is a sign of Judaism, not Judaism itself. III, 2274. Circumcision of the flesh has no merit. III, 2241. If it had been a sign of salvation, Jewish women would not have been saved either. VIII, 1154. Rather, it was given as a sign of shame and disgrace. VIII, 1154. The sacrament of circumcision erased the guilt of original sin. X, 1652, 1781. And it carried the grace of baptism. X, 1653. The circumcision of the Samaritans was not repeated. IX, 764. Why circumcision was performed on the eighth day. III, 2232; X, 1652. Christ received circumcision in order to abolish it. V, 1999. Circumcision, since it was a sign of Christ’s promise, ought to have ceased when he was born. III, 2250. Circumcision of the heart: the spiritual sign of those who are born spiritually. III, 2250.

Circumstances that constitute a question. I, 1442.

The Field of the Martyrs at Cirta. IX, 798. The larger house. IX, 798, 799. The place, date, and proceedings of the Council of Cirta. IX, 774.

Two cities have existed from the beginning of the world, composed of the humble and the proud. V, 2311. One city belongs to the world, the other to paradise. V, 1877. Two loves make two cities. IX, 1877. The origin of the citizens of the earthly and heavenly cities. X, 1872. A citizen of heaven is a pilgrim in the world. X, 1860.

What a cry to God is. X, 1867. The cry of the saints is heard by God without a voice. V, 1792.

Clarius, presbyter. IX, 801.

Claudianus, Donatist bishop. IX, 805.

Claudius Saturianus. IX, 780.

The keys of Peter. VI, 766. Those entrusted with the keys of the kingdom of heaven require clemency. V, 1899.

The ladder of the cloister. VI, 997.

Clement, taught by blessed Peter, corrected the errors of the ancients and consecrated the faith by martyrdom. X, 1719. The basilica of Clement. X, 1719.

The distinction between clemency, mercy, and compassion. VI, 1275. Whoever gently forgives those who sin against him will most certainly receive the clemency of God. V, 2329.

[Col. 0707] The clerical militia, belt, and stipend. V, 1905. Why clerics shave their heads. VI, 1215. Why they retain a small portion of their hair. VI, 1216. They ought not to wear hair, mitres, or other coverings of the head while chanting the psalms. VI, 1216. It is unlawful for clerics to possess anything as their own. VI, 1215. When Christ deprived them of earthly possessions, he took up arms against his own enemies and theirs. VI, 1216. Clerics received a portion of gifts made to the bishop when these were distributed to the poor. IX, 799. The ecclesiastical order uses a white garment in administering the sacrifices. X, 1704. The insufflations and exorcisms of clerics at baptism. X, 1759. It is greatly feared that a dispute between the bishop and the deacon may become known outside. IX, 796. The clerics and elders of Cirta are instructed to reconcile peace between that bishop and deacon. IX, 795, 796. The stability of clerics. X, 1761, 1762, 1763; see 1771. Clerics who give themselves over to mourning are, as it were, insulting the will of God. VI, 1166. A cleric is not a non-cleric. V, 1905. African churches suffer from a shortage of clerics. IX, 806, 808. What things prevent someone from being ordained a cleric. VIII, 1219. Who obtains the office of pontificate, presbyterate, or diaconate unworthily, and who worthily. V, 1804. Whether the honor of clerics ordained among the Donatists should be preserved. IX, 806, 809. The Council of Carthage preserves their honor, subject to the respect due to the transmarine council; afterward it is denied them by that council. IX, 808. Those who ordain clerics in heretical errors, as well as those ordained, are fined. IX, 806, 812. Constantine frees Catholic clerics from the office of decurion and other burdensome public functions. IX, 792. He wishes them to be exempt from all public functions whatsoever. IX, 777. Constantine grants Caecilian three thousand folles to be distributed among the ministers of the churches, and permits him to request from the administrator of his estates whatever may be necessary. IX, 777. Privileges abolished for clerics and churches are restored. X, 1751.

Nothing is coeternal with God. III, 2218.

Coddeus, lector. IX, 795.

Pope Celestine protects Augustine and restrains the renewed heresy of Pelagius. X, 1684. His letter to Nestorius rebukes the Pelagians. X, 1730. He also wrote to the bishops of Gaul concerning the faith of blessed Augustine. X, 1730. He defended Augustine’s writings against certain Gauls. X, 1755. Celestine’s letter for restraining the presbyters who were pursuing novelty in Gaul. X, 1755. He is praised. X, 1831. Through Celestine’s efforts, Caelestius is driven out of Italy and Britain is freed from the Pelagian error. X, 1831. The remnants of Pelagianism are also suppressed in Gaul. X, 1831. A response is indicated to Celestine’s writings to Tuentius. X, 1756.

Caelestius. X, 1646. Noble by birth and a forensic scholar of that period. X, 1681. Born a eunuch from his mother’s womb. X, 1686. A man whose intelligence was that of a little fox. X, 1725. While still a young man, before joining Pelagius, he wrote three moral letters in the form of little books from the monastery to his parents. X, 1679. He was his [Pelagius’s] auditor around the year 420. X, 1686. Note (a). By incredible loquacity he made many people share in this madness of his. X, 1681. When Caelestius came from Rome to Carthage, he taught the Pelagian heresy there. X, 1682. Paulinus, a deacon of the church of Milan, resisted him. X, 1682. Paulinus accused him before Aurelius in a written statement. X, 1686, 1687. What had been debated at Carthage in 411 concerning the name of Caelestius was reviewed there in 416. X, 1711. In 412 Caelestius was brought before the judgment of the church of Carthage and condemned by the sentence of the bishops. X, 1691. He had already begun to insinuate himself into the honor of the presbyterate when he was brought before the episcopal judgment. X, 1692. Yet he is said afterward to have attained that honor of the presbyterate. X, 1711. In Asia, namely. X, 1712. When at Ephesus he dared to seek the honor of the presbyterate by underhanded means. X, 1687. This underhanded action was noted by the assembly at Jerusalem. X, 1699. Nevertheless, Zosimus calls him a presbyter. X, 1719, 1721.

Caelestius was the first to write against the transmission of sin. X, 1682. He denies original sin. X, 1719, 1725. At Carthage he taught that human beings could be without sin by nature, through unaided human nature alone. X, 1682. Then, when a synod was assembled there, he was forced to confess that redemption was necessary for infants. X, 1692. He also professed that he was uncertain about the transmission of sin, but nevertheless agreed with the better opinion. X, 1692. More convicted than corrected. X, 1692. For this reason he was condemned. X, 1691, 1692. Aurelius was present and Augustine absent. X, 1692. In a written statement Caelestius confessed that the redemption of infants takes place through baptism. X, 1712. In what sense he granted this. X, 1719. How much he loved and defended his error. X, 1619. He is proved from his own books to be an advocate of heretical doctrine. X, 1682, 1723. In 417 he was deprived of ecclesiastical communion together with Pelagius by Innocent. X, 1714. Even after being condemned in this way, he did not cease defending the heresy. X, 1682, 1723. The seven chapters of errors that he disseminated among the peoples. X, 1682, 1686. Seven others opposed to these in the synodal proceedings. X, 1687. Frequently heard in those same proceedings and ordered to condemn his own opinions, he refused to comply and was deprived of ecclesiastical communion. X, 1687, 1699. Convicted at Carthage, he appealed to the Roman [Col. 0708] bishop. X, 1687, 1723. But when he had appealed to the Apostolic See, he failed to appear. X, 1725. Thus, neglecting the appeal, he went to Ephesus. X, 1787. From there, after several years, he made his way to Constantinople and was expelled by Atticus. X, 1787. Atticus also sent letters concerning him to Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage. X, 1787. From there he withdrew to Rome and mocked Zosimus. X, 1787. Zosimus examined his case: the whole course of events. X, 1719, 1721. How kindly Zosimus dealt with him. X, 1719.

Caelestius presented Zosimus with a statement of faith, about which no question was being raised against him. X, 1718. How craftily he submitted himself to the judgment of the Apostolate. X, 1718. Zosimus charged that the Africans’ judgment concerning him had been hasty. X, 1720. He judged him to be sound in the faith. X, 1720. He also wondered how so great a man, and Pelagius likewise explaining his faith in the same way, could have been defamed. X, 1721. Nevertheless, Zosimus warned Caelestius and the others that these disputes arose from perverse curiosity. X, 1720. Yet he gave him a letter, which Caelestius afterward abused. X, 1687. The African bishops complained that Zosimus had accommodated Caelestius in every respect. X, 1726. What Zosimus replied to their complaints. X, 1726. Ordered by Zosimus to condemn everything that Paulinus had charged against him, Caelestius evaded the command. X, 1724. When the bishops from Africa wrote back, he was summoned to a fuller hearing, fled from Rome, and was condemned by Zosimus. X, 1687. Thereafter Zosimus’s Tractoria was sent throughout the whole world and strengthened by the signatures of the holy Fathers. X, 1689. Those who refused to subscribe to it were deposed under imperial laws and priestly statutes. X, 1689. The decree of Constantius in 421 ordering that Caelestius himself be driven farther and farther from the City. X, 1750. He is praised. X, 1730. The prefect’s edict against him and those who provided him with shelter. X, 1751. When Caelestius sought a hearing from Celestine, he was expelled from the whole territory of Italy. X, 1831.

The Caelestian heretics. X, 1613, 1622. For some time they entertained hope concerning the Council of Ephesus. X, 1761. They must be driven from all human society. X, 1761. Though condemned so often throughout the whole world, they disturb the distant provinces. X, 1761. He whom they persecute for his faith persecutes them everywhere. X, 1761. They adhere to Nestorius. X, 1761. See Pelagians.

The Caelicolans, followers of some unknown doctrine. IX, 815.

“Heaven” derives from *celare*, “to conceal.” VI, 1028. What is commonly understood by the name “heaven.” VI, 1027. By “heaven,” which God created first, all invisible things are signified. III, 2218. Three heavens historically and three symbolically. VI, 1028. The heaven to which Paul was carried up. VI, 1028. In which Stephen saw Christ. VI, 1028. Why angels and the righteous are called heaven. VI, 1028. Heaven is where guilt has ceased. V, 1907. The Church is the heaven of the elect. III, 2419, 2422. The heaven of heaven: the pure mind most harmoniously united with God. VI, 915. The heaven of heavens is God himself. VI, 1030.

The kingdom of heaven lies beyond this corporeal heaven, indeed beyond every place. VI, 1012, 1029. If the saints take delight in the corporeal heaven, that condition is better for them. VI, 1025. Nor will the bodies of the saints be sustained by the corporeal heaven. VI, 1029. The kingdom of heaven has various names: what they are. VI, 1013. Christ is heaven, he who alone ascended. V, 1884. Christ led with him to the heavenly homeland those whom he freed from hell. V, 2195. Heaven was not dishonored but honored by the entrance of the thief. V, 2049. The gate of heaven, closed by Adam, is now open. V, 2085. The martyrs are honored with heavenly rewards even before the judgment. V, 2155. Vincent rejoices in heaven and in the vision of God. V, 2097, 2098. After this life has passed, the righteous seek heaven with God. III, 2371; VI, 1165. Holy souls rejoice in heaven while the flesh is devoured by worms. VI, 1183. To long for the heavenly homeland, where the saints await us. V, 2160. How many who have already been granted it may be awaiting us there. V, 2137. The carnal conception of the heavenly kingdom. VI, 1007. The glory and happiness of this kingdom. V, 2136; VI, 820, 822, 861, 915, 954, 958, 966, 993. At what price it is purchased. V, 2136.

Imperial heavenly writings. IX, 778. Constantine’s heavenly command. IX, 790.

What thought is. VI, 809. Two kinds of thoughts continually try to implant themselves in our hearts. V, 2345. Holy thought preserves; unholy thought destroys. V, 2344. When thought concerning food and clothing is holy. V, 2344. Superfluous thoughts are signified by hairs. VI, 1215. One ought to be ashamed to think what one is ashamed to say. II, 1114. What should be set against shameful thoughts. VI, 1175. Nothing excludes useless and lustful thoughts so effectively as meditation on the word of God. I, 1461. Evil thoughts must be shaken off at their very birth. VII, 1358. This is shown by many comparisons. V, 2345. How one may become unaccustomed to the habit of evil thoughts. V, 2344, 2346. To direct every thought toward Christ. VI, 956. Toward God himself. VI, 964. Pious thoughts do not arise from free will without God’s inspiration. X, 1816. By ourselves we can think and desire human things without grace, but not divine things. X, 1774, 1780, 1786. The origin of all good thoughts, and their agreement with one another, is from God, through the inward operation of the Holy Spirit. X, 1775, 1786. A good and sudden thought is like a guest from heaven. V, 1911. Good thoughts are always from God. VIII, 1221. Not all evil thoughts are stirred up by the devil. VIII, 1221. God alone knows the inner thoughts of the soul. VIII, 1221. The devil infers these from bodily movements. VIII, 1221.

Whence our knowledge of creatures that are not seen comes. X, 1896. The morning and evening knowledge of creatures. VI, 741. Through the senses we perceive substance, and through mind and reason, accidents. I, 1423. Nothing is better than knowledge of God. V, 2323. This very knowledge is the blessed life. V, 2323. Knowledge of oneself. See Knowledge.

The method of cultivating the earth. V, 2327. A person worships what he loves. X, 1879. Superstitious worship of various things is touched upon. VI, 1172, 1174. Veneration is to be offered to no creature except God and his saints. VI, 1173. In the worship of God, no reward other than God himself is to be sought. X, 1861.

The time of the Collation. 1456.

The place and complete procedure of the Collation of Carthage. II, 819.

“Collect” for an ecclesiastical assembly. V, 1757.

Bands worn around the neck. VI, 1172.

Colobium. II, 1125.

The colonicus, assistant to the commentaries. IX, 816.

The comes of Africa. IX, 808. The name of *comes* and *dux* was applied interchangeably to one and the same person. VI, 1046. In the *Admonitio*: the seat of the *comitiva*. IX, 816, 842.

All our affairs are commended to God. VI, 938.

The rules of the commentaries. X, 1995.

Those conscious of crimes avoid ecclesiastical communion. V, 2216. Thus they accumulate guilt and avoid the remedy. V, 2216. The Apostles expelled Simon, Philetus, and others from communion and from the thresholds of the church. IX, 835. To suspend oneself from communion on account of guilt. V, 2221.

The *competentes*. V, 1821. As though seeking together. V, 2242. What they seek, and what they must do or avoid in order to obtain what they seek. V, 2242. The *competentes*, whom the womb of Mother Church conceived under the inspiration of Christ, must beware of miscarriage. V, 2243.

The hour of Compline. II, 1122, 1124, 1141.

Jerome is called a fellow presbyter by the Synod. X, 1712. A bishop calls presbyters only fellow priests or fellow presbyters, but does not likewise call deacons fellow deacons. III, 2302.

What compunction is. VI, 816. The praise of compunction. VI, 1254. Every excess prevents compunction. VI, 1062.

The Council of Arles: when the bishops had been summoned, public conveyance was provided together with imperial travel warrants. IX, 785. The bishop of Syracuse was ordered to go there with two second-order clergy and three servants. IX, 786. The council was held in the secretarium of the basilica. IX, 808, 809, 827, 828; X, 1728. The bishops were seated, with the deacons standing nearby. IX, 808; X, 1728. Tribunus invites the bishops gathered at Carthage to sit. IX, 827. Pelagius sits among the assembly of presbyters at Jerusalem. X, 1699. One bishop subscribes to the council’s letters on behalf of all. IX, 813. The chapters of the Second Council of Orange. X, 1785. Why they should be subscribed not only by bishops but also by laypeople. X, 1789. They were sent from the Apostolic See. X, 1785. And they are confirmed by that same see. X, 1791. At the request of Caesarius, who presided over it. X, 1790. Two clerics of the church of Carthage are sent from the council to the imperial court. IX, 814. Likewise, two are sent with a *Commonitorium*. IX, 811. How highly Constantine valued the council’s judgment. IX, 788. A plenary council. X, 1731.

Every human being conceives, but one conceives from Christ and another from the devil. V, 1891.

God is the author of concord among human beings; the devil is the author of dissension. IX, 791.

The frequent practice of taking concubines before wives. V, 2290, 2292. So that it is not even thought a sin. V, 2290, 2340. Because of their number, a bishop cannot excommunicate them all. V, 2290, 2293. Whoever takes concubines, either before or after taking a wife, commits adultery—indeed, a sin worse than adultery. V, 2290, 2293; VI, 1179. The gravity of this sin is shown by the fact that only slaves are born from such unions. V, 2291. And by the fact that it is done publicly, whereas adultery is done secretly. V, 2291, 2293. The concubinage of certain old men. I, 1461. A man who takes concubines could and should be suspended not only from communion but also separated from the banquets and conversation of the Christian people. V, 2293.

Desire is sometimes directed toward good and sometimes toward evil. III, 2413. Every human being conceives either from Christ or from the devil. V, 1891. The threefold form of desire. VI, 1316. The threefold desire in the sin of the first parents. VI, 1051. Desire is not antecedent to the nature of the human being as created, but consequent upon the punishment of the condemned. X, 1885, 1896. The struggle against desire is the just punishment of sin. X, 1674. The guilt of desire is remitted through baptism. X, 1674. Its struggle assails those born again, so that they may implore divine help every day. X, 1674. Desire must not be offered peace but war. X, 1867. By free will alone a human being cannot overcome the desires of the flesh. X, 1615. To overcome them, daily help from God is also necessary even for those born again. X, 1757. Stronger foods are nourishment for desire. VI, 768, 777. Desire is born through the senses, aided by demons; we can overcome it, and when we are occupied it grows quiet. III, 2351. It is lulled by the withdrawal of food. III, 2351. For this, however, God’s help must be implored. III, 2351. The whole world is full of the snares of desire; and who can escape them? VI, 873, 878. What the arts of those who desire what belongs to another are. V, 1890. See Lust.

How many extortioners there are. V, 1905.

Confirmation, a sacrament. VI, 794. It is indicated that this is conferred immediately after baptism. VIII, 1217, 1220. Also upon those who, having been baptized among heretics, come to the Church. VIII, 1217.

God must always be confessed in prosperity and adversity. VI, 859. Confessing to God alone is not sufficient for salvation. VI, 1154. Those who think otherwise are marked as superstitious. VI, 1154. One must continually confess not only to God but also to human beings. V, 2212. Otherwise there is no return to God. V, 2213, 2215. The devil’s efforts to deter us from confession. V, 2212, 2214.

The necessity of confessing sins. V, 1851; VI, 1288, 1289. God desires our confession so that he may have a just reason for forgiving. V, 2213, 2215. Whoever accuses himself before the just and merciful judge excuses himself. X, 1875. God commanded confession so that the devil might hear us repent and no longer accuse us on that account. VI, 1288. Adam’s confession preserved him; Cain’s denial condemned him. V, 1928. Confession is a plank after shipwreck. V, 2226. The beginning of healing. V, 2214. Confession of a hidden sin heals the sick person in two ways. VII, 847. The usefulness and fruit of confession. V, 2050, 2215, 2216; VI, 1289; X, 1879. Confession must not be postponed until the last day of Lent or of one’s life. VI, 1289. Offenses should be washed away more quickly through confession and repentance. VI, 1049. Confession should precede reception of the Eucharist. VI, 1059.

What the demeanor of one confessing ought to be. VI, 1289. The person confessing must beware of offering excuses for sins. VI, 1126. Confession of sins should be made humbly. VI, 1056. Humble confession of vices. VI, 945. Confession in the priest’s ear. VI, 1148. To confess very frequently to priests. VI, 1252. One must confess with one’s own mouth, not through a messenger or in writing. VI, 1122. When someone confesses to several people, he obtains the grace of remission all the more easily. VI, 1122. If anything is concealed or cleverly glossed over, it strangles the soul. VI, 1156. At least in thought, daily sins should be added to the general collect. VI, 1156. To divide one’s confession among different people is always to remain without forgiveness. VI, 1125. To which priests one must confess. VI, 1156. Each person should confess to the best priest he can find. VI, 1123. To one who knows how to bind and loose. VI, 1122. The error of priests who bound penitents even after death. VI, 1157. How the person hearing confessions ought to conduct himself. VI, 1289. What I know through confession I know less than what I do not know. VI, 1289.

The unusual birth of Christ did not condemn marriage. V, 1981.

Three conjunctions worthy of the angels’ wonder. VI, 788, 1339.

What conjunction is. I, 1405. Figure, order, and power belong to conjunction. I, 1405.

By the law of marriage, men too are not permitted whatever is not permitted to women. VI, 1179.

How far a good conscience is not sufficient. VI, 1222. The happiness of a pure conscience. VI, 1252. Tribulations contribute to it. VI, 1252. How conscience should be examined. VI, 817. A bad conscience diminishes the confidence of one who prays. VI, 903. The misery of a bad conscience. VI, 945.

[Col. 0711] Nothing is consecrated without the sign of the cross. VI, 1192.

Consentible. VI, 1146.

Constans, consul. IX, 842.

The emperor Constans sends alms to the poor throughout Africa and ornaments to the churches. IX, 800. The Donatists reject them insultingly. IX, 800. Four kinds of controversies. I, 1445. Four figures. I, 1446. What knowledge of these contributes. I, 1447.

*Cortis*, used for paradise. X, 1629.

Dacianus. V, 2096, 2097. Demons, by the sharpness of their perception and the speed of movement of their aerial body, anticipate the perception of earthly bodies. VI, 799. A small florilegium. VI, 984.

Democrates. I, 1445.

Demosthenes, an obscure Pelagian speaker. X, 1705.
