How great an injury it does to God. VI, 961, 1158. One must not despair of the wicked. X, 1874. See *Sin*.

No one is to be despised. VI, 1179.

[Col. 0716] Spiritual betrothal. V, 1754, 1756.

The purposes of the commandment [reading uncertain: *Destina*]. V, 1737.

Detractors are reproved. V, 1845. How someone becomes a detractor. V, 1978. The detractor and the willing listener carry the devil on their tongues. VI, 1056. For both, detraction is food for the death of the soul. VI, 1056. Detraction is fornication of the soul. VI, 1058. It is characteristic of worthless people. II, 1112. It must be avoided no less by the ears than by the tongue. II, 1112. So that the detractor may learn not willingly to say what he has learned is not willingly heard. II, 1112. The freedom of just correction is opposed to detraction. VI, 1095. No opportunity for defamation is to be given. VI, 1097.

What devotion is. VI, 816.

That God exists. VI, 1010. Yet He cannot properly be expressed in any words, and no predicates properly apply to Him. V, 1008. Human speech cannot suitably explain divine realities. III, 2368. It explains them in one respect, but not in another. III, 2366. What God is, or how great He is, cannot be known. V, 1969. By what method knowledge of God is to be acquired. VI, 812. In order to conceive God, all created things must be removed from the mind. VI, 974. God is not found through the senses. VI, 887. The testimony of creatures concerning God. VI, 887. God deigns to draw us to knowledge of His own things through things that are ours. VI, 973. In what respect our knowledge of God surpasses that of philosophers and pagans. V, 2173. Ignorance of the divine nature earns pardon; rash assertion incurs punishment. V, 2173. The angels know more of God than human beings, and the archangels know more than they, just as the cherubim and seraphim know more than the archangels. III, 2214. To investigate God’s essence rationally is to hasten toward life; to neglect it through ignorance is to hasten toward death. VI, 1005. God is not to be scrutinized by us, but believed. VI, 1191. God’s essence is known in a marvelous way when it is believed that He exists. VI, 973. Let no human being attempt to comprehend God, when he cannot even comprehend himself. VIII, 1120. “Do you wish to know what God is? Know this: that you do not know—and that not even the angels have known.” V, 2173. God alone knows His own essence in its entirety. VI, 924. He is fully known only to Himself. VI, 889, 974. Therefore He is worthily worshiped by us. VI, 974. By what way and to what extent He becomes known to human beings. VI, 889, 890. A considerable part of knowledge of God is knowing what He is not. X, 1864.

God lacks matter, not form. VI, 924, 978, 980. He is not corporeal. VIII, 1206. Whoever believes that bodily members or human emotions exist in God makes idols in his own heart. VIII, 1200. How the bodily members Scripture attributes to Him are to be understood; each is explained individually. VIII, 1200. God’s walking in paradise took place through a creature. VI, 745. God’s breadth, length, and depth. V, 974. The nature of God and of bodies or spirits is one and the same. VI, 762. What kind of God the teaching of the Manichaeans makes Him, and what kind the Catholic faith believes Him to be. VIII, 1152. The Church’s teaching about God. VI, 923.

What God is. III, 2214; V, 1969; VI, 827, 1010, 1011. God is the universe of things, and none of its individual parts. V, 788. God’s supreme excellence. VI, 889. God’s perfections. VI, 909, 951, 970, 971. God’s perfections, which appear to conflict, are described fully and clearly. VI, 922, 951, 971, 978. God’s perfections as related to us. VI, 982. How great a good God is is shown by this: no one who departs from Him fares well. X, 1884. How He is wholly good. VI, 965. God’s supreme simplicity. VI, 761; X, 1893. For God, to be, to live, to understand, and to be able are the same. VIII, 1174. In God foreknowledge is not an accident but an essence. X, 1657. In God substance itself is knowledge for Him. III, 2373. Everything in Him is called substantive. III, 2373. There is nothing concerning God that is not called God. III, 2251. God Himself is number, measure, and weight. VI, 745. He moves Himself without time or place. VI, 746. For God, foreknowing, doing, and choosing are present at one and the same time. X, 1668. God’s existence is eternal. VI, 996. God did not precede the world in time, but in eternity. VI, 995. God’s immutability. VI, 982. The argument for God’s immutability. VI, 762. Times and moments do not vary for God. VIII, 1109. Words about God such as “always,” “when,” and “never” are to be spoken only with qualification. VIII, 1185, 1188. In what sense it can be said, “He was, is, and will be.” X, 1893. How God is to be believed to be the same both when He is at rest and when He is at work. X, 1871. Or when He is said to become angry or to repent. X, 1872.

God’s essence is incorporeal. VI, 976, 978.

God is an immeasurable spirit, wholly present everywhere. VI, 969. He ineffably fills and contains all things. VI, 762. He can nowhere be defiled. VIII, 1146. How He is outside, beneath, above, and below all things. VI, 982. God Himself is His own place. VI, 982. That God is in all things and everywhere, and remains in Himself, is demonstrated through many questions. VI, 1019. God is now everywhere; how He will be all in all. VIII, 1787. Why He is said to be rather in heaven. VIII, 1174. How His descent is to be understood. V, 1749. God dwells in the soul that desires Him. VI, 887. Signs of God dwelling in us. V, 2009. God is absent nowhere; but He is said to be there where He appears and wishes to be seen. III, 2322. By a certain mystery He is in all things; through providence He appears where He wishes. III, 2322. He touches all things unequally. VI, 971.

[Col. 0717] God’s mind. VI, 1141. Knowledge. VI, 996. God’s wisdom is no more wisdom than truth, and conversely. VI, 996. Nothing is hidden from Him. VI, 775. God knows not only what is said and thought, but also what is to be done and thought. V, 2034. Some falsely suppose that God’s foreknowledge is the same as His will. X, 1840, 1843. All things are present to God. X, 1668. This occurs without impairing our freedom. VI, 995. God did not see the creature outside Himself. VI, 746. How “not knowing” is to be understood of Him. V, 1749. God’s speech. III, 2367; VI, 995. God begot the coeternal Word, in whom He spoke all things timelessly. VI, 740. He speaks to us in three ways. VIII, 1204. How He speaks to the saints. V, 2155. What is meant by the praise of the saints in God’s mouth and God’s praise in the mouth of the blessed. VI, 995.

God’s omnipotence is established by many arguments. V, 2182. God’s power is the same in small things and in great things. VI, 871. God’s will is always fulfilled. X, 1783. It is absurd to say that God’s will is unchanging throughout all ages, while His dispensations vary according to the mutability of human free choice. X, 1836. In what sense He is said to wish all to be saved. X, 1783. God can do all things, but does only what accords with truth and justice. III, 2291. And with reason. III, 2278. What He does, He does justly. III, 2278. God needs nothing. VI, 792. He made His works out of beneficence, not out of need. VI, 740. He created us for His goodness and our benefit. VI, 850. He could have made everything simultaneously, but did not; why. III, 2320. Some foolishly say that there is something that does not belong to God. III, 2318. Whatever is praiseworthy in creatures has God as its author. X, 1895. God foreknows everything of which He is the author, yet He is not the author of everything He foreknows. X, 1895. God is the author only of those things that have being. VI, 729. He is not the author of evil, but its arranger. VI, 1018. He did not arrange sin, but punishment for those who love guilt. VI, 1126. He does not will sin, yet does not restrain it. VI, 1126. God is said to do what He permits. III, 2269. How He is said to kill without having made death. X, 1885. God is to be believed to have done what, even if it is not apparent, is recognized by right understanding as something He ought to have done. X, 1896.

God’s concern for us. VI, 792, 854, 875. The words of those who deny that God cares for our affairs. III, 2386. They are refuted. III, 2387. We must acquiesce in God’s ordering. VI, 853. God leaves to human beings what belongs to human virtue. V, 1928. Divine providence, unchanged in itself, changes its remedies according to our condition. X, 1896. God’s kindness toward humanity. V, 2244. God always grants more than He promised. V, 1806. God’s diverse gifts are possessed in one God. X, 1888.

God’s mercy is commended. VI, 902, 946, 949. God’s inclination to forgive. V, 1851. God does not abandon anyone unless He is first abandoned. VI, 793. He does not desire the punishment of the guilty, but orders it justly and calmly. X, 1860. In a certain sense He avenges unwillingly. V, 1895. God’s sentence against sinners is not unchangeable. V, 1802. God’s mercy would be injustice unless it belonged to God. VI, 1150. How great God’s mercy is, and how necessary His justice. VI, 1187. God cannot be called only just, or only merciful. X, 1658. God’s severity in punishing the Israelites deserves close attention. V, 1801, 1802. It is not permitted to investigate God’s ways—that is, the gifts of mercy and truth—by judgment. X, 1852. God’s justice or wisdom is not to be debated according to the law of human wisdom or justice. X, 1667. Why He retains one person or frees him, while He does not retain another, is impossible to comprehend and not lawful to investigate. X, 1848. Without injustice, God grants one person undeserved grace and returns to another a deserved punishment. X, 1867. In condemning a human being He is just; in redeeming one, merciful. V, 2202. God is merciful here and just in the future. V, 1963. God’s mercy and justice could have been demonstrated without the wretched or the reprobate. VI, 1017.

How God alone is immortal and invisible. VI, 1022. He has never appeared to anyone according to His essence. III, 2411; VI, 973. No mortal living person has seen, or will be able to see, God in His essence. VIII, 1206. To see Him is to believe Him rightly and love Him from the heart. VIII, 1206. The Son of God appeared to the fathers, but the one who is the Father was never seen except by the Son. III, 2266. The Son also was never seen according to substance, but according to reason. III, 2265, 2411. And this through surrounding appearances. III, 2411. No one is worthy by nature or merits to see God the Father, except His true Son, in whom the saints in heaven see Him. III, 2369. God cannot be seen by bodily eyes except through a creature placed before them. VI, 737; VIII, 1196. To seek God is good; to seek His face is the full good. III, 2334. For what purpose God’s face is sought, since it cannot be seen by mortals. III, 2334. The heart must first be purified for the vision of God. V, 2083. What it means to see God’s face, and that it is the complete blessedness of the human being. VI, 895. The many names for the blessed vision of God. VI, 1012. God can be seen by angels and the souls of the saints, but not fully, neither by saints nor by angels. VIII, 1173. How angels and the souls of the blessed see God. VI, 1023. In three ways the blessed will enjoy God. VI, 829. What we shall receive from the vision of God. VI, 981. The saints will possess it unequally. VI, 980; VIII, 1173. Yet in such a way that no one lacks anything to desire. VIII, 1173. Each person will see God more clearly in proportion to the purity of the life he has lived here. VI, 980.

The mystery of the one and triune God. VI, 974, 975, 976. One God is proclaimed throughout all the Scriptures, but His mystery is adored in the Trinity. III, 2296. God is one by nature. V, 2151; VI, 769, 770; VIII, 1213. One, but not solitary. V, 2180, 2188. One, but not singular. III, 2280. One in the Trinity of coeternal persons. VIII, 1213. In the one there are three, and the three are one. III, 2280. God is one, or unity in essence, and triune, or Trinity in persons. VI, 1260; VIII, 1193. Triune and undivided. III, 2151. The Trinity is one true God. VI, 769. One everlasting God, one immutable God. VI, 770. The sole creator of all things. VI, 770. One God, immeasurable in power, not in bulk. VI, 771. One God, three persons, one image of the three. III, 2244; VI, 1210. One power of the three. III, 2374. The Father and the Son have one and the same omnipotence. VIII, 1181. The Son’s work is not other than the Father’s, but one and the same, so to speak, movement in all things. VIII, 1183. There is no other goodness in the Son than that alone which is in the Father. VIII, 1183. When it is said, “No one is good except one God,” Christ or the Holy Spirit is not excluded. VIII, 1183. Christ is signified in the sacred books in such a way that He does not exceed the measure of the one. III, 2285. There is no difference between God and what is from God; but He who is another in person is the same by unity of substance. III, 2408. God’s unity is commended by the fact that one human being was made by the One, from whom the others would arise. III, 2217. The unity of the Godhead in the Trinity is confirmed through the unity of grace and gift. V, 2088. The God of the Law and of the Gospels is one. V, 2176; VIII, 1175.

There is one God, not three gods. VI, 924. Pagans and Sabellians accuse us of not worshiping one God because He is triune. VIII, 1101, 1102. They admit that God is without marriage and that nothing at all like it can be found in Him. VIII, 1102. Hence they deny the Son. VIII, 1102. God the Father and God the Son are one God. VIII, 1103. The Son and the Father are distinguished in such a way that the Father is the one from whom all things are, and the Son the one through whom all things are. III, 2266. Because the Father and Son are undoubtedly one, they are not two gods but one God. VIII, 1116. Although He is God from God, day from day, light from light. VIII, 1119. God is Trinity. VI, 733. The Father is other than the Son and the Holy Spirit, not something else. VI, 734. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons. VI, 734. Not three gods or three essences, but one God. VI, 735. The coeternity of the Father and Son is demonstrated by Isaiah’s words, “Before me no god was formed, and after me there will not be one.” VIII, 1111. Likewise from the likeness of fire and radiance. VIII, 1111. Likewise from the fact that the Son is the Word and reason of the Father. VIII, 1110, 1119. Duality in offspring, unity in deity. VIII, 1112. “God” is a proper and natural name for each person, whereas “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are appellative names. VIII, 1208. Therefore we say three persons, not three gods, because there is distinction in the persons, not in the Godhead. VIII, 1209. To triple the Godhead is a sacrilegious offense worthy of spitting upon. VIII, 1209. The Father, Son, and Spirit are one charity, not three charities. VIII, 1174. Nor are there three good beings or three omnipotent beings. VIII, 1172. Nor three gods, because there is one substance and not three substances, and not three wisdoms. VIII, 1174. Not three lights. VIII, 1174. God does not admit the plural number at all in names of nature. VI, 924. In God all things are one, except what pertains to relation. VI, 996. Therefore only relative names may be expressed in the plural number. VIII, 1172. And names of nature may be predicated of each individual person. VIII, 1174. The unity of God and the Trinity of the persons are demonstrated by the example of light, radiance, and heat. VI, 1013. Whether the Father acts, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is the Trinity that acts; and whatever the three do is the operation of the one God. III, 2251. Just as the Father is said to act through the Son, so the Son acts through the Holy Spirit. III, 2244. By the likeness of fire—in which, although there is one substance, radiance does one thing and heat another—the incarnation of the Son alone is demonstrated. VIII, 1175.

God’s kingdom is everywhere undivided. X, 1655. To know and love God here is the privilege of few. X, 1860. What great grace it is to have God as Father. V, 2193. How God is to be sought. VI, 804, 814, 827, 827, 964, 966, 969. The method of finding God. VI, 1221. By what way one approaches God or clings to Him. X, 1879. Nothing is more present to us than God, and nothing more hidden. VI, 822. We are near to or far from God through our actions. X, 1867, 1869. God has no enemy except the sinner. VIII, 1149. God’s presence keeps sins away. VI, 1188. A person ought never to forget God. VI, 806, 964. How one should recall His presence. VI, 964. Whoever does not remember God, understand Him, or love Him is not with Him. X, 1864. Whoever does not have God appeased will by no means escape Him as an angry God. VI, 924, 978. There is nowhere to flee from God except from Him to Him. X, 1878. A burning desire for God. VI, 865, 894. And throughout the entire treatise. The ardent affections of one thirsting for God. [Col. 0719] VI, 930, 942, 944, 953, 981. How God’s radiance is to be contemplated step by step. VI, 1011. How God is to be contemplated in prayer. VI, 1011, 1020. How God’s goodness and majesty nurture contemplation. VI, 1137.

God alone is to be adored. VI, 1173. The religion of the true God has God as its author, holy laws, and authority derived from the testimony of virtues. III, 2342, 2344. One must necessarily yield to these. III, 2344. The integrity of His laws and ministers is compared with the disgracefulness of the laws and ministers of the pagans. III, 2343. Why the Godhead is not worshiped under the names of justice, mercy, or other virtues. VI, 1016. Honorius orders everything toward the true worship of God, whether through the labors of war or the counsels of peace. IX, 816. How the worship of the one God was transferred to many. V, 2001. Human beings are the authors of the gods; their worship was not commanded by the gods themselves and is supported by no testimonies. III, 2341. It is disgraceful and dishonorable. III, 2342, 2343. It is celebrated in darkness. III, 2342.

The divine hand of the Emperor. IX, 817.

Deusatelius, priest. IX, 794.

Deuterius. IX, 816, 827.

The right hand is understood as the love of God; the left as vanity or desire for the world. V, 1863, 1865. The right hand signifies the intention of eternal life. V, 1867.

The devil is a name derived from his work, not from his nature. III, 2282, 2298. The distinction between “devil” and “Satan.” III, 2298. The Church teaches that the devil exists, but not who or how he is; this is the common opinion concerning him. VIII, 1177. What the devil is. VI, 1071; VIII, 1117. Some say that he was either made evil by God or has an origin of his own. III, 2299. The devil was not evil by nature. III, 2217. Inflated by his own excellence, he wished to be called God. III, 2216. Humanity was made for his accusation, and therefore he became humanity’s enemy. III, 2217. The devil is one of the created things to be detested. VI, 1183. He is the author and inventor of evil. VIII, 1218. How many good things he has taken from humanity, and how many evils he has brought upon it. VI, 1071. He seduced the woman through the serpent, and when the sentence was pronounced upon the serpent, he himself was condemned. III, 2232. In what language he spoke. III, 2232. Statements concerning death are referred to the devil as its author. X, 1618. The devil is the author of death through the suggestion of sin, not through the power of retribution. X, 1779. He is the author and inflictor of punishments by divine permission, not through his own power. X, 1779. Among human beings he is the author of lust. X, 1639. In the crimes of sinners he assists through temptations, but does not generate their wills. X, 1847. He has power over the flesh, not over the soul. VI, 1074, 1332. He does not see the soul’s inner thoughts, but gathers them from certain indications. VIII, 1221. He does not arouse all evil thoughts. VIII, 1221. He does not enter the soul substantially through an energetic operation. VIII, 1221. He is present where the person whom he deceived is. V, 1908. Abandoned in the idols, he lay hidden in the temples as though enclosed there. IX, 802.

Every unredeemed human being is the devil’s captive. X, 1845. It is insane to say that God wishes the devil to be served. X, 1846. The sinner deservedly suffers the punitive domination of the devil. X, 1846. Before Christ there was neither the courage to fight him nor the strength to conquer him. V, 1819.

The figure of the devil envying us Christ’s coming. V, 1819. The figure of Christ freeing us from his hands. V, 1819. It was unjust for the devil, the victor, to have his spoils taken away by force. III, 2277. By what stratagem Christ deceived him in hell. III, 2277. How justly and fittingly the devil was deceived and overthrown by the divine human being. V, 2053. How the human being was justly snatched from him. III, 2359. The devil conquered by Christ’s cross. III, 1820. And slain by his own sword. V, 1820. He justly fell by the right through which he rejoiced over humanity. V, 1808. The works of the devil that Christ removed. X, 1624. The devil’s pomps, which must be renounced. V, 2235; VI, 1170; VIII, 1118.

The devil’s deceptions and arts by which he destroys us. VI, 877, 878, 879, 1319. Why a certain monk was permitted to soil his garments through repeated filth. VI, 1104. It is exceedingly difficult never to be struck by the devil’s cunning. V, 2076. The devil always gives himself away when he fabricates things inconsistent with the persons through whom he tries to deceive. III, 2231. He is always tormented by the peace of the brethren. IX, 802. There is nothing that gives him greater joy than when a person makes him the author of his sin. V, 2213. The devil prefigured in Laban. V, 1763. In Pharaoh. V, 1776. He is both lion and dragon. V, 2349. The hammer of the whole earth. V, 1844. How he batters the just and the unjust, and what different effects he produces in them. V, 1845. The devil was loosed before Christ’s coming and bound afterward. V, 1819. He can bark, but cannot bite unless one wishes it. V, 1820. He can invite to evil, but cannot drag anyone to it. V, 1979. He harms not by force but by persuasion; he does not extort consent but solicits it. II, 1117; V, 1820, 2213. He does nothing unless permitted. VI, 1175. The devil customarily harasses those who depart from him. VI, 1175. And those who despise his deceptions. V, 2269. But even this he cannot do unless permitted. V, 2270. He is permitted for two reasons. V, 2270, 2272. The devil persecutes only the good. V, 1775. He usually does this through the wicked. V, 1775. He does not seek Jews, pagans, or people of evil life, but servants of God. III, 2217. The devil’s hatred grows against those in whom devotion to virtue grows. II, 1116; II, 1117. How he tempts novices. II, 1118. The nearer he sees the end of the world to be, the more cruelly the devil rages against us. VI, 1182.

Having the devil as an enemy is more useful than having him as a ruler. X, 1870. He does not fear him who entrusts himself to God. V, 1909. Nor need one who is joined to God fear him. V, 1917. Whoever follows Christ declares war on the devil. V, 1796. How one must contend with him. V, 2076. With what weapons he is to be defeated. V, 1797. Let us not help the devil, and we conquer him. II, 1117; V, 2213. Let the devil always find us full of the Spirit of God and occupied with good works. V, 1821. He must be driven away by devotion to the Scriptures. II, 1117. Everyone feeds either the devil or Christ in his heart. V, 2347. Whoever is separated from God joins the devil. V, 2348. The devil’s angels are those who do his will. VI, 1071. How wretched the devil’s slavery is. V, 1773. The devil howls when a sinful soul departs. VI, 1356. How he will accuse the guilty at the judgment. VI, 1072. That is, those who have not wholly renounced his spectacles and pageants. VIII, 1118.

## Deacons

Deacons were first established to serve the mysteries—I do not wish to say, the tables. III, 2302. The office of deacons is to receive from the priest and then distribute to the people. III, 2302. With the exception of priests, they are placed before everyone else. III, 2303. A presbyter is made through the testimony of deacons. III, 2302. Those being ordained are led forward by deacons. III, 2303. The deacon calls out so that the people may humble themselves for the blessing. V, 2286. He announces the prayer, crying, “Let us bend our knees.” V, 2285. He ministers Christ’s chalice to believers. V, 2096. Deacons stand while the bishops sit in council. IX, 808. The deacon’s dress. VII, 838, 846.

Falcidius contends that the deacons of the Roman city should be made equal to, not to say preferred over, the priests. III, 2301. As though they were more honorable than in the other churches because of the city’s magnificence. III, 2301. The deacons of the Roman Church should not presume to claim the dignity of sitting in church. III, 2301. The multitude of clerics causes them not to pour water over the priest’s hands, as is done in all the churches. III, 2301. Why should the priests not receive the same deference as they do? III, 2302. At banquets they perform what belongs to priests; and they wish what is permitted only to priests—to have responses made to them in the prayers. III, 2302.

## Dialectic

Dialectic is the science of arguing well. I, 1409. The principles of dialectic. I, 1409. One thing belongs to the capacity for dialectic, another to the discipline of dialectic. I, 1411. The dialectician and the orator have their own proper limits in the use of words, but neither should despise the other. I, 1414.

## Diapsalma

Diapsalma. III, 2334.

## My dedication

My dedication. IX, 819, 820.

## Dicible and diction

How *dicibile* (“sayable”) and *dictio* (“diction”) differ. I, 1411.

## Didymus

Didymus. IX, 781. He contends that there is a third element in human substance, the spirit. VI, 815; VIII, 1216.

## Day

Day and night began with the world and will cease with it. III, 2321. Night is always subject to day. III, 2321. The first day itself is the angelic nature. VI, 740. How the six days of creation are to be understood. VI, 741. Evil days are made by wickedness and misery. V, 1964. The days of the Roman city. VII, 841. Superstitious observances of days. V, 2269. One should not say “the day of Mars, Mercury, or Jupiter,” but “the second day, the third day,” and so forth. V, 2005. The Lord’s Day is every day for Christians. V, 1757. What the great day is. III, 2440.

## Difference

What difference is. I, 1424.

## Worthy

Worthy. IX, 778.

## Dignities and offices

The various titles and grades of dignities and offices. IX, 808, 816, 818, 820, 828, 841, 842. In positions of dignity some are made better and others worse. VI, 1082.

## The Flood

The universal Flood of the whole world under Noah. III, 2175. The Flood was an effect of divine mercy. V, 2028. It was an image of baptism and the Lenten fast. V, 2028. Why only terrestrial animals perished in the Flood, and not aquatic animals. III, 2155. What happened to those that cannot live solely either on land or in water. III, 2156. Various opinions concerning the bursting forth and retreat of the waters. III, 2156. The Flood destroyed humanity but could not destroy sin. V, 1984.

## Diocletian

Diocletian, eighth consul. IX, 794.

## Diocese

The diocese of Egypt. X, 1687. The pope holds the greater dioceses. IX, 787.

## Dionysius

Dionysius, the source of Arius. VIII, 1214.

Dionysius, consul. X, 1686.

Dioscorus. X, 1778.

The Diospolitan synod. X, 1685, 1688. Whatever Pelagius denied having said there, he later said more openly. X, 1749. See *Palestine*.

## Learning

The learner’s condition is safer than the teacher’s. X, 1891. We are led to learning in two ways: by authority and by reason. X, 1897.

## Discipline

What discipline is. VI, 1087. The difference between discipline and virtue. I, 1433. The necessity and usefulness of discipline. V, 1799. Discipline also exists among animals. VI, 1221. Discipline is the teacher of religion and true piety. VI, 1219. By it all things are contained and ordered. VI, 1219. All vices are restrained. VI, 1219. The punishments of crimes are avoided. ## Wealth

Wealth is naturally good, but for the wicked it is evil. V, 2153. True riches. V, 1786. True and false riches. X, 1866. True riches are those by which poverty is removed; false riches are those by which it increases. V, 2153. Everyone has his riches where he has his delight. X, 1878. Whoever entangles himself in riches distances himself from the love of God. VI, 1345. They can never be acquired here without sin. VI, 1345. One must not confine the soul, together with silver idols, in a wretched purse; under the weight of money it will never be able to fly across to heaven. I, 1471.

Although money does not come to an end for the rich, life does. V, 2342. Hell belongs to the rich if the kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor. VI, 1218. The changed lots of the rich man and the poor Lazarus. V, 2332. The rich redeem themselves from their possessions while they are still theirs. V, 2332, 2333. The same act of a rich and a poor person deserves greater praise or blame in one than in the other. III, 2372. Pelagius said that the rich could not possess the kingdom of God unless they renounced everything. X, 1709. But he was compelled to condemn this. X, 1709. The rich can be good; their dignity is not to be blamed, but their arrogance is. V, 1843. It does the rich no harm that they are rich if they strive to maintain humility, mercy, or justice. V, 2311. Earthly abundance is more usefully held humbly than abandoned proudly. X, 1887. Christian rich people, if they are truly Christians, are altogether poor. X, 1878. The rich man who despises in himself what ordinarily causes pride to swell is poor before God. X, 1879. The rich before God. III, 2233. How a rich person may exist with some hope. V, 2248. The rich man is poor without charity, while with charity the poor man is rich. V, 1957, 1968. Charity is the good disposer of riches. V, 1957.

Why God made rich and poor. V, 1980. What they contribute to one another is illustrated by the likeness of the vine and the elm. V, 2334. The poverty of the poor serves the rich. V, 2331. What remains beyond their needs was not given to the rich, but transmitted through them to the poor for distribution. V, 2338. God appointed the rich man a steward of his goods. V, 2341, 2342. And because he takes some care that food should reach the poor man in safety, he is therefore first permitted to take from the common supply what is sufficient. V, 2248. The crime of the rich who distribute nothing to the poor. X, 1866. The rich man who does not distribute his surplus is guilty of as many murders as poor people have died of hunger in the places where he lives. V, 2268; VI, 1176. For this he will plead his case with them on the day of judgment. V, 2265. The rich man without mercy is an abuse. VI, 1246. The conduct of rich misers. VI, 1346. A truly rich man is now scarcely found. V, 1938.

From the evening of Saturday until the evening of the Lord’s Day one must abstain from agricultural work and every business. V, 2275. The curses he uttered against the emperor Constans and the prefect Gregory. IX, 801. Constans had sent ornaments for the houses of God and alms for the poor, but nothing to Donatus. IX, 801. ## Donatists

Teachers of a wandering populace. IX, 811. Heretics belonging to the party of Donatus. IX, 811. They regarded Catholics as Samaritans. IX, 763. They themselves, with better right, are to be regarded as Samaritans. IX, 764. Constantine calls them the devil’s agents. IX, 788. Unspeakable deceivers of religion. IX, 789. Standard-bearers of a most wretched quarrel. IX, 791. They built unnecessary basilicas. IX, 800. They contemptuously rejected the ornaments sent by Constans to the churches and the alms sent to the poor. IX, 801. In the city of Constantia they invaded the basilica built for the Catholics by Constantine and, though repeatedly warned, refused to return it. IX, 792. The Donatists have neither regard for their own salvation nor reverence for God before their eyes. IX, 785. The Catholic Church suffers much from them against divine and human laws. IX, 811. The Donatists commit murders. IX, 803. They give the Eucharist to dogs and throw the chrism out of the window. IX, 804. They violate girls. IX, 804. They break altars. IX, 804. They depose bishops. IX, 804. They spare no ecclesiastical order. IX, 804. They wash walls without cause. IX, 804. They exorcise the faithful and subject all the Orders of penitence to regulations contrary to the laws of the Church. IX, 804. This is done with partiality toward persons. IX, 804.

The earlier Donatists held that those who had belonged to the other party should not be rebaptized or reordained, but reconciled through penance. IX, 774. The violence of the Circumcellions causes hatred toward their party. IX, 801. Some of them, in their desire for a false martyrdom, threw themselves headlong. IX, 801. The Church tolerates the things carried out through the madness of the Circumcellions, although it would be lawful to restrain them. IX, 811, 812. Protection is sought against their violence. IX, 812.

The Donatist Church exists only in a corner of Africa. IX, 771, 773. They had no basilica in Rome. IX, 805. Instead, outside the city they chose a certain cave where they could meet. IX, 805. The schismatic bishops whom they had sent there from Africa are listed. IX, 805. They were called Montenses. IX, 805. This was because of those who met in the cave outside Rome. IX, 805. It is not unusual for the party of Donatus to falsify records. IX, 784.

## Donatus condemned by the Roman Council

Donatus was condemned by the Roman Council under Miltiades because he confessed that he had rebaptized and laid hands on fallen bishops; he appealed. IX, 779. Although struck by the judgments of the Roman Council, he nevertheless returned to Carthage first of his own accord. IX, 780. This was despite his promise that he would not go there. IX, 779. The seditious party of Donatus at Carthage did not accept the judgment of Miltiades and the nineteen bishops. IX, 780. What they bring forward against the acts of the Roman Council. IX, 785. They are ordered to meet at Arles. IX, 785. Constantine detests the Donatists’ obstinacy and their appeal from ecclesiastical judgment to his own. IX, 788. He orders those appealing from the synod of Arles to be sent to his court. IX, 789. He withdraws permission for them to return to Africa. IX, 789. They are ordered to prove, in Caecilian’s presence, the charges they bring. IX, 789. He promises to believe the rest if they prove even one charge. IX, 789. They withdrew by fleeing Constantine’s presence. IX, 789. Constantine promises that he will come to Africa and judge the entire matter. IX, 790. He urges the Catholics to tame their insolence by patience. IX, 791.

The Donatists defame the Catholics on account of their deeds. IX, 768. Many harsh acts carried out by the agents of unity must be attributed to the Donatist leaders. IX, 800. They accuse Macarius in vain of the harsh deeds he carried out. IX, 803, 804. They complain without cause about the persecution by Paul and Macarius. IX, 800. The Donatist cause was settled before the Carthaginian conference by ecclesiastical and imperial judgment. IX, 829, 832. In the year 348, Gratus gives thanks for the end of the schism. IX, 802. Some Donatist bishops were exiled far away. IX, 800, 802. They petitioned Julian and obtained from him permission to return. IX, 803. They were given liberty by the same proclamation by which the temples of idols were opened. IX, 803. Their desperation appears in the rescript they obtained from Julian. IX, 808. Their dreadful crimes after Julian restored their liberty to them. IX, 803. Those who rebaptize are judged unworthy of the priesthood by the constitution of the emperor Valentinian in 373. IX, 806. By the constitution of Gratian in 377 they are ordered to be expelled from the churches, their basilicas being restored to the Catholics. IX, 806. The places where they met secretly are handed over to the treasury. IX, 806. The decree of the Council of Hippo in 393, confirmed at Carthage in 397, provides that no Donatist cleric be received into his order but only among the laity. IX, 806. Those are excepted who evidently did not rebaptize, or who cross over to the Catholic Church with their congregations. IX, 806. Concerning these, Aurelius with his council in 401 dares to define nothing. IX, 809. The transmarine Council does not approve preserving the Donatists’ honors. IX, 809. Subject to this decree, the Council of Carthage in 401 receives them in their former honors. IX, 809.

From what they did against the Maximianists, a way is prepared by which they may be brought back to the Church. IX, 809. They, three hundred and ten in number, at Bagai pronounced sentence against Maximian and his ordainers and associates. IX, 807. By judicial orders they drove the Maximianists from their seats. IX, 773, 811. On their return they received them in their ranks and accepted their baptism. IX, 772, 809. Decree of the Council of Carthage in 403 concerning the summoning of the Donatists, and the form of this summons. IX, 810. Donatist bishops who have been summoned dare give no reply. IX, 812. But they rage against bishops, clerics, and others, and invade certain churches. IX, 812. The Council of Carthage in 404 seeks the enforcement against them of laws that fine heretics who ordain, or deprive them of the right to make a will or to receive anything by inheritance or donation. IX, 812. In 405 Honorius punishes those who rebaptize by confiscation of all their property and deprives them of the right to make a will or receive anything under the guise of a donation. IX, 813. The Council of Carthage in 405 gives thanks for the unity effected and the exclusion of the Donatists. IX, 814. Decree of the Council of Carthage in 407 concerning the extent to which the imperial law enacted for unity is to have force. IX, 814. In 408 and 409 Honorius decrees against them the penalty of due punishment. IX, 815.

## The Donatists and the conference at Carthage

The Donatist bishops likewise demanded a conference. IX, 818, 830. Nevertheless, they are said to have refused it. IX, 829. Those who replied that they would come were promised the return even of the churches that had been taken away. IX, 818. Those who came were promised a free and safe return to their own places. IX, 818. The proceedings of the Carthaginian conference. IX, 816. Representatives from all the African provinces were present at the Carthaginian conference. IX, 816. They were summoned by the order of Honorius, who had granted this at the Catholics’ request. IX, 817. The Donatists call themselves bishops of sincere Christianity and of Catholic truth. IX, 821. And defenders of ecclesiastical truth. IX, 828. They insist that it is a lie that their opponents often boast that they are few. IX, 821. They indicate that they do not wish to consent to Marcellinus’s second edict. IX, 821. Hence there is anxiety among the Catholics. IX, 821. The Catholics call them brothers, while they deny that the Catholics are their brothers. IX, 824.

They say that the Church of Caecilian and his associates perished through their sins, and that its remnants remained in the party of Donatus. IX, 824. From this point their error must be refuted. IX, 824. It is refuted especially by their judgment concerning Maximian and his associates. IX, 825. It is also refuted by their accusation that Catholics accept baptism administered in another communion. IX, 826. Or by their complaint that Catholics hand them over to earthly authorities. IX, 826. They refuse to sit at the Carthaginian conference. IX, 827. They attempt to create delays. IX, 829. They do many things so that nothing may be done. IX, 829. When summoned for the conference, Primianus replied: “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs should meet with the offspring of traditors.” IX, 831.

The Donatists habitually cast the crime of betrayal upon the Catholic Church. IX, 831. The case of Caecilian and his colleagues. IX, 832. How empty it is. IX, 833. They vainly wish Caecilian to be the father, root, or head of the Catholics. IX, 832. They contend that the parables of the dragnet and the like are to be explained only of hidden and unknown evils. IX, 835, 839, 840. And that the prophets were among the wicked by residence, not by communion. IX, 836. They complain that they and their fathers have been harassed continuously for a hundred years or more. IX, 838. They list the atrocities they suffered and those by whom they suffered them. IX, 838. Especially in the town of Bagai. IX, 838. They say that nothing similar was done by their own Maximianists. IX, 838. The Donatists are condemned by Marcellinus’s judgment. IX, 840. The Donatist bishops are allowed to return from the conference to their own places without any harassment. IX, 841. The laws of Honorius issued against them after the conference. IX, 842. The baptism of the Donatists must not be repeated, just as the circumcision of the Samaritans was not repeated. IX, 764.

## Drunkenness

Drunkenness is like the pit of hell. V, 2306, 2307, 2325. It is nothing other than a most evident demon. VI, 1060. The effects and evils of drunkenness. V, 2302, 2308; VI, 1106, 1107, 1108, 1111. They are demonstrated by examples and words of Scripture. V, 2305. The evils of drunkenness among women. VI, 1110.

Drunkards are like shipwrecked vessels. V, 2307. They are like marshes from which nothing useful grows and nothing comes forth that does not produce horror. V, 2304. How ridiculously they mock sober people as though they were not men. V, 2303, 2307. Drunkards lose themselves and their possessions. V, 2304. While they think they are drinking wine, they are being drunk by wine. VI, 1060. A priest close to drunkenness is close to punishment. V, 1107. Drunkenness is so common that it is not even considered a sin. V, 2303, 2308. Some clerics are subject to this vice. V, 2306. Even clerics of higher rank. V, 2308. Drunkenness alone, if frequent, casts a person into hell. V, 2309. It is a grave sin and hateful to God. V, 2304, 2308. It must be punished by eternal punishment. V, 2305, 2308. The friendship of drunkards is an enemy, by which they compel one another to drink. V, 2303, 2304. Even if someone says, “Either you will drink or you will die,” it is better for the sober flesh to be killed than for the soul to die through drunkenness. V, 2307. If no one wants to have a drunken slave, why do you wish God to tolerate drunken servants? V, 2308. The lavish waste and drunkenness of certain peasants wherever they have wine. V, 2309. Those who seek inducements to thirst are blamed. V, 2308. Drunkenness is imposed by friends only on mourners. VI, 1107. Just as someone gradually becomes accustomed to drunkenness, so he should gradually become unaccustomed to it. 2306. Let drunkards store in heaven through almsgiving what they were going to lose through excessive drinking. V, 2309.

Sober drunkenness with the love of Christ. VI, 933. The spiritual drunkenness of martyrs and of those who send a message to the world. V, 2090.

## Church

The Church was called after the Synagogue, but was promised before it. V, 2171. Namely, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to the peoples who became their sons through imitation of faith. IX, 822. The Church was to succeed the Synagogue, as Rebecca was brought to Isaac after Sarah’s death. V, 1754. Other figures of the same matter. V, 1800, 1814. Just as Rebecca’s arrival consoles Sarah’s death, so the faith of the Church consoles the Jews’ unbelief. V, 1754. The dispute between the Church and the Synagogue. VIII, 1131.

Adam, Noah’s ark, and Sarah prefigured the Church, but especially the queen of the South. V, 2171. Rebecca did likewise. V, 1758. Pharaoh’s daughter. V, 1776. Moses’ Ethiopian wife. V, 1777. The widow who received Elijah. V, 1824, 1825. The Church is from the saints; the ark is made of squared wood. VI, 749. The Church from the Gentiles is foreshadowed by a sinful woman. V, 1906. Figures of the Church’s union with Christ through baptism. V, 1754, 1763. The Catholic Church existed in Abel, Noah, Abraham, and the others. V, 1854. At one time it was hidden; now it cannot be hidden. V, 1853. It is known to everyone. IX, 829. What was promised concerning it to Abraham can no longer remain hidden: it strikes the eyes of the blind and breaks into the ears of the deaf. IX, 829. Scripture commends Christ and the Church as a holy marriage, Christ as bridegroom and the Church as bride. IX, 830.

The Church is the virgin and bride of Christ. V, 2166. She is Christ’s mother, virgin, and bride, in the likeness of his own mother. V, 1989. Why she is the Lord’s bride and wife. VIII, 1128. The Church arose from Christ’s side as he died on the cross. V, 2067, 2068. She becomes Christ’s spouse by sharing in Christ’s body and blood. VI, 748. The Church’s marriage with Christ was confirmed on the cross. V, 1987. In the present Christ gives the Church the pledge of his blood, and later will give her the dowry of his kingdom. V, 1761. He gave the pledge when he was promised through the Law, and the dowry when he was sacrificed. V, 1918. We may also understand the pledge as present grace and the dowry as eternal life. V, 1918. The Church alone is Christ’s bride. VIII, 1130. The only lawful bridegroom of the Catholic Church is Christ. V, 1779. The Apostles received her as one abandoned and raised up children in the name of Christ. V, 1780. The Church’s beginning and progress. IX, 832. Who is properly her father. IX, 833.

The Church is a winepress. V, 1816. A little boat. V, 1884. Unshaken against the storms of the world. III, 2204. The more she was tossed, the more regions she reached. V, 1884. The Church continually gives birth to Christ through her members in their sufferings. III, 2434. The devil first attacked the Church as a lion, now as a dragon. V, 2349. Within, false Christians, and outside, heretics or pagans, persecute her as though they were one body because they are of one spirit. III, 2442. How the Church’s enemies benefit her. X, 1872.

The Church is Christ’s body. V, 1940. She is enlivened everywhere by one Spirit. X, 1773. Spiritually, she eats those who are incorporated into her through faith. III, 2446, 2447. The Church’s gate is the gate of paradise. V, 2059. It is certain by faith that the Church is to be extended into all parts of the world. X, 1812. Scriptural passages that establish that the Church will be spread throughout the whole world. IX, 822. We believe the Catholic Church, not “in the Church.” V, 2193. Her unity. VI, 1197, 1201. The one Catholic Church is signified under the name of the seven Churches. III, 2418, 2420. Only in the Church are sins forgiven. V, 2189. Only there is baptism beneficial. VI, 767, 776. Repentance. VI, 766. Every good work. VI, 768, 776. Only there are true faith, peace, and salvation. VIII, 1331. And the place of the true sacrifice. X, 1860. Outside it there is no salvation. VI, 776. Only eternal condemnation. VI, 776. Who belong to the Church. V, 1939. The churches of heretics are not Catholic. V, 2193. Whoever does not feel the evils or goods of the brethren shows that he has been cut off from the Church’s body. VI, 1066. The Donatists wish the Church of Caecilian and his associates to have perished through their sins, with its remnants remaining in the party of Donatus. IX, 824. From what points they are to be refuted. IX, 824, 830, 831. Testimonies collected by the Donatists concerning the Church’s purity. IX, 835. The Church’s cause must be distinguished from the cause of human beings. IX, 832. How it is to be distinguished. IX, 833.

The Church is black and beautiful. V, 1777, 1823. She is foreshadowed by ravens. V, 1822. Likewise by the widow to whom Elijah was sent. V, 1824. Likewise by another widow whom Elisha freed from debt. V, 1828. She carries good and evil people, colliding with one another, in her womb. V, 1758, 1759. How the wicked serve the good. V, 1759. The Church has good and wicked members. III, 2431. They are mingled in every profession. VI, 777. She has carnal and spiritual members; both were foreshadowed by Abraham’s sacrifice. V, 1745. The Church has three states: repentance, righteousness, and glory. VI, 1337. The Church has four kinds of heads: bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the faithful. IX, 804. The Church was given by God so that she might assist everyone with all her goods. VI, 1127. For whose remission of sins the Church’s faith is beneficial. VI, 1119. Public penitents must be assisted by the Church’s tears. VI, 1123. It must be believed that the good works of the whole Church assist penitents. VI, 1123. Therefore no one can repent worthily outside the Church. VI, 1123. When the Church is at peace through the appropriate labors of penitents, she obtains life for them. VI, 1126. Those enriched by the Church’s goods do not experience purgatory when they are baptized at the end of life. VI, 1127.

The Church is Christ’s house. V, 1849. A beehive where spiritual bees prepare honey. V, 2077. Those who love the Lord come to her quickly and leave slowly; others do the opposite. V, 2077. The Church is to be frequented. V, 2079. One must not come to church without alms. V, 2330, 2331. Those who attend church only on feast days are rebuked by Origen. V, 1755, 1756, 1757. Whoever withdraws from the church on days appointed for prayer is a deserter of the heavenly camp. V, 2076. Whoever does not withdraw for six hours from the church’s assembly acquires a great remedy for the soul. V, 2079. In church one must either pray or sing psalms. V, 2286. The crime of those who devote themselves there to idle conversations. V, 2287. Those who behave immodestly there are rebuked. V, 1785. The vessels and furnishings of the Church are listed. IX, 794. The Church’s many ornaments of gold and silver. IX, 775. Who was to guard them. IX, 775. Ornaments sent by Constans to the churches of Africa. IX, 800. How great a sin it is to withdraw what has been offered to the Church is shown by the death of Ananias and Sapphira. III, 2200. Violation of the Church’s immunity is avenged by excommunication. II, 1096. The law of Honorius concerning intrusion into churches. IX, 807.

An ecclesiastic may not engage in trade. III, 2385. Ecclesiastical law and power. III, 2287. By the author’s grant, ecclesiastical law permits both the imposition of penance and the reception of someone after penance. III, 2310.

## Almsgiving

Almsgiving is a better good than fasting. V, 2023. No one is easily excused from it. V, 2023; VI, 1175. How each person is to fulfill the command of almsgiving. V, 2024. Those who are exempt from giving alms. V, 2331. A recluse is not permitted to possess anything for the sake of almsgiving. I, 1453, 1465. If, however, she has anything left over from her own labor, let her give it not by her own hand but by another’s. I, 1453, 1465. What kind of almsgiving is permitted to her. I, 1465. There are two kinds of almsgiving: one of the heart and the other of money. V, 2252, 2259, 2261, 2331, 2336, 2337. These are of no benefit apart from one another. V, 2266. A third kind of almsgiving is good will. V, 2337. This kind lies within the power even of a poor person. VI, 1177. Our God is nourished not only by the giver’s abundance of generosity but also by his benevolence. V, 2230. He desires not so much our possessions as ourselves. V, 2261. How he draws us to himself through almsgiving. V, 2261. Even one who punishes gives alms. V, 2329. How almsgiving may be secret while being public, and public while being secret. V, 1864. How it may be done by the right hand or the left. V, 1865.

Almsgiving is urged for many reasons. V, 2343. Almsgiving is a kind of pious loan. V, 1912. Incomparably more is received on behalf of the poor person than is given to him. V, 2331. Whoever does not give alms for the sake of his children looks after his children, not himself. V, 1912. We are invited to almsgiving when we hear, “Lift up your hearts.” V, 1912. Whoever refuses almsgiving will knock at heaven without cause. V, 2332. He will demand the end of punishments without cause. V, 2333. What confidence the giver of alms will have on the day of judgment. V, 1899, 2331, 2337. What reward there will be. V, 2333. Sins must necessarily be redeemed through almsgiving. V, 1895. Daily minor sins are redeemed through daily almsgiving. V, 2339. Daily adulteries are not consumed. V, 2339. Almsgiving for sins is greatly beneficial if those sins are abandoned. V, 2239. Whoever gives alms but does not cease sinning is like someone who offers his possessions to God and himself to the devil. V, 2018. He feeds another’s flesh but strangles his own soul. V, 2226. He offers money to God and hands his soul over to the devil. V, 2338, 2339. He loses his money and does not redeem himself. V, 1846. Those who distribute alms from plunder are brought before judgment. V, 2340. God abhors alms given from unjustly acquired possessions. VI, 1042, 1058, 1067, 1345. Whoever makes alms from plunder wishes to have God as an accomplice in the spoils, as though he were a corrupt judge. V, 1846. Any almsgiving outside the Church is of no benefit for salvation. VI, 768, 776.

Almsgiving: how much is needed for sins to be redeemed. V, 1892. What things, and when, are to be set aside for almsgiving. V, 2337. What each person should give to the poor. V, 1879; VI, 1175. Their tithes are to be given to them. See Tithe. Each person ought to give alms as much as he is able. V, 1898. Only that almsgiving is pleasing whose excess is pleasing. VI, 1227. From all income and profits, besides the tithe, something additional is to be set aside for the poor. VI, 1348. To make a portion for oneself and for Christ, together with one’s children, from one’s substance. V, 2217, 2218. After reserving here what is necessary for the flesh, something is to be sent through almsgiving from which the soul may live in heaven. VI, 1335. Whoever uselessly keeps what would benefit the poor is, in a sense, a retainer of another’s property. X, 1866. Whoever does not give away what remains to him after taking a moderate and reasonable quantity of food and clothing takes away what belongs to others. V, 2265, 2267. Food and clothing are to be restricted for the sake of almsgiving. V, 1879. No one should come to church empty-handed. V, 2331. One should give to a beggar so that one may receive from Christ. V, 2330. Alms are to be given willingly. VI, 1225. And with a cheerful spirit. VI, 1176. Everyone ought to give cheerfully, because much profit comes to him from this. V, 1898. Prayer together with fasting should accompany almsgiving. VI, 1228. Almsgiving itself prays effectively. VI, 1225. The proper order of almsgiving. V, 2264. The error of those who think that charity should not be given to the wicked. VI, 1227. The righteous are to be preferred, but the wicked—even enemies—are not to be despised. VI, 1227. The command not to receive a sinner is reconciled [with this]. VI, 1227. Those to whom we give are not to be selected. VI, 1176. Something is to be given to all who ask, according to one’s ability; but to God’s servants it is to be pressed upon them even when they do not ask. V, 2335. What benefit returns from these things to the rich. V, 2334.

The four elements. VI, 729. Their order. VI, 741. The elements are not to be destroyed by fire, but changed into something better. VIII, 1219. The pagans serve the elements; the Jews are under the elements; Christians, above the elements, serve God. III, 2275.

Men who are about to receive the Eucharist wash their hands; women present clean cloths in which they receive Christ’s body. V, 2168.
