Matters of faith are taught by divine testimonies rather than by reason. VIII, 1158. Faith first believes, then labors to understand what it believes. III, 2340. It is then stronger when it can give an account of its belief. III, 2340. Faith is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you have believed. X, 1891, 1892. The praise of faith is to believe what has not been seen; its reward is to rejoice in attaining what was believed. X, 1880. The vision of God is to be earned by faith. X, 1897. The virtue of faith compared with a mustard seed. V, 1914. The foundation of the Christian faith. V, 1999. A certain rule. VI, 1189. Its prerogatives and duties. III, 2376. Its limits. X, 1777, 1778.

The necessity of faith. V, 1959; VI, 753, 775. Many things concerning God must be believed for salvation. VI, 1152. Without faith no good work is ever begun or completed. V, 2234; X, 1791. Noah’s faith for salvation is the same as ours now. X, 1633. The faith of Abraham is the offspring of Abraham. X, 1878. How Abraham’s faith is to be imitated. X, 1955. By no other faith than the one now existing were all those saved who preceded Christ’s coming. X, 1637, 1638. Faith was bestowed by grace on the Saints who preceded Christ. X, 1789. Faith lost in Adam is not recovered except by God’s gift. X, 1851.

Faith is God’s gift. X, 1638, 1895. Nor is it God’s gift only because he gave human beings freedom, by which they have the capacity to believe or not believe. X, 1851. Whoever believes that faith is given closes the way to Pelagian frauds, and conversely. X, 1851. A human being does not possess faith by nature, but possesses the seed of faith, as a stone possesses fire. III, 2359. Those who speak of natural faith define as faithful even those who are outside the Church. X, 1786. These are weighed down by the remnants of an ancient error. X, 1791. [Col. 0732] The beginning of faith originated in grace. X, 1770, 1774, 1786. Augustine once said that faith came from the human being, but later retracted it. X, 1850. All merits begin from faith. X, 1781, 1850. Faith does not precede grace if merit does not precede it. X, 1826. If faith is denied to come from grace, no good thing will be attributed to grace. X, 1791. Faith, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift; and this gift has not been given to everyone. X, 1852. Why it is given to some and not to others may not be investigated. X, 1853. Faith is received only by the will. X, 1804. How this happens together with grace. X, 1805. Faith exists only through God’s gift and human will. X, 1841. Some believe by their will, others do not believe. X, 1851, 1852. Believing itself—that is, giving assent to the truth—is given to us by God. X, 1774. An objection against this opinion and its solution. X, 1774.

What faith ought to be like. V, 1959. The faith of a Christian and the faith of the devil. VI, 1190. The necessity of inward and outward faith. VI, 1189. Many falsely believe that the sins of the faithful are to be purged through a passing fire. V, 1946. Those who believe that the faithful cannot be condemned are refuted. VI, 1118. Likewise those who say that faith without works is beneficial and that God will be the avenger only of faithlessness. VI, 1042, 1043. Faith alone without works does not commend a person before God. III, 2412. It is not sufficient for salvation. III, 2333; V, 1855. It is useless. V, 1896, 2235. Without faith good works are of no benefit, nor is faith without good works. V, 1959. Complete faith believes both what God promises and what he threatens. V, 2234, 2236. True faith acts so as to avoid the threats and attain the promises. V, 2234. Faith can also be endangered by an idle word. V, 2234. The faith of Christ does not belong to those who trust in themselves. X, 1891. It belongs neither to one who hopes wrongly nor to one who despairs wrongly. V, 2235. Faith is nourished by hope as the body by food, and animated by love as the body by the soul. VI, 1025. Faith is now lacking in human beings. V, 1934. The death and resurrection of faith. V, 1886.

How great a grace it was to have been imbued with Catholic faith from childhood. V, 1855. True faith. VI, 1025. The rule of true faith written by Fulgentius. VI, 753. The brief confession of faith sent by Pelagius to Innocent. X, 1716. Another written by those who adhered to Pelagius. X, 1732. The broad confession of faith. VI, 890. An exposition of the Catholic faith. V, 2175, 2180, 2181. Right faith is especially required concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and the Eucharist. VI, 977. What the Catholic faith gains from heresy. V, 1804. The Donatists imply that people were compelled against their will to communion with the Church. IX, 838.

There are four kinds of the faithful. VI, 1308. How fervent was the charity of the earlier faithful. V, 1937. How cold it is now. V, 1938.

Christ’s Passion gives confidence to one who prays. VI, 907. An evil conscience diminishes it. VI, 903. How great will be the confidence on the day of judgment of one who gives alms. V, 1899, 2331, 2337. Whoever trusts that he is sufficient for himself falls away from the one who truly suffices for him. X, 1872.

The Potter: God, by whom we were formed for life and, through Christ, re-formed for glory. V, 1901.

The distinction between figures and forms. I, 1433. One and the same thing can be a figure of different things. V, 1818.

Filetus, attendant. IX, 816.

The Son has life not by participation, but by being born. X, 1889. By nature, everything belonging to one substance is properly the Son’s. V, 1880. The distinction between natural and adopted sons. VIII, 1161. The care of enriching one’s children is to be entrusted to God. V, 1912. Everyone is called the son of the one whose works he does. VI, 1324.

The opinion that there are sons of God among Greeks and barbarians appears to have existed. VIII, 1183. Mercury acknowledged the Son of God as born from God alone, not from marriage. VIII, 1104. The Sibyl proclaimed another God from the Father. VIII, 1103. The Son always appeared to the Patriarchs and Prophets. III, 2411. He was seen by Nebuchadnezzar in the furnace of fire. III, 2234. By what arguments the pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians deny that he is God. VIII, 1101. What answer is to be given to those who say that the Son is lesser in divinity. V, 2176. The divinity of the Son and his distinction from the Father are established by several testimonies of the Old Law. VIII, 1104. The Son’s mission proves him different from the Father, but not lesser. VIII, 1112. The Son’s being taught by the Father means his being begotten. X, 1889. The Son’s eternal generation is shown from his temporal birth. VIII, 1162. It cannot be expressed by any comparison or thought. VIII, 1178. To what extent our word corresponds, or does not correspond, to him, and human generation to his generation. III, 2366, 2367. The Son’s various names and their explanations. V, 1970.

The Son of God is the Father’s vicar. III, 2329. After God the Father he is second, not in nature but in order. III, 2341. He is Son by nature, not by adoption. VIII, 1178. He is not from things that did not subsist. VIII, 1187. He is not an emission or a part of God’s substance. VIII, 1187. He was begotten without any bodily suffering. VIII, 1187. He must either be believed to be from the Father’s substance, or else both Son and God must be denied. VIII, 1161, 1164. What distinguishes him from a created thing. VIII, 1162. It is not absurd to call him the son of love, just as he is the son of will. VIII, 1187. The Son proceeds from the mind as the will does. VIII, 1179, 1181, 1187. He was born from the Father without any beginning, even of reason. VIII, 1177, 1181. Why he is called Wisdom created at the beginning of the Lord’s ways. VIII, 1177, 1180. He is the truth, life, and way of all that exists. VIII, 1178. He was born so that through him creation might come into being. III, 2228. When God wished to create the creature, he generated for himself the Word whom he held mysteriously within himself, consubstantial with himself. III, 2249. The Son has subsistence nowhere except in the one from whom he was born. III, 2249. He subsists in his own proper identity. VIII, 1181. He is not the one from whom all things are, but the one through whom all things are. III, 2366. Why he is called the Word of God. III, 2366; VIII, 1177, 1180. Why he is the Son, Word, power, and wisdom of God. III, 2367. By being born he obtained everything that belongs to God. III, 2367. Although he is God from God, he and the Father are nevertheless not two Gods. III, 2366. He proceeded properly from God’s substance, not created externally by command or will. III, 2367. He is not a creature. III, 2368. He has life in himself, since he can also give life to whatever he wishes. III, 2368. He himself is nothing other than life. III, 2368. He is the image of God and invisible like the Father. III, 2368. An example from an example. III, 2369. He alone sees God the Father, and in him, as in his image, the Saints in heaven see the Father. III, 2369. He differs from the Father in no substance, but in the degree of causality; therefore the Father is greater by authority, not by substance. III, 2369. He is the image of the Father. VIII, 1179. He is truth in relation to the Father and image in relation to us. VIII, 1179. He proceeds inseparably from the Father, as radiance from light. VIII, 1179. He is the figure of God’s substance or subsistence, insofar as he made God, known in himself, known to us. VIII, 1180. How he is called the power of God, glory, eternal light, spotless mirror, activity, and goodness. VIII, 1180. He is power from power. VIII, 1181.

The Father begot the Son not by necessity, not by will, but by nature. V, 2180; VI, 736; VIII, 1196. The Monad generated a Monad differing in nothing from it, except that the Monad is taught to exist. VIII, 1165. The Son’s birth was called an “exit” so that he might be shown both to be without beginning and to be from the Father’s essence. III, 2293. The Father and Son are not two gods, but one substance. III, 2293. They are one not in persons but in nature. III, 2293. The only difference between the Father and Son is that the Father is unbegotten whereas the Son is begotten. III, 2292. The Son’s eternity. III, 2413. If there was a time when he did not exist, there was something that he did not make. VIII, 1110. If the Father did not beget an equal Son, he is either not good or not omnipotent. V, 1822. The Son is co-eternal and equal to the Father. VI, 976. And with him one in reason and substance. V, 1971. He is contained in no place, but is absent from no place, even though he is not present in the same way in all things. VIII, 1187. In the assumed body he was wholly present, and wholly present everywhere. VIII, 1189. The Son assumed a human body and a soul like ours by nature, but made like himself in purpose. VIII, 1189. He was incarnate, not because he was unable to redeem humanity from the devil’s power through others. III, 2340. But so that he himself might claim the dominion that the devil had usurped from him. III, 2340. The Son alone was born both according to divinity and according to the flesh. VI, 755, 770, 771. Why the Son’s humility did not pass over to the Father. VIII, 1163, 1164. The Son’s subjection. X, 1895.

Adopted sons of God. III, 2370, 2375. They do not possess merely the name without the reality. III, 2375. That human beings can become sons of God is a great benefit and pure grace of God. VI, 871. It is heretical teaching that no one can be called a son of God unless he has been entirely without sin. X, 1709. We are sons of Abraham not by birth, but by imitating his faith. V, 1745. Everyone is either a son of God or a son of the devil; and who is a son of God or of the devil. III, 2273.

We are sons of the devil through imitation of his wickedness. V, 1742, 1776.

Filtanius, bishop of Gaul. X, 1755.

Filuminus. IX, 779.

What the end is. I, 1440. What the end of good or evil is. X, 1872. Christ is the end of the faithful. X, 1875, 1876.

The firmament, which was made firm by the waters gathered together by God. III, 2317. Heaven is so called from concealing or hiding. III, 2317. It stands in the midst of the waters. III, 2318. It is not reached by the eyes. VI, 1027.

Firmus, presbyter of the church of Uzala. VII, 853.

The necessity and usefulness of scourges. V, 2322. God’s scourges are benefits and remedies. V, 1851. They benefit sinners for correction and the righteous for testing. V, 1852. Why Pharaoh became harsher under the scourges, while Nebuchadnezzar repented. X, 1675. The scourges would cease if sins ceased. V, 2077. When God removes them from sinners, he is said to harden them. V, 1787, 1788.

*Flagitare* for *jactitare*. X, 1623. For “to defame.” X, 1657 note 1.

What a disgraceful act is. V, 1869.

Flavianus, Vicar of Africa. IX, 806.

Flavitus, consul. IX, 809.

Flavius Constantinus, consul. X, 1721.

Flavius Marcellinus. IX, 816, 827, 834. Judge at the Carthaginian Conference. IX, 816–819. He permits another judge to sit with him. IX, 818. He pronounces a judgment against the Donatists. IX, 840.

When weeping is effeminate, and when it is inhuman. VI, 1147. One’s own sins, those of others, and the delay of the homeland are to be mourned continually. VI, 1253. Earthly things are not to be mourned. VI, 1253.

Florentius, consul. X, 1686.

Florentius, administrator of public funds. X, 852.

Florentius the Donatist. IX, 807.

Florentius, Catholic bishop. IX, 816, 827. Legate against the pagans and the Donatists. IX, 815.

Florianus of Caesena. IX, 779.

Florinus the Jew. VII, 829.

Florinus taught that our flesh was created for the sake of evil. VIII, 1220.

Florus, to whom Julian sends his books. X, 1735. He wishes to be regarded as bishop of the Western regions. X, 1754. He is regarded as deposed by the synod. X, 1760.

The custom of refusing the *focus* (hearth) on the Kalends of January. V, 2002, 2004.

*Covenant* (*foedus*), said to derive from the foulness (*foeditas*) of the pig by which a covenant is made. I, 1413.

It is not enough not to demand interest, if one is troublesome to the debtor. V, 1913. Cyprian groaned over the cruelty of interest among certain of his colleagues. IX, 825. Interest is punished by death. VI, 1300. Pious interest. V, 1912.

The Church’s threefold fountain: the Trinity. VI, 1203. The fountains to which prayer is offered according to pagan custom. V, 2271.

The form of the baptismal sacrament. VI, 750.

Fornication is thought permissible for men, but not for women. V, 2292. It is no longer even counted among grave crimes. V, 2292. Nevertheless, it makes those who commit it liable to eternal punishments. V, 2292. The fornicator injures the body which Christ assumed from us. V, 2046. Therefore he sins against his own body, because the whole Adam—that is, man and woman—is polluted. III, 2405. Fornication is the same thing as sacrilege for Novatian. III, 2405.

Letters of Fortis, the bishop, to Silvanus and his clergy. IX, 796. Likewise those of Sabinus to him. IX, 796.

A brave spirit chooses rather to endure a troubled life than to flee from it, and also despises popular judgment. X, 1863. Worldly desire produces the courage of pagans; charity, that of Christians. X, 1788, 1884. A sermon on courage. VI, 1256.

Unequal use of fortune in good and bad circumstances. X, 1863.

Fortunatianus, bishop. IX, 814, 816, 827.

Fortunatus. IX, 783.

Fortunatus. IX, 816, 827.

Fortunatus, bishop, an exile in Sardinia. X, 1772, 1779.

The opinion of Fortunatus, according to which he believes that God is visible to creatures. VIII, 1214.

Fortunius. IX, 807.

Gravediggers. IX, 794. Marcuclius, Silvavanus, and Carosus are called gravediggers, as are also the subdeacons. IX, 794.

How long the kings of the Franks endured: the Roman Empire did not cease. VI, 1133. It is reported that one of the kings of the Franks will be the last and greatest of kings. VI, 1133.

Who is properly to be called a brother. V, 1938. Christians are signified by the name “brothers.” V, 1861. He is also called a brother who belongs neither to one Church nor to the same sacraments. IX, 833. Constantine calls the bishops “brothers.” IX, 788. Every human being is a brother. V, 2139, 2259; VI, 1178. The brotherhood of Christ is greater and better than that of blood. V, 1937. Spiritual generation is nobler than bodily generation. V, 1960. The concord of brothers is praised. V, 1858. Dangers from false brothers will never cease. V, 1965. An attack on brotherhood is a sin unto death. V, 1860.

The pretext of fraud is cut away. VI, 1100.

The catechumen’s forehead is signed. V, 1821. Let the forehead be signed with the cross. V, 1820.

Fructuosus, a gravedigger. IX, 794.

To enjoy the world. III, 2319.

“We have fled.” IX, 793.

Fulgentius, bishop, an exile in Sardinia. X, 1772. His book *On Faith to Peter*. VI, 753. Also three books *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, and seven against the two [books] of Faustus, are praised. X, 1784.

Fulgentius the Donatist, and a book against him. IX, 763.

The sacrilegious art of fumigation. V, 2273.

The spiritual foundation is on high. X, 1868.

Certain funeral rites are noted. VI, 1166.

Furni. IX, 781.

The distinction between a thief and a brigand. VI, 1231. A thief caught in the act is condemned to fourfold restitution according to the Law. III, 2277, 2278. The sacrilegious method of identifying a thief is condemned. V, 2273.

The pretext of theft is cut away. VI, 1100. What sort of harm theft is. V, 1783.

Fuscius, duumvir. IX, 781.

[Col. 0735] G.

Gaianus, bishop. X, 1731.

Another Gaianus. X, 1731.

Galatius. IX, 781, 782.

The Africans demand Gallic judges from Constantine. IX, 778. Constantine sends them to Rome to be heard by Miltiades and the appointed Gauls. IX, 778. Certain Gallic priests, stirring up innovations, are restrained by Caelestine. X, 1756. The charges of the Gauls who slandered Augustine, and the replies to them. X, 1833. The bishops of Gaul attribute the beginning of faith to nature. X, 1790. They stir up hostility against Caesarius of Arles, who resisted them. X, 1792. Little by little they accepted the Catholic doctrine concerning grace. X, 1792. What Prosper had declared that he hoped for. X, 1795.

Gallicus. IX, 791.

Gallienus, duumvir. IX, 780.

Gamaliel, wearing the *stola*, revealed the relics of Saint Stephen. V, 2147. How he revealed them. VII, 807, 809, 815.

Gamalius. IX, 807.

The Ganges, second in size after the Euphrates, divided by Cyrus into 460 channels. III, 2173.

The peoples of the Garamantes. III, 2350.

The Gargilian Baths. IX, 815, 827, 828. A most suitable place for the Conference. IX, 819.

Gaudentius of Pisa. IX, 779.

Gaudentius, Donatist bishop. IX, 828, 830.

Joy is always found in one thing. VI, 846. To rejoice is good, but not if someone rejoices in what he ought not. VI, 1050. One kind of joy is right, another wrong. V, 2132, 2133. The joy of iniquity, the joy of vanity, and the joy of the Holy Spirit. VI, 963. Joy abominable to God. VI, 1050. True joy. V, 1917. It is the fruit of justice and peace. V, 1917. It does not belong to one who lacks a pure heart or a chaste body. V, 2169. True joy neither was, nor is, nor can be in this world. V, 2159. What constitutes the Christian’s joy. X, 1868. It is found in hope. V, 1961. For the present, let our joy be in hope; one day it will be in reality. V, 2160. Joy in Christ is eternal. X, 1867. How great the joy will be for those who enjoy God. VI, 966. “The joy of the Lord.” VI, 894.

Gideon, chosen for grace. V, 1816. He foresaw the abolition of the sacrifices of former times. V, 1816.

Gelasius, bishop of Rome. X, 1684. Two of his letters against the Pelagian heresy. X, 1763–1765. A third, concerning an old man who had fallen into this heresy. X, 1766.

Ice, when the storm of wind and rain has ceased, occupies the lower regions of the air. III, 2166.

Gehenna was made on account of the devil, not on our account. VI, 1200. Some are freed from Gehenna, though not into glory. III, 2224. Some merit, if not a crown, at least pardon. III, 2224.

To beget: it was possible for God alone that the simple should beget. III, 2229.

Two generations: their ways of life. III, 2334. A superstitious observance of Genesis. VI, 1173.

The people of the nations represented in Naaman. V, 1833. A figure of the nations raised up by Christ. V, 1825.

The courage of pagans is produced by worldly desire. X, 1788, 1884.

Gervasius and Protasius lived the life of monks in their own house for ten years. VI, 1104.

The proceedings before Zenophilus, the governor. IX, 793.

Geniscus. VI, 1172.

Gennadius and Felix, ancient martyrs. VII, 835.

Excerpts from Augustine sent from the city of Genoa. X, 1849.

What genus is. I, 1424.

Germanus of Auxerre is sent by Caelestine in his place to Britain. V, 1753. He is sent together with Lupus of Troyes by a numerous synod. X, 1753. There, with the people watching and judging, they dispute with the Pelagians. X, 1753. Germanus restores a girl’s sight by applying the relics of the saints to her eyes. X, 1753. He restores the soundness of the faith throughout Britain. X, 1753. Then, when the heresy revived, he returns there a second time with Severus of Trier. X, 1754.

Giesi, a figure of the Jew or of the Jews. V, 1832.

The two-edged sword by which the just are defended and the unjust punished. III, 2445, 2447.

Glory derived from nature is not genuine. VIII, 1184. Human beings have no ground for glorying in themselves. X, 1787, 1880. One who seeks glory for himself is a thief. VI, 876. Those who love empty glory place good things before their face and bad things behind their back; the opposite must be done. V, 1846. The conflict between empty glory and the fear of the Lord. V, 1093. The power to do harm possessed by love of human glory is perceived only by one who has declared war against it. X, 1887. Pride must be guarded against in despising earthly things. X, 1887. The vain glory of knowledge must be avoided. X, 1891. Our glory ought to be our conscience. V, 2350.

[Col. 0736] The glory of a pagan who dies as a Christian will not be that of one who has completed life as a faithful Christian. III, 2378. The glory prepared for us is not grasped by faith, not reached by hope, and not seized by charity; it surpasses our desires. V, 2172. The glory of the saints is diverse. II, 1130. God will be all in all when the glory of the head fills the entire body. X, 1895.

Gorgias. I, 1441.

Rome trembled at the cry of the Goths. II, 1120.

The Greek pronunciation by which εἰρήνη (*eirēnē*) is rendered in Latin as *irini*. III, 2420.

Grammar. A book *On Grammar*. I, 1385.

Grace, the kingdom of God. V, 1908. The tree of life placed in the middle of paradise was an image of God’s grace. III, 2320. The mystery of grace is a cause of fear for the saints. V, 2009. The doctrine of predestination, grace, and God’s foreknowledge must be preached as the doctrine of the Church. X, 1858. Some say that grace was not rightly defended by Saint Augustine. X, 1801. Because of their rank, talent, and reputation for learning, they possessed no ordinary authority in the Church. X, 1801. In attacking the one Augustine, they inflicted an injury upon everyone, and especially upon the pontiffs of the Apostolic See. X, 1802. They lead matters to the point that the enemies of grace are unjustly thought to have been condemned by the Church. X, 1801, 1803. They draw many to themselves. X, 1801. Among them Cassian excels in knowledge of Scripture and practice in disputation. X, 1803. The Church’s faith concerning grace and free will is contained in Augustine’s books, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper. X, 1778, 1784. Pope Boniface commends Augustine’s doctrine of grace. X, 1790. Certain chapters preserved in the ecclesiastical archives. X, 1778, 1784. They are sent from the Apostolic See to the bishops at Arles, to be observed and subscribed by all. X, 1785. Many authorities containing the doctrine concerning grace. X, 1811, 1824, 1825.

Julian requires the help of grace only for acting more easily. X, 1740. Therefore he compares it not to a hearth that kindles a flame, but to wind, which spreads the flame more widely. X, 1742, 1745. Grace would have been necessary even for our unfallen nature. X, 1886. Even with God’s help, it would in no way have preserved itself. X, 2452. Those who were just before the Law were saved by grace. X, 1633. No saint ever was or is without grace. X, 1635. How the time of grace was prepared by God. V, 2203. A figure of the grace to be granted at Christ’s coming. V, 1825. Before Christ, grace rescued a few from the whole world; now it saves countless people from every class of humanity. X, 1853.

The necessity of grace for overcoming temptations. X, 1757. Whoever does not fail in tribulations should not doubt that he is being helped by God. X, 1823. We cannot serve or please God except by God’s gift. VI, 913, 928. Without God’s help our building neither stands nor is preserved. V, 2032. Our sinful nature always needs God, its author, cultivator, and preserver. X, 1646. Without grace a person cannot do good or persevere in anything. VI, 818. There is no good in a human being that is not God’s gift. VI, 876. We owe it to grace that we have not committed whatever evil we have not committed. VI, 819. It is by grace that we do not fall into every sin. VI, 876. By perpetual grace the creature is kept from returning to nothing. VIII, 1162. Every good thing—of deed, speech, and thought—is from grace. X, 1780. Without grace no one can will, begin, or complete any good. X, 1791.

The continual help of grace is necessary for us. VI, 915. God’s assistance must always be implored. X, 1787. It is necessary that in each individual work we rely upon and be guided by the help of grace. X, 1693, 1694. What Elias was like when grace briefly abandoned him. V, 2263. What is a human being without God’s grace except what Peter was when he denied Christ? V, 1899. Pelagius’s arguments against the necessity of assisting grace for each individual work. X, 1694, 1706. The Catholic Church has always held that grace is given for each individual act, and given freely. X, 1709.

What Pelagian grace is that is necessary for beginning, advancing, and persevering in the good. X, 1794. The Pelagians understand by the name “grace” free will and knowledge of the Law. X, 1693. They say that Christ bestowed upon us not gifts but examples of virtue. X, 1743. Knowledge of the Law was not sufficient for acting rightly. X, 1673, 1787, 1880. Unless God’s help is present for observing it. X, 1674. Grace helps not only so that we may know what must be done, but also so that we may love and be able to do it. X, 1729, 1758. It belongs to grace to illuminate and govern free will. X, 1779. To give good speech and zeal for good action. X, 1780. It has been established by the agreement of the whole world that God’s grace helps us not only to know but also to do justice in each individual act. X, 1723, 1807, 1837. With Pope Innocent leading the way. X, 1807.

The Pelagians preach grace in such a way that it is understood to be given according to merit. X, 1762. The most subtle of the Pelagian errors is that grace is given according to human merits. X, 1793. If it is repaid for merits, and is not itself the creator of good things, it is called grace in vain. X, 1794. Grace is preached as something that must be preceded by good works. V, 1882. And as something added by God to merits. V, 2045. The opinion that we begin and are afterward helped by God’s mercy is rejected. X, 1789. According to Cassian, it is an error to want either grace to depend upon good will or good will upon grace. X, 1807. Of these definitions, one has been overthrown by the Church and the other defended. X, 1807. Grace, acquired at the price of Christ’s blood, is given to us freely. V, 1822. It is donated, not repaid. X, 1631. It precedes us; we do not precede it. X, 1625, 1659. It precedes all human merits. X, 1757, 1759, 1776, 1781. The free grace of Christ is not bestowed because of the evil merits of many, nor preceded by the good merits of anyone. X, 1845. Grace is for each person the beginning of justice, the fountain of good things, and the source of merits. X, 1762. It is the beginning of salvation, faith, and every good thing. X, 1770, 1791.

If merits do not precede grace, neither does faith precede it. X, 1826. Through grace preceding faith, and the beginning of every good will, definite impulses are inspired. X, 1791, 1792. The beginning of good will belongs to grace. X, 1812. Grace is the glory of God, not the merit of the one set free. X, 1814. No movement of good will exists unless created by the Holy Spirit. X, 1815. So that the will may both know God and live according to his will, it always needs the illuminating grace of the Savior as its help. X, 1625. Through grace faith was bestowed upon the saints who preceded Christ. X, 1789. And also upon the thief, Zacchaeus, and Cornelius. X, 1789. Cornelius’s good works began from the grace of God. X, 1796. The fallen angels prove that the beginning of good will and thought does not arise from the human being himself. VI, 764. The beginnings, growth, and perseverance of good will belong to grace. X, 1791. The prayers of the Catholic Church prove this. X, 1759. Cassian himself professes this. X, 1603, 1804. There is no doubt that a person doing good receives from God both the completion of the work and the beginning of the will. V, 2009. Grace makes us believe, ask, and be humble and obedient; it is not itself added to human humility, obedience, and so forth. X, 1786. No wretched person is set free unless first preceded by God. X, 1787, 1876.

The medicinal grace of the Redeemer was necessary for fallen humanity. V, 1866. It belongs to grace alone to restore the human heart. V, 1812. Even the desire for health in the soul does not exist without grace. X, 1806. We are Christians by the grace of God. X, 1712. What grace of God first exists in us. X, 1868. The second grace is the gift of living rightly; the first is calling. X, 1672, 1773. Calling belongs to God who has mercy, as does the fact that those who are called do something good. X, 1671. Our conversion to God is from God. X, 1796. The grace of conversion, and the grace that gives a person the means to please God. X, 1783, 1789. God’s free mercy precedes our repentance. VI, 775. Grace must precede a person so that he may both will and be able to do God’s commandments. VI, 775. The person blind by himself and enamored of his blindness is preceded by God’s light. VI, 892. Grace amid complete ignorance and need, a guest in the night. V, 1911. By free grace Christ turns those who have turned away from him back to himself; so that they may please God through good works, he works in them both willing and ability, and by preceding and following their course with mercy he brings it to completion. X, 1623. He prepares in them a suitable will for believing, by which they may carry out the divine work. X, 1624.

The strength of endurance is a gift of God’s grace. X, 1823. Knowledge and charity. X, 1808. Faith and charity. X, 1796. What we rightly vow to him. X, 1787, 1864. What we rightly think, or how we restrain ourselves from evil. X, 1787, 1861. That we ask for love. VI, 944. Grace is not conferred through human invocation. X, 1785, 1786. We ask God for the virtue by which we may be able to do his will. V, 1870. How much grace benefits our wills. X, 1886. Whenever we do good, God works in us and with us so that we may act. X, 1787, 1861. The Holy Spirit enables us to believe, giving sweetness in assenting to and believing the truth. X, 1786. “Breathe into me the holy work, so that I may think; compel me, so that I may act.” VI, 1076. Grace not only increases virtues but also bestows them. X, 1819. It belongs to grace to begin, complete, and crown. X, 1741. Through grace God lifts up the one who is falling, heals the sick, and crowns the victor. V, 1999. How the love of God for us precedes our merit. X, 1787, 1789, 1864.

The manifold grace by which God precedes the sinner. VI, 857, 877. God does many good things in a person without the person; no person does anything without God. X, 1788, 1886. The helps of divine grace are supports of the human will. X, 1827. God’s grace is ineffable, so that the guilty may be justified. X, 1845. By grace the person who had been changed for the worse through iniquity is changed for the better. X, 1787. Justifying grace does not make good people better; it makes good people out of bad people. X, 1797. Afterwards, having made them good, it makes them better. X, 1797. The grace of justification is effective not only for the remission of sins committed but also for help so that they may not be committed. X, 1729, 1758. Chrysostom does not place heavenly grace solely in the remission of sins, while others hold different views. X, 1736. The grace of justification is not given merely so that we may fulfill God’s commandments more easily, but also so that we may be able to fulfill them. X, 1729, 1759, 1824. Grace removes the sickness of inability and the guilt of disobedience. X, 1887. With the Spirit of God both teaching and helping, the commandments can be fulfilled. X, 1642. Those reborn through baptism can and ought, with Christ helping and cooperating, fulfill what pertains to salvation. X, 1789. God has deigned to promise his grace to the faithful. X, 1783. There are two gifts of grace. X, 1870. According to Basil, grace makes us good and enables us to persevere in goodness. X, 1775. The vessels which creative Wisdom forms so that they may exist are filled by assisting grace so that they may not be empty. VI, 784. Stability in faith and efficacy in action are attributed to grace. VI, 927. Our entire salvation is a great mercy of God. VI, 928. It is piously believed that grace, which destroys former evils, also rewards good things. VI, 1125.

It is falsely preached that grace removes praise and merit. X, 1824, 1826, 1827. They complain that free will is removed in vain if the beginnings, progress, and perseverance in good things are called gifts of God. X, 1827. When a person does not resist God’s grace but becomes its co-worker, he merits. X, 1636. Grace does not abolish human free choice but cultivates it. X, 1841. It does not remove it but liberates it. X, 1712, 1759, 1776. Grace does not take the will away from us when it forms, governs, orders, and imbues it. X, 1809. For grace does not work so that wills may cease to exist, but so that they may become better. X, 1811. The various ways in which the Spirit of God draws us to Christ. X, 1809. In every good movement of the human will, and in each such movement, our free choice is not absent, but God’s help is more powerful. X, 1731, 1758, 1808. Let no one trust in God’s grace as though God did not require the works of his free will. X, 1631. Grace is compared to a rider and free will to a beast of burden. X, 1632. Thus grace and free will together complete the journey of faith. X, 1632. Baptism confers grace upon infants without any voluntary work of theirs. X, 1800. Grace makes infants possess blessed life without the exercise of free will. X, 1633. Grace precedes and teaches those who are capable of reason, so that they may will and be able to do good. X, 1633. It causes, governs, and perfects them so that good works may abound in free will. X, 1636. In every holy work, God’s will is first and free will second: that is, God works and the human being cooperates. X, 1631. The believer has one cause and the unbeliever another: of the unbeliever it was said, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs”; of the believer, “By my will I will confess to him.” X, 1630. God works deeds in us, yet not entirely without us. VI, 1002. Because we are living stones, the hand of the author builds us in such a way that the one who is being restored also works together with him. V, 2032, 2033. Grace precedes, and by following we become its co-workers. X, 1779. God does not wish the gifts of his grace to remain idle in us. X, 1759. For he acts so that we may both will and do what he wills. X, 1759. And so we may be co-workers with grace. X, 1759. To will and to do good belongs to the human being who wills and acts; but in this God himself works the willing and acting. X, 1782, 1827. How this happens. X, 1788. Grace must precede, but it also requires our labor and zeal. X, 1671, 1672. Human obedience must not withdraw itself from God’s grace. V, 2033. Preceding mercy confers the beginning of salvation, and the will, followed by that same mercy, becomes the co-worker of its own salvation. X, 1782.

Cassian suggests a general grace of Christ. X, 1804. He says that some come to Christ by their own will and others are dragged unwillingly. X, 1804, 1809, 1826. It is equally foolish to say that someone comes to grace either unwillingly or without being moved by the Spirit of God. X, 1804, 1810. Grace does not compel the unwilling, but makes a willing person out of the unwilling. X, 1805, 1817. Grace does not draw one who is ignorant, but precedes one who understands and follows. X, 1817. God’s grace is common to all—and this is said of the Law. III, 2243. The grace of knowledge of God, faith, and evangelical preaching has been denied to some. X, 1798, 1799. A way of escape from this doctrine is blocked. X, 1799. How the grace of calling has not been granted to all. X, 1836, 1841. Why Pharaoh became harder through the punishments, and why Nebuchadnezzar repented. X, 1675. That we are preceded by grace, so that we may be able to believe, is the Catholic faith; why this grace does not work in everyone is not ours to investigate. X, 1626. If the sin of the first human beings is taken into account, God’s judgments will be recognized as most just. X, 1627. The Tyrians and Sidonians, to whom the gift of faith was denied, and likewise Chorazin and Bethsaida, in whom God did not perform what would lead them to believe, ought to move us to give thanks for his grace. X, 1855, 1856. Grace is not granted to all. X, 1780, 1782. Nor is it granted equally to those to whom it is given. X, 1782. It is necessary that it be unknown to those to whom it is not granted, and acknowledged by those to whom it is given. X, 1780.

Grace. By what signs God’s indwelling in us may be recognized. V, 2009. We show that grace is in us when we are concerned for our brothers. X, 1779. As long as grace is not in a person, it is necessary that he resist it in word or deed. X, 1779. From where it receives increase. X, 1836. The helps provided by God to preserve grace in a person. VI, 1126. If someone lacks something good that is necessary for salvation, let him not accuse God. VI, 860.

Prosper approves Cassian’s demonstration that grace can be resisted. X, 1804. A person can freely hold fast to grace and, by retaining it, avoid guilt. VI, 1126. Grace always departs unwillingly. VI, 1127. For it is always present and never fails unless expelled. VI, 1127. It continually and necessarily inspires what belongs to it, if there is someone to receive it. VI, 1127. God is compelled by the necessity of just mercy to abandon no one unless that person first abandons him. VI, 1127. Grace abandons only those who have deserved it. X, 1839, 1841, 1845. Let a virgin not doubt that grace will abandon her if she utters even one word against modesty. I, 1459.

Thanks are to be returned to God for works of piety whose activity is seen in servants. V, 2034. Thanksgiving for God’s benefits. VI, 940. For each of the mysteries of the incarnate Son of God. VI, 916.

The constitution of Gratian against those who rebaptize. IX, 806.

Gratus gives thanks for the extinction of the schism. IX, 802.

Gregory of Nazianzus. X, 1725.

Gregory. IX, 787.

Another Gregory. IX, 787.

The episcopal patience of Gregory the prefect. IX, 800. What he did to subdue the Donatists. IX, 801.

Grunnius. X, 1695, 1696.

Griffins. VI, 1229.

Gudila. II, 1097.

The *Scala Claustralium* of Guigo the Carthusian. VI, 998.

What gluttony is. VI, 1090.

H.

*Habitation.* A treatise *On the Threefold Habitation*. VI, 892.

A habit is a disposition of the mind persisting for a long time. I, 1433.

An immodest bodily bearing is the messenger of an adulterous heart. V, 1888. What adulterous bearing is like in either sex. V, 1888. It is injurious to the Creator and condemned by the Fathers. V, 1888.

Hadrianus, P. F. P. IX, 808, 813.

Heresy is not the bride of Christ. VIII, 1130. Rather, it is from the devil, at whose instigation whatever is done by heretics is done. IX, 791, 792. How gnats signify the cunning of heretics. V, 1781. Frogs, their talkativeness. V, 1783. The philosophers are the patriarchs of heretics. X, 1692. It belongs to heretics to call peoples by their own name, not Christ’s. V, 1780. Heretics do not have the Holy Spirit. V, 2092. The letter of Scripture kills them. V, 1799, 1804. The impious doctrines of heretics ought to be refuted by all Catholics; failure to do so. X, 1710. The Church does not regard as heretics those who have thought rightly concerning heretics. X, 1723. What they contribute to the Church. X, 1611. Which of them are to be baptized. IX, 787.

The Synod prefers heretics to be healed within the Church rather than, unless necessity compels, cut off from the Church. X, 1712. Public laws against the Manichaeans. VIII, 1153. The law that permitted heretics their rites is revoked. IX, 815. Those assembling publicly are threatened with the penalty of proscription and bloodshed. IX, 815. Those who provide heretics with a place in which to attempt forbidden practices are fined. IX, 806. Heretics who ordain clerics, and those who are ordained, are fined ten pounds of gold, etc. IX, 806, 812. Heretics are deprived of the right to make a will or receive anything from an inheritance. IX, 812. Honorius confirms laws enacted against heretics. IX, 814, 815. And decrees against them the punishment of just correction. IX, 815. Valentinian III orders all heretics to be banished even from the very sight of the cities. X, 1751. No heretic can be either advocate or judge. X, 1700. A Latin heretic in Latin regions is to be judged by Latin judges. X, 1700. The Pelagians are deprived of office and deposed by imperial laws and priestly decrees. X, 1689. By submitting to the Apostolic See, they recovered their churches. X, 1689, 1691.

Sand-workers. IX, 798, 799.

Heber perhaps worshipped idols. III, 2323.

Ebion. VIII, 1217. He says that Christ was born from sexual intercourse with a man. VIII, 1213.

The Hebrews are called from Heber according to some. III, 2323. They are called from Abraham. III, 2323. The Hebrew language. See *Language*.

The name of Eli is erased from the book of life. V, 2321.

Eli and Joseph were sons of brothers. III, 2233.

Helius, deacon. IX, 794.

Aelia, which is Jerusalem. VII, 809.

Heraclianus, Count of Africa. IX, 815.

The odium of the tyranny of Heraclianus. X, 1708.

Heraclidas, procurator of Constantine’s estates. IX, 777.

[Col. 0740] Heraclius, bishop. X, 1790.

Christ’s inheritance is as great for many as for few; as great for each as for all. X, 1875. Ambition for another’s inheritance is blameworthy. V, 1783, 1784.

Hermes. See Mercury.

Hermagoras. I, 1441, 1442, 1443, 1444, 1447.

Herod’s cunning and cruelty. VIII, 1122. His foolish error and terror. V, 2150.

Heros is spoken ill of by Zosimus. X, 1721. Note (e): see Lazarus.

Herpas the Goth. II, 1095.

Ireland. III, 2158.

The churches of Ireland are imbued with Pelagian doctrine by Agricola. X, 1753.

Hibernius. IX, 787.

Jerome. III, 2163; VI, 1270. A priest of Bethlehem. X, 1683. He does not condemn marriage. X, 1696. He suffers the calumnies of Pelagius. X, 1696. He is compelled to reply to him. X, 1697. Jerome intends to write against Annianus the Pelagian. X, 1697. Jerome published the dialogue of Atticus and Critobulus when Julian was still a little boy. X, 1746. Jerome, a pillar of the Church. X, 1697. He is praised by the Synod as a chief defender of God’s grace against Pelagius. X, 1712. A distinguished eulogy of Jerome. X, 1685. His modesty and high esteem for Augustine. X, 1708. Orosius is entrusted by Augustine to Jerome for instruction in the fear of God. X, 1698. Those living under Jerome’s care are most cruelly harassed by the Pelagians. X, 1710. Eustochium and Paula lament such harassment before Innocent without naming its authors. X, 1710. Jerome himself does the same. X, 1711. Gelasius considers it unjust that Jerome and Augustine, lights among ecclesiastical teachers, should be attacked. X, 1771. Jerome teaches that Christians, if overtaken in sin, are to be saved after punishments. X, 1704. Nor does he allow it to be said that the wicked are not to be spared on the day of judgment. X, 1704.

Jerome’s letter to Rufinus is praised. VI, 833. [His letter] to Ctesiphon. X, 1699, 1730. His book against Pelagius. X, 1699. A work falsely bearing Jerome’s name is circulated. II, 1132. Some rashly attribute to him Julian’s letter to Demetrias. X, 1745, 1746. A statement is cited under Jerome’s name which occurs in the commentaries on Mark ascribed to him. V, 1751. Jerome’s praises and miracles written by pseudo-Augustine and pseudo-Cyril. II, 1121. Jerome held Christ in the altar many times with his own hands. II, 1152. Fables concerning Jerome’s cardinalate and other matters. VI, 1274. When Jerome’s body was brought to Rome. II, 1152.

Hieroprepes. VII, 809.

Hilarion. VI, 1104.

Hilarius, prince. IX, 790.

Hilarius. See Prosper.

Hilarus, recorder. IX, 816.

Words of Hildebert of Le Mans concerning the complaint of flesh and spirit. VI, 826.

A little hind. To practice obscenity with a little hind. V, 2339.

Hippolytus, Lawrence’s keeper, and converted to the faith by him. V, 2351.

Decree of the Council of Hippo of the year 393. IX, 806.

Hippo of the Zaritani. VII, 839.

All Spain is ravaged by an enemy spread abroad. VII, 805.

Silken baptismal garments. V, 2211.

What a human being is. I, 1438; III, 2369; VI, 727, 811. *Homo* from *humus* (ground). III, 2323. A human being is dust and ashes. VI, 818. As a rational and moral animal, he has something divine and something bestial. VI, 800. In what he surpasses beasts. VI, 727. What he has in common with the four kinds of animals. VI, 729. Demons cannot change human beings into beasts of burden. VI, 798. What they accomplish in order to appear to do this. VI, 798. One part of the human being is heaven, the other earth. VI, 833. In a human being there is one person of flesh and soul. VI, 810. How body and mind are united in a human being. VIII, 1166. In a human being there is no third spirit as to substance. VI, 815. Endowed with sense and intellect, a human being goes outward for pleasure and returns inward for happiness. VI, 790.

Human dignity and excellence. VI, 805, 1047, 1328; X, 1883. The human being, a microcosm. VI, 1025. A great portion of God’s creation. VI, 926. A dear and beloved possession of God. V, 1843. By whom, why, and for what he was created, and what was created on his account. VI, 849. The world was fashioned for the sake of the human being. III, 2378. All things serve him, that he may serve the Creator. VI, 881. The human being is placed between the world and God. VI, 814, 850. He possesses God for consolation, and all lower things for service. VI, 881. A human being’s good consists both in what he renders to God and in the service he receives from the whole world. VI, 850. The human being was made for the devil’s accusation, and therefore finds him his enemy. III, 2217. He was created from things above and below. III, 2217. He was made by God for heaven, not for Gehenna. VI, 1199. According to a pagan pronouncement, he was made to contemplate heaven and the lights of heaven. [Col. 0741] VI, 1338. Three wondrous conjunctions in the human being. VI, 1339. It is not stated with sufficient accuracy that some human beings were created only for the adornment of the age and the usefulness of others. X, 1812. In what respect the human being is now inferior to angels, when equal, and to what extent superior. VI, 870. A human being seems to have power over God. VI, 853. Through Christ he has obtained more than Adam had possessed. III, 2370. Christ exalted the human being above angels. VI, 1152. “I would not wish to have the place of an angel, if I could have the place due to a human being.” VI, 1153. God’s various relations to the human being. VI, 866.

How different are the dispositions of the human being and of God. VI, 866. God’s benefits toward the human being. VI, 792, 962. How God gives himself to the human being in many ways. VI, 962. How dear the human being is to God, how much he is worth, and how much he owes the Redeemer. V, 2042, 2043, 2045, 2065. It belongs to our nature to be with God. X, 1870. Whence God’s delight with the human being. VI, 886. Holy human beings on earth and angels in heaven have the same office and the same dignity. V, 2017. The portion of every human being that is in Christ has already risen, reigns, and is glorified. VI, 912, 957.

Man made in the image and likeness of God, insofar as he was so made. III, 2319; VI, 786, 806. How he becomes threefold. III, 2370. Man is the image of God in that there was one man on earth from whom the others would have their carnal origin. III, 2244. Those who wish the image of God to consist in dominion are refuted. III, 2244. Man was made in the image of God according to the soul, not according to the flesh. V, 2021; VIII, 1207. He ought to treat the soul as mistress and the flesh as servant. V, 2021. How the inner man was formed in the image of God, and the outer man according to the pattern of the world. VI, 1023. The likeness of God is referred to the work of righteousness. VIII, 1207. Why man was made in the image of God, and to what extent that image was abolished. VI, 964. Man is far from God insofar as he is unlike him. V, 2000. How he becomes like the devil. X, 1871.

The carnal and spiritual man. III, 2353. How he becomes wholly spiritual through contemplation. VI, 1000. He becomes wholly spirit when he lives according to the law, and wholly flesh when he lives according to the world. III, 2404. The exercises of the spiritual man. VI, 997.

The pagans think that man is bound by the violence of fate and the necessity of sinning. X, 1749. God did not implant an evil will in man. X, 1845, 1846. The distinction between wicked men and demons. X, 1846. Human nature was left to its own free choice. III, 2215. No one was created by God in order to perish. X, 1845. No one was created in order to do the devil’s will. X, 1845. Men are born neither sons of God nor sons of the devil. III, 2272. Some say foolishly that man ought to be born perfect and know everything in its entirety. III, 2369. He knows nothing except what he learns here. III, 2369. He does not even know himself. III, 2369. Our nature is capable of learning the truth. III, 2272. So that we ourselves may in some manner be responsible for good and evil, and may not unworthily glory in ourselves. III, 2272. Every man’s nature is such that he can resist evil. VI, 1126. All men are capable of every virtue, both that which is commanded and that which is advised. X, 1747, 1749. The human heart is naturally assigned to virtues, not vices. V, 1812. When virtues succeed after vices have been expelled, they occupy not so much foreign territory as their own. V, 1812. The defect of nature must be distinguished from the author of nature. X, 1845. Man is nowhere well except in God. VI, 874, 914. From the one by whom man has existence, he also has the means of existing well. X, 1879.

The first state of man. X, 1743. The state of his descendants. X, 1743. Who taught that the first men were created mortal and harmed only themselves by sinning. X, 1681, 1682. By what arguments. X, 1682, 1688. The first man was created both mortal and immortal. VI, 739. So that he would neither grow old nor fail, he possessed this through the tree of life. VI, 739. He was created in blessedness, from which he could not have been expelled unless he had lost his own good. X, 1769. In this blessedness he is never read to have sought divine assistance. X, 1769. He worked for delight, not from necessity. II, 744. What would have happened to an innocent man is shown by Enoch’s translation. III, 2154. How the beasts would have obeyed is shown by the raven feeding Elijah. III, 2181. Even men close to God in this life cannot show what sort of beings they were originally made by God. X, 1747. Even human nature, while sound and whole, would not have preserved itself without God’s help. X, 1788, 1836.

The misery of fallen man. VI, 866, 1328; X, 1769. What man lost through sin, and what he found. VI, 964; X, 1812, 1813. How many good things the devil snatched from him, and how many evils he brought upon him. VI, 1071; VIII, 1117. Fallen man has been placed between paradise and the lower hell. V, 1875. He was cast down from eternal things to temporal things, from abundance to poverty, from firmness to weakness. X, 1896. Through sin he became wholly worse. X, 1773. When the first man sinned, not a part of nature but the whole of nature sinned. X, 1624. The nature of all men was preformed in Adam; all were condemned in him. X, 1845, 1851, 1853. Through pride the human race received a mortal wound. V, 1843. Men died on the day on which they were made mortal. X, 1767. Human nature sinned in them [Col. 0742] and became corrupted. X, 1767.

How the first man became bound to the devil together with his offspring. VIII, 1117. Every unredeemed man is the devil’s captive. X, 1845. This slavery is not God’s institution but his judgment. X, 1845. Man is not moved in vice by a natural impulse but by the impulse of captivity. X, 1846. God is not the author of the destruction of men. X, 1845, 1848. A slave could beget only slaves. X, 1773. Iniquity sold man and prevents him from being redeemed. V, 1945. To free him against his will would have been both evil and unjust. V, 1945. The deserter from the good is justly tormented. X, 1883. Conceived in guilt, born in punishment, he lives in misery and dies in anguish. VI, 1332. We are born in mourning, live in labor, and die in pain. VI, 1351, 1353. Men without heads, with eyes in their chests. VI, 1304. Others having only one eye in the forehead. VI, 1304. Certain philosophers mourned at man’s birth and rejoiced at his death. VI, 1152.

The punishment of condemned man, not the nature with which he was created. X, 1885, 1896. Human miseries arise not from the Creator’s institution but from the Judge’s retribution. X, 1813. Human nature, although evil, is not itself an evil. X, 1885. It has been corrupted, not extinguished. X, 1814. What still remains to it. X, 1817. Pelagius is accustomed to commend, and does commend, the powers of human nature from the beginning. II, 1100, 1104. Teaching that it is sufficient unto itself to avoid sin. X, 1682, 1701. Therefore assistance is sought in vain for avoiding sin. X, 1682. Man’s insufficiency for salvation without God’s grace. VI, 883. Man, having fallen by himself, was unable to rise by himself. V, 1866; VIII, 1168. What he is without God’s grace. VI, 877. Man’s inclination toward evil before grace. VI, 943. No one is good by himself. X, 1757. No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin. X, 1788, 1887. Man is nothing except evil. VI, 876. Before grace, human nature is in condemnation, blindness, and woundedness. X, 1829. By Adam’s sin all men lost natural possibility and innocence, and no one can rise up by himself. X, 1757. It does not belong to man to will what he can, or to be able to do what he wills, or to know what he can and wills; these belong to God. VI, 883. By the powers of nature man can do nothing that pertains to salvation. X, 1786. By free will alone he cannot attain the grace of baptism. X, 1786. The human heart is reformed by the operation of grace alone. V, 1812. Without God man does no good, but in man God does many things without him. X, 1788. Man has neither life, liberty, nor salvation except in Christ. X, 1846. Orosius is accused as though he had said that man cannot be without sin even with God’s help. X, 1700. Certain people slander Augustine by saying that he taught men to have been created from two masses and two natures. X, 1794, 1800. One man is condemned by God’s blameless justice, another is justified by his ineffable grace. X, 1845. Man, justly condemned, can be healed only by God’s mercy and by repentance. V, 2202.

The lost man ought not to have been helped so quickly. III, 2278. The figure of the fall and restoration of the human race: the axe-head recalled from the river by Elisha. V, 1834. How greatly we must beware lest we fall again. V, 1835. To restore the human race, humility could not do so without majesty, nor majesty without humility. V, 2009. The whole human race is, in a certain manner, two men. X, 1885. Each person has two men within himself. VI, 1340. Two things in us restore the divine likeness. VI, 819. He fell through pride and empty pleasures; let him rise through obedience and daily lamentation. V, 1866. The fortunate fault of man. VI, 853. Man must first of all attend to the dignity of his condition and the excellence of his restoration. V, 1866. In Mary human nature recovered the propitiation of divinity. VI, 1139. To man the Father gave the Son as the price of redemption, the Holy Spirit as the privilege of adoption, and he preserves himself wholly as an inheritance for those adopted. VI, 784, 820. Because of creation man owes himself wholly to God; because of redemption he owes him more than his whole self. VI, 938, 943. All this that I am, Lord, is yours by creation; make it yours by love. VI, 943.

What one who is conscious of homicide ought to do. V, 1979.

How homonyms and paronyms differ. I, 1422. What homonyms and synonyms are. I, 1421. Various kinds of homonyms. I, 1421.

Homoousion, “of one substance,” divided into two, has one sound. VIII, 1161. The Arians reject homoousion as not expressed in Scripture. II, 1157. Yet they themselves preach, apart from Scripture, that the Father is unbegotten and incapable of suffering. II, 1158. Homoousion is defended and explained. II, 1158. The Son is homoousios with the Father; the Holy Spirit is homoousios with the Father and the Son; the one Son is homoousios with God and man. VIII, 1114.

Homoousian. II, 1157. There is no reason to be ashamed of this name. II, 1161.

Honesty is the friend of justice. V, 2003. When it is violated, it becomes a pleasing sacrifice to demons. V, 2003.

The praise of honor is the virtue of humility. 2314.

Honorius, in the year 417. Consul. X, 1714. Tenth consul. VII, [Col. 0743] 809. Eleventh consul. VII, 832; X, 1721. Twelfth consul. X, 1726, 1727, 1728. Law of Honorius against those who break into churches. IX, 807. Against the rebaptizers. IX, 813. Another law confirming the constitutions enacted against heretics. IX, 814. Abolishing the freedom of religion permitted to them. IX, 815. Honorius’s command concerning the holding of the Carthaginian Conference. IX, 816. And the laws issued against the Donatists after the Conference. IX, 842. Sacred rescript of Honorius and Theodosius against Pelagius and Coelestius. X, 1726. Honorius and Theodosius again wrote to Aurelius against the same men. X, 1730. Their letter. X, 1731.

Two letters of Gelasius to Honorius, bishop of Dalmatia. X, 1763, 1764, 1765.

The book On the Knowledge of Life is shown to be by Honorius of Autun. VI, 1006. The title itself is so marked. VI, 1007.

A saying of Horace. X, 1708.

What one gains by not withdrawing for six hours from the church assembly. V, 2079. One must assemble at Terce, Sext, and None. V, 2019.

A letter of Hormisdas to Possessor. X, 1777. It is called into question by John Maxentius. X, 1778. It is praised by the African bishops. X, 1784. The profession concerning the grace of God delivered to Hormisdas’s legates. X, 1771.

Hortensius’s slander concerning the ambiguity of words. I, 1415.

Hosius. IX, 777.

Praise of hospitality. V, 1747, 1748; VI, 1325; VIII, 1104. Hospitality is not without reward. V, 1714. Abraham received God as his guest. V, 1714, 1748. Guests are allowed more sumptuous food. VI, 1101. Their feet are to be washed. VI, 1212. See Washing. A guest: grace. V, 1911. A good thought. V, 1911. Christ. V, 1911.

The treatise On the Seven Vices, etc., is attributed to Hugh of Saint-Victor. VI, 1088. Admonition. His book On the Substance of Love. VI, 843. A large part of the book On the Soul’s Earnest. VI, 851. The Magnificat is expounded in his words. VI, 1137.

The human race needed the medicine of humility. V, 1843. We could return to God only through humility. V, 1996. Praise of humility. V, 2133. Its praise and fruit. VI, 1058. God considers and tests humility in every creature of his. V, 2313. God made humble puts the proud man to shame. V, 2314. The practice of humility is honorable even among human beings. V, 2313. Truth eludes the mind which it has not found humble. V, 2314. Nor can the grace of the Holy Spirit dwell in it. V, 2314. Whoever performs good works without humility carries dust into the wind. V, 2314. Humility is the daughter of charity and cannot exist without its mother. V, 2312. Humility is necessary for charity. V, 1875. Humble weakness is more sweet-smelling to God than exalted virtue. VI, 854. Humility alone approaches God’s height. X, 1866. The high God looks upon the lowly from near at hand, and upon the lofty from afar, a great miracle. V, 2083. God the Most High is reached through humility. V, 2313. Whoever preserves humility cannot perish. V, 1926. Humility makes men like the holy angels. VI, 1053. Many follow the shadow of humility, few its truth. II, 1113. Among God’s servants there is sometimes humility without humiliation, but never humiliation without humility. VI, 1140. The distinction between true and false humility. V, 2133. True humility. X, 1866. Who is humble. VI, 1344. The humble person is himself poor in spirit. VI, 1084. The first degree of humility is to hear the word of truth humbly, retain it in memory, and carry it out willingly. V, 2314. In the highest honor, let humility be of highest importance to you. V, 2314. The conflict between humility and pride. VI, 1098. The humble and the proud have constituted two cities from the beginning of the world. V, 2311. What Christ said and did through humility, and what the devil did through pride. VI, 1053.

The Huns. II, 1095.

Whom hyacinth represents. VI, 1230.

Where the name “hypocrites” comes from. V, 1863. Almost no one, or only a rare person, lacks the stain of hypocrisy. V, 1863.

Subdeacons. IX, 792.

Hypomnesticon. X, 1614.

How hypothesis and thesis differ. I, 1441.

## I

How Jacob represented the type of God the Father. V, 1765, 1818. How he represented Christ. V, 1760, 1761, 1763, 1764. How he represented the Jews. V, 1764. The words with which he blessed his sons refer historically to the division of the Promised Land, and allegorically to Christ and the Church. III, 2199.

The translation of James the Greater. VI, 1277. Note (a).

When James was being stoned by the Jews, he knelt and prayed for them. V, 2258.

The opinion of James the Syrian concerning two souls in one man. VIII, 1216.

The boasting of the powerful is beaten back. X, 1780. The Jews do not dare to live in Fammona. VII, 822. There neither wolves nor foxes are seen. VII, 822. Serpents and scorpions have no power to do harm. VII, 822.

Januarianus the Donatist. IX, 821, 834.

Januarius of Flumenpiscensis, the Donatist. IX, 803.
