Superstitions of the Kalends of January. V, 2001, 2002, 2003; VI, 1172. A public fast was proclaimed throughout all the churches on the Kalends of January. V, 2002, 2004.

Who Janus was. V, 2001. Why he had two faces. V, 2001. Thus, while they wished to make him a god, they made him a monster. V, 2001.

What jasper signifies. VI, 1229.

At the coming of the Lord’s law, the flight from idolatry was prefigured by Dagon with his back broken. III, 2174.

A public fast proclaimed. V, 1865, 1872, 1948. The public fast on the Kalends of January. V, 2002, 2004. Fasts before Easter. III, 2364. Why fasts were instituted on certain vigils of the saints. VI, 1276. During the fasts of the four seasons, on the vigils of the saints, and likewise on Wednesday and Friday, one should fast from food during Lent. I, 1458. The necessity of fasting. III, 2364. Its virtue. I, 1456. Its fruit. V, 1887. The usefulness of fasting is shown by several examples. V, 2025, 2026. Fasting is the humbling of the soul. V, 2080. It is the fitting satisfaction of all the limbs. VI, 1274. Fasting and food are twofold. VI, 1064. Fasting on dry foods. VII, 811, 812. The principal fast is from vices. V, 2025, 2079. Fasting is useless for those who do not turn away from iniquity or devote themselves to pious exercises. V, 2029. Whatever you do beyond God’s commandment, although you abstain, you are not fasting. V, 2030. Fasts acceptable to God. V, 2080. They are then acceptable to God if we refresh those who fast from necessity. V, 2026. Fast in such a way that, when another is eating, you rejoice as though you had dined. V, 2027. Let our fasts be made full and well-supported, nourished by the richness of almsgiving. V, 2027. Prayer is the refreshment of fasting. V, 1887. Let prayer accompanied by mercy be the companion of fasting. III, 2364. What would have been eaten at table should be distributed to the poor. V, 1760; VI, 1178. Fasting with almsgiving is a twofold good; without almsgiving it is no good. V, 2023. Without almsgiving it is like a lamp without oil. V, 2024. Fasting without almsgiving is a kind of commerce. V, 2029. The days of fasting are days of reconciliation. V, 1906. Days for showing mercy to one’s neighbor. V, 1906. When the fast is at hand, one should approach the Lord’s table. V, 1906. See Lent.

Jephthah’s character, deeds, and vow are altogether condemned. III, 2239. His daughter gained the profit, dying innocent amid her father’s evils. III, 2239.

Jeremiah, prophet of the nations. III, 2242.

Jericho means “moon.” X, 1628. It had the type of the world. V, 1814; X, 1628.

Jerusalem was besieged for two years in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion. V, 1827. How many Jews were then gathered there, how many were killed, and how many taken captive. III, 2441; V, 1827. It is reported that the relics of Saint Stephen were transferred to Jerusalem. VII, 817. Jerusalem, “vision of peace.” X, 1628. Description of the heavenly Jerusalem. VI, 919, 958. This city has walls built of peace. V, 2255.

The proceedings of the Jerusalem assembly in the year 415 in the case of Pelagius. X, 1698.

Joshua, the figure of the true Jesus. V, 1813. He alone is able to lead into the Promised Land. V, 1812.

The name of Jesus, the sinner’s trust. VI, 939, 946. Where the name Jesus is first mentioned in Scripture. V, 1797. Why Isaiah saw Jesus sitting and Stephen saw him standing. III, 2281.

Fire is in the higher region. III, 2181. From there it cannot descend unless mixed with heavier matter. III, 2182. It is understood to be of incorporeal nature. III, 2190. It can live in nothing except water or the substance of some liquid. III, 2190. Its life consists in air and moisture. III, 2190. Incorporeal fire is declared in Moses’ bush. III, 2163. Fire is twofold: one external, the other internal. V, 2127, 2128. There are two fires: those of charity and of desire. V, 1779, 2170.

Transitory and purgatorial fire. V, 1946. It is like a river of fire. V, 2212. It will be harsher than anything that can be felt or imagined here. V, 1947. It will purge only minor sins. V, 1946, 2212. It will purge those sins that have not been expiated here. V, 1947, 2212. We shall remain in it as long as the sins mentioned above are consumed. V, 1947, 2212. Perhaps for months, or even years. V, 1948. For a long time. V, 1949. Those who are free from sins will pass through that fire without any injury. V, 1948. That fire is called the judging fire. V, 1772. A wise punishment and a rational discipline of flame [Col. 0745]. V, 2212.

The ignorant. Not everyone who is ignorant is free from punishment; but the person who had no one from whom to learn can be excused. III, 2262. Ignorance is sin in those who did not wish to understand, and the punishment of sin in those who were unable to do so. X, 1886.

Whoever refuses to forgive others does not consider what he himself owes to God. V, 2162.

No one ought to avoid what is illicit more than the person who rejects what was permitted. V, 2340. Whatever is illicit for women is also not permitted for men. V, 2290, 2340.

What imagination is. VI, 802, 808. How it is formed in us. VI, 802, 808. The distinction between imagination and sensation. VI, 786.

In Scripture, the names of things are often assigned to imagined objects. III, 2179.

The twofold character of images. VIII, 1179. A perfect image is equal to the thing of which it is the image. VI, 783. The image of God insofar as it exists in man. VI, 1047; X, 1889. When man is truly called the image of God. VI, 739. It is suggested that the image is not in woman. VI, 739. The image of the triune God in the soul. VI, 805, 827. Who bears the image of the heavenly Adam. V, 1889. The story of Jerome’s struck image. II, 1138. The power of another image of the same kind. II, 1142, 1150.

Imitation of the wicked is easier than imitation of the good. XI, 769. What it means to imitate Adam, and what it means to imitate Christ. VI, 1051. How we can imitate the martyrs and Christ himself. V, 2161.

Strictly speaking, only God is immortal. VI, 1022. Intellectual natures are immortal, and why. VIII, 1216. The cup of immortality prepared for us from our weakness and divine power. X, 1844.

Wherever there is bodily impurity, there is the dwelling of the devil’s spirit. V, 2296.

God alone is immutable in nature. VIII, 1218.

Change occurs in three ways. I, 1439.

Impatience in awaiting God’s promises is praiseworthy. VI, 861.

The emperor’s writings are received and worshiped. IX, 778. His hand is called divine. IX, 817.

The Roman Empire is already destroyed for the most part. VI, 1133. It did not wholly cease as long as the kings of the Franks endured. VI, 1133. At the end of the world it is to be obtained in its entirety from one of these kings. VI, 1133.

There is no empire except where something unjust is commanded. VI, 1219. The empire of the just is slavery. X, 1873.

God cannot restore the unrepentant to his former state without injustice. V, 2202.

The impious person is one who does not acknowledge or denies the true God. III, 2336. The virtues of the impious are false. X, 1818, 1819. All their works are unclean. X, 1818. Their wisdom is diabolical. X, 1818. How the wickedness of the impious may be useful. V, 1804. How the impious contribute to the adornment of the world and the benefit of the saints. X, 1839, 1842.

The imprecations of the prophets are not wishes of those hoping for something, but prophecies of future events. V, 1860.

Impunity. God decrees more severe punishment for the person from whom correction is withheld. X, 1866, 1870.

Persians wear women’s earrings. III, 2349. Moorish women also wear them in their nostrils. III, 2349.

The rainbow bears the type of the incarnate Word. III, 2419. The incarnation of God from the Virgin neither exceeds faith nor dishonors God. VI, 1191. The necessity of the incarnation. X, 1880. Without the incarnation of the Word man could have been freed, but it would not have been fitting. V, 2062. God could have acted otherwise, but no more advantageous remedy could have been procured for us. V, 2201. How fitting the incarnation of God is to our need. V, 2009. The causes of the incarnation of the Son of God. VI, 962; X, 1887, 1888, 1889, 1894, 1896. Above all, two: our restoration and our instruction. V, 1982. The purpose and fruit of the incarnate God. V, 1988, 1997; VI, 1065. By worshiping the mystery of the incarnation from afar, the just before Christ received the remedy of eternal salvation. X, 1770. No one from Adam onward was saved except through faith in the name of Jesus. X, 1772. All the saints burned with desire for the incarnation, since they knew that they could be saved through it alone. VI, 1153.

The mystery and benefits of the incarnation are expounded. VI, 910. This mystery is illustrated by a similarity of sound. V, 2202. The incarnate Word was served by the Holy Spirit. III, 2284. Spiritual nuptials were celebrated in the virginal womb. VIII, 1122. The Son became incarnate through the whole Trinity acting together. VI, 891. 801. The Son alone assumed flesh, not the Father or the Holy Spirit. VI, 755, 770, 772; VIII, 1213. How flesh pertains to Christ alone. V, 2196. Although the substance of the three persons is one. VI, 1015. How the whole Trinity fashioned man, while only the person of the Son assumed him, illustrated by the example of soul and reason. VI, 1195; VIII, 1196. Why only the Son is said to have become incarnate. VIII, 1175. Why he is not called the son of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1175. Whether divinity was conceived, born, and suffered together with the flesh. VIII, 1175. By assuming flesh, the Son of God neither diminished anything belonging to himself nor added anything to himself. V, 2200, 2201. An incomprehensible nature so united the substance of the body to itself that it was neither less in the body nor itself lessened. VI, 1140. God the Word did not take a human person but a human nature. VI, 772. Thus God, by an altered exchange, was made in our image and likeness. V, 1982. How much remembrance of the incarnate Lord helps toward virtues and against vices. V, 1979. Various heretical opinions concerning the incarnation. VIII, 1213.

An undefiled substance. VIII, 1146.

The provocations of self-indulgence. V, 2291, 2298.

Nothing is incorporeal by nature except God. VIII, 1215. There can be no division of the incorporeal. VIII, 1189.

“Blameless,” as though liable to blame. V, 2203.

Indicula. V, 1780, 1788, 1825, 1873.

Hardening follows upon the absence of grace. V, 1787. It arises from despair. V, 1786. It begins when small sins are first neglected. V, 1786. It is brought about not so much by God’s power as by his patience. V, 1786, 1788. Namely, while God removes the scourges. V, 1787. God is said to harden the person whom he has not wished to soften. X, 1668. Or when, by a just judgment, he does not remove hardness. VIII, 1205. That is, not by driving him toward iniquity, but by not rescuing him from iniquity. X, 1782.

They say that the infant is formed in the womb in forty-six days. VI, 742. Pelagius does not dare openly to confess that infants are without sin, lest he be stoned. X, 1707. The infants of the Sodomites are free from hell, having been killed in another’s cause. III, 2224.

No misfortune breaks the person whom no prosperity corrupts. X, 1879. There are two hells. V, 1875. The ancient saints were detained in the lower regions when they departed from this world. III, 2316, 2371. Although in the bosom of tranquility. V, 2059. There they had necessarily to await Christ’s birth. III, 2276. Christ became the bite of hell, and how. X, 1617. From there Christ snatched those whom he recognized as his own by faith and works; he left the others. V, 2059. Those detained in hell for original sin alone were freed when Christ descended there. V, 1193, 1194. The voices of the infernal ministers at Christ’s descent into hell. V, 2060. The entreaty of the righteous captives in hell to Christ. V, 2060.

The punishments of hell. V, 2211, 2215; VI, 1064, 1280, 1355, 1356. Their inequality. VI, 1280. The evils of hell and the goods of God’s kingdom are compared. VI, 991. The flames of hell are called spiritual. III, 2258. Infernal fire is incorporeal, or the condemned soul is not without a body. VI, 1026.

The unbelief of believers is not predestined but foreknown. X, 1840. It arises solely from the human will. X, 1841, 1843. The worst example of unbelief, cut off as though at its very root in Ananias and Sapphira. V, 2264. Unbelievers possess a certain wisdom from the remnants of nature created by God. X, 1814. Through it they can order temporal life, but not find justification. X, 1814. In them there can be many things that bear the appearance of piety but not its truth. X, 1797. The righteousness of unbelievers is false. X, 1796, 1818, 1819. Their whole life is sin. X, 1868.

Bodily infirmities, and how they are gifts of God. XI, 1150. They should be received joyfully. VI, 1150. Sacrilegious remedies against diseases. V, 2272. The sick should avoid them. V, 2238; VI, 1173. It is more salutary to receive the body and blood of Christ, and faithfully to anoint oneself and one’s household with blessed oil. V, 2273. Let the sick receive Christ’s body and blood, and then anoint their own little bodies. V, 2238. With blessed oil. VI, 1173. Two books on visiting the sick. VI, 1148.

What natural ability is. VI, 787, 809.

Ingentius, a public scribe. IX, 780. Scribe of Augentius. IX, 782. Decurion of the Ziquenses. IX, 784. He came suborned with letters supposedly from Felix. IX, 782. He was sent through Mauretania and Numidia as an envoy from the opposing side. IX, 782. He stirred up sedition against the Catholic Church. IX, 784. He was thrown into prison and reserved for a stricter interrogation. IX, 784. Under torture he confessed what he had fabricated to gain the favor of Maurus. IX, 783. He was convicted of lying when he denied having traversed Numidia. IX, 784.

An ungrateful mind revives dead evils, kills living works, and blocks the fountain of grace. VI, 879.

By the name “enemy,” the spiritual Jews understood the devil. V, 1860. The enemies of man. VI, 946. Why enemies are permitted, and what should be prayed for on their behalf. X, 1876. The fruit of Christ’s prayer for his enemies. V, 2052. We should pray for our enemies, following the example of Christ and Stephen. V, 2052. How prayer kills enemies. V, 2251. It is not lawful to desire their death in any other way. V, 2251. In an enemy two things must be distinguished: the human being and the sinner. V, 2251. The human being is our neighbor, and the enemy is the devil. V, 2254. Enemies must be loved, so that we may be superior to the nations and the beasts. V, 2258. Whoever loves his enemy is a friend and son of God; whoever does not love him is a murderer. V, 2161. Love of enemies is not advice but a commandment. V, 2258. We have no other hope unless we forgive whatever people have done to hurt us. V, 2252. The person who does not forgive an enemy is first an enemy to himself. V, 1882. Whoever gives alms but does not forgive his enemies offers earthly substance to God and subjects his soul to the devil [Col. 0747]. V, 2261.

To forgive enemies is an almsgiving from which no one can excuse himself. V, 2336. No one can excuse himself from loving enemies. V, 2161, 2252, 2255, 2256, 2260. We are shown that the injuries of enemies can be endured patiently. V, 2139. We are bound to love them, since we were loved by God when we were enemies. V, 2250, 2251. Whoever says that he cannot love an enemy who harms him daily does not consider what he owes to God. V, 2139. Nothing in Scripture opposes the commandment that enemies be loved. V, 1860. Joseph, Moses, and Job observed it. V, 2253. This commandment seems hard, but it has a great reward. V, 2139; VI, 1170, 1178. There is no stronger medicine for healing sins. VI, 1178. No action brought David into closer intimacy with God than love of his enemies. V, 2253. Enemies are delirious, for while they persecute us, they suffer a greater persecution from the devil. V, 2257. Enemies can be converted. V, 2252. In what manner they are to be loved. V, 1859. They are to be loved more than friends. V, 1862. It is not enough merely not to stir up the enmities of others with kindness, unless one also extinguishes them. X, 1874.

Iniquity is not a slight sin. III, 2336. It harms the person who commits it before harming the person who suffers it. X, 1870. It is better to suffer iniquity than to commit it. X, 1881. The sorrow of one who suffers injustice is better than the unjust joy of the one who commits it. X, 1876. Correction or condemnation brings iniquity to an end. X, 1864. The depth of iniquity. X, 1878. Another’s iniquity torments the just person as much as he himself departs from his own. X, 1869.

Whoever inflicts an injury bears the greater one himself. V, 2152. Injuries must be forgiven before prayer. VI, 1057. What constitutes imperfect and what constitutes complete forgiveness of them. VI, 858. Many forgive the Lord’s injuries more quickly and their own more slowly. VI, 1097. Or, on the pretext of avenging the Lord’s injuries, they avenge their own. VI, 1097.

The innocent ones were Leah’s sons, not Rachel’s. III, 2258. The innocent victims are owed to the God who was born. V, 2151. The contentious judgment of the Innocents against Herod. V, 2151. Herod benefited them more through hatred than he would have benefited them through obedience. V, 2152. The flowers of the martyrs. V, 2152. The first fruits of the martyrs. V, 2155. They are returned from their mothers’ embraces to the laps of angels. V, 2150. They were given eternal life by Christ. III, 2258; V, 2151; VIII, 1123. They confessed him through the testimony of their death. VIII, 1123. Not by speaking but by dying. V, 2154, 2155. They are rightly honored. V, 2151. They intercede more than the other martyrs. V, 2154.

Praise of innocence. VI, 1040. True innocence neither harms itself nor another. X, 1859. God does not approve innocence which love of justice does not produce. X, 1869. Simulated innocence is a twofold sin. X, 1877.

Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome. X, 1842, 1684. He reproaches John of Jerusalem for negligence in restraining the crimes of the impious. X, 1710. He writes to Jerome about that matter. X, 1711. The case of Pelagius is referred by John of Jerusalem to Pope Innocent. X, 1700. Innocent condemns Pelagius and Coelestius. X, 1682, 1683. He was the first to condemn the Pelagian heresy. X, 1723, 1724. He struck the heads of that unspeakable error with the apostolic sword. X, 1830. What reason Innocent had for condemning Pelagius. X, 1687. The Carthaginian and Milevitan synods, together with five bishops, write to Innocent against the errors of Pelagius and Coelestius. X, 1711, 1712. Innocent replies to them. X, 1714, 1715. Innocent’s letter to the Council of Carthage is cited. X, 1757, 1807. Likewise his letter to the Council of Milevis. X, 1757. Innocent wrote the decree issued against Pelagius to the Western and Eastern Churches. X, 1715. The Africans base their position on Innocent’s judgment concerning the necessity of grace for each individual act. X, 1724. Letters of Pope Innocent stating that bishops should not easily travel overseas. X, 814.

The vain pretexts of disobedience are rejected. VI, 1094.

The difference between an unwise person and a fool. VI, 892.

One Spirit inspired the prophets and apostles. VIII, 1176, 1183. The grace of inspiration. V, 1824. Everyone who acts well is inwardly inspired by God. V, 1824.

The term “insubstantial.” X, 1618.

The origin of islands, and where their animals come from. III, 2158.

What intellect is. VI, 787, 809; X, 1889. Faith opens a path for the intellect; unbelief closes it. X, 1869. The person who understands correctly what ought to be done and does it has a good understanding. X, 1860, 1861.

Intellectual vision. VI, 752. Through this the soul is never deceived. VI, 797.

The intelligible and the intellectual. VI, 729.

What intelligence is. VI, 787, 808, 809.

Intemperance is discouraged. VI, 1059.

Intention is discerned only from the end of the work. VI, 817. What it ought to be. VI, 819.

What an interjection is and how many kinds there are. I, 1408. The Greeks do not distinguish the interjection from the adverb. I, 1404.

The sweetness of the interior life. VI, 791. Its commendation. [Col. 0748] VI, 801, 804, 814, 827, 891, 922.

Envy is like rust and vipers. V, 1769. It is a devilish vice. IX, 825. A sin leading to death. V, 1979. It arises from pride. X, 1884. What it is. VI, 1089. The misery of envy. V, 1769, 2004; VI, 1055. Its remedy. VI, 1095. The envious person must be cut away like bodily decay. V, 1950. Or like a dead limb. V, 1950. A discourse on envy. VI, 1264.

Calling upon God does not imply that God is outside us. VI, 951, 970. Grace is not conferred by human invocation. X, 1785, 1786. Assistance must always be sought even by the reborn and the saints. X, 1787. Invocation of the saints. V, 2146, 2147; VI, 916, 918, 938. Saint Stephen is invoked as though he were present to the person praying. VII, 844, 846. Invocation of the martyrs for temporal benefits. V, 2161. The saints must recognize something of their own virtues in us, so that they may deign to intercede for us. V, 2159. On what condition Saint John can obtain whatever we ask. V, 2116.

John is interpreted as “the grace of God.” III, 2417. John the Baptist bore in himself the form of the Law. V, 2112, 2114. He surpassed the other prophets. V, 2112. He is the clasp between the Law and grace. V, 2117. Mediator of the New and Old Testaments. V, 2112. He is called a lamp for Christ. V, 2017. Why he is called a lamp and sent before Christ. V, 2111, 2114. He was delayed until the sense of desire had fled from his parents. V, 2117. Sanctified before he was born. V, 2112. He received the divine Spirit before the human spirit. V, 2118. While his body was delayed, by the spirit alone he fulfilled the office of an evangelist. V, 2118. The one Holy Spirit fills the hearts of the father, mother, and son. V, 2118. John was the first to recognize the Redeemer of the human race. V, 2017. He understood that the Lord’s mother had come to his own mother. VIII, 1125. He prefigured Christ in his birth and manner of life. V, 2115. The birth and passion of John and Christ are full of mystery. V, 2114, 2119. John was born from an old woman, as the end of the old Law; Christ from a young woman, as the beginning of the New Testament. III, 2193. John did not doubt, but wished to strengthen his disciples in faith when he sent them to Christ. III, 2394, 2395. Before Christ’s baptism he knew him, but because Abraham’s faith had to be fulfilled through him, he did not know him. III, 2254. John was the guardian of chastity. III, 2384. With complete and perfect freedom, he preferred to suffer injustice rather than fail to speak what was just. V, 2116. Whoever is born of a woman is inferior to John. V, 2113. John escaped the measure of human merits. V, 2115. He is greater than man. V, 2117. Whatever we ask, he will be able to obtain for us. V, 2115.

The nativity of John the Baptist is marked by a vigil among believers and unbelievers. VI, 1276. Superstitious rites at his solemnity. VI, 1172. At this feast, the custom of bathing, which arose among the pagans, is forbidden. V, 2268. In that sacrilegious bathing, bodies very frequently also died. V, 2268.

John the Apostle was chosen as a virgin; and he received the special privilege of virginity, so that he might recline on Christ’s breast. I, 1469. The Apocalypse is his. III, 2286. Written while he was exiled on the island of Patmos by Domitian. III, 2266, 2267. What Christ granted John on the cross. I, 1463.

The apology of John of Alexandria addressed to Gelasius. X, 1684.

John of Antioch is accused of having received the deposed Pelagian bishops along with the others. X, 1760.

The translation of John Chrysostom’s commentaries on Matthew was sought by a certain Annianus, a Pelagian. X, 1749. The Pelagians praise his statements as favorable to themselves. X, 1749. Nevertheless, he is acknowledged to commend the continual assistance of grace. X, 1749. A passage of his praised by the Pelagians. X, 1736. John Chrysostom opposed the Pelagians. X, 1755. John Chrysostom’s homily on the cross. V, 2047, note 6. Two other sermons by the same author—very probably—on the consolation of the dead. VI, 1161.

A work by John of Fiscannus, as is believed, addressed to Agnes, the widow of Emperor Henry. VI, 909.

John of Jerusalem. VII, 809, 813, 812, 817. How he favored Pelagius. X, 1699. Nevertheless, he agrees that Pelagius’s case should be referred to Innocent. X, 1700. He receives Orosius, who greeted him, with harsh words. X, 1700. Innocent reproaches John of Jerusalem for negligence in defending the devout and restraining the impious. X, 1710, 1711.

A booklet issued in the name of John Maxentius and his associates. X, 1771. Likewise, a letter in defense of the Scythian monks. X, 1778. He himself excerpted chapters from the books of Faustus and Augustine, whose opposition becomes apparent by comparison. X, 1779. John the presbyter and archimandrite is thought to be the same person as Maxentius. X, 1779, note (b).

John the monk and John the lector sent to Rome in the matter of the faith. X, 1772, 1776.

A Psalter attributed to Pope John. VI, 1135.

Job cannot be called by any worthy name. V, 1842. Job, a “ductile trumpet.” V, 1844. Evangelical before the evangelical precepts. II, 1103. Before the Law, he displayed in his works a model of the Law. III, 2361. His eulogy. III, 2361. Why Job was handed over to the devil. V, 1739. He was afflicted for the cleansing of minor sins. V, 1844. Job’s patience is praised. V, 1813. In the dung he was better than Adam in paradise. V, 1844. His wife was an Eve to him, but he was not an Adam. V, 1813, 1844. He had learned to forget his wife in his children. V, 1841. When his limbs were endangered, Job preserved his breast for the author of the wounds. V, 1841. Justice, remaining unharmed, guarded him in his shipwrecked body. V, 1841. Job was victorious over the devil both in prosperity and adversity. V, 1842. In himself he showed that the rich can be good and the poor blessed. V, 1842. Cassian attempts to prove the strength of free will by Job’s example. X, 1820. How futilely. X, 1823. The Latin version of the words of Job from the Greek Septuagint, and another from the Hebrew. X, 1652.

Jonah is reported by the Hebrews to have been the son of the woman of Zarephath whom Elijah raised from the dead. III, 2181.

The Jordan was consecrated by Christ’s baptism. V, 1812, 1833.

Joseph is interpreted as “increase.” V, 1766. Joseph is a figure of Christ. V, 1924. In how many ways he prefigured Christ. V, 1765, 1773. What he saw in a dream was fulfilled in Christ alone. V, 1766. The translations do not agree on the price for which he was sold. V, 1765. Though sold, he did not know a servile spirit. V, 1768. Why Joseph did not make known to his father what had happened to him. V, 1770. Joseph’s kindness. V, 1769. Foreseeing that the Egyptians would worship him, Joseph ordered that his bones be carried away from there. III, 2163. Nevertheless, when an image of an ox had been set up beside his tomb, they worshiped him. III, 2163. For this reason the children of Israel cast a calf for themselves in the desert. III, 2163.

Joseph is incorrectly said to have had two fathers. III, 2252. He is of royal and priestly descent. V, 2110. His disturbance when he saw his betrothed pregnant is explained. V, 2108. Joseph survived Christ’s resurrection. V, 1766, note (a).

Joseph of Arimathea’s affection for Christ was no less than Mary’s. V, 2204. Joseph places the Lord in the monument of his heart. V, 2205.

Joshua was formerly called Auses. III, 2273.

Thursday should not be spent idly by anyone, even in May, apart from holy festivals. VI, 1172.

Jovinian equates virginity with marriage. VIII, 1219. He believes that those who abstain from wine and meat gain no increase of merit. VIII, 1219. He wishes there to be no distinction of merits in the future. V, 2183; X, 1718. He asserts that a human being cannot sin. V, 2183; X, 1718. That is, after baptism. X, 1735. Jovinian’s second question is a product of Pelagian ingenuity. X, 1693, 1696, 1697, 1706.

Iphidamia. VIII, 1150.

What anger is. VI, 1089. No one thinks his own anger unjust. X, 1887. The futile pretexts of anger. VI, 1096. Its stages. VI, 1251. Its effects. VI, 1251. Anger harms those who will cause harm before it harms those who will be harmed. V, 2301. The flames of anger are kindled by false suspicions. V, 2346. Sudden anger is straw; long-standing anger, a beam. V, 1872. Anger disturbs the eye of the heart; hatred blinds it. V, 1872. The saints did not act to satisfy anger when they exacted punishments from the impious. V, 2262, 2263. What the anger of God is. X, 1872.

Irenaeus hopes for what pertains to food and drink after this life. VIII, 1818.

The rainbow is produced not only by the sun but sometimes also by the moon. III, 2157. The rainbow bears the type of the incarnate Word. III, 2419.

Irregularity with respect to the clerical state. See Cleric.

Isaac bore the type of God the Father. V, 1760, 1818. And also of Christ. V, 1758, 1818. Of Christ suffering voluntarily. V, 1954.

Jesse bore the type of God the Father. V, 1818.

The son of Isaiah, Rabshakeh. III, 2187.

Isidore of Hispalis. V, 2130.

Isera. X, 1792.

Isis. III, 2343.

By what right the Israelites obtained the land of Canaan. V, 1811. Their ungrateful attitude toward God’s benefits. V, 1797.

Superstitious observances of travelers, opposed to pious practices. V, 2001, 2002, 2269.

Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise.” III, 2201. Judah’s final blessing applies to Christ. III, 2203.

Judah prefigured Gehazi. V, 1832. Incest is attributed to Judah, and health was miraculously restored to his father and mother. VI, 1285. Judah’s hardening. V, 2036. The Lord gave him his body. III, 2311; VI, 1285; IX, 766. And washed his feet. VI, 1285. Judas was the severest judge of himself. V, 1901. He could not bear the new wine of the Holy Spirit, and therefore burst. VI, 1069. On what day or at what time he ended his life is uncertain. III, 2288.

The Jews were named from Judas Maccabaeus. III, 2274. They are called the sons of the legislators. VI, 974. A person is made a Jew by birth, not by circumcision. III, 2274. Cain is the father of the Jews. III, 2282, 2298. The Jews were prefigured in Jacob’s final words to Reuben. III, 2203. And also in Esau. V, 1758. How they serve Christians. VI, 1758. The Jews’ efforts against Christ were signified by Jacob’s wrestling. V, 1758. The Jewish people are thorny. V, 1779. Figures of their unbelief and weakness. V, 1750. A figure of the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles. V, 1821. An excellent figure of Jews and Christians. V, 1800. Another. V, 1801, 1814. Leprosy clung to the Jews when grace passed over to us. V, 1833. Gideon’s fleece as a figure of the Jews. V, 1817, 1818. The solemnities of the Jews. III, 2276. Why they were commanded to make vows or sacrifices in only one place. V, 2048. From the beginning of Judaism, no Gentile who came forward was forbidden to join himself to the Law. III, 2240.

The Jews are ready to read, blind to understand, and hard to believe. V, 2008. They sinned against the Holy Spirit. III, 2307. Their madness in Christ’s passion. V, 1827. Punished through Titus and Vespasian. V, 1827. How many were then killed and how many taken captive. V, 1827. The Jews were dispersed throughout the world so that, like wooden lampstands, they might supply the Gentiles with the lamp of the Law. VIII, 1128. The Jewish race is the archivist of the Christians. VI, 751. Our codex is preserved in a Jew’s archive. VIII, 1113. Laws against the Jews. IX, 815. Valentinian denies Jews permission to bring lawsuits, serve in the army, or hold Christians in their service. X, 1751. There is no access for them to the rank of count, the senate, the prefecture, military service, or the tables of the rich. VIII, 1133. In one town of Minorca they are not permitted to live with impunity. VII, 822. The Jews wish to acknowledge one God, but not a triune God. VI, 974. They are convicted by many testimonies concerning the truth and divinity of Christ. VIII, 1123. Likewise concerning the truth of the Church. VIII, 1132, 1133. The remarkable conversion of the Jews in the town of Magona. VII, 824.

A judge who presides over a province. IX, 813. At the Carthaginian conference, Flavius the tribune sits as judge in the foremost place. IX, 817, 818. Among those by whom, as he admits, he ought to have been judged. IX, 816, 819. African judges. IX, 808, 809, 810, 813.

What is proper for judges. VI, 1297. Mercy and discipline should not be separated in a judge. V, 2328. For a judge, this is the security of faith: not to fear being judged himself. IX, 820. The absent and unheard should not be condemned. X, 1735. The accusations of absent witnesses against absent persons should not readily be accepted. X, 1720, 1722. It is more tolerable for an innocent person to be discovered later than for an innocent person to be quickly condemned as guilty. X, 1772. He was never reluctant to turn a judgment toward the better. X, 1720. It is a sign of the best mind to believe wrong things with greater difficulty. X, 1720. The moderation of secular judgments teaches what ecclesiastical judgments ought to be. X, 1722. Judges may not revoke a sentence pronounced against the accused. III, 2352. The banditry of judges. VI, 1292, 1297. Many unjust judges here received the punishments with which they had unjustly afflicted others. VI, 1035. Why judgments were formerly held at the gate. VI, 1231. Bringing or hearing cases is forbidden on feast days. V, 2275.

One judgment concerns discernment, another condemnation. V, 1925. Open evils should be judged, not unknown or doubtful ones. V, 1871, 1873. Open evils ought to be judged, but with charity. V, 1871. It is better to judge well concerning the wicked than badly concerning the good. V, 1871. To judge the good always badly is naturally implanted in the common people. VI, 1221. To judge rashly about the hidden matters of another’s heart is a sin. X, 1861. Rash judgment is no small sin, even though it is a common one. V, 1873. A brave man despises popular judgment in the light of conscience. X, 1863. We ought not to be moved by the judgments of others, since we cannot judge of ourselves—not to say what we shall be tomorrow, but even what we are today. V, 2350.

How deep are God’s judgments. VI, 887. They are always just. X, 1885. They are generally hidden, but never unjust. V, 1771, 1788, 2262. We are not to investigate them. X, 1658, 1660, 1663. Both the mercy by which God freely liberates and the truth by which he judges justly are unsearchable. X, 1887. God commands us not to examine his judgments but to believe them. V, 2192.

The distinction between an earthly and a heavenly judge. V, 2050. Angels lead the souls of the saints to worship the true Judge. VI, 1061. The soul departing from here is brought by angels before the awe-inspiring Judge. VI, 1183. Sinners are judged unjustly if they did not sin freely. VIII, 1142.

Because the day of judgment is unknown, it is called midnight. V, 1892. How Christ can say that he does not know the day of judgment. III, 2410. How Christ is understood as Judge of the living and the dead. V, 1805. On the day of judgment, those who are then alive will be caught up together with the resurrected dead in the clouds to meet Christ. VI, 1161. It is consistent with reason that there will be a final judgment. III, 2219. One judgment was through water in the Flood; another will be through fire at the end of the age. III, 2419, 2422. The fire of judgment is the arbiter. V, 1772. The blazing furnace seen by Abraham is a figure of the final judgment. V, 1746. How just is the severity of judgment. V, 1803. The basis of our judgment lies in our own power. V, 2139, 2162, 2252, 2259, 2260, 2329. From this will come either our condemnation or our crown. X, 1869. The sentence of the future Judge must be anticipated. V, 2221. How we ought to forestall the day of judgment. V, 1846. The day of judgment should be frequently recalled. VI, 1169. Caesarius frequently preaches this. V, 2206. The reading of Matthew 25, in which judgment is discussed, is sufficient by itself to make one flee every evil and do every good. V, 1897. Forgetfulness of the future judgment is a great punishment for sin. V, 2045. How great will be the terror of the final judgment, and how exact its examination. V, 1893. What its basis will be, and how useful daily remembrance of it is. V, 1963, 1964. Consideration of the final judgment. VI, 1185.

Judgment will not begin immediately after the death of Antichrist. VI, 1134. Concerning the lot of sinners on the day of judgment: the differing opinions of Pelagius, Origen, and Jerome. X, 1704. The threefold lot of those to be judged. V, 1949. What the judgment will be concerning the impious, sinners, and righteous. III, 2332, 2333. Sinners will not be able to endure the Lord’s face. III, 2333. The city of Jerusalem descends from heaven at the Lord’s coming. III, 2333. Pagans, heretics, and Jews do not come to judgment. V, 1896. The faithful will not be subjected to judgment in order to receive a sentence, but so that they may be praised for the merit of faith. III, 2376. The faithless will see the glory of the faithful, just as the faithful will see the torments of the faithless. III, 2376. Even infants will come to God’s judgment. X, 1652. How the devil will accuse the guilty on the day of judgment. VI, 1072. Good and evil works are to be placed on a balance, as it were, in the judgment. VI, 1202. Sinners must act so that on the day of judgment, even if they do not deserve to receive a crown, they may at least obtain forgiveness of sins. V, 1835, 2340. Three sermons on the final judgment. V, 2206.

“To lay the necks down,” meaning “to subject to the yoke.” VII, 846.

Everyone is subject either to the yoke of Christ or to that of the world. V, 1800. Christ’s yoke is light. V, 2316. The light yoke is charity. X, 1651. The heavy yoke is sin. X, 1650. The yoke of avarice is most harsh and bitter. V, 2317.

Juliana, wife of Alexander the senator. VII, 819.

Juliana and her eulogy. X, 1738.

Julian, prefect of the praetorian guard. IX, 790.

Julian, proconsul of Africa. IX, 805, 844.

By an edict Julian granted women the power to dismiss their husbands. III, 2349. In the city of Rome. III, 2349. Everywhere, by his edicts, he testified that he was an apostate. IX, 802. From a servant of God he became a minister of the enemy. IX, 802. When asked by the Donatists, he permitted their return from exile. IX, 803. The profane and sacrilegious emperor died. IX, 803. His rescript obtained through the Donatists. IX, 809.

Julianus Hamartolus. X, 1790.

Julian. X, 1681.

Julian of Campania. X, 1857. Born of devout parents, Memorius and Juliana. X, 1738. A man vigorous in intellect, learned in the divine Scriptures, and scholastic in Greek and Latin. X, 1736. He is a most accomplished rhetorician. X, 1740. Extremely insolent. X, 1830. Mercator calls him the former bishop of Eclanum. X, 1739. Bede calls him the bishop of Celanum from Romania. X, 1740. He wrote on the Song of Songs. X, 1740. He composed a booklet on love. X, 1740. Likewise, one on the good of constancy. X, 1745. Likewise, to Demetrias, on the education of a virgin. X, 1745. His style has the sweetness of pleasing eloquence. X, 1746. His books would contain much that could benefit those devoted to virtue, if only he taught them in those books to implore grace. X, 1746.

Julian was ordained by Innocent and remained in his communion as long as he lived; he condemned Coelestius and Pelagius. X, 1689. He became a follower of Pelagius and Coelestius. X, 1684, 1686. Refusing with others to subscribe to Zosimus’s *tractoria*, he was deposed. X, 1689. He is warned to identify by name those whom he believes to hold the correct view. X, 1690. Many defect from him and his associates. X, 1691. Julian’s complaint before the emperor after being expelled from the West. X, 1754. Julian’s deposition is confirmed. X, 1760. Having attempted to insinuate himself into the episcopate and communion of the Church, he is rejected by Sixtus at Leo’s urging. X, 1761. He instructed two sisters in his errors; what one of them charged against him. X, 1738. Alms distributed to the needy during a famine attached many people to his heresy. X, 1737. He defends the Pelagian chapters; hence Augustine’s books against him and his own against Augustine. X, 1737. He filled his parchments more with insults and abuse than with any sound argument of faith. X, 1737. The entire substance of that foolish labor of his. X, 1737. Marius Mercator also replied to him with annotations. X, 1737. When summoned to condemn Pelagius and Caelestius together with the universal Church, Julian refuses. X, 1738. He also sends a letter to Zosimus, which he first arranges to have circulated throughout Italy. X, 1739. With what deceptive meaning he declares that all die in Adam and all rise again in Christ. X, 1738, 1739. Or how he says that Adam harmed not himself alone but the human race. X, 1738. How he understands that infants are not in the state in which Adam was before his transgression. X, 1738. He admits that Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin, but says this without any firm reasoning. X, 1738. By what sophistries he proceeded at Rome to diminish the transmission of sin from Adam. X, 1739. He spreads his errors in Cilicia. X, 1739. He goes there to Theodore of Mopsuestia. X, 1739. Returning from there, he writes eight books against Augustine. X, 1740. Theodore, whom he praises most highly, condemns him at an assembly of bishops. X, 1740. Julian’s opinions, extracted by Bede from his brief works, together with their refutation. X, 1740. A booklet of faith apparently written by Julian. X, 1732.

Excerpts from Julian Pomerius. VI, 1050.

Julius, bishop, sent to Innocent by the African councils. X, 1714.

Why Junius was called Brutus. III, 2357.

Junius Quartus, consul. X, 1714, 1715. See Palladius.

Junius, registrar. IX, 794.

A sermon by Ivo of Chartres. V, 2200.

The Savior forbade swearing. III, 2411. The formula for swearing. IX, 783. Another. IX, 784. Yet another. IX, 818.

The right of the soul and of the flesh. V, 1916. By the law of the forum, not by the law of heaven. V, 2293.

The grace of justification. III, 2370. Which works are excluded from justification. X, 1633. No one can be justified by the resources of natural reason alone or by knowledge of the divine Law. X, 1743. How heretics slander Catholics on this point. X, 1743. Justification through faith in Jesus Christ has been given, is given, and will be given to believers. X, 1637. God does not await our will but prepares it, so that we may be cleansed from sin. X, 1786. God justifies the ungodly without being anticipated by human will. X, 1659. In justifying, God freely anticipates those whom he intends to glorify through righteousness. VI, 765, 767. The righteous of the Old Testament were justified through their own labor and faith in Christ. X, 1734.

Justice, in the sense of the power to administer law. II, 1138. Justice derives from administering law between two opposing parties. V, 1916. Justice is the teacher and governor of human beings. III, 2327. It is God’s work. III, 2327. When justice is removed, kingdoms become banditries. VI, 1292. Through the rigor of justice, as by an iron rod, the good are corrected and the wicked broken. III, 2421. Excessive justice incurs sin, but tempered justice makes people perfect. III, 2226. God’s justice is hateful to the unjust, like light to diseased eyes. X, 1874.

The beauty of justice. VI, 994. The praise of justice and how it is to be maintained. VI, 1258. The commandment of justice is general for everyone. II, 1105, 1106. Justice alone can make the soul blessed. VI, 830. Justice produces peace, and peace produces joy. V, 1917. Justice has always pleased God, and injustice offended him. VI, 1037. When justice does not reign in us, iniquity rules. X, 1818. Whoever wishes to learn justice hungers for justice. V, 2317. Justice is nothing other than not sinning. V, 1863. All this is justice: virginity, priesthood, and martyrdom. III, 2154. Justice is the whole of truth. III, 2232. True and perfect justice. V, 1915. Justice exists neither by nature nor by the Law. X, 1887. The justice of unbelievers is false. X, 1796. The justice of the Law is earthly; the justice of faith is divine. III, 2412. True justice exists only through Christ. X, 1796. Sin was made by abandoning God; justice is not made without God. X, 1880. Abel was the first in justice, and Enoch second after him. III, 2154. What our justice is like here. X, 1873. How true justice is perfect and imperfect in certain people. X, 1886. The twofold function of justice. VI, 1050; X, 1867. That justice is lost by many. X, 1834, 1836, 1848.

Whence the righteous are so called in Scripture. X, 1695. One cannot be just toward others if one is unjust toward oneself. V, 1916. One just person is dearer to God than many sinners. VI, 1037. Pelagius wishes there to be many righteous and perfect people. X, 1702, 1705, 1706, 1707. In what sense this may be said. X, 1705. The righteous crown Christ, but are adorned by him. V, 2058. How a righteous person can be his own accuser and yet be righteous. III, 2232. Just as the righteous are not without minor sins, so they need to be cleansed through tribulation. V, 1771. The minor sins of the righteous are cleansed through tribulation. V, 1771, 1844. The affliction of the righteous is not punishment for a crime but a test of virtue. X, 1863. The rewards and labors of the righteous. VI, 1065. The great labor of the righteous is to endure contrary dispositions. X, 1869.

To make a heifer. V, 2004.

## K

Keayea. VII, 815.

The Kalends. See January.

## L

Laban bore the type of the devil. V, 1763.

Honest labor consists in reading. V, 2324.

By what harm monks may be occupied with manual labor more than usual. V, 2334. The labor of the devout is exercise, not condemnation. X, 1882. No labor here is comparable with our hope. X, 1881. Or with the labors of Christ. X, 1882. There will be no end to labor unless what cannot be taken away is loved. X, 1870.

Whence false tears arise. III, 2161. Whoever sheds tears over temporal things but does not shed them over sins is culpably hard-hearted. VI, 1122. Tears are signs of love. VI, 930. Their continual grace is earnestly requested. VI, 931, 935. What tears of contemplatives accomplish for them. VI, 1000. The Lord’s tears are the joys of the world. V, 1928. Tears are a substitute for Christ’s passion. VI, 1254.

Lactantius hopes for what pertains to food and drink after this life. VIII, 1218.

Whence foolish joy should be restrained. VI, 1101. See Joy.

Laetus, registrar. IX, 810.

The excuse of the laity when they are urged to study the Scriptures or to attend churches frequently. VI, 1060. It is equally appropriate for laypeople, clerics, and monks to preserve faith, hope, charity, and humility, and to practice repentance. VI, 1061.

Lamech did not kill Cain. VI, 2221.

Lampadius, bishop. IX, 787.

Lampadius, consul. X, 1792.

What wool and flax signify. V, 1854.

Landuleus of Capua, bishop. VI, 817.

Stones from water. III, 2169. A heap of stones as a testimony of mourning. VII, 815.

“A stoned deacon,” meaning “a degraded deacon.” IX, 795, 796.

Masked persons. See Persons in masks.

Licentiousness is always joined to satiety. V, 2026.

The thief who, hanging on Christ’s right at the cross, merited paradise is said to have rescued Christ himself from thieves when he was fleeing into Egypt. I, 1466. Thief and thief. V, 2049. The thief blasphemed Christ from his own standpoint but believed in the Spirit of God. X, 1810. He was the first after Adam to enter paradise. V, 2044, 2049. The thief’s absolution is the hope and consolation of the world. V, 2043. He did not merit it without cause. V, 2044. The thief’s faith is extolled. V, 2044, 2046, 2049, 2054. The thief was confessor and martyr. V, 2044. A teacher. V, 2049, 2050. The thief’s devotion is to be imitated. V, 2070. The thief’s example should not become an occasion for a more lax life. V, 2046.

### Intellectual freedom

Human freedom. V, 1873, 1875, 1878. It is proved by the commands given to humanity and by the punishments inflicted for neglecting those commands. VIII, 1142. Likewise, by the future judgment. God does not take away the possibility of good from the sinner; the sinner himself takes it away from himself. X, 1848. Adam sold his own freedom and ours. V, 1944. Christ restored to us the condition of our former freedom. X, 1758. The author of restored freedom must be followed. X, 1770. True freedom. VI, 732.

### Free will

What free will is, and from where the term derives. X, 1623. It is the spontaneous desire for something pleasing to oneself. X, 1813. The capacity of free will produces different degrees of participation in the Word of God. VIII, 1190.

How the free will of the first human being was fashioned. V, 2214. What it could do before the fall. X, 1771, 1773. Before guilt, the first ancestor alone was sufficient, through free will, to accomplish whatever he wished. X, 1621. At that time he possessed the good of possibility. X, 1621, 1623. But through guilt he lost it. X, 1621, 1623, 1628, 1629. In the first human being it became clear what human free will could accomplish with regard to death. X, 1880.

Free will, sound in Adam and weak in us, is strengthened by greater grace. X, 1783. The free will of the first human being was injured by sin. X, 1813. It was corrupted and weakened. X, 1786. What remains in us is wounded and lame. X, 1621, 1828. It needs the medicine of gratuitous grace. X, 1622. To what extent it was bent and weakened. X, 1789. When free will is corrupted, a human being is by himself able neither to begin nor to complete anything pleasing to God. X, 1625, 1631. A human being can fall by himself, but cannot rise again by himself. X, 1622. He has ample ability of his own for sinning, but is not sufficient for doing good unless he is justified by God. X, 1869. By free will alone a human being cannot overcome the desires of the flesh. X, 1615. It is necessary that, by the help of the one through whom we conquer, we should again be overcome if he does not help us. X, 1757. Free will is now capable of discerning and desiring what belongs to the world, but not what belongs to God. X, 1623, 1772. Without grace it is in no way fit to choose or desire the good. X, 1812. When God abandons it, it can do nothing toward virtue; for sin it is sufficient unto itself. X, 1671, 1672, 1673, 1675. It is useless to object: “God should not be believed to have made such a human being, one who neither ever wishes nor is able to do good.” X, 1813. Free will does not possess within itself the capacity to recover what it lost. X, 1840. What was lost in the first human being cannot be restored except by the one from whom it could have been given. X, 1787.

How Manichaeus and Jovinianus abolish free will. V, 2183. How Pelagius professes it. V, 2183. The exaltation of free will. II, 1104. No other cause makes doing good difficult for us than the long habit of vices. II, 1104. Julianus vainly exalts free will. X, 1745. He subjects all movements of the mind to it, except sexual pleasure alone. X, 1745. Cassianus attributes to free will not only the will but also the possibility of good. X, 1815. And he denies that only what is evil should be attributed to it. X, 1815. How the same Cassianus attempts to establish the strength of free will by the example of Job. X, 1821. How empty this is. X, 1823. The powers of free will without grace are vainly commended by the example of Cornelius. [Col. 0756] X, 1796. Where Gennadius places the weakness and strength of free will. VI, 814; VIII, 1216, 1218.

It is wrongly said that free will is nothing or does not exist. X, 1836, 1841. Whoever denies free will is not a Catholic. X, 1631. That a human being acts by the free choice of the will, and not by some necessity of nature, is shown by the law that was given. III, 2347. By the praise of the good and the blame of the wicked. III, 2317. By their reward and punishment. III, 2318. By the fact that no one is always good or always wicked. III, 2318. Likewise, by the fact that whoever acts against the law seeks hiding places. III, 2318. By the judgment of the will, through which many have turned from vices to righteousness. III, 2318. By the subjection of demons and the commendation of prayer. III, 2358. By those things that Christ entrusted to human faith. III, 2358. Free will is established by the struggle against desire. III, 2409. An example of free will in Balaam. V, 1810. Each person subjects himself to evil by free will, and nature does not compel him to it. VI, 1126. Each person can freely retain grace and, by retaining it, avoid guilt. VI, 1126. It is within human power to consent to the devil. V, 2213. God commands on the right, the devil deceives on the left, and the human being is placed in the middle. V, 2213.

Free will remains in nature, but its quality and condition are changed through Christ. X, 1827. What it is before being enlightened and liberated, and what it is afterward. X, 1836. Before grace it exists in the human being, but it is not good. X, 1780. Without grace it is like an eye without light. X, 1780. Just as the eye always needs light in order to see, so the human being needs grace for goodness. X, 1780. Free will is compared with an animal, and grace with its rider. X, 1632. Thus free will and grace complete the journey of faith together. X, 1632. To be able to have faith or charity belongs to human nature; to possess them belongs to the grace of the faithful. X, 1887. Free will obeys the exhortation of the one who calls when God’s grace has produced in it the inclination to believe and obey. X, 1796. When it has received the Spirit of the Lord, it will possess freedom to undertake the commandments. X, 1630. How the case of one who believes differs from that of one who does not believe. X, 1630. We therefore say that free will, through the operation of grace, conceives an inclination toward good will and the beginning of faith, so that through these gifts—which were granted to it without any preceding merit—it may merit those things that have been promised to the one who will act; always asking from the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing,” for the ability to do some good. X, 1821. Which works of free will are approved for justification, and which are rejected. X, 1636. God works in free will in such a way that every movement of a good will comes from God. X, 1758, 1759.

They foolishly say that through grace nothing remains to free will. X, 1800. The will is free even if it needs divine help. X, 1709, 1710. How it is not taken away by God’s gifts. X, 1804, 1827. How God’s assistance does not hinder it. X, 1731. Free will is not taken away by God’s gift, but liberated. X, 1759, 1776, 1797. By God’s grace it truly becomes free. X, 1712. The will is not taken away when it is formed, governed, ordered, and imbued by the Spirit of God. X, 1809. Why. X, 1811. Those destroy free will who abuse it against the beneficence of the giver, not those who always turn back to him. X, 1694.

The proper use of free will. VII, 732. No one uses it well except through Christ. X, 1757. Free will can do nothing better than commend itself to the one who cannot do evil. X, 1886. Our free will is healed and restored by Christ’s wound. X, 1623. How. X, 1623. Even once liberated, it is not sufficient for itself to remain in the good. X, 1797, 1798. It does not yet enjoy such perfect health that it does not need the help of its physician. X, 1800. It needs Christ’s grace to preserve it by acting, breathing, helping, and leading it all the way to the end. X, 1801. So that Peter might not appear to stand by free will, although he had made great promises about himself, he was permitted to be put to the test. X, 1798. The supports of the human will are the aids of divine grace. X, 1827.

### Sexual desire

“Libido” derives from *libendo*, “to take pleasure.” X, 1640. In a good inclination it cannot be called *libido*, but only in a bad one. X, 1640. For the Pelagians, sexual desire is a natural good, and there is nothing shameful in it. X, 1639. They openly praise it. X, 1640, 1644, 1648. To what extent it ought to be called and considered a natural evil. X, 1641. It is proved to be evil from the words of the Apostle. X, 1646. “If sexual desire is condemned,” the Pelagians say, “marriage too will be condemned.” X, 1644. Among married people who use an evil rightly, sexual desire is venial. X, 1645, 1646. Among adulterers and fornicators who use an evil wrongly, it is condemnable. X, 1646. The author of sexual desire is not God but the devil, after the prior sin of the human being. X, 1648. If he had not sinned, human beings would have been begotten from human beings without sexual desire, through voluntary intercourse. X, 1646. Parents transmitted sexual desire to their descendants by hereditary right, as a testimony to their sin. X, 1645. What a human being suffers from sexual desire. X, 1641. Sexual desire can be called the hammer of the whole earth. V, 2302. How it drags a human being to death unless the antidote of grace comes to his aid. X, 1639. Sexual desire conceives pain, [Col. 0757] gives birth to sin, and generates death. X, 1644. How foolish it is to satisfy sexual desire with the hope of repentance. V, 2302.

How the incentives of sexual desire are to be resisted. I, 1459, 1460. The solitary will cannot restrain it unless Christ’s grace comes to its aid. X, 1647. All the saints fought against sexual desire, relying on grace and chastising their bodies. X, 1641. Sexual desire must be conquered by fleeing. V, 2301. Lustful thoughts must be rejected without delay. V, 2345. That sexual desire does no harm if dealt with immediately, but that after delay it cannot be shaken off without injury, is shown by the example of burning coals. V, 2303. The fear of those who worry that bodily mortification may cause them to fall into weakness is empty. I, 1461. No medicine is as effective against sexual desire as the death of the Redeemer. VI, 961.

The Magi are the firstfruits of the Gentiles. V, 2005, 2008. They came from the farthest part of Ethiopia. V, 2150. They are called kings. VI, 1318. Three kings. V, 2018. The Magi observed the course of the stars without evil intent. III, 2258. Having received a tradition from Balaam, they understood that the king of the Jews had been born. III, 2258. ### Evil

Evil is not a nature or substance. VI, 1018; VIII, 1142; X, 1874, 1878. It is either sin or punishment. VIII, 1142. We call people evil by nature because we are born in sin. VIII, 1142. V, 1737. The one who loves is not evil, nor what he loves, nor the love by which he loves, but the fact that he loves wrongly. VI, 845. ### Manichaeus

Manichaeus arose outside the Church. IX, 766. He boasts that he is the genius of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1146. His book is called *The Treasury*. VIII, 1141, 1143. It is a treasury of every indecency. VIII, 1149. The *Epistle of the Foundation*. VIII, 1141, 1147. It is the source of all vain fables. Manichaeus says that there are two natures: one good, which made the world, and another evil, from which the world was made. VIII, 1153. He introduces a prince of the race of darkness, equally opposed to God and uncreated. VIII, 1141. If he is uncreated, the nature of evil is in many respects shared with God. VIII, 1141. Manichaeus says that the kingdoms of God cannot be shaken, yet introduces a God who fears that they may be shaken. VIII, 1143. He says that a part of God’s substance was given out, and that, having been mixed throughout all bodies, it cannot be wholly recalled. VIII, 1143, 1144. How shameful and disgraceful are the methods he devises for liberating this part. VIII, 1144. This part is in calamities, captivity, and subjection. VIII, 1144, 1147. God is in mourning. VIII, 1143, 1144. His God has been swallowed up and mixed by necessity into his own substance; part of him is held there, and part will always be held in the globe. VIII, 1148. This is refuted. VIII, 1153.

Manichaeus does not know that Christ came in the flesh. III, 2267. He says that if Christ had flesh, the woman was not a virgin; and if a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom. V, 2197. This is refuted. V, 2197. He says that the prince of darkness, together with his companions, suffered and was crucified by the Jews. VIII, 1147. He says that Christ is born, suffers, and dies every day in pumpkins, leeks, and similar plants. VIII, 1148. In this way he wishes human beings to be freed from sins now through the sufferings of demons, now through the sufferings of vegetables. VIII, 1148. He says that the part of God in the fruits and herbs of the earth knows its beginning, middle, and end, but that in the flesh it is foolish; therefore a teacher was sent to human beings, not to melons. VIII, 1149. His disciples say that the souls of pigs are of the same kind as human souls. VIII, 1149. Manichaeus taught that our flesh was composed of good and evil. VIII, 1220. He condemns first marriages. V, 2183. He closes the entrance to marriage and encourages indiscriminate intercourse. III, 2266, 2267. He says that a human being cannot avoid sin. V, 2183. He says that his Elect cannot sin even if they wish to. X, 1693. His opinion concerning free will is rejected. X, 1623.

The two principles of the Manichaeans. X, 1735. Manichaeus could not avoid admitting that souls sinned by their own will. VIII, 1141.

Manichaeus the Irishman. III, 2176.

The Manichaeans take pleasure in being called by this name. III, 2381. They seem to affirm nonexistent things in place of existent things, consequences in place of principles, and common things in place of contraries. VIII, 1170. They make God corruptible, timid, full of ignorance, cruel, evil, rash, and so forth. VIII, 1152. The Catholic faith is opposed to this. VIII, 1152. The Manichaeans say that God could not create the world except by necessity and with the assistance of uncreated matter. VIII, 1151. They assert two principles, and say that the soul is from the good and the flesh from the evil. X, 1735. The Manichaeans maintain that the soul is from God’s substance. VIII, 1207. They call themselves omnipotent gods when they claim that their souls are parts of God. VIII, 1146, 1153. They say that the human being was made by Satan, but not this world. III, 2218. They deny that the will of the soul can be liberated. VIII, 1142. [Col. 0760] They attribute sins to the race of darkness. V, 2213, 2214. How absurdly they say, “We do not sin; we are souls of light.” VIII, 1154. How absurdly they teach that sinful souls are condemned to guard the globe, so that security may be provided for the divine kingdom. VIII, 1151, 1154. They alone bend the knee. VIII, 1146. When they consider him to be Christ. VIII, 1120. They wish Christ to be God alone, not human. V, 1855. Why. VIII, 1101. They say that Christ had a body just as angels did when they appeared. VIII, 1145. Their fear that he might have been defiled in the Virgin’s womb is refuted. VIII, 1146. The Manichaeans deny the resurrection of the flesh. VIII, 1151. How they explain the liberation of souls. III, 2381. It is demonstrated to them that the flesh is God’s work, not the devil’s. V, 1937. The Manichaeans condemn marriage and believe that foods are evil or the cause of evil. VIII, 1219. By condemning marriage, they secretly devote themselves to impurity. III, 2381. This was exposed by imperial edicts. III, 2381. Marriage is defended against them. III, 2379. The Manichaeans deny that alms should be given to the wicked; why. VI, 1227. How they lend authority to falsehood. VIII, 1150. They abuse passages in which God is said not to know. V, 1749. They accept or reject the Scriptures as they please. VIII, 1145. They accept the New, not the Old, Testament. VIII, 1106. In vain. VIII, 1106. They assert that the New Testament, not the Old, can be understood figuratively. VIII, 1150. Merits of one’s own, without grace, may possess leprosy, not health. V, 1833. God’s grace precedes all human merits. X, 1757, 1759, 1775, 1781, 1788, 1885. Nor are things given on account of human merits, as the Pelagians wish. X, 1625. God loves us as we shall be through his gift, not as we are through our own merit. X, 1787, 1864. Without any preceding merit, a person receives the gift by which he may acquire merit. X, 1836. All merits begin from faith. X, 1850. Merits arise from grace; grace itself does not arise from merits. X, 1826. All the merits of the saints are to be referred to God’s glory. X, 1757, 1775, 1808. All the merit of the saints throughout their earthly life was grace. X, 1637. My merit is the death of Christ; the Lord’s mercy. VI, 961. God is so good that he wills our merits to be his merits, and for what he has bestowed he will bestow eternal rewards. X, 1759. A reward is owed to good works. X, 1788, 1885. But grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be done. X, 1885. Jovinianus says that there will be no distinction of merits in the future. X, 1718. The merits of the same works are different in different people. III, 2372.

Merocles, from Milan. IX, 779, 787.

If “mine” and “yours” were removed, human life would be peaceful. VI, 1238.

Miccius, a secretary. IX, 781.

Migelius, a monk. VII, 815, 816.

Miggines, a gravedigger. IX, 794.

The term “military service” embraces several things. V, 1905. The earthly and spiritual soldier are compared. VI, 1054. The difference between worldly and Christian military service. V, 2159. How unbecoming it is for a soldier to be a slave to sexual impurity. V, 2294. A Christian’s military service ought first of all to be one of honor. V, 1904. The ornaments of an earthly soldier. VI, 1050, 1054. The common excuse of soldiers for their sins, and how empty it is. V, 1904. Just military service. V, 1879. Valentinian denies Jews and pagans permission to sacrifice. X, 1751.

The prison at Mileum. IX, 773.

The Council of Milevis in the year 416. It writes to Innocent against the heresy of Pelagius. X, 1712. In imitation of the Church and province of Carthage. X, 1712. Innocent writes back to it. X, 1714.

The teaching of the Millenarians and of those who approach them closely. VIII, 1218.

Miltiades, bishop of the city of Rome. IX, 778, 779.

The ministers of God are good for every good, while evil men are ministers of the devil for every evil. V, 1775. Whoever considers merit necessary in God’s ministers does an injury to God’s gift. III, 2312.

The situation, size, and towns of the island of Minorca. VII, 821.

“Minute,” used improperly for “small.” I, 1412. A diminished people. IX, 799.

Miracles are not contrary to nature. X, 1883. The distinction between true and magical miracles. VI, 726. Some miracles are visible, others invisible. X, 1870. Only those whom they benefit see the miracles of God. X, 1868. Miracles make a person famous, not holy. VIII, 1221. They were even performed by sinners. VIII, 1221. That wonders were performed through the Apostles was due to the grace of the time, not of the persons. III, 2288. These were seeds of faith. III, 2288. Miracles require not example or reason, but faith. V, 2072. The miracle of the Eucharist thrown to dogs. IX, 804. And of a flask of chrism thrown through a window. IX, 804. The greatest miracle is the conversion of a sinner. V, 1919.

Miserable are those who either do not have what they want or have what they do not rightly want. X, 1864. The misery of humanity is common to all, and the extent to which regeneration frees us from it. V, 1965. The misery of a person who departs from God. VI, 809. Great is human misery: to be without him without whom one cannot exist. X, 1864, 1869. The greatest misery is not to hope in God and to promise oneself second-best things from oneself. X, 1866. God willed the Israelites to be afflicted with many miseries so that they might learn to show mercy. VI, 1037.

No works are devoid of God’s mercy, when he provides both through indulgence and through the scourge. X, 1859. God’s mercy precedes us so that we may be freed from every misery. X, 1787, 1876. God’s mercy would be injustice unless it belonged to God. VI, 1150. God’s prolonged mercy is patience, not negligence. V, 1802. How he now asks us, and how he will later judge. V, 1803. Here God grants mercy; in the future he exercises justice. V, 2273. God’s mercy is wrongly invoked as a pretext for remaining in sins. VI, 766. The bosom of God’s mercy is always open to penitents. VI, 1187. Yet it can never remove God’s justice. VI, 1187. A person especially needs mercy. V, 2328. The appeal for God’s mercy. VI, 946, 949. The commendation of mercy. VI, 1246. The necessity and manner of fleeing to God’s mercy. V, 2265.

A person first owes mercy to himself. V, 2328. There is no hope of mercy except for the merciful. V, 1882. Whoever does not forgive others closes the door of divine mercy against himself. V, 2242. Where God stretches out the bridge of mercy for us, it is unjust to wish to withdraw it from others. V, 2251. It is an arrangement of divine mercy that some are in need and others abound. V, 2336. Whoever bestows mercy is an executor and minister of the divine work. V, 2036. He keeps Christ’s bond of caution. V, 2331. By showing mercy to others, each person wins mercy for himself with God. V, 2328. Mercy is in heaven; it is reached through earthly acts of mercy. V, 2330. Mercy is present to the merciful. V, 2036. Mercy averts God’s anger, redeems from sins, and extinguishes future fires. V, 2341. Mercy alone will save, or its absence will condemn. V, 1898. One must persist unceasingly in works of mercy. VI, 768. After this life there is no place for them. V, 2230. Mercy is signified by oil. V, 1828. The distinction between mercy, clemency, and piety. VI, 1275. Mercy and truth must not be separated. X, 1868. Mercy is to be closed to no one, nor are the sins of any sinner to be released without punishment. VI, 1230. Mercy in a judge ought not to exist without discipline. V, 2328. Even one who rebukes and punishes bestows mercy. V, 2329.

Mass is solemnly celebrated on Sunday at approximately the seventh hour. VII, 829. During Masses one must stand for one or two hours. V, 2277, 2278, 2279. Everyone should attend the celebration of Mass each Sunday. V, 2275. Powerful people compel the presbyter to shorten the Mass. V, 2275. Masses are celebrated when offerings are made and the body or blood of the Lord is consecrated. V, 2276. Nor does this take place except in the house of God. V, 2277. Those who leave the church before the mysteries are completed are reproved. V, 2077. On Sunday or other major feasts, no one should leave the church until the divine mysteries are completed. V, 2276, 2278. This means until the Lord’s Prayer has been said and the blessing has been given to the people. V, 2276, 2279. Almost everyone leaves after hearing the readings. V, 2276, 2277. How bitterly Caesarius endured this. V, 2276, 2278. He who leaves hurriedly truly does not know how much good is accomplished in the celebration of Masses. V, 2276. What is this good? V, 2279. Reading at Masses. V, 1793. The prayer of the sacred altar, published by Blessed Basil, which almost the whole East regularly uses. X, 1775. In the celebration of the mysteries, prophetic, apostolic, and Gospel readings are recited. V, 2276. Likewise, “Lift up your hearts,” the “Holy,” and the Lord’s Prayer. V, 2277. Then the blessing is given. V, 2277, 2279.

Mission does not show the one who is sent to be lesser, but indicates the unity and harmony of the one who sends. V, 2188. The Father alone is nowhere read to have been sent. VIII, 1197. What the mission of the Word is. X, 1890. The mission of the Son or of the Holy Spirit is not spoken of according to the substance of divinity. VI, 737. The mission of Christ is the work of the whole Trinity. VI, 910.

The mitre, from which a bishop is called “father.” IX, 804.

The Monad (Monas) begot the Monad (monadem). VIII, 1165.

Protasius and Gervasius lived the life of monks in their own home. VI, 1104. Three kinds of monks in Egypt. VI, 1268. It is impious for a monk to change his purpose. VI, 1344. “Since I have become a monk, either I shall be saved as a monk or I shall not be saved.” VI, 1243. It would have been better for a proud monk to marry. VI, 1224. A monk who attacks the rule of his own order is an antichrist. VI, 1131. For a monk nothing is so deadly as going around villages, cities, and crowds of peoples. II, 1147. A monk can be perfect in his own homeland. VI, 1104. Monks withdrawing into the desert ought not to despise the synaxis of the brothers. VI, 1224. Brothers in monasteries are rightly compelled to visit one another. VI, 1224. Nor are those to be reproved who do this willingly. VI, 1224. It is certain that brothers may have, possess, give, or receive nothing without the superior’s permission. I, 1449. Gifts for monks. I, 1455. Under what condition gifts are to be accepted. I, 1449. No one will be able to retain for himself what by agreement belongs to all and has been consecrated to God. I, 1450. It is contrary to the monastic profession to adorn a cell with various paintings and images. I, 1462. Let the image of the crucified Christ, attended on either side by John and Mary, suffice. I, 1463. An unheard-of temptation involving the clothing of a certain monk. VI, 1104. Time assigned to reading or labor. I, 1450. They should work in silence unless the necessity of the work requires otherwise. I, 1450. For monks silence does what water does for fish. II, 1146. Outside the monastery no one should eat or drink without an order. I, 1450. Let those who wish take wine on Saturday and Sunday. I, 1450. Those living in the cloister ought not to be distracted by the care of the poor and guests. I, 1464. Against coenobites who, seeing others occupied with temporal matters, envy and slander them. I, 1464. If monks are not assisted by the alms of the faithful, they must occupy themselves more than usual with earthly work, to the greater detriment of the faithful. V, 2334.

She is not a nun who possesses anything beyond necessary food and clothing. I, 1453. The prescribed Rule for an enclosed nun. I, 1452. See Enclosed woman.

Monasteries contain both helpers of Christ and ministers of the devil. V, 1893.

Monaxius, prefect of the praetorium. X, 1727. Consul. X, 1731, 1732.

Montanus, a Donatist. IX, 839.

Montanus, a presbyter. IX, 794.

The Montanists introduce two contrary principles. VIII, 1218.

To mount into the air. III, 2173.

Why the Donatists are called Montenses. IX, 805.

The royal disease and various others are named. VII, 815, 816.

Customs. The earliest years are the best for the formation of character. II, 1108.

A certain man feigned madness for thirty years. III, 2357.

Death takes its name from “bite.” X, 1617. Why it is called sleep. V, 2063. What it is. VIII, 1771. Death is deprivation, possessing only a name and not an essence. X, 1616. If it is nothing, how can it see, hold, insult, be conquered, and be condemned? X, 1618. The Pelagians teach that Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin. X, 1613, 1614. Death is not from God, but occurred through sin from the devil’s envy. X, 1613. Death is not from God, but from contempt of the divine command. V, 1739. It is not a condition of nature but the punishment of sin. X, 1667. It was not made in the tree, but discovered through human beings. V, 1737. Death is truly a debt. VI, 1159. God cannot be called the author of death unless he is also called the author of sin. X, 1649. How it can be said that death and life are from God, and yet that God did not make death. III, 2234; X, 1885. The devil is the author of death in one way, God in another. X, 1680. That human beings die is the punishment of sin; that they return to life is the work of the merciful Lord. X, 1616.

There are many deaths of mutable things. VI, 732. Four deaths according to Scripture. VI, 741. Death and life are spoken of in three ways. X, 1679. There are two deaths, and two parts of the first death. V, 2074. The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body; the second unwillingly holds it in the body. X, 1873. The first death, not the second, is owed to the just. X, 1614. The first death may be called good, but not the second. X, 1871. It is called good for the pious, although it is also the punishment of sin. X, 1871. The second death. III, 2334, 2248. Why death comes quickly to the good, and why to the wicked. VI, 1036. The Lord’s Prayer represents the uncertainty of death to us. V, 1870. Whether those whom the day of judgment finds alive will die or not is free to either interpretation in faith. VIII, 1215. Those who survive Christ’s final advent will not die. VI, 1161.

The day of death must be anticipated, since it is accustomed to anticipate us. V, 2046. Death should be considered whenever we lie down in bed. VI, 1061. The thought of death restrains desire. V, 2152. Consideration of death. VI, 987. By this admonition the sinner is struck so that, dying, he may forget himself, since while living he forgot God. V, 2153, 2221. The prayer to be said to one who is dying. VI, 1152. For the dying person it is pleasant and salutary to speak of Christ’s humanity and be satisfied with it. VI, 1153. Not to mourn the common death is philosophical; to take consolation in the death of the soul is irreligious. VI, 1199. Not to fear death because of a clear conscience is better than all the delights of the world. I, 1471. Death is feared even by the servants of him by whom it was conquered. III, 2268. Our death has been conquered by Christ’s death. III, 2359. How death dies. V, 2065. It could die only in life. V, 2349. How Christ became the death of death. X, 1617. By an unjust death Christ conquered a just death. V, 1808. Christ’s single death paid our double death. VI, 1193. Death is now more to be desired than mourned, though it must not be inflicted upon oneself. VI, 1162. It is to be preferred to the present life. VI, 1151. For the good it is a door that presents them to life, not one that removes them from it. V, 1957. It is the beginning of blessedness, the goal of labors, and the destruction of vices. I, 1471. Angels attend the death of the righteous and offer assistance; the worst spirits deliver the impious, dragged from the body, to the fires. I, 1472. Those devoted to pious works do not perish by an evil death. VI, 1319, 1320, 1321. It is not death that makes death evil, but what follows death. X, 1863. Many walk about dead within, and while living carry their own funerals. V, 1785.

Spiritual death is necessary for the believer. V, 1824.

Dead to sin. VI, 1052. Once Christ has come, it is no longer permitted to mourn the dead, although it was permitted formerly. VI, 1160. The response of an unbelieving father to one announcing the death of his only son. VI, 1166. Christ raised the dead in one way, the Apostles in another. V, 1927.
