A resurrected dead man tells what he saw. VII, 838. In what manner the dead appear. VI, 799. They do not know what is happening here while it is happening. VI, 799. By what means they can learn it. VI, 799. They care for us just as we care for them. VI, 799. See Deceased.

The necessity and usefulness of mortifying the flesh. VI, 1075.

There are three kinds of motion. I, 1439. God moves himself without time or place; a created spirit temporally without place; and bodily creation temporally and locally. VI, 746. How this is to be understood. VI, 746.

The mystical name of Moses. V, 1789. Moses bore the type both of Christ and of the Law. V, 1813. He himself is understood as the Law. V, 1781. He avenges an injury done to God; he does not satisfy anger. V, 2262. He saw the Lord. V, 2026. Since the Jews were unable to endure Moses’ face, it was shown that sinners do not deserve to behold God’s glory. III, 2222. Where and when Moses took an Ethiopian wife. III, 2171. Moses’ life is divided into three periods of forty years: first, in Pharaoh’s household; second, as an exile from Egypt; third, as leader of the people through the desert. III, 2174. Moses’ unbelief at Kadesh. III, 2172. Why no one knew of his death and tomb. III, 2174. Many think that he took away with him the staff with which he had performed many signs, so that it would not be worshiped. III, 2174. Why Moses’ sons did not succeed to his priesthood. III, 2170. The authorities agree that Moses was seen at Christ’s Transfiguration with his true body, but that afterward this body was again committed to burial. III, 2198.

“Woman” takes its name from softness. V, 2292. She is a portion of man. III, 2405. Woman is not the image of God, but man is. III, 2228, 2229, 2244, 2319; VI, 739. Woman is the cause of all evils. V, 2032. Adam could have stood firm amid the delights of paradise if Eve had not been there. V, 2032. How much woman contributes to the devil’s victory. V, 2032. The devil captures no souls in such numbers by any snare as by that of women. II, 1141, 1142, 1147. Familiarity with women is to be avoided by all, especially monks and clerics. V, 2301. Not only with strangers, but also with maidservants, neighbors, daughters, and foster-daughters. V, 2302. The lower their condition, the easier their ruin. V, 2302. How Christ wiped away women’s reproach by being born and rising again. V, 1993. At the world’s beginning a wife led a man to death; in Christ’s Passion a wife calls him to salvation. V, 2038. Through a woman death was announced; through a woman life is restored to humanity. V, 2040. Julian’s edict gave women the power to divorce their husbands. III, 2349. In the city of Rome. III, 2349. The use of wine was unknown to Roman women. III, 2350. A certain woman in the city of Rome had eleven husbands, and a man had twelve wives. III, 2357. Another woman bore five children. III, 2356. A woman who has acted so as to be unable to conceive is guilty of as many homicides as children as she could have borne. V, 2298. The nuisance of women chattering in church. V, 2275.

Multicolae. VIII, 1101.

Munatius. IX, 794.

Purity of heart is required beforehand for the vision of God. V, 2083.

Why the world is so called. VI, 895. In Scripture it is sometimes spoken of in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense. IX, 839. The twofold meaning of “world.” X, 1891. Various opinions concerning the world’s origin. III, 2316. It is highly inappropriate to say that the world has existed from eternity or will be eternal. III, 2231. The world had a beginning. VI, 1011. That it began and must be dissolved is certain; what existed before it, or what will exist afterward, is not equally certain. VIII, 1177. The Manichaeans deny that God could create the world except by necessity and with the help of matter. VIII, 1151. The world was created by the true God. V, 2176. From nothing, and as it were not from nothing. VI, 1019. At the spring equinox. III, 2317. The Kalends of April. III, 2252. Why it was made, and that it was made in God. III, 2216. The world lies between the kingdom of God and hell, possessing something from both. VI, 891. Why no one before Moses explained the world’s beginning, and why Moses began to do so. III, 2218. God prescribed laws for the world, not for himself. III, 2355.

The age of the world. V, 2048. The Law was given more than three thousand years after the world’s creation. III, 2349. The world is now passing through its sixth thousand years. III, 2357. The works of the six days bear the figure of the world’s six thousand years. III, 2320. Christ came in the world’s sixth millennium. III, 2320. There will be rest in the seventh millennium. III, 2320. The world’s six ages. V, 1920; VI, 742, 749. The end of the world is imminent. VI, 1187. The end of the world will be near when the Gospel has been received throughout the whole world. X, 1836. The form of the world, not its substance, is passing away. VIII, 1219.

This world is our prison and exile. VI, 1350. The sea that is crossed in many ways. VI, 1309. It is like a flood over which faith floats. VI, 847. Whether a person ought to love anything in this world. VI, 1083. Three things are worst in this world, and three best. VI, 1065. Jericho represented the world. VI, 1290. The world’s deceitfulness. V, 1814. The dangers with which it is filled. V, 2033. The world’s weapons are earthly estates. VI, 1216. The world either laughs at and tramples us, or is laughed at and trampled by us. V, 2020. It is bitter, yet it is loved; do you suppose that if it were sweet, it would be loved more? V, 2315. The world does not know how to love; it is an artisan of hatred. VI, 1226. It must hate those whom it sees hating what it loves. X, 1891. Love of the world is an evil region. V, 1891. Love and fear of the world lead to every sin. X, 1879. The lovers of the world are ground and turned by time like a millstone. III, 2446. Their wretched occupation is always beginning. III, 2446. The person who belongs to the heavenly city is a stranger in the world. X, 1860. A sermon to clerics on contempt for the world. VI, 1215. The whole world was redeemed, at a price surpassing its own worth. V, 2042.

Gifts pleasing to God. V, 1919. A gift pleasing to God, by which he acquires grounds for rewarding. V, 2015. He considers everything to have been offered to him by us if we act so that everything may be offered to us by him. V, 2015. God loves us ourselves more than our substance. V, 2017.

Murmuring usually arises either because unjust things are commanded or because the person giving the command is less worthy. II, 1110. Those who murmur are displeased with God. V, 1916.

The day of the walls. VI, 1172.

The weasel is hostile to the serpent. VI, 1241.

The mute sand-digger. IX, 798, 799.

## N

Naaman’s cleansing. V, 1830.

Nabor, a centurion. IX, 775.

Nebuchadnezzar saw Christ in the furnace. III, 2391.

Nagarbae. III, 2169.

Namatius, an illustrious man. X, 1790.

Nampius, a secretary. IX, 816.

Nasoon. VII, 816.

Nassutius, a Donatist bishop. IX, 778, 790.

Natalis. IX, 787.

Birth is like a tree that is grafted. III, 2382. It is wrongly accused by the Manichaeans. III, 2382, 2384. The three remarkable kinds of birth in Adam, Eve, and Christ. V, 1989. The Arian definition of birth. VIII, 1166. A human birthday is rightly celebrated. III, 2381. With what solemnity it is celebrated by the powerful. V, 1973. On their birthday feast the rich customarily give exquisite gifts to take home. III, 2371. There are two human births. X, 1888.

No one’s nativity is celebrated except John’s and the Lord’s. V, 2111, 2113. What should be done as the solemnity of Christ’s birthday approaches. V, 1973, 1975. As Christ is born, light increases and darkness diminishes. V, 1989, 1995. The prerogative of this day. V, 1994. Its sweetness and grace. V, 1977. Christ’s birthday is his nuptial day. V, 1975. What virtues in particular are commended on Christ’s birthday. V, 1990. Something should be vowed to the newborn Lord. V, 1978.

Navigius, an assistant in numerical matters. IX, 816.

The archbishop of Nazareth. II, 1133.

What nature is. VI, 810. Nature is everything that God made. X, 1639, 1883. Therefore nothing in miracles is contrary to nature. X, 1883. Nature can exist, and does exist, without any evil, but it cannot exist without every good. X, 1872. Nature contains nothing that is not good. VI, 773. Change of nature is the work of the devil. V, 1888. Nature is not always opposed to grace. X, 1880. What is understood to be observed through faith is said to have been fulfilled by nature. V, 1743. The seeds of justice are inherent in our nature. III, 2361. The principles of the Law. III, 2362. Nature is foul without grace. X, 1796.

When necessity excuses one from observing the Law. III, 2257.

Negligence in sacred matters is sacrilege. VI, 1207.

Worldly business must at least be interrupted so that time may be devoted to prayer and reading. V, 2266.

Neporus. See Lazarus.

“Grandson” signifies the son of a son and a lustful person. I, 1418.

The absurd doctrine of Nepos concerning Christ’s and the saints’ reign for a thousand years. VIII, 1218.

Nestorius, an impious man of empty understanding. X, 1883. Deceived by Theodore of Mopsuestia. X, 1739. He blasphemously declared Christ either to be a man with God or to exist apart from God. VIII, 1215. He denies that the Word was brought forth from Mary, but says that the one born from her had the Word accompanying him. X, 1684. Thus he was regarded at the Council of Ephesus as though he wished to renew Pelagius’ doctrine. X, 1683. The Caelestians adhere to Nestorius. X, 1761. Nestorians and Pelagians form an alliance with kindred errors. X, 1831. The Nestorian and Pelagian heresies are the same. X, 1683, 1686. To cut out Nestorian impiety, Caelestine assisted Cyril with the apostolic sword. X, 1831. Two letters of Nestorius to Caelestine concerning the Pelagian bishops who had withdrawn to Constantinople. X, 1753. Caelestine intimates that Nestorius held something worse than they did. X, 1754. Nevertheless, his opinion concerning original sin was correct. X, 1755.

Nicasius. IX, 785.

Nicodemus, a priest of the Jews. V, 2148. His relics. VII, 807, 809, 811, 815.

Nicolaus, archbishop of Crete. II, 1145.

To wear black clothing on account of mourning is foreign to a Christian. VI, 1165.

Nothingness. Nothing created from created things returns to nothingness. VI, 728.

It snows. III, 2396.

Ninus is said to have been the first to wage war against neighboring peoples. III, 2353.

Ninus. IX, 803.

Nitentius. IX, 806.

Evil nobility, which through pride makes a person ignoble before God. V, 2035.

It is false that no one can be harmed except by himself. X, 1745.

Noah is the voice of one preaching the destruction of the world. V, 2028. Noah is an example of charity that endures all things. V, 1952, 1953. Noah signifies God’s rest in the saints. V, 2068.

The various terminations of names. I, 1385. The names of numbers that are ἄπτωτα [indeclinable], and those that are declinable. I, 1408.

“Notary” has the same meaning as “recorder.” IX, 820. The notaries of the Catholic Church and the notaries of the Donatists. IX, 816. Flavius, tribune and notary. IX, 816.

The notices of the apparitors. IX, 807. The Donatist notice. IX, 821. Another as well. IX, 828.

Novatianus. VIII, 1221. He considers a fornicator sacrilegious, as one who sins against Christ’s members. III, 2405. He pretends that penance must be performed, although he does not dare deny that it should be granted. III, 2304. He abuses the Lord’s words, “Whoever denies me, I will also deny him.” III, 2304. He wants the one meaning to apply both to denying the Lord and to sinning against the Holy Spirit. III, 2304. He holds that fornication is not to be forgiven. III, 2305. Although God granted forgiveness for adultery and murder, and promised it to repentant idolaters. III, 2305, 2308. Indeed, for all sins except one against the Holy Spirit. III, 2307. Novatian’s twofold error was to deny idolaters the fruit of repentance and to preach that the good are contaminated by the wicked. III, 2309. He denies that there are good and wicked people in one Church. III, 2310. How he excuses his separation. III, 2310. He says that the crime of idolatry can be forgiven only by God, against whom it was committed, and not by him. III, 2310. He says that he urges the guilty to do penance in the same way that Peter urged Simon Magus. III, 2310. He condemns the fact that the Lord’s body is given to sinners. III, 2310. He denies that those who do not belong to his society are Christians. III, 2311. He placed his own name above the name of Christ for his followers. III, 2312. The error of the Novatians is refuted. VI, 1197.

Novatus. IX, 816, 827.

Whenever the universal Church is assailed by novelty. X, 1756.

“New creation” is spoken of in three ways. VI, 1027.

Consideration of the last things is urged upon many. VI, 980.

Night is the mother of the wicked. VI, 926. See Day.

The perfection of the number six. VI, 741. The mystery of the numbers seven and eight. VI, 749, 750. And of fifty. III, 2335; V, 1822.

Numidia. IX, 784, 785.

Nundinarius the deacon. IX, 774. He presses before the governor that Silvanus be proved a traditor. IX, 793. Several bishops attempt to reconcile his disagreement with Silvanus. IX, 795.

The Manichaeans condemn even first marriages, and the Cataphrygians second marriages. V, 2183; X, 1718. Jerome condemns not even second or third marriages, and so forth. X, 1696. Second and third marriages are entered into without sin. VI, 768, 777.

Those who assert that marriage is a sordid and defiling work are refuted. III, 2379. The tradition of this matter remained both in the Synagogue and is now observed in the Church, so that God’s creature may be joined under God’s blessing. III, 2379. Why Christ attended a wedding. V, 1922. God the author of marriage. X, 1733. In what respect marriage is good. VIII, 1219. These are not condemned, as the Pelagians claim, when sexual desire is condemned. X, 1645. The lawful use of marriage was not instituted for the wantonness of lust. X, 1645. It owes offspring not to lust but to the good proper to its nature. X, 1646. The freedom of marriage is very good; wicked desire in married people is condemnable. X, 1646. When women take husbands, they should not presume to enter the church for thirty days. V, 2299. Cerinthus and Marcion expect marital intercourse after this life. VIII, 1218. The wedding banquet to which we have been invited. V, 1976.

Comparison of the nut and the Law. V, 1805.

O.

Whoever lives with a hardened heart. VI, 766. See Hardening.

Commendation of obedience. VI, 1242, 1248. The great usefulness of obedience, even blind obedience. X, 1883. How great a good obedience is. X, 1879. Why it is better than sacrifices. VI, 1249. One obedience is worth more than all other virtues. VI, 1221. Where there is disobedience, there is pride. VI, 1221. Obedience is the mother of all disciplines. VI, 1881. It requires great exercise. VI, 1881. It took the norm of its pursuit from Christ. VI, 1881. Christ assumed flesh in order to teach obedience to those who could obtain salvation in no other way than through obedience. VIII, 1186. The one who has fallen through the foot of pride must rise through the foot of obedience. V, 1866. Through the merit of obedience Christ’s yoke is gentle. V, 1866. How pleasing obedience to parents is to God. VI, 1221. God will comply with our prayers in proportion to the way in which we ourselves obey our parents. VI, 1344. What obedience ought to be like. VI, 1345. Who is fit or unfit to maintain the discipline of obedience. VI, 1344. Obedience must be honorable and discerning. VI, 1249. He receives the world’s prosperity solely at command and embraces adversity out of devotion. VI, 1243. The beginning of obedience is wanting to know what is commanded, and part of submission is learning what one should do. II, 1105. Each person ceases to obey by his own will, not because God compels him. X, 1839, 1842.

One ought voluntarily to offer God what is better. III, 2313. Those who act unjustly, when they offer God what is unworthy, become guilty of a double injustice. III, 2313. An offering is good if justice is maintained and mercy is not neglected. III, 2313. Offerings to be consecrated on the altar must be offered, so that whoever can do so may not share in another’s offering. V, 2238, 2241. The person in whose name the priest acts is said to offer. III, 2246. The sacred liturgy is called an offering, and the prayer in which, after the consecration, the high priest Melchizedek is mentioned is designated by that name. III, 2329. See Sacrifice.

The distinction between obscure and ambiguous things. I, 1414. Three kinds of obscure things. I, 1414. How all these may be avoided. I, 1415.

The dreadful calamity of a siege and its hostile devastation. V, 2315.

Detractors are sea-dogs. V, 1885.

No one except a judge is permitted to kill anyone with a sword. III, 2314.

The Octavensis passage. IX, 801.

The eye is the door and messenger of the heart. VI, 1991.

Hatred is deadly poison. V, 1977. The devil’s poison. V, 1977. Through hatred of even one person, whatever good we do becomes fruitless. V, 2139; VI, 1178, 1180, 1188. Pretexts for empty hatred. VI, 1095. How can one hate a person whose nature one sees in God’s humanity? VI, 962. Hatred of the sinner is to be reconciled with love of the human being. VI, 1229. The devil alone is to be pursued with hatred. V, 1860. A thunderclap against those who retain hatred or anger. V, 1975. Perfect hatred. X, 1865.

What the fragrance of Christ is. X, 1891.

I offer. See Offering.

Public officials. IX, 782.

[Col. 0770] The official whose function is to torture by interrogation. IX, 783. See Exceptor. “Office” in the sense of a judicial place. IX, 781.

The order of the divine office. I, 1449. The people are summoned to Vigils, Terce, Sext, and None. V, 1760. An office in honor of the Virgin. I, 1456.

The threefold power of oil. VI, 1312. Oil is understood as mercy or charity. V, 1892. The oil of the righteous is the Spirit of God. IX, 767. Blessed oil, with which the body of the sick person is anointed in the name of Christ, provides healing not only for the body but also for the soul. VI, 1773. See Sick. Consecrated oil brought from the shrine of a holy martyr. VII, 844, 848. From it the limbs of the sick are anointed. VII, 845. And in it a morsel is dipped and taken daily before other foods. VII, 848.

The Mount of Olives. They relate that the Antichrist will be killed there. VI, 1134.

Olympius the bishop. IX, 779.

Olympic victors. I, 1446.

A burden. “If your brother has been overtaken in something, let it be carried by you; and if you have been overtaken, let him support you.” V, 2262.

Opilio, a distinguished man. X, 1790.

Four kinds of opposites. I, 1437.

What is done superstitiously and what is done as a Christian at the beginning of a work. VI, 1722. The two roots of all good or evil works are charity and desire. V, 2312. Evil works are bars and bolts by which the door of the heavenly kingdom is closed; good works are keys by which it is opened. V, 2166. Good works produce delights through brief hardships; evil works prepare everlasting bitterness through passing sweetness. V, 2019. Commendation of good works. VI, 1347. Their barrenness alone will condemn us. V, 1895. For a Christian, faith without works is of no benefit. V, 1896. The necessity of good works. VI, 768. They alone will be carried with us to heaven—or rather, they will carry us. VI, 1188. Those devoted to works of mercy do not perish by an evil death. VI, 1319. Good works must be done; it is not enough not to do evil. V, 2331, 2236. A good work gives confidence when it is not merely anticipated but accomplished. V, 1854. God speaks to every person who does good. V, 1824. Works that are not excluded from justification. X, 1634. In matters relating to bodily exertion, no Christian is compelled unwillingly: charity itself is sufficient. V, 2246.

One should place one’s good works behind one’s back and one’s evil works before one’s face. V, 1846. How a hidden good work may be made public, and a public one hidden. V, 1864. Whoever acts for God performs a good work behind a closed door, even if he does it publicly. V, 1829. A good work becomes more a work done to you than one you do, if you do it sadly. X, 1868. They are not good works unless they are done through faith and love. X, 1878. No good work is ever completed or begun without faith. V, 2234. A reward is owed to good works; but grace, which is not owed, precedes it. X, 1788. God both gave and prepared good works. X, 1781. The work of God is the work of the righteous. X, 1663. All the works of the impious are unclean. X, 1818.

The Ophians wish our flesh to be evil. VIII, 1220.

An excerpt from Optatus of Milevis. IX, 773.

Optatus. IX, 807.

What an oracle is. VI, 798. “Oracle” in the sense of the Law. IX, 815, 817.

The custom of applying a *orarium* to the sacred relics. VII, 840. It is then given to the sick person to embrace. VII, 844.

Praise of prayer. VI, 1228. Several incentives to pray to God. V, 1909. What prayer is. V, 1887; VI, 816, 997. The fruit of prayer. V, 1887; VI, 1057. The devil is beaten and conquered through prayer. V, 1797. The prayer of the righteous is the key of heaven. V, 1838. Whoever knows how to pray rightly truly knows how to live rightly. V, 1849. One must pray before and after every work. VI, 1057. How we ought to be disposed before prayer and during prayer. VI, 1057. One must pray not with a resounding voice but with a conscience crying out to God. V, 2281. Let only roaring and sighs or groans be heard. V, 2281. God hears tears more quickly than voices. V, 1838. It is more useful to pray briefly more often than once at excessive length, unless inspired devotion prolongs the prayer without the one praying knowing it. I, 1456. How God should be contemplated in prayer. VI, 1012. How the saints should be contemplated. VI, 1012.

What prayer ought to be like. VI, 1316. It should not be made while one’s neighbor is injured or appeased. VI, 1096. How a bad conscience diminishes the confidence of the one praying. VI, 903. Christ’s Passion arouses this confidence. VI, 907. Humility is necessary for the one praying. X, 1865. When prayer has been announced and the deacon cries, “Let us bend our knees,” the knees should be bent—or, because of weakness, the back should be bowed or the neck humbled. V, 2284, 2285, 2286. This utterance of the deacon is directed especially not to the clergy but to the people. V, 2286. Those who then stand upright are rebuked. V, 2284, 2285. Why we turn toward the east when praying. V, 1867. During prayer the devil is accustomed to attack us most intensely. V, 2287. Wandering thoughts in prayer are called captivities of the soul. V, 2282, 2287. How great are God’s offenses. V, 2281; VI, 964. Whatever a person thinks about more attentively during prayer, he establishes for himself in place of God. V, 2281. If he is thinking about the forum, he [Col. 0771] worships the forum. V, 2281. Prayer should persevere. V, 1909. Almsgiving and fasting are the wings of prayer. V, 1864. How effective the invocation of the Father through the Son is. VI, 904. Christ’s Passion is represented to him. VI, 905. What sons ask, what hired servants ask, and what they receive. VI, 1090.

One must pray for everyone and for whatever God himself knows to be useful for our soul. V, 2282. Forgiveness of sins and God’s grace must be sought with all one’s heart and mind. V, 2281. That one must pray with the body humbled is shown by many passages. V, 2285. One asks for what pleases God to hear and is useful for us. VI, 939. That God may complete what he has begun, grant what he causes us to will, and enable us to love him as much as he commands. VI, 940. Whoever asks for eternal things prays with the door closed; whoever asks for temporal things, with it open. V, 1865. In what place temporal things may rightly be requested. V, 1865. From what source our prayers are ineffective. II, 1128. Whose prayers God hears or rejects. VI, 1041. God refuses Saul the forgiveness sought in his prayers, which he grants to David when he pleads, because the disposition of heart was not the same in both. III, 2225. Prayer for the necessities of this life is mercifully heard, and mercifully not heard. X, 1876. Whoever asks for what God commands and promises will receive what he requests. X, 1877. When something is wrongly requested, or something for which one will make bad use is requested, God is angered by granting it and shows mercy by not granting it. X, 1880, 1892. A person devoted to magic is heard to his own punishment. VI, 726. An example of meditation following prayer. VI, 1000. A prayer in which the soul asks that the virtues be freed from vices. VI, 1076. A prayer asking that vices be cut away and virtues granted. VI, 901, 938. Prayers in which God is called one who contains all things, whom no one contains. II, 1159, 1161. A formula of prayer to God, on one’s own behalf and that of all, through the merits of all the saints. VI, 939. Prayers celebrated uniformly throughout the world for idolaters, Jews, and others. X, 1759. In almost the whole East God is asked to make us good. X, 1775. The practice of commending ourselves to the prayers of others. VI, 939.

The Lord’s Prayer must be said by the one praying before all else, because the one who instituted it willingly hears it. V, 2282. The Lord’s Prayer contains every kind of prayer. V, 1867. How much Christians are taught by its opening words. V, 1867. Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer. V, 1907. The most sacred covenant of the Lord’s Prayer. V, 2035.

Every place has been made an oratory by Christ. V, 2048. A place suitable for prayer: the inner parts must be clean. X, 1889.

The only parts of a sentence are the noun and the verb; the remaining elements should be called its connections rather than its parts. I, 1419.

The function of an orator. I, 1439. The end of an orator’s function. I, 1440. See Dialectician.

Orca. IX, 794, 797, 799.

Grace is infused into those ordained through tradition. III, 2287. The rule and form of this discipline is handed down by the Lord to the apostles. III, 2287. The apostles were ordained bishops by Christ through the laying on of hands. III, 2296. Presbyters and the other ranks are initiated by the sign of the cross. VI, 1192. The blessing of ordination is nothing unless the ordained priest performs the ministry. III, 2223. The priest’s will can neither hinder nor benefit it. III, 2223. Donatus confessed that he had laid hands on fallen bishops, an act alien to the Church. IX, 779. Defects in ordinations are noted. X, 1720. What things prohibit a cleric from being ordained. VIII, 1219. By the canons, bishops are not permitted to ordain someone else’s candidate. X, 1771. Those wounded by penance cannot be ordained. IX, 804. Those ordained by heretics, as well as those who ordain them, are penalized. IX, 806, 812. Whether those who had been baptized as children by the Donatists may be ordained. IX, 807, 808. Twenty purses were given by Victor the fuller so that he might be made a presbyter. IX, 795, 798, 799. The bishops divided this money. IX, 798. The higher order contains the lower within itself and can perform its office. III, 2302.

Orders; magistrates. IX, 807. Men of rank. IX, 818, 841.

The proper order of rational creation and how one falls from it. VI, 1018. Nothing disturbs the order of God’s rule. VI, 972. Whoever does not preserve the order of divine institution will not escape the order of divine vengeance. VI, 773.

Orestes the consul. X, 1792.

Orontius, an African bishop exiled in Sardinia. X, 1772, 1779.

Orontius, a Pelagian bishop. X, 1749, 1754. His deposition is confirmed. X, 1760.

Augustine handed Orosius over to Jerome at Bethlehem so that he might learn the fear of the Lord. X, 1698. Summoned to the Jerusalem gathering, he fought vigorously against Pelagius. X, 1698. He was badly received by John of Jerusalem. X, 1700. Sent by the African bishops, he came to the holy places. VII, 806. He brought relics from the body of Saint Stephen to Braga. VII, 806. Orosius, carrying the relics of Saint Stephen and unable to cross into Spain, decided to return to Africa. VII, 823.

The Oriental. IX, 787.

Origen holds that there is something in God invisible even to himself. VIII, 1214. In the Trinity there is something uniquely belonging to one person and not communicable to another. VIII, 1214. He says that Christ’s flesh was brought from heaven. VIII, 1214. He imagines that human souls were created all at once. [Col. 0772] VI, 814; VIII, 1216. He holds that another new body will be given in place of the flesh at the resurrection. VIII, 1214. Another of his ravings concerns the restoration of demons or the impious after the day of judgment. VIII, 1215. He denies that all rational creatures will be destroyed and attributes repentance to the devil. X, 1704. Pelagius’s teaching is a little branch of Origen’s. X, 1693, 1696, 1697, 1699. A homily of Origen. V, 1755. The two books on the Incarnation consist of mere scraps of his work. VIII, 1175.

The ortygometra is a new creature among birds, recently indeed displayed, but not newly created. III, 2170.

When a bodily kiss is to be used. VI, 835. What a spiritual kiss is. VI, 835. We kiss God whenever we are pierced with love for him. VI, 961.

Osiris, the husband of Isis. III, 2343.

Idleness must be avoided. VI, 1262. Its harmful effects. I, 1455. Idleness is the burial of a living person. VI, 1263. The idle person not only acquires nothing new but consumes what has been acquired. II, 1118. Desire troubles the idle, whereas it rests in those who are occupied. III, 2351. Love of truth seeks holy leisure; let the necessity of love undertake just business. X, 1873.

Oxyrhynchus. VI, 1104.

Uzzah was punished for a preceding sin. III, 2180.

P.

God’s covenant with us. V, 2139. The covenant written in baptism with Christ. V, 2235, 2243; VI, 1170, 1209. Whoever observes superstitious practices, after rejecting Christ, makes a covenant with the devil. V, 2272.

To repent is to hold on to punishment. VI, 1128. God’s repentance. VIII, 1205; IX, 1872.

How the preaching of repentance appears to many as an exhortation to the religious or monastic life. V, 2208, 2222. Baptism is the sacrament of repentance and faith. VI, 775. Repentance is necessary for all adults together with baptism. VI, 775. Those who assert that repentance is useful only before baptism and is ineffective afterward are refuted. VI, 1114. Repentance is granted after baptism. X, 1733. The Novatians deny it to the lapsed. X, 1735. There is a place for repentance and, through repentance, for forgiveness. VI, 1198. If the old law receives penitents, how much more the new. III, 2303, 2306, 2308. If repentance is denied, no one will be able to be saved. III, 2307, 2308.

Repentance is a second baptism. VI, 1066. It is beneficial if practiced in the Catholic Church. VI, 1123. Outside the Church it has no validity. VI, 766. The foundation of repentance is faith. VI, 1113. All repentance concerns liberty badly used. VI, 1120.

Repentance is necessary for everyone. V, 2033, 2220, 2223. For without it only original sin is forgiven. VI, 1119. It is continually necessary for those who continually sin. VI, 1119. For without spontaneous repentance there is no return to one’s former state. V, 2202. It must be practiced as long as we live. V, 2020, 2221, 2223. Even priests should not spend a single day without repentance. III, 2420. The sorrow of repentance should end only with life. VI, 1124, 1128. What is the subject matter for our repentance and sorrow. VI, 1120. The fruit of daily repentance. V, 2224. What difference there is between the repentance practiced continually and that received at the end of life. V, 2217. What difference there is between sorrow and repentance. VI, 1120. What difference there is between one who turns toward repentance and one who is converted. VI, 1127.

True repentance is measured not by years but by contrition of heart. V, 2216. It is true repentance when one does not admit what must be repented of and mourns what has been admitted. VIII, 1218. Or when a person is so converted that he does not return to sin. V, 1977. What should be imposed as satisfaction on penitents placed at the point of death. VI, 1157. The error of priests who bound them even after death. VI, 1157. Those at the point of death are to be absolved if they ask. VI, 1158. But if they recover, they must undergo the censure of the canons. VI, 1158. What is rightly imposed on them then. VI, 1157. Those doing penance in the Church should learn to mourn wisely. V, 1980. And to pass from fear to love. V, 1980. Nothing makes repentance certain except hatred of sin and love of God. V, 1977. Repentance that does not proceed from faith and charity remains barren and does not wash away crimes. VI, 1121. Without the love of God no one finds grace. VI, 1121, 1128. Forgiveness of sins after freely received mercy is to be obtained through the penitent’s groaning and not without cost. III, 2306. The devout disposition of the penitent. V, 1977, 1979; VI, 949. Repentance must grieve over absolutely every sin. VI, 1121, 1128. He is culpably hard who shows sorrow over temporal things with tears but does not show sorrow over sin. VI, 1121. Repentance is vengeance, punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed. VI, 1120.

The effects of repentance. V, 2229; VI, 1113. Sins are quickly forgiven one who practices true repentance. VI, 1323. Before repentance no sin can remain. VI, 1114, 1116. Repentance restores the defective to perfection. X, 1631. It is a gift of God. X, 1630. Repentance both merits forgiveness and brings reformation. III, 2304, 2305. God not only [Col. 0773] forgives the penitent’s faults but also promises rewards. VI, 1350.

How dangerous it is to corrupt repentance once undertaken. VI, 1201. Nevertheless, it was not undertaken without fruit. VI, 1201. Those who contend that repentance benefits only once after baptism and is not to be repeated are refuted. VI, 1116. The earliest Fathers forgave sins up to seventy-seven times—that is, always. VI, 1117. The bosom of mercy is always open to penitents. VI, 1187. Examples of sinners who obtained forgiveness through prompt repentance. V, 2222.

Repentance must not be postponed under hope of God’s mercy. V, 1802, 1969, 2208, 2218, 2219, 2226; VI, 766, 1189. The remedies of repentance should be applied while the wounds of sins are still warm. V, 1803, 1974, 2219; VI, 1177. The folly and impiety of one who delays repentance. VI, 1061. How dangerous, foolish, unjust, and hateful to God it is to reserve repentance for old age. V, 2046, 2220, 2221. Why late repentance is rarely true and useful. VI, 1127. It is subject to the fire of purification. VI, 1128. Repentance during illness can benefit some people. V, 2220. Here, whenever and by whomever it is practiced, it obtains forgiveness. VI, 766. Even in the final breath of life. VIII, 1220. It cannot be denied at the point of death, but how uncertain its fruit is. V, 2217. I can give repentance to the sick person, not security. V, 2218. There will be repentance in hell, but it will be fruitless. V, 2211, 2215; VI, 765, 1189, 1200. Fruitful repentance should precede fruitless repentance. V, 1963.

The fruits worthy of repentance. V, 2215; VI, 1125. Repentance should be proportionate to offenses. V, 2229. The same penalty should be imposed for the same fault. IX, 805. The Donatists did not take account of this rule. IX, 805. In satisfaction for enormous sins, not words alone but actions are required. V, 2217. God does not seek the sinner’s gifts but souls. VI, 1067. The sinner’s soul itself must make satisfaction on its own behalf; it must not ransom itself from outside. III, 2339. Whoever has taken pleasure in sins must be afflicted in repentance. III, 2339. The sinner must bid farewell to every consolation. VI, 949. The penitent must either abandon the world or relinquish what he administered not without sin. VI, 1125. Whoever voluntarily committed unlawful things should abstain from many lawful ones. VI, 1125. He should depend entirely on the priest’s judgment. VI, 1125. He should first offer his mind, and then whatever he can from his possessions. VI, 1125. He should not approach the Lord’s body until he has strengthened his good conscience. VI, 1126. He should restrain himself from games and spectacles. VI, 1126. He should not divide his confession out of shame among different people. VI, 1126.

Repentance granted by priests must be completed. V, 2209. God accepts repentance even when a person has been unable to complete the entire order of satisfaction. VI, 1199. Repentance should be private for private sins and public for public sins. VI, 1123. Mortal sins committed after baptism must be expiated through public repentance. VIII, 1217. Though they may be absolved through secret satisfaction. VIII, 1218. Public repentance. V, 1948. It is not to be regarded with shame. VI, 1187. How wretched it is to be ashamed of repentance. V, 2219, 2223. Repentance should not easily be entrusted to the young. V, 2218. Note (a). Children wounded by penance by the Donatists, so that they could not be ordained. IX, 804. Crimes subject to public repentance. V, 2229. Those who have observed superstitious practices need harsh and prolonged repentance. V, 2240, 2269. A magician was shut up in a cave as a form of repentance. II, 1142. Repentance is publicly requested so that one who destroyed himself along with many others may redeem himself through the edification of many. V, 2226. And although it could be done more privately, it is requested publicly so that he may be helped by many. V, 2227, 2228. For penitents are to be helped by the Church through public tears. VI, 1123. And the hair shirt with which the penitent is covered is in itself an effective supplication to the people. V, 2227. Not to sympathize with one who asks for repentance from the heart is excessively inhuman. V, 2228. There should be no doubt that God hears the prayers of the whole people on behalf of the penitent. V, 2228.

The penitent should not rely so much on the prayers of the whole people that he himself ceases from good works. V, 2228. If illness permits, he should not drink wine. V, 2228. The person who desires or presumes to eat meat without being compelled by illness receives repentance without sufficient compunction. V, 2229. Some ask to be reconciled quickly so that they may eat meat. V, 2229. Even after reconciliation, if the penitent can find vegetables or little fish either at his own table or at another’s banquet, he should not eat other meat. V, 2229. The penitents are to be mourned who consume meat and wine even to drunkenness. V, 2229. Whoever asks for repentance begs to be excommunicated. V, 2228. Whoever has received it is put outside, covered with a hair shirt. V, 2228. As long as fornicators are doing penance, one must not communicate with them. III, 2308. When repentance is imposed, their heads are shaved and coverings are spread over their heads. IX, 804.

Pagans call Christians fools. III, 2342. They criticize their faith, but do not deny that nothing can be reproached in their commandments. III, 2344. They have *cinaedi* as ministers of their religion, men made into women. III, 2342. The obscenity of these people. III, 2343. They are concealed out of reverence for Christian majesty. [Col. 0774] III, 2343. Because they suffer obscenities in darkness, they think they can remain unknown. III, 2343. Having found depraved human beings, the devil added magical tricks. III, 2344. Through custom, what was shameful began not to appear so. III, 2344. But this was exposed by the holy Christian faith. III, 2343. The devil instituted the celebration of their mysteries for the pagans in the first month. III, 2279. Remnants of pagan customs on the Kalends of January. V, 2001, 2003. At the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, around the graves of the dead. V, 2101, 2102. At the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. V, 2268. At any festival of the saints. V, 2239. On Thursday. V, 2239. Or when the moon is eclipsed. V, 2239. Other customs of those setting out on a journey. V, 2004, 2269. Of those who sneeze. V, 2269. Of those dining together. V, 2306. Of those from whom something has been stolen. V, 2273. Or of those who suffer some illness in themselves or in their family. V, 2238, 2273. Arguments of the pagans against faith in the Trinity. VIII, 1101. Those who deny that God can have a Son or deny the resurrection are refuted. III, 2345. Laws against pagans. IX, 815. Valentinian forbids pagans to plead cases, serve in the army, or keep Christians in their service. X, 1751. Imperial laws concerning the breaking of idols. IX, 814.

The Palestinian synod at which Pelagius was acquitted. X, 1684, 1685, 1708. It is commended. X, 1808, 1812, 1831. The twelve propositions that Pelagius anathematized there. X, 1709.

The Palatini. V, 2087.

Palatinus the bishop. X, 1731.

Palchonius, pope of Braga. VII, 805.

The *palla*. V, 1978. The sacraments are carried in a *palla*. VII, 838. A *palla* over the relics. VII, 836.

Palladius, prefect of the praetorium. X, 1726, 1727.

Palladius the deacon. X, 1753.

The cause of pallor. I, 1433.

The branches benefit from the vine, not the vine from the branches. X, 1788.

We read of three loaves in Scripture; what are they? VI, 1316. The multiplication of the loaves is explained. V, 1903.

Pannonia devastated. III, 2353.

Pantagathus, a distinguished man. X, 1790.

Pantius. IX, 791.

The pope holds the larger dioceses. IX, 787. Pope Sylvester. IX, 786.

Papias is the source of carnal hope for many. VIII, 1218.

Paradise in the sense of a garden. V, 2041. The paradise of God promised to us is not the one in which Adam was commanded to work bodily. III, 2381. It was opened to all the righteous by Christ’s Passion. V, 2048, 2054, 2059. The thief entered it first after Adam. V, 2043, 2045, 2049.

What *παράδοξον* (“paradox”) is. I, 1446.

The day of Preparation is a feast day. V, 2047. On the authority of Paul himself. V, 2047. No one should withdraw from the church on the day of Preparation. V, 2036.

I spare. To be unwilling that God spare the wicked, as though this were a characteristic of all wicked people. V, 2251.

The leopard. IX, 787.

Honor and love are always owed to parents, and assistance in their needs. V, 2264. Alms should be given to poor parents before strangers. V, 2264. Those who disdain their poor parents are censured. V, 2264. Christ taught by his own example that earthly parents are to be renounced for God’s sake. VIII, 1146. They are owed not even burial if they prevent service to God. VI, 1055.

Parmenian’s see. IX, 775.

Paronyms. I, 1422. How they differ from homonyms. I, 1422.

Rules of frugality in food. VI, 1101.

That which takes part of a noun and part of a verb is called a participle. I, 1405.

According to one Chrysostom, infants are in the confusion of sin but not defiled by sins. X, 1736. Whoever denies that infants should be baptized, or says that they derive no original sin from Adam, is condemned. X, 1728, 1730. If infants have no sin, God is unjust when he takes life away from them. X, 1649, 1652. Or when he allows them to be tortured by various pains and sufferings. X, 1651. Or when he brings them before himself for judgment. X, 1652. The Pelagians promise eternal life to unbaptized infants. X, 1653. Catholic faith permits no alternative for them except Gehenna. X, 1654. Infants who die without baptism are condemned; nor should they be said to have been taken away by God’s kindness before they could become impious. X, 1781. They will be punished with the penalty of eternal fire. VI, 774. Nor is there an intermediate place in which they may live blessedly. X, 1654, 1728, 1730, 1769. But their punishment or condemnation will be the mildest. X, 1748.

Easter derives its name from the Passion. III, 2359. Its mystical meaning. III, 2359. Easter was celebrated only once. VI, 725. The individual rites of eating the paschal lamb are briefly explained. VI, 725. Easter was observed by the Jews on the evening of the day on which Christ died. III, 2288. The Council of Arles decreed that Easter should be celebrated throughout the world on one day. IX, 783. When it should be celebrated. VIII, 1221. The time at which it is celebrated and the mystery of that time. V, 2068. The preparation owed to the paschal solemnity. [Col. 0775] V, 1801. The history of Isaac’s sacrifice is reserved for the vigils of Easter. V, 1749, 1750. As Easter approaches, temptations usually grow more severe. V, 1775. Praise of the day of Easter. III, 2368. Easter is the solemnity of solemnities. V, 2068. How Easter is to be celebrated spiritually. V, 2067, 2068. The paschal Lamb is eaten in the one Church. VI, 1196, 1201. At the conclusion of the paschal solemnity the dress of the neophytes is changed. V, 2075. The days of Easter are days of indulgence and forgiveness. V, 2075.

Passerius the presbyter. X, 1699.

How passions and passive qualities differ. I, 1433.

How profitably Christ’s Passion should be contemplated. VI, 960. It is expounded. I, 1468, 1469. Its mysteries are explained in several sermons. V, 2036. How the devil imitates the sacraments of Christ’s Passion. III, 2279.

Even lengthy passions were customarily heard standing in church. V, 2320.

The shepherd announces the judge’s commands like a herald. V, 2077. His danger if he neglects to cut away vices by preaching. V, 2206. Goodness without discipline or knowledge is not sufficient for him. V, 1849. Christ our shepherd carries and refreshes, rules and guards. VI, 1070.

The book *The Shepherd* is praised by Cassian. X, 1817. It is considered to have no authority by Prosper. X, 1819.

“Father” is said in Scripture in four ways. VI, 1080. Honor is always owed to either of them. VI, 1080. One person is called father as a matter of honor; another is designated father with respect to faith or salvation. IX, 833. I recognize no father of salvation except God. IX, 832.

The heavenly Father is the special Father of Christ alone, whereas he is our Father in common. V, 1907. Abraham is a figure of the eternal Father. V, 1753. Isaac. V, 1760. Jacob. V, 1765. Isaiah. V, 1818. The Father is called the monad. VIII, 1165. Principal goodness. VIII, 1183. The beginning of the whole Godhead. VI, 976. It is his peculiar property not to be called “sent.” III, 2295. He never existed without the Son. VI, 1014. He was not God before he was Father. V, 2192; VI, 1191. It is better to say that he is wisdom than that he possesses wisdom only in the Son. VIII, 1174. He is omnipotent through the Son. VIII, 1181. Through Wisdom, who is Christ, he exercises dominion over all things. VIII, 1182. He is wrongly proclaimed to be incomprehensible and alone invisible. II, 1159. The Father declares himself through his Word. V, 1880. Thinking of himself as he is, he begets the Son. VI, 1014. And by that same thought he spoke the whole form of the world. VI, 1013. The works of the Father and the Son are inseparable. X, 1887, 1895. See God, Son, Trinity. Concerning the manner of divine generation, it is enough to know that he begot light from light’s radiance. VI, 1091.

A certain person called “Father of fathers” by the Jews. VII, 823. The Son of God appeared to the fathers in the angels, the bush, and so forth. III, 2270. Abraham is the father of the faithful, not because they are born from him but because they imitate his faith. V, 1745. The devil is our father, not by nature but by imitation. V, 1742.

The consulships of Paternus and Torquatus. III, 2176.

The Pelagians, together with the philosophers, teach that *πάθη* (“passions”) can be eradicated from the mind. X, 1692.

God’s patience is instruction in repentance and an offer of correction. X, 1859. To abuse it and not understand God’s kindness is already a great condemnation. X, 1870. To criticize God’s patience toward the wicked is characteristic of the wicked. V, 2251. The imitation of Christ’s patience is recommended. V, 1956. God wills those who love him to suffer something, so that he may justly seem to advance them. III, 2239. To bear adversity patiently. VI, 1188. Whoever does not sympathize with one who suffers is cut off from the Church. V, 1951. Heretics and schismatics must be subdued by patience. IX, 791, 792. Although patience loves to endure, it does not love what it endures. X, 1874. The strength of endurance is from God. X, 1823. A prayer for requesting patience. VI, 936.

Our homeland is heaven: how foolish not to yearn for it. VI, 1351. Those who think that the homeland of perfection must necessarily be abandoned are refuted. VI, 1104. It is better to leave one’s homeland in one’s affections than in one’s steps. VI, 1104.

Patricianus wishes our flesh to be evil. VIII, 1220.

To hang estates from one’s ears. II, 1116. Whoever wishes to increase his estate is wicked, if not by robbery, at least in desire. V, 2248.

The Patripassians. VI, 733; VIII, 1101. See Sabellius.

Patritius, vicar of the prefects. IX, 777.

Patroclus of Arles. X, 1751.

Paulinus, Saint Ambrose’s deacon, accuses Coelestius at Carthage. X, 1686, 1692. He resists Coelestius at the gathering of priests. X, 1686. He is summoned to Rome by Zosimus. X, 1725. His pamphlet against Coelestius is presented to Zosimus. X, 1724. Coelestius says that from the charges brought against him by Paulinus, Paulinus could be proved a heretic. X, 1724. Nevertheless, Zosimus orders him to condemn all those charges. X, 1724.

Paulinus Aelius. IX, 780, 782.

The book of Paulinus of Aquileia, *On Salutary Teachings*. VI, 1047.

[Col. 0776] Paul, the Jonah of the New Testament. V, 2122. “A wolf ravaging in the morning and dividing the food in the evening.” V, 2098. He stoned Stephen with the hands of everyone. V, 2251. Having wholly stained himself with the blood of martyrs, he became an Apostle. VI, 1099. Paul’s conversion. V, 2098, 2125. He was caught up into the third heaven. VI, 1028. Paul saw God in this life as the saints see him after this life. VI, 752. He suffered the evils that he had inflicted upon Christians. V, 2124. How fittingly milk flowed from Paul’s neck instead of blood. V, 2120. Paul is simply called “the eminent Preacher,” without his proper name being mentioned. VI, 1095, 1100. See Peter.

Paul the Hermit. VI, 1104.

A persecution arose when Paul was bishop of Cirta. IX, 797. What he answered those who were asking about the Scriptures. IX, 794.

Paul and Macarius. IX, 838. Workers for unity against the Donatists. IX, 800, 804. Ministers of the holy work. IX, 802.

Paul of Samosata. V, 2200.

The Paulianists. VIII, 1217.

The poor are blessed throughout the Scriptures. V, 2310. Here “the poor” does not mean all those in rags, but the humble. V, 2310. Poverty benefits many poor people nothing, since they are rich in vices and evil habits. V, 2311. Nothing is more foolish than a proud poor man. VI, 1084. The kingdom of heaven is promised only to those poor whose lack of riches is accompanied by humility of spirit. VI, 1085. He is poor in spirit who is humble. VI, 1084. Noble poverty is humility of mind. VI, 1084. Heaven is promised to the poor in spirit alone. VI, 1084. To preserve equity in poverty is perfect justice. III, 2363. The virtues or vices of the poor compared with the corresponding virtues and vices of the rich. III, 2372. The poor can be blessed. V, 1842. The poor must not be despised. V, 1842. Rather, they must be honored. VI, 1065. Why God has permitted them to exist. V, 1980, 2230, 2336, 2341; VI, 1176. Namely, so that the poor through patience and the rich through almsgiving might be able to merit God’s grace. V, 2330. The poor as merchants. V, 1892. Commerce between the poor and the rich. V, 2335. The misery of the poor is medicine for the rich. V, 2331. A poor man can make you rich. V, 1843, 2231. The poor man’s hand is Christ’s treasury. V, 2024, 2335. What is given to the poor is kept for us in heaven. V, 1881. No one can possess heavenly treasure except the poor, or one who provides relief to the poor. VI, 1081. On the day of judgment the poor will intercede for those from whom they received alms here. VI, 1076. What condemnation it will be to have despoiled a poor person whom one is supremely guilty of not having fed. V, 2231, 2232. The poor are to be invited to the banquet. VI, 1183. At holy solemnities. V, 1976. Caesarius publicly accuses himself of having sometimes neglected to give his little garments to the poor. V, 2024. The bishop acts as ambassador for the poor. V, 2170. The custom of dismissing the poor with the words, “Go on your way; God gives to you.” V, 2305.

Five kinds of poverty. VI, 1313. The worth of evangelical poverty. V, 1934, 1935. The vow of poverty. VI, 1099. He does not permit subjects to accumulate possessions under the pretext of distributing them to the poor. VI, 1099. What crime is committed by those who violate it. VI, 1084.

Little poverty. V, 1898.

In what way the peace of God and the peace of the world differ. III, 2286. What domestic peace is. X, 1872. Peace among the wicked is a matter greatly to be deplored. VI, 1239. Peace must not be called peace if it does not arise from the root of charity. V, 1916. Peace and justice are two dearest friends. VI, 1338. From justice comes peace, and from peace joy is born. V, 1917. Peace is not complete so long as the vices are being resisted. X, 1873. The first peace is that we may be at peace with God. V, 1055. Peace is perfect when we are at peace both with others and with ourselves. V, 1916. Praise of peace. V, 1858; VI, 1237. The benefits and effects of peace. V, 1931, 1933. Peace is Christ’s inheritance. V, 1932. Not to preserve peace is to despise Christ. V, 1858. The peace of Christ is the perfection of every pious intention and action. X, 1894. The blessedness of the peacemakers. VI, 1894. Whoever does not want peace does not want to be a son of God. V, 1933. Peace must always be maintained with the good, and war waged against the vices. V, 1933. Without peace, neither prayer nor offering is acceptable. V, 1933. Peace, to which the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem stand open on every side, and without which they are closed on every side. V, 2255. In time of peace, defenses against adversity are to be sought. X, 1875. The observance of peace with the enemies of peace. X, 1861. The peace of the times is to be secured by peace with one’s neighbors. V, 2078. By the word “peace,” the unity of the Trinity is explained. VIII, 1210.

The sinner is more his own enemy than God’s. VIII, 1149. When a person sins and separates himself from the Word, he becomes nothing. VI, 869. He is abandoned by the Holy Spirit, and darkness takes possession of him. V, 1821. The sinner’s bonds are prison, darkness, and weights. VI, 947. A threefold abyss. VI, 948. The sinner is a blind man who sees. VI, 948. While alive, he carries his own funeral. V, 1785. What evils threaten him everywhere. VI, 947. The sinner rouses every creature against himself. VI, 856. That the whole world arms itself together against those who rebel against God is shown by the plagues of Egypt. III, 2163. Why God does not immediately avenge himself upon sinners. V, 1963. Why he does not punish some of them here. V, 2322. For two reasons God does not immediately punish them. VI, 1033. Even to them he does not deny a father’s tenderness and the name of son. VI, 1034. Many sinners are punished in this life once the accumulation of their sins is complete. VI, 1034, 1035. Why nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners. X, 1862. The joy of sinners is a stroke of God’s anger. III, 2439. It is impossible for a sinner not to weep, either here or in the future. VI, 949. The sinner is destined either for the continual pains of a repentant life or for eternal torments. VI, 945. Every sinful soul has two punishments: ignorance and difficulty. X, 1896. Unable to remain within himself, the sinner turns to other things, but increases his restlessness. V, 2224. This too is brought about by the multitude of minor sins. V, 2225. Whoever turns away from God has taken away from himself both the will and the ability to do what is good. X, 1848. It lies within the power of evil to sin, but not to commit this or that sin unless God permits it. X, 1854. How God orders their darkness. X, 1854. Human transgression could not disturb the order of creation established from the ages. X, 1845. Sinners serve God’s disposition unwillingly, while those who willingly submit are not subject to his command. VI, 1139. God abandons no one except those who deserve to be abandoned. X, 1839. He abandons no one before being abandoned. X, 1841, 1846, 1848. God abandons those who transgress, hardens those who resist, and condemns those who despise him. X, 1671.

Every sinner is without excuse. X, 1886. No condition excuses him. V, 1904. The sinners’ empty excuses. V, 2213; VI, 1126. They can no longer shift their guilt onto the devil. V, 1979. The crowd of sinners is an unhappy consolation for you. V, 2321. The sinner accused by the devil at the judgment. VI, 1072. How sinners are not to be flattered. V, 1814, 1815. Whoever flatters them supplies fuel for sin. V, 1872. Sinners are not to be despised, but their feet are to be anointed with oil as Christ’s feet were. V, 1907. How they are to be led to repentance, and how penitents are to be received. V, 1772. The distinction between sinners and demons. X, 1846. “Sinner” and “human being” are two names. V, 2251. How the two are to be distinguished. VI, 1229.

All the saints truly declare themselves sinners. VIII, 1221. Every human being is a sinner. IX, 767, 769. No sin occurs that another could not commit if God were absent from him. VI, 877. In how many ways God has preserved us from it. VI, 877. The sins forgiven us by God are those which, under his protection, we did not commit. VI, 818, 856. God preserves us from sins in three ways. VI, 856. How often he recalls us from them. VI, 857. It does no good to call oneself a sinner if one still takes pleasure in sinning. V, 1977. In the sinner God hates negligence in returning and despair of salvation. VI, 1049.

Sinners are counseled against despair. VI, 1098. No sinner should despair of pardon. V, 1960, 2216, 2222. Under the hand of the almighty Physician, it is never advantageous for any sinner to despair. V, 2273. God loves to lead sinners to amendment. V, 1851. God seems slower to grant him pardon than the sinner himself is to receive it. VI, 784. Sinners must beware either of despair or of confidence in obtaining pardon without repentance. VI, 1118. The sinner should fear justice in such a way as to seek mercy, and trust in mercy in such a way as to tremble before justice. V, 2219. The sinner is between God and sin like a sick person between a physician and an illness. V, 1876. His first remedy is to know that he is ill and to desire the physician’s help. X, 1836. Sinners are given hope by what Christ did and suffered for them. VI, 907, 910, 956, 960. Sinners who know what God promised to those living well, yet live badly, judge him a liar. III, 2336. They justify God when they flee to his mercy. III, 2336. The prayer of the sinner who flees to God’s mercy. VI, 946, 949. From an angry God to one appeased. VI, 949. Another prayer mingling fear and confidence. VI, 936. Another addressed to Christ out of longing for tears. VI, 930. The sinner ought to mourn his soul as a mother mourns her only dead son. V, 2226, 2230. The sinner’s conversion is the greatest miracle. V, 1919. The sinner’s mirror. VI, 983.

Every sin is a lie. X, 1871. To sin is not to remain within the precepts of truth or within truth itself. VIII, 1142. Sin occurs when either what is forbidden is presumptuously undertaken or what is permitted is done disorderly. III, 2215. The Pelagians deny natural sin. X, 1734. They call those who think otherwise Manichaeans. X, 1735. Yet the Pelagians affirm that natural and original sin are one and the same. X, 1772. Those who say that natural sin, or some substance, is sin must be anathematized. X, 1772. Sin is not nature, but a vice of nature desiring what does not belong to its order. X, 1878. It is against nature. X, 1845. The Pelagians deny that original sin can be defended without saying that God is its author. X, 1767. This is refuted by many arguments. X, 1767. God is not the author of sin. X, 1833, 1835, 1839, 1841, 1842, 1846, 1848. Not even a Manichaean dared to make God the author of sin. X, 1739. Some have said that only death, and not sin, passed into the human race. X, 1772, 1773. God is the author of sin if he is the author of death. X, 1649. If human beings sinned by God’s will, there would be no judgment of God. X, [Col. 0778] 1847. Sin does not occur without the devil’s activity. VI, 1177. Yet it cannot be attributed entirely to the devil, still less to God. X, 1847. God did not ordain sin, but punishment for those who love guilt. VI, 1126. Even the Manichaean was compelled to confess that sin belongs to the will itself. VIII, 1141. This is also demonstrated by many arguments. VIII, 1142. Sin consists not in loving evil, but in preferring a lesser good to a better one. X, 1896. All sins have two origins: error and pride. V, 2003. Sin began with the soul. III, 2382. Adam sinned not through bodily desire but through hope of divinity. III, 2382. The soul does not sin except through the flesh. VI, 1075. By what steps Adam and Eve fell into sin. VI, 1051. In those two, the whole human race was originally condemned. VI, 1051. Eve borrowed sin from the devil; Adam, by his consent, made the guarantee, and interest increased it for posterity. X, 1649. Christ paid the debt. X, 1649.

The Pelagians teach that the sin of the first parents harmed only them. X, 1617. Some Syrians, and especially Theodore, first denied original sin. X, 1680. Then Pelagius, instructed by Rufinus. X, 1681. Afterwards Coelestius. X, 1681. Many of Julian’s opinions undermine faith in original sin. X, 1743, 1748. By what arguments heretics deny the transmission of sin. X, 1689, 1739. Christ found all the dead subject to original sin. V, 2257. Original sin is demonstrated against the Pelagians. X, 1647. The necessity of regeneration proves it. X, 1812. The death of all human beings also proves it. X, 1667. So too does the misery of the human race. X, 1882. For punishment would not have passed over unless guilt had passed over. X, 1617. Guilt is therefore evident where punishment is not hidden. X, 1813. It would indeed be easier for punishment not to follow sin than for punishment not to be preceded by guilt. X, 1667. Whoever denies original sin has against him many ancient Catholic teachers. X, 1725. Zosimus’s words clearly expound the faith concerning original sin. X, 1730.

By sin Adam made the human race liable. III, 2336, 2339. Hence the devil received power to mingle himself with his flesh and suggest the pleasures of wrongdoing. III, 2337. Original sin is present in every human being conceived through the intercourse of man and woman. VI, 774. Christ alone is without sin. V, 1977; X, 1650, 1773. All are subject without exception to the law of sin. V, 1944. The only one born without sin is he whom not the lust of the flesh but the obedience of the mind brought forth. V, 1997. The flesh contracts original sin and transmits it to the soul. VI, 810. Nor can it be attributed to God. VI, 810. In infants sin passed over not through an act but through uterine conception. X, 1650. It is not propagation but lust that transmits sin to children. VI, 758. The sheep of Jacob demonstrate the power of desire to alter nature. X, 1768. The stain of the corrupted root was transmitted through propagation. X, 1667. It passes through the shedding of semen, yet the semen is not the vice but is corrupted. X, 1619, 1623. Christ alone was born without seed and free from wrongdoing. X, 1619, 1620, 1623. We all draw the sin of the first-created human being through conception by seed, not through imitation of conduct. X, 1620. Hence we also imitate the wicked. X, 1620. When the first human being sinned, he sinned as nature, which was thus made sinful and corrupted; nature itself was not the vice or sin. X, 1619. At that time Adam and Eve were the nature of the human race, and therefore in those two alone we were all present. X, 1619, 1621.

Pelagius denies that infants have any sin. X, 1707. It is futile to deny that those born of two baptized persons ought to be free from original sin. X, 1683. Its guilt is transmitted even by one who has been baptized. X, 1885. Infants draw original sin from Adam, although they have not yet been able to commit any sin. X, 1728. The sins forgiven infants are not their own but another’s. X, 1725. Infants dying without baptism will be punished with eternal fire for original sin alone. VI, 774. The sin of the first parents made a wound for them and wounds for us. X, 1628. Some parents aggravate original sin, others lessen it. X, 1885. The first sin was remedied by that through which it was committed. III, 2389. Circumcision erases the guilt of original sin. X, 1781. By the merit of original sin the righteous before Christ were held in hell until he released them. V, 2060.

Original or actual sin could not be forgiven without Christ. V, 1830. Against the wound of original sin, the true, powerful, and unique remedy is the death of the Son of God. X, 1814. The guilt of original sin is in all Adam’s descendants. VI, 764. It is absolved by the gratuitous grace of the liberator. VI, 764. All original and personal sins are forgiven in baptism. VIII, 1129. The faith of everyone maintains this. VI, 1043.

The distinction between necessary and voluntary sins. VI, 945. No sin is necessary. VI, 1120, 1126. The original sin in Adam was voluntary. VI, 1120. Three reasons for sinning. V, 1869. A human being sins even when unaware. III, 2390. Even those to whom the discipline of the law has never come are guilty. VI, 1220. An abomination has been admitted among many, as though it were an image of innocence. IX, 776. But the one who does not think that he is sinning gravely sins more dangerously. V, 2285. Sins are more serious in proportion to the eminence of the sinner. III, 2304. Sin rebounds upon the one who does not wish to prevent it when he can. V, 2004. What harm the sins of others do not cause. VI, 777. Sins of the heart must not be neglected. VI, 159. Which sins are capital and which minor. V, 1946. Mortal sins. VI, 1121. The sin unto death. V, 1860. What and how great are the sins distinguished from capital sins. V, 2220.

The Pelagians deny that sins can be avoided without God’s grace. X, 1735. What sort of grace they mean. X, 1733. That a human being can, if he wishes, be without sin, and that some in fact were so before Christ’s coming, is Coelestius’s teaching. X, 1681, 1687, 1692, 1693, 1694, 1699. No adult lives here without sin. VI, 776. It is impossible for a human being not to sin. III, 2306; V, 1895, 1898. It is impossible that a nature capable of sinning should never sin; otherwise it would be better than God. III, 2326, 2333. The saints confess their sins not only humbly but truthfully, and pray for their remission. X, 1729. No one ever was or can be without minor sins; we can and ought to be without crimes. V, 1947, 1949, 2020, 2219, 2220. In small matters, the faithful and diligent person will obtain mercy. III, 2333. Minor sins do not kill the soul but disgracefully defile it. V, 1946. If they are numerous, they overwhelm it. V, 1946, 1947. How dangerous it is to pile sins upon sins. V, 2221. How neglected small sins produce hardening. V, 1787. How one who sins in one matter becomes guilty of all. VI, 1124.

The foulness of sin. VI, 945. Its effects. V, 1974, 2224, 2225. Sin grows when neglected; no sin is small with respect to God. VI, 1119. God will permit no sin to go unpunished. VI, 1350. None can remain unpunished. X, 1876. Human beings spare sins because they are widespread; but then they are avenged all the more severely by divine judgment. V, 2290. Why God does not punish the sins of certain people here. V, 2322. God sometimes waits for the measure of sin to be filled. V, 1811. After guilt there is no place for impunity, since the guilt itself becomes the punishment. II, 1101. For some, the punishment of sin turns into guilt. X, 1839. So that the punishment of sin itself becomes their sin. X, 1842. As a just God, he avenges sins, though in his foreknowledge he does not compel them to occur. X, 1895. Some think that an earlier sin of Uzzah was punished through the guilt for which he perished; and that it often happens that lesser faults bring vengeance for preceding sins. III, 2180. The punishment endured by the people because David numbered them proves this. III, 2180. The same conjecture applies to the captains of fifty consumed by fire at Elijah’s word. III, 2182. To what extent Achan’s sin harmed others. III, 2234. When sins cease, scourges cease. V, 2077.

The punishment of sin is the devil’s domination. X, 1845. Once the habit of sinning has arisen, one must fear that a person may be unable to free himself from the devil even if he wishes. V, 2222. Sins have easy entrances and difficult exits. VI, 944. Sin is evil in guilt and bitter in punishment. VI, 986. The punishment of sin must be preferred to sin itself. VI, 948. No one ought to sin, even if it were necessary to perish rather than to do anything that is not God. VI, 950. How grave and harsh the condition of sin is, the magnitude of its remedy reveals. V, 2014. The cross of sins is more grievous to Christ than the cross he took up for us. V, 2207. In baptism we swear to renounce the devil, his pomps, and all sins. VI, 1066. Those who postpone accepting the faith in order to sin more freely are rebuked. III, 2376. Four stages of sin. VI, 1231. To recall sins with joy is hateful to God. VI, 1050.

To sin is human; to desist from sin is Christian; to persevere in sin is diabolical. VI, 1155. No sin is so great that repentance cannot obtain pardon for it. VI, 1179, 1182, 1187, 1189, 1199. The forgiveness of sins must always be contemplated until it is obtained. VI, 1199. This is often necessary even for the righteous. VI, 1117. The sins contracted daily by the righteous must be expiated by continual good works. VI, 768, 776. Sins must be redeemed daily. V, 2221, 2224. Whenever they creep in, medicine must be provided for them without delay. V, 1788. The wound of sin must be treated while it is still fresh. V, 1803, 2219, 2348. God has provided remedies for sins that the rich and the poor can use. V, 2259. And from what else could we redeem our sins without great labor? V, 2335. So that no one can now say that he had nothing from which to redeem himself. V, d252. Their remedy lies with us. V, 2162. Remedies for sins. V, 1877; VI, 1348. Three remedies. V, 1869. Sins must necessarily be redeemed by good works, especially almsgiving. V, 1895, 1898. We can redeem them through charity. VI, 1066. The indulgence of brothers hastens forgiveness of sins. V, 1869. A condition so kind to human beings must be embraced that, by forgiving the sins of others, one may wash away one’s own. X, 1892.

How minor sins are cleansed here or after this life. V, 1947. They cannot be redeemed except by good works and the preponderant mercy of God. V, 2220. By what works they are redeemed. V, 1948. They were remitted through the ceremonies of the old law. VI, 1129. The minor sins of the righteous must be consumed by the fire of tribulation. V, 1771. By what works capital sins are to be erased. V, 1948. Capital and mortal sins committed after baptism must be washed away by public penance. VIII, 1217. Nor must it be denied that they can be resolved through secret satisfaction. VIII, 1218. They must be expiated through truthful confessions and worthy fruits of repentance. VI, 1066. Our sins should find us judges, not advocates. V, 1788. How great an evil it is to defend them. X, 1878. Sin is shown in the likeness of a monstrous serpent. VII, 846. It is destroyed by confession. VII, 847. Whoever accuses his sins is united to God. V, 2227. The remission of sins has two causes: one of gift, the other of repentance. III, 2377. It is hard to forgive those who intend to sin. III, 2377. A Christian must arm himself against sins; but because it is impossible for him always to conquer, if he grieves at being defeated, he restores himself. III, 2376. He runs well toward the remission of sins who is displeasing to himself. X, 1875. Past sins do not harm us if they do not please us. V, 1891, 2208.

The Church has been given the power to forgive sins. VI, 766. How much the Church contributes to the remission of sins. VI, 1119. What people do against us must be forgiven; what they do against God must be punished, lest we become participants in it. V, 2162. Whoever begins to redeem sins must not commit capital sins. V, 2337. Almsgiving benefits nothing those who do not abandon their sins. V, 1846. Nor do praises of God. V, 1847. The person who intends to sin is scarcely to be admitted to pardon. III, 2216. Certain sins are mortal in themselves but become life-giving through penance, though they are not immediately healed. VI, 1128. What it means to die to sin. VI, 1052. How the kingdom of sin is destroyed. V, 1861; VI, 822. By sinning we destroy God’s temple. V, 1835. We must beware lest, once restored, we fall again. V, 1835. How dangerous this is. VI, 1073.

Sin against the Holy Spirit. VI, 766. It is not forgiven. III, 2304, 2307. In what way it has no pardon. VI, 732. Only the impenitent sin against the Holy Spirit. VI, 1119.

Sins; sacrifices for sins. VI, 774. Christ is said to have been made sin for two reasons. III, 2268.

Beating of the breast. VI, 1148.

Pegasius. IX, 807.

Pelagius the Briton. X, 1679, 1684. “A white dog,” of the Scottish race, from the neighborhood of the Britons. X, 1696. Overloaded with Scottish porridge. X, 1696. Large and corpulent. X, 1696. Nourished by baths and banquets, he carried broad shoulders and a sturdy neck. X, 1696. Note (a). He was a monk. X, 1681, 1730. A layman. X, 1699. He persuaded two young men to abandon the world. X, 1713. Bound to Jerome by an old friendship. X, 1697. Known to Augustine by name and with great praise before he was known for his heresy. X, 1691. Augustine saw him once and again face to face at Carthage. X, 1691. Before he was exposed as a heretic, he wrote three books on faith in the Trinity and one on the actual Christian way of life, entitled *Eulogiarum*. X, 1679. On account of this he said that he was an imitator and completer of Cyprian’s work *To Quirinus*. X, 1704. Deceived and instructed by Rufinus the Syrian. X, 1781. He published commentaries on Paul. X, 1683, 1781. Before the sack of Rome. X, 1687. He attacks the commentaries that Jerome had written on the same Apostle. X, 1695, 1696. Pelagius’s letter to Demetrias. II, 1099. Words from his book to the widow Livania. X, 1690, 1707. How flattering they are. X, 1707. He and his associates habitually swore that these words were not theirs. X, 1707. Pelagius’s books contained brilliance of style and the elegance of Tullian eloquence. X, 1707. He entrusted them to his disciples alone to copy. X, 1707. His disciples admired the divine genius in him. X, 1703.

Pelagius, heir of Jovinian. X, 1706. A disciple of Antichrist. X, 1646. He acquired Coelestius as a disciple. X, 1730. He revives Judaism. X, 1690. He holds the doctrines of the Manichaeans. X, 1683. He himself calls those Manichaeans who preach that there is a shadow in the Law and truth in the Gospel. X, 1704. He could not endure Augustine’s words, “Give what you command, and command what you will.” X, 1691. He contends that free will is removed in reality if a human being can do nothing by himself. X, 1707. And that God is the author of our sins. X, 1706. He asserts that all are governed by their own will. X, 1691, 1703, 1708. He teaches that a life which can be praised on its merits must arise from us and exist in us. II, 1107. He denied that any human being was harmed by Adam’s transgression, but only by imitation. X, 1681, 1688. Subscriptions sought from the bishops of the plenary council against Pelagius and Coelestius in the year 419. X, 1731.

How Pelagius denies that the first human being was the author of death. X, 1689. He wants infants to be baptized for the kingdom of heaven, not for the remission of sins. X, 1708. He does not dare to profess this openly, lest he be stoned. X, 1708. His opinion concerning impeccability is expounded and refuted ironically. X, 1705. When Pelagius says that we can be without sin, he deceptively adds, “not without God’s grace.” X, 1693, 1694, 1699, 1701, 1703. By “grace” he understands the precepts of the law and free will. X, 1693, 1701. Therefore he teaches that those who lack knowledge of the law cannot avoid sins. X, 1693, 1703, 1708. How one should interpret what he said: “No one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law.” X, 1708. In what sense his claim that a human being can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments is tolerably misleading. X, 1713. Several of his opinions are quoted piecemeal. X, 1703. His teaching is expounded from Prosper’s poem and chronicle. X, 1684, 1691. The places and persons by whom it was rejected and refuted. X, 1685. Aurelius, Augustine, and Jerome refuted Pelagius’s teaching without naming him. X, 1697. Cyprian, Hilary, and Ambrose published many works against it. X, 1697. Jerome spares Pelagius’s name. X, 1695, 1697. He is an enemy of error, not of persons. X, 1697. Nevertheless, he did not think he needed to be cautious lest he seem to injure an old friendship. X, 1697. Augustine refutes the book that Pelagius gave to two young men, at their disclosure and request. X, 1698, 1713. Innocent likewise judges that it must be condemned and trampled underfoot by all. X, 1715.

Pelagius and Coelestius were neither bishops nor clerics, nor members of the sacred order at all, but wandered about like monks. X, 1683. Pelagius lived for a long time at Rome. X, 1713. When he arrived on the shore of Hippo in Augustine’s absence, he did not remain there. X, 1691. After the sack of Rome he lived in Palestine. X, 1689. Then, after his books had been sent to Africa, he was deprived of ecclesiastical communion, together with Coelestius, by three councils and subsequently by Innocent. X, 1689. He deceived some people at Jerusalem. X, 1712. There he encountered many more opponents, especially Jerome. X, 1712. Pelagius, a layman, sits among the presbyters at Jerusalem. X, 1699. How Bishop John protects him in this assembly. X, 1699. Nevertheless, John refers him to Innocent. X, 1700. Pelagius, accused by Neporus [reading uncertain] and Lazarus, is acquitted at a Palestinian synod. X, 1684. Some of the charges brought against him. X, 1688. While Pelagius was at Jerusalem, he deceived the Diospolitan synod, but at a later synod he was expelled from the holy places. X, 1689. By what art he deceived the fathers of the Palestinian synod. X, 1708, 1709. The twelve propositions that he anathematized there. X, 1709. The letters of the Carthaginian and Milevitan synods, and of five bishops to Innocent, together with Innocent’s replies, after Pelagius had been acquitted by the aforesaid synod. X, 1711.
