The Africans ask that, if he seemed rightly acquitted to Innocent, he at least restrain the serpent of impiety. X, 1712. They hope and piously believe that he has been cleansed and corrected. X, 1712, 1713. Innocent doubts the truth of the proceedings, but even more Pelagius’s correction. X, 1714. He condemns Pelagius and his followers with an anathema. X, 1714. Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned by Innocent. X, 1723, 1724. They were also deprived of ecclesiastical communion. X, 1689. This was done in response to the report of nearly all the African bishops. X, 1682. By Honorius’s rescript to the African council in 417, they were expelled from the city. X, 1727, 1731. At Aurelius’s instigation. X, 1731. Anyone was permitted to accuse their followers, and the penalty of exile was decreed against them. X, 1727.

The heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius was condemned by the universal council of Africa in 418. X, 1728. In condemning Pelagius’s teaching, the African bishops showed moderation toward its authors. X, 1712, 1713. Innocent wrote the decree issued against Pelagius to the Western and Eastern Churches, and Zosimus promulgated it more widely. X, 1715. Julian refuses to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius and writes to the Apostolic See. X, 1738. Namely, to Zosimus. X, 1739. His letter, in the name of several who appeal to the plenary synod. X, 1732, 1735. How they excuse themselves for refusing to subscribe. X, 1735. Various writings of emperors and pontiffs against Pelagius and Coelestius are noted. X, 1730. Although condemned by the universal Church, they did not cease defending their errors. X, 1730. The devil found no one so fond of his own error as Pelagius. X, 1619. Pelagius sent letters with a statement of faith to Innocent; these were delivered to Zosimus. X, 1715. From there they were sent to the Africans. X, 1716. How in them he attempted to deceive the Apostolic See concerning the baptism of infants and free will. X, 1716. The aforesaid statement of Pelagius’s faith. V, 2181; X, 1716. When Pelagius’s letters were read publicly, Zosimus and others were deceived. X, 1721. Zosimus and the Palestinian bishops, deceived by the counterfeit faith of Pelagius and Coelestius, are nevertheless treated and honored as Catholics. X, 1723. Pelagius was acquitted in the East because he said that he confessed God’s grace. X, 1713. Yet elsewhere he replied that he called nothing grace except the nature in which God created us. X, 1713. He is shown by the proceedings themselves to have evaded the judgment of the Eastern synod through equivocation. X, 1715. Afterwards he professed what he had denied saying to the Diospolitan synod. X, 1749. What he condemned in the Eastern judgment, he attempts to establish in the assembly of the Apostolic See under Zosimus. X, 1725. How Zosimus followed Innocent’s judgment. X, 1724. With Zosimus presiding, the priests of God condemned Pelagius and Coelestius. X, 1739. To mutilate them, Zosimus armed the right hands of all the bishops. [Col. 0782] X, 1731. Pelagius was condemned by Zosimus, together with Coelestius, on the basis of his own commentaries on Paul. X, 1687. After Pelagius’s doctrine had often been condemned, the Catholic faith enjoyed peace in the days of Celestine. X, 1754.

The Pelagian heresy is supremely proud. X, 1761. Through feigned humility it teaches pride. X, 1692. It embraces all the poisons of the heretics that flowed from the source of the philosophers. X, 1692. Which philosophers and heretics are the parents of the Pelagians. X, 1692, 1693, 1696. Origen, Priscillian, and Jovinian live in them. X, 1697. The authors of the Pelagian sect are eloquent. X, 1767. Pelagius and Coelestius are indiscriminately called disciples of Theodore of Mopsuestia. X, 1772. The Nestorian heresy is the offspring of the Pelagian heresy. X, 1686. The Coelestian and Nestorian heresies are said to be the same. X, 1684. Pelagians and Nestorians are allied in kindred errors. X, 1831. In what way they are kindred. X, 1683. In their interest Nestorius writes two letters to Celestine. X, 1754. As though unaware of what had happened. X, 1755. The Pelagians are said to have been received by John of Antioch. X, 1760. They praise John Chrysostom as though he favored them. X, 1750. Yet Celestine praises Atticus as a worthy successor of John because he persecutes the Pelagians. X, 1754. The followers of Pelagius and Coelestius are hostile to the Scythian monks. X, 1771. Through their faction Constantius, who lived in Rome as vicar, suffered much. X, 1724. After the Palestinian judgment, the supporters of Pelagius cruelly harass those living under Jerome’s care. X, 1710. The Pelagians have their own presbyters and bishops. X, 1682. They have no other Church. X, 1682. Therefore they do not reject communion, saying, “We are distinguished by the question, not by communion.” X, 1682. They deceive the simple and uneducated, but not ecclesiastical men versed in God’s law. X, 1693. They are publicly ashamed to say what they do not fear to teach secretly. X, 1695, 1697. They teach secretly and deny publicly. X, 1696. They first cleverly put forward their doctrine through their disciples. X, 1695. To expose their propositions is to refute them. X, 1695. This is also a victory for the Church. X, 1695.

The question between the Pelagians and the Catholics concerned the principles of faith and charity, and the origin of holy volitions. X, 1808. The Pelagians say that Christ, coming in the flesh, bestowed upon us not gifts but examples of virtue. X, 1741. They say that each person, according to the merit of his will, both summons and repels the Holy Spirit. X, 1684. They maintain that a human being can naturally do whatever he wishes. X, 1622, 1624. And consequently that Christ rendered us no service at all. X, 1623, 1624. They claim equality with God for themselves. X, 1692. And they attribute it to all human beings. X, 1696. They say that a human being is without sin, but do not dare to say ἀναμάρτητον [“sinless”]. X, 1693. How they interpret, “No living person shall be justified in your sight.” X, 1692. In saying that nature alone is sufficient for them to live without sin, they are refuted by the customary practice of imploring assistance. X, 1682. Those who teach that a human being, through free will as though sufficient in himself, fulfills whatever he wishes—or even that by the merits of works God grants grace to each person—are refuted. X, 1621. How contrary to the faith is their wish that a human being should become blessed through free will, with the support of the good of nature. X, 1769. The Pelagians are the most ardent praisers, and perhaps also practitioners, of obscenity. X, 1648. With shameless speech they publicly praise lustful conduct. X, 1641. By what words they defend it. X, 1644. How they interpret, “See another law,” etc. X, 1705. Or, “No one is clean from pollution,” etc. X, 1705. Those who teach that sexual desire is a natural good in human beings, and that there is nothing in it of which one should be ashamed, are refuted. X, 1639. The Pelagians say that sin entered the world through one human being by imitation of conduct, not by transmission of seed. X, 1619, 1681. Those who teach that Adam’s sin harmed no one except Adam himself are refuted. X, 1617. Their principal argument against original sin. X, 1767. It is refuted. X, 1767. It is also refuted that they say infants cannot be condemned for original sin alone. X, 1768. Or that they deny that infants contract original sin, or that they will perish from eternal life if they depart from this life without baptism. X, 1647. The Pelagians ordinarily reply, “God is just in judging.” X, 1653. Likewise, that an uncircumcised infant will perish because of the evil deeds which God foreknew he would commit when he reached mature age. X, 1953. They baptize infants also—but with what faith? X, 1656. They have two faiths and two baptisms. X, 1656. They brand the defenders of original sin with the name of Manichaeans. X, 1735, 1743, 1745. And they attribute to them the Manichaean doctrine of different natures. X, 1694, 1706. As though they were assigning our origin to the devil. X, 1735, 1741. The name “Manichaeans,” with which they usually stigmatize the Catholics, properly belongs to the Pelagians. X, 1650. What view of predestination they falsely attribute to the Catholics. X, 1657, 1662.

Five propositions of the Pelagians. X, 1614. Almost the whole Pelagian doctrine: that nothing is worthy of praise or merit if it does not originate from oneself but from God’s gift. X, 1824. The Pelagians say that grace is given according to our merits. X, 1807. And they strive for nothing more than to establish this. [Col. 0783] X, 1851. This is the most wicked of the Pelagian errors. X, 1793. Pelagius was compelled by the Eastern bishops to anathematize this proposition. X, 1808, 1812, 1831. In what sense the Pelagians professed that God’s grace assists and accompanies them in beginning, progressing, and persevering in the good. X, 1793. By what arguments they reject the necessity of grace for each individual act. X, 1693, 1701. In what sense they admit it. X, 1701. Their cunning in acknowledging grace. X, 1762. According to them, God’s purposes are not hidden if both grace and wrath arise from merit. X, 1852. They vainly protest that free will is destroyed by those who assert that we need God’s help for each individual act. X, 1694. They distinguish between existing and being able to exist. X, 1694, 1702, 1703. In vain. X, 1694. He who believes that faith is given blocks the way to their frauds. X, 1851.

The adherents of Pelagian teaching admit the necessity of baptism. X, 1733. And they declare that certain contrary propositions charged against Caelestius and Pelagius were condemned in their own writings. X, 1735. They acknowledge a grace that is always the helper and companion of every good act. X, 1733. Nevertheless, they equally wish one person to become just and another unjust through the human being, not through God. X, 1733. Declaring every human being, and then marriage as well, to have been created by God, they deny that sin is therefore natural. X, 1733. They detest those who say that human beings can avoid sins without God’s grace or assistance. X, 1735.

How subtle the Pelagian plague is. X, 1764. If some germ of this heresy is tolerated, it will be able to restore itself in its entirety from a small part of itself. X, 1832. Writings published in various places against the Pelagians. X, 1776. The councils and Roman pontiffs are praised by whom they were overthrown. X, 1830, 1831. Against the enemies of grace, the necessity of grace for each individual act was decreed by 214 bishops in the year 412, with the agreement thereafter of the whole world. X, 1808, 1837. With Pope Innocent taking the lead. X, 1808. The Eastern bishops, the Apostolic See, and the African councils detected the Pelagians’ cunning. X, 1794. The Pelagian heresy flourished in the East, spread in the West, was detected at Carthage by Aurelius and Augustine, and condemned by many councils. X, 1684. Its supporters were expelled from the Church by the Roman, African, and other bishops of the West. X, 1684. After Augustine’s death, this heresy was suppressed by Caelestine and thereafter, through the care of Septimius, by Leo. X, 1684. It was also condemned by the Council of Ephesus and by John of Alexandria. X, 1684, 1760. It was overthrown by Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Caelestine, Sixtus, Leo, and the laws of the Roman rulers. X, 1764, 1767, 1776. Under Augustine’s leadership the Catholic army defeated the Pelagians. X, 1802. From there they were expelled, deprived of pontifical favor and communion. X, 1803. They persuade people that they were unjustly condemned, although they wish to maintain that grace was not rightly defended by Augustine. X, 1801, 1803.

The Pelagians should now be resisted not so much by disputations as by authorities. X, 1832. Some people in Rome favor Pelagius for various reasons. X, 1713. Unknown to Innocent. X, 1715. The decree of the Emperor Constantius ordering that the Pelagians be expelled from the City and not permitting them to remain within one hundred miles. X, 1750. Another decree of Valentinian III ordering them to be deposed from the priesthood and expelled from the Gallic provinces unless they renounced their error within twenty days. X, 1751. When the Pelagian plague had occupied almost all Britain, it was cured there through the care of Lupus and Germanus. X, 1753. When it had again been brought back there by a few supporters, the authors of the depravity were expelled from the island through the efforts of Germanus and Severus. X, 1754. The Pelagians, expelled from the western regions, approach the Emperor every day at Constantinople with tears. X, 1754. Atticus did not allow them to remain at Constantinople. X, 1755. Pelagius’ teaching increases in the East and West, especially in Sicily and Rhodes. X, 1696. It is reported to Gelasius that it has spread through Dalmatia. X, 1764. Clerics of various orders, Pelagians, were rashly received into communion within the province of Aquileia. X, 1761. They are forbidden to be received unless they approve, by full and explicit protests signed in their own hand, the Church’s decrees against them. X, 1762. In the provinces of Picenum an old man who disseminated Pelagian opinions and tore apart Jerome and Augustine was tolerated. X, 1770. Many Pelagians return to the Church. X, 1691. Leo the Pope wished returning Pelagians to be received under a condition. X, 1730. Pelagius’ wise explanation of the Father drawing people to the Son. III, 2272. Likewise, the account by which the birth of human beings and their power for good and evil are explained. III, 2273. A certain heresy arising from the Pelagian source said that Christ alone lived without sin, and that every human being could do the same; and that Christ came to us not for redemption but as an example. X, 1751. Leporius, the principal defender of the Pelagian heresy in Gaul, is corrected. X, 1752.

Caesarius sent Pope Boniface a letter full of the absurdities of Pelagian error. X, 1792. There were some who, through simplicity and insufficient caution, held views about grace and free will that did not accord with the rule of faith. X, 1785. The presbyters—namely, those of Gaul—who, bringing undisciplined questions into public discussion, taught things contrary to the truth. [Col. 0784] X, 1756. And who remained in the condemned opinions of the heretics, whether through depravity or through ignorance. X, 1757. Nevertheless, they did not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Caelestius. X, 1757. And they professed that they approved what the See of Peter had decreed concerning grace. X, 1757. But they contradict our teacher Augustine, as though he had exceeded the proper measure, and they strive to scatter the memory of him, now at rest. X, 1756, 1757. Reported by Prosper and Hilary to the Apostolic See, they are sternly restrained by Caelestine. X, 1755. These were condemned among the Pelagians. X, 1830. Taking up again little questions from the school of the condemned, they disturbed the peace of the victorious Church. X, 1828. They renewed Julian’s insults and slanders against Augustine. X, 1830. Namely, so that the impiety of Pagans and Manichaeans might be attributed to a man of such great piety. X, 1794. What they were secretly spreading about him in particular. X, 1794. They wished to raise up the freedom of human choice against God’s grace. X, 1779. From these men Cassian teaches that the seeds of virtue are naturally present in every soul, but that the growth toward perfection is lacking unless they are awakened by God. X, 1817. And although elsewhere he admits that the beginning both of good actions and of good thoughts is from God. X, 1803, 1828. Nevertheless, he says that a human being can sometimes extend himself by his own impulses toward the desire for virtue, but always needs to be helped by the Lord. X, 1806, 1811, 1828. Thus he wishes these two propositions to be accepted together. X, 1807. So that in some cases a good will precedes grace, while in others grace precedes a good will. X, 1807, 1809, 1826. So much so that if free will is removed when grace precedes it, grace is removed when free will precedes it. X, 1829. Cassian’s entire teaching is contained in twelve definitions. X, 1828. From this follows the restoration of the already condemned proposition that grace is given according to merits. X, 1805, 1812. And, with all people divided into classes, that some are saved by grace while others are justified by law and nature. X, 1805. So that Christ is the protector of some and the savior of others. X, 1826. Other errors consequent upon Cassian’s teaching. X, 1830. Some Gallic bishops, also reported by Caesarius to Pope Boniface, wished faith alone to belong to nature, while all other good things belonged to grace. X, 1790. Faustus in particular is said to add the assistance of grace to human labor. X, 1776. And impiously to profess that the ancient saints were saved not by the same grace as we are, but by nature’s capacity. X, 1776. Several passages give off the same doctrinal odor. V, 2044, 2045, 2062, 2122. It was customary for them to say: “Unless I first will, grace does not come to me.” X, 1774. They make God a spectator and witness of Job’s patience, rather than his helper. X, 1824, 1830. They recoil from confessing God’s grace lest they later be compelled to acknowledge a definite number of the predestined. X, 1798. They vainly think that the statement “God wishes all human beings to be saved” contradicts this doctrine. X, 1774, 1798. They vainly use the example of Cornelius, as though he had merited grace by the powers of nature alone. X, 1796. Their statement is refuted by which they attribute the beginning of righteousness and charity to us, and only their increase to God. X, 1796. Those who say, “It is ours to will, but God’s to help or perfect,” are rejected. X, 1772, 1774. So also are those who imagine for themselves that, regarding the salvation or calling of the whole human race, God’s will has remained entirely indifferent throughout all ages. X, 1836. The synodical letter of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia. X, 1779. The Second Council of Orange. X, 1785. Pope Boniface. X, 1790. Prosper, in many books. X, 1793. Against these same men the bishops residing beyond the Isère assembled at Valence. X, 1792. Since they are not yet divided from one another by fraternal fellowship, their intention should rather be tolerated than their correction despaired of. X, 1832. This is hoped all the more because danger has arisen for them concerning their zeal for virtue, and a crisis concerning moral uprightness. X, 1795. Meanwhile charity must be shown them. X, 1784. And they should be advised to read Augustine’s books to Prosper and Hilary. X, 1784. But Faustus must not be received. X, 1777. And since his books are contrary to Augustine’s books, they are plainly heretical. X, 1779. Three classes of those who favor Pelagius, and how each class should be treated. X, 1832. Special care must be taken lest some evil germ arise from the doctrine that has been cut away. X, 1762. For such are its cunning devices that, if it is allowed, it can restore itself in its entirety from a small part of itself. X, 1832.

The condemnable doctrine of the Pentapolis. VIII, 1215.

The day of Pentecost is solemn above all others in every age. V, 2094. It is always to be observed on the Lord’s Day. III, 2289. By whom it is celebrated, not without reason. V, 2092. Many think that Christ ascended into heaven on the day of Pentecost. X, 2093.

Pilgrimages, so that assistance may be given to the dead. VI, 1321. The reception of pilgrims is commended. V, 2023. Their feet are to be washed. V, 2035, 2219, 2228, 2241. Pilgrims are devout Christians. V, 1902. Christian pilgrimage. V, 1877, 1879.

All created things were made perfect and, at the same time, imperfect. III, 2370. Some foolishly say that a perfect human being ought to be born and to know everything completely. III, 2369. Perfection does not consist in years. VI, 1062. [Col. 0785] When something is lacking for perfection. VI, 1120. How Jerome affirms and Pelagius denies that anyone can be perfect in this life. X, 1702. Let us never believe that we have arrived at perfection here. II, 1118. When we have begun to stand, we descend; and for us not to advance is to turn back. II, 1118. Consider that you must begin anew every day. II, 1119. There is no perfection here to which no ascent remains. X, 1867. There is none to which the labors of enduring the old person do not still belong. V, 1868. There is none upon which the disturbances of vanity do not intrude. X, 1868. All our thoughts should strive toward the rewards of the future homeland, since that is the perfection of our course. VI, 1062.

The dangers with which this world is full. V, 2033.

Persecution against the sacred books. IX, 781. Persecutions are not lacking for a Christian. VI, 1342. What the devout suffer in a time of peace. V, 1965. The persecution which these people suffer is that of vices. VI, 1092. The persecution of the wicked is not lacking for the good. V, 2249, 2272. The usefulness of this persecution. V, 2249, 2272. The persecution of the wicked is compared to a dream. III, 2442. What should be considered in the persecutor. V, 2348. When the wicked persecute the just, they suffer a greater persecution from the devil. V, 1862, 2257. The person who inflicts persecution on another in the body first endures it in the heart. V, 2159. To persecute the wicked is not evil. IX, 772. The final persecution will be throughout the whole world. III, 2426. Then the whole Church will withdraw from the place. III, 2426.

Perturbations: see πάθη [passions].

The Persians wear earrings in the manner of women. III, 2349. They consider it permissible to have intercourse with their daughters. III, 2349. Their ancient kings were not even seen by the peoples. III, 2350.

One must persevere in a good resolution. VI, 1188. Praise of perseverance. VI, 1249. The life of someone who begins well and ends otherwise is monstrous. VI, 1250. There is no perseverance in someone for whom his own progress is already sufficient. X, 1878. Perseverance is the virtue of a good work. VI, 931. How certain people perversely interpreted Augustine’s teaching on perseverance. X, 1836. Perseverance in the good is a gift of God, which in mercy he gave to some and in justice did not give to others. X, 1836. Why it is given to one and not to another cannot be comprehended, nor is it lawful to investigate. X, 1848. The fact that some do not persevere is not God’s fault. X, 1841. How the gift of perseverance is to be hoped for and obtained. X, 1857. Perseverance in a good manner of life must be received through God’s daily assistance. X, 1757.

The deposition of Persidius is confirmed. X, 1760. The colors of Persis. VI, 1110.

When someone calls them persons in the Trinity, do not suppose that he means human persons. V, 2174. See God; Trinity.

The art of actors in theaters. V, 1863. Those who put on the appearance of wild animals or women are noted. V, 2001, 2003. Nor should the eyes be polluted by looking at them. V, 2003.

The feet of guests and pilgrims are to be washed. V, 1748, 1760, 2034, 2209, 2228, 2241; VI, 1046, 1171, 1212. According to our promise in baptism. V, 2220. According to what was said to us in baptism. V, 2071. They are to be washed and kissed. V, 2195. When we fulfill this through faith and humility, we cleanse not only minor but also capital sins. V, 2035. Whoever Christ has not washed will have no share with him. I, 1468.

Worse. VI, 1076.

Plague. Concerning a Punic proverb about keeping the plague away from the doorway. V, 1966.

Petilianus, bishop. IX, 828. He speaks on Donatus’ side. IX, 827, 832, 840.

Petronius, P.P. IX, 790.

Petronius, ducenarius. IX, 816.

Peter, standard-bearer of faith and piety, and pillar of the human race. V, 1900. A stone for the foundation and a pillar for support in building up the peoples in God’s house; a key to the kingdom. V, 2123. Interpreter of the Law, defender of grace, destroyer of the synagogue, restorer of the Church. V, 2123. Chief among the Lord’s disciples, and the first suitable person to call the Jews to salvation. V, 2123. First among the Apostles. III, 2269. And their head, in whom all are contained after the Savior. III, 2270. He received primacy among the Apostles. III, 2384. He represented and symbolized the Church. V, 1940. Peter’s fishing and calling are explained with rhetorical skill. V, 2125. Peter’s walking upon the waters is recounted. V, 2102. Peter knew of Christ’s resurrection before the crucifixion. V, 2087. Peter was sterner by nature. V, 1899. He justly struck the high priest’s servant. III, 2314. And he was permitted to do so. III, 2314.

Peter’s most ardent faith would have failed in the temptations unless the Lord had prayed for him. X, 1797. Why he was disturbed even after the Lord’s prayer. X, 1797. Peter’s rash promise of love. V, 2035. But he could not stand by human strength, since this depended upon divinity. V, 2036. What is a human being without God’s grace except what Peter was when he denied Christ? V, 1899. The Lord abandoned Peter for a little while so that in him the whole human race might recognize that it can prevail in nothing without God’s grace. V, 1899. And so that a certain rule might be established for the future ruler of the Church concerning forgiveness of sinners. V, 1899. Thus, in view of his own fall, he might temper a harsher judgment toward sinners. V, 1899. Peter’s fall. V, 2037. Peter’s fall, a slight fault. V, 1900. Peter denied Christ the man. V, 2039. Peter advanced through his errors. V, 2102. Peter’s weeping. V, 2037, 2039.

Peter, prince of the Church, is to be followed not by imitating his denial but by imitating his repentance. X, 1892. The pastoral care of the whole Church was entrusted to Peter. VI, 853. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to him. V, 1899. We honor Peter’s episcopate when we celebrate the anniversary of his episcopal see. V, 2100, 2101. Power over the Church was conferred on Peter by the Lord. X, 1725. Equal power was given to those who obtained the inheritance of that see itself. X, 1726. Peter’s dissimulation, reproved by Paul, was a crime. III, 2407. Why Peter punished Ananias and Sapphira so severely. V, 2264. He pursued Simon Magus for so long that he brought about his death. IX, 772. He was struck with death chiefly because he had overthrown that magician. V, 2121. He was hung on a cross with his head turned downward. V, 2126. Emperors now worship Peter on bended knees. V, 2125. Namely, those who bend their knees in memory of him. V, 2127. Peter and Paul, two most powerful leaders, chosen for the salvation of two peoples. V, 2122. Two most illustrious merchants. V, 2122. Most devout parents of souls, differing in the pursuits of their parties but equal in the merits of their works. V, 2121, 2122. They suffered on one day, but through different deaths. V, 2120. They suffered not in the same course of time, but at the same recurrence of the returning year. V, 2126. Peter is famous everywhere through miracles, Paul through letters. V, 2119. The finest names of the Apostles—rock and vessel—necessary to the house of the Savior. V, 2119.

Peter Marcellinus Felix Liberius, prefect of the Gallic praetorium. X, 1790.

Peter, a most devout man. IX, 828.

Peter, domestic protector. IX, 816.

The letter of Peter the deacon and his companions to the bishops exiled in Sardinia. X, 1772.

A sermon of Peter Chrysologus. V, 2117, note a.

A rhythm by Peter Damian. VI, 930.

The hardening of Pharaoh. X, 1669, 1675. Pharaoh was hardened less by God’s power than by his patience. V, 1786, 1788. Pharaoh’s cruelty and drowning. V, 1789.

Philagrius, bishop. X, 1790.

Philippus, consul. IX, 815.

The philosophers are the patriarchs of the heretics. X, 1692. The philosophers who did not know Christ possessed no true virtue. X, 1747.

The division of philosophy into three parts and their subdivision. VI, 728. To philosophize is nothing other than to meditate beforehand on death. VII, 1274.

Phinehas’ zeal without carnal hatred. V, 2263.

The death and resurrection of the phoenix. VI, 1264.

Photinus, a bishop exiled in Sardinia. X, 1779.

Photinus. III, 2266, 2267, 2407; V, 2200; VIII, 1217. He wishes there to be in Christ only a bare and mere human being. V, 1855, 2182; X, 1717. And against Photinus, who denies Christ’s existence before Mary, by what arguments one should respond. III, 2282.

The Photinians. III, 2229. Their baptism is invalid. VIII, 1217.

Photius, concerning the Pelagian heresy. X, 1683.

Diabolical phylacteries. V, 2239; VI, 1171, 1173, 1174.

A work on physics. VI, 808.

The bishops of Picenum are reproved because, contrary to apostolic discipline, they indiscriminately mix everything together. X, 1771. And because they tolerate a supporter of Pelagian error. X, 1771.

Picridia. VI, 726.

The exercise of piety against vices. X, 1884. It would not have existed in paradise. X, 1884. Various degrees of piety. VI, 1323. The wicked persecute the devout in life and conduct. V, 1965.

A comparison of Pilate and Daniel. V, 2041.

The art of a cupbearer for increasing a small quantity of liquor. III, 2184.

The city of Pisa. VII, 840.

Fish were worthy to be blessed first. V, 2056. They represent the faithful who live in the water of baptism. V, 2056. Aelred permits fish to the recluse. I, 1458.

No one is pleasing to God except through what he has received from him. X, 1775. Unless God is working in him. X, 1783.

Placidia. X, 1730.

The mystical meaning of the plagues of Egypt. V, 1781. Their comparison with the Ten Commandments. V, 1783.

How to lament wisely. V, 1980.

Empty honor bestowed upon the planets. V, 2004. Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are said to have been born while the children of Israel were in Egypt. V, 2005.

Plato. I, 1441.

The undisciplined common people: an abuse. VI, 1087.

A plenary council. X, 1731, 1732. The plenary council of Bagaia. IX, 810.

[Col. 0787] Plinta, consul. X, 1731, 1732.

There were no rains before the Flood. III, 2157. Just as now there are none in Egypt. III, 2157. How rain and clear weather alternate. III, 2158.

What punishment is. VI, 1128. It is unjust to inflict punishment where there is no fault. X, 1768. It is more fitting for an unjust person to suffer in punishment than to have rejoiced in wrongdoing. X, 1872. How punishments inflicted by God bring benefit. V, 1947. Eternal punishments will be suffered by souls that lived even for a single hour without being released from the bond of sin. VI, 764. The guilt of one year among the people of Israel, compensated by punishment lasting one year, instills fear of eternal punishments. V, 1803. Eternal punishments. V, 2167, 2210, 2211. How just they are. VI, 1128. How severe. VI, 821, 993, 1186, 1200. The chief punishment will be not to see God. VI, 821. The absence of Christ. VI, 993.

Voluntary pollution excludes one from the kingdom of God. VI, 1102. After pollution, which usually occurs against our will, it is not permitted to receive communion unless contrition and almsgiving have first preceded it, and, if illness does not prevent it, fasting as well. V, 2299.

The pomp of the devil. V, 2235.

Pontianus, a fictitious prefect. VI, 1330.

Pontius. IX, 807.

Pontius, a senator who became a catechumen. VII, 845, 846.

What the people of God ought to be like. VI, 1038.

Human beings can keep God’s commandments. II, 1110; V, 2257. No one knows how much we can do better than the one who granted us the ability itself. V, 2257. The first human being possessed the good of capacity. X, 1621. By sinning he lost it for himself and for us. X, 1621, 1623, 1628, 1629.

How God may become our possession. VI, 1050.

Possessor, an African bishop, the chief of those who defend Faustus’ books. X, 1779. His letter to Hormisdas on this matter, and Hormisdas’ rescript. X, 1776, 1777. This rescript is praised by the African bishops. X, 1784.

Possessor, a presbyter of Donatus. IX, 796.

Possidius. IX, 816, 827. An envoy against the Donatists. IX, 815.

Possidius, assistant in the commentaries. IX, 816.

What natural power is. I, 1433.

A ducenarius of the eminent officials. IX, 816, 828. Attendants. IX, 816. The judgment of illustrious officials. IX, 818. The wicked opinions of those possessing power are set forth. VI, 1067.

Prebends. VI, 989, 1302.

Why the Church reads the Jewish commandments. V, 1930. The Ten Commandments, medicines corresponding to the ten plagues of Egypt. V, 1783. The commandments are observed in two ways. V, 1862. What is forbidden by laws because it is criminal is always illicit; other matters are otherwise. III, 2257. God’s commandments are not impossible. V, 1860, 2183. They apply equally to all Christians. VI, 1063. Those reborn through baptism can and ought to fulfill them with Christ’s help and cooperation. X, 1789. The commandment of love admits no excuse. V, 1860. He who is just could not command something impossible. II, 1110; V, 2257; X, 1746. A human being receives the commandment to seek divine assistance. X, 1807, 1815. By this very fact he is reminded of what he lost through his own fault. X, 1815. The commandments of the Law cannot be fulfilled except by charity, that is, through the action of the Holy Spirit. VI, 749. They can be fulfilled not by carnal will alone but by the Spirit both teaching and helping. X, 1642. God commands; indeed, may he bring about what he commands. X, 1643. Free will is not capable of fulfilling the commandments unless it is divinely assisted. X, 1783. God promised this grace to the faithful. X, 1783. By commanding, God makes useful whatever he wishes to command. X, 1883. God’s commandments are burdensome to the unwilling and light to the willing. VI, 1049. The burden of Christ’s commandments does not weigh one down by pressing upon him; rather, through grace it helps him fulfill them. V, 1867. Every commandment of God is light to one who loves. V, 1877. A person is not a friend of what is right if he would prefer, were it possible, that what is right not be commanded. X, 1877. The commandments of righteousness are fulfilled to the extent that the spirit of grace helps. X, 1877. God gives commandments in order to awaken desire and provide assistance. V, 2032. If anyone experiences something in them as impossible or difficult, he should not remain within himself but should turn to the one who helps. V, 2033. See Mandates.

How ancient the dogma of predestination is. X, 1670. An outline of predestination. V, 1816, 1817. What predestination is. VI, 775. Predestination derives from foreseeing or foreordaining the future. X, 1657. God merely foreknows evil things, but both foreknows and predestines good things. X, 1657. The statement that God hardened Pharaoh concerns God’s foreknowledge, not God’s action. X, 1669. God’s predestination is always directed toward the good. X, 1840, 1841, 1847, 1848. It in no way makes people wicked. X, 1841. It is not the cause of anyone’s falling. X, 1841, 1848. Unbelief is not predestined. X, 1840, 1843. Rather, faith, works of charity, and perseverance are predestined. X, 1840. God mercifully foreknows, not on the basis of merits, those whom he predestines to life by the election of grace. X, 1660, 1662. He foreknows that the others will perish through their own fault, but he did not predestine them to perish. [Col. 0788] X, 1663. Thus we rightly confess that punishment is predestined for them. X, 1661. Heaven, not hell, is predestined for us. V, 1895. Those who believe that some are predestined by divine power for evil are anathematized. X, 1789. Sinners are foreknown, before they existed in the world, as being destined to perish through their own evils, but they are not predestined to perish; their punishment, however, is predestined according to what was foreknown about them. X, 1662. Unbaptized infants too are subject to predestined punishment. X, 1662.

There is one predestination to glory and another to punishment. X, 1680. Some are predestined by God to punishment. VI, 1069. Some absurdly understand the vessels of mercy or dishonor with reference to the dignities of this age. X, 1783. From the condemned mass, God’s gratuitous goodness frees some, while eternal condemnation holds others in an unbreakable bond. VI, 764. From the condemned mass God prepares those whom he foreknows in his mercy—that is, predestines them—for eternal life; the others he punishes with the punishment they deserve. X, 1658, 1660. How he does this without partiality. X, 1660, 1663. In Jacob’s election there is God’s gratuitous goodness; in Esau’s rejection there is just severity. X, 1780, 1781. Nothing can be referred to predestination except what belongs either to the due retribution of justice or to the undeserved generosity of grace. X, 1847. What view of predestination the Pelagians falsely attribute to the Catholics. X, 1657, 1663. The Gauls complain that, through God’s predestination, human beings are driven to death as though compelled by a fatal necessity to sin. X, 1833, 1636. It is commonly reported that Augustine denies the remission of original sin through baptism to those who are not predestined. X, 1834. Likewise, that the necessity of perishing is imposed upon those who are not predestined. X, 1834. Both claims are refuted. X, 1834. Faith in predestination is certain. X, 1833. As long as we are here, predestination is uncertain to us but certain to God. X, 1847. It in no way makes children of God into children of the devil, but does the opposite. X, 1847. It is a cause of standing for many and a cause of falling for no one. X, 1847. It is not a fatal necessity. X, 1833. It does not impel anyone toward good or evil. X, 1836, 1840. It is in no way lawful to attribute to God the evil actions committed by human beings. X, 1833. A person is not disobedient because he is not predestined; rather, he is not predestined because he is foreknown to be going to be disobedient. X, 1839. In creating and choosing human beings, God has power like a potter over clay. X, 1668. Although predestination to death is evil for a human being, it is both just and therefore good in God’s sight. X, 1678.

Some predestinations concern binding and power; others, condition and justice. X, 1677. The cause of predestination to death is sin. X, 1677. How this is so. X, 1677. Some are saved by God’s goodness and grace, while others are abandoned by a just and hidden judgment. X, 1774. From those for whom just severity had decreed punishment, he absolved some from the coming wrath and abandoned others. X, 1673. The elect have no basis for boasting, nor do the abandoned have grounds for complaint. X, 1673. That many perish is the merit of those who perish; that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. X, 1845, 1655. The predestined person lives by faith given to him; the non-predestined perishes through voluntary unbelief. X, 1844. The predestined are those who are never erased from the book of life. VI, 1141. Predestination does not exist only among the Apostles, as the Pelagians wish. X, 1664. Whoever denies that Christ and his saints were predestined attacks the apostolic faith. X, 1783.

What the predestination of the saints is. X, 1854. It is gratuitous. VI, 767; X, 1886. This is demonstrated from infants. X, 1798. It is foolish to say that the Apostles were not permitted to go to certain peoples to preach the word because God knew that those people would not believe. X, 1659. Jacob was predestined through God’s mercy, not through merits or foreseen works. X, 1670. The predestined are called vessels of mercy, since they owe to God everything that they are. X, 1670. In predestination, no human being should exalt himself on the basis of merits. X, 1662. God gives his predestined grace and perseverance. X, 1785. The predestined must be especially diligent in good works. X, 1662. Predestination to reward is ordinarily made on the basis of foreknown virtue. X, 1678. The disadvantages that follow from predestination based on foreseen merits. X, 1855. The number of the predestined is definite and determined before God. X, 1798. God knows the number and names of the predestined and the reprobate. VI, 886. None of the predestined to the kingdom can perish, nor can any of those who are not predestined be saved. VI, 776. Why those who have lived damnably die holy, and conversely, is a hidden but not unjust counsel of God. X, 1663, 1664. The reason for this distinction is sought beyond the capacity of human understanding, and is unknown without any diminution of faith. X, 1798. Nor should we impatiently endure the fact that we do not know what or how great the vessels of election are. X, 1799. The profound mystery of God’s predestination and foreknowledge. VI, 886. Let us marvel at this in such a way that we hold it certain that there is no injustice with God. X, 1678. If God had condemned some to eternal destruction without any preceding sin, who would say to him, “Why have you done this?” X, 1676. Let us believe only that the guilty person’s death depends upon the judge’s will. [Col. 0789] X, 1664. The fact that not all are saved does not result from any fault in God. X, 1664. Let us interpret what is said about God’s will in such a way that we understand God to be neither weak, nor unjust, nor partial. X, 1665.

A passage on the predestined concerning Pelagius and Caelestius. X, 1682.

The preacher, distributor of spiritual jewels. V, 2319. And like a mother devoted to adorning her daughter. V, 2320. A priest is obliged to preach and to cry out vehemently. V, 1814. The power of priestly preaching for conquering wickedness. V, 1815. A priest should not seek to preach his own opinions. V, 2206. How necessary harsh preaching is. V, 2320, 2323. He provides medicines for the sick and arranges ornaments for the healthy. V, 2321. Timid preachers are reproved by the example of John. V, 2116. They may sometimes refrain from rebuking evil people. V, 2116. And by the artifice of charity they may lead them, through praise that is undeserved, to shame over their way of life. V, 2116. When preachers are like ascending or descending angels. V, 1761. Truth is heard more safely than it is preached. X, 1891. How the people ought to recall to one another the bishops’ sermon. V, 2327. The disadvantages of a preacher without the good works that should follow. VI, 1079.

The offices of prelates are sought indecorously. X, 1873. A bishop must always perform the ministry of preaching for the people entrusted to him. VI, 1169. More lenient prelates often foster great pestilence. X, 1763.

The guardianship of superiors is beneficial, when the Spirit guards both the flocks and the shepherds themselves. X, 1862.

Some prepositions govern the ablative, some the accusative, and some either case. I, 1406.

The distinction between God’s foreknowledge and His will. X, 1839, 1840, 1843. God merely foreknew, but did not also predestine, those things which He Himself neither did nor required us to do. X, 1844. God knows sin either as something to be forgiven, to the praise of mercy, or as something to be punished, to the praise of justice. X, 1841. God both foreknows and predestines good things; but He merely foreknows evil things and does not predestine them. X, 1840, 1844. God foreknew to whom He was going to give the gift of believing, and what benefits He was going to bestow upon them. X, 1855. With God, foreknowing, doing, and choosing are present at one and the same time. X, 1668. God’s foreknowledge compels no one. X, 1675. Nor does it impose necessity. X, 1840, 1848.

The presence of the Judge who sees all things is a great necessity for us to live rightly. VI, 876. The effects of God’s presence. VI, 854.

How faithful governors are to be admitted to or deprived of communion. IX, 783.

Presidius, legate against the Donatists. IX, 815.

“Had provided.” III, 2178.

Nothing is to be presumed without God’s help and will. V, 2035.

Bishop Praetextatus. X, 1790.

Praetextatus, registrar. IX, 816.

Praetors and palace officials: messengers of the king’s arrival. V, 2087.

Pragmatici [legal experts]. IX, 842.

Praxeas presumes God to be solitary. VIII, 1215.

Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem. X, 1689, 1721.

Presbyters are subordinate to bishops in dignity. X, 1756. They must not hold the highest authority in preaching. X, 1756. They have the third place within the Church. X, 1756. A presbyter’s seat in the basilica’s baptistery. VII, 807, 808. “Presbyter” is understood to mean “bishop.” III, 2302.

Priapus always depicted with Liber. III, 2344.

Primate bishops. IX, 820, 827, 834. Primates among judges. IX, 815.

Primianus. IX, 807, 821, 828. The condemnation of the Maximianists could not harm him while he was absent. IX, 841. His statement when he refused the conference. IX, 830.

“To begin” [principiare]. I, 1448.

What “beginning” means. III, 2365. Cerdon and Marcion introduce two principles unknown to one another; Mani, two contrary principles; the Sethian and Theodosian, three barbarous principles; Valentinus, many principles. VIII, 1217.

Principius, bishop. X, 1790.

Priscillianus was a branch of Manichaeism. X, 1693. Revived among the Pelagians. X, 1697. The Priscillianists wish the soul to be of God’s substance. VIII, 1207. The Priscillianists are restrained by the severity of the laws. IX, 815.

Priscus. IX, 816, 827.

Privileges revoked from clerics and churches are restored. X, 1751. He who abuses a privilege forfeits it. V, 1888.

“Prior” is said of one thing in relation to another in five ways. I, 1438.

Probatianus. IX, 787.

Probianus, proconsul of Africa. IX, 784.

On the day of a procession, certain things are not permitted that are permitted at other times. III, 2360, 2380. Relics carried with hymns and choirs of singers. VII, 815, 816, 835, 839.

Proclus of Constantinople. X, 1730.

The Proclians. VIII, 1217.

The proconsul’s assistant in the records office. IX, 816. Registrars. IX, 816.

Proculus of Marseille. X, 1721.

Procurators. IX, 818, 843.

God demands progress from us; and those are not approved who wish to be found on the day of their death in the condition in which they emerged from baptism. V, 2232, 2233. One must always make progress. X, 1878.

Three professions in the Church. V, 2327. Every profession contains both good and bad people. V, 1893.

Projectus, lector. IX, 795.

The promises of Scripture. V, 1889, 1891. What God’s promises are, and that they cannot be desired excessively. VI, 861. The promises of Christ and of the devil. V, 1878. God promises what He Himself does. X, 1863. The promises, especially those of baptism, must be fulfilled. V, 2234.

The Church of Promontorium. VII, 838.

Pronouns are either definite, indefinite, or more than definite. I, 1394.

Pronunciation, a matter belonging among the first—or the only—duties of oratory. I, 1441.

The prophets were despised in Judaea in the time of Elisha. V, 1826. The Manichaeans oppose the prophets in vain, since the Apostles agree with them. VIII, 1107.

The figure of prophecy leading to Christ: Naaman’s girl. V, 1832. A type of the prophetic word: the boy sent by Abraham to seek a wife for Isaac. V, 1753, 1756. Prophecies already fulfilled provide evidence for those not yet fulfilled. X, 1877. Merits are not increased by prophecy toward better things unless good works are present. III, 2178.

The fourfold nature of property. I, 1426.

What is one’s own. Only that is ours which reasonably suffices for us or for those belonging to us. V, 2264, 2268.

Property prohibited to monks. I, 1450.

Prosper and Hilary report certain innovators from Gaul to Celestine. X, 1756. Prosper, a man of God, disperses certain shoots of the Pelagian heresy at Rome. X, 1684. Prosper’s poem *Against the Ungrateful*. X, 1684. *Epitaph of the Pelagian and Nestorian Heresies*. X, 1686. Prosper of Aquitaine’s letter to Rufinus on behalf of Augustine. X, 1793. *Book Against the Collator*, on behalf of Augustine. X, 1801. *Replies on Behalf of Augustine to the Chapters of the Slandering Gauls*. There is no third substance in the human being called spirit. VI, 815; VIII, 1216. A corporeal spirit. VI, 803. The word “spirit” signifies wind. III, 2254.

Where “Spirit of God,” “Spirit of the Lord,” or “Spirit of Christ” occurs in Scripture without an addition, the Holy Spirit is undoubtedly signified; when “evil” is added, the devil is understood. III, 2179. Whenever the name “Spirit” is used simply in the New Testament, the Holy Spirit is indicated. VIII, 1184. The same may be said of the Old Testament. VIII, 1184. Some say that the Holy Spirit is the Father himself. III, 2387. Some think that the Holy Spirit served as the seed in the formation of Christ’s body. X, 1717. The Arians want him to be lesser than the Father and the Son. VIII, 1129. Heretics say that he is subject and obeys God who commands. V, 2092. They are refuted when they call him lesser or more ministerial than God. V, 2178. Eusebius vainly denies that the Holy Spirit knew the Lord’s birth. III, 2373. For he is not denied to possess the same divinity, substance, and knowledge. III, 2373. His substance is the substance of the Son and therefore the substance of the Father. III, 2374. If he does not have the same divinity, he has been placed foolishly among the Father and the Son. III, 2375. Christ’s statement, “No one knows the Father except the Son,” does not imply ignorance in him. III, 2374. Nor does the Apostle’s statement, “The Spirit searches all things.” III, 2374. The Holy Spirit may be understood as the star that led the Magi to Christ. III, 2195. The Holy Spirit is the priest of the Most High God, not the highest priest. III, 2329. See *Melchizedek*.

The Holy Spirit, second after Christ and third after the Father, is to be adored in the Trinity. III, 2280. He is third in order, not in nature; in rank, not in divinity; in person, not in ignorance. III, 2376. He is above all powers. III, 2318. The Spirit governs material substances. III, 2318. The Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son. VI, 820, 959. The indissoluble bond of the Trinity and of love. VI, 820. He binds together the indissoluble mystery of the Trinity. V, 2017. Charity is substantial, consubstantial with the Father and the Son. X, 1894. He is joined to the Father and the Son in nature and dignity. VIII, 1176. He is equal to the Father and the Son and inseparable from both. VI, 976; VIII, 1128. Whatever has been said of the unity or equality of the Father and the Son has also been said of the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1116. The Holy Spirit is to be adored like the Father and the Son. V, 2176. He is to be worshiped with equal reverence. V, 2088. He always existed. VIII, 1185. Many Scriptures teach that he is the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1184. He is nowhere called a creature. VIII, 1184. His dignity. VIII, 1184. The Holy Spirit is shown to be God. III, 2294; V, 2087, 2089, 2187; VIII, 1194, 1207. He is truly and properly from the Father. V, 2176. He proceeds from the Father. VIII, 1207, 1210. Therefore he is of the Father’s substance. VIII, 1210. How procession can be said to have conferred divinity upon him. VIII, 1210. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son. VIII, 1213. He is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son. VI, 734, 737, 770. He is from the Father and the Son as something given, not as something born. VIII, 1196. He cannot be called a son. VI, 737. He is neither begotten nor unbegotten. [Col. 0802] VI, 734; VIII, 1171, 1193. Rather, he proceeds from the Father and the Son. II, 1160; V, 2175, 2180, 2195; VI, 734, 737, 976; VIII, 1193, 1196. He alone proceeds essentially from the Father and the Son. VI, 755, 770. In what sense he is understood to proceed from the Father and the Son. VI, 1016. Because he receives from the Son, who is life, he is therefore life. III, 2237. He is from God and consubstantial with him. III, 2238. For the Holy Spirit, to know and to hear is the same as to exist. X, 1894. The Holy Spirit is a good teacher; what he teaches. V, 2093. He must be of one substance with Christ, since he is of one doctrine with him. V, 2094.

“Holy Spirit” is an appellative, natural, and personal designation; his proper name is “God.” VIII, 1210. The name “Holy Spirit” is relative. VIII, 1173. Yet not by reciprocal relation, as are the names “Father” and “Son.” VIII, 1173. Where the Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete, the distinctive character of his operation is expressed. V, 2188.

The Holy Spirit is not separable from the Son. V, 2091. Why he could not come unless Christ departed. V, 2091. He is the fruit of Christ’s Passion. VI, 963. His effect in us. VI, 963. To what extent he appeared in the form of a dove or fire. VI, 1016. The Holy Spirit did not assume a dove or fire. VI, 737. He did not appear in the form of a dove or fire in the same way that the Word appeared in a human being. VIII, 1196. Because of these bodily forms he is said to have been sent, but he is not lesser than the Father. VIII, 1197. He is another, but not lesser than the Son. V, 2088. He is like him in nature and of the same substance, and a companion of his majesty. V, 2088. The Redeemer’s vicar. V, 2088. No longer a sudden visitor, but an eternal inhabitant. V, 2088. Through the substance itself, not through operation alone. V, 2088. When the Holy Spirit appeared, Christ was present; and while Christ was with the Apostles, the Holy Spirit was present. III, 2287. If this is referred not to the person but to the nature. III, 2287. What he added to the Apostles’ perfection. V, 2088. The Apostles alone were not intoxicated with the new wine of the Holy Spirit. V, 2090.

The Holy Spirit seems to be more closely ours, as the gift of the Father and the Son. VI, 783. He is properly called God’s gift and charity. VIII, 1174. He is the pledge of immortality. III, 2371, 2375. He makes it possible to call God Father. III, 2372. Through him the sign of adoption is possessed; it was not so with the ancient saints as it now is among believers since Christ’s coming. III, 2371. Yet he was in the prophets for the sake of the dispensation, and in the righteous as the cause of holiness. III, 2371. He is the sign in a human being of Christ’s victory, and does not allow the one in whom he is to be held in the underworld. III, 2371. Those who think he was given to Adam do not know what kind of gift he is. III, 2372. The gift of the Holy Spirit is evidence that Christ reigns in heaven. V, 2093. Why those who receive the Holy Spirit do not now speak in all languages as formerly. V, 2091. Thus we have not lost Christ when he departed; we retain him by faith and possess the Spirit who comes. V, 2093. There is one Spirit, but he has many gifts and offices. III, 2286. The threefold form of the Holy Spirit’s offices shown to the Apostles. III, 2287; VIII, 1196. The gifts of the Holy Spirit against the seven vices. VI, 1261. They are compared with the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer and the beatitudes. V, 1868. The gifts of the Holy Spirit, now diverse in individuals, will be common to all in eternity. V, 2189. The Holy Spirit is said to groan because he makes others groan. VI, 738. He governs, teaches, consoles, and leads the Church to Christ. VI, 783. He inspired both the prophets and the Apostles. VIII, 1176. The words of the Holy Spirit are assessed independently of the merit of those who speak them. III, 2178. Nor are the merits of those who utter them increased if they do not have good works. III, 2178. The Holy Spirit appears not to be whole when he loses us. III, 2404. He must be invoked by us daily. V, 2090. Invocation of the Holy Spirit. VI, 908.

God often withdraws himself from his betrothed; why. VI, 1001. How carefully they must then conduct themselves. VI, 1001.

The conflict between stability and instability. VI, 1098.

A stationarius. IX, 780. See *apparitor*.

Stephen, also called Celeliel. VII, 816. Young and handsome. V, 2148. Endowed with most sincere chastity. V, 2137. Possessing wondrous charity. V, 2138. Given to the Church as an example. V, 2137. Chosen as deacon from the laity. V, 2138. Christ’s archdeacon. VII, 813, 814. Called an apostle. V, 2052. He first waged the Lord’s battle against the Jews. VII, 814. Why he prayed standing for himself and kneeling for his enemies. V, 2141, 2144. Saul’s conversion is owed to Stephen’s prayer. V, 2124, 2144, 2146.

Stephen makes himself visibly present in the form of a handsome young man. VII, 838, 840, 841, 853. He wears the habit of a deacon. VII, 838, 846. Stephen’s body was revealed to the presbyter Lucianus. VII, 806. His relics were transferred on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. [Col. 0803] VII, 815. When they were discovered, seventy-three souls were healed of various diseases. VII, 815, 816. A part of his body, given by Lucianus to Avitus, was sent through Orosius to Braga. VII, 807. Stephen’s relics, placed on the island of Minorca, produce the remarkable conversion of the Jews. VII, 823, 835. They are carried into the city of Uzalis with hymns and songs, the bishop carrying them in his arms. VII, 835. They had likewise been carried into the Church of Zion with psalms. VII, 815, 816. Invocation and protection of Stephen. II, 1097. A painting on a veil depicts Stephen carrying his cross on his own shoulders. VII, 851.

The cause of barrenness is harshness toward the poor. V, 2341.

Sacrilegious and ridiculous sneezes. V, 2269. They are prohibited. VI, 1172.

III, 2318. What are called second substances. I, 1426, 1427. Substance is not evil; rather, certain things are called evil and unclean by comparison. III, 2215, 2222.

One should not hang amber amulets around the neck. VI, 1172.

What pride is. VI, 1089; X, 1884. Its various forms. I, 1462. The characteristics of arrogance, insolence, pride, and obstinacy. VI, 1256. The nature and evil of pride. VI, 1058. How difficult it is to correct the proud. VI, 1223. By the vice through which a person was first overcome, he conquers last. X, 1869. The root of pride must be uprooted; it is not enough to remove only the branches through feigned humility. V, 2312.

What is superfluous, and what does not belong to us. V, 2265, 2268. What remains beyond necessities has not properly been given to us. V, 2338. God does not need your superfluous possessions, but he wishes to preserve them for himself. V, 2336.

[Col. 0804] “Lift up your hearts.” V, 1891, 1912. To have the heart lifted up toward oneself is pride; toward God, obedience. X, 1872. To lift the heart toward the Lord is refuge; not to the Lord is pride. V, 2083.

Susanna defended by her chastity. V, 2041.

Those who have been received. X, 1654.

No penitent from whom death is feared is to be suspended from communion with the faithful. VI, 1158.

The Creed is simple, brief, and complete. V, 2190. Brief in words, though great and extensive in its mysteries. V, 2191; VI, 1190. To recite the Creed at the beginning of a journey or undertaking. VI, 1172. One commanded to recite the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer returns from death and is soon restored to life. VI, 838. Several expositions of the Creed. V, 2183; VI, 1189.

The type of the synagogue in the bush seen by Moses. V, 1777, 1778. The dead Sarah prefigures the synagogue’s unbelief. V, 1754. The Church seizes the kingdom from the synagogue. V, 2113. The dispute between the synagogue and the Church. VIII, 1131.

Synodical proceedings are to be embraced, since the authority of the Apostolic See confirmed them. X, 1762.

The bishop of Syracuse is summoned to the Synod by a letter from Constantine. IX, 786.

T.

The letter T expresses the mystery of the cross. V, 1817.

A temple of God: our body is better than one constructed from stones. III, 2381. Spiritual temples are more precious to God than visible ones. V, 2169. Anyone bringing dogs into temples would be judged worthy of flogging. V, 2345.

The world is somewhat earlier in time. VI, 995. Time began from creation rather than creation from time. X, 1883. The Creator of times possesses all things without time. X, 1862. The times are not simply more unfortunate than those before them. V, 1965. How the harshness of the times benefits the good. V, 2249.

Terminatius. IX, 787.

Tertullian does not reject everything corporeal from God. VIII, 1214. He holds that something from the essence of the Trinity was brought down into the nature of creatures. VIII, 1214. After this life he hopes for what pertains to food. VIII, 1218. Tertullian’s book Against the Jews. III, 2243.

The two Testaments signified by two men carrying grapes. V, 1799. How Christ is in the midst of both. V, 1799. The type of the Old and New Testaments in the births of John and Christ. V. John. What was figured in the Old Testament we see completed in the New. V, 1762. The change from the Old Testament foretold and fulfilled. III, 2241. A splendid image of those who store up treasure in this age and those who store up treasure for the future. V, 1794. The treasure of the righteous is faith. V, 1842.

The points of agreement and difference between fearing and loving. X, 1879. Whoever fears Christ but does not love him has the faith of a demon. VI, 1190. The Timotheans wish the natures in Christ to be confused. VIII, 1213.

The day of Tiniarum. VI, 1172.

Tobis and Tobias. V, 1838, 1839. The encomium of Tobias. III, 2361.

The Trinity alone exceeds every understanding. VIII, 1188. This mystery must not be investigated. VI, 1259. Nor are the angels able to investigate it. VI, 1260. Or able to know it. V, 2173. Various heresies concerning the Trinity are noted and rejected. VIII, 1213. How many things there are in this mystery that humanity cannot grasp. VI, 979. The unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity are explained and proved. VI, 974, 976. The Trinity manifests itself in Christ’s baptism. V, 2011. The Trinity expressed in the words, “I will ask the Father,” and so forth. V, 2088. The faith concerning the Trinity is explained. V, 2175, 2176, 2178, 2180, 2181; VI, 891, 892, 909, 925, 967–984; X, 1716, 1732. The Trinity alone has no beginning. III, 2367. The Trinity has one incorporeal nature. VIII, 1190.
