The Trinity of unity and the unity of the Trinity. V, 2017. The unity and inseparability of the Trinity in the persons. VI, 924, 977. The unity of the Trinity is coeternal and inseparable. VI, 1195. The coeternity and properties of the persons are illustrated by fire, from which brightness and vapor arise. VIII, 1160. The equality of the three divine persons is proved. VI, 1016. Christ and the Holy Spirit have the same substance. III, 2195. The whole Trinity has the same will. III, 2196.

The one deity of the Trinity exists not merely through the charity of concord but, more profoundly, through this very united deity. V, 2179. The Father and the Son have one and the same nature. VIII, 1198. Such unity cannot exist in a human family in which the father is separated from the son. VIII, 1198. In the divine Trinity the unity of substance is so great that it preserves equality and admits no plurality. X, 1878. The Trinity is one God. X, 1894. One God, not three gods. V, 2194, 2196. We venerate the whole Trinity under the designation of one God. VI, 1209. Let us believe in one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity. V, 2092. To deny three persons in one deity is a Jewish error; to suppose three gods is pagan impiety. V, 2188. Whoever says that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are gods, and not one God because there is one divinity, one kingdom, and one will, is anathema. V, 2176. The Father, Son, and Spirit are three, yet one life. III, 2237. Three days, and one day. V, 1791. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are to be believed one God, three persons, not three substances. V, 2014.

We confess one and the same substance of the Trinity against Arius, and distinguish three persons, explicitly marked by their individual properties, against Sabellius. V, 2181, 2182. There are three persons and one substance, not three essences or three gods. VIII, 1194. The Trinity is the one sole true and good God. VI, 753, 769. Yet the Father is not the same as the Son and the Holy Spirit. VI, 769. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, not one person. VI, 754. They are distinguished by the property of their persons, but not separated by diversity of nature. VI, 754. See also more illuminating material on this subject. VI, 769. Only the proper persons of the Trinity are distinct. V, 2179. Cursed is the one who wishes there to be, according to the three persons, three substances divided among them, or three principles, or three gods. V, 2179. The Church judges it impious either not to distinguish the Trinity in its persons or to worship three gods. VI, 975. The distinction and unity of the Trinity. X, 1732. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not divided in divinity but in the quality of their persons. V, 2174. They are divided by their properties but united in nature. V, 2174. Substance is always predicated of individuals existing in plurality, whereas person is predicated of an individual rational creature. VI, 1014. The Trinity exists in the one who begets, the one begotten, and the one proceeding. VIII, 1209. “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are appellative and relational names. VIII, 1209. Each has the proper name “God.” VIII, 1209. The Trinity of persons is signified by relational names, and the unity of nature by the singularity of the name. VIII, 1209. In each case “Father and God,” “Son and God,” and “Holy Spirit and God” are joined together. VIII, 1209. In the Trinity we confess not only names but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons—or, as the Greeks express it, ὑποστάσεις (*hypostaseis*), that is, substances. VI, 979. The properties of the persons, which are designated by various names. VIII, 1171; VI, 981. “Unbegotten” is the same as “begotten,” but is not the same person as the begotten. VIII, 1158. The same through communion of substance, another through the property of person. VIII, 1159. If you seek the substance, the Trinity itself is one God; if the person, the Son is another. VIII, 1159. The Father and the Son are not two unbegotten beings. VIII, 1159. Yet the Son never had a beginning. VIII, 1159. Otherwise, if he had a beginning, time and place existed before him. VIII, 1159. Three degrees of the three persons in unity. III, 2369. Christ is the Father’s vicar and chief priest; likewise the Holy Spirit is called, as it were, chief priest and priest of the Most High God. III, 2329.

The Trinity is one and the same supreme good. VI, 827, 861. What each one individually is, the whole Trinity is together. VI, 861. Each individual person of the Trinity is fully God, and all three together are one God. V, 1748. Each person is fully God in himself. VIII, 1172. In the Trinity there is neither less nor more. V, 2092. Although the Father alone is not from another, no inequality is to be imagined. V, 1893.

The Trinity operates inseparably. VIII, 1173. As it is inseparable in its works, so it must be said to be inseparable in its persons. VIII, 1173. The works of the Trinity are common. VI, 770. The operations of the Trinity attributed to the individual persons. VIII, 1185. All things have their being from the Father; their rationality from the Word; their holiness from the Holy Spirit. VIII, 1185. The works of the Trinity are inseparable, even though creation is ascribed to the Father, redemption to the Son, and sanctification to the Holy Spirit. VI, 927. The whole Trinity raises the widow’s son. V, 1825. The whole Trinity made the human being, but the person of the Son alone assumed him. VI, 1195; VIII, 1196. How this is so. VI, 1195. How the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, yet all are not incarnate. V, 2196. Rather, the Word alone was made human. VI, 1015. Why the Father is not called mother, and why the Son is not called daughter. VI, 1014. The statement that Christ is one of the Holy Trinity. X, 1778.

The names of the Trinity are names of piety. VI, 820. The benefits of the Trinity to humanity. VI, 784. Invocation of the Trinity, by which we may be granted to believe and think worthily concerning God. VI, 967. Its explanation and invocation. VI, 820, 925, 927, 981. The one and indivisible essence of the Trinity illustrated by the example of light. VI, 1013. By the sun and fire. VI, 1321. Again, by the sun, brightness, and heat, and also by a vein, spring, and river. VI, 1195. Likewise by fire and the soul. VI, 979. Traces of the Trinity in the soul. VI, 783, 819. In it there is the image and likeness of the Trinity. VI, 805, 827, 1025. The unity of the Trinity and the distinction of the persons explained by the word “Peace.” VIII, 1210.

Two kinds of sadness. VI, 1097, 1159. Why excessive sadness produces death. VI, 1160. Sadness over worldly matters forbidden. VI, 1232. It is better to be sad while suffering injustice than joyful while committing injustice. X, 1876.

Tripolitana. IX, 785.

What force the sound of the trumpet has. V, 1815.

The writings of Tuentius. X, 1756.

What Tullius is. I, 1417.

*Tulta*, from the verb *tollo*. VI, 925, 967.

Turbantius. X, 1737.

Tysedi. IX, 804.

V.

Vacarianus. IX, 1244.

Vadianus conceives God as bodily represented. VIII, 1214.

[Col. 0808] The bishop of Vaiana. IX, 827.

The Synod of Valence on grace. X, 792.

The constitution of the elder Valentinian is praised. IX, 806.

The father of the younger Valentinian was Constantius. X, 730.

The constitution of Valentinian III against heretics, Jews, and pagans. X, 750.

Valentinus. VIII, 1217. He wishes Christ’s flesh to have existed only in appearance (*δοκήσει*, “according to appearance”) and imaginatively. VIII, 1214.

Valentinus of Vaiana. IX, 827.

Valentinus, a fictitious bishop of Carthage. VI, 1336, 1339.

Valerius. IX, 797.

Valerius. X, 1737.

A certain form of vanity. I, 162.

Varanes, consul. IX, 815, 817, 827, 828, 842.

When taxes are just or unjust. V, 1905.

Divine transportation. V, 1988.

Hunting is forbidden on Sunday. V, 2275. Nor are those to be approved who devote themselves to it during Lent. V, 2029. Dangerous hunts. V, 2225.

The hunter and the charioteer. II, 1109.

Venerius of Milan. IX, 808.

Venerius, bishop. X, 1755.

Venerius, deacon. X, 1779.

The province of Venetia. X, 1763.

What gluttony of the belly recommends. VI, 1101. How it is completely overcome. VI, 1101.

What wind is. VI, 1009.

To be wordy. V, 2238, 2275, 2281, 2287.

Where “word” comes from. I, 1441. The Word, as though “truly good.” VI, 1015. What it is. VI, 812. It is thought itself. V, 2112. “Word” is understood in three ways. VI, 1015. The Romans principally call *verba* the words with which we speak; properly speaking, they are those that we decline by moods and tenses. I, 1418. Every word produces a sound. I, 1410. It is a sign of a thing, so that the thing does not cease to exist. I, 1410.

What a word is. I, 1410. One may inquire into a word’s origin, force, declension, and arrangement. I, 1411. To inquire into the origin of a word is excessively curious and not very necessary. I, 1411. Cicero mocks the Stoics because they think that no word exists whose definite explanation cannot be given. I, 1412. What the force of a word is, and how many kinds there are. I, 1413. One kind is for explaining truth, another for preserving propriety. I, 1414. Some words are simple, others compound. I, 1409. We understand words in four ways. I, 1396. Five kinds of words. I, 1396, 1397. Why neuter verbs are so called. I, 1397. Some are so called through misuse. I, 1397. They are, as it were, semi-neuter. I, 1401. Common verbs. I, 1399. Why deponent verbs are so called. I, 1400. The class of verb called neuter-passive. I, 1401. Impersonal verbs. I, 1401. Inchoative, frequentative, and desiderative verbs. I, 1402.

The generation of the eternal Word. VI, 812. It is ineffable. V, 2000. To conceive it, we must transcend all created things. V, 2000. The Father declares himself through his Word. V, 1880. How the Word is his own and not his own. VI, 975. God is shown through the power of creating. VI, 975. The Word is the food of angels. V, 2035. Why the Word of God does such different things for different people is a secret known only to God. VIII, 1188. In a certain manner it extorts the conversion of some. VIII, 1187. All things are preserved through the Word through which they were made. VI, 869. Participation in the Word is granted to all in proportion to the affection of love by which they cleave to it. VIII, 1190. The Word of God is in Christ like fire in iron, and in the saints like heat proceeding from it. VIII, 1192. In Christ it is like the substance of ointment in a vessel; in others, like a scent received from proximity to the vessel. VIII, 1192. What it means to be separated from the Word. VI, 868. How the Word of God descended to us without leaving the depth of the Father’s breast. V, 2112. How he is always with the Father, always from the Father, always in the Father. VI, 975.

A splendid hunger for the Word of God. V, 2317. The people demand the preaching of the Word of God from the priest as something rightfully owed to them. V, 2317. Those who neglect to listen to it are rebuked. V, 1755. Whoever willingly hears the Word of God receives the ears of the soul sent from the homeland of paradise. V, 2320. The Word of God is customarily heard while standing. V, 2319. When the readings are lengthy, Caesarius asks that those unable to stand because of weakness sit down. V, 2319. He rebukes healthy women who also make use of this permission, especially those who lie on the ground as though on a bed. V, 2319. The Word of God is no less than the body of Christ. V, 2319. Nor is the one who hears it negligently any less guilty than the one who allows Christ’s body to fall to the ground. V, 2319. The Word of God is rain and light. V, 2284. It is light and food for the soul. V, 2325. The Word of God is manna. V, 1794. It tastes to each person according to that person’s desire. V, 1795. For the sinner it becomes a worm. V, 1795. The Word of God must be cherished with the ardor of the heart. V, 1853. Meditation on the Word of God excludes useless and wanton thoughts. I, 1461. The word shows what each person does or suffers. I, 1419. Good words are from God, evil ones from the devil. V, 1777.

The worms of covetousness. V, 1795.

[Col. 0809] Truth is the law of all arts. X, 1896. It permits no one to use either speech or talent for deception. VI, 1101. It flees the mind in which it has not found humility. V, 2314. What knowledge of truth is. VI, 962. Participation in truth, like participation in light, is common to all. X, 1879. Reason uncovers certain truths not expressed in Scripture. VI, 1143. There is no greater proof of truth than virtue. III, 2287. How hatred of truth is punished. X, 1874. Truth should prevail for the correction of the willing; for it will also overcome the unwilling. X, 1876. It is more advantageous to be conquered by truths than to conquer truths by falsehoods. III, 2328. What is true is better than what is false, although an evil truth may be worse than a falsehood. VI, 995. True things please good and religious people more, even when expressed in faulty language, than false things expressed in polished and ornate language. VII, 833.

Verus. IX, 787.

Vespasian. III, 2243.

Little garments. V, 2024.

The white garment of clerics in the administration of the sacrifice. X, 1704.

To make old women. V, 2001.

The way of Christ must be traversed on the feet of the twofold love, with humility accompanying it. V, 1874. The way to salvation is the head and body, Christ and the Church. VIII, 1130. Those afraid to enter the way of life are encouraged. V, 1956. The way of life is both narrow and broad. X, 1860. We are given the choice of narrow or broad ways. V, 1874, 1878. Both are to be judged not with the eyes of the flesh but with those of the heart. V, 1874. Christ presides over the narrow way, the devil over the broad. V, 1874. The sweetness of the broad way is brief and false, and its punishment long; the opposite is true of the narrow way. V, 1874, 1876, 1878. The broad way leads to the lower hell, the narrow to paradise. V, 1875. Who walk along the broad way and who along the narrow. V, 1876. The royal way is the law of God. VII, 1088.

The Vicar of Africa. IX, 789, 790. Acting as prefectural vicar. IX, 780, 781, 789. The vicar of the prefects throughout Africa is so called. IX, 784. The one who is called the proconsul. IX, 780. The vicar’s assistant in the office of the *numeri*. IX, 816. The vicar’s recorder. IX, 816.

Victor, who attended the Council of Arles. IX, 787.

Victor, bishop. IX, 791.

Victor, bishop, killed. IX, 814.

Victor of Busiccada, a traditor. IX, 768.

Victor of Garba. IX, 775, 805.

Victor, African bishop exiled in Sardinia. X, 1779.

Another Victor, likewise an exile. X, 1779.

Victor, presbyter. IX, 793, 794.

Victor Samsuricus, gravedigger. IX, 794, 797. Craftsman. IX, 797.

Victor of Aufidius. IX, 794.

Victor, fuller. IX, 795, 797, 798, 799.

Victor, grammarian. IX, 793, 797, 798. His interrogation concerning the tradition carried out by Silvanus. IX, 793, 797.

Victor, notary. IX, 816.

Victorianus, bishop exiled in Sardinia. X, 1779.

Victorinus, bishop. IX, 791.

Victorinus, bishop. X, 1731.

Victorinus, lector. IX, 795.

The three kinds of widows. VI, 1045. What a widow of Christ ought to be like. VI, 1046.

Bent, an old man. I, 1413. The wood of wheels. I, 1413.

Vigilantius denies that the relics of the saints should be honored. VIII, 1219.

We must always keep watch, but more fully in peacetime. V, 1852.

What a vigil is. V, 1886. Excessive and disorderly vigils are censured as intemperance. II, 1115. Funeral vigils. VI, 1009. The fruit of Christian vigils. VIII, 1117. To attend vigils frequently. V, 1977, 2019, 2022, 2029. People are to gather in church for vigils before dawn. V, 2275, 2280. Those who arrive late are rebuked. V, 2284. Men and women gathered for vigils, and a sermon was then delivered. V, 2320. During Lent women came to vigils with little children who were to be baptized. V, 1751. It is indicated that the poor and artisans attended vigils even on days that were not feast days. V, 2284.

A fragment of Vigilius of Thapsus from Book VI, On the Trinity. V, 2178. The book On the Unity of the Trinity against Felicianus. VIII, 1157.

The villa of God and the villa of humanity. V, 2326.

Vincentius, unconquered amid various tortures. V, 2095. He is healed by God and refreshed by angelic hymns. V, 2097. Placed on a soft bed, he dies. V, 2097. When his body is exposed to wild beasts, a crow guards it. V, 2097. A wolf venerates him. V, 2097. Then, thrown into the sea, his body is returned to the shore. V, 2097.

Vincentius, consul. IX, 809.

Vincentius, bishop. IX, 816, 827.

The objections of Vincentiana against Augustine’s teaching on predestination. X, 1843.

Commendation of Peter’s bonds. V, 2123.

Vindemialis, bishop. X, 1790.

The person eager for vengeance is restrained. V, 2140. How dangerously he prays. V, 2034. He provokes God’s vengeance against himself. VI, 1357. [Col. 0810] While wishing to conquer another, he is conquered by anger. VI, 1357. How he may rightly conquer it. VI, 1357. If someone takes revenge for a time, not bitterly and not with bloodshed, he does not sin; nevertheless, it is better to leave the matter to God the judge. III, 2262, 2264. When vengeance is left to God, harsher punishment is inflicted on enemies. IX, 792. How the saints seek vengeance. V, 2155. The vengeance sought by holy men in the Old Law against sinners arose from divine zeal and love, not carnal hatred. V, 2262. What the martyrs ask when they pray for vengeance. V, 1861. Vengeance should be sought for correction, not condemnation. VI, 1252. The Church avenges itself upon its enemies by killing error in them and raising faith. V, 2349. In a certain sense God avenges himself unwillingly. V, 1895. Divine vengeance ceases if human conversion precedes it. X, 1876.

Wine and youth are a twofold conflagration. VI, 1348. The use of wine was unknown among Roman women. III, 2350. What wine is useful for. VI, 1106. Wine is medicine; taken beyond what is proper, it is poison. VI, 1106. It is permitted to drink wine on Sunday; the elderly are compelled to do so. VI, 1236. What wine signifies mystically. V, 1919.

Violence. A person cannot live rightly without violence. V, 2112.

“Man” (*vir*) receives his name from virtue (*virtus*). V, 2292.

The rod belongs to rulers. V, 1805. How Moses’ rod was turned into a serpent. III, 2164.

Virgil, the poet. VI, 815. The noblest of poets. VI, 743.

The Virgin alone could provide medicine for our wound. V, 1998. The cause and miracles of the virginal birth. V, 1985. By being born from a Virgin, Christ consecrated virginity. VIII, 1146. Virginity bears in the mind the one whom Mary carried in her womb. V, 1988. The praise of virginity. I, 1458. Its excellence. VIII, 1219. Virginity is never bare. V, 1992. Virginity of the flesh and virginity of the soul. X, 1863, 1866. Bodily virginity is of no benefit without integrity of heart. V, 2165. How precious the gift of virginity is, and with what care it must be guarded. V, 1980. Virginity is gold; the cell, a furnace; the devil, the refiner; temptation, the fire; the virgin’s flesh, an earthen vessel. I, 1459. The treasure of virginity, once lost, cannot be recovered. I, 1459. Virginity is generally violated without intercourse with another’s flesh. I, 1459. The vow of virginity. II, 1105. Consecration. II, 1112.

The adornments of secular virgins and of Christ’s virgins. II, 1116. What vices virgins must avoid and what virtues they must pursue. V, 1893. The first care and primary pursuit of a virgin. II, 1105. How familiar meditation on the Word of God ought to be to her. I, 1461. Many useful precepts are handed down to the virgin. II, 1109. The virgin of the Lord is instructed in sacred precepts for right living. VI, 1108. She is contrasted with laywomen. VI, 1108. How a virgin and bride of Christ can also be called married. V, 2166. In the inner person we can become virgins either through baptism or through penance. III, 2437. Some invent that the Antichrist will be born from a virgin. VI, 1131. Virgin earth. V, 1993, 2031.

A shrub (*vigultum*) is that which is not consumed by burning but is rendered purer. III, 2163.

Virtue is principally God. X, 1818. The mind is not virtue but the dwelling place of virtue. X, 1818. Civic, purgative, and exemplary virtues. VI, 729. Sacramental virtues. VI, 794. The virtues of the soul. VI, 794.

Discrimination between virtue and discipline. I, 1433. What virtue is. VI, 782. The heavenly four-horse chariot of the virtues. V, 2289. The four cardinal virtues. VI, 781. How the soul may be instructed by these against vices. VI, 794. Possession of the heart is native to the virtues. V, 1811. The soul should possess virtues through exercise, just as it possesses their capacities by nature. VI, 782. Cassian teaches that the seeds of the virtues are implanted naturally. X, 1817. What was implanted by the Creator’s gift was overturned by the transgression of the first parent. X, 1818. The chain of virtues. VI, 1031. That the good things found individually in individuals can here all be present in everyone is false. X, 1747. No one possesses all the virtues in this world. X, 1702. The Peripatetics said that the virtues are intermediate. I, 1438. Virtues cannot dwell together with vices. X, 1818. When virtue receives vice, it is not vice but virtue that is abandoned. X, 1827. In what way virtues are harmed by a sin that does not appear to be opposed to them. VI, 1125.

The species of virtue exists among the impious, but not the truth of virtue. X, 1818, 1819. False virtue even in the best conduct of unbelievers. X, 1868. The virtue of the philosophers lacked goodness. VI, 1256. See Grace. The gift of grace is every true virtue. X, 1747. Grace not only increases virtues but also grants them. X, 1819. A prayer asking to be freed from vices. VI, 1076. The conflict of virtues and vices. VI, 1092. Whoever has learned through knowledge of virtue how far he is from virtue has made no little progress. VI, 833. Before God, weak humility is better than lofty virtue. VI, 854. The three virtues to be embraced by one who proposes to live honorably. VI, 1105.

Certain customary and human visions. VI, 797, 798. The soul forms within itself images of seen bodies with marvelous speed; it is not the bodies that are seen that produce them. VI, 798. Visions occasioned by the relics of Saint Stephen. VII, 807, 834, 835, 836, 838, 841, 846. Others foretelling the conversion of the Jews. VII, 824. Three kinds of visions. VI, 751, 796, 1028.

The vision of God is the complete blessedness of humankind. VI, 895. Its many names. VI, 1012. The blessed vision of God, wherever it occurs, is itself the kingdom of heaven. VI, 1113. The ineffable sweetness of the vision of God. VI, 994. What it confers upon the blessed. VI, 996. What it will be like in them. I, 1474. The vision of the blessed is threefold: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual. VI, 997.

The insensible life of the earth. III, 2171. The life of the soul. X, 1873. The several degrees of bodily life, by which it imitates spiritual life. VI, 790. How mercifully God has dispensed both our lives. V, 2231. The four degrees of the spiritual life. V, 1807. The great necessity for living rightly implanted in us. VI, 876. The rule of living handed down in two verses. VI, 986. He truly knows how to live rightly who rightly knows how to pray. V, 1849. The origin of an evil life. VI, 764. Practices. V, 2209. The knowledge of life treated in a special book by Honorius of Autun. VI, 1005. This title is marked by the author himself. VI, 1007.

Who may possess the true life. X, 1616. The falsity of the present life. VI, 1332. The distinction between eternal and present life. VIII, 1129. A comparison of the two. VI, 1350, 1353. The miseries of this life. VI, 917, 955, 981, 982. The thought of eternal life alleviates its labors. II, 1119, 1120. How useful frequent reflection upon it is. VI, 917. The joys and punishments of the future life must always be meditated upon. VI, 1061. The happiness of eternal life. VI, 917, 954, 958, 981, 1184. See Blessed, Heaven, Kingdom. Eternal life consists not in difficult commandments but in good will. V, 1915, 1920. It is to be attained through right faith and works worthy of faith. VI, 927. To change one’s life is one thing; to endure life is another. V, 2339. Repentance prepares one for eternal life; Christ leads one to it. VI, 1147. A guest here, God everywhere: if he is received by us, he will receive us after death. VI, 1149.

Vitalis. IX, 787.

Vitalis the presbyter. X, 1700.

Vitalis the notary. IX, 816.

Vice can exist neither in the highest good nor except in some good. X, 1871, 1874, 1884, 1885, 1896. All vices are enemies of God. V, 2083. What vice is, how many kinds there are, and when it constitutes guilt. VI, 1189. Vice is contrary to nature. X, 1870, 1896. Vices are partly born with us and thereafter nourished. V, 1742. Every vice is to be located in the will. V, 1936. The alliances of vices are bound by a stronger glue. X, 1761. The conflict of vices and virtues. VI, 1191. Vice had to be demonstrated by the law and healed by grace. X, 1863. Three vices to be feared. VI, 1354. Three things to be avoided by one who proposes an honorable life. VI, 1105. Our vices will make a ladder and raise us up if they are beneath us. V, 2082.

The piety of Vitula, a noblewoman. VII, 843.

Among the Jews, the anointed are only priests, prophets, or kings. VI, 1033. Anointing with blessed oil obtains bodily health and remission of sins for the sick. V, 2238, 2273.

Sabellius takes the Father and the Son as a union. III, 2267.

Personal union of the soul with the body, and of God with the soul, explained. VI, 789.

The benefit of a gratuitous calling. VI, 853, 943. Why it has not been granted to all. X, 1835, 1841, 1842. All who hear the word of God are called alike. X, 1835, 1841. Why one of these believes and another does not: in the former, the operation of divine grace prevails; in the latter, an aversion of the will. X, 1835. Works are the reason why God calls one person and does not call another. V, 1882.

Vocius. IX, 787.

What the will is. VI, 729. Nothing is richer than a good will. I, 1465. How rich a good will is. V, 2248. It is itself called charity. V, 2248. Its value and merit. VI, 962. Isaac’s will, as a just man, was good; if it was good, why was it not fulfilled in Esau’s blessing? III, 2223. God sometimes gives the will to do good but prohibits its execution. X, 1816. A perfect will to do something is reckoned as the deed itself. V, 2025. Every movement of a good will is from God. X, 1758, 1759. The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily and spiritual movements. X, 1864.

Human free will must be subjected to grace in all things. X, 1785. A good will is so truly human that it is conceived under God’s inspiration. X, 1817, 1827. When the will is to be called ours and when God’s. X, 1788. In good actions the will is from grace; in evil actions it is to be understood as acting without grace. X, 1836. It falls through human action; it stands through divine gift. X, 1836. Whether it is God’s will that any of those who say, “Your will be done,” should ask for something against themselves. X, 1848. It is not God’s will that human beings fall away from salvation, holiness, and so forth. X, 1846, 1848. Nor that a human being should do the will of the devil. X, 1845. The will to do what the highest and inmost Truth forbids is the soul’s first vice. X, 1896. An evil will is also punished when it receives the power to accomplish what it desires. X, 1863. Those who have despised God’s will when it invited them will experience it when it takes vengeance. X, 1850.

The pleasures of the world are compared with the dream of people condemned to the mines. VI, 1200. Julian makes an exception only for sexual pleasure, which does not move by the decision of our mind. X, 1740. See Lust.

Volusianus, prefect of the City, while serving as envoy at Constantinople, is baptized by Proclus. X, 1730. The threat of execution is made against him unless he expels the Pelagians from the city. X, 1750. His edict against Coelestius. X, 1751.

A vow owed to God. X, 1860. It is of no benefit outside the Catholic Church. X, 1860. No one would rightly make a vow unless he received from God what he was to vow. X, 1787, 1864. “Let us vow to the Lord”: he will grant the ability to fulfill the vow. V, 1978. Our guardian angels offer our vows to God. V, 1979. The vow of virginity. II, 1106. The obligation of a vow of continence. VI, 768, 777. One vows a cloak, another oil or wax, another abstinence from wine or meat. V, 1978. The best vow of conduct is conversion. V, 1978. The fruit of this vow. V, 1979.

The voice is the sign of thought and, as it were, a vehicle of the word. V, 2112, 2115.

U.

Urbanus of Caris. IX, 774.

Urbanus of Formae. IX, 803.

[UNPUBLISHED SERMONS.]

[Col. 0813]

TO THE AUGUSTINIAN READER.

[Col. 0813] The writings of the divine Aurelius Augustine have always been held in the highest esteem by all worshipers of the Christian faith, except those who have fruitlessly sought their own opinions in them. Yet after the extensive editions of Johann Amerbach, Johann Froben, the theologians of Louvain, and the monks of the once flourishing Congregation of Saint Maur; after the contributions of Jacques Sirmond, Jean-Baptiste Mari, Hieronymus Vignier, and Godfrey Bessel (*Συμβολαί*, “Contributions”); and even when, toward the very end of the eighteenth century, one might have thought that further additions could scarcely be made, since those highly learned and industrious men seemed to have spared no labor in examining the libraries of Europe, I nevertheless regard the gleaning left to me after so rich a harvest as, among divine gifts, a part of my own happiness. For I do not think that I deserve nothing from the Church of Christ, since I am once again awakening the voices of so great a Doctor, with which it resounded more than thirteen hundred years ago, after they had lain suppressed for easily six hundred years. How this came about, hear briefly.

After completing the first volume of the *Recensions*, which contains nearly a thousand theological manuscripts brought to the Viennese Palatine Library in the time of Emperor Charles VI, and which is now at the press, as I was undertaking the second volume, which was to contain the manuscripts acquired from that time to the present, a Codex numbered Ten was offered to me at the end of November of the past year. It was written on large-format parchment in two columns in the twelfth century, neither inelegantly nor inaccurately; for whatever the first hand had at times got wrong, a second, more learned though contemporary (*σύγχρονος*), had for the most part diligently corrected.

As soon as I examined it, I encountered at the lower edge of the first page the following note: “This book belongs to the Congregation of Saint Justina of Padua; assigned to the Monastery of Saint Severinus at Naples.” You may perhaps have read in Volume I of Lambecius’s *Commentaries*, Kollar’s edition, Supplement, column 763, that in the year 1717 quite a few manuscript books had been presented to Emperor Charles VI, then King of the Two Sicilies, as gifts from various Neapolitan monasteries. At once there came to mind the illustrious Bernard de Montfaucon, who, while his associates were laboring in Paris on the edition of Augustine, had reached Naples in October 1698 during a literary journey to Italy. I consult his *Diarium Italicum*, printed at Paris in 1702, chapter XXI, p. 319. “Before we left Naples,” he says, “we copied the following note from the library of manuscripts of the Monastery of Saint Severinus.” He then lists the codices, and in seventh place: “Certain sermons of Augustine, and the *Retractations* in a twelfth-century codex.” Here is our very codex (*αὐτότατος*), which also contains the *Retractations*. Thus that most celebrated man, either relying only upon the catalogs of the Severinati monks or falsely persuaded that nothing more of Augustine’s sermons survived that had escaped his brethren, deprived them—without even opening the codex—of this supplement, which they could at least have added to Volume XI, and handed the torch, as they say, to me, which I gladly accept.

I shall not here investigate with you, Reader, how it could have happened that this exceptional codex remained hidden for so long, nor shall I burden you with the aids by which it was necessary—and by which I diligently endeavored—to uncover and establish beyond doubt the authenticity (*γνησιότης*) and unpublished character (*ἀνέκδοσις*) of the material I publish from it. Scholars know these matters. I come to the point.

I first share with you the list of fifty-six sermons that the scribe placed before the codex. You will see in it that unpublished sermons run alongside published ones in sequence. For each published passage I note where it is found in the works of the holy Doctor; here I always wish the Maurist Paris edition of 1689–1700 to be understood. So that you may immediately distinguish the unpublished sermons, I have placed in the margin beside each the number under which it will appear; what I thought should be observed about them I have deferred to the beginnings of the individual sermons. Here, then, is the list.

I. Sermon on the Praise of the Paschal Candle. Chapter I.

II. Likewise, another sermon by the same author—namely Augustine—at the Easter Vigil. Chapter II. Another by the same author on Easter Day. Chapter III. Volume V of the Maurist edition, Sermon 228.

III. Another on the sacraments on the same day. Chapter IV.

IV. Likewise, another on the same day. Chapter V.

Another by the same author on the same day, concerning the fact that before baptism the priests anoint the ears and nostrils of the newly baptized with holy oil. Chapter IX. Volume VI, Appendix, column 288. The editors followed Jacques Sirmond, who was the first to publish it and removed it from Augustine, although in the Fleury Codex from which he published it, it was attributed to Augustine and cited under his name by Ivo of Chartres and by another very ancient, Remigian, codex—and this sermon and the following two as well. Add that our codex places them amid the genuine sermons. Another by the same author on the mystery and holiness of baptism. Chapter X. Volume VI, Appendix, column 289. See what I noted below. In the cited volume, Sermon 330. Chapter XXXIX. In the cited volume, Sermon 153. In our codex a folio has fallen out, so that the text breaks off at the words: “Because it is dead, he said, it lies hidden: not ap . . .”

Another by the same author on original sin and on the Apostle’s reading: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not,” and so forth. Against the Pelagians. Chapter XL. Another by the same author on the Apostle’s reading, where he says: “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.” Against the Pelagians and the Stoic and Epicurean philosophers. Chapter XLII. In the cited volume, Sermon 156.

A sermon by the same author on the Apostle’s reading: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance, because Christ Jesus came into the world,” and so forth. Against the Pelagians, Nestorians, and Eutychians. Chapter XLIII. In the cited volume, Sermon 174.

XVIII. Another by the same author on what the Apostle says: “I speak humanly because of the weakness of your flesh,” and so forth. Chapter XLIV. [Col. 0817] XXIV. Likewise another on the Gospel, where the story of the rich man and the beggar Lazarus is related. Chapter LII. Likewise another, continuing the preceding subject. Chapter LIV. In the cited volume, Sermon 163. XXV. Sermon fifty-six, and the last, although written by the same hand as the preceding sermons, was omitted from the list, at the end of which is written: “The chapters end.”

The remaining matters that I thought should be prefaced are these. Whether you consider the exposition of passages from the sacred books, the force of the reasons and arguments, or the very modes of expression, you will find in these sermons much that occurs in other writings of Augustine long known. These were evidently the things that seemed especially effective and appropriate to the holy bishop for impressing repeatedly upon his hearers or readers; and examples of such repetitions are already present in the works long ago printed, nor can they entirely be avoided by a person of even the most abundant talent amid so great a number of works.

I have taken the liberty of correcting the text only with the greatest restraint, even when obvious scribal errors (*παροράματα*) invited it. Nevertheless, I understand that I should wish older copies (*ἀντίγραφα*) of my sermons to be found when the libraries are searched again, from which unstable readings might be confirmed, interpolations detected, and my conjectures either overturned or approved. Perhaps a second volume, twin to our Palatine volume, is somewhere wrestling with shadows and contains selected sermons for the remainder of the year, together likewise with certain unpublished (*ἀνέκδοτοι*) ones.

Besides the sermons whose list I have given, the codex contains Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 118, consisting of a prologue and thirty-two sermons, found in the Maurist edition, Volume IV, column 1277; likewise his two books of *Retractations*, as in the cited edition, Volume I, column 1, although the parchment leaves beginning at Book II, chapter 24, have fallen out; finally, commentaries on the Gospel of Mark, formerly attributed to Jerome, here acephalous (*ἀκέφαλα*), but rejected by the illustrious Vallarsi in Volume XI of Jerome’s works, at column 783. I thought these works should be listed because, as is evident, no one has hitherto consulted or used this codex to complete their text.

As far as permitted, I have endeavored to adapt this edition to the Maurist edition, so that it may more conveniently be joined to the works of the holy Father in libraries.

Finally, while certain counselors of an enraged Wisdom do everything in their writings to diminish the faith and authority of the ancient Doctors of the Christian Church, I commend these remains (*λείψανα*) of a writer of whom, as Erasmus testifies, the Christian world possesses nothing either more golden or more august to the judgment of pious and learned lovers of sacred antiquity; and I withdraw to the Palatine Library to resume the labors I mentioned at the beginning.

[Col. 0817]

UNPUBLISHED SERMONS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO. SERMONS WITH SOME DOUBTFUL ITEMS MIXED IN. (G, S)*

SERMON I. On the Paschal Candle

[Note: [Col. 0817] In the codex, folio 1, page 2, it is inscribed: “Sermon of Saint Augusti[ne], [Col. 0818] bishop. On Holy Saturday.” Let the learned judge. I attribute it to Augustine with less confidence, moved by those concise comparisons and by the style itself, although chronology would not stand in the way. For the ancient published liturgical books of this rite make Pope Zosimus, who died in 418, its author, apparently following the *Liber Pontificalis*, where one reads: “He granted permission throughout the parishes to bless the Paschal Candle.” Amalarius adds, in Book I, chapter 18 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: “Since the Romans did this, it is also known that Pope Zosimus ordered the Candle to be blessed.” This command, therefore, could have passed to the Gallican Church and also to the African Church, since Canon 2 of the Council of Toledo IV, celebrated in 633, asserts that this rite was in use throughout many regions. In addition, the blessing of the Candle—“Let the angelic host now exult,” and so forth—is attributed to Augustine in the Gothic and Gallican Sacramentaries, when he was still a deacon; and the holy Doctor himself, in Book XV, chapter 22 of *The City of God*, quotes verses composed by him in praise of a certain candle. But was it this Paschal Candle? It is more certain that the letter to Praesidius on the Paschal Candle, formerly attributed to Jerome and rejected by Vallarsi in Volume XI, p. 154, comes close to Augustine’s time; after it came the two Blessings of the Candle by Ennodius of Ticinum, the hymn of Florus Drepanius, and other documents that confirm the antiquity of this rite. See what the distinguished Martin Gerbert, prince-abbot of Saint Blasien, has gathered on this subject in Part II of *Ancient Alemannic Liturgy*, Dissertation VI, chapter 1. I name him here out of respect, learning, and friendship, and especially wish this Augustinian appendix to be commended to him. If anyone decides in favor of Augustine, this sermon may be inserted into the Maurist edition after Sermon 223.]

SUMMARY

I. He makes them attentive. II. The candle, an image of the righteous person and of Christ. III. The bee, an image of the righteous person; the honeycomb, of the Scriptures. IV. Samson killing the lion, a figure of Christ.

I. In paying honor to God and our almighty Lord, the creator of visible and invisible things, I believe that I must be aided by your prayers, so that what I have undertaken to say in praise and glory of the most indulgent Creator I may be able to unfold not so much by my own strength as with the help of the Lord’s mercy. Attend, therefore, now with concentration, dearest brothers, so that, after carnal thoughts have been driven from your hearts as though they were nighttime darkness, and the light of Christ has been kindled in the chambers of your consciences, you may be able not only to receive with your ears but also to grasp in your minds what the Lord will deign to provide you through our service.

II. The candle is a light in the night, and the righteous person is a light in this dark world. The Lord says to those whom he himself justifies: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). Three things are seen in the candle: wax, papyrus [Note: [Col. 0819] In place of a torch or candle wick. Compare Du Cange’s *Glossary*, s.v. “Papyrus.”], and flame. In the righteous person there are likewise three: flesh, soul, and wisdom. The flame gives light, the papyrus is kindled, and the firmness of the wax is dissolved. The teaching of wisdom holds the mind; the hardness of the flesh is overcome. The flame burns, the papyrus is burned, and the wax drips in drops. Wisdom teaches, the soul grieves, and the flesh pours forth tears. The flame shines above, the papyrus is changed within, and the wax runs outward. Wisdom is preached on high, the soul is secretly converted, and the flesh cooperates visibly.

The beauty of the candle is praised by day; its brightness is honored by night. Thus it shows us the image of that pillar under whose guidance the people of Israel walked through the desert and were not permitted to wander. For a pillar of cloud appeared to them by day and a pillar of fire by night (Exodus 13:21 and Numbers 14:14). Day signifies security in this world, and night tribulation in this world. This is the day of which the Prophet sings and says: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Psalm 41:9).

In this carnal life, when the Lord Christ came, he did not display his glory; rather, veiled in mortal flesh, he appeared in the wilderness like a pillar of cloud. But when the end of the world comes, when the joys of all visible things will be taken away, then the Lord himself, bright and shining without any veil of mortality, will shine like a pillar of fire. The pillar of fire burns and gives light. What burns belongs to power; what gives light, to honor. What burns judges; what gives light illuminates. What burns is the punishment of the impious; what gives light is the blessedness of the righteous.

III. But we must properly declare the meaning of the name “candle,” since it belongs to the mystery of so great a celebration. [Col. 0820] We carry it in our hand, look upon it with our eyes, behold it with our heart, and praise it with our mouth. The bee is the maker of wax; concerning it Scripture says this [Note: [Col. 0820] The author seems to have made a lapse of memory, substituting the bee for the ant of Proverbs 6:6. A little below, however, he alludes to Sirach 11:3.]: “Go to the bee, O sluggard, and learn how industrious it is. How holy a work it has, whose labors kings and ordinary people take for their health. It is pleasing to all and glorious, and, though weak in strength, it has advanced by honoring wisdom.”

What do you remind us of, Christ? What do you command us to observe in the bee? It is a small and winged animal. This is because humility is exalted. It flies with two exceedingly bright wings. And what is brighter than charity? There are two commandments of charity: that we love the Lord and that we also love our neighbor. By these, as by two wings, the righteous person is lifted to heaven.

The bee produces sweetness; the righteous person has truth in his mouth, for the Lord cries out: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The Prophet also cries out: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). Bees love their king; the righteous love their Christ. Bees make honeycombs; the righteous work for the Churches. Bees gather their riches from flowers; so all the righteous gather the beauties of the Scriptures, through which God is understood and honored. These are the flowering meadows of the righteous.

Without lust, bees produce offspring; the righteous likewise produce Christians through the chaste preaching of the Gospel. For Paul addressed his children when he said: “Though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

There are three things in the honeycomb: wax, honey, and the young bee. In the Church there are likewise three: Scripture, understanding, and hearing. Just as honey is enclosed by wax, so understanding is guarded by Scripture. Just as the nest of the young bees is in the wax, so the breast of the hearer is in Scripture. Just as the openings of honeycombs that still contain young bees do not yet contain honey, so the secrets of Scripture, before they are understood, contain the faith of little ones.

Just as the young bee, after it has flown out, fills with honey the wax receptacles in which it was nourished, so the faithful little ones, when they have grown in faith and begun to guide themselves on the wings of charity, make fuller the defenses of Scripture by whose reverence they have been guarded, and guard them with greater reverence.

Just as, when honeycombs are pressed, honey flows and vessels receive it, so the Passion of the Lord pressed out the writings of the Law and the Prophets, knowledge flowed forth, and the hearts of spiritual people received it. Just as after the honey has been pressed out, wax without the taste of honey is more suitable for receiving impressions, so the rulers of the Jewish people, holding fast in the Law and the Prophets to Sabbaths and circumcision, new moons and unleavened bread, and other things of this kind, retained only the traces of the signs, like wax without honey, as though the sweetness of the Law had been lost.

## IV.

But the honeycomb, wax, honey, and the swarm signify much more clearly [Note: [Col. 0820] Read *evidentius* (“more clearly”).] the sacraments of the Church and the good works of her fruitfulness. Therefore Scripture prompts me to say something also, from the Book of Judges, about that honeycomb which was found in the mouth of a dead lion.

For when that exceedingly strong Samson was going to marry a wife, a young lion met him on the road. He seized it as though it were a kid and killed it, and the strength of so great a beast came to nothing in his hands (Judg. XIV). He continued on his way, married the woman, and departed. On his return he turned aside to inspect the lion’s corpse. Then he found that bees had gathered and made a honeycomb of honey in the mouth of the dead lion.

This is a great mystery; but what we have so far briefly related will suffice for the circumstances of the present time. Now, brothers, attend as much as you can. What do Samson, the lion, and that honeycomb signify? I shall explain what the Lord suggests.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself, wondrous in beauty and almighty in strength, summons the Church gathered from the nations, as a bride from among foreigners, and comes to marry her. To this Church the Apostle was speaking when he said: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. XI, 2).

The young lion is this world: the lovers of this age, the son of the devil, the people of the ungodly, whose fury dared to meet and resist the Lord, so as to obstruct the evangelical preaching concerning the salvation of believers. For gentile fury raged through the kings and powerful men of this age; and, inflamed as though by its father the devil against the Gospel of God, it burned like a young lion. But it raged only until it came into the hands of the strong man.

The persevering faith of the Martyrs broke the entire savagery of the nations and the fiercest assaults of persecution. Through such truly most courageous members, Christ the Lord conquered the world. Since we now see its monstrous pride extinguished throughout the whole earth, who would not gladly look upon the slain young lion lying upon the ground?

# SERMON II. On Holy Saturday

[Note: [Col. 0821] In the manuscript it is entitled: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, at the Easter Vigil.” Sublime and worthy of its author, it expounds the creation of the world, the mystery of the Incarnation and the Trinity, the existence and nature of God, and our hope of immortality. It should be placed in the edition after Sermon CCXVIII.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. God created all things through the Son. II. The manifestation of the Son through the Incarnation. III. The mystery of the Trinity. IV. The existence of the human mind demonstrates the existence of God. V. The true conception of God, and in it our hope of immortality.

## I.

We have heard many divine readings, whose length neither are we able to match with an equally extended sermon [Note: [Col. 0821] Perhaps *exhibere* or *proferre* (“to present” or “deliver”) should be supplied.], nor, even if we were able, would you be able to contain. Therefore, insofar as the Lord grants it, we wish to speak to Your Charity about that very beginning of Scripture where, when it was read, we heard: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1).

Attend and consider who made them; but I know that you cannot consider who made them. Consider what he made, and praise him who made it. “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Behold, the things that were made are at hand, are seen, and give delight. The work is open to view; the Craftsman is hidden, because both the source from which it is seen is open, and the source from which it is loved is hidden.

When, therefore, we see the world and love God, surely what we love is better than what we see. We see with our eyes; we love with our mind. Let us therefore place the mind before the eyes, because he whom we love from what is hidden is better than his work, which we see from what is open.

Let us ask, then, if it pleases you: when God made so great a mass, by what instruments did he make it? The instrument of the maker is the word of the one who commands. Why are you surprised? The work belongs to the Almighty. If, then, you ask who made it: God made it. If you ask what he made: he made heaven and earth. If you ask through what he made it: he made it through the Word, which he did not make.

The Word through whom heaven and earth were made was itself not made. For if it was made, through what was it made? “All things were made through him” (John I, 3). If everything that was made was made through the Word, then clearly the Word through whom all things were made was not made.

Finally, Moses, the servant of God and narrator of these works, says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Through what did he make them? Through the Word. Did he also make the Word? No. But what then? “In the beginning was the Word” (ibid. 1). The one through whom he made them already was; therefore he made what was not. We can understand—and rightly understand—that heaven and earth were made in the only-begotten Word himself. For through whom they were made, in him they were made.

This can be, and can be understood as, the beginning in which God made heaven and earth. For this Word is also the wisdom of God, to whom it is said: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24). If God made all things in wisdom, and his only-begotten Son is undoubtedly the Wisdom of God, let us not doubt that those things which we have learned were made through the Son were made in the Son. For the Son himself is plainly the Beginning.

When the Jews asked him, saying, “Who are you?” he answered: “The Beginning” (John VIII, 25). Behold: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

## II.

Now, as for the remaining things—whether they are arranged and ordered, adorned, or created when things that had not existed in heaven and earth are brought into being—God speaks and they come to be. “And God said, ‘Let there be,’ and it was made” (Gen. I, repeatedly). And so, for each individual work: “He spoke and it was made”; “He himself spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII, 9).

With what language did he speak? Did he speak so that someone might hear? We must not always be nourished with milk. Raise your minds with us to solid food. Let no one imagine God as a body; let no one imagine God as a human being; let no one imagine God as an angel, although he deigned to appear in this way to the fathers—not through his own substance, but through a creature subject to him. For otherwise he could not have appeared to human eyes, since he is invisible.

Let us seek what is better in us, and from there let us try to reach what is better than all things. What is better in us is the mind. What is better than all things is God. Why seek a better reality through an inferior one? In you, the body is lower than the mind; among all realities, nothing is better than God. Raise up what is better in you, so that, if you can, you may reach him who is better than all.

For even I, when I speak, speak to minds. I certainly see visible faces, and I myself am visible in the body; but through what I see I address what I do not see. Within, I carry a word conceived in my heart, and I wish to bring it forth in your ears. What I conceived in my heart, I wish to tell you, to bring to you what is within. What lies hidden—I seek how it may reach your mind.

First I approach your ears, as though the doorway of your mind. Since I cannot draw to you the invisible word that I conceived in my heart, I provide it, as though a vehicle, with sound. Behold: the word is hidden, the sound is open. I place what is hidden upon what is open, and reach the hearer; thus the word goes out from me, comes to you, and does not depart from me.

If, then, it is permissible to compare great things with small, lowly things with highest, and human things with divine, God did this also. The Word was hidden with the Father. In order to come to us, he assumed, as it were, a vehicle: he took flesh, came forth to us, and did not depart from the Father. Yet before his Incarnation, before Adam himself, the father of the human race, before heaven and earth and all that are in them, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “in the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

## III.

God made the earth before it was adorned, before its form was laid bare. It was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss. There was darkness where the law was not; for light had not yet been made. “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 2), and he himself was the Craftsman, not separated from the Father and the only-begotten Word.

For behold, let us attend carefully: the Trinity is intimated to us. Where it says, “In the beginning he made,” the *ousia* [Note: [Col. 0823] Greek: οὐσία, “essence.”] of the Father and the Son is understood: in “the beginning,” the Son; in “God,” the Father. The Spirit remains, so that the Trinity may be complete: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

“And God said.” To whom did God speak? Before the creature existed, was there anyone to hear? There was, he says. I ask: who? The Son himself. God therefore spoke to the Son. With what word did he speak to the Word? For if the Son already existed—as no Christian doubts—then surely this Word also already existed. The Son was the Word, and the Father was speaking to the Word.

Were words, then, passing between God and the Word? Far from it! Remove, brothers, the impediments of carnal thought. Think of invisible things invisibly; do not allow bodily likenesses to move before the eyes of your mind. Pass beyond whatever is seen in you. Transcend whatever in you is not seen as well. The body is seen, but the soul is not seen; nevertheless, the soul changes. Now it wills, now it does not will; now it knows, now it does not know; now it remembers, now it forgets; now it advances, now it falls back.

This is not God; this nature is not God; the soul is not a portion of God’s substance. Whatever God is, is immutable Good; incorruptible Good. God is invisible, and the soul is invisible, but the soul is mutable and God immutable. Transcend, then, not only what is seen in you, but also what changes in you. Transcend everything; transcend yourself.

## IV.

A certain lover of invisible goodness, a certain lover of invisible eternity, said in his sighs and the groans of his love: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI, 4).

How could tears not truly become the bread of one whose tears are offered to love, so that he may somehow feed upon them as upon the pleasure of food, and gladly weep as long as he does not see what he loves, when he is told every day, “Where is your God?”

If I say to a pagan, “Where is your God?” he will show me idols. If I break the idol, he will show me a mountain, or a tree, or a worthless stone from a river. For whatever he has taken from among many stones, placed in a more honored location, and worshiped by bowing down, that is his god. “Behold,” he says, pointing with his finger, “behold my god.”

When I mock the stone, remove it, break it, throw it away, or despise it, he points his finger at the sun, at the moon, or at some star. He calls one Saturn, another Mercury, another Jupiter, another Venus. I ask what he means, whatever he points at. He answers me: “Behold, this is my god.”

And because I see the sun but cannot break it, cannot cast down the stars, and cannot overturn the heavens, he seems to himself superior by displaying visible things and extending his finger toward whatever he chooses, saying, “Behold, this is my god.” Then he turns to me and says, “Where is your God?”

When I hear, “Where is your God?” I have nothing to show to his eyes, and I find blind minds barking at me. I have nothing to show to the eyes he has for seeing. Yet when I truly have one whom I could show, he has no eyes with which to see. I am willing to weep, as though feeding on bread in my tears.

For my God is invisible; the man speaking to me demands visible things when he says, “Where is your God?” But in order to reach my God, I did what is said in that very psalm: “I meditated on these things and poured out my soul within me” (Ps. XLI, 5). My God is not beneath my soul but above my soul. How do I reach what is above my soul unless I pour out my soul above myself?

Yet, with the help of my God, I shall try in some way to answer this insolent man who demands visible things, displays visible things, and exults in visible things. You certainly say to me, “Where is your God?” I answer you: “Where are you yourself?”

I answer, I say, and I think not improperly. You asked where God is; I ask where my questioner himself is. He will say: “Behold where I am. You see me; I am speaking to you.” And I say to him: “I am looking for my questioner. I see his face, I see his body, I hear his voice, I observe his tongue. I am looking for the one who directs his eyes toward me, moves his tongue, emits his voice, and desires to know by asking.”

All this of which I speak is the soul. I shall not therefore deal with you any longer. You say, “Show me your God.” I say, “Show me your mind.” You struggle, grow weary, and become fixed when I say, “Show me your mind.” I know that you cannot. Why can you not? Because your mind is invisible. And yet it is better in you than your body. My God, however, is better than your mind. How, then, shall I show you my God when you do not show me your mind, through which I show you that my God is better?

Behold, if you say to me, “Recognize my mind from its work,” because I direct my eyes to see, my ears to hear, move my tongue to speak, and bring forth my voice to sound, from this I understand and recognize my mind. You see that you cannot show it itself, but command me to know it from its works.

Behold, I too shall show you my God from his works. I shall not go farther, nor perhaps refer your unbelief to things you cannot grasp. I do not recall my God’s works in this way: “He made invisible things; he made visible things—that is, heaven and earth, the sea, and all that are in them.” I do not send you through many things. I return to yourself.

You certainly live. You have a body; you have a mind. The body is visible; the mind is invisible. The body is a dwelling; the mind is its inhabitant. The body is a vehicle; the mind is the user of the vehicle. The body is, as it were, a vehicle to be directed; the mind is the charioteer of your body.

Behold, your senses are manifest, like doors in your body through which something is announced to the mind dwelling within: eyes, ears, smell, taste, touch, and limbs arranged in their places. What is that within from which you think, from which you give life to these things? The one who made all that you marvel at in yourself is my God.

## V.

Therefore, my brothers, if I have addressed your minds and your inward souls with some suitable conversation, insofar as I could; if by speaking I have reached those who dwell within houses of clay—that is, your souls inhabiting your bodies—do not infer divine things from what you know about them.

God surpasses all things, heaven and earth. Do not set before your eyes some great craftsman assembling, arranging, contriving, turning, or revolving something; nor imagine him like an emperor seated upon a bright, ornate royal throne and creating by command. Break the idols in your hearts.

Consider what was said to Moses when he inquired into God’s name: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14). Seek what else “is.” In comparison with him, nothing else is. That which truly is does not know how to be changed in any respect.

Everything that changes and fluctuates, and does not cease changing at some time, was and will be. You do not grasp “is” in it. God, however, does not have a “was” and a “will be.” What was is no longer; what will be is not yet. And what comes in such a way that it passes away will therefore exist so as not to exist.

Consider, if you can: “I am who I am.” Do not be rolled about by your desires; do not be shaken by voluntary and temporal thoughts. Stand fast at “is.” Stand fast at that very “is.” Where are you going? Stand, so that you too may be able to be.

But when we grasp a flighty thought, when can we fasten it to what remains? Therefore God had mercy. He who is, and he who said, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you,’” after declaring the name of his substance, later declares the name of his mercy.

What is the name of his substance? “I am who I am. You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (ibid.). But Moses was a human being, and he existed among those things which, in comparison with God, do not exist. He was on earth, he was in the flesh, and in that flesh was a soul; he was a mutable nature, under the burden of human frailty.

For when could he grasp what was said, “I am who I am”? Through what appeared to his eyes, the invisible God was speaking to him, and the hidden God was using what appeared as an instrument. For what Moses saw was not the whole of God. Likewise, neither is the sound by which I say that I am a human being the whole Word [Note: [Col. 0826] The word *tu* (“you”) is redundant.]. I have in my heart a word that does not sound. The sound passes; the word remains.

Therefore, when the invisible God spoke to a human being through what he deigned to make visible, the eternal spoke temporal things, the immutable spoke fragile things, saying: “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” It was as though Moses could not grasp what “I am who I am” and “He who is has sent me to you” meant—or perhaps, if Moses himself did grasp it, it was we who could not grasp it. Immediately after the name of his substance, God spoke the name of his mercy.

It was as though he said to Moses: “You do not grasp what I said, ‘I am who I am’; your heart does not stand firm; you are not immutable with me, nor is your mind unchangeable. You have heard what I am. Hear what you can grasp; hear what you may hope for.”

Again God said to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. You cannot grasp the name of my substance; grasp the name of my mercy. I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (ibid. 6).

But “what I am” is eternal. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were indeed eternal—or rather, I should not say eternal, but made eternal by him. Finally, the Lord himself also refutes the Sadducees who were arguing against the resurrection, and from this passage he gives the testimony of Holy Scripture.

Read what the Lord said to Moses in the bush: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. He is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. XXII, 32; and Mark XII, 26–27), “for all live to him.”

Accordingly, here too, after saying, “I am who I am,” God did not add: “This is my name forever” (Exod. III, 15). Here no one doubts, because what is is so precisely because it is eternal. But when he says, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” there he adds: “This is my name forever.”

It is as though he were saying: “Why are you afraid concerning the mortality of the human race? Why perhaps do you tremble lest, when you have died, you should no longer exist? ‘This is my name forever.’ The name ‘God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob’ could not be eternal unless Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived forever.”

Turned toward the Lord, etc. [Note: [Col. 0826] It is sufficient to indicate once this formula, familiar to Augustine and appended to several sermons. Sirmondus presents it in full in the note to Sermon XL of his edition of the works, vol. I, col. 337.]

# SERMON III. On the Sacrament of the Altar, to the Infants

[Note: [Col. 0826] In the manuscript, folio 4, page 2, it is entitled: “Here begins another sermon on the Sacraments [Col. 0827] on the same day.” I think this is the sermon referred to by Augustine, Maurist edition, vol. V, Sermon CCXXVIII: “Today we ought to speak to the infants [newly baptized Christians] at the altar of God about the Sacrament of the Altar.” Perhaps it is also the sermon which Possidius records in his Catalogue of Augustine’s Works, vol. X, chapter 10: “On the Eucharist.” It is a beautiful preparation for Holy Communion and should be placed in the edition after Sermon CCXXVIII.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. The commendation of the sacrifice of the New Law. II. This sacrifice is Christ. III. He is truly and really present in the Eucharist. IV. The effect of the Eucharist. V. Conditions for worthy reception.

## I.

The duty of delivering a sermon, and the concern with which we have brought you to birth so that Christ might be formed in you, compels us to admonish your infancy. You have now been reborn from water and the Spirit; with new light you behold this food and drink upon this table of the Lord, and with newly awakened devotion you receive it. We must teach you what is meant by so great and divine a Sacrament, so bright and noble a medicine, so pure and accessible a sacrifice.

It is not sacrificed in one earthly city, Jerusalem; nor in that tabernacle built through Moses; nor in that temple constructed through Solomon—though these were shadows of future things. Rather, as the Prophets foretold, it is sacrificed from the rising of the sun to its setting, and according to the grace of the New Testament a sacrifice of praise is offered to God.

No longer is a bloody victim sought from flocks of sheep; no sheep or goat is now brought near the divine altars. The sacrifice of our present time is the Body and Blood of the Priest himself. For it was foretold long beforehand in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

That Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, brought forth bread and wine when he blessed our father Abraham, we read and retain in the Book of Genesis (Gen. XIV, 18).

## II.

Christ our Lord, therefore, who in suffering offered for us what in being born he had received from us, having been made High Priest forever, gave the order of sacrifice which you see: namely, that of his Body and Blood.

For when his Body was pierced by the lance, it poured out water and blood, by which he forgave our sins. Remembering this grace, and working out your own salvation—for it is God who works in you—approach this altar with fear and trembling.

Recognize in the bread what hung upon the cross; recognize in the chalice what flowed from his side. For those ancient sacrifices of the people of God prefigured, in a single reality represented through manifold variety, the one sacrifice that was to come.

Christ himself is both a sheep, because of the innocence of his simple spirit, and a goat, because of his likeness to sinful flesh. Whatever else was foretold in the sacrifices of the Old Testament through many different forms refers to this one reality revealed in the New Testament.

## III.

Receive, then, and eat the Body of Christ—you yourselves, already made members of Christ in the Body of Christ. Receive and drink the Blood of Christ. Do not be dissolved: eat your bond. Do not regard yourselves as worthless: drink your price.

As this is changed into you when you eat and drink it, so you too are changed into the Body of Christ when you live obediently and devoutly. For when his Passion was already near and he was celebrating Passover with his disciples, he took bread, blessed it, and said: “This is my Body, which will be handed over for you” (Luke XXII, 19).

Likewise, he gave them the blessed chalice, saying: “This is my Blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. XXVI, 28).

You were either reading or hearing this in the Gospel, but you did not know that this Eucharist was the Son. Now, however, with hearts wiped clean [Note: [Col. 0828] I read *abstersi* (“wiped clean”).] in a pure conscience and bodies washed with clean water, “Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. XXXIII, 6).

For if you receive this worthily, which belongs to the New Testament through which you hope for an eternal inheritance, and if you hold to the new commandment—to love one another—you have life within you.

You receive that flesh of which Life itself says: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,” and, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have life in himself” (John VI, 52–54).

## IV.

Since, therefore, you possess life in him, you will be one flesh with him. For this Sacrament does not commend the Body of Christ in such a way as to separate us from it. The Apostle recalls that this was foretold in Holy Scripture: “The two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32).

Elsewhere, concerning this same Eucharist, he says: “We, though many, are one bread and one body” (1 Cor. X, 17).

You are therefore beginning to receive what you have also begun to be, provided that you do not receive it unworthily, lest you eat and drink judgment upon yourselves. For he says: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the Body and Blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. XI, 27–29).

## V.

You receive worthily, however, if you avoid the leaven of evil teaching, so that you may be “unleavened in sincerity and truth” (ibid. V, 8); or if you retain that leaven of love “which a woman hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matt. XIII, 33).

For this woman is the wisdom of God, made flesh through the Virgin in mortal flesh. Throughout the whole world—which he restored after the Flood through the three sons of Noah—she spreads her Gospel, as though in three measures, “until the whole was leavened.”

This is that “whole,” which in Greek is called *holon* [Note: [Col. 0828] Greek: ὅλον, *katholon*.], where, while guarding the bond of peace, you will be according to the whole, which is called *katholon*, and from which the name “Catholic” is derived [Note: [Col. 0828] The word *Ecclesia* (“Church”) seems to have dropped out.]

# SERMON IV. On Easter

[Note: [Col. 0828] In the manuscript, folio 5, it is entitled: “Here begins another sermon on the same day, a sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop.” Perhaps it was delivered extemporaneously, arising from sudden inspiration, such as Possidius relates in the Life, chapter 7, that the holy Doctor sometimes gave; nevertheless, it is worthy of his genius. It should be included in the edition after Sermon CCXXIX.]

## SYNOPSIS

Christ the Lamb and the Lion.

As the truth sounded forth through the Apostles, and “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5), “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (Rom. X, 18).

Of him the Prophet had earlier foretold: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before the one who shears it he was without a voice; so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7).

Who is this? Surely the one of whom what follows says: “In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him. Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. ibid. 7).

I see an example of such great humility in a King of such great power. For this one, who like a lamb before the shearer did not open his mouth, is himself the Lion from the tribe of Judah (Rev. V, 5).

Who is this Lamb and Lion? He endured death as a lamb; he consumed it as a lion. Who is this Lamb and Lion? Gentle and strong, lovable and terrifying, innocent and powerful, silent when judged, roaring when he comes to judge.

Who is this Lamb and Lion? Is he a lamb in his Passion and a lion in his resurrection—or rather, both lamb and lion in his Passion, and both lamb and lion in his resurrection?

Let us see the Lamb in his Passion. It has just been said: “Like a lamb before the shearer he was without a voice; so he did not open his mouth.”

Let us see the Lion in his Passion. Jacob said: “You have gone up, reclining; you have slept like a lion” (Gen. XLIX, 9).

Let us see the Lamb in his resurrection. Revelation, speaking of the eternal glory of virgins, says: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV, 4).

Let us see the Lion in his resurrection. The same Revelation says what I have already cited above: “The Lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered to open the book” (ibid. 5).

Why is he a lamb in his Passion? Because he accepted death without iniquity. Why is he a lion in his Passion? Because, when killed, he killed death. Why is he a lamb in his resurrection? Because innocence is eternal in him. Why is he a lion in his resurrection? Because power is eternal in him.

Who is this Lamb and Lion? How do you ask who he is? If you ask what he was, “In the beginning was the Word.” If you ask where he was, “And the Word was with God.” If you ask what sort of Word he was, “And the Word was God.” If you ask how great his patience is, “All things were made through him.” If you ask what he himself became, “And the Word became flesh” (John I, 1–2, 14).

If you ask how he was born either from the Father without a mother or from the mother without a father: “Who shall declare his generation?” Begotten from another, he is coeternal with the one who begets him.

The Word, remaining what he was, became flesh. The Creator of all times was created at the proper time. The prey of death, and the predator of death. Disfigured in appearance beyond the sons of men, knowing how to bear weakness, exalted in making lowly things, humbled in making lofty things. God-man, and man-God. Both firstborn and creator of the firstborn. Only-begotten, and brother of all. Born from the substance of the Father, and made a participant in the adopted. Both Lord of all and servant of many.

This is the Lamb “who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid. 29); this is the Lion who conquers the kingdoms of the world.

I was asking who this one is. Let us ask for whom he died. Perhaps for the just and holy? The Apostle does not say this; rather, he says that “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 6). Certainly not so that the ungodly might remain ungodly, but so that, through the death of the Just One, the ungodly might be justified, and through the pouring out of blood without sin, the legal bond of sin might be erased.

# SERMON V. Again on Easter

[Note: [Col. 0830] In the manuscript, folio 5, page 2, it is entitled: “Another sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the same day.” Excellent and composed for moving the hearers, it concerns the Passion and death of the Savior and should be placed in the edition after Sermon CCXXX.]

[Col. 0830]

## SYNOPSIS

I. Christ’s death is our hope. II. Christ’s death was voluntary. III. How Christ was sorrowful in death. IV. The necessity of the Incarnation, so that we might be redeemed. V. The Redeemer’s words to the redeemed. VI. How Christ is understood to have died for us. VII. The errors of Apollinaris and Arius refuted. VIII. Exhortation.

## I.

We have heard the Gospel. The Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ has been read. Christ rose again; therefore Christ died. The Resurrection is a witness to death; but Christ’s death is the destruction of fear.

Let us not fear to die. Christ died for us. Let us die with the hope of eternal life. Christ rose again so that we might rise. In his death and resurrection we have a work commanded and a reward promised: the commanded work is suffering; the promised reward is resurrection.

The Martyrs fulfilled this work. Let us fulfill it through devotion if we cannot through suffering. For it is not granted to everyone to suffer for Christ and die for Christ. Yet dying itself comes to everyone.

Blessed are those for whom what had to happen—that is, death—happened for Christ! Death was necessary, but death for Christ was not necessary. Death will come to everyone, but death for Christ will not come to everyone.
