Those to whom it was granted to die for Christ in a certain way returned what had been given to them. The Lord had given himself to them, to die for them; they returned it to him by dying for him. But from where would the poor and needy man repay, if the blessed Lord had not given first?

Thus what Christ had given to the Martyrs, he gave them as the means by which they could repay Christ. For the voice of the Martyrs is: “If the Lord had not been among us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. CXXIII, 1–2).

The persecutors, he says, “perhaps would have swallowed us alive.” What does “alive” mean? Knowing that we would do wrong if we denied Christ, yet, while alive—that is, knowingly—we would commit so great an evil; and thus they would have swallowed us alive, not dead.

What does “alive” mean? Knowing, not unaware. By what power, then, did they not do what the persecutors were forcing them to do? Let them be asked; let them speak for themselves. Behold, they answer: “If the Lord had not been among us.”

Therefore he himself gave what was to be returned to him. Thanks be to him. He is rich. And what is written of him—that “he became poor so that he might make us rich” (2 Cor. VIII, 9)—we have been enriched by his poverty, healed by his wounds, exalted by his humility, and given life by his death [Note: [Col. 0830] Supply *sumus* (“we have been”).]

## II.

The Martyr said: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV, 12). Hear what follows. He considered and sought what he should render to the Lord. And what did he say? “I shall receive the cup of salvation” (ibid. 13).

“This I shall render to the Lord: the cup of salvation, the cup of martyrdom, the cup of suffering, the cup of Christ.” This is why he says, “The cup of salvation,” because Christ is our salvation.

“Therefore,” he says, “I shall receive his cup and repay him.” Christ himself spoke of this cup to the Father before his Passion: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39).

He had come to suffer; he had come to die; he had death in his power. Or, if I am lying, hear him himself: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, and I take it up again” (John X, 18).

You have heard the power: “No one takes it.” The Jews boast without cause. From this they have sin, not power. Christ died because he willed to die.

He himself says in the Psalm: “I slept, and I began my sleep” (Ps. III, 6). They shouted, “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke XXIII, 21; and John XIX, 6); they seized him and hung him up. Thus they helped, because they were able to do something.

“I slept.” And what follows? “And I began my sleep.” Truly, it was a sleep lasting three days. What follows? “And I rose again, because the Lord took me up.” He speaks according to the form of a servant: “The Lord took me up” (Ps. III, 6).

As he says elsewhere: “Will not one who sleeps rise again?” (ibid. XI, 9). The Jews boast as though they had conquered me. “Will not one who sleeps rise again?”

They hung him up in order to kill him; but “I slept,” because when I willed, I laid down my life, and when I willed, I rose again.

### III.

Therefore he himself is the cup which he wished to pass from him, the cup which he had come to drink. What, then, Lord, is the meaning of what you said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”? You said to the disciples, when you were about to suffer and die: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

I therefore seek in these words of yours those other words: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again.” From where, then, do I hear: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death”? “No one takes it from me.” Why is it sorrowful? You have power to lay down your soul. Why do you say: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”?

He answers the one who asks and says to you: “O human being, in my flesh I have taken you up. If, then, I have taken you up in my flesh, have I not also taken you up in my voice? When I say, ‘I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again,’ I speak as the maker. When I say, ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death,’ I speak as the thing made, as you. Rejoice because of me in me; recognize yourself in me.

“When I say, ‘I have power to lay down my soul,’ I am your helper. When I say, ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death,’ I am your mirror.”

### IV.

Have you not read that he died? Are we to deny it? If we deny his death, we deny his resurrection as well. He died in that by which he deigned to be human. He rose again in that by which he deigned to be human, because we too are human, and we shall die, and we shall rise again.

Did the Word die in him? Could anything be suffered by that which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:2)? What can such a Word suffer? Yet it was necessary that the Word should die for us; it could not die, and yet it was necessary that it die. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Where is the blood? Where is death? Is there death in the Word? Is there blood in the Word? If there is neither death nor blood in the Word, where is our ransom? Is not his blood our ransom? From where, then, would he give this ransom, if the Word remained alone?—unless the Word assumed flesh; and flesh living from a human soul, so that, since the Word could not be killed, only the flesh that lived from its own soul would be killed.

For not even the soul could be killed, since, by clinging to Divinity, it was one spirit—only the Lord himself clothing himself with it [Note: [Col. 0832] Read: “it,” referring to the soul.], not itself believing in him, as it is written concerning us: “He who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). For when we were unbelievers, we were unworthy and alienated from God; but by believing we clung to God. That soul, however, was created worthy of union with God when it was assumed, new and unformed, into the unity of the divine person.

When this unity, in the singularity of two unequal spirits, departed, the flesh died. It had lived in a new manner and by a new kind from that very unity of the two spirits—that is, possessing a twofold and wondrous life—and for only a short time was it left behind. For God is spirit, and his image, the human spirit, are immortal.

### V.

Thus, in a certain manner, our Lord and Savior addresses us, saying:

“O human beings! I made the human being upright, and he made himself crooked. You departed from me and perished in yourselves. But I will seek what had perished. You departed from me,” he says; “you lost life. And life was the light of human beings” (John 1:4).

Behold what you abandoned when, in Adam, you all perished: “Life was the light of human beings.” What life? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (ibid. 1). Life existed, while you lay in your death. I did not have, as a human being, that by which I might die; you did not have, as a human being, that by which you might live.

(Because the Lord Christ deigns to take up my words, I have taken up his. If he takes up mine, how much more may I take up his.)

In a certain manner, speaking in silence through the realities themselves, our Lord Christ says: “I did not have that by which I might die; you did not have, as a human being, that by which you might live. I took from you that by which I might die for you. Take from me that by which you may live with me.

“Let us celebrate an exchange. I give to you; give to me. I receive death from you; receive life from me. Awake and see what I give and what I receive.

“Exalted in heaven, I received from you humility upon earth. Your Lord, I received from you the form of a servant. Your health, I received from you wounds. Your life, I received from you death.

“I, the Word, became flesh, so that I might be able to die. I did not have flesh with the Father; I took it from your mass, from which I might distribute it to you.”

(The Virgin Mary was of our mass; there Christ took flesh from us, that is, from the human race.)

“I received flesh from you, by which I might die for you; receive from me the life-giving Spirit, by which you may live with me. Finally, I died from what was yours; live from what is mine.”

[Col. 0833]

### VI.

Therefore, brothers, when you hear: “He was born of the Spirit from the Virgin Mary,” and “he suffered, was scourged, and received blows upon the face”; when you hear: “Christ suffered these things,” do not suppose that the Word who was in the beginning with God could have suffered anything of this kind in his own nature and substance.

But can we say that the Word of God, the only-begotten God, did not suffer for us? He suffered, but according to his soul and his passible flesh. For he assumed the form of a servant, so that as a human being he might suffer. He possessed both a soul and flesh, because he had come to redeem the whole human being—not by losing life, but by giving life.

To offer an illustration, so that you may grasp more quickly what we are saying: when, for example, the martyr Stephen, or Phocas [Note: [Col. 0833] It is difficult to say which of the three Phocases Augustine has in mind here—namely, the Antiochene or the two from Sinope. The Belgian hagiographers, as usual, discuss them carefully under 14 July. Yet it is clear from the monuments cited there that none of them was known or venerated in Africa. Meanwhile, knowledge of Phocas “the sea-worker of wonders” (τοῦ θαλασσόθαυματουργοῦ) could have come from sailors frequenting the African coast; and that this was Phocas of Sinope we learn from the Encomium of Asterius, bishop of Amasea, published by Fr. Combefis, Paris, 1648, together with other works.], or someone else, suffered, was killed, and was buried, only their flesh was killed and buried; their souls could neither be killed nor buried. Yet we rightly say: “Stephen died,” or “Phocas died,” or “so-and-so died for the name of Christ.”

So also, when the only-begotten Son of God suffered, was killed, and was buried, only his flesh was killed and buried; his soul, and still more his Divinity, could not be killed. Therefore we confidently say that the only Son of God—that is, God’s only-begotten God—died and was buried for us.

Accordingly, the Lord Christ himself, who is Truth without falsehood, truly and not falsely said: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). The Apostle likewise says of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

Do you wish to know what Christ is? Do not consider only the flesh that lay in the tomb; do not consider only the soul of which he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death”; do not consider only the Word, because “the Word was God.” Rather, consider that the whole Christ is Word, soul, and flesh.

### VII.

Do not, however, take anything away from Christ’s soul. For the Apollinarian heretics said that he had no mind, that is, that this soul had no understanding, but that the Word took the place of its mind and understanding. This is what Apollinaris said. The Arians, however, say: “He did not have even a soul of any kind.”

You, therefore, hold faithfully that the whole Christ is altogether Word, soul, and flesh. And when you hear, “My soul is sorrowful,” understand a human soul, not an animal one. For a soul without understanding is the soul of an animal, not a human soul. If he did not come to redeem the mind, he did not have a mind.

Thus there is one Christ: Word, soul, and flesh. What is a human being? Soul and flesh. What is Christ? Word and human being; and therefore Word, soul, and flesh—one Christ.

When you strike a human being with your fists, what part of him do you strike? His soul, or his flesh? You acknowledge that it is his flesh. Yet the soul cries out: “Why do you strike me? Why do you beat me?” If you were to say to the soul: “Who touched you? I am striking the flesh, not you,” would not everyone who heard you say this laugh at you and judge you foolish or insane?

So, those who scourged the flesh of the Word of God or struck it with blows upon the face cannot say: “We scourged the flesh,” or “we struck the flesh with blows,” but not the Word or the soul of Christ. For they scourged or struck the whole Christ—that is, Word, soul, and flesh.

Although they could neither kill his soul nor his Divinity, which is true life, upon the cross, they nevertheless delighted in trying, in their hearts and evil will, to destroy the whole Christ. For whoever persecutes someone in order to kill him wishes him to be extinguished entirely, just as the whole light of a lamp is extinguished when it is dashed upon the ground, so that it no longer shines at all, when a wicked person sees that it obstructs him [Note: [Col. 0834] I read: “when each wicked person sees himself obstructed by it.”].

This cannot in any way happen to a human being, namely, that he be extinguished entirely, since he possesses one mortal substance and another immortal one. For nothing in him is mortal except the flesh.

The only-begotten Christ of God could much less be extinguished entirely, when the Jews thought they had extinguished him. In his three substances—namely, one eternal and divine substance and two temporal, human substances—he had only one that was mortal, namely, his flesh. His soul, and above all his Divinity, were certainly immortal.

Therefore, by his brief death he alone could redeem us from our eternal death: he was not merely human flesh and soul, but God and soul and flesh, the one only-begotten Son of God. For “he who descended into the lower parts of the earth is the same who ascended above all the heavens” (Eph. 4:10), something that a human being alone could not do.

### VIII.

Therefore, with confidence let us rejoice and be glad, beloved brothers, because he redeemed us by his death—the one who, though killed, triumphed over his enemies. For when he was killed, he killed death and freed us forever from its power. “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (ibid.), and, having sent the Holy Spirit to human beings, he gave them his gifts. Even while lying in the tomb, he was able to bring the believing thief into paradise.

## SERMON VI. Also, on the Sacrament of the Altar, to the Infants

[Note: [Col. 0834] In the manuscript, fol. 7, it is entitled: “On the Sacraments of the Altar. Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the same day.” It is a brief instruction for those approaching the sacred assembly for the first time, such as our Sermon III above and the printed Sermons 227 and 272. The Maurists published a fragment of it from Bede’s and Florus’s collection as Sermon 229. Here we give it in full.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. The Lord’s body is both on the altar and ourselves.  
II. The Eucharist as a symbol of unity.  
III. Explanation of the eucharistic liturgy.

### I.

This which you see, beloved, on the Lord’s table is bread and wine; but this bread and this wine, when the word is added, become the body and blood of the Word.

For that Lord who “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), because of his mercy, by which he did not despise what he had created in his own image, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid. 14), as you know. For the Word himself assumed a human being—that is, a human soul and flesh—and became human while remaining God.

Because he also suffered for us, he commended to us in this sacrament his body and blood, which he also made us ourselves. For we too have been made his body, and by his mercy we are what we receive [Note: [Col. 0835] Here begins the fragment that was published, mentioned above.]. Remember that this substance was once in the field: how the earth brought it forth, rain nourished it, and brought it to the ear; then human labor carried it to the threshing floor, threshed it, winnowed it, stored it, brought it out, ground it, mixed it, baked it, and only after all this finally brought it to the form of bread.

Remember yourselves also [Note: [Col. 0835] “You” is in the accusative case. It was therefore incorrectly punctuated in the published fragment.]. You did not exist, and you were created; you were carried to the Lord’s threshing floor; you were threshed by the labor of oxen—that is, of those who proclaim the Gospel.

When you were being deferred as catechumens, you were kept in the granary. You gave your names; you began to be ground by fasts [Note: [Col. 0835] The published fragment inserts: “and”], by exorcisms. Afterwards you came to the water, you were mixed, and you became one. When the heat of the Holy Spirit was added, you were baked and became the Lord’s bread.

### II.

Behold what you have received. Just as you see that what has been made is one, so you too must be one [Note: [Col. 0835] The published fragment has: “be one, you.”], loving one another, holding one faith, one hope, undivided charity.

When heretics receive this, they receive testimony against themselves, because they seek division, whereas this bread signifies unity. So too the wine was in many grapes [Note: [Col. 0835] The same source has: “clusters.”], but now it is one. It is one in the sweetness of the cup, but [Note: [Col. 0835] The same source omits “but.”] only after the pressure of the winepress.

And you, after those fasts, after those labors, after humility and contrition, have now come in the name of Christ as to the Lord’s cup; and there you are at the table [Note: [Col. 0835] The same source has: “at the table, and.”], there you are in the cup. You are with us in this [Note: [Col. 0835] The same source has: “you instead of this.”]; for together we are this [Note: [Col. 0835] More correctly in the same source: “we receive together.”], together we drink, because together we live [Note: [Col. 0835] Here the published fragment ends, vol. V, col. 976.].

You are about to hear what you also heard yesterday; but today what you heard is explained to you, and what you answered—or perhaps, while the answer was being given, you were silent—you learn today what ought to have been answered.

### III.

After the greeting that you know, namely, “The Lord be with you,” you heard: “Lift up your hearts.” The whole life of true Christians is “lifted up,” not merely of those who bear the name Christian, but of those who are Christians in reality and truth: their whole life is “lifted up.”

What does “Lift up your hearts” mean? Hope in God, not in yourself. You are below; God is above. If you place your hope in yourself, your heart is below; it is not lifted up.

Therefore, when you hear the priest say, “Lift up your hearts,” you answer: “We have them with the Lord.” Strive to answer truthfully. For you answer in God’s official proceedings [Note: [Col. 0836] Elsewhere: “in the Action.” A synonym for the Canon, the Secrets of the sacrifice of the Mass, as below: “the things that are performed.”]; let it be as you say.

Let not your tongue sound one thing while your conscience denies it. And because God himself grants you this very thing—that you should have your hearts lifted up—therefore, when you say that you have your hearts lifted up to the Lord, the priest follows and says: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

Why should we give thanks? Because we have our hearts lifted up, and unless he had lifted them, we would be lying upon the earth.

And then there follow [Note: [Col. 0836] Supply: “there succeed,” “there follow,” or something similar.] the things performed in the holy prayers that you are about to hear, so that, when the word is added, the body and blood of Christ may come to be. For remove the word: it is bread and wine. Add the word, and now it is something else. And what is this something else? The body of Christ and the blood of Christ.

Remove the word, then: it is bread and wine. Add the word, and it will become a sacrament. To this you say: “Amen.” To say “Amen” is to subscribe. “Amen” is translated into Latin as “True.”

Then the Lord’s Prayer is said, which you have already received and recited back [Note: [Col. 0836] That is, you recited it from memory to the priest. Thus they were not reciting back only the Creed. See our Sermon 58, vol. V, col. 337.].

Why is it said before the Body and Blood of Christ are received? Because, given human frailty, if perhaps our thought has conceived something improper; if our tongue has uttered something it ought not; if our eye has looked upon something it ought not; if our ear has heard something too pleasing that it ought not to have heard; if perhaps such things have been contracted from the temptation of this world and the frailty of human life, they are cleansed by the Lord’s Prayer, where it says: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), so that we may approach with confidence and not eat and drink what we receive to our judgment.

After this it is said: “Peace be with you.” The kiss of peace is a great sacrament. Kiss in such a way that you love. Do not be Judas. Judas the betrayer kissed Christ with his mouth, but plotted against him in his heart.

Perhaps, however, someone harbors hostility toward you, and you cannot convict him; you are forced to endure him. Do not return evil for evil in your heart. He hates; you love, and you kiss with confidence.

You have heard little, but it is great. Let it not be despised because of its smallness, but let it be precious because of its weight. At the same time, you must not be burdened with too much, so that you may retain what has been said.

## SERMON VII. On Easter

### SYNOPSIS

I. Who celebrates Easter, and how it should be celebrated.  
II. The “alleluia” of the rich, the poor, and the afflicted.  
III. God acts as a father; the Devil as a slave-dealer.

### I.

It is known to everyone on which days we celebrate Easter, namely, the days on which we sing “Alleluia.” Therefore, brothers, we must carefully attend to this: what we celebrate visibly must be held in our minds.

For we say that we celebrate Easter. Easter is a Hebrew word, interpreted as “Passover” or “Crossing”; in Greek, *paschein*, “to suffer” [Note: [Col. 0837] Πάσχειν. This seems to be a frivolous interpolation.]; in Latin, *Pascha* means “to feed,” as is commonly said: “I will feed my friends.”

Who celebrates Easter except the one who passes from the death of his sins to the life of the righteous? As the Apostle says: “We have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren” (1 John 3:14).

Who celebrates Easter except the one who believes in Christ, who suffered on earth so that he may reign with him in heaven? Who celebrates Easter except the one who feeds Christ in the poor? For he himself says concerning the poor: “Whatever good anyone has done to one of the least of mine, he has done to me” (Matt. 25:40).

Christ sits in heaven and is in need on earth. He intercedes with the Father for us, and here he asks bread from us.

Therefore, brothers of the Lord, if we wish to celebrate Easter profitably, let us cross over, suffer, and feed. Let us cross over from sins to righteousness; let us suffer for Christ; let us feed Christ in the poor.

Let us celebrate feasts honorably, so that with Abraham we may enjoy a heavenly banquet in the kingdom of God.

Let us therefore sing “alleluia” to God, which in Latin sounds as: “Let us praise him” [Note: [Col. 0837] Rather: “Praise him.”], the one who is. Let us praise him both in prosperity and in adversity. In the prosperity of riches, let us not be lifted up; under the scourge of losses, let us not grow weak.

Let us say “alleluia” with Job, who said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Let us therefore bless the Lord at all times. We always sing “alleluia” if, at the sound of our tongue, our limbs are moved to the performance of righteousness; if what sounds in the mouth of the singer shines in the conduct of the one who lives.

### II.

Hear how the rich and the poor are commanded to sing “alleluia.”

“Command,” says the Apostle, “the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment. Let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–18).

What the poor should sing, Tobit teaches: “My son, do not be afraid, for we lead a poor life. Many good things will abound for you if you fear the Lord your God and do what pleases him in his sight” (Tob. 4:3).

Most beloved members of the Body of Christ, let us await our Head, who is to come from heaven. Clinging to him, we shall remain steadfast, so that, having celebrated his passion on earth, we may reign with him in heaven.

Let us endure his discipline, so that we may be corrected, because God deals with us as with children. For who is there, the Apostle says, to whom his father does not give discipline? (Heb. 12:7). If you separate yourselves from God’s discipline, then you are bastards and not sons.

Let us endure the father’s scourge, lest we encounter the judge’s severity.

### III.

God and the Devil are father and slave-dealer [Note: [Col. 0838] Similar expressions occur below, Sermon XXI, no. 4.]. God, as a father, scourges, corrects, and takes us to himself; the slave-dealer flatters, seduces, and sells. The father carries a scourge, and the slave-dealer carries a little sack [Note: [Col. 0838] Instead of *sacculus*, “little bag.” The word also occurs in Petronius, Celsus, and others, though nowhere in the printed works of Augustine. It recurs below, Sermon XX, no. 12.].

If you run beneath the wings of the one who scourges, you will be freed from the iniquity of the seller. See by whom and where you are to be stored: in the kingdom of heaven, or in the little sack of Gehenna.

If you desire the kingdom of God, you will rejoice in the payment of freedom; but if you desire the little sack, you will receive the bondage of servitude, and, bound hand and foot, it will be said of you: “Take him and cast him into the outer darkness. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13).

A loud cry is made to us: “Let anyone who has ears to hear hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 3:22).

## SERMON VIII. On the Octave of Easter, to the Infants

[Note: [Col. 0838] In the manuscript, fol. 14, it is entitled: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on Easter Saturday.” It is worthy of the author and treats the sacrament of baptism exceptionally well. Certain passages from no. 1 are read in vol. V, Appendix, Sermon 172, col. 296, but there they are badly pieced together. Ours should be inserted after Sermon 260, which perhaps alludes to it in these words: “A brief but weighty sermon must be delivered to those regenerated in baptism who today are to be mingled with the people.”]

### SYNOPSIS

I. The power and effect of Baptism, and the hope placed in it.  
II. Baptism outside the unity of the Church is of no benefit.  
III. Against schismatics who boast of Baptism.  
IV. Exhortation to the newly baptized.

### I.

My sermon is addressed to you, infants newly born, little ones in Christ, new offspring of the Church, the Father’s grace, the Mother’s fruitfulness, a godly shoot, a new swarm, the flower of our honor, and the fruit of our labor, my joy and crown—all of you who stand in the Lord. In the words of the Apostle I address you:

“Behold, the night has passed; the day has drawn near. Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day—not in reveling and drunkenness, not in chambers and impurities, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:12–14), so that you may also be clothed in life with him whom you have put on in the sacrament [Note: [Col. 0838] I read: “so that you may put on life, him whom you have put on in the sacrament,” namely, Christ.].

For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ. “There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:27–28).

This is what the very power of the sacrament accomplishes. For the sacrament is of the new life, which in this present time begins with the forgiveness of all past sins, but will be perfected in the resurrection of the dead.

“For you have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so you too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4).

You now walk by faith, as long as, in this mortal body, you are pilgrims away from the Lord. But Christ Jesus himself, according to the human nature which he deigned to assume for us, has become the sure way for you to the one toward whom you are journeying.

For he has kept much sweetness for those who fear him, intending to open and perfect it for those who hope in him, when what we have now received in hope we shall also receive in reality.

“For we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

He himself also promised this in the Gospel: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments. And whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

Certainly they saw him to whom he was speaking, but in the form of a servant, in which the Father is greater, not in the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father. The former he displayed to those who feared; the latter he kept for those who hoped. In the former he appeared to those journeying as pilgrims; to the latter he summoned those who would dwell with him. He spread the former beneath them as they walked; he promised the latter to those who arrived.

### II.

Since we have these promises, beloved, “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7:1).

I beseech you to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility of mind and gentleness, bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:1–3).

What a thing this is, from which we have received such a pledge!

But there are some who have put on Christ only in the sacrament, while they are naked with respect to faith and conduct. For many heretics also possess the sacrament of baptism itself, but not its saving fruit, nor the bond of peace: “Having,” as the Apostle says, “the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5).

They are either marked by deserters, or are themselves deserters, carrying the sign of the good king upon damnable flesh. They say to us: “If we are not faithful, why do you not give us baptism? But if we are already faithful, why do you seek us?”

As though they did not read that Simon Magus both received baptism and yet heard Peter say: “You have neither part nor lot in this faith” (Acts 8:21).

Behold, it can happen that someone possesses the baptism of Christ but does not possess the faith or love of Christ; that he possesses the sacrament of holiness but is not counted among the lot of the saints.

As far as the sacrament itself is concerned, it makes no difference if someone receives Christ’s baptism where the unity of Christ is not present. For even one baptized in the Church, if he becomes a deserter of the Church, will lack the holiness of life but will not lack the sacramental seal.

For it is shown that what he could not lose when he departed is not given back to him when he returns. Just as a deserter from military service lacks lawful fellowship but does not lack the king’s mark. If he himself also marks another with the same sign, he does not make him a companion in life but a companion in punishment.

But if both the deserter returns and the other comes to the lawful and properly ordered service, once the king’s severity has been appeased, the deserter is forgiven for his departure, and the one who has come is received.

In both, the fault is corrected; for both, the punishment is remitted; to both peace is given. In neither is what was marked repeated.

### III.

Therefore let them no longer say to us: “What will you give us, if we already have baptism?” For they are so ignorant of what they are saying that they do not even wish to read what Holy Scripture testifies: within the Church itself, that is, in the communion of Christ’s members, many baptized in Samaria did not receive the Holy Spirit, but remained in baptism alone until the Apostles came to them from Jerusalem (Acts 8).

On the other hand, Cornelius and those who were with him were found worthy to receive the Holy Spirit before they received the sacrament of baptism (Acts 10).

Thus God taught that one thing is the sign of salvation and another is salvation itself; one thing is the form of piety and another is the power of piety.

“What will you give us,” they say, “if we already have baptism?”

O sacrilegious vanity! They think so little of the Church of Christ, which they do not possess, that they suppose they will receive nothing if they join themselves to its communion.

Let the prophet Amos say to them: “Woe to those who do nothing for Zion” (Amos 6:1) [Note: [Col. 0840] Greek: Τοῖς ἐξουθενοῦσι Σιών. The Septuagint has: “Those who are wealthy in Zion.”].

“What will I receive,” he says, “if I already have baptism?”

You will receive the Church, which you do not have. You will receive unity, which you do not have. You will receive peace, which you do not have.

Or, if these things seem worthless to you, fight, deserter, against your Emperor, who says: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23).

Fight against his Apostle—or rather, against the one who spoke through him, and in this way against Christ himself—who says: “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3).

Count what he said: forbearance, love, unity, Spirit, peace. The Spirit works all these things that have been named, and you do not possess him.

Did you bear with anyone, having departed from the Church? Whom did you love when you abandoned Christ’s members? What unity do you have in your sacrilegious severance? What peace in your wicked dissension?

Far be it from us to say that these things are nothing; rather, without them you yourself are nothing. If you disdain to receive these things in the Church, you may indeed possess baptism, but whatever you possess without them you possess for greater punishment.

For the baptism of Christ, which together with these things would be a helper of your salvation, is without them a witness to your iniquity.

### IV.

But you, holy children, Catholic members, have received not another baptism but another result from baptism. You have received it not for punishment but for life; not for destruction but for salvation; not for condemnation but for honor.

Together you also received the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace—provided that you, as I wish, hope, exhort, and beseech, both preserve intact what you have received and advance toward greater things by making progress.

Today is the eighth day of your birth. Today the seal of faith is completed in you, which among the ancient fathers was made in the circumcision of the flesh on the eighth day of bodily birth.

The stripping away of mortality was represented in that human member through which a human being is born to die. Thus the Lord himself, stripping away the mortality of his flesh by rising again, and raising up not another body but nevertheless a body that would die no more, marked the Lord’s day by his resurrection. It is the third day after the day of his passion, but, in the reckoning of days after the Sabbath, it is the eighth and also the first.

Therefore you too, not yet in reality but already in certain hope, since you will possess the sacrament of this reality and have received the pledge of the Spirit, should hear:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:1–4).

## SERMON IX. On Psalm 117, verse 1: “Give thanks to the Lord,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0841] In the manuscript, fol. 17, verso, it is entitled: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop.” It deals with the confession of sins and is mentioned by Possidius in the Index of Works, chapter 9. It should be inserted after Sermon 29.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. What it means to confess to the Lord.  
II. How and why confession should be made to divine Goodness.  
III. How much confession made to a human judge differs from confession made to God.  
IV. Exhortation to confess sins to God.

### I.

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 117:1).

The Holy Spirit has exhorted us through the voice of the Psalm, and with one mouth and one heart we responded: “Alleluia,” which in Latin is interpreted as “Praise the Lord.” Through our voice that same Holy Spirit exhorts you:

“Confess to the Lord,” he says, “for he is good; for his mercy endures forever.”

Whether you sing in praise by celebrating his gifts, or pour out your sins with groaning, “Confess to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endures forever.”

For not only the remembrance of our sins but also the praise of our Lord is called confession, because if we do either one of these, we do it without the other. We accuse our iniquity with hope in his mercy, and we praise his mercy while remembering our iniquity.

Let us therefore confess to the Lord, “for he is good; for his mercy endures forever.”

Some think that certain creatures are evil because they offend the understanding of the ignorant, but this is false. For God made all things “very good,” because he is good.

Some think God is unjust because his faithful often suffer many harsh and difficult things in this temporal life; but those who think this are deceived. For he scourges every son—not one whom he rejects, but one whom he receives—because “his mercy endures forever” (Heb. 12:6).

## II.

Let us therefore confess to the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” Let us say to the Lord our God: “Your works are marvelous; for you made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). “Your judgments are just; for because of iniquity you have disciplined mankind” (Tob. 3:2). “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Ps. 118:67).

Let us say these things in confession, because, [Col. 0842] if certain things are adverse to us through the penalty of our mortality, he nevertheless does what is good, for he is good. And even if we are corrected by temporal pains and labors, “he will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 102:9).

What is as good as our God? Human beings blaspheme, and not only are they not humbled, but they even grow proud in their crimes; yet he “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). What is as merciful as our God? Human beings persist in their wickedness and crimes, and he does not cease to call them to conversion.

What is as good as our God, from whom we receive such great consolations even in distress? What is as merciful as our God, whose future sentence we cause to change by changing ourselves? Let us confess to the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Not every praise is a confession, but the praises of the Lord our God are. For if it was said most truly, “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1), he certainly seems evil to those who are perverse in heart. But who among human beings becomes upright except from perversity, so that, as one convicted, he begins to praise what he previously reproached, and to marvel at what he previously despised, confessing to the Lord that he is now good to him, once made upright, though he had seemed evil to him when he was perverse?

And since he was perverse through his own wickedness but was corrected by God’s grace, he must confess at the same time: “For his mercy endures forever.” We are evil; he is good. We become good through him; through ourselves, evil. He is good to us when we are good; he is good to us when we are evil. We rage against ourselves; he is merciful toward us. He calls us, so that we may be converted; he waits until we are converted; he forgives if we are converted; he crowns us if we do not turn away.

## III.

Let us therefore confess to the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” The confession of sins has always seemed something to be feared by human beings, but this is true in the presence of a human judge. Very often, to extract a confession from the mouth, people are subjected to lashes and various beatings, even hooks and fires; and sometimes the limbs yield to torments before the soul yields to pain, so that the structure of the body is broken apart before the secret of the crime is revealed.

The executioners press on; every kind of torture grows more intense. Yet the entrails are torn and punished in vain when the conscience is closed by denial. Why, then, does a person fear confessing amid such torments, unless because those who confess are accustomed to being punished? Whoever confesses to a human being is punished. Whoever confesses to God is set free.

Nor is this surprising. A human being asks another human being about what the one who asks does not know; but God, who urges us to confess, knows what we were unwilling to confess, and he does not learn it at the moment when we have confessed. How much more, then, does he free those who confess from eternal death—the one who, although he already knew our iniquities before we confessed them, spared us temporal death—

[Col. 0843]

## IV.

Perhaps you say: “What does God ask of me, that I should confess what he already knows?” For when one human being asks this of another, he does not know. What do you suppose is the reason, except that God wishes your sin to be punished by your acknowledging it, and to be released by his forgiving it? For how do you wish him to forgive what you do not wish to acknowledge?

Listen to the Psalm, and, if you are awake, notice your own voice and where it is found: “I acknowledged my sin,” it says, “and I did not conceal my wrongdoing. I said: I will confess my transgression to the Lord against myself, and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Ps. 31:5).

Hear this in another Psalm: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (ibid. 50:5). Thus he did not shamelessly say to God: “Turn your face away from my sins” (ibid. 50:11). God deigns to turn his face away from a person’s sin when the person himself takes no care to turn his face away from his sin, so that he may say in God’s ears: “My sin is always before me.”

Nor is it said to God, “Turn your face away,” because he does not know, but because he forgives. If, then, you fear, human being, to confess to a human judge because he is evil, or because he is compelled to enforce the severity of the law, confess confidently to the Lord: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

## SERMON X  
### On Psalm 149, verse 1: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” etc.

**[Note: [Col. 0843] In Codex fol. 19 it is entitled: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop.” It belongs to the Easter season, inspiring love and desire for future blessings, and should be inserted in the edition after Sermon 34.]**

### Synopsis

I. The two songs: the old and the new.  
II. What the Church of the saints is on earth.  
III. What the true Zion is, and what its condition is.  
IV. In Christ, the faith and hope of our blessedness.

### I.

The days have come for us to sing “Alleluia.” Attend carefully, brothers, to receive what the Lord offers for our exhortation and for the nourishment of that love by which it is good for us to cling to God.

Attend carefully, good singers, children of praise and of the eternal glory of the true and incorruptible God. Attend attentively and praise God; for this is “Alleluia.”

**[Note: From the following passage up to the words “because it never grows old,” Augustine repeats almost word for word—*κατὰ λέξιν*, literally “according to the wording”—in his *Exposition on the Psalms*, volume IV, column 1683, in the edition of the cited Psalm.]**

But praise God not only with your voice, but also with understanding and in good works. As the Psalm exhorted us, let us sing to the Lord a new song. For it began thus: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. 149:1).

The old person sings an old song; the new person, a new song. The Old Testament is an old song; the New Testament, a new song. In the Old Testament the promises are earthly; in the New Testament the promises are heavenly.

Whoever loves earthly things and is absorbed in earthly pleasures sings an old song. Whoever wishes to sing a new song should love eternal things. Love itself is new, because it never grows old and renews the one who loves.

Therefore, brothers, we commend to you that you love God; indeed, he himself commends this to all of us. We love him for our good, not for his; for we do not love him because of our evil, nor because of any evil in him. God will not have less divinity if a human being does not have love in him.

**[Note: Perhaps: “love for him” (*in illum*).]**

**[Col. 0844]** We grow through God, not he through us; and yet he loved us first so greatly, before we loved him, that he sent his only Son to die for us. He who made us was made among us.

How did he himself make us? “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). How was he made among us? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

### II.

Therefore, brothers, if we were previously reluctant to love, at least now let us not be reluctant to love in return. He loved us when we were foul, because he loved us as sinners. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6). He who gave the ungodly his death—what does he reserve for the righteous except his life? (Rom. 5:16)

Consider, then, where, or by whom, this new song is sung to the Lord. For when he said, “Sing to the Lord a new song,” he added: “His praise is in the assembly of the saints” (Ps. 149:1). And can there be an assembly of the saints on earth?

For the Prophet says: “The land has been defiled with blood, and adulteries and murders have been poured out upon the earth” (Ezek. 9; Hos. 4:2). How, then, can the assembly of the saints be understood to exist on earth?

The Apostle teaches, saying that, although we walk on earth, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Thus the saints, while placed on earth, constitute a heavenly Church.

“Let Israel rejoice,” he says, “in him who made him” (Ps. 149:2). Let Israel—that is, the righteous and the saints—rejoice in the Lord; but let the unrighteous rejoice in the world. When the world ends, the exultation of the unrighteous ends, because, while the Lord remains, the exultation of the righteous will remain.

Therefore, if we belong to Israel, and if we wish to be Israel, let us not rejoice in the things that have been made, but in him who made them. Let our hope be our God. He who made all these things is better than them all.

What is Israel? “Seeing God.”

**[Note: Jerome, in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, chapter 32, verse 28, more correctly interprets it according to the Hebrew sense as “prince,” or “one prevailing with God.” See in that passage whether he may also be alluding indirectly to our author.]**

How are we Israel if we do not yet see? There is one kind of vision belonging to the present time, and another kind belonging to the future. The vision that exists now is through faith; the vision that will exist in the future will be through sight. If we believe, we see; if we love, we see.

What do we see? God. Where is God himself? Ask the Apostle John. “God,” he says, “is love” (1 John 4:8, 16). Whoever possesses love—why do we send him far away to see God? Let him attend to his conscience, and there he sees God. If love does not dwell there, God does not dwell there. But if love dwells there, God dwells there.

If he wishes to see God seated in heaven, let him have love, and he will dwell in God.

### III.

“But let the children of Zion exult in their King” (Ps. 149:2). It is worthwhile to know who they are.

Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.”

**[Note: This is also found in Jerome, in the *Hebrew Names* and elsewhere, although the etymology rather suggests “a dry place.”]**

A watchtower is a high and elevated place from which one looks far ahead at what is to come. Therefore, if through the virtue of faith we place our life [Col. 0845] higher than the earth and far above human vices, we shall rightly be called children of Zion.

The King of Zion is without doubt the one who says: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6). Zion is itself Jerusalem; but it is the true Zion and the true Jerusalem—not that one which fell in war, which was set before us in mystery, but the one that is in heaven: “Jerusalem, which is our mother” (Gal. 4:26).

She gave us birth; she nourished us—partly a pilgrim in the world, and for the greater part dwelling in heaven. In the part that dwells in heaven there is the blessedness of the angels; in the part that is a pilgrim in this world there is the hope of the righteous.

Of the former it was said: “Glory to God in the highest”; of the latter: “And on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Therefore, those who groan in this life and desire that homeland should run—not with the feet of the body, but with the affections of the heart. Let them not seek ships, but seize the wings of love.

What are the two wings of love? Love of God and love of neighbor.

For, as the Apostle says, we are pilgrims: “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6). But letters have come to us from our homeland, reminding us of our return. These letters are read to us whenever the divine Scriptures are read.

Blessed are those who are there! They are no longer wounded by any desires, nor tormented by any iniquities, whether their own or those of others. Their only occupation is to praise God.

They do not plow; they do not sow. Those are works of necessity; there necessity does not exist. They do not steal; they do not plunder. Those are works of iniquity; there iniquity does not exist. They do not break bread for the hungry, clothe the naked, receive the stranger, or bury the dead. Those are works of mercy; there is no misery in which mercy may be exercised.

### IV.

O blessed ones! Do we think that we too shall be like this? Come, let us sigh; from our sighing let us groan over what we are and where we are.

And where are we? In a vain and passing world.

And what are we? Mortal, cast down, rejected, and, as a certain saint said: “Earth and ashes” (Gen. 18:27).

But the one who promised us immortality and eternity is almighty. If we look at ourselves, what are we? If we look at him, he is God; he is almighty.

Will God not make an angel from a human being, when he made a human being from nothing? Or does God truly regard as something insignificant the human being for whom he was willing to let his only Son die?

Let us attend to the sign of love and promise: from where have we received such pledges? We hold the death of Christ; we hold the blood of Christ.

Therefore let human weakness lift itself up. Let it not despair; let it not turn away. He who promised is God, and he came in order to promise. He appeared to human beings; he came to accept our death and to promise his life.

For God wished human weakness to be secure concerning his promise, so that he would not merely speak but also write. He spoke to believers; he took precautions for those who doubted; and behold, everything is held in a kind of bond-document, in Holy Scripture.

He therefore came to the region of our pilgrimage to receive what abounds here: reproaches, lashes, insults, a crown of thorns, the cross, and death.

**[Col. 0846]** These things abound in our region. He brought a commercial exchange: he came bringing us good things from that region, and in our region he endured evil things.

Yet he promised us that we would be where he came from, and he said: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

Such great love went before us: where we were, he was with us; where he is, we shall be with him.

Therefore hold fast to Christ, brothers; hold fast to faith; hold fast to the way. It will lead you to what you cannot see now. For in the Head it has appeared what the members are to hope for. In the foundation it has been shown what is to be built in our faith, so that afterward it may be brought to completion in hope.

## SERMON XI  
### On the Nativity of John the Baptist

**[Note: In Codex fol. 26 it is entitled: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop. On the Feast of Blessed John the Baptist.” An excellent and lofty treatise, also concerning the mystery of the Trinity, noted by Possidius in the *Index of Works*, chapter 8. On the response from Psalm 131: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” etc. It should be placed after Sermon 293.]**

### Synopsis

I. Who prepared a lamp, for whom, and what kind of lamp.  
II. The modesty of John the Baptist.  
III. The dignity of John the Baptist.  
IV. The mystery of the Trinity and the co-eternity of the Father and the Son.  
V. The Trinity manifested at Christ’s baptism.  
VI. Who the hidden enemies of Christ are.  
VII. Who the open enemies of Christ are.  
VIII. Recapitulation and exhortation.

### I.

We speak to Your Charity in the house of God about what the present Psalm has brought to our attention.

**[Note: Namely, the verse soon to be cited: “We will enter into his tabernacle,” etc., verse 5.]**

Who is it who says: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. I will clothe his enemies with confusion; but upon him my sanctification will flourish” (Ps. 131:17–18)? What is the lamp he prepared for his Christ? Who are the enemies of his Christ whom he clothes with confusion through that lamp? And what is the sanctification of the one who prepared a lamp for his Christ, which will flourish over his Christ?

Among all these words, only this seems plain and clear: “my Christ.” For nothing else is to be understood than Christ the Lord and our Savior.

Searching, then, as far as God grants us, into the depth of this meaning, we find that God the Father is speaking. God the Father—that is, the person of God the Father—speaks through the Prophet: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

That the same one is both the Son of God and the Christ of God need not be explained to Christians. Having identified the person who is speaking, let us see what lamp was prepared by God the Father for Christ the Son.

The Lord himself says about John the Baptist: “He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light” (John 5:35).

Therefore he called John a lamp kindled from the source of light, so that he might bear witness to the truth. For people lay in this blindness, in this weakness of the inner eye, so that the Sun of righteousness might be sought through a lamp.

If anyone had a pure eye of heart, he would look first upon the Sun himself and would not seek a lamp for his testimony. For after saying of that [Col. 0847] lamp, “You were willing to rejoice for a time in his light,” he added: “But I have testimony greater than John” (John 5:36).

The lamp, then, was kindled for the weak in the night. And how did he kindle it? The Father says concerning John, to Christ his Son: “Behold, I send my angel before you, who will prepare the way before your face” (Mal. 3:1; Matt. 11:10). “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131:17).

### II.

How did he clothe Christ’s enemies with confusion through this lamp? First, consider what we said: that the lamp was kindled from the source of light.

John himself bears witness: “But we,” he says, “have received from his fullness” (John 1:16). John possessed such outstanding excellence that, although he had been sent before Christ, he himself was thought to be Christ.

But if he had been a lamp extinguished and smoking with the stench of pride, when the Jews sent to him and said, “Who are you?” (ibid. 1:19)—“Are you the Christ? Are you Elijah? Are you the Prophet?”—he would have said, “I am.”

For he had found an opportunity for self-display, with human error spontaneously offering him a false honor. Was he struggling to persuade them of what those who questioned him were already saying?

But he was sent in humility to prepare the way for the exalted one. Hence he was the friend of the Bridegroom, because he was the servant who acknowledged the Lord.

And he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord; make his paths straight” (Matt. 3:3). “I am not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet.”

And they said to him: “Who then are you?” And what did he say? “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord.”

Isaiah had already foretold this (Isa. 40:3). Concerning whom he had prophesied is understood there. “You have read this,” he says, “in Isaiah, and perhaps, although it was read, you did not know of whom it was spoken. I am the one of whom it was said.”

Consider how greatly he humbles himself, having been so exalted that he was thought to be Christ. “I indeed baptize you with water; but he who comes after me is greater than I” (Luke 3:16).

“And he might be said to be greater than I by some degree.” **[Note: The sense is unstable here, and I see no remedy.]**

He says that the other is greater than himself. Say how much greater. “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen the strap of his sandal” (ibid.).

### III.

From this point understand why John was sent before Christ. You see how much less he is, and how greatly he confesses the other to be greater, saying that he is unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal.

How great is this one who says he is unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal? How great is he? Where shall we seek the answer?

If we ask John himself how great John is, we do not find the answer; for he humbles himself and says nothing about himself, whether truthfully or boastfully.

How great, then, is John, who is not worthy to loosen the strap [Col. 0848] of the sandal of the one who was thought to be a human being? From whom shall we hear this? Let us ask the Lord himself and say to him:

“Lord, John bore great witness concerning you. When his great excellence appeared among human beings, so that he was thought to be the Christ, and when he was asked who he was, he said that he was not the Christ. He said that one greater than himself would come, and so much greater that he was not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. Like a faithful lamp he spoke of your excellent light. This is what John said about you. Let us see who he is—the one who said these things about you. How great is the one who so humbled himself before you and confessed you to be so much greater than himself? Who is he?”

“That is what he says about you. You, tell us something about him.”

Hear the Lord’s voice concerning John: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11).

But what does he say? “Yet the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

**[Note: More correctly, if I understand it, Saint Augustine punctuates this differently from the majority of Greek and Latin copies, which here and at Luke 7:28 read: “Yet the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” For who would that lesser one in the kingdom of heaven be who was greater than John?]**

He is speaking of himself; for God is not arrogant when he commends his own greatness.

What does “the one who is lesser” mean? The one later in age, but greater in majesty. The Lord Christ was born later than John, but this is true in what he became for us, not in what we were made through him.

Of the one who was born after John, hear the Father: not “before John,” not “before David,” not “before Abraham,” but “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

If, then, something was accommodated to our weakness so that the day might be preceded by a lamp, and the lamp was believed concerning the day, how much more must the day be believed concerning the lamp, since “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist”?

The human being than whom no one greater had been born says that he is unworthy to loosen the strap of someone’s sandal. What, then, is the one whose sandal strap this human being, than whom no one greater had been born, is unworthy to loosen?

If John is already so great a human being that no human being can be greater, whatever is greater than he is more than human. If John is already so great a human being that no human being is greater than he, whoever is greater than he is more than human.

And the one who is more than human nevertheless became human for the sake of humanity. Rightly, therefore, the sanctification of the Father flourishes over him.

### IV.

For the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. The flower of holiness, manifested then in the form of a dove, simple and innocent, was shown more fully to John himself, so that this might be fulfilled: “And upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

“I did not know him,” he says, “but the one who sent me to baptize with water himself said to me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. And I,” he says, “have borne witness to what I saw, that he is the Chosen One of God” (John 1:33–34).

Concerning whom does he bear witness? Concerning the one upon whom he saw the Father’s sanctification flourishing.

From where did he see the Holy Spirit descending? For the Holy Spirit never at any time departed from the Son, nor the Son from the Spirit, nor the Son from the Father, nor the Father from the Son, nor the Spirit from the Son and the Father.

But these things are understood one way by a purified mind and demonstrated another way to the eyes. At no time does the Father precede the Son; at no time does the Son follow the Father—at no time, because there is no time there.

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, creator of time, are one God. Therefore there is no place there for saying, “The Father is earlier, the Son later.” From the time that the Father is, the Son is.

Ask: “From what [Col. 0849] time is the Father?” By thought you surpass earth, heaven, the angels, visible and invisible things, and the whole of creation, and you ask: “From what point did the Father begin?”

Eternal things are not sought in this way. Do not ask “from what point” except of what begins. Do not ask from whom that from which everything that began begins has its beginning; what begins from no one does not begin.

Just as the Father does not begin, so the Son does not begin, but the Son is the splendor of the Father. The splendor of fire comes from fire; the splendor of the Father comes from the Father.

From what time is the Father? From eternity to eternity. Therefore the splendor of the Father is also from eternity to eternity; and yet, because it is his splendor, it is his Son. Did it not therefore begin in time, so that he was begotten by the Father?

Who can see this? Polish the heart; shake off the dust; wash away the stain. Whatever disturbs the inward vision must be cared for and healed, and what is said and believed before it is seen will appear.

### V.

For now, however, we believe, brothers. What do we believe? That the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit do not precede one another in time.

Although, then, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit do not precede one another in time, I could not name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit without these names occupying time and being held within their respective temporal sequence.

The Father is not earlier and the Son later, yet I could not speak except by naming one first and another afterward. All the syllables occupied their own times, and the second syllable in my words could not sound until the first had passed.

Time was completed in my syllables while I was saying things that have no time.

Thus, brothers, when that Trinity was shown perceptibly to this flesh, the whole Trinity appeared at the river where the Lord was baptized by John. For he was baptized, he came up from the baptism, the dove descended, and a voice sounded from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

The Son in the human being, the Spirit in the dove, the Father in the voice. An undivided reality was shown distinctly—if it should be called a reality, or rather the cause of all realities, if indeed it is a cause.

For what do we say when we speak about God? And yet we speak, and he allows himself to be spoken of, though he is not as he is conceived. He cannot be spoken of in the manner in which he is conceived, nor conceived in the manner in which he is.

But as far as human beings are concerned, brothers, behold, he appeared through the dove, and this was fulfilled: “And upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

For “will flourish” was said to mean “will appear clearly.” Nothing in a tree is clearer than a flower, nothing brighter.

Come, then. We have reached the final words of the hypopsalm.

**[Note: Augustine also uses this word in *Retractions* I.20 to designate the portion of a Psalm that is more frequently repeated by those singing responsively.]**

“Upon him my sanctification will flourish” (Ps. 131:18).

I remember that I omitted who the enemies are who were confounded through the lamp.

### VI.

“I have prepared a lamp for my Christ”—the Father said this concerning his Son. What lamp? John.

Ask the Son himself: “He was a burning and shining lamp.”

“I will clothe his enemies with confusion.” Who are Christ’s open enemies except the Jews?

For Christ also has hidden enemies. All who live unjustly and impiously are Christ’s enemies,

**[Col. 0850]** even if they are marked with his name, even if they are called Christians.

To whom will he say: “I do not know you,” while they say to him: “Lord, in your name we ate and drank, and in your name we performed many mighty works” (Luke 13:26; Matt. 7:22–23)?

“What did we eat and drink in your name?” They were not boasting greatly about ordinary food and saying that this was why they belonged to Christ. There is a certain food that is eaten and drunk, and it is Christ.

And Christ is eaten and drunk even by enemies. The faithful know the spotless Lamb on whom they feed—and would that they fed upon him in such a way that they did not become liable to punishment!

For as the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

Therefore Christ’s enemies are those who prefer to live unjustly rather than obey him, and, when it is said that he will come to judge the living and the dead, fear that he may come.

If it were permitted to them, they would make him not come. Since they could not make him fail to come, they would make him not return.

The Jews already wished to do this—to prevent his return. For a son was sent to those wicked tenants, those wicked leaseholders unwilling to render the payment, who stoned the servants sent to them.

Then the master of the household, the owner of the vineyard, said: “I will send my son” (Luke 20:13). “Perhaps they will reverence even him.”

But they thought, saying: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (ibid. 20:14).

They could not prevent him from coming from the Father, and they attempted to prevent him from returning to the Father. But to what avail?

They saw and despised a mortal, but in him they could kill nothing except death. In Christ’s death, death itself died.

Rising, he ascended to the Father, and he will come. What do you fear? Love, and you will be secure.

Do we not pray: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10)? Therefore, brothers, do we pray and fear that we may be heard?

### VII.

But these, as I began to say, are the hidden enemies. Let us speak of the open enemies, who openly envied, raged, seized, scourged, mocked, crucified, killed, and guarded him after he had been buried.

Let us see how they were clothed with confusion through that lamp.

When these same enemies saw the miracles performed by the Lord, they said: “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?” (Luke 20:2).

They asked with hostile intent, so that, if he confessed his authority, they might hold him as guilty of blasphemy.

But consider how he dealt with the coin when they wished to slander him. If he said, “Let tribute be paid to Caesar,” they would accuse him of cursing the Jewish nation, which he would thereby have made subject and tributary. But if he said, “Let it not be paid,” they would accuse him before Caesar’s friends and officials of forbidding its payment.

He, however, said: “Show me a coin. Whose image and inscription does it have?” They answered: “Caesar’s.”

“Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:19–21).

This is like saying: If Caesar seeks his image on the coin, does God not seek his image in the human being?

Thus here too these enemy slanderers “spoke evil in their heart and heart” (Ps. 11:3). They would have spoken in one heart if those who said such things had not possessed a double heart; and hence [Col. 0851] shortly before it was said that the heart was joined together, not simple.

Consider how great the difference is. Of many servants of God who had one heart it was said: “They were of one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32) toward God.

Many simple people have one heart; one deceitful person has two hearts.

Therefore, because they spoke in heart and heart—“Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?”—that is, “If you say it, we honor you; if you say it, we venerate you; if you say it, we entreat you”—this seems to come from one heart.

But from the other, since there was a double heart: “If you say it, we slander you; if you say it, we will find something by which to seize you; if you say it, we will find something of which to accuse you.”

Such are Christ’s enemies. But let them be confounded by the lamp.

Now you will see them confounded. And rightly so: since we are holding the service of the lamp, let Christ’s enemies be confounded by the lamp that the Father prepared for his Christ.

For the Lord himself says that he was a burning lamp.

What, then, did he answer these people who said, “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?”

I too will ask one question. Tell me: “The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?”

They, however, were troubled among themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’”

That is: “Why do you ask me by what authority I do these things, when the one whom you questioned bore witness concerning me?”

“Therefore, if we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ we fear the people; for they all held John to be a prophet” (Matt. 21:24–27).

Fearing the people on one side and fearing the truth on the other, timid here and envious there, blind everywhere, they answered: “We do not know.”

The lamp was brought forth; the darkness fled. For although they were bodily present, they fled in heart by saying that they did not know what they knew.

The evidence of flight of heart is fear. They feared being stoned by the people if they said that John’s baptism was from human beings; they feared being convicted by Christ if they said that John’s baptism was from heaven.

They fled in confusion. When John was named, they were afraid, became disturbed, and fell silent.

And he said: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

### VIII.

John the Baptist, then, was prepared as a lamp for Christ our Lord. When the light of the lamp was brought forth, his slanderous interrogators, the enemies of Christ, departed in confusion.

This was fulfilled: “I will clothe his enemies with confusion.”

But we, brothers, recognizing the Lord through John the Baptist, his forerunner—or rather, recognizing him through the testimony of the Lord himself, of whom he said, “I have testimony greater than John”—by believing in Christ, may become the body of his Head, so that there may be one Christ, Head and body.

And when all of us have been made one, this will be fulfilled: “Upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

## SERMON XII  
### At the Vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul

**[Note: In the Codex, fol. 28, it is entitled: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop. At the Vigil of the Apostles.” An elegant and weighty sermon against the schism of the Donatists. It should be inserted in the edition after Sermon 294.]**

### Synopsis

I. Peter questioned three times by the Lord about his love.  
II. Against those who divide the Lord’s flock.  
III. Against the Donatists, who confine the Lord’s flock to Africa.  
**[Col. 0852]** IV. The Donatists blinder than the Jews.  
V. A warning against schism.

## I

Everything that has just been read from the holy Gospel took place and was said after the Lord’s resurrection. We heard the Lord Jesus Christ questioning the Apostle Peter—questioning whether he loved him (John 21). The Lord was questioning a servant, the teacher a disciple, the Creator a human being, the redeemer one who had been set free, firmness one who was trembling, the knower of all things one who was ignorant; and where he presented himself as asking questions, there he was showing himself as teaching. For Christ did not fail to know something that Peter held in his heart.

He asks once. Peter answers, but that is not enough. He asks again; Peter gives no different answer, but answers the very thing he had been asked. The question is repeated a third time, and love answers a third time. For he was questioned three times because of love, who had denied him three times through fear. When the Lord was dying, Peter was afraid—afraid—and denied him; but when the Lord rose again, he implanted love and drove out fear.

What, then, would Peter fear now? When he denied him, he certainly denied him because he was afraid to die. Once the Lord had risen, what would he fear in one in whom he had found death itself dead? Surely the living one who was asking was the very one who had been buried dead. The one who had hung upon the wood was present.

When our Lord Jesus Christ was being judged by the Jews, Peter was questioned and—what is worse—by a woman, and—what is more disgraceful—by a maidservant; he was afraid and denied him. Before a maidservant he trembled; before the Lord he stood firm. Yet to the one who confessed his love once, again, and a third time, he entrusted his sheep.

“Do you love me?” he said. “Lord, you know that I love you.” And he said to him: “Feed my lambs” (ibid. 16). This once, this again, this a third time—as though Peter had no place to show his love for Christ except as a faithful shepherd under the Prince of all shepherds.

“Do you love me?” “I love you” (ibid. 17). And what will you, who love me, do for me? What will you, a human being, bestow upon your Creator? What will you, who have been redeemed, bestow from your love upon your Redeemer, or, at the most, you who are a soldier upon your king? What will you bestow? This alone I require: “Feed my sheep” (ibid.).

## II

Yet consider, brothers, the evil servants who, for their own benefit, have made private possessions out of the Lord’s flock and divided what they had not bought. For certain unfaithful servants arose; they divided Christ’s flock and, in a manner, by their thefts made a private possession for themselves out of his flock. You hear them saying: “Those are my sheep. What are you looking for among my sheep? I will not find you among my sheep.”

If we too say “mine,” and they say “theirs,” Christ has lost his sheep. Place before your eyes the Prince of shepherds, the Lord standing beside his flock, distinguishing and judging among his servants.

“What do you say?” “These are my sheep.” “And what do you say?” “These are my sheep.” “Where are those whom I bought?”

Evil servants! You call them your sheep and claim for yourselves what I bought, although, if I had not bought you, you would perish. As for us, far be it from us to call you our sheep! That is not a Catholic voice; it is not a genuine voice; it is not Peter’s, because it is against the Rock.

You are sheep, but of the one who bought both us and you. We have one Lord. He is a shepherd, but not a hired man. He feeds his own and, unlike anyone else concerning sheep, both paid the price and prepared the document.

Ask what the price was: it is his blood. Ask what the document is: it is the Gospel, which you heard just now when it was read.

What did he say to Peter? “Do you love me?” “I love you.” “Feed my sheep.” Surely not your sheep? Do you wish to know to whom he says “your sheep”? Hear it in the holy book called the Song of Songs. Holy love-poems are read there: the Bridegroom and the Bride, Christ and the Church. That whole book is, as it were, a wedding song, what they call an epithalamium—but of a holy bedchamber, a chaste bedchamber.

“For he placed his tabernacle in the sun,” that is, in the light, in public, where it could be open and not hidden. “And he himself, like a bridegroom, came forth from his chamber” (Psalm 18:6). For he took a spouse, human flesh. His chamber was the virgin womb. There he joined the Church to himself, so that what had previously been foretold might be fulfilled: “And the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:5).

## III

These lovers, Christ and the Church, were therefore speaking with one another. The Church says to him:

“Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday. Why do I want you to tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at midday? Otherwise I may become like one covered among the flocks of your companions.”

“That is why,” she says, “I want you to tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, so that when I come to you I may not go astray—otherwise I may become like one covered among the flocks of your companions” (Song of Songs 1:6), that is, I may rush upon flocks that are not yours but your companions’, as one covered.

What else does “covered” mean except as though hidden and unknown?

[Note: Thus the Hebrew. Greek: *periballomenē*, “clothed/covered.” The Vulgate, however, has *vagans*, “wandering,” as though [lacuna].]

The Donatists usually give these words their own meaning, not the meaning of the Scriptures. For they commonly say this: “Africa is the south; Africa is the south of the world.
