Therefore the Church asks the Lord, ‘Where do you pasture, where do you lie down?’ and he answers, ‘In the south’”—as though he were saying, “Do not seek me except in Africa.”

Read and understand, heretical mind. A mirror is being held up to you now. Here I have found you. Understand that the Bride is still asking. Why do you make the Bridegroom answer already? Or recognize the feminine gender: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday? Otherwise I may become like one covered.” “Covered,” I think, is feminine, not masculine.

Therefore, O Lord, let Africa be the south. Let it be understood as they understand it. Africa is the south. Here the Donatist party was formed [Note: So the manuscripts read; but I think “of Donatus.”]. Here a great division occurred, and the saw of dissension was drawn through Christ’s flock.

Therefore she asks, like the Church overseas, where this division did not occur: “Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” For I hear that there one speaks of the party of Donatus, others of Catholics, others of Donatists. Tell me where you pasture, lest I come there and go astray. I seek news about where I fear uncertainty. “Tell me, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday. Why do I want you to tell me?”

“Otherwise I may become like one covered,” because to the party of Donatus I am like one covered, like one unknown. I am preached there, and they do not know me.

## IV

The Scriptures say this:

“In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, prepared on the top of the mountains; it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall come to it” (Isaiah 2:2).

It is called a mountain, yet for the party of Donatus the mountain is covered. One who stumbles against a stone may be forgiven. But one who stumbles against a mountain—what sort of eyes does he have?

My brothers, the Jews are more excusable. The Jews stumbled against a stone; the heretics stumble against a mountain.

How did the Jews stumble against a stone? Because, while Christ was suffering, he was still small, and it was said: “They stumbled against the stone of stumbling” (Romans 9:32).

The holy Daniel saw a vision, wrote what he saw, and said that he had seen “a stone cut from the mountain without hands” (Daniel 2:34). Christ came from the nation of the Jews. It too was a mountain, because it possesses a kingdom [Note: I read *illa*, “it”—namely, the Jewish nation.].

What does “without hands” mean? The stone was cut without human work, because no masculine work approached the Virgin, so that he might be born without human work. “A stone cut from the mountain without hands”; and it shattered the statue in which the kingdoms of the earth were signified.

And what was said? “This is the stone against which the Jews stumbled: ‘They stumbled against the stone of stumbling.’”

What is the mountain against which the heretics stumbled? Hear Daniel himself: “And that stone grew,” he says, “and became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth” (ibid. 35).

The Psalm rightly says to the risen Lord Christ: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth.”

What does “your glory above all the earth” mean? Your Church above all the earth; your Bride above all the earth. And yet she says:

“Tell me, you whom my soul has loved.” “I am already everywhere; I already possess all lands, and among the Africans I am covered. Therefore tell me, lest I become like one covered among the flocks—not of your sheep, but of your companions.”

For the companions created schisms. Who are the companions? Those who approached the Lord’s table, of whom the Psalm says elsewhere: “He who ate my bread” (Psalm 107:6); of whom it says:

“If an enemy had reproached me, I would surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food, in the house of God we walked with accord” (Psalm 40:10; 54:13–15).

Once with accord, now with discord, because without understanding. These are the companions whom she feared, lest she fall among them.

“I fear,” she says, “that I may go astray; I fear that, like one covered, I may rush upon the flocks of your companions; that by going astray I may perish; that I may wholly lose the baptism I received by repeating it.”

## V

You have heard the Bride’s concern; hear the Bridegroom’s answer. When the Bride had said this, the Bridegroom immediately replied:

“Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women” (Song of Songs 1:7).

Catholic woman, beautiful among the heresies! Unless you know yourself; unless you take care to know yourself there where you learned about me; unless you place my Scriptures before human rumors; unless you know yourself, because you are everywhere; unless you know yourself, because you are the one designated where it was said: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8).

Unless, then, you know yourself—what? “Go out!”

Unless you know yourself, go out! A bad word, a sorrowful word: “Go out!” May God turn it away from us!

See of whom it was said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). To the evil servant it is said: “Go out,” because “the servant does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever” (John 8:35).

Do you wish to see that “go out” is said to the evil servant? What is said to the good servant? “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21).

Therefore everyone who hears, everyone who is a member of his Bride, should fear what is said: “Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the footsteps of the flocks” (Song of Songs 1:7).

What does “in the footsteps of the flocks” mean? Through the errors of human beings, not in the voice of the Shepherd.

As for us, brothers, shall we go out in the footsteps of the flocks? We have the Shepherd’s footprints; by following them we do not go astray. “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21).

Therefore: “Unless you know yourself, go out in the footsteps of the flocks, and pasture your kids” (Song of Songs 1:7). Both “kids” and “your own.” You know that the sheep are on the right and the kids on the left.

“And pasture your own kids.” Why “your own kids”? Because when you go out, you pasture, like Donatus, your own kids. But if you do not go out, you pasture, like Peter, “my sheep” (John 21:17).

# Sermon XIII. On the Feast of Laurence the Martyr

[Note: In the manuscript, folio 31, page 2, it is inscribed: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the feast of Saint Laurence.” The opening suggests that something had been disturbed by certain persons who were profaning the feast days of the martyrs with untimely revelry; this is also relevant below, section 4. The rest concerns various subjects. In the edition, the sermon should be placed after Sermon 305.]

## Synopsis

I. Praise of Saint Laurence, and how the feasts of martyrs should be celebrated.  
II. The example of the martyrs as a stimulus to live well and to keep watch against the devil.  
III. We are rather children of Abraham than Jews.  
IV. Against those who profane the memorials of the martyrs through intemperance.  
V. Paul’s example is set before the afflicted.  
VI. Maternal love in Paul, and still more in divine Wisdom.  
VII. Necessity gives birth to good works.  
VIII. This life is a perpetual struggle with death.  
IX. The goods of eternal life exceed our capacity.  
X. Mutual assistance through prayer is commended.

## I

The sermon had to be shortened because of the hearer’s weariness, but it had to be delivered out of devotion to the Martyr. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, it will be moderated so that it is neither burdensome nor perhaps excessively abridged, [Note: Perhaps *sed*—“but”—has fallen out.] to the extent sufficient for what is enough.

A most solemn day has dawned in Rome, celebrated with a great gathering of the people. We join our brothers there, although absent in body, yet present in spirit, in one body under one head. For his merit is not remembered only where his body’s tomb is. Devotion is owed everywhere. His flesh is placed in one location, but the victorious spirit is with him who is everywhere.

The blessed Laurence was, as we have received, a young man in body, but grave in spirit; his younger age greatly commended him, and his crown was still more unfading. He was a deacon, inferior to the bishop in office but equal to the Apostle in his crown.

This solemnity of all the glorious martyrs was instituted in the Church for this purpose: that those who did not see them suffering might be led to imitation by faith, and might be reminded by the solemn celebration [Note: I think *commoneantur*, “be reminded,” should be read.]. For perhaps what the annual observance did not repeatedly recall would fall from human hearts. Nor can solemn celebrations of all the martyrs be kept fervently everywhere, since they would be lacking no day: indeed, not even one day can be found in the course of the year on which martyrs were not crowned in different places.

But if fervent solemnities were continuous, they would produce weariness; intervals renew devotion. Let us hear only what has been commanded; let us attend to what has been promised. At the solemnity of any martyr, let us prepare our heart for his festival in such a way that we are not separated from imitating him.

## II

He was a human being, and we are human beings. He was made by the one by whom we too were made. He was bought at the price by which we too were bought. Therefore a Christian ought not to say, “Why, then?” Rather, he ought not to say, “I cannot,” but: “Why can I not also?”

You heard the blessed Cyprian, both an example and a trumpet of the martyrs: “In persecution there is warfare; in peace conscience is crowned” [Note: Thus the holy Champion concludes his treatise *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, which, since it was customarily read publicly in the churches of Africa, appears to be cited from that work here by Augustine.].

Let no one, then, think that he lacks the time. The time of suffering is not always present, but the time of devotion is always present. Nor should anyone consider himself weak where God is at work giving strength, lest, while fearing for himself, he despair of the one who is at work in him.

For this reason God wished examples of martyrs to exist in every age and in both sexes. Old men were crowned, young men were crowned, adolescents were crowned, boys were crowned, men were crowned, women were crowned. Every age among women was crowned, and no woman said: “I am unequal in sex to defeat the devil.” She looked instead to the enemy who was to be cast down, the enemy by whom she had been cast down, and to be conquered by faith, to whom she had assented through deception.

Did women, then, presume upon their own strength? For it has been said to every human being: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

The glory of the martyrs is therefore the glory of Christ who goes before the martyrs, fills the martyrs, and crowns the martyrs.

Nevertheless, although peace belongs to one time and persecution to another, is any time without hidden danger? Never. That lion-dragon neither always rages nor always lies in wait, but it always persecutes. When its savagery is open, its snares are not hidden. When its snares are hidden, its savagery is not open. That is, when it roars like a lion, it does not creep like a dragon; when it creeps like a dragon, it does not roar like a lion. Yet because it is either a lion or a dragon, it always persecutes.

When the growl is silent, beware its snares. When the snares are exposed, avoid the lion in its growl. Both lion and dragon are avoided if the heart is always kept in Christ.

Whatever is to be feared in this life will pass away. In the other life, however, what is to be loved does not pass away, and what is to be feared does not pass away.

## III

Just now, in the Gospel, the Lord was addressing the Jews and saying to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees! For you build the monuments of the prophets and say: ‘If we had lived in the time of our fathers, we would not have joined them in killing the prophets.’ Certainly you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets. And you will fill up the measure of your fathers.”

When they said, “If we had lived in the time of our fathers, we would not have joined them in killing the prophets” (Matthew 23:29–32), they confirmed that they were their sons.

But we, if we keep to the right path, do not call those who killed the prophets our fathers. Rather, we call our fathers those who were killed by their fathers. For just as each person degenerates in character, so he becomes a son in character.

Certainly, brothers, we are called children of Abraham, although we have neither seen Abraham’s face nor derived a bodily branch from his lineage. How, then, are we his children? Not in flesh, but in faith. For Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6).

If, then, Abraham was righteous because he believed, all who after Abraham imitated Abraham’s faith became children of Abraham. The Jews, born from his flesh, degenerated; we, born from foreigners, attained by imitation what they lost by degenerating.

Far be it, then, that Abraham should be their father, although they came from Abraham according to the flesh. Their fathers were those whom they themselves confessed to be their fathers. “If we had lived,” they say, “in the time of our fathers, we would not have joined them in killing the prophets.”

How can you say that you would not have joined those whom you call your fathers? If they were fathers, you are a son. If you are a son, you would have joined them. But if you would not have joined them, you are not a son. If you are not a son, they are not fathers.

The Lord therefore proves from this that they will do what those men did, because they called them their fathers. “Certainly,” he says, “you yourselves testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets,” because you called them your fathers. “And you will fill up the measure of your fathers.”

## IV

And now let us consider who are the sons of those who were killed and who are the sons of those who killed. You see many running to the memorials of the martyrs, blessing their cups at the memorials of the martyrs, returning satiated from the memorials of the martyrs; yet examine them, and you will find them among the persecutors of the martyrs.

Through their very riots, seditions, and dances of every kind of luxury—which God hates—even now, since they cannot stone those who have already been crowned, they persecute them with cups.

Whose were those people, and whose sons were they, whose dances were recently and almost yesterday prohibited at the place of the holy martyr Cyprian [Note: Compare Sermon 311, *On the Nativity of Cyprian*, in the Maurist edition, volume V, column 1252, section 5, where he says that this plague was removed through the bishop.]? Certainly they were dancing there and rejoicing there. They eagerly awaited the solemnity itself as though they were rejoicing, and always desired to come on that day.

Among whom should they be counted: among the persecutors of the martyrs or among the sons of the martyrs? They revealed themselves when, after being prohibited, they swelled with sedition.

Sons praise; persecutors dance. Sons sing hymns; those others prolong banquets. It therefore does not matter how they appear to honor them. Those who honor are of the same kind as those who said: “If we had lived in those times, we would not have joined our fathers in killing the martyrs or the prophets.”

Join the faith of the martyrs now, and we shall believe that you would not have joined the killers of the martyrs. By what means were the martyrs crowned? I believe it was by walking in God’s way, enduring, loving even their enemies, and praying on their behalf.

This is the crown of the martyrs; this is the merit of the martyrs. You love, imitate, and praise them: you are a son of a martyr. You live a contrary life; then you will bear a contrary hand [Note: I think “left hand” is intended at the final judgment.].

## V

Therefore, dearly beloved, since persecution, as I have said, is never absent, and the devil either lies in wait or rages, we must always be ready, with our hearts fixed upon the Lord. As far as we can, amid these troubles, tribulations, and temptations, let us ask the Lord for strength, since of ourselves we are small and nothing.

What shall we say about ourselves? You heard the Apostle Paul when he was read: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (2 Corinthians 1:5). As it is said in the Psalm: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, O Lord, have made my soul rejoice” (Psalm 93:19).

Just as the Psalm says, “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, so your consolations make my soul rejoice,” so the Apostle says: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation abounds.”

We would fail when persecution came if the Comforter were absent. And because the strength either to endure or to obtain some temporary relief in life for the sake of necessary ministry did not come from themselves, observe what he said:

“I make known to you, brothers, our tribulation which occurred in Asia: we were weighed down beyond measure and beyond our strength” (1 Corinthians 1:8).

That tribulation surpassed human strength—but did it also surpass divine assistance? “Beyond measure,” he says, “and beyond our strength we were weighed down.” How far beyond our strength? See that he is speaking of the strength of the spirit: “So that we were even weary of living.”

How was the Apostle affected by the multitude of his pressures, so that the love that urged him to live was checked by weariness of life? How did love compel him to live—that love of which he says elsewhere: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:24)?

Behold, persecution had grown so great, and tribulation so great, that he was even weary of living. Behold, fear and trembling came upon him, and darkness covered him, as you heard when it was said in the Psalm. It is the voice of Christ’s body, the voice of Christ’s members.

Do you wish to recognize your voice there? Be a member of Christ. “Fear and trembling,” he says, “came upon me, and darkness covered me. And I said: ‘Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and rest?’” (Psalm 54:6–7).

Does this not seem to be what the Apostle said when he declared, “so that we were even weary of living”? In a certain sense he suffered weariness from the glue of the flesh, when he wanted to fly toward Christ.

The abundance of tribulations harassed the road, but did not close it. He was weary of living, but this was not in that eternal life of which he says: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

But because he was held here by love, what follows? “If living in the flesh is fruitful labor for me, and what I should choose I do not know. I am compelled by both desires: to depart and to be with Christ.” Who will give me wings like a dove? “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (ibid. 22–24).

He had yielded to the chicks who were chirping, covering them with outspread wings and warming them, as he himself says: “I became a little one among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

## VI

And observe, brothers: just now it was read in the Gospel: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

Look at the hen; look also at the other birds that build nests before our eyes. They warm their eggs and nourish their chicks. You will see none of them grow weak with its young.

Observe the appearance of a hen when she feeds her chicks, how her voice changes and breaks into a kind of hoarseness. Her feathers are not gathered and lively but rough and languid, so that if you saw another bird whose nest you did not know, you would not recognize whether it had eggs or chicks.

But when you see a hen, even if you do not see her eggs or chicks, from her voice and the appearance of her body you understand that she is a mother.

What, then, did our mother Wisdom do? She was made weak in the flesh in order to gather, beget, and warm her chicks; yet what is weak in God is stronger than human beings.

Under the wings of the weakness of her flesh, but beneath the hidden power of her divinity, she wanted to gather the children of Jerusalem. He had taught this to his Apostle, because he himself was doing it in him.

For the Apostle himself says: “Do you wish to receive proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). And he says that the sufferings of Christ abounded in him—not his own sufferings, but Christ’s sufferings.

For he was in Christ’s body and was a member of Christ, and whatever was being done in the Apostle, his member, for the warming of the chicks, the Head was doing.

This Apostle, therefore, attentive to the weakness of his chicks, desired and longed to fly like a dove; but through love for his children he remained like a hen.

“We had,” he says, “within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead, who delivered us from so great deaths and will deliver us, in whom we have hoped, for he will still deliver us” (ibid. 1:9–10).

What does “he delivered us and will deliver us” mean? He preserves this life of ours for your sake. For he delivered us from many deaths, so that we would not be overwhelmed by our persecutors and crowned sooner than the chicks needed us, in accordance with what he says: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.”

But, confident in this, “I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and the joy of faith” (Philippians 1:24–25).

Desire was carrying him elsewhere; necessity was holding him here. “To depart,” he says, “and to be with Christ is far better” (ibid. 23). He did not say “necessary,” but “better.” For what is better is desired for its own sake; what is necessary is taken up from necessity. That is why it is called necessary.

## VII

Necessity gave its name to a necessary matter. Therefore this food, which we now use, is necessary for us. Food is necessary for sustaining temporal life. But that best food—virtue and wisdom, the living bread, always producing and never failing—is the best food.

That one is best; this one is necessary. Therefore, when this necessity of hunger and of sustaining the mortal body has passed, this food will no longer be necessary.

For what does the Apostle say? “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians 6:13). When will he destroy them? When this animal body, rising again, becomes spiritual.

There will be no need there, and there will be no works of necessity. For all these things, brothers—the good works spoken of here, and the very works that we are daily urged to perform—are works of necessity.

What is so good, so excellent, so praiseworthy for a Christian as to break bread for the hungry? To bring the needy person without shelter into one’s house? To see the naked and clothe him? To see the dead and bury him? To see people in conflict and reconcile them? To see the sick and visit or care for them?

All these are praiseworthy works. Attend and see that necessity gave birth to them. You break bread because you see someone hungry. If no one were hungry, for whom would you break bread? Remove the necessity caused by another’s misery, and your mercy will have no task.

Yet through these works, which necessity has brought forth, we reach that life where there will be no necessity—just as by a ship we reach our homeland.

A ship will not be needed in the homeland, where one will remain forever and never again be a traveler; but the very ship that will not be needed there brings us there. When we have arrived, these things will not exist; but unless they are fulfilled here, we cannot arrive there.

Therefore be eager in the good works of necessity, so that you may be blessed in enjoying that eternity where necessity itself now dies, because the mother of all necessities, death itself, will die.

For “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” When it is said to death, “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Corinthians 15:53–55), it will be said to death, now consumed and conquered: “The last enemy, death, shall be destroyed” (ibid. 26).

## VIII

Now, through all the works of necessity, we struggle with death. For every deficiency draws toward death, and every act of sustenance recalls us from death. The body is so changeable that, in a certain sense, different deaths are driven away by other deaths.

Whatever is taken in, since one cannot remain in it for long, is in a certain sense the beginning of death. Now consider this life. If whatever is taken in is something in which one cannot remain longer, and if, by remaining in it longer, one dies, it is the beginning of death; yet unless it is taken in, another death is not driven away.

For example, a person does not eat. If he eats and digests, he is restored. When he does not eat, he takes up fasting so as to repel from himself the death that excessive eating would have caused. Unless he takes up abstinence and fasting, he will not repel it.

Again, in this fasting that he has taken up to repel the death of excessive eating, if he wishes to persist in it, he will fear another death, the death of hunger. Just as he took up fasting to avoid the death of excessive eating, so he must take up food to avoid the death of fasting.

Whatever of these things you take up, if you persist in it, you will fail. You were tired from walking; if you persist in walking, you will fail from the fatigue itself and die. Therefore, so that you do not fail through walking, you rest by sitting. Persist in sitting, and you will die from that.

Heavy sleep had weighed upon you; you must wake up lest you die. You will die from staying awake unless you sleep again.

Give me something that you can take up as an aid to drive away the evil that was weighing upon you, something in which you can be secure enough to wish to persist. Whatever you take up, that very thing will have to be feared.

Therefore, amid all the movement and change of failures and remedies, we struggle with death. But when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality, it will be said to death: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting?”

We shall see, praise, and remain. There will be no need there, and no aid will be required. You will find no beggar for whom to break bread, no stranger whom you must receive into your house. You will find no thirsty person to whom you must offer a cup, no naked person whom you must cover, no sick person whom you must visit, no person in conflict whom you must reconcile, no dead person whom you must bury.

All are nourished by the food of righteousness and the drink of wisdom; all are clothed with immortality; all live eternally in their own homeland. The health of all is eternity itself—eternal health, eternal harmony.

No one quarrels; no one seeks a judge, an arbiter of settlement, or a sentence of vengeance. There is no sickness, no death.

## IX

We have been able to say what will not be there; but who can say what will be there? “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

The Apostle therefore rightly says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

Whatever you may have suffered, O Christian, know that it is nothing compared with what you will receive. Certainly we hold this by faith; let it not depart from your heart.

You cannot grasp this or see what you will be. What, then, must that be which cannot be grasped by the one who will receive it? Certainly we shall be what we shall be, and we cannot grasp what we shall be.

It surpasses all our weakness, surpasses all our thought, surpasses all our understanding—and yet we shall be it.

“Beloved,” John says, “we are children of God”—already, certainly, through adoption, faith, and the pledge. We have received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, brothers. When does the one who gave such a pledge deceive?

“We are children of God,” he says, “and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

He said, “It has not yet appeared,” and he did not say what has not yet appeared. What we shall be has not yet appeared. He could have said: “We shall be that, and we shall be such!” Whatever he might have said, to whom would he have said it?

I do not dare to say, “Who could say it?” but certainly: “To whom would he say it?” Perhaps there was someone who could say it, because he is the one who reclined on Christ’s breast and drank wisdom from his breast at that banquet; filled with that wisdom, he poured it forth: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1).

Therefore he said this: “We know that when what we shall be appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

Like whom? Certainly like the one whose children we are. “Beloved,” he says, “we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when it appears, we shall be like him whose children we are, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Now, if you wish to be what the one to whom you will be like is, if you wish to know whom you will resemble, look at him himself, if you can. You cannot yet. Therefore you do not know whom you will resemble; for that reason you do not know how greatly you will resemble him.

In not yet knowing what he is, you do not know what you too will be.

X. Therefore, beloved, meditating on these things, let us always await our everlasting joy, and let us always pray for strength amid temporal labors and temptations—whether we pray for you or you for us. For do not suppose, brothers, that our prayers are necessary for you while your prayers are not necessary for us. Our prayers are mutually necessary for one another, because these prayers for one another are formed by charity, and this sacrifice, as though arising from the altar of devotion, exhales the sweetest fragrance to the Lord.

For if the Apostles said that prayers should be offered for them, how much more should we, who are far unequal to them, though desiring in some measure to follow in their footsteps—and unable either to know or to dare to say how much we attain to them. Those men, then, such as they were, wished the Church to pray for them, and they said: “For you are our glory, just as we are yours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Cor. I, 14). They prayed for one another before the day of our Lord Jesus Christ: glory on that day, weakness before the day. Let prayer be offered in weakness, so that there may be joy in glory.

For although we shall arrive there at different times, nevertheless we shall all arrive at the same time. The times for departing from here are different; there, the time for receiving is one. For once and together we shall be gathered, to receive what at different times we have both believed and desired. It is like those laborers in the vineyard: some were brought at the first hour, others at the third, others at the sixth, others at the ninth, others at the tenth (Matt. XX). They were called at different times, but the wages were paid to all at one time.

Turned toward the Lord, etc.

# SERMON XIV. On the Feast of Cyprian the Martyr

[Note: In the Codex, fol. 36, p. 2, it is inscribed: “Likewise, a sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, On the threefold struggle of Christians, and strongly against the spectacles of the pagans.” It should be inserted in the edition after Sermon CCCXIII.]

## Synopsis

I. Praise of Saint Cyprian in the Lord.  
II. With whom the Christian must struggle.  
III. Against the spectacles of the pagans.  
IV. Against pride.  
V. Cyprian’s praise repeated.

## I

The holy solemnity of the most blessed Martyr, which has gathered us together in his name, requires that something worthy be said about the merits and glory of so great a Martyr. Human speech might perhaps suffice for his virtues and glory if he himself had wished to praise himself. Nevertheless, let us praise him more through devotion than through ability—or rather, let us praise the Lord in him, the Lord through him, and him in the Lord.

For what could he be without the Lord? The voice of the Martyrs was heard just now from the Psalm, when it was read: “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXIII, 8). If the help of all of us is in the name of the Lord, how much more so is that of the Martyrs! Where the struggle is greater, greater help is necessary.

There are two things that make the way of Christians narrow: rejection of pleasure and endurance of suffering. You conquer, whoever you are who struggle, if you conquer what pleases and what frightens. I say: you conquer, Christian, whoever you are who struggle, if you conquer what pleases and what frightens. One is what pleases; another is what frightens. But now we are dealing with the glory of the Martyrs. It is easy to celebrate the solemnities of the Martyrs; it is difficult to imitate the sufferings of the Martyrs.

## II

The Christian way, narrow and constricted, as I had begun to say, is made so by two things: contempt for pleasure and endurance of suffering. Therefore, whoever struggles should know that he is struggling against the whole world; and in struggling against the whole world, let him conquer these two things, and he conquers the world. Let him conquer whatever flatters; let him conquer whatever threatens.

Pleasure is false, punishment transitory. If you wish to enter through the narrow gate, close the gates of desire and fear. For by these the tempter tests the soul in order to overthrow it. Through the gate of desire he tests by promising; through the gate of fear he tests by threatening. There is something for you to desire, so that you may not desire these things. There is something for you to fear, so that you may not fear these things. Desire must not be taken away, but changed. Fear must not be extinguished, but transferred to another object.

What did you desire? To what did you yield before the world’s flattery? What did you desire? The pleasure of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, the ambition of the age. I do not know which of these three heads is the hell of the flesh. But hear the Apostle John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast and belched forth in the Gospel what he had drunk at Christ’s banquet. Hear him say: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (I John II, 15–16).

The world is also called this heaven and earth. He does not condemn the world itself who says, “Do not love the world.” For whoever condemns this world condemns the world’s maker. Hear the word “world” mentioned twice in one passage with different meanings. It is said of the Lord Christ: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. The world was made through him” (John I, 10). “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXXIII, 8). The world was made through him.

“I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Ps. CXX, 1–2). “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” This world was made by God; yet “the world did not know him.”

You who love the world, lover of the work and despiser of the maker: let your love migrate. Break the cords binding you to the creature; bind yourself to the Creator. Change your love; change your fear. For nothing makes good and evil conduct except good or evil loves.

“Someone is a great man,” someone will say; “he is good, he is great.” “From what source?” I ask. “He knows many things.” I ask what he loves, not what he knows. Therefore, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world”—that is, among those who love the world; the things that exist among the lovers of the world—“is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.”

In the desire of the flesh there is pleasure. In the desire of the eyes there is curiosity. In the ambition of the age there is pride. Whoever conquers these three has no remaining desire at all that he must conquer. There are many branches, but a threefold root.

How many evils the appetite for carnal pleasure contains, how many evils it produces! From it come adulteries and fornications; from it, wantonness and drunkenness. Whatever illicitly tickles the senses and penetrates the mind with destructive sweetness subjects the mind to the flesh, casts down the one who is exercising himself, and causes the one who ought to rule to serve. And what can a person do rightly when he is himself perverted?

## III

What evils are produced by shameful curiosity, the empty desire of the eyes, the eagerness for trivial spectacles, the madness of the arenas, and the contests of combatants when no reward follows! Charioteers compete for some reward; the crowds quarrel over the charioteers for some reward.

[Note: Concerning such contests, see various passages in Martial’s Epigrams and in the writers of the Augustan History.]

Yet the charioteer delights people, the hunter delights them, the stage performer delights them. Is it honorable to take pleasure in disgrace? Change, too, your desire for spectacles. The Church presents to your mind spectacles more honorable and worthy of reverence.

Just now the Passion of blessed Cyprian was being read. With our ears we heard it; with our minds we watched it. We saw him struggling; in a certain way we feared for him in his peril, but we hoped in God’s help.

Finally, do you wish to know quickly what difference there is between our spectacles and those of the theater? As far as a sound mind is active within us, we wish to imitate the Martyrs whom we watch. I say: we wish to imitate the holy Martyrs whom we watch struggling.

An honorable spectator! In the theaters, when you watch, you go mad if you dare to imitate the person you love. Look: I watch Cyprian; I love Cyprian. If you grow angry, curse me and say, “May you be such as he!” I watch, I delight, and as far as I can I embrace him with the arms of my mind. I see the combatant; I hear the victor.

Grow angry, as I said, and say to me, “May you be such as he!” See whether I do not embrace him; see whether I do not wish it; see whether I do not desire it; see whether I cannot call myself unworthy. Yet I cannot shrink back or turn away. You watch; you delight; you love. Do not grow angry if I say, “May you be such as he!” But I spare you; I do not say it. Recognize a friend.

Change your spectacles with me. Let us love those whom we desire to imitate as far as we can. But the one who is watched is infamous; the one who watches is honorable. Let the buyer’s desire cease, and there will be no disgrace for sale. By watching, you confirm the disgrace. Why do you provoke what you condemn? I am surprised that the disgrace of those you love does not splash upon you.

But let it not splash upon you; let your honor remain unblemished—if it can—while you watch lust and purchase shameful pleasures. Do I dare prohibit spectacles? Do I dare prohibit them? I certainly do. This place gives me confidence, and the one who established me in this place gives me confidence. The holy Martyr was able to withstand raging pagans; should I not dare to instruct listening Christians? Should I fear silent offenses when he despised open furies?

I shall speak plainly. Certainly I shall be refuted in the hearts of my hearers if I speak falsely. The ancient Roman discipline does very well—indeed, it does exceedingly well—in assigning every kind of stage performer to a dishonorable status. No honor is granted to them in the Senate, nor even among the plebeians.

[Note: In some assembly of the plebs.]

They are removed from honorable people on every side, and household slaves are set over them.

[Note: I read *vernales*, that is, household slaves and those born within the household.]

What have you removed from yourself because of the dignity of the decurionate—

[Note: Or decurionate, an office which in colonies and municipalities was comparable to a senatorial office.]

—and placed in the theater for your pleasure? Let your pleasure correspond to your dignity. Those wretched people themselves are enslaved to the desires of the spectators and to the spectators’ frenzied pleasures. Remove all these things, and they will be freed. The one who refuses to watch shows mercy toward them.

## IV

Let this be said about the desire of the eyes. How much evil does the ambition of the age contain! There is all pride there. And what is worse than pride? Hear the Lord’s judgment: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

Therefore, the ambition of the age is also evil. Someone will say: “Without it, the powers of the age cannot exist.” They certainly can. I do not know which author of theirs says: “Each person transfers his own fault to the affairs themselves.”

[Note: Perhaps Seneca, *Epistle* 50 to Lucilius: “That you may understand that the faults you think belong to circumstances are yours.”]

They certainly can. A ruler has been appointed to authority. Let him rise up—and let him rule. But the human mind advances into self-exaltation. Let exaltation be restrained. Let the person who judges another recognize that he himself is a human being. Their dignity is unequal, but fragility itself is shared.

Whoever piously and reverently considers this, even if he possesses authority, does not proceed into self-exaltation. Cyprian conquered all these things. For what did he not conquer, since he despised life itself, a life overflowing with every temptation? The judge threatened him with death; he confessed Christ, ready to die for Christ.

When death has come, no ambition remains, no curiosity of the eyes, no appetite for filthy and carnal pleasures. By despising one life, everything is overcome.

## V

Therefore, let blessed Cyprian be praised in the Lord, because he conquered all these things. When could he have done so if the Lord had not helped him? When would he have conquered if the spectator who prepared the crown for the victor had not supplied strength to the laborer?

He himself plainly rejoices—he rejoices for us, not for himself—when he is praised in the Lord. For he is exceedingly gentle, and it is written: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised. Let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. XXXI, 3). He was meek. He wished his soul to be praised in the Lord. Let his soul be praised in the Lord. Let his body also be honored, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. LXXII, 1).

Let him be solemnly celebrated, as Christians should celebrate him. For we do not set up an altar to Cyprian as though to a god; rather, we have made Cyprian an altar to the true God.

[Note: Compare the end of Sermon CCCXIII and Sermon CCCX, no. 2, vol. V of the Maurist edition.]

# SERMON XV. Likewise, on the Feast of Cyprian the Martyr

[Note: In the Codex, fol. 37, p. 2, it is inscribed: “Likewise, a sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, On the Martyrs and the victory of the Church in them.” The sermon may perhaps be the one noted by Possidius in the *Catalogue of Works*, chapter 8, “On the Hunters of God and of the Age.” For the verse of the Psalm cited above is explained as referring to the teeth of the persecutors and to the teeth of the Church, as becomes clear in the course of the sermon. It should be placed in the edition after the preceding Sermon XIII.]

## Synopsis

I. Joy at the religious gathering of the people and the victory of the Martyrs.  
II. The Martyrs’ thwarting of the persecutors’ plans.  
III. The Church victorious over the persecutors.  
IV. As in the case of Christ, so in that of Cyprian, many persecutors converted.

## I

We sang the Psalm: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth” (Ps. CXXIII, 6).

Due thanksgiving is owed for God’s gifts. “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.” This is certainly a voice of thanksgiving, and a worthy thanksgiving. Yet when is human thanksgiving sufficient for such great divine gifts?

When the most blessed Martyr shed his sacred blood in this place, I do not know whether there was here so great a crowd of those raging as there is now a multitude of those praising. I say it again—for I delight in seeing the people gathering in the house of the Lord with such devotion in this place, and in comparing one time with another. Therefore I say it again, repeat it, and commend it to your minds with as much devotion as I can:

When the most blessed Martyr shed his sacred blood in this place, I do not know whether there was here so great a crowd of those raging as there is now a multitude of those praising.

But even if there was such a crowd, still: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.” When they were killing, they believed that they were conquering. They were being conquered by those who were dying, and they rejoiced if they were being conquered. They were certainly raging.

The crowd of those raging has departed; a multitude of those praising has succeeded it. Let the multitude of those praising say—let it say: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.”

Whose teeth? The teeth of enemies, the teeth of the impious, the teeth of the persecutors of Jerusalem, the teeth of Babylon, the teeth of the hostile city, the teeth of the crowd raving in its crimes, the teeth of the crowd persecuting the Lord, abandoning the Creator, turning to the creature, worshiping what human hands have made, and despising him by whom it was made.

“Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.”

## II

This is the voice of the Martyrs. It is certainly the voice of those who preferred to be killed for Christ’s name rather than live by denying Christ. If they wished to kill, and these were killed—if those did what they wished while these suffered—how is it that we say, “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth”? What kind of thanksgiving is this: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth”?

Because the persecutors did not wish merely to kill but to devour—that is, to transfer them into their own body. They were pagans, they were impious, they were worshipers of demons and idols. This is what they wished to make us when they desired to devour us.

Consider what we do with food when we eat. What do we do except transfer it into our own body? There was the body of the impious; they devoured those who consented to them in impiety. Without doubt, those people passed into their body.

Therefore, when the Martyrs were being pressed to deny Christ and worship an idol, they stood firm, rejected the idol, confessed Christ, and by consenting did not pass into their body. Let them say—let them say it gloriously, let them say it happily, let them say it truly: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.”

The nets are faithlessness; the nets are impiety; the nets are the denial of Christ. The nets have been stretched out. You hear the hunters. If you wish to avoid the hunters, despise those who frighten you. You know what hunters do: from one side they stretch the nets, and from another they frighten the wild animals, driving them into the nets.

Do you fear the evil by which you are frightened? Worse is the evil from which you flee. Therefore, when the holy Martyrs saw where the hunters had stretched their nets—for this was why the persecutor threatened death, so that the Savior might be denied—they suffered, but by suffering they were not captured.

With what rich fat of prey, with what abundance of spoil, would impious Babylon have fed if the Lord had been denied by Bishop Cyprian—by Cyprian, that great man, teacher of the nations, frustrator of idols, betrayer of demons, gainer of pagans, confirmer of Christians, and kindler of Martyrs? If the Lord had been denied by such a great man, how joyfully would impious Babylon have feasted upon such prey!

“Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth. They raged, they persecuted, they tortured, they imprisoned, they bound, they struck, they burned, they went beneath the beasts [reading uncertain].”

[Note: So the manuscripts read. Perhaps: “They subjected them” or “laid them beneath.”]

Christ was not denied; the Lord’s Confessor was crowned. They lost their cruelty; the Martyrs found glory.

Let the Christian people say, let them say it altogether—it is fitting that they say it: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.”

Now let them say it. This place is filled with a people confessing; it is filled with a people worshiping the one true God. Let this place say it. For the harvest was being sown then, when this place was being watered with the Martyr’s blood.

Do not wonder, O earth, at your fertility, if you have been watered so that you might bring forth this growth.

## III

Therefore: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.” By what strength have we been snatched from the teeth of the impious? We claim nothing for ourselves; we do not attribute this to our own power. “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth.”

For what were we when the weak were being frightened by the strong, the lowly by the exalted, the poor by the rich, and the needy by those who possessed abundance? What were we, unless our help were in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Ps. CXXIII, 8)?

Rejoice, rejoice, Jerusalem; rejoice, you who were not given over to the teeth of the hunters. Rejoice, you too. You also have teeth. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep. You also have teeth, holy Jerusalem, city of God, Church of Christ; you also have teeth.

It is said to you in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song IV, 2; VI, 5).

Well done—well done, because you did not fear the teeth of Babylon. The teeth of Babylon were the powers of the age; the teeth of Babylon were the teachers of unlawful rites. You were not given over to these teeth.

Recognize your teeth. Do what they wished to do. Turn yourself. You too have teeth.

“Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep.” What does “shorn” mean? Those who lay aside worldly burdens. What does “shorn” mean? Those who lay down their fleeces, as burdens of the load of this age. They were your teeth, of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that “they sold all their possessions and laid the prices of their goods at the feet of the Apostles, to be distributed to each as there was need” (Acts IV, 35).

You received the fleece of your shorn sheep. That flock ascended from the washing of holy Baptism. They all gave birth, because they fulfilled the two commandments of charity.

You remember; you recalled them, and, as though instructed, you applauded when I mentioned the two commandments of charity. I did not say what they were, yet I received an indication of your hearts through your voices. You recognized them.

Nevertheless, I shall say them for the sake of those who come to the Church less frequently. The Lord says—the most truthful Teacher says—the Prince of Martyrs says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 37–40).

Therefore, your teeth have conquered in God, because they have borne such twins. To you who possess such teeth, to you, O Church, it is said in the figure of the blessed Peter: “Rise, kill, and eat” (Acts X, 13).

“Rise.” This was said to Peter when a vessel descending from heaven, carrying animals of every kind as a figure, was brought to the hungry Peter—that is, to the hungry Church: “Rise. Why are you hungry? Rise; food has been prepared for you. You have teeth; kill and eat.”

Kill what they are; make them what you are. Kill what they are; transform them into what you are. Well did you hear, possessing such teeth; well did you kill; well did you eat.

You drew to yourself the very judges whom you had not feared. You transformed into yourself the very powers of the age whom you had not feared. You despised those who raged; you made them honor you.

What was promised to your Lord has been fulfilled: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI, 11).

## IV

The persecutors did not believe these things when they raged. How many of those persecutors who saw the most blessed Cyprian shedding blood, bending his knees, and offering his neck to the executioner saw him here, watched him here, rejoiced here at so great a spectacle, and here—here—insulted him as he died!

How many of them, as I do not doubt, later believed. This must not be doubted; it must be believed without hesitation.

The Jews, the killers of Christ, who, while he was hanging there, shook their heads in mockery and joyfully spoke against him whatever words they wished, later believed in the very Lord whom they crucified.

For could the voice of the Physician hanging upon the cross, who from his own blood was preparing medicine for the deranged, have been useless? Could that voice have been empty: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34)?

It was certainly not useless. A multitude of those for whose sake this voice resounded from the mouth of Truth was present there. Later, after a miracle had occurred and the Holy Spirit had come from heaven, when the Apostles spoke in the languages of all nations, those people, astonished at the sudden miracle, were suddenly pierced in heart. They turned to the one whom they had killed and, believing, drank the blood which they had shed in their rage.

The same must by no means be doubted concerning the blessed Cyprian, the holy Martyr of Christ: many of those who impiously watched him being killed believed in his Lord, and perhaps even imitating him shed their blood for Christ’s name.

Finally, let the matter concerning those people remain uncertain. Let it be uncertain whether those who were present at this place then, who saw holy Cyprian struck down in this place, believed. Certainly all these people—or nearly all of them—whose voices I hear rejoicing are children of those who insulted him.

# SERMON XVI. On the Feast of the Scillitan Martyrs

[Note: In the Codex, fol. 39, it is inscribed: “A sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, On the Feast of the Holy Scillitan Martyrs.” These Martyrs suffered at Carthage around A.D. 200; they appear to have numbered twelve and to have originated from the town of Scilla, or Scillium, in the Proconsular Province of Africa. Other Acts of theirs are extant in Baronius under A.D. 202, and others from the Library of the Church of Toledo among the Bollandists, vol. IV of July, under the seventeenth day, on which their memory is celebrated. Augustine preached a sermon in their basilica at Carthage, in edition CLV. Since Possidius notes two treatises in the *Catalogue of Works*, chapter 9, “On the Hunters of God and of the Age,” William Cuperus writes as follows in the cited volume of the *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 206: “Since this sermon appears nowhere among Augustine’s works, not even in the most recent edition, I think that it has either perished or is still somewhere struggling with the dust.” Behold, now the worship and relics of the Martyrs are no longer soiled by dishonorable dust: they have spread through Spain, Gaul, and Italy, and some rest at Rome in the Church of Saints John and Paul on Mount Caelius. While I was writing these comments, that titular church was adorned by Joseph Cardinal Garampius, a man truly eminent in piety, learning, love of learned men, and sacred dignity, and one who had favored me from the time when he served as legate of the Supreme Pontiff at the imperial court. He was eagerly awaiting these relics of Augustinian thought. But before they could be completed in print, he was, as we piously hope, brought closer to the fellowship of Augustine at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of May. This sermon, moreover, could be placed in the edition after the preceding Sermon XIII.]

## Synopsis

I. By the example of the Martyrs, Christ must not be denied either for the world’s superfluous goods or for its necessary goods.  
II. From where love of neighbor arises, and what kind it is.  
III. Health and a friend, the two necessities, and how they should be regarded.  
IV. The Martyr’s struggle with the persecutor over superfluous things.  
V. The Martyr’s struggle with the persecutor over necessities.  
VI. The ways in which Christ is denied.  
VII. The reward of steadfastness in heaven.

## I

The holy Martyrs, God’s witnesses, preferred to live by dying rather than die by living; lest by fearing death they should deny life, they despised life by loving life. To induce Christ to be denied, the enemy promised life—but not the kind of life Christ promised. Therefore, believing what the Savior promised, they laughed at what the persecutor threatened.

Brothers, when we celebrate the solemnities of the Martyrs, let us recognize that examples have been set before us, which we may attain by imitation. For by assembling this gathering we do not increase the glory of the Martyrs. Their crown is known to the peoples of the angels. We were able to hear what they suffered when it was read. But what they received is something “neither eye has seen nor ear heard” (I Cor. II, 9).

The goods of this world are partly superfluous and partly necessary. Attend for a little while, so that we may speak, and let us distinguish, if we can, which goods of this world are superfluous and which are necessary, so that you may see that Christ must not be denied either for superfluous things or for necessary things.

Who can enumerate the superfluous things of this world? If we wished to mention them, we would cause great delays. Let us speak, then, of necessities. Whatever other things there may be will be superfluous.

There are two necessities in this world: health and a friend. These are the things we must value highly and not despise. Health and friendship are natural goods. God made the human being to exist and live. That is salvation. But, lest he should be alone, friendship was sought.

Friendship therefore begins with spouse and children and extends even to strangers. But if we consider that we have had one father and one mother, who will be a stranger? Every human being is near to every human being.

Ask nature. Is he unknown? He is a human being. Is he an enemy? He is a human being. Is he hostile? He is a human being. Is he a friend? Let him remain a friend. Is he an enemy? Let him become a friend.

## II

To these two necessities in this world—health and a friend—foreign Wisdom came. It found everyone foolish and wandering, honoring superfluous things, loving temporal things, and ignorant of eternal things.

This Wisdom was not a friend to fools. Since, therefore, it was not a friend to fools and was far from fools, it assumed what was near to us and became near to us. This is the mystery of Christ.

What is as far apart as folly and wisdom? What is as near as one human being and another human being? What, I repeat, is as distant as wisdom from folly? Wisdom therefore took up the human being and became near to the human being through that which was near.

And behold, since Wisdom itself said to the human being, “Behold, piety is wisdom”—and it belongs to human wisdom to worship God, because this is piety—two commandments were given to us: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” The second is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Luke X, 27).

And the one who heard this said: “And who is my neighbor?” (Ibid. 29). He thought the Lord would say: “Your father, your mother, your wife, your children, your brothers, your sisters.” He did not answer in this way. Rather, wishing to commend every human being as near to every other human being, he constructed a story.

“A certain man,” he said. Who was this certain man? Nevertheless, he was a human being. “A certain man.” What kind of human being, then? A certain one, but nevertheless a human being.

He was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke X, 30). Those who pursue us are themselves called robbers. Wounded, stripped, half-dead, and abandoned on the road, he was disregarded by those passing by, by the priest and the Levite; but he was noticed by a passing Samaritan.

The Samaritan approached him, examined his wounds, lifted him onto his animal, brought him to an inn, ordered that care be given him, and paid the expense.

The one who had asked the question is asked: “Who was near to this half-dead man?” Since two had disregarded him—and those two were his neighbors—an outsider approached. This Jerusalemite had priests and Levites as neighbors, but regarded Samaritans as foreigners. His neighbors passed by, and the foreigner became his neighbor.

Who, then, was near to this man? You, who had asked, saying, “Who is my neighbor?” now answer what is true. Pride had asked the question; let nature speak.

What did he say? “I think, the one who showed him mercy.” And the Lord said to him: “Go, and you do likewise” (Ibid. 37).

## III

Let us return to the matter. We now see three things: health, a friend, and Wisdom. But health and a friend are also from this world; Wisdom comes from elsewhere.

For health: food and clothing, and, if illness occurs, medicine. The Apostle, speaking soundly to those who are sound, says: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these things.”

These are necessary for health. But what is for superfluous things? “Those who wish,” he says, “to become rich”—for superfluous things, certainly—“fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition.”

Where, then, is health? Therefore, for health: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these things” (I Tim. VI, 6, 9).

What is for a friend? What more could have been said to you than, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”? Therefore, let health be yours, and let health also be your friend’s.

For your friend’s clothing: “Let the one who has two tunics share with the one who has none.” For your friend’s food: “And let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke III, 11). You are fed; feed others. You are clothed; clothe others. These things are from this world. But from elsewhere—from Wisdom—you learn and teach.

## IV

Now set the Martyrs’ contest before your eyes. The enemy comes and compels Christ to be denied. But let us first introduce him as one who flatters, not as one who rages. He promises riches and honors. These are superfluous things.

Those who are tempted by such gifts to deny Christ have not yet entered the contest, have not yet encountered the struggle, and have not yet challenged the most ancient enemy in genuine combat.

[Note: I prefer: “have not yet entered it” (*inierunt*).]

But the faithful man to whom such things were promised despised them and said: “Shall I deny Christ for riches? Shall I deny riches for riches? Shall I deny the treasure for gold? Is this not the one who, although he was rich, became poor for us, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (II Cor. VIII, 9)? Is this not the one of whom the Apostle likewise says: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3)?

You attend to what you promise, because you cannot see what you are trying to take away. By faith I see what you wish to take from me; you see with the eyes of the flesh what you wish to give. Better are the things contemplated by the eyes of the heart than those seen by the eye of the flesh. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

“Therefore,” says the faithful soul, “I despise your gifts, because they are temporal, superfluous, fragile, fleeting, full of dangers, and full of temptations. No one possesses them when he wishes; he loses them even when he does not wish to.”

The promiser has been despised; another approaches—the persecutor. The flatterer has been despised; he begins to rage. The serpent has been despised; he has been changed into a lion.

“You do not wish,” he says, “to accept greater riches from me? If you do not deny Christ, I shall take away the riches you have. You still rage against my superfluous goods.”

“You have acted deceitfully like a sharp razor” (Ps. LI, 4). You shave the hair; you do not cut the skin. Take these things from me as well.

“Indeed, since you saw that I gave these things to the poor and received strangers, I was doing what Paul had commanded. ‘Command the rich of this age,’ he says; ‘command them not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment. Let them do good, let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may seize true life’” (I Tim. VI, 17–19).

“If you take these things from me, I shall not be able to perform those works. Shall I therefore be less before God because I wish to do them but cannot? Or am I so utterly deaf to the voice of the angels: ‘Peace on earth to people of good will’ (Luke II, 14)?

“Take away, then, my superfluous possessions. We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything out of it. Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI, 8).

### V.

But the persecutor says: “I am taking away your food; I am taking away your clothing.” The contest has begun. The enemy raged more fiercely. The superfluities have been passed over; we have reached what is necessary. “Do not depart from me, for tribulation is very near” (Ps. 21:12–13)! Nothing is so near to a person’s soul as his flesh. You feel hunger, thirst, and heat in the flesh. There I want to see you, good Martyr! Witness of God! “See,” he says, “see! Who will separate us from the love of Christ? What is it that you threaten? I am taking away your food; I am taking away your clothing. Tribulation? Or distress? Or hunger? Or nakedness?” (Rom. 8:35).

Let him threaten from the other side: “I am taking away your friend; I will kill your dearest ones before your eyes; I will slaughter your wife and children!” “Do you kill them, do you kill them? Let them not deny him, and you do not kill them. What is this—that, because you do not frighten me concerning myself, you frighten me concerning my own?” If they do not deny him, you do not kill those who are mine; if they deny him, you kill those who are not mine.”

Let the persecutor add still more, rage, and say: “If you do not care about your own, I will take you yourself away from this light.” “From this light? Surely not from the eternal Light? From what light will you take me away?” The light that I share with you? It is not a great light, the one that you too see. For this light I will not deny the Light. “He was the true Light” (John 1:9). I know to whom I shall say: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” [Col. 0873] (Ps. 35:10). Take away life; take away light. I shall have life; I shall have light. I shall have life where I will not suffer you to be my murderer; I shall have light which, I will not say you, but not even any night, can take away from me.

The Martyr has conquered. Or is there something else in which we ought to behold a greater contest? He does not threaten death; he rages against salvation, tears with claws, tortures with torments, burns with flames, brings beasts against him—and here he is defeated. Why is he defeated? Because “in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:37).

### VI.

Therefore, my brothers, let Christ not be denied for the sake of superfluities; let him not be denied for the sake of necessities. No one is more necessary than he. I was speaking of necessities: Salvation and a Friend. You sin for the sake of Salvation, and deny Christ. By loving Salvation, you will not have Salvation. You sin for the sake of your friend, and, so as not to offend him, deny Christ.

Alas, miserable me! Sometimes he is denied through shame. The persecutor does not rage; the plunderer does not strip you; the torturer does not bear down upon you. Merely so that you may not displease your friend, you deny your Lord. I see what your friend has taken away from you; show me what he will give. What will he give? Those very friendships through which you sin, through which you are entangled, through which you become an enemy of God. This man would not be your friend if you were your own friend. But because you yourself are your own enemy, you think that your friend is your enemy.

And why are you yourself your own enemy? Because you love iniquity. “But the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). Christ is not denied so as to please a wicked and perverse friend; rather, he is reviled by the wicked person, accused by the wicked person, and, through the shame of the faithful person, is not defended, is abandoned, is kept silent about, and is not proclaimed. The tongue of the blasphemer rages, and there is no tongue to praise him.

How many evils are committed as though for the sake of necessities—for food, clothing, salvation, or a friend—and all those things that are sought perish even more! But if you despise present things, God will give you eternal things. Despise salvation, and you will have immortality. Despise death, and you will have life. Despise honor, and you will have a crown. Despise a human friend, and you will have God as your friend.

But there, where you will have God as your friend, you will not be without a neighborly friend. There your friends will be with you—those whose deeds and confessions were read a little earlier [Note: [Col. 0873] Namely, those of the Scillitan Martyrs.].

### VII.

We have heard men acting bravely and confessing manfully. We have also heard women [Note: [Col. 0873] In both of the Acts cited above, women are introduced as speaking.] who held fast to Christ not as women, having forgotten their sex. There will be with them that friendship in which there will be no desire of the flesh, and in which the only pleasure found with friends will be wisdom.

See what we lose if we love such things here and deny Christ! There our neighbor does not terrify us if he dies. There is no mourning where eternal life will be; nor is that necessity present there: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.” Our clothing will be immortality; this food will be love; it will be eternal life. Nor shall we there perform the good works that are called such by these things. We shall not reach them if we have not done them here.

You will not be told there: “Share your bread with the hungry” (Isa. 58:7), where there will be no hunger. You will not be told: “Receive the stranger into your lodging,” where you will find no traveler. You will not be told: “Set free the oppressed,” where there will be no enemy. You will not be told: “Reconcile the quarrelsome,” where there will be eternal peace.

See, my brothers, how it is endured here while it is being sought. There we shall have it, where we cannot perish. Do you seek Salvation? Despise it, and you will have it. You deny Christ, fearing to offend human friendships. Confess Christ, and the city of the Angels will be your friend; the city of the Patriarchs, the city of the Prophets, the city of the Apostles, the city of all the Martyrs, and the city of all faithful and good people will be your friend. “Christ himself founded it forever” (Ps. 47:9).

## SERMON XVII  
### On the Solemnity of the Holy Maccabees

[Note: [Col. 0874] In the Codex, fol. 40, p. 2, it is inscribed: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the Feast of the Holy Maccabees.” This distinguished Sermon, after the exposition of Luke 14:28 and Matthew 19:16, attacks profane spectacles and exhorts the faithful to perseverance. It was delivered at the request of the bishop of Bulla Regia. For, as Possidius says in *The Life*, chapter 8, Our Bishop preached not in one region only, but wherever he had been invited to come. It should be inserted into the edition after Sermon 301.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. The sayings of the Gospel pertain to every age. II. Explanation of the parable about building a tower and about two kings. III. The rich young man’s encounter with Christ. IV. After the Apostles, the converted Jews, and afterward many Christians renounced their possessions. V. How faith in Christ must be proved, even in daily matters. VI. Promises ought to rouse us to prove our faith. VII. The Maccabees: their contest compared with profane spectacles. VIII. A warning against profane spectacles. IX. The warning continued.

### I.

The Gospel, the living word of God, penetrating the marrow of the soul and searching out the heart’s hinge, is beneficially proclaimed to all of us; it flatters no one unless a person flatters himself. Behold, it has been set before us like a mirror in which we should all look at ourselves; and if something perhaps blemished on our face should come before our eyes, let us wipe it away with careful attention, lest we blush when we look into the mirror again.

For the crowd was following the Lord, as we heard when the Gospel was read, and he turned and spoke to those who were following him. If he had said what he said only to those twelve Apostles, each one of us could say: “He said it to them, not to us.” One thing seems to concern pastors, another the flocks. He spoke to the crowds who were following him; therefore he spoke both to all of us and to all of you.

We must not think that, because we did not yet exist then, it was not said to us. For we too believe in the one whom they saw; by faith we hold the one whom they beheld with their eyes. Indeed, seeing Christ with bodily eyes was not a great thing. If that had been great, the Jewish people would have been the first to find salvation. Certainly they too saw him, yet they despised him, and after seeing and despising him they even killed him. But we certainly did not see him, and yet we believe; though we did not behold him with our eyes, we have received him into our hearts.

Hence he said to one of his own who at that time was among the Twelve: “Because you have seen, you have believed. Blessed are those who do not see and yet believe” (John 20:29). For if the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ were now present in the flesh and stood silent, what benefit would that be to us? But if he benefited us by speaking, he also speaks now when the Gospel is recited.

Nevertheless, as God he bestows many benefits through his presence. But where is God not present, or when is God absent? Do not be absent from God, and God is with you. This is especially so because he himself promised it, and we hold, as it were, his written promise as a bond: “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20). But he foresaw us and was making the promise to us.

### II.

Let us therefore return and hear what he said; and, as I said, let us look at ourselves and, whatever we find lacking in us, cultivate it with complete diligence according to the pattern of beauty that pleases his eyes. And because we are not sufficient by ourselves, let us invoke him for help. Let him reform us who formed us; let him renew us who created us, so that he who established us may restore us to perfection.

This, then, is what he said: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish it, all who see it may begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish.’ Or which king, going to engage another king in war, does not first consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while the other is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for peace.” And he concluded these two comparisons in this way: “So therefore, whoever does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:28–33).

If only those Disciples were called, it would not have been said to us. But since, as Scripture testifies, all Christians are Christ’s disciples—“For one is your teacher, Christ” (Matt. 23:10)—let only the person who denies Christ deny that he is Christ’s disciple. Nor, because we are speaking to you from this higher place, are we therefore your teachers. He is the teacher of all, whose chair is above all the heavens. Under him we gather into one school, and both you and we are fellow students; but we admonish you as the older members of a school customarily do.

The tower is faith, and the cost is patience. Faith is the tower; patience is the cost. If someone is impatient in bearing the evils of this world, he has run out of the cost.

The wicked king with twenty thousand is the devil; the king with ten thousand is the Christian. The onefold against the twofold; truth against falsehood, because simplicity is against duplicity. Be simple in heart. Do not be a hypocrite, displaying one thing and doing another, and you will conquer him who is double and transforms himself into an angel of light.

Where, then, are the resources for these people? Where is that perfect simplicity, entirely steadfast and persevering with complete firmness? In what follows, which seems harsh. This is what I said: The word of God flatters no one [Col. 0876]. “Thus,” he says, “whoever does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple.”

Many have done this and examined themselves [Note: [Col. 0876] I think this is a scribal error for *exinaniverunt*, “emptied themselves.”] before the time of persecution pressed upon them; they renounced all that belongs to the world and followed Christ. Among them were the Apostles, who said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Luke 18:28).
