Nor had they themselves left anything very great, since they were all poor; but those who conquered every desire are judged to have left truly great possessions.

### III.

The Disciples said this, finally, when that rich man departed sadly after hearing from the most truthful Teacher the counsel concerning eternal life, just as he had requested it. For a certain rich young man came to the Lord and said to him: “Good Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?” (Matt. 19:16).

I believe that amid the most abundant pleasures of his riches he was being pricked by the goad of future death, wasting away; and, because he knew that he could carry none of what he possessed with him into the underworld, his soul groaned in poverty amid the great abundance of his flesh.

As we may suppose, he said to himself while surrounded by the abundance of his riches: “They are good, beautiful, delightful, sweet; but when that final hour comes, everything must be abandoned. Nothing of these things can be taken away from here. Life remains, and conscience alone; after the body, the soul’s life remains, and conscience alone. If conscience is [Note: [Col. 0876] “Evil” appears to be omitted.] present, this is no longer life, but must be called another death, and a worse one. For there is nothing worse than that death in which death does not die.”

Because he was thinking about this amid his pleasures, possessing so many good things, he came to the Lord. For he said to himself: “After possessing all these great goods, if I also have eternal life, who will be happier than I?” Thus he was concerned, asked about it, and said: “Good Teacher, what must I do to obtain eternal life?”

The Lord first answered him: “Why do you ask me about what is good? No one is good except the one God” (Matt. 19:17). This means: “Only the one God can make you blessed.” What the rich possess is indeed good; but those goods do not make people good. For if those goods made people good, each person would be better in proportion to his abundance of them. But when we see that many are worse in proportion to their greater wealth, without doubt we must seek other goods that make people good.

These are the very things that cannot be possessed by the wicked: justice, piety, self-control, religion, love, the worship of God, and finally God himself. We must hasten toward that good. We shall not attain him unless we despise these things.

### IV.

Should I flatter you, when the Gospel flatters neither you nor us? Therefore, brothers, I exhort Your Charity, as the Apostle says: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it” (1 Cor. 7:29–31).

The Apostles therefore left behind what they had at that time, and for this reason Peter said: “Behold, we have left everything.” What did you leave, Peter? One little boat and one net? He would answer me: “I left the whole world, since I left nothing for myself.” The poverty of all—the poverty, that is, of all poor people—has few possessions but great desires. God does not consider what a person has, but what he wants. It is the will that is judged, and it is searched invisibly by the one who is not seen.

Therefore they left everything, and truly left the whole world, because they cut off whatever they hoped for in this world. They followed the one by whom the world was made, believed his promises, and afterward many did the same.

And it is remarkable, my brothers: who did this? Those who killed the Lord himself did it. There in Jerusalem, after the Lord had ascended into heaven, and after ten days, having sent the Holy Spirit, he fulfilled his promise: filled with the Holy Spirit, the Disciples spoke in the languages of all nations (Acts 2).

Then many Jews who were in Jerusalem heard them and, terrified at the gift of the Savior’s grace, wondered and were perplexed among themselves about its origin. They received from the Apostles the answer that the one whom they themselves had killed had granted this through his Spirit, and they sought the counsel of salvation.

For they had despaired and did not think that such a great crime could be forgiven them, since they had killed the Lord of all creation. And they received consolation from the Apostles. Having been promised pardon and promised immunity from punishment, they believed; and, selling everything they had, they placed the proceeds of their possessions at the Apostles’ feet. The more frightened they were, the better they became. Greater fear tore pleasures away.

Those who killed the Lord did this; afterward many did it, and many still do it. We know the examples; we see them; in many we are consoled, and in many we rejoice, because the word of God is not ineffective in those who hear it faithfully.

But did some fail to do this and were tested when persecution came? They used the world “as though they did not use it.” Not merely common people, not merely ordinary craftsmen, not merely the poor, needy, and insignificant, but also many great and wealthy men, senators, and even women of the highest rank renounced all they possessed when persecution came, so that they might complete the tower and, through the simplicity of courage and piety, conquer the double and deceitful devil.

### V.

Therefore, exhorting us to martyrdom, the Lord Christ said to all: “Thus, whoever does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple.”

I ask you, Christian soul: if I say to you what was said to the rich man, “Go, sell all that is yours, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Christ” (Matt. 19:21), might you too depart sadly? For that young man also departed sadly.

Yet only a Christian can hear these words. When the Gospel was read, were you able to close your ears against your salvation? You heard: “Whoever does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple.” Consider within yourself: You became faithful, you were baptized, you believed. You did not abandon your possessions, but I ask you about your faith. How did you believe?

Behold, the danger to faith has arrived. You are told: “If you persist, I will take away what you possess.” I ask your soul. If you say within your soul, “Let him take what I have; I will not abandon my faith,” then you hold fast, and you have renounced. Because you hold fast, you are not held captive. For holding something is not evil; being held captive is evil.

But persecution is absent, and there is no way for you to prove what you promised the Lord. Daily affairs test people. What if, at some time—I do not know who—someone summons you to give false testimony, and he is powerful enough to be feared for the moment, and, if he threatens you, able for the moment to do you harm, and persuades you to give false testimony? He does not say to you: “Deny Christ”; for you had prepared yourself for that. In another way that double deceiver has crept up on you, with something you had not considered and had not set before yourself.

“Give false testimony,” he says. “If you do not, I will do this and that.” He threatens confiscation; he threatens death. There prove yourself; there pay attention to yourself. Do you give false testimony? You have abandoned Christ, because he himself said: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). You gave false testimony; you acted against the truth; therefore you abandoned Christ.

And what was that man going to do to you by threatening confiscation? Make you poor? What would you lack when you had God with you? But he threatened something more. What is that “more”? He threatened to kill you. Your flesh. Surely not your soul?

You consider what he threatened; you do not consider what you do. He threatens to kill the flesh. “But the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

There are two of you: the enemy and you; yet he too is a human being, just as you are. Both are corruptible according to the flesh; both are immortal according to the soul; both will pass away in due course; both are guests and travelers on this earth.

He threatens death, not knowing whether he will die before carrying out what he threatens. But suppose he does carry out what he threatens. I examine the two of you; let us see which is the worse enemy to you, he or you. He draws a sword to kill your flesh; you bring forth a lying tongue to slaughter your soul. Which sword struck more forcefully [Note: [Col. 0878] “More forcefully” appears to have fallen out.]? Which killed more grievously? Which penetrated farther inward? His reached the bones; his reached the entrails; yours reached the heart. You left nothing of yourself intact when you lost your heart. “The mouth that lies kills,” he said—not the flesh, but the soul.

### VI.

Such are the daily temptations of human beings. When the matter comes to iniquity, so that either you commit iniquity or suffer what God wills you to suffer for the time being, then pay attention to that double deceiver; then pay attention to the resources of that tower.

But you fail through thinking alone. Invoke the one who gave the command. May he help his commands in you, and from himself grant you his promises.

For what does God promise us? My brothers, what shall I say to make us desire it? What shall I say? Is it gold? Silver? Estates? Honors? Is it whatever we know on earth? It is worthless. “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—these are the things God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

I speak briefly: he promises not his gifts, but himself. He is greater than all things, because he made all things. He is more beautiful than all things, because he formed all things. He is more powerful than all things, because he gave strength to all things. Whatever we love on earth is nothing in comparison with God.

It is little to say: whatever we love is nothing—and we ourselves are nothing. The lover ought to become worthless in his own eyes in comparison with the thing that is to be loved. This is the love that is commanded: “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” But he added and said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40).

Thus, when you have loved the Lord, know that you love yourself then, if you love the Lord. But if you do not love God, you do not love yourself either. When, therefore, you have learned to love yourself by loving God, seize your neighbor for God, so that together you may enjoy the Good—and so great a Good, which is God.

### VII.

Just now we watched the great contest of the seven brothers and their mother. What a contest, my brothers, if only our minds know how to watch it! Compare with this holy spectacle the pleasures and delights of the theaters. There eyes are defiled; here hearts are cleansed. Here the spectator is praiseworthy if he becomes an imitator; there the spectator is disgraceful, and the imitator infamous.

Finally, I love the Martyrs; I watch the Martyrs. When the sufferings of the Martyrs are read, I watch. Tell me, “Be such as they are,” and you have praised me. You watch a mime, you watch a pantomime; I will say to you, “Be such as he is,” and do not be angry. But if I say to you, “Be such as he is,” and you become angry, it is not my words but your anger that makes you guilty. By becoming angry, you pass judgment on yourself. Behold what you love and what you fear to be.

It has seemed appropriate, on the occasion of this spectacle of the holy Maccabees, whose victory we commemorate today, to admonish Your Charity concerning theatrical spectacles.

O brothers of Bulla [Note: [Col. 0879] Bulla, called Bulla Regia, was an African city between Hippo and Carthage, according to Pliny, Book 5, chapter 3; in Ptolemy, Βουλλάρια (*Boullaria*). Augustine mentions it in Book 7 of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 24, and in the Second Council of Carthage, A.D. 390, and the Third, A.D. 397, as well as in the *List of African Provinces and Cities*. Some attribute references to it to Victor of Vita, in volume 1 of Sirmond’s works and volume 8 of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*. It is thought to be the city now called Bejie, between Tunis and Constantine. Compare Baudrand’s *Geographical Lexicon* and Wesseling’s edition of the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, p. 43.], in nearly all the neighboring cities around you, piety has silenced your wantonness. Are you not ashamed that among you alone disgraceful things remain for sale? Or does it delight you, amid grain, wine, oil, animals, cattle, and whatever is sold in Roman markets [Note: [Col. 0879] Perhaps “in the open market” has fallen out.], also to buy and sell disgrace?

Perhaps travelers come here for such commerce, and it is said: “What are you looking for? Mimes? Prostitutes? You will find them at Bulla.” Do you think this is glory? I do not know whether it is a greater disgrace.

In every respect, my brothers, I say this out of sorrow: the neighboring cities condemn you in the sight of human beings and in the judgment of God. Whoever wants to imitate evil holds you up as an example. At our Hippo, where such things have now almost disappeared, these shameful persons are brought from your city.

But perhaps you say: “We are like Carthage.” At Carthage there is a holy and religious populace; yet in such a large city there is also such a great crowd that everyone excuses himself by pointing to others. Pagans do it; Jews do it; one can say this of Carthage. Here, whoever does such things is a Christian.

We say these things to you with great sorrow. Would that your correction might one day heal the wound of our heart! We say to Your Charity: We know, in the name of God, how great a multitude and how large a population there is here, both in your city and in the cities neighboring you. Can all of you be anything but known to the one appointed over you as administrator of the Word and the Sacrament? Who excuses himself from this disgrace?

Behold, there are games. Let Christians not go, and let us see whether there will not be such solitude that the disgrace itself will be ashamed. Let us see whether those shameful persons themselves will either turn to the Lord and be freed, or, if they remain in their disgrace, depart from this city.

Christians, do this for yourselves. Do not enter the theaters.

### VIII.

But I see few of you. Behold, the day of Christ’s Passion will come; behold, Easter will come, and those spaces will not contain your multitude. Will those who now fill the theaters themselves then fill these places? Or will you compare the places and beat your breasts?

Perhaps you say: “You abstain from these things properly, since you are Clerics and Bishops, but we are Laypeople.” Is this truly a just statement in your eyes? For what are we if you perish? What we are for ourselves is one thing; what we are for you is another. We are Christians for ourselves; we are Clerics and Bishops only for your sake.

The Apostle was not speaking to Clerics, nor to Bishops and Presbyters, when he said: “You are members of Christ.” He was speaking to the people, to the faithful, to Christians: “You are members of Christ.” Pay attention to whose body you are members; pay attention under whose head you live within the unity of one body. See the one Spirit whom you received from him.

I repeat the Apostle’s words: “Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” (1 Cor. 6:15). And do our Christians not only love prostitutes, but even make prostitutes? They not only love those who already were such, but make prostitutes of those who were not, as though they too did not possess souls; as though Christ’s blood had not also been poured out for them; as though it had not been said: “Prostitutes and tax collectors go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 21:31).

Since, then, we ought to win them, choosing to perish with them—and this is done by Christians! I do not wish to say, “by the faithful” as well. Perhaps a Catechumen despises himself. “I am a Catechumen,” he says. You are a Catechumen? A Catechumen. One forehead of yours has received the sign of Christ, and you raise another to the theater? Do you want to go? Change your forehead and go. Therefore, do not lose the forehead that you cannot change.

The name of God is invoked over you; Christ is invoked over you; God is invoked over you; the sign of Christ’s cross is painted and impressed upon your forehead.

I exhort everyone; I address everyone. You will see how much more honorable you will be in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### IX.

I dare to say: imitate the city neighboring you. Imitate the neighboring city of Simittu [Note: [Col. 0880] Simittu, a town mentioned by Pliny, Book 5, chapter 4, and by Ptolemy as Σιμίσθου (*Simísthou*), six miles from Bulla Regia. Among the names of bishops cited above by Victor of Vita occur Deuterius of Simminum and Florentius of Seminensis; I think one of these two names belongs here. Compare Baluze, *Collection of Councils*, notes to the *Carthaginian Conference*, and Baudrand’s *Geographical Lexicon* and the *Itinerary of Antoninus* cited above.]. I say nothing else to you.

I speak to you more plainly, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. No one there enters the theater. No disgraceful person remains there. An official wanted to stage such disgraceful performances there. No leading citizen entered; no commoner entered. No Jew entered.

Are they not honorable? Is that not a city? Is that colony not all the more honorable because it is all the more empty of such things?

We would not say these things to you if we heard good things about you. But if we remain silent, I fear that we shall be judged together with you. Therefore God willed, my brothers, that I pass through here. My brother [Note: [Col. 0881] The bishop of the place.] held me back, ordered me, begged me, and compelled me to speak the word to you.

From what else could I speak, if not from what I fear most? From what else could I speak, if not from what causes me the greatest sorrow? Do you not know that I and all of us will have to render a most serious account to God concerning your praises [Note: [Col. 0881] Apparently the praises with which they welcomed Augustine on his arrival.]? Do you think that these praises honor us? They burden us; they do not honor us. A very weighty account will be required concerning those praises.

I greatly fear that Christ will say to us in his judgment: “Wicked servants, you gladly accepted the praises of my people, and you kept silent about their death before them.”

But our Lord God will grant that from now on we may hear good things about you and, through his mercy, be consoled concerning your correction. For our joy will be all the greater because our sorrow is now great.

## SERMON XVIII  
### On the Feast of Quadratus the Martyr

[Note: [Col. 0881] In the Codex, fol. 57, it is inscribed: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on amendment of life and progress toward God, with praise of Saint Quadratus the Martyr.” From its very opening it is clear that this Sermon too was delivered not at Hippo but elsewhere; where the memorial shrine of Quadratus was located I am at least unable to say. Possidius mentions the Sermon in the *Index of Works*, ch. 9; it may be inserted in the edition after the preceding sermon.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. Three kinds of persons on their way to God. II. Paul’s example set before those who are walking. III. One thing is the perfect traveller, another the perfect person who has arrived, as shown in the example of Saint Quadratus. IV. At least as much must now be given to righteousness as was formerly given to impurity. V. Indeed, more must be given to righteousness than to impurity. VI. And this with every regard for human opinion laid aside. VII. Especially in relation to pagans who insult Christians.

### I.

Our Lord God, to whom we jointly give thanks, has granted that we should see you and be seen by you. And if this is the reason why “our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation” (Ps. 125:2), because we have seen one another in mortal flesh, what will our joy be when we see one another there, where we need fear nothing about one another?

The Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12:12). Therefore our present joy is in hope, not yet in the reality. “Hope that is seen,” he says, “is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience” (Rom. 8:24–25). If fellow travellers rejoice with one another on the journey while they are pilgrims, what joy, then, will there be in their homeland?

On this road the Martyrs contended, and by contending they walked; by walking they did not remain fixed. For those who love are walking. We do not run to God with steps, but with affections. Thus our Way seeks us while we walk [Note: [Col. 0882] The following sentence occurs word for word in Codex Bibl. Palat. theol. XIX, among the spurious *Sermons to the Brethren in the Desert*, Sermon 19, not published by the Maurists. Therefore the present Sermon was known to the impostor who pieced together those spurious sermons.].

There are three kinds of people whom God hates: the person who remains still, the person who turns back, and the person who goes astray. May our step, with the Lord’s help, be rescued and defended from these three evil kinds. But when we are walking, one walks more slowly, another more quickly; yet both are walking. Therefore those who remain still must be stirred up, those who turn back recalled, those who stray led onto the way, the slow encouraged, and the swift imitated. Whoever makes no progress has remained on the road. Whoever perhaps declines from a better purpose to that worse condition which he had left behind has turned back. Whoever abandons the faith has strayed from the way. Let our concern be with the slow, but our standard with the swifter—yet with those who are walking.

### II.

Who is the one who makes no progress? The person who thinks himself wise; who says, “What I am is enough for me”; who does not heed him who said: “Forgetting the things behind, and stretching forth to those before me, I press on according to my aim toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:13–14). He called himself one who was running; he called himself one who was pressing on. He did not remain still, he did not look back—far be it that he should have gone astray, who both taught, held, and showed the Way itself.

That we might imitate his swiftness, he said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:6). Therefore, dearest brothers, we think that we are walking with you on the road. If we are slow, go ahead of us. We do not envy you; we seek persons whom we may follow. But if you think that we walk quickly, run with us. There is one goal toward which we all hasten, both those who walk more slowly and those who walk more quickly. The Apostle himself says this: “But one thing: forgetting the things behind and stretching forth to those before me, I press on according to my aim toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.” The order of the words is: “But one thing I press on toward.”

But in order to say this, what had he said above? “Brothers, I do not reckon that I myself have attained it” (Phil. 3:13). Behold one who does not remain still, who does not reckon that he has attained. Behold one who does not wish to be a pilgrim [Note: [Col. 0882] Perhaps *lente* [“slowly”] or *diu* [“long”] has fallen out.]; behold one who does not cling to the road; behold one who will rejoice in the homeland. “I,” he says. Who is this “I”? The one who “laboured more than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). Yet where he says, “I laboured more than all of them,” he did not say, “I do not reckon that I have attained.” Properly does he say “I” where there is a place for humility, not for self-exaltation. “I,” he says, “so far as concerns myself, do not reckon that I have attained.” This is of himself. But where he says, “I laboured more than all of them,” he adds: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” Did the grace of God not attain it? Rightly, then, is “I” used there. For not attaining belongs to our weakness; attaining belongs to the help of divine grace, not to human weakness.

Who, then, can show us? Who can teach us? Who can worthily make clear to us how this is true—yet true beyond doubt—that nothing in us is ours except sin? Let piety know this; let weakness accuse this in itself; let love desire to be healed of it! “Not that I have already received,” he says, “or am already perfected” (Phil. 3:12). Then he added: “Brothers, I do not reckon that I myself have attained”; and when he was exhorting them to run and to stretch out their heart toward the things before them, he said, “But as many as are perfect, let us think this way” (Phil. 3:15). Above he had said, “Not that I have already received, or am already perfected”; afterward he says, “But as many as are perfect, let us think this way.” And you had called the Apostle himself, so great as he was, imperfect; now you find many already perfect, and say: “But as many as are perfect, let us think this way.” Therefore there is perfection and perfection.

### III

A traveler is perfect who has not yet arrived perfectly. The perfect traveler approaches well, walks well, keeps to the road, but is nevertheless still a traveler and has not yet reached his destination. For surely, if he is walking, he is walking on a road, and he is walking toward somewhere, and is trying to reach something. The Apostle, then, had not yet attained that destination toward which he was striving. And he exhorts the perfect to know that they are not yet perfect, to know their own imperfection. The perfection of the traveler is to know that he has not yet arrived at the goal toward which he is advancing. For he knows how far he has progressed and how much remains for him.

Let us therefore know that we are not perfect, however many of us are perfect, lest we remain imperfect. What shall we say, brothers? Was not the martyr Quadratus perfect? [Note: [Col. 0883] The account of Saint Quadratus’s commemoration is found in Godfrey Henschenius, *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. VI, May, for May 26, p. 369. After Usuard, Ado, Notker, and other later writers, it has been inserted into the Roman Martyrology as follows: “In Africa, Saint Quadratus the Martyr, on whose solemnity Saint Augustine preached a sermon.” Baronius adds that this sermon is mentioned in Possidius’s *Index*. Would that it might someday appear! And thus the excellent old man’s wish has been fulfilled.] What could be more “square” than a square? Its sides are equal, its form is equal on every side; whichever way it is turned, it stands firm rather than falling. O beautiful name, displaying a figure and indicating a future reality!

Quadratus was already called by that name, although he had not yet been crowned. He had not yet appeared in the trial through which he was to become “square”; yet, when he was called by that name, his predestination—established before the foundation of the world—was being announced. So that he might be called by this name, this quality was already being formed in him so that it might be fulfilled. And yet he was walking; he was still on the road. As long as he was in this body, everything was feared: that he might remain behind, turn back, or stray from the road.

But now he has run his course, completed the road, stood firm on solid ground, and been built into the structure by the craftsman of the Lord’s ark, which was commanded in its symbolic form to be made of squared timber (Exod. 27:1). Now he fears no temptation. He heard the one who called him, and he heard that same one as his invoker; he followed the Savior and carries the Indweller. [Note: [Col. 0883] This expression is taken from the Greeks, among whom various saints are called Θεοφόροι, Χριστοφόροι—“God-bearers,” “Christ-bearers.” See Cotelerius’s notes on the epistle of Saint Ignatius the martyr.] He despised the world when it flattered him, conquered it when it threatened him, and escaped it when it raged.

Great, brothers, is the glory of the martyrs—the first glory in the Church. Whatever other glories there are follow after it. For it was not said without reason to certain people: “You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” (Heb. 12:4). When will one who cannot despise a flattering world endure and withstand a raging one?

### IV

The same Apostle says: [Col. 0884] “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members to serve impurity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

What he appears to urge is very great indeed. Let each person measure himself by these words of the Apostle. Let him not flatter himself hypocritically; let him weigh himself and tell himself the truth. What does he expect to hear from me? Let him tell himself.

I have decided to place before you a mirror in which each person may examine himself. I am not the gleam of the mirror that reports its own face to the one looking into it. For I am speaking now of the faces we have within us. I can address them through the ear, but I cannot see them. I am certainly placing a mirror before you. Let each person examine himself and report to himself.

Take the very words of the Apostle that I have recalled as the inscription of the mirror: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members to serve impurity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification.”

What does “so” mean? As that was, so let this be. When you presented your members as weapons of iniquity to sin and impurity, did it give you pleasure? I ask you. Pay attention and answer. Did it give you pleasure? I hear the one who answers—even the one who remains silent. For you would not have done it unless it had given you pleasure.

As, then, you presented your members to serve impurity for iniquity, and did this with pleasure, so let righteousness at some time give you pleasure. “I do not want you to do it out of fear,” God says to you. Did you do that other thing out of fear?

“So,” he says, “so: just as you presented your members to serve impurity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification.” You were compelled toward righteousness by fear; toward impurity you ran out of love.

What is more beautiful than wisdom? I ask you. It deserves to be loved even as impurity was loved. When you ran toward impurity, you were forbidden, and still you went. You offended your father, and still you ran. You were prepared to be disinherited rather than separated from that depravity.

What will you say? Righteousness demands from you what impurity possessed from you. You have heard the Gospel: “I have not come to send peace on earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). He said that he would separate children from their parents. Therefore, pay attention to that sword.

Perhaps you wish to serve God, and your father forbids you. When you loved impurity, you ran even though your father forbade you. Now righteousness forbids you, its lover. Here too you have found a father who forbids you. Exercise your freedom, you who then exercised your desire.

You were then prepared to be disinherited rather than separated from the depravity of that impurity. Be prepared to be disinherited rather than separated from the beauty of righteousness. It is a great demand, but a just one. Who would dare say: “Impurity deserved to be loved more than righteousness”?

For the moment, righteousness makes a beginning for you. “Certainly,” she says, “I am unlike it; certainly there is an immense difference between the darkness of that impurity and my light, between that depravity and my beauty, between its glory and mine. Certainly there is an immense difference. For the moment, I am making a beginning. This is what I want. For I owe more—indeed, I owe far more. The greater the distance between us, the greater my obligation.”

But I speak and defer in human terms. Why should I defer in divine terms? “I speak in human terms because of the [Col. 0885] weakness of your flesh.” That is why he says “so”: because he is still sparing your weakness. That is why: “Just as you presented your members to serve impurity for iniquity, so now”—though you certainly owe more—“at least walk in this way; reach this point, but also pass beyond it.” For the moment, “I speak in human terms”; but as that was, so let this be.

### V

Was Quadratus like this? Not at all like this, but more—and deservedly more. Consider those impurities and see what piety, charity, the beauty of righteousness, and the sweetness of sanctification demand more from you. Pay attention to what they demand more from you.

The lover of impurity does not want his evil deeds to be known. He fears being condemned because of them; he fears prison, fears the judge, fears the executioner. He desires another man’s wife’s chastity, deceives the husband, seeks darkness, dreads an accomplice, fears the judge, fears being discovered because he fears being punished for it.

But now hear from the Lord that greater demand which the beauty of righteousness makes upon him—what the Apostle postponed for the moment when he said, “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh”:

“What I tell you in the darkness”—that is, in secret—“speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27).

Does the adulterer proclaim his crime upon the housetop? But why does he not merely fail to proclaim it upon the housetop, but seek to hide beneath a roof? Why does he do this? Because up to this point the love of impurity has been able to go. [Note: [Col. 0885] Perhaps *huc*, “to this point.”] For he fears being exposed; he fears being punished.

But these lovers of that invisible beauty, lovers of that splendor in which is “the one beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3)—why do they not fear proclaiming upon the housetops what they have heard in the ear? Ask why that man fears being known and punished; ask why this one does not fear.

The Lord himself continued by adding the reason. For after he had said, “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops,” he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28).

Thus, in order to speak in the light what you hear in the darkness, and in order to proclaim upon the housetops what you hear in the ear, “do not fear those who kill the body.”

Let the adulterer fear those who kill the body. For when that adulterer has lost his body, he loses the workshop of his pleasures. Let the one who lives by the body fear losing the body. Everything he desires he accomplishes through the body; therefore, [Col. 0885] pleasure does not suffice for him, but he burns with desire until he reaches the body’s most filthy pleasure. [Note: I think the reading should be *voluntas*, “will,” rather than *voluptas*, “pleasure.”]

But you, man of God, if you have the eyes of the heart with which to see the beauty of charity, with which to see the beauty of piety—if you have the eyes of the heart, see by what means you may enjoy what you love. For in order to enjoy it, you do not seek the members of the body.

Let the lover of filthy pleasure fear the destruction of the body; but “peace on earth among people of good will” (Luke 2:14)!

### VI

How far you are from this love, Christian! Would that you might reach at least that human level, and do good with pleasure, just as before you sinned with pleasure. [Col. 0886]

For if you do good with pleasure, if you believe in Christ with pleasure, if you enjoy his wisdom with pleasure according to your capacity, if with pleasure you hear and carry out his commandment, then that “human” quality has begun to exist in you because of your weakness.

You have already begun to possess a good gift, but you have not yet fulfilled the “square.” Yet, as I said, if you have reached this point, come forward; there is still a road ahead. Do not remain where you are. There is still something for you to do. Do not fear and hide your good deeds out of fear.

What do your critics and persecutors say to you? “You are a great Apostle! Your feet are hanging down from heaven. Where have you come from?” And you are afraid to say, “From the Church,” lest someone say to you: “Are you not ashamed, bearded fellow, to go where widows and old women go?”

You are afraid to hear this, and afraid to say: “I was in the Church.” How would you endure a persecutor when you shudder at an insulter? And certainly this is a time of peace; they ought to be ashamed.

Are so many who have come forward ashamed, while so few who have remained behind are not ashamed? And where have these come forward to? Where have those remained? These have come forward into the light of peace; those have remained in the darkness of confusion.

Are you not ashamed to be ashamed of what should be gloried in? They are not ashamed of what should cause shame, while you are ashamed of what should be gloried in? And where is what you heard: “Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. 33:6)?

### VII

I have said these things, my brothers, because I know—and I am deeply grieved—that people fear the tongues of a few pagans who are not raging but merely insulting, and that they hold back the minds of those who wish to believe, when these do not yield to the exhortations of Christians.

And what more shall I say? Or what am I to say? You see some pagan—I do not know whom—being harassed so that he may not become a Christian, and you, a Christian, remain silent. You count it a great thing that he spares you—that is, that he does not insult you.

When he frightens that other man, you say in your heart: “Thanks be to God! He said nothing to me.” You flee—not in body, but in mind. You stand there, and you flee. You fear that his abusive tongue may turn against you, and you do not help the one whom you ought to win for Christ.

You do not help him; you remain silent. As I said, you flee—not in body, but in mind. You are a hired servant: you see the wolf coming, and you flee (John 10:12).

And what more am I to say? We have all just heard it. Let the Lord inspire fear. The one who is to be loved is himself to be feared.

“Whoever has confessed me before men.” (And see when he said this: when the world did not believe but raged.) “Whoever has been ashamed of me before men, I will put him to shame before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever has confessed me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32–33).

Do you wish to be denied by Christ, or do you wish to be confessed by Christ? You will have the insulter far from you when you find that Christ is your denier. What he promises will come to pass. Will the one who has provided so much be found deceitful only concerning the day of judgment? Far be it from us.

Let them keep their faithlessness—or rather, let them also be rid of their faithlessness—but offer yourselves to them as examples to imitate in confession, not as people to be overcome by their silence.

For if they find Christians stronger in defending the weak, in asserting the faith, in the freedom to confess, in the wisdom to teach, and in the charity to instruct, they will fall silent—believe me. They have nothing to say [Col. 0887]. Their voice is empty. The ringing cymbal (1 Cor. 13:1) that ceased in their temples has remained in their mouths.

## SERMON XIX

On the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 12:31: “I show you a still more excellent way,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0887] In the manuscript, fol. 64, it is entitled: “A sermon of Saint Augustine the bishop, *On Charity*.” It is an excellent treatise, directed especially against the Donatist schismatics, whose latter part is historical. Possidius mentions two treatises *On Charity* in his *Index of Works*, chapter 9. The present one should be inserted in this edition after Sermon 162.]

### Synopsis

I. Charity is greater than all gifts, which can also be possessed without it.  
II. Prophecy without charity in Saul and his attendants.  
III. Prophecy without charity in Caiaphas.  
IV. Faith without charity in the demons.  
V. An example of mutual charity in the members of the human body.  
VI. Different dignity among the members, but health is to be valued more highly.  
VII. The Donatists as diseased, severed members.  
VIII. The condemnation of Crispinus, and the earlier Donatist case concerning Caecilianus and Majorinus.  
IX. A way of return is open to those severed from the Church.  
X. The Church, spread throughout the whole world, is Catholic and true.  
XI. The gift of tongues given to the first believers signified that the future Church would be παντάγλωσσος, “of every tongue.”  
XII. He urges the Donatists to return.

### I

It is good to speak about Charity to those who love it—the Charity by which whatever is loved is rightly loved. For, according to the Apostle, Charity is the most excellent way. It was just now being read; we heard it: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31).

Then he recounted many gifts, gifts indeed that were splendid and not to be undervalued; yet he said that none of them benefits people who do not possess Charity. Among these gifts he mentioned speaking in the tongues of human beings and angels, possessing all prophecy, all knowledge, and all faith, so as to move mountains, distributing all one’s possessions to the poor, and handing over one’s body to be burned (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

All these things are great and divine, if they are placed upon the foundation of Charity and arise from the root of Charity. But we would not dare to say that many people possessed many of these gifts without having Charity, unless we were taught by the examples—not of just any people gathered from anywhere, but from the holy Scriptures themselves, without faith in which no one can have Charity.

Among the chief gifts mentioned, Prophecy and Faith especially appear great. What, then, shall we say of the others? If prophecy benefits no one who possesses it without Charity, and if no one who possesses Faith can reach the kingdom of God without Charity, why should we speak of the rest? What is speaking in tongues compared with Prophecy and Faith? What is distributing all one’s possessions to the poor compared with Prophecy, or handing over one’s body to be burned? Reckless and rash people often do such things.

Those two, then, are the great gifts about which we should truly be astonished [Col. 0888] if we could find someone possessing Prophecy without Charity, or possessing Faith without Charity.

### II

The Book of Kings gives us an example of Prophecy. Saul was persecuting holy David (1 Kings 19). While he was pursuing him and sending attendants to seize him for punishment, those who had been sent to bring David to his death found him among the prophets. There also was the holy Samuel, son of barren Hannah, whom she had asked of the Lord, received from the Lord, and given to the Lord.

Samuel, then, lived at the same time as David, that outstanding prophet, for David had been anointed by him. When David was suffering persecution from Saul, he fled to Samuel, just as, for example, someone who is suffering persecution outside may now flee to the Church.

He had therefore fled to the place where not only Samuel, the foremost of all the prophets, was present, but also many other prophets. While they were prophesying, Saul’s men came among them—those who, as I said, had come to seize David and put him to death.

The Spirit of God rushed upon them, and those who had come to lead a holy and righteous man of God away to the sword and remove him from among the prophets began to prophesy. Suddenly they were filled with the Spirit of God and became prophets.

Perhaps this happened because of their innocence. They had not come of their own accord to seize David; they had been sent by their king. Perhaps they had indeed come to the place where David was, but were not going to do what Saul had commanded. Perhaps they too were going to remain there. Such things happen even today.

Sometimes an official is sent by a great authority to drag someone out of the Church. He does not dare act against God, and, lest he too fall beneath the sword, he remains where he had been sent to seize the other person.

Someone, then, might admire the fact that these men suddenly became prophets and say that, because they were innocent, the prophecy itself bore witness to their innocence. They came as men sent on a mission, but they were not going to do what that evil man had ordered. Let us grant this concerning them.

Others were sent. The Spirit of God also rushed upon them, and they too began to prophesy. Let us count these also among the innocent on the same grounds. A third group was sent. The same thing happened to them. Let us suppose that all were innocent.

When they delayed and what Saul had commanded was not done, Saul himself came. Was he also innocent? Was he himself sent by some authority, rather than acting perversely of his own will?

Yet the Spirit of God also rushed upon him, and he began to prophesy. Behold: Saul prophesies. He possesses Prophecy, but he does not possess Charity.

He became a kind of vessel touched by the Spirit, not a vessel cleansed by the Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0888] Read *illum* (“him”), as a little earlier: “upon them.”]

### III

For the Spirit of God touches certain hearts so that they may prophesy, yet does not cleanse them. And if it touches but does not cleanse, is the Spirit itself perhaps polluted? Since it is the substance of God, it touches everything and is polluted nowhere.

Nor should you be amazed that this light, which is poured down from heaven, touches everything unclean while scattered everywhere, yet is nowhere darkened by what is unclean. And not only that light which comes from heaven: even the [Col. 0889] light sent forth from a lamp touches whatever you direct the light toward. Perhaps someone passing through a sewer is himself polluted if he touches it; but if he carries a lamp, the lamp’s brightness passes over everything and contracts no stain.

If God was able to grant this to bodily lights, can the true, eternal, and unchangeable Light itself be polluted anywhere? Or can the light of God be absent anywhere, of which it is said: “It reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1)?

It touches what it wills and cleanses what it wills. It does not cleanse everything it touches; rather, it touches what it has cleansed.

The Spirit, then, did not cleanse Saul, the persecutor of God, but nevertheless touched him so that he might prophesy.

Caiaphas, the chief priest, was a persecutor of Christ, and yet he spoke Prophecy when he said: “It is expedient that one man should die, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50). The Evangelist then explained the prophecy and said: “He did not say this of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied” (ibid. 51).

Caiaphas prophesied; Saul prophesied. They possessed Prophecy, but they did not possess Charity. Did Caiaphas possess Charity, when he persecuted the Son of God, whom Charity brought to us? Did Saul possess Charity, when he persecuted the one by whose hand he had been delivered from his enemies? He was not only envious but ungrateful.

We have therefore proved that Prophecy can exist in someone without Charity. According to the Apostle, Prophecy cannot benefit such people. “If I have not Charity,” he says, “I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). He does not say: “Prophecy is nothing,” or “Faith is nothing,” but: “I am nothing if I do not have Charity.”

A person who possesses great gifts is nothing, however great the gifts he possesses. For the great things he has are not possessed for his assistance but for his judgment. It is not great to possess great things; it is great to use great things well. But one who does not possess Charity does not use them well. For no thing is used well except by a good will, and there can be no good will where Charity is absent.

### IV

What shall we say of Faith? Do we find someone possessing Faith but not Charity? There are many who believe but do not love. We need not enumerate human beings. We find that the demons believed what we believe, but did not love what we love.

The Apostle James was rebuking those who thought it sufficient for them to believe and did not wish to live well—a thing impossible without Charity. For a good life belongs to Charity, and one who possesses Charity cannot live badly, since living well is nothing other than being filled with Charity.

When certain people boasted that they had believed in God but did not wish to live well, James compared them to demons, in keeping with the greatness of the Faith they had received, saying: “You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe—and tremble” (James 2:19).

If, then, you merely believe and do not love, you still have this in common with the demons.

Peter said: “You are the Son of God,” and it was said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. [Col. 0890] 16:16–17).

We also find that the demons said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” (Matt. 8:29). The Apostles confess the Son of God; the demons also confess the Son of God. Their confession appears equal, but their love is unequal. Both believe, but some love while others fear. Love expects a reward; fear expects punishment.

We therefore find that someone can possess even Faith without possessing Charity.

Let no one, then, boast about any gift of the Church—if perhaps he excels in the Church through some gift granted to him—but let him see whether he possesses Charity.

For the same Apostle Paul spoke and enumerated many gifts of God in the members of Christ, which is the Church (1 Cor. 12). He said that particular gifts are assigned to particular members, and that it cannot happen that everyone possesses the same gift. Yet no one will remain without a gift.

The Apostle mentions prophets, teachers, interpreters, speakers in tongues, those possessing gifts of healing, helps, administrations, and kinds of tongues. These things have been stated, and we see some gifts in some people and others in others.

Let no one therefore grieve that he has not been granted what he sees granted to another. Let him possess Charity; let him not envy the one who possesses the gift. In that person he has what he himself does not have.

Whatever my brother possesses, if I do not envy him but love him, is mine. I do not possess it in myself, but I possess it in him. It would not be mine if we were not one body under one Head.

### V

For example, the left hand has a ring on the body, while the right hand does not. Has the right hand therefore remained without adornment? Look at the individual hands and you will see that one has it and the other does not. Look at the body’s structure, to which both hands are attached, and see that the hand which does not have it possesses it in the hand that does.

The eyes see where one should go; the feet go where the eyes look. The feet cannot see, nor can the eyes walk. But the foot answers you: “I too have light, but not in myself—in the eye. For the eye does not see for itself but fail to see for me.”

The eyes also say: “We too walk—not in ourselves, but in the feet. For the feet do not carry themselves without carrying us.”

Thus, the individual members, each assigned its own particular functions, carry out what the mind commands. Yet, established in one body and preserving unity, they neither claim for themselves what the other members possess, if they themselves do not possess it, nor regard as foreign to themselves what they possess together in the one body.

Finally, brothers, if some trouble befalls one member of the body, which members will refuse their assistance? What seems so lowly in a human being as the foot? And in the foot, what is so lowly as the sole? And in the sole, what is so lowly as the skin itself, which treads upon the earth?

Yet this lowest part is held within the structure of the whole body in such a way that, if a thorn is stepped on at that point, all the members rush to help remove it. At once the knees bend, the spine curves—not the part that has been pierced, but the spine that supports the entire back—and the body sits down so that the thorn may be removed. Sitting down for this purpose is already the work of the whole body.

How small a place is involved in the pain! The place is only as large as the thorn could prick, and yet the whole body does not abandon the pain of that lowly and tiny [Col. 0891] place. The other members feel no pain, but in that single place everything feels pain.

The Apostle himself gave this as an example of Charity, exhorting us to love one another just as the members love one another in the body. “If one member suffers,” he says, “all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Cor. 12:26–27).

If members whose head is on earth love one another, how ought the members to love one another whose Head is in heaven?

Certainly they do not love one another if they abandon their Head. But since that Head is truly Head, and has been so exalted and placed in heaven at the right hand of the Father that he nevertheless labors on earth—not in himself but in his members—so that at the end he says, “I was hungry, I was thirsty, I was a stranger,” and when he is asked, “When did we see you hungry or thirsty?”—as though he were answering, “I was the Head in heaven, but on earth the members were thirsty”—he says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me”; and again, concerning those who did not do such things: “Whatever you did not do for one of the least of mine, you did not do for me” (Matt. 25:35–45).

We are joined to this Head only through Charity.

### VI

Thus, brothers, we see the individual members performing their own work according to their functions: the eye sees but does not work; the hand works but does not see; the ear hears but neither sees nor works; the tongue speaks but neither hears nor sees. Though each member is distinct and separate in its own function, all are joined together in the one structure of the body and share something common.

Their functions are different, but their health is one. Thus, in the members of Christ, Charity is what health is in the members of the body.

The eye occupies the better position, placed on high and established, as it were, in a citadel for counsel, from which it may look out, see, and point the way. Great is the eye’s honor—in its position, its perception, its keener sense, its agility, and a certain power that the other members do not possess.

For this reason people commonly swear by their eyes rather than by any other member. No one says to another, “I love you as I love my ears,” even though the sense of hearing is almost equal and close to the eyes. What shall I say of the other members? Every day people say: “I love you as my own eyes.”

And the Apostle, indicating that greater love is held for the eyes than for the other members, said, when he declared that he was loved by the Church of God: “I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have plucked out your own eyes and given them to me” (Gal. 4:15). [Note: Better: *haberi*, “to be held,” or “to be considered.”]

Nothing in the body, then, is higher or more honored than the eyes; and perhaps nothing in the body is lower than the little toe. Yet, although this is so, it is better for the body that the toe exist and be healthy than that the eye exist and suffer from inflammation.

For health, which is common to all the members, is more precious than the functions of individual members.

So, in the Church, you see one person possessing some small gift and nevertheless possessing Charity, while another perhaps excels in the Church through some greater gift and nevertheless does not possess Charity. Let the former be the little toe and the latter the eye. [Col. 0892] The one who has been able to preserve health belongs more truly to the structure of the body.

[Note: Instead of *compaginem*, read *compagem*, as in Ovid, Celsus, Seneca, Pliny, and others.]

Indeed, whatever becomes diseased in the body troubles the rest of the body. All the members work together to heal what is sick, and usually it is healed. But if it is not healed and has contracted such a degree of corruption that it cannot be cured, provision is made for all the members by removing it from the structure of the body.

### VII

Suppose, then, that a certain Donatus was an eye in the body—although we do not know what sort of man he was, except that he was certainly as he is said to have been. What benefit did his eminence of honor and glory bring him? He could not preserve health, because he did not possess Charity.

In the end, these people became so corrupt that they necessarily had to be severed; and those whom they say belong to them are worms of corruption. They are severed worms, and they cannot receive health.

For a member admits health only so long as it has not been severed from the body. Health flows from the other healthy members to the place of the wound; but once the member has been severed, where and from what source can health reach the place where the wound is? No source can be found.

For this reason they are also compared to severed branches, and the Gospel reading agrees with the apostolic reading. There too, when the Lord urged us to remain in him, he commended nothing to us so strongly as Charity:

“I am the vine; you are the branches; my Father is the cultivator. Every branch in me that bears fruit, he cleanses it so that it may bear more fruit; but the branch that does not bear fruit in me, he will cut away” (John 15:1–2).

The fruit comes from Charity itself, because fruit does not come except from a root. The Apostle says: “Rooted and grounded in Charity” (Eph. 3:17). There, then, is the root from which all fruit arises.

One who begins to dissent from the root, although he may appear to remain for a while, has either been secretly severed or is plainly destined to be severed; for he cannot possibly bear fruit.

These people once belonged to the unity. They have been severed. From what were they severed? From unity.

“But you,” they say, “have been severed.” What are we to do? I say: “You have been severed.” You say: “You have been severed.” Let God judge.

Have we therefore postponed the question and referred it to God’s judgment? Certainly not. We do this in many matters when God’s verdict has not yet become apparent. But where it is apparent, let us use it and not delay.

I produce Scripture, and I see who has been severed and from what. If Scripture bears witness to the party of Donatus—to some Church established in some part of the earth, just as the Party of Donatus is established in part of Africa—then let them call us severed and say that they themselves are rooted.

But if Scripture bears witness only to the Church spread throughout the whole world, why do we seek a human judge for our dispute? We have God. He does not yet preside in judgment, but he already presides in the Gospel.

## VIII

The heretic Crispinus has just been judged. [Note: [Col. 0892] In the year 404. See Augustine’s *Life*, Book V, chapter 11, vol. XI of the Maurist edition, column 259, and Augustine himself in various passages.]

But what does he say? “Have I perhaps been defeated by the evangelical judgment?” He asserts that he has not been defeated because the Proconsul judged against him, not Christ. If, then, he thinks a human judgment of little account, why did he appeal from the Proconsul to the Emperor? He himself demanded the Proconsul’s judgment; he himself said, “Hear me. I am not a heretic.” Does the judgment of the man whose judgment you demanded now displease you? Why? Because he judged against you? If he had judged in your favor, he would have judged well. Because he judged against you, he judged badly. Before he judged, he was a good judge—the one to whom you said, “I am not a heretic. Hear me.”

“But,” he says, “the Proconsul judged according to the laws of the Emperors, not according to the laws of the Gospel.”

Let it be so: let the Proconsul have judged according to the laws of the Emperors. If the Emperors judge wrongly against you, why did you appeal from the Proconsul to their judgment? Were the imperial laws already against you, or were they not yet against you? If they were not yet against you, the Proconsul did not judge according to them. If they were already against you, surely the Emperors will not judge in your favor against their own laws?

Furthermore, I ask you: which laws of the Emperors are against you? What happened? Teach me! For it is manifest and cannot be denied that many imperial laws exist against them. How did this come about? From where did this happen? Perhaps we persecuted them and said many evil things about the Emperors concerning you?

This is what they say to those unfortunate and uninformed people whom they deceive. For they completely conceal from those whom they wish to deceive the circumstances of how the matter was conducted at that time. But however much they conceal it, it is extracted, revealed, made public, and brought to the knowledge even of those who resist and refuse it. Let the very light strike their closed eyes, since they do not wish to see it. Let them not be permitted to disguise what is manifest; let them not be permitted to turn away from what lies open; let them not be permitted to cover over what is plain! I will press them with manifest truth.

“You demanded the Emperor’s judgment.”

“You lie!” he says.

Public documents remain. [Note: [Col. 0893] Those, namely, of the earlier case under Constantine the Great, between Majorinus and Caecilianus. See the Letter of the Clergy of Hippo among Augustine’s letters, no. 88, vol. II of the Maurist edition, column 213, and the holy Father himself in more than one passage.]

The Donatists themselves, belonging to the Party of Majorinus—the one who had first been ordained—approached the Proconsul Anullinus at that time against Caecilianus. They submitted written accusations concerning Caecilianus, sealed in a thin leather covering, [Note: [Col. 0893] A thinner skin, apparently like parchment, in which the written petitions were wrapped. It also occurs in the previously cited Letter of the Clergy.] saying that they had charges against Caecilianus, which they had written in that document, and asking him to send their accusation itself to the Emperor’s court. [Note: [Col. 0893] That is, to the palace. See Ducange, *Glossary*, under this word.]

There survives the report of the Proconsul Anullinus, addressed to the Emperor Constantine. He writes that men from the Party of Majorinus had come to him with written accusations against Caecilianus, asking him to send those same documents to the Emperor, and he says that he did what they had requested.

The Emperor wrote to the bishop Meltiades [Note: [Col. 0893] Melchiades, or Miltiades, Roman pontiff. But who was the Marcus added here? Was he the man who subsequently held the pontificate after Melchiades? Or one of the three Gallic bishops assigned to assist him in the judgment?] and to Marcus, transferring the ecclesiastical case to them and removing it from himself. In the same letter the Emperor writes that he had sent the documents sent by Anullinus, and in that letter he does not know [Note: [Col. 0894] I would read: “it is not known,” and shortly afterward: “is contained.”] what those documents were, but that from Anullinus’s report it could be recognized what is contained today in the public records.

Then the same Constantine wrote to Anullinus that he should direct the parties to Rome for episcopal judgment. At the end Anullinus also reports that he had sent the parties.

You, therefore, brought these matters to the Emperor; you brought the Church’s case before human authority. He was better than you. You brought it before the Emperor; he brought it before the bishops.

The case was heard in an episcopal judgment, with those men bringing the first accusation. Judgment was delivered in favor of Caecilianus. Not content with the ecclesiastical judgment, they began to murmur and again approached that same Emperor, seeking an imperial judgment after the episcopal judgment.

He granted another ecclesiastical hearing at Arles. [Note: [Col. 0894] In the year 314, a second hearing after the Roman condemnation.]

From that judgment also they appealed to the Emperor himself. Overcome by their persistence, he too wished to take up and investigate the case. He took it up, investigated it, judged Caecilianus completely innocent, and also issued all the imperial orders against them.

What is surprising? Do you dare reject the sentence of the one whose judgment you demanded? Why did you wish to bring the judgment before him? Did you have the Church in Africa but not throughout the whole world?

But where were they going, they who had already cut themselves off? They no longer clung to the Church, but the Emperor clung there, to whom the judgment was being referred. Therefore he most gently wished to judge the bishops, and afterward yielded to them so that he himself might also judge.

Hence there are laws against you; see whether they are not against you. First, you yourselves were the accusers; you were the first accusers, the final appellants, and the last murmurers.

“But surely,” he says, “I have not been defeated by the Gospel.”

You have been defeated by the judgment which you yourself chose.

## IX

But we do not reject the evangelical judgment. Indeed, even if he had not said it, we would read it, extract it, and demonstrate it. Let the Gospel be recited! Let us see where the Lord Jesus Christ says that the Church is.

Certainly, our ears and our hearts ought to be open to him. Let us hear him himself. Let him tell us where the Church is. If he says that his Church is in Africa, let us all flock to the Party of Donatus. If he says that his Church is throughout the whole world, let the severed members return to the body; for the branches have not been broken in such a way that they cannot be grafted in again.

You have the Apostle Paul saying this. But you say: “The branches were broken so that I might be grafted in.” Good. They were broken because of unbelief; but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you (Rom. 11:19–21).

The Jews had been broken off as natural branches, and the Gentiles had been grafted in like a wild olive into an olive tree. From these grafted branches, and from this grafted wild olive, we all share in the olive tree. But just as the Apostle had threatened the branches of the wild olive that were becoming proud, so these men became proud, with the result that they deserved to be cut off by pride along with those natural branches that had previously been cut off.

But what does the Apostle say? “And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in” (Rom. 11:23); and you, “if you do not remain in faith, will be cut off.”

Let no one be proud in the vine; let no one outside the vine despair. If you are proud in the vine, take care lest you be cut off. If they have been placed outside the vine, let them not despair; let them dare to be grafted in. For they are not to be grafted in by their own power. He says: “God is able to graft them in again” (ibid.).

Let them not say: “How can a severed thing, a broken branch, be grafted in again?” You rightly say that it cannot happen if you consult human ability, but not if you consult the divine majesty.

What then? Can any farmer do what has already been done by the Lord? He took a wild olive and grafted it into an olive tree, and the wild olive grafted into the olive tree did not produce bitter berries but olives. Let someone do this now: let him graft a wild olive into an olive tree, and he will see that nothing comes forth except the berries of the wild olive.

God, therefore, was powerful enough not to graft the olive into the wild olive, but the wild olive into the olive, and to make the wild olive share in the richness of the olive, so that, stripped of its bitterness, it might be clothed with richness. Will he not be powerful enough to graft you, cut off through pride, by means of humility?

“Good,” he says, “you exhort me; but first show me that I have been cut off, lest perhaps you ought to exhort yourself to come to me, rather than exhort me to be grafted into you.”

I dare to say, “Hear me,” and yet I fear to say, “Hear me.” For I fear that he may despise a human being. Rather, I exhort him to despise a human being. If he despised a human being, he would not belong to the Party of Donatus. For Donatus was a human being.

Therefore, if we speak our own words, let us be despised; but if we speak Christ’s words, let him be heard—he who is not heard without reward, and is not despised without punishment. He is heard for a reward; he is not heard for punishment.

Let us hear him himself. Let the Lord himself speak to us.

## X

He shows the Church in innumerable passages, but let me recall one. After the resurrection, as you know, brothers, he showed himself to his disciples and displayed his scars, offering himself to be touched, not merely seen. Yet even while holding him, touching him, and recognizing him, they still hesitated for joy, as the Gospel teaches us—the Gospel which must be believed, and which it is impious not to believe.

But while they were still hesitating for joy and doubting, the Lord gave them firmness from the Scriptures and said: “These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you: that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”

Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:44–47).

You are not there. I am there. What are you waiting for—a human being to judge you from a tribunal? Hear Christ from the Gospel. “Among all nations,” he says, “beginning from Jerusalem.”

Are you there? Do you share with all nations? Do you share with that Church which has been spread among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem? If you share with it, you are there; you are in the vine; you have not been cut off.

For this is the vine that grew and filled the whole world, the body of Christ, the Church of Christ, whose head is in heaven. But if you share only with Africans, and from Africa secretly send wherever you can people to console the exiles, do you not find that you have remained in a Party and have been cut off from the Whole?

What did you say in the judgment of the Proconsul? “I am Catholic.” Those are his own words. It is read from the official records: “I am Catholic.” Hold the Whole.

*Holon* [Note: [Col. 0896] Greek: ὅλον. Shortly afterward: *meros*, μέρος. From this, just as *katholikē* was formed, so *katamerikē* was formed.] means “whole”; and the Church is therefore called Catholic because it exists throughout the Whole. Was it perhaps called *Catamerica*, and not *Catholic*? *Meros* means “part,” while *holon* means “whole.” The word Catholic comes from the Greek expression meaning “according to the whole.”

Do you therefore share with the Universal? “No,” he says.

Then you are in a part. How are you Catholic? There is a great difference between the Whole and a part. From where does it receive the name “Catholic”? You received your name from the Party of Donatus; the Catholic Church received its name from the entire world.

But we say that it exists throughout the whole world. Perhaps God does not say this? I have recalled the Gospel; I have recited it from the Gospel: “Among all nations,” he says, “beginning from Jerusalem.”

Did it not come from there to Africa? If it began from Jerusalem, then, in filling everything, it came to you—not by drying up.

Who would say, “A stream was led from its spring so that it might come to me; it dried up on the way and reached me”? If it dried up on the way, how did it reach you? Certainly it reached you by filling everything.

Ungrateful stream, why do you blaspheme the spring? Unless it flowed, you would not be filled. But I fear that you have dried up. For every stream cut off from its spring must dry up.

They speak harshly against the Church out of their dryness; they would speak gently if they were being watered.

“I am Catholic.”

What does “Catholic” mean? A man from Numidia? At least ask the Greeks. “Catholic” is certainly not a Punic word, but a Greek word. Seek an interpreter. You rightly err in language, since you do not agree with all languages.

## XI

When the Spirit came from heaven and filled those who believed in Christ, they spoke in all languages; and at that time this was the sign that someone had received the Holy Spirit: that he spoke in the languages of all peoples (Acts 2, 10, and 19).

Surely the Holy Spirit is not now given to the faithful? Far be it from us to believe this, otherwise we will have no hope. They too certainly admit that the Holy Spirit is given to the faithful; and we say this, we believe this, and above all we discern that this happens in the Catholic Church alone. [Note: [Col. 0896] Thus the manuscripts; but I would correct it to *attestamur*, “we attest.”]

“But let them be Catholics; there the Holy Spirit is given. Let us be Catholics; here the Holy Spirit is given.” For the moment, let us not ask what the difference is or who the Catholics are; it is clear that the Holy Spirit is given.

Why do those who receive the Holy Spirit not now speak in all languages, unless it is because at that time something was represented in a few people which afterward was to be manifested in everyone?

What did the Holy Spirit announce, moving the hearts of those whom he had then filled and teaching them all languages? A person scarcely learns two or three languages—whether from teachers or from the regions in which he lives with some familiarity, perhaps at most three or four languages.

But those who were filled with the Holy Spirit spoke in all languages, and they spoke them suddenly, not gradually learning them. What, then, was the Spirit showing at that time? Tell me: why does he not do this now, unless he did it then to signify something?

What did it signify, unless that the Gospel would exist in all languages?

I dare to say that even now the Church speaks in all languages. For the Gospel cries out in all languages. What I was saying earlier about the members, I say also about the languages. Just as the eye says, “The foot walks for me,” so the foot says, “The eye sees for me.” In the same way I say: “My language is Greek; my language is Hebrew; my language is Syriac.”

For one faith holds them all together, and one bond of charity joins them all. What was demonstrated through the Lord was foretold beforehand through the Prophets:

“Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

See how far the Church has grown—the Church called Catholic from the Whole. And observe that all languages have gone throughout all lands:

“There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard” (ibid. 18:4).

## XII

This Church, then, I hold; you do not hold it. If you have been cut off, acknowledge from what you have been cut off. Return and be grafted in, lest you wither and be thrown into the fire.

The Prophets speak; the Apostles speak; the Lord speaks about the Church spread throughout the whole world. All these pronounce judgment against you.

From the Proconsul to the imperial judgment—but from the Gospel to whom? Perhaps to Donatus? Will Donatus judge against Christ? Or does Christ judge Donatus?

What will Donatus say to you? “I preached my Christ from Africa.” What will he bring forward? Perhaps: “I set myself in Christ’s place,” and “I succeeded Christ”? This is what remains for him to say, since he dared to cut people off from the body: that he succeeded Christ.

Here is Christ’s judgment; here are the Gospels: “Among all nations,” he says, “beginning from Jerusalem.”

It began from Jerusalem. There the Holy Spirit came; there the Apostles were when he descended upon them; from there the Gospel began to be preached; from there it was spread throughout all nations; from there afterward it came to Africa.

Where did it come afterward? Did it abandon them? No, it did not abandon them—if they are unwilling to abandon it. For we too are Africans.

The Gospel that came to Africa certainly remains here among the Catholic Africans, just as it remains among all nations. For, as there are heretics throughout all nations—some there, some here—so Africans who belong to them were not born in all those nations. They have been cut off from the vine.

For the Catholic Church knows them all, while they do not know themselves. Indeed, the vine from which the branches have been cut knows all the branches—both those that remain in it and those that have been cut off from it.

The Catholic Church has been spread everywhere. Those branches remained where they were cut off and could not reach other regions and other regions. But the Church spread everywhere holds its own everywhere and everywhere mourns those who have been cut off. It cries out to all that they should return and be grafted in.

Its cry is not heard, yet the breasts of its charity do not cease to pour forth through exhortation. It is concerned for those who have been cut off. In Africa it cries out against the Donatists; in the East it cries out against the Arians, against the Photinians, and against others and still others.

Because it has been spread everywhere, everywhere it finds those against whom it must cry out—for they were in it and were cut off from it. The branches began to be fruitless and were cut off. “If they do not remain in unbelief, they will be grafted in again.”

Hear this, brothers, with fear, lest you become proud; with charity, so that you may also pray for them.

Turned toward the Lord, etc.

# SERMON XX

## On the words of Psalm 38, verses 1–5: “I said: I will guard my ways,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0898] In Codex folio 68 it is entitled: “A sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop.” It deals chiefly with the use of the tongue and with the end of the human being. To conceal nothing, some things seem to me less coherent, some beneath Augustine’s dignity; the words of the Psalm are also repeated more than once inappropriately and inserted, and I therefore suspect an interpolator. Let those who are more deeply nourished by the reading of the holy Doctor weigh the matter. In the edition, this passage should occur after Sermon XVI.]

## Synopsis
