I. Concern for daily progress, and consequently the invocation of divine assistance.  
II. The use of the tongue is both necessary and dangerous.  
III. The tongue is governed by the mind.  
IV. The deceitful tongue of the Jews confounded.  
V. The good use of the tongue in the adulterous woman.  
VI. The adulterous woman’s confession as instruction for us.  
VII. How one should deal with an abuser.  
VIII. Abusers should be forgiven, and prayer should be offered for them.  
IX. The end of the human being is investigated.  
X. Christ is the end of the human being.  
XI. This end is attained through faith and works.  
XII. The purpose of temptations, and how one should conduct oneself in them.  
XIII. Repetition of what has been said.

## I

It is characteristic of Christians to advance daily toward God and always to rejoice in God or in his gifts. For the time of our pilgrimage is very short, while our homeland is outside time. There is a great difference between eternity and time. Here piety is acquired; there rest is enjoyed.

Therefore, on each day, like good merchants, let us know what progress we have made. For we must be not only diligent in listening but watchful in acting. This school, in which God alone is the teacher, seeks good pupils—not deserters, but diligent students. The Apostle says: “Not sluggish in zeal, fervent in spirit, rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12:11).

In this school, then, brothers, we learn every day. We learn one thing through commandments, another through examples, and another through the sacraments. These are the medicines for our wounds and the supports of our studies.

A moment ago we answered: “Hear my prayer and my supplication, O Lord!” “Give ear”—[Note: [Col. 0898] An unusual formation of the verb *inaurior*, after the Greek ἐνωτίζομαι, which the Septuagint has in this passage.] that is, “Perceive my tears with your ears” (Ps. 38:13).

What do you think this man will ask, who first desires God to be favorable toward him? What will he seek from him? Let us see; let us learn. Perhaps he will ask for riches; perhaps some happiness in this life.

Let him tell us, then, what he will ask who first beseeches God. For he saw that he could not possess something from himself, but could possess it from God. He had heard: “Ask, and you will receive” (John 16:24). He therefore knew what he would ask, since he first begged God.

“Therefore, O God, hear my prayer!” And as though he were asked: “What do you want? What are you knocking for? What are you crying out for? What are you calling upon me for? I will listen. What do you want?”

“What do I want?” he says. “Hear my desire, and complete your works.”

“What is my desire?”

“I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue” (Ps. 38:1).

He is undertaking a difficult task, but he does not doubt, since he first beseeched the Lord. For he knew Paul’s teaching: “Not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

## II

I said, then: “I will guard my ways.” Which ways? Earthly ways. Do we walk on the earth by means of the tongue? We walk on the earth either with our own feet or with the feet of others. We are carried by animals, or we go on our own feet.

What, then, is the way he seeks? That he may not sin with his tongue.

This is great teaching, brothers; pay attention. Surely we cannot, just as we can take food in one hour and depart refreshed, speak for a moment and then be silent? For just as we have eyes for seeing, ears for hearing, and the other senses for perceiving, so likewise we have the tongue for speaking.

The tongue is a great necessity for us. Either you are going to hear something so that you may answer, or you are going to say something so that you may teach. Are you going to speak with the eye and not with the tongue? And if you are going to hear with the ear, you are going to answer with the tongue.

What shall we do with such a useful member? Through it we ask God; through it we make satisfaction; through it we utter praises; through it, singing together with one voice, we sing to God; through it, day by day, either we become merciful when we speak with others, or we give counsel.

What are we doing now? Our tongue itself is providing you a service. What shall we do so that we may not sin with the tongue, especially since it has been said: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21)?

And again it has been said: “I have seen many fall by the stroke of the sword, but not as those who have fallen by the tongue” (Sir. 28:22). Again it is said: “The tongue is set among our members, and it defiles our whole body” (James 3:6).

Again the same Lord says: “They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood” (Jer. 9:5). “They have taught it”! For the habit of speaking falsehood creates the practice. Even if you do not wish it, it speaks falsehood.

Just as, if you turn a wheel once (James 3:6), then, when you have pushed it with your hand, it runs by that same shape and roundness, or by its own unstable and almost natural course, so our tongue does not need to be taught to speak falsehood; it now runs spontaneously toward what it can do more easily.

You have one thing in your heart, while it sometimes rolls out another according to habit. What will you do? You see, brothers, what a balance of the heart must be established before the tongue says anything! For it does not move spontaneously. There is one within who moves it.

## III

There is a certain power that moves itself and its other instruments. It is necessary that the one who governs be good, and that, aided by grace, he overcome however bad a habit.

Let the minister be good, and the ministry rests. A soldier has weapons, but if he does not strike [Note: [Col. 0900] Thus the written text, in place of *fecerit*, which is found in the parchment manuscripts.], the weapons accomplish nothing.

So too the tongue among our members is the weapon of our soul. Of it it is said: “An restless evil” (James 3:8). O restless evil! Who made this evil except one who is restless? Do not be restless, and this evil does not exist. Do not stir it up [Note: [Col. 0900] Perhaps more correctly: “do not be stirred up.”], and there is nothing to stir itself up.

For it is not the mind that is being moved; it is the body. It lies still. Do not move it, and it is not moved. But see how you move [Note: [Col. 0900] “The tongue” seems to have dropped out.] it.

This is the tongue with which many who devote themselves to fraud and serve greed, when they begin to conduct some business, bring forth a member made for the praise of God, and there blaspheme God, saying: “By Christ! I bought it for so much; I sell it for so much.”

“When did I ask you: ‘Swear to me how much you are selling it for?’ I asked you: ‘How much are you selling it for?’”

“I am selling it for ten *folles*, for twenty *folles*.” [Note: [Col. 0900] Either for purses containing a fixed sum of money, as in Juvenal and Vegetius, or for a particular kind of coin. See Sirmond’s note on Augustine’s sermons, vol. I, Paris 1696, column 344. The holy Doctor himself mentions *folles* in vol. V, columns 219 and 1499.]

Do you swear by Christ? Swear by your eyes; swear by your children—and at that very moment your conscience trembles.

O the impiety of the tongue! You despised the Creator but guarded the creature.

O restless evil, full of deadly poison! With it we bless God and the Father—God on account of nature, the Father on account of grace. And with it we curse the human being, who was made in the image of God (James 3:8–9).

Pay attention, brothers, to what you bear. Behold, I tell you what we bear. For I too am a human being together with you. But let us return.

## IV

“Hear my prayer, O God.” This concerns those Jews whom we have just read about in the Gospel. Their tongue led them to death.

For we have just heard in the Gospel: “The Jews brought a certain woman, although she was an adulteress, to the Lord, testing him and saying: ‘Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. In the Law of Moses it is written that any woman caught in adultery should be stoned. What do you say?’” (John 8:4).

The tongue was speaking this, but it did not recognize the Creator. These men did not wish to pray so as to say: “Deliver my soul from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119:2). For they had approached deceitfully; this was what they intended to do.

The Lord had come not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17), and to forgive sins. The Jews therefore said among themselves: “If he says, ‘Let her be stoned,’ we will say to him: ‘Where is your claim that you forgive sins? Are you not the one who says, “Your sins are forgiven you”?’” (Matt. 9:5; Mark 2:5–9; Luke 5:23).

“If he says, ‘Let her go,’ we will say: ‘Where is your claim that you came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it?’”

See the deceitful tongue directed against God.

He who had come as redeemer, not as condemner—for he had come to redeem what had perished (Matt. 13:11)—turned away from them, as though unwilling to look at them. This turning away from them is not without significance. Something is understood in that turning away.

It was as though he were saying: “You bring me a sinful woman, you sinners! If you think that I ought to condemn sins, I begin with you.”

And he himself, who had come to bestow forgiveness of sins, said: “Let the one among you who knows himself to be without sin cast the first stone at her” (John 8:7).

O what a response, or rather, what a challenge! If they had wished to cast a stone at the sinful woman, the saying would immediately have been recited again: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:2). You have condemned; you will be condemned.

Yet although they did not recognize the Creator, they knew their own consciences. They placed their faces one behind another, so that in their shame they did not even wish to see one another, and all went out, from the elders—as the Evangelist says—to the youngest.

For the Holy Spirit had said: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless. There is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. 14:3).

## V

And they all went out. He remained alone, and she alone. The Creator remained, and the creature; misery [Note: [Col. 0901] Might “misery” (*miseria*) be more correct?] remained, and mercy; the one who acknowledged her guilt remained, and the one who forgave sin.

For this is what he was writing when he bent down and wrote on the ground. He wrote on the ground. For when the human being sinned, it was said to him: “You are earth” (Gen. 3:19).

Therefore, when he was granting forgiveness to the sinful woman, he was writing on the ground as he granted it. He was granting forgiveness; but when he granted forgiveness, he raised his face toward her and said: “Has no one condemned you?” [Note: [Col. 0901] Here, and below, the scribe absurdly wrote *lapidavit*, “stoned,” instead of *condemnavit*, “condemned.”]

And she did not say: “Why? What have I done, Lord? Surely I am not guilty?” She does not say this, but says: “No one, Lord.”

She accused herself. They had been unable to prove the charge and withdrew, but she confessed. Her Lord did not fail to know her guilt; he was seeking her faith and confession.

“Has no one condemned you?”

And she: “No one, Lord!”

“No one,” because of the confession of sins; “Lord,” because of the granting of mercy. “No one, Lord! I acknowledge both. I know who you are; I know who I am. For to you I confess. I have heard: ‘Confess to the Lord, for he is good’ (Ps. 106:1). I know my confession; I know your mercy.”

This woman said: “I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.” They sinned by acting deceitfully; she acquitted herself more fully by confessing.

“Has no one condemned you?”

She said: “No one.”

And he, remaining silent, wrote again. He wrote twice. Let us hear what this means! He wrote twice: once in granting forgiveness, and again in renewing the commandments.

For both take place when we receive forgiveness. The Emperor has signed the document. When another form [Note: [Col. 0901] That is, a rescript or imperial decree, whence also *formulae*, formal letters.] is issued again, it is as though other commandments are given again.

These are the commandments through which we first heard in the Apostle that charity was imposed as a law. [Note: [Col. 0901] The Letter of James was evidently read before the sermon, where at 2:8 it calls charity the “royal law” (*νόμον βασιλικόν*), alluding to the word “imposed” and to the whole comparison with an emperor.]

First we heard that reading; afterward the Lord himself said this: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40).

## VI

So that none of us might have difficulty, two things were named: God and neighbor—the one who made you, and the one with whom he made you.

No one said to you: “Love the sun; love the moon; love the earth; love whatever has been made.” In these things God is to be praised, the Maker is to be blessed.

“How greatly your works have been exalted!” we say. “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 104:24). They are yours. You made all things. Thanks be to you!

But you made us above all things. Thanks be to you! For we are your image and likeness. Thanks be to you!

We sinned. We were sought out! Thanks be to you!

We neglected you. We were not neglected. Thanks be to you!

When we were despising you, we were not despised. Lest we forget your divinity and lose you, you also took on our humanity. Thanks be to you!

Where is there no reason for thanksgiving?

I said, then: “I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.”

That woman, when she was brought forward on the charge of adultery, received forgiveness and was freed. Is it burdensome for us that, through baptism, confession, and grace, everyone receives forgiveness of all their sins?

But let no one now say: “She received forgiveness; I am still a catechumen. I will commit adultery, since I am going to receive forgiveness. Regard me as one who, like that woman, [Note: [Col. 0902] I insert here: “who.”] confessed and was freed.”

“Our God is good, and if I sin, I will confess to him, and he will forgive me.”

You attend to his goodness, but consider his justice. As goodness applies to forgiveness, so justice applies to punishment.

I said, then: “I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.”

I would like to know whether, during this time in which we are ministering the sermon to Your Charity, no one is sinning with his tongue. During the time we are here, perhaps none of us has said anything evil, but perhaps someone has thought something evil.

Pay attention.

“I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.”

Say truly: “I placed a guard over my mouth while the sinner stood before me” (Ps. 38:2).

### VII

Pay attention. “I set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.” Someone wicked stands against you, reviles you, and says things that you do not know to be true. You set a guard over your mouth. I said: “I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.” Let him speak; you listen and remain silent.

There are two possibilities: he is speaking the truth, or he is speaking falsely. If he speaks the truth, you have caused him to say it, and perhaps this is mercy. For when you do not wish to hear what you have done, God, who cares for you, tells you through someone else what you have done, so that, overcome at some point by shame itself, you may have recourse to the physician.

Therefore do not repay evil with evil; for you do not know who may be speaking to you through him. If, then, he says something that you have done, acknowledge that you have received mercy: either you may think that you had forgotten it, or judge that this was said for your confusion. If you did not do it, your conscience is free. What are you seeking? Why are you angry about something you did not do? For what does he say to you? “Thief! Drunkard!” Quickly, go back within to the secrets of your conscience. Look within yourself. Be your own judge; be your own examiner. Search there. Where do you think I have placed my sins, the sins I committed? Or, if they are not there, say: “I did not do it.”

If your conscience tells you, “I did not do it,” say: “This is our boast, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). When your conscience has told you this, remain silent; grieve for the one who says it to you. Say also to God: “Father, forgive him, because he does not know what he is saying.” Pray to God for him.

“I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.” “I set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.” Do not think that you appear holy when no one tests you. You are holy when you are not moved by some insult, when you grieve for the one who speaks, when you do not care about what you suffer, but nevertheless grieve for the one from whom you suffer it.

There is all mercy in this. You grieve because he too is your brother, your member. He is out of his mind against you; he is delirious, he is sick. Grieve for him. Do not rejoice; rejoice only in the security of your own conscience, and from that security grieve for him. For you are human; take care lest you too be tested. For it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

For now, while he is speaking, remain silent; afterward, when he has calmed down, say to him: “Brother, for the sake of your salvation, why did you tell me that I did something I did not do? You have sinned against me; I ask God on your behalf. I do indeed forgive you, and I ask my God on your behalf—the God whom you wronged when you sinned against me. Do not do this again; do not become arrogant!”

I do not say: “Repay him, God, who told me what I did not do.” I do not wish to say this. “I set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.”

### VIII

“I became deaf and was humbled” (what follows), “and I was silent from good things” (Ps. 38:3). I became deaf. I did not listen to him speaking. How much this spirit has advanced—one that, even amid its brother’s error, rejoicing inwardly in the security of its own conscience, does not know what is being barked at it from outside! What sort of soul is this—how secure, how joyful! It is the soul that says to God: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of your house” [Note: [Col. 0903] I emend: “my house.”] (Ps. 100:2).

The burglars were pounding at the doors, but the house was sound. “I became deaf and was humbled”; I did not become arrogant against him. And, humbled, I was silent from good things; for it was not the time for me to say anything good. It is time for you to be silent now; afterward, once he has become sincere [Note: [Col. 0903] A little farther below: “they became sincere.” I find no such form in the Glossaries, except the participle *sinceratus*.], speak, and then he will understand.

Often sick sons have beaten their fathers, yet, because of their sons’ weakness, those fathers both endured the blows and wept. What affection people show toward their children so that they may not die, awaiting the children’s recovery! But you say: “He is not my son?” He is God’s work, God’s image, God’s son. If you despise him because he is not your son, do not despise him because he is God’s son; he is your brother.

Therefore: “I became deaf and was humbled.” I was not arrogant, but “I was silent from good things,” and my grief was renewed—not because of myself, but because of him, because I had not done what he said. I felt grief; but because he said this, I felt grief. Since I cared for my brother, grief was renewed in me.

This is the way. For this is what the Lord himself, our Father, did—he who is also called the Bridegroom. “The sons of the Bridegroom will not fast,” he said, “as long as the Bridegroom is with them” (Luke 5:34). He was beaten by delirious sons; delirious sons killed him. He prayed for them.

Afterward they became sincere, recognized and believed; and those who had refused to be healed by the physician were healed by the physician’s disciple—for they were healed through Peter. When Peter rebuked them, they said: “What shall we do?” Then Peter said: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38).

A moment before they were raging; a moment later they were believing. You see what weakness and health do. When they were sick, they were tolerated; when they were made well, they were redeemed.

Therefore, brothers, whenever we suffer such things, let us remain silent, so that we may hold fast to this: “He is either speaking the truth or speaking falsely.” Even if he has not said it, and I did it, what then? Since he does not say it, though I did it, it is to be desired that he say it, so that I may be put to shame because I did it. This is God’s mercy.

But if he says what I did not do, let me rejoice in my security and grieve over my brother’s weakness.

“My heart grew hot within me” (Ps. 38:4); my heart burned within me from the love I have for my brother, but I was not able at that moment to make it the time for speaking. Hence Paul himself says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1). Yet he did speak to them.

How did he speak? “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire blazed up.” The fire of charity is within me. I have no one to whom I can speak, because he is weak. Therefore let me humble myself. Perhaps at some time there will be an opportunity for me to say something.

Nevertheless: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). I will forgive him something that I do not have in my conscience. It is little that I have nothing in my conscience; let me pray for him because of his conscience.

### IX

This man had already passed through: “I said: I will guard my ways. I will set a guard over my mouth.” “I was humbled,” and “in my meditation the fire blazes up.” I do not know what it is; suddenly he brings forth something greater. After so many struggles and such great labors, listen to what he says: “I spoke with my tongue” (Ps. 38:5).

There is a tongue of the soul, namely the movement of the will itself. Just as the tongue is movement in the body, so the will is movement in the soul. There is the first tongue. From it, and through it, one speaks to God. The bodily tongue performs its service for people who are outside; the other tongue, which consists in the movement of the will, performs its service for the one who dwells within his own temple. It is the true tongue.

Therefore the Lord said that those who worship him must worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). This is the true tongue.

“I spoke with my tongue: Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack” (Ps. 38:5–6). If Your Holiness pays attention, understand the meaning first; then the Lord, in his mercy, as he often does, will grant us through your prayers that we may examine it, for it is sufficiently difficult.

“I spoke with my tongue: Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack.”

See what he prays for: “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” The end, brothers, is where we are heading, where we shall remain. Our leaving our homes in order to come to the church had an end. Thus our journey ended here. From here each one again has as his end the return to his own house. It ends where it was heading.

Now, therefore, as we are situated in this pilgrimage, we have an end toward which we are heading. Where are we heading? To our homeland. What is our homeland? Jerusalem, the mother of the faithful, the mother of the living. We are heading there. That itself is our end.

And because we did not know the way, the citizen of that city himself made himself the way. We did not know where to go. Some winding paths—thorny, rocky, altogether difficult—lay along the road. He himself, who is supreme there, came down here first, seeking the citizens of that city.

For we had gone astray. Although we were citizens of Jerusalem, we had become citizens of Babylon; we had become children of confusion, for Babylon means “confusion.” He came down here seeking his citizens and became our citizen. We did not know that city; we did not know that province. But because we did not come to it, he came down here to its citizens and became himself a citizen—not by consenting to our condition, but by taking it upon himself.

He came down here. How did he come down? In the form of a servant. God-Man walked here among us. For if he had been merely man, he would not have led us to God; if he had been merely God, he would not have been joined to human beings. He took upon himself with us an equal condition, while possessing divinity with the Father. He took upon himself with us temporality, while possessing eternity with the Father. Here he is our equal; there he is equal to the Father.

Our fellow citizen came down here and said: “What are you doing here, citizens of Jerusalem?” The image and likeness of God is not raised up except in Jerusalem. Statues of God are not established in this life. Let us labor; let us return!

By what way do we return? Behold, I spread myself beneath you; I become your way; I will be your end. Imitate me! “Make known to me, Lord, my end!” We believe that he himself is our end.

### X

God the Father is now speaking. “I say to you, O soul whom I made, O human being whom I made: You had come to an end.” What had you come to? You had perished.

I sent you one who would seek you; I sent you one who would walk with you; I sent you one who would forgive you. Hence he walked with his feet and forgave with his hands. Therefore, when he ascended after the resurrection, he showed his hands, side, and feet: his hands, by which he granted the forgiveness of sins; his feet, by which he announced peace to those who had deserted; his side, from which flowed the price of the redeemed.

“Christ is therefore the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” Your end has now been made known to you.

How has your end been made known to you? Your end was poor; your end was humble; your end was struck with blows; your end was covered with spittle; false testimony was spoken against your end.

“I set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.” He himself became your way. “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). He is the way. Let us now walk; let us not be afraid lest we go astray. Let us not walk outside the way. For it is written: “Around the way they placed stumbling blocks for me, and around the way they placed a snare” [Note: [Col. 0906] The Hebrew and Greek have παγίς (*pagis*), “snare”; Augustine, both here and in *Enarrationes in Psalmos* II, on Ps. 30:5, has *muscivula*.] (Ps. 140:6).

And behold that mercy: lest you fall into the snare, you have that very mercy as your way. “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” Behold, you have the end. Imitate Christ the Redeemer. “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. 3:17).

How did Paul imitate Christ? Pay attention to what he said: “In hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness,” and so on, continuing to: “Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:27–29). “I became all things to all people, so that I might win all” (1 Cor. 9:22). “I set a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stands against me.”

These are Paul’s words, brothers: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” Pay attention to the end: “Who will separate me from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or nakedness, or danger?” (Rom. 8:35). O man who loved, who burned, who ran, who arrived! What was this soul suffering? How it burned, how it taught!

“Who will separate me from the love of Christ?” Distress? And so on, continuing to: “Or the sword?” What did this man suffer! And lest anyone think that he was proud because of these things, he says: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended” (Phil. 3:13).

### XI

Why this? “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days”: how long I have to live here. Why do you want to know the day? “So that I may know what I lack”—what I lack, with respect to eternity.

Now pay attention to Paul. After so many labors had been counted, he still says: “I do not consider that I have apprehended.” Hear him saying: “What I lack.”

Therefore let no one say: “I have fasted much, labored much, given much. I have already fulfilled all God’s commandments. Yesterday I did it; today I did it”—and there will still be a “today” if you have ever done it. Yesterday always has a today. If you reach tomorrow, it will have a today; and if you reach ten years from now, it will be today. Always say today: “What do I lack?”

For if Paul was a heavenly soldier amid such great labors; if, after such great exercise and such great revelations, he was caught up even to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words; and yet, lest he be exalted by the revelations, he received a thorn in the flesh to humble him—who is there who can say, “It is enough”?

Therefore: “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” And behold, Christ, the end, is before you. You no longer have anything to seek. Once you have believed, you have already recognized him. But the matter does not lie in faith alone; it lies in faith and works. Both are necessary.

For demons also believe—as you have heard the Apostle say—and tremble (Jas. 2:19); but their belief does not profit them. Faith alone is insufficient unless works are joined to it. “Faith that works through love” (Gal. 5:6), says the Apostle.

“Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days.” This is not said because, if each one of us knew when he would die, he might decide, for example, to live well until then. Therefore the Teacher himself, wishing us to become watchful, was asked about the day and hour, and said: “No one knows that day and hour” [Col. 0907] (Mark 13:32). He did not want them to know. Hence he said: “Not even the Son.” This means: It is not expedient for you to know, for you would become negligent rather than watchful.

You will live well all the more when you are watchful—not because I do not know the day, for “all that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days.” Make this known to me so that I may always be watchful, because I do not know when the thief will come, so that I may know what I lack.

### XII

Therefore, brothers, let us be cautious there, so that we may know what we lack. The testing of Christians is the proving of Christians. For when someone is tested, what he lacks is shown to him.

There are two possibilities: either what he possesses is shown to him, or what he lacks is shown to him. Abraham was tested—not so that what he possessed might be shown to him, but so that what we ought to imitate might be shown to us.

He was tested in his son. What sort of testing was it? He had desired a son in advanced age, when hope of one had already been abandoned. Yet, when he heard God’s promise, he did not hesitate at all; he believed, received, merited, and took possession. The child was born, nourished, brought to maturity, was weaned [Note: [Col. 0907] I confidently restore: *ablactatus* (“weaned”).], and it was said to him: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). He knew in whom that seed was found. For we have testimony in the Gospel: “Abraham desired to see my day; and he saw it, and rejoiced” (John 8:56). Therefore he knew.

After all these things that he had believed, he heard from God: “Abraham, offer me your son as a sacrifice.” He was tested (Gen. 22). Why? Did God not know his faith? But God graciously chose to show these things for our sake.

For we are told: “Offer me the sacrifice of your purse” [Note: [Col. 0907] As above, Sermon VII, no. 3; see note 6, p. 169.], and we hesitate. What sacrifice? “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). And again: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Matt. 9:13; 12:7).

“You are told to give something from your purse,” and you tie it shut. What if you were given a command concerning your son? Behold, you hesitate over your purse; what would you have done concerning your son? “So that I may know what I lack.”

I am going to speak with grief and shame. Many women perhaps wish to serve God; and, if they are bold, they say to their parents: “Let me go. I wish to be God’s virgin,” or “I wish to be God’s servant.” And they hear: “May you neither be saved nor prosper.” “You certainly will not do what you wish. You will do what I wish.”

What if it were said to you: “Kill”? You are alive, eternal life is promised to you, it is before you, and yet you resist, hesitate, and oppose it? Certainly you are a Christian. Why? “Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0907] An address not unusual for the holy Doctor.] “Because I am a Christian, therefore I ought not to have grandchildren?” You ought to have grandchildren? You know how much you lack.

As for the fact that you fasted yesterday—sing what this man said: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack.”

For may God, and his mercy, grant that we may be stirred daily, tested, proved, exercised, or make progress [Note: [Col. 0907] Perhaps: “so that we may.”]. “Tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proving, proving produces hope, and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:3).

### XIII

Therefore, my brothers, let us desire to know daily what we are, lest, when we are secure, the day come afterward and nothing be found of what we supposed, and it be said to us: “Who will confess you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6).

Therefore, my brothers, let us make every effort each day to advance toward God, not sparing the fleeting things that we shall leave behind here. Let us attend to Abraham’s faith, for he too was our father; let us imitate his devotion, let us imitate his faith.

If we are tested in our children, let us not be afraid; if in our purse, let us not be terrified; if some affliction is inflicted upon our bodies, let us place our hope in God. We are Christians; we are pilgrims. Let no one be terrified: this is not our homeland.

Whoever wishes to have his homeland here will lose this one and will not reach the other. Let us press on toward our homeland as good children, so that our course may be approved and brought to its destination.

Turned toward the Lord, etc.

## SERMON XXI

On the words of Psalm 32, verse 1: “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0908] In Codex fol. 71, p. 2, it is entitled: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, On the Rich Man and Lazarus.” From this sermon and from the history of Job, our author argues that a righteous man ought not to cease praising God either because of the happiness of the wicked or because of the misfortunes of the righteous. The place of this sermon in the edition is after Sermon XV.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. Who ought to praise God.  
II. God must not be judged by the temporal happiness of the wicked.  
III. God is praised by the upright of heart even amid adversity.  
IV. Divine chastisement is paternal.  
V. Use makes riches good or bad.  
VI. Job is proposed as an example to Christians.  
VII. Job’s uprightness of heart in every trial.  
VIII. God’s purposes are to be worshiped, not examined.  
IX. Nevertheless, God is to be implored in adversity.

### I

What we have just sung urges us to rejoice in the praise of God and, by our way of life, to conform to God’s praise: “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord. Praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32:1).

For if it befits the upright, it does not befit the wicked. Those who are upright are also the righteous, to whom it is said that they should rejoice in the Lord; praise befits them. But who are the wicked except sinners and unjust people, who cannot rejoice in the Lord because praise does not befit them?

It is rightly said in another Psalm: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16). Since praise befits the upright, and since the Lord’s justifications and the Lord’s covenant are found where the Lord’s praise is, it is rightly said elsewhere: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9). For where it does not befit, it is not beautiful; and where it is beautiful, there it befits.

### II

Yet, seeking to discover who properly are upright men, so that each person may recognize whether the praise of God is beautiful in his mouth, we find the following in the Scriptures.

A certain Psalm says: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright of heart.” And it continues: “But my feet almost slipped, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72:1–3).

The speaker confesses not indeed his turning away and falling, but nevertheless his danger. He does not say that he fell, but that his feet wavered so that he might fall. For this is what he says: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright of heart. But my feet almost slipped.”

By distinguishing himself from the upright of heart through his turning away, he confesses that at some point he was not upright of heart, and therefore that his feet almost slipped. “The God of Israel is good,” he says, “to the upright of heart; but at one time he did not seem good to me, because I was not upright of heart.”

He did not dare to say, “God did not seem good to me,” but nevertheless he said this. For when he says, “God is good to the upright of heart; but my feet almost slipped,” he shows that his feet slipped because God did not seem good to him.

And why did God not seem good to him? “My steps almost poured out.” What does “almost” mean? They almost spilled over. Why? “Because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.”

“I looked,” he says, “at sinners who did not worship God, who blasphemed God, who provoked God. I saw that they abounded in peace, that they abounded in happiness, and it seemed to me that God judged wrongly, granting happiness to those who blasphemed him.”

While he was looking at this—that is, at the happiness of the wicked—he said that his feet had wavered, so that God did not seem good to him. But afterward he came to understand, as he says in that same Psalm: “I undertook to understand,” and he added: “This is labor before me”—why the wicked are happy. “This is labor before me,” he says, “until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny” (ibid. 16–17).

For those who are wicked now and are granted happiness for a time, eternal punishment is being reserved at the end. When he learned this, he became upright of heart and began to praise God in everything: both in the labors of the faithful and in the very happiness of the wicked. He considered that God is a just retributor at the end: now he gives certain people temporal happiness, for whom he reserves eternal unhappiness at the last; while he exercises certain faithful people in present unhappiness, for whom he again reserves eternal happiness.

The order of things must be reversed, as happened with that rich man “who feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19), and with that poor man covered with sores who lay at the rich man’s gate and desired to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table.

When both had died, the rich man began to be in punishment in hell, while the poor man rested in Abraham’s bosom. When this seemed intolerable to the rich man, and he wished a drop of water to be dripped onto him from Lazarus’s little finger—in return desiring a drop from that person’s finger, from whose table the other had desired a crumb—he heard the judgment of the righteous God from Abraham:

“Son, remember that you received good things during your life, while Lazarus received evil things. But now he is comforted here, and you are tormented” (Luke 16:25).

The man to whom God did not seem good, because he was jealous of sinners when he saw the peace of sinners, directed his gaze toward these final destinies as he entered the sanctuary of God. He recognized that God’s judgment is true and just: it is indeed being carried out now, but secretly; it will be in the end, in manifestation.

And, as though his heart had been corrected from its own crookedness by the application of the rule of God’s justice, by which the twisted heart might be straightened, he burst into this cry and said: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright of heart!”

“Now I understand what good means, because I have become upright of heart. Before, he did not seem good to me, because my feet were wavering. For I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.”

### III

If, then, God now seems good to you even when he gives happiness to the wicked—on account of which you used to murmur against God—then you have become upright of heart; praise befits you. “Praise befits the upright.”

But if you are wicked, praise does not befit you. Why does it not befit you? Your praise, by which you praise God, will not endure. You praise God when things go well for you; you blaspheme God when things go badly for you. He pleases you when he gives happiness, but displeases you when he chastises.

You are not upright of heart; you will not be able to say the words of another Psalm: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2). How can it be “always” if you praise him when things go well for you, but not when things go badly?

For what is called “things going badly for you” is also good, if you understand that he who chastises is a father. An unintelligent boy generally loves a teacher who flatters him and hates one who beats him; but an intelligent boy understands that the teacher is good both when flattering and when beating. He flatters so that the boy may not fail; he beats so that he may not perish.

When someone has such a heart—that is, an upright heart, so that God does not displease him even when God does what may seem temporarily adverse to him—he praises God securely, because he will praise him always. Praise truly befits him, and he truly sings faithfully: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth.”

“He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). What, then, do you choose: to be scourged and received, or not to be touched and not to be received? Consider what sort of son you are. If you desire your father’s inheritance, do not reject the scourging. If you reject the scourging, renounce the inheritance.

For why does he instruct you, except to give you the inheritance? Was it not so that you might be your father’s heir that he reproved, rebuked, chastised, and beat you? Why did he do this? So that you might succeed him in a house that would one day collapse, an estate that would one day pass away, and gold that would not remain in this world longer than you yourself, who possess the gold.

For either you will lose what you have while still alive, or you will leave it behind when you die. Yet for the sake of this temporal inheritance you endured your father’s blows, and you murmur against God as he instructs you so that he may give you the kingdom of heaven?

### IV

When, then, you are such that God pleases you—even when he chastises you—then either there is something in you that needs correction through the scourge, or your very uprightness is being tested by the scourge. When you are such, praise him; for you praise him securely.

Why do you praise him securely? Because you praise him fittingly, because you praise him perseveringly. I am not afraid that you may praise him now and shortly afterward blaspheme. I am not afraid that you may praise him when healthy and blaspheme when sick.

I am not afraid that, from the mouth of a healthy person, the praise of God will emerge, but from the tongue of the sick person a mathematician, or diviner, or incantation-maker, or a maker of demonic remedies will be sought [Note: [Col. 0911] “Mathematician,” that is, astrologer or diviner, as often in the works of the holy Doctor. For *Sortilogus* I prefer *Sortilegus*, as in vol. III, part II, *On the Gospel of John*, Tractate 7, col. 344, where *Praecantores* also occurs. The remedies mentioned are elsewhere repeatedly called *Ligaturae*, that is, amulets.].

I am not afraid, because you have now understood that God is good both when he chastises and when he spares, and you know that the one who strikes a son also knows when to spare him.

It will befit you to praise him, because you will always praise him perseveringly, and the praise of God will always be in your mouth. You willingly receive a father when he flatters you; you willingly receive a father when he scourges you. You do not run to him when he flatters you and flee from him when he scourges you.

For if you do this, you will be like the boy who, while fleeing from his father who was scourging him, ran into a flattering slave-dealer [Note: [Col. 0911] Similar passages occur above, Sermon VII, no. 3.] and thought that man good and his own father bad. By preferring the deceit of flattery to the truth of blows, he lost his inheritance and fell into servitude [Note: [Col. 0911] “Into slavery.” This is relevant to the meaning of the obscure word in Suetonius, *Julius*, and in Capitolinus and Lampridius.].

Change your mind, then, and make your heart upright. God has not changed because he scourges you; you are the one who is changeable. Through change he does something so that, changed for the better, you may receive the inheritance.

For if he leaves and neglects you when he seems good to you, then he is exceedingly angry. Let Your Charity attend to what the Scripture of God says in another Psalm: “The sinner has provoked the Lord.” Why did he provoke him? See where it speaks of the angered God. Surely the sinner provoked the Lord to greater anger. “Because of the greatness of his anger, he will not seek [him out]” (Ps. 10:4).

### V

In contrast, holy Job blessed the Lord at all times, and his praise was always in his mouth. When he was rich, he blessed the Lord in his riches, using them for all the good works enumerated in his book: breaking bread for the hungry, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, and so forth. These are the only things that the rich gain from their riches, the only things from which they derive profit.

For they do not gain, nor do they presume upon, the profits that they leave to their children. They do not know who will possess their labors after their death. Scripture also called this vanity: “Nevertheless, every living human being is altogether vanity. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. 38:6–7).

Therefore all the profit made from riches is a treasure of the kingdom of heaven. Hence the Lord gave counsel—not that you should lose your gold, but that you should change the place where you keep it. He did not say to you: “When you give it, you will lose it”; rather: “Though you keep it in a bad place on earth, I will keep it for you in heaven.”

Why are you afraid that you will lose it? You are placing it in heaven, with Christ as its guardian. If the place concerns you, heaven will be the place; if the guardian concerns you, Christ will be the guardian. Why are you afraid that you will lose it?

When Job did such things with these riches, he was indeed at work; God was praised in his works, and he blessed the Lord for what he had received.

For, truly, brothers, riches are not being accused. Do you think that, when you see wicked rich people, riches are therefore wicked? Riches are not wicked; those people are. Riches are gifts of God. Give them to a righteous person and see what good he will do with them.

Is wine bad because someone or other gets drunk on it? Give it to a sober person who uses it well, and see God’s gift. In the same way, give gold to a greedy man: so that he may increase what he has, he seeks to undertake every crime. Give gold to a righteous man, and see how he distributes it, how he shares it, how he helps the needs of people wherever he can.

Therefore riches are not evil; the person who uses riches badly is evil. Job, then, used riches well, just as Abraham used them well.

Certainly, brothers, that poor man covered with sores who lay before the rich man’s gate was so needy that dogs licked his sores. This is how we read it; this is how it is written. And yet where was he carried? Into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22).

Review the Scriptures and see whether Abraham was poor here. You will find that he possessed much gold, much silver, many flocks, many servants, and many estates. Thus the poor man was carried into the bosom of the rich man.

If poverty had earned him merit, Abraham himself would not have gone before him into rest and received him as he came after him. But because Lazarus the poor man possessed what Abraham the rich man possessed—that is, humility, devotion, worship of God, and observance of God—riches did not harm the one, nor poverty the other; rather, the merit of the poor man was his devotion.

Therefore, in that rich man who wrongly exchanged their circumstances, it is not his riches that are reproved, but his attitude. “He was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19).

And he allowed a poor man covered with sores to lie before his gate? In his arrogance he despised him and did not satisfy his need. What do you think the rich man said as he looked upon the beggar with disgust? “Why is this fellow lying here?” But deservedly that tongue, which despised the poor man, desired a drop from his finger.

### VI

Since holy Job, as I said, possessed many riches, he praised God—tested so that he might be proved, proved so that he might be revealed. For this was hidden not only from human beings, but even from the devil himself, who observes more attentively than any human being. It was therefore hidden from him who Job was, but it was not hidden from the Lord. The Prover permitted the tempter—but the Prover did this not for himself, but for us, so that he might reveal to us what we ought to imitate. For he did not wish to show Job to the devil himself, but through the devil to us, so that, once the devil had been conquered, we might have something to imitate.

Therefore, after losing everything—not gradually, but suddenly—he said:

> “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened” (Job 1:21).

What pleased the Just One cannot be wrong. What pleased the Good One cannot be evil. For “God is good to Israel, to those who are upright in heart.” Job was upright in heart; therefore praise was fitting for him.

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened.” He confessed while praising: “Blessed be the name of the Lord.” The Lord gave, and the Lord took away. There was abundance; now there is poverty. My circumstances have changed; he has not changed. I am sometimes rich, sometimes poor. He is always rich, always just, always Father. Blessed be the name of the Lord! Surely the name of the Lord was not blessed in my abundance and will be cursed in my poverty. Far be this from me.

This is what Job said, enriched with inner riches. He had lost his entire house, but his breast was full. He had lost his house and his gold, but he had filled his breast. God himself was present in place of all that he had given. “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.”

See how he understands the supreme power. Perhaps you wish to worship God, Christian, because of the kingdom of heaven, and fear the devil because of earthly goods. Entirely and supremely, all power belongs to him. The devil wished only to cause harm; without permission, he could not. Power therefore belongs to God.

But if the devil were permitted as much as he wished, which Christian would remain? Which worshiper of God would be left on earth? Do you not see his temples falling, his images being shattered, and his priests being converted to God? Do you not think that the devil grieves and is tormented by this? If, then, he also had power equal to his grief, what Church would remain on earth?

Accordingly, when holy Job had lost everything through the devil’s plots, he does not assign the devil any power. When he praises God, he does not say, “The Lord gave; the devil took away,” but he says, “The Lord gave; the Lord took away.” Let the devil claim nothing for himself. When I was rich, that belonged to God; and when I am poor, that belongs to God. And although he was permitted to test me, he was not permitted to suffocate me.

He would have suffocated me not by seizing and crushing my throat, but by constricting my spirit. For if that man, suffering the pressures of tribulation, had uttered a single blasphemous word from his mouth, then, suffocated as the spirit of life was shut out from him, he would have breathed his last. He did not do this either in that sudden poverty or in that final wound.

### VII

For it was not enough for the devil to have taken away everything that Job possessed; he also took away the children whom he possessed, leaving only his wife. He did not take her away, and this certainly because he knew what he was doing. He knew that Adam had been deceived through Eve. He therefore preserved for himself a helper rather than a comforter for her husband.

When he had taken away all those things and left one person through whom he could test Job again, this was still not enough for him: he also asked to take away his bodily health. He was permitted to take that away as well, so that Job, placed even in that wound, might praise God, upright in heart and unchanging in anything, for praise was fitting for him.

The woman who had been left for this purpose approached him and urged—or rather, advised—blasphemy. For she said:

> “How many evils we suffer! Say something against God, and die” (Job 2:9).

At first Eve was deceived by the devil, who invited her, as it were, to life, and she found death. For the devil said:

> “You shall not surely die” (Genesis 3:4).

Thinking that she would possess life, she found death, because she acted against God’s commandment and persuaded her husband to act against God’s commandment.

Now, by contrast: “Say something against God, and die!” Let this suffice for Eve, because she persuaded him to act against God’s commandment. She is still Eve; he is no longer Adam. She was filled by the devil; he was corrected by the example. Job on the dung heap was better than Adam in Paradise.

So that you may know how great a thing it is to have an upright heart, consider how Job overthrew the devil in that poverty and in that wound. He answered the woman and said:

> “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10).

He blessed the Lord at all times; his praise was always in his mouth. For he was upright in heart, and therefore praise was fitting for him.

Be upright in heart. If you wish to be upright in heart, do not be displeased with God in anything. Either you see the reason why he does what he does, and, seeing the reason, you do not reproach him; or, if the reason is hidden from you, know that the one who does it is he who can never be displeasing in anything.

### VIII

Someone brings down his house—I do not know who—and is reproached. If you knew the reason, perhaps you would not reproach the person who was doing it. We are now in this Basilica, and it is cramped and somewhat small. It has pleased the Lord that another should be built, and this one will have to be demolished.

Whoever happens to see those bringing it down, when it begins to be demolished, will say: “Was prayer not offered here? Was the name of God not invoked here? What are these people suffering, that they should demolish it?” The work is displeasing because the plan is hidden.

So God also does something. Why he does it: either you know and praise him, or you do not know and believe—if you are upright in heart. For that person is upright in heart who praises God both in those causes which he knows and in those which he does not know, and does not attribute folly to God.

A human being, the governor of your own household, would be reproached unjustly and foolishly by one ignorant of his reasons and plans—and you dare to reproach the Governor of the whole world and the Creator of heaven and earth because the wind blew and the vines dried up, or because a cloud arose and poured down hail?

Do not reproach him. He knows how to govern and number all his works. You certainly could not create heaven and earth, and yet, if you were permitted, you would say to God: “If only I were governing, I would not do what you do.” For whenever something done by God displeases you, would you not wish to be the governor?

Be ashamed. Consider whose place you would wish to take. A mortal wishing to replace the immortal, a human being wishing to replace God! It is better for you to yield to him than to seek to replace him. Yield to God, because he is God; and although perhaps he has acted against your will, he has not acted against your benefit.

How many things do physicians do against the will of the sick, and yet they do not act against their health. A physician sometimes makes a mistake; God never does. If, then, you entrust yourself to a physician who sometimes errs, you entrust yourself to human judgment—not merely so that he may apply a poultice, which is mild, or a plaster that causes you no pain, but often so that he may cauterize, cut, or remove a limb from you, a limb born with you.

You entrust yourself to him and do not say: “Perhaps he is making a mistake, and I shall have one finger fewer.” You permit him to remove one finger lest the whole body perhaps rot from that place, yet you do not permit God to cut away something from your fruits, if perhaps, in that very moderation, he is giving you discipline?

### IX

Therefore, brothers, be upright in heart—that is, so that God may not be displeasing to you in anything. I do not say that you should not ask him. Ask as much as you can in affliction. He has withheld the rain; he should be entreated. But if it rains, he should also be praised; and if it does not rain, he should be praised, though still entreated.

For we are not saying that you should not ask. Sometimes he is moved and grants the requests of those who ask, and he does not wish to grant to those who do not ask. God is exacting, so that he will not grant unless he is asked. But the small soul will then advance toward the greatness of God if it comes to his aid in tribulation, so that he may give consolation to us who ask and are afflicted.

He wishes to become sweet to us for our good, not for his. Consider what an evil it is that the world should have become sweet to you, while God, who made the world, is bitter. Must you not change? Must you not be corrected, so that you may have an upright heart? Rather, let the world be bitter and let God be sweet.

Therefore, let our Lord God mingle bitterness into this world. Let him surely mingle it!

[Note: [Col. 0915] A copyist’s error for *frui* (“to enjoy”). The following passage—“If he has … he spends money”—appears to have been inserted.]

Here, to enjoy oneself, to overflow, to abound in pleasures, and to forget God is delightful. If someone has somewhat more money, he wishes to squander it on trifles; he does not wish to use it to do something useful or to acquire something heavenly. He wishes to destroy both the money and himself and the others on whom he spends the money.

Do you therefore not wish God to remove what is excessive, lest, because of the rottenness, everything should rot? He knows what he is doing. Let us leave him to it; let us merely present ourselves to be healed, and not give the physician advice.

Turned toward the Lord, etc.

## SERMON XXII  
### On the words of Psalm 51, verse 10: “I have hoped in the mercy of God”

[Note: [Col. 0915] In Codex folio 74 it is entitled: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine the Bishop. He discusses human and divine hope with great distinction.” The Opening shows that it was delivered at the evening Office. I do not know who that bishop was who preferred tranquil charity to restless charity. Possidius notes Augustine’s sermon *On Restless Charity* in the *Indiculum* of his works, chapter 8. It may perhaps be found if investigators of libraries are not content merely to run through catalogues of manuscripts or to inspect only the backs of codices. In the same chapter Possidius also mentions the present sermon, which could be inserted in the edition after Sermon XX.]

### Synopsis

I. How long our hope ought to last.  
II. Human hopes: long, empty, and deceptive.  
III. What our true hope is.

### I

First I shall answer my brother and colleague. This morning I said that charity ought to be restless—not sluggish. But since he wished this, let us obey both him and God through him, and you also; and may he grant obedience in you.

We sang: “I have hoped in the mercy of God” (Psalm 51:10). Let us say a few things about our hope. The words of our sermon will indeed have an ending suited to the occasion; but hope itself, which is the subject of the sermon, ought to endure and not cease with our sermon. Let us speak and cease speaking; it continually cries out to God.

But even hope itself—for what I am saying may perhaps seem difficult, but it will not offend if I show why I say it, and I believe that it will not offend—even hope itself will not be eternal. For when the thing has arrived, there will be no hope. Hope is called hope only so long as the thing is not yet possessed, as the Apostle says:

> “Hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Therefore, if hope that is seen is not hope, because who hopes for what he sees, and if it is called hope because we hope for what we do not see, then, when what we may see has arrived, there will no longer be hope, because there will be the reality.

Nor will it then be a curse to be without hope. But now, for anyone to be without hope is a curse and a reproach. Woe to the one who is without hope now! For it is bad to be without hope, because the person is not yet with the reality. Hope ceases when the reality is possessed.

### II

But what is the reality itself—the reality that will be possessed? What will succeed hope? We now see people hoping for many earthly things, according to the world. No one’s life is without hope, and no one is without hope until he dies.

There is hope in children: that they may grow, be educated, and know something. There is hope in young men: that they may marry wives and beget children. There is hope in parents of children: that they may nourish and educate them and see them grown, the children whom they used to caress when they were little.

To name human life itself as the chief hope—the hope which is, as it were, more natural, more excusable, and more ordinary [Note: [Col. 0916] I read: “To name the hope of human life itself as the chief hope.”]—there are many common hopes that are highly blameworthy; but let us hold to this one, which is civic and natural.

For each person is born for this: to grow, to marry, to beget children, to educate them, and even to be called the father of children. What more does he seek? Yet hope is not finished. He wishes to arrange marriages for his sons, and he still hopes. When he has achieved this as well, he wishes for grandchildren. When he has them, behold, there is already a third generation, and the old man is slow to make room for the children.

He still searches for something to wish for, searches for something to hope for, and appears benevolent. “If only,” he says, “that child would call me grandfather, and I could hear it from his mouth—and then die!” The child grows, calls him grandfather, and he still does not consider himself a grandfather. Surely, if he is a grandfather, if he is old, why does he not recognize that he ought now to depart, so that those who have been born may succeed him?

When he hears from the child’s voice the title of honor, he himself wishes to educate the child. Is there nothing left for him to hope for—a great-grandchild? Thus he dies hoping, hoping for one thing and then another, even after receiving what he had hoped for. Yet by receiving what he hoped for he is not satisfied; he gapes after other things.

Why has what you hoped for arrived? Surely now, so that you may finish—where are you going? The ending is not extended. How many people this hope deceives—this ordinary hope! First, it does not satisfy when it arrives; and for how many does it not arrive at all!

How many hoped for wives but could not marry! How many hoped for someone with whom they might be happy, but married someone by whom they would be tormented! How many desired children but were unable to have them! How many groaned over the children they did have! So it is with everything.

Someone hoped for riches; if he did not obtain them, he was tormented by desire; if he obtained them, he was tortured by fear. No one stops hoping, and no one is satisfied. So many are deceived, yet they do not cease from the hope of this age.

### III

Let our hope at last be not deceptive but satisfying, and let it be something so good that nothing greater can exist. What, then, is the reality for which we hope, which, when it arrives, will cause hope to cease because the reality will succeed it?

What is it? Is it earth? No. Is it something born from the earth, such as gold, silver, a tree, a crop, or water? None of these.

Is it something that flies through the air? The soul recoils from that. Perhaps it is heaven, so beautiful and adorned with lights? What among visible things is more delightful or more beautiful than these? Yet this is not it either.

And what is it? These things delight; these things are beautiful; these things are good. Ask who made them. He is your hope. He is now your hope; afterward he will be your reality. He is the hope of the believer; he will be the reality of the one who sees.

Say to him: “You are my hope.” You rightly say now: “You are my hope.” For you believe; you do not yet see. It is promised to you; you do not yet possess it. As long as you are in the body, you are away from the Lord; you are on the road, not yet in your homeland. He himself, the ruler and founder of your homeland, became the way in order to lead you there.

Therefore say to him now: “You are my hope.” What afterward?

> “My portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 113:6).

What is now your hope will afterward be your portion. Let your hope be in the land of the dying, and it will be your portion in the land of the living.

Turned toward the Lord, etc.

## SERMON XXIII  
### On the words of Psalm 145, verse 1: “I will praise the Lord in my life,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0917] In the codex, folio 74, part 2, it is entitled: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine the Bishop. On the brevity of life and transitory happiness, once again remarkably illustrated by the example of the Rich Man and Lazarus.” It should be placed in the edition after Sermon XXXIII.]

### Synopsis

I. God’s praise is to continue beyond this life.  
II. Nothing in this life lasts long.  
III. Transitory happiness should not deceive the Christian.  
IV. The end of the Rich Man and Lazarus should teach us.

### I

May the Lord grant us the ability to speak to you about the words of this Psalm, which we have just sung. For we said:

> “I will praise the Lord in my life. I will sing to my God as long as I live” (Psalm 145:1).

With these words let us first admonish Your Charity, lest, when you hear or say, “As long as I live, I will sing to my God,” you suppose that, when this life has ended, our praise of God will also end.

Rather, then we shall praise him, when we shall live without end. For if we praise him in the pilgrimage from which we are passing, how shall we praise him in the home from which we shall never depart? As it is said, read, and sung in another Psalm:

> “Blessed are those who dwell in your house. Forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

When you hear “forever and ever,” there is no end: to live the blessed life, where God is seen without doubt, loved without offense, and praised without end. This will entirely be our life: to see, love, and praise God.

If, then, we praise him when we believe, how shall we praise him when we see? How shall the vision be praised if faith is praised in this way? For the Apostle says:

> “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:6–7).

Now, therefore, we live by faith; then, by sight. Now we believe what we do not see; then we shall see what we believed. The one who believes is not put to shame, because what he will see is true.

But our Lord first built faith in us so that, if the reward of faith is granted, it may not be sought prematurely, before faith itself [Note: [Col. 0918] In place of *ubi* (“where”), *ut* (“so that”) should apparently be restored, meaning that the reward of faith ought not to be sought prematurely, before faith itself.].

### II

Someone says: “Why, then, did the Psalm say, ‘I will sing to my God as long as I live,’ and not, ‘I will sing to my God forever’?” For when it says “as long as I live,” it seems to indicate an end—unless it is not understood [Note: [Col. 0918] Apparently it should read: *etsi* (“even if”).].

If you think that “as long as I live” was spoken about this life, examine this life: does it last long? However long you live here, it does not last long. How can something last long if it does not satisfy you?

A child says that someone has lived a long time when he sees an old man; but when he reaches the age that the old man reached, then he sees how short that time was. Indeed, age flies so quickly, and moments run through themselves so rapidly, that we see ourselves as having been children the day before yesterday, young men yesterday, and old men today.

Why, then, do you suppose that “as long as I live” was said of this life? Precisely because he said “as long as,” the true interpretation is that it was not said of this life. Truth would never say “as long as” of this life, in which nothing lasts long.

Could the wise men of this world see this, while Christians cannot? One of the most eloquent men among the wise men of the world said:

> “For what is this ‘long’ at all, in which there is something that is its end?” (Cicero, *Oration for Marcus Marcellus*, 28).

He entirely denied that something could last long if at some time it could reach an end. At some time, certainly—not merely as long as you have lived, even if you have reached extreme old age.

For the life of one human being, especially in this present age, is “a vapor that appears for a little while.” Divine Scripture said this to people who were exultant, exceedingly powerful through pride, and unaware whether they might die immediately. Scripture admonished them in their pride and confidence in things that pass:

> “What is your life? It is a vapor that appears for a little while and afterward will vanish” (James 4:15).

The one who raises himself in boasting trusts in vapor, is lifted up by honor, and perishes with the vapor. Pride must therefore be restrained and trampled down with all the force we can muster. We must understand that we live mortally on this earth and must think about the end where there will be no end.

For if you, whoever you are, have grown old—as I began to say—and exalt yourself greatly, thinking that you have lived a long time, although you will eventually come to an end, even Adam himself, if he were still alive and were to die not now but at the end of the age, would have nothing lasting in which there was an end [Note: [Col. 0918] I think the ill-suited *epiphonema* that follows has entered from the margin.]

This has been said most truly, understood most wisely, and is recognized as true not merely because it is proclaimed, but also by the hearers themselves.

### III

Let us turn our attention to the Psalm that we sang, and discover that he would not say, “I will sing to my God as long as I live,” unless he were speaking of that life in which duration is long.

For if there is nothing lasting in this life precisely because it has an end, we are not called to desire this life when we become Christians. We do not become Christians in order that things may go well for us in this life.

If we suppose that we become Christians so that things may go well for us here according to this temporal life, according to its fleeting, vaporous happiness, we are greatly mistaken. Our feet will falter when we see someone possessing such dignity that he surpasses others among whom he lives, being healthy in body and reaching extreme old age.

The poor Christian sees this person—the poor Christian who is obscure and sighs daily amid labors—and perhaps says to himself: “What does it profit me that I have become a Christian? Am I therefore better than the one who is not? Better than the one who does not believe in Christ? Better than the one who blasphemes my God?”

The Psalm admonishes him:

> “Do not trust in princes” (Psalm 145:3).

What delights you in the flower of grass? “All flesh is grass,” says the Prophet—not merely does he say it, but he cries it aloud. The Lord cried out to him: “Cry out,” he said. And he replied: “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is grass, and all the honor of flesh is like the flower of grass. The grass withers; the flower falls. Is everything therefore lost? Far be it! But the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40:6–8).

What delights you in grass? Behold, the grass has perished. Do you wish not to perish? Hold fast to the word.

So also in this Psalm. Perhaps the poor Christian was looking at the flower of grass in some rich and powerful pagan, and was perhaps choosing to have him as a patron rather than God. The Psalm addresses him:

> “Do not trust in princes, or in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation” (Psalm 145:3).

He immediately replies: “Does he mean this man, who has salvation? Behold, he is healthy. Today I see him vigorous. I am constantly sick and miserable.”

Why do you look at those things that please you and delight you? There is no salvation in them.

> “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth” (Psalm 145:4).

Behold the whole of his salvation: a vapor that appears for a little while. “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth.”

Let some years pass. Let the river shift its course, as usually happens. As it runs through various places, let it uncover the bones of the rich man among the tombs of the dead; distinguish the bones of the rich man from the bones of the poor.

When his spirit goes forth, he returns to his earth. The Psalm says nothing at all about his spirit, most appropriately, because while he lived he thought nothing spiritually. He will return to his earth according to the flesh, of course, according to the body—the place where he was powerful, where he was exalted, where he deceived you, through whose fleshly happiness he deluded you.

> “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth. On that day all their thoughts will perish” (ibid. 4).

Those thoughts were earthly:

> “Behold, I do this; behold, I complete that; behold, I reach this. Behold, I buy that; behold, I acquire that; behold, I attain such and such an honor.”

“On that day all his thoughts will perish.”

But if, because the word of God remains forever, you hold fast to the word so that it may give you eternal life, not only will your thought not perish then—it will then truly come into being. When his thought perishes, yours will come.

For he was thinking about temporal and earthly things: adding wealth to wealth, increasing his financial resources, striving after honors, swelling with power. Since he was thinking such things, “on that day all his thoughts will perish.”

But if you were thinking, because you had become a Christian, not about temporal happiness but about eternal rest, then, when your body returns to its earth, your soul will find its own rest.

### IV

Attend to the Gospel, and observe and examine the thoughts of two men. There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day (Luke 16:19). Every day: grass, and the flower of grass.

Do not let the happiness of the one who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day deceive you. He was proud; he was impious; he thought vain things and desired vain things. When he died, on that day all his thoughts perished.

But there was a poor man before his gate, named Lazarus. He kept silent about the name of the rich man and spoke the name of the poor man. God kept silent about the name of the one whose name was proclaimed, and spoke the name of the one whose name was ignored.

Do not be surprised. God recited what he found written in his book. For it was said of the impious:

> “They will not be written in your book” (Psalm 68:29).

Likewise, when the Apostles were rejoicing because the demons had been subjected to them in the Lord’s name—and although this was a great matter and an outstanding power, so that they would not exalt themselves like human beings and boast about it—he said:

> “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

God, who inhabits heaven, kept silent about the rich man’s name because he did not find it written in heaven. Yet he spoke the poor man’s name because he found it written there—or rather, because he had ordered it to be written there.

But look at that poor man. We have spoken about the thoughts of the impious rich man, the distinguished man who wore purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day: when he died, all his thoughts perished.

The poor man, however, Lazarus, was before the rich man’s gate, full of sores. He longed to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything. But dogs also came and licked his sores (Luke 16:21).

There I want to see you, Christian. For the ends of these two men are related. God is indeed powerful enough in this life to give health, remove poverty, and grant sufficiency to a Christian. Yet if even this were not so, which would you choose: to be poor like that man, or to be rich like the other?

Do not be deceived. Hear the end, and observe the evil choice.

Without doubt, because that poor man was devout, although placed amid temporal hardships, he thought about the life that would one day end and about attaining eternal rest. Both died, but the thoughts of that poor man did not perish on that day.

It happened that the needy man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. On that day all his thoughts were healed.
