Since *Lazarus* is interpreted in Latin as “Helped” [Note: [Col. 0920] Jerome likewise gives this interpretation in *Interpretation of Hebrew Names*. Evidently, “helped by God,” from [lacuna] and [lacuna], the same as [lacuna] or [lacuna].], the Psalm rightly admonished us:

> “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob” (Psalm 145:5).

When his spirit goes forth and his flesh returns to its earth, his thoughts will not perish, because his hope is in the Lord his God.

This is learned in the school of Christ the teacher; this is hoped for by the soul of the faithful hearer; this is the truest reward of the Savior.

## SERMON XXIV  
### On the words of the Gospel, Luke 16:19–31: “There was a certain rich man,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0921] In the codex, folio 80, it is entitled: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine the Bishop, on the Rich Man and Lazarus. The truth of the Christian religion is demonstrated from the promises of God already fulfilled and those still to be fulfilled, with an exhortation to patience.” Possidius mentions this notable sermon in the *Indiculum* of Augustine’s works, chapter 8. It should be placed in the edition after Sermon CXIII.]

[Col. 0921]

### Synopsis

I. The Jews still do not believe the prophetic oracles concerning Christ and his Church.  
II. The unbelief of the Jews is refuted by the example of the rich feaster.  
III. The rich feaster is a salutary example for us.  
IV. Having been sufficiently warned about the future, we have no excuse.  
V. Our faith must be confirmed by what has already been fulfilled and by what has been promised by God.  
VI. God’s promises among the Jewish people, beginning with Abraham, whose faith is commended.  
VII. God’s faithfulness in fulfilling his promises, and the madness of idolaters.  
VIII. God seeks his image in the soul, just as Caesar seeks his image on a coin.  
IX. How many of God’s promises have already been fulfilled.  
X. Abraham’s faith as an example for us.  
XI. Two comparisons concerning the endurance of adversity.  
XII. We must make use of God’s patience and imitate it.  
XIII. In adversity we must entrust ourselves to God without complaint.  
XIV. An exhortation to patience.

### I

The faith of Christians, which is mocked by the impious and unbelieving, is this: we say that there is another life after this life, that there is a resurrection of the dead, and that after the age has run its course there will be a judgment at the end.

When this was not believed in human affairs, although it was proclaimed and announced by the Prophets, the servants of God, and by the Law given through Moses, and although it still seemed incredible to human beings, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ came to persuade humanity of this.

Although he is the Son of God, born invisibly and ineffably from the Father, coeternal with the Father, equal to the Father, and one God with the Father; although he is the Word of the Father through whom all things were made, and the Counsel of the Father by which all things are governed; he laid aside his great magnitude, incomprehensible majesty, and power—which could not be known by human beings—and came down to earth [Note: [Col. 0921] I think this should be corrected to: “for a time.”] by taking flesh and appearing to human eyes.

Since God—that is, divinity itself—was not seen in Christ, his flesh was despised. Yet he demonstrated his inner divinity by miracles [Note: [Col. 0921] In the parchment manuscripts: *approbat* (“demonstrates”).]. Although he appeared as one who could be scorned by human eyes, he did such great things that in those very works he was seen to be the Son of God.

When he was doing great things, giving beneficial commands, correcting and chastising vices, teaching virtues, and even performing healings of bodies in order to heal the minds of unbelievers, the enraged people among whom he had been born and raised—and among whom he had done all these things—killed him.

But he who had come to be born had certainly also come to die. Nor did he wish the death of his flesh, which he had accepted in order to demonstrate the resurrection by example, to be without fruit. Rather, he permitted it to fall into the hands of the impious, so that, although they did not wish to do what he commanded, he would suffer what he willed.

It happened. Christ was killed and buried; he rose again, as we know, as the Gospel bears witness, and as the Gospel is now proclaimed throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0922] Evidently “the Gospel.” Perhaps it should read: “is now being proclaimed.”]. Yet you see that the Jews still refuse to believe in Christ, even after he rose from the dead and was glorified in the sight of his disciples and ascended into heaven, while the proclamations of the Prophets are already being fulfilled throughout the whole world.

For all the Prophets who foretold that Christ would be born, die, rise again, and ascend into heaven also foretold that his Church would exist among all nations. If the Jews did not see Christ rising and going into heaven, they could at least see the Church spread throughout the whole world. When this was fulfilled, the sayings foretold by the Prophets would certainly also be fulfilled.

### II

What we have just heard from the Gospel is happening among them. They do not hear Christ, who rose from the dead, because they did not hear Christ while he was present on earth.

Abraham said this to the rich man who was being tormented in hell and wanted someone to be sent up to the living, so that he might announce to his brothers what was happening in hell. Before they came to those places of torment, he wanted them to live well and repent of their sins, so that they might deserve to go instead into Abraham’s bosom, and not to those torments where the rich man had arrived.

Although that rich man had late become merciful—he who had despised the poor man lying before his gate and had perhaps therefore been proud toward him—his tongue itself was burning, and there he desired a drop of water.

Since he had not done among the living what he ought to have done so that he would not come there, he belatedly began to be merciful on behalf of others. But what does Abraham say?

> “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded if someone rises from the dead” (Luke 16:31).

It is entirely true, brothers. The Jews today are not persuaded to believe in him who rose from the dead because they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets [Note: [Col. 0922] Perhaps it should read: “because they listen.”]. For if they wished to listen to them, they would find there that what has now been fulfilled was foretold, yet they still refuse to believe.

What we have said about the Jews, let us apply to ourselves, lest, while we look at others, we fall into the same impiety. Beloved, the Gospel is not read to the Jews; Moses and the Prophets are read to them, and they do not wish to listen. If they wished to listen, they would believe in Christ, because Moses and the Prophets foretold that Christ would come.

Therefore, let us not be like them when the Gospel is read to us, as they are when the Prophets are read to them. Among them, as I said, the Gospel is not recited; among us it is recited.

### III

Behold, you have just heard from the Gospel about two lives: one present, the other future. We possess the present; we believe in the future. We are in the present and have not yet reached the future. While we are in the present, let us acquire merit for the future; for we are not yet dead. Is the Gospel read out in the underworld? Certainly, if it were read there, the Rich Man would hear it in vain, because repentance could no longer be fruitful. It is read to us and heard by us here [Col. 0923], while we are living and can be corrected, so that we may not come to those torments.

Do we believe what is read, or do we not believe it? Far be it from us to suppose this about Your Charity—that you do not believe! For you are Christians, and you would in no way be Christians if you did not believe the Gospel of God. Since, therefore, you are Christians, it is clear that you believe the Gospel. We heard it; it has just been read aloud.

The Rich Man was certainly proud, certainly exalting himself in his wealth. He “was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day” (Luke 16:19). At his gate, however, there lay a certain poor man covered with sores, named Lazarus; even the dogs licked his sores, and he desired “to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table” (ibid. 21), but he could not.

Behold the Rich Man’s crime: the poor man desired to be filled with the crumbs, and could not, although the Rich Man ought to have shared his humanity with him. If that Rich Man had pitied the Poor Man lying at his gate and had wished to be merciful from those riches, he too would have gone where the Poor Man went. For it was not poverty that led Lazarus to rest rather than humility; nor did riches keep the Rich Man from that great rest, but pride and unbelief.

Now, brothers, so that you may know that this Rich Man was unbelieving while among the living, let us prove it from his own words, which he spoke in the underworld. Pay attention. He wanted someone to go from the dead and announce to his brothers what was happening in the underworld. When this was not granted him, Abraham said: “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.” But he replied: “No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from here, from the underworld, they will be persuaded.” He showed that he himself, while he was among the blessed, did not believe Moses and the Prophets, but desired that someone rise for him from the dead.

Pay attention now to people of this sort, and see where we are warned by the example of this Rich Man—if you have faith. How many there are who say now: “Let us live well while we are alive! Let us eat and drink and enjoy these pleasures! What is it that they tell us will happen afterward? Who has come back here from there? Who has risen from there and come here?”

Such things are said. That is what the Rich Man said, and what he did not believe while alive he learned by experience after death. It would have been better for him to be corrected fruitfully while alive than to be tormented fruitlessly after death!

### IV

Now, then, let us change those very words, if perhaps there is anyone among us who is accustomed to say such things. God does not now show us what he commands us to believe. He does not show it for this reason: so that faith may have its reward. For if he were to show you what merit you have because you believe, it would no longer be believing but seeing. God does not show it to you precisely so that you may believe. He commands you to believe; he reserves for you what you are to see.

But if you do not believe when he commands faith, he does not reserve his appearance for you; rather, what is reserved for you is that in which the Rich Man was tormented in the underworld.

And when our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ comes—he is now proclaimed as having come in such a way that he is also hoped to come—he will come with recompense for the faithful and the unfaithful: to give rewards to the faithful and to send the unfaithful into eternal fire.

He said in the Gospel how he will judge at the end: he will place some at his right hand and others at his left, and he will separate all the nations, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. The righteous will be at his right hand, the ungodly at his left. To the righteous he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” But to the ungodly and unbelieving: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34–41)!

What more could the Judge have done for your benefit than to tell you his definitive sentence, so that you might avoid falling under it?

Brothers, everyone who threatens does not wish to strike. For if he were to overwhelm someone at once [Note: That is, bury him immediately; a term familiar to Africans, used by St Cyprian in Epistle 57 and by Pontius the Deacon in his Life of Cyprian, as well as more slowly by others.], he would strike. Whoever says, “Take care,” does not wish to find someone to strike. People bring blows upon themselves; people procure punishments for themselves when they refuse to believe God, who says for so long: “Take care.”

Indeed, the punishment of one who errs—the affliction or scourging that exists here—is perhaps corrective or testing. Someone is corrected for his sins so that, if left uncorrected, he may not fall into greater punishments; or each person’s faith is tested, to see with what endurance or patience he remains under the scourge of his father, not murmuring against the father who chastises him, and rejoicing in the one who caresses him, but rejoicing in the one who caresses him in such a way that he gives thanks also to the one who chastises him, because “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

How much the Martyrs suffered, how much they endured! What chains, what filth, what prisons, what tortures, what flames, what beasts, what kinds of death! They trod everything underfoot. They saw something with the spirit, so that they did not care about what they saw with the body. The eye of faith was in them; their eye was stretched toward the future; they despised present things. But the person whose eye concerning the future has been extinguished is terrified by present things and does not reach the future.

### V

There is, then, a faith that is being built in us. Now, whoever does not wish to believe that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, that he suffered, and that he was crucified, should believe the Jews, because he existed and was killed; let him believe the Gospel, because he was born of a Virgin and rose again. There is indeed a basis for belief.

Even the hostile Jews do not dare to say: “Christ did not exist among our people,” or: “This man—whoever he may be, whom the Christians worship—did not exist.” “He did exist,” they say, “and our ancestors killed him, and he died as a man.”

If we find that the things which followed his death were foretold [Note: I think: “foretold.”] by the Prophets—that the whole world was going to run in his name [Note: Perhaps: “run into his name,” or “believe in his name,” instead of “run.”], that all nations and all the countries of the nations were going to worship him, and that all kings were going to be placed under his yoke—and if we see that after Christ’s death the things foretold before Christ’s birth have been fulfilled, how do we deceive ourselves if we refuse to believe the rest, when we see many things fulfilled among us?

For we ourselves, brothers—not merely we who are Christians here, but the whole world—are now Christians. A few years ago we were not so. It is astonishing how it has happened that what had not existed for so many ages now exists. We read this in the Prophets. We should not think that it happened by chance; we find that it was foretold.

By this our faith is increased, by this it is built up, by this it is strengthened. No one should say: “It happened suddenly.” How so? Behold, this is something that had never existed on earth. Sometimes in those Scriptures God was regarded as a debtor [Note: Either “in those” is superfluous, or “the things foretold” or “the promises” are understood]; yet in his own time he was going to repay the debt.

But from whom was God in debt? Had he received a loan from someone, when he gives everything besides to everyone? Who existed for him to whom he could give? Human beings themselves, to whom something might be given, did not yet exist.

Can someone say: “God granted these good things because of my merits”? Suppose he granted these good things because of your merits. In order that you might exist, to whom did he grant them? Since you did not exist, what did he give you? He gave you existence freely. You had not earned that before you existed. Believe him, because he has also deigned freely to give you the rest.

We therefore possess the grace of God, and the whole world somehow held God as a debtor. Rather, it did not hold him, because it did not know the bond that he had made. He made himself a debtor by promising, not by receiving a loan. For someone is called a debtor in two ways: “Repay what you received,” or “repay what you promised.” Since what God promised cannot be called “repay,” for he received nothing from humanity, having given everything to humanity, it remains that he is a debtor only because he deigned to promise.

### VI

This promise existed in the Scriptures, and these Scriptures were among the one Jewish people, from whose flesh God chose to be born—the flesh of his faithful servant, who believed in him.

And how was that people born? From the old Abraham and the barren Sarah. That Isaac should be conceived and born—from whom the Jewish people came—was a miracle (Genesis 17 and 21). The old man expected nothing from his own limbs; he did not dare hope for anything from his wife’s barrenness. God offered him what he did not at all reckon on, and he believed the God who offered it, although he had not dared to hope for it from God.

When he had believed, and a son had been born to him—the son concerning whom he had believed that innumerable offspring would arise—God asked him to offer that very son as a sacrifice (ibid. 22). Abraham possessed such great faith that he did not hesitate to sacrifice his only son, concerning whom he had received the promise.

Did he hesitate and say to God: “Lord, you granted me a son in my old age as a great gift, in response to great prayers, for great joy; a son was born to me unexpectedly. Are you demanding that I kill him? Would it not have been better not to give him than to take away what was given?” He did not say this. Rather, he believed that whatever he saw God willing was beneficial.

This is faith, brothers. Certainly, that Poor Man was carried into Abraham’s bosom, and that Rich Man went to the torments of the underworld.

So that you may know that riches are not at fault, Abraham was rich, and Lazarus rested in his bosom. Abraham was rich on earth, as Scripture teaches us. He possessed much gold, silver, livestock, and household servants. He was rich, but he was not proud.

To show you that in the rich man only pride was tormented, and only vices were tormented: those things had deserved punishment, not God’s substance. For God’s substance is good for whoever receives it [Note: I read: “is given”]. But for one who uses it well, a reward is acquired; for one who uses it badly, punishment is repaid.

Consider, however, how Abraham possessed riches. Did he preserve them for his sons? If he offered his very son at God’s command, how did he despise riches?

### VII

This Scripture, then, in which God had made himself a debtor by promising, lay hidden among the Jews. Our Lord Jesus Christ came, born according to that same Scripture, because according to that Scripture he was given [Note: Perhaps it should read: “promised.”]. According to that Scripture he suffered, because in it he had been foretold as one who would suffer. According to that Scripture he rose again, because in it he had been foretold as one who would rise. According to that Scripture he ascended into heaven, because in it he had been foretold as one who would ascend.

After he had ascended, unknown to the Jews, he began to send his Apostles to the nations, and, in a certain sense, to awaken those who were sleeping and say: “Rise up; receive the debt that was promised to you long ago!”

Who is it who awakens his creditor and offers him what he owes? The nations did not rise because they considered God their debtor. They were called; they began to attend to Scripture; and there they discovered that what they were receiving had long ago been promised to them.

They received the promised and manifested Christ; they received the grace of God, the promised and manifested Holy Spirit; they received the Church itself, dispersed throughout all nations, promised and manifested.

God had promised that the idols worshiped by the nations would be overthrown. This is read in the Scriptures; there you find it (Isaiah 2:18; Ezekiel 6:6; and Micah 1:7). You see how in our own times God did what he had promised many thousands of years before.

Human beings had turned away from the one by whom they had been made toward what they themselves had made. Since the one who makes is always better than what he makes, God is better not only than the human being whom he made, but than all Angels, Powers, Authorities, Thrones, and Dominions, because he himself created all things (Ephesians 1:21; Colossians 1:16). Thus whatever a human being makes is inferior to the human being himself.

Human beings had been led into such great madness that they worshiped the idol which they ought to have condemned. If they worshiped the craftsman who made the idol, it is clear, brothers, that the craftsman is better than the idol he made. And although people would be detestable if they worshiped the craftsman, they worship the very idol made by the craftsman. They would be detestable for worshiping the craftsman, but they would be better than those who worship the idol.

If, then, those who are better are condemned, how am I to mourn for those who are worse? But if I said that the worshiper of the craftsman ought to be condemned, what must be said of the one who abandons the craftsman and worships the idol—who, having abandoned the better, turned to the inferior? How is he to be condemned?

Whom did he abandon first as the better? God, by whom he himself was made. He seeks the image of God. He has it within himself. The craftsman could not make an image of God, but God could make an image for himself. He did not make something else for you; he made you yourself in his image.

By worshiping the image of a human being, which the craftsman made, you destroy the image of God that God impressed upon you. Therefore, when he calls you to return, he wishes to restore to you that image which, by rubbing it away, as it were, through earthly desire, you yourself have lost and worn out [Note: So Tertullian, Augustine’s compatriot, has *obsoletant* in *Apologeticus* 5 and *obsoletassent* in *Scorpiace* 6.].

### VIII

This is why, brothers, God seeks his image from us. He recalls those Jews when they offered him a coin. At first they wanted to test him, saying: “Lord, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” (Matthew 22:17). If he said, “It is lawful,” they would accuse him of wishing Israel to be under a curse, since he wanted it to pay tribute and be subjected to the king. But if he said, “It is not lawful to pay tribute,” they would accuse him of acting against Caesar and authorizing them not to pay the tribute they owed, since they were subject to him.

He saw those who were testing him, as truth sees falsehood, and briefly convicted the lie from the mouths of the liars. He did not pronounce judgment against them from his own mouth; rather, he made them pronounce judgment against themselves, because it is written: “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned” (ibid. 12:37).

“Why are you testing me?” he said. “Hypocrites, show me a coin.” They showed him one. He said: “Whose image and inscription does it have?” They answered: “Caesar’s.” And he said: “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (ibid. 22:18–21).

Just as Caesar seeks his image on your coin, so God seeks his image in your soul. “Render to Caesar,” he says, “the things that are Caesar’s.” What does Caesar seek from you? His image. What does God seek from you? His image. But Caesar’s image is on the coin; God’s image is in you.

If you lose a coin, you mourn because you have lost Caesar’s image. When you worship an idol, do you not mourn because you do injury to God’s image in yourself?

### IX

Hold fast, then, brothers, to the promise of our Lord God, and now count from the number of his promises how much he has repaid.

Christ had not yet been born; he was promised in Scripture. God repaid this: he was born. He had not yet suffered or risen again. God repaid this also: he suffered, was crucified, and rose again. His Passion is our reward; his blood is our redemption.

He ascended into heaven, as he had promised. He repaid this also. He sent the Gospel throughout all the lands. For this reason he wished there to be four Gospels, so that by the number four the whole world might be signified: from east and west, from north and south.

For this reason he wished to have twelve Disciples, so that they might appear to be distributed, as it were, three by four, because the world was called in the Trinity—in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

He repaid this. He sent the Gospel, as he had foretold:

“How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize, of those who announce peace, of those who evangelize good things!” (Romans 10:15).

As he foretold:

“There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:4–5).

As he said, so he sent it. The Gospel is being written throughout all the lands.

The Church also first suffered persecution. He repaid this, because he had promised Martyrs as well. Read the bond: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15). He repaid the Martyrs also, because he had promised them.

What remained to be repaid afterward? “All the kings of the earth shall worship in his presence” (ibid. 71:11). The kings believed—the very kings who had first made Martyrs by persecuting them. We therefore see that kings have now come to believe as well.

He also repaid what he had promised: that, at the command of kings, the idols for which Christians had previously been killed at the command of kings would be broken. He also removed the idols, because he had promised: “There shall be no regard for the idols of the nations” (Wisdom 14:1).

Since he has repaid so much, brothers, why do we not believe him? Is God a debtor of insufficient means? Even if he had not yet repaid us anything at all, we would have held him to be a debtor of sufficient means, since he made heaven and earth. He would not become poor and lack the means to repay; nor does he deceive, since he is Truth; nor is God’s power so limited that he could be superseded and have no time in which to repay.

### X

It is right, brothers, to believe God before he repays anything, because he cannot lie or deceive. He is God.

Our fathers believed him in this way. Abraham believed him in this way. Behold a faith truly worthy of praise and proclamation! He had received nothing from him, yet he believed the one who promised. We do not yet believe, although we have already received so much.

Could Abraham have said to him: “I will believe because you promised this to me and repaid it”? He believed at the first command; he had received nothing else of the sort.

“Go out from your land,” he was told, “and from your kindred, and go to the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). He believed immediately. God did not give him that land itself, but reserved it for his offspring; and what did he promise his offspring?

“In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

His offspring is Christ: from Abraham came Isaac, from Isaac Jacob, from Jacob the twelve, from the twelve the Jewish people, from the Jewish people the Virgin Mary, and from the Virgin Mary our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ became the offspring of Abraham, and we find that what was promised to Abraham has been fulfilled in us: “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed.”

He believed this before he had seen anything. He believed, and did not see what was promised. We, however, see what was promised to him. And everything that was promised to him was still future.

What has God not yet repaid? He foretold that there would be labors in this world, and that his saints and faithful would be in labors and would bring forth fruit with endurance (Luke 8:15). He foretold it, and we see it. We are worn down by those very labors.

What labors that were foretold have not yet appeared? Do not think, brothers, that what you see now—the wearing down of human affairs—is not written in God’s Scripture. Everything is written, and endurance was enjoined upon Christians; the future good things are all the more to be believed because the evils foretold as coming have come. If they had not come, they would have taken away our faith even in the good things; but the evils came first so that we might believe in the future good things.

### XI

Now the world is like a winepress under pressure. But if you are *amurca* [Note: Greek ἀμόργη (*amorgē*), from ἀμεργώ (*amergō*), “I press out”: the first dregs of olives beginning to be pressed. See Pliny, Book 15, chapter 18. Our author mentions it elsewhere as well.], you go through the sewers; if you are oil, you remain in the *gemellarium* [Note: In Columella, *Gemellar.* Book 12, chapter 50. Our author says in Psalm 136, volume 4, column 1518: “May you not see oil in the *Gemellaria*.” Perhaps *Gemellarium* or *Gemellaria* is more correct; possibly a double vessel named from *gemelli*, “twins.”].

For there must be pressure. Consider the *amurca*; consider the oil. Pressure sometimes occurs in the world—for example, famine, war, want, poverty, mortality, robbery, greed, the oppression of the poor, and the hardships of cities. These things exist. We see them. They were foretold as future, and we see that they exist.

We find people murmuring amid these pressures and saying: “Behold how many evils there are in Christian times! How many good things abounded before the Christian era! Such evils did not exist then.”

From pressure the *amurca* emerges; it runs through the sewers. Its mouth is black for that reason: it blasphemes. It does not shine. Oil gleams.

But you find another person in the very same pressure and from the very same crushing that has crushed him. Is it not the same crushing that has crushed him? You have heard the voice of the *amurca*; hear the voice of the oil:

“Thanks be to God! Blessed be your name! All these evils by which you crush us were foretold. We are secure, because good things will come. When both we and the wicked are corrected together, your will is done. We know you as a Father who promises; we know you as a Father who chastises. Instruct us, and restore the inheritance that you promised your saints at the end. We bless your holy name, because you have never been a liar. Everything, just as you foretold, you have manifested.”

In these praises flowing from the very pressure, the oil runs into the *gemellarium*.

Yet because this whole world is a winepress, another comparison is also drawn from it [Note: The passage is corrupt. Perhaps read: “Yet, although it is a winepress—from it another comparison is also drawn.” A similar interpolation seems to be present in what follows.].

Just as gold and silver are tested in a furnace, so trial through tribulation tests the righteous; and an illustration is drawn from the goldsmith’s furnace.

In a narrow pot there are three things: fire, gold, and straw. There you see an image of the whole world. There is straw, there is gold, and there is fire. The straw is burned, the fire blazes, and the gold is tested.

So in this whole world there are righteous people, ungodly people, and tribulation. The world is like a goldsmith’s furnace; the righteous are like gold, the ungodly like straw, and tribulation like fire.

Would the gold be purified if the straw were not burned? What happens is that the ungodly are reduced to ashes. When they blaspheme and murmur against God, they become ashes.

There the righteous, purified like gold, who bear all the troubles of the world with endurance and praise God in their tribulations, are stored in God’s treasuries. For God has treasuries into which he may place purified gold; he also has filthy places into which he may send the straw’s ashes.

From this world he demands everything. You must see what you are. For the fire must come. If it finds you to be gold, it will remove your impurities; if it finds you to be straw, it will burn you and reduce you to ashes.

Choose what you are. For you cannot say: “I will be without fire.” You are already in the goldsmith’s furnace, and the fire must come to it; indeed, you must be there, because you cannot be without fire.

### XII

Why, then, do we not believe, brothers, both that the end of the world will come and that the day of judgment will come, so that there each of us may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil?

When we see so many things promised, manifested, and given, why do we not choose, while we are living, that in which we may live forever?

Suppose we have been negligent; today let us become diligent. We must not always be negligent [Note: “Not always” here means “never.”]. You do not know what tomorrow will be. God’s patience urges us to correct both ourselves and our life, if it has been evil, and, while there is time, to choose better things.

Do you think that God sleeps and does not see those who do evil? Perhaps he is teaching us patience, and first displays patience himself.

But he may find that someone has perhaps made progress and no longer does what he used to do—that is, evil. Such a person bears patiently with some malicious individual, wishes God to remove him, and murmurs against God because he keeps that person—his strong enemy, who does evil—and does not remove him.

He has forgotten that God dealt patiently with him, and that if God had wished to act severely earlier, there would be no one to speak. You demand God’s severity? Because you have crossed over, let another cross over too. You have not, merely because you have crossed, cut off God’s bridge of mercy. There is still someone to cross.

He made you good when you were evil; he also wishes another to become good from evil, just as you became good from evil. Thus all come in their appointed order. Some refuse to come; others do come.

To such people the Apostle says: “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works” (Romans 2:5).

Moreover, if an evil person wishes to persist in evil, he is not your companion but will be your tester. For if he is evil and you are good, by enduring evil you are proved good. You will receive the crown of your testing; he will have punishment for his persistence in evil.

Let us patiently await what God is doing—his good patience, his fatherly discipline. He is a father; he is kind; he is merciful. If he were to let us drift away, that would be when he would be angry with us.

### XIII

Pay attention, brothers, and see these amphitheaters that are now collapsing. Luxury built them. Do you think piety built them? Nothing built them except the luxury of ungodly people.

Do you not want what luxury built eventually to fall, and what piety builds to rise? When these things were being built, God permitted it so that people might at some point recognize the evils they were committing. But because they refused to recognize them, the Lord Jesus Christ came, began to proclaim their evils to them, began to overturn what they held in such great esteem, and they say: “These are evil times, the Christian times.”

Why? Because the place where you were dying is being overturned for you.

“But,” they say, “all good things abounded when these things were being built.” Certainly—so that good things might come from them. If, then, you know that God once gave you abundance, and that you used it badly and for your destruction, see that this abundance made you overflow and lose your soul.

Did not a strict father come and begin to say: “This boy is undisciplined. I entrusted this or that to him. How did he lose this, and that as well?”

If we do not sow seed in the earth unless it is good, lest the seed perish, how do you wish God to give his abundance to us, undisciplined and negligent in our lives, so that we may use it badly? And you do not want God to cut off the overflow of human beings?

My brothers, he is a physician, and he knows how to cut off a gangrenous limb, lest other parts become gangrenous from it as well. “One finger,” he says, “is cut off from it, because it is better for one finger to be missing than for the whole body to become gangrenous.”

If a human physician does this through his skill, if the art of medicine removes some bodily part so that everything may not become gangrenous, why should God not cut away whatever he knows to be corrupt in human beings, so that they may attain salvation?

### XIV

Therefore, brothers, do not grow weary of God when he chastises [Note: *taediare* occurs in Vegetius, Lampridius, Tertullian, and others.], lest he abandon you and you perish eternally. Rather, let us ask him to moderate the very scourges and temper them so that we do not fail under them; and let us ask him to correct us with salvation, to measure out his chastisement, and afterward to restore what he promised his saints.

See what Scripture says:

“The sinner has provoked the Lord. According to the greatness of his anger he will not inquire” (Psalm 10:4).

What does “according to the greatness of his anger he will not inquire” mean? Because he is very angry, he will not inquire—that is, he will let them perish.

If, then, he is greatly angry when he does not inquire, he is also greatly merciful when he disciplines. He disciplines when he chastises, when he fastens our heart to himself.

Let us therefore hold fast to his saving hand and not flee from his scourge. This is what he teaches us; this is what he admonishes; in this he builds us up.

His own Son, who came for this purpose, to console us—what good did he endure here? Tell me. Certainly he is the Son of God; he is the Word of God, through whom all things were made. What good did he endure here?

Is he not the one who, when he was casting out demons, heard such insults that they said to him: “You have a demon” (John 7:20)? The Jews said to the Son of God, who was casting out demons: “You have a demon.” The demons who confessed the Son of God were already better than those men (Luke 4:41). For the demons confessed him, but those men did not.

Yet his power, greatness, and patience were so great that he endured everything. He was scourged; he heard insults; he received blows; he was spat upon in the face; he was crowned with thorns; he was mocked and derided; finally he was hung upon wood and killed; afterward he was buried.

The Son of God endured so much here. If the Master did, how much more the disciple! If the one who created us did, how much more we, his creatures! He left us patience in order to give us an example.

Why do we fail in that very patience, as though we had lost our head, which went before us into heaven? For this reason our head went before us into heaven, as though saying: “Behold the way. Come through hardships, through patience. This is the road I have handed over to you.”

But where does the road lead, on which you see me ascending? Into heaven. Whoever does not wish to travel by this road does not wish to reach that place. Whoever wishes to come to me must come by the road I have shown.

You cannot arrive except by the road of hardships, sorrows, tribulations, and distress. In this way you will reach the rest that will not be taken from you.

But if you desire the rest that lasts only for a time and wish to withdraw from Christ’s road, consider the torments of that Rich Man who was tormented in the underworld. He too desired present rest and found eternal punishments.

Dearest brothers, choose rather the harder things, which will have rest without end, forever.

Having turned toward the Lord, etc.

## SERMON XXV

On the words of the Gospel, Matthew 12:41–50: “Behold, something greater than Jonah is here,” etc. [Note: In the manuscript, folio 89, it is entitled: “Wednesday of the first week of Lent. A sermon of Saint Augustine against the Manichaeans.” The latter part argues subtly against them. The earlier parts concern the blindness of the Jews, the relapse of sinners, and the duties of parents and children. This treatise should be inserted after Sermon 72.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. The Jews are worse than the Ninevites and the Queen of Sheba.  
II. How the last state of a person liberated from an unclean spirit becomes worse than the first.  
III. Christ teaches parents not to hinder their children in good works.  
IV. Since Christ honored both sexes by his birth, the duty of children is taught.  
V. The Manichaeans’ assertion that Christ had no mother is refuted.  
VI. It is concluded against the Manichaeans that Christ had a mother.  
VII. The excellence of the Virgin Mary.  
VIII. How a Christian can become the mother of Christ.

### I

Dearest brothers, if we wished to treat everything contained in what was read from the holy Gospel, scarcely would there be enough time for each individual point—how much less enough for all of them.

The Savior himself showed that the prophet Jonah, who, after being thrown into the sea, was received into the belly of a sea creature and brought out alive on the third day, prefigured the Savior who suffered and rose again on the third day.

The Jewish people were accused in comparison with the Ninevites, because the Ninevites, to whom the prophet Jonah was sent to rebuke them [Note: The manuscripts incorrectly read: “but to rebuke.”], appeased God’s anger by doing penance and deserved mercy.

“And behold,” he says, “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41), wishing the Lord Christ himself to be understood. They heard a servant and corrected their ways; these people heard the Lord and not only failed to correct themselves but even killed him.

“The Queen of the South,” he says, “will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it. For she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (ibid. 42).

It was not a great thing for Christ to be greater than Jonah or greater than Solomon. He was the Lord; they were servants. Yet what kind of people are those who despised the Lord present among them, when foreigners listened to his servants?

## II

Then follows:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through arid places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says: ‘I will return to my house [Col. 0933], from which I came out.’ And when it comes, it finds it vacant, swept clean, and adorned. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering in, they dwell there. And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. So will it be also for this most wicked generation” (Matt. 12:43–45).

If this is to be understood and explained consistently, the discussion would occupy a great deal of time. Nevertheless, I shall touch on it briefly, as far as the Lord grants, so that I may not send you away ignorant of the meaning of this matter.

When the remission of sins takes place in the Sacraments, the house is cleansed; but an inhabitant—the Holy Spirit—is necessary. The Holy Spirit, however, dwells only in those who are humble in heart. For God says: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest?” And the answer to the question follows: “Upon the humble and quiet one, and the one who trembles at my words” (Isa. 66:2).

When he is the inhabitant, therefore, he fills, governs, directs, restrains from evil, arouses to good, and makes righteousness sweet, so that a person does what is good out of love for what is right, not out of fear of punishment. What I have described a person is less capable of doing by himself; but if he has the Holy Spirit as an inhabitant, he also finds him to be an assistant in all good things.

But certain proud people, after their sins have been forgiven, if they presume to live well by the mere freedom of the human will, by that very pride exclude the Holy Spirit from themselves. The house remains, as it were, cleansed of sins, but empty of every good thing. “Your sins have been forgiven; you have been deprived of evils. But none other than the Holy Spirit will fill you with good things.” Pride drives him away. You presume upon yourself, and he abandons you. You trust in yourself, and you are handed over to yourself.

But that desire by which you were evil, driven away from the person—that is, from your mind—when your sins were forgiven, wanders through deserts seeking rest. And when it does not find rest, that desire returns to the house, finds it cleansed, brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.

It brings seven others with it. What does “seven others” mean? Is the unclean spirit itself, then, sevenfold? What does this mean? Through the number seven, totality is signified. The whole thing had gone away; the whole thing returns—and would that it returned alone!

What does “It brings seven others with it” mean? Those whom it did not have when it was evil, it will have when it is falsely good. Pay attention, so that, if I can, with whatever help I receive, I may explain what I am saying.

The Holy Spirit is commended through a sevenfold operation, so that there may be in us the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of God (Isa. 11:2–3). Set against this sevenfold good, by way of contrast, a sevenfold evil: the spirit of folly and error; the spirit of rashness and cowardice; the spirit of ignorance and impiety; and the spirit of pride in opposition to the fear of God. These are the seven wicked spirits.

Who, then, are the “seven others more wicked”? The seven others more wicked are found in hypocrisy.

One evil spirit is the spirit of folly; another, worse, is the pretence of wisdom. The evil spirit is the spirit of error; another, worse, is the pretence of truth. The evil spirit is the spirit of rashness; another, worse, is the pretence of counsel. The evil spirit is the spirit of cowardice; another, worse, is the pretence of fortitude. The evil spirit is the spirit of ignorance; another, worse, is the pretence of knowledge. The evil spirit is the spirit of impiety; another, worse, is the pretence of piety. The evil spirit is the spirit of arrogance [Col. 0934]; another, worse, is the pretence of fear.

Seven were scarcely bearable; who could bear fourteen? It is therefore necessary that, when pretence of truth is added to wickedness, the last state of the person should be worse than the first.

## III

While he was saying these things to the crowds—I follow the Gospel—his mother and his brothers were standing outside, wishing to speak with him. Someone announced to him, saying: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are outside, wishing to speak with you.” But he answered: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand over his disciples, he said: “These are my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:46–50).

I should like to speak only about this, but because I did not want to pass over what came before, I have consumed, as far as I can tell, no small portion of the time. For what I have now proposed contains many recesses and knots of inquiry: how the Lord Christ could piously disregard his mother—not just any mother, but, the more she was a virgin mother, all the more such a mother; a mother to whom he brought fruitfulness without taking away integrity; a virgin conceiving, a virgin giving birth, a virgin remaining perpetually so.

Such a mother he disregarded, lest a mother’s affection intrude upon and impede the work he was doing. What was he doing? He was speaking to the peoples; he was destroying the old human being and building the new; he was freeing souls, releasing the bound, illuminating blind minds, doing a good work, and burning with fervor in good work both in action and in speech.

Amid these things, a carnal affection was announced to him. You have heard what he replied; why should I repeat it? Let mothers hear this, so that by carnal affection they do not impede the good works of their children. For if they wish to hinder them, and rush upon those engaged in such works so as at least to interrupt what ought not to be postponed, they will be disregarded by their children.

I dare to say it: they will be disregarded—disregarded out of piety. When her son is intent in mind upon a good work, and for that reason disregards his mother who comes to him, when will a woman—whether married or widowed—be angry, when the Virgin Mary was disregarded?

But you will say to me: “Are you therefore comparing my son with Christ?” I compare neither him with Christ nor you with Mary. The Lord Christ, then, did not condemn maternal affection; rather, by disregarding his mother for the sake of God’s work, he gave in himself a great example of the mother who must be disregarded. He was a teacher in speaking, and he was a teacher in disregarding; therefore he deigned to disregard his mother, so that he might teach you to disregard even your father for the sake of God’s work.

## IV

For the Lord Christ could not become human without a mother, although he could without a father. If it was necessary—indeed, because it was necessary—for the one who made humanity to become human for humanity’s sake, consider and recall from what he made the first human being.

The first human being was made without father and without mother. Could he not afterward adapt something of the same kind to himself for the restoration of human affairs, just as he had been able to adapt it at first for the instruction of human affairs? Was it difficult for the Wisdom of God, the Word of God, the Power of God, the only-begotten Son of God, to make for himself a human being from whatever source he wished?

Angels presented themselves to human beings in human form. Abraham fed holy angels and invited them as though they were human beings; and he not only saw them, but also touched them [Col. 0935], for he washed their feet (Gen. 18). Were those things done by the angels as if in the playful illusions of phantoms?

If, then, an angel could, whenever he wished, present a true human appearance, could the Lord of angels not make a true human being, from whatever source he wished, whom he would assume? But he did not wish to have a human father, lest he come to human beings through carnal desire. Nevertheless, he wished to have a mother, so that he would have among human beings a mother whom he might teach human beings to disregard for the sake of God’s work.

He wished to assume the male sex in himself, and he deigned to honor the female sex in his mother. For in ancient times a woman had sinned and had given sin to the man to drink (Gen. 3). Both sexes had been deceived by the devil’s fraud. If Christ had come as a man without commending the female sex, women would have despaired of themselves, especially since through a woman the man had fallen.

He honored both, commended both, assumed both. He was born of a woman.

[Note: [Col. 0935] I add: “as a man.” The following seems to require this.]

Do not despair, men: Christ deigned to be a man. Do not despair, women: Christ deigned to be born of a woman. Let both sexes come together for Christ’s salvation. Let the male come; let the female come. In faith there is neither male nor female (Gal. 3:28).

Christ therefore teaches you to disregard your parents and to love your parents. You love your parents in an ordered and pious way when you do not place them before God. “Whoever loves”—these are the Lord’s words—“father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

By these words he seems, as it were, to have warned you not to love. Rather, if you pay attention, he warned you to love. For he could have said: “Whoever loves father or mother is not worthy of me.” He did not say this, lest he speak against the law that he himself had given. For he himself gave that law through his servant Moses, where it is written: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12; Deut. 5:16).

He did not promulgate a contrary law; rather, he commended that law and taught you the proper order. He did not overturn filial piety. “Whoever loves father or mother—but more than me.” Let him love, therefore, but not more than me.

God is God; a human being is a human being. Love your parents, obey your parents, honor your parents. But if God calls you to something greater, where parental affection could become an impediment, preserve the order; do not overturn charity.

## V

In the midst of so great a truth in the teaching of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who would believe that the Manichaeans sought a pretext for slander, by which they might attempt to assert that the Lord Jesus Christ had no mother at all?

This is what they think—or rather, what they foolishly think: that the Lord Jesus did not have a human mother, contrary to the Gospel and contrary to the light of truth itself. And observe the basis of their argument.

“Behold,” they say, “he himself says it.” What does he say? “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12:48). “He himself,” they say, “denies it, and you wish to impose upon him what he denies. He himself says: ‘Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?’ and you say: ‘He has a mother.’”

O foolish, contentious, and deservedly hateful man! Answer me: how do you know that the Lord said, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” You deny that Christ had a mother, and you try to prove [Col. 0936] what you intend by the fact that he said, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?”

Suppose another person were to appear and say that the Lord Christ never said this at all. How would you convict him? Answer, if you can, the person who denies that Christ said this. By the same means by which you convict him, you yourself are convicted.

Did Christ himself whisper into your ear that he had said this? Answer, so that you may be convicted by your own mouth. Answer so that you may prove that Christ said it.

I know what he is going to say: “I shall take up the Codex, open the Gospel, and recite his words written in the holy Gospel.” Good, very good. With that very Gospel I shall hold you fast together with him; with the Gospel I shall bind you; from that very Gospel I shall strangle you.

In the Gospel itself, read what you think supports you. Open it; read: “Who is my mother?” Why did he say this? Above, you will read: “Someone announced to him: ‘Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside’” (Matt. 12:47).

I am not yet pressing you, not yet holding you, not yet strangling you. You can still say: “That messenger was false; he did not speak the truth; he suggested lies. Therefore the Lord rejected a false report.”

After the messenger’s announcement, he replied: “Who is my mother?” As though he were saying: “You say, ‘Your mother is standing outside.’ I say, ‘Who is my mother?’ Whom do you wish us to believe—the messenger making the report, or Christ rejecting what was reported?”

Listen, then. I question you again. Hold fast to the Gospel alone. Do not throw the Codex behind you. Hold it; grant authority to the Gospel. Unless you grant it authority, there will be no basis for proving that the Lord said, “Who is my mother?”

But when you have granted the Gospel worthy authority, see what I am asking. A little earlier I had asked where you knew whether Christ had said, “Who is my mother?” What had preceded it? Someone had said to Christ: “Your mother is standing outside.”

Before the messenger said this—or, rather, in order that the messenger might say this—what preceded it? I compel you to read.

[Note: [Col. 0936] Perhaps: “I ask you.”]

I see that you are already afraid to read. Read it. The Lord answered and said. Who said this? I am not asking who said, “Who is my mother?” You will answer: “The Lord said it.” The Lord answered—which person said it?

You will answer: “The Evangelist said it.” Did this Evangelist speak the truth or falsehood? You will say either that he spoke the truth or that he spoke falsely.

[Note: [Col. 0936] In the manuscripts: *an* (“or”), which seems illogical (ἄλογον).]

“The Lord answered and said to him”—what the Evangelist said: did he say it truly or falsely? If you are going to say that the Evangelist falsely stated that the Lord answered, how do you know that the Lord said, “Who is my mother?”

But if you prove that the Lord said, “Who is my mother?” because the Evangelist said that he said this, you do not prove that the Lord said it unless you believe the Evangelist. Now, if you believe the Evangelist, why do you say nothing? If you do not believe the Evangelist, read above what the Evangelist himself said.

## VI

How long am I delaying you? How long am I holding you suspended? It is a benefit that you should be defeated quickly. Pay attention, look, read. I see that you do not want to. Give me the Codex.

I read: “While he was saying these things to the crowds.” Who says this? The Evangelist, and if you do not believe him, Christ said nothing. If Christ said nothing, Christ did not say, “Who is my mother?”

But if Christ said, “Who is my mother?” then what the Evangelist wrote is true [Col. 0937]. See what he said before. “While he was saying these things to the crowds, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, wishing to speak with him.”

That messenger has not yet announced anything—someone whom you can claim was lying. See what he announced; pay attention to what the Evangelist stated beforehand. While the Lord was speaking to the crowds, his mother and his brothers were standing outside.

Who says this? The Evangelist, whom you believe when he says that the Lord said, “Who is my mother?” But if you do not believe that this was said, then the Lord did not say, “Who is my mother?”

Yet the Lord truly did say, “Who is my mother?” Believe, therefore, the one who said that the Lord said, “Who is my mother?” For the one who said that the Lord said, “Who is my mother?” is the same one who said: “While he was saying these things, his mother was standing outside.”

Why, then, did he deny his mother? Far from it! Understand. He did not deny her; he placed something he was doing before his mother.

The only remaining question is why the Lord said, “Who is my mother?”

[Note: [Col. 0937] Perhaps: “only.”] The first question is to see that he had someone of whom he could say, “Who is my mother?” He had a mother; she was standing outside; she wished to speak with him.

Tell me, how do you know this? The Evangelist says so, and if I do not believe him, the Lord says nothing. Therefore he had a mother. But what does “Who is my mother?” mean?

“With respect to what I am doing, who is my mother?” If you say to someone who is in danger and has a father, “May your father save you,” although he knows that his father is not capable of saving his son, would he not answer you with complete piety and undiminished truth: “What is my father?”

“With respect to what I wish, with respect to what I now feel I need, what is my father?” So, with respect to what Christ was doing—releasing the bound, illuminating blind minds, building up the inner human being, constructing a spiritual temple for himself—who is his mother?

But if you think that Christ did not have a mother on earth because he said, “Who is my mother?”, then his disciples also had no fathers on earth, because the Lord himself said to them: “Do not call anyone your father on earth.” These are the Lord’s words: “Do not call anyone your father; for one is your Father, God” (Matt. 23:9).

They did not have no fathers; rather, when the matter comes to regeneration, let the father of regeneration be sought. The father of generation is not to be condemned, but the father of regeneration is to be placed before him.

## VII

Behold, my dearest brothers, pay closer attention—pay closer attention, I beg you—to what the Lord Christ said while stretching out his hand over his disciples: “This is my mother, and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father who sent me is my brother, sister, and mother.”

Did the Virgin Mary not do the will of the Father? She believed by faith, conceived by faith, was chosen so that salvation might be born from her among human beings, and was created by Christ before Christ was created in her.

She certainly did the will of the Father, holy Mary. And therefore it is greater for Mary to have been Christ’s disciple than to have been Christ’s mother. It is more blessed to have been Christ’s disciple than to have been Christ’s mother. For this reason Mary was blessed: because, even before she gave birth, she carried her teacher in her womb.

See whether what I say is not true. As the Lord passed by with the crowds following him and [Col. 0938] performed divine miracles, a certain woman said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you.”

[Note: [Col. 0938] This sentence appears redundant.]

“Blessed is the womb that bore you.” And the Lord, so that blessedness might not be sought in the flesh, what did he answer? “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:27–28).

Mary, then, is also blessed because she heard the word of God and kept it. She kept the truth more fully in her mind than she carried flesh in her womb. Christ is truth; Christ is flesh. Christ is truth in Mary’s mind; Christ is flesh in Mary’s womb. What is in the mind is greater than what is carried in the womb.

Holy Mary, blessed Mary—but the Church is better than the Virgin Mary. Why? Because Mary is a portion of the Church, a holy member, an excellent member, a pre-eminent member; yet she is still a member of the whole body. If she is a member of the whole body, then surely the body is greater than the member.

The Lord is the head, and the whole Christ is head and body. What shall I say? We have a divine head; we have God as our head.

## VIII

Therefore, dearest ones, pay attention. You too are members of Christ; you too are the body of Christ. Pay attention to how you may be what he said: “Behold, my mother and my brothers.”

How will you be Christ’s mother? “Whoever hears and whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:49–50).

Suppose I understand “brothers”; I understand “sisters.” For there is one inheritance, and therefore Christ, in his mercy, although he was the only one, did not wish to be alone: he wished us to be heirs of the Father and co-heirs with himself. For this is an inheritance that cannot be narrowed by the multitude of co-heirs.

I understand, then, that we are Christ’s brothers and that holy and faithful women are Christ’s sisters. How can we understand “mothers of Christ”?

What, then? Do we dare call ourselves mothers of Christ? Indeed, we dare call ourselves mothers of Christ. I have called you all his brothers; would I not dare call his mother so? Yet I would be even less willing to dare to deny what Christ said.

Come, dearest ones, pay attention to how the Church is plainly Christ’s bride and, more difficult to understand but nevertheless true, Christ’s mother. In her type, the Virgin Mary went before us.

How, I ask you, is Mary the mother of Christ except because she gave birth to Christ’s members? You to whom I am speaking are Christ’s members. Who gave birth to you? I hear the voice of your hearts: “Mother Church.”

This holy and honored mother, like Mary, both gives birth and is a virgin. That she gives birth I prove by you. You were born from her, and she gives birth to Christ, for you are Christ’s members.

I have proved that she gives birth; I shall prove that she is a virgin. Divine testimony does not abandon me; it does not abandon me. Come forward, blessed Paul, to the people. Be a witness to my assertion. Cry out and say what I wish to say:

“I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Where is this virginity? Where is corruption feared? Let the one who called her a virgin speak: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear,” he says, “that just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted,” he says, “from the purity that is in Christ.”

Preserve the virginity of the mind in your minds. The virginity of Catholic faith is its integrity.

[Col. 0939]

Where Eve was corrupted by the serpent’s speech, there the Church ought to be a virgin through the gift of the Almighty. Therefore let Christ’s members give birth in the mind, just as the Virgin Mary gave birth to Christ in the womb; and thus you will be Christ’s mothers.

This is not far from you, not outside you, not alien to [Col. 0940] you. You were children; become mothers as well. You were children of the mother when you were baptized; then Christ’s members were born.

Bring to the baptismal washing those whom you can, so that, just as you were children when you were born, so by leading others to be born you may also become mothers of Christ.

# Sermons

[Col. 0939]

To Our Most Holy Lord, Pope Pius VII

## Most Blessed Father,

Since I clearly see that it has fallen to my lot to bring to light for the first time, rescuing from the moths and granting the use of daylight, certain new sermons of the divine Aurelius Augustine lying hidden in the manuscript Codices of this Archicenobium of Cassino and hitherto inaccessible to all eyes, I beg you, Most Blessed Father, to allow me to present to you a specimen of them, which I have taken care to prepare for publication in advance, not rashly indeed.

This specimen of sermons, I thought, ought rightly and deservedly to be presented to Your Beatitude, both because it displays the most precious monuments of that great Doctor and Teacher of the Church, whose excellence of doctrine and a certain divine sublimity have always claimed as their chief bulwark the summit of Your Apostolic See, and because these sermons have been drawn from the place from which the Benedictine offspring has spread—an order among whose humbler members Your Holiness was once enrolled, and of which you are now both Parent and Glory and Defense.

May you therefore receive them with a more smiling countenance than anyone else and cherish them, as it were, in a more kindly embrace, providing them with your immediate protection, so that no opportunity may be left for criticism or envy—especially since the Benedictine Family may fairly claim for itself almost the privilege that the works of so great a Doctor should be examined, illustrated, and published principally by its own pupils.

Do you therefore assent to my prayers and undertakings, Most Blessed Father. The Christian world has long honored and revered you as its public Father; at the same time it looks up to and admires you as a most generous Maecenas and patron of the sciences and arts. Finally, prostrate at your most holy feet, I most humbly ask that you bestow the pledge of your paternal blessing upon me, upon this Archicenobium of mine, and upon the whole Congregation.

Your Holiness’s most humble and obedient son,  
D. Octavius Fraja Frangipane, Cassinese monk.

## Editor’s Preface

[Col. 0939]

When I undertook to arrange the manuscript Codices of this Cassinese Library in a new catalogue, weighing as fairly as I could both the subjects of their contents, the form of their script, and the ages themselves, nothing more welcome or auspicious could ever have happened to me than to come upon a considerable number of sermons of the great Doctor Augustine. I saw that these were either entirely absent from the printed editions, even from the most approved copies, or interrupted by numerous lacunae.

Although I found some of them listed in the Medicean Library, both the Laurentian and the Leopoldina, in that of Saint Mark at Venice, and in others whose catalogues of manuscript Codices have been printed, I nevertheless read that each of them had been specifically noted there as excluded from the edition.

More recently, I found twenty-five of them published among the Germans in the year 1792 by the distinguished Michael Denis, Prefect of the Vienna Library. I lamented that the rest still lay hidden in darkness. Since I could not bear that they should continue to be deprived of the light, I had no task more urgent than to investigate whether there might be fragments from which one or another apparently patched-together piece could be formed.

For I was not unaware of that perverse practice which had become especially prevalent in later ages: namely, the practice of fashioning from excerpts of the Fathers some kind of bastard offspring and rashly assigning it to whichever author one wished. I feared that I might waste my labor, or undertake something too bold, beyond the diligent and scarcely comparable work of the most learned monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur in their Paris edition. I also rightly suspected that I might in some slight degree detract from the dignity and renowned excellence of other, much more celebrated libraries.

For fuller confirmation of the matter, I therefore decided to consult distinguished men of learning, men virtually beyond all criticism, as well as other excellent judges of such matters living in various Italian cities and connected with me by correspondence. Among these, the foremost place certainly belongs to the very learned Aloysius Vincentius Cassittus of the Order of Preachers. I testify both to the honor due to his insight and diligence in this matter and to my gratitude toward him.

All of them pronounced nearly unanimously that these sermons—those, at least, which they had before their eyes—were new, and that they also bore the character of Augustine’s manner of expression. Indeed, I confess that they added their own encouragement to mine, urging me to make them public as soon as possible.

Unable any longer to resist the encouragement and wishes of these most serious men, and confident that I would thereby render an excellent service to the republic of letters, I complied with them. I resolved to guard against one thing alone—a precaution that we know every good man must observe: that I should dare neither to assert anything false nor to fail to assert anything true.

And indeed it was neither some ill-considered desire to hunt fame, nor a rash eagerness to judge, nor finally mere devotion to the great Doctor that led me to claim these works for Augustine. Rather, supported by all the other resources of sound criticism and relying especially upon the authority of the Codices—which I observed to agree in every other respect, down to the smallest detail, with the printed copies—why should I not submit to their authority?

If some of them should perhaps be found unworthy of the name of so great a Doctor, whether because of the difference of style, as it is called, or because of the slightness of their subjects, or for any other reason, and should therefore seem either to be expunged as apocryphal or relegated among the doubtful, I do not obstruct the judgment of wiser men. I only wish that those judges might be equipped with lynx eyes, which both Verlinus and Vindingus themselves would envy.

Whether, however, a sufficiently certain argument for determining the author can be extracted principally from style is a matter on which the water remains unsettled. I should call it exceedingly difficult and arduous, other things being equal. Let this serve as an example.

In Father Combefis’s Homiliary there is a sermon beginning, “Today the true sun” (vol. 1, p. 519). He himself reports it as assigned to Origen; Father Bruni, on the contrary, claims it for Saint Maximus (fol. 413); Vallarsius thinks it should be relegated among Jerome’s apocrypha; but the Laurentian Library, in Bandini, assigns it to Saint Ambrose.

Does the style of the Fathers transform itself like a new Proteus into new and varied forms?

The editors themselves, the monks, vividly explain how greatly and for how many reasons Augustine’s own style is varied and manifold in their Preface to volume five. At the same time, as they are accustomed to do, they most learnedly persuade us that there is one and the same spirit of Augustine throughout, by which his style is, as it were, animated.

For, they say, Augustine is everywhere recognized by a certain distinctive kind of grave and serious eloquence, which subjugates the minds of readers—not through the charm of polished and affected expression, but through a certain effectiveness of judgment, prudence, and piety.

Nor should this be passed over here: the very expressions, sentences, and almost entire periods that occur in Augustine in one place are frequently repeated in these new sermons as well. Yet beware of calling them patchworks or of treating them as doubtful in authenticity. The editors mentioned above repeatedly found the same thing even in Augustine’s authentic works; and anyone who reads Augustine encounters it everywhere, especially in the books *On Questions*.

For some things to be present in certain sermons that are also found elsewhere is something altogether different from stitching sermons together out of his words. Who could deny that the holy Doctor, delivering or committing to writing almost innumerable sermons extemporaneously, could very easily at times express the same thoughts in the same words?

If someone should inquire more curiously how it happened that those most learned monks nowhere remembered these sermons, allow me to ask in return how they could ever have remembered them, when they did not even greet the Cassinese Codices from the threshold while preparing Augustine’s edition? This is especially clear from the fact that, among all the manuscripts they individually reviewed and diligently collated, ours are passed over in complete silence.

Nor should you argue that they were therefore disregarded because they were considered either less trustworthy or altogether apocryphal. At least they would have counted the Homilies among the apocrypha, as is easy to infer from the threefold classification of sermons that they established: those which the unimpeachable editors chose to divide into authentic, doubtful, and apocryphal.

If anyone should further be seized by a desire to know more precisely why the Cassinese Library was given no consideration at all in that edition, this could have happened either because before Mabillon, Montfaucon, and other men of that station bore witness to its distinction, it had enjoyed less celebrated renown among the French, or because the wars then raging everywhere—at that time, namely, when the wars of Louis the Great, Most Christian King, were exhausting almost the whole of Europe—deprived them of the freedom to communicate and perhaps obstructed the very means for the exchange of letters.

If you regard this as an absurd conjecture, I could easily prove from the list of Codices they consulted that their purpose was to consult, among all the Italian libraries, only the Vatican and the Library of Saint Croce in Jerusalem at Rome, while setting aside all the rest, even the most famous Medicean Library.

I would not deny that Mabillon, Montfaucon, and the others who repeatedly stayed among us in search of monuments of learning and antiquity seemed almost blind to these sermons; nor does this surprise me. Since those exceedingly learned visitors came here only after the Paris edition had already been completed, they thought it not worth the effort to devote greater attention to these sermons, which they easily supposed had been published along with all the others.

It is also reasonable to suspect that the Codices themselves, being of a later age than the much more ancient ones, were not shown to them. Or, finally—and much more probably—they ran out of time to examine individually our more than five hundred Codices.

This is clearly demonstrated by the example of Montfaucon himself, who, in reviewing and listing the Codices of the other libraries, including the Cassinese, enumerates them all while omitting any individual analysis.

Moreover, in the Library of the Monastery of Saints Severinus and Sossius at Naples, belonging to the Order of Saint Benedict, he himself lists and describes, among the other Codices, Codex no. 7, yet neither produces anything new nor repeats anything old from that treasure.

I mean the Codex then assigned to that monastery and for many years now transferred to the Vienna Library. From it, of course, the aforementioned exceptionally perceptive Denis most auspiciously drew new sermons of Augustine. In this matter, by heaven, Denis deprived us of the glory only a few years ago, although he seems to have paved the way for confirming the authenticity of our Codices.

But in order to review the entire matter with renewed care, and so that, in accordance with Horace’s precept, the work might be kept back until the ninth year, I have resolved at present to commit to print only ten of these sermons—which I have been fortunate enough to discover many of—as a specimen.

I have done this all the more because it would no longer be permissible to frustrate the public hope, lest someone deservedly mutter against us:

“If only the fortunate knew their own good fortune.”

I thought it appropriate to support them with modest and strictly necessary notes and observations. It should also be noted in advance that they come from parchment Codices, for the most part of the tenth and eleventh centuries, displaying Lombard script. Their script corresponds to that of the Codices presented by Mabillon in *De re diplomatica*, vol. 1, no. 4, from Codex Chisianus, shelfmark no. 1521, and no. 5, from a Medicean Laurentian Codex; to the script also noted by Father Bruni in the Roman edition of Saint Maximus; to that which Trombellius describes in his *Art of Distinguishing the Ages of Latin and Italian Codices*, p. 79; and finally to that mentioned by Father Blasi in the list of princes who ruled at Salerno during the Lombard period, table III, no. III.

Although those highly skilled masters of diplomatics assigned no age to any of these Codices, since Lombard script remained in use for a long time, nevertheless, when they are compared with the Cassinese Codices—especially with the one externally marked no. 148, which internally gives the year 1010—one can scarcely distinguish one from another.

This indicates sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, that all Codices displaying the same script ought to be assigned only to the tenth or eleventh century.

Just as these Cassinese Codices contain many works of Augustine, so it was also possible to distinguish two classes of sermons.

The first restores to their integrity sermons already published in mutilated and imperfect form, and repairs the fragments and lacunae for which the Maurist editors had wished to obtain more complete copies. Thus, concerning the sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, which also appears here in fourth place, they wrote with regret:

“There are also certain other passages that may be less complete; but the copies necessary for healing them are lacking to us.”
