The second brings out of darkness sermons which both Possidius in his *Index* and other equally certain indications, drawn from the rules of sound criticism, establish as having been composed by Augustine, although, since they were lost, only hopes of recovering them had remained.

The specimen of these classes may be discerned in these ten Homilies: the first four belong to the former class, while the remaining six are assigned to the latter. It remains useful to give advance notice that these Codices are precisely those said to have been written at the command of Theobald and Desiderius, Abbots of Cassino. The latter, later taking the name Victor III, held the helm of the Church and deserved to be enrolled among the Saints. For this fact there is the ample testimony of Leo of Ostia (*Chronicle*, Book 2, chapter 51, and Book 3, chapter 63), who is described by Baronius as a man of unimpeachable trustworthiness and who enumerates each Codex individually, although several had perished through the ravages of time, the Cassinese Library having been plundered more than once. The form of the scripts, and the dates themselves added by some in the same hand, seem to settle the matter.

These Codices, however, although they have nothing preferable in the elegance of their script or in the splendid ornamentation of their large letters, were not copied with sufficient accuracy. For although the copyist himself, or someone else almost his contemporary, corrected errors here and there, whether by writing between the lines, by marking the margins, or by erasing letters, nevertheless the sense of the discourse is often interrupted either through the omission of words, or is blemished by an error or a solecism. In correcting these matters, I was able, by comparing the Codices with one another, to attain the genuine reading. So that it might more easily be recognized, in the sermons already published by the Parisian editors but restored on the authority of our Codices, what is now being made public for the first time, it seemed appropriate to indicate that material in the letters called italics [Note: In the present edition, however, we have placed the passages drawn from the Codices within brackets.]; and I have carefully marked with suitable observations everything that the Parisian edition either reads differently or supplies in addition to the reading of our Codices. Such matters as require annotation, as we have said, are either placed at the beginning of the sermons or relegated to the margin of the page. For it was of the greatest importance to promote, so far as possible, the clarity and dignity of these sermons; nor has moderate diligence been devoted to the task.

Whether the undertaking has succeeded according to our intention, let the judgment of a stricter Censure decide—would that it neither harass the Doves, as I shall say with Juvenal, nor spare the Crows!

[Col. 0943]

WE, DOM STEPHANUS ALESSANDRI, ABBOT OF SAINT BENEDICT OF SUBIACO, PROCURATOR GENERAL AND APOSTOLIC DELEGATE OF THE CASSINESE CONGREGATION.

[Col. 0943] Since Dom Octavius Fraja Frangipane, a monk of our Congregation and, in the Archicenobium of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino, keeper of the archives and custodian of the Library, has made it known to us that he found the following ten Sermons, attributed to the holy Doctor Augustine, written in the manuscript Codices preserved in the aforesaid archives, by these presents we grant him, insofar as it concerns us, permission in the Lord to make them public.

[Col. 0945] Given at Rome, from the residence of Saint Callixtus, on 6 December 1819. Dom STEPHANUS ALESSANDRI, Abbot, Procurator General and Apostolic Delegate. L + S. Dom ALOYSIUS BELMONTE, Pro-Chancellor.

[Col. 0945]

TEN SERMONS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, RECENTLY EDITED FROM THE CASSINESE CODEX. (G)*

## SERMON I

[Note: The Maurists identify this sermon as being about the ten plagues and the Ten Commandments. Eugipius’s Codex has: “An exposition of the Ten Commandments, preserving the firmness of its literal foundation, from the exposition of the Decalogue to the People.” Augustine mentions it in *Psalm* 77, no. 27, where he briefly explains it.]

On the ten plagues and the ten commandments given through Moses to the Jewish People.

The Maurists published this sermon (*Vol.* V, col. 41) as a fragment found in Eugipius and in the manuscripts of the Royal Library and of Victor. The Cassinese Codex no. 17, entitled *Augustine’s Sermons on the Words of the Lord and on Other Matters*, restores it to completeness; but Codex no. 13, entitled *Extracted Sayings of Eugipius from the Books of Augustine*, corrects its careless transcription. In that Codex, however, only the published fragment is present, with a few variant readings. If any errors remain, I have left them untouched, since I obtained only one Codex among all the Cassinese manuscripts that presents this sermon in full. That Codex contains twenty-six sermons on the Words of the Lord, arranged in the same order, which the Louvain editors published. These are followed by fifty-eight others, of which twenty-seven appear in the Maurist edition, twenty-three in Denys’s recent appendix, and eight had until now been concealed, either in part or in their entirety, beneath the ashes.

### I.

[“To the Lord our God, whose worshippers we are, it is said in praise in a certain passage of Scripture: ‘You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight’ (Wisdom 11:21). Then, through apostolic teaching, we are instructed ‘to contemplate with understanding the things that have been made, and through visible things to investigate the things that are hidden’ (Romans 1:20). [Note: Augustine here quotes the scriptural text according to the ancient, or Italic, version, which in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 2, chapter 15, he judges preferable to the others. Would that the distinguished Denys had noticed this! He would not so rashly have judged, in his note (b) on the Sermon on the Praise of the Candle, that the author seems to have erred in memory by substituting the bee for the ants of Proverbs 6:6; for in the Italic version after the Septuagint he would have found examples of both bee and ant.] Thus creation, as though questioned everywhere, answers by the very voice of its form that it has the Lord God as its craftsman. Then the Apostle Paul recalls that the things written in the books of the Old Testament occurred in a figurative manner: ‘These things,’ he says, ‘were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come’ (1 Corinthians 10:11). Therefore, dearly beloved, when the things that seem to arise fortuitously in the order of nature are carefully questioned and examined, wisely investigated and discovered, they proclaim the praise of the Creator and the divine Providence spread throughout all things, ordering everything gently, as it is said: ‘It reaches mightily from end to end’ (Wisdom 8:1).

“How much more, then, must we attend to things that not only have been favorable [Note: Thus in the Codex.] but are also commended in the divine Scriptures? Accordingly, we undertake, in the name of the Lord our God, with his help and gift, and with the pious intention of your hearts joining us, to explain as far as we can the question—or rather the inquiry and discussion—proposed to us by the brethren: what is signified by the Egyptians being struck with ten plagues and the people of God being instructed by ten commandments? For we believe that this very assistance has been granted, if not on our account, certainly on yours, so that we may say what I have learned and may be heard as he is to be heard, in order that, walking together in the way of his truth and hastening together toward our homeland, we may deserve to avoid the ambushers along our road by recognizing the will of the law.”

[Note: The passage is obscure; a scribal error has plainly entered the text.]

There are ten plagues with which Pharaoh’s people were struck; there are ten commandments with which the people of God were instructed. Let us therefore see, brethren, how things accomplished bodily are to be understood spiritually. We do not deny that they occurred, so as to suppose that they were merely spoken and written, not done; rather, we believe that they happened as we read that they happened, and yet we recognize from apostolic teaching that those very events were shadows of things to come.

Let us therefore investigate spiritually what happened, while nevertheless believing that it happened. Let no one say: “It is indeed written that the water was changed into blood in the plague of the Egyptians, but this signifies something; it could not really have happened.” Whoever says this seeks God’s will in such a way as to do injury to God’s power. For if he could signify it by speaking, could he not also accomplish it by doing? Surely he could. Was Isaac not born, or Ishmael not born? They had been born; they were human beings; they had been born from Abraham—one from a slave woman, the other from a free woman (Galatians 4:22). Although they were human beings and had been born, they nevertheless prefigured the two Testaments, the Old and the New.

Thus, after first establishing the firmness of the historical events as a foundation, we must seek their significance [Note: The Maurist edition has “signification.”], lest, with the foundation removed, we seem to wish to build in the air.”

[Note: These words begin the Maurist edition and the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts, which very often agree. The edition has “significance.”]

“I believe that all who despise and do not observe the ten commandments of the Law suffer spiritually what the Egyptians suffered bodily. Until I explain this subject with God’s help, I want you to remain attentive and to pray for us, so that we may speak to you. For what concerns us, perhaps we think; but what we speak, we render as a service to you.

“First, then, understand this, so that you are not misled in the number: the first event, which occurred as a sign, namely that the rod was changed into a serpent, does not belong to these ten plagues.” [Note: The edition reads: “But the first event does not belong to the ten plagues.”] “For this was the approach [Note: The edition reads ‘this very approach.’] to Pharaoh by which Moses was commended as the one who would lead the people of God out of Egypt (Exodus 7:10). The rebellious were not yet being struck; they were already being frightened by a divine sign.” [Note: The Cassinese Codex consistently reads *Moses*, whereas the edition reads *Moyses*; it is enough to note this once.]

[“There is no need, nor is it our purpose, to say anything about the rod itself being changed into a serpent. Nevertheless, since necessity has made us mention it, so that no one may err in the number and no difficulty about an unintelligible matter remain in any hearer’s mind [Note: He had discussed it more fully in Sermon 6, no. 7, and in *Psalm* 73, no. 5.], we say briefly that the rods signify the kingdom of God, and that this kingdom is certainly the people of God, while the serpent signifies the condition of this mortality; for death was introduced through the serpent.” [Note: The edition reads: “The rod signifies the kingdom of God, and this kingdom of God is certainly the people of God; but the serpent …”]

“Thus, as though falling from the hand of the Lord, they became mortal when they reached the earth; hence, when Moses’s rod was cast from his hand, it became a serpent. Pharaoh’s magicians [Note: The edition reads “Pharaoh’s magicians.”] did the same: when their rods were cast down, they became serpents. But Moses’ serpent—that is, Moses’ rod—first devoured all the magicians’ serpents; then, when its tail was seized, it again became a rod, and the kingdom returned to the hand.” [Note: The edition reads *therefore* instead of *and*.]

“The rods of the magicians are the peoples of the ungodly. And who are the peoples of the ungodly? Those conquered in the name of Christ; when they are transferred into his body, they are swallowed, as it were, by Moses’ serpent. Until we return to the kingdom of God [Note: The edition reads: “until the kingdom of God returns to the hand of God, but at the end.”], at the end of the mortal age—which is signified by the serpent’s tail—the great sign will be accomplished. You have heard what you ought to desire; hear what you ought to avoid.”]

### II.

The first commandment in the Law concerns the worship of one God: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3). The first plague of the Egyptians was water changed into blood (ibid. 7:20).

### III.

Compare the first commandment with the first plague. Understand the one God, from whom all things are [Note: The edition reads “in the likeness.”], in the likeness of water, from which all things are generated. But to what does blood pertain, if not to mortal flesh [Note: The edition has: “What, then, is it?”]? What, then, is the changing of water into blood, if not this: “Their own foolish heart was darkened” [Note: The edition reads *eorum* (“their”) instead of *ipsorum* (“their own”).]? For, claiming to be wise [Note: The edition reads *se esse sapientes* (“that they were wise”).], they became fools, and “they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God [Note: The edition reads *incorruptibilis* (“of the incorruptible one”); compare Romans 1:21.] for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Romans 1:21–23).

The glory of the incorruptible God is like water; the likeness of the image of corruptible man is like blood. [Note: I have supplied “The glory of the incorruptible God is like water; the likeness of the image of corruptible man is like blood” from the Codex of Extracts; one can scarcely doubt that the eye wandered from the earlier occurrence of the word to the same word repeated later, the mind being distracted from the sense and intent only on copying.] And this indeed takes place in the hearts of the ungodly, for God remains unchangeable. The Apostle’s saying, “They exchanged,” does not mean that God himself was changed. [Note: The edition has: “For the Apostle also says …”]

### IV.

The second commandment: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for he who has taken the name of the Lord God in vain shall not be cleansed” (ibid. 20:7). [Note: The edition reads: “whoever takes the name of the Lord his God.”] The name of our Lord God Jesus Christ is truth, for he himself said: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Truth therefore cleanses, while vanity defiles.

And since whoever speaks truth speaks of the truth of God [Note: The edition reads “speaks of God.”—for whoever speaks falsehood speaks from himself], to speak truth is to speak rationally; to speak vanity is to make a noise rather than to speak [Note: The edition has: “But to speak vanity …”]. Rightly, then, because the second commandment concerns love of truth, to which love of vanity is opposed, this is called speaking. Truth speaks; vanity makes a noise. [Note: The edition reads: “Vanity makes a noise.”]

See [Note: The edition reads “See the second.”] that the second plague is contrary to this second commandment. What is that second plague? An abundance of frogs.

[Col. 0949] You have vanity plainly expressed and signified [Note: The Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts reads: “vanity more expressly signified.”] [Note: The edition has “signified.”] if you attend to the loquacity of frogs. Consider the lovers of truth, who do not take the name of the Lord their God in vain [Note: The edition reads: “not taking the name of the Lord their God in vain.”]. They speak wisdom among the mature, and even among the immature—not indeed speaking what the latter cannot grasp, but without departing from the truth and proceeding into vanity. Although [Note: The edition reads: “Although the immature do not grasp …”] the immature cannot grasp what is said somewhat more sublimely about the Word of God, who is God with God, through whom all things were made, they can grasp what Paul speaks among them as among Christ’s little ones: “Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” Yet the former is Truth, and the latter is not vanity.

Vanity would be involved if we said that Christ had not truly undergone death but had merely pretended to do so; if we said that those wounds had been phantom wounds, that blood had flowed from them not truly but artificially, and that he had displayed false scars as though after false wounds. [Note: The edition reads: “If we were to say that Christ had not undergone death but only feigned it; if those wounds had been a phantasm, if the blood flowing from the wounds had been not real but simulated, if he had displayed false scars …”] But when we say that all these things happened, we declare and believe them to be real, manifest, and accomplished. [Note: The edition reads: “When we say these things are true, we say that the events are certain.”] Although we do not speak of that sublime and unchangeable truth, we nevertheless do not proceed into vanity.

Those who call all these things in Christ false and fabricated are frogs croaking in a swamp. They may possess the din of a voice, but they cannot impart the teaching of wisdom. Finally, in the Church they speak while clinging to the truth: the truth through whom all things were made [Note: I have supplied “through whom all things were made, the Truth—the Word made flesh and dwelling among us” from the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts; this lacuna too was caused by the eye’s skipping between similarly repeated words.], the truth—the Word made flesh and dwelling among us, the Truth—Christ, born God from God, one from one, Only-Begotten and Coeternal; the Truth, born of the Virgin Mary after receiving the form of a servant, having suffered, having been crucified, having risen, having ascended; Truth everywhere, and Truth which the immature cannot grasp [Note: The edition adds: “and which the mature can grasp”], Truth in bread [Note: The Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts reads: “the Truth which is in bread.”] and in milk—in the bread of the mature, in the milk of the little ones. For the same bread is conveyed through flesh so as to become milk.

Those who contradict this truth and, deceived by their own vanity, deceive others [Note: Bede, commenting on 1 Corinthians, chapter 2, reads: “and by their own vanity.”] are frogs, bringing weariness to the ears [Note: The edition reads *inferentes* (“inflicting”) instead of *offerentes* (“bringing”).], not nourishment to the minds. Hear, finally, people speaking rationally: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard; but their voices are not empty, for ‘their sound has gone out [Note: The Codex of Extracts reads “has gone forth.”] into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’” (Psalm 18:4–5). If you also wish to understand frogs in the opposite sense, recall the verse of the Psalm: “They spoke vain things, each one to his neighbor” (Psalm 12:3).

### V.

The third commandment: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exodus 20:8). In this third commandment a certain cessation is prescribed, namely tranquility of heart and of mind, which a good conscience produces. There is sanctification there, because there is the Spirit of God. Finally, observe the cessation—that is, the rest: “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2). [Note: In the edition, the question precedes the word “upon.”]

The restless therefore recoil from the Holy Spirit: lovers of quarrels, sowers of accusations, more desirous of contention than of truth. Through their restlessness they do not admit [Note: The edition reads “do not admit to themselves.”] the spiritual Sabbath rest [Note: The Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts has: “that is, the spiritual Sabbath”]. Against this restlessness it is said—as though so that they may have the Sabbath in their heart—in the sanctification of the Spirit of God: “Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand.” [Note: Ecclesiasticus 5:13.]

“What shall I understand?” God saying: “Cease from your restlessness; let there be no tumult in your heart, with fantasies [Note: The edition reads “phantasms.”] flitting about through corruption and pricking you; let it not be so.” [Note: The edition punctuates the passage differently, but the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts agrees with our reading.] For you will understand God saying to you [Note: The edition reads: “Be still and see that …”]: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11). You do not wish to be still because of your restlessness, and, blinded by the corruption of your contentions [Note: The edition has “of your disputes”], you demand to see what you cannot see.

### VI.

Attend, then, to the third plague, which is contrary to this third commandment. Gnats were born in the land of Egypt from the mud—tiny flies [Note: The edition reads: “they are certain tiny flies”; compare Exodus 8:18.], exceedingly restless, flying about disorderly, rushing into the eyes, not allowing a person to rest as they are driven away and rush back, and as, once driven off, they return again, exactly like the vain fantasies of contentious hearts. [Note: The edition has: “Hold fast … beware.”] Hold fast to the commandment; beware of the plague.

### VII.

The fourth commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The fourth plague of the Egyptians, contrary to this, is the *cynomia* [Note: The edition has Κονομνία … Κονομνία.].

What is *cynomia*? *Cynomia* is a dog-fly; it is a Greek word. It is canine not to acknowledge one’s parents; yet nothing is more canine than for those who begot one not to be acknowledged. Therefore, rightly, puppies of dogs are also born blind.

[Note: I supplied “What is *cynomia*?” from the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts. Jerome, in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela, maintains that the word denotes every kind of fly and should be written κοινομυία (*koinomyia*, “common fly”), with the diphthong *oi*, rather than κυνόμυια (*kynomyia*, “dog-fly”), with *y*.]

### VIII.

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid. 14). The fifth plague is the death of the livestock of the Egyptians (ibid. 9:6).

Let us compare them. Consider a person committing adultery, not content with his own marriage [Note: The edition has: “To commit adultery is to meditate upon it, not being content with one’s own marriage.”]; he refuses to control within himself a certain appetite of the flesh, which we share with animals. For to lie together and generate offspring is also swine-like; to reason and understand is human [Note: The edition has: “To lie together and generate offspring is characteristic of animals; to reason and understand is human.”].

Therefore reason, which presides in the mind over the lower movements of the flesh, must restrain them as a reigning and ruling power, not release them without measure or law, everywhere and indiscriminately. For this reason, by the Creator’s ordering, animals themselves have been given a natural pattern whereby they are not moved toward females and intercourse except at fixed times. An animal does not restrain itself through reason at other times; rather, when the movement itself cools, it becomes entirely torpid.

A human being, however, can therefore always be moved because he can also restrain the movement [Note: The edition reads *refrenare* (“rein in”) instead of *frenare* (“restrain”).]. The Creator has given you the dominion of reason; he has granted you commandments of continence as reins for the lower beasts. You possess what the animal does not have [Note: The edition reads “cannot have” instead of “does not have.”], and therefore you hope for what the animal cannot have. You may labor somewhat in restraining yourself [Note: The edition reads: “You labor in restraining yourself; the animal does not labor, but you will rejoice forever in the eternity which the animal does not reach.”], whereas the animal does not labor; but you will rejoice forever in what the animal does not reach.

If the task tires you, let the reward console you. For patience itself consists in restraining the inward movement and in not releasing without limit [Note: The edition reads *laxare* (“to loosen”) instead of *relaxare* (“to release”).] what you share with the animal, as an animal would. But if you despise yourself [Note: The edition has: “and in yourself the image …”] and neglect in yourself the image of God in which he made you, overcome by the desire of beasts [Note: The edition reads *insinuatarum rerum* (“of things impressed upon the mind”) instead of *bestiarum* (“of beasts”).], you will be a beast, as though you had lost your humanity—not transformed into the nature of a beast, but bearing in human form the likeness of a beast, since you do not heed the saying: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9). [Note: The edition adds: “Perhaps …”]

Perhaps you choose to be a beast for yourself, free to wander in lust [Note: The edition reads *libera* rather than *liber*.], restraining the appetite of the flesh toward continence by no law. Attend to the plague. If you do not fear being a beast, at least fear dying like a beast. [Note: The Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts reads: “If you are a beast and do not fear …”]

### IX.

The sixth commandment: “You shall not kill” (Exodus 20:13). The sixth plague: boils on the body, and blisters swelling and bursting, and the burning of wounds [Note: The edition reads “bursting forth.”] from the ashes of the furnace (ibid. 9:10). Such are murderous souls: they burn with anger, because through anger brotherhood is destroyed. People burn with rage [Note: The edition reads *ira* (“anger”) instead of *iracundia* (“wrathfulness”).], and they burn with favor as well. But one heat belongs to health, another to an ulcer.

Burning pustules throughout the body burst forth with conceived murders, and what burns is not healthy. It burns, but not from the Spirit of God. For both the person who wishes to help burns and the person who wishes to kill burns; the former according to the commandment, the latter [Note: The edition reads “the latter.”] through disease; the former in good works, the latter in foul ulcers. [Note: The edition has “the latter in notorious deeds”; Eugipius reads with our Codex.]

If we could see the souls of murderers, we would grieve more than over the ulcerated bodies of the putrefying.

### X.

The seventh commandment follows [Note: The edition places “There follows” before “commandment.”]: “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15). The seventh plague: hail upon the crops (ibid. 9:23). What you take away contrary to the commandment, you lose from heaven; for no one has unjust gain without just loss.

For example, the thief steals; by stealing he acquires a garment [Note: The edition reads: “For example, the thief acquires a garment.”], but by heavenly judgment he loses good faith. Where there is gain, there is loss: visible gain, invisible loss; gain from his own blindness, loss from the Lord’s cloud.

For nothing happens without Providence, dearly beloved. Or do you really suppose that people suffer the things they suffer while God is asleep? These things seem to happen at random: clouds gather, rains pour down, hail is hurled, the earth is shaken by thunder [Note: The edition has “by thunderclaps”], people are terrified by lightning. They are thought to happen at random, as though they did not pertain to divine Providence.

Against such thoughts that Psalm keeps watch: “Praise the Lord from the earth”—after praises had been spoken of things in heaven—“you dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which do his word” (Psalm 148:7–8). Therefore those who steal outwardly through an evil desire are inwardly pelted with hail by God’s just judgment.

Oh, if only they could inspect [Note: The edition reads *possent* (“could”) instead of *possint* (“can”).] the field of their heart! They would certainly mourn when they found nothing there to put into the mouth of the mind [Note: I have supplied from the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts: “Although in their theft they might find something to put into the greed of the belly”; the lacuna was clearly caused by an error similar to those above.], even though in their theft they might find something to put into the greed of the belly.

The hunger of the inward human being is greater [Note: The edition reads: “The hunger of the inward human being would be greater, a greater hunger and a more dangerous plague.”]; greater is that hunger, and more dangerous the plague, and more severe the death. Many dead people walk about, and many famished people [Note: The edition reads *facinorosi* (“criminals”) instead of *famelici* (“famished people”).] exult in empty riches. Finally, Scripture calls the servant of God rich within: “The hidden person of your heart, who is rich before God.” Not rich before human beings [Note: The edition has: “Not rich before human beings, but rich before God, and rich where God sees”], but rich before God, rich where God is.

Look at yourself, rich man: what does it profit you? [Note: The edition has: “If where …”] Where no human being sees, you steal; and where God sees, you are pelted with hail.

### XI.

The eighth commandment: “You shall not bear false witness” (Exodus 20:16). The eighth plague: the locust, an animal destructive with its teeth (ibid. 10:13). What does a false witness seek except to harm by biting and consume by lying? Accordingly, the Apostle warns the people of God not to attack one another with false accusations: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).

### XII.

The ninth commandment: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:17). The ninth plague: dense darkness (ibid. 10:22).

For there is a certain adultery against which the commandment given above [Note: The edition reads simply “the commandment.”] also applies, namely, not desiring another man’s wife in one’s pursuit of chastity. The man who is not content with his own wife is an adulterer, even if he does not go to another’s wife. But to sin not only after having one’s own wife but also to assault another’s is truly dense darkness.

Nothing hurts so much in the heart of the person who suffers this, and the one who does it to another would not want to suffer anything so much himself. [Note: The edition reads: “would wish to suffer it. To another’s wife …”; the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts agrees with our reading.] Every person is more prepared to endure other things; but I do not know whether anyone has been found who can bear this tolerably. [Note: The edition has: “whether anyone has been found who would tolerate it.” The Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts agrees with our reading.]

O dense darkness of those who do such things and covet such things! They are truly blinded by terrible fury [Note: The edition has “horrible fury”], for unrestrained fury is to defile [Note: The edition reads *conculcare* (“to trample”) instead of *commaculare* (“to defile”).] a man’s wife.

### XIII.

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor: neither his livestock, nor his property, nor his servant, nor anything at all belonging to your neighbor” (Exodus 20:17). The plague contrary to this evil is the tenth: the death of the firstborn (ibid. 12:29).

In this plague I seek a certain comparison. [Note: The edition reads the grammatically irregular *cum comparationem quamdam* in place of *cum comparatione quadam*.] For the moment, nothing occurs to me; perhaps something better will occur to those who inquire more carefully [Note: The edition reads: “unless it is because everyone who has property preserves it for his heirs and is censured. But here cries out the man who covets his neighbor’s property, and the one who takes it by theft; and whoever steals anything belonging to his neighbor can only steal his neighbor’s property.”]. Perhaps it is because people preserve all the property they possess for their heirs. But the person who covets his neighbor’s property is condemned [Note: Eugipius’s Extracts read: “is found to preserve what he has for his heirs. But here he cries out …”]: the one who takes it by theft also covets it; and whoever steals anything belonging to his neighbor cannot steal it except by coveting his neighbor’s property.

But the commandment concerning theft was already given above, so that there you may understand robbery as well. [Note: The edition reads *ubi intelligas* (“where you may understand”) instead of *ut ibi intelligas* (“so that there you may understand”).] Scripture would not give a commandment concerning theft and remain silent about robbery unless it wanted you to understand that, if it is punishable to take something secretly, it is punishable by a much greater penalty to seize it violently [Note: The edition has: “to take it unwillingly.”]. To take from someone unwillingly, whether secretly or openly, has its own commandment.

But to covet one’s neighbor’s property—a matter that God observes in the heart—is not permitted, even if you seek a lawful succession there. Finally, those who wish to possess another’s property as though justly seek to become heirs through the deaths of the owners.

For what seems more just than to possess what has been left to one, to hold it by common right? What does the man say to you? “It was left to me” [Note: The edition has “by inheritance”]; “I have obtained the inheritance; I am reading the will.” Nothing seems more just than this voice of avarice [Note: The edition has: “You praise him as though he possessed it by right.”]. You say: “You hold it justly,” and you praise him as though he possessed it lawfully. God condemns the person coveting unjustly.

Consider what kind of person you are when you wish to become someone’s heir: you do not wish him to have heirs [Note: The edition has: “But among the heirs …”]. Among heirs, none is dearer than the firstborn. Therefore, in your firstborn, you are punished [Note: The edition reads *punieris* (“you will be punished”); Eugipius confirms our reading *puniris* (“you are punished”).] because, by coveting another’s property, you seek what was not lawfully owed to you under the shadow of a supposed right [Note: The same Extracts read: “under the shadow of legal right.”].

It is easy, indeed, brethren, to lose one’s firstborn bodily. People die, whether before or after their parents; those destined to die do die. But what is grievous is that through this hidden and unjust covetousness you lose the firstborn of your heart.

For the firstborn in us bears the image of God’s grace: newly born, born first, among all the offspring of our heart, faith is the firstborn. No one performs good works unless faith has gone before, as the Apostle says: “Without faith,” he says, “it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 9:6). All your good works are your spiritual children, but among these faith is born first [Note: The edition has “the firstborn.”]

Whoever therefore secretly covets another’s property loses inward faith [Note: The edition has “inwardly.”]. For first of all he will undoubtedly be a hypocrite, showing obedience not from love but from deceit, as though loving the person whose heir he desires to become. In loving him, he seeks his death [Note: The edition lacks the conjunction, which is nevertheless found in Eugipius.]; and, in order to see himself in possession of his property, he envies him a successor.

### XIV.

[Note: Our Codex has: “These ten commandments and ten plagues having been traversed, brethren, comparing the contemptuous with the obstinacy of the Egyptians, we shall make you cautious.” I have placed before this perhaps less complete reading another taken from the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts.]

Come, brethren, having gone through the ten commandments and the ten plagues, comparing those who despise the commandments with the obstinacy of the Egyptians, we have made you cautious, so that you may safely keep your possessions in the commandments of God—your possessions, I say, the inner possessions of your treasury, the inner treasures of your chest [Note: The edition reads “of the inner person … of the inner person.”]; your possessions, which neither thief, nor robber, nor powerful neighbor can take from you, where neither moth nor rust is to be feared, and with which even the shipwrecked person endured [Note: The edition reads: “and the shipwrecked person comes forth with them.”].

Thus you will also be the people of God among unrighteous Egyptians, while they suffer these things in their hearts and you remain unharmed in those very inner persons of yours, until the people are led out of Egypt [Note: I have supplied from the Codex of Eugipius’s Extracts: “while they suffer these things in their hearts and you remain unharmed in those very inner persons of yours, until the people are led out of Egypt.” The eye clearly wandered from “Egyptians” to the later “Egypt,” as in the preceding instances.] by a certain Exodus [Note: The edition has “by their Exodus.”]. This too is happening: that event happened once, but this does not cease to happen.

### XV.

[“For if we pay attention [Note: See Book 22, *Against Faustus*, chapters 71 and following.], we also despoil the Egyptians. For it was not without mystery that this happened. How do less intelligent people dare accuse God because he commanded the Israelites to ask the Egyptians for gold, silver, and clothing, and these things were given and taken away (Exodus 12:35)? These people would have been thieves if they had done it without God’s command. Let Your Charity attend: I say, they would have been thieves if they had not done it at God’s command; but because they did it at God’s command, they were not thieves.

“You no longer accuse them; you are ready to accuse God himself. It was their part to obey [Note: See Book 2 of *Questions on Exodus*, Question 6.]; with God lay the counsel of the one who commanded, for he knows what each person ought to suffer, who ought to suffer what, and for what merit.

“It would have been the clearest and most dreadful parricide for Abraham if he had struck his son of his own accord. But he did it laudably because he obeyed God’s command; and what would have been cruelty arising from spontaneous will became piety under God’s command” (Genesis 22).]

### XVI

[I wish to say something about the Acts of the Apostles. When Peter was confined in prison, an angel of salvation came to him and commanded his chains to come away from his hands (Acts 12).]

[Note: [Col. 0955] Something has certainly been omitted, perhaps an addition involving the word “chains.”]

He went out and followed the angel. He was freed from prison by the Lord’s command, by God’s authority. The next day the judge sought him in order to hear him; when he learned that he had departed, he ordered the prison guards to be led away. I mean, he ordered the soldiers, after they had been interrogated, to be led away; he pronounced against them the sentence, the law which seemed appropriate to him, unless they found Peter.

What do you say? Was Peter responsible for their death? Would he not have been perversely pious if he had opposed God’s will and said to the angel commanding him to leave: “I will not go out, lest these wretched men, the prison guards, die because of me”?

The answer would be made to him: “Leave these matters to the Creator. Since you are not the maker of a human being, you cannot be the judge of how he is to die. No one dies except one whom God wills to die.” The decision concerning death is left to God the Judge; nevertheless, the murderer’s desire is condemned. For here one must not consider what God judged, but what the evil people intended.

[Note: [Col. 0955] The words that follow are found repeated in Psalm 93, up to “our redemption.”]

Judas, after all, handed over the Son of God to suffering, and through the suffering of the Son of God all the nations were redeemed for salvation. Yet Judas was not given a reward on account of the salvation of the nations; rather, the punishment he deserved was repaid to him for his wickedness.

For if one considers Christ’s handing-over and not the intention of the one who handed him over, Judas did what God the Father did, of whom it is written: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32). Judas did what our Lord Christ himself did, of whom it is written: “He handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing fragrance”; and again: “Christ loved the Church and handed himself over for her, in order to sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:2, 25).

And yet we give thanks to God the Father, who did not spare his only Son but handed him over for us all. We give thanks to the Son of God himself, who handed himself over for us and thereby fulfilled the will of the Father. But we detest Judas, through whose deed God bestowed so great a benefit, and rightly we say: “The Lord repaid him according to his iniquity, and according to his wickedness he destroyed him” (Psalm 93:23).

For he did not hand Christ over for us, but for the silver for which he sold him, although Christ’s being sold is our redemption.

### XVII

[Therefore, brothers—no one, no one should question God. It is proud, impious, foolish. Restrain your desires; do nothing with an evil intention; be ready to obey, not to harm. Thus those men acted, and God acted. If they had committed theft, even then perhaps God would have wished Christ to suffer what they suffered, since he permitted those who acted to act. Yet he would have reserved punishment for thieves and would have imposed some temporal vengeance upon those who had suffered the theft.

But as it is, they did not act of their own initiative; God, in his just judgment, willed that it should happen. For if you weigh the matter, perhaps they did not take another’s gold, but demanded the wages due to them. Unjustly oppressed while making bricks in Egypt, they did not leave without compensation for the harsh labor of their servitude. Nevertheless, God did this for a definite reason.]

[Note: [Col. 0956] In the second book On Christian Teaching, they are said to have been enriched by the wealth of the Egyptians. Cyprian, Hilary, Victorinus, Optatus, and others say the same.]

If we are, like the people of Israel in Egypt, in this world, I dare to say to you—for I think that I am speaking to you by the Spirit of God—“Take gold, silver, and garments from the Egyptians.” Their gold is their wise men; their silver, their eloquent men; their garments, the variety of their languages.

Do we not see all these things in the Church? Does not the Church do this every day? How many wise men in the world believe in Christ? The gold has been taken from the Egyptians.

[Note: [Col. 0956] Perhaps he was speaking at the table of Cyprian, who had taught rhetoric before he was converted by Caecilius.]

The holy man whose table this is called was once either the gold or the silver of the Egyptians. The garments of the Egyptians, by which the senses are clothed in a certain manner, are their various languages. You see them migrate from Egypt to the people of God: “There are neither speech nor languages whose voices are not heard” (Psalm 18:4).

Here is the gold; here is the silver of the Egyptians. We leave, carrying what is ours as payment; for we did not labor in the mud of Egypt without cause.

Thus, brothers, whether there are things that can be explained by us or things that cannot yet be explained; whether you are able to understand them or are not yet able; whether they are understood in the manner in which we have expressed them or in some better manner—believe absolutely that “all these things happened to them figuratively, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10).

Would I, then, not pay attention to these matters? And would you, any spiritual Christian, not pay attention, and say that it happened without cause—that the magicians of Pharaoh failed at the third plague?

Would I seek nothing here? Would I think that it had been done or written in vain? Pharaoh’s magicians contend with Moses over rods becoming serpents, over water becoming blood; they make frogs, they do these things. They come to the third plague—that is, to those flies which are called *ciniphes*—and there they fail. Those who made serpents fail; those who made frogs fail; they fail before the flies.

It is certainly not without cause. Knock with me.

[Note: [Col. 0956] See Sermon 9.6; Sermon 251.5; and also Book 4 of On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis, chapters 13–20, where the sanctification of the seventh day is discussed.]

To what is this third plague opposed? To the third commandment of God, where the Sabbath is prescribed to the people, where rest is proclaimed, where sanctification is commended. For there it is said: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.”

Finally, even in the first works of the world God made the day, made heaven, earth, the sea, the lights, the stars, the animals from the waters, and man from the earth in his own image. He made all these things, but nowhere does anything sanctified sound forth. These things are completed in six days; the seventh day of God’s rest is sanctified. He does not sanctify the works; he sanctifies the rest (Genesis 2:3).

What shall we say? Just as, when we labor, rest is often sweeter to us than work, do we suppose that the same is true of God? We must not suppose this. We must not suppose that he made by laboring and did not create by commanding: “God said, ‘Let there be,’ and it was made.” If he made things in this way, man himself would not labor either.

Rather, on that day a certain rest from all our works was commended to us, so that after our good works we might understand that we would rest without end. For all the days there have an evening; the seventh does not. We work with an end; we rest without end.

There sanctification resounds with a great mystery, referring to the Holy Spirit. But as I say this, brothers, receive it with indulgence, I beg you: consider more what I am attempting than what I explain. I know who I am and to whom I speak: a human being speaking divine things to human beings (Isaiah 66:25).

Behold, strive with me; labor with me, so that you may rest with me—as much as the Lord grants, as much as he opens, as much as he signifies, as much as that Wisdom itself intimates, showing herself gladly to those who love her in her ways and meeting them in every providence.

The Sabbath day, the rest of God, is sanctified. There sanctification first resounds, as far as I perceive, as far as you too understand, and as far as we believe.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Here the reading of the edition resumes.]

No divine and true sanctification exists except from the Holy Spirit. For he was not called the Holy Spirit without reason in a particular sense. Although the Father is holy and the Son is holy, this name was nevertheless received as the Spirit’s proper name, so that the third Person in the Trinity might be called the Holy Spirit.

He himself rests upon the humble and quiet person, as upon his Sabbath. For this reason the number seven is also assigned to the Holy Spirit. Our Scriptures sufficiently indicate this. Let better people see to greater matters; let the better explain better things and the greater explain greater things, and let them say and explain something more subtle and more divine about this number seven.

Yet what is sufficient for the present, I see and remind you to see: this arrangement of the number seven is properly assigned to the Holy Spirit because sanctification resounds on the seventh day.

[Note: [Col. 0957] The edition reads: “to be found properly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0957] The edition reads: “on the seventh day.”]

And how do we prove that the sevenfold enumeration is assigned to the Holy Spirit?

[Note: [Col. 0957] The edition reads: “the arrangement of the number.”]

Isaiah says that the Spirit of God comes upon the faithful, upon the Christian, upon the member of Christ: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, the Spirit of the fear of God (Isaiah 11:2).

[Note: [Col. 0957] If you have followed the seven things, I have supplied the phrase “I traversed them,” as though the Spirit of God were descending to us, from the manuscript of the *Excerpta Eugippiana*. The lacuna was evident.]

If you have followed the seven things, I traversed them as though the Spirit of God were descending to us, from wisdom all the way to fear, so that we might ascend from fear to wisdom. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 1:7).

Thus the sevenfold Spirit and the one Spirit are one Spirit in a sevenfold arrangement. Do you want something more evident? Holy Scripture records that Pentecost, the feast day, was made from the weeks. You have this in the Scripture of Tobit, where it is also clearly said that this feast day comes from the weeks.

[Note: [Col. 0958] Tobit 2:1, according to the Old Latin version after the Seventy Interpreters.]

Seven times seven amounts to forty-nine; but, as though one were to return to the beginning, we are gathered into unity by the Holy Spirit, not scattered away from unity. Therefore, to the forty-nine is added one, the honor of unity, and they become fifty.

It is not, then, without cause that on the fiftieth day, through the Lord’s Ascension, the Holy Spirit came.

[Note: [Col. 0958] The edition reads: “rose again.”]

The Lord rises again; he ascends from the underworld, though not yet into heaven. From that resurrection, from that taking up from the underworld, fifty days are counted, and the Holy Spirit comes in the number fifty, as though celebrating his birthday among us.

For the Lord remained here with his disciples for forty days; on the fortieth day he ascended into heaven; and when ten days had been completed there—as though they were the ten signs of the commandments—

[Note: [Col. 0958] The edition reads: “the tenth sign of the commandments.”]

the Holy Spirit came, because no one fulfills the law except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, brothers, it is clear that this number seven belongs to the Holy Spirit.

But whoever does not adhere to the unity of Christ

[Note: [Col. 0958] I have supplied from the *Excerpta* manuscript: “and rebels against the unity of Christ.”]

and rebels against the unity of Christ must be understood not to possess the Holy Spirit. Contentions, disagreements, and divisions are produced only by those who are natural persons, of whom the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Then it is also written in the Epistle of the Apostle Jude: “These are the ones who separate themselves,” natural, not having the Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0958] The edition adds: “rebuking them, he was speaking”; “these are the ones who separate themselves.” Jude 1:19.]

What could be clearer, what more evident? Let them come, even if they believe the same things as we do, in order to receive the Holy Spirit; yet they cannot possess him so long as they are enemies of unity.

The Apostle compares these people to Pharaoh’s magicians: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:5 and following). By possessing the appearance of piety they performed similar things, but by denying its power

[Note: [Col. 0958] The edition reads *qui* instead of *in*.]

they failed at the third sign.

### XVIII

[But continue to ask with me why at the third sign. They would have failed at the second; they would have failed at the fourth. What difference does it make where they failed, since they were destined to fail? Why, then, at the third?

[Note: [Col. 0958] This explanation is often abrupt, perhaps also longer than it is here. Those familiar with Augustine know that this does not weaken the sermon’s authenticity—or at least they know it from reading Erasmus’s preface to Augustine’s works.]

But first see whether the Apostle Paul compared those heretics with those magicians, as I promised. “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power—and avoid these people.” Among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, driven by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.

For they continually hear testimony about the Catholic Church, and they do not wish to come to the Catholic Church. They are always saying—for they do indeed always hear it—“In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 1:2). Do they not always hear: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8)? Do they not always hear: “All the families of the nations shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm 21:58)? Do they not always hear: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:18)?

They always hear these things, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.

Now see what I promised. What follows does the Apostle say? “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth; people corrupted in mind, rejected with regard to the faith. But they will make no further progress, for their folly will be evident to all, as that of those men also was” (2 Timothy 3:8 and following).

Now see why they failed at the third sign. Remember that those who oppose unity do not have the Holy Spirit.

The first three commandments of the Decalogue are understood to belong to love of God, while the remaining seven are understood to belong to love of neighbor. Thus, on the two tablets of the law and in the ten commandments, those two commandments are held as summaries: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matthew 22:37–38).

Let us therefore refer the first three commandments to love of God.

Which three are first? The first: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” The plague opposed to this is the water changed into blood, because the highest principle of the Creator was brought down to the likeness of human flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0959] The edition reads “water changed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0959] The edition reads “to an imitation,” and in the annotations, “imitation.” Eugippius agrees with our manuscript.]

The second commandment: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” As I understand it, this pertains to the Word of God, who is the Son of God. For “there is one God, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist” (Romans 11:36). Against the Word: frogs. See—against the word, frogs; against reason, noise; against truth, vanity.

[Note: [Col. 0959] The edition reads “See.”]

The third commandment concerns the Sabbath and pertains to the Spirit because of the sanctification that first resounded on the Sabbath, which shortly before we commended to you with all the force we could.

The plague opposed to this commandment is the unrest of the flies, born from corruption and rushing into the eyes. Therefore those who were enemies of unity and did not possess the Holy Spirit failed at this third sign. For the Holy Spirit produces this as punishment: grace produces one thing, punishment another; one thing is produced by filling, another by abandoning.

Finally, so that we may now recognize clearly, with Pharaoh’s magicians themselves confessing it, by what name the Spirit of God is called, let us see what name he receives.

[Note: [Col. 0960] The edition adds “receives.”]

When the Jews were reviling the Lord and had said, “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons,” he answered them: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:24).

Another Evangelist relates the same saying in this way: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 10:20).

[Note: [Col. 0960] The edition reads “by the finger.”]

What one Evangelist called the Spirit of God, another called the finger of God. Therefore the Spirit of God is the finger of God.

For this reason the law was given, written by the finger of God. This law was given on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after the killing of the lamb, when the Jewish people celebrated Passover.

Fifty days after the killing of the lamb had been completed, the law written by the finger of God was given. Fifty days after the killing of Christ had been completed, the Holy Spirit came.

Thanks be to the Lord, who conceals providently and opens gently.

Now see that Pharaoh’s magicians also confess this most clearly: when they failed at the third sign, they said, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:10).

Let us praise the Lord, the giver of understanding, the giver of the word. If these things were not generated by mysteries, they would not be sought diligently; and if they were not sought diligently, they would not be found so sweetly.]

## SERMON II

[Note: [Col. 0960] The edition gives the title: “On the Day of His Ordination.” That “birthday” means the annual anniversary of a bishop’s consecration, and that it is a solemn day, is attested by Saint Paulinus in Letter 20 to Delphinus; Pope Sixtus in his letter to Cyril, in the year 430; Leo the Great in Sermons 1 and 3; Pope Hilary in Letter 2 to the bishops of Tarragona; and Augustine himself in Letter 255 and elsewhere.]

### On His Personal Birthday

The manuscript codex numbered 17, mentioned above, indicates that Sermons 339 and 40 of the Maurist edition have been torn apart from this single sermon.

As I considered how it happened that these codices—especially those in Gaul—are scattered and incomplete, and that Amerbach, Erasmus, the Parisian editors, the Louvain editors, and the Maurists arranged their editions according to them, this thought occurred to me, perhaps not implausible.

Since, as the Maurists themselves admit (preface to volume 5), Caesarius of Arles, already advanced in age, was accustomed to order the priests and deacons to have read not only his own sermons but also those of Augustine—sometimes mutilated, and at other times furnished with a new beginning and conclusion—it may be that one of them separated the principal arguments of the sermon according to what was convenient for him, omitting those passages that connected the portion he had reproduced with what had been omitted.

Since this was not done with the requisite intelligence, there still remain indications that support the authority of our codex, which joins those separated members into one whole.

Meanwhile, the sermon, abbreviated at Arles and thus transmitted publicly, first spread through the Gallic codices and then through distant regions to which Caesarius, as is read in Book 1 of his Life, sent the same priests to instruct them in what they should preach in their churches.

It will therefore be worthwhile to restore to the sermon its original integrity, which has until now been lacking in the printed libraries.

### I

[Note: [Col. 0961] The edition reads “this day.”]

Today, brothers, reminds me to think more attentively about my burden. Even though I ought to think about its weight day and night, I do not know how this anniversary day presses it upon my senses, so that I cannot entirely avoid thinking about it.

And the more years are added—or rather, taken away—and bring us nearer to the final day, which will certainly come one day without question, the sharper my thought becomes and the more full of goads: what account will I be able to render to the Lord our God on your behalf?

[Note: [Col. 0961] The edition reads “as the years increase.”]

For this is the difference between each of you and us: you are concerned almost exclusively about yourselves when you will render an account; we are concerned both about ourselves and about all of you.

Therefore the burden is greater. But when it is carried well, it wins greater glory; when carried unfaithfully,

[Note: [Col. 0961] The edition reads “when it is performed.”]

it plunges one into the most terrible punishment.

What, then, must I do above all today except commend my danger to you, so that you may be my joy?

My danger is this: that I should pay attention to how you praise me and disregard how you live.

He knows—before whose eyes I speak, indeed before whose eyes I think—that I am not so much delighted by popular praise as stimulated and troubled by the question of how those who praise me live.

I do not want to be praised by those who live badly; I shrink from it, I detest it; it is a grief to me, not a pleasure. But if I say that I do not want to be praised by those who live well, I lie; if I say that I do want it, I fear that I may be more desirous of emptiness than of substance.

What, then, shall I say? I neither wholly want it nor wholly reject it. I do not wholly want it, lest I perish through human praise; I do not wholly reject it, lest those to whom I preach become ungrateful.

My burden is the one you have just heard about when the prophet Ezekiel was read. It is too little that this day itself reminds us to think about that same burden; in addition, such a reading is recited that it strikes great fear into us, so that we may consider what we are carrying—for unless the one who imposed it carries it with us, we fail.

Behold, you heard: “The land upon which I bring the sword,” he says, “and it appoints for itself a watchman who sees the sword coming upon it, and he speaks and gives warning.”

[Note: [Col. 0961] The Greek of the Seventy is: ἐφ’ ἣν ἂν ἐπάγω, “upon which I may bring,” with which the Old Latin version very often agrees.]

[Note: [Col. 0961] The edition reads: “When it comes.”]

“But when the sword comes, if that watchman is silent, and the sword comes upon the sinner and kills him, that sinner will indeed die for his iniquity, but I will require his blood from the watchman’s hand.

“But if he sees the sword coming, and blows the trumpet and gives warning,

[Note: [Col. 0961] The edition reads “and announces.”]

and the one to whom he gives warning

[Note: [Col. 0961] The edition reads “to whom he announces.”]

does not take heed, that person will die in his iniquity, but the watchman will have saved his own soul.

“And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the children of Israel” (Ezekiel 33:2 and following).

He explained what he meant by “the sword”; he explained what he meant by “the watchman”; he explained what he had meant by “death.”

[Note: [Col. 0962] The edition reads “what he had said.”]

He did not allow us to excuse our negligence in the obscurity of the reading.

“Therefore,” he says, “I have appointed you as a watchman. If I say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you remain silent, and he dies in his sin, he will indeed die in his sin deservedly and justly, but I will require his blood from your hand.

[Note: [Col. 0962] The edition reads “I will require.”]

“But if you say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he does not take heed, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your own soul.”

[And he adds in words what he wishes to be said to the people of Israel: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘Why do you say among yourselves, “Our iniquities are upon us; we waste away in our sins; how can we live?”’ Thus says the Lord: ‘I do not desire the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked turn back from his evil way and live.’”

This is what he wanted us to announce to you. If we do not announce it, we shall have to render a bad account of this watchmanship. But if we announce it, we have done what pertains to us.

You must look to yourselves; we are now secure.

But how are we secure? You are in danger and dying. We do not want our glory to consist in your punishment. Security has indeed been given, but love makes us concerned.

Behold, we speak, and you know that I have always spoken; you know that I have never kept silent: “Thus says God: I do not desire the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked turn back from his most evil way and live.”

What was the wicked man saying? He spoke the words of the wicked and sinful: “Our iniquities are upon us; we waste away in our sins; how can we live?”

The sick man despairs, but the physician promises hope. The human being said to himself, “How can I live?” (Romans 3:4). God says, “You can live.”

If every human being is a liar and God alone is truthful, let what the human being said be erased and let what God said be written.

Do not despair. You can live—not on the basis of your past evils, but on the basis of your future good deeds. You will erase evils if you turn away from evil. Everything, whether good or evil, is erased by a change.

From a good life you turned toward an evil one: you erased the good. From an evil life you advanced toward a good one: you erased the evil.

See what you attend to, what you take in. Two treasures have been prepared for you. Whatever you deposit, that you will find. God is a faithful custodian; he will return to you what you have done.

But there are others who do not perish through despair. They do not say to themselves, “Our iniquities are upon us; we waste away in our sins; how shall we be able to live?” Rather, they deceive themselves in another way.

They flatter themselves because of God’s excessive mercy, so that they may never be corrected. For this is what they say: “Even if we do evil, even if we commit iniquities, even if we live luxuriously and criminally, even if we despise the poor and needy, even if pride exalts us, even if we feel no sorrow of heart over our evils—is God going to destroy so great a multitude and save only a few?”

[Note: [Col. 0962] See Sermon 20.3–4, where similar material occurs.]

There are therefore two dangers: one that we have just heard from the Prophet, and another that the Apostle did not leave unmentioned.

For against those who die in despair—like gladiators already assigned to the sword, panting after pleasures and living wickedly, as though they already despised their condemned souls

[Note: [Col. 0963] Something may be missing.]

—he says that they say to themselves: “Our iniquities are upon us; we waste away in our sins; how shall we be able to live?”

But concerning the other danger the Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience?” (Romans 2:4).

He speaks against those who say: “God is good; God is merciful. He will not destroy so great a multitude of sinners and save only a few. For if he did not want them to exist, they would not live. Since they commit so many evils and yet live, surely, if God were displeased with them, he would immediately remove them from the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0963] See Sermon 18.3; and On Psalm 101, Sermon 1.10; and On Psalm 144, section 11. See also Book 1 Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 17, section 34.]

Against such people the Apostle says: “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works.”

To whom does he say this? To those who say, “God is good; he will not repay.” He will most certainly repay each person according to his works.

What are you doing? You are storing up—what? Wrath. Add wrath to wrath; increase the treasure. What you store up will be repaid to you; the one to whom you entrust it will not cheat you.

But if you deposit good works in another treasure—fruits of righteousness, or self-restraint, or virginity, or conjugal chastity; if you keep yourself free from fraud, murder, and crime; if you remember the needy, because you too are needy; if you remember the poor, because you too are poor—no matter how abundantly you possess wealth, you are clothed in the rags of flesh.

If, thinking and acting in this way, you deposit these things in the good treasure for the day of judgment, the one who cheats no one and will repay each according to his works will say to you: “Take what you deposited, because it has increased. When you were depositing it, you did not see it, but I was keeping it in order to repay it.”

For indeed, brothers, each person knows what he deposits in the treasure because he deposits it, but he does not see it after he has deposited it.

Imagine a treasure buried in the earth, with a single entrance or a small opening through which you can put things. Little by little, whatever you acquire you deposit, and you do not see it. If the earth preserves what you deposited without your seeing it, will the one who made heaven and earth not preserve it for you?

## II.

Therefore, brothers, relieve me, relieve my burden, and carry it with me; live well. Today we must feed our fellow poor, and we must share human kindness with them.

[Note: The edition adds “the Nativity of the Lord is approaching.” Is this to be attributed to the negligence of the copyist, who omitted the words “the Nativity of the Lord is approaching” from the manuscript? Or were they introduced into so many Gallican codices by some minister of Caesarius, or by someone else—who knows?—speaking about the bishop’s ordination around the feast of the Nativity? I shall say what I think; the following conjecture seems probable. The Maurists relegate to an appendix in volume 5 a Sermon 116 attributed to Caesarius from the Corbie Codex. In section 6 it reads: “The Nativity of the Lord is approaching . . . invite the poor more frequently to your banquets,” and in section 3: “Let us frequently invite the poor to the banquet before all else.” The fact that Caesarius was proclaimed bishop in December is not ruled out by the writer of his life, who, after saying that Aeonius died on 17 August, states that Caesarius was placed over the Church of Arles not long afterward. By these words I would rather understand an interval of a few months than the space of a few days, as the Bollandists have conjectured. Accordingly, one of Caesarius’ deacons or priests, speaking about his ordination as Christmas approached, stitched the bishop’s saying together with Augustine’s sermon, changing the word “today” into “the Nativity of the Lord is approaching,” so that he could speak about banquets for the poor, taking the opportunity from the metaphor of spiritual nourishment with which Augustine had played so humanely. But, you may ask, why do I deny this to the bishop of Hippo? Nowhere, so far as I know, did the holy Doctor speak of this particular preparation for the Lord’s Nativity; this would therefore be the one place in which he insisted upon it. Yet who, even minimally acquainted with Augustine’s reading, would say that he could have urged the necessity of such a preparation furtively and hurriedly in a single clause, rather than dwelling on it at length? For anyone reading his writings sees that the very man who, in speculative matters, demands attentive hearers also requires in practical and moral matters people capable of sustained effort—I shall use Erasmus’ words (Preface to Augustine’s Works)—so that the judgments on which he himself thought one must insist might always please them equally. Moreover, I shall find it difficult to believe that the holy Doctor preferred, on that day, to borrow the burden of spiritually feeding the faithful from a coming solemnity rather than from the ministry of a shepherd, about which he had said so much beforehand. Yet, without realizing it, I offend Pagius, the Bollandists, the Maurists, Tillemont, and all the leading critics, who most willingly support the edition’s text, so that from it they may conclude that the bishop of Hippo’s ordination took place in December. For determining this date, I quote not an opinion from my own storehouse but that of Saint Prosper, followed by Cassiodorus in his Chronicle and by Hermannus Contractus in Canisius. Tillemont himself admits it to be certain on the authority of Dom Pontac (Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire ecclésiastique, vol. 13, note 24, §85). That worthy disciple of Augustine testifies in the second part of his Chronicle that, while Theodosius was still ruling with his sons Arcadius and Honorius, and while Olybrius and Probinus were consuls—that is, in the year 395—that illustrious ornament of the Church was raised to the See of Hippo. But since Socrates says in Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 1, that Theodosius died on 17 January of that same year, and all the chroniclers agree unanimously, Augustine was certainly proclaimed bishop of Hippo in January. All these considerations therefore establish the truth of the Cassinese Codex, which reads “today” instead of “the Nativity of the Lord is approaching.”]

As for you, my dishes are these words. I am not sufficient to feed everyone with substantial and visible bread; I feed from where I myself am fed. I am a minister, not the master of the household; I set before you what I too live on, from the Lord’s treasury, from the banquets of that master of the household who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9).

If I were to set bread before you, each of you would take away a piece after the bread had been broken; and if I set out a great deal, very little would reach each person. But now, what I say is possessed wholly and entirely by all, and each person possesses it all. Have you divided among yourselves the syllables of my word? Have you each taken away individual words from the sermon itself as it was delivered? [Note: How is the sermon said to have been “delivered,” when it has scarcely extended to half a page of the edition? Passages had therefore been removed which the Cassinese manuscript restores.] Every one of you heard the whole of it. But let him consider how he heard it, because I am a distributor, not a collector.

If I do not distribute and keep the money, the Gospel terrifies me. For I could say: “Why should I weary myself for human beings? Why should I say to the wicked: Do not act wickedly? Live this way? Act this way? Stop acting this way? Why should I burden myself for human beings? I have received instructions about how to live. I shall live as I was ordered, as I was commanded. I shall dispense what I received [Note: The edition reads: “how”]; why should I give an account concerning others [Note: The edition reads: “that I should give account concerning others”]?” The Gospel terrifies me.

No one could defeat me in this utterly idle security: nothing is better, nothing sweeter than to examine the divine treasury without any disturbance. It is sweet; it is good. But to preach, reprove, correct, build up, and be concerned for each person is a great burden, a great weight, a great labor. Who would not shrink from that labor? But the Gospel terrifies me.

A certain servant came forward and said to his master: “I knew you were a difficult man, reaping where you did not sow. I kept your money; I did not want to distribute it. Take what is yours; if anything is lacking, point it out and judge me [Note: The edition reads: “point it out”]; if it is intact, do not trouble me” (Luke 19:21 and following). But he replied: “Wicked servant, I condemn you from your own mouth” [Note: The edition reads “I shall condemn you.”] (Luke 19:22). Why this? Because you called me greedy; why did you neglect my profits?

“But I was afraid to give it away, lest I lose it.”

“Is that what you say?” For this is often said: “Why do you reprove him? What you say is wasted on him; he does not listen to you.”

“And I,” he says, “did not want to give it away, lest I lose your money.”

He says to him: “If you had given my money, and I had come and demanded it with interest, I had appointed you as a distributor, not a collector. If you undertake the distribution, you would leave the collection to me.”

Therefore, with this fear in mind, let each person consider how he receives. If I, who distribute, am afraid, should the one who receives be secure?

Let the one who was wicked yesterday be good today. This is my distribution: let the one who was wicked yesterday be good today. He was wicked yesterday, and he has not died. If he had died wicked, he would have gone where he could not return [Note: The edition reads: “If he had died, and had been wicked, he would have gone …”]. He was wicked yesterday; he lives today. Let the fact that he lives benefit him; let him not live wickedly.

Why, then, does he want to add today’s evil to yesterday’s? Do you want to have a long life, but not a good one? Who can endure evil for a long time—or even an evil meal? So deeply has the blindness of the mind grown callous, so deaf is the inner person, that he wants to possess every good thing except himself.

Do you want to have an estate? I deny that you want to have a bad estate. Do you want to have a wife? Only a good one [Note: The edition has “you do not want” in place of “only.”]. A house? Only a good one. Why should I go through each item? You do not want to have a bad shoe, yet you want to have a bad life—as though a bad shoe harmed you more than a bad life.

When a bad and constricting shoe hurts you, you sit down, take it off [Note: The edition reads: “you unshoe yourself”], discard it, repair it, or change it so that it does not injure your toe, and then shoe yourself [Note: The edition adds: “A bad life is …”]. You do not take care to correct the bad life by which you lose your soul.

But I clearly see where you are deceived. A harmful shoe causes pain; a harmful life gives pleasure. The one hurts; the other delights. But what delights for a time later causes worse pain, whereas what causes salutary pain for a time later makes one rejoice with infinite pleasure and abundant joy [Note: The edition adds: “According to what is written: ‘Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.’ And: ‘Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be filled.’”].

“Look at the one rejoicing and the one suffering: that rich man rejoicing, and that poor man suffering. The one feasted; the other was tormented. The one was surrounded by servants and honored; the other was licked by dogs. The one was made more brutal by his banquets; the other was not filled even with crumbs” [Note: See Sermon 1 on Psalm 48, section 10, and Sermon 36, section 6.].

Pleasure passed away; need passed away. The rich man’s good things and the poor man’s evils passed away; evils came upon the rich man, and good things came to the poor man. What passed away could not be recalled; what followed did not diminish.

The rich man burned in hell; the poor man rejoiced in Abraham’s bosom. Earlier the poor man had desired a crumb from the rich man’s table; afterward the rich man desired a drop from the poor man’s finger. The former man’s want was ended with the completion of his satisfaction; the latter man’s pleasure was followed by pain that was completed without end. Thirst followed banquets, pain followed pleasure, fire followed purple [Note: Perhaps something is missing, for there is no antecedent to which the words “This is the banquet” may refer.].

This is the banquet which Lazarus appeared to possess in Abraham’s bosom. This is what we want you all to possess; this is what we want us all to possess together.
