Would it be a banquet that I presented to you if I invited you all and this church were filled with tables of banqueters? These things are transitory. Think about what I say, so that you may come to those banquets which you will never finish.

For there no one is made ill by feasting, nor are the banquets themselves of such a kind that they nourish us by their corruption and restore us by their exhaustion. Those banquets will remain whole, and we shall be restored by them.

If our eye is nourished by light, while the light itself does not fail, what will those banquets be like: the contemplation of truth, the sight of eternity, the praises of God, the security of happiness, a stable mind, an immortal body, our flesh wasting away under no old age, and no hunger loosening our soul?

There no one grows, and no one diminishes. There no one is born, because no one dies; and there you are compelled to perform none of the works which we now urge you to perform.

For today you heard [Note: The Gospel read that day was Luke, chapter 14, as is frequently recorded in ancient lectionaries.] the Lord saying—and he said it to all of us: “When you hold a banquet, do not invite your friends.” He showed where you should be generous: “Do not invite relatives who have the means to repay you; instead invite the poor, the weak, the blind, the lame, and the needy, who have no means to repay you” (Luke 14:12).

And will you lose your reward? “It will be repaid to you in the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14:14). You distribute, he says; I receive, record, and repay. God said this, and he encouraged us to do these things, and he will repay us.

When he has repaid us, who will take it away from us? If God is for us, who is against us (Rom. 8:31)? We were sinners, and he gave us the death of Christ as a gift; if we live justly, will he deceive us? For Christ did not die for the righteous but for the ungodly (ibid., vv. 5–6).

If he gave the death of his Son to the wicked, what does he reserve for the righteous? What does he reserve for them? He has nothing better to reserve for them than what he gave for them. What did he give for them? He did not spare his own Son (ibid., v. 32). What does he reserve for them? The Son himself—but God to be enjoyed, not a human being to die.

Behold what God calls you to. But how do you attend? To what do you deign to attend [Note: Thus in the Codex], and how? But when you come, will this be said to you: “Break your bread for the hungry; if you see someone naked, clothe him”? Will this passage be read to you? “When you hold a banquet, invite the lame, the blind, the needy, and the destitute” (Isa. 58:7).

There no one will be destitute; there will be no lame person, no blind person, no weak person, no stranger, no naked person. All will be healthy, all vigorous, all abounding, all clothed in eternal light. Whom will you see there as a stranger? Our homeland itself is there; here we are strangers.

Let us desire it, let us do what is commanded, so that we may receive what is promised. Rather, I did not put that well; I correct what I said: far be it from us to demand what is promised; we shall receive it freely. For if we demand it, it would be as though God did not wish to give it. He certainly will give it; he will defraud no one.

Consider this, my brothers: see how many good things our Lord God gives to the wicked—light, life, health, springs, fruits, generations, and often honors, high positions, and powers. All these things he gives both to the good and to the wicked.

Do we think that he reserves nothing for the good, who gives so many good things even to the wicked? Let no one bring this thought into his heart. My brothers, God reserves great good things for the good, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9).

You cannot think of it before you receive it; you will be able to see it when you have received it. Before you receive it, you cannot think of it.

What is it that you want to see [Note: Something has been omitted, as is clear from Sermon 331, section 3: “The eye does not see, because there is no colour; the ear does not hear, because there is no sound,” etc.]? It is not a cithara, not a flute, not a sound that produces pleasure in the ears. What do you want to think about? It has not entered the human heart.

“What shall I do? I neither see, nor hear, nor think. What shall I do?”

Believe: there is a great shortcut. Faith is a great vessel in which you can receive a great gift. Prepare a vessel for yourself, because you must approach a great fountain; prepare a vessel for yourself.

“What does ‘prepare’ mean?”

Let your faith grow; let your faith increase; let your faith be strengthened. Let your faith not be slippery and made of mud; let your faith not be broken by the tribulations of this world, but fired and hardened.

When you have done this and possess faith like a suitable, capacious, firm vessel, God will fill it. For he will not say to you what people say to someone begging and saying, “Please give me some wine,” and the other replies, “I will; come, and I shall do it.”

The man brings a jar and says, “I have come as you ordered.” The other says, “I thought you would bring one small flask; what have you brought, or why have you come? I am not able to give so much. Take back the larger vessel you brought, and bring something small. Bring me something that my poverty can supply.”

God does not say this. He is full, and you will be full; and when he has filled you, he himself will possess as much as he possessed before he filled you. God’s gifts are abundant; you will find nothing like them on earth. Believe, and you will discover this.

“But not now?”

“And when?” Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, so that when you have received you may say: “You have put gladness in my heart.”

[Note: Here begins Sermon 40 in the edition, entitled “On the same passage of Ecclesiasticus 5:8: Do not delay to turn to God,” concerning those who postpone conversion from day to day, some of whom perish through false hope and others through despair. This sermon is produced by the same codices from which Sermon 339 had been drawn.]

Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.

[Note: The edition begins Sermon 40 as follows: “Frequently, brothers, we have sung with the Psalmist: ‘Wait…’”]

What does “wait for the Lord” mean? It means that you should receive when he gives, not demand when you wish. The time for giving has not yet arrived. He endured you; endure him.

What do I mean by saying, “He endured you; endure him”? If you now live justly, if you have now turned to him, if your past deeds now displease you, if you have now chosen a good and new life, do not hurry to demand your reward. He endured you so that you might change your bad life; endure him so that he may crown your good life.

If he had not endured you, there would be no one for him to give to. Therefore endure, because you have been sustained.

[Note: Let sharp-nosed judges read, reread, and finally explain the connection between this first period, as it lies in the edition and serves as the beginning, and the remaining parts of the sermon. If they cannot do so by any effort, let them admit that the sermon is lacking in the edition’s completeness; that this first period is connected with what precedes it; and that the discussion of excessive confidence and despair is here urged anew—both because it was a moral subject and because he had already said that the whole rationale of his pastoral concern lay in announcing it.]

But you who do not want to be corrected—O whoever you are here who still do not want to be corrected! As though there were only one, I should rather have said: “Whoever you are here.” Nevertheless, you who are here—if indeed you are here—and who have not decided to be corrected, I shall speak as though to one person.

Whoever you are who do not want to be corrected, what are you promising yourself? Do you perish through despair, or through hope?

Whoever perishes through despair, you say this in your heart: “My iniquity is upon me; I waste away in my sins. What hope do I have of living?” Hear the Prophet saying: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his most evil way and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

Do you perish through hope? [Note: The edition reads: “Whoever perishes through hope says this in his heart,” omitting the questions.]

What does it mean, to perish through hope? You say this in your heart: “God is good; God is merciful; he forgives everything; he will not repay evil with evil.”

Hear the Apostle saying: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?”

What, then, remains?

[Note: The edition adds: “For if we have gained anything with you…”]

It is as though you have accomplished something if what I said has entered your heart. I see what answer is made to me [Note: The edition reads: “you answer me”]:

“It is true. I do not despair, so as to perish through despair; nor do I hope falsely, so as to perish through hope. I do not say to myself, ‘My iniquity is upon me; I have no hope’; nor do I say to myself, ‘God is good; he will repay evil to no one.’ I do not say that; I do not say that. The Prophet presses me; the Apostle presses me.”

[Note: The edition reads: “The Apostle presses me.”]

And what do you say?

“For a little while longer I shall live as I wish.”

These are the people who weary us. They are numerous; they are troublesome.

“For a little while longer I shall live as I wish; afterward, when I have corrected myself”—for what the Prophet said is certainly true: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his most evil way and live.” When I have turned, he will erase all my evils. Why should I not add something to my pleasures and live as long as I wish, as I wish, intending afterward to turn to God?”

Why do you say this, brother? Why?

“Because God promised me forgiveness if I change.”

I see it; I know it [Note: The edition reads: “God promised”]. He promised forgiveness through the holy Prophet; he promises it through me, his least servant.

[Note: The edition reads the following words thus: “God promised forgiveness through the holy Prophet; he promises it through me, his least servant. It is true, etc.”]

Does he promise? What he promises is true; he promised it through his only Son.

But why do you want to add evil days to evil days? Let the evil of the day be sufficient for it. Yesterday was an evil day; today is also evil; tomorrow also will be evil.

Or do you think the days are good when you satisfy your pleasures? When you nourish your heart amid luxury? When you lie in wait for another’s chastity? When by fraud you distress your neighbor? When you deny what has been entrusted to you? When you swear falsely for money? When you provide yourself with a good meal?

Do you think that, because you enjoy a good meal, you are therefore having a good day? How can a day be good when the person is bad? Do you want to add evil days to evil days?

“Please let me have some time,” he says.

“Why?”

“Because God promised me forgiveness.”

But no one promised you that you would live tomorrow—or show me where it is written. You show me the Prophet, the Gospel, and the Apostle, because when you turn, God erases all your iniquities. Show me where tomorrow has been promised to you, and then live wickedly tomorrow.

Although, my brother, I should not have had to say this to you. Perhaps your life will be long. If it is long, let it be good. Why do you want to have a long and bad life? Or perhaps it will not be long. The long life that ought to delight you is the one that has no end. Or perhaps it will be long; and what harm will there be if you have lived well for a long time?

You want to live wickedly for a long time; you do not want to live well. And yet no one promised you tomorrow.

Correct yourself. Hear from Scripture [Note: These are the words deliberately omitted by the person who mutilated the discourse so that he might speak only of conversion. The word *natalitiarius* is absent from the glossaries.].

Do not despise me as though I were a *natalitiarius* (“anniversary preacher”; the precise term is uncertain). I am speaking to you from Scripture. “Do not delay to turn to the Lord.”

These words are not mine, but they are also mine. If I love them, they are mine; love them, and they are yours as well. The sermon that I am now delivering is holy Scripture. If you despise it, it is your adversary.

But hear the Lord saying: “Come to terms quickly with your adversary” (Matt. 5:25).

[Note: Here again are words deliberately omitted; meanwhile, observe that “Nativity” means the anniversary of the ordination. It is clear from what follows that the terrifying sentence here was spoken from Ecclesiasticus, not from Matthew.]

[“What is this terrifying saying? You have come for joy; today is said to be the bishop’s anniversary. Should I put forward something that would sadden you? Rather, I put forward something that will make the one who loves rejoice and the contemptuous person grow angry. It is better for me to sadden the contemptuous person than to defraud the faithful.”]

## III.

Let everyone hear. I recite words from Scripture—

[Note: The edition reads: “Words of divine Scripture.”]

O bad procrastinator, O wicked seeker of tomorrow, hear the Lord speaking; hear holy Scripture proclaiming. I am a watchman concerning this passage:

“Do not delay to turn to God, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will suddenly come, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclesiasticus 5:8–9).

[Note: The edition reads the following words in this way: “Did I write this? Can I erase it? If I erase it, I fear being erased…”]

What have I done? Can I erase it? I fear being erased. Can I keep silent about it? I fear that it will be kept silent.

[Note: The edition reads: “Can I keep silent?”]

I am compelled to proclaim it. Terrified, I terrify others. Fear with me, so that you may rejoice with me.

“Do not delay to turn to God.”

Lord, see that I am speaking. Lord, you know that you terrified me when your Prophet was being read. Lord, you know my trembling in that chair when your Prophet was being read.

[Note: The edition reads: “My fear.”]

[Note: See Augustine saying that he was a watchman, that he had been terrified, and that he had been terrified by the Prophet when the passage was read. But nothing is said about the watchman or about that reading from Ezekiel in this Sermon 40 of the edition, but only in Sermon 339. Therefore the two sermons must be joined; therefore the reliability of our Codex, which connects them, is certain.]

Behold, I say: “Do not delay to turn to God, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will suddenly come, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” But I do not want him to destroy you. I do not want you to say to me: “I want to perish.”

Because I do not want it, what I want is better than what you want.

[Note: The edition reads: “Therefore what I want is better.”]

If your lethargic father were ill in your hands, and you, a young man, were attending an old man who was sick, and the doctor said, “Your father is in danger; this sleep is a kind of deadly stupor. Watch him; do not allow him to sleep,” then if you saw him sleeping, you would wake him. If waking him were not enough, you would pinch him; and if that were still not enough, you would prick him, so that your father would not die.

You would be present, a young man burdensome to an old man. As he sank into the sweet illness and closed his eyes under the pressure of that stupor, you would cry out to him:

“Do not sleep!”

But he would say: “Leave me; I want to sleep.”

And you would say: “But the doctor said that if he wants to sleep, he must not sleep.”

But he would say: “Please, leave me; I want to die.”

“But I do not want you to,” you say, a son to his father.

To whom? To one who, of course, desires to die.

And yet you want to postpone your father’s death and to live somewhat longer with your old father who is dying.

The Lord cries out to you: “Do not sleep, lest you sleep forever. Wake up, so that you may live with me and have a Father whom you will never carry out for burial.” And you are deaf.

What, then, have I done as a watchman? I am free; I do not burden you. I know that some will say: “What did he want to say to us? He terrified us, burdened us, and made us guilty.”

Rather, I wanted to free you from guilt.

It is shameful; it is disgraceful. I do not want to call it evil; I do not want to call it dangerous; I do not want to call it destructive. It is disgraceful for me to deceive you if God does not deceive me.

The Lord threatens death to the wicked—to the most depraved, the fraudulent, the criminal, the adulterous, those who pursue pleasures, those who despise him, those who grumble about the times and do not change their ways. The Lord threatens them with death; he threatens them with hell; he threatens them with eternal destruction.

What do they want me to promise, when he does not promise it?

Behold, an administrator will give you security.

[Note: The edition reads: “He will give.”]

What good is it to you if the master of the household does not accept it? I am an administrator; I am a servant.

“Do you want me to say to you: Live as you wish; the Lord will not destroy you?” The administrator has given you security. The administrator’s security is worthless.

Would that the Lord gave you security and I made you anxious! For the Lord’s security has value even if I do not want it; but mine has no value if he does not want it.

What security is there, brothers—whether mine or yours—except that we listen attentively and diligently to the Lord’s commands and faithfully await his promises?

In the things by which we are wearied, because we are human beings, let us implore his help; let us groan toward him. Let our prayers not be for secular things, things that pass away, things transitory and vanishing like vapor. Let our prayers instead be for the fulfillment of justice itself and sanctification for the sake of God’s name—not for conquering our neighbors, but for conquering lust; not for satisfying it, but for subduing greed.

[Note: The edition reads: “For healing the flesh.”]

Let our prayers arise from this. Within us, let them help us as we struggle, so that they may crown us when we conquer.

## SERMON III

[Note: The Maurists entitle it “On Contempt for the World.” It was delivered during the Easter season and on the solemnity of the holy martyrs of Thuburbo, who are two according to Sirmond—Felicity and Perpetua—and three according to Henri Valois—Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, as the same Maurist Fathers testify.]

### On Contempt for Temporal Things

Manuscript Codex no. 173, entitled *Volume 12 of Augustine’s Works: Treatises and Sermons*, contains works and sermons, the greater part of which agrees in every respect with the editions, while the rest, besides variant readings, exhibit passages absent from the editions.

From among these latter materials I selected one filled with almost innumerable variants. Since I do not dare to decide whether these passages arose from notaries who copied too hastily and later revised what they had written, or whether Augustine himself introduced them—perhaps having first delivered the sermon ex tempore and afterward written it down, as he acknowledges having done elsewhere in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*—I thought it better to leave the judgment to learned readers, so that from this one example they may determine what should be thought about the other sermons written in the same Codex.

Codex no. 219 as well, entitled *Didymus on the Holy Spirit and Other Works*, contains this sermon, differing in no respect from the earlier codex. The Maurists published it in volume 5 as no. 345, copied from the Colbertine and Sirmondian manuscripts, without in any way suspecting that it had been deprived of its integrity.

The solemnity of the Martyrs and the Lord’s Day also admonish us to speak to Your Charity about something [Note: In the edition, the opening is: “I shall speak to Your Charity, brothers, of what pertains, etc.”] pertaining to contempt for the present age [Note: In the edition, this is absent, etc.] [Note: The opening is made more explicit here by the addition of the temporal circumstance than in the edition.], and to hope for the future [Note: The edition adds “age.”]. Are you asking what you should despise [Note: The edition prefixes τὸ quaeris.]? Every holy man, and every devout Martyr as well, despised the present life. Are you asking what you should hope for [Note: The edition adds: “I mean the resurrection, because today…”]? Today the Lord rose again [Col. 0972] [Note: The edition adds: “O man, if…”]. If you waver in the matter, be strong in hope [Note: The edition has “firm” instead of “strong.”]. If the task troubles you, let the reward raise you up [Note: The edition has “the reward itself.”]. [Note: By “the first reading” is meant the Epistle of Paul, followed by the Psalms and the Gospel. Augustine clearly indicates this in Sermon 177, where he calls all three indiscriminately “readings.” Although the same order is retained in the present Liturgy, only the Epistle retains the name “reading.”]

The first Apostolic reading, in the Letter that he writes to Timothy, also admonishes us; for he commands him, saying [Note: The edition reads: “The Apostle also admonishes us when he commands Timothy, saying”]: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who grants us all things abundantly for our enjoyment. Let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share, let them store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may lay hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17 and following) [Note: The edition reads “in the living God.”].

And let this reading not seem less appropriate to the solemnity of the blessed Martyrs; for it contains contempt for the world. For when the rich are commanded to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future and to lay hold of the true life [Note: Augustine frequently, when commenting on this Pauline text, considers the falsity of the present life. It is especially appropriate here, so that there may be no suspicion concerning the authenticity of this passage. See, above all, Sermon 39, §5.], there is no doubt that this life is false.

And above all, the rich ought to hear this [Note: The edition adds: “Hear this, you rich who possess gold and silver and yet burn with desire; when…”], those whom the poor, when they look upon them, grumble at, groan over, praise, envy, wish to equal, and lament that they are inferior; and amid their praise of the rich they commonly say: “These alone exist” [Note: The edition has “they themselves” instead of “these.”]; “these alone live” [Note: The edition has, in place of these words, “by which men…”].

Because of these words, then, by which the poor flatter the rich [Note: The edition reads: “when they say, ‘These alone live’; do not be puffed up by the words of flatterers, O rich men, but rather listen to the Apostle, a physician of sickness and not a flatterer of words: ‘This life…’”]—because they live, and live alone—lest they, inflated by these flattering words, think that they truly live, “Command,” he says, “the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who grants us all things abundantly for our enjoyment” [Note: The edition has a similar thought and order of words in Sermon 39, §5.]. Let them be rich—but where? In good works: let them give readily, because they do not lose what they give; let them share with those who have nothing. And what follows from this? Let them store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may lay hold of the true righteousness, not agreeing with the flatterers who tell them that they live, and live alone.

This life [Note: The edition adds: “This life is your sleep.”] is a dream; these riches flow away as in dreams [Note: The edition adds: “Paul says: ‘So that they may lay hold of the true life.’ Listen to Paul and do not be proud.”]. Hear the Psalm: “O most wretched rich man” [Note: “O you most wretched rich man, what do you have if you do not have God? Or what do you not have if you have God? Concerning the rich the Psalm says: ‘They slept…’”]: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

Sometimes even a beggar lying on the ground [Note: The edition adds “and trembling with cold,”], trembling with cold, yet overcome by sleep [Note: The edition reads “overcome by sleep”], dreams of treasures, and rejoices [Note: The edition adds “exults”] and is proud in his dreams; and he does not deign to acknowledge his ragged father [Note: The edition adds: “is indignant at seeing him in rags. What you see, O beggar who are sleeping and rejoicing, is in a dream. Nevertheless, until he wakes up he is rich; when he sleeps he finds something real to grieve over.”]. He remains rich until he wakes. When he has fallen asleep, then, does he find something false over which to rejoice? When he wakes, he finds something true over which to grieve.

A rich man, therefore, when dying, is like [Note: The edition reads: “like that poor man who was awake while dreaming of treasures”] the poor man who was awake and saw treasures in a dream. For that rich man also was clothed in purple and fine linen. A certain rich man, neither named nor to be named, who despised the poor man lying before his gate, was clothed in purple and fine linen, as the Gospel testimony records, and feasted splendidly every day [Note: The edition adds: “afterward he died.”]; he died [Note: The edition adds: “and was buried.”], he was buried; he awoke and found himself in the flames [Note: The edition reads “in the flame”] (Luke 16:19).

He therefore slept his sleep and found nothing [Note: The edition reads “after sleep, nothing”] in his hands, that man of riches, because he had done no good [Note: The edition reads “had accomplished nothing with his hands”] with his hands [Note: The edition adds: “that is, from his riches.”]. Riches are therefore sought for the sake of life, not life for the sake of riches.

How many have made a pact with their enemies that they should take everything and leave them their life [Note: The edition reads this as a question: “that they might redeem only their life”], whatever they possessed [Note: The edition adds: “They gave everything to the barbarians, only so as not to lose their lives. ‘You gave the barbarians everything you had, brother?’ ‘Everything,’ he says; ‘I was left naked—and if I live, naked.’ ‘And why?’ ‘I was going to be killed outright, and therefore I gave everything.’ ‘And why did this happen to you? Shall I tell you? Because, before the barbarian arrived, you did not help the poor, so that through the poor your alms might reach Christ. You gave Christ nothing, and you gave the barbarians everything you had—and you gave it with the sacrament. Christ asks and does not receive; that man tortures and takes everything. If you bought a perishing life at so great a price, at what price must it be purchased…’”], and at such a price they bought their lives. At what price must eternal life be purchased, if perishing life is so precious [Note: The edition reverses the commas in this conditional sentence and reads “who,” rather than “if”]? Give something to Christ, so that you may live blessedly, if you give everything to your enemy so that you may live as a beggar.

From your temporal life, which you redeem at so great a price, estimate how much the eternal life is worth which you neglect, merely so that you may live a few days, even if you are destined to reach old age [Note: The edition reads: “You do what the enemy demands, and despise what Christ demands?”]. For all the days of a man, from infancy to old age [Note: The edition reads “to old age”], are few days [Note: This same reading occurs in Sermon 301, §9.]. And if Adam himself were to die today, he would have lived only a few days, because he had completed them all [Note: The edition adds: “Although he had lived six thousand years, they were nevertheless few, because he had completed them all.”].

Do you redeem a few days—and those laborious, in such poverty, amid such temptation [Note: The edition reads: “full of temptations, so that you may possess a little land, that is, an estate”]? At what price? You wish to possess nothing so that you may possess yourself. Do you wish to know how much eternal life is worth? Add yourself as well.

Look: the enemy who had taken you captive [Note: The edition reads “says”] said to you: “If you wish to live, give me whatever you have”; and, in order to live, you gave everything—redeemed today, perhaps to die tomorrow; released by this man, perhaps to be slaughtered by that one [Note: The edition adds: “redeemed from the barbarians, only to be killed by another. See how much people suffer at the hands of barbarians for temporal life, while we are reluctant to suffer anything for eternal life.”]. Let these dangers teach us, my brothers. What people are so unlearned amid the words of God and the lessons of human experience? Look: you gave everything and went away rejoicing because you are alive [Note: The edition adds: “and you rejoice”], even though poor, even though naked, even though needy, even though a beggar [Note: The edition adds: “‘I rejoice because I am alive and have not lost this sweet light.’”]. Yet you rejoice because you are alive, and the light is sweet.

Let Christ appear and make a pact as well—not the one who took you captive [Note: The edition reads “with you himself, not a barbarian”], but the one who was taken captive for you; not the one who seeks to kill you, but the one who deigned to be killed for you [Note: The edition adds: “the one who gave himself for you—he himself says to you”], who gave himself for you. What is the price? The one who made you [Note: The edition reads: “he himself says to you, ‘With me’”] says to you: “Make a pact with me: do you wish to possess yourself and lose everything? If you wish to possess yourself, you must possess me, so that you may hate yourself [Note: The edition has “and” instead of “so that”], love me, and, by losing your life [Note: The edition places a full stop before “your life” and thus reads: “you will find your life by losing it”], find it, lest by holding on to it you lose it” [Note: The edition adds “it.”].

Concerning these riches of yours, which you love to possess and which nevertheless you are prepared to give for your present life [Note: The edition reads: “I will give you advice about what you should do”], I have already given wholesome advice [Note: See Sermon 38, from §7 to the end. All the statements of this sermon are repeated there.]. If you love them as well [Note: The edition adds “them themselves”], do not lose them [Note: The edition reads: “if you love them here”]; but where you love them, they will perish with you.

I also give advice concerning them: Do you love them? Send them ahead to the place where you will follow them, lest, while loving them, you lose them on earth while alive [Note: The edition reads “lose them while alive”], or leave them behind when dead. And here, he says [Note: The edition reads “he has now given advice”], I have given advice: I did not say, “Destroy them,” but “Preserve them” [Note: The edition reads: “I have now said, ‘Do you wish to store up? Good…’”]. Do you wish to store up treasure? I do not say, “Do not”; I say, “Where.” Accept me as an adviser [Note: The edition reads “accept me”], not as one who forbids.

Where, then, do I say that you should store up treasure [Note: The edition reads: “It is written: ‘Store up…’”]? “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches, nor moth nor rust destroys” (Matt. 6:20).

“But,” you say [Note: The edition reads: “But perhaps you say”], “I do not see what I put in heaven” [Note: The edition adds: “what ladder, what device shall I seek that may reach heaven, so that I may see where to put my money [Col. 0975]? What do you say? Do you see on earth the place where you bury it? ‘I do,’ he says. ‘That is good enough—if it is secure.’”]. For you see what you bury in the earth. You are confident when burying it in the earth [Col. 0975], yet anxious when giving it to the one who made heaven and earth [Note: The edition reads “why” instead of “and”; it adds: “Give it securely to God. Entrust yourself to him who preserves your money in heaven, because he also governs you on earth as long as you live. Do you wish to preserve your money? Preserve it…”].

Preserve it where you wish, if you find someone better than Christ [Note: The edition reads “a guardian better than Christ”]; entrust it to him, commit it to his keeping [Note: The edition reads “entrust your money to him.”] [Note: The edition adds “he says.”].

“I entrust it,” you say, “to my slave” [Note: The edition adds: “Good, O Christian man!”].

“How much better to your Lord [Note: The edition reads “your slave”]? A slave perhaps takes it away [Note: The edition adds “and flees”], and flees [Note: The edition reads “Will Christ do this? Many…”]. Amid all the evils that have already occurred, it would at least have been desirable that a slave should take it away and flee, rather than lead enemies to his master [Note: The edition reads: “Many slaves suddenly…”]. Many slaves suddenly became enemies to their masters and betrayed them, together with what they possessed, to the enemy [Note: The edition reads “handed them over” instead of “betrayed them.”].

To whom, then, do you entrust it? “For the present,” you say, “I entrust my gold to my slave” [Note: The edition adds: “I know the faithfulness of my slave, and therefore I entrust my gold to my slave.”].

You entrust your gold to your slave—but your soul to whom [Note: The edition adds: “O man, to him…”]?

“I entrust my soul to God.”

How much better to entrust your gold as well to the one to whom you entrust your soul? Or is he perhaps faithful in guarding your soul but unfaithful in guarding your money? Does he not preserve for you who preserves you? Therefore show faith.

A slave takes care not to steal it; does he also take care that it not be lost? His entire faithfulness consists in not defrauding you. You consider his faithfulness [Note: The edition reads: “Look: he put it away, and…”], but do not consider his weakness? He put it away; it was not hidden [Note: The edition reads: “another found it and took it”]. Another came and took it away [Note: The edition adds: “Give to Christ who is hungry; store up in heaven. Is it really a labor to store up in heaven?”].

Can anyone do this to Christ? Shake off your laziness and accept the advice: store up in heaven. And why did I say, “Shake off your laziness”? As though storing up in heaven were a labor! Even if it were a labor, it ought to be done [Note: The edition adds: “to place your money in a secure place”], and the labor ought to be undertaken, and what we consider valuable ought to be deposited in a secure place from which no one could take it [Note: The edition adds: “Nevertheless…”].

Yet Christ does not tell you, “Store up in heaven” [Note: The edition reads “Christ tells you”], “seek ladders” [Note: The edition reads “tie together devices, attach wings”], “fit out wings” [Note: The edition reads “This is what he says to me”]. Rather, he says to me: “Give it to me on earth, and there I shall preserve it” [Note: The edition reads “and I shall preserve it for you in heaven.”]. “Give it to me on earth,” he says. For this reason I came to be poor here on earth [Col. 0976] [Note: The edition reads: “For this reason I came to be poor on earth”], so that you might be rich there [Note: The edition reads “so that you may be rich”].

Make a transfer [Note: The edition reads “Perhaps you are afraid.”]. Are you afraid of a thief, lest you lose it [Note: The edition reads “take it away,” removes the question, and adds “and you seek…”]? You ask who will carry it to the place to which you are moving [Note: The edition reads “who will migrate”]. Christ is present to you in both respects. He does not perpetrate fraud, but he does make the transfer [Note: The edition reads “will make the transfer as well.”].

“But where do I find Christ,” you say [Note: The edition reads: “‘But where do I find Christ on earth?’ ‘I find him there so that I may give to him.’”], “when my faith has received what I heard in the Church? This I learned; this I believed; with this sacrament I was instructed [Note: The edition adds: “He suffered, died, and was buried”]: he was buried, he rose again on the third day, after forty days he ascended into heaven [Note: The edition reads “into the heavens”] before the eyes of his disciples, he sits at the right hand of the Father [Note: The edition reads “at the right hand”], and at the end he will come. When, then, do I find him here? To whom shall I give it [Note: The edition adds “so that he may carry it to him?”]?”

Do not be anxious; hear the whole matter—or, if you have heard it all, tell it all. I know that you have received this: Christ was suspended on the cross, taken down from the tree, placed in the tomb, rose again, and ascended into heaven [Note: The edition adds “or have read it”]. But you have also read this: when Saul was persecuting Christ’s Church—proud, cruel, breathing out slaughter, thirsting for the blood of Christians—when he was raging and persecuting, carrying letters to Damascus so that he might bring bound to punishment the men and women of this discipline whom he found (Acts 9:2) [Note: The edition reads “Have you not heard what he shouted to him?”].

Have you heard what he cried out, whom you confess to be seated in heaven? Recall, then, what he said, what you heard, what you read: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” [Note: The edition adds: “Paul did not even see him.”] Paul neither saw him nor touched him [Note: The edition reads: “From heaven he cries out.”], and yet he said: “Why are you persecuting me?” He did not say: “Why are you persecuting my household, my servants, my saints”—add “my brothers” as an honorific [Note: The edition reads “or brothers?” and adds: “He said none of these things. And what did he say?”]. He said none of these things. What did he say? “Why are you persecuting me?” [Note: The edition reads: “He said, that is, my members.”] That is, my members, for whom, trampled on earth, the head cried out from heaven; for if your foot is trampled on earth, your tongue cries out from your head [Note: The edition adds: “and says: ‘You are not trampling my foot, but you are trampling me.’”].

What, then, makes you hesitate about to whom you should give [Note: The edition reads: “You who say, ‘What then?’ He who said to Saul: ‘Why me…’”]? The one who said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”—he himself says to you: “Feed me on earth” [Note: The edition adds: “On earth Saul was raging”]. Saul was raging, and yet he was persecuting Christ [Note: The edition reads “touching Christ in heaven”]. So you too give on earth, and you feed Christ [Note: The edition reads “feed Christ in heaven.”].

For the Lord himself foretold this question that troubles you. Those who will be placed at his right hand will also be moved, and when he says, “I was hungry and you gave me food,” they will answer: “Lord, when did we see you hungry?” And they will immediately hear: “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:35) [Note: The edition adds: “If you had heard this clearly, say: ‘I do not want to give,’ and you will have no excuse, but will condemn yourself with your own voice.”].

If, then, you do not wish to give, you have grounds on which to accuse yourself, for you have nothing with which to excuse yourself.

Concerning these riches, then, your Lord says to you: “I have given you the most wholesome advice” [Note: The edition reads “what you should do”]. Do you love them [Note: The edition reads “You love riches”]? “I do,” he says. “Then transfer them.” And when you have transferred them, you will follow them [Note: The edition reads “transfer them and follow them”]; follow them meanwhile in your heart [Note: The edition adds “while you live: for where your treasure is…”]. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” [Note: The edition reads “there” instead of “there also.”].

If you entrust your treasure to the earth, you bury your heart in the earth as well. But when you have buried your heart in the earth, be ashamed [Note: The edition adds: “Be ashamed, because you lie when you answer after hearing ‘Lift up your hearts.’ For it is said, ‘Lift up your hearts,’ and you immediately answer, ‘We have them with the Lord.’ You lie to God. In one hour in the Church you do not speak the truth; you lie to God, as you always do to men. You say, ‘We have them with the Lord,’ while you have your heart buried in the earth, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”] when you answer, after hearing “Lift up your hearts,” “We have them with the Lord.”

“I,” he says, “have given wholesome advice” [Note: The edition reads: “If you do with your riches what you have heard, if you are such a rich man as the Apostle describes, not being high-minded…”] concerning your riches. If you do it, if you listen, if you are such a rich man as the Apostle describes—so that you are not high-minded, do not place your hope in the uncertainty of riches, give readily, and share [Note: The edition adds “so that you may store up treasure”]—store up for yourself a good foundation for the future, so that you may lay hold of the true life.

“Now,” says your Lord, “ask me” [Note: The edition reads: “Ask God and your Lord, and say there: ‘Behold, Lord, I have now moved to heaven; what I possess I possess as though I did not possess it.’ It is worth this much.”]. “Behold, I have moved to heaven what I possess, whether by giving it all away or by holding what remains as though I did not possess it, using this world as though I were not using it. Is the kingdom of heaven worth this much?” (1 Cor. 7) [Note: The edition adds: “As much as my patrimony? Let it be worth more.”]

Behold: if I have done this, it is worth this much. Is it dear? It is worth more. For it is not truly such that it ought to be worth this much [Note: The edition reads “worth this much.” It adds: “This is what your Lord says, whom you asked about your patrimony: ‘You will live for a time and afterward die; in my kingdom you will never die, but you will live forever. There you will be truly rich, where you will never be in need.’”]. You will live forever. You would give all these treasures for the sake of a few days of life; there you will be truly rich, because you will not be in need.

But you act this way because you wish to be rich, so that you will not be in need on earth. And for that reason you heap up and pile together a dense mass of mud by which you are weighed down, pressed down, and, when it has dried, more tightly enclosed [Note: The edition adds: “For this reason you seek many animals for transport, lest you fail; for food…”].

Therefore, so that you may not be in need, you seek many animals for transport, lavish feasts for food, and the most costly garments for clothing [Note: The edition reads “costly”]. But lest, by possessing much, you be rich while my angel is poor [Note: The edition reads: “In truth, by possessing much you are rich, while my angel is poor: he has nothing, not even a horse…”], who uses neither a horse nor rides in a carriage, nor fills a table with respectable furnishings [Note: The edition reads: “nor fills a table with respectable equipment”], nor has a garment woven for him, because he is clothed with light [Note: The edition adds “eternal”]—learn to desire true riches [Note: The edition adds: “Learn, O rich man, to desire true riches.”].

You wish to possess these things [Note: The edition adds “riches”] so that you may have something with which to soothe your throat and fill your belly; but the one who gives you the gift of never hungering makes you truly rich [Note: The edition adds “forever”]. Not to be in need at all means not to hunger. For however much you possess, when the hour comes at which you are to dine [Note: The edition reads “the fifth hour, before…”], or before you approach the table, when you are hungry, you are needy [Note: The edition adds: “you are hungry and failing, because you are miserable. Does the angel endure this? Far from it: the angel neither hungers nor fails.”].

Finally, when the feasts have been removed [Note: The edition reads “when these feasts…”], you pant proudly. This is not the satisfaction of needs but the smoke of anxieties [Note: The edition adds: “when you think about increasing your riches—look…”]. Consider what you think about increasing these riches of yours. See whether you sleep easily when you are thinking either about not losing what you have stored away or about increasing what you have stored away [Note: The edition reads: “If I am not mistaken, when you found riches, you lost rest.”].

You found riches, then, when you found rest. When you are awake, you think about increasing your riches; when you sleep, you dream of thieves. By day anxious [Note: The edition adds “and by night”], by night fearful, always a beggar [Note: The edition reverses the words in this clause].

He who promises you the kingdom of heaven wishes to make you truly rich. And for how much do you think you will purchase those true riches, that true [Note: The edition adds “true and blessed life; for how much are you prepared to redeem these wretched and laborious days?”] and eternal life? What? Do you think it is true because you will purchase it at the price at which you were prepared to buy these few laborious and wretched days? Something that is far greater must be worth more [Note: The edition reads: “which is much more, because it is the kingdom of heaven.”].

“And what shall I do?” you say [Note: The edition adds: “Behold, holy Bishop, I have heard your admonitions, obeyed your advice, and not rejected the Lord’s commandment. What I possessed…”]. “I have given everything I possessed to the poor, and I share what I have with the needy. What more can I do [Note: The edition adds “to do?”]?”

You have more: yourself. You possess yourself as something greater; you yourself remain among your possessions; you must be added to the gift [Note: The edition reads: “You still have yourself; you yourself are more; you are lacking to your possessions.”].

Attend to the advice of your Lord [Note: The edition adds: “Have you done what he gave to the rich man? ‘I have,’ he says. ‘Why do you lie? You have not done everything: you have done it on one side, but on the other you have touched nothing. Hear what he commands: Go…’”], which he gave to the rich man: “Go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor.” And did he dismiss him after saying this? To prevent him from thinking that he had lost what he loved [Note: The edition reads: “what he had given to the poor,” and adds: “He made him secure by saying: ‘And you will have…’”], he first made him secure, because he had not lost it but stored it away: “You will have,” he said, “treasure in heaven” [Note: The edition adds: “Is this enough?”].

Is this enough? No. What then? “Come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21) [Note: The edition reads: “He says. ‘You love him and wish to follow him; whom?’”].

Have you loved him? Do you wish to follow him? He ran; he flew. Seek where? I do not know where. O Christian! Do you not know where your Lord went? Shall I tell you the way by which you may follow him? Through hardships, through insults, through false accusations, through spittle in the face, through blows of slaps and lashes [Note: The edition reads “through slaps and the blows of scourges”], through a crown of thorns, through the cross, through death.

Why are you sluggish [Note: The edition adds: “Behold, the way has been shown to you. ‘But it is a hard way,’ you say; ‘who can follow him along it?’”]? You wished to follow him; the way has been shown. And you ask: “Who follows him?” Be ashamed, bearded man [Note: The edition adds: “Be ashamed: you are called a man from virtue.”]. Women followed him, whose birthdays we celebrate today.

Today we celebrate the solemnity of the women Martyrs of Tuburbitana [Note: The edition has “Suburbitarum”; in the annotation, “Suburbitanarum,” from Sirmond.]. Your Lord, our Lord, their Lord, the Lord of all, the Redeemer of our life, by going ahead along the narrow and harsh way made it a road [Note: The edition reads: “made it a road for you—a level, secure, fortified road. Christ our Lord, who reigns forever and ever. Amen. Thus the sermon ends.”], a royal road, fortified [Note: See Sermon 235, §1; there you will recognize the restored mutilated passage.],

[and pure, in which he would make it delightful for women also to walk—and are you still sluggish? Do you not wish to pour out blood for so great a shedding of blood? Your Lord says this to you: “I suffered first for you; give what you received, return what you drank.” You cannot? Boys and girls could. Delicate boys and delicate girls could. The rich, and the very rich, could; when the temptation of persecution suddenly assailed them, they were not held back by their abundance of riches, nor captured by the sweetness of this life. They thought of that rich man who ended his riches and found torments; they did not send their riches ahead, but rather went ahead of them in martyrdom. Are you sluggish with so many examples going before you? And yet you celebrate the feasts of the Martyrs.

Today is the birthday of the Martyrs. “I will go before them,” you say, “perhaps even in a better tunic.” Consider with what conscience you act; love what you are doing; imitate what you celebrate; do what you praise.

“But I cannot.” The Lord is near: “Be anxious about nothing” (Phil. 4:6). “I cannot,” you say. Do not fear the fountain itself: from where those women were filled, you too can be filled, if you approach eagerly; if you do not swell up like a hill, but humble yourself like a valley, so that you may deserve to be filled.

Let us not, then, find these things hard, brothers, especially in these times, when affliction is increasing [Note: I judge that the sermon was delivered after the year 427, when the first Vandal persecution was beginning. See Sermon 296, §§6–11. There, however, he speaks of the devastation of the city of Rome; here he says that Africa itself is being afflicted.]. The world was despised by the Martyrs when it was flourishing. Truly, it was a great act of praise to despise it while flourishing, and it is loved while perishing. They despised its flowers, while you embrace its thorns.

If you are sluggish about moving away, perhaps even a collapsing house frightens you. But a pagan taunts you. Why does a pagan taunt you? In truth, it is time for the pagan to taunt you, because the predictions of your Lord are being fulfilled. He would taunt you more rightly if what he predicted were not being fulfilled.

He denies the God whom you worship; from what the world suffers, show that he is truthful, and, without being saddened by the predicted events, rejoice in the promises. For he came at the time when the world, as its age was declining, was already becoming such that it was destined to end, and was to abound in disasters, calamities, distress, and troubles [Col. 0980].

He who came then came for your consolation. So that you would not fail amid the pressures of a life that is perishing and passing away, he promised another life.

Before the world labored under these afflictions and calamities, the Prophets were sent; servants were sent to this great sick man—to the human race, stretched out and lying there like one sick man extending from East to West. The powerful Physician sent his servants. The time came for such attacks to befall this sick man, attacks under which he was going to suffer greatly. And the Physician said: “This sick man is going to suffer greatly; I am necessary.”

Let the foolish sick man say to the Physician: “Lord, I have been suffering ever since you came.” Fool, you are not suffering because I came; I came because you were going to suffer.

To be brief, brothers, why say much? “The Lord, completing and shortening his word, has cut it short upon the earth” (Rom. 9:28). Let us live well, and because of our good life let us not hope for the good things of earth, which pass away [Note: This conclusion is very closely connected with the rest of the sermon and completes its integrity.]. Earthly happiness is a paltry reward for a good life. That you live well here is not worth as much as what you desire here; indeed, if you desire such things, you do not live well. If you wish to change your life, change your desires.

You keep faith with God, and therefore wish to be happy on earth—and this is everything for you. Why do you keep faith with God? Is your faith worth only this much? Do you value it at this price? Is this how you bring it forward? If you have something for sale on earth and make an agreement with a buyer, you name a higher price, while he names a lower one. “It is worth this much,” you say, because you exaggerate the value of what you are selling. He says: “It is not worth that much, but this much,” and sets a lower price for himself, wishing to buy more cheaply.

The Lord Christ corrects you. You say to your Lord Christ: “Lord, I keep faith with you, and you give me something on earth.” Fool, what you are selling is not worth only this much; you are mistaken and do not know what you possess. You keep faith and seek earth? Your faith is worth more than earth, and you do not know how to value it.

I know its value, for I gave it to you. It is worth as much as the whole earth; add heaven to the earth: it is worth more. And what is greater than earth and heaven? The one who made both earth and heaven.

Let us turn to the Lord [Note: The published sermons append various clauses after these words “Let us turn to the Lord”; it is therefore uncertain which wording Augustine used whenever nothing further is added. See Sermons 67, 100, 141, and others.]

## SERMON IV. On the Nativity of the Lord

The Maurists regret that they have nowhere seen Sermon no. 189 in volume V in a manuscript, so that they might repair passages that were less complete or badly joined. I have copied it restored to its original completeness from seven codices, three of them ancient lectionaries that the monks used in the choir for solemn liturgical recitation; among these, Codex no. 106 is especially notable, copied with great elegance in the hand of Leo of Ostia, who added his date and name and adorned the codex with illustrations.

Two other codices are Breviaries in Latin characters from the fourteenth century, before the time of Urban V [Col. 0981]; for they read the Psalms from the Roman edition, not from the Gallican edition that that pontiff prescribed for the Cassinese monks.

The remaining two contain sermons by various authors, and are so entitled as well. In all seven of these codices the sermon has one consistent reading and one consistent title, agreeing with the Maurist edition. The Laurentian Medicean Library reports that this same sermon exists complete in Codex 1, Plutarch XIV, just as it does in our codices.

THE DAY that made every day has sanctified this day for us [the edition adds “Brothers”], the day of which the Psalm [the edition reads “sings”] sings: “Sing to the Lord a new song, sing to the Lord, all the earth; sing to the Lord, and bless his name” [the edition reads “to his name”] (Psalm 95:1–2) [the edition reads “bless”]. [The Old Latin version has: “Sing to the Lord, bless his name, proclaim from day to day his salvation.” The Maurists therefore supposed that this verse of the Psalm could be restored by the manuscripts to that reading. But our codices do not suffice to establish the conjecture. The learned Sabatier notes in his Old Latin Version of the Bible that Augustine used that reading only once, whereas elsewhere he always wrote “from day to day,” or “day out of day.”] “Announce his salvation from day to day.” What is this “day from day,” if not the Son from the Father, light from light? But that Day begot the Day who was to be born of the Virgin on this day [the edition reads: “begot this Day, who was born of the Virgin today”]. That day, therefore, has neither rising nor setting. I speak of God the Father as Day. [For Jesus would not be “day from day” unless the Father also were Day.]

What is day if not light? Not the light of bodily eyes, not the common light of human beings [the edition reads *cum* (“with”) for *et* (“and”)] and animals, but the light that shines for the angels, the light by whose vision hearts are purified. For this night in which we now live is passing—the night in which the lamps of the Scriptures are kindled for us—and that will come which is sung in another Psalm [this is an entirely unusual passage. Although Psalm 36, Psalm 58, Psalm 148, and *Tractate* 34 on John read, “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will contemplate,” here alone the pronoun “you” is added]: “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will contemplate you” (ibid. 5).

That day, therefore—the Word of God, the day that shines for the angels, the day that shines in that homeland from which we are exiles—clothed itself in flesh and was born of the Virgin Mary. He was born wondrously. What is more wondrous than the birth of a virgin [the edition reads “conceives”]? She conceived and is a virgin; she gives birth and is a virgin. For he was created from her [the edition reads “from her”] whom he created, and he brought her fertility without corrupting her integrity [the edition adds “her”]. Mary, from where? From Adam. Adam, from where? From earth [the edition reads: “If Mary is from Adam, and Adam from earth, therefore…”]. If Adam is from earth, and Mary from Adam, then Mary too is earth. If Mary is earth [the edition reads “but if”], let us recognize what we sing: “Truth has sprung up from the earth.”

What a benefit he has bestowed upon us [the editions punctuate this differently, treating what precedes as a question]: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (ibid. 84:12). For the Jews, as the Apostle says, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own, were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3). From where can a human being be righteous? From himself? Who gives himself bread when he is poor? Who clothes himself when naked, unless he has received a garment? [We had no righteousness; here there were only sins.] From where comes righteousness—and what righteousness is there without faith? “For the righteous person lives by faith” (ibid. 1:17). Whoever says that he is righteous without faith is lying [the edition says “he says, without a question: because he lies”]. How can one in whom there is no faith not lie? If he wishes to speak truth, let him turn toward the truth.

But it was far away [the edition reads: “Truth was far away. You were sleeping; it came to you; you were oppressed by heavy sleep; it awakened you”]. Truth has sprung up from the earth. You were sleeping; it came to you. You were snoring; it awakened you. It made a way for you through itself, so that it would not lose you. Therefore [the edition reads: “Therefore truth has sprung up from the earth, because Christ was born of the Virgin, etc.”], because truth has sprung up from the earth, our Lord Jesus Christ was born of a Virgin; “righteousness has looked down from heaven” [the edition adds: “so that through righteousness human beings might recover their senses, who through unrighteousness had lost them. Mortals…”], so that human beings might have righteousness—not their own, but God’s.

What condescension! What indignation preceded it! What indignation preceded it? We were mortal, weighed down by sins [the edition reads “oppressed”], bearing our punishments. Every human being, when born, begins in misery. Do not seek a prophet; question the newborn and see him weeping. Since, then, there was such great indignation of God on earth, what sudden condescension there was! Truth has sprung up from the earth.

He created all things and was created among all things; he made the day and came into the day; he existed before the ages and marked out the ages. The Lord Christ is eternally, without beginning, with the Father [all this is absent from the edition, which has only the following in its place: “He also has a nativity in the beginning, the Word, who, unless…”]; [and yet today ask what he is. It is a birthday. Whose? The Lord’s. Does he have a birthday? He does. The Word was in the beginning, God with God—does he have a birthday? He does.] Unless he had a human generation, we would not attain divine regeneration: he was born so that we might be reborn. Let no one doubt rebirth: Christ has been born. He was generated, not to be regenerated. For whom was regeneration necessary except for one whose generation had been condemned?

Let his mercy, therefore, come to be in our hearts. His Mother carried him in her womb; let us carry him in our hearts. The Virgin was made pregnant by Christ’s incarnation; let our breasts be made pregnant by faith in Christ. She gave birth to the Savior [the edition adds “the Virgin”]; let us give birth to praise. Let us not be barren; let our souls be fruitful for God.

The generation of Christ from the Father without a mother [the edition has different wording in place of “the generation of Christ”]; the generation of Christ from a mother without a father: both generations are wondrous. The first generation is eternal, the second temporal. [When was he born from the Father? What does “when” mean? Are you asking “when” there, where you will find no time? Do not ask there when. Here ask when: you ask properly when speaking of his mother. You do not ask properly when speaking of the Father; he was born, and he has no time.] He was born, eternal from the eternal, coeternal. Why are you amazed? He is God.

When the consideration of his divinity is made, the cause for amazement disappears. [And when we say, “He was born of a Virgin”—a great thing! Are you amazed? He is God; do not be amazed.] Let amazement pass [the edition reads “rise”]; let praise draw near. Let faith be present; believe [the edition reads “that” for “because”] because it happened. [If you do not believe that it happened, you remain unbelieving. He deigned to become human; what more are you seeking?]

Was God humbled too little for your sake? He who was God became human. The lodging was narrow; he was wrapped in cloths and placed in a manger [the edition reads “was placed”]. You heard this when the Gospel was read. Who would not [the edition reads “admire”] marvel? He who filled the world found no room in the lodging; placed in a manger, he became our food [the edition reads “our food”].

Let two animals, two peoples, approach the manger [the edition reads “recognized”]. For “the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.” Look toward the manger; do not be ashamed [the edition reads “to be God’s beast of burden”] to be the Lord’s beast of burden. You will carry Christ and will not go astray [the edition reads “walking along the road, he sits upon you”]. Walking along the road, [he sits upon you; the road itself sits upon you. You remember that little donkey brought to the Lord? Let no one be ashamed: we are that donkey.]

Let the Lord sit upon us and call us wherever he wishes [the edition reads “direct us”]. We are his beast of burden; we are going to Jerusalem [the edition reads “let us go”]. When he sits upon us, we are not crushed [the edition reads “we are not oppressed”], but lifted up. When he leads us, we do not go astray; we go to him, through him we go, and we do not perish [the edition reads: “we shall not go astray; through him let us go to him, that with the Child born today we may rejoice for ever”].

## SERMON V. Preached at Carthage at the Table of Blessed Cyprian [for the nature of Blessed Cyprian’s table at Carthage, see Sermon 310, section 2], on the sixth day before the Ides of September, on what the Apostle says to the Galatians: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual…” 

The following sermons, not yet published and constituting a second class, are now seeing the light for the first time. They will, I think, find as defenders all who have spent even a little time reading Augustine. I copied this first one from Codex 17, mentioned above, and gave it the same title that it bears in that codex. I did not find it in the published libraries; if you wish to insert it among the sermons of the Maurist edition, place it before Sermon 164. It is clear to readers of Florus’s commentary that he drew from this source the sentences with which he explains the earlier verses of chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Galatians. The Maurists, unaware of this sermon, thought that Florus had transferred these same passages from the aforementioned Sermon 164. But there only the bearing of one’s own and another’s burden is treated, whereas here the first six verses are expounded, and Florus’s commentary does not disagree with this exposition.

### I

RECALL the reading of the apostolic Epistle as it was proclaimed: “Brothers,” he says, “if a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. Let the one who is catechized share the word with the one who catechizes him in all good things. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person has sown, that he will also reap; because the one who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, while the one who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit. Let us not grow weak in doing good; for in its season we shall reap without weariness. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Galatians 6:1 and following, according to the Old Latin version).

Up to this point the passage from Paul’s Epistle was read; up to this point I have been a reader for you. But, my brothers, if the reader has been understood, what need is there for an interpreter? We have heard, we have understood; let us also do and live. And why should we burden your memory? Hold on to these things and think about them from there.

Perhaps one of you is troubled by how we should understand what he says: “Bear one another’s burdens,” and shortly afterward: “Each person will bear his own burden.” You say in your hearts—you who have noticed this—“How do we bear one another’s burdens if each person will bear his own burden?” [To understand the Carthaginian liturgy, observe that on that day chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Galatians and chapter 8 of Matthew’s Gospel were read.] If we bear one another’s burdens, how do we do so? I confess: this is a question.

“Knock, and it will be opened to you”: knock by paying attention, knock by studying, knock also by praying for us, so that we may say something worthy of you. By knocking in this way you help us, and this question will quickly be resolved. Would that, as quickly as it is resolved, each person might also put into effective practice what he understands!

In the burden of weakness we bear one another’s burdens; in the rule of piety each person will bear his own burden. What have I said? What are all human beings except human beings—and therefore weak, and not entirely without sin? In this respect we bear one another’s burdens.

For if you grow weary of your brother’s sin, and he of yours, you neglect one another and commit a truly great sin. But if you tolerate what he cannot tolerate, and he tolerates what you cannot, you bear one another’s burdens; and because you bear one another’s burdens, you fulfill the most sacred law of charity. For this is the law of Christ: the law of Christ is the law of charity. That is why he came: because he loved us. There was nothing in us to love, but by loving he made us lovable.

You heard what it means: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” What, then, does “Each person will bear his own burden” mean? Each person will give an account for his own sin; no one will give an account for another’s sin. Each person has his own case; he will give his own account to God.

Even the overseers themselves, who give an account for Christ’s flocks, give an account for their own sin if they have neglected Christ’s flocks [Col. 0985]. Therefore, brothers, “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual”—all of you who are spiritual—“instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness.”

And if you cry out, love inwardly; exhort, coax, rebuke, rage: love, and do whatever you wish. A father does not hate his son; and yet, when necessary, a father beats his son and inflicts pain in order to safeguard his health. This, then, is “in a spirit of gentleness.”

For if a person is overtaken in any offense and you say, “It does not concern me,” and I say to you, “Why does it not concern you?” and you reply, “Because each person will bear his own burden,” I will answer you: “Certainly you listened willingly and understood: ‘Bear one another’s burdens.’”

Therefore, if a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness. He himself will give an account for his own sin, because “each person will bear his own burden”; but if you neglect his wound, you will give a bad account for the sin of your negligence. Thus, if you do not bear one another’s burdens, you will have a bad account in the very matter that “each person will bear his own burden.”

Do this, then, so that you may bear one another’s burdens, and God will spare you because each person will bear his own burden. For if you bear another’s burden when he is overtaken in an offense, so that you may instruct him in a spirit of gentleness, you will come to the place where you heard, “Each person will bear his own burden,” and with a good conscience you will say to God, “Forgive us our debts.”

Therefore, brothers, remember: “If a person is overtaken in any offense”—do not take “person” as meaning a passerby. He could have said, “If anyone is overtaken,” or “if whoever is overtaken”; he did not say this, but said “a person.” It is very difficult for a person not to be overtaken in some offense, because what is a human being?

But these spiritual people whom he admonished to instruct in gentleness the person overtaken by an offense perhaps said in their hearts: “Let us bear the burdens of those who are overtaken by offenses, because they have nothing in us that they could bear.” Listen, so that you may not be secure: “Looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted.”

Let the spiritual not become proud or exalt themselves. Yet if they are spiritual, they will not exalt themselves. I fear that they exalt themselves for precisely this reason: because they are carnal. Nevertheless, let the spiritual person also pay attention, lest he too be tempted.

Is a person not human because he is spiritual? Does he not, because he is spiritual, carry a corruptible body that weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15)? Has he, because he is spiritual, finished this life, which is entirely temptation upon the earth (Job 7:1, according to the Old Latin)? Therefore it was rightly said to him—entirely rightly: “Looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted.”

And after admonishing them—that is, the spiritual—he immediately added that general statement: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” What does “one another’s” mean? Let the carnal bear the burden of the carnal; let the spiritual bear the burden of the spiritual. “Bear one another’s burdens”: do not neglect one another’s sins. Where you have confidence, rebuke; where you do not have confidence to rebuke, admonish (2 Corinthians 7:4); and if this is necessary to prevent someone from sinning, pray and entreat.

Perhaps I have humbled you by saying “entreat”? Hear the Apostle: “Commanding,” he says, “we also entreat you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (ibid. 6:1, from the Old Latin).

If a physician finds strength in a sick person, he rebukes him; but if he does not find strength and fears that the person may collapse under the bitterness of correction, he begs and entreats him to listen, act, and live.

It is clear, then, that the Apostle said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” for he had admonished the spiritual person and said, “Looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted”—lest this spiritual person claim so much for himself that he should think he has no burden that ought to be supported by another.

Hear him again, concerning arrogance, swelling, and inflation: “If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” Nothing could have been said better: “He deceives himself.” The devil must not always be blamed; sometimes a person is his own devil. Why must the devil be avoided? Surely so that he may not deceive you. Are you not therefore your own devil when you deceive yourself?

What follows? “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another.”

When you do something good, if you are pleased with yourself because another person praises you, but if that person did not praise you, you would cease doing the good work, deprived of the praiser’s words, then you have glory in another, not in yourself. If he praises you, you act; if, perhaps, your good work displeases a foolish person, you do not act.

Do you not see people pouring out their possessions on actors while giving nothing to the poor, and being praised by the mouths of many? Is what they do therefore good because they are praised? Wake up at last: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul.”

You all applauded because you know the Holy Scripture from which we recall this testimony. Let those who do not know it also hear. Holy Scripture said, Holy Scripture foretold: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Psalm 9:24).

Now, if the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the one who acts wickedly is blessed, seek praisers. Are evil desires tearing you apart? Commit iniquities every day to satisfy your desires, and seek praisers. Believe me, you will find no one except flatterers or seducers.

How are they seducers, and how flatterers? I must give an account for my words. Flatterers are those who know that you are doing evil and nevertheless praise you. But those who praise you when you are doing evil because they think what you are doing is good are not flatterers, since they praise you sincerely; they are seducers, however, because by repeatedly praising you they seduce you into committing those evils, and do not allow you to recover your breath.

You rush into empty airs and imagine that what you are doing is good. You squander your goods; you empty your household; you leave your children naked. Those praises have made you insane. You run, wave your hands, receive applause, raise it to your mouth, spend your household’s resources, and gather wind.

“How,” you ask, “are these people my seducers, when they praise me sincerely?” They are your seducers because they first became their own seducers by going astray [Col. 0987]. Will someone who deceives himself labor to set up a ladder to you so that he will not deceive you?

Therefore, “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed.” Beware such a praiser; avoid a person who blesses this way of life.

Rather, you do good. But you will say, “If I do so, I will displease such-and-such a person.” Then displease him and please God. For if you displease him and please God, you will have glory in yourself and not in another.

But evil people slander the good, and lovers of this world curse those who despise the world. They speak insults and seek something to criticize. As soon as something evil has been said, they immediately believe it; if something good has been said, they refuse to believe it. Your heart is troubled, and you cease doing good because no praiser, flatterer, or deceiver has been found.

Is the testimony of your conscience not enough for you? In the theater of your breast, under God’s eyes, why are you troubled? I ask you: why are you troubled?

“Because many evil things are being said about me.”

Is this what you say? You would not be troubled in the ship of your heart unless Christ were sleeping [perhaps this second question is superfluous in the codex].

You heard this when the Gospel was read: “A great storm arose, and the boat was being tossed and covered by the waves.” Why? Because Christ was sleeping (Matthew 8:24).

When does Christ sleep in your heart, except when you forget your faith? Faith in Christ in your heart is like Christ in a ship. You hear insults; you grow weary; you are troubled: Christ is sleeping. Awaken Christ; awaken your faith.

You have something to do even when troubled: awaken your faith. Let Christ wake and speak to you: “Insults trouble you? What insults have I not first heard for your sake?” This is what Christ says to you; this is how your faith addresses you. Listen to it, and see whether, when it addresses you, you have perhaps forgotten that “Christ suffered for us” (1 Peter 2:21).

Before he suffered such great evils for us, did he not hear insults? He cast out demons, and it was said to him, “You have a demon” (John 8:48). Through the Prophet it was said of him: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen upon me” (Psalm 68:12).

Awaken Christ, therefore, and he will say to you in your heart: “When people insult you and say every evil thing against you because of me, rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew 5:11, from the Old Latin). [Believe what has been said, and great tranquility will come to be in your heart.]

Therefore, if a person thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another.

Whether someone praises or criticizes, you have glory in yourself, because your glory is your God in your conscience. You will be like the wise virgins who took oil with them in their vessels, so that they would not have glory in another but in themselves (Matthew 25:8).
