For those who did not take oil with them begged it from the others, and their lamps went out; they said, “Give us some of your oil.” What is “Give us some of your oil” [the holy Doctor often interpreted this same passage from Matthew as referring to empty glory; see *Expositions on the Psalms* 140.13] except “Praise our works, because our conscience is not sufficient for us”?

What seemed obscure in the apostolic reading I have explained, as the Lord granted. The rest is clear; it does not need explanation but action.

So that we may do what we have heard, let us ask him, without whose help we can do nothing good, since he said to his disciples, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:15).

Turning toward the Lord, etc.

[Such additions are frequent in the published sermons. The opening words, however, belong to some notary or shorthand secretary. This passage confirms what Possidius testified in Augustine’s life: that the bishops and people among whom the holy Doctor stayed not only begged him but even compelled him to preach. This is an outstanding proof of the excellence of his learning and the flourishing reputation of that illustrious man.]

And after the sermon:

Because the people requested that he not depart before the birthday of blessed Cyprian, he added:

“Truly I say to Your Charity: we cannot even bear our desire and complaints through letters. But because the holy Elder has now commanded this very thing that you request, I conclude the sermon thus: The birthday of blessed Cyprian is already near. For the sake of that solemnity you wished to keep me here by force; therefore, since we devote ourselves to the word, it is good that we should also fast in body.”

## SERMON VI. On Several Martyrs

[Although the sermon’s title speaks indiscriminately of “Several Martyrs,” it is clear from the reading of the acts—which is said to have preceded it with the words, “When the passion of the saints was being read”—which martyrs are being praised here. I believe that Augustine is speaking here of the Carthaginian Martyrs whom he mentions in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day three, chapter 17, where we read: “They confessed in their sufferings that they had held an assembly and conducted the Lord’s service.” Optatus of Milevis, Baluzius, and Ruinartus report that they numbered forty-eight and suffered martyrdom on the day before the Ides of February in the year 304.

Indeed, the assemblies are reproached here by the judge as though they were the sole cause of their guilt, while the Martyrs confess with thanksgiving that they had carried them out. It is scarcely credible that Augustine preached no sermon on these Martyrs, who were celebrated throughout Africa, since the Carthaginian Calendar records five distinct solemnities of theirs, to which a sixth was later added after the Emperor Justinian built in his palace a church for the famous Virgin Prima, as Procopius reports (*On the Buildings Constructed by Justinian* 6). Baronius holds that this famous woman was one of these Martyrs.

In the published collections available to me, no sermon on these Martyrs had yet appeared. Two Cassinese codices, numbers 12 and 17, preserve one, perhaps preached at Carthage, where their more celebrated memory compelled Augustine to warn the faithful with special severity not to dissolve into drunkenness and feasting in their excessive joy. He ended his speech in this way: “Let us celebrate the day of the Martyrs by honoring the sufferings of the Martyrs, not by loving our drinking.” He gave nearly the same warning at the solemnities of Saint Cyprian at Carthage and at the festival of the Twenty Martyrs at Hippo Regius.

Wherever the truth of the matter lies, the Donatist compiler cited by Optatus and Baluzius must be accused of falsehood (vol. 1 of the *Miscellanies*, p. 14, 1761 edition). In his additions he reports that the holy Martyrs died while still detained in custody through the cruelty of hunger, whereas here the judge orders at least some of them to be executed by the sword. Baronius and Ruinartus had already rejected those additions, disapproving of the history of Mensurius and Caecilianus. It is therefore not unreasonable that, if the Donatist author was false in one matter, he was also false in the others.

Finally, the Colbertine, Compendian, and Pratellian codices used by Ruinartus lack those additions; but in the title of the acts they state that those holy Martyrs shed their blood on different days and in different places. From that title we can also understand why their memory was celebrated individually at Carthage on separate days of the year. Let us therefore acknowledge the Cassinese codices as preserving the truthful history of the martyrdom, a history that also establishes the reliability of those codices.]

From Codex 12, entitled *Sermons of Augustine and Others*, this sermon emerges bearing Augustine’s name and mingled with his genuine works. In the published libraries that I was able to consult, no mention of this sermon appeared. In the Maurist edition it should be placed after Sermon 326. Its opening and its principal thought are repeated in Sermon 286, in nearly the same words. See also Sermon 328, section 2, after the middle.

The word *martyr* is Greek; in Latin they are called *witnesses*. If, then, they are witnesses, they suffered so greatly for the truth of their testimony. Truth served God; iniquity lied to itself. For it is written—the body of Christ, which is the Church, speaks in the Psalm: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied to itself” (Psalm 26:12).

Witnesses and witnesses: unjust witnesses and righteous witnesses; witnesses of the devil and witnesses of Christ. We saw, awaited, and heard both kinds of witnesses when the passion of the blessed Martyrs whose solemn day is being celebrated was read.

When questioned, they answered that they had held an assembly because they were Christians. This is the testimony of truth. The judge said, “Because you have confessed to a crime.” This is the testimony of iniquity. God was being proclaimed, and it was called a crime. In proclaiming God, truth obeyed God; in calling it a crime, iniquity lied to itself. For what the judge said turned back upon them, and a false crime was condemned by a true crime.

Our Martyrs were not committing a crime. Christ’s Martyrs were not committing a crime by gathering in an assembly to praise God, to hear the truth, to hope for the kingdom of heaven, and to despise the present, most wicked age. These people were not committing a crime. The name of this act is piety. The name of this act is religion. The name of this act is devotion. The name of this act is true testimony.

What crime, then, were those committing who even killed people who had confessed their piety? “Let this one and that one,” said the judge of iniquity, the witness of falsehood, “let this one and that one and that one be executed by the sword.” There is the crime.

Hear also the voice of piety: “Thanks be to God,” said the first witness [something appears to have been inserted here by a figure which rhetoricians call the notation of a name; the words “to conquer” and the repeated “victory” perhaps establish the point. In Sermon 325, on Fidantius and Victoria, the holy Doctor used the same figure: “The beginning is from Faith, the end toward Victory.” It is certain that one of these Carthaginian Martyrs was named Victoria, and, unless I am mistaken, Augustine had her in mind here.]

Primus closed his testimony with perpetual victory. I believe Your Charity noticed, when the passion of the saints was being read, who confessed first: before becoming last, he was called Primus; at the end was perpetual Victoria.

O victory without stain! O end without end! For what is perpetual victory except victory without end? It is conquering the allurements of the flesh, conquering the threats of the perverse judge, conquering bodily pain, conquering love of this life.

I shall say, if I can, with the Lord’s help, my brothers, what I feel: in the holy Martyrs, love of life was conquered by love of Life.

Those of you who applauded understood; but for the sake of those who did not understand, bear with me who have understood, for a little while, as I explain what I said. I said this: in the holy Martyrs, love of life was conquered by love of Life.

By loving life, they despised life. Who despises silver by loving silver? Who despises gold by loving gold? Who despises estates by loving estates? No one despises what he loves.

We find Martyrs who loved life and despised life. They would not have reached that other life if they had not trampled upon this one. They knew what they were doing: by giving out, they were acquiring. Do not think, dearest ones, that they had lost their judgment when they loved life and despised life; they had not lost their judgment. They were scattering seeds and seeking a harvest.

I see the farmer’s reasoning and recognize wisdom in the Martyrs. A farmer, loving wheat, scatters wheat [the same comparison is found in Sermon 331.1]. If you do not know what a sower is doing, you may rebuke him and say: “What are you doing, madman? What you gathered with such labor you bring out, scatter, remove from your eyes, throw onto the earth, and even bury?”

He answers you: “I love wheat; therefore I throw down wheat. If I did not love it, I would not throw it down. I want it to grow, not perish.”

This is what our Martyrs did, incomparably wiser than farmers. Sowers scatter a few grains, and reapers gather many. But both what they scatter and what they gather have an end. What is scattered is not much; what is gathered is much, yet both come to an end.

And you did not want our Martyrs to scatter a life that would eventually end in death, so that they might receive a life that has no death? Good lenders, good sowers—and God is the one who multiplies. He himself multiplies crops in the field; he himself nourishes whatever is produced from the earth. God can multiply grains, but cannot preserve his Martyrs?

I say to you: listen to what they heard. You also heard it just now when the Gospel was read; you received what was promised to them [two scriptural testimonies are blended here, although Augustine declares that he is speaking of the Gospel appointed for that day in the liturgy. This is precisely what I noted with the distinguished Sabatier in the preface to his *Ancient Biblical Versions*: the holy Fathers did not always recite scriptural texts from books, but sometimes retained only the sense of the words, sometimes offered an abbreviated form, sometimes spoke as memory suggested, and sometimes even conflated similar texts. You see that happening here]:

“They will hand you over,” he says, “to councils and to their synagogues; they will scourge you, and some of you they will kill.” “But I say to you: not a hair of your head will perish, and by your endurance you will possess your souls” (Matthew 10:19; Luke 21:18–19).

You will possess them, and you will not lose them [you will find this statement repeated six hundred times, especially in sermons on the Martyrs]. No enemy persecutes anyone there; no friend dies. You will be where perpetual day has no yesterday preceding it and no tomorrow following it.

There you will be good lenders, where the devil cannot follow you. Endure for a time; rejoice forever. Hard are the things you endure, but the seed you sow bears a great harvest.

Read what was said about you when you were sowing: “Going, they went and wept, scattering their seeds” (Psalm 125:6–7). With what fruit? With what end? With what consolation? “But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.”

From those sheaves crowns are made. Let us therefore celebrate the day of the Martyrs by honoring the sufferings of the Martyrs, not by loving our drinking.

Turning toward the Lord, etc.

## SERMON VII. On Saint John the Baptist
This sermon survives in four Cassinese manuscripts—namely, Codex no. 12 and three lectionaries of the twelfth century, all consistently attributed to Augustine. In the Leopoldine library of Blandinius, however, it is assigned to an anonymous author. I transcribed the beginning of the sermon from Codex 12, for in the Leopoldine manuscript and, perhaps, in the lectionaries, it is read in abbreviated form, apparently because it seemed somewhat unrelated to this feast. I have retained the conclusion supplied by the lectionaries, so that the sermon would not appear mutilated; for, instead of a conclusion, Codex 12 appends a question about word and voice, which, interrupted by lacunae, was left wholly unresolved by the careless scribe.

Moreover, the Maurist editors frequently provide examples of such alterations in lectionaries. In Sermon 44, *On the Words of Isaiah*, chapter 53, they aptly note: “For the treatises of Augustine that were to be read in church were generally shortened of necessity; a suitable beginning was attached to them, as well as an appropriate conclusion.” Possidius’ Index lists several sermons on this feast (chapters 8, 9, and 10), among which this sermon and the following one must be included; this is confirmed by the Maurist edition, volume V, numbers 228, 293, and following, since the words and ideas of these sermons often correspond closely with them. In that edition you will insert this sermon after Sermon 293, and it will be VIII, *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*.

**Since** [Note: [Col. 0991] In the Leopoldine manuscript and the lectionaries, the beginning reads as follows: “Today, dearest brothers, a solemn day has dawned: the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist and the Lord’s precursor. What, I ask, should I first admire, dearest brothers—the nativity of the Savior or that of the precursor? John’s mother was barren and did not know how to give birth, etc.”]

The Lord wished on this day to restore to Your Charity our voice and presence, and he did so not according to our arrangement but according to his own will. Together with you we give him thanks, and we render you the service of preaching, which is our ministry, in which it is both our duty and our honor to serve you. It is your task, dearest ones, to receive with charity whatever dispensation the servants of God provide and to give thanks with us [Note: [Col. 0991] Perhaps these words indicate that he is speaking extempore and outside his own church; for he would speak too deferentially if he were addressing his own people.] to him who has granted us to celebrate this day together with you. Of whom, then, should we speak today except of him whose nativity is celebrated today?

Saint John, therefore, born of a barren woman, was the precursor of the Lord born of a Virgin; he became the greeter of his Lord and announced him from the womb. John’s mother was barren and did not know how to give birth, while the Savior’s mother was a virgin and had no means by which to give birth: the barren woman bore a herald, the virgin gave birth to the Judge.

But the Lord Jesus Christ himself had sent many heralds before him, before he was to come to humanity from the womb of the Virgin. All the prophets were sent beforehand by him, but he himself was speaking through them. He who came after them was before them. [Col. 0992] Since, therefore, the Lord sent many heralds before him, what did this man merit so greatly? What greater excellence did he possess, whose nativity is commended today? For it is not without a sign of some greatness that the day of his birth is not hidden, just as the day of the birth of his Lord is not hidden. We do not know when the other prophets were born; in John’s case, we were not permitted not to know when he was born.

His great merit also appeared in this: the others foretold the Lord and desired to see him but did not see him; and if they saw him in the spirit, they saw him as one who was to come. They were not here to see him present. The Lord himself says of them to his disciples: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:17). Was it not he himself who sent them? Yet there was in all of them a desire, if it could somehow be, to see Christ here in the flesh. But because they preceded him in death, just as they had preceded him in birth, Christ did not find them here; nevertheless, Christ redeemed them for eternal life.

And so that you may know how great was everyone’s desire to see Christ here, remember that old man Simeon, to whom the Spirit of God announced as no small benefit that he would not depart from this world until he had seen Christ. Christ was born; Simeon recognized him as an infant in his mother’s arms, took him, and held him in his hands—him by whose divinity he himself was being carried. Holding the infant Word in his hands, he blessed God, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

The other prophets, therefore, did not see Christ here; Simeon saw him as an infant; John recognized him while still conceived and greeted him. John announced him and saw him, pointed him out with his finger, and said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). This man, then, was more excellent than all the others.

Hear the testimony of the Lord concerning him, where the Lord set himself above him, and no one else. John was so great that, apart from Christ, there was no one who could be set above him. Thus the Lord himself says: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). And in order to place himself above him, he immediately added: “Yet the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” He called himself lesser and greater: lesser in being born, greater in ruling; lesser in age, but greater in majesty.

The Lord was born after John—but in the flesh, and from a Virgin; before him, however, “In the beginning was the Word.” Great is Christ, who came after John, and yet John was made through Christ: “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

Why, then, did John come? To show the way of humility, so that human presumption might be diminished and the glory of God increased. John came, therefore, a great man commending the Great One; John came as the measure of humanity.

What is “the measure of humanity”? No human being could be greater than John. Whatever was greater than John was already more than human. If the measure of human greatness had been established and completed in John, you would no longer find a greater human being; and yet you did find one greater. Confess, then, the God whom you were able to find greater than a human being. [Col. 0993]

John was human, and Christ was human; but John was only human, whereas Christ was God and human. Insofar as he is God, Christ himself made John; insofar as he is human, he was born after John.

Yet consider how much that precursor of his Lord, who is both God and human, humbled himself. He than whom no one had arisen greater among those born of women was asked whether he himself was the Christ. He was so great that people could be deceived: there was doubt about whether he was the Christ, and the doubt was so serious that he was questioned about it.

If he had been a son of pride rather than a teacher of humility, he would have aligned himself with the people who were mistaken and would not merely have acted in such a way as to make them think this, but would have accepted what they thought. Perhaps it would have been too much for him to wish to persuade people that he was the Christ? If he had tried to persuade them, they would not have believed him; he would have remained rejected and cast down, despised among human beings and condemned before God.

But he had no need to persuade people: he already saw that they thought this. He could have accepted their error and increased his own honor. But far be this from the faithful friend of the Bridegroom—that he should wish to be loved by the bride in place of the Bridegroom. He confessed that he was not what he was not, so as not to lose what he was.

For John was not the bridegroom. When he was questioned, he said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but he who comes after me is greater than I” (John 3:29; Matt. 3:11).

How much greater? “Of whom I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.” Consider how much lesser he would have been if he had been worthy; consider how greatly he would have humbled himself if he had said: “He is greater than I, whose sandal strap I am worthy to untie.” For he had said that he considered himself worthy to bend down to his feet. But now how greatly did he commend humility, when he declared himself unworthy even of his feet—or rather, of his sandals!

John came, therefore, to teach humility to the proud and to announce the way of repentance. The voice came before the Word.

How does the voice come before the Word? Of Christ it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). But in order to come to us, “the Word became flesh, so that he might dwell among us.” Since, therefore, we have heard that Christ is the Word, let us listen because John is the voice.

For when he was asked, “Who are you?” he replied: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make ready the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Let us listen to John crying out, and let us prepare the way for the Lord, so that the Word may come to us [Note: The following passage was transcribed from the lectionaries and from the Leopoldine Codex. Codex no. 12 instead appends the following in place of this conclusion: “Let us therefore, dearest brothers, discuss for a little while—for as much as the Lord grants—word and voice. Christ is the Word, the Word that does not sound and pass away; voice is not word. The Word of God, through whom all things were made, is our Lord Jesus Christ. The voice of one crying in the wilderness is John. Which is prior, voice or word? Let us see what word is and what voice is, and there we shall see which is prior. What do you think word is, brothers? Let us set aside the Word of God, through whom all things were made, and speak for a little while about our own words, if we can take from them some steps toward the highest by way of resemblance. Who can comprehend the Word of God, through whom all things were made? Who is worthy even to think of it, much less to express it for a little while? Let us therefore set aside his ineffable majesty, eternity, and co-eternity with the Father, so that by believing we may deserve to see.” What person, moreover, does not see that here so many stones have been laid without mortar and heaped together confusedly, without even presenting to the mind’s eye the image of a hut?]

because [Col. 0994] “all flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls; but the Word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6–8).

## SERMON VIII. On Saint John the Baptist

The Maurist editors observed that this form of address, placed at the beginning of the sermon (Sermon 243, Appendix, vol. 5), is solemn and customary in spurious sermons. But since Augustine is plainly revealed here, I would prefer to say that the beginning in lectionaries nos. 115 and 123, from which I transcribed it, was altered for precisely the reason that I borrowed from the Maurist Fathers in the preceding case. If there I happened to discover the genuine beginning while remaining uncertain about the conclusion, here, on the contrary, the beginning is doubtful to me, while the conclusion is entirely certain.

The sermon should be valued very highly on account of what is placed near its end: it warns of the superstition customarily observed by the common people on the eve of this feast, which no sermon of this holy Doctor had indicated up to now. I searched for it in vain in the published libraries. You may transfer it to the Maurist edition under number 295; it will be the ninth sermon *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*.

### I

Dearest brothers, today we celebrate the birthday of a great man; and do you wish to know how great he was? “Among those born of women,” Scripture says, “no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). The one born of a Virgin said this about him; he gave this testimony concerning his witness; the Judge pronounced this judgment about his herald; thus the Word wished to honor his voice, as you know and heard today also in the morning Sermon [Note: It is clear that the sermon was delivered during the evening office. I would not dare speculate which sermon was delivered in the morning, for there is no sermon on the nativity of John in which Augustine did not state this Gospel testimony and adorn John with the titles of witness, herald, and voice.].

### II

Christ is the Word; John is the voice. For it is written of Christ: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). But when John spoke about himself, he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (ibid. 1:23).

The Word pertains to the heart; the voice to the ear. When the voice reaches the ear but does not carry the word to the mind, it has an empty use but no useful result. But for the Word to be born in my heart, it does not need a voice. To carry to your heart what has already been born in my heart, however, it assumes the ministry of the voice.

A word can precede a voice [perhaps: “a word can precede the voice.” But in the manuscripts: “voice”], but the Word cannot proceed without a voice. The voice is created for this purpose—not to give birth to the Word, which it already knew, but to emit what already existed.

Let us therefore see what sort of Word Christ is and what sort of voice John is, in accordance with what we have said about Word and voice, that is, about Christ and John.

“In the beginning was the Word.” Where was it? “And the Word was with God.” How far before us! How far above us! “And the Word became flesh” so that he might dwell among us (John 1:1, 14). And how would we know this if we did not hear the voice?

Christ was already walking among human beings clothed in mortal flesh, yet people came to John and said to him, “Are you the Christ?” John replied: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid. 1:29). Listen to him; recognize him. I go before him; I announce him.

Remember what he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make ready the way of the Lord”—not for me, but for the Lord. When I cry out, I announce him, because the voice of the herald signifies the arrival of the Judge. When he whom I announce has come and has found rest in your heart, “he must increase, but I must decrease” (ibid. 3:30).

You know this, do you not? [Note: Perhaps these two words were recorded by the stenographers: “They said, ‘We know.’”]

They said, “We know.” When the Word, having taken up the assistance of the voice, flows more closely through the narrow paths into the region of the heart, the Word grows in the heart, while the voice diminishes in the ear. The sound that struck the ear does not remain, because it does not remain indefinitely; it descends into the mind. Why? Because “he must increase, but I must decrease.”

John baptizes, and Christ also baptizes. It was said to John: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matt. 3:15). You know this, brothers. It happened when Christ was baptized.

Behold, now throughout the whole world he is the one who baptizes. The baptism of Christ has increased everywhere. Although the baptism of John possesses a mystery in the recollection of the past, it does not possess a mystery in present celebration. The baptism of John has ceased, and the baptism of Christ has increased. Hence he says: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

We find this statement also in the births and in the passions of both men. Although John said this about John—that is, John the Evangelist about John the Baptist—although he said of him, “There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light” (John 1:6–7), nevertheless today John was born, brothers, when the night grew longer and the day began to diminish.

Christ, however, was born at the winter solstice, as you know, when the losses of night begin to be transferred into the mourning of light: “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

Why were they born in this way? Because “he must increase, but this man must decrease.”

The same is true in their passions. John is beheaded by the sword; Christ is exalted on the wood. The one is raised up; the other is laid low. This man was beheaded so that he might decrease; the other was exalted on the gallows of the cross so that he might increase.

These two are the Lord and the servant: the Lord on the cross’s gallows, the servant in the death of decapitation. Hence we say: “He must increase, but this man must decrease.”

Not without reason, I think, are even the ages of their parents chosen. A woman advanced in years gives birth to John; a young Virgin gives birth to Christ. He was carried in the Virgin’s womb and adored by the angels in heaven. The hopelessly barren woman gives birth to this one; the untouched virgin gives birth to that one. Finally, the young woman gives birth to the one who grows, while the declining old age gives birth to the one who decreases.

And what of this, my brothers? How great is the dignity of this man, since an angel announced to his parents that he would be born, just as he announced the birth of the Lord Christ! Why did he merit this? Because “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11).

As you know, the angel Gabriel was sent both to the Virgin Mary; a son was promised to each woman, and each gave a response. Zechariah replied to the angel who promised a son: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is barren and advanced in years” (Luke 1:18). Mary also replied: “How shall this happen, since I do not know man?” (ibid. 1:34).

Both answer out of doubt, and yet he is punished while she is blessed; I think they did not yet know that, when the gift of God’s grace intervenes, the law of nature ceases.

Thus both respond from doubt, yet one is punished and the other is blessed. To him it is said: “Behold, you will be silent.” To Mary it is said: “Blessed are you among women” (ibid. 1:42). Zechariah loses his voice; Mary conceives the Word.

What happens after this? The Word becomes flesh in the Virgin, and the voice is born from the one who was silent. John is born and restores his father’s voice; the speaking father gives his son a name.

Everyone wonders, everyone is astonished, and they murmur among themselves, mixing their words back and forth. They say to one another: “What, do you suppose, will this child be?” (ibid. 1:66). Let us speak from the Gospel [Note: The liturgy of that church prescribed the same Gospel that is read today at Mass.]. “For the hand of the Lord was with him.”

What, do you suppose, will he be who has begun in this way? He is still so tiny, and already he is great. And if this one who has just begun will be great, what will he be who always was?

He whom John, while still enclosed in the secrecy of his mother’s womb, recognized even as he lay within the chamber of the Virgin’s womb, and whom he greeted by movements since he could not yet do so with words—what, then, will he be?

Do you wish to know what he will be? I shall say it briefly; hear the Prophet: “He himself,” he says, “will be called the Lord of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:6).

Therefore, as we celebrate with heavenly festivities the birthday of blessed John, the Lord’s precursor, that great man, let us ask for the assistance of his prayers. Since he is the friend of the Bridegroom, he can also obtain for us that we may belong to the Bridegroom and deserve to find his grace.

### III

But if we wish to find his grace, let us not insult his birthday. Let the sacrilegious religious observances cease; let the pursuits and games of vanity cease. Let those things not be done that are customarily done—things that are already, in a certain sense, in honor of demons, but still according to the custom of demons.

Yesterday, after evening, the entire city was aflame with rotting fires in the ancient manner of demons, and was itself decaying; smoke had covered the whole air. If you pay little attention to the religious aspect, at least consider the common injury.

We know, brothers, that these things are done by the poor, but they ought to have been forbidden by those of higher rank. For someone has said: “Whoever does not forbid sin when he can, certainly commands it.”

Brothers, in the name of the Lord and of our God Jesus Christ, since the Church advances year by year, this practice and every diminution of it are certainly tending toward nothing; but they have not yet been so completely exhausted that we may safely remain silent.

Antiquity and newness are nothing unless they reach their proper ends, the old superstition is consumed, and the new religion is brought to perfection.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory and power, together with God the almighty Father and with the Holy Spirit, now and always and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. On Luke 17:4: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven”

From Manuscript Codex no. 170, entitled *Volume IX of the Works of Saint Augustine*, I transcribed this treatise—for that is how it is entitled in the Codex—which is mixed in that Codex with other works already published. Augustine had spoken elsewhere on this same chapter of Luke at the table of Saint Cyprian, in the presence of Count Boniface, as Sermon 114 of the Maurist edition testifies. Our sermon should be placed after that one. When the two are compared with one another, the same hand is recognized in both.

I did not find this sermon in the published libraries. I think it was composed after the year 429, after the blessed Prosper had written to Augustine about the heresy of the Semipelagians, which was already flourishing in Gaul and in which the presbyters of Massilia denied that grace was necessary for the beginning of faith. For, taking the occasion from praise of God, Augustine raises the question for himself whether the first beginnings of faith come from God; he confirms the answer from the Apostle’s Letter to the Philippians.

In any case, this is a truly excellent sermon, containing doctrines of the greatest importance concerning faith and morals.

We heard a most salutary command from the holy Gospel: that we should forgive a brother who has sinned against us. Nor is it enough to do this once; rather, whenever he sins, he must be forgiven if he asks pardon. Thus it says: “If he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him” (Luke 17:4). If you understand “seven times in a day,” then it means “whenever,” for the number seven is customarily used to signify totality. Hence the saying: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24:16)—that is, whenever he has been humbled by some tribulation, he is not abandoned, but is delivered from all his tribulations. Hence also the saying: “Seven times a day I praise you” (Ps. 118:164). “Seven times a day” here means “always.” What is said elsewhere as, “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2), is the same as “seven times a day.” For we do not merely sound forth the Lord’s praises with our tongue, and cease to praise him when we are silent. Rather, in all our good thoughts, in all our actions and good conduct, we praise him from whom we rejoice to have received these things.

We see, moreover, that the Apostles themselves ask that their faith be increased (Luke 17:5). Did they give themselves the beginnings of faith and ask the Lord for its increase? Far be it from us to think so. They asked that the one who began the work might himself complete it, according to the Apostle: “For he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Phil. 1:6).

[Note: [Col. 0997] Of the three readings set in the Liturgy for that day, he mentions only two: the second, from Psalm 85, verse 11; and the third, from Luke chapter 17, on which he is preaching. He omitted the first, unless perhaps by the words, “we see also that the Apostles ask that their faith be increased,” he intended to suggest that a passage from the Epistle to the Philippians had been read, whose testimony he cited.]

And what else does what we have just sung demonstrate, beloved, than this: “Lead me, O Lord,” he says, “in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. 85:11). He does not say, “Bring me to your way”; for he himself does that too. But once he has brought us there, he must not abandon us. It is little, therefore, to have brought someone to the way unless he goes before him on the way and brings him to his homeland.

Since, then, we have all good things from God, [Col. 0998] whenever in all our good works we think of the giver of every good, we praise God without end. And when we praise God without end while living well, then “let us bless the Lord at all times, and let his praise always be in our mouth” (Ps. 33:2). “Seven times,” he says, signifying totality by the number seven.

Therefore, if your brother sins against you seven times in a day and comes saying, “I repent,” forgive him. Let it not weary you always to forgive one who repents. If you were not a debtor, you might with impunity be an importunate creditor; but since you have a debtor and are yourself the debtor of one who has no debt, see what you should do with your debtor—for God will do the same with his.

Listen and fear: “Let my heart rejoice,” he says, “that I may fear your name” (Ps. 85:11). If you rejoice when you are forgiven, fear in order to forgive. How greatly you ought to fear, the same Savior shows by setting before us in the Gospel that servant with whom the master settled accounts and found him to be a debtor of a hundred thousand talents. He ordered that he be sold, together with everything he had, and payment made (Matt. 18:32). The man fell at his master’s feet and began to plead that he be granted an extension; and he obtained remission.

But when he went out from the presence of his master, with his entire debt cancelled, he himself found a fellow servant who was his debtor and owed him a hundred denarii. Seizing him by the throat, he began to drag him away for payment. When his own debt had been forgiven, his heart rejoiced; but not in such a way that he feared the name of his Lord God.

The servant said to his fellow servant what the servant had said to his lord: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you.” But the other replied: “No; you must pay today.” The matter was reported to the master of the household. And what you know happened: he not only threatened that he would no longer forgive him if he found him with a debtor, but also revoked everything he had forgiven and ordered him to repay all that he had granted.

[Note: Although this is not read in the Gospel, Augustine nevertheless draws it out by a legitimate inference in order to suggest the moral point, treating it as though it were stated in the Gospel. Hence, in Sermon 5, no. 2, of the edition, speaking from the same inference, he says: “Let them beware lest, if someone sins against them and they themselves are unwilling to forgive, not only will they thereafter not be forgiven, but everything that had been forgiven will also be recalled.”]

How greatly, then, my brothers, must we fear, if there is faith in us, if we believe the Gospel, if we do not think the Lord a liar? Let us fear, observe, take care, and forgive.

For what do you lose by forgiving? You give pardon, not money. Yet even in distributing money you ought not to be dry trees. In distributing money, you give to one in need; in granting pardon, you forgive one who has sinned. The Lord sees both and rewards both; he commended both in the same place: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37).

But you neither forgive nor distribute: you hold on to anger and preserve your money. Consider anger, from which you cannot be freed by money:

[Note: [Col. 0998] See, in accordance with Sixtus of Siena’s critique, Augustine’s manner of speaking, which at times carries very many things along with it in a mixed fashion and requires a reader who is familiar, keen, attentive, and of good memory. (*Bibliotheca Sancta*, under “Augustine.”) For, having taught one whose anger could not be relieved by almsgiving to restrain it, he thought it fitting, on the occasion presented, first to speak of the use of riches, so that afterwards he might establish that first proposition by contraries, resuming from the words, “This is what you say when you wish to preserve your money,” the period which the extended digression had interrupted.]

“Treasures will not profit the wicked.” This is not my judgment, but the divine judgment. Those who have read it know it. I read it in order to speak it; I believed it in order to proclaim it: “Treasures will not profit the wicked” (Prov. 10:2). It seems to profit them, but it will not profit them. Perhaps in the present life? Perhaps—if indeed it profits them at all. But on that day it will not profit them. Let it be held onto, and it will not profit; let it be despised, and it will profit.

You will use justice well if you love it, because if you do not love it, you will not possess fortitude, temperance, chastity, or charity. You use other goods of the soul well if you love them; you use money well if you do not love it. Finally, if money [Col. 0999] is loved, let it be stored up in heaven. If it is feared that it may be lost, let it be guarded in a safer place.

For surely your servant keeps faith with you in preserving your money—does your Lord deceive you? Do you not hear him saying: “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven”? See: he did not command you to lose it, but to transfer it: “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where the thief does not approach and the moth does not destroy; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:20–21).

You store up treasure on earth; on earth you place your heart. What will happen to your heart on earth? It wastes away, rots, and turns to ashes. Lift up what you love, and love it there; do not think that you will receive back what you deposit here. You deposit mortal things and will receive immortal things; you deposit temporal things and will receive eternal things; you deposit earthly things and will receive heavenly things. Finally, you distribute what your Lord gave you, and you will receive your reward from that same Lord.

But you will say: “How am I to deposit anything in heaven? By what machines shall I climb into heaven with my gold and silver?” Why do you seek machines? Transfer it.

[Note: The Maurists show that this expression, *laturarii*—“carriers”—and another, *trajectitium*—“a transfer” or “transferred property”—were customary with Augustine. See Sermon 18, no. 4; Sermon 38, no. 9; Sermon 60, no. 8; and elsewhere.]

Your carriers are the poor, and they have become carriers through the breaking down of the world. Finally, you make a transfer: you give here and receive there. Indeed, if you give here, you will receive there; and from the one to whom you give, you will receive.

Do not merely bring to mind some ragged beggar; bring to mind the saying: “Whenever you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40). He receives in the poor who made the poor; he receives from the rich who made the rich. For he receives from it what he gave: you give to Christ from what is his, not from what is yours.

Why do you boast that you found many things here? Recall how you came. You found everything here, and, having found many things, if you use them badly, you have become swollen with pride. Did you not come forth naked from your mother’s womb? Give, then; give, lest you lose what you have. If you give, you will find it there; if you do not give, you will leave it here. Whether you give or do not give, you will depart nonetheless.

Yet sometimes avarice, though unwilling to distribute to the poor from what it possesses in abundance—a reluctance foolish, reprehensible, and to be rejected by the ears of the faithful—nevertheless has some excuse. It says to itself:

“If I give, I shall not have anything. By giving much, I shall become needy. Afterwards I shall seek someone from whom I too may receive. I must have enough not only for food, clothing, my house, and my household, but also for unforeseen circumstances, so that I may have something to spend on an accuser, something with which to redeem myself. Human affairs are full of accidents; I must preserve enough to free myself.”

This is what you say when you wish to preserve your money. What will you say when you are unwilling to give forgiveness to one who has sinned? If you are reluctant to distribute money to one in need, distribute pardon to one who repents. What do you lose if you give?

I know what you lose; I know what you forfeit. I see it—but you forfeit it for your own good. You lose anger; you lose indignation; you remove hatred of your brother from your heart. Should these things remain there? Where will you be? Anger, indignation, and hatred remain forever. What do they do to you? What evil do they not do to you?

Hear Scripture: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Therefore, even if he sins against me seven times in a day, shall I forgive him? Forgive him. Christ said this; the Truth said it—the one to whom you sang: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.” Do not be afraid; he will not deceive you.

“But,” you say, “there will be no discipline; all sins will always go unpunished. It is pleasant always to sin when the sinner thinks that the one sinned against will always forgive.”

It is not so. Let discipline remain vigilant, and let benevolence not sleep. Do you think that you repay evil with evil when you give discipline to one who has sinned? Far be it from us. You repay evil with good, and you do not act well if you do not give discipline. Sometimes discipline itself is tempered by gentleness; nevertheless, it is given. But is extinguishing discipline through negligence the same thing as tempering it through gentleness? Let discipline remain vigilant; forgive and strike.

[Note: This sentence is interrupted by another digression and resumed in the words, “But since we were speaking of discipline.”]

Look at the Lord himself; [Col. 1000] listen to the Lord himself; consider whom we, as daily beggars, address when we say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). And you are weary when your brother repeatedly says to you: “Forgive me, for I repent.” How often do you say this to God? Do you ever omit this petition in any prayer?

Do you want God to say to you: “See, yesterday I forgave; the day before yesterday I forgave; for so many days I forgave. How many more times shall I forgive?” Do you not want him to say to you: “You always come with those words; you always say, ‘Forgive us our debts’; you always beat your breast, and, like hard iron, you do not reform”?

But since we were speaking of discipline, does our Lord God not forgive us because we say in faith, “Forgive us our debts”? Yet although he forgives us, what has been said about him? What has been written about him? “For whom God loves, he chastises.” But perhaps only with words? “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

Let not the sinner be indignant that a son is corrected when scourged, when he who alone was without sin nevertheless deigned to be scourged. Therefore give discipline, but forgive anger from the heart. For the Lord himself says, when speaking of that debtor whose entire debt he revoked because he had been inhuman toward his fellow servant: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18:35).

Where God sees, there forgive; do not lose charity there. Exercise salutary severity; love and strike; love and chastise. Sometimes you flatter and yet rage. How do you flatter and rage? Because you do not rebuke sins, and those sins will destroy the one whom you perversely spare under the pretext of love.

Let your word at times be harsh, at times severe; consider what will wound and what it will accomplish. Sin lays waste to the heart, destroys the inward parts, suffocates the soul, and ruins the soul. Have pity; strike.

[Note: Augustine uses nearly the same comparison in Sermon 82, no. 2, of the edition.]

Set before your eyes, beloved, so that you may understand more clearly what I am saying, two men. A heedless little boy wanted to sit where they knew that a serpent was hiding in the grass. If he sat down, he would be bitten and die.

The two men knew this. One said: “Do not sit there.” He was ignored. The boy went to sit down; he went to his death.

The other said: “This boy does not want to listen to us. He must be rebuked, restrained, dragged away, struck with a slap. Whatever we can do, let us do it so that we do not lose the boy.”

Another said: “Let him be; do not strike, do not offend, do not hurt him.”

Which of these is merciful? The one who spares him so that the boy may die from the serpent, or the one who rages so that the boy may be saved?

Understand in the same way those who are subject to you: correct them and impose discipline upon their conduct. Preserve benevolence; forgive from the heart; let there be no anger inwardly. For fresh anger is a splinter, slight and seemingly contemptible. Fresh anger troubles the eye like a splinter in the eye: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8). But that splinter is nourished by suspicions, strengthened by the passage of time, and will eventually become a beam.

When anger grows old, it will become hatred; and once there is hatred, there will be murder: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer,” he says.

[Note: This is a brief digression, but it reveals Augustine’s style. See Pope Blount, *Censura Auctorum*, p. 271, edition of 1710. Augustine repeats the same sentence very frequently, especially in Sermons 5, 42, and 82.]

And sometimes people who harbor hatred in their hearts rebuke those who are angry: “You hold hatred while rebuking one who is angry? You see the splinter in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own” (Matt. 7:3).

Let the sermon conclude. Let the Lord be invoked, so that he may deign to grant us what he commands: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.”

[Note: At the end of the sermon the Codex reads: “Here ends the treatise on the Gospel of Luke 17.”]

(Luke 6:37–38)

# SERMON X. On the Dedication of a Church

From manuscript codices nos. 98, 115, 123, and 543—two of which are entitled *Collections of Augustine’s Sermons*, while the other two are lectionaries containing various sermons—I copied this sermon, marked with Augustine’s name and worthy of so great a Doctor. The same sermon, likewise attributed to Augustine and divided into three readings, VI, VII, and VIII, is also found in Codex no. 2 of the Library of the Pomposa Monastery of Saint Benedict of the Ferrara Charterhouse, whose complete catalogue is preserved in the Casinensis Archive among the *Miscellanea*, folio 77a [reading uncertain].

That codex is a parchment folio written in Latin characters in the eleventh century and containing seventy-nine pages. On the margin of the first folio a later hand has written: “This book belongs to the monks of the Congregation of Saint Justina of Padua, assigned for the use of the convent of Saint Mary of Pomposa, marked no. 5.” I did not find it in the printed libraries.

In the Maurist edition it should be inserted after Sermon 338 and will be Sermon IV, *On the Dedication of a Church*. Those familiar with Augustine’s reading, observing the thoughts that fall together, the various figures which the holy Doctor delighted in, and the transitions, circumlocutions, and clever turns with which he used to entertain his hearers, will recognize it as a genuine work of Augustine.

## I

I exhort you, beloved, to strive to be God’s house and to have the Lord dwelling within us; for if we have God dwelling within us, we shall always have him as our helper.

Let us rejoice together over those good works which Christ has worked in his faithful people, and let each person continually imitate the progress in good works to the extent that he is divinely assisted.

It is necessary, brothers, that everyone build a house for God. Let the rich build; let the poor build. Let the exalted build; let the lowly build. Let the master build; let the servant build.

But how can we say this simultaneously to the rich and the poor, to the exalted and the lowly, to the master and the servant, since they do not possess equal means, dignity, or power?

The rich man can confidently reply: “I build a house for God because I possess abundant resources.” The exalted man replies: “I build a house for God because I have attained high dignity in this world.” The master replies: “I build a house for God because I have great power over my subjects.”

How well we rejoice in those who gladden us both by their words and by their good works! But for these people to answer us in this way, the rich man relies on the abundance of his resources, the exalted man considers the eminence of his honors, and the master considers the multitude of his subjects.

We have heard, then, the answer of the rich man; let us hear that of the poor man. We have heard the answer of the exalted man; let us hear that of the lowly. Finally, we have heard the answer of the master; let us hear that of the servant. The former have something they can promise; the latter perhaps have something they can offer as an excuse.

The poor man undoubtedly says to us: “How can I build a house for God, since I am constrained by the neediness of poverty?” The lowly man says to us: “When can I construct a house for God, since I am held down by the ignobility of my low station?” Then the servant says: “How can I construct a house for God, since I am bound beneath the yoke of servitude, and, since my master scarcely grants me enough food for a single day, where can I obtain sufficient means for building a house for God?”

They seem to have answered reasonably. But if they are willing to accept our answer, they will have no means whatsoever of excusing themselves from building God’s house.

First, then, we reply to the poor man with what the Lord has given, so that he may rather be built up himself when he is salutarily admonished to build a house for God.

Listen, whoever complains about poverty and therefore declares that he is unable to build God’s house. Why do you consider only your poverty and despise your inward substance? It is there that you must build a house for God; there you must abound in spiritual riches.

Therefore, if you are poor in earthly possessions, be rich in the abundance of charity. You do not possess an estate, but you possess wisdom. There is no coin in your purse, but let God be in your spirit.

Let your mind be radiant in poverty, which is much better than shining in costly garments. You do not have luxurious [Col. 1002] foods with which the body is nourished; let good conduct be yours, by which the soul is fattened. For what else do luxurious foods know how to do except nourish lust in the body? Good conduct, however, nourishes holy charity in the heart.

Do not therefore seek as something great the riches that will remain here. If you possess spiritual riches, you will not be poor. Indeed, if you are such a person that through bodily riches you seek spiritual riches, you will truly be rich in this very respect, because you will be a praiseworthy poor person. Thus you will truly build a house for God, because you yourself will be God’s house.

For building God’s house does not require an abundance of money. God is not pleased by a multitude of coins, but by purity of souls. True charity builds God’s house, not material resources.

We have answered the poor man with what God has given us. It is time to answer the lowly man as well. He presents as his excuse that he has received no lofty dignity in this world.

## II

Listen, and be, beloved, humble in heart, so that you may believe for this reason that you can build God’s house. Here your struggle must lie more in your will than in necessity. Be humble in heart and begin to build a house for God within yourself.

For he himself says: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Therefore, to the extent that your will has made you humble, recognize that to that extent you have become exalted; and to the extent that you preserve humility of heart, to that extent you will build the holiest dwelling for God.

## III

Now let us answer the servants, who, when they set before us the condition of servitude, think that they have no means at all for constructing a house for God.

Listen, whoever you are who are temporally a servant, whoever is bound by any law of domination, whoever is subject to any condition: in order to build a house for God, be a servant and be free.

Be a servant by obeying humbly; be free by serving faithfully. Be a servant of your Lord, and do not be a servant of sin. When you serve a human being, think of God; preserve God’s commandments; always obey God’s will; expect from God the reward of good service.

Keep faith; flee fraud; recognize that you must render an account to God for every deed of yours. Let laziness not make you contemptuous; let sluggishness not make you negligent.

In this way, while you offer good service, you will receive everlasting freedom from God. Let there be freedom in your body—the freedom that contains true and great riches, not those by which mortal man is puffed up, but those from which a pleasing house is built for God.

For with God, where there is neither slave nor free (Gal. 3:23), the one builds a true house for God who preserves good conduct in the fear of God.

As I judge, brothers, by the Lord’s gift we have answered the poor, the lowly, and the servants, so that they may recognize that they ought to build a house for God not outside themselves but within themselves.

Yet because in Christ we are servants both of the rich and of the poor, of the exalted and of the lowly, of masters and of servants—for he commanded this and first did it himself—since he is truly rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9); since he is truly Most High, “he humbled himself for us, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8); and since he is truly Lord of all things, he made himself a servant when he took the form of a servant, not only for us but from us.

Therefore, since in Christ we are servants of all, just as we owe the service of our speech to the poor, the lowly, and the servants, so we owe it to the rich, the exalted, and the masters. For wealth more easily puffs up the rich, dignity makes the exalted arrogant, and power raises up masters.

They must therefore be instructed with particular care, so that the zeal they show in constructing churches they may always apply to good works and may build a true house for God within themselves—a holy building that will collapse through no old age and succumb to no reproach.

We therefore address you now; in the charity of that same builder we exhort you who abound in riches, excel in honors, and rejoice in the power of domination. Take care to build [Col. 1003] God’s house in yourselves, not with stones and wood but with holy conduct.

Your building will be of the same character as your activity. First, then, stand firm upon the foundation and remain in Christ. Then, in the midst of your abundance and plenty, guard suitable caution of heart.

You build a true house for God when you suffer no loss to your soul. Flee pride if you do not wish to suffer ruin. “Do not hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17), and you will always have a stable foundation for your building.

Be rich always in good works, so that your riches may contribute not to your destruction but to your building. Be inclined toward mercy, and do not be quick to robbery. Let your resources not be violent; let your dignity not be proud; let your power not be unjust.

Therefore let all the faithful build a house for God by living well.

Let us attend, brothers, to what blessed Peter admonishes us and how he entrusts us with the care of this building. For he says: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2:5).

Look, brothers, at this church that we see. How pleasing to us are its light, its newness, and its firmness! Therefore let us also, who are God’s house, shine through good works; let us put off the old man (Eph. 4:22) and commendably put on the new; and let us continually possess the unfailing firmness of holy charity.

Look: we see columns upon which walls have been set; we also see stones in the building joined to one another. Who are the columns in God’s house [Col. 1004], by which the multitude of stones is carried, if not spiritual men through whom the multitude of the faithful is governed?

Who are the stones joined together by mutual connection, if not all the faithful who are bound together by the bond of unity, who, possessing one soul and one heart turned toward God, build within themselves an everlasting dwelling for God?

Therefore let living stones be joined to living stones in the building of God’s house. Let holy stones adhere to one another and be inseparably united, not by the mixture of mortar but by the sweetness of charity.

Whoever you are, then, who enter God’s house, be God’s house. Keep the faith; hold fast to the charity of the Church’s unity. “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:28). Flee avarice; love mercy. Flee fornication; love chastity.

And if you are not yet able to be a column in God’s house, so as to carry the burden of many stones, be a stone clinging to stones, so that you may persevere in the building.

It is indeed good that you build a visible house for God on your own property, on your own ground, on your own estate; but it is much better that you build an invisible house for God in your spirit.

Outside you there is a house of human prayer; within you, let there be a house of your prayer. Have it frequently there and carry it continually within yourself. There God will hear you all the more readily, the more freely he deigns to dwell in it.

Therefore always build a house for God in your heart. Cleanse it; prepare it for God, so that you may always have God present there and he may salutarily hear you as you pray.

To him be honor, kingdom, and supreme power forever and ever. Amen.
